sermons.title: Feed My Sheep
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. We are continuing our look at Acts. We are in Acts chapter 20. Before we get there, I'd like to Read to you some excerpts from a news story that appeared in a March Edition of a Miami newspaper. Quote Pastor Mark Gardner Left his church members out in the dark. Last Wednesday, he filed an injunction and locked the doors of the church. To shut out longtime outspoken members and board members who had ousted the pastor under evening skies on an empty lot across the street. Suddenly, members discovered the property they were standing on was no longer theirs. The pastor sold it. To members, that was Gardner's last straw. They fired the controversial, defiant pastor who has come under fire for allegedly running up hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt from loans and other expenses without the approval or knowledge of church members. They used flashlights to read financial documents and sign statements before unanimously voting to terminate the pastor, hoping to end a nasty battle to put away Gardner. The pastor defied a suspension and continued preaching after leaders of the Florida State Association of the Church of God, an organization to which the North Side belongs temporarily stripped Gardner of his duties after he failed to give account for his personal and financial affairs at the church. He didn't want to give up or be honest, said Janelle Masek, a member of fifty-one years who is considered the church's matriarch. It's not fair to the majority of the church that this continue. Gardner's injunction against the members cast a dark shadow on the meeting. Leaders said a police officer called them hours before the meeting to inform them of the order which was taken out that day. Members were told if they held the meeting of the on church grounds, they would be arrested for trespassing The church building was closed and locked up to keep out outspoken members who f filed a petition seeking to remove Gardner. At the meeting, members, some of them in their 70s and 80s, were forced to stand in the dark as they signed public statements listing personal loans they said Gardner borrowed from them to pay his personal bills Members hope the statement will help them take legal action against the alleged losses. They also seek to force Gardner to turn over documents that may explain the status of the church's financial condition. Oh, what a sad way to end a church relationship with a pastor. But that is a different church, right? A different denomination, even, right? Well A few years back, after a number of frustrated parishioners left a particular Reformed Episcopal Church that will remain nameless And after several years of the pastor of the said church, spending more time in Washington, D. C. than he did his parish ministry. And all the while speaking against the recurring changes in the Reformed Episcopal Church, the pastor resigned without warning. Before he left, however, he replaced the old REC prayer books with the new ones, the ones that we use today, without explanation or warning to the congregation. Then he was gone, and the congregation's identity was unknown, and his future unclear. Each of these instances is an example of pastors leaving their posts poorly. So very, very poorly. And they show what can happen when separation in an ungodly manner takes place. In our reading today from Acts chapter 20, we have an example of a godly manner Of a pastor saying goodbye to his church as Paul bid goodbye to the church at Ephesus Remember last week that Paul was traveling to Jerusalem, and in the midst of this traveling, he has this encounter. The clear details of his travels are given in verses 13 through 16, you will note. And then we have verse 17, and it might appear a bit confusing. It says that he was to sail past Ephesus. That was his plan. But then he ends up meeting with the leaders at Ephesus. And so we find that it is described that he is meeting with the elders of the church together at Malitas And it was there that he was giving them instructions on how to say goodbye to the church and how they are to lead the church after his departure. In verses 18 through 21, there is a summary testimony of what St. Paul practiced amongst the Church at Ephesus while he witnessed to them the gospel. The manner that Paul lived among men, the serving in humility that he practiced. The suffering in reputation, and the physical fear that he suffered because of Jewish persecution, and how he gave them all that he had to give Holding back nothing of importance. All of this was evidence to them of his sincerity in preaching the gospel. And sincerity. Sincerity is so, so very, very important when it comes to sharing the gospel. Consider an extreme example of a man holding in one hand the gospel and in the other hand a ronco-begomatic. And he tries to sell one along with the other. The effect is the receiver being distracted by the other. And such distraction speaks of an apparent ulterior motive of selling the gospel. The seller seems to want to make money in the same manner he wants to share the gospel, distracting attention from the gospel This is more blatant when an evangelist, so-called, wants to sell something like a prayer cloth. With the promise of praying for your salvation, or the salvation of someone you love, or perhaps healing. That prayer cloth can be bought for a price Thus it is the same as simonizing, which is described in Acts chapter 8. Simonizing the belief that God's blessings can be bought and sold. Such offerers, we are to be wise as serpents, knowing that it is money for the prayer cloth that the evangelist desires, not actually to pray for your needs. By sharing his sincerity, Paul is exposing his conscience. It is a conscience that all ministers of the gospel must have. Must have. Or it is promised that they will be judged more harshly because they are entrusted by God to teach the truth. What St. Paul is sincere about is the good news of Jesus Christ, which we call the gospel. Look at verse 21. In verse 21, he describes it, that gospel, as repentance towards God and faith toward the Lord Jesus Christ. Oh, how wonderfully simple. Repentance toward God and faith toward the Lord Jesus Christ. Repentance toward God, because it is against God, only that we can sin. Remember from David's Psalm 51. And faith toward the Lord Jesus Christ, because He is the only one that can provide forgiveness. Repentance and faith. Oh, how wonderfully simple. It is faith in the atoning work of Jesus, it is faith in his holy words, it is faith in the efficacy of all. All that he has done that saves us from sin and shame. Oh, how wonderfully simple This sincerity toward the ministry of the gospel by St. Paul is further explained in verse 24 after he describes the suffering the Holy Spirit promised that he would endure. I read that to you now. He says, None of these move me, nor do I count my life dear to myself, so that I may finish the race with joy and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus. To testify to the gospel of the grace of God. And this he is describing that in the end it is all worth it. In the end, it will all be worth the suffering. In the end, testifying to the grace of God will be worth it. It will all be worked. Can I get an Amen? St. Paul uses the descriptive of a race to describe his journey in this world just as he did, you remember, in his letter to the Corinthian church. Where he further describes that he buffets his body so that he might run that race as best as possible, buffering his body. He then says that such a race is done with joy. And to that I say, oh my! Racing is hard. Bucketing one's body is hard. He just described past humility and trials along with future chains and tribulations. He knows he's going to be jailed. He knows he's going to go through future tribulations. And he dare uses the word joy. Because of Paul's circumstances, such joy cannot be underlined, highlighted, cannot be happy, clappy outward expressions. It has to be inward and untouched by the circumstances of life in this world. This is Christian joy. Christian joy is a joy that lies deep in the heart as something permanent Something that establishes a person in the heavens and thus helps them walk the trials and tribulations in this life. It is a joy that the world cannot touch. It is the joy of salvation that knows nothing can separate us from the love of God. It is in a place where God continues to make us new. It is in the heart, the very place of our essence. The honest heart is shared in verse twenty-five, and that is one a heart as a father to his children. As a father, he must be strong by stating the truth of the matter, even though that truth is hard to face. Even if hearts ache, it is best to be strong against such heartache, so that that heartache does not overwhelm us. They will not see him in this life again. That is hard. But it needs to be said. It needs to be confronted. Like death that needs to be confronted. It needs to be confronted because it is a reality And Paul needed to be clear with them about what the future held and what he had done to show his sincerity. His words are what every minister should strive to be able to say. And I would add, every parent should strive to be able to say to his or her children. He first says that he was innocent of the blood of all men. That does not mean that he is not guilty of any physical confrontations with men. He's referring to being like a watchman. Responsible to warn of coming danger. He stayed awake and did the job of warning all men that would hear him about the judgment of God and the grace offered through Jesus Christ. What men then did with what he told them, the truth, he was no longer responsible for. There is great freedom in such a work. Some pastors, slash leaders, slash parents Will spend much of their days trying to have people like them, speak highly of them. Or some just want to keep their jobs. Or some just want to have friends. But such an approach is not the work of a watchman. How St. Paul is not guilty of the blood of men was explained in verse 26, where he refers to preaching the whole council of God. The whole council of God. And this, I bid to you, is where the modern church is failing, failing God and failing us Christians. Mega church pastors are focused on the positives of the gospel only. Prosperity preachers on television are focused on earthly wealth primarily. But ministers who are innocent of the blood of all men preach and teach all that the Bible has to say. All of it. Such includes positive, such includes prosperity, along with, along with suffering, persecution Warnings of eternal judgment and inevitable death. The whole council of God Gives the correct understanding of God so that people can be truly saved. Saved from sin and the second death. And I say truly saved, because if a person hears the positives only, or the prosperity primarily, they will not be moved away from the sins of greed. The sins of the pride, sins of self-glorification, which are blatant sins of our day The next essential content of a godly farewell is a commission to shepherd the church He says to the elders, Shepherd this church. The shepherding St. Paul describes here is one of protection of the sheep. Because, he reminds the church, there are savage wolves that seek to destroy the sheep, seek to destroy God's people, you and me. And they are not wolves only, but savage wolves. They want blood. Their intent is the death of sheep, your spiritual death. And they come not only from without, but from within. Of course, we know that Judas was from within. We know that Simon was from within Aries. Those of you who remember your church history was from within. Nestorius was from within. Sibelius was from within. Now, did you know that Frederick Nietzsche was from within? Having been baptized in the faith, and having a grandfather and an uncle who were pastors in the Lutheran Church? Did you know Karl Marx was from within, having been baptized in the triune name of God at the age of six? Charles Darwin was from within, even beginning to pursue a pastoral calling when he entered Cambridge. These men and others have either tried to corrupt the faith like Arius and Astorius, or tried to tear it down, like Nietzsche and Marx. The warning provided to the church by Paul is akin to the message Jesus had to the seven churches in the book of Revelation, and that message was to hold on. To hold on. To protect against savage wolves and to hold on takes a great deal of effort and fortitude. When I was preparing for the ministry in seminary, and in my early years as a pastor, I could be characterized as but Has been called a thunder puppy. Thunder puppies are people who get excited and aggressive about convictions to the point of looking like a puppy Who growls like he is big and strong and can take all comers like he is a big dog We think of such puppies as cute as they raise their upper lip at bigger dogs and growl with their high-pitched growls. And they are cute. But Thunder Puppy pastors are not cute. When in seminary, a requirement for graduation was to be interviewed by a number of professors. They would put forth to you ethical dilemmas that will occur in the pastoral ministry, and they require you then to verbally, before them, give a defense of the decisions you would make regarding all the things that you had learned in your three years. at seminary excuse me. My answers to each of the scenarios that were presented to me were quick. Decisive and way, way too confident. I remember one professor responding to me with a compliment that my answers were thorough. but warning me that my confidence would be a detriment in my ministry. And he was right. Of course he was right. Early in my ministry, I treated problems like they were recipes. You have the problem, and then you take this verse, and then you take this verse. And then you add this wisdom, and you add this wisdom, and you put it in the oven, set the timer, and be it all comes out solved. Through much wrestling, humility, and more humility. I have been transformed to see parish problems and people problems much much differently. And the primary difference is how much work it takes. It takes a great deal of effort and fortitude to not compromise the truth, but to compromise your pride, your understanding, your subjective perspective. And your willingness to meet people in troubles as they are, not as you want them to be. The diligence that it takes to remain faithful and to fight off the enemy from within and from without is great. So great it is difficult to overstate. But the necessity of such diligence is found in the number of churches that lie on the side of the road to the celestial city. The following excerpts are from a farewell address that I recently heard. These statements were given under the heading Reflections and Encouragement. Quote There are a number of things which the Lord has at least been trying to teach me. Lessons which might prove to be of benefit of each of us. The first of those lessons is simply this: that keeping Christ central and the proclamation of his gospel paramount is the essence of what we are called to do and be as a people. A second and related lesson is this: submission to the ultimate authority of the Holy Scriptures, of the Old and New Testaments As the Word of God written, both in precept and in practice, is the rudder that maintains the ark of the church on a steady course. And prevents it from foundering on some reef of cultural relativism, pseudoscience, or some fashionable philosophy visual These farewell words are from our former presiding bishop, Leonard Riches. And there are words the Apostle Paul is proud of. There are words that our Lord Jesus Christ is proud of. Their words I would like to leave behind if I am ever given the opportunity to say a farewell. The reaction of the elders of Ephesus to these farewell words of St. Paul is emotionally touching and emotionally moving. They wept, they hugged him, they kissed him, they were emotionally invested in him as their spiritual father. And his departing was painful, emotionally painful for them, as it should have been. Mature faith and mature spirituality allows for such emotional expressions because those who are mature in faith and mature in spirituality are not focused on the minor issues of life. You know, a minister can be tempted to complain to God about the people he serves, about the minor issues. They don't listen. They can be a petty. They don't listen. I said that twice. I shouldn't say any more. And I am aware that people can complain about the minister or ministers But upon examination of those complaints, if none of them are about the gospel, if none of them are about the authority of the Word of God, then from a minister's viewpoint, And from what St. Paul describes to us in his words to the elders at Ephesus, there is nothing to complain about, but much to be grateful for I lead a people who believe the gospel of Jesus Christ and want to hear his word proclaimed, preached, and taught. Nothing could be better. In summary then, St. Paul's farewell to the church at Ephesus shows us what is most important for the church. It is the gospel, and it is the Word of God. And it always will be. Amen and Amen. Let us pray

sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Rather warm for a Christmas Eve. All that up and down gets a little hot. We can uh open some of the windows if possible. I don't know if you are aware, but there is a video available made by a man named Frederick Larsen. who is a lawyer who has investigated whether or not the Bethlehem star, or what some call the Christmas star, can be historically verified. Historically verified. Using modern knowledge on how planets move Larson invested in software that enables anyone with basic knowledge of astronomy, now again we're talking about astronomy, not astrology, astrology is uh a sin in scripture, but astronomy. If you're able to follow the patterns of the past guys, then you can determine what planets align with what planets at certain times in history. What Larson found was that Jupiter and Venus, the two of the brightest planets in our solar system, came into alignment. displaying unequal brightness in the sky in 3 BC. Now Larson also adds that prior to the aligning of Jupiter and Venus creating this bright star, there was movement of Jupiter seemingly across the sky in a backward and forward motion. over the star Regulus. Three times in fact. One, two, three. Well, this movement of Jupiter over regulus three times occurs prior to these planets aligning, that is the aligning of Jupiter and Venus. And Larson points out that Jupiter, being the largest planet in our solar system, has been called by the Greeks and the Romans the god of the universe. While Regulus is the name for a king. And all of this occurred, get this now, in Leo, the star constellation, Leo. After the movement of Jupiter over Regulus, then the star Virgo seems to follow Jupiter. Now Larson brings all of this together by pointing out that Jupiter represents God. And God crowning the king star, Regulus, or Jesus, within Leo, the lion. Jesus is of the lion of the tribe of Judah. And then you have the star Virgo, which means virgin, appearing after in the skies. Now all of this seems to come together from a verse from Revelation chapter 12. It reads as follows. A great sign appeared in heaven. A woman clothed with the sun and the moon under her feet. And on her head a crown of twelve stars, and she was with child, and she cried out, being in labor and in pain to give birth. Of course, all of this is very interesting and would confirm, if accurate, what we already know to be true about a star leading wise men to the place where Jesus died. I hope I've done this justice. I'm not uh obviously an astronomer. Um but you can go online and you can watch this video. It's about an hour long and it's very interesting Now the Bethlehem star is fun to speculate about as it is one of the more prominent symbols during our Christmas season Stars adorn trees. They are a top to remind us of that star of Bethlehem. But we first read of the importance of a star in Holy Scripture in the book of Numbers of all places. There you'll find an account where the Israelites had escaped from Egypt, been delivered from Egypt from slavery And they come upon the Moabite people. Now the Moabite people, you will remember, were related to the Israelites as they were descendants of Abraham's nephew, Lot. They became frightened that Israel was at its borders. Oh, children at Christmas time. And so Balach, the king of Moab, he called for Balaam, who was a well-known prophet, to come down and curse the Israelites to protect his people. Balaam was an interesting fellow, for we know that he had a prophetic gift, but he did not fear God, and so he did not use his gift always in a righteous manner. Essentially, he was a prophet for hire. But try as he did, he could not speak a curse upon God's people Because if God wants to tie up a tongue of a man, he's going to tie up a tongue of a man. If he wants to loose a tongue, he's going to make it loose. Now the following passage is from Numbers 24. It reads, Then Baloch's anger burned against Balaam. He struck his hands together. And said to him, I summon you to curse my enemies, but you have blessed them these three times. Now leave at once and go home. I said I would reward you handsomely, but the Lord has kept you from being rewarded. And Balaam the Prophet answered Balak. Did I not tell you the messengers the messengers who you sent to me Even if Balot gave me all of the silver and gold in his palace, I could not do anything of my own accord, good or bad, to go beyond the command of the Lord. And I must say only what the Lord says. Now I am going back to my people, but come, let me warn you of what this people will do to your people in the days to come. Then he spoke this message. The prophecy of Balaam, son of Boor, the prophecy of the one whose eyes sees clearly, the prophecy of the one who hears the words of God. Who has knowledge from on high, who sees a vision from the Almighty, who falls prostrate and whose eyes are opened. I see him, but not now. I behold him, but not near A star will come out of Jacob. A scepter will rise out of Israel. He will crush the foreheads of Moab. The skulls of all the people of Shech, Edom will be conquered. Saire, his enemy, will be conquered, but Israel will grow strong. A ruler will come out of Jacob and destroy the survivors of the city. Interpreting the prophecy from this side of the incarnation, we know the scepter mentioned is a promised king, and we can either understand the star to be metaphorical Or actual. For a prophecy to be true, we know that it has to be fulfilled fully. And for it to be miraculous, it must go beyond what you and I can explain in this world. The difficulty of the star of Bethlehem Is that it doesn't just shine brighter than any star in the sky, it moves. And then it rests, and by rest I mean it stops. It had to for the wise men to know where to go to find the child. To take a literalist approach on this is risk-taking. And by risk-taking, I am referring to looking like a fool because you are believing a star could stand still over a town. Now what we know about stars, they cannot do what the Bible is describing this particular star did. In Matthew chapter 2, we read that the wise men saw the star in the east, but followed it west to Jerusalem first, and then to Bethlehem, which is about six miles south of Jerusalem. So the star, excuse me, the song, star of wonder, star of bright, uh star of might is accurate when it says westward leading, still proceed. Matthew also says that the star which appeared in the east before the wise men went before them. Again, it moved. It guided their movement. I recall in seminary there were certain students and professors who would try to guess which miracles described in Holy Scripture were for metaphorical use and which ones actually occurred. Miracles like Jonah being swallowed by a fish and being in his belly for four days and and the sun stopping for Joshua, those two most agreed upon were metaphorical. They could not have actually occurred. And all of the doubt was and caused by fitting miracles into our so-called enlightened experiences. It seems that when we experience life for a certain amount of days, we are less and less convinced that miracles occur. A man living in a fish four days cannot be imagined to have occurred. The sun standing still until a battle is won would throw the whole solar system out of balance. Thus they could not have happened because we can't imagine that they could have happened. But I wish for us to consider That doubting miracles, such as a star being brighter than any star and moving and then standing still at a particular place and a particular time To doubt such things is the breaking of the first commandment. For it is placing ourselves at the judgment seat of creation and the judgment seat of time To determine what God can pull off and what he can't pull off. What is missing? When imagining how a miracle the star moving and then resting To point to an even greater miracle. What is missing is mystery and awe. There is great mystery in our world and in our galaxy and in the universe that should leave us with a continuing sense of awe and wonder. Consider what we have become familiar with that should cause us to pause and to wonder. Philosophers think it is fascinating to imagine a beast, a creature like a unicorn. But unicorns are boring. They're just horses with a horn. Compare that animal to a giraffe. What is a giraffe? What can you compare a giraffe to? Imagine never having seen a giraffe before and someone describing it to you. You would laugh. You would call them silly, thinking that nothing like it exists or ever would exist. But they do exist. We can see them and interact with them when we're in the right place. And if you did interact with a giraffe, would you know it better And if you knew it better, would you lessen your wonder about such an animal? I doubt it. It lessens our wonder only when we try to control it. When mankind gains knowledge about things, it is then that he is tempted to try to control them, those things. Evolutionists, for example, speculate that giraffes have long necks because their choice of food was leaves in trees. And for many years they spent straining their necks to get to these leaves, and so that eventually evolved into a need to grow a longer neck, and therefore they are these creatures with very, very long necks And that sounds plausible. Therefore, giraffes, well, we now know them, they're no longer mysterious. Therefore, we can move on to something else that we can find out about and then control. But how is such speculation actually knowing anything about the essence of a giraffe? It is when mankind comes to the conclusion that he really can't know anything fully that he has the opportunity to wonder. And when we are in a state of wonder and awe, we are then open to picturing a bright star appearing in the sky to guide men to a baby boy in Mary's arms. And when we picture that, when we open our minds and our hearts to believing that that baby boy could be in Mary's arms Then we can also then believe that he is King of Kings and Lord of Lords. I don't know if Mr. Larson's speculation about the Star of Bethlehem is accurate or not, It is fun to speculate about and certainly makes some sense. Regardless of what happened in the sky. It was all done to shine upon the greatest wonder and awe of all, God becoming man. Amen and Amen. Let us pray

sermons.title: Christmas Morning
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Like to extend my preaching topic from last night into this morning by learning and being blessed by the story of the wise men following that Bethlehem star or that Christmas star I first want to mention the contrast between the wise men and Herod. Herod did not make a big deal about the star in the sky that shined brighter than any other star Herod only made a big deal about the wise men making a big deal about the bright star in the sky. For all that we don't know about the wise men, the one thing that we can say positively about them is that they looked up. They marveled at the sky, they wondered at the sky. Herod, on the other hand, looked down. Looking down, looking down is being concerned first and last about the things of this world, and not acknowledging that there's a world beyond you That Herod would do anything to maintain that world that was his is not an exaggeration. As many of the slain infants of that region testify. Because there were so many charlatans and impostors that claimed power to tell the future and read the stars. No one in a high government position like that of Herod's would have paid attention to the magi coming to them saying, we're reading the stars. Unless unless they actually came from the Magi College in the East and there was such a thing. Those of the Magian College were learned men. They were considered both astronomers and astrologers. Astronomers measure the celestial bodies and note the laws of physics occurring between the planets. Astrologers are people who believe that they can predict human behavior by reading the stars in heaven. Astrology is condemned in Scripture again, mentioned last night, for two reasons. The first reason is that it is false. Stars in the sky don't tell the future. It is that simple. The second reason is that God wants his people to look to him and to him alone for their future. So, what is the reason or purpose for this magi visiting Jesus? Well the church calendar tells us it's because the Gentile world is included, and that's that's true when we celebrate that But there is even more to it, and we'll try to discover that this morning. But this is what we know about the Magi, little history lesson. The ancient historian Herodotus tells us that they were a priestly tribe for the Medes. They were priests, much like the Levites were priests for Israel. They were priests for for the Medes and then the Persians and then the Babylonians. And they considered they were considered to be providing divine information on daily matters for government affairs. Kings will look to them literally for advice. We see them interacting, most assuredly, in the book of Daniel. And it is quite likely that Daniel, being among the Magi in Babylon, helps to explain why those in the Magian profession actually cared about or thought about or predicted when a Jewish king would come. We remember That this is the very thing that Daniel prophesied would happen, a king would come. Daniel prophesied the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the Babylonians destroyed it in the 6th century. He also said, you remember our study from Daniel, that 490 years would pass from that command to rebuild Jerusalem until the world-embracing messianic kingdom would emerge in the region of Palestine. Well, there is assuredly lack of specifics in Daniel's prophecy, and that led to a lot of speculation as to when this Messiah would come. Most Jews were certain enough about the prophecies of Daniel to believe that it would occur sometime around the first century. And the Jewish historian Josephus confirms this, for he lived in that time and knew of that expectation. And there can be no doubt that the Magi in Mesopotamia would have been aware of the prophetic indications among the Jews. In fact, scholars today are able to see that there was a great deal of mingling between the Jews and the Magi in that period of time. This was because, again, that connection of Daniel in the 6th century BC. Interestingly Most Jews respected the Magi in the East, and this was not only because of their former association with Daniel the prophet, but also because they were not idolaters. Though the Magi believed in the power deities that were manifested, let's say in water and air and earth and fire, what set them apart from all the others around them is that they did not make images to worship. Thus the Jews of the first century respected the Magi. The Jewish philosopher by the name of Philo, who lived in Alexandria, Egypt during the time of Jesus, spoke of the Magi with warm praise. The Bible said they were men who gave themselves to the study of the laws of nature and they contemplated the divine perfections. Philo considered them worthy counselors of the kings of the region. Now when you examine the text in Matthew that describes the Magi coming, When you dis when you examine it carefully, you find that when the Magi speak to Herod, they don't just say we have seen a star, but the Greek word actually means we have seen a rising star. The plain meaning is that the Magi had witnessed a star rise above the eastern horizon. It was a moving star, and thus could match what we said last night concerning the alignment of Jupiter and Venus Also there must have been some unusual relationship with the star with other celestial bodies The Magi were so impressed that they made their long, difficult journey to Jerusalem with costly gifts to present to this new king. After hearing their account, King Herod and all Jerusalem were equally persuaded that something was very important about this star. And there is no doubt that the New Testament is using normal astronomical terms to describe this event. The narrative clearly shows that the magi observed this ordinary star or planets aligning Above the eastern horizon, and they interpret it as the sign of the king of the Jews, now in his nativity period. It was one star that intrigued them. And it was the Holy Spirit that moved on their hearts, that moved on their minds to go and see what this symbolized. You should know also, if you remember your history, that this was a period of time when astrological interpretations were made by first-class professionals. Every nation used the stars to try to figure out whether they would win a battle or lose, whether they should go out and conquer or remain in protection. So confident was the Roman government about predicting the future in the skies that 60 years before Jesus was born The Roman Senate ordered that all boy babies must not be allowed to live in 63 BC Because an astrological forecast said that a king to the Romans would be born. This earlier event would have been well known by Herod and the people throughout the Roman Empire. And indeed, Caesar Augustus was born in 63 BC. And this is very likely witness. stirred Herodons realized if that was true about Caesar Augustus, it's going to be true again, only it means that I'm the one on the outs. And this is the purpose now to the star, the purpose of the magi. Their purpose was to pronounce the presence of a king. Of course, he was not just any king or just another king. He was and is the king of kings. He is what all earthly kings want to be, but cannot be. The importance of the birth of Jesus is underlined and highlighted by the visit of the Magi and by the response of Herod to this newborn king. As the book of Revelation describes, the devil sought to destroy the one born of a virgin. Herod became a tool, a vehicle that would destroy the child if it were possible. It is most certainly sad and very true and real that the devil uses people to do his bidding. And they don't know it. Men and women who give themselves over to emotions like anger and bitterness then become a tool of the devil to use that anger and bitterness to hurt people. Those who have given themselves over to hate think that they are making their own choices when in fact their choice to be given over to anger and bitterness, well that was their last choice What they do afterward is guided by the devil. Herod had given himself over to pride and vainglory. Before the birth of Jesus, he had declared himself king of Judea. He has been described as a madman who murdered his own family and a great many rabbis. Also described as an evil genius of the Jewish nation, and prepared to commit any crime in order to gratify his unbounded ambition. Thus the devil could use Herod in any way he wanted, and he wanted to kill the Son of God. The feast of the Holy Innocence. Is to be celebrated three days from now, in remembrance of that massacre ordered by Herod for all the boys of Bethlehem in the region, ages two and under, to be killed. Such is the nastiness of the devil. And it should be noted that such nastiness is evidence that the devil really had no true knowledge of God's will. He did not know where the baby Jesus was born. He could not find the Son of God. His powers only extended as far as God allows them. And even now they're minimized because Jesus has overcome sin and death. Now, this hate of Herod reminded me of a story that I read this past week. In Lansing, Michigan, the Detroit chapter of the Satanic Temple set up a snakeity scene. Snake Tivity scene. Near the Capitol building. It featured a snake offering a book called The Revolt of the Angels as a symbolic gift. The snake is wrapped around a satanic cross, a cross upside down. It was a three feet by three feet display. The group says it does not worship Satan, but promotes individuality, compassion, and views outside of Christian and many conservative beliefs, explained Jex Blackmore. What an appropriate name, Blackmore. Satanic Temple Spokesperson. A picture of the group has them all wearing black. And gray, and every word that comes out of their mouth is an expression of anger and hate. The group is an example of what the devil continues to try to do when the birth of the Son of God is celebrated But of course, it does not matter. It doesn't matter what the hered types do. They can lust for power all that they like. The devil can use them in whatever manner he thinks will promote hate, evil, and bring forth death. He can use ordinary people living ordinary lives to try to distract the world. From true joy, beauty, and unconditional love. But it does not matter. Jesus was born. He was born King of kings And the visit of the Magi tells the world he is king of kings. He was not king of the Jews only, but king of all creation. And so I close with this following poem written by Cecil Francis Alexander, titled The Adoration of the Wise Men. Saw you never in the twilight when the sun had left the skies, up in heaven, the clear stars shining through the gloom like silver eyes? So of old the wise men watching saw a little stranger star, and they knew the king was given, and they followed it from afar. Heard you never of the story, how they crossed the desert wild, journeyed on by plain and mountain till they found the holy child How they opened all their treasure kneeling to that infant king, gave the gold and fragrant incense, gave the myrrh in offering. Know ye not that lowly baby was bright and morning star, he who came to light the Gentiles and the darkened isles afar? And we too may seek his cradle. There our hearts' best treasures bring love and faith and true devotion for our Savior, God. And king Ahmed

sermons.title: Sermon Dec 28
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Okay. I don't know what I'm saying. Yeah, okay. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. If you are a Ravens fan this morning, it's good news for you. Today is the fourth day of Christmas, and that is a good sign for Ravens fans. Four calling birds. Fourth day of Christmas. Evidently, I ran across this information. Evidently, the four calling birds from the Twelve Days of Christmas song is actually an Americanization of the original wording, which was for caulibirds. C-O-L-L-Y. For collie birds. And that originally means blackbirds. And could very well be referring to ravens. So four raven birds in the twelve days of Christmas This morning I want to point your attention to two days ago. Two days ago was the feast of St. Stephen's. You are aware, of course, that certain days have been set aside in the Western Christian tradition to honor specific saints on specific days. The Feast of St. Stephen's is appropriate for us to acknowledge for the simple reason that that is our parish name. We are named after St. Stephen. Understand, please, that such names are not chosen arbitrarily like a mascot would be chosen. Proverbs says that a good name is to be preferred rather than great riches. Names in Scripture have meaning, eternal meaning. People were named according to what their parents wanted that child to be, or What that child reminded the parent of when the when the child was born. Remember Esau being born, and he came out all hairy and and red, and so he was named Esau And then Jacob came out, grasping his brother's heel. Well, Jacob means surplanter. And that's what Jacob was trying to do, and that's what he eventually did to his brother. These names represent characteristics. Historically, the naming of churches has followed the same principle, at least in terms of wanting a parish to emulate the characteristics of the saint. That they were named after. Now I have asked around and I've talked to Reverend Godman and I've talked to Bishop Cox trying to find out why this parish was named St. Stephen's. And there's not a an agreement as to how they came about that name. But I got suspicious because, well, Bishop Cox was instrumental in helping start this church and and His son is named Stephen, and so I thought maybe maybe it was to honor Stephen and And then I heard about what type of child Stephen was. And I said this to his face, so I'm not saying anything And realize that there's no way this was named after Stephen Cox. If such were true about this parent, that is that it was named after the saint that we are to emulate, well, what does that mean for us? St. Stephen, we find his story in Acts chapter 7, is called the first martyr of the church. And that is true in one sense. He is the first person to die, a martyr's death, in history, for proclaiming Christ as his Savior. In another sense, it can be said that Stephen was not the first martyr of the Christian faith. In fact, he is not the first martyr of the New Testament. You will remember the story of Jesus' birth as recorded in St. Matthew. The Magi were told in a dream not to return to Herod Not to tell him where the Christ child could be found. And Herod became enraged. Herod was a crazy man. And so he gave orders to kill all the boys in Bethlehem and its vicinity who were two years old and under. The cries of weeping caused by these murders were so great that it is said to have been heard in the next town next to Bethlehem. Today is that holy innocence day we remember innocent children dying. These children, these young boys, were the first martyrs of the New Testament The word martyr means witness. Its original meaning did not relate to dying for one's faith, but to testify to one's faith. Those who followed Christ in the first few centuries did so. They testified wonderfully, powerfully, inspirationally They faced death also. And thus the word martyr became associated with witnessing to the faith in Jesus and also dying for that faith. Because the word martyr literally means witness, it is fitting to call the children who died by Herod's order martyrs, for they testified that the Messiah had come. In Jeremiah 31, we read it, I'll read it again. The voice is heard in Rama weeping and great mourning. Rachel. Jacob's beloved wife, weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted because they are no more Such was a prophecy 500 years previous to the day in which Herod would take his vengeance out on children. The prophecy, as painful and heart-wrenching as it became, was a witness that the Messiah had come and dwelt among men. Being a martyr, such as Stephen, or the children who died by Herod's sword, can also be said of someone like Abel. Abel was the first man murdered, we know. He was murdered by his brother Cain over jealousy because God favored Abel over him. And this jealousy parallels the emotion of Herod that he had towards the Christ child, and that the Pharisees had towards the Christ. God favored him over them, and they hated him for it. Abel offered unto God the firstborn of his flock. And this was a precursor to the offering of Jesus himself. Who was the fulfillment of the perfect sacrifice that you and I need for the forgiveness of our sins? Abel was then a martyr, a witness to the coming Christ because of that offering. After he was murdered, the Lord confronted Cain. Again, you will remember asking Abel Asking Cain, excuse me, where Abel was. And then Cain uttered that famous lie, am I my brother's keeper? The Lord then revealed that Abel's blood had been crying out to him from the ground. And we find that same crying out in the book of Revelation. Where the martyrs are under the altar and they are crying out to the Lord, how long? How long? And that question is about vengeance. To be taken upon those who are guilty of their murder. How long? So St. Stephen is one of the many who cries out, How long? One of the many early Christians who was martyred, unless it is fitting for us on December 26th to wear red. To remember those who are martyred and to wear it today for those children who were murdered and martyred. The Holy Scripture, of course, reveals more about Stephen than him being a martyr. He was the first of the seven to be set aside to serve as deacons in the church. The book of Acts, you will recall, describes how deacons were chosen from among the members of the Church of Israel to serve the needs of the poor, the weak, and the elderly. Stephen was one of those men chosen. His duties were humble and they were necessary. Along with Stephen's character qualifying him to be one of the first deacons, he is described to be a man full of God's grace and full of God's power. The evidence of that grace and power were great wonders and miraculous signs done through him. And they were a witness, a powerful witness to the people of Jesus Christ. Stephen was also a man of courage, speaking aggressively to the Jewish people that the law had been fulfilled and the temple was no longer necessary because Jesus the Messiah had come. When Stephen was put on trial for his life before the Sanhedrin, he did not blink, he did not falter. He clearly pronounced to those who were listening that Jesus is the fulfillment of the prophet's words. He is the only hope for Israel. Although he knew his aggressive speech would lead to his death, he spoke bravely, calling his accusers stiff-necked people and uncircumcised in heart. and ears. In the same manner that Stephen stood before the Sanhedrin, without blinking and faltering, he stood before the stone throwers. He took his blows while crying out that the Heavenly Father would receive his Spirit and then in the Spirit of our Savior ask God to forgive those who were murdering him. St. Stephen was a remarkable man. And we are his namesake. His type of character we are to exhibit. We have a very tall order force. This parish is now 32 years old. If it were a person, if St. Stephen's Paris was an average American adult, he would likely be established in a career and raising children. To be established in a career and raising children meant that there had to be a lot of important decisions made in the past to get where it is now. Some of those decisions were good and some were not. But they are all used to give us an identity, to give St. Stephen's an identity that we have now. There have been people in St. Stephen's past who were insisting that St. Stephen's be like the popular churches that embrace a contemporary style of music only contemporary style, and that the order of service should be more like a concert than that which is traditional To such suggestions, we settled on the wisdom that, first, there is no reason for us to emulate churches that are contemporary in their music style and worship style Because our place in the body of Christ in this region would become unnecessary. We would have nothing to offer others that they couldn't find elsewhere. Those churches that are more contemporary are usually larger, and we and they have, excuse me, more at their disposal to entertain. We recognize that we should not attempt to do something that someone else is already doing because they they'll do it better than us anyways And second, we simply need to point to the sign that is outside our church near the road. It marks our identity. It says St. Stephen's Reformed Episcopal Church. We, according to the Sign Outside, are Reformed Episcopalians. Being a Reformed Episcopalian means we have history dating back to eighteen seventy-three, and even farther, because we are inheritors of the English Reformation. And our history gives us identity. It is very important to realize that as we define ourselves, we put limits on ourselves And that's not a negative thing. That word limit I am using in a positive sense, where it allows us to know who we are, and not to be confused or drawn away by fad or pragmatism. Besides those who were telling us who we should be, there were others in our past who have told us what we should not be. That advice comes in the form of what is called Romophobia. Romophobia is the fear of the Roman Catholic Church. And those who tried to tell us we should not be like the Roman Catholic Church, we're not so much concerned about what we were, just what we shouldn't be. They didn't want us to be like the Roman Catholic Church. Well, the reason for Romophobia affecting so many within the Reformed Episcopal Church is that our history is a reactionary history. In the beginning, Bishop Cummins was concerned about the Roman Catholic influence on the American Episcopal Church. When he believed that the evangelicals were being squeezed out of the church by the tractarians or those who wanted us to move closer to Rome, well, he decided to start a new denomination. The name, Reformed Episcopal, was chosen because those who started the denomination wanted us to go back to the practices of the original American Episcopal Church, reforming it Back to its original ways. Thus, the Reformed Episcopal Church. It is my take on history that we have spent too much time as a denomination identifying ourselves with what we are not. That is, we are not Roman Catholic. And that is opposed to identifying ourselves for what we are, or better said, what we should be. The Reformed Episcopal Church will never be Roman Catholic. Again, the logic would have it that if that is what we want it to be, well, let's just close our doors, take a left on Liberty Road, go down to St. Joseph's and join them. No reason for us to exist. Instead of becoming Roman Catholic, we have become like the Church of England is supposed to be We have become Catholic in our understanding of the Word, the universality of the gospel. And we have embraced the Protestant ideal of holy scripture being our first and final authority. In its beginnings in the 16th century, the Church of England made a bold statement, like St. Stephen made to the Sanhedrin. The church said the Pope is not infallible. Church tradition was not equal to Scripture, and that men are saved by grace through faith alone. What the English reformers would not do is abandon the liturgical order of worship that does not really identify with the Roman Catholic Church, but has been with the church, the Christian Church from its beginning. By us embracing the practices of the reformers, we are also not going to abandon our liturgical order. For again, it has been handed down to us, a gift to us from our fathers, from our fathers in the faith. Our identity then is strongly grounded in two primary areas. First, We strive to be reverent in our worship as our order follows biblical ideals that God has put before his people on how he wants to be approached and worshipped and called upon. Second, we are Bible believers. We believe all that the Bible teaches. We believe its teachings are first and primary to any traditions of the church. We preach it, we teach it, and attempt to live it out in our daily lives. And I, for one, have a godly pride in that identity. I do not apologize for using the prayer book to direct our prayers for corporate worship. To be more bold, I would challenge any church. to compare the wording of their extemporaneous prayers to the wording of the prayers that we pray from the prayer book. Not only would our prayers contain so much more, but they would be more beautiful. And I also with you do not apologize for the manner we uphold Scripture in our services and in our time of training. I would match our teaching and application of biblical principles against any church, any church who would consider us to be like Rome. I could go on, but I'm certainly aware that I'm preaching to the proverbial choir. The purpose of this sermon has been to bolster our courage, to be who we are It is also my goal to more precisely define who we are, allowing those who wonder to know, to know better. And to those who have questions, well, some answers. I also want us to consider how much work it takes to maintain what we have. I am repeatedly moved by Jesus' words to the seven churches in Revelation to hold on. And if he keeps repeating it, it means it must be pretty hard to do, to hold on. We are told to hold on to the truths that make us pleasing in the sight of our Savior. There have been people in the past who would like us to see us let go. And there are people in our future who will want us to embrace other things. To embrace the next spirit of the age, the siegegeist that comes along. And I am becoming more and more aware that to hold on, we are going to have to be courageous. We're going to have to stand strong when false accusations are made about us When we are accused of abusing women because we do not ordain them to the ministry, we are going to have to stay strong. When we are accused of waging war against women because we strive to protect the unborn, we are going to have to stay strong. When we are accused of being abusive toward our children because we brainwash them by telling them that there is one truth, and that we don't spare the rod, we are going to have to be strong. When we are accused of being prejudiced because we believe homosexuality to be a sinful behavior and not a state of being, we are going to have to be strong When we continue to say that marriage is between a man and a woman only, we're going to have to hold on and stay strong. When St. Stephen stood before the Sanhedrin, he had to decide who he was, and he had to decide whether his identity was worth the sacrifice he was about to make. He had to choose whether he would go back to Judaism or be counted a follower of Christ and die at the hands of his accusers. We of course do not face such an obvious choice now. And yet it takes similar courage. To go the opposite way of what is popular or what is perceived about you that is negative by others. We have decided, we have to decide, excuse me, we have to decide whether our identity is worth the sacrifices we will have to make. When the stones start to fly, each of us as individuals, and then as families, and then as a church family. We'll have to decide what we want to live for, and thus what we want to die for May we be able to say, as Saint Stephen did on that day, his last, look I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God. Amen and Amen.

sermons.title: The Love of God
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: A good preacher points the congregation he is addressing away from himself and to the Savior. If he talks about himself, it must be for the purpose of pointing to the Savior. That is the purpose of telling you the following story. 31 years ago, I was given a Bible for Christmas by my sister Dana. It was a living Bible translation. The Living Bible is a paraphrase of the American Standard Version of the Bible written by Ken Taylor for the purpose of children understanding God's Word. Even though I had received my first communion and had been in a local C C D program, it was the first Bible I had owned and read. At the front of the Living Bible translation I was given, there was a table of content that informed the reader where they could go to read about certain topics. One of the topics was love. During the Christmas season of 1982, at 17 years of age, I sat on my bed in my bedroom and picked up my living Bible and turned to the topic of love and read the following. Love is patient and kind. Love is not jealous or boastful or proud or rude. It does not demand its own way. It is not irritable, and it keeps no record of being wronged. It does not rejoice about injustice, but rejoices whenever the truth wins up. Love never gives up, never loses faith is always hopeful and endures through every circumstance. After reading those words, my heart was warmed And I recognized that I had not known or ever experienced the type of love that was described in those words. There are many solid arguments for the existence of God, and I have shared them from this pulpit with great conviction in the past. But the greatest argument that convinced me of God's existence was a realization that love, as is described in 1 Corinthians 13, is real. It exists. I had not known love as described in 1 Corinthians 13 before I believed Jesus Christ as my Lord and Savior. Before I read of God's love, I had known what author C. S. Lewis calls need love. Need love is best understood in the relationship between a child and its mother. Need love comes from an appreciation for what is provided. Every child needs the love of its mother for food, knowledge, and protection. It is a selfish love on behalf of the child, but unnecessary selfishness, where it is needed to survive. I knew that love, but always felt it was not enough, for as a child who had lost his birth mother at the age of three I always felt that I needed more need love than I had known. On the other side of need love is gift love. which is a love that is providing the love others need. Interestingly, Lewis explores how such a love that sounds so very unselfish can actually be turned into a perversion. He describes this perversion through a character called Mrs. Frigid. Mrs. Frigget was sent by her neighbors to live for her family. She did everything for the family. The laundry, the cleaning, and the cooking, even when no one wanted her to, and even begged her not to. She was so insistent, Betsy, that she sacrificially cared for her family, that she would wait up to the wee hours of the night and early morning to make sure her family returned home safely. But she did so with a sacrificial judgmental expression that what she insisted was love was not felt by those she smothered. When she cared for her children who were sick, she wanted them to stay that way so that she might always be needed. Thus. Thus Mrs. Fridget turned gift love into need love, for in her giving she revealed her need to be needed. Such a character as Mrs. Fridget reveals that love, as mankind understands it, is always tainted with self. And before I'd read of God's love, I had also known friendship love. Many of you met a childhood friend of mine named Jay Ward. He graciously came to surprise Me on my 40th birthday party ten years ago. I have known Jay since I was three years of age. We were close friends throughout our childhood. Our friendship has continued because well because of life experiences. Friendship love usually arises when two people discover that they have some common insights or experiences in life or tastes that they share. If two people who are not friends find something important that connects them, they say, What? You two? And then they begin a conversation that will very likely lead to a friendship if what they agree upon is important. A healthy friendship is inclusive. For although it is based on certain and necessary commonalities, it invites others who are of the same commonality to join in, to be a part. Unhealthy friendships are exclusive. They insist that only certain persons can be included based on very specific criteria. It has been argued that friendship love is the least needed of all the types of love human beings experience, which is to say that you don't need friendship love to survive. But friendship love is also the most productive of loves This makes perfect sense when compared to something such as need love, for such a love as one person receiving from another or one person giving to another. Erotic love, which I have yet to mention, is also not productive because it focuses on two persons and no one else, and is also a love that has but one end goal. These, compared to friendship love, are unproductive. Friendship love is a shoulder-to-shoulder love that can work towards goals and accomplish much. The Book of Proverbs speaks of friendship love as being superior even to familial love because it is entered into voluntarily and continues because of common goals. Proverbs says, there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother. And before I read of God's love, I had also known erotic love. Erotic love is affectionate love, for it is expressed by the way of the body. It is a love that can be both selfish and selfless at the same time. It is neither holy nor sinful in and of itself, for its value is determined by its context. Erotic love outside of a marital context, a marital covenant, is perverted, plain and simple. In the context of marriage, it is an important and necessary part of a covenant bond. When in its godly context, erotic love can be a taste of heaven. The negative on erotic love is that it is first limited in that it is between two persons only. And as a negative, it distracts people from caring about others beyond the persons providing putting. There's also a distracted love, as is evident by the poems and songs it produces. It clouds the mind of a person as it puts everything else in the background, focusing on the one that is the object of affection. Well this is not a bad thing at all, I and I hope I'm not communicating that it is. But erotic love has its limitations and it Its emotional swings, making it unpredictable and even unruly. Too many people confuse erotic love with happiness. This is found in the writings of the father of psychoanalysis Sigmund Freud, who defined happiness in terms of sexual pleasure only. Such happiness is fleeting, of course, and therefore it is not happiness as God has described it in His Holy Word. Happiness. True happiness. Well, that is like joy. It is a fruit of the Holy Spirit, and therefore fasting and deep within the human soul. After need love and after friendship love and after erotic love, there is but one more type of love. The type of love is actually the first type of love. And that love is also called charity. Modern Bible translations such as the New King James Version in your pews translate charity in 1 Corinthians 13 as love. And that is acceptable, although if we were to be critical, we should choose the word charity because the word separates the type of love being described from all other types of love. In the Greek language, the language of the New Testament, the word love or charity is agape. What is unique about the word agape, as it is used in the New Testament, is that it is only used in reference to God. Agape love or charity only comes from God. Therefore, if we are commanded to use it, that love toward one another as we are in 1 Corinthians 13, then we must get it from God and then pass it on. Therefore, unless a person has the love of God within him or her, it cannot be passed on to another person. Of course, need love and friendship love and erotic love can be passed on from one person to another person at any time by a person's own will and own strength. But to pass on God's love, a person needs to have God's love within him. And it was God's love that I knew I did not have. And so desperately needed when I sat on my bed at seventeen years of age and read for the first time what God's love was. Let us then reread the verses about God's love from 1 Corinthians again, this time from the New King James Version. Love suffers long. If we were to stop here and not continue We already have a great deal to work on when it comes to loving one another. Love that suffers long puts up with a lot of garbage, for lack of a better adjective. And it puts hook with a lot of garbage over and over again. That is what long suffering is. It is enduring weaknesses and wrongdoings and neglects again and again and again without ever giving up. To love in such a manner is to love like God, for God refers to Himself as long-suffering. And it does not take long to understand God's long suffering when reading the Old Testament and know how God endured the sins of Israel, his people over and over again If we are tempted to think that there is a limit to our long-suffering, we only need to consider how much and how many times God has done long-suffering for us. Next. Love is kind. That sounds so simple and easy, doesn't it? Love is kind. Well, of course it is kind. We should all be kind to one another. And yet being kind is not easy. For some of us, it is actually very hard. A dismissive look is not kind. An unwillingness to speak to another person is not kind. Not taking the time to acknowledge another person's presence, another person's needs, another person's worth. is not kind. Being kind takes work. It takes investing in other people's lives. C. S. Lewis said somewhere that when we work at being kind to someone, we find that we grow in our love for that same someone. That is a very true observation and includes the realization that being kind takes work. It takes a determined will and it takes effort No one else can do the work for you. You have to get up and get to the task of being kind. Next. Love does not envy. We learn here that we can know love from not only saying what it is, but what it isn't. What it isn't tells us that it is the opposite. Love does not envy. To envy is to want what someone else has. It could be, yes, earthly wealth, social standing, authority, respect, possessions, etc. , etc. Envy includes jealousy and coveting. It is selfish. It is not rejoicing for what others have, but concerned about what the loveless person would prefer to have. You know you are full of love when you rejoice regarding the success of others. You know you are full of love when you are glad for your neighbor's promotion, his son's scholarship, his wife's weight loss, his new car, etc. , etc. You know you are full of love when someone is good at what they do and you praise them for it. Any other response is not of God. Next. Love does not parade itself. In this description we have the other side of envy. Whereas love does not envy, when it finds reasons to rejoice, it does not behave like a braggart. It does not participate in tempting people to envy It recognizes that whatever gifts, earthly wealth, and earthly success a person obtains are from God and not because that person is better than others. For a person to think that he is or she is better than other people who are also made in God's image is to be puffed up. Love, instead of being puffed up, is humble, weak, and always grateful. Next, love does not behave rudely. We don't often consider the subject of love in the context of social manners, but the Bible does. Consider where a person's thoughts are focused when he or she behaves in a rude manner. Rude manners come forth from selfish motives. Interruptions, careless words, ignoring another person, being indiscreet, being inappropriate are behaviors that occur when the welfare of other people is not considered. The opposite of behaving rudely is thinking of the comfort and needs of others first and primarily. Love, God's love, the love he commands us to share with one another, considers first the comforts and needs of others. Next. Love does not seek its home. This description of love is an underline to the previous description of love not behaving rudely. Before my eyes were opened to believing truly, believing with all of my heart that Jesus was Lord and Savior, I am quite confident that everything I did in my life was based on what I was seeking for myself. I am not aware of putting anyone else's needs before my own, and I am quite sure that if I ever did, it was so that it would be to my benefit in the long run As a young man, reading this description of what love is, I knew. I did not know that love. But I desperately wanted to. Next. Love is not provoked. When our anger is set off at another person We can immediately conclude that it is what the other person has done that has provoked our anger. It's their fault. Actually, it was not an action of another that provoked us, but what is inside of us already that was waiting to come out. Anger and bitterness are nasty demons that when harbored in our hearts come out of us in a very unholy way. When love resides within us, it overwhelms anger and bitterness to the level of casting them out. Therefore, another person's actions do not phase us even when those actions are careless and thus thoughtless because love dominates. Next, love thinks no evil. When we are loving one another as God has commanded and equipped us to love, We are faking the best of one another. We are assuming that people have good motives and not bad. We are remembering the good they have done for us and not keeping record of wrongs. To think no evil is to only think good about an individual. Such thinking I had never dreamed of being possible before I gave my life over to Christ. I wanted it though. I needed it. Next, love does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices in the truth. Truth. Truth. I'm a product of the American public school system. I didn't know that truth, objective truth, existed. I would easily rejoice in iniquity if iniquity was to my glory and my pleasure. But it was the existence of truth that I never knew, and that I wanted to know. When I first read the cont and contemplated the existence of truth, I needed faith to accept that it existed and was therefore possible to know. In verse 7, we read the summary of the love of God just described. The summary is couched by two words. Conveying the same meaning. Those words are bears and endures. Love bears all things and endures all things. And these descriptions can be brought together with verse 8, where we are told that love never fails. When need love passes away, there will still be God's love. When friendship love is no longer needed to produce anything, there will still be God's love. When erotic love passes into only our memories, God's love will remain. That is why believing all things and hoping all things are couched in between, bearing and enduring. Consider all that each of us need to live happy lives in this life and to live forever. We need the love of God. The love of God is the only love that lasts. With it comes faith and hope. The three things that remain, the three things that matter, faith, hope, and charity. The beauty of the sacrament of baptism that we have witnessed today is that it is a tangible expression of God's love for us, his people. It is a tangible sign of Jesus washing away our sins and making us new. And the importance of baptism is seen in the relationship that now exists between Roman Catholic the Roman Catholic Church and many Protestant churches such as our own. That is, that both groups recognize the legitimacy of one another's baptism And we do so. How? We do so by charity. You could go to a Roman Catholic Church, transfer over there, and they would recognize your baptism. Those who come in from the Roman Catholic Church to us, we recognize their baptism. And why? Again, because of charity, because of love, God's love. The love of God I have described, I want all of my children to know, and all of my grandchildren, starting with tax. But what I want cannot be assured. It is most important that God wants Jackson. He wants you. And he wants me to know his love. Then we can through Jesus. Amen.

sermons.title: Preparing for Tests
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated Today, we are beginning a new series of sermons based on the letters written by St. John. This means, of course, that we are interrupting our study from Isaiah. We are doing this for two reasons First, when we continue our study of Isaiah, it will be near Passion season and Easter season and therefore appropriate for where we have left off as we are close to Reading of the suffering servant. Second, I want us to study The letters of John, because they contain the greatest teaching of the apostles regarding how Christians are to love one another. The sermon last Sunday on the overall topic of the love of God was very purposeful for this congregation. In the past year, and even the past two years, and then certain years before that, when relationships have been severed in this parish I'm not awa uh aware of anyone asking the question, where is God's love and all of this? Well precisely the question would be, where is the love of God and the way I am responding to my authorities in Christ? Where is the love of God in this the decision I am making? Where is the love of God in my attitude? Where is the love of God in my response to the decision people make? And such questions I have not asked, and I have repented For not asking them. And part of my restitution is to preach this series of sermons I mention the following in my annual report, but it is worth repeating, so I say it here. Jesus said to his disciples, A new commandment I give you, that you love one another, even as I have loved you, that you also would love one another. By this, all men will know that you are my disciples. We must note first, in order to apply this commandment in our lives, That it is not new for God to command us to love one another. What is new is the type of love. We are to love one another as Jesus loved us. Now stop in your tracks for a moment And contemplate the love that Jesus has for us. It is 100% selfless As it culminated in him sacrificing himself for us. That is the love standard we are to have toward one another. That is what is new. And then there is this add-on that Jesus puts in his words as he continues to explain that the non-Christian world will know that we are his disciples by our love for one another Now let's stop again and contemplate what that means The world, which is a descriptive of those who are not born again, they are not a part of the kingdom of God They will know, which is to say that they will understand, it will make sense to them that Christians are indeed followers of Jesus. By the manner, the way in which we love one another. Wow How are we doing? How well does the world know we are Christians by the manner we are currently loving one another? I preached a message in early November about the priority of the church and what it should be. I argued it was worship. Worship of the one true God is the priority of the church. And so it is. I also mentioned that some denominations put evangelism and outreach as the top priority of the church. I have always been skeptical about such a priority, especially when I received criticism that St. Stephen's Parish under my care doesn't have an outreach or evangelism program. I have been skeptical about such criticism, and I finally figured out why. It is because of what Jesus said. The best outreach, the best evangelism tool we have to reach the lost, the lost and dying world is loving one another as Jesus commanded. Consider what we are asking people to be a part of when we are not loving one another, as Jesus commanded We are asking them to be a part of God's people by coming to Christ and then coming into his church where there is bickering. Holding of grudges, gossip, slander, disobedience, stirring up dissension, becoming bitter, becoming angry, and just no longer talking to one another. Why would anyone want to be a part of such a people? All of us already have such people in our extended families. No one needs to become a part of another dysfunctional group. And next consider how much easier it would be to share the gospel to people who are witnessing self-sacrificial love that Christians practice toward one another. Who would not want to be a part of a people that spoke kind and caring words to one another and about one another? Who would not want to be a part of a people who were always long-suffering, always kind, never provoked to anger? Always thought best of one another. Always forgave, always sought out forgiveness I don't think anyone in their rational mind and heart would refuse to be a part of such a community. So let us begin with St. John's first letter. And let us begin by looking at the author, John. We first remember that John was a fisherman, along with James his brother, along with Peter and Andrew. He was one of the men Jesus called to follow him, saying, I will make you fishers of men. John was also, as I said, the brother to James, and together the two brothers were known as the sons of thunder. They were rough, hewn guys, very likely colorful of character. Being compared to thunder means that they would not back down from a confrontation. In fact, they might even have looked forward to a confrontation. They were socially aggressive, and such people can usually be very insensitive. To get a better idea of John's thunderous personality, recall that when the people of the village of Samaria were not responsive to the message of Jesus It was James and John who wanted fire to come down from heaven and destroy them. It was John and James, who were insensitive enough to ask for a position of political power just after Jesus prophesied about his own death. But God transformed James and John. And at the end of their lives, these men, who were known as sons of thunder, became known as something else. James was the first apostle to be martyred. John became known as the apostle that Jesus loved. John refers to himself as the apostle Jesus loved. He did not do so because Jesus loved John more than all the other apostles, or loved him more than anyone else. He did so because he keenly felt that the love of Jesus marked him. It gave him an identity that established his purpose for the rest of his life. John, therefore, is an obvious choice by the Holy Spirit to teach and to propagate love among Christians. Turning to the text, John, 1 John chapter 1. The opening statement of the letter is quite unique. There is no greeting as most New Testament letters have. Thus we do not know if specific recipients were intended. What we do know is the purpose of the letter. And that comes out in a very forthright manner. The purpose is the gospel of Jesus Christ. And there is no mistaking that how the opening is worded is to draw immediate and obvious parallels to the opening of the Gospel of St. John. In verse 1, we read, That which was from the beginning. From this we conclude that Jesus always existed. There was never a time when the Son of God was not. The pre-existence of Christ is the presupposition of the incarnation.
