To say that he came into the world is to say that he was somewhere else before he was born of the Virgin Mary. Of course, John began his gospel in the same manner. Both are strong affirmations that God became flesh. The eternal God, the creator of heaven and earth, entered the world and dwelt among men as a man. In verse 2, that which was from the beginning, John says, he and others have seen and have even touched Jesus. In the first chapter of the Gospel of St. John, you remember John says that this one who created the world And the word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen, seen his glory. The point being that John was an eyewitness to Jesus. And John, as an eyewitness, was quite important to the church. There were already, already false teachers who came and said, no, God would never come in the flesh. And John was given the mission to refute this denial and establish what is so fundamental to our Christian faith, God becoming flesh and dwelling among us. And regarding that person, Jesus Christ, John says that he was and is life. John saw life itself with his own eyes, and he touched eternal life with his own hands, because he saw and he touched Jesus of Nazareth. The author of all that lives. Verse 3. We are to highlight that three times in the first three verses, John says that he saw The incarnate Son of God. He is an eyewitness. And that is where the authority of what he is about to say in this letter, that's where it comes from. He was an eyewitness. He was there. He saw it all. That is the point he is establishing. Of course, what John saw, he touched, what he tasted, what he felt, that was not just for his benefit only. It was for the salvation of the world. And accordingly, he was commissioned, along with the rest of the apostles, to proclaim to the world the world of their day. What they heard, what they saw, what they tasted, what they touched. And so they had proclaimed it to these Christians to whom John was now writing. That should also be recognized. Jesus I mean excuse me, John was writing to Christians That is a reminder that conversion is only the beginning for Christians when we use words like saved. When describing our conversion, phrases like, I was saved at 17, it communicates that we are a finished product. Well hardly. And that's why John's writing. They are hardly finished. John and the rest of the apostles came to understand that their fellowship with the Lord Jesus was not simply for themselves, but for something to share with the world. They did not get that at first, but the words of Jesus at his ascension, you remember, made it very clear The love of God, as we examined and took heart to last week, does not exclude, it includes. God's love is meant to be used to bring others into the fold. And fellowship in Christian love is fellowship with God the Father and Christ Jesus the Savior. It all comes together. And John wants that for his audience. Verse 4, John says he wants the joy of Christians to be full because he loves them. The joy John is speaking of is the establishment or re-establishment of these believers in the confidence of the gospel and in their fellowship with John and other believers. Out of love for fellow Christians, John is writing to Christians who have been damaged by false understandings of the gospel, and therefore it put them out of fellowship with other Christians. Living in the age we now live is no picnic. And I am not saying that it's any worse than living in any other age. That would be chronological egoism, and I don't want to be accused of any such thing. But the age in which we live calls us, as Christians, to be insecure. Popular culture wants us to have trouble knowing what's right and wrong, what's evil or what's righteous. We are to question all of our teachers, not trusting anyone has a has a corner market on truth. And actually we're told that truth is unattainable by us. And along with our cultural insecurity is insecurity that comes from being a part of a church When we are part of a church body, we we see things we would rather have not seen. We hear about things we would rather have not heard about. We discover that people are not always who we thought they were. Sometimes our relationships with people are revealed to be conditional and really insincere. When our insecurity is at its limit, we might question whether anyone we know is living out the Christian faith in the manner that is pleasing to God. It might feel or be perceived that everyone is compromising in some manner or form Nothing can be more dangerous to young faith than the insecurity of wondering whether the blood of Jesus and the power of the Holy Spirit and faith Of mankind, that that blood and that power, that it's real, that it actually works. John has recognized this insecurity in Christians, and so he writes to them to strengthen them, to strengthen us. In the first place, John wants to strengthen is the certainty that the Christian religion is true. He wants Christians to know for certain that they can and they will inherit eternal life. John has already argued in the first For verses that the historical event of Jesus was real, witnessed, and it's behind us. It's part of his stream. And the accounts of the eyewitnesses of the apostles of that death and that resurrection and that ascension is to be known and trusted and heard and proclaimed throughout the world. And second, we can know the truth because the Holy Spirit is present to confirm the truth in our minds and in our hearts. Sometimes it's so intangible. We can't understand why that makes sense, but we know it's true. John also recognizes that such confidence he wants is primarily head knowledge. There is an insecurity tempted to reside in all Christians that would cause us to wonder, if we admit it, are we really heaven-bound? We know that the Bible presents the fact that there are many people who will believe themselves to be Christians and find out in the end that they were not. And we can't help but wonder Is that me? Does that include me? To one degree or another, most of us have had a doubt, perhaps fleeting, perhaps far more serious, about whether we ourselves are Christians, or maybe we're just playing a part. Am I part of the chaff and not the wheat? Am I the one who will not have the proper garment at the wedding feast? Am I the one that did not fill my oil lamp in time? Am I the one that will be placed on the side of the goats on the day of judgment? John. John will tell us that there is a way not to worry In 1985, an English scholar by the name of Robert Law published a study on 1 John, a study that still holds up today. And he entitled that study, The Tests of Life. The Tests of Life In that book, Law summarizes John's lesson for insecurity in what he calls the three cardinal tests. Three cardinal tests by which a man or a woman may judge whether he or she possesses eternal life. The three tests while said are, number one, the doctrinal test. Do you believe the teachings of the Word of God concerning Jesus Christ, the God man, and his saving work? Number two, the moral test. Do you live as a Christian is to live? And number three, the social test. Do you love God? And because you love God, do you love your Christian brothers and sisters? Such tests are not to be seen as arbitrary, forced, or separate from the gospel, but they actually naturally flow out of the gospel. These are what the gospel does. The gospel either separates men from the truth or it establishes them in the truth. The gospel either forms the way we live or it condemns the way we morally live. And the gospel either engenders in our hearts an ever-increasing love for God and our brothers and sisters in Christ, or it shows us guilty of harboring bitterness, envy, and strife. We find the summary of what John is after, what his end goal is, in this letter in chapter 5, verse 13. It is there that he says that he wrote this letter that Christians might know that they have eternal life. But we have to pass his test before our confidence can be secure. So are you ready to be tested? We will in the coming weeks. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Test 1 Part 1
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. You would be well served to turn to first John. We are covering verses five through ten. And we are to remember that in the backdrop of covering 1 John is 1 Corinthians 13 and those instructions for us to love. In particular, to love one another. Love is patient, love is kind. Love is long-suffering. These types of words of descriptive love are to motivate us to understand how important it is for the church to exemplify the love of Christ. That's in the backdrop of our study of 1 John. To begin with a story, an ancient story, of narcissists. Narcissist was a hunter from the territory of Thespiae. He was renowned for his beauty. He was the son of a river god named Syphesus and a nymph named Liriope. He was exceptionally proud as he had the audacity to disdain those who loved him. Nemesis noticed this behavior and coerced Narcissus to a pool where he saw his own reflection in the water. For the first time saw his reflection and fell in love with himself, not realizing it was merely an image. Unable to leave the beauty of his own reflection, narcissist drowned. This Greek myth is where we get the term narcissism, which is a psychological diagnosis of a person. This is official now. who pursues gratification from vanity or egotistic admiration of his own attributes Psychologists Drew Pinsky and Mark Young argue that at the heart of the problem of a narcissist is a lack of self-awareness. a lack of self-awareness. Those who lack self-awareness don't recognize how they are coming across to people, how people are understanding what they're communicating. Psychologist Dr. John Meisner tells the story of being in a conversation with a friend, and the friend telling him to stop doing what he is doing. Dr. Meisner is shocked and befuddled because he didn't know what his friend was talking about. His friend told him that he always checks out in the middle of a conversation having glossed over eyes and staring off while only being concerned about what is going on, excuse me, what he is going to say next, and no longer paying attention to his friend. Dr. Meisner was stunned by this observation and turned to his wife for support against his friend's accusation. Instead of support, his wife said, Oh he's right. You do that a lot. Well Dr. Meisner felt he had to stand up for himself, so he asked why this is the first time he was hearing of this. His friend responded that he had not brought it up before because Dr. Meisner was so very defensive that he would turn the discussion into an argument. That settled it in Dr. Meisner's mind. He realized for the first time his lack of self-awareness. Examining oneself to achieve some level of self-awareness is not easy. Even when some people try to evaluate themselves, they are so very deep into their lack of self-awareness that they conclude they are perfectly normal. When normal is only accurate if lacking self-awareness is normal. Last week We were challenged to be tested as to whether we are truly Christian, whether we are truly in the faith. The accepted the categories that commentator Robert Law identified as being the tests St. John provides in his first letter. These tests were one holiness of life, two, right belief regarding Jesus Christ, and three, the love of God and one another. It is healthy to remember that John does not come up with these tests to say definitively who is in and who is out. So once the test results are in, we have to accept them and go on our merry or our disappointed way. No, instead he wants to provide stability in the life of Christians so that we do not doubt. And if we don't pass one or more of the tests, then we are to get right with the Lord so that we can qualify as the first test will show us. Let us now look at verses five through ten of first John chapter one. Verse five. This is the message which you have heard from him and which we have heard from him and declare to you that God is light and in him is no darkness at all. We remember from our study of verse 1 through 4 that John made his personal and historical connection to Jesus. He made it clear, and that is done again in this verse. John says, this is the message we have heard from him that is from Jesus and proclaimed to you. It has been a strange charge upon Christians that they have been a people of secrecy. Those who have been in the Eusebius class this past Sunday school semester have heard about this accusation Early Christians were accused of doing secret heinous things when they gathered together. It is a strange charge because there is nothing hidden or secret about the gospel. It is a shoudeth from the rooftop faith. It is the very nature of the gospel to shine light and to illuminate truth. The false teachers had apparently brought what they described as some kind of hidden secret knowledge, but there is nothing secret about the gospel. As the gospel is light, it is also a symbol of purity, as darkness is a symbol of evil. Remember how we read in the Gospel of John that when the light came into the world in the person of Jesus Christ, Jesus is identified as the light. In 1 John 1. 9 it says, men loved darkness rather than light because their deeds were evil. This is why Jesus said that he did not come to bring peace, but instead a sword. The gospel provides peace only when it is received as true. When it is rejected, darkness and light are at odds. It must be that way. Verse 6. If we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth. The phrase, if we say, almost certainly indicates that what follows is what the false teachers had said. The false teachers have been saying that you could have fellowship with God and walk in darkness. Paul is now the aggressor here. When it came to truth. And when it came to protecting the people he loved, he went on the offensive. Going back to the three tests that we have identified, The right doctrine, moral, and social tests are all identified by the use of the word liar. This will help us organize the letter in our minds. Here in verse 6, we read that if we say we have fellowship with Him while we walk in darkness, we lie. The same point is made in chapter 2, verse 4. Whoever says, I know him, but does not keep his commandments is a liar. That is an example of what we are calling the moral test. In chapter 2, verse 22, we read. Who is a liar, but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ. That is an example of what we are calling the doctrinal test. And then in chapter 4, verse 20, we read, if anyone says, I love God and hates his brother, he is a liar. That is what we are calling the social test. Verse 7. But if we walk in the light as he is in the light We have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ, His Son, cleanses us from all sin. We might expect for John to say that if we walk in the light as Jesus is in the light, then we will have fellowship with God. That sounds right. It's true. Of course it's true. But as in verse 7, John goes further. He says we also have fellowship with other believers, who are likewise walking in the same light. To walk with Jesus is to walk with his people. This point cannot be missed. It is consistent with the summary of the law Jesus gives when he says it is to love God with all of our heart, soul, mind, and strength, and then to love our neighbor as ourselves. They are connected. You cannot separate them in terms of them being the whole law. Love for God and love for people go hand in hand, especially love for our fellow Christians. The point of love for God equals love for our fellow Christians is so very important. That he next mentions the blood of Jesus, the blood of Christ, removes not simply the guilt of our sin. Not simply our exposure to punishment for it, but delivers it, delivers us from its stain, its defilement in our lives. And it is appropriately mentioned here because of the failure we continue to repeat when it comes to loving one another as Jesus loves us. The next verse, verse 8, addresses a problem that is likely a result of the false teachers who had influenced these new Christians, and it is related to the manner Christians were treating one another. Verse 8. We say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. The claim of the false teachers appears to have gone so far as to say that Christians have no sin. This may have been the beginning of what the church wrestled with regarding the Gnostics, who taught that once you were forgiven, your very spirit The essence of who you are, well that is cleansed and forgiven, and therefore it didn't matter what you did with your body, what you did with your hands, with your tongue. With your fists. All this is in the physical realm, and we are to worry about the spiritual realm only. Verse 9. If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. Note please that Christians are to be assured of forgiveness from God, not because he is easy-going, not because he is indulgent, but because he is faithful to his promise. and just in the application of the sacrifice of his son. It is also important for us to remember that this verse is in the present tense. God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins now He is faithful and just to cleanse us from our sins, from our unrighteousness now. This message was and is for those who already believed in the Lord Jesus Christ. This is not a message for people to be converted, but for those who are converted and who continue to need the forgiveness the Heavenly Father offers in Jesus. Now the closing verse of this chapter is a direct blow to the false teachers. And a clear marking of who are true believers and who are not. Verse 10. If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us. Again, the word liar. It is an aggressive distinctive regarding who are the true and who are not. In summary, what we have here in these verses, verses five through ten, is a part of that moral test. John says in verse 5-7 that real Christians live godly, obedient, and faithful lives. They reflect the character of their Heavenly Father and His Son, their Savior. John is teaching us that the deeds of the body matter, and they matter a great deal. They are important, they are an important mark of God's presence in our lives. If a person has been born in the light, he or she will live in the light, and as the light. It's very much the same as James teaches when he says, true faith produces righteous works. The verses which immediately follow, verse 8 and 10, amount to a description of the first way a believer walks in the light and reflects the light, is what separates true believers from counterfeit. A true believer lives, John says, always facing, always recognizing, always confessing his or her sin. He does not deny it. She does not try to hide it. They confess it to God and receive forgiveness from the Heavenly Father through Jesus Christ the Savior. Their sinful deeds are not ignored as irrelevant, but confessed as unworthy of a Christian, so that they can be forgiven. Wow. That sounds so simple, and yet we make it so complicated. An objection to all of this might be, well, if that is the Christian life, then it sounds like we are to accept sin in our lives and Not worry too much about it because we can simply repent and be forgiven over and over again John is going to address this type of thinking in a very forthright manner later, so we need not do so here. It is suffice enough to say at this time that the main point against the false teachers is that Christians do indeed sin and are in need of forgiveness on a regular basis. It must be realized that Christians lead a paradoxical life. Real Christians will live to please God, and that entails their ready admission of how often they fail to please him. And as they ought, and as they want to. Consider how true this is for any relationship in life. Any rift in a relationship begins to be healed when bad behavior is acknowledged and confessed so that it can be forgiven. I don't want to run down any other Christian group or denomination in my following remarks, but it is good for you to know that my involvement in the Church of the Nazarene brought me face to face with the doctrine of perfection. That doctrine is a denial of what St. John is teaching here. And early Methodism there was a teaching of a possible second work of grace for Christians to experience. It was called entire sanctification. The Church of the Nazarene came out of the Methodist Church. The belief was that a Christian could experience an anointing by the Holy Spirit that would enable him or her, no gender preference here It would enable him or her to never sin again. I recall sitting in the kitchen of an older couple who were believers in this doctrine of entire sanctification. The husband was a retired preacher, and he claimed to have not sinned in decades since the Holy Spirit entirely sanctified him. My patience was not great back then, so I challenged him and asked if he had always loved his wife just as Jesus loves the church. He was visibly taken back by the question, and he had to admit, as every husband would, that he had not always loved his wife as Jesus loves the church. And he realized that such was a sin. It was falling short of God's will and command. In my more mature days, I don't think I would have asked that question so forcibly as to put an elder of mine on the spot. But the point is a necessary one. Sin is in every Christian and among every Christian gathering. In Anglican churches, there is no such doctrine as entire sanctification. But there is, like every body of Christ, whether it be Protestant or Roman Catholic, whether it be evangelical or liberal, a type of legalism that projects that Christians behave in a certain manner and not behave in a certain manner. Christians are not immune to behaving like Pharisees with the belief that certain things should be avoided, certain attitudes towards certain subjects should or should not be taken. Christians ought not to dress like this or have their hair like that. Christians should look a certain way or not look a certain way. Christians should like this entertainment and not that entertainment. Christians should never struggle with this or that sin. Christian marriages should not have problems. Christian children should commit no lies and never get into trouble. Christians should never have bad days. Christians should never be depressed, etc. , etc. There is without a doubt a perfectionism that Christians can fall into without much difficulty. The false doctrine of sinlessness, of getting to the place where the Christian is above and beyond his or her sin. Of no longer having moral failings has been with the Christian Church in the days of John up to today and will continue until we are perfect in heaven While I am preaching, what I'm preaching here has been labeled joyless by some who want to always be pop polyana positive. Perhaps because our modern day provides so many moral failings around us, we can't bear to hear about our own sinfulness. Also, perhaps because polyana positives do indeed tickle the ears, it can appear ungracious to address sin and our need for holiness. But it should be recalled that this is the loving, warm-hearted, gentle apostle, the one whom Jesus loved, John, who brings these necessary words to us. And it is love that moves him to not hesitate to say that people who make this claim that Christians no longer sin are self-deceived and neither know nor practice the truth. They also make God out to be a liar. True love reveals this. The actual truth is that if we think in such a manner, we are lying to ourselves. As Droyszevsky once wrote. The important thing is to stop lying to yourself. A man who lies to himself and believes his own lies becomes unable to recognize truth, either in himself or in anyone. That is John's point here. It may or may not need to be said, but enacting love is not easy. It need not be said because God never promised that loving one another would be easy. Loving Christ is hard work. It may need to be said because we may have come to the understanding that loving others is easy. But that is false. If it were easy, it would not be a command. And he commands it. That it is a command, and it is a new one at that. Those who Love, live in the light. And in the light, there is kindness, there is patience. There's long suffering. There's forgiveness. There's joy for other successes. There's politeness. There's keeping record of right. Thinking the best and hoping the best. When you compare such living, there really is no other place a Christian ought to be. So Christian, pass the first test. Love one another. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Differences in Maturity
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. Our attention is upon 1 John chapter 2. We're looking at verses twelve through 14. 1 John 2, 12 through 14. The passages that we are looking at today are unlike any that John, that Paul Or Peter or any other New Testament writer has written. It is unique in the manner it addresses three different groups regarding their maturity level. Biblical scholars dating as far back as we have commentators on the Holy Scriptures agree that the designation of children Young men and fathers, as not references to different ages, chronological ages, but instead a reference to different maturity levels. And if you are female, please resist the temptation to feel slighted because of these male references only. Remember that under the new covenant there is neither male nor female in Christ. And the times that the male gender is referred to are for the sake of referencing the fact that all Christians Regardless of gender, our inheritors and males are inheritors. Considering the juxtaposition of these verses Saint Saint John reveals a very big pastoral heart. Very big pastoral heart. He had just finished teaching in a very direct manner the first two tests that Christians are to do inventory to ensure they are indeed Christian and that heaven is indeed their future home. The first test was the moral test, the second was the social test. In the moral test, we were to examine ourselves to see if we were walking or Living as Jesus did. And the social tests, we are to examine ourselves to see if we are loving our fellow Christians as Jesus loved. And if we are not living as Jesus did, we are to be understanding ourselves to be liars. And if we are not loving as Jesus loved, we are to consider ourselves to be living in darkness. Those are tough words. No doubt about it. With understanding of those words being tough, John then softens his blows, if you will, with these verses, with verses 12 through 14. It is with these verses that Christians are to realize that there is a maturation process that takes place in the Christian life. And all of us are going through it. And that maturation process takes longer for some than it does for others. The positive point is that all Christians are maturing in some way. We are to be on the scale of Christian maturation on some level. The first maturation level John addresses are those who are children. In 1 Corinthians 13, Paul said, when I was a child, I thought as a child. Children think differently. Of course, they do. As a young child, I was like most other boys, and that I I thought in terms of simplicity. As young boys tend to do, the silliest and the most crass jokes are hilarious. Like, hey, did you hear about the new series of books coming out? The first one is titled Life Under the Grandstands by I. C. Morebutt. That's funny. Or what about the next one titled Yellow River Sam by I. T. Freely. I know they're terribly crass, and I'm leaving out a number that still make me giggle. For a young child, especially a young boy, those are hilarious When our boys boys were young, we would allow them to watch television, or better said, videos. We didn't bother with Teenage mutant ninja turtles or power rangers. No, we bought the three Stooges and the Little Rascal videos And our boys laughed and laughed when they watched them. And when I sat down, I laughed too, and their mother, as she would walk by, would simply roll her eyes at all of us. You see, laughing at silly pranks and pratful pratfalls and puns is easier when your mind is not so complicated. And that is why John refers to those who are at the child level of maturity to know at least one thing. He wants them to know at least one thing, and that one thing is a most important thing. He wants them to know that their sins are forgiven. I write to you, children, that you would know your sins are forgiven. That statement is so very simple and yet so very profound and necessary. It is where all Christians must begin. Because humanity is in a fallen state, and because we have our own immoral baggage, our own immoral weight that we carry around, our guilt that we carry around. Even with the maturity of children, we can know that we have our sins forgiven, and that is a wonderful thing. If we can be eternally grateful to God through Jesus for the very wonderful thing of having our sins forgiven, of having them no longer define us or weigh us down, that is a wonderful place to be It is a wonderful place from which we can grow, from which we can mature. Now the next maturation level address is to fathers. It's interesting he doesn't go on chronological order, he goes to the fathers. The fathers in a nuclear family are to be the most mature. They have the greatest responsibilities within a family, and they are expected to be the most mature. If the reference to fathers was chronological, Only the most mature among us are simply those who've lived the longest, while not necessarily learning anything about life. Consider some of the following wise sayings about getting old chronologically. Age doesn't matter unless you are cheese, said Billy Burke. Time and tide wait for no man, but time always stands still for a woman of thirty, said Robert Frost. Inside every 70-year-old is a 35-year-old asking, what happened? That's Ann Landers. You don't stop laughing because you grow old, you grow old because you stop laughing. Michael Pritchard. Always be nice to your children because they are the ones who will choose your rest home. Phyllis Dillard. Retirement must be wonderful. I mean you can suck in your stomach for only so long, Burt Reynolds. The secret of staying young is to live honestly, eat slowly, and lie about your age. Lucia Ball. You're only young once, but you can be immature all your life. Charles Scoggins Old age is no place for sissies, Betty Davis. It's no longer a question of staying healthy, it's a question of finding the sickness that you like, Jackie Mason And this is my favorite, my favorite. A man is as old as the woman he feels. Groucho Marx. Instead of simply knowing what it is like to be older, the fathers John addresses are said by John to know. To know him who is from the beginning. To know him who is from the beginning. And who is from the beginning. Well, as John said earlier in this very letter, Jesus is from the beginning. So the fathers are to know Jesus. To know him is to correctly identify both his character and his nature. Is also to have a personal relationship with him. Fathers know the character of Jesus to be holy, true, and good. The nature of Jesus known by the mature, by being one substance with the Father. Fully divine and fully human. He was dead and now he is alive forevermore. And to have a personal relationship with Jesus is also something a person grows into, especially if he or she is of the second or third generation Christian. And John was indeed writing to second and third generation Christians. We have already started our confirmation class for this year, and again it is a wonderful group of students Who are, for the most part, having grown up in this parish. As I've seen time and time again, they are learning, learning to know Jesus as their personal state savior They're learning to walk with Jesus on their own as opposed to holding the faith hand of their parents. And it takes a while to grow accustomed to walking with Jesus alone. It doesn't feel quite the way it used to, and that takes time to feel right. And as a person growing into adulthood, these comframans are going to look back on the days in which they were 12 and 13 years old and say to themselves, I knew very little of myself and Jesus back then. And they will say that because they have matured. The next group that John writes to is the young men. And these are the vigorous Christians. These have energy of faith, strength of faith. They are ready for battle. They are ready to take on mountains and move them. Such persons certainly do not have to be young of age, but most certainly strong of spirit. To think of this group addressed as only young in age is to make a grave mistake A mistake that both Hollywood and juvenile Christian churches make. Targeting an age demographic can be all the rage when a group is concerned about the bottom line. Young adults have passions, lustful desires, and their parents' money. The Christian Church should Cease worshiping the youth age and appreciate the vigor that energized Christians of every age bring to the church No better example has been produced to reveal the flaws of the modern Christian church. And it's idolizing of youth that a video parodied that parodies a youth pastor named Ignatius the Ultimate Youth Pastor. This parody opens up with the great anticipation of this speaker, famous speaker coming to a small church. This speaker has a reputation for being on fire for Jesus. He even calls himself a flamer, not recognizing the double meaning of that. The parody then shows Ignatius that This great youth speaker preparing for his presentation while balancing on a workout ball and sipping his non fat latte And when he enters the youth meeting, he he has rock music blaring in the background as he tries to give high-fives to all the students who are rather hesitant to do so. He then has the students chanting, Who's your daddy? Who's your daddy? pointing up to the sky. And then he has them hold up their Bibles. Hold up your Bible, he says. And chant after me. This is the Bible, it is God's Word. This is the Bible, it is God's Word. It is powerful, it is powerful. And finally, it's too much for you to deal with at your young age, so put it underneath your seat. We're not going to use it. He then has the students. Excuse me. He then begins his talk by retelling of a story from the movie The Dark Knight, a gory story that he admits has nothing to do with what he came to say, tell them Ignatius then talks to the teens about sex, telling them that for the teens, sex is wrong. But for him and his smoking hot wife, it's so right. The Winning Nations wants the teens to know that God loves them. He shows them the slideshow of pictures from the Hubble telescope. And he has photoshopped a picture of Jesus at the end of this famous galaxy. He ends with having all teenagers who struggle with having impure thoughts, even about his smoking hot wife, to stand up. And he promises he won't reveal them. Then he ends it by revealing all of them to all the rest of the students. Finally, he is ushered away from the podium by a parent who can't take it anymore. The idolization of the young age in our culture and in many churches has created a lot of silliness and a lot of compromise. What God would have us focus on is not being young in terms of age, but being young in faith, being strong in faith. It is those who are young of faith who will speak words of faith first. They will fast and they will pray and they will believe. They will confront evil and do good first and look for the kingdom of God to be established on earth as it is in heaven. The young and faithful march for life. They will call sin. They will share the good news of Jesus with their neighbor. They will, as John says, overcome the wicked one. Now John returns back his attention upon the children again, so he's repeating his cycle in the same order. And the NIB translation read doesn't do this passage justice. So if you use your King New King James Version, you'll get the point. Turning back to the children, he says, They know the father. They know the father. Now this again is a gentle and pastoral way to refer to a level of maturity that needs to know God as Father first. God as Father defines the very relationship a father is to ideally have with his children. God as father is the standard by which all fathers can be measured. God as Father is perfect love, perfect patience, perfect kindness, perfect endurance, perfect wisdom, perfect security, perfect discipline, and so very much more. All Christians come to God the Father as children, children needing a hug, needing security in his love, needing a pat on the back, a shoulder to cry on. And that is what God the Father is for all who love him, those who love him as sons. And once John has addressed the children, he again addresses the fathers in that order, and then young men. He does it in the same order he did previously, only this time when he addresses the father and the young man. Notice it in the New King James, he does it in the past tense. He did the children in the present tense. He does the young men and the fathers in the past tense. I have written to you, fathers, he says. I have written to you, young men, he reiterates. Have written. And so we must consider why does he write in the past tense and why did he write in the present tense when he referred to the children for a second time? Why are only the father and the young men referred to in the past tense this second time? What makes the most sense when considering these designations of children, fathers, and young men being maturation levels? is that he wants Christians who are of the child maturation stage of faith to be concerned about the here and the now, the present. He wants them to know that their sins are forgiven and that God is their Heavenly Father. Those are enough for the moment. They are very important foundation stones for the moment. And God can build on those foundation stones. But why the past tense to the fathers and the young men? Well, I believe that it focuses on what has been written in the letter thus far, and how what he has been writing to the fathers and young men is particularly for them. More precisely, excuse me, the phrase I have written, he's referring to the moral test and the social test that we are to be taking. We recognized earlier that the moral and the social test were difficult to hear. Excuse me. To call someone who is not living as they should a liar. And those who are not loving as they should to be in darkness. Those are hard words. Hard words. And those who need to hear those words are not children. Not children in the maturation stage. They are fathers and they are young men. The mature and the vigorous in faith can handle those words. They need to accept, that is the young man and the fathers, they need to accept and respond well to hard words. By accepting the truth of test, John has prescribed the fathers as showing that they know Jesus. By being admonished by John's words, the young men are showing that they have overcome wickedness What St. John exemplifies when he designates people in the Christian faith as being mature as a child, and then mature as a young man, and then mature as a father, is the very love that he teaches Christians to have for one another. Excuse me. Each of us is at varying degrees of maturity in our Christian faith. And love begins by recognizing the reality of those varying degrees of maturity that each of us are at. I hope we all can see that being varying degrees of maturity is not what is most important. What is most important is that we are all in Jesus. We are all in the family of God, having been adopted according to his mercy, according to his sacrifice, according to his love for each of us. People at varying degrees of maturation are not different in the Lord's eyes, certainly not different in regards to his love and the pleasure he takes in each and every one of us. If we are tempted to see one Christian of a certain maturity level as being better or more holy than another person at a different maturity level, Then we are misunderstanding how holiness is wrought in our lives. We are misunderstanding the love of God. Our holiness, and please never forget this. Our holiness is based on what Jesus has done on the cross, not based on what we do at any time. And I pray from time to time before the service begins that the Holy Spirit Through his word read, through it sung, through it preached and prayed, that he would convict the comfortable and comfort the afflicted. It's such an old phrase I heard many years ago. It made sense to me. But I don't have any way of knowing all of your present spiritual conditions as you come into worship each Sunday. But the Holy Spirit knows. Of course, He knows. He knows who our children in the faith. He knows those that need to know that their sins are forgiven and that God is their Father. He knows who are fathers who need to be steeped deeper in theology and called higher in morality. He knows who are young in the faith and therefore need to be challenged to work harder, be more brave, more outspoken, willing to fight the good fight. Thankfully our liturgy touches on all maturity levels. The same can't be said for sermons, I am humble to say. Beloved, the kingdom of God, the Christian church, is made up of Christians who struggle with this sin and don't struggle with those sins. It is made up of people who are emotionally strong in most areas, but emotionally weak in one or two areas that seem to overwhelm them. It is made up of people who don't allow love to win out all the time, but are to be loved just the same. It's made up of impatient people who need patient people. And patient people who need impatient people to sanctify them It's made up of people who sin in thought, word, and deed. It's made up of those who have not done what they ought to have done and have done what they ought not to have done. And all of it to varying degrees and varying maturation bubbles. That is the church. And it will be until Jesus returns. Meanwhile, love one another. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Love not the World, OK?
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Of Jen, our organist, from the burning of the noontide day, sun, heat, sunshine. Sounds so nice. We are looking at John chapter 2 verses 15 through 17. I encourage you to join me there, especially in the New King James Version, your best helps. On Monday morning again it's first John two, fifteen through seventeen. On Monday morning this week We woke up to hear stories from the mainstream media about 21 Coptic Christians being beheaded by Islamic terrorists. In case you were not aware, the word Coptic means Egyptian. And this wing of the Christian faith broke away, separated itself from the mainstream of Christianity at the Council of Chalcedon in 451 A. D. The issue was over whether the natures of Jesus were two or one. The Orthodox position is that Jesus is one person sharing two distinct natures. Divine and human. Whereas the Coptic understanding is that he had one nature made up of two natures fusing together. Now the difference in these positions is important and it is not. For Egyptian Christians in 451 A. D. , it was important enough to separate themselves from what is considered mainstream Christian Orthodoxy. The Coptic Christians today are very similar in their worship practices to Roman Catholic churches and Eastern Orthodox churches. Now, whether these 21 men were actual Christians, were true believers in Jesus Christ as the Son of God is impossible for us to know. We are all aware that there are people who consider themselves Christians because they are a part of a sect or because it is part of their culture. But they do not have a personal faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. But I bring the tragedy of this beheading to your attention because it was the first thing that came to my mind. When I read these words this week from John, do not love the world or the things of the world. There is a great divide that John is drawing between Christians and people of the world. And it reminded me how we need to know, be ready. We need to know of ourselves and be ready. To die for our faith. We are to be ready to prefer having our heads cut off than to deny Jesus as our Savior. In reference to the 21 men who were savagely treated by Islamic terrorists, I do not pretend that they had a choice to deny Jesus or not. Likely they were going to be beheaded regardless of what they professed or denied. But I like to put myself in their position. If it is at all possible to imagine. But I want to check myself to try to be certain as much as I can be that I would be willing to die for my Savior. And it seems to John that the best way to know if a person would indeed give up his or her life for Jesus is whether or not he or she does or does not love the world. I mentioned a few Sundays ago that John didn't write this letter as orderly as I would have preferred him to write it, and that's my problem and not John's. What he seems to do in chapter 2, verses 15 through 17, is go into a digression He wrote some hard words to hear at the beginning of chapter two regarding that moral test that we are to take and then that social test that Christians are to take of themselves. And then he became rather pastoral to be sure that those who were hearing these tough words were not being overwhelmed So he doesn't want them to be discouraged, so he he talks about different maturation levels Christians find themselves in throughout their lives. One level not being holier than another, it's just that we are on different levels. But in pulling back, so as not to overwhelm or discourage his listeners, He does not want to give them the impression that the issues he is discussing are not serious enough. He does not want to pull back so as to in any way be cavalier about what is at stake. The eternal souls of his audience are at stake. And so he returns again to some serious, very serious discussion, so that those he writes to will not miss his point. Preachers who are of any value in the kingdom of God at all have this dilemma on a regular basis We have to ask how hard we should drive a difficult thing to say, and then how much we should then pull back. We have to decide whether or not we have made the point God wants us to make without browbeating or downgrading. Now no doubt there are some of you who believe you can identify when I have understated a point or overstated a point in a sermon. You believe maybe you could even do it better? I don't find fault with such thinking at all. I have done that many times when I hear the sermons of others. I'm just trying to take up the challenge John seems unsure as to whether he made his point sufficient enough, and so he returns to hard words. He draws that clear line between those who are of the world And those who call themselves Christians Now before I refer to any application of what John is telling Christians, we need to do a short word study of two words from these passages. The first word is love, and the second word is world. Love and world. Christians are not to love the world. The word love, initially surprising me, is agape. It is not Phileo, as if John was telling Christians not to have brotherly love. It was not Eros, as if John is telling Christians not to have passionate love for the world. Instead, it is adopted. Which is used, you remember, to describe God's love and then the love we're to have for one another. It is fully devoted in its love. It is unhindered and unconditional. But on further review, contemplating a little bit more, it is not surprising it is agape used here, because after all, Christians are to live in the world. We are told that we can enjoy the things of the world. God wants us to enjoy the things of the world. And yet we are not allowed to enjoy them unconditionally. We have conditions placed upon us. They need to be placed upon us so that we do not pervert what God allows us to enjoy. And so do not love the world. Love agape. Unconditionally love the world. Next, we must examine that word, world. The word world is used differently in the Bible and in particular by John. For example, world can mean the entire created order. John used it in his first chapter of his gospel, where he wrote that Jesus, the Son of God, is the creator of the world, creation, all that exists. Also in John chapter 21, we find that the gospel writer says that the world is a big place that can hold a lot of books. So we're talking about space. The term can also refer to the nations. It is where people dwell, it is where we have communities. Jesus, you remember, said that he would not return to the earth until the gospel had been preached throughout all of the world. Communities, nations, people. But here in John's epistle, the word world doesn't mean any of those. It means fallen humanity. It means the ways fallen humanity lives and thus remains alienated from God, from the truth. The word world is therefore the community of men and nations, insofar as they are in rebellion against God. The world hates me, Jesus said. The world that hates him includes all persons, such as social and political powers that are alienated from him. That world could not and does not accept Jesus and does not see or know the Father who sent him. Jesus told us that the devil, he's the prince of that world, the world we are not to love. We read in John's Gospel that There is the whole world lying in the power of the evil one. That's the world we are not to love. Jesus said in his pastoral prayer, I pray for my disciples. I am not praying for the world, but for those you have given me, he says to the Father. Making a clear distinction between the world and those who are citizens of God's kingdom Commentator D. A. Carson sums up the meaning of the word world by concluding, quote, therefore, when John tells us that God loves the world, John 3. 16, Far from being an endorsement of the world, it is a testimony to the character of God. God's love is to be admired not because the world is so big, but because the world is so bad. Well said, Dr. Karst. John uses the term world in this very characteristic way here in our text. This world contains that we are not to love contains non-bel no believers. There's no believers referenced here. Those who come to believe Jesus The Lord Himself said later, they are no longer of the world. When you are converted, you're no longer of the world. He says they have been chosen out of the world. Now that we have love and world satisfied, to best understand what John doesn't want God's people to love about the world, Is described in verse 16. And it's best stated in the New King James, not in the NIB. Verse 16. The lust of the flesh The lust of the eyes and the pride of life. Lust of the flesh, lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. Now, this is where application gets addressed. All that is in and all and all of the world of the evil sense can be classed under one or the other of these three categories. Lust of the flesh, lust of the eyes, pride of life. Let's first look at the lust of the flesh. Lust of the flesh, this is the seat and the source of our lower animal nature. We read of Satan first trying to tempt Jesus in the desert those 40 days. Command this stone to be turned into bread. Such was an appeal to the flesh. Youth especially is liable to fleshly lusts, but older generations can make it an idol as well. Perhaps there is no greater idol today in our culture than the lust of the flesh. Excess alcohol and drugs is bowing to the lust of the flesh Excess eating is bowing to the lust of the flesh. Sexual gratification outside of the marital covenant is bowing to the lust of the flesh. And if the lust of the flesh is the most bowed to idol in our day, sexual gratification has to be at the head of that idol. If you are plugged into any type of media, you are inundated with sexual images. What used to be risque is now mainstream. What used to be viewed only in CD movie theaters is now played on laptop computers. I read a study last week that stated that the average age a child is exposed to pornography is 10 years old. And we should say to that, Lord have mercy upon us. The popularity of a movie now playing in a theater near you. that presents sexual intimacy as deranged psychodrama is more evidence of just how high we raise the idol of lust of the flesh and how low we are willing to bow to it. As if sexual intimacy is not enough of a privilege, fallen humanity has to find ways to degrade it and to make it To make it, I don't know what they're trying to make it. Let it be understood, dear Christian, consuming excess food and drink is loving lust of the flesh. And therefore loving the world. Seeking and indulging in sexual acts outside of the marital covenant is loving lust of the flesh, and therefore not loving God. We cannot equivocate about such things. The next is lust of the eyes. The avenue through which outward things of the world, riches, pomp, beauty, power, and influence that excite us come through our eyes. Satan tried this temptation on Christ, showing them all the kingdoms of the world in one moment. But the lust of the eyes were David's undoing. Lust of the eyes were Achan's undoing. And you compare these undoings to David's prayer from Psalm 119. He said, Turn away my eyes from looking at worthless things and revive me in your way. Here Job's resolved, I have made a covenant with my eyes. Recall the parable that Jesus told of a certain man having a great supper, but he could not find guests who would come to him. One made the excuse that he had bought a piece of property and he had to go see it. Lust of the eyes is the heart of the sin of coveting. It is discontentment with what God has provided. It's where we allow greed and envy to enter our hearts. Again, our culture is bowing to this idol as well. We are the richest nation in the world, and yet we want more. Our economy is at its best when we are our greediest. People gamble. And play the lottery so that they can have all the riches, the pomp, the beauty, the power, the influence, without working for it, without having the discipline to care for what they have Surely you have read stories of lottery winners who regret they had won anything at all. They've lost their friends, they've lost their family, and they lost all their money. To love the world is to pursue riches in this life. To love God To love God is to pray as the proverbial writer does in Proverbs 30, where he said, Give me neither poverty nor riches. Feed me with food allotted to me, lest I be full and deny you and say, Who is the Lord? Or lest I be poor and steal and profane the name of my God There is soul-saving wisdom in such a prayer. And finally, to love the world is to have pride of life. The pride of life literally means having arrogant assumptions. It is vainglory on display. Pride was Satan's sin. He authored it. Satan tried the temptation of vainglory on Jesus by setting him on that temple pinnacle. And having the spiritual pride, the presumption that God will take care of him no matter what he does, so go ahead and jump off and let's see The appeal of pride the devil knows so very well that he used it to bring human beings down to the dust. It was unsanctified knowledge that Satan convinced Eve she needed to have Here again is an idol of our day that cast a large shadow over us, the idol of vainglory Note that there is a subtle but necessary distinction between wanting to do your best and wanting to be the best. To pursue being the best, you have to compare yourself to others. And it is in the comparing ourselves to others that ignites vain glory. Vainglory is the praise of mankind. It is doing whatever it takes to be socially elevated. What causes a man to compare his job to another man's job or his paycheck to another man's paycheck? Pride and vainglory. What causes a woman to compare how she looks in her dress, comparing herself to a woman she doesn't even know, and how that woman looks in her dress? Pride and vainglory. What causes parents to brag, not just tell people, but brag about their child's grades or athletic accomplishments? Pride and vainglory. What is it that rises up in us when we feel put down? Pride and vainglory. What is it that causes us to be defensive when we make a mistake in public? Pride and vainglory. It was the praise of men that the Pharisees wanted, and Jesus said that would be all of their reward. In summary, we can say that these three listed are the world's awful anti-trinity: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, the pride of life. So, after such an examination, has John done his job? Has he sufficiently warned us how serious we must take all of this? The fact that the world is passing away is to cause us to take a step backwards and evaluate what is most important for us to pursue. A world that will pass away is certainly not worth investing in. Perhaps what is most difficult about being a pastor is to watch persons or families even. Make decisions that look very much like they are pursuing lust of the flesh, lust of the eyes, pride of life. And as they go, you hope that your teaching and your preaching somehow, some way has warned them enough. But alas. I have seen families pursue sports for their children that caused them to no longer attend any worship on a regular basis. I have witnessed couples choose work and thus money over worship and even family time. I've known of persons who were going to pursue happiness in this life, even if it meant breaking a marital covenant and causing insecurity in their children. I've been made aware of parents who encourage their children to be as popular as as they want to be, no matter the cost. Now the opposite of all this is what John says at the end of verse 17. It is to do the will of the Father. And we must consider that the only way to achieve any eternal reward is to do the will of the Father. I found the following online. It is by an author named Beth Fisher. There's no other description of her person, so I can't give any more credit than that. But she does well in capturing this temptation of lust of the flesh, lust of the eyes, pride of life. The poem is entitled Two Visitors. Two Visitors. Two visitors came to see me both at the same time. Both were trying to win control of my body, heart, and mind. One was dressed quite plainly, one dressed fit to kill. I couldn't see the battle. They were raging for my will. One promised to give fame, friends, and riches beyond compare. Anything I wanted, it seemed, and while I was standing there, he showed me how life could be for a little while at least I couldn't see beneath the clothes to recognize the beast. The other told of hard times, of sacrifice and pain, ridicule and persecution, nothing much to gain But there was something deep in this visitor's eyes that made me feel to choose him somehow would be wise. I guess you know the outcome, I hope my life reflects, the one I picked, the path I chose, the one that he directs. But now at least I see him as he truly is the king. So did I choose so poorly? I wonder as I sing. Eternal praises to my God, at last in heaven's city. Could I have been richer, more popular? What a pity. For now all I have to show for the pain and unkind laughter is a crystal mansion on a street of gold, living happily ever after. The one necessary addendum to that poem is that the two visitors don't come just one time. They come each day, and sometimes several times a day. And each time we are to choose not to love the world. Amen. Let us pray

What John establishes in this short section of Scripture are doctrines that define what it means to be Christian. Lewis's The Line which in the wardrobe where he talks of, it was always winter and never Christmas. Life without heavenly hope is winter always. It is death, and it is more death But that is not us. That is not not that is reason enough not to sin. There's more to this life. We have the hope of heaven. And beloved, I plead with you, do not choose what you are told is happiness in this life over a heavenly reward. Do not choose immediate gratification over and against eternal peace and rest. Whoever first spoke such words as, everyone deserves to be happy That person was foolish. And all who repeat such words are being foolish. First, we don't deserve anything but the punishment for our sins. And second, the happiness that is being referred to in such a statement is earthly happiness. And even that is not guaranteed. For how can a person be happy in this life if they are not at peace with God? That's a rhetorical question. No one can truly have peace in this life or the next without having peace with God. Hope of life everlasting, that this is not all there is keeps us from sin. Another means provided is to avoid sin. To avoid sin is to abide in Jesus. John says, whoever abides in him, the hymn is Jesus, does not sin. To abide is to do something. It's an action word. It means to stay, to dwell, to endure, to be present, to remain It is to choose to be with Jesus where he is and what he is doing. It is to endure temptation. Trials, tribulations, without abandoning your post. It is to remain faithful But when you are abiding in Jesus, you don't want to sin. You don't want to disappoint a Savior that you love and who loves you. And when you are abiding in Jesus, you have all that you need. Sin does not have an appeal worth considering. The next means to avoid sin, he says, is to practice righteousness. This teaches us that righteous living has to be intentional. You've got to think it, you've got to do it, you've got to work at it, you've got to stay with it. It has to be worked at willfully and conscientiously. The first time that I played the game of football, organizational-wise, was in eighth grade. At the first week of practice, the head coach called me over. I want to see the size of my hands. He then asked me to stand about 15 yards away from him, and he told me, I'm going to throw balls at you. Try to catch him with one hand. And so I did as he ascribed me. He came on glowing about my ability to catch a football. And for me, literally, it was almost as easy as breathing. Not because I was born to catch a football, but because I played catch with my brother and my best friend year-round. Year-round I dreamt of being a wide receiver. I was obsessed with catching footballs. So when the time came for me to do it in an organizational way, I was ready. To practice righteousness, it has to be something you do year out. We have to work at it. Think about it. For some of you, you might not get this. But for some of like me, it's true. Some of us have to work at being nice For some of you, Betty Moore is an easy. But some of us have to work at it. We have to work at putting others before ourselves. We have to work at thinking the best of other people. We have to work at forgiving. We have to work at controlling our tongue, etc. , etc. Christianity, beloved, is no social or emotional crush. It is work. And it is hard work at that. The final means that enables us not to sin takes us right back to the first, which is our identity. It is being born of God. It is being part of God's family. It is having the mark of God on us that we are his and his only. And so I close with this plea to each and every one here. If you find that sin has the best of you. If you fail the moral test, you need to be born again. You need to be born of God. And that doesn't take much. You simply need to confess that you are a sinner and in need of the forgiveness of God by the blood of Jesus. You simply need to tell the Father that you would like to be born anew. And he will do it. He wants to do it. He wants you to be born anew so that you will live without sin. Remember, beloved, God the Father, Jesus the Son, God the Holy Ghost wanted John to write these words to you so that you do not sin. And we face we say thanks be to God. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Lines in the Sand
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: We don't know we don't want to be going through all the time. In the name of the Father and of the Son of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated Turn with me if you would to first John, first John chapter three, beginning at verse eleven. The challenge of studying John can be best understood perhaps by contrast. Picture a scene in a movie comedy or a television comedy where a false hero tries to prove he is tough. By drawing a line in the sand, endaring his foe to step over that line or suffer the consequences. When the foe is undaunted and steps over the line, the false hero, who is actually a coward, and the audience knows he's a coward. draws another line in the sand. And says, okay, now step over that line. Well, we can predict what the foe will do. He will step over the next line and over the next line and again and again until our hero runs for his life. As you picture this familiar comedic bit, play out almost the opposite. Is what John is doing in this first epistle. We are not necessarily his foes, but he is putting us to a test or test. As if he is drawing lines in the sand to see if we are or are not his foes He has put out the social test, and then the doctrinal test, and then the moral test, and now he's back to the social test to see if we measure up And John is relentless. He has already spoken frankly about the need for Christians to love one another, and now he pushes the point even harder. It is as though John is drawing a line in the sand and telling us that we better not step over it. And when we don't, when we stay behind the line, He then has us move back farther. And then he draws another line and says, now you can't step over this line even. It's all a rather bit intimidating, we have to admit. When the Lord places it upon my heart to preach a particular book of the Bible And I should say I perceive that the Lord places it on my heart. I am not infallible when it comes to the the topics or the books that I preach through I don't know what those sermons will look like or sound like or feel like until I'm in the midst of such a series. I have had a few of you tell me that for you, these series of sermons from 1 John have been hard-hitting and yet good. And I concur with that. That is my experience. They have hit me hard in terms of being convicted of sin and provoking me to strive harder against sin and my flesh. And I can feel, and it can feel, excuse me, and it can feel while we are in the midst of confessing our sins and striving harder that we become a bit. Weary. The convictions can come so hard and fast that we don't think we can keep up. And so we want the preacher to ease up a bit. Let us catch our breath, you say. And I again concur. But John doesn't. He keeps going and he keeps on the same subject. He drives the point home over and over again. And so I ask you, what am I to do? What is the preacher to do? Do I preach God's word as it is written and at the pace it is written, or do I modify it so that you and I would feel a little bit more comfortable? Well for this preacher it is unthinkable to let to let up, for if St. John was truly inspired by the Holy Spirit And was given these messages in such a rapid succession as he presents them, who am I, or any man, to edit the Holy Spirit? I assure you, dear parishioners of St. Stephen's, that God has gifted me with the ability to speak every sermon so that no one is ever offended or uncomfortable. I could write those sermons, deliver them without much difficulty. He has also gifted me to speak. with emotion and triumph and with a whimsical spirit that I could sound quite convincing and yet say absolutely nothing He has also gifted me to match the cadence of those slick salesmen who convince the audience that there are earthly treasures, earthly fame. For anyone who calls upon the name of the Lord, if you would just ask, then God would give. All you need to do is give that thousand dollars just as a sea face. And if you do, you will see a money tree grow. You will see a health tree grow. You will see a success tree grow. It just takes that one seed. I could preach in such a manner. And yet, and yet, none of these things would I preach, for I'm convinced it is only the Word of God that must go forth. Because it is only the word of God that does not return empty. This is as opposed to the words of men, which have such a short lifespan. It is only the words of the Holy Scripture that are life-giving. I therefore cannot alter them or silence them because I or anyone else feels that the weight is a bit too much at the moment. A preacher has to be like a coach who gets his team to running and gets his team to running and they're running and running and pretty soon they feel like they can't go anymore. And yet by his words, by his admonition, by his life, he tells them you can indeed go farther. And they take another step. And they run another lap. And so it is with the church. We walk again by faith. We are convicted again and we receive God's forgiveness again. Because we can. And God wants us to realize that we can. This is necessary to experience in order to pass this social test. This passage from 1 John is fitting for Palm Sunday. It addresses what occurred on that faithful day when the words of praise were spoken. Regarding Jesus being the Messiah of the Israelites, and then just five days after. Perhaps those same people that praised him with their lips, then cursed him with their tongues Or if they heard people cursing Jesus, those tongues, those lips that praised him now fall silent. John knows this type of lip service about love, and he states in verse 18 Chapter three, my little children, let us not love in word or in tongue, but in deed and in truth. Actions of love are indeed more holy than words, especially words only. Well, the background of this instruction by John regarding Christians loving one another is, of course, that God loved us first. With our profession, when we turn to God, we know it's because he loved us first. He has already told us in this letter that we cannot say that we walk in the light of Jesus and at the same time not love our fellow brothers and sisters in Christ. It is with that background that we examine John's line in the sand, pushing us back a little bit further to be humble, to be more obedient than we were even before. In verse 11 of chapter 3, John mentions that the command to love one another was from the beginning. The beginning point John is referring to is when the good news of Jesus was pronounced. The beginning of the preaching of the gospel had its foundation in love. And it included us loving one another. It was from the beginning of knowing who Jesus was. The need for God's people to love one another is now essential to the gospel. The contrast of such love is in verse 12 with the mention of Cain and his wicked heart toward his brother Abel. Such a grave sin of murdering a brother reveals the basis of hate. The basis of hate is enemy. Cain envied Abel because God favored Abel. This is in line with the Epistle of James. The same point is made When there is fighting among Christians, it is usually because of jealousy and envy that turns to bitterness and hate. The devil tempts Christians to find objects of their hate, and so we turn on one another as if the person we are angry at has the problem, when it is the angry person that has the problem. The reality of hate is accepted in verse thirteen. The world will naturally hate us if we are true followers of Christ. Consider that it hated Jesus, who is a perfect man. It hated Jesus and still hates Jesus. even though he offers forgiveness and love and everlasting life. And if the world hates Jesus who is perfect, well then it is bound to hate us who are imperfect. And the world hates us because our sins are forgiven, and it hates us because we are still sinners. And thus we are hypocrites in their eyes. All of this can be summarized in regards to our response from the prayer book It has us praying, Lord, give them repentance and better minds. But such hate, Christians are not to have. In this reminder of how the world hates us, John is saying that it is difficult enough to suffer the hate of the world, that Christians should not have to suffer the hate from one another. I recall speaking to an ordained minister of the Christian church. Who was so frustrated by a parishioner that he started to run words against this man that were purposefully unkind and condemning, even though the man to which he spoke did nothing that was immoral or disparaging against the gospel This preacher simply did not like the man. And I was shocked by his words, and I shuddered when I envisioned the devil speaking the same unloving words right along with this man who was to represent Jesus. Let us commit to not being a mouthpiece for the devil In verse 14, we have the social test placed before us. And as I said, it's placed before us again. Recall that John is calling all Christians to test themselves as to whether they are true followers of Jesus, and here the social test is repeated to make sure He mentions passing from death to life, and that is being born again. John is then saying that those who love fellow Christians are the ones who are truly, truly born of God, born again. And those who do not love remain dead in their sins. That, good listeners, is a line drawn in the sand. This is not feel good preaching by John. It is not benign teaching. It is not health and wealth preaching. This is true, truth stated emphatically with no non-zero qualifications And to show you how aggressive John is with this teaching, may I remind you of God's definition of love that we are to have towards one another. We are to suffer with one another, which means we are to put up with one another. We are to be kind to one another without exception. We are to be humble before one another. We are to be polite towards one another. We are to seek the best for each other before being concerned of our own needs. We are to rejoice in the truth for the sake of one another. We are to bear up the burdens of one another. We are to believe the best about one another. We are to hope the best for one another. We are to endure the worst from one another. We are to forgive one another. If you do that, if you are doing that, if you are committed to doing all that love is for one another, then you can know that you are born of God. Remember this example I gave of John drawing this line in the sand and telling us not to step over it and then forcing us back a little bit farther and then drawing another line with the same instruction. Well, that is what he is doing in verse 15. He is telling us to back up some more, and then drawing another line and telling us that if we do not love a brother or sister in Christ, we are a murderer. A murderer? Really? Just because I Withhold forgiveness just because I keep record of wrongs done to me by fellow Christians? I'm a murderer. Really? How can such actions as being unkind be equated with the actions of the likes of a Charles Manson? If such reasoning is your own, then I answer such questions with a question. If John is not saying such actions are indeed A line in the stand in line with murder, then what is he saying? What is he saying? My point is that it is easy to dismiss John's words because they seem too extreme. But if you do that, you have to replace it. And what do you replace it with? But the plain meaning of what he said. I submit there is nothing else to replace it with. The plain meaning of the words is good enough. Is this preaching lacking joy? Is there no joy in what I am articulating? If you conclude that there is a lack of joy in these words, then I would ask if these words are my words only or are they the words of John? And as the words of John, are they not inspired by the Holy Spirit? And if they are inspired by the Holy Spirit, do you want to say that the words of the Holy Spirit lack joy? Is it not true that when words of truth are preached, when they are received, when there is repentance, that the response is joy, that is true joy, that is internal, that cannot be snatched away? I submit to each of you that if you repent to God for not being kind, for not being polite For not putting up with one another, for not believing the best of one another, for not enduring each other, for keeping record of wrongs, for not forgiving, for not bearing the burdens of others, if you repent from such actions, or from your failures of such actions, and receive God's forgiveness, having the burden of such sins lifted off of you, so that you are free. Free indeed. Then you will have joy that no preaching can provide. Do you hear me, good Christians, or am I whistling through the graveyard? I trust you are alive. And want a joy that is natural to the Christian life. In verse 16, we have the standard for love that all Christians are to aspire to attain. And the logic in that verse is straightforward. We know Jesus loves us. We know this by the fact that he laid down his life for us. No greater love can a person have. Then if we love, we are to act in the same manner as our Savior and lay down our lives for one another. And all of us here would say, without question, I'm sure, that we would lay down our lives for our loved ones, those who are closest to us, our spouses, our children, our grandchildren. We would lay down our lives readily. But what about one another? Would we do the same for one another that are not our closest relatives? The challenge is to know if I would lay down my life for any of you. To know whether or not we would give our lives for the sake of one another, who are not our immediate family. We are to examine our hearts. We are to examine our actions to see if we are really loving one another Recognize that the likelihood that I would ever have to lay down my life for someone like an Austin Foreman or a Matt Trail, pretty unlikely. Probably never. And so maybe I can't know But I can though. I don't need to prove it physically. I can prove it by believing the best about Austin or Matt, and each of you. I can know whether or not I would give my life for each of you, as I would my wife and my children, if I am forgiving you, if I am enduring you, if I am thinking the best of you, if I am wanting the best for you. If I'm not keeping record of wrongs, if I'm hoping the best for you, when such love is practiced, the giving up of my life for yours is already determined. And if my love is not being practiced, if that love is not being practiced, then the not giving of my life, well that's already determined as well. Do you see from these words of John how directly connected our witness to the gospel is to loving one another? I remind you of Jesus telling the world that they will know we are his followers, that we are Christians by our love for one another.
