John explains here that by us loving one another in the manner Jesus loved us, the world will be witness, hear this, to the atoning sacrifice of Jesus. Did you hear that? Our loving one another is a picture of dying for one another, which is a picture of Jesus dying for mankind. Oh, what power there is in loving one another as God has commanded us to do. The devil knows well the power of us loving one another. And so he works very hard to thwart such love. C. S. Lewis well captured how the devil works to thwart the love of Christians toward one another in his book titled The Screw Tape Letters. For those of you who have not read the book, it is a clever take on looking at the threats of Christianity from the viewpoint of a demon. The book is a fictitious set of letters from a senior demon writing to give advice on deception and temptation to a junior demon who happens to be his nephew. In one letter, the human being, the junior demon, is assigned to deceive. This human being has started to attend a particular church. And this has the senior demon concerned. And so Screwtape, the senior demon, advises Wormwood, the junior demon, to first get the human to be dissatisfied with his church that he is attending and to bounce around to a series of churches. with a critical spirit rather than being satisfied with the truth and the accountability he can receive from one church. And if that doesn't work, next, the devil wants this demon to deceive the human to attend another church, a church that has come lukewarm. or one that has looked for causes to stand up for rather than the gospel and the holy scriptures The senior demon then advises the junior demon on how to stir up dissension within any of the churches this human attends. The real fun, Screwtape says to Wormwood, is working up hatred between those who say Mass and those who say Holy Communion When neither party could possibly state the difference between, say, Hooker's doctrine and Thomas Aquinas', in any form which would hold water for five minutes. And all the purely indifferent things, candles and clothes and whatnot, are an admirable ground for our activities. We have quite removed from men's minds what that pestilent fellow Paul used to teach about food and other such unessentials. Namely, that the human without scruples should always give in to the human with scruples. You would think they could not fail to see the application. You would expect to find the low churchman genuflecting and crossing himself, lest the weak conscience of the high churchman, brother, should be moved to irreverence. And the high churchman refraining from these exercises, lest he betray his low brother into idolatry. And so it would have been, but for our ceaseless labor. Without that, the variety of usage within the Church of England might have become a hotbed of charity and humility. Beloved, let it be our end goal to make this church a hotbed of charity. And humility. Amen. Amen. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Baptismal Vow Renewal '15
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Begin tonight with a personal story. When I was fifteen years of age, I was eligible, just like in the state of Maryland, I was in the state of Washington, I was eligible to get my driver's permit. When at the desk of the DMB, the processor noted that I had documentation from my high school that my name was Eric Williams. It was Eric Williams because my uncle and aunt who raised my three siblings and I Had us use their last name so as to make it easier when it came to dealing with the school district. But they never adopted us The processor then asked if I wanted to go by Eric Williams or by my birth record name, Eric Jorgensen. I am not sure if the processor was asking me if I wanted to go to the whole rigmarole of changing my name legally. I didn't even know that that was possible. Or She simply put down whatever name I chose. I recall looking at my father to help for some guidance, and he simply shrugged his shoulders. It was a memorable moment because I felt I was choosing my identity for the rest of my life. It would be an identity that I had not known before, but would forever be known by. My second thought was that I wanted to honor my birth father. I wanted to carry on a name that I believe, from my limited vantage point, was taken all too quickly from this earth. And so I made a confident decision that I would go by Eric Jorgensen. And today I'm very glad that I did, but not for the reason I originally made that decision. You see, I came to learn in my adult years that my parents were devout Roman Catholics. In fact, my father converted to Roman Catholicism so that he could marry my mother whose family was staunch Irish Catholic, and so that he could raise his children in a home under the Roman Catholic tradition. Thus, when I was baptized as an infant, I was baptized with the name Eric William Jorgenston. Yes, there is great irony in that my middle name was William, and I did go for a time by Eric William Williams. A further irony was that I was named after a grandfather on my mother's side who was Roman Catholic. It's an English name, but So today I'm glad that I chose at the age of 15 to go by Eric William Jorgensen, because that was the name given to me at my baptism. And thus it is a name that identifies me with the Christian Church. Today I am strengthened when I remember my baptism. I am confident that at my baptism, God marked me as His and He used that baptism to regenerate my soul. I use the word regenerate or regenerate. Because it is a word used several times in the Book of Common Prayer service. for baptism, and it is a word that has caused great consternation among and between Christians. The word regenerate has a biblical link to the phrase born again. Which you will recall was uttered when Jesus had that intimate conversation with Nicodemus, and Jesus explained, except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. The criticism that is placed on the church against using the word regenerate or regeneration within the baptismal service is that it appears It appears to convey more than it should convey regarding the sacrament of baptism. It appears to convey that something takes place that we cannot be sure of. It appears to Protestant ears that regeneration wording presumes a great deal too much upon God. It appears to Protestant ears that the word makes the same mistake that the Roman Church makes when it assumes that every ritual it practices automatically supplies the grace needed. The Latin phrase we learn it in confirmation class, ex operato. Which is translated by the works performed. The Roman Church position is that because Jesus gave the church authority on earth, Whatever the church practices regarding its rituals, the very same is done in heaven as it is done on earth. In practical terms, if the church baptizes someone, then that same someone is saved, is born again by the work performed by the church. It was not until the Reformation that voices that objected were publicly heard. And what was heard by the Protestants was that faith had to be enacted. It had to be present for a person to be saved. We are saved by grace through faith, of course. And the Protestants continued arguing that no person can presume upon God. A person, whether an infant or an adult, cannot be pronounced born again and saved unless God does the work. Spiritual work. And that can only be known by the fruits of the life of the person that was baptized. Now the Roman Church tries to counter that argument with the words of Jesus, who told the church before he ascended, whatever you bind on her shall be bound, and whatever you loose on her shall be loosed. Thus, the church is supposedly given the authority and responsibility to claim salvation for those who have received Christian baptism. In summary, the debate goes on. In Bishop J. C. Ryle's wonderful book. Addressing subjects that are controversial in the church, the book is titled Knots Untied. He addresses the subject of regeneration in the baptismal service, in the prayer book, in the following manner. First, first, he argues that the word regeneration communicates a change in the nature of a person who has converted to the Christian faith And such a change of nature is consistent with the verbiage in the Bible that describes conversion, calling people born again. putting on the new, becoming a new creation, and even partaking partaking in the divine nature Second, Bishop Ryle concurs with the critics that there is only one evidence of knowing whether or not or not a person is regenerate, and that is by the fruits of their life. godliness that comes out of their everyday life. Every tree is known by its own fruit. This is in line with the words of St. John that we have been studying. Whoever is born of God does not live in sin. Everyone who does what is righteous is born of God. Third, Bishop Rile accepts that baptism and regeneration do not necessarily go together. The Book of Acts reveals that a person can be full of the Holy Spirit and not yet be baptized in water. It also tells us stories of persons who were baptized in water, but had not yet been made new or born of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit does indeed move as He pleases, and when He pleases. Fourth, Bishop Rile rejects the doctrine of ex opera operato for the same reasons already mentioned. When the church performs such a sacrament, it does so out of obedience and as the instrument of God For such ritual is God's hand upon the church and upon the individuals in the church. But as the church is obedient, the church is also dependent upon God to renew the spirit of the person being baptized. And so it's not the church performing the act, it's God performing, using the church. Now you would think, by stating these four points regarding the verbiage of regeneration in the baptismal service, that the book of the Book of Common Prayer, that Bishop Ryle would reject the use of the word. But he doesn't. He does not. He does not for the overriding truth of the love of God. The word regenerate is to be used by Christians in baptism, whether the baptism be an infant or an adult, because of the overriding commandment By God for Christians to love one another. Yep, there I go again, talking about loving one another by God. Now perhaps if we use the word charity it would sound better. We are to use the word regenerate or regeneration in relation to a person, a child being baptized out of Charity. In other words, we are to accept a person who has been baptized as being part of the Christian faith and thus the Christian church as an expression of charity. We accept them as a brother or sister in Christ, as an act of charity, and we continue to do so until that brother or sister, that little biggie baby, proves otherwise. If this is difficult to understand, first consider the alternative. The alternative would be to be uncharitable. Which would be to doubt that someone is actually born of God. To doubt that someone is born of God is to not think the best, but instead the worst. It is also not to hope the best for an individual. And to not think the best of someone and to not hope the best for someone is not obeying the love of Jesus. Now let us let us put a case study before us to see different sides of this issue Let us say that a child is born into the home of two parents who love God and worship him through Jesus the Savior. They both have been baptized themselves, and they want their now new daughter to be a part of the covenant that they have with God. And so they have the child baptized, but they they have doubts as to whether the child is truly born again. And so they wait to see if the child will follow their example in life and faith. They try to be consistent in not presuming upon God. And so they are cautious about referring to the child as a Christian. They wait to see fruit in the child's life. Child, like all children, exhibits some good and some bad personal habits And as the child grows, she does not have a confidence as to whether she is a Christian or not, because although she has been baptized, no one confirms to her whether she is in the family of God or not. With a lack of identity with Jesus or in Jesus, the child wanders in and out of obedience to God. And with every disobedience, the parents become more and more concerned that the child is not exhibiting fruits of righteousness. And the lack of fruit causes the parents to see their daughter as an unbeliever. And thus an unregenerate person who needs to be saved. Meanwhile, the daughter identifies less and less with her parents and their faith, and more and more with people who don't know Jesus. Now let us back up and try the same beginning point. Only this time, let us have parents practicing charity toward the child. The child is baptized as an infant, and the parents enact charity by calling their daughter a child of God. The parents teach the daughter how to pray the Lord's Prayer, how to sing to God in sincerity, how to trust God in difficult circumstances. Because they believe in the charity of Christ Jesus that their daughter has been born again. With such charity given to the daughter, she grows up, knowing who she is and who God wants her to be. She has every confidence in her identity with God and in Jesus. Even when she does wrong, she knows how to find forgiveness and freedom from her guilt. And her parents. Get this. Her parents view her disobedience as opportunities for the daughter to be sanctified. Thus, the daughter identifies less and less with the world, and more and more with the kingdom of God Perhaps our case study is oversimplified. Perhaps But within it are truths that are consistent with the biblical testimony. It is consistent with the power of charity. It is consistent with the promises God gives families who raise up children in His nurture and in His admonition, in His covenant. It is consistent with the biblical teaching of what baptism means for each and every Christian. Is every person that is baptized automatically regenerate, born again? We say, in the spirit of love, spirit of charity, we say yes That is not presuming upon God. It is lovingly obeying Him. And it is enough. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Maundy Thursday '15
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. The sermon that you are about to hear is over sixteen hundred years old. The sermon was preached by the Golden Mouth, known also as Bishop or St. John of Chrysostom. This sermon is from John, the Gospel of John, chapter 6, based on verses 52 through 69. I encourage you to turn in your Bibles and follow along. John is a heady man. He was an eloquent man, a wise man. The best preacher probably the church has known, but he was a heady man. Jesus therefore said unto them, Verily, verily I say unto you, except you eat of the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have not eternal life in yourselves. Whosoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood. hath life in himself. When we converse of spiritual things, let there be nothing secular in our souls, nothing earthly, let all such thoughts retire and be banished. And let us be entirely given to the hearing of the divine words only. For if at the arrival of a king all confusion is driven away, much more when the spirit speaks With us do we need great stillness, great awe. And worthy of awe is that which is said today. How it is so, here, verily I say unto you, except a man eat my flesh and drink my blood, he has no eternal life in him. Since the Jews had before asserted that this was impossible, he shows not only that it is not impossible, but it is absolutely necessary. Wherefore he adds, he that eat my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life. And I will raise him up at the last day. For since Jesus had said, He that eats this bread shall not die forever, and it was likely that this would stand in their way. Just as they before said, Abraham is dead, and the prophets are dead, and how do you say that you shall not taste death? In this discourse, Jesus brings forward the resurrection to solve the question and to show that the man who eats shall not die at last. He continually handles the subject of the mysteries of Holy Communion, showing the necessity of the action and that it must by all means be done. Jesus continues in John 6, verse 55. For my flesh is true meat, and my blood is true drink. What is it that he says here? He either desires to declare that this is the true meat which saves the soul or to assure those who listened concerning what he had what had been said, that they might not suppose the words to be mere enigma or a parable, but might know that it is by all means needful to eat the body And then he says, verse 56, he that eats my flesh dwells in me. This he said, showing that such a person who eats is blended with him. Not what follows seems to be unconnected, unless we inquire into the sense, for, says someone, after saying, he that eats my flesh dwells in me. What kind of consequence is it to add? Verse 57. As the living Father has sent me, and I live by the Father. Understand that the words harmonize perfectly, for since he continually spoke of eternal life, to prove this point, he introduces the expression, dwells in me. For if he dwells in me, I live. And it is plain that he will live also. Then he says, as the living father has sent me, And this is an expression of comparison and resemblance. And its meaning is of this kind. I live in like manner as the Father lives. And that you not deem him unbegotten, he immediately subjoineth by the Father. Not by this to show that he needs in order to live any power working in him. For he said before, to remove such a suspicion, as the Father hath life in himself, so he has given to the Son also to have life in himself Now, if he needs the working of another, it will be found that either the Father has not given him so to have it, and so the assertion is false. And if he is also given it, then he will need no other one to support him. What then means Jesus by the phrase, by the Father? He here merely hints at the cause. And what he says is of this kind. As the Father lives, so I live. And he that eats me shall live by me. And the life of which he speaks is not life merely but an excellent life. For in those words he spoke not simply of life, but of that glorious, ineffable life. It's clear from this, for all men live, even unbelievers and uninitiated, who eat not of that flesh. Don't you see that the words relate not to this life, but to that other life? And what he says is of this kind, he that eats my flesh, when he dies, he shall not perish nor suffer punishment. He spoke not of the general resurrection, for all shall rise again, but according to the special, the glorious resurrection, that which has a reward. Verse 58. This is that bread which came down from heaven, not as your father did eat manna and are dead. He that eats of this bread shall live forever Continuing, Jesus handles the same point so as to imprint it on the understanding of his hearers. For the teaching on these points was a kind of final teaching. And to confirm the doctrine of the resurrection and eternal life. Wherefore he mentions the resurrection, since he promises eternal life. Showing that that life is not now, but after the resurrection. And when someone would say, are these things clear? From the scriptures to them, Jesus everywhere refers to the Jews, bidding them to learn these things from them, and by saying, which gives life to the world. He was inciting them to jealousy so that he was frustrating them that others should enjoy the gift that they may not stay without. And continually he reminded them of that manna showing the difference between it and his bread. And guiding them to the faith. For if God was able to support their life for forty years without a harvest of corn or other things in course, Much more now will he be able to do so as having come for greater ends. Moreover, if those things were but types, and yet men collected what came down without a sweat of labor, Much more shall this be the case where the difference is great both in never dying and enjoying the true life. And rightly has Jesus spoken often of life, since this is desired by men, and nothing so pleasing to them as not to die. Since even under the old covenant, this was the promise, length of life. And many days, but now it is not length merely, but a life that has no end. Jesus desires at the same time to show that he now revokes the punishment caused by sin, annuling that sentence which condemned mankind to death And bringing it not to life merely, but life eternal, contrarized to those former things. Verse 59. These things said he in the synagogue as he taught in Capernaum. The place where most of the marvels of Jesus had been done, so that he ought there especially have been listened to, but why did he teach in the synagogue and in the temple? As well, because he desired to catch the greatest number of them, and because he desired to show that he was not opposed to the Father. Verse 60. But many of the disciples, when they heard this, said, This is a hard saying. What do they mean by hard? Rough? Laborious? Troublesome Yet he said nothing of this kind, for he spoke not of a mode of life, but of doctrines, continually handling the faith which is in him. What does it mean to say is a hard thing? It is because it promises is it because it promises life and resurrection? Is it because he said that he came down from heaven? Or that it was impossible for one to be saved who did not eat of the flesh? Tell me, are these things hard? Who can assert that they are? What then do they mean by hard? It means difficult to be received. Transcending their infirmity, having much terror, for they thought that he uttered words too high, too high for his real character And such words were above his station. Therefore they said, Who can hear it? Perhaps making excuses then for themselves, since they knew they were about to leave him. In verse 61 and 62 we read, When Jesus knew in himself that his disciples murmured at it, for this is an attribute of his Godhead to bring secret things to light. He said unto them, Does this offend you? When and if you shall see the Son of Man ascend up where he was before In like manner Jesus spoke to Nathaniel, saying, Because I said unto you, I saw you under a fig tree, you believe? You shall see greater things than these. And the same to Nicodemus. He said, No man has ascended up to heaven but the Son of Man which is in him. But then does he add difficulties to difficulties? No, that be far from him. But by greatness of the doctrines and the number of them, he desires to bring his listeners over to a true understanding For if only he had simply said, I have come down from heaven, and added nothing more, he would have been more likely to offend them But he said, My body is the life of the world. He said, as the living Father has sent me, so I live by the Father. And he said, I have come down from heaven. You see, he solves the difficulty, for the man who utters any one great thing concerning himself may perhaps be suspected of feigning. But he who connects together so many truths, one after another removes all suspicion All that Jesus does and says in John 6 is intended to lead them away from the thought that Joseph was his father. And it was not with a wish to strengthen, but rather to do away with a stumbling block that he said these things. For whosoever deemed that Jesus was Joseph's son could not receive his sayings, while one that was persuaded that he had come down from heaven and would ascend to the same might more easily give heed to his words. Skipping down to verse 66. From that time many of his disciples went back and walked no more with him Rightly has John the Evangelist said, not that they departed, but that they went back. Showing that they cut themselves off from any increase of virtue. And that by separating themselves they lost the faith which they had of old. But this was not the case with the twelve. Wherefore he says to them, verse 67, Will you also go away? Again, showing that he needs not their ministry and service, and proving to them that it was not for this that he led them about with him. For how could he, when he used such expressions even to them, but why did he not praise them? Why did he not approve them? Both because he preserved the dignity befitting a teacher, and also to show them that they ought rather to be attracted by this mode of him dealing with them. For had he praised them, they might supposing that they were doing him a favor, having had some human feeling But by showing them that he needed not their attendance, he kept them to him more. And observe with what prudence he spoke. Will you also go away? The expression of one who would remove all force and compulsion, and who wished not that they should be attached to him through any sense of shame, but with a sense of favor. By not openly accusing, but gently glancing at them, he shows what is the truly wise course under such circumstances. But we feel differently, with good reason, since we do everything holding fast to our honor, our own honor, and therefore think that our state is lowered by the departure of those who attended on us. But neither flattered nor repulsed. He asked them a question. Now, this was not the act of one despising them But of one wishing them not to be restrained by force or compulsion, for to remain on such terms is the same as to depart. And what does Peter say next? Verses 68 and 69. To whom shall we go? Thou hast the words of eternal life. And we believe and are sure that thou art the Christ, the Son of the Living God See you that it was not the words that caused offense, but the heedlessness and sloth and wrong-mindedness of the hearers For even had he not spoken, they would have been offended. They would not have ceased to be ever anxious about bodily food, ever nailed to the earth. Besides, the disciples heard at the same time with the others, yet they declared an opinion contrary to the others, saying, To whom shall we go? An expression indicating much affection, for it shows that their teacher was more precious to them than anything, than their father or mother, or any possessions And that if they withdrew from him, they had not a place to flee. Then lest it should seem that Peter had said, To whom shall we go? Because there was none that would receive them, he straightforward added, Thou hast the words of eternal life. I end here Bishop John Chrysostom's words, for they go on a bit more. And I find it much easier to simply point out why we are here to receive the bread and the wine. I speak to why you and I don't walk away at hard sayings. It's because Jesus and only Jesus has the words of eternal life. I thus liken Jesus' words to natural law. When I'm teaching students in philosophy about the idea of natural law, I explain to them it's something like you know it to be true. You know it to be true, and the only reason you don't admit it is because you simply have stuffed down falsehood. You've denied the truth Things like admitting that there's a God. You know it's true. You just have to be honest with your conscience. Something like there are absolute moral values You know there is a right and a wrong. You know it. You know it's in there. You just have to admit it. When it comes to Jesus having the words of life, You know he is the only one that does. You know it. You know it when you hear it. You know it to be true. And you simply have to admit it. Our inner person is touched, is quickened, is grounded. And only Jesus' words. All other words of men fate. Jesus are the only words that give us life, that quicken us to know that we are indeed alive spiritually. And so we come to him. We come to him to receive eternal life. We come to have our souls touched, our souls quickened, our souls grounded. And so the Lord Jesus bids each of us to come. To come tonight, to come to his table, to receive the bread and wine. That represents his body and his blood, that are a means of grace to us, like no other means of grace. And so we tonight receive. Receive asking the Lord once again to touch us, to quicken us, to ground us. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Easter '15
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Maybe seated. It is my privilege and honor to welcome you into the house of the Lord on this glorious Easter Sunday. We especially welcome those who are part of the Secret Service. I once heard of a man who came up to the minister on Easter Sunday. And commented about how good it was to be in the army of the Lord. The pastor could not help but be bold and inquire of the man, saying If you are in the army of the Lord, how come I only see you on Christmas and Easter? Well, I'm in the Secret Service. Now I know that many of you here are visiting because of family, and we're glad to have you in the house of the Lord. I want to speak a little bit about Easter Sunday as I Many of you know grew up in the Roman Catholic Church, and although I attended Mass, C C D, and had my first confession and Holy Communion in the church, we eventually became Christmas and Easter attendees. And Easter was always a big deal We boys were given new blazers. I've got a picture. Blue, white buttons, got a little derby hat, sporting. Looked quite good. Girls given new dresses We always received baskets of goodies on Easter morning, followed by an egg hunt around the house. My parents would take money on the eggs and we would try to find them. For these reasons, the Easter holiday was a grand and glorious thing to experience as a young child. The holiday was also in stark contrast to the Friday previous. Being with my Roman Catholic grandparents on Good Friday, well that was a dark experience. The solemnity and the introspection. It's quite contrary to the gaiety of Easter Sunday. In fact, my grandmother treated all Fridays on the calendar as a solemn day. Beyond Roman Catholics, many Western Christians historically have approached Friday and Fridays in the same manner. The tradition of refusing red meat on Friday reflects the desire to remember that one Friday in history. When God's Son was placed on the cross as a sacrifice for the sins of the world This solemnity for every Friday has its merits for if we wish to celebrate the resurrection of our Lord every Sunday. Well, it seems appropriate to recognize the death of our Lord every Friday. Because our culture is no longer driven by religious convictions were more driven by economic concerns. The work week has been segmented and divided up according to the workplace. Monday now begins the week and is perceived as drudgery because we have to get back in the work mode Wednesday has been given new attention because of that humorous commercial. We now call it Hump Day. And the hope is that we might get over Hump Day, that we might get to Friday. Friday is understood as the end of the week and hence a day of celebration. Saturdays and Sundays are me time, from which we have to recover and start the week on Monday. Needless to say the biblical ideal of approaching the weak conflicts with our modern age It will be our attempt this morning to go back in time and in our minds so that we can better understand the weak days according to our redemption. From our gospel text, we receive an emotional description of how the women reacted when they came to see Jesus. In John chapter 19, prior to our reading, the events of Friday are described, and they were fast, and they were furious, and they were gut-wrenching. The man that these average men and women had put their hopes in for not only their happiness in this life, but for the life to come. That man had been arrested Beaten, ridiculed, and mocked. Most of the followers of Jesus did not see him After his arrest, it was not until that Friday came that they saw what the Sanhedrin had reduced him to. A common criminal. And no moment in their lives could have been more surreal than to watch helplessly as Jesus was placed in front of Pilate and then in front of a multitude who were given the power to release him or have him die. And when the crowd was swayed toward crying out for the death of Jesus, what could these lowly, average, non-influential followers, what could they do? Such days like that can haunt us. There are days when it seems as though we are the only sane person on the planet. We desperately seek for people who understand and see the situations in our lives the same way that we do, but there is no one. We feel alone. The insanity of seemingly everyone around us makes us feel as though we ourselves are going insane Can I be the only one that can see this? Or maybe I'm the only one that is blind There are some days when Christians can call them Fridays that can be haunting. There are certain days when we face the reality that we are powerless. We may wake up each day believing ourselves to have a handle on our lives. And those around us that we love a handle on their lives. But an event, an event can shake us so deeply that we recognize that we really had no control at all. In John chapter 19, the scripture says that the soldiers took charge of Jesus. Someone else took charge of Jesus? Who can take charge of the Son of God? And yet take charge is what they did. They made him carry his cross to the place of his designated death. They placed a mocking sign above him, they nailed him to the post, and then they stuck it in place. They stripped him naked and then gambled for his clothes. During all this, there was nothing. Nothing any man opposed to this treatment could have done to stop it. All of us can fall into the trap of believing we actually control our individual lives. One day our future is sad, and the next we find we have no job. One day our home is established, and the next we find that the government or the bank is taking it away. We feel in tip-top shape one day, and the next the doctor tells us that we are desperately ill. These are but a few examples of moments when we come to realize that we have no control, at least not the control that we thought we had. These moments are like a certain Friday. Then there are days, and these are the worst days, when you simply want to die. And I'm not speaking about those days where we suffer from a cold. And by we I mean men like myself who act like when they're dead, when they're sick, they are dead. The actual days you want to die happen when you lose hope. Depression is a nasty experience for anyone to go through. Consider when Jesus died on that cross, what hope did his followers have? When you lose hope The purpose for continuing just another moment in a day can vanish. The hope of the disciples of Jesus for that fateful day, that hope was taken from them. And their hope for tomorrow was taken from them. And their hope for yesterday was taken from them. Vanished when their Savior breathed his last. And this happened on Friday. And it did not get any better Well they took Jesus down and hurriedly buried him in the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea because the Sabbath was approaching. The spiritual dark world, well that was they they they were having a part. Satan was dancing on the rooftops. He was mocking the host of heaven. He ruled the world. It was Friday. The Friday was beautiful to him. Darkness covered the face of the earth. It was Friday. Satan had stolen who, even stolen faith from the hearts of men. It was Friday, and the day belonged to hell. The scripture does not speak of Saturday. It was obviously a quiet day after the death of Christ. The Jewish people according to custom and law, they could do nothing regarding the body of Jesus. They had to let him by. As far as his followers were concerned, Saturday was no different than Friday. Worship in the synagogue, painful, joyless. But the future of the followers of Jesus every day, from the rest of their lives, was going to be the same as Friday. How true it is that the difficult flights that men find themselves in seem unending An ending while you're in the midst of them, an ending because there is no hope after them. From the small same things such as financial debt, To the more significant tragedies such as a debilitating illness, it is hard to see beyond the moment. A new day dawning does not seem possible. When the first day of the week came, as described by Saint John. It could not have come sooner for the women who were closest to Jesus. John said, while it was still dark, Mary of Magdala, she was the first to go to the tomb. Now her mission was simple. She was going to complete the anointing of Jesus' dead body that it might be fully prepared for burial. For this woman, on that Sunday morning, it was still Friday. Nothing had changed. No flicker of hope was present. No doubt the images of her dead Savior burned in her mind. Yet when she arrived at the tomb where the body of Jesus was placed, a still small voice whispered Whispered from the evidence of the rolled away stone, whispered, it's no longer Friday. The voice was not audible, of course, but the evidence, it stated it clearly. The hangover from Friday was obviously great because Mary didn't hear the small voice For her, the glass was half empty. Friday had stolen her optimism. She continued to think in her heart and in her mind, it's still Friday. She ran as fast as she could to one of the disciples she knew would do something, Peter. She ran to Peter and told him that someone had taken the body of Jesus out of the tomb. And now that still small voice was whispering to Peter, It's no longer Friday. Peter was a man whom desperately needed to hear this news. His Friday began, we know, on Thursday, when Jesus was arrested. That night he denied the Savior three times. From then on, Peter was in the background of the disciples. He was ashamed and he was shamed publicly. For him, Friday was tragic on another level. He had denied knowing Jesus, and now Jesus was dead. Dead along with his hopes for reconciliation. Unlike Mary, Peter heard the voice, and a glimmer of hope stirred within him. He and another disciple, whom we believe was John, ran to the tomb. When they arrived, the voice was louder. It is no longer Friday. Each of them saw the burial close as evidence that this was a new day. The strips that were around the body were just lying there as if the body had been removed and the strips just simply collapsed. The burial cloth placed around his head was neatly folded, like a good Jewish boy would do. Placed to the side. Someone had tidied up before they left. The voice now spoke even louder. It is no longer fine. The Gospels make it clear that Peter and John did not grasp all that they had witnessed. They still did not understand that Jesus had risen from the dead. They did not know, they did know, excuse me, one thing. They did know one thing. It was indeed no longer Friday. The scene next shifts back to Mary. She still has no hope. And while she is weeping outside the tomb, two angels, one sitting at the head and the other at the feet where Jesus' body once lay Ask her, why are you crying? What is implied to Mary by the angels is to look. Take a look, Mary. She was to see the evidence for herself. Jesus was not there. It was no longer Friday. There was no longer a reason to mourn. And Mary justifies her tears by describing the treachery of someone having stolen the body of Jesus. At her words, she turns around and Jesus is standing before her. Unfortunately, Mary's eyes are blinded by her tears. The evidence around her is confusing, so much so that she does not see that hope is alive. It is no longer Friday. We cannot be so busy feeling sorrowful not to understand how glorious a day it is. It is no longer Friday. Because it is a new day, we can see things for what they really are. The empty tomb means hope has returned with a vengeance. And such hope is to be applied to this light and to the next. The folded burial clothes mean that the sorrow I experience on Friday is but a passing moment. And the sun s o N has come up to never go down again. It is no longer Friday, which means that all of us can be as Mary Magdalene and go back to loved ones and say, I have seen the Lord It is no longer Friday. Sunday has come. Because it is no longer Friday, Christians are not to live as if it is Friday. I challenge you to consider what cataclysmic events, what painful news, what poverty, what illness can occur on Friday that cannot be overcome by Sunday. Church, regardless of what Friday has brought you, regardless of what Friday has brought you, you must understand, getting the tears out of your eyes, that it is no longer Friday. Sunday has come. And because you now live in Sunday, you must put all your Fridays behind. From our first reading this morning, we received the instructions from Paul to the Colossians. Since then you have been raised with Christ. We must stop here to comment that if it is Sunday, that means Christ has risen. And it also means if it's Sunday that you have risen. Death shall no longer have dominion over you. Death and all of its pretenders shall no longer sting your soul. We continue from Paul. Set your heart on things above where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. And here we are reminded that the only place that will grant us the ultimate healing, the ultimate joy, the ultimate peace is the presence of God. Set your mind on things above, not on earthly things, for you have died and your life is hidden now with Christ in God. Church this morning, the words of the apostle cry out to us that it is no longer Friday. Even though we are in the midst of events that remind us of Friday, Sunday has come. Your life is now hidden with Christ and God. Rejoice. And again I say rejoice. Church, this is the day we are to put on our dancing shoes. The devil danced and body owned the world. And now he knows what the truth is. He who wants to dance because he thought he ruled the world now has to watch God's people dance because Sunday has come. On that one Friday in history, the devil mocked the hosts of heaven. And now it is Sunday. And by our praise to the one who has overcome death, we mock the demons. The demons who shiver behind the gates of hell, knowing that the church will prevail against it. It is no longer Friday. Sunday has come, and it's time to celebrate. And all of God's people said. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Doctrine and False Teachers
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Please turn in your Bibles to First John chapter four. 1 John chapter 4. I want you to follow along in your Bibles this morning, especially at the beginning of the sermon. And I I I want you to know Listening to a preacher this week, he talked about the goal for a minister in a sermon is to get the people to look down. That sounds rather strange. What do you mean look down? What he means is you want to get the people to look down in their Bibles and read what is being preached. That you might know the Word of God, that it might be alive to you. And so I encourage you during this part of the sermon, look down. Let's see what God has written to us. We begin this morning by examining each verse of 1 John chapter 4. And we see in verse one that he is teaching us that behind every human teacher is a spirit. And behind each spirit is God Himself or the devil. Now, John doesn't mention the devil in this verse or in this section, but it is most certainly implied. And he will plainly speak it in chapter 5, verses 18 through 19. To test a human prophet, therefore, was in effect to test the Spirit By whom this so-called prophet spoke: of God or of the devil? Verse 2. Here there is an emphasis on two things. First, the necessity of confession The Apostle Paul said the salvation is procured by what we profess. Here, John says that the details of what we confess are vital to eternal life. And that leads us to the second emphasis. Which is to confess that Jesus was of the flesh. He was of human form. Verse 3. Here explains further about the thinking that was apparently proving attractive to some circles in this young Christian church. Years later, before the end of the first century, this thinking would be termed, given a term, docetism. This comes from the Greek, which means to seem or to appear The idea was taught in various forms, but the central thought was that Jesus only seemed or appeared to be a man. You see, not just the reality, but the idea that Jesus became a true human being with a physical body and a physical life that was actually repugnant to many in the first century. The reason for this It was a position that presented the physical or the material world, which included human flesh, to be inferior to that which was supposedly truly important, which is the spiritual world. In fact, it was believed that the physical world or the flesh, that was actually a source of mankind's trouble. It was believed that if the spirit could be free from the body, then it would no longer fail morally. Therefore, such teachers could not believe or not even imagine that God would make himself flesh. To these first century philosophers, God would not bother with the flesh, but would want to be free from the flesh and only be concerned about the spirit. Hear a lot of Gnosticism in that belief. Now John, as we read, will have nothing to do with that type of thinking. He uses a strong word for flesh to describe what Jesus coming from heaven came to be. We recognize that flesh is a term that highlights the physical nature of humanity. That's what it means. We're physical. Although there is a shade of influence of docetism today, it is not as prevalent as it was in the first century. But what is prevalent, beloved, what is prevalent today are false teachers. False teachers that you and I don't even know we're paying attention to. No, we don't call them false. In fact, they insist that they are the honest ones. They're disinterpreting the scientific facts. The Christians are not to be fooled. It will be my objective this morning to point to some false teachers. And to show from John's instructions here how we are to be careful not to have false teachers influence us, but to see them for what they are. John has the courage to call false teachers antichrists. By using such a label, John shows that there are many, many who stand against Christ in the world. In verse four, John claims that Christians have overcome Antichrist And the logic is obvious, for if the Spirit of Jesus overcame the devil, overcame the nature of sin, overcame the punishment of sin, which is death. How easy it is for his spirit, which is within Christians and in the church, to overcome false spirits, any false spirit. Stated more plainly, the spirit behind Christians overcomes the spirits behind any false teachers Now examining verse 5 and 6 together, we can summarize that there are two camps, and the two camps do not understand each other. The camp of God knows the voice of God, and to put it simply, the camp of the world does not. The camp of the world does not want to hear the voice of God, but instead loves falsehood, and the camp of God only wants to hear God's voice and thus wants to hear the truth. We have been examining John's letter in terms of a series of tests, and this set of verses would fall under the doctrinal test. Christians are to believe rightly about Jesus. And to believe rightly about Jesus is to believe that he was fully manned And to believe he was fully man is to believe that he lived and he died and lives again in human flesh. We have spoken on several occasions about the importance of knowing Jesus as fully man, fully of the human flesh. God created the physical world, and God called it good. The physical world is part of God's plan of redemption. For he says that although it is under the curse of man, the actual world cries out, the physical world cries out to be free and to praise God. Even the rocks would cry out God says that his plan is to make heaven and earth new. He also plans to make the bodies of Christians new, giving us bodies that will never see corruption. To do all of this, God must see the physical world as good, and he does. So instead of focusing on the importance of God redeeming the physical world or the importance of Jesus being fully human, I want our attention this morning to be more focused on the reality of false teachers. Why false teaching is so important to identify and then to avoid Consider the doctrine of docetism, that Jesus only appearing to be in the human flesh. Consider what it has distorted. Docetism has contributed to the denial of Jesus being a historical figure. We hear that a lot today. It has contributed to the belief that Jesus was never crucified. In fact, that's a belief of the Islam religion, that Jesus was a historical figure, but was never crucified. And of course, because Jesus was never crucified, he was never raised from the dead, because after all, what is not killed does not need to be raised from the dead. Docetism has also contributed to people claiming themselves to be Christian and yet denying the sacraments of baptism and the Lord's Supper. They do this because these are done in the flesh, and supposedly, supposedly, Christians are to concern themselves with only the Spirit. And so it's the baptism of the Spirit. And it's the communion in the spirit that is the most important. Such a listing of wrong thinking is only a sample of the damage that a false doctrine can do to the truth. Those of you who have sat in on my confirmation classes know that I have a powerful dislike For churches that use the slogan, we have no creed but Christ, sounds so pious. Such a statement shows no respect For the blood that has been shed by Christians over the centuries, because of what they have said they believe about Jesus, born of a virgin, being made man. These are statements that embrace that Jesus was a man, was a man in human flesh, just as the holy scriptures describe. To not confess what the church has always believed is to be set up to believe anything and everything except the truth. And what are some other beliefs that are not the truth? Consider with me the doctrine of evolution We can call it a doctrine, because like statements of the Christian faith, it consists of statements of belief. The doctrine of evolution has contributed, hear this, has contributed to accepting divorce in the West It has contributed to sexual promiscuity in our culture. It has contributed to the acceptance of the horror of abortion. It has contributed to the acceptance of euthanasia. And it has contributed to the moral relativism in general. And finally, it has contributed, even contributed, to the rise of Islam. Now that sounds all crazy, doesn't it? I suppose it's with in my responsibility to show you how these things relate. Now, mind you, I will do that, but this is just an example of how a wrong doctrine, where it can lead. Just an example, how a short statement of belief could have many great and terrible ramifications. Consider it. The evolution teaches that the survival of the species is the highest good. Survival is the highest good. Thus mankind has reason that monogamy is an unnecessary practice and is in fact an enemy of that highest good of evolution. Therefore, mankind can be more promiscuous and less responsible, leading to more frequent immoral sexual expressions of all types. And because we are thought to be merely products of the genetic world, if our genetic makeup has us be more attracted to the same sex or both sexes or a new sex, Then nature has to be obeyed. That's the law of evolution. All of these accepted beliefs show a close connection to divorce rates. And moral relativism. Regarding issues related to life and death Unwanted babies. The sick elderly are members of the unfit category And because evolution upholds the standard of survival of the fittest as the greatest good to achieve, then unwanted, unborn babies and the sick elderly persons have to die because they fit in the category of being unfit. They are not the fittest. Do you now see how one lie can have many great and terrible ramifications? I mention Islam, so I will bring it up. Evolution has led to the rise of Islam because mankind is a creature. That needs absolutes and needs to worship. When evolution rejects moral absolutes and claims no need for God, then those things have to be replaced. And Islam offers a replacement. This semester I once again put my philosophy students at the university into an ethical dilemma An ethical dilemma that requires of them to choose likely starvation or to participate in cannibalism. Even though, in this fictitious dilemma, even though they are to have a religious conviction against cannibalism, And even though, if when they were rescued, their cannibalism would be revealed And even though the victims they would have to eat also did not believe in the morality of cannibalism And even though after all of the arguments against cannibalism, and after upholding the virtue of dying with dignity, which is that they held on to their moral convictions The majority of the students chose cannibalism. And they do every semester, every year. And the answer to the why they choose cannibalism, it's simple. Survive, man. That's what I get. I just want to survive. For me, staying alive is what matters most. That is a product of a doctrine of evolution. When survival is all that matters to a human being, then such persons have nothing to die for. When the meaning of life is based on personal survival, anything goes and nothing else matters. This is why moral relativism is so rampant, and I am greatly concerned that Christians today accept moral relativism as truth. When it is anything but true. Someone tells us that morality is relative, and we shrug our shoulders in defeat, as if there's no challenge to such a statement. But there most certainly is a challenge, and challenges. I believe we better know those challenges to such a statement, or our culture is going to consume, our children is going to consume our grandmother. grandchildren and maybe even ourselves if we don't hurry up. I want to give you some challenges to this idea that moral relativism is truth. The first challenge against moral relativism is that every moral statement, every moral statement, has a truth value to it. A statement such as adultery is immoral. That has a truth value to it The statement that adultery is immoral is either true or it's false. And the truth value remains In that statement, regardless of who says the statement, regardless of where the statement is made or when the statement is made. And no, there is no such thing as moral for some people, but not moral for others. Notice that I did not say that I believe Or that I think or that I feel adultery is immoral. If I had used such personal references, then another person could say that it was immoral for me, but not for them. But I didn't use personal references. I said adultery is immoral. And that statement either has a true truth value or a false truth value. It can't have both and it can't have something else Now, a detractor might interrupt and argue that there have been statements about morality that have changed over the years in some cultures. And that is true, but it doesn't change my point. In fact, it strengthens my point. Take for example, such a controversial topic, take for example, man stealing. There was a time when even some Christians thought they were being moral by stealing people from a foreign land and enslaving them. They justified it as moral because the Bible speaks about in the law allowing slavery. But that is half a truth. The Bible allows for slavery when a person is in debt. If a person had a debt they could not pay, they could offer themselves as a slave until the debt was paid or until the year of Jubilee. Regarding man stealing, the Bible clearly and forthrightly forbids it. Thus, when people said slavery in America was moral or biblical, Well, the truth value of that statement was false. And it always was false. And it will always be false. Those who said it was moral were false. They were wrong. So again I say that adultery is immoral. And I say it because God does. And he is the authority source for me saying it. The second challenge to this moral relativism Is when people say that morality is obviously relative because it's different for different cultures. That is a lie. And it's too readily accepted among us. Oh, that's true. Yeah, you're right. No, they're not. You hear someone say something like, homosexuality has been accepted in some cultures like Greece in the days of Plato and unacceptable in others like Israel, therefore its relative. It's all based on preference. First of all, know your history And second of all, don't accept the logic that since it's been accepted by some cultures, then it's just based on personal preference. The truth is that morality is actually universal. Morality is universal. And being universal is evidence that there is a primary initial source for the universality of morality, and that primary source is God. The basic argument to prove there is a universal morality is to properly label what we call differences in morality. We need to call those differences moral opinions. And what we morally have in common should be called moral principles. For instance, a person could argue that suicide is honorable in some cultures and in others it is not. Which is true. In some cultures, women go go topless and it is acceptable. In other cultures, it is not. But those examples are examples of, hear this now, opinions about applying morality and not recognizing the moral principles that support opinions. Consider that every culture has moral principles such as honor, justice, and modesty. Every culture has those. No society prizes honor over dishonor, injustice over justice, or immodesty over modesty. Dr. Peter Craith makes this point in his book, The Best Things in Life, and he prefers to call what cultures have in common as principles. All cultures share the same principles with differing opinions about their applications. Dr. Crafe also argues that opinions about morality are actually the same in different cultures if we define opinions about how we feel about morality. The point is that we feel the same about such principles as justice and modesty. We feel that they are important. All cultures do. It is only the rules that we come up with to honor justice and to honor modesty. Those things differ I hope you see that the argument refuting relative morality is quite simple. It's easy to find when we stop accepting lies. So rather. We give up the fight before we even begin. Believing lies has consequences, and some of them very great. Also, what have we learned today? We learn that followers of Jesus Christ must believe truth. We learn that a modern lie to avoid is that a moral statement can be true for some and not for others. No, in fact, moral statements are either true or false and nothing else. And moral statements that God makes, the ones that God makes, those are the true ones And third, we learn that the different moral standards in different cultures is not proof of moral relativity. We learn this because moral standards are actually not different. They're the same We understood what is different is moral application, moral rules, but not morality itself. Folks, you and I know that our culture is dying around us. And the only salt that is there is the church. We need to stop giving up these arguments as if they're already lost. These lessons are to be used. We can stand up for truth and expose lies. These lessons are for the church to actually preserve the world, change it, maybe even save some people along the way. So let's do that. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Three Times Love
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be preceded. Turn in your Bibles to First John chapter four, beginning at verse seven. I remind you of my responsibility to get you to look down. That is to get you to look down. at God's word and to see if what this preacher is saying is what God is saying. And so we look down, first John chapter 4. If something is repeated, then it's important. It is repeated twice, then it is real important. Something repeated twice is said three times. Three matches the number of the Godhead. Three refers to our triune God. Thus we can say That the Father says for Christians to love one another. The Son says for Christians to love one another. And the Holy Spirit says for Christians to love one another That is what we read again today from John's letter. We read for the third time that we as Christians are to make it a priority in our lives to love one another. This repeated referencing of the need for Christians to love one another reminds me of a story, a story I heard rather early on in my ministry. Coming now upon sixteen years here and three years prior. The story goes as follows. A pastor preached one Sunday On Christians being commanded by Jesus to love one another. He preached on the same subject the next week. And then the next week after that. And then the next week after that. It was after the fourth time of this sermon that the congregation started to grumble. It was put upon then the junior warden to speak to the pastor about his choice of topic of sermon. The junior warden sheepishly asked the pastor When are you going to stop preaching to the congregation about loving one another? And the pastor didn't hesitate to respond by saying, until we start doing it. And of course the answer to that is out until we start doing it. Perhaps we shouldn't be surprised that the Apostle John is given the task of calling Christians to love one another. Obviously, Jesus had placed it upon his heart, for it is in John's Gospel that we find that wonderful verse, for God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son. And it was John who referred to himself as the disciple that Jesus loved. And we understand that he referred to himself as such, not to say that Jesus loved John more than he loved the other disciples. No, no, no. And it was not to say that Jesus gave him the title himself, the one whom Jesus loved. No. John referred to himself as the one whom Jesus loved because he keenly felt the love of Jesus. It was the love of Jesus that moved him, that motivated him to dedicate his life, to share that message of God's love. That is why the following story about John, although extra-biblical, seems likely to have occurred. Jerome of the fourth century, a church father, relates what was obviously well known about St. John at the time. The great man was near the end of his life, and he used to be carried into the church of Ephesus by the arms of his disciples. He was weak, unable to speak but a few words at a time. But when he was given the opportunity, he would repeatedly say, Little children love one another. At last, growing weary of the repetition, his disciples asked, Master, why do you always say this? Because, the old apostle replied, it is the Lord's command, and if this only is done, it is enough. Whether that story is true or not is unnecessary to know, for what it communicates is most certainly true. To love one another, as Jesus displayed, and as 1 Corinthians 13 describes, that is indeed enough. Jesus said as much when he summed up the law, we heard it this morning in our gospel reading. The second commandment, love your neighbor as yourself. So let us now look at 1 John, beginning at chapter 4, verse 7, at what John has to say again about loving one another. Consider God loved us first. Love begins with God, as verse 7 and 8 explain. There are natural and necessary connections between us loving and us knowing God. Love is God's nature. It is his attribute. To understand God, it is not enough to know that he is all-powerful, omnipotent, that he is. everywhere present that he is all knowing. We must know him as love, or we do not know him at all. To love one another is to be a people of action. We are to do something about the love we have. We are to act it out. Love is a verb for God loved and then he gave his son. Verse 9 And we are to do likewise when we love one another, and thus the first thing we must do is to make a willful choice to love, and that is to be done in an action. Verse 11 And God then brings these two points together, the point of his loving first, and then presenting love as a verb, by mentioning Jesus as a propitiation. Propitiation is a big word. Theologians love to discuss and debate its meaning. And the book nerds, for them it represents all sorts of interesting dilemmas. But I will not repeat those dilemmas. They will do an injustice to this point. The meaning of the word is best summed up in Paul's words. That he said to the Corinthians, quote, God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself. The word propitiation tells us that God satisfied his own wrath. That is the love he has for us. It is a love of which there is nothing greater. And it is the love we are to have toward one another. The next point that John makes about the necessity for Christians to love one another is how we can measure our place before God In terms of the Holy Spirit being present in our lives and our confession. Remember now that this is part of John giving us three tests. That we might know and be positive and confident about our place in Christ. We are to know that we are Christians if we pass these tests. And Christians are children of God. God is to be in us and therefore enabling us to love, verse 12. And his presence within us is verified by the Holy Spirit being in us. Verse 13. And the truth we confess about God and Jesus is evidence that the Holy Spirit is within us. Verse 14 and 15. And then we come to verse 16, summarizing the point quite nicely. God is love, and no one else is. To be in God is to be in a relationship with him as his child, and thus to be in God is to be a byproduct of his love. Naturally. When a Christian knows he or she is in God, there is evidence, evidence of his love that leads to a boldness about God's judgment. And he then tells us that such boldness casts out fear. Verse 17 and 18. When the fear is cast out, we can know that we have passed the social test. Which is the test of loving our brothers and sisters in Christ. I would like us to consider To consider that the love of God that casts out fear is not just in terms of God's judgment upon us. but in also allowing us to be vulnerable with one another When we are vulnerable to one another, we allow others to know our inner struggles, our inner hopes, and our personal weaknesses. The casting out of fear is accepting that people can use, they can, if they wanted to, can use that knowledge about us against you. Spreading rumors, keeping score, and condemning you, and yet you still choose to love. You choose to love to show that the love of God is so strong within you. Such love overcomes those fears. Such love allows you to be vulnerable. Verse 19 takes us back to the first point, which was that love begins with God. It is at verse twenty where we will spend the remainder of our time. Verse 20 Verse 20 is presenting a person who says one thing, I love God, and then does another thing that does not match up with the first thing said. And that other faith is not loving a brother or sister in Christ The remaining argument is that it is easier to love people that you can see and that you can know in everyday life, and not so easy to love those you cannot experience with your senses. Therefore, God tells us that we cannot truly love Him who we do not experience with all of our senses. And then not love our brothers who we see face to face. Our eyes witness people in his image. And if we are going to love God, we have to include people, especially God's people, church people. The examination we are to have with ourselves is to ask, am I doing this? Am I loving God's people? If I am not, then I cannot say I am loving God. John is insisting on this point. Dr. Robert Rayburn is a Presbyterian minister That I use as a resource from time to time because I both respect his scholarly work and his pastoral heart. And regarding this section in 1 John, he says the following. This is a personal testimony of his own. He says I don't think nearly enough about what the Bible is actually saying to me and what it means for my life today, and how it ought to change the way I live my life today. And I certainly don't nearly often enough turn that truth into an argument with myself An argument that I will not allow to be concluded until I have embraced and obeyed the truth as God has taught it to me in His Word. Now if Dr. Rayburn is not examining himself well enough, I wonder about the rest of us. And this has been a reincurring conversation between Bobby Leon and myself during this last month. We have been wondering how many Christians today, my own children included, how many Christians have conversations with themselves and with the Holy Spirit in terms of examining themselves and listening to what God is saying to us. What I am concerned about is how many Christians have a genuine relationship with God via the Holy Spirit in the name of Jesus. Where we are asking God to examine us, asking God to show us how to love in this situation. And then in this other situation. And then still in this other situation. I fear, and I use the word fear purposefully I fear that many who call themselves Christians view God as a rule maker and a scorekeeper. I fear that he is understood to be more as a referee in our lives instead of someone who is our God and we are his children. As a referee, he knows the rules and he watches us to make sure we don't break them And if we do, he blows the whistle or throws a flag and writes the infraction down, keeping a running record. I fear this is happening too much among us because I don't witness often enough great concern about offending God or offending a brother or sister in Christ. Eyewitness people defending themselves for their actions or justifying themselves for their temper and not being concerned about how their choices reflect upon God and his church. I see a lot of that. I have done a lot of that And I have finally been paying attention to what my responsibility is when it comes to loving people. I recall when I was in a conflict with an individual, it wasn't that big of a deal, but it was an argument. And I was about to make a point to defend myself, and my heart was quickened. And I felt a deep conviction from a question in my conscience that went something like this, what are you trying to prove right now? What are you trying to prove right now? It's amazing how in a conversation your mind can be going and you're talking to yourself And the answer to that question was that I was trying to prove myself. And proving myself had nothing to do with showing the love of God to the person I was talking to. Consider this next statement and the ramifications of this next statement. John never tells us to consider how we are being loved, but instead tells us how we are to measure how we are loving his people. Let me repeat it. John never tells us we are to consider how we are being loved. Most of you have heard of the love language theory, which I believe was expounded upon by author Gary Chapman. The love language theory is that each of us receives love differently. Whereas I Feel love when someone engages me in a deep conversation. I'm not much on small talk. Deep conversations, they move me. Others feel love by means of gift giving And others by affectionate touching. Well, one of the dangers of examining our love language is that we can focus on how others are paying attention to our love language. Instead of examining ourselves to see if we are paying attention to the logic language of others. I repeat it again. John never tells us we are to consider, to take inventory, to examine how others are loving us. We are only to examine if and how we are loving others. To know whether or not we are loving, as John is describing in this letter, we are to talk to ourselves. We are to examine ourselves, talking to ourselves, in the manner I described previous. In a conversation. Why am I talking this way? What am I trying to gain when I counterpoint my sister's perspective? What is my agenda when I become irritated by a brother? Now, such questions, when answered, lead me to be able to know whether the love of Christ is within me in my words, in a conversation. Whether the love of Christ is within me in my attitude, in my actions, or whether the love of Christ is within my emotions in a response. I have been practicing, talking to myself as of late, and I begin with a conversation that goes something like this. Look and see how you can express the love of Jesus to this person. Pay attention to what this person needs to know about the love of Christ. Just asking those simple questions, they help, it helps a great deal to say something to yourself, to put the priority in front of you. Now, if you are hearing me as if I am leaving out God or the person of the Holy Spirit by talking about talking to yourself, that's not what I'm saying. Such questions and such coaching of myself naturally leads to asking the Holy Spirit to speak to me, to lead me. Let us be reminded of examples in Holy Scripture. Some of my favorite verses are when David talks to himself, coaching himself. Why, my soul, are you downcast? Why are you disturbed within me? Put your hope in God, for I will yet praise him, my Savior and my God. I love such passages because they are so very honest, vulnerable, and what I find myself saying to myself. David's conversations are not limited to him talking to his own conscience or his own soul. They include him talking to God. Search me, O God, and know my heart. Search me. Try me and know my anxious thoughts. And see if there be any hurtful way in me, hurtful towards others in me. And lead me in the everlasting way. As we can see In the Psalms, David models how people can be after God's heart. It can be by speaking to ourselves what is right. And what is good to be, what is good to do. It is asking God to reveal within us the need to confess, to guide where we need to go. In the context of this action from John's first letter, we are to speak to ourselves regarding what is and what is not loving towards our fellow Christians. It is to ask God to reveal within us why we are not loving when we fail to love and what we need to do to express more love. Amy Carmichael served our Lord and Savior Jesus As a missionary in India, ministering to orphans for 55 years during the early 20th century. She wrote several books on her mission work, but no book or booklet has been more popular from her work than the one titled If It just so happened that Mrs. Jen Fry loaned that book to me earlier this week. She was not aware how I could have used it. She just thought it fit with covering 1 John But the Lord knew how I could use it. I have quoted Miss Amy and have read some of her mission work before, but I had not read this booklet if in its entirety And when I read it this week, I immediately thought of the book The Imitation of Christ by Thomas Akempis, because both of them present the Christian life as, don't mean this to be negative Demanding. The Christian life is demanding. Here are some examples of Miss Amy Carmichael's writings from the booklet If If I belittle those whom I am called to serve, talk of their weak points in contrast, perhaps, with what I think of as my strong points. If I adopt a superior attitude, forgetting who made thee to differ, and what hast thou that thou hast not received, then I know nothing of Calvary love. If I can easily discuss the shortcomings and sins of any, if I can speak in a casual way even of a child's misdoings Then I know nothing of Calvary love. If my attitude be one of fear, not faith, About one who has disappointed me, if I say just what I expected, if a fall occurs, then I know nothing of Calvary love. If I take offense easily, if I am content to continue in a cool unfriendliness, though friendship be possible, then I know nothing of Calvary love. If I refuse to be a corn of wheat that falls into the ground and dies, is separated from all in which it lived before, then I know nothing of Calvary love. And these quotes are but a small sample of the demanding self-examination that all Christians must practice. And Miss Amy wisely advises that each examining point is to be taken in slowly because of the weight that each carries. And she points out the following. She says, some of the ifs appear to be related to pride, selfishness, or cowardice. But digging deeper, we come upon an unsuspected lovelessness at the root of them all. The Apostle John would agree. I close with the words of John verse 21. And this commandment we have from him, that he who loves God must love his brother also. Let us pray

sermons.title: The Sufficient Gospel
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please turn in your Bibles to 1 John chapter 5. We are beginning at the first verse this morning. First John chapter five, before we look at the passage, I want to share with you a couple of stories. There's a local radio morning show that regularly presents three strange stories. And only one of them is made up. Callers call in to guess which one is the false story, and they win some simple prize. Well, I would like to try something similar this morning, but I only present two stories. One is true and the other is bogus. And I don't have any prize. Story number one. Story comes to us from Suncook, New Hampshire. Betty Lynn Monroe Believes her dog, Rambler, has had a conversion comparable to what humans experience. Monroe says that for months Rambler had been sitting in a corner and listening to her Bible study group discuss the Bible. Then last week during the prayer time, Rambler ran into their midst, lay down on the floor, and looked up at them with a quote a look of pure regret and sadness. Monroe says, it was as sincere as anything I've seen among humans at the altar of a church. The group laid hands on Rambler and prayed that God would make him a born-again creature. Rambler then leapt up and pranced around the living room. It was the most joyous display of freedom in Christ we'd ever seen, said one woman said one woman. I teared up. Well since his conversion Rambler is more helpful. He doesn't chase squirrels into bushes, and he tolerates the neighbor's cat. He even has corrected his owners. Monroe says she and her husband fought one night and retreated to separate rooms. Rambler came to one room. Then another with a disapproving look. He wouldn't stop until they reconciled before bed. It was like he was reminding us not to let the sun go down on our anger, she says Rambler seems to wait all week for the home Bible study. He runs around excitedly when people gather. He yips and howls when the group worships. He loves the presence of the Holy Spirit as much as we do, says one Bible study member. He also lays on Monroe's lap every night and whines until she reads to him from the Psalms. His favorite passage comes from Psalm 145, verse 21.
