Personally, I believe that is the fault of the parents, but we will address that on a later day. Verse 8 also informed us about this original audience. of the original audience of these Proverbs. It was written to the Son of a King. Of course, he's not named because it's supposed to represent all of God's children, us, you and I. And to appreciate how important this book is, do you know that Proverbs is quoted in some part 100 times in the New Testament? Certainly in application for us Christians. Now for all children hearing me now, if you are somewhat awake, note the importance in this verse of both the father and the mother in the life of a child. This is a parallelism. The instruction of the father and the law of the mother are saying the same thing. The basic message, heed the teachings of your parents, both of them. Next, in verse 9, it explains how wisdom has an ascetic reality to it Just as Holy Scripture can be viewed in the lives of people as joy and hope are exhibited in a person's countenance. So too can wisdom be revealed in a person. It adorns a person. Wisdom is aesthetically pleasing. It is viewed as confidence and trust. And when people see it in us, we become in their lives a sight for sore eyes. Moving on to verse 10, we have the opposite of listening to one's parents, and here we have a straightforward instruction. We are to understand that there are necessary components when we are being enticed by sin. We're going to hear a lot about these necessary components in this book. But one of those components is other sinners. Sinners who do not know God. Many foolish decisions made begin with whom we are friends with. I heard a minister give an example about this. He was counseling with a young woman, and uh the woman had fallen again and again into abusing drugs. And he made the observation to her, you know, I've never been offered drugs in my entire life. And he wasn't saying that to be braggadocious, he was simply pointing out to her that he didn't hang around people who had drugs to offer him. But of course the people that she chose to be around had the drugs and always brought her back in And then we see this connection, another component. Sinners is one, and making our choices is another. The other component is being tempted to evil by our will. It is implied in terms of who we choose to be friends with. We make choices. Now the wording of verses 11 through 13 require us to recognize that it is unlikely that our peer group would describe their intentions so blatantly. Not even a fool would say, let's go ambush the innocent without reason. So why is he wording it this way? What's he wanting the children to understand? He's trying to get them to see through the through the outer veneer of temptation and to go and look at what is at the core of the temptation toward evil. He wants his children to realize that temptations that seem so exciting and attractive at a given moment lead to very ugly and awful things. The blatant description of what is really going on with peer temptation forces the child to see the brutality, the injustice, the callousness that these people are intending to do. And with this warning, we are to compare the devil's mode of operation. Doesn't he make things appear so benign? Even a little fun because they're daring, because they tempt fate. But what is really going on is a battle for a person's soul. And with verse 14, we hear the deceptiveness that tries to make a person believe that the devil actually has good intentions. Let us share the same purse. The devil never shares equally, and neither do his followers. If he can get a person to believe He does share equally, well, he has succeeded in convincing the deceived that good is evil and evil is good. And such a deception forces the father to be unequivocal in his warning for his son not to walk the same road as his tempters. The Father who's riding this knows that road. He himself has been on it. And then to verses 16 through 19. Here we have described where it all leads. When tempters are followed, where it all leads. When selfish gain is the end goal. The end loss is a person's soul. Consider all the decisions that you make in life. Consider which ones are the most important. The first one, of course, is to follow Jesus. That's the main one. The second one, you've heard it from this pulpit before, it's who you marry. Remember that, young ones, it's who you marry. That's the second most important decision you make. And the third one is much like it. It's who you choose to influence your life. Who you choose to influence your life Consider that the following wisdom to help children grow up, to follow Jesus, and thus not follow the wrong crowd, consider how this also applies to adults as well. As Christians, we are to have instill within us a certain identity. An identity that makes us distinct from those who do not know God There should be something different, dare I say, odd about us People might even call us weird. Weird because we do not have their same priorities. We're because we actually believe in what cannot be seen. And because of that distinct identity, we are to expect And you should tell your children that they should expect to feel different and to be treated different by their peers. Christians, beloved, are the called out ones. We do not follow the path of the crowd. We need not expect to fit in. It is necessary for godliness that we don't fit in. This does not mean that we need to be antisocial, but it does mean that when attempters come at us and plea for us to fit in, That we see the words for what they really are. They're trying to get our soul. I witnessed I have witnessed parents who don't want their children to experience feeling weird or feeling different. Maybe they themselves, by following Christ, have not enjoyed the times where they didn't fit in. And so I've watched these parents encourage their children to fit in. To have fun. To go ahead and do those things. Beloved, as I watch these parents, I also see their children going the way of the world. Now, of course, I don't know what their end game will be. None of us do. But we are to understand that our souls are at stake. Our children's souls are at stake. To be different for Christ needs to be understood as a privilege. A privilege to carry his name. So here we are. Our first lesson from Proverbs. Go the way of wisdom. Don't go the way of the world. Sounds like pretty good advice, don't you think? Let us pray.

sermons.title: Heart of the Matter
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. Always appreciate reciting the Affination Creed. Thank the Lord we don't have to memorize it. So our second installment in the book of Proverbs. And thinking about the second epistle from John and the commandment once again to love one another. One of the most difficult, if not the most difficult aspect of loving one another is thinking the best of one another. Thinking the best of one another. It is both natural and habitual to question another person's motive about anything and everything. A person may ask us a question, and because we don't immediately understand the context of the question, we might wonder what the motive is behind the question. Why would he ask me that question? What is he trying to get at with that remark? The natural and habitual response of not trusting another person's motive is likely caused by the reality that we humans understand the importance of motive. We understand motive to be at the heart of who a person is I purposefully used the word heart in that last sentence to introduce you to the subject matter we will be exploring in this sermon from Proverbs. According to Strong's concordance, the word heart is used in the book of Proverbs 80 times. For you mathematicians, that means that the word occurs 2. 58 times on the average in each chapter of the book. So it's important The importance of our hearts is underlined by the teachings of Jesus. In the Sermon on the Mount, he explained that the heart is where sin begins. Thus, when you lust in your heart, you have already committed adultery. When you hate in the heart, you have already committed murder. And from a separate teaching moment, similar to our gospel reading from Mark chapter 7, verse 20 through 23, Jesus said, What comes out of a person is what defiles him, for from within, out of the heart of a man, come evil thoughts. sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, coveting, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, and foolishness All of these evil things come from within. They defile a person. And so sin is inside out. And therefore, the place of the heart, that place of the heart is to be protected, it is to be cultivated, it is to be strengthened. Matured, nurtured, given wisdom, built up with fortitude, and I run out of descriptives of how important it is to take care of our hearts. But what is the heart? How would you define the heart? Well, you and I tend to use the word heart to refer to our emotions. When we say that we feel something from the heart, that means that we really feel it. It might surprise some of you to hear For me to say that our heart really is our emotions. It has been said by some that I I disregard the importance of emotion in my preaching and my teaching, and so I may have But I would edit that opinion by pointing out that I focus my criticism on emotions that carry the day, not emotions themselves Getting back to the proper understanding of the word heart, the Bible uses the word to describe our emotions, indeed, our feelings. But it also uses it to describe our thinking, our minds. And then also our choosing or our wills. And so simply put, the heart is the mind, it is the emotions, it is the will of a person. In the Bible, when a person lacks inside or judgment, he is said to lack heart. The heart, in other words, thinks. But the heart also plans, the heart makes decisions, the heart renders judgment. The heart also feels In the book of Proverbs, we find that the heart has anxiety, the heart has bitterness, it has peace, it has good cheer, it's attracted to a beautiful woman, it envies, it loves, it hates. All of this is found in our heart. The heart, as commentator Bruce Watke described, is the center, quote. All of a person's emotional, intellectual, religious, moral activity. Some have called the heart, as used in the Bible, our core personality, our inner self. I like to say it is the very essence of who we are. Our heart. Who a person truly is. And when you take this definition of the heart and you place it back into the teachings of Jesus, where he warned against lust and against hate, you can see why those teachings are so dramatic. Persons who lust in the heart haven't simply noticed a pretty girl, but are giving their essence over to wanting something that is not holy, that is not right, that is not good. The person who hates is giving their very selves over to an emotion that only cares about destruction. Such persons are lost to God. Our definition of the heart also brings us back to the importance of our motivation. Motivations stem from the heart. Our motivations are who we truly are, and therefore they matter a great deal, why we do what we do. Let us now look at some samplings from Proverbs referring to the heart. This first one is from Proverbs 3, verse 1. He says, My son, do not forget my teaching, but let your heart, your heart, keep my commandments. In order to not forget the teachings of a father, the son must give himself toward duty. Commandments in the heart, when they're in the heart, those are the commandments that are not forgotten. And then from Proverbs 3, verse 5, you know this verse: trust in the Lord with all of your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding. To trust in the Lord with a person's very essence, his or her true self, is to be given completely over to the Lord. And this is why the Christian life cannot be lukewarm about anything. Following Jesus is not a category in our lives that is practiced only at times It is not an instrument in our lives to be picked up and put down whenever it is seemingly needed or not needed. No. It is to be who we are at all times This verse is seen in the teachings of Jesus, who said, You shall love the Lord your God with all of your heart. From this we can say that we are to love God with all that we truly are. Nothing less. From Proverbs 15 verse 13. A glad heart makes a cheerful face, but by sorrow our heart of the Spirit is crushed. And here is a truth that we all know very well. When the heart is truly touched by whatever emotion it can be seen on our countenances A man or woman happy at their very essence cannot help but reveal their happiness in their face, excuse me, in their posture and their conversation. It comes out of them. naturally, organically, out of them. And the same is true for a man or woman who is hurt to the core. Such hurt is also seen in the face, in the posture, in the conversation. From Proverbs chapter 20, verse 9. A rhetorical question indeed. Who can say I have made my heart pure? I am clean from my sin. This is similar to the truth spoken in 1 Samuel. For the Lord sees not as man sees. Man looks at the outward, but the Lord looks upon the heart. This quote from Proverbs is a rhetorical question because no one can make his own heart pure. No one can clean his own heart of sin. It has to be done by another. It has to be done by the only one who can look upon the heart. From Proverbs chapter 21, verse 1. The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the Lord. He turns it wherever he will. And such is a helpful verse, for it teaches us that the events of the world that are seemingly controlled by men, whether they be good or bad, Are in truth controlled by the very one who created all things. Whenever you consider that you're worried about what men are doing in this world, what leaders, what choices they're making, and how it's affecting the world, all Always remember as we pray that the Lord has them in his hands, and he will turn them as he wills. And from Proverbs chapter 21, verse 2. Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, but the Lord weighs the heart. This verse teaches us that we have a viewpoint, even of ourselves, and a viewpoint of the world that is not always helpful. We don't always see ourselves or the world as it is. I repeat what I have confessed before. I like you with every argument that I have when it's inside my head. But here is the reality. The Lord judges the heart of a person, and that judgment is the truth. And what the Lord weighs and what the Lord judges, he judges our motives. He cares about not just what we do, but why we do it. A Christian ought to know that he or she can be in the right for the wrong reason. For example, I could be in the right regarding a stand I take against a person gossiping. But my motivation could be that I don't want others to know what I said or what I did The gossip is wrong, but I am most concerned about other people knowing my sin. God knows that heart, and he condemns the motive. It is sin unto him. From Proverbs 27, verse 19. As in water, face reflects face. So the heart of man reflects man. Now here is a verse that verifies how we are defining this word heart. Remember, it's it's who we truly are. It is our emotions, our wills, our mental faculties, our very essence. What makes you you? It is our essence, and our essence is going to be revealed. It may take time, but our essence is going to be revealed, and that is to be good for Christians. It will be bad for some, but to be revealed is to be a good thing for Christians. And one might wonder how much issues of the heart are controlled by the wills of men. How much determination do we have over our own hearts? How much can we actually control when it comes to our own hearts? We first need to be reminded that a heart that does not know God is a heart that is dead to God. And thus that heart needs to be awakened. The Bible uses the metaphor of a circumcised heart to describe what needs to happen to a person who is still dead in their sins. The circumcision of the heart is the cutting away of what is dead to God and thus allowing a new, freshly beating heart to replace what was cold, what was hard, what was dead. And such cutting away only God can do. And so we are completely dependent upon Him to give us new hearts. And after our hearts are awakened, only after our hearts are awakened, then it is for us to care for our hearts. To see that they do not become diseased, clogged, strained, weakened, and near death. That's on us Here from Proverbs chapter 4, verse 20 and 21. Solomon says, My son, pay attention to what I say, turn your ear to my words, do not let them out of your sight, keep them. Within your heart. In these instructions, it is inferred that there is a place In place, the ability for God-fearing people to have control over their hearts, to pay attention and to keep words of wisdom within the heart is up to us And also inferred in this is a will. That is a choice we make or choices we make. We choose to pay attention. We choose to keep words of wisdom within our hearts. And so we accept this ability, we accept that we have a will to be stewards of our hearts, and therefore we must consider how to protect them. And what follows is the least of what we should be doing. The very first thing we need to do, to be stewards of our hearts. is to examine our hearts. Just as St. John taught us, you will remember those sermons. We are to be examining our love for one another, our doctrine, and our personal morality. And such examining is not a one-time procedure, of course. We are to be in the examining room on a regular basis. This is an insisting on an honest reckoning of ourselves to be sure that we are not just professing Christians but have a faith that is living, that we are an embodiment of Jesus Himself to the rest of the world. It sounds lofty. I know that that sounds lofty, but it is the only Christianity that the Bible knows. And to say this is simply to say that keeping the heart, keeping the heart is one way of saying the same thing that the Bible says. That we are to be growing in grace all of the time. A Christian keeps the heart by putting sins to death. Practicing faith, all in the heart. Keeping the heart is not something other than to practice the Christian life Taught throughout the Bible. There is no other type of Christianity, beloved. There's only one. And it gives all of the heart. The second thing we should be doing for our heart is protecting it, protecting it from all influences that would distract us. That would give us a wrong motive, that would change our priorities. This requires of us to stay away from things that promote bad habits, bad thoughts, and bad actions. The heart is influenced and shaped, formed by what we put before our senses. And we find that wisdom prominent in Proverbs, it is here for us in chapter 21 to verse 27, chapter 4. A man who keeps his heart listens to the right kind of instruction. Preserves the truth in his heart. He puts all devious talk from himself We are to be a people who make sure we are concentrating on the right things, keeping focus on the right things. That's what somebody does when he's guarding, keeping his heart. He's keeping out of his heart all the things that would damage it. Consider in chapter 5, verse 8. And there the father warns his son to keep his foot from the door of a wayward woman. Stay away from her and from her influence, lest in later life you will have to say, oh, how I hated discipline and how my heart despised reproof The wrong sort of influences will misshape the heart and it becomes hardened and it will stay that way. Well our society repeatedly debates the effects of pornography, violent movies. violent video games upon young people. They ask whether such images and portrayals cause minds and then actions to become perverted and more violent. For the Christians, that decision is already decided. If you want a pure heart, you can't look at pornography. Or give yourself to daydreams over sexual images. If you want a soft heart that doesn't think violently against others, you cannot be entertained by a celebration of violence You see, the matter is decided for the Christian. It's not a matter of mind or actions, but a matter of the heart. This principle also applies to matters of faith. If you want a believing heart, you cannot expose that heart constantly to unbelieving minds and unbelieving influences, unbelieving teachings. Unless you are able to refute every single one of them. This is how so many young Christians get led away from the Lord. They start to trust in their teachers who are non-believers, whether it be high school or college. They're swayed away from the truth by these charismatic teachers. As we spoke last week, a major choice in each of our lives is who we allow to influence us. The third thing we can do for our hearts is to feed and exercise them. What works for the body also works for the spirit. Remember the Apostle Paul saying that bodily training has some value, but the training of the heart The training of the heart that gives us eternal value. We feed our hearts by being in the Word of God. We read it daily, study it weekly, memorize it monthly, apply it always. We feed our hearts by prayer. Pray the Lord's Prayer daily. Pray the Psalms when you have no words yourself. Pray by talking to the Lord because He is always with you. We feed our hearts by being at corporate worship, religiously at corporate worship. Our hearts need to sing with the saints. Our hearts need to hear the prayers of others. Our hearts need to hear the gospel sermons. Our hearts need to taste the bread and wine. We need to be fed. And then after we get fed, we need to exercise. If you don't apply God's word, that's the exercising. If you don't apply God's word to your heart, you will become weak and you'll become flabby. You have to strengthen it by working it out, which means you have to have to work at being kind, you have to work at forgiving others, you have to work at getting away from the addictions of the flesh. You have to work at believing truth as God has revealed it. The Christian life, beloved, is not for whims. Finally, finally, remember that the Lord measures our lives by our hearts, by what is truly inside of us. He measures it by who we truly are, our very essence. Thus, we need to heed the call to protect our heart. Protect it from what will defile or weaken or distract it. We need to feed it. We need to train our hearts with our thoughts, with our feelings. We need to do all that is pleasing to the Lord for the sake of our hearts. Recall that the Tin Man and the Wizard of Oz didn't realize that the very fact that he wanted a heart meant that he had one. Before Christ was known to us, we didn't have one. Not one that beat for the Lord. But he gave us one. He gave us a new heart, to beat for him and to beat for eternity. It is then for us to protect, to feed, to exercise our hearts. To love our Lord our God with all of our heart, with all of who we are. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Money Problems
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. For what profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world and loses his own soul? Jesus asked that rhetorical question in the context of all who follow him to pick up their very own cross if they were to continue. To follow him. The rhetorical question forces us to conclude that there isn't anything that is worth gaining in this life That would cause us to lose our souls to the punishment of hell. No pleasure, no power, no prestige, no position No amount of money is worth the loss of one's own soul. But in saying that How does this reflect, this truth reflect in your life? You see, I have been moved in the Spirit to address a habit that I believe too many of us have. It is one thing to hear that we are to pick up our own cross in order to follow Jesus. It is one thing to agree that there is no profit in this life worth losing our soul over, and yet it is another thing to answer the question, how does this apply to me? I'll ask it more directly. How does the agreed fact that there is nothing in this life worth losing your soul over, how does that affect you? How does it change your priorities? How does it change your daily living? Well, such questions need to be asked because Jesus' rhetorical question has to have an effect on us. That has to change us, each of us. It has to be applied to each of our lives every day. You need to ask yourself, how is your life being changed? Daily changed by the necessity of you not being concerned about what you gain in this life But instead living a life that is sacrificial. That's what picking up a cross is, sacrificial. And what you are going to hear this morning is the rhetorical question of Jesus asked. The question that he asked repeated in the context of what the Proverbs, the Book of Proverbs, has to say about money. And it has a great deal to say about money. First, a couple of stories, quick ones. Andrew Whitaker, at 55 years old, bought the winning lottery ticket for $315 million. Powerball ticket in December of 2002. But soon after he cashed in his ticket, his life began to unravel. Legal problems and personal demons pushed Whitaker towards heavy drinking. He also liked to frequent strip clubs. He reported that he had $545,000 stolen from his car when he was at a strip club. In 2007, Whitaker told police that the thieves had emptied his bank accounts Whitaker also suffered several personal tragedies after winning the jackpot. His granddaughter died of a drug overdose. His only daughter died five years later. He was quoted to have said, I wish I'd torn that ticket up. Janet Lee. She won $18 million at age 60 from a lottery in 1993 in Illinois. She spent much of her yearly $620,000 installment payments on philanthropic causes. Her generosity saw her dining with then President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore. She got her name on a reading room at the Washington University School of Law. Later, she sold the rights to her annual payment for a lump sum. She wanted it all in the moment And soon later, in 2001, filed Chapter 7, where it was said that she had $700 to her name and was $2. 5 million in debt. For what profit is it to a man who gains this whole world and loses his own soul? There are, as you like me know, many more stories like these, these tragedies, lead us to mention that prayer of augur Found in Proverbs 30, verse 7 through 9. I'll read it again. Two things I ask of you, Lord, do not refuse me before I die. Keep falsehood and lies from me. Then hear this. Give me neither poverty nor riches, but give me my daily bread. Otherwise, I may have too much and disown you, and say, who is the Lord? Or I may become poor and steal and dishonor the name of my God. Well there is in this simple prayer an admission that money provides a great deal of things in this life. Money makes a very big difference. It is acceptable to admit that rich people physically live more comfortable lives. They travel more often and to more interesting places. They eat better, they dress better, they drive better cars, and worry less about monthly bills. That is the attraction of money. There is no denying it. Also in the prayer is an acknowledgement that being poor stinks. Consider Proverbs 10, verse 15. A rich man's wealth is his strong city. The poverty of the poor is their ruin. Of course, the Bible speaks very fondly of the poor because they tend to be more receptive of the gospel But this proverb from Proverbs 1015 describes how things are from the point of view of the world. Some proverbs are descriptive rather than prescriptive. They describe as people are, not necessarily as they should be. And so the proverb reveals the way rich people think about money. It is not accurate, but that is what people think. In fact, both rich people and poor people tend to think the same, perceive the same about money. Wealth is a strength, and poverty is a weakness. But this next proverb, being similar, again reveals a false understanding The poor is disliked even by his neighbor, but the rich has many friends. Again, it is descriptive. It is not how it should be, but it is how things usually are. In certain Proverbs, God uses wealth as a metaphor for blessing. From Proverbs 14, 24. The crown of the wise is their wealth. From Proverbs 10, 22. The blessing of the Lord makes rich, and he adds no sorrow to it. So we can conclude from this that it is not money that is evil, and God does bless people with wealth. But although God uses wealth as a metaphor for blessings, he also has some grim warnings about the love of money and what that can do to a person. As the prayer of Augur expresses, the worst money can do to people is give them a sense of security apart from God. That is the idea behind the world describing security as a rich man's wealth being his strong city. He thinks himself secure behind his money. He thinks that he has all that he needs. He needs nothing else. But of course, that is untrue. Dangerously untrue. That it is untrue is plainly stated in this next Proverb, Proverbs 18, 10. A rich man's wealth is his strong city, and like a high wall in his imagination. That's a truism. The security of a rich person is imaginary, as anyone knows, who has faced a disaster in life. There are tragedies in life that money cannot prevent, nor can money heal. And yet the world falls prey. To the belief that money is the answer, always the answer. If there is trouble in the inner city, give them more money. If there are schools that are not producing, give them more money. The economy, not doing well, give incentives to the citizens. Give them more money Money is the security blanket for the godless. For what profit is it to a man? He gains the whole world and loses his own soul. But next in Proverbs, God warns that money, ironically, creates a desire for more money. From Proverbs 17a, a bribe is like a magic stone in the eyes of the one who gives it. Wherever he turns, he believes he prospers. Notice today that we do not become wide-eyed when we hear that there is corruption in businesses, in governments, in sports. We don't get wide eye because it occurs so very often. On those of you who follow professional soccer Have known that the leaders for FIFA who have been in the news of late have been on the take for years. It was clear to all that the leaders of FIFA were awarding the World Cup to host cities because they would give them bigger bribes. And the men, interestingly, who ran FIFA were bringing in salaries individually well over a million dollars. And they had all the perks that they wanted for their travels, and still they wanted more money Their most obvious sin, love of money, lust of money. For what profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world and loses his own soul? So after hearing the warnings about the dangers and the love of money Let's now turn to some wisdom that the Proverbs gives us in regards to handling our money, giving us a skillful approach to money that brings the Lord's blessings and rewards and does not harm the soul. First, we are given the wisdom, do not make a pursuit of more wealth than you need as a priority. Here are these proverbs from chapter 23, verse 4. Do not toil to acquire wealth. Be discerning enough to resist. Again, from chapter 10, verse 22. The blessing of the Lord makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it. With the first verse read, we are to recall that Jesus is telling his disciples to seek ye first the kingdom of God. And again, when we hear that, we have to ask ourselves the question, how does that apply to me? Now I know he said it generally. But how does seeking first the kingdom of God apply to your individual life right now? And affect all the decisions you make in your life today, tomorrow, and the next If we pursue anything else, it is an idol to us as money is to so many. The second proverb read tells us that Jesus did when he told us to seek first the kingdom of God, then he said, All these things shall be added unto you. Given to us all that we need by the Lord. You see, we are told here that when the blessings come from the Lord, there is no sorrow in it. No guilt comes with it. No one in your life is bitter or angry at you because you forgot about them or you mistreated them as you were pursuing to acquire wealth. When it comes from the Lord, it is to be used to rejoice in the Lord. And this leads us to another point that Proverbs makes about wealth. There is only one safe way to acquire wealth, and that is by the blessing of the Lord, the blessing of the Lord upon your hard work and your faithfulness to him. Remember in the law of Moses, the Lord tells his people, do not muzzle an ox while he is treading the grain. Such is a cruel way to treat an animal. The animal needs strength from the grain in order to continue to tread. But then St. Paul uses that same axiom. That same principle to teach Christians how a minister of the gospel is to receive his just due by spreading the gospel. And the same can be said for all who work hard at what they do. They should receive their just due. St. Paul says as much to Timothy when he quotes the law again, and he says, a worker is worth his wages. That is a truism. You should get What you receive from the Lord according to your work, according to your effort, according to your success. At the beginning of the book of Proverbs, after describing about the ruin that comes from those who steal to acquire wealth, we read this from chapter 1, verse 19. Such are the ways of everyone who is greedy for unjust gain. It takes away the life of its possessors. Those who care only to acquire wealth, that's all they care about, and are not concerned about how they get such wealth. Do not realize that their behavior is slowly eroding away their humanity. They don't feel the erosion. No one says anything to them about it. But they become less and less human as they use people to achieve material wealth. And so we hear again, for what profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world and loses his own soul? But love of money is evident when a person or a couple live above their means, and thus they become dependent upon the money of others. This is from Proverbs 22, verse 7. The rich rule over the poor, and the borrower is slave to the lender. And to become a borrower is to become dependent or in debt to another. When St. Paul instructs Christians to owe no man anything, He is talking about our Christian witness. When we become indebted to others, we no longer come to them in the name of Jesus, but we come to them in the name of duty that we might not have our debt called into account. Our witness becomes obscured by our ability or our inability to have a true motive with our lender, a pure motive. And along with warning against borrowing, Proverbs instructs us to be careful with our investments. From Proverbs 11:5, whoever puts up security for a stranger will surely suffer harm. But he who hates striking hands in pledge is secure. And this from Proverbs 6, verse 1 through 5. My son, if you have put up security for your neighbor, have given a pledge for a stranger, then do this, my son, and save yourself, for you have come into the hand of your neighbor. Go, hasten, and plead urgently with your neighbor. Give your eyes no sleep and your eyelids no slumber. Save yourself like a gazelle from the hand of the hunter, like a bird from the hand of the fowler To put security into someone else is to invest your money in them. Because Christians Care for their fellow man, and because we love our fellow Christians, it is tempting to invest in others' endeavors because they seem genuine It is not sinful to do so because the Lord wants us to love one another and trust one another, but it is also not wise. I know of a man who entrusted himself to a fellow Christian on his business endeavors. He was told his $30,000 investment would be returned in a few months' time with great interest. They both attended the same church. They worshiped the same Lord. They had been in each other's homes. The businessman boasted of great wealth, and it could be seen in his home and in his toys. But it was a risky investment. The businessman eventually saw no return on his friend's investment, and in fact, the entire $30,000 was lost Proverbs teaches that the right use of money requires the good sense, the good sense not to throw money away on something perhaps kindly intended, but all too risky. Even if we're trying to help someone, we have to realize that we don't have the money to risk. Again, for what profit is it to a man that he gains the whole world and loses his own soul? Next, Proverbs teaches us that a wise use of money includes having self-control when spending it. From Proverbs 21, verse 17, whoever loves pleasure will be a poor man. He who loves wine and oil will not be rich. Consider these statistics on pleasure spending. Beer. Americans spent approximately $83 billion on beer in 2013. $83 billion. And that is expected to rise to $95 billion by 2018 annually on beer. Lottery tickets. U. S. consumers in 43 states in the District of Columbia spent $69 billion in 2012 on lottery tickets. Smut. The U. S. porn industry race an approximately eleven billion dollars annually. Somebody's watching it. Somebody's buying it. Taco Bell! Americans in two thousand thirteen spent roughly six billion dollars at Tacovell. Now, I hesitated to call these things pleasures. They are certainly extracurricular And so we hear again, for what profit is it to a man if he gains the whole world and loses his own soul? Finally, a righteous handling of money shows up supremely in the practice of using one's money not only responsibly But generously. A generous heart of giving money reflects a generous heart toward God. From Proverbs 28. 8. Whoever multiplies his wealth by interest and profit gathers it for him who is generous to the poor. The Lord came for the poor in spirit. And so it is natural for those who have been saved by the grace of Jesus to give freely to people who are in need. From Proverbs 11, verse 24 and 25. One gives freely, yet grows all the richer. Another withholds what he should give and only suffers want. Whoever brings blessing will be enriched, and one who waters will himself be watered Now, such is the way of the kingdom of God. This is how God governs his kingdom. God does not forget about those who give freely. He does not forget about those who give to the people in need because they bear his nature. And when we give, we bear his nature. And from Proverbs 3, verse 9-10. Honor the Lord with your wealth, and with the first fruits of all you produce, then your barns will be filled with plenty, and your vats will be bursting with wine. Again, this is not a promise, but a truism. It is how God runs his kingdom. We can be free to give because we have been given so freely by God. For what profit is it to a man who gains the whole world and loses his own soul? Nothing. None. There is no profit when money is loved, when money is a priority. Christians are stewards of money. All you and I have is from the Lord and is the Lord's A faithful steward is wise with his money. That is all the Lord asks of us. To be good stewards and wise with what he has given us to use. Let us pray

sermons.title: The Danger of Anger
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Our readings this morning were not from Proverbs, but we are looking at Proverbs. And we're looking at Proverbs in terms of the subject of anger. I purposefully chose the topic of anger from the book of Proverbs for Father's Day. One of the things you as a congregation have become accustomed to is hearing sermons on Father's Day that instead of celebrating Fathers, I wish to challenge them And some of my challenges can be a bit of a bop in the nose. And there are reasons for that. I have believed and continue to believe that fathers slash husbands Our key to reviving our culture with the gospel. How husbands slash fathers lead in terms of living the gospel Is the direction this parish and our culture will go? I will never back away from that belief. But why address anger? Well, I cannot explain my reasons any better than a blog post that was written a couple of weeks ago by the Reverend Doug Wilson. It was titled or is titled An Open Letter to an Angry Husband. Wilson explains that the letter is fictional. So that no one man would think it was directly to him, but the letter is very personal. And any man who struggles with anger and struggles expressing anger can find himself in that letter. It is a letter, I believe, that every God-fearing preacher could write, because there are many fathers slash husbands who fit the description. In Wilson's letter, he describes a scene of the husband barking at his wife and children in a cruel manner in public at a church picnic. The pastor has heard of the man's temper before, and now he has witnessed it himself. And the pastor concludes, rightly I believe, that what is seen in public is a sign of something much worse going on in private. Wilson also makes the point to the angry father slash husband that he is hiding behind behind his machoism. And he's hiding behind the biblical teaching of a wife needing to submit to her husband. The angry man knows those verses well. And thus justifies the bullying of his family with the Bible. I know such men. And I could be such a man, but by the grace of God. Anger can be a serious problem for both men and women, but when it is a problem for a man, it has serious Devastating consequences. And I use the word problem. Anger is more than a problem, it is a damnable sin And we read from Colossians chapter 3, verse 6 through 9. Paul says, Because of these, the wrath of God will come on the children of the disobedient. In which you also walk in these, when you lived in them, but now you also put off all of these: anger, wrath. malice, blasphemy, filthy communication out of your mouth. In that verse, Paul leaves no doubt the seriousness, the sin of anger. I try to recall stories of human anger expressed in the Bible. Recall Cain killing his brother Abel. Recall Saul becoming angry at David to the point of trying to kill him. Consider what these two stories express of expressed anger, what they have in common. The first thing we should learn from Proverbs regarding anger is that anger is the fruit or expression of other sins. The fruit or expression of other sins. Underline and highlight that point. That we don't condemn ourselves like we should for being angry when we fail to see the connection that anger has with other deplorable sins. When it comes to anger, there is always something underneath or at the heart of that anger that needs to be addressed. Consider these two proverbs from chapter 27, verse 4. Wrath is cruel, anger is overwhelming, but who can stand before jealousy? And from chapter 29, verse 8, scoffers set a city aflame, but the wise turn away wrath. Now ponder what is similar about these verses. Each mentions causes of anger. Causes of anger. Note this next point, please. Much anger, much anger is produced by envy or jealousy. And Proverbs is so very helpful to show us that connection. Rarely does anyone want to admit that he is jealous or that he is taken over by envy. Such allows others to know that a person is insecure. Or at least subconsciously aware of his shortcomings. And there is something pathetic about a person who is jealous or envious His constitution is weak, and he tries to make up for it by being angry. In the second verse read, we find that there is also a connection between anger and scoffing. Scoffing means to ridicule. A person who ridicules is a person who displays a critical spirit. And a critical spirit and an angry spirit are one and the same. We often don't connect cruel and critical speech with anger But the one is an expression of the other. Again, there is something pathetic about a cruel person, even though no one wants to admit that he or she is cruel Consider that it is easier to admit that you are angry if you are able to excuse your anger with some type of righteous indignation. In truth, angry people are often jealous or cruel, and thus their anger makes them pathetic. Is that too harsh? Does that make you angry? I am horrid for the purpose of keeping us away from anger. The very real problem with the repeatedly angry person is that he or she does not see what everyone else sees so well. Anger displayed reveals a sorry condition of the mind and heart and makes a person appear small, very small. They appear small because we all know how easy it is to give ourselves over to anger. We can all do it at any time. We all feel it and are tempted to give into it, but a person who is small in character gives into it all of the time. Hear this next proverb. If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small. If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small. Anger is not mentioned in the passage, but a person who faints at a time of adversity is giving into the emotions like anger instead of rising above it. And thus, if you can't control your anger, there is again something very small about you. And the only way to grow from your smallness is to admit that you are behaving in an angry manner. If you are a jealous person, an insecure person, a cruel person, you must be willing to admit it. And most importantly, to admit it to your wife and to your children To scare you even further away from anger. Here are these proverbs. From chapter 15, verse 8, verse 18. A hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but he who is slow to anger quiets contention. From chapter 29, verse 22. A man of wrath stirs up strife, and one given to anger causes much transgression. Both passages teach that an angry person causes others to sin. Anger begets anger. It begets bitterness. It begets hatred. Over time, anger, especially in a Christian home, results in unbelieving children. From Proverbs chapter 22, verses 24-25. Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man, lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in his snare. How many times have we seen an angry father resulting in an angry son, and an angry daughter resulting from an angry mother? Sin is anger is like a nasty genetic disease. It is a sin that is passed on to the next generation. Now I've been focusing on the male species, but Proverbs doesn't. From chapter 21, verse 19. It is better to live in a desert island than with a quarrelsome and fretful wife. But pay careful attention how serious Solomon is about living with a quarrelsome woman. It would be better to live alone in complete isolation than to live with an angry woman. And why do women get angry? Well, from this pastor's experience, women get angry primarily primarily because of bitterness wrapped up in their heart. Bitterness is caused by withholding forgiveness, and forgiveness is withheld because when a woman has expectations and they're not met, well, that's the first cause. She expects to be treated a certain way, and soon she becomes disappointed. And the devil tells her that she deserves to be treated a certain way, so she agrees and she refuses To love unconditionally, and therefore she withholds forgiveness. As time passes, unforgiveness becomes bitterness, and bitterness becomes anger. And when a woman lives with anger, she becomes unbearable. She becomes so unbearable that living with a volleyball is a better companion than the woman. An unexamined result of anger. It is a a number of people get hurt. From Proverbs chapter 30, verse 33. For pressing milk produces curds, pressing the nose produces blood, and pressing anger produces strife. In short, anger is destructive and harmful to others. Consider what is needed for a person to be angry. What is needed is an object of their anger. Bitterness, envy, resentment, and other such sins are so deep-seated, people don't know why they're angry anymore. And then transference occurs. Angry people let their anger out on others who emotionally remind them of the sin that started their anger. As a pastor, I have noticed people becoming angry at their spiritual leader for some cockamami excuse when the real target is angry at God. The angry person may think himself or herself simply venting strong feelings or expressing his or her sense of injustice, righteous outrage. But when he or she is really examining themselves, they are hurting other people. Always. Anger always results in the hurting of other people. When anger is embraced and people are harmed, the next result is a destruction of relationship. Anger puts people and keeps people in adversarial relationships Just as important as admitting that anger is caused by jealousy, insecurity, and a heart bent toward cruelty is the admission that anger is an attack on people. An attack. And this is why Jesus likened anger to murder in his Sermon on the Mount. The two include the same principle. It is a desire to destroy another person. And that that something like this could happen, that one person could be angry at another person to the point of wanting to witness the other person's demise. That's why Jesus addressed the sin. It is why the apostles used so many words to teach the people and implore the people to love one another. And if you are to love and care for others as Christ loved and cared for us, that means we can never justify darkening the lives of others with our anger. Our selfish pride and our small resentments. Anger in this way is seen as a repudiation of virtually every Christian principle, everything that we are to be about as Christian. And thus it is fair to ask an angry man, are you a Christian or are you not? Here is another proverb regarding anger from Proverbs chapter 19, verse 19. A man of great wrath will pay the penalty. For if you deliver him, you will only have to do it again. The reality identified in this proverb is rather sad. We might want to believe that an angry person simply needs to be heard and have love expressed to him in order for him to be rid of his anger. But the sin of an angry person isn't the anger only, as we have seen Until a person deals with the sinful habits of sins like jealousy and envy, withholding forgiveness and alike, there is no rescuing him. The wisdom of these proverbs has been eye-opening for me as a pastor I have practiced the being slow in being contentious with an angry person, and it did help calm the situation. But being kind and being slow with emotions does not save someone from their anger. The only thing that saves a person from anger is the blood of Jesus. The blood of Jesus does not atone for a man's sin until he confesses that sin and repents. An angry person needs to know that if he does not deal with his habitual anger, it will be forever too late. Because anger is such a dangerous sin, and a sin so easily fallen into. It becomes so very difficult to get out of it. Therefore, it is a praiseworthy achievement when it is rooted out, when anger is rooted out. Consider this next proverb from Proverbs 16, verse 32. Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city. Ruling your spirit, controlling your emotions. The wisdom here first is that being slow to anger is preferred. And most important message is that it is greatly difficult to be slow to anger. Consider the energy, the resources, the sacrifice of an army that it must use and make to overthrow a city. Lives are lost when a city is overtaken. People have to die when a city is overtaken. For a man to control his anger, he must die. Die to himself Die to his pride, die to his self-righteousness, die to his jealousy, die to his callousness, die to his perception that he is right and everyone else is wrong. But this is why the Christian life is referred to as a great race, a battle to fight, a cross to bear. A person who is angry is not a lost cause, but there is a great deal before him to overcome. And so when a man does overcome his anger, we can glory in such achievements, just as we glory in the achievements of great military men. And the fight to overthrow anger is always a just war. Always From Proverbs 19, verse 11. Good sense makes one slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook an offense. When a man has control over his anger, he is not provoked even when the offenses are real. Even when someone truly has wronged him, he's still in control. And such self-control is an example of how a man is full of the Holy Spirit. Such a man is to be admired and to be held up as an example. From Proverbs 15, verse 1. A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger. This proverb puts the subject in full view for me. Soft words reflect a soft heart, for from the heart the mouth speaks. Harsh words come from a hard heart that is full of anger. And as we have learned, anger is the result of other deplorable sins. And harsh words result in more anger. And more anger. And so what can be done for a person who has given over to anger? I believe the answer is obvious. It's obvious because it is what any person needs to do in order to have his or her sins forgiven and to be filled with the Holy Spirit. What does the scripture say? If we confess our sins, confession begins with acknowledging our sin, the sin of anger. And then after acknowledging anger, we must acknowledge the sin underneath the anger. Are you jealous and envious that someone has a job you think you should have? Confess your your coveting. Are you callous towards the needs of others? Confess your cruelty. Are you withholding forgiveness from someone? Confess your failure to love. When you do this, the scripture goes on to say he, God, will be faithful and just to forgive us our sins. And so we are to believe we are forgiven. The sin of anger and all the sins that led to our anger is no longer who we are. Your identity has changed, for you are now a person of Christ. And once that happens, what's a Christian to do next? I believe a person of anger has some reparations to pay Not for the atonement of their sins. Please don't ever hear me say that. His reparations need to be to those his anger has harmed. If you are a man of anger, you need to apologize to every person who has been hurt by your anger. You need to apologize with no excuse, no expectation of people needing to apologize to you But only seeking with a humble spirit that your relationships be restored I said earlier that fathers and husbands are the key to bringing revival to our culture. And I say it again. With the vision of men being humble in spirit, confessing their sins, receiving the love and mercy of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, and exemplifying that love and mercy first to their families. And then to the church, and then to their neighbors, and then to all whom God places in their path. Of course, there is an anger that is not sinful. Jesus got angry. There is a righteous anger. But that is not the sin that Proverbs is warning against. Don't let the devil fool you into justifying your sinful anger by identifying it as righteous anger. Righteous anger is under control. Anger is a serious sin that needs to be acknowledged and confessed and washed by the blood of Jesus. Christian men, put anger far from you. Don't allow it in your home. Do not entertain the emotion. Stay away from venues that tempt you toward anger. Christian fathers, Christian husbands, Christian men, the kingdom of God needs you. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Taking a Stand
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: It's In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Those of you who receive email announcements from the church Are aware that today we are veering away from our series on the book of Proverbs to address the devastating news. That the Supreme Court of these United States handed down a decision that makes it legal for our nation To sanctify marriage between a man and another man, between a woman and another woman. Perhaps my reaction was like yours. I received the news of the Supreme Court's decision through my Twitter feed. I clicked on the story to read more of the headline, and I was struck dumb. I knew it was possible, but I was struck dumb. I've always been an idealist about this country I always remember believing that the United States was the greatest nation. Not only in the world today, but the greatest nation the world had ever known. I know that conclusion is debatable, but it is what I believed as a young boy. And such idealism has always been with me. But my idealism was shattered on June 26th. This nation is no longer the nation I once loved. And don't be angry with me for saying that. It's just a gut reaction, a knee jerk reaction, and I hope to recover After reading about the Supreme Court decision, I prayed that the Lord would give me some living words. I was by myself, front porch. Of the house we were staying at. I needed living words to feed and calm my troubled soul. And I found two readings from the daily lectionary that spoke to me. The first one was from Psalm 107, verse 33-43. And it reads this: God turned rivers into a desert, flowing springs into thirsty ground. And fruitful land into a salt waste because of the wickedness of those who lived there. He turned the desert into pools of water, and the parched ground into flowing springs. There he brought the hungry to live, and they founded a city where they could settle. They sowed fields and planted a vineyard that yielded a fruitful harvest. He blessed them, and their numbers greatly increased, and he did not let their herds diminish. Then their numbers decreased, and they were humbled by oppression, calamity, and sorrow. He who pours contempt on nobles made them wander in a trackless waste But he lifted the needy out of their affliction and increased their family like flocks. The upright see and rejoice, but all the wicked shut their mouths. Let the one who is wise heed these things and ponder the loving deeds of the Lord. These words remind us that God is sovereign, and that means he will judge the nations as he sees necessary. And when a nation sins, he will in turn make their ground dry. And when he chooses to be merciful, he will turn their dry land into pools of water. Nations can do nothing outside of God's plan, and his plan is for his kingdom to come and his will to be done. The epistle lesson for that same day was from Acts chapter 7 The starting point was verse 37, which is right in the middle of St. Stephen's sermon before the Jews, before he was about to be stoned. He was recounting to them a story of God choosing them as a nation, but they rebelled again and again. In the section cited, Stephen reminds the Jews of the time when Moses was on Mount Sinai, waiting upon the Lord, receiving God's commands, and the people became so impatient that their leader had not returned. That they turned to Aaron and asked him, told him to make a golden idol so that they could worship a false god The lesson reminds us, a very simple lesson. People do that. People choose false gods, and when they do They choose evil and they call it good. These readings calmed my soul because I once again knew that God was indeed still in control, but it also started within me a determination that has only grown. God has called me to be a voice of dissent. Dissent in these days And I know this because I live in these days and I'm anointed to preach the gospel. And the gospel is a descent from the ways of the world. I am thus required as a preacher to be a voice of descent to any spirit of the age, and now that spirit of the age is up in our face. I also know that I am prepared to be a voice of dissent. I recognize that in being a voice of dissent, I may become an enemy of the state. If they have come after cake bakers and photographers for not supporting homosexual wedding ceremonies, the clergy are likely next. I raised five boys who fear God and thus honor their father and their mother. I have no doubt that they will take care of their mother and sister if I am persecuted, incarcerated. I am ready to fight. I truly am. And I realize that as I raise my voice in descent, I may cause some of you, parishioners of St. Stephen's, to be uncomfortable. You may have some sympathy for the issue of homosexual marriage. You may not like that your pastor takes a stand against the spirit of this age in regards to this issue. You may become tired of me speaking against people that you like, that you care about, even respect. I understand that that may happen, but you need to know that I fear standing before God and having to give an account for my silence. During an age that celebrates sin, I fear that more than I fear looking out at empty pews. If you are uncomfortable with the proclamations I make against the morality of our time, I only ask That you give me your ear and hear my arguments and judge them against the opposing views and judge for yourself who is speaking the truth. Well first, I want to be grateful for our denomination, both for the REC and the ACNA. The REC has clear definitive statements about what constitutes marriage and what does not Archbishop Foley and the ACNA bishops gave a statement immediately after the Supreme Court ruling that was a message of dissent. Warning and faith in God's sovereignty. It is a great comfort to know that we are not alone in our descent And to know that we have ordained leaders of the church who are courageous. Grateful to God for that. But their leadership will only be effective if we lead in South Carroll County. We need to stand firm on our own. We are responsible for our little corner of the world. Second, I need to speak prophetically in regards to what this ruling means for the future. The downgrade of our culture toward becoming godliness tipped in the 1960s with the embracing of the sexual revolution. The degree of that downgrade increased dramatically in 1973 when the Supreme Court here they are again Ruled that the mother's womb was no longer a safe place. The domino effect of that decision Continues today. We are a culture that gives birth to monsters who kill people at prayer meetings. who sell their children for drugs, who abuse the handicapped and the elderly because human life is not cherished, and the commandment thou shalt not kill has no authority. The degree of the downgrade of our culture as a result of the Supreme Court ruling regarding homosexual marriage has once again increased to a near 90 degrees. And note the lie that my prophetic words confront. It is the lie that this ruling will not affect the average person. You might say or heard it said, doesn't affect me. The reality is it will affect all of us. Our society is already greatly troubled because of the breakdown of the home, primarily because fathers are absent and thus too many children are raised in single-parent homes. Statistics clearly show that children are more healthy and happy when raised with a father and a mother. The Supreme Court ruling accepting homosexual marriage is another blow to the home because it further erodes the traditional family, a father and a mother. A most obvious argument, obvious, against homosexual unions that should be readily accepted. Is that such a practice does not need Christian revelation for a person to see how destructive such unions are Natural law reveals that for societies to thrive, for the human species to continue. The bedrock of such societies and for the human species is heterosexual unions. Human society since the creation of man have understood the necessity of upholding the sanctity of heterosexual unions. Even cultures that homosexual apologists uphold as accepting of homosexuality, such as the ancient Greek culture Such a culture never condoned homosexual marriage or unions. And they may have looked the other way, away from homosexual acts, but they always defended and upheld heterosexual homes. Important and necessary for the health and prosperity of a society. It's so obvious. Evidently not. Because of the Supreme Court ruling, no longer are we as society going to be able to identify what is a family. No longer are we going to be able to provide what is best for our children, the children born in this nation. The fundamental understanding of what makes up a home has been dismantled. Confused. And so what has been a bed-off for every every civilization of mankind is no more in these United States. Prophetically, we can know what the future holds, not by special words from God, but by common sense. Common sense he provides for us. Now this ruling by the Supreme Court is going to challenge our religious freedom. I have already mentioned how it has challenged small businesses, how I anticipate it's going to challenge pastors to perform homosexual marriages. As it is now in Canada. And we can also anticipate how it will challenge any religious institution who hires employees Gives housing to students, provides benefits for employees, gives financial assistance to the needy, chooses couples for adoption, and other provisions and outreach ministries. For one example, let us imagine a small Christian college that provides married student housing for its married students. The housing is low cost as an encouragement for young couples to avoid sexual temptation and instead be married. It is low cost to encourage young married couples to continue their college education. It is a ministry to young married couples. But that college accepts government loans for its students to attend. And because they accept government loans, the government believes it can have a say on how the college is run And the government becomes aware that a homosexual couple who is married in the eyes of the state and federal government has been turned down by said college to receive a place in married student housing. Because of this Obergfell v. Hodges case, that Christian college doesn't have a law to stand on. Third, Christians need to be willing to accept derogatory titles given to us as we take a stand against homosexual marriage. Jesus warned, we heard it this morning, Jesus warned his disciples that the world that hated him would hate those who follow him. It shouldn't be a news flash that the world hates Christians. It always has. Oh, it may personally like you, because you're nice. But when you profess Jesus as your Lord and Savior It reminds the godless that you believe in moral absolutes. It reminds the godless that you believe in a heaven and a hell. It reminds the godless that people who believe in Jesus as their Lord and Savior are to receive a heavenly reward, and those who cling to their sin Their sexual sin, they will receive hell as their eternal punishment. That offends That causes people to call to call Christians prejudiced, mean, and hateful. The accusation of being hateful is the primary derogatory title given to Christians who stand against homosexual marriage. The hateful label appears to be the trump card argument against or for the godless. Once a person is identified as hateful, then everything he or she has to say can then be dismissed. But we are to fear God and not men. We are to fear the one who can throw both our bodies and souls into hell. The labels of men should not, cannot, and must not detour us from the road we are on or dissuade us from the moral stands that we take. Let them call us haters. That the goddess would label Christians hateful reveals where their arguments rest. Their argument rests in their emotions. Even in Justice Kennedy's remarks on behalf of the majority, there is an emotive plea when Kennedy states That it diminishes a homosexual's personhood to deny him or her the right to marry. But he fails to decide how it diminishes personhood. He does not explain himself because to him and the rest of society the emotion is obvious You're hurting them. Last year I listened to a public debate between a Christian minister and a college professor on the subject of homosexual marriage. The debate was good-spirited and the Christian minister was getting in some pretty good points until the college professor shared his own story about loving his homosexual partner. He challenged the Christian minister to state that the love he and his homosexual partner shared wasn't real. Well, as soon as the college professor used an emotional argument, the debate was won I don't mean to say that the college professor won because he was right, of course not. But the audience went his direction because they were emotionally moved that this man had a love for someone else. Time and time again, Christians are emotionally moved to side with the homosexual agenda because someone they love, someone they care about, claims to be a homosexual. And we think that if we're going to love them, we have to side with them Christians too often fall into stories where people talk about they just want to be happy, as if that's the most important thing. Emotions are not where Christians are to take their stand. We know that, but you need to hear it. Christians are to take their stand on the Word, the Word of God. And that Word of God became flesh and dwelt among us. We are to take our stand on Jesus, and Jesus fulfilled the law. And we are to be doers of the moral law of God. And God's law says That it is an abomination for a man to lie with a man and for a woman to lie with a woman Where emotions contribute. Where emotions contribute is that we are to love that a man wants to be loved, and we are to emotionally love by telling a man that wants to be loved That Jesus is the only one that can fulfill that voice that you have. And Jesus' love is sufficient for you. That you don't need the love of another man. True love, God's love, tells the truth, knowing that the truth of Jesus, that's what sets a person free. This third point can be summed up by saying that Christians need to be willing and prepared to be legally and socially persecuted for standing against homosexual acts and homosexual marriage. Fourth. Fourth, it is finally time that we stop fooling ourselves about how the world has influenced the Christian church away from biblical morality. Christian parents need to be diligent at counteracting the sexual propaganda that is being taught in public schools and private secular schools. I highly recommend parents not send their kids to public schools. No place is the homosexual agenda being taught without a filter more than the public schools. Most of my children attend or have attended a secular private school where they heard the same agenda. We have been diligent parents by asking and talking with our children about what they have heard and how they are understanding it all in light of what we have taught them. If you send your children to public schools, you must, must be diligent in counteracting what they are being taught about sexual orientation. When St. Paul instructs Christians to keep every thought in captivity, every thought in captivity, no place do such words apply more than what our children are being taught about sexuality. It is time for us to audit what our schools are teaching, to audit what each family member is listening to in music, watching, and reading for entertainment. Don't be fooled, dear Christian, by a good joke or a sentimental story that upholds a sexual agenda that goes directly against your Christian faith. Bringing every thought into captivity means every thought Finally, we must acknowledge before God that the sins of our nation are our sins. Like Isaiah, we must confess that we as individuals have unclean lips, and we live amidst the people of unclean lips. Our nation was founded on God-fearing principles, and yet from the beginning we were a people of unclean lips. The sin of slavery continues to haunt us, and such a sin cannot be atoned for by getting rid of a flag or renaming a road. And that sin of slavery is doubled by the sin of abortion, which continually places us under God's judgment. And now we have the spin of sanctioned scholarly to add to the pile. These are not the sins of others only, as they are ours as well, for we are members of a nation that sanctioned all of these sins. The only atonement possible is by the blood of Jesus. And we as the church are responsible to tell our neighbors that truth. If you are tempted to critique my words this morning by pointing out that there weren't any words of love, I challenge you. Words of love can be words that are a loud warning. I critique your thoughts by countering that silence is an act of condoning, and condoning sin is practicing unrighteous hate. For it is allowing another person to go to his or her demise without any warning from you. So what are we to do now? What's our next move? Well We need to be better examples of what true marriage is. We need to work harder at being better husbands and better wives and better parents So that the world can know that we are Christian. We need to be better churchmen by loving one another as Jesus taught us. We need to stop being petty and forgive one another. We need to focus on what is essential for being the church Jesus died for instead of infighting about nothing that has to do with the gospel. And we need to take a stand. We need to be willing to be persecuted for the stands that we take. I am willing, and I am calling you to join me in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.

sermons.title: Proverbs: Pride vs. Humility
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost, Amen. May be seated. Before I dive into the sermon proper, I feel like I need to make a comment, um, clarification. Some of you see me rebuking a little child down here, you're probably wondering, what's the problem with that guy? Um that's my grandson, and I'm actually getting a kick out of him. I'm not really Rebuking him. I believe wholeheartedly that it is better, as they say, to have a crying or babbling child in the service than a snoring old man. So uh prefer the child. When a person takes a moral stand against a particular sin, a sin that is being paraded around as good and just It is ironic that the person taking the moral stand is tempted by another sin. That is similar to the sin that he is standing against. Last week We agreed to words of determination that we would not be moved off of our stand against homosexual marriage. Those who want to destroy our culture and eventually this country, and want to silence the Christian Church They can try to redefine marriage, but it won't stick, and true, true Christians will always defy them The idea of homosexual marriage reminds me of an old parable. A man in a small town bought himself a pig for a pet. When he walked his pet pig down Main Street on a leash, people would stop and comment about the man's pig. And the man would persistently interrupt the passerbys, telling them that his pet was not a pig, but a dog. As days passed and the man with his pet pig kept calling his pig a dog, it eventually caught on. And the people from the small town also started to call his pig a dog, not only in front of the owner of this pet pig, but to one another when they would refer to the pig as a dog. The lesson of the parable is that it doesn't matter that everyone calls the pet pig a dog because the pig remains a pig. The same is true for homosexual marriage. People can call it marriage if they so wish. And everyone, including the Supreme Court of these United States, can call it marriage, but it remains a perversion and not marriage Now in saying that, there is a temptation to sin that comes into my heart. I just gave A logically sound argument, and that puts the opposition in their place And as I stand here with my personal bravado and tell you where I'm going to take a stand against the spirit of this age and Encourage you to take that same stand against the spirit of this age. There is a temptation to embrace another sin. And that sin is the sin of pride, pride And consider this irony. I recently read an argument that at the heart of the homosexual lifestyle is the sin of pride. It is prideful to look at God and to say, I know what your word says regarding a man lying with another man, and I know what your word says regarding. a marriage being between only a man and a woman, but I choose to define such things by my terms That indeed is pride. But that also means, and here is the irony, it also means that the sin of a homosexual is my sin. It's my sin as wealth, for when I am arrogant, when I am taking my moral stance, and I embrace the fact that I am standing hard, and I embrace the fact that I'm brave. I'm actually having the same sin of pride as the one that I am rejecting. Ironic indeed Now I refer to the sin of pride in terms of personal pride, which is pride in self. There is a pride. There is a pride that is good, is holy. We can have pride in our loved ones when they are practicing their God-given gifts. We can have pride in our God, in our faith, in our Christian church. That is pride in others. It is pride in self that is sinful. And by pride in self I mean a pride that understands self to be better than others. It is the pride that evaluates self as worthy of the praise of other people It seems necessary to admit that being prideful because I am taking a stand against the idea of homosexual marriage, that's rather foolish Because I am taking a stand in front of people who, as far as I can tell, agree with me. There's nothing courageous about that. It is also foolish to embrace personal pride because of taking a moral stand, because it is the power of the Holy Spirit that enables us to be courageous. St. Paul said that the Holy Spirit gives us power or courage as opposed to timidity. We did not receive a spirit of timidity, but of power. And so any stand that you and I take is by the courage, the strength of the Holy Spirit. Certainly nothing personal to brag about there. But regardless of how foolish personal pride can be, it is very provocative as a sin. It is easy to pick up, even subconsciously pick it up. Because the sin is so easy to pick up, the book of Proverbs, which we are studying Provides many warnings and much wisdom on staying away from personal pride. Consider this proverb from 16, verse 19. Better to be of a humble spirit with the lowly than to divide the spoil with the proud. First, this proverb provides a contrast between pride and humility. The Hebrew definition of humble is abase, to be down, to bring low. It is how people can feel about themselves. People feel abase or low about themselves, and when they do, they carry a certain countenance, a down countenance. You can see the loneless in their personal in a person's face. And if you have the heart of Jesus, you see that loneliness and you feel for them. You want to lift them up Then you realize when you are at that position, that loneliness, there are few, if any, worse emotions to feel The word pride in the Hebrew means to rise, to be majestic, even glorious. It is then to think of yourself in a manner that is only given to God. And so humility and pride are far from one another. The second thing we learn from this proverb is that the company we keep will affect whether we are humble or prideful.
