sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. The story of Hansel and Gretel As first told by Brothers Grimm, is an awful, awful tale Consists of a mother who in the story is named woman because she does not have the heart of a mother. The woman, when she realizes the famine has caused there to be almost no food in the home. She forces her husband to send the children out into the forest so that they will be lost and the remaining provisions would be kept by the parents to keep them alive. The father is a weak man. For although he loves the children, he does not stand up to the woman. But Hansel is aware of the woman's plot. So as he leaves to the woods, he leaves a trail of pebbles behind. As they are taken into the woods to find their way back home. And it works. They do find their way back home. Well the next time a famine hits, the same events occur, only this time Hanselk must leave a trail of breadcrumbs behind, and those end up being eaten. So they cannot find their way back home and are literally starving in the forest. As they are searching around for a few days, they find a gingerbread. house. And it just so happens that there is a witch inside the house, and the witch wants to eat the children. The witch tries to fatten up Hansel while locking him in a shed, and in the meantime, Gretel To her credit, has some quick thinking and shoves the witch into the stove so that she is burned to death. When the children finally make it back home, they find their father who is joyous, and they find that their, well, the woman is dead. After reading the original story this past week, I wondered how any child would be able to go to sleep. If that were their bedtime story, it is some nasty stuff. But I want us to zero in this morning on following. Following. Hansel and Gretel needed to have a trail to follow to get them back home. And their trail needed to be of rock. Nothing else was dependable enough. Consider that we are following something or someone always. All of us are following whether we like to admit it or not. Just like we are created to worship, so are we created to follow. In fact, what we follow is usually what we worship. It can be something Silly as a sports team that we allow to give us emotional highs and emotional lows Could be a politician that we find ourselves agreeing with on practically everything they say, and so we start to see them as some sort of political savior. It may be an entertainer that we must see when she has a movie that is coming out, or we must read about when the tabloids follow her around. It may be a moral movement that we follow, believing that what is being fought against is so very important it becomes a priority in our lives And therefore we devote our time and our money, our resources to fight the cause. It may be material wealth that we follow. We may want a bigger house, more prestigious job, nicer clothing, nicer cars, and so we follow after it, believing that if we catch it, catch it all, we will be satisfied. I wonder if you can identify what you personally are following today. What we follow is what we put our trust into. Hansel put his trust in those rocks to lead him home. And it worked. He put his trust in crumbs, and it failed him. And so it is with us. There are things that we follow and thus things that we trust that will lead us home. And other things that will fail us if we follow them. And this sermon is going to take a large chunk of scripture passages at one time and thus make for a big task. But the central theme of following is so very strong at the end of chapter one in John's Gospel that we must look at all of them in one sitting. Turn with me then in your Bibles to John chapter 1. And we are going to be looking at the first section, or first big chunk, is verse 14 through 34. Verse fourteen through thirty-four, John's Gospel, chapter one In these verses, we learn that John the Baptist followed Jesus without knowing Jesus was the Messiah. But first we learn that John the Apostle followed Jesus and thus was able to testify that Jesus was the word made flesh. He was able to know that Jesus was made flesh because John and the other apostles beheld his glory. The phrase we beheld is to mark a definite moment that is assured. It is very important this we beheld, for it places John as a historical eyewitness. This is not what someone told John. This is what he was an eyewitness to. His glory is his manifestation. His manifestation of God's very presence and power at work. His glory. And then the good news. Here the good news. Jesus was full of grace and truth. Grace and truth. The grace and truth is what will be unfolded throughout this gospel. And next, we are reintroduced to John the Baptist John the Baptist's own words regarding his call in life, we understand that he was a follower of Jesus without knowing he was a follower of Jesus. He knew that it was the Messiah he was preceding, and so the one he was following was was greater than him Which is to say, greater in position in the universe and greater in his call to serve God. The knowledge that John has about who he is following without personally knowing who he is following, and isn't that curious because Jesus was his cousin? But he doesn't know if Jesus is the Messiah, the marked one yet. John knows that what he follows is grace for grace. Look at that at the end of verse 16 in the New King James, grace for grace. What a glorious expression is that. Grace for grace. We too follow grace for grace. We too follow Jesus, who is grace, for grace. As he offers grace, unmerited forgiveness for all of our sins. Amen and amen. The exchange that John has, John the Baptist has with the priests and Levites about his identity. Reveals what it means to follow Jesus. Notice how the priests and the Levites want to pigeonhole John. They they were literalists who were looking for the historic Elijah to precede the Messiah. Not a man who is like Elijah or Not a man who has the same Holy Spirit as Elijah, but Elijah himself. They wanted God to do what they wanted God to do, not what God wanted to do. But John the Baptist, he was different. John the Baptist deferred to Jesus. And that is what it is to follow Jesus, to defer to Jesus. Those who follow Jesus are to defer. When John is asked who he is, he starts with who he is not. He is not the Christ. He is not the Messiah And that is John's focus. It is about who the Messiah is, not who he is. And so it is to be for all who follow Jesus. It is to be about who the Messiah is, not who I am. When next John is asked straightforward who he is, his answer is what he is called to do. He was the voice of the one crying out in the wilderness. Make straight the way of the Lord. His identity then is the call that he had. What God called him to be, which was that voice that prepared for the coming Messiah, Jesus. When John the Baptist is asked about who he is compared to Christ or compared to Elijah or the prophet, which might be Moses, might be Jeremiah, we don't really know. John the Baptist again points not to himself, but to the man who was coming. A man that John does not deem himself worthy enough to do the task of a servant, which is to untie the master's sandals. To bolster the point that John is following Jesus without knowing Jesus, John says, who is coming after me is preferred before me. Following Jesus is to defer and then prefer. We are to defer priority in our lives to Jesus. We are to defer any praise we would receive by men to Jesus. We are to defer our wills to God's will. And we are to prefer the teachings of Jesus. His truths, his ways, prefer them against our own The Christian life, a life of following Jesus, is a life that demands a great deal, a great deal of us. With an insurmountable amount of benefits that follow. We are asked to give up much, and yet we are promised so very much more, the Christian life. Now I want us to note that in John telling us this story of the interaction between John the Baptist and Jesus, he does not mention, notice here, Jesus being baptized. But rather assuming the reader understood as much from likely the other gospels, he instead focuses on what John said about Jesus. John tells his followers that Jesus is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit. And then he says that Jesus is the Lamb of God. For those who had ears to hear, those who knew the scriptures Knew that John the Baptist was saying to his followers, follow Jesus, he's the Messiah. They were to follow Jesus because they needed to be baptized in the Holy Spirit. They were to follow Jesus because they needed the sacrifice that Jesus would make so that their sins could be forgiven. They needed to follow Jesus. We need to follow Jesus. This next section we look at. Is a series of quick stories about those who choose to follow Jesus The first two that followed Jesus were first disciples of John the Baptist. That is confirmed in verse 37. We learn then in verse 40 that one of the first two followers of Jesus was Andrew. What we see from the first instance of following is that followers in Jesus respect Jesus. By calling him Rabbi. Andrew calls Jesus Rabbi. That is accepting him as a teacher. They want to learn from him. Followers of Jesus want to learn from him. They are committed to following his teachings. Now mentioning that following Jesus includes respecting Jesus might seem unnecessary. But I put forth to you today that Christians today could do a better job at respecting Jesus. When we hear his name abused, lies told about him, if we respect him, I believe we should say something. Consider that if you or I heard the name of a loved one being misused, abused, lies told about him or her. We would most certainly speak against it, and maybe it might even come to blows. So why not have the same emotions when people speak so poorly about our Savior? I know that Jesus could handle himself. But it is time, I believe, that we need to stop apologizing for loving our Savior. Amen? Respecting Jesus also includes living as a Christian should live. By calling ourselves Christians, we need to respect That we have the name of Christ as we walk this life. We carry the Messiah's name. As Christians, we love and support the Savior's church. As Christians, we pray faithfully. As Christians, we love our spouses, honor our parents, love our neighbors Repent when we sin, seek reconciliation when relationships are broken, and we love one another. Well, next we see that to follow Jesus we need to tell somebody. Andrew told his brother Peter right away. Have you told someone lately that you are a Christian? That you have found the Messiah? Ask God whom you should tell, and then tell them, just as Andrew did. Next, we see that to follow Jesus is to be given a new purpose in life, a new meaning for our lives. Jesus renamed Simon Cephas or Peter, which means little rock. Jesus is the big rock and Peter is the little rock, who will remind people of Jesus when Jesus is gone. Peter did that. He was a preacher of the gospel and a man who was hung on a cross upside down because he accepted the role of being a little rock. What role or meaning in life is Jesus calling you to fulfill? Whatever it is, pick up your cross and fill it. And next we learn that to follow Jesus, you have to have a sense of humor. Jesus found Philip and said, follow me. Philip went and found Nathanael and told him to follow the one whom Moses wrote about. Nathanael understands Jesus to be from Nazareth and remarks sarcastically, can anything good come out of Nazareth? It's kind of like saying, can anything good come out of Dundalk? You've heard me say that before. And we know that Nazareth was an unimportant place religiously. Most thought the Messiah was going to be coming from Bethlehem. There might have been more insights to Nathaniel's comment that those first century folks would have picked up on, but we we cannot. But sarcasm, humor, double takes on words are very healthy To understand the gospel. Because the gospel has a great deal of jaw-dropping realities that are humorous, allowing us to envision our God smiling. Next, we learn that to follow Jesus is to have everything about you known, and to know everything about you is known. In Matthew's Gospel, you remember the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus tells his disciples that the Father even numbers every hair upon our heads. That is told to us so that we understand how detailed God knows us. And that is to comfort us regarding how much God cares for us to the minor details And finally, from this chapter, we learn that to follow Jesus is to be a witness to remarkable truth. A witness to remarkable truth. Nathan was amazed that Jesus would have been able to see him under a tree even before they met. That is indeed a remarkable feat. But Jesus says there is much more that he will see. Seeing the heavens open. That's either in the literal sense, which happened at Jesus' baptism, you remember. Or it might have been the mystical sense, that there should be a clearer manifestation of heavenly truths revealed in Jesus' words and in his actions. It might be that Jesus himself is heaven open to mankind. While Christians continue to debate about the cessation of spiritual gifts, I am thankful that our denomination has come to no such conclusion. Our denomination leaves it open. Let God perform miracles as He wills. But Jesus wasn't talking about seeing miracles in his phraseology. He's not talking about physical healings or bread multiplying. He was talking about seeing him as the Messiah. Seeing him as the Messiah. Thus, we can say that followers of Jesus see Jesus. See Jesus. We see Jesus And because we see Jesus, we see everything else. We see Jesus in our lives, working, teaching, guiding. We see Jesus in our families as we love them, and He loves them, cares for them, sanctifies them. We see Jesus in our brothers and sisters in Christ. This is why we are to love one another. Love one another through our problems in getting along together The first pastor that hired me to work in the church full-time to minister to youth, he was a simple preacher, nice guy. He used to say on a regular basis, you gotta love me if you're gonna get to heaven. And I first thought he was being a bit flippant. But in retrospect, he was quite right. We have to love one another to get to heaven. And so finally, we need to see Jesus in our fellow man. Followers of Jesus, see Jesus in their fellow man. And that is easier, of course. In some than it is opposed to others. But the lesson Jesus teaches us when he talks about the difference between the sheep and the goats, remember from Matthew 25? The difference is how the sheep care for their fellow man. And as they care for their fellow man, they care for Jesus. And one last point to make about following Jesus, as described here by John, there is no mentions of hesitation. Nobody hesitates. John the Baptist didn't hesitate for following Jesus was what he was conceived to do. And he didn't hesitate decreasing his existence while Jesus increased. Andrew didn't hesitate. John the Baptist told him that Jesus was the Messiah, and so without hesitation, he followed him. And he didn't hesitate to tell about Jesus. He went right to his brother Peter, telling him the good news. And then Peter didn't hesitate. He believed and followed, not even hesitating to take on a new name. And then Philip didn't hesitate. And then Nathaniel didn't hesitate. They knew he was the Messiah. Why hesitate? They knew in their hearts, just as you and I know. And thus we need not hesitate. To follow Jesus is to defer ourself to the other. To follow Jesus is to prefer the Son of God, the Father. To follow Jesus is to respect his truth. To follow Jesus is to share the good news. To follow Jesus is to receive purpose leading to a hereafter. To follow Jesus is to enjoy good laughter. To follow Jesus is to be known by the one who truly knows. To follow Jesus is to see him wherever one goes. To follow Jesus is to respond without hesitation. To follow Jesus is to live out revelation. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Why A Wedding and Wine?
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We are in the John chapter 2, the gospel according to St. John chapter 2, our gospel reading this morning. One might ask Why this story is told? Why do we need to read about Jesus turning water into wine? The answer to that is threefold at least. The first twofolds are Number one, the miracle was for the disciples of Jesus to more firmly and deeply believe in him as the Messiah. That is what verse eleven of chapter two plainly states. The second reason for telling this story Is that it is the first of the seven miracles that John records Remember from our introduction, we noted that John was going about this telling of the gospel much differently than Matthew, Mark, or Luke. John is being emotionally poetic in telling his account And so he only tells seven miracles. For seven is the perfect number, and that number confirms Jesus and his life to be perfect. Many more things John could have written. He explains that in the latter part of his gospel. But he chose only seven. And the first of the seven is this wedding at Cana. The first miracle at a wedding. And the mentioning of a wedding leads us to recognize All of the typologies that are occurring in this story. Read along with me from John chapter 2. We'll read verse 1. On the third day, there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Now, since chapters are were not original to John's writing of the gospel, we can understand the third day to be a reference. To after Nathaniel spoke to Jesus, which we talked about last week, the third day is after Nathaniel spoke to Jesus in chapter 1. The manner that the Jews counted the days, we might have said, well, it was two days later. But we can also see that the mention of it being the third day is not by accident. And of course, John knows what the third day means. For Christians, the third day is always the day of resurrection. And this miracle that's about to be told is the beginning of a new era, a day of new revelation. And so let's identify it as the third day. Verse 2 and 3 together. Now both Jesus and his disciples were invited to the wedding. And when they ran out of wine, the mother of Jesus said to him, They have no wine. It is not illegal to understand that Jesus was related to the wedding party. Family was naturally invited to Jewish weddings. It is also not a leap to understand that his mother Mary was part of the wedding preparations, for she has intimate knowledge of the catering arrangements. And this is all very common, even for us today, as we can imagine a family member putting on a wedding celebration. and catering it themselves while being helped out by other family members who love them and want the whole celebration to go off well. We can imagine ourselves, perhaps we've even been there ourselves. The fact that it was a wedding in which Jesus began his public ministry should not be lost on us. He begins and he consummates his ministry toward mankind with weddings This wedding and everything Jesus does publicly points to that final wedding when Jesus welcomes his church, his bride, into the mansions of glory. That's what we're all looking toward. Now there are a lot of customs going on in the story that we need to be privy to. In Jewish culture in the first century, running out of wine, being unable to provide for the guests that you invited And thus guests that were expecting to be well fed, to run out, was greatly embarrassing. There is even more evidence to suggest that a bridegroom's family could have been sued in certain circumstances for inadequate provisions at a wedding. So this was important. In order to avoid embarrassment, Mary does what any loving family member would do, which is to try to solve the problem. Again, talking about customs, that she approaches Jesus likely tells us that Joseph, her husband, was now deceased. For it would have been more appropriate for her to approach Joseph first before Jesus Mary instead approaches Jesus, her firstborn son, which again, according to custom, was the thing to do, because Jesus, being the firstborn son, would have been the head of Mary's household. In her words to Jesus, Mary says they've run out of wine. Wine. Now let us be clear. Regardless of what Mr. Welsh would have us believe, the word wine meant what it means today. A fermented drink produced from grapes that has the potential to intoxicate There have been teetotalers for a long time who have sought to argue that the word wine in the Bible is only grape juice. I used to dwell in circles that heard men yelling from pulpits that the drinking of wine was a sin. And such men would never accept that Jesus would provide wine to intoxicate, nor that Jesus would ever drink wine that would intoxicate. And such preachers, I will say kindly, are poor in their Greek and even poorer in their history. When in verse 10 the steward speaks of people at such a feast as to have well drunk, as the New King James says He uses the word that refers to inebriation. Now Paul did not say to the Ephesians, do not be drunk on grape juice, as we just heard. Nor did he rebuke those who were abusing the Lord's table for drinking too much grape juice. No, what they ran out of was wine that intoxicates. But in making the point, let it be clear that there is no justification for being intoxicated. Just because wine is provided, there's not requirement for anyone to drink too much of it. That point we made on to verse 4. Jesus said to her, Woman, what does your concern have to do with me? My hour has not yet come. Well, this reply by Jesus to his mother has received all sorts of unnecessary speculations regarding the relationship that Jesus had with Mary. Because of this manner, it seems that he speaks to her. But the title woman, here Woman is not used in the same manner as the brothers Grim use the word in Anselm Gretel that we heard last week The title woman by itself was not a harsh greeting as it might sound, and we simply need to consider that Jesus addressed his mother And with the same words, woman, when he was hanging on the cross and commending her to John, the writer of our gospel, that he might take care of her. He called her there, woman. And because of this, we can hear the term as one of respect or one of affection. But what we can also hear Is that by not calling her mother, his public ministry had begun. And this caused him to put a bit of personal distance from his mother, as he becomes more a man of the people than her son. And we are to make no mistake that his next words, what does your concern have to do with me? That is a measured rebuke. That is a measured rebuke. His mother is his mother. And she could have easily taken advantage of that relationship, and he wants her to know that he knows that, and that there is a definite change that is happening between them. And Jesus next gives his explanation for the rebuke. He says, my hour or my time is not yet come. And this is the first in a series of similar remarks throughout John's Gospel Here he says, my hour is not yet. He says the same thing in chapter seven, verse six. In chapter 8, verse 30, the Jews were not able to seize Jesus. And John explains to the reader, he says, because his hour had not yet come. It is only when the cross is immediately in sight that we hear Jesus say, the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Thus, we are to hear that Jesus is telling his mother that the time for him to be revealed so that men might believe or deny him. is not upon them, and she was not to hurry it along. Verse 5. His mother said to the servants, Whatever he says to you, do it. Interestingly, that is similar language to when the famine struck in Egypt. And Pharaoh, having Joseph at his right hand, told the Egyptians, Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you. Same language. For Mary, it is a statement of faith in her son. And we will see this interaction pattern happen again in other places of the gospel. Here we have Jesus At first refusing a request, and then proceeding to help in a manner that is more fitting to God's timing, not man's. Verse six. Now there were set there six water pots of stone, according to the manner of purification of the Jews, containing twenty or or thirty gallons apiece. Now the number six can be understood to be parallel to the six days of creation, when God made and then filled. Remember the first three days God creates, and then the next three He fills with that which He creates for those days. We've been studying this on Wednesday, Wednesday study. So pots are made, but not filled. And the purpose of them we know to be part of the Jewish custom of ceremonial washing, to present themselves as pure before God and before men. These washings we learned from Jesus went beyond what the law required. Verse 7 and 8 Jesus said to them, Fill the water pots with water, and they filled them up to the brim. And he said to them, Draw some out now, and take it to the master of the feast. And they took it Now this is all very natural. Servants are told what to do, and they do it. No questions asked, it was not their place. Verse nine. When the master of the feast had tasted the water that was made wine, and did not know where it came from, but the servants who had drawn the water knew, the master of the feast called the bridegroom. And we realize that John does not tell us how this miracle occurred. He doesn't tell us when the water was turned into wine. He simply mentions it. And we are not told precisely how much, we're to assume that it was all of the water pots To realize that this is a substantial gift. Jesus is giving this wedding party a substantial gift. Verse 10. And he said to him, Every man at the beginning sets out the good wine, and when the guests have well drunk, then the inferior. You have kept the good wine until now. Well the logic here is evident. The host starts off with better quality wine. And when faces are happy and voices are raised, the lesser quality wine is introduced, the less expensive wine is passed around because the taste buds are not as sharp anymore. But Jesus does not go cheap. Jesus does not do a miracle halfway. Jesus did not turn water into box wine. Jesus gave the best, for he is the best given. Verse eleven This beginning of signs Jesus did in Cana of Galilee and manifested his glory and his disciples believed in him. Well, the mention of the miracle having been done in Cana of Galilee is to put a frame around this story, the beginning and the end. John said that he along with the other apostles beheld the glory of Jesus. And now he has just finished giving us an example of what he meant. Jesus manifested his glory here, John says. Now for unbelieving years This story of the first miracle could easily be dismissed as a sleight-of-hand trick. It could be dismissed as a magician's trick. Just like pouring the milk into a rolled up newspaper, only having the milk leave no wet mark. So too seemingly can a magician have an audience first see water and then see wine But Jesus did more than perform a trick. Jesus gave. And in giving revealed his true identity, who he really was. Jesus manifested his glory by turning water into wine in, I believe, at least three ways, and here they are. The first way that Jesus is revealing his glory is most obvious. Jesus marked his public ministry by increasing the celebration. Increasing the celebration. And the revelation that God became man and was now dwelling among mankind and had started speaking words of eternal life, that is something to celebrate indeed. Perhaps it cannot be emphasized enough that drunkenness is a sin. It always has been. Drunks are fools. They do foolish things and therefore reveal their sinful hearts. But drinking wine to make the heart glad is not automatically equal to drunkenness Consider Psalm 104. Wine gladdens the human heart. And from Ecclesiastes, go eat your food with gladness and drink your wine with a joyful heart. For God has already approved what you do. You know, one of the goals of our annual winter ball is to demonstrate to our young generation That Christians can celebrate responsibly. And as it has been said from this pulpit before, Christians of all people should know how to celebrate. Amen? For Christians have the best reasons to celebrate and the freest of spirits to celebrate. The people who attended that wedding in Cana were celebrating much more than they knew. And Jesus wanted them to celebrate. The second way Jesus manifested his glory by turning water into wine. was by marking the beginning of the new covenant. Marking the beginning of the new covenant. This is as contrasted to how Moses marked the old covenant Consider when the plague of blood struck Egypt by Aaron holding Moses' rod over the Nile. All water, including drinking water, turned to blood Such was fitting, for under the old covenant, that blood was repeatedly being spilled to atone for the sins of God's people. But the new covenant only needs one blood offering, and that is the blood of Jesus. And so, what represents that blood is wine. For wine makes the heart of men glad, and is a type of what the blood of Jesus does for the heart of every person who calls upon the name that will save them. Wine is also imagery used in the Old Testament to describe a messianic age. Consider these passages. Jacob from Genesis 49, 11, pronouncing upon Judah what will happen to him and his seed. Judah's royal descendants, Jacob said, would bring in an age in which wine was so abundant that they could wash their clothes in it. Amos speaks of the great day of salvation as the day when new wine will drip from the mountains and flow from all the hills. Jeremiah the prophet looks forward to a day when, quote, they will come and shout for joy on the heights of Zion. They will rejoice in the bounty of the Lord, the grain, the new wine, and the oil. The days of the wedding at Cana were days that were described by the prophets here And the third and final way to see the glory of Jesus manifested in this miracle is actually related to the first in terms of celebration. Jesus with the gift of wine shows us, shows us how to look forward to heaven. How to look forward to heaven. The gift of wine is a glimpse of heaven. Now, full disclosure time here. I am not a wine expert I have attended wine-tasting venues. I have spoken to Somaliers. I have tasted high-tier wine, expensive wine. And I get that there is a difference between highly regarded vintages and, say, the Sutter Home brand, but a love for wine I do not have People with more sophisticated palates love wine. They love swirling it around in their glass, smelling it Tasting a little bit and talking about what might be in it. Those type of people are above me. They appreciate the beauty of it. They enjoy it. Jesus is giving something that people can enjoy. A taste, a bit, just a taste of that which we will enjoy forever. Whether people appreciate it or not, God gives us moments, just moments Of heaven. Just little tastes of those things that we will look forward to to share for eternity. I vividly remember riding a lift chair to the top of Crystal Mountain, which sits on the end of the Cascade Mountains in the state of Washington. And I remember riding that chair on a beautiful blue and sunny day, and coming over a ridge, and there standing in all its glory, 15,000 feet of Mount Rainier Majestic. With a blue, bright sky behind it. It was the most glorious thing I had ever seen on this earth. That is a heaven moment. I remember, although not vividly enough, the first time I tasted a Ruth Crisp Steakhouse steak. I knew at that moment that what I was was served was how steaks should be cooked. But I get a lot of amens on that one. And I also concluded that this must be what steaks taste like in heaven. Although there's no animals in heaven, right? So never never mind, we'll not go there. There have been times In our home living room, when Bobby Lynn and I have sat with all the children, talking freely, laughing freely, enjoying the conversation so very much. That I imagine heaven must bring such joy, more such joy. I've had more times than I can count when I look at my beloved's eyes. See that she loves me and I love her and it literally touches my soul. That most certainly is a heavenly moment Jesus gives those to us. And we need to count them more, don't we? He gave them to a wedding party in Canaan. And he gives them to us. Jesus gives our heavenly hope. Let us pray

sermons.title: Strengthening our wrists
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I very much encourage you to grab a Bible and to follow along with me this morning. Help keep you awake. We are in John chapter 2, beginning at verse 13. We're going to be walking through our approach to the gospel text this morning is twofold. Comments will be made on the text that I referred to, and then we will find application that the Holy Spirit has for us this morning. This is from the gospel reading starting at verse 13. We find the feast of the Passover. was kept on the 14th day of Nisan in commemoration of the Lord passing over the houses of the Israelites when God slew the firstborn in Egypt This is called the Jews Passover. The date corresponding with our calendar would have been this past year, April 3rd. For Christians, we know the Passover is satisfied by Jesus. He is now our Passover. Now the second Passover that's mentioned in this gospel is thought to be the feast of which is found in John chapter 5, verse 1. And then the third mention is John chapter 6, verse 4, and then the last being the suffering of our Lord, John chapter 18. It is interesting because John is the only writer that refers to these three Passovers, or four, excuse me, and it seems to be to tell us just how long our Savior served, we roughly estimate three and a half years. Of course the Passover tells us that Jesus did all that the law required. He came to fulfill all righteousness, and therefore he strictly obeyed all the ceremonial laws and, of course, all of the moral laws. Verse 14. The place in the temple Jesus first comes to is not the holy place. It is not the court of the priests where the sacrifices were offered. It is not the court of the women, nor the court of the Israelites, where the chosen people of God worshiped, but the court is of the Gentiles. This is where all the strangers might come. And the Passover now being at hand, there were sold there oxen and sheep and doves, changers of money, changing that which is Roman currency into Jewish coin. Verse 15. The scourge used by Jesus might have been the thongs cut out of hides of beasts slain in the sacrifice. Or the cores which the owners of the sacrifices use to bring these cattle to their place. The scourge seems to be made and used not so much as a force of terror, but to symbolize that these persons are violators of the holy place and thus deserved a scourge from the divine And this also shows Jesus' miraculous power. This is Christ driving out a number of men with such a small and insignificant weapon. Verse 16. We find there in verse 16 the phrase, my father's house. How close this is, right here, his words to when he was just a boy. Luke chapter 2, where he is in his father's house, seated amongst God's people, for sacred worship The temple, of course, was the symbol of God's presence on earth. And it dictated how men are to approach him. Of course, when Jesus was a youth, he was simply a son in his own father's house. And now in this moment, he is a son who rules over his father's house. He is the proper representation. He is the flesh. He is the heir of his father's rights, his father's rights to his house. Well note, please, that the house of merchandise that he mentions does not condemn buying and selling. The problem was it was brought to a place of worship. It was there for their convenience into a most sacred and holy place. It was so high-handedly profane, Jesus could not endure it. Verse 17. Here is one of many verses that his disciples come to realize that this man is the fulfillment of all the prophets. Whether it be afterwards or in the moment, they understood Jesus to be the fulfillment of the Messiah. Verse 18 What is here being argued by his opponents is either Jesus did these things of himself, that is, by his own authority. Giving him no claim, his actions would be unjustified, or he had to show them proof of his authority, either in writing, a fulfillment of the scriptures, or in the miraculous. They were ready to dismiss him, dismiss his zeal, especially a zeal they did not have, in order to keep their pride, to keep their self-righteousness. Verse 19. The manner Jesus speaks here is enigmatic, hidden. Those who had ears to hear would know what he was talking about, or at least later they would know what he was talking about. He was talking about, of course, his body. He is the temple of God. God is in him. Yet only the chosen knew it to be true. Verse 21 through 22. John here is making it clear to the reader what Jesus was talking about. It appears That no one fully understood what Jesus had said until after the resurrection, and thus after the greatest proof that his body was indeed holding the very presence of God Verse 23. This verse may slip by us if we're not careful. John mentions miracles Jesus did, but does not tell us all that Jesus did. Remember, John is purposefully telling us only part of the story. As for the miracles We know that the Jews looked for them to be fulfilled. What the Messiah was to do, everyone knew. Give sight to the blind, cause the deaf to hear, the dumb to speak, the lame to walk. And such miracles were expected of the Jews who were looking for the Messiah. And Jesus fulfilled them, just not here. Now verses 24 and 25 I want us to read together, so I will read this to you But Jesus did not commit himself to them because he knew all men And had no need that anyone should testify of man, for he knew what was in man. To say that Jesus did not commit himself to the people is to say that he did not want to reveal more of his nature to them. He was holding back. Then he tells us why, John tells us why. To say that he knew all men is the same thing as saying he knew what was in man. And that is to say, he knew the weaknesses of the spirit of humanity. We can say that Jesus had no faith in their faith. Jesus had no faith in their faith. Now to say that last statement is not easy. It is not easy to say that Jesus had no faith in their faith. Because not so many people like to hear it. Not many people like to hear or even consider that Jesus might not have faith in their faith. In our present culture, in this present day, people do not flock to hear a preacher say to them that Jesus has no faith in their faith. No. Instead, people by the thousands, literally by the thousands, attend churches even this morning. Where they are told only positive things about themselves and positive things about how God feels towards them And by pointing out what Jesus said and what he meant, and then applying it to us today, I risk people being mad at me. It is difficult for all of us not to associate the messenger with the message, especially when the message is bad. But that doesn't happen with the positive message. I suppose you've noticed that in life. You tell something, someone, someone positive, a story or an experience. And that person goes on to tell another person that positive story or experience. And the person secondhand hearing it says, well, where did you hear that? And the person says, I don't know But it is when the bad news comes, they remember who told them, and they associate the bad news with the messenger. And so I can be labeled a bad guy, a downer, a negative preacher, yet it is my concern That there are far too many negative warnings in Holy Scripture, that to ignore them or to candy coat them so that they go down easier, well that's to be disingenuous to the Holy Scriptures and to my own conscience. Let us consider why Jesus did not have faith in their faith. Jesus did not have faith in their faith because he knew that as soon as the wind direction changed Those who said they believed in him as the Messiah would leave him and follow something else. One of the serious repercussions of the sin of Adam, of the fall of mankind away from God. Is the greatly weakened constitutions of individuals. Weakened constitutions. We As fallen human beings who have marred the image of God due to our sin, we give up on things too easily. We quit. We walk away. We walk away from relationships. We walk away from commitments. We even walk away from convictions. And we make excuse after excuse after excuse to justify our quitting. And it is greatly disappointing to say to you that ministers of the gospel are some of the worst offenders at quitting. Another reason Jesus didn't have faith in their faith was because he knows how overly sensitive people are. People were overly sensitive then, and I would argue we are more overly sensitive today Anytime Jesus said something that was hard-hitting, people would stop following him. Or they'd plot to kill him. He said, unless you eat of my flesh and drink of my blood, you cannot meet be my disciple. And they left him. They walked away from him. They didn't understand him. What he said sounded too odd, too difficult to comprehend, maybe even offensive to their palates, so they just left him. They quit Jesus confronted the Pharisees for their hypocrisy in order to give them a chance to repent and be forgiven, and they hated him. Hated him for it. They hated him so much they talked of murdering him. But let's compare. Let's compare. I have heard of people who call themselves Christians leave churches to go to other churches because they were offended. I have heard of people who call themselves Christians stop attending Christian worship altogether because they were offended And these people I'm thinking of were not offended because someone was mean to them, someone was unkind to them. No, they was truly nothing wrong done to them. They left because hard decisions were made by the leadership to stand against sin, and they took it personally and left. People leave because sermons are too harsh, teaching too dogmatic, and because they don't like to hear of such sins as homosexuality or abortion. It's too hard, too difficult. We are offending people outside these doors. We may be disgusted and disheartened by the political correctness that continues in our culture, resulting in a child being sent home from a public school because the little girl girl wore an Air Force badge to honor her father. And the school was not going to have it. No honoring of military there. We hear of reports of policemen not being allowed in restaurants in their full uniform because he's carrying a gun And when we hear it we feel like our culture's lost its way. A Muslim who is following Sharia law really shouldn't be a president before it goes against the constitution and the Political correctness of the mass media malign him, a man who's simply being rational. We can become so Frustrated by the political correctness around us, yet we as Christians are not immune to being overly sensitive. Christian politically correct We can become so sensitive about certain music styles or worship formats or what programs a church should should or should not have or should or should not support, what ministries we should or should not support. Beloved, we play the devil's game when we allow such things to upset us. When we understand why Jesus did not have faith in the people's faith, We can see what type of faith he expects of us. The faith he expects is in contrast to the faith that cannot be trusted. It is a faith that is in a perfect juxtaposition to the faith that cannot be trusted. It is a faith that Jesus had when he turned over those tables. It is a zealous faith. I said that Jesus did not have faith in their faith because it would change with the wind. Well, a zealous faith is the opposite. A zealous faith stays the course, regardless of what the outcome is going to be. A zealous faith is not moved even when the circumstances are not going to be good to the person's liking. A zealous faith is a faith that says, I am Christian, while staring down the barrel of a gun, just like those saints in Oregon. Showing courage to not deny Jesus even when the consequence is going to be their death. The zealous faith stands up against the sanctioning of sodomy, even when it might cost a job, a friend, a family member, or even being labeled homophobic. When I was in college, I joined a group of folks who wanted to picket and advertise gay and lesbian dance. Now I don't know if we were altogether wise in doing so, but by golly we were zealous. We wanted to engage them, and so we did when they came out to argue with us. And I doubt if any of them changed their lives because of those encounters, but I look back and I remember how deeply we felt seeing this advertisement and thinking how many people might be drawn to that which they shouldn't be drawn to And so we felt like we needed to do something. And so we picketed, walking outside. Now I have marched a few times against abortion as well, but it's been too long. And I want to challenge all of us this coming January to clear our schedules and do our best to get down to Washington, D. C. in March for those unborn children that are literally being brutalized in the womb. I said Jesus did not have faith in their faith because mankind is so very sensitive and that we are too easily offended. But note here that Jesus didn't care about the people being offended when it came to the worship of the one true God. The place they were exchanging goods was a place of worship. It was a place that the Gentiles were privileged to stand and to say their prayers and to seek God. No one, not one thing is to be a greater priority than to worship God. And such zeal Jesus showed was no limp-wrist faith. He didn't care what people thought when it came to assuring priority, the priority of worshiping the Heavenly Father. Beloved, recall that the Apostle Paul warned that the gospel would be offensive. It was offensive to the Greek ears, it was offensive to the Jewish ears, and it's offensive to modern secular ears. Those who are too sensitive emotionally to hear that they are sinners in need of a savior are going to be offended. Those or who are too politically sensitive to be told there is absolute truth. And Jesus is that truth, and that he will exclude people from his kingdom who do not believe. Such people will be offended by you. They'll be offended by your life and what you believe. Expect it, have a backbone about it, strengthen your wrist, and be zealous for the Lord. What Jesus does to the money changers and the sellers is so hard for fallen mankind to understand. Even Christians struggle to understand how Jesus could be said to be loving and yet be angry. But that is the beauty of our Savior, and it's the example for us Christians to walk in. To live up to. We are to be righteously zealous when that includes being angry at times, while at the same time being loving. And that is something the world cannot do. The world either hates or it loves. You either love or you hate. But the Christian life is a life of following Jesus, the Savior, and thus it is a life that is zealous for the things of God, angry at times against sin, while being loving, always loving. Beloved, this dying world doesn't need more people who are blown around by the wind. This cursed world doesn't need overly sensitive people that become offended even when someone calls them overly sensitive. It doesn't need any more limp wrists. This dying, cursed world needs people who are zealous for the Lord Jesus. That is your charge today. Be zealous for the Lord Jesus. Amen. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Just to See the Kingdom of God
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.source_file: Just to See the Kingdom of God.txt
sermons.text: You would to the gospel according to Saint John chapter three. Follow along in your Bibles, be most helpful. Those of you who are near my age or older will appreciate this reference. A man named Roland Stewart, aka Rainbow Man. made his first public debut on the American sports scene in nineteen seventy-seven, the NBA Finals. Initially, he merely wore a large colored afro wig and he danced around wildly in front of the camera. In 1980, Stewart was sitting in a hotel room watching a televangelist by the name of Charles R. Taylor. Stewart says that his heart was warmed by the message of the gospel, and he decided then and there to follow Jesus. Thus he became what he called a born-again Christian. Stewart then went on a mission to share his new faith. He chose to continue his Rainbow Man antics. While coming up with the idea of adding a large John 3. 16 sign to his repertoire. And those of you like me remember watching Monday night football and seeing this guy always in the end zone. with his John 3. 16 sign. For the next decade, he traveled the globe to display John 3. 16. Among the events he attended, the Olympics, the World Cup, NFL playoff games, the Indy 500. The Masters, Horse Races, and even the wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diane. I would love to see a picture of that again He claimed he drove over sixty thousand miles a year to attend sporting events. He was able to figure out the prime positioning where he should stand for his sign to be seen by carrying with him a portable television, seeing where the cameras were focused, and he made his way to that point. Sports television producers began to loathe him, believing his antics detracted from the action on the field. Some producers asked cameraman to refrain from showing Stewart, going so far as to threaten their jobs if they showed him on television. Unfortunately, for Stuart and for those who were impacted by his John 3:16 sign. Stewart started acting irrational and eventually even cruel. He began practicing more negative tactics to get attention. He blew horns at golf matches while men were putting. He detonated stink bombs where large crowds were gathered for events. His personal life became a wreck as well. He was broke from traveling to so many events, and his wife claimed physical abuse, and she left him. By the 1990s, he was homeless and living in his car. Finally, Stewart went over the edge. When in September of 1992, Stewart locked himself in a hotel room in Los Angeles, a Hyatt region, and made threats to shoot airplanes as they were landing and taking off. He held a Hyatt Mage hostage. He plastered religious verses on the windows and held a standoff with the police for eight hours. The SWAT teams were eventually able to break in his room. They found handgun with two ammunition clips and 47 live ammunition rounds. Stewart is currently serving out three life terms at Mule Creek Prison in Iwn, California. Now, such is not a story that you would think would describe a man who is truly born again. It is not a story of any man who believed that God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son. Now understand please that I am in no way saying that I know the spiritual state of Roland Stewart. That would be arrogant for anyone to make such a judgment I only say that such an outcome is not expected when you hear of someone who claimed to be born again. And what Roland Stewart's life choices reveal is that the fallen condition of humanity shows that we have a lot of needs In this section of scripture from John chapter 3, verse 1 to verse 21, there is revealed the needs of humanity. The needs that we have that we might have our new birth stick, and by stick I mean remain, that our newborn life would carry us through to the end of our days That we would not leave our Savior. From verse 1 through 8, it is revealed that we need to be born of Spirit. That is our first need, to be born of Spirit. From verse 19, 9, excuse me, verse 9 through 17, it is revealed that we have a need for understanding. And in verses 18 through 21, it is revealed that we have a need for faith, and how appropriate that is on Reformation Sunday. And let us now look first at the need to be born of Spirit. If you have Heard Bible studies, read commentaries, and heard sermons about Nicodemus coming to Jesus, described here by John You know that the detail of him coming at night to see Jesus indicates the angst that he felt. After all, he was a Pharisee who was supposed to be challenging Jesus, and yet he was a man who had his conscience moved by the teachings of Jesus. He comes at night to talk to Jesus so that he is not seen by his peers But let us not look down on him for the simple reason that at least he comes to Jesus. Very few Pharisees did. Nicodemus was challenged by the miracles that Jesus did. He knew the scriptures. He knew what was expected of the Messiah. The Messiah was to do such miracles. They were signs. And Jesus fit those signs. But the manner Nicodemus mentions signs indicates that he needs more. And Jesus, knowing that he needs more, tells him what he needs. Every person who wants to see the kingdom of God must be born again. The word C indicates a beginning point. It's not finished when you've been born again. It's not finished. But it must start there. The kingdom of God will not be realized in a person's life until that person is born again. The response that Nicodemus gives to Jesus is really more of a challenge. What Jesus said sounded ridiculous to him. His question back to Jesus was more rhetorical. He knew that no one could re-enter their mother's womb, and thus he knew That such could not be what Jesus was saying. What do you mean, Jesus? But Nicodemus was not yet born anew himself. And so he could not at this point see. He could not comprehend. He didn't know that he was not alive spiritually, that he didn't yet have the ability to understand what Jesus was saying. Christians continue to be tempted towards frustration when we cannot communicate with those of the world. We cannot get through to them. We try logic and it doesn't work. We share our testimonies and it doesn't work. We declare God's word and it doesn't work. It doesn't work because people of the world are spiritually dead. They cannot see or hear God. And being spiritually dead, they do not have eyes to see what the Spirit reveals. Being spiritually dead, they do not have ears to hear the truth. They are like what we were, or how we would be, if the Spirit of God had not breathed life, spiritual life, on us, into us We know the sin of Adam caused spiritual death within the human race Although each earthly child that is born breathing is breathing in the oxygen of this world, they are not breathing in the breath of eternal life. Such breathing only happens when God gives such life, utterly dependent upon Him. Historically, the church has interpreted the words of Jesus in his response to say that a person must be born of water and spirit as a reference to be being born in baptism. And then born by the Holy Spirit. In the book of Acts, we see a connection between being baptized in water and being born again by the Spirit. And there is a great mystery in all this. The words of Jesus reveal that mystery when he describes the Holy Spirit being like the wind. It is unpredictable. And yet you are very much aware when that wind does blow. Do not our life experience reveal this unpredictability of the Holy Spirit Where from our vantage point, a person seems far from God, and the Holy Spirit moves upon him, giving him new birth. New birth, a sinner being born again, is the greatest miracle we are privileged to experience and to witness. I want to underline that. Consider that to he to heal a knee, well that's remarkable. A person had a bad knee, they now have a good knee, we prayed, they're healed, that's remarkable. To calm cancer cells and bring them in line, that's glorious. They had cancer, they don't have cancer anymore. But to move the will of a human being, to move the will into humility, repentance, into faith, that is the greatest of miracles. And Jesus is still doing them. The next part of the conversation reveals the human need to understand We have to love the Lord with our mind to understand. Dicodemus is honest regarding his inability to comprehend what Jesus has said to him. And I would say that this is a good sign for Nicodemus, admitting he doesn't understand. It has been said that learning, the simple act of learning, is like conversion. Each person must begin by admitting that they are inadequate before he or she can accept or receive new knowledge. Each person must acknowledge that he or she does not know, and thus they have fallen short. Each person must confess that he or she needs to know. And the rebuke Jesus gives to Nicodemus might be hard for sensitive ears. But not for ears that are truly wanting to know. But Jesus tells Nicodemus. All Pharisees, all Sadducees needed to hear, needed to accept. They thought of themselves and presented themselves to their fellow man as leaders, teachers. As leaders and teachers, they were to be in the know. They were to be the one that people ask questions of. They were to be the source of truth, and yet they could not understand what is basic to knowing the kingdom of God. Let us be reminded of what blinded these Pharisees and these Sadducees. It was the sin of personal pride. Pride, personal pride, is the most base of sins. Pride is looking at oneself as not needing outside help, as If self is a finished product, and thus no need for further revelation. It is Most helpful to know that anytime someone is telling us that we don't know, and we lie and we say that we do know, that it is personal pride that has won over our soul. When we are asked a question that we should know and we don't know, and we try to cover up our lack of not knowing. It is the sin of pride to which we have submitted. Overcome the sin of pride within you, and a Pharisee you will never be. And Jesus continues his explanation of what the kingdom of God really is. And I want us to note that Jesus doesn't make it easy for Nicodemus. Remember that Jesus is recorded in Math, in Mark, excuse me, and Luke. To quote Isaiah for an explanation of why he taught with parables. The simple teacher Assumes that Jesus teaches in parables so that people could understand more clearly. As if a story approach works best. Fact is the exact opposite. Jesus told his disciples that he taught in parables so that, quote, seeing the people may not perceive. And hearing that they might may not understand. Jesus did not make it easy for people who allowed personal pride to rule them. He did not make it easy to follow him. They had to get rid of that personal pride. Those of us who have been given eyes to see and ears to hear, because we have been given new life by the Holy Spirit, can readily see how basic these teachings are to Nicodemus. The one coming down described, the one coming down from heaven, well that's Jesus Jesus is the Son of Man, he calls himself. That is the title the prophet Daniel gave the one that we hoped for, the Messiah. The day Moses lifted up a bronze serpent, so that all that looked upon that staff with the bronze serpent would be healed from those snake bites, poisonous snake bites. Guilty they were because of idol worship. That scene was a setup for what Jesus was to do for all of mankind. That scene in the desert with Moses was a shadow of what all persons need to look up to. It was a sign to say that all need to look up to Jesus on the cross in order to be healed from the poison venom of death that has infected all of us. And next described is the good news that the only requirement of mankind is individual belief. By grace, we are saved through faith. That is all that is required to receive the gift of eternal life. And the reason why individual belief is all that is required is summed up in that wonderful John 316. It is because God did it all. God loved This is the true God. He is the God that loves. Not just love itself, but God's love starts it all. Not just love itself, God's love. God is always initiating relationship with humanity. And the reason he does that, the reason he initiates relationship, the reason that he wants to be our God and for us to be his people His love. God so love. Next, after love, God gave his son. You realize that is what the story of God instructing Abraham to sacrifice Isaac, that's what that story shouts to us It was always the plan of God to offer his son. And it is his only son. Adam was the firstborn of humanity, but Jesus was always God's son Here is the mystery of the Trinity displayed. God is one, but the Father and the Son are two different persons. The Son Jesus always was and always was to be given for humanity. Belief in the Son of Man is specific. Faith does not save if faith does not have the correct object. Faith must be in God's Son to be a saving faith. And it is faith that there be no mistake in Jesus alone. There is no other way to the Heavenly Father, thus there is no other way to heaven. Last week, in a conversation during Sunday school, I remark that there are certain entertainers that I boycott. One of those is Oprah Winfrey. I realize that some of you here might listen to her, respect her, maybe even heed her. I will not say that she is not a good person. I will say that she preaches a religion that resembles universalism. She denies that Jesus is the only way to heaven. Understand, please, that to say such is in direct opposition to what we are hearing from Jesus in this passage. For anyone to believe that there is a different way to heaven than by Jesus as the Son of God, that's just blasphemous. It is saying that God is a fool. He didn't need to send his son, there's other ways. Such is false teaching and nothing less. And Jesus follows the succinct gospel of John 3. 16 by saying it a little different in John 3. 17. God did not send Jesus to condemn the world because he loves the world. God sent his only son to save the world, because without him it cannot be saved. Now the last portion of the teaching of Jesus in this section of Scripture reveals the need of faith for humanity. You remember the book of Hebrews telling us that faith is the substance of things hoped for and the conviction of things not seen? Faith goes beyond empirical evidence. Faith is otherworldly. Faith is from God. Faith is a gift from God. Faith is a gift from God, but it must be practiced by us. That's part of our job. Faith in Jesus as the Son of God and the Savior of humanity saves us from condemnation. Without faith, Jesus says here, we are condemned, not only in the future, where we will give account for all of our sins. But we are condemned now. Even now. Those who do not believe stand condemned now. To be condemned now is to be under the curse of Adam. It is to remain dead in spirit. And Jesus now closes his words to Nicodemus by declaring a great contrast between those who are born of the Spirit and those who remain dead. To the Spirit. Those who remain dead in spirit hate the light. They hate the light because it exposes their sin. Under the light, they have to see themselves for who they truly are. And they don't like to see themselves for who they truly are. In contrast, those who are born of the Spirit, well, they want the light. They want the light so that they might see themselves. They want to see themselves so that they can repent, have sins revealed, and then have them cleansed. That is being alive in the Spirit. They want to see themselves because their good deeds are done for God. And when people see their good deeds, God is pleased because God is honored. A very great gift for those who are born of the Spirit is a guilt-free conscience. Amen. I don't know. I don't know what happened to Rainbow Man Roland Stewart. Listening to that televangelist where he claims to have been born of the Spirit of God. According to the words of Jesus to Nicodemus, a man born of the Spirit will not hold a maid hostage at a hotel room with a loaded gun. What we know from these words of Jesus is that God has done so very much for us to be forgiven. That we who claim to be born of the Spirit, well, we're to live out that new life. Live out being born again. John 3. 3, John 3. 16 are very much more than signs to be held up or slogans to recite. They are the good news of salvation. If you have never felt alive in the Spirit. If you have avoided the light, today is the day of your salvation. Believe that God sent his only Son. Believe Jesus is the Messiah and new life in the Spirit is yours. Let us pray

sermons.title: Different by Nature
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: I don't know, man. In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. You'd be seated. Turn in your Bibles to the Gospel according to St. John chapter 4. We are finishing up the story of the Samaritan woman, the woman at the well. I want to begin by pointing out that Christianity is a faith that goes against the grain. It actually goes against many grains. The grains that goes against are the expectations of contemporary society Every contemporary society. It goes against the impulses and desires of the flesh It goes against the grain of peer conformity. It goes against what is considered normative by society. And it does not go against all of these things to get attention to itself Christians are not like persons who color their hair as a rainbow and put many piercings in their nose and their ears and their tongue. Such people are putting on costumes, costumes to be different from societal societal norms Only they don't recognize that their attempt to be different just places them in another category of society. That category is the category of those who want to be different. And those who want to be different seem to dress an awful lot alike. There appears to be a conformity to non-conformity. No, Christians are not different by putting on a costume. Christians are different by nature. It is our nature to be different. We are, after all, born anew. We are born again. But we are born anew in life as a light We have living water within us that the rest of the world does not have. We cannot help but be different. But we can be tempted to not want to be different. We can be tempted by the devil and our own flesh to not want to stand out, but rather to fit in. And that is why a message like today is so very needed. We need to embrace our distinctiveness as Christian. When I was in the fifth grade, the school I attended was trying to assimilate handicapped students into the traditional classrooms. And my class was to receive Jonathan. Jonathan had several handicaps. He was born with one finger on one arm with no true hand On his other hand, he had what resembled a palm with two toes sewn on that were added to one finger, giving him three digits to work with. He was also born without a right leg from the knee down. We were prepared by our teacher and the counselor. To receive Jonathan and all of his differences. And as I recall, we did well receiving him, accepting his differences at first. But Jonathan was an angry boy. He was nasty with his tongue as he tried to get you to fight him every recess. He was angry because he was different. He was angry because of the manner people treated him because he was different. And we might say, who can blame him? But I remember Jonathan here because I fear Christians can also become angry. bitter, resentful, when they are treated differently. So it is my call today for all of us, young and old, to embrace our differentness. Let's go to this continuation of the woman at the well, seeing how different we are. From the part of the story of the woman at the well that we looked at last week, we learn from that conversation that she had with Jesus. That Jesus wants a new understanding about worship. Worship is a heavenly activity, it's a place And it is led by Jesus, our high priest. That is spirit and in truth. We then learn that the gospel is for everyone, all walks of life, as we compared that first discourse with Nicodemus the Pharisee and the second discourse with the Samaritan woman. And we found them to be so, so very different that they are very much alike. We continue the story with the disciples returning and seeing Jesus converse with this woman. Having a conversation with this half-breed, cast off, ignorant, adulterous woman Of course, the disciples and all who witnessed Jesus talking and disapproved of him talking to her were too cowardly to say anything. But they condemned the conversation in their hearts. It is true that no rabbi in Jesus' day would have carried on the conversation With not just that woman, but with any woman, let alone an adulterous Samaritan woman. One of the sayings of the day was this, I quote. A man shall not be alone with a woman in an inn, not even with his sister or his daughter, on account of what men may think. A man shall not talk with a woman in the street, not even his own wife, and especially not with another woman, on account of what men may say. This norm, this too was expected of Jesus. But Jesus didn't follow cultural convention. No, he did not He did not do what others expected of him, especially when it came to presenting the good news of forgiveness and the mercies of God. As Christians, as little Christs, we too cannot be shackled by what modern convention expects of us. Modern convention says that people don't really live out their religion in all aspects of their lives. But Christians know differently. Modern convention says that it would be that to be in the world, you have to be like the world. But Christians know differently. Modern convention says that if it offends anyone, anyone at all, except Christians, then it ought not be said. Ought not be done, ought not even to be thought. Christians know differently, and we cannot be silent when truth needs to be heard. The next important detail, as told by John here, is that the woman left her water pot. Having forgotten all about the reason why she came there to begin with in the first place, and she went to tell others what she had heard and from whom she heard it. It is this evidence that a deep impression had been made upon her, for she left the business at hand and left left something of value behind her. To tell others. And by the simple things that Jesus had told her about herself and about worship She had this everlasting hope that he was indeed the Messiah, the Christ. And this is another manner in which Christians are different. Christians know the eternal without empirical evidence. We recognize the eternal. The scientism of this modern age is perhaps the largest false idol that mankind has ever built. We are pouring millions of dollars into climate models that have no proven track record, but because a supposed majority of scientists agree on an issue, full speed ahead. One study of a minutiae of specimens and one conclusion by one scientist allows us to conclude that our sexuality is not according to our anatomy, but according to a supposed gene of desire. Now hear this list of historic scientific theories proven wrong. There was a theory in the 19th century, I didn't know about this one, that there was a planet named Vulcan between Mercury and the Sun. Wrong. The theory of spontaneous generation, the organic things could simply pop up out of nowhere. Wrong. That the earth was and is expanding, getting bigger and bigger. Wrong. The Fotisthan theory That all things combustible contain the element of phlogiston, making burning possible. Wrong The blank slate theory stating that people are born not born without a priori knowledge. Wrong. Einstein's theory of a static universe. Wrong. The theory of cold fusion, believing that nuclear energy could be created at room temperature. Wrong. The theory that red MMs cause cancer. Wrong. The list is longer and the list will be added to. And this is not a criticism of science at all, not the least. It is a critique of our culture that puts its whole trust in any scientific theory that would prove what they want it to prove. But Christians do not walk according to theory. Christians walk by faith and not by what a scientist concludes from a scientific experiment. Christians know that there is a world, a reality that cannot be measured by a scientist. There is a spiritual reality that we cannot deny, for it is as real to us as our own hands that we look at and that we use. We know God is real because His Spirit speaks to our Spirit. We know the gospel is true because once we were shackled and chained and blinded and now we are free and we can see. We know what it is to be forgiven when before all we knew was guilt. The woman at the well, who ran to tell others of her hope, even when she had not seen Jesus do anything miraculous But merely speak to her and speak to her intimately. We have no reason to believe her, but we get her. We relate to her hope. Well next, Christians are different because we understand metaphor and miracle. Metaphor and miracle. Having returned to Jesus, verse 31, the disciples are concerned for Jesus. They have not seen him eat anything, and they're bringing him food, and they want him to eat to regain his physical strength. So they urge him to eat something, something that they bought But Jesus tells them that he has consumed food that they do not know about. And this confused the disciples. Maybe it even made them insecure, wondering, well, who else is Jesus talking with and in our inner circle with. The disciples were too immature in their faith to think beyond the physical world Just like Nicodemus before, who could not understand a spiritual birth, only understood the natural birth And like the woman at the well who could not understand living water, but only understood water coming from a well So too, these disciples of Jesus did not understand that there was a food that was different than that which you consumed with your mouth. Now we, being on the other side of the resurrection, we now understand how Jesus uses concepts of the natural world to explain truths of the eternal world. Christians understand metaphor. Meat you do not know. Water you need to have. A birth that is spiritual. I heard a minister wrongly state that Jesus used story so that people could better understand and remember his teaching. Well, I said, should say the minister was partly wrong. Recall that when the disciples didn't understand the parable of the sower, they come to Jesus. And he says to them that all things are told in parables, so that those who hear will hear but not understand. And that sounds to the sensitive ear that Jesus didn't want people to actually know what he was talking about.
