Lewis, which he popularized in his BBC radio broadcast during the Second World War, and popularized it in his writings. It is sometimes this trilemma is sometimes called the lunatic, liar, or lord, or mad, bad, or god argument. It takes the form of a trilemma, a choice between three options, each of which is an option regarding who Jesus was and who Jesus, of course, is The argument, interestingly to me, was not new to Lewis, for it can be found in the writings of St. Augustine and some other fairly well-known preachers in their day The argument was widely cited in various forms in the 19th century. It was used by an American preacher, Mark Hopkins, in his book, Lectures of the Evidence of Christianity. It was also used by a Scots preacher, Rabbi John Duncan, in 1859, and he said this. Christ was either deceived, either deceived mankind by conscious fraud, or he was himself deluded and self-deceived, or he was divine. There is no getting around out of this trilemma. Other preachers have used something similar as well, and even G. K. Chesterton used something similar in his book, The Everlasting Man. By following this argument, I read directly from Lewis himself, from his book Mere Christianity. He said, I'm trying here to prevent anyone saying the really foolish thing that people often say about him, meaning Jesus. I'm ready to accept Jesus as a great moral teacher, but I don't accept his claim to be God. That is the one thing we must not say. A man who was merely a man and said the sort of things Jesus said would not be a great moral teacher He would either be a lunatic on the level with the man who says he is a poached egg, or else he would be the devil of hell himself. You must make your choice. Either this man was and is the son of God, or else a madman, or something worse. You can shut him up for a fool, you can spit at him and kill him as a demon, or you can fall at his feet and call him Lord and God. But let us not come with any patronizing nonsense about him being a great human teacher. He has not left that open to us. He did not intend to Now it seems to me obvious that he was neither a lunatic nor a fiend, and consequently, however strange or terrifying or unlikely it may seem I have to accept the view that he was and is God. End quote That Lewis was responding to those who presented Jesus as a moral teacher only is a necessary point to underline while examining this argument. Surprising to me, there are some Christians who don't like this trilemma argument. According to Bart Ehrman, he said there could be a fourth option. Legend And Lewis, of course, denied accounts of Jesus being a legend akin to mythology, stating, I have read a great deal of legend and am quite clear that they are not the same sort of thing. N. T. Ride, a leading New Testament scholar, has commented that Lewis's argument, based on a simplistic understanding of the incarnation in Judaism. doesn't work as history and it backfires dangerously when historic critics question his reading of the gospels Another criticism raised is that Lewis is creating a false trilemma by insisting that only three options are possible. Philosopher John Beverasulis comments, quote, he deprives his readers of numerous alternate interpretations of Jesus that carry with them such odious implications. For example, it is logically possible for Jesus' claims, if any, as to his divinity, to have been merely good faith mistakes. Resulting from his sincere efforts at reasoning, as well as for Jesus to have been deluded with respect to specific issues of divinity. This is also agreed upon by William Lane Craig, an apologist. And yet I find it interesting that a well-known atheist The late atheist Christopher Hitchens sees some positivity to the trilemma argument He argues that Lewis's contention is right, but offers a different interpretation. Hitches writes, I am bound to say that Lewis is more honest here, absent a direct line to the Almighty, and a conviction that the last days are upon us. How is it moral to claim a monopoly on access to heaven, or to threaten waverers with everlasting fire, yet alone to condemn a fig tree, persuade devils to infest bodies of pigs? Such a person is not divine. He would be a sorcerer and a fanatic. And so now we can count six options. Jesus was either a lunatic, a liar, a lord, a legend, a sorcerer, or a fanatic. But note, none of these objections, none of them, none of these objections address what Jesus said about himself. Rejecting or accepting what Jesus said makes all of the difference. If what he said is true, if what he said is true, you cannot respond with half of your heart. You cannot respond with half of your will. You cannot respond with half of your emotions. If it is not true Then just walk away, be done with it, if it is not true. Whatever a person decides, let it be understood that because of what Jesus said, it is either all in or all out. That is what the words of Jesus about himself force us to decide, all in or all out. I trust, you will say with me, as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. Amen and Amen. Let us pray

sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Those of you who have hearing aids probably think if your hearing aid is not working well today Because our microphones are not working today, our system is down, we apologize, try to make up for it We're going to do something a little different. So in your Bibles, as you follow along, in John chapter 6 We are not going to be going verse by verse through 1 through 14, the story of the feeding of the 5,000, but actually We're going to be looking at the teaching of Jesus at the end of John chapter 6, really starting at verse 24 and following. So be ready to go back and forth in your Bibles. A little personal story to begin with, and my wife is not here, so that's always the safest time to tell a story about her The first time I brought Bobby Lynn to my home, my family's home, was the fall of 1984, because her brother had married my sister. She had been to our family home before, but not as my romantic interest. And wanting to be a gracious host, I had her sit down in the living room, and I asked her if I could get her anything to eat. She paused, looked thoughtful, and said, I would like some bread. It is helpful to understand that Bobby Lynn and her father are both bred connoisseurs. Her father's love for fresh baked bread and multi-grain breads was passed on to her. So she liked bread. Okay. However, in the Jorgensen poem It was a home that rarely saw any fresh baking, any good cooking, and the only bread that we had was oven joy sliced white bread. For those of you who do not shop at Safeway, Ovenjoy is their base brand. It is a step lower than Wonder Bread. But because this beautiful creature asked me for bread, well, I'm going to get bread. So I bring her a slice of Northwest Oven Joy white bread. I next ask her if she wants something to drink. giving her the option of coke and milk lemonade, she says, or asks, could I have some water Sure, sure, I say so I go and flip on the faucet and fill her glass up with tap water and I bring it to her and then it hits me. She thinks she's in prison. Either she thinks the house is a prison Or this relationship is a prison and she's ordering a suitable meal for a prisoner, bread and water Thankfully that was not the case, and she told me much later that if she had known that I was going to bring her oven joint bread, she would not have had the order, and and I was relieved Isaac Watts, the great hymn writer and theologian, but also a logician, in his book on logic, he makes the point that if a boy grows up Having a thatched roof for a home, and that's all he's ever seen, then anytime that he hears the word home, he's going to think of a thatched roof Well, when I heard the word bread, I only thought of oven joy white sliced bread And such is not the image that Jesus would have us have in our minds when he makes the statement that he is the bread of life. In our gospel reading, we once again heard the story of Jesus feeding 5,000 men and more. We say more because only the men were counted, and we assume that some of them had wives and some families had children. And so we say that there was 5,000 and more. And I say that we read it again because we have heard before from the three other gospels this same story In fact, this miracle of Jesus feeding the 5,000 plus people is the only miracle that is told in all the four Gospels. The only miracle that is told in all the four Gospels. That includes, it is quite curious, that it in John includes it is quite curious to me, because we know by now that he is so very picky as to the discourses and the miracles that he tells. And we know, because we know the end of John's gospel, that he only tells us about seven miracles. So it is curious again Why he would tell us this one when all of the other gospels already have this and John is the last gospel to be written. Why would he include this miracle? It is curious until we read the discourse that Jesus has with the people about himself, as I said, starting around verse 24 in chapter 6 For in there he is teaching them about how he is the bread of life. And we find this again later, starting at verse 24. And I have concluded That you cannot tell the story of Jesus feeding the 5,000 plus without including the teachings of Jesus teaching about himself afterward. Explaining the meaning of the feeding of the five thousand. Like the woman at the well And like Nicodemus, before the woman at the well, the people who are trying to find Jesus, they're looking for him in verse 24. The people who are trying to find him thought only in terms of the material world. Nicodemus could only consider being physically born again. The woman at the well could only consider quenching her thirst physically. And now the people who ate of the bread that Jesus multiplied could only think about being fed physically And Jesus confirms this in verse 26 of chapter 6, when he says that they are following him, following after him, because they physically ate the bread and were physically filled. Jesus then points them to a different world, a world they did not know about, points them to a different world or a different understanding of their world by pointing The fact that he has food that will not perish. Food that is not earthly Food that does not of enjoy white sliced bread. Bread that satisfies forever The people respond by asking Jesus, well, what should we do to get this bread? How can they get involved? How can they work to earn it? It is much like the disciples wanting to know how they are going to feed this many people. Only thinking in the material world. We can at least now give the disciples credit that they recognized that several days wages would not pay the bill for feeding so many people. That they got. But still they were thinking that they could work and make it dumb. That they could physically do work, earn wages, and then possibly pay the bill to feed this many people in the material world And so Jesus next reveals to them the glory of the gospel. The people are seeking him. He tells them that he is the bread of life. They say, How can we get this? They want to work for it. And then he reveals to them the gospel. He reveals to them The truly good work. Work is actually belief. Work is belief. Work in the kingdom of God is having faith in Jesus. That is it. Nothing more required. Nothing more to be seen here. That is it. That is all that is needed. It is exactly what was needed by the disciples who told the people to sit down. Even though they had but five barley loaves and two small fish. Now only John, interestingly, mentions that the boys' loaves were barley loaves And that was because it was inexpensive bread for the lower class. The fish, no doubt, were more than a tidbit. You can think of pickled small fish. This was added to the lunch to make it more flavorful because bread isn't that flavorful by itself. So you picture this scene, and you think to yourself, well, this is a joke that you can feed 5,000 plus with five loaves and two small fish. That's a joke to consider. But you also need to realize that it's also a joke to consider that mankind can be saved from hellfire and the guilt for sin simply by believing in Jesus And yet, as a joke, these both are, both occur, both are true. In the discourse of chapter 6, verse 31, the people are still thinking of this physical bread that fills their belly. When they mention that Moses fed the Israelites with manna in the desert, and we are to remember that that manna bread was given daily, except for the Sabbath day. It was a daily meal. And perhaps that is what the people wanted from Jesus. They wanted perhaps a daily meal. They wanted a handout every day. And so this mention of Moses is a bit of a challenge to Jesus Because the prophecy said that one like Moses would be raised up. Moses said this himself in Deuteronomy 18. And it also says that the people are to listen to this one that is raised up like Moses. But the people here want Jesus to show them how he is like Moses. How these people represent themselves here shows a great lack of self-awareness. They are not aware that they actually would not believe, even if Jesus multiplied bread for them every day. They still would not believe Their forefathers didn't believe, and they are no different than their forefathers. Recall the story of the rich man and Lazarus. Recall that the rich man is being tormented in hell and he asks of Abraham for some relief and he doesn't find it. And then he says, Well then could you send someone up? from the dead to tell my brothers how horrible it is down here. And of course, the lesson is, as Jesus teaches, that No. Even if you were to send someone up from the dead, they still would not believe. Of course, Jesus is that someone. Who rose from the dead. And people today still do not believe. Some even today questioning if Jesus ever existed. When Jesus next in verse 32 says that he himself is the true bread that has come down from heaven. He is then here comparing himself to manna, the manna of Moses, the manna that Moses called down, and he's comparing himself to the bread loaves he recently multiplied. He is the true bread. Those breads all fall short. Those breads are not lasting, but Jesus is, of course, everlasting. Those breads were types and shadows of the true bread. The true bread is food for our spiritual sustenance. Bread that will save our souls alive. Bread that is assimilated within us conveys a consciousness, a reality of eternal blessedness. Not immediate fullness, but eternal blessedness. The kind of strength that will arise within us when once the true bread is consumed Is an eternal possession, an abiding advantage, the satisfaction that is not exhausted by short intervals like lunch to dinner. Instead, it remains forever. The true bread, the true bread is veritable heaven for you and in you. Consider this also. That Moses was not the actual giver of the manna. God, of course, was the giver. And this is much like the feeding of the 5,000, for it was the disciples who handed the bread to the people who gave out the bread, but the bread was multiplied, coming from Jesus. All the giving then was the work of God. It was the work of whom God had sent. On whom we have to believe. Jesus, he is the veritable giver of this true bread coming from heaven The giver then, the giver then and the gift are the same. Jesus. And Jesus next explains the unique relationship he has with the Heavenly Father And that those who come to him, those who follow him, who consume him as eternal bread, are the same people the Father gives to him. Those who follow him are given to him by the Father. And then Jesus says, because the people the Father gives him are such a great gift that he will lose nothing. Verse 39. The people God gives him, he will ensure they are forever with him. Have you ever wondered why God told the disciples After the feeding of the 5,000 plus, after they were all filled, why he told them to gather up the fragments of bread that remained. Ever wondered that? Why not just let the birds eat the remains? Or just let it feed the soil? What's the big deal? Well, it is because the collecting of the bread is symbolic of what Jesus will do with the people the Father gives to him. He will collect them all. No matter how scattered, no matter how small the fragment, he will gather them all. We know this is what is meant to gather up the bread fragments because they were able to fill how many baskets? Twelve in number? And what does twelve represent? People of God. Twelve tribes of Israel, the 12 apostles, the people of God, chosen by God, the New Testament church. And just as Jesus didn't leave one fragment of bread on the ground that day that he fed the 5,000 plus, so he will not leave one of God's people in the grave. He will rescue all who believe in him by raising them, by raising us from the dead, giving us life eternity. Hallelujah. Amen. When we hear of doubters who are talking amongst themselves, you see that in verse 43? Doubters were talking amongst themselves, their reasoning that Jesus could not be who he said he was. They know his family. They know the town that he came from. They know his home. There's no mystery here. He's just a man like us. But this is to remind us of what just happened in the feeding of the 5,000. How did that happen? How did that happen? That is a reasonable question Can we imagine that one loaf morphed into another and then another? Can we imagine the matter of one fish morphing into another fish and from that fish another fish and so on? Can we imagine that where there was once nothing in a basket, all of a sudden there was something and it was very full indeed? Something coming from nothing? And this type of inquiry has been done by many. Consider this commentary coming from Hilary, an early church father from the fourth century. He said this about this miracle. The method eludes our powers of observation. Five loaves are offered and broken. While the apostles are dividing them, a succession of new created portions passes. They cannot tell how. Through their own hands. The loaf which they are dividing grows no smaller, yet their hands are continually full of the pieces The swiftness of the process baffles sight. You follow the eye, a handful of portions, and meantime you see that the contents of the other hand is not diminished. And all the while the heap of pieces grows. The carvers are busy at their task, the eaters are hard at work, the hungry are satisfied, and the fragments fill twelve baskets. Sight or sense cannot discover the mode of so noteworthy a miracle. What was not existent is created What we see passes our understanding. Our only resource is faith in God's omnipotence. Amen. But so is the same for us accepting who Jesus is. He does not pass the eye test. He is more than what is seen, just as the five loaves and the two fish were more than what was seen. But those who don't have eyes to see and ears to hear can't accept it. They see just another man. And that is why the Father and the Holy Spirit are necessary, so that eyes can be open and ears can be open to believe, to know the truth. After Jesus explains this, he says to those, these most difficult words, perhaps the most difficult words that Jesus says in all of the Gospels. Verse 23. I mean verse 53. He says this, most assuredly I say to you, unless you eat of the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood. You have not life in you. And then, as if that is not provocative enough, and instead of Jesus saying, Oh, of course I'm speaking metaphorically Jesus once again doubles down. He does not back away from this hard saying, but stays with it. And he emphasizes that his flesh they must eat and his blood they must drink. It is him that they are to feed on, he says, if they are to live forever. And with this doubling down, we must consider the dietary sensitivities of the Jewish life in the first century. Their dietary laws were one of the clear ways they were able to separate themselves from the Romans and from the Greeks as their overlords. And their dietary laws strictly forbid the drinking of any blood from any animal, especially a human, and any thought of cannibalism was near blasphemy. So it is not a wonder that we are told in verse 66 that many of his disciples went back, meaning they went back home, and walked with him no more. They left. They quit. They walked away from the hope of eternal life. And Jesus didn't go after them. He didn't explain himself in a in a different, less offensive manner. He let them go Knowing that whether a person stays to follow Jesus or leaves to go their own way, it is the Father's will. When Jesus next asks if his disciples will also leave, Peter gives that wonderful response that is on our lips as well. Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life. And so Jesus does. And those words of life are why we come to him, for in him only do we receive such life. So now, do you see that the miracle of the feeding of the 5,000 plus was to lead to a moment of a decision? It was to lead the people to eat of Jesus or reject him completely Just as it was last week, we have an all-in or all-out moment That is what John is communicating with these narratives, with these discourses. It is all in or all out. Now of course there is a great deal more to be said about these words of Jesus in John 6 regarding the consuming of his body and blood, when you compare them to the words that he gives in the Lord's Supper. Saying, take, eat, this is my body while holding the bread. And saying, take and drink, this is my blood while holding up the wine. We don't believe in the doctrine of transubstantiation. The bread at Holy Communion turns into the actual flesh of Jesus, or that the wine turns into the actual blood of Jesus. But we do believe that the very presence of Jesus is in the bread and in the wine in a manner that we do not try to explain. As Bishop Sutton has pointed out, to believe in the real presence is to believe in the real presence is to believe in the real absence, and that is no belief at all. And so when we take of the bread and eat, we are doing just as Jesus had said. We are consuming his flesh. Is the bread the flesh? Well, no. And yes. Is the wine we drink his blood going down? Well, no. And yes. These are representatives of his flesh and of his blood like nothing else we do in life. And as we consume them, we are consuming them in light of his command to eat of his flesh and drink of his blood. For what we do in the physical world points to a reality of a greater world, an eternal world. We are what we eat, and we eat Jesus. Taking the bread, beloved, and drinking from the cup, dear church, is the most profound thing you will do each week. The most profound thing you will do each week. Believe that. And one last point. When you see ministers up here trying to consume the rest of the bread, trying to drink the remaining portions of the wine in a timely manner And you realize the service is almost over and you're thinking to yourself, hurry up, man! Or that seems so unnecessary. Consider. Consider when you see it the next time that it is pointing to what Jesus said, so that nothing is lost. So that nothing is lost. Amen. Let us pray

sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Turn in your Bibles to St. John's Gospel chapter 6, the story of Jesus walking on water. Those of you who are astute Bible readers, those of you who might like to read ahead, knowing which part of the scripture I'm going to be preaching on, recognize That last week I skipped the story of Jesus walking on water. I did so. Because I argued last week that we can best understand the miracle of Jesus feeding the 5,000 plus If we hear him teach on what he means by saying that he is the bread of life And so we come back to the event of Jesus walking on water, which we find between him feeding the 5,000 plus and him teaching on being. the bread of life. Understand that with the Sea of Galilee, the surface of the waters lies some 600 feet below sea level. And up to a 2,000 feet below the tops of the hills that surround the sea. The difference in temperature at the top of those mountains to the surface of the lake is so considerable That evidently it causes air to rush downhill through the ravines to the water. And this allows for storms to come up quickly. Some can be quite severe or fierce for a small lake. And we learn from the other gospels that Jesus had sent his disciples away across the lake ahead of him while he remained back in order to pray. And that's an important point for us to remember that Jesus told them to get into the boat. With a measurement given And the knowledge that we have of the Sea of Galilee, it's supposed to be 61 stadia in length. They were about halfway through, which places them in the middle of the lake. Which is, as you can imagine, the worst place to be when a storm comes up. The mention of it being night is a c to cause us to remember that darkness in the Bible is a symbol of evil and a symbol of ignorance Light and the ability to see clearly are righteous in nature, and so the inability to see what was exactly happening, and being ignorant about the whereabouts. of Jesus and being in the midst of the storm, a storm that could capsize their boat, well, all of this is understandable. Why would make the disciples afraid? That Jesus walked on this tumultuous sea is almost presented by John as an afterthought. Of course, he's walking on water. And John leaves out the fact, you remember from other gospel accounts, that Peter tried to do the same And was successful for a time, you remember the story, and until he looked around him and realized he really shouldn't be able to be doing this, and therefore he went down We cannot know why John left out such an inspiring story, and yet a disappointing story as well. It is as though John wants us, his readers, to focus on Jesus calming the fears of his disciples in the midst of a very scary situation. And from verse 21, it is not clear whether we are to understand that there is a second miraculous effect of this speeding up to get the boat to shore or was this just as Mark points out something that naturally happened they went through the storm they got on to the shore It is good for us to remember that the Bible uses the sea and its storms, its waves, as symbolic of chaos and disorder in general. And that chaos and disorder is that which represents our own tribulation, our own troubles in life. All the waves and breakers have swept over me, the psalmist says in Psalm 42, verse 7. I sink in the miry depths where there is no foothold. I have come into the deep waters, the floods engulf me. Psalm 69, verse 2. And such verses are used to describe our emotions when life appears to overwhelm us. Consider the case of Jonah the prophet. The sea and its waves were both his literal peril and the symbol of the trouble that God had visited upon him on account of his sin. You hurled me into the deep, into the very heart of the seas, and the currents swirled about me. The engulfing waters threatened me. That's from Jonah chapter 2, verse 3 through 5. But such powers don't act on their own, of course. They're subject to the Lord. He rules them and he controls them. God himself makes this clear in Job when he says you remember him challenging Job Who shut up the sea behind the doors when it burst forth from the womb? When I made the clouds its garment and wrapped it in thick darkness. When I fixed limits for it and set its doors and bars in place, when I said, This far you may come and no farther, here is where your proud waves halt. Job 38, 8 through 11. So the most obvious application for Christians of Jesus walking on water. and calming the sea has been that the Lord delivers his people from the trials of life by calming what is seemingly out of control all around them Consider that if you or I, any one of us, were in that boat. Any one of us, all of us, would have been terrified, just like the disciples were We all have had terrible trials in our lives that move us to first try to grow vigorously, to save ourselves by our own strength. And as we do, we find we are going nowhere, unable to save ourselves. All of us have times in life when we found ourselves in some trial Some darkness, some storm, and we felt entirely alone, trusting in our own strength We were unaided, so we thought, by God's grace, we were completely unaware of his presence. We doubt during such times in a manner that reveals that we have not grown much in our faith from the last time the Lord brought us through a trial, through a tribulation, through a storm. We felt then that we were alone, and we feel again that we're alone. And consider that these men just witnessed a great, great miracle at the feeding of the 5,000 plus. They just came from that moment. They just came from a most dramatic moment that they witnessed with their own eyes and with their own hands. They touched the bread and then passed that bread along while it multiplied And yet, because of darkness, rain, and wind, they panic They do worse. They doubt. They have great fear for their lives, not knowing how they are going to be saved. They do not apply their faith in Jesus to all things. Instead, they compartmentalize their faith, only applying it here but not over here. Here but not over here. Do you ever do that? Do you automatically apply your saving faith in Jesus to all of your life circumstances? When you face a trial, do you take the lessons learned from your previous trials and apply them? This trial of the disciples in a storm is to teach them that they are to take the faith that they were given to feed the 5,000 plus with five barley loaves and two fish and use it. In that moment, even and especially in dark and stormy circumstances And next comes Jesus. Consider that Jesus could have most easily calmed the storm from the hillside and then continued to pray. He could have done it from a distance and gone back to praying to his heavenly father. But Jesus wanted to be with his disciples. He wanted to be with them in the midst of the storm, in the midst of the darkness, in the midst of the trial. And so he comes to them. He feels the battered rain and battered wind. He experiences the darkness. Jesus does this. Because he identifies fully with his people, not just partially, fully with his people's suffering He does not leave us alone in the midst of our trials and tribulations, but goes through them with us. That is what his love is. It is an everlasting, abiding love that never leaves or forsakes. And just because we don't feel his presence in the midst of a trial means nothing to the actual fact that he suffers, that he strives with us, always with us. Of course, Jesus calms the storm because he can. That's what he came to do. He came to calm the storms in our lives. Lives that rage with sin. Lives that live in darkness Jesus calms the inner storms, the inner storms by forgiving, loving, and giving his Holy Spirit. If that was all that this miracle meant, it would be enough, wouldn't it? Is it not enough to say, to understand how Jesus is with us during the storms in our lives? It would be enough to know that he calms the storms in our lives by forgiving us. Forgiving us our sins, repairing our broken hearts, repairing it with his love. That's enough, isn't it? It is enough. But there is more here for us. Very often The Bible uses bodies of water as representative of nations of the world that are enemies of God. The psalmist says, When the waters roar and be troubled He will still the noise of the seas, the noise of the waves, and the tumults of the peoples. When it describes such, it is describing foreign nations who are in rebellion against God. God also uses bodies of water to judge his own people. We know that of course from the flood. But from Isaiah, God warned that although he is the rivers whom streams make glad, the city of God, when they reject his word, he is much different. When they reject his word, he becomes the flood. And the flood is allowing foreign nations to overwhelm Israel. Jeremiah does something similar while describing Nebuchadnezzar as a sea monster who will swallow up the Lord's people. So let us take the Bible's use of bodies of water as foreign nations. And apply it to this story of Jesus walking on the water and calming the storm. What are the nations now doing? What do you see when you turn on your television and watch the news? What are the nations now doing? What are the nations who have rejected the gospel and have chosen a false God doing in the world today? Are they raging? Are they roaring? Are they overflowing? Are they storming? Are we in the midst of a storm? In Syria alone In Syria alone, as of December 5th this year, ISIS has killed 2,157 civilians, not troops, civilians. including 150 children and 154 women. Al Qaeda has killed 279 civilians, including 31 children and 53 women, again just in Syria. Boko Haram in Nigeria is estimated to have killed over 8,000 civilians In the year 2014, last year, they abducted 1,123 citizens while enslaving 536 females. 129 gunned down in Paris, France. 14 killed and 21 wounded in San Bernardino, California. Are the nations raging? France is now bombing Syria and Iraq. Russia is now bombing Syria and Iraq. Britain is bombing Syria and just started bombing Iraq after a spirited debate in Parliament. We are well I think we're involved somehow. Anyways, are the nations storming? You may have noticed That I don't spend a lot of time talking about current events behind the pulpit. I have, in the past, taken time to address current events when they are so much on our minds, and there's such great curiosity among Christians about what is the proper Christian response, what is the appropriate Christian response. 9-11 is the most obvious example. I share my political thoughts in Sunday school or Wednesday Bible studies or in my blog if I get around to blogging But I need to preach the everlasting living word of God when I stand here behind this pulpit. I cannot justify exchanging God's word for my words. My words are not everlasting. They are not living and sharper than a two-edged sword. No, these descriptions only apply to God's word. It is my calling to bring you to the foot of the cross, to give you the hope of heaven. To call you to greater holiness, to warn you of the devil's schemes, to hold the truths of God up high and help transform your mind to think like the kingdom of God. I cannot do any of that if I focus on the news of the day. But here we have a text. A narrative that allows us to bring the contemporary world and its troubles into the story of Jesus walking on water and calming the storm. Today, we are those disciples in that boat. And this sanctuary is our boat. It is our ark that is taking us to the heavenly shore. And outside the nations are raging. The nations are roaring. The nations are storming. The nations are trying to overflow into our boat. And where is Jesus? Where is Jesus? I get to tell you. Jesus is on the water. Jesus is on top of the water. Stop and consider what that means for Jesus to be walking on water. To be on water means that he is not subject to its properties. He's not subject to its rules. To be on water means that he does not have to obey the water, but the water obeys him. And if the nations that rage and roar and overflow are the water that Jesus walks on, Well then Jesus is not subject to their properties. He does not obey them, they obey him. Certainly, you turned on the news to hear the story of the many people being gunned down in Paris and thought to yourself, What is man doing to himself? And you likely said the prayer, Jesus, have mercy on those people. And then you didn't dare ask that question, where was God when this happened? Because you hate that question. But now you can answer that question. Jesus was on the water. When you heard the news that 14 people were killed in California, obviously gunned down in a terror act. You had the same thoughts and prayers as you did with the news in Paris. And we had the same answer. While 14 people were being killed and 21 injured, simply trying to enjoy a holiday lunch, Jesus was on the wall Many of you have heard that after the shootings in California, the New York Daily News came up with the headline God isn't fixing this. He was to cleverly, in their eyes, challenge the politicians who put out press statements for praying for those who had suffered as victims The paper believes that such men to be hypocrites because they fail to decrease or excuse me increase gun control. And you know the logic of this is that if you increase gun control, then radical terrorists will stop killing people. The headline is not inaccurate in that God is not, God is not at this time fixing this, but God is on the water. He's on the water. Now a cynic might, to my words, might say, well, if Jesus is on the water, why doesn't he calm the storm? It's a fair question. But those who ask such things usually don't like the answer. Jesus will calm the storm according to his will. Which is to say, according to the day and the hour that he chooses. But you notice that the nations that rage are not crying out to him. They are not willing to receive him in the boat, as the disciples did. And that is the root of the problem in this world. The nations want God to be real, they want Him to be benevolent, and thus save them from themselves, at the same time, they want to keep Him out of the boat. Of course, there will come a day when he will get in the boat, invite it or not. And that is what we focus our attention on in this Advent season. Jesus is coming again. Beloved, I know. That we feel the nations raging, roaring, and storming. It's a very dark time in the news today. It's hard to see. And it may be this way for a good while longer. Who knows? But Jesus is on the water. And Jesus will calm the nations. And Jesus will get into the boat. Believe that, and your soul will be calm. Amen? And Amen. Come, Lord Jesus. Let us pray.

sermons.title: They will hate you
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Encourage you to turn in your Bibles to St. John's Gospel chapter 7. We read uh through the first section of that chapter, but we'll be covering all of 1 John, I'm excuse me, all of John 7. So uh please turn there and follow along. They will serve you well You may or may not know that I attended the Ravens game last Sunday. Some members of my family. I'm not going to talk about the score. That's not the point of this story. At halftime, Jared invited us over to sit with them, for several seats around him were vacated, and he was sitting with Katie's father and brother. And when we sat down with them, I noticed, Caddy cornered to me across the aisle, the steps, was seated a man. At the end of the row, wearing a Pittsburgh Steeler jersey and a Pittsburgh Steeler hat with dark sunglasses on I asked Kevin, Katie's father, what's the deal with that guy? For it seemed to me rather ridiculous for a Pittsburgh Steeler fan to be wearing a Steelers jersey at a stadium of their arch enemy when the Steelers weren't even playing. In response Kevin shook his head and said, typical Pittsburgh Steeler fan. And then he told me that during the first half of the game There was a loudmouth Seahawk fan sitting in their section, and he was talking up a big game about the Seahawks when he then noticed this Pittsburgh Steeler fan sitting there And he got right in the guy's face, stopped everything, and said for everyone to hear, Ravens and Seahawks fans together, well, we can all agree to hate that guy. Nothing personal, Larry, about that at all. But I think that story is appropriate Because it is what is occurring in the world today toward Christians. The Muslims hate us The atheists hate us, the secularists hate us, the religious liberals hate us. They are all pointing to us and saying to one another, well, at least we can all agree to hate that guy, the Christian. In John 7, we have a number of people pointing to Jesus and saying virtually the same thing. But we can all agree to hate that guy. Recall that in John 6, Jesus had said some very hard things to understand and then accept. Unless you eat of my flesh and drink of my blood, you cannot be my disciple. And many who were following him, the scripture says, all except the twelve, stopped following him. They quit. They went home. So the following of Jesus had dwindled significantly as we come to John 7. But the reputation of Jesus and the hate for Jesus appears to have grown. We are going to examine John 7 in three parts. The first part is his discussion with his brothers, which we read for our gospel reading. The second is Jesus teaching in the temple. And the third is that last day of the Feast of the Tabernacles. I understand John should choose each of these three sections as examples of division that Jesus caused simply by being who he is. And what I hope that we all get out of this sermon is an appreciation for what for why Jesus offends And in anticipation that you too will offend as you walk the Christian road to the city of God. In John chapter 7, verse 1 through 9, we have an exchange with Jesus and his brothers. The occasion is the Feast of the Tabernacles. Let me remind you that the Feast of the Tabernacles is the last holy day celebrated in the Jewish calendar. Jewish families were to build a sukka or a hut to remember the 40 years wandering in the desert before entering the promised land. The celebration was to be seven days of worship and eating and enjoying, with the eighth day, the last day, as a Sabbath day for all to gather. The Feast of the Tabernacles took place in the month of Tishri, which for us is in our fall, and thus the feast also celebrated the year's harvest, like we do every year as well. Like every other Jewish feast, the best place to be for worship on such a celebration was the temple, which meant the city of Jerusalem. Which is where Jesus ended up in the middle of John 7. To understand this exchange that Jesus has with his brothers, it is best to point out That they are not believers in Jesus as the Son of God. They do not believe He yet is the Messiah. And I will not speak to the issue of whether these are Jesus' actual brothers or cousins. Much of early tradition has them being cousins But the text gives us no reason to understand them to be other than brothers, sons of Mary and Joseph. That these men knew Jesus as a man from Galilee, a man just like them, is likely why they had not yet believed in him as the Messiah. We have no evidence that Jesus did any miraculous things while growing up. We do have evidence about him being very wise in his teaching in the temple and wise beyond his years. That wisdom may have given his relatives a reason to envy him, seeing that he was one that you could resent. Because of his favored status. But again, we don't know. They just didn't believe. In verse 3 and 4, the brothers are challenging Jesus And that challenge amounts to basically saying this. If you are who you think you are And if you are who many say you are, then prove it to the world or stop this nonsense. Put up or shut up. Well this type of criticism of Christianity has not ceased. Repeatedly the secular world and the religious liberals challenge Bible-believing Christians to prove themselves. If Jesus can heal, well then you go ahead and heal for crying out loud. If Jesus performed miracles, then you too should be able to perform miracles. If your God truly is benevolent, then let us see him stop the violence in the world And such challenges are not actually looking for miracles or for God to stop the violence, but they are actually trying to get us to stop professing, to stop believing what they consider to be nonsense. The response of Jesus to his brothers is quite telling, very insightful in regards to the unbelieving mind. Jesus first says that he has not made his claim as the Messiah known to the world because it was not yet his time. He lays down his life and he takes it back up on his own terms, not theirs. Second, He points out the nature of his unbelieving brothers, and this is where we get into the mind of an unbeliever. They are always ready. They want the miraculous to occur now. They want the truth to be revealed now. And that is what the flesh insists upon. They want their pleasure, they want their satisfaction, and they want it now. But the nature of God's people, the character of God's people, is to wait The promises of truth revealed, of strength to overcome, are made to those who wait on the Lord. As we celebrate another Advent, which is to say, as we look forward to Jesus coming again, Jesus returning, we realize that we have passed many, many advents. And while the world says, well, where is he already? And shouldn't he have returned by now? We know that we are to wait, wait on the Lord. And here is a reason to hate Jesus. A reason to hate Jesus. He does not give what the flesh wants when it wants it. He is not a genie that grants wishes. He is not a miracle machine that allows some incantation to be uttered and then bam someone's healed. Bread appears or water divides. And he is not the Messiah people were looking for because who they were looking for would bring them military might That would overcome Rome, bring Rome to its knees, and that was to occur now, in their lifetime. They want it all. The unbelieving mind wants it all now. They did not want a Savior who said, My time is not yet fully come. For the unbeliever, I'll serve for the believer, for the believer, the word yet is so very important to us. My time is not yet fully come. The word yet tells us that there will come a time. And it will not only be Rome that will be bending its knee, but all of mankind. Yes Well the next section of the passage of this John 7 has Jesus teaching in the temple For he delayed coming to Jerusalem, let his brothers go ahead, and he came on later, arriving after his brothers And in verses 11 through 12, we find that the people are divided over who Jesus is and if he's really any good for the Jewish people. Is this a man that is worth for all of us to care about? For them, Jesus was anywhere from being good to being a deceiver. And that's quite a contrast, good or a deceiver. But that is the way it has to be. For Jesus taught and said many challenging things and confronted deep-seated sins of the religious leaders of his day. That there is no doubt that he would cause people to either be for him or against him. It has been Rightly noted, that the religious liberals have presented a Jesus that would provide no reason for him to be crucified The religious liberals have given an interpretation of Jesus that does not confront the sin of anyone, that does not teach anything unique about himself Make no claim of the divine. Does no miracles that reveal the divine. He says loving things only, so they say. That's it. We know that those loving things that they say he says are really not loving, because love confronts sin. Love roots out falsehood. At best, the Jesus presented by the religious liberals says only the benign. And why would the Pharisees and the Sadducees want to kill a teacher who said nothing of consequence? Why would Rome agree to murder a man who posed no threat to anyone at any time? Well, the answer to those questions is they wouldn't. And so it is ridiculous to teach of a Jesus in such a manner. The actual Jesus divides That is the way of it. Those who hated Jesus once again challenged his authority because he taught with authority. In doing so, they reveal how weak they actually are. Those who are bold in their personalities can cause a dislike of those who are not. Those who are bold can appear threatening to those who are timid. Add to a bold personality a teaching that is black and white in its contrast that draws lines and upholds holy standards, and says things that are a true revelation, as in never having been said or claimed before. And the result is a great many people not liking said person. Add to that boldness, the ability to see into their hearts And the hatred for Jesus could only increase. When Jesus told them that they wanted to kill him, They thought that was their chance to prove that Jesus is the crazy one. Because they could act incredulous, as if Jesus had no basis for making such a claim. But again, Jesus knew their hearts. And they did not know that Jesus knew their hearts, or at least they didn't want to admit that Jesus knew their hearts. And so they put up a front that tries to make Jesus seem to be the demented one. But because Jesus was correct about their motive That gave them another reason to hate him. And their hatred for Jesus blinded them to understanding the plain truth about the law. Jesus then gives them example of how they're not even seeing the plain truth about the law they say they follow. They had accused, remember, Jesus of healing on the Sabbath day, thus Jesus working on the Sabbath day. But Jesus points out to them that they too work on the Sabbath day when they circumcise. You see, the law says that you are to circumcise a young male born into the covenant of Abraham on the eighth day And if the eighth day fell on a Saturday, the Sabbath, for the Jews, well, then they went ahead and followed that commandment the eighth day and circumcised a child. Jesus points out this exception, not condemning them for it, but simply points out that they too do some work on the Sabbath, just like he did some work on the Sabbath. The commandment of God says to love your neighbor, and Jesus loves his neighbor by healing on the Sabbath. It was an exception. Of course. The law isn't contradictory. You simply do as the law commands, as Jesus did. But exceptions, according to the hearts of those who hate Jesus, are for them to choose. Such grace is what they give to themselves, never considering giving such to Jesus. And this is how Jesus can challenge them to stop looking outwardly and to look at the heart. See what's going on in your heart. But they don't want to admit the righteous heart of Jesus, even though it's plainly obvious. And because they know it's obvious and they don't want to admit it, that makes them more mad and gives them another reason to hate Jesus. There is a consistency of those who hate Jesus. They only look on the outward. meaning the physical world. These were the first century empiricists, insisting that all knowledge comes from their sensory experiences only. They talk about where Jesus is from. They could only know that Jesus physically was from Galilee, to them only from Galilee. They could only understand that Jesus could go to a place they could not go to, because Jesus said that and they didn't understand it, so they only understood it in terms of, oh, he must be talking about going amongst the Greeks, and we wouldn't want to go amongst the Greeks. They could only understand the world in terms of their own experiences with the world, never considering that there is an entirely different world altogether. But a funny thing happens, if you read that text, a funny thing happens when Jesus teaches. Regardless if there are people around him that hate him, some people can't help but believe in him. His words are so full of life and truth, some stop denying the obvious and believe him to be the Messiah. As verse 31 tells us, many people believed on Jesus as the Messiah because they stopped denying the obvious. What more could be expected for a man claiming to be the Messiah than what Jesus has already done? Nothing is the answer, and this is where we come to this what I call the the come on moment We can say, come on. When someone is acting like they don't really understand something that they simply have chosen not to understand, rather than admitting it's understandable We can say, come on. When we see a person denying the obvious It was not the Pharisees, not that the Pharisees didn't have the evidence in believing in Jesus right before them. Thus we can say to them, come on. For they knew the evidence was there. Jesus divides, and they chose the side of unbelief. Well, the last section of chapter seven is the last day of the feast of the tabernacle. Verse 43, look at that verse. Verse 43 sums up this sermon and thus all of the events that have happened in this chapter. It says, so there was a division among the people because of him. The him is Jesus. In this section, you have people arguing about interpreting Scripture properly to better identify the Messiah. Jesus caused that argument. You have soldiers disobeying orders to arrest Jesus because they were in awe of his teaching. Jesus caused that. You have the Pharisees claiming the crowd to be accursed. Because they're believing him. Jesus caused that. You have a Pharisee sticking up for him. Jesus caused that. You have Pharisees accusing that one Pharisee of siding with Jesus. Jesus caused that too. Jesus divides. And this should have been expected. When God said that there would be strife between Ishmael and Isaac for generations, We see that literally in their descendants as Arab states and the Jewish state cannot remain at peace It seems that since 1948, the center of the world has been the Middle East, where Arab states and the Jewish state are in repetitive tension. And that tension will not be resolved with any type of peace agreement. Don't ever get happy about one. For the Arab states and the Jewish state are under the curse of God, as descendants of Ishmael and Isaac, respectively. Therefore, and understand this well. The only way such a curse can be overcome is by the blood of Jesus. Know that and believe it. But Jesus divides. So here is the great irony of God's redemptive plan of God Almighty The redemptive plan of God Almighty, the greatest irony, is that the man who divides is the only one who can bring peace That the world hates us should then not be a surprise. The world is under a curse, and the only one who can lift that curse is Jesus. And Jesus divides. The only one who can bring peace is the one who divides. Jesus will say later in John, if the world hates you, remember that it hated me first. There is no question, now more than ever in any of our lifetimes, that Christianity and us Christians are under attack. Recall that I have said from this pulpit that the devil wants to do one of two things to each and every one of us. He wants to either deceive us, to deny the faith in Jesus Christ, or he wants to kill us. One of the other. And that is where the hate comes from. And our challenge, and it is a great high calling indeed, Our challenge is that we are to love those who hate us. We are to pray for our enemies. As we profess Jesus, the Jesus who divides, let us accept that there will be hate toward us. But our response is no jihad. Our response is not a sword for a sword. Our response is to love as Jesus loved and to pray as Jesus prayed. So following Jesus is like sitting at a Ravens game in a Pittsburgh Steeler Troy Palomalo jersey. With a Pittsburgh Steeler hat on and sunglasses. People are pointing, they're whispering, what's the deal with that guy? And someone is pointing and saying, well, we can all agree to hate that guy. We should expect such a response because we follow the one who divided, the one who men hated. But we love him. And so we endure for him. Not because we like to be different for different sake. Or not because we want to be obnoxious and bother Ravens fans. We expect it. Because the world hated Jesus first. And we are to love our enemies because Jesus loves us. Amen and Amen. Let us pray

sermons.title: The Authority to Forgive Sins
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. I want to express my uh sincere gratitude to Bishop Cox for filling in on Christmas Day As I was on my fifth hour of worship worshiping the porcelain throne, I realized I couldn't uh depend on anybody else but him. And uh So grateful for his fatherly graciousness to all of us, but including me. Grateful for him and Bill Bowles and everyone. And thankful this morning for the three winds to come out and play for us. And Tim playing his trumpet makes me feel like I didn't miss Christmas Day. So grateful for that. Today I prayed a prayer, a call-ex for St. John the Evangelist, and we are staying in the Gospel according to St. John, so we'll take that as providence. Today is the Feast of St. John. Yesterday was the Feast of St. Stephen. And I do want to encourage you before I get into the sermon that all of our families would make note that tomorrow is the Feast of Holy Innocence. And in that day we remember that Herod did order all children to be killed. Of course, we live in a time when uh children are tossed away in s in a similar manner. And so please make note of that. Your family should be having devotions of prayer, asking God to forgive us for the sin of abortion, and also pray that we always be mindful of those who sacrificed for our Savior. We are in John chapter 8, and uh we are looking more closely at the woman caught in adultery, but also we're looking at the challenge that was given upon Jesus Growing up in the Roman Catholic Church, I have a distinct memory of my first communion That usually occurs for a young Roman Catholic at the age of seven. The required task for a seven-year-old is to attend his or her first confession. What I remember about my first confession is that I was, and I think most of you growing up Roman Catholic will recall this, I was making stuff up. My conscience, which is to say my awareness of my sinfulness, had not much developed, and so my ability to identify my personal sin was inadequate for that moment. It was not until my teenage years that I started to realize just how sinful my heart was. And I will spare you the details of that sinful heart, only to say that what other people were doing outwardly, I was likely doing inwardly. My brother and brother-in-law remember a conversation we three had on our way back from a workout when I was the age of 17. They were talking about life priorities and what should be most important to us as young men, and they agreed that God should be first in our lives. Even though neither of them were walking on the road to the city of God. And then they asked me, what was my first priority? According to them, because I don't remember the conversation well, according to them, I said football was my first priority. They remember that conversation more clearly than I do, but I do remember that my own arrogance and the sport of football were indeed God's to me. Add to that my lust of the flesh, and I was a true secularist. But I was not without a conscience. I knew my life was not respectful. I knew that I was not living by God's standards. And I also knew that I was not even living up to my standards. In the culture we now live that seemingly will not will not acknowledge absolute truth, thus will not acknowledge absolute moral truth, There is still one thing that we all have in common. We all have guilty consciences. Such a statement I make to my philosophy class each semester during my lecture on natural law. And the non-verbal communication, when they hear that they too have a guilty conscience, the non-verbal communication they give back to me tells me that they agree We all have guilty consciences. And if someone says that they don't, well, just understand that he or she is lying. We all have guilty consciences. And I believe that is why the story of the woman caught in adultery, as told in John 8, is so very, very important. Let us now look at that story. I encourage you to turn to John chapter 8. Before I begin, I am forced to mention that the story found in this section of Scripture is not accepted as inspired scripture by many evangelicals, for it is not found in some of the most trusted manuscripts for which we receive our English translation. I preach about the story today, however, in the context of what follows. For I contend that the story of the woman caught in adultery is connected to the challenge made to Jesus regarding his authority. And most importantly, about that authority is his ability to forgive sins. The setting of the story. The setting of the story of the woman caught in adultery has Jesus once again inside the temple walls teaching. The word taught here is in the imperfect tense and thus could be translated was teaching. And that indicates that it was something that Jesus did frequently and was ongoing. It is interesting that this is the only place that John mentions the scribes Whereas the expression scribes and Pharisees occurs in all the other three Gospels. It's the first time it occurs, and the only time it occurs in John's. By the manner the adulterous woman is brought to Jesus, we can interpret immediately that their purpose, their main purpose, was not to attain justice. As has been pointed out by many commentators and preachers before me, the absence of the male counterpart in this story is the most obvious of proofs that these scribes were not after justice. To state it plainly, if you were able to catch someone in the act of adultery, there would have been two persons present. That the woman is the only one brought to Jesus reminds us of how women were treated in the first century, and it tells us that the trapping of Jesus was the main goal. And thus the male sinner was not needed. The scribes and Pharisees invoke the Word of God to Jesus as if that was necessary. They want to see if Jesus would fulfill the law of God as it is written. Notice these men, these educated men, these religious leaders. They would not fulfill the law themselves. They would not pick up a stone. They would not enact justice in the moment. But that point evidently is not important. What is important for them was to expose Jesus as a hypocrite. Remember that they hated him at this time, and this story is an example of how they hated him. The Mosaic Law says that the penalty of stoning a woman caught in adultery is to be applied when the woman is either a betrothed virgin or an already married woman. And so we assume that this woman was either one of the two. The problem was that in the days of Jesus, the carrying out of the Mosaic law, as it is written, was forbidden by Roman law. Under Julius Caesar, the Jews were given permission by law to perform their religious practices, and that continued under Caesar Augustus. But judicial law was overseen by the Romans. Thus, she would have to be turned over to the Romans to be punished. So these men are putting Jesus in another conundrum where he was to choose to go against God's law and be labeled a religious hypocrite, thus a sinner. Or against Roman law and be considered a subversive of the state. In case there is any doubt about the motive behind this case, John makes it clear in these verses, especially in verse 6. That they were indeed doing all of this to test Jesus. And of course, not just testing him to see what he would do, but testing him so that he would fail. The next move Jesus makes is to stoop down, which means that he went from sitting, which is normally the posture when someone was teaching, to then kneeling. As has been pointed out by many, the act of Jesus riding in the dirt on the ground, apparently with his finger. is the only recorded writing that Jesus ever did. Why that is significant, I don't know, but every commentator mentions it And there have been many speculations regarding what Jesus wrote. Some guess he was writing the accusation that was being made towards the woman, like writing adultery. Others claim that it was the sins of her accusers that he was writing down. Others guessed that he wrote out what he eventually said. My conclusion is that because the story does not tell us, well, then that information is not important. Perhaps Jesus was writing as a as a technique of pausing before he spoke. That it seems to be the interpretation of the storyteller. As commentator Joseph Mayfield describes, Jesus' response to their accusation was a coup de grace. The key word was anamartetos, which we translate without sin. With such a word, Jesus addresses the consciences of these men, these accusers. Consider how easy it is to condemn a revealed sinner While ignoring your own heart. A man lashes out in anger and stabs another man. And we condemn that man as a violent criminal. When there have been times when our anger has been so high in a level that if we had something sharp in our hands, we very well could have stabbed someone ourselves. A woman is pregnant out of wedlock and she is looked down upon for her lack of self-control when many a man has undressed many a woman in his own heart and mind. A politician can be caught in a lie and become a pariah to the talking heads in the media, whereas those same talking heads have told so many lies, they go uncounted. The point is that if a person is going to be a representative of God's law, he or she better not have sin in his or her life. But we all have sin in our lives. Serious sin. Not the sin of a seven-year-old at first confession. But sin in which we knew what we wanted to do and we knew it was wrong. We knew it was a sin against God and a sin against man, but we did it anyways. Such makes us no more righteous than a person having been caught in the act. That is Jesus' main point. It is rightly noted by most commentators that the elders leave the scene first because they are the most aware of their own personal sins, having lived long enough to sin much. But all leave. All must leave, for all have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God. And because Jesus knew the hearts of men, he knew that none would be left to condemn the woman. And so he does not condemn. But, but Jesus does more than not condemn, because he is the only one in the story, you note. That has the moral authority to condemn her. She was a sinner. That was clear. The problem was there was no one who had the moral authority to judge her, that is to say, condemn her, except Jesus. Thus, for Jesus not to condemn her is for Jesus to forgive her. This is the coup de grace. And let us not think that the forgiveness of Jesus is a license to go on sinning, for Jesus makes it clear in his command to her, go and sin no more. This was truly a dramatic moment, a dramatic scene in the life of Jesus. And it brings Up the necessary revelation that Jesus has the authority. In fact, Jesus is the only one who has the authority to forgive sin. It is similar. You remember to the scene of the paralytic. You remember the story of the man being lowered by his brethren. Down to the roof of Peter's house and Jesus seeing their their faith, he says, your sins are forgiven. And the Pharisees object And in response, Jesus challenges them to understand what is more difficult, to forgive sins or to heal such a man. Of course, they don't answer because they're really cowards. And Jesus, showing that his authority extends from earth to heaven, heals the man on the spot. Such is what Jesus is revealing here when he is focusing on his authority, the most important authority, to forgive sins. The story of Jesus forgiving sins of this adulterous woman then flows into a teaching of John once again about Jesus being the light of the world. Jesus says of himself, I am the light of the world. As light of the world, he can help people walk in the light. Which is a life that has sins revealed and has sins forgiven. That's walking in the light. Those who walk in darkness Think that their sins are hidden from others, while also thinking that their sins cannot be seen by God. Those who brought the adulterous woman before Jesus to test him were examples of those who were walking in darkness. They thought the rest of the story didn't matter, that God didn't care They hide their sins behind the sins of others. They are fooled by God's silence. No thunder rolls, no lightning strikes when they commit their sins, and so they conclude that God must not know. Thus they show that their reasoning and their consciences are in the dark.
