Because the disciples tend to understand statements that Jesus made in the most plain of meanings, they are hopeful that his illness is something that he can recover from. And this gives opportunity for Jesus to confirm why he delayed and what his primary purpose is in this moment. He wants them to believe that Jesus is the Messiah. That's why he wants to bring forth the glory of God so that he might convince them. I love this part of the story because it teaches us that belief is something that we grow in. You see, the disciples already believed Jesus was the Messiah. They've already confessed it. But they needed to believe more and more. They needed to have greater faith. Don't we all? Don't we all? We need to grow and grow in our faith, and we do so by having God's word confirmed in our lives and by experiencing the grace of God through Jesus again and again and again. And next in verse 16 we have a heroism espoused by Thomas, a very unique verse, and it shows us that he's more than a doubter. Thomas is a brave man, loyal to the end of his life. And because of the proximity of Bethany to Jerusalem, we read that so many friends and family from the Holy City were able to come to the aid of Mary and Martha. And when Jesus arrives, Martha has an exchange of words that we can read into a bit. Martha is second-guessing the timing of Jesus. O good Christians, too often we question the timing of the Savior regarding answering our prayers. We pretend often that we have divine eyes that can see what is best to happen and what time it should happen. And yet the delay of our Savior is not that he does not care, it is not that he has not heard from us. It is because it is according to his timing. It is according to his will. And it is for us to humbly accept such timing, for we are servants. His servants and thus called to wait on him and not he on us. Well Martha's faith is re- is real and honoring of Jesus, but it also reveals that she is immature and needing to grow Martha believes in the resurrection of the dead. Many Jews do, did, excuse me, many Jews did, and many Jews do. And our trip to Jerusalem, we embarked up on the Mount of Olives. And there you see scores of graves. Great markers. And there are there many on the Mount of Olives and then at the foot of the walls of Jerusalem. And they house Jews and Christians and Muslims, all who believe that their bodies will one day be raised from the dead. Yet it is only the Christian that has the testimony that such has already been done, and why we know it will happen many, many times again. Now the further explanation Jesus provides to Martha is the actual glory of God that Jesus came to reveal. These words of Jesus, I am the resurrection and the life, our everything in terms of God's glory to be revealed for the salvation of mankind. It is what he wants to reveal to us, within us, and through us. And Jesus asked Martha, do you believe this? And I say, wow, what a question. What a question to be asked. And it is necessary for any good preacher to point out that each of us is asked that same question. Each of us is asked, do you believe this? And each of us is to answer in the affirmative: if we want to live forever, never die. The confession of Martha is what needs to be said by all who want to live and never die. Yes, Lord, I believe in you. You are the Christ, the Son of God. And beloved, that is what we are each of us saying whenever we recite one of the creeds. Whenever we bow our heads and pray in the name of Jesus, we are confessing what we believe. The next part of the story has Mary coming to Jesus. St. John is telling the story to clear up the movements of the characters. Martha had met with Jesus, talked with him, and then had gone back home, shared with Mary what had they had conversed about. Mary didn't know Jesus was there, so Mary makes her way to Jesus. Sure why Jesus stays in that spot, but he does. And so Mary comes to him, and here she is more forthright than Martha her sister, for she tells Jesus plainly That if he had arrived earlier, Lazarus would have been healed, and thus would not have died from the illness that had overcome him. Verses 33, 34, and 35. I want you to see those verses as one verse. They are to be treated as one thought or one description of one event that is so very unique, but a necessary part of the entire story. Jesus, wanting to know where Lazarus' body was laid, asks, inquires, and while he does so, he looks around and he sees people mourning, and he identifies with them. In his identifying with the mourners, he joins them, joins them in their emotional pain, and the result is Jesus left. God cried. And let us utterly reject the notion or any teaching that suggests That Jesus cries here as if displaying his humanity or his human nature. That is completely false. What he is displaying is everything that he is. He is displaying that he is the Savior, the Good Shepherd, the light of the world, the bread of life, the resurrection, and that means He identifies fully, completely, unreservedly with the pain of humanity. God cried Let us all have faith and know the Savior well so that we know that when we cry, He cries. He does not just know of our pain, but knows our pain intimately, and therefore does not leave us to ourselves in our times of need, but experiences our hurts with us. Beloved, God cries. And Jesus then made his way to the tomb where Lazarus lay, and there were people observing this drama who second guessed Jesus. They too thought he should have arrived sooner and done his healing thing, and Lazarus would have been healed. But they are not looking for the glory of God to be revealed. Jesus is. And John tells us that when Jesus orders the stone to be taken away, that he is still emotionally hurting because of the pain of those that loved Lazarus. Now regarding this tomb, maybe you've seen pictures, but we assume this tomb is very much like those of the first century, either carved out of a stone or carved out of a hill. And uh such were in the first century the way that the Jews were buried. They would be placed in a uh cave-like tomb. And they would wait for their bodies to decay, and then once that had occurred, they would go in and collect the bones and put it in an ossuary. Like a little tiny casket. And then those ossuaries were placed in a uh a larger tomb for the family if the family had the means to own such a tomb Some bodies decomposed or decomposed just after 24 hours. And this had been four days. Unfortunately, because of Jesus' instruction to move the tombstone away, Martha reveals her weak faith, and the result is Jesus repeating the purpose of the whole drama that they were in at that moment. The whole purpose of Lazarus getting sick, the whole purpose of Jesus waiting two days before eating, starving toward Bethany The whole purpose of Jesus speaking to Martha and then speaking to Mary, the whole purpose of emotionally suffering with the mourners, the whole purpose was to reveal the glory of God. Jesus next prays, and his prayer exemplifies how he and the Father are one. One. He prays for the sake of those who were around him. He prays for the sake of you and I who read this story He prays to show that he that what he does, he does because of the Heavenly Father who calls him to raise the dead. And Jesus then gives the command, Lazarus, come forth. Now John tells us that this was done in a loud voice, so we can imagine Jesus shouted, Lazarus, come forth. Now this shouting was done by Jesus not for dramatic effect Because of the prayer that Jesus just prayed for the purpose of those around him, we might think that Jesus is shouting also for the people around him as if he is acting out a play And this also comes from the reality that you and I can both imagine, all of us can imagine, that Jesus could have whispered, or he could have said nothing at all, and Lazarus still would have come forward. But Jesus did say something. And in saying something, we are reminded that all of creation came into being because God spoke. And we are to recall that all creation came under a curse because of the sin of mankind that he brought into the world. Death. Thus, when Jesus shouts for Lazarus to come forth, he is remaking his creation. He is bringing life back into his creation. By Jesus shouting, he is also exhibiting how far his authority goes. It goes down to the bowels of the dead. It goes to the gates of hell. And finally, Jesus shouts because what he did for Lazarus was a precursor to what he will do for every person who believes that he is the resurrection and the life. Jesus will shout us out of our graves. He will shout to all of creation to give up the dead. He will shout so that all of the flesh will be restored on the day of judgment. And the very loving thing Jesus did for Lazarus, he will do for all who believe in him. He called Lazarus from the grave by name. And he will call each of us who believe in him by name from the grave as well. And so all that is done in this story of Lazarus being raised from the dead was for the glory of God to be revealed, and the glory of God to be revealed is that Jesus Is the resurrection and the life. In closing I want us to think of Paul Lazarus just for a moment in regards to what he experienced, what he suffered. He suffered an illness, we don't know what it was, likely, difficult. He then in that illness faced his mortality. I'm going to die. And then he died. He then was raised from the dead. And no doubt celebrated his new life. And yet, sometime later, nobody knows when, but sometime later, he died again. So he faced death twice. I love this quote by C. S. Lewis. Who contemplated the possibility of his wife Joy returning from the dead? Lewis said this I never raised the question whether a return, if it were possible, would be good for her. I want her back as an ingredient of my past. Could I have wished for her anything worse? Having got once through death, to come back, and then at some time later, having all of her dying to do over again? They call Stephen I martyr. Hadn't Lazarus a rarer deal. That's a rather whimsical way to describe the situation of Lazarus. But for the Christian, the point is not that we face death once, twice. The point instead is knowing that Jesus is the resurrection. That was the point of all the details of this story, even for Lazarus, who had to die twice. And for those who mourned him twice, it was all to reveal the glory of God, which is that Jesus is the resurrection and the life. It seems to me that someone ought to break out in song whenever it is proclaimed that Jesus is the resurrection and the life. When I was writing this sermon, every time I wrote Jesus is the resurrection in the life, I thought of trumpets and of choir and beauty. The trumpet shall sound, the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. St. Paul's words to the Corinthians are the words chosen by Handel. He used for his masterpiece, the Messiah. And during this move in the Messiah, as a male tenor is proclaiming those words of St. Paul, of the resurrection The trumpets sound as one along with the tenor. Trumpets are the only true instrument this side of heaven that can adequately announce the resurrection. Jesus is the resurrection, beloved. Feel how real that is. Believe it, and it will be oh so very real for you now and in that day. Amen and Amen. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Decisions, Decisions
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Leave me seated. We're looking at our reading from the Gospel according to John this morning. Always good to open your Bible and read the words therein. I want you to take inventory of how many decisions you have made today already You decided to get out of bed. You decided to eat breakfast. Or not eat breakfast. He decided to wear that tie. Or no tie at all. Or that dress. Or not that dress, that skirt. Or not that skirt, but slacks. Women have it a lot tougher than men, to be sure. You decided to pick up after yourself after getting ready Or wait till you got home from worship. You decided to attend Sunday school, or not Because, well I don't know why you would not. And you decided to come to worship? I know, because you are here. If you are listening to this sermon for the first time over the internet, then you either could not attend worship this morning or you decided not to go, and again, I for a reason I would not understand. There are a lot of decisions and important ones at that, and I didn't mention the lesser decisions we make at the beginning of our day. And all the of this decision making is just this morning. Many, many more decisions will be made today and tomorrow and the next day. And all of them add up to a number that none of us want to spend time counting. And in all of these decisions made, I next ask you. To consider how much of your thought process in making that decision was about yourself How much of your decision making was based on what you thought was best for you In other words, how much of your decision making was motivated by selfishness? Note that I am not condemning you for being selfish. When I take inventory about my own decisions and force myself under the same scrutiny Well, I am undone. I have to conclude that I am selfish in my decision making most of the time And this is why our liturgy has us confessing sins of what we have done and what we have left undone, recognizing it's usually because of self. It is why we confess we have followed too much the devices and desires of our own hearts. I am aware that the selfishness I practice is so very common that I don't know all of the times that I am practicing it. And I confess that for your sake as well as my own. The subject of decision-making is pertinent to our passage from the Gospel of John As we are made privy to a discussion amongst the Sadducees and the Pharisees about how they were going to address what they considered the problem of Jesus. And Jesus does present a problem to anyone who does not believe. Jesus was a problem when he walked this earth, and he is a problem today to anyone who hears his name and has yet to decide to believe in him as the Messiah, the Son of God. That hangs in their consciences, you know, as it did some of us when we didn't know him or confess him. As we examine this exchange between the priests and the Pharisees, we must keep in mind that a miracle has just happened. Someone got raised from the dead. And it was a miracle of astounding proportions. And the miracle, hear this now, could be verified. There were witnesses. There were people that you could go and ask. You could go to them and ask, did you see Lazarus sick? And then did you see him dead? Did you see him buried in that tomb? Did you see him come out of that same tomb alive again at the command of Jesus of Nazareth? And they would say, yes, I saw every moment of it. They could go to a doctor who could verify the illness and the death and then the life, the life given again. Such was the same in John 9, when the blind man was healed and his blindness could be verified by his parents at the pool of Siloam. And the man who was blind and then could see could testify. Any one could ask him, and he could tell them, Jesus is the one who healed me. Such verifications are not like the healings we hear about that occurred in foreign lands somewhere else. We hear about a healing and nothing is verified. Jesus didn't just do things for the point of doing them. He did them as a testimony to himself. Jesus did it to prove his miracles were real, and thus he was really the Messiah. And yet, and that's a underlying, and yet, and yet, such matters not at all, such matters not at all to these men Who meet together to figure out what to do about the problem of Jesus. Forget about all of his miracles. Let's talk about what we need to do to get him out of the way. What causes such stubbornness? What causes such blindness to the truth? What causes such obstinence to be without hope? They are insisting they don't want to have hope. These men in their conversation, they're going to tell us what causes this. The chief priests and Pharisees were the principal members of the Sanhedrin, which was the religious body that was given just a little bit of clout by Rome. They were responsible to settle religious matters only because Rome didn't want to have to. The discussion begins with the confessing of the miracles of Jesus. and then expressing what their two options are as seen by them The first is to think that if they let Jesus alone and thus let him continue what he was doing, Which is to convince people that he was indeed the Messiah of Israel, that they had waited for for oh so many years. If they let him continue, all the people would go to his side. And we know that Jesus was convincing the crowds by what he said, by what he did, and what type of man he was. It is a natural part of creation. Something that God has embedded into creation That the most convincing of leaders are those who make logical sense, who live by high ethical standards, and those who empathize with those they lead. And Jesus did all of that, and certainly much more. So their train of thought continued, concluding that if Jesus convinces people in the manner he was doing, then the people would make him king after King David, in the line of King David. And thus this would cause Rome to bring in their armies and destroy their land That is what they mean by, quote, the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation. The Greek word translated here to be placed in the New King James Version as in take away our place is literally land, and thus many translators replaced temple. The temple for land, interpreting in their translation that the leaders are concerned that the temple would be taken away, destroyed. Now the fear of the Romans taking away their nation must refer to the independence they perceived that they had. And this is quite unfortunate for these religious leaders to think that they had any meaningful independence. They had settled, evidently, on the occupancy of Rome. They were not crying out to God for forgiveness and for deliverance as the prophets had done before them. These religious leaders were still in captivity and they did not know it. They were prisoners in the covenantal land God had promised them, and they were satisfied with their state of being. That tells us something, doesn't it? We could get satisfied with our state of being not realizing that we're in captivity The second option this impromptu council thought they had was articulated by Caiophys, who was the high priest at the time. John says he was high priest that year. Interestingly, that phrase is unique to John and his writing, and it is believed he is referring to that year being the year that Jesus died. The option, rudely put by Caiophus, was for one man to die, and the rest of them, the leaders and the nation, to be spared. There is, of course, great irony in this utterance by Caiophus. The first is that he was indeed the high priest And as the high priest, it was his responsibility to offer a sacrifice once a year, the atonement sacrifice, for the salvation, for the forgiveness of all of God's people. Caiophas thus was fulfilling his priestly duties by offering up Jesus, but he didn't realize he was offering him up for the sins of mankind. And thus the other part of the irony is Jesus was indeed being offered up for the sins of many, not so that other people won't get hurt by Rome. And John adds a very pastoral word in verse fifty-two. He includes us. He includes believers that will follow. He includes us today. Those who hear his gospel will know that Jesus did indeed die for them. Not just those who were alive at Jesus when Jesus was alive, but for all who would come after. Of course we know that the wisdom of Caiophas was the winning plan. They plotted to put Jesus to death. Of course they did. They put only two options before themselves. Which was ridiculous to begin with. There were plenty of more options, but they put only two before them, only two choices, and they chose the most evil one. Of course they did. I asked earlier what makes people so stubborn, so obstinate, so truly terrible. And we can answer such a question from the very words of the Sadducees and the Pharisees. Look with me again at verse 48. There the members of the Sanhedrin are reported to saying to one another that if Jesus isn't stopped, the Romans will come, take away both their land and their nation. And yet there's an unusual wording in the Greek, and scholars say it is a result that the emphasis falls especially on the pronoun our. As in our place and our nation. It occurs very frequently in the Greek, but first in this phrase. In other words, they fear that the Romans will take these things away from them personally. Not for the nation or all of us together, but for them as leaders personally. They are, in other words, less worried about the well-being of the nation and its people Than they are about their own positions of power and prestige. The second instance of this emphasis occurs in verse 50. And there John quotes the priest Caiophas as saying, It is expedient for us that one man should die for the whole people. Now what Kyophus was doing in case you did not catch it was making a naked appeal to their own self-interest. The emphasis again is on us. And the us are the Sadducees and the Pharisees. It was expedient for them. And he knows. He knows that the rest of them listening to him want to hold on to their privilege, to their rank, to their status, to the economic benefits. He knows they want it as bad as he does. And so he frames his option in those terms. He essentially says to them, Make the decision that is best for you. And of course, they did. They did not consider how many more lame people could walk if Jesus was still alive. They did not consider that more blind could see, that more dead could be raised, that more hungry could be fed. No No. This whole matter in their eyes was about them And so we have our answer as to why people are so obstinate to the truth. It is because of selfishness. It is because of self-love, which is plain hate toward others. But it is too easy, isn't it, to condemn these men for their selfishness. Yes, we must identify it, absolutely, and call it for what it is, absolutely. But they are not alone in their self-love. In a recent study done by the University of California researchers on recently published books in the United States and Britain. They show that the word get has increased significantly in our writings. And that is compared to the word give, which has significantly gone down. That subtle difference is evidence to psychologists that we have become a more self-absorbed, self-serving society. But of course, scientific studies are unnecessary. We only need to look at what entertains us to see a reflection of ourselves and what we see In movies is that we celebrate looking out for ourselves. We celebrate pursuing fame, pursuing power, pursuing money, all for self It is blatant today. No one apologizes for it because no one is ashamed of it. I say no one for dramatic effect, but it certainly does seem that that selfishness dominates our airways But we don't need studies or critique of what entertains us to know how self-absorbed, how selfish, how self-loving we are. We only need to look at ourselves. Amongst ethical theories, there is a category officially called egoism. It is a theory that proposes, argues, that it is perfectly ethical, meaning perfectly moral, for a person to think of themselves first when they are faced with a moral dilemma. The argument goes that if we all think about ourselves first and foremost, then we don't have to worry about one another. You take care of yours, I'll take care of mine. We will remain separate and responsible. And there are even different subcategories under egoism. Such as individual egoism, which states that all persons are morally responsible to think about themselves And if one does not put him or herself first, then he or her is being immoral. It is your moral duty to be selfish. Then there is personal egoism, and that says that every person is to think about his or her own best interests first and not be concerned about what everybody else is doing. And finally, there is universal egoism, and that says that we should all think about ourselves first when facing a moral dilemma. But If you do have a chance to do something for others, go ahead and do it as long as it will come back and help you later. As I said, this is an actual accepted ethical theory on how one should live his or her life. The critique I have with all forms of egoism is that it does not have to be a theory in order to be practiced. Egoism comes naturally to all of us. Those who perceive egoism to be a theory like that of utilitarianism or or Kantian ethics, they are kidding themselves. For all they have done is put a labels on behaviors that human beings do without thinking. To call this a theory seems to be motivated by wanting to justify selfish behavior. And I believe it is within every human being the knowledge that altruistic motivation is morally right and thus righteous. I believe it is within each of us to recognize that to put another person's needs in front of our own is a good thing to do. And thus, as Christians, when we hear Jesus say that we are to die to ourselves, when we hear him say that we are to pick up our own cross. When we hear him say, do unto others as you would have them do unto you. When we hear him say, That we are that a man who tries to save his life will lose it, and a man who loses his life will retain it. When we hear him say all of these things, we say to ourselves, of course, of course, that makes sense. We know as followers of Jesus Christ that to make decisions based on what is best for others and not ourselves is the righteous thing to do. When self-love is identified as immoral and something we ought not to do if we are followers of Jesus. It is hard for the modern mind to accept that because we are told that it is necessary to love ourselves in order to have good mental health. I recall my mother attending an Al-Anon meeting to learn how to cope with my father's alcoholism. And one of the first lessons she learned was how to love herself. She was told that when the Bible says, love your neighbor as yourself. It is to teach us that we must learn to love ourselves before we can ever start learning to love our neighbor. Well, that is poor biblical interpretation. The instruction to love our neighbor assumes we love ourselves. Like most everything else it does, the secular world misconstrued conclusions about mental health. For they contain only partial truth. It is true that no human being should hate his or herself. But the reason why we should not hate ourselves is not because we are worthy of self-love. It is because God made us. And God loves us, each and every one of us. God's purpose for us is the basis for why we should think positively about ourselves And God's love for us is the reason why we don't need to learn about how to self-love or think of ourselves first. The motivation behind the decision made by the Sadducees and Pharisees to murder Jesus was out of selfishness and self-love. It came naturally to them. But that decision, beloved, is to be in contrast to what Jesus was doing and the decision he was making at the same moment. We ought to remember that Jesus said that no one takes his life from him, but he lays it down according to his own will. He lays it down himself. So while these Sadducees and Pharisees were thinking they were making a choice to end the life of Jesus for their own sake. The truth was that their plans meant nothing because Jesus was doing it by his own will. And Jesus willed it because he put the needs of others before his own. Of course he did. And so Christians are to make decisions as Jesus did. We are to think of others before self. Of course we should. Amen.

sermons.title: Pour out your oil
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. You will do well to open your Bibles to John chapter twelve. That's where our focus is this morning. I got into an argument with a student in one of my college classes last week. And he was visibly upset at me. We were talking about determinism versus libertarianism Libertarianism believes that human beings have free will in all things, and thus are able to choose their own destiny. Determinism, and in particular hard determinism, states that our choices are only illusions. And that the choices we think we make are actually caused by outside sources that we cannot control. Every decision has causes before it, and thus what we choose is really the only choice we had or have. The problem with hard determinism is that it takes away human responsibility. The reasoning goes that if all things are determined, then no human is morally culpable, responsible for his or her actions. Thus, to punish a person for acting immorally is unjust because the guilty person did not have a choice. Philosophers try to answer this objection by introducing a soft determinism theory. which identifies internal causes as part of the equation when it comes to decision-making, and thus providing personal responsibility back in to when immoral choices are made. Now, if all of that doesn't interest you, then I simply point to the point I made that caused this student to become so angry with me I suggested that freedom to make choices is not true freedom, because all of our choices are restricted by the options themselves. Consider that if I put a candy bar before you in one hand and I put an apple before you in the other, and I say you can choose which one you wanted. And you chose the candy bar, most people probably would, and I asked you how you came about to make that choice, you could answer by your own free will But I could argue that your will was not free to choose because your options were restricted to the apple or the candy bar, candy bar apple only. And thus if you define freedom as having no restrictions, no restrictions, then you cannot say you chose freely because you were restricted to one of the two options. Now the student who got upset insisted that whenever we make choices, we are doing so freely because the one no one No one forces us to choose one thing over another. I countered with the point I originally made that the options themselves limit us in our choices, thus, because there is restrictions on our options, there is no true freedom. He made his point again without addressing my definition, and so I challenged him to do so. Challenge my definition His counterpoint was no, and that ended the discussion. My main point in telling you that story is to give us a working definition of the word freedom. Freedom having no restrictions. And when I say no restrictions, I mean just what that universal negation says. Zero restrictions. When we examine the actions of Mary pouring out oil on the feet of Jesus, we are to understand That she was a woman who loved Jesus without restrictions. And such love is the standard that we are to love the Savior as well. The story told by John in chapter 12 is also told in the Gospel according to Mark, and that means we're going to use both of those stories to inform us. Because John calls immediate attention to Lazarus, we can rightly assume, and he actually says in there, that people wanted to see Lazarus. So as much as this was for Jesus, it was likely also a dinner for Lazarus as well. And we are told also that Lazarus reclined at the table, and this informs us that Lazarus was of good health. Mark tells us that the meal was held in the home of Simon the leper, who very likely was someone that Jesus had healed and possibly was related or at least a close friend to Mary, Martha, and Lazarus. Lazarus being raised from the dead was so very much on everyone's mind who were at this dinner party that Mary being so close to Lazarus as his sister, and having sat at the feet of Jesus, taking in every word he spoke, was rightly Overcome by the greatest of loves, and found a way to express herself to the Savior with no restrictions. A Roman pound of spikenard would have been approximately twelve ounces, we are told. Mark tells us that the oil was in an alabaster flask, and this would have been evidence to those viewing this moment that this was expensive inside. While Mark focuses on the oil being poured on the head of Jesus, John focuses on it being poured on his feet. And being wiped upon his feet, spread upon his feet with Mary's hair. John's memory has Mary in a most humble position. A position that every Christian should take before the Savior. And another reason while kneeling to receive bread and wine at communion is so very appropriate. For we believe we are kneeling before Christ when He offers us that bread and that cup. He is in our midst, like no other time, when we partake. Thus kneeling is most appropriate. By John informing us of the perfume filling the room, he is describing an aesthetic moment that was beautiful to the senses. And while Mark makes the point that others in the room thought the costly perfume to be wasted, John tells us the objection was led by Judas Iscariot. John fingerpoints him. And by John's commentary about Judas being a thief and caring nothing for the poor, We can understand, I believe, the one whom Jesus loved had no pity on the man who betrayed his Savior. As a side note, it is interesting to hear of a man who was a disciple of Jesus. use a claim to care about the poor as a cover for his love of money. Such is so very common within our political circles today. It doesn't seem to matter if the populace knows our politicians are pretending to care about the poor. They know it's a facade for re-election. And I would also like us to notice that Judas' love for money is a great contrast here to Mary and her love for Jesus. She was unrestricted, free to love Jesus, just as Judas loved money, and that love was unrestricted. Only his bound him and Mary set her free. Because a denare was a day's wage, Judas calculated that what was poured out on Jesus was nearly a year's wage. It would have been nice for him to skim off the profits of that perfume if it was sold and he was given the authority to distribute to the poor. Now mind you, the answer uh that Jesus gives to this objection about the poor is not to be used to justify not caring for the poor, as some have done. It is simply a declaration. A declaration that the moment was greatly unique. And such a unique moment necessitated a unique gesture of love. There has always been, until Jesus returns, always will be, opportunities to help the poor. But there was only one opportunity to anoint the feet of Jesus. for his burial. Anoint him out of unrestricted love. Now when Jesus refers to his burial here, we naturally wonder what his disciples were thinking. They had heard him speak of his death a few times before, but they didn't understand the necessity of his death. It was not in their psyche. And we all may also wonder what Mary actually understood. Did she know she was anointing Jesus for his burial? Did she herself intend this act of symbolism? To know Jesus' death is coming, we cannot know. Well we can conclude Is that she either had an understanding or that the Holy Spirit moved her to do an act, the only act she knew how to do or what to do, out of pure, free love for him. That is what the Holy Spirit moves upon those who follow Christ. Now what John leaves out is a It's fair for us to add in because John's gospel was written later, and he probably thought Mark covered that, I'll cover something else. Mark tells us Jesus saying, wherever this gospel is preached in the whole world, what this woman has done will also be told as a memorial to her. Now consider with me how many acts of love and kindness and mercy have been done by people who follow Jesus. How many things have been done to sacrifice for their Savior? And ask yourself, what made this act of Mary anointing Jesus with expensive oil so worthy? of being remembered. Why this? We've noted several times during our examination of John's gospel That the purpose of John writing was to show all who would hear his words that Jesus was the Christ, the Son of God. That was his purpose. That is sung loudly from the stories and teachings John chooses to tell about Jesus. The actions of Mary are unique. The actions of Mary are described by John with a different purpose. Her actions are to be an example to us as to what it means to be a follower of Jesus. Little detour here for a moment. While preparing confirmation new members class last week I was struck by a necessary understanding about being a disciple of Jesus that I have failed to emphasize in my preaching and teaching all these many years. I was looking up several metaphors to use to describe how the church is described in the Bible. You know, metaphors that the church is a body and that the church is a bride. And that the church is a city on a hill, and the church is a family, etc. My plan was to use those metaphors as I have in the past. To help the class understand how the church can be a benefit to them. That is the way I have taught the confirmation class since I have served here as rector. What the church can do for you. See? And the Holy Spirit moved upon me that I was doing this all wrong. Parishioners should not be sold on how the different ministries of the church could benefit them Instead, they should be considering the planning and planning how they can benefit the ministries of the church, how they can show their love for Jesus through the church. Christians are not to look to the church to see how the church will benefit them. That is wrong thinking, and it's Western Christianity thinking. Christianity today, Christians today are so consumer-minded that they go to this church over here because it does this for them, and this one over here because it does that for them That is not picking up your cross daily. That is not putting others before self And we ministers speak a similar language when we present the church in these terms of what it can do for you. Or even when we present a sermon in a manner of what this information can do for you. I'm convinced that this way of thinking and presenting the church is all wrong. And Mary would agree. For Mary, following Jesus, was doing what would show Jesus her love for him. Following Jesus is showing unrestricted love for him. It is showing freedom in expressing love for Jesus. This thought of unrestricted expressions of love led me to consider the Song of Solomon. Contemporary Jews read the Canticle of Canticles or the Song of Songs during Sabbath of the Passover. For they understand it to be an allegory for describing God and his relationship with Israel. Christian interpretation understands it to be between a man and a woman, seeing love back and forth. But it also in certain circles is understood as the relationship that Christ has with his church. Well I believe whatever the actual intended meeting, I believe all three of those understandings serves God's purpose well. The Song of Songs is a model of unrestricted expressions of love. It is a song that Mary could have sung because of its passion. I have read that ministers of the gospel should not refer to the Song of Songs as an allegory between Christ and his church because it turns away men in the pews. For they see such imagery as effeminate, for it makes them out to be the bride. But I say that that is foolishness If the Bible uses the metaphor of the church being the bride of Christ, then this imagery of unrestricted love must include Eros. And if there is any passion that men understand most, a passion that drives them to be unrestricted in expressing love, it is Eras. The first lover to speak in the song in Solomon's song is the bride. She speaks first as a response to what her man has already done for her. His love has moved her, and she must say something, or the rocks will cry out. She must speak how his love for her has moved her, causing her to lose grip with reality. Resulting in only seeing him and thus only serving him. She said, May he kiss me with the kisses of his mouth. For your love is better than wine. Your oils have a pleasing fragrance. Your name is like purified oil. Therefore the maidens love you. Bernard of Clairvaux, who I saw was the writer of our last hymn we sang, he was a French abbot from the 11th century. And in his commentary on the Song of Songs, and in particular these verses I just read from the Song of Psalms, he describes what I believe Mary would understand as she poured out that oil on the head and the feet of Jesus. Bernard of Clairvaux says this about the bride. Quote, She loves more chastely who seek him whom she loves and not some other thing which belongs to him. She loves in a holy way, because she does not love in fleshly desire, but in purity of spirit. She loves ardently, because she is drunk with love, so that she cannot see His Majesty. What? He it is who looks on the earth and causes it to tremble. And she asks him for a kiss? Is she drunk? Indeed she is. And perhaps then when she burst forth, thus she had come out of the wine cellar. She said afterward that she had been there, glorifying in it. For David too said to God concerning such, they shall be intoxicated with plenty of your house, and you will give them the torrents of your pleasure to drink. Oh, what force of love, what great confidence of spirit, what freedom Did you hear that? Freedom. Unrestricted expression of love because of having been so loved. As scholar Anthony Esselin states, quote Only love, so ardent that it supersedes prudence and logic could presume to ask for a kiss. Logic must yield in humility. The seraphim burn in love. The cherubim burn in wisdom. The seraphim are closer to the divine vision than the cherubim. The wedding feast of the Lamb will be no meek affair. And indeed it will not. The freedom to love in an unrestricted manner is claimed by the bride in the Song of Psalms and by Mary, who pours out her oil. Both are free with either actions or speech. Both toss caution to the wind. Both love and receive love in return. The freedom in love that they both claim are to their credit. They make free before the Lord because the Lord they love wants them to be free. This is from Essalin again. And he, Jesus, is not prim. So does he not want primness in return? Her freedom. Sets her free. Jesus, setting Mary free, makes her free to express her love for him And that is why she is to be spoken of wherever the gospel is preached. You want to know how to follow Jesus? Do as Mary did. Unrestricted love. She is what every follower of Jesus is to be. We are to be free, unrestricted, to express our love for the Savior. And thus, it is no longer what is in this relationship for me. Everything has been done for us already. Mary was not there to get from the Lord. She was there to give. And she gave the greatest gift we fallen humans can give to God, and that is unrestricted expressions of love to him who first loved us. Notice how brazen a heart is when the love of God is received and then needs to be, needs to be expressed. This is from John Dunn to our Saviour. Take me to you. Imprison me. For I, except you enthrall me, never shall be free. Nor ever chaste except you ravished me. Beloved the Lord has ravished you. Pour out your oil. Amen and Amen. Let us pray.

sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. We are moving away from the Gospel of John this weekend because it doesn't quite match up with uh With a Palm Sunday next weekend that our text will finally match up uh according to the calendar. So I'm going a different uh direction this morning And I do want to say f first of all because we've lost an hour of sleep, might not be as sharp as normal. But I told my wife that uh Minister has one uh thing to consider and be appreciative of, uh, neither will you be a sharp. So we're both in the same boat. We're in Colossians three We're going to be challenged this morning about loving one another, and I don't think we can be challenged enough on that. One of the more memorable victories from my college football playing days was beating Oregon State. By a score of forty-one to twenty-two, way back in nineteen eighty-four. Wow. Oregon State that year was not a good football team, but they were part of the mighty Pac-10 And they had lost only by eight points to the number six Ohio State Buckeyes two weeks prior. The game was supposed to be a blowout by the Beavers. The University of Idaho was from the Lowly Big Sky Conference. And when walking on the field to see our opponent, it was obvious that they were bigger than us. It was obvious that they had all the confidence in the world that they would beat us. And to make it worse, our starting quarterback went down early in the first quarter. He now coaches in the NFL. He was very good. Rick Sloan, a transfer, came in and he told us to start running those backside routes, which you're not into football. That simply means we're going to be throwing this ball all over the field. Well, I caught three balls that game, my sophomore year. They could not stop our passing attack, and our defense played stout enough to slow their running game down so that they could not keep up. We won, beat them by 19 points. It wasn't close after the second quarter. Tough games. Games you are supposed to lose and lose to a bigger, stronger, and faster opponent, those are the best games to win. They are the most satisfied to find a victory. The battle is tough. You have to rise to the occasion and be tougher than the battle. Overcoming odds, overcoming doubters, overcoming your own limitations and the limitations you put on yourself makes a victory all the more sweet. St. Paul's charge to the Colossians to love in the manner he described is a tough challenge to take on. It is tough, a tough charge to complete. But what makes it all the more sweet is when you complete it, when you love in this manner. A minister I know was preaching at a council where half the congregation consisted of fellow preachers. He decided to preach about the necessity for Christians to love one another because he had experienced some animosity from his fellow clergy recently And felt that St. Paul's charge here in Colossians and in 1 Corinthians 13 needed to be rehearsed. Such love requires men to set aside unnecessary squabbles and opinions, and to think the best of one another, and to forgive harsh words of offense. The sermon was so effective, read sarcasm into that comment, five ministers chose not to participate in communion after the sermon because they were mad at the preacher for preaching about love. Think about that. Ministers of the gospel. Men who are called to preach the love of God in the person of Jesus Christ. chose not to love a fellow minister of that same gospel. Such as a shame, a disgrace, a travesty, and an embarrassment. And here is yet another reason why the Christian Church is so impotent in preserving our culture from rot and from getting the masses to turn from their sins and their wickedness. We can't even love each other in the clear manner described in Scripture. Because we see too many Christians failing to love one another, And because Jesus prayed and taught about the need for Christians to love one another, and because Paul believed it necess a necessary topic to teach in detail about We can conclude that this is indeed a tough thing to do. Loving one another in the manner God insists is a tough thing to do. But that is what makes it all the more sweet when we do it. The tough tasks are the sweetest tasks to accomplish. So if you turn with me to Colossians, we find there in chapter 3, Paul being led by the Holy Spirit to remind these Christians at Colossae what they were like. before Jesus gave them life. What their lives were like, living day to day before Jesus came into their life He reminded them of their sinful lifestyle, how God had taken them out of such immoral mud. The sins are specifically listed at the beginning of the chapter, and they seem to apply to most men and only some women. For they focus on the sins of sexual lust and the love of money. And such sins tend to be the greatest of struggles for men as opposed to women. We men are more easily pulled away from God by the temptation of sexual pleasure That is our weakness, and it is why the advertising industry bombards the airwaves and print media with half-nude women and suggestive slogans. Sex does indeed sell. Add to this the desire for money which allows men to buy things they do not essentially need, and you have what most men are willingly led astray. by. Such realities need to be mentioned from time to time in the church, for they do indeed are, they are indeed every man's battle. These are the sins that result in broken marriages. They are the sins that keep young men away from committing their lives to Christ. At the point of temptation, the pull of such sins is what makes Christian men no different than godless men in terms of how strong that pull is. Well, the rhetorical device St. Paul uses to get these Christians at Colossae and us to flee from such sins of the flesh is to speak about them as in our past. As Christians, we have died to ourselves, Paul explains. We have chosen Christ instead of ourselves. Therefore, just as we die to self, then we are to die to the desires of the flesh now, which are those sins of sexual pleasure and the love of money. Or what money can buy. Next, Christians are to put off, as Paul says. Sins that start internally and then find themselves expressed in the manner we treat or speak to one another. Anger, wrath, malice, blasphemy, filthy language, and lying Are sins that become natural when a man lives a life pursuing sexual pleasure and earthly goods. Men who live in sexual immorality are men with black hearts. And the only thing that comes out of a black heart are evil speaking from the tongue. These are to be put off. And that phrase, that phrase put off, is usually found referring to clothing. Thus Paul is providing an image of Christians regarding how we are to think about removing sin in our lives. We have to think of it as physically doing something, which makes us no longer a part of our the sins of our past. The older sinner we once were is like an old garment to be removed and discarded. We are not that person anymore. When the image of putting on comes next in verse ten When it does, it uses the phrase, put on the new. And then most translators add on, put on the new man. That's not what the Greek says. There's no word man there, but translators put that word there. Put on the new man. And that word is put there because it seems necessary for the word who follows it in the New King James. New Testament scholar F. F. Bruce believes Paul is referencing Christ Jesus as if he is saying, put on the man, put on Christ. And this makes so much more sense because when verse 12 tells us to put on tender mercies, kindness Humility, meekness, and long-suffering, those are indeed characteristics of Christ Jesus. Thus, we are to have a visual image within our imaginations that we are putting on Christ Jesus. He is now our identity. And when we do, we are to put on tender mercies. Put on, Jesus, put on tender mercies. Tender mercies are feelings of pity toward other Christians Not the pity that makes us perceive another person to be less fortunate than ourselves, but a pity that helps us identify with another person. I know your struggles, your failings, your needs, because they are my own. And therefore, when I see you struggle, I have tender mercies toward you. I empathize with you. And when I put on Jesus, I put on kindness. Kindness is easily one of the most overlooked godly characters by Christians in that it is not upheld as important as it should be. It is caring about what another person needs in any given moment, kindness. It is searching for what care another person needs in a given moment. Kindness is put on by being conscientious of the needs of others. It is looking for needs to be met, even if the moment is contentious. Being kind is as simple as seeing a person struggle and carrying boxes and offering to help Being kind is as difficult as having a harsh word spoken to you and you return it with a soft one. is asking the Holy Spirit to show you what you can say and how you can say it in a moment that will calm the storm and break down those emotional barriers that are dividing people If we ask, if we ask in any given moment, Holy Spirit, how can I be kind in this moment? He will tell you. Believe that. Believe it. Putting on Jesus is to put on humility. Such a characteristic is what Jesus is known for. Jesus defines humility, for he made himself of no reputation and took on the form of a servant. Living out humility is to internally, inside, internally believe that I am not what is most important in the world Thus I am not what is most important in any given moment. Humility is more internal than it is external. It is telling yourself, what I want does not matter right now. It is choosing to perceive others as more important than self. It is to lose your life for the sake of others just as Jesus told his followers to do Putting on Jesus is to put on meekness. Meekness comes from humility. Meekness is speaking gently and working gently with others. It is being quiet and careful so as not to offend unnecessarily It is speaking the truth only in love. A meek person does not boast. A meek person does not bluster. A meek person does not speak to be noticed. A meek person does not insist that his or her opinion must be counted. And with this characteristic, it might be harder to see Jesus as meek. For we read a great deal of his aggressive words uttered to the Pharisees and to the Sadducees. We might conclude that a meek person does not call a group of people hypocrites or false teachers. But a meek person is not a weak person. For a meek person says what needs to be said, and to whom it needs to be said. A meek person does not speak softly to a person who is burning in a building. If the Pharisees and Sadducees were teachable men, they would not have been spoken to harshly. They were not teachable men. Putting on Jesus is to put on long suffering. Long-suffering is a characteristic of God underlined in the Old Testament. It is an act of taking it on the chin time and time again and still staying in the relationship. It is putting up with people again and again. It is being hopeful that a person is going to change. Maybe this guy. Change for the good, maybe this time, even if there's no evidence of any change coming. It is Jesus Waiting to come again, but waiting until all who are his come to repentance. Long suffering Long suffering goes along with being not quickly or easily provoked to wrath. It is not doing what what can be so easily done. Like quitting on another person or blowing up on another person. Putting on long suffering should never be difficult for any of us. Well we all know how much long-suffering our Savior has done for each of us. Next, we are told to put on Jesus That is bearing with one another. Bearing with one another. And we might be tempted to conclude that bearing and long-suffering are the same, and certainly they take the same humble position to practice. But bearing with one another is in the context of forgiving one another. This means that we are to have forbearance about the sins of one another. And that includes forgiving one another, and that includes if someone has wronged us, or we simply can't stand to be around said person, we are still to forgive. And Paul doesn't say we need to wait for the person who has wronged us to ask for that forgiveness. The person who drives us crazy to ask for that forgiveness, being a forgiving person, is putting on Jesus, for that is what Jesus came to do, was to forgive us. That we must forgive each other is what Jesus has already taught us. Paul is simply repeating what Jesus emphasized. Our character, our identity as followers of Jesus are to be persons of forgiveness. Let us read verse 14. But above all these things, put on love, which is the bond of perfection. And there is our summary. It is consistent with what Paul defined as love to the Corinthians. Remember there in 1 Corinthians 13, Paul begins with love and then follows with the most challenging definition to live to, to live up to. And here he describes holy living that is challenging and difficult to live up to, and then reveals what he is actually describing all along is God. It's God's love. As we would expect, this is the word agape, the love of God. Thus to forgive. Forbear, practice long suffering, behave meekly, humbly, to be kind and grant tender mercies to one another is to love one another And here we can bring together the sermon from last week, and with this one, we are to pour out unrestricted love for Jesus, and part of that unrestricted love for Jesus is to practice loving one another. We know this because God has told us that we cannot say we love Him unless we also love our brothers and sisters. The book titled To End All Wars, and the movie by the same title Is a true story of British troops, young men, who endured great suffering at the hands of the Japanese in Thailand during World War II. These men were part of the slave builders that built the bridge over the river Kwai. The story is told by an officer named Ernest Gordon, who was captured along with some men of his battalion by the Japanese. And taken to a prison camp deep into the Thailand woods where they would suffer from disease and physical torture. After suffering great hardship while working on the bridge, Gordon became ill with diphtheria, and he was in its latter stages. Gordon became so ill so quickly that he was ordered to be placed in the death house where bodies of already dead soldiers and those who were certain to die were sent before their bodies were either cremated or buried. Gordon stirred enough in that death house for someone to notice him and insist that he go to a hut to see if he can recover. It was in that hut that he met a man by the name of Dusty Miller. Dusty was a gardener from Great Britain. He too had survived from diphtheria as he was recovering himself. It was at that first meeting that Dusty committed himself to helping Gordon recover. And what he had to do to help Gordon recover was out of the ordinary. Gordon writes He came to my legs and we both looked down at them. They were not a pretty sight. Skin ulcers had laced them with an ugly pattern and open sores, half-formed scabs and dry blood. Hmm, quite a mess, aren't they? said Dusty. I think I'd better wash them first. Then I'll clean out the pus. And that began a daily routine. Dusty would work the evening in the kitchen and tend to Gordon in the morning with repeated cleaning and rebandaging of Gordon along all along, because the necessity of his duties meant that he had to be with him whenever he was not working. He massaged those infected legs routinely. And through conversation, Gordon learned what motivated Dusty to be so kind. It was because he believed kindness came back to you, and because kindness spreads. But there was also what caused him to believe this about kindness. It was his love for the Lord Jesus Christ that freed him to love others in such a sacrificial manner. Dusty put on love. Dust he put on Jesus. And he rolled up his sleeves, and he cleaned another man's wounds day after day until the man was healed. I think we should think about acts like Dusty's, when we are tempted to be trite, when we are tempted to withhold forgiveness. When we are tempted to be mad at someone for telling us that we need to love others. We should think about the Son of God, creator of the universe, wrapping a towel around his waist. And washing the feet of men, even men who would betray him. That image kept in our hearts, in our minds. Will not allow us to be unkind, to be impatient, to be unforgiving toward one another. Thus he chose what was most difficult. We are to choose what is most difficult. Love one another. The reward is oh so sweet. Amen.

sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Our text is from the Gospel according to Saint John, chapter 12, beginning at verse 9. It is rare. It is rare when both a novel and a movie A movie made to represent the same novel have the same artistic impact Harper Lee, may God rest her soul, her novels Who Kill a Mockingbird and the movie titled with the same have equal artistic impact. And my favorite point in the book and in the movie is the final scene in chapter 21 of the book. As you are aware, it is tradition in a court of law for people of the court to stand as the judge enters or leaves the room. In order to show respect to that judge as the one and only arbiter of the law in the room. But people of the court never stand for attorneys as they enter or leave the room. Attorneys do not have the same legal authority as judges By the end of chapter 21, Judge Taylor has read the jury's tragic, unanimous, guilty verdict on poor, innocent Tom Robinson. And Atticus, the white lawyer defending a black man in the Deep South, proceeds to exit the courtroom by taking the South exit. The exit choice is noted by Scout, his daughter, as she looks upon him, taking what she calls the lonely walk down the aisle. Amidst the courtroom of spectators. Now, since Scout, Atticus's daughter, whose real name was Jean Lewis, kept her eyes glued on her lonely father She failed to notice that all of the people in the so-called colored balcony had risen to their feet. It wasn't until Reverend Skyx called it to her attention saying, Miss Jean Louise, Miss Jean Louise, stand up. Your father's passing. The scout was naturally very surprised by the behavior, since this was not the first time She had been in a courtroom during her father's career, and she was well aware that no tradition exists for standing for an attorney as he leaves the room The surprise tone in Scout's narrative so shows that she was well aware of the symbolic meaning of the Negroes getting to their feet, the importance of that moment. Not only does the action of the Negroes rising show their respect for Atticus, it shows that they saw Atticus as the true symbolic arbiter of the law, not Judge Taylor. And through his cross-examination, Atticus had proven to the court, including proving to Judge Taylor, Tom's innocence. Judge Taylor had the legal authority to dismiss the case when the physical evidence showed that Tom Robinson could not have committed the crime he was accused of. But the judge chose to go the way of what was expected of him. And so the people who knew the truth stood when Scout's father was passing. If judges are considered the symbolic arbiters in court in courtrooms in these United States I think it is fair to say that Jesus of Nazareth should be understood to be the only true symbolic arbiter of the law in all of creation and beyond. Thus it was most certainly appropriate for the multitude that was coming to Jerusalem for the feast of the Passover, as recorded in John's Gospel, chapter 12. To put down palm tree branches, and to cry out as Jesus passed by Hosanna. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, King of Israel. Certainly, if the King of Israel is passive, it is most appropriate to stand up. If the Savior of Israel is Pasan, it is most appropriate to sing his praises. And if it is the King of Kings of the Lord of Lords, the great I am, Pasin, then it is most appropriate to stand, to cheer, to sing his praises. A passing Jesus is a present Jesus. And it will be my task on this Palm Sunday to increase our faith about the passing presence of Jesus in our lives. And that will be a call for you to stand when Jesus is passing, when he is present. John tells us that when the events of this first Palm Sunday occurred, the disciples did not understand what it all meant. They didn't understand the palm branches being laid down. Probably seemed like a bit too much fuss being made. They didn't understand how quoting the words from Psalm 118 by the people applied to that moment and applied to Jesus in that moment. We didn't understand that Jesus riding into the city on a donkey was Jesus entering symbolically as a king, coming in peace. They didn't understand that all of this took place to fulfill what was prophesied about Jesus, to verify to them that Jesus was the fulfillment of all that was promised of the Messiah. Jesus was everything that the Father intended him to be at that moment and beyond. It was only after Jesus was glorified and these events were remembered that it was seen as God's plan fulfilled. Understanding and then believing in the presence of Jesus among us will cause us to stand, for to stand is to pay attention To stand is to be ready to listen, ready to relate, ready to obey, as a servant should. Jesus is passing, beloved. Jesus is present, first of all, when we gather together for corporate worship. In the book of Revelation, chapters 4 and 5, we hear first of the four creatures, and then the elders. And then the many creatures, numbering ten thousand times ten thousand and thousands of thousands, singing to the Lamb, who is Jesus, at the center of their gathering. That is why tradition encourages us to think of our worship as heavenly. We go somewhere else. For when we worship corporately, we are gathering around the throne room in heaven, where Jesus is. Where he sits, and we join the course that has already begun and continues We worship with the saints in the presence of Jesus. Crucifers lift up the cross. Ceilings are elevated in the church so that crosses on the wall are elevated. Our chancel is elevated, and we are called to come up to the feast because we are to understand our worship to be occurring in the presence of Jesus, who is seated in heaven. Because we are in the presence of Jesus at our worship, there is nothing selfish. Uncharitable, lustful, prideful, or hateful to be in our hearts Because Jesus is in our midst in a unique manner like no other time when we ascend to his throne for worship. He tells us that if we come to him offering a gift, and that gift could be songs of praise, words of prayer, our wills And we remember that a brother or sister in Christ has something against us, we are to leave our gift. And be reconciled to our brother or sister, and then come back to worship, and then come back to heaven Jesus will have no gods before him. And when we hold on to our pride, When we hold on to our uncharitableness, our selfishness, our pettiness, then such is acting as our own God in the moment. And it needs to be repented of and thrown out. It cannot come to the throne of heaven. When Jesus is passing, we are to stand. We are to stand. Next, Jesus is passion. Jesus is present when we agree together. When we agree together. Now you might have expected me to say that Jesus is passing, that Jesus is present in our midst when we pray together. But the verse Christians commonly use to refer to the presence of Jesus in their midst, that when two or more are gathered in my name, when they pray, we think it's when they pray. But it's not actually referring to prayer only. The promise of the presence of Jesus is in the context of describing how to save another Christian who is caught up in sin. You remember from Matthew 18, Jesus explains that if you see a person in sin, you are to go to them and tell them that they need to repent. And if they refuse, then you're supposed to bring a witness to help the person bring them to repentance. And then if that doesn't work, you're supposed to bring them to the church. And if the church presence doesn't help them, then you are to cast them out as an unbeliever, Jesus says. In that context, Jesus then instructs, again from Matthew 18, he said, Truly I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound. in heaven. And whatever you loose on earth shall have been loosed in heaven. Again I say to you that if two of you agree on earth about anything that they may ask It shall be done for them by my Father who is in heaven.
