And these may have been God-fearers who were interested in Judaism, but had not gone so far as to become circumcised and thus become Jews. The words that they speak, the words that they speak, sir, we wish to see Jesus. Those words should be written on every Christian pulpit for the preacher himself to see each Sunday, and thus be reminded that the people you come to see Jesus. You don't come to hear simply another man's opinion. You don't wish to see a man bluster on about himself or about his views on politics or his favorite sports team. You come to see Jesus, and every preacher needs to be convicted by that In verse 22, we read that Philip went to tell Andrew that the Greeks wanted to see Jesus, and then Philip and Andrew go together to tell Jesus. And then Jesus begins to speak. He begins to teach. One commentator I read believes that Jesus doesn't respond to what Philip and Andrew tell him. According to this commentator, Jesus practically ignores the news that some Greeks wanted to see him. But the phrase that begins verse 23 says that Jesus answered them Answered them, Philip and Andrew. He answered them. He responded to them. He responded to what they told him. The New King James Version, which is in your pews, chooses to translate the Greek conjunction day as the word but. And that's certainly reasonable. However, but that word indicates that Jesus wants to talk about something different than what they told him about. The word day, however, can also be translated simply and, the conjunction and. The reading would then be, after hearing the news that the Greeks were present to see Jesus, and Jesus answered them, and then followed by his teaching. We read with the word and in place of but we can understand that Jesus began to teach this way because he heard that there were Greeks that wanted to see him. So I conclude, what he taught on hearing that the Greeks had come wishing to see him was that what it meant to truly see him, he was about to teach To see Jesus. To see Jesus is to see an innocent man suffer at the hands of jealous men. It was to see a man needing to die so that many, many others could live. To see Jesus was to understand what it meant to follow Jesus. To see Jesus was to hate one's own life. To see Jesus is to live as Jesus lived, which was a life of sacrifice for the sake of others. To see Jesus is to gaze upon the Son of God lifted up and to know it must be done. And to be humbled by it because your sins are what caused him to be lifted up. To see Jesus is to walk in the light and live in the light of Jesus, being always wary of darkness. To see Jesus is to understand and live out what fundamentally makes a person a Christian. For me, this passage is much like when Jesus was courted by the Pharisees asking if he was in favor of paying the Roman tax. And you remember being cornered, they wanted to know, do you support Rome or do you support the independence of Israel? And Jesus asked for a coinage and he asked whose image is on that coinage. When he was told Caesar, he said, give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's. And of course it was a brilliant answer in that it showed he was not cornered after all. But it was also an answer that showed that Jesus didn't want to talk about taxes It was not important to him because it was not the point of his life. It was not the point of his death. It was not the point of his resurrection. It was not the point of his ascension. Taxes were not about the good news, the gospel of Jesus Christ. You remember when he was asked about paying the temple tax. First of all, he thinks it's kind of ironic, it's my father's house, therefore it's my house. Why should I be paying a tax on my house? But he says to Peter, in order not to offend In order not to offend, go catch a fish, you'll find money in it, and pay the tax. Peter does that. Goes and catches a fish, pays the temple tax. The spirit behind that story is that paying the temple tax or not paying the temple tax was not the point. It was not important. It is focusing on that which is not the gospel. And it is the gospel and the gospel alone that matters. When I described how I felt upon hearing of Christians being martyred in Pakistan, because they were celebrating the resurrection of Jesus. No doubt you identify with some of my anger, guilt. When I said I was disgusted by how the media tells us how we should respond to Muslim terrorists, you could also identify with my disgust. Such emotions are justifiable. There is nothing wrong with such emotions. And there is nothing wrong with wanting to do something about these injustices. And dare we say Support candidates in offices that might help protect the innocent from fanatical murderers Our next men's meeting will be about candidates and who Christians should support. Such things are good for Christians to talk about and be wise about and thus be involved. But but and you have to know this on the other hand point needs to be said But we are to be essentially about, as Christians, the gospel It is good and right to support candidates that you believe in that will be just. It is good and right and necessary to speak out against the sins of abortion, sodomy, and sex trafficking. All of these sins are inhumane and they plague our country. It is good to insist that something be done to defeat terrorists, both foreign and domestic. But as Christians, our primary energy, our priority is to be about the gospel. Who knows what those Greek men wanted to see Jesus about? Nobody does, for they are not in the picture after they are mentioned. We know not what they wanted to see Jesus from Jesus for Jesus never spoke about them afterwards. We don't even know if Jesus ever spoke directly to them But what we need to know is what Jesus thought they needed to see. They needed to see what was important. And that was the truth, which was that he must be sacrificed in order for the sins of men to be forgiven, and those who follow him must give up their life in order to receive eternal life back. That is the gospel, and to know the gospel is to see Jesus. Beloved, this Easter season challenges us to live a resurrected life. And the resurrected life is about the gospel. It is amazing. Amazing how strife ends in relationships, how easy it is to think the best of others How quickly we can forgive a wrong done to us, how sweet it is to be kind to others when you make your life about the gospel. I want to briefly describe very practically how this works. Someone talks to you and disagrees with you, and they're not nice about it. In fact, you perceive that they might be baiting you into an argument, and if they successfully do that, they will have another reason not to like you. And what you ask yourself before you speak, what you ask yourself Is this about the gospel? Does getting into this discussion honor life? The life suffering, death, resurrected, ascended life of the Savior? If the answer is no, then you don't get into this discussion, then you don't get into an argument, and you don't give people reason to be mad at you. And this works when it comes to things that bother you. It works when people are making decisions that you would not make. You ask yourself, does having the women's tea in a different location matter to the gospel? And if the answer is no, then you don't sweat it. To ask such questions is to make your life about the gospel. And it works for the bigger things as well, such as wanting revenge on terrorists. Make your life about the gospel. Do it because Jesus did. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Mystery of the Will
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. Please turn your Bibles to Gospel according to Saint John chapter twelve, beginning at the thirty-seventh verse. Sadly to say, sadly to say, there are Christian young adults that I personally know of today that are in a state of outward rebellion against their parents One person is still a member of this parish. Such rebellion is a mystery for me for one reason. That reason is the human will. The human will is a mystery It is especially a mystery when it comes to knowing where the human will, which is the power to make individual choices, Where that ends, and the will of God begins But to put it even that way isn't well stated because God's will is always playing a role. Even if it is just the role of allowing a person to make individual choices. And an even greater mystery about the human will is to try to understand why people choose to destroy themselves. Why does a person make decisions that are self-destructive? For instance, why does a man choose to abuse his spouse and thus destroy his marriage and scar his children? Why does a young man reject the love of his parents to chase after a girl who neither fears God nor really cares about the young man? Why does a woman choose to have a sexual affair instead of having peace with God? Why does a Christian choose to be constantly angry? And thus damage every friendship in his life. In general, why do people choose to be angry instead of happy? Why do people choose hate or bitterness rather than love? Why do people choose pleasure in this life in exchange for the hope of everlasting life? You and I could go on and on asking similar types of questions. And make no mistake about it. All of these are choices people make. They, and they alone, are morally responsible for such choices. In John Bunyan's most famous allegory, Pilgrim's Progress, a man by the name of Christian is a pilgrim who has set his sights on making it to the celestial city. Heaven for you and me The first stranger Christian meets on the way is named Pliable. Christian tells Pliable about the hope and beauty of the celestial city. And Pliable loves to hear about it and immediately decides to join Christian on his pilgrimage. And Fiable wants to go fast on the road, but Christian is weighed down by what we would say is a backpack, which is his sin. While strangely enough, Pliable has no such burden on his back. Unfortunately, shortly after Pliable joins Christian, They fall into a sort of quagmire called the slew of the spawned. When Pliable questions Christian as to what has happened to them, Christian admits that he does not know. He's just trying to stay afloat. This offends Pliable. And he responds angrily, asking, Is this the happiness you have been telling me about? If we have such miserable misfortune at the beginning of our journey, what may we expect when we reach the end of our journey? Pliable promises that if he gets out of this flu of despawned alive, Christian can have his heavenly country. After that, Pliable finds a shallow area near his home and climbs out, never to be seen or heard from again. With that conversation, Bunyan allows us to know why Fiable gave up. It was too hard of a road for him. Too hard of a road for him to walk. He did not have the fortitude for the walk. He was weak, and he therefore gave up In the interpreter's house, Christian meets a man in an iron cage. By questioning him, Christian learns that the man was once a flourishing professor, on his way, mind you, to the celestial city. But the man flirted with sin and ignored the commands of Holy Scripture. The man says of himself that I laid the reign upon the neck of my lusts. Instead of controlling his passions, he allowed them to run wild, and his lack of confessing his sin hardened his heart. From the words of the man himself, also called hopeless, we learn why he turned from God. He wanted pleasure in this life, and thus he knowingly, knowingly exchanged it for the hope of heaven. That is supposed to be answer enough for us of why he did it. But I say it still begs the question, why was earthly pleasure more appealing to this man than heavenly reward? Bunyan doesn't provide such an answer. And I wonder So let us turn to the scripture, and specifically our reading from the Gospel according to St. John, for some answers regarding how the will of man works with and or against the will of God. In verses 37 through 41, I want you to note that these are commentaries by John. These are not the words of Jesus, but John himself is writing, giving us commentary on what had happened. John wants us to know that enough signs and wonders were done in front of people in public. That those who do not believe that Jesus is the Messiah, they are without excuse. They have plenty of opportunity. To explain why they didn't believe, and thus to explain how their wills worked against God, John quotes from Isaiah. The first quote is from Isaiah 53, which is the section, you remember, of the suffering serpent. This shows that Isaiah prophesied that there would be widespread rejection of Jesus. John next quotes from Isaiah 6, which is that introduction, you remember, of Isaiah's great vision. That is where he is called to be the prophet of God. And when God gave him that call, God warned him that the message that he would preach would not be received. And he said, because God had already passed judgment on the guilty, who was Israel, and thus they were blinded spiritually and made hard of heart. The same then, John is saying, applied to those of Jesus' day. They too had been found guilty by God, and thus they too were blinded in spirit and hardened of heart. John next explains that some people actually did believe, but among the Pharisees it was very few. And the main issue was their choice to love the praise of men as opposed to to love the praise of God. Now this is all well and good and helpful, but it does not help us understand why they loved the praise of men rather than the praise of God. We can all well imagine why we love the praise of men. Everyone likes to be appreciated. Everyone likes to be encouraged. Everyone likes to be told how good he is. But again, why is such praise better than God saying to a person, well done? John doesn't take it that far. He doesn't explain it that far. He just says this is the way it is. John's commentary is in contrast to what Jesus says next And you and I are supposed to connect what Jesus says next with what he said in verses 23 through 36 that we covered a few weeks ago. In verse 35, Jesus told the listeners that the light was with them. That light was Jesus himself, as he says more plainly in verse 46. Verses 44 through 46 explain the unity that Jesus has with the Father, and that believing on one is believing on the other. Believe in the Father, you believe in the Son, believe in the Son, you believe in the Father. Verse 47 and 48, verses 47 and 48 imply that believ Sing in Jesus and hear this now implies that believing in Jesus is a choice. A choice that each person makes according to his or her own will Believing and rejecting are presented as that which each person does, and it is easy to surmise that people make choices. According to their will. Jesus then finishes this section of teaching by confirming that his authority comes from his father, and that Jesus is the epitome of an obedient son. So while we understand what Jesus is teaching and confirming, again, we are not helped to understand the issues in regards to the will of individuals. With and against the will of God. On the road to the celestial city Christian meets up with a pilgrim named Faithful. Faithful came from the same city of destruction as Christian did, and thus he was able to catch him up on what was going on in the town after. Christian left. The people, he found out, hated him for leaving them. They wished him to stay. When Faithful tells of his own travels, Christian learns that he avoided the slew of Despond, but came upon a woman named Mrs. Wanton. Faithful recounts of how difficult that temptation was. You cannot imagine, he said to Christian, unless you have similar experience. What a flattering tongue that woman had. He continued, I suspected that she was trying to attract me to her trim figure by her behavior and sympathetic understanding of the human nature. She was so attractive, especially when she spoke of human freedom and natural love. Just a little way, she said. Just a few moments of pleasure. Thank God you escaped her, said Christian. He then quoted Scripture: The mouth of a strange woman is a deep pit, and he that is aboard of the Lord shall fall therein. But I don't know if I wholly escaped her or not, said Faithful. I closed my mind to her subtle, seductive suggestions. Yet I cannot say I have acquired a holy pure mind since. Such a confession can be made by every man. So why did faithful not give way to the lust of his flesh? Why did he choose God instead? His words tell us that he made a conscious effort to remember the dangers that Scripture warns about of such lust. But why did he choose it while others do not? Why did he take the warning while so many do not? The author of Pilgrim's Progress is John Bunyan, as I said. John Bunyan was a Calvinist, as his other writings and his preachings indicate. As a Calvinist, he embraced the doctrine of predestination, that God had predetermined individuals to be saved. That God had made choices for individuals, woken them up to the gospel. Bunyan also embraced the doctrine of irresistible grace. That doctrine states that when God reveals his mercy to a person, well that person cannot refuse, but will only repent and believe. But Bunyan's characters, as we have seen, behave as if their choices are part of the equation when determining a person's salvation. One critic wrote that Bunyan presented these characters in his story, not discounting the doctrine of predestination, but to present them in a more relatable manner for his intended readers. Who he hoped were non-Christians and who would come to the faith. That sounds like a fair explanation, but it doesn't help us understand how the human will works. With or against and or against the will of God. I don't have a segue here, so I'm just going to go into it. We have a very strange dog. If you have not met our dog, his name is George. The surname Jorgensen literally means son of George, and so we name the Jorgensen dog George. If you have heard our family stories about the appetite of our George, you have heard how he has taught himself to open a refrigerator And to open a slide in the garbage drawer, all because of his stomach compelling him to do so. But the appetite of George is not what makes him weird Bobby Lynn and I used to have a bed in the master bedroom that was put on risers. From the time George was our only dog, thus from the time that our other dog Rex had passed away, George has loved to sleep under our bed. He became so obsessed with sleeping under our bed that he would sneak into our room in in the afternoon and stay there in hopes that we would not know or recognize that he was there in the evening And we didn't like him under our bed for two reasons. First, George snores while he sleeps. And when he would sleep under our bed, and I'm not making this up, He would shake our bed with his snoring. And then he had this type of chain stoking, that type of noise. And he would wake you up. The second reason why we didn't like George to sleep under our bed was that he would steal things of ours, our possessions, to sleep with them I have found socks, shoes, and t-shirts, even found a watch under my bed that he had taken under my bed to sleep with. He doesn't always chew on them, he just likes to sleep with them. Well after Christmas, Bobby Lynn and I bought a storage bed. We became adults. We have a bed with a headboard for the first time in our marriage. It is a bed that has a headboard but also with drawers underneath. We've always wanted one, we finally bought one. But George can't fit under the bed anymore. And we are thrilled with that. But George did not give up easily. George has now found a way to crawl under one of our dresser drawers that has only eight inches from the from the bottom drawer to the floor And he is too fat to fully fit under that dresser. And so he always has to have a part of his body sticking out. Well, it all came to a classic moment this Monday. Watching TV in our bedroom, I get up Stand up from my bed. I look down, and there is George. Half of his body is underneath the dresser. His head and his paws are sticking out. And in his paw is an old pair of broken glasses that I had, holding them, not chewing it, but just holding on to it. And for me, that's when I said, my dog is weird. Now I tell you all of this about my weird dog, George. Because of why he believe why he behaves in such a manner. He doesn't choose to behave weirdly. He doesn't choose to behave in that manner, only the manner that comes natural to him. What he does is innate He has an innate need to be under his master, connected to his master in some way. This is how he was created. The same can be said about each of us regarding sin that is innate. Because each of us has been born under the covenant of Adam, and that covenant, because of original sin, is cursed, we are all born under the curse of God. We are all born dead in our trespasses and sins, and thus, because of the sin we are born into, and with, we make decisions in life that are self-destructive. Remember when David said in Psalm 51, the Psalm that is a prayer of repentance because of his adultery with Bathsheba and the murdering of her husband Uriah. David said to the Lord, In sin did my mother conceive me With some ears that may sound like David's mother committed sin by having sexual intercourse, and the result was David. But the true meaning is That from the time that David was only a newly fertilized egg, David was under the covenant of Adam, which is cursed. And thus David was sinful even in the womb, as we all are, in our mother's womb. It is, as my sister loves to say, when she holds up one of her newlyborn grandchildren, oh, you're such a cute little sinner. And so it's true. We are all cute little sinners. Because we are born cute little sinners, we have wills that naturally go against God. And because our hearts are set against God, it is first nature for us to make decisions that are self-destructive. Thus the question I have been insisting to be answered by God regarding how the human will interacts with or against God's will, that's the wrong question The question should not be, why do people make poor decisions that ruin marriages and scar children and alienate friends and corrupt their bodies, etc. , etc. The question should be how do we not make decisions that ruin marriages, scar children, alienate friends, and corrupt our bodies? How do we not? Such is the right type of question because doing self-destructive things is natural for us. To understand the subject of the human will through the reality that it is first nature to be self-destructive is to deny what is obviously true about human nature. Human nature has fallen from perfection. The human nature under Adam falls short of the glory of God. The Greeks even understood this. Without biblical revelation, the Greeks understood this. Plato believed the human condition to be the soul struggling to control the appetites of the stomach and the genitals. The plight of man, according to Plato, was to pursue virtue so that the flesh would become submissive to the soul. If the Greeks could get it, we who have Holy Scripture ought to get it all the much more. The fallen human nature is why people do not believe in Jesus, even though they were eyewitnesses to his miracles. The fallen nature is why the Pharisees preferred the praises of men. The fact that John mentions that there were people who believed even among the religious rulers, that is the true miracle. That is the will of man being overcome by the will of God so as to be saved. So what are we to say? What are we to do to the truth that our need that our wills have to be overcome by God's We are to thank him with our lives. Did not Jesus say He who loves his life will lose it. And he who loses his life for the sake of Jesus will receive eternal life. Beloved, God has overcome your will for your salvation. You owe him your life. Jesus has pulled us out from under the bed. Jesus has pulled us out from under the dresser. Given us hearts. That chose him. Chose him over self-destruction. Such rescuing deserves our full devotion. Amen and amen. Let us pray

sermons.title: Practicing the Virtue of Humility
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Exceeded. Turning your Bibles to Saint John's Gospel, chapter thirteen Maya Angelou, an African American poet and author, now deceased. Answered when she was asked what was the most important virtue. Courage is the most important of all virtues, she said. Because without courage, you cannot practice any other virtues consistently. It is a thoughtful answer, but it has problems. A person can be an angry person and still practice the virtue of courage. A person can be a bitter person and still practice the virtue of courage. And a courageous, angry person, well that's a dangerous person. Dr. Andrew Taggart, a philosophical counselor, said in an article back in 2012 That the three most important virtues were patience, courage, and phonesis. Phonesis is good judgment. This helps because the virtue of good judgment would tell an angry person or a bitter person that it is not wise to be angry or bitter. But a patient person, a courageous person, and a person of good judgment can be all three at the same time and still be a jerk Yes, being a jerk isn't necessarily showing good judgment, but that is the weakness of virtue ethics as a theory. For words such as good and judgment are honestly ambiguous. A person of a certain mindset can convince him or herself that being a jerk to a certain person in a certain situation is indeed good judgment. Another weakness of upholding virtue as an ethical theory is that you have to choose which virtue is the most important depending on a given situation. For instance, a man facing an enemy on a battlefield is going to need much more fortitude and courage than he will need justice or honesty. And so the most important virtue is a virtue that is depending on a given situation. Some have argued that love is the most important virtue. And I would agree, because love can apply to every given situation. But I don't agree that love is a virtue. Love, properly defined as unconditional, selfless caring, Is instead not a virtue but a characteristic of God. Love is of God. Love is not a virtue, but is to govern all virtues. And so, with the challenge of identifying the most important virtue in the context of human relations, I conclude that the most important virtue is humility. Humility, governed by love, is the most important virtue we can practice as we relate to one another. That humility would be our focus should not be surprising, for we are studying the act of Jesus washing his disciples' feet. Which is the model regarding Christian humility, the model we are to display to one another? Let us look at the passage itself. From verse one, we learn That the foot washing took place before evening dinner on the Thursday, before what we now call Good Friday And this is why we recognize Bondi Thursday as it follows the same timeline of Jesus and his disciples, the same one they walked on his last week. You recall that it is called Mandi because Mandi means commandment. And Jesus gave a new commandment. He said it was new. Love one another. Also, in this verse, we are to note that John uses the word world, and he's going to use that word world 40 times in the next five chapters. He's using that word world to draw a contrast between those who followed Jesus and those who did not of the world. And this whole idea of being in the world but not of the world is alluded to here The end of this verse indicates that what follows is a demonstration of what it means to follow Christ instead of the world. Verse 2 provides further commentary by St. John as he is able to understand what had happened here and what he's describing post-resurrection, post-ascension. Verse 3 is another commentary by St. John, and it links back to the end of chapter 12, where Jesus explained where his authority came from. It came from the Heavenly Father. John calls it this authority, power over all things. And this is to leave us to conclude that nothing, nothing that happens next has caused, is caused by anything other than the will of Jesus. He is in total control. Verses 4 and 5 begin a play-by-play of what happened next. Now catch this, please, if you would. It's fascinating. While the New King James Version that we have in our pews translates John's description in the past tense, Jesus got up. The original Greek is actually in the present tense The present tense. It is as if John is seeing the image of Jesus standing up in his mind as if he's right there. For John actually wrote, he rises. Present tense. As if he's looking at it, he rises. Describing Jesus getting up from the table. Then he says, he places Describing Jesus putting aside his own garments, like he was right there. By describing it in this Present tense, John is communicating how momentous this occasion was. For him, he could go right back there and see it as it all was. His mind's eye could take him there, and it was real to him at that moment. And the meticulous manner he describes Jesus serving It reminds us of what's going to happen when they come to the tomb, and he has laid his bedclothes, his graveclothes folded to the side neatly, meticulously. Before Jesus came to Peter in this washing, we can imagine how stunned the disciples were watching Jesus serve them in such a manner. The washing of someone else's feet was a menial chore. Ceremonial washings were practiced on a regular basis, so it was common that only the feet needed to be washed because of a day of walking. But the job of washing another's feet was so menial, so menial that some Jews thought it beneath the dignity of any Jew of any stature. They thought it was worthy of a Gentile slave. This was the Christ, the Messiah washing their feet. They did not know what Jesus was going to do for them on the cross, but they knew that he was their Messiah. For the Messiah to wash their feet must have been an embarrassment, for they desired that the roles would be reversed, as Peter states. And as everyone came to expect, Peter was the first to speak. And he says what everyone else wanted to say. The reply of Jesus shows that he is giving an illustration, an illustration that doesn't speak much to them now, but will speak to them volumes. Later on. The foot washing is an example of how the suffering servant would be obedient unto death, even death on the cross. He tells us. It was also an example of how the disciples were to serve one another. By serving one another, they then are serving Jesus. In verse 9, Peter takes a step too far, again as expected. Peter exaggerates, but with gusto. The logic is, it's fair logic. If you need to wash my feet, then wash all of me. All of me needs to be washed by Jesus. But the reply of Jesus is more than expected etiquette. Jesus is teaching a theological truth. Even though a person is made right by God and justified by faith in Christ, having confessed Jesus as Savior, having been baptized. There still needs to be forgiveness sought each and every day. And this is why John writes in his first letter to those who are already saved that they are to continue confessing their sins and then be forgiven. Daily. In verse 11, we have to understand that Jesus washed the feet even of his betrayer. He knowingly washed the feet of his betrayer. And we will say more about that in a little bit. Jesus goes on in verse 12 through 16, explaining what he has done, and it is what we have already pointed out. As their teacher, they are to do as he has done, and they are to do the same to one another. This is stated plainly in verse 17. Now there are some Christians who have taken these words of Jesus in verse 17 to mean that Jesus wants his followers to literally and thus physically wash each other's feet. I don't have a problem with that. None of us should. I participated in a foot washing when I was 19 years old, and I can attest it is a very humbling act. Then any group would make it such practice a right, as in a ritual, as in baptism, like baptism or holy communion. Well that's going beyond the church historic. But again, there is no harm in doing this act. It is. It is, however, what the act represents that all Christians are to practice. And what it represents is the virtue of humility toward one another In the collect prayer of the second Sunday after Easter that we prayed last week, I remind you that we prayed That as Jesus lived an ensample life, that we would daily endeavor ourselves to follow in his blessed steps of his most holy life. And this Sunday, from the third call-up after Easter, we prayed that we would follow all such things that are agreeable to our profession of Christ Jesus. Thus, the virtue of humility that Jesus displays for us, we have prayed that we would follow, that we would do the same. And that requires us to examine his humility more closely. In the narrative written by John here Jesus got up from where he was reclining. He took the initiative to humbly serve his disciples. Thus, practicing the virtue of humility, beloved, is looking for opportunities to serve. It is not waiting to be asked. It is not waiting to be told. It is getting up on your own initiative and doing something for someone else. And this is a very stark contrast to the disciples of Jesus who were still talking among themselves regarding who is the greatest, who is going to be sitting next to him when he had his earthly kingdom. When he claimed his earthly rule, they didn't get they didn't get it until after the resurrection that the role of Jesus was much greater than any political rule It was to take his rightful place as ruling over all that there is. And to rule in such a manner, he had to be a humble servant. Recall St. Paul describing it to the Philippians, but made himself of no reputation by taking on the very nature of a servant. We are to emphasize today, made himself, as if it was his choice to become a man and to serve humanity. We heard from John 10 Jesus say that he laid down his own life. It was all his choice, as any humble service should be. You know, one of the more strains that occur between a husband and wife is motive behind an action. A man can take out the garbage, clear the table, pick up the living room because his wife told him to do those things. Or he can do it. Because he saw such things needed to be done and he wanted to be a help to his wife. I ask you, which motive receives the most praise from his wife and the most kisses at night? It's the latter. It's the latter because we see behind it a motive that cares, that wants to show love. Such is naturally received as an act of love. That is what Jesus did. Now if a husband takes out the garbage, clears the table, and picks up the living room just because he wants more kisses at night, I can't speak about that this morning. Next, Peter objects to Jesus washing his feet. And as was noted, Peter spoke for all of the disciples with this objection. And Jesus responds with kindness, honesty, and patience. You are already clean, Jesus tells Peter. And this says to Peter that your sins have already been forgiven. Here, Jesus shows that the virtue of humility practice includes patient instruction. Patience is long-suffering, and long-suffering is practicing love. It is recognizing that not all people are gifted with the same spiritual gifts. Not all have the same learning abilities, the same spiritual sensitivities, the same attention to detail, or the same maturity level. Humility practice motivates a teacher to adapt to the strength of a student, to the strength of a disciple. Jesus is understanding where Peter is in regards to his maturity. And so Jesus adapts. Now the response of Peter to Jesus adapting is a warning to us what humility is not. Humility is not exaggerating the situation. He did not need to be so overt as to say, Jesus, then wash all of me. Humility practice is not drawing attention to oneself publicly by loudly showing how humble you are. It is not rejecting praise when people are already giving you praise. It is not confessing sin and then when someone else confesses more sin, you try to top them by confessing even more than them. Of course, we call this false humility because it actually brings more attention to the person as he as he tries to display a greater humbleness, which actually causes more praise to come his way. For the Christian, the follower of Jesus, as our example, humility is to be genuine. When Jesus says to Peter, You are not all clean, we know now what Peter did not. Jesus was referring to Judas who would betray him. Well the first part of verse 12 says, so when he had washed their feet, plural, John was using such as a segue to what Jesus would teach next, but it is also told to us That the one who was unclean also had his feet washed. Jesus washed the feet of his betrayer. And by doing such, Jesus shows that the virtue of humility practice bends the knee and serves the lowest of sinners. The humility of Jesus served a sinner who would never repent. You know, you and I identify more easily with the imprecatory psalms. The impregatory psalms are those psalms that call God to curse the enemy. They are psalms that invoke the justice of God. Here are a few examples from Psalm 5. Pronounce them guilty, O God. Let them fall by their own counsel. From Psalm 6, let all my enemies be ashamed and greatly troubled. From Psalm 12, may the Lord cut off all flattering lips and the tongue that speaks proud things. From Psalm 35, let those be put to shame and brought to dishonor who seek after my life. These are the type of words that you and I would pray regarding Judas. And yet Jesus washes his feet. Jesus humbles himself before his enemy and serves him. Consider when Jesus taught in the Sermon on the Mount that his followers were to love their enemies, and pray for those who persecute them. Such teaching could easily be dismissed as hyperbole. Jesus doesn't actually expect his followers to pray for their enemies, right? That requires great humility. No one can be that humble, right? Jesus was. Jesus was humble before Judas, his betrayer. Psalm 41 is a prophecy of what Judas would do to Jesus. It says, All who hate me whisper together against me, against me they devise my hurt. Even my own familiar friend in whom I trusted who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me. I wonder, have you ever had people whisper about you? They talk low, and when you enter the room, they even talk lower. And then their eyes divert back and forth between you and their co-conspirator. Sure you have, we all have. Now let us say that those who whisper about you are planning your death Do you want to love them? Do you want to pray for them? Do you want to wash their feet? Thus, the remarkable humility of Jesus. I found a poem. That summed up this sermon so well, you would have thought I wrote the sermon after I found the poem. It is by Wayne Van Horn, a professor at Mississippi College, a Christian college. It goes as follows. Jesus wrapped a towel around his waist that night, and then gave his disciples an unforgettable sight. The King of Glory knelt and washed their feet till clean. He loved these men dearly and wanted his love to be seen He washed the feet of Peter, who protested all the while, but Jesus did it anyway, wiping and drying with a smile. Unless I wash you, you have no part of me. Wash my whole body, Lord, for I must be with thee He washed the feet of John, the disciple whom he loved, knowing this one would someday write about his saving love. For John one day, for Jesus' cause, would live in long exile, and write the revelation there on Patmos Isle. He washed the feet of Thomas, the one noted most for doubt, who yet had come to know that Jesus with God had clout. For Jesus had told him, Thomas, you must believe. So Thomas turned to Jesus, his soul from sin relieved. He washed the feet of James, the brother of dear John, and knew that he would serve well but not live too long. Just fourteen years past Calvary for faithfulness to God's word, King Herod had James killed, putting him to the sword He washed the feet of Andrew, who brought his brother Peter to the Lord, and knew that his disciple would be a man of his word. And so it was. Jesus made his way, washing the feet of all these men. The cross of Calvary growing near, where he would die for sin. And then one last disciple, thirty pieces of silver was his pay, this devil of disciples, whom his own Lord would now betray. What were his thoughts when Jesus knelt to wash his cruel Judas' feet? He knelt and washed and dried with care and then took his seat. Do you understand tonight what I have done for you? You must take a towel of your own in order to be true. And when this world, one by one, in humble service fare as you, my saving love, with poor lost sinners share. You must serve and share with everyone, not just the ones you like or love. Share even with your enemies and point them to me above. Let us pray. Our Father, we hear the call to be humble, and we recognize that it is a call for each and every one of us that we cannot ignore. And so from this place and from this hour, Father, remind us each and every moment to take that position of kneeling before our fellow Loved ones, before our fellow Christians and before the world. And may you win them one by one by such love. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen

sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
