In our culture, in our era, we experienced the temptation toward fear Toward fear, as acts of terror occur more frequently and more heinously And the media intensifies its coverage of said acts of terror from every possible angle of blame that they can come up with. These two ingredients, the media and terror, can make it seem as though the world is crumbling around us. Thus, we are tempted to shut our doors and windows and stay home, hoping that the world does not come into our lives. But that is not what the apostles did. They went out and they spoke up. And that is what Jesus told his followers to do. Did you notice that in the descriptions I gave of the apostles who were martyred, that some of them were martyred far from Jerusalem? Having traveled as far east as India and as far west as Europe. They did this knowing the words that Jesus spoke to them. The world would hate them, persecute them, and kill them. Beloved, we should not need the guilt. Of Jesus walking past us out of our homes into the world while we are going into our homes to shut our doors and windows so that the dangers of the world cannot reach us. Yes, the world can be a dangerous and scary place because there are evil people who have made themselves tools of the devil. Yes, when we speak the truth of the gospel in that same world, we make ourselves a target of evil people. But St. Paul's words, his words, to die is gain, to live is Christ. They are to ring true for us if we call ourselves Christian. Jesus taught the disciples what was ahead of them What was ahead of them so that they would not cower, so that they would not be paralyzed by fear. It is our responsibility to take those same words of Jesus and apply them to our culture, our era, our today. As we stay in the truth, as we stay in the church and speak up And live out the gospel. Our days in God's hands are in God's hands, and no one can or will touch us. And thus God wills it. And if God wills it, we are to say, so be it, for we know in Christ our death will never be in vain. I prepared this sermon not really thinking that it was Father's Day, but it struck me This morning, that such a sermon, if it needs to be preached to anyone, is the Fathers For who needs to be the bravest in a family? Who needs to cast away fear? Who needs to stand up and speak out? But our fathers. Our fathers to lead, and for our families to follow. For the world, this slogan is for them. To fear, to fear is vain, and to live is following the Zeitgeist. For the Christian To die truly is gain, and to live truly is Christ. Amen and Amen. Let us pray

sermons.title: A Little While
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: My sin, oh the bliss of this glorious thought, my sin Not in part, but the whole, is nailed to the cross, and I bear it no more Praise the Lord. Praise the Lord. O my soul. Have any better words been written in a hymn than that? In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. May be seated. We've been walking through the gospel according to Saint John, and I once again encourage you to turn there. You will Most certainly benefit by following along. It's always good to have your Bibles open when a preacher is preaching. Need to make sure he's telling the truth. You need to be checking on me We start at verse 16 in John 16, and in verses 16 through 22, Jesus explains to his disciples. That there will be seasons ahead of them that will include both sorrow and joy. The confusing phrase for the disciples was a little while. A little while How much is a little while? And how do you not see a person and then see a person? The manner that John describes the scene causes us to picture Jesus saying that he would not be seen in a little while, and then he would be seen, and then not seen again, and after such a saying, the disciples whispered to each other what in the world Jesus could have meant. Jesus, we are not told he didn't hear that what they were saying to one another, but he knew their thoughts because he's God. And therefore went about answering a question that they were not willing to speak up about. Their future weeping and lamenting will be because of the suffering that Jesus would endure and because of his tortured death. A woman in childbirth is the chosen analogy to describe being in great pain in one moment and then in great joy in the next because of what is borne out of suffering. And it is a very interesting choice as an analogy For women give birth in great pain because of the curse God placed upon women because of the sin of Eve. But by suffering for the curse, the woman receives great joy because she endures the suffering and has a child. In like manner, Jesus suffers the curse, Adam and Eve's curse, for us by his wounds and by his death, and yet the same wounds and death bring about new life. And thus a reason for great, great joy. Jesus wants his disciples to consider how seasons of sorrow turn to seasons of joy. Because all of the seasons are grace to us. That we are even in a season is grace to us. As commentator Matthew Henry stated, the Holy Spirit would be their comforter. And neither men nor devils, neither sufferings in life nor in death would ever deprive them of their joy. But notice, if you would, the source of a Christian's sorrow and the source of a Christian's joy. A believer in Jesus has joy or sorrow according to his or her sight of Christ. The presence of Jesus in our lives is a source of sorrow and joy. Sorrow when we do not heed Him, when we do not obey Him. When we do not act as if we know him. And joy when he is followed, when he is trusted, when he is honored, when he is loved. Jesus then moves his teaching regarding his absence, appearance, and absence to how his disciples' relationship with the Godhead would change after he ascends to heaven. After he is seated at the right hand of the Father. Because Jesus was our offering to God for our sins, he is forever our access to the throne of the Godhead. Thus, when we ask of God, when we need anything of God, it is to be asked in the name of Jesus And in asking, that is an acknowledgement that without him and without what he has done for us, we have no access at all. In fact, without him, our deserved place is hell. Jesus continues teaching, saying that our prayers, by way of Jesus the Father, confesses that we are in need. Just by praying in his name says we are in need. And it says we have a desire for spiritual blessings. And it also confesses that we can get neither by no other means but Jesus. Let us recognize that the necessity of Jesus to be our mediator is to impress upon us the deep sense of our sinfulness. And the great power and the great merit procured by Jesus because of Calvary. And next is a plain declaration of Jesus coming from the Father and his return to the Father. And this plainly teaches that the entrance of Jesus into the world was God manifest in the flesh, and his departure would be a return to the glory from which he came. By learning this, the disciples are improving in their knowledge and thus improving in their faith. But the disciples were not aware of their own weaknesses. They weren't ready for what was ahead of them. We know that they will shirk in their trial to betray. They will bail. They will leave instead of face what Jesus was about to face. Their recent understanding will not result in a faith strong enough to overcome their cowardice. And Jesus, this is remarkable, Jesus knows that And Jesus knows that and still promises them peace. The world will not provide for them peace. Jesus most recently warned them that the world will hate them, even unto the death of each of them. But Jesus will provide the peace they need to endure the hatred of the world and to overcome their own cowardice. In these words of warning, beloved, Jesus is preaching the gospel. Jesus is offering forgiveness to his disciples even before they desert him, even before one denies him. Jesus has peace ready for them, unmerited peace. It is a peace that touches the soul, the very essence of who a person is. And it is a peace that Jesus offers to each and every human being who would confess their sins to Him and confess Him as their Savior. And there is no sin that Jesus will not forgive as his sacrifice is sufficient to overcome all sin, all death. Don't pretend to be more righteous than Jesus by insisting that your sins cannot be forgiven. They can and they are if you confess Jesus and thus peace that only he can offer is yours. Believe that with all of your being Now I have summarized the gospel reading and clearly preached the gospel to you as it is here. So now I want to focus on a phrase in this whole passage. A phrase that was very curious to me when I read it. That phrase I want to examine is in a little while. In a little while. When Jesus says, in a little while, he is referring to a short amount of time as it is measured on earth. In the most practical interpretation, we understand Jesus to be referring to a literal few days, for the teaching of Jesus, as recorded by John in this chapter and in these verses. All have occurred within the final week of Jesus' life. Right before the cross, Jesus is saying these things In fact, it is immediately after Jesus prays his high-priestly prayer, which is in our next chapter, chapter 17, that he and his disciples enter the Garden of Gethsemane. But we all have experienced that a little while can feel like a more than just a few days. A little while can feel like a very long time. It can feel like a very long time when you have lost a loved one in death. It can feel like a very long time when you wait for a loved one to come out of surgery. It can feel like a very long time when you wait for that doctor to call you and tell you the test results. A little while. A very long time. It can seem like a long time when you repeatedly pray for a sinner to come to repentance. Jesus calls his time of suffering, death, and descending into hell to be a little while. So that his disciples will remind themselves that pain, the pain that they experience while he is away from them, it will pass. It will have an end. There will be an end, and the ending will be what they had hoped for. Jesus will be alive When we are when we are not told that there will be an end to suffering, an end to a trial, we are tempted to lose hope. I remember reading about Navy SEAL training and what it described must be one of the most difficult and demanding training that any special forces are required to endure. It was one Navy man's perspective regarding marching and running that I recall best when he stated That it is one thing to be told that they were jogging, going to jog ten miles with all of the gear on their backs and after being soaked to the bone, coming out of a cold ocean. He could endure that That was much easier, he said, than being told to start running and have no idea how far or how long. Three miles of such running feels as it is twice ten miles I believe that well describes our human condition. We feel linked to time. We feel confined by time. It has us. Yet time helps us understand what we conclude about our reality. But I remind you that time of any length is a created thing Time, like the rest of creation, will come to an end. Even when the Bible refers to concepts such as eternity. That is not time forever, but that's the way God communicates to us because that's all we can understand. Time will cease when there is a new heaven and a new earth. I try to teach my philosophy students that even though we use the concept of infinity to measure things, An actual infinity of something, anything, including time, does not actually exist. I do this because modern science having no empirical proof for how or when the universe came to be throws out the argument that the universe has always been here. Always. And therefore does not need evidence of how it came to be. But that claim means that the universe has existed for an infinite number of days And I think if I can prove to the students that the concept of infinity is not real, then I can say that the scientists are wrong. Now the following argument is not mine. We can use many different items to show this, but we're going to use a timeline. So I need you you to imagine a time not a timeline, excuse me, a number line Imagine a number line, and I'm going to go like you would on a board from left to right. Imagine a number line And the numbers are listed, and it goes to infinity, and I put an arrow on the end of it because that indicates infinity. And so we have a traditional number line in front of us. And you recognize that you can remove all the even numbers and you can remove all the odd numbers, and when you do that, it still goes on to infinity. You remove the even numbers, all the odd numbers go on to infinity. You remove the odd numbers, all these even numbers go on to infinity, right? Okay. So if you have a traditional number line that goes on to infinity, and then you remove all of the odd numbers that would go on to infinity if they were on there. And you just have the even numbers left, then you have an even numbered line that goes on to infinity Are you with me? And so you have the first number line, the traditional number line, infinity. You take away the odd numbers, infinity, and that leaves you with infinity. Right? And so you conclude that infinity minus infinity equals Infinity. That doesn't make any sense. Of course it doesn't. It doesn't make any sense because infinity is a concept. It's not a reality. And so we recognize that if you were to respond by saying that that equation is absurd, you are correct. The point of such an exercise is to show that infinity is abstract. It's not reality. Days do not go on forever. Days and nights and time have a beginning and they will have an end. And for the Christian, that means two things at least. We are to redeem the time we have been given, and we are to endure the trials, knowing that they have an end. St. Paul instructed the Ephesian Christians to redeem the time, for the days are evil. The NIV interprets Paul to say, make the most of every opportunity. The warning there is to keep Christians away from the sins that make us deaf to the Holy Spirit and sins that enslave us in time. Our time in this world is so very short. Even if a person lives to what we call an old age, the time span is nothing compared to all of creation. Recall how the book of Ecclesiastes describes our lives. We are, it says, as vapor. Like a vapor, we suddenly appear. We barely have substance. We can be seen, and then we fade, just as a vapor fades. This is our life, and the depiction of it is to humble us. In confirmation class, I usually hand out a copy of a timeline. that shows the important dates in the life of the Christian church. The timeline is long and cumbersome. It has so many events on it that That took place, events that were quite dramatic, but even something dramatic like the Reformation is but a tiny dot. Well, we are all tiny dots on the timeline. But the shortness of our lives is not to humble us so that we feel sorry for ourselves or sorry of how seemingly insignificant we are. No It is a call for us to redeem our days, which is to use each day God has ordained for us to live in, doing that which matters. When St. Peter explained why Jesus had not returned as quickly or in a little while, like many of the first century Christians expected, remember these words Peter said. With the Lord, a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day. And then he explained that the Lord is waiting to return because he does not want any person to perish but for all to come to repentance. Now we don't have time to discuss the difference between God's ordained sovereign will and his desired will. We will save that for another time. But what we can do is underline how God uses these days before he returns to redeem people. That's the purpose of the days, to redeem people. He uses these days so that the unbeliever will believe and so that the believer will obey. God wants all the time we have been given in each of our short lives to matter and to matter for an eternal reward. He wants us to use our lives to make us more holy, more like him, and to help others know him and to be more like him. God redeems the time by using his church to redeem the time. And the church redeems the time when all of its members as individuals redeem their time. This will not be a surprise to many of you. I hate stoplights. And I hate traffic jams. I hate such things because they seem to waste so much time. I would not want to know how much of my life has been spent in a car at a stoplight or at a traffic jam. That would be depressing. But I need to hate other sections of my life just as much. Like when I don't redeem the time to love someone. When I don't redeem the time by being kind to someone. When I don't redeem the time by forgiving someone or asking for forgiveness. When I don't redeem the time by telling someone that Jesus loves them, the gospel's real and true A little while longer, Jesus said. That's all we have. Whether we are an infant just born or 92, a little while longer is all you and I have. Second, as I said, being aware of the shortness of our lives enables us to walk the trials of God that He has for us to experience. St. Peter said to the Christian church, Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice in so far as you share Christ's suffering, that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed. And we are to believe that his glory will be revealed in a little while. To consider That we, when we go through our trials, are sharing in the sufferings of Jesus. That is a great mystery and should be very humbling We are not worthy, but he makes us worthy. We don't have the faith, but he gives us the faith. When we suffer in a trial, we share in the sufferings of Jesus because he suffers with us also, promising never to leave us or forsake us. If you have prayed for a cup to pass from you, and it has yet to pass, hear the words of Jesus for you in a little while. If you have asked the Heavenly Father for a person you love to come to repentance and have faith in Jesus, and there seems to be no movement with that person, hear the words of Jesus to you. In a little while. If you have long for his second coming as you see the world going after false hope and false gods, allow the words of Jesus to calm your heart. In a little while. I close with a poem from John Milton. That describes how time, like an enemy of God, will be placed under our feet. Fly, envious time, till thou run out thy race. Call on the lazy leaden stepping hours, whose speed is but the heavy plummet's pace, and glut thyself with what thy womb devours, which is no more when what is false and vain. and merely mortal dross, so little is our loss, so little is thy gain. For when as each thing bad thou hast entombed And last of all by greedy self consumed, then long eternity shall greet our bliss with an individual kiss, and joy shall overtake us as a flood When everything that is sincerely good and perfectly divine, with truth and peace and love shall ever shine. About the supreme throne of him to whose happy making sight alone, when once our heavenly guided soul shall climb, then all this earthly grossness quit Attired with stars, we shall forever sit, triumphing over death and chance and thee, O time. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Prayer for Priests
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. Encourage you to turn to John seventeen. Following along there with me this morning. A man and a woman, having been married forty years, sat on a couch together in the office of a marriage counselor. The wife was teary and sad. The husband was grumpy and stared at the floor. The wife began the session by telling the counselor that she does not feel loved. She cooks for her husband. She cleans for her husband. She serves her husband by providing every need that he has ever had, and yet she did not feel loved. And she revealed to the counselor that the husband does not even tell her that he loves her. Is that true? The counselor asked the husband. You don't tell your wife, you don't say to your wife that you love her? The husband glared at the counselor for an uncomfortable ten seconds and responded Forty years ago on our wedding day, I told my wife, I love her. If anything changes I'll let her know. Now it's hard to argue with that logic. But the story informs us of how important speaking words of affection in a relationship, especially a marital relationship, how important it is. But have you ever wondered why? Why is it important, why is it necessary for the health of a relationship with my wife that I tell her on a daily basis that I love her? I agree with the grouchy man. I said it when we got married, it should stand until something changes. That should be enough, shouldn't it? But it is not, and I wonder why. We will come back to that question. The prayer by Jesus in John 17 is labeled by some to be the high priestly prayer. That is because Jesus serves here as our high priest, in that he offers to God what is needed for our forgiveness. He is our intercessor who goes to the Father for our sake, that we might obtain forgiveness for our sins. But as you know, there is a uniqueness about Jesus, for he is both the one who offers to God the sacrifice for our sins, and is himself the offering. Thus he is a high priest like no other high priest. The high priest normally stands in an objective position between God and the sinner as a mediator. Well he takes the name of a the the life of a nameless animal. Jesus is both the high priest and the sacrifice, and this causes his mediation to be very, very personal. We are to realize, having the very words of the high priestly prayer revealed to us, that it is very rare for us To know what Jesus prayed. We are told, of course, that Jesus did pray, but this is a privilege for us to hear what he prayed. And consider this, and I did not realize this until studying for this sermon, that Jesus never prayed with his apostles. It's not recorded that he prayed with them. And also it is not recorded that Jesus corporately worshipped with his apostles. Although we can reason that he likely did, it is not recorded. It can be argued, I believe, that when Jesus was teaching his apostles, he was, in a sense, praying with them. But that is not how you and I normally think about the traditional way of praying with one another In not praying with the apostles, or at least not recording it, it seems to be exemplifying that prayer is a very personal thing between the believer and God. In John's Gospel, we have three accounts of Jesus praying out loud. In each of these occasions, it is evident that Jesus wanted to be heard. He wanted these words to be heard and remembered. In fact, when Jesus prays outside the tomb of Lazarus, you'll remember we covered that story, he overtly prays out loud and he states that he's praying out loud for the benefit of those who can hear him, those who are standing around. Thus, we can understand this prayer to be the same. It's prayed out loud for our benefit, to hear it and remember it. And John provides an eyewitness detail of this prayer as he begins describing that Jesus looked toward heaven and prayed. We know, of course, that you do not need to look to heaven to pray, as we can bow our heads and close our eyes like we normally do, and pray to God in our own minds. But we should also acknowledge that posture for prayer helps us in making what we want to be true on the inside to be led by our outward position. Thus, if I want to be humble inside, I take the posture outside of kneeling. There are three postures of prayer as described in the Bible. The first is kneeling, which is our willingness to humbly serve God. Another is standing, symbolizing our readiness to serve God, and finally lying prostrate. Which communicates our awareness that we are not worthy in and of ourselves to approach God or His throne. John, our gospel writer, places the high priestly prayer after recording a lengthy teaching by Jesus, which we have covered in most recent weeks. And thus we can understand this prayer as a summation of the teachings of Jesus up to this point. I see three themes in this prayer. Three themes. The first is the obedience of Jesus to the Heavenly Father. The second is the glorification of the Son through his death and resurrection. And the third is God being revealed to his disciples, the disciples of Jesus then and disciples in the future, to separate us from this cursed world in which we live. We could, and some would argue, we should hear sermons about each of these three themes, breaking it up into three different sermons. As so often with the great texts of Holy Scripture, one could preach many sermons on many different themes from some few verses. We have the doctrine of predestination in this prayer. We have the kingship of Christ. We are to see how he reigned even when he was on the cross. That even in his greatest humiliation and suffering, he was exercising the authority the Father had given him, conquering sin and death. We also have in this prayer the nature of eternal life, the doctrine of two states of Christ, the doctrine of the Trinity. And each of these could be preached about, of course. But instead, I want us to focus on what our Lord Jesus did in this prayer, and I want to communicate it to you as something that you and I should be doing. how we should pray. And I don't always like to do that, for I perceive Christians make the mistake. Of looking at the life of Jesus and concluding that we're to do whatever he did. Remember the pop popularity of the WWJD initials? What would Jesus do and try to live out our lives? We can figure out what he would do in our situation And I always appreciated the intent of such initials so as to remind us of how we are to live Christian lives all of the time But the truth is the WWJD missed the mark, specifically missed the mark. For what would Jesus do is that he would humble himself He would be born as a servant. He would live a life of sacrifice. He would die the death of a criminal, and he would rise again. That's what Jesus would do. That is what Jesus would do, and we know that because that's what he did. We are to copy what Jesus did. We are not to copy what Jesus did, excuse me, but we are to live our lives in honor of what Jesus did But Jesus prayed this high priestly prayer out loud for a reason. He prayed it so that we might learn from what he prayed and so that we might follow the example in our own prayers. So again, start with looking up. As was said, we do not need to look up But looking up symbolizes that we are dependent and that our help comes from above. It does not come from beside us, it does not come from below us. If you need help overcoming sin, look up. If you need help forgiving someone, look up. If you need your heart to be calm, look up. Make your body do what needs to be done in your heart. Second, pray for the glory of God to be revealed Oftentimes we say that we do not know what to pray when we hear of violent outbursts, another mass killing. Another act of terror or a natural disaster. What do we pray? But a simple yet profound place to start is to pray for the glory of God to be revealed. Notice how Jesus wants to be glorified so that he can return the glory right back to the Father. Each of them wanting to glorify the other is the unity that we are to practice as we follow Jesus But here he wants first to glorify the Father. And so we pray. From the fires in California that have taken land and lives, God, let your glory be revealed. From the floods in West Virginia, Lord, let your glory be revealed. From the shooting in San Bernardino, in Paris, in Orlando, and now the bombing in Turkey, Bangladesh. Baghdad, Heavenly Father, let your glory be revealed. We do not know how it should be revealed, and we do not know when it's going to be revealed, but we do know without any shred of doubt. That the best thing for mankind is for the glory of God to be revealed. God's glory being revealed This is what we pray when we pray the Lord's Prayer. We say, Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. In heaven, God's glory is revealed, and that needs to happen on earth. For the sake of the unborn children, God, let your glory be revealed. For the sake of abused children, Lord, let your glory be revealed. For the sake of abused women, Jesus, let your glory be revealed. For the care of the poor and the downtrodden, Holy Trinity, one God, let your glory be revealed. Do you hear how such prayers resonate with the mind and the spirit? Do you feel how appropriate and fitting such wording is in every given situation? Praying God that your glory be revealed is saying little in terms of word count, but a great deal in terms of what needs to be done. Next, we are to pray for one another. That's what Jesus does. Prays for his disciples. After he declares the glory of God being revealed as he lived a holy life, he then asks the Father to keep his disciples. Keep them By keeping, he means sustain them. He means protect them. He means that he wants the Heavenly Father to protect them from leaving the faith, their faith in Jesus. Remember folks, the devil wants to either lead you to deny Jesus or kill you. And he can't have you dead unless the Heavenly Father allows him to do so. And since God does not allow your death yet. The devil works instead to tempt you toward non-belief. That is the devil's goal. It is what he works for daily. To have you give up your faith in Jesus as your Savior and as your God. And Jesus knows this, and so he prays that those who believe in him would not be lost. And Christians, we need to pray for one another. Of course we do, and of course we practice it. But we often limit those times of prayer when someone is sick. Here Jesus prays for his followers to remain faithful, and he does so before his disciples are not faithful. Again, we too often pray for one another when we hear of a person struggling in his or her faith, and we pray for people who have walked away from Christ. And we should keep doing that. But Jesus gives us an example of praying for one another before the struggle begins and before someone walks away. And Jesus next praise, and this is this, I feel humbled that I never have seen this before. Jesus prays next for his followers to be sanctified, to be made holy. Have you ever prayed for someone to be holy? He prays for his followers to be holy both in their heart and in their behavior, for by living in such a way they glorify God, and such living keeps them in the faith. Jesus wants the good work that God has begun in his disciples to continue until it is completed and they enter into their rest. Do we pray like that for one another? Do we pray for one another to live holy lives? I know that I pray for my children not to get into trouble, not to do foolish things that they will regret later. I pray for the physical safety of my grandchildren. But I have yet to pray for any of my children to be holy. At least I hadn't until I studied this. To pray in the manner that Jesus prayed. Our children, our loved ones, one another, to be holy. And Jesus next prayed for us. He prayed for those who would come after the first disciples. And he prayed for us to be kept in the fold, to not walk away. And he prayed for us to be holy. Thus, we should be praying for those who will follow us. We should be praying, of course, for our children and our grandchildren, and even our great-grandchildren, yet to be born, that they might know Jesus. We should be praying for the spouses of our children, our grandchildren, our great-grandchildren, that they too would have eternal life. We should be praying for parishioners, yet to be known. I should be praying for the next pastor of St. Stephen's parish, that he might be faithful and true to the gospel. All of this, of course, is for the glory of God. And finally, what I want us to learn from this prayer of Jesus So that we would pray in a similar manner is how Jesus prayed for certainties. Jesus prayed for certainties. A certainty is that which will come about, regardless of how or what or if we pray. We are to pray for certainties. Praying for a certainty is, for example, when Jesus prayed that he would be glorified. Even though he already knew how things would come to pass in terms of how he would be glorified. He knew it was going to happen, yet he prayed it anyways. He had told his disciples often enough what was to come, how he would die, how he would rise again, how he would ascend to heaven And yet he prayed to be glorified. A certainty. Another example is how he prayed that he might give eternal life to his disciples. Even though he had often said before that he would indeed give them eternal life, and that no one would be snatched out of his hand. And yet he prays that they might have eternal life, a certainty. And yet we see in that action of praying certainties that words need to be spoken. In fact, the praying for certainties is characteristic of Christian prayer. We pray for God's will to be done. In the certainty that it will be done, regardless if we pray that or not. We pray for Christ's return in the knowledge that the day is already fixed and nothing in the world can prevent it from coming to pass. Well let me ask and answer the obvious question: why does someone pray for things that are certain to come to pass? Sounds unnecessary. The simple answer is that prayer is not a formula. Do you remember that faddish book, The Prayer of Jabez? And how it presented prayer as a formula, like a spell that needed to be said in a specific manner for it to work? The book was a fad because it did not communicate what Christian prayer truly is, which is an act of love between God and his people. It is a conversation with the one true God that we love and trust. This takes us back to the older couple in our marriage counseling. While the logic of the husband was sound, it was still foolish. For he did not understand that he was in a relationship, and that was to include all that he was as a person And all that his wife was, and that includes emotions and the inherent need for expressed affection. Words of love need to be heard, and so they need to be stated, for that is how God created humanity. We are relational. And just as words of love need to be spoken, so do words of prayer need to be spoken. For they are a part of what it means to be in a relationship with God. Yes, what we pray can be certain. What we are praying to someone that we love, that we trust, that we revere. This takes us to what it means to be a Christian. Fundamentally, being a Christian is to have a loving, trusting, and eternal relationship with God. Who, of course, is Jesus Christ, our Savior and our Lord. And to be in relationship is to be in communication with God. And we are privileged to speak with him, to speak with him in constant prayer. Pray without ceasing, Paul instructed. And we do that by talking to God, talking to Jesus all day, every day. Prayer can sound like a daunting task because we think we have to come up with something beautiful, something right, and something theologically astute. Sometimes words like that don't come to us. But Jesus modeled a prayer for us here. First, in what we call the Lord's Prayer, and hear how he prayed to the Father. He prayed for the glory of God to be revealed. All of us can do that. He prayed for his disciples to be holy. All of us can do that. Praying for one another to be holy. And he prayed for those who would come later. All of us can do that. Prayer doesn't sound so daunting when it is summarized like it is here. And we are to pray to a God we love, we trust, we revere, meaning that He's someone we already want to talk to. So with that said, let us pray.

sermons.title: Women who fear God
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: He is brilliant for the power of the Lord. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We begin this Lord's day starting on a new journey. We're going to be hearing sermons from the book of Exodus. You may wonder why we are not finishing John and the Gospel of John after chapter 17 that we heard from last week. We are told about the Passion of Christ and his resurrection. Since we have recently come out of Holy Week and Easter Sunday and Ascension Day and Pentecost I conclude that we can wait another cycle year before we rehearse it all again. So I have chosen the book of Exodus. Now I call it a book, but it is really a continuation of Genesis. They are one story continuing But historically, they have been broken up for the sake of keeping shorter scrolls in order to make it more easily to preserve them. Our introduction for this Exodus is actually going to begin in Luke 9, verse 31. Strange place to begin, but that's where we're off, where we are. For there in Luke chapter 9 is the story of the transfiguration of Jesus. And you remember that with him was Elijah and Moses. And Luke tells us what Jesus, Elijah, and Moses were talking about. Again, what a privilege to know what they were saying. The New King James says that they spoke to one another about the decease of Jesus. The decease. That is an awkward translation for me. The New American Standard translates deceased to be departure. They talked about the departure of Jesus, and the NIV uses the same. These words are chosen for understanding, but Bible readers are robbed a bit by the great insight and irony of the word that Luke actually chose. The word Luke used for decease, for departure, was Exodus. Not the concept of Exodus or the idea of Exodus, but the actual word Exodus. Moses and Elijah spoke to Jesus about his Exodus. Yes, Exodus can refer to one leaving this life and thus refer to a person's death. And it can refer to a departure as in leaving this world. But the word Exodus for the Bible student allows for so much more meaning. For we know Exodus to be meaning free from bondage. We know it as being given the moral law as a standard for living under God's covenant We know Exodus as a word that describes what a Christian experiences when his or her sins are forever forgiven, and he or she is freed from the bonds of sin and eternal death. As we study the book of Exodus, we are going to be pointing and hopefully better understanding and thus building our faith up. Regarding what Jesus has accomplished by providing for our Exodus. Let's look at the text. Exodus chapter 1, beginning at verse 1. And as I said We could treat this as actually Genesis chapter 50, verse 27, for it is a continuation of the stories previous. And where Genesis left us off was the death of Joseph, the son of Jacob. That Joseph had secured the lives of his family, Israel, by serving Pharaoh for many years. And so we are given the names of the tribal leaders who have built up a large household and each generation having more and more children. And the heads of those tribes were the sons of Jacob as red, which we know to be twelve in number. Only the names of the sons are listed because, as we know, the sons were the inheritors of their father's wealth. But women ought not feel slighted in the least, for in the New Testament, under the covenant procured by Jesus Both genders are one, and both are referred to as sons, for all are inheritors of eternal life from Christ Jesus. Now the number given to us of the family of Jacob is 70. And we don't need to read that literally. You can if you want to. But understand that you have a combination in that number of perfection and completion. And 7 times 10 is 70, so the number could very well be being used as symbolic. It is a number that communicates that these are all the people that God had intended there to be before he moves his people on to another chapter, another book, another stage to make them his people. Now, the increase of the number of family members, as it describes in verses 6 and 7, is to be understood as a blessing. I'm grateful to serve in a parish that understands offspring, growing families, children to be a blessing. Bobby Lynn and I have a few stories of people who responded quite ungraciously when we announced that she was once again pregnant. The first parish I served as a youth minister, the congregation gasped when we announced that she was pregnant with our third child. We have even had family members who would show their disapproval with our announcement with a sigh. And some who would say, Well, if if that's what you want And strangers would even chime in one day at in a mall. For those of you who are younger, that's a big building. It's got a lot of different stores in it. One day in a mall we lost track of Joel, who had wandered a bit. He was with a young man who was holding his hand and Bobby Lynn thanked the man and he thought he needed to tell her that she had too many kids. Such a sentiment cannot be found in Holy Scripture. Children, all children are a gift from the Lord. And as believers, they are to be as arrows in a quiver that we shoot out into the world for the glory of God. Bear with me, for I need to stay on that topic a little longer because of the times in which we live. Every young Christian couple needs to do their part in having children and raising them in the Christian faith. And by children I mean more than the replacement rate. The replacement rate is obviously two, and actually more, when you consider childhood mortality. Statistics say a couple should have at least three children in order to replace themselves But the birth rate in the United States is below two per family, and is significantly lower in Europe. The greatest cause of population growth, and I checked this out twice, in the US and Europe, is immigration. And I don't have a problem with that. Only the immigration consists of a large number of number of people who are not Christian. And I don't have a problem with that. If the church is able to reach out to them, present to them the gospel. But that is the problem. The Christian population is shrinking in both America and in Europe as families are smaller and the faith is not carefully passed on. Young families need to have more children to increase the size of the church and thus increase the workers in the church to be able to convert the many immigrants To have large families and worship a different God. And that means that it is not virtuous by itself to have three or more children He must be willing to work at training them in the Christian faith, which takes a great deal of effort, sacrifice, sincerity, and of course faith All of this is why young Christian families need to be supported by older generations. We are told that Israel as a people were fruitful and multiplied, and that made a difference. Their numbers alone made them formidable. And that cannot be said for the Christian church today. We are not formidable because of our numbers. But we can work to get there. The population of Israel, the growing population of Israel is what started the exodus. Perhaps when the number of Christians multiplies exceedingly, our final exodus will begin. Now, because of the population of the Israelites, the new king, the new Pharaoh, who didn't know Joseph, became afraid. To say he did not know Joseph is not to say that he did not know of him, but that he did not consider what authority and influence Joseph once had. It didn't matter to him. And that is natural for a new dynasty. Remnants of the old dynasty would be thrown out and even discredited. Now it says here that they dealt truly, or the Pharaoh dealt truthly, and that's a nice way of saying dishonestly. And we see that this type of politicking is not old. In studying ethics and sociology They've come to realize how easy it is for politicians to justify their behavior of being dishonest. It's called act utilitarianism. And it believes in the greater good. But it believes that you can get to the greater good by whatever means possible And so you have politicians just politicians justifying their lying, their cheating, their stealing, because they believe at least they're getting after the greater good. Of course, what the greater good is actually is debatable. For the Egyptians, the greater good was not to be overrun by the Israelites. The shrewdest plan was to make the lives of the average Israelites miserable, as they were to work as slaves to build cities where their taskmasters would rule over them. The problem was it didn't work. At least it didn't work in slowing down the population growth. The more they were afflicted, the more fruitful they became. Historically, that's usually what happens in the church. The more we are afflicted, the more fruitful we are. But the Egyptians continued thinking that they were not making life hard enough The New King James uses the word rigor twice. And the Hebrew word rigor means to break, to fracture with severity. They wanted the Israelites to be a people with broken spirits, losing even the will to live. Now the other part of the plan was to kill all male infants at birth Do we not see that the devil's methods have not changed as he continues to lie to women, having them conclude that abortion is better than life? As Matthew Henry summarized, the enmity that is in the seed of the serpent against the seed of the woman makes men forget all pity. It most certainly does. But what Pharaoh did not anticipate, because he had no understanding about what it meant to have devotion to the one true God He did not understand the midwives who had been ordered to kill these infant sons, for they were women who feared God over the Pharaoh. He did not anticipate it and it did not make sense to him when they did not carry out his instructions. And we should consider how courageous these women were to defy the king's orders. Their lives would mean nothing to Pharaoh and his henchmen. They could have been easily cut down and replaced. But they feared God And the midwives were shrewd themselves, for they told a believable lie to Pharaoh in order to continue to save the babies and to preserve themselves. And this elaborate lie, the idea of the Hebrew women giving birth so vigorously that they gave birth too quickly before the midwives could arrive That was a guess easily believed by the Pharaoh because the women were having so many babies. But it was still a lie, right? And lies are bad all the time, right? How can a person be said to fear God and tell a bold faced lie? Well, much has been discussed and debated about such instances, and I'll only mention a few points here. You will remember that Rahab hid the spies in the book of Joshua. And not only was she not rebuked, By the Lord for doing so, but she was instead saved from death and is labeled in the book of Hebrews as a hero of the faith. Such lying has been labeled by some to be dutiful lie. A dutiful lie. And that seems to soften it a bit. But the reasoning behind the acceptance of such lies is actually simple. People who are looking to do evil are not deserving of the truth. The wisdom, courage, and faith of those midwives and of Grey Hab and the family of Corey Tenboom Who did not allow the Jews to find the Nazis they were hiding in their home? The Kurds was a Those who were bent on evil did not deserve the truth to be told, and thus these people would not contribute to the evil intent. Such wisdom we too can follow. God, being pleased with the midwives, is said to deal with them, which is to say he ministered to them according to their faith. Verse 21 says that God provided households for them, meaning that he gave them husbands and he gave them children for their own. Realize that these women were slaves to the orders of Pharaoh's court. They had no hope in having their own families, but only to help others have children. But God overcame whatever man-made obstacles were in place in front of them, and God rewarded them, making them contributors to the fruit of Israel. And why? Why did God reward them? It wasn't for the lie. The midwives feared God. Now the Hebrew word feared has two essential meanings. The first is what we would call being scared, and the second is being reverent or in awe. The ear-tickling preacher doesn't mention the first part, being scared of God. That doesn't fit his narrative. He does not want it heard, he does not want it understood. God is our friend. God is all-loving. God is safe. And to be sure, he is all of that and more. And the more includes a God before whom we ought to be scared. It is the preacher to the Hebrews that said, It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of a living God. It is Jesus who said, Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Instead, fear the one who can destroy both the soul and body in hell. It was St. Paul who said, therefore, since we know what it means to fear God, we try to persuade men. We are to fear God because He is the final judge of each of us. We are to fear God because by ourselves we have no justification. We are to fear God because He is holy, pure, righteous, and we are not, but by the blood of Jesus. And because of the blood of Jesus, we live in the tension of fearing God, actually being scared of him. While at the same time calling him our Savior, even our friend, our beloved, benevolent God. In this story in Exodus, we hear for the first time in Holy Scripture people being rewarded by God because they feared him Now in Genesis, people fear other people. And when someone fears God, they do so in a convoluted manner. Remember that story of Abraham denying that Sarah was his wife. He gives the justification that he feared the king of Abimelech. And so he lied about Sarah. And then when he was confronted, he said that he knew that he was amongst the people that didn't fear God. But in doing so, Abraham's actions showed that he did not fear God, as he should have. The fear of God should have been his motivating factor to protect his wife, to shield her from those who would steal her away. Fear of God is to be a motivating factor in deciding our behavior, our actions. The Hebrew midwives feared God, and that caused them to place themselves in danger of their lives being taken from them to save babies being born. This story causes us to pray, O dear God of heaven and earth, give us more women like these Hebrew wit midwives. Who would risk their lives, their own lives, to save children born and unborn I couldn't help but think and considering the events this past week that are being aired all over our televisions and Our computers. What would happen in every situation that was tragic if the people involved feared God first? We know everything would be changed. And this story of these midwives is a cause us to ask, where in our lives. Do we need to fear God more than we fear men? And thus use that fear to act as God would have us act. Where in our individual lives do we need to behave in such a manner that distinctively shows that we fear God first and foremost? I've been speaking of the Hebrew midwives in general, when in full disclosure there is but two of them mentioned. Shifra and Pua in verse 15 identify. Shifra means beautiful, and Pua means one who cries out. Let us consider as motivation that each of our lives might be used to the glory of God. That the Exodus, one of the greatest events in the history of humanity, began with two women who feared God and acted accordingly. Two women, starting the Exodus. Dare we imagine the great things God will do in our lives and in the lives of people that we care for. If we foremost fear him and live according to that fear. As stated at the beginning of this sermon, We all have our own exoduses. The first is our exodus from the sins that bind us, which Jesus provides for us, forgiveness. And the second is our exodus from this world, where Jesus waits for us. In between those times, there are a lot of lives that need their own exodus from sin, from eternal death. Let us then fear God and do what is right, and let Him lead the way for our excellence. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Charge for a Priest
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Thank you all for coming out tonight. Thank you for this honor. Reverend Bowles to preach this charge for you. At the dinner table our son Joel mentioned the 40% rule. I had not heard of the 40% rule, so I did some reading. And came across a story of a rich executive and a Navy SEAL. The young executive met this particular Navy SEAL while participating in a 100-mile run. The executive was in the run as a member of a six-person relay team. The Navy SEAL was running the hundred miles by himself. After the race, the executive introduced himself to the Navy SEAL and asked him to come live with the executive and his family, that they all might receive from the SEAL greater mental toughness. Now the first day together, the executive learned what the forty percent rule is It is when your mind is telling you that you are done, and yet you are really only 40% done. To prove it, the SEAL asked the executive how many pull-ups he could do. The executive said eight. And so he went about doing eight pull-ups. He rested 30 seconds and the SEAL asked him to do eight more. He could only do six. He rested another 30 seconds, and he asked him to do eight more, and he only did four. The CEO then told the executive to do 100 pull-ups. The executive thought that he had no strength left in his arms. He couldn't even move them. But the SEAL insisted they keep going. And although it took a bit of time that day, the executive did a hundred more pull-ups. That he never would have believed he could have done. But that story is not hard evidence that the 40% rule is real. The following quote is from an exercise magazine. Quote, in a 2008 study, researchers found that subjects who were given a placebo, but told that they were given caffeine were able to lift significantly more weight than those who were really given caffeine. The article goes on. Of course, this doesn't imply that our bodies and minds are limitless, but it does confirm that to the extent of those limits need revising. Often we limit our abilities, but stories like the Executive and the Navy SEAL are numerous and show the capability of exceeding those limits. St. Paul's letter to the Corinthians, the second letter He was concerned about who was influencing these new Christians, and he was concerned that these Corinthians were rejecting his influence. And so he lists what he had endured for the sake of the gospel. His resume, if you will. And I wondered how the list would read if it was used as a job description for leading God's people, a job description to be a pastor. Imagine this, listening for a job. To be our pastor, five times you will need to receive 40 lashes less one. Three times the Presbyter will need to be beaten with rods. Once he is to be stoned, by the biblical definition of being stoned. Three times he is to experience a shipwreck with one night and a day adrift at sea. On journeys of visitation, he is to suffer dangers from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from saints. Danger from sinners, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers. The Presbyter is to have toil and hardship through many sleepless nights. in hunger and in thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure. And apart from other things, there is the daily pressure to suffer anxiety for all persons in the church. The Presbyter is to be weak, he is to be made to fall, and he is not to be indignant about it. For the sake of Christ, then our pastor, is to be content. with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. All serious candidates send their resume to the senior warden, and the address is listed. Any fakers? When St. Paul heeded the call to follow Jesus. And to be an ambassador of the good news of Jesus, he had no way of knowing what would be his journey No man stands up and says, here I am, send me, can know what is in store for him, how God will use him, what he must endure. And oh yes, Paul knew some of it. He was one of those persons who dished it out. He was a persecutor, making him fully aware that he too would be persecuted. But the manner and repetition and the situations he found himself in the middle of could not have been prepared for. Even the rest of the apostles, who were told by Jesus that the world would hate them because it hated him, and he specifically told them that they would die for Jesus They were not ready for what was going to be their moment. Last month I read to our congregation the summary of the apostles and their martyrdoms. And we told the story of Saint Peter, who was counseled to leave Rome to save his life, and as he was leaving, saw a vision of Jesus coming in to be crucified once again. Peter, even Peter, was not ready. You can be told often that you will face many difficulties as an ordained minister of the gospel. And you cannot anticipate how gut-wrenchingly hard it can be. Now, of course It can be easier for some men than others. Those who tickle the ears of their parishioners and who work hard not to take over any of the devil's territory, well they will find it easier The devil leaves such men alone. Such men are always already doing the work of the devil. But a man who truly loves God and loves the gospel will be harassed by the devil, and the biggest harassment will come from within, not from without. And oh yes, it will come from without, as is being proved in more and more in our culture. But for now it will first come from within. And it will appear to you that everything that you dreamed of your calling is just the opposite. Even in the church, yes, in the church, you will find what love is not. Consider the listing that Paul has in 1 Corinthians 13. In the church, it can happen the opposite. People will suffer shortly with you. Some people will not be kind to you. Some people will envy you. Some people will parade themselves and be puffed up. Some people will behave rudely, seek their own, be provoked, and think evil thoughts about you. They will rejoice when your sin is revealed. They will not believe the best of you and they will not endure you. And the question you have to answer, and I sincerely mean you have to answer it and answer it every day What are you gonna do about it? Are you going to run and hide like too many pastors do when they get roughed up? And so they go to another parish with their three years worth of sermons to preach them all over again, only to be roughed up again and to leave that church. The Christian Church has plenty of that type of man. Are you going to roll up your sleeves and fight for yourself? Are you going to make it about you against them and see who comes out ahead? You can prove them wrong and showing how their sin is actually worse than yours And you can win each scuffle, and you can raise your own right arm and the symbol of victory, and you can do so while your congregation is walking out the door, never to return again. Young ministers, such as myself, need to learn sooner than later that winning an argument is not winning people. And to be a fisher of men, which is what we are called to be as ministers of the gospel, is to win people. And I realize thus far that I have described uh what I've described about being a Presbyter is not positive. So, I'm going to double down. Recall in the book of 1 Kings When Elijah had defeated the prophets of Baal, and the Lord had answered his prayer to end the drought, and the rain came upon the land. And although all of his actions were good for the children of Israel, still King Ahab, that big baby, went and told his mommy wife Jezebel what Elijah had done. And this caused her to swear that she would see Elijah dead. When the news reached Elijah, he fled. He ran. He was scared for his life, and he was a day's journey into the wilderness before he sat and prayed that his life would end then and there. He was alone, or he felt alone. Elijah was at his forty percent. He thought he was drained. He thought he was alone. Do you psychologists say that being alone is one of mankind's greatest fears? And those that are before it are rejection, death, and failure. And all those include feeling alone. A minister, a teacher, a preacher of the gospel will have times of feeling alone, all alone. There are instances when even our spouses cannot get to us. And oh, a bit of personal advice. Don't ever tell your spouse, when she is not understanding you, that she sounds like the rest of your parishioners. I've heard that doesn't go over very well. The problem with Elijah when he reached his 40% is that he had been depending on his flesh, as was evident by him running into the wilderness, and his flesh let him down. He was depending so much on his own courage, his own strength, that he had a breaking point. And what he discovered not too long after was that he was never alone. And that God was with him always, as he proved being that still small voice. Things were not as Elijah thought they were, for God had other men he had saved and other men he had called. And Elijah could trust in God's sovereignty and the plan of God's salvation, even though he was looking through that glass dimly. Again, I understand that I have painted a gloomy picture of what it means to be called, to be ordained into the Christian ministry. But what I have said is true. And it is perhaps why, according to our prayer book, at the deacon ordination, this is the Presbyter ordination, at the Deacon ordination When the bishop asks the candidate if he is truly called, the appropriate response is, I think so. And I know I put the accent in the wrong place. To imply that there's some doubt, but it seems to fit. For we who save those vows truly don't know what we are going to experience So allow me to provide sage advice that was given to me before I entered the Christian ministry. Make your ministry about the gospel of Jesus Christ first and last. The bishop will ask you if you believe and will teach the holy scriptures, and you will say that you are persuaded And you are persuaded because the holy scriptures teach the gospel. The Bishma will ask you to perform dutifully the sacrament. And you will say you will do so because the sacraments and the water and the bread and in the wine preach the gospel The bishop will ask if you will protect the church from false teachings and other dangers. And you will say, I will, because you want to maintain an environment within the parish that will be easier to hear the gospel. You will be asked to commit to study, and you will say, you will endeavor to do so because you will teach and preach from your study the gospel. You will be asked if you will pursue a holy life, and you will say you will apply yourself to do so, so that your life will not be a hindrance to teaching and preaching the gospel. You will be asked to commit to maintaining love in the church, and you will say you will do so because it is by the love that is expressed from Christian to Christian that the world will see the gospel When your pride is hurt and you have feelings of anger, remember your calling is about the gospel. When your opinion is not appreciated, your sermons are questioned, your office is not respected, remember it is not about any of that. It is about the gospel. When you are attacked for your personality, your manner, or whatever it is that someone doesn't like about you, it is your responsibility to remind yourself that it is not about any of that anyway. It's about the gospel. The second and last stated advice is to have faith that you are not alone. The last question the bishop will ask is if you will obey your bishop and other ministers whose charge you are placed under. And you will say, I will do so. But that statement is for your benefit. That promise is for your benefit. The church is in existence for your sake. You have men over you, under you, and beside you to help you and be helped by you. That is what the body of Christ is for. Helping the needs of each other as part of the body. And your bishops and your fellow presbyters and deacons are in your life to be what you need for them to be for you to minister the gospel. And also the Holy Spirit is with you and will never leave you or forsake you. And when you are at your 40%, Jesus will be that extra 60%. And because Jesus gives you the first 40%, well, he's pretty much 100% of what you need When you feel alone in your ministry, recall that Elijah did as well. And the devil works hard to place a lot of noise in our lives so that we don't hear the truth. And the truth is we need to remember that God is with us and that still small voice. And to complete the point that you are not alone, I charge you to believe in this process. Believe in the church's process of vetting you, and believe in the church's authority to ordain you When hands are laid upon you and prayer is made for you, believing that, believe, believe that something happens to you that doesn't happen to all other believers. You will be given special authority. Set apart authority so that you will be able to carry out the duties as a priest. Don't ever forget it. The anointing is real. It is most very real. And it keeps us from doubting our call. Believe me, the devil will continually cause you to doubt your call. Don't let him. God speaks through his church. He empowers by way of his church. And at the laying on of hands, he will empower you. With every wedding that I have officiated here at St. Stephen's, I stand with the groom in the back room just before the ceremonies, right through that door. And the room has a door that leads out of the building. And every room that I have had back there, I tell them that this is the moment, your last chance, you can get out of here And I am not joking. I am not joking because the vows they are about to make are life-binding. And I want them to understand the gravity of the moment Well that is what I've tried to do in this sermon. I've tried to present the gravity of the moment, but the bows made here are powerfully important. They matter for eternity. Heed them, and God will use you for the coming of his kingdom. Amen.

sermons.title: The oddity of God choosing men
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.source_file: The oddity of God choosing men.txt
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son of the Holy Ghost. Amen. God does many things. God does most things Maybe he does all things differently than we would do them. He picks the weaker man before the stronger one. He chooses vulnerable land instead of land that is easy to secure. He chooses a shepherding people as opposed to a warrior clan. He chooses to serve rather than be served. He chooses to die instead of all others dying. Again, not how we would choose. I wonder if you know them. Probably not by name. The husband's name is Amram, and the wife's name is Yaquet. They had three children, Aaron, Miriam, and Moses. There was nothing remarkable about the family. They were not politically known. They had no royal blood. They were, by what we read in Scripture, a typical Hebrew family from the tribe of Levi And yet from them came a leader like no other before him, and like no other until the Son of God walked the earth. I would not choose a leader from an unknown family, an unconnected family, but God did. Evidently, what was remarkable about Moses was that he was physically beautiful. At least that's what the New King James Translation says. But the word beautiful in Hebrew can mean healthy and strong, which describes a child who could survive as opposed to a frail newborn. Let's summarize Exodus chapter 2. Turn there if you would in your Bibles. And there we have a narrative that begins really at the end of chapter 1. Which tells us that the newborn sons of the Hebrew women were to be thrown into the Nile The warped justification of these Egyptians was that the Nile to them was a god, and the god, the Nile, would determine the life of a newborn child. Ya Kobed takes advantage of this warped mind of the Egyptians and hides her son where they would not look for him. Which was in the Nile. Ironically, she was actually doing precisely what Pharaoh had commanded her to do. She put her infant son in the Nile. Interestingly, this papyrus reed container is called, in the Hebrew, an ark. Yes, the same word used to describe what Noah built. And only two places in Scripture is the word ark used. Noah's account and this account. It's hard to avoid the conclusion that there is a parallel to the stories The narrative, in other words, tells the story of God saving a chosen people by way of Noah's Ark, and now by the Ark of Moses. And we should notice also that the heroes in the story thus far from chapter 1 and chapter 2 are all women. The midwives, Moses' mother, his sister, and next the princess are all people of faith and thus heroes All are used of God to bring about this great exodus. And this is a wonderful example of how God can use people of for his kingdom's sake to come without those people having to be leaders. They're just doing as God would have them The women were second-class citizens in their particular societies, but to God they were vessels for his glory. Verse 6 informs us that the princess knew the child was of the Hebrews. Thus each person in the narrative knows that what they are doing is dangerous. Each put their own life in danger for the sake of this one child. Their courage is inspiring as they are willing to sacrifice themselves for the sake of one. Verses ten and eleven tell us very little about how Moses was raised, but we hear from Acts chapter seven, that's where Stephen, our patron saint He gives his sermon, and in that sermon, he summarizes the life of Moses. And in there, he tells us in that sermon that Moses was educated in all of the wisdom of the Egyptians. Now, such is a reasonable conclusion to draw from the fact that he was raised in the court as a member of the royal family. And such training was important, as we can imagine, for the role that Moses was going to play in the future for Israel. He was a chronicler of their history. He was a lawgiver. All needing an education. There's an example of parallels between the law of Moses and the Code of Hammurabi. And of course, that is what the Egyptians study for their law. When the events occur in verses 11 through 15, Stephen tells us again from that sermon in Acts that Moses was 40 years of age. Forty years. And that gives him plenty of time to see the injustices being done to his people, to be concerned about helping his people out of their plight. But the justice for one people does not deserve injustice upon another And Moses is naive to believe that his action of killing for vengeance sake a man he thought was being unjust would not be known. And that if it was known by his people, surely they would accept him. But what was he to them? But a spoiled man who got lucky in life not to have been enslaved as they were enslaved. And so he is turned against by his fellow Hebrews, and his actions become a reason for Pharaoh to no longer ignore the heritage of Moses, and now Pharaoh wants him dead. Fleeing to Midian meant that he likely traveled as far east as the Dead Sea, but the Midians were nomads, so they could have been anywhere in the promised land. And again, we read of a man and his future wife meeting at a well. That happens a lot in the Old Testament. The scene described as historically astute, as Midians were known to be ruthless to women. It is very likely Moses would have had to come to their rescue. Moses again is a man of bravery and a protector of injustices. Maybe the casting of Charlton Heston as Moses was an astute choice. Now the rest plays out very quickly. Moses is accepted by the father of the women, the women he saved, the women he protected He is understandably brought into the family, for we are not told that Ruel, also known as Jethro, that he had any sons. Moses is given a wife, and with his wife, Zipporah, he is given a son, whom he names after his plight of being forced to live in a foreign land. It has also been suggested that Moses named his son to reflect the reality that he had been living in a foreign land when he lived in Egypt. And if that is so, then Moses knew quite well the need for Israel to leave Egypt. At the end of the chapter, the story gets to where it wants to be. And we can conclude this because of how fast the narrative goes. It wants to get somewhere. The king of Egypt has died, and later we are told all men who were after Moses are dead, and that makes his return to Egypt a safe one. But the most important part of the narrative, the part that it has been pushing towards, is that God has heard the cries of his people And in accordance with his covenant with Abraham and Abraham's seed, God acknowledges them, which is a way of saying he understood their plight and their need to be delivered from bondage. I say the ending verses are what the narrative was pushing for because we have to reason how fast these things are happening in the life of Moses. His parents met, they get married, while the children of Israel are going through a genocide. Moses is hidden, he's protected He's adopted by royalty, he's educated, he's called as a protector, he kills a man, buries the man, rejected by his people, runs away to live with foreign people of whom one he marries, takes a new life, and starts a family. I don't know about you or I just know that if someone's going to write my life story, I I hope it lasts more than 25 verses. But that's how quickly we get to where Moses is. And because we will spend a great deal of time discussing what it meant for God to finally Hear the cries of the Hebrews and begin the great exodus of history. I want instead for us to focus on something unique. That which is God choosing a man. If I was to choose to lead an Exodus, I would have chosen an angel. He would have had wings the size of mountains. He would have been able to shoot lasers from his eyes. He would be able to breathe fire from his throat. His commanding voice would shake the ground. He would strike fear into Pharaoh so quickly and easily that the Egyptians would become the slaves and the Israelites would become the rulers of the land of Egypt and any other land that they wanted to conquer. But God chose a man. He chose a man. Men are difficult to follow. Two years ago, our son Isaac was taking a course for his master's degree that taught about different styles of leadership. The instructor pointed out that most people think that there is only one type of effective leadership, and it turns out to be usually the type of leadership that same person likes to follow. Simply stated, we tend to follow those leaders that lead in the way we would lead. Good leaders for me There have been men who are no nonsense, they get to the point, and they get things done. And because I respond to such leadership, I find myself leading in the same manner. But there are other types of leaders, very similar to there being other types of personalities. There are leaders who like to build consensus to be sure everyone is on board before the project is started. before the task at hand is is is tackled. And then there are the analytical who need to have all the fallout possibilities examined before a step forward can be taken. A great example of leaders like myself who see a mountain and say, oh, let's overcome it. Run up the mountain. Meanwhile, better leaders are at the bottom saying that's the wrong mountain. Leaders. All men except one are hard to follow. Leaders except one have faults. Men are inadequate. Men are inadequate in that there is always a weakness in their leadership. Moses was a poor public speaker. We will learn more about it later, but I can say without hesitation But I would not choose a man to lead a people on the greatest exodus in human history who could not do well speaking publicly, but God did Consider what men we remember most and how important their public speaking was to their leadership. Winston Churchill came to mind first in writing this It has been said that Churchill during World War II quote, he mobilized the English language and sent it into battle. Here is a quote from the Churchill Archives. Winston Churchill is viewed as a paradigm of public speaking, the epitome of a great orator New leaders try to emulate him, copying his phrasing, voice projection, rhythm, and language. His voice is still recognizable by many from frequently heard recordings of his speeches. When people talk about the great power of speech, many will mention Churchill and his famous broadcast during World War II in the summer and autumn of 1940. when he consolidated his reputation as a war leader, with memorable and iconic phrases such as, Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few. Such are words that are part of history and which have been passed down to our usage today. Well, that's the type of leader I would choose. That's the type of leader I want. Such leaders for such times need to speak to all in the presence of God. But such was not the kind of leader God wanted. And men, men are inconsistent. Men are inconsistent in that they are strong one minute and weak the next. They say one thing and then do another You can count on them in one moment and then be abandoned by them in the next Moses could be brave, one of the bravest, but at times he was a coward. He was brave in that he would stand up to men who were unjust and violent and meet their violence and give them more. Moses was brave in that he did as God told him and stood before Pharaoh to call God's people to be released from bondage. And Moses was a coward. And that he could not muster up the bravado to speak before Pharaoh at length. And he didn't want to go alone before Pharaoh. And so the Lord provided his brother Aaron to come along and to speak on his behalf. Perhaps it is surprising that a man who is so brave in so many manners and circumstances is found to be a coward in certain instances. We likely expect a person we deem brave to be brave in all circumstances. But men are inconsistent. They don't always match up to the personae that they portray. They don't always do what they say. Consider how some of the greatest blows to the witness of the Christian Church to the world has been when Christian leaders didn't live the way they said they lived. You remember those charismatic preachers from the 80s having affairs and using money sent to their ministry to cover up those affairs. That allowed the public church, the Christian church, to be mocked. whether we were related to them at all or not. The bishops, covering up crimes of pedophilia, have allowed the universal church to be rightfully scorned. And every now and again we hear of small churches who have pastors caught up in some type of affair or Some type of money laundering scheme, and the unbelieving world shakes its head And confirms to themselves that religion is all a bunch of nonsense, anyways. With such potential for men to be inconsistent, I wouldn't choose a man to lead, but God would. God did. And God does.
