Finally, in general, I wouldn't choose a man to lead, because in general, men are sinful. Men are sinful in that they sin in every way and in nasty ways. God is the one who concluded that the heart of man was continually bent toward evil. Our nature looks to find perverted ways to practice sexual intimacy. We can cheat an elderly woman, widow, out of her last dollar and not ever think about her again. We can distort the truth until we think we are virtuous for trusting ourselves. And we can physically tear another human being apart in or outside the womb. And wipe the blood away just like we wipe away sweat. That's what our natures can do Thus, because man is sinful, a man who leads is going to sin. He is going to do something selfish. He's going to do something unholy. Something he probably wishes he could do more of. And we are going to be disappointed in him. We are going to feel betrayed by him and maybe even disgusted by him. And still, God chooses men to lead. He does so. God chooses men to lead, because all before Jesus and all who come after Jesus are to point us to Jesus. As the only true leader and really the only true man, God chose men to lead because he chose Jesus to redeem mankind from their sins and live forever with him. God chooses men to lead because each leader is to remind us in both his weaknesses and strengths that there is a perfect man who is a perfect leader. And we who choose to follow him, know him, and love him. Jesus is the leader who charges the hill. He is the leader who builds consensus. He is the leader who counts the cost. Now all of this questioning I have done of God choosing men was indeed to set us up, to give praise to Jesus. And I did so because God chose Abraham. He chose Moses. He chose David. He chose Peter. He chose Paul. He chose all of his twelve. So that all of those people can point to Christ and say He is the true leader for all of us to follow. This passage of Scripture was chosen by God for us today to prepare us for the ordinal vows this evening. God chooses men. I don't know why, but that's what he does. The only thing we know of is that those men are to point us to Jesus. God chooses men. And he wants men to choose Jesus. And the charge for each of us is to follow Jesus. Let us pray. Our Father, you choosing a man such as Moses Reminds us, dear Lord, of choosing Jesus to die for our sins and the call for us to choose to follow him. As simple as that, and we accept it as that. We thank you for choosing men, but most of all we thank you for Jesus. It is in his name that we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: You gotta have faith like Abraham
sermons.speaker: Rev. William Vowles
sermons.source_file: You gotta have faith like Abraham.txt
sermons.text: Let us pray. May the words of my mouth and the meditations of our hearts be acceptable in thy sight, O Lord, our strength and our Redeemer. In the name of the Father and the Son The Holy Ghost may be seated. I'd like to begin this morning with a word picture, an image from our great church father, St. Augustine. In one of his most best-known works, The City of God, which some of you went through this Sunday school year, Augustine tells of two roads leading to two very different cities. One road leading to the earthly city, which has as its end destruction and eternal misery. The other road leading to the heavenly city and eternal bliss. Augustine divides the entire human race into two groups, each with Very different values and very different destinies. Everyone, he says, belongs to one city or the other. Those belonging to the first city love their own strength. Seek glory from men and make their way on their own to God or salvation. Those from the second city love God, glory in him, rely in his strength, and find salvation by grace through faith. And true faith is a chief issue for the writer of Hebrews. The book of Hebrews was likely written to a select Jewish congregation somewhere in Israel. We gather from the message of the book that there appeared to be a segment of this congregation who very much had difficulty in this matter of salvation by faith. This for many would have been a dramatic change for them as they were steeped in the legalism of Judaism, believing that salvation came to those who earned it. So the writer's emphasis was to convey to his audience that salvation was by faith and not by works. We are naturally taken to Ephesians 2, 8 and 9. As a connecting passage, for by grace you have been saved through faith, that not of yourself, that is the gift of God, not by works, lest any man should boast. But Hebrews chapter 10 ends also with a similarly famous quote from Old Testament prophet Habakkuk, verse 38: the just shall live by faith. The writer is now going to illustrate this in chapter 11 with all these faith heroes. But before we get there, let's look for a moment at the first few verses. Of the first chapter of Hebrews, we see there a lot of the same truths that Augustine brought out in his journey to that great city. One of the most important things we need to remember in our Christian journey to that heavenly city Is that we must trust and understand the preeminence of Christ. So the first couple verses of chapter 1 of Hebrews speaks of this. When I think of the preeminence of Christ in the beginnings of Hebrews, I am reminded of St. Patrick's poem Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me, Christ beneath me, above me, to my right, to my left, as I rise, as I sit. Christ in every heart of every man who thinks of me. Christ in the mouth of everyone who speaks of me. Christ in every eye that sees me, Christ in every ear that hears me. These are realities of Christ's preeminence in our lives of faith. So let's look at chapter 1, the first couple verses. God, who at various times in various ways spoke in time past to the fathers by the prophets, has in these days spoken to us by his son. whom he has appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the worlds, who being the brightness of his glory and the expressed image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power When he had by himself purged our sins, sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. Certainly we see here The preeminence of Christ. He is our high priest. Again and again the writer reminds his readers of Christ's preeminence. So that they can not only understand who Christ is, his position, what he did for them, but also That they can be secure and trust that his accomplishments are effective and complete. First 24 of chapter 9 says, For Christ our high priest, has not entered the holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence. of God for us. It is only by the grace of God, through faith in the accomplished work of Christ, that any of these Jews Can make a claim on salvation. So it is with us. So let's look at Hebrews 11 and our faith heroes When we look at these heroes, especially the patriarchs, it seems rather obvious to see that they are not considered heroes necessarily because of their great righteous deeds or because of their extreme high moral character. In fact, we re- as we read their stories, sometimes we just are left shaking our heads, aren't we? Yet we see in their human flaws. Our own flaws, and thus we can relate. Maybe that is why they are such good examples for us. But in the end, when all the dust had cleared, they trusted their God for the promises that he had given to them. And it's that faith and trust that I believe the writer wants his readers and us to emulate as we take our journey's walk down that road to the heavenly city. So the first patriarch we come to is the father of them all, Abraham. For time's sake, he's really the only one we'll be able to touch on this morning. It's of him, of course, that we have the great quote from Genesis, of which the Apostle Paul uses in Romans 4 to defend justification by faith Genesis 15, 6. Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him for righteousness. So let's look at the faith of Abraham. There are three components of his faith that I would like to explore this morning. The pilgrimage of his faith. The patience of his faith, the promises of his faith. First component I wanted to look at this morning is his pilgrimage. Verse 8, by faith, Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, obeyed and went, even though he did not know where he was going. Look first at this important little phrase. By faith, Abraham, when he was called, obeyed. Literally, a better way to translate this might be Abraham, while being called, was obeying. It's active. There's an immediacy to his response. And it's faith because he didn't know where he was going. How strong is this faith? Strong enough that when he has no idea where he's going, when he's leaving everything familiar to him, he just goes. He has no other thought but obedience. He didn't go to Canaan because he saw this great brochure of the land of Canaan. He didn't go because someone told him of this wonderful shoreline of the Mediterranean. He didn't even go because of the great pictures in the portfolio that he saw of the great estate he was going to get when he got there. As a matter of fact, as we heard in chapter seven of Acts and Stephen's Great Address He tells the Jews present that Abraham never owned anything even when he got to the promised land. He just trusted God to the end. Trusted that he and his family would receive the promised inheritance. Notice that this pilgrimage also is one of separation. Remember, Abraham comes from a very pagan culture. He was the product of the scattering of the people of the Tower of Babel. In Joshua 24:2, we read the father of Abraham, whose name was Terah, served other gods. He wasn't just a pagan. He was a polytheist. He served multiple gods. So why did God choose Abraham? In the words of Isaiah, God appeared to Abraham and quarried him, if you were, out of stone Similar to what Stephen said in Acts 7, the God of glory appeared to our father Abraham. God showed up and said, Abraham, leave your country. Leave your relatives and come to a place that I will show you. And he left. What a marvelous expression of grace. There's no real explanation given for God's choosing Abraham. We're left to believe that is God's sovereign intention, his sovereign purpose is what we might call election A man surrounded by iniquity, coming from a family immersed in idolatry. And God singles him out and gives him a command to see if he would follow him. Nothing is said about Abraham's morality. Really, it's almost irrelevant in response to salvation. God doesn't come along and sovereign grace to save the most righteous. As a matter of fact, in Romans, in the section where Paul is talking about Abraham, he says that God justifies the ungodly. Abraham responded in faith. He believed God, and a separation took place. He separated his family ties. He left his loved ones and abandoned those things which were comfortable, which were familiar, and he embraced total uncertainty. Jesus said we are to hate our father, hate our mother, our sister, our brother, even our own lives. We're to pick up our cross and follow Him, Luke 14. A life of faith starts with a willingness to separate from everything that is familiar. That is where the Christian pilgrimage begins. When we can separate from the world. When we, as Paul says in 1 Thessalonians 1. 9, where he characterizes the church at Thessalonica as those who turn to God from idols to share And serve the living true God. And then in verse 10 he says, to wait for his son from heaven. At the end of Galatians, Paul talks about being crucified to the world. In other words, Paul, when he came to Christ, died to his interests in the world. The world no longer had a grip on him. James tells us, friendship with the world is enmity with God. It makes us ask in our own pilgrimage. Does the world still have a grip on you? Are we crucified to it? What ways might we identify with being friends with the world and thus at enity with God? Well let's look a little closer at this separation. In Abraham's day, a new era of human history begins, really. Remember, when men built the Tower of Babel, which was a manifestation of human pride and idolatry, at that time the general relationship that God had with mankind was shattered. Languages were confused. People could no longer understand one another in different groups. That was the price for revolting against God. God was openly available to them, but they revolted against him, and they were scattered. Man had been given over to his idolatry. As Paul says in Romans 1, God had abandoned them to immorality. Homosexuality and to a retrobrate reprobate mind. Sound familiar? Mercifully, however, God had a plan. He always has a plan. God is going to reveal himself, but not in a broad sense as he once had. Now he's going to reveal himself in a very specific sense. He's going to reveal himself through one man and through the loins of that one man, that one man being Abraham. Abraham became the father of the people of God, Israel. And Israel becomes the nation that is the receiver of his divine revelation. So in a very real sense, Abraham becomes a central figure in salvific history. His life becomes for all who come to God by faith a pattern to follow. His is one of completely one of faith. Back to verse eight again. He went out not knowing where he was going. So it is with us. We too have not seen our final inheritance We don't know exactly where our journey is going to take us next. We walk by faith and not by sight And by the way, the journey Abraham took took a long time. He spent five years in a town called Haran, waiting for things to unfold. But his faith never on never never wavered. Abraham had patience in his pilgrimage. Look at verse 9. By faith he made his home in the promised land like a stranger in a foreign country. He lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise. For he was looking forward to the city with foundations, which architect and builder is God. By faith he lives as an alien in the land that was promised to him Just as we in our own right are pilgrims. He has accumulated wealth and servants along the way, but ultimately he's still an alien. He's in the land of promise, but he never really possesses anything So here's Abraham. God's promise is never seen by him in this life. He wanders around Canaan as a tent dweller, but never abandoned his faith in a future promise. This is the challenge for us as well. As we are reminded certainly of this We should remain faithful and strong. We should be joyful and full of anticipation. In that period between, sometimes long period between our moment of salvation and our ultimate moment of glorification. Abraham didn't give up hope. He continued to hold God's promises high. God's promises drove him. They motivated him. They pressed him forward. A person of faith isn't always one whose faith is like a shooting star. Instead, rather often a strong faith is like a beacon. Steady, relentless, even sometimes when there's nothing to do but wait. Waiting when perhaps there's pain in your life. Disappointment in your life, where fear can set in and test your faith, but instead it is sustained or even strengthened. Waiting can be a trap for some of us, can it not? But Abraham never grows impatient. He never tries to grab what the world has to offer like his nephew Lot did. Lot pitched his head towards Sodom, remember? Do you remember why? Because he had intrigue with the world. Lot's story is one of monumental tragedy. Not so with Abraham. His is a patient faith. And we really see it with each of the patriarchs if we look at them. The covenant promises given to Abraham was repeated to Isaac and then repeated again to Jacob. The promise that they would receive a land and ultimately an inheritance in a heavenly city. They all died in faith without receiving those promises here on earth. Yet faith is patient. Past it to endure all the lack of fulfillment of this life because it has as its focus a promise of the future. The promise that lies ahead. All these heroes gained approval through their faith and yet didn't receive that promise, at least not here in this life. Yet they had much confidence in that promise. So much so that verse 15 tells us that they really never had a fleeting thought of returning to their old country. To their own life, their old life. They desired a better country. They desired a heavenly country. And then verse 16 ends with an awesome statement. I think one of the most comforting statements in all of Hebrews. Therefore, because of this faith, God is not ashamed to be called their God. For he has prepared a city for them. Now that's a promise, right? I'm pretty sure I have given God plenty of reason to be ashamed to be called my God. But by grace, through faith in the accomplished work of Jesus Christ, he is not ashamed. Hallelujah. Hallelujah. Praise his name. Amen.

sermons.title: God wants you to be delivered
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.source_file: God wants you to be delivered.txt
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Leave me seated. We are continuing our study of the book of Exodus. We are, as our reading took us through in Exodus chapter three. The story here of Moses standing before the burning bush is known by people who have never read the Bible or cared to know the one true God. For more than one reason, this story is a part of Western culture. Moses stood before the burning bush, and God spoke to him, and told him to go to Pharaoh and demand that he set the Israel slaves free. Bible readers know more detail about this story, and yet the gist of it is understood. To be the same by those who know the story in more detail and those who simply know it as some type of fairy tale Because we are familiar with the narrative of Exodus 3, I am approaching it this morning from the point of answering curious questions about some of the details found in the narrative. Questions such as, number one, what is a priest of Midian? The text says that Jethro Moses' brother-in-law was a chief priest of Midian. Was Midian a cult? Well, to answer that, we must remember that the book of Exodus is a continuation of Genesis. They are really one book. And when you read Genesis 25, you find that after the death of Sarah, Abraham took on another wife named Keturah, and she had three sons. And one of them was named Midian. And so the Midianites are those who come from the line of Midian, Abraham's son. And this means we can Assume that they knew the God of Abraham. But if the Midians were like all the other tribes in that region, they mixed in the God of Abraham with the other gods, thus making him part of many gods. Second question. What is Mount Horim? The name Horib in Hebrew possibly means to glow or heat Because of the manner that the sun appeared upon the mountain from a distance, making it glow. But the evidence for the exact meaning, the evidence is scarce. The mountain is later named Sinai, and again with scarce evidence, it is possible that the new name is given after Senet. Which is Hebrew for a particular kind of bush found in the region, and thus likely the type of bush that was burning and not consumed. The greater curiosity, then the origin of the name of the mountain, is its location. Where is it? In 1 Kings, we learn from the story of Elijah that the location of Horeb was still known with certainty. But strangely, strangely, there are no biblical references after the story of Elijah as to where Horeb or Mount Sinai is. Some even speculate that it's outside of the Promised Land. Third question: What is the point of a burning bush? I recently heard a comedian make fun of this story saying how unimpressive it must have been for God to appear in the form of a burning bush. Of course we know God was not the burning bush, but instead was using the burning bush as a sign. It is said that bushes in the region would catch fire seemingly spontaneously because of the heat. What we who have faithful minds are to understand is that God would again use something simple, something ordinary, as a symbol of his presence, just as he does bread. and wine. And we are to meditate on the most important part of this sign, which is the bush was burning but not consumed. Such is the condition of all who believe, such is the condition of the church. For the very presence of God is within us by means of the Holy Spirit, and we are not destroyed. Think about that. The God of all creation is within us, and we are not destroyed. The presence of Almighty God, who made heaven and earth, is in the church, and it is not destroyed. In fact, it's just the opposite. The church is empowered, empowered to do great works to bring in the kingdom of God. Fourth question. What does Moses have to take? Why does Moses have to take, excuse me, why does Moses have to take off his sandals? Of course, the obvious answer is because God told him to do so. But why did God tell him to do so? Well, God says he told him to do so because Moses was standing on holy ground. But this is a challenge for our modern minds, for we don't think about the material world as holy. Really very important. There's still some Gnosticism going around amongst Christians. I remember visiting my sister and family a few years ago, they would house college students. And they were housing one particular college female who wore ratty clothes all of the time, as did her friends who came and visited her. I mean ratty clothes And they wore the same to the church services, to worship on Sundays. And I questioned what is the meaning of this, and I was told that these young people were protesting protesting by what they were wearing that Christians cared too much about material things. So they were trying to show how unimportant material things were Some Christians today, who haven't fully grown out of their college protesting ways, dress down for worship because they want to show it doesn't matter what you wear. Thus which with such understanding about the material world some would question God As if he's being unnecessarily snobbish. Maybe God is being a little bit too legalistic, caring too much about the material material world when he instructs Moses to remove his sandals. It shouldn't matter what Moses wore, right? Well, it did matter, and it does matter today. God came into the material world. God became matter himself as Jesus took on flesh and blood. Recall that the material world, the physical world at creation was named by God to be good. It longs to be redeemed from the curse placed upon it by man. And it will be made new, the scripture says. Thus we Christians are to understand that there are certain ways we are to treat certain parts of the material world, because they are used to represent the presence of God. We kneel at the communion rail rather than put our feet up on it because Moses removed his sandals. We clean off the communion table when it is not being used, and we only put vessels used for the Lord's Supper upon it, and not our coffee mugs, because Moses removed his sandals. We don't show movies in the sanctuary or perform secular entertainment for applause from the chancel because Moses removed his sandals. God does inhabit the material world, and we are to appreciate it by taking off our sins. Fifth question. Why was Moses reluctant to lead the Israelites out of bondage? I asked that question to myself this week because I thought we needed to be reminded that Moses did not know, even though we are told in chapter 2 that all the men who are after Moses are dead. Moses didn't know that. And so he thinks he's risking his life. And also you remember that Moses was rejected. His leadership was rejected when he tried to defend an Israelite and killed an Egyptian and then tried to make peace between two Israelites, they rejected him and he ran. Moses has no idea that they would accept his leadership now as opposed to then. The sixth and final question I want to answer from this chapter Why did God name himself I am? To understand this name better, we must first realize That Israel was in bondage as slaves to the Egyptians for 430 years. 430 years Consider that the United States as a nation has been in existence 200 years less than Israel was in bondage. And the majority of citizens in the US have forgotten God already. Add 200 more years to our culture. And how much will God be remembered if we continue the path we are on? Thus, how easy it would have been for Israel to forget God, to forget his covenant with Abraham, and to worship anything that they thought could relieve their suffering. Israelites. They would have identified with Moses saying that he is coming in the name of the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. They would have remembered that. But this name, this name, this new name, I am, they would not have heard that before. Now, in case you are not aware, The translation I am in the English is not accepted by Jewish scholars. In fact The name of God, the name God gave to Moses, is thought to be so very holy that it is not to be spoken by human lips. The faithful Jewish scholars don't even add vowel sounds to the name because they do not want it pronounced. The majority of Christian scholars say it should be pronounced Yahweh, but in truth we have no way of truly knowing. Translators use the phrase I am as an acceptable translation because it reflects what God is seemingly trying to convey here. Which is that he cannot be defined by one name. One name, one adjective sets parameters around God and that would take away from him being the God as he is And so simply saying that God is, that God exists, sets no parameters It allows God to define Himself, which He is about to do to the Israelites, which He will do to the Egyptians, and He has done throughout the ages, and continues to do And with these questions I have chosen to answer now complete, I want to get to the main message I see in this chapter for us. In verse 7 of chapter 3, we read of God using the same loaded verbs that he uses in chapter 2, verses 24 and 25. Look at chapter look at verse 7. God saw, God heard, and God knew. God saw, God heard, and he knew. The repetition from chapter 2, verses 24 and 25, to chapter 3, verse 7, indicates that what God is doing, speaking to Moses from the burning bush, Is taking steps to address the suffering of the Israelites in Egypt. Moses is not yet told how the deliverance of Israel will take place. But he is told that it will be so. And he set it set up by saying God saw, heard, and knew For the Christian, the story of Israel being delivered from slavery in Egypt has been a typology, a metaphor. for how each of us is delivered by God in the person of Jesus from our own slavery. And it is also a typology of how the church universal will be delivered from the bondage of death. As we will one day rise, be made new, eternally new. We see in St. Paul's letter to Colossae, how Paul uses Exodus language to describe how Christians are made new. Giving thanks to the Father who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in light He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins. And so let us look how God began delivering Israel from bondage in the context of how he will deliver the church. And with the needed message that God sees the plight of the church. God hears the plight of the church, and God knows the plight of the church. I would like to tell you, I'd like to think that God sees and hears and knows the plight of the United States. But let's be honest. God never made a promise to save the United States of America. God made a promise to save his church. We must confess, I believe, that we are unable to know how bad the times really are in which we are living. We can only compare it to other times that we have experienced or other times that we are told about. How difficult was it to live through World War II? I have heard the stories as you have from people who are still with us. And it sounds like it was pretty bad. There were there was fear, excuse me, of the Germans, and there was fear of the Japanese. Each empire wanted world domination. And each empire had great success for such a time as it seemed possible for them to dominate the world. That sounds scary to me. It sounds more scary than what today's terrorists have successfully done. But what our culture seemed to have during World War II that we do not seem to have today There's a unity in identifying our enemies and agreeing that they need to be defeated. And the result of what we do not have is confusion and fear. And the church is seemingly powerless at influencing almost anything in our culture today Do you know what the Christian position is on war against Islamic terrorism? What's our position? Do you know what the Christian position is on gun control? Do you know what the Christian position is on abortion? Oh, we can say we have our personal positions, but who is speaking for the Christians as a whole? One minister, such as myself, or even a bishop of the Reformed Episcopal Church, says that the United States should declare war on militant Islam and no one pays attention. One clergy speaks out against abortion, and another claiming the same faith speaks in favor of it. And this is what should bring the most fear in our day. It is that the church does not have a voice that our culture will heed. And it is our fault. We as a church, Christians Universal. are in bondage to our own sins, sins such as gluttony, passivity, greed Envy, strife, jealousy, and even unbelief As our response should be the same as our prayers from the litany, knowing all of this, good Lord deliver us. And he will. He will separate the sheep from the goats. He will return by way of the eastern sky with those who were faithful to him unto death. And Jesus will collect those who are still alive, and he will return, and his church will be revealed. It will be revealed as one, as holy, as universal. And as much as we can say that the deliverance of Israel from the bondage of slavery is akin to the Christian church being delivered. So we can say that such deliverance is akin to our personal deliverance from sin and death. Before each of us came to a saving faith in Jesus, God saw us, God heard us, God knew us. And having seen, heard, and known us, he had a plan on how we would come to a saving faith in Jesus. And I want each of us to believe today, hear this now. I want each of us to believe today that with every sin that we struggle to overcome, God sees us, God hears us, and God knows us. God has an awareness of our plight. God has a plan to deliver us from our sins. Sins that we cannot overcome by our own strength. Let us be reminded by humble confession that sin is not outside these walls only But also inside. Christians struggle to overcome dependency on alcohol just as many in the secular world do. Christians can and do become dependent on drugs, prescribed or not, just as people outside these walls do. Christians do bow to the pleasure of sex. Christians can be motivated by greed. Christians can surrender to anger and bitterness. Christians can struggle with sins of sloth, lust, selfishness, pride, etc. , etc. We can repent of our specific sins and be determined to commit them no more and find ourselves confessing them again and determining again, only needing to confess them again. The wonderfully good news in all of this failing is that when we cry out to God for our deliverance, we can be confident that God sees, God hears, and he knows us. And he has a plan to deliver us. The devil wants us. To perceive God as the deists do. The devil wants us to understand God Be way up there in the sky, giving us his commandments and remaining above us, looking down upon us, watching us fail, with no regard to what we are experiencing down here If there is any perception for you that God is like that, get it out of your mind. Repent of it The actual God, the only God, the one true God, sees us, hears us, and knows us And gives us his only son, who was like us in every way, only he overcame sin. And because he overcame, he enables us to overcome. I originally plan to close with an anecdotal story Of a Christian struggling to overcome sin and soon finding victory But I concluded that such stories can appear distant because we don't know the person and we don't know if they're struggling in the same manner that we do. I cannot know how God will deliver you from your sins, your struggles that you struggle to overcome, but I can know that he will What you need to know as you stay in the fight to be delivered is that God sees you God by definition is omnipresent and on the present and so he sees all things at all times And because he does, and I know this is going to sound strange at first, but because God sees all things at all times, it allows us not to try to hide from him what we are embarrassed for others to know about us. In fact, God's omnipresence brings us to not be ashamed before Him. Now, of course, it is never good to be indifferent about your sins. There should be some shame. But because God sees everything we do, it is ridiculous for us to pretend we are any different a person than what God has watched us be. That God sees has freedom for us. God knows all of my weaknesses, all of my struggles, and all of my propensities to sin, and I'm glad that He does not, that He does see it. As God sees, he also hears us. He hears us when we confess our sins. He hears us when we bemoan our sins. He hears us when we cry out to overcome. And he hears us when we pray to him to give us a desire to want to overcome. Because God hears us, he also expects us to speak to him. It's part of the relationship. Asking of him, crying to him, telling him our passions and our fears is what he desires from us. He requires us to ask. He wants us to speak to him. That is all a part of God hearing us. And so we speak to him. Finally, as God sees and hears us, so he knows us. He knows our sincerity and our insincerity. He knows when we are genuine and when we are disingenuous. He knows our mixed motives and he knows our insecurities. And because Jesus is God, God knows how to overcome what is weak within us and how to make our motives righteous. All of this is good news for us. It is good news that God sees you, that God hears you, that God knows you He not only can deliver you, but he will deliver you. That is the God he revealed himself to be. And that is the God we will watch him perform for Israel, a God of deliverance. Let us pray.

sermons.title: God Takes His Covenant Seriously
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We are in Exodus chapter four, and you will do well to turn there with me. Exodus 4, we read from the lectionary, we read the latter half of the chapter, but we will be covering all of Exodus 4. This is not new, but needs to be repeated. God takes his covenant promises seriously. All covenant promises God takes most seriously. We have sponsored college boot camp here at St. Stephen's for the past several years. Because God takes his covenant promises seriously. Because these young people have been baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. They have placed been placed into God's everlasting covenant. And God desires. He wants He wills and he expects that his covenant will be fulfilled. And for it to be fulfilled, young people must live their lives as having been baptized. as being believers in the Lord Jesus Christ. According to the Barna Institute, reported in the USA Today paper, Over 70% of Christian youth leave the church after high school. Over 70%. As most of you know, it is my greatest passion as a pastor to reverse such a trend. Too many Christian churches place an emphasis on mission, on reaching the lost with the gospel, and that is good and part of what Jesus commissioned his church to do. But mission and outreach and other forms of ministry cannot continue in the church to grow the kingdom of God When new people are walking in the church and our children are walking out of the church. I don't see the point of rejoicing over a new convert being saved. While a child of mine is renouncing the faith and choosing the road that is wide on which many, many people travel. What makes the difference, I believe, for the sake of our children staying in the faith and us staying in the church. Is for each of them to understand that they are in and under a covenant with God. A covenant A covenant is a binding contract of sorts that is based on promises made. Now, because God is the superior in the relationship, the covenant we have with him is determined by him, of course. He sets the parameters of the covenant, and we agree to the stipulations of the covenant, or we perish. Israel. Israel was in covenant with God. Through Abraham, God set the parameters. And you recall what those parameters were? He only instructed that they believe that he is the one true God. And he insisted that they believe in his promise of the promised land. That was it. That was all that was required of them. The law had not yet come. They simply needed to believe in the one true God and trust that the promised land would be theirs. Oh, and there was one more thing. One more thing. There was to be a symbol of the covenant God made with Abraham. That symbol was circumcision. Each male born into the family of Abraham and his descendants were to be circumcised on the eighth day of their life. It was to be the males, because the promise given after the sin of Eve would be that a male, a male, would be born that would crush the serpent's head, the devil It was circumcision because reproduction was to be the means by which the male would be born, only we know that it was conceived by the Holy Spirit. It was also circumcision because the cutting away of flesh would be a symbol of how God would start his new covenant, which was a cutting away of the stony heart. And it was the eighth day because the number eight would come to represent the new covenant, the new Sabbath, a day of celebration. Before we hear how serious God takes his covenant and his covenant symbols, we read in Exodus 4 at the beginning of that chapter. How Moses was given confidence by God by enabling Moses to perform miraculous signs. The first three miraculous signs Moses was to present to Pharaoh, when Pharaoh would refuse to let Israel as slaves go free. The first was a rod turning to a serpent and then back again to a rod, a hand becoming leprous, and then healed from leprosy. And water turning to blood. And it is, of course, I think, natural for us to ask, why would God choose these three miracles as a sign of his authority given to Moses? Consider the rod turning to a snake and then back to a rod. was symbolic of Moses having control and authority over evil. What is a snake but a serpent What did the devil inhabit in the Garden of Eden? But a serpent. And so God uses that symbol that Moses can manipulate such a creature. Tells us that Moses, and it tells Pharaoh as well, that the evil one was not the being that was in control. It was Moses. Jesus in his ministry revealed the same. He revealed that the devil was not in control, he was. At his presence, the demonic obeyed his commands. Even the most difficult demonic possession cases that the disciples could not handle, they were subject to the voice of Jesus. And then this hand turning to leprosy. And then healed. This had to show that Moses was being given authority over the flesh of men. God would cause the Egyptians to suffer in the flesh in different ways if they did not repent and let Israel go free. Jesus also came, showing the same authority over the flesh of men. He could heal them of any and every sickness that humanity could come up with. The outward healing of Jesus was also a sign of an even greater healing that was the healing of the soul and giving the body and soul of mankind eternal life. And then the water turning to blood. sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Seed it. Before we get to Exodus 6. I want to uh discuss what it means to know someone Now I don't know if this first story actually occurred, but there is a story circulating amongst clergy of a funeral. Where some family members spoke very kindly of their father, who was recently deceased. And the pastor spoke so glowingly of the man as well, causing the new widow to get up out of her pew in the middle of the eulogy She walked to the casket which was closed, opened it up at the headside, looked in, closed it, and returned to her pew The preacher was baffled and asked the widow if everything was alright. The widow said with calmness, after hearing such glowing words, I had to be sure it was my husband we were speaking about. Obviously she knew him much better than anyone else. The reality of not truly knowing someone reminded me of a story I read just a couple of weeks ago In late July of this year, Leroy Blast, that was his nickname, Blast, Leroy Blast Bill Black died of lung cancer at 55 years of age. Unlike most people, Leroy had two obituaries in the local newspaper, the New Jersey's Atlantis City Press. It's a true story. His wife wrote one and his mistress wrote the other. Both obituaries list similar information, except one says that he is survived by his loving wife, Beretta. Harrison Black, and the other says he is survived by his longtime girlfriend, Princess Hall. And so we have to ask who actually knew who Leroy Blast Bill Black was. In an article in the New York Times about people leading double lives, it is stated like this, but psychologists say that most normal adults, now consider their definition of normal. That most normal adults are well equipped to start a secret life, if not sustain it. The ability to hold a secret is fundamental to the healthy social development, they say. And the desire and the desire to samples other identities, to reinvent oneself, to pretend can last well into adulthood. And in recent years, researchers have found that some of the same psychological skills that help many people avoid mental distress can also put them at a heightened risk for prolonged, covert activities. And the article goes on. This is a quote. In a very deep sense, you don't have a self unless you have a secret. And we all have moments throughout our lives when we feel we're losing ourselves in a social group or work or marriage, and it feels good to grab for a secret or some subterfuge to reassert our identity as somebody apart. says Dr. Daniel Wegner, a professor of psychology at Harvard. And we now know, he continues, We are now learning that some people are better at doing this than others. End quote. Here we can agree and say, indeed, some people are. What I want us to do when considering stories of not truly knowing someone is for us to extend that difficulty. That difficulty of knowing our fellow human beings extended to how difficult it is to know God, maybe even an inability to know God. What is most important, I believe, about Exodus 6 is the focus that God has in his words to Moses that he wants his people to know him. So turn in your Bibles if you would and read along with me. Exodus chapter 6. We'll be reading verses 1 through 9 again Verse 1. Then the Lord said to Moses, Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh, for the strong hand he will let them go, and with a strong hand to me. For with a strong hand he will let them go, and with a strong hand he will drive them out of his land. Now this is new information for us. We are told that the Lord will harden his heart and that he will not let the people go. But now Pharaoh will not only not let them go, God will make the situation so miserable, Pharaoh will literally kick Israel out of Egypt. Verse two. And God spoke to Moses and said to him, I am the Lord. We can best understand this section of God's Word having an appreciation Of Hebrew narrative artistry. And this has been gained through recent scholarly study. And this text is best understood as a repetition, taking us back to what God said to Moses initially. And so these words are necessary for him. It is also interesting to note that it was an expected practice of ancient Near Eastern kings to begin their proclamations with the formula, I am so-and-so, even though the name of that king was well known. I am Mesha, son of Kemosh, king of Moab, reads one such proclamation. The Bible and the works of Moses in particular seem to employ this language as a linguistic practice to help the people in those days. To do so is another manner of grace God is relating to what they understand. The same phrase, I am Yahweh occurs many times in the law of God. And when God uses such phrasing, he is announcing his name in the sense of declaration and in the sense of his authority. The force of the words makes it clear that because of who he is, he is to be heard and he is to be obeyed. Now, soon the exodus of Israel will take place, and that will bring about a greater force for the use of God's name. Along with the name of God as I am, being so holy, you remember from last week that it cannot be pronounced in Hebrew. It also means that God is the one who is. That is, he is the one who is present with his people. It is a name that itself speaks of God's personal faithfulness to his people get this as their Savior and as their Lord. Because of the phrase, I am the Lord, opens and closes this paragraph, starting at verse two and ending at verse eight. It speaks of God being actively present, confirming what he has said and what he will do. And Moses needed that, and the people needed that. Verse 3 I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty. But my name Lord was not known to them, Lord being the I am. Verse three is fundamental to biblical theology. And any understanding about the history of salvation, how God saves. It is also, I would say, fundamental to understanding how I preach to you. And it goes against what has become so popular and I would say so wrong regarding a proper understanding of the covenants being actually one and not two. God's revelation to Moses and his deliverance of Israel from Egypt was a fulfillment of that covenant God made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And God sending Jesus to die for our sins is a fulfillment of the same covenant made to Abraham, even made to Adam and Eve. A besetting sin of mine is a sarcastic tongue, in case you didn't know. It all goes together Looking back at the verse, verse 3, we see that God introduces himself here as Almighty. That's an important revelation. In the Hebrew it is El Shaddai. El is a shorter version of Elohim, the standard name for God. No one, however, is entirely entirely sure how to translate Shaddai. For example, in Genesis 17 we read, I am El Shaddai, I will multiply you exceedingly. Fruitfulness In Genesis 28:3 we read, and El Shaddai will bless you and make you fruitful and multiply you So that name was used and spoken to the patriarchs was not new. But the name I am, that was a new revelation. And what we can conclude from this in terms of God withholding this new name from Abraham is that God is patient in how he reveals himself. He does not give all of his identity at once, and we can suppose that he does not do so for many reasons, including the fact that we couldn't handle it if he did He is too great. He is too holy. He is too wonderful. He is too ancient. He is too marvelous for us to behold him as he truly is. And so we have to receive him in stages, as Israel does. Verse 4. I have also established my covenant with them to give them the land of Canaan, the land of their pilgrimage in which they were strangers. So verse four allows a connection with the patriarchs. Realize that they were given the promise of the promised land, but they never possessed it. God was now giving the land to Moses and the people fulfilling that promise Thus we are to relate this new name, Yahweh, I am, to be associated with a God who fulfills promises. Verse 5. And I have also heard the groaning of the children of Israel, whom the Egyptians keep in bondage, and I have remembered my covenant. Verse 5 then allows us to know God as the one who is present and paying attention. It is a love expressed when a person pays attention to your plight. If you have ever shared your sorrow with another person And that same person made it clear that he or she doesn't really care what you are experiencing. It is hard to not feel emotionally bruised. But God has paid attention to what Israel was experiencing. He knew of their groaning due to the oppressive whips and chains of the Egyptians. And he calls them children. Notice here he calls them children. Because that is how he views them, for he sees them as needing care, needing protection as children do, and he knows himself to be the only father who can care for them. Provide for them. Provide for their every need. And here God says he remembers And when he says he remembered his covenant, he does not mean that he forgets a lot of things, but it finally came to him that he recalled that he made a covenant with them. This is what is called an anthropomorphism, describing God acting in a way that can be understood by the people he speaks to. And he wants them to understand that he is a promise-keeper, that he knows what he has said. And when God says this, it is directly connecting these people with the promises of Abraham. Again, he is taking on the identity of as a God who keeps his promises. Verse 6 Therefore, say to the children of Israel, I am the Lord. I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians. I will rescue you from their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great judgments. Here in this verse are divine actions that are emphasized, underlined, highlighted. God is to be known by his people as a God who will. A God of action. We see in verse 6 through 8 the phrase, I will, is stated by God a total of seven times. This is an emphatic statement that God's people are to be, it's to be embedded in their psyche, that their God is their deliverer. They can depend on no other, and he will be true to his word in delivering them. Verse 7. I will take you as my people, and I will be your God. Then you shall know that I am the Lord your God, who brings you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians. Here we get to hear the heart of God. And this is understanding, this understanding of God is repeated both in the Old and the New Testaments, making it clear as to why God would deliver his people. God is relational. Not because he has to be, in terms of having to have a relationship with his creation. For the relationship with the Father that he has with the Son, and the Son has with the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit has with the Father and the Son, these are most certainly sufficient. But God, as a God of love, shares himself, and therefore he wants to share himself with more and more persons. And so God wants to be in relationship with a people that he truly knows and a people that truly know him. Such is the good news of the gospel right here in the Old Testament. The good news is right here in the book of Exodus, chapter 6, verse 7. The same book where we receive the law of God, that God wants to be intimate with his people. Is seen when he sends his son. And so Exodus 7, verse 6, I mean sorry, Exodus 6, verse 7 is the same as John 3. 16. For God so loved the world. Verse 8. And I will bring you into the land which I swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and I will give it to you as a heritage. I am the Lord. So verse 8 tells us where God wants to have this intimate relationship with his people. He wants to have it in the land that he promised for them. And I have shared this with you before, how remarkable it is that God would choose this land. Remember that it is right in the middle of two major civilizations, making it a trade route that everyone wants to control And it had to be that God chose such a land so that Israel would not just be a player on the world stage, as we like to say today. But it was chosen because for them to survive as a nation, they would have to depend upon God solely. God was the only power that could keep Israel from becoming a vassal state or from becoming overrun. And later we know that they will become a vassal state. They will be overrun and even made slaves. But that's not our focus here. Our focus is to be on what God wanted for his people. He wanted to them to be safe and he wanted them to truly trust in him. And to be in a situation where they had to trust in him. Verse nine. So Moses spoke thus to the children of Israel, but they did not heed Moses because of the anguish of spirit and cruel bondage. And we end our study at verse 9. Because I want us to use the sadness of that verse. To jar us into realizing how privileged we are, and to help us to commit, not to commit the same sins as Israel Moses told the people what God said, and that means that Moses told them who God was. Moses was able to tell them that they were of a special dispensation and that they were privileged to know a new name of God that no one else had ever known. God was the great I am, and thus he was present with them. And God as the I am was a promise-keeper. He is their Savior because He is the I Am. And because God was present with them, He is also compassionate, knowing their fight, their pain, their struggle. Their need for hope, their need for deliverance, and and a God of love. He wanted to be intimately involved in their lives. He wanted to be their protector and their provider so they could love him back. And after Moses tells the people all of this, we are told the people did not heed Moses because of anguish of spirit and cruel bondage. Let us pause and consider what these people just did God revealed himself to them in all the gracious manners I've described, and the people did not listen to Moses. Why? Because of their personal suffering And let me state it another way. God expressed his love for these people, and they were so focused on feeling sorry for themselves they did not hear that love expressed. and therefore turned the opportunity down to be saved. Beloved, is that not what every person does who refuses to believe on the Lord Jesus Christ? Every person who hears the good news of Jesus has the opportunity to know God, to be loved by God, for Him to be their God, and for them to be a part of His people. And they turn them down because they are focused on themselves. But we can't point fingers, can we? No, no, no. We can't point fingers. We have to take inventory on the privileges we have to know God. The Israelites in the day of Moses were privileged more than Abraham to know God as Yahweh, as I am. And we all the more, much more blessed that we know God in the person of Jesus of Nazareth And we get to know the love of God by way of the Son of God hanging on the cross and dying so that our sins can be forgiven. And we get to know the power of God and that he did not stay in that grave but was raised from the dead and now lives forever. And where he went, we too can go. We get to know all of this about God, and yet too many times we listen to the devil's voice and get focused on ourselves. And it is our fault when we listen to the lives of the devil and believe the lives of the devil to focus on ourselves and not the love of God, the love he has for us. The devil says, you don't have enough friends. People don't include you like they should. You have it rough. And we say, yeah, that's right. People should be nicer to me. And the preacher is saying, God loves you. He knows you. And you know him. You know Jesus. Isn't that fantastic? And we say, well, people should be nicer to me. What? Seriously? Or maybe it's an illness, or the illness of someone you love. And the devil has us focus on that and get us down on that to where we think about that first. Meanwhile, the Bible is saying God wants you to know him and for him to be your God, your Savior. We say, yeah, well, things are tough for me right now, so that doesn't really help me. What? What again? Or maybe it's a relationship that is broken or a job that is lost or bills that are not paid or whatever the devil is using to get us to focus upon that Our anguish, our cruel bondage, instead of focusing on the God who knows our flights, knows our needs, and can meet them and more. I hate the way our culture treats celebrities. I know you do too. I hate the way people will go out of their way to meet a celebrity and then tell everyone that they met that celebrity and that now they know the celebrity personally as if that makes them more special or their lives more meaningful. I hate such things, not because it is not cool to meet someone who is well known, but I hate it because we get to know and be in the presence of the Creator of the universe. Each time we gather together to hear his word, to eat of his flesh, and drink of his blood. A time like no other time in our week. And yet too many treat it like it's not a privilege. Nothing special here. Like it does not help because my personal plights are just too difficult. People, we get to know God in a manner that is by his grace and his mercy alone. We are privileged to know him as we know him. And so let us stop focusing on our plights, on our anguish, on ourselves, and focus on the God who wants us to know Him and wants to save us. God does not have a double life. How he has revealed himself is who he is. And it is our privilege to know him by his name, Jesus. It is for us then to take advantage and not for granted. Every opportunity to know him better. Let us pray

sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. We are in Exodus chapter seven. Get into a car accident. It's bad. Both cars are totally demolished. But amazingly, neither of the clerics is hurt. They crawl out of their cars And the rabbi sees the priest's collar. And he says, So you're a priest? I'm a rabbi. Just look at our cars. There's nothing left. But we are unhurt. This must be a sign from God. God must have meant that we should meet and be friends together in peace for the rest of our days. The priest replies, I agree with you completely. This must be a sign from God. Miracle as a descriptive in the Bible is referring to events that are not explainable Solely by the natural process, but which require a direct causal agency that is supernatural, we would call him God. Bible commentator Matthew Henry calls such men who do not believe as they witness miracles, they are quote, bent to disobey and willing to object. Such persons have their minds and their hearts made up even before they witnessed the miracle. Consider the story that Jesus told Lazarus and the rich of Lazarus and the rich ruler.
