But he said to him, If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded through one who rises from the dead. Such is a sobering story that Jesus tells. He, of course, is the one who would rise from the dead, the greatest miracle there ever was or will be. And still people choose not to believe, even now today, going so far as to question whether Jesus was actually a historical figure. This for the purpose of not having to address the truth of his resurrection. No, a miracle does not automatically result in belief. As we turn to examine the miracles performed by Moses and Aaron in Exodus 7, we are to keep in mind that although Pharaoh and his court would not believe in the one true God, these miraculous events can have a great effect upon those who want to know and love God, us. The first miracle was that of a rod being thrown down and turning into a serpent. The serpent, interestingly, was one of the first living creatures that God created upon earth. As recorded in Genesis. It was one of those creeping things the New King James describes. Here it is a serpent using a different Hebrew word, the same word used to describe the type of creature that Satan inhabited in Genesis 3. Since Jesus as the Son of God has been revealed to us, we can have a fuller picture of why God would choose this as a first miracle before Pharaoh. The rod of Moses was to be thrown down and turned into a snake, you remember, and then picked back up again by its tail and turning back into a rod This was to symbolize to the people of Israel and to Pharaoh if he was paying attention and to Pharaoh's court if they were paying attention that God had given authority to Moses over the devil himself. And when the ministry of Jesus started, the same proof was made. In Mark 3, Jesus is recorded to have healed many and cast out many demons. And when they accused, he was accused by his enemies of having a demon himself to enable him to do all of these things that he did, you remember they challenged him in such an evil way, Jesus said the following. How can Satan cast out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. And if a house is divided against itself, the house cannot stand. And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is at an end. No one can enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods unless he first bind the strong man and then he will plunder his house. Clearly in those words in Jesus' teaching, the strong man in this parable is Jesus. I'm sorry, sorry, the strong man is Satan And thus clearly the person plundering the strong man's house is Jesus. And he's doing so by healing the sick, by casting out demons. And how did Jesus get this authority to plunder, to bind the strong man? Where did that come from? We might not answer that question by thinking, well, simply because he's the son of God, right? But Jesus actually earned his authority over the devil when he withstood temptation in the wilderness those forty days, being tempted in every way, and yet he did not sin. The devil was thus bound by Jesus after those 40 days, and he could do nothing to stop the kingdom of God. And it was the kingdom of God that was arriving every time Jesus arrived at a place or said a word. Such an understanding of the ministry of Jesus is so very, very important to a greater understanding of the importance of Jesus' ministry on earth. Bishop N. T. Wright, speaking in Baltimore last winter, made the point That if the ministry of Jesus was all about the atonement, only about him dying for our sins, that he simply merely needed to die for our sins. Then he might as well have died with the rest of those children that were killed by Herod on that horrible day. And that would have been enough. But it was not enough. The salvation procured for us by Jesus needed to include having authority over the devil. Just as Moses was able to grab the serpent by its tail and use that rod as he desired, so too is Jesus able to grab the certain the serpent by the tail and bind him to do God's will. And of course, this means everything to those who follow Jesus. It means everything to us. It means everything to us because our victories over sin and temptation, our victories over the demonic and demonic temptation, those can be practiced now. In our times of desperation, in our moments of weakness, and in our most vulnerable hours, we have authority over sin and temptation. Every Sunday, if you look up to the chancel area at all, you might see me pray before I preach. And I not only ask God to bless my mind so that I can think clearly and bless my lips that I might articulate clearly in my heart, that I too would be convicted by the word I preach. That I might increase my own faith. I also rebuke the devil in the name of Jesus so that he would have no place in this house of worship And I believe the devil must make his way out of this place so that the word of God can be preached effectually. And I believe it because Moses grabbed that rod, that serpent by the tail. And it became a rod again. For that means to us that Jesus bound the strong man and he must submit to the authority of Jesus. I trust you believe that as well. After the rod of Moses was thrown down, we read that the Pharaoh and his sorcerers threw down rods as well, and those rods became snakes. Verse eleven says, they also did so in like manner with their enchantments. So Pharaoh completely missed the symbolism of the miracle Moses and Aaron performed, overcoming evil. He saw it as a magician's trick that could be duplicated. Matthew Henry again sums this up better than I can. Quote, the magicians were cheats, trying to copy the real miracles of Moses by secret slights or jugglings. which to a small extent they succeeded in doing, so as to deceive the bystanders. But they were at length obliged to confess they could not any longer imitate the effects of divine power. In provoking Pharaoh and his sorcerers to imitate a true miracle. The devil gives away his most prominent technique at deceiving people away from the truth. The devil imitates. In fact, the devil is not original in anything that he does. Ponder that for a later time. The devil is not original in anything that he does. He can only distort what God has done. He cannot do anything that is of his own. But we must give him credit Just as the Pharaoh's magicians were able to deceive the bystanders, so too is the devil successful at deceiving many. Many Consider how many imitations of Christianity there are in today's world. Consider the most prominent one, the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. A little bit about that faith. The originator of the Mormon Church you might know is Joseph Smith. Who was known in his days as a self-proclaimed prophet, but also a poor salesman and a teller of tall tales. He began as a religious leader, claiming that all who had followed Jesus from the time of the apostles till Joseph Smith's day had it all wrong. And that God had come to him in a special revelation, chosen him as a prophet to receive special revelation and to turn the people of God back to the truth. And so he claimed to have been given golden plates that revealed all sorts of new things, such as Jesus and Satan were actually brothers in heaven. He taught that each male who was faithful in the Mormon faith would receive his own earth to populate. And in order to populate his own earth, he must have many wives to give birth to spiritual children that would inhabit his planet. Ladies, you realize that heaven for you then is perpetual pregnancy. Sound like a heaven to you? And so polygamy was justified and wholeheartedly practiced on this planet in preparation for those faithful Mormon planets in the future. Smith also taught that the golden plates revealed how the African race was cursed because of a particular sin, and therefore blacks would not be allowed to become Mormons. Smith also proclaimed that there were ten lost tribes chosen by God to be his people And that they were on the American continent originally, and that John the Apostle is still alive even today preparing those lost ten tribes to return to prominence It goes on. While serving as mayor of a small town in the state of Illinois and at the same time running for president of the United States, Smith was jailed because he destroyed a building of a local newspaper that revealed he was practicing polygamy. While in jail, a mob was formed. That mob stormed the jail and shot Joseph Smith dead. And there was no clear line of succession to the leadership of the Mormon religion, and thus with some political maneuvering and some strong armed tactics. Brigham Young took the lead as the new self-proclaimed prophet and set them on a journey toward Utah. And we could spend the rest of the day talking about his distorted version of the faith. Bobby Glenn and I were watching a television program that did not portray Mormonism in a positive light, and she asked rhetorically Why anyone would follow Mormonism? She grew up with Mormon friends and has known their way of faith for many years, and she still does not understand what the draw is. I believe such a rhetorical question can be answered here in the story of Pharaoh's magicians turning their rods into snakes. It does not take much for the devil to twist a truth and make it believable, because, and here's the answer, because people who are dead in their trespasses and sins are already deceived. They think they are controllers of their own destiny, and any religion that tells them that they can earn their eternal reward appeals to what is already deceived in their minds and in their hearts And so they will seemingly believe anything. Consider that although Africans were said to be cursed All of a sudden, a new revelation came to the leaders of the Mormon church, and such teaching became an embarrassment, and in 1978 their doctrine was changed to allow blacks to enter into the priesthood. Consider that the doctrine of allowing polygamy, which was from the beginning of the religion and was said to be in those golden plates that no one has ever seen that that didn't go out of style or taken out of the law of Utah until they would not be allowed into the Union unless it was taken off their books. Consider that Brigham Young, a man who said that all of his sermons were as holy scripture, that Brigham Young taught that the God of this earth, the God that we worship, the God who sent Jesus and who called Joseph Smith, was actually Adam. Of Adam and Eve fame. That understanding, that teaching has been plainly discarded by the church as early as 1981. These are the most prominent examples of what the Mormon faith has changed about its doctrine, and I believe they prove that a people deceived will indeed believe anything. Consider the existence of the worldwide Church of God, Jehovah's Witnesses, Christian Science, United Pentecostals, Unitarians. And many independent churches or independent movements that claim the name of Jesus in some shape or form, but always preach a salvation that is earned by good works. Leading people back to the same sin of Adam and Eve, wanting to be like God, wanting to determine their own destiny And just as Pharaoh's magicians wanted to pretend their rods were the same as the rod of Moses and Aaron, so too Do these false religions, these cults, want to believe that Jesus they claim is the same one who died, who rose again, and who was seated at the right hand of the Father, offering salvation? Well we know by grace through faith. And we should embrace the argument that imitation is the greatest form of flattery. The devil knows that the best way to deceive is to imitate and distort the truth. After all, it does no good to distort a lie. Distorting the truth is the devil's modus operandi. Now I want to take you back to Exodus 7 again. For after these magicians of Pharaoh throw down the rods to be like the rod of Moses and Aaron. We are told that Aaron's rod or staff, as the NIV said, swallowed up the rods or staffs of Pharaoh's magicians. Medieval Jewish commentator Rashi notes that the language used here to describe this event are rod and rods as opposed to snake and snakes. Thus the rod of Moses and Aaron swallowed up the rods of Pharaoh's magicians. And Rashi calls this a miracle within a miracle. Because rods don't normally swallow anything. A rod in the days of Moses and the days before and up to today represented authority and were used by shepherds to beat off the enemy. To protect the sheep. And the authority of Moses, then, by that rod, swallowing, Pharaoh's rods, was authority, swallowing authority. And it would be used to beat Pharaoh down. And Moses was doing so with the humble symbol of a shepherd. Which, according to the Egyptians, was an embarrassing work, an embarrassing trade. But God took on that lowly trade, that lowly position. He himself as the chief shepherd. Chief Shepherd. And the point for us today is that what the devil tries to do in turning Pharaoh's rods to be like the rod of Moses and Aaron, he continues that today. And the mode of operation is the same in that he wants to look us to look the other way, away from the authority of God, away from the authority of Christ Jesus. He wants us to look away from how we are saved by grace and faith alone and not by any human good deed. He wants us to look away from the truth that without Jesus our works are filthy rags to be thrown into the fire. The devil wants us to believe we can earn our own salvation by just being good persons He wants us to think we can balance the scales of justice by doing something good after we have done something bad. His tactics are so old they would be laughable if they were not so very effective. For they work on many who travel on that wide road. And we should be assured that every time we throw down a good work before God as a claim to righteousness, it is eaten up by the rod of the good shepherd, Jesus. Beloved, I want us to see and I want us to believe that there is authority in the doctrine of being saved by grace through faith. It is a doctrine that overpowers the devil. It is a doctrine that swallows up anything that tries to be like it. We proclaim that by grace, the grace of Jesus, and faith in the sacrifice of Jesus That our sins are forgiven, and heaven is our true home, and the devil is grabbed by the tail and thus is controlled by the truth. And I want us to see that every time a soul is saved by grace, the grace of God in Christ Jesus That is a true miracle. It goes against our nature, and the only explanation is God. To him be glory. Forever and ever. Amen. Amen. Let us pray

sermons.title: A Bloody Mess
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Please be seated. Before I get to my sermon proper, I want to say struck as we were singing that moving uh response Orial song of what we believe. Last week I was coming from Bel Air to get to church on time. And as we drove through neighborhoods, I saw people getting ready for kayak trips and other family outings on a Sunday morning, and I remarked to my wife how I wonder what people think Sunday is. And it struck me as we were singing that song, what a privilege it is to believe, to have faith. To believe there's something more in this life. There's something more we have to look forward to. The gift of faith is a wonderful, wonderful thing that brings us here this morning. We are in Exodus 7. I begin by sharing with you my childhood when I was a wee lad. I was running in the house as I should not have been doing, likely chasting the dog, when I came around the corner in the kitchen and caught the corner of a pullout cutting board with my head. The result was a bloody mess requiring stitches. My very first stitches. When I was a bit older, the family was playing baseball in the backyard. My mother was up to bat. She was not a very good athlete. I was the catcher. So when she swung at the ball, she swung all the way around and caught me in the back of my head with the baseball bat. The result was a bloody mess and several more stitches. My father, who took me to the hospital, loved to tell the nurses when they asked what happened that his mother hit him in the head with a baseball bat. When I was a bit older, riding my bicycle in the neighborhood, when I came upon neighborhood kids, one my age, who was picking on some girls. I decided to step in, not because I'm courageous, not because I like the girls, but I did not like that kid So I stopped and bullied him a little bit. He stopped and ran away, but came back, picked up the rock, threw it at me and hit me in the head. The result was a bloody mess, several more stitches. The age of thirteen, my friend Jay and I were playing on an embankment full of ivy. Because we could dive for football passes better and not get hurt. Well, I only only I did get hurt. I fell with a broken bottle beer bottle embedded in the ivy and a jagged edge went into my knee I sent Jay for a band-aid because we were closest to his house. Only when I stood up, the blood gushed and washed away the band-aid. I found out later that I a had actually cut a tendon and the result was a bloody mess, surgery, and several stitches. Now each of those incidents had a shock level for me, as I would either look at the bloody hand from feeling the back of my head from the new wound there or watch as blood poured from my knee I put these incidents together for you to explain how the shock value of each of those moments never diminished. I didn't say to myself, oh, I've been through this before, like we say about so many other experiences No, for me each event was as shocking as the other, and I believe that is because of the blood All of us have heard of people becoming sick to their stomach at the sight of blood. And I speculate That shock and sickness at the sight of blood are caused by the innate knowledge that blood is life. The blood within us carries our lives. And it is dramatic to see your own life oozing out of you because of trauma. And it is the direct relationship that blood has to life that piques our curiosity to ask why God would choose blood as the second miracle and the first plague. We usually refer to them as ten plagues, but in truth they were eleven miracles and ten plagues, as the first one, the rod turning into a snake and back to a rod again, was a miracle, not a plague. And in case you were wondering, if we're going to use each Lord's Day to talk about each plague, the answer is no. Um full disclosure, I had actually planned on preaching the snake and the blood on the same sermon last week, but It intrigued me so much that the rod of truth was swallowing up rods of duplication, of false duplication, that I had to make that one sermon. Today we look at the plague of blood. Next Sunday we will examine all the plagues or the next eight together, and then the final Sunday or the Two Sundays from now we will look at the last plague, the death of the firstborn. Now before we look at the text of Exodus 7, I want to underline to you just what the Egyptians thought about the Nile. how the Nile River was so important to them. Egypt became a great salvation, or sorry, civilization because of the Nile River. The rising and falling of the Nile's waters enabled the people to use the river for irrigation. And this enabled them to stay put in the desert, which was very unusual. And not only stay put in the desert, but to build. To build what we now call wonders of the world. It also enabled them to go papyrus, where we get the name paper, which became leaves where they could record their history and pass that history down and pass their culture down to the next generation. The river, the Nile River, became so important to the Egyptians that they assigned several gods to it, and they developed an understanding of the afterlife. Because of the man of the river repeated its cycle every year, rising, flooding, and then falling again Physically, spiritually, and culturally, we can say that the Nile River was the lifeblood of the Egyptians. And in saying such, we are getting to the reason why God would turn this Nile to blood, why the first plague was blood. Let's look at the text starting at verse 17. We have there God telling Moses and Aaron what he is going to do. And let there be no mistake what God wants the Egyptians to know. Not what, but who is the true giver of life. And not just the giver of life, but the taker of life. For blood inside a creature means life, but blood outside means death. He is a god of power and of vengeance. No matter what a person prefers, he is both. Well verse eighteen warns of what's going to happen to the fish. And it would be of course a natural result for fish to die since the water turned to blood. And the stench of both blood and dead fish truly would have been miserable to endure. And this would have been a great blow to the average Egyptian who depended upon fish as a staple food. And it would have made daily living and sweeping an aroma hell, for such a bad smell could not have been avoided without retreating a great distance from the Nile And this would mean that the average household would have to move their homes while the river was blood. Verse 19. God gives instructions on how they are to go about turning all of the water into blood. And considering the size of the Nile, we expect that there would be branches and canals derived from it, including lakes, pools, and ponds. Consider that there is no other stream of water but the Nile in that whole country. Everything comes from the Nile. And there are no natural springs, fountains, or brooks. Water may at times in all parts of that Nile Valley be obtained by digging wells. But historians say that the soil was would not have provided good drinking water, at least drinking water that would have tasted anything that you would want to consume. And also note that the vessels of wood and the vessels of stone were used to bring that Nile water from the banks into the houses. For houses did have tanks and cisterns also made out of wood and stone. Verse twenty. This is the verification verse That tells us that Moses and Aaron did as the Lord commanded, and it tells us the result of doing what God commanded them to do. It is odd in reading some commentators about this section of scripture that some speculate that it didn't really turn to actual blood. It just looked like blood. Have an appearance of blood. And I say to that sarcastically that it apparently is perfectly legitimate that God could create the universe by means of his spoken word and also include creating humanity with all the intricate detail of the human body, keeping it alive, keep it functioning by including a system in the body that creates blood, and that same blood flows throughout the body to keep all tissues alive. I guess God could do that, but turning the Nile to actual blood seems a little bit too difficult, according to some Bible commentators. Which I say such is rather silly. Verse 21. This is a verification verse. That the plague took away basic life sustenance. It took away both eating and drinking, and thus the blood was death to them, not life. I believe this is God shedding his blood for them. Shedding his blood for them to see that the Nile God they worship And the gods they worship in relation to the Nile are no gods at all. And there was a chance to believe in the one true God. And we don't get a lot of chances. Verse 22. Here's a reference to these magicians, Pharaoh's magicians, repeating the miracle. We need to be careful here, for we don't want to conclude that the magicians actually imitated the plague of blood, for the scope of the plague could not have been duplicated. This again was a cheap imitation. But they did something that was similar. They found some water that had not turned to blood, and they did something to make it look like blood. And that gave Pharaoh enough evidence to once again dismiss Moses and Aaron. And we are to conclude also that Pharaoh was implicit. In the hardening of his own heart, as he dug in even more in his resistance to the demands of Moses and Aaron. And such is the heart of men. Men who are dead in their trespasses and sins. They don't look for God. They look for arguments to disprove God. They don't look for evidence of a creator. They look for evidence to deny a creator Verse 23. This is a continuation of verse 22. It describes the will of Herod. And I think it describes him like a young boy with a ball. He takes his authority and he goes home. He doesn't want to play anymore. Verse 24 seems to describe how they might have gotten a little water from digging wells. And this might have been how they survived these seven days of the plague. These Egyptians had never had to dig before, so this was new to them. And apparently the water was drinkable, but again, likely not very agreeable, since we noted the soil in the region did not suit for making good wells. And so we go on to the next plague. It didn't work. Moses and Aaron tried. It's a nasty plague. But it didn't work. It didn't change Pharaoh. It didn't change the Egyptian people. And Israel is still in bondage. But the blood plague still has shock value. It has a shock value to those who have eyes to see and ears to hear. It has shock value to those who believe. Consider God's focus and preference for blood. Recall Genesis 4, where we read of God accepting the offering of Abel, but rejecting the one, the offering of Cain. And the book of Hebrews in the New Testament discloses that God preferred the offering of Abel because it was a more excellent sacrifice. It was a blood sacrifice, as Abel offered the first sheep of his flock, as opposed to Cain offering his grain. And the preciousness of blood, particularly human blood, is revealed by God in that same story when Cain kills Abel, and God says to Cain, I hear Abel's blood crying from the ground. The importance of blood being shed for forgiveness And blood crying out for justice is next found in the instructions God will give for that Mass F. Exodus from Egypt. And the instructions there we will get to later are very specific as to what to kill and when to kill and where to place the blood on the doorposts of each entrance. And the lamb slaughtered was to be consumed inside that same house with the blood door with the blood on the doorpost? That has to symbolize the reality that blood was for protection from judgment, as well as marking God's people, and the consuming of the sacrifice was that they identified fully with the blood sacrifice. Of course, it was also a precursor to the new covenant, where consuming the body and blood of Jesus is found in the taking of the bread and the wine. And of course, the use of blood and worship of God, as prescribed in the book of Exodus, and especially then in Leviticus, has many usages. The blood covering the sins of the priests first, and then covering the sins of the people, to even sanctifying the altars on which the offerings laid. And of course, all of the sacrifices and the rituals related to the sacrifice commanded by God to be fulfilled all were precursors to the sacrifice of Jesus upon the cross. As his blood was spilled for the atonement of the human race. St. Paul was assigned by God to properly explain to the church what that sacrifice meant, that blood sacrifice. In Romans 3, 24 and 25, St. Paul wrote. being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation, an atoning sacrifice. Through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins that are passed through the forbearance of God. Jesus an atoning sacrifice. Jesus freely giving his own life to appease the wrath of God. Jesus, the only sacrifice, the only blood spilled that can redeem all the blood that was spilled before him and all the blood that was spilled after for the sake of justice and atonement. St. Paul says it again in the same letter, Romans 5, 8, and 9. But God commendeth his love toward us. And that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Much more than being now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from the wrath through him. The blood of Jesus makes us righteous before God because God considers a debt paid. And the blood of Jesus saves us from future wrath because it is sufficient not only to forgive our sins of the past, but to forgive them in the present And the future as well, so that we are never not justified. Have you ever considered what happened to the blood of Jesus Have you ever thought what happened to that blood spill? Have you ever pondered where his blood spilled on earth ended up? As it was being, as he was being whipped and his back torn apart, what happened to that blood? Where did the blood go that came down upon his head as those thorns were pressed into his skull? Where did the blood go that surely splattered when the nails went into his flesh? Where did the blood go that spilled from his pierced side? Where did the blood go that was wiped and washed from his body by those who prepared him for burial? Where did it go? Did you know that scientists describe the Earth's biosphere as maintaining itself by carbon recycling? If scientists are right in describing the Earth's biosphere as a sealed container, that's what they say it is. A sealed container into which nothing new is ever added except the energy of the sun. then it is essential that living things today be able to reuse the existing matter again and again Now process what that means in terms of the blood of Jesus. Meditate on where the blood that colored the dirt on Calvary and tainted the wood that bore the weight of Jesus as he hung on the cross. Consider where that went. Consider where it is. It would mean that the blood of Jesus is still on the earth In several forms, even today, being used and reused again And for us, used again and again to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. I say that such pondering of the blood of Jesus still being used and reused on this earth is quite shocking and marvelous at the same time. The challenge today, after contemplating the sacrifice of Jesus and the blood spilled by Jesus for us. is to be moved emotionally and and spiritually, moved by it, so that we are not the same person that we were when we came into this building this morning. We leave a different person because we're moved by it. Just as a little boy is shocked To feel the back of his head be warmed by blood from a fresh wound, and shocked as he brings his hand to his face. And sees his blood life coming out of him on his hand. So too are we to be shocked To contemplate the life Jesus let pour out of him. And why? For the sole purpose that you and I be righteous. Such a shock silences voices who tell us that we take our faith too seriously. Go to church way too often. We care too much about that. Such a shock silences doubts of unbelief and weak faith that are whispered in our ears by the devil. Such shock awakens our spirits to what truly matters in our lives. And the rest we need not get upset about. Beloved, the blood plague was to awaken the spirit of the Egyptians who were dead in their sins, and it did not. But the shock of the blood of Jesus awakens those who believe. It awakens those who have faith. Those who confess. And it will make every sacrifice we make for Jesus seem insignificant. Beloved, I simply ask, see the blood of Jesus and be shocked, shocked to love him more and more. Amen and Amen. Let us pray

sermons.title: Their plagues, our trials
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I want to start off by confirming that the Scripture is breathed by the Holy Spirit and is truly our authority. And by golly, I would love to preach a sermon on Leviticus eight. But that was the wrong reading. And that's my fault. Evidently my brain froze when I typed in what the reading was for this Sunday. It's Exodus 8, which is what we've been covering. So If you would turn in Exodus 8 and 9, is what we're going to be going through, and I apologize for those who expected a sermon from Leviticus 8. Exodus 8 and 9. The Ipuhr papyrus Epuer papyrus is an ancient document That arguably provides an independent record of some of the Ten Commandments that God bringed down upon Egypt. I'm sorry, plagues that got bringed up upon Egypt. The oldest copy of the Ipuhr papyrus dates to around 1400 BC Around the same time that we believe the exodus took place. The Ipua papyrus is the sole surviving manuscript of an ancient Egyptian poem officially designated the papyrus Laden. The poem is known as the Admonitions of Ipuhr. We closely examine the blood plague last Lord's Day, and this is what the Ipur papyrus says. Quote, Plague is throughout the land, blood is everywhere, the river is blood, men shrink from tasting. human beings and thirst after water. This is our water. This is our happiness. What shall we do in respect thereof? All is ruin. The fifth plague was the death of livestock, and here is what the Ipur papyrus says. All animals, their hearts weep, cattle moan. Behold, cattle are left to stray, and there is none to gather them together. The seventh plague was hail and fire. The Ipur papyrus says, Forsooth, gates, columns, and walls are consumed by fire. Lower Egypt weeps. The entire palace is without its revenues. To it belong by right wheat and barley, geese and fish. Forsooth, grain has perished on every side. Forsooth, that has perished which was yesterday seen. The land is left over to its weariness like the cutting of a flax The ninth plague was darkness on the land for three days. The Ipur papyrus says plainly, the land is without light. And the tenth plague, the last plague, was that death of the firstborn males. And the Ipur papyrus dramatically described it as follows. Forsooth, the children of princes are dashed against the walls. Forsooth, the children of princes are cast out in the streets. He who places his brother in the ground is everywhere. It is groaning throughout the land, mingled with lamentations. Is such a document proof of the historicity of the ten plagues God placed upon Egypt? Before Israel was freed from bondage? Is this a historical account? The answer depends on what you're looking for. The eight plagues we examine this morning, we accept as historically accurate a historical depiction And so as a people of faith, we look at them not just to see what happened in terms of history, but also to hear and understand the message that is contained therein for each of the plagues. The Egyptians were a people who worshipped many gods, false gods. And so we are to notice that God did not choose these plagues randomly He chose them orderly and purposefully. And remember God's objective in this Exodus. Sure, it is to free his people from bondage. Yes, of course. But also and just as importantly, he wanted Egypt to confess that he and he alone is the only God. Remember a focal verse from last Sunday's sermon, Exodus 7, 17. The Lord said, By this you shall know that I am the Lord. The this in that statement was the blood plague, but the same is said for all of the plagues to follow. God was showing the Egyptians and the Israelites and the Christians who is the Lord only. Having examined the plague of blood last week and planning to examine the plague of death upon the firstborn males next week. We start today with examining the second plague and working to the ninth. Let's look at each The second plague, the bringing of frogs from the Nile, was a judgment against Heget, the frog-headed goddess of birth. The Egyptians thought their frogs sacred because they supposedly brought forth life God's answer then was to give them more and more frogs until they could be viewed as, so they no longer could be viewed as sacred. Which took place when the frogs died and their stinking bodies were heaped up in offensive piles all through the land, stripping the frog of any sacredness. The third plague was that of Nats, and this was a judgment upon the false god, the desert god named Set. Set was thought to be a god of war and chaos. And if you have ever had gnats swarming around you, you know how they are related to feeling chaotic. Interestingly, unlike the previous plagues, the magicians were unable to duplicate this one, and they came to Pharaoh confessing that this is the finger of God. The fourth plague was that of flies, and this was a judgment on Uachit, the fly god. Believe it or not, Egyptian mythology has flies as giving protection against disease and misfortune. With this plague, the Lord makes it clear that what the Egyptians suffer, his people will not. For the flies did not swarm the area where the Israelites lived. The fifth plague The death of livestock was a judgment on the goddess of Hathor and the god Apis and other gods, for the Egyptians seemed to worship many animals. Interestingly, today archaeologists have uncovered burial chambers of mummified bulls. Mummified bulls. Showing the obsession the people had with their livestock. As with the previous plague, God protected his people from this plague. While the Egyptian cattle died, God preserved The Israelites cattle. And by these plagues you can see God steadily destroying the economy of Egypt. And showing the ability to protect and provide for those who were faithful, who believed, and who obeyed. And even when Pharaoh learned that the Israelites were not suffering like his people were, we are told again that he hardened his heart and would not let the people go. The sixth plague of ashes, dust, and boils was also a judgment on several gods who were believed to reign over health and disease. Sek met sunu and ISIS. This plague was so very nasty That Pharaoh's magicians were crippled by it. They could not physically go and stand before Pharaoh to perform the same. And even with the crippling of his magicians, Pharaoh would not let the people go. Now before God sent the last three plagues, Pharaoh was given a special message by God. The message was that the next three plagues would be more severe than the others previous, and they were designed to convince Pharaoh and all the people, as God said himself, That there is none like me on the earth. Exodus nine fourteen And there is commentary in this text that is as much for all who have ears to hear today as it was for Pharaoh's day. Pharaoh was a man chosen for that day, for that hour, as it is clearly stated, he is for God's purpose That God would show the world who was God and who was not. As St. Paul would later say, Pharaoh was a vessel chosen by God for destruction. For the reason of revealing to the lost and dying world and deceived world that there is but one God, and He is the I Am. But let us not think of God as only wanting to dominate his pretenders. As an example of grace. God warns Pharaoh to gather whatever cattle and crops remained from the previous plagues and to shelter them from the coming storm. The seventh plague was hail and fire, which was an attack on Nutt. Nutt, the sky goddess. Who was a supposed mother of Osiris, the crop fertility god, and Seth, the storm god? Because of this hail being accompanied by fire, it was like nothing they had seen before. Everything it touched was devastated. And again, it is important to note that the children of Israel were miraculously protected as no hail damaged their land. And before God brought the next plague, he told Moses that the Israelites would be able to tell their children of the things they had seen God do in Egypt and how it showed God's power. There were many gods associated with the crops of Egypt. Archaeologists have uncovered amulets in the shape of locusts. As these were supposedly used to ward off swarms of locusts. And that tells us how much they feared swarming locusts. If the later crops, wheat and rye, had survived the hail, they were now devoured by these locusts. Obviously, there was no harvest in Egypt that year. Amun Re, Amun Re was the chief deity of Egypt. He was the sun god. The night plague, darkness, was aimed at the sun god Rey, but it was also directed personally at Pharaoh himself. Who thought himself to be a divine representation on earth of the sun god. Darkness for three days. Darkness for three days was to show who actually controlled the sun and its effect on the earth. As Christians, we cannot look past the fact that the darkness was for three days. Jesus was in the grave three days. Three days of darkness proved that Pharaoh was not the divine representation of the sun. And three days in the grave and out of the grave Proved that Jesus did not only represent God, he was God Evidently this personal attack was too much for Pharaoh, and he agreed to let the people go and worship their God in the desert, but he said they had to leave their animals behind Moses pointed out that they needed their livestock to worship as God would have them worship. And besides, God was not going to bargain with a false God. And of course, the hardening of Pharaoh's heart continued, making the final plague necessary. And the hardening of Pharaoh's heart makes for quite an interesting speculation how much God was responsible for that hardening and how much was Pharaoh responsible. But there is truly no reason to speculate. God hardened Pharaoh's heart first. God started it, and God finished it. It does not matter if Pharaoh contributed to the hardening of his own heart. Every time his heart was hardened, it gave another opportunity for God to defeat the most prominent false gods of the Egyptians. And to prove that the God of Israel, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, is the only true God. Now I want us to go down the road that some of us may be afraid, a little afraid, to travel on I want us to go down the road of examining ourselves to see if there is any hardening of the heart within us. My premise is that if a man of such personal pride and false faith hardens his own heart to the one true God, even under the most punishing of circumstances, as Pharaoh did. Then people who have their hearts circumcised and given themselves to Jesus would not turn away from God revealing himself as the one true God, would they? Is that true? God does not plague his people, to be sure. But God does have his people experience trials and troubles for a time And perhaps we need to be reminded that God is deeply involved in our trials and troubles. Hear these words from Saint Peter, 1 Peter 1, verse 6 and 7. In this you greatly rejoice, even though now for a little while, if necessary, you have been distressed by various trials. That the proof of your faith be more precious than gold, which perishes, even though tested by fire, may be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus. Christ. Here it is plainly stated then that our trials and troubles that we experience in this life have at least one purpose, likely more. But the one purpose is for Jesus to be revealed in us more and more. And the result of that is that our praising and giving him glory more and more. But too often Christians see their trials and their troubles as events to get through as fast as possible, get past as quickly as possible So that we can go back to doing what we were doing before without considering that God maybe doesn't want us to keep doing what we were doing. God wants instead, through our trials and our troubles, for Jesus to be revealed to us Christians are to utter what King David said. Try me and know me, God. Search me in all my ways. See if there is any offensiveness in me, and lead me to an everlasting way. We should know, as I said, that God is not about making his people go through plagues He made Egypt go through plagues because they were so very steeped in their false religion and false gods. They needed the two by four treatment to wake them up. And that didn't even work. If you don't know what the 2x4 treatment is, it is when some people, you know, they just need a tap on the shoulder to get their attention. But other people need a little slap on the back to get their attention. And still others need a two by four to the side of their head to get their attention. And we should examine ourselves and ask what it takes for God to get our attention. What does it take for God to get your attention? Do you need trouble at work for God to get your attention? Do you need kids acting up and being disobedient for God to get your attention? Do you need unexpected bills for God to get your attention? Do you need sickness, a troubled marriage, emotional stagnation? A child who has lost his or her faith, a loss of friends, troubling neighbors, natural disasters, for God to get your attention Fifteen years ago. Fifteen years ago today, God used human evil to get the attention of every citizen in the United States. And you and I can still tell fresh stories as to where we were, what we saw, what we felt, what we thought, and how we prayed on that day. That same morning I made a hospital visit, and it felt like every person who saw me and my clerics asked me to pray Pray for our country. Pray for the victims. Pray for the families. Pray for the future that we might have one. The terror happened on a Tuesday, and the details were all too sketchy to know exactly how to pray. But the next day we had Wednesday evening prayer, and some people attended here that I have never seen attend the Wednesday evening. They wanted to pray and they needed to pray, and so we prayed. And it was a joy for this pastor to see and to hear of many churches across our nation that were filled because people wanted to pray. But it faded. It faded very fast. And I heard Christians lamenting that it had faded, that it had faded, and were even questioning the faith of those who wanted to pray that day or maybe that week, but didn't want to keep praying. That day was like a plague for us. And too many people looked quickly for something else to blame. Just as Pharaoh looked to his magicians. And soon we saw an enemy that was a worshipper of a false god, and we were told to look away. And blame the things that make terrorists angry like Jesus, like the Christian Church. It really was a missed opportunity for our nation. But I ask us as individuals, are we any better? Do we all pray a little harder, show up at Bible study more regularly when crisis is right in front of us? I confess to you. I try. I work hard at obeying St. Paul's instructions that we pray always without ceasing. I talk with God throughout the day. I but I never prayed more fervently like I prayed for my son Isaac when the doctor said he had cancer. And I would have been a fool if I did not ask in those days, try me, God, know me, see if there is any offense within me, and lead me to an everlasting way. I at least knew that God wanted all of us who loved Isaac and wanted him to be healed, that Jesus needed to be revealed in all of us in a deeper way. And I knew Jesus like I had not known known him before in those days. And that has been true when I have been hated as a pastor, ignored as a pastor, maligned as a failure as a pastor. I need a deeper revelation of Jesus in all of those times so I could give him glory and give him more praise. The challenge from this text is to move beyond condemning Pharaoh for not heeding the warnings that came with the plagues. It is to move beyond condemning those who only pray when they fear death. It is to examine ourselves and to want God to examine us. The challenge, beloved, is not to get through a trial, not to get through trouble, but for Jesus to be revealed in the midst of the trial, in the midst of the trouble. And when we know him like we have not known him before, that is when we can give him more glory and give him more praise. And beloved, that is the Christian life. That is the Christian life. Not an easy one, but one that God, by his grace, has chosen us to live. Let us pray

sermons.title: Christ OUR Passover
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: I can do screen if there are any. In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. That most appropriate hymn considering the funerals of this past week and also our topic today in regards to the Passover. We are in Exodus 12 Watching common Jewish families celebrate the Sabbath is both inspiring and convicting. We watched a few families celebrate in the hotels that we stayed while visiting in Israel. Women wear fine dresses. Men put on a talus that looks something like a shawl. There is wine for specific moments in the meal. Special bread is shared, and a blessing is said by the father for first the young boys and then the young girls. It is inspiring because the event is about celebration with family and devotion to God. They focus on passing their faith in God to the next generation. It is convicting because not enough Christian families show such devotion to God and effort to passing on the faith to their children. On what we identify as the Lord's Day, the day of our Savior's resurrection And if you think the average Jewish family makes a big deal about the Sabbath, well, you should observe them celebrating the Passover. Those of you who participated in the Haggadah or Seder meal we hosted during Lent this year, you know a little of that celebration. Regarding our scripture reading and really uncovering the whole chapter of Exodus 12 What we are looking at today is a pivotal text or section of Scripture that reveals God's plan of salvation, not just in the Old Testament. But in the new. It is pivotal because it is historic in the way that Israel was saved from God's divine wrath, in which they were given hope of a new life in the promised land. It is also pivotal as an event in that it served as the great anticipation of God's ultimate redemption, which was to save mankind from his wrath by Jesus becoming the Passover. St. Paul said it this way, Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed for us. Therefore, let us keep the feast. Also, for Christians, it is pivotal as an event because the Passover as a feast at the night that Jesus was betrayed, he turned it into the Lord's Supper. Which is the central point of our Christian worship. By chapter 12 in Exodus Pharaoh is essentially forgotten. Played such an important role, now forgotten. Instructions for that first Passover night are given in verses 1 through 13 and instructions for its perpetual celebration in Israel in verses 14 through 28. And then the narrative turns and tells us that they indeed escaped, exited Egypt. The specific instructions regarding the slaughter of the lamb will point to the perfect Lamb of God who would be slain. The bitter herbs are understood to represent the bitterness of Israel's toil as slaves and to represent our sin. We read as much in Exodus 1. The unleavened bread is a symbol of the readiness, readiness and haste. Israel was to leave Egypt Symbolize that there was no time for waiting, no time for the dough to rise, and this is explicitly explained in Deuteronomy 16. When we read in verse 14 of chapter 12 that the day of Passover was to be a day of memorial, we Christians naturally turn to the words of our Savior. Who said, do this in remembrance of me, which is the same as saying, do this in memorial of me. And what follows in Exodus will include the slaughter of the Passover lamb, and then it was to be roasted, and the family was to eat it together with those bitter herbs and unleavened bread. But at the Lord's Supper, Jesus only needs bread and wine, for he is the Passover meal. It is of interest to note that the instruction about staying inside all night, which is found in Exodus 12, is applied only for that first Passover And we know this because Jesus, after he celebrated the Lord's Supper, went with his disciples to Gethsemane. Some other interesting observations. Are the Israelites asking the Egyptians for proper clothing for their journey? Apparently, as slaves, they would not have sufficient clothing for a long journey. There are also not many verses given to describe the Exodus. Apparently, even though we've been working towards this and working up to it, apparently we are to know that they got out. And that was enough. Also, because of the numbering in Hebrew for a thousand, it could actually be describing units and not actual people. Thus the number could have been smaller. We don't really know. But we know that a lot of people got out. A lot of people were saved. And let us now underline and highlight the importance of the Passover in the history of Israel. And as I said, in the story of God redeeming his people as a whole, because God tells Moses that the celebration of the Passover is to begin Israel's calendar year. There is a real sense in which the Passover marks the beginning of Israel as a nation. It gives them their first identity. This then leads naturally to God after the Exodus giving his law shortly after, his law that would govern God's people. The teaching of the New Testament is that the death of Jesus is the fulfillment of the Passover. The event which the Egyptian Passover anticipated, typified, and really actually only began. Consider the words of John the Baptist, who identified Jesus as the Lamb of God, the Lamb that takes away the sin of the world. It was, as you recall, during the feast of the Passover that Jesus was crucified. And the night before, he turned that Passover feast that he shared with his disciples into the new commemoration of his death, our Lord's Supper. And then Paul makes that point explicitly in 1 Corinthians 5, Christ, our Passover Lamb. has been sacrificed. It is not then difficult for theologians and preachers to tie the events of the Passover and the sacrifice of Jesus together. In fact, if we do not do so, we don't then know the story of God redeeming his people. In Egypt, God revealed himself to be judged. He passes through Egypt exacting punishment as he himself says in Exodus 12. I will pass through Egypt. I will bring judgment. It is God who is the destroyer. That judgment was passed over, however, for everyone who was protected by the blood of the lamb that had been sacrificed. And for every family that followed God's instructions on how to apply that sacrifice to each of their homes. It is important to note that Israel, they were not to leave their homes that night. As they were to be sheltered under the blood. In the commemoration of this event, in the annual Passover ritual as we read in 1227, is done to fix the mind and the heart on how God redeems his people from judgment. By this act of judgment, God is forthrightly revealing his manner of redemption. And hear this, know this. His manner of redemption is substitutionary atonement. Someone in our place. Christians have never had any difficulty understanding how Jesus Christ is the true fulfillment of the Passover. The God and Savior of the Passover and the God and Savior of the cross are the same. And believing that is what it means to be Christian. The God of the New Testament is the God of Exodus. It was He who visited judgment on the Egyptians as he will visit judgment upon the whole world at the end of the age. And it was he who passed over the Israelites' homes. It is the same God today who judges the nations while giving peace to those who follow Jesus. It was the same God who provided the means for Israel to be passed over in judgment, a judgment that was so destructive to the Egyptians physically, emotionally, and spiritually. And it is the same God who raised up the living and the dead, dividing them as you would divide the sheep and the goats. The means that God enabled the Passover of Israel to take place is the means by which the final judgment of God will be stayed. For those who follow Jesus, and that should be meditated upon. The people of God were delivered from this judgment again by substitution. And we today, who know Jesus as Lord and Savior, are delivered from eternal damnation, which was assuredly our destiny and our just desert by substitution. Again, only the homes that were spread with blood were those in which the lamb had died. A lamb's blood had been shed. As we studied the use of blood in the Bible, we have seen it as a symbol of life given up in death. To put blood of the lamb on the doorposts of a house was to demonstrate in a public way that a lamb had been killed by this household. And killed for those who occupied the house. And the application was more as the lamb's blood was to be sprinkled after it was shed. There had to be then an individual appropriation of the blood for it to serve its purpose. It was not enough simply to kill the lamb. One had to take the blood and put it on the doorpost of his home. And there is so very much to learn about the manner the blood of the lamb was to be applied to each Jewish household. Consider that it was the father who sacrificed the lamb. It was the father who bled the lamb. It was the father who cut up the lamb. It was the father who sprinkled the blood and painted the blood upon the doorpost of the house for his own family. The application for us today, I hope you do not miss. For the fathers, the application today is for the fathers to take responsibility It was the spiritual welfare of their homes, and in particular their children. You cannot be with your children all the time. No. You cannot protect them from temptation No. You cannot protect them fully from the many things that will snare them or be a snare to them, and we shouldn't want to. But as fathers, you are the covenant head of your children. God made a covenant with you, and then gave you children to raise under that covenant. To know and love Jesus. And thus, fathers, you have to do the dirty work. Just as the Jewish fathers did, who chose the lamb as God instructed, and who cut its throat. And who bled it and spread the blood on the doorpost of his home so that his family might be saved A Christian father needs to get his hands dirty. A Christian father gets his hands dirty. By checking on his young sons to see if they are keeping their lust of the flesh, their sins of youth, under control. A father gets his hands dirty by assuring that his daughter is loved by him first, and thus does not look to the opposite sex for desperate affection. A father gets his hands dirty by doing battle with teachers who are godless, peers who are rebellious, and fads that are careless. Many, many times when children don't keep the faith of their parents, it is because of the father. And not just because the father is a hypocrite, although that is the worst scenario. It can be that the father did not get his hands dirty and thus allowed godless influences into the lives of his children that went unchecked. And the result is the devil having his way. We next Learn that obedience of the Father by providing the covenant sign God commanded of blood on the doorpost, the result is the salvation of his whole family. By redeeming his people in this manner, God is showing us the ideal of how salvation can be done. God redeems his people by families first. The father being obedient takes on the faith himself and then applies that faith, the blood of the Lamb, to his whole family, preserving them all. And then when his family is saved, he joins up his family with the rest of the people of God, and they make their way to the promised land. Today, the Father applies the blood of the Lamb to his household by having all of his children baptized. He then, with his wife, trains the children to know the Lord, teaching them the Lord's Prayer, the Ten Commandments, the Creeds, all things a Christian ought to know. And then the family joins God's people, the church, and they travel together to reach the promised land, which for us, for Christians, is heaven. I say that it worked first for the Exodus and it can work for the covenant of Christ And a major point to be made regarding this manner of salvation, this ideal pattern of God, how he can save his people Is that he does so as families, and he does so as the body of people who we would call the church. In other words, the salvation is procured by God by way of the Passover, not by individually. It is done corporately. God saved each household first and then saved an entire people Beloved, I perceive that the devil has been working an angle in the Christian church, especially among evangelicals. That has convinced many who claim Jesus as Lord and Savior, that a faith, a faith that I call just Jesus and me, is sufficient. Just Jesus in me is believed to be sufficient for salvation A just Jesus in me faith believes that a personal relationship with Jesus is the most important aspect of the Christian life. And I'm aware that some of you are uncomfortable if I am going to say that it is not the most important aspect of the Christian life. I will qualify my point by agreeing that because of the presence of the Holy Spirit in the lives of Christians, we can have and we need to have a personal relationship with God. But that personal relationship is not biblical if it is outside of the church The Christian life, as prescribed in the Holy Scriptures, is a relationship with God within the context of the body of Christ. Just Jesus and Me faith has wreaked havoc on the Christian church, especially at the end of the 20th and into the 21st centuries. Just Jesus and me has resulted in too many independent churches starting up with no affiliation with the larger body of Christ and thus no accountability. Just Jesus and me has resulted in faith based on emotion, as it promotes how we feel, how we feel about worship How did you feel about the sermon? How did you feel about the style of music? How did you feel about the people in the church? As if how we feel about any of it is important compared to the objectivity of the gospel and the fact that the only audience that matters in worship is God. Just Jesus and me also wreaks havoc and that it allows for Christians to refuse labor in the church or to submit to authority in the church. And it allows people to church hop when issues are too difficult to work through, because we can always say We prayed about it. Such phrasing allows us to blame our decisions on the Holy Spirit. Because when we say we prayed about it and leave a parish or turn down an opportunity to serve or reject authority in a parish, it is implied that it was a decision of God and not our own. And such practice is a cheap way to blame God for decisions that we make as individuals for the individual as opposed to the kingdom of God. Beloved, we quoted earlier. The words of Saint Paul Christ, our Passover, is sacrificed for us. Let us keep the peace. And hear those words again. It is our Passover collectively. It was for us. Not as individuals, but individuals within the community. Jesus passes over his people, and because they are under his blood, under his covenant, they are given life. Yes, life. For individual believers, but always in the context of being part of something greater than themselves Beloved, our individual salvation has always been greater than our individual self. Only in the context of the church, the church sitting down with God's people, only in that context can we keep the feast. Let us pray

sermons.title: The First Born Consecrated
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. You'd be seated. Turn in your Bibles to Exodus chapter eleven. We're dealing with the final plague. At Christian ThinkTank. com, ChristianTinktank. com, author Glenn Miller Does extensive number crunching of the infanticide that appears to take place with God killing the firstborn males in Egypt. He does this because, Glenn Miller does, because some people have tried to justify their rejection of the God of the Bible because they say He is a vengeful God who preys on the weak. And the accusation is based on the events such as God killing the firstborn in Egypt. Such thinking has been rightly labeled being more righteous than God. The text says that every firstborn of every household will die from the richest household to the poorest of the poor. God is no respecter of persons. God does not show favoritism as men do. And the plague included the firstborn of Egypt's livestock. Conclusions from Miller's crunching of numbers says that only 25% of the households in Egypt would have had a male who was a firstborn. Next, Miller argues that the wording in the text allows only for daughters and sons And that is a conclusion that children were the only ones who would die, not adults who were once a firstborn, but are now themselves heads of households. Next, Miller says that the average household would have been approximately six in number, making it four out of every 100 children that would have been a victim of this plague. The total number dead, from what we know, of the size of the Egyptian population, would have been 69,000 or 3% of the population. Miller then compares the plague to the infanticide that Pharaoh was doing or practicing upon the Israelites. That infanticide was an all-out onslaught upon Israel's children as they were ordered to kill all male children born in Israel or to the Israelites. And it was to be done by Israelite women, the midwives. And Miller makes the point that the infanticide could have been going on all the way up until Moses did his returning. Which was eighty years. Eighty years of trying to kill Israel's newborn males. The number dead would be staggering compared to the number dead at the hand of God at this tenth plague. But what point does such a comparison make? It seems only to say that what God did here was not as bad as what Pharaoh did. But God does not do bad. So there must be some other way to look at this tenth plague. We know of course that this was the last resort, this tenth plague. God had judged the false gods of the Egyptians with the first nine plagues, and that miracle of the rods swallowing the rods. Pharaoh would not believe that the God of Israel was the only true God, and the people of Egypt would not believe that God of Israel was the only true God. And so it had to come to this point. to where the Egyptians would actually kick out the Israelites, not wanting to see them anymore, just as God had prophesied to Moses. And then there is the purpose of God choosing the firstborn. The purpose. Please hear these later passages, passages that God spoke later after the Exodus. In order to confirm the value of the firstborn. From numbers God says, I have taken the Levites from among the Israelites in place of the first male offering of every Israelite woman. The Levites are mine. For all of the firstborn are mine. When I struck down all the firstborn in Egypt, I set apart for myself every firstborn in Israel. Whether man or animal, they are to be mine. I am the Lord. He continues in numbers. The Lord also said to Moses, Take the Levites in place of all the firstborn of Israel. And the livestock of the Levites in place of their livestock. The Levites are mine. I am the Lord. Continuing on in Numbers. Have the Levites stand in front of Aaron and his sons, and then present them as a wave offering to the Lord. In this way you are to set the Levites apart from the other Israelites, and the Levites will be mine After you have purified the Levites and presented them as a wave offering, they are to come and do their work at the tent meeting. They are the Israelites who are to be given holy to me. I have taken them as my own in place of the firstborn, the first male offering from every Israelite woman Every firstborn male in Israel, whether man or animal, is mine. When I struck down all the firstborn in Egypt, I set them apart for myself. And I have taken the Levites in place of all the firstborn sons of Israel. Of all the Israelites, I have given the Levites as gifts to Aaron and his sons. To do the work at the tent meeting on behalf of the Israelites, and to make atonement for them, so that no plague will strike the Israelites when they go near the sanctuary. And then this from Exodus chapter 13, the Lord said to Moses, Consecrate to me every firstborn male. The first offspring of every womb among the Israelites belongs to me, whether man or animal. And again in Exodus. After the Lord brings you into the land of the Canaanites and gives it to you, as he promised on an oath to you and your forefathers. You are to give over to the Lord the first offspring of every womb. All the firstborn males of your livestock belong to the Lord Redeem with a lamb every firstborn donkey. If you do not redeem it, break its neck. Redeem every firstborn among your sons. In days to come, when your son asks, What does this mean? Say to him, With a mighty hand, the Lord brought us out of Egypt, out of the land of slavery. When Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the Lord killed every firstborn in Egypt, both man and animal. This is why I sacrifice to the Lord, the first male offspring of every womb, and redeem each of the my firstborn sons. And finally from Leviticus. No one, however, may dedicate the firstborn of an animal, since the firstborn already belongs to the Lord, whether an ox or a sheep. It is the Lord's. These verses tell well how important the firstborn is to God. Another word for setting apart or consecrating a firstborn is to make holy. God makes holy the firstborn. And some hymns try to convey something, they could also convey something else. Take that hymn, the old rugged cross. The line I will cling to the old rugged cross is not a good line. Jesus died on the cross, yes. But he was buried and he was resurrected. We bring our sins to the cross, but we get up, born anew. We do not cling. If God is our audience, He does not want us to cling to anything but the gospel, which is the hope we have in Jesus alone. That is why he tells us to hold on to, hold on to the gospel. And let us mention patriotic hymns. Oh, don't go there. God is not the audience of America the beautiful. And I love the song. We should sing it. But it's not a song suitable for corporate worship. Consider that the audience in that song is us. The subject is how we love our country. God has only mentioned that he might shed his grace on our nation, the nation we love. And without question, we are to love God first and foremost. So first, God is the audience of Christian singing, and next, we are to sing about what God has done. This is what we find in the lyrics of Israel's first recorded hymn. God triumphed gloriously over the Egyptians. God drowned Pharaoh's army in the sea, the sea that he used to save his people. God did it. God was the strength of Israel. God was the source of Israel's salvation. And he is the God of strength and salvation for generations, as they sing. He is God of our fathers. The songs then that we sing in corporate worship should proclaim what God has done to save us. Our songs should rehearse the binding of the devil, the healing of the sick, making the lame walk. The resisting of temptation, the scourging, the cross, the grave, the empty tomb, the ascent to heaven, and the baptism of the Holy Spirit, all done to save us. We are also to sing about who God is. Our lyrics are to be a public acknowledgement. Of what the Lord has done and who he is for his people. Moses saying that God is a man of war. He fights for his people. But such lyrics are for the sake of the people of Israel. Here's the other audience. Although God is the primary audience in our singing and worship, he knows who he is. He knows he is strong, that he is holy, that he is the God of war, that he is a God who saves. But we who sing such words need to be reminded of such truths and be reminded of them over and over again I have mentioned this before, but it bears repeating here. A consistent theme in the Old Testament is a warning for the people of God not to forget. He says it over and over again, not to forget. They were not to forget what God had done for them, and they were not to forget his law, so that they would not willfully or ignorantly sin against him In the New Testament, the theme is similar, but worded in a new way. In the New Testament, we are to hold on. We are to hold on to the truth of the gospel lest it become corrupt. We are to hold on to our first love of Jesus lest we got get caught up in earthly desires. We are to hold on to the teachings of the apostles, lest false teachers lead us astray And so our music, the songs that we sing in corporate worship, are to be used to help us not forget and hold on. And this is another reason why we need to cautiously, consciously, excuse me, keep ourselves focused at worship. Keep ourselves focused when we are at corporate worship. The devil would have us pay attention to anything and everything that is going on in our minds or physically around us. Instead of what we are praying, what we are singing. When we are singing, we are to engage in spiritual warfare. And when you are in warfare, you better pay attention. Pay attention to the context of singing, the words you are singing. This allows those words to help us hold on. Hold on to the truths of the gospel and the teachings of the apostles. Like Paul says, we teach and admonish one another with songs, with hymns and spiritual songs. In the second stanza, we find interesting lyrics in that they mock the enemy. They mock the Egyptians. They rehearsed what the Egyptians said to themselves when the waters were parted. They thought they could use God's means of salvation for their gain. They thought victory was theirs. They were arrogant in what they thought. They were prideful. They assumed that they could take advantage of the God who parted the sea. Mocking the devil? Do not the Psalms mock in the same manner? Does not David repeatedly taunt the enemies of God? He reminds them of how God put them down and how God will be his defender. I believe Christians should mock in the same manner. We should sing with mocking words how the devil thinks he can snatch us out of the loving arms of God, but he cannot We should mock the devil in that he tempts us in vain to fear. He tempts us in vain to lose hope. The love of God casts out fear. The gospel itself is hope. We should mock the enemies of God because they claim that there is no God, that they can do as they please with no consequences. When they find out differently, it will be too late. We should mock the enemies of God who think that they control their own destiny. We should mock the enemies of God who think that they are free when they are mere lackeys of the devil. Now mocking in such a manner does not do much for or against the devil or the enemies of God. But instead it helps those who believe, for it puts the spiritual world in perspective. We are able to see by way of mocking that the devil isn't as formidable as we might fear that he is. And the enemies of God are not actually winning when it seems like they most definitely are. Mocking the enemy reminds us that the enemy is already defeated. And as time passes, the truth will be revealed and all blasphemy will forever be silenced. In the third stanza, final stanza, Israel sings of what God will do for them. The people who inhabit the Promised Land will hear of what God did to the Egyptians and will feel sorrow because of what awaits them. The chiefs and kings of the tribes that then lived in the Promised Land will tremble because their destruction is near. God will place his people where he wants them, and that place will be a holy place because God will dwell with them. This shows us that Christian worship singing should communicate God's wonderful promises for the future of his people. We should sing of death conquered, of sin vanquished, of the devil thrown in the lake of fire, of mansions, of streets of gold, crowns cast before Jesus. Tears dried up and joy, joy forevermore. I believe I believe that if Israel had kept this song before them, if they had sung it regularly and meditated on why they were singing regularly, they would not have made so many. so many unfaithful decisions they were about to make. We must appreciate and obey Paul's instruction to the Christians at Colossae to use song. To use singing, to impart wisdom, provide teaching, and give admonishment And this means that we are to be purposeful with our Christian worship singing. I know Jen is purposeful when she chooses songs for us to sing each Sunday, but I challenge All of us to be purposeful when we sing those songs. We are to be purposeful in working to understanding the words we sing, to believe them, to hold on. to hold on. And we should be bold when we sing. I don't have a pleasing pleasing singing voice. I know that. But I attempt to sing out because of what I am singing. And to whom I am singing. I want God and I want my fellow worshipers to know I am proud to follow Jesus. I sing to show I am not ashamed of the gospel. I seem to show that I know I know it is a privilege to call God my God And so let the heavens hear us sing, and let the devil cover his ears. Let us sing with Moses and Miriam. I will sing unto the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously. The horse and rider fell into the sea. Amen.

sermons.title: God Meets the Need
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Leave me seated. I want to start off by voicing dissent. Voicing dissent. Disagreeing with the Bible. Well, not really disagreeing with the Bible, but disagreeing. With the chapters that were chosen way back in the early thirteenth century. And one of my disagreements is with this Exodus 15. It's ending at a wrong place. Should end at verse 21, and chapter 16 should pick up at chapter 15, verse 22. In fact, uh and I and we can do this, of course, because the chapters and the numbered verses are not inspired, of course. The words that are in the Bible are the inspired ones, so I can feel comfortable uh dissenting with choosing to start the chapter later than chapter 15, verse 22. You see, I believe that we must take chapter 15, verse 22, and chapter 16 in its entirety, and then into chapter 17 as one message, as one lesson. There is a pattern in these sections of scripture. The pattern we are going to recognize, and then we're going to break down. The pattern goes as follows. God tests Israel, his people. Israel complains to their leadership. Moses cries out, God hears the need, and then God meets the need. And I want to examine this pattern step by step. First of all, God tests Israel. God tests his people. He tests them to begin with by having them make their way through the desert, toward the promised land, with no natural water made available for three days. When they did come upon natural water, it had been contaminated and thus not fit to drink. The next test was traveling through the desert after being well watered and running out of their food supply likely that they had brought from Egypt The next test in chapter 17, traveling again through the desert and again having no natural water supply God tests his people. God tests his people And let us hear that carefully. God does not tempt his people, he tests them. God would not tempt his people because God is good, he is holy, he is just and he loves his people. He loves them so much, he tests them. Hear what Moses said to the people as his last testimony in Deuteronomy, Deuteronomy chapter 8, verse 2.
