He was boisterous, opinionated, quick with an answer, unwise in his decision making A coward in one moment, and a very brave man of faith at another moment. He was first, chosen by God, to preach the gospel after the anointing of the Holy Spirit. He was a Jewish man, yet chosen to be the first to share the gospel officially with the Gentile. And yet, while sharing the gospel with Gentiles, he was wrongly influenced by the Judaizers. As he would not fellowship with Gentiles for a time, because they were uncircumcised When St. Paul confronted Peter about his inconsistent understanding of being saved by grace through faith Peter was gracious enough, mature enough, and thus a man of faith enough to take the rebuke. And finally, Peter was a leader of the Christian church in Rome. And from these epistles We learn he had a great concern for Christians who felt as though they were out of place in this world. because of the displacement Christians had experienced, both physically being forced out of their homes and out of their hometowns, and socially displaced. Christians, first persecuted by the Jews and then by Rome. Here I want to take what may seem like a drastic 45-degree turn in the sermon. I want to talk to you briefly about suicide. And hopefully why I do so will make sense to you as we consider how St. Peter greets these Christians who have been dispersed both physically and socially. Having taught ethics, general ethics, as a college-level course for four semesters, I became familiar with the secular arguments against suicide. And perhaps surprising to you, or perhaps not, the college textbooks that I was exposed to take the side that suicide is an immoral act. And that conclusion does not include acts of suicide that are actually of sacrifice. such as a soldier jumping on a grenade in order to save his fellow soldiers. It does not include jumping from a burning building that if stayed in would bring certain death And if jumped from would also bring certain death. And the stance that suicide is immoral does not include issues of assisted suicide where person is diagnosed to be suffering certain a an illness that will lead about to certain death Instead, what most secular ethicists address is suicide based on how a person feels feels about his or her given situation in a given moment. It is an argument that says that a person who is desiring And then considering, and then committing or trying to commit suicide is making an immoral decision Because he or she cannot see his or her life as objective as he or she ought. It is the conclusion that when a person is caught up in a moment or moments of despair He or she cannot think clearly enough and thus know well enough the value of his or her life. And it is that argument that most closely resembles the Christian ethical argument of the sinfulness of suicide. Christian ethics first says that a life that was given to us is not a life we have the authority to choose regarding when it should end The Christian ethic also says that a person who concludes that his or her life is not worth living has tried to take the position of God. Who is the only one who can have an objective perspective on the value of life Along with the inability of a suicidal person to be objective regarding the value of his or her life. There are other perspectives to consider regarding how the death of a person committing suicide will affect the lives of those who love him or love her. There are moral obligations of love and care and kindness being abandoned by the person who commits suicide. There are unforeseen effects morally, emotionally, and socially, when a person commits suicide. All are good arguments against suicide, but the most important one seems to be embedded in God's creation. It appears to be that the person who wants to commit suicide does not have the necessary perspective, the objective perspective. to determine the value of his or her life. And it is that inability to have the right perspective about ourselves that I want us to grab on to. So we go back, taking another 45-degree turn to get us back on that road less traveled, that narrow road that few travel. And underline and highlight what Saint Peter describes Christians to be, and to make the point. But what we think of ourselves, what our perspective is about our individual lives, or even maybe your perspective about everybody else's life Maybe that cannot be trusted. And maybe we have to be trusting in what God's holy word has to say about us as individuals. And about everyone else that is around us. So, looking back at the epistle, looking at St. Peter's first letter. As we look at verses one and two, which were read to us, some scholars are surprised At the depth of St. Peter's theology, as he expresses so well in the opening two verses. There I say, nowhere in the writings of either Saint Paul or St. John do we find a more full or more instructive teaching concerning the Holy Trinity. Look at verse 2. In verse 2, Saint Peter has been guided by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit to choose The holy order, revealed obviously in the ministry of Jesus on this earth, regarding the triune God. And perhaps we need to confess that when we read of the Trinity so clearly stated, we take it for granted. We read first our election is of the foreknowledge of God the Father. We read and then we yawn a bit Our election is continued by the sanctification work of the Holy Spirit. Yawn and yawn again. The work of the Father and the Holy Spirit is procured for us by the obedience to the shed blood of Jesus Christ. Well, yawn, yawn, and yawn. We have heard it before. We confess it each Sunday. Okay, yes, God is three and he is one. God. Let's move on. If this is at all our attitude, then we don't understand or appreciate as we should. The need for the creeds, the need for Saint Nicholas to punch Arius during the Council of Nicaea. The need for councils to spend months debating and then needing to gather years later to debate again to get it right. And what they needed to get right is what Saint Peter so easily describes Which is the work of the Father, and then the work of the Holy Spirit, and then the work of the Lord Jesus Christ. In this introduction by St. Peter, each person of the Trinity gets a position in the redemption of mankind, gets a title for that redemption. And gives it's given authority for that redemption. They are all separate, but yet they are one God. And this is the God we are to know, for this is the God who has revealed himself to be such. As the Athanasian Creed rightly and boldly states, this is the Catholic The universal faith, which except a man believe faithfully, he cannot be saved. And we say Amen I skipped over verse one purposefully. Forgive me. So as to set the scene for what I believe our focus is to be, as this epistle relates to us today. In verse 1, Peter begins by identifying himself as an apostle of the Lord Jesus Christ. That's important. The title makes it clear that Peter is one of the chosen ones, the twelve, that Jesus chose, to be around him, to hear him, to know him best. Now, other epistles would be later written and claimed to be written by the apostles, so it was necessary in this first century that the apostles set it straight, who they are. What he writes is of authority. He is one of the twelve. He is half of the 24 elders that surround the throne of Christ in the book of Revelation. And so, Peter is as a symbol for God's people. He is the authority to reveal God's will. And once the author has been established, and thus the authority as to what he has to say established, we are next to take what he says to the church, to us, as God's word. And what Peter communicates to Christians is what they needed to hear in the first century and what we need to hear and believe today. He writes to them as, quote, Sojourners of the dispersion. Sojourners of the dispersion In the minds of the Jews, this description as sojourners would connect them, no doubt, to sad realities of life under the covenant of Moses. Israel's experience as sojourners of the dispersion was the time of the Babylonian rule and Israel's disobedience. And even when some of the Israelites were allowed to return to their land to restore the walls of Jerusalem, they suffered painful periods. As they served as a vassal state for Persia, and then the Greeks, and then Egypt, and then Syria, and then Rome. The Jews as a people were made the sport of the world powers as those powers rose and fell. Times in which Israel would see few evidence of the divine favor God had said about them, not even hearing the voice of a prophet to encourage them or guide them. But then, at the time of Peter's writing, to those who had accepted the gospel of Christ, those dark years. would have been seemed to be empty or silent at once, at one time, or so they thought What happened was, truly, that the scattered Jews had carried much of their faith abroad, among the nations. Creating schools and teaching had arisen, the Jewish faith had arisen among Gentiles. This dispersion allowed Jews to adopt other languages and to understand other cultures. And thus the outcome of those sorrowful times had been a preparation for the gospel. A wider field was opened for the Christian harvest to come. And as the expositor commentary puts it, The dispersion of Israel had been made, as it were, a bridge over which the grace of God passed For publishing the glad tidings of the gospel and to gather Jew and Gentile alike into the fold of Christ. Of course, God's providence But St. Peter's letter is written to Christians, not Jews, even though many of them would have had a Jewish heritage. And so it would be a mistake to restrict the word dispersion here to be of Jewish converts alone. The apostle speaks more than once in his letter of those who had never been Jews, men who had been fashioned according to their lusts of ignorance. Who had at times not shared the gospel of Christ, who did not know Christ, but yet from a distance, even the hope of Abraham. These former Christians were people walking in lasciviousness, in lusts, in abominable idolatries. Such labels would only refer to converted Gentiles. The point being that we are to take this descriptive dispersion. Sojourners and place it upon Gentile Christians, Christians converted from paganism. They were now, as the Jews were before, Christians here in this world, although they were among heathendom. And their acceptance of the faith of Jesus must have given them their lives a different perspective. A different identity to set them apart as they were dwelling among people that were not their own And such must have been especially true for these Christians in Asia. They could only be strangers and sojourners. Their true home could never be made among the heathens around them. As Jews in the old days sighed for Jerusalem, so Christians of the first century centered their hope on the Jerusalem above. Now, connecting the identity of being sojourners during the dispersion and knowing how God used Israel during the dispersion. We can see how God has set a mission for the Christian church in this world. That mission is a special portion of St. Peter's message. As scattered Jews of old had opened the door for spreading the covenant of Abraham, so the Christians of the dispersion were to be witnesses. To the fulfillment of that covenant and that fulfillment with Jesus. And their election I emboldened that word. Their election had made them a peculiar people, but they were peculiar in that they might show forth the praises of him who had called them out of darkness. Called them into his marvelous light, and by their good works the lost might be won to glorify God When in his time he would reveal himself as that day star, even a day star to the Gentiles. Let us next look at that important identity mentioned by Saint Peter about all Christians, about you and I. It is that large charity of hope, which is stamped upon the whole of the New Testament. As he calls the scattered Christian converts the elect of God, the elect. And just as St. Paul calls many in the church to be saints, even though they were still lacking a great deal, much reproof needed to be made, they were still saints. So too does Peter call the church the elect, even though there was much sanctification to be done. The knowledge of the election of the saints by God is to give a sense of a mighty power. It is to bind the saints, wherever they may be scattered, into one communion in Christ. Throughout the world they are dispersed, but in Christ they constitute one people, united, the elect. Such a sense of this reality is to lift their hearts above any sorrowing, any sorrowing due to isolation in the world. For through Christ, an inheritance, a home, a claim of sonship, and a claim of their salvation is ready to be revealed. For they are the elect Now we will not spend time debating the difficulties some have about that word election. Instead, we are to focus upon the purpose of Peter using that word in an attempt to put the same purpose of our lives before us. The identity of a Christian of every age is that we are sojourners dispersed throughout the world. And yet elect of God, and therefore bound by him and to him, and bound to all who are of him for eternity. When we bring verses 1 and 2 together, we see that the election of believers is connected to the various stages of the three persons of the Trinity. The elect are chosen according to the foreknowledge of God, sanctified by the Holy Spirit, having been procured by the obedience of the blood of Jesus. Take now that given identity, given to every Christian, and apply it to how you perceive yourself. Or how you perceive others. Like a person in dispersion or despair or both or more, who does not know how to value his or her life, we can say that such a person's perspective of self and the value of his or her life is incorrect It is a lie, for it is defaced and covered by the feelings of despair, of self-hate. So too, Christians are lied to when they use their success in life or position in life. or physical beauty they have been gifted with, or a spouse they have won, or children they have raised, or any other such thing to identify who they are. And it can be reversed. Christians are lied to when they use their failures their low position in life, their lack of physical beauty, or lack of a spouse, or their disobedient children. And say that that is their identity, or those things are their identity. That too is a lie. St. Peter said it so simply, so plainly, so succinctly, so truthfully, that all the counseling in the world cannot compare. To the sojourners of the dispersion, the elect, according to the foreknowledge of God and the sanctification of the Spirit, for the obedience of the sprinkling of the blood of Christ. The hat is who you are. That is the identity of a Christian, every Christian. And the rest doesn't matter. All the rest that the world will tell you is important about self-identity is a lie. It is a lie from the devil. To know yourself as a sojourner of the dispersion, having been elected by God in the covenant of Jesus Christ, is enough. Consider this child we've just baptized, Lindsay Shay. Is her identity going to be her earthly beauty? Is that what you will tell her? Is her identity going to be her earthly success? Her social popularity? Her natural gifts? Beloved, I cringe this week. I have a cousin. If sh she's listening, I love my cousin. But she I have a cousin. Who works at a Christian school and she proudly put forth on social media these pictures of a seven set second grade class, each of the children standing behind next to a chalkboard And each of them having an individual statement. And it said this, something like this. Child standing there proudly next to a chalkboard that says, God loves me because I am good at soccer. God loves me because I write poetry. Etc. , etc. How horrible is that? God loves you because you do something, have something, are able to do something? Bad theology. Bad theology being put in the minds of our children. Why does God love us? God loves us because he loves us. What does God do for loving us? Sends us his son. We don't do anything to earn it. We don't have to be anything to receive it. God loves us. And our identity is as a sojourner, as in the dispersion, as the elect Not as a soccer player, not as a successful businessman, not because I have a nice car, a wonderful wife, none of it. God gives us an identity as a sojourner in the dispersion as the elect and beloved know it to be true. That is enough. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Begotten Again
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Oh you love the I dump and I'm going to let you wrong. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Let us all play like a Berean and open up our Bibles. Turning to 1 Peter chapter 1. We are covering what was read this morning, verse 3 through 9. Verse 3 through 9. Walk with me. We are going to be reading this like a commentary. As we walk through these verses of scripture, so written by the Holy Spirit through the Apostle Peter Peter begins by blessing God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Just like our song this morning, we are blessing God, our Father. God is the only one to be blessed in this manner by us. Such a blessing by us is to be compared to humanity who is blessed by God, a position we are already in. God has already blessed us, and so we turn around in that state of being blessed and bless his name. Our blessed state of being was by God's abundant mercy. And God's abundant mercy is described by St. Peter as begotten us again. Peter is the only one in the New Testament to author that phrase, begotten us again. The phrase, evidently, is his way of describing being born anew, born from above, born into a new creation. It is what God has done, what must be done, what will be done for those who will receive a heavenly reward. All persons must be, as Jesus said, born again. What Peter calls a living hope is usually the only hope for humanity. There is no true hope outside of Jesus as the Christ. Now we recognize that the secular world tries to give us hope. Hollywood would want us to believe that there is hope and simply being human beings. And if we could possibly be more politically correct, we could create a utopia on this earth. And that possibility of a utopia is supposedly hope, or at least hope for those who don't know God. And humanity pretends to put hope in nature, hope in politics, hope in social causes But none of these have any relevance to the true hope. We even have those who want to put hope in God. But redefine him as a God who would never judge, therefore a God who would never condemn If the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ is true, then none of what the godless world puts as hope has any meaningful value. In fact, it is all false hope. The Christian hope, according to verse 3, hinges on the resurrection of Jesus. Hinges on the resurrection of Jesus. If you ever want to be an outcast in a social gathering, not that you would want to be, but in any case, you want to be an outcast in a social gathering Just for fun and a conversation, bring up the fact that you believe in the resurrection of Jesus Christ. They could do go something like this. Someone says, did any of you see that championship game last night And you say, why, yes, I saw it. And you know, it reminds me of a wonderful victory that I believe in, which is Jesus Christ over the grave. I guarantee you will be alone alone in a corner within five minutes of that conversation And that reminds me of a social experiment I have to share with you that was on social media a few years ago. It was a demonstration on how you can get yourself and your car through any border stop, whether coming in or out of the United States. To avoid having his car searched and being stopped, this young man put a camera in his passenger seat And so we can all see his point of view. And he pulls up to the station where a patrolman was there, and the patrolman asks for his passport. And the young man said, you know, before that, uh, can I share with you the truth about my Lord and Savior Jesus Christ? The Border Patrolmen said, What? And he said it again. Can I tell you about my Lord and Savior Jesus Christ? And then the trollman literally went, move along, move along. And the gentleman looked at the camera and went, huh? The point being, people who are not looking for God are uncomfortable with the statement that Jesus Christ has been resurrected or that Jesus is your Lord and Savior. Because even the secular mind realizes that everything hinges on the resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ. Verse 4 Here is a near repeat of Jesus' teaching when he taught his followers that they were to seek the kingdom of God first. And then we are to, as seekers, put all of our treasures in heaven. And this is that which is most important to us. That which is ourselves and what we care about most and what we love most. Those are to be placed into the heavenly realm, where as Peter described and Jesus said They are not corrupted, they are not defiled, nor does their shine fade away. Our treasures are to be our love for God, our love for his people. Our good deeds for the sake of his kingdom. It is called our inheritance here because each of us is given the title Sons. Having nothing to do with our gender, but everything to do with the fact that we are all inheritors, all who believe In verse 5, our position as inheritors is stated to be secure because, as Peter says, we are kept by the power of God. The salvation spoken about in this verse is our final salvation. Hence the phrase ready to be revealed in the end. And we Christians, we talk about being saved. As a Christian, I might say, I am saved by grace through faith. Well, in one sense, we are saved, but that salvation is not complete. We are still, all of us, alive yet to be saved fully. When we are saved fully, we shall be raised from the dead, ourselves having received eternal bodies. And that, Peter is saying, is still to be revealed. Verse 6 discloses where Peter is going with the message, which is a Christian's hope of heaven. And he says, because of that hope, we need to greatly rejoice, which is to show great enthusiasm for our hope of heaven. And that enthusiasm is to combat to combat times of grief. We need enthusiasm at certain times because many of us in this life suffer through seasons of grief because of our various trials. The phrase various trials has also been translated manifold temptations. Various trials, manifold temptations. And those two phrases sound distinct, distinctly different from one another. But we may tend to think that trials are difficult times that come upon us. And manifold temptations are those things that pull us towards sin. But putting them together, we recognize that difficult times Very much pull us towards sin, for they tempt us to distrust God. They tempt us to despair, to lose heart, to have a fainting faith. The phrases then are actually compatible And that phrase, various trials, that I believe is a gift to the church down through the ages. It's not one specific trial. For the first century, Christians certainly various trials was persecution even unto death But that also could occur to Christians living today, as it does in regions of this earth. And yet there are other trials that, as just described, Can tempt to weaken our faith. The devil would love for Your financial despair to lead to your distrust in God as your provider The devil wants marital strive to separate us from our spouses. The devil whispers to us To choose bitterness over forgiveness and thus divide the body of Christ. And such trials can be just as effective as threatening persecution resulting in death. For they all can lead to a personal denying of faith in Jesus. Whether the denial is outward or even inward, whether it is abrupt or subtle, subtle and over time. And I hope that we catch that warning subtle over time. The devil uses trying times to get us to deny the Savior over time. He slowly chips away at our faith until we abandon it and not fully realize what we have done in making a decision. We simply stop praying. We stop hoping in Jesus. We stop believing. Verse 7 continues the explanation of how God uses trials in our lives, manifold temptations in our lives. So that our faith could become more and more genuine, he says, so that our faith could become more precious than gold, for gold, even though of great value, perishes. But faith purified by fire, fire of trials in this life, makes for a faith that does not perish. That is genuine. The understanding that our faith can and needs to become more genuine should not be new to our knowledge of the Christian faith. Every Christian should be living an examined life, and every Christian who examines his or her life will see That our motives for serving God, regularly serving God, have mixed motives. Some very good motives and some very selfish motives And the more we get selfish motives out of our psyche and instead live to serve others, well, the more genuine our faith is. The less we concern ourselves with how we are not being loved by others, which some people focus upon. As we think we should be loved, but instead focus on how we can do better at loving others, the more genuine our faith is. Consider how mixed our motives are when we turn down an invitation to celebrate with someone else Or an opportunity to serve someone else, or an opportunity to be at a Bible study with someone else Someone invites you to a luncheon, and you think to yourself, I don't really need to spend time on a luncheon. I have better things to do And when we examine such thinking, we should see that we are thinking about ourselves. It sometimes does not occur to us that others may need to see us at the luncheon, whether we think we need to be there or not. We may not attend Sunday school because we don't think we need to study the scriptures with somebody else. We have no need of man, but perhaps others need to see us in Sunday school. Youth groups provide the same example. Our ecclesiology is evident in the manner we choose to be involved in parish life or not be involved in parish life. And genuine faith makes decisions based on how others need me, not what I can get from others. Those are hard words, I I know, but that does not make them false Trials allow us to change our motive for the sake of others, unless and less for self. Thus, we are to acknowledge and accept the benefits of various trials as they can become a glory to God as we live them out in faith. We are able to see God more and more, His image more and more, as we work through our trials, trusting and believing. Verses 8 and 9 point us to the crescendo of our trials and our faith being more and more genuine. And our joy being more expressive as it brings glory to God. And that crescendo is the salvation of our souls. The Greek literally being translated the salvation of souls. Plural. And allow me to bang the drum that I like to bang. Allow me to bang it this morning. It is a drum that says the end. The end is always to be before us. It is always to be in our horizon, and that end is our eternal salvation. I promised you, young man, in school, if you get out of bed every day with the purpose of your eternal salvation before you Then every day is going to be a great day. Young dad, every day you get out of bed with the goal of your eternal reward. Then every day on the job will be short, and the love of your wife and children will be more pure as the days go by. Young mother, get out of bed every morning with the salvation of your soul as the first goal And you will love more purely, live more sacrificially, and your children will indeed praise you at the gates. Old man, old woman, get out of bed every day, thankful for another day, to serve God for the eternal reward of your soul. And those words Well done will indeed be said to you. The end is to always be before us. And with the end before us, I now turn us back to two points made by Saint Peter that we need to have established in our thinking and in our believing We first must go back to that phrase that is unique to Saint Peter, begotten us again. And we confirm that such a phrase is another way of saying that we have been given new life, new birth, born again. It also carries with it the important understanding that God does it. God does the birthing. As St. John states in his first chapter of his gospel, he says we are God's children, quote, children born not of natural descent, nor of human decision, or a husband's will. But born of God. Thus God is responsible for us being born anew. Now please hear me. If you are among us who has the understanding that every human being born into this world since the second generation of mankind until the coming of Jesus again, that you believe that we all have total free wills, and thus we are able to choose for ourselves whether we wish to be born again or not. Not only does logic from experience teach us that no one chooses to be born into this world. But phrases like, begotten us again, clearly state that God is responsible for our new birth. Any Christian that describes his or her salvation as a decision that he or she made simply does not understand how salvation is one. Too many Christians today speak of their salvation in Jesus as me and only Jesus matters It is described as an experience with Jesus based on his or her decision to follow Jesus. If a person thinks in such a manner, I am going to be provocative and say that such an experience wasn't real. And it wasn't real because it wasn't your decision. Any person born of God, begotten again, experienced the decision of God. And to solidify how dependent we are upon God for our salvation, there is the phrase in verse 5 where Peter says We are kept by the power of God through faith for salvation. The word kept also means sustained. We thus remain in the faith, having faith in Jesus, by the power of God holding us there. And so we not only don't choose to be born again, we also don't choose to remain children of God, for God does the choosing for us. And this is where it must be pointed out to us something that is likely so obvious that we overlook it. We shouldn't want our new birth, our staying in the faith, to be dependent upon our own choices or our ability to stick by our choices. Consider with me the many dumb choices you have made throughout your life. And if they turned out with a good ending, consider how that was by the grace of God and not by your good decision making. With your and my track record of making decisions, can we honestly say that you would want your new birth in Christ Jesus to be based on your ability to make decisions? I know that I wouldn't and I don't. Those of you who might insist That you need to have total free will in order to have a relationship with Jesus based on you choosing to love him Please don't think so highly of yourself. Reconsider that your ability To love selflessly and thus to love Jesus selflessly is not possible by your own strength and your own will. Before Jesus made you alive, you were dead in your trespasses and sins. All of us were We needed Jesus to speak to us out of the grave like he did Lazarus and to give us new life. And we need him to continue to give us new life. We are all too weak at keeping our promises, keeping our commitments. Self-examine yourself and count how many relationships you have discontinued, how many people you have disappointed in your life. And now consider that same person you disappointed, those same people you've left behind, consider them now that they were Jesus. Apply the reality that you cannot be dependent upon your own ability to make decisions or keep commitments. Are you sure you want staying in the faith or being in the faith based on your will, on your constitution? I know I don't Understanding and embracing the decision God makes for us that we might be born anew, that we might stay in the faith. Increasing our appreciation for the decision he has made for us increases our love for him more and more. And so we are told by Saint Peter to rejoice exceedingly, even in the midst of our trials, because of what God can do for us. And in the midst of our trials, because we have been begotten anew by God, and we are sustained by the power of God. And because of that, we cannot be lost. And everything we do in this life, because we are in him, everything matters. Everything has meaning. Rejoice exceedingly. Amen.

sermons.title: God Motivates our Will
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles. To First Peter chapter one. We'll be finishing up the chapter this morning. Before we get to the text, I want to allow you into the family courtroom of the Jorgensen household. Where you can help us solve a cold case. We were living on Jennifer Way in Sykesville, Maryland The year was 1999. The crime committed, the burning of several matches. And the evidence was a number that were quickly lit and quickly put out, placed in a pile on an ashtray stand. The father of the household primarily used the matches to light his tobacco pipe that he smoked two or three times a week. The children of the household, six in number, knew the rule that they were not allowed to light the matches without permission and supervision, regardless of the matches being available. And the crime or sin that the father of the household hated more than the burning of matches unsupervised was the sin of lying. And so all of the sons were lined up, and each of them interrogated, and the father does the interrogating. And thinks he knows well when his son, each son, is lying to him And so he goes down the line. Did you commit the deed? Each being interrogated, and each one denied. No sign of lying from the first son, no sign of lying from the second son, no sign of lying from the third. The fourth sign is at the age that it becomes more precarious. The case gets a little tougher. The fourth son is of the age of having the motor skills to light matches, but he doesn't have the track record or shall we call it a rap sheet, long enough, long enough for the father to know for sure if he is lying And the two younger children don't have the motor skills to light matches from a matchbox. So when the fourth child is accused, He immediately denies any wrongdoing with no expression at all The father has a hunch it is the fourth child, only because the three other possibilities seems more unlikely. And so the fourth child is taken into a room alone, light shining on his face. The father bends down and asks again, did you do the deed? And once again, a denial with no expression. The Father gives dire warnings for lying. offers a reprieve of punishment if the truth is told, and still denial with no expression The father asks the older sons, each alone, for their testimonies, and each deny, and each accuse the fourth son. But there is no corroborating evidence. The father, wanting to punish the fourth child for lying, chooses not to do so. Not to do so because he cannot get a confession. And so the case of the burn matches remains to this day unsolved. Who did it? If you are wondering, I can update you by saying that each child today still denies that he was responsible for the crime Perhaps the guilty party was so traumatized by the interrogation that he has put it out of his conscience, perhaps It is likely that every household present here has a similar story. And the mystery is not who burned the matches. The mystery that I want us to all identify is the mystery of the human will, the mystery of the decisions we make and why we make them We spoke at length last week about God's will overriding our will to get us to be in the Christian faith and to keep the Christian faith. But there is still a will that God has given every human being that makes choices regarding behaviors that we practice. And it is a great mystery regarding where that will begins or ends, and where the will of God begins or ends. I don't present the mystery of the human will before us as if we're supposed to uncover that will and understand it completely. It remains a mystery to all It is a mystery to understand the human will in regards to the choices we make, to sin or not to sin. To speak the truth or not to speak the truth. And today we come to a passage of Scripture. at the end of chapter one of 1 Peter, where we read of certain expectations and motivations regarding the human will. The Holy Spirit here uses Saint Peter to motivate Christians, to influence the will of Christians to live holy lives. And the words he uses, the teachings he provides, the insights we are granted are to motivate our wills. So that we would want to be holy, so that we would strive to be holy. Let us now see If the revelation pen by Saint Peter can be a motivation for us to live holy lives, Peter begins the motivation by informing that the prophets of the Old Testament spoke about the grace that God was going to send upon mankind. Peter says they searched intently and with the greatest of care. to discover specifics regarding how God was going to send the Messiah, the Christ, the Anointed One. And they appear to have understood a little regarding the need for the Messiah to suffer, and that glory would come after the suffering. But they didn't know the whole picture. And we can assume that they were looking at biblical passages such as from Isaiah 53. There we hear of a servant that suffers at the hands of men, and he suffers because of the sins of God's people. He suffers even though there was no deceit found in him, even though he was innocent, yet he was tortured And the prophet Isaiah also promises days ahead, resulting from that suffering, that many shall have their sins forgiven. And we can assume that the prophets looked at Psalm 22, and they were informed that the suffering servant would be publicly ridiculed, that his bones would be out of joint. His hands would be pierced and his clothes gambled over. They could see such events, but in no way could they know him as Jesus Until those specific events and those specific days came to pass. The point being That Christians can look to the prophets as favored men of God, having a part in God's plan of salvation. But they can also see themselves as favored. And so the motivation comes into play in verse 12 when Peter says to the first century Christians, That the prophets of old did not prophesy and look into the scriptures to help themselves. Peter says they did so to help you. Or specifically the first century Christians. Is there any greater motivation to love another? than when you come to know that someone has done something truly wonderful specifically for you. Our children celebrated their mother's 50th birthday, flying and driving long distances, preparing a meal, gathering all together, and they formed a memory book. With letters from each of the children, with also sharing their favorite pictures. Bobby Lynn thought we were gathering to celebrate all of our birthdays in January, but no, it was a night, a day specifically for her. That moves us when someone or a number of people do something sacrificially for you And we should acknowledge that the first century Christians were specifically chosen to be the first to have the truth of Jesus as the Messiah revealed. They were the first to be to understand and accept that a man dying on a cross could and did provide forgiveness for all who believe in his name. Such was a privilege that no other generation will ever know. But that truth doesn't mean that you and I are not privileged. Remember the words of Saint of Jesus to St. Thomas. That the people of future generations who believe, believe without seeing, believe without touching, they will be blessed. Blessed in a different manner that is no less important. And so when we read Peter's words about being privileged, And such words are to inspire us, to motivate us to live holy lives. We are to be motivated personally in our own lives. Knowing that the prophets spoke and searched for the sake of you. And to underline the privilege of first century Christians and all Christians down through the ages. Peter closes his thought by stating that angels, angels longed to look into the plan of salvation that God had for mankind. Can we imagine angels looking over the shoulder of God as God's will played out down through human history? It could not have made sense to those angels that a savior would be conceived by an unwed mother. It could not have made sense to them that the lineage of Jesus would have the sins of incest and prostitution It could not have made sense that the Savior would be of the lineage of King David, an adulterer and a murderer. It most certainly could not have made sense that Jesus, the perfect man, the Son of God, would be betrayed, mocked, and beaten, and killed. They didn't know of what C. S. Lewis called in The Lion Witch and the Wardrobe a deeper magic And so as we know of the humility Jesus took on by being born of Mary, being born of the line of David being mocked and beaten and killed We are to see the privilege that we have of knowing what is more profound, a more profound mystery, a more profound miracle. God can raise the dead. Most English translations begin verse 13 with the word therefore. And in the discipline of logic, the word therefore clearly identifies that what follows is a conclusion, as it does here in St. Peter's reasoning. To make the statement more clearly, we could read into the words therefore the following. Since you know, since you now understand that you are privileged, Privileged to know what you know about the plan of salvation that God has revealed through the life and death and resurrection of Jesus. Such knowledge is to motivate your will to do what I am about to tell you. That's what therefore means. And so next, we are told what to do. Now, our NIV reading didn't capture this. Our New King James does. We are told to gird up our loins, the loins of our minds. And this is a metaphor of picking up our oriental dress and being ready for activity. And it is our minds that we are to be ready for activity. We are to be thinkers. This instruction is a manner by which we are to love God with our minds. We are next told to be sober, which is a metaphor for being clear-headed. And our minds are to be ready for activity and clear. So that we can place our hope completely in what has been revealed to us in the person of Jesus. Dare we not underestimate the importance of our minds and how we think regarding our salvation? Not in that it is complicated, but that it rests in what has been revealed. And we are to protect our minds regarding what has been revealed. Has not our study on Tuesday nights and a study of Timothy in the mornings on Sunday shown that Christians were constantly in the need of protecting their minds Protecting them from false teachers who would have them believe anything but the simple fact that Jesus was God And Jesus was man. And Jesus actually died. That he actually rose again. And that he would actually raise us who believe again. The verses that follow next are the primary teaching, the primary influence of the will that St. Peter has been building up to. And that primary influence is that Christians live holy lives. Lives that are worthy of the revelation that it is a privilege to know. The first metaphor used for holy living is that all Christians are to be as obedient children. As obedient children we are to do as the Father says. Again, the Christian life is not complicated. We are to live as obedient children. The Father says, love him and love our neighbor, and we obey. The Father says, don't worship other gods, don't hate, don't lust, don't steal, don't covet, and we obey what the father says. How is that anyway complicated? It is not complicated until our former desires, our sinful habits Come against what God has told us to do and not to do. So that is what the address it what is addressed next Christians are to conform to the commands of God and not conform to the sinful desires that pull them towards sin. And another way to motivate us is to just do just that, set up a standard And so the standard set up, Peter says, is to be holy as God is holy. Jesus said in Matthew 5, 48, be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect. But we can't do that, can we? Well, it doesn't matter how many times we fail to meet the standard. The standard is still the standard. We are to be holy as God is holy, no compromise. Imagine if the standard were compromised. Imagine if we were to read Be holy as the Father is holy, but if you cannot, no big deal. If something as such were written, we would all settle for the no big deal clause. But there is no compromise. And because there is no compromise, we are given another motivation. We are told that God will judge each Christian according to his or her conduct. Well, I thought we were saved by grace through faith. Yes, we are. And God will judge us by our works. Not save us, not redeem us by our works, but judge us. And yes That is to cause us fear, and that fear is to motivate our will to holy living. So we have been motivated toward holy living by realizing we are privileged, and then by giving us the highest of standards, and then by fear of judgment And in case those motivations are not enough, we are next motivated by the passion of Jesus. He here next described his precious blood being spilled. This satisfactory atonement of the most precious blood is to motivate us to know how much Jesus gave for us. And then Saint Peter brings the motivation back to the privileged position we find ourselves. Verse 20 says that although Jesus was from the foundation of the world, he was manifested in the days of the first Christians for their sake. Peter says, for you. And in verse 21, all that God did in the life and death and resurrection of Jesus is stated to be, for what purpose? Their faith. Peter says it was so that your faith and hope are in God. Verse 22, Christians are said to have purified souls, and that they own true love for one another, just as they ought. And that they have been born again, begotten again, as Peter described earlier. And this new life gives each Christian a new identity. And that identity is also motivation to live holy lives. And the final motivation is what lasts, he says, and what does not last And he brings in this poetic prophecy from Isaiah, telling us that what is true, God's word, will last. And everything that is not true will wither and fade All of this is to be motivation. But a question remains Is all such motivation enough for each Christian to choose by their own will to live a holy life? What was in the will of a child to light matches and quickly blow them out and place them in a pile when they were clearly told not to do such a thing? What was in that will? What was in the will of a child not to tell the truth regarding his guilt of lighting those matches? What was in the will of a child never to do the same lighting of matches again, for the crime that was never solved was also never again committed. What we know from knowing ourselves is that what motivates our wills vary and likely involves several factors. The Holy Spirit knows this about us. God knows we need several motivations to live holy lives. We need several motivations because our sinful desires pull us to sin even when the Holy Spirit is motivating us to be holy. The motivation or motivations God uses for us to choose holiness are summed up in the truth that God wants us. He wants to be our God. In going after our wills, God is pursuing our hearts. For where our will goes, so does our heart. And God will wait for us to return as rebellious sons, or he will stand outside with us and wait till we want to go into the party. He'll do both because he wants us. I say, let's give him us. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Are Your a Disciple?
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: With my heart of dealing with In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Leave me seated. I invite you to turn in your Bibles to 1 Peter chapter 2. We will be working as was read through verses 1 excuse me. Verse 1 through 3. Are you a disciple? Are you a disciple? Jesus said to the leaders of his church, Go into all the world and make disciples, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. This commission Jesus gave to the church has a beginning point, the point of baptism. When the old is washed away, And the new person is born. Born into the kingdom of God. The commission also tells us that disciples are made. Go make disciples. Thus, being a disciple is the process of being made. But by whom? Well, disciples are made by the leadership of the church. For example, this sermon is for the purpose of making disciples. We are the disciples as we hear, say, and do that which is pleasing to God each Sunday. But if we are being made disciples Shouldn't we know what disciple means? Of course we should. The word disciple literally means a learner. A learner. A learner is one who is gaining knowledge and never stopped gaining knowledge. Being a disciple is learning and then learning some more. Thus, Sunday school is a part of the process of making disciples. Catechesis, teaching and learning the catechism, is part of the process of making disciples. Confirmation class and confirmation itself are establishing essential Christian truths in the hearts and minds of God's people, and these are part of the process of making disciples. And Bible studies of most forms, of all books of the Bible, are part of making disciples. And finally, as stated, hearing the Word of God expounded upon, preached, and receiving the sacraments on a regular basis are very important parts of being made a disciple. Because disciples are made, and because being a disciple is being a learner There is no end to human beings learning about the truths of God, including the depth of his nature. So we cannot say that being a disciple is a fixed or a finished state of being. You're constantly being made disciples of Jesus. It was shared with me recently at a Tuesday Bible study that a friend of one of our parishioners had said to her that she's got it. She's figured it out. She understands she's supposed to believe in Jesus. She's supposed to be baptized. She's done all that. She doesn't need to do any more. Of course, by saying that, she reveals she actually doesn't get it at all. She got the starting point, but failed to see the need to pursue holiness. Which is what St. Peter is trying to help these people do who read his letter. Now I mentioned last week That the word, therefore, indicates a conclusion is about to follow. And this is used in the first verse of 1 Peter 2. It is following both the instruction in chapter 1 for Christians to be holy as God is holy. And it's then followed by St. Peter praising these Christians as they are said to be loving one another as they should. To say that Christians are loving one another as they should is high praise, high praise indeed. It means that Christians are being patient with one another, being kind to one another. That they are thinking the best about one another. That they are not keeping record of wrong, but instead they are enduring one another. To live in such a manner is worthy of praise, for it pleases God the Father, brings praise to God the Son, and is evidence of the Holy Spirit being in the hearts of his people. And so we can read verse one again and translate it by reading it this way. Because you are to be holy as God is holy, and because you have been loving one another as you should be doing, you are next To be rid of all malice, all deceit, all hypocrisy, all envy, all slander. That list of sins should be interesting to us because if they were loving one another as they should. Then they would not have had malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander between them. Therefore, the call to get rid of such sins must, and hear this Must go beyond their relationship with one another. It must go into their relationships with other people, believers and unbelievers. That is a tall order, but one that is consistent with the love of Jesus. Now the New King James Version says lay aside these sins. The ESV says put away the sins of malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander. Both of those phrases that indicate getting rid of malice, deceit, envy, and slander means we are to remove them. From our minds and hearts, and to do so, we are to think of it as a physical act, like picking up Clearly evil attitudes and placing them outside of our lives so that we do not have access to them. We cannot reach over and get them. Laying aside, putting away evil is the same as repenting of evil, turning ourselves around the opposite way And repenting is akin to being a disciple. For to learn is to repent. You ask how To learn is to repent because when you learn you must acknowledge that you are missing something, that you're falling short. And to learn you must receive an understanding from someone else. The end point, being a disciple, is repeatedly putting away things. And receiving truth. Now the sins to pick up and put far from us, we need to look at more closely. The first is malice. And we can all agree that malice is a nasty sin. It is having ill will toward another human being. It is to want unfavorable events to come upon another person. It is to want the hate that is within our hearts to play out in some form of punishment or pain upon another person. And in order to have malice, a person needs to have stored up a great deal of unforgiveness. And stored up unforgiveness makes for a lot of bitterness, and bitterness poured out is malice. Love is the opposite of malice because it wants the best for other people, as opposed to wanting the worst, which is what malice wants. And people with stored up anger and unforgiveness and bitterness and malice have it all spill out when their emotions are bumped into. And such persons are literally dying inside as their sin resulting in malice eats them away inside out. Hear these proverbs. Do not say, I will repay evil. Wait for the Lord, and he will deliver you. Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses. The next sin to pick up and put far from us is translated in the New King James to be deceit And the Greek word can be properly rendered wickedness, which includes all sinful tempers and simple practices led by our tempers. And such sinful practices include guile. Well, guile is deceitfully cunning. And this is sinning in a purposeful manner. This is planning and waiting with the purpose of harming another person. It is one thing to cause harm to another in a moment of anger, and quite another to lie in wait to harm a person. Evil has taken over the heart, and the devil has been given the reign of power over the will of an individual if such a one lies in wait to hurt someone And hear this warning from the Prophet Micah. Woe to those who plan iniquity, to those who plot evil in their beds. That morning light, they carry it out because it is within their power to do so. And from Proverbs we read Will they not go astray who devise evil? But kindness and truth will be to those who devise good. The warning of those who practice deceit is that there is a strong likelihood that they will do as they plan to do, and in the end, it will not go well for them. The next sin to pick up and put away far from us is hypocrisy. Hypocrisy includes types of dissimulation. Dissimulation is when you hide your true self. And it is in this context it would be to hide how you feel about something or what you think about someone For the purpose, hiding it for the purpose of eventually doing evil to that person. Hypocrisy can include envy Which would be resenting any good that would or has come upon someone you do not like And whereas love rejoices in the blessings of others, hypocrisy seeds with envy. In fact, hypocrisy does not only seed, but actually grieves Grieves because the good that comes upon another is seen as an injustice. The sin next and the last listed to pick up and put far from us. Is all slander. Slander is reproaches and unkind speaking about others. The tongue is indeed a hard muscle to control. It seems that it has a will of its own But it does not. Even though it's hard, we do control our tongues with our hearts and our minds. It is we who choose to speak uncharitably about another person. It is we who allow our tongues to express the malice, the deceit, the hypocrisy, the envy. If we allow those things to dwell in our hearts and minds, they will come out with our tongue. Is it necessary? Is it kind? Is it true? And do you know for sure it's true? If no, then don't say it. Taming the tongue takes conscientious practice. You have to work to be quiet. To be quiet unless what you have to say is good, is charitable, is improving the conversation And I speculate that of all the sins the devil uses to divide and conquer Christians, the one of slander, with the tongue as the weapon, is the one he uses the most. But let us not forget that God wants us to put away slander from our lives as it relates to Christians and non-Christians alike. And here is the truth. If there is no malice, deceit, hypocrisy, or envy in our heart, there will be no slander on our tongues. Know that to be true. Let us next confess that the putting off of these sins is not easy. It is not easy because the enemies of God, the people who hate God, even though they say he doesn't exist, they say some nasty things about Christians, and they say some nasty things about the Christian church. And they know what hurts us most. They know that to call us hateful, hateful because we believe, for example, certain sexual behaviors to be sinful To call us hateful hurts, because we are drawn to our Savior because of love. And we are commanded to love others, even love our enemies. And so they say that we do not. They know to call us hypocrites, herds. It hurts the most because we want to be genuine and honest and forthright in our faith, and that includes our lifestyles. To say we are hypocrites is to say we do not have faith. And we are not a people of faith, yet we know we are saved by grace through faith. And so we hear these accusations and we want to fight back. We want to express malice. We want to use deceit. We want to call them hypocrites. To slander them. To sting their consciences. But God. God tells us to put down the weapons of the devil. And take up the life of Jesus as our example and respond by turning the cheek, by giving up the coat, by walking the extra mile, by being meek. If there is any time that those very instructions given by Jesus are to be applied to our lives, it is when we are hated for our Christian faith. Like any good teacher should. But what we should replace with malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander. He tells us to replace such things with pure milk. Pure milk of the Word of God. And here then is the good news as he describes it, good news within the good news is that we Christians can behave sometimes like babies. Not all the time and not in every way, of course. But in places, in place of sin, we are to behave as babies. As infants, we are to replace such sins with the Word of God as infants. And how does an infant behave that we should replicate? Well, we have a few infants among us, so we can easily observe infants are in constant need of nourishment. And they are dependent upon someone else to feed them. And this brings us back to what it means to be a disciple. For us to learn, and in order to learn, we need to be humble, for we need to receive from another what we are lacking. The word pure in the New King James can be translated unadulterated, which is the opposite of being adulterated with human mixtures or with human opinions. A very, very serious problem that plagues the Christian church is the mixing in of opinions of the people with the authority of God's Word. The Christian church is plagued with individuals who think that they can decide for themselves what the scripture teaches and therefore what they want to believe. Whereas exegesis is critically interpreting the Holy Scripture, theologians have used the term isegesis to describe how people will interpret God's word using their own presuppositions and their own agenda. agendas in order to get the Bible to say what they want it to say. And Peter, by using the word unadulterated, is combating such interpreting of God's word and is therefore saying that a true Christian, that is a person who is not just Christian by title, but by the living faith, will want to be taught the word of God rather than be exposed to the words of men. That is why Peter ends his point on the importance of learning the Word of God as a baby receives milk. From its mother. And he says in verse 3, if indeed you have tasted, that the Lord is gracious. Which is another way of saying, if indeed you are a Christian. A Christian is a learner. A disciple who was ever saying, excuse me, never saying, oh, I already know that. Never saying, I believe what I want to believe. But instead saying, Teach me. And I believe, but help my unbelief. Now allow me to be vulnerable before you. My uh very first paper Written for a seminary professor, was returned to me without a grade But with a question written on the top of the page, which read this, What is this? Question mark. I was mortified. I came to seminary with a bachelor's degree. I had three years of studying the Bible and theological subjects by correspondence. I was a youth leader. I was a Bible study leader. I was a Sunday school teacher. I was ready for seminary, or so I thought. The truth was I didn't know how to write a theological paper. I didn't know how to rightly articulate a theological argument And I didn't know the Bible. The most important lesson I learned in seminary was that I was ignorant about the Bible and ignorant about God. I learned that I didn't know very much at all. And as soon as I could admit that, that was the time I started to learn. As soon as I became a babe, I was ready to receive unadulterated milk. Naturally, my next question is, where are you? Do you think you know the Bible? Do you think you have enough knowledge of God? Are you a babe in need of pure milk, which is the unadulterated word of God? As we have confessed, it is a difficult task to put away malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander, especially in regards To how we wish to retaliate to unbelievers who criticize us for our Christian faith. But it is not so difficult. Not so difficult when we replace such things with the Word of God. As the psalmist has said. Thy word, O God, I have hid in my heart that I might not sin against you. Are you a disciple? The most fitting answer I can come up with is, gladly I am. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Being a Holy Priesthood Today
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be be seated. You do well to turn to First Peter chapter two starting at verse four. First Peter two starting at verse four. It is I believe unfortunate that modern cynics and critics of Christians Equate political conservatism with Christians and with Christianity. This may be a leftover Cause and effect from the days of the nineteen eighties when some of the more popular and outspoken Christian evangelicals aligned themselves with political conservatives and took on the title moral majority. The presumption behind the name moral majority was that the majority of American citizens were Christian, and because they were Christian They accepted the morality of the Bible as the standard by which the United States should be governed. The problem with the presumption was that it was incorrect. The majority of American citizens were not Christian, and therefore they did not accept the Bible, the Bible's morality, as the standard in which they wished to be governed. Yes, it is true that the majority of American citizens in the 1980s claimed to be Christian and some and had some type of Christianity in their family background. But we know from Holy Scripture that that does not make you a Christian. But the equating of political conservatism with Christians in the United States has remained. And thus has made for some very unjust criticism laid at the feet of Christians today as if the hypocrisy of Christians and the Christian Church Can easily be spotted in political issues that are at the forefront of our modern media and present politics. An example is the issue of abortion. Critics challenge Christians that if you are going to insist on caring for the life of the unborn, then we should start caring for the lives of those already born. The argument is based on a presupposition that Christians are not caring for the already born, even while that presupposition has no argumentative merit to stand on. In our little corner of the world, we offer education at an affordable price for children already born. And we offer an education that teaches children about the world and about the God who created them and died to save them. And we offer scholarships to children who come from families that can't afford sending their children to our academy. And we do so because we care about the least among us. That is just a small example of how Christians are caring for children already born. The next example is the critique that Christians don't care for refugees. Evidently When a Republican president signs an executive order to halt the acceptance of refugees from certain countries that are currently harboring Islamic terrorists That such an act is actually the Christian church or individual Christians signing the order. Therefore, Christians hate refugees and especially hate Muslims. That conclusion then leads to the accusation of hypocrisy, for we are not living up to the standards, they say, of the Bible. As it instructs God's people to accept foreigners into our homes and to love all people as Jesus did. The Bible really doesn't say that exactly. And if you and I are similar, we don't know what correct approach should be used regarding immigration and refugees. Just as the Right Reverend Foley, presiding bishop of the Anglican Church in North America, recently wrote in regards to these issues, he said they are too complex And we don't have all the information that is being used to make decisions for us to know what the Christian thing is to do. Thus, we simply need to pray for our leaders. And for the average citizen to pretend that they have all the information needed is just plain arrogance. That last part is my commentary, not the bishop's. What we can know for sure is that any refugee That we have the capability of personally helping is to be treated as our Good Samaritan moment For he is our neighbor, no matter his religious faith. And at the same time, we are to pray for our government leaders who make complex decisions For their biblical responsibility is to protect the citizens they serve, no matter their party. It is this preacher's evaluation that those who criticize the Christian Church and criticize Christians are suffering from a narcissistic sentimentalism. A narcissist is someone who is intensely and unhealthily thinking about themselves. And adds sentimentalism to the diagnosis And we see and hear people believe themselves to be more caring, more loving, and thus more sensitive to the needs of others than anyone else, especially more than Christians. It would be a failure, I perceive, for us to try to outsentimental them. You cannot outdo a narcissist. For he perceives himself as a narcissist to be the standard of caring, and you can't outdo his perception. Instead, we are to do as Peter is doing in this epistle and in this section that we are examining. With St. Peter's description of the uniqueness of Christians, here in this section, we are then to act as we are described. And how we are described is separate from the world. We are in the world, but not of the world, which is to say, we are not products of this world. But instead we are citizens of the kingdom of God, and that's how St. Peter wants us to live. You'll note in this section that St. Peter has a few metaphors that he's mixing together, and the one overriding metaphor is the temple of God. Which we recall in the Old Testament, the temple was the place where God dwelt to meet with his people. But the temple Peter describes is spiritual. It is similar to the house that Jesus said he will build in three days. You remember that exchange between the Pharisees. He was looking at Herod's temple and made the challenge to to break it down and he will build it in three days. Of course, he was not talking about the physical temple, but himself And his resurrection was the rebuilding. And the people he saves. You and me are the stones that he uses to build that spiritual temple that Jesus will reign in forever. And such a building we are to understand as a privilege to be a part of. Such a building is unique. And only inhabited by Jesus and those he has redeemed by his blood. The metaphor of being a part of the temple breaks down if we are mere cold stones. St. Peter then corrects it by calling Christians living stones. But what is a living stone? Well, it is firm and it is in place, but it is also living in that it grows and that it is relational. And next, St. Peter refers to Christians again as elect, as he did in chapter one, elect. Another way to understand the uniqueness of being Christian is that you were chosen by God to believe. Again, not by human decision, as St. John told us. In the context of being a part of the elect, is an emphasis on being different than the rest of the world around us. Being elect is like being Israel of the Old Testament. They were the elect of God. And this moves Peter to use another metaphor that should be surprising to us. He calls Christians a holy priesthood. That should surprise us because the priesthood, as described in the law of Moses, is quite a unique and special calling that was limited to only the tribe of Levi, but also limited in regards to who could be a priest to enter inside the temple and even enter inside the Holy of Holies but once a year. Considering the priesthood's regulations and restrictions and requirements in regards to dress, in regards to how they were to move about in worship. It was a very small number who could be a holy priest. But that highlights for us what Jesus accomplished for all who believe in him. His atonement, his resurrection, his ascension makes us, each of us, a holy priesthood. And we have to be, in order to enter that spiritual temple that Jesus is building, we have to be a part of the Holy Priesthood. But there is more to being a holy priesthood. The priests in the house of Levi were given a restriction. And that they were not to be given any land. No property were they to own. Even if they didn't enter the temple, they still could not have property. And consider why. If you own property, you spend a great deal of time and energy and your attention on caring for and protecting the land you own. And what was the responsibility of the Levites? It was to serve the Lord Thus they didn't have property, so that their attention would be on serving the Lord, not serving any land. And when we take the metaphor of Christians being a holy priesthood and apply it to our Christian lives in this world, We can recognize that just as the Levite priests were not to have their time and energy taken away from serving the Lord, So too are Christians not to have their time and energy taken away by the things this world would have us be doing, that would take us away from our primary duty, which is to serve the Lord. I realize I must qualify what I just said because it can sound sound like I'm dissuading you and other Christians who hear me To not get involved with political or moral issues or movements. And that is not at all what I am saying. What I'm saying is that our involvement in anything that is of the world is to be for the sake of the gospel, which is the purpose of the kingdom of God. Christians are to approach issues that involve us in this world in a different manner than everyone else. And so we care about political issues from the vantage point of being holy priests. We get involved in moral issues as holy priests. So I trust that you can see that our calling to be involved in the world is a higher calling rather than a lesser calling. Consider for a moment what you expect of me. And try to apply that to your place in the world. In a time of crisis, you expect me to be available And that when I arrive to have living words, God's words, to heal and to point to what matters and to lift up, that is what the world needs of all of us. In times of confusion, you expect me to have an eternal perspective and a calm that provides trust. That is what the world needs from Christians. In times of depression or times of elation, you expect me to pray and to know what to pray. That is what the world needs Christians to be And you can't choose this role of holy priest. That is what you have been made if you believe in Jesus. You have been made holy priest in this world. The call is what all of us are. We only need to decide how well we are going to do what we have been ordained, if I can use that word, to do. To be holy priests in the world by providing living words to heal, truth that calms, and prayers that give peace. To do so is to offer up ourselves As spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. Isn't that what Peter says? Such offerings, St. Paul says, are our reasonable duty, considering all that Jesus has offered up for us. Well, St. Peter continues his metaphor of the temple and moves into describing Jesus as the chief cornerstone. And we should all note the irony here of Peter referring to Jesus as the cornerstone, for Peter was that rock that Jesus said he would build his church upon. But Peter here acknowledges there is no rock that is like Jesus. Jesus is the rock that has been carefully cut and carefully placed so that the kingdom of God could only be built with him. as the chief or necessary cornerstone. Jesus is that cornerstone the prophet Isaiah described. And all who believe in him to be that cornerstone will receive the hopeful promises he has made. And yet there is a problem. Peter recognizes it through the prophets. Not everyone believes. Many will reject Jesus because they are offended by him. And they will stumble, being offered by him, stumble because of him. And it says here by Peter, because of their disobedience. And this is where the line is drawn with every generation that chooses not to believe. It is the line that is made when people insist that they are going to do what they want to do. They're going to live their lives if they want to live their lives. They aren't going to be like in judges doing what is right in their own eyes. You know, the Barna group, the Barna group did a study last year that examined American public attitudes towards Christians. And the overall finding was that more people than ever, on average, find Christians, believers in Jesus, to be extremists, simply because they believe. The Barner Group speculates that American society on average is growing increasingly uneasy with any person or persons who take their religious faith seriously. Concluding that anyone who says he or she believes in something is automatically susceptible to become radical. And as a radical, he or she is then capable of acts of terror on behalf of his or her beliefs. And while it may be true as to why more Americans don't trust professing Christians I counter that there is no difference in reasoning as to why secularists dislike Christians and dislike the Christian church. No difference than it has been since the first century. It was then because Jesus claimed that there was absolute truth and that he was the absolute truth. The predominant mind of the Jewish Pharisees in Jesus' day was that no person had a grasp on absolute truth. Many rabbis had good points, but they didn't get at the truth. And Jesus said not only did he get at the truth, but that he was the truth. And people followed him and they hated him for it. And I say it is the same today Jesus, as we say and preach of him today, is the truth and speaks the truth. I see this play out in my logic class every year as I introduce the law of non-contradiction. The law of non-contradiction states that a statement cannot be true and false at the same time. There's any aught with another Christian it should be taken care of before the service would continue and we would partake of Holy Communion. The word aught is also translated something against you. It is from the teaching of Jesus. Who was instructing his followers that if they were to bring an offering before the Lord, an act of worship, and someone had something against you You are to go to that fellow believer and find forgiveness and reconciliation before the worship of God is to take place. So after the employee of the preacher, a fellow student from across the sanctuary approached me. Now, mind you, I did not know this young man personally. He introduced himself to me and stated something like the following. I need to ask your forgiveness. When I first saw you, I didn't like you. I thought you were a jerk. Please forgive me. Now again, I did not know this fellow college student. I was obliged to forgive him But as you are hearing now, I have not forgotten that moment. Can you agree with me that this apology didn't need to be stated? I didn't need to know what was going on in his heart toward me if he had slandered me. gossiped about me, done something unkind to me, I would have appreciated the apology. But he didn't. He had mere thoughts in his head and feelings in his heart that were unkind and he felt like he needed to unburden himself by telling him about his unkind thoughts towards me. Thanks a lot He goes away feeling better, having unburdened himself, and I feel depressed. I have had a hard enough time in my life to get people to like me when they know my personality and they know what I think, let alone people who have never heard me speak before Depressing indeed. Well, having heard a solemn, a solid sermon last week covering verses 1 through 3 in 1 Peter, 1 through 7, and 1 Peter chapter 3. We continue in the same with a better understanding of the context of Peter's words. In chapter 2, you will remember, Peter encouraged Christians to focus on the gospel as the priority when it came to being under authority. And then he taught us how to make the gospel a priority in our marriages, and this all makes our testimony of the gospel the centerpiece of our lives, the center of the most important relationships in our lives. He then moves here in the section we are covering this morning on how to relate to other Christians. And what he tells us here allows us to say that we are to be gospel-centered in our lives, missionaries, in all of our relationships. Even with people who already claim to know the gospel. As I read this Week this section of scripture we are examining this morning. I thought of St. Paul's letter to the Corinthians.
