And that great love chapter in chapter 13, where Paul sets the standard of love that is higher than we can reach, but is a standard we must always be reaching for. I also thought of the first epistle of John, where the apostle emphatically states that we cannot say we love God. While at the same time we are showing indifference to a brother or sister of the same faith. And of course, all of this teaching is based on the teachings of Jesus. Who first said for us to love our neighbor as ourself, and then told us that as followers, others, people who are non-believers, will know us by our love for one another. Here in 1 Peter, Peter begins with the admonition to be of one mind, Christian to Christian. We can dismiss any exaggeration that would have us conclude that we are to be of one mind about everything. A pointless comment to make to someone, I think, is that you say you don't agree with everything that they say. You know, you should know that I don't agree about everything that you say. Of course you don't. We are blessed if we still agree with ourselves after five minutes. We state a personal opinion. And with that fact, there is no chance we can agree with others on everything. But we can agree on the essentials. And that is one reason why we confess the creeds in corporate worship. The rubric in the Book of Common Prayer could appropriately read before we recite one of the creeds. Quote, so what do you agree on, dear Christians? And we could respond in kind. The answer would be the Apostles or the Nicene Creed, most appropriate. Next, we are instructed to have compassion on one another, which literally can be translated sympathetic. This is similar to Paul instructing the Romans to rejoice with those who rejoice and mourn with those who mourn. It is being at the place emotionally, if possible, with a fellow believer, especially those who are going through a difficult time. It is, interestingly, the same word that the preacher to the Hebrews uses to describe what Jesus does for us as our high priest. He is sympathetic towards us. We then can conclude that in expressing our sympathy, we are to do as a high priest would do, we are to intercede for one another. We are to pray for one another. And in our sympathetic manner, and in our praying for one another As a people of compassion, people of sympathy, we are the continuation of the presence of Jesus on this earth. As we are his body being present with people, his people in need. And next St. Peter says that we are to love the brethren. This surprised me, by the way. The word for love used by Peter is not agape, as Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 13. It is not God's unconditional love. Now Peter will use that word later in chapter 4, but here he uses the word phileo. Which we know to be fraternal or brotherly love. Because Phileo is chosen, we must do further study to understand Why such a love is to be important for Christians to express to one another. C. S. Lewis Does the best job, in my opinion, of flushing out the meaning of Phileo love in his book titled The Four Loves. He calls Phileo love friendship love. Well, there are several reasons for friendships, and let's face it, some of them are quite selfish. We be we befriend the cleaning lady for the sole purpose that she might not charge us for the bad stains she has to remove on our clothes. But there are also very good reasons for loving another person as a friend Lewis describes friendship love that Christians are to share with one another as a friendship of exclusivity without excluding. Excivity without excluding. And here is an example of how that works. Let us say that you were at a New York Yankees baseball game in New York. And in the sea of people wearing pinstripes, you spot a person wearing your beloved orange and black. You will likely want to know that person and befriend that person because of what you have in common. And so you strive to meet the person and talk with the person. And you are exclusive in your relationship because your gathering and your sharing with this new friend is based on your love for the Orioles. And the Yankee fans don't love the Orioles. But you are not entirely exclusive because if you spot another person wearing orange and black You quickly invite them into your group because they share a love for what you love. And so you are being exclusive. While not excluding, because you welcome anyone into your friendship group who has a love for the Orioles For Christians, this type of exclusivity without excluding is something vital for survival. We Christians go many places where we find we do not fit in. And when we find other Christians who are at the same place, And who are like us not fitting in, we want and need their friendship Lewis makes the claim that friendship love, as Christians are to have for one another, is to be seen as superior to eros or romantic love. And also romantic love just focuses on one individual to another, where friendship love gets things done. Friendship love is productive. It roots for its team. It expresses itself in building and producing and worshiping as friendship love centers on what matters most to the friendship. Christians who are living out the love of God are always looking to become a friend with other people who love the Lord Jesus. Finally, about friendship love, Lewis warns that friendship love has its dangerous counterfeits. There are people who are exclusive in their friendship because they perceive themselves to be part of the elite, and the elite do not allow anyone else in. And so they exclude, with no intention of including anyone else. Friendship love can also be dangerous as a counterfeit when it is based on being rebellious Or based on hating the same thing, or, shall we say, hating the same person. Such friendship or friendships are counterfeit because they do not fit the meaning of God's love, or the meaning God has placed upon all love. We continue with Peter. He goes on to say that we are to be tender-hearted toward another Christian. The disposition means the same as being kind. Being kind is being gentle to the sensitivities of another human being who calls Jesus Lord. Combining kindness as gentleness with love, it must also include forgiveness. And so being tender-hearted is to be a person of forgiveness. And such forgiveness is what we pray that we would do in the Lord's Prayer. Forgive us our trespasses, as in the same like manner we forgive those who trespass against us. Jesus said in the same way we forgive others so we will be forgiven. I need to be forgiven a lot. And therefore, I need to forgive a lot. And if we become focused on how people Who we are quite sure are not forgiving us as they should, well then we need to be forgiven even more as we need to forgive people for not forgiving us Next, we are told that Christian to Christian we are to be courteous. When a person is courteous, he or she or she is considering the needs and importance of another as opposed to self. To put another person's needs before our own, you need to pursue the virtue of humility. When pursuing the virtue of humility, we find it is much easier to put other people's knees before our own. An internal question we can ask ourselves on a regular, consistent basis is the following. How can I die to myself in this particular moment? In a conversation with another believer, I can ask, how can I die to myself in this moment? With the purpose of allowing the needs of the other person to be expressed rather than my own. In a work situation, I can ask myself, how can I die to myself in this moment The answer to the question will point me to a job that I can do that will ease another person's load And in a conflict, in a conflict I can ask, how can I die to myself in this moment? The answer to that question will help me discern what is important in the conflict and what is not If it is a conflict that is the result of protecting my image of myself. What I think is my reputation, protecting my pride, then the conflict can end because I choose to die to myself Such is being courteous. Now the word courteous for Peter we can know is focused on conflict between Christians. For that is evident in the next few verses. He warns next against returning evil for evil or reviling for reviling in a conflict. is when you return evil for evil and reviling for reviling. In a c in a fight. In a fight with a fellow believer. Evil can be done in act as railing is done in words. Evil includes undermining. Undermining another person is an evil act. Entrapping another person. It includes setting up another person to fail. Railing includes unkind words and words that provoke to get a counter-reaction. Such things should be far from the Christian life, and Peter is saying, especially from Christian to Christian. Instead, the opposite is to be practiced. We are to be a people of blessings. We are to bless one another. And as people who bless others, we are to be motivated that by blessing others we are further assuring ourselves an eternal blessing. That's what Peter says A home in heaven where death will be no more and peace will be in our hearts and peace will be with one another Now the remainder of this section of scripture is a quote from Psalm thirty-four. Which sums up St. Peter's teachings on how Christians are to treat one another. Before we get to the Psalter, it is necessary, I believe, for us to confess How difficult it is to live in the manner St. Peter is here describing. It has been my experience, both as a Christian and a pastor. For years long enough to garner precious experience, that living out the instruction about how Christians are to treat one another as St. Peter describes Living out the love Saint Paul describes and being united with one another as Jesus prayed we would be is one of the hardest, if not the hardest, duties of the Christian life. The hardest is not just one of the hardest. And this we must confess, and this we must be honest about. It is much too easy today to simply walk away from a relationship in Christ. Than it is to labor to be of one mind focusing on the essentials of the faith. Easier to walk away It is hard to have compassion on someone who doesn't seem to have compassion toward you. It is hard to love another as a close friend when he or she hasn't loved you as a friend. It's hard to be tender-hearted and courteous when I want someone, anyone to be tender-hearted or courteous toward me. It is much easier, much easier to simply get away from certain Christian relationships and go find new ones and try it all over again Here is a statistic that startled me when I read it. From the Fuller Institute and Barna together. A study last year reveals that 3,500 people a day in the United States Left the church they were attending three thousand five hundred a day That is 1,246,000 people left the church they were attending last year. Because of the experience we have all had, we can guess that the majority of those left because they did not heed the words of St. Peter as we have heard them today. The world will know we are Christians, but that we are little Christs when we love one another, which includes how we work through conflicts with one another. It is likely that most of you do not know A. W. Pink. He was a British theologian that made an impact on the Christian church with his writings, especially his book entitled The Sovereignty of God. In that book, Pink argues quite persuasively about the doctrine of predestination from an ultra-Calvinist perspective. Many have read Pink's book and have come away with a new perspective on how far God's sovereignty reaches, especially into the wills of human beings that He has chosen. But Pink's ministry in the church was a lot less influential. He tried being a pastor, but he could not find a people who would follow him in the manner he insisted upon. He tried to pastor five different churches, most of them in America, with no success. He came away from his pastoral failures convinced That there are more goats in the Christian church than there are sheep. He then convinced himself that his ministry should continue in written form only. He inherited enough money to buy a home in Stornoway, Scotland, and hide away from fellow Christians and society itself. It was said of him that no one in the nearby town knew of him, only to see him take a stroll once a week through the town. When fellow Christians would travel long distances to see and speak with him, he left them disappointed, turning all visitors away. He lived alone with his wife, dying at the age of 66. His wife lived ten more years and enjoyed some travel and fellowship with other Christians. Because it was taken away from her because of her husband's attitude toward other Christians and toward the church. Such is a sad, sad tale. But all of the sad parts could have been prevented if Arthur Pink would have lived out the words given to us here by St. Peter. And so, we close this section of teaching by Peter by doing what he did. We are going to recite the passage from Psalm 34, and we're going to recite it together. We are going to do so as a pledge that we will live lives toward one another as the psalmist describes. So grab your pew Bible, New King James Version, turn with me to 1 Peter 3, beginning at verse 10, and stand with me. First Peter chapter three, beginning at verse ten, reading through verse twelve. Together, for he who would love life and see good days, let him refrain his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit. Let him turn away from evil and do good. Let him seek peace and pursue it. For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to the praise. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil. Let us pray. Father, for this standard, we ask that you would continue to enable us by the power of the Holy Spirit That we could walk in its light and its strength to overcome ourselves, that we could live out these instructions by Saint Peter, to live out the love that you have been required of your people So that we would be good testimonies to the world about who is our God, and so that we could secure our place in your heavenly home. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Estimating the Suffering of Jesus
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. Turn to your Bibles to 1 Peter chapter 3. Beginning at verse thirteen, and as the reading guided us, we'll be going through chapter four or into chapter four A couple of weeks ago, I attended the showing of the film Is Genesis History? Is Genesis history? I tended it with Mr. Mark Hammett, Mr. Dan Nevius, Mr. Josh Devers, and Mr. Larry Cavra. And I can summarize for all of us that we came away inspired, encouraged I'm much more curious regarding science and creationism than we were going in. One of the premises that the scientists operate from in the film is how the effect of the flood, as described in Genesis chapters 6 through 8, how that is understated. And this allows the scientists to operate from the theory that the sudden rise and fall of great waters That effect would have had an enormous and profound effect upon geological structures. And this theory answers more questions than does the theory of these geological structures forming over a long period. The theory of a sudden rise and sudden drop. Matthews Psalm 104. Which states to God, You laid the foundation of the earth so that it should not be moved forever. You covered it with the deep as with a garment. The waters stood above the mountains. At your rebuke they fled. At the voice of your thunder, they hastened away. They went up over the mountains. They went down into the valleys to the place that you founded for them. Now, contemplating the result of underestimating the effect of the flood and its receding waters Caused contemplation of the many things we likely underestimate in regards to God's redemption of mankind. The effect of the flood is one underestimation. And the effect of the suffering of Jesus, I believe, is another. We likely contemplate the suffering of Jesus only in light of his sacrifice. Yes, he suffered, but his death is more important in our focus. And then we leave the suffering behind. But the suffering of Jesus is everlasting. Not everlasting in terms of that it continues. For as scriptures clearly teach, Jesus died once for all. Instead, the sufferings of Jesus are everlasting in terms of what they accomplished. And in terms of how his followers, you and I, are to join ourselves to his sufferings. And before I open up that spot, I want you to walk with me through 1 Peter chapter 3 and into chapter 4. We start at verse 13, and here Peter has admonished Christians up to this point. that they are to be missionaries of the gospel in all aspects of their living, but primarily focusing on relationships that Christians have First with governing authorities, then inside the home, and then inside the church Verse 13 asks the rhetorical question that recognizes that our testimony regarding our faith, if lived out as Peter instructs, This will lessen the possibility of Christians being falsely accused of doing evil. Of course, there will always be those who will try to detour and persecute Christians, but Peter's point still stands. If you live a dutiful life, the detractors will be less But if and when there are detractors in a Christian's life that cause us to suffer Peter says we are then to consider ourselves blessed because we are suffering for the sake of righteousness. The quote from Isaiah is to remind us that God's people, down through the ages of his story of redemption have faced the same persecutions for righteousness' sake, and they persevered. Thus the conclusion. Therefore, do not be troubled by what you face in this life. Pretty simple. The next instruction is for each Christian to be ready when detractors arise in our lives and persecutions come. We are to be ready. We have to be ready with an explanation or a defense as to why we remain a people of hope even while being persecuted. Each of us then is responsible to be able to explain the faith that we have in Jesus It does not have to be an airtight defense. It does not need to be prepared for all philosophical questions that counter what we say we believe. But it must be true, as we must trust, that the Holy Spirit will take care of the rest Did not Jesus say that when his disciples would be dragged before the magistrates, that they need not worry but to say for the Holy Spirit would give them the words that they need in that hour. They need not worry, but they need to be ready. We need to be ready. Verse 17 deserves a question. The question is, why is it better to suffer for doing good than for doing evil? The answer When a Christian suffers for doing good, he suffers as Jesus did. When we suffer for doing evil, we suffer as the pagans. Thus we carry no witness with us at all. Next is an emphatic statement that Jesus suffered once and for all, which includes for all people of all time. And this goes against any doctrine that would have Jesus needing to be sacrificed repeatedly on an altar of holy communion. Jesus as the pure sacrifice was sufficient for all time and for all sins committed and yet to be committed. Again, here is a place where we can say we underestimate the sacrificial offering of Jesus. It was sufficient and more. And this leads to one of the more interesting and debatable pairs of passages in all of the New Testament, verses 19 and 20. What in the world is going on here? Verse 19 and 20 allude to a place That Jesus went after his death and apparently before his resurrection, where he was able to preach the truth Regarding who he was and what was about to be accomplished by him rising from the dead. He preached to an audience made up of sinners. Who apparently were part of the problem that caused God to flood the earth during the days of Noah. After reading for years about these verses, I have settled on the following. The audience Peter alludes to here are the sons of God, named in the book of Genesis, chapter 6. These are said to have corrupted the women on earth, bringing forth generations of men who loved evil and turned away from God. The larger debate over whether these sons of God were men or angels has caused a great deal of angst, especially when people interpret them to be angels. I'm not going to get into that. I'm not even going to guess. The important linchpin as to what Peter is referring to Has to be from the book of Enoch. You say, hey, I know my books of the Bible. That's not in the Bible. And you would be correct. The Book of Enoch is a part of the Apocrypha, which most of Protestant Bibles do not have. In the book of Enoch, it describes Enoch. You remember him from Genesis? He was and was no more, for God took him, is what the scriptures say. In the book of Enoch, it is said that Enoch went and preached the truth to the same sons of God who were in Hades or the dwelling of the dead. Peter knew that these Jewish converts coming to Christ, being in the past Jewish, knew the book of Enoch. They knew the story of Enoch. And so it appears that Peter is addressing them and proving to them who knew the story that Jesus was superior to Enoch. He was superior to Enoch in that he not only preached to the dead as Enoch did, but then he overcame death itself, as Enoch did not. That is the most sensible reading of these two verses I have come across. But Peter doesn't dwell on that point, and so we're not going to dwell on that point. Instead, Peter moves on to the flood. And how the flood is an anti-type or an opposite type of our baptism. As all of the people of the world were judged by the death of the flood waters, the baptism of Christians is the opposite, as we are forgiven and given life because of the baptismal waters. And Peter adds a reference to the removal of guilt and not the removal of flesh. And this might be linking circumcision again to baptism. Circumcision removes flesh, whereas baptism removes guilt. And this next leads Peter to combine both Jesus as superior to Enoch in his resurrection and ascension. as well as to our blessed fortune of being raised with Jesus in our baptism. Peter is mixing a lot of metaphors and analogies together. And he's keeping us Christians on our mental toes. Well, in chapter 4, Peter comes back to the subject of Christians suffering in this life. With the comparison that Christians, when they suffer, are to suffer as Jesus did, for his suffering resulted in righteousness, which includes the overcoming of the lusts of the flesh. Overcoming the lust of the flesh is what Christians are predestined to do, for men had spent many days prior to their conversion pursuing the sins of the flesh. Whereas such sins are now to be overcome. In the meantime, those who still pursue pleasures of the flesh will wonder why these Christians have turned away, why they are no longer joining in. They, in their jealousy, will speak evil of Christians who have turned away from their flesh. But in the end, those who speak evil will be judged by the Christians who live righteously. Chapter 4, verse 6 brings us back to the understanding of Jesus being greater than Enoch. As it explains that the dead, such as were preached first by Enoch and then by Jesus, will be judged by men who chose to walk by the Spirit and not by the flesh. Those who mock Christians for living righteously will be judged by the same men and women they mock. That is the end of our reading. And as a side note, after giving an overview of these verses, I contemplate how preachers are criticized for being all over the place in sermons. Well, Peter seems to be in a lot of places at once in this section of Scripture. And so we dig out the main point. The main point from all of these passages of scripture is that there is a great deal of testimony. Witness, power, hope, justice, and Christ's likeness. All of that is available for those who suffer for righteousness' sake. And that point takes us back to my first point, which is that we underestimate the power of the suffering of Jesus. This underestimating of the suffering of Jesus has by God's providence Come before us from this first letter of St. Peter, comes before us today near the release of the movie The Shack. Based on a best-selling novel from ten years ago by the same title. I don't normally address Christian novels or movies and sermons But here I am mentioning two in one sermon. I address the movie The Shack because I am aware how well the sentiments of that story mesh with modern Christian sentiments. Sentiments that I prophetically proclaim steer modern Christians away from Orthodox Christianity. For those who don't read my blog, the following is a quick setting of the story found in the shack. The story tries to show how God, the Christian God, can help a distraught and spiritually bankrupt father, his name being Mac. How they can help Mac work through the pain and find something redeeming from the horrible death of his younger daughter. His younger daughter was abducted, tortured, and killed by a serial killer as a result of the father needing to leave his young daughter alone at a campsite in order to save one of his sons from drowning. Quite a difficult scenario After four years, the father is summoned back to the shack where his daughter suffered at the hands of this serial killer. At the shack, God supposedly appears to Mack in various personal forms. In order to help him deal with not only the hellish death of his daughter, but also the abuse that Mac suffered by his own father. In the Shak, God is described as appearing as a papa or father figure, Tumak. by the personae of an overweight black woman. In other scenes, God is described as appearing as Jesus, who has the personae of a Middle Eastern male carpenter. In other scenes, God, the Holy Spirit, is described as appearing with the persona of an Asian woman named Sarayu. Any Christian with minimal exposure to Christian church history can identify that the movie commits the heresy of modalism. Modalism presents God as three different modes or visions of the Godhead as opposed to being three distinct persons, Father, Son, and Holy Ghost. But I have tried to identify an even more serious problem with how God is presented in this story, the Shack. And this serious problem dominates Western Christianity in our day. The problem is identifying our personal suffering in this life. As something that God needs to adapt to for our individual purposes. This is in contrast to the purpose of the suffering of Jesus and how our suffering in this life Is to be adapted to the suffering of Jesus and not his suffering adapted to us And who is to blame for this understanding that God needs to adapt to our suffering? We can start by blaming the health and wealth preachers as they present Jesus as some sort of vending machine. You put an offering into the slot, you pray a prayer that might be something like A5, and soon enough, Jesus, the bending machine, drops down an answered prayer that could be anything from a healing. To a new cause. And the end lesson is that God's redemptive work is about you as an individual. We could blame the modern Christian worship churches who have decided that the best form of evangelism is to market Jesus as something cool. Something that represents modernity or postmodernity or millennialism, whatever category the greatest number of consumers occupy And in this marketing strategy, Jesus and the Christian faith is like the world, but not the world. Jesus has songs that are like the top 40, but they have Christian words. The church has sermons, but with a Tony Robbins approach. So that your business runs better, your marriages are more streamlined, and you know how to meditate through a stressful day. All of it is focused on the goal of serving the individual as a consumer. The end lesson is that God's story of redemption is all about you as an individual. And we could blame the liberal churches that have a form of godliness but deny its power Such churches have redefined God by denouncing past revelations of himself and instead wanting God to be known as a God who cares. What makes you different is what God loves about you and that he is accepting of you even when your uniqueness goes against his holy law The law of God be damned, they say. The denominations of this liberal persuasion feel that the individual must feel comfortable in his individualism. And that's what matters. The end lesson is that God's story of redemption is all about you, the individual. We could even blame the conservative Christians, for although they believe God's law and all of Scripture to be God's word, and thus necessary to believe, in all of its revelation. They merely stand by in a neutral gear, not saying anything that would challenge the false teachings of all these other groups who call themselves Christians. They allow so-called Christians to conclude that God's story of redemption is about the individual. Of course, blaming someone else never accomplishes anything. The first blame was Adam blaming Eve, and that didn't help. Instead, what we can learn and use from Peter's teaching about suffering is that as we suffer in this life, We are to more fully identify with Jesus and his suffering. As we suffer for righteousness, we are becoming more and more like him. He doesn't need to further adapt to us because of our suffering. His adaptation was more than an adaptation. It was an incarnation. And that was for eternity as he is now and forever human like us. And that reality then calls us to be conformed to be like him. If we embrace suffering as a vehicle or a means by which we become more and more like Him, then our suffering will never be in vain. If we suffer only to expect God to accommodate to our situation, we remain the same, and our suffering is an empty endeavor. As the false and lying spirit of the age tells you that in your suffering Jesus adapts to identify with you. The Holy Spirit tells us that in your suffering, you are to adapt, to identify with Jesus. Jesus has already identified with us in everything. It is now for us to identify with Him. So that as we do, our identity is more and more like him and less and less of ourselves. A man who saves his life will lose it. But a man who loses his life will save it in the end. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Covenant Childrearing
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Принудь, привет, связанный голодный. I think that's the first time. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. Today we are veering away from our study of 1 Peter because of the occasion of a covenant child being baptized And yes, because it's my grandchild, I get to veer off. But first a riddle. A riddle. An Arab sheikh tells his two sons to race their camels to a distant city to see who will inherit his fortune. The catch was that the one whose camel is the slower will win and receive the fortune. What to do. After wandering aimlessly for days, because neither wanted to be first, the brothers ask a wise man for guidance Upon receiving advice, they jumped on the camels and raced to the city as fast as they could. What did the wise man say to the two brothers? Hopefully that riddle will keep you awake the entire sermon. If Jesus of Nazareth died and rose again from the dead, Everything changes. Every priority for every human being changes if Jesus was dead and then alive. You want evidence? Empirical evidence? What do you need? We have eyewitnesses, not just the apostles. Jesus being alive after dying on the cross was seen by over 500 people. You want historical evidence? The claim of Jesus having overcome death was never publicly disputed by any person of the first century. There was every chance for the people to debunk the story of Jesus rising from the dead, from Jews and Gentiles alike. They could have simply gone to the dead body of Jesus and said, here is his body. He's obviously not risen from the dead. Now you followers can stop your claims But no one did that because his body was no longer in the grave. So if Jesus did rise from the dead and then Everything he taught is true. Every law that God gave was fulfilled in him. Every hope for humanity is found in him. And every priority we have in life is going to need Jesus to be first place. And the greatest priority we have given to us Is our children. Some of you grew up like me where going to church and believing in God is just what you did. It was very much like being an American. You were born in America. You were taught the great history of the United States, and you identified yourself as an American. Along with everyone else that you went to school with and that you played with in the sand lot. It's just who you were. You were an American. And going to church was part of that. Of course you believed in God. You said, one nation under God every day at school during the Pledge of Allegiance. It appears that for many of us, we were raised to believe in God in the parental style of osmosis. Our parents seem to have the child-raising strategy of putting us in the environment of other people who believed in God, and we were to simply soak in those same beliefs by being present in the midst of others who thought and lived in the same manner. But religious faith can become habitual. You can easily go through the motions without there being any true belief, no true faith within you. Remember that God rebuked Israel for doing the same, for going through the motions. In fact, he even told them through the prophets that he didn't want their rituals and their sacrifices. And he was the one who gave them the very rituals and sacrifices he no longer wanted. He didn't want them because the people's hearts were not in it. The rituals were not the problem. The hearts of the people were the problem. They were performing religious ceremony out of habit and maybe even superstition. As have many who consider themselves religious. And going through the motions can sustain some sort of faith for a while, but soon another generation grows up. and says that they are tired of the ritual and they want something real for themselves. And so many walk away from their parents' faith. Well, instead of parenting by osmosis, there is another type of parents who have for themselves a living faith in God. They pray daily. They study their Bibles. They worship Jesus as their Savior corporately on a weekly basis. They model a God-fearing life to their children, and they raise their children with the hope and with prayers that their children will someday come to a faith in Jesus. And yet they have said hope with the understanding that the decision is completely up to the child. And this approach to child rearing is quite inconsistent because the child is told that he or she can make a decision to follow Jesus whenever he or she wants to But in the meantime, the parents are going to teach the child how to pray, read Bible stories for the child to believe. But how can the child pray when his or her prayers to be heard, she or he must be a believer. And she or he hasn't made the decision to be a believer And how can the Bible stories have any value if the child does not have the Holy Spirit to guide him into all the truth of the Bible? And so sometimes the child is treated as a believer, and sometimes she is not. And again, it appears to be all up to the child. And notice how odd such a parenting approach is when a parent will tell the same child when he or she should go to bed. or eat his vegetables, or that she should brush her teeth. Those behaviors aren't a choice. But to believe in God is a choice. The obvious question is if eating one's vegetables is important enough to demand it of a child, isn't believing in God even more important? Then there's something a child should be Forced to do, make their own decision, getting ahead of myself Another type of parenting does not so much concern itself with waiting for the child to believe in God, but instead waits for God to give faith to the child. Such parents place so much reverence in the doctrine of predestination that they raise their child with the curiosity as to whether God has chosen the child to be saved or to be damned. Let's see. Such parents model the Christian life to their children, but they don't want to presume upon God's will that their child is a part of the chosen people. These parents point their children to the right way to believe, but seem willing to accept that if their children do not believe, if they choose to live a life of debauchery, oh well Such was according to God's will, and there was nothing we could have done to change it. I trust you can see that each of these parenting approaches I have described, each of them is wanting. There is a great importance missing in each of them, and yet such are the primary parenting approaches within Christian homes. That you will find today and have been practiced, dare I say, for several generations. The question that needs to be asked Is there a biblical model for raising children to believe in God all of their days? Is there a model that works? And by works, I mean that their children actually believe and grow up in the faith always. The answer is yes. And none of the parenting approaches I have described fit that model. The biblical model, the only manner of child rearing that is consistent with what God has revealed has been called covenant child rearing. Covenant child rearing. Covenant child rearing doesn't raise children by osmosis by just being around God-fearing people with the hope that the child soaks in that environment and becomes a good person. Covenant childbearing does not put hope in a child making a decision to believe in Jesus, for no child has the fortitude or has the wisdom to make such a decision for his or herself. Covenant child rearing doesn't wait to see if God is going to give the child faith and merely shrug the shoulders if the child rejects. No, covenant child rearing is loving, teaching, training, modeling, guiding, and doing everything. within a parent's capacity to ensure a child born into a Christian home knows nothing other than loving God and trusting in Jesus as their heavenly hope. Remember, if Jesus has risen from the dead, then everything must be different, including and in particular how we raise our children. Covenant child learning is Christian parents raising their children as if the salvation of their children is their responsibility. It is raising children to believe in God and to trust in Jesus as their Savior, in the revelation that God is a God of promise, and God fulfills his promises. Consider that when God proclaimed the curse upon Eve, for believing the words of the serpent rather than believing the words of God. In that curse, God made a promise. He promised that the seed of the woman that is Her descendants, from her descendants would come a son who would crush the serpent's head And of course the promise was fulfilled in Jesus, who was born of the Virgin Mary, who stomped the head of the serpent, the devil, while overcoming death. God is a God of promise. A major part of God fulfilling his promises were those that he made to Abraham, who would be the father of many nations. Not just the father of Israel, but of many nations. And although Abraham only had two sons as his descendants, the promises of God made to Abraham were many, many, many people Connected to Abraham as his descendants, not just by blood only, but by faith. Yes, many have been born in the line of Abraham, who are now Jewish people and Arabic people. But St. Paul explained to us that the faith of Abraham that he had in God That was awarded to him as righteousness. And then Paul says that the same faith Abraham had in trusting in God's promises is the same Christian faith that you and I have, that Jesus is our Savior. And thus we are all children of Abraham because we believe that Jesus is the fulfillment of the promises God made to Abraham and Abraham's descendants. God is a God of promises fulfilled. God being a God of promise Commanded Abraham and his descendants to be given a sign of the promises. The sign was circumcision. Such a sign not every ordinary man would choose. But God wanted his people to be separate from the pagan tribes around them and to no longer worship false gods. God wanted his people to be marked as his and not another. But there was also another reason God commanded circumcision. He knew that the real trouble of humanity was the problem of the heart. It is the heart that is cold and hard against God. And so the circumcision became a symbol of the promise that God would cut away the stone that covers the heart of humanity and give people hearts that beat freely. And it was then revealed in the promises made by Jesus, who said that Abraham saw his day and was glad. It was the promise of Jesus that said, excuse me, that people who confessed their sin and confessed him as the Son of God and were baptized in the triune name of God that said people would be given hearts. That beat freely. And so baptism. Water baptism became the symbol of God's promise to set his people free, free of heart. It was Jesus who said that a person must be born of water and the Holy Spirit to enter his kingdom. It was St. Paul who brought circumcision and baptism together when he said to the Church of Colossae, In him, Jesus, You were also circumcised with a circumcision not performed by human hands. Your whole self, ruled by the flesh, was put off when you were circumcised by Christ. having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the working of God who raised him from the dead. It was natural for the Jews who had converted to follow Jesus, for them to have their children baptized. With the promises of Jesus, just as they had their children circumcised with the promises of the Father, so they had their children baptized with the promises of Jesus. And when you add the ministry of Jesus who called children to come unto him and to bless them, and when Jesus healed the sick child of the centurion and healed the sick child of a gentile woman, We learn of the heart that our Savior has towards children. And then when Jesus instructs his disciples to be witnesses, To first to Jerusalem, and then to Judea, and then to Samaria, and then to the uttermost parts of the world. We see a principle of starting first with those closest to you. And there was no one closer to us that we are to disciple, to train, to become a believer in Jesus. There is no one closer than our own children. After all, did not the prophet Joel say that the promises of God were for our children and our children's children? Yes, he did. Children born into a home where his or her parents are believers in Christ Jesus are covenant children. They are covenant children because they are born into the covenant that God has with the child's parents. And a major part of covenant means promise. God has made promises for our children and for our children's children. And it is for us to keep the covenant alive. By doing our part, which is to purposefully train our children to know Jesus and to believe in Jesus and to have never a never-ending faith in Jesus And this next point is just as important, if not more, for them to pass their faith to their children. Their children to their children. Not by osmosis, not by hoping the child makes the right decision, not by waiting to see if God gives faith to the child. No. It is by training the child, each child, in the way he or she should go. And the way each child should go is to believe in the Lord God with all of his heart, soul, mind, and strength. It is to confess Jesus has risen, he is risen indeed. And such teaching and training must go against all odds and overcome all enemies which are in the world and of the devil. The enemies of God want our children, instead of believing, to be wasting away in a drug house, or blaspheming God in a courthouse, or living by their fleshly desires in a frat house. But the greatest most effective enemy or tactic of the enemy that I have witnessed as a pastor is not the dangers that lie outside the home, but rather inside. The greatest deterrent that would cause a covenant child to turn away from the faith in Jesus is to be a witness to hypocrisy in his or her parents. It is not that a child will witness his or her parents' sin, that's going to happen and happen a lot. No, the deterrent that is hypocrisy is when a professing believer in Jesus does not own up to their sins, does not admit when he or she is wrong, does not model repentance and confession. Many times the greatest testimony a parent can display to a child is humility and the receiving of God's forgiveness. Well beloved, what you have heard today is my heart. It's what God put in me when He called me to be a father the first time. is what he put in me when he called me to be a pastor. So tired of seeing Christian families have their children walk out the door of the church never to come back. Why? Why? Does it have to be? And God's word says no All of this is why I made my sons still think that I gave them stupid rules that would not allow them to date as their peers dated. It was why we started the academy. It was why we monitored and prayed desperately over each child's high school choices and college choices. It's why we started the college boot camps, why we stay up late with a son or a daughter who is fighting off the devil. It is why we continue to prod and plead for our children to be earnest about the manner they raise their own children. It is why I rejoice today at the baptism of Jameson. Remember, if Jesus has been raised from the dead, everything changes. Oh, the riddle. What did the wise man say to the two brothers who were trying to figure out How to come in second place in order to gain their father's fortune? What did he say? He said to them, switch camels. Christian parents need to change camels and run the race to win. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Suffering? Serve the Church
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. You will be well served to turn to First Peter chapter four. Beginning at verse seven, covering a good deal of material this morning. First Peter four, verse seven. It has been over a four-year battle that not many of us have paid much attention to other than Feeling sorry for those fellow Christians who have been sued. Sued for not making wedding cakes or not catering For homosexual weddings, weddings, so-called. Or not being a photographer at such weddings, so called. In 2013, Melissa and Aaron Klein, owners of sweetcakes, by Melissa Cited religious beliefs when they refused to bake a wedding cake for Laurel and Rachel Baumann Cryer. The homosexuals, Laurel and Rachel, were awarded damages in July of 2015 by the Oregon Labor Commissioner for emotional suffering saying the owners had violated the women's civil rights by discriminating on the basis of sexual orientation. They were also slapped with a gag order that prohibited them from speaking publicly about their refusal to participate in or bake wedding cakes for same-sex marriages. Tough on them. Tough on a family bakery in Colorado, facing the same charges. Tough on another family bakery in Texas going through something similar. Tough on a photographer in New Mexico. And then in the spring of this last year, I became aware of a late-night comedy show on a major television network. Who did a parody called A Small Town Baker, where a Christian woman refuses to make a wedding cake for a homosexual couple. The Christian baker is then sued with the goal, to be funny, with the goal of the plaintiff dropping the suit if the Christian bakery owner will simply say that God is gay. The portrayed Christian in the skit then sets out to prove that God is not gay, he's straight, and so in doing so they commit vulgar language to describe God's sexual desires. Evidently, some people laugh. Such parodies can be helpful to the Christian church if we get to see how the secular world views us. It can be helpful to get a glimpse of how we are displaying ourselves to the unbelieving world. Of course, betrayals like this will fall short. But what seems to be consistent is that many unbelievers view Christians view Christians as too serious We are not relaxed enough about our convictions. We can't seem to have fun If the critics with such charges attended a Christian wedding, a winter ball, or just a family getting together to tell stories I'm guessing the charge of Christians not having fun could be debunked quite easily. But the charge would also remain because it's an easy critique As if being critiqued for being too serious isn't enough. Here Christians are charged by Saint Peter to be serious. In your New King James Version, 1 Peter reads, But the end of all things is at hand, therefore be serious and watchful in your prayers. And yes, the grammar of the charge is focused on being serious in our prayers because the end is near, but Peter has been serious in this whole epistle. He wants us to be serious, you remember, about our missionary work with our everyday vocations. He wants us to be missionaries in our homes, and he even wants us to do mission-type work in the church. And then he instructs us on how to suffer properly. And it is not near possible not to take suffering seriously. In our suffering, we are to identify with the suffering of Jesus. And then we are to identify with him in overcoming sins of the flesh. All which must be done in a very serious manner. So it seems that Christians are to be serious by their very nature. By the nature of our calling to be separate from the world, to be like Christ Jesus in our daily living, we need to be serious. And in the context Peter is in, when he writes such instructions, being serious was an absolute necessity. The necessity comes from Peter understanding that the end of all things, he says, is at hand. And it is accepted interpretation by faithful Bible readers and scholars that the first century Christians believed that the return of Jesus would occur in their lifetime. So Peter could very well mean that he believed that the end of time was near, and therefore Christians ought to be serious about all aspects of their life. But there is a different, plausible interpretation of Peter's warning. Jesus not only prophesied, you remember, regarding his second coming, he prophesied about the fall or destruction of Jerusalem. And we know by our dates from history that as Peter was writing, the end of Jerusalem and the destruction of the temple was very close at hand. And for the Jews of Jerusalem, some of the Christians to whom Peter was writing, to them, the end of all things as they had known them was about to come to an end. And again, another event in Scripture that we underestimate in its influence is the destruction of Jerusalem. I was just made aware in my studies this week that a great deal of the Roman Colosseum, in the part that still stands today. was funded by Rome sacking the city of Jerusalem and stealing the values from the temple. Peter very well could have been referring to the imminent fall of Jerusalem when he refers to the end being near, for the destruction of Jerusalem was a big deal. And so what of us? What big deal is going on around us Is there anything going on in the world that should make the life of Christians more earnest and thus more serious? Another news story that seemed not many Christians have noted as a concern was that two street preachers in Britain who were recently convicted by a court of law for being a public offense because they quoted parts of the King James Bible. They were arrested by officers who considered their language abusive and criminal. And in case you might think that the words that they were espousing off were purposefully foul The main prosecutor argued that the preachers were saying that Jesus was the only way to God, and that such a pronouncement is considered hate speech by people of other faiths. Should such a story concern us, is there need for us to be serious Professor Daniel Philpot at the University of Notre Dame recently identified Christian persecution in the modern Western world. He called it polite persecution. Polite persecution in the West says to Christians, if you don't think like us If you don't vote like us, if you don't condemn like us, then you will lose your job, your social standing, your overall relevance in society. There are no laws that need to be passed against Christians. There is no need to give them any type of identity tags that say they are Christian. The persecution simply needs to be at the hands of bureaucrats and bosses and judges, public officials. Students, fellow employees, these will all inform who should be fired, who should be fined, who should be shunned, who should be shut down and ignored. Ignored until Christians don't matter in society. And I can sound like an unnecessary alarmist If I say that such persecution is happening now and that it will get worse. But the stories of family bakeries and street preachers are very real and very close to home. In the context of our contemporary setting of polite persecution, let us jump ahead in St. Peter's epistle here to hear his instruction. In verse 14, he says, if you are reproached for the name of Christ, blessed are you, for the spirit of glory and of God rests upon you. And in verse 16, yet if anyone suffers as a Christian, let him not be ashamed, but let him glorify God in this matter. The qualifier in both verses is that the suffering for which Christians are blessed and are to give glory to God for are sufferings that come because of Christians Living out their Christian lives. To suffer as a Christian is to suffer because you are a Christian And the life you lead as a Christian becomes an offense to someone around you. And Peter wants us to differentiate between sufferings that are brought about by our own sins and sufferings that occur because we are Christians. A person who calls himself Christian and yet is a murderer or a thief or a person who practices evil doings or simply becomes a busybody concerning himself with everyone else's business and stirring up trouble. These are not to be identified as suffering with Jesus. Most certainly not identifying with Jesus suffering. I believe Peter is being hyperbolic when he says that suffering because of an act of murder should not be considered suffering as Jesus did. And he is allowing a long range of sins that could be included between being a murderer and a busybody. The point being that to suffer because of your own moral failings or sinful habits is not suffering in the manner Peter is addressing in this epistle. If we suffer the consequences for our sins, those sufferings are deserved and are likely necessary to bring about repentance and better minds. A Christian can feel that nobody likes me, everybody hates me, and I might as well eat some worms. But it is likely because such a person is being a jerk, and people are simply responding to him being a jerk. Again, the sufferings Peter is concerned about is a suffering for being a Christian. And by being a Christian, he means living out the Christian life. Our study of First Peter comes at an interesting time in certain Christian circles. Three books have been released recently, three books that attempt to show how Christians are to respond to days in which the Christian faith has not only been labeled as politically incorrect But a faith that needs to be shouted down and then discarded on the trash heap of history's marginal worldviews. The one book is by the writer-blogger Rod Durr, who has journeyed in his Christian faith from evangelical theology to Roman Catholicism and now Eastern Orthodoxy. Another book was written by Roman Catholic bishop and scholar by the last name of Sheput. And the third book was written by Catholic scholar and professor Anthony Eswin. And what is interesting about all these three books at the same time is that all of these authors agree that the task for the Christian church today is the creation of a distinctive Christian culture. Distinctive amid the ruins of what each of them say is the lost American Republic experiment. All agree that a recovery of America's greatness is secondary to the first goal. The first goal being the church to build up Christian communities that are separate from the corrupt social orders of today. Well, there is no time in this sermon to unpack each of these writers' thesis, and I don't want to misrepresent their arguments. What I do want is for Peter, Saint Peter, to have some words into this discussion, into this climate that is politically I'm sorry, that politely persecutes Christians. Well, we have already noted that St. Peter wants Christians to be serious and watchful in their prayers. You are to be watchful and anticipating that events of persecution will take place. You are to be serious because the persecutions will not be light, even though they are polite. This is the devil pushing back, and the devil pushes back. And so what are Christians to do? Well, St. Peter next instructs that in the midst of suffering, politely or not, that Christians are to concern themselves about loving one another. And the love Peter refers to here is not that phileo. Love we talked about from chapter 2 This love instructed here is agape. It's unconditional. It's it's the origin the love origin from God, originated from God It is God's love to be expressed Christian to Christian with the end result, he says, of sin being covered. Covered a metaphor for forgiven. And we say, okay, Peter again talking about love and love Christians need for one another. But notice the end primary goal. Christians are to forgive one another. Withholding forgiveness holds the church back. That from being an effective witness to the unbelieving world around us. Your individual unwillingness to forgive holds the church back. Any bitterness, envy, and strife occurring in the Christian church is the result of Christians withholding forgiveness for other Christians. And the answer, or the only thing that will overcome withholding forgiveness, is practicing love toward one another. But what is practical loving of one another? Well, St. Peter says that Christians are to be hospitable to one another. Hospitality is a frontline way to practice love, Christian to Christian When a person or family practices hospitality, it is realized that a person is investing in another person, and the result is that, lo and behold, we start to care about each other And the more Christians care about one another, the more they love one another. But hospitality is not easy. And because it is not easy, St. Peter adds, without grumbling. He adds that clause because he knows the fallen nature of humanity. Christian or not. What we struggle with inside. We struggle to die to ourself. And being hospitable is dying to self. By being more concerned about the needs and the personalities of others than your own. And after speaking about hospitality, St. Peter next adds that Christians are to use their spiritual gifts to minister to one another. And again, such is Christian loving one another. Each of us, a steward of what God has given us, gifts to express to one another. There is the gift of a stronger faith that some have over others. There is the gift of workmanship with the hands, the gift of coordinating events. The gift of industrious labor, the gift of organization, the gift of friendship, the gift of teaching, the gift of artistry, the gift of service, the gift of building, of repairing. of patience. The list is seemingly endless as to what Christians are to contribute to the church and to their fellow Christians. And each of us is to be responsible for the gifts we have been given, responsible to use them toward one another. And speaking of needed gifts, the last described is the ability to speak publicly the Word of God. God's primary means of spreading the gospel is preaching the Word, preaching Jesus. And men who are gifted to do so are to speak the gospel, the words of Jesus, with every confidence. That what is being spoken is God's word. The Christian church needs men who will speak the word of God the word of God without flinching. Amen. The end of verse 11 summarizes all that St. Peter has instructed regarding what Christians are to be doing. Regarding living out their faith. And it is interesting that the focus is what Christians should do within the church. And what is done in the church is what brings the most glory to God. I did not anticipate that such would be how Peter would want Christians to deal with suffering. Work in the church. But here it is. I've tried to bring together all of these instructions in this section of scripture So that they remain in the context of what the church is to be doing while it suffers, politely or not. And I have perceived Saint Peter in a scenario of a conversation. As a wise old man who would talk to a young whippersnapper about the following events, politely being persecuted. The young whippersnapper says to St. Peter, hey, St. Pete, we are being persecuted here because of our Christian lives. Because we have stood against falsehood and we are getting mistreated for it. Tell us what we should do And old wise Saint Pete says, Well, I can appreciate what you're going through. Tell you what, the first thing you need to do is pray. Pray in seriousness and in watchfulness. Well, the young whippersnapper gets a little impatient. with that answer. And so he explains to St. P that Christians today are mobilized. We are we are energized. We're ready to take a stand. And St. Pete says, well, I can appreciate how you are feeling, so what you need to do is work on loving one another. That will be a great weapon against polite persecution. In fact, old St. P says, work on loving one another and provide hospitality toward one another. Such is frontline love. Well that answer makes the young whippersnapper even more impatient, and so he tries to explain that Christians today are ready to fight We've got legislation we can get passed. We've got protests we can organize and people to march about Our lather is up. And say peanut stands again the emotion that is being communicated. And so he advises a way even more love can be practiced, Christian to Christian, which is using our gifts to serve one another. The young whippersnapper now is sorry he even asked old St. Pete anything at all. It's obvious that Saint Peter does not appreciate our modern predicament as Christians And so as the young whippersnapper starts to walk away, St. Pete adds, one more to combat this polite persecution. He tells the young Christian that those who preach the gospel are to do so with the confidence and authority that they are speaking God's very words. And as they do, God will be glorified. Such is the same strategy the prophets used, the same strategy of John the Baptist. The same strategy of Jesus of Nazareth, the same strategy that Peter used on the day of Pentecost. So the young whippersnapper has a choice, and so does the contemporary Christian Church We can do as the Jews did, rise up when we're being persecuted, only to find that we are defeated and dispersed. Or we can do as Saint Peter did, as Saint Paul did, as Jesus taught. We can live out our Christian lives with faithfulness and commitment and leave the outcome to the Heavenly Father. It's worked before. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Leaving it up to George
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Vitor, Vitor Olhos In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. Turn your Bibles to First Peter. First Peter chapter five. Allow me to begin with a commercial. Are you feeling lost? Searching for meaning You need a change. Online ordination Through the Universal Life Church opens doors to a fresh start in your life. A ULC ordination is completely legal throughout most of the U. S. And increasingly internationally. The Universal Life Church offers a number of helpful tools that can help you expand your ministry and your mind. As you explore their website, you'll find a great deal of content designed to train you as a minister. Aid you in performing better ceremonies and help you to navigate and understand your world The Universal Life Church Monastery, also known as the ULC, has been serving our online church community for over 40 years. Our fundamental tasks are to promote freedom of religion and to do that which is right. Core tenets that underscore everything we do. The ULC appeals to a worldwide audience through our online church services and our overarching belief that we are all children of the same universe. Over 20 million ministers worldwide have become ordained with the Universal Life Church. The ULC is open to people of all faiths, offering everyone the religious freedom to become an ordained minister and to practice your beliefs. Those who get ordained with the ULC are empowered to take control of their own spiritual lives and to do good in their own worlds. As a minister, you have the authority to perform weddings, funerals, baptisms, or even start your own ministry. Join the active ULC community by completing your free online ordination. I took the challenge. I answered the call. And here is proof. I am an ordained minister in the Universal Life Church. I can now preside over weddings, funerals, bar mitzvahs, baptisms, and I also had my dog become ordained. George Jorgensen was an ordained minister. He also can preside over weddings, funerals, barmitmas. And you can reach us at the same number. That my dog and I can be ordained by the click of the computer button doesn't make me feel all that well about my three years in seminary What is the cause of ordained ministry becoming so poorly respected that it takes barely any effort at all to become an ordained minister? I cannot think of any other profession that so easily allows people to become certified or licensed. Even professions that pay minimum wage insist on some type of training. You cannot flip hamburgers without some training. You cannot sweep floors without some training. But evidently you can preside over weddings with no training at all. According to the Fuller Institute and the George Barna Group, a recent survey revealed that the profession of pastor Is near the bottom of a survey of the most respected professions. It was just above car salesman. Over 1,700 Christian pastors leave the ministry in the United States each month. On average, 4,000 new churches are started each year, while 7,000 close their doors. It has been many, many years since the Christian church was respected in local communities and the pastors were community leaders. I did some research, found these articles on August 12, 1883. August 12, 1883, a featured article In the Daily Ocean Newspaper in Chicago, Illinois, there appeared for the purpose of explaining the distinctiveness of a new denomination, an article about the Reformed Episcopal Church. On October 28, 1901, on page 20 of the Brooklyn Daily Eagle There appeared an article that reported that the Reformed Episcopal Church was not going to reunite with the Protestant Church until changes had been made in the Episcopal Church. That was considered important news. Even as recently as nineteen ninety-three, there was a positive article in a Delaware newspaper reporting the ordination of a pastor into the Reformed Episcopal Church in New Jersey These proved that there were years gone by when most anything good that would happen in a local community from the Christian church was considered newsworthy to the surrounding community. Now, what is newsworthy is scandal, especially sexual abuse and sexual misconduct What is news is a television preacher claiming that God wants him to own a private jet. If there is a primary cause for why the pastoral office of the Christian church is looked down upon in our culture today, we need look no further than the church itself. Peter told us in chapter 4 that judgment begins in the house of God. And so it does in regards to the pastoral office. Being called pastor has become a byword for hypocrite, a title to scoff at. We need not blame the devil for this. We must blame ourselves and thus confess our sins and turn away from unrighteousness. Men of the colour must recommit themselves to live holy lives, holy lives for the sake of the gospel itself, for the gospel first and foremost. And if a man will not repent, then he should resign and get out of the way. Churches must insist upon leaders with good reputations. And churches must have the courage to discipline men who sin against their calling. Before I continue along this line, I want you to turn with me to what St. Peter instructs in those four verses of chapter 5. And there, of course, he's addressing what it means to be called an elder of the church In 1 Peter 5, verse 1, Peter uses the word elders to refer to men who are serving as officers in the church. And I use the word officers meaning men who have been ordained to the work of the ministry It is good to remember that Peter is not writing to one physical church, but many churches, and thus the plural elders he's writing to. The word in the Greek, as you might know, is presbyter, and it is used in St. Paul's letters to pastors. as a title designated for men assigned by the apostles themselves to do the work of pastors When referencing the men who officially minister in the church, Peter then refers to himself as one of them. And this is a very humble posture for Peter to take. Remember, he was an apostle and a leader of the apostles. He was of the inner circle with Jesus. And yet he wants to be considered one of them. Peter wants those who pastor to see him as their peer. Then Peter confirms his apostolic position with the referencing of himself being an eyewitness to the sufferings of Jesus. And that mention seems to prompt him to remember the words of Jesus. That whatever a person suffers for Jesus on this earth that will be returned to them in an uncountable way regarding the glory they will experience in heaven. In other words, the suffering we endure in this life will be all worth it and much more. The instruction for the presbyters or the contraption priests, we shouldn't be offended by that word, the instruction is to shepherd the flock. Of course, Jesus used the image of a shepherd and of sheep several times when he described his own ministry. He was that shepherd that went out and found that one lost sheep and carried him back to the fold. He was the shepherd that was opposite the hireling. The hireling runs away. Jesus was the shepherd who stayed and died for the sake of his flock. As shepherds, presbyters, priests, are not to serve the sheep out of compulsion, the New King James says, but willingly. Not out of compulsion, but willing. If a man serves by compulsion, he does not have an inner call of the Holy Spirit and therefore would serve but by his own strength. And a man who serves by his own strength doesn't last very long. A man serves by compulsion. He is serving because others have pressured him to serve. Other men have called him rather than God. And that again falls short. Such a scenario would be a man building his ministry on the strength of other men and himself, and again, it would not be fruitful. To serve out a compulsion in St. Peter's Day would be to give your life as an offering For it was the leaders of that crazy Jewish sect called Christians. The leaders were the first targets for the persecution. So instead of compulsion, elders are to heed the call Willingly. And willingly would include having an idea of what you are facing when you take the call. It did not take long for the first century Christians to understand the cost, the cost that they needed to pay if and when they followed Jesus. And even though Christians today don't face near the persecution that Christians did in the first century, there is always a necessary counting of the cost for anyone who puts on a collar. The cost, again, just for a general disciple, is that we all die to ourselves. And for the minister, that's even more. The pastor is called to die to himself in an even greater stint. And where Jesus says that all who follow him must pick up their cross, the pastor picks up a cross that's significantly heavier. And you have known me long enough to conclude that I don't say that to boast or to get any sympathy. It's just an obvious reality. And my best advice I give to anyone who desires to serve the church as an ordained minister is that he must be at a place mentally and emotionally that would cause him to conclude that he can do nothing else because the word of God burns within him If he would do something else, he would never be at peace because he was not being the man God was calling him to be. Any doubts, any doubts at all, and the caller should not be pursued. Next, a Presbyter priest is not to be in the office if he is pursuing financial gain. This warning should not surprise us, for whenever there are people who are open to God, they are also vulnerable to men. And greedy men take advantage of the vulnerable. And greedy men can take all shapes and sizes and put on all different types of uniforms, and the worst being a collar. As a man of the caller, everything is to be done as a representative of Christ. And when a man takes advantage of a widow's might, he blasphemes the name of Christ. He discredits the office he swore to uphold, and he silences the church's testimony of the gospel. The world turns a deaf ear to a hypocrite. Such a man may as well have a millstone tied around his neck and be thrown into the depth of water so that he drowns instead of becoming a scourge upon the body of Christ. Now in a positive sense we are told that the minister must serve eagerly That is a positive for a presbyter, a priest, to serve eagerly is to serve for the sake of the work itself. It is to believe firmly that the ministry being done is the most important thing a man can be called to do. And therefore it is satisfying because the call cannot be any greater. And yet while a minister may feel at times that his own cross is heavier, he is also a man who receives great perks. He gets to be with couples at their most joyous times, such as preparing for marriage, presiding over weddings. Also the great joy of celebrating a child being born into a covenant home, followed by baptism, followed by confirmations. A minister finds it a great privilege to share in such joys in families' lives. And he shares in times of awe, in times of great meaning, such as at the bedside of an ill person, a loved one. At the deathbed of a saint, at the graveside of a life that profoundly touched many people Such moments allow a minister to eagerly, eagerly serve the church. Uh my next instruction is for presbyters, priests, to not lord over God's people, but to be examples to them as they are sheep. The nature of a sheep is to follow, and they best follow in herds and in step as opposed to being pulled along A godly older woman said to me many years ago now, before I became pastor here. She said, remember that God's people are sheep, not cattle. Don't drive them, but lead them. Such wisdom could not be better spoken. To lord over is to lead by force. And while doing so, forgetting that you are leading a people who have weaknesses as fallen human beings and a people who have rights. As children of the king. The instruction to not lord over God's people reveals the inherent temptation within the office of a presbyter, the temptation to love the power over people. Leadership in all circles tempts a leader to love power. For a Christian minister, the temptation to love power can be perceived even greater because the authority is of God. And people need to fear God. And the temptation to love power was the reason why St. Paul instructed that presbyters should not be new converts. The temptation to pride is too great if you're seeing yourself elevated over others who have been believers for many years. Power can indeed corrupt, and power within the church can corrupt leadership and the reputation of Christ Himself. Excuse me. I was doing pretty well so far. Well The need for humility is evident, and we will talk more extensively about that next week For now, we need to underline that a presbyter presbyter is to show God's people an example. A minister of the gospel must exemplify to the people he shepherds that the church and his ministry is not about him. It is to always be about the gospel first. It is to be about bringing glory to Jesus first and last. And if such is the focus, the humility of a presbyter will be duly noted. I see it as necessary that we conclude our study of Peter's instructions regarding the office of presbyter, of priest, in the church. With examining ourselves to how we treat the office. Consider these challenging rhetorical questions. Do men who hold the office of presbyter, of priest aspire to the office? To treat it with necessary fear and trembling? Do we treat God's people as ministers with care and gentle leadership that sheep need? in order to remain safely within the herd? Do we serve eagerly by finding what we do to be a great privilege as opposed to a great burden? Do we resist the temptation to lord our authority over God's people? Do we strive to be examples of humility to young and old alike? And then for you as parishioners, do you as parishioners uphold the office of priest, of presbyter as an honorable position Not based on the men who hold the position, but that God ordained the office himself Do you use your pastor as a spiritual father who is placed in your life by God to be God's voice to you when needed? Do you uphold the office of deacon, presbyter, and bishop so that your sons aspire to be so? In your dreams as parents, do you hope that your son will become a priest as much as you hope he becomes a professional sports star? Consider that restoring the reputation of the Christian church within communities has to include restoring our respect for the office of pastor. And that restoring begins in the church. In nineteen forty A book titled One Foot in Heaven was published. It was written by Hartzell Spence, a son of a pastor. His father, William Spence, had an undergraduate degree, and he had just finished four years of medical school, planning on becoming a physician Before he attended a revival and heard the call of God in his life to become a pastor. William Spence served God in the Methodist denomination. back when the Methodists believed the Bible to be the Word of God. And Hartzell Spence tells of the many humorous stories that occurred while his father served many different parishes, moving essentially every three years. And although the stories of the ministry of William Spence are interesting, and his son is a good storyteller, they're not all that unique. Any son or daughter of a preacher could tell many stories of sacrifice, heartache, triumph, peculiarity, all that occur within a pastoral ministry. The trouble the church has today is not that is that many young people do not aspire to the office. But that is the fault of the church, and that's the fault of the home.
