And the result is many mainline denominations being fooled by God's silence. When it comes to false teaching, the church must take the advice of Deputy Party Five When it comes to false teaching, nip it. Nip it in the bud. May God have mercy, that we are never fooled by his silence. Instead, we will fear the Lord. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Resist Evil, Receive the Holy Spirit
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.source_file: Resist Evil, Receive the Holy Spirit.txt
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. You be seated. We are in Second Peter chapter two, our epistle reading for this morning. And I will be going through that section of Scripture verse by verse in a few moments. We continue our study of 2 Peter, having established in our minds That false teachers have always been a threat to the Christian Church, and having established that false teachers will be judged by God Which is to say, they will be condemned by God just as surely as God has condemned evil and evil men in the past. And that brings us to his next point, St. Peter's next point stressed, which is That evil exists in the world, and that evil is expressed in people, and therefore evil people exist in the world. But why does St. Peter need to make such a point that evil exists and evil people exist? Isn't that obvious? Both obvious The honest answer to that question is no. It is not obvious to all that evil exists and that evil people exist. There are times when cultures redefine good and evil so that good is now evil and evil is now good. We have this occurring before us today. There are also people who are naive When they can imagine false teachers purposefully being misleading, because they themselves would never be misleading. And they cannot imagine people doing unmentionable harm to another human being, well, because they would never do intentional harm to another human being But false teachers who are purposefully false and cruel people who are purposefully evil, these do exist. A new documentary titled The Keepers has been made available online recently. The documentary exposes the perverted behavior of a Roman Catholic priest in the city of Baltimore in the late 1960s and early 70s. The stories of the behavior of this priest are so appalling and perverted That men with any amount of testosterone who watch this documentary respond by wanting to beat that priest up and then have him thrown in prison or worse. Several years ago I read a book titled Sacrilege, which describes many Detailed testimonies about pedophile abuses committed by Roman Catholic priests And these include hebophilia, which is the attraction of pre-pubescent boys, and then epobophilia, an attraction to mid-pubescent boys. As if the accounts of the molestations and rape are not bad enough to hear about, what is included in these testimonies is how these perverted priests would include false teachings as part of their method to draw in their victims and then to keep them quiet. But Roman Catholic priests are not the only people, of course, who practice perversions in the name of Jesus. The number of Protestant pastors who have raped, molested, adulterated is just as numerous as in the Roman Church, just as numerous in the Jewish religion, and the number of abusers of Muslim And the Muslim religion is impossible to know because it's tolerated. And the reason why I am exposing these sins before you is to do as St. Peter did, which is to tear away any facade that would tempt us to see a neutral world where there is neither good nor evil. There is evil. And there are evil people. There are people who give themselves over to sin, and that sin takes a hold of them. and corrupts them further and further until it no longer satisfies, but still seeks gratification Until the most innocent victims in society become a target. And the only way to get to those victims, for some, is in the name of Jesus. And what is implied by Saint Peter exposing evil excuse me And evil men among Christians is to warn them against evil in general, and we can add to that warning against evil A call to receive the Holy Spirit. Because this is Pentecost Sunday It is most appropriate for us to emphasize the receiving of the Holy Spirit. For it is the Holy Spirit that enables us to overcome sins of the flesh. It is the Holy Spirit that enables us to bring words of Jesus to our minds that those words might be used to combat the temptations of the flesh and the temptations of the devil. It is the Holy Spirit that leads us to all truth, and therefore the Holy Spirit helps us resist false doctrine. And remember that the Holy Spirit is a gentleman. He is a gentleman and that he does not force himself upon us, but waits to be asked. And so we can hear first this morning, resist evil, and second, receive the Holy Spirit. Let's look at verse 12 of 2 Peter 2 To speak like natural brute beasts is to speak according to the flesh Which is to teach according to basic animal desires, which is to promote the giving into those desires. And so greed and lust and envy and rage and jealousy and the like are the motivations of these false teachers. To perish in their own corruption is to reap what they have sown in this life and in the life to come. As the writer of Ecclesiastes expresses, we too might think that the unrighteous don't get their right judgment in this life as we think they should And we are tempted to complain to God that justice should be immediate rather than those who do evil enjoying their rebellion. But we are under the sun. Our advantage point our vantage point is so very limited. God will condemn the wicked. We just need to know he will do it in his way in his time. For now, resist evil and receive the Holy Spirit. Verse thirteen. I remind you of the phrase that we used two weeks ago. Which was be not fooled by God's silence. The people being described in this verse They are fooled by God's silence. They conclude that they are getting away with their sins because they have not been punished in this life. Their carousing in the daytime is evident that they are fooled by God's silence. In Romans 13, St. Paul describes men who sin in the evening, and they sin in the dark because they are trying to hide from God. They're trying to hide from their fellow man. They're trying to hide from their own conscience. But these sinners, Peter describes, are past worrying about their conscience. They are living among the Christians to whom Peter writes. They're doing it out in the open. The enemy is in the gates. Resist evil. Receive the Holy Spirit. Verse 14. The description of these evildoers is further given as adultery being in their eyes. Now adultery can be both sexual activity and it can be linked to idolatry as they were linked in the Greek and Roman worlds. Having been given over to their sin, as St. Paul describes in Romans 1, these adulterers cannot help themselves. Their sin has become who they are. Their sin is their identity And they prey on the weak who are unstable souls, the new King James Version. Unstable souls can go either way, and these adulterers make them go their way. Their hearts are bent towards sin and that continually, just as the people who were before the great flood. And it doesn't matter how nice they are on the outside. Inside, they want what is not theirs to have. They are accursed. They are not simply non-believers, understand that. And they are not even demon-possessed. They are accursed. Meaning that they are so given over to sin that the possibility of redemption, the possibility of being forgiven of their sin, has passed by them As Bobby Lynn and I learned of the sins of the priest from Baltimore watching that documentary. And the manner that he took advantage of young boys and young girls, it could only be fathomed in our minds that such a man had lost his soul, having given it over to the devil years before. He truly lived a life that was accursed, which is to say a life that was absent from the presence of God. Beloved, that happens. Resist evil. Receive the Holy Spirit. Verses fifteen and sixteen. Here we are to be sure that these evil men and their evil ways, that they are their own. Peter says, they forsake. It was their choice. The way they went is the way of Balaam. Balaam, you remember, was the prophet that sold his gift of prophecy to King Balach, who wanted Israel to be cursed. But God intervened through the voice of a donkey. It is a short, simple story with a great moral lesson. God will speak the truth even if it be through a donkey. Resist evil. Receive the Holy Spirit. Verses 17 and 18. Now here is a metaphor that any traveler in Israel knows is very cruel. Israel is a very dry land. A well of water seen at a distance is oh so very desired and very needed and so the pace of the journey quickens only to find the well dried up and useless So too were these false teachers. They were giving hope that happiness and holiness could be found in the flesh. A teaching that was known by the second century Christians that matches up what St. Peter is describing is from the claims of the Simonians. A heretical group that followed Simon Magus, who was mentioned two weeks ago. The Simonians came to believe that Simon himself could bring them salvation As he was believed to be God the Father in human form. Simonians were perhaps the first. in a long line to come that would deny the truth of Jesus as the Christ and instead choose another Messiah type Who speaks great swelling words of emptiness? Great swelling words Of emptiness. Resist evil. Receive the Holy Spirit. Verse 19 The real message of these false teachers is to promise on how to become free from righteousness, to become slaves to sin. The freedom promised by false teachers is a freedom from guilt. It is an argument that says that the Bible's teaching on sin, well that's archaic. Such teaching says that Jesus was simply a man of peace, a type of guru for social justice. St. Paul, on the other hand, was a misogynist, prejudiced, homophobic, and a hypocrite who turned Christianity into a religion instead of a movement. Once Jesus and Paul are placed in such categories, their teachings become weakened and even irrelevant to modern humanity. And so the guilt of their teachings is removed, and don't we all feel better? But St. John's teaching, I mean St. Peter's teaching here is the same as St. Paul's in Romans, where he said, everyone who continues to commit sin is a slave to sin. And you and I know the drill, but it is necessary to keep the warning before us The drill is, a person is told by the evil spirit of the age that rules and laws restrict and bind the human spirit. Instead of being bound, we are meant to be free, says the spirit of the age. To be free is to be able to do what you want to do when you want to do it. And so if it feels good to you, then do it for you. That's the freedom we all need, we are told. And so said person takes the hit from the bong or sleeps with a woman that is not his wife. Or gets drunk at a party, or views pornography, or steals a candy bar from a corner store Or tells his parents to go to hell, or moves in with his girlfriend, or vandalizes his neighbor's car, or place your pleasure here, and he does it all in under the banner of freedom. But such sins demand more. Getting high on drugs creates a desire to get even higher the next time. Salacious sex desires more salacious sex. Rebellion against the establishment necessitates more rebellion. And the supposed freedom a person started with has become a series of false gods served. The whole thing was a trap. And now the person who thought he was free can only find true freedom in Jesus. Who breaks the power of canceled sin and sets the soul free. Resist evil. Receive the Holy Spirit. Verses twenty through twenty-two. For every person who has suddenly lost a close loved one in this life especially a parent losing a child. Describing such a loss as painful is not enough. But what will be much more painful is when human souls are cast into the lake of fire. Weeping, wailing, and gnashing of teeth will be experienced by all who choose to cling to their sin. And hell is especially maintained for the devil, his angels, and all persons who claimed Jesus as his or her savior. But chose to teach lies, to believe lies, and to live in shackles of sin. Recall that Simon Magus was baptized by Philip the Evangelist. He was supposed to be a follower of Jesus. But he soon returned to his sorcery and he created his own following. There is no repentance for the likes of such people. They are gone Their souls have been sold to the lowest bidder, and the lowest bidder is always the devil. If you have ever owned a dog, you likely have witnessed it eating its own vomit. The reason why dogs do so is simply because they smell a source of food. They think they are eating food that will fill their bellies. Such a simpleton reason is why sinners return to their sin. To them, it is a way of pleasure for self. That is all. Nothing more complicated. And just as there is no nourishment for the dog who eats its own vomit, so there is no pleasure, no true pleasure, in returning to one's sin. But the Spirit of God is so far removed from such sinners that it doesn't matter. It is all that they know to do. But we say resist evil and receive the Holy Spirit. It must be acknowledged after hearing these verses expounded upon that you might wonder if you know A person or people that have been described, people who have been given over to evil to the point where there is no longer a chance for them to repent? Well, let us know first that we ought not to come to such conclusions. For while there are indeed people walking the streets and in our lives and yes even in the church who have reached the point of no return. It is never for us to hunt them down, to point them out, or to come to conclusions about them. Instead, we are commissioned to go and make disciples. We are commissioned to baptize new believers. We are commissioned to love the brethren. The condemnation is God's responsibility. So the reason of St. Peter's words is not for us to have hunting parties and round up all the false teachers, false believers, and sinners trapped in sin. Instead, it is for us to fear. And yes, I said fear. We are to fear enabling false teachers We are to fear believing false teachers. We are to fear encouraging the trappings of sin. We are to fear ignoring the trappings of sin and fear choosing ourselves to live in sin. Fear is necessary when it comes to sin because fear causes us to fight or flight. It causes us to go away from what is dangerous and to cling to what is good. When you read about heinous crimes done to people, do you ever wonder to yourself if you are capable of acting out something similar? Bobby Lynn and I talked early last week, asking ourselves, are we capable of, am I ever capable of doing something that is being described? And I said I was capable, at least. I was before I knew Jesus as my Savior. Before then I had a lot of rage in me. I remember wondering then what I was capable of doing in my anger. And now I say I am not able because the Holy Spirit lives in me. But what if my circumstances change? Like Job. What if I lost my calling? What if I lost my income, my children, my health, and my wife is counseling me to curse God and die? What would I do then? Would I be capable of harming another person? Would I be capable of choosing pleasure over righteousness? And the answer to that is I would be capable. I would be capable, and you would be capable if you allowed your circumstances to determine your emotions. Feelings of unfair treatment easily turn into bitterness, and bitterness to anger, and anger to rage, and rage to doing harm to others. And then the guilt comes and it will come. And that needs to be drowned out by pleasures such as drugs, alcohol, adultery. And because such pleasures of the flesh never last, they need to be repeated over and over again. And the next act of sin becomes slavery to sin. And the end is a dog returning to its own bonnet. Resist evil, receive the Holy Spirit. Are you scared? I hope so. I hope we are all scared of the wrath of God so much. So much that we resist evil and receive the Holy Spirit. Let us pray.

sermons.title: The Heart of God
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. We are in Second Peter chapter three, covering verses one through nine. Before we get to the text, I trust you have heard stories of men who live double lives By double lives, I do not mean men who have secret sins. I am using double lives to describe men who are married. Hold a job and raise children in one city, and also have a completely different wife and children in another city. Their stories are truly remarkable in terms of their seared consciences and in their ability to maintain such deception for long periods of time. Because I have only heard such stories occurring with men, I searched to find if there are women who have lived such double lives. Sure enough, I found something similar in a 2007 column appearing in the Chicago Tribune. Describes a woman named Warren leading a double life. She was happily married, or what appeared to people on the outside as happily married. Until she met an old classmate. She started to exchange emails with him and then share lunch with him and then share a bed with him. He too was married. The two came to an agreement that they did not want to leave their families, but they did want to be husband and wife. And so they chose to remain married and see one another on a regular basis. And this is a quote from Lauren. I hate the word cheating. Cheating denotes wrong and shameful behavior. But I don't feel wrong and shameful. I feel married to the man. In fact, I feel more married to him than I do my husband. End quote. We could, if we were given the chance, point out to Lauren that how she felt didn't change the objectivity of the truth. She was cheating, and we would call it something different. She was committing adultery. She was breaking God's commandment. And what was just as bad is that she was bearing false witness to her husband and to her children, breaking her marital vow. She was leading a double life as she was not who her husband and children thought her to be When double lives are discovered, there is a sorrow that comes over the spouse cheated upon, as she or he feels that their whole life with the guilty party Maybe has been a lie. And we can understand how the victim of said deception would question whether any laugh Any intimacy, any memorable conversation or shared experience? Was it real at all? It could all have been a lie, and it has to make them sick, to think about that The conclusion has to be that he or she never knew her husband or wife. He never truly knew his wife, the man in the article. Years can seem wasted as love was never truly shared. Life gives its greatest meaning when we know, truly know, those whom we have our closest relationships with. Interesting that the word no in the King James Version is a euphemism for sexual intercourse. That is because the word is relational in its most intimate forms. To know in the Bible, to know is to perceive. Learn, understand, be willing, performing, and experiencing To know God, according to the Bible, is to enter into a saving action. To know God is to recognize and accept his claims. To know God is to walk in obedience with Him. Thus, the opposite of having a knowledge of God is to live in rebellion. Our focus this morning is to know God and to know him in the manner he is described in verse 9 of our reading. And I want to read that verse again. 2 Peter 3 verse 9. The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some count slackness. But is long-suffering toward us, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. We need to know the God that is described in this verse. But before we examine him more closely, by way of verse 9, We need to look at the verses that lead up to that verse, verses 1 through 8. In chapter 2, it was taught to us that there are evil teachers and thus evil people who live among us, and we are to be confident that they will be judged by God. St. Peter next wants us to address the presence of mockers among us. Mockers who challenge a fundamental Christian belief, the belief that Jesus will come again. That second coming is fundamental to our faith. Recall that in the Apostles' Creed, we state that Jesus will come from heaven to judge the quick and the dead. In the Nicene Creed, we say that Jesus will come again in glory to judge the quick and the dead. The creeds are the summary teaching of what a Christian needs to believe to be a Christian. Therefore, believing in the second coming of Jesus is fundamental to the gospel. You must believe in it. But where is he? It has been a long time since Christians have been saying that Jesus is coming again. At the writing of St. Peter, it was but a few decades. As we stand today, you know it is almost 2,000 years. To understand the delay and to respond to these mockers, Peter first wants Christians to have their minds stirred up. That's the language in the New King James, stirred up. Interestingly, the Sunday before Advent season, the Book of Common Prayer has a callette, a prayer, for the occasion. And because Advent means coming, and we celebrate the first coming of Jesus in Bethlehem, and then we celebrate also his second coming. We pray this prayer. It starts out like this. Stir up. Stir up. We beseech thee, O Lord, the wills of thy faithful people. Stir up. Thus, when we talk about the second coming of Jesus, according to Peter and our collect, we need to be stirred up, woken up. The stirring up that St. Peter wants is within the mind, as Christians are to be stirring, remembering the words, he says, spoken by the holy prophets. The words of the commandment and the words of the apostles. I admit that other translations write out that verse a little bit better. than the New King James. We could read as the NIV does, recall the words spoken by the holy prophets. And the command given by our Lord Jesus and Savior through the apostles The words spoken by the holy prophets, these are such as Isaiah, describing a new heaven and a new earth, where the wolf will lie down with the lamb. Also in the prophets Isaiah, references to the day of the Lord. These are scattered throughout the Old Testament. If such references are referring to the day of the Lord that is a local judgment, it is also referring to a day of the Lord that is the ultimate or final judgment. And we find this day of the Lord phrase in Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Joel, Amos, Obaniah, Zephaniah, Zechariah, and Malachi, all referring to the last day, the day of the Lord. The words of the holy prophets are also describing heavenly signs involving the sun, the moon, and the stars. These are linked to the last day, the day of the Lord. And these same heavenly signs are then picked up in the New Testament, referring to the day of the Lord Regarding the command given by the Lord to the apostles, the context of the second coming of Jesus would mean that St. Peter is referring to the command Jesus gave to go and make disciples. Baptize him in the name of the Father, the Son, and Holy Spirit until his coming again. In the meantime, or as the apostles and the church as a whole are preaching the gospel and baptizing the Christian church, is to remember the warnings of Jesus who said, scoffers will come. They will stop you, mock you, to walk according to their lusts, such people will do whatever they want in whatever manner they want. Lust, after all, is unpredictable. It desires one thing in one moment, and another thing in another moment. And people who live according to their own lust will say whatever they want to say. They have no filter. And they will make fun of you, Christians. They will ridicule, they will mock. And in their mocking, they claim that the gospel is not true. Well, because Jesus hasn't returned. Where is he? Their argument is that everything since the beginning of time is still the same. Nothing has changed. But that argument is willfully ignorant, as St. Peter points out. He says, For before the lands were formed and the earth populated, the globe was in chaos, as Genesis describes And it was from chaos that the Lord God raised up the land from the water and gave each its boundaries. And after mankind corrupted the earth, there was a flood where God judged mankind and judged the earth. Still today, interestingly, mockers forget the flood and its continuing effect upon creation. And this point in the sermon gives me an opportunity to plug again the showing we will have of that documentary is Genesis history. In the documentary, you will be an eyewitness to the continuing effect the great flood has upon the earth today. The flood was real and it was devastating. The scientists today look past it because, well, it doesn't fit their narrative about how they think the earth was formed and how old it is. Evidence for a flood would mean the story of Genesis is true. And if Genesis is true, then God is real. And if God is real, then each person has to answer to him. And because the majority of humanity in the West do not want to answer to God, God is not real. The flood did not happen. And any other theory about how the earth came to be today is what's accepted. That is modern science. Peter continues to defend against the mockers by explaining that each day that passes Is a day where the earth and mankind are being preserved or protected until judgment But the next judgment won't be a flood, but a judgment of fire And the fire will be an eternal one, torturing the devil, torturing his angels, and torturing ungodly men. Perdition, the New King James uses, perdition is a fate of final spiritual ruin, resulting in a state of eternal punishment. That is the fate of all who refuse to repent and believe. The next explanation allows us to spend some time out from under the sun. For we get a glimpse of the nature of God. It is to be remembered by believers that time itself is part of creation. Time was created and is maintained by God. God called the sun, light, the sunlight day, and the starlight night. Those are his designations. And all of creation is governed by time, but God is not a part of creation. He is that by which nothing greater can be conceived. So he is above time and therefore not limited by it or constricted by it. So when the Lord delays When the Lord delays his coming, the delay is from our perspective, not his. And let us be careful when we consider this thousand years as a day, a day as a thousand years. Let us not think that since Over 1,000 years has passed since Jesus ascended into heaven that such is almost two days passing. The phrasing is not literal, it is figurative. It could say that God to God a day is as 2,000 years or 10,000 years. And the message would be the same. His days are not ours. But it's fair to ask, why would God wait 2,000 years? Why would he wait a thousand years, a hundred years, or even a decade before Jesus returns? In verse 9, That question is answered. And in verse 9, we are privileged, privileged to know the heart of God. The Lord is not slack. Meaning the Lord God does not delay. He is not slow concerning fulfilling his promises. The promise of his second coming, to fulfill that, as if the time fixed for the fulfillment of it were past. For it will surely be fulfilled. It will be fulfilled in its proper season. But instead of slack, God is long suffering toward us, or all of humanity. Not willing that any should perish. That is any human being, any soul that he has made in his image. His first will, with regard to the whole posterity of Adam, has been and is that they should be eternally saved. And as proof of it, he has given his son as a ransom for all Has commanded his gospel that the glad tidings of salvation be preached to all, to every human creature. Not willing, not wanting, that any should perish. That is, he does not desire it. He does not wish it to be His nature is benevolent, and he sincerely desires the eternal happiness of all. And his patience towards sinners proves that he is willing, desiring, wanting them to be saved. If he were not willing, it would be easy for him to cut them off and exclude them from hope immediately. Now, this passage, this verse cannot be spoiled by asking rebuttal type questions. But why doesn't he just do it then? Why doesn't he just save everyone? But what of all his rhetoric that condemns sinners But what if his predetermined plan to save those who are chosen and the language he uses to express his sovereignty over the salvation of every human being? Those are good questions, but they are not questions that appreciate this verse. And what we are privileged to know from this verse about God, about his heart. When it comes to God's will, God's will, theologians have given it several categories. And these categories can help us understand this verse. There is God's sovereign will, which is what will happen because God controls all things, and we are to be assured that nothing can thwart His sovereign will Then there is the category of God's permissive will, which is when God allows you and I to make choices that we make and enjoy the rewards or suffer the consequences of those choices. But his permissive will never allow us to make choices outside of his sovereign will. And then there is God's desired will, His expressed heart. It is what he would prefer. It is what he wants for everyone. That is the will expressed in this verse. But many people don't understand a verse like this because they conclude that God is like men. For us, for every human being, because we are under the sun, because our lives are like fleeting vapor of smoke We know what we would do if there was something that we wanted, something we preferred, and we could make it happen. We would do it. We would make it happen. And so we conclude that God is such that He should do what we would do. Make it happen. But God is not like men. God instead controls his desires. God is perfect God is both righteous and benevolent. His character is made up of a perfect charity and a perfect justice. But here, we Christians are to focus on God's charity, his benevolence toward us. Beloved, God is love. He is love in action. Love and caring emotionally and sincerely, caring about your soul Last week we spent a great deal of time hearing about the presence of evil in this world and the presence of people who are evil in this world. And such is not easy to hear, but such is contrasted and overwhelmed by what is said in verse 9. God wills that no one should perish. God wills instead that all would come to repentance, which is a turning away from evil. God wants that for you. And I know he wants that for you because you are listening to my words, and my words are God's words. And his word says he desires you to be saved. And because he desires you to be saved, I can say that he desires you to forgive all who have wronged you in your life. He desires you to seek forgiveness from all you have wronged. He desires you to overcome addiction. He desires you to love and be loved by your fellow man. He desires you to believe on the Lord Jesus Christ as your Savior. All of that can be said of what God desires, all of it. And more is what it means to live a life of a saved person Beloved, with the knowledge of what God desires, of what his heart wills. We are as Moses allowed to see God. Only Moses was allowed to see God from behind. Because of the revelation of Jesus, who is the heart of the Godhead, and because in Jesus God so loved the world. And here in Peter, we get to hear what God's heart is towards humanity. We get to see God as he is, be inside of him. Let us be humbled as Moses was, and emboldened. Emboldened by this knowledge of God. God wills that you all come to repentance. God wills that you be saved. Let us love that heart of God. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Use a Net
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. I want to first thank Reverend Landboy for filling in the pulpit last week. And uh for those who helped serve, much appreciated. We are in 2 Peter chapter 3, and we are finishing up our series on first. and the second Peter do very well to turn in your Bibles to those to that section 2 Peter 3, 10 through 18. For our last reading from Saint Peter's epistle, our focus is going to be upon personal holiness. And I will meld that call for personal holiness together with what was The primary message of general counsel a couple of weeks ago, how I will do so remains to be seen. But first let us address the subject of personal holiness. Personal holiness can sound to me like a subject matter afar off. By that I mean it can appear to be something we cannot achieve ourselves and as something we cannot control and something perhaps we will never be. Consider these words spoken by Jesus. Be perfect as your heavenly father is perfect. A likely response to that command is not stated by us, but because it would be unfaithful. But an understandable, unstated response to this command of Jesus for his followers to be perfect as the Heavenly Father is perfect, a natural response is to think Well, that's impossible. I cannot be holy as God is holy. I simply cannot. I am a fallen creature. I am born in sin. I am weak in my flesh. I am under the sun. I am mortal as I am under the curse of death because of my father Adam. All and more are reasons why I cannot be perfect as God is perfect But, but, regardless of our sinful state of being, the command of Jesus still stands. Be perfect. And then there are directives like we have in 2 Peter 3. We are told to live lives in holy conduct and godliness. Which is to say, lives that are as God is. And we are to do so because Jesus will indeed return, and we are to be ready for said return, verses eleven and twelve. 12. And again, because there will be a new heaven and a new earth, verse 13, we are to be diligent in being certain that we are in peace with God and man. And we are to be without spot and blameless. To be without spot is to be without sin. To be blameless is to have nothing in your your life's ledger to be counted against you. And with the reality of God's long suffering regarding his second return, verse fifteen We are to be warned and aware that we do not fall into believing the errors of the wicked. Verse 17 In between that thought is a verse that has been very much appreciated by Christians down through the ages. It is the admission that St. Paul confirms God's long suffering. Even though what he writes can, at times, admitted by Peter, be difficult to understand. And such difficulty has allowed many lively discussions in Bible studies down through the ages. As PhDs earned because of Paul's words, misunderstood. And unfortunately Paul's words misunderstood have led to Christians dividing. But we appreciate St. Peter acknowledging St. Paul's difficult words because we are not alone in the matter. Thankfully also, the epistle ends with the encouragement to grow in grace. That is something we all can admit to be able to do. Grow in grace. If we think we cannot be holy, as God is holy, at least we know we can grow in grace. Now I say that we cannot be holy as God is holy, only in terms of our perspective and specifically our perspective of ourselves. Not in terms of how God sees us and what he does for us in Christ, but we will get to that at a later time. Personal holiness. It is living a life of holy conduct and godliness. It is living without spot, a life that is blameless. But what does that mean for each of us individually? It seems that there is a subjective aspect to personal holiness. And an objective aspect. The objective aspect is that God is the standard. Jesus is the human form of that standard. We are to be as Jesus. And yet it is a personal, subjective call on our lives to be holy. Because each of us struggle with personal sins. What may not be hard for you to overcome might be hard for me, and vice versa. What might be a vice to me might be over. be ignored by you and vice versa. What sin or sins I need to repent of right now might be sins in your long past, covered by the blood of the Lamb. Or sins in your future or sins you will never practice, and vice versa. That is the subjective aspect of the call of God upon his people to be holy. But I wish to step away from the subject of personal holiness. I'm interrupting myself with a description of what was presented at the General Council. And as I said, I will attempt to bring back personal holiness and tie it all together. Let's see if I can do it. Bishop Sutton who was officially elected and consecrated as presiding bishop of the REC, presented a three-part lecture titled Veritas. Those of you who remember your Latin know that that means truth. The lectures were a main part of the theme of the council. The council itself was called REC 100. You already know what the REC stands for. Mark shared with you that the 100 refers to the goal of planting 100 new churches in the next 10 years. This is a lofty goal, for as of now, as was mentioned, the REC has only 113 churches total in the United States. There are more in Cuba and Germany and Croatia. But 100 is still a lofty gold. However, what Bishop Sutton presented to us made the goal seemingly attainable, because it was material regarding growing the kingdom of God that was fresh. Fresh, at least to me. It was material I had not heard before. Over the 21 years of my ministry as a pastor, I have heard many church growth models. models, plans, strategies that others were doing, and supposedly with success, but none of them appealed to me In fact, I have been arguing that the more popular models for church growth accomplish Nothing in terms of bringing forth the kingdom of God among us. Church growth models of the past have sprung up megachurches with their thousands of members and big buildings and big productions, but none of them, none, none of them have ushered in the kingdom of God. And by ushering in the kingdom of God, I mean the evidence of God being among men. And by evidence I mean holy lives and changed lives, resulting in a change of culture. A culture that fears and loves God. Answer me these questions. Is the Christian culture better now than it was before the era of televangelism? Is the American culture more holy now than before the era of mega churches? What challenge did telechurches and mega churches offer? offer against homosexual marriage, against divorce, against abortion, against adultery, against fornication, against the casting out of God from the public schools. What did these people, these leaders, these churches offer to any of that? My answer is that they have done nothing to change personal lives and then change our culture. Nothing. Now hear me, I am not blaming telechurches or megachurches for our cultural problems. We are to blame. But the model of bigger is better is not accomplishing anything worth noting in terms of the kingdom of God being established on earth as an is in heaven. Another poor part of previous church growth models is the focus on decision making. Preachers of the gospel for too long have had the goal of getting people to make decisions to follow Jesus. And they count those decisions just as a World War I pilot. Pilate would count the kills that he had in the air. But such decisions were never an indication of true growth for the kingdom of God. After all, Jesus instructed the church to go and make what? Disciples, not decisions. The result of decisional Christianity has been an individualistic faith that ignores the necessity of the local church. and the universal church. And the result of that is a weak Christian church that has a bunch of individual popes who worship as they like, believe as they like, and live as they like. How is that working out? How is that working out? Is seen in every community in the United States and in Europe As Bishop Sutton pointed out, we are not just living in a post-Christian era, but a repaganized age. This age is worse off than the days of the pagan Roman Empire because they had not yet heard the gospel of Jesus Christ. Whereas our culture has heard it and has openly rejected it. Was it not Saint Peter who said that it would be better for those who left the faith if they had never known the faith at all? The same can be said for a culture. So what do we do to grow the kingdom of God in this age? The image put forth by Bishop Sutton was so helpful and meaningful to me. It is called the net approach. It is fishing with a net. It is fishing with a net as opposed to fishing with a hook A fish hook approach is where a bait was put on a hook, and there we are waiting to see who would bite. The fish hook approach was and is a poor way to grow the kingdom of God, because it was the same as the decision approach, with all of its weaknesses. The bait and hook approach focuses on individuals evangelizing individuals And debate always focused on the prospective fish and what Jesus can do for them. With such an approach, it is hard, hard not to sell the gospel or sell Jesus and to focus on the sinner as the consumer of the gospel or of Jesus. As a Pope, as opposed to focusing on Jesus and the truth of the gospel The fish hook approach also put a great deal of onus on Christian laity to go out and evangelize. We preachers can too easily tell laity that it is your responsibility to go evangelize. If the kingdom of God is going to grow, it is your job to see that it is done. So we tell you to witness to your family members, to your co-workers, to your neighbors, to your fellow citizens in the street. Until they are all tired of hearing from you about religion and choose to walk away when they see you coming. Thanks, Pastor. Again, that hasn't been very effective, and it certainly won't be effective today. And it doesn't matter how guilty our pastors make us feel, because many of us are ill. equipped to offer a bait on a fish hook that is it going to be challenged. Very few are well read enough to answer objections to the faith, and that reality causes most of us to fear offering At all. Fear of it simply sharing what we believe. In contrast, the fishnet approach doesn't see sharing the gospel as an Individual responsibility, but instead the responsibility of the local church. After all, did not the disciples fish with nets? They used a method of spreading a wide parameter that would make it more likely to catch fish and to catch several fish. The Vishnette approach to growing the kingdom of God is the community of God's people reaching the communities of the world that are around them. And a great passage that communicates the positive effect of community faith is read from the paralytic story found in Mark chapter 2. Recall that story. For Jesus had come back to Capernaum, a small town on the shores of Galilee. A large crowd had gathered to hear him teach. It was so large That a few men carrying a paralytic man could only access Jesus by digging a hole on the roof of the house and to lower the paralytic down in front of Jesus. When describing the scene, Mark says that Jesus saw their faith. Plural, their faith. Not the faith of the paralytic only, but the faith of the community. And it was the faith of the community that caused Jesus to say to the man, Your sins are forgiven. And then, to impress upon them all that Jesus could forgive sins, Jesus healed the man of paralysis based on their faith. Community faith, of course. Of course. A great example for us on how community is used to reach the lost for Jesus is given to us by enemies of the faith Julian, Emperor of Rome in the fourth century, wrote of a concern that he had about how Christians were influencing the culture. when he complained about how they were reaching the non-believers. He said, quote, we must pay special attention to this point and by the means effect a cure. For when it came about that the poor were neglected and overlooked by our pagan priests, then I think the impious Galileans, Christians Observed the fact and devoted themselves to philanthropy. And they have gained ascendancy in the worst of their deeds through the credit they win for such practices. For just as those who entice children With cake and throwing it to them two or three times to induce them to follow. By the same method, I say the Galileans, the Christians Also begin with their so-called love feast or hospitality. End quote Now remember, beloved the love feast, as mentioned in 1 Corinthians, was where the community gathered together to share a meal before worship. And so what Julian is complaining about and describing is simply that the early Christians included non-believers in the community before they led them to believe in Jesus. They shared a meal with them. They invited them to have a meal. They acknowledged them as worthwhile, as in God's image. And I underline that they did so as community, together. As an example, and I don't want to embarrass them, but it's such a good example. This example of approaching kingdom building by way of community, we can look at Bill and Betty Moore's. Bill and Betty love on people and their apartment community and they bring them to church. People in church love on those who come by befriending them. Then others, such as myself, teach the word of God to them and feed them by way of sacrament. Then the church provides times of fellowship and even ministers ministers food and company when needed. Therefore, it is not just one person helping to save another person, but one or two people, in this case Bill and Betty, doing one thing. and working with others who do what they do good at, and resulting in the building of the kingdom of God, the community of faith, building the kingdom of God. By the way, uh Bill and Betty, the vestry is meeting this afternoon to decide whether we're going to buy you a passenger van or not. So uh be ready. Consider that some of us feel inadequate to explain our Christian faith. But we can always invite someone to church, and if not church for worship, then do a Bible study or a worship. Woman's tea or breakfast on Thursday mornings or a men's meeting or special service And we should expect that when we bring someone into the Christian fold, that others will do what they do best. Help said persons either find Jesus as their Lord and Savior, or if they are already Christian, to be built up. And encouraged in their faith, or grow in grace, and just as Peter here describes Now this approach to kingdom building has many, many possible applications, but we cannot focus on those this morning. What I am stressing is kingdom of God building by way of community. With that, it is important to point out that there is a flaw in this system. The flaw is when there is not a healthy church community to where a new person can be brought into the fold. A sick church community is revealed when it is not kind to visitors, or when it is infighting, so much so that it doesn't see the importance of adding anyone new. Or when it is unforgiving, to the point when no one wishes to fellowship together. Such is like fishing with holes in one's net The holes need to be mended. The church needs to be a healthy place for it to be effective at catching fish and thus building the kingdom of God on earth as it is in heaven. But being unhealthy, honestly, is not our problem. And that is not bracking. St. Stephen's is a healthy parish. It is not perfect, and it is necessary to say that and to ask God to help us grow in grace as a community. With that said, I have every confidence. that when a new fish enters our midst, we have resources among us to love them, include them, feed them by God's word and physical food, and hence disciple them. Every confidence left. And yet, and yet Here is where I bring back into the sermon our call by St. Peter for personal holy lives. Here is the truth. Churches are only as healthy as the individual members of said church are living holy lives. Say it again. Churches are only as healthy as individual members of said church are living holy lives Thus the call to personal holy living is a call that recognizes a domino effect. Personal holiness lives to community holiness, and community holiness leads to growth in the kingdom of God. But we tend not to think of our belief in such a manner as we tend to view our faith as personal and our holiness as personal between me and Jesus. Hear this in plain language. Personal holiness has an effect upon the local church. And the holiness and effectiveness of the local church determines how effective it is for the kingdom of God. And how effective it is for building the kingdom of God is how effective it is in bringing back the coming of our Savior. Believe that. It is how God has planned it. So we have a goal of a hundred churches being started in ten years. Where do you start? We start with personal holiness. We start with resisting temptation, fleeing from evil, resisting the devil, confessing sin, receiving forgiveness. And forgiving others. Our marching orders are before us. Let us get to it. Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful Father, we thank you for the truth of how to grow the kingdom of God revealed in your holy word and to be practiced by your church. But we also hear the call of St. Peter. Live holy lives. Be prepared for the coming of the Savior. Be prepared for the coming of the kingdom of God. And so we individually take that challenge, and may your church grow, and may your kingdom be established. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Repentance from Dead Works
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. You be seated. As a child, it was discovered early on that I was completely deaf in my left ear. I have never been diagnosed as to what the cause of my deafness is, but I was told that it seems to be inherited from family, as I have ancestors who are also born deaf in one ear. It is easy to recognize that having youths of all our senses gives us important foundation stones so to live healthy and vibrant lives When you are without one of the senses, or when one of your senses is weakened, you have to compensate. Because I had full hearing in my right ear growing up, the deafness in my left ear was not so debilitating, although it created for some awkward moments, as it still does. Like most of us here, I was giving I was given hearing tests in elementary school And even though my hearing chart informed the testers that I was completely deaf in one ear, they would always say, okay, now let's try the left ear. Raise your hand, remember, when you hear the beep. And so I would try to guess when they were beeping in my left ear. And I wasn't messing with them. I was truly trying to hear a beep. And so I would raise my hand when I thought I heard a beep. And I could always sense a lot of fidgeting going on with the testers, as they would test my left ear, for I am sure I guessed right once in a while, and I'm sure that made the tester quite confused. But I wanted wanted to hear out of my left ear, so I wanted to pretend I could hear something. And today I continue to stand at a disadvantage. I have been accused of being rude because I don't respond to someone who has greeted me when, in fact, they were on my left side and I simply did not hear them I have carried on conversations with people at a dinner banquet who sit on my left-hand side, and I find myself nodding and And smiling, probably too much, because I am pretending to hear them and agree with them and think that they're funny when I really don't have an idea what they're saying But turning, turning my right ear to someone who's on my left side literally does make it look like I'm trying to go in for the kiss. And that can be most awkward. of all. And I tell you all of this not as a complaint, but as an example of when something fundamental to the human experience, such as hearing, is not what it is meant to be. And I wish to apply the struggle of what is fundamentally lacking in a particular person's senses. And the results of what is lacking to what occurs when a Christian is lacking certain fundamental faith principles That should be established and should have been established a long time ago. What I want us to focus on is what is needed in the Christian life that is fundamental. In order for a Christian to function in a healthy manner in this life. And I want to prove to you Then unless what is fundamental to the Christian life is established, that what we are, what we have in ourselves Is a handicap. We're handicapped in terms of what our Christian lives could be as we wait for our Savior to return. This sermon is the first in a series of what I will be preaching this summer in this common season in the church calendar. And I'm hoping these sermons will help us Re-establish ourselves so that we might grow in grace all the better, as St. Peter instructed us last week For just as, let's say, a marriage needs time of returning to first loves, time to reconnect with one another. So too do we Christians need to refresh, to renew, to reestablish what is fundamental to our Christian lives, to be disciples of Christ. And so I point us to what was read from our epistle reading and to what is, from my perspective, a text in Holy Scripture. That is underappreciated and often overlooked. In Hebrews chapter 6, the preacher Tells his parishioners that the discussion of the elementary principles of Christ Jesus needs to be left so that the Christians can go on to perfection. And such a passage fits well with our sermon last week that reminded us that Jesus instructed his followers to be perfect as the Heavenly Father is perfect. The preacher of the Hebrews is saying the same thing, only he is using a rhetorical technique that assumes, assumes, fundamental principles in Christ are already established. Causing the listener to do an inventory, to assure that such is the case for self. And it is, if it is not the case, then we are to examine ourselves and reestablish those things that need to be in place. And so we see the phrase not laying again. This implies that those things should be applied and only need to be applied once. And if they are not applied, then they need to be applied and only applied once. And so we will be working with these foundation stones this summer with the purpose of assuring that each of these is established in our individual lives The first foundation stone, as listed in Hebrews chapter 6. The first foundation stone to be established is repentance from dead works. Repentance from dead works. You for certain know what repentance is. It is turning away 180 degrees to go the opposite direction of where our sin was taking us. But what about this phrase dead works? The phrase dead works is full of meaning. And the first most basic meaning in Scripture are sins that lead to death In Adam Clark's commentary on Hebrews, he defines dead works as works that deserve death. Works that deserve death, according to Romans 6. 23, are all sins and trespasses. Sin in all of its forms is breaking God's commandments, and the penalty of such sin is everlasting death. Hence dead works are our individual sins. As those sins lead to death. Adding to the meaning of dead works being sins that result in everlasting death is an understanding that a person might think his good deeds are going to earn God's favor when in fact the opposite is true. They will earn God's wrath. Twice in the book of Proverbs it says this There is a way that seems right to a man, but in the end the way is death. It seems right, but in the end, it's death. Thus, dead works includes those things that human beings do that they think will earn them favor or merit before God, but in the end are actually acts done That contain no righteousness at all. The most prominent example of this type of thinking and then actions Is the primary purpose of St. Paul writing to the Galatians? We recall that soon after St. Paul left Galatia They were exposed to the teachings of the Judaizers, who were false teachers, claiming that Christians needed to not only believe in Jesus, but be subject to the ceremonial laws of the Old Testament. in order to be in right standing before God. And so some Gentile Christians were circumcised and began to follow Jewish customs because they believed By doing so they would be better received by God. And when Saint Paul heard of their practices, he quickly wrote to them, and remember what he said, Who has bewitched you? The epistle then spells out how Christians are forgiven their sins and promised eternal life, not for what they do in fulfilling the law, but instead. What Jesus did, solely did in fulfilling the law. Dead works in such a context are works where a person believes he or she can do something. Anything to earn the forgiveness and earn even the kindness of God. The belief that God forgives or finds favor with people who do good in this life Is a serious problem and a serious curse that is a consistent plague upon all people of all cultures and all of history of the human race. Consider that it was Cain who first believed that he could earn God's favor by what he offered to God. Consider that when his good works were rejected, because they were dead works, his countenance fell, his personal pride increased to the point of killing Abel, his brother. Consider that every every religion that mankind has ever developed in all corners of the globe throughout all the ages of mankind, every religion incorporates Good works for finding favor with God or many gods. The Greeks believed their good works would stave off the wrath of the gods. The Romans believed their good works held off the angry gods. The pagans believed their good works satisfied the wrath of their gods, bribing them to send rain and provide healthy harvests. Consider how all of the organized religions of the history of mankind have good work clauses in them When satisfied, these good work clauses promise either worldly blessings or otherworldly blessings. And then comes Christianity. Jesus comes into the world saying that it is impossible for anyone to do good enough, to be good enough. In order to be forgiven or even liked by God. The plan of salvation was not that humanity would perform well enough to be forgiven. But that so God loved the world that he gave his only son. And the only son would offer himself as a sinless sacrifice. So that all who believe in him as their Messiah would be forgiven, would be saved. And so it was revealed that the only good works done by anyone are the good works of Jesus. And anything that we do that is good is good because it is done in the name of Jesus. For only he is good, and only works done for him for his glory are good. Every other work is death. What I have just spoken to you is truth from Holy Scripture, but there are objections to such words. And one of the objections is legitimate in that it asks, what about when people do nice things for other people? Because they are emotionally moved to do so, to just be nice. Do such actions constitute good? The simple answer is yes, if by good, we mean only that a need of a human being is being met. If a man is hungry and someone feels for that man and gives food to such a man because of empathies. Then good has been done so far as feeding a hungry man. But in terms of good meaning eternally good, well the answer is no. No, because whatever a person does in this life is not done for the glory of God. Those things have no value. Only that which is done for the glory of God in Christ's name has eternal value. Good. Now I mentioned that the belief that God forgives and finds favor with those people who do good things in this life is a serious problem, and So I point to evidence that when the average person mourns the death of a friend or a loved one. A mention of good works of the dead is always heard. Consider How many eulogies you have heard, whether given by a minister presiding over the funeral or a layperson speaking at a funeral? Consider how their words convey that the dead person is now, quote, in a better place, or at peace, or with grandma, or simply in heaven. Because of the type of person he or she was while living When a person dies, we naturally feel empathy, and so we want to think what is good about the person, and we want to say nice things about the person. And so we choose to remember only the good, and then the person is presented to all who mourn to be only good. And we think the good has to outweigh the bad in this great scale of eternal justice. Bringing us to the conclusion that heaven is this dead person's final resting place because of the good done in this life. But such good done are dead works. They don't account for anything that brings about the forgiveness of God Consider, please, that if it were so, if a good work done in this life did bring about forgiveness and favor by God, Then the suffering and death of Jesus was completely unnecessary. And therefore the Father sending his only son, that was a sadistic act at best. But God is not a sadist. God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. God satisfied his own wrath as Jesus was the propitiation for us. Another evidence that reveals how dangerous it is to believe that good works earn God's favor. Are the copycat religions that have sprung up over the centuries using the name of Jesus while including good works? The Mormons and Jehovah's Witnesses are the most prominent examples. As each of these false religions include the name of Jesus and their confession of faith, While denying the divinity of Jesus, and while insisting that their good works do earn God's favor. That's why the Jehovah's Witnesses work so hard at going door to door to share their false words. They believe God favors them the more they do so. And the Mormons add good works on top of good works as they teach that the more children a woman has, the greater her heavenly reward. And the more faithful they are at wearing their undergarments and abstaining from caffeine and fulfilling their mission requirements and increasing their tithe, the more holy they are seen by God. Of course, it is all nonsense, and most certainly contrary to Holy Scripture Which is why each group has their own version of the Holy Scriptures, as these versions enable them to describe Jesus not as God. But a man of good works as well, just as they are trying to be. The final example for us to look at that reveals the danger of believing that our good works earn God's favor. is the necessity of the 39 articles of religion as in the back of your prayer book listing the subject of the works of supererrogation. Works of supererrogation. These are godly actions lived out so as to receive excess merit from God. The necessity to make a statement against such works takes us back all the way back to the first century of the church. When it was taught by some that Christians could earn God's favor, score extra points with God by way of martyrdom or by voluntary celibacy. By doing either of those two things, a Christian was supposedly satisfying God's commands and even exceeding them. Hence, works of supererrogation were practiced within the monastic system of the church, where monks taught that their mode of life was a state of perfection. Because they not only observed God's precepts, but also followed his counsels, making themselves out to be a sort of super Christian. But while we can say there is a difference between precepts, which are commands given by God, and his counsels, which are directives to Christians to help them live out this life The scripture provides no defense that says that good works go beyond what God commands, granting a person any extra merit from God. The scripture only confirms that each person who is saved from the judgment of sin and from eternal death is saved only by the works of Jesus and his works. That is why the 14th article of the 39 articles calls extra works arrogant and impious. Not arrogant and impious because the good works are done, but only because that by doing them it is believed that God would ever grant us extra favor. With these examples, let us ask if there is evidence among us that reveals that we believe we can perform good works to earn God's favor. Consider the language some Christians carelessly use. For example, when something disappointing happens in a person's life, and it is said by such person What did I do to deserve this? Does not such a question reveal a belief that blessings in this life are a result of being good and curses are a result of being bad? And when one Christian describes another person as a really good Christian, oh, she's a really good Christian, or simply good Christian. Does not such labeling reveal that the person speaking believes a Christian is made good by the works he or she does? And when a person beats herself up or himself up over personal failings, does not such personal abuse reveal that he or she believes that if she works hard enough If he can do just a little bit more, that he or she is then worthy of more blessings. Beloved, the foundation of repentance from dead works turns away from any action or statement A belief or belief in thought that what we practice in this life earns God's favor. Repentance from dead works has us believing the opposite. And the opposite is that there is nothing we can do to earn God's favor, but only what Jesus has done. For what Jesus has done is the only thing that grants us forgiveness, that gives us hope. Repentance from dead works is a foundation stone that must be a part of our Christian foundation for anything else to be built upon us. If it is not, we are handicapped. If repentance from dead works is not established in our lives, if we are not confessing the sin of thinking we can earn God's favor. Then we are like a man with one deaf ear who is trying to compensate and it looks like he's trying to get a kiss. Don't be that guy. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Foundation of Faith
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: May the words of my mouth and the meditation of our hearts be acceptable in thy sight, O Lord, our strength. And our Redeemer, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. Foundation. Foundation. What is to be laid to enable a structure to be built up and remain sturdy? Foundation. The element of an architectural structure which connects it to the ground and transfers loads from the structure to the ground. Foundation A skin-colored makeup applied to the face to create an even uniform color to the complexion to cover flaws. Which definition do we need for our second foundation stone? I suppose either the first two will suffice. And what is to be built on the foundation stones that ought to be laid in the life of every Christian? The preacher to the Hebrews says that the end goal we are to build toward in our lives is perfection. And perfection is holiness. And holiness is a state of being sinless. And the state of being sinless is our heavenly reward Laying these foundation stones, then, is a part of our journey to the celestial city, heaven. This is the second installment of our summer series of sermons based on Hebrews chapter 6, verses 1 through 3. There you recall we are given six foundation stones that are to be already established in a Christian's life. And if they are not already established, then they need to be immediately. The challenge for this preacher is coming up with something that is new or interesting to be said about the foundation stone of faith I tend to think that it needs to be something new or something interesting so that it will stay with us. But sometimes nothing new needs to be said because what has already been said is worth repeating. Faith. We read it in our epistle lesson. Faith is best defined in the book of Hebrews to be the substance of things hoped for and the evidence of that which is not seen The substance of faith is the ground or the base upon which we rest our hope. It is the reason for our hope. It is to be the confidence of our hope. Thus, faith is not something that abides on its own But it has to be attached to something greater than itself. And in the case of a Christian, Faith is grounded in the person of Jesus of Nazareth. It is the person of Jesus upon which our faith is grounded. Jesus is who gives us confidence in what we hope for And the hope consists of things that we have not experienced, but only desire to experience. And it is faith that makes those things real to us before we experience them. The early church fathers used the promise of our resurrection. Jesus raised and we are to be raised, and they said that we have faith in our resurrection, even though we have not, of course, experienced it as of yet. But faith allows our resurrection to be a reality. To us, even before we die. Faith The evidence of things not seen. Evidence is demonstration. The demonstration of things not seen Evidence is convincing proof. Convincing proof of what The answer is things not seen. Faith is convincing proof of things not seen. And what are things not seen? Well, the the spiritual world is not seen, not seen by the human eye Christians have convictions that the spiritual world exists, and that means, yes, there are angels, and yes, there are devils They are real, and there is a heavenly realm, and that God is spirit, and that the Holy Spirit is as real as the Son and as the Father. All of it is unseen, and yet we are to be convinced of its being real, just as everything else in life we experience as being real. In um in my teaching I use a sleight-of-hand trick to help my students understand that although we depend a great deal upon our senses to understand the world in which we live That does not mean that our senses are always reliable. I put a substance, sometimes a coin, in this case just a Top of a pen in my hand and I take my other hand and people watch the other hand, right, and it makes it look like you're picking that thing up and you didn't It's the easiest slide of hand trick there is, once practiced. It looks like the objects transferred to this hand when in secret it was actually dropped into the other hand. And it's supposed to make you realize that what you think you see actually didn't happen. And what happened was actually hidden from your eyes. And that's very much like the spiritual world. We do not see what is actually before us. Unless we see it by faith. Understanding that there's a world out there going on that we cannot see, that we do not know so much about But think about that there are other things that we do not see. We do not see love, for example. And I know we see expressions of love, a good hug, a good kiss. We see examples of love, of people doing service to another. But we do not see the substance of love as if it is a physical being. And we do not see forgiveness. We do not see sins being tossed physically as far as the East is from the West. We do not see actual blood washing away the debt of sin. But love and forgiveness are as real as any other reality that we you and I can know. And yet, love and forgiveness are only real to those who know Jesus, who love Jesus. For it is only knowing Jesus as Savior that a person can know true love, not the love they sing about on the radio. But the true love of God, an actual forgiveness, eternal forgiveness. And so faith is the evidence of love And forgiveness. Both are not seen. But faith, faith gets a bad rap, doesn't it? Faith is spoken about in unfriendly tones, in even judgmental tones. Faith is said to be A cheap way to justify a belief in God when there is no empirical evidence to prove that God exists. To underline the bad rap faith is given, the word blind is tacked on. And so a person is accused of having blind faith. But blind faith in reality is just faith given a first name when it is ridicule. To the unfaithful, the people who claim faith, who claim no faith, those who have faith to them are ignorant. They are said to believe in God because they need to believe in something greater than self in order to understand the world and their purpose in the world. God was described by Sigmund Freud, that most famous of psychoanalysts. He described the belief in God as a belief in a Superman figure A Superman figure that weak-minded people need to have in order to believe that they can be saved from my circumstances. And such is the same argument against Christians as the crutch that we have heard for centuries. Jesus is said to be a crutch for us. And with that character, we are to be embarrassed because anyone who uses a crutch Well, they're less than whole, and they're dependent upon the help of something other than self Of late, however, Christians have begun to accept this character of having Christ as a crutch with pride. I recently saw a bumper sticker that said, Jesus is not a crutch. If anything, he is a stretcher. Such accepts the identity of being weak, of being wounded, of being in the need of help. But does not the scripture say that we are dead in our trespasses and sins? And when a person is dead, he needs a stretcher. Jesus is our stretcher, and we say that by faith If anything, Freud was identifying what nature reveals to us, which is that we need a Superman. It is true that we need somebody to save us. And so faith is positively divine as substance of things hoped for. And evidence of things not seen. And then after the positive definition We can even do better if we recognize that faith has its counterfeits. If we look at Hebrews chapter 6, and you can turn there in your Bibles to be helped along, in Hebrews chapter 6, 1 through 3. We can see a different angle about faith when we see that it is presented to us as a parallelism. Now, scholars have long marked the use of parallelisms as a foundation for Hebrew poetry. And we find parallelisms all over the Psalms, and I'll give you a brief example. Here in Psalm 24, Verses 1 through 2 it says, The earth is the Lord's and everything in it. The world and all who live in it. For he established it upon the seas and established it upon the waters Now to say the earth is the Lord's and everything in it, that is stated next by the line, all who live in it. It's a parallelism, a repeat. To say God established it upon the seas, and next to say he established it upon the waters is to say the same thing, only in a different manner. That's a parallelism. Parallelisms are also stated to contrast two things. And so we look at Hebrews 6, verses 1 through 3. With parallelisms in mind, And we can learn that faith is not as it is contrasted against dead works. Faith is not dead works. Remember, the first foundation stone is repentance from dead works. And then the next is faith toward God. And we learned two weeks ago that dead works consist of things that we tried to do to earn God's favor. To repent from such works can also be said to be having faith in God. It's the opposite. Thus, the parallelism is that instead of trusting in works to find favor with God, we do the opposite, which is to have faith in God. Perhaps the most fundamental understanding of faith is found in St. Paul's words to the Christians at Ephesus, where he states. By grace, you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, it is a gift from God. From these words we learn again that faith is something attached to something greater. Christians, and hear this now, Christians don't have faith in faith. Christians have faith in Jesus who procured our salvation. Our faith in Jesus then acts as a conduit that enables grace to flow to us. Faith, then, is a means by which God's grace, his forgiveness, his blessings are given to us. A necessary means. Next, Paul clears up a possible misunderstanding and thus a misapplication of being saved by grace through faith by informing Christians that faith that each of us has For God flows to us as a gift from God The faith we have then is not our faith as if we own it ourselves or conjured it up ourselves, came up with it ourselves, as if we can get more if we desire But instead, it comes from God. As a Christian, I believe because God enables me to believe by giving me faith. The gift of faith is why one group of people will hear the good news of Jesus living and dying and rising again and they give their life to him because of it. And others hear the same message and find no reason to believe and yet turn away from the gospel instead and continue as their own God. The group that turns away does not have faith given by God to believe Let me add more to this. Faith as a gift is further explained in Scripture. As a special gift given by God to certain Christians for the edification of the church. It is listed as a gift by St. Paul in his first letter to the Corinthians. He lists faith along with the gift of tongues, the gift of healing, and others. And because of this faith that is given to all who believe in Jesus as Savior, that faith is titled Saving Faith. Whereas the gift of faith that edifies the church is called the spiritual gift of faith The spiritual gift of faith is displayed when Christians respond with strong and unshakable confidence in God in the midst of very trying times. Consider whereas I could hear, God forbid, that my wife has been stricken with cancer, and I could crumble emotionally My daughter or sons could hear the same news and remain joyful and steadfast with the hope for healing. And that joy and that hope displays the spiritual gift of faith. When someone displays the spiritual gift of faith, it strengthens God's people. It strengthens those who are struggling to trust God, to trust His providence. And it also reminds each of us to pray, asking God for more faith. As we realize faith only comes from Him. He made us, He saved us, and He continues to save us by faith. Faith is something we ask for, just as that father who had that possessed child, Jesus asked him, Do you believe? And he said, and we must repeat it. I believe help my unbelief. Ask for faith As you know, the Bible is filled with stories of men and women of great faith. And their stories are told again and again as encouragement that you and I would apply the faith given to us in moments that try us and tempt us. We must apply the courage faith like that of Daniel who slept with hungry lions. We must apply fearless faith, that of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. Who were confident that a fiery furnace would not take them from the presence of God. We must apply the undaunted faith of Moses, who could see a path through the Red Sea before it parted. We must apply the curiosity faith of Rahab, who did not know the God of Israel, but knew that he was mightier than any God the people of Jericho worshipped. We must apply the against all faith of David, who believed a rock could bring down a great giant. We must apply the counter-cultural faith of Elijah, who alone challenged the prophets of Baal to a duel and saw God destroy them by fire. And we must have the personal faith in Jesus practiced by the apostles, who believed every word that he said, and went out and about. Making disciples in the known world.
