And I viewed a particular picture of the conflict in Charlottesville that had an old Soviet Union flag being carried by a young man on the left for the viewer. As he was yelling across to a young man who was carrying a Nazi Germany flag, also yelling back at the first man. The fact that such was being done on American soil 72 years after World War II is a great irony to all of us. Because of the gospel and thus because of the love of Jesus, we can't hate anyone simply because of their race, gender, or even their creed. And because of the gospel and the reign of Jesus, we cannot put our trust in man or his government structures that say they will wipe out all hate and all classes and all creeds. By way of hate and by way of violence. As Christians, we cannot seize such a conflict and take sides. But again, the devil loves the chaos. He loves the division. And he would love for Christians to take sides. The reality is there is no side for Christians in such a conflict. Well, you may want to stand with one side because they say they are standing against racism. You end up standing with a group of people who don't want any good but the state, and they want the state to be established by violence And when you stand on the other side, because you don't want historic monuments irrationally and ignorantly taken down, you will also be standing on the side of racists and supremacists. Who look at their fellow man as inferior to their kind. So the truth is, no one is on the right side of such a conflict, and both sides are without a father. Such is what happens when fathers are forgotten. Well, I want us to be aware of all the bad that can happen when fathers are forgotten Even the failings of the fathers. If we conclude that our culture is divided, I propose that the Christian church is even more divided. And much of that division is from forgetting the fathers. And by fathers I mean the church fathers. The evangelical church has thrown off memories of their Christian fathers as they pursue being relative to the culture. Church buildings don't like don't look like church buildings anymore, but rather cathetimatoriums, all to be relatives. And the churches that have nice church buildings don't preach the truth anymore, but rather self-help or hatred of all who believe in absolute truth. All of this is a byproduct of forgetting and purposefully ignoring the church fathers. Denomination after denomination has forgotten or purposefully ignored what their founding fathers believed and practiced. And independent churches behave as if the church hadn't existed until they came along. Again. It appears obvious that the reason that secularists want to throw off their fathers and forget them forever is that they don't know what to do with the sins of their fathers. They don't know what to do with the sins of their fathers because they don't know the gospel. The gospel that forgives sins of the past. And saves a person by grace through faith, and not by what a man did or did not do. The two passages come to mind both in the Old Testament that speak to the hope of the gospel that the secular world does not have. The first passage is from Ezekiel chapter 18. It reads, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge. Now this is a challenge given by God to Israel through the prophet Ezekiel. The problem was a common one. The proverb was a common one. That meant that what a father does will have a negative effect upon the children. And God was telling Israel through Ezekiel that such a proverb would no longer be true under the new covenant. Which is under Jesus, the Savior. Each person will be free from suffering a direct guilt for the sins of his or her father. Thus a father's sins do not have to count against his children and their children and their children. This is good news. And to insist that sins of the Father do count against us if we remember them. is to accept the opposite of what the Christian gospel offers. The second verse are actually the last words of the Old Testament from Malachi. The Lord said, and he, God, will return the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to the fathers. Well, this verse assumes the brokenness that sin causes from generation to generation. And the worst but most common brokenness is in the home from father to child and child to father. And God's plan through his son Jesus is to set that right. For under his covenant, forgiveness is freely given and freely received. So that the sins of the father are not counted against him and the father's desires and cares for his children. And this is true for the community as it is for the home. To not want to be in good fellowship is to not want to forgive the sins of the past generations. And such is also rejecting what the Christian gospel offers. It is then the church's role, the Christian's responsibility. To tell the culture in which the Christian lives that the gospel and only the gospel can reconcile one generation to another. It is the gospel, and only the gospel, that allows us to forgive the sins of our fathers, while at the same time allow us to honor our fathers. Christians and only Christians know this good news. And thus it is for us to tell it to a world A world that needs a father. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Our Father
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. I suppose every minister that's worth anything Any preacher that's worth anything thinks that the sermon that he is preaching this day is perhaps the most important ser important sermon he's ever preached. And he probably thinks that every week. I know I But then there's times when he says it, and now he's on the line. And I do feel As I shared with you last week that God had put a burden upon my heart about fatherhood, that these three sermons I'm preaching on the subject are the most important that I've preached. I hope last week reflected that, and I hope you will see it again today. I once feared that Sigmund Freud was right I say feared because I thought that if he was right, that humanity was irrevocably messed up, and God is not necessary. But I can now say that Freud was right, right on some things. And it is understandable That he would be right on some things because any person who is smart enough and works hard enough is able to discover truths about the created order and human nature that are observable. Just watch, pay attention, write some notes, and draw conclusions. Whereas Freud concluded that all human behavior is expression of sexual desire, it can be agreed That most human behavior is an expression of the lust of the flesh. Lust of the flesh may or may not be sexual There is lust for power, lust for influence, lust for material wealth, etc. These all can play a powerful role in motivating a person to make choices in life. It was also Freud who speculated about the great influence fathers have upon the mental health of their children. Freud observed impulses in persons to either seek out a relationship with their father or run from such a relationship as fast as possible. The impulse, whether positive or negative, was based on how a child was treated by his or her father. Unfortunately, Freud's observations became clouded because of his sexual obsession, resulting in the Oedipus complex theory. But this being, but this beginning observations about people having strong impulses toward their biological father, that is spot on. And that impulse, both positive and negative, has far-reaching repercussions. When I was ministering to youth, my first official assignment in the church, Kennewick, Washington, sits right central of Washington State. A young father approached me wanting to start a Bible study for young fathers. We decided we would read a book that would encourage Christian men to be better fathers. We decided to meet every Tuesday morning as early as possible. The total number of men that met were about eight, again, primarily consisting of young fathers. And one particular man, a husband and a father, he was quite outgoing in his personality and very faithful to the Bible study. Well, it was less than a year from when the Bible study started that we moved so that I could attend seminary And it was in my first year in seminary that I learned that one of the men from our Bible study was arrested. The same man who was outgoing and faithful to the Bible study, he was arrested for molesting his daughter. And he had been molesting her for over two years I know of a young man who was involved in his church's youth program, quite active, and when he went to college he was involved in campus crusade ministry He started pursuing a girl who was also a part of that same campus ministry. They went out a few times, and then the last time they went out, he forced himself upon her. And he date raped her. The act resulted in her being pregnant. When the young man learned of her pregnancy, He berated her and coerced her into having an abortion because he wanted to keep up his Christian image. Months later, the young girl dropped out of school, fell into a deep depression until she confessed to her pastor that she had killed her baby. Her exact words were, My baby is dead, I killed my baby I have heard of a husband who chose to attend a certain church only because the pastor preached about submission of wives to their husbands. And the need for fathers to discipline their children. This father-husband walked and talked like a macho Christian. Who knew how to keep his children and his wife in line. And he knew what Bible passages to quote to justify his leadership. But cracks started to develop in the family life, as people noticed that the wife did not simply submit to her husband, but she cowered in his presence. And finally, a call was received by the pastor late one night as he was informed that the submissive wife was on her way to the hospital. Because her macho husband believed he had a right to physically abuse her when she didn't obey as he felt she should. I ask you to suffer me one more story. A young woman came into a pastor's office so afraid she couldn't sit. She shared with the pastor, pacing back and forth. Shared with the pastor because she needed to share with someone That her brother had molested her throughout her childhood, and she finally got up the courage to tell someone, so she told her aunt. And her aunt directed her to a family priest who decided the girl was so vulnerable that he too could molest her. Thankfully, with this new pastor, the suffering in silence stopped. Such behaviors are a small sampling of sins that occur amongst people who call themselves Christian. Such sins are practiced by earthly fathers who claim to have a faith in Jesus. And it is painful to make such a statement. And such sins occur in every church because every church houses sinners. And sinners can behave in reprehensible ways. And such sins are tough to point out and to talk about because we are tempted to wish that they did not happen and we want to believe that is not us. But there are women and children who suffer in homes by abusive husbands and fathers, and they do not find refuge in the church. Because the church won't address the sin. And all of this suffering eventually falls to the Heavenly Father. As he is eventually understood to be ultimately responsible for this suffering The questions sound as follows. Why didn't God prevent this from happening? Why didn't God stop it? Of course, no person can answer such questions. They are specific to specific persons and events that only a few know of. But Scripture does provide answers, answers that open up a reality that leads to reprehensible sins. The first reality is that all of humanity are sinners. You know that, but Recognize that all of humanity are sinners and thus capable of doing reprehensible things. We are all sons of Adam, as Adam is our first covenant head, and under his headship is sin and death. Isaiah states, Isaiah 43 states, your first forefather sinned, and your spokesman transgressed against me. Well that verse is another parallelism. It says the same thing, but differently. Our first forefather Adam sinned against God. Our spokesmen who represented all of humanity transgressed against God And to add to the poor headmanship of Adam is the moment he was confronted by God, hiding in the garden. God asked Adam, who told him he was naked. Adam replied, the way all fallen, sinful men respond, he passed blame. He blamed Eve. Our covenant head sinned against God, having all of humanity thrown out of the Garden of Eden, and then he denied responsibility. And it is a pattern that all men but one have since followed. And what were Adam and Eve rejecting when they were heeding the words of the serpent instead of the words of God? We often talk about what was in their heart when they first sinned, and we easily identify that as pride. But what were they rejecting? They were rejecting the fatherhood of God. And just as there were serious repercussions, For sinning against God, so too were their serious and unsuspecting repercussions for rejecting the fatherhood of God. Let us consider the serious repercussions of mankind and his sin, and then draw that parallel to see how much we have lost by rejecting God as our Father. Before the floods, the earth as judged before the floods that judged the earth because of sin. We learn of the diagnosis that God gave of the situation. In Genesis 6 It says, the Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great on the earth. And we stop and consider that no one gave God a summary or a report. He was the witness to this. And he was the deciding factor in the evaluation. The evaluation continues. And that every intent of the thoughts of man's hearts was evil continually. Continually. The word every is a universal affirmative. It leaves no room for the existence of something different. It cannot read every intent of the thoughts of the hearts of mankind where evil continually accept Sissy or Susie or Frank or George No, Sissy, Susie, Frank, and George have to be included. Now I ask you to consider what has changed in the hearts of humanity since God gave such a diagnosis. Are the hearts of men any better than they were with this original diagnosis? The only answer that makes sense is that the hearts of men are better because God made them better by the works of Jesus and the presence of the Holy Spirit But what about people who don't have their sins paid for by Jesus and who do not have the Holy Spirit? Where are their hearts? Now, you might know some people who are upstanding citizens and who are really, really nice folks, nicer than many Christians you know And you say, well, they have good hearts, even though they don't know of Jesus. But it is required for me to respond, how do you know? How do you truly know another person's heart There is a very real possibility that any nice person that you know is not nice for the right reasons. And by right reasons, I mean holy reasons. I mean selfless reasons Many people can be nice, really, really nice, and their motive is selfish pride by the fact that they want people to think of them as really, really nice. By pointing this out, I am merely agreeing with God and his diagnosis that humanity is bent toward evil. But we have many mixed motivations for doing nice things, really, really nice things. We still have selfish motivation. And our motivations are really messed up when we do wrong things. Our hearts are bent toward evil continually unless Jesus changes our hearts. And therefore, we shouldn't be surprised when people in our world do evil things. We shouldn't utter such a ridiculous phrase as, I can't believe he did that. I can't believe they believed that. We should be able to believe that he did that or they believed that because we know the hearts of men at least enough to know they are bent. In which direction they're bent. We know God's diagnosis. Now let us take that diagnosis and apply it to our rejection of God as our Father. Our hearts are bent on rejecting the fatherhood of God and that continually. And such a rejection can be seen in a society's rejection of fatherhood in general. Think of in times past, such a rejection of fatherhood was done quietly, personally, and now it is blatant and it's publicly sanctioned. We have groups in our culture that promote that a child only needs a mother. We have paternity suits that declare that a father is a donor and nothing more. We have lesbian couples using artificial insemination to put together a pseudo-family that tells the children and the culture that fathers are not needed. In fact, in this world, new world culture, the only use for men, seemingly, are for props on television sitcoms. So that they can be the dumb ones in the family who only pass gas, watch television, and want sex from their wives. And we also have among us a rejection of fatherhood of our heritage, which we heard about last week. And that rejection, again, is because we do not know what to do with the sins of our fathers. We don't know what to do with the sins of our fathers because our culture has rejected the gospel. And so the rejection of fatherhood in general, and the cultural conclusion that fathers are not needed Eventually leads to the rejection of God. It is the rejection of God in the home and in the public square Because just as fathers are not needed, so God is not needed as he is the definition of father. But it is a lie. It is a lie And it is one of the biggest lies ever told and ever believed. We all need God as our heavenly Father. All of humanity from the beginning to the end of the world and beyond needs God as Heavenly Father. I mentioned last week that our besetting sins Our psychological problems, our emotional issues, our relational struggles are rooted in our need to have a better relationship with our Heavenly Father. And as a pastor who knows himself enough, and who knows the troubles of others, I believe that such to be important To acknowledge and to do something about. Modern Christendom found in what are called evangelical circles. Doesn't understand our need for the Heavenly Father This is another way the church, yes, even the conservative church, has failed our communities as we don't see the basic impulse of all human beings to know the Heavenly Father. Evangelicals get that title by claiming to preach and teach and believe the evangel or the gospel. They are differentiated between them from the mainline liberal churches that have abandoned the authority of the Bible Evangelicals claim to believe all that the Bible teaches with an emphasis on the good news of Jesus And a major emphasis of this gospel for evangelicals is that each of us can have a personal relationship with Jesus Christ. But I ask you this. Is that what the scripture teaches? Is that what the scriptures teach? Consider from our reading from Galatians what the end goal is God sent his son, born of a woman, born under the law, so that The phrase sets up the real reason for it all, so that those under the law, all of us, might receive adoption as sons. Did you hear that? Do you understand that? God the Father sent his son to die and to rise again so that so that we could be adopted into a family in which we call God our Father. That is the end goal for God to be our Father. It continues in Galatians with the explanation that the Holy Spirit is in the hearts of the believer to enable the believer to cry out, Abba Father. In fact, a good argument can be made that calling God Abba, as it is the only Aramaic word for Father Is primarily used in the context of expressing a personal relationship with the father. So it is having a personal relationship with the Father that is the gospel. Now I realize it may sound like I am preaching against having a personal relationship with Jesus. I am not. Check my notes. Check the tape Jesus is the only means by which we can call God our Father. Jesus is the only means which our Father hunger can be satisfied and our relationship with the Father healed. Jesus deserves all of the praise. Jesus deserves the glory, and the Father desires to give his son the glory. But it was the goal of Jesus to bring us to the Father, his Father And that is proven by the way he taught us to pray and the desire for us to see the Heavenly Father in him, saying that if we've seen Him, we've seen the Father and known the Father. Read your Bibles again and look for the Heavenly Father Here he is, providing good gifts to those who ask of him. He is here seeing you pray in secret. He is here seeing your kind deeds that are going unnoticed. He is here knowing your needs before you ask of him. He is here counting the number of hairs on your head. He is here pitying us as we strive against ourselves and against him. He is here wanting to give his mercy to his children and to their children. He is here waiting for his prodigal to come home. And for his prideful son to come inside and join the celebration. Beloved, I confess to you that before I prepared this sermon, I did not see the importance of the relationship we are to have with our Heavenly Father. All of my preaching before was about getting right with Jesus. And now I see that the preaching of Jesus was about us getting right with the Father. The father impulse that Freud identified is real. The fact that our heavenly fathers have let us down time and time again, well that's real too. And because our covenant head Adam rejects God's fatherhood, we are born with a nature that rejects the fatherhood of God without thinking. But God the Father was in Jesus, reconciling the world to himself. Jesus was sent and was obedient and overcame death and hell so that you and I could know the Heavenly Father. And call him our father. And doesn't it feel good to call him your father? To know the Heavenly Father calms the psyche, heals damaged emotions, and puts our relationships in right order. I love our liturgy for many reasons, but we follow the 1662. And in that order of service, we hear God's word preached and we say, Oh woe is me. We hear God's word read and we see our lives that we don't match up to God's word. And we confess our sins and we need the grace of God. Forgive us our sins. We receive the means of grace as a memorial of our sins being forgiven. And then, and then we get to say, our Father. We are privileged to say our Father. Let us pray. Our Father, we are grateful to you. For opening up your word in this manner. We pray, dear Lord, that those hearts that need to be healed, knowing you as Father, That a relationship that Jesus wants needs to develop between us and you. May it be so. May our understanding and privilege grow and grow till we get to call you our Father. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Earthly Fathers
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: My hands have for you. In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. They are called PSAs. Stands for Public Service Announcements. And I hear them on the radio on a regular basis in my travels, as well as that they appear on television. And the ones I hear a lot promote adoption. One particular PSA on television shows a daughter lying in bed and she's obviously depressed, and there is a father sitting next to her in a chair trying to console her. It appears that she has lost her boyfriend. He struggles as to what to say until he comes up with an analogy. He tells her that dating is like the stock market. It has its ups, and then it has its downs, it has its ups, and then it has its downs He pauses, looking around as if trying to find something more to say. He finishes by saying so by low. He then gets up, looks at his watch, walks out of the room, and the daughter rolls her eyes. The scene ends with a voice over saying, you don't need to be perfect to be a perfect parent And the premise of the ads are effectual, although I don't know if it's improving anybody's interest in foster parenting This sermon is the third and last in the series of sermons I told you three weeks ago that I believed God was laying upon my heart. The first look at what to do with the sins of our fathers, as in the fathers of our heritage. As Christians and as the church, we have the answer to a culture who does not know what to do with the sins of our heritage. Because we know the gospel, we know how to forgive and to honor at the same time Next, we look at the need of each human being to be in right relationship with the Heavenly Father And we learned that the gospel is about Jesus placing us in right relationship with the Father, thus making us privileged to call him our Father. Today, we are looking at earthly fathers. Earthly fathers who are not perfect. That need to strive to be so. This series is on fatherhood. Last week, I told four stories that described reprehensible sins done by earthly fathers. I did so to acknowledge that such sins occur in the church and to show how the Heavenly Father gets the ultimate blame. Because we think he should have done something to stop such sins. We humans, you know, want it all. We want freedom of the will to be able to choose our behaviors, and yet we want God to thwart the will when chosen behaviors will harm us or harm others. But we can't have it both ways, for we are in a world where people suffer because of the sins of others and because of their own sin. That is the way of it. But God intervened into that world so that one man could suffer for the sins of many, so that the many could become sons of God. Amen. But I also told you those stories with the knowledge that most of us have had bad experiences with our earthly fathers. And some of those experiences are so bad, they remain having damaged us today. And for some, the damage is so great, they just seem to can't get over it. You still feel damaged by your earthly father. And what I'm about to say to those who feel that way is unpopular but necessary. Those of you who feel you can't get over the sins of your father. Don't die a victim. Don't die a victim. I have counseled men and women who can't get past the hurt done to them by their earthly father. Every problem of today goes back to the pain that they feel from the treatment they received from their earthly father. Their hurts of the past have turned into permanent bitterness. Unless such bitterness is relieved, unless they are delivered from the bitterness that they choose to pick up and make a part of their identity, they will go to the grave a victim. And victims who choose to remain victims only feel sorry for themselves. They feel sorry that they were victims of their father's failures. What they fail to see in their victimhood is that their father was a victim of his father's failures. As was his father's father. And all of us can trace the failures of our fathers back to Adam. But a believer in Jesus has been adopted as a son of the Heavenly Father. The fatherhood in our lives is not limited to earthly fathers. And our heavenly father is perfect He never fails us. He is not fickle. He certainly will never abuse. He is intimate. He is a friend who sticks closer than a brother, and he is the one who can deliver us from our bitterness. And so I repeat, don't die. A victim. And once we get beyond our earthly fathers having failed us, we can next look to the Bible as it teaches fathers how to be pleasing to the Lord. And the first biblical teaching fathers are given is to take responsibility. Fathers are to take responsibility, all responsibility in the family. By responsibility. I do not mean that a father is to micromanage the household, nor do I mean that the father is directly responsible for all that goes on in the household. By responsible, I am referring to bracing embracing the role as covenant head As covenant head of the home, each father is to take on the responsibility of the household, especially when that responsibility has overwhelmed his wife and his children. Now the principle of taking responsibility for a household is found in Genesis. You already know the story of the first couple sinning. But we are to notice that even though it was Eve who first sinned and then Adam, the description of their fall is that Adam sinned. In Adam, all mankind sinned. Thus Adam is given the responsibility of his household, even though Eve was to blame as well. That is what covenant heads do, and that is what covenant heads are to embrace, because it is not like the fathers have a choice. Fathers are responsible for their households even when the father doesn't want to accept the role of responsibility. I have counseled men who threw off my instruction that they take responsibility for the condition of their home. I've even had men argue back to me that God doesn't take responsibility for the fall of Adam and Eve, so why should he take responsibility for the sins of his wife and his children? I hope you can guess how I responded. The beauty of the gospel is that God did take responsibility for the household of Adam by Jesus becoming the new Adam. As the new Adam, Jesus was able to start a new household. And he took responsibility for that household by paying, by sacrificing for the sins of that household. Men have to love their wives, love their children, and that means taking responsibility for them. Covenant responsibility. Well what does that look like practically? Well practically a father takes responsibility when his son throws a rock through his neighbor's window. He takes responsibility in that he did not teach him well enough the importance of respecting other people's property. He still punishes his son while taking responsibility. When siblings fight and it gets quite heated and physical, a father takes responsibility He has not trained his children well enough to restrain their emotions and to love their brother and sister as they should. The children are still punished for fighting, but the father takes responsibility. When a husband and wife are not getting along, the father takes responsibility. He confesses his weakness in expressing his temper. He confesses his inability to forgive. He expresses that he has not loved his wife as Christ has loved the church. And when a father sins, when a father sins, he takes responsibility. He is to confess his sins to his children if his sins have harmed his children He's to confess his culpability when he has done things against them that he should not have done, or when he has not done things for them that he should have done. And that includes times when his children have witnessed his mistreatment of their mother. He needs to apologize and seek the forgiveness for his children for not loving his mother as he should, their mother as he should. And I prophetically state that many relationships can be healed today if a father would apologize to his children. Even if the children have grown and have their own households, many disorders and emotional disturbances and bitterness can be overcome. If children are able to hear from their father such words as, I am sorry for failing you and for hurting you, please forgive me. There is covenantal gospel power in such words. Believe it Well, next, a God-fearing father is to embrace and promote fruitfulness He is to love being a father, a grandfather, and a great-grandfather if he is allowed to live that long. After all, if the Heavenly Father is fruitful, so should the fathers who follow his lead be fruitful. Of course, God's first instruction to Adam was to be fruitful and multiply. God gave a similar instruction to all his covenant heads, to be fruitful. They were to be fruitful, which meant having many offspring, and not just themselves, but their children as well. Having a fruitful family is being a Christian. That has been lost in some Christian circles As couples speak about collecting earthly goods and affording college and having time to themselves. But such speaking is not biblical. Decision to have few children and be concerned about earthly goods is not included in the teachings of Jesus. Who told us not to worry about tomorrow, and that his followers were to seek first his kingdom and righteousness, and that all the earthly needs will be taken care of. Jesus said those things not being indifferent or in opposition to God's command to be fruitful, but in light of that command. But there is a catch to this. There is wisdom still to be shared. It is not a righteous virtue to have many children as if the number of those children itself has a righteous value. There are plenty of men and women who are capable of having many children. In the Christian covenant, there is a catch of having covenant fruitfulness. Which means that we are to have children who know the Lord. We are to have children that we can capably raise to love Jesus and to worship Him alone. As was stated to me many years ago, there is no virtue in populating hell. Christians shouldn't have a lot of kids just to have a lot of kids. There must be a determined and planned means to pass the faith along to the next generation, with no child missing out on covenant blessings. It is thus a part of a father's love of fruitfulness to raise his children, all of them, in and under the covenant of Jesus. Next, to raise children in and under the Christian covenant, a father must be a teacher. God's first instruction to Israel as a people, being under his covenant, was for fathers, fathers to diligently teach their sons about God's commandments. They were to talk of them when they sit in their house, when they walk by the way, when they lie down and when they rise up. They were to bind God's law on their hands and on their foreheads and on their doorposts and on their gates. So that God's law was a part of their identity and the identity of their children. Isaiah the prophet said to God, a father tells his sons about your faithfulness. A child's education is the responsibility of the father. Well, practically we know that fathers cannot spend the time needed to teach their children all that they need to know. But the father most certainly can assure that his children are being taught by those who have the time and the resources. And practically we can also say that a child should learn directly from his father, by hearing the reading of Holy Scripture, by catechism recitation. And by being an example as a learner himself. I have told my sons that a godly man is always reading a book. It may take him some time to finish a book, but he is always reading a book Next, to be a father that pleases the Heavenly Father. A father must be a good churchman. He must submit to his church fathers as he expects his wife and children to submit to his leadership. He is a good churchman who serves the local church where his gifts are best utilized and where he is working where no one else is willing to work. He is a good churchman who accepts the church discipline when needed, or who simply heeds the word of God as it is preached and taught by those ordained to lead. He is a good churchman who gives his tithes and his offerings so that the church can minister to all who are in the household of faith. He is a good churchman who encourages his family to do their part in the church, so that the body of Christ is using all of its body parts to maintain good health. Next, to be a father that pleases the Heavenly Father, a father must be a disciplinarian. He first must be disciplined in his own life. He cannot be given to vices that ruin his health or compromise his morals. But his own life is disciplined. The father then is better able to discipline his children, for they follow his example. And the Bible cannot be more clear about a father's role to discipline his children. If a rod is spared. Not used to discipline child, that a child becomes spoiled by his own impulses. With hearts bent toward evil and that continually, our children need to be disciplined so that they learn how to say no to their impulses, the desires of the flesh. To say no to a heart that wants to rebel against the Heavenly Father. As the writer of Proverbs warns Apply your heart to discipline and your ears to words of knowledge. Do not hold back discipline from the child. Although you strike him with the rod, he will not die. You shall strike him with the rod and rescue his soul. It was such a passage I had in the back of my mind when I first became a father, and still do today as a grandfather. It always hurt me to see my children give in to their fleshly impulses so easily. Someone need to help them be saved from that. If a father truly loves his children, he will work to rescue them from their fleshly impulses by disciplining them. Proverbs says the same. He who withholds his rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him diligently. Beloved, that is the word of God to us. It is his holy word as he uses stark and dramatic language to get across to us how important it is to discipline our children. Next and finally, at least for our time this morning. A father that pleases the heavenly father loves his children. And his love is phileo, brotherly, and it is agape, heavenly. A father loves his children, meaning that he cares for them as they are. He values them unconditionally, and he will never give up on them or forsake them. The love of an earthly father provides security and peace to the soul of a child all of his or her days. Such a love is provided to a child like no one else can give. For a person to know that he or she is loved by his or her earthly father is a power Is a gift, is something that every child needs, and the most precious gift to receive. A father who takes responsibility for the family without love is of no use. A father who is fruitful, without love, leaves nothing of value behind. A father who teaches many wise things without love has wasted his knowledge. A father who is a good churchman but does not love is a dangerous witness to the gospel. A father who disciplines his children but does not love trains an army for the devil. A godly father is a loving father. I close with a charge to all of you who are not fathers. What fathers are called to be and to do by God is a great, great task, as you have heard. But it is much more difficult when men are expected to act like women and thus not be fathers. Wives, children, allow the father of your home to be the father God wants him to be. Mothers and mothers-in-law allow fathers to be fathers. Don't expect them to be like mothers. Don't expect them to be like you. Pray that you might control yourself in allowing fathers to be fathers. Allow the Holy Spirit to show you when you are trying to control a situation that actually needs a father. Now, perhaps more than ever before, perhaps more than ever before, in the history of Western civilization, we need fathers. We need our forefathers as we understand their sin and their virtue We need the Heavenly Father as the end goal is to be in right relationship with Him and thus call Him our Father. And we need godly fathers in our Christian homes to lead as God has called them to lead. And if this happens, By His grace, in our lifetime, if this happens, the church will indeed be a city set on a hill. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Introduction to Ezra
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. And what an appropriate hymn to sing during this time of upheaval, weather-wise. Truly is the awesome God that we serve, even when his little finger moves. How did we get here? No fault divorce that allows couples to leave their vows made before God and men With no repercussions besides the deterioration of a foundation stone for a society and its culture, which is the marriage covenant. How did we get here? Homosexual marriage being upheld by as lawful by the Supreme Court of the United States. Resulting in a culture that sanctions sodomy and in general sanctions sexual intimacy that can bear no fruit. How did we get here? Transgenderism has been changed from a very serious mental disorder to a suppressed minority group. That needs their own bathrooms and special laws that protect such people so that they can serve in the military. How did we get here? We fail to label things properly. A parent uses a rod to discipline his child, and he is a child abuser. A parent lets a child express his temper by throwing tantrums and getting his way, and that is called patient parenting. A person of moral conviction expresses concern about the moral failings of a culture that has allowed sexual expression to become unhinged, and he is called bigoted A homophobe and an oppressor. A person who promotes unhinged sexual expression is called open-minded and free. A news reporter blatantly lies to promote his or her political agenda, and he or she is said to be promoting the greater good. A spokesman points out the lie, and he or she is called divisive. Trying to help someone out of a sinful lifestyle is called being judgmental. While encouraging destructive behavior is being understanding. And it is ironic that one of mankind's first responsibilities given by God was to properly name things. And now we name things the opposite of what they are. How did we get here? Politicians and religious leaders point out that there is much suffering that is occurring within minority communities that is self-inflicted. And such people then are called racist. While organizations like Planned Parenthood kill more and more minorities every year, and they are called promoters of choice. How do we get here? Churches with deep Christian roots who once proclaimed Jesus and only Jesus as God and Savior today don't even mention his name. While allowing false gods to be prayed to in lust of the flesh to be promoted from the pulpits. How did we get here? Gender is taught to be no longer determined by one's biological makeup, but by a decision of the will. And thus some parents Don't call their sons sons or their daughters daughters, but wait to see what the child wants to be. How did we get here? I repeatedly ask, how did we get here to bring our current state of being within today's Western culture? To be in contact with and in relationship with Israel at the end of the 6th century BC. They too were asking themselves, how did we get here? The book we are venturing into in this series of sermons is the Book of Ezra. The person of Ezra was a descendant of Hilkiah, the priest who was given the responsibility to restore true faith. to Israel under the leadership of King Josiah. Ezra, like Hilkiah, was chosen by God to return to Jerusalem after being a prisoner in Babylon. So that he could teach the people about God and about God's laws. He went from Babylon to Jerusalem 80 years after the return of Zerubbabel. Who was the leader of the first return of Israel back to the promised land, just as Jeremiah had prophesied Israel went into captivity and the majority of the people were taken to Babylon in 586 BC around there. The end of that first return led by Zerubbabel was 516 BC, matching the 70 years promised by Jeremiah. Unfortunately, from the time of the first return to this time where Ezra is called, the people of Israel had made little or no progress, restoring the temple Nor had they done well in practicing their Jewish faith. When Ezra arrived and took inventory of the state of God's peoples Initially he would have asked, how did we get here? If Ezra did ask such a question, the question could be answered. Israel got there by repeatedly breaking the covenant God had made with them. Hear what was clearly stated by God from Deuteronomy chapter 29. God said, Your children who follow you in later generations and foreigners Who come from distant lands will see the calamities that have fallen on the land and the diseases with which the Lord has afflicted it All the nations will ask, why has the Lord done this to the land? Why this fierce burning anger? Then the answer will be, it is because this people abandoned the covenant of the Lord, the God of their ancestors, the covenant he made with them when he brought them out of Egypt. Therefore, the anger of the Lord burned against that land to bring upon it every curse which is written in this book. And the Lord uprooted them from their land in anger and in fury and in great wrath, and cast them into another land. Well, the warning of God could not have been more clear. And yet, it was not that simple. Because God is a God who is slow to anger and merciful And so Israel would break the covenant it had with God, and God would punish them with other nations, but he would not cast them out of the promised land. Even though they deserved to be cast out. And then they would sin again as a people, and God would punish them again, only not cast them out of the promised land, even though it was just Such was the repeated case until the sin stench of Israel became too much, requiring that they be cast out into another land until they can start all over again. Ezra is this instrument for starting again. It is then appropriate to ask about the level of our stitch. Are we at the point of no return? Now when I say our stent Or ask, if we are at the point of no return, I do not use the pronouns our and we to refer to citizens of the United States of America. Beloved, I know that the following is a reminder, but it needs to be said again. God has made no promises when it comes to the United States of America. Too often, well-meaning Christians apply promises that God made to Israel as if he made it to the United States. For example, too often Christians have quoted this verse from Second Chronicles. If my people Who are called by my name will humble themselves and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways. Then I will hear from heaven and I will forgive their sin and will heal their land. The context in which those words were spoken was at the dedication of King Solomon's temple. Those beautiful words of promise by God to Solomon were spoken about the nation of Israel, not the United States of America. If any application of said verse applies to us today, it would be in the context of the church. For the church is a part of God's covenant with Israel. And as such, it is the church where we find God's people who need to seek his face and turn from their ways so that God can figuratively heal their land. Now we ask, how did we get here? Concerning the craziness that is our culture today. And that question also can be answered We got here today because the church has been impotent in changing the culture in which we live. And the church is us. Instead of changing the culture for the better, the majority of people who call themselves Christians have been busy assimilating into the culture. instead of being salt and light as Jesus intends for us to be. We got here by being silent when no-fault divorce became a part of our culture's identity. We got here when sex outside of marriage was being practiced by professing Christians as much as it was amongst unbelievers. And the church had no clear voice about such behavior. We got here when the sexual revolution began and the church was muzzled because of her hypocrisy. We got here when the culture said, let us have women be as men. And so the church, wanting to be relevant, ordained women to holy orders. We got here when the culture said rock music speaks to the younger generation, so the church, seeking to be relevant, should duplicate such music, only replacing drugs with Jesus. We got here when a lie was told that sexual orientation is genetic and thus normal. And therefore what the Bible says about it is archaic and prejudice. And the church said, okay, we got here because Christian leaders began to care more about how many people were attending their services. Then they cared about fearing God and making disciples. We got here when Christians divided more quickly and more dangerously than cancer cells because they wanted their own type of worship. They wanted the type of church government that they wanted and the type of teachings that they wanted. And all of it was a genuflect to relativism. But relativism is a false God, never satisfied. Relativism is always changing, and the church is never catching. Relativism always has new experiences that lead to inevitable compromise. What Ezra is going to teach us is that God's people are only relative to the world when they start acting as God's people. After all, the Greek word for church is ekklesia, meaning the called out ones. Called out for what? The world. It is a people called out to be away from the world. We are to be a city on a hill so that when people seek life, they find it. We are to be the salt on this earth, so whoever seeks health, flavor, and preservation to life will find it. Ezra is going to tell us that we, as God's people, are to rejoice in being different. And what makes us different will give us a voice in the world that is spiraling to its demise. I ask you, where else can you hear the words, the body of the Lord Jesus Christ? Spoken for you. Where else can you hear the words, the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ shed for you? The answer is, nowhere but the church. Where else do you adjust your posture to show adoration, especially kneeling to pray? Nowhere else does anyone ask you to kneel to make a request. For nowhere else is there someone worthy that is present. Who is owed your allegiance, complete allegiance? Nowhere else are you asked to sit and listen. To someone who provides you no entertainment value, offers you instead something you may not want to hear, that is not always easy to hear. Where else but the church? Nowhere else are you reminded that from dust you came and to dust you shall return. Nowhere else but the church. The most relative actions a church can take, the most relative things a church can do to and for a dying world is to be different, as the Lord intends us to be. Embrace being different as God has called you to be. Embrace as your identity that you do not pray as those without hope. Embrace that you do not sing only that which is popular. Embrace that you pray to a God you cannot see. And believe a story about a man who claimed he was the Savior. A story that is beyond your physical experience. Embrace that you are a sinner in need of a Savior who offers you forgiveness without any expense to you. Embrace that the world sees you as wasting your time attending church each Sunday. Embrace that the world sees you wasting your money when you tithe to the church. Embrace that the world sees you as a fool who thinks there is a God who cares anything about your life. As stated, Ezra wants Israel to embrace being God's people. And we are going to apply that to us. And embrace being God's people under the covenant of Christ, which is a people who make up the church. Also, what Ezra brings back to Israel that is so prevalent, was so prevalent among Moses and needs to be prevalent among us. Is a collective thinking and a collective being. Collective thinking and collective being is understanding yourself as an individual that is part of something greater than self. So that your identity is what you are as a part of something greater. And thus your state of being is more profound. Because of this collective way of thinking and being, Ezra confesses and laments the sins of the people as his own sins. He sees the sins as his own sins even though he was a new arrival. Even though he was not personally involved in committing those sins, he confesses and then laments over them. And this is going to be a challenge to our modern manner of thinking, for we are trained in our culture to think individually. What is mine is mine, and what is yours is yours. Your problems are your problems, and my problems are my own. Evangelicalism promotes such individualism, speaking about personal salvation and a personal relationship with God. Me and Jesus theology, it dominates so-called Christian media. But Ezra does not think in such terms, in such categories. And he will challenge us not to think about the importance of the individual over the importance of the collective whole. As I have said from this pulpit before, Jesus is not coming back for you or for me. He's coming back for his church. The church as a whole, the church that we are privileged to be a part of. Ezra is going to challenge us to not simply condemn liberal churches who have abandoned the Bible as their authority. But he's going to challenge us to see our part and how that came to be. Ezra is not going to merely point out how other Christians are compromising their faith. He will include us examining ourselves to see where we have compromised or where we have contributed to others compromising. After all, we need to be rebuilt just as Israel needed to be rebuilt in the days of Ezra. I close with a current news topic to hopefully show how challenging this will be for us to rebuild. Many of you have likely heard of the Nashville statement. If you have not, I will summarize this statement. The Nashville Statement is a document most recently has come out that articulates a conservative Christian stance on the issues relating to sex and sexuality It defends the institution of marriage being between one man and one woman. It also teaches that sexual behavior is clearly prescribed in the Bible. And such behavior should not be determined by whether a person identifies himself or herself to be a homosexual or a transgender. And those who agree with the statement are encouraged to sign it online. And many Christian leaders that you know of have done just that. It may sound like a no-brainer. I should sign, you should sign. But wait There has been some valid criticism of the statement, as some argue it does not go far enough. For example, the preamble of the statement identifies a spirit of the age that has led to the sexual moral confusion that we have in our culture today. What the statement does not mention is all that can be included within that spirit of the age. For instance, is the spirit of the age actually being addressed by pastors and denominations That allow people who are divorced to be remarried in the church when there is no justification for the first divorce. Is the spirit of the age being challenged when Christian families see children as something to be protected from? by artificial means rather than a blessing, as the Bible describes them. Is the spirit of the age truly being rebuked while Christians use in vitro fertilization Which removes God-ordained sexual intimacy, taking procreative work outside of the covenant union. Consider that an argument can easily be made that connects easy divorce and remarry. contraception and in vitro fertilization, connecting those to the sexual immorality and the sexual confusion our culture wallows in today. Such an examination and challenge is what Ezra does for Israel and what I believe the Holy Spirit is doing for us. How did we get here? Do we really want to know the answer? What if the answer points to our culpability? Who is willing to be challenged in such a manner? There are plenty of churches who won't talk about this, won't examine themselves. How many are willing to be challenged in this manner? The world would say not many. We shall see. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Stirring the hearts of kings
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Do well to turn in your Bibles to Ezra, one of the historic books of the Old Testament. They're in Ezra chapter 1. To best appreciate what we are studying from Ezra, we must put on our history hats. So put on your history hats. Somewhere in the attic of your mind, you recall hearing and learning about the Greco-Persian wars. At first hearing the relevance of these wars to your life was likely not apparent For young men, the reason why these wars are interesting is because of the story of the 300. The 300 is the supposed number of Spartan men who are part of the Greco army. Who fought to the death at the hot gates during the Battle of Therm Thermopylae. The story has been glamorized by Hollywood But that should not take away from the fact that there were some 300 Spartan warriors who almost for three days held off a Persian army to most certainly outnumbered them vastly. The end of the battle saw a Persian victory, but not before Greek heroes were immortalized. The Greco-Persian War began after Darius, one of many Dariuses, put down an Ionian revolt. And decided he was going to assure Persian Greek loyalty to the Persian Empire. By insisting that each Greek state gave a contribution that he called earth and water. These were tokens of their submission Most Greek cities obliged, except for Athens and Sparta. In Sparta They threw the Persian official down a well. Darius put together a naval presence that would impress today as he forced the Greek island cities to submit to his rule. When the Persians attacked Athens, we hear of another great heroic tale of the Battle of Marathon. Where we get the legend of Pelepides, who was said to run from Marathon to Athens to deliver the news of the Greek victory against the Persians. The Athenian victory turned the tide of the war. It bolstered the confidence of the Greeks that the Persian army could be defeated. And it bolstered the Athenians that they could win a battle without Spartan men. For beforehand, Sparta was instrumental in all of Greek victories. The dates of the Greco-Persian War were approximately 499 to 449 BC. The date of the Holy Spirit moving on Cyrus, king of Persia, moving upon his heart to allow Israel to return to the promised land And Jerusalem specifically was just one generation previous to that Greco-Persian war, or wars. Darius' rule over Persia was so expensive because of the rule of Cyrus the Great, whom we read about from Ezra. And Cyrus was called the great, not only because of the expanse of the Persian Empire under his rule, but because of his manner of ruling. He was the first of rulers who embraced the cultures of the civilized states that he conquered. He thus became a model for establishing a centralized administration that was comfortable to allow foreign states to continue their customs and their religions. And this attitude toward other cultures led to this edict of restoration Which is what allowed the people of Israel to return to Jerusalem and restore the temple for worship. How does that happen? How does a ruler who ruled amongst other barbaric rulers How does he have a different mind and heart that would allow strange customs and unknown religious practices to continue? After all, those were difficult days. Rulers didn't just have to defeat their enemies, they needed to murder them. And all of their family members. They cut off the head of anyone who could claim any part of their throne. And they had to be on constant alert for those who would usurp them, even those in their own court. How does a man living in such a time have a different attitude of being open and amiable toward those he conquered? Especially, especially as compared to those who ruled around him and ruled against him The answer is obvious trust. The difference is caused by God Verse 1 of chapter 1 says, The Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus, King of Persia. The Lord stirred up. Recall the story of King Abimelech. King of Gerar, who took Sarah in to make her his wife, until God interrupted his dreams and warned him not to touch her. That is God stirring up. We call the story of Balaam The four higher prophets who was sent to King by King Abimel by King Balak of Moab to curse the Israelites. Only to be met by God and to do exactly the opposite, which was to bless Israel instead of cursing them And when King Balach interrupted Balaam, he confessed that the Lord compels him, compels him to bless Israel. He could do no other. That is God stirring up. Recall the dreams of King Nebuchadnezzar, those that haunted him in his ruler, rulership over Babylon. Remember that dream God gave him an image, a great image, that was made of fine gold, silver, and bronze and iron, and then clay. Each represented kingdoms that would rise and fall, including the king of Babylon. It was a dream only God's prophet Daniel could interpret That is God stirring up. Consider this proverb from Proverbs chapter 21, verse 1. A king's heart is like streams of water in the Lord's hand. He directs it wherever he chooses. But to best understand this verse, we have to think of little channels of water used by a farmer for irrigation. And such channels bring water under the gardener's control where he wants it to go. So then, too, are the hearts of kings, who seem quite superior compared to their fellow man, but are in no way superior to the God who directs them. by hidden influences, by providential arrangements, by turning a heart to go a different direction without being conscientious of that change God directs the monarchs as he designs. The king may or may or may not fear God or even acknowledge God, but he will do God's bidding. And if he is stubborn enough, and his heart is prideful enough, he will take credit for the decisions he thinks he's making on his own. Decisions that fall perfectly in line with God's will. God still stirs up. Do you believe that? Do you believe that God still stirs up the hearts of kings? So to bring them under his sovereign will. Consider the men and women today who are in powerful positions, similar to that of those kings in Ezra's day. A conversation that occurred with friends recently caught me by surprise We were eating dinner at a restaurant with friends and one of the friends at our table was asking another if he knew anything about Kim Kim Kim Jong-un And the tensions between the United States and North Korea. I was surprised that the person was asking the questions as She evidently knew very little about the tensions and what the leader of North Korea is capable of doing, considering his mental state and his nuclear capabilities. And I began to wonder how many people don't pay attention to current events like this particular person. And in conversing with my family, I realized likely a great many of people don't pay close attention to current events. I didn't mention any names, so don't look over there. And I began to wonder what it would be like for people who don't pay close attention to current events if they woke up one morning To turn on the news and find that one of our allies had been bombed by a nuclear warhead, forcing the United States into a nuclear war that very morning. And I imagine their minds scrambling to wrap their head around the devastation and the danger that millions of people were facing in the days ahead when they knew nothing of it before that day. But I also know amongst my family members that there is a deep faith that understands that God does indeed have the hearts of kings under his control. And they can do nothing except what God wills for them to do. Nothing outside of his sovereign will can be done. By me keeping up with current events, I am not able to control the hearts of kings any more than those who are ignorant. But there is something else that Christians should consider. Christians should consider knowing current events. Such as intended acts by political leaders for the purpose of praying for them. Leaders like Kim Jong-un should be prayed for. Have you thought of that? We should pray for his repentance and for him to come to a faith in Jesus Christ, which would save him and his family. And that new faith would have a great impact for the good for the people of North Korea. After all, we have an example of God transforming the heart of a king in the story of Nebuchadnezzar. Remember him going mad, becoming like a wild beast? Only to come to his senses and acknowledge that the God of Israel was the only true God Such can be done for Kim Jong-un and any ruler like him if God so wills it to be. And we should speak the same about our own leaders. Whether you voted for Donald Trump or not, it is a Christian's duty to pray for him. And to pray for all of our political leaders. And part of our prayer and our faith is to trust that God will stir up their hearts, as He wills to do, for the sake of His kingdom. As we are to be confident that God will stir up the hearts of earthly rulers and move them toward his sovereign will, So too are we to have even more faith on what God can move, considering moving the kings of the earth on his behalf and moving upon the hearts of the masses as well. Look again at what God was able to do, able to get King Cyrus to do. First, he was able to include all of the Persian kingdom in his proclamation. And that kingdom was quite large, covering over three million square miles, spanning over three continents, Asia, Africa, and Europe. Second, he was able to get King Cyrus to confess that the extent of his kingdom was due to the one true God of heaven and earth. Third, he was able to get the king to follow his command to allow Israel to return to Jerusalem in order to rebuild the temple so that the Israelites could properly worship the one living God. Fourth, God is able to influence King Cyrus to influence all of the population of the exiles. Even the once slaves in Persian land to return to Jerusalem, their home, and rebuild Fifth, God is able to influence King Cyrus to allow all who return to Jerusalem to plunder the places in Persia where they find themselves By telling the Jewish people to take silver and gold and goods and livestock with them. And the Persian people were going to help them do it. Let us consider how remarkable such an order is, and remember it is similar to how God brought Israel out of Egypt. They plundered that place as well before they came into the Promised Land. God is once again taking control, sovereign control over a foreign enemy. of his people and giving Israel a victory that was not earned and required no bloodshed. That is amazing. It is unheard of. It is a miracle. As we read on, we see that the people did just as King Cyrus instructed them to do. And the text, the end of verse 6, says that the plunder was willingly offered to God's people. Willingly offered. Take it. Yours. We'll help you load. Willingly offer it. How does that happen? It happens only when God moves the hearts of people. It happens when God enchants the will of man, even having them think it's their idea. And to top all that God had influenced so far, King Cyrus brings out the articles from his treasury that King Nebuchadnezzar had stolen from the temple. And gave them back to Sheshbazar, who was given the responsibility to take them back to the temple for worship. He did not have to do this. King Cyrus didn't have to do this. According to his law, those items were his. They were proper booty from overthrowing the Babylonians. His justice was to keep the gold for his own wealth, his own prosperity, to use it as he saw fit. Instead, he gives it back. He freely gives it to honor the God of Israel. And why? No one else would do such a thing. It is hard to imagine anyone doing such a thing today. Why? Why did he give it all back? Because the hearts of kings is like streams of water in God's hands Consider the words of Jesus in our gospel reading. He explains to his hearers that he is the good shepherd. He is not like the hirelings who run away when danger is present, but instead he is a shepherd who loves his sheep and who lays down his life for his sheep. And he does not lay his life down by compulsion of someone else No, he lays it down by his own will. No one takes his life from him. He tells us that. He alone has the power to lay it down and the power to take it up. But we would have seen it that way if we didn't know him. It looked like his life was being controlled by politics and leaders like Kyophas. Who tried and condemned Jesus. And then it looked like it was controlled by Pilate, who had the authority to set him free or to call for his execution. And then it looked like it was controlled by the people who could cry for his release or cry to crucify him It looked as if everyone but Jesus had power to take his life. And yet the truth was that Jesus had the power all the time. Jesus had the hearts of Ciophus and Pilate and the people sifting through his hands like streams of water being directed by a gardener. Considering what God controls, considering what God controls, perhaps we lament too much about the condition of the world that we live in. Without confessing that our God has the hearts of rulers sifting through his hand. Not perhaps. We do lament too much. Without confessing who controls all of them. When you worry about what type of world your children and your grandchildren will inherit, we are to have faith that God sifts the hearts of kings through his hands. When you decry the state of the country and the state of the church with no evidence of good coming soon, snap out of it. Believing that no one has control of life or death but Jesus who is Savior of the world But it all seems out of control as mankind destroys itself and brother fights against brother. Increase your faith that God is directing the will of men where he wills for the sake of his kingdom to come. You know, on Thursday mornings, we still meet for breakfast at the Harvest Inn. When I arrived 18 years ago, the men were meeting after mowing the church lawn. I involved myself with these old men. Now I am one of them. Although I have resisted about talking about visits to the doctor. But we still meet and talk about the ravens, the Orioles, stories we have seen on the news, and some still talk about doctors' visits. And about restaurants where we had eaten recently. We talk about politics and leaders that make us upset, and the media that makes us upset And a culture that thumbs its nose at God and how bad it all is today. And there's nothing wrong with such conversations, unless Unless we fail to mention who controls the hearts of men, and who is working for his kingdom to come and his will to be done. God's will is going to be done, and Christians need to say and believe it more and more. The darker it gets, the greater the light of Christ can shine. And it is for the Christian church to shine it. God has shown us here in Ezra how he does it. He changes the course of history. He changes the course of history through the hearts of men. He stirred up Cyrus the Great. He stirred up Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar and Pilate. And he will stir up Kim Jong-un and Donald Trump and bishops and pastors. And whoever else it will take for his kingdom to come, for his will to be done. Believe it. Be faithful to the truth of God being sovereign over the hearts of men, no matter what happens. No matter what happens. Let us pray. Our Father and God, we confess today That we have not always trusted that you have the hearts of kings sifting through your hands like water, but today we do And we pray, dear Lord, that our faith might increase to believe it all the more as the days get darker. And Father, as the days get darker, we want to be light. And so help us in our righteousness and our faith be light to this world and to trust and believe your kingdom is coming and your will is being done. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen

sermons.title: Name Written
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. See it. I want to start off by apologizing to you On behalf of Ray, Ray, you pronounced every one of those names incorrectly. Kidding Ray, you did not pronounce them incorrectly. Who knows how they're pronounced? I'm sure when you saw that reading you went, oh my goodness. We are in Ezra 2. Want to start off by Reading a song. I learned how to write it when I first started school. Some bully didn't like it. He said it didn't sound cool. So I had to hit him. And all I said, when the blood came, it's my last name. Grandpa took it to Europe to fight the Germans in the war. It came back on some dog tags nobody wears no more. It's written on a headstone in the field where he was slain. It's my last name. Passed down from generations too far back to trace, I can see all my relations when I look into my face. May never make it famous, but I'll never bring it shame. It's my last name. Daddy's always told me far back as I recall, son, you're part of something. You represent us all. So keep it how you got it, as solid as it came. It's my last name Passed down from generations too far back to trace, I can see all my relations when I look into my face. May never make it famous, but I'll never bring it shame. It's my last name. So, darling, if you're wondering why I've got you here tonight, I want to be your husband. I want you to be my wife Ain't got much to give you. What I've got means everything. It's my last name. Oh, it's my last name. What do you know? Country music isn't only about trucks and breakups The song is by Dirks Bentley, and it communicates what we all recognize. We each inherit a reputation with our last name. And we can keep it, that reputation, ruin it, or improve upon it Having lost my father at a young age, I never received a sense of what Jorgensen was to mean. My grandfather never tried to pass on any tradition that defined what it meant to be a Jorgenson, so I've had to make it up. What Jorgensen means has to be restarted with me and established with my sons, every one of them. I have to put it in writing I have put it in writing to my sons what I want Jorgensen to mean. The uh Name comes from George, which originates with St. George. Legend attributes Saint George to slaying a dragon. Another legend has him as a Roman soldier of Greek origin who was sentenced to death under Emperor Diocletian because of his Christian faith. We choose to embrace both legends and say that Jorgensen stands for maintaining faith in Jesus while slaying dragons. I started thinking about last names and family names when reading the names recorded in Ezra chapter 2. It would have been, would it not, a privilege and an honor, and generate much glee From generation to generation to have a family name on the list, a list, like Ezra chapter 2. Remember that these families were part of the first wave of Jewish families to return to the Promised Land after being in exile for seventy years. around 535 BC. These people were before Ezra returning, which we will read about later. The privilege, the honor, the glee about having your family name, that would have been something. But that glee would have been tempered with the mention of those families that did not have records that identified them as to what house they were from. They knew they were Jewish, but they did not know from which tribe they came. That is terribly, terribly sad. I read one commentator who believed it should be understood that it it it's more remarkable that anybody had any records at all because of the time that had passed and because they were driven out of Jerusalem But that is not how this should be understood. Instead, it was so very important to Jewish families that they connect themselves back to Abraham. And all that was promised to Abraham and to each tribe under Joshua. Their records and their inheritance, proven by their family records, was an essential part of their identity. It was so very essential that family records were memorized one generation to the next generation, carefully memorized. With each family treasuring where they fit in in God's covenant as God's people, to lose your family records was devastating. And speaking of being devastated, consider what it would have felt like to understand that your family was of a priestly lineage. And therefore, you had priestly duties. And therefore, thinking you are going to play an important role in restoring God's house, the temple. that you are going to be able to go into the temple and to touch holy things according to the law of Moses, only to find out that there are no records of your family's heritage. Verse 62 says that they sought their names among the listing of priestly families only to discover their names were not there. And because it was so very important that priestly families only feat priestly families do certain jobs and certain duties amongst the people, amidst the temple and before God. The governor of Jerusalem would not allow these families for them to eat amongst the priests until their identity was solved. The passages mention using Urm and Tuman, but these are not easily identified as to their nature. We don't know what they were. What is clear from their usage here is that the high priest would use them to speak to God directly. With the hope that God would speak back somewhat directly, giving the priest a sign as to from what family these people came, using Urim and Tumun. And because not the temple nor the sacrifices to God had been restored, the ability to hear directly from God was down the road if it would ever come again. To not be able to find your name on a list that would identify you as to who you thought you were. Had to be devastating and somewhat demoralizing. But such a loss of identity Which was a loss of family records, is the fault of the family heads. It is the fault of family members from one generation. to the next for not passing handing down that family lineage that record Now such could happen because of tragedy, or such could happen because of lethargy But men could die leaving no son behind and therefore carrying no lineage forward. But that is rare. So we need to talk about lethargy. This was discussed during our Sunday hour last week. And a great deal of wisdom was shared regarding how lethargy has damaged our culture and damaged the Christian church in general. And so we need to examine ourselves regarding lethargy within families and what steps we are taking or not taking. To assure our family names and each name of a family member is written in the records and by records. I mean the book of life I spoke at length a few weeks ago about the importance of Christian fathers taking their role very seriously, so I won't take much time here. Although I must mention that a common sin among fathers is lethargy. We can easily be lazy when it comes to fatherhood. We can watch our child misbehave, and because we don't want all of the drama and all of the time it takes to discipline the child, we turn away. Act like it didn't happen. And it takes time and much effort to talk to our children about why we believe what we believe, why we embrace the traditions that we embrace, why we don't behave like the godless. And because it takes time, and because it takes effort, and there's a good game to watch right now, we put it off to tomorrow, and it never gets done. Lethargy is a sin practiced in all aspects of our lives. We get tired of remembering what God has done for us just as Israel did. Although the prophets warned not to forget what God had done, the Israelites took for granted their deliverance from Egypt, took for granted God's protection of them from their enemies. And that gave opportunity for the devil to sneak in false gods and lead Israel into idolatry. To not forget, God's people must tell stories. The stories of God's work of delivering his people need to be heard. Our children today need to hear God's stories. Our children need to know of Abraham offering Isaac. Of Moses being hid in the Nile in a basket. Of Joshua and his people marching around Jericho.
