Does that soften what it meant to put away these wives? In verse 3, we have the character Shechaniah. He makes the general confession for the people And he includes in his confession the children of the wives as part of all that should be put away or sent away after the divorce. In verse 44, the last verse of the chapter and of the book, we are told after the listing of all the families that had wives taken away and sent back to their pagan tribes, that some of the couples did indeed have children. The note that some had children tells us that children were involved in possibly a few of these family situations. Does that make us feel any better? There's just a few. The one commentator I read believes that because verse 11 mentions only the wives being sent away, that that allows the reader to conclude that the children born in these marriages were able to stay with their fathers. He even speculates that the children were taken care of, which to him means that they were educated in the religion of Yahweh and entered the Jewish faith as converts. Does that make us feel any better? Even if the happy ending proposed by this commentator occurred There were still mothers who had empty arms the rest of their days. Beloved, we are to remember. That the wages of sin is death, always death. And with death, there is pain. The pain is an unnatural tearing away of life from a body, whether the life is spiritual or physical. But the people of God, but for the people of God to return to God, meaning to be in right relationship with God They were to return to Jerusalem and to worship God as God had prescribed in his temple And to follow his laws that he had given, so that the people of Israel would be his people and they would be his God, their God, and they would be his people. And to do all of that, they must first repent for the sin of marrying pagan wives. And to do so was painful. Relationships had to die. And a question for us today is how we are like the Jewish people of Ezra's day. Are we like the Jewish people of Ezra's day? What influences are we married to in our individual lives that lead us away from worshiping the one true God? Now the most obvious example is the same one Israel faced. The problem is and has been Christians who desire to marry non-Christians To do so is to do the same as the men in Ezra's day. It is to go against what God has clearly forbidden, and even repeated in the New Testament through St. Paul, who said Christians are not to be unequally yoked. Meaning joined together with unbelievers. To even consider such relationships is a revelation As to who or what is being served as a God in a particular life It has been said from this pulpit before that besides choosing to follow the Lord Jesus Christ, The most important decision anyone can make is whom he or she will marry. And that decision will greatly affect how serious you follow the Lord Jesus Christ. Do not turn away your ears from such a prophetic statement. Another example as to who we allow to influence us is who we allow to teach us. Government schools can be similar to pagan spouses as they tell us who we are to believe, and they want us to believe them first and last. Who we are to trust as our sources, and even what we are to conclude about the beginning of time and the existence of God. These schools want to own our children from pre-K through graduate school. By then they believe they have succeeded in filtering out any notion of a benevolent God. And have replaced it with a trust in a supposedly all-caring government bureaucracy. Every teacher we allow to influence ourselves or our children, we are responsible for, which means we will answer to God for them. It is no longer an acceptable excuse that we send our children to school just like our parents sent us to school. Times have changed, and schools have changed, and changed to the detriment of the souls of our children. I must also mention what teachers in the Christian faith we allow to influence us There are preachers who will not preach certain sections of the Bible because the content is too controversial. There are Bible teachers who will not speak sound doctrine because they don't know it when they read it. For some teachers the word doctrine is too divisive Whenever we choose a teacher to influence our understanding of God, we must examine ourselves as to what motivates or causes us to choose such an influence. If there is pride, jealousy, ignorance, or immaturity, in our decision-making, we must confess it and put it away. Another example of who we allow to influence us is who we allow to inform us about our daily news, and who helps us understand the news. A survey finished this past summer found that nearly 70% of millennials get their daily news from a source on social media. That should concern us all no matter what source that is. Older folks such as myself still rely on newspapers online or hard copy and television news And too many, by my count only, get their news from the Opras and the Ellens of the world, especially their understanding of the news. And what can be said that is absolutely for certain is that none of these sources are trustworthy For their God is the devil. And none of these provide wisdom, for they have not the Holy Spirit to guide them in their comments towards the truth. Now a list of all possible influences in our lives cannot be exhausted here But each can be examined regarding its effectiveness to our faith in God and our confession of the Lord Jesus Christ. Of course, it is easier to separate ourselves from a news anchor as opposed to a teacher that we love It is easier to stop reading news on Twitter than to give up our favorite talk show that makes us laugh every day And that brings us back to Jehosiah and his like-minded buddy Jonathan, verse 15 These did not agree with Ezra, and the decision to have the guilty men of Israel divorce themselves from their pagan wives was rejected by them. Jahazia may have been in a profound romantic love with his pagan wife, and that meant that the answer of divorce was not obvious nor a reasonable option in his heart. Emotions can play a very, very big part in a person's decision-making and how serious they are at following God. Emotions of the heart can appear to have the power of a thousand men, causing us to feel like we can do nothing but follow our heart. But when we hear words of Jesus who said that his followers must love him before they love their own families, can we not conclude that what we feel at times Must be disobeyed. When our emotions tempt us to do what is in opposition to God's law, the Holy Spirit says, put them away. When Jesus instructed his followers that they must pick up their own personal cross, their own dying instrument, and follow him. Does that not mean that for each confessing Christian, that our closest friends who do not have faith in God, that they cannot be a source of counsel to us? When friends tempt us to follow the wide road where many travel, we must hear the Holy Spirit say, put them away. When St. Paul instructs believers in the Lord Jesus Christ to be transformed by the renewing of their minds He expects Christians to challenge every way of thinking that they had used before, as well as questioning what had been accepted as group think. Usual ways, popular ways, conventional ways of thinking, when such goes against Holy Scripture, must be put away. That requires Christians to go counter culture. And yet Going counter-culture today is like sticking a wet finger in the air to see which way the wind is blowing only ten minutes later that the wind has changed What Christians need to trust is that to go the way of the Savior is to go the way of counterculture, no matter which way the wind is blowing. We take the example of the daily headlines that we have been reading News anchors and male politicians being exposed because of their sexual abuses, even though these same people have been praised multiple times as defenders for the causes of women. The wind blew one way and then another. And all the while there's this vice president who says that he won't be alone with another woman and that is not his wife. And all of a sudden he seems like a stable source. That is what the church can be to a lost and dying culture. the culture we have around us, if we put away the proverbial pagan wives To put away the proverbial pagan wife is to put away any influence that would pull us, tempt us, counsel us against Jesus as our Savior and our God. Put it all away. This Advent season, a season of preparation. There is a good message for us. Put it all away. As the preacher to the Hebrews stated. Let us throw off everything that hinders. Put it away. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Advent Prep for a Wedding
sermons.speaker: Rev. William Vowles
sermons.text: Let the words of my mouth and the meditations of our hearts be acceptable in thy sight, O Lord, our strength and our redeemer, in the name of the Father, and the Son and the Holy Ghost. Amen. All of us have had those moments when, sometimes of great importance, when we were needed to be prepared for something, right? Well have you ever found yourself miserably ill prepared at that moment Found yourself totally unprepared for the moment to come. I have, and it's not a very good feeling. Maybe you've been there Well, preparedness is exactly the parable for which I'm going to talk about this evening. We're going to look at Matthew 25, beginning at verse 1. Passage known as The wise and faithful I mean wise and foolish uh virgins. And it's the preparedness that this parable is exactly about. It's taken from the great Olivet Discourse, the last of five celebrated discourses given by Jesus during his earthly ministry. And in a sobering way, it teaches us that we ought not to be caught unawares by the inopportune appearing of our Lord. It is a warning parable, one of several warnings found in this discourse. As a backdrop, Jesus had just been giving the Pharisees and the Sadducees a big rebuke in chapter 23 of Matthew. And then coming out of the temple and walking up to the Mount of Olives, his disciples pointed out the grandness of the temple buildings. To which Jesus begins telling them about the destruction of the temple, the end times, and the timing of his second coming. In chapter 24, Jesus gives the signs of his coming. And in the light of that, he warns the world to be ready for when that happens. The passage begins with a question from his disciples in verse 3. They ask, When shall these things be? Four times in this passage, in verses 32, 42, 44, and 50, the Lord tells them that his coming will be at an unknown moment. And then he concludes the parable of the wise and foolish virgins, our parable, by saying, Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour which the Son of Man comes. The disciples asked, when will it be? And Jesus said, no one will ever know. It will be sudden, though, and unexpected. You will know the general time because I've given you the signs. But the reality is, many generations, even our own, have said these are the last days, right? Each generation seems prone to think that the evils of their time have reached the utmost limits. Jesus must be coming soon. But are we really prepared? Things that may look for a moment out of control to us are yet within God's purposes and providence. So we do well to remember that the time of the end is in God's hand alone. The exact moment we will never know. But another reading of our first week of Advent in our readings is 1 Thessalonians chapter 5. Of which we read, the Lord will come as a thief in the night. So what we have in this parable is a call to preparedness. And it should also be an alarm for us as we enter into the Advent season. After all, Advent is a time for us to be expectant, is it not? It's a time of anticipation. As we look back, we are reminded to look ahead and to be awake and prepared for our master's return. Let me point to four things in our passage. First, there is a wedding. Secondly, there are ten virgins or bridesmaids. We have a bridegroom, and lastly, we have a warning. Notice in verse 1 of Matthew 25, the parable starts with the word then, which takes us to a time. What time? The second coming of our Lord, which he had just talked about in chapter 24. So verse 1, then the kingdom of heaven shall be likened to ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom. So there's a specific time when the Lord will come, a time when he calls for his servants to be ready. It's a time to reward his faithful servants. And to punish those unfaithful servants. Now that doesn't seem like a very kind and loving thing to our world, harsh as a matter of fact. But we must remember that while our Savior came to save the world from their sins, only those who believe in his name will enter into the feast. 1 John 5. 1, whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God. John 3. 16, for God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son that who should ever believe in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. In John 1, beginning in verse 10, John says, he was in the world, which he made, but what? The world did not know him. He came into his own, and his own received him not. But as many as received him, those who believed in his name, to those he gave the right to become children of God. So the second coming of our Lord will be the calling of his children to come into his feast. The intent then of The opening verse one is to tell us that there is a specific time when the Lord calls for readiness, for preparedness, and alertness on the part of all his children. For that time will come unexpectedly and suddenly. So the theme of this parable is really very simple. It's not very complex at all. It teaches us that Jesus is coming and he's coming to judge sinners and to reward his children. It teaches us that he is coming at a sudden and unexpected moment, and that we should be prepared. Because afterward there will be no more second chances. People may look, they may knock, they may want, but the door will be shut. The day of opportunity will have come and gone forever. So let's look again at the text. First, again, Matthew 25, verse 1. Opens with a wedding scene. And a wedding in that culture was maybe the greatest event of the life of a town or a village. It was a great social celebration One of which everybody got involved, friends, family, extended family. It was a festive time. So that's the scene as the curtain opens on this parable. Now it's important to remember that a Jewish marriage in that culture was very much different from what we experience today. While historians differ in some of the timing of those activities, including Josephus. He states that there were three chief components. First, the engagement, which would have happened long before the scene here in verse 1. That is a time when the official contract would have been agreed on between two fathers, likely, and things like the dowry would have been discussed. The next phase of the wedding was called the betrothal. This was the official ceremony where the couple would come together before friends and family and community and make their vows and promises. Here they were officially considered married. Yet their marriage was not yet consummated. It was then that the young man had up to a year, sometimes even two, to get his house in order for his bride Perhaps he would build an addition on his father's house or go out and buy land of his own, build his own house. Maybe he would cultivate a field for crops. All this to prepare a home for his bride. So as the time would be passing, you can imagine the anticipation in the hearts of the bride and the bridegroom as they wait for their marriage to be finally consummated. We will rehearse this over the next few weeks because that's exactly the place of the marriage process that Joseph and Mary were in when the angel came to Joseph with that wonderful proclamation. Which brings us to the scene of our parable, phase three of the wedding, the w actual wedding feast. The wedding celebration itself, where the bridegroom comes to the bride's house where she is waiting with her bridesmaids. He collects his bride and her maids and they go out with torches, parading the night throughout the streets in the village, celebrating with song. He leads the whole party back to his home that he had prepared for her. And there is a celebration for days And then finally, when the festivities have ended, the friend of the bridegroom takes the hand of the bridegroom and the bride and puts them together, and everybody would leave, hopefully. So that's the wedding in all of its festivities, with a wonderful picture it is for us, the Bride of Christ, to be ready for our bridegroom and enter into his marvelous feast. It's a grand picture. Now let's look quickly at a couple other features of our story. First, the bridesmaids. We are told that there are ten of them Jesus calls them virgins. We are told that they took their lamps, actually torches, probably on a pole. And then when the call has gone out, they go out with their torches to meet the bridegroom. They would also bring a little flask with some extra oil in it so that they could keep the torch going as long as would be needed until they would meet the bridegroom. So who are these bridesmaids? From the context here, it would seem obvious that they are those who claim to belong to Christ. They profess to be Christians. They represent those who have gathered with the church to await the coming of the Lord. They have on their wedding garments. They have their torch in hand. They show all the outward marks of being committed to Christ. But as we look at the ten of them, while they seem to be indistinguishable, they are not alike. And this is an important message of the parable. Jesus says in verse 2 that the five of these bridesmaids were wise, and five others were foolish. While we see on the surface Jesus sees the hearts of these ten. And according to verses three and four, the differentiation between them was their preparedness. Here is where their wisdom or foolishness manifests itself. The wise carried along the extra oil needed. The foolish had no oil when they needed it. They made no provision for the arrival of the bridegroom. They all made a profession, but only the wise bridesmaids had the genuine oil and faith of preparedness. The oil could be likened to the garment in Matthew 22. Remember the wedding feast? The king calls a wedding for his son and sees among the guests the man without a wedding garment. He too was unprepared. He tries to crash the kingdom party, if you will, but without a prepared heart, he is cast out And so the oil is a necessary grace without which no person can see Jesus Christ for who he is, our true salvation. The oil is a transformed inward life. The foolish virgins are like those whom Paul writes of in 2 Timothy 3, where he says that they had a form of godliness, but were without power. The theme is repeated over and over again by Jesus. In another parable, he tells us that in the kingdom there will grow together wheat and tares together. And they will look so much alike that you dare not pull any of them up for lest you pull the wheat instead of the tares. But rather we are to wait until the coming of the Lord when he will make that distinction. So in verse 6, there is a cry. A cry at midnight, behold, the bridegroom is coming. Go out and meet him. Up the bridesmaids go, they trim the lamps, and verse 8 tells us that the foolish bridesmaids' lamps were going out. And so they asked the wives for some of their oil, to which they said no. Not because they were mean or unloving, lest they would have enough for their own lamps to keep burning They tell them to go out into the marketplace and buy them. Apparently you could buy oil any time of the day. It would have been there for them anytime they wanted it. The sellers of the oil represent the scriptures, the apostles and the prophets and teachers. So when the foolish virgins went to buy more oil, the bridegroom came. He, of course, being Christ. And those who were ready and prepared went into the wedding feast with him, and the door was shut behind them. This might be a good time to sing the Left Behind song that Pastor Eric gave us a couple weeks ago. Good pu good time, but I'll refrain But the fact remains, the foolish were shut out. This is a beautiful parable for those prepared. Yet it is a sobering and alarming reality for those who are ill-prepared. For those who are outwardly going through the motions but have no oil of true inward faith. Again, verse 13, Jesus gives us the warning: watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour in which the Son of Man is coming. Simple yet profound. We are to be prepared. We are to be found practicing our faith, giving our lives as a living sacrifice. So as we move through this Advent season, may we have a true sense for the loss, a true sense for the cares of others, shining our lamps in the darkness around us. Remembering what it is that we are to be known for, our love. So let us go forth this Advent season, being prepared. Loving God and loving others as ourselves. Amen

sermons.title: Advent Ready
sermons.speaker: Deacon Ricky McCarl
sermons.text: A few years ago there was a man, a very sincere man, by the name of Harold Camping. Mr. Camping had a radio broadcast and a very small but loyal following. In 2010, Mr. Camping made the claim, based upon his reading of the scriptures, that Jesus would return on Saturday, May 21, 2011. I remember the date quite well because my wife and I were guests at a college friend's wedding My friend is a Presbyterian, so we found ourselves in good company for the end of the world. I remember we spent the whole afternoon joking at Mr. Camping's expense. and the impending doom of the world. But then it happened. Right at the moment that the second coming was supposed to occur, there was a loud boom. The rooms stopped. We were all in complete silence and shocked. What were the odds the air conditioning would come on right at the moment of the alleged end of the world? My friend Jared, a Presbyterian minister up in North Carroll County, loves to tell people the story of the look of fear on my face. conveniently leaving out the bit about the look on his face, but I digress. Mr. Camping isn't the first person who has predicted the second coming. And he hasn't been blessed. If you ever watch CBN or TBN or any of those lame Christian television networks with the tongue-speaking preachers, you might occasionally hear someone try and make these claims. There's nothing new under the sun The problem is that Jesus told us that only the Father knows the time and the hour. He hasn't hidden the date and time in some secret Bible code. He hasn't shared it with anyone in a dream, and the truth is clear that none of us know That's what St. Paul's getting at in 1 Thessalonians 5. But he's also saying that we don't need to know either. He starts off his discourse in verse 2 by explaining that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. How do thieves come? By surprise. We don't know when the thief comes, nor do we know when the Lord comes. But those aren't the things we're to worry about, because we are awake. We are alert. No need to worry about a thief when you're awake, because you're prepared. You might not know when the thief comes, but you'll know what to do when he does come. Or at least that's how it's supposed to work. That's the whole point of verse 4 when he writes, but as for you, my dear family, you are not in darkness, that day won't surprise you like a thief He goes on to say, You are the sons of light, sons of day. We are not of the night or the darkness. Therefore let us not sleep as others do, but let us watch and be sober. You see, we aren't like those who are asleep and unaware, those who go through life in a drunken stupor. We are to be people who are wide awake and of sound mind. That's how it's supposed to work. Unfortunately, this isn't always true of the church. This is why St. Paul has to remind the church that they need to be alert and sober. There have been times in history, and now is one of those times, dare I say, when the church has acted more like children of darkness than children of light. They've acted more like they were asleep than if they were awake. We need to be reminded That's why we have times like Advent, times to regroup, reflect, and re-evaluate in preparation for that great day of judgment. St. Paul wants us to be what we are, children of day and children of light, alert and awake, waiting for the coming of the Lord. Now, I hope you notice the imagery here. St. Paul places his illustration at night, at a time of darkness This isn't a mistake. If you don't think we live in a time of darkness, then I might suggest you live under a rock. St. Paul sets his illustration at night, because the night is a metaphor for the current times in which we live. A time in which most people have no knowledge of the gospel, asleep and unaware. A time when morality is up for grabs, walking around in a drunken stupor. We aren't to be like this though. No, we're to be children of light and day, awake and sober in this dark night of human history, prepared for the imminent return of our Lord. How do we do this? St. Paul tells us in verse 8 when he says, put on the breastplate of faith and love and the helmet of the hope of salvation. He tells us to arm ourselves, to prepare for battle, because battle is what we're engaged in at this present time. This is another fascinating word picture. The children of night are sleeping peacefully as if nothing is happening, whereas the sons of light prepare for war. because they know of the impending doom. How many people do we know who live lives as if everything will be alright? They live as if there is no God or no consequences for what they've done. They go through life thinking that they'll never be judged, but we know better. And so we are preparing ourselves with the weapons God has given us weapons of faith, love, and the hope of salvation. How do these weapons protect us? Bishop Wright puts it this way in his commentary on 1 Thessalonians. Faith and love are the breastplate to ward off frontal attacks. The hope of salvation is the helmet, protecting the head itself. If we put these things on, then the attacks of the enemy cannot prevail. Our hearts are kept safe by our faith and love, and our minds to the hope of eternal salvation. This is where St. Paul reminds us that we are, as children of light and day, not appointed to wrath, but salvation. Which was purchased for us by our most blessed Savior, Jesus Christ. Here he reminds us once again that we are different from those who slumber. They're going towards destruction, but we're going towards our blessed hope and reward purchased for us by the blood of Christ. That's the good news of the gospel that awakens us to the world around us. So, what does this look like practically? First, we have to stay awake. What does this remind us of, this idea of staying awake? It reminds me of the story of Jesus in Gethsemane found in Mark chapter 14. Jesus instructs his disciples to keep watch, but repeatedly returns to find them sleeping. And verse 38, Jesus says, watch and pray so that you might not fall into any temptation. That's exactly what St. Paul's saying. Be awake, be alert. Jesus, of course, directs us to prayer. He wants us to be alert and in prayer so that we might not be tempted. Tempted with drunkenness and sleep, which I believe in St. Paul's writing is a metaphor for all sin and rebellion. The solution Jesus gives us to such temptations is to be in prayer. So children of light and day are first and foremost a people of prayer. Praying as our Saviour taught, lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. We must daily be in prayer, seeking forgiveness and deliverance from all of our sinful tendencies. We also, as the psalmist David wrote, must hide God's word in our hearts. Children of light and day are also students of God's word, studying it to show themselves approved. If we want to be awake, then we must allow God's word to awaken us, to let it reveal who we actually are, sinners in need of a Savior. And we must also let it direct us and how we are then to live our lives as a redeemed people. In modern times, most people have forgotten the Word of God. Some have outright rejected it as archaic and outdated. Even some who are supposed to be children of light and day, but not us. Not if we're truly awake. How else can we actually be awakened if not by the scriptures? Now, some might point to the direction of special revelation. God is still speaking, as one liberal church puts it. Yes, but how is God speaking? It's always been through His Word. So if God speaks, then it must be in accordance with what his word has already revealed to us. Nothing has changed. Children of light and day aren't led by the light of some special revelation that they receive subjectively, but instead they are led by the objective light of God's Holy Scripture. What the Bible says is sin is sin, and we don't have the ability to change that. No matter what feelings we might have deep down in the pits of our stomach Now, anyone who's had a healthy portion of a good port wine knows that wine leaves a good feeling in the pit of your stomach. And not to take this illustration too far, but maybe the feeling that these people feel isn't so much a direct revelation from God. But it's the result of their lack of sobriety. And now I can hear Pastor Eric saying, what do you mean, maybe? Of course that's what it is. Which brings me to my second and final point of practicality. We must stay sober. We can't go through life in a drunken stupor, completely oblivious to the world around us. Just the other day I was talking with a young mother who has behavior problems with her son. I jokingly said that maybe her son has ADHD, which is overdiagnosed these days, and she said in response, he's three. All three-year-olds have ADHD. I gave her just one example of a three-year-old who was better behaved than hers. I can sometimes be uh a little too bold in such conversations. And her response, I kid you not was, that's because he has more discipline. You could see the clarity come over her. That moment she realized what I was getting at was both eye-opening and humiliating. But instead of saying, you know you're right, which are words I love to hear, she said, Well, I'll raise my child the way I want. Sleeping and in a drunken stupor. The world around us can't see what's going on because they aren't sober. They don't have the ability to see that they're on roads to destruction because they aren't awake or sober. Let's not be like them. Of people who are more influenced by what they watch on TV, read in the tabloids, or see on social media than what God has revealed in His Word. If you can come to a church service once, be confronted with your sinfulness, hear the good news of the gospel, and walk out angry at God and unchanged by his radical grace and love Then there's a problem. If you can walk about this life thinking that all of your sin and dysfunction are perfectly good and normal, and that you don't need Jesus Then there's a problem. The whole point of Advent is to remind us that Jesus has come and that He's coming again, and that we must prepare ourselves. Not just for a day of festivities and merriment, but for that great day in which the Lord comes like a thief in the night. Let's pray. Heavenly Father, we ask that you will work in our lives this Advent season to prepare us. Help us to put on the breastplate of faith and love and the helmet of hope. Help us to be awake and alert for the coming judgment, remembering always that Jesus, what Jesus has done, all the work that needs to be done All that you require of us is faith. Thank you, Lord, for revealing this to us and our needs, and in the good news that we can have salvation through Jesus Christ. And that you have appointed us to obtain this salvation. In the name of the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost. Amen.
