We cannot say creation was loud because of the so-called Big Bang. That was made up. That's man-made, not according to Scripture. But recall some other stories, perhaps of Israel, walking silently around the city of Jericho, until the trumpets were blown and the walls came crashing down. Certainly that was a story that ended being loud. But it is worthy to note, is it not, that there was silence before it was loud. Gideon's army is another story. They were quiet, quiet as they surrounded the enemy, and then And then they began to break pots and to yell to confuse the enemy. Certainly that was loud. The angels that proclaimed the glory to God and the highest at the birth of the Savior were loud enough for the shepherds to hear them. But that proclamation didn't go beyond the fields in which they lay. So none of these stories depict God as unnecessarily loud. Unnecessarily. In fact, we can find stories that speak of God being purposefully quiet. He quietly walked in the garden looking for Adam and Eve. He appeared to Moses as a mere burning bush. No sound. He appeared to Abraham and to Jacob in dreams. When he spoke to the prophet Elijah, he did so In a still small voice, to be in contrast with earthquakes and great winds Even when he entered the world as a man taking on the form of a vulnerable infant, he did so first privately. Speaking to Mary and quietly instructing Joseph in a dream On the other hand, in the book of Revelation, God seems very loud. Trumpets are blown Thousands upon thousands sing praises to God. There is fire and there is earthquakes brought about by the wrath of God being poured on the earth. And we anticipate that all of it is very loud. And God is loud without noise. He is loud in the grandeur of the mountains. He is loud in the vastness of the universe. And such creation proclaims his presence, shouts his presence It displays part of his nature which is objectively beautiful and vast. But most people don't hear God's creation as loud. In fact, most people don't hear God at all. And so how could he be loud and people not hear him? A mystery indeed. I believe we can get a better understanding of God being both quiet and loud in the story of Eli and Samuel. You remember that Eli was the high priest over Israel, and Samuel was the answer to the prayers of his mother, Hannah. And he was also a promise to God from Hannah that he would be raised as an offering to God. And so Samuel lived with Eli, and Eli had two sons. Hafni and Phineas. Both of those sons were wicked priests. They kept the best portions of the offerings for themselves, and they seduced women at the sanctuary entrance. They were wicked indeed. And God was loud to Eli about his sons. He was loud in his holy word that condemned, clearly condemned their behavior. He was loud to Eli in the chances he gave Eli to call his sons to repentance, and he was loud. Loud to Eli when a prophet came and personally rebuked Eli and warned of his son's imminent death. But Eli did not listen to God being loud. And then there is Samuel. He was a young boy with a strong conscience. God called Samuel at night in a whisper. Samuel thought it must be Eli calling him, and so he went to Eli as any dutiful servant would, but it was not Eli who called. The sweet voice at night calling Samuel was heard again. And Samuel again went to Eli. And it was Eli who finally realized that it was God calling Samuel. And so he instructed Samuel, and Samuel replied, the next time he heard the voice, Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening. And from this story, in this comparison, can we conclude that it is God's manner? His way of operation to quietly call his people while also yelling at those who are afar off. I think we can. Along with God being quiet, we are also to note that God, I know this might sound surprising to some of you, that God hides. God hides. And by hide I mean that he does not make himself obviously known. And many times makes it difficult for him to be found or noticed. And such is an understanding about God that young minds in the faith don't easily grasp. I remember hearing of a young man protesting at a Bible study where he heard the teacher say that Although many people are called to repentance, there are only a few that are actually chosen to be saved. That was not the God of this young man, the God that he believed in The very idea of many people being on a wide road that leads to hell and only a few on a narrow road that leads to heaven, well, this was denied by this young man He argued with the Bible study leader because his understanding of God was such that God does everything so that he can be known so that people can believe, so that people can follow, as many as possible, follow God. But that is not the God revealed in the Bible. And such an image of God needed to be shattered for the young man to believe in God as he truly is, as opposed to a God that we want him to be. It is not a question of if God hides himself, it's a question of why God hides himself. The prophet Isaiah states it plainly in chapter 45, where he says, Truly, you are a God who hides himself. Consider that God hid himself from humanity until the wickedness of man became so great that he flooded the earth. He hid himself from humanity until the people built a tower to make themselves like God. And so God then confuses their languages and scatters them from one another. He hid until the tribes and families replaced him with idols of the earth and the idea of multiple gods. He then revealed himself to Abram, but only Abram. Even though his covenant was to be passed on through Isaac and Jacob, he hid himself from Isaac and Jacob until they searched for him. Until they found him and realized he was also their God He even hid himself, consider this, for ten generations while Israel worked as slaves in Egypt. Ten generations He did not reveal himself until their cries for freedom reached his patients. God hides. A most remarkable passage of Scripture is found in both the Gospel of Matthew chapter 13 and the Gospel of Mark chapter 4. Same story, same events. It is after Jesus tells the parable of the sower, the sower who sows the seeds on various types of ground. Some plants that grow are choked, some have no roots and are easily plucked up, and some seed falls on good soil and grows large and healthy. Jesus then takes his closest disciples aside and explains the parable. He tells them that the seed is the word of God. He himself is the sower, and the various soils are the hearts of men. Jesus finishes his explanation with why he uses parables. Why he uses parables when teaching instead of speaking plainly? He explains it by using the words of Isaiah. He says this. So they may indeed see and not perceive, and may indeed hear, but not understand. Lest they should turn and be forgiven Well, for most of us, such a statement is confusing at first reading and then second reading and all the readings because this is not the Jesus we were first told about He uses parables, he is saying, in order to make it difficult for people to understand him. That is exactly the opposite of what many of us expect of Jesus. In fact, I have heard preachers Say that Jesus used parables to help us understand. But that is not what Jesus said. He said the opposite. And to solidify his explanation for using parables, Jesus teaches his disciples that what is truth or light will eventually be revealed. But at first it is hidden. But hidden for the purpose of being revealed. Then he tells the parable of the kingdom of God being like a man who casts seed upon the soil and then he goes to bed. When he awakes, he sees evidence of the seed sprouting and growing. But Jesus points out that the man doesn't know how it all works. So it is to be understood about the kingdom of God. Who believes and how the kingdom grows is unknown to man because it is done in secret. It is done outside of any man's ability to control it It is grown by the will of God in a manner hidden by humanity, hidden from humanity. The ways of God are hidden. God hides. So what does this practically mean for Christians who believe? What does it mean to us for God to be a God who moves and speaks quietly to us? And who at times hides from us. To understand more fully what it means for God to be quiet and for God to hide. We must answer why he is quiet and why he hides. In summary We can know that God is quiet and that God hides in order not to be found where humans want to hear and find God. But God is quiet and hides in order to be heard and found where God wills to be heard and found. Thus it is his will and not ours. Consider the game of hide-and-seek. I think this apropos. When we played as children, there was a time given by the seeker that required him or her to count to ten or more, while the rest of the participants scrambled and hid themselves. And the purpose of hiding oneself was not to remain forever hidden But to come out of hiding and to get to a particular agreed-upon safe place before being seen by the seeker Hence the game made sense not when a person hiding remained forever hidden, but that the person hiding controlled when he or she was found. And such in a similar manner is how and why God is quiet and why God hides. The quiet hiding of God is very much connected to the first sermon of Jesus. Where he instructed all people to seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness. To seek God's kingdom, which is to seek righteousness, was to seek God who had been hiding. To become a seeker under the instruction of Jesus is to humble one's self by becoming obedient to the instruction and to accept that God is found according to his terms rather than the terms of any individual This lesson is very appropriate to learn and accept during the Advent season. When we both examine how God revealed himself in the Christ child and how he promises to reveal himself at his second coming. We have already seen how God was quiet at the coming of Jesus by way of speaking to Mary and appearing to Joseph in a dream. And we can say that God hid when he was born in a stable, in a small town, Bethlehem. It was not allowed place to be born. He further hid when he escaped to Egypt in order to be safe from the spear of Pharaoh. He further hid when he lived his days of development in a lowly town in the region of Galilee we know as Nazareth. Nothing good came out of Nazareth, so the people thought. And even after Jesus publicly displayed his words of life and his ability to perform miracles, He had those moments. We read about it in John, those maddening moments, at least maddening according to immature eyes like my own. where crowds were ready to make him king and to follow him to Rome and Jesus would slip away and go hide Demons would start to speak his identity as the Messiah, the Son of God, and he would quiet them. Those calls for quiet and times of hiding were done because Jesus said it was not yet his time. By saying that he meant it was not time for him to be found. For he was to be found on his terms. on his father's terms, as opposed to the wills of men. And the same can be said for his second coming. Yes, we can understand the delay of his second coming because God wills that more should come to repentance. Yes, indeed. We can understand the delay by facing the truth that God's time is not our time, for we see a thousand years and he sees a day. All of that and many more reasons for his delay are true. But what is also true, as we have seen God chooses to be quiet at times, and God hides at times. And as God is quiet, and as God hides, we are to know that He only reveals Himself and makes Himself heard on His terms. And not on the terms of anyone else. And it is for us to continue to seek his kingdom. And that means to seek righteousness. One of the debate points that I recall made by Christopher Hitchens, now deceased, and other atheists who were popularized at the turn of the 21st century. They made the point of asking the rhetorical question as to why the God of the universe, if he exists Would not manifest his existence in a more obvious manner so that people, more people, would easily believe Well personally, I cannot help but read into this challenging question a kind of complaint being offered as an excuse as to why people choose not to believe in God. The challenge, seems to me, implies that if certain proof criteria were met, then the challenger would, as a result, believe in God. The most obvious problem with this implication is that there are no stated standards to be met. What exactly do you mean by a sufficient evidence of manifestation? And it implies, to me, begs this question, why is the person of Jesus his teaching, his death, his resurrection? Why is that not obvious enough? The second problem with the implication is the assumption that God has an obligation to meet any person's standard of manifestation. And we should ask who is man, that God should be mindful of him, especially mindful in meeting personal and thus arbitrary standards of manifestation. Now a great ironing to all of the questioning about and doubting of God Because of the manner that he does not manifest himself, is that in the beginning it was mankind, Adam and Eve, who hid from God. Our representatives, our kin, our likenesses, those who are with our nature, after they sinned, they hid from God. Is it then not an obvious relational ploy that God would speak softly and hide quietly so that he is found on his terms? Is it not poetic justice that humanity that hid from God would now be required to seek God? Beloved, it is never, never for the created thing, us, to question the creator As to why he made us, or made us the way we are made, or why he chooses to be quiet, or why he insists on being found. It is for us to accept what we are, who God is, and what he instructs of us. And what he instructs of us is that we seek Him. Advent gives us a new start to do just that. Let us pray.

sermons.title: God Hidden in Joseph
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Leave be seated. Again I ask that you keep in mind the readings That we're done today, both from Genesis 45 and from the Gospel according to Saint John. And I anticipate that my message last week was confusing to some of you who had not considered that God would be purposefully quiet and purposefully hidden I qualify that message only in terms of underlining a point that might not have been obvious enough. That point is that God does indeed wish to be found. He doesn't hide for the sake of hiding He isn't quiet because he does not want to be heard. Being quiet and hiding are done to be heard and to be found on his time. To be heard and found in his time, that is the point to underline. That is what you need to get. The Reverend Dr. Martin Luther, the most famous of the reformers, spent a good deal of time writing about God hiding. One of the ways Luther noted how God hides is the manner that he moves among people. Specifically, his call upon some people to be saved and others he leaves to their own devices. Luther argued that when God does not awaken the heart of a person who is dead in his sin, God is then choosing to be hidden from that person. The simple logic is that if God is not revealing himself, well, then he is hiding himself. In Luther's understanding of God's will, he matches up well with John Calvin and John Knox and other theologians that we now call Reformed. The reformed understanding is that the Bible teaches that every human being is born under the covenant of Adam, which is the covenant of death. Because every person is dead in their trespasses in sin, no person can decide to believe in Jesus. As his or her savior, or can confess sin and receive forgiveness. Dead people can only do dead things. Thus, for any person to believe and confess and be forgiven, he or she must be awakened by God, out of that death position, and alive to faith. Faith, after all, is a gift. But since not everyone believes Since the road to hell is wide, since many are called but few are chosen, it needs to be accepted that it is the will of God for some to be saved and others. not to be saved. So for Luther, God choosing to remain hidden is a way to describe how some are saved and some are not What I want us to develop in our faith in God is connected to the will of God. But not in terms of who God chooses to be saved and who he leaves to their state of spiritual death. But rather the will of God in terms of how he interacts in our lives, the lives of Christians, while seemingly hidden from us. Seemingly For every Christian, the greatest mysteries, or the greatest of mysteries, is the location of God in our everyday lives. Especially his location when life is hurtful, confusing, dangerous, sick. Scary, dark, when the future is unknown. Where is God? The revelation our faith needs is the reality that God is present while hidden. Present while hidden. The presence of God while being hidden makes the most sense in the context of Advent season. Advent season where we say that Jesus is going to come again. And yet he has not. And he has not for many a great time. But he is with us just as he said he would be. That was his promise that he would never leave or forsake his church. So he is present. But he is hidden. And the best example I have heard for God being present amidst his people while also being hidden is the story of Joseph. Not the story of Joseph, of Mary and Bethlehem, the story of Joseph as we read in Genesis. It is the story of Joseph and his interaction with his brothers, who do not recognize him and him being the second one in authority in Egypt. Do not recognize him, yet he is the one who is in control. And I remind you of the story only to point out some necessary details So that God being present while hidden can be better understood. So first let us recall that Joseph, in his early life, was a type of Christ. He was a type of Christ in that he was favored by his father. He was a type of Christ when his brothers were jealous of him. He was a type of Christ when his brothers plotted to kill him. He was a type of Christ when his brothers sold him to a foreign authority to decide his fate. He was a type of Christ when he was falsely accused of sin. He was a type of Christ when he was sent to the lowest of prisons. He was the type of Christ when he was found to be blessed of God and thus raised from prison and seated at the right hand of Pharaoh. Such was the life of Joseph early, and that life was to pair, to prepare those who had ears to hear. That a savior named Jesus would follow a similar pattern, only to be seated at the right hand of the Heavenly Father. And to remain there, to rule over all forevermore. But as Joseph is a type of Christ for our understanding, So too is he a type of God the Father. He's a type of God the Father in his dealing with his brothers, before he reveals himself to be very much alive and very much in control. Again, let us be reminded of some important details of that part of the story. The events begin in Genesis chapter 42, where the drought had taken its toll. And the family of Jacob and his eleven leftover sons had no more grain to feed themselves. Jacob sends his sons to Egypt to buy grain, but he does not send Benjamin because he fears something dreadful might happen to Benjamin. When the other ten brothers arrive and stand before the second most powerful man in Egypt to buy grain, they do not recognize their brother Joseph. But they bow before him, just as Joseph's dream had told him they would. Joseph, however, recognizes his brothers, but does not reveal himself to them. Joseph next quizzes his brothers with very specific questions regarding the welfare of their father and the welfare of their brother, not with them. Joseph next tests them to see their loyalty toward family. He wants it displayed. He challenges them to prove their loyalty to family and their loyalty to his authority by going home and bringing back the one brother not with them. On their way back, they express their guilt regarding how they treated their brother Joseph. And they believe the treatment that they have been receiving from this Egyptian Lord That it is a type of karma coming back to them because of their guilt. Secretly Joseph seemingly, seemingly, made the situation worse for them by slipping in money into their grain bags. When the money is discovered, the brothers fear that they are going to be accused of stealing. When they arrive home, they tell their father their side of the story. But with massive holes in their accounts because they did not know what Joseph had been doing for them. And when the famine continued and the grain purchased from Egypt ran out, the brothers needed to go back to the Lord of the country. That's what they called Joseph, the Lord of the Country. And purchase more grain. The problem was that they had promised the Lord of the country that they would bring Joseph or Benjamin back with them. But Jacob wouldn't allow it because he had lost Joseph so close to him, he feared losing Benjamin, and he feared he could not handle or endure such a loss. But the brothers promised with their lives that Benjamin would return to their father, and so they all went back to Egypt together. When Joseph met them and saw Benjamin, he was overwhelmed with emotion because of his love for his younger brother, but he would not let them see his emotion. He then took special care of his brothers and their donkeys and their slaves. And then Joseph arranged for a great feast. He could not sit with them, but he arranged the feast and he had his brothers sit in order of their age. A special knowledge that no one would have known except a person who had a personal relationship with the status of these brothers. The next day after the grain is purchased and the brothers are on their way home, Joseph plans another way to test them. He places his own cup, a royal cup, in the sack of Benjamin. And when his brothers are away from the city, Joseph has men go after them. Catch up to them and search them. When it is found, this cup in the bag of Benjamin, the brothers know that they are accursed. For the punishment will go to Benjamin, and thus they would have broken the oath they gave to their father Jacob. It is then that Judah, who speaks and offers himself as an offering to the Lord of the country in place of Benjamin. Judah's words are a foreshadow of the Messiah who will come from the tribe of Judah and take place of the sinner to set people free. After Judah's speech to be enslaved in place of his brother, Joseph is overwhelmed with emotion of joy and forgiveness. He then reveals himself to his brothers, but only to them. He tells all of his court to leave, and then he reveals himself. At the revelation of who Joseph was, the brothers could come to the realization that Joseph was present among them while being hidden. Joseph was controlling the situation while being present among them, all the while being hidden from them. And we can see then that the part that Joseph played in the narrative was a type of God the Father figure. He was the one behind the scenes, controlling all major events, with an end goal of reconciliation. Reconciliation in mind, and yet hiding in his presence and in his authority from his brothers. Deus absconditus is what Martin Luther used as a term to describe God, insofar as God hiding himself. And not explaining himself to man. Consider how these events in the story of Joseph and his brothers are very Much similar to how God works in our individual lives and in our corporate life. It is at at at very many times impossible to know what God is doing in our own lives or in the lives of the world in general He rules over all. He sifts the hearts of kings through his hands. He has an end goal in his plan. But is more oftentimes mysterious, it is hidden from us. As we addressed last week, so carefully does God hide himself from men that atheists can be quite confident in their unbelief. And even for those of us who know God and thus have faith that God sees the end from the beginning of all things. That he knows precisely what he is about to do and where he is going, we still discern cannot discern all of God's purposes and all of God's plans even as they unfold right before us. That has certainly been true throughout history. Consider that the last thing Joseph's brothers thought when they sold Joseph into slavery 22 years prior, was that that they were arranging the provision of their family in a famine A famine that would come upon the world two decades later. Nor did they imagine that their terrible crime of selling their brother into slavery The terrible crime of faking his death to their father, that that would someday, that those acts would someday mean their spiritual renewal. But God had all of these outcomes in mind when he employed those sinful attitudes and intentions of the brothers to send Joseph ahead to Egypt. A primary message of the story is how Joseph became himself a type of God the Father figure in history. Orchestrating the events in the lives of his brothers behind the scenes in order to bring about their spiritual renewal, even a reconciliation with them. And we must also realize this as well: that the brothers were completely ignorant of all that was going on around them. Not only did they not recognize the purpose that lay behind the various things that happened to them, not only did they fail to completely imagine that the Egyptian was dealing with them in some purposeful way. They in fact ascribed completely different meaning to all their events. As it turned out, completely false meanings. Their interpretation of the events as they unfolded was completely wrong 100% of the time. Have you ever done that? Have you ever wrongly interpreted events in your life concluding that they were all against you, when in the end you could finally see that they were actually working for you Joseph's brothers got it wrong because Joseph all the while hid hid himself and his intentions. He did it on purpose. He was Joseph Abscondiken. Joseph in hiding And it was necessary. It was necessary for the achievement of his purpose that his brothers neither recognized him nor knew the reason for what was happening to them. But in the end, Joseph's purpose had been achieved. The hidden Joseph became the revealed Joseph, all for a greater purpose. God always has a greater purpose. If Joseph is to be understood as a typology of God the Father and the manner that he related to his brothers, What may we conclude about the manner God the Father relates to each of us as his children? We can say at least that what was most obviously learned by Joseph's brothers can be learned by us. In the midst of living with guilt, because of sin committed and not confessed, God is present with us, but hidden from us. He is hidden from us because we have hidden from him, just like Adam and Eve hid from him. We have maybe even tried to hide our particular sin from him. As if we could hide it, as if he doesn't know us. But no matter how we cover the sin up or try to ignore it We receive reminders when bad things happen to us and we think that, well, we deserve those bad things because we haven't confessed our sin. Even in such times, God is present while hidden. Next, in the midst of our faith being tested, God is present while hidden The hidden money and the hidden cup and the bags of the brothers were tests to see if Joseph's brothers were still the type of men who would sell their brother into slavery. When they offer themselves as a replacement, they show Joseph and to themselves that they are indeed new men. And this is what God does for us when He puts us through various trials. We likely don't even see them as trials, we just see them as tough times trying to get through But our our faith revealed in those tough times shows that we have faith we didn't even know about One of the reasons why coaches can be necessary in life is that they will require of us to work harder than we know we could. To require more of ourselves than we know we had. Team sports can do that as well because the team's needs can push a player farther than he thought he could go. And God is like a team or a coach in that He takes our faith to depths we did not know we could reach, and we are so much the better for it. Next, in a journey where the end is scary because the destination is unknown, God the Father is present while hidden. For the brothers of Joseph, the events took them from one scary moment to another. And those events focused them on survival in the moment, with no good thought that there will be a good outcome. And yet where it ended was glorious. It ended in a full family reunion, full forgiveness of all past sins. And a safe place for Jacob's family to live and survive the famine. Now we began by saying, God is hidden from us at times when life is difficult. In the hiding of Joseph from his brothers, there is typology, an enacted prophecy. That God leaves his fingerprints in history, as in the story of Joseph and his brothers, and in our individual life stories. And in these stories, God has woven into the lives of his people a pattern, a meaning. The nature of our holiness, of our salvation. And such is a repeated and most important subject of the Bible. Our holiness and our salvation. And so it is not surprising that it is taught in many different ways. And what lesson is all of this? But however the mysterious, the mysterious providence of God, however opaque the purposes of God remain from our perspective. For the people of God, for their pilgrimage through this world, however torturous the road, however difficult the climb, God will bring them at last to a wonderful destination. Joseph's brothers Had no idea what that destination was. Joseph says to his brothers, what you meant for evil, God meant for good. St. Paul said the same when he said to the Christians in Rome, all things work together for the good, to those who love God and are called according to his purpose. Believe that. Let us pray. Our God, we are truly grateful for this lesson in the story of Joseph to his brothers. For we do identify so very well that we don't see you when we think we should. And you don't seem to be where we think you ought to be. And yet, by faith, we hear this story and we know that you are there. And that you are working things to the good. And for this we simply say thank you and bless your name. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: John the Baptist Observes Advent
sermons.speaker: Phil Lambooy
sermons.text: Let us pray. Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you for this opportunity that we have to gather here in the House of Worship. To sing songs and to offer up prayers unto you, to hear your word and to sing it, and later on to partake of the body and blood of your Son. And we pray that as we Do all of these things and participate together, that we would bring honor and glory to your name. We pray all this in Christ's name. Amen. As we heard this morning and as Pastor Jorgensen mentioned a little bit here with regards to the candle It is the third Sunday of Advent. It's called Gaudete Sunday, the day when we light the pink candle on the Adventry, sometimes it's referred to as Pink Candle Sunday God means rejoice. This day reminds us of the joy that is to come and serves amid the season of penance as a kind of a break. When we recall the hope we have because of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Filling us with a sense that a time is getting short, and soon our joy will be complete in the celebration of our Savior's birth. In John's mind, incarcerated as he was, time was getting short. And his earlier joy in anticipating Jesus' messianic advent, his coming, had given way to restlessness and uncertainty. Our gospel reading from Matthew 11 today centers on John the Baptist and his imprisonment by Herod Antipas in the hilltop fortress of Macarius. rising even today as it does on the eastern shore of the Dead Sea. And while the Bible does not give us its name, we learn of it from the Jewish historian Josephus. Macarius, the name means black fortress, was one of a series of hilltop strongholds established by Herod the Great, the father of Herod Antipas of this evening's story. It afforded seclusion and safety in times of political unrest, as did Herodium, and a more famous palace and fortress that you are aware of, Masada. On top of Macarius, Herod the Great had built a palace and a courtyard. The palace was breathtaking in size and in beauty, according to Josephus. And it is in this palace, possibly in the courtyard, where the dance of death by his stepdaughter Salome or Salome, the daughter of Herodias, was played out. Today, the royal courtyard where Salome did her entertaining dance has been partly reconstructed by the Hungarian Academy of Arts. The stones where biblical figures once walked, John and Herod the Great and Herod Antipas, are visible once again. A couple questions we might want to ask. Why was John incarcerated at Macarius? And how did things end up for him there? Familiar as you are with John's life in the early chapters of the Gospels, we know that John's ministry was characterized by proclaiming both a message of repentance and baptism for the forgiveness of sins, and a foretelling and heralding the news of the coming one. The one who was greater than he, the one who would bring a baptism of fire and of the Holy Spirit, and the one who held the winnowing fork in his hand to exercise judgment During John's ministry, the gospels tell us that many of the common people heard him gladly and responded to his call to repentance. But what you might not be as familiar with is that John was a direct and no-nonsense kind of guy. A man who called sin a sin and a sinner a sinner. Like his predecessor Elijah had done. And so he also called out and took to task the clergy and the rulers of his day. And one ruler in particular was Herod Antipas, the governor of Galilee and Perea, for unlawfully marrying his half-brother Philip's wife, Herodias. And it was this charge, this accusation against Herod and Herodias that eventually led to John's imprisonment at Macarius, the black fortress. And while the Gospel of John makes only a passing reference to this imprisonment of John, the other Gospels tell us more. Luke states, but Herod the Tetrarch being rebuked by John about Herodias, his brother's wife And about all the evil things Herod had done, added this to everything else, he locked John up in prison. Matthew and Mark give us considerably more detail, explain that Herod's wife Herodias wanted John put to death, but could not do this on her own Herod personally desired to execute John as well, but ultimately protected him because he was afraid to harm John, knowing that John was a righteous man. And fearing that the crowd, what they might do to him, Herod, because they regarded John as a prophet. As you can imagine, the sort of public condemnation did not sit well with Antipas or his unlawful and awful wife Herodias. And so in order to shut him up, Herod shut him up in Macaris to get his accuser out of the public eye. Poor John, it must have seemed like the reincarnation of Ahab and Jezebel, who were the sworn enemies of the prophet Elijah. Two prophets, Elijah and John, hounded and hated by powerful women. Which calls to mind the predicament of Sir Thomas More in the 16th century, who likewise was sent to prison for not condoning the marriage of Henry VIII to Anne Boleyn. Of course, Henry and Ann did not take kindly to Moore's non-support of their marriage. Moore said the marriage was wrong, called it a sin. With the same result, he too lost his head. But I hope, like John, kept his soul. So here we find John languishing in prison after defying his ruler. Standard procedures for that time would have meant that John would have had a lonely and mostly isolated experience in his prison, aside from a few conversations with Herodantipus and sporadic visits from his disciples. He would have lived in a small, sometimes extremely cramped, dirty, and deteriorating space. As bad prisons go, though, Macarius was not alone. For comparison, there is a prison in Rome that was contemporary with Macarius. It was called the Mamertine or Mamertine prison. It was described as the house of darkness. And most likely you've never heard of Mamertine, but of his pasan pro prisoner prisoner as you have For did tradition has it that it was the prison where later on, possibly, both Peter and Paul were holed up While they were awaiting trial. Its neglect, its darkness, and stench gave it a hideous and terrifying appearance, according to the Roman historian Seleuce. So you have the Black Fortress for John? And possibly the house of darkness for Peter and Paul, man who proclaimed the truth, and were willing to die telling it In the environment of the Black Fortress, I wonder, was John hoping for a pastoral visit from Jesus? Wouldn't you, if you'd been in John's place? John would have longed to see Jesus, but he had to be content with hearing of his work through the sporadic visits of his followers. John's earlier confidence in Jesus seems to be wavering in our passage. He's now questioning whether Jesus is the one. He could see no definite sign from the perspective of his limited context and knowledge that Jesus was the one whom he had expected. And of whom he proclaimed to appear with a winnowing fork in his hand, in order to burn the chaff with unquenchable fire. Was it just that things weren't progressing as quickly as John had expected? Was it the arrest itself that had thrown him off? Had he not expected that? Was it Jesus not quite living up to the fiery character that John had envisioned? Or was it just the normal effects of imprisonment taking its toll on John? Deprivation, depression, and disease would be common in John's situation. Jesus did not seem to be the type of Messiah that John had proclaimed, nor was he the type of messiah. the people were expecting. Both John and the people were expecting looking for a military type of ruler who would drive out the Romans and restore Israel to the glory days of King David. Have you ever been in a situation where people or events did not live up to the hopes and expectations you had for them? Work, health, retirement, family, friendships And you were left discouraged, confused, questioning? If so, you can probably understand why John would be confused His expectations had not been met according to his expectations. Uncertain times can shake us up and cause us to question our expectations and our faith. And as the months dragged on, and they think John was Macarius for a year to a year and a half, but as they dragged on, John started having second thoughts. In modern parlance, have I backed the wrong horse? Was Jesus truly the one who had come after John, whom he had boldly proclaimed was more powerful than he? Was Jesus the one, or should John and all of Israel look for another? So wondering if he had backed the wrong horse, he sent two disciples here direct from the horse's mouth himself, so to speak. And when his disciples arrived, they repeated John's question. John the Baptist has sent us to you to ask: are you the expected one? Or do we look for someone else? In response, Jesus did not preach a sermon about belief. Jesus simply continued to perform miracles Then he told the two disciples to return. Go and tell John. The blind receive their sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed. And the deaf hear and the dead are raised and the poor have good news preached to them Which were the expected acts and the deeds of the Messiah as spelled out in the book of Isaiah, for instance, in chapter 35 and chapter 61. These deeds shed light on who Jesus was. And even more so. And as for the raising of the dead, as he had done for the widow of Nain, Jesus' actions went beyond what the prophet's words had foretold. Yes, John, I am the expected one, the one whom you have foretold and to whom you pointed others to. These deeds prove, demonstrate, shed light, John, and who I am. Interesting though, Jesus left out one significant messianic work in his response to John. The Messiah would set the prisoners free. And now possibly we begin to see another unmet expectation of John. He'd heard that Jesus was doing the works of the Messiah. But then why was he still languishing in prison? Why was he not set free Jesus' answer to John confirmed that he was the Messiah. But his silence regarding the prisoners being freed indicated whether John fully understood it or not that John would remain in prison. Jesus perceives that John's question is most likely doubt fueled by lack of consistent and reliable information. That was skewing and clouding his thinking and his expectations, which highlights even more the importance of John sending his disciples straight away to Jesus. John knew that Jesus would tell him the truth, and that it was only to Jesus he could go for his answers. Is there a mild rebuke to us here in this passage? Do we often run to and fro seeking to life's, seeking qu answers to life's questions rather than first seeking out Jesus? To hear what he has to say to us through his word? You know, some have said that John did not have doubts. They believed that John wanted the question asked in order to help his disciples believe in Jesus. But John was the one who had doubts, as indicated by Jesus' words. Go and report to John. John's disciples may have had doubts. Because their leader was having doubts. But the message of Jesus was for John. To strengthen his weak knees, to strengthen his faith, with the added assurance that he was the one. John was made of the same flesh and blood as we are. Jesus' words to John and to us was reminded that the scriptures had foretold two comings and two advents. of the Messiah. The first Advent, as outlined above, and the answer of Jesus to John, was that the Messiah would come with mercy. Healing and the proclaiming of good news. This first advent to secure our redemption by way of the cradle to the cross. And that is what John is hearing about, and that is what John is realizing now. But that at the second advent or the second coming, he would come as a conquering king. At that advent, he would indeed clean house to bring about the full consummation of his kingdom. John's expectations had been skewed because he allowed the latter coming, the second advent, to cast a shadow over the first. The coming crown to obscure the present cross. As it were, he was looking through the lens of a telescope where the distant things dwarf the things that are near. But I wonder, have we skewed the life of Christ from the opposite perspective? As through the lens of a microscope, where we only see the now and the near. And neglect and minimize the far and the not yet. And though John's hand wavered As do ours at times, we take hope in the expectation that the one born in Bethlehem is truly a Messiah, the anointed one. This is what the scriptures foretold, and this is what the scriptures promised. The one that John had foretold and promised was the one Messiah, the one who brings forgiveness and salvation to all who come to him and believe to him to be the one. On the day when John lost his head at Macarias, at a young girl's bequest, he died a man who I believe fully understood and knew what Jesus' mission was all about. And that he, John, had indeed accomplished his mission as well. For John could look back, remember that Jesus was the one born in Bethlehem. The one pointed out by John himself to his disciples, behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. The one spoken by the Father, this is my son, listen to him. The one confessed by Peter, you are the Christ. To be able to answer yes when you and I are confronted with John's question about Jesus, are you the one? Is to have a truly experience what the Advent season is all about in his promises to transform Our lives, and yes, our expectations. Advent is a season that prepares us to gaze on the whole life of Jesus Christ From cradle to Calvary to the final consummation. It is all of one piece, all of one fabric, and it's all about one life. The vision of life that Admin gives us is twofold. It looks back to the first coming of Christ in Bethlehem, and it looks to the future when Christ will come again. And in between that which has come and that which will come again, in between, you and I never stop seeking and looking to Him to complete His work in us. To paraphrase the interaction between Herod the Great and the wise men, where is the one who is born king of the Jews? The answer is why he's right over here. He's closer than you think. Let us pray. Heavenly Father, we thank you for the two advents. One we can celebrate in the past and give us the heart and the joy to do so, and the second Advent that will come in the future. And may we do all that we can to be prepared and to prepare others for that great and glorious day as well And as we look forward to Christmas Day and celebrate the birth of Christ in Bethlehem, the house of bread, we pray that we might feed upon you. And that you will guide and direct us to be the people you want us to be between both your Advents. We pray in Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.title: Finding God Amidst the Humble
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. The following are actual bumper stickers. I kid you not. Bumper stickers. Quote, if Jesus had a gun He would still be alive today. End quote. Along that same thing see theme, another bumper sticker is a picture of a cross Where the post is made out of bullets, and the crossbeam is made out of pistols. I don't know what that means. Next, it says, Jesus is my co-pilot, and we are cruising for chicks. And this try Jesus. If you don't like him, Satan will always take you back. And then this clever outreach Jesus loves the hell out of you. And back to the gun theme. Stuff to do. Pray, check box, vote, check box, buy more ammo, checkbox. Now what is curious to me about these stickers and many others like them is what the persons were thinking when they wrote those stickers and what the persons were thinking who placed them on their cars. Do people actually conclude that if Jesus was fully armed, that he would not have died on the cross? And by the way, he is alive today. Considering the bullet and pistol cross, are guns the type of cross that people actually want to die for? And the holiness of Jesus to be treated with such disdain that it has to be included in a joke about cruising for chicks. Finally, I wonder if people actually believe that a person is going to be converted because of their clever turn of the word hell. What is most curious about such bumper stickers is what people are thinking when they consider God. A concern is that they think of him as trite, as silly, as thuggish, as violent, as being like them in their sinfulness. And I've been wondering, can a parallel be drawn between what a culture upholds as enviable and what it thinks to be a God? Is there a correlation between what people uphold as praiseworthy and what type of God they want to follow? If there is a parallel, if there is a correlation, then what does our culture think to be a god? What type of god do they want to follow? Well, according to some of these bumper stickers just read, violence is something to uphold, something to emulate. There are some, a great many it seems, because of the mass media always giving them a prominent place. There are some who practice violence when they don't get their way. They take to the streets and demand justice, justice as they define it, and power as they describe it, and therefore serve a God of violence and of power. And power and fear go hand in hand. So these people violently strive for power while attempting to strike fear in anyone who opposes them. The violent take it by force, Jesus said. He said it in the context of how John the Baptist was received, how he was treated. He was killed by violence to quiet his message. And that is what carnal minds, minds of the flesh, think of doing first. They think of violence. They plan violence and they carry out violence. And such violence is not sequestered within liberal gatherings or socialist gatherings only. Religious men have tried to procure their way of thinking and living and believing by violence. There were Jews during the days of Jesus who wanted to take it by force. And there were Christians after the days of Jesus who thought the same. And we are all aware of the Muslims today who think and practice the same. But regardless of how the violent take it by force The kingdom of God is not established by physical force. The birth of Jesus in a stable in Bethlehem makes that point emphatically. On the last two Christian Sabbaths, I have been explaining the manners in which God has been quiet in history and at times how he hides It is most appropriate then and necessary that we understand this morning where God can be found. After all, we know that he does not want to stay quiet or hide so that no one can hear him and no one can find him. We have confessed that he wants to be heard and he wants to be found, but on his terms and his time. And he wants us to listen for him and search for him. Remember, that is the first teachings of Jesus to his disciples. Seek ye first the kingdom of God. But where do we look? Where do you start? Well before I answer that question, let it be known that God does not hide so that he makes it difficult to be found. God hiding is very much like playing Huckle Buckle Beanstalk. Anybody here play Hucklebuckle Beanstalk? Just my family. Our granddaughter Shera loves Hucklebuckle Beanstalk. Hucklebuckle Beanstalk is a hide and seek game, only it is not people who hide, it is an object, usually somewhat small. The game begins by the seekers either closing their eyes or going and being sequestered in a room while the object is hidden by the person responsible. Now a necessary rule is that the object hidden has to have a portion of it visible, so that those who begin looking for the object cannot or not to remove anything within the room or touch anything in the room, but merely look for the item When a person sees the object hidden in sight, he or she calmly goes to a chair or a couch and after sitting down declares Huckle Buckle Beanstalk. An important strategy in the game is not to give away to the other players where you were when you saw the object in question. That is because the last person that sees it is out of the competition. So each player that views the object must sit down and declare Huckle Buckle Beanstalk. Until there is but one person standing. And I use that as a simple explanation to how God hides. He hides so that he actually can be seen. You just need to look. And so let's look for him. Where do we start? Where to start is to know that God leaves behind a pattern, a way in which he hides places where he can be found in history. And so it is for us to go back and find the pattern. And so let us start at the garden. A good place to start. Where was God in the garden? Well, Genesis tells us that God walked in the Garden of Eden in the cool of the day. Now while while some have wondered what time of day that would have been, or what does that mean for the climate in the Garden of Eden It is better for us to focus on the fact that God was in the Garden of Eden at all That the creator of all would choose to be walking amidst the garden, the garden that housed Adam and Eve, should be amazing grace to us. And thus should give us the clue that God chooses to dwell amongst humanity. Us. That pattern will most certainly be repeated. The next major clue about where God would be is his choosing of Abram, who we later know as Abraham. Abram was a shepherd, and shepherds were of low estate. Abraham wasn't necessarily a poor man, he was not yet a rich man, but God chose him. Abram also had faith in what God told him. Faith necessitates a teachable spirit and a trust that is beyond a person's senses And we know that that faith of Abraham was put to the ultimate test by the offering of his only son. And God stopped that sacrifice because God was still dwelling amidst humanity, and God is found amidst faith. He is found amidst a people of faith. When Abraham's, or Abram's name was changed to Abraham, Sarai's to Sarah God was placing himself within their name. The Yah was with them. In them. The next place of we prominently find God is in the life of Moses. Consider that Moses was with God was with Moses when Moses was a baby. Even as a condemned baby, God was with Moses. Even as a passionate killer, God was with Moses. When God makes himself known to Moses, he does so in the form of, we know, a burning bush. Not a burning wildfire, forest fire, mind you, not even a burning tree. But a bush. What does that tell us about where God can be found? Have you noticed any patterns yet? Consider this clue. When the authority of and leadership of Moses was questioned, questioned by those closest to him, his brother and sister. God said of Moses, now the man Moses was very humble, more than any man who was on the face of the earth. With that, let us continue our search and follow Israel into the promised land, led by Joshua, very similar to Moses in leadership. But who or what was Israel? What had they done that made them a people that could frighten nations and conquer lands? The answer is they were nothing. They had not contributed to the world in terms of new resources, better weaponry, better tools. They had no knowledge of better strategies for war. They most certainly did not have better fighting skills to overrun tribes. And they didn't have a greater population than their enemies either. They were nothing Nothing unless God was everything for them. And when that was true, they could not be stopped. And the land was easily theirs. Well after failing to obey all that God had commanded them to take possession of the promised land, God, and again watch this pattern, God continued to dwell with Israel Through the leadership of a woman, because no man would take responsibility. It was after Deborah, forty years later, that they had to be rescued again from a foreign enemy, the Midianites God chose Gideon, whose name was Jerubabal, which indicates that his parents were idol worshippers. Gideon was chosen while being a frightened and timid man. And God insisted that Gideon lead only a few 300 into battle instead of a large army. Again, are you noticing the pattern? There are repeatedly a few people that God chooses to be with. The characters of the individuals are mixed. But what is common is that they are all either starting off humble or God makes them humble. Even Samson was humble in the end. Our search for God continues next in the person of David. David was always the one God was after. King Saul was merely an example of who God did not want to be with, which is a man of pride and a man of excuses. When we meet David, we learn that he is a shepherd. A shepherd like Moses when God found him. A shepherd like Abram when God found him. Interesting, the profession of shepherding was not a well-thought-of position. In the ancient Near East, shepherding was as low as tax collecting and dung sweeping There were a few reasons for this. First, the wealthy owned land. The wealthy farmed land, while the poor were nomads owning no land. Thus, herders were poor nomads. Second, herds, such as sheep and goats and bulls, destroyed the land by grazing. Such land could not be cultivated and therefore cost landowners money when they were not utilized. And finally, the Egyptians, well, they viewed sheep herding As a lowest state, because to them sheep were worthless food and they did not use them for sacrifice. And so God chose men who practiced shepherding. Men who were looked down upon by the cultures around them. And Jesus would later identify as a shepherd. Interesting. That God chose David and stayed with David, even through David's egregious days of sinning Again, that continues a pattern that God has set. Even when Israel is led by a series of kings who were false worshipers of their various idols. God stays with Israel. Then even after the people of Israel are taken into exile because of their repeated and blatant disobedience to God and his laws, God stays true to them. And brings them back to the promised land. And we know next what happens. That's why we're here today. God is then found in a lowly stable, coming in the form of a servant, taking on human flesh. And revealing himself as Jesus, the Son of God, the Messiah, God incarnate. So what patterns are consistent? What have we found? Where does God dwell? We can say that God dwells among men. His choice is to be in the midst of humanity. We saw this in the Garden of Eden, and God gives no explanation other than He loves. And so He consistently dwells with men. Consider how easily you and I give up on people. Especially people we think they don't want us in their presence, so we save faith, we save hurt emotions But God stays with humanity. He persistently dwells among us. Second, we can say that God dwells among sinners. When the King James Bible states that God is no respecter of men, we are to interpret it that God does not take into account our outward appearances, our social standings, our personal talents. He does not show favoritism to anyone because of who they are personally. Or what they can do outwardly. He treats all people the same because all sinners and thus all people need his grace. When the psalmist asks the rhetorical question, What is man that thou art mindful of him? It is implied that God is not required to be mindful of humanity. It is not God's duty to save humanity, because humanity has turned away from God. But God dwells among humanity, despite the nature of humanity. God dwells amid sinners, and aren't we grateful? We are to recall that the one of the greatest scandals of the presence of Jesus on earth is that he ate with sinners. He allowed prostitutes to touch him. He cared for those in society that had been abandoned because society determined that the lame The blind, the leprous, the poor, and the sick, they were all cursed of God, either because of their own sin or the sins of their fathers. The self-righteous repeatedly failed to understand that when Jesus was among them, it was the same as being among the abandoned. Because all persons since Adam and Eve have sinned, all are sinners before God. Third, we can say that God is found amidst the humble. You know, one of the most beautiful passages in all of Holy Scripture is found in Philippians chapter 2. Where Paul pens a poetic description of Jesus regarding, not regarding, equality with God, a thing to be grasped. But made himself of no reputation by becoming a man. As God is humble, so does he dwell with people who are humble Remember these words of the prophet Isaiah. For thus says the high and lofty one, who inhabits eternity, whose name is holy. I dwell on a high and holy place. And also with the contrite and lowly spirit. A contrite and lowly spirit is a humble man or woman. He or she knows that God owes nothing to them, but they owe everything to him. Amidst such people, God chooses to place himself The psalmist says it this way, Psalm 113, for though the Lord is exalted, yet he regards the lowly. The lowly are those who are self-aware of their sinfulness and their need for a Savior. God wants to be with them. I ask us now to contrast where God chooses to dwell, where he chooses to be found. Against our culture and what it upholds as praiseworthy and deserving of imitation. Our culture upholds the proud, the violent, the loud, and the self-righteous. And yet God cannot be found among them. They don't believe they need God, and thus they are left to their devices. And their devices result in injustices that they claim are just Their devices lead them to judge God and to judge his saints. Their devices lead ultimately to destroying themselves. And that is what happens when God is not found amongst humanity. Like demons, humans turn on themselves and become their worst enemy. As the prophet Isaiah warns, seek God while he may be found. And he may be found because he chooses to be. Where is God? Again, let us start with where he has been. One of those places is in a stable lying in a manger. Let us go there. Let us pray.
