sermons.text: Music, where is it coming from? asked George Handel. As he and his wife, Dorothea, quickly sat up in bed. It was the middle of the night, and they could hear melodies floating through the house. After a thorough search of their home, they failed to find the source of it. As a last resort, they decided to go to the attic where their son slept. There, sitting on his bed, they found him playing a clavier clavier, a small keyboard instrument It had been secretly given to him by his uncle, who knew that George loved music. George Frederick Handel was born February 24, 1685, in Halle, Germany, to a family of no musical distinction. However, his own musical talent manifested itself so clearly that before his tenth birthday, he began to receive from a local organist his only formal musical instructions. Handel's mother, the daughter of a Lutheran preacher, made sure of his early spiritual training. However, His father, a surgeon, insisted that he study law. He was able to continue his music career after his father's death, which occurred while he was still in college. Handel's first job was as a church organist, beginning just after his 17th birthday. However, his musical preferences lay elsewhere. By age 19, he had mastered most of the orchestral instruments. While continuing his musical adventures, he was also rapidly becoming one of the greatest composers of the world. Handel's crowning achievement, of course, was Messiah. But it was not an immediate success. In 1741, Handel was heavily in debt following a string of musical failures. It seemed that his career might be over, and he may even be forced to go into debtor's prison. On April 8, 1741, Handel gave what he believed to be his final concert. Later that year, two key events changed the course of Handel's life and the landscape of music forever. His friend Charles Jennings wrote a libretto taken from the Bible based on the life of Jesus and gave it to Handel. Then Handel was given funding by a group of charities from Dublin, Ireland, given to compose a new work. For a benefit performance that would help free men from debtor's prison. Handel would also receive his own commission for composing the work. which in turn helped him on his path to reversing his own misfortune. The composition of Messiah, the complete 260-page oratorio. began on August 22, 1741, and was composed in just 24 days. When Handel finished the final orchestration on September 14th of that same year A second account of the behavior of Handel while writing the Messiah is as follows. In a small London house on Brook Street, a servant arranges a tray full of food. For more than a week he has faithfully continued to wait on his employer, an eccentric composer Who spends hour after hour isolated in his own room, morning, noon, and night The servant delivers meals to the composer and returns later to find the food basically untouched. Once again, the servant forces himself to go through the same routine complaining under his breath about the strange behavior of the musician. As he swings open the door to the composer's room, the servant stops in his tracks. The startled composer, tears streaming down his face, turns to his servant and cries. I did think, I did see all heaven before me and the great God Himself. George Frederick Handel had just finished writing a movement that would take its place in history as the Alleluia Chorus. Although Handel received wide recognition as a music composer in Italy and Germany, his greatest fame came from a concert in Ireland In Dublin, April 13, 1742, Neil's Music Hall. A choir rises, and the Alleluia, Alleluia, Alleluia fills the auditorium. A great crowd had gathered, which included King George II of England. He, the king, was so moved by the exhilarating music, he sprang to his feet. An action which seemed to prompt the whole audience to do the same. From that day, whenever the world Whenever in the world the hallelujah chorus is presented, audiences stand. In the hours just before his death, Handel said, I want to die in the hope of rejoining the good God, my sweet Lord and Savior, on the day of his resurrection. Included in the lyrics of the Messiah are these words, and he shall reign forever. And forever. Hallelujah. King of kings and lord of lords, forever. Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end. I was anxious to read about the story behind the handle the composer and the writing of that hallelujah chorus because during this Advent season I happened upon online A video of a choir singing that chorus, and I was emotionally moved I teared up during that singing several times. It is true for me, as I have heard for others. that I find myself weeping the older I become. I recently watched a uh a the movie Field of Dreams and Those of you who don't know me, my father passed when I was three, and sure enough, it comes to the end of the movie, have a catch, Dad, bawling my eyes out I suppose that the passing of time allows a person to reflect and then appreciate small moments more and more than when we were younger. But most of all, appreciate people and the love for people in your life, and the most important people, as we can call him, our God. To express our love for him. Now, I remind you of the words of the Alleluia Chorus Not going to sing them, thanks be to God. But the words, the words. I can't say them all, but hallelujah, alleluia, alleluia, hallelujah, hallelujah Four more times. For the Lord God omnipotent reigneth. Hallelujah. Hallelujah. Hallelujah. For the Lord God omnipotent reigneth. And it repeats and it repeats and it repeats and it builds and it builds. The kingdom of this world is becoming the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. And he shall reign forever and ever. And he shall reign forever and ever. Again and again, repeat it King of Kings forever and ever. Hallelujah. Hallelujah. And Lord of Lords forever and ever. Hallelujah. Hallelujah. And these are repeated again and again, and he shall reign, and he shall reign, and he shall reign King of Kings and Lord of Lords. Hallelujah, Alleluia, Alleluia, Alleluia Rod Capolo, a renowned composer and conductor of today, along with Fred Chile took a deeper look into the structure of Handel's popular chorus to discover why the music had such a powerful grip on singers and listeners, all the way back to King George II. Much of the power of the peace, Cappello says, lies behind the rhythm of the word hallelujah. Handel could have assigned the four syllables of the word to four notes of equal length, but that would be boring. And it wouldn't be handled, Capolow says. What makes handle great, Capolot says, is that that first note is lengthened and then we explode at the end. We have this Alleluia. Another key to the course is the power, is the power what Kiplow calls the King of Kings section. The thing that is so amazing about it, Capolow says, is that it's actually based on one of the simplest ideas you could possibly imagine. A single note repeated over and over again. One note per syllable, King of Kings, and Lord of Lords. But Handel keeps repeating the mess the passage in higher and higher registers. Each one seems to be the highest you could possibly get, Capolow says. That's the climax of the piece. Now I know that reading the words cannot, and talking about Handel's style does not in any significant way compare to hearing it sung by a choir. And I have no doubt that my emotions, let my tears flow because of hearing the beauty of the arrangement that I saw on that video. But I also know what was in my mind and what was swelling up in my heart when I was listening. It was a desire and a prayer that Jesus would indeed reign forever and ever. And it is the declarative manner the singing of the music is done that stirs the soul. To know that Jesus reigning forever and ever is not only a hope for the future, but a reality for the present. The fact that he shall reign forever and ever means that he shall reign now. For now is a part of forever. The only issue is the reign of Jesus is fully in heaven and not fully on earth. And so we pray, Thy kingdom come, thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. But our hearts ache on this side of heaven, because the kingdom of God is not fully realized. We desire so very much to see Jesus reign over our nation and thus bring the proud to their knees. The rebellious to confession and the hurting to be spiritually healed. We long for our tears of pain and fear to be wiped away. We want the sting of sickness and death to be as far as the east is from the West We want the truth of Jesus known and our faith in him vindicated We want Jesus to reign in our hearts and the hearts of those we love, with the casting out of lies, of confusion, of doubt, anger, deceit, and anything that leads to death. We want our hearts to be free, free from the fear of men, from the concerns of the temporal, free from what keeps us from expressing unconditional love. And that will happen when all lips confess that Jesus is King of kings and Lord of Lords. And working on my dissertation and studying the eulogies of early Christians It was a consistent part of a sermon to say that we can praise God that this person in Christ has been saved from all the misery in this life. Because there is much misery in this life. And so we wait for that King of Kings and Lord of Lords to reign here and now Until God's kingdom comes on earth as it is in heaven, until then we have the hallelujah chorus. To bring us close to where we long to be and what we long to experience, fully experience Until then, we get to hear words from heaven sung. In honor of the Alleluia chorus, I found a couple of stories about how it has moved people. The first one is is is a simple one. It's by a woman named Leslie Weatherhead She said, I once attended in the Royal Albert Hall, London, a magnificent rendering of Handel's Messiah by a choir of several hundred. The friend who accompanied me was a dear saint of God, then in his 70s, when the Alleluia chorus rose to its stupendous height. King of kings and lord of lords. My friend could hardly contain himself. The tears were streaming from his clear blue eyes, and he whispered to me That was my Savior, they were singing about. I shall never forget the meaning that he put into the word my And then this story that is from one of Baltimore's own, a story that is quite goose pitle chilling. During a long and complex surgery to separate another set of twins from Zambia, Dr. Carson reached a particularly challenging point in the operation that involved separating a tangle of blood vessels Carson began to feel frustrated and fatigued. He said, I began praying desperately that God would take over and simply use me to accomplish what only he could do. Despite the exhaustion that had almost paralyzed me a short time earlier, I now sensed a remarkable steadiness of my hands. I felt a strange calm. an almost detached awareness, as if I were merely watching my hands move and someone else had actually taken over the surgery. God's hands seemed to move, providing inspiration and guidance through the gloves of Ben Carson. Quote, I don't know that I have ever experienced anything quite like what happened in that operating room that day. When I separated the very last vein connecting Joseph and Luca The stereo system at that very moment began playing the Alleluia chorus. From Hanel's Messiah. I suspect every single person in that OR felt goosebumps and knew that something remarkable had taken place. And it was not our doing, he said, giving all praise and glory to God. Such, beloved, is true that God inhabits the praises of his people, and this day and this night and tomorrow of all days. We get to say King of Kings and Lord of Lords. Amen.

sermons.title: Go Tell it on a Mountatain
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.source_file: Go Tell it on a Mountatain.txt
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Our text from the gospel reading this morning, I hope, surprised you. It is not a common Christi or Christmas text. But what do you expect of a preacher who's been preaching Christmas Eve sermons and Christmas Day sermons for 19 years now Actually that is not why I chose the text, and hopefully you will see why uh in a due time. But let us consider what's happening in this story There was a poor and wretched man being possessed by a legion of evil spirits, and they had been driving him to madness. His home became the tombs, the dwelling of the dead, where he dwelt day and night, only to become a terror to anyone who passed his way. The authorities from the nearby village attempted to curb his madness, this madness of the possessed man, by by chaining him But he tore the chains from their bindings and threw off anything they used to bind him. He could not be tamed. He was worse than a wild beast. He became a misery to even himself as he cried and howled day and night. It appeared that whatever semblance of sanity was within him wanted to be dead As he cut himself with sharp flints and bruised himself in a frightful manner It was not until Jesus passed this man's way that there was a glimmer of sanity. Jesus simply said to the devils that possess the man, come out of him. And the man was healed that very moment. The man next fell at the feet of Jesus, and when reason came back to him, and gratitude filled his heart and soul. He said to Jesus, Lord, I will go wherever you go. I will be your constant companion and your servant, if you will permit me. But Jesus, a bit surprisingly, turned the man down. He is moved by the man's devotion, and yet Jesus wants something else from him. He wants the man's devotion to be displayed by him going home to his friends and family. And telling them what great things the Lord had done for him, and how he had compassion on him. Such may be a surprising request by Jesus because such a dramatic series of events would make a for great storytelling And any circuit preacher knows how well good stories sway crowds. This man could have been a great example of what Jesus can do for any man or woman who calls upon him to be. saved. He could have been the opening act for Jesus as he went from town to town telling his story and then introducing Jesus as the main attraction who can make it all happen. Many a Christian has thought so well and profoundly of their own conversion that they think they need to start a worldwide ministry to express their profound gratefulness. Gratefulness for their conversion while desiring to tell others about their personal story of what made them believe in Jesus And here, instead, as a man delivered from possession by demons, he is told to go home and tell his friends what God has done for him. Going home brings another aspect of this instruction by Jesus for what was true during the days of Jesus is still true today. Jesus himself, you recall, was not accepted as a prophet in his hometown of Nazareth because they knew Jesus as a child. And it was not that Jesus had a bad reputation as a child, but only that they knew him as a child. They knew him to have been small and thus weak and thus vulnerable They knew him to be like their own children, who soiled their garments as infants, and who needed instruction and protection as innocent babes. And they knew the family of Jesus. Joseph was like any other man. He needed to work with his hands to provide for his family, as well as performing menial tasks, tasks of everyday living. Nothing was special about the family of Jesus, so what would make him special as a grown man That was their reasoning. And the reasoning of all people who become surprised when any hometown child becomes influential on a greater stage For many families, because home is a place where everyone is viewed the same, and no one can have meaningful conversations about politics or religion because every man's opinion is thought to have the same weight or value. And such is being magnified today in social media sources Thus you could think that there would be no effective testimony received if this man goes home and tells his story. Even a story as wild as being possessed by a legion of demons. But that does not detour Jesus. from instructing the man to go home and tell people from his home what Jesus had done for him. The primary reason this text is appropriate for Christmas is the anticipation of many conversations that will take place within the next few days. And the subject matters will that will be broached. Politics and politicians will be discussed and debated. And feelings will be hurt and invitations will be regretted, and the peacemakers will do anything to get our guests off the topic. And then sports will be mentioned and frustration with the local teams will be discussed and who should get fired and who should get hired and who should be signed and who should be cut And although there is disagreement, there is consensus that the team stinks and another season is lost. With that, the spirit of the gathering is brought low, and the host again tries to steer the conversation to a more joyful topic. The next conversation centers around Christmases long ago. And that reminds someone in the party of an argument that took place fifteen years ago that was never settled And some in the family get riled up all over again and try to settle it. The host is once again at a crossroads regarding how to make the occasion a happy one instead of a contentious one. What will not be heard as often as it should, our conversations centered around what Jesus instructed this once possessed man and now sane man to do. Which was to go home and tell his friends what the Lord Jesus had done for him and that the Lord had compassion on him. Of all the anticipated conversations you have around your dinner tables and living rooms this Christmas season Ask yourself if you have planned to tell your friends and family what the Lord has done for you. You ask, but what should I tell? We can answer that from the story, Red. First, you are to know that the Lord has given you a story of personal experience The Lord does not require you to preach. There is no requirement for you to take up a doctrinal topic and expound upon it so that you are shown to be wise and you are able to make others wiser. Instead, you are to tell what you have believed and what you have felt because of what you believe, and therefore you are to tell what you really know to be your own. Such as not what great things you have read, but what great things the Lord has done for you Not alone what you have seen or done in a great congregation, and how maybe great sinners you know have turned to God, but what the Lord has done for you. And mark this, there is never a more interesting story told than when a man tells about himself. Note next that what you should tell should be a story of free grace. It is not instructed, tell your friends how great things you have done yourself, but how great things the Lord has done for you. It should not take long for any person with any sense of self-awareness. The telling of your own accomplishments thins a crowd. A person who is aware of God's amazing grace says nothing about his own doings or willings or prayings or seekings, but instead ascribes it all To the love and grace of the great God who looks on sinners in love and makes them his children, heirs of everlasting life. Go home and tell that story. Another part of the story that we can tell is a story in which we are grateful. Consider the likely story of the previously possessed man. His tale was undoubtedly a grateful story. We can know he was grateful because the man will say, I will tell thee how great things the Lord has done for me. A person who better knows his or her own sinful ways always thinks that what God has done for him is immensely good and supremely great. The more you know your sin, the more you know the grace of God. Now it should be acknowledged that as freely and openly as I have described this storytelling There will be those who will think of it not particularly exciting or interesting But that is not to detour you. You must take the challenge to look such persons in the eye and say, if you knew the Savior as I know him, you would not think little of what I am telling you. Say it with the hope that they may see that you have what they need, which is freedom from the burdens of sin that weigh every man down. It is true that I have spoken in generalities regarding what you should tell others. And you may think that nothing much has happened to you in the last months or the whole year that is worth telling But to conclude such a thing is to disregard the mercies of God that have been great in your life A life in which you are able to call him Lord and Savior. Take inventory of the sins the Lord has forgiven you. In just the past days, not counting months and the year. Take account of your ability to forgive others because of the new heart God has placed within you. As opposed to the grudges and bitterness you so easily carried earlier in the year. Consider how many times you have made foolish decisions, such as to speak when you should have listened And to make haste when you should have waited. And the Lord saved you from the consequences of these matters. And consider the sorrows and cares you have for others and how the Lord has allowed you to weep with those who weep and to mourn with those who mourn. And thus God has used you for the sake of others. All of us have such stories. That can be shared. And all of us have people in our lives who need to hear such stories, who need to be Convinced of the experience that can be theirs because of the presence of God in your life. And that last point brings us to the conviction as to why others need to hear what the Lord has done for you. People do not hear the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ enough today. Too many people do not know the Savior Jesus because they do not know who Jesus is or what Jesus can do for them. There is a comedy movie, I won't give the title, starring Will Farrell, shows him praying with his family to baby Jesus That is how they address God in their prayers. They pray to baby Jesus. As much as such a depiction might border on blasphemy, it also tells a hard truth. Which is that people are very comfortable to hear stories of Jesus as a baby born in a stable, but that is as far as it goes. The hard teachings of Jesus are just that. They are hard. The reality of heaven and hell are just that. They are polarizing. Betrayal, hypocritical behavior, gory death, impossible resurrection are aspects of the story that are not easy to hear and harder to believe for the sake of salvation But they must be told. And the story each of us has to share as to what the Lord has done for us leads to the greater story of the gospel of Jesus Christ. And this brings us to a necessary discussion on the responsibility of every believer to publicly confess the Lord Jesus. Publicly. It is one thing, a minor thing, for we Christians to greet people on the street and in the stores with Merry Christmas! Instead of seasons greetings, the greeting of Merry Christmas can be a witness to your religious beliefs. But to tell other people about what the Lord Jesus has done for you, that is another great step. And a necessary step to fulfilling what Jesus said himself, which was that if we acknowledge him before others, that he would acknowledge us before the Father who is in heaven. To acknowledge him is to say he is our God, our savior. And for him to acknowledge us is to say that we are his family. Now I mentioned I must mention a caveat here, which is that I am not preaching that you should tell what the Lord has done for you to people who don't want to listen. The Lord never places it upon followers to be obnoxious storytellers The wisdom of not casting pearls before swine includes not sharing the story of the grace of God with people who have made it clear that they don't want to hear it. But such a caveat should not outweigh the words of the Lord Jesus, who said, go home and tell your friends what the Lord has done for you. Now I end with the hope of convincing you that there are people who need to hear what the Lord has done for you. As you know, during this time of year it is heard that people struggle with depression and hopelessness because the season is a time for family and for friends to gather, and when family members and friends have been lost in death, it seems like the time for grieving has been extended. And so there is not a focus on the gift of God and giving his son, but instead a focus on self and personal loss. Such people need to hear what the Lord has done for you. And there are people this time of year that are reminded that they have no faith. The story of the Christ child is but a fairy tale, no different than Peter Pan or the Princess and the Pee. Those without faith have no hope and thus remain in their sin. They too need to hear what the Lord has done for you. So on this day, this Christmas day, it is good to heed the hymn which instructs us to go tell it on a mountain. Over the hills and everywhere that Jesus Christ is born. And I say, yes, do that. And while you're at it, tell family and friends what the Lord has done for you, how he has had compassion on you. Amen. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Letting Christmas Touch Us
sermons.speaker: Deacon Ricky McCarl
sermons.text: Let us pray. May the words of my mouth and the meditation of all our hearts be acceptable and pleasing in your sight, our rock and our redeemer. In the name of the Father, and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Amen. I was recently having a discussion with a relative about the theological significance of Christmas. My relative is an evangelical whose church has largely abandoned the liturgical calendar in all of its feast days. He had explained to me that from his perspective Christmas was just a repurposed pagan festival and that Jesus had probably actually been born in April or May. This conversation perplexed me because it revealed in my relative a lack of understanding of what's being communicated in the church calendar. It isn't about linear dates and making sure we know exactly when things happened, but instead the celebration of feasts and holy days were designed to communicate something important to us about the gospel. namely that Jesus' life Jesus' life from his birth to his ascension Each event is crucial in communicating to us just who Jesus is and what he's done for us in our salvation. And this is why I don't like to rush Christmas. It's why we're still talking about Christmas today instead of moving on. We need to take our time and let Christmas touch us and prepare us for what comes next. If we slow down and take that time, we get the full picture of what Jesus has done for us. Because the church calendar, just like the gospel in written or verbal form, is an unfolding story with twists and turns and different perspectives. It's important that we take this time to pause and to get a full view of the whole story. A few years ago there was a film by the name of Vantage Point. The film centered around an attempted assassination of a fictional president. Each scene captured the different perspectives of each person involved. It showed the vantage point of the Secret Service agent. the news reporter, the bystander, and even the terrorists. Each scene gave a little bit more to the s as the story unfolded and as the end comes together and the mystery surrounding the assassination attempt is revealed. Each of the storylines are then neatly wrapped up and the story comes to a close. The Gospels are written in a similar sort of way. Each one captures a different vantage point. As we read through them, we get more and more of the story until the climax comes together, and the wonderful news is revealed that Jesus has died for our sins and risen again. bringing about the hope of salvation from sin, death, and the devil. Now some have pointed to this and they've claimed that these different vantage points reveal contradictions in the narrative, that the stories don't match up with one another, so they must then be fabrications. Actually, I would argue that the opposite is the case. The differences in the narrative are actually a testimony to their reliability. Because, as we all know, anyone who witnesses an event witnesses it differently than those around them. I'll give you an example from my year of teaching last year A fight broke out in my classroom. Two friends had spent too much time together and gotten into a little argument. I broke up the argument and the fight and asked the students around them what had happened. And each of my students had a different version of the events, because they each had a different vantage point. Some were close to the fight and saw one thing, and some were farther away and saw something slightly different. It's not that they were lying or fabricating a story, they just saw something from a different perspective If their stories were all exactly the same, then one might conclude that they had gotten together and discussed what they were going to report. It would indicate that they crafted a narrative instead of just reporting on what they actually saw. Similarly, If each of the Gospels were exactly the same, then it would indicate that the authors had gotten together amongst themselves and fabricated their accounts The differing details of the story actually lead the critical thinker to conclude that they are truthful and that they are the same stories from different vantage points. This is the case of the birth narratives found in St. Matthew's and St. Luke's Gospels. In St. Luke's Gospel, Mary is overjoyed to learn that she will have a child, and that that child is the long-awaited Messiah. She receives the news joyfully and reveals it to her family who also receive the news joyfully. St. Matthew's account starts off on a much more somber note. Instead of joy, we are greeted with a man in a perplexing situation. Joseph is betrothed to this seemingly faithful Jewish girl They share the same faith, values, and morals. But it all comes to a screeching halt when it is discovered that she is with child, and that that child isn't Joseph's. So Joseph doesn't respond to the news with joy and jubilation like Mary or Elizabeth or Zacharias. Instead, he has some thinking to do. He has to figure out if he's going to divorce Mary quietly. Or openly shame her in front of all their neighbors and family. Initially, it looks as if Joseph's hopes and dreams have all come to an end. Joseph, being the upright man that he is, decides not to bring shame to Mary, but to divorce her quietly. That is, after all, the logical thing to do, and he spent a great deal of time thinking through these things and what's the best decision for both him and Mary. Or so he thinks at the time. Because as we learn further in the story, God has other plans for Joseph. And that night he has a dream in which the angel of the Lord comes to him and says Do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit, and she will bring forth a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he will save his people from their sins. Now there's a lot going on in just these two brief passages, and I think we would be amiss not to discuss them First, the angel says, fear not. But why does he say this? What is there for Joseph to be fearful of? Well, basically, Joseph had a lot riding on this betrothal to Mary. His reputation and the reputation of his family were all on the line. First century Palestine wasn't like 21st century America, where you had common law marriage and unwed mothers running around. Fornication was taken seriously, and it brought shame upon you and your household. Joseph couldn't possibly marry Mary, because he would have to say that the baby was his. which was not only a lie, but that it would make him admit to uncleanness. This is a huge problem for him, but the alternative wasn't much better. If he publicly divorced Mary, then there was this very real possibility that she would be stoned for adultery. And Joseph, being the upright man that he was, couldn't bear to see that. I imagine that Joseph must have spent a great deal of time weighing his options and worrying about what was best for him and for Mary. And so he makes his decision and he goes to bed. The problem is that Joseph doesn't have all of the details, and his plan is based in fear. fear of humiliation, fear of shame, and fear for the life of his betrothed. But Joseph doesn't need to be fearful, and the angel goes on to explain why. When he says, For that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit, and she will bring forth the Son, and you'll call his name Jesus. What's the angel doing here? He's preaching the gospel. Joseph doesn't have to fear because the Messiah is coming, and his betrothed is about to deliver him into the world. What better way to dispel fear and anxiety with the good news of the gospel? There is no need to fear, no need to despair, no need to worry or to be perplexed, for the Messiah is coming to save us from our sins. That's the good news. That's the gospel. It might not be framed the way we expect, but it's right there summed up in one simple sentence. Simple and yet very profound, and more than enough for Joseph to arise, throw caution to the wind, and take Mary as his wife. The word is preached, a call is issued, and faith is exerted. All of the elements of an effective proclamation of the gospel And so Joseph rises, takes Mary as his wife, and heeds God's call to provide, defend, and protect the little Messiah and his mother. Interestingly enough, when the birth narrative in Luke and the narrative in Matthew are compared, the two things, other than the angelic encounter, of course That tie these two things together is this exhortation to fear not and a proclamation of the good news. But this is also what ties our own stories with that of the biblical narrative. When we first heard the gospel, we were in some way exhorted to fear not and told that Jesus had died for our sins. We might not have had angelic encounters. We might not have even heard the exact words, fear not. But the good news always compels people to have no fear, but to trust in Christ And this takes me back to my own conversion. It was at a VBS, Vacation Bible School, the local Baptist Church. And our teacher told us all in good fundamentalist fashion that we were all sinners destined to hell, and that we needed to believe the gospel. I was all of nine years old. Perhaps this wasn't the most subtle form of evangelism, but God used it in my life. No angelic messengers No dreams, just the knowledge that I had broken God's commands and that he was justly displeased with me. I had great fear of God's wrath for my sins, and so I trusted in Christ and found the peace that only He could give. The fear of God's wrath subsided because I heard the message that Jesus came to save me from those sins. And I, like Joseph, found this message to be the best news, and it radically changed my life. Which brings me to my next point. The gospel also compels us, like Joseph, to rise and serve the Messiah. That's what faith looks like Faith isn't just a sent to a list of facts or an emotion or a feeling. Real saving faith is a faith that changes us from the inside out. It empowers us to think, say, and do things that we once couldn't and or wouldn't do. Joseph goes from a man who is led by his fear of disgrace and humiliation to a man who could care less about his reputation and his family name. Because of how valuable and important the call of the gospel was. We also go from selfish sinners who have willingly broken God's commands to a people who hate our sin and desire to live new lives of service to our Lord and Savior. Faith brings about transformation in our lives. It makes us different people. Just as it changed the lives of Joseph and the Blessed Mother of our Lord And so Saint Joseph stands as an example to all of us of faith and commitment to the gospel Though he might not have understood the gospel as fully as we do today, it was clear that the good news of Jesus' birth caused a great faith to be kindled in his heart A faith that led him to serve God faithfully by protecting the incarnate son and his most blessed mother. So let us, like Saint Joseph, allow ourselves to be shaped by the gospel, whether it be in written form, oral form, or even the church calendar. Let us pray. O God, who from the family of your servant David raised up Joseph to be the guardian of your incarnate son and the spouse of his virgin mother. Give us grace to imitate his uprightness of life and his obedience to your commands. Through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

sermons.title: Following the Magi
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. As everything around you indicates, this is the day. after the feast of Epiphany. Therefore it is most appropriate that we spend this Christian Sabbath learning and being sanctified about the story of the three wise men visiting the Christ child. As you know, Epiphany refers to manifestation or the revealing of the person of Jesus to the Gentiles, the non-Jews. It is the time identified by the Christian Church to celebrate that God has revealed Himself having included the Gentile world into his everlasting covenant and therefore allowing non-Jews to be inheritors of his eternal kingdom. The three kings of Orient traveling afar. Symbolize the revelation that God desired all the world to know about the nature and purpose of his son, Jesus, coming into the world. Now if you are bothered by me referring to the visitors that came from the east bearing gifts to celebrate the birth of the king by following a star If it bothers you that I have referred to them as three kings, well then jolly good for you. Yes, let us set the record straight. We don't know how many there were, and we only say that there were three of them because of the number of gifts they brought. Being Westerners, we have accepted the custom that each guest to a party, especially a birthday party, is expected to bring a gift. And so three gifts must have meant three men. But it could have been more than three and no less than two. As far as calling them kings, it is not likely that they were kings. For kings rarely traveled far distances because of the likelihood of a coup in their absence. And most of the kings would not have traveled without a large army to guard and protect them. So the song We Three Kings doesn't get it exactly right, although I hope we will see that it has the right intention. And so we use the word that St. Matthew chooses for his gospel, which is magi. And here are some facts about these magi. The word magi comes from the word magus, which is of Persian origin. Magus is associated with royal authority in various countries. because they participated in helping men get to political powerful positions by interpreting omens, signs, and in particular, signs from the heavens. We find such men described as both wise and royal at all places the Book of Esther. There we read that King Xerxes spoke of wise men who knew the times, the men next to him, the seven princes of Persia and Media. who saw the king's face and sat first in his kingdom. Such men were like the Magi in Matthew's gospel, as they were learned men who were advisors to their respective kings. And very well could have traveled as ambassadors for their kings. Because such magi could have traveled as ambassadors for their respective kings The early church fathers were most comfortable referring to the magi as kings. They liked to do so because they believed that such visitors were a fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies. Prophecies of the like from Psalm 72, where we read, May the kings of Sheba and Seba present him gifts. And in Isaiah 60, where we read, nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn. And all from Sheba will come bearing gold and incense and proclaiming praise to the Lord. What else could such passages be pointing to other than the Christ child being visited by three kings of Orient? To best understand the authority given to the magi, we need to recognize the magi from the Old Testament. Consider the person of Joseph, born of Jacob, sold into slavery by his brothers and imprisoned by the Egyptians Only Joseph practiced the arts of the magi. He was called by the Pharaoh of Egypt to interpret his dreams. Which were prophecies of seven years of prosperity and seven years of famine. Because of his correct interpretation, he was elevated second in power over all of Egypt. the place of a king. Daniel was another member of the Magi, as he too was able to interpret dreams for King Nebuchadnezzar. And he was also elevated to a high position of authority within the kingdom of Babylon. Such other world wisdom gave Joseph and Daniel positions of power like princes, princes described in the book of Esther. Such advisors were highly respected within their respective kingdoms and were thus given envoys to represent kings, their king. Thus the song, We Three Kings, is a reasonable representation of who visited the Christ child. Now examining the three wise men searching for the Christ child is quite fitting, I think, as it goes with our series of sermons preached during the Advent season. We first learned how God was quiet and how God hides. We next learned how God How God's providence is practiced in a similar way, and how he worked through the life of Joseph to providentially lead his brothers to repentance and reconciliation. We then learn how God wishes to be found, but on his terms and in his time, and what I hope we receive from observing the magi. From observing the magi is what seekers have to do to follow Christ, the Jesus of Nazareth. What can be noted first regarding the Magi looking for the Christ child? Is that they were maybe two, but they were few. They were the only ones who followed the star that led to Jesus. The only ones. Presently, there is a website and a documentary devoted to the phenomenon of the Bethlehem Star. And what scholars show from these sources is first how to use the three laws of planetary motion, mathematician Johannes Kepler identified As early as the 17th century. The three laws are used by astronomers, NASA, and European space agencies today. They are used because the three laws do not change. Because the laws do not change, it is possible For astronomers to draw up sky maps to show exact positions of all the stars over the planet Earth in space back through human history. Kepler himself was a devout Christian who desired to identify the mystery of the Star of Bethlehem. But he failed, and he failed because he was using wrong data in regards to the birth of Jesus. As we know, Jesus was born shortly before the death of King Herod. The only problem is Christian historians got it a bit wrong. in dating when Jesus was likely born. In truth, he was likely born between 2 and 4 BC. Which is two or four years earlier than medieval scholars thought. Now, with the advancement of computers, It is now much easier to map the movement of stars down through history and find and confirm the star of Bethlehem. It is not possible for me to walk you through all of the evidence that points to said star, and I would encourage you to look it up yourself, but I will get to the end game for us. The event was likely what astronomers call a dancing star, which is a star that is actually an alignment of stars with the planet Jupiter. The visual effect of watching Jupiter come together with a star of Regulus and then pass and then come together again and then pass, switching directions. is a phenomena that when viewed by men who are seeking wisdom from the stars, they would have noted and noticed it was actually a threefold coronation. Back and forth, back and forth. Because of the laws of physics, what appears to be a celestial coronation And a star stopping over a particular spot on Earth is what scientists call retrograde motion. Which is an effect on our human sensory because, you know, we are moving through space just as other planets are moving. Making it look like a star in the heavens is standing still. I'll stop. Because I don't even know if I understand that. Probably too much to share. But what's the point? The point is that what occurred in the heavens that caused the magi to seek the meaning of this celestial crowning was easy for all mid Middle Easterners to witness And yet only a few of them witnessed it and did anything about it. Thus following Jesus Coming to Jesus is represented in the Magi as a decision that few act upon. Few It is similar to the words of Jesus saying that many are called but few are chosen. It is the same as Jesus explaining that the road to perdition is wide and many travel on it. But the road to heaven is narrow with few travelers. Coming to Jesus, following Jesus, is automatically going to go against what is popular, what is faddish, what is considered the consensus. It is doing what most other people are not doing as the Magi themselves understood. To seek out the kingdom of God, to find Jesus, and fall at his feet as he sleeps in a manger and or hangs on a cross. is to do what the majority of people you know are not doing and unfortunately will never do. And it is a story like that of the Magi that gives us the expectation to be different It prepares us to be different and gives us the confirmation that we will be treated as different. Being different breaking is breaking the mold. It's going against the grain. And that is the Christian life. For the Christian life is destined to occupy a new heaven and a new earth, and this means this is not our home. Thus we will act differently than those who have this as their home. As has been noted, we are just passing through. And so because this is not our home, we must not act like this is our home. And in fact, if we are acting like this is our home Then we must repent and get back on the narrow road. And the only way back on the narrow road is to repent. Repent from being like everyone else. Repent and take the next step to pursue what is different. Christians are to be aware. that the devil loves to use the temptation of following the crowd. In informal logic it is called in Latin odpopolum. Which simply means appealing to the people. In colloquial terms, it is called bandwagon, as in everybody jump on the bandwagon. Consider that Adam and Eve were tempted by the devil to be like God. Israel was tempted to be like other nations around them. The persecution of Christians from the first century into today has occurred because Christians were not and do not behave like everyone else. And this is just as Jesus prophesied. The enemies of God hated Jesus, and just as they hated Jesus, they hate all who follow Jesus, and thus Christians And Christianity cannot appeal to the people or can never be a fad bandwagon on which everyone will jump. And as a side note, because Christianity is anti-faddish by its nature, As a pastor, I cringe when Christian communities create and follow their own paths. It could be a thad about worship styles, or a fad about trinkets to wear, or a thad about clothing, or a thad about certain books to read, whatever. From the vantage point of this pastor and as a father, I find it helpful that Christians train themselves not to follow any fat. So that they become accustomed to going against what the world says is natural, common, or popular Another behavior of the magi that identifies what it means to be Christian. Is how and what they worshipped, how and what In both the how and the what of their worship, we are to identify a mystery. A mystery in what they were experiencing versus what they were believing. Consider what they were experiencing. They were experiencing when they arrived a baby. Now again, I know the controversy regarding the question of Jesus being an infant lying in a manger or a child in his home in Nazareth when the Magi visited him. The sticking point seems to be this word in the Greek for child that St. Matthew uses It could be a representation of someone older, not quite an infant or in infant stage. But the logistics of whether Jesus was an infant or older are confusing. If the family was in Nazareth at the visit of the Magi Because Matthew makes it clear that the family purposefully fled to Egypt and seemed to only travel to Nazareth after Herod is known to be dead. So we're sticking with the Magi visiting the holy family in Bethlehem, and perhaps it was somebody else's home after they were in the stable. Anyways, what did they see? What did they witness? We don't know if they saw a donkey or sheep or shepherds like our comfortable manger seems. What we do know is that they saw Jesus as a baby. They saw a human child with human parents of no recognizable royal distinction. What they witnessed then was a mystery, as Jesus was nothing to the naked eye other than a human child. What their experience told them was that they were before a common human baby. But their standing and then kneeling, for Matthew says that they fell before Jesus, that went beyond their senses. What their souls understood was what their senses could not dictate. What they fell in front of went a great deal beyond their outward experience. Thus they worshiped by faith in that moment by mystery. It was a mystery because it was greater, much greater than what their senses told them. It was a mystery because they could not explain how they could know that the child they fell in front of was King of Kings and Lord of Lords. They could not explain it, and yet the inability to explain it, the true identity of Jesus, made it all the more convincing of who he was And I trust you can apply this practice of worshiping beyond our senses. Worshiping in terms of mystery when we partake of Holy Communion. It is more than what your senses tell you that it is. I was lamenting with the Reverend Lamboy recently how similar evangelical Christians have behaved compared to secular society today, who have decided to desecrate monuments and protest statues Recent desecrations and protest of statues are caused by the protesters Saying what the monument and statues represent. And what they represent is what the protesters experience Rather than something beyond what they can see or what they can know. The ridding of statuary symbols is thus egocentric Because the protesters are only concerned about what the symbols mean or don't mean to them And in a similar manner, modern Christians, we can call them evangelicals today, they have cast off symbols of the church That are supposed to represent a great deal beyond their physical appearance. The result is a pragmatic approach to the Christian faith that makes decisions regarding corporate worship, church government, and church ministry based on what is most practical And what is most practical is what brings in the greatest number of people and the greatest amount of money. We know that to be true The end game is no different than the strategies of corporations like Walmart, Target, Amazon, and the rest. And end result are buildings that are called Kafajima sanctatoriums Such buildings have no inherent beauty, but only a practical use. And end result are corporate worship services that entertain rather than exalt Jesus. And then results are pastors who dress up like an Apple CEO while leading corporate worship. And then results is placing in the dumpster crosses That once lie center on the communion table. It is the selling of the communion table, because after all, it's only used a few times a year. It is getting rid of pulpits from one side of the chancel, lecterns from the other side of the chancel. It is even getting rid of pulpits that are the center of chancels, you know, like the Baptists and the Presbyterians arrange. When the lectern on one side and the pulpit on the other side represented God's word and authority read and word and authority preached. Now the central focus is not even where the Baptists and the Presbyterians put it. The central focus is now placed on a man who places himself at the center, representing man. And nothing more. What the Magi fell before was a man who represented all of mankind, as only Jesus could. What the Magi fell before was God who became man in a manner only he could do. What the Magi fell before was both fully God and fully man, who could only be explained by mystery And the result of mystery was awe. And the result of awe was falling before him. Beloved, please mark my words as prophetic, which means to say, applying to God's church today. What is missing among Christians today that we need to bring back is a zeal to be different from the world and an embracing of the mysteries of God Going beyond what our senses tell us. A result of being different from the world, a result of embracing the mysteries of God will be a revival of the church. And a revival of the church will mean the church is no longer pragmatic, but supernatural. Corporate worship and serving Jesus within the church cannot possibly be boring or insignificant or irrelevant to each generation. If Christians embrace being different, going the opposite direction of the culture around us, and believing in mystery that creates both awe And anticipation within the heart of every Christian. In summary, for this day, we need To heed the call to follow the magi, who follow the star, who come to Jesus. The world will think that you are stupid for doing so. Let it be so. The road to heaven is narrow, and few travel on it. Let us pray

sermons.text: So In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Leave me seated. You may have speculated what my sermon topic is this morning from the readings I have chosen to preach today in reference to the Right to Life Sunday, even though it is one week early than its designation. I do so because the March for Life in Washington, D. C. occurs this coming Friday. And I want us as a parish to be as supportive as possible on that effort. The ruling was January 22nd, 1973, when the Supreme Court ruled that babies in their mother's womb could be killed. The first March for Life was January 22nd, 1974. This means that this year is the 45th March on behalf of the unborn. My responsibility as a pastor, preacher, is to do my very best to convince God's people, people who claim Jesus as Savior, that the unborn Are persons who are worthy of life. It is my responsibility to confront every attempt at a reasonable argument to justify abortion And to give you, God's people, arguments that affirm what the Bible teaches, which is that life begins at conception And therefore, every human being in a womb is to be celebrated as a bearer of the image of God. I will do so, but first a qualifier. There are likely women in this congregation who have been a part of the sin of abortion. That needs to be acknowledged. We cannot pretend that abortions only take place outside of Christian homes or that women who love Jesus today do not have broken pasts. That include abortion. Therefore, it should be said again and again that abortion is a sin that Jesus can and does forgive. His blood, his righteousness, his love is sufficient to overcome all sin, and therefore that includes abortion. This sermon then is not to make anyone feel guilty all over again, but instead it has the focus of convincing all who follow Jesus. That the least of these among us, the unborn, are worthy of life. Because the Bible is our authority For all things pertaining to life and godliness, we must start there. And from the Bible, We can say that unborn children are the epitome of the least of these You recall in Jesus' parable in Matthew 25 of the sheep and the goats. The sheep are rewarded heaven, and the goats rewarded the punishment of hellfire because of what they did and did not do. For the least of these. The least of these are the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the unclothed, the sick, and yes, even those in prison. What the list represents are the least that are cared about in society In the first century, when a person was homeless, jobless, or too ill to contribute to society or to take care of his or herself, Or destitute or in prison for any particular crime, he or she was considered an outcast by God He or she was reaping, evidently, what was sown in this life as is evident by their current condition. The reasoning was that to help such persons would be to thwart God's judgment and that they would not do. The thought process was very much like the idea of karma found in the Hindu religion. It is the same thought process that is endemic to our fallen natures, which is to believe That every situation in which we find ourselves indicates that we have done something in our past to deserve our present. We find this communicated in the Gospel according to St. John, where it records Jesus coming upon a blind man, blind since birth. His disciples assume the thinking that this man must have done something or his parents must have done something to cause him to be blind. Another example of this way of thinking is described in the gospel according to Saint Luke. Jesus knows what the people are thinking. News has spread that some Jews from Galilee had been put to death by Pilate, and that Pilate took some of their blood and mixed it with the sacrifices in the temple. Because the people think that all tragedies are somehow deserved, they question Jesus as to why these Galileans suffered such a fate. Who was at fault? In both instances, Jesus explains something quite different than their thinking and ours. He helps the people understand that such tragedies are not necessarily related to anything any individual did. But that all tragedies can reflect, in the end, the glory of God, as God works to redeem each moment and redeem each person affected by a tragedy. As we think upon who are the least of these, we can conclude that a child conceived who is unwanted and whom the mother of the child and the father or both would rather see the child dead than living, even if it was with someone else to care for that child. Can we not see that such children are the epitome of the least of these? And if we can, then we can also conclude that the sheep are faithful when they care for the epitome of the least of these. Next, along the same lines as the first point, we can say that unborn children are a part of society that Christians are called to give the most protection. In the Epistle of James that we read this morning, we are told that pure religion is where the orphans and widows are protected. Orphans and widows represent those in society that are weakest and most vulnerable. They are the weakest and most vulnerable because they do not have anything to offer of economic value to society A widow, most likely an elderly woman, could not contribute to the welfare of a society beyond her own household, and if she's widowed, she has no household. An orphan was just as bad because such children were too young to be a part of the workforce. They had no inheritance because they were orphaned. Thus, they were a drain on society. They required the resources of others to be clothed, sheltered, and fed. While societies of all generations look negatively upon such people, God refers to them as his own. In Deuteronomy, God reveals his heart by commanding that what is left in the fields is to be given to the widows, to the orphans, to the stranger. And this, mind you, is from the law of God. Not supposed to find grace in the law of God, but there it is. And the psalmist knows this heart of God as he sings of the Lord watching, the Lord watching over the alien and sustaining the fatherless and sustaining the widow. Through Isaiah, the Lord instructs his people to have the same heart when he tells us to seek justice. Encourage the oppressed, and defend the cause of the fatherless and the widow. When we defend the right to life for the unborn, we are defending the cause of the fatherless We are defending those who cannot defend themselves. We are defending God's children, as he identified himself as the father of the fatherless. Next, we can conclude from scripture that the unborn children represent life that only God can give and God can take away. Arguments about abortion usually center on the issue of life. Questions such as, what is life? And when does life begin? These are answered in such a way in the Scripture as, well, excuse me, in the defense of the arguer, as a presupposition People answer what is life according to what they have already concluded about abortion. In contrast, the Bible teaches that such arguments are not to be had by men because men have no place in deciding what is life because men are not creators. Because only God can create. He is the only one who can determine what life is and when it begins. During a summer in college, I volunteered for an organization called Youth for Christ. And part of their mission was to minister to pastor youth that were troubled in a detention center. We led Bible studies, worship services, did some counseling, and so on. And before one particular Bible study, the director told the young men there that we were going to play out a scene from the Bible. And as soon as this was uttered, a wise-mouthed youth stood up and shouted, I get to play God! And without a pause, even before that sentence was finished, the director shouted back shouted back, you can't play God. Sit down. Well, a similar shout needs to be made to any person who thinks he or she can determine what is life. Those who think they have the right or responsibility to decide what is life and when life begins need to hear that same retort. You can't play God It is God who says that He knits us in our mother's womb. It is God who says that we are fearfully and wonderfully made. It is God who baptizes children in the womb with his Holy Spirit. It is God who says, of the children in the womb, this is life. Well these are biblical arguments against abortion. And I know that you know And you know that I know that such arguments from the Bible regarding the unborn do not have authority within the world in which we live, the culture in which we live. They don't carry much weight outside of the church. Sadly, they don't even carry much weight for many who say they are Christian, but their faith has been so liberalized that they no longer regard the Bible as relevant. And because of this rejection of the Bible as authoritative, both in the secular world and in liberal Christianity, we should know some arguments from natural law. These can be helpful when engaging the unbelieving world about the sin of abortion. And so we do. There is an argument learned from the principles of biology. We start with the acknowledgement that every human being has 24 chromosomes. No more and no less. We could argue that because an unborn child has 24 chromosomes and the mother has 24 chromosomes. That they are two separate beings, not one. If a mother is going to claim the fetus as another part of her body, she's going to have to explain why she has an abnormally inhuman amount of chromosomes. Of course she can't explain that, so she has to admit, if she is honest, that she is carrying a separate human being Next, we could argue that if a child is born alive is considered to have the right to life, which all laws and states Tell us if a child born has the right to life, then a child unborn has the same right because geography does not determine personhood Consider that you are still a citizen of the United States, even though you step over the southern border and into Mexico. Even if you spend a day in Mexico, your citizenship in the Americas does not change. So too is a child, a person, in the womb or outside the womb. Geography doesn't change the nature of anything. Next, we can argue from the concept of potentiality. The potentiality principle was formerly identified by that Greek philosopher Aristotle. Who identified the value of objects that exist in terms of their potentiality and their actuality? First, there is the nature of an object as to what it presently is, but that should also be added and accounted for is the potentiality of what that thing is. Aristotle argued that potentiality is an intrinsic value to that which should be respected as part of its objective nature. Consider that social programs that we accept embrace this potentiality principle This principle justifies why poor children should receive a free education and free health care and alike. Because such aids provide a child's potentiality. That same argument can be applied to the unborn because what they need are aids that would help them achieve their potential. And the first aid that they need is the right to life. Giving them the right to live is aiding them toward their potential Next, one of my favorite. Next is the Horton Hears A Who argument If you recall the story from Dr. Seuss about Horton here's a who, there is a community of human beings, like human beings, that inhabit a speck of dust. Horton the elephant is the one who first hears the voices of the community that no one else can hear. The community is called Huville. And therefore the mayor of Houvil asks Horton to protect them from harm Horton agrees to do so, proclaiming throughout the story that a person is a person, no matter how small. And it is with that same logic as Horton and that of Aristotle that we can argue that a fertilized egg contains all that a person is going to be in the future. A fertilized egg is genetic, genetically speaking, is everything that person can and will be. Therefore, you and I and all persons alive today are made up of the exact genetic makeup that we had in the wombs of our mothers at the moment of conception. Therefore, we were persons in the womb of our mothers, just as we are now persons, because a person is a person, no matter how small. The next argument to address is one that I heard from a theology professor in seminary. And I confess that I was greatly disappointed when I heard it. He said that if abortion is immoral, then God must be immoral because of all the miscarriages and stillbirths. That women have endured over the ages. Ages in which God was sovereign. Beloved, such an argument. Takes us back to the example of a young man wanting to pray God. No man is God And because no man is God, any action we take that behaves like God is, of course, a violation of the first commandment. It is for humanity to trust in God's will when there is a miscarriage or a stillborn. To trust in God's will. It is never for us to replicate what God is sovereign over. Now I hope I have convinced you that arguments like these are valid and sound, and arguments before are biblically based. However, what must be admitted is that no matter how well we articulate our argument, those arguments don't change the hearts of men and women. As a church, we must be honest with ourselves and ask, what can truly save the unborn? Is it reason? Is it legislation? Is it electing the right people? By themselves and of themselves the answer to all is no. But that does not mean we should not be reasonable. It does not mean that we should not fight for righteous laws and work to elect people who will stand for righteousness. All of that is good, and the Holy Spirit will use our argumentation to change hearts. And that is the reality we must accept, it's the heart that must be changed Any argument, any reasoning is dependent on the Holy Spirit to change the hearts and wills of human beings. One story about the Holy Spirit changing a heart will suffice. This is the testimony of Dr. Beverly Macmillan. Dr. Macmillan performed numerous abortions before she was confronted by the Holy Spirit. Her conversion was not directly related to being an abortionist, as she sought God during a difficult time in her life. It was after she gave her life to Christ that she soon realized what she had been doing After performing an abortion and examining the remains of the child, she awoke to the reality of a life being taken. And these are Dr. McMillan's own words. She said, standing at that sink, I guess I just started seeing these bodies for the first time. I don't know what I did before that. I remember very clearly seeing an arm and seeing the deltoid muscle. And it struck me how beautiful this was. The thought just engorged my mind. Here is this beautiful piece of human flesh. What are you doing? Beloved, I know that such descriptions are graphic and hard to hear What I want us to note is that what brought Dr. Macmillan to this revelation was not reason. It wasn't legislation. It wasn't politics. It was the Holy Spirit. It was the Holy Spirit let loose in the heart of an individual after she heard the gospel of Jesus Christ and believed. I hope by saying that I I don't want to discourage you from reasoning. Of course not. I I'm presenting you arguments for reasoning to the world and to one another. And I present these arguments that you too would be convinced that the unborn are worth protecting. They go to the very heart of our being Christian. Abortion as a sin is a great mark of blood guilt upon my generation and each generation that follows until it is no longer acceptable. You know, we are very much like Israel, suffering because of the sin of Achan. You remember that story in Joshua? God promises to take Israel on victory after victory over the promised land, and yet they lose their their second battle. They lose and lose people. And Joshua speaks the Lord and asks him what has happened, and the Lord reveals that a man named Achan had kept some of the spoils of war for himself, going against what God directly commanded. And it was not until Achan's sin was atoned for that Israel could move on, fight on, and win. We cannot expect as a church God's blessings while we do not care for the least of these. The most vulnerable among us. God's people. Be convinced that the unborn are the least among us. The fatherless that God calls himself father over. And therefore, and therefore, as the least of these, when we fight for them, when we stand for them, when we work for them, We do it unto the Lord. Let us pray. Our God and Father, we confess that we too were once fatherless. Dead in our trespasses and sins, but you found us, woke us up, gave us your spirit, and made us your children. And so with that grace and mercy, we now are called to protect those who are the least, those who are the most vulnerable, those who are the fatherless. So, Father, increase our courage all the more. Help us to heal wounds of our past. Help us to move beyond the sins of our past, and to stand for those who are the weakest among us. And as we do, may we always be mindful that in doing so, we are standing for you. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen

sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Ladies, wives Former wives want to be wives. Which one of the following descriptions describes your man? Or was your man or would be your man? Is he Mr. Command Man? Is he a born leader? Gets big jobs done. Strong, forceful, bossy, less tolerant, less intimate or vulnerable than other men, not into sharing his feelings He sees the big picture and expects his wife to be there for him whenever he needs her. What about Mr. Visionary? Mr. Visionary is a shaker, a dreamer, a changer. He tends to focus on peripheral issues like whether it's okay for Christians to smoke marijuana. These men love confrontation and they hate the status quo. They love to communicate their feelings and thoughts with writings and music and signing and singing And other arts. They love to experience new things. Well, how about Mr. Steady? He is a natural servant. He knows the value of peace and safety. He is not easily disturbed and usually cautious. He is dutiful and loyal, sometimes to a fault. He doesn't create tension and looks to calm every situation where needed. He may look indifferent at times, but there is a depth to him that is greater than other types of men. So which man is yours? Is he clearly one? Or is he a mix of two? Gentlemen, husbands, former husbands, want to be husbands, which of the following descriptions is your woman, was your woman, or would be your woman? Is she a dreamer? A dreamer is driven, focused, often creative, not always patient with less efficient people. She would rather do something about a problem than sit around thinking. She wants to make everything work and look good. Or what about the woman who is a servant? A servant is extroverted, friendly, and warm to others. She loves to get to know people. She is emotional and very compassionate. She is understanding, sympathetic, and quick to take blame. She can serve to the point of exhausting herself. She wants to make everyone happy. Or what about the go-to girl? Is she a go-to girl? A go-to girl takes life and most moments seriously. She has great attention to detail. She is cautious about what is appropriate and what is not. She thrives on consistency and is driven by principles She does not express her feelings easily. She expects everyone, including herself, to live up to high ideals. So man, which woman is yours? Is she clearly one or a mixture of two? Well, what if I told you that a Mr. Command man should not be married to a woman who is a dreamer because their personalities collide? And a go-to girl should not be married to a visionary. And a Mr. Steady should not be married to a woman who is primarily a servant. These personalities do not make good marriages. So if you are caught up in such a marriage, what should you do? Well, the spirit of the age says, get a divorce. The spirit of the age says that you are not compatible. He or she is not your soulmate. But what does God say? What God says is what the Bible says. And I invite you to take the challenge of finding anywhere in the Bible any teaching or any narrative that describes the concept Or existence of a soulmate. No, don't bother. Don't bother because it isn't found in Holy Scripture. According to several sources, the concept of soulmates comes from Greek mythology. Our ancestors are said by the Greeks to have had two heads and four arms and four legs, etc. But they did something to offend the gods. So the gods decided to punish them by splitting them down the middle. Thus, humanity was created and automatically given the task of each person finding their other half, their soulmate. Perhaps that is where the saying, better half, comes from. So the origin of soulmate is most certainly not Holy Scripture. God never directs any of his followers to find his or her soulmate. And in fact, the only concept of soulmate in the scriptures is to identify the person you are married to, the person on your wedding day that you said, I do to. That person, God says, he has made you and her, or him and you, that person, God has joined together. Without considering personalities or Greek myths. That is your soulmate. That is the one no man should separate. This lengthy introduction is for the purpose of proclaiming the need of Christians to treat their marriages and marriage itself As a sacrament. As a sacrament. I am compelled to preach this because of the sermon last week, and this is officially Right to Life Sunday. Last week we addressed the plague of abortion that continues to wreak havoc among us. And because one major aspect or cause of abortion is how the institution of marriage is treated, even amongst Christians. There was a time in our culture when pregnancies occurred before marriage, and instead of aborting the child, a couple would get married. And they would make said marriage work for the sake of the child, and thus for the sake of the institution of marriage. And thus for the institution of a nuclear family, and really for the sake of the wellness of society as a whole. As you know, that has altogether changed, and we are all worse for it. At the root of the problem, as I see it. Is the failure of Christian people to treat the institution of marriage in a sacramental manner I say sacramental because we Protestants don't go so far as to say that marriage is a sacrament in the same manner that the Roman Catholic Church says it is a sacrament. Because what we call sacraments are those things that Jesus commanded and are things that all Christians are to participate in, and of course Jesus himself was not married. The intriguing part of marriage as a sacrament is that although Jesus was not married, he himself uses the image of marriage to describe his relationship with the church. So in a very important image communicated by Jesus himself, he does participate in marriage. So it is at least fair to say that for Christians, marriage is sacramental, having all of the qualities of being a sacrament. If Christians were to treat marriage as sacramental, divorce would be very, very rare. And children would be a blessing, not a burden, not mere tissue to dispose of, and the church would be a better witness to the unbelieving world and to societies, making them morally stronger, having given a higher standard, a Christian standard to live. I truly believe such to be true. So this remainder of the sermon is to convince you to agree with me. Of course, like last week, I must provide a qualifier. Divorce in the Christian Church is a reality. Spouses do sin against one another. Husbands and wives can be unfaithful to their marriage vows in terms of infidelity and or abuse. And thus they break their vow and give the right of the innocent spouse to leave the marriage. Jesus and St. Paul recognized such realities. And Christians have divorce in their past before they knew the mercies of Jesus or before their eyes were open to the truth. The good news is that divorce, like abortion, is a sin that can be forgiven. The blood, righteousness, and love of Jesus is sufficient. And that is qualifier enough. And let it also be heard that if you are presently single because of divorce or death or have never been married You too need to be convinced of the importance of marriage, or you too have a voice that needs to be heard. Well let us then return to establishing in our minds and hearts the truth that the institution of marriage is sacramental. First, we must be reminded of our accepted definition of sacrament. This comes from the office of instruction. in the Book of Common Prayer. You can find it in your pew, page 481. The question reads, What do you mean by this word sacrament? And here's the answer. Although the Bible goes to no great length to describe all that angels do and are, when it does speak of them, people usually take notice, we perka, about angels. For some reason. And the superiority of that which we will eventually receive in Jesus Christ is compared to that which we receive from the world around us. A statement of superiority is followed by a number of citations of scripture.
