And I'm guessing you won't go beyond four seconds before the shot changes. Because they don't trust that you can pay attention long enough And in case you're wondering just why I'm concerned, in a recent lecture I gave to students in the logic classes that I teach at Stevenson University I was showing my notes on the screen for the lecture, and I was reading to them those same notes, rewording it So they could understand it differently. And then I wrote on the whiteboard an example. And the simple lesson was to show them how to find the middle term in a syllogism Now the middle term is one of three terms in a syllogism. A syllogism can only have three terms, and the middle term is the one that's not in the major, not in the conclusion, but is found in both the major and minor premise. Basically I'm going to sum it up to say there's only three terms and the middle terms not in the conclusion but in the other premises. Well after I get done with this lecture, and it happens every cross A student will raise his or her hand and say, yes, I understand what you said, but but how do you find the middle term? Now, I do not hide my emotion to such questions very well, and I need to get better at that, but I kind of give this, you know Didn't I just say that? But I I I answer and I just repeat myself exactly what I said before, and then I'll have someone else. I get that. Yeah, thank you, Professor, but can you help me find the middle term Well there are times that I wonder in those moments if I'm on the old candid camera show, I'm looking to be pranked or punked, or someone surely is trying to pull one over on me But in reality, they don't have the attention span. They're not paying attention Consider the likely reason why so many people do not attend church each Sunday, especially the young. For them, it's boring. Many churches have attempted to accommodate by entertaining. The result are worshipers becoming audiences and ministers and song leaders becoming entertainers. I've spoken about this enough times from this pulpit, I will not elaborate further. What the preacher to the Hebrews has said is important. And those who have heard are in danger of not paying attention. And they didn't have televisions or phones to distract them. The preacher to the Hebrews understood that if they do not pay attention, they will drift away, literally float away. And this takes us back to the opening story. The truth of salvation is like the ski tube floating downstream. It goes by us, and if we do not jump in the water and climb onto that tube, there is no guarantee another will come by. This may sound like a warning of doom because it is. Again, he's being urgent here The picture is not so much the truth floating away, but of a person who says he is a Christian and not paying attention to the truth right in front of them. The way of the world, the spirit of the age, is a stream flowing hard and flowing rugged. It dashes the weak and unattentive upon its rocks. If we don't jump on the tube of truth, we will smash against those rocks. If we do not pay attention by believing and living what we have heard, we will float away. and suffer at the consequence of that current. The reason for the warning is given in verse 2 and following Warning in verse 1, the reason in verse 2 and following. Verse 2 describes the message spoken by angels, he says. The law given to Moses was understood to have been delivered by angels. Thus, the message spoken by angels is the law of God. The law of God, of course, is binding upon all men, even those who have not heard it. No one is without excuse, the Apostle Paul tells us in Romans that the evidence of God is ever-present. The law being binding upon all men must be obeyed. If not obeyed, a just punishment is assured for every violation, every act of disobedience. This is not qualified. There are no exceptions. If the law of God is binding and the disobedience to such law is to be punished, the question that follows must be asked. And we need to answer it. He says, how shall we escape if we ignore such a great salvation? How shall we escape? Escape what? Escape punishment. Because all have sinned, as we hear in Romans, all have fallen short of the glory of God The only way to escape from the punishment of such sin is what we are to pay attention to. It just went by us. It's floated by us. It is to trust in Jesus as our Savior. That is what the word escape is trying to help us understand, to save us from what is our Destiny in our sin. Now consider that there is no weight to the warning unless what is escape is harmful. Unless we escape. Escape what? Oh, it's no big deal. Oh, it is. In this text, the warning is in reference to eternal damnation. And we need to use the word hell. That's what we are to escape. Hell. The Bible teaches us. Orthodox Christianity confesses that hell is a real place. Weeping, wailing, gnashing of teeth. Consisting of torment, excruciating pain, unsatisfied desires. That's hell. It is not a place where demons in red suits and pitchforks wander around making men work, nor is it a place where partiers go to be uninterrupted by the morally uptight. Hell is described in Scripture as eternal, a fire prepared for the devil and his angels, a place of divine punishment everlasting. And the reality of hell should be spoken of more often in the church today. Although Christians do not need to dwell upon hell, it should be in our consciences and it should keep us from going astray. I recalled in preparing this a story that my oldest nephew told when he first started college He said he shared a dorm room with what he called likable pagans, I thought was a nice description. He said they sat around to get to know each other, and of course the topic came up was sex And one of the gentlemen there said that he had three heroes, God, angels, and Hugh Hefner. And when my nephew was asked what he thought of Hefner He responded as a Jorgensen might, stating bluntly, well, Hugh Hefner's going to hell. Well, after the group's initial shock at that statement, they actually started to agree with him And realizing that Hugh Hefner had probably broken every commandment with no repentance, and today we know that he is now deceased, and I have no knowledge of him repenting. But what is positive about that story to me is the effect that the truth of hell and even mentioning it, the effect it had upon these young men. If we truly believe the words of our Lord and understand hell to be an actual place of actual punishment for sin, that it should be on our lips and it should be part of our conversation. A main concern is just how literal people understand the place of hell, or they don't understand it literally. I know my children have told me as they attended McDonough School that many times they were asked by their fellow students, am I going to hell? And then they would point to someone else, is he going to hell? Is she going to hell? And of course they'd get a kick if one of my sons said yes Yes, they are going to hell. But those questions easily were asked because the hell to them wasn't a real place. It was just something to laugh at. It is to be for us something that scares us into God's kingdom. According to a decade-old survey conducted by Barna Research Group, Only three out of ten adults in the United States believe that hell is a literal place. Three out of ten is significant because four out of ten claim to be evangelical Christians. And even more revealing than that is that Christians generally in general think that a good person gets to go to heaven and a bad person to hell. We should recognize the result of this type of thinking is catastrophic, for if we take away the threat of eternal punishment and allow the entrance to heaven being for those who are generally good. Then we take away the whole purpose of Jesus and his sacrifice and the whole meaning of salvation itself. There is no need to escape, for there is nothing to escape from. There is no need for Jesus to die on the cross, for there is no wrath of God to be satisfied. This is what John Henry Newman was concerned when he wrote the following: Quote: Hell is the turning point between Christianity and pantheism. It is the critical doctrine, you can't get rid of it, is the very characteristic of Christianity. It is my contention that many Christians do not believe in the literal hell simply by the evidence of their unfaithful living. If hell were truly understood and accepted as a real place, it would be a deciding factor in the prevention of purposeful sin by Christians. If the place of hell was in our minds and conversations when we are tempted to please ourselves over obeying God's commands, the fear of such a possible torment would move us toward the cross. As we considered the alternative. But alas, it is not on our minds, on our tongues, as much as it ought to be. And furthermore, we are tempted to believe that God would not do that to anyone, would He? We have heard he is too loving, too loving to punish in such a manner Well, God's love, of course, does not contradict his punishment. The presence of hell and the punishment we all deserve makes his love toward us all the more amazing and all the more merciful. Well the question asked in verse 3 is really a question that cannot be answered. It cannot be answered by men or by angels. No one can say they escaped if he neglects so great a salvation. If you neglect it, there is no hope. There is no other way to prevent the fires of hell but by faith in the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. That's what's going by us. That truth should always be on our minds and on our lips. The remaining words of verses 3 and 4 give reason as to why this great salvation should be believed. It was spoken first by Jesus. That is first in that Jesus revealed these truths to us. God bore witness to the truth of what his son was and did and said by signs and wonders. And thus we can ask again. How shall we escape if we reject so great a salvation? Hell is our destiny. The lake of fire is our eternal place of residence if we reject Jesus as our Messiah. And this message, this truth, should not be silenced, it should not be hushed. Our Savior placed it before us. The apostle placed it before us. It is there, whether we acknowledge it or not, whether we are comfortable with the subject or not. And finally, I fear that the topic of hell falls on too many ears like so many other cliches. Hell is like a cliché. The devil wants it to sound sophomoric, imaginary, cartoonish, or anything else but a real place. Because he is evil. And he wants the souls of humanity to dwell there with him. The devil wants you to neglect your salvation. He wants you to leave your faith in Jesus or die. He inhabits false teachers who deny the faith. Those who are professing Christians, teaching falsely, and leading others astray. And he inhabits Cray's gunman. who go into schools and take the lives of too many. Either way, he gets what he wants. The preacher in Hebrews wants to scare us, scare us away from the plans of the devil. And the way for each of us to resist him is to pay attention. Because the salvation message is going by us. Let us pray. Our Father, we want to take the urgency of the preacher here, and we want to apply it to each of our lives. And you know, and Holy Spirit, we ask you to speak to each of us. Where we are not paying attention. Father, restore us, forgive us, restore us, and Father Keep our attention upon the truths as they are in Jesus, because we do want to enter our heavenly home. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Humility in Obscurity
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. And please turn in your Bibles to the book of Hebrews, chapter 2. Starting at verse 5, you will be well served to follow along at the first half of this sermon You'll note that we have bitten off a big chunk of Scripture today, but our focus is going to be upon one particular aspect of that chunk. Recall that the preacher to the Hebrews has made definitive statements regarding the superiority of Jesus as compared to angels. Angels that some believed would play a prominent role in Israel being saved from their enemies in Israel, having the crown returned to the promised land. The belief in the importance of angels in the salvation of Israel, an importance even over the promised Messiah, was discovered in the writings of what we know as the Dead Sea Scrolls. It appears that the preacher to the Hebrews is addressing those who were once of the Qumran community who kept such scrolls, taught from such scrolls and had developed their understanding of God's plan of salvation from said scrolls. The entrance of Jesus onto the scene turned this teaching upside down, but as time passed, apparently. These new converts to Christianity began to experience the difficulty of living the Christian life Especially amidst their Jewish communities who were hostile to the Christian message And well, the difficulties gave the devil an opportunity to tempt them, these new converts, to go back to their old teachings. And that meant to go back and look for an archangel instead of accepting Jesus as the Savior. In verse 5, we have a repeat of the preacher's argument regarding the superiority of Jesus over angels. The verse also mentions the world to come, which is a world fully redeemed. He is alluding to the new heaven and the new earth that would be ruled by Jesus, and we who are his followers will be the benefactors of that rule. Verse 6 asks a rhetorical question, and that question will eventually be our focal point. Mankind, in general, isn't anything that God should be mindful of him. Humanity is depraved. Humanity is fallen. Humanity is guilty and therefore under the curse of death. But the psalmist who is David, anointed by the Holy Spirit, changes the focus away from humanity in general to one man, the Son of Man. God is indeed mindful of the Son of Man. And the Son of Man is a clear reference to Jesus. It is Jesus, in Jesus, that the true dignity of humanity is revealed. And it is the title Son of Man that Jesus prefers when he refers to himself. It is another way of saying that Jesus is the second Adam or the Adam as Adam should have been, which is sinless. The exaltation given to Jesus is because of his willingness to become fully man while being fully God. And this passage of Scripture in Hebrews 2 is the closest in kind to the great poetic description given to us by St. Paul to the Philippians. Where he tells us that Jesus, although being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but made himself of no reputation taking on the form of a bondservant and coming in the likeness of men. Verse 8 makes the same claim as St. Paul does to the Philippians by declaring Jesus to have all things subject to him. As he stands above all of creation in heaven and on earth, he is the sovereign one. The curious statement is the last one in verse 8. It informs us that not yet are all things placed under the feet of Jesus. And what does that mean? Well we're going to come back to it. Verse 9 is the reason why Jesus made himself lower than angels. It is the reason why he became man. He did so to die, and to die is a sacrifice that the preacher will fully proclaim in a few verses ahead. And he died so that he could be glorified Having overcome sin and death, and he was glorified so that he could glorify his followers who will come after him and who will be like him Verse 10 makes the point perfectly clear as Jesus is proclaimed to be the captain, or we could even say the trailblazer. Who leads the way to heaven by suffering, so that those who come after will not suffer the second death, but will instead become inheritors of his kingdom. And as inheritors, this is why the followers of Jesus are called here brethren. Not that we are all male, but that we are all made children of God and thus heirs of Jesus. Any idea that an angel could share in our humanity or make us his brethren or make us follow or excuse me make us fellow heirs That is preposterous, it is absurd, it is unimaginable. In verses twelve and thirteen We have a series of Old Testament references that verify how Jesus shared in our humanity. There is reading from Psalm 22 and then from Isaiah 8. Messianic promises are listed as only being fulfilled by the Son of Man. Verses 14 and 15 are restatements of all that has been said thus far, and we're going to see in Hebrews that they repeat and restate quite a bit, so that there is no doubt as to what the preacher is saying. The description of those who, through fear of death, were all their lifetime subject to bondage. That is an attempt to identify with Christians who have suffered persecution for their faith. And it is also an identification with all of humanity who have had a sense of their own depravity, a sense of in their conscience that they cannot escape the guilt of their past sins. All persons who have had their consciences awakened to their own sin and guilt have a fear of death. Because they cannot overcome their sinful behavior and they cannot face God who would hold them accountable. Jesus knows such people. And he says that he has procured one their release. Verse 16 drives the point of Jesus releasing humanity from bondage by explaining clearly who benefits. Angels are not the benefactors of Jesus overcoming sin and death. Only humanity. And for the sake of his audience, the preacher specifically says, the seed of Abraham. The Jews Who are now Christians, they are the ones who benefit for what the Messiah has procured for them. The conclusion in verse 17, while summing up the preacher's points, also adds a new element to all of these truths, and that is that Jesus was also their high priest. And to describe his work as high priest, we hear again that word propitiate. We hear that in Romans, we hear that in 1 John. It means to placate or satisfy wrath. God's wrath In other words, Jesus as our high priest offers himself as a sacrifice to turn away God's wrath. And God's wrath must be satisfied, for his justice is established, and thus evil must be atoned for. For such evil is not a mistake An accident, but the destruction of what God made and called good It is the opposite of God's love and goodness, and therefore it, evil, must be put down, never to be reprised. We have now received the message of the preacher regarding the superiority of Jesus over any other heavenly being. In terms of his atoning work for the salvation of all who put their faith in him. Angels don't have what it takes. No other creation has what it takes. It is only the God man, who is Jesus the Christ, who has what it takes. This has been clearly established. But what is in these verses for us as well is a picture of Jesus that we are to admire. and is a cause of our worshiping him, and is also a cause of our emulating him What I am referring to is Jesus humbling himself. Jesus as a model for the Christian life. is a necessary topic of constant discussion, as well as some necessary qualifications. I have stated in some years past from this pulpit before that I was not really a fan of the WWJD bracelets. And it was placed on bracelets and other paraphernalia on which Christian publishers use that acrimon to sell the idea You remember what that meant for those of you who have fading memories or for those of you too young to remember in the 90s. The acronym WWJD stood for the question, what would Jesus do? It was derived From a book titled In His Steps by a Christian preacher named Charles Sheldon. But interestingly, the phrase actually goes back to the great preacher Charles Spurgeon. And Spurgeon claimed it was based on the work of Thomas Akempus in his book, The Imitation of Christ. Those are pretty big names in Christian history. Charles Spurgeon and Thomas Akampus And I certainly have no standing to question their understanding of the usefulness of the question, what would Jesus do? In general, the question was to be a challenge to Christians to attempt to act in a way that personified the teachings of Jesus from the Gospels. And that is most certainly what the Christian life is to be. And so the acronym meaning definitely captures the essence of Christian ethics. But also it is an interesting acronym because it implies, or can imply, that whatever Jesus would do, we who follow him should do it as well. And that is where it fails, as the preacher to the Hebrews would agree. Because the preacher has just proclaimed that what Jesus did No one else, including heavenly angels, can or could or would do. What Jesus would do is become lower than the angels. He would suffer pain and sorrow and death by being our high priest and our propitiation, our offering to God. And he would be exalted by overcoming the bondage of death while making his followers holy and making them his brethren. Jesus and only Jesus could do that and did do that and therefore there is no one like him in that no creature in heaven and on earth can do what Jesus did. But although it is only Jesus who would do such things, it is the Spirit The love, the principled actions that Jesus took upon himself that we are to follow and do as he did. And that spirit, that love, those principled actions, began with humility Jesus making himself low so that his followers can be raised high is what Jesus would do and what he would have us do. As I mentioned, the passage in Philippians 2 is very much like the description that the preacher to the Hebrews gives in Hebrews chapter 2. And when St. Paul writes this to the Philippians, that same idea, before he tells us about Jesus taking no reputation and taking the form of humanity St. Paul says that believers in Jesus are to have the same mind. The same mind. We are to have the same mind of humility as Jesus did. Thus you and I are doing what Jesus would do when we humble ourselves. And to humble ourselves in a similar manner as Jesus is to take on the form of a servant, which for us is to serve other people before we serve ourselves. Consider what happens when you serve others, not begrudgingly, for that's not true service. When you truly serve someone else, you have less opportunity to think about yourself. When you serve others, truly serve, you have to concentrate on their needs and not your own. And when you do, you are doing what Jesus would do. And each of us, each of us has a place in life where we are called to serve. Children are to obey their parents in all things, and that means children are to serve at the behest of their parents. How often is that heard in our culture today? And wives are to submit to their husbands in all things. That's Paul's qualifier. Not some things, not certain things, in all things. And to submit is to serve as requested. And husbands are called to love their wives as Jesus loved the church, not as he wants to love her. not as he is comfortable with loving her, but as Jesus loved, which was loving by atoning for sin Thus husbands serve by loving their wives so that they cover a multitude of their wives' sin. And each of us is to submit to our governing authorities. We are just to submit to magistrates and to the rule of law We are to submit to governors who have been placed in their positions of authority by God. We are to submit to bosses who own companies we work for. We are to submit to teachers and instructors commissioned to lead us. We are to submit to the church leaders who have been ordained to the task of teaching God's Word and helping us apply His Word to our everyday lives. Even when we don't like the application, and even when we don't like the man who's teaching it. The only way we can submit and love and serve is to be humble. To be humble. And being humble before people we may not like, we may not respect, is very, very difficult. To be humble before leaders who might not be as gifted as we are, or who don't lead in the same manner we would lead. That's asking a lot. And yet it it it must be done, and it must be done in faith. And there is said a key point. You're still with me, hang with me. Humility and service must be done in faith. Consider a woman who strives to serve her husband by way of submitting, as the Bible instructs, and her husband makes a few decisions that she does not agree with Most certainly would do differently and is afraid that these decisions will hurt the family financially. What is she to do? Well, God doesn't tell her to nag. God doesn't tell her to pitch a fit God tells her to submit in faith and trust that God will be faithful to her and to her family. Consider that when Jesus submitted himself to the guards who arrested him, and to the Sanhedrin who unjustly accused him And to Pontius Pilate, who decided his execution, that Jesus did it all in faith. Now perhaps we don't think of Jesus enacting faith because he personifies faith. But Jesus acted in faith just as the preacher to the Hebrews says in verse 17. Jesus was faithful, and the result of his faith was turning lies into truths, sufferings into healing, and death into life. But it didn't look that way in the eyes of those who lacked faith. To take on the form of a servant, to humble self before others, requires a living faith that God will respond to us in our humility and he will lift us up. The problem, however, is that God might not lift us up on our preferred timeline. God might not even lift us up in this life. That reality is the application of the phrase from verse 8. where we are told, but now we do not see all things under him. This is the Christian reality that theologians have called the already And the not yet. Which is to say that we have victory in Jesus, for we are in him and he is in us, but the full reality of that victory is still to come. And so we wait and we serve. And while we serve by taking humble postures before our fellow man, we may suffer injustices. We may be treated unkindly and unfairly, but that too is how Jesus was treated. And that continues to be how many treat Jesus even when they say they don't believe in him. While preparing this sermon, I ran across a book titled Embracing Obscurity. Embracing obscurity. It teaches Christians to serve without fanfare or recognition Under authorship it reads Anonymous. And I thought that was quite clever. And a challenge For Christians to embrace humble servanthood that by definition should be anonymous Hear this quote. Quote, He who would learn to serve must first learn to think little of himself. This is the highest and most profitable lesson, truly to know and despise ourselves. And to think always well and highly of others is great wisdom and perfection. Who said that? Does it matter? There was once a woman Who in the name of Jesus nursed people stricken with leprosy while starting nine elementary schools to educate the poorest of the poor. She did this before anyone in the general public knew her name. What was her name? Does it matter? I know the man that is said of him That he preached the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ to more people than any other man in the history of the world. You may think you know his name, but doesn't matter. Doesn't matter. There is a woman right now that is home with a sick child. She serves the child as if the child is the most important human being on earth. Who is she? There is a man who loves Jesus, and after each Sunday service, when Christians leave to go to their homes, they leave messes behind, and this person cleans those messes up. Who is it? When all is said and done, Christians know that their service is not for their own sake. The Christian life and thus humble Christian service is done for the glory of one name only. And yes, that is the only name that matters. Oh, and I have one more example. In the readings through the New Testament this past week, we read we read of a woman who anointed Jesus For his death and burial with an alabaster jar. Jesus said that wherever the gospel is preached, what she did will be told. What's her name? Let us pray Our Father, we thank you for the example of the Savior to lead by humility. But that is the first step in the Christian life as Jesus took it. And so we take the challenge to follow him in humility. To die to ourselves, to consider others as more important than ourselves, and to not look for fanfare But look for your glory. May that be done. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Did I say Daily?
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: May the words of my mouth and the meditation of our hearts be acceptable in thy sight, O Lord, our strength and our Redeemer. In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We are covering Hebrews chapter two. Verse 18, the very last verse of the chapter, and then into chapter three of Hebrews. Some of you will remember that I helped start a high school football program made up of high school students. who otherwise would not have been able to play football in high school because of homeschoolers not being allowed in Maryland to play by law, play at local high schools, even though their parents pay the same taxes as public school families. It's not a just system, but that's not the point of my story. One of the teams we played that first year were the Maryland Saints, who had started their program a year earlier We had based much of our program off of what they had started. In fact, both groups came under the Ministry of the Fellowship of Christian Athletes. We based our program on all players participating in Bible study, team prayer, and Christian discipleship in general. When we played the saints that first year, we gathered with them before the game to pray. We gathered with them afterwards after the game to pray. And it was at that after game prayer That the Saints team gave each of our players and coaches an SCA copy of the New Testament That was their practice after every game to give their opponents a copy of the FCA New Testament. What was odd to us is that we are a part of the same program and we already had copies of the FCA New Testament. And so we all we needed to do was just say thanks and be done with it, but I could not end with a thanks only I tried to be humorous, and when it was my turn to speak in front of both teams, I decided to tell them that we look forward to playing them The next year so that perhaps we could get copies of the Old Testament. I don't remember if many of them laughed, like not many of you did either. But I was trying to say something about the importance of the Bible in its entirety. I once heard a story that I have no way of verifying because I do not know who told it to me, and I only heard it once. The story goes that there was once a missionary to a foreign land who had worked very hard to understand the language of the tribe he was ministering to. And the result was that he was able to take their language and translate the New Testament into their language, much like the Wycliffe ministry does so well. Well, evidently, when the leaders of this tribe read the New Testament in its entirety, they returned it to the missionary. And after handing him back the New Testament book, they said something like, may we now read the first half of the story. Now again, I don't know if the story is true or if it's made up to make a point, but I love the point. The preacher to the Hebrews does not see the gospel of Jesus as the Messiah standing alone without the revelations within the Old Testament. The preacher to the Hebrews instead sees the gospel as a fulfillment of what was promised in the Old Testament. And thus anticipated about the gospel, and most specifically anticipated about Jesus of Nazareth. The preacher sees the Old Testament through the lens of his faith in Jesus. And therefore sees that Jesus was always there in the story of God redeeming Israel. But they needed faith to see him. I have documented in many ways from this pulpit the failure of modern Christianity to rightly interpret the New Testament. Because of the failure of modern Christians to properly know the Old Testament. Baptism is the most obvious example. Modern Christians only understand baptism from the New Testament perspective, and they expect to see some type of verse that commands them to baptize their infants. And therefore, since there's no such command, infants should not be baptized. But a proper understanding of circumcision And how God uses outward signs of his covenant with his people would allow us to see that a man with a family Who believes in Jesus to be the fulfillment of God's covenant with Abraham, he is going to expect that his family is included. With that fulfillment that his family is added to the faith through Abraham and his descendants. To not understand the Christian covenant as a fulfillment of God's covenant with Abraham is a terrible and costly mess. And the Christian church continues to suffer because of that miss. Unfortunately, infant baptism is just one example. Now getting back to our text specifically, I will summarize the point of chapter 3 by dividing into two headings. The first heading is the preacher describing what Jesus did. And the second heading is describing what believers are to do in response to what Jesus did. We begin by answering, what did Jesus do? Well, according to the preacher, he tells us that Jesus was tempted in every way, and that purposefully. Without sinning, and therefore he is able to aid us who are tempted. Now during lent season, we are to be reminded Daily, about the time Jesus spent in that desert fasting 40 days and 40 nights. We cannot fully know or understand what Jesus accomplished. By not eating for 40 days while facing every type of temptation in the flesh and the spirit, but we can know that while doing so, that he bound the strong man. The strongman was the devil. Jesus explained to his disciples that he bound the strongman, the devil, In order to plunder what was once the devils. The strong man thought he ruled the earth, and that included all flesh upon the earth Until Jesus came along. By Jesus resisting temptation, he proved that the devil did not have jurisdiction over him. And in fact, Jesus proved himself more powerful than the devil, not just in regards to overcoming sin, but also having authority over spiritual forces, evil forces. Again, where Adam failed and therefore made himself and all mankind subject to the devil and his angels, Jesus succeeded. And therefore place humanity in the position where the devil and his demons necessarily submit themselves to humanity who have placed their trust in Jesus. It is, after all, a part of the prophecy of Jesus that his followers would heal the sick and cast out demons. So, resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Believe that to be true. Practice casting out the devil from your presence. And next, next, watch God give you strength over every temptation. Believe that to be true. Two, next, the preacher tells us that Jesus was faithful to the Father. As he fulfilled his appointment to be the sacrifice of mankind, he was faithful. And again, as last week, we are to understand that concept of Jesus himself being faithful. Enacting faith. And he calls us to enact that same faith. After all, the same Holy Spirit that dwelled in him dwells in us. And that being so, we too can face death with the full confidence that God will raise us also from the dead. 3. Next, the preacher tells us that Jesus was faithful over his house, and that faithfulness was greater than the greatest of men before him, Moses. It is not easy to overestimate how important Moses was to the Jewish people. He was their first redeemer. And he was given a role by God of putting forth God's law. His covenant and his people as a whole were led by him. Moses was given more responsibility than any man before him, and yet he was also called the most humble of men. For Jesus to be greater than Moses, he needed to be great indeed, and of course he was. To say he was faithful over the house of God is to say that he was faithful at delivering God's people, for the people of God are the house of God. So as Moses was faithful to deliver God's people out of Egypt, Jesus was also faithful, only his deliverance of God's people was a deliverance from sin and death. To such a deliverance nothing can be compared, and therefore no man can compare to Jesus, not even Moses. Not even Moses. And we now turn to the preacher's admonition regarding what believers are to do in response to what Jesus did. What are we to do in response? Well one, the first thing we are to do is told by implication, for it is because of Jesus overcoming every temptation that we are to lean on Him when we are tempted. This should be a no-brainer, but it is likely that we don't call upon Jesus to deliver us from temptation for a variety of reasons. One reason may be that we invited the temptation into our lives purposefully. That may be embarrassing to admit, but it is likely true for all of us at one time or another, imbiting in sin purposefully. In the epistle by James, you remember, we are told that the sin that we practice is the result of being led away by our own lusts. We can't blame the devil, and we can't blame the object of our desire. We can only blame ourselves. We must all confess that our deliverance from evil is just a short prayer away. We only need to call upon Jesus. Two. Next. We are to do, what we are to do is again stated by implication. We are to give Jesus more honor and glory than would be given Moses. This expectation is more directed at those of Jewish descent who had naturally honored Moses. But it can be also received by us Gentiles as we acknowledge the temptation to give glory to men that is meant only for Jesus. The last three expectations, these are the ones that are overtly given as compared to the first two that were implied. And it is these last three that I want us to give our full attention. They are to get our full attention because they point to the main warning of the entire chapter. Which is that Christians must renew their covenant with God every day. Every day. Consider that what we are told to do next in response to what Jesus has done. The third thing we are to do is what we are not to do. We must not harden our hearts. A hardening of the heart will eventually, eventually lead to disbelief. The fourth thing we are to do is exhort one another daily. Thus, our need to renew our covenant with God each new day includes the need to encourage one another in the faith. And the fifth thing we are to do in response to what Jesus has done is to hold on to what we understood from the beginning. Consider that the only reason a person is told to hold on is that something might easily be let go, either by not much effort or not much thought. These last three expectations remind me of a phone call that I received a few years ago. when our third son Isaac was starting his new job in Tampa, Florida, at a private Christian school. He told me he was about to go into a meeting where each of the teachers was asked to share their testimony about when they became a Christian. Isaac was looking to me for advice as to how he was to articulate his Christian faith, even though he had never had a conversion story or experience. What some call a born-again experience. He asked almost verbatim, how do I tell them about when I came to know Jesus when I perceived that I have always known Jesus? Such a dilemma happens when Christians only understand the faith in terms of personal conversion experience and not faithful covenant succession. Handing down the faith to our children and our children's children. Well, my answer to Isaac was similar to these last three responses. We are to have as to what Jesus has done for us. It is the understanding that a person living the Christian life Whether since birth or since a conversion experience, said persons need to renew his or her covenant with God on a daily basis. Those of you who have known Jesus as your Savior and Lord for many years can attest that you don't just have one Made a new, born again experience, but you have many. Those many are times when you have a heightened sense of both your guilt And your need for the mercies of God. And when you seek out Jesus in those moments and you repent and you know that your sins are forgiven You are also given a refreshing by the Holy Spirit, and that makes you feel alive all again Such is the Christian life as I have known it, and I trust many of you as well. I mentioned last week that the Hebrew preacher describes the humility of Jesus very much like St. Paul does in his letter to the Philippians. Well, this description of the Christian life as a daily renewal of our covenant with God is also similar to Paul's words to the Philippians. where he told them that they are to work out their own salvation with fear and trembling. To work out one's salvation is to do these three things listed by the Hebrew preacher. It is to not harden our hearts It is to exhort one another daily, and it is to hold on to what we know to be true. A person hardens his or her heart when he or she refuses to repent when confronted with sin. I recall an older woman calling me to her house to tell me that she will not be attending church any longer. When I asked why, she told me that one of my sermons taught that Christians must forgive in order to be forgiven. She applied that to her life and concluded that she could not forgive her brother who had wronged her years prior. She insisted that she would never forgive him. That, my friend, is a hardened heart, a heart left alone in her bitterness. It is the daily duty of Christians to guard their hearts from pride, envy, bitterness, strife. particularly from withholding forgiveness. Each day should begin with checking the heart That no bitterness is within against any other person, and each day should end with the same examination, so that the devil is never granted a foothold to the door of our souls. Next, a person is to receive and give exhortation daily. We all need our souls fed by the Word of God, the truths of the gospel. To exhort is to encourage, and we are most encouraged by God's holy word. It is One of my greater joys as a pastor to sit around on Tuesday nights or Wednesday mornings with you people and read God's Word and talk of God's Word. These are when the deeper truths of God are exchanged and our souls are privileged to exchange them We also have such conversations in Sunday schools and even in moments of working together, just this past Saturday, not this past Saturday, the one before Where some of us came together to clean up and put things away from the winter ball. During that time we talked of our Bible readings and recent sermons and about articles we recently read. about the sins of our culture, about the call of the church to lead. That was exhorting one another. And doing so naturally because we love Jesus And we are amongst his people. And I can recount many faith-based conversations that I had the night of the winter ball with people who do not attend our church but who love Jesus. That is exhorting one another. And the point being that to exhort and be exhorted daily, we must be amidst believers. We must be in the presence of one another, God's house. Finally And our response to what Jesus has done is to hold on to what we have been taught, to what we know is true about the Christian faith. With this instruction, we can recall the same message being repeated in the book of Revelation. That message to hold on. And we need to hold on because people will try to take it from us. It is very similar to the warning that God gives throughout the Old Testament, which is for his people to never forget. Not forgetting and holding on are the same message from the same holy book about the same God who loved so much that he gave his only Son. And we are not to forget and to hold on because God does not change. And yet the devil will tempt He will pry, he will try to mislead, and he will send his false teachers, if possible, to lead us astray. Hence we are to hold on to the truths that we know. That's why we confess the creeds, folks. We're holding on when we do. These last three things we are to do in response to what Jesus has done for us is for the purpose of keeping us in the faith. And they are necessary. We must do them. Doing these things does not save us. Only the work of Jesus saves us. But we are to work out what Jesus has done for us, and that means guarding our hearts daily, exhorting one another about our Christian faith daily. And we are to hold on to the truths daily. Daily. Did you hear me say daily? Let us pray. Our Father, we see the urgency of the preacher Wanting his household, the household of faith, to keep the faith. And so we receive that message. And we pledge to you to do it daily, to guard our hearts, to exhort one another, and to hold on. Father help us. We pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Fear from a double edged sword
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.source_file: Fear from a double edged sword.txt
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We are doing something a little different this morning to begin, so I encourage you to open your Bibles to Hebrews chapter 4. We will be walking through that reading again, and I will be commenting as we go, just to keep us all on track. From the New King James Version starting at Hebrews chapter 4, beginning at verse 1 Therefore, since a promise remains of entering his rest, let us fear lest any of you seem to have come short of it. This is a continuation of the argument that was started in chapter 3 regarding the danger of people not holding on to their faith to the end. The mention of fear as a motivation is because fear is necessary. A person who does not hold on is a person who needs to fear. Verse 2. For indeed the gospel is preached to us as well as to them, but the word which they heard did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in those who heard it. Them are the Israelites, and that's clear in chapter 3, the Israelites with Moses who were not allowed to enter into the promised land. We are to notice that they were to have faith, just as we are to have faith. By grace through faith, they were saved, and by grace through faith we are saved. The Old Testament was not law and the New Testament grace. No, God is the same always, and therefore faith was reckoned as righteousness under the Old Covenant and is now reckoned as righteousness under the newly revealed covenant of which Jesus is the Savior. Verses 3 through 5 For we who have believed do enter that rest, as he has said, so I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter my rest. although the works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he has spoken in a certain place of the seventh day in this way And God rested on the seventh day from all his works. And again, in this place, they shall not enter my rest. The quotes are from Psalm 95 and from Genesis 2. The rest he's referring to refers to the promised land and a Sabbath-day rest Each is understood as a shadow or a type of the true promised land or the true Sabbath, which is where Jesus went to prepare a place. It is heaven for us. Verse six through ten. Since therefore it remains that some must enter it and those to whom it was first preached do not enter because of disobedience. Again, he designates a certain day, saying in David, today. After such a long time as it has been said. Today, if you will hear his voice, do not harden your hearts. For if Joshua had given them rest, then he would not afterward have spoken of another day There remains, therefore, a rest for the people of God. For he who has entered his rest has himself also ceased from his works as God did from his. Again, a quote from Psalm 95, and it is a warning now to Christians. The reference to Joshua is the acceptance that there was another generation that did indeed enter the promised land, and it was a sort of rest But because the people had to work to occupy the Promised Land, it could not have been the final rest. The preacher to the Hebrews is pointing the hearers, the Christians of all ages, to keep before them the eternal rest that awaits all of us. The emphasis on belief is the foundation in the explanation as to why the Israelites did not enter into the rest. For it was their disobedience. Their disobedience was unbelief. Verse eleven through thirteen. Let us therefore be diligent to enter that rest, lest anyone fall according to the same example of disobedience For the Word of God is living and powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit, and of joints and morrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. And there is no creature hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and open to the eyes of him to whom we must give account. The diligence that's being exhorted here is a reference back to Hebrews chapter 3 from last week. That's where we were told to guard our hearts, to exhort one another, and that we were to hold on to what the Lord had revealed to us of Jesus dying, living, dying, and living again. The description of the Bible being a double-edged sword and thus able to dissect the essence of humanity, the soul, the heart, the mind, the body of every person. That is for the purpose of God's people using that tool to enable them to believe. The preacher is telling us that God's word, the scriptures, are vital to us entering into our eternal rest. And in case we are not yet motivated to allow the Word of God to dissect and then heal us, there is another plea by the preacher to the need for fear. To say there is nothing hidden from the sight of God is to assure us that no sin is hidden from his sight. No unbelief can go unnoticed. If a life is not lived by faith, such persons will be required to give accounts, to explain themselves before God. Yes, fear here is to be a great motivator to get right with God. Fear. The preacher next explains how Jesus is our high priest, and that's going to lessen our fear, but we must fear God first before we can trust in Jesus as our high priest. When reading through the New Testament during this Lent season, and specifically the Gospels The Pharisees and scribes stand out as people who did not fear. And oh they thought they feared God. But the reality was they feared people. And because they feared people, they could not truly fear God. Consider how costly fearing people is in Scripture. Herod had the head of John the Baptist cut off because he feared the opinions of his guests more than he feared God. The Sadducees challenged Jesus regarding the source of his authority. Jesus answered them back about the origin of John's baptism. When the Sadducees reasoned between themselves, they confessed that they feared the people, and that if their response wasn't popular enough, that the people would come after them and reject them. Saint Peter, the first of the apostles, denied that he knew Jesus because he feared that the people who recognized him would punish him as they were punishing Jesus. And all such is misplaced fear. Jesus said not to fear those who could harm the body But instead fear him who could cast both the body and soul into hell. He said this, but still most people fear other people. We can fear what they might do to us physically, but we fear as much what they might do to us socially. What if each of us did an inventory of our lives regarding times that we have compromised what we would say in a moment, what we would stand up to be morally right in a moment, because we feared the peers that were around us. Such temptation to fear our peers seems strongest when we are in adolescence. Our hormones are running amok and therefore we are emotionally and physically on hyperdrive And so everything seems to matter more than it should, and therefore seems that the worst thing that can happen is to not have friends. But to have friends of this world, you have to be like everyone else of this world. And to be like everyone else, you cannot fear God. You have to ignore God. You have to keep a belief in God quiet. And you will likely have to deny that you know Him at all. All because a fear of people overwhelms any fear of God. And such fear of people carries over into adulthood Where many live their whole lives fearing people over God. No, the great awakening, as it is called was an evidential moving of the Holy Spirit amidst the American colonies dated approximately 730 to 755, 17, excuse me, 1730 to 1755. It is recorded that the Holy Spirit converted many to the Christian faith, awakened many more that attended church services with little or no change in their lives before. With the preachings of George Whitfield, John Wesley, Jonathan Edwards, people finally began to look at their lives. And they saw their own sin and they understood finally their need for a personal savior. One particular sermon preached by Jonathan Edwards, you'd like you heard of it titled Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God, is held up as the epitome of revival preaching during that era. The sermon itself is broken up into ten considerations, which focus on the realities of God having the right authority. the right and authority to cast anyone at any moment into hell. The wicked deserve hell, and many wicked are now at this very hour suffering in hell The only way a person can be saved from hell is if he or she repents. But as of now, until such repentance, hell is assured and the pains of death are eternal. And God has no obligation but his own will that anyone should not go to hell Speaking of the unrepentant, Edwards preached the following: quote: The wrath of God burns against them. Their damnation doesn't slumber. The pit is prepared. The fire is made ready. The furnace is now hot, ready to receive them. The flames do now rage and glow. The glittering sword is wet and held over them, and the pit hath opened her mouth under them. The devil stands ready to fall upon them and sees them as his own At what moment God shall permit? They belong to Him. He has their souls in His possession and under His dominion. The sermon goes on with repeated warnings about the reality of hell and the justice of God for such a punishment. Now, on its own, the sermon does have some problems because it only preaches one part of the reality of hell. It doesn't convey that God does not will that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. But that point was not needed in the days of Edward. What was needed when Edwards preached was a revival, and the revival needed to start with fearing God Now in comparison to the preaching of Edwards is the preaching we have here in Hebrews chapter 4. There was also in the days of the Hebrew preacher a need to fear God for that need to be revived, but the fear needed was not held explicitly. But a fear of missing out on heaven. The alternative is indeed hell, but the preacher to the Hebrews did not see that as a needed focus at the time. He is appealing to a people. Who at one time, at least one time said that they were Christian. And if at one time they said they were Christian, now they are second-guessing their commitment to Jesus as their Savior And it is the preacher's calling to point them to their ancestors in order for them to see their failure to enter the promised land because of unbelief. But what these Christians would miss is far greater than the promised land. It is heaven. Eternal life, eternal rest. Yes, the opposite is mentioned, and we read it. It is the fact that nothing is hidden from the eyes of God. All will be judged and judged rightly. That is a reference to eternal judgment, which is justly eternal damnation. Both need to be considered. The point is that humanity, individual persons, need to fear God. Now what has been curious to me about the need to fear God is the placement of verse 12. Look at it again. It states the usefulness of God's word. And I have preached on and referenced verse 12 several times in other sermons, but I am not convinced as to why that verse is here in chapter 13. If you read the chapter as a whole, it does seem like it's out of place. Just stuck in there. I didn't understand it until I read author Eric Matax's book on reformer Martin Luther. What Metaxis carefully lays out is a description of a time in history when within the Christian church, before there were Protestant churches, during the days of the Middle Ages, There was not only blatant sin and corruption within the leadership of the Christian church, there was a profound disinterest in having any fear of God. The laziness of many, many priests was rampant and known by the laity. The Pope, Pope Leo X, thought it perfectly acceptable that he use his leisure time to be entertained by making public fools of those in his service. Greed, superstition, and ritual for the sake of ritual governed the church life. Priests didn't speak Latin and yet led Latin Mass. Monks didn't read Bibles and most of them didn't have one to read. Paying for forgiveness was more common than praying to God for forgiveness. And there is a story told that highlights the foolishness of this time. Tetzel, the most famous of monks selling indulgences, was asked by a nobleman if he could purchase a certificate of forgiveness for future sin. Tetzel quickly said yes and eagerly took the man's money. When Tetzo left town, he was accosted on the road, beaten, and his money from his indulgences collection was stolen. Stolen by the nobleman who told Tetzel that the sin he had paid for in the future was the very sin of robbing Tetzel From such events it is easy to conclude that there was no fear of God among men inside and outside the church. It was not until Father Martinus Luther began studying the Bible and carefully interpreting it in contrast to the spiritual life of confessing Christians and the church of his day, and realize how sinful he was and how lost the church was It was the Bible, the truth within the Bible, that cut into him, dividing his soul and spirit, piercing his joints and marrow. And when soul and spirit and joints and marrow are dissected by the Word of God, a healthy and needed fear of God returns to an individual and to the church. The people of God. And what I am saying is that the preacher to the Hebrews knows that when the Word of God is not before us, When it is not dissecting us and thus healing us, we lose a desire to know God. And when we no longer know God, we turn to anything that is not God, and we are lost eternally. I want you to consider why the following prayers are included in the litany of our prayer book, the larger litany. We pray that God would deliver us from all sedition, privy conspiracy and rebellion, from all false doctrine, heresy and schism, from hardness of heart and contempt of God's word. And commandment. We pray such a prayer because of the danger of losing out on heaven if we ever had contempt for God's word. We also pray that it would please God to illuminate all bishops, presbyters, and deacons with true knowledge and understanding of God's Word. And that both by their preaching and living they may set it forth and show it accordingly. Set what forth? God's Word. Not traditions, not customs, not ritual, not superstition, no We need set before us leaders living out the Word of God We also pray that God would give to his people an increase to hear meekly his word and to receive it with pure affection and to bring forth fruits of the Spirit. We pray this because hearing the Word of God is one thing, and believing it, so that all of God's people live it out. That's the ultimate thing. All such prayers we need to have answered by God because if we lose our love for God's word, we lose our fear of God, and if we lose our fear of God, we lose our heavenly reward. And to underline all of this, we can examine the downfall And the outright blasphemy occurring within mainline churches today. Churches that were at one time primary banner waivers for the Christian faith Clergy presiding over unions of sodomy would not occur if God's word was believed and feared. Allowing a Muslim prayer service within our National Cathedral, a cathedral built by Christians for Christians Such would not be allowed by leaders who knew God's word and feared God. Ministers who condone abortion rights sexual perversions, unbiblical divorce, fornication, and who teach polytheism blatantly Do not know God's word and or believe God's word and most certainly, most certainly do not fear God And they are to be like the Israelites who roamed in the desert for 40 years, not being allowed to enter the promised land. For their unbelief, those were to be examples to the Hebrews, not to follow, not to replicate, be warned because of them How are we to be warned by those denominations who have gone before us, abandoned God's word, have lost their fear of him, and have lost their hope of heaven? May it not be so. May it not be so of us. Let us pray. Our Father, we come humbly before you, acknowledging that without you preserving us Without you stirring up within us a desire to know and to replicate your word, that we too would be going away, astray. And so, Father, we ask, in your mercies, keep us and help us to hold on. In Jesus' name we pray.

sermons.title: Sufficiency and Resistance
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles to Hebrews chapter four, picking up at verse fourteen. Hebrews chapter four Two weeks ago, we were exhorted to fear God and to use our Bibles as a tool to dissect our lives, that we would continue to fear God So that we would not lose out on heaven. The flow of argument of the Hebrew preacher is to talk next about Jesus as our high priest. But we noted that the teachings of Hebrews 4 require believers to first fear God. And fear the possibility of losing out on eternal life. It is only as we fear God that the teaching of Jesus as our high priest makes any difference in our consciences. To further appreciate Jesus as our high priest, we need to understand the place that the office of high priest had in Judaism. The Jewish high priest had a unique responsibility to enter the Holy of Holies once a year on Yom Kippur, or we know it as the Day of Atonement. He did so to burn incense and to sprinkle sacrificial animal blood to expiate his own sins and the sins of the people of Israel. On such an occasion, he wore only a white linen garment, foregoing the elaborate priestly vestments worn whenever he chose to officiate the services any other time of the year. The high priest had overall charge of the temple finances and administration, and in the early period of the Second Temple, He collected taxes and maintained order and was essentially the political head of the nation. The high priest could not mourn the dead. He had to avoid defilement incured by being in the proximity of someone that was dead, and he could only marry a virgin. The office was first conferred on Aaron by his brother Moses and was normally hereditary and normally for life. And Jesus needed to be the high priest in order for him to make the offering of atonement for our sins. The problem with Jesus was that he was not of the line of error. Therefore, his high priesthood had to be legitimate, and it was legitimate because it came from the order of Melchizedek, and we will hear about him more on a later date. Now as our high priest, Jesus goes before us to make offering to God, and yet Jesus himself was the offering. And so he plays a part of representing us as priests before God and as our atonement offering before God. And this most unique position of Jesus allows him to sympathize with us as our priest, who represents us to God, and as our offering, who suffers for sin. Our need to understand the uniqueness of Jesus is because we are tempted, all of us are tempted from falling away from the faith. We struggle to fear God more than we fear this world. We can too easily get off of our eternal hope that we have in Jesus and become again what we once were, which was a sinner in the hands of an angry God. The reasoning of the preacher and our epistle reading is as follows. We need to hold on firmly to the faith we have been given. We can hold on firmly because Jesus ascended to the right hand of the Heavenly Father and is therefore our intercessor, our representative. He pleads our needs. And Jesus can be our intercessor because he empathized with us, with our great weaknesses. Jesus was tempted in every way, which means in body, in soul, and spirit, and yet, and yet Even better than the first man who had no sin nature, Jesus did not sin Because he was tempted and did not sin, he can convey to the Father what it is like to be man and be tempted by the world, the flesh, and the devil. And he can convey to us What it is like to resist the temptations and overcome sin. Because of all this that Jesus did and is We can approach God the Father with confidence that as we do, we will receive mercy and grace at our time of need, which is all of the time. We are to do at least two things, I believe, with these facts. These facts of what Jesus is and what he did. We are to use them to overcome our own sins, those sins that tempt us and those sins that we habitually practice. And we are also to have faith in the acceptable priesthood and the acceptable offering that was Jesus. Now I wish to address the fur the second part first, and that is we are to Can't help but notice that voice We are to focus our attention on the acceptable sacrifice of Jesus as our high priest and as our atonement. Now, regarding the sufficiency of Jesus as our offered atonement for sin of humanity, there can be no doubt. His sinless life is evidence of his sufficiency. And along with his sinless life, the Hebrew preacher wants us to be aware of the temptations he suffered. And the full identification he made with humanity by humbling himself to the point of needing to learn obedience And to accept his fate, even though it was full of suffering and full of sorrow. It is a great curiosity to most of us how Jesus grew in wisdom and stature as the Bible describes, and yet he was God. Just how God becomes man is a great enough mystery, and it deepens significantly when we consider that Jesus had to be potty trained. He had to learn how to read. He had to learn the Ten Commandments and learn obedience. And we wonder if all such things were already known to him because he was God. But that is not revealed to us. We are told that because he was fully man, he had to learn such things and much more. And he did. In fact, it was as he was learning such things that the Hebrew preacher tells us he was made perfect. And so we have to understand that he was perfect and he learned perfection. How does that work? We have no way of knowing, but only to accept what the preacher says is true. Of Jesus as an accepted atoning sacrifice. We must have no doubt. And I propose that it has been a great problem in the Christian church down through the ages when God's people do not have full assurance of Jesus as an acceptable sacrifice for sin. During my studies for my dissertation on the origin of Christian eulogies, I Notice a great deal of concern within the early church regarding what happens to sinners after they have been baptized and again fall into sin. There was a fear that sin that occurred in a life of a believer after his or her baptism would remain sin counted against him or her. Because there was no second, third, or fourth baptism to wash away the sin. Truly, great men of God chose not to be baptized. until much later in life, for the very reason of wanting to have their baptism in the closest of proximities to their death Thus the faith seemed to be placed in the baptism as washing away sin as opposed to the atonement of Jesus. And this grave misunderstanding about the atonement of Jesus is, I believe, a major factor in the development of beliefs such as purgatory. It was thought by many that because people sinned, and some did so egregiously after their baptism, a place was needed to have those sins purged and ultimately forgiven. With the idea of a holding place for Christians, you know, Abraham's bosom after they die and wait for the resurrection, and with the Bible mentioning offering prayers for the dead A purgatory was an understandable answer to how sins after baptism could be forgiven. But a purgatory is not needed when we understand and have faith in the sufficiency, the sufficiency of Jesus as the atonement once offered. As our consecration prayer makes clear. We only need to add to our knowledge of Jesus as the perfect sacrifice, that God is the creator of time. And there will be a moment when time, as as we experience it, as we know it, time will be no more. And because God is above time, meaning that he is not limited by it, It can be true that Jesus as an atoning sacrifice is sufficient when he was offered, all times after he was offered, and all times before he offered himself. Just as it describes in Revelation, that Jesus is the Lamb that was slain before the foundation of the world above time. The atonement sacrifice of Jesus is just as sufficient now as it ever was, making the doctrine of such as purgatory and transubstantiation unnecessary. We only need to confess with our mouths and believe in our hearts, and we will be saved. Now another way people do not trust in the atonement of Jesus is to think about their sin as too great and their soul as too unworthy to be forgiven. But such thinking is of the devil, and such thinking is thinking about self too much To think of one's sin as too great is to grossly and embarrassingly underestimate the atonement of Jesus. What sin could be greater than the perfect sacrifice of Jesus, the Son of God, the God-man, the creator of heaven and earth? It is absurd to ask such a question. To think of one's sins as greater than Jesus giving up his life would be laughable if it wasn't so sad. Such thinking is made up of false humility. No person can be unworthy of God's love when God says he loves the world, for that world includes all who are part of the world. For those people who are genuine in their feelings of guilt, let it be heard that the atonement of Jesus was specific for you. There is no sin that cannot be forgiven. There is no past that cannot be healed. There are no memories that cannot be conquered. And all of this is true because of the atonement offered by Jesus and made by Jesus, and all of God's people said, Amen. Now another response we are to have to what Jesus did for us and to who Jesus is for us is to fight against sin. It is to resist temptation. And let me say up front on this point that most of us do not work hard enough at resisting temptation. Whether that temptation be temporary temptation or besetting temptations, we do not. We are not working as hard as we are able to work against what tempts us. Consider what Jesus did. As a man of the flesh, like we are, flesh, Jesus offered up prayers when he was tempted. With his prayers, he cried out to his father. With his cries to the father, he shed tears. All of this the Hebrew preacher reminds us, and later he will remind us that Jesus resisted temptation to the point of shedding blood. Such is the standard Jesus set for us, and that means that none of us has any just complaint before God when we give in to our temptations. Realize how easy it is for us to blame everything and anything for our own outbursts of anger and careless speech. We say that the person we blew up at is responsible for our anger, and yet we have been carrying around bitterness and envy for months, maybe years. And when we say something about someone that is not our place to say or even think, we quickly cover it by explaining that we brought it up because we care and we're concerned. No, we are being busybodies, and that is all, and that is too much. Maybe our s your sin is sexual lust. And your excuse is the outfits that women wear or television shows that they're the ones obsessed with sex. Maybe your sin is gluttony, and we blame a glandular problem or fast food advertisers Maybe your sin is bigotry, and we blame it on government programs and a race that we don't understand. Maybe your sin is a lying tongue, and we blame it on being misunderstood. The truth to such sins are that no one forces you to oval women. No one forces you to turn on the television. No one holds you at gunpoint to go through a drive-thru burger joint. No one else cultivates your heart to act in prejudiced ways against your fellow man No one else uses your tongue to mislead the truth. The person who sins needs to look no farther than the person responsible, and that is in the closest mirror. The Epistle of James says it plainly. But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own desires. And enticed. Then when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin. And sin when it is full-grown, brings forth death. We are to blame for our sins, and thus we are responsible to resist temptation. Our efforts to resist temptation are similar to what I see in exercise gyms I have been a member of three different local exercise gyms, and I have witnessed a particular type of person in all three gyms who regularly exercise with no results. Because I exercise regularly. I see these people. They are there several times a week and they are exercising diligently. But they don't look any different from the time I first noticed them, identified them as regulars years earlier. And the reason why these people who exercise regularly don't look any different is because they don't strain themselves when exercising. I have watched them. Let's say that they are on a curl machine, you know, working on the bicep. And these people on such a machine will have it set on the lowest of settings to move the lowest of weights, and they're doing it multiple times. And they talk with their partner, workout partner, they smile, they sip water. There's no grid on their face. There is no strain on their muscles. Now I understand that I shouldn't stand in judgment of such people. They might need to exercise to improve their joints or to get in their socializing. It's none of my business. But in exercising as they do, they should not expect to grow muscle or burn fat. And there I say, when there is no pain, there is no gain. Folks, there's a reason why that saying is catchy, because it's true. When it comes to exercising, there must be pain to get gain. If you want to lose fat on your body and build muscle, you must suffer pain. Pain is necessary. And the same can be said about resisting temptation. Going through the motions of resisting temptation is not truly resisting, and it is certainly not resisting as Jesus did. Some of you will remember the 40% rule that I described over a year ago. The 40% rule is the belief that we think that we are at our physical limit when we are actually only at 40% of our limit. And it takes grit and great effort to work beyond that limit that we've placed upon ourselves. But when we overcome that limit, we will discover that we can physically endure much, much more. When you are faced with the choice of resisting temptation, we must be confronted by the fact That where we have placed a limit on our endurance of temptation, we're only at 40% of what we can resist. We can go further. We can resist more. We can resist longer. We can So those are our two responses to Jesus as our high priest, our mob for resisting temptation. We are to increase our faith in the atonement of Jesus, and we are to work much harder at resisting temptation. These things to do are quite fitting as we begin our holy week Holy Week gives us sharper focus on what Jesus has done for us as we do We will be all the more ready to rejoice that his atonement was accepted by the Heavenly Father. And this will allow us to rejoice all the more on Resurrection Sunday. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful Father For this message from the preacher to the Hebrews, we thank you. For we find ourselves therein, needing to increase our faith in your atonement and needing to resist temptation. May it be said of us that we went beyond our 40% because we know you did. We ask this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Show and Tell
sermons.speaker: Phil Lambooy
sermons.text: Let's break. Heavenly Father, we thank you for the opportunity that we can gather this evening for this special time of remembrance. And of renewal. And we pray that as we meditate on your words, not only of the scriptures, but of the readings that are laid out before us this evening. May the reality of our relationship with Christ become whole, and may our the reality of the relationship we have with one another in Jesus Christ be made more manifest. And we pray this all in Christ's name. Amen. This past Sunday, the Clistus stood at the baptismal found holding Hudson and Savannah between them. They are surrounded by family and friends scattered throughout the church. Why are they standing there? They're there to experience God's rite of passage, the public administration of baptism. Who here played show and tell when they were a child? And if you did, can you remember any of the items that you brought into school, yo, those many years ago? Or have those memories faded away over time like old soldiers who never die, they just fade away. Show and tell is a common game about showing an audience something and then telling them something about it. It's a common classroom activity at early elementary school. It's used to teach young children the skills of public speaking. For example, a child will bring an item home or bring an item to school from home and will explain to the class why they chose that particular item, where they got it, and other relevant information. Or they will stand there and stare and freeze up, too afraid to say anything I have to ask, do students today, this is a real question, do students today still play show and tell In their schools. In this school, I don't know. I hope so. But to come to think of it, do you know show and tell us a game that we actually never outgrow? Adults today still play show and tell, except we no longer call it show and tell, do we? We we now call it Facebook. And since we are all in need of a constant reminder, again, what is a sacrament? Question 66 of the Heidelberg Catechism, the question, what are sacraments? Sacraments are visible holy signs and seals They were instituted by God so that by our use of them he might make us understand more clearly the promise of the gospel and seal that promise. I like that phrase, sacraments are visible, the show, to make us understand the tell. Or this from our own 39 articles. The sacraments instituted by Christ are not only badges or tokens of the profession of Christians. But are also sure witnesses and effectual signs of God's grace and goodwill towards us. Again, witnesses and signs. So the sacraments are visible. They're there for all people to see, given to us by God, and they tell us About God, His grace and the benefits we derive from Him. And as we read through the Bible, you notice that God shows and tells us often A lot of the major components of who he is and who we are in relationship to him. God loves show and tell. The Bible is full of signs To Noah, God gave the bow and the cloud, signifying his covenant with mankind.
