To Abraham, God gave circumcision, sniff and clip, to signify his covenant with Abraham and his posterity. To Moses and the Israelites, God gave the Passover lamb to signify his covenant with his elect people. To the church, he gave baptism and the Lord's Supper to mark, sign, and seal the covenantal promises to us who are the spiritual seed of Abraham. All of them visible signs that speak to us of inward. reality. So what about the sacrament of baptism? Chapter twenty-eight and the Westminster Confession of Faith states baptism is a sacrament of the New Testament ordained by Jesus Not only for the solemn admission of the party baptized into the visible church, but also there be unto him a sign and seal of the covenant of grace. Article 34, the Belgian Confession, has this to say about baptism. Baptism also witnesses to us that God, being our gracious Father, will be our God forever. So, in general, we can say that baptism has meaning on multiple levels. On the historical level, within a few weeks of Jesus' resurrection, the apostles are preaching the gospel. to people by the thousands baptizing them in Jesus' name. And think of the long line of people who've come before you, parents, maybe your grandparents Your spiritual ancestors who were welcomed into the church by baptism. On the theological level, you know baptism is a powerful sacrament that signifies the washing away of sin. It gives us a new identity as being engrafted into Christ's body. It connects us to a new community of believers. It's also a gateway that initiates us into a new way of living. And provides a clear mission in life. And the Mishnah life is to be a disciple of Jesus Christ Jesus said, baptize in order that they might be disciples. But I like that one phrase, and it's not my phrase. I I got it from one one of the authors I was reading. It's the gateway that initiates initiates us into a new Way of living. On the physical level, like any sacrament, baptism makes visible and invisible reality. In other words, we see physical signs and rituals to express our experience with God. The symbols you see at a baptism ceremony include some of the following. The sign of the cross that Pastor Jorgensen did on Sunday. Do you remember when he did the sign of the cross? Did you see him do the sign of the cross? I had to stand up because I couldn't see from the back. But he does the sign of the cross. It's traced on the forehead of the one being baptized. This ritual action expresses that the mystery of the cross is at the heart of our faith And that by this mark the child visibly and publicly is now one of Christ's own. Speaking of marks, If you want to have a little enjoyment of a play on words, we could say that the mark of the cross in baptism replaces the mark of Cain. on the believer's life. You know, you and I are born in and we enjoy living in the old man Adam and his son Cain. We love that life. Until we experience new life in Christ, we are his new children. He's our new owner, our new master, and then we become men and women of the line of the new Adam and his later son Seth, and then his descendant, Jesus. The water used in baptism, whether it's sprinkling, whether it's pouring, whether it's immersion, the mode is not important. But when the person is being baptized reminds us that we die and are buried with Jesus in order that what we rise up with him. Freed from the slavery of sin, and then we start the conquest of sin as servants of Jesus Christ. And this action that you see when it's been being performed with the water The dying and being buried by the water, it's a reminder of how Moses led the Hebrews on their escape from Egypt, and how God parted the waters of the Red Sea as a gateway to their new liberation away from slavery and into the promised land. Now as an aside, you may not know this, but many new churches or remodeled churches Have the baptismal font near the main entrance to symbolize that we are all entering and have entered the church through the waters of baptism. Personally, I think that's a real powerful symbol. You can't come in church and avoid the fount. Another symbol that we can see at baptism, sometimes a white garment, reflects that in baptism we put on Christ, taking on our new identity as sons and daughters of God. And then in some ceremonies they have a baptismal candle. It represents the one true light of Christ, a light to guide the new believer throughout his or her life. And then finally, on the cultural level, baptism has meaning. Families often celebrate, they affirm all that happened at the altar by gathering after the ceremony, in the gymnasium to enjoy one another's company, right? Share a meal, celebrate. So it happens here and then it continues on there as the family of God So, what happens in a baptism? The church rejoices because we have welcomed the new covenant member, and because we have once again celebrated the mysteries of God's love for us and our salvation. So tonight we gather together for the reaffirmation and renewal of our baptismal vows, taking hold of the promise, what? That the Holy Spirit who has begun a good work in us will continue it to the completion in Jesus Christ. Are you reminded of any of this while you are observing a baptismal ceremony? Do you use this time to hearken back and think about your own baptism? Did you do this past Sunday? When you think of the ceremony of what you were witnessing, do you think of what happened to you, yoga's many years ago? So anyone here this evening who knows their date of their baptism I see some hands raised. To reaffirm your vows, wouldn't it be easier, I suppose, if you knew what it was when you took the vow? I did not know the date of my baptism until earlier last week. Why? Because well I had chosen, I guess, just to forget, to remember. Which begs the question, is the baptismal anniversary date an important date to remember? That's kind of why we're here this evening. I now think it is, but I do not always think so. In the same way, some churches they hold it in high esteem, Roman Catholic Church, while others do not, many Protestant bodies What do you think? Is your baptismal vow important to you and to remember it? Which brings me to the topic of vital records and show and tell So look at this. I was born. Me, Philip John Lamboy, September 14, 1955. I just told you I was 62 years old. Oh well So I have a baptismal record on September in September I can come up here and stand w when we do that every month, you know, when September comes around. So I have this record, I know I was born My family celebrates my birthday, whatever. I have a record of it. Actually I used to have two baptism uh two birth certificates, but I'll go into that another time. But we celebrated September 14th It is set in stone. It's history. Well at least it's my history. And then Marga and I got married on uh December 23rd. Nineteen seventy eight. And so in December, come up here, we celebrate the anniversaries, right? We we do this as a church, don't we? Birthdays, anniversaries Well then I found out I also had this, my certificate of baptism. Wow. I thought when was I baptized? Well, June 24th. 1973. I was seventeen when I was baptized. You'd think I could have remembered when I was seventeen when I was baptized, but I couldn't. I might as well have been three. I wouldn't remember. But I was baptized I have a birth certificate, I have a marriage certificate, I I I have a baptismal certificate. So what what are your vital records? Where are you keeping your vital records? Isn't it safe to say that we all have a birthday? We can all agree because we're sitting here. Isn't it also true to say that many here will have or already have an anniversary day? Days that for the most part we look back on, remember, and celebrate. But what about our baptismal day? Is not this day also rooted in history? In the same way as the other two days that we celebrate, birthday and anniversaries? And like the other two, isn't it a cause to continually celebrate? And if you say, well, I can't remember that day since I was an infant when I was baptized. Now you may be thinking that. Well, you were a younger infant when you were born, but that didn't stop you from celebrating that day It all has to do with what we consider important, does it not? We place more importance on the physical than we do on the spiritual John Calvin is very wise when he says this. The benefit which we derive from the sacraments ought by no means to be restricted to the day. when they are ministered to us. The benefit of baptism lies open to the whole course of life, because the promise which it contains in it is perpetually enforced. More recently, Hughes Oliphant Old Statement stated baptism is a sign under which the whole of life is to be lived. Our baptism is always with us, constantly unfolding throughout the whole of life. And so for us who have been baptized, you and I should remember and think upon our own baptism. Whenever we are shown and told another baptism, And if you were baptized as an infant, see in the infant before you the state that you were once in. And thank your parents, thank your godparents, who made the promises for you in your stead, that they desired for you to be set apart for Jesus Christ on that day. Baptism is an outward and visible action that connects a person to God in a covenant relationship, so it belongs in public worship. Baptism is the ritual of the faithful that speaks to becoming a member of Christ's church. Baptism, it could be argued, is the root and foundation of the Christian life. I recently read that the entire season of Lent, while it's an extended meditation on the suffering and death of Jesus, is also preparation, is it not, for our remembrance of our baptism. I am reminded of Jesus' questions to disciples regarding John the Baptist. Matthew 11, verses 7 through 9. This is what Jesus says As John's disciples were leaving, Jesus began to speak to the crowd about John. What did you go out of the wilderness to see? A reed swayed by the wind. If not, what did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? No, those who wear fine clothes are in king's palaces. Then what did you go out to see? A prophet, yes I tell you, and more than a prophet. In the same way we could ask ourselves, what do you and I go out and see when we watch a baptism during the service? The water, the sign of the cross. You even see in here words of institution, the vows and the promises. A white outfit, maybe a candle, the baby or the person. You know, yes, we see all those things. And it's the perpetual reenacting of God's covenant. Faithfulness and love to his elect sons and daughters. A love handed down from generation to generation to the next generation Visible public reminder that Jesus is with us and that he is always working out his will in each one of our lives. Set apart as his sons and his daughters to belong solely to him. So go home and find your baptismal certificate. Put it alongside your birth certificate. They both equally testify to you who you are. Born of the flesh, born of the water, and the spirit. In the end, you and I are ultimately God's finest show and tell. By the way, we live out our lives between these two great events, the first birth and the second birth. Celebrate both of them when you see a baptism Remember yours because your life is sandwiched between the two. Let us pray. Heavenly Father, I ask for your forgiveness for me and any of us here. So taken our baptismal vows, well, maybe not at all, but very loosely, maybe quietly, and very nonchalantly. Do we pray that we would once again be restored to fellowship with you and that when we think upon our baptism, we can use it as once again the knot that ties us even closer to you. And the next time, Father, we do see a baptism as a congregation. May we as one not only celebrate with them, but be very thankful and very glad. That you also chose us, marked us, and set it apart in our lives as well. And we pray all this in Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.title: Remember Me
sermons.speaker: Deacon Ricky McCarl
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and the Son and the Holy Ghost. Amen. You may be seated. A few months ago I had a hospice patient who suffered from dementia. as most of my hospice patients do. And she had a very difficult time remembering how old she was, how many children she had, and where she was most of the time. She was, how should I say this, not one of my uh most warm and fuzzy patients. She was a straight shooter and someone who didn't really like to beat around the bush. And when I would visit her, I would often feel as though I was more of an annoyance than a help to her. One day I stopped in to visit, and she was working on a craft as she was usually doing And I interrupted her craft as I usually did. And I got this what do you want now look? I asked her if she knew that Jesus loved her, and she looked at me as if I was a complete fool. And she said, Of course I know that. I used to go to Sunday school. This poor lady didn't even know her own children most of the time, but she remembered who Jesus was and that he loved her. Because it was part of who she was at her core. It wasn't about cognition or memory, but about who she was as a person. She knew Jesus loved her because that was her identity. So what does it mean to remember? The dictionary defines it as the mental process of retrieval of information from the past. It's a very scientific definition. And it looks at the concept of memory and remembering from a very cognitive perspective. Remembering is about taking a past event and recalling it in our minds. I remember the things that my wife asks me to get at the grocery store. I remember the way to get home from work in the afternoon. And most of the time I remember where I put my car keys. And I remember my loved ones when I look at their pictures. That's the idea of memory that I grew up with. Memory was about me thinking about things and about recalling them in my mind. Memory was cognitive and oftentimes nostalgic. This is how I was taught to think about remembering, and it's also how I was taught to think about remembering in the context of Jesus' words in the Gospel, which St. Paul quotes for us in 1 Corinthians 11. The common view amongst our evangelical brethren is that when we remember Jesus at communion, it's chiefly a mental exercise. When we receive the elements, we're recalling all of the things that Jesus had done for us. This is what is known as the Memorial View of the Sacrament The memorial view of the sacrament, specifically the Lord's Supper in this case, is the belief that the elements of bread and wine, and for you, Larry, grape juice, Are only symbolic of the body and blood of Jesus, and that communion is simply a commemorative meal. It is to remember cognitively the things that Jesus has done for us using symbolic things like bread and wine to communicate the truth of the gospel. For some who hold this view, communion is nothing more than an object lesson, but a very important one for sure. That's the view of communion that I grew up with, and maybe you did too. But is that what Jesus means by remembering? Is that what St. Paul is describing in 1 Corinthians 11? Is it just simply a very important object lesson using bread and wine as tools to communicate important truths? No. It's so much more than that. St. Paul writes verses 23 and 26 of 1 Corinthians in the context of sacramental abuses in the church. The Corinthians didn't seem to understand the significance of what was happening, and they began to use the communion service in inappropriate ways. St. Paul's correcting their errors because it's led the church and Corinth in some pretty dark directions. People are sick and even dying because it's being used improperly It's easy for us to look down on the church at Corinth and judge them for their failure to understand the sacraments. But do modern Christians really do any better? If people were dying at Corinth because it was being abused, if they were in danger of judgment, then is the memorial view of the sacraments. Which is the general view of the modern American church? Really a proper understanding of them. If people were getting sick and dying, don't you think there's something important about them That it's something more than a spiritual object lesson. And shouldn't it lead us to try and get them right? So what does it mean to remember biblically? What is Jesus saying when he commands us to do this in remembrance of me? Cognition can certainly be a part of it, but biblical remembering goes much further, especially when a covenant sign is involved. When the Bible calls a Christian to remember, it's not just a nostalgic recollection of the events of the Bible or a symbolic object lesson, but an actual participation in salvation history. So when we participate in the act of taking communion, we aren't just subjectively recalling the events that took place in the scriptures, but are actually actively taking part in those events. That have taken place in history past. So, where does this idea come from? Reformed theologian Michael Horton has this to say. In our Western intellectual heritage, remembering means recollecting, recalling to mind something that is no longer present reality. Nothing could be further from a Jewish conception. For example, in Jewish liturgy, remembering means participating here and now in certain defining events in the past and also in the future. So according to Horton, for the first century Jew, remembering isn't just an object lesson or a recollection of events. but a real, live participation in those events. The prime example of this from Scripture is the Exodus, which is remembered in the yearly Passover meal that Jewish people have celebrated for millennia. They'll be celebrating that tomorrow night. This Passover meal is closely connected with the meal that we come to celebrate tonight because it was the Passover meal in which Jesus institutes our Eucharistic meal, which was most certainly a purposeful act on the part of our Lord. But for the first century Jew, the Passover isn't just an educational exercise or object lesson. It's not just a memorial. It's a participatory rite in which they are called up in the redemptive story of God and his covenant people. By celebrating the Passover, they are living out year after year the benefits of their redemption as God's covenant people. Likewise, we as Christians celebrate our own exodus each time we come to the Lord's table to partake in his most precious body and blood. By celebrating communion each week, we are living out the benefits of our redemption as God's covenant people. This, of course, would have been the understanding that Jesus' disciples had as they sat around the Passover table. They weren't coming to Passover looking for an educational experience But as participants in God's redemptive story, little did they know that the story was about to take a dramatic turn. With all of that in mind, it would have been difficult for the it would not have been difficult rather for them to understand what Jesus meant when he said, Do this in remembrance of me. They had been celebrating remembrance rites all of their lives. They knew what it means for a Jew to remember. Now, if remembering isn't a cognitive exercise, but has more to do with participation, then why shouldn't our children participate? What is it that is set after the consecration, the gifts of God for the people of God Which people? Is it for some of the people? Or is it for all of the people who bear the name of Christ given to them in the baptism? The Jewish custom of Passover was a family meal. The entire home took part, and it affected them all. They grew up knowing that God had brought them out of Egypt and that they belonged to him. Shouldn't our children grow up in the same manner? If communion is just a memorial and a cognitive act designed to be a spiritual object lesson Then I guess it makes sense for children to be barred from the table. I guess. But if it's a participatory right Like the Passover, then we really have no excuse for refusing to bring our children to the table. In fact, I would argue we owe it to our children. I would also argue that this understanding of remembrance actually accomplishes more cognitive good than a simple memorial view does, because it actually affects the heart. Which of course changes our minds. The Eucharist changes us from the inside out And this is compelling to me as an Anglican because the sacraments are what we call effectual signs of grace That is to say, that they aren't empty signs, things we do just for the sake of doing them, but they actually do something for us and to us. They change us. The Catechism of the Anglican Church defines the sacrament as an outward sign of an inward and spiritual grace given by Christ as a sure and certain means by which we receive that grace. In other words, the sacraments are God's gifts to us. In them we receive, through faith, God's grace. God actually delivers to us what the sign promises. Take baptism for an example. Holy baptism, as the catechism says, is the sacrament by which God adopts us. Adopts us as children and makes us members of Christ's body and inheritors of the kingdom of God All of that is promised in the sign of baptism according to the catechism. It's also delivered to all those who live their baptisms, who participate. Who participate in their baptisms through faith on a daily basis? Baptism is not an empty sign, and neither is the Eucharist. It actually does something to us. The catechism goes on to say: the outward sign in communion is the bread and the wine. But the inward spiritual grace is the body and blood of Christ. The benefits of communion Our forgiveness of sins, the strengthening of our union with Christ, and one another, and the foretaste of the heavenly banquet, which is our nourishment to eternal life. All of that we receive through our participation in the sacramental rite of communion when we come to the table in faith. And all of that changes who we are at our core. But I do anticipate objections to all of this. Jesus does, in fact, call it a memorial in the Gospels. Yes, and I'm not suggesting that it's not a memorial. What I'm suggesting is that our view of memorials and remembrances don't necessarily go far enough. And that for a first century Jew, the idea of remembering and memorializing was much deeper. It was about being brought into what was being remembered and living it out sacramentally. Then of course someone might say, but how do we participate in something that happened 2,000 years ago? Well that's a mystery. I'm not sure that that can be completely comprehended by our 21st century Western minds, but that doesn't make it untrue. And we need to be comfortable with mystery. We need to come to the realization that mystery is good and that we don't have to have all things figured out I don't believe that we can begin to scratch the surface of what God does for us in the sacraments with our finite minds, but what I do know is that they are more than just empty signs or educational symbolism Meant to teach us subjective truths. They actually do something to change who we are. They touch us in our inner being. So the Eucharist doesn't leave us the way we are. It changes us from the inside out. It's one of the things that forms us into the image of Christ. In the Eucharist, we are reminded that God so loved the world that He sent His only Son to die for our sins, so that we might be reconciled to the Father, adopted as His children. And become inheritors of his kingdom. And from those truths flow the grateful hearts, which are bold to say, Our Father who art in heaven. The Eucharist reminds us that our citizenship has changed, that we have a new people and a new family. We are God's children. Our sins have been forgiven, and we have been raised to new life in Christ. Life without the fear of death. Life with the crucified and risen Messiah. Let's pray. Our gracious and merciful Father, we're thankful for this meal that you have given us. This gift of the sacrament, that we can come to it and be objectively told that we belong to you and that you love us and that you forgive us. I pray, Lord, that as we come to this meal instituted on this night, that you will use it to work in our lives and to change us in the inner man. We pray this all in Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.title: My son who was dead is alive
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.source_file: My son who was dead is alive.txt
sermons.text: It's In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. You be seated. The Bible passages read this morning, especially that of our gospel reading, are not the usual passages read on Easter Sunday That is because this is not going to be a typical Easter Sunday sermon. I'm not going to preach about the proofs of the resurrection of Jesus. I have done that before. I will do it again, I suppose, but not today. I am not going to proclaim the authority that Jesus established because he overcame sin and death. I have done that before. I will do that again, but not today. Instead, we are working from the presuppositions that Jesus has risen From the dead, and that Jesus does indeed reign. We are starting with those realities in place And then we are going to focus our attention on the last thing the father in the parable read from Luke, the last thing he said to his oldest son. It was during my reading, during this Lent season, reading through the New Testament, that I came across this phrase in Luke's Gospel where the father says about the younger son Your brother was dead, and now he is alive again. That is what we say about Jesus, and that is what needs to be said about each one of us And so each of us must answer, can it be said of you that you were dead and are alive again? Let's start by looking at the parable, usually referred to as the prodigal son, as we need to look at it more closely. It is important to note that the father had two sons. The parable is about two sons, not just the prodigal, as most people tend to think. We need to recall that at the beginning of the chapter, Luke 15, we are told that the Pharisees and scribes were complaining that Jesus was receiving sinners. From that it is clear that the older brother represents the mindset of the Pharisees, who complained because Jesus was welcoming and having fellowship. With people that they judged to be unworthy. It is important to know that according to Middle Eastern thinking The young man showed appalling disrespect for his father, as well as disrespect for the honor of his family and for his community. by asking for his inheritance before the death of his father. The family and the village would have been aghast at the behavior of this son. It amounted to him basically saying that he wished his father was dead Making his actions unthinkable, making them repugnant. He had proved himself radically selfish, a man without honor It should also be noticed that the father granted the son his request when he did not have to. He could simply have said to his son that he needed to wait till his father's death before he received his inheritance. Most fathers would have rebuked their son at such a request. And here, the father, in effect, lets the sinner go his way. And with that, we are to see how perfectly this parable is describing the rebellion of humanity before God. God lets us go our way. Examining the actions of the youngest son in a culture that measured wealth by how much a person owned land, the young man proved himself Very foolish, by turning all of his inheritance to quick cash, taking a great loss so that he could literally take the money and run And we can well imagine that everyone in the village would have heard of what he had said and what he had done by sundown. It has been noted by biblical scholar Kenneth Bailey that most Middle Easterners at this point in Jesus telling this parable They would have already wondered what happened to the older son, asking why he did not intervene. Why did he not seek to mediate between the father and the young son and restore the relationship? The lack of action makes the older son complicit in this disaster that was overtaken the family. It is also a surprise that the father did not at some point disown his son. He had every right to do so. It is what people would have expected him to do. With the people of the families in the nearest towns, they would have expected the son never to return. A final departing. Not only the family, but the entire village would have refused to receive him back. The description of the young man struggling to come to his senses is for the purpose of every human creature to identify with him. Sin Sin so easily entangles us even to the point where we become out of our minds. Sin bankrupts us. For the young son, his most obvious bankruptcy was financial. For others, it can be a moral bankruptcy, and still others an emotional bankruptcy. What is common with all is being broke and broken. Broke and broken Feeding pigs was a job no Jew and no Middle Easterner would have ever wanted to do Nothing could be more degrading for a Jew than to care for the pigs of a Gentile. The young son is bankrupt in every single sense of a person's life. But being bankrupt to such an extent has its blessings. It can bring a person to the possibility of finally, finally coming to their senses. That the young man knew that the only place he could go to find help was the household of his father, says a great deal about the character of the father. What is hopeful about the young man, the young son coming to his right mind was that he knew he wasn't deserving of the forgiveness or love of his father, but he was determined to go to his father anyways. Because mercy was his only hope. And we must have, he must have known his father to be a merciful man. The determined words of the Son, I will arise, is all what repentant sinners are saying when they look to the God of mercy. All who confess Jesus as Savior and Lord can say, I will arise and go to the Father. And when that is confessed, it has quite the double meaning. For we arise to confess our sins with the hope that we too will arise from the dead and see God face to face. Now there are so many great details in this story to inform us of the character of our God, who is clearly represented by the Father. The father sees the son afar off. In order to see the son who had gone into a life of debauchery, the father needed to be looking for him. And in order for him to see him on the day he was returning, the father needed to be looking for his son every day We are reminded from this that God is indeed slow to anger and abounding in love. God does have a will that wants no one to perish but for all to come to repentance. God does so love a lost and rebellious world. Then there is the description of God running. He doesn't wait for the sinners to come begging at his feet He goes to the sinner and embraces him, embraces her, embraces any and all who come to him. And next God pours out his affection upon the repentant sinner, for repentance is what the Father waits for. After the father's affection, we hear the confession of the Son. All he said was true, all of it. The son had sinned against God. He had betrayed his father. He was not worthy. No one is worthy. But the Father knows that. God knows that. That has been established. What needs to be established next is how a sinner is made a son again. The Father's response is full and total forgiveness and reception. The Son has returned in rags and next is dressed in the best of the best. He's given sandals when servants typically went barefoot, given a ring, which in all likelihood indicates that he has been restored to the family. And then he was a guest of honor at a feast thrown for the whole town. The killing of a fattened calf was reserved only for the most important of occasions. For meat. Meat was rarely consumed in the first century Palestine. And it most certainly couldn't be consumed by a family of four, allowing us to imagine the people of the nearby town were invited. This was a big deal. With so much food, the feast would have included surrounding neighbors. And therefore, the banquet restores the son not only to the immediate family, but to the larger community that would have been, as we have noted, known the transgressions of the son Verse 25. Verse 25 says that the older brother was in the field when he heard the sounds of the celebration in the family home. A son of a rich man would be in the field only to supervise work. He would have been treated as the owner in the eyes of the slaves, for it is the older son who would receive the sick a significantly larger inheritance compared to his younger brother. His refusal to enter the banquet would have been a great insult to his father and to the guests. Obviously, he was furious about what his father had done. But in a very significant and ironic twist, The insider, the older brother, insider has become now the outsider The older brother's decision to remain outside of the celebration was a choice to be farther away from his father than his younger brother had ever been while living in debauchery. The son who had remained at home was now outside, not enjoying the feast with his family And indeed, he is the Pharisee. He is the scribe. He is the unbelieving Jew. Very clearly, Jesus makes the point that it is the Pharisee who is standing outside while God is rejoicing in the repentance and the coming home of the tax collector and of the sinner. The response of the older brother to the news about his younger brother returning reveals a great deal about the heart of the older brother. He reveals that his obedience to his father was motivated by self-interest. He had obeyed all of that time in order to be rewarded. Rather than out of love or thankfulness. His lack of love for his father is noticeable as he kept track when he felt that his obedience was not recognized properly. And next he thinks the worst of his brother as he accuses him of sleeping with harlots. Whether it was true or not, he had no way of knowing. The words of the older brother reveal that he does not know his father, just as the Pharisees didn't know the father. He does not know his father as the one who loves all of his sons. He does not know his father as slow to anger, merciful, abounding in love. The older brother only knows or thinks he knows his own value. And it most certainly is greater than his brother and greater than honoring his father, even at the request to join the celebration. The fate of the older brother is untold. We don't know how the older brother eventually responded to his father's appeal. And that is so very fitting, as it reveals that just as the Father awaits the decision of his oldest son, so too does Jesus wait the decision of the self-righteous. Those who think that they do not need mercy, Jesus gives them a chance still to receive mercy and join the celebration. According to the account that Jesus tells, the Father is still standing outside waiting for a decision. The parable truly does give every person, every human being, every image of God bearer, an opportunity to be made alive. Every human being fits into the category of either being aware of their unworthiness because of their own sins. Or the category of being self-righteous, as they refuse to acknowledge their sinfulness. There are no more categories. There are subcategories, but no more categories. You are one who knows your sins and your need of forgiveness, or you deny your sin and see yourself according to your own righteousness. For those with a conscience about their personal sins and guilty verdict that hangs over them, they can easily see themselves in the younger brother. They are the ones who wished their father, wished God to be dead, so that they could live a life as they so willed. Many of us are old enough to remember the generation of people in the 1960s who proclaimed that God was dead. And the result was free love, so-called, getting high, living casually, throwing off the morality of their forefathers that they claim bound them and oppressed them and depressed them But in order to throw off those morals while keeping the conscience clear, God had to be dead And people who deny the existence of God today do so because they want to live as they will. And they can't if God exists, if God is alive. To have a conscience restored. And for a person to become aware of personal sin and guilt is also to need a father. A God of mercy, who can be approached with the hope of being forgiven The younger son came to his right mind. He became aware of his need for a father of mercy. And all of us can as well. For those who don't acknowledge their sinfulness, there is the example of the older son who didn't believe he needed the mercy of his father. He was just fine living by his own standards. And as long as his own standards were met, he lived believing that he deserved to be celebrated. Also amongst the people who are self-righteous are those, like the older brother, who are angry at God. Even those who say they don't believe in God are angry at God because they are living lives they don't think they deserve. They think things should be better for them. Like the older brother in the parable, they stand in judgment of God, believing their fate should be according to their choosing. And when it is not, they then become angry with God, and then they say they don't believe in God. So too did the older brother. Today is a day that celebrates that there was a man who lived and then died and then lived again Jesus did so in order for those who would have ears to hear would also live again. And so there are two resurrections offered to each and every one of us. The first resurrection is when we are dead in spirit because of our sins, whether they be sins of debauchery or sins of self-righteousness, they are all sins that keep our spirits in the grave. And yet, when Jesus pronounces forgiveness, we are raised from said death. The Heavenly Father says of us, just as the Father in the parable said of his youngest son, That we who were once dead are alive again. And for those who are alive again, there will be a second resurrection. For Jesus has risen from the dead to be first, and if he is identified as first, it implies there are more to follow Jesus promises those who believe in him as Savior in God that they too, you too, will overcome death. Finally, consider this reading from the prophet Hosea. Just the first three verses from chapter six. Hear this. Come, let us return to the Lord, for he has torn us that he may heal us. He has struck us down and he will bind us up. After two days, he will revive us. On the third day, he will raise us up, that we may live before him. Let us know, let us press on to know the Lord. His going out is sure as the dawn. He will come to us as the showers, as the spring rains that water the earth These words uttered our encouragement that after God disciplines his people That he will do as he wants to do for them, which is to restore them to their rightful place as sons and daughters. The language of the prophet alludes to that resurrection to come 500 years later, on the third day, he will raise us up. Thus from the prophet Hosea we get the promise that by returning to the Father, just as the prodigal son did, is to have our self-inflicted wounds healed. And for ourselves to be raised up. We claim the resurrection of Jesus today While it is asked of you, have you been raised up? Come to the Father, having faith in Jesus, and God will make you alive again. And all of God's people said, Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful Father. We thank you for the proclamation we can make today that sin and death have been overcome But we also see it needs to happen in our individual lives. For any and all who need to be made alive again, may it happen this day. And may you receive the glory. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen

sermons.title: Practicing the Word of God
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. You will be aided if you turn in your Bibles to Hebrews chapter five. Working from verse twelve to verse fourteen I wonder how many of you know that the Bible does not speak of or describe people as good Christians or bad Christians. I wonder because I've heard such descriptions. She is a good Christian, someone has said. He is a bad Christian, someone else has said. To describe a person in such a manner is to use extra-biblical language. It is to use categories that God does not use. What God uses is Christian or unbeliever. A person is a Christian only by the grace of God and through faith in Jesus Christ as the Son of God. A person is an unbeliever by rejecting the grace of God, thus also rejecting Jesus as God's son. When it comes to categories for describing Christians, the Bible does not use good or bad, but rather weak versus strong, or mature versus immature. Recall that in St. Paul's letters to the Corinthians and Romans, they was concerned about Christians dividing from one another because they felt They did not feel free in their faith to eat meat offered to idols, while others did not feel guilty eating that same meat. Because there is a principle in Christianity that Christians are to do things by faith A person who would eat meat offered to idols needed to do so by faith, or not at all. Paul called such persons strong who could eat Meat offered to idols in faith. They could do so in faith because what they were doing, they believed, was honoring Jesus, believing that Jesus makes all things new. They are strong because their faith in Jesus sees the efficacy of the blood of Jesus making all things clean. All those who have a heavy conscience about eating meat offered to idols must not eat such meat because they would not be doing so in faith. They are called weak. But Paul doesn't correct those called weak. He doesn't make fun of them. He doesn't look down upon them. Just like we do not look down upon young children who have a much-needed way in which they need to grow up. In fact, Paul instructs the strong to respect the weak. By not eating idols offered, I mean meat offered to idols in the presence of those who are weak, so that the devil doesn't pinch their conscience so that the devil doesn't challenge their conscience. Such a standard of living is truly Christian. It is what Christians are to do. Who follow Jesus, we have to care for the weak in the faith among us and put them as a priority before our own rights and our own freedoms. That is what Jesus did, and so we replicate him. Another set of categories the Bible uses to describe Christians is found here in Hebrews chapter 5 and then into chapter 6. They are the categories of mature and immature. And these are different from weak and strong because the Hebrew preacher. is not happy with the immature. And his unhappiness is revealed in the sarcasm that he uses for them, which is a little bit like looking down on them. But he is not looking down on them by way of sarcasm because he thinks he is better than them or that he is simply cruel. No, he uses sarcasm with them to get them riled up. So to get them to realize that To walk away from the faith, well that's serious business. And their conscience needs to be stirred Now, like my example with understanding the weak and comparing them to how we understand the behavior of a young child. It can be understood that some people are immature, to be sure, because they have not had time enough to grow into their maturity. But this was not the case with those the Hebrew preachers addressing no. He clearly says that they are a people who should have matured to the standpoint of being able to teach others about the faith, but instead they be continue to behave as children And next comes the sarcasm. These immature Christians are like children who can only drink milk. Because they are unable to properly chew and swallow solid food. Ouch! That's offensive. But he wants to be. What does a young child do who has not yet learned how to eat solid food when he or she puts solid food in his or her mouth? Why, she or he chokes on said food and spits it out. That is what these Christians are doing with the solid food that is the Word of God These Hebrew Christians are still only able to consume the easy parts of the Word of God while choking on the meatier parts of the Word of God because of their immaturity. And how does that immaturity manifest itself? Good question According to the Hebrew preacher in chapter 5, verse 14, the immature Christian does not have the ability to discern both good and evil. And note the explanation of the Hebrew preacher as to why these Christians remain immature, resulting in the inability to know the distinction between good and evil. It is because they have not worked at practicing the Word of God. Practicing the Word of God. They have not used the Word of God in their life to better understand it and mature with it. The reality of the Christian life is that if a person does not practice his faith in everyday life situations, And by practicing his faith, I mean properly applying God's word, the teachings of the Bible, to his everyday life He is not going to mature in the faith and he will remain only drinking milk And the result of only drinking milk is to be stunted in growth to the point of abandoning the faith, a topic that he will address in chapter 6. Now, this point of not being able to discern good and evil because of not having practiced the Word of God in everyday life is where we need to spend our time today. We must spend time here because eternity is at stake. That's why he's writing to them It can be argued that this point is where personal holiness is met. It is where victories in life are decided. Where a person works out his or her salvation with fear and trembling. The topic of applying God's Word to your everyday life so as to be able to discern good and evil can start by applying a sermon just heard. What do you do with sermons you hear? Last week we heard how we can either identify with the younger son in the parable of the two brothers, or we can identify with the older son. If we identify with the younger son, we are able to come to our right mind and realize how sinful we have become. We then are to confess that we are sinners who are not worthy to be called sons or daughters. But that we are seeking mercy so that we can be forgiven. If we identify with the older son, we are to confess our self-righteous attitude and behavior. And instead see that we also need the mercy of the Heavenly Father, just as much as the younger brother. And if we have been angry with God, we need to confess such anger to be a great sin. And we are to humble ourselves before God, for He is in the right, and we are not To do either of these is to apply the Word of God to your life. Applying God's word to everyday life. is to read in the Epistle of James. He tells us, be quick to listen and slow to speak. And then when we walk out of our home and we engage people, we are to practice listening to others. Before we speak, and when we speak, we are to bridle our tongue so that we are controlling it that we might not sin against God or harm our fellow man To apply the Word of God to your life is to remember the teachings of Jesus, who said we are to seek the kingdom of God first. His kingdom coming is to be the first priority in our lives. So that if I am pursuing a job in another state or another town, I want to be assured that there is a church there that I can be fed. in word and sacraments and be held accountable for my faith. I do not compromise my convictions in order to make money My day is to be structured so that it resembles that I have put God first and his kingdom. To apply the Word of God to my life is to use the wisdom of Proverbs that tells me to avoid the house of a harlot. Such houses today can be in the flesh or a website. I must avoid such houses so that I do not get sucked into one of them and make sexual satisfaction an idol To apply the Word of God to my life is when I do not let the sun go down on my anger. So when I perceive that I have been wronged, I I do not let it fester in my mind or in my heart But that I go to the person I think has wronged me and I tell them and I give them opportunity to apologize and then I forgive them And even when they don't apologize, I apply the Word of God to such a situation, forgiving them regardless of what they do or do not do And from these examples, I trust you can see that there are seemingly an unending number of ways the Word of God can be practiced and applied Realized in your life so that you grow in your ability to discern good and evil. They also show the silliness of anyone who would describe Christian life as a bore It is anything but boring and quite demanding actually, causing a great deal of energy and stamina and being awake to one's self and our fellow man. It is listening, remembering, working, resisting, confessing, receiving, and repeating the cycle. And all of that is from applying the Word of God. In fact, one of the evidences of Christianity as a true faith Is that no one would make such a faith up if one could make up such a faith. Consider that if you and I were to make up a religion, we certainly wouldn't have such high standards to try to live up to. We would make life much easier if Christianity was something to be made of. And so we stand before the teachings of the Bible with humility and awareness that what is written therein must be practiced in our individual and corporate lives, or we suffer to lose everything eternal. And this brings me to my final focus point, which as a pastor I am most concerned about. Regarding the Word of God and how it is being practiced or not practiced in our midst. What I am most concerned about is our practice of what the Bible instructs regarding the family. The family. And how those teachings are being practiced. Let us consider what the Bible teaches about parents raising their children. We know this proverb, right? Raise up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old, he will not depart from it. This has been understood by some to be a promise by God It is taken to mean that if I raise up my children to be Christian or raise them in the Christian faith, then God will be sure to keep said children in the faith. Not departing from it when said children are older. Now, I can understand why people would interpret such a passage in such a manner. They want it to be so. Of course they do. Unfortunately, or in reality, such a passage is not a promise. Much of Proverbs, much of the Proverbs in the book of Proverbs are truisms or maxims If we read the reference proverb as a truism, we interpret it to mean that in whatever way you raise your child, that is the way the child will go. Therefore, if you raised your child in the Christian faith but did not exemplify the Christian faith in your own life, or when you did, your child saw you as a hypocrite Because of what you said you were in public was not what you were at home, your child is going to go the way of understanding the Christian life as hypocritical. Recall the law given to Moses in Deuteronomy 6, verse 7. He said, You shall teach them the laws of God. Diligently to your sons, and you shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up Consider that with this verse from Proverbs 3, verse 1. My son, do not forget my teaching, but let your heart keep my commandments. We must combine the instruction to teach of God diligently to the warning of not forgetting such teaching. The word diligently in the Hebrew is a verb, it's an action, and it can be translated to inculcate Which can be interpreted to give persistent instruction. Persistent instruction. And the need for persistent instruction is because of how easily a child can forget. Consider this wisdom, which is found in these two verses and in life experience. As a parent Every practice you live out in your life that you consider to be good will be replicated by your children, but to a lesser degree. to a lesser degree. For example, the manner you keep your bedroom, if you clean your bedroom once a week, your children will clean their bedrooms once a month. If you make your bed every once in a while, your children will never make their beds. Whatever your convictions are regarding housework will be passed on to your children, but to a lesser degree. Unless, unless they are persistently taught your beliefs about your housework. Then and only then is it possible that they will at least replicate your housework practices It is because of our fallen natures, our proclivity to fall short, that we need persistent instruction. Now take the example of housework and apply it to your Christian faith. Unless you are persistently instructing your children about God and Jesus and the whole of the gospel, your children will believe but to a lesser degree. And I hope that unnerves you. I hope that jars you. Examine yourselves. Take inventory of your faith habits. How disciplined you are at reading the Bible, your children will be as you, but to a lesser degree. How dedicated you are to attend worship services at church, your children will be also, but to a lesser degree. How well you obey your ecclesiastical authority, your children will also, but to a lesser degree. How well you listen to the Word of God preached, your children will do the same, but to a lesser degree. How often you pray, how long you pray, how faithful you are in your words of prayer, your children will be, but to a lesser degree. How you forgive others, how well you speak of others, how you ask for forgiveness of others will all be practiced by your children as well, but to a lesser degree. I hope that unnerves you. I hope it jars you. Unless why you do what you do is persistently taught, your children will only replicate you. But to a lesser degree. And if your children are you in the faith, but to a lesser degree, what does that mean for your grandchildren? God forbid, where they could end up if the cycle is not broken. The extra-biblical proverb is true. What is a grandfather's conviction becomes a habit for his son and a discard of the grandson. But none of this has to be There are two ways to break such a cycle. The first way is that God intervenes God can intervene and transform a grandson or a great-grandson or a great-great-grandson so that there is faith in the family once again. That is what he did in my Jorgensen line. My grandmother's uncle on my father's side was a Luther minister. I am the first since him to be ordained. The other way to break the cycle is to persistently train our children to believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. And to know the Ten Commandments, the Lord's Prayer, the Creeds, and to apply the Word of God in our daily lives so that we continue beyond milk. I have planned to say much more about the family, and in particular how important it is to apply the Word of God to our lives as husbands needing to love their wives as Christ loved the church. And how important it is for wives to submit to their husbands in all things. But there was too much to say about parenting, about raising children. Beloved, this concern by the preacher to the Hebrews for Christians to apply the Word of God to their everyday life or lives. Was a concern for them not leaving the faith. And the need for us to apply the Word of God to the raising of our children persistently Has the same concerns. The concern of the salvation of our children. There is nothing, nothing that I can think of that is more important. Let us pray. Our Father in Heaven

sermons.title: Foundational Baptism
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. A true blessing in life, especially for my children, was when we stumbled upon the comic characters of Calvin and Hobbes. In case you are in the dark about Calvin and Hobbes, they are from the imagination of Bill Watterson, who tells stories of the life of Calvin, a six-year-old boy of great mischief. and his stuffed tiger friend Hobbes, who is very much alive in the imagination of Calvin. I loved them and my children devoured those comics We collected every book that was published and never failed to laugh and be entertained. One of the running gags in the series was when Calvin would inform his father that he was slipping in the poles. Of course, Calvin was the only one polled for his polls, and he wanted to inform his father that he needed to improve his ways for Calvin to approve of him. Recently, I learned that Watterson believed that modern politicians were governing by polls instead of by common sense. So the witty retorts Calvin's father would give to Calvin about the polls was Watterson's way of making political statements about modern politics. One particular strip shows Calvin discovering that his father could not be removed from office or impeached, but was Calvin's father for life. Calvin yells in protest, demanding to know who wrote the constitution that ruled his home. And his father calmly says that he wrote it with some help from Calvin's mother. Now I'm not sure what Watterson political comment is with that particular strip. Perhaps there isn't any. Watterson's focus on Calvin is being as Calvin being raised and my children's love for Calvin and Hobbes series are curious to me because of our focus this morning. Which is on baptism. In our study of Hebrews, we arrive at chapter 6. And I hope you are able to recall That I preached several sermons on Hebrews chapter six last summer. I hope you remember because They mention the foundation stones that must be in place in a Christian's life in order to move toward perfection. Because it would not be fruitful to duplicate those sermons so quickly, I will just focus on one of those foundation stones, which is baptism. And I focus on baptism because it appears to be one of those practices, one of those teaching subjects that is not so easily passed on to children My children, at least. And I question why. Consider my reference to Calvin and Hobbes comic series. I never told my children to like Calvin and Hobbes. I never taught them why Calvin and Hobbes is funny. I just read them and I laughed. And because of them, when my children pick them up, they laugh as well. But when it comes to the subject of Christian baptism, my beliefs My practices regarding it are not so easily communicated and received by my own children. It could be said of me that my failure to pass on a clear understanding of Christian baptism has me slipping in the poles as a father, a grandfather, and a father-in-law. And this is related to last week's sermon, when I challenged us to better train our children in the Christian faith. If to diligently teach our children means to persistently instruct, ask yourself what you have taught your children regarding Christian baptism. What have you taught them? That answer may challenge you to ask yourself what you believe and understand about the subject yourself. Here are a number of questions that should have immediate and clear answers. What happens at a Christian baptism? Who should do the baptizing? What mode or manner should be practiced? Should a person be dunked, sprinkled upon, or poured upon? Should infants be baptized? If so, why? If not, why not? There are sub-questions to these, such as Is a person automatically saved because he or she has been baptized? You know, baptismal regeneration. Do both parents of a child need to be a Christian in order for a child to be eligible for baptism? Can a person be baptized twice or three times, or is there a limit? Perhaps because there are so many questions to be answered, it is understandably difficult To pass on to our children all that needs to be known, especially when we don't know the answers ourselves. So let's get at it and hear some answers. First, what happens at baptism? Well we can all imagine that there is much that happens that we do not know What we can know is what the Bible says. It says in Romans chapter 6 that we are buried with Christ in our baptism. Such a metaphor is why some insist on immersion or dunking at baptism to replicate this burial. But the point of the metaphor is to say that the baptized identify with the death and resurrection of Jesus Meaning that the old person, the person under the sin covenant of Adam, that person is now dead and buried. And a new person is alive by the power of Jesus as their Savior. The Bible also says that baptism, in baptism, we have been circumcised. But not circumcised physically, but spiritually. which is to have our hearts of stone, again, hearts that we have received by being born as part of Adam's race. And then we are given hearts of flesh, being born anew in the race of Jesus. Finally, what we can know that happens at baptism is that a person baptized is received into the church. And by church I mean with the big C. of the Catholic Church, the universal church. I distinguish that if you get confused between Catholic and Roman Catholic. What is important to notice is what happens at baptism, is what God does to and for the person being baptized. This is why mode and other practices thought about by Christians, between Christians, are non-issues Baptism is not, as many Christians understand, it is not something we do for God. We don't bury ourselves, we don't circumcise ourselves, but it is rather something God does for us. And we are to receive all of what God does for us at our baptism by faith. That's important. We trust God does things for us at baptism by faith, but we say it is by faith we are saved. Now that faith is involved naturally leads to what is the most controversial question, which is should infants be baptized? You know what I'm going to say, but you don't know why I'm going to say it. It was the Anabaptist coming out of the Reformation who argued That a person who is baptized must have their own faith in order for them to be baptized. What they were reacting to Is the practice of the Roman Church to put faith in the ritual of baptism itself? which came to be described as ex operato, which is translated by the very work performed. Meaning that the act of baptism or the work of baptism was what a baptized person could trust in, which seemed to exclude the need for faith in Jesus. And we can understand why the Anabaptists would be concerned about the exclusion of faith in Jesus. Any baptism that is not done in faith in Jesus is not a Christian baptism. What Martin Luther and others correctly argued, I believe, in response to the Anabaptists, was that the faith of the parents is transferred to the child. Transferred. Examples are plenty in Holy Scripture, as we see the faith of a father sufficient to heal his daughter. And faith of friends helped heal a paralytic, and faith of a woman to give her last meal to a prophet to provide bread for her and for her son throughout a famine Faith is transferred from people to people throughout Scripture. After all, the faith of Jesus is transferred to all of us. Add to that the circumcising of infants under the covenant of Abraham, and the Christian covenant being a fulfillment of the covenant of Abraham. And you have a natural transitioning of how marking infants with circumcision of heart, as Paul describes in Colossians 2, which again is marking them with baptism. Add to that the practice of Christians baptizing their children from the time records were kept in the church, the only aberration to that practice occurring with the Anabaptists. As I have explained before, there is no need for there to be a specific teaching regarding infant baptism in the New Testament as it was naturally for the Jews who converted to Christianity to include their children in that rite, just as they had done with circumcision under the covenant of Abraham. Again, seeing the Bible as one whole book and not too divided. Unfortunately The position of the Anabaptists, who are known today as simply as Baptists, places children who are not baptized in some space limbo as they are raised to know Jesus as Savior and Lord, but not given the very right that marks them as a Christian. The position to not baptize until a person can confess for their own faith also leaves out people who You know, by reason of accident or illness, cannot confess and cannot understand enough to know that they are confessing. To leave such people out is not the gospel. And it certainly is not expressing the love of Jesus. Now, a related question to the subject of infant baptism falls under what happens at baptism. Is a person saved at their baptism? The answer to that by Christians down throughout history is a bit nuanced. It is nuanced because we cannot make the mistake of trusting in the ritual itself to save from sin and death. But we also must recognize the plain statement of Saint Peter, who said in Acts chapter 2, that to be saved, a person is to repent from his or her sins and Be baptized. The rite of baptism is then connected to converting to Christianity, which is another way of saying describing a person becoming saved. And you will notice that in our baptism rite in the prayer book, it uses language to describe a person baptized as being regenerated or made new. Such a word describes conversion or procured salvation. Thus we are saying that a person baptized is a person who is saved from sin and death. But again, this is not the same as saying that the ritual itself saves anyone. As Bishop J. C. Ryle describes in his wonderful book, Knots Untied. We use language to describe a person newly baptized that they are regenerate because of charity. It is in love that we say a person that has been baptized is a new person, having the old sinful manner put away and the new person washed and cleansed. We think of one another having been baptized as fellow Christians until he or she proves otherwise. Christian charity calls us, calls us to do so. And when it comes to Christian charity, related to the sacrament of baptism, The Christian church today falls short, which is to say that we have sinned and continue to sin against God. Christian baptism was designed by our Lord to unite his people. He plainly said that whoever would follow him must be born of the Spirit and of water. And that water is baptismal water. In the context of imploring Christians at Ephesus to be united with instructions for Christians to forbear one another in love St. Paul makes the observation that there is one body, one spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father of us all. Baptism, therefore, is to be a mark that we all have in common. It is what makes us all a part of the family, of the same body, of the same bride, of the same church. Those who divide over the sacrament that is meant to unite us do so to dishonor God. If we cannot worship with other Christians because we think a person being baptized must be baptized by immersion or they're not baptized, well, we have divided over what is to unite us. If we insist on pouring because the Holy Spirit was poured out amongst God's people, well, we too have divided over what is to unite us. If we insist on sprinkling the water at baptism because that was done on the altar of God when a sacrifice was offered, then we too have divided over what is to unite us. The mode or manner we are to be baptized does not and therefore should not divide us, for there is but one baptism. If we cannot worship with other Christians because of who did the baptizing, we again divide over what should unite us. It has been since Vatican II that the Roman Catholic Church recognizes Protestant baptism as being the Christian baptism we all share. Although the Eastern Orthodox Church and all of its branches do not have a particular dogma on the subject There are many Eastern Orthodox bishops who recognize both Protestant and Roman Catholic baptism as being legitimate Christian baptisms. Our tradition recognizes all baptisms from every Christian tradition as legitimate The only requirement is that the baptism must be done in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, and it must include water. The primary group among Protestants who do not accept baptism of others as legitimate Christian baptism are the independent baptistic churches. Unfortunately, for such churches and their leaders, there is a disconnect from other Christian churches as well as the historic church I was a part of such a group during my college days, as most of you know. And what that group insisted was that I be rebaptized Because my baptism as an infant in the Roman Catholic Church, they said, was not a true baptism. And I had not considered then, as I do now, just how arrogant that position is. It is arrogant because it presumes certain leaders can decide, apart from God and apart from the historic Christian church, what God has done or what God has not done. It also reveals that such churches understand and therefore believe about their baptism. They believe it is not something God does, but what they do as believers for God. And I do not and have not for some time looked at that second baptism as a legitimate baptism. I instead trust in the baptism over which my parents spoke words of promise to raise me to know Jesus as the Savior. That was my baptism. That is when God marked me The meaning of St. Paul, proclaiming there is but one baptism, unites us, as I have said, and excludes for there to be a second. A third, or however many baptisms someone would want to practice. This position is very much found in our Book of Common Prayer. You'll find that there's a place where the minister, if the person about to be baptized, doesn't know whether he or she was baptized as a child The minister may say, if this person has not been baptized, then I baptize you. And such an approach does not presume upon God, but respects the work God may have done in the past, and having faith that it does not need to be done again. A great problem with independent churches is the disconnect they have with denominations like our own who are practicing the Christian faith as it was first practiced In the early church and the church victorious. Independent churches can be easily tempted and swayed by the devil that their leaders have got all the doctrines correct Well the church historic and triumphant were very wrong. I'd like you to hear this true statement regarding the Bible teaching on independent churches versus the church universal. This is from the former Archbishop of Canterbury, Michael Ramsees, back in 1935. He wrote, There is no Christian community mentioned in the New Testament that is not behind it some authority responsible to the larger whole And there is no letter in the New Testament, except the Epistle of Philemon, that does not show that the local society, local church, owes obedience to someone who addresses it in the name of the larger whole. End quote. Baptism. Christian baptism makes us a part of the larger whole, whether we want to be or not. I preached the sermon because I was slipping in the poles I have been slipping in the polls because my children have difficulty passing on to others what I thought was already understood regarding something so fundamental as Christian baptism. It is not their fault. I have assumed that because of what I believe about baptism and what I explained during confirmation, that they would have embraced it and be able to explain it. Perhaps I have done that with other important topics as well. Baptism and all of its particulars is foundational And yet what it stands for, what God does in it and with it, can be easily obscured by the devil if we are not careful to pass it on. And so this day I pass it on to you, so that you can pass it on to others. Let us pray. Our Father, we thank you for this foundation stone. We thank you for its mysteries, and we thank you for that which is concrete about it. We identify with being buried with Christ and raised with Him. We identify with having our hearts circumcised so that we beat freely for you. And we identify with being a part of your body, your church. May all of us know it, and may we pass it on to our children. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: The Point of No Return
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We are in Hebrews chapter six, working from verse four through verse twenty. I'd like to start off by talking about titles. The historic titles given to men of great fame and influence are fascinating, if not curious. We know of Alexander the Great, King of Macedonia. There was Catherine the Great, Empress of Russia. We all should have heard of Charles the Great, aka Charlemagne, King of the Francs. As you might have guessed, there is no set of criteria for giving someone the title Great. There is a large number of people in history who have been given the title, and quite a few who have called themselves great. When they were alive, but no one called them great after their death. There are other nickname titles given to people of history They include titles like The Blessed, such as Alexander the Blessed or the Bold Such as Philip the Bold, and then the Conqueror, such as William the Conqueror. And there are negative nickname titles as well Such as the devil Robert, Duke of Normandy. And the one title that has for a long time intrigued me, Julian the Apostate. Why was Julian called an apostate? Well, Julian was born into the Constantine family. After Emperor Constantine made it legal to be Christian and to spread the Christian faith within the Roman Empire, Christianity was spreading rapidly When Flavius Claudius Julianus was made emperor of Rome, Julian was raised to be a Christian. Having been tutored by Eusebius, the bishop of Nicodemia. But when Julian was older, he decided to study the ancient philosophers. And as a result, it turned him to Neoplatonism. By his own admission, Julian despised his Christian heritage as he perceived the faith was forced upon him during what he described as a bitter and lonely childhood. Julian thus made it a priority to turn Rome back to its pagan gods while targeting Christian leaders and churches with laws that restricted their influence. He became a true enemy of the Christian faith and of Christians. Hence the nickname given to him by Christian historians, Julian the Apostate. The origin of the word apostate is from the Greek, originally meaning a runaway slave. It was also used as a synonym for defection, desertion, and rebellion. These are all appropriate descriptions of someone who has known the Christian faith And has at one time claimed to be Christian and then turns away from the faith so much to the degree of denying all of its truths. When the preacher to the Hebrews turns to the dark reality of apostasy in verse 4 of chapter 6, of people turning away from the Christian faith, he does so abruptly. However, his abruptness is necessary. Consider that the first part of the chapter he is encouraging these Hebrew Christians. to have certain beliefs and certain practices of their faith established so that they can go on to perfection Which is to say, to be made holy, walk with the Holy Spirit while following the life of Jesus, their Savior. But if those foundations are not established, there is great risk of turning away from the truths of the Christian gospel. And once that truth is turned away from The great scandal is that there is no turning back to the faith. You are forever lost. Now, before we examine that warning in greater detail, I ask that you follow me as we follow the argument of the preacher from verse 5 through 20 of chapter 6. For a person who has once tasted the heavenly gift to leave the faith only to return again is the same as saying That the suffering, death, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus was insufficient the first time, therefore it must be done all over again. That is putting Jesus to shame. The metaphor in verses 7 and 8 Compare the unbelief of someone who turns away from the faith to growing thorns and briars when what was planted was herbs. Although the preacher has to give warning like he has, he also wants these Hebrew Christians to be positive because of how God views them. God knows of their love for one another and for their fellow Christians. They have practiced this love and God knows about it. But the concern is in verse 11, where we understand that the same works that they have been practicing toward their fellow Christians That work needs to continue to the end, which means there is concern that they are faltering The warning against becoming sluggish emphasizes the concern of the preacher that they are faltering. Next is the reason why the Hebrew Christians should not be sluggish in their faith. It is because God is the keeper of promises. His covenant promises are certainties. And people who trust in God's promises to the end of their days are most certainly rewarded. Abraham is then the prime example of one who trusted in God's promises and did so to the end of his days. And the reasoning of the preacher continues by comparing how we treat the promised words of our fellow man to how we should trust the promised words of God all the more. He then describes two characteristics about God that are underlined to increase the faith of believers. The preacher calls them immutable things, the New King James Version, immutable. What is immutable does not change. It is a certainty. And as it relates to God, we can say that it always was, always is, and always will be. We can be certain that God does not lie, and because God does not lie, and He has said that He has an eternal refuge for us, it is there that we can place our hope. Thus we are what are immutable are what God has promised and his oath to assure that it will be done. And what will be done is our heavenly reward if we remain faithful to the end of our time in this life. The problem is, not everyone is faithful to the end of their days This, of course, is not the only place in the Bible that refers to people losing faith. We must remember that Scripture is best interpreting itself, or as some have said, Scripture interprets Scripture. One place that helps us understand how a person is lost to the Christian faith, never to return Is 1 John chapter 2, where St. John describes apostates in the following manner. He says, They went out from us. But they did not really belong to us. Such a statement works like a proverb. For we all know people in our lives For a time, and they were very much a part of our lives for a time, but then decided to no longer be a friend And we can best handle such abrupt departures from us, accepting that such a person or such people were never truly friends. Because after all, friends don't just leave friends. What John is describing, however, is more than a proverb. It is a reality check that if a person once believed in Jesus and next denies the faith entirely, Such a denial proves that said person was never a true believer, with the consequences being much more than a lost friendship.
