Jesus taught the saying. When he used the parable of the sower, you will recall that in that parable, the seed that is the Word of God Falls on rocky soil and springs up, but it has no root. And so when the trials and tribulations arise, the plant dies. Now remember, it was a plant, or it looked like a plant like all the other plants. It was a person who said that he believed and did so with a glad heart Only to find that the faith was not set deeply enough in the heart. And then there is a seed that grows amidst thorns. Again, the plant grows and at one time looked like all the other plants, only to have the thorns choke out the plant. Jesus explains that the thorns and thistles that choke the plant are cares of this world and the deceitfulness of riches. In plain speech, the enjoyments of this life become more important than the promises of God. And we know such people They may be people we are very, very close to, people we love. We watch them and we don't like what is happening, but we don't see how we can stop it. They trade eternal life for this life. They insist that they deserve to be happy. And so they abandon their marital vow, or they abandon a moral standard, or they just stop pursuing God, and they decide to pursue earthly pleasures or earthly wealth. What they define as earthly happiness has become their God, and they serve it well. It is thought by some when God says that apostates cannot turn back to the faith, then it means that God won't let them. But that is not consistent with Holy Scripture. God says He desires that no one be damned, but instead all come to repentance. That is his heart. It doesn't mean that is his sovereign will, but it reflects his love for all he created in his image. The cannot. The cannot return commit then communicates that they will not return It is the nature of apostasy not to want to return. It is the nature of salvation that if you truly have it, you will not deny it, and if you deny it, then you never truly have it. And that point reminded me of a law in Deuteronomy that states that a man who has divorced his wife and then she marries another man And he divorces her, that the original husband is forbidden to take back his wife again. His original wife again. Commentators believe that such a law is for the purpose of punishing fickleness in marrying and divorcing frequently and abruptly. And that does make sense. But there is something deeper being represented in such a law. The very nature of marriage is an abiding covenant that is not to be broken because two have become one. If a man does break it and then tries to restore it, then he never understood the nature of marriage the first time. In the same way, a person who commits his life to Christ Jesus and professes to be a disciple and later departs from said faith, and then later wants to return to the same faith, he cannot, because it never was a faith that he claimed to have He cannot return because he will not return, for he never was there the first time Some preachers have connected this teaching by the Hebrew preacher as the same as the unpardonable sin described by Jesus in the Gospels. During our study of difficult sayings in the Bible, during our midweek Bible study, we tried to tackle this sin against the Holy Spirit, aka the unpardonable sin. And we discovered that there are difficulties to know precisely what it is. Some are convinced it is referring to a person who once was a professing believer and then turns to be an apostate Others like myself believe it is specifically against the Holy Spirit. It is attributing what is godly to be evil and what is evil to be godly in a blasphemous manner. What is consistent with either interpretation of this unpardonable sin is that there is a line that is crossed. A point of no return that is past, leaving no opportunity for repentance or restoration. The Hebrew Christians were to be fearful of such a line, such a point, and so are we. The prophet Hosea described the Israel people of his day in a similar manner. Hear this from Hosea chapter 5, verse 4 through 6. They do not direct their deeds toward turning to their God, for the spirit of harlotry is in their midst, and they do not know the Lord. The pride of Israel testifies to his face. Therefore, Israel and Ephraim stumble in their iniquity Judah also stumbles with them. With their flocks and herds, they shall go seek the Lord, but they will not find him. He has withdrawn himself from them We are to be warned here that once harlotry is embraced, i. e. , acknowledging other gods, the line is crossed. There is no return. Such warnings against leaving the faith seem to come to a contradiction with the doctrine of predestination. Again, we studied said doctrine about two weeks ago during our weekly Bible study, and we were able to conclude that predestination is a doctrine taught for Christians to be confident that their salvation is in the hands of God, not in our own hands, which we should be very glad for. And it is a doctrine that because of God's will being assured, it casts out fear. We cast out fear of the devil who cannot reach us. We cast out fear because we cannot be separated from God. But if we are predestined in our salvation from sin and death, why do we need to be warned against apostasy? And while such is a reasonable question, it tries to venture into a field of understanding that we are not privy to. There are certain understandings that we are not given light to know. The subject of where the will of God overlaps with our personal wills Where we make our own choices, that overlapping, that place of it is mysterious, and it's not revealed in Scripture What we know from Scripture is that God is holy. He is fully, He is completely sovereign over all of His creation. And that we, as his creatures, created in his image, are fully responsible for our choices. That is what we know, and that is enough. Therefore, the warning against apostasy, those warnings are needed. Now what I anticipate is necessary is to distinguish what is apostasy and what is rebellion, resulting in disobedience Where we might wonder is whether a person choosing to live in sin is a person who is also apostate. There is in Scripture a description of people living in egregious sin against God, who are also able to repent from such sin and be restored to God. Jesus told us, you remember, the parable of the two sons, the young man who wanted his father dead, living a sinful life according to the flesh, squandering his inheritance. And was still able to return to the arms of a loving father. The sin of David was worthy of earthly death. For he committed adultery going against his vow to his own wife, and then the vow of another man's wife. And then he tried to cover his sin by having that other man killed But when he was confronted with his sins and confessed his guilt and prayed for God's mercy, he was forgiven, fully and completely forgiven. So living in rebellion against God is not apostasy. But it very well may turn into apostasy. That is the warning for all of us. There is a line. There is a point of no return. And it is foolish for any person to test where that line, where that point is. Well, beloved, the topic of apostasy is a difficult part of the faith. It is difficult because there are no warm feelings that come with it. There is no positive mental attitude imparted when addressing the warning against apostasy. But it is real and it is necessary. For we all know people who seem to be living very close to that line, very close to that point of no return. We need to pray for them. And we need to pray for ourselves. That we will always abide in Christ. It is only by abiding in him that we will not be led astray. I close with this Poem by Joseph Addison Alexander from the 18th century. I'm sorry, 19th century. It reads. There is a time we know not when, a point we know not where, that marks the destiny of men to glory or despair. There is a line by us unseen that crosses every path, the hidden boundary between God's patience and his wrath. To pass that limit is to die. To die as if by stealth. It does not quench the beaming eye or pale the glow of health. The conscience may be still at ease, the spirit lit and gay. That which pleases still may please and care be thrust away. But on that forehead, God has set indelibly a mark, unseen by men, for men as yet are blind and in the dark. And yet, doomed man's past below may bloom as Eden bloomed. He did not, does not, will not know, or feel that he is doomed. He knows, he feels, that all is well, and every fear is calmed. He lives, he dies, he wakes in hell, not only doomed, but damned. Oh, where is this mysterious born by which our path is crossed, beyond which God Himself has sworn that he who goes is lost? How far may we go on in sin? How long will God forbear? Where does hope end and where begin the confines of despair? An answer from the skies is sent. Ye that from God depart, while it is called today, repent, and harden not your heart. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful Father, we thank you for this warning from the preacher of the Hebrews. These are hard words to hear, but we hear them, we acknowledge them. Father, save us, save us from ourselves, and keep us in your family all the days of our lives. This we ask in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen

We are in Hebrews chapter eight, working through verse one through six. I begin With the following dialogue from a movie. And I'm not endorsing the movie. Gotta be careful with that. You see it, see it through the television version The movie title is Planes, Trains and Automobiles. It starred Steve Martin and John Candy. The basic plot of the story, two guys are trying to get home for Thanksgiving. Only everything that could go wrong does go wrong. And so they have to work together to uh Use various forms of transportation to get home. In a scene toward the middle of the movie, Steve Martin's character is fed up with John Candy's character Resulting in a tongue-lashing by Steve Martin. John Candy's character is named Dale Griffith, and the following are Steve Martin's lines He says, you got a free cab, a free room, and someone who will listen to your boring stories. Didn't you notice on the plane when you started talking, I started reading the vomit bag? Didn't that give you some clue that this guy's not enjoying it Everything's not an anecdote. You have to discriminate. You choose things that are funny or mildly amusing or interesting. You're a miracle. Your stories have none of that. They're not even amusing accidentally. Honey, meet Del Griffith He's got some amusing anecdotes. Here's a gun so that you can blow your brains out. You'll thank me for it later. I could tolerate any insurance seminar for days. I could listen to them go on and on. They'd say, how can you stand it? And I'd say, because I've been with Dale Griffith, I can take anything You know what they say? I know what you mean, the shower curtain guy? It's like going on a date with a chatty Kathy doll There should be a string on your chest that I pull. Except I wouldn't pull it out. You would. Ah ah ah ah By the way, when you're telling these stories, here's a good idea. Have a point. It makes it so much more interesting for the listeners. Those lines are something similar to what many people would like to say when someone starts a story that doesn't seem to have an off-ramp. And the FYI, the writers of the movie, do a good job of getting the viewers to feel sorry for Del Griffith after he is berated and And yes, E. Barton's character apologizes for what he said, and all is eventually forgiven The point of me quoting movie lines is because of how the Hebrew preacher gets to the point after taking a few detours of his explanation of how Jesus is our high priest. You have noticed, I trust, that we skipped all of chapter 7 of the Hebrew Sermon, and we did so because at the beginning of chapter 8 The chief point of chapter 7 is stated. All that was said in chapter 7 is to lead up. to the main point, which is that Jesus is our high priest, and that is a very, very good thing. There is great importance for us as Christians to understand Jesus as our high priest. For Hebrew Christians, the importance is heightened because they knew the law of God and that it required a high priest to be the only person eligible to offer an atoning sacrifice. We heard earlier in this sermon to the Hebrew Christians that Jesus is that high priest. in the order of Melchizedek, as opposed to being of the line of Aaron, and that Jesus was himself the atoning sacrifice. In chapter 7, we are told how Jesus is of the order of Melchizedek. The preacher reminds us of the story in Genesis Where Abraham goes to battle against tribes who had taken his nephew Lot for hostage. God gave Abraham a great victory over his enemies. And while he returned home from the battle, he meets up with Melchizedek, who is called there King of Salem, while also being referred to as a priest to whom offering is given. This is the first and only mention of Melchizedek in a biblical narrative. And the first mention of a priest of any type. The first mention. When the Hebrew preacher helps us see, what the Hebrew preacher helps us see is that the character of Melchizedek was a type of priestly king. He was a precursor, a type or a shadow of the priest king to come, who is of course Jesus of Nazareth. The argument next explains why being of the order of Melchizedek is superior to being of the order of Aaron. The genealogy of Aaron is of the tribe of Levi, and all priests were to be born of the line of Levi. What the preacher shows is that because Levi was of the loins of Abraham, who was Levi's great-grandfather, When Abraham paid a tithe offering to Melchizedek, it was as if Levi was making that offering payment. Making Melchizedek and his priesthood greater than that of Levi, including first high priest of the line of Aaron. Greater than those priests. And because of the change in the priesthood line, there is also a change in the law. For Jesus fulfilled the law both sacrificially and morally. Thus, there is no more need for a daily sacrifice offered, no need for an annual sacrifice on the Day of Atonement. Jesus satisfied all sacrificial needs, once for all. This gets us to the main point. Chapter 8, verse 1. We have a high priest. We have a priest that is of the greatest priestly order. And what is our priest, what is our priest doing? Right now, what is he doing? Verse 1 of chapter 8 says That our high priest is seated at the right hand of the majesty in heaven. Our high priest sits. Jesus is able to sit because his work is finished. He is able to sit because his work of overcoming sin and death is done, and he sits and waits to come again. Being seated means he is victorious. To be at the right hand of the Father means that Jesus is given the highest place of honor in heaven. And this is what we see in the book of Revelation, as Jesus sits enthroned on high, and all the elders surround him singing his praises, casting their crowns. After comparing the priesthood of Jesus to the human priesthood here on earth It is emphatically stated in verse 6 that the ministry of Jesus is more excellent in every way to that which was under the covenant of Moses. Jesus is mediator of a better covenant and better promises. But we need to stop there for a second. We cannot misinterpret what that means. Using words like more excellent or better. The preacher is not saying that the covenant and the promises are different. and superior, because they are separate from that which is of old. That would go against the teachings of Scripture elsewhere, that the new covenant being a fulfillment of the old And that Jesus Himself was the fulfillment of the old. He was that which with Abraham and Moses both saw in the future. Both saw in the future and had faith in it and trusted in it. So by using the more excellent, the better, the preacher is referring to a fulfillment or an apex of all that was being pointed to in the Old Testament. That's how it's better. That's how it's more excellent. Because it is established that Jesus is the superior high priest. And that means his ministry as mediator between God and man is superior, and nothing can be better We as followers need to increase our faith in Jesus as our mediator and the one who fulfills all the promises in which we put our trust. There is a problem with believers that I witness and I have a burden for regarding Some people who don't believe fully that Jesus is indeed mediating for them. And so we must start with an understanding of what it means for Jesus to mediate, intercede for us. In the first sense, Jesus is our mediator, and that he stands between us and the wrath of the Heavenly Father. Now let us not understand that to mean that God is angry and he needs to be held back before pulverizing us. But instead we are to know that God is a God of justice. And we are to know the Heavenly Father as a God who wants to separate our souls from the sin that entangles us and condemns us. That is why he sent his son so that we could be separated from sin and guilt So then Jesus as our mediator allows the Heavenly Father to have a relationship with us to where he calls us his children and we call him our Father So when there is a problem, when there are times we don't trust that God wants to forgive us and wants to heal us and wants us to be separated from our weaknesses The cause of that problem, the cause of our lack of faith, is us. The cause is our unbelief Consider this scenario. You are angry with someone, and you know that you should forgive this person, but you choose not to. You hold it within your heart and you hold it within your mind, bitterness toward this particular person. And then something happens in your life, such as your car won't start, and you have to have it towed And when you hear from the mechanic, he tells you that you are going to have to pay a few thousand dollars. And when you hear the news, you consider why such a difficult thing is happening to you And then you conclude that your difficulties are the result of you not forgiving that certain person you chose not to forgive, and you conclude that God is punishing you Such a scenario may not be yours specifically, but the principal parts are your story. You think that because you did something you know in your heart you should not have done, every troubling thing that happens after it must be God punishing you. What I say to such a line of thinking and concluding, I want to be very clear. God is not punishing you. That is not the God of Holy Scripture. If it were, then the suffering and death of Jesus was for no purpose. The truth of the gospel God has revealed in Jesus is that God forgives because Jesus paid the penalty for the sins of the whole world, and that means your sins and my sins. The only thing we have to do is repent by way of our mediator, Jesus, and in him and in him alone do we find forgiveness. And as stated, God wants to forgive you all of your sins. That is a major part of what it means for Jesus to intercede, to be our mediator. Our sins are not counted against us. Thanks be to God. I I know I I must say the caveat to the scenario I I just used. For God very well may use events in your life, events that are not pleasant to experience, to awaken your conscience about a sin from which you need to turn away from. That may happen. But again, such events are not punishments. They are calls upon our consciences, calls upon our souls that need to seek God and find freedom. Next, we can know that because Jesus is our mediator, our intercessor, our prayers are heard by the Godhead. And this is the point where we need to embrace our Protestant perspective. The Bible teaches us that we do not need an earthly mediator for God to hear us. We do not need a clergyman to speak God to speak to God on our behalf. We do not need an earthly priest when we have the high priest of heaven. You and I can speak to God in every moment of our lives, and God hears us whether we feel it or not And God not only hears us audibly, but he wants to hear from us as he wants to hear from Jesus, his son. Jesus has enabled by his life, death, and resurrection, ascension, enabled us to be heard by the Father and the Holy Spirit in his name. But these are some statements that I have heard from you over the years. Statements like, I don't know what to pray. The answer is, yes, you do. Jesus gave you precise words to pray. And once you pray what we call the Lord's Prayer and you don't know what else to say, we are even told that he hears our groans. The God of heaven hears our groans and the Holy Spirit interprets them. Or you can just talk to God like you would a good friend, because after all, He calls us friends. I have also heard, I don't like praying for myself. The answer to that, you need to get over that. You need to pray for yourself. And you could start by confessing your false humility. If Jesus prayed for himself, which he did, you need to pray for yourself I have also heard, I don't feel that God hears me. Answer to that: of course He hears you. He hears everything and he responds to everything done in the name of Jesus. What we feel is not relevant to what is objectively true. Feeling the presence of God is a blessing, but it is not what confirms God hearing or caring. I believe a most beautiful image is given to us, given to the church regarding prayer. It's from the book of Revelation, chapter 8. And it reads as following. And the angel of the Lord came and stood at the altar with a golden censor, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar before And the smoke of incense with the prayers of the saints rose before God from the hand of the angel. Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it on the earth. And there were peals of thunder, rumblings, flashes of lightning, and an earthquake. Beloved, our prayers. Do not rise to the heavens only to dissipate into the atmosphere, but they are collected to be used by God to bring forth his kingdom now and in the future. This we are to believe as a conviction of things not seen. Believe that of your prayers. I wonder if any of you have heard of Rabbi Baruch Kahin. Rabbi Baruch Kahin. Almost two years ago, Rabbi Baruch Kahin was elected by the nascent Sanhedrin in Israel. To be the next high priest over Israel. The choice was made as a precaution That if political conditions would suddenly change and the Jewish people were allowed to worship on the Temple Mount The high priest could re-initiate the Day of Atonement sacrifices as the law of Moses requires. In fact, Rabbi Baruch Tahaim has been leading Israel in performing certain rituals according to the law of Moses, such as offering an omer or barley offering to God in the heart of the old city of Jerusalem Isn't that interesting? Isn't it curious? What if we witnessed in our lifetime Israel offering sacrifices in the temple once again? Well, it may be interesting, but it will mean nothing. It will mean nothing in terms of the fulfilled covenant God has accomplished in Jesus. You and I don't need Rabbi Baruch Kahin, regardless of how nice of a man he is. Jesus and only Jesus is the high priest that is needed. What is the point? So that it is more interesting for you, the listener. Jesus as our high priest stands before God as the one who offered himself so that justice is served and you do not have to be punished in this life or the life next That is the point. What is the point? Jesus, as our high priest, enables our prayers to be heard. We can talk to God. We can call God our Father because Jesus is our mediator. We can speak to God without a priest, without a rabbi, without a pastor. And those of you who struggle submitting to ecclesiastical authority, here is a place where you can embrace your individuality, for you have the ability to speak to God with no help from clergy. That is the point. What is the point? Jesus as our high priest means that no one can Not only can we talk to God, but we can know that our prayers are participating in His kingdom coming and His will being done. Our prayers by the authority of Jesus are incense in heaven and fire and storm on the earth. Our prayers. That is the point. What is the point? The curtain of the Holy of Holies, used to keep all worshippers but the high priest on one side and God on the other, that has been torn into. And we have direct access to God. All because Jesus is the true high priest and always was. That is the point. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful Father, we confess you today as our high priest. And that all that we offer unto you, especially ourselves, we have every confidence it is received by the Father, it is wanted by the Father because of you. High priest lead us. High priest, always be with us. We pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: One not Two
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. We are covering Hebrews chapter eight, starting at verse seven, through chapter nine, verse fifteen. I state that there is a problem among us, and it is not a problem just among us as a local congregation of Christians It is a problem among Christians today all over the globe. It is a problem of proper understanding. Now you might think that such a problem warrants much concern, not warrants much concern, because it does not seem to be a doctrinal problem, it's not a moral problem But I argue that it is of great concern because it leads to problems that are doctrinal and moral I dare say it is a problem that has the fingerprints of the devil all over it. And I realize that when saying I see the devil having responsibility to the problem I am referring to, then I'm going to offend some. But I have to risk being offensive to address the problem. The problem I have been describing is the understanding among Christians. That the covenant of God to his people, as found in the Old Testament, is different than the covenant of God found in the New Testament. Yes, after hearing me state the problem, you may be saying to yourself, well, that's not a serious problem. You may even be saying to yourself, but they are different. So there is no problem. And so I realize that I need to convince some of you that they are not. Two separate covenants, and I need to convince you that to think in such a manner is a serious problem. And finally, I need to show you how fruitful the kingdom of God can be if we see them as one covenant. We begin by addressing the passages from our epistle reading in the Hebrews that appear, I say appear. To separate the covenants. Look at chapter 8, verse 7. There describes the first covenant. The covenant given under Abraham and then Moses. It describes that covenant as being clearly flawed, and said flaws are to make the second covenant better. But that is not what the preacher to the Hebrews is stating. Recall three weeks ago that we learned that Jesus was superior as a high priest compared to the Levitical Order, because Jesus was of the order of Melchizedek, to whom the Levitical Order paid tribute. Thus, Jesus was a part of the old covenant. Not separate, but a part of the old covenant, and that is revealed in the new. What was at fault in the old was not the covenant itself, but was instead the unbelief of the people of Israel. That was the problem. That was the fault. A flaw was their lack of having faith in God. The preacher of the Hebrews is here and before here warning these Jewish Christians not to make the same mistake, the same sin. as their ancestor, that is repeating their unbelief. In chapter eight, verse thirteen The preacher uses the term new covenant to distinguish what Christians understand after Jesus appeared compared to what they understood before. The term new covenant is fitting because it was in the prophecy of Jeremiah as being different because the law would not be written on stone, but on the hearts, on the consciences of God's people. The fact that such a writing will occur will have the result of God's people not needing teachers of his law, because each person will know God intimately. But to interpret these words to mean that this new covenant is separate from the old is to ignore that the law of God is found in the Old Testament That law written upon our hearts is from the old covenant and is now a part of the new. And therefore, what is truly new is that again the people of God will actually believe. Now, we cannot interpret the preacher to be saying that all of Israel didn't believe, because we know that in chapter 11 he's going to list A host of people in the Old Testament who had faith, and that faith we Christians are to emulate. What is new is that the people as a society, as a people, as a group, We'll believe the church. It's similar to the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is in the old covenant, but when it was dispersed amongst God's people and they had the Holy Spirit as a group, That was new. Also, to interpret the preacher's words as treating the new covenant separate from the old. is to fail to examine the content of Jeremiah's prophecy. Answer to yourself, has the prophecy of Jeremiah been fulfilled in the new covenant? Asked another way, is the law of God written on the hearts of Christians so that we don't need teachers? If so, I am certainly not needed and you are wasting your time right now. But we need teachers. I need teachers so that I can teach you, and you need me so that you can learn and teach others. So what must be meant by Jeremiah's prophecy that there is going to be a place A place, a heaven, where the law is written on the hearts of God's people, requiring no teachers and no preachers. That is the place where we will truly be God's people and he will truly be our God because there will be no hindrances There will be no unbelief, no sin of any kind. That place is heaven. And next, I need us to consider the dangers and the negative repercussions of treating the covenants as separate. The first danger is what theologians have labeled antinomianism, which means against the law or being against the law. It is the belief that draws the conclusion that because the new covenant under Jesus fulfills the old covenant and thus is superior to the old covenant. that the law of God as found in the old covenant needs look no longer to be a concern. This casting off of the law of God is first proposed to be a good thing because the believer lives by faith and love and such things prevail over the law. But the truth is that faith and love within each Christian in this life under the sun is not perfected. It is not perfected until heaven is our reward. Until then our faith and love are to grow, are to mature, while we discipline our lives, ourselves By following the moral law of the Old Testament and confessing and repenting when we fail to do so. For those who have insisted on faith and love against the moral law of God, they have gone the way of moral liberalism. Which is accepting rebellion against authority, sexual impurity, gluttony, and a host of other sins as personal choices rather than offenses before God. As St. Paul has warned in several places, woe to those who live by the flesh. Such a fallout from separating the old and new covenants is clearly seen in what are called the mainline Christian denominations. Such groups have publicly stated their willful abandonment of the Bible as their authority. And even when said groups claim some respect of the Bible They pick and choose their own canon or passages of Scripture that they will give authority to while openly rejecting other passages that do not match their lifestyle choices. Woe to them indeed. Another negative repercussion for separating the covenants. is an individualism that slowly separates Christians from the fathers of the faith in the Old Testament while separating modern Christians from early Christians in the church, while separating Christians even from one another today People separate with the understanding that their faith is only in terms of their personal relationship with Jesus and nothing more is needed And the result of that faith, individualism, this only Jesus and me needed creed Is a major, major contributor to the impotence of the Christian church today. An impotence toward making a positive effect on the cultures that surround the church. The only Jesus and me needed creed allows for individual Christians to interpret the scripture as they please. But all the while confessing that they believe that the Bible is fully inspired. This is different, you'll note, than the liberal confessing Christian Who state their distrust of much of the Bible. Instead, these individualist Christians state a positive confidence in the Bible, being the Word of God. With the caveat that it is the Word of God as they interpret it. So where the Bible clearly instructs Christians to submit to their church authority, They believe that they can make a particular situation, their particular situation, an exception because, well, they don't like their church leadership. Same can be said for praying for governing authorities. They don't like their governing authority, so they don't pray for their governing authority. Same can be said for wives submitting to their husbands. They don't think their husband can be trusted, so he doesn't deserve my submission. The individualist Christian can ignore such instructions because they interpret their situation as an acceptable exception. I have heard them. You have heard them. We have heard them People who say they are Christian, who exempt themselves from laws against adultery, because, well, God wants them to be happy They exempt themselves from tithing because well they they can just can't afford it right now. They exempt themselves from the sin of gossip because, well, their situation demands a lot of counselors so that everybody can know who really hurt them. They exempt themselves from faithfully attending church worship because their application of the Sabbath is their own. They exempt themselves from loving their neighbor because their neighbor is the most difficult neighbor in the history of humanity. And such confessing Christians have an exempt stamp in their hand for when the more difficult teachings of the Bible are applied to their life. Only they own this exhibit stamp, and only they can use it as they see fit. They prayed about it after all, and Jesus said they could use it. And Jesus is their Lord and Savior. Sure He is. Sure He is This only Jesus and Me needed creed eventually leads to ignoring how God has moved in the lives of Christians in the Old Testament. and Christians who lived and died for the faith since Jesus walked this earth. And yes, I called those Jewish faithful Christians. Because Jesus referred to them as believing in him. He said, Abraham and Moses saw his day and they were glad. He said David understood God to be the God of the living, even as his old ancestors were all dead. Even our preacher to the Hebrews preaches the faith of those of the Old Testament as the same faith that you and I have to be saved. The same faith. The faith of the only Jesus and Me needed creed crowd concludes that the faith of the Jewish fathers is not needed because it's not as good as their contemporary faith. The faith of the only Jesus and me-needed creed crowd also doesn't need the faith of Christians who live with threats of loss of life and even died for their faith, died for formulating the creeds, died for developing orderly Christian worship. No, these individualistic Christians believe that their age is the true church age and their worship is more sincere. And so they replace sacraments that the church has practiced from its beginning with pseudo-sacraments that are based on emotion rather than the institution of Jesus. They dedicate children instead of baptizing them into the covenant because they ignore the covenant under Abraham that circumcised children while allowing children to participate in the feast that God established. They dedicate children because it is about their choices and the choices of their children. They want their children to have a personal experience with Jesus over being raised as a full member of the covenant that God made with Abraham and fulfilled in Jesus They prefer the subjective over the objective. Thus, many children are raised with an identity that is about self. Self apart from God's covenant, self apart from parents, self apart from the church local and universal, self apart from Christians victorious. And this focus on self, when it comes in contact with the words that Jesus tells him or her to die to self, well that will not happen. It will not happen because children focus on self when growing into adults only know about self. And so to die to self is is to just die. Remember that I said this is a problem and it's a serious problem There are dire effects that have specific causes, and a major cause is believing that the covenants are separate when in truth they are one. There are some key words in the passages in chapter nine and and in the New King James Version. For us to properly understand the relationship of the covenant of Abraham, Moses, and David compared to the covenant under Jesus. Those words are three: manifest Symbolic and more perfect. Manifest symbolic and more perfect. As a material lesson to show the connection between what we unnecessarily label as old and new, the preacher to the Hebrews describes the tabernacle, not the temple yet, but the tabernacle. In verse 8, we read that the way to the Holy of Holies was not yet manifest. The word manifest is to make something clear or obvious to the eye or the mind. What needed to be made manifest is what had previously existed, but the existence was not known. It was present, but not clearly seen, not clearly understood. Jesus was the tabernacle. He was the offering. He was the veil. He was the one who offered the offering. And he was the one who received the offering. They couldn't see him until he made himself seen. But he was there, always there. Verse 9 says that the tabernacle and its furnishings were symbolic. What is symbolic represents something greater than the symbol itself. Thus the tabernacle represented the body of Christ, which was more fully understood by the symbol of the temple And then revealed to its fullest in the very person of Jesus, who was the Christ, whose body was destroyed only to be rebuilt in three days. The tabernacle and the temple were symbols of the man who would truly house the Spirit of God, God Himself. That Jesus was more perfect, that all the symbols, shadows, and types before him is stated in verse 11. And this explains just how Israel was forgiven of her sins as a people and as individuals. For the offering, offerings made in the tabernacle and then in the temple were effective. Why Because they pointed to Jesus, who would be the Lamb of God slain from the foundation of the world. Already. Jesus as a sacrifice for sin is sufficient for all sins before him and after him And for these Hebrew Christians who are struggling to continue in the faith, they needed to know that Jesus is the only means to cleanse their guilty conscience. If Jesus is not believed, then the past sins, the present sins, the future sins are not forgiven, even if sacrifices in the temple continued. Beloved, we, God's people, must see cause and effect relationships. We must see them For the devil has blinded the minds of unbelievers who cannot see such connections. For example, We should see that shootings in schools, how tragic again this week. We should see of all people that shooting in schools and death in the inner cities Have a cause that leads back to the way we view life in a mother's womb. We must see that. And we must see the connection of how we value life for the sick and the feeble. How quickly we are now to vote to pull the plug. We need to see those connections. If we do not value life in its most vulnerable circumstances, we're not going to value life in any circumstance. And we should see cause and effect of the believing of God's covenant to be two and not one. I'm sorry, to be one and not two. The evidence of them being one is overwhelming. Consider that Jesus said he came to fulfill the law, not to do away with it. Jesus said that Abraham saw his day and was glad. Luke tells us that after the resurrection, Jesus explained the scriptures to the apostles, and the only scriptures were the Jewish scriptures, the Old Testament. Also, the first two sermons preached by the apostles in the book of Acts tell of Jesus fulfilling the promises of God through King David. And how the same God of their father Abraham and the original covenant is the same God who sent Jesus. And then there is the sermon preached by Stephen, just before his martyrdom, that shows how the salvation of God's people started with Abraham and culminated in Jesus of Nazareth. We can add to this mountain of evidence the letters of Paul, which clearly teach that people of the Old Testament were saved by grace through faith. just as they are under the revealed person of Jesus by grace through faith But the devil has done well. We can acknowledge his success in getting false teachers to separate the covenants. while disregarding the moral law in some circles or promoting individualism in other circles. But it ought not. It cannot be said of us. We are to be a people who embrace the whole council of God. According to respected theologian D. A. Carson, to embrace the whole council of God is to do the following. To embrace God's purposes in the history of redemption, truths to be believed, and a God to be worshipped It is an unpacking of human origin, the fall, redemption, and destiny, a worldview that shapes all human understanding, and a savior without whom there is no hope. The conduct expected of God's people, commandments to be obeyed, and wisdom to be pursued, both in our individual existence and in the community of the people of God. And finally, the pledge of transforming power both in this life and in the life to come. Promises to be trusted and hope to be anticipated. That should be enough to keep us busy on this side of the sun. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God, we ought to be a people grateful for this revelation, to see the connection of old and new and what it truly means to be new To truly have faith, to truly trust to the end. Father, forgive us, for any times our minds and hearts separate. The one covenant you've kept with your people and will fulfill to the end of our days and to the hope of heaven. Keep it before us, Holy Spirit, we ask. In Jesus' name. Amen. Okay.

sermons.title: Blood is Needed
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We continue in the book of Hebrews, our epistle lesson from Hebrews 19, chapter 9, beginning at verse 16. Peter Hitchens, a columnist and part-time theologian, recently wrote an article in First Things. But examine the modern influence of the martyrdom of Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley These were reformers of the Church of England during the time of Queen Mary, aka Bloody Mary. The martyrdom of these Two faithful Christian men is mostly remembered by the line that Latimer is heard to have said to Ridley on their way to be burned. Quote, play the man, Master Ridley, and by God's good grace we shall this day light such a candle in England as may never be put out. That the candle was never put out was quite true for a long, long time, but sadly it is not true today. The Church of England has worked very hard to put out the candle of the gospel of Jesus Christ, and the result is a mere flickering of sparks like a dick lighter running out of fluid. When describing the suffering of these two martyrs, Hitchens speculates as to why the form of punishment, capital punishment, was so brutal. He considers that the burning of men who were found to be enemies of the state, that it was done because beheadings were too clean and too quick. Burning someone alive provided an extra warning against anyone who would consider following the martyrs to a similar end. Hitchens speculates that the crown knew the need for such cruel executions because they knew the toughness of their citizens. Their lives were sustained by hard labor and hard rations. Their hands were tough and their hearts were tougher. They plowed their own fields, butchered their own meat, and suffered the death of many loved ones caused by disease, malnutrition, and childbearing. Beheadings wouldn't scare them and therefore would not dissuade them from rebelling against the crown. Burning, perhaps, had a better chance of instilling a second thought. Now I accept Hitchens observation and I accept his next point Which is that those of us who live in first world cultures today are not as tough as our ancestors. We have soft hands. Few of us slit the throat of the meat we eat. We don't see blood spilt. And whenever we do, we panic and cringe and hide our eyes. We are sheltered from sacrifices it takes to enjoy the few foods we enjoy. and to wear the clothes we wear and to live with the freedoms we have been given. I am soft. I know I am And so when we read of how Jesus procured our salvation by way of blood sacrifice, I fear that I don't get it well enough. I fear that I am too squeamish to appreciate the seriousness of such a sacrifice I read too quickly the description the preacher gives in chapter 9, because any image I might have, I don't like. Images of bloodletting, of blood sprinkling, of necessary death, well, I want to avoid those But I speculate that if we avoid such realities, we lessen the seriousness of it all. And that is where my concern as pastor lies. We are not serious enough about our faith. Which is to say we are not serious enough about the sins we commit, the blood it takes for our sins to be forgiven. And the lives we owe to the Savior who shed his blood. The preacher's point is the seriousness of the blood of Jesus spilled. He has been proving in this sermon the superiority of Jesus above all that came before him, making the clear point that all that was done before him was an anticipation of his perfect sacrifice. The Hebrew Christians were being tempted to go back to their Jewish ways, which consisted of trusting in temple sacrifices. The preacher responds by showing them that the many sacrifices were insufficient in and of themselves They needed the blood of Jesus for them to be fulfilled, for them to have a perfect effect. And we must appreciate what it means to say that the blood of Jesus was needed needed a very common way In which we do not take sins, our own sins, serious enough, and thus not appreciate the blood of Jesus enough Is that we at times can consider it all unnecessary. We can reason that if we were God If we were given the role of satisfying justice because of the sin of humanity, well, we would simply call for a do-over. Let's try again. We would simply pretend like the past is in the past and it doesn't not need to be brought up again In doing so, we would be communicating that God has made a bigger issue about sin, well, bigger than he should have. After all, teachers allow students to retake tests all the time. Parents allow children to have another attempt at cleaning their room before they truly get into trouble Bosses have patience for their employees who make mistakes. Why can't God be like teachers and parents and bosses and give a do-over to humanity? Such reasoning is done by people who see through the glass dimly. It is done by people who are under the sun. We don't comprehend the need for God's justice to be satisfied because our minds are clouded by our own definition of justice. We don't see the devastation that sin causes in the spiritual realm. Therefore, we have no way of appreciating how or why sin cannot be overlooked. It cannot be ignored. Besides, does anyone actually believe that if humanity was given a do-over, that we would do better than Adam and Eve? Please, please do not believe that for a second. We wouldn't do better, and we couldn't do better. Adam and Eve are us, and we are them. Another way we do not take sin serious enough is how we enter into it with the expectation that God will forgive us later. I recall a philosophy class where a student of mine was presenting a paper on how cannibalism can be justified. And I challenged her that the scenario I had given her said that she needed to work through the subject with the background that cannibalism was against her religious faith. She easily responded that she would eat her fellow travelers so that she could remain alive and simply ask God for forgiveness when she was rescued. And what I reviled at was not her answer, but rather how quickly and glibly she gave the answer. And my reviling could not be toward her alone, but had to include myself. For I too have responded in a similar manner within my conscience To sin willfully, to enter into it willfully, and then expect to ask God for forgiveness afterwards Another way we do not take sins serious enough is how we compare ourselves to others. Gossip is not as bad as murder, right? The slander of a person is not as bad as adultery, correct? Withholding forgiveness is not as serious as stealing, right? Judging others is not as serious as worshiping false gods, correct? The next time you read a listing of sins given by Saint Paul, whether it be to the Romans, Galatians, Corinthians, Ephesians, Colossians, to Timothy, I encourage you to slow down. Slow down and realize that gossip is listed as serious a sin as murder. The sin of slander is listed alongside the sin of adultery. Withholding forgiveness assures forgiveness being withheld. Haughty judgment and idolatry have the same, the same eternal results. The number of sins listed in total covers a great deal of human interaction that does not allow any one of us to escape the guilt and the deserved punishment. There are the top ten, of course, but to them we are to include anger, slander. Greed, malice, sexual perversions of every kind, envy, rivalry, treachery, faithlessness Foul language, spite, being boastful, insolent, heartless, ruthless, jealous, causing dissension. Bitter, ungrateful, reckless, and conceited For him who is without sin, let him cast that first stop. Also consider how each of these sins is related to one of the top ten. Jealousy is a cousin to coveting, as is envy and rivalry. Jealousy asks why other people's children do better in school. It's not fair. Or have more friends or are better looking or more athletic. It's not fair. It's not fair. Jealousy says nobody is watching out for them or people are thought of first before them. Such is the same as being ungrateful for what God has given. And both tell God and other people that God is not fair. Being angry, bitter, and causing dissension are cousins to committing murder Jesus taught us that murder begins in the heart, as it is the person's emotions where anger and bitterness and desire to see other people suffer. That's where it takes seed and that's where it grows Beloved, if we condemn the big sins while overlooking their cousins, we are no better than the unbelieving world that worships sexual perversions in one moment and then pretends to condemn them in the next. We are no better than hypocrites who want to save the lives of children in classrooms while marching for the right to kill children in the wombs of their mothers. We are to be the people set aside from a lost and hypocritical world and included in being set aside is to see what are normally viewed as lesser sins Or not sins at all, we are to view such sins as just as serious and that they are just as damning as the more salacious sins. And finally, for for now, I say that we don't take sin serious enough When we are able to use the same tongue and lips we use to worship God while so quickly speaking evil of a person who is a brother or sister in Christ. That's a problem. As St. John pointed out, we cannot say we love God while hating our brother in Christ. Let service to Christ while not practicing love to one another does not fool God. He knows better. He knows what's in the heart of every individual. And he knows that much better than we do. There are certain behaviors That Christians are to identify with regarding personal holiness, about their personal choices for righteous living. They are in a sense Christianity 101, for they are the first things we are to learn to live as Christians. An example of Christianity 101 is to trust God for our daily bread, which is to say to have faith that God will provide for you all that you need and more. So there is no need to fret, no need to stir, no need to be anxious, because God has promised all that you need. That is Christianity 101. Another fundamental part of living the Christian life is forgiving one another. And a forgiving heart does not keep record of wrong. It does not envy. It does not get jealous. It does not boast. It does not take self-serving or self-righteous posture. If any of or all of such behavior is part of a person's life, he or she has not forgiven and therefore is not forgiven. My point in delving more deeply into the specific sins that we don't take serious enough is the principle that the more we understand the seriousness of our sin, hear this, the greater our love and appreciation for that blood spilled for our sins. And this point allows me that our love will be greater the more we appreciate the blood spill. This point allows me to segue into addressing the homily of Bishop Currie, who addressed the grand crowd who attended and viewed the most recent British royal wedding. I didn't. I do not disparage any of you who liked the sermon. It received high praise by many. I listened to it this past Monday. Good oratory skills were displayed. Love was preached. But it is part of my calling to listen with discernment. Jesus was mentioned, yes. Sacrificial love was mentioned, yes. And then the social gospel snuck in. And the ideal of love as a conquering champion over poverty and social injustice, that was lifted up. Love itself was hailed as the Savior. It is a problem when love is hailed as a victory or a victor. With no acknowledgement of sin, death, and shed blood You see, if Jesus would have come into this world to promote and exemplify social justice, he would have demonstrated and taught as much. If Jesus came into this world so that no child would ever go to bed hungry, then he would have said more than 5,000 and he would have done it on a daily basis. Perhaps it is hard to imagine that a child went to bed hungry even while Jesus walked this earth, but it is perfectly reasonable to imagine that one did. And there were sick people who did not get well and who died while Jesus lived. There were slaves mistreated. women abused in the home while Jesus preached the Sermon on the Mount, walked on water, and ate bread with his apostles. You must see that Jesus didn't come down from heaven being in the likeness of men. God didn't send his only begotten son to stop hunger or to stop diseases or to stop oppression wherever it may be found. Jesus came down from heaven to pay justice for what is at the root of the cause of hunger, disease, and abuse. Jesus came down to shed blood for the sins of many. God hates sin. Sin brings forth death. Sin destroys souls. God's love can only be rightly understood in the context of Jesus sacrificing for sin. The love that Bishop Curry preaches doesn't die for sin. It dies for the right of the homosexual to stay in his sin. Or the adulterer to stay in her sin, or the abortionist to stay in his sin, or even for the idol worshipper to stay and worship a false God. That's not love. That is not the love of the God of Holy Scripture. God's love is to pull us out of sin that so easily entangles us God's love rescues us from sin by the blood of Jesus so that we can go to a place where there will be no hunger, no injustice, no abuse, no sin. You know the place. It is heaven, and heaven is not here That does not mean that we look the other way when we can do something about an injustice or about a hungry child We can care for such who are before us with the belief that this is not our home. And it is the love of Jesus dying on the cross that will get us to where we belong. It is because Jesus shed his blood for the sins of humanity that we are able to acknowledge that it is reasonable, a reasonable requirement to leave our former lives in order to follow Him. The requirement is that we give up our lives to follow him. And dare we not think that to give up our lives is to do equally what he did for us? No. Giving up our lives, our self, can be in no way equal to what he gave for us. In truth, what we give up is what we need to give up because it weighs us down. What we need, what we do not need, and what weighs us down are our weaknesses. Our prejudices, our selfishness, our personal pride, our judgments of others, while we have grace for ourselves, our greed, our self-righteousness, our foolishness, etc. , etc. Our shed blood is no good. It pays for nothing. It is tainted by sin, our own sin. The only shed blood that matters is the blood of Jesus. It is his atonement that we trust in for our sins to be forgiven and for heaven to be our hope. The seriousness of the blood of Jesus cannot be overhyped or overpreached. What can wash away my sin? Nothing but the blood of Jesus. What can make me whole again? Nothing but the blood of Jesus. This is all my hope and peace. Nothing but the blood of Jesus. This is all my righteousness, nothing but the blood of Jesus. Let us pray. A Father, today we try to grasp what the preacher to the Hebrews is saying and how Your atoning work goes to everything we believe in, anything we can hope for. May we never be ashamed of the blood of Jesus. May it be that which saves us to our eternal home. Thank you, Father, for sending your son. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Please open your Bibles to Hebrews chapter ten, as was read for our epistle lesson. I'm going to be sharing notes from the particular verses read, and I want you to follow along. Beginning at verse 1 As has been argued and explained prior, the Levitical sacrifices only foreshadowed the future salvation which Christ has guaranteed by his death and resurrection, and which will someday come to its completion. And the problem with those sacrifices is again that they cannot take away sin and they cannot make the worshiper perfect before God. Verses 2 and 3 This is counted as the third of the three contrary conditional statements around which the preacher has formed his central argument. The first is chapter 7, verse 11, and that reads, If perfection could have been obtained through the Levitical priesthood, what need was there for another priest to come? The answer is that it was needed. Another priest was to come, and that priest is Jesus. The second conditional statement was in chapter 8, verse 7, and that reads: If there had been nothing wrong with the first covenant, no place would have been sought for another. The answer to this is that what was new about the new covenant was that it was believed. The third conditional is here in chapter ten. It says that if the sacrifices could deal definitively with sin, why did they have to be offered over and over again? The answer is that Jesus offered a sacrifice that was forever. Verses four through six Here it is stated that what the scriptures already teach, what he is not saying is that the sacrifices were supposed to take away sin, but failed to do so. He is saying that they were never capable of doing so, and that the people of the ancient epoch never imagined that they could take away sin. And thus he quotes from Psalm 40 Indicating what Jesus taught. And of course, we remember that Jesus said all of the Psalms speak of him, and we could argue that all of them speak of him. The citation of Psalm 40 perfectly suits the preacher's use of it here because it compares the Levitical sacrifices unfavorably with the work of Christ. It was a truism of the Old Testament revelation that the Levitical ritual served no good purpose, no good purpose without faith and obedience on the part of a worshiper. It wasn't the act itself. And this is not a New Testament teaching only. It is in both the old and the new, making them again one covenant. Verse 8. Modern interpreters need to be careful about verses like this one. It needs to be understood that David is speaking categorically when he says, sacrifice and offerings you do not desire. For what he means is that what comes first, what is most important, is the offering of the heart and faith that one puts in God. What he is not saying is that God did not desire ritual and sacrifice. And that should be obvious because God commanded them in the first place. Modern Christian worship innovators read into such passages to justify their modern worship styles, and that should not be. Verse 9 through 10. Stated straightforwardly, Christ's sacrifice of himself has just the saving power that the Levitical sacrifices lack. The will of God mentioned here is that Jesus came to fulfill that will. And that was, of course, the offering of himself for sinners. And what need would there have been for him to do that, to offer himself if the Levitical sacrifices were adequate to take away sin and guilt? They were not adequate, and so Jesus was necessary. Verses 11 through 14 The point made earlier in verses 1 through 4 is given several times in the argument, and it is recapitulated and summed up here. It is that the ineffectuality of the Levitical sacrifices is demonstrated by the fact that they had to be performed over and over again. They fare poorly in regard to comparison with the once-and-for-all sacrifice of Jesus, the effectuality of which is attested by the singular place of honor that he has granted. When he has finished his mission to the world. Consider that the Levitical priests must continue to stand and Jesus as Christ sat down. And where? But the place of honor, the right hand of the Father. It is to Christ, therefore, and not to priests and rituals that sinners must come to attain forgiveness and entrance into eternal life. Verses 15 through 18, here the author is Returning to a citation of Jeremiah 31, he did the same in chapter 8. And this is to provide a dramatic climax to his argument that began as far back as chapter 4, verse 14. The true salvation that God promises and Christ has guaranteed results in a permanent and full absolution for the forgiveness of sins. I'm going to hold off my comments on verses 19 through 22 for the end of the sermon. It is truly the greatest of rewards serving as pastor to have the freedom and responsibility to announce that Jesus forgives all sin. It cannot be said enough when it is believed. Such announcements can only get old when it's not believed. You and I have been to funeral services, even here at St. Stephen's, where attendees sing hymns, Amazing Grace. And the law and the like. And it is obvious who doesn't believe the words of those psalms. Funerals bring people to church who otherwise never attend. And when it is time to participate They don't. They don't pray. They don't recite. They don't sing. It's not in their hearts to do so. They hear the grace of God forgiving their sins, and it is like they have just heard a weather report and they never plan to go outside anyway. It is like they just heard an old song on the radio. They know the words. They perhaps liked it when they first heard it, but now it means little or nothing to them. And so they observe. They just watch. Amazing grace is not sweet to them as a sound. They don't see themselves as a wretch. And therefore don't know their need to be saved. They don't know they are lost, and so they don't know they need to be found. They think they can see just fine without Jesus. A true believer, the person who has had the guilt of his sin cast away as far as the East is from the West, will always sing heartily of God's amazing grace. And will always want to hear from the preacher that their sins, although many and ugly, are no more counted against them as they are justified by the blood of Jesus. You can hear it every Sunday and it doesn't get old. It doesn't get old because it is eternally true and it makes the difference for your eternal life. And it doesn't get old because we sin. Again and again we sin. And so every week our souls long to hear that our sins are forgiven by the means of Jesus. As mentioned, Jeremiah 31 is quoted again, and he ends the quote with the same verse. And that verse must be important as it's repeated, so I read it to you again. It says, their sins and their lawless deeds I will remember no more. And so your sins and your sins and your sins and all of our sins collectively, God will remember no more. It is like they didn't happen. It is like they are not us, and therefore they do not define us. It is like they no longer control us, they no longer mark us, they no longer scare us. They are not us, and we are not them. Because they have been removed from us by the blood of Jesus, and we always have to remember it is by the blood of Jesus. The world we live in, the world we live in does remember. You know that as well as I do. The world remembers and it keeps track of our past sins. Some people don't like to go back home to their hometown because people remember your sinful past and they will bring it up just like it happened yesterday. Some people avoid family gatherings because of someone in the family that likes to bring up sins of the past Most college students experience that first time back home after being away and thinking of themselves much more mature than when they left, and there's always that sibling that reminds them, no, you're the same person you always were Some family members insist that you are the same old knucklehead you always were. That is the world. This world keeps record of wrong. That is the devil's way. The devil and his angels take advantage of the weak-minded and the weak-willed and use them to mention past sins just like a bragging athlete points to the scoreboard to remind you that you are losing Now this next point is a side note, but it reflects the ways of this world I read an article recently about the information on the internet about you, how it is kept Supposedly, every search you have ever made on the internet has been stored. Every email you have received or sent has been stored. Every product you have looked at on the internet, there is a record of. Every item purchased, there is a record for, and it is used to encourage you to purchase more. Every map search you have used has been stored. Last year, during the summer months, Bobby Lynn and I, along with Jared and Josiah, took a two-grafting trip on the Susquehanna. Through a rafting company that donated to our winter ball option. This past winter, Bobby Lynn and I took a trip That had us drive by the same water rafting company. And as we were driving, bam! As we were driving, Bobby Wynn received an email advertisement from the same river company. They know where you are right now. Such is a creepy example of the spirit of the age in which we live. And such should not be us. Of all people, we should not keep record of wrong. God's way, and therefore the way of his people, is to be free from records of wrong. And shame on us if we ever talk of other people's past sins. Shame on us. And each of you should know that you have every right to rebuke the devil in the name of Jesus when he whispers in your ear the sins of your past. God is for you and the blood of Jesus is sufficient and your sins are not you. Believe that. Believe that On another topic, separate but related, is our awareness of our personal day-to-day sin. And the objective truth of God's forgiveness because of the blood shed by Jesus. We have here in Hebrews chapter 10 What Protestants have used to challenge the Roman Catholic belief that the sacrifice of Jesus for sin is offered again and again and again at Holy Communion services. Roman Catholics also understand the reality of day-to-day sin, of course they do, but they believe it's taken care of by the renewal of the sacrifice of Jesus at Holy Communion. They believe that bread changes into Jesus' flesh and the wine turns into his blood as the priest consecrates the elements. Hence, God is able to remember our sins no more because Jesus renews his offering on a regular basis And yet in Hebrews chapter 10 verse 14, it clearly and unashamedly states that the offering of Jesus was once One offering that perfected forever those who believe in him. And we say this with certainty in our liturgy that Jesus was once offered. I have explained it various times before that it makes perfect sense when it is understood that God is above time. Time is a created reality that we operate within, but God does not. So when Jesus is offered once in a time, The effectiveness of that offering is not bound by time, but covers sins past, present, and future. Enabling John the Revelator to say that Jesus was slain from the foundation of the world His sacrifice made all sacrifices before him understandable, yes, but effective at washing away sin. As his sacrifice applies to the past sins, it also applies to future sins as well, making the doctrine of transubstantiation unnecessary. However, however, there is still the problem of day-to-day sin Sin that mucks up our minds and hearts to the point where we wonder if we are truly saved. We fall short every day and we know it. No, we don't worship idols every day. We don't take the Lord's name in vain every day or dishonor our father and mother every day. But we practice the sins that are cousins to those sins. And we can speak more generally about our guilt when we point to the fact that whenever we are not loving the Lord our God with all of our heart soul, mind, and strength. When we are not loving our neighbor as ourselves, we are falling short, we are sinning every day. And so while Jesus obeyed and died that we might be perfect forever, sin is not out of our lives this side of heaven. And this is hard to understand. Our reality, this side of heaven, is that in one case, a very important case, God in His mercy removes the guilt of our sins entirely, once and for all When he gives us faith to trust in the atoning work of Jesus. And in another case, a very honest case, we are liable and culpable for our continued sin. We are the cause of ugliness and unworthiness in our lives. And that is why I believe familial language God uses is so very important. Consider that God insists on being our father. And as his children, we are to know that we are a family. And just as loving families do not cast off their children when their children are disobedient, so too does God not cast us out when we sin, even when we sin every day. God has sent his son, who by his obedience and sacrificial blood paid for our sins forevermore. And so we stand perfect before God as sons and daughters. We are all sons and daughters who do foolish things for which we suffer in this life, and these things we confess daily and strive to overcome and even weep over them when we Don't and sometimes we have to just accept the consequences that we cannot escape in this life Not too long ago, I was exchanging emails with a young woman who no longer attends here, but she was still seeking my counsel. She was struggling with a particular sin that she found little victory over. Her struggle made her question if she truly did have faith in Jesus with a more general concern about doubting whether this Christianity thing actually worked. And by work I mean that it had power to overcome sin. I assume that there are many in this congregation like her who not only struggle to overcome particular sins, but struggle to want to overcome particular sins. If we would examine ourselves more closely, we would see, I hope, that we have overcome many sins that weighed us down in the past. There are sins in our past that we are no longer tempted by. And they are evidence that the sin in front of us can be overcome as well. And as we strive, we are to do as St. John tells us, which is when we do sin, we are to confess our sins to God. Who is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. And so I finish my point by recalling verses 19 through 22. For you look at those words again. We are told to have boldness when we enter into God's presence. It is our daily sins, our sins that we have not overcome, those are what make us timid. But we are to come to God boldly because of the blood of Jesus. For that blood overwhelms the reality of our past sins, our present sins, and our future sins. And look at verse 22. Verse 22. And see how God wants us to have hearts full of assurance of His mercy and a guiltless conscience because, not of what we do, because of what Jesus has done. The objective reality of our salvation. It is the preacher's dilemma To boldly proclaim the forgiveness of sin in Jesus while acknowledging that sin remains in the life, and to try to communicate that without accepting complacency. Without accepting daily sin. But we will never be complacent in our sin if we truly love God. May we always pray the prayer of that anxious father in Scripture who said to Jesus, Lord, I believe. Help my unbelief. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God, for these powerful words of the preacher, to tell us that God remembers our sin no more, to tell us you do not remember our sin, how grateful we are. Now we all come boldly to your table, ever confident that you want to forgive us. You want us to be a part of your family. Thank you and pray to you in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Why We Hold On
sermons.speaker: Phil Lambooy
sermons.text: Let us pray. Heavenly Father, we thank you for the opportunity that we have to be here this morning to sing your praises, to partake of your table. To fellowship with one another and to hear your word. We pray that the meditations of our hearts would be acceptable in thy sight And we pray all this in Christ's name. Amen. Please be seated. John Tolly Hood Worthington was born on November 1, 1788 at Shawan, near Baltimore, Maryland. He was the son of Walter Tolly Worthington and Sarah Hood, daughter of John Hood, by Hannah Barnes. Worthington was elected as a Jacksonian to the 22nd Congress in 1831. He was also elected as a Democrat to the 25th and 26th Congresses, where he served from March of 1837 to March of 1841. After Congress, he resumed. Agricultural pursuits. Worthington died at Shawnee in Baltimore County, Maryland, and was interred in a private cemetery on his farm. He was reinterred in St. John's Episcopal Churchyard in Worthington Valley, Maryland. So last evening I was sitting in that churchyard, one of my favorite graveyards. Preaching through my notes, preaching out loud to see what actually sounds like with or without my hearing aid, but alas, my words fell on deaf ears because everybody is dead. Seeing John Tolly's Memorial Stone, though, I hoped he lived a life of love and accomplishment. But more so I hoped he listened and loved hearing God's word, and that he persevered to the end. May you and I, as living stones, as Peter would tell us, listen and take to heart all that God says to us, not only this morning but each day of the week. And picking up on verse 22 as we go through the end of the chapter, a chapter that's very long and detailed, a chapter that has a lot of information that can be put into 10 sermons, about an hour each, you're going to Get in one sermon less than an hour. But it begins with let us. Let us, you and I, draw near to God. And that'll be the first let us In these passages. In your English translations, let us is only mentioned three times, but in the Greek there is five opportunities for us to read let us. So let us approach him Get close to him, let us draw near, many of your translations say. You know, we see that same word used in the wilderness temptation of Jesus. On the front end of the temptation, we are told that Satan drew nearer. Came to him. And on the back end of the temptation, where we are told, angels then came or draw near to him to minister to him. And yet Satan and the angels eventually departed from him. Which is the case even among ourselves. Each day we draw near to one another physically, and yet eventually we do depart. And we go our separate ways. And this is in the physical realm. It happens all the time, coming and going, drawing near and drawing apart. But this drawing near in this passage is not a physical act. It is an invisible act of the heart Hebrews 4, 16, let us draw near with the confidence to the throne of grace. Hebrews 7, 25. He is able to save forever those who draw near to God. Hebrews 11, 6, which passes Jorgens. And we'll teach on next week. Without faith it is impossible to please him, for he who draws near to God must believe that he is, and that he is reward of those who seek him. The great passion Of this writer to the Hebrews is that you and I draw near to God. That we come to his throne to find all the help that we need. That we come to him confident that he will reward us. With all that he is for us in Jesus. The great aim of this writer is that we get near to God, that we have fellowship with him, that we not settle for a Christian life at a distance from the world. From God, that God would not be a distant thought, but a near and present reality that we experience, what the old Puritans called communion with God A communion with God, first of all, in our hearts, but a close second would be a communion with God in the context of worship. And in order to draw near to God, we must go through his Son's body and blood. We must go through the cross of Jesus Christ. He is not only our great high priest, which we've learned over the weeks We come to him and he ministers to us, intercedes for us, but he is that cross in that way that we finally get to the Father. You know, in the same way that the curtain of the temple was torn asunder at the hour of Christ's crucifixion And thereby allowing access to the Holy of Holies, if only for a short period of time before they sewed it back together. Now we are given access to the throne of God's presence through the torn body of Jesus Christ on. Calvary's tree. And this not for a short period of time, but for all eternity. Christ is the only way to the Father. All other religions are dead ends. So let us draw near, the writer says. Let us draw near to God through his word and through his church. The second, let us hold fast. Let us hold fast unswervingly to the hope we profess. To hold fast means keep a firm grip. Come into full possession. Hold down and not let go. What sport comes to mind when you think of a firm grip holding down and not letting go? Any Sport of wrestling. It's all about a firm grit. It's all about speed. It's all about strength and the ability to hold down and pin your opponent. I don't think I'm alone. I hated wrestling in high school, junior high school, gymnasium. Why?
