Well because I I would lose When you play baseball, you can throw a ball at somebody, hit them with the bat, hit the ball, but in wrestling you got a grip and hold and all this stuff and I didn't like it. We hated it Well, at least I did. But it's all about a firm grip, holding down. But it's all it's right there in the Bible, is it not? Genesis 32. Look at a striking picture of this in Genesis thirty two of the story of Jacob. The same night he arose and took his two wives, his two female servants, and his eleven children, and crossed the ford of the Jabak. He took them and sent them across the stream and everything else that he had. And then it said, and Jacob was left alone Whenever you read in the Bible that a man is left alone, you know there's going to be a struggle here. With David on the hilltop or on the top of his fortress, his palace, he struggled with temptation. Temptation got a firm grip on him, and he fell. Peter was left alone in the courtyard. He was tempted, was he not, by even the words of the maid in the courtyards to let go of his grip on Jesus? He failed, but not Jacob. Jacob is left alone And a man wrestled with him, we read, until the breaking of the day. When the man saw that he did not prevail against Jacob, he touched his hip socket, and Jacob's hip was put out of joint as he wrestled with him Then he said, let me go, for the door, for the day is broken. But Jacob said, I will not let you go Unless you bless me. And he said to him, What is your name? And he said, Jacob. And then he said, Your name should no longer be called Jacob But Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed. Jacob's steadfast grip led to his blessing. He encountered the angel of the Lord and would not let him Let him go. You know, in the same way, the writer to the Hebrews was exhorting his readers, and you and I this morning to hold on to the hope that we have in Jesus Christ. And based on the psalm. foundation of that hope, our confession as a church stands. God's word never wavers His confession is sure. God is not man that he should lie or son of man that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it? Or has he spoken and will he not fulfill it? Numbers 23, 19. Our hope is in him. Our confession is his Hold fast to that hope. Hold fast to that confession. And that grip, the blessing of assurance. comes. So let us draw near. Let us hold fast. And then he says, and let us consider how to stir up one another in love and good works. How to not neglect meet meeting together as is a habit of sin. Let us encourage one another all the more as the day draws near. Let us, let us, let us. This is a communion message, a corporate message for the people of God Here he stresses Christian fellowship and the church's role in helping believers persevere until the end. We cannot have confidence and full assurance of faith apart from the church. We cannot endure in isolation. Each Christian desperately needs the body of believers for encouragement, to obtain assurance, for continual reminding from other saints. The older in the church to mentor to the younger, the younger in the church to To model the older. Each Christian needs one another, do they not? You need each other. I need you. We need to be encouraged Question, why are so few men in church nowadays? Well, on any given Sunday Is a 1999 American sports film directed by Oliver Stone, who actually makes things up as he goes along in his life, depicting a fictional professional American football team. It's partly based though on a novel, any given. Sunday by famed NFL defensive player Pat Tumey. Some of you gentlemen may remember Pat Tumey. The title, on any given Sunday, is derived from a line in the book, but it's also used in the film that a team can win or lose on any given Sunday. But then again, on any given Sunday, all across the world, churches are likely to have more women in the pews than men. Some estimates place the gender gap as 61% women versus 39% men. That means that on any given Sunday, there are millions more women attending church than men. Many theories have been put forward for that, why so few men attend church. As I read a few of these theories, I I was just commenting out loud all the time through some of these, and I will refrain from those kind of comments now. One theory is that church's teachings emphasizing humility, holiness, and introspection are seen by some men as weak and as somehow less than masculine. So because of that, men don't come to church. Men are looking to be challenged with a bold message of adventure, danger, and aggressiveness. Not me when I go to church, but some people must. Find the right activities to attract men is also a challenge for many churches. Some congregations make an effort to provide times of fellowship and bonding for men by adding Hunting expeditions. I could do that. Fishing trips. Larry, you could plan that. Sports to their schedules. Another theory is that many churches knowingly or unknowingly create a feminine atmosphere with their decor. Did you know that? Men stay away because I guess of colors and decorations and I guess. Another explanation for why there are so few men in church has to do with the stereotypical masculine ego. Men are naturally self-reliant, headstrong, and proud. The theory goes, and are therefore naturally more resistant to the divine call to humility and submission. The gospel confronts are need, and men are often averse to admitting neediness So there are many hypotheses, such as upbringing, men were reared by fathers who did not attend church services, and so have no role model for masculine involvement in a church. There might be a grain of truth in many of these, especially in that one, but none of them fully explain the gender gap in modern churches. Men avoid church for a variety of reasons. Church leaders should be aware of those possible reasons and they should reach out to young men, husbands, and fathers. And that is why men need each other to challenge and to encourage one another. And so do you men sitting here today? It was so great to see that insert in the bulletin about the beginning of men's ministries. So for you men sitting here today, this message isn't necessarily for you, is it? The message is for those who are not here today. And so I'm all for going hunting. Let's go hunting. Hunting for other men. And the rewards of Tokens, Lord of the Rings, and out of the mouths of the orcs We need man flesh in the church. Guys, you're an instrument of reconciliation in the lives and family of the men you know who are neglecting worship. Maybe that's one of the biggest reasons men don't go to church. Other men don't pursue them. They want to be pursued themselves, but they won't pursue others. Men whom you know need the presence of Christ and the fellowship of the saints. Men who need you. And you, by the way, need them. Ladies know this. I just thought I would bring it up in the context of encouragement. Men we need to be encouraged, do we not? So all of us though must n not neglect gathering together for corporate worship. Times of prayer and encouragement. Those who neglect assembling together cut themselves off from the very means whereby Christ feeds and assures and protects his people To say I can do this alone is to defy the very command of Jesus Christ. Some may claim that they can hear better preaching on the internet. But that they're too busy to attend church. But these excuses reveal the reality, men, women of our disobedient hearts. Instead of searching for an excuse We should be doing everything within our power to meet together. Not only because we need to be fed by the preaching of God's Word, but also because it's part of the faith to stir one another up as believers to loving good works. And so the challenge would be not to forget that many out there need to be encouraged and brought back to the fold. And then we get to verse 26. Does Hebrews 26 mean that a believer can lose salvation? You've been ready for this one? You all excited about this one? Can the believer lose salvation? I must say, when I looked at this passage last week, I thought to myself Pastor Jorgensen's going on vacation. We're going to talk about apostasy. And I get that opportunity to talk about apostasy That's alright. The time will come and other passages will delve upon other men. And so I did a lot of reading on apostasy. It's only used two times in the scripture, but we'll make a big deal out of it But it's only used two times in the Bible. So does Hebrews ten twenty six mean that a believer can lose salvation Willful sinning, deliberate sinning maybe you have. Willful sinning in this passage carries the idea of consciously, deliberately, rejecting Christ. I've been using that word a couple of times. Deliberately, deliberately, consciously rejecting Christ. To know God's way, to hear it preached, to study it, to count oneself among the faithful, and then turn away is to become apostate. Sinning willfully carries with it the idea of sinning continuously and deliberately Such a person does not sin because of ignorance, nor is he carried away by m momentary temptations. He is too weak to resist. It's not that. The worldful sinner sins because of an established way of thinking and acting, which he has no desire to give up. The true believer, on the other hand, is one who lapses of his sin, loses temporary fellowship with God, but he will eventually Come back to God in repentance. Why? Because his Heavenly Father will continue to woo him and convict him until he can't stay away any longer. The true apostate will continue to sin Deliberately, willingly, and with abandon. John tells us, John tells us in 1 John, no one is born of God, practices sin because his seed abides in him. And he cannot sin because he is able to be in the world. is born of God. Apostates have knowledge but no application of the truth. Judas Iscariot is the perfect example. He had knowledge but he lacked true faith No other rejector of the truth had more or better exposure to the love and the grace of Jesus Christ than Judas. He was a part of Judas's, Jesus' inner circle of disciples. He ate with them, he slept with them, he traveled with them for several years. He saw the miracles and heard the words of God from Jesus' own lips, and yet he not only turned away, but was instrumental in the plot to kill Jesus. Having turned his back on the truth, with full knowledge, choosing to willfully and continually sin, the apostate is then beyond salvation. Why? Because he has rejected the one true sacrifice for sin, the Lord Jesus Christ. Christ. To turn away willfully from this sacrifice leaves no sacrifice. It leaves only sin, the penalty for which is eternal death. This passage is not speaking of a believer who falls away, who stumbles, who doubts, etc. Many things that we experience. But rather someone who may claim to be a believer, but truly is not. And that is ultimately between God and that person. Whether it be your son or my son, your daughter, my daughter, my father, your father, your mother, my mother. It is ultimately between God Between God and that person. First John two tells us, you know, they went on from us, but they were not of us So if they had been of us, they would have continued with us. But they went out, then it might be plain that they are not of us. But our hearts and our minds and our prayers should not be focused on that. And directed to this. We should be directing our hearts and minds and prayers to the gloriously inspired certain words That out of the mouth of Jesus and his apostles. First John 5. 13, I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life. Philippians 1, 6. And I am sure of this that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ. John 10, 27. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life. And they will never perish, and no Everyone will snatch them out of my hand. This last verse tells us and promises that Jesus' hold on us is as strong as the angel of the Lord's grip was on Jacob and Jacob's was on his. It's a nice parallel, actually, between the first Israel, Jacob, and the theophany of Christ in the Old Testament, and we, the spiritual children of Israel today, in the grip of Christ today. And in his grip, in the grip of Jesus Christ, the blessing of assurance will come. So no, a true believer cannot lose their salvation because those who are truly in Christ will persevere because of the keeping presence and the keeping power of God. And if you want some extra reading, you go ahead and read number 17 of the Articles of Religion, and we'll talk about the predestination of God's And now to summarize the rest of the passage, because there's so much here It does close with the last few verses, 32 through 39, with an exhortation to fidelity and perseverance. The writer reminds those who he wrote that they've already endured. He encourages them by the commendation by what they've already been through. He says that they need to be patient. That the time of their deliverance from all trial was not far off For that he who was to come would one day come. Having thus the close of this chapter eludes the subject of faith, he will proceed in the following chapter, chapter eleven, to illustrate the value and the strength of that faith. The object of the whole is to encourage and exhort them to bear their trials with patience and with submission to the will of God. But my righteous will live by faith. We read that in Habakkuk. It's also here in the end of Hebrews chapter 10. The righteousness. They should live by continued confidence in God. They should pass their lives not in doubt, in fear, in trembling apprehension, but in the exercise of a calm trust in God He is exhorting the Christians whom he addresses to persevere in their religion, even in the midst of the persecution, the same lesson and the promise we can hear today in the midst of our trials and tribulations. So therefore, let us draw nearer to God. Let us hold fast to our hope and confession. Let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works. Let us not neglect to meet together as is the habit of some. Let us encourage one another and all the more as you see the day drawing near. This fabulous five is needed in the church today. And where Christ is preached, they shall be found. And speaking of the preaching of Christ, I could not end but read you a short blurb from Spurgeon. He says the doctrine of Christ crucified is always with me. As the Roman sentinel and Pompey stood at his post even when the city was destroyed, so do I stand for the truth of the atonement, though the church is being buried Beneath the boiling mud showers of modern heresy. Everything else can wait, but this one truth must be proclaimed with a voice of thunder. Others may preach what they like. But as for this pulpit, it shall always resound with the substitution of Christ for our sins on the cross. God forbid that I should glory save on the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. Some may continually preach Christ as an example, and others may perpetually speak upon his sec second coming to glory. We also preach both of these things. But mainly we preach Christ crucified. To the Jews a stumbling block. And the Greeks foolishness But to them that are being saved, Christ, the power of God, and the wisdom of God. And Jude knew this in his one-chapter book when he says, to him who is able to keep you. From stumbling and to present you before his glorious presence without fault and with great joy, to the only God our Savior, be glory, majesty, power, and authority through Jesus Christ our Lord. Lord, before all ages, now and forevermore. Amen. Let us pray. Heavenly Father, we thank you that you do keep on keeping on us. Father, thank you that your true children will not wander away forever. Thank you too, Father, that you know those who belong to you. And to our eyes, if we know people who seem to be Avoiding you, departing from you, deserting you. You know the hearts. May we focus on the encouragement and the exhortation that you call the church to do. And we leave to you, Father. Thank you, Father, for the writer to the Hebrews That he reminds us of the corporate fellowship we have in Christ. And we pray in his name. Amen.

sermons.title: Necessity of Faith
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Join me turning in your Bibles to Hebrews chapter 11 beginning at verse 1. Hebrews 11 beginning at verse 1 From what we heard last week regarding Hebrews chapter 10, we are to see what led the preacher To address the subject of faith directly and more fully here in chapter 11. The argument from the end of chapter 10 flowed as follows. We are to hold fast to our hope, to enter the presence of God, and a major part of holding fast is to encourage one another And in order to encourage one another, we must not neglect corporate worship, for those who do find themselves headed towards apostasy. The ultimate apostasy is losing faith in Jesus. And so faith needs to be defined as well as exemplified So that we who are disciples of Christ Jesus can live our faith ourselves in every circumstance of life. But what is faith? You are to have it, and you are to have it in the object of Jesus, but what is it? Well, it is the substance of things hoped for. Substance can be translated competence, even sure competence The meaning can also be foundation or the very essence. It is then what everything rests upon and is connected to. Faith, the essence of what it means to be Christian, is connected to what we hope in Not what we hoped for, as in saying, I hope it doesn't rain again. That type of hope is what we wish for. What we hope in are the promises God has made in the Bible. St. Peter said Set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ The hope of a Christian is in God promising to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. Christians hope in God's mercies being new every morning. Christians hope in Jesus being the Messiah So that all he promised regarding our sin, regarding eternal judgment, that all of it is true and all of it will come to pass. Our hope is in living eternally in the presence of God instead of suffering eternally in the presence of our sin and the devil. Our hope is in the living God being a loving God towards sinners who call upon Him for salvation. And hear this now. Hear this now. Our hope is in what is objective. Objective Our faith and our hope are in what is objective, and the object is God, who is revealed more fully to us in Jesus. I say it in this way to address a problem in the modern church, which is to present the Christian faith as subjective, a subjective experience rather than an objective reality. Reason with me that any false religion can claim the same subjective experiences modern Christians put their trust in When all the while what is not seeking stand is the objective reality of Jesus of Nazareth, of his death, his resurrection, his ascension. Even godless philosophers have recognized that personal experience does not determine truth. Experiences don't determine truth because they vary from person to person and they cannot be verified. But Jesus is verified. The disciples knew him intimately. Many Jewish leaders heard him teach and witnessed his miracles. Witnesses saw him suffer and die. Over 500 witnessed his resurrected body. And yes, you say, but we don't see him today. We don't have sensory proof of Jesus. And true, true, hence the next part of the definition of faith. Faith is also evidence of things not seen. Evidence is demonstration regarding the subject It is convincing proof to the believer to what the senses cannot detect. Hence it is proof of what is not seen. And with this understanding, we are to recognize faith to be a mystery It is not a mystery in a confounding way, as though it does not provide answers, but it is a mystery in the manner of us not knowing from which it came, how it came to us, or even why we have it That mystery is solved somewhat, and that we are told that faith is a gift from God. St. Paul said, you remember to the Ephesians, by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, it is a gift of God. Both grace and faith, a gift. Elsewhere, Paul says that spiritual gifts are given out by the Holy Spirit, and one of those gifts is faith. The context there, mind you, cannot mean that saving faith is a gift that some believers have and some others do not, for all believers have the gift of saving faith, initial belief. It must mean instead a faith to trust in God during various trials and tribulations. When some people break down and allow life circumstances to overwhelm them, others are able to trust in God through various trials and tribulations. And with this understanding, it is easier to recognize those Christians who have this gift of faith. They are the ones that we call when we need prayer in the midst of trouble. They are the ones we look to to lead us when we don't know where to go. The point is that faith is a mystery, for it is determined by God both to save us and to sanctify us. The how, the when, and why questions about faith are mysteriously found in the will of God and are therefore part of the relationship we have with Him as potter and clay. He is the potter, we are the clay, and therefore we have no position to question him on how, when, and why he molds us the way he does. Related to this definition of faith being evidence of things not seen is then moved into with our first example of faith given by this preacher in Hebrews. It is by faith that Christians believe that God is the creator of the heavens and the earth And notice that it is not required of believers to disassociate with modern scientific views of how the world came to be. That's not in here. There are Christians who believe in the theory of evolution in its entirety while still believing that God planned it all Other Christians believe in the literal sixth day creation with understanding evolutionary evidence to be diluvian in reality. The truth that needs to be confessed by all theories of creation is that nobody was there. And thus nobody can be certain how it all came to be. What the Christian is to believe is that God is the creator and the only creator. The next example in faith is Abel. Abel's story is curious. Because it could be understood that his offering was accepted by God and Cain's was rejected because Abel offered a blood sacrifice while Cain offered only grain. It might be taught that Abel had an understanding of what was required because of sin, which is sacrifice, while Cain did not. But that is not what this example says. This example is about faith. Dr. Robert Rayburn points out that while Cain brought, the text actually says, some of the fruits of the soil, some, Abel brought the fat portion. on the first of his flock. What each brought was according to their faith. And therefore what Cain brought was a token rather than what is best. His tokenism was an expression of his faith, which was no faith. Tokenism offerings to God are a problem throughout the Old Testament and in every generation of people who call themselves Christians. Today, tokenism places a $5 bill in the offering plate while spending disposable money on frivolous items because, well, you can. Tokenism is attending corporate worship once or twice a month when nothing better is planned for Sunday Tokenism is reading the Bible when you are sad, when you are panicked, when you are stressed, so that you can use God's word rather than submit to God's word. Tokenism is doing unto others as you would have them do unto you, except when it causes you to go out of your way. This is to be contrasted to Abel, who, like Jesus, gave his best because God deserves nothing less. Such giving trust that no matter how much I give, God will provide in response to what is hoped for and to what is unseen. The next example of faith is Enoch, who is a quite curious character in the Bible, for he is the only one that is described as being taken by God. Now, yes, you good Bible scholars remember that Elijah was another one that was taken, but we know how he was taken. It was witnessed by Elisha. He was taken up in a whirlwind Enoch is described simply as being taken. And why did God take it? The Genesis account tells us that Enoch walked with God. The phrase walked with God is interpreted to be that Enoch was faithful to God all of his days. Note that it does not say that Enoch was more obedient than other people. It does not say that he did righteous works better than other people. Instead, it is implied in Genesis, and it is said clearly here in Hebrews, that it was because of his faith. As it was his faith that pleased God. Recall that Enoch was the father of Methuselah, who is reported to be the oldest man who ever lived. Because Enoch was his father, there is this brain twister that asks, who is the oldest man who ever lived who died before his father did? Ask that one around and see who gets the right answer. Enoch, of course, left behind quite a legacy. And being the man who God took and took because he was a man of faith. Again, he was not a man of good works or of great personality, but a man of faith. He pleased God because he had the substance of things hoped for, he had the conviction of things unseen. Fathers, can that be said of you? Are you leaving a legacy of faith to your children Will your children say of you that you were a man of faith? It is providential Providential that we would come upon in our study of Hebrews this chapter, chapter 11, on the day we celebrate fathers. As we will see next week, there are all sorts of personalities and circumstances where God's people have expressed true faith. Regarding all who are listed, their actions, their personalities, those could easily condemn them, but their faith is what saved them, and they are to be copied by us all. Fathers, will your children copy your faith and be saved? It is a very important question, and one that is related to what Reverend Lamboy preached last week It is quite fun to do a search about epitaphs, what people who have died or loved ones have set upon the tombstones of a dead loved one It is, after all, the last word in a person's life. It is what can be said about them Bobby Lynn has always loved the one that says, I told you I was sick. She thinks that that fits her quite well I I want you to enjoy these. There are a number of them, but they're just fantastic. This is on the grave of Ezekiel Akel in East Dalehousie Cemetery, Nova Scotia. Here lies Ezekiel Akel, age one hundred two, the good Dyeung. In a Fermont, Maryland Cemetery, here lies an atheist, all dressed up and no place to go. In a London Cemetery, England London England Cemetery. Here lies Anna Mann, M-A-N-N, who lived an old maid, but died an old man, M-A-N-N. In a Riversford, England cemetery, the children of Israel wanted bread, and the Lord sent them manna. Old Clerk Wallace wanted a wife, and the devil sent him Anna. Playing with names here in in New Mexico Cemetery. Here lies Johnny Yeast. Pardon me for not rising. This is in memory of an accident in Uniontown, Pennsylvania. Here lies the body of Jonathan Blake, stepped on the gas instead of the brake. In Silver City, Nevada Cemetery, here lies Butch. We planted him raw. He was quick on the trigger, but slow on the draw. This widow wrote for her husband, sacred to the memory of my husband John Barnes, who died January 3, 1803. His comely young widow, aged 23, has many qualifications of a good wife and yearns to be comforted. From a lawyer's epitaph in England, Sir John Strange, here lies an honest lawyer, and that is strange. From uh Lester Moore, a Wells Fargo Company station agent in Naco, Arizona, in the cowboy days. He was buried at Booth Hill. In the tombstone, Arizona, here lies Lester Moore, four slugs from a 44. No less, no more. In a cemetery at Heartham, England, on the 22nd of June, Jonathan Fiddle went out of tune. From Winslow, Maine, in memory of Basel Wood, departed this life November 2nd, 1837, age 45. Here lies one wood, enclosed in wood, one wood within another. The outer wood is very good. We cannot praise the other. Oh let's see, I'll skip a couple of things. I like this. Okay. Ellen Shannon, who was fatally burned march twenty-first, eighteen seventy, by an explosion of a lamp. filled with R. E. Danfors non-explosive burning fluid. And finally, Harry Estel Smith, Albany, New York, born 1903, died 1942. Looked up the elevator shaft to see if the car was coming on the way down. It was. Now these are fun and yet they are also sobering. What is also sobering is to consider what we are leaving behind, what will be said about us I submit that it does not matter what will be said of us if only we are a person of faith. Recently I was asked to do an outline for a seminar on Christian parenting. And I started off with what it means to live in a Christian marriage, including husbands loving their wives as Christ loved the church. Wives submitting to their husbands, I brought next the topic of infant baptism, marking a child, raising the child as Christian I finished with some practical advice on proper spanking methods, the need to work as a team, the time to choose the right battles, so on. And when I finished, I was quite pleased with myself, perceiving that I had covered what was most important, only to realize there was a glaring omission. All that I planned to say about parenting was the work of the parent and the application of biblical principles with the expectation that if you do it all, then the child's going to come out and be a Christian. When in truth, when all that is said and done, it is faith, it is by faith that we raise our children in Christ, it is by faith that we trust they will be the Lord's. And if it is not done in faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, it will be in vain. Parenting is just an example. We are to be a people of faith in all aspects of our lives. When it comes to who we will marry or who our children will marry, we are to be a people who apply the substance of things hopeful. When we are sick or a loved one is sick, we are to practice having conviction about what is not seen. When someone threatens our livelihood or our well-being, we enact the substance of things hoped for. When the bills are more numerous than our bank account, it is time to trust in what is not seen. When people are unkind to us or we feel alone, it is then that we are to focus on what is hoped for. And when our sin is ever before us and the devil wants us to feel like a constant failure, it is then that what is unseen by faith can be seen. And this sermon cannot end without being reminded that it is not faith in faith that a Christian practices It is faith in God, who embodied himself in the person of Jesus, who leads us to the Father, who ministers to us by the Holy Spirit. And I close with an assignment for you. I assign you to recall an incident when you enacted faith. When you had confidence toward God about what is hoped for, when you had conviction about what is not seen, and God answered favorably, answered your faith favorably. Recall that incident and tell it to somebody today, preferably a father to a child. May it be that people think about, when they think about you, may it be that they think of you as a person of faith. Let us pray. Our Father, it is to you that we collectively give thanks, because we know that any faith we have Any faith is from you. And so with that thanksgiving, may we all take the charge to repeat times in which you have answered our faith, to build up one another that we too might grow in that faith. It is in Jesus' name that we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Faith as Our Responsibility
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I encourage you to turn in your Bibles to Hebrews chapter 11. We're picking up at verse 6. of that chapter. And we actually read through verse 16 for our epistle reading, but we will be going all the way through the chapter this morning. So Hebrews chapter 11, 6 through 40 And as you turn there, I just want to give a word of admonishment. I know, as I said, a number of families are on vacation and some of you come back and so on. I just want to encourage you, admonish you That we do not, as Christians, take vacations from the Lord's Day. I have heard of people who go to church on a regular basis and then go away on vacation and don't go to church. I think that's that's such a tragedy and it's it's great to be as we are traveling, to be in the house of God, wherever that is, and to worship with God's people. So encourage you to do that. I I was encouraged this morning our son Jared and his wife Katie are in Ireland. They are uh there with uh Katie's family enjoying their uh homeland And he sent me a text today of an Anglican church that they attended, and it encouraged my heart that they were in church on the Lord's day. Hebrews chapter 11, starting at verse 6. As a child, I remember looking for Romals. I suppose that losing my biological father early in life was a big factor in wanting role models But I didn't choose just one person I wanted to be like. I chose several. I developed, for instance, a love for the game of football because my grandpa Jorgensen loved to watch it I tried to dress myself with popular clothing and shoes because my older sisters would tell me what the older kids in school were wearing. When I was 13 years old, I recall observing closely how a very popular 16-year-old walked and talked. as he was very popular with the ladies, and I wanted to be popular with the ladies. When God snatched me out of my slew of despond and set me on dry ground with a saving faith in him I've started to look for role models in the Christian faith. I found many, and I am grateful for most of them as they helped me be helped me become a better Christian man. Ultimately, ultimately, that is the purpose of people being listed here in chapter 11 to the Hebrews. Their faith, the way they enacted faith, is a role model for us. Last week we heard of the importance of faith to maintain our place in the kingdom of God so that we might receive that ultimate hope which is heaven. Today we look at the rest of the examples of people of faith after Enoch. And the example of Enoch must be seen as playing a role in the example of Abraham, a man of faith. But first, we are to notice that faith is given a more complete definition in verse 6. Now recall in verse 1 of chapter 11, we heard that faith is the substance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen. In verse 6, that definition is added to by the statement that to please God, a Christian must believe that God is, which is to say that he exists. And even more, he exists as the great I am, and as the I am, he is a rewarder of those who diligently seek him. The rewarder part refers back to what we hope for, which ultimately is forgiveness of sins and then heaven. The diligently seeking him communicates, and hear this, there is personal responsibility when it comes to faith. We have a responsibility. We understood last week that faith is a gift. It is a gift of saving faith. It is a gift of sanctifying faith. But like any other gift, it must be utilized. It must be applied to life situations. Faith given must be enacted by every believer for it to be effective faith, useful faith. That looks like or is practiced by diligently seeking God. Faith enacted is seeking God, and seeking God means calling upon Him, working to know His Word, and applying His Word to our lives. And so that we know what it means to have faith and what it means to diligently seek God, next we are given some more examples of people who lived by faith. The first up, Noah. We know the story of Noah. He was told it was to rain before he knew what rain was. He was told of a flood before any part of the earth had ever flooded. He was told of God's judgment upon the people of the earth, and he believed it. to the point of building a boat so big that it would hold hundreds, maybe thousands of animals of the earth But Noah had a character flop. He was a drinker of alcohol and became drunk to the embarrassment of his sons. Next is Abraham. We read about him this morning. Abraham, who enacted faith in a number of ways. He left his home to follow an earthly path that he had not known before. He believed the promised land would be his before he saw it, and even when he never owned it He believed he would have children, although his advanced age and Sarah's advanced age said differently. He believed he would have many, many descendants, even before he had one. And in verse 16, in verse 16 we learn what Genesis does not tell us Abraham had faith regarding a heavenly reward, which connects him to Enoch For he would have known of a man who pleased God, and that God took that man, allowing Abraham to have faith in a place that is beyond this world. This allowed Abraham to have faith, to offer his only son as a sacrifice for If he went through with it, he believed that God had the ability to resurrect the dead. There seems to be no man until Moses who had faith as Abraham But Abraham was a coward at times. Abraham put the fidelity of his wife in danger twice Abraham publicly offended God twice, and still he was a man of faith. Isaac is listed next, for he had faith in God when he blessed Jacob as the chosen descendant of Abraham. And yet Isaac sinned in the same manner his father did. Jacob is next, as he blessed each of his sons to carry on the promises of God. And yet Jacob, Jacob was a coward and a deceiver. Next was Joseph. Who had faith while imprisoned and while being a slave with the hope of returning to the promised land, even if it was in the form of his own bones. And next, by faith, the parents of Moses raised him with confidence that their son's life would be spared. And that faith became the faith of Moses after he chose to suffer rather than receive the benefits of being a part of the Pharaoh's court. He did this with a faith in the Holy Savior, the preacher tells us. He identified with the coming Christ, both in his suffering and in his hope. By faith, Moses obeyed the practice of the first Passover. By faith, he led Israel up to and through the Red Sea as he watched the army of Pharaoh drown. And yet Moses, Moses, even Moses had moments of doubt, of fear, and even anger toward God. By faith, Joshua led Israel around Jericho seven times, and by faith the people shouted, and at their shout the walls of the city came down, and it was due in part to Rahab. Who gave the spies the knowledge they needed? But Rahab, she was a harlot, a prostitute, an adulterer. Next are the names of some judges who had faith in God, and this hurried listing of them is a hint again that this was not a letter, this was a sermon. Gideon had faith in God as a victor, even though he had to have his concerns verified in really truly demanding ways. Barak was a man of faith in battle, but he was also a man who feared to lead. Samson was a man of faith in God's vengeance, but was also a man of unbridled lust. Jesta is next, for he was a great warrior who had faith in God against great odds, but he was a fool. A fool in promising to sacrifice what he first saw when he returned to war, and what met him was his own daughter. Then there is David and Samuel who have whole books dedicated to their lives in faith, lives in faith, even though Samuel was a very poor father. And David was also a poor father, an adulterer, and a murderer. The one who stopped the mouth of lions is surely Daniel. The ones who quenched fire, escaped the sword, became strong from weakness, turned armies away while bringing the dead back to life. These are likely descriptions of Elijah and Elisha. The remaining ones who suffered are likely the numerous prophets whom God raised up to speak the truth, even though the people would not hear them and even worked, strived to silence them. And even the greatest of these prophets like Elijah and Elisha, even they had times of doubt and of frustration and physical weaknesses. I have balanced all of these who are named in this hall of faith listing I have balanced it with their character flaws because I want to convince you that it was not, and hear this now, it was not their moral character, it was not their mental state that prevented them from enacting faith. Also among this list are landowners and slaves married women and harlots, kings and farmers. So social standing makes no difference when it comes to enacting faith in God. Character flaws, egregious sins, are no factor when it comes to having the substance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen. And it is for all of us who hear my voice to take these examples of faith in all of their situations and in all of their personalities. And in all of their personal struggles, and to know that what each experience what we each experience and and what we each have at our disposal with our own personalities and our own struggles is that we too, we too can enact faith in God in all of our life situations. And this is this is where I must linger. Because it is important for each of us who say we believe. That we take responsibility to enact the faith we have been given in all of our life circumstances. I feel like I need to convince you of that. I wonder if you can name this next man I describe. While most preachers and teachers speak of his dramatic conversion to believe the gospel Even after his conversion, he doubted that he had saving faith. He had many disputes with both his friends and enemies. Many of which divided his friendships. When it came to siding politically with the poor versus the rich, he sided with the rich. When he mocked his fellow Christian ministers for their varied theological perspectives, he did so with vulgar language. In his old age, he is described as being cantankerous, while he struggled with depression and anxiety, which caused him to wonder if God was displeased with him Do you know his name yet? Who am I describing? I am describing Martin Luther. The great reformer, who brought the heart of the gospel back to the church. He was the man Who had faith to stand up to false teachers and false doctrines that took people away from the gospel. His ministry over the years abound with blessings But he struggled with faith up to the end of his days. You see, even the greatest of faithful men struggle with faith I wonder if you can name this next woman described. She is known as one of the most giving human beings that has ever lived. She cared for the least of these, as Jesus called them. And yet after her death Some personal letters were found that showed a very different woman than everyone thought she was. She frequently wrote of loneliness. Of not hearing God, of personal hypocrisy, and doubts of her own faith Here is one example. She wrote, quote, darkness is such that I really do not see, either with my mind nor with my reason. The place of God in my soul. It is blank. There is no God in me. When the pain of longing is so great, I just long and long for God. The torture and pain I can't explain. In another letter she confessed that That she needed prayer because certain moments heaven meant nothing to her. Do you have her name? She is best known as Mother Teresa. How can a woman experience and then endure the depth of human suffering while doubting her own beliefs, beliefs that moved her in the first place to care for the least among us? Her faith may have wavered, but her compassion never did. Again, I wonder if you can name this next man. who is considered one of the greatest preachers of the gospel. In one sermon he said, quote, I think when a man says, I never doubt, it is quite time for us to doubt him. It is quite time for us to begin to say, ah, poor soul. I am afraid you are not on that road at all. For if you were, you would see so many things in yourself and so much glory in Christ, more than you deserve. That you would be so much ashamed of yourself. End quote. In another sermon, he explained that even the strongest of believers may face seasons of depression. Being stripped of joy by faith, wounded. He said, quote, the strong are not always vigorous, the wise not always ready. The brave not always courageous, the joyous not always happy. The man who preached these words was Charles Spurgeon. who was called the Prince of Preachers. Spurgeon preached in London, England, in the middle of the nineteenth century to several thousand parishioners each Sunday, and his sermons were being printed and sent around the world. But Spurgeon did not preach about struggling faith in the midst of trials from the outside looking in. He experienced struggles firsthand. He experienced it in personal relationships when toward the end of his life he went through what is called the downgrade controversy. Which is when Christian ministers were downgrading or compromising essential Christian doctrine for what they thought was popular. Anybody do that today? Because of the direction of this Baptist Union, Spurgeon withdrew himself from the union, and that sparked betrayal of many of his closest friends, including 80 alumni from his own pastor's college. And the deepest dagger was when his own brother voted publicly to censor him. Spurgeon also wrestled with deep depression. Some depression was brought on by life circumstances, such as during a worship service at Surrey Hall. There were 12,000 people gathered to hear him preach, and 10,000 outside in the garden trying to get in. And shortly after the service got underway, some cruel men shouted, fire, and panic ensued. The result was seven people dead and 28 hospitalized with serious injuries. That haunted him the rest of his life. Depression was also a result of Spurgeon's many physical illnesses. He suffered with gout that caused him multiple occasions of great pain and weeks being laid up in bed suffering. He also suffered from Bright's disease, which was a chronic inflammation of the kidneys, and that too caused him great pain. Spurgeon wrote to several friends doubting words, questioning whether he could go on living because the pain was so great. And what is striking about Spurgeon is that with all of his suffering in body and spirit, while being aware of his weakness of faith When he would come out of his lingering times of suffering, he would look back with much thankfulness. At one time he wrote, It would be a very sharp and trying experience to me to think that I have an affliction which God never sent me That the bitter cup was never filled by his hand, that my trials were never measured out by him, nor sent to me by his arrangement of their weight and quantity. To see his affliction as coming from God is a trust in God that very few have. It does not match with any of our definitions of God being loving, but Spurgeon saw it as the opposite. In another place, he said this: I am afraid that all of the grace that I have got of my comfortable and easy times and happy hours might almost lie on a penny. But the good that I have received from my sorrows and pains and griefs is altogether incalculable. Affliction is the best bit of furniture in my house. It is the best book in a minister's library. And let us say together, wow, to such faith, especially faith that comes from suffering. Beloved, what I have tried to get at is what I believe the preacher to the Hebrews is striving for. He wants us to see that faith A living and applicable faith in God is available to all of us. It has been given to us by God and then placed before us as our responsibility to enact in our lives. Which means in the moments of our lives that are most difficult, we can believe That God will deliver us, even when the devil whispers to believe the opposite, even when circumstances around us scream for us to disbelieve. We are to see that the past sins of a man or a woman does not dictate how faith in God can lead us forward. Our applied faith in God does not need to be thwarted by our social or economic status. Even an awareness of the weaknesses of our character, to apply faith, will not stop faith from being victorious And the end victory for all of us, for the saints of the Old Testament, for the saints of the new, is all the same. It is to go to a place that Jesus has prepared for us. So let us go there, by grace, through faith. Let us pray. Our Father, we do thank you for the gift of faith, and we embrace the responsibility for each of us to live in it, to enact it, to practice it. even in life's most difficult circumstances. Holy Spirit, we welcome your leading, guide us, strengthen us. May we hold on to that faith all our days. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Encouraging Chastisement
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: All my God is all In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated and turn in your Bibles to Hebrews chapter 12. Hebrews chapter 12, covering verse 1 through 13 Quick story, back in 2006, Bobby Lynn and I were picking up our oldest son Jared from a recruiting trip to Westchester University. One of the events before leaving campus was the head coach speaking to the parents of the recruits. As the coach spoke, he talked about toughness and hard work, overcoming the odds and the value of winning. When he was finished, I said to Bobby Lynn, I want to play for this guy. I was inspired, I was emotionally and physically motivated, I wanted to strap on the gear and play again That's what a good coach does. He motivates his players to go beyond themselves. When I was coaching the Crusaders, for those of you who don't know what that is, it was a football program that I helped start. consisted of either homeschool students or Christian school students that didn't have a football team. And I soon noticed that something was missing in these boys that first year They were afraid. They lacked courage. They were afraid, most of them, to hit another player or to be hit by another player. It could be seen in them being unwilling to run their hardest down the field and to tackle an opponent. In tackling drills, they would turn and received the blow on the side of their bodies rather than the forefront of their forehead and squared shoulders At first I didn't know what to do. I was very confused. You see, in the Jorgensen household, tackling was a fundamental skill of survival. I played tackle football in the house and in the yard with my boys hundreds of times, and I thought every Christian father did that. To overcome this fear in these young men, I had to come up with some inspired coach speech myself. And so I told the players of the story of Hugh Latimer and Nicholas Ridley, a story I repeated to you several sermons ago. A part of that story of martyrdom during the reign of Bloody Mary was when they were on their way to be burned at the stake for believing and preaching the gospel. Latimer told Ridley, quote, play the man, Master Ridley, and we shall this day light such a candle by God's grace in England as I trust shall never be put out. The first part of that statement, play the man. That was earlier said to the martyr named Polycarp A second century Christian bishop who, when he was faced with his own martyrdom, heard that phrase by the Holy Spirit, telling him to face his martyrdom by playing the man. And that phrase, play the man, has biblical connotations and is actually used in the King James Version when Joab and his brother Abishai In the book of 2 Samuel, when they are surrounded by Syrians and Ammonites, Joab says to his brother, Be of good courage, let us play the man for our people. The meaning then was to be a man of courage, facing fear head on Now, when we take our understanding of the man and place Jesus in that picture who embraced being called the Son of Man, We can see that we are to play the man means to us that we are to imitate Jesus when we face our fears, when we face adversity. So after I explained this to my players, the phrase became a rallying cry when I would see them give in to fear. I would yell to them, play the man! Our team huddles would be broken with that chant, play the man on three, one, two, three, play the man. All was done so that young men would learn to be courageous men. And I have hoped and prayed that the phrase play the man reminds them to this day and to the rest of their days what it means to live fearlessly for Christ. All of this to say what the Hebrew preacher is doing in the beginning of chapter 12 is a follow-up to what he did in chapter 11, where he set before us people of faith to be imitated. And we learned that we too can have faith just as those listed had faith. We can live too by faith And we can live by faith in every life situation, regardless of our personal failings, regardless of our personal struggles. In verse 1 of chapter 12, what we are seeing is an encouragement to do just that This verse, chapter 12, verse 1, is both poetic and inspiring. It allows us to view saints around us, seeing us, watching us, and saying, we did it. Now you do it. Live by faith. The cheering is not only for us to have faith all the way to heaven, but to have faith to overcome sin. Sin that is repeated and thus sin that pulls us down into discouragement. This says to us that we not only can have faith all the way to heaven But we can also overcome sins, sins that once we thought were always going to be a part of us. And finally the verse reminds us That we are not in a marathon. I'm sorry, that we are in a marathon, not in a sprint. Therefore, we need endurance in order to finish well. Verse 2 is a most helpful reminder that Jesus is responsible for the faith that we have and that he started it and he finishes it. And we say, thanks be to God. Thanks be to God that our salvation is not dependent solely on us, but is dependent upon what Jesus did and continues to do for us. What is to be motivation for us is to continue in faith while suffering in this life. And that our motivation comes from Jesus, who endured the cross of shame, doing it so that joy could come after. Doing it so that after the cross, after the shame, there is joy forevermore. And that is what we are to do as well. Verses 3 and 4 make the point of verse 2 more plainly, as we who suffer physically, or maybe we suffer socially by the scoffing of others. must not become weary from the scoffing, but realize that Jesus suffered so much more, even to the point of bloodshed. Jesus did it for our sins, and as our example we are to do it also for our sins, that we would be willing to resist sin to the point of bloodshed Verses 5 through 8 put suffering into perspective and are in line with what we read from the great preacher Charles Spurgeon. You remember last week Recall that for Spurgeon, it was important for him to understand that his afflictions, all of them, all of them, as coming from God. For he saw how much his faith had been strengthened because of those afflictions. And here the preacher gives us the perspective of seeing our sufferings as from God. For God is our Father and we are his sons. Although I have stated the following Before I recognize the need to address it here again, the idea of sonship, referring to both genders. And by the way, I take a detour off of my detour, to note that the idea that there are more than two genders is absolutely and positively absurd. And evidence that our culture has gone off the rails and is no more a culture but a tabloid magazine giving attention only to the salacious and the absurd. But I digress. Back to our original detour. All females are to understand themselves as sons in the kingdom of God. And that it is used as an identity as sons, pointing to the fact that God makes all of his children inheritors of his kingdom. And because sons, according to the law, were inheritors, he refers to all of us, male and female, as his sons, inheritors. Remember that in Christ there is neither male nor female when it comes to eternal salvation. So both male and female are to see themselves as inheritors, sons. In the verses we are examining here, the idea of us being sons is in the context Of God our Father, and it does refer to us as inheritors, but also in the fact that he's rebuking us for sin. And as a father of five sons, I certainly understand why the title sons goes beyond being inheritors. I know for certain that I did not chasten my one daughter near as much as I chastened all of my five sons. I recognize that my simple or my sample is small when it comes to raising daughters, but I also know how much foolishness is wrapped up in the heart of a young boy Boys repeat the same sins over and over, expecting a different outcome each time. Boys let their flesh lead them time and again And personally, I saw it was my responsibility before God to spank their foolishness out of them so that they learn to say no to their impulses. If I did not chasten them as the book of Proverbs warns, I would have been leaving them to themselves, to their own discipline, which was no discipline. And according to Proverbs, such a parenting of leaving a child to himself is actually child abuse. Now I know the world, the devil, says differently, child abuse to the world, and the devil is staking a child. But what does God say? From Proverbs 29. The rod of reproof gives wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother. As Christians, we are to trust the Word of God as a double-edged sword. We must resist a lost and dying world that tells us that a child is innocent at heart. And that a child is good at heart when we know, whether born to a Christian home or a non-Christian home, the child is under the curse of Adam. The child needs a savior The child needs Jesus to give it a new heart. Some parents use timeouts to discipline a child. The timeouts can be leaving a child to himself. For it is not chastening the child so that the child is humbled and therefore teachable. Oftentimes parents give their children timeouts because they just want peace and quiet in the home. But disturbing the peace can be part of a lesson for a child. One of the charted punishable offenses in our home was a child taking peace out of the home. It was a spakeable offense to disturb the peace of the home. So that when a child did so by Starting a fight with a brother, hurting a brother, taking from a brother. We would chasten and then require the guilty party to apologize to everyone for disturbing the peace of the home. Leaving a child to himself does not teach the child anything about taking responsibility for one's actions and the results of those actions. From Proverbs 13. Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him Notice that word diligent. Discipline takes diligence. All parents have witnessed foolishness in their child and are aware that when they witness this, there is a choice to be made. When said foolishness is witnessed, you can either ignore it and again leave the child to himself Or you can address the foolishness, getting up out of your comfortable chair and discipline the child. But that discipline takes energy. For it to be done properly, you need to bring the child under control, then teach the child why his behavior is wrong. And then just discipline the child to bring him back under your authority, and then follow through with proper apologies and then praying with the child. All of that takes diligence. And let us be honest, that it is much easier to ignore the behavior of a child or freak out as if the world is coming to an end. And freaking out teaches the child that you yourself have self-control issues. From Proverbs 23. Do not withhold discipline from a child. If you strike him with a rod, he will not die. If you strike him with a rod, you will save his soul from Sha'ol. Now this lesson is to help us see that disciplining a child has spiritual and then eternal implications. It helps us step back and see that discipline is not just in the moment. It's not just for the moment. It is for eternity. And consider this, parents, what you do not help your child learn when he or she is young, God will have to teach when he or she is older, and those lessons are much harder. Because we are both body and spirit, bodily discipline has spiritual ramifications. And it works both ways. When bodily discipline is abusive, the spirit of a child is broken and damaged. When bodily discipline is done properly, which is teaching and praying, while disciplining, a child's spirit is strengthened and matured Remember that these words come from God, who practices the same principles, not allowing his children to stay in their sin, but instead he chastens them. Those he loves, he chastens. He's working to save their souls, our souls, from eternal death. Going down to verse 8. The truth of verse 8 is the other side of the chastening Which points out that a person not being chastened is not a legitimate son of God and therefore left to his own outcome. We may look to persons who lead non-chastened lives and be tempted to be jealous of them. But we are jealous only if we do not see that chastening is a loving act of God. Verses 9 through 13 explain what I have been trying to do, which is to compare earthly parenting to the parenting of our Heavenly Father. And so we go back. Let us go back and look at each of those proverbs that we applied to earthly parenting and see through how God the Father parents us. Again, from Proverbs 29, the rod and reproof give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother. God does not leave us Christians to ourselves. When He does leave humanity to itself, we destroy ourselves. Men exchange their passions for other men and women for other women when we are left to ourselves. Human beings left to themselves become like devils, and that devils devour each other. I saw a headline this past week of a quote from a Hollywood producer. He claims this, quote, humanity is an expletive disaster, an expletive disaster, end quote. The Bible agrees. And humanity does bring shame to God as our creator. And yet he so loved us that he sent his son. And we who follow his son believe him to be the Savior and God, and are not left to ourselves, but we are chastened. And when we receive such chastening, we are given wisdom. And hope for eternity. Again from Proverbs 13. Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him. God does not hate us. And so God does not spare the rod upon us as needed. And God is diligent at disciplining us. He is not lazy like we are lazy. He does not grow tired or weary so that he would ever overlook a transgression that we need to confess, that we need to turn away from The simple saying that God loves us so much that he will not let us stay the way we are is true. And we are to be thankful for it and motivated by it so that we see the purpose of his chastening and we desire to grow in grace from it. Again from Proverbs twenty-three. Do not withhold discipline from a child. If you strike him with a rod, he will not die. If you strike him with a rod, you will save his soul from Shaol. The chastening of God is truly and ultimately about receiving a heavenly reward. The preacher to the Hebrews has said as much, and so as this proverb presents it, withholding the rod is to withhold heaven, and God will not do that to us. He wants us to receive our heavenly reward. And to do so, we are to receive his chastening as it is truly for our eternal good Now I anticipate that as you've heard my words and we've walked through these verses, that you're wondering what parts of your lives God is chastening you in, even now. And as I believe Spurgeon, his words have been hanging in my heart and mind this week, to believe that every struggle in our lives is from God. Knowing that he wants to mold us and make us better than we are, certainly. But for the sake of heaven, knowing that, well, that gives me greater faith. Not thinking the devil's to blame, not thinking someone else is to blame, but understanding whatever we're struggling in, it's God's chastening hand. And he's using it to make us like him. That's a gift to understand. I started by saying that the phrase play the man is used to motivate us to have courage to practice faith. We can end by recognizing that to properly receive the chastening of God, we must also play the man. We must play the man for receiving chastisement effectively. We must have courage that whatever God uses to chasten us, it is necessary. And we are to receive it by faith. And so we say, let us play the man. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God, we thank you for these encouraging words to have the confidence that what we go through That what we suffer in is from you. And that you are using it to make us like your son. Increase our faith all the more to know that whatever we are in, you are there with us. You are our Father, and you are guiding us and chastening to make us again like your Son Increase our faith all the more we ask in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: After Chastisement
sermons.speaker: Deacon Ricky McCarl
sermons.text: Let us pray. May the words of my mouth and the meditation of all our hearts be acceptable and pleasing in thy sight, our rock and our redeemer. In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. Amen. My wife and I sometimes keep our niece at our home for extended periods of time. It gives her mother a break and thus an opportunity to practice parenting for a long time. little bit. It's also lots of fun to have small children around. One time we had her for an extended period of time and I noticed that she had recently learned some bad habits from her older sister. One of the habits that I disliked greatly was that she had started to spit. I personally believe that young ladies should not do that. But what irritated me more was that when she we had all sat down for dinner, she decided This was unacceptable behavior, and I made sure that she knew that it would not be tolerated in my home She doesn't spit at Cool Cool's house. That's what she calls me. A few months later I noticed that she did it at another relative's house. She spit on the floor. And I fussed her, and the relative and I I entered into a debate about sending mixed signals to my niece. He said that others encouraged it, finding it cute, so it would be confusing for me to fuss her over it I disagreed and believe firmly that what my young niece will learn at the very least is that while others might approve, her uncle does not. She has learned what I expect of one of my nieces, and she diligently works to be obedient, though not always perfectly. My ultimate goal with all of my nieces and nephews is that they might grow up to know Christ and what's expected of them, not only as my nieces and nephews, but as children of the Father. That's why I chastise them, and it's why he chastises us. Last week we established that fathers who love their children chastise them. We also learned that the reason for the chastisement is so that they might learn how they are to behave as Christians. Fathers, or in my case, cookools, don't discipline their children because they dislike them or enjoy inflicting pain, but rather do so for the good of the child. Chastisement teaches them how they are to live and behave as sons and daughters of their fathers. Discipline is the result of a godly love. This is why God disciplines us, not because he enjoys punishing people or because he has some sort of hatred for his children. But rather he disciplines his children so that they might learn how to behave and live as sons and ultimately attain heavenly peace. This morning, the preacher to the Hebrews is going to teach us what that looks like in our daily lives as sons of God Turn with me to Hebrews chapter twelve, and we will be starting in the fourteenth verse. In verse 14, the preacher to the Hebrews begins with an exhortation, imploring the Hebrew Christians to live in peace and to pursue holiness. He goes on to tell them to make sure that no one fails to seek grace, and that no root of bitterness might come up among them. He wants them to avoid sexual immorality and to not be ungodly like Esau. All of these things are directly related to what the preacher said in the previous verses about chastisement. This is how our Father wants us to conduct ourselves as sons of the living God. This is why God disciplines us, so that we might learn to do these things. And these are the things that our Father expects from us. Christians are to live in peace. Just like Jesus said, Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the sons of God. God does not wish for us to quarrel with others. He does not wish for us to fight andor bicker. He wants us to live in peace with everyone. Christians are to pursue holiness. God wants us to be what we have been declared to be. For if we live in peace with others and strive for holiness, we will see the Lord. Christians are also to seek grace and to see it that others seek it too. We are our brother's keeper. And finally, we are not to be sexually immoral and ungodly, because we are different from the rest of the world. We have been bought with the precious blood of Christ and set free from those things. But this isn't how the world lives. And in fact, the world thinks living this way is backwards and unenlightened The world teaches that we should dislike the other and treat them with scorn. It teaches them that we should pursue individuality and personal freedom, oftentimes at the expense of holiness. Whatever makes you happy, they say. Just follow your heart. Never mind that true happiness is found in the law of the Lord, or that the heart is desperately wicked and deceitful above all things. The world teaches that sexual immorality is not only okay, but that's how real men behave. Never mind that true virtue is found in honoring women instead of using them. Or the fact that sexual morality is bad both for physical and spiritual health. The world teaches that Sexuality is for our own gratification, but it's actually so that we might be fruitful and multiply, and so we can enjoy our marriage and a family. So should the preacher to the Hebrews not encourage such behaviors, since it sends conflicting messages with what the world says, like me telling my young niece not to spit? Or should we be held to a higher standard? The answer is clear. The Father chastises those whom he loves, so that they might learn how to behave the way that he expects. Character matters, and despite what the world says, God has given us the model to live by. His name is Jesus Christ. But all of this comes with a warning. Don't be like Esau The preacher to the Hebrews is reiterating his warnings from previous chapters, specifically Hebrews 6, 4-8 and 10, 26-31. He says, don't be ungodly like Esau and sell your birthright for a single meal. Now the Hebrews would have immediately known what the preacher was talking about. Esau was Isaac's oldest brother, or Isaac's oldest son. son and Jacob, later Israel the younger. Esau, due to his place in his family, was set to inherit everything from Isaac. We aren't just talking about worldly goods and inheritance. He was to inherit all the covenant promises and blessings given to his grandfather and father. But Esau was worldly and didn't care about such things. All he wanted was a meal. And so his younger brother Jacob made a deal with him. Jacob would provide him with a meal, and Esau would hand over his birthright. So Esau not caring about all that he was to inherit, gave Jacob everything for a simple meal. When it came time for the birthright to be given, Jacob entered into some trickery and inherited what was supposed to be given to Esau. Esau realizes the error, but it was too late. And all that God had promised to Abraham and Isaac went to Jacob. No tears of repentance could change what had happened. It was in the past. Likewise, for us, there is always a real and great danger looming that we might put ourselves in similar positions The preacher to the Hebrews makes it clear that we are to avoid that at all costs. How? By making sure that we all seek to obtain God's grace. Now there are people in every church who are just along for the ride, who enjoy being around God's people because perhaps they are neat and tidy, clean-cut as it were. Perhaps they like the church for its perceived political views, whatever they might be, or perhaps because they are looking for some social outlet that encourages them to be better people. These are people who experience the fringe benefits of the gospel and God's grace, but have never done business with Jesus. They have not sought out and truly obtained the grace of God. They just go through the motions and have never been changed by the undeserved grace that God gives and changes us from the inside out. These people are always in a great danger. There are people who have not taken seriously the call of God on their lives. And it would be easy for these people to give up the covenant promises that God freely gives us for something worldly and sinful when it comes along. If that describes you, it's not too late. Gonna go back to my Baptist roots here. There comes a time when the opportunity to receive grace passes. Like Esau, there won't be any chance for tears or repentance because the chance that chance has come and gone. Perhaps you missed out because you were too busy loving the world, or perhaps you never saw it as important in your life. Regardless if that's you today, the chance has not yet passed. All you must do is believe the gospel and live out your baptisms in true faith and repentance. But if that's not who you are, if you have received God's grace and continue to do so in your daily lives, then you have a responsibility to see to it that everyone receives God's grace. The command is, let us make disciples, teaching them to obey all the things that I have commanded. If we fail to do this, if we fail to be about the business of showing people the gracious love of God, then there is, as the preacher to the Hebrews says in verse 15 A real danger that a root of bitterness might rise up causing trouble and defilement I had the unfortunate opportunity to witness this the f um the first church I served. Um I was the youth pastor there And a man and his wife started attending our church and had shared with the pastor that he had a difficult time finding a church where he fit in. That's kind of a red flag, I think. So he thought he would give that church a try and see what it was like, and time went on and some off-putting things were said, some strange and peculiar theological statements were made and ignored. And after a while, these things started to take a more sinister turn, and he began to try and turn the elders of the church against one another. He made some false accusations against the pastor and some of the people the other elders, and he started to wreak havoc in the church He began to get a following, people who he could get on his side, and it got really ugly after that. Relationships were damaged and people got hurt along the way. A root of bitterness had sprung up. And this is always a danger, and we must guard against it by diligently making sure that all of those around us have obtained the grace of God by preaching the gospel. But these things aren't works that earn us favor with God. Remember that these things flow out of God's discipline of us, and that God disciplines us because He loves us already. Discipline is actually an act of grace. When we do these things, it's not because that's how you work your way to God, but rather how God's love changes our lives. All of this was revolutionary in the 1500s. These truths were rediscovered by a German monk named Martin Luther, and they made. in all the way to England through our Archbishop Thomas Cranmer and down through him to us. The reformers realized that the medieval church had it all wrong You don't practice obedience to earn God's love. Obedience flows from God's love and is the practical application of grace in our life. And it's lived out in faith in Jesus Christ. The Roman Church had been teaching that it was impossible to earn God's love without really good works. The people were beat down and oppressed by their own sinfulness, and obedience was ironic. Ironically, in short supply. I mean, why try if it's impossible, right? But the reformers discovered that's not how the Bible works. That's not what the Bible teaches. Instead, the Bible teaches that God gives us grace freely, and that it is obtained through faith in Jesus Christ alone. It is out of a grateful heart that obedience flows. So the preacher to the Hebrews is explaining that one, God loves us. Two, that because of the love of God, he disciplines us. And three, that these things Peace, holiness, sexual purity, and a grateful heart come from that loving discipline. Obedience and faithfulness are what Christians are called to do, and we must guard against any Esau-like tendencies in our own lives. The preacher continues to encourage his readers to persevere in peace and holiness in verse 22, not with a warning like before. But rather with a reminder of all the good things we have in Christ. He writes, But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the innumerable angels in feastal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the Judge of all, And to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks better word than the blood of Abel. Where are all all of these things? Where is the city of God? Where are the angels in feastal gathering? Where do we find all of this wonderful stuff? Here. Right here in this gathering of God's covenant people. This is a foretaste of what is yet to come. This is just a sampling of what we will see when Christ returns. When we come together as the church, we are surrounded by the heavenly host. We come into the very real presence of the living God and His Son Jesus Christ. We receive the benefits of His grace and are transformed with grateful hearts. We would never turn back to the world. The world only gives us anger and hatred. It gives us unholy desires and wickedness. It encourages sexual immorality and bitterness. As we go from work and interact with people on a daily basis, I am constantly reminded of the fact that the only time I ever find true peace and holiness in this crazy world is when I come here to worship with you fine people. For about two hours every week, I am surrounded by all of these things and the preacher that the preacher mentions. But also I'm surrounded with like-minded people who strive to worship God in spirit and in truth. The world doesn't agree with my values, my morals, or my worldview. In fact, they despise it But when I come here, I find what the preacher to the Hebrews is talking about. For two hours each week, we leave the world together as a body of like-minded people.
