And we enter into the very presence of the Holy Trinity, and we become just a little more like Jesus and less like the world around us. This is why the preacher to the Hebrews exhorts us not to forsake the coming together of the brethren. It's why he reminds us of all the wonderful things we have in Christ and his church. It is through the preaching of the Word, the right administration of the sacraments, and godly discipline that we are changed, transformed, and made into Christ's image. It is here and only here where you will be exhorted to seek peace and holiness, to be reminded, to not be sexually immoral and unholy like Esau. The whole reason God disciplines us, the whole reason he disciplines his sons, is so that they might learn how they are to behave as a redeemed people. The world says that this is in conflict, that it violates our freedom, and that it is restrictive and unhealthy. But God is the arbitrator of what is freedom and what is healthy. And his people learn that this is what he expects from them. And we give thanks because we have been called out of the old, sinful, and dead world into a new and better world with a new and better promise. So let us give thanks for the fact that God loves us enough to discipline us. Let us give thanks for His love and grace in all things and diligently seek to obtain it. Let us strive to be at peace with everyone and live lives of holiness each and every day. And let us never be like Esau, giving up our birthrights for temporary things of the world. But instead let us give thanks for all of God's goodness and loving kindness and all the blessings of this life. Let us pray. Our Father, we do thank you for your chastising hand. We are mindful of your love for us and that your desire is for us to grow in faith and obedience. Help us, Lord, to fight the good fight, to run the race, and to attain the prize. Make us, we humbly beseech thee, to be obedient and faithful in all things, and to continually remind us of your grace. Let us not be unholy like Esau, but help us rather to seek peace and live holy lives, living faithfully in your grace until the last day We pray this all in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. And open your Bibles to Hebrews chapter 12. Hebrews chapter 12, our epistle reading. You'll want to follow along. A couple of notes need to be underlined before we get to the specific verses that we are covering today First, we need to remember that the chapters and verses placed upon Scripture are man-made, and therefore they are fallible. Now that's from the New King James Version. The NIV does not translate it that way. The translations vary from having grace to living thankfully. And we are to live in grace in that we give grace to others And thus we live as a person who both has grace and gives grace by the same measure. Then I realize that I have that that to have been given grace and to give grace to others by the same measure, that's asking quite a lot. But that is the standard. The need for brotherly love next stretches to a warning against the sin of covetousness. That's verse 5. And we shouldn't see this stretching too far. For in St. James's letter, you will remember, he makes the point that when when there is quarreling among the brethren, among Christians Many times the problem is jealousy. We want the spouse or or the job or the children or the house. or the spiritual gifts that someone else has, and when we can't get what we want, we take it out on one another. The simple response against the temptation to covet is to be thankful for what you have and let God be enough for you. Next comes the quote from Psalm 118, and I hope you see it as a defiant proclamation against the devil and against our own personal doubts. The Lord is indeed our helper. Because he is my helper, I will indeed not fear. I will not fear because I have reason that if God is my helper, man can do nothing to me that cannot be overcome. And so we finish through our verses this morning. And I want to come back then to the point made from verse 25. That point, which is that no person should refuse God in what he says. The Hebrew preacher Again, has us looking to Israel as a model of failure for not wanting God to speak to them And it should be pointed out that the generation that asked God not to speak to them audibly, but only through Moses They robbed. They stole from generations after them that would have well benefited from hearing God's voice. It was a selfish and foolish request to fear God in such a manner that they would rather not hear him at all. But let us examine how something like that happens. How do you get there? Consider the history of the Episcopal Church in the United States of America, who just this past month were meeting for their general council and they were addressing They were addressing, changing the prayer book to be gender neutral, so that God is neither referred to as a male nor a female. How did they drift so far from where they started Could their downfall have started in 1784 when Samuel Seabury of Connecticut was consecrated to be bishop in America by Scottish bishops? Who were at political odds with England's bishops making the consecration invalid according to the Church of England? Could it have started then? Little rebellion Well, no. No, that was rectified when Samuel Provost of New York was consecrated as Bishop to America by the Church of England in 1787. All that officially occurs within the Episcopal Church in the United States after 1787 reveals a faithful expression of Christian truth and love. They started to ordain black men to the priesthood. The Chicago Lambeth Quadrilateral was adopted, making the Holy Scriptures the final authority of the church. And the creeds, their statement of faith. Next came the 1928 prayer book, which is a faithful expression of the Christian church And then the 1940 hymnal, which is considered one of the greatest hymnal achievements in all of Christendom. It was not until 1974 that the Episcopal Church moved away from its Christian heritage by ordaining women into the priesthood. They did so despite nearly two millennium of history before them that believed the priesthood was God's call only upon men. They were able to justify such a massive shift in direction because they started to believe the educated higher critics That started to examine the Bible as a 20th century text rather than a first century text. Because a first century text doesn't have proof required for validating what was required for a 20th century text. Scholars, and we'll say so-called, began to question the authority of much of the Bible and concluded that such letters as 1 Timothy where it clearly forbids women to have leadership over men. They conclude that that could not have been written by Paul And therefore, it no longer has apostolic authority. And therefore, Paul's instruction not to have women as leaders in the church thrown out. All other references to men as leaders in the church only are explained as prejudicial for the times, and since we live in a much more enlightened time, so they believe about themselves. We can excuse those Bible verses as well. So when certain passages of Scripture are erased, And others reinterpreted or just plain ignored due to prejudice, the church could then say that women can be ordained in the priesthood. But women being ordained to the priesthood is not the problem. No, the problem is not wanting God to speak anymore. The problem is not wanting to hear God's voice. And when you don't want to hear God speak, something has to fill the void. What follows after women's ordination is truly a slippery slope. After women are ordained in the Episcopal Church in America, a new prayer book is now adopted. A prayer book that is much weaker and effeminate in its language against sin and against the devil. It is a prayer book that was never recognized as usable by any other official Anglican body outside the Episcopal Church. Again, God's voice muzzled. Sadly, there are some ACNA churches using this prayer book today, and they should not be. What follows next was the non-disciplining of Bishop Spong, spelled S-P-O-N-G. Bishop Spong openly taught from 1979 to the year 2000 that understanding God as Christians have done for centuries is meaningless to the modern mind. He denied that Jesus was God, he denied any concept of creation, he denied the virgin birth, he denied miracles of the New Testament, and he viewed the idea of Jesus being sacrificed for sin as barbaric. All in all, he rejected God speaking. He rejected God's voice. And yet, with such teachings being contrary to the essential doctrines that make the church the church. Spong was never charged for heresy. He was never censored by the Episcopal Church. The bottom of the slope gets faster. When in 2003 an openly gay man was ordained to serve as a bishop in the Episcopal Church in the Diocese of New Hampshire, God's voice ignored. And this brings us to today when we have the church debating whether God should be called Father anymore Some have even joked that the Episcopal Church in America is going to vote next whether to remove any belief regarding the Trinity from their worship so that Muslims can feel more welcome. That joke sounds more likely to happen with each decision made by the church. And why did all of this happen? It happened because people didn't want to hear God speak. And when we request not to hear God's voice, Something must fill the void. And what usually fills the void is our own voice, or a voice that the devil has inspired. Consider how much God has spoken to us today. Examine yourself, inquiring if you plan to heed what God has said. With the summary of the law read, God has said for you to love him with all of your heart and to love your neighbor as yourself. Did you hear it as God's voice You have heard from the preacher to the Hebrews to continue in brotherly love, to entertain strangers. To remember prisoners who are suffering unjustly, to honor the marriage bed, and to not covet. Are you committed to obeying these instructions as God's word to you? If the latter, I'm sorry, if yes Then you want God to speak. And if no, then you'll ask God, just like the Israelites, to be silent If the latter is the case, then you are warned here this morning, just as the first audience to this sermon was warned. If you do not obey God's word, you will not hear God's most important words. Well done, good and faithful servant, enter into your rest. Please be warned that those words you will want to hear. Let's hear it again. Do not refuse him who has spoken. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God We have heard the warning. We have heard it read. We have heard it preached. And now it is up to each of us individually. We confess that. We are responsible Father, give us the strength, the constitution, the wisdom, the will to hear your word at all times. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: We All Submit
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. May be seated. Please turn in your Bibles to Hebrews chapter 13. Well benefit by following along. Hebrews chapter 13, starting at verse 7. Now the main point of this letter to the Hebrews which we are treating as a sermon, is a warning against apostasy. And that point is pretty much concluded at the end of chapter 12 However, we noted a connection between having grace, which is receiving it and giving it in the same measure Two Christians needing to love one another. And then that moved us into how we treat strangers, and then how we treat the prisoner. How we treat the marital bed, and then the warning against covetousness. The majority of chapter 13 is a listing of several instructions the author wants to get in before the epistle ends. It could be that the entirety of chapter 1 through 12 is the sermon And the closing remarks of chapter 13 are what makes it a letter. So we pick up at verse 7 of chapter 13. Now in Hebrews chapter 2, verse 3, the preacher gives a passing reference To the preachers who first brought the gospel to these Jewish Christians, it is then likely that the instruction for these Christians to remember those who ruled over them. While considering the outcome of their conduct, that that is referring to the first gospel preachers that they heard These first men may or not be with them, for they may have passed on as in died, or they may have moved on and preached elsewhere. Their conduct, to be exemplified, it may have been that they were faithful to the end of their days, believing the gospel Or that they lived godly lives and that was to be followed and that was to be imitated. Verse 8. Here is a clear statement of faith that contains the eternal nature of Jesus And the proclaiming that Jesus was not a new addition to the Old Testament covenant, but was always in the covenant that God made with Abraham and to Abraham's descendants. And so I say it again, as boldly as I can, the Christian faith and the Jewish faith are not two covenants. They are one. Jesus is the fulfillment of all that was promised to the Jews and then the Gentiles. Faith in Jesus is true Judaism. In that he is the one that God pointed to from the beginning. He is the seed that was to crush the serpent's head. He is the Melchizedek. He is the offerings, all of them. He is the message of the prophets, the one in whom all who have a saving faith believe in. Teachers and preachers and lay people who say there are two covenants are misunderstanding the gospel. And such teaching contributes to the ignoring of the Old Testament law known as antinomianism, big word. And it contributes to Gnosticism, which again is the heresy that denies the physical part of the world has any good merit. And just those two misunderstandings, antinomianism and Gnosticism, lead to a great many false understandings, and all of those false understandings lead away from Jesus. Please accept my warning about seeing the covenants as one and not two Verse 9. These next verses confirm the warning. The strange doctrine mentioned is only one example of the many that had come forth. Anything that pretends to earn God's favor is to be opposed. Christians are people established by grace. It is by grace we have been saved, not of any of our works. A persistent insistence on works for God's favor in the first century seemed to always come back to food. And to obey the Jewish law of food restriction. Such a subject was cleared up in Acts, it was cleared up in several of St. Paul's epistles, yet it kept surfacing. Verses 10 through 12. The point of these three verses is that the Jewish restrictions on food and their continued practice of making animal sacrifices in the temple Does not make them worthy. For the only thing that makes a person worthy before God is accepting the sacrifice of Jesus who was rejected by the Jews as they murdered him outside the gates of the old city. Verses 13 through 14. Going outside the camp as Jesus did is a metaphor for making the choice to be different from those who deny Jesus is Savior and Lord. It is always helpful to use metaphor to describe how the Christian life is lived differently than the rest of the world. Christians need to expect to live differently than the world and then be treated differently than the world and even to accept such differences with a righteous pride that says we choose to stand with Jesus. Being different by standing with Jesus allows us to identify with a particular city that is not of this world. Again, a metaphor. After all, the underlining purpose of this Hebrew sermon and the underlining purpose of this sermon I'm preaching right now And the underlying purpose of living the Christian life every day is the hope of heaven That goal, that goal, heaven, must never be out of our sight. Ever. Ever. Verse 15 Here is a primary responsibility of Christians as we travel the narrow road to heaven. We are to be worshipers of God. We are to give him and him alone our praise and our thanksgiving. It is best summed up with that Westminster Shorter catechism question, what is the chief end of man? Which is to ask what is the final purpose or the end goal of a life of a human being? The catechism says to glorify God and enjoy Him forever. And that can be summed up even more by saying the chief end of man, the chief purpose of man, is to worship God and to go to heaven. Verse 16. Here is a good reminder that although our lives are separate from the world, and although our end goal is heaven, We must not forget to live out our lives on earth by doing good. Doing good is living righteously. It's caring for the needs of others. It is loving our fellow man. Our last verse is verse 17. And I want to tell you some stories before I break down verse 17. When I accepted the call to pastor St. Stephen's, the bishop who worked with me and installed me was named Hotchkiss, Gregory Hotchkiss. Hotchkiss resigned his position as bishop when, after the mainline Episcopal Church consecrated an openly gay bishop in 2003 The Reformed Episcopal Church put out a statement of strong disagreement about such a concentration. And next, Hotchkiss declared his disagreement with the leadership of the Reformed Episcopal Church. He claimed he could no longer continue in good conscience with the Reformed Episcopal Church while agreeing. with the homosexual lifestyle and its place in the church, as you can imagine. It was a great disappointment for me to have a leader directly over me who rejected the leadership over him and, as I view it, chose apostasy. When Bishop Hotchkiss left, there was only Bishop Riches serving as leader over this diocese, the Northeast Diocese. I never connected personally with Bishop Riches. To me, he was aloof and appeared to have no time for me. And trust me, I always respected him. I never spoke ill of him, but he never knew me, and I never knew him. He was and is a great man who has done a great deal for the church, but I did not have a meaningful relationship with him. When Bishop Hicks came along, he was a refreshing change because he was more engaging as he worked to have a relationship with me. He went out of his way to have a relationship with me But I have not only seen eye to eye with Bishop Hicks, his leadership over the Holy Orders Committee for the ACNA, that was a disappointment to me For his conclusions of the committee, I strongly disagreed with, and I told him so. And he was not shy in telling me how wrong I was on some of my points. But that disagreement never interrupted my obedience to him and my ability to enjoy his company and to receive from him his teaching, leadership, and friendship. By telling you these stories, I am relating to you that each of us has leadership over us in the church And each of us knows disappointments, missed connections, and disagreements with the leadership of the church. The preacher to the Hebrews knows such things as well. It was Very good timing that a reading from the lectionary this past week, this past Monday, was from First Corinthians chapter four. That is where Paul defends himself against people in the church who accuse him of not being a man of his word, and therefore a poor leader, and therefore someone they could not trust. Paul recognized such negative talk about him as from the devil, and it was and always is. But he worked to explain himself in order to protect the weak in faith who may not know how to deal with negative accusations. And Paul's main point, back to those naysayers, is that there are many things that a person does that cannot be judged by another. It is a kind of not able to walk in another man's shoes type of defense He then humbles himself to say that with some of the decisions he has made, only God knows if they were right, and only God will judge in the end. The point of reference is to show that the best of disciples have contentions with followers and with leaders. And so we come back to verse 17. Obey those who have authority over you. To obey includes submit, which is to comply with their wishes and requests. We are to comply with the wishes of those who have leadership over us in the church. The reason is that church leaders, bishops, priests, and deacons will be required to of God to give account of you, which means to give a report of their care Each of us is going to want our church leaders to give an account with joy rather than grief. The word grief literally means with a sigh. If it is with a sigh that a church leader gives an account to God for you, then it will not be good for you. How will it not be good is not stated. Whatever it will be, it will not be pleasant. There is, of course, a warning given in this verse to church leaders. The warning is that they are responsible for each person under their care. I have to give an account to God about each one of you. And Bishop Hicks and Bishop Gillen will be given an account about me. That is a serious burden to take on, for as James warns in his epistle, he says, Not many should become teachers in the church, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness. Paul says that to desire to be a leader in the church is a noble task, but one that requires a higher standard of accountability. The story examples I gave before examining verse 17 get to the biggest problem we have regarding submitting to church authority. The problem is we are submitting to fallible people, and we are fallible ourselves. We are sinners. We all see through the glass dimly. We are all under the sun. With a subjective perspective. Hence, we are limited in our wills and in our judgments about others, even ourselves. But God knows this, of course he does, and yet he tells us to obey, to submit to church authorities. Submit. That's a tough word for us who are in the West. Consider the irony that it is hard for us to obey the instruction for us to obey. When I provide premarital counseling, I begin with Ephesians 5, verse 22. There it reads, wives submit to your husbands as unto the Lord. And I begin there because I anticipate that the woman is going to have trouble with that word, submit. And therefore, I need to address the trouble right away. After all, being a submissive woman goes against our Western culture, at least what we have left as a culture. A submissive woman is contrary to what educators, entertainers, and the media want women to be today. Because men are said to be coarse, narrow-minded, perverse, and oppressive, women need to break the chain of abuse and usurp the roles of males wherever they can So they say. Even we who claim to be Christians struggle with requiring women to submit. We only need one example of a husband abusing a woman to make that word submit ugly and unusable And when we read again the standard that a woman is to submit to her husband in the same manner she is to submit to God Himself, well we conclude that St. Paul has to be exaggerating here. He has to be exaggerating. No one can submit to another human being to such a high standard. No one. And yet there it is. Of course, the future husband can sit quietly and happily while I instruct the future bride to submit to her husband just as she submits to the Lord. Until I get to the future husband and show him his standard. He is to love his future wife in the same manner Jesus loves his church. And how does Jesus love his church? Well, he serves it, he suffered for it, and he died for it. And after I make that standard clear to the husband, I then point to verse 21 of Ephesians 5. And I purposefully ignored that verse. To bring home the point as dramatically as I can that God instructs both the wife and the husband to submit. Verse 21 reads, Submit to one another in fear of God. Therefore, in a good marriage, a godly marriage, the husband and wife are both submitting Only differently. Hence, hence, the Christian life is a life of submission for everyone Without embracing submission, a person cannot be a Christian. For following Jesus requires submission to the Triune God and submission in all of our relationships Children must submit, they must obey their parents to be in proper relationship with God. Parents, as I mentioned, husbands and wives, must submit to one another for their marriage to be honoring to God. The family must submit to their church authority to be pleasing to God. The church leadership is to submit to one another for the church to be without spot, and all the church must submit to God. For his kingdom to come, for his will to be done on earth as it is in heaven The finishing point to make for the Christian life being of submission is the fact that Jesus himself lived in submission as he submitted to the Father's will. To follow Jesus, to claim him as Lord and Savior, is to submit as he submitted. But, but, but what if, what if? What if the leadership we are to submit to is bad? You know, I'm not talking about bad as in he is fallible and he sees through the glass dimly just as I do bad. I mean bad that he is teaching falsely or behaving immorally or both Well the answer to that is actually simple. Ministers can be charged with heresy or immoral living, and they can be stripped of their ordination rights. And those men who are found guilty of such things should be charged and convicted and defrauded. It is the responsibility of both lay people and clergy to rid the church of false teachers and false livers. And evil livers, excuse me. But but but what if what if what if he is a bad decision maker? What if my leader is a bad decision maker? What if he hasn't convinced me that he the church should be run the way he's running it? What then? The honest answer is there is no provision for such a problem. The instruction to obey your church authority is not conditioned on whether you agree with the decision that he makes or not. Again, we can look to the marriage example. A wife who has a husband who she disagrees with his decision-making ultimately has to submit, and by faith Trust that God will protect her and the family in the end. The same is true for a parishioner who disagrees with church leaders Faith must be applied as we trust God will protect all involved that are hoping in Him. Yes, today, more than any other time in the history of the church, people can disagree and walk away. Ultimately, that will not be good for them. That is what the preacher says. How is it not good is again not stated. And I assume it's not stated because it can manifest itself in many ways. I would not want to find out. Yes, submission requires faith, a great deal of faith. When we submit, we have to focus on what we hope for and what is unseen. I think the best way to end A sermon like this, and our series on Hebrews, is to turn to Hebrews chapter 13 To Hebrews chapter thirteen and read from verse eighteen through twenty-five. Pray for us, for we are confident that we have a good conscience in all things, desiring to live honorably. But I especially urge you to do this that I may be restored to you the sooner. Now may the God of peace, who brought up our Lord Jesus from the dead, that great shepherd of the that great shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant, make you complete in every good work, to do his will. working in you what is well pleasing in his sight. Through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. And I appeal to you, brethren, bear with the word of exhortation, for I have written to you in few words. Know that our brother Timothy has been set free, with whom I shall see you if he comes shortly. Greet all those who rule over you, and all the saints, those from Italy, greet you. Grace be with you all. Amen. And Amen

sermons.title: Strange Fire
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. You have heard from this pulpit the saying that goes something like this A man's conviction can become his son's tradition, which can become his grandson's elimination This usually occurs because the first man who had the conviction did not pass it down well enough to his son and then to his grandson. A common example is a man's patriotism. Imagine a father, sorry, a grandfather, who loved his country and expressed it By hanging his U. S. flag on Flag Day, Veterans Day, Memorial Day, and Independence Day. He hosted a family picnic every year on the 4th of July. He prayed to God to bless the United States and its citizens. He was proud to vote every year, and he rooted heartily for the good old US of A for every Olympic Games. And his son then does the same. His son loved the traditions of his father, and so when he had a family of his own, he displayed his U. S. flag on the day his father did. He hosted his own 4th of July picnics, and he prayed for his country, and he called himself blessed to be living in the greatest country in the world. But his son, which is the first man's grandson, isn't so sure about the greatness of his country. He hears from his teachers that the history of the United States is not honest, and that generations before him overlooked the sins of their forefathers. Our forefathers' treatment of Africans and Native Americans was abusive at best and murderous at the worst. When his son asks his father about why he thinks the US United States is the greatest country in the world, when it has such a terrible founding in its sins, his father cannot answer Because he loves the country because his father did. And his father never explained what was the foundation of that love that he so richly displayed. Conviction to elimination happens quickly A year ago, I preached about our culture's failure to address the sins of our forefathers because we have lost a sense of the gospel of Jesus in our country. And my intent is not to repeat that series of sermons, so I will only mention that we can only address the sins of our forefathers with an understanding of the Christian gospel. But back to my point. Passing on conviction requires explanation, cogent explanation. For those traditions, for without understanding traditions, they become dead on arrival to the third generation. That reality is very easily seen in Christian traditions, especially traditions in terms of Christian worship. Take this quiz. Why do older older churches use pews for sitting? And why are they placed in rows of two or four, one behind the other? You don't know? Well then change it. Why not? Why is the pulpit on one side and the lectron on the other? You don't know? Well then change it. No, don't don't just change it. Just get rid of them both. Why not? Make it all practical. Why is communion, the communion table in the middle? Why is it behind the lectoran and the pulpit? Why do ministers wear dresses? Why is everyone so somber and serious when they receive the bread and the wine? And what really is the Lord's Supper? You don't get your hunger or your thirst satisfied, so what good really is it? Then if you don't have these things that are practical, get rid of them, change them, after all, God doesn't care how he is worshipped He only cares if we are sincere and honest when we worship. Stop. Stop right there. There it is. That statement is where it is. There is an understanding in that statement that God only cares about our sincerity and our honesty in worship. That is where we question everything in regards to our traditions. It is the belief That God doesn't care how he is worshipped, but only that he is worshiped in sincerity of heart and of mind. The problem with that belief is that it has no biblical merit. It doesn't come from Scripture. God never says that it does not matter how he is worshipped, and he never said that he's only concerned about our hearts and our minds. Such an interpretation is reading into Scripture what we want it to say rather than what it does actually say. People who have argued that God does not care how we worship, but only that we do so in sincerity of heart and mind, they go to passages such as Psalm 51. You know this Psalm well, we actually recite it a number of times. David is there saying, quote, You speaking to God Do not delight in sacrifice, or I would bring it. You do not take pleasure in burnt offerings. My sacrifice, O God, is a broken spirit. A broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise. Now some people these words teach that, again, God doesn't delight in any sacrifice at all. But that conclusion doesn't wrestle with the reality that God is the one who commanded those sacrifices to be offered to begin with. For some people, the latter part of the verse reveals what God actually wants, which is a broken spirit and a contrite heart. But that conclusion doesn't take into account what David says next in the very same psalm. He says the following. Then you will delight in the sacrifices of the righteous, in the burnt offerings offered whole. Then bulls will be offered on your altar. Well this last verse makes it clear that it is not sacrifices that God is displeased with, but sacrifices made without broken and contrite hearts. God wants both from his people. He wants sacrifice as he commanded it, and the hearts of the people as they obey. The problem with Israel is that they either repeatedly trusted in the rituals without their hearts being given to God, or they did not obey as commanded. Another passage often quoted by those who think God does not care about the form in which his people worship is Hosea 6, verse 6. That says, For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. To conclude that God does not like the very thing that He commanded to be done, well that's simply illogical It fails to take into account what God is truly after when he asks for those sacrifices and where he commands them to be performed. His end goal has always been for the people of Israel to be his people and for him to be their God. And what that looks like is a people who love him and accept his love, and that would be expressed by obeying his law. Not out of trust in the law itself, but out of love for the giver of the law. That is called faith. Worship in faith. In case you are being tempted to think that such is my own interpretation, listen to these words of the prophet Jeremiah. Jeremiah says Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh For in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, I did not speak to your fathers or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But this command I gave them, obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people, and walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well for you. Of course, the offerings are essential to worshiping God because they all point to that great fulfillment, which is the sacrifice of Jesus upon the cross. That is essential to our worship. Their faith, the faith of the Jews, pointed towards Jesus. Ours points backward. All to the same thing. The Christian life is to be what God wanted for the Israelites, which is forgiveness of sin, and that includes sacrifice. And obedience to his will. And all of this means that the Christian life is a life of worship Another biblical argument against the worship of God in any manner we choose is the number of times God rejects worship that is not commanded We learn very quickly in the Holy Scriptures that God does not indiscriminately accept all forms of worship. Remember from our study of faith in the book of Hebrews, how God accepted the offering of Abel, but not of Cain. Cain did not bring forth the first fruits, and he did not bring them because he lacked faith. Abel brought the firstborn of his flock to worship God, and yet it wasn't the fact that he brought forth the firstborn, but that he did so in faith that God would receive it and forgive sin. This example teaches us that God does discriminate when it comes to the worship that he will accept. Interestingly, the offerings of Cain and Abel can be considered both private worship and corporate worship It is private because they each brought separate offerings, and it is corporate because they were the only people beside their parents that were alive. Now the next example comes from the book of Leviticus, where the Israelites received commandments primarily. Leviticus is about primarily corporate worship. This is from Leviticus 10, verses 1 and 2. It reads, Now Aaron's sons, Nabab and Abihu, took their censors. Put fire in them, placed incense on them, and offered unauthorized fire before the Lord, contrary to his command. So fire came out from the presence of the Lord and devoured them, and they died before the Lord There are several points of information we can identify in these verses that were violations of God's law. A law that he just gave them as leaders for corporate worship. First They each took his own sensor, his own sensor, rather than the sacred utensil that was to be used in the sanctuary. Individualism. Second, they both offered their censors together, whereas incense was to only to be given by one person Third, they performed an action that was only to be performed by the high priest, and in that case it was their father. Fourth, they offered incense at an unauthorized time. Fifth and finally, they offered these incense offerings as worship directly in front of the Holy of Holies, which was a breaking of a specific commandment. So in summary, Nadab and Abihu worshipped in a manner that they were not instructed to do, and in a manner they were instructed specifically not to do. But they were worshiping. They were worshiping. That should be in their favor, right? At least they were at church. They were calling upon God, the right God, not some idol, but the right God. That should count for something, right? Apparently not. You see, by worshiping in a manner that God did not command, they were presuming upon God that any way God is approached is sufficient and acceptable. It wasn't and it isn't. If you are still convinced that sincerity of heart and mind is what God is most concerned about when it comes to The worship of him, let us reflect on the story of King Saul and the Israelites' victory over the Amalekites. At the beginning of 1 Samuel chapter 15, God speaks to King Saul through the prophet Samuel. Telling him to go and fight the Amalekites, to avenge the manner they attacked Israel when Israel had been freed from bondage while escaping Egypt. God instructs Saul to kill every Amalekite as well as their oxen, their sheep, their camels, and their donkeys. Nothing of the people was to be left. The directives were clearly stated and agreed to. And yet, after God gave Israel a resounding victory, We read that the people took the plunder they were to destroy, particularly the sheep, the oxen, and used them as sacrifices to worship God. Let that be underlined. The people used the best of the livestock from their plunder of the Amalekites to worship God. That sounds like a good thing they were doing. That sounds like they were praising God for the victory. They acknowledged that God was responsible for their victory. That all seemed so very right because they were worshiping God in sincerity. But here is what Samuel the prophet says to them after discovering what the people had done. Samuel says, Has the Lord a great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in or comparing to obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice. And to heed, that is, heed God's word, is better than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Note that the sincerity of the people is not in question. And it is quite a statement to compare witchcraft and idolatry to the people offering sacrifices to God. We would be shouting for Israel's condemnation if they were turning blatantly to witchcraft and idolatry. It seems like a sincere mistake. But not to God. No, not to God. Such disobedience, regardless of sincerity, was an abomination. From that example in 1 Samuel, let us not next make the mistake of thinking that God must only be concerned about obedience when it comes to corporate worship. We get another example from the prophet Malachi. Malachi brought forth God's word to the Israelites while the temple was being rebuilt under Ezra and Nehemiah. He begins his prophecy by condemning the priests for their defiled offerings. That's what he calls them. Defiled offerings. But the offerings were defiled not because the priests were worshiping an idol or a false god. They were worshiping Yahweh. And they were worshiping in the right location. They were offering the sacrifices according to the law. All was good. But all was not good, because the poor were being oppressed, the starving were not being fed, the widows were not being cared for, the lame and the sick were being ignored. Thus the rituals of corporate worship were being followed by the laws of not being followed by the laws of loving God and loving one's neighbor as oneself. Corporate worship had become ritual for the sake of ritual, which can happen in any form of worship that does not include loving God and loving our neighbor. I anticipate that by now some of you might be frustrated at the points I have made because It can appear that there is no way to please God when it comes to corporate worship. If God is concerned about our hearts and minds as we worship, but not to the point that it's the most important thing. And then he cares about obedience, but not that that is his only concern. And then that obedience is not just what we do in worship, but what we do outside of the temple Well, then it appears that God is easily offended if we lean too far one way as opposed to another. And if you perceive God is too easily offended when it comes to worship of his people, I emphatically say that he is not. But getting you to the point of questioning whether God is easily offended, well that was a goal of mine this morning The very least I want us to conclude is that God does not accept any and all worship that uses his name. That should be clear enough by the examples given in Scripture. I can say that God is not easily offended by the worship of his people because our worship, our corporate worship, is not for God. It's for us. God is concerned about our manner of corporate worship because he cares for us. Hear this now. How we worship God is how we think about God, and how we think about God is in what we put our faith If we view God as only concerned about our hearts and not our obedience, then we worship God by way of our emotions. And when our emotions change, so does our God. If we view God as being most concerned about obedience, then we put our faith in ritual, and ritual becomes death. If we view God as only concerned about what we do within the walls of his sanctuary, then we fail to love our fellow man, and that means we don't love God either. We have spent a lot of time in the Old Testament today, but remember the point made from the book of Hebrews. That Jesus is in all of the Old Testament, and therefore he is the model of worshiping God. He is the epitome of us of a sincere heart and mind, while being fully obedient and while loving his fellow man. So we look to him today in our worship, and we will look to him in this series of sermons regarding how to properly worship. I started by talking about a grandfather's convictions becoming a son's traditions becoming his grandson's eliminations. Because I am concerned that such will occur in my own family and in the families of St. Stephen's. I've started By trying to convince you that sincerity and effort to worship God is not enough. My end goal is to convince you that the traditions we have been given within the Anglican way, which is part of the great tradition, are actually convictions. Convictions worthy to be passed on. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God, we begin by thanking you for the traditions passed on to us and how they are a part of the great tradition given to the Church. Father, may we be good stewards of it, both in our lives and to that which we pass on to our children, taking ever the examples of your word, which shows us that you do care about how you are worshipped. For the sake of your people. Again, Father, help us to be good stewards. We pray. In Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Relevant to whom?
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I started this series on corporate worship two weeks ago Making the simple point that the God of Holy Scripture does not accept just any form of worship, but is instead is insistent that our worship be by His commandments. with a heart that loves him fully, and a love for our fellow man. Any worship that falls short of said standard is worship rejected. A number of years ago, I visited a home of a parishioner who attended this parish, but her husband did not. I visited the home because I wanted to see if I could convince the husband to believe in Jesus and then become a part of St. Stephen's. For the sake of his own soul and for the soul of his wife, who so desperately wanted her husband to be a Christian and to worship with her The husband thought himself a good thinker, and so he posed to me this question. Why does God need to be worshipped? It appears, he said, that God has an ego problem when he commands that he be worshipped. Up to that time I had not been asked such a question, but I have surmised since that many people who struggled to have faith have asked or thought something similar. Certainly, if any human were to demand to be worshipped, we as Christians would be appalled as that sinful ego was being expressed. And we look back at the pharaohs of Egypt, the Caesars of Rome, and the likes of Hitler and Mussolini, and we rightly disdain their egos. And their insistence on being praised by their followers. And then we make the mistake of thinking that God Might be worthy of similar disdain because of his commandments to be worshipped. That type of thinking is a very serious problem, for it reveals that we are tempted by the devil to understand God. In the same categories as understanding ourselves and as understanding our fellow man. It is a struggle For human beings to comprehend that God is wholly different. W-H-O-L-L-Y and H-O-L-Y. Wholly different from humanity. And in being wholly different, he is beyond our comprehension. And yet, because he's beyond our comprehension, That means that him coming to be like us is even more profound. But being our comp beyond our comprehension is what it means to be God. If we who are finite could understand God fully, then he would also have to be finite. But we can only understand fully what is finite and not understand that which is infinite. To realize God is beyond our comprehension Helps our faith to increase again as we contemplate his revelations to us, especially his glorious incarnation. Christian apologists have rightly described God as separate from his creation by explaining that everything that has existence Either exists as being caused by something else, or by the necessity of its own nature. I'll say that again. Everything that exists has come into being by the cause of another thing. Or it exists by the necessity of its own nature. Thus it is argued that while all things that exist require an outside agent that caused its existence. There is the possibility of God because God exists by the necessity of his own nature, which is eternal. To put it another way, God does not have to have a beginning, because the word beginning implies the existence of time. And it was God who created time, making God before time, and we only say that To help us comprehend God's eternal existence, since there could not have been a before, before time, because the word before only makes sense in the context of time. Hang in with me? What I said makes sense, only you might have to listen to it a few times to follow the track of logic. But my point to go on in such a manner is to show how difficult it is for finite minds like ours to understand the full nature of God. The great mind of St. Anselm of Canterbury, the 12th-century theologian, put forth his famous ontological argument for the existence of God By defining God as that by which nothing greater can be conceived. That by which nothing greater can be conceived Such a definition works well within the ontological argument, but it has a flaw. In that it seems that God's existence is based on what man cannot fully comprehend. Of course, God's existence isn't dependent upon anything that humanity can or cannot understand, but the definition of God being that which is nothing that nothing greater can be conceived At least gets to the point that to compare God to humanity or any one man ever but Jesus Is to fall embarrassingly and shamefully short of coming close, close to knowing God It is only after we try to comprehend just how much we cannot comprehend that we can reasonably see why it is necessary for us who are created beings To worship the one who created us. So God is beyond our comprehension And yet there are truths that God has revealed to us about Him that He wants us to focus upon. But we find it difficult to focus upon God, what he has revealed to us, because we who are worshipers by nature are also sinful due to our fallen nature. Having established the argument that God, because of his nature, is worthy of praise, our praise, It is next necessary for us to examine the nature of humanity, and in particular, examine our nature as compared to God. Interestingly, it was mentioned to me a couple of times before service that some people are having a hard time staying awake during my sermons. And I assure you that God does not have a hard time staying awake. God reveals to us that we are worshipers by nature, telling us of our first parents, Adam and Eve. You remember who were placed in a perfect environment where food was plenty, temperature was such to where no clothing was necessary, and because there was no sin, there was no shame, requiring nothing to be hidden. All of it was given by God, and therefore God was to be thanked and honored for giving such gifts that required no toil of humanity, but only to enjoy the fruits of the garden. Except one. Except one. The fruit of the knowledge of good and evil. By the way, it's not in my notes, but as a Washingtonian, that fruit of the knowledge of good and evil was not an apple We don't know what it was, but we from Washington take offense if you say it's an apple. Apples are good for you. The fruit of the knowledge of good and evil was the only fruit God instructed Adam and Eve not to eat, and with that instruction they were placed in a position of possible failure. Interesting. God knew they could possibly fail. To not eat would require them to fully love God, as God would reign supreme in the hearts of Adam and Eve. And to disobey by eating said fruit would bring the curse of death. From the choice that our two parents made, it was revealed that they loved something other than God. And we know from the sermon two weeks ago that obedience is an act of worship and disobedience a rejecting of proper worship. When God curses Adam and Eve because of their disobedience, he reveals then what is meant for Adam and Eve to know good and evil. No one, to my knowledge, has better explained what it meant for Adam and Eve to know good and evil better than C. S. Lewis. In the second installment of his space trilogy titled Paralandra, Lewis describes a planet that has been recently occupied by two human-like creatures, human-like. They are male and female, but something different than human. They are given the duty by God to procreate and to fill this new planet with their own kind. But they were not alone, for a demon-possessed man who on Earth was a scientist named Weston had created a ship that enabled him to land on Paralandra. With the goal of corrupting these undefiled creatures and eventually corrupting the whole planet. This plan of corruption was interrupted by another scientist named Ransom. And you should note that from the theories on atonement. He is the hero of the story who works diligently to expose Dr. Weston to the innocent creatures while helping these new creatures resist temptation to disobey God. And just like the biblical story, the possessed Dr. Weston tempts the female creature while she is unwillingly separated from her mate. Now the story is more complex than I am able to describe for this sermon. But what Lewis brilliantly shows from the conversations the female creature has with both both the possessed Dr. Weston and the hero Dr. Ranson, is the difference between, and here it is, The difference between knowing good and evil from the devil's perspective versus God's perspective From biblical narrative of the fall of Adam and Eve, some have interpreted it that God did not want humanity to know good and evil at all, or ever. What Lewis explains is that God did and does want us to know good and evil only from the side of obedience and holiness. rather than from the side of disobedience and sin. Because of the choice of our first parents, all of us know good and evil from the side of disobedience and sinfulness. And that perspective makes our knowledge of good and evil distorted, limited, and corrupt. Remember in our covering of the book of Hebrews, when the Hebrew preacher teaches us That Jesus knows our weaknesses because he was tempted in all ways like us without sin. And we learn that Jesus as a human being Then is first to know good and evil as God intended it to be known. Again, from the side of obedience and holiness. From such a side, it can be said that Jesus is the only person to ever truly know good and evil. For the devil himself only knows it from the side that we are on. Now, because we know good and evil from the wrong side, the distorted, limited, and corrupt side Everything we do, every act we perform, even listening right now, even my preaching right now. Every thought we have, every project that we complete, every relationship we have, every motive that we use, all of it is tainted by sin. All of it. This is the same as where it says in the Bible that all have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God. This is, as I have described, is confirmed by the prophet Isaiah, who said, that all we like sheep have gone astray. The Apostle Paul said of humanity, there is none righteous, no not one. Now reminding you of the fallen state of our humanity is Depressing? I must interrupt your thoughts to say that it is not my goal, of my words, to depress you or the goal of the words of scripture to depress us, but rather to awaken our consciences to the need for God's forgiveness. Every time we are reminded of our fallen condition, our sinful condition, it is to awaken our souls. So that we might utter the same words spoken by the crowd that heard that wonderful sermon by St. Peter on Acts 2. And hearing that sermon, they say, What then shall we do? If you are a Christian, you know the answer. It is to repent and be baptized. And if you are a Christian, then you have been baptized, then you know your next duty is to repent. The Christian life is indeed a life of repentance. Thus, repentance plays a central role in Christian worship. And God help all those churches that worship today who do not repent in their service. It is central to our worship. And after we repent of our sin, we are to believe that God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. It is when we have believed that God has forgiven us that we next give him thanks. We give him praise. We give him our worship. And we must give him our worship because if we do not, then we will give it to something other than God To be convinced that we humans are by nature beings that must worship, allow history to teach you For there is no civilization known to history that does not have some form of worship of some form of God or gods. If history is not enough, then examine people you know and observe their obsessions. If a person is not a follower of Jesus, he or she is a follower of something else. People give themselves over to anything to serve as their God. Substances we refer to in the context of addictions, they are worshipped. Money is worshipped. Fads are worshipped. Material goods are worshipped Social causes are worshipped. Politicians are worshipped. Sports, athletes, celebrities are worshipped Recreation is worshipped. Even laziness is worshipped, as there are people who work hard for the purpose of avoiding work. We can also see how emotions are worshiped as people, on one end of emotional expression, pursue a high of joyfulness, while others pursue a high of anger and bitterness. Every emotion in between can also be made a God to follow and to submit to. If history and observation is not enough, then be convinced by Bob Dylan, who you've heard before, you've got to serve somebody. It might be the devil, it might be the Lord, but you have to serve somebody. Now putting this sermon puzzle together, you need to see that the piece that shows that the nature of God is naturally to be worshipped. And the human nature's need to worship, those two things go together. The troubled piece that doesn't seem to fit is that we are sinful in our natures, our fallen natures. So the missing piece that helps our fallen nature fit with the creator of the universe is, of course, Jesus, who fits perfectly between us. So that we are no longer estranged from God, even while we have yet received our heavenly holiness. Before we do receive that heavenly holiness, we are to be acting out the task of worshiping God. The question remains, how? How are we to worship God? That question is going to be answered more fully next week, as this is a sermon series. And two weeks ago we were shown biblically how God is not to be worshipped. And what I want to end on in this sermon. is how modern worship has failed to answer the question of how God is to be worshipped, so that he accepts it There is a British satire television series. I think it's older. I've only seen it on YouTube. It's called Yes, Minister. And they performed dialogue skits giving humorous insights into the British culture, including politics. In one particular scene, the Prime Minister is to appoint a new bishop, but is having trouble choosing from the candidates. He discovers that all of the politically acceptable candidates are not true churchmen, but rather politicians. He learns that the primary candidates for bishop no longer dress for their position as Christian ministers, but instead for social status. The Prime Minister is told that their modern dress is for the purpose of relevance. The Prime Minister responds to this by asking, relevant to God? The answer comes back, no, of course not, Prime Minister. I meant relevant as a sociological term And it is that term, relevant, that has dogged the modern church as many bodies of believers have worked hard to be socially relevant. There is the attempt to be relevant in terms of society, resulting in what are called liberal Christian churches. These churches, as you know, have abandoned Judeo-Christian morals set forth in Holy Scripture and instead have adopted moral standards that set no standards at all Except the virtue of tolerance, and even that virtue is rejected if it is tolerance for those who still uphold Judeo-Christian morals. The other group that wants to be relevant are the independent Christian gatherings who confess to abide by Judeo-Christian morals. but who worship in a manner that they think is appealing to the greater masses of people, especially younger people. And so these groups replicate popular music styles while placing Jesus in the lyrics. Some even use light shows and fog Because, well, such staging is thought to make worship more relevant The begging question is relevant to whom? Relevant to God? No. And there lies the very serious problem. I submit that the more relevant Christian worship becomes to humanity, especially particularly Western humanity, The more God begins to look like Western humanity, and such a picture is not worthy of any worship. I also submit that if you examine the worship as commanded by God in both the tabernacle and for the temple, and the worship that is described in the book of Revelation You will realize that corporate worship of the one true God is to be heavenly relevant, not earthly relevant. Christian worship is only relevant when it ascends into heaven where the Father and the Son reign. I submit that we are only relevant to the kingdom of God when our worship is relevant to heaven. That should be our goal, our standard, and nothing less. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful Father, we come confessing that our worship being received by you is a privilege And it is not to be offered lightly and unseemly in any manner. And we thank you for the high standard. And Father, as we pray that your kingdom would come, your will be done, may that occur in our worship. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: The Order Given
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I ask you to turn in your Bibles to Exodus chapter 24. That was not part of our reading this morning, but I'd like you to turn there. Exodus chapter 24 It would be quite useful for you to follow along. So far in this series of sermons on Christian corporate worship, we have established that God rejects worship that does not obey his commandments. That does not love him and that does not love our fellow man. Last week we learned that God, because of his nature, is to be worshipped, and because of our nature, we are to be worshipers of God. And finally, our worship of God is to be heavenly relevant. Today we focus more closely on answering how we are to worship God so that we would be heavenly relevant. When I arrived in Pullman, Washington to serve as pastor of Pullman Nazarene Church, fresh out of seminary. I was handed a worship bulletin of the prior Sunday and was told by the Secretary that the content in the bulletin is how they've been worshiping, but I could make changes and do as I preferred. And my initial response was panic. The moment I remember overwhelmed me because I questioned by what authority I was to decide how the God of the universe, the only True God, how I am to decide how He is to be worshipped. No one in seminary had taught me that there was a preferred order of corporate worship, and by preferred I mean preferred by God. When I was a senior in seminary, I was given a book by a local pastor, not a professor, but a local pastor. The book was titled Worship, Old and New by Robert Weber. That book became my first source of guidance. In that book, Weber shows how early Christians used to worship From the temple and from synagogue order of worship. And Christians use that to bring about a new covenant understanding of worship He argues that the orders provided from the temple and from the synagogue each incorporate what we find in Exodus chapter 24. What is so special about Exodus 24? Well, it describes the very first order of worship. of God that He commands, that He directs His people to follow, when they for the first time collectively gather together. Exodus 24 is the first description of corporate worship. Before Exodus chapter 24, God was worshipped by individuals. He was worshipped by heads of families, but never before was there an organized worship of all of God's people gathered in one place. Weber argues, and so do I, that Exodus chapter 24 provides a format, an outline for worship that includes basic essentials for all of God's people to incorporate when they approach God for corporate worship. Hence, this morning we are going to break down each verse of Exodus chapter 24. That is why I want you to follow along with me in your Bibles. So Exodus chapter 24, beginning at verse 1. Now he said to Moses, Come up to the Lord, you and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of his elders of Israel, and worship from afar. The very first thing we are to notice is that God initiates the relationship. God calls his people to worship. And as we established last week, he doesn't call them because he needs to be worshipped, but rather the people need to worship him. If they do not, they will worship something else as they do indeed do, not too long after this moment. We also see that God calls his people to come up. The people of God are to come to him. He is where he should be, and we are to go to him. Next, we see that there is a hierarchy that calls certain men to perform certain duties that other men do not and must not perform. Moses and Aaron, along with Aaron's sons, are chosen by God to represent all of the people at God's throne. Verse 2 And Moses alone came, shall come near the Lord, but they shall not come near, nor shall the people go up with him. In this verse, we recognize that Moses had a unique role that we are to see as a type of Christ. Moses was a mediator chosen by God to bring forth God's word to his people. He is also privileged to see God as no other man did. And we are to recall later that Jesus tells us that he is the only one that has seen the Father. In comparison to Jesus, Moses again was a tight, only a tite, as he was more privileged than any other man, but not as privileged as the son of man. Verse 3. So Moses came and told the people all the words of the Lord and all the judgments, and all the people answered with one voice, All the words which the Lord has said, we will do. What Moses told the people was how God had instructed them to worship. Prior to this, the people had feared God, you remember, so terribly that they asked that God no longer speak to them audibly, but that they only hear the voice of Moses. So the here, Moses is speaking for God, and the people upon hearing God respond in agreement. Now scholars speculate that this was a covenant ritual that the people would have understood or experienced before, for God was acting as some type of king or tribal leader as he was dictating them the standards of the covenant agreement, and the people according to the agreement must make public acknowledgement of their assent And that understanding that if they break their word, they would rightly suffer at the hands of their sovereign, in this case, God. Verse 4. And Moses wrote all the words of the Lord, and he rose early in the morning, and built an altar at the foot of the mountain, and twelve pillars according to the twelve tribes of Israel. What Moses wrote were the Ten Commandments and other commandments that God had given from Exodus 20 to through 23, chapter 23. That the altar built by Moses was at the foot of the mountain, allows for the people to see and learn by repetition. That it is by blood sacrifice that they are allowed to hear from God and be in covenant with God, and it is a covenant with all the people of Israel as a whole, together. That is the symbol of the 12 pillars representing the 12 tribes that are God's people in the line of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Pillars highlight God's use of symbolism. We will talk a great deal about that next week. Verse 5 He sent young men of the children of Israel who offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings of oxen to the Lord. The offered animals were according to the law, and we again point to the fact that they were offered before the eyes of the people. So that they could see that there was no misunderstanding that death was necessary for sin to be forgiven and for them to stand righteously before God. The fact that young men were involved was taking advantage of their aggression to do the slaughtering. The burnt offering represented the removing of the guilt of sin. And the peace offering expressed man's gratitude for the mercies of God received. Verse 6. And Moses took half the blood and put it in basins, and half the blood he sprinkled on the altar. Now, this sprinkling of blood is unique to this corporate worship moment. Only here For after, according to Levitical law, it will be done by the high priest and not sprinkled upon the people as a whole. That the blood is shared by God and by the people shows how God is both receiving the sacrifice and then using it to cleanse his people of sin. Verse 7. Then he took the book of the covenant and read it in the hearing of the people. And they said, All that the Lord has said, we will do, and be obedient. Well, this book read must most certainly contain the laws that we have mentioned, and there is no reason why it didn't include the stories of Genesis Where God first laid out this same covenant with Abraham, then Isaac, and then Jacob. Also, once again, we have this pattern, you notice Moses the leader, reading the word of God to the people, and the people responding with assent to all that God has said. Verse 8. And Moses took the blood, sprinkled it on the people, and said, This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you according to all these words. The blood sprinkled was likely upon the heads of each tribal leader to represent the people as a whole. It is likely it was not sprinkled on all of the people, for there were possibly two million Israelites at this time. Being touched by the blood will become consuming the blood in the form of wine. Verse 9 and 10. Then Moses went up also Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and 70 of the elders of Israel. And they saw the God of Israel, and there was under his feet, as it were, a paved work of sapphire stone, and it was like the very heavens in its clarity. These verses have God's leaders back upon the mountain. They went up to see God and to eat with God. Let us get out of the way any idea that what the leaders witnessed was the same that Moses witnessed when God walked before him. This is different for several reasons. The most obvious reason being that Moses was given a privilege of seeing God's backside like no other man had been given. And second, God was conveying something to these leaders when he manifested himself in this manner. Before the people knew God in the form of smoke, fire, thunder, lightning. Here they are able to see his loveliness. His beauty. His beauty as more blue than any sky they had ever seen. Verse 11 But on the nobles of the children of Israel, he did not lay his hand. So they saw God, and they ate and drank. The first part of this verse reminds us that no man, no man had seen God and would expect to live. It is implied that they could have justly had God's hands laid upon them in judgment. But that was not why God called them to himself. He wanted to be their God and for them to be his people, making this moment very unique, profound, and a holy other. The scholars share in majority agreement that the wording of verses nine through eleven Has God revealing himself to the leaders of Israel while they ate and drank? Why? It was most certainly fitting that the end of the worship of God's people would end with a meal that celebrated the covenant agreed upon. And we are given the importance of a meal finalizing God's gracious work when we are given a picture of our heavenly reward, beginning with a feast at God's banquet table. You are likely ahead of me by thinking that a Christian worship service ending with a meal, Holy Communion is also connected to the meal here in Exodus 24 and to the heavenly banquet feast described in the Gospels And the commandment of Jesus to his disciples to take the bread and eat, to take the cup and drink until he returns. If you are thinking ahead, you are quite correct. This point, this point then brings us to a contemporary application of all of this, what it means to us today. Consider what our tradition, our Anglican tradition, does that embraces the principles revealed in Israel's first call to corporate worship. In our liturgy, God initiates. When we read the first sentences in the prayer book, we are speaking the voice of God. For God's people to come forth and to give him praise. He dictates the time of our worship. Not the time on a clock, but time in terms of our worship starting with his word being spoken. The main and most important point is that God initiates everything in our relationship with Him. From calling us out of sin and guilt to giving us new names and placing his very self, the Holy Spirit, within us. With the Holy Spirit within us, God is always calling us to worship Him and particularly for corporate worship each Sunday. Also within the call, we recognize a necessary hierarchy that calls some men to come up closer to God in order to relate God's word to his people. We call such men clergy, coming from the Latin clericus, which is actually from the Greek Referring to a man who had no inheritance, no inheritance but the Lord. Next comes the reading of God's word by the clergy to the people, and the people responding to the same word by committing themselves to following what they had heard. And we do the same with our readings from the Psalter for every morning and evening prayer, followed by the glory of Hatha. Glory be to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. which is the Christian expression of accepting what is written as coming from the triune God We have the same pattern in the first and second readings when after we hear them, we in unison say, thanks be to God. Which is also a way of stating our agreement, our agreement to that word read that we will heed what it said. And finally, we have a very special moment in our full Holy Communion service where we have the gospel read down amid the people. It is at that time that we celebrate the incarnation of God becoming as we are, yet without sin. We read amidst the congregation, believing that Jesus lived amidst humanity. We praise, glory be to thee, O Lord, and thanks be to thee, O Christ. In great gratitude of God condescending to us. Next in Exodus comes the sacrificial offerings. Which for the Christian Church is both confession of sin and the preparation of the Lord's table Our confession of sin places our trust in the one and ultimate sacrifice of Jesus, to whom we put our trust for our sins to be washed by his blood. And for us to be worthy to sit at the table that God has laid out for us. That God has said He will withhold His hand from us. He wants to eat with us and we with him. It is hopeful to know That the confession of sins occurs in the Book of Common Prayer purposefully after the reading of the commandments. And after the reading of the scriptures, and after the sermon, so that the Holy Spirit can use God's word read and preached to move upon our hearts to confess what we need to confess. It is after we confess our sins and receive words of expiation and propitiation that we are next free to eat at the Lord's table. As I said earlier, we are to read verses 9 through 11 of Exodus 24 as happening simultaneously. As the men are eating together, the Lord God appears to them. This we believe occurs at Holy Communion. When we understand Jesus to be present among us as we break the bread and drink from the cup. His presence is uniquely with us. A glimpse of his glory is available to us like no other time within our gathering together. Thankfully, the Anglican tradition doesn't apply specific words to the very presence of Jesus among us while we partake of the bread and of the wine, the bread, his body, the wine, his blood. For whenever specific descriptions are given, lines are drawn and Christians divide. Holy communion is to bring God's people together as one, never to divide, unless those who divide are willfully disobedient. I wonder If you have noticed the many narratives in Holy Scripture that tell of a meal being eaten to mark the very unique presence of God. Remember that after Abraham gave tribute to Melchizedek, the priest that Jesus comes from, the order that Jesus comes from, remember what they did afterwards They sat down breaking bread and drinking wine When the two angels came to judge Sodom and Gomorrah, knowing that the angels were a special manifestation of God, Abraham immediately sat them down before a feast where they broke unleavened bread together. After making covenant with each other, the presence of God's peace was marked by Laban and Jacob by sitting down and eating together. And of course, the central part of the Passover is the breaking of unleavened bread and the drinking of wine, marking God fulfilling his covenant promises to save Israel from the angel of death. Early Christian worship, and worship that has been passed down in the Roman tradition, Anglican tradition, Eastern Orthodox tradition. all recognize the appropriate order of Christian worship to end with the breaking of bread and drinking from the same cup. This last spring, during a men's breakfast, the Reverend McCarl shared his appreciation for our liturgy. And during the question and answer time, a gentleman from another Christian church local asked if the Reverend McCarrell was arguing that our liturgy was the only proper way to worship God. I am aware that many Christians ask similar questions, and I understand that it can appear as if Some of us defend our use of Anglican liturgy with earthly pride. An appropriate response to such questions and concerns. That we have as Anglican Liturgy, the Book of Common Prayer Liturgy, what we have is very similar to early Roman worship, Eastern Orthodox worship. And then Lutheran worship, which came later, and then Methodist worship, which came even later than the Lutheran worship The point being that modern Christian worship, modern Christian worship in the West, that is practiced in independent churches today, or churches that want to appear to be independent. That worship is a diverging away from the principles revealed in Exodus 24, with no biblical warrant for doing so. Their diverging has no biblical warrant. When our Anglican liturgy is upheld as a model of how God is to be worshipped It is only in light of how God has commanded that he be worshipped. And what is upheld by us is not what is unique about our worship But actually what we have in common with all other ancient Christian traditions that see that see the same principles here in Exodus 24. After all, God is the same yesterday and today. He is the same God that revealed himself here in Exodus 24. We are privileged to know him today as Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, who calls us to worship, who sets up a hierarchy, who gives us his word, and we respond. Who provides atonement and we repent? Who reveals his real presence when we sit and eat with him I ran across this quote that's actually in your bulletin that for me sums up this sermon in just three sentences It is from G. K. Chesterton. He says, tradition means giving votes to the most obscure of all classes, our ancestors. It is democracy of the dead. Tradition refuses to submit to the small and arrogant oligarchy of those who merely happen to be walking about. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful Father, for our tradition we give you our thanks, not because of its uniqueness. But of what it follows, which are the principles we find in your holy word as you call your people for the first time to worship you. May we, as good stewards, appreciate with all of our hearts, and may we keep it as your will be done. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.
