sermons.title: Heavenly Relevant symbols
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. In this series on corporate worship, Christian corporate worship We have established that God does indeed reject certain forms of worship We learn that there is a preferred order of worship, God Himself established in Holy Scripture. We have seen how our Anglican traditions follow what God established. Making our Anglican traditions heavenly relevant. Today we look at the power of symbolism and how God has used symbols in the context of his people worshiping him. But first, a joke. I have to tell you ahead of time that it's a joke so that you'll know you're supposed to laugh A Jewish father was very troubled by the way his son had turned out, so he went to see his rabbi about it. Rabbi, I brought my son up in the faith, gave him a very expensive barmitsa, and it cost me a fortune to educate him. Then he tells me last week he's decided to be a Christian. Rabbi, where did I go wrong? The rabbi strokes his beard and says, Funny you should come to me. I too brought up my son as a boy of the faith. sent him to university, and it cost me a fortune. And then one day he comes to me and tells me he wants to be a Christian. What did you do? asked the man of the rabbi. I turned to God for the answer, the rabbi replied. What did he say? asked the man. He said, funny, you should come to me. I have some of you laughed at that. My wife didn't think it was funny at all. I like the joke because it mixes together the old covenant and the new covenant. Recently I have been reading Bishop NT Wright's book titled Paul, a biography One of the bishop's arguments that I so much appreciate is that the Apostle Paul did not have a conversion experience To Christianity on the road to Damascus when Jesus appeared to him in that blinding light. Bishop Wright argues that it wasn't a conversion But a proper right progression. For it was God's plan all along for the Jewish people to follow Jesus as their Messiah. God promised a Messiah to the Jewish people within his covenant promises, and Jesus was and is that Messiah. To believe in Jesus was to believe in the covenant that God made with Adam and Noah and then Abraham and through Isaac and Jacob and Judah and then Moses and then David and then Jesus That Jesus is the fulfillment of what is meant to believe in God's covenant with the people of Israel is dramatically stated in the book of Revelation. Where Jesus calls Jewish people who reject him as being members of the synagogue of Satan. Quite a dramatic way to put it. This oneness of the Old and New Testaments allows us to glean from the Old Testament principles regarding how God prefers to be worshipped And we did that extensively last week looking at Exodus chapter 24. Today we peek into the tabernacle, into the temple worship To understand powerful symbols and how God's people can use them to worship Him. And to appreciate symbolism, we first need to address the second commandment. Remember, it condemns the making of raven images, and that such images should not be bowed down to nor worshipped. Here is the commandment in full. Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them. For I, the Lord, thy God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me And showing mercy unto the thousands of them that love me and keep my commandments. Now the middle part of that commandment is important. For some Christians have interpreted the first part of it so stridently that they believe it is a grave sin for any Christian to make any image at all of any likeness of heaven or earth. Historically, such people have been called iconoclasts, for they were of the conviction that it was their duty to destroy images that Christians used to worship God. And it would not be useful for us, or possible for us, to address all of the issues regarding sacred images, for that issue still divides the church today. What we can know for sure is that God was not commanding that no images of any kind should be made And we can know this because God Himself commanded that cherubim should be made of gold and placed on top of the Ark of the Covenant with their wings pointing at one another. Also, the curtains of the tabernacle were to have been decorated with elaborate embroidery depicting heavenly cherubim, which were angelic-like creatures that symbolized God's protection. God therefore was not hypocritically commanding that there be no graven images whatsoever, and next commanding that images of cherubim be used in the holy tabernacle and then in the holy temple So God allows for images to be used for worship. What we need to underline is worship Him as opposed to worshiping an image. Reflect with me how God uses images, symbols for his people to worship him The Ark of the Covenant. The Ark of the Covenant was a profound symbol for God's people as it represented God's very presence among them, amidst them. It contained, you remember, the Ten Commandments, the central doctrine of God's covenant with his people. It contained Aaron's rod that budded so that God's wrath would be turned away It contained a pot of manna reminding the people how God provided for them in the desert. Each item was a reminder of God establishing covenant with his people, Israel, as a whole. Regarding other furnishings that served also as symbols, there was that outer wash basin In the temple court that was used to ceremonially clean so that the priest could properly present the offerings It also pointed to the watching that God would give believers at their baptism when Jesus the Messiah was revealed. There was also the altar where the sacrificed animals were bloodless because the wages of sin is death. That altar pointed to the cross. Inside the curtains of the tabernacle and later the temple was the table of showbread containing twelve loaves representing the twelve tribes. It was an offering to God in thanks for the grain that was received by him every year, and that God was their provider. It also pointed Israel to the Messiah to come who would offer himself as the bread of life Then the lampstand across from the showbread table served as a source of light, of course, while also representing God's presence as he went before the Israelites as a heavenly flame. It also refers to God revealing himself to Moses as a fire in a bush not consuming. And then, of course, more importantly, it pointed to the Messiah who would come as the light of the world. Then there were the garments to be worn by the priests, and especially the high priests, who wore a breastplate of precious stones that were symbols of God's commandments to his people and symbols of what God thought of his people, that they were beautiful, and he was making them beautiful. All of these reference symbols are related to what God has done and was doing and is doing to bring the salvation for his people. The use of symbols representing God bringing salvation to his people is tenfold in the book of Revelation. Where Jesus is exalted with feet of brass, eyes like fire, upholding the seven churches around him, surrounding him like lampstands. In Revelation, we are next in a throne room where Jesus is on the throne, and then he also appears as a lamb before the throne. The 24 elders surround that throne singing, holy, holy, holy, and then taking their crowns and throwing them at the feet of their Christ, their Savior, their God. In the scriptures, a violent sea is a symbol of troubled nations. In heaven, in the book of Revelation, the sea is smooth as glass. Representing Christ having brought peace to the nations. Also, a rainbow can be seen only, a rainbow that's not a half circle, but a full circle. Meaning that God has fulfilled his promises, all of them, to his created order Each depiction of the heavenly scenes tells us a portion of the story of how God saved and is saving his people. All of these symbols from the tabernacle worship to the throne of Christ Jesus are heavenly relevant The question is, are we? Are we heavenly relevant Remember, I quoted a proverb of sorts at the start of this series that says that a grandfather's conviction can become a son's tradition and eventually his grandson's elimination. An example is a trend within contemporary Christian worship that has pastors wearing casual clothes while standing on a stage speaking to the congregation like Tony Robbins at a you can do it positive mental attitude seminar How did that happen? Notice that our traditional setting of chancel furniture has the pulpit on one side of the sanctuary, the lectern on the opposite side. the Holy Communion table in the center, in the back of the chancel. That is purposeful. For it gives a cruciform shape, the shape of the cross, more clearly seen from a bird's eye view. The shape of the cross is thoughtfully made, for it is the cross that enables us to call upon the name of God. The central position of the Holy Communion Table communicates the primary importance of the Holy Meal. That we eat each week to commemorate our covenant with God and where God is manifested to us as we eat of the flesh and drink of the blood. As an overreaction against Roman tradition. Certain Christian gatherings from the time of the Reformation Decided that the Holy Communion table should not be the central focus, but instead it should be the preaching of the Bible. The result was placing pulpits at the center of the chancel And such placing of the pulpit communicates priority, the priority of preaching. With some modern churches, the pulpit is altogether removed, communicating a different priority. What or who is the priority when a man stands in his by his lonesome with his microphone headset, his blue jeans, his untucked shirt, and his talking points. What is the focus? The answer is the man, the man himself. And we should be asking, is the priority of a preacher's personality, is that heavenly relevant? And I submit it is not But it sells. It markets well. There are even Christian gatherings that display a video of a man. Who is in another city, maybe even another state, wearing his blue jeans, his untucked shirt, cordless microphone, displaying his talking points. It is modern church on the big screen. Thousands of professing Christians appear to prefer such a setup, for they attend most Sundays to watch the church service. To watch it. These things have happened. Because nobody knew why the pulpit was placed in the middle of the chancel to begin with. Because no one remembered that preaching of the Word of God was to be a priority The pulpit was placed at the center because people didn't understand why Holy Communion was so important. Because they didn't hear it taught that God preferred to end his time with his people and worship by eating and drinking. And I submit also that the Holy Communion table was removed from the center of the chancel and the focal point of the worship service Because people stopped believing that Jesus was present among his people when they broke the bread and shared the cup. An absence of faith in the real presence of Jesus at the communion table has resulted in placing the personality of a man center stage. And we we can call it a stage because it is not treated as a chancel. The word chancel is from the Latin meaning crossbars. It describes the barriers that were used to distinguish the area that the clergy and the choir worshiped from the nave where the congregation worshipped, and from the altar where the bread and wine were consecrated and consumed. The chancellor. was treated like the holy place in the temple and the altar, the communion table, like the holy of holies. What was done in the chancel area was the leading of worship of God's people with the utmost reverence. Because the clergy pursued reverence, it was necessary that their vestments not represent themselves, but represent the office that they held, or more specifically, the God that they worshipped. Clergy in the Middle Ages learned how effectual their vestments could be at helping the worshipers of God. Wearing two cloaks for warmth turned into wearing a cassock, which is black, representing the sinfulness of the preacher. And then a surplus ovary representing the purity that Christ gives all of us The tiffit or stole worn over the surplus came to represent a yoke that is placed on oxen to plow a field. It was to help the clergy know he is first and last a servant. When leading a full holy communion service, a white robe became, called an owl became a clear choice, for it symbolized the presence of Jesus. The presence of Jesus as the congregation broke bread and drank wine. I have said it many times before Holy Communion proper. That it is Jesus who offers us the bread and the wine, and the white being worn by the clergy symbolizes that reality. And I mentioned the knave, which is where the congregation worships. The knave comes from the Latin nabis, which means shit. Traditionally, Christian sanctuaries lined their knaves with rows of seats or pews to replicate a galley of a ship where the servants would row in unison. To keep the ship moving toward the heavenly shore. The concept of a sanctuary being like a ship comes from Noah's Ark. Which was the vessel God used to save his chosen people from his condemnation of humanity by the flood The church then serves just as the Ark of Noah did for each are vessels by which God's people are saved. Consider that if you remember each time you enter this sanctuary or another like it That you are on this journey toward the heavenly shore together with other Christians. And if you remember that, you are less likely to be selfish, to be unkind, to be unforgiving. Because you know you can't row alone. And we need one another. And we need to stay in the boat. There are other important symbols that when understood add to our appreciation for what God has done for us that we might receive salvation. The fine linen cloth on the communion table is to remind us of the cloth that was used to cover the body of Jesus at his burial. The veiling of the chalice and the patent are symbolic of the cloth that were once covered Jesus when it was found were folded and placed to the side because he was no longer there. He's risen. If you pay close attention, you will see water being poured into the communion wine. That symbolizes that at the suffering of Jesus on the cross, Both water and blood poured from his side as his side was pierced by a spear. Interestingly, it It has been speculated that the water that poured out of Jesus was from the pericardian sac that surrounds the heart, meaning that Jesus died of a broken heart for the sake of his people. There are other symbols and movements you might witness the clergy performing that are part of Anglican custom, that are they're not prescribed in any book of the church order or book of common prayer. They include crossing oneself or bowing while professing the names of the Trinity You might see clergy and laities striking their chest while confessing their sin as a reminder that we are the same as that publican in the story that Jesus told Of the Pharisee who stood before God with a self-righteous heart, while the publicans stayed back of the room, pounding his chest, recognizing he was a sinner in need of God's grace. There are other symbols that are too numerous here to review. But the point of it all remains that each contribute to telling the story of how God has redeemed, is redeeming, and will redeem his people. Are they necessary for worship? No. No. Are we better Christians for using symbols? No, and there's no such thing as a better Christian. Can they be useful tools to heighten our attention upon God while we worship? The answer to that is that God thought so. Let us pray Our Father, once again, for the traditions that have been handed down to us, we do not make them idols And Lord forbid that we ever would. But we thank you that we can look beyond those symbols to the truths that they represent. To your salvation that you have given to us, are giving to us, and will give to us. And so, Father, heighten our attention that we might worship you better all the more. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Embracing the Peculiar
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. One of the characteristics Bobby Lynn and I tried to instill in our children was the embracing of that of being peculiar. By peculiar I don't mean socially awkward. I mean peculiar in the sense of standing out because they did not follow the crowd in terms of what was popular Or what was expected. I wanted them to get used to being thought of and treated as different or odd because as Christians living in a secular world If we are being faithful to the Holy Scriptures in our day-to-day living, we are going to stand out. We are going to be seen as being different. When you don't join the mob think, people will notice and they will pass judgment. When you don't curse or gossip or slander or complain People will notice, and they may even accuse you of being arrogant. When you bow your head in public to pray before each meal, people will notice And they will murmur about your piety. When you simply obey your parents, people will notice and think that you are some type of suck-up. When you don't smoke weed, don't do drugs, don't get drunk, don't commit adultery, people will notice and conclude you are either under the thumb of your parents dying to get away from them, or you are self-righteous and will soon, like the rest of us, be a hypocrite. That is what my children faced when they attended a secular school, and I wanted them to be prepared for it. I prepared them by telling them how different Christians are to be. And how people will notice and by standing out in the manners I just described, they could be a witness to the truth of Jesus Christ without saying a word. By my children embracing being peculiar, they were able to park with pride a rusted $300 pickup. Next to the Mercedes, Luxes, and Jaguars that their school parking lot was filled with. They were able to with humor drive a to school a twenty-five-year-old Cadillac that drove like a boat and wouldn't go in reverse. They were able to laugh at their peers who had asked what they thought were trapping questions such as, what would your dad do if you told him you were gay? They were able to say yes when peers would ask, hey, if I die not believing in Jesus, am I going to hell? Yes. When you know you are different and expect for others to treat you differently, it keeps reality before you and it helps you stay different. Mind you, yes, there is a danger in being different because people can be different for the sake of being different. But Christians are different because of our nature. We are awake. We are no longer dead in our trespasses and sins, but are instead awake. To the life giving Holy Spirit to be able to know God, to love God and to love our fellow man We have God in us, animating our spiritual selves while those who do not believe remain crippled and yes, dead in sin. My premises are that if we are different by our nature, and that we are to embrace being different Leading to the conclusion that our worship of God should be different as well. This is the last in this series of sermons on Christian corporate worship. And here I am espousing a very simple point, which is that our worship should embrace being peculiar. Being different. The logic from the opposite view, I am espousing, goes something like the following. Christians need to corporate worship with God. Many Christians do not attend church services to corporately worship God. Many Christians don't attend because church services are boring The answer is to then make church services more exciting. The church services are more exciting when the people are entertained. No one knows entertainment better than the secular world, so the church should replicate what the secular world does, only make it Christian by adding Christian words with a secular style Fundamentally, the logic of this approach to corporate worship is not flawed. Worship as entertainment can and does draw a crowd. The problem with this type of reasoning and worship is not the logic applied, but the question it fails to address which is whether or not God is pleased with worship that is focused on entertaining. We know that God would not be pleased by worship that is entertaining if it contained the pornographic or the barbarous. But what about circus-type stunts or having special effects? Such things don't break any of God's commandments, do they? What some people are not questioning is whether such questions should be asked. The point is not whether God would allow circus stunts and special effects in a Christian corporate worship service. It is instead to determine whether or not what is being done in a Christian corporate worship service, whether it is heavenly relevant We have established that God does indeed, does indeed reject certain types of worship We have concluded that our worship of God must include obeying Him and loving Him and our fellow man. We have learned that God has given us an order of worship in Exodus 24, which is the very first time Israel worshiped as a people. And we have seen how our Anglican traditions follow that given order. And what I want to accomplish again with this sermon is for all of us young and old to embrace what it means to worship God as a peculiar people. Let us look where Christians are described as peculiar. This is from our epistle reading from 1 Peter. The Apostle Peter has exhorted Christians to lead lives that are morally separate from the unbelieving world. Christians are told to put aside malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, slander, for all are sins of their former lives and sins of the people around them. What they are to replace such sins with is the Word of God. To further implore Christians to live a different kind of life, Peter uses several metaphors such as Christians being as babies longing for pure milk, or hungry so as to want to taste the kindness of the Lord. And because Jesus is the cornerstone, he is to be approached by us as a living stone, that although rejected by men, he is precious before God. And as Jesus is a living stone, so too are Christians to see themselves as stones who are being used by God to build a spiritual house in order to offer up spiritual sacrifices. To Jesus. Jesus as the cornerstone of all that is built up is either the rock upon which all earthly and heavenly lives is built upon or are built upon, or a rock upon which all who do not believe stumble or crash into. And after mentioning those who do not believe and therefore stumble and crash upon the eternal rock of Jesus St. Peter wants to get back to the reason why Christians are to live separate moral lives away from the unbelievers around them. He gets there by identifying them as a chosen people. According to St. Peter, Christians are to identify themselves with Israel, for he quotes here Exodus 19 verse 5. Where God called Israel out of bondage in Egypt to be his very own people, they are chosen by God. And just as God chose Abraham and credited Abraham's faith as righteousness, in the same manner God has chosen an entire people to be his very own. It is God's choice and no one else's. Christians are next called a royal priesthood. As royals, Christians belong to one king. As priests, Christians have been washed clean of sin and are able to stand before God as clean and are able to hear God speak. that are able to serve him as his representatives. Christians are next called a holy nation. The term holy is to be consecrated or set aside, to be used by God for his glory. The term nation reminds us that Christians are not believers separate from other believers, but are instead an entire people who must love one another to continue. As God's people. We are chosen. We are part of a royal priesthood. We are holy and a nation only Only if we are a body and not mere individuals. Christians are next and finally called a peculiar people. That word peculiar does come from the King James Version translation The word or phrase literally in the Greek means a people of special reservation. It is a very personal word. It describes what God owns and what God personally takes care of. He will not share us with anything else. We are his And what are Christians to do with this unique identification, St. Peter gives us? The why question? The why question needs to be answered. What is the point of being chosen, royal, priestly, a holy nation of peculiar people? The answer is in the next phrase in the text. He says, to declare the praises of God. That's the why. To proclaim the excellencies of him who called you to worship God. So if Christians are chosen, royal, priestly, a holy nation, a peculiar people, it follows that the worship of Christians should reflect who they are To put it another way, Christian corporate worship should reflect the people God has made us to be. It should reflect that we are chosen, royal, priestly, a holy nation, and peculiar. To put it another way, Christian worship shouldn't reflect who we are not. We are not unbelievers, and therefore our corporate worship shouldn't look like we are unbelievers. A glaring flaw of the Christian Church for at least the last three decades, probably more. has been an inability to differentiate between Christian corporate worship and outreach And outreach. Modern Christian churches have made times of Christian corporate worship a time of outreach to justify worship styles in terms of recharching, professing Christians, and sharing the gospel of Jesus with unbelievers. They have done so because they understand the purpose of the church is to grow its membership. It is to evangelize. And while evangelism is a responsibility of the church, it is not the why, it is not the purpose of the church. I say again, the purpose of the church, the end goal of the chosen people of God is to glorify God and enjoy him forever. It is to worship God. Christians from every tradition, East or West, should have no problem whatsoever with Christian bands playing music that sounds like secular music, only with words devoted to Christ. when it is played and used as outreach to unbelievers who might like such music. Christians from every tradition should not have a problem with a pastor wearing a cordless microphone and blue jeans and an untouched shirt with his talking points when it's in the context of outreach. There are indeed unbelievers who are more apt to attend gatherings of people who play rock music and who speak in a casual manner and who entertain. It seems to work. But when such settings are called Christian corporate worship, The Bible does not know of such worship, and the church historic does not know of such worship, and those are the only sources of authority that can teach us the proper Christian corporate worship what it should be. Let us consider the words Saint Peter has chosen for God's people in worship Being chosen means that we are going to have a security in our salvation and a trust in God that an unbeliever is not going to have. Being chosen means we are able to celebrate that our salvation is not determined by our ability to keep promises, but by But it's determined by God's ability to keep promises, and wouldn't you rather have it that way Being a royal priesthood means that we are going to take our corporate worship seriously by behaving in a proportionate manner to our status. A royal does not behave like a pauper because the privilege demands more. The priesthood with its privileges calls for dignity to be shown and seriousness to be maintained. As St. Paul has said when addressing Christian corporate worship, Let all things be done decently and in order. As a peculiar people We are going to have verbiage that we only use when we gather together. This is one of the reasons why we use the old text for our book of common prayer. Those who prefer a modern language version have put forth the purpose that no one today uses the language used in those old prayer books. The fact is, no one used said language when the prayer books were first written, for no one used it as a common vernacular. The formal language of the prayer book was chosen because it reflected corporate worship as a unique time for God's people to gather. And it communicated the formality the church believed was needed for those unique times. Admittedly, some of the words are quite archaic to us, and some of them can sound strange and even funny. Do you hear the word succor and chuckle because of the way it sounds and wonder what it precisely means? It means to give assistance or to aid someone. How about dissemble nor cloak? Don't use that very often. Dissemble means to hide true motives. Cloak is to cover rather than reveal. How about absolution and remission? Absolution is a declaration of God's forgiveness, and remission is a canceling of debt owed. How about inestimable? It means too great to calculate What about the use of thou so often when reading the Ten Commandments? To be sure, Thou is an archaic form of the more simple word you. But when it is used in the context of God's founding document for his covenant with his people, and is expected to be followed without excuse, Thou is most appropriate. What about the word oblation? It refers to the thing that is being offered to God. And the mouthful word propitiation. What does that mean? The word propitiation is a mouthful word. And yet there is not another word in the English language that can express that God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself to appease his own wrath. Yes, there are certain words that we use in our Christian corporate worship that unbelievers have a hard time understanding, as do Christians who are not a part of our tradition. The hope is that an unbeliever who worships with us will at least know that our attention, as we gather here, is upon God. And if they are seeking God, and our attention is upon God, then they will find him, for we shall be pointing to him. I recall an advertisement in a local newspaper several years ago. This is a while ago. where a church was starting up and they were meeting at the local freedom hall, just as this parish did many years ago The advertisement showed a cartoon drawing of a church setting where a man was asleep in a pew. Had little Z coming out, you know. And the caption read something like, If this is what you think church is, Come visit us where you will never know you are in church. Any reasonable person Could respond that there is no purpose of going to church if you don't know you're in church Obviously, I am taking the position that when Christians worship, they should know they are attending church Because what we do here is altogether different than what we do at other times and in other places each day of each week. What we do here reflects that we have been chosen and made royal priests and made a holy nation and are a peculiar people. And I began this series warning that if we do not pass on the justifications of why we worship in the manner that we worship, The manner will be lost and replaced by the practical. And what is and will be practical will be less and less meaningful. A parishioner last week sent me a link that provided the following quote that I believe summarizes the burden that God has laid upon my soul. The quote is from the Reverend Dr. Kerr Markwort, Kerr Markwort, a Lutheran theologian who has since passed on. He said the following. Quote, if the liturgy is boring to children, it is usually because the parents do not find it interesting either If children saw adults treating the Sunday service as the most important activity of their lives, they would respect it too. and would never dream of treating it as a pop event to be tinkered with by every Tom, Dick, and Harry. A church which has won the conscientious loyalty of parents, particularly fathers, will have the devotion of their children too. But a church which abjectly capitulates to the whims and tastes of adolescents will have and deserve neither. In this series, I have strived to gain the conscientious loyalty of parents so that you would pass on the principles of corporate Christian worship to the next generation. So that a standard can be maintained that is received by God because it is heavenly relevant I will continue to do so by various means provided to me. But what I have put forth in these series of sermons is the best I have. Let what is true be established in the hearts of God's people, and let what is manufactured burn with the chaff. Amen. Let us pray. Our Father, to you we give thanks for the revelations in your word. that show the manner that you receive that is heavenly relevant when your people gather to worship. Help us to embrace them evermore. And to trust that as they honor you, that we are changed to be like you, for that is what we desire. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Beginning of Beginnings
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: It is a terrible feeling to come up to the pulpit and not see your sermon sitting there. Sorry to disturb like that. I've had to retrieve my iPad. Uh you would be well served to turn to Genesis chapter one So we are going to be covering Genesis chapter one. I begin by making an observation That there is great comfort, a feeling of inner warmth, that comes with the realization that our lives are connected, that there is purpose in our comings and in our goings, our living, our dying. Seeing interconnections and relationships that give our lives meaning and seeing that the meaning of our individual lives is part of a greater meaning, that's marvelous to understand and to behold. I will describe what I mean by way of example. I love my wife. I cannot imagine life in this world to be more complete with anyone else. And as I trace the events that led to our union, I marvel at what apparently needed to take place in order for us to meet, to fall in love, to be married. And the results of our marriage are children who believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and who will live eternally with God And the Lord is now blessing them with love and help meets and children, and those children by the grace of God will believe and live eternally. Bobby Lynn and I are not the centerpiece of the story, of course not. To think otherwise would be arrogant and half-witted. But we are apart. Our lives fit within God's plan for His eternal kingdom. To know, to understand such a truth about our life brings great comfort Now nothing in the story of my life or your life happens by chance. Everything matters. Everything has a reason and a meaning. We might not see it in the immediate. We might not even see it in this life. But it is true. I believe it with all that is within me. And I wish for us to take that belief, that way of thinking, that everything has a reason and a meaning into the context of our next study. I will be preaching over the next several months, the Lord knows how long, from the book of Genesis. It was not too many years ago that we did a Bible study on Genesis. The preaching series we will, in this preaching series we will not be a verse-by-verse study, but instead a recognition of how the stories in Genesis describe how God will save his people. I do so anticipating that you have preconceived ideas about this book of beginnings. Many of the stories are so familiar you might think that you will not hear anything new. However Most sermons preached through Genesis have a moralistic tone about them. For example, Cain was jealous regarding Abel, and that is why he killed him. Thus we should learn from his actions and not be jealous. Those types of lessons are fine, of course, but moralizing everything has limited appeal and does not take much imagination. What I will be adding or attempting to add, you will have to judge for yourselves regarding my success, is a connection between the stories we are told in Genesis to the redemption of mankind through the person of Jesus Christ. Simply stated, I will attempt to reveal the gospel in its various forms within the stories told in Genesis. In doing so, I hope to show an interconnection in relationships, convincing you further that everything has a reason, everything has meaning, everything matters. As we walk through the book of Genesis, my overall goal is for our faith to be increased. We start our study in the beginning, not at, but in the beginning, for that is the first sentence in the text And it is the very meaning of the word Genesis. Genesis means beginnings. In the beginning, God created. We note that such a statement is a definitive statement, and it is one that can only be said about God. No one else creates but God The Hebrew word for creator is bara and is only used in reference to God. We can carelessly use the language of creation when we describe something like a piece of art or architecture. We might say that a certain building is the creation of a certain architect, or a painting is the creation of a certain painter. But in reality, they are simply reconfigures of what has already been created The adjective creator and the verb create can only be attributed to God. God, it says, created the heavens and the earth. The heavens are plural. The heavens are layers. What those layers will be used for will be discovered later. There appears, to the perspective of some, that there is a gap between verses 1 and 2. And verse 1, God created. In verse 2, the earth was without form and void. Is it possible that something happened to make it without form and empty? Of course, it is possible, but we can only speculate. The purpose of the text is not that we might speculate, but accept the fact that the earth was Form was without form and void. It is interesting that words like without form and void and darkness are used by the prophets. particularly Isaiah to describe God's judgment, making it possible that the earth at that time was under God's judgment. Although the earth is described in terms used for judgment, it is not left alone. It is not uncared for. God's Spirit broods over it. The Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters. This is the state of the earth before God's second stage of work begins. Now, before we examine that work, we must pause and notice that the description of the earth is very much like the description of every man who was born to inhabit the earth, who is under the curse of Adam. The soul of a man is without form because he is under the broken covenant of Adam and therefore born a sinner. Our souls by themselves are utterly lifeless. The soul cannot respond to goodness, but is only prone to evil, and that continually, the scripture says. There is no one good, no not one. All we like sheep have gone astray. Each has turned to his own way. Men are dead in their trespasses and sins. The condition of mankind led the writer of the Ecclesiastes to pronounce that life is vanity, vanity of vanities, says the preacher, vanity of vanities, all is vanity. Empty. The life of mankind is absurd. It is futile. It is even nonsense. It is without form. It is void, void of meaning. And darkness. Darkness covers the life and heart of a man. His heart is blackened by sin, and the blackness overwhelms his environment. The heart of man is so very black that he cannot do good for his fellow man without being motivated by his own interest. Everything man does is smudged by the black that is on his hands. And yet, although man, like the earth at the time of creation, was without form and void, and blackness covered the deep. So it covers the deep of the heart of man. But God's Spirit hovers. God's Spirit hovers over the heart of man The creature is helpless, but God is very near. Theologians call the hovering of the Spirit of God prevenient grace. Such grace is that which comes before. It is grace that is present while the sin of man is present. It is present before a man is forgiven. It reveals that God must be first to break man out of his sin. God must go before. God must initiate. Man cannot change his own formless, empty, darkened state. For man to be born anew, to be born again, as Jesus described it, he must be born from above. To change the earth's form, to fill its void, and to pierce the darkness. Genesis tells us that God speaks Then God said, Let there be light, and there was light. There is power in God's word spoken. When God speaks, it is true. It cannot be other. God speaks a word and it pierces the darkness. This is why in John's Gospel Jesus is described as the Word. To give the world form, to fill its void, and to pierce the darkness, God spoke words To give form to the dead souls of men, to fill the emptiness of the hearts of men, and to pierce the darkness brought on by sin, God spoke the word. He spoke Jesus, and there was light. In both the creation of the world and the redemption of man, the new transformation is the work of the word. Speaking of Jesus, we are told in him was life, and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness. As the creative work of God began, so it continues. God speaks and forms. He speaks and fills void He speaks and divides. As his work of transformation is described, we notice that it is progressive. Not culturally progressive, mind you. But that it was done not all at once, but in six successive days was creation perfected In nature, we we first have the first the blade and then the ear and and and then the full stock of corn to progress. So it is with grace. The birth of a new man is the beginning point. And there is much to grow into, and we should not forget that such growth takes time. A man is not fully mature, showing the glory of his Creator until he has grown, until he has endured. We cannot rightly judge another or even ourselves while we take shape, while we progress. St. Paul said as much when he told the Corinthians just that, that he did not even judge himself Each step, each phase is moving us closer and closer to the image of our Creator. Let us wait in patience. Knowing that he who has begun a good work in you will be faithful, faithful to complete it. The final thing we will notice about God's work of transformation is that it occurs in two great parts The first work of the first three days, which we read in our Old Testament reading, is certainly connected, but differs from the work of the last three days. In each half the order is the same. We are to notice that. The difference is that in the first three days the work is setting boundaries and dividing. In the last three, the work is furnishing and adorning. The setting of boundaries is like restraining. It is God placing parameters upon his creation. The character of each of his creations is then marked with a name. With the giving of each name in creation, we are privy to the thoughts of God. On the first day, light shines out and is divided from darkness. Thus, darkness at once is bound or is given parameters. Then light and darkness are each given a name. God called the light day and the darkness night. On the second day, God made the firmament and divided the waters. The firmament is separated from the earth, as it is, as it were, and is a boundary is set. It is divided within itself, leaving waters below and waters above. And God called the firmament above heaven. On the third day the land appears and is divided from the seas, but are given their boundaries as they are divided. God did this. He gave the dry land a name, earth, and the waters he called the seas. After each of these days he pronounces that what he has done is good. All is good, but not all is finished. After God has set boundaries and divided, he begins to furnish and adorn. The fourth day, he works to furnish what he created the first day. With the objects of illumination. In the firmament of the heavens, he made two great lights, one to rule by day and the other to rule by night. These objects are not merely practical, but beautiful in their own right. Their illuminating effects cause effects cause the rest of creation to sing, to call out. Since the first time mankind has experienced these heavenly effects, they have brought men and women to tears, inspired sonnets, and melodious compositions, because of their beauty. On the fifth day, God fills the firmament he divided on the second day with living creatures. He created creatures that fly above the earth, and great sea creatures that live within the waters. Each according to its kind God created. He did not make one like the other, but created them with numerous shapes, sizes, and colors. Their forms and colors became standard bearers for what is beautiful, bright, and cheery. On the sixth day, God furnished and adorned what he created the third day: the land, the earth. He made every living creature according to its kind. He made creatures that creep, that crawl, that walk on four feet and two. He made some with fur and some without. He made some with toes, some with hoofs, and some with slit hoofs He made some pink, some gray, some yellow, some orange, some spotted, some striped, and some with no markings whatsoever. And he made the most beautiful creature, wonderful creature of all. A creature made in his own image. God made man on the sixth day. In the image of God he created him, male and female, he created them. And when he was finished, God looked upon all that he had created and said, it was very good. The division of the six days of creation into two parts, each consisting of three days, is to be understood in light of our spiritual regeneration. Those who follow Christ, who who press on to the perfect man, as Paul calls it, will readily know the importance of three days. Just as creation must be bound to set boundaries and then divided so that every man be there be for there to be much about ourselves that needs to be bound. Parameters must be placed upon us so that we will not be led astray. We are warned by the apostle to flee from the sins of our youth We are to no longer live for ourselves, but to die the self, to live to God. The body and the spirit are at odds. The body needs to submit to the spirit Our minds and our tongues are to be placed in parameters as well. We are to be renewed in our minds and bridle our tongues, being quick to listen, slow to speak. As new creations, we are submitting to have what was once natural to us restraint. At the same time, we are taught to call things as God calls them. And after this, when we have submitted and called things as God does, it is the third day. It is resurrection day. The work to fill and to adorn is ready to begin. Jesus told the parable, and we read it in our New Testament reading. of the man who had multiple evil spirits cast out of him. When the evil spirits left, they roamed for a time, failing to find a body to inhabit. They decided to go back to that man again, although they found his body clean, swept clean He had not been filled by the Spirit of God. And so they entered him, more numerous than before. Jesus uses the parable to teach us of the importance of being filled with the Spirit of God. Getting rid of evil, placing parameters in one's life is only the beginning. We must be filled with the Spirit, the Spirit of God. We must replace evil vice with good. We must be adorned with good works. Just as there is variety in the shapes and sizes and colors of God's other creative works, and within those works is natural beauty So does God adorn man with the beauty of righteous works. A man who has been adorned by God is a beautiful man. He is aesthetically pleasing to look upon, being righteous in all of his ways. God looks upon him and says, it is very good. I have tried to speak somewhat poetically to what I will now state plainly. The creation account in Genesis chapter 1 is a parallel, a parallel to the new creation account of a man's soul. God's pattern of work seen in creation is the same pattern as what he does in redemption. It all fits. The same God who creates makes us new creations. We are darkened by sin, and yet his spirit broods over us. We are formless and void, and he speaks the living word Jesus Christ to give light and life to our souls. He places boundaries to restrain us And once resurrected with Christ, he adorns us with righteousness. And as he does with all he creates, he gives us, the scripture says, a new name. From now on, when we think upon God as creator, I trust we will include our salvation. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God, we thank you, Holy Spirit, for opening our eyes to see a story of creation Of this earth that we live and enjoy, see also the new life you give to each one who calls upon you. May we praise you all the more to realize you have made us new creations. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: The Lord Provides
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We continue our preaching through the book of Genesis. We are in Genesis chapter 2, which is where our epistle reading came from. It is well discussed and defended that the basis for the fall of humanity by way of our first parents Is and was the sin of pride. Eve wanted to be like God, and then Adam wanted to be like God, and then Humanity became much less like God than before because humanity sinned, all of humanity sinned when Adam and Eve sinned. But chapter 2 of Genesis reveals a sister sin to pride at the fall. The sin of choosing to be discontent. Consider how more subtle being discontent is to the sin of pride. The sin of pride is usually outwardly manifested. It has to be because at the heart of pride is selfishness. And that means the person is concerned about him or herself first and last, resulting in decisions being made, thoughts being focused upon, while figuring out the question, what is in this for me? Choices are made in accordance with the prideful person, what they perceive is best for him, and the selfish acts that follow can be viewed by others. Choosing to be discontent in comparison starts and can stay within a person. It can reside in the mind and the soul without anyone else noticing. It is only after a person acts out his or her discontentment that anyone can know that the sin was present. Without being seen. And the acting out may not appear to be discontentment. It can look instead like lust or greed or simple disobedience But it starts in the heart with being discontent. Consider a woman who has a broken marriage because of the sin of her husband. He is a habitual drug user. The woman and mother is a professing Christian and is protective of her children and she wants to stay away from the influence of the father so she separates from her husband to protect her children and herself from her husband's blatant lawbreaking. She lives in celibacy and provides for her children. God helps her into a good-paying job and a nice home. But loneliness grows within her as she longs more and more for companionship, both physically and socially. She meets a man who is not a Christian, but offers the companionship that she craves. God has said that she should not be unequally yoked, and that he can be sufficient for her during her time of trial. But what she wants, she wants now. And what she has, she wants more of. And so she ignores the scriptures. She ignores the authority of the church, such as not only ignoring the church but her own conscience. And she chooses the unbeliever. And such is not a made-up story, but one of many that I have witnessed as a pastor. The devil is most certainly aware of the enticement, the enticing power of the sin of being discontent. God is well aware of the enticing power of the temptation to be discontent, and so he gives us what can easily make us content. He first gives humanity rest. After six days of created work, God establishes his creation with a day of rest. He didn't have to rest, for he tells us through the prophet Isaiah that he does not grow weary or tired He does not sleep. Sleep is for the temporal. God is not temporal. He is eternal. The eternal does not need to rest And yet he rested on the seventh day. And by doing so, he sanctified the seventh day, making it holy, making it a day for being holy, for us practicing to do holy things. The seventh day being holy is later solidified as being part of God's covenant with his people. It is the fourth commandment where God says, honor the Sabbath day and keep it holy. It is to be understood as a day for humanity. It is a day every human needs to be able to find reprieve in order to be well in serving God in the next six days that follow. It is a day, Jesus taught, that is for mankind. The Sabbath is made for man, not man for the Sabbath. The Sabbath then serves us. It enables us to be more physically healthy, more mentally healthy, and more spiritually healthy. The Sabbath puts our human lives in proper order regarding priority. God's order of time is regarded as right and necessary. When we remember the Sabbath, we remember God and we remember the one who created the day to remember Him. From the revelation of Jesus as Messiah, we learn that the Sabbath is not only a day that enables us to rest and therefore to properly prioritize our lives. It is also a type of eternal rest that God promises for those who follow Jesus as Lord and Savior. And not only is the Sabbath a type of heavenly rest, but we are to understand that Jesus himself, his person, is a Sabbath rest. For he gives rest to the souls of men. Souls that before the forgiveness of God through Jesus, souls are blotted, marred, scarred, troubled, and in turmoil. What Jesus provides the soul is rest, a rest that is better experienced than described, for it brings a calm to the seared conscience and a hope of a guilty heart. These aspects of the Sabbath as it serves us are targets of the devil, prime, prime targets. The devil has worked on you and will continue to work on you to tempt you to be discontent with all that the Sabbath means to your understanding of time. He tempts you to be discontent with the era you live, as you contemplate that the decades before you, this before this present day, were much better and you would have been much happier if you would have lived only in those times. He makes you discontent with the time you spend at work, trying to get you to think about jobs you don't have or that would be a lot better than the one you do, even though it provides all that you need. The devil tries to make you discontent with time in terms of your social and recreational life. He tells you to live for the weekends and then complain about how fast they go when Monday comes around. The devil and his demons tempt you to find something, anything to do on Sunday besides worshiping God. The devil loves football on Sundays. He loves soccer on Sundays, basketball on Sundays, baseball on Sundays, fishing on Sundays, air shows on Sundays, traveling on Sundays, visitors on Sundays, and for you to feel that there is not enough Sunday fun days in your ear. He entices you to want every day to be a Sunday fun day, and that they don't have anything to do with God Because the Sabbath day is a type of heavenly rest for believers, the devil next tempts us to be discontent with the hope of heaven. The promise of heaven for those who believe in Jesus is to be one of the greatest motivations for us to remain faithful to our God. And so the devil attacks it. He attacks it by getting us to imagine heaven as boring, probably like listening to Pastor Eric's sermon. Who wants to do that? He attacks it by getting us to imagine heaven as merely existential or too difficult to attain. He wants heaven to be so very surreal to us that it is unreal, and that we should want something more or at least something different. He tempts us to be discontent with heavenly hope. And the third way we are tempted to be discontent with the Sabbath. is for us to be discontent with Jesus himself. Immature Christians can sound a great deal like an atheist And that atheists spend a great deal of time arguing against something they say doesn't exist. In the same manner, immature Christians will complain about the manner God loves them while not believing God loves them at all. The devil works to get us to ask the why questions. Why did this have to happen to me? Why don't I feel different? Why does everything happen to me or not happen to me? The devil tries to convince us that we can stand in judgment of God, for we can do a better job at running the universe better than he is doing. When professing Christians take such a posture in front of God, he or she is saying that Jesus is not enough. What Jesus did was not enough. What Jesus said was not enough. What he taught was not enough. How he loved with his arms stretched wide was not enough. And we should be reminded here of the disciples that we read in our gospel reading who no longer followed Jesus because what he was teaching was too hard for them to understand. For them, Jesus wasn't what or who they thought he should be and they walked away. If people can be discontent with the man who spoke living words, then people can be discontent with anything. In Genesis chapter 2, not only did God provide the Sabbath for his people, he also provided a help meet for Adam. Male and female, he created man. When Adam named the creatures of the earth, he realized that he was alone. He didn't have a mate, like all the other creatures did. Now, consider that this is actually a good discontentment. This is a righteous discontentment. For Adam sees that that his soul needs something. Just like a man when he realizes he needs God, that's a righteous discontentment. And so man can righteously be be discontent in recognizing his need for companionship. In this case, a woman. God wants us to want more when it is applied to his will. He wants us to be discontent about not having enough of his kingdom, not having enough of his righteousness. For Adam, it was God's will that he would want more and that he would get more, and once he got more, she alone would be enough. The poets and theologians have recognized how appropriate it was for the woman to be created from the side of Adam. She is not of his head to rule over him, or of his feet to be under him, but by his side. She is his helpmeet. Adam needs help and Eve needs help, needs to be helped, excuse me, needs to help. She is for him and he is for her. She is from his side also, for she is from what is closest to his heart. She thus becomes a source for his love and unity and wholeness. And God gives them unity and wholeness by making the two become one. We should be careful here, for man by himself does not need a woman, nor does a woman need a man to bear the image of God. Each bears the image of God within themselves, by themselves. When God makes them one, it is a spiritual unity that cannot be broken in this life. It cannot be broken because the word God made is based on covenants. And a man and a woman becoming one is a covenant designed and blessed by God. St. Paul writes of an interdependence men and women have for one another. Woman comes from man in the beginning and then men come from women in every birth since the beginning. The interdependence is where true equality resides, as well as being in Christ, for we are told by Paul, in Christ there is neither male nor female, but all are one under Christ Jesus. But humanity isn't content with male or female, nor with one man and one woman. No, humanity thinks it can do better than God, so we make up new categories. Most have heard of the LBGT categories, standing for lesbian, bisexual, gay, or homosexual, and transgender. Today there is a gender, which uses the A as a negation to stand for not identifying with any gender There is the big gender that supposedly allows a person to identify as both male and female at the same time. There is gender fluid, which supposedly allows a person to identify with either male or female, depending on the situation and how they feel. There are other categories, but these I have listed cover most people who used extra categories Now let it be clearly understood that people who struggle with identity issues are not to be laughed at. scorned, mocked, jeered, or treated in any way as less than a person who in them has the image of God. Compassion should be given for a person who struggles with his or her identity. But such persons who struggle with identity do not have the right or the authority to make new categories of gender. To be discontent with what God has established might be a great deal of the problem they are having, or a cause that they are having, a cause of their identity struggle. So there they were, Adam and Eve together in a garden that contained all that they needed for life and for godliness. It was all at their disposal to feast upon, to frolic, to be free with one another and with all of God's creation. All but one thing. God had set parameters around them so that when they stayed within those parameters they could enjoy it all. And with peace of conscience and heart, all but one thing. And it is the one thing that the devil used to entice with feelings of discontentment. Now I say feelings of discontentment because it could not have been anything else. For Adam and Eve to succumb to the temptation to be discontent could not have been physical because everything they needed was provided for them. There was no physical need. It could not have been a logical temptation for being discontent while having everything needed does not make logical sense. It had to be an emotional temptation. Adam and Eve were tempted by the devil to feel discontent, leading them to want what they could not have and did not need. It is an irony of the human condition that what we feel, the emotions we have, are a great deal of what it means to be human. And yet, they are the least trusted part of us as humans. Our feelings cannot and should not be trusted as authoritative. And yet all of us allow them to rule us from time to time, and sometimes even to the point of sinning because of what we feel. The devil is aware of Genesis chapter 2, in that he knows it presents the building blocks for human societies. The building block of man and a woman becoming one, having children and subduing creation so that their family can grow and flourish. The building block then is attacked. If the devil can break up the man and the woman, he can control societies and the cultures they built. And he attacks the building block of a man and a woman who are one flesh by tempting them to be discontent with one another. God counters by telling men to enjoy the wife of your youth. He speaks of love between a man and a woman as a beautiful example of his love for his people. He instructs men to love their wives as Jesus loves the church, and for wives to respect their husbands as they are to respect the Lord. He then instructs through Paul that women should give their bodies to their husbands and their husbands, their bodies to their wives, so that the devil cannot tempt them to want desire someone else. It is all there for married couples to be content. And yet the temptation to be discontent has a hold on many. Many who even claim that Jesus is their Lord and Savior. A clear message in Genesis chapter 2 is that God is always providing enough for his people to be content. But it is it is by faith that God's people, we as God's people, are to trust that what He has given us is enough. Hear these many passages of promise and have faith. From Philippians chapter 4, verse 19. And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in the glory of Christ. From Matthew 6, verses 31 and 32. Therefore do not be anxious, saying, What shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or what shall we wear? For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. From Matthew chapter 7, verse 11. If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your will your Father, who is in heaven, give you good things to those who ask of him? From Luke chapter 12, verse 24, consider the ravens. They neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds? From Psalm 34, verse 10, the young lions suffer want of hunger, but those who seek the Lord lack no good thing. And finally, from 2 Corinthians 9 verse 8, and God is able to make all grace abound to you So that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work. May we abound in every good work. Let us pray. Our Father, we at this time together acknowledge your goodness, your provision, that you have given all that we need for life and godliness. Father, forgive us for times of being discontent. Remind us of its danger. Remind us of the way the devil attacks us to tempt us to be discontent. And may we always remember and focus upon the promises you give and have fulfilled. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Adam is us as Eve is us
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.source_file: Adam is us as Eve is us.txt
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We are continuing our series for the book of Genesis, and I want to commend Mr. Ray Harmer for his reading of the book of Genesis this morning. And then I want to apologize that I wrote down the wrong chapter. But we can we we can make the best of this By simply saying that you receive a commercial for next week's sermon. You'll have an opportunity to look forward to hear about Cain and Abel Actually, we are in Genesis chapter 3. So if you would turn there, Genesis chapter 3 The book of Genesis, studied from a sterile view, can be understood as etiological. Etiology is the study of causes, origins, or reasons why things are the way they are. If you want to know why a week consists of seven days, the answer is in Genesis. If you want to know how sin entered the world, the answer is in Genesis. If you want to know how different languages started, the answer is in Genesis. If we want to know how certain men are skilled to perform different callings in life, the answer is in Genesis. If we want to know how and why God chose the nation of Israel as his people, the answer is in Genesis. And there are other questions answered, of course. Of those other questions, I wish to answer two of them. The first is, how are we similar to Adam and Eve in that their sin becomes our sin? Ask in a less mature fashion, how is it fair that we who come after Adam and Eve are said to be guilty of their sin? The second question I wish to answer is how did God provide for Adam and Eve and for us to be forgiven of sin? I will attempt to answer these questions in a non-sterile manner. The first principle to understand when asking such questions is that God does not allow his creation to consider at any length what could have or would have happened in either history or our personal life. It is not for us to know what might have been, but to accept what is and respond accordingly. For example, we could spend a lot of time speculating about what the world and humanity would be like if Adam and Eve had not sinned. To do so would be a silly endeavor, for sin is such Has corrupted so much that we would be trying to explore the counsel of God, and such counsel of God cannot be contained by the human mind. It is enough for us to acknowledge what is, not what could have been. And what is, is that Adam and Eve sinned. But how or why is their sin our sin? That is the question we begin with. Within the characters found in the garden, each of us should see ourselves. Every person can see himself or herself in the garden doing the very thing that Adam and Eve did when they disobeyed God, his one, one negative commandment. When I am finished explaining myself, you will see that whenever a person sins, whether it be a sin of commission or omission, things done or left undone. What is here set forth in Genesis is also within all of us, within us. In the Garden of Eden, man, or Adam, for Adam is translated man. Adam represents understanding. The woman, Eve, represents the human will. And the serpent represents animal faculties or the emotions that are within us. When someone, anyone, male or female, is tempted It is the will that is first addressed, what you want to do. Eve represents the will of a person, and she is approached by the serpent, which represents the emotions within us. Because of the will, emotions are felt. We choose. The will, mixed with emotions, become passions. The first passion stirred up by emotion within Eve was independence. She wanted to be independent. If the will stood firm, the temptation would be overcome. But the will yields, and that becomes self-will, doing what I want. If humanity embodied in Eve could have been stopped at that moment, preventing the will from influencing the understanding, then Eve, and then Adam would not have been, would not have eaten the forbidden fruit. Yet the will seduces understanding, Adam. In every fall, which is to say every sin, the heart perverts the head. Unfortunately, we learn only after a fall, a sin, just how we have been overtaken by our passion. It could be a simple instance of yearning for peer approval, and the emotion of pride rises in us. We choose to follow it, and a passion of selfishness overcomes our understanding, and the result is Something as simple and yet hurtful as saying something to someone hurtful that we have said before that we loved. St. James in his epistle described it this way: that each one of us tempted when he is drawn away by his own desires and enticed. Then when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin, and sin when it is full grown brings death. Simply identifying the serpent as emotions, the woman as the will, and Adam as understanding Does not help us recognize as deeply as we should what is happening when a person sins We need to further identify how the devil appeals to our emotions, thus making them passions and then influencing our wills. The serpent, an embodiment of the devil in the garden, challenges the strongest emotion of all. God's love. The serpent tempts Adam and Eve to doubt God's love. He does this with great subtlety, suggesting that God's commandment not to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, that that was imposed upon man by God's power. He's making you, he's forcing you Rather than it being ordained and given in love. By saying, has God said, You shall not eat? The devil is as much saying begrudgingly, God cannot really love you To inflame the woman's doubt of God's love, the serpent keeps out of her sight what God has done. His countless gifts and the proofs of his love that are all around her. He fixes her instead on the one thing denied. And again, this is subtle. He does not come out and say, God does not love you, or don't pay attention to the many blessings that you have received around you. He instead poses his temptation as a question, and by doing so awakens hard and evil thoughts within Eve she didn't have before. She does it within Eve, and he does it within us. We thus come away thinking that we have come to the conclusion on our own when we truly haven't. The hard truth is, if we question what God does, we judge God. We get out of our place as worshipers and as servants, and we put him out of his place. As simple as the question of the serpent was, did God really say? He was drawing Eve to judge God rather than to worship him. For we learned from our study in worship that obedience is a form of worship. Instead of worshiping God, the woman chooses to interact with Satan. This sounds dramatic, and it was. The ultimate goal of the devil is first to have men cease worshiping God and then turn and worship him. He can accomplish the first part by asking simple questions that distract. Where was God when that hurricane struck? How could God allow a crazed gudman to kill those people? What kind of God would allow my loved one to contract cancer? These questions are worth answering if they come from a troubled soul looking for hope. When they come from within To usurp God's authority, they should be recognized as the temptation to distract us from worshiping God. If ever you need to be convinced about how easily we humans are distracted, simply drop a hymnal on the floor in the middle of a solemn portion of a worship service. Heads turn in that direction from where the sound came as soon as the waves strike the ear. It is unfortunately necessary for me to lecture sometime in the year our students of the Academy who have a hard time sitting still and paying attention for a mere 30 minutes each morning for morning prayer. I have to remind them that loud noises, whisperings, constant movement, and so forth are distractions that take other students' attention away from God and place it on the noisemaker. You are aware, I trust, how important I believe our time of worship is every Sunday. I attempt to limit the distractions as much as possible, for I know how easy it is for us to focus our attention on on something, anything, other than the one that deserves our full attention. And each of us should be wary of this for our actions, our words, our postures and so forth can be distractions to worship if we draw attention to ourselves rather than to God When we do so, we are doing as Eve did, which is dialoguing with the serpent rather than speaking to and listening to God What we can see by examining Adam and Eve in this way is that the passions stirred up within them that overwhelmed their understanding and resulted in sinful actions follows the same example, same pattern of our experiences. We identify with Adam and Eve because we are led to sin in the same manner. When Adam sinned, we all sinned. Now genetically, we can say we sinned because his makeup is our makeup We should be humble enough to say that what happened in the garden would not have happened differently whether it was Adam or a man named Mark or Jeb or Tom. Besides, genetically, we are also guilty of sin because we are under God's covenant with Adam. Adam represents the human race. God's manner, his pattern is such that he relates to his creation by way of covenant. God made a covenant with man that if he sinned, he would die. Man sinned, and so all who are born into the covenant God made with man, all of them die. To ask further questions such as, well, why can't each man have their own covenant with God instead of falling under Adam's covenant? Or why did God create man with a capacity to sin in the first place? To ask such sins, uh questions, excuse me, is to go beyond our comprehension Questions like these can only be answered in the manner of St. Paul, who said, You remember, O man, who are you? To reply to God. Will the thing formed say to him who formed it, Why did you make me like this? Does not the potter have the power over the clay? From the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor? The questions are rhetorical because the answers are obvious. Again, we are to accept how things are, not how we think they should be. The amazing grace of God in his response to the sin of man after Adam and Eve sinned, they immediately became aware of their nakedness. Have you ever wondered why? We can understand this revelation in two parts. First is the physical realm, where we can imagine That the glory of God that once shone upon them as a result of God walking amidst them, that that glory is gone. We can reasonably assume that just as the face of Moses shone brightly when he came down from the mountain after being in God's presence. And you remember Jesus coming down from the Mount of Transfiguration, glowing with God's glory. So did Adam and Eve. But it was after they sinned, the glorious glow left them. The second part we can understand in terms of exposure Their sin exposed their mortality. They are mortal when they do not have access to the tree of life They are mortal in and of their own strength. The sowing of fig leaves to make for themselves aprons is an understanding of their lack of strength. Man cannot bear his sinful condition as if to carry it. He cannot change his sinful condition. The only thing he has left is to try to hide himself. But of course, hiding himself is not repentance. Modern man does not sow fig leaves to hide, but we hide just the same. We hide behind excuses. We hide behind others. We hide in our own psychological world. Of course, hiding does nothing before the eyes of Almighty God, who sees everything The description of God looking here for Adam does not mean that he fails to see, like he doesn't know. It is a relational act on God's part to reveal to Adam, to all of mankind, that God seeks out the sinner. God is like the woman who looks for the lost coin or the shepherd who goes after that one sheep. He is the father who looks for the wayward son to come home. God looks for Adam. He calls out to communicate what? To communicate his love. Where are you? This also is God initiating relationship. His voice is drawing men back to him. It is a first step, and God makes that first step. His call is to convict of sin in order to lay a foundation for full restoration. The response of man to God's call for him and God's question for him, well, his response is quite embarrassing. He blames the woman. And he even blames God for giving him the woman, that woman you gave me. The response of the woman is embarrassing as she blames the serpent. But we are to notice that she follows the lead of the man in her response of blame. Therefore, each of their punishments fits their crime. For Adam, the curse is upon his work, and thus upon the world. For Adam, instead of creation, that is the ground, the creatures of the ground and the creatures of the sky. that they all provide for Adam for all of his needs, they now become a source of his suffering. The curse is why we have disasters. The curse is why we have disease. The curse is why life is difficult. The woman's curse is that she would first be in subjection to her husband. You recall that she was created to be a helpmeet. She was to be by his side as his most important ally. Instead, she decided to usurp her husband's authority by first conversing with the serpent and then follow his lead rather than the lead of her husband. Adam in turn follows her lead and eats instead of leading her away from the serpent. The result is a curse upon the woman, desiring Her husband's place, her husband's position in the marriage. But as the Lord says, the husband will rule over her. If you wonder why there is stress and strife between the sexes and why marriage has marriages become troubled, here is your answer. When a woman desires the authority of her husband and he acquiesces his God-given duty to lead, there is a strange spirit in the home. A spirit that confuses children and manifests itself in subtle but significant ways and that carries on to the next generation. Although God curses, he also provides. He first provides a promise.
