Failures, too, are seen, such as we never see in the prudent, worldly man. The pilgrim learns what is in his heart He cannot easily forget what his pilgrimage has taught him of his own weaknesses. Once he might, like Eve, have believed the word, ye shall be gods. Pilgrimage has proved that even faith is not a God, but only a vessel to receive God. While it is confirmed that Abram was a pilgrim, he is more also. Abram builds an altar. He is a worshiper. He worships in the midst of his trial, his wanderings, and in response, God appears to him. God has to. God promised he would. God appears to strengthen the call he first gave Abram. The land will be given to Abram's descendants. And the focus upon that promise is the word descendants. Abram is to understand that the changes he goes through, the experience he has, the trials he faces, and the seclusion he will know because he is different than any other man Is to be done not for his personal benefit in this life, but for the benefit of his descendants It is a man or woman of strong character who can sacrifice his or her pleasures in this life to better the lives of his or her descendants. It should be the way of every Christian to work toward benefiting those Christians who follow after us. And after God appears to Abram, another trial comes. A famine is in the land of promise. The land that will be known as flowing with milk and honey suffers famine. This is not the way it is supposed to be. Abram could easily have convinced himself that he's made a mistake. It's all been a big mistake He did not hear the voice of God like he thought he did when he was called to leave his city of Ur. And in response to his trial, Abram goes down to Egypt. He goes down to a land he hears has food. He walks in the steps that Jacob will soon take after him. And before he goes to Egypt, Abram prepares for the worst. And so he conjures up a lie to protect himself and leave his bride, his beloved bride, exposed. Abram fails here. Isn't that an understatement? There is no other way to look at it. He fails. He does not protect his bride. He does not think of her well-being before his own. He sins. As you know, God reveals what Abram has done by cursing Pharaoh's household. God's grace restores Sarai to Abram. God's grace restores her. It is an unmerited favor of God toward Abram that not only is Sarai restored, but Abram is not killed by Pharaoh and was allowed to keep his possessions. The only thing Abram has done, the only part he has played to be blessed like this, and for his descendants to be blessed, the only thing he had done right was get out As the years passed on, and the line of Abram became the line of Abraham, a child was born to one of his descendants. The child and his parents went to Egypt, like Jacob, before them, like Abram, only to flee, not to flee, excuse me, a famine, but to flee death, for Herod was after him. When it was saved, the child, the Christ child returned. While in Egypt he was not a slave like his ancestors, but came from there. To free the descendants of Abraham from their sin. While in Egypt he did not deny his beloved, but came from there to call his bride, to call his church to himself. Just as God revealed himself to Abram, calling him out from among a fallen world, and promising that he would make him a great nation. So he continues to call us, to call us out, to tell us to get out. To come out, to repent, and to follow. And when he does, he also says, I will. I will give you rest. I will be with you. I will never leave you or forsake you. We only have to get out. So let us get out. Amen. Our gracious and merciful God, we thank you for this call. And I pray, dear Lord, for these in this congregation who have not gotten out Who have not put to death those things that are of the flesh behind them. May this day be that day. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen

sermons.title: Separating from immaturity
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated If you'll join me turning in your Bibles to Genesis chapter 13, we will actually be coming chapter 13 and chapter 14. Chapter 13 and 14. A most difficult decision to make is choosing the right school for your child. And each child being unique means that one particular school might not meet the needs of all of your children I emphasize to every parent here that giving your children an education where Jesus is at the center is a duty God has given you, and you must not fail in such a critical area of life. The most difficult problem for all of us is where to send our children to school when they are of high school age. There is the homeschool route, which usually includes some sort of co-op arrangement to get to those classes where mom and dad might not be able to teach so well It may be a private Christian school. You may choose a private secular school or the public school. Each choice has its own pitfalls, and the most dangerous pitfall when it comes to a Christian school or a Christian co-op school is for the parents and students to expect Everyone else that attends to have the same morals and the same faith that you do. They don't, and they won't. And if you let your guard down, the devil will throw a pretty nasty left hook. When we sent the majority of our children to a private secular school for high school, we knew That we could not expect all of our Christian values to be upheld or even respected. They were not, but we were able to use those to our advantage. By talking openly to our children regarding what to expect and how to combat it, how to keep Christ at the center of their understanding. And this helped when we sent some of them away to college, for we knew we had given them the mental and spiritual tools to fend off the sins that are so prevalent among today's young. What you cannot be sure of, however, when your children move away to college or get a new job and move uh out of your home What we cannot be sure of is whether he or she will follow the faith that you have so diligently trained them to believe when they are on their own. What will be determined is if they will follow Christ or no And I say or no, because if they do not follow Christ, it does not matter what they follow, because all other roads lead to damnation. This is not to say that your children are not now following Christ, but only to say that with the greater freedom With the greater freedom, there is more opportunity to set priority that is different than what you have taught them. When they are on their own, they determine what their daily and weekly schedules will be, and they will be making the moral decisions. And moral dilemmas will be flying at them at the speed of sound, and the decisions they will make will determine whether they continue to follow Christ or no. On the one hand, that is a burden for parents, and we may repeatedly impress upon our children the gravity of their upcoming independence While on the other hand, knowing that such separations are necessary in order for them to mature into God-fearing men and women And such is what we want for all of our children. All believing parents want this. We want our children to take up the faith, not just while they're living in our homes. But when they establish their own homes, if just one of my children chooses to follow another road other than the one that is that narrow road I would consider my parenting, and yes, even my life, to be a failure. And that statement places pressure upon them, I know, and it places pressure on me Yet that is the pressure a pastor is to have, for as the scriptures say, if a man cannot lead his own family, most assuredly he cannot or is not capable of leading the people of God Because the burdens and pressures can be great upon parents to get it right with their children owning the Christian faith for themselves. Some parents go overboard in parenting, resulting in what you've heard of called helicopter parenting. I came to know about this uh some time ago, but it actually was a phrase coined in nineteen ninety describing parents who hover over their children Hovering parents are those that watch and guide almost every aspect of a child's life. In the most extreme cases, a child is full-grown. And he does not know how to do anything of meaning for himself. He does not have close friendships with anyone of the same sex or opposite sex, because mom has always manufactured them, those friendships, with planned play days and arranged prom dates. He does not know how to talk to adults because mom and dad have always run interference with coaches and teachers He does not even know how to complete a project because mom or dad has written papers for school, arranged employment, and made excuses when things didn't go well And this manner of parenting carries over into the spiritual life. A young man or a young woman can find that they don't know what it means to call upon the Lord in their time of need. They don't know what it means to depend upon the Lord when they are alone. For they have become familiar with mom or dad doing the saving. In such cases, separation must take place. And this sets us up to examine the needed spiritual growth for both Abram and Lot. We learned last week from Genesis twelve that for a person to be saved, he must first get out. Abram, like us, was called to get out, get out from among the environment of idolatry and adultery. For him to get out completely, the old needed to die and be left behind. And here in Genesis 13 The call for Abram to separate continues in regards to his relationship with his nephew Lot. Where Abraham's father represented the old things in life, Lot represents immaturity. Abram must separate from his immaturity. We notice first that Lot is a follower of Yahweh, the one true God. But he is a follower only insofar as he is a follower of Abram. Abram was called out of Ur, and Lot went with him. Abram buried his father in Haran and then went on to Cana and Lot went with him. Abram went to Egypt to escape a drought and Lot went with him. We now read in Genesis 13 that Abram left Egypt and again Lot went with him. Abram is following God, and Lot is following Abram. That's not a bad thing. Please don't hear me recounting it as if it's a bad thing. Lot is following Abraham, and he's wise to do so. We remember the story of Ruth and Naomi. Naomi's God became the god of Ruth because Ruth followed Naomi. In like manner, Abram's God becomes Lot's God. Whether we are young in age or young in the faith, it is necessary for us to follow godly people. They know better. They know where they're going. Follow me, Jesus said. Paul said the same, adding, follow me, for I follow Christ. The virtue of humility must be in a person that is willing to follow So following is a righteous act, and yet there are times when there must be separation Abram was ready to separate from Lot, but Lot was not ready to separate from Abram, as we will see. In the case of Lot and Abram, the separation was necessary because of quarreling. We read about that, increasing tensions between the families. Lot's family was growing. He was becoming wealthy by following Abram. Their livestocks were grazing on the same land. Fights were breaking out between the herdsmen. Passions were being kindled. This happens. This happens. It does not necessarily happen, meaning that the passions do not need to flare up into fighting. Lot could have acquiesced and given Abram the right of way. Instead, he spoke as an equal to his elder and wanted to divide the land. Abram, being a man of faith and less of passion, allows Lot to have things his way. This tension between Abram and Lot is not unlike many conflicts within the church. We remember the words of James, who said, There are fights among Christians because of our lusts. We want and cannot have, and so we quarrel. In the home, it could be a son wanting to have freedom and more power over his life. In the church, it could be and often is over influence. Who will have the greater influence upon music and worship upon the youth group, upon outreach, upon decor, and so on. The fact that tensions rise and passions flare over various issues in a home or in a church does not mean anything more than the fact that we struggle to walk by the Spirit But instead rather walk by our flesh. And what is most important is how such tensions are resolved Abram takes the higher robe, which in this case is the lesser ground. He allows Lot to choose. Abraham does this because again he was a man of faith. As a man of faith, he knows that however the land is divided, God will provide. God is not limited by climate, elevation, soil problems, or any number of issues that could make the land useless. God has told Abram that the land is for him and his descendants. Abraham believed God and such gave him the confidence that God would provide. Now Lot is different than Abram. Lot is an outward man, meaning that he bases his decisions on what he sees. He puts his trust in his outward physical senses. Inwardly, he might represent an upright mind. Inwardly, he might take a few steps in faith toward heavenly things. But outwardly, he represents those whose outward mind rules their life, whose soul lives religious things outwardly. It is inevitable that the outward man is going to come into a collision with the inward man. And for the Christian, the outward man comes into collision with the inward man many, many times. Too often, like Lot, the outward worldly-minded Christian will choose the lower ground, where their natural tastes find more that is in accordance with them, more what they like. Where outward things keep them from coming to themselves from self-examination. Whether their weaknesses are mistaken for strengths and circumstances, well that's to be seen. Lot chooses according to sight. He fails to understand that he sees through the glass dimly, like we all do. What looks right to the eyes is not always right, and in some cases is very, very wrong. An immediate result of his choice is that he no longer communes with the godly And instead, he more intimately communes with the ungodly. And this happens all too often as God's people pursue riches and greater rewards in this life With the choice of a new job, a so-called better job, maybe better schools, we move and we no longer commune with the godly Too often when people move, church life, the gathering together with the saints, that's an afterthought. Churches that preach the truth and honor the author of all truth and sincerity do not abound as they once did. Soon churches church shopping ends and the family no longer attends and ceases to commune with the godly. As communion with the godly decreases, communion with the ungodly increases We must notice that Lot did not commune with the ungodly immediately. The pool was gradual The King James says that Lot, after choosing the plain of the Jordan, that he pitched his tent toward Sodom. Toward Sodom. Verse 13 makes it clear that the men in Sodom at that time were wicked and rebellious, sinful. Lot knew this and still pinched his tent toward Sodom. By pitching his tent towards Sodom, he could see from a distance their indulgences and still remain separate from them. And such is the position of many young Christians who are raised under the covenant of Christ. They're sheltered in certain ways to protect them from the pain and suffering that sin brings. And this is good, but it does not remove the curiosity, a curiosity that is deep-seated. Lot wants to know what it is like to live a wicked and sinful life. It is not enough to be told of the pain there seems to be a pull in some young people that They would have to experience that pain for themselves before they believe it is real. The devil convinces young minds that What they are being sheltered from, well that's actually a lot of fun. It's freeing, it's pleasurable Lot is being convinced, or is convincing himself, that he can both be a follower of Yahweh, as is Abraham, and experience the lifestyle of Sodom. He is also convincing himself that he can live next to the wicked without becoming a part of them, without becoming a citizen of Sodom. Now those who are wiser due to life experiences that suffer the same sins, well, we are not surprised that the next time we hear of Lot He is no longer pitching his tent towards Sodom, but living within the city and living amongst the wicked. Christian parents are desperate to know how they can prevent their children from living among the wicked Although there is no recipe that will be successful for every child in every circumstance, there is one principle that I believe, if embraced, will be of great reward. What Lot fails to see as he looks outside of his tent towards Sodom, and what most young minds fail to see as they wonder what it is like to be high. To be unchaste, to experience pleasures of the flesh. What they fail to see is the sin they experience every moment of their lives. Sin in its essence is the falling short of God's perfection. Christians must understand that even as they are sheltered, they are experiencing sin. They are continually falling short of God's perfection. If they want to know what a sinful lifestyle is, they only need to look within their own heart. Their sin is not as overt as those committed by the citizens of Sodom, but it is sin nonetheless. Perhaps the pull of the sin occurring in Sodom would have less strike upon Lot if he was to recognize it was already being experienced within his own soul. As the narrative shifts at the end of chapter 13 and the whole of 14, as it shifts to the man of Abram We are able to contrast what blessings come upon a man who trusts God. After Abram separates from the immature, he is visited by God and given another assurance Of the land that will be given to him. Abram then worships. We then read that cities and tribes are going to war, and yet Abram is able to live in peace. While Lot gets caught up in the battles and becomes a slave because he was a citizen of Sodom, Abram is able to be a free man and strengthen his own household. Because of his faith, because of his maturity, and because of his strength, Abram is able to act as a savior for Lot. In chapter 14, verse 15, he gathers an army of 318 of his own household and overruns a band of kings and armies. that neither the cities of Sodom or Gomorrah could defeat. And after his victory, Abram meets this mysterious character named Melchizedek. We learn later, you remember our study from Hebrews, that he was a priest in the order of the Most High God, and we learn a type of Christ to Abram. It does not surprise us that when Abram would eat bread and drink wine with Melchizedek, that that's the same meal that we we eat with Christ when we worship. In the last godly act of this story, Abram refuses a reward from the king of Sodom And he does so because he does not want the king to have any opportunity to claim that he is responsible for Abram's wealth. And we see from this that where Lot could not refuse the influence of Sodom, Abram, a man of faith, a man of maturity, he could. What we learn overall from the stories told here is that separation occurs and is at times necessary. Although there is nothing wrong with separation, whether it be a physical separation of a child from his parents or a family from its home church, or an emotional separation where a person becomes less dependent upon another. It matters where you pitch your tent. We can only imagine what would have happened if Lot would have chosen the land he left for Abram. We can only imagine what would have happened if he would have pitched his tent toward Abram instead of Sodom. We can only imagine how the pull of the sins of Sodom would have been lessened if Lot would have noted that there was sin within himself that he needed to deal with. And when we do imagine, when we do imagine, we can only come up with good things. For Abram, as he separated from the immature, he only experienced good things. And so let that be said of us. If you are immature and need to separate, pitch your tent toward the godly. If you are older and God is calling you to separate from the immature, do so. Do so with the faith that you will only experience good things. Amen. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God, we thank you for this story and stories. To show us how our need to separate, our need toward maturity, our need to pitch our tent toward the right place is clearly spoken. Father, we thank you for the hope of good things. May that be our sole desire. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Combating Doubt
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: God in angels has our hope for years to come, for we are God was God will stress man. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated and turn to Genesis 15, if you would. We're going to be going through that story, the whole chapter there, Genesis 15. Becoming tired, depressed, and struggling to keep faith is part of the human condition. And perhaps we Christian leaders don't mention that enough. If I don't remind you enough that traveling on the narrow road can become wearisome, please forgive me. It is helpful for each of us to admit that we can go from an emotional and spiritual high to a low very quickly When in college, the church I attended held a retreat that they called Heartbeat Retreat. Quite a clever title. The sessions were highly emotional as we confessed our sins to one another, and in the end wrote our sins down on a piece of paper and then threw them into a roaring fire to represent our sins burning away. The games and the singing and the praying and emotional healing all made for an emotionally high weekend. And stood in great contrast to getting home Sunday evening with homework to do, studying to do, and practice to prepare for. It was like living two different lives It became evident that the Christian life, a life of faith, is not a continuous retreat. Instead, the Christian life faces the realities of everyday life that consist of more downtimes than up times. We all have experienced similar letdowns after a great wedding celebration or a great Christmas party or other types of celebrations. In these letdowns is revealed our human weaknesses. The silence can be deafening, and we may wonder what there is to look forward to on the calendar after the highlight of the year is over. Thankfully, by God's grace, He does not leave us to ourselves while we are in such a low state. In the midst of being downtrodden, God, via the Holy Spirit, picks us up. In chapter 15 of Genesis We read of God picking up Abram, who was coming off a high, a high caused by a great victory over several kings and tribes with just over 300 men. Abram has learned at this point in his life that trials, what he thought was a trial, can be a blessing. What we think will hurt us actually turns out to be what is best for us. And now, after achieving a great victory Abraham must learn, or Abram must learn, that blessings can be trials. What we initially see as a blessing turns out to be a trial. So far, for Abraham's God's God's promises have been blessings. All that Abram has achieved since God's promises have been blessings. And at this point in his life story, Abraham is tried more deeply, perhaps than any other time that had befallen him. When Abram learned that he must depart from his home, you will remember, depart from his extended family, he listened and obeyed. When he learned that he must part from Lot, his nephew, because their herds were too large and fighting with one another, the Lord's promises came to life, and he made a clean break. When he learned that Lot was in trouble against tribes that the kings of Sodom and the kings of Gomorrah could not defeat, he did not hesitate, but believed in God and came to the rescue. And now, after the victory, a word from God comes to Abram saying what God has already proven God said, Do not be afraid, Abram. I am your SHEOL, your exceedingly great reward. Abram knows this to be true about God, but the blessing The blessing which was the promise, which was the promise for a child, that becomes a trial Abram looks and does not see how God will fulfill what he has promised because Abram doesn't have a son of his own. Abram's answer expresses a deep soul trial. As we note, after what God had done for him, now he wonders if anything more will be done. At this point in Abram's spiritual walk, he is looking beyond the joy of his initial conversion. Many who come out of a sinful life and are born anew in Christ experience an initial joy like nothing they had ever known before. It is like the seed in the parable of the sower that springs up quickly. For the seed to become a lasting flower, the roots must be dug deep. What tasted sweet as honey to Abram initially as he learned that he was chosen of God and he obeyed God cheerfully has now become bitter in his belly. Much like that scroll you remember eaten by John the Revelator. We start with joy. But years pass on, and if we have not yet seen the fruit of the promise, we are tempted to waver It is not a waver outwardly. We don't leave the church or renounce the faith. Instead, we struggle inwardly. Unsure if we understood God correctly. At such a moment of need, God speaks again. God's next words are no less a trial than the first, for they are words of promise that are not fulfilled in the immediate, but will take some time before they are fully realized. And this is what makes them a trial. They are words from God regarding salvation, but they are yet to be fulfilled, causing us to be tempted to question whether they will ever be fulfilled. And please understand that Abram's desire to see the promises to him fulfilled is in no way sinful The soul of a believer longs for that which God has promised. In this we should recognize our kinship with Abram. For as he longed for the promise of his son to be fulfilled, so we too long for Christ to be revealed in us and before us regarding his second coming. We long for our flesh to submit to the Spirit, and that the Spirit of Sonship might fully grow within us. We long to see the eastern sky split and for Jesus to come in all of his arraignment so that our faith can be vindicated and be no more. And God replies, like he did to Abram, that such too is his will, but like Abram, it takes time. To inspire Abram and us, God has him go outside of his tent. His tent represents his earthly body. It is limited. It is temporal. Abram needs to see beyond his earthly limits. And so God directs his attention to the sky, to the heavens. For that is from where the promised seed will come. Count the stars, God challenges him. Abram is to understand that just as the stars cannot be counted, so his descendants will not be able to be counted. As an in inside, by the way. As an inside, it is important to realize why the Lord becomes upset at David when David takes a census. Practically speaking, counting the people can can be a help, but it is an attempt to do what God said you will not be able to do, and thus it is not trusting in the covenant being fulfilled. And as another insight, I have had the privilege of looking up at the sky near the equator while in Brazil. And the stars seen from the naked eye are more bold and bright and numerous than I had ever seen before. And that is what I think of when I read Abram looking up, told to count the stars that he cannot count. As Abram looks upon what God is pointing out, something happens within him. Perhaps it is The awe that most men feel caused by the immensity of the heavens as they testify of the Creator. Perhaps he is inspired by the hope of being the father of so many descendants And what we can be sure of is that he is given the gift of faith. He believes. He believes, although there is still no fulfillment in front of him. He believes what God has promised. And that faith was counted to him, God says this, counted to him as righteousness. This type of faith, the faith that is counted as righteous, is the same faith that saves us Faith comes from hearing, hearing the word of God. Abram heard God's word and believed. He believed in the promised seed as we do. As Abram was reckoned as righteous, so are all persons who believe on the Lord Jesus Christ. All of this is good news, and there should be great rejoicing by Abram and us who stand on the other side of God's revelation. However, there is still more to believe without seeing. God follows up his promise about Abram's descendants with another word about giving Abram land. Although Abram now truly believed the promise of the descendants, he is once again skeptical about this promised land. And here again we are akin with Abram. We believe, we have confidence that we are forgiven, but not all of what will happen to us is understood, and therefore we waver. We are like the man who had a son who was possessed by an evil spirit. It was our second reading. He brought his son to the Lord Jesus for healing. Jesus asked the man if he believed. The man responded, Lord, I believe. Help my unbelief. That is what we say, is it not? As Christians, we believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Messiah We believe he is the Son of God who died for the sins of mankind. We believe that he rose again on the third day and that he ascended into heaven. It is the rest of God's promises that we too will ascend to heaven that confuse us. Can we admit that? The promised land to Abram and his descendants is a type for a shadow of God's heavenly promises to us. Heaven is our promised land. That is helpful, but we wonder how it all works. Where is it? Is it a physical place? If so, where does it now reside? We are told elsewhere that when we die we will be with Christ, but not our bodies, for they will still be in the grave. When Jesus comes again, he will raise our old bodies and give us new ones. In the meantime, we will be with him, but in what capacity is not clear. And what type of bodies will we have when he gives us new ones? The Apostle Paul says that they will be incorruptible bodies, but we still wonder whether we will look at all like we do now. Will we be recognizable to others as we are now? Will we recognize our loved ones? The unknown causes some angst within us. We like Abraham ask, how shall I know? I will inherit it. How shall I know? God is merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in love. He knows well that we see through the glass dimly. He is not angered by Abram's questions, nor is he angered by ours. His response to Abram's question is one of instruction. Abram is to cut into a three-year-old heifer and a three-year-old goat. He is also to sanctify a three-year-old pigeon, but not cut it in half. He is to place each half of the carcasses of the heifer and the goat opposite sides of himself. In doing this, Abram is giving the substance of Abel's offering and a figure of the offering of Christ. The particular animals instructed by God to the sacrifice are important for what they represent. The heifer is a service animal. It is used to till the ground and grind wheat, bread. The goat is a sin-bearing animal, chosen by God as an acceptable sacrifice for sin, blood. The dove is a symbol of innocence and peace. Each of these sacrifices is an outward sign of what is to occur inwardly within each of us. We are to be as a heifer and offer our services to God as a sacrifice. We are to be like the sacrificial goat and die to self. We are to be like the bird and be a people of peace. Peace with God and peace with our fellow man. We are to be living and holy sacrifices, for such is our reasonable service. After Abram offers the sacrifice as the Lord instructed, vultures come down upon the carcasses No sooner are the bodies of the beasts offered as worship unto the Lord than fowls come down flying to mar the offering. How true this is for every person who attempts to offer himself or herself to the Lord. The fowls or vultures symbolize evil spirits, powers who are subject to the wicked one. These are angels of the devil himself who come to distract or mar our communion with God. We are told by James, are we not, that the devil prowls, seeking whom he may devour? Peter warns the same. We are to resist the devil, and he will flee. Abram gets up to drive the vultures away. We must learn from this story of Abraham giving an offering unto the Lord that it does not result in the safety from the from the enemy. The enemy will come and tempt us to become bitter and jealous of our brother. He will tempt us to satisfy the flesh by withholding a part of our lives from God. Once the sacrifice is made, once the worship is offered, it is not over. We still need to resist, we still need to drive the enemy away. After the vultures are driven away, Abram becomes tired from offering these sacrifices The cutting in half of a heifer and a goat was a laborious, bloody task that would have taken great energy and strength. As he falls asleep, a great darkness, a terrifying darkness, comes over where he rests. His lesson is not over. His offered sacrifice is not complete. Whether it is in sleep or in awakened state, the text is not clear, but Abram becomes scared. Next, the word of God comes to him. His descendants will indeed inherit the land, but by trial and suffering. Abram learns from this that God's chosen way of salvation is through trial and suffering. His people will go through trial and suffer slavery because of their own sin. God's Son will go through trial and suffer because of the sins of others, the sins of all of mankind. In the end there will be a morning, a new day. There will be a dawn that will never end. Israel will inherit the land after the fourth generation. In like manner, followers of Christ will inherit their heavenly reward. This will happen, but not yet. In the meantime, a burning torch passes in between the carcasses, the offered sacrifices. We learn in the New Testament that light is symbolic of the Son of God and that fire represents the Holy Spirit, which baptizes and purifies the souls of men. God is thus in the midst of Abram's sacrifice. The Spirit of God is dwelling in the midst of a man's life as he offers himself unto the Heavenly Father. Man is not left to himself in his offered service, his confessed sin, or his need for peace. God is present. He is always present. That is what the torch in the midst of the carcass means. It means that God sets the parameters of his covenant with Abram and then fulfills the covenant himself. But all of this is not a simple answer to Abram's question. How shall I know? He asked. This is the answer. Instead, it is complicated and something that Abram is going to have to accept. It reminded me in the book of C. S. Lewis called A Grief Observed. Lewis said of asking God about the great mysteries of his will, quote, when I lay these questions before God I don't get a no answer, but rather a special sort of no answer. It is more like a silent, certainly not uncompassionate gaze As though he shook his head, not in refusal, but waving the question. Like, peace, child, you don't understand. What I hope we will take away from this part of Abram's story is how common it is to believe. To have faith in God and yet have areas of doubt and confusion. Abram did, and so do we I have experienced the doubt myself, and at times it has scared me. I have questioned whether I truly have faith. I have heard the doubt in the words of my children and in the words of many of you. The doubt we have regarding God's promises may lead us to doubt whether we are saved at all. We are tempted to think there is something wrong with us because we can't wrap our minds, even with our own imaginations, around all that God has promised to those who believe. What the Lord answered Abram and what he answers us is not necessarily comforting. It consists of sacrifice, of trial, suffering. In the suffering, we must accept the unknown, but do so with the confidence that God is with us. He is in the midst of a life offered as sacrifice. The Bible says that faith is the substance of things hoped for, the conviction of things unseen. We cannot always immediately see what good comes out of our trials or how effective our lives are as living sacrifices. And we will not know exactly what our heavenly hope is, what it is like, until we are there. And so we walk through this life, living the rest of our days like Abram. Acknowledging that there are things we don't know. We can't know. And that is okay. It has to be. Let us pray. Our gracious God, we thank you for the faith given to Abraham that overcomes unanswered questions. that overcomes not experiencing your promises in the now. And because we identify with these readily, we confess that at times we waver, but you know that. And so, dear Father, we thank you for your grace, your mercy, your forgiveness. We thank you for faith that goes beyond this life. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Law vs. Grace
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn if you would to Genesis chapter 16 in your Bibles. Our reading, our first reading. Came from Galatians 4, and maybe you're wondering, I thought we were doing a series on Genesis. And we are. I wanted us to hear how St. Paul interpreted Genesis 16. I want to take a look at the chapter a little differently by contrasting two different ways to interpret the stories that are told therein. The first way is what we could call the moralistic way, and by that I mean we could examine the moral lessons contained in the story. This is the approach that we take with fables. We look for the moral of the story. So, what are the moral lessons to be learned from Genesis chapter 16? Well The chapter begins with Sarai, Abram's wife, concerned that she has yet to bear a child. Because she and Abraham are getting along in years She decides to give her servant Hagar to Abram, and the child Hagar bears will be considered a child of Sarai and of Abram. That's the plan. From this, the first moral lesson is do not commit adultery. Or as a commentator has taught, at the very least, the couple was guilty of the sin of polygamy. Practicing polygamy isn't wise. After Hagar becomes pregnant, we are told in verse 4 that Sarai is despised in Hagar's eyes, meaning that Hagar looked down upon Sarai because she was pregnant and Sarai was not. The moral lesson here is the danger of the sin of pride. We should not become prideful for something that God has blessed us with. We should be kind to others who are not as fortunate as we are. When Sarai recognizes that Hagar looks down upon her, she realizes her mistake of letting her husband sleep with her maid. She next confesses her sin, well, sort of, and decides to take her anger and frustration out on Hagar. All the while, Abram is described as a bystander. He gets to have sex with a woman that is not his wife, and his wife blames herself. When the women start fighting, he leaves the issue to his wife, allowing her to pass the judgment. When Sarai is given the authority, she beats Hagar, who naturally runs away from the abuse Now I can see at least two lessons here. First, Abram should take greater responsibility for his home. He is to lead rather than follow his wife's every suggestion The second lesson involves Sarai. She is not to be bitter, for bitterness results in anger, and that's expressed in an ungodly manner. She sinned in her anger by physically abusing Hagar, and that was wrong. You see how easy it is to find moral lessons in the Bible? When Hagar was alone in the wilderness after having fled from Sarai, she was visited by an angel who tells her to go back home to her mistress, promising that God will bless her with a son. The angel even goes as far as to name the son. Hagar's response is one of faith. She believed what the angel told her, and she obeyed. The lesson here could be, well, first, the importance of being alone so that God can speak to you and you can hear him. It could be that God takes difficult situations and turns them into something good. It could be that submission to authority works for the greater good. All of these are important lessons. And so we could end our study of Genesis 16 by learning all of these valuable moral lessons. And yet it should be obvious that something is missing. The Bible is not Aesop's fables. It is the story of God redeeming his people. Thankfully, a reading of Galatians 4 helps out to reveal that Serai and Hagar represent more than their individual selves As do Ishmael and Isaac, which are yet to be born. So let us go back and look at the characters and the situations they find themselves in and see if there are deeper lessons. Commentator Andrew Jukes states that women in Scripture can be symbolic of the affections of the human will. The affections of the human will. Applying this to the story here, Hagar can be seen as the natural self-will. And Serai is the submissive spiritual will. And these two are parallel to law and grace. As the the apostle explains to the Galatians Hagar and her offspring are symbolic of the law, which is our natural will, and Sarai and her offspring are symbolic of grace, which is symbolic of submission and our spiritual will. Where Abram finds his trouble is that although he is a man of faith, and his wife Sarai is that means by which he is to go through, that means of grace for God's promise to be fulfilled There is temptation to force the issue. Enough though, even though, excuse me, even though we are people of faith We can force God's promises along by our own works, which are our efforts to aid the cause. Interestingly, the attempt to add works to faith is not peculiar to Abram or his day. You remember Cain tried to earn God's favor? Moses will try. So will Saul, so will David, so will Solomon, and others. Even we who uphold the doctrines of sol fide, faith alone, sola graptia, grace alone, even we are guilty of adding works to our salvation. Let me give you a few examples. In the Christian circles I was in prior to coming to the Reformed Episcopal Church, It was required of all members to abstain from the consumption of alcohol and tobacco. We were also forbidden to attend a movie theater or a dance hall. Not that they even had dance halls anymore. If one were to look in Scripture for a condemnation of such behavior, he would find warnings against drunkenness, a call to moderation, and a warning against evil influences. But there would be no specific words against such things listed. And yet many I knew placed their confidence in their salvation because of what they did not do. And it was rarely examined how such abstinence could be works-oriented salvation. Another form of adding works can be in the manner a person dresses or doesn't dress. I know a time in certain Christian circles when women wore only long dresses and long hair, believing that that was the only way a Christian woman should show femininity. I know of Christian circles that believe homeschooling is the only way to go to educate your children. I know of families who place great pride and extra pride in the size of their family Yet to do so is to be no different than Abram and Sarai, for it is adding works to faith. The Anglican branch, our branch, in the 39 Articles of Religion, Article 14, condemns what are called works of superarrogation Such works are besides or over and above God's commandments and are believed to be incapable of being taught and practiced without arrogance and impiety. The adopted article was a reaction to the many Roman Catholic doctrines that teach righteousness by doing extra works. As we have seen, however, it does not have to be a Roman Catholic doctrine. Many fundamentalists and Calvinists have unwanted similarities with the Roman Church And as was said, similarities with Abram and Sarai. The only relation that works and grace have is that works must follow grace. What that means is that we obey the law and perform works because we are saved, not to be saved. If the order is reversed, works before grace, trouble is the result. We learn from the apostle in his epistle to the Romans that when the law comes first It brings forth sin and then death. He explains that when the law comes, he wants to do the very thing he's told he should not do. His next actions then bring about guilt. The result is sin and then guilt when Abram and Sarai put the law first. Remember that Hagar is symbolic of the law and Sarai of grace. The law, or Hagar, mocks grace or Sarai. The law can mock in this way because it can require that which man cannot attain. Sarai cannot attain a child on her own. Hagar, like the law, hangs that truth over Sarai. In response, Sarai feels guilty first because she cannot bring forth a child by her own will, and second because She tried to do so in an ungodly manner. Her extra work failed her, and now she has to deal with the consequences. Now, before we get to the manner of how she deals with the consequences, we are to note that God, interestingly to me, does not condemn anyone in this story. No condemnation is spoken about. Sarai is the woman who represents a means of grace, and she is married to the man of faith, Abram. But because of her decisions, she experiences difficulties in life. She begins to reap what she has sown. I believe Sarai to be a good example of our many brethren in Christ, in the fundamentalist camp, all the way to the Roman Catholic camp. These people are believers in Jesus Christ. They confess Him and have been baptized in the name of the Triune God. They are Christian. And yet, because they too often add works to the law, to their salvation, they experience difficulties in this life, difficulties caused by their legalism or their ritualism. Sarai's response. Sarai's response to her difficulty is also common to us. Her response is technically known as antinomianism. Anti-nomianism is a mouthful word that means a rejection of the law in its entirety. Sarai, who is still a means of grace, is married to faith, loses sight of what she is and attempts to cast out the law, cast out Hagar completely. She first abuses it and then drives it away as if by doing so she is not bound by it. But she is bound by Hagar, for Hagar is her bondwoman. Sarai is responsible for the fruit of the work she attempted. The law which Hagar represents cannot be thrown out. The law is good, the scriptures say. It is good if it is used lawfully. Where Sarai has erred is the exalting of the law out of its proper place. And here we have another example of an extreme within the church. And we first described those who believed that they could add works to their salvation. And now there are those who believe they can throw out the law altogether. Those who attempt to throw out the law, they are a variety in and of themselves. These antinomians ignore the Old Testament laws, believing that Jesus would have us not be concerned about Regulations of property rights or a due process or just punishment or Sabbath restraints Ironically, these who preach such things as ignoring the Old Testament law, they always have the exception of tithing. That law, that's in place, all the others should be removed. Another group of antinomians throughout the law, believing that Jesus would have his followers, concern themselves most importantly with brotherhood, unity, coexistence. While believing that the laws of Scripture are a product of man in his environment being influenced by all of his prejudices The teaching says that such moral laws restrict people from being happy in this life. And so they are rejected as old-fashioned and irrelevant. People in this group have abandoned the traditional morals that the Bible clearly teaches while still claiming to be Christian. And what both Antonomian groups share with Sarai is the attempt to cast the law out. But as we see by the words of the angel, God does not want the law cast out. He wants it in submission to the Spirit of grace. He therefore instructs Hagar to go back to Sarai, to go back and to go get back to grace and submit. The law is perfect, the psalmist says, reviving the soul. The law in its proper place is perfect in what it is supposed to do. It is to lead a man or a woman to Christ. The law allows us to see God's standards and compare it to where we are, and notice that we fall woefully short The knowledge that we fall short then causes us to conclude that we need a Savior. Thus, to cast the law out is to cast out what would convict us and lead us to Christ. Hagar in obedience goes back to Sarai, confirming to us that the law has a place under grace. Even as she does, so, however, difficulties are not ended, for there is a son to be born, who, as the angel prophesied, will be a wild man. Having every hand against him, even while he dwells among his brethren. This is not good, and yet it is according to God's will. When men look to the law for their hope, look to the law for their salvation, meaning that they look to their obedience of the law and their own works to earn God's favor, the law becomes wild. It becomes wild in the sense that its standards cannot be obtained, and it is wild because it is never-ending. By never ending, I mean that men add on law on top of another law, on top of another law ad infinite. We see from this that it is all too easy to take the road of the Pharisee as we trust more in our own man-made laws and move farther and farther away from understanding, even believing that it is by grace. We are saved through faith, not by our own works. We do not have the time to list all of the laws we add, but I will mention a few. A number of years ago I preached on idols of our day, and included in that series was a sermon on ceremonialism. Ceremonialism was the placing of faith in the customs and traditions of the church, believing that when we do them, we are then more pleasing to God and thus more righteous. I bring this to our attention again because we have spent time this morning pointing out the errors of certain Christian camps, and yet to examine what could be our own. As much as I am in favor of more ritual, so that our senses might be more engaged and attentive, better focused as we worship. I am also careful to realize that we are just as apt to put our trust in those things in and of themselves, not what they point to. The Latin phrase ex opera is literally translated from the work worked. From the work worked. It is used to describe that a ritual practice in worship is only done because of the work of Christ, not our own. But reformers fairly criticized that the worshiper, practicing his ritualism, his ceremonialism, seemed to be trusting in the ritual itself rather than Jesus to whom we are to place our faith. This can be what we do with our rituals. The story of Abram, Sarai, Hagar, has a dramatic number of tense moments. The moral lessons within can be good and helpful if we're only seeing the Bible and the Christian faith as just another option for what kind of moral standards we want to emulate for our lives. The greater lessons for Christians, however, is to understand the relationship between law and grace and our works versus the work of God. Such lessons about our redemption, such lessons help us to think and believe rightly about God. As Abram and Sarah reveal, even as a people of faith and grace, it is hard to wait on God and let him do his work on his own time and in his own way. In our haste we add works, righteousness to his grace, which actually mars and covers his grace. Even the elect can be misled to trust in their own resources instead of waiting on God. What results from the effort is fruit, but not fruit of the promise. What results is a seed, but not the seed. Ishmael is a seed of Abram. He is a wild seed. And his descendants, understood today to be mostly Islamic, will be a constant thorn in the side of God's people. Thus not only has the work efforts of Abram and Sarai been to no avail, but actually has caused them pain. And so does the same happen to all who put their work before grace, who put law before gospel. And this is the lesson, the most important lesson from the text. The law can lead us to grace, but when grace is taken over the law, then our works of the law must become submissive to the covenant of grace. And this is to be more than a moral lesson to us. It is what we believe. We believe we are saved by grace through faith. And that not of our own works, but our salvation is a gift of God, lest anyone should boast. Let us pray. A gracious God, we thank you for this important story of Sarai and Hagar. And how it all reveals very well your plan all along to save your people by grace through faith May that always be kept before us, and may we be mindful whenever we try to put our works in front of grace that is not to our benefit nor to your glory. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Several Reasons to Laugh
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: I think for less morning, more morning, you mercy thy hands. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turning your Bibles to Genesis chapter seventeen, there are many lessons in this chapter. I'm going to try to summarize them with three in kind of four. They can be broken up into what we could call three edible sections. The chapter is essentially a three-course meal. The first course is the promise of what God will do. The second course is the changing of names The third course is the circumcision. And I use the word course to describe the third, for it would be hard to explain circumcision as a dessert. Speaking of circumcision, you wouldn't think that such a topic would lend itself for joking, but some of the best jokes that I have heard are containing the subject of circumcision Here's one you may not have heard. It seems that there were two little boys who were in the hospital at the same time, and they struck up a conversation. The first one asked what the second was in for. And he responded that he was there to get his tonsils taken out. The first responded that he had that procedure done and that it hurt only for a few days and he was able to eat all the ice cream that he wanted. The second boy then asked the first what he was in for. He responded that he was to be circumcised The second boy lamented, saying, Oh, tough break. I had that done just after I was born, and I couldn't walk for a year Now that's a good joke. And if you didn't laugh, I bet you're gonna tell it to someone else when you leave here. Well after the damage, if we can call it that, after the damage has been done of Abram and Sarai attempting to force the hand of God with their own work Which resulted in a wild son being born that they named Ishmael, God graciously reveals his will to Abram in a more specific manner. We learn that the promised seed or the promised son is to be born from Abram. Abram's and his wife will give birth in God's timing and in God's way. He has chosen Abram as the father, even though Abram at this time is 99 years old. He has chosen Sarai, a baron. And yet, free woman who is beyond natural childbearing years, she is chosen to be the mother. This is God's way. And we know him better when we understand his manner of doing things. He makes the crooked paths straight. He causes rivers to run and overflow through deserts. He chooses the second born rather than the first. He chooses a man who is a of weak speech to speak to Pharaoh. He chooses an army of 300 to defeat an army of thousands. He chooses a boy to become king, a virgin to bear the Son of God, and a man from Nazareth to save the world from sin and death. Thus, it is consistent for God to choose Abram and Sarai at such a time in their lives. God does this. He works in this manner. So that there would be no doubt that he is the cause, that it is his will that is being done. The circumstances of the stories I have just referred to require us to conclude that they were determined by God by divine will. He had to be involved for these events to take place in the manner they did. When Abram takes a kneeling posture before God, There's an emphasis of him, God, that is, being the one responsible for the coming birth. God is revealing himself as God Almighty. And it is repeated seven times in this section, the phrase, I will. God speaking, I will. The number seven, you remember, symbolizes fullness or completion, and by its use here, confirms that God will complete what he is promising. He said, I will make my covenant with you, I will multiply you, I will make you exceedingly fruitful, and I will make the nations of thee, and I will establish my covenant with your offspring and I will give to your offspring the land where you are a stranger, and I will be their God. By this repetition and the exact number, God repeats the phrase, I will, seven. He is saying, thou child of grace. Do you not realize that my I will is what makes you fruitful? It's what God does. He explains as is needed that Hagar, the self-will, the will of man, is not the means by which the promised son would be born. And this is just as the Gospel of John states. Those who are born of the Spirit are not born by human decision or the will of man, but, you remember, by the will of God. We can easily see through our Christian lenses that Isaac is a type. He is a shadow. He is a precursor to the Messiah. Jesus, like Isaac, is born to a previously barren womb in an unexpected and miraculous manner. Jesus, like Isaac, is a son of promise, only Jesus is not a son, but the son of the promise. Jesus, like Isaac, is the second son. The first in Isaac's family was Ishmael And the gospel explains that the first in Jesus' family was Adam, and that Jesus is to be understood as the second Adam. Thus, what Isaac pointed to is what Jesus fulfilled. And we now look at the second course, which is the changing of names. Proverbs says that a good name is to be preferred over great riches. Under a covenant, a person's name is to describe his or her personality or their physical characteristics or their calling in life. Under the covenant of Abram, a child's name was to give them their identity under God. It told others what their parents hoped for their children in relation to God So the name Abram originally meant of elevation, of elevation, and it describes where Abram came from, where he was derived. The name Sarai originally meant diminutive, that is she has dominion. And it is an adjective emphasizing and exercising control, which is a bit ironic because she is used in scripture to model what it is to be a submissive woman. As Abram takes the posture of facing down, he is next blessed by God. And the blessing is to make Abram and Sarai sufficient for the task that God will accomplish through them. Thus far, the pairing of faith, who is Abram, and the Spirit of Grace, who is Sarai, has not yet borne fruit. For God to bring forth fruit from this marriage of faith and grace, he must endue them with the power from on high, which we know as the Holy Spirit. God does so by changing Abram and Sarai's name. He changes their names by adding to each a letter which is most significant. Abram was changed to Abraham or Abraham, and Sarai to Sarah. What the Lord is doing here is adding an H in the English alphabet or a He in the Hebrew. And that is part of God's divine name, Yahweh. You will remember that God's name, the name he gave to Moses on Mount Sinai, was Yahweh spelled Y-H-W-H, which by the very sound emphasizes the ha sound. Thus, their new names are giving them new character, namely the character of God. It is also interesting to note that the hay sound is only formed by outbreathing, and an outbreathing that is emphasized. Upon hearing this, we should flash back in our memories to how God brought mankind life. After he created Adam from the dust, he breathed into him life. And this acting of breathing life into an individual is then replicated in the Gospel according to St. John chapter 20. You remember where it is recorded that Jesus is in the room after his resurrection, and he's greeting the disciples, and then he commissions them to go out in the name of the Father. And next he breathes on them and says, Receive the Holy Spirit Both then at creation and the Gospel of John, they reveal that the breath of God carries a giving power both physically and spiritually. Thus by giving Abraham and Sarah a letter or a sound in which God breathes, he is empowering them with his Holy Spirit. They are both thus baptized by the Holy Spirit, and their names reflect that baptism. Until we are so breathed upon, though beloved and elect, until the Holy Spirit is given to us, we too will be barren. Remember these words of Jesus. Most assuredly I say to you, unless one is born of the water and spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. That which is born of flesh is flesh, and that which is born of spirit is spirit. The Holy Spirit needs to be breathed upon every person who would be saved, and it must be breathed upon every person who would bring forth fruit in his or her life. And such fruit is righteous for living. Such fruit is a faithful marriage, faithful children, loving others as yourself. It is living as God has commanded. Typologically, we could say that in order to bear fruit, we must obtain a new name. A new characteristic must be born within us as a result of the Spirit of God breathing upon us. Let us consider how this applies to the context of the church. A number of years ago, a parishioner was invited to a christening. And she wanted to know from me what the difference was between a baptism and a christening The question relates to our topic because a christening occurs within the baptismal service. It occurs when the minister says to the sponsors, name this child. The minister then baptizes the child by the name given. Thus a christening is when a child is given his or her Christian name. Then it is by that name that we claim Jesus as our Savior, and that we live our lives as followers of Jesus, bearing that name given to us when we were marked by Christ. There was a time, believe it or not, when Christian parents did not name their child until the child was baptized. At the same time, a child's name was not officially acknowledged within a community until after its baptism. Today, we put all our legal trust and confidence in a state-issued birth certificate of a child A birth certificate in the United States grants the privilege of a Social Security card, a driver's license, little league eligibility, and such Showing how times have changed, it was not all that long ago, maybe maybe 70 years, that a person's baptismal certificate was just as legal. If not regarded as better than a birth certificate, there was an age within our country where being identified as part of the Christian covenant after being baptized And receiving one's Christian name was held in the highest esteem that when the state declared to you to be a living soul, so the Christians had already done so. Unfortunately, these days are long gone. But they should not be for us. We should continue to make a big deal about a child being given his or her Christian name. For in being given such, we recognize the Holy Spirit empowering a life and godliness, just as it was for Abraham and Sarah. The third and final course of our analogous meal, the course that most certainly is not a dessert, is circumcision. God commands Abraham to perform circumcision upon himself and the male children of his household. In chapter 17, verse 10, the Lord says to Abraham, This is my covenant, which you shall keep. The meaning of that phrase is that God will do all of the rest. Of what is required to fulfill this covenant that he is making with Abraham, but Abraham must do this one thing. He must circumcise his male offspring. And the one question that all of us wonder is why? Why that? Well, there are actually several parts to the answer of that question. First, there is the relation of the procedure upon that which bears the seed within the male. If the promise is the seed that will crush the serpent's head, it makes sense that a sign would be in relation to the male anatomy. Second, as a pledge of Abraham's entire dependence to the promises of God, he must submit to a certain level of suffering. Which circumcision most certainly entails. Because the Lord has covenanted with him, he has breathed on him, and so he has changed him. Abraham must suffer for his part, suffer in his flesh. In doing this, he is Another precursor to Christ, who most certainly we most certainly know suffered in the flesh for the sake of the covenant. Third answer, the sign of circumcision is but a shadow of the circumcision that all Christians are to experience. Which is, as St. Peter said, putting away the filth of the flesh, which are the sins of the flesh. The Apostle Paul described it in Colossians 2, where he said that Christians are circumcised with the circumcision made without hands, in the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh. So under the new covenant, then our circumcision is one of cutting away of the sins of the flesh from our lives and having the Spirit reign over us. I have a a fourth point here. It's not necessarily well, we'll just call it a second dessert. And it's the mentioning that the child should be circumcised on the eighth day. The instruction was for children born under Abraham to be circumcised on the eighth day. And the eighth day is related to the fourth commandment regarding the Sabbath. The Jewish week was made up of seven days, as you know, as our week. God introduces the concept of counting to the eight-day here And later he expounds upon it when he instructs Israel how to celebrate the Feast of the Tabernacles. He told them that seven days they were to worship God by resting and offering sacrifice. On the eighth day, they were to gather together, all of the people in one place to worship. They called it a holy convocation. It was the final day of celebration. Thus, the eighth-day celebration was a precursor to Resurrection Day. For if we count a week of days plus one, we come to Sunday And Sunday we know as the Christian Day that celebrates resurrection. Therefore, even though circumcision is a sign of the old covenant, we can see by the fact that that it pointed to the sinful flesh of Christians being circumcised and making the eighth day a part of our worship, that it is an old sign that pointed to the new covenant which we are under Now the final point I wish to make regarding this chapter and the one that wraps up all of the other points together, I believe Is Abraham's response to laugh when he hears that he and his wife Sarah will have a son. And that laughing Is to be an example to us. We will note later that when Sarah hears this news and laughs, God is not pleased with her. When Abraham laughs, God is not offended in the least. And this allows us to conclude that Abraham is laughing in a different way, most different way, than Sarah will. As John Calvin remarked, Abraham laughs not from doubt or disbelief, but in gladness and wonder. The Lord, in response, in order to perpetuate that wonder, names the son to be born Isaac, which you know means laughter. It is remarkable to me, after considering all that we have in this chapter, that there is room for laughter. A natural reaction when we learn that God is responsible for all that is to be fulfilled in the covenant after he says, I will seven times, a natural reaction is having great assurance that this will come to pass. A natural reaction when we receive the power of the Holy Spirit as he changes our names is great humility. Because we note that we are not worthy of such a gift. A natural reaction when we understand our part in the covenant is to be circumcision, for Abraham, a circumcision of the flesh. For us, a cutting off of the sins of the flesh, well, the natural reaction is resolution. It must be done We become resolute that to be circumcised in such a manner is the least we can do for our part in order to receive our heavenly reward. included with these quote-unquote natural responses is a is a theme of seriousness and and even awe in the moment That God would allow laughter, levity, or express joy reveals a part of his character that needs to be a part of ours. An appropriate response to the covenant we have with God is laughter. We laugh At our foolishness for thinking that we could be saved, ever saved by our own works. We laugh at the devil for his foolishness in thinking that he could keep the Son of God in the grave. We laugh because our hearts are free to enjoy life's ironies and whimsical moments. We laugh in gladness and wonder at what God has done for us. So here at the outset of Israel as a nation, beginning with this family, we have three new names. The first two are indicative of the power of God, and the third of the levity and joy that the power of God brings with it. This was the covenant of Abraham, which is later to be revealed as the covenant of Christ. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God, we want to see everything that is in this chapter. For in it is again, once again, the redemptive story that you have for your people, setting its foundation and pointing to Christ. May our faith be increased by it, and may we enjoy the laughter. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Faith Compromised
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. To serve yourself well, to turn to Genesis chapters 18 and 19. Genesis 18 and 19. Our reading only came to us from 19. But we are going to be covering all of that story and focus on one particular message. Like the introduction here, we Christians can waste a considerable amount of time in our lives judging people. By judging people, I mean we try to determine within our own minds whether or not certain people are Christian or not. Because the majority of people in the Western hemisphere of this world claim some relation to the Christian faith We can perceive it to be our duty to decide who are the true believers and who is not. This is a foolish thing to do, for we are never given the responsibility to judge others in terms of their faith. In fact We are warned not to judge others, for we will be judged in the same ungracious standard we judge others. The biblical instructions on how to determine whether a person is a believer or not is to do what the church did in the first three centuries. It is to discover whether a person has been baptized in the name of the Father, and the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, and whether they confess doctrines such as you find in the Apostles' Creed. The first requirement of baptism is in line with that testimony of St. Peter you remember from Acts 2, when they all cry out, What shall we do to be saved? Peter said, Repent. and be baptized. The second requirement is to confess doctrine as summarized in something like the Apostles' Creed And that is in the language and the teachings of St. Paul, who said to the Corinthians, Confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus Christ, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead and you shall be saved. Combining these two proclamations, I can be assured, at least in this life, That if a person has been baptized and confesses Christ as Lord and Savior, he or she is a Christian. Now, before you think of objections to that conclusion, let me clarify what I mean by Christian. I mean that the person has done all the things outwardly to verify their standing within the church, and therefore I am to treat said person as a Christian. I do not mean that I can verify with all certainty that every person that has been baptized and confesses right doctrine is going to receive a heavenly reward. I don't know that. Only the Lord knows that. And when it is time, he tells us that he will indeed separate the sheep from the goats, the tares from the wheat. Until then, we can and we must have charity towards others who have been baptized and who confess what we confess. Charity to one another. Thus we should not conclude that because a person does not attend services as much as we think they should or they have friends that we think they shouldn't have, or raise their children in a certain way that we wouldn't, or have marriages, or even dress the way that we think they should or should not. That we could determine that they are a Christian or not. From this we should recognize that by judging people in the manners described We ourselves, we ourselves are not acting like Christians. I have no doubt That when we stand before the Lord on judgment day, we will be surprised who is called to come up to their heavenly rest and who is judged to be tormented for eternity. Now putting the subject of final judgment aside for a moment, I want to discuss another very important aspect. of the Christian faith, which is the aspect that affects, even determines our well-being in this life. A life that is in some ways victorious in this life. What we will do in this sermon is compare Lot to Abraham while identifying the outcomes of their lives. While noting that there is a difference in their behavior, and that difference determines the health and the happiness with God and with men in the world, and that there is A difference in their behaviors. And all of this, even though they both have the hope of heaven, their lives in this world are definitely different. And we will need to remember this: that Lot is a believer. Lot is a man of faith. It is not a strong faith, but it is a faith. And yet, because of the poor decisions he makes, his life on earth is much more difficult than it should be. And for those of you who find your life on this earth more difficult than it should be, this message is for you. Now, before we examine Lot and Abraham, I wish to recognize the many directions that we could have gone in studying all of Genesis 18 and 19. We could have studied the unfaithful laugh of Sarah and her failure to confess her laughter when she was confronted. Sarah laughed because she thought it was absurd that she, at her age, could conceive and bear a child. And this we could compare to Abraham, who you remember, laughed in wonder and in awe. Next, we could have learned about how God revealed his plan regarding the disruption of Sodom to Abraham In order to cultivate within Abraham a heart that is compassionate and slow to anger, just as God is. We could have learned how God wants to converse with us in prayer just as he does with Abraham. And that when Scripture says that God changed his mind What that means is that he is changing the mind of his followers to be like him. Where the liberals want God to change his mind so that they can change the Holy Scriptures and allow them to say what they do not say, we are to remember that God is forever the same Next, we could have studied, if we had the stomach, the sexual depravity that men can descend to when they ignore God. This is seen in the homosexuality of the citizens of Sodom. It is seen in the willingness of Lot to have his daughters abused. It is seen in the incestuous behavior of Lot's daughters in the end. The whoredom within the city of Sodom reflects the fruit resulting from their rejection of God's revelations. Next, we could have learned about the judgment of God and his chosen use of fire and brimstone, understanding that fire is used to consume, to punish, and also to purify. And finally, we could have learned about the danger of looking back. Looking back in the fondness of the sinful life that God has brought us out from And that looking back can result in a state of preservation for salt preserves, and Lot's wife preserved her longing for sin. Although these are all worthy of our time and attention, I believe the Lord would have us focus on comparing Lot to Abraham and then both of them to us. As we do, please remember again that Lot is a man of faith. He is part of Abraham's family. We are to recall what St. Peter said of Lot. St. Peter from 2 Peter 2, verse 7. He said, God delivered righteous Lot who was oppressed by the filthy conduct of the wicked. End quote. Inwardly, Lot was who we are. And yet he leans towards outward things or things of this world. He believes, but he has surrounded himself by those who oppress him, unbelievers. The outward mind concerns itself with pleasing the flesh. The outward mind is focused on self-love. And thus is able to receive only inferior revelation. Because we focus on self-love, we receive inferior revelation And that point is very important. By inferior revelation, I mean that the whole truths, or at least the whole truths of God that needed to be understood and embraced in in order to provide healthy fruit of the Spirit and good morsels of meat to feed on, well, they are limited. They are limited to lot. People who receive inferior inferior revelation about God are similar to a plant that just gets enough nourishment from the soil and from the rain, from the sky and the sun But remains small and unappealing. There are many Christians like Lot who are caught in the world and thus receive inferior revelation. They walk around in a spiritual fog, being confused as to why their marriage is not as they know it should be, or their kids are not as they know they should be, or their peace of mind. is not as it should be. The other party of our comparison and contrast is Abraham He is a type of those who live and are ruled by the Spirit of faith. Thus, the fruit of Abraham in his life is full of colorful and nourishing events. He is living an appealing life. Things are in Abraham as they should be. Now it is easy to compare Lot and Abraham because their paths are so similar in these chapters. First, there is the comparison in the form of divine manifestation In Abraham's case, we read that the Lord appeared to him in midday in the form of three men. Midday, three men. In Lot's case, there were only two, and it was in the evening. In Abraham's case, the Lord appeared in human form, and we saw three persons. In Lot's case, only two were seen. It is quite easy for us to understand that what Abraham saw was a type or representation of the Trinity, the three and one. He saw three persons. Lot, while being a man of the world, only saw two, and thus received a lesser manifestation of God. Understand that it was the same God, but Abraham was able to understand three lot, only two. The light of day is also noted here. The Apostle Paul commissioned the Christians to walk properly as in the daytime. In the day, the works of men can be seen for what they truly are. This is as opposed to the night, where men hide themselves and even hide from themselves. Abraham received the heavenly visitors by day because he lives by day. Lot received them at night because he lives by night. For us, living in the day means that we are allowing others to know who we are, who we truly are Living in the night means we are hiding ourselves, or at least part of ourselves, because we are either embarrassed or we know we are doing what we should not be doing. Another point of comparison is the ground on which Abraham and Lot stand when the visitors come to them. And remember that coming to them is God revealing himself. Abraham is in the plains of Mamre, in his tent door. Lot is sitting at the gate of Sodom. Mamre was the place where Abraham made a sanctuary. He called it Bethel, meaning the house of God.
