It was also where he received the promise from God about Isaac. Thus, Abraham receives the three messengers in a place of communion and vision. As for Lot, a person who sat at the gate of an ancient city was considered the judge of that city. Unfortunately for Lot, he was not a self-judge, but one who judges others. This is what sinners and the immature in the faith, this is what they do. Instead of judging themselves, instead of looking inwardly to acknowledge their own shortcomings, they occupy their guilty minds by judging others, putting the spotlight on someone else. Another contrast between Abraham and Lot may be seen in the manner that they receive the guests and the circumstances around each receiving. True enough, in both cases there is the same desire for communion, but in one man's case that communion is immediate, and the other man it is at first denied. When Abraham is visited by the three messengers, he requests that they do not pass by, but that they remain and sit and eat bread with him. The immediate answer of the three is yes. In Lot's case, he requests that the two visitors would come into his home and they first reply, no. And they actually say they would prefer to sleep in the streets. The two visitors then must be convinced before they decide to be entertained by lot. And from this we see that being in fellowship with God and in good relationship with other men is cause for good company, good company to want to be together. In Lot's case, when the company he keeps is considered, and the surrounding he chooses to be a part of is seen, there is no reason that the righteous would want to dwell with him. What Lot shows is that his attention to fellowship with God is genuine. But his understanding that his surroundings are discouraging that fellowship, that understanding is lacking Furthermore, regarding the fellowship that each man has with the heavenly messengers, we notice that in Abraham's case, the communion is unbroken. Whereas with Lot there is disturbing disruption. With Abraham, there are no rude alarms from without There is only quiet discourse. In fact, it was so quiet and calm that an eavesdropper like Sarah could hear the conversation. Because Abraham has but one master, the Lord God Almighty. He can stand before God in peace. Lot, on the other hand, having two masters, the Lord and the world, he cannot satisfy either one. Lot's communion with the heavenly messengers is interrupted by the people of the world that he has chosen to make close friends with. Those friends do not see the messengers as they are. They do not see God. They only see what they want to see, which is an opportunity to debase what is holy and what is righteous. Lot's response to his friends is forceful and ironic. He tells them to not do the wicked that they intend. He is forceful because he knows their impure intentions and of the righteousness of his guests His worlds are clashing, and he understood, at least at the moment, that they could not coexist. His words next are ironic because the message to not do the wicked is the message he himself has not yet listened to. Just as he asks them to turn aside, so he should have turned aside from them and from Sodom. He should have gotten out of Sodom a long time ago. The messengers had come to tell him to get out in order to save himself. Instead, he chooses to preach to others What he himself has not yet been strong enough to do. From his actions we can examine the church and its members And count how many self-righteous lots attempt to speak the Lord's message against the dangers of sin, the sins of Sodom, while they linger in it. All, including Lot, need to be separated from it. Only for Lot it's going to have to be by force against his will. The final comparison we will make is the difference in the words spoken by the heavenly messengers to Abraham and then to Lot. To both, the Lord declares the city's fate. But he communicates it in a very different manner. To Abraham the Lord speaks as a friend. He says, Shall I hide from Abraham the thing I will do? To Lot, who lingers in Sodom, he says, We will destroy this place. Escape for your life, or you too will be consumed. We learn from this that those who walk with God can in the quiet hear his voice and learn from him. Those who walk in the world, however, must be spoken to as an alarm, so that they might wake up and get out. Carnal Christians, Christians of the flesh, who spend much of their time in the world, tend to hear God's voice primarily in tones of warning and alarm. Some might even become frustrated, piercing, perceiving, excuse me, that the minister is always preaching at them. That sermon he must have meant, just for me. Or that the focus of Scripture seems to be always negative. Of course, it is not always negative. But that will not be known unless they flee from the corrupt world they have befriended. In the end, Sodom is judged. It is condemned. And Lot, although he escapes from judgment, he does not escape from the pain that sin causes in this life. He first loses his wife and then the purity of his daughters. Now I remind you again that Lot is a believer. He is called righteous by St. Peter. The heavenly promise is his, and yet there is much pain and heartache experienced in this life. He is saved, but only as the apostle states, saved as by fire. Perhaps you have recognized yourself or someone you love in the description we have of Lot in comparison to Abraham. There is one foot in the world and the other in God's kingdom. There is love for God. There is a profound faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. But there is also this lingering in Sodom. The message of these two chapters is that a life lived like that of Lot does not have to be. You can get out of Sodom. You can have fellowship, sweet, peaceful fellowship with God, as Abraham did. But you must, and I repeat, must get out of sun. Anticipating the question of how, as to how do I get out My response to that is that you know. You know the answer to that. You know how to get out. You know whom you need to separate yourself from. You know what life situations you need to stop walking into. But to separate, you need to have courage. But such courage is a choice. No one but you can make that choice. Come out from among them, the Lord has said. Come out and be free. Let us pray. Our gracious God, we confess at this time the privilege it is to know the truth. To be believers, to be considered righteous, and yet, and yet, some of us have our foot in Sodom. May we take this message as you speaking to us and know that yes, indeed, we can be courageous. And put both feet in your kingdom. May it be so. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: The Power of Submission
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I feel like I need to say something. Apologize maybe for that response. Oreo, I was singing the Benedictus Which was on page 15. I didn't look at the page numbers, and you were all singing Benedictus S. Domine, so I was very confused. I don't know if anybody else was with me, but uh we'll have to straighten that out We are in Genesis, in Genesis chapter 20. We're continuing our series in Genesis. If you are like me, you are greatly disappointed when reading Genesis 20. We want Abraham to be flawless, and he is not. We want him to have learned from his past sins, and he did not. We want it so for the same reason we want heroes. We want to aspire to greatness, and we are spurred on by those that we know who have achieved greatness. Their success allows us to believe that we can achieve the same. When they fail, as Abraham did, it causes us to pause and wonder whether obedience is possible. Does the faith we claim actually work? And can anyone follow it? Abraham was not able to remain faithful in all areas of his life Thus, if we are tempted to see Abraham as a complete type of Christ, we should be dissuaded because of his actions in Genesis 20. He sinned by denying his wife yet again. What Abraham does for us then is highlight the uniqueness of Christ Jesus. For if the man of faith, Abraham, did not remain faithful when hard-pressed, it is all the more remarkable to note that Jesus did. And did so while suffering, enduring greater temptations and hardships. So Abraham's faithful Failure is used in Scripture as a means to glorify Christ, even if it was unintentional. Included with the glorifying of Christ in this passage, there is also the remarkable faith of Sarah and the response of God in meeting her with protection. And that is our focus this morning. There is or are dilemmas that each person faces multiple times in his or her life, and women face such dilemmas even more, many more times. It is the dilemma of doing something, it doesn't matter what, but doing something that you are not comfortable with, and yet that something has been ordered by your superior. Simply stated, the dilemma is either obeying the authority over you or going your own way. As you can well imagine, women face this dilemma more often because what the Scripture instructs, which is for wives to submit to their husbands. And before we go further into the text and understand the message therein, I want to dispel unnecessary objections to what I am about to proclaim. I am not under any circumstance preaching that we should obey an authority that would ask us to do something that is salaciously immoral. For example, if a boss were to ask an employee to steal, a husband were to ask his wife to commit adultery, a parent were to ask a son to sell drugs Such instances require a response, just as the apostles who said, when commanded to no longer preach the good news of Christ, they said, it is for us to obey God rather than men. And I use the descriptive salaciously immoral in order to convey that there are certain acts that if we are commanded to do by our authority over us, we simply cannot do because The sin is that is requested is plainly evident. It's wrong. And I realize that it can be argued that Abraham, what he asks of Sarah, is plainly immoral He asks her to lie and for her to accept the consequences of her lie, which is the possibility of committing adultery with Abimelech. And because of the gray area, however, in their familial relationship, which you heard that Sarah is Abraham's sister, his half-sister, the request for Sarah to say that she is Abraham's sister is not so plainly immoral. It is how we should deal with such gray areas that we need to consider. In chapter 20, verse 2, Abraham tells Abimelech, the king of Gerar, that Sarah was his sister. After Abimelech discovers the truth, which again is that she is his half-sister and also Abraham's wife, he confronts Abraham, and Abraham explains his lie, saying, Because I thought surely the fear of God is not in this place. and they will kill me on account of my wife. We are to remember at this point what was said of Sarah when the couple entered Egypt. She was said to be very beautiful. At this point, evidently, age has not affected her beauty, and although She was beyond childbearing years, her looks had evidently held up quite nicely, at least at this point in the story. Abraham anticipated that her beauty would again be noticed, therefore making it likely that the king of the region would try to take her as his own to be his wife. Abraham also justified his lie by explaining to Abimelech that she was his, as we know, half-sister. She is of the same father, but not of the same mother. We then learn an insight into the conversation between the couple. When Abraham explained that he and Sarah had made an agreement. He requested of her as an act of kindness to say that wherever they went, that she was indeed his sister. All of this was done to protect Abraham. It was done to protect himself. It was a very selfish thing to request. As we have stated, he is not a hero in this story. In fact, he is the anti-type of Christ, for Christ Would never give up his life, uh excuse me, would never give up his bride for his life, the church. In fact, he gave up his life, indeed, for the church. But again, that is not our focus. What is to be noted in Abraham's explanation is that Sarah made no objection. She didn't protest. And that does not mean, of course, that she did not have an objection. It means that her predominant attitude was obedience. Sarah's life as a whole stands as a beacon for all women. She is an example for all women regarding faith and submission. Sarah is appelled to all Christians as an example of faith, for in Hebrews 11, verse 11, we read, by faith Sarah herself also received strength to concede the seed, and she bore a child when she was past the age, because she judged him faithful who had promised. That is, she judged God faithful. And along with her faith, the New Testament holds up Sarah to all women as an example of obedience. To Christian women, St. Peter states, quote, As Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him Lord, whose daughter you are if you do good, and are not afraid with any terror. Now the context of these words by St. Peter to wives is that wives should submit to their husbands. And such a call we know as part of the household codes that we find in other books of the Bible. Now, the household cold here focuses in, St. Peter does, more than anyone else, on wives submitting to their husbands. This household code part is, for Peter, essential. After he calls wives to submit He then compares that a wife submitting could actually win over her husband to the faith if he is an unbeliever. And that says a great deal about the power of submission. And we don't often think of submission as a position of power. Submission, according to St. Peter, also involves chastity. A woman who is sexually faithful to her husband is being submissive. The apostle then describes submission in terms of how a wife adorns herself. While many women concern themselves with their outward appearance. He describes the importance of inward beauty and calls such beauty incorruptible and precious in God's sight. Stating that truth leads St. Peter to uphold Sarah as an example to all women. Sarah's obedience to Abraham, the fact that she called him Lord as in master, is all the more remarkable when we understand and remember the story here in Genesis 20. Abraham is asking her to come in harm's way of what he thinks is a godless king, and she submits. Her obedience is more than borderline in our day. And I assume that most women would not agree with Sarah's obedience here, but again, here it is upheld as an example for all Christian women. The subject of wives submitting to their husbands inevitably moves to discussing instances of abuse. The logic is that if there are examples of men abusing their wives, and that those examples render the whole subject of submission impotent. But the discipline of logic would rule that such a conclusion does not follow. Logic insists that a part does not determine the whole What is true for a part of something is not necessarily true for the whole of something. For example, just as a seat A seat cannot drive down the road by itself does not mean it cannot drive down the road when it is part of a car In the negative, just because a part of a plane fails does not mean the whole plane is going to fail and not be able to fly. And we apply this rule to submission, just because a particular man abuses his wife does not mean that the general call for wives to submit to their husbands is faulty The problem is with the man who abuses, not with the command to submit. What should be emphasized is the power of submission. As I have already pointed out, submission by a wife may lead to her disobedient husband coming to the faith And such power within the act of submission is confirmed in the Lord Jesus, who submitted to the will of the Heavenly Father. That submission gave him authority over sickness, evil spirits, and death itself. We can conclude from this evidence that submission has life-giving power. Sarah's submission to Abraham's ungodly request had life-preserving power. In response to Sarah's faith and because of his mercy, God intervenes. Before anything unholy occurred between Sarah and Abimelech, God appeared to the king in a dream, as we read. And said to him, You are a dead man because of the woman whom you have taken, for she is a man's wife. God then commands the king to return Sarah to Abraham, or his whole family will die. Abimelech does so that following morning along with gifts. The appearance of God before Abimelech had obviously shaken the king. Afterward, he was a man who gave rather than took. And what is curious is verse 16 Rabimelet states that his gift of silver vindicates Sarah, followed by a comment by the author that in such actions she was rebuked. This rebuke, we must remember, is not from God, but from the king, who was obviously embarrassed by the situation. So we must not conclude that Sarah was rebuked by God, but instead God protected her purity and life. Along with Abraham's life, and he did so in response to Sarah submitting. That is confirmed in the words of St. Peter already discussed. It is especially clear in his words where he says that women who obey, this is St. Peter now Women who obey like Sarah are daughters of Sarah, if they are not afraid with any terror. Sarah, in her obedience to Abraham, was not afraid. She believed God would be working all things to the good, even if her husband was being unwise, unsafe, scared, and foolish. And this brings us to practical examples. For if Christian women are to be daughters of Sarah, they must recognize scenarios in which they are to obey as Sarah did. If, for example, a husband wants to make a large item purchase that his wife believes they cannot afford. It could be a boat, new car, new home, and the wife believes the cost will stretch their budget to the breaking point. If her husband hears her objection and listens to her reasoning and still decides to make the purchase, what is a wife to do? Staying within the subject of finances, it may be a scenario where a husband is tired of his job and he wants to quit and he wants to start his own company The wife fears that the company will not be a success and that she will have to go out into the workforce to provide for the family and she'll have to leave her young children at home. She expresses her fear, but the husband is not deterred. Three months into his business, he tells her she needs to find a job so that his business can continue. What is a wife to do? In the realm of relationships, a husband could be harsh and overbearing towards his son, and the wife responds by counseling him to let up. The husband does not listen, being stubborn and continues to be overbearing, telling his wife to stay out of it. Does she stay out of it? Even though her son is hurting? What is she to do? Another likely scenario is a rift occurring between a husband and extended family members, the in-laws. In an angry state, the husband tells his wife she is not allowed to be in contact with her parents, should she obey Well these are just few examples of how women get caught up in the dilemma of either obeying their husbands or doing what they believe is right. It may be simply a mistake a wife believes her husband is making or a concern that he is doing something immoral, ungodly, unchristian. If Sarah would have focused on all of the negative things that could have happened because of her husband's request, she would have been without hope. But the person of Sarah is one that all can look up to because Sarah aspired to obedience and trusting God over the mistakes of her husband. Sarah, by God's grace, was able to trust that God would do something good when she obeyed her husband. She was able to obey without fear, we are told. Such is the power of faith and of submission. Faith casts out fear. A wife who is placed in a difficult dilemma must first and foremost choose to live by faith, to submit by faith. She must not be subject to fear, for in the state of fear, she will not submit. And I can hear the many but what-if scenarios that are going through your minds. I anticipate them. There is no possible way anyone can answer what is right to do in all possible scenarios. I believe the point of the passage we have heard, and the corresponding words of St. Peter, is the principle of submission. We are to respect the power of submission. It gives power to life. It gives power to preserve life. We are to have faith that to obey those who have authority over us is to obey God. And when that is done, even in moments of concern and consternation, we need to believe He, God, will protect us. He protected Sarah, and he will protect all who obey without fear. And all of this leads me to address an issue that I have never broached before from the pulpit or even in a Bible study setting. But the issue is so very pressing in these days that I must speak about it. Two weeks ago A parishioner sent me a link to a story about the decline of the Christian churches in the United States. An alarming statistic shows that on the average in the United States, 100 Christian churches are closing their doors every week. 100 every week. And I speculate that a major cause of these door closings can be traced back To parishioners who are unwilling to submit to the ecclesiastical authority that God has placed over them. And no, I don't have statistics to back up my claim. I only have wisdom from experience that tells me that I am right. Let me paint a picture on how it develops. A man is called by God to a local parish, and the parish confirms the call, and he is installed as the pastor, the priest. He teaches honestly and dutifully the Word of God while making staff decisions, decisions on the direction of youth ministry, women's ministry, men's ministry, Sunday school ministry, etc. Not all of these decisions are agreed upon by the local members or longtime members. The decisions are not questionable in terms of being unbiblical or unwise. They're just not what the former pastor did or not what the current leadership positions want him to do. Next is grumbling, complaining to others, holding grudges, and then a lack of cooperation. With the spirit of discontent invading the set and settling in in the parish, some people leave for less contentious bodies, while others only involve themselves in the parish on Sunday mornings. It doesn't take long for the pastor to realize that he is losing his congregation. Well, he needs to keep his job. So he becomes less direct, less forthright in his preaching and teaching. He becomes soft in order to be, well, likable. In short, he compromises, and it is a compromise on the very word of God that he was ordained to preach and teach. When his sermons become fluff and his teachings lack conviction, well, people don't see the need to come to services anymore. They receive nothing of life from the church, so they remain home lifeless The church is soon empty, and the church is soon closed. This, of course, is just one example of how a once vibrant parish becomes available on a realtor's website. But we don't think or nor hear enough about the power of submitting to our church authorities and the power, the negative power, of not submitting to our church authority. And to be sure, to be sure, clergy will be held accountable by God on Judgment Day for not submitting to God's word in order to tickle the ears of his people. But so too will parishioners be held accountable who did not submit to their ecclesiastical authority. Here is the biblical truth. Submission can be powerful when it is done in faith. And it is not just women who are called to submit. All of us, which is each of us, is called to obey those who have authority over us in faith. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God. Here we can all find ourselves in the story of Sarah submitting to Abraham. For each of us are called to submit in some way to authorities both in this world and in the church. Father, may each of us take an account for our submission, and may we uphold Sarah as our example. To trust and faith that you will protect us, that you will meet us where we are needed. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Humility and Being Born Again
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. You do well to turn to Genesis chapter 21, which was our first reading this morning. And I want you to be aware that I will be preaching this sermon in two parts, and they may not seem connected. The first will be shorter than the second. And I've chosen to proclaim Genesis 21 in this manner because the lesson to be learned in the first part is simply too important to pass over before the primary lesson of the chapter. The first lesson focuses on Sarah, but in a different way than last week. Not only is Sarah a model of faith, as Hebrews proclaims, and a model of obedience, as Saint Peter describes She is here a model of humility. To see this, I would like you to examine Sarah's reaction to the birth of Isaac. While remembering her response to the angel's words to Abraham that she would give birth to a son in her old age. I am referring to the verbal exchange that occurs in Genesis 18, where Sarah, after hearing the words of the angel, laughs to herself And says, within herself, shall I surely bear a child since I am old? We remember that her laugh was unlike Abraham's laugh, whereas he laughed to express joy and awe, Sarah's laugh is one of doubt. The angel, knowing what Sarah had done, questioned Abraham as to why Sarah doubted, and then proclaimed that nothing is too hard for the Lord When confronted by her laughter, Sarah denied it and then lied and said, I did not laugh. The angel responded factually, saying, No, but you did laugh. The subject is then dropped, and we hear no more about Sarah's doubt. And I would say on a side note, whether we be children or adults, If someone confronts us with the truth, no matter how embarrassing, it is always best to confess rather than to deny. In Genesis chapter 21, where the birth of Isaac is described, Sarah and laughter are once again part of the story, only this time in a much different manner. Sarah conceived, she gave birth to a son, and Abraham called him Isaac, meaning laughter, just as the Lord had instructed. Sarah's response, as recorded in verse 6, was as follows. God has made me laugh, and all who hear will laugh with me. It is Sarah's testimony that the laughter of doubt she initially had was now a laughter of joy and awe, just as her husband had laughed. She is also now willing to accept what she could not admit initially when confronted by the angel. She was wrong to laugh at first, and now she is able to laugh at herself, at herself, for doubting. She is able to laugh in a joyful manner because the Lord had favored her while she was undeserving. This musing with humor by Sarah can be compared to Mary, mother of Jesus, who has said Of her after hearing the pronouncement about her newborn son, she it is told us that she pondered all of these things that she witnessed in her heart. Sarah's son was not given the same praise and proclamation as Jesus, but their contemplation regarding what God had done was profound and quite humble. True humility is a gift from God, and all who receive it no longer concern themselves with what others think about them. They are no longer ashamed of their sin, for God has blessed them. God has forgiven them. God has turned their laughter of doubt into laughter of joy. He has turned their moments of embarrassment into moments of honesty and openness. When the Bible speaks about freedom in Christ, It is speaking about an openness and honesty about who you are, who you really are. As a person, and the willingness to allow others to see who you are, sins at all. Sins and all People are able to be open about their lives because they care first, and primarily, about what God says about them. God's blessing told Sarah that he had shown her favor. His favor was an act of mercy. And then those who confess Jesus Christ as Savior have been shown that same favor, that same mercy. And thus they may know, you and I may know, the same freedom in which she laughs, the same godly humility. which includes the ability to laugh at oneself, can be known to all And this may seem odd, but I have at times envied those who have been publicly embarrassed because of sin. Their sin being publicly revealed. I watch such people being forced to cling to the mercy of God and his love for them as their means of identity and their means of self-worth. Because they have been stripped of all pretensions God has to be. He has to be their identity. I'm convinced that such identity is true freedom. There is no easy way to segue from that point to the next, so I'm simply going to leave that truth hanging and move on. We now come to the second point, which proclaims the birth of Isaac. And I am paralleling that birth, that birth of the second birth of every man Who would follow Jesus Christ? Isaac is the second birth to Abraham. Jesus is the second Adam as God's son And each of us needs to have a second birth. Each of us needs to be born again. The birth of Isaac is a birth of sonship. Isaac is the firstborn under the covenant of Abraham, which I have argued. in many different ways over these 19 years is the same covenant we have with Christ. Thus he is born a son of the covenant. Jesus said, of all who followed him, that we too, that we too are sons of God. Sonship is what we are afforded when we are born into the kingdom of God. How Isaac's birth parallels that of our second birth, if we follow Christ Jesus. It is first seen in the fact that he was born outside of the common course of nature. Born outside of the common course of nature. The Bible says, as you know, that Abraham and Sarah were both as good as dead. For we remember Abraham was 100 years old and Sarah was barren past the age of Calburth, way past the age. Similarly, the Bible says that all men, that includes females of course, when they are born into this world, are born into sin and under the curse. It is to be understood that all persons are born spiritually dead, where the Bible says the wages of sin is death. It also says that all have sinned. And we put those two truths together and it forces us to conclude that we are born dead in our sins. King David in Psalm 51 describes this truth when he laments, In sin did my mother conceive me. And by this he means not that his mother committed sin at conception, but that he himself was a sinner at conception. Jesus describes the dead state of men when he said, No one can come to me unless the Father draws him. Now the the Greek word translated draw in most English translations, well that word is actually drag. And thus it could read, no one can come to me unless the Father drags him. Drag is appropriate when we're talking about moving a dead man. In order to move a dead man where you want to be, and you're doing it by yourself, you have to drag it In order for any man to come to a saving knowledge and confession of Jesus Christ, he must be dragged to the right place and then awakened by the Spirit of God. St. John describes such an awakening as a new birth. When he said that men who are born of God are not born of blood. Not of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but born of God. Jesus said the same in his conversation with Nicodemus You remember it, a man must be born again to enter the kingdom of God. The concept of new birth or being born again implies that there has been an initial birth. And we take that to be our physical birth. But because we are born spiritually dead, we must be born of the Spirit. Only can God do this for it is out of the common course of nature. Just as Abraham and Sarah having a son was out of the common course of nature, God must do it. The descriptive of being born again makes sense to persons like me who had a conversion experience later in life. For me, it was as if a light came on in a dark room. It was as if I was seeing life through new and clearer and hopeful glasses. It felt like I was given, as the saying goes, a new lease on life. It felt like I had been born again. For others, it is not so dramatic, especially for those who grow up in the faith. Yet there is a need for all to be born anew, born out of the common course of nature. For some, that birth occurs at baptism. For others, it occurs at confirmation. For others, it occurs outside of a formal venue and in the privacy of one's daily life. Such births are marked by a new attitude, a greater understanding of a personal commitment that causes the person, young or old, to say within himself that the faith of his parents Will be his faith. And it will be his face, faith for the rest of his days. There does not need to be an altar call, as some traditions would insist It doesn't even have to be dramatic, but it is needed. All who follow Christ must be born again An understandable question in response to what I have just said is, well how how do you know if you've been born again? Well the Bible provides plenty of tests Simply calling Jesus Lord and Savior and meaning it, that's evidence enough. Publicly confessing Jesus as Lord is another Attending to the teachings of Holy Scripture and receiving the sacraments is another. Exhibiting the fruits of the Spirit, still another. With the outward evidence, we can include what the Apostle Paul describes as God's Spirit, confirming within our own spirit, so that we might call him God Abba, Father. Which means a very intimate father. The second similarity of Isaac's birth to our own is the mark of circumcision On the eighth day of Isaac's life, he was circumcised just as God had commanded. And in a similar matter, similar spiritually Those who are born again are baptized, for as St. Peter instructed, repent and be baptized, everyone. And the Apostle Paul describes baptism as spiritual circumcision. It is the cutting away of a sinful heart. Specifically, he said of Christians, in him, Jesus, you were also circumcised with the circumcision made without hands. by putting off the body of the sins of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, buried with him in baptism. in which you also were raised with him through faith and the working of God who raised him from the dead For the children born to Abraham, the ritual was a literal mortification of the flesh. It is by the flesh that men walk, rather than by the spirit. It is the flesh that must be put to death. Jesus chose out of love to mortify his own flesh. as a perfect atoning sacrifice that men would no longer have to do so to themselves. Instead, we are baptized. Which is the washing away of the flesh that Jesus put to death. Whereas circumcision physically marked you as sons of Abraham So baptism marks you spiritually as sons of God. This is the mark that is upon those for whom Jesus will return as Revelation describes. Whereas the sons of disobedience are marked by the number of the beast, the sons of God are marked by the baptism in the name of the triune God. Also, just as the dead skin cut away at circumcision was tossed out, we who follow Christ, who have been baptized, are to toss out the sins of the flesh. Sins such as fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which we are told is idolatry. Well, the third similarity between Isaac's birth and that of our own is the manner that he is greeted by the world. After he was weaned from his mother, Isaac was honored with a celebration marking his maturation. At the celebration, he was mocked by the son of the bondmaid, the son of the flesh, Ismael. He that was born after the flesh persecuted him that was born after the spirit. As it was then, so it is today. Christians who are immature, who remain upon milk, are not bothered by men of this world, men of the flesh. It is when they begin to feast on solid food, becoming stronger, that they become a threat. The men of this world mock men of God because they are jealous of the favor that God has upon them. Ismael knew that Isaac was the true heir, and that he would always be regulated as a servant within his father's house. In like manner, the Pharisees saw that Jesus was able to perform miracles that they could not. He was loved and praised by the people, and they were not. He was wiser and more knowledgeable than they were, and at times made them look foolish. They knew he was favored by God and they hated him for it. Today the men of this world continue to be jealous of the men of God. They see joy and peace in a man's life, and because they had none themselves, it makes them angry. They see Christian families that genuinely love each other, compare such families to their own And they know they do not have such love. This is why they rejoice when Christians fall. When Christian families fall apart or when Christian men suffer, men of this world smirk because they want Christians brought down to their level The men of this world, men of the flesh, also mock men of God because of the guilt that they feel. A righteous man causes an unrighteous man to examine his life and see for himself what he really is. The unrighteous surround themselves with other unrighteous people because such company makes them comfortable in their sin. A righteous man forces an unrighteous man to acknowledge a higher standard of morality and acknowledge how woefully short he himself is from that standard. The unrighteous cannot live with the righteous. Ishmael cannot live with Isaac. They must be separated. The Pharisees could not live with Jesus. They could no longer be with him in the same synagogue or city or even the same geographical region. They must be separated from him by death. His death. And Jesus warned that the way in which he was treated would be the way of his followers. You will be brought before rulers and kings for my sake, Jesus said, and you will be hated by all for my name's sake. He reminds us a disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master The meaning is that if he experienced rejection, mocking, and persecution at the hands of men, so too would those who followed him receive the same. And so many Christians have, and many Christians will, and many are, suffering, suffering because their righteousness stands out. The summation of the second point is that in the birth, circumcision, and weaning of Isaac, we have a description of every Christian's experience. Those who are sons of God are born again by unnatural means. They are then marked as sons of God, inheritors of his kingdom, and they are mocked by this world. This is the life of the Christian. It is to be the life of every Christian. And I suppose we can bring the two points together now by noticing that within the Christian life, even with the unrighteous mocking us, But we can laugh. We can laugh with inner joy that we are not our own. Our identity is not found in what the unrighteous say or think about us. It is found only in God who gave us new birth. And because of that new birth, we will be laughing, laughing through the end of time. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful Father, we are grateful that we have eyes to see this reality and this narrative, to see our own individual lives and our need to be born again in the life. of Isaac, the birth of Isaac, and the reaction of Sarah, truly powerful messages that you carried out in Jesus. May our faith be increased all the more, knowing that as we walk, we walk in the manner that you have directed. Father, I thank you for helping me get through this sermon. In Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: God offers His Son
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. We continue in our series in the book of Genesis. And I ask if you are moved By stories that express unconditional sacrificial love. By moved, I mean, are you motivated to be a better person? after you hear to read or watch of such stories. Even the staunchest evolutionist Must admit that human beings separate themselves from other living beasts because we can be motivated by love Stories of expressed love reveal that human beings have souls, and those souls or spirits aspire to virtues other beasts never know. And it is true that some beasts are loyal, other beasts work diligently, but these virtues are instinctive. Human beings make choices about the practice of such virtues, making such virtues noble. I remember reading a number of years ago about a father and his remarkable love for his disabled son. What follows is an abridged version of the story. Dick and Judy Hoyt were blessed with a son named Rick in 1962. Unfortunately, the umbilical cord was wrapped around Rick's neck while in the womb for an extended period of time, causing Rick to be born with brain damage. At first, doctors gave the parents no hope for Rick to be able to function or communicate. The doctors were wrong. Rick communicated quite well through modern technology, and after a classmate in high school of Rick's high school was paralyzed People organized a five-mile run to raise money for this young man and his family. And Rick communicated to his father through a MIDI computer that he wanted to participate Dick, Rick's dad, had never run a mile in his life. But wanting to please his son, he participated by running and pushing his son along. That day changed the lives of Rick and his dad. Dad, he typed, when we are running, I felt like I wasn't disabled anymore. And from that day on, Rick and his dad became marathoners. And not just marathoners, for they have also completed triathlons. As of 2016, the hoist had completed 1,130 endurance events, including 72 marathons and seven triathlons. They had run the Boston Marathon 32 times. They have also gone cross-country skiing, mountain climbing, and biking across the continental United States. Such a story is one of love. It is of a father loving his disabled son. It is a story that first causes other fathers like me to feel guilty about how much I do not do with my sons. But it also inspires us to do more for our sons. What I hope we will see within our text this morning is the story of love. It is also a story of the love of the Father, and it is to inspire us to our very core, who we are. As read, our story begins with Father Abraham. We are to understand Abraham as a type or a shadow of a new convert. Remember, he was called out of the pagan land away from pagan people. He was converted to the truth that there was but one God only. His son Isaac, we are to understand, as a type of sonship in relation to God. Isaac is a type of what happens to all who are converted, for they become truly sons of God. And once this happens, after a man is converted and adopted as a son into God's kingdom, there might be a temptation to believe that that is enough. You're adopted, you're a son. Coast all the way. It may be thought that a person can merely sit back and wait for the Lord to call him home. But that is not what God has in store for Abraham and Isaac, and is not what he has in store for us. In the Gospels, Jesus teaches us to count the cost of discipleship. He does so by telling the story of a man who is about to build. And if you are a builder, it is wise to count your costs. He projects, a builder does, as to whether he will have enough money to start and finish the work. If he fails to finish, men will see him and mock him for his failure. And rightfully so. Bunyan teaches this lesson in Pilgrim's Progress after a Christian sets off from the city of destruction to follow that road to the celestial city. A man named Pliable joins him. Pliable, we are to understand by his name, is a sort of character that bends in the direction of the wind, blowing. After hearing his testimony, Pliable believes that Christian is right about the hope of heaven. And so he joins him on his travels. But not far into their travels, both Christian and pliable fall into the slew of despond, which is depicted as a type of muck. It is difficult for both men to get out, and once they do, because Pliable experiences difficulty early on in his travels, he decides to turn back. When he arrives back at the city of destruction, the men of the town, well, rightfully, mock him. One mocks him for being a quitter, another mocks him for starting out in the first place. What is agreed upon by those of the city of destruction and those who are on the road to the celestial city is that there is no virtue in not finishing what one has started. It is apparent that Abraham counted the cost of discipleship. The first account, you remember, was leaving all that he knew behind him. The next accounting, well this one has a greater cost still. A greater cost even than his own life In Genesis 22, we read that God said to Abraham, Take now your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love. And go to the land of Moriah and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you. Ishmael, Abraham's first son, the son born into the bondsmaid, he is not offered, but cast out. Isaac is to be offered up as the sacrifice. And this is what God asks of men that he has chosen. This is what God asks of a man of faith. He is to give up what is most precious to him, his only son. Indeed, this is a test. Can faith, Abraham, give up the son so long waited for, the son that spurred him to leave his homeland when God first called him? And we expect a pause in the story so that the tension might build as we anticipate what is Abraham to do. In our touchy, feely era, a writer of such a story would use a pause here to describe Abraham's troubled mind. He would want the reader to know about the anguish that Abraham is going through inside. But the Bible is not touchy feely. The next sentence of after God's instruction describes Abraham making preparations to offer his son. We are to understand from this that there is no hesitation, at least none, in Abraham's actions. He has heard and he obeys. As he obeys, we are to notice that this is Abraham's sacrifice. He, Abraham, saddles the donkey He coordinates the men who will go with him. He splits the wood for the offering. He leads the party to the place that God told him. And he is the one who lifts the knife. It is the same for all who follow the Lord Jesus Christ. The sacrifices we offer unto God are to be our own. When Jesus says to all who would follow him, pick up your cross, we know that what we give up for him must be very personal. It is not someone else's cross. It is your own. When he says that those who come to him must hate their mother, their father, their sister, their brother, yes, even their own life. We are to understand that there is nothing that is to come between us and the Lord He takes his relationship with us very personally, and we are to do the same as well When a great leader like the Apostle Paul says, Follow me, for I follow Christ, and then he says, It is no longer I that live, but Christ that lives in me, and the life I now live, I live for him. We know that the Christian faith is not simply getting a membership to a gym or becoming a brother in a lodge. What we are to give up is everything we hold dear, and we are to entrust it to the one who commands us to give it up. And again, what we give up is very personal. Although we may be able to empathize with one another regarding our own earthly sacrifices, we cannot truly be in another man's shoes when we offer off what is most dear to us. We can only wear our own shoes, making any trouble or any anguish that we go through personal. Personal indeed. As Abraham obeys, we also notice that the sacrifice is not self-chosen. When following Christ, we are not on self-chosen ground. It is God who chooses Isaac as the sacrifice, not Abraham. The sacrifice required is not like the choices we make when we decide to give up something for let We may decide, hmm, this this year I think I will give up chocolate. Yeah, that would be a good sacrifice, chocolate Such a sacrifice is not this sacrifice. We may get more serious than chocolate, as we may give up the internet. Wow, that's tough. Television, even sex. And yet self-chosen penance, self-inflicted pains, are not the sacrifice faith offers upon Mount Moriah. As great as those sacrifices may seem, which are imposed by self-will, much more precious are those which God calls us to offer. Faith does not choose its type of cross or when or where it will endure suffering. God makes that decision. What is remarkable about the spirit of faith making such an offering is the expectation that whatever sacrificed God will make it right and bring it to life again. We are to notice that when Abraham gave instruction to the servants about what was to take place, he told them The lad and I will go yonder and worship, and we will come back to you. Now Abraham did not misspeak when he said, We will come back to you And he didn't correct himself by saying, Oh, I'm sorry, I mean I will come back to you. He believed that God is the God of the living and the dead, and that whatever God would take from him, he would also replace. Whatever God would bring low, He would also bring up. I'll interrupt the flow of the narrative here to address what has become a common argument used by modern atheists, to argue that the God of the Bible is not worthy to be worshipped because of this very story. Modern atheists say that the story of God requiring Abraham to offer up his son as a sacrifice reveals the God of the Bible to be both barbaric if he actually expected Abraham to go through with the sacrifice. Or if not, then he's a sadist for making Abraham go to the very edge of the sacrifice of his son only before God stops him and basically says, just kidding. What we know about ancient Near East tribes in Abraham's day is that it was common, common. For fathers to appease their false gods by sacrificing one of their children. It is from that knowledge that we can understand that God was actually walking Abraham through a process of sacrificing his son to reveal to Abraham that he was not like any of the gods of his ancestors or his neighbors. Instead, he is a God that will ask for a heart of full obedience, but never harm the innocent. Back to the narrative. When Isaac surveys all this necessary for an offering, but no lamb, he inquires of his father. Once again, there is a possibility for tension. A melodrama would provide a voiceover at this point in the story. Maybe imagining Abraham asking, do I tell him the truth? Do I couch the truth? Do I say nothing? But there is no drama here. For Abraham responds factually. God will provide for himself a lamb for the burnt offering. Faith being the substance of things hoped for and the conviction of things not seen, faith is able to see a sacrificial lamb where the eyes see nothing. As the rest of the story is told, we can speculate as to Isaac's emotions as he is tied to the wood, just as a sacrifice would be. We can speculate that Abraham's emotions were what they were as he raised the knife and looked into the eyes of his son. But the Bible does not have us do any such thing. What was felt is not recorded because it's not the point of the story. Obedience to the point of ultimate sacrifice is the point. God interrupts Abraham by calling his name. Remember that he called the name of Adam, when Adam was sinful and hiding. In the case of Abraham, he is obedient and out in the open. God is moved by Abraham's obedience. He is moved to provide another sacrifice. He is moved to bless Abraham with multitude of descendants, because Abraham would give up his son, his only son. God is moved by Abraham's obedience because he understands. He knows the love Abraham has for his only son, for God has that same love for his only son. It is therefore not by accident that Abraham has but one son to offer. And yes, Abraham had a son of the bondwoman, and so did God with Adam, who was a son of the earth. Neither Adam nor Ishmael was a true son, for a true son is a son of the covenant, a son of freedom. Isaac is true sonship, for he is the son of the promise. And Jesus, of course, is the promise of God. The parallels of the two sacrifices are not by accident. It is not by accident that the third day is mentioned in both the offering of Isaac and the resurrection of Jesus. It is not by accident that a lamb was provided for the sacrifice and Jesus is referred to as the Lamb of God. It is not by accident that by that by Abraham raising his hand Isaac was as good as dead. And when God held his hand back, Isaac received new life. It is not by accident that Mount Moriah becomes a place where the first temple is built, and on that same hill region, Jesus is offered as a sacrifice. Thus, in this story of Abraham and Isaac, there is the story of the cross of Christ. Only the cross of Christ was much more. Whereas it may seem cruel for God to demand so much of Abraham, consider how much more he demands of himself. In the story of Abraham offering up Isaac, the focus is upon his willingness to make the sacrifice. The story of the gospel is God being willing and caring through the offering of his only son. When comparing the two, we note that Abraham offered his son in response to a command. God offered his son voluntarily as a response to his love for us. Abraham had his hand withheld from sacrificing his son. God carried through. His hand came down. His wrath came upon his sinless son. Because Abraham's arm was held back, we are spared that gut-wrenching emotion that he would have experienced by watching his son die. God did not hold his own hand back, and thus he had to hear, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Although we may compare these two offered sacrifices, it is not possible for us to know all that the Heavenly Father experienced when he offered his only Son, our Savior, upon the cross. The story of Abraham offering Isaac is God giving us a glimpse from a human perspective as to what it was like to offer his only son as a sacrifice. And as we have noted, the remarkable love and faith of Abraham and Isaac by and for one another and for God. We can multiply that love to its ultimate end to know the Heavenly Father's love for His Son and His love for us expressed by the sacrificing of His Son. If we are moved to be better people when we hear stories of a father pushing, pulling, and carrying his disabled son and marathons How much more should we be moved to be better people when we are told that God sacrificed his only son so that we could be forgiven? But the story of God giving his only begotten Son is not about being better people. It is about placing our faith in his Son, in Jesus And then picking up our own cross. We are to do what Abraham did. We are to sacrifice what is most important to us. Believing that God will bring it to life again when He chooses. We are to do this because our faith in our Heavenly Father Well I close by remembering this is the last Sunday of Advent, and because our place in Genesis allowed me to tell of God offering his only son on the cross. I want to challenge you in the same way that I challenged you 20 years ago giving my first Christmas sermon. Then I preached that the Christmas story is not as much about the cross I'm sorry is as much about the cross as it is about the incarnation Thus I challenged you in, at least for those of you who were here at the time, to see if you had a cross on your tree. Today I say the same. Is there a cross on your tree? Are you celebrating the Christmas story while including the suffering Savior? If not, you need to. Tell the gospel story. The whole story. Tell that story on Christmas. Let us pray. Our gracious God, we thank you for the clarity of you offering your son in this story of Abraham offering up Isaac. And we thank you for the glimpse that we get from a human perspective of what that actually meant. And we pray, dear Lord, that we would always, always be so very, very grateful for that love expressed. Yes, for your incarnation, and yes For your death and resurrection. May this whole story be before us this season. We pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Christmas Eve 2018
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. No doubt most of you adults have heard about the controversy over the song Baby It's Cold Outside For the awake generation, it is supposedly a prelude to date rape. They call themselves awake or woke. Because they see things in American culture that older generations did not and do not see They see racism and gender disparities and homophobia in places the rest of us have conveniently and willingly overlooked. Now they are aware of such social sins, and they are going to point them out in order to change them. Well this got me to questioning if there are other lyrics in Christmas songs that are politically incorrect or just plain odd. Let us examine, if you haven't heard, Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer. The woke generation says it is a dangerous song because it describes bullying. However, if they use the other side of their brain, they can notice that it sings about overcoming bullying. But that's not what stands out to me. I question, why are we asked if we recall the reindeer Rudolph? You know the line, but do you recall But yet he's supposed to be the most famous reindeer of all. Why are we questioning whether we recall him if he is so famous? It doesn't make sense. Especially since we are told that we already know the names of the other eight reindeer And then there is the song Jingle Bells, a song that my grandson Jackson says is his favorite. Christmas song. When I told him it isn't a Christmas song, because it does not use the word Christmas or the name of Jesus, he was baffled and upset. He broached the argument with his mother, who told him that it has the spirit of Christmas in it, and he understood that. And the next time he came to me He challenged me again on my argument. Remarkable. But what Jackson doesn't know, I haven't told him is that not only does the song Jingle Bells not mention Christmas or Jesus, it actually contradicts itself. For in the first line it says that it is fun to ride in a one-horse open sleigh. And yet the second line, the most that most people don't know, goes like this. Miss Fanny Bright, seated by my side, the horse was lean and lank, misfortune seemed his lot. He got into a drifted bank and we got upstot. Which apparently means tipped over So a fun sleigh ride into a turns into a slamming into a snowbank and sprawling all the riders across the road. Are we awake now? Others that have some strangeness about them, perhaps you've heard these, Santa Claus is coming to town, where we are told that he sees you when you are sleeping. That is indeed creepy. And then there is the too often played Seed the World Right? Feed the World Christmas song that has millionaires telling us how to give our money away while being motivated to describe the poor as so thirsty that they don't that their only water is the stinging tears that they drink. And then, and then they mock us by saying, well, tonight, thank God, it's them instead of you. And while we are in a depressed mood, did you know that the song Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas with its original words actually goes like this Have yourself a Merry Little Christmas. It may be your last. Next year, we may all be living in the past. If that is being awake, I think I'd rather stay asleep. But the idea of being awake and woke was first a biblical metaphor, not a millennial metaphor Christians are the ones to be awake. We are awake because we were once dead in our sins and trespasses, and now made alive in Christ Jesus, as the Holy Spirit came into our souls and gave us life. God has given his very self to us in the spirit, and thus we have victory in Christ evermore, and thus we are awake. As people who are spiritually awake, the celebration of Christmas is focused on the miracle of God becoming man. And that means God in Jesus. condescending himself to be like us so that we can be like him. To know as Mary did That Jesus was the Son of God, the Lord of all creation, is to be very much awake. Now, speaking of Christmas music and being awake. There is no contest when it comes to the greatest Christmas music ever to be written. It is, of course, Handel's Messiah. In Messiah, there are lyrics that are direct quotes of Scripture, such as describing God as the everlasting Father, the Prince of Peace And there is also the line quoted from Isaiah that says, unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given. Isaiah prophesying over 700 years before the birth of Christ told us that Jesus would be human just as any other child born to humanity. But the full person of Jesus was not born because he did not have a beginning. He was instead begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father. As much as we proclaim it true that Jesus was born to Mary, we should realize that there is a great mystery in what we say, in what we sing, in what we hear. It is a mystery that remains only in the understanding of the Godhead, and we are simply privileged to believe that it is true. Jesus was not born into this world as God's son, but instead Jesus was given. Unto us a child is born. Unto us a son is given. And I must, as a preacher of the gospel of Jesus, while I'm proclaiming that God became man, and that is what we are celebrating here and now. I must also bring a challenge to you all as listeners. The challenge is for you to question whether or not you can honestly say That Jesus was not only born unto us, but can you include that he was born unto you? Unto you. Is it so? Is Jesus born to you You know, religion is a word, as it is used in our culture, that encompasses a great deal. A person can speak and think upon God as an afterthought and call himself religious. And some in the Christian religion can hide themselves in the church by attending large churches where tr no one truly knows one another unless a concerted effort is made to get involved and to be held accountable. When I was in the Roman church as a young man, it was easy to show up in the service, greet no one, and be greeted by no one. And then leave directly after the one-hour service, no more time and no less time, one hour, with no contact with another human being, and think that I was being religious. But the Christian faith requires a great deal more than thinking you are religious. It requires that you know if Jesus is born to you. It is required of us to self-examine. Do I believe in Jesus as Savior and God? If the answer is yes, then Jesus is born to you. If the answer is no, then you remain dead in your sins, and hell is your destiny. Sorry to seem as I am ruining Christmas for you, but actually I'm trying to make this the best Christmas ever for you, with the opportunity to repent for your sins and believe and be saved For those of you who are confident that Jesus is born unto you, there is the question of what to do next. What is to be done next is to grow in wisdom and grace before God and men. What is done next is to be sanctified by the Holy Spirit within us, as it convicts us of wrongdoing, of wrong thought, of wrong deed, while leading us to maturity in both our speech and in our behavior. This is the tough part of living in the Christian faith. It is easy to start in the faith. It is easy to confess when you are finishing the last days of your life. But it is the in-between time that many find themselves sliding back to their old ways. It needs to be confessed that living the Christian life can be wearisome and require a great deal of effort. It requires effort to bring your thoughts under captivity by the Holy Spirit. It can be painful work to bridle your tongue when speaking. When speaking your mind is so much easier. If you are susceptible to alcohol, it can take a great deal of concentration and discipline to say no to that bottle that is so easily picked up. If you are susceptible to temptations of sexual pleasure outside of biblical marriage, it can require great effort to remain faithful to your spouse and your mind and in your body. If you are prone to be selfish, the call to pick up your cross daily and to think of others before yourself might seem impossible, but strive for it, you must Ah no, I am not presenting you a fun advertisement to sell you on living the Christian life of being a disciple of Jesus But it is the way that Jesus taught us, it is the way for those who believe that unto them a child was born. Now the next there is the irony of the Christian life. For if you are able to say that indeed Jesus has been born unto you, and if you can next say that you are striving to have Jesus revealed inside of you and to others from you, what is required next is that you are to become a child. I say this as an irony, because what describes the Christian life takes discipline and the constitution of a mature adult. Thus, how can mature adults be as a child? When Jesus tells his followers that they must be as a little child, he is not putting forth before them immaturity. But he's instead focusing on what it means to trust and to wonder. There is no doubt As all adults can attest, that Christmas is a great deal more enjoyable when we see it through the eyes of children. We can live our wonder of Christmas all over again, watching our children and our grandchildren. That wonder is wrapped up in a mystery. In the mystery that there is hope and joy and all the fuzzy warm feelings we could stand. Regarding trust, children have to trust because they can't provide for themselves. They can't protect themselves, they can't even discipline themselves. They need to trust that you are going to buckle them in their car seat, that you are going to feed them and help them grow in their bodies, that you are going to train them from right and wrong. That trust is necessary for their survival. And it is the same type of trust we are to have in God. We are to trust Him for needed things while we seek His kingdom first. We are to trust him for our protection while we turn the other cheek. We are to trust him for our emotional well-being when we forgive our enemies. We are to trust him for our overall well-being when we live lives counter to our culture, for we will be hated for it. In summary, our trust is the substance of things we hope for and the conviction of things we cannot see. People today who think they are woke think that the family of Mary, Joseph, and baby Jesus, that there in them is an example of homelessness and immigrants. Well, for the woke, Mary and Joseph and Jesus were neither homeless nor immigrants. For the woke, Parson Brown has no business asking if you are married And by the way, with that song, you ever wondered why they say, No, but you can do the job when you're in town, when he's actually in town right then? Very strange For the woke, Christmas today is about pointing out all of the hypocrisy of everyone else. Why they should focus on instead is the question, is Jesus born to me? And if Jesus is born to you, then it is for you to grow in wisdom and grace. And to grow in wisdom and grace must include becoming a child. A child that trusts and stands in wonder before God. And there is no better time for Jesus to be born unto you For you to commit to maturing and growing in grace, to be a child this night, this most holy night. May this Christmas be Christ born to you. Amen. We take this time now to worship the Lord in the giving of our tithes and our offerings, ever being reminded that God loves a cheerful gift. Gentlemen

sermons.title: Christmas Day 2018
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: The name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Merry Christmas to you all. Christmas and Easter seasons can be frustrating for a preacher like myself, for I feel like I am responsible to put out small fires that spring up seemingly every year. These fires must be put out because if they are not, they will spread quickly and and do great damage. The type of fires I'm referring to are caused by modern scholars and secular writers who purposefully set to destroy Christmas lore or the history of Easter. The best example of such fires is the too often repeated lie. Lie That Christmas was designated to be celebrated by the Christian Church on December 25th to replace a pagan festival. Yes, it is alive. Evidence that it is alive goes back to 500 A. D. when a Scythian monk named Dionysus moved to Rome and when there proposed that the calendar system no longer follow Julian dating but instead identified the birth of Jesus as the distinguishing mark of years. So that all years that were before would be labeled before Christ, and all that follow be labeled Anodomini, which means, as you know, in the year of our Lord. And Dionysius the monk also started each year marking the birth of Christ on March 25th. which was the day that the church was already celebrating the Feast of the Annunciation, which was the announcement to Mary that she would be with child. And since the church recognized life inside the womb as being a human being at the moment of conception That made the date of March twenty-fifth the true day of the incarnation, and also made it natural for to be celebrated the birth of Jesus nine months after, which falls on December 25th. As I said, to insist that Christians chose December 25th as the date to celebrate Christmas in order to replace a pagan holiday is a small fire. That if spread can cause doubt in the hearts and minds of weak and immature Christians in the faith. They are tempted to see Christianity as nothing more than Like all the other religions, simply borrowing from other religions, making their traditions our own Now the small fire started this year, and it may have started earlier, but I embraced or came in touch with it this year It is the doubting that Mary gave birth to Jesus in a stable. The questioning surrounds the word for in as an I-N-N. As in there was no room for them in the inn. When I was a youth minister back in 1992 The church where I served put on a Christmas play, and I was chosen to be the innkeeper. And as the innkeeper I was essentially in charge of a a you know Turn of the century hotel, which included meals, so it was really like a bed and breakfast. And since Bobby Lynn was pregnant with our third son Isaac being eight months along, she was cast to play the part of Mary And so the innkeeper that I was was forced to turn away his own wife from the inn Not allowing her a place to sleep. But back to the small fire. Evidently, the Greek word for in is kataluma. Cataluma, which is often translated in, but also is translated as a guest quarters. Guest quarters. And he followed this. And since Joseph was from the region of Bethlehem, it is likely, they speculate, that when he traveled back to pay taxes, that he would stay with a relative, not a bed and breakfast. So, the no-room in the inn can be translated, that there was no space for them in the guest room. The fact that there was a manger or trough in the main space of the house is said to be common because it was used for many things, such as feeding livestock. And sometimes the livestock needed to be stored in the house to protect them from the elements. The seeming need for scholars to try to change narratives We have come to know and understand is odd, but yet is done quite often. What I question is why this new narrative of Mary giving birth in the living room rather than a guest room is a better interpretation than of Matthew and Luke talking about a stable Consider what the new scholars want us to believe. They want us to believe that Mary and Joseph stayed in Joseph's family, with Joseph's family, while she was nine months pregnant. And when they arrived, the other extended family that was staying in the home in the guest room would not give up their room to a pregnant relative. That narrative tells us, they tell us, is more believable than burying Joseph and then Jesus to find comfort in a stable. We are supposed to ignore that the fact that hospitality in Judaism is a godly virtue and that it would be they want us to believe a regular practice to not give a guest room to a pregnant family member That is ridiculous. Whether it was December twenty-fifth or another date Whether it was a stable or a living space, whether it was three kings or three star seekers, whether it was two Or four star seekers. Whether the wise men came to Bethlehem shortly after the birth of Jesus or to Nazareth a few years later. All of the second guessing, changing of the narrative, is used by the devil to take us away from the fundamental reality that God became man in the form of an infant to save us from sin and death. And when I ponder why scholars would try to change the Christian, the Christmas narrative We know so well, I am reminded of the question that Jesus asked his followers when they brought up the faith of John the Baptist. He asked them to examine when they first heard of John and when they decided to go out and listen to John, what did they go out to see? In other words, what was their motive? What did they expect? What were you looking for? What were you expecting? And so let us ask that question in relation to the birth of Jesus. When each of us comes to a crush or a manger scene, what are we expecting to see? Do we come expecting to see cattle lowing? Do we come to see hay and mules and sheep and a trough that can be used to place an infant or to eat from? Or when you read the story of the birth of Christ, do you read it in order to picture the wooden stable, a lot of hay, some cows and stable stuff? Or if you have visited a live nativity, why didn't you go? What were you hoping to see? Does an older Caucasian man pretending to be a Jewish man named Joseph and a Caucasian woman neatly dressed and looking a long time past just having a baby And a Caucasian baby trying to play Jesus when the real parents are only concerned about him being out in the cold. Do each of these allow you to feel what it was like for Joseph and Mary and the Christ child over 2,000 years ago? Do real animals in a fake barn give out the aura of what it was like on that holy night? And of course I describe it in such a manner to help us realize that those are poor motives, poor motives for seeking out manger scenes or simply envisioning them in our minds. What is worthy to come and see is how simple and common it all was. It was a woman having a baby with her husband by her side in a simple place that was not their home. It is very likely that there were other babies born that night in Bethlehem and all over the known and unknown world. They were born in similar fashion with a woman suffering the pains of birth, a father worrying about the life of his wife and the child, with the need for God's preservation for the woman and the child. It was also familiar because of how many children have been brought into the world in the same manner. We know We know it was different because we are made aware of the spiritual realities that were going on in and around Mary and the child. It suddenly became less common when angels appeared to shepherds and told them about the newlyborn child that was not like any other child. And yet, what did the shepherds see? When they went there, what did they expect to see? Did they expect to see a glowing child like those paintings made of Christ with glowing halos around his head? No. It's just an ordinary child. We cannot know what they expected to see, but we can know what they saw. They saw a baby lying in a manger and a woman next to the child having just given birth. And a father, quite proud and concerned, protecting woman and child from the elements around them. That is what they saw. Again, it was so very common, even though it wasn't. And what of the wise men coming from the east, following a star? What did they come to see What were they expecting to see and following this star? They came to see a king, a great king, a king above all kings. And yet what did they see? They saw a child looking like any other child. They saw a family of three, like any other family of three. But they knew by the signs of God that it was not just any other family because the child wasn't any other child. But he didn't look different. As he was begotten in the form of an average man, having nothing physical, Isaiah tells us, about him that would draw men to him. It was also plain, it was regular, so simple. And yet it wasn't. The moment demanded gifts, great, gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh, gifts for a king. But he wasn't a king. At least he was not a king like the world elevates kings. He was a commoner, born into a lower-class home, born under Roman rule and law. Just like every other Jewish person around him. It was all so simple, so common, so ordinary, but it wasn't And thus the ordinary allows us to come back to this day, this day that is an ordinary day. It is the 25th of December. And yesterday was the 24th, and tomorrow is the 26th, just dates on a calendar Time moves on in the manner that it always has in our lives and will continue to do after we are gone. It is all so simple, so common, so ordinary, but it isn't. It isn't because this day is set aside to celebrate the birth of our Savior and our Lord. This day isn't like any other day, even though it looks like it is. Even though many do not believe that it is unique, that it is high, that it is holy, understand that it takes eyes of faith and and ears of believing that allow us to see a common day. as not common at all. And if you believe in Jesus as the Messiah, if you celebrate God's incarnation on this day, Even though you look ordinary and common like other human beings, you are not. You are a child of God. An inheritor of the kingdom of God. You are part of God's own people. On the outside, you and I are ordinary, but our souls, our souls are reborn to live forever with God. You don't feel it. You can't tell the difference. You don't need to. You just believe. You just have faith. And this clarity about things being very common, ordinary, and simple describes well what we do here on this ordinary but not ordinary day. We come to eat bread and drink wine. That is such a very simple, common, and ordinary thing to do, except it is not. Just like every other thing that God has ordered and sets apart, being blessed by God, bread is no longer common bread, and wine no longer common wine. They are instead a means of grace to us. Which is to say, physical matter that God uses to bestow to us a portion of his grace that is very unique and holy in the mystery of his very presence among us His very presence as we eat common bread, but not common bread, and drink common wine, but not common wine. And so I asked you this morning, what did you come here to see? What were you expecting? The great irony of our Christian worship is that everything you came to see today is common, but not common at all. And we say thanks be to God. Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God, we do thank you for making this day not so common. and for making us not so common, and that we might receive the means of grace that we believe is here your presence. Continue to bless us with that knowledge until we see you face to face. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Another New Year
sermons.speaker: Rev. William Vowles
