sermons.text: Let us pray. May the words of my mouth and the meditations of our hearts be acceptable in thy sight, O Lord, thy strength and our Redeemer, in the name of the Father and the Son. And the Holy Ghost. Maybe seated? Well, here we are at the end of another year Looking to the new. But as we look forward, I believe it is helpful to evaluate where we are now, as well as to look back with reflection where we've been. I wonder if you, like me, have ever been convicted by the rebukes to the churches in the beginning of the book of Revelation. Where to the church at Ephesus, the Apostle John tells us that they had lost their first love. Or to the Laodiceans who were labeled as lukewarm. These churches had lost their intimacy toward God. The Old Testament passage read this morning is one Well, if not of obscurity, certainly not one that is widely turned to or often quoted. But the story involved depicts a condition that is well rehearsed Throughout the Old Testament as well as the New. It is in direct contrast to the condition spoken of by the Apostle Paul in his letter to the To the Galatians, which brings forth the emphasis of sonship, or to the oneness in God that Jesus speaks of in the culmination of his high priestly prayer read this morning in our gospel reading in John 17. This brings out a oneness in God That we are all to keep in mind of, that we are to cherish and to think through as we go through this next year. He says that beginning in verse twenty-two, the glory which you have given me, I have given to them, that they may be one, just as we are one. And then in verse twenty-four says Father, I desire that they also whom you gave me may be with me where I am, that they may behold my glory which you have given me, for you love me before the foundation of the world. Jesus tells us that he will share the same intimacy that he had with his father before the foundation of the world. He will share that with all those who the Father has given him. But the prophet Hosea brings to God's people another message. His is more like the messages sent to the churches. That we spoke of earlier, one that reveals our tendency to wander and to seek our own identity and agenda. While Hosea is the first of the minor prophets that we come to in our Bibles chronologically, his message comes just before or just after that of Jonah and Amos. Like those two, his ministry occurred during the reign of King Jeroboam II in the north. Yet his work continued well beyond Jeroboam's death. as he served on through King Hezekiah. In total, Hosea prophesied for about 40 years. In the beginning of his ministry, the northern kingdoms experienced prosperity that was unsurpassed other than the reigns of David and Solomon. Yet things changed dramatically under Jeroboam II when he died. Over the next 20 years, there was an upheaval in Samaria, the capital of Israel Over the next 20 years, six of the of the of the or of the six kings that followed, four of them were assassinated. Some of these kings had made relationships with the more powerful Assyrian Empire. to secure their own positions. This influence essentially turned Israel into a pawn state until they ultimately were taken into exile in 722 BC. But God sent Hosea to Israel to warn his people against these foreign alliances But more importantly, to confront them with their unfaithfulness to a holy and faithful God This morning I'm going to whisk through a portion of the first three chapters of Hosea with the intent of noting the loss of intimacy on the part of God's people. But also with the hope of increasing ours. So chapter one begins with a seemingly very odd command given to Hosea by God Look at verse 2. He says, When the Lord first spoke through Hosea, the Lord said to Hosea, Go take to yourself a wife of harlotry. and have children of harlotry, for the land commits flagrant harlotry forsaking the Lord. Now we could easily spend all our time this morning just trying to unwrap that command and its meaning If you read ten different commentaries on this passage, each one will, in some way or another, have a differing view. Some say that this entire passage is allegorical, meaning that it has a hidden spiritual meaning that overrides the Literal text itself. Others say that we are to take it completely literal. Others have somewhat of a blending of the two views, but one thing is certain. The overall meaning and theme of this passage is much agreed upon by all, and really is true for the whole book. It is a prophecy that condemns an unfaithful covenant people for their waywardness and loss of intimacy toward God. A loving God. So let's look for a moment at this command. As mentioned, there are several different views on this. One being that God told Hosea literally to go take a prostitute for his wife at This gets difficult for some because in chapter three, verse one, God tells Hosea to go again. Love a woman who is loved by a lover and is committing adultery. But then in verse 2 says, so I bought her for myself, and then gives detail of the payment. Questions that come forth are several. Is this woman in chapter 3 the same woman in chapter 1 or a different one? Is the first incident in chapter 1 just a foretelling or an introduction to what happens in chapter 3? Or is it that Hosea went and married Gomer, a prostitute? Had children with her and then afterwards saw her abandon them only to go back to her old lifestyle. Yet another view is that because Hosea's wife and children would covenantly have become Israelites, they are by association connected to a people of prostitution. because of their disloyalty as a nation to Yahweh. The presumption then is that any woman that Hosea married and any children that he would have had with them would have been tainted by this national prostitution. So great was Israel's corruption and religious unfaithfulness at that time. But no matter the literal or allegorical reading of this passage The message and imagery are clear. God is the husband of his covenant people, his bride. This imagery is seen throughout Scripture, culminating in Revelation 19, where the people cried out, Let us rejoice and exalt and give him the glory. For the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his bride has made herself ready. This is a picture of great intimacy. Conveying a deep love that the Lord has for his people. And Israel was called to return that love to him as we are. This oneness mirrors that which occurs in a good and healthy godly marriage. I have to ask myself, you ought to ask yourself, am I pursuing the Lord in this manner? Well, Israel certainly wasn't, and because of that, judgment would come. In verses four through nine of chapter one, the Lord gives names to the children of Hosea and Gomer And names, as we know, had a significant place in the culture of the ancient world. Names were often chosen after the birth and were given according to events or circumstances that surrounded the birth. For instance, Jacob's name meant Sir Planar, sitting as he grabbed the heel of his brother Esau coming out of the womb. Or Moses, whose name meant drawn from water. In this case, there was no doubt that the children's names were given for a purpose. They were given as a prophetic judgment against Israel. And in each name there was, as I see it, a progression of judgment that got deeper. The name of their first child was Jezreel, meaning God sows. Jezreel, of course, was the site of many historical battles. It was the scene of great victory for the Gideon army. It was also the location of judgment in which the Israelites, led by King Saul, were defeated by the Philistines. It was also the place used by God to eradicate the house of Ahab. by the hands of Jehu, where Jezebel was thrown out of her window to her death and left her dogs. This name would have struck an accord with the people of Israel. The second name, Lo Rahama, or No Mercy, Her name signified the imminent withdrawal of compassion and mercy which God had shown to Israel over and over again, despite their covenantal unfaithfulness. Then in verse 9, we have the birth of their third child, whose name was La'ami, or Not My People. This was the high point of judgment and a low point for the condition of the people whom God had given so much and loved so completely. In this name, God basically declares his covenant with his people null and void. Israel's entire identity was that they were a people of the living God. Who were they without them without him? Who would they become? When I read the second chapter of this book, I am struck with awe at the great compassion, though, of our God. But I'm also struck with sorrow at the adulterousness of his people. Listen carefully as I highlight a few verses from chapter 2, beginning in verse 7. She will chase her lovers but not overtake them. Yes, she will seek them but not find them. Then she will say, I will go and return to my first husband, for then it is better for me than now. For she did not know that I gave her grain, new wine and oil, and multiplied her silver and gold, which they used for Baal. Israel had been given so much as we have. They had been rescued. They had been delivered. They had been loved. And yet, where did they turn? They turned to other gods, to Baal. Hosea says in verse seven She, meaning Israel, will chase her lovers. Her lovers are, of course, the Baals, but she will never overtake them. Israel will seek after the intimacy that they had with Yahweh, but they will never attain it. And that is the difference between a relationship with the living God and the hollow worship of idols. Only when she repents and turns to her loving husband will she be fulfilled. I asked this question. With the hope that you have a good answer to it, and I have a good answer. Where does your true fulfillment come from? Does it come from the world and its idols? Or from a living and loving God? Notice again in verse 8. Then she will say, I will go and return to my first husband, for then it is better for me than now. Isn't that the way we are as a people? God supplies us with blessing upon blessing. We use them for our own means and for our own idol worship, forgetting our great provider. He gives us pantries that overflow, homes with all the latest gadgets and convenience, comforts certainly beyond our needs. And do we use these resources and provisions to honor Him, to advance His kingdom? Well, certainly some individuals do. But as a culture and certainly as a nation, would you say that we do? Sadly, as a whole, I would say that we are much more concerned about advancing our own agendas, our own little bayals. But what happens when things get really difficult for us? Like Israel We will get on our knees seeking the love that we have left, knowing that if we return to our first husband, things will be better for us then than they are now. Kind of like the prodigal son. Can you see how the message this marriage of Hosea and Gomer would have been convicting to Israel? Imagine every time Hosea strolled through the town with Jezreel, no mercy, and not my people. Could anybody miss the message? I'm quite sure they understood the message, but what was their response? We know that there was no great revival. In fact, we know that the Assyrians fulfilled the prophecy and eventually took an unrepentant nation into captivity. So what causes a people to leave a loving relationship with their husband, the Almighty Living God, the creator and preserver of every living thing? How is that intimacy lost? By chasing after other gods. So how do we as individuals protect ourselves from losing this intimacy, assuming we have it? How do we get back what we once had? The same way that we protect the loss of intimacy in our marriages and other close relationships First and foremost, to have intimacy, someone must spend time with you You've heard it said. You know what someone cares about by looking at their checkbook, right? Well the same could be said about our schedules, can it? If you lay your calendar day by day, week by week, month by month, down in front of you, how much time is developed? And put aside for intimacy with our Savior. What are the things on that schedule that squeeze out our availability for prayer, for studying and reading His Word? For service to him. Staying connected has long now been a real thing of importance to much of our society. Smartphones, Facebook, Twitter. Instagram, I probably don't know the note the the the the modern ones for you young people but they all give us immediate access to friends family work and the world around us But with these advances, how much time is spent actually building meaningful face-to-face relationships with one another, with other people around us? Let me go a step further. How much time and effort is invested in connecting with our Lord and Savior? I dare to even guess how much time is spent by the average Christian in a week cultivating these intimacy-building activities. Sadly for many, I fear it's one hour on Sunday, if that. Well, like us, the Israelites were consumed by the culture around them. And many had no desire to nurture that relationship. Thankfully, like us. They were fortunate to have been called and redeemed by a faithful and loving covenantal God. So we see in chapter 3 in the Return of the Prodigal Wife that no matter how far we stray, our faithful husband is there to redeem us. One thing stands out loud and clear in this third chapter. There is a cost to redemption. Verse 2 says, So I bought her for myself with fifteen shekels of silver and one and a half homers of barley. Apparently Hosea didn't have enough cash or silver to redeem Gomer, so he had to use all the resources available to him. So he dipped into his barley stash. And the measurements here are very interesting. One and a half homers of barley came to a value of 15 shekels. Plus fifteen shekels of silver totals 30 shekels of silver that was paid for her. The same amount it took to redeem a slave. Also, sounds a lot like another transaction that took place later on in the history, doesn't it, of Israel? What was the price the religious leaders paid Judas for the betrayal of Jesus? 30 shekels. So as we enter into this coming year, let us remember through God's prophet Hosea the valuable cost of redemption. And in so doing, may we not ignore the loving desire he has for us to be intimate with him. With each of us each and every day, knowing that we are bought with a price, perfected in unity, so that the world might know who Jesus is. That Emmanuel has come, and that he has come as Savior and Lord. Let us pray. O Holy Father, our Creator, Protector, Husband, Guide, may we, your people, be ever mindful of Your loving desire for intimacy, and that while we are made in your image, we are yet fallen and weak. So through your Holy Spirit, help us to respond in kind to your love, shining the light of your son, Emmanuel, to a dark and needy world around us. In your name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Suitable Marriage Suitable Doctrine
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We continue on in the book of Genesis, even though it is Epiphany, that'll simply be mentioned. But we are actually covering Genesis 23 and 24 today, even though the reading was only from Genesis 24. So Turn there in your Bibles, if you would, and we can uh touch on each chapter. There is a practical way and a theoretical way to approach these two chapters The practical way teaches the reader to be careful where one is buried and who one marries. In chapter 23, Abraham goes to great lengths to secure a place for Sarah and later himself to be buried. The first part of the chapter depicts Abraham following the customs of the land. He's bowing and doing other gestures in order to secure a proper place for his burial. Because Abraham is respected, he is given a field that contains caves, and these caves would provide a proper burial site. And we have to understand that a proper burial is a burial. It is not cremation The Christian tradition takes its lead from Abraham and has promoted burial rather than cremation because we believe in the resurrection of the body. In our Western Christian past, belief in the resurrection of the body has also encouraged parishes to provide and care for their own cemeteries with the hope that on that day of resurrection we would all be raised together in force. I describe all of this, not to condemn cremation. But as a minister of the gospel, I do frown upon it. The Lord can and will raise up those he has chosen in whatever form he finds them. I do say this to promote Christian burial because as we practice it, we make a positive statement, a proclamation. about the righteousness of the body in its original form, and we make a statement about the resurrection. The hope that we have of the resurrection, that our bodies will indeed be raised, and when we bury them, we proclaim that resurrection. Now, the practical lesson regarding who one marries is learned by the way that Abraham goes to great lengths to ensure that Isaac, his covenant son would marry a woman from proper religious stock. Both Isaac and Abraham realized that no suitable wife would be found among the Canaanites where they lived. If Abraham was going to provide a wife for his son, who would be open to the instruction of there being but just one God, one true God, he reasoned that he must go back to his own people. Being a man of faith, Abraham trusted that he could send his servant and that God would use his servant to identify the right woman for Isaac. The romance of the story, as it begins in verse 10 of chapter 24, shows us the faith of Abraham being expressed through the prayer of the servant. The prayer that he trusted God would answer. It is romantic because the circumstances make the uniting of Isaac and Rebekah one of destiny God's hand was clearly involved. God's will was being done. From the writings of poems and songs, it appears that All lovers want to know that the man or woman they have fallen in love with is the one they are destined to be with forever. In truth, Rebekah is chosen for Isaac in the manner described here because they are of the covenant line of Abraham. And Abraham is called the father of the faith. The line, the family, is specific. Your love story and mine are not going to be like this one. Most of our love stories are pretty mundane except to ourselves. The Bible doesn't teach any such thing as a soulmate. It's not in the scriptures. If you are married, the person you are married to, well, he or she is now your soulmate. Be thankful for him or her, and that would be enough in this life. So Rebecca we find is ideal for Isaac because she was first, it says, a virgin. Second, she has a servant's heart, and that was evident by her watering of the camels. Third, she was of Abraham's household. That God's hand was leading Rebekah to marry Isaac is further seen by the manner Abraham's servant was received by the family. The story he told of Abraham and Isaac convinced all of them that this Rebekah was an obvious choice for Isaac. Biblical commentator Henry Morris says that the typological teaching in the story of Rebekah being chosen for Isaac, well, to him, it's very clear He says that Abraham's servant is like the Holy Spirit, who is in the world working, seeking a bride for the Son of God, who is Jesus the Christ. Isaac is like Christ, for he is the son of the promise. Rebecca is like all those who would receive Jesus as Savior, making them a part of the bride, which is the church. We can take the typological even further by noting that the servant adorns Rebekah with jewels, silver and gold. He beautifies her just as the Holy Spirit beautifies the church, making those in the church righteous. When Isaac and Rebekah finally meet, the scripture says that Rebekah became Isaac's wife, and he loved her. Well that is what our Savior does. He loves his church. Now all of this typology is very good and useful to point us to the direction of the Son of God to be revealed, who will seek out his church and love it as he does his own life. Such parallels confirm to us the truth of the gospel. Such parallels confirm that the way of salvation is and always will be through Christ. And there is more. There is more typology in this story than what I've mentioned thus far. We have just seen how the story teaches us how we are to be careful who we marry. Yep. We have also learned in another sermon that women in Scripture are symbolic at times Regarding the passions of mankind, or our emotions. In placing these two thoughts side by side, I conclude that the story of Isaac Seeking for and marrying Rebecca contains a lesson for all Christians to be careful, to be careful as to what doctrines they hold to, what teachings they believe As was said, Abraham and Isaac knew that there was not a suitable woman for Isaac amongst the women of the Canaanites. The Canaanites, you remember, were a polytheistic people, and they did indeed worship idols. Abraham and his family were like new converts, for they were the only ones worshiping the one true God. In order for Abraham's family to continue to worship the truth that had been revealed to them, Abraham knew, he knew, that his son could not, should not be influenced by idol worshippers. Remember, remember that the law restricting God's people from marrying women from Canaanite lands had not yet been given. But Abraham, the man of faith, did not need such a law, for the law of God was written here on his heart. He needed to protect the primary doctrine of his faith, which was and is that there is but only one God. The law that restricted intermarriage between the children of Abraham and the people of other faiths was given when Israel was to re-enter the land of Canaan after the exodus under Moses. Or service, after Moses. By then the people of God had swelled to over a million, necessitating the need for a clear statement about who they should marry and who they should not. This is from Deuteronomy chapter 7, verse 1. When the Lord your God brings you into the land which you go to possess, and has cast out many nations before you, the Hittites, and the Gergeshites, and the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jibusites. Seven nations greater and mightier than you, and when the Lord your God delivers them over to you, you shall conquer them and utterly destroy them. You shall make no covenant with them, nor show mercy to them, nor shall you make marriages with them You shall not give your daughter to their son, nor take their daughter for your son, for they will turn your sons away from following me to serve other gods So the anger of the Lord will be aroused against you and destroy you suddenly. I underline that it is not just the primary reason, but the only reason that this commandment is given Is to protect God's people from false doctrine, from false belief, from false worship. The only reason The law is not racially motivated, it is not economically motivated, it is not culturally motivated, it is doctrinal. God is protecting his people as to what they believe. Now the ultimate example we know of is, of course, King Solomon. Who is recorded in 1 Kings to have taken over 700 wives, including wives from the Moabites, the Ammonites, the Edomites, the Sidonians, and the Hittites. From the nations, the scripture says, of whom the Lord had said to the children of Israel, you shall not intermarry with them. It has been explained to us that when Solomon was older, these very same wives turned his heart to other gods. All Christians are to heed the warning from this example, for it is weighted by the fact that Solomon was considered the wisest of kings, and yet. He did not have the wisdom to protect his heart from falsehood. Now, the New Testament provides a similar warning. When St. Paul tells the Corinthians, do not be unequally yoked together with unbelievers. For what fellowship he reasons has righteousness with lawlessness And what communion has light with darkness? Or what part has a believer with an unbeliever? In case you are unaware, the yoke metaphor refers to two oxen joined together in a yoke, in a restraining, so that they can plow together. And if one oxen is much stronger than the other, well, they start to go in circles, making them ineffective. And so it is with Christians who are yoked with non-Christians, they go in circles. Again, on a very practical level, we can be certain that a Christian should not marry a non-Christian. Beyond that, we should recognize the warning against marrying ourselves to false doctrine. For that is what one is doing if he or she marries a non-Christian. Now, to avoid confusion, I want to be clear what I am saying. We can learn from the choosing of Rebekah for Isaac that it is important for us to be careful who we marry. Because the warning about marriage refers to being led to worship false gods, we can take the example a step further and heed the warning to be careful about the doctrines we believe. Consider that the number the number of warnings that Jesus gave regarding false teachers He said the following: be aware of men. Take heed of the leaven. Beware of false prophets. And these and other examples are how Jesus starts off several teachable moments. He warns them first of false teachings. And of course, several epistles also deal primarily with the warning against false teachers and false doctrines. Upon hearing that the Galatians had been persuaded by Jews to keep the law for their salvation rather than trust in Christ Jesus, the Apostle Paul warns. He says, I marvel that you Have already turned away so soon from him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different gospel, which is not another, but there are some who trouble you and want to pervert the gospel of Christ. Later in the same letter he challenges them. He says, Are you so foolish? Having begun in the spirit, are you now being made perfect by the flesh? For that's what they were being taught. With the Church of Thessalonica, the apostle is concerned that the people are not ignorant about what happens when a Christian dies. He says to them, but I do not want you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning those who have fallen asleep, lest you sorrow as others who have no hope. He then explains that those who have died in Christ will be raised first when Jesus comes his second time. In St. John's second letter, his main purpose is to give a general warning against false doctrine. He says, many deceivers have gone out into the world who do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh. This is a deceiver and an antichrist. Whoever transgresses and does not abide in the doctrine of Christ does not have God. Doctrine. What we believe. St. Jude, in his one and only epistle, encourages Christians to contend for the faith because, he says, men have crept in among the church who had turned the grace of God into lewdness. Then, after a warning of how God will judge such people, he admonishes Christians. He says, Remember the words which were spoken before the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, how they told you That there would be mockers in the last time who would walk according to their own ungodly lusts. But you, beloved, building yourselves up On your own most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life. Urgency, safety, protection of what we believe The comparison between how one is to be careful about marriage and being careful about doctrine is appropriate considering how loose we view the commitment of marriage in our Western culture. We practice our affiliation with the church bodies and church teachers with the same loose commitment. When we become dissatisfied, we believe it is within our right to go to another church or align ourselves with a teacher without making what is believed, what is practiced, what is taught, the most important issue. What many underestimate is how important doctrine is in forming us, in determining our relationship with God. It is difficult to give examples about how doctor informs us and determines our relationship with God without referring to churches around us. I don't believe it is appropriate for me to downgrade other churches, for it serves no purpose. So the best way to handle this is to speak in generalities. In general, we should know that the manner a church worships forms and determines how God is understood by us. The teachers or churches' position on the authority of Scripture also forms and determines The way in which Scripture is read, taught, preached, forms, and determines. The frequency of observing the sacraments forms and determines. The creeds and confessions of the church form and determine. And if you agree with all these statements, then you agree how important it is to be careful, extra careful regarding who you marry yourself to. In regards to the many churches who claim to be Christian. Now, this may shock you. Nonetheless, it should be said All churches or teachers who claim to be Christian may not be Christian. And even those that passed certain tests, such as confessing the Apostles' Creed or observing the sacraments, may not teach sound doctrine. And I must add that much of what you read on the internet that claims to be Christian is not sound doctrine. What social media reveals is how gullible people can be in what they will believe. The devil knows this. And therefore fills your inboxes and your social feeds with hat-truths, poor reasoning, to keep Christians ignorant and keep them chasing doctrinal rabbit trails. To be sure, as I have already said probably too many times in the sermon, the lesson to be learned by the marriage of Isaac and Rebekah is how careful we are to be regarding who we marry, but What also we should have learned is to be careful in what we are believing. And we must be warned against false teachings. We also must be pointed to truth. What you hear from this pulpit and in our Sunday school and in our Bible studies in this parish is carefully planned to match up with what the scriptures teach, and this is important. And what the church has taught that the scriptures teach. For one can say, I believe in the scriptures, but their interpretation is much different than Christians have believed for thousands of years. What I am preaching is being careful in our doctrines to know the Holy Scriptures While also knowing of our church fathers and how they have interpreted the scriptures that we say we uphold as our authority. Abraham was careful for his son and was even careful regarding the burial of his wife. Such carefulness should challenge us to examine all that we do in light of Scripture. Parents should be challenged to know what your child's teachers believe. Do you know what your child's teachers believe and what they practice? Radio listeners should be challenged to know what the preachers on the radio believe and practice. Church shoppers should know all that they can know about the people and its leaders before jumping in. When St. Paul tells Christians in Rome to bring every thought into captivity, he was not just talking to the church leaders. He was talking to every one of us who believe. He was expecting all Christians to work at properly understanding God, which is properly understanding God's word. Because it is epiphany, we Gentiles are especially thankful today that God has included us in his story of redemption. And we can show our thankfulness by how we know the holy scriptures that He has given so freely to us. To know the Bible, to know the Bible is to avoid false doctrine. It is to be careful on who you marry your faith to. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God, for this typology, for this lesson, and seeing how careful carefully we must be and who we marry our faith to. Father, bring us all into conviction to examine all that we allow to come into our minds and to believe in our hearts, that we might not turn to any other God. We pray this in Jesus' name

sermons.title: The Fruitful
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. May be seated. Genesis chapter 25. And our reading picked up at verse 19, but we are actually going to be covering the entire chapter. So if you want to turn there, we'll make some comments about the first part of the chapter. Genesis 25. One of the obvious typologies in Scripture is children being a type of the fruit of the Spirit. Remember that children are called the fruit of a man's loins. The effect of the Holy Spirit on a person's life is also called fruit, and are various fruits as you know them, love, joy, peace, patience. and so on. Thus, when we read Genesis 25, that Abraham took on another wife, and by her had more sons Thus with them we are to understand that there was more fruit in Abraham's life. The fruit, or sons, He has from his new wife Katurah, however, are not the same as Isaac. Isaac is the promised seed. Isaac is the only son of the covenant line. The fruit of Abraham that he has from Keturah Can be identified as earthly fruit or fruit that benefits him in this life, but does not have anything to do with the life to come. Now this typology is true in our lives as well, as there is fruit that we produce after being born anew that is Eternal, like Isaac, that fruit is being under the covenant of Christ, knowing that heaven is our inheritance. The most important fruit There is also fruit we enjoy in this life that is not eternal, but a byproduct of living godly lives. A good paying job can be a fruit, as it can be a byproduct of a hard-earned education and a good work ethic. A good marriage is a fruit in this life. Jesus said that in heaven men and women will not be given in marriage, but in this life, Proverbs says that a good woman is from the Lord. A good church, good friends, good meals, etc. , are fruit in this life that we are free to enjoy They are not eternal, but we are allowed to enjoy them. Abraham's sons born to Keturah are enjoyed, but they will not receive the inheritance of Abraham. And by this I do not mean to say that heaven will not be their home. I do not know that. The scripture doesn't go there. But I mean that they are not chosen. They're not of the chosen line from whom the Savior will come. Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac because Isaac was of that line The sons born to Keturah are not heard from after Abraham's death other than Midian, and Midian will be a type of what Ishmael was to Isaac and Esau was to Jacob. Although the fruit of Abraham is mentioned, it is not the focus of the chapter. The focus of chapter 25 is the birth of twin brothers Jacob and Esau to the parents of Isaac and Rebekah. But before we go there, however, we need to compare the lives of Ishmael and Isaac as it is described in this chapter. Look at verses 12 through 16, and there we are given the names of Ishmael's sons, 12 in all. Each of these sons were princes. They were leaders who settled their own towns and were successful, each of them, in this life. But number 12 symbolizes a complete people, just as the 12 tribes of Israel represent all of Israel, and the 12 apostles represent all of Christ's disciples. By Ismael having twelve sons, God's promises fulfilled. You remember that he gave to Hagar, saying that he would make her son into a great nation. It should be underlined, if only to shore up what I have previously explained that Ishmael had twelve sons. I've argued that sons are fruits of the Spirit, and it just so happens that there are twelve fruits of the Spirit, twelve sons, twelve fruits. A coincidence? I think not. After Ishmael's twelve sons are listed, we learn that Isaac, his wife Rebekah, was barren. We then learn from verse 20 and 26 that she was barren for 20 years, 20 years before she gave birth to her twin sons. This is not what was expected. This is not what we would expect when comparing the fruit of the flesh with the fruit of the spirit. We would not expect that Ishmael, who was not of the chosen seed, would be more fruitful in this life than Isaac, who was the chosen seed. What is expected is that all who worship the only true God, that they would be blessed more abundantly than pagans in this life and the life after. Because we expect this, we get disappointed time and time again. The pagans have more. The enemies of God triumph in this life. Examples abound. The backstabber climbs the corporate ladder. The perverted obtain mansions and yachts. The deceiver successfully steals from the poor and the widow. The godless are voted into high political positions. The Patriots win Super Bowls. And the pause on that one These are just a few examples of the wicked succeeding in this life. And yes, they succeed either on the backs of the godly or as the godly struggle. Ishmael has twelve sons, while Isaac, for the first twenty years of marriage, has none. The preacher in Ecclesiastes announces the reality of the wicked, seeming to triumph in this life when he says There is a just man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who prolongs life in his wickedness. It doesn't seem fair, and it isn't, at least in this life. This 20 years was a trial for Isaac But not just Isaac. Is it it is a trial for many who are called children of God King David, who, you know, wrote most of the church's Psalter, was repeatedly disappointed and expressed his disappointment in his songs to the Lord. He wrote, For I was envious of the boastful when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. For there are no pains in their death, but their strength is firm. They are not in trouble as other men, nor are they plagued like other men. Behold, these are the ungodly who are always at ease They increase in riches. Men of the world are those who have their portion in this life and whose belly God fills with hidden treasure. They are satisfied with children and leave the rest of their possessions to their babes. Again, we think this is not how it's supposed to be. The righteous should be more blessed. The children of God should be less troubled. How is it that the barren couple asks that we should be desperate to have a child and the sinner is able to procreate without love, without commitment, without scruples? How is it? The man out of work asks that so many men hate their jobs and speak unkindly of their bosses when there are men like me who would be grateful to have an opportunity to provide for my family. How is it? That a man can smoke like a chimney, eat like a goat, and drink like a fish, and live to be a hundred. And there are men who have never smoked that contract lung disease There is no denying that in this life the godless prosper. Thankfully, there is a solace that Should be apparent in regards to these discrepancies in prosperity. We are to remember the words of our Savior Who told his disciples that none of them had left anything that would not be returned to them a hundredfold in the life to come? Heaven is our place of retribution. It is the place where all will be made right. It is where the martyred saints under the altar will have their prayer answered as they ask, How long, O Lord, how long? Another solace is the virtue of patience. The children of God must often say, It is not yet my time. We are weak, but you, O God, are strong. We are despised, but you are honorable. The flesh, like Ishmael, has no such delay. The flesh brings forth its fruit of wrath and envy and emulation while the Spirit of God waits. The Spirit waits from year to year. Isaac and Rebekah waited twenty years. But when it is time, it is the fullness of time. It is the perfect time, meaning that it is as God would have it. The flesh, in contrast, has it immediately. It has it now, just as it wants it, and it is imperfect. It is fallen. The Spirit instead waits, waits until the fullness of time has come. The Spirit waits until after Isaac prays. Notice that. We should not understand that this is the first time Isaac has prayed. such a prayer, but we should understand that it is the first time the Holy Spirit responds positively to the prayer. When God answers prayer, it is again not as we would expect. No sooner had Rebecca conceived that she felt trouble within her. This cannot be It was enough that the son of the covenant, Isaac, and his lovely wife Rebecca, had to wait so long and watch while the unrighteous prospered. When that time is over, it should all go well. But it does not. If all is well, Rebecca asks, why am I like this? After she inquires of the Lord as to what is going on within her, the Lord answers her and says Two nations are in your womb. Two peoples shall be separated from your body. One people shall be stronger than the other, and the older shall serve the younger. What could possibly possibly worse for a mother to hear? Her family will be divided, and it is certain because the Lord has told her And once again we ask, how can this happen to the family of God? The family that God chose to be a great nation, to proclaim the truth that Yahweh is the only true God. Well perhaps it is the term chosen that the Israelites became enamored with. The word chosen can imply privilege. The word privilege implies blessings and blessings that are expected in this life In a similar way, I have observed Christians being enamored by the word saved To find out if another person is before the Lord as a believer, we might ask, are you saved? Answers vary, but sound something like, yes, I was saved at the age of twelve. But we are to notice that the word saved has a finality to it. It is used as if all is finished regarding a particular person's salvation. And we seem to assume a person who is saved has the blessings of heaven at his or her disposal. When the trials come, when prayers are not answered, when sickness, accidents, and many other troubles occur, we don't say it out loud, but we wonder Is he really saved? We think it because we are assuming that a person who is chosen or a person who is saved Would never do anything bad, and nothing bad would happen in his life. Isaac and Rebecca would tell us differently. The struggle that goes on within Rebecca is a type of that which is in every Christian and in every Christian body, which is the church. Within her are a child of the spirit and a child of the flesh. And like Ishmael and Isaac, the two are opposed to one another. And as we have already learned by studying Ishmael and Isaac in an earlier sermon, there is first the natural and then the spiritual. Ishmael and Esau are the natural, and they are first, making them men of the flesh. And Isaac and Jacob are spiritual, as they came after the flesh, being born second, making them men of the spiritual. And from this example of Isaac, we have to admit that seed from a chosen man of God results in both the carnal and the spiritual. It is honest to admit that what each of us produce in this life is mixed, mixed being of the flesh and of the spirit. And we should not be surprised by this. But I am afraid once again we are. People of God commit acts of sin while being marked as holy and righteous. People of God live at times according to their flesh. If they live all the time according to their flesh, they are not people of God as their works prove. But there is not one man of God beside Jesus who does not live from time to time according to his flesh. Too many Christians have placed Christian leaders on pedestals, expecting them never to produce acts of flesh, only to be sorely disappointed when it happens. Some even become disillusioned with the faith because sinful behavior of a man of God is unearthed. It's revealed. Of course, if there is egregious sin practiced by a church leader, he must be removed from his office. But church leaders will always practice sins of the flesh because they too, like all of us, see through that glass dimly and therefore make foolish decisions, careless comments. And commit unwise practices. That is the way of it In addition, not only does carnal seed come from men of God, the carnal seed is mixed in with the seed of the Spirit. Esau and Jacob were together in the womb. This fact forces us to acknowledge that even acts that we perform for the sake of God's kingdom are mixed with influences from our flesh. That is to say that when a person acts in obedience to God's commandments and loves his brother, He may be doing so with righteousness and selfish motivation mixed together. The selfishness may be small, but it is there. For instance, a man may give to the poor, but do so congratulating himself that he is more thoughtful than others. A man may risk his physical well-being to save a woman in distress, and at the same time praise himself that he is braver than all the rest who are around her. The seed of the flesh, in such instances, is undetectable, but it is there. The fact that Esau and Jacob were together in the womb also forces us to acknowledge what is in the church. Rebecca is a type of the church, for the church is a mother to the people of God. The church nurtures God's children. Within the church, within its womb, are sons of the flesh and sons of the spirit. Jesus used the analogy of tares and wheat. Thus the very nature of the church, while upon earth, involves the presence of flesh and spirit. There are men within the church who, although called Jesus Lord, Lord, are actually men of the flesh. And there are men and women of the flesh who pray side by side. With men and women of the Spirit, who will be separated from one another when the Lord returns and judges. And this is hard for the Mother Church, as it was hard for Rebecca. It is hard to know that the family will one day be split. Splitting of the family occurs in this life, of course. We know it well here at St. Stephen's, as we do, as most churches do that strive to worship in spirit and in truth. At times it is hard. What is to be learned from this passage of Scripture is that this is how God has planned it. We should then not be shaken when we experience the struggles within us as individuals. The carnal is still present and it is in conflict with the Spirit of God. We should not be shaken when we see the struggles within others, even men to whom we have given high esteem. We should not be shaken when we see it in the church. For it is as God said it would be, and it is for us to work through it. through the days of conflict, knowing that better days are always ahead. When there is strife We are tempted to say that something must be wrong with that person who is struggling or wrong with that church because they have conflict But there is nothing wrong, because it is as it should be. In fact, if there is no strife, then there might be something wrong because the devil doesn't need to stir up anything allowing a person or church to remain in a state of being lukewarm. Strife can be sanctifying where stagnation is a sign of death. So this entire chapter teaches us to accept our struggles as part of the Christian life. And to be faithful while struggling to know that God's will is being done. It may take 20 years, as it did Isaac and Rebekah. It may take even more, as it did with Esau and Jacob. But God's will is being done, and his will will be done that we can lean upon. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God We thank you for the stories in this chapter that truly do describe the lives that we are living. Describe the church as it is striving to honor you. May all of us, may all of us recognize the struggle and not back away from it, not shrink from it, but walk through it, knowing that there is a better tomorrow. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Holding to the Birthright
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. The sermon this morning comes from Genesis twenty five. As always, it would be useful for you to turn there There appears to be purposeful ambiguity in the narrative as it ends in Genesis chapter 25. We made effort last week to understand the difference between Esau and Jacob. Esau was a man of the flesh, and Jacob a man of the spirit. And just as flesh is said to be first in this life and then the Spirit, so it was that Esau was born first and then Jacob. Just as flesh and the spirit are contrary to one another, so were Esau and Jacob. And that contrariness to one another is evident by them wrestling in their mother's womb The typology is very, very clear, as we have seen, and as we will see What is not clear, what is ambiguous, is the ethical behavior of the godly characters in this narrative. The first ethical ambiguity is in the favoring of Esau by Isaac and the favoring of Jacob by Rebekah We know such favoring is wrong because the Bible says so. Show favoritism to no man, commanded the Apostle Paul. The command is based on the fact that all men are created in God's image, making them each worthy of the same esteem. The similarity between the rich and the poor, Proverbs says, is that the Lord made them all. There is to be no partiality shown because of social or economic status. There is to be no estimated value of worth for one person over another. For there is neither male nor female, Jew nor Greek, but all are one in Christ Jesus. We also know that the type of favoritism being shown by Isaac and Rebecca is wrong because of the damage that it does psychologically to the health of a child. Children have a difficult enough time fitting into their peer groups, finding their place in the world If a child has to add a perception that he or she is not particularly liked by a parent, but the same parent prefers a sibling Such a thought could send a child over an emotional edge from which he may not recover. We can only imagine how difficult it was for Jacob to be less in his father's eyes for the simple reason that Esau cooked, or killed and cooked, venison. Thus it would appear that Isaac's standard for favoritism was his stomach. The second ethical ambiguity is the conniving way that Jacob obtains the birthright from Esau. The story seems to put Jacob in a planned thought-ahead geographical position where he is making a particular stew and he knows that his brother will desire it coming from his expedition knowing he would be naturally tired and hungry. Thus he takes advantage of his brother's weakness in the flesh and makes a deal with him in such a manner that we would expect the devil himself to do As people of God, we are actually called to warn other people of temptations and the sins that result. It is better, Jesus said, for a man to have a millstone tied around his neck and to be thrown into the sea than to be guilty of leading someone astray. If we are to pray, Lord, lead us not into temptation, we most certainly are not to be responsible for tempting anyone. And yet, here Jacob tempting Esau and succeeding. These ethical scenarios are ambiguous. Because the Bible does not condemn any of these actions mentioned, at least not in this story. Nowhere do we read that it was wrong for Isaac and Rebekah to show favoritism to a particular son. Nowhere is Jacob condemned or even spoken of in a negative way for tempting his brother. In fact, it is just the opposite. Hebrews chapter 6 condemns Esau, condemns him with fornicators and the profane for selling his birthright. And there is reason, I believe, for this ethical ambiguity We can look back on these stories and condemn the parents and Jacob for what they did, but we should remember that the law had not yet been given That the revelation of Christ had not come to them. We can conclude that their behavior was wrong, but that's not the point of the story. The point of telling the story, the reason why it is part of holy writ, is not for us to judge the characters and their moral or ethical standards through our New Testament eyes. It is to look beyond the ethics to what each character and scenario represents. Ultimately, we are to come to understand the privilege of the birthright. The privilege of the birthright. Undoubtedly, the purpose of the narrative style is to contrast Esau and Jacob, and so that's what we need to do. The few deep details given are for the purpose of that contrast. We learn of their birth and shortly after their adult lives with no information about their development. The story gets to the point immediately, and the point is that these two men are different, and the point is why they are different. The differences begin with God's prophecy to Rebecca. Remember that he tells her that within her are two nations, not just two children, two nations. As descendants of Abraham, nationality was intertwined with purpose, identity, and faith. To be different nations meant that you were a people of different faith. So Esau and Jacob are of a different faith. That the older would serve the younger was in contrast to the culture and the time. The oldest son had the birthright to receive the primary inheritance of his father. The scripture later describes it as a double portion of both spiritual blessing and material wealth. That God is reversing this order is another instance of God pointing to the person of Jesus. Remember that Cain was born first but was rejected. Ishmael was born first, also rejected. Esau born first, and he too rejected. These are all in the same line of Adam, who was that first man, but was rejected because he sinned, requiring there to be a second Adam who we know is Jesus. He is the secondborn and the true son of the promise. From the moment of the twins' birth, each child Revealed its ultimate role or character in life. We read that Esau was ruddy, or as the New King James states, red and hairy. The word ruddy describes natural health and strength. Interestingly, I find this stuff interesting. His hue, his redness is like the red horse. or the scarlet beast that is described in Revelation 6 and 12. The responsibility of the red horse is to take peace, to take peace from the earth by sword Thus the color red communicates physical strength and violence, as was Esau. Esau is also described as hairy. Long or abundant hair communicates strength along with wildness. The Lord through Ezekiel used the description when referring to Israel growing in strength. We remember Samson's strength associated with hair. The wildness is in the line of Nebuchadnezzar, who you remember, when he went mad like a beast, let his hair grow long. Thus Esau is described to be like a fierce animal. In contrast is Jacob. Nothing about him physically is noted other than he does not look like his brother We should note also that if Jacob is born like most children, we should note that Jacob was likely hairless, or at least not hairy like Esau. In Numbers 8, and again, these contrasts or these connections fascinate me, in numbers eight, the priests Who were consecrating themselves to serve in the temple were required to shave all of their flesh, all of their hair off of their flesh, symbolizing cleanliness In order to go into the temple. At birth, Jacob was set apart from Esau. The one description of Jacob at birth was his action, what he did. Jacob, we will find is a man of action. He is born grasping his brother's heel. And as this is seen, he is then named Jacob, which the word means surplanter. A surplanter is a person who wants to take over for or take place of the person who is ahead of him. Jacob is not only destined to receive the blessing of the firstborn, he has wanted it since birth. The next paragraph in the story describes the brothers as men. As men, they are vastly different regarding the trades that they choose. Esau became a skillful hunter, and Jacob became a tent dweller. It might appear by this translation that Jacob is a homebody and that Esau is a man's man. This is not the case. Describing Jacob as a tent dweller means that he was as his father was, and as his grandfather was. He was a shepherd. He herded and cared for livestock. Esau, in contrast, was unsettled. He was an unsettled man wandering in and out. He was a man who was uncomfortable in his own skin. He went out to hunt when it was not necessary to hunt. He honed the skill of hunting that was not needed, for there was plenty of livestock to eat. To prefer to hunt What is not needed could be a sign of an unsettled soul. The Bible warns men against leading unsettled lives. The warning is in line with the command not to covet. Unsettled men look for other women besides the one that God has given them. They look for thrill or adventure as if providing for and raising a family is not thrilling and adventurous enough. They pursue sport for the sake of distraction. Distraction so that they do not have to face the reality that their youth is gone and the end of their days on earth is coming closer and closer. Instead of leading unsettled lives, the scripture commends the pursuit of peaceable and quiet lives. Paul said to the Thessalonians, aspire to a quiet life, to mind your own business, and to work with your hands as we commanded you. While these two brothers had nothing in common that was noticeable, they did come in contact, and the most important moment of their encounter, that is told to us. And as I described earlier, it appears that Jacob placed himself in a position to bribe his brother, whom he knew was likely to come through where Jacob was cooking his stew. And perhaps like no other time before, Esau would come, like every time before, Esau would come back hungry after spending a good deal of time in the fields. And if we can look beyond the ethical issue that is presented of Jacob bribing his brother, it is there that we notice the primary point. Jacob wanted the birthright of his brother, and he worked to get it, while Esau cared more for his appetite than his birthright. It is this contrast of the two brothers where the greatest lesson and warning, warning is found. Jacob cherished the birthright, whereas Esau did not. This is the important difference between men of the flesh and men of the spirit. It is the difference between the wheat and the tares, the sheep and the goats. When Esau is presented with a bargain, his logic is based on the immediate. In the moment. He is hungry, so hungry that he feels famished. He reasons that a birthright will do him no good if he dies, so he willingly sells it. Of course Esau would not have died, but he felt like it in the moment, and that was enough. Perhaps he felt even too weak to beat up his brother and take the school for himself But whatever the case, his immediate hunger was most important to him. After having eaten both the red lentil stew and bread Jacob had made, Esau went his way, apparently thinking nothing about what he had done. The Lord, however summarizes what he did by stating, thus Esau despised his birthright. To understand how serious this is, we must understand birthright. The birthright, as was said, is a right to a blessing. It was for the firstborn male in a family, and it consisted of the right to a blessing of the father for prosperity. As well as receiving a double portion of all that the father had owned compared to the rest of the siblings. What distinguished the birthright is that it was given to the oldest son based on the fact that he was born first, rather than having worked to earn the blessing, to earn the inheritance. The birthright then was ordained by God, meaning that God chose who would be born first, and thus who would receive the blessing, the double inheritance. To despise a birthright then was to despise a gift from God This is what Esau did, and it is what Israel did when they rejected the Messiah. The parallel of Esau despising his birthright and the people of Israel despising Jesus as God's son is before us in this story. God chose in the fullness of time to present his son before the people of Israel. Jesus said that he came first for the Jews He referred to them as God's children, and you remember he referred to the Gentiles as dogs under the table. He confirmed the Jews as God's chosen, as a people who were privileged by birth to have the law and to be the first to hear the gospel of Jesus. He even prayed up to the end of his life that the Heavenly Father would forgive them because they know not what they were doing. And yet they rejected him. They despised him. By rejecting the Son of God who came to save them, they were rejecting their birthright as children of Abraham. As we recognize these parallels, and as we gawk at the audacity of Esau and the Jews to reject their birthright, we also must be warned. If you have been baptized in the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, you too have been given a birthright. You too have been given a blessing and a double portion inheritance. For all who claim Jesus as Savior are called sons of God, and all are inheritors of his kingdom. Having been adopted as sons, we are each to understand ourselves as firstborn, because as believers in Jesus, we all share in the inheritance from the least to the greatest. All of us, male and female, are to see ourselves as adopted sons, for sons are the inheritors. And as a son of God, you too can be tempted to sell your birthright. It is what the devil would have you do. This can be done in various ways, of course, and it is usually not as blatant as Jacob's offer to Esau. As God's children, we are privileged to call upon the name of the Lord. So the devil would have us believe it is more of a privilege to do something else. As God's children, we are promised that our daily bread would be provided. But the devil tempts us to want more than we need. And to pursue temporary wealth before pursuing the kingdom of God. As God's children, we are called to give up our lives in this life. with the promise of an eternal life after death. But the devil tempts us to pursue pleasures in this life, or pleasures in the moment, just like Esau. Esau gave into temptation. He settled for pleasure and satisfaction in the moment. This is the most common of temptations. And as I was writing this sermon, I recognized that I have I have preached like this before. I have given many warnings over the years regarding the dangers of exchanging pleasure in this life, exchanging it for the hope of heaven after? And some people who are no longer with us did not heed that warning. You and I know of people who consider their personal happiness, their personal pleasure in this life to be worth more than their birthright in the kingdom of God. I am honest with you about this because I want you to be warned and then raise the warning to a higher level. So that when you are tempted to exchange your birthright for pleasures in this life, that you will remember this day, remember this sermon, remember Esau. Remember those who have done so only to lose their souls. As you have seen, the story of Esau and Jacob is more than a moral story. It is more than the ethics described. It is a confirmation that when Israel rejected Jesus, they rejected their birthright. Which allowed the Gentiles to be like the second born son and claim it for themselves. And the story is a warning, and perhaps this is the most important purpose of this story. Those who now have the birthright, we are to do whatever we need to do to keep it. Nothing is more valuable, and nothing in this life will compare to God's promises for eternity. Amen. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God, for this story, for the example herein, that points us to the birthright you have given each who call upon you Father, may our souls be quickened, may our hearts be charged, may our consciences be seared, may we truly, truly seek you first And may we always hang on to the wonderful gift of being born into your kingdom. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Higher Ground is Mercy
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. May be seated. The reading, uh the first reading in the Old Testament, uh, we took a big chunk out of chapter 26, but I'm actually going to be covering the whole chapter, at least Not the last two verses, but everything before that. So if you turn to Genesis 26, follow along with me. Dr. Peter Lyhart, in his book, A House in My Name, makes the observation that the Garden of Eden must have been on a mountain. The evidence is in the description of the region which has a river coming from the land of Eden and through the Garden of Eden. Eden itself then is higher than the garden, but since the water runs through the garden, it too is on high ground. The ideal uh idea of a higher ground and the people of God meeting with God on such high ground, that is constant throughout Scripture. In fact, the city called the City of God, Jerusalem, is built on a mountain that we know as Mount Zion. If you were to stand on the outside of the city of Jerusalem and you were to walk all around it from every side, you would see how high it is raised up above the valley around it It appears, Dr. Lighthart noted, that ever since Adam was kicked out of the garden, his seed, his descendants, have been trying to get back there. In the garden were a man and a woman on a mountaintop with all the water and food they needed to sustain a peaceful life. The themes of a man, a woman, mountain, and water play a vital role throughout Scripture. Thus, it is not by accident that the men of God meet their wives by wells. They come togethers in a similar manner as Adam and Eve. And in the Genesis 26 narrative, we see the importance of water, elevation, and family. So here we have another famine coming into the land where Isaac and his family are dwelling. And Isaac is first tempted to go down. Go down to Egypt where there is grain. Before he can do so, the Lord appears to him and instructs him Not to go down to Egypt but to stay up and live in the land the Lord chose him The land the Lord had to show Isaac was the same land he promised Abraham and Abraham's descendants. The words God uses to describe the promise are similar to those that He spoke to Abraham, and this makes it clear that God is showing that the covenant promises are passing through the person of Isaac. The reason the Lord gives to Isaac for continuing his covenant is the obedience of Abraham. He said, Abraham obeyed my voice and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws. implied in those words is that Isaac is to do the same. Follow suit. Follow the path that Abraham started. For the promise to continue, obedience must continue as well. Thus Isaac is connected to the covenant by blood offspring of Abraham, and by obedience, and that obedience is of his father, who we know obeyed out of faith, the man of faith. The narrative regarding the covenant being passed on from Abraham to Isaac is interrupted by an event that is eerily, eerily similar to the events experienced by Abraham. Just as men of the region lusted after and inquired after Sarah, so now they do with Rebekah. And just as Abraham feared for his own life, rather than protecting the purity of his wife Isaac shrinks and called Rebecca his sister. Such behavior is a sad reminder of how men of faith, men of faith, They too can shrink in fear, and they too can fail at times to trust God These moments cause us to view Isaac and his behavior as really an anti-type of Christ, for we know that Christ would never deny us as his own. Now the similarities between Abraham denying Sarah and Isaac denying Rebekah, they must be there to teach us who hear and every generation About the dangers of the sin of a father. The sin of a father. Being a father or parent is the scariest thing most of us have done. Being a father was appealing to me at the moment I said I do. And my experience was that being a father of young ones was a blast. Life in the eyes of young ones is vibrant. Everything is cool. Everything is fun And no matter what type of day I had, I could come home to my wife and we could put those buggers to bed at 8 p. m. and have the rest of the day or night to ourselves. Unfortunately, or fortunately, depending on your vantage point, the young ones, well, they grow up. Their moods change. No longer is everything exciting. In fact, most everything is boring. Whereas we used to hear, this is fun, you next hear, this is boring. And they don't go to bed at 8 p. m. anymore. In fact, teenagers stay up later than their parents do. But among these differences is not what it is most difficult about being a parent. What is most difficult is noticing your sins in the lives of your children. It is more than sobering to watch the ugliness of sins that you have struggled with most of your life being practiced by your children. First there is the guilt you feel for passing such a sinful trait onto your child, and then there is a bit of a panic For you wondered that if you've been struggling with this your whole life, how are you ever going to be able to help your child? Very, very humbly. I have read the story of Isaac denying Rebekah and compared it to Abraham denying Sarah. several times with with an attempt to find a lesson from the Lord that would help a father from passing on his personal sins to his sons, and I have not found one. In the story of Isaac, we see that God is merciful and that he reveals the lie before Rebekah is defiled. And like Abraham, Isaac is blessed with material wealth by the Lord even after the lie was revealed. So what I believe the blessing teaches us is what we will discuss after we get through the rest of the narrative. So we continue that although Isaac sinned, we are told that his household continues to prosper. He gets livestock, and he gets to harvest. And a man living in such a time in history was truly wealthy if you were able to raise livestock and to farm the land. The Philistines then envied Isaac because of the wealth he had accumulated, and because he was blessed, and they were not. A common reaction by the ungodly toward the godly, toward those who are blessed, is to make life more difficult. This is why the wells are filled in. The wells were rightfully Isaac's as they were given to his father, but the Philistines did not honor that right. They filled in the wells, which was symbolically appropriate. For as we have seen, the wells remind us of the water from the garden. And they point to the Savior, Jesus, who will be called living water. The ungodly want nothing to do with the garden because they do not want to walk with God. They do not want to drink from the living well who is the Savior. They want to stop up the water and not allow anyone to drink. Like demons, the ungodly are miserable in their sin, and their only joy, if you can call it joy, is to bring low as many souls as they can to be with them in their misery. Isaac's response to this mistreatment is to move on. Move on. He is in his right to resist, and by the testimony of Abimelech, Isaac's household is mightier than all the other households For the godly, however, it is not about personal individual rights. It is not about providing, proving, excuse me, who is mightier, stronger. It is only about the persecution of the righteous. So Isaac moves on, and he settles in the valley of Gerar. Where Isaac fails, or what makes this decision poor, is that he is dwelling in a valley where dwells the ungodly. Remember that the garden is on a mountain and the people of God are called to go higher up. When Isaac settles in a valley, he is bound to be in conflict with the ungodly. We read that the herdsmen of the region quarrel with Isaac's herdsmen, and they claim that the water dug up by Isaac's household, they say it's theirs. Once again, Isaac is within his rights. These wells that he dug up were his father's wells His household first dug those wells. But once again, Isaac moves on. Isaac digs another well. The ownership of that well is disputed, and again, Isaac moves on. Finally, he moves on far enough away that the Philistines no longer care if he finds water. They have theirs, and that was most important. Similar to Isaac choosing to move on, we remember that Jesus would go from town to town, village to village, preaching the good news. He would, in a sense, dig up well waters by healing the sick and casting out demons, demons that had conquered the deranged. When the people of the towns and villages saw what he had done, some of them asked him to move on. They did not know what to make of him, but only concluded that he was not like them. And therefore should not stay among them. And what did Jesus do? He moved on. He claimed no ownership. He moved on. The plight of all who dig for water in the name of the one true God, the plight is contention and hatred by those who do not know God. Because this is not our home, and because those who are born of God are born, or excuse me, not born of God are born of the devil, there is going to be contention and hatred. Did anybody feel contention when you see lawmakers in New York applauding abortion? Feel any contention Isaac's response and Jesus' response to contention and hatred should be ours. We should not be quarrelsome or insist what is rightfully ours Need to move on. As is possible with you, the scripture says, be at peace with all men The calling of God's people is not to win court cases or to ensure that we get what is ours in this life. It is to return a curse with a blessing. It is to return a harsh word with kindness. It is to turn the other cheek or give an extra coat. The behavior of Isaac eventually becomes a noticeable testimony of his faith. Abimelech comes to him After the contention and after noticing that Isaac is once again blessed, and he convinces Isaac that, or he is convinced, excuse me, that Isaac is a man to be at peace with. Abimelech and the other men conclude that Isaac is a man blessed of God, and therefore he should be a friend, not an enemy. The words of Abimelech reveal that he comes to Isaac for the purpose of self-preservation Isaac is surprised at first and reveals his suspicion by pointing out that every time that he was among them, he was kicked out. They sent him away. Abimelech explains that they have seen how God has blessed Isaac while insisting that they have done nothing wrong. By saying they did nothing wrong, he meant that they had not physically harmed Isaac. With fear that Isaac just may do them physical harm, they seek a covenant with him. And notice the words of Abimelech. That the covenant is for the protection of the Philistines, not the protection of Isaac's family. They say, let us make a covenant with you, that you will do us no harm. This is a one-sided covenant if there ever was one. Isaac certainly knows this, but it doesn't matter to him. In fact, Isaac says This is, oh Isaac decides that he's going to have a feast for them to celebrate the covenant that is not in his favor. Isaac gained nothing from the covenant that he made with these men, but he still made it. And as a confirmation that the Lord's will was being done, and the Lord's blessing was upon Isaac, the news that there was another well found and supplied him plenty of water. And these events juxtaposed cause Isaac to name the new water supply the Well of the Oath. Now the last two verses of the chapter, verse 34 and 35, they are to be studied with chapter 27. So we're just going to notice how all of these stories are sandwiched together. The primary message of this chapter, and the hope, the hope for parents not to pass on their sins to their children, the primary message Is the mercy of God. And I don't want to sound glib or oversimplify this text. I truly believe that the mercy of God is to be highlighted in all of these stories. We first see the mercy of God in the reason God pronounces the covenant to Isaac. Remember that he said it was because of Abraham's obedience that the covenant was passed through Isaac. Now, I've spent a good deal talking about the sins of the Father being passed on, but I've yet to speak about the blessings passed on because of obedience. Whereas God curses generations because of the sins of the fathers, he also blesses because of the obedience of the fathers. Whereas Noah's family was blessed because of the faith of their father. Abraham's family was blessed. David's family was blessed. Even in the New Testament, we read of children being healed because of the faith of their father The reason that Isaac is blessed is due to the obedience of his father, making the covenant passed on through Isaac, an act of God's mercy. He didn't have to do it. The second place we see God's mercy in the narrative is in the fact that Isaac was not punished after he denied his wife. We see mercy in the fact that Rebekah was not defiled by being forced into adultery. We see mercy in the fact that instead of being punished, Isaac is then blessed. His household was actually made stronger after his sin. And we might ask, how can this be? And the only answer is God's mercy. If we understand this in terms of Isaac simply being lucky or favored more than other men, we need to think again. All of us must be honest when examining our moral choices. How often, hear this now, how often How often we are not punished in the manner that we certainly deserve How often that we do not get what should be coming to us It is not remarkable that a drunk driver gets pulled over or arrested, but it is remarkable how many times the same drunk driver is never caught. It is not surprising that a student gets caught cheating, but it is surprising how many times his cheating went unnoticed. It is not a shock that someone is caught in a lie, but it is a shock how many times her lies have gone unchallenged. The list can go on and on of examples of how often we are not punished for our sin as compared to the times that we are. It is not mentioned anywhere in the text what Isaac's thoughts were as God was merciful to him Instead, what we find in Isaac were actions. After not being punished for his sin, but blessed beyond other men, Isaac's behavior Tells us his reaction to God's mercy. Because of God's mercy, Isaac is merciful. As was noted, he had he had the lawful right to those wells he dug, but instead of fighting, he moved on. Each time he dug, he had a right, but instead of conflict, he moved on. His response then to God's mercy was to be merciful. He was a forgiving man. Even when the covenant he made with men of the region favored them and not him, he was merciful. For these reasons he is like our Savior and like us. He is like our Savior as he was merciful to those who did not deserve mercy. He is like us in that much mercy was given to him and therefore much mercy was required of him. Instead of accounting for all the times you perceive God to be punishing you for your sins Take inventory of the times that you did wrong and were not required to pay a justified consequence. Most certainly, that number is exponentially greater than the times that you have had to reap what you've sown After we account for the mercies of God, there is but one response. We ourselves are to show mercy. The call for God's people to not go down and live among amongst the pagans Is a call for us to go higher and to live higher. We are to go higher up where the river runs through the garden We are to go higher up when men count the mercies of God and act out mercy toward their fellow man.
