We are to go higher up, for that is what Isaac did in his character, and we are to do as well. Remember the words of our Lord, to whom much is given, much is required. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God. You who have shown us such great mercy, we now take the call to be merciful. To not return evil for evil, but to do as you did for us. Show mercy. Father, help us to be creative and courageous in showing that mercy to a world who would hate us, and would hate truth. Father, empower us to do that, we ask in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: To God be the Glory
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. We read only a portion of Genesis chapter twenty-seven. We will be covering the entire chapter So you will be well served to turn there in your Bibles to Genesis chapter 27. The narrative in Genesis 27 Is rather hard on preachers. I do not say this as a complaint, but as an admission, that I am weak in my ability to garner the good that is recorded In the lives that are described and the behaviors described herein, it's difficult to find redeeming value. Just look at the characters and look at their actions The last two verses of chapter 26 tell us that Esau married two Hittite women. His choice in wives Grieved his parents because they feared, just as Abraham feared, such women would take Esau away from worshiping the one true God. We again from this have the opportunity to point out that one that who a person marries is the second most important decision one makes in his or her life. Chapter 27 begins with Isaac wanting to bless his oldest son, which no doubt grieved the Lord, for the Lord clearly revealed to Rebecca that the oldest in her womb would serve the younger. Isaac seems to disregard the prophecy by secretly telling Esau to prepare a meal in the celebration of the blessing. The planned deception of Rebecca to deceive her husband, no doubt that too grieved the Lord, because she wanted to control the situation. rather than to trust God that the prophecy he gave her would be fulfilled. The behavior of Jacob, no doubt, grieved the Lord For Jacob not only went along with the deception, but did so in the name of the Lord when he assured his father that he was Esau. As we examine the sinful behavior of these characters, we must remember that they are, were, God's chosen people. Isaac was chosen. He was a man of God. Rebekah is chosen. She is the right woman for Isaac. She is the one from whom the promised seed continues. Esau and Jacob are their children. They are thus covenant children, born in a covenant home. The problem is not that these people don't know God, for they know him quite well. Thus we cannot dismiss their behavior as simply a result of them being unbelievers. They know God and still they behave in this manner. The reason for their behavior should be familiar to us, for it is the cause of our misbehavior as well. The family strives to achieve by the flesh what can only be achieved by the spirit. Even though we are sons of God, we are still tempted, and yes, even practice trusting in the flesh to achieve God's favor rather than living in the spirit. In the first place, Isaac, if possible, tries to give a blessing to the son that is of the flesh. In like manner, many Christians desire the acts of their flesh to be blessed. In spite of our knowledge that the flesh is fallen and thus under the curse, we work to redeem it in this life. We want to have an abundant life in the flesh as well as the spirit, even though we have been clearly told that the flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God. The Apostle Paul explained this to the Corinthians when he was teaching them about the new bodies that we will inherit at the resurrection. Because of Adam's sin and the ensuing curse that all men are born into, the flesh we currently live in is corrupt, and thus it cannot inherit the kingdom of God. God must and will change us, giving us new bodies that are called incorruptible, because the kingdom of God is incorruptible. But still, even with this knowledge, many children of God want God to bless our works in the flesh. Now so as not to confuse, I need to clarify how I'm using that term flesh. The Apostle Paul uses the word flesh in two different ways. The first way refers to the natural flesh or our physical bodies. The second way refers to works or acts that we perform in order to earn God's favor. In this sermon, I am using the term in both ways. We want God to bless our physical flesh for doing good works. We want them to be counted as righteous works and by such receive physical rewards for them. We do this even though the scripture clearly teaches that our works are as filthy rags unto the Lord. They are filthy rags because everything we do, regardless if it is good to the outward eye, everything we do is tainted somehow by selfishness and pride It's always in there somehow. Because our works can never be pure, never holy, as God's works are, they are to God filthy rags. The sons of God may stir up the flesh to seek a blessing, but it will always be in vain. Whereas Isaac in his old age attempts to bless the flesh, Jacob, the youngest in the story, attempts the same by energy and cunning. He is young and eager to be blessed. He first desired that birthright and then he pursued it. He now desires the blessing of the firstborn and will do what is necessary in his eye to get it. The idea of waiting on the Lord is not in Jacob's understanding. Patience is not in his vocabulary His sin is the sin of youth. Youth wants the pleasures of marriage without the covenant responsibility. Youth wants the wealth of its elders without working and saving. Youth wants to have a say and make an impact on society without wisdom. that only comes from living many years and having life experiences. Such sins are not just the sins of millennials today. Such sins are the sins of all who are, who were, and who will be young in life. Sins of youth. Indeed, Jacob wants what the Lord wants. He wants the blessing, and God wants it for him as well. But Jacob is willing to compromise his principles to get it. He succumbs to the spirit of compromise, what we call situational ethics. As circumstances change, so does his sense of right and wrong change. In fact, the goal of the blessing becomes so important to him he is willing to present himself as a man of the flesh. He dresses like Esau. He even places animal skin on his hands and neck to impersonate Esau. Thus the chosen son, the spiritual seed, puts on the manner and appearance of a carnal seed. of an unbeliever. The use of such animal skin before him is strikingly different Remember when Adam fell, God gave him a coat of animal skin to cover his nakedness, his flesh, which was noticed because of the fall, the curse. That skin covered the shame of Adam and Eve. In like manner, the prophets would wear hairy garments, testifying the same truth that mankind has fallen. But Jacob is not wearing such a garment to cover his sin, but actually in order to sin, in order to deceive. And I cannot shy away from identifying how the compromising of Jacob is similar to the compromising of many Christian churches today. Some compromise by taking or not taking moral stands based on what the spirit of the age dictates. When the present culture condemns sexual deviancy, well, the church follows. When the same culture begins to embrace sexual deviancy, the church not only follows But consecrates the deviancy with special wedding services for homosexuals and baptisms for the transgender. And for what? For what? What is the purpose of such compromising? They argue that it is out of love. They love the sinner, they say. But they don't love the sinner. They hate the sinner because they want them to stay in their sin. And that means the sinner will suffer eternity for it. That is not love. Another way Christian churches compromise is by the manner they evangelize. And I'm quite certain in these instances that the reason for such compromise is for the blessing of being relevant. Like Jacob, these churches are young and eager and thus try to get people in their doors by being energetic and cunning. Just as Jacob dressed like Esau, so these Christians dress like the world. The music they produce, the auditoriums they build, the programs they institute are an attempt to look like the world The flesh, in order to reach out to the world. Like Jacob, they desire for a blessing, but their manner of achieving it is faulty And note, please, that I am not saying these people are not Christian. I am simply drawing parallels between the behavior of the chosen son Jacob and the many modern churches. In contrast to this approach, the Apostle Paul described the proper manner of evangelizing when he said this to the Corinthians. But we have renounced the hidden things of shame, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the Word of God deceitfully, but by the manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God. Rebecca Acting like her husband and her favorite son Jacob, attempts to earn God's favor as well. She was the one who personally received the promise regarding Jacob, and yet, instead of simply trusting in the promise, she attempts to do just as her grandmother-in-law Sarah did To control the manner that God fulfills His promise. There are results, very negative results, that occur. Because Isaac, Jacob, and Rebekah walk according to the flesh and not the spirit. A tragic result is that Isaac's family is forever torn apart. His sons are at odds as Esau hates Jacob and makes plans to kill him. Another result is Jacob living in fear of his brother We shall see this later as he must face his brother and the possibility of his death. And Rebecca experiences a painful result as well, for Jacob, her favorite son, must leave home. When he does, Rebecca does not realize that she will never see him again. Never again. All of this occurred because the people of God walked by the flesh rather than by the spirit. They pursued works of the flesh rather than having faith in the promises of God. Now, in the end, God's will was done. Jacob became the one that Esau served. Jacob became the man that would be called Israel, and from him we know the twelve tribes of Israel come. God's will was not thwarted by the behavior of these people, but was realized through their behavior and better said, despite their behavior. Let us now look at the manner God works through the lives of ordinary and even disobedient servants. Isaac was stubborn, wanting to bless his oldest and favored son. God used his old age, his large stomach, and blindness to have him bless the chosen son. As stubborn as Isaac was, he still was a man of faith, because he served the only true living God who made the universe by a spoken word. Isaac knew that he himself, once he had spoken a word of blessing upon Jacob, could not go back on it. Like God's word, Isaac's word was to be fulfilled, thus he would not recant his blessing or allow a blessing upon Esau to supersede the one he put upon Jacob Even though he was stubborn, God got through to Isaac as is evident by the blessing he gave Jacob and the prophecy he spoke to Esau. And I want you to look at these verses, noting that the word order is carefully changed. In verse 28, Isaac blesses Jacob, saying, Therefore may God give you the dew of the heaven, of the fatness of the earth, and plenty of grain and wine. Contrastingly, in verse 39, Isaac gives a prophecy regarding Esau, saying, Behold, your dwelling shall be of the fatness of the earth and of the dew of heaven from above. Did you hear or see the reverse of order? Did you see in reading it? The order is switched, whereas Jacob is the chosen son, the son of the Spirit. He is to receive dew from heaven and then the fatness of the earth. Esau, the son of the flesh, will receive fatness of the earth before the dew of heaven. The eternal difference is that Jacob will be a man who is first and foremost a man of the spirit. The blessing he receives in this life will be a residual effect. of his primary place, which is in heaven, his home. Esau, however, will be a man of this earth. The blessings he received will be only of this earth, and anything of heaven will be only a residual effect. Isaac's words to his son confirm that there are men of the flesh and men of the spirit. And the difference between men of heaven and men of the earth remains. There are Jews who continue to look for the Messiah, whom they believe will make them inheritors of this earth. They yearned for the re-establishment of the temple on Mount Sinai and the re-establishment of the Davidic throne. But for the spiritual Jews, we call them the church, they believe the Messiah has come, and the true temple is in heaven, where the Son of God, Jesus Christ, sits at the right hand of the Father. And like Esau, the earthly Jews are satisfied with their earthly inheritance. Like Jacob, those born from above will only be satisfied when the kingdom of God is on earth, becoming the kingdom of heaven. Like he did with Isaac. God works through the life of Rebekah as she panics for fear of Jacob's life. She learns that Esau is angry and intent on killing Jacob. She decides that Jacob must flee from the family, not knowing when Isaac would pass and how long Esau would wait before he took vengeance. In her haste, Rebecca makes a wise decision. She sends Jacob to live amongst her family, which is Abraham's family. It is the same family that Abraham sent his servant to to find a proper bride for Isaac. And although she sends Jacob away to preserve his life, the real purpose is God's purpose. Although her reasons are not pure, Rebecca acts as the Christian church should. Instead of keeping her best loved son, the mother church must send them out. Jacob is sent forth to toil, to win flocks and herds. So too should young men, our best young men, be sent forth. We remember that Jacob lives with his uncle Laban. As he does, he becomes an owner of literal sheep. But the Bible uses sheep as a metaphor for winning over men and women to the gospel. Young men of the church are to be sent out to win, young men and young women, to the gospel. We must keep this in mind as we raise boys. We are to send them out, send them to win the world. Because of the narrative of Genesis twenty seven It has taken us and me a number of different directions. So I want to summarize my points First, works of the flesh, which are works that we try to achieve God's blessing, they never achieve that desired end. Second, regardless of what men do, whether with good intentions or ill, God's sovereign will always be accomplished. We can see this in how God works to his end through the simple behavior of these who are his chosen people. And after stating these truths, I am aware that there is a rational thinking that goes like this. Why bother worrying about or even praying about our behavior or choices? Because God's will is going to be accomplished in the end. The answer is in the lives of Isaac and his family. As we pointed out, there are repercussions for being stubborn as Isaac was, or impatient as Jacob was, or persistent regarding her own ways as Rebecca was. When we consider that God sees the stubbornness, impatience, and selfish persistence of his people. He uses them, despite how sinful they are, he uses them to accomplish his righteous and holy will. And to this we are to respond with, to God be the glory. Last week we highlighted God's mercy. And today we highlight the glory, the glory that is owed to God from us. Because he assures his sovereign will despite what his servants do. Thus Genesis chapter 26 and 27 teach that salvation is in the hands of God. We don't choose it, and we don't keep it, for it is to God and God alone. In the narrative of Genesis, there is no mention of how the wills of people, the choices that people make, mix with God's plan of salvation. That will be a mystery to us on this side of the sun. Seeing what God does through sinful and incompetent men and women We understand him a little more. He conveyed himself in the same way through the prophet Isaiah, where he said, But now says the Lord who created you, O Jacob. And who formed you, O Israel, fear not, for I have redeemed you. I have called you by your name. You are mine. Everyone who is called by my name, whom I have created for my glory, I have formed him. Yes, I have made him Again, because God uses us for his kingdom, despite our behavior. Again, we say, to God be the glory. Amen. Let us pray. Our God, we thank you for working through the lives of sinful people That means working through our lives. And so we say, to you be the glory for all that is good, that is righteous, that is hopeful in our lives and hereafter. Is all from you. We thank you in Jesus' name. Amen

sermons.title: Get off the Ladder
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: I don't know what they can mean or they're gonna have to run a pretty much In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. There is a respectable theory regarding the greater meaning of the lives of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The call of God upon the lives of this grandfather, father, and son is parallel to God's call on the lives of any who would follow the Lord Jesus Christ. Abraham represents the spirit of faith, as he is noted for believing in God, and that belief was reckoned to him as righteousness. Therefore, Abraham represents the new believer. Isaac represents the spirit of sonship. Just as all who profess faith in Christ are said to be sons of God. Therefore, Isaac represents how every Christian is to learn how to live out being an inheritor of the kingdom of God. And finally, Jacob represents the spirit of service. He is like all Christians who need to work out their salvation in fear and in trembling. His life is a lesson regarding how works interact with faith. Now I call this perspective about the lives of these three men as a theory. But it seems so obvious now that we are to understand these men in this way that I would prefer to call it a truth rather than a theory. But just as in all typology, nothing is as clear-cut as we first would like. Jacob's life, as well as we will see in the coming weeks, is a life of works But before the works to earn his wives and then his flocks, he must understand, and you and I must understand, how God saves Christianity has struggled since the first century to understand how to work out the difference between works and faith. You remember, of course, that the Reformation was caused in part by abuses in the Roman Catholic Church as it had begun to insist that a man's work within the context of the church could earn God's favor. The insistence of the reformers was that men can only be saved by grace, and any work performed by men is to be in response to God's grace, not to earn God's grace. It was not and is still not that simple As I've just described, for there remains a debate as to what constitutes a work. The Roman Catholic can concede the point that men are only saved by grace. But insists that grace is distributed through the church, and those who desire such grace can receive it if they participate in the sacraments of the church. Participation in sacraments is not a work to earn grace, according to the Roman Church. Reformed Protestants respond by insisting that anything, and they mean anything that would involve an effort by man, that constitutes a work, and therefore cannot contribute to a person's salvation, for the scripture is clear. We are saved by grace through faith alone. The Roman Catholic rebuts saying that reformers contradict themselves by insisting that men are saved without works while at the same time saying that men must confess the doctrine of grace alone, making such a confession a work The Reformed respond by stating that even the ability to confess is given by God, thus it is not a work of man, but of God. They continue their argument by noticing that the error of the Roman Church is the same that was made by the Jews of Jesus' day who believed that they could keep the law of God, and the better they did that, the more they received mercy from God. Well, fairly recently, there has been a new discussion, it may even be called an argument, among leading Reform Protestants. That have brought the question into play as to whether the Jews of Jesus' day have been rightly understood by scholars. A leading voice of this so-called new perspective is Anglican Bishop N. T. Wright. He argues that the Jews of Jesus' day believed that obeying the law was a sign of being in covenant with God and not a means to earn God's favor. He then argues that Paul understood this about the Jews as well, and we should read his epistles with this in mind. The bishop has received strident disagreement from well-known reform clergy, causing sides to be chosen. Now I aired the dirty laundry of the church before you to give you an idea of how difficult and divisive this issue is of how we understand works and grace. And my hope of our study of Jacob, we can reconcile the two. Now we are in chapter 28 of Genesis, and we only read part of it, but I encourage you to turn there. We're going to be covering the whole chapter. and uh and and focus on something more specific. This section of scripture, this chapter, is more commonly known for the reference here of Jacob's ladder. Many know Jacob's ladder more by the spiritual song than they do the details of this story. The song contains the following verses We are climbing Jacob's ladder. We are climbing Jacob's ladder. We are climbing Jacob's ladder, brothers, sisters, all. Every rung goes higher and higher. Every rung goes higher and higher. Every rung goes higher and higher. Brothers, sisters, all. Every new one makes us stronger, every new one makes us stronger, every new one makes us stronger, brothers, sisters, all. The song includes another stanza repeating the phrase, We have toiled in dark and danger, and ends by repeating, we are climbing Jacob's ladder. The song is believed to date back to the 19th century, sung by black Americans who worked as slaves on southern plantations. The song reveals the hardships they endured and their focus on heaven that helped them get through each day. Although popular, there is something, unfortunately, to point out that's very wrong with this song, and I hope that some of you have already heard it After we get through the narrative of the chapter, I will point it out to all of us. So the chapter begins with Isaac confirming Rebekah's instruction. For Jacob to go to his mother's house to find a wife, rather than finding a wife amidst the Canaanites. The idea first came to Rebekah so that he could be safe, again because his brother Esau was going to take his life Now Isaac is in agreement, and with his agreement comes another blessing. The blessing is similar to the one given to Isaac by the Lord, who in chapter 26, verse 3, and verse 24 Promised to give him the same land that he promised Abraham and to multiply his descendants. This was the blessing that God had intended all along for Jacob. The same blessing that was revealed to Rebecca when the Lord told her that the younger son would serve the older. Now an interesting side story to what was going on in the life of Jacob was the reaction of Esau when he saw Isaac blessing his younger brother. Before sending him to find a wife amongst his mother's family. Esau, you will remember, had taken wives from the Hittite tribe, Hittite tribe. And we are told in chapter 26 that these women grieved Isaac and Rebekah because they worshiped false gods. Esau, understanding, or so he thinks. The reason why Jacob was blessed and he was not, he decides to go amongst his grandfather's other son, the family of Ishmael, and take another wife. And I say that his actions are typical to what the carnal mind attempts to do. Instead of repentance and atonement for sins committed A man of the flesh tries to make up for the wrong that was done. Since he married two wrong wives, he tries to marry a right one. If the sin is different, the manner of making up for it, balancing the scales is different as well. If something wrong was said, well then something right said is attempted. If there has been an insult uttered, a compliment will follow. If a lie was formed, an honest truth is told to cover up the lie. By trying to make up for wrong done, men of such carnal minds reveal that they do not understand God. Sin is not made up for by good deeds. The only payment of sin is death. A life sacrifice must be made, but the carnal mind, the carnal mind does not want to have to die. It only wants to try to make things even. While Esau attempts to balance the scales of this wrongdoing, Jacob makes his way to Haran, which is approximately five hundred miles from his home in Beersheba. About 70 miles into the trip, Jacob arrives at Bethel, although he does not call it Bethel yet. Bethel is the same place where Abraham built an altar after the Lord had appeared to him. That Jacob came upon the same place, we need to read, is not by chance. God ordained it to be so, and it should teach us that God does not change. The same covenant he made with Abraham, he makes with Isaac, and with Jacob. It is the same for those who follow Christ. We are under the same covenant. We are children of Abraham. And all children of Abraham are part of the same baptism, having been baptized by the same Spirit. The stones that Jacob uses for his bed are likely those that Abraham used to build an altar to God. Consider that God uses the worship of the grandfather Abraham as a means to pass on the covenant to the grandson Jacob. Providing that a proving that a man never knows how his worship of God is going to bless his children's children. While Jacob's head rests upon a stone, he dreams a dream like no other dream. He dreams of what is translated to be a ladder. Another possible word is staircase, but what makes this word so difficult to translate is that it is the only place here where this word occurs in Scripture. The root of the word is actually a verb which means to exalt or raise up. The only conclusion I can draw from the literal meaning of the word is that this is whatever he is seeing, it is very unique. What is also unique about the dream is the manner that this so-called ladder was used. Angels, multiple angels of God are ascending and descending on it. What the angels were doing besides going up and down, that's not revealed to us in the story. But it is revealed elsewhere. Hebrews 1 verse 14 says that angels are ministering spirits sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation. That's us. Psalm 34, 7 describes angels as protectors. Quote, the angel of the Lord encamps all around those who fear him and delivers them. In Psalm 91, verse 11, the promise is made, for he shall give his angels charge over you to keep you in all his ways. In Genesis 28, at the top of the ladder, which is the entrance into heaven, it tells us is the Lord. He is said to be standing above. The words the Lord speaks to Jacob are greater than the blessing given to Jacob by his father Isaac. God will give to Jacob and his descendants the land that he was laying upon. This was the same promise that God gave to Abraham. And like Abraham, Jacob is told that his offspring will be a blessing to all the families of the earth. What is unique about the Lord's promise to Jacob is the description of his offspring being scattered. Scattered as dust to the four corners of the earth in order to be a blessing. We can say with great assurance that such scattering was fulfilled at the spread of the Christian faith. The book of Revelation describes the fulfillment as the four corners of the earth being gathered together. But more important Then the four corners is the mention of Jesus in Jacob's dream. If you did not notice it, let me remind you of a seemingly unrelated story. It's recorded in the Gospel of John. Just as after Jesus begins his public ministry, Philip invites a guy named Nathaniel to join them, to meet Jesus When Jesus sees Nathaniel coming towards him, he comments about the sincerity of the man. Nathaniel asks how Jesus could know him. Jesus explains that before Philip had talked to Nathaniel, he saw Nathaniel sitting under a fig tree. And since Jesus was not in the same geographical vicinity, Nathaniel heard that statement and was alarmed and was convinced then that Jesus could see all, and thus Jesus was the Son of God. And Jesus replied in this way, You shall see greater things than these. More assuredly I say to you, hereafter, you shall see heaven open And the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man. Now, any God-fearing Jew listening to Jesus would know their Old Testament stories and know the application of the description of angels ascending and descending. Jesus in his conversation with Nathaniel was identifying himself with the latter in Jacob's dream Essentially, Jesus is saying he is the means, he is the means by which heaven meets earth and earth meets heaven. The angels descending at Jesus' birth, they continued ascending and descending to minister him while he was on earth They descended to announce his resurrection, and they ascended to take him to heaven at the Father's right hand. Jacob, of course, did not fully understand what the latter represented. He did, however, know that he had seen and heard God. And the natural response for him, like his grandfather, was to build an altar and name the place Bethel, or House of God, or the place where God dwells. Now let us go back and take another look at the spiritual song Jacob Ladder, keeping in mind the symbolism of the dream. The song describes the climbing of Jacob's ladder. It describes how the ladder goes higher and higher. It also describes the great toil of climbing. While it is true that the Song of Toil describes well the plight of black American slaves, they do not describe how man is saved. What should be asked of anyone who would sing such a song, what should be asked is, what are you doing on the ladder? What are you doing on the ladder? Although Jacob sees a ladder, he himself never gets on it, nor are we ever told that he thought about getting on it. Those who are on it are ministering spirits. Those who are on it are bringing the aid of heaven down to us and taking our petitions, our needs up to heaven. Thus, the manner of a person's salvation, the way in which we are saved, is not by climbing a ladder or climbing Jesus. But for heaven to visit us upon earth through the mediator of Jesus Christ. In fact, the one who ascends to heaven and descends upon the earth for our salvation is none other than Jesus Himself. Jesus said of himself, No one has ascended to heaven but he who came down from heaven, that is the Son of Man who is in heaven. After quoting Psalm 68 regarding Jesus' ascension, Paul, the Apostle Paul, explained the following to the Ephesians. He said, Now this, he ascended, what does it mean? But that he is also first descended into the lower parts, descended into the lower parts of the earth He who descended is also the one who ascended far above the heavens, that he might fill all things. This, beloved, is how we are saved. We are saved by the works of Jesus, who is the mediator between God and man. He is the only mediator. He is the only means by which a man can be saved. Jacob understands the dream enough. To know that his blessings on earth originate in heaven. He responds by committing to the Lord a tenth of what the Lord will bless him with in the future. And this is the beginning of understanding the combination of works and faith. God initiates with Jacob. He initiates with all men that he chooses The response of every man with whom God initiates is to perform an act of worship. This is to be our primary act. There are other works to be sure, but worship is the initial and primary work. In response to God's mercy, we are not to get on a ladder, but we are to worship. After that, he will show us what else we are to do. And I hope you see as you think back these last few sermons how this all comes together Two weeks ago we highlighted the mercies of God in the lives of Isaac and Rebekah. Last week we saw how God goes forward with his will, despite the sins of those he has chosen. So that we might all look to him and say, To God alone be the glory. This week we are able to highlight that our salvation is never earned by our own works. But only by the works of Jesus, for he is as the latter who brings heaven to earth and earth to heaven. Dr. Jordan Peterson, who we will use as a springboard for our men's meeting next Saturday. In a conversation about religion, he quoted Jesus as saying, quote, No one comes to the Father but by me. And his response to those words of Jesus was, that's a hell of a thing for anyone to say. I had to laugh at that. And I assure you, he didn't say it as a criticism of Jesus, but instead was trying was trying to express how serious a statement Jesus was making when he used such words. And Jesus used such words to provoke a serious response because forgiveness of sins is serious business. And Jesus is the only way God the Father has chosen for the sins of mankind to be forgiven. So I close by saying, get off the ladder. Get off the ladder and trust that Jesus is the means for heaven to be yours. For in Jesus alone are your sins forgiven you. And all of God's people said, Amen. Let us pray.

sermons.title: His love is enough
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Christ is God, God is for us, God's glory, Christ, glory long, great. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Instead of being perplexed and quizzical When God appears to judge mankind by way of flood, earthquake, fire, or wind Asking why God, we should be just as interested as to why God allows us to get away with as much as we do. I mentioned this a few weeks ago by calling each of us to recount the many times that we have done something wrong, but received no consequence. Taking such inventory a step further, I ask you to notice the beliefs and behaviors that you have exhibited over the years. beliefs that are superstitious, behaviors that are contrary to the Word of God, and to notice how God has been patient with you. If we are going to ask why God, when referring to so-called natural disasters, why should we not ask why God when we do not receive the punishment and rebukes that we so justly deserve. By accounting for the many times God overlooks our sin, both in our behavior and in what we believe. We can better understand how the behavior of Jacob and his family is overlooked. In summary, the story of Jacob and his family as told in Genesis 29 and 30, and I want you to know that we'll be covering those two chapters entirely. We only read a part of chapter 30, but we're covering Genesis 29 and 30. That we notice in these stories of these two chapters that these stories include deceit, polygamy, adultery, and superstition. Not to mention jealousy, backbiting, and shallowness. Now before we get to the types and lessons of these two chapters, I want to quickly summarize each primary scene in the narratives of these two chapters, since we didn't take time to read the entire chapters this morning. So we start off noticing the first 14 verses of chapter 29 are the most benign of the two chapters. Jacob arrives at Haran. He is introduced to shepherds, and since he is a shepherd himself, he quizzes them on regarding their watering practices. When Rachel arrives, Jacob is excited because she is family and she is beautiful, which confirms God's hand upon his quest to go find a bride amidst his mother's family. The description of Jacob kissing Rachel is not to be understood as romantic, it's familial affection. Laban, Rachel's father, receives Jacob in the same hospitable manner he received Abraham's servant when he was looking for a bride for Isaac. In verses 15 through 30, here begins the soap opera of sin between these family members. Laban offers to pay Jacob for his labor. Jacob wants to marry the pretty daughter, Rachel. So the two men come into a covenant. Jacob will receive, will serve, excuse me, the household of Laban for seven years, and afterwards receive Rachel as his wife. After the seven years, Jacob requests his payment, and Laban pretends to honor the agreement Now say pretends because we know that he deceived Jacob and gave him Leah instead. And I need to stop here and mention to you that I have gotten in the habit of calling her Leah, and my wife reminds me that this is not the Star Wars story, this is in the Bible. So it's Leah, but if I say Leah, you know who I'm referring to. Leah is described as being weak-eyed or having delicate eyes. Most commentators agree that the description means that simply she was not as pretty as Rachel. The text tells us that the wedding occurred in the dark, and we know of the customs of the day that Leah was likely veiled, so we are able to imagine that Jacob did not detect this deceit. We are also not told how Leah and Rachel felt about this deceit, and so we're to assume that however they felt doesn't matter to the story. When the deceit is discovered, Jacob confronts Laban, who attempts to justify his actions by claiming a higher moral ground because he was honoring a custom. The obvious rebuttal is that he should have told Jacob about this custom before Jacob asked for Rachel. And what else is obvious is the what some call the come-uppins, the come-uppins received by Jacob. He was the original deceiver. He deceived his father by pretending to be Esau, and now he is the one, justifiably, to be deceived. Jacob next insists on the original agreement that it be honored to receive Rachel as his second wife. Here is polygamy. The manner the story is told does not make it clear if Jacob was given Rachel as his wife after he served another seven years or as a down payment for the seven years to come. The latter scenario is natural to the text, so we'll think it that way that he received Rachel and then worked for another seven years. And it's natural because of the strife and the jealousy that is experienced by these two sisters. Although the text does not condemn the behavior of Laban or the taking of a second wife by Jacob, the Lord will list such sin when the law is given to Moses. The book of Leviticus will contain a law that prohibits false witness, as well as a man marrying sisters, calling it incest. Once again, just as we had seen so many times in Genesis, man goes against God's will And he's not eternally condemned, but he will suffer consequences in this life. And they will. Although Jacob is in covenant with both women, he favors Rachel over Leah. Leah. But the Lord has revealed himself as a God full of compassion. He loves the unloved. And so as he sees the pain of Leah, he blesses her over Rachel. The fullness of Leah's womb begins, a bitter rivalry between the two sisters. Leah had four sons consecutively, and she named them after the manner the Lord answered her prayers and the desire she had to be favored by her husband. Instead of rejoicing for Leah and Jacob, Rachel is filled with jealousy and desperation. She confronts Jacob, and then Jacob confronts her back. Confronts her because he recognizes that Rachel's closed womb is of the Lord. God is doing something to her. It's not his fault. Rachel decides that she will get a child immorally if she cannot have one morally. And so she gives Jacob her maid Bilha. This can only be described as adultery, but Jacob, typical man, doesn't protest. Billha does conceive and has a son. Rachel believes that the son of her maid is proof that God has judged her side to be right. Although nowhere does God agree to her assessment. After Bilha gives birth to a second son, we learn what Rachel's motivation was. Look at chapter 30, verse 8. It says, then Rachel said, With great wrestlings I have wrestled with my sister, and indeed I have prevailed. So she called his name Naphtali. She's not wrestling with God, she's competing with her sister. Leah is not to be outdone in the competition, and she responds by giving her servant Zilpah to Jacob so that she can have another son. Zilpah gives Jacob two more sons, confirming to Leah that God is on her side. The minds of modern men can only imagine what it would be like to have your two wives insisting that you sleep with other women. Jacob does not protest. The silliness in the narrative continues regarding the mandrakes. It seems that Rachel believed there was fertility in the mandrakes And that is why she insisted on having some for herself. She was so desperate for the mandrakes that she agreed to tell Jacob to sleep with Leah Once again, Jacob obliges, and Leah becomes pregnant with another son. According to verse 22 of chapter 30, It was not the man drakes, but the Lord who opened Rachel's womb. In God's time, he gave her the privilege of having a child of her own The name she gave her son Joseph means literally, may God add or increase, which is a prayer for Rachel to have another son, revealing that Rachel was not focused on raising sons, but having sons. Again, reminding us that it's not a virtue to have children, it is a virtue to raise them in the Lord. The playing of musical beds slows considerably after the birth of Joseph, and this moves the narrative back to Jacob's relationship with his father-in-law, Laban. Once again the two men enter into a covenant. By now they know each other well, and this makes the covenant a little bit cunning on both ends. Jacob wants to go back home, so he asks permission from Laban to take his wives and children. This probably seems strange to us. To ask permission to take your wives and children, but it reveals the confusion regarding the relationship between these two men Jacob was both a son-in-law and he was a slave. David essentially denies Jacob's request for the selfish reason that he noticed that he was being blessed, his household was being blessed, because Jacob was amongst him. However, because he knows Jacob is blessed, he also recognizes that he might not be able to stop him from leaving, and so he offers him a deal. And it might sound noble of Laban to say to him, name your wage, which is what he said to Jacob. But we will see later that the wages change several times, according to Laban. As was said, Jacob knows Laban, and so he presents him a deal that seemingly entirely is to Laban's advantage. Normally in the region the sheep were white and the goats were black. It is rare to have a black sheep or speckled or striped sheep or speckled goats No more than 20% in a flock. So Jacob offers to take the sheep and the goats that are striped and speckled. The end result would be Jacob taking no more than 20% of the flocks as they multiplied. And this would clear the gene pool for Laban's flock. But to be sure that he is not taken advantage of by Jacob, Laban journeys three days away from Jacob so that their flocks aren't intermingled. And this move turns out to be to Jacob's benefit as he is able to breed his flock in secret. Now regarding Jacob's reading method, it must be said that it is absurd. It's absurd. Jacob, like Rachel, is superstitious. He believes that his flock only needs to look at something speckled or striped while mating, and the result will be offspring that is striped and speckled. That is, as I said, absurd. It is not absurd as the liberal mind would say, believing that the whole story is fiction. This is not fiction. What is absurd is that Jacob would believe his method is responsible for God's blessing. What is going on in the story is the same that occurred with his father Isaac. God is blessing Jacob while he is in exile, while he is a stranger among strangers. While Jacob believes it is the work of his ingenuity, God has simply chosen to bless him for the greater good. And the greater good is God's sovereign will being done, not Jacob's. The primary lesson of these two chapters is like the one we learned in the life of Isaac and Isaac's family. God blesses those he chooses despite their actions. He does so for the sake of his sovereign will and for the sake of his deserved glory. It is the secondary lesson, however, or lessons, that I wish to focus on as we come near the end of this sermon. First of all, Jacob is a type of Christ. Certainly not entirely, but in a very important part, Jacob is a type of Christ. Jacob loved Rachel and he worked to get her fourteen years. Remember that seven is the number of completion, and Jacob worked to completion to marry Rachel the first time. He was duped by his father-in-law into marrying Leah. So Jacob, because he loved Rachel as much as he did, worked another completed term. He worked another seven years to have Rachel as his wife. Rachel is a type of the bride of Christ, the church. She was a shepherdess and the fairest among women. For her sake, Jacob served, and for the church's sake, Jesus served. Jacob served seven and seven again. Jesus served in his life and then into his death. In a world of conditional love where affection is given only if affection is returned, we yearn to hear stories of true love. In a world where the word love is spoken just as quickly as it is taken back, we yearn to hear of a love that is eternal. The story of Jesus loving his church is the love we yearn for. He is the one who suffers for and with his church. He remains at the door and knocks, wanting to commune inside with believers. He continues to seek out individual sheep that have wandered into danger, and he rejoices when he has just returned, just one, just one to the fold. For love Jacob served fourteen years. For the love of the church, Jesus gave all he was by taking on the form of a servant. And hear this. the form of a servant for eternity. Other types in this passage are Leah and Rachel, where Leah represents Judaism and Rachel Christianity. Leah is the old covenant and Rachel is the new. Leah, like the law, like Judaism, must be first, not just by custom, as Laban explains, but by the sovereign will of God. The law comes first, for it reveals the holiness of God and the depravity of men. As the law reveals these things, those who have their consciences pricked, those people look for a Savior. The law, however, again, like Leah, is also veiled. The new covenant is veiled in the old. Jesus, the Savior, must be revealed When the new covenant is revealed, we see that it is beautiful like Rachel. That Leah must be first, besides referring to the law, also refers to Jesus coming first for the Jews. His message and his sacrifice was first for them. It was only after he was rejected by the Jews that the message went to the Gentiles. The strife between Leah and Rachel is akin to the strife that Judaism and Christianity has had and continues to have. It was the Jews who first persecuted the Christians, yes, even before the Romans. It was the Christians who persecuted the Jews during the Middle Ages as they tried to take back Jerusalem Leah and Rachel were at odds, having their focus upon being jealous each of the other. Where they failed is where Judaism and Christianity continue to fail. Jesus did come first for the Jews. The first Christians were of the Jewish race. Just as Leah gave birth first, so too were the first born-again Christians of Jewish descent. But after having gone to the Jews, the Lord then went to the Gentiles, and from them brought forth many children into his kingdom. This is Rachel. Instead of being bitter and envious, each should have humbled themselves to the point of appreciating that God would choose them from among all other women. Please don't hear me speaking negatively against the Jews, simply pointing out how These types, these shadows of Leah and Rachel fit in our context. Christians worship the Triune God, the God who has revealed himself as the Father, as the Son, as the Holy Ghost. Judaism rejects the Son. They reject our Savior, Jesus the Christ. This rejection is most serious because Jesus was always a part of the covenant that God made with Abraham. Jesus completes that covenant. To reject him is to reject the covenant God made with Abraham, and then Isaac, and then Jacob. But of course, the religious Jewish people don't see it that way. Attempting now to bring these two types together, which is Jesus' love for his bride, and Judaism and Christianity being at odds. I believe we are able to see it in the words of Jesus, if you remember, as he was making his way to Jerusalem, looked upon the city as he stood on a hill. And he said, Jerusalem, Jerusalem, I wish that I could take you under my wing. This is knowing that he is about to die. God's love for Israel was expressed by choosing her and sending his son first to her. God's love for the new Israel, the Christian Church. is the same. Only the Christian faith has received his son, making her, that is, the church, more beautiful. Rachel. What the Jewish people need is what Leah and Rachel needed in their relationship with Jacob. Each of them needed to appreciate that they were loved. And each of us needs to appreciate that we are loved. Appreciate that God has chosen you Learn from Leah and Rachel. Stop concerning yourself with how another appears to be favored and blessed and loved more than you. Appreciate that you are loved, and that will be sufficient. For the Christian, we are to appreciate being loved above all things. And never, ever concern ourselves with someone who appears to be more favored or blessed than we are I personally have struggled with such concerns in the past, as I have seen numbers swell in other churches while I labor to remain faithful and receive a smaller return While we should not compare the number of attendees in different churches thinking that larger is better We are tempted to do so, even though such logic would mean that cults are being blessed, and we would be ignoring the truth that Scripture reveals, which is that it is God. Who gives the increase? What I miss, where I sin, is any time I become jealous of someone else. It is then that I failed to appreciate the love of the Heavenly Father, the love He has for me. His love for us, His people, is more than Jacob loved Rachel. Of course it is. He worked hard to express that love. And it is never appropriate for us to be jealous or wish that we were someone else. God's love in Christ is enough. It is truly enough. But it is not enough for me to say it to you, for each of us needs to confess it to God. Each of us needs to say to God, your love is enough for me. The more you say it, the more you will believe it The more you believe it, the more you will be content in that love. And the devil's temptation to be discontent will weaken and weaken. Confess to God that his love is enough for you. Say it to him. Say your love is enough for me. And it'll be so. Let us pray. Our gracious and loving God. We thank you for the images found in these two women, in the dealings of Jacob and Laban, and we thank you for the revelation. That you do love us, and that love is enough. May we never stop telling you that. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Kill the Old Man
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated Turn in your Bibles, uh, Genesis, we're gonna be covering actually the entire story of Jacob and Laban And at first reading the story, it may seem like it's simply a disagreement, two conniving men, infighting family members But it is much, much more than that. When I was a boy, about the age of ten, A neighbor boy, my same age, and his younger brother, were making faces and ugly sounds at me as I walked by their house And I reacted in an angry manner by taking some tomatoes that were in a nearby garden and throwing them at the boys and hitting their screen door. I didn't realize their father was home He came to the door and yelled at me, informing me that he was going to tell on me to my old man. Gonna tell your old man Well, that was the first time I had ever heard the descriptive old man. So to get my dad on my side, I thought I was telling on our neighbor by telling him that he he said you were old, Dad He laughed it off and made me go clean up the mess on the screen door. The Christmas before my 18th birthday My sister had become a born-again Christian just six months prior, and she gave me a Christian rock album. If you don't know what an album is, it's a circular piece of vinyl. It's quite remarkable advancements there. The album was by a group named Tetra And one of the songs on the album was Kill the Old Man. The title of the song seemed Rather drastic, as I did not anticipate I would need to kill my father if I was going to become a Christian. I soon realized that there are several usages for the descriptive old man. The first is a label for a father, anyone's father. A father can be called an old man whether he's in his twenties or in his 80s. The only requirement is that you need to be a father. The second use of old man is simply for a man who's past his prime. I will not give a particular age, but I believe I am numbered of those who is past his prime. The biblical use of old man is different than the first two. Of course it is The biblical old man is the man or person that used to exist, but no longer. He is the man that a person was before becoming born again. He is the man that a person was before he knew Christ as Savior. Thus, every Christian has an old man. The old man's power of persuasion and the memories he provides depends upon when a person was converted Even little babies among us have an old man. It is also called the sinful nature. Even if they've been buried in baptism, they have an old man. They will not have the memories of their old man like I will have memories of mine, but they still have an old man. Romans chapter 6 verse 5 describes what happens to the old man of every person who is baptized in Christ Jesus. Having identified with Christ at baptism, our old man was crucified with Christ in order that the body of sin might be done away with. That Christians should no longer be slave to sins. The wording of the passage is interesting. The old man is dead. He is crucified. But his full demise is still in question in this life. Ephesians chapter four, verse twenty-two assumes the continuing influence of this old man. He says that you put off, Paul says, concerning your former conduct, the old man which grows corrupt according to the deceitful lusts. Colossians chapter 3 verse 9 is a command to live differently than the old man. Do not lie, Paul instructs to one another, since you have put off the old man with his deeds. From these three passages and from the story of Laban and his relationship with Jacob's family, we will see. That the old man in each of us who have been baptized in Christ, that old man is dead. He is powerless. In his position, but his ways still linger. And by position I mean that the old man does not reign as he used to, but his influence is still present. We must therefore continue to work, whether we have walked with the Lord for one hour or 80 years. We must work to kill the old man. But what does all of this have to do with Jacob and Laban? Notice that Jacob desires to get out from under the influence of Laban just as each Christian desires to get out under the influence of his or her old man Jacob learns from Laban's sons and from his own observation that Laban is unhappy with Jacob's success and believes that Jacob has taken what is his. The Lord speaks to Jacob, calling him back home. And he does the same for all who follow Christ. He calls us away from the sins of old. He calls us away from our old man. As Jacob explains his reasoning for moving away from Laban to his wives, we are to identify with what makes living with our old man so difficult. The first thing we learn of our old man is that he is unreasonable. He is unreasonable because he is never satisfied. Jacob explains to his wives that he faithfully served their father, but the response of Laban was anything but gratefulness. Laban changed Jacob's wages ten times. Nothing satisfied him. He agreed to a deal with Jacob, but did not fulfill his end. He agreed to another deal and once again failed to pay. Time and again, Laban made an agreement and then changed the agreement when it did not come out to his advantage. Our old man, like Laban, is never satisfied. He always wants more. He tempts us in the following manner. He says to us, do it just once, and you will be satisfied. And so we do what we are tempted to do once, but afterward we come to know that doing it once makes us want to do it again. The simple bargain has changed. Another bargain is made, but couched in different language and in a different context, and so we think the outcome will be different. But it is not. The old man wants us to do the things we used to do. He wants us to become angry at the drop of a hat He wants us to hold grudges and become embittered by those who have wronged us. He wants us to lust after what is not ours. thinking that we can get away with it because no one knows what goes on in our minds, right? The deal is that if we withhold forgiveness Our personal pride remains intact, forgetting that that same pride has never earned us anything of value. The old man also wants us to satisfy our cravings. After all, he tells us God would not give you those cravings if he didn't want you to satisfy them. We remember those days of satisfying our flesh with fondness, not recalling how we were slaves to our own flesh. The old man makes a deal with us. You can satisfy your flesh and remain a Christian, he convinces us. The deal sounds good, but it is inconsistent with our Savior's wisdom when he tells us that we cannot serve two masters. Once that inconsistency is revealed, the old man has another deal. He always has another deal. Leah and Rachel side with Jacob's explanation, which does not say much for their old man Laban. Neither daughter perceives herself to be a daughter to Laban because their father treated them as goods to be sold. Their response is not an insult to Jacob. Laban has treated him like a hired hand, paid for by the labor, paid for because of the labor with wives. With his wives firmly behind him, Jacob sets out to rid himself of the old man. He was able to do this because there was already three days of separation between the camps. Again, this is like the Christian. We already have separation from our old man because of baptism, but still we must work to get further distance away from his influence. While Jacob's family packs and leaves, we learn that Rachel was busy stealing and hiding away what are called household idols. We will soon learn why this was a mistake. But before that discussion, it must be said that the old man will not allow us to leave quietly. Laban certainly checked in on his closest family from time to time, and when he had gone out to shear his sheep, he learned that Jacob and his family had departed. That the old man does not let us go quietly is frustrating to us. We think that because all things become new after we have been converted to Christ, that we should not have to deal with the troubles that we dealt with before. But Christianity in this life, on this side of glory, is not like that. Jesus never promised a life following him would be easy. What he promised was eternal life for all who journeyed through the valley of the shadows of death And remain faithful when coming to the end. If any man preaches that the Christian life is nothing but joy, wealth, and health, he is a liar and a thief. The way to the kingdom of God is narrow, and few travel on it. Victories are small and incremental for the Christian life. They are but a taste, a taste of the ultimate victory that awaits us in heaven. Until we reach that heavenly shore, the old man follows. Laban pursues Jacob and after seven days catches up to him. Laban's intentions are obvious. He wants his household idols back. He also wants his extended family back. He wants to continue to use Jacob's standing before God so that he himself might be blessed. God knows the intentions of the old man. And because of that knowledge, we should be comforted God is well aware of our struggle with our old man. In the case of Laban, God appears to him in a dream, verse 24. And warns him not to speak to Jacob in a good way or a bad way. The literal meaning is that he should not speak to Jacob with a peaceful greeting or a bitter reproach. He is not to praise Jacob or use bitter words. For the Christian, God sends the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, to intervene with our old man. The Spirit bears witness to us that we are not controlled by the old man, but instead we are children of God. The Holy Spirit helps us in our weaknesses, teaching us to pray and have confidence in the new man, the man that God has made us. The Spirit helps us to know that we do not face the old man alone. He is there for us. When Laban meets up with Jacob, he questions him as to why he left in secret. He then puts on, we'll call it heirs. The old man, Laban, speaks to Jacob as if he has nothing but good intentions His soul properties are now referred to as his daughters. Finally calls them his daughters. He suddenly becomes a caring grandfather Who wanted to send off his extended family with wealth and with blessings and have the opportunity to kiss his grandsons and granddaughters, which he never did before. The old man. The old man's ways are very old indeed. His ways are as old as the serpent. For he puts on a different character in order to deceive. Where the old man Laban has Jacob, where he is able to accuse him in truth. And that's due to the fact that Rachel did indeed steal the household idols. Household idols are to be understood as statues representing the gods, not the gods who control nature, but gods that are family ancestors. These were at first to memorialize and honor ancestors, but were soon turned into idols that were looked to for guidance and protection, and every family had them. Now I said that Laban's accusation was true, and so it was. And this is where each of our old men has a bit of a hold on us. He knows our sin. He knows what we have done. We all have sins that our old man knows about, but our closest loved ones do not. And if he can use that knowledge to exploit us, to get us back to obeying him, he will. He threatens to expose us. Early church fathers, such as St. Ambrose, believed that Rachel did not take the household gods for herself. But for the sake of her father, that she might help him to trust in God alone and not trust in the family idols. Such a conclusion you should see is very charitable to the character of Rachel. If we can agree with such an assessment about Rachel, there's another point to be made. The old man, no matter how you try, the old man cannot be converted. He is by his nature the old man. You can take away all of the idols he currently worships and he will find others to replace them And this is where many Christians fail because he continues to believe that some things of his old man can be salvaged. And this is where Ephesians chapter 4, verse 22 instructs us. If we believe that there is something about our old man that can be changed, that can be converted. Paul counters with the instruction, he says, put off concerning your former conduct, because the old man which grows corrupt, the old man grows corrupt. He does not rejuvenate. There is no life in him that can be restored. He only grows corrupt and cannot be saved. So put off, Paul says, your former conduct or the ways of the old man. That is the only option for a Christian. Well, after giving a tongue-lashing to Laban, Jacob is able to do just that. He is able to put off the old man. Finally separating from him. And so I asked, what have we learned here? What have we learned? We've learned that I was a delinquent child when I threw tomatoes at my neighbor's home. We have learned that the phrase old man in Scripture refers to our human nature before we are born again. We have learned that even though the old man has power over us after our baptism, every Christian is followed by his old man being tempted to walk in those old ways again. We have learned that the old man cannot be satisfied and we should not even try. Once he gets you to follow your old temptations, he will want you to follow again and again. The old man wants to make deals, but each deal is a trap that leads us to another deal, and then another deal, just as Laban made with Jacob. We have also learned that when we begin to leave the old man, he does not let us go quietly. He lives on because we let him. And if we listen to him, we give him more days to live. Notice, please. How the instructions in Ephesians require us to be active in denying and killing our old man. We are to be active. We are to be doing something about it. It tells us we are to put off the old man, which is to stop him from continuing on. We are to put on a new man, which is to live by the power of the Holy Spirit, enabling us to keep the old man quiet. We are to put away lying and instead speak the truth. We are not to let the sun go down on our anger. We are to no longer steal. We are to speak edifying words. We are to let all bitterness, wrath, and anger, clamor and evil be put away, not apart. We are responsible to do this, each of us to do it and do it again and do it again. And we are to be kind to one another, which must include forgiving one another And finally, we have learned that the old man cannot be redeemed. We can do nothing to help them, and we should not want to. It is the new man, the new man we are in Christ that we are to nurture so that he might mature. The less influence the old man has upon us, and the more corrupt he becomes to us, the better off we are. Just as Jacob had to work to separate himself from that old man Laban, so too do we need to work to separate ourselves from our old man. From the newly baptized to the oldest parishioner among us, we are all commissioned today to putting off the old man. It is a lifelong process, but one that is necessary to do if you want peace with yourself and more importantly, peace with God. Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious God We thank you for this picture of what it means to put away the old man. And as we've seen this type, this shadow in Laban and Jacob, May we recognize it in each of our individual lives and take that challenge to put him to death each and every day. It is in Jesus' name that we pray, and all of God's people said, Amen.

sermons.title: Wrestling Match
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated and turn to Genesis chapter 32. We read a portion of it, but we are going to be covering all of the chapter, Genesis thirty-two. I attended a junior high school that consisted of students between seventh and the ninth grade When I was in eighth grade, a monumental moment occurred that remains in my psyche to this day, at least the emotions that I felt. While at my locker to get books for the next class, a ninth grader pushed me back against the wall with a fellow eighth grader lurking over his shoulder. With glee, I would say. I quickly surmised that the fellow eighth grader had it in for me and he was getting this ninth grader to do his dirty work I was ordered to get down on my knees and kiss the ground, or I would receive a beating. As you can imagine, the commotion brought about a gathering of fellow students Wherever a fight is likely, a crowd of junior high and high school students are quickly to gather. After examining the ninth grader in comparison to myself, both in build and experience I concluded that I could not win this fight. I did not want to receive a beating, but there was no way I was going to get down on my knees and kiss the ground. I would not do it for him or any man. So there I stood, red-faced, a bit shaky, but very determined. Just in time, because we were in between classes, a teacher happened by and ordered everyone to break it up and get back to class. I was spared, but I knew it was only for a moment. The next class period was a blur as I concluded that my fate was sealed. I could only think of the pain that I would feel while losing a fight. After the class, that same ninth grader who had threatened me Was quickly approaching, only in a non-threatening way. And he told me he was just kidding. Behind him was my older brother, who had persuaded him who had persuaded him that bodily harm would come to me to him if bodily harm came to me. I thought of that story when I reread the story between Jacob The younger brother, and Esau the older brother. Jacob feared that bodily harm would come to him, not from an outside enemy, but from his older brother. And I wondered what that would be like. Last week we learned that Jacob was able to make distance between himself and his old man. Just as Christians are to make distance between their new man in Christ and the old man, the old man who was the person we were before our conversion, before our baptism. We now learn that to get to the promised land, Jacob needs to do more than separate from that old man. He must also face his fear of bodily harm and death while also facing the sins of his past. Not everyone has to face bodily harm in the manner that I did, and maybe there's among us some bullies yourself who uh probably wish you weren't as you were back then Threats of bodily suffering and death do not come from bullies alone, but also from accidents and disease. Most of us have been white knuckled on a plane when we are that we are riding and it takes a unexpected dip Many of us have been in automobile collisions that were serious and could have been much more serious All of us, I assume, have been diagnosed or know someone close to us who have been diagnosed with a terminal disease. Those moments when the diagnosis is heard are very similar to where we find Jacob in Genesis chapter 32. He is facing bodily harm, and he is well aware of it. The chapter begins with Jacob first becoming aware of angels as he makes his way toward the promised land. Remember that God had told him that he is to go back home, which is the promised land. The angels, the messengers of God, are there for him to help him along the way. The messengers are a sign that God is with him. They are to prepare him for what he is about to face on his way. When Jacob learns that his travels are going to take him into the land of his brother Esau, the same brother who vowed to kill him, he is understandably fearful for his life. Now he could have simply stayed where he was, or gone a different direction, or even gone back to his old man Laban. But the Lord told him to travel to his home. And if he was to be an inheritor of the promises of God, he was to go the route that God had assigned him. Jacob needed to press on. To go the route he was assigned is similar to the manner that we Christians press on. And walk the journey that God has set for us. I believe there is something innate, something that God has placed within each of us. We could call it a conviction or an intuition, whatever. It is personal knowledge that God wants you to go down a particular road and accept whatever you have to experience. For some, that road is not so obvious. It is more like a hunch that we should keep going. For others, their path is before them and they can do no other. Like a confirmed diagnosis. You have been told you must go down there and go you must. Jacob's first response is to see what possible deals he can make with Esau. He wants to bribe away his fear. Jacob was smarter than I was standing at that locker. I could have tried to feel for the ninth grader to bribe him in some way. Instead I simply tried to hold my position and hold my bladder. Moments before possible bodily harm or death, we may try to make a deal with God. The saying is in war, foxhole conversions, or there is no atheist in foxholes. These are true because people find it easier to turn to God when they are facing their own death, their own demise. And such immediate conversions, however, usually last as long as the threat. As soon as the threat is gone, well, the conversion is forgotten. This might have been true for Jacob if the Lord would have ended the threat shortly after it began, but the Lord allows the threat to remain. Esau does not respond to the knowledge that Jacob has wealth. Instead, he continues his march towards his brother. Destined to cross paths, and he even allows Jacob to know that he has 400 men with him. This raises the angst of Jacob even more. It is made clear in verse 7 that Jacob was greatly afraid to the news that he had heard. In this fear, he sets a plan in motion That seemingly is the only thing he can do to assure that he and his family will remain alive. Jacob divides his family up separates them from one another in order that if one part of his family is attacked, well, the other part might be able to escape. Again, the plan is wise if he just is focused on surviving somehow. The reality is that if Esau is bent on destroying Jacob's family, He will succeed, regardless of what Jacob does, attempting to stop him. The second part of Jacob's three-part strategy is to pray, and we see that in verses 9 through 12. We are actually privy to the prayer Jacob prayed. He begins by referring to God as the God of his fathers. And I want you to notice that he did not say, my God. Not his God, but the God of his fathers. He then appeals to God's command that Jacob continue going the way he is going. In other words, you told me to go this way. If God was going to deal well with Jacob, Jacob felt like, well, he had better start pretty soon. Jacob is next humbled in verse 10. He recognizes God's favor upon him and that he started with nothing and now he was a very well-to-do man, both in family and in property. Jacob is specific in verse 11. He asks to be delivered from the man who appears to be his enemy. Jacob next appeals to the promises that God has made, believing that in order for the promise to be fulfilled, his family must be spared. We can step back and look objectively at this prayer and say this is a good prayer. In many ways it models what our prayers should consist of. He is humble, he is specific in his request, and he appeals to God's promises. And that is to pray for God's will to be done. Appealing to God's promises is like saying, thy will be done. Despite the good prayer, there is still a problem. The God he prays to has yet to be called his God. The third part of Jacob's strategy begins the next morning. Jacob no longer investigates about a bribe, he actually makes one. His plan again, if it works, is a good one. He loads some servants up with great wealth, for all the flocks and cattle were worth a fortune in that day. He sends them ahead in order to appease Esau. This strategy is clearly stated in verse 20. It is there he says. I will appease him with the present that goes before me, and afterward I will see his face, and perhaps he will accept me. Although Jacob was a tent dweller and saw himself as no match for his brother in a fight. He was still a true man. And as a true man, he attempted to protect his immediate family one last time by separating himself from them. He sends his wives and children away so that he can face Esau alone with the hope that his life might be enough to satisfy the anger of Esau. After Jacob separated himself and was alone, a man wrestled him. The man seems to have come out of nowhere. As far as reading stories go, we were expecting Jacob, if we were to expect Jacob to be in a wrestling match, we would have been told that there was another person there. But Jacob is alone. Now I've heard of men putting on wrestling exhibitions by wrestling against themselves. And Kathy, I believe you know what I'm talking about. Your father wrestled himself, or Joe the ghost, if I remember the article about him But Jacob was not wrestling himself or a ghost. Jacob was wrestling a man, even though he was alone. Now, in order for Jacob to be alone and yet with a man, this means that the man was no ordinary man. For the identity of this man, we can go in two places. First, Hosea the prophet says that Jacob had power with God by having power over an angel. We know from the story of Abraham that angels do appear in the form of men, and we remember that in the story of Abraham they actually ate food with him. So we can speculate that Jacob Jacob wrestled with an angel in the form of a man. What makes the identity of the man even more interesting is Jacob's confidence that he had indeed wrestled with an angel. With God. It is possible then that the man Jacob wrestled with was none other than the pre-incarnate Jesus. And this possibility can be further defended by the exchange between Jacob and this man The man, the name of the man, excuse me, the name of the man is not given after Jacob asks for it, presumably because Jacob already knew in his heart who he was wrestling. The power of the man is evident in that although he allows Jacob to win the match, he is capable of injuring Jacob with just one touch. After getting insights into the narrative, we can now ask the question: what are we to make of all this? What is this really about? Jacob was facing the most fearful time in his life. He was not just facing his own demise, but the demise of his entire family. Because Jacob is alone, and because the man he wrestles with is to be understood to be God in some form, whether the pre-incarnate Christ or an angel representing God We are to understand that this wrestling with God is a crisis in prayer and in faith. Jacob's crisis Comparing what Jacob is facing the next morning and his actions of separating himself from his family to do this wrestling. First, we are to see Jesus, the Christ himself. In our gospel reading Jesus was faced with physical and emotional pain. He knew the scourge and he knew the cross were ahead of him, and he also knew that his heavenly father and earthly mother would suffer with him. And he separated himself from his disciples, knelt down in the garden to wrest with the will of the Father, and then to say, Thy will be done. The greatest struggles between men and God occur in prayer and are best described as wrestling duels. We as humans, not having the ability to see in the future or control our own destiny, attempt to grab hold of God and either retrieve knowledge of what is to come or force him as if we could. To take our lives in the direction that we prefer. God, not wanting to destroy us, but rather conform us to his will, wrestles back. by placing us in holds that require greater fortitude and determination on our part. More fortitude and determination than we have ever demanded of ourselves It is a powerful testimony to God's mercy that he allows such wrestling instead of robotically controlling us to do his will. There is confirming evidence in Scripture that God loves for his people to wrestle with him. According to the prophet Hosea. Jacob's wrestling involved weeping and supplication as well as physical tenacity. Hosea compared Jacob's holding on to the angel to his tenacity of holding on to Esau's heel when he was born.
