These actions reveal Jacob's desire to be a recipient of God's blessings. And God desires that we, his people, persist in prayer, pray without ceasing. He even appears to delight in yielding to such prayers, our prayers. I ask you to consider the parable of the unjust judge. It is there that Jesus explains God's desire to wrestle with these words. He says, And shall God not avenge his own elect who cry out day and night to him, though he bears long with them? He wants to bless us. He told this parable, he says, so that men would always pray and not lose heart. But it is easy to lose heart, to give up, especially when bad news repeats itself. We seemingly, and I seemingly, we seemingly move from one disappointment to the next. And when hope raises its head from the rubble, another disappointment follows. I have told the story before about my niece Lindsay, who has suffered a great deal of disappointment while she battled cancer. And even when cancer was no longer a threat, her lungs had deteriorated so greatly from the cancer treatment That she suffers every day, fighting to breathe, as she awaits a lung transplant that they told her will only come when she is near death. She and her husband, Jacob, interestingly, have wrestled with God for over a decade regarding her health while accepting that such is God's will for them. Some of you have and are wrestling with God, perhaps over your future, as you are not employed the way you want to be Some of you are wrestling with God over sin that re- that you return to even though you don't want to. And some of you are wrestling with God over past sins. I mentioned this earlier in the sermon, and I need to get back to it. Jacob facing Esau again is like many of us dealing with past sins that haunt us. The old man in us wants to return to those sins. The devil wants us to continue to feel guilty about past sins. We remember them like Jacob remembered Esau. We think of them as having power and authority over us. We are scared to acknowledge the past sins as if when we do they can now cling to us once again. But look what happens to Jacob when he finally meets up with Esau. While Jacob was strategizing how to survive the meeting with Esau, God was going before him. While Jacob was wrestling with God, God was healing the heart of Esau. So much work was done by God that when Jacob meets his threat, his elder brother Esau. Esau sees him from a distance and runs to his brother and expresses his love for him by embracing him, kissing him, and weeping with him. Beloved, wrestling with God is a good thing. It is telling him with all the honesty that you have within you that you are scared That you are nervous and that you see yourself as weak. It is expressing your fear about your past as well as your future. The result of such wrestling may not be as immediate as Jacob's was, but it will be a similar outcome. God goes before you to calm your enemies, to make a path for you, to strengthen your weaknesses, to weaken the pull of your past sins, and to make straight your celestial road. God answers prayer in a way that is best for you. Believe that. Have faith that God cares for you even when you don't feel cared for and you don't feel worthy of His care. And he will wrestle with you. He will wrestle with you because Jesus wrestled for you and won. God the Father wants you to win. He really does. Considering these last two sermons, I have noticed how powerful these narratives in Genesis can be, providing us mental health. They point us to overcome our mental and emotional weaknesses. They do what no psychologist or counselor can do. They call us to kill that old man that is no longer our identity. And they call us to wrestle with God when we are at our weakest point There is nothing but great things to happen when we actively kill the old man and wrestle with God. Believe it, and it will be so. Amen. Let us pray. A gracious God, we thank you for this narrative. We thank you for the truths therein that apply to each and every one of us. All of us have, are, and will wrestle with you. And we take from this narrative that that is what you want. That is what you want. May it be so, and may you win every one of those matches. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: We Must Press On
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. You'll be well served to turn to Genesis chapter thirty-four. Genesis thirty-four We read part of it, but we will be covering the entire story. Christian life. was likened to a pilgrimage long before John Bunyan's A Pilgrim's Progress was penned The term was originally used in the Middle Ages to refer to travelers who made the arduous trip to the shrine of St. James in northern Spain. The English word pilgrim comes from the Latin peregrinus, which literally means somebody who wanders across fields. Plural. We Americans know the word primarily from the story of those Christians who came to America on the Mayflower to flee religious persecution and to find freedom in the New World. That a follower of the only true God is considered a pilgrim predates all these references As the patriarchs in Genesis were in principle pilgrims. In principle, all believers are pilgrims until they reach their heavenly home. Adam and Eve began the journey when they were forced to walk out of the garden. The whole world was before them to inhabit, and yet their journey and those who follow Appeared to be attempting to get back to the garden. Dr. Peter Lighthart makes the observation that the east end of the garden was blocked Making entrance into the garden on the opposite end. If you want to return to the garden, you have to travel west. Those who are not of God travel east, and those who seek God walk travel west. Consider that after Cain was cursed, he traveled east to Nob. Lot moved east when he settled near Sodom. When Israel entered the promised land, they crossed the Jordan, moving west, when it would have been easier for them, coming from Egypt, to travel north. When Israel was taken into exile, they were taken east where their foreign captors were, requiring them to head west if they were going to return home to the promised land. It was not an accident that God had the temple built with walls on the north, south, and west sides. And that the Holy of Holies was on the west side, meaning that all who sought after God in the temple had to travel through the east gate, traveling west to get to the courtyard to get to the most holy place. Also in the New Testament, the wise men traveled west to see the Christ child, for he is truly the tree of life. And of course, Jesus will split the eastern sky, traveling west, coming from the east at his second coming. That's a call to follow God, is a call to be a pilgrim, and it's a call to head west God's call for Abraham to leave his family and to travel a land that God was giving him was a call to be a pilgrim and go west. Abraham, even though he received the call and obeyed, this is important, never settled in one spot, but continued to travel throughout the promised land. We recall that due to the arguments over water and flocks, Isaac in the Promised Land also remained on the move. Because of Esau's threat, Jacob remained on the move as well, at least at first That God's people are called to be pilgrims is seen in the traditions of the Jewish people who ate that great Passover meal in haste. As it were in haste, with their loins girded and their staffs in hand, ready for a journey. That was to be their mindset whenever they celebrated the Passover, ready for a pilgrimage. From our study of Genesis, we have read that Jacob has been on a pilgrimage. God told him to go back to his homeland, to be separate from that old man Laban. He was to go toward the promised land, and according to chapter 33, he overcame his fear of death after his confrontation of Esau and started to make his way to that promised land. The problem with Jacob is that when he comes to the promised land, he does what God did not tell him to do. When he comes to the promised land, he rests. He rests because he chose to rest. And the events that follow occur as a result of that choice to rest. And this is to be a warning to all of us regarding the dangers of stopping in our pilgrimage. Dinah, Jacob's daughter, by his first wife Leah, decides to go wander in the land while her father is resting. She goes out to see the other girls of the region. As she does, she is found alone by that Hivite prince named Shechem. And just as a wolf looks for wandering sheep that are a fair distance from the shepherd, so does a pagan prince look for young girls who are a safe distance from the protection of their father. Shechem spots Dinah and takes from her what he desires. He takes her virginity, he defiles her. The law of Moses later reveals that God's perspective is that fathers take responsibility for the virginity of their daughters. Fathers are morally and spiritually responsible for the purity of their daughters. Jacob was then responsible for Dinah's purity, her virginity. But Jacob was resting. Jacob had stopped the pilgrimage and decided to rest, not fully realizing that such a decision put the purity of his household at risk. I pause here in order for you to clearly understand what I mean by rest when referring to Jacob and his pilgrimage. There is certainly nothing wrong with physically resting. When we are tired, we should rest. But in resting, we should be building up strength so that we might press on again. Jacob was not resting as a man who is leaning upon a stick. To relieve his weary legs, Jacob was resting as in settling, with no immediate plans to press on. This decision gives his daughter, who is his purity, time to wander amongst the dangers of the world. All of us like Jacob, all of us are like Jacob, and that we are tempted to do the same. We are tempted to rest and to remain at rest. After striving for many years in the flesh, we are tempted to rest, to take a break from our pilgrimage, and our resting comes in many forms. At this moment in the sermon, I am going to be doing some meddling more than preaching, but meddling will help get to the point that we need to hear. Some of us rest in that we consider our prime days behind us. We think it, if we do not say it out loud. That it is time for us to step aside and for the younger generation to step in and do the work of the church. But the scripture says that older men are to be honored, and to be honored, you need to be around. Need to be present. The older women are to train the younger. And neither of these things can happen if the older in Christ stay home. In fact, there are certain things that those who are older in Christ can do that the younger generation cannot The older can care for the children in the nursery, while young parents are given a rare moment together in Sunday school or a Bible study. The older can tutor a young child during the day at the parish school while parents are at work. The older men and women of the church can provide wisdom from years of trial and error that younger generations need to hear. These things can only be done by those who have been granted that crown of gray, as the Bible describes. Another way to rest is to conclude that our current knowledge of God and His Word is now sufficient. Believe it or not, some perceive that they know enough about the scriptures that there is no need to make future efforts to for personal devotions or or regular Bible studies or attendance to worship and hearing sermons regularly Of course I cannot convince people who think this way. Most of the reason is because they're not here. But in the case of some who have been tempted to think in such a manner, please think again. God's ways are unceasingly revealed to us in Holy Scripture and in the sacrament. I could preach a series of sermons through Genesis again and again, and if I am a man of good study, each series would be as lively and insightful as the first. This is because God's word, you know it, is living. It's a living word. The Holy Spirit brings it to life each time it is read and preached amongst God's people who are seeking Him. In regards to reading and studying the scriptures, there is never a time to rest, but we are to always be pressing on. Always And there is also the command repeated in the New Testament for Christians to hold on. Hold on to the truths of the gospel. And it is necessary for us to work to hold on because we so easily loosen our grip and forget what is necessary for salvation The church calendar allows us to rehearse the gospel story every year, and we must rehearse it lest we let go, as so many liberal churches have done. Another way to rest is to conclude that once we have made it through a particular temptation, that we can relax. Many a young man has struggled with sexual lust and believed that marriage would cure him of his sin. Only to find that sexual temptations come into the covenant of marriage as well. Other men overcome one vice. only to find that there is a character flaw that lies deep within them, resulting in them embracing another vice The devil knows our weaknesses. Now, note he is not powerful enough to get us to do what he wants us to do, but he is cunning enough to know where we are vulnerable. And when we let our guard down. The devil roams around, the scripture tells us, like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. Fools we are if we let our guard down. And not surprisingly Resting occurs not just with individuals, but also with bodies of believers, with churches. Churches having all that they need can become fat, dumb, and lazy. They begin to go through the motions after being satisfied with how far they've come. But God calls his church forward, ever forward. The Great Commission, that instruction of Jesus to go forth to all nations and make disciples, preaching and baptizing, that is an ongoing command. It is not a command that is done one time and then finished. We are to continue to go and to preach and baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost until Until Jesus returns, until that eastern sky is split. Without question, the Reformed Episcopal Church lacks missionaries. Our denomination at this time supports five missionary works. Yes, we are a small denomination, but five works doesn't come close to taking the gospels of all nations. Thankfully our reach is a longer one, more spread out with the missions of the Anglican Church in North America, of which we are members, but there is always a need for more mission work. We must do more and we should not wait for someone else to do it. After all, just giving money doesn't solve anything or reach anybody. It could start with us. It could start with you. Why not? Now leaving these challenges for a moment, we we get back to examining our text Jacob had rested, and the result is that his purity, his daughter Dinah, is defiled. When Jacob learns of the treachery of Shechem, he decides to tell his sons. Jacob's sons were grieved and angry because of what they had heard, as we would expect a brother would be. Notwithstanding the moral standards of Jacob's family, Amor, the father of Shechem, makes the request for Shechem to take Dinah as his wife. Evidently Shechem enjoyed Dinah and wanted her legally. Hamar's request goes even far further as he suggests that Jacob come into an agreement. that his families would exchange sons and daughters. Again, Hamor does not know what he is asking. Jacob is a product of a family that has taken great care regarding who they marry. Intermarrying amongst a family that does not respect their morality nor recognize the God of Abraham and Isaac, that is not an option. However, although Haymar does not know what he is asking, he cannot be blamed for asking Jacob is the one who chose to dwell, to rest among these pagan people Jacob's actions led him or to conclude that Jacob is like him, that there is really no difference between them. The same occurs when Christians dwell amidst the ungodly. If we choose to live as the non-Christian lives in regards to our priorities and our proprieties, we will be expected to be in covenant with them. But it cannot be. It cannot be because it is easier to push someone down than to pull someone up. It cannot be because bad company does indeed corrupt good morals. It cannot be because it is much easier to worship the gods of this world than the only true God who demands that his standards are met. It cannot be because a little leaven does in fact Corrupt the whole dough. Jacob's sons respond deceitfully to Hamor's request. For in his eager words they see an opportunity to enact revenge They assent to the request, but it insists that due to their custom, they cannot enter into an agreement with the Hivites until they are the men circumcised. Shechem is desperate enough for Dinah that he and the rest of the Hivite men agree to the circumcision. And the remainder of the narrative describes how the sons of Jacob, led by Simeon and Levi, kill the Hivites. As they recovered from their circumcision. According to verse 30, Jacob was not in favor of their actions believing that they would make the name of his family obnoxious among the other tribes. And just as many other sins in Abraham's line are not immediately condemned by the Lord. So too are the acts of the sons of Jacob not immediately condemned. It was not until later That we read the Lord's condemnation and the prophecy of Jacob, their father, on Jacob's deathbed When he blessed and prophesied over each of his sons, he said the following of Simeon and Levi. Simeon and Levi are brothers Instruments of cruelty are in their dwelling place. Let not my soul enter their council. Let not my honor be united with their assembly For in their anger they slew a man, and in their self-will they hamstrung an ox. Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel. Andrew Jukes, Bishop Andrew Jukes, in his commentary, points out that judgment is easier than confession. In their anger, the brothers enacted revenge, but they failed to examine themselves to see what part they played in the defiling of their sister. We are mistaken if we think that their zeal was righteous, for in their zeal they acted with poor judgment and self-righteousness. Now this does not mean that the sword should never be used. Judgment and excommunication of offenders is warranted when a person is rightly judged. This case is different because the Hivites acted like Hivites. They did nothing that they were not known to have done. The real problem was that Jacob and his family rested amongst them. What was needed was for the brothers to watch out for their sister. so that they would not be alone, their sisters, so that they would not be alone, so that no one could defile them. What was needed by Jacob and his sons was not judgment. It was confession. There needed to be a confession that the problems of the family had encountered the disgrace they all felt was caused in part by the fact that they had stopped being pilgrims. They rested. They had rested instead of passing through. And confession, confession is a good thing to highlight on the first Sunday of Lent. If you are here this morning feeling tired in your pilgrimage, there is no sin in resting. But that resting must be done to prepare you to press on. Regardless of age, length of trial, or number of trials, rest is only for a time. We are not to rest because of age, or because we think we understand enough, or because we have overcome temptation or vice Nor are we to rest as a church, for there are always people who need to hear the gospel and places on the globe that have failed to embrace the truth that Jesus Christ is Lord. I think the beauty of a message like this is that it is not focused on one particular group This is not for males only or females only or the young only or the old only. Each of us are being challenged by God's word to continue our pilgrimage. If we are Christian and we are breathing, the message of God's word to us is to press on, to continue our pilgrimage. Let us do so as long as God gives us strength. Now the picture John Bunyan gives us at the end of Christian's life, Christian is the main character in the story of a pilgrim's progress, is that Christian must walk through the waters that represent death Experiencing all the fear and the doubt that death provides before he reaches the celestial shore. If he were to stop in the waters, he would surely drown. He needed to continue his pilgrimage until he was on that celestial shore Through death, we all must do the same. Let us pray Our fathers for the story of Jacob and the defiling of his daughter, and the revenge sought by his sons. We do see that warning of the dangers of stopping, of resting to the point of not continuing on. May you find us each of us where we are now. And as a congregation, places where we are resting. May we receive your strength and press on. We hear this message. And we heed it. In Jesus' name. Amen. Love because

sermons.title: Gone Fishing
sermons.speaker: Phil Lambooy
sermons.text: Think back to the times of fishing you have had. With your dad, maybe your mom, and then later, maybe with your own children. Or maybe because of the other two you've always fished alone. There are many emotions felt and expressed before, during, and after fishing. Disappointment and exaltation Anger and joy. To be a good fisherman is an art. But one of the keys in catching fish is Getting a line in the water. Whether in a river, stream, pond, lake, or ocean, the line has got to go down. Off the coast of New England, eighty miles from Gloucester, Massachusetts, lies an ecosystem that is unexpected, beautiful, and unrivaled in the North Atlantic. Biologists and fishermen have long been aware of its existence because the rich ecosystem serves as a nursery for many species of fish. It is one of the few places on the East Coast considered by scientists to be unique, flourishing, and in need of permanent protection. It has been dubbed the Yellowstone of the North Atlantic. It is the underwater mountain range called Cassius Ledge. One hears stories about Cassius Ledge from the 80s, when schools of cod and cusp and pollock and mackerel and paddock and other fish could be seen with myriad sharks and whales. Anybody know what this is? What do you do with it? Put it in the water, right? The line. And so now I will share with you my story of fishing at Cassius Ledge in the 80s before they wanted to make it a national protection park. It began in a pub, as all good fishing trips should. In Gloucester, I was with two of my best friends from seminary, Gary Laterno And a man named Tim Bailey, who some of you have heard of. We threw darts. We threw back a few pints. Of course, we were witnessing to the fishermen. And around ten o'clock, we had to board our chartered fishing vessel to begin an overnight excursion out to Cassius Ledge. It was a journey of about 80 or 90 miles, and we arrived there early the next morning. At around 5 or 6, we got out of our bunks I guess, but I don't remember the night. We had breakfast, and I assumed coffee. And then we went up to the deck to start our day of fishing. It was a bright and sunny day. And here is what I had to do. All the work I had to put into that fishing excursion at Cash's Ledge. I had to stand at the rail, lower my line over the rail into the water. I had a crewman who attached the hooks. They attached the lures. Some of these guys are big too, these lures. They gave me the pole. They made sure the line was there. And I started to fish. I put my line into the water. I guess that would be called boutique fishing. Don't do they'll do anything except And so I stood at that rail with occasional breaks for about seven hours, lowering my line into the water. So for of course, after all, I'm a real fish in it. Now we'll fast forward seven hours. I had caught cusp, cod, mackerel, pollock, and haddock The fish never seemed to stop biting. Except when one of the guys snagged a shark and he messed up all of our lines, we cut the shark off so we could keep on fishing. Sometimes my line would be rigged with two large lures. You lay it down. These fish were sacrificing themselves. You catch two at a time and you pulled the line. There were two large mackerel or coll cus a cusp on the line. And you load it in, you pulled it up. It was a fantastic day. It's never a day I'm sure I will ever experience again. On the way back to Gloucester, boat hands filleted our fish. And I went home with about 47 pounds of fillet of fish that day. Yeah. You cut off the head, the fins, the tails, and everything else that you don't want. 47 pounds a lot. And so it went into the freezer. I think we had to borrow somebody else's freezer. But it was there ready to we we just fished out for a good old while. Fish and chips was the order of the day On that trip, the crew did 95% of the work. I did five percent. That was my contribution. I told you what that was, right? I lowered the line into the water. I did have to pull it up too, I must admit But once they got the fish up, they took it off, they cleaned it, I took care of it, and then I just lowered it in the line. The boat captain took us to where we had to go to fish, right? He knew We had the right equipment. We had the right attitude. We wanted to catch fish. We knew we would catch fish outdoor starter. But here's the key. I lowered my line into the water, and that is how I caught fish. In our gospel reading from Matthew 4, we find that Jesus walking on the shoreline outside the city of Capernaum, which had become his adopted home. Not far from where in 1986 a first-century fishing boat was discovered and buried in the sand off the shore of Galilee. It's the only boat of its kind ever found in antiquity, and it's an excellent example of the type of boat the disciples would have used that day on Galilee. It dates to the first century BC through the first century A. D. It's about 27 feet long. It's sometimes referred to as the Galilee boat, or maybe you've heard of it being referred to as the Jesus boat. Though there is no evidence, of course, that Jesus ever rode in it. So go online, take an example, take a look at what the Jesus boat looks like with the remains of it today. The hull is pretty much intact You can see the planking, etc. But as Jesus is walking along the shoreline, he comes across his first disciples who was read to you this morning. Simon, Andrew, James, and John. Ordinary men at an ordinary place going about their business as they did every day. For them, fishing wasn't recreation as it had been for me. It was serious business Life or death enterprise for them. Being fishermen on the Sea of Galilee was their vocation. It was their livelihood and would be ultimately their legacy, so they thought So while walking along the shore, Jesus calls on to these four men, men whom he had met earlier, we see in John chapter 1. But he called out to him to them to follow him, and he would make them fishers of men. So they stop what they are doing. They get up and follow him. There seems to be no reservation and no hesitancy in responding to his call. They follow him. Leaving what is known for the unknown, what has become familiar for the unfamiliar. What they were doing though, not fully understanding it, was going after bigger fish. A bigger prize. To be disciples of Jesus, they were willing to give up all that they knew, all that they loved. And entrust their lives and future into the hands of one whom they believed was the Messiah, though they were beginners only at that time in their beliefs. They wanted to be fishers of men. And nothing less is expected of you and me this morning. To be able and prepared and willing to give up all that we know and love in order to entrust our lives to follow Jesus. The call is still the same. The question for us is: what kind of fishers of men are we? Instead of fishing for men and women, we often busy ourselves by attending fishing seminars. Telling fish stories or fixing up the fishing camp, the church. It has been well publicized that 70% of all of our churches are plateauing or declining. And it begs the question, are we truly fishing or wetting a hook? In many instances our fishing today consists mainly of Transferring fish from one church ice chest to another church ice chest down the street or across town. Few churches are impacting the fish pond and reaching your God-given potential. After all, can a person or a church really be a follower of Jesus if they never fish? In Luke 5. 10, we read of another aspect of this call of the first fisherman. And here Jesus tells Peter. Do not be afraid. From now on, you will be catching men. So point one would be Jesus says, follow me. I think that's difficult, right? Point two is fear not. That's also difficult, especially in the area of fishing for men. And he says, fear not to Peter after Peter recognizes his sinfulness when he's in the presence of Jesus. And to be fishers of men demands that we follow Jesus and we trust ourselves to Him to combat our fears. Catching men is an interesting phrase there. In the Greek this means literally to take captive, to take alive. As is done in the course of war rather than killing. So in the fishing for men that Jesus is calling the disciples to, they are fishing no longer to hook, neck, capture, and kill the fish to eat or sell But catching men so that they might be rescued from the bondage of sin and be restored to Christ's kingdom. Consider this You and I are called to fish for men to save men and women. In a sense, we are really a catch and release fisherman. The devil fishes for men to capture them, to condemn them for eternity. We catch them so that God can release them from sin and bondage. A couple weeks ago on March 11th, Pastor Jorgensen, while preaching on Genesis 34, made mention of the fact that the RE Church currently supports five missionaries. Who here heard that? Who here is awake? You can listen to it on the web site. Spied missionaries. The denomination and birth in 1873. My old pal Ulysses S. Grant is president at that time. Five active missionaries. Is that the legacy that we are leaving on the mission field after 146 years? The legacy that we are leaving in the minds and hearts of the next generation in the RE Church. That is, if there is a next generation. As you heard the number five two weeks ago and you just heard it again when I spoke it, are you a little disappointed and embarrassed? The church has been around for 146 years has five missionaries. Seems pretty pathetic, one could say. And if you want to go out on the limb, does God wonder what we are doing or have not been doing with the resources, the Holy Spirit, and the Word that He's been given to us? It seems to me that as a denomination, we are pretty lukewarm. When it comes to our reach, missions, and evangelism. By contrast, a denomination that was founded 100 years later, in 1973, the PCA, Right now they have over 310 overseas missionaries and counting. Then the pastor went on to say that just giving money does not stop anything nor reach anyone He says resting in our laurels occurs not only with individuals, but also with bodies of believers as well, as is the local church. Churches, he said, become fat, dumb, and lazy. They, we, go through the motions, but God causes church always to move forward As outlined in the Great Commission, what Jesus charges and commands his church to continue in preaching, baptizing, and discipling of all nations. That means fishing for converts. It is an ongoing, timeless command, and it extends to the old world. And as he finished up, he said. We are to continue to go. sermons.title: Shame Redeemed
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. It's good to be home. It's good to be in God's house. If I had to choose what was one of the more embarrassing moments of my life, the following account would compete for first place. I was just out of college working at a local church ministering to college students. I was invited to a college social that was hosted by an older couple in the church As I got out of my vehicle, I needed to tuck in my shirt, so I unbuckled and did all that. And uh after entering the home, I made my way to each of the college students and shaking their hands and introducing myself. And each of them carried a strange look that I attributed to the fact that I was just new to them. After about 10 minutes of introduction and hogging the conversation, a note was handed to me by the host telling me that I was unzipped and actually unbuckled With my shirt tail hanging out of my fly. To this day I cringe with embarrassment thinking of that moment Embarrassing moments stay with us a long time. Moments of shame stay with us even longer. Shame is different than embarrassment. Shame is the result of sin. We are shamed when our sin was found out, and what is worse We should be ashamed at our sin, but we're ashamed because we've been caught. And this relates to our study in Genesis 35. That Jacob and his family were shamed. Jacob's resting led to the grievous defilement of his daughter, Dinah, you remember. The defilement of Dinah led to the sons of Jacob taking cruel revenge. The cruel revenge of Jacob's sons led to an unholy reputation among the people of the land. Shame came upon shame at this time in Jacob's life. What is remarkable is how God ministered to Jacob in the midst of this shame. Jacob's rest brought on shame, but that shame eventually God used to advance him and even free him. And that is what God does. He does it not because of our shame, as if our shame is something that has earned God's mercy, but by overcoming our shame with his mercy. The devil's logic would tempt us to go ahead and commit that act of sinful shame because after all, God will forgive you after you do it. To believe such logic is to not understand mercy. For if mercy is taken for granted, it is not mercy. Mercy is when we deserve suffering, we deserve punishment, even hellfire punishment, and we do not receive it. Amidst the shame of resting and the result of Jacob's daughter being defiled and the conflict of Jacob's sons taking revenge, Jacob could no longer rest where he was. His inability to rest was again a means of grace to him, for it forced him to press on, and we learned three Sundays ago that God's people must always be pressing on Jacob is helped, literally helped, up by God, as God comes to him directly, commanding him to go to Bethel. Such a word from God comes when his servants are faint and when they are frail. It comes when we think that we have shamed ourselves into exile. It comes when we cannot even look upon ourselves and we wonder why another someone else would bother with us. It is at such a low moment that God comes Miraculously to us, and lets us know who we are to him As long as we migrate in this world, we are tempted to determine the value of others and even ourselves by what we see around us. Which is to say that we compare our value as a person to the value we think we see in others. We walk by sight. We look at our outward appearance and make an evaluation of what is good and bad in comparison to what is upheld in our culture as good or bad. And we don't measure up. We don't measure up. Not even those who pose for ads that tell us how skinny and good-looking we should be, not even those same people measure up Their pictures are doctored and their physique is a result of unhealthy obsessions. The most wonderful time, the most freeing times we get to experience in this life. are not when we have lost some weight and think that we are closer to measuring up or when we have achieved a certain status in our social circles That fool us into thinking that we are more important than we are? No, the most freeing time is when we have found our identity in God and what He has said about us. In Jacob's case, although his family had been shamed, God had called him. And that's all that mattered. To comfort Jacob more, God calls him to a place identified with mercy. Jacob is called back to Bethel, and we should remember that place. That is where God met with him and that ladder appeared and angels were ascending and descending to minister to him, ministering from heaven and taking what is on earth to heaven. For anyone who is suffering from emotional scars that sin leaves, he or she is called back to a place where God has made his mercy evident. That place is different for each person, but for all of us, a common place to go back is our baptism. It was at our baptism that God marked us as his own. And where we were assured that no one could snatch us out of his hand, we are always forever his. Although God has initiated his relationship with Jacob at every step, Jacob must necessarily respond. Jacob must lead his family back to God by ridding his household of false gods. The New King James uses the term foreign gods. These foreign gods are not described. And that is helpful to us. We can assume that these gods were idols used to worship by the Hivites. And other tribes that occupied the land. When we were in Greece, we saw artifacts of similar worship as household carvings of Greek gods have been found in archaeological digs of average Greek homes The literal translation in this passage mentioning foreign gods from Genesis is actually gods of strangers. Gods of strangers. Well the reason why we lack specifics to the description, the reason why it is helpful is that it allows us to understand in principle That the gods used for prayer and worship by Jacob's family were anything but the true God. Too often, specifics of false gods and specifics of sin bog us down. We hear a scripture passage that lists a number of sins that are damnable, and because the sin that we are involved with is not specifically described, we can think, well, we're exempt The thinking is that if Genesis doesn't identify false idols that I worship, then the condemnation of such worship doesn't apply to me. This also happens when we hear a preacher spend time attacking this or that sin And because the scenario he describes does not match with our own in precise detail, we think that God is talking to someone else. Because these gods are generally described as gods of strangers, forces us to acknowledge that anything that is not of the true God That is, in common with his holy word, anything that is not is to be put away. If we allow the Holy Spirit to speak to us rather than wait for men to precisely name the sin that we are involved with, We will hear, we will hear the Holy Spirit say, put anything away that is not of the true God. And dads, fathers, listen to this more intently. Jacob led his household to put away foreign gods, and you need to do the same. You are the leader of your house, you are the priest of your home. You must help your family see that what needs to put what needs to be put away in your home is anything that takes us away from our attention to God. And please don't let this admonition fall on deaf ears. Don't wait for your specifically identified idol to be named. Rid your house of idols that do not align with God's word, and that will be enough. Jacob acts as priest in his home and he takes the foreign gods away from his family while explaining that the only true God is worthy of their worship because that God has always been with them. In verse 5, we are told that Jacob and his family journeyed to Bethel, that as they did, the terror of God was upon the cities they passed by. The terror of God and likely generated a reputation given by his family because they slaughtered the Hivite men. We remember that Jacob rebuked his sons because of their actions, and he was concerned about this reputation that it would be a stench to the tribes around them. God, by his merciful care over them, takes what was meant for evil and turns it to their advantage. He works all things together for the good. No man in his wisdom can do this. Man simply piles evil on evil Only God can turn around what was once a stent and make it a sweet aroma. God uses the sin of Jacob's sons to cause fear in the hearts of would-be enemies. And this does not make the actions of Jacob's sons good in any way. Instead, it highlights that God is always good to his people. When Jacob arrives at Bethel, he builds an altar which is a monument upon which he worships and uses to honor what God has done for him. Now notice, church, that the response of Jacob is the only appropriate response of God's people when grace has been received. Jacob worships. Moments of worship occur quite often in Genesis because the patriarchs respond to every act of God's mercy by worshiping. But I remind you that as we are in Genesis, the Ten Commandments had not been given yet. We have not heard the fourth commandment. There's been no setting aside of a day to worship the Lord. All worship prior to this has been done by individuals or families, but not by a people as a whole. It is not until God brings forth that law that a day is designated. The Sabbath law is established. And those Sabbath laws were established to remember that God had delivered Israel out of slavery. to something new and free that they had not known before. In like manner, Christians are expected to continue worshiping on a day designated by God because we as a people have been given freedom, only better freedom. Freedom from the guilt of sin. What is difficult for Christians is what was difficult for the nation of Israel, which is the ability to stay motivated to worship regularly. Jacob was motivated to worship then and there after having an emotional experience with God's mercy For those of us who were converted to Christianity decades ago, the emotional experience is far removed. For those who were baptized as infants and raised in the church, an emotional experience is less understood, making it farther removed. And with the lack of emotion, the temptation to stay home from worship or find something else to do, that temptation is all the more stronger. As more generations of Israel were removed from the Exodus experience, the greater likelihood that they would forget the one true God and turn to false gods. The only thing that would turn many unfaithful back to God was a crisis in life that would force them to call out for God's mercy. Once received, they would go back to true worship, but the cycle was seemingly destined to start over as generations would follow. We Christians, we Christians know this cycle well. We know of families to have God-fearing grandparents and and parents who are seemingly somewhat believers and then Grandchildren who have just gone wayward. So often it is only two generations removed that wander from the faith. And we ask again, how do we prov prevent this? As you have heard from this pulpit and elsewhere, I have often questioned what I can do as a pastor to protect my own family first and then the families of this church The generations that follow will not go away from the faith. And my attempt the past year was to offer a series of sermons to address this terrible cycle, and still I know of people who have rejected those sermons. And unfortunately a crisis in the future may be necessary. There are some other principles I have identified in Scripture to prevent this, and I've decided to go ahead and give them here with the disclaimer that nothing is foolproof Nothing is foolproof but the mercy of God. There is no formula that produces faithful worshippers. I am simply identifying what the scripture clearly teaches. And so I say that first, Christians are to count the mercies of God. Literally, not figuratively, we are to count the mercies of God. We are to note them when they are evident. If a person has been sick and we prayed for healing and they recovered, that is mercy of God to be counted. If I have health, if I have safety, if I have food, if I have shelter, warmth, if I have loved ones, all of these are to be counted. Even if I have just some of these, they are to be counted. Lamentation says that God's compassions, his mercies, are new every morning. Indeed they are, and we should count them every morning. Second, we are to tell of the mercies of God. We are to tell them to our children and friends, just as we tell jovial stories and exciting adventures. Telling of God's mercies reminds us of what motivated us to worship God in the past and keeps us motivated in the present. If you have a story of physical healing, tell it. If you have a story of reconciliation, tell it. If you have a story of God's provision in difficult circumstances, tell it Each ritual followed, and the Passover meal was commanded by God so that the children might know what he had done many years ago to deliver Israel from slavery. God's acts of mercy are kept fresh when they are told. Third, rehearse the law of God regularly. The Israelites were to instruct their children regarding God's law systematically. And there are two primary purposes for such a rehearsal. First, we are to know what pleases God and we are to attempt to live accordingly. Second, we are to recognize how far-reaching God's standards are and how far short we fall of those standards and how much we need. A Savior. And this is a vital point. Ingrained in our liturgy is a rehearsal of the Ten Commandments as we did today. Followed by the Word of God being preached to us as it is now, followed by prayers of confession of sin, so that we can see how God saves us and what he saves us from. God gave us this order of worship. He did it for each of us. Fourth, and this one takes us back to our text in Genesis. Worship is to be part of who we are. It is to be our identity. It is to be who we are as individuals and as a people. Notice that God changed Jacob's name to Israel, as told in verse 10, and along with that change, he gives him a new identity. Jacob was no longer the supplanter, that's what his name originally meant. But God now says he is one whom God contends and preserves, for that is what Israel means. As Christians, our identity changes. Having been marked by Christ, we are forever linked with the universal church, its past, its present, its future. Is now a part of our identity. And what have Christians done and continue to do? Well, they worship God. In spirit and truth, they worship God. Worship for us and for our children needs to be a natural part of our life routine. If it is missed, it needs to nag us as like unbrushed teeth at bedtime. It needs to cause pangs within us as our stomach does when we miss a meal. It is to be such a part of who we are that if it is not done, something is missing. Something is not right. The last principle we need, I do not list as the fifth, because it is not one of many, but must be included in all that has been discussed so far. That principle is faith. We are saved, after all, by faith Our motivation to worship begins and ends with faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. Faith is having trust in God's promises. We have faith in what he said to be true. We have faith that Jesus was who he said he was, that he accomplished what he said he accomplished, and that if we give ourselves to him, we will receive eternal life. Jacob's worship was offered because God had taken his shame and the reasons for his shame and used it to Jacob's favor. The emotions of the moment were expressed in Jacob's offering of worship. Those who are in Christ are to understand that what happened to Jacob in that moment happens to each of us. Each day of our lives. Jesus takes our shame upon himself and uses it to our favor. So as we do better at counting God's mercies, as we do better at telling of his mercies, as we do better at rehearsing his law, and identify ourselves as worshipers. the more faithful we will be at worshiping. After all, God has taken our shame and He works it together for the good. As he continues to do so, may we continue to worship him. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God, we do mark this time of you taking on the shame of Jacob and his family and working it to the good. And in it we see the cross, we see your son, we see our confession, and we believe. Father, keep us as worshipers all of our days We ask this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: God intended it for good
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. If you would open your Bibles to Genesis chapter 20 or 37, Genesis 37, we'll be walking through that chapter this morning. What makes the Bible such a compelling book? What makes it interesting literature even To those who do not believe that it is divinely inspired. What makes it all these things is the transparent humanity that it offers. Few, if any, of us, when we write our family history, include stories of jealousy, lust, rage, attempted murder. We prefer to forget such things, but Jacob's family tells the story in details because the Holy Spirit wants us to see ourselves in these stories. Their sins are our sins. The preferential treatment of Joseph and the jealousy of his brothers is one of those stories. In Genesis 37, we will see two types that I hope will increase our faith. The first will be ourselves We will see our sinfulness through the words and actions of these ten brothers who become jealous of the one. And seeing our sinfulness is not fun. It is like looking in the mirror when you know you have a blemish. It is hard to look at at first, but then when you do you become a little fascinated by it, like a big old zit on your nose And that is because what will happen to us is that we will have a hard time looking at the reality of our sin, but then become fascinated by it that it is our image, that it looks so much like us The second vision will be of Christ. Joseph is like Christ. He is like Christ in many ways. What we will focus on in this sermon is how he is like Christ in the manner that he was despised by his brothers. With this story, I also want to jump ahead in the story of Genesis to that moment when Joseph reveals himself to his brothers. And then Joseph sums up their family tragedy by stating that what they meant for evil, God meant for good. And we must apply that truth to every aspect of this story. And so we begin by examining Genesis 37 with the scene set for us in the first few verses. Jacob and his family have been dwelling in Cana just as God instructed him. Joseph was about 17 years of age. He was the son of Rachel, who had recently died. Joseph had assigned, was assigned, excuse me, to serve as a shepherd alongside his brothers, who were the sons of Jacob's other wives. And it is clear from verse 3 that Jacob had greater affection for his son Joseph, who was the firstborn of his beloved Rachel. He preferred Joseph more than he did the rest of his children. That is not good. We could say it's even evil. To show greater affection, he made this coat or tunic, as the New King James uses, this tunic of many colors. Such a tunic was special primarily for two reasons. First, it was expensive, for it took a great deal of time to make such a tunic. Second, a colorful coat signified superior rank, meaning that Joseph was being given greater responsibility over the sheep than his brothers who were older than him. And it is here that we can again apply what man meant for evil, God meant for good. Thus far, the description of Joseph can be likened to Christ in that he was favored by his father. We know that Christ was favored by his heavenly father. Jesus was said to be having found favor with both God and man. He was the firstborn of God. He was the Son whom God said he was well pleased. Joseph can also be likened to Christ because of his coat of many colors. You remember from eighth-grade biology that light is made up of a bunch of different colors and you see it through a prism? Well, Joseph's coat is like a prism. He is showing that Christ to come will be a light as well. Now these types are interesting, but they will become quite dramatic. The reaction of Joseph's brothers to his favorite status reveals the frailty of the human psyche That all of us can relate to. All of us are tempted to be jealous. And most of us have moved past jealousy from time to time Into sin, especially when it involves jealousy of siblings. Joseph's brothers hated him, and they committed murder in their heart because he was favored. What they do to him later began the moment they hated him inside. There is no doubt that Joseph knew his brothers hated him by the evidence that they would not speak a word of kindness to him. They would speak kindly to one another, but not to him, because he was favored by his father, and he was a tattletale. But Joseph either didn't care that he was not liked by his brothers, or he enjoyed seeing them be jealous. He even told them about his dreams. Dreams that had obvious interpretations The brothers knew that they were the sheaves, bowing down to the sheave of Joseph in the dream, and that Joseph would rule over them. And again, naturally, they hated him. We can say of Joseph at this time, what Joseph meant for evil, God meant for good. Evidently the telling of the first dream was not enough, for Joseph told them of another dream, and that same dream had heavenly bodies bowing down to him again, and this time it included his father. When he told his father of this dream, his father rebukes him, but then the scripture says that he held it with in his mind, in the back of his mind, remembering that it would come to reference in the future. Now the story is less emotionally charged in verses 12 through 17. They describe Joseph being sent by his father to travel a few days and to check on his brothers. The emotion picks back up in verse 18, where the brothers are said to have seen Joseph from afar, and they began plotting to kill him. And we remember, we remember what men mean for evil, God means for good The original plan agreed upon was to kill him by their hands, bury him in a pit, and claim to their father that a wild animal had killed him. The whole while they were planning their killing, they were stirring up their jealousy, reminding themselves of Joseph's dreams. Evidence that this is all under God's control. Is that for unstated reasons, Ruben interrupts the plan. He interrupts the plan and insists there will be no bloodshed. Reuben, you remember, was the firstborn of all the sons. He was leader of the brothers, and so it was natural that they heed his counsel. Although they do not kill Joseph, they did everything just short of murder. They stripped him of the coat that they were jealous for. Then they threw him into an empty pit, planning for it to be his grave. And then we are told that they sit down and have a meal. Truly, their hearts were callous, as evident by their ability to mistreat their own flesh and blood, and then enjoy a meal. Their jealousy and hatred continued after they spotted slave traders from among the Ishmaelites. If they are not going to get full satisfaction for their hatred, they reason that they might as well make some money off of their brother, so they sell him into slavery. And we are reminded once again what men mean for evil, God means for good. Once Joseph was sold and the money shared, the brothers decide to stick to the original story And they plan to tell their father that he's dead. Wild animal killed him. Here's his coat with blood on it. All of it to look quite innocent on their part. What men mean for evil, God means for good. As I argued in the beginning of this story of transparent humanity, we look at Jacob's response. And as you read it, you get the idea of how much he was grieved at this loss. We can imagine him mourning the loss of his son in the way it is described. But the greater lesson for us is not found in the manner that Jacob cries. No, the greater lesson for us today is the jealousy in these brothers. Joseph was favored, as was evident by his coat and by his dreams. But he was not just favored by his father, he was favored by God. His two dreams were not doubted by his brothers. They just hated the fact that he was favored. By rejecting Joseph, the brothers failed to see that they were rejecting God's rule, his sovereign plan for all of their lives. But rejected as they may, they could not accept it. God's will would be done. His purpose would be carried out. And here is a fact of life that we all struggle with in one way or another. We struggle with it just as brothers struggle with it. God does not treat all of us the same. He does not give us all the same things. He does not favor us with the same blessings. Some Christians are smarter than others. Some are better looking. Some are more athletic, more financially successful. Some are married to lovelier wives or more impressive husbands. Some have better jobs than others. Some have higher achieving children. Some have children with greater faith. Some live healthier and longer lives. Some people seem to step from one triumph to another, with others seeming to walk into one trouble or another. Some have seemingly natural virtue. Some have greater self-discipline. Some have a naturally kind disposition. Some have a greater work effort. Some are more at ease in front of people. Some have the ability to teach, and a smaller few have the ability to teach well. Samuel Elliott Morrison, an American historian and essayist, once wrote that life is like a card game. God deals the deck. He gives some a very good hand. He gives to others a very bad hand. But everyone is required to play by the same rules. It is a hard truth, but truth it is. And we see it not only in the case of Joseph and his brothers, but in our own lives, and then the lives of everyone we know. A man can squander a good hand, and a man can play a poor hand in life very well. But if a great hand is played, well, played well, it is unbeatable And because we know the end of this story, Joseph was dealt eventually a great hand, and he played it well. The trouble for us is that it is hard to accept when we know that another is holding a better hand than our own. The Tenth Commandment makes the top ten because it is the root of evil that all of us struggle to resist. Struggle against coveting. I know a man who at one time would do anything to serve the Lord in his church. He had a will and a desire to make a difference in the kingdom of God. He served on parish committees, he volunteered to teach Sunday school, and even made his way to the pulpit a few times when there was seemingly no one else available. As the church leadership changed, however, his services became less and less requested. His ideas were no longer heeded. The direction of Sunday school had changed and he was replaced with better teachers. He was also no longer an option for pulpit supply And as he saw others take positions of leadership that he once had, as well as others he coveted, the jealousy overwhelmed him. And he did what most do in that situation. He left his home church. To my knowledge, there was no malice intent on anyone's part to discard this man. Simply put, there were people who were more gifted at doing the jobs he once did. But that is hard for some to take For some, they cannot take it at all. For some, it is nearly impossible to admit that it was God who chose others, who gave greater gifts to others. But this topic of jealousy and God giving more to some people as compared to others is greater than one person, one person having more talent than another. Some people are given more breaks in life than others. Some people are awarded what appears to be blessings when we know that they are scoundrels. To these types of scenarios, we also must be able to say what men mean for evil, God means for good. Consider our political arenas today, and notice the many jealous, envious, those who hate, those who have hearts that idolize power When they rant, rave, protest, lie, slander, and get headlines, we can identify their jealous rage and be concerned about them ever being in charge. But Christians are not to fear the politically progressive. Christians are to have faith that what men mean for evil, God will always mean for good. And that truth, that truth will always be the case. Joseph was despised by his brothers, and Jesus was despised by his Jewish brothers. The Gospel of John tells us that Jesus came unto his own, and his own were his fellow Jews. He came to his own people, he came to his brothers of faith and flesh, and his own brothers did not receive him. He was rejected and despised, said the prophet Isaiah. And why? Why was he rejected and despised? In part, a big part, was jealousy. The Pharisees and the Sadducees were jealous of the crowds that followed him. They heard of the miracles and they saw the evidence, and instead of rejoicing that the Savior had come, they tried to dissuade the crowd from listening to him. When Jesus' words put the religious leaders in their place, they privately seized and plotted to kill him. And like Joseph, Jesus was sold. Like Joseph, Jesus' robe was torn off of him. And like Joseph, what man meant for evil regarding Jesus' death God always meant for good. But we cannot yet get to that good news this morning until again we focus on jealousy. I would like you to go back and just glance through the passages in chapter 37 and notice how many times the word brothers is used, especially at the beginning. There is a purpose for its repeated usage. We the readers are to understand that the crimes committed against Joseph weren't done by brothers. And who is supposed to be there for him? Who is supposed to protect him? Who is supposed to support him but his brothers? And they do the opposite. The reason the scripture uses familial descriptive terms like brother is to describe the Christian relationship in reflecting what we are to be to one another. Brotherhood is the ideal. Thus the sin of Jacob's sons is all the greater, not simply because they were jealous, but they were jealous of a brother. Again what they meant for evil, God meant for good I need, as I trust some of you need, to believe that what men mean for evil, God means for good. And you might wonder how this can be true all of the time. What men can do can be very mean and nasty And because of this, it is hard for us to think that God would allow such meanness and nastiness to occur all so that he could turn it around to the good. Why doesn't God just stop the meanness and nastiness of people? And this is similar to the question to what theologians call the problem of evil. It is argued by some that God should have made all of us incapable of sin to prevent evil from ever invading his created world. But we are not privy to the whole mind of God. We are mere creatures who have no right to question the will of Almighty God. What we are to do instead is to believe, which is to have faith, which is to trust that when men have meant, do mean, and will mean evil That God has meant, does mean, and will mean the good. We don't know how it works with the wills and choices of people who aren't intent to hurt us But that is not to matter. We are to believe that God will make good of what is meant for evil. Not only are we to believe this in general, we are to apply it to our everyday life situations. I need to apply it to my everyday life situation. I need to believe that when people who are supposed to honor choose to do the opposite and to only think about their desires, That when they are doing such, God has planned to turn such sin around for his good. I am to realize that I don't deserve for him to do that. None of us do. We don't deserve it. But that's why it's called grace. I just stated that God seems to allow for meanness to occur so that it can be turned to the good. It seems that way. But he never tells us that. He allows it so that he can turn it around. He never says that He just knows that it does happen that men do things that are mean and mean it for evil. God knows that. And he wants us to know he turns that around. What we are to trust is that within the mystery of God is the love of God overcoming the sins of others, so that in the end, in the end, There is good. The good end may not be immediate, and it may not even happen in this life. But it will come. It will come. That is what we hope for. That is the convictions we have that are unseen. Let us pray. Our gracious God For this great lesson in the lives of these patriarchs, we are grateful. For we get to hear those words. We get to know that in every situation, no matter what men mean to do, You can turn it around, and it can be good. And so we say those words of Joseph, and we believe them. And we thank you for that faith. In Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Not Being Nice
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I am ready to get into trouble today So you are now forewarned. What if the Jesus you worship in your mind The one you envision, both in how he looks and his type of personality as you sing to him and pray to him and listen to him. What if That is not actually Jesus. What if you were confronted with the fact that Jesus, the Jesus you had understood him to be, was not only incorrect, But in some ways, the opposite of what you thought him to be. Would you stop having faith in him? Would you stop worshiping him Or would you repent from thinking about him the way you used to think, and instead think upon him as the Bible describes him? Those are a lot of questions to answer. I read recently that a besetting sin among Christians today in the West is the sin of believing that being a Christian is being nice. Being a Christian is being nice. And that our idea of nice comes from what our culture defines as nice. Nice in our culture is non-confronting. Nice in our culture is letting be what will be. Nice in our culture is coexisting. I trust you have seen those bumper stickers with the different religious symbols within it, a word that says coexist. That message is absolutely ridiculous. And if you have one, I cannot apologize for criticizing it because I forewarned you that I was going to get into trouble today How can Islam coexist with Judaism when Islamic teaching purposefully targets the destruction of the Jewish faith? How can Christianity coexist with Muslims when we proclaim Muhammad is not a prophet of God? And the Muslim faith demands that those who deny Muhammad as a prophet be put to death There is no coexisting with those realities. But back to what is nice in our culture. Nice is letting others sin how they want to sin. Nice is letting people marry who they want to marry. Nice is sanctioning sodomy. Nice is letting people feel comfortable in their sin, sin that the Bible says will lead to their eternal damnation. And because people are allowed to feel comfortable in their sin, and because the Bible says that those who cling to such sin are going to be sent to hell. Our culture's definition of nice is not nice after all. Here is another question to add to the many so far. Was Jesus nice? Was Jesus a nice person? I found a story two weeks ago by a Christian writer who tried to put the personality of Jesus as revealed in the Gospels Tried to put it through a personality test. The author used the Myers-Briggs test. That test identifies people as either extroverts or introverts. Sensing or intuition, feelers or thinkers, and judges or perceivers. This writer's conclusion was that Jesus was an introvert, intuition, feeler judge. Or, he said, an introvert, intuition, feeler, perceiver. In other words, because Jesus was most certainly an introvert and a feeler, he was nice. Of course, what information the writer put into the Myers-Griggs personality test determined its outcome So I think we should look specifically at certain passages that describe Jesus interacting with people to see how well he comes across according to our modern definition of nice. In your Bibles, you can turn to John chapter six, the Gospel of John, chapter six. At the beginning of the chapter, Jesus feeds a great multitude of people who have been listening to him all day. He feeds them using five loaves and two five loaves of barley and two small fish. This miracle put Jesus at the height of his popularity. And if you look at verse 15, he becomes aware that the crowd is ready to claim him as their king. He next shows the apparent introvert side of his personality and hides away to be alone. More people had arrived, having heard that Jesus was feeding so many people, and yet when they arrived, they couldn't find him. Then they heard that he went across the sea to Capernaum, and so the great crowd went after him, and they found him again. And when Jesus sees the crowd and he becomes aware of how much they have done to catch up with him, he does the nice thing and fixes another bread and fish meal After all, it drew a great crowd the first time, so why not do it again to draw even more people? That is what we would have done, right? We would have had done what works to draw the biggest crowd. After all, that is what all the church growth books state. Give the masses what they want. But you know I'm kidding when I say that Jesus fed the crowd again. Not only did he not feed them, He turned to them and told them that they were only following him to get their stomachs filled. Instead of believing, instead of trusting that he was the Christ, the Son of God. He told them that their motive for following him was wrong. Jesus then explains that he is indeed the bread that they need. The people don't understand. And he explains further how he is what God has sent from heaven, so that they might have their sins forgiven. And they thought that he literally was telling them to eat of his flesh as if it was bread. Someone nice today, someone nice today, in such a circumstance where people misunderstood him, would say, oh no, no, no, that's not what I mean. No, no, no. Don't take me literally. I'm sorry that you took it that way. I am only using metaphor. But that is not what Jesus did. Instead, Jesus turns the screws tighter. That is a metaphor. Jesus wants them to be more appalled Jesus next says, unless you eat of the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you. Since Jesus did not back away from the literal meaning of his statement, the crowd acknowledged that he was not who they thought he was, and he was not who they thought he should be. But Jesus continued, recognizing that he had indeed offended many of them, and he tightens the screws even more. He says that no one can come to the Father but by way of him. That was too much. John says that many followers left him that very moment. And here is the kicker for me. Always has that. Regarding Jesus' approach to church growth. He doesn't go after them. He doesn't say anything to them. They leave, he says nothing, and he does nothing. He doesn't try to explain himself further. He lets them go to find another church None of these actions fits our definition of nice. None of this behavior is what we expect from our local pastor. Consider what adjectives we want to use to describe our local preachers. We want them to be accessible, approachable, and understanding. While their teaching is to be understandable, palatable, and easy to receive. Is that the person of Jesus? Is that the Savior of the world? If it is not, then why do we expect it of our local pastors? That question is rhetorical. In truth, the person of Jesus was a troublemaker Today we mark the time he stepped into the city of Jerusalem to begin what would be his passion week. When he stepped into that the city, he went straight to the temple and saw what was happening in the Gentile courts. Now the temple of Herod was massive, much larger than Solomon's temple. Scholars say that the Gentile court itself was about 35 acres of space. 35 acres of space. That is huge. And it was there for the Gentiles to worship God, even though they could not enter farther into the temple, nor could they offer sacrificial offerings. What the Jews of Jesus Day realize is that they could use the massive space of the Gentile court To sell the needed offerings to their fellow Jews for convenience so that the travelers who came from a distance didn't have to bring their own animals It made sense. But that is not what it was designed for. And because the zeal of Jesus was for the purity in worship. He got angry at what he saw, and he tipped over the tables that traded goods while interfering with the worship of the Gentiles, or by the Gentiles. And we shouldn't think that Jesus turned over but one or two tables. Within a 35-acre space, there were likely tables scattered throughout the entire space. It would have taken a good amount of time for Jesus to complete this task, but his zeal insisted upon it. And Jesus would know without a doubt that such zeal would make the Pharisees and Sadducees, whom he knew already hated him and were plotting against him. He knew the turning over of the tables would make them more angry. After all, such selling in a place of worship had occurred before under their self-righteous eyes And their silence before was an approval. The Pharisees and the Sadducees could not allow people to think that they were not righteous Or that Jesus was more righteous than them. And to add to the anger Matthew's gospel describes the children continuing to sing into the Gentile court. So it wasn't just he got off the donkey and went in and they stopped singing. They kept singing while he was going in. Maybe even while he was tipping over the tables. Some described it as a bunch of teenagers cheering him off. And as we picture that scene, we have to know that the Jewish leaders became even more angry at their singing. And Jesus knew it. He knew what it would do to them and he allowed the singing, he allowed the praises. He allowed them to get more angry Such behavior in no sense fits with our modern definition of what it means to be nice. Jesus was a troublemaker and would not have been crucified if he wasn't. We need but one more example. In John chapter 8, you can turn there. Jesus is in the temple area teaching. John makes it clear in verse 31 that there were Jews listening and believing what Jesus was saying. John says that. They were believers. They were listening to what Jesus was saying. But Jesus wouldn't make it easy for them. He explained that they were slaves, and they resisted what he was saying by saying that they were Abraham's descendants and they were not in bondage. Jesus explains that their slavery is to their sin, and the proof was that the more he provoked them, the more they wanted to hurt him. He then refers to the devil as their father. Now allow me to save you some time in searching. by telling you that you will not find this type of an approach to church growth in any book or any seminar on the subject. Every book written on how to grow a church does not advise us to offend the audience that we already have. It doesn't tell us to make it more difficult for the hearers to receive what we are saying. But these are examples of church growth that Jesus gave us. Church growth is a subject the Lord helped me smell out when I was first a pastor. The methods of gathering crowds into church buildings were becoming more and more absurd, having nothing to do with calls to repentance from sin and faith in Jesus as Savior and God. Christian rock and Christian rap and Christian pop music and Christian magicians, Christian dancers, even Christian wrestlers were being used to draw crowds And the bigger the crowd drama, the more the Holy Spirit was moving, or so we were told. But does the Bible actually teach that? Does the Bible teach that when crowds grow, it is automatic evidence that God is well pleased? You say to me, isn't the report in the book of Acts of 3,000 being added to the Christian church, isn't that a sign of God's Spirit moving? And I answered, yes. Yes, it is. And what did those 3,000 respond to? Did they respond to a Christian concert? Did they respond to any type of Christian entertainment? Did they respond to a health and wealth message? Did they respond to a positive mental attitude message? What did they respond to? They responded to these words Repent and be baptized. Repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the taking away of your sins. That and only that is to be the message which truly grows the church. All other presentations are smoke screens that hide truth. I told you I was going to get in trouble today. If there is a church growing not based on the message of Jesus as the only way to God the Father while calling people to repentance You better be suspicious of it and you don't want to have anything to do with it. But back to John chapter eight. So Jesus tells them that their father is the devil. Now remember, Jesus, John started this by telling us that these people at one time were believing what Jesus was teaching. Their response to Jesus next was to claim that he, Jesus, has a demon. Jesus then describes himself more clearly as a servant to the Heavenly Father only And then he really steps over their line of patience, their line of offense, when he says, before Abraham was, I am. Your Bible should have those words, I am, in capital letters. For that audience of Jesus would have known immediately. That Jesus just then had taken the name of the God of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses. And he used that name to describe himself. That is why they picked up stones to kill him right in that moment. And seeing the stones, John says that Jesus hid himself. That I guess is what most introvert feeling type people do when they try to avoid death I hope you agree from these examples that the personality of Jesus was one that could and did adjust to the moment he found himself in And not to make himself popular or to draw a crowd for the sake of drawing a crowd. His personality fits the need in the moment without compromising truth. And that is key. Jesus was at odds with the establishment, and everyone knew it. Jesus ruffled feathers purposefully. And Jesus also befriended sinners. He healed the sick. And he loved the impoverished. It must then be said like a conclusion to a syllogism that what is obvious to follow is that the people who call themselves the body of Christ are to do as their head did when he walked this earth, which is to adjust to the moments we find ourselves in, not to draw a large crowd. but to bring the truth of the gospel of Jesus into the world so that those who seek God can find him That means that we are going to need to poke our culture in the side and provoke it when it embraces sin, when it calls evil good and good evil. We are to be at odds with the establishments outside and inside the church that are compromising truth. We need to ruffle feathers purposefully when self-righteous people tell us that the truth we proclaim is oppressive or bigoted or prejudicial to those who want to live out their flesh. Personally, I am done with unbelievers publicly telling Christians what it means to be Christian. It is time we started to be disagreeable with such people.
