And we are to challenge the establishment that call themselves Christians. Call themselves Christians, but do not teach what Jesus taught and are therefore teachers of the devil. And you have heard from this pulpit Then I get frustrated with Baptists who don't know how the Old Testament works within the New Testament. You know how I see the dangers of the traditions celebrated by the Roman Church and Eastern Orthodoxy that are not scriptural. But I have no problem with them as compared to denominations. Who no longer claim Jesus to be the only way to God the Father, and who make sinners comfortable in their consciences while they practice wantonist sins. Such churches need to be rebuked and chastised for the falsehood that they teach and allow in the name of being of and allow such sins in the name of love, of being accepting. Of being nice. And there's that word again, nice. Have I been nice in this sermon? That's rhetorical. Let us agree that instead of that it is nice, truly nice, to wake up a people out of their Christian slumber Let us agree that it is nice to warn against false teachers. Let us agree that it is nice to actually not want people to spend eternity in hell so you tell them the truth You tell them the truth, so they repent and are forgiven. I close with this simple observation. Jesus said, Woe to you when people speak well of you Woe to you when people speak well of you. He gives such a warning in the context of describing what it is to be his follower. It is in the context of being different in the world, different from the world. He follows it up with the prophecy that men will hate, insult, ostracize, and scorn his followers. If the world likes us, if we are popular, we are not the body of Christ that He has called us to be. Let us repent from not being the body of Christ and poke our culture and make trouble when needed. Let us pray. Our Father, I ask that what is true in these words would stick within our consciences and our hearts. That you would improve our bravado, that you would increase our determination to stand for what is right no matter the consequence, to speak truth. so that people who are seeking truth may find. And Father, may your will be done, for we want your kingdom to come among us. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen

sermons.title: Easter 2019
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Oh, it's a little bit more than a little bit. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. The leaders of the Soviet Union in Russia Recognize even before they came to power that the Russian Orthodox Church could not coexist with a socialist regime. The state could not share power or influence with the church, so the leaders of the church were to be persecuted and eliminated where possible. The state's form of accusations, trials, and punishments upon Orthodox Christians came to be called the Red Justice. Although few, some bishops and churchmen remained faithful to Christ even while facing death. The following is an account written by a modern-day bishop about a group of martyrs who died for Christ. At dawn on the 25th of April, 1922, the sentence of the just and impartial People's Court, that was written in sarcasm. was handed down. 18 men were to be executed by a firing squad. The rest were to be imprisoned for terms of various lengths The suggestion of the presiding judge was to appeal for more leniency But that was responded to by Archbishop Zayo Zertsky in an ardent speech, as the recommendation was rejected by all who were sentenced. Only a deep sigh was audible in the hall at the punishment of the sentence, the pronouncement of the sentence. Not a groan, not weeping. A great redemptive sacrifice was to be offered up for the sins of these Russian people, and the people dispersed in silence. Yet not to their homes, but to the square, where all night more and more awaited the fatal moment It was already light, the sun had already risen, when the heavy doors of the court opened, and those sentenced to death emerged onto the square surrounded by a forest of bayonets. They walked bareheaded, their arms crossed upon their breasts their eyes upraised to heaven, where the good Redeemer of the world awaited them, where all is forgiven, all is forgotten, where there are no sufferings, no evil. And a loud voice, an exultant hymn, poured forth from these soon-to-be martyrs. Christ is risen from the dead. Estatically the people responded to them crying, truly he is risen. They kissed their hands and the hems of their garments. The guards fended off the crowd with their rifle butts, yet they swelled in number, pressing against the soldiers. Mounted detachments appeared and pushed the people back with their horses. They beat them back with their rifle butts and whips, all to no avail. The ecstatic singing poured forth. The ecstatic people hurled themselves at the martyrs. A truck carrying soldiers of the Red Army forced its way into the crowd. They seized the convicted and literally threw them into the truck. The truck rumbled and sped off. Yet the joyous Christ is risen was long heard, was long audible in the clear air of the sunny spring morning. The red courts and show trials clearly revealed the astounding moral purity and religious struggle of the true believing Christians. and the loathsome baseness and treachery of all the renovationists. End of story Such a story is one of many that could be told of people who find strength in saying and in singing that Jesus is risen. The souls of Christians need to boldly proclaim what is true. Jesus is no longer dead. He is living. That point, the point that such a proclamation is able to stare down death, is made from a passage of scripture that most have trouble interpreting. I'll read it here from 1 Peter chapter 3. He said, For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous. To bring you to God. He was put to death in the body, but made alive in the spirit. After being made alive, he went and made proclamation to the imprisoned spirits To those who were disobedient long ago when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built. This passage tends to give Christians trouble because there seems to be many questions that are left unanswered. Who are these spirits in prison? To what prison is he referring? Does this mean that people get a second chance after death The context of the passage is important. Peter is writing this first letter to the first persecuted Christians. Christians were being persecuted, and they are to identify when they are persecuted with Jesus, who was persecuted, even unto death, but of course overcoming death and conquering Jesus was put to death and as far as the world is concerned he is dead forever, having been executed as a criminal. Yet the church knew that on Easter Jesus came alive, not only in the human sphere, but in the spiritual realm as well. His body was raised, but not as Lazarus, who was who himself died again. Jesus was raised with an immortal body. This is why we can find stories of the immortal Christ doing things that he could not do before his death, such as appear and then disappear, enter into a locked room. But it was in the spiritual life, the spiritual realm, that Jesus went to these spirits in prison. We learn from the next verse that these spirits were those who were guilty of disobedience during the days of Noah. In Genesis, we are told that God looked down upon men and noted that their hearts were turned toward evil and that continually. We remember that. There was no one good, no one but Noah. Because of this, besides Noah's family, all who were alive on the earth died And we might want to conclude that the spirits referred to are the people who were drowned in that great flood. What complicates matters is that the word translated spirits used here is not used anywhere else to describe dead people. Humans who have died are elsewhere referred to as souls, not spirits. Another clue, interesting, on identifying these spirits is actually found in the Apocrypha, 1 Enoch. There the fallen angels are said to be kept in prison. Such angels are also described in the Epistle of Jude, verse 6, as having abandoned their homes, and in 2 Peter described as guilty of sin. It is quite possible then that the spirits referred to in 1 Peter are fallen angels. Their relation to the days of Noah is their involvement in tempting man towards evil. But what are we to make of Jesus preaching to them? Is he trying to convert them? The term for preach is normally used in the New Testament for just that, for claiming the gospel so others would believe, but it also means to announce, to state a truth. When we turn again to 1 Enoch, which is cited in Jude, we discover that Enoch proclaims to these spirits, these fallen angels, their doom. Not good news. They're doomed. We can conclude then that Jesus is doing the same and he is adding with clarity as to why they are doomed. They are doomed because he has overcome death. They are doomed because he is in the midst of rising from the dead, vanquishing sin and vanquishing death. Now this victory of Jesus over the spiritual world is proclaimed in several places throughout Scripture. I will only read a few. From 2 Corinthians chapter 2, Paul said, But thanks be to God, who always leads us as captives in Christ's triumphal presession and uses us to spread the aroma of the knowledge of him everywhere. That triumphal procession is what we are part of because of him. From Ephesians chapter 6, we are to put on the full armor so that we can stand against the devil's schemes. And then he tells us that our battle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of the dark world in the spiritual realm. And from Colossians 2, and having disarmed the powers and authorities where in the spiritual realm He made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross. And finally, from Revelation 12, we read that a war broke out, not here, but in heaven. Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon and his angels. But the angels of the devil were not strong enough. And they were cast out. The great dragon hurled down that ancient serpent, the devil, who leads the whole world astray. He was hurled to the earth and his angels with him It is this victory described in these passages, the victory of Jesus over the grave, the resurrection of Jesus, that Jesus himself proclaimed to those spirits. It is that victory, that victory that we are to proclaim as well. We are to announce it. Jesus has risen. That is our announcement. And no, it does not satisfy the skeptic. But then again, what will? Saint Peter tells us to be ready to give reason for the hope that lies within us Our reason. Our reason. Our Lord is risen. He is risen indeed. If that was enough for Jesus to proclaim, then it is enough for us to proclaim. And it is for us to proclaim that the resurrection of Jesus marks his victory over the spiritual world. and the physical world, even if such is not yet fully realized. However Although the truth of the resurrection of Jesus is known to us, we know that there are skeptics who choose not to believe. And it is not because of the wisdom of men that an unbelieving heart is going to be changed. It is not an irrefutable argument that is going to cause contemporary atheists to give up their book deals and their late-night talk show appearances and for them to confess, oh, he really is Lord What will affect the atheist today, or anyone who considers themselves a skeptic of the resurrection, is a bold affirmation that Jesus is alive. When we announce it and believe it, we can cause doubt in the heart of doubters, or should I say, the Holy Spirit will cause doubt in the heart of unbelievers. The type of person that unnerves the doubter is a person who is bold and confident in what he believes. I believe that is why the modern atheists have had success and been influential. Their confidence alarms many. It even alarms Christians. Knowing this and with Jesus' example of announcing to the spirits in prison that he is alive, that he is victorious over death We too are to be bold and confident when we say that he is no longer dead, but risen. Beloved, we have not been given a spirit of timidity, but of boldness. We have every right and every duty to say boldly and announce triumphantly that Jesus is alive. But we must not stop at only proclaiming that Jesus is alive, that Jesus has risen. We must not stop there because the apostles didn't stop there. Certainly that was their primary message as recorded in the book of Acts. The main message to the Jews was that Jesus was crucified and made alive again and never to see corruption. But as the church grew and spread into the Gentile world, questions were being asked regarding what the resurrection of Jesus means for believers, besides the fact that Jesus himself is alive forevermore. It is saying quite a lot that Jesus is alive forevermore, and that is well, and that is good for him. And certainly it is good that my sins can be forgiven. Because his resurrection means that his sacrifice for my sins was accepted by the Father. But what about my resurrection? What about me seeing beyond the grave? Such a question was on the minds of the Corinthians, and St. Paul addressed it in his first letter, chapter 15. In that chapter, Paul spends the first part verifying the evidence that Jesus was raised from the dead by reciting the number of people who witnessed his resurrected body. He appeared to the women at the tomb. He then appeared to all of his apostles. He then appeared to James, his brother. And then Paul says he appeared to 500 people. And then finally, to Paul himself. The fact of the resurrection of Jesus meant that the dead can and do rise. And the fact that the dead can and do rise means that the followers of Jesus will also rise. That is why Paul refers to the resurrected Jesus as the first fruit of all that will rise. Those who will rise are believers in the Lord Jesus. Hence, what Christians are to proclaim is indeed the resurrection of Jesus and the resurrection of all who believe in the Lord Jesus. When you and I confess the Apostles' Creed that we believe in the resurrection of the body, We are not saying we believe in the resurrected body of Jesus because we have already said that Instead, saying we believe in the resurrection of the body means we believe in our body being resurrected, as well as the bodies of all who believe. The Nicene Creed, we say it more plainly, and I look for the resurrection of the dead. That's us. Whose resurrection, our resurrection, all who believe in Jesus' resurrection St. Paul finishes the chapter about resurrected bodies by describing what our new bodies will be like, focusing on the fact that they will be incorruptible. They will be immortal. And you and I say, What does that look like? And he doesn't answer. He simply ends on the note that death will have no more sting after the final resurrection and reward, new bodies. There have been others who have tried to imagine what our resurrected bodies will be like. Jesus, being the first, allows us some observations. He himself, he was himself. That is, he didn't change his body, but it did change. He was himself and that it was his body, but he was not recognizable initially to those who believed in him. He wore his scars, yet he was able to walk through buildings. He ate food, but nowhere are we told that he needed to. The theologian origin of the third century used such information to speculate what our bodies will be like being resurrected. In regards to our physical substance, we know that we are always in a stage of transition Origin didn't even know what we know today, which is that every atom and molecule in our bodies changes pretty much every seven years. We maintain a semblance of ourselves even though we are in a constant state of change. In our resurrection, there will be continuity of form to our bodies. But a discontinuity in matter and what we are made of. With this, we can say that the bodies we will be given will be like us, but a better us. Enti Wright says, what we are now is a is a shadow of our future self There will be a strength and beauty of the new bodies given that we have not known before. There is a real, glorious, astonishing you. A real and glorious astonishing you to be recreated at the resurrection. And we will be to one another what was good and right in our relationships. And perhaps, perhaps. Our scars, whether they be in our consciences or on our physical bodies Our scars might be there as a reminder of what was used in our lives to sanctify us, to make us holy, so that we could inherit eternal life. All of this is speculation, and yet the Heavenly Father gives us enough information so that we can speculate. So this Easter, I am calling on all of us to boldly proclaim that Jesus is alive, that he has risen from the dead. But I add that we should also proclaim that we believe that we too shall be raised, and that all who believe in Jesus' resurrection will be raised themselves. That there is a real, glorious, and astonishing physical reality that you and I are yet to experience. But that is what our souls cry out for. That is what our souls want. So let us cry, cry out with the martyrs. Christ has risen from the dead. Truly he has risen. And all of God's people said, Amen. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Embracing Guilt
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Just last week A conservative Roman Catholic philosopher was scheduled to speak at Middlebury College in Vermont. But the event was canceled because the speaker was labeled a billiberal activist to be homophobic, racist, xenophobic, and misogynistic. The speech was to be about the dangers of totalitarianism within a democracy. And the irony is that totalitarianism defined is a system of government that allows the state to dictate to its subjects on issues such as what speeches can and cannot be given in public. These liberal activists were acting like a totalitarian state without admitting it. And don't worry, this is not a political sermon. I use the example of liberal activists to point to a fundamental flaw in their worldview Such people so easily point out the sins of others, even when said sins are not present, while ignoring their own sins, while also denying that they are sinners by nature. The people who consider themselves woke quickly, eminently, and self-righteously condemn the sins of their moderns and their patriarchs, even their matriarchs. Like Kate Smith singing God Bless America. If you haven't heard about that, you should look it up. It is at best ignorant In summary, people are condemned for their sins, past and present, while accusers remain blind to their own pathologies and narcissistic ways. This blindness to not owning one's sin leads us into examining the events in Genesis chapter 38. Now before we get there, um just a reading of that I'm sure was just un uncomfortable I remember a professor in seminary who told the story of uh him gathering around his children to read the Bible and they got to Genesis thirty-eight and he began reading and his wife said, Stop, stop, stop! And he says, Why? And she said, I don't want them to hear this. And he said, It's in the Bible. And she said, Well, I wish it wasn't But we have a family in Genesis 38 and individuals who are not aware of their sinfulness until that sin catches them. And when it does When it does, God is gracious to enable confession, to understand guilt, and to enable restoration. Judah at the beginning, leaving his family and going down from the higher country of Hebron to the foothills Is probably an indication that there has been some spiritual disintegration of Jacob's family. There was no longer a sense of importance of being God's chosen covenant people. There was no transcendent value holding the family together at this time. And let us be mindful that these events in this chapter overlap the events of the following chapters where Joseph is living out his life in Egypt. And some have wondered again why this chapter is in the book. If if Genesis were to end at chapter 37 and you and I were to speculate what happened after that, we would likely guess that Joseph is the man chosen from which Christ would come. That Joseph is so much like Christ in in many ways of his actions of his life that we would be assured that Jesus would come from him. But no. No indeed. Judah is the man. Judah is the one from whom Christ will come, as we will see. We learn next that Judah married a Canaanite, and we remember the great lengths that Abraham and Isaac went to so that their sons would not marry such women. Because of this marriage, we can conclude that again the family has lost its spiritual identity. The manner in which this marriage is described is literally Judah saw and took. Judah saw and took. The New King James is very soft in its translation. This this action suggests what we see Eve do. Eve, when she saw the fruit, saw and took. Shechem, when he saw Dinah, saw and took The death of Judah's firstborn son reveals an ancient custom of ancient Near East marriages. But this custom, Tamara's first by this custom, Tamara's first child, although was would be conceived by Onan, would legally have been born to the oldest brother who died, who was Ur. Heirs would bear his name and receive his property. Thus, what Onan was to do was a sacred obligation. This was a way for protecting widows in the ancient Near East. The Old Testament law to come later would enforce this very tradition. Now, because the law reveals the custom to be godly, Onan's sin was a serious one. He enjoyed Tamar sexually, but refused to honor the custom that was expected of him. And this is very much like modern behavior of many men of the West today Who take advantage of the promiscuity of women while wanting nothing to do with the repercussions of their adultery. To God, the sin was worthy of Onan's death. And so that is what the Lord did. And God does that. He takes lives at his will. And although we grieve and wish it were not so, we all have to submit. Now the wording of verse 11 gives us insight that Tamar did not have. Judah made a promise that he had no plans of keeping. He actually believes that Tamar is the problem or cause of his son's death. She was labeled in his heart a cursed woman. Judah again, very much like modern man here, he does not see the connection between sexual immorality and the evil that is within his sons. And from this we can examine ourselves. Let us not be fooled by failing to see that when sexual promiscuity became mainstream in our culture, in terms of acceptable behavior That the dominoes fell, as we have now accepted abortion in order to keep our sexual freedom, just as we have accepted no-fault divorce pornography, incest, and any other perversion humanity can come up with Tamara's actions next reveal that she knew enough of Judah's character to believe that he would consort with prostitutes. And she knew that Judah, despite his assurances, would never make provisions for her. She knew his character, and so she knew what That she would have been lied to, and that the obligation that Judah owed her meant nothing to him. Tamar herself was consumed with her right as a matriarch. Judah's admission in verse 26 will indicate just that. Whatever the justice of her means, her effort to secure was hers by right, and it was to her credit. She is, despite our doubts about what she did, she's actually the heroine in this story. The only one who seemed to care about the Covenant family and it continuing on Now realize that sex with a prostitute was sinful. Sex with a daughter-in-law was a crime punishable by death. The fact that there was characteristically a lot of wine drinking in the sheep shearing time may explain why Judah did not recognize Tamar's disguise. Tamar's hard bargaining, together with Judah's lust, resulted in him giving things that would have unmistakably belonged to him. as each item had a seal and each seal was unique to its owner. When tomorrow's actions are revealed, an extreme penalty, burning to death, is announced by Judah. Now remember that she was still betrothed to his younger son Shelah. Her crime then was adultery, and the extreme punishment by Judah was his hypocrisy. Thankfully, when all is revealed, Judah cannot escape his hypocrisy, and it is what he does by confessing where our focus needs to be this morning. As I started to explain at first reading, it is difficult to see how chapter 38 fits within the entire narrative of Genesis. What will become clear later is how these characters and these events are fundamental to our understanding of the entire history of Joseph and Judah. Again, what is surprising to most is that the real hero in this story is not Joseph. It's Judah. The very Judah who is described in such a despicable manner, in despicable terms, in this chapter. It is Judah at the end of Genesis that the great promise is made. It will be from Judah that will come the seed of a woman that will crush the serpent's head. From Judah Will come the Messiah, through whom all the nations will be blessed. Now, the Pharisaical, legalistic, self-righteous side of some of us Could not see Judah being a hero at any time. When we take inventory of his life, we identify a man motivated by lust Greed, pride, envy, and contempt. His lust led him to sleep with a woman he did not identify, who would later be revealed to be his daughter-in-law Although a member of the only covenant family God had chosen at that time, he showed his contempt of said covenant by going down and living amidst the Canaanites obviously not caring how they could lead him to idol worship. This slide toward a worldly abyss began when he envied his father's love for his brother. When he allowed that envy to turn him to plotting murder, selling his brother into slavery and pretending to his father that his brother was dead had no emotional effect upon him Other than hardening his heart. That Judah's son would be so wicked that God took their lives when they were young shows the effect his sin had on the entire family. A man like Judah can live in such a manner only for so long before his conscience is seared and silenced. Only selfish interest remained to guide Judah. So no, he does not seem like a possible hero in this story, and certainly not a hero that would be used to bring forth the Son of God. We spend time describing Judah and how despicable a man he was, because of how it will all end. And where it started to turn around. We see at the beginning the turn in verse 26. Look at that verse again. Where Judah's acknowledgement of his sin and the justice of Tamar's cause and even of her actions were to be interpreted as if she had no other alternative. He says, she has been more righteous than I. That confession is actually different in the Hebrew. Hebrew scholars agree that it should be read not as a simple comparison, but as what is called a comparison of exclusion. in which the subject alone possesses the quality of the adjective. In other words, Judah did not say, She has been more righteous than I, but rather said, She is righteous, not I. A comparison. She is righteous and not I. A contrast. This means that Judah made no claim of righteousness at all. He was not asserting merely that she was more righteous than he, but that she has been righteous while he has not been. And this I trust you can see is a far better thing for a man to say who had behaved the way Judah had behaved. Remember in Proverbs chapter 28, verse 13, we read, He who conceals his sins does not prosper. But whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy. Such wisdom was finally understood by Judah. And we know that the Lord must have revealed it to him because the direction Judah was going showed no indication that he was softening toward righteousness. And we can be assured that his confession included repentance, for we read in verse 26 that he did not sleep with Tamar again. Though he had done so before, though the ice had been broken as it were, though we have found Judas so thoroughly a sensual man A man with a little regard for the sacred honor of the family, or for his responsibilities to preserve honor To preserve purity. Though we might well have expected Judah to do something to tomorrow just like Onan did, Judah did nothing of the kind. The Lord was at work in his heart. His conscience had been awakened. His behavior now troubled him. He stood self-condemned on account of what he had done. Finally he could live as he had before. I'm sorry, finally he could not live as he had before, because sin had become sin to him. And that, as would be the case for so many multitudes of others, was the beginning of something new in this man. When sin became sinful to him, when he began to reckon with his moral failure, his need for the forgiveness of God, when he got there, his life changed. He had been a moral failure for long years, but he never admitted it or reckoned with the fact until now. And so what we find here, in what is called the most sordid chapter in the Bible, what we find is the grace of God. The grace of God abounding where sin had abounded, and God's grace beginning to cover a multitude of sins. That Jesus Christ himself is in this physical line through Joseph and Mary, through this disgusting incest. is as grand a picture of God's grace overcoming man's sin, as grand as can be imagined. Now what can possibly come of lives like these? Of history like this What could possibly come of cruelty, infidelity, hardness of heart, sexual promiscuity, even incest, and in general plain stupidity? What can come of all of that? Well, the grace of God, by the blood of Jesus Christ, and heaven itself can come of that. What we have in Genesis 38 is the person of Judah, a picture of Judah, of what we all are without the grace of God. All of us, whatever our sins, however polite, however little, however sins we have that people do not take notice of. No one took notice of Judah's sins either in that corrupt day until the Lord Himself brought them to light. But no matter our sins, ugly as they are, the rest of the Bible tells us what God's grace can make of us. But for it to be so, for it to be so, there must be an honest admission of our sins and a serious reckoning which says, no excuses, no one else to blame. We know that God is responsible for the confession and repentance of Judah because He tells us that only He can turn the heart of a sinner. Only God can give the gift of faith. Only God can create a righteous sense of guilt that demands confession and repentance. Unfortunately, for some of us, a sense of guilt is a scary thing to experience, let alone embrace. When someone wants to talk serious to us, you know, we need to talk. We turn into our childhood selves as we were trying to prepare for that talk with mom and dad when they called us up. Every possible sin recently committed or sin hidden in the past is reviewed in our minds with the question: which sin has now been revealed to them and what excuse is now best? But godly men and women learn that it is best to fear God more than to fear the feelings of guilt before men. The Quaker leader, George Fox, was so bold as to say that he thanked God more for his sins than his righteous works. Puritan preacher John Bunyan said the same thing, only more directly. He said, the guilt of sin did help me much. Of course, Puritans are known to have been gluttons for punishment. But if we were to examine our lives more closely I wonder if we could see how much having sins revealed has changed us and changed us for the good Mark the times when you embraced the guilt and shame of your wrongdoing, even if it was only revealed to yourself. The freedom found in times of confession and repentance cannot be compared to the fear and pain of ignoring hidden sins. Would not Judah say that his sin revealed was the most life-changing moment that he had yet experienced? His revealed sin and his guilt, when faced with it, and his need to confess and repent, it meant his salvation. Judah's sin being revealed as a child of the covenant of God teaches us that the people of God have more than one born-again experience. We can compare Judah to the many of us who were baptized as children and who have grown up to know the Lord and in the church, but have never had a born-again experience. Until we come to see our sins, whether they be petty and small or loud and obvious, and we realize That we too are undone. We too are undone The guilt can be difficult, but it is quite necessary to face what is true and what needs to be done in response. The faith given to us to confess said sin and repent from it gives us a feeling of being made new, of being born again. And later in life, when a habit has become addicting, or an emotion has become controlling, or an attitude has darkened the heart, and God shows it to us so much so that we can't escape the truth. We are called to embrace it. Embrace the guilt, confess the sin, repent, and be born again again. We all have those times, and we all need those times. Consider the type of people I described at the beginning of this sermon. They are too busy embracing the guilt of others, so they do not see their own sin and their own guilt. And so their sin and their guilt remain. For the Christian, embracing the guilt of our sins leads to a freedom from sin that the woke among us do not have. An awareness of our own sin is something our culture has lost, but the church cannot Part of what it means to be salt of the earth is to know our guilt and to be a people who confess and repent. May that be true of us. Amen. Let us pray. Our Father, we thank you for this story as sordid as it is. And we thank you for the truth that embracing our true guilt also brings to us true freedom. Father, help us remain a people who do not fear our guilt, but fear, but fear disappointing you. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: God With Us
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. May be seated. It would be good for you to turn to Genesis chapter 39, where we continue our series on the book of Genesis. Genesis 39, and I begin by asking several questions of you. What does it mean for you that God has said that He will never leave you or forsake you? What does such a promise mean to your everyday life? How does it affect your prayers? How does it affect your work or school situation? How does it affect your relationships? The statement that God will never leave you or forsake you is found in Hebrews 13, verse 5. And it is based off of God's promise to Israel in Deuteronomy chapter 31, and the promise of Jesus that he would be always with his followers. The context of the Hebrew preacher is where he is making closing remarks in what we call a sermon slash letter. He tells the listeners to be free from the love of money and to be content with what they have in regards to material wealth And he follows it up by saying that God will be with them always, never leaving or forsaking them. So the verse prior means that because of the ever-abiding presence of God, his people will be provided for regarding essentials to everyday life. This is backed up, of course, by the Sermon on the Mount when Jesus tells his followers to seek ye first the kingdom of God, and all that they need will be added unto them. All their personal needs will be met. But in the book of Hebrews there is more, for the verse after the quote that God will never forsake his people, he says, so we had so we say with confidence The Lord is my helper, I will not be afraid. What can man do to me? This puts the promise of God's presence in the lives of believers beyond basic needs of life to the realm of some type of safety. Thus, the presence of God is to mean to us, at the very least, that our basic needs will be met and that we need not fear men bodily harming us because we Can be assured that they cannot do to our souls only what God can do. Again, Jesus said something very similar He said, I tell you, my friends, do not be afraid of those who can kill the body and after can do no more, but fear the one after you have been killed who has the power to throw you into hell. Therefore, God's presence being always with us means that He is the only one who has the authority over our life after this earth. So I asked the questions regarding what it means for each of us that God is with us always, never forsaking us. Because I want to do battle with the devil, who has placed lies in our thoughts and in our expectations regarding God's promises. Take the story of Joseph in the house of Potiphar as an example of what we might wrongly expect when we say that God is with us always. There is an emphasis by the writer of Genesis that God was with Joseph. Look at verse 2 and in verse 3. It is stated there the same way in verse 3 to underline the point that God is with Joseph in a very special way. That God was with Joseph was evident to his master, for there was proof of God's presence in his success. And it was noted by the master that Joseph was successful in this life, and that had to mean God was with him. But I pause I pause here from that main point that I will get back to in regards to what it means for God to be with his people, because in this story of Joseph and Potiphar's wife. We have the best example for Christians and how to understand, to resist temptation, sexual temptation here, but temptation in general We are told first that Joseph was a handsome man, and that makes him appealing to Potiphar's wife. That he was made an overseer of Potiphar's household necessitated that Joseph be a daily presence before Potiphar's wife. It is the master's wife who takes the initiative, asking Joseph to lie with her. We must understand at this point in the story that although Joseph was an overseer, he was still a slave. For a slave to say no regarding anything asked of his master or the master's wife, that was putting his life in danger. We see in verse 8 that Joseph was a principled man. He would never betray his master as his master had been good and trusting of him. And we see he forthrightly states that to lie with the master's wife would be a sin against God. That, of course, is reason enough not to commit adultery. God has said it is a sin, and that is to be enough for those who say they believe It doesn't matter how lustful you feel. It doesn't matter that you have sexual desires that make you want to lie with the same sex. Or the underage, or anyone who is not your spouse. God's commandment is enough for believers to know that sex outside of a marriage covenant between a man and a woman is not to be practiced. That is the principle that Christians are to live by Now, as read, Joseph's initial resistance and reasoning did not stop Potiphar's wife from pursuing Joseph in lust. Verse 10 tells us that she tempted him day after day, and yet day after day Joseph resisted. And he resisted not only having intercourse, but to do anything sexual with her, as that phrase, to be with her, communicates. Potiphar's wife's next move was to physically force herself onto Joseph, resulting in her being able to pull off his garment, which means that he forcefully resisted her. But she had him in her net because no one was around to see her come on to him, and thus she could enact revenge for being refused by falsely accusing Joseph of trying to rape her. The garment left in her hand tells us that Joseph made haste, running away from her. And it is this act of running away It can be applied to a multitude of temptations that Christians face every day. When Jesus said that if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off He was using hyperbole, but not excessive hyperbole. Christians, followers of Jesus Christ, are to do what is within their power to resist temptation. And the most obvious temptation to resist temptation, a most obvious way to do it, is to run away from it. How do I resist sexual temptation? The answer: flee. Flee from places that allow you to express your lust Flee from the bars. Flee from the clubs. Flee from parties. Flee from the internet. Flee and get as far away as possible for what calls you to sin. Not what causes you to sin, but what calls you to sin. From what else and where else can we flee in order to resist temptation? Flee from friends who do not know God and want you to live as they do. Flee from schools that teach the non-existence of God and openly teach sexual promiscuity. Flee from work situations that tempt you to express a different personality that your spouse and God do not know. Flee from any source of entertainment that requires you to be lazy and half-minded. Flee Fly away, make haste, and allow God to be your defender from the fallout of you. Flee. Remember that God will not leave you just as he did not leave Joseph in the dungeon. But that's for a future sermon. So Joseph and his actions provide an excellent example for all of us, any of us of any age, to imitate. But we need to get back to the truth that God was with him. The author made it clear, as we have said, that God was with Joseph. But let us remember that God is said to be with Joseph when Joseph was a slave. If God was with Joseph, then why was Joseph made a slave in the first place? I know the answer that is his brother sold him to be a slave, but that does not answer the heart of the question. For when we read that God was with Joseph, don't we assume that Would mean that Joseph wouldn't be made a slave? Doesn't God's presence with his people mean that they will lead a blessed life? With little to no troubles from the devil or their fellow man. If you say I have got it wrong when I expect blessings in my life, because God is always with me If that is wrong, then why do so many Christians call out to God all too quickly when life gets a little difficult? Why? Why God? When something negative happens in our lives, we say, Why God? I believe it is absolutely to our benefit that we are honest with God. And honest with ourselves, that we confess that we do have expectations. That we do have expectations that are not warranted in Scripture. And is it easy for you to recognize my false expectations when I say that I expect that God's presence in my life means that I will have blessings overflowing It is easy to note that that's wrong-headed. But it is harder, much harder to see the devil, how he has used your false expectations of God in your own conscience to dent and weaken your faith. Let's examine Joseph's life again. As was asked, do we expect That when God is with someone, that he will not make them a slave, and yet Joseph is a slave, and God was with him. We do expect that because God was with Joseph, that everything he did, everything he put effort to was a success. That sounds right. That Joseph was made an overseer is also what we would expect when we say that God is with someone. Yes, he's going to bless you in that way. Success is a natural part of what it means for God to be with someone, right? But then Joseph becomes a target of a wanton woman who has the power to destroy his life. That isn't what we expect when God is with someone. We expect God to keep such people away from us, if He is truly with us. Deliver us from evil, we pray. And Partipher's wife was evil. And yet there is Joseph in a dangerous situation. You know, there could have been other rich places, other homes in Egypt that Joseph could have gone to that didn't have a wanton wife. If God is with Joseph, he isn't working very hard to protect him. Am I right? And the temptations are every day. We pray to God to not lead us into temptation And there was Joseph placed in a situation that he did not control except to remain chaste. If Joseph is not in control, While living the life of a slave in the house of Potiphar, then God. If God is with Joseph, then God is in control. So is God leading him into temptation? It seems that way. I trust some of you have heard the upheaval caused by the Roman Catholic Pope Francis. who over a year ago wanted to change the Lord's Prayer because he says that the phrase, lead us not into temptation, is confusing Because it contradicts other teachings of Scripture that says that God tempts no one. Pope Francis has shown himself to be more of a humanitarian than a theologian or a Bible scholar. The phrase, lead us not into temptation, is a parallelism in the Lord's Prayer, and what follows it, deliver us from evil That is the explanation of what the phrase means. God indeed does not tempt anyone. What our problem is, where we need help, is when we unknowingly find ourselves in a situation where the temptation to sin is the strongest. Our prayer is that we could avoid such situations as much as possible, but when we do find ourselves in one, because that does happen, We are asking to be delivered from that same situation. But maybe Pope Francis has the same false expectations of God that many of us do. Maybe he too expects that if God is with us, we would never be put into a situation of being tempted. But that is impossible. Temptations are not only all around us, but as you know, they are inside of us To lead us away from all temptation would be to lead us away from ourselves But wait, isn't that what Jesus is trying to tell us when he teaches his disciples that we are to be last? When he tells us to pick up our cross and follow him. But let us continue on with Joseph and God being with him. When Joseph finds himself in a trap set by Potiphar's wife, we again wonder why God would not rescue him if God is truly with him. His only rescue is to flee, and still God's presence doesn't stop him from leaving behind evidence that will wrongly convict him. Now God could have stopped that also because he was with Joseph, but he didn't When Joseph was confronted by Potiphar for his crime and believed the testimony of his wife, he became angry and threw Joseph into prison. Some suspect that Potiphar may have been in charge of the prison himself. But if God is with someone, how is that same someone wrongly accused and thrown into prison? But it must have meant something. It must have meant something for God to be with Joseph. A slave accused of trying to rape a free woman, who was a master's wife, would certainly have been put to death in Egypt and in any country in the ancient Near East. For God to be with Joseph meant that it was not his time to die. And read verse 21 with me. This is the key verse. Verse 21, after Joseph had been thrown into prison, it reads, but the Lord was with Joseph and showed him mercy. And he, God, gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison. So for the Lord to be with Joseph is to show him mercy. If there was a spreadsheet of what God owed to Joseph and what he owes to every human being, that spreadsheet would be blank. If there was a spreadsheet of each of our sins, the libraries of the world could not contain the amount of paper needed. Thus, when God is with us, it is an act of mercy. And when He does something, anything that relieves our suffering or changes our situation, it is always an act of mercy. Which is an act of unmerited forgiveness where harsh punishment is due. For God to be with Joseph never meant Never meant that Joseph would not suffer at the hands of men. It never meant that injustices of a government would not be bestowed upon him. God's presence with Joseph was not a promise that he would not face temptations or unkind people or evil people or times of disappointment or heartaches or prison cells. The same is true with the presence of Jesus with us. Jesus never leaving us or forsaking us is true. But it does not promise warm, fuzzy feelings, and it does not mean we are protected from the sins of mankind or the diseases of this world that are caused by the curse placed upon man and the earth at the first sin of our parents. It is the devil who has given Christians the idea that God's presence with us means we have a spiritual shield that protects us from all sorts of evil. Evil we can see and cannot see. It is the devil who has told us that God's presence with us means we won't get sick. And the sins of others won't hurt us, and friends won't forsake us, and family won't betray us. All of that is a lie. And we need to know this just as the early Christians did. For if the stream keeps flowing, like it is now, against Christians, there will be a day just as there was in the first 300 years of Christianity. When believers will be outwardly persecuted for what they believe and how they live. And when such a day comes The devil will have us believe that it ought not be so, because God is with us and therefore none of this should be happening. The devil's schemes are old. He whispers again, just as he did to Eve. He whispers again. God didn't really say God didn't really say he would always be with you, did he? But God did indeed say it. The testimony of martyrs, knowing the presence of God, began with Stephen in the book of Acts, you remember, our patron saint. Who looked up at his death by stoning and saw the Lord. The Lord was with him. But it began earlier than that with Shadrach, Meshach, and Abendigo, who, when thrown into the fiery furnace, had another man, the Son of God, with them, delivering them from the flames. But it began with Abel, whose blood cried out and was heard by the Lord. The Lord was with him But the Lord is not with us to make life easy, to make life soft, to make it comfortable, to have us avoid suffering. No, the Lord is with us to be merciful, for his mercy is everlasting. Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious God and Father, we thank you for the truth of your everlasting presence. And we thank you for what it truly means, your mercy. And so may we focus upon that, how grateful we are for that mercy. And never expect things you didn't promise, but truly believe in all that you did promise. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Joseph's life in tension
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. Turning your Bibles to Genesis 40 as we continue in Genesis. Genesis 40, quite a few years ago I preached on the subject of the necessary tensions in holy scripture regarding such doctrines as predestination versus free will of humanity, and God's sovereignty versus human responsibility Yes, we can say that God predestines those who would be saved, and yes, we can say that God calls us to choose to follow Him. Both realities are taught in Scripture, and thus we are to acknowledge and accept the tension that they have with one another. The teachings are also true for God being sovereign over all things, including the wills of men, and God warning us that we are responsible for the choices that we make. That too is intention in Holy Scripture. Now such tensions in Scripture were identified By the Reverend Dr. Robert Rayburn, a Presbyterian minister, and I confess I am indebted to him Because since reading his teachings, I have been able to reconcile my struggle with certain passages in the Bible by recognizing the purposeful tension that God has placed in his holy word. My inability to reconcile certain passages that seem to contradict was caused by me being under the sun and seeing through that glass dimly. Apparent contradictions will not be able to be explained on this side of heaven, and that must be acceptable to us. And one of those apparent contradictions is the description of us made by Jesus in John chapter 17, where it is recorded the prayer of prayers. Which is God praying to God, or Jesus praying to the Heavenly Father. In that prayer, Jesus says the following I do not pray that you should take them out of the world, but that you should keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. And so we can summarize this part of the prayer by saying that Christians are to be in the world, but not of the world. That is a position of tension. And that was the position of Joseph in Potiphar's house and of Joseph in prison. In Joseph's life of being in Egypt and yet a child of the covenant, in that we find the Christian life. The Christian life is a life of tension, and we need to acknowledge and adjust our approach to life to fulfill our Christian journey. One of those tensions in the Christian life is the pursuit of success in this world while not being concerned about worldly wealth. Joseph was successful outside of prison as a slave and inside the prison as a convict. What he was assigned to do, he did well, and what he touched was successful. The writer of Genesis wants us to know that the success of Joseph was caused By God's presence with Joseph, and we identified that last week. But that must have also included Joseph working hard and using the blessings and gifts God had given him. Christians are to work hard for their daily bread. Christians are to have a strong work ethic where our work is done for the glory of God. Christians are to use their earthly gifts as good stewards. And when we work for God's glory and when we use our gifts to his honor, we are going to be successful in this world. That is nothing to be ashamed of, but instead we are to be grateful to God for that principle in life The United States continues to be blessed because many of our founding fathers practiced the principle of hard work to the glory of God using their gifts to honor God, and there is a residual effect of that still in our culture, even though most of our citizens do not recognize it. The principle of hard work and earthly success is in tension with another teaching of Jesus who instructed his followers not to be concerned about their daily bread or the clothes that they wear, but to seek first the kingdom of God, saying that all things needed will be provided to us. Yes, we can seek first the kingdom of God by working hard at our vocation, and we can be blessed in an earthly manner because of such work. But it is very easy to get our eyes off of the kingdom of God and onto worldly wealth, material things. We are easily susceptible to temptation of seeking our daily bread and the trappings of a material life. It is required of us to continually examine our hearts and minds to see if we love the world more than we love God. We need to be able to say always that the Lord gives and the Lord takes away, and blessed be the name of the Lord. Another tension of the Christian life is how we are blessed to have spiritual knowledge while being earthly bound. Joseph was given the ability to interpret dreams. Dream interpretation is knowing the mysteries of God. Because of his ability, Joseph could know the future. And when others knew of Joseph's ability, they would look to him for wisdom. As Christians, we know the mysteries of God. St. Peter describes the gospel, the truth of knowing the time and suffering of salvation through Jesus. He knows these truths that Peter says angels longed to look into, longed to understand. We then are privileged people to know the plans of God that angels and prophets did not understand. We are able to understand why the human race struggles to do right by its own conscience and by the laws of God. We know the human condition to be sinful and thus guilty before God. We know that human beings, because of their fallen nature, are prone to sin. We know of our sinful pride, anger, lust, greed, envy, and malice, person to person, we know. We are aware of how debase a person can become. We of all people should not be surprised by the sins of human beings, even the sins of our own children. What we are capable of doing can be identified as pure evil. And with the knowledge of our sin nature is also the knowledge of how we can be forgiven, of how we can be people who are changed. In Christ Jesus, a zebra can change his stripes. Because of what God has revealed to us in Jesus, we have the knowledge of how the conscience can be freed from guilt. Because of the Holy Spirit in the lives of believers, we can resist temptation and therefore not be the person we once were. We can change. Our character can be made different. It can be made more like God. Every day can be new in Christ. All things can pass away, all things can become new. We have this knowledge from the testimony of our own lives and from the lives of one another. The truth of Jesus can and does set people free. The gospel works, and you and I have the knowledge that it does. But St. Paul said to the Corinthians. That the truth of Christ Jesus was a stumbling block. Stumbling block to the Jews because they could not understand how God could become man And foolishness to the Greeks because they could not accept a God who would sacrifice himself. So the unbelieving mind doesn't care what we know They do not think it's worth knowing. They don't respect what we claimed to be essential to our lives. But they come to us. They come to us just like they did Joseph when life doesn't make sense. They come to us when they don't know who to talk to or how to interpret life. They hope what we have is an answer, just as they hope Joseph had an answer. They come to us because we are different, and that is how God intended. They come to us to know the future, their future. And we know the future. Not in detail, but in a general trajectory. The future contains a time when Jesus will return and raise up all who have died and judge all according to their faith. And those who believe will receive eternal life, and those who reject Christ will be thrown into the eternal fire. That is the future we are to speak of, even when no one is listening. That we know the future plays into the tension that we have good news and bad news for the world. Joseph knew the good news of the butler's dream and the bad news of the baker's dream. That is living intention. Such attention has been lost to people who claim to be Christian, but who have focused on attracting crowds rather than preaching and teaching the gospel. Preachers and teachers who focus on the good news of Jesus only reminded me of an episode of the Andy Griffiths show. The best television show ever. It is when Aunt B is feeling sad and lowly because of a recent death of a friend. She is listless and without energy until a handsome man named Colonel Harvey comes to town hawking a tonic that will fix all ailments Aunt B buys two bottles, and by the time Andy gets home, she is singing and happy-go-lucky. Andy the sheriff is suspicious of the salesman, but his permits are in order. Later Andy has the elixir analyzed and finds it is eighty-five percent alcohol. As the uh bumbling deputy Barney Fife describes the elixir was why Aunt B and her friends were so tiddly. Tiddly The medicine man who sold Aunt B and her friends, the tonic that cures all ills, is very much like a preacher who speaks the gospel in terms of wealth and health and happiness without telling the truth of suffering and eternal damnation Aunt B's initial sadness was brought on by the reality of her mortality. The alcohol allowed her to forget about her mortality and to focus on how she feels in the moment. It is curious how anyone would receive the good news of Jesus without understanding the bad news that every human being is sinful and destined for hell unless his or her sins are forgiven. Without the reality of the bad news, the good news makes little sense. That Jesus loves and forgives us and gives us new life only makes sense when we understand our sin and understand our guilt. The only way the good news of Jesus makes sense is if we are aware of our need of our sin to be forgiven. What the positive health and wealth preachers put forth that provides any type of good news is how the world has let us down. It is the environment in which we live that is to blame for our sorrows. And it is the positive mental attitude that Jesus can give that will help lift you out of your environment. That is 85% alcohol truth. That allows us to escape the real truth and brings us to feel good in the moment. But such moments pass and we are still in our sins. Instead, we have been gifted to know the truth. Our individual sins are real and need to be atoned for if we are going to find any freedom for our souls. Our sinful natures are real as we cannot escape from falling short of God's standards and even our own standards. The good news is that Jesus paid the penalty for our failures by dying on the cross, by rising again, which was the overcoming of the penalty of sin. This is the real and true good news that we confess as true gospel believers. All other preaching and teaching is a lie. And all who preach and teach are liars, destined for hell themselves. Surely the revealing of the dreams of Joseph didn't win him any friends, and the butler himself forgot Joseph, even though his interpretation of the dream was good. And that is what Christians are to expect. Even when we speak the truth, it will likely not be appreciated. But speak it, we must The reality that Joseph trusted the butler and the reality that he forgot Joseph is another tension in the Christian life. We desire to trust humanity and yet we accept human failing. Joseph deserved to be remembered for he helped encourage and provided hope for the butler But it was not initially reciprocating. We might think we deserve the faithfulness of friends, and yet friends fail us and even betray us. We might think we deserve honest and openness from our family members, and if they lie to us, withhold from us for selfish ambition. We might think that we are owed fairness and justice from our governing authorities, and yet they continue to convict the innocent and ignore the guilty. These are realities of what it means to live in this world. And we must escape these realities while not being of the world. Which means not being a product of the world, which means the world cannot produce us. Thus, while others betray, Christians are to be loyal. While others lie, we are to be truthful. While others are unfair and unjust, we are to be fair and uphold the virtue of justice. Such character will likely not be rewarded in this life. But that's not our goal. Finally, the tension of the Christian life is revealed in Joseph, as he knows that God knows the future, but he still needs to live in the present. Joseph knew the end of the baker's life. He knew it was near. And he believed that what man intended for evil, God would make for good He knew that, but he had to wait. He had to wait in his cell. He had to serve under the jailer. He had to be in consignment, waiting for God's timing. And isn't that what Christians do every day? Do we not know the future in terms of our heavenly hope and that God will judge all men and make all things new? And yet we wait. We wait in the confinement of our bodies and in the limitation of our minds, waiting to escape this world and to be delivered to a new world to come. Joseph was a slave who lived in Egypt, but was not of Egypt. Just as Christians are in the world, but not of this world. The following content is from a letter to a teacher by the name of Diognetus. Diognetus. The writer is unknown, but the writer is writing a description of Christians from the 4th century, likely the 4th, 5th century. And it reads as follows. It's a little long, but painted. Christians are indistinguishable from other men either by nationality, language, or customs. They do not inhabit separate cities of their own, or speak a strange dialect, or follow some outlandish way of life. Their teaching is not based upon reveries inspired by the curiosity of men Unlike some other people, they champion no purely human doctrine. With regard to dress, food, and manner of life in general, they follow the customs of whatever city they happen to be living in, whether it is Greek or foreign. And yet there is something extraordinary about their lives. They live in their own countries as though they were only passing through. They play their full role as citizens, but labor under all the disabilities of aliens. Any country can be their homeland, but for them their homeland, wherever it may be, is a foreign country. Like others, they marry and have children, but they do not expose them. They share their meals, but not their wives. They live in the flesh, but they are not governed by the desires of the flesh. They pass their days upon the earth, but they are citizens of heaven, obedient to the laws They yet live on a level that transcends the law. Christians love all men, but all men persecute them Condemned because they are not understood, they are put to death, but raised to life again. They live in poverty, but enrich many. They are totally destitute, but possess an abundance of everything. They suffer dishonor, but that is their glory. They are defamed, but vindicated. A blessing is their answer to abuse. Deference their response to insult. For the good they do, they receive the punishment of malefactors. But even then they rejoice as those receiving the gift of life. They are attracted by the Jews as aliens, attacked, excuse me, by the Jews as aliens. They are persecuted by the Greeks, yet no one can explain the reason for this hatred To speak in general terms, we may say that the Christian is to the world what the soul is to the body As the soul is present in every part of the body, while remaining distinct from it, so Christians are found in all the cities of the world, but cannot be identified with the world. As the visible body contains the invisible soul, so Christians are seen living in the world, but their religious life remains unseen. The body hates the soul and wars against it, not because of any injury the soul has done to it, but because of the restriction the soul places on its pleasures. Similarly, the world hates the Christian, not because they have done it any wrong, but because they are opposed to its enjoyments. Christians love those who hate them just as the soul loves the body and all its members despite the body's hatred. It is by the soul enclosed within the body, that the body is held together. And similar similarly, it is the Christian detained in the world as in prison that the world is held together. The soul, though immortal, has a mortal dwelling place, and Christians also live for a time amidst perishable things While awaiting the freedom from change and decay that will be theirs in heaven. As the soul benefits from the deprivation of food and drink, so Christians flourish under persecution. Such is the Christian's lofty and divinely appointed function, from which he is not permitted to excuse himself. May such a description be able to be written of each of us. Let us pray A gracious and merciful God, for the example of Joseph living a life in Egypt but not being of Egypt. So we find ourselves living in this world, and as you prayed, not being of this world. So may we live like that May we continue to be challenged to live like that, that what is written of us may be the same that was written to this teacher, that as Christians we really are different, and heaven is our home. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Joseph like every man
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I encourage you to turn in your Bibles to Genesis chapter 41. We read a portion of that passage or that chapter, but I will be covering the chapter as a whole. As you do, let's talk about the parallels of Joseph and Jesus The parallels cannot be avoided. Joseph was a type of Jesus to come. Joseph helped prepare for the coming of Jesus. Joseph and Jesus were favored sons. Of each, their respective fathers would say, This is my beloved son, in whom I am well pleased. Because of the favored status of Joseph and Jesus by their respective fathers, their brethren were jealous. Joseph's brethren, his immediate familial brothers, were jealous, and the jealousy ended in a plot to kill him. Jesus brothers, his Jewish brethren, were jealous, and the jealousy led to a plot to kill him. Joseph's brethren decided to throw him into a pit and then sell him as a slave. Jesus' closest of brethren, an apostle named Judas, sold Jesus into the hands of those who would next place him in a deep cell of what today is called the Tower of David Where you can, when you visit the old city of Jerusalem, stand in the likely place that Jesus stood before they took him to stand before Pilate. So each man was sold, and each man descended below the ground. After each man came out of their respective pits, they were falsely accused. Joseph came out of the pit only to later be accused of attempted rape and was thrown into a prison even deeper than the pit he was in. Jesus was also falsely accused of blasphemy and was thrown into a deeper pit known as hell. I preached on an Easter morning several years ago regarding the hell that Jesus was thrown into. We confess it in our creeds, but I think we don't think about it much as to what it means. When we confess that he descended into hell Some think we are simply confessing that Jesus descended into the place of the dead. But I interpret it to mean the place of torment and punishment. I do so because in the Apostles' Creed we have already confessed that Jesus died. We say crucified, dead, and buried. If he descended into hell only means the dwelling of the dead, then we're just repeating ourselves But if it means torment hell, we are saying that Jesus identified with sinners fully. But hell could not keep him. It could not contain him. And that meant that the spotless lamb slipped through the fingers of torment. And burst out of hell and burst out of the tomb. So each man descended as low as can be in their particular state of being followed by each man ascending to the highest of positions according to their particular state of being As Joseph was placed at the right hand of Pharaoh, and Jesus sits at the right hand of the Heavenly Father. These are striking similarities indeed. Another similarity that I only discovered recently is how Joseph and Jesus represent every man. And by man I mean person, no gender excluded. Jesus, of course, wasn't every man And that he sacrificed his life on the cross for the sins of every man, every person who was, is, and will be. And Joseph was an everyman, but not of course in the meaningful and dramatic way Jesus was everyman. Joseph was every man, and that he did what every man is to do who calls himself Christian Joseph was an everyman because he needed to be obedient to God as every man must. I ask you to look further with me now, looking at Genesis 41 and just how every man comes out of this text. We read in verse 1 that it was two years since Joseph interpreted the cupbearer's dream Thus two more years Joseph was in prison with no end in sight, as far as he knew. And this means that he was raised out of the cell on the third year. Another type. From the dream of cows, we must know that throughout the ancient world, seven was a sacred number, and the cow was both a symbol of Egypt and of one of their gods. The fact that the cows come up out of the Nile is not an insignificant detail, as the Nile was Egypt's lifeblood, the source of its power, its everyday life provisions. Next in the dream, we have heads of grain. Seven ears on one stalk is an image of great abundance. That the wind came from the east assures that it was a hot, dry wind coming off the desert. Egypt was considered the breadbasket of the ancient world. It was famous for the grain that was able to grow there. The Roman Empire would depend upon Egyptian grain for centuries. And perhaps these dreams were so vivid that they were unnerving and forced Pharaoh awake. Some things in such dreams are obvious. Abundance always meant a good thing. Famine always meant bad things. Thus, the magicians would have known some of what the dream meant, but they would not want to be the one to give Pharaoh any bad news. And they didn't have any wisdom to help Pharaoh, even if they got the dream correctly interpreted. That the butler finally remembered Joseph is caused by God through the anger of Pharaoh. The mention of Joseph shaving is because Egyptians were typically clean-shaven, unlike other men of Asia, like the Hebrews. We are to notice that Joseph was fearless, as he did not hesitate to correct the mistake of the king's opinion. And he knows that it is God alone who knows the future and can interpret Pharaoh's dreams. As the king retells of the dreams, he embellishes on what we had heard before, and this is to tell us, the readers, that Pharaoh had strong feelings of fear because of these dreams. Joseph next responds in the role of a prophet. And we are to understand that to be consistent with his family line. Abraham was called a prophet in chapter 20, verse 7. Both Isaac and Jacob predicted the future in the matter in which they called their sons together and told them of their blessings in the future. The double dream with a single meaning confirmed there was certainty of the prediction. And it's very similar, interestingly, that Joseph received two dreams, and both of them were interpreted to have the same meaning, that he would be raised above his brethren. Joseph not only predicted the future to Pharaoh, but gave wise advice on what to do to overcome the famine years. Again, Pharaoh's magicians would not have considered giving such advice because if they were at all mistaken, it would have meant their life. But Joseph. Joseph was speaking for God. And Joseph feared God first and last So it was natural for him to speak the wisdom he spoke of keeping food reserved during the years of abundance. So Joseph is elevated to a position of great authority as Pharaoh sees such reward as meritorious. Joseph earned the position as did Jesus earn his. But being seated in such a place of authority isn't an everyman reality. So how is Joseph and every man in this story? Well, I believe the answer is found in verses 47 and 48. 47 and 48. I read with you. It goes as follows, now in the seven plentiful years the ground brought forth abundantly. So he, Joseph gathered up all the food of the seven years which were in the land of Egypt, and laid upon the food in the cities, he laid upon in every city the food of the fields which surrounded them You see it, I hope. Joseph was an everyman, and that he did what every man, every person, no gender excluded, needs to do. Every man like Joseph needs to be a doer of God's word Consider how useless all that Joseph had experienced so far would have been if Joseph failed to store the grain grown in abundance during those seven years. His first two dreams that started his burdensome life would have been for no good. His descent into the pit His being sold as a slave, his rise and then fall because of a false accusation, his second descent into a jail cell. his interpretation of the dreams of the butler and the baker, his ascension from jail to the right hand of Pharaoh, would all have been for no good Had he not followed through with the wisdom that he was given by the Holy Spirit, Joseph is in every man, every person, in that he needed to follow through with what he knew to be true. Take the example of myself as a preacher, and you as parishioners. In the Epistle of James, the same epistle that teaches us to be doers of the word and not just hearers. We read in chapter 3, verse 1, My brethren, let not many of you become teachers, knowing that we shall receive a stricter judgment What that means is that I will be judged by God in regards to what I teach and how I live what I teach. In my office as a Presbyter priest, I have to be judged by God in terms of the truthfulness of what I teach regarding God's Word, and then like you I will be judged in regards to how I live the same word I teach. Thus the preacher is every man, like Joseph was every man, and that he has to live what he says is true. Otherwise, what I teach, even though it is true, is of no value to me if I do not live it. The Apostle Paul had this same reality in his mind when he wrote to the Corinthians regarding why he lives a disciplined life according to his flesh. He said, I discipline my body and make it my slave, so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified. That is Paul being every man. For every man, every person who claims to be Christian must live a life in the same manner that he or she says he believes We can hear this in the truth of King David's words, to obey is better than sacrifice. Let us take inventory of our character to see if we are living in the same manner we confess to believe. A fundamental example is the fifth commandment, honor thy father and thy mother, that your days may be long upon the land which the Lord thy God is giving you. So the command, and thus the principle for life, is that we who believe in the one true God are to honor our parents, and if we do, we are promised To live a long and prosperous life. And by prosperous I mean keeping our land. We all know this commandment. We all believe it is the right thing to do when we have opportunity to honor our parents and so we speak well of them and we speak uh well to them we care for them as needed and we do not rebel against them If you don't honor your parents as you obviously should, then you should not expect your days to be long or for your property to remain your own. To say it more simply, you need to do what you know is right to do in order to receive the blessings of a long and prosperous life. To live differently is to expect different and negative results. Consider St. Paul's instructions for wives Wives to submit to their husbands as they are to submit to God. And for husbands to love their wives in the same manner Jesus loves the church. Those are similar instructions to Joseph storing up grain during abundant years. It has to be done in order to survive the lean years. In marriages there are abundant times and there are lean times. It is necessary for the wife to submit to her husband in the same manner she submits to God, and for the husband to love his wife in the same manner that Jesus loves the church. For there to be abundant grain in times of lean circumstances. When Bobby Lynn and I were married First married, we never considered the times that our parents would die, my parents, or become gravely ill, my parents and her parents. Or children would be diagnosed with cancer, or trouble in school, or any of them to publicly sin, or have trouble in their own marriages, etc. etc. But when you do go through such times and even worse times, and the husband is sacrificing himself for his wife. And the wife is respecting and trusting in her husband's wisdom and leadership, through, through those times you will go and be better on the other side. Joseph knew it to be true that to obey the truth you know is necessary. And we know that also. To submit and sacrifice in marriage is storing up grain in abundant times, being ready for the lean times. Now take inventory of your life on forgiveness, fundamental to the Christian faith. Consider Jesus instructing his followers to forgive one another as they want to be forgiven. Consider Jesus warning us that as we judge others, so we will be judged.
