Now take these principles and carry them forward as if they were not obeyed, as if they were not heeded. What does a life look like of not forgiving those who have sinned against you? What does that look like? What is the end game of withholding forgiveness? By experience, we know that it leads to bitter hearts. We know it leads to us not being forgiven by God. We know it, and all the while we say we don't want our hearts to be bitter, and we don't want God to harshly judge us. So we must be every man and do what every man must do, and that is to forgive, no matter what it is. To forgive is like carrying through with storing grain in abundant times, being ready for the lean times. Consider the warning of Jesus, such as not to pursue earthly riches or lusts of the flesh, or to allow personal pride to control you. When any man, any person sets his mind and heart on things of this earth, it never goes well Such persons become like the things of this earth, which fade, which rust, and become destroyed. To pursue first the kingdom of God, that is storing up grain in abundant times, being prepared for the lean times. How many more examples do we need to expound upon and be convinced that every man, every person has a duty as Joseph did? To follow through with the knowledge you have been given about God and the world, the world He has placed you in. All this reminded me of the parable of the two sons that was read our second lesson A parable that I have never expounded on before in a sermon, and I haven't done so because I thought the meaning to be too obvious Therefore, not as thoughtful as other parables that Jesus used to teach. But I see now how I have been dead wrong. In the parable that we read this morning as our second reading, the first son is told by his father to go and work in the family vineyard, and initially he refuses. He didn't honor his father and mother. And then later he regrets his refusal and goes into the vineyard to work. The father goes to his second son and asks the same, and the son agrees to go to work. In the vineyard only, he never goes. He never works. Jesus asked a question that has an obvious answer. Which son obeyed the Father? The Pharisees and elders answer the first time. And we say, duh. But wait. The question is an every man question. Any man, any person can give lip service to faith and living out their faith. Yeah, I'll do it. Yeah. And every man is to live out their faith. But the reality is not every man, not every person does. Beloved, each of us is every man. Each of us is to do as we know to do. And when we don't, when we don't, we are to repent and ask forgiveness from the one who was also every man, Jesus. As he died for every man, so that every sin can be forgiven when honestly confessed. And then we are to go back into the field and work like every man, do the work we know to do. And when we fail, again, we confess our sin and once again go to the everyman Jesus. That is the Christian life. It is the life of every man, every person who says he or she loves Jesus We have here in this story a man who Obeyed the Word of God, and God blessed him. God does that for each of us. If we simply obey. Our gracious and merciful God, we thank you for the type that is here. We thank you that we can see Jesus. Well, we also thank you that we can see every man. We can see us. And our need to do as we know to do, to follow through with the truths that you have revealed to us. Father, give us that strength as we know you do. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Ministry of Reconciliation
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. In your Bibles you can turn to Genesis chapter 42. Genesis chapter 42. I hope I have convinced you that Joseph is a type of Jesus Just as Seth was, but in a small way, and Jacob was in a small way, and David will be in a very large way. Joseph also is a type of Jesus in a large way, but I think it's best to say that Joseph is like Jesus in a more profound way. On this Sunday after ascension, we underline how profound it is that Joseph sat at the right hand of Pharaoh. And Jesus ascended to sit at the right hand of the Heavenly Father. Last week I listed the several ways that Joseph is like Jesus And then we focused in on how Joseph is like every man. For like every man, every person, Joseph needed to be obedient. Because Joseph needed to obey the truth that was revealed to him. He needed to be a doer of the Word of God for the Word of God to do any good. It is the same for us. We need to do the good we know to do, for that is how God has ordained human life. What God has called us to do must be done in order for us to receive the blessings He desires to bestow upon us. As we come to Genesis 42, I have actually decided to cover chapters 42, 43, 44, and 45 in one sermon. Not because each chapter isn't deserving of a full sermon and even more. I am covering four chapters at once. Because our focus has been on the typologies in Genesis. And Joseph here, again, is a type of Jesus And this is better seen by examining these four chapters together. You likely don't see it how he is a type of Jesus here, even if you have read these stories several times in your life. I am guessing you don't see it because I didn't see it until this very week, and that is my calling to see it. Have you ever wondered why Joseph went to all the trouble he did before he revealed himself to his brothers? Why all of the back and forth? Why not reveal himself immediately? Clues as to why Joseph is once again a type of Jesus are first found in chapter 42 with the use of choice words. For example, look in verse 7. We find the verb in the New King James translation, recognized, where Joseph recognized his brothers. That is the same verb used in chapter 37, verse 32, where Joseph's brothers asked Jacob For their father to uh identify or recognize the bloody cloak as belonging to Joseph In verse 17 of chapter 42, the word prison, where the brothers were placed those three days, is the same word used for Joseph's imprisonment in chapter 40. Such connection of words are to stir our memories to the crime that was committed against Joseph by his brothers. A crime that was never confessed, never repented of, and still not known by Jacob, their father. Also, the comment in verse 9 that Joseph remembered the dreams he had about his brothers bowing down to him. Further indicates that Joseph recognized the Lord's hand in his brother's appearance before him, and he intended By his actions to serve the Lord's interests into this whole affair. What interest would that be? It was and must have been the interest of reconciliation. And that is how Joseph is a type of Jesus in this story. Joseph does all that he does in order to orchestrate needed reconciliation. That reconciliation was Joseph's motivation is revealed in the emotional reactions Joseph has towards his brothers Look in verse 24 of chapter 42. He turns his face away from his brothers so that they do not see him weep. At their second return in chapter 43, he goes to another chamber to weep in private. Also, he repeatedly asks about the health of their father. And in chapter 45, when he reveals himself to his brothers, he does not lord it over them of his high position, but instead he wept openly. Each of these moments reveals a heart that desires his brothers to be at peace with him and to be at peace with their father, having confessed their wrongdoing. And if the purpose of Jesus' life and death and resurrection can be summed up in a sentence, one possible sentence might be that Jesus lived, died, and rose again, and ascended. to reconcile humanity to the Heavenly Father and to one another. Now before we examine more fully how Jesus works to reconcile us to the Father and to one another. I want to provide a summary of the events in these chapters in order to see how the events are orchestrated. Beginning in chapter forty-two, the attention of the narrative shifts from Joseph, the individual, and from the Egyptian Empire back to the family of Jacob. the family from which Joseph was torn. As Joseph had risen to power in Egypt, now he will rise to rule over his family. And you remember that was his two dreams. that he would rule over his brothers. The shift is back to Jacob and Canaan, where 20 years have passed. Joseph, we read in chapter 41, verse 51, named his first son Manasseh, because he said, God has made me forget all my troubles and all my father's household. That is, God has made me forget the trouble I had at home. What we see in the next four chapters is actually he hasn't forgotten. And that it's been in his heart to be reconciled to his brothers and to his father. And we see both of them, Jacob and Joseph, yearning for reconciliation. So the story unfolds in three journeys to Egypt. The first was made by Jacob's ten sons, minus Benjamin, who came to Egypt to get grain. There they were met and were understandably in awe of the authority figure that was Joseph, although they didn't recognize him. Joseph recognized them and accused them, again, he's orchestrating, accused them of being spies, and then placed them in prison. And here is the beginning place of reconciliation. The brothers had to be in a humble state, a humble state in order for them to hear what they needed to hear. Next, Joseph makes a deal with his brothers to give them a chance to prove their integrity. And this is another part of reconciliation. Those who wish to be reconciled must be honest. At the end of their first journey, all of them returned home except Simeon. Simeon was kept back to ensure that Benjamin would return with the brothers the next time. That Simeon is held back allows us to speculate. that Joseph held him responsible for what happened to him. And you need to remember that Reuben is the oldest of brothers. And Reuben was against killing Joseph. And Reuben wasn't present when they sold Joseph into slavery. So with Reuben absent, the second oldest would have been the authority amongst the brothers when Joseph was sold. Knowing the heart of Joseph as we do, we should not think that he held Simeon back out of spite, but only to help Simeon know that he must take responsibility for what happened to Joseph. When they return to their father, they also find money in their bags. The money they paid for the grain was returned to them. And this caused them great fear, for they expected the Egyptian authority to accuse them of being thieves. They wouldn't want to go back. Again, this is another step toward reconciliation, the step of fear. Fear motivates. The second journey was made by all ten remaining sons, that is Benjamin included, and this caused fear on Jacob's part because He was so desperate not to lose his second favored son, having lost Joseph, his favored son. When Benjamin appears before Joseph, Joseph is overwhelmed with emotion, and he cannot yet show it. He serves his brothers a feast, and he gives Benjamin five times the portion compared to his brothers. This places the brothers in a position of confrontation as they are confronted with their sin, their first sin to Joseph, the sin of envy. The envy they originally had against Joseph. And here is another part of reconciliation. It is being confronted with our sins past and on an emotional level. When they start off to return to their father, Joseph has his servants put their money back again that they used to pay the grain, and to put Joseph's cup back In one of their bags. To steal the cup of Pharaoh's right-hand man would have been instant death as a punishment And yet Joseph has the guards chase after them, has them all empty their bags, and they find the cup in Benjamin's bag. And what happens next is a powerful display of selfless love. Judah, of all people, remember our stories about Judah and his incest ways. Judah of all people steps up and offers himself to be punished in place of Benjamin. Judah, of course, is the head of the tribe that will give birth to the seed promised, for Jesus is in the line of Judah. This sacrificial offering of Judah, the offering of himself, causes Joseph to reveal himself in a manner that rejoices in the redemption, the reconciliation he has with his brothers. Can we say from all of this that Joseph orchestrated the events that led to the reconciliation of his brothers and to their father? That so too does Jesus orchestrate the events in our lives so that we can be reconciled to the Heavenly Father and to one another. Can we say that? I believe we can. I once again extol to you That the work and sacrifice of Jesus that he made for us was first and foremost, so that we could be reconciled in right and good relationship with the Heavenly Father. Consider the letter to the Galatians. What the end goal is. What does Paul say is the end goal? He says God sent his son born of a woman born under the law, so that so that that phrase sets us up for what's going to happen so that Those under the law, all of us might receive adoption as sons. Did you hear that? Did you understand it? God the Father sent his son to die and rise again so that we could be adopted into the family of God and call him our Father. That is the end goal for God to be our Father. It continues in Galatians with the explanation that the Holy Spirit is in the hearts of believers, enabling us to cry out, Abba, Abba Father. In fact, a good argument can be made that calling God Abba is the only Aramaic word for Father. And it is primarily used in the context of a personal relationship. So it is having a personal relationship with the Father, that is the gospel. Of course, Jesus is the only means by which our Father's hunger can be satisfied and our relationship with the Father be reconciled. Just if Joseph was the chosen means by which the sons of Israel would be reconciled to their earthly father, Jacob, Jesus is the only means by which we can be reconciled to the Heavenly Father. Because of this, Jesus deserves all of our praise, Jesus deserves all of the glory, and the Father desires it to be placed upon him. Yet it was the goal of Jesus to bring us to the Father, His Father, and that is proven by the way He taught us to pray, and the desire to see the Heavenly Father in Him Having seen him and knowing him, we are to know the Father and see the Father. Read your Bibles again and look for the Heavenly Father. He is the one providing good gifts for those who ask of him. He is there seeing you pray in secret. He is there seeing your kind deeds that go unnoticed. He is there knowing your needs before you ask of him. He is there counting the number of hairs on your head. He is there pitying us as we strive against ourselves and against him. He is there wanting to give mercy to his children and to their children. He is there waiting for the prodigal to come home and for the prideful son to come in to the celebration. And just as the prodigal son needed to get to the point of great humility, as did the brother of Joseph before reconciliation to the Father could occur. So too. So too do we need to be humbled, and to be humbled, we only need to confess that we are unworthy of the love that we so desperately need. Along with humility, we need to have a sense of fear to be reconciled We need to fear God, God who can cast the body and soul into hell. We need to fear what our lives on this earth would be like if God was ever, even for just a smidgen of a moment. Would remove his sustaining hand. We need to fear that we would ever be left to our own end. Along with humility and fear, we need to be confronted with our past sins that we have neither confessed nor repented from. Sin does not go away by being ignored or forgotten because of the passing of time. Sin that we are responsible for must be owned up to. This is the honesty part of reconciliation. Joseph's brothers could not make an excuse for what they did to their brother Joseph. For what they did was evil. Evil. Jesus summed it up in the simple message, repent. Repent for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. Repentance includes acknowledging of guilt for the sin committed and turning away from that path and going the opposite. And finally, we learn from these stories of Joseph and his brothers that reconciliation means offering self as sacrifice. Judah did it to save Benjamin, and we are to do it to save ourselves. Jesus said to each person who would follow him, pick up your own cross. He said it in another way when he said, he who would save his life will lose it in the end, and he who would give up his life will gain it in the end. To die is gained, St. Paul said. That is true in this life and the life after. As these truths apply to being reconciled to God, they also apply to being reconciled to one another. And we are to be reconciled to one another. You remember that Jesus said the world will know us by our love for one another. We are not called to love in general, just love. We're not called to love our immediate family or even our extended family. Even the pagans do that. But we are called to love one another in the body of Christ. And to love one another is to be in good relationship with one another, which is to be reconciled. Joseph's brothers needed to be in good relationship with Joseph, just as we need to be at peace with one another. To be in good relationship with one another starts with humility, which is to say that we do not think that we are more righteous than our brother or sister in Christ. It is acknowledging that whatever righteousness I have is not my own. It's been given to me by Christ. I have none of my own. Instead, I am to think of myself last, never first. Next, to be in good relationship with one another, we must have fear. Our fear should be that we would be judged by God harshly because we harshly judged others. It should be a fear that if we don't forgive and love one another, we will be left alone. Alone in our self-righteousness. To be in good relationship with one another, we need to acknowledge our past sins towards one another. And that takes honesty. People do not get hurt by what we don't say, but by what we say. People get harmed by what we do and what we don't do. They need our confession to be reconciled, and we should be thankful for the opportunity to confess and to be forgiven. Finally, to be reconciled, we need to live sacrificially. This is a true saying for all of us. The needs of my friend in Christ are more important than my own. The first will be last. And so we are to compete to be last, in order that in the end we would not be forgotten. I did not anticipate that I would have a hard time convincing you that Joseph is a type of Jesus in how he works to assure this reconciliation. You are here because you believe in reconciliation between you and God and between you and your fellow Christians. What I anticipate being hard is to convince you that God orchestrates the events in your life to move you toward reconciliation either to him or to one another. We know that God doesn't tempt any person to sin, and that is good to know and always good to remember. But at the same time, we are to acknowledge that God tests people He tests people. He says, he does in Deuteronomy 8. 2, he says, God tests the people to know what is in their hearts. Now, you say, well, if anyone's going to know what's in my heart, it's God, and yes, that's true. Of course God already knows what's in your heart, but do you know what's in your heart? We need to know what is in our hearts. For we can say, as Joseph's brothers did, that they were honest people, men of integrity. But we will only know that to be true when we are tested and we pass the test. The work of the Holy Spirit guiding us to all truth is a work of taking us through various tests while providing us the faith and the strength to pass each test. St. Paul recognized the importance of being tested, of Christ Jesus orchestrating his life. He said, through weaknesses and hardships, learning that when he was weak, Then he was strong, for it was Jesus who was his strength. So as Joseph orchestrated the events of his brothers' lives For the sake of reconciliation to their father and to him, so too does Jesus orchestrate the events in our lives. So that, so that, the end goal, so that we would be reconciled to the Heavenly Father and to one another. This is what St. Paul means when he says that God has given us a ministry of reconciliation. So take opportunity. Take opportunity whenever it is given to be reconciled to God and to fellow Christians. For God has ordained it. Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious God, we thank you for the clarity of your word to show how Joseph was inspired by you to work towards reconciliation. And you, you working in our lives, bringing us through tests and trials that we might also be reconciled to you and to one another. Father, help us all embrace that ministry of reconciliation. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Accepting the not Understood
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. For this installment in our series in Genesis, we are covering actually chapters forty-six and forty-seven. We are doing so because the narrative continues through chapter 46 and into chapter 47, so it really didn't need to be two chapters, but one. I give the following summary with commentary because we did not read the entire verses for each chapter. So we begin. We see that from the promised land, Jacob and his family travel toward Egypt, only they stop in Beersheba. The very place his father Isaac met with God and heard God's promises to him God gives Jacob a vision also connecting him to the promises he gave to Isaac his father and Abraham his grandfather. After the vision, all of Jacob's family traveled to Egypt because the famine we are told in the land of Canaan was so severe. Their traveling moves the author to name each of the sons of Jacob and number their family members. The total number he gives is 70, but that has to be symbolic As the number listed did not match up to the numbers counted. The meaning then is the number 70. It's a perfect number, 7 times 10. It means the whole. So the whole of Jacob's family traveled to Egypt. When Jacob's family arrives in Goshen, which is northeast of Egypt Proper. Joseph sees his father again, and the reunion is dramatic and emotionally moving as Jacob, or going by his other name, Israel. Proclaim that he was then ready to die, having seen Joseph was alive What follows is an interesting exchange as Joseph prepares his brothers to meet Pharaoh and he coaches them to tell Pharaoh that they are shepherds. This appears to be done so that the Egyptians are not fearful of the Hebrews interfering with the Egyptian economy. Because the work of shepherds is actually something the Egyptians look down upon. The reason for such work looking being looked down upon is simple and it continues to this day. People who live settled lives do not like wandering clans because of what they are used to being interrupted. And their goods, such as grass and crops, could be destroyed by the herds guided by the shepherds. Joseph, the orchestrator, also wants his family to be proud of what they are doing, recognizing that to do what they do is a gift of God, and it should not matter who looks down upon it. And many a Christian man should have the same attitude. It matters not who looks down upon your profession As long as you know that you are able to provide for your family and honor God and what you are doing. Doing what God has called you to do. After Pharaoh meets five of Joseph's brothers and provides them the land of Goshen to live and to prosper, Jacob is then brought before Pharaoh for a meeting. The meeting is a reversal of authority, as the Egyptians thought that anyone who had reached the age of 120 is to be honored. Jacob had reached 130, which likely had the king of Egypt bowing before Jacob, who then blesses Pharaoh. And we should see this as a meeting of God's promise, where he said to Abraham that the seed of Abraham would be a blessing to many nations, and so Jacob is to Egypt. The narrative next takes a turn toward Joseph and his work in Egypt as it is described to us the severity of the famine. resulting in a greater dependency on the Egyptian government for breath, resulting in the Egyptian government by way of Joseph buying and controlling all the land of Egypt except the land owned by the priests of Egypt. Thus, big government came to Egypt by what appeared to be necessary circumstances. The people gave up their land and their rights because they thought that to do otherwise they would die. Chapter 47 closes with Jacob preparing to die at the age of 147 He asks Joseph, who has the authority to keep a promise, to bury him in the promised land. The oath is assured in the same manner Abraham's servant swore to Abraham. You remember by placing a hand under the thigh of the person in authority Which many scholars believe was actually placing the hand under the testicles of the person in authority And that gesture meant that the promise was being sworn by under the covenant of circumcision. And for those of you who tend to picture stories in your mind, I apologize for telling you that, but not really. Within these two chapters lies one of the more significant mysteries for me, and all of Holy Scripture. For what these two chapters describe is God purposefully and necessarily leading the nation of Israel, which at that time was Jacob's immediate family, into Egypt. With the foreknowledge that their favored status would die with the death of Joseph and would lead to their enslavement by the Egyptians for 400 years. Said enslavement would result in the calling of Moses, who would initially would cause the people of Israel more grief, for Pharaoh punished them because they wanted to leave. That would lead to a great deal of suffering by the Egyptian people by way of ten plagues, leading to the letting of Israel go, only to have Pharaoh and his army chase after them and then be drowned in the sea. And the people of Israel will suffer greatly as well, for they will be unfaithful in the wilderness, and that will result in God judging many of them, some by snake bite And the others by the earth opening up and swallowing them whole. That is followed by forty years of wandering in the same region until the entire generation dies off. And it is easy for us to ask, was it all necessary? If we are Bible believers, which we are, and we trust that what God does is good, which we do, Then we can conclude that nothing else but that it was all necessary It occurred how God wanted it to when he led Jacob and his family to settle in Egypt because of famine. It must be acknowledged that Israel as a people did not do anything against God that warranted the punishment of slavery. At least they didn't do anything that God condemned them for and called them to repent from, but enslaved the people of Israel were. Under suffering and bondage they remained. Was it fair? Was it good? We can ask such questions and be troubled by the lack of answers. From one angle, it doesn't seem fair because the people again didn't do anything specifically to warrant enslavement There was no warning by God to tell them you better shape up or you're going to go into slavery for 400 years. Nothing like that. From another angle it can be argued that it was fair and good because Israel, like all of us are in the line of Adam and Eve, and thus we are under the curse of sin and sin brings forth death. Enslavement is deserved because we are already, all of us, enslaved to sin. We do the bidding of sin and its tempter in thought, word, and deed. We do it by what we have done and what we leave undone. Thus, a physical state of being, slavery, can justly look like our spiritual state, which is also slavery. To ask such questions as to whether the suffering of Israel was fair or good or both To ask such questions, we invite the same answer St. Paul gave to the Romans when he anticipated they would wonder, was it fair for God to love Jacob and hate his brother Esau? It is similar to the response given to Job when Job asked God why about his sufferings. The simple and straight answer is, who are you to ask such questions? An answer to that question is not expected, for it is rhetorical. We accept, like we learned last week, that God orchestrates the lives of his people toward holy and righteous ends. That we may not see this side of heaven. To ask if God could have done it differently is very much like asking the like the pot Asking the potter why he was made the way he was made. We are but an inanimate object compared to the wisdom and reality of God, and thus we have no position. From which we can rightfully second guess God. An unbeliever cannot accept such an answer. For to them, the faith needed for that answer, that faith is too blind, and the lack of autonomy is frightening to them But that is why they are unbelievers. They are too blind to their present lack of autonomy As their master is the devil who allows them to believe that they are in control of their destiny when nothing of the sort is true. It takes a good deal of humility to accept that we are not in a position to second guess God. And it takes even more humility to be ridiculed by unbelievers who think us to be double foolish To not only believe in God in the first place, but to accept the things that God does that don't come with an immediate explanation But the Christian knows, which is to say, we are keenly aware, that although we cannot answer the why to all that happens in our lives, Regarding all that God allows to be done. We are following the person named Jesus. And that person has the words of eternal life. As the disciples confessed, where else can we go? That also is a rhetorical question. There is no other place to go, for it is only Jesus who has the words of eternal life. So we now turn to the second part of the mystery in Israel being enslaved in Egypt, for me anyway, and that is the amount of time it took for Israel to become free. Four hundred years is a very long time by human standards Consider what was taking place on American soil 400 years ago. 1619. 1619 In 1619, three major events that shaped American history happened in Jamestown alone. The first event occurred between July 30th and August 4th Where the Jamestown residents formed the first representative assembly in America. The second event happened later in August when the first African slaves 20 people arrived and were sold in Jamestown. The third event in Jamestown occurred in early December. when 39 settlers arrived from Britain, and as they did, they marked their arrival date, December 4th, as a date that they would celebrate years to follow, as a day of thanksgiving to God. This day was celebrated, as I said, several years after. It was before the landing of the pilgrims And the only reason pilgrims are associated with the Day of Thanksgiving is due to President Lincoln, who decided to honor the Plymouth colony rather than this one in Jamestown. We do not have the time to highlight, of course, all the major events in America and in world history that happened between 1619 up to today. Again, what is obvious is that 400 years is a very long time by human standards. Forced slavery as an is an evil no matter how it came about, but it is important to compare just for providing a greater understanding of the plight of these people of Israel That the African slaves in America, by law, were slaves from 1619 to the end of the Civil War, which is approximately 246 years Approximately 154 years less than the Israelites were slaves in Egypt. And I only note the difference, not to trivialize American slavery. But to underscore that four hundred years of slavery is a very long time. And this lengthy period of Israel's slavery in Egypt leads to the second mystery for me of this story, which is how and why the Lord waited so long to free Israel out of this bondage. Yes, I know to ask why and to ask how is to do what we just talked about, not doing. It is to try to enter the mind and will of God and we have no business entering But it teaches us something about what it means to be the people of God. I believe it teaches us what it means to be Christian. What it means to be Christian from Israel being in captivity 400 years is that the life with God, the Christian life, is a life of waiting. The people of Israel waiting to be delivered from their bondage in Egypt is a type or shadow of our needing to be delivered from the perils of this life by the return of our Lord and Savior. And the return of our Lord and Savior is nearing now 2,000-year wait. Thus the Christian life is a lifetime of waiting. But that is not all that Christians wait for. Consider how much you and I wait for the with the responsibility and thus the expectation That what we wait for is to be waited for with faith that it will come to pass. The faith we are to have is in God to provide to us the substance of things that we hope for. All of us have waited for a person to come into our lives that would be our spouse for the rest of our lives. Some wait longer than others. Some go through greater heartache than others. All of us wait. We next wait for our marriage union to bear fruit by way of children. We hope to be pregnant only to get a negative test, and then we wait again and then again and then again. For some the blessing of a child is fulfilled, for others the wait goes on And every couple, no matter how long the wait, is to wait with faith in God's will We next wait for our children to walk and then talk and then read and then learn and then develop and to mature and to go out on their own while we wait to see if they will follow the Lord Jesus all of their days In the meantime, we wait on acceptance to schools, we wait on financial help to attend those schools, we wait on grades, we wait for them to return home from break. All the while we wait and faith until they too find that someone special to be their spouse for life. We wait and we pray. But chronological life events are not all that we wait for. We wait for the test results from the doctor to come back. We wait for the end of a surgery that could mean life or death. We wait for on mortgage loan approval, we wait on job openings, we wait on hearing back from a job interview We wait on news from loved ones. We wait on prayers to be answered for people to be converted. We wait on prayers to be answered for rebellious loved ones to come to repentance. We pray and wait for broken relationships to be mended. We pray and wait for our elderly to no longer suffer, but to find peace for their souls in Christ. And finally, we wait for the coming of our Savior to return and to take us home to glory where we are told that Thieves cannot break in and steal, rust and moth cannot destroy, where there is no more sorrow because there is no more death. We wait for it. Yes, the Christian life is a life of waiting. And that is how God has ordained it. There is no sense, no sense at all in fighting against it. It is as God has ordained it to be. We wait. But you may say, doesn't all human life wait? It is not simply Christians that wait, but all of humanity waits. And yes, that is true. The difference, however, should be obvious. We are to wait having faith. Faith in Christ Jesus that all of God's promises will be fulfilled All too often we identify the people of Israel as unfaithful, and to be sure, that generation that wandered for forty years in the desert, they were unfaithful. But it takes a great deal of faith to be enslaved for 400 years and to continue passing on stories of hope That the God who chose Abraham and his descendants is still listening to our prayers and still willing to free us from our bondage. It takes an inherent, although not clearly articulated, faith that says that perhaps my years on earth are but a short time compared to God. And therefore, what I perceive to be long waited for is in fact, for God, quite short. And we learn that indeed to God a day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as a day. Our life is but like vapor, as the writer of Ecclesiastes says. We are here and we are gone. But God is everlasting to everlasting, therefore we wait. I have often wondered How our culture would react. If we started to advertise the Christian life as honestly as possible, We could start by putting on our reader board out there for people to feel welcome to come on in to worship services and hear how degenerate by nature they are And how the only way to reverse their degenerate state is to confess their guilt as sinners and to die to themselves the rest of their days in this life. Would we have to sell tickets to get into the church building each Sunday because the demand would be for reserved seating only? Or what about the two simple messages today? What if we advertise the Christian life? Only in terms of accepting the mysteries of God, even when it means your enslavement. And that the Christian life also consists of a great deal of waiting. Waiting for what you hope for, but you cannot see. What type of rush to the door would we see with that advertisement? Advertising agencies would tell us we would get no response at all. But I wonder. I wonder if there are hungry souls that are looking for something to die for, so that they have something to live for. Maybe so. Let us pray. Our Father, these great mysteries you pronounce. They're there. We know it. We don't avoid it. They are there. Your willingness to allow your people to be enslaved for 400 years. And we say thy will be done. Your quietness, you're allowing for those years to be long and for our lives to be that which we wait, and we continue to wait. Father, we confess all of this, knowing that we see through the glass dimly, knowing that we are on this side of the sun. And so we put our faith in you and trust in you that you overall your will is being done and that is good. And we say, thy will be done in Jesus' name. Amen. sermons.title: And Still He Uses Us
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles to Genesis chapter 48 and 49. We are coming very close to ending our series in Genesis. It's been since September that we started this series What a wonderful journey it has been. I shared with you last week two great mysteries for me that are not directly addressed in the Bible. The first is why God allowed Israel to be enslaved without the people having done anything against his law that warranted such slavery. The second is why God allowed Israel to remain in slavery for 400 years. We can get hints at the answers to these questions, but no more than hints. Just before I graduated from seminary, a number of students that included myself got into a lively discussion or conversation. at a senior social on the subject of what the world would have been like if Adam and Eve had not sinned Some believed that sin would be brought into the world eventually. Others speculated that Eden would have stretched out over the whole earth to expand with the human population. Others questioned whether a human could live on forever if he or she did not have access to the tree of life. As this discussion went on, a well-regarded professor sat in and listened for a time. A student soon turned to him and asked, What do you think, Dr. Deasley? And Dr. Deasley turned up his nose at the question as you can imagine any British scholar doing, and simply said, it is not for us to consider what might have been, but only to address and deal with what is Well, you can imagine that just kind of deflated the whole discussion, and we all departed. I remember that moment well because of how profound and simple Dr. Beasley's statement was And I have tried to pattern my life and ministry by the truth that is within that comment Great theological minds have spent a great deal of time and energy thinking and speculating on topics that the Bible does not address. So as to fill in holes that they see in Scripture, while not spending enough time, as far as I see it, on what can be known from the Scriptures. I have chosen to work hard to know what the scriptures teach as opposed to what they don't teach. And it would take many lifetimes to know all that the scripture teaches, and even with many lifetimes, all that the scriptures teach could not be exhausted. But I think it is important for you to know that I am aware of the difficulties Holy Scripture contains I want to model to you that we can be honest with ourselves, with one another, and with God That there are some things we wish were a bit more clear, with the thinking that perhaps our faith could be stronger if we could understand things more clearly. And in chapter 48 and 49 of Genesis, we are challenged by what is perhaps the greatest mystery of all. That mystery is where the will of God and the will of humanity meet. And what is the determining factor that has God's will or man's will Determining an outcome in life. And this mystery is brought to light in the manner Jacob speaks forth his blessings upon his sons and grandsons. They're not blessings as you and I think of blessings, but are actually prophecies. And will set forth the future of the nation of Israel and the future of specific tribes of that nation. With these prophecies, are we to understand them to be set in stone so that they cannot be changed? Or is there any room for the human will being expressed? Is everything predetermined by prophecies such as these? Or is there any leaning towards the ability to make choices? Addressed in a more general sense, we ask: how much of our lives are predetermined by God and how much is according to our choices? Now, before I try to fake answering such a question, I want us to look more closely at Jacob and what he does in these two chapters. And so we look at chapter 48 to begin with. And here Jacob musters enough strength at his deathbed to speak and to bless Joseph's sons. What is not clear to the average reader is that Jacob is doing more than blessing Ephraim and Manasseh. He is legally adopting them. This is understood by his repeating of the names of Reuben and Simeon, his two oldest sons. He is saying that just as his two oldest sons have a right to the inheritance of Jacob, So too will Ephraim and Manasseh. They will be to Jacob as his two oldest sons are. And this is a great honor to Joseph. For what Jacob is saying is that instead of Joseph being one tribe like the rest of his brothers, he will now be two tribes in the names of his sons. And we know from our reading of the Old Testament that Ephraim Emanasseh are prominent tribes in Israel, and in fact, when the nations divide and the ten tribes of the north are by themselves, Ephraim takes the lead. And we also see in this story of how Ephraim and Manasseh come into the nation of Israel and how Jacob instills his own will, which he believes is God's will. Jacob gives the blessing of the firstborn to Ephraim instead of Manasseh. And Joseph doesn't like it, for Manasseh was the firstborn. Joseph is a product of the Egyptian culture. And in the ancient Near East, the law of primogeniture was sacred. Primogeniture insisted that the firstborn is blessed of the gods because of his firstborn status, and thus he is owed all that is his father's. But Jacob being as God was for, but Jacob knowing God, knowing that God was the God of Abel. whom God chose over Cain, or the God of Isaac, who he chose over Ismael, or Jacob over Esau, or Rachel over Leah. This choosing of the younger over the older went against all human wisdom and is for us to be seen as a practice of God's grace. Where God shows that he identifies with the weak, with the outcast, with the unexpected, what we call the underdog. That is our God, and Jacob knows that God. St. Paul spoke of God choosing men in the same manner when he wrote to the Corinthian Christians and said this. Brothers, think of what you were when you were called. Not many of you were wise by human standards. God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong. He chose the lowly things of this world and despised the things and the things that are not to nullify the things that are, so that no one may boast before him. Therefore, as it is written, let him who boasts boast in the Lord. Such is God's grace, known by the actions of Jacob given to the Christians at Court and shown to us and all who know him What we next find in chapter 49 is Jacob providing both prophecy and reckoning. Which communicates that the future of each tribe is determined by the will of God and the choices of Jacob's sons made in the past. Reuben loses his favored place as firstborn because of his past sin. And you will remember in chapter 35 of Genesis where we are told that Reuben tried to assume the leadership of the family in the same manner that the pagan nations did around him by sleeping with his father's concubine. Jacob was silent about that until now, where he pronounces a curse and judgment. And history will see Jacob's words take root when Israel takes possession of the promised land and the tribe of Reuben settles outside of the border of Canaan. and phase out of the nation's history, giving it no prophets, no kings, no judges. What was done by the will of Reuben sealed the fate of those who would bear his name after. Simeon and Levi are addressed together because their treachery was practiced together. You remember when they tried to avenge the rape of Diamond? Neither of them are deserving of any ruling position. Simeon essentially disappears as an insignificant tribe. And Levi is given the responsibility for the priesthood, but will inherit no land We remember it was Judah who stepped forward to be a sacrifice for Benjamin, even though his past was quite reprehensible. His willingness to sacrifice brings blessings, for he will be the tribe from whom King David would come forward, and the same tribe that brings forth the King of kings, Jesus, who will reign forever. The remaining sons of Leah and the two concubines are spoken briefly. Each of them played an important role by way of important people. Dan would be a tribe that would serve the entire nation by its military victories. The Gadites also were famed for their military exploits, and their name became a byword for military prowess. Joseph, we have already mentioned, and Jacob goes even farther to express his love for this favored son. Benjamin is described as a ravenous wolf, and that is surprising because he has always been protected by his father. It was likely a description of his descendants, which would be Saul and Jonathan, and these two men were great warriors. Now it has been said about these two chapters, Genesis 48 and 49, that they lay a foundation for the national life of Jacob's descendants. Here are the lives of the people of Israel who will follow in a similar pattern to what Jacob has described. Some will follow in a general sense, and others, like Judah, as Judah, the description given will be followed to the most important details. And what should be clear is that these two chapters are linking us back to the call of Abraham, where God made a promise to a man who had no children. That he would be a father, the patriarch of a great nation. And here is that great nation promised at its beginning point. All of the promises of God will be fulfilled through this nation, and they are promises to us as well. Therefore, it should not surprise us to understand that these two chapters in Genesis give us a picture of the life of the Christian church as well as the overall kingdom of God. When we think back on the stories of Jacob and his sons, those stories include rivalry, cruelty, envy, and sins of passion. And we learn of the grace of God making something redeeming out of all of the evil that we see in ourselves. And all Christians down through the ages. And we know what is ahead for God's people here. We know of the slavery, of the exodus Of the idolatry and God's judgment and his compassion and the man he calls to deliver his people time and time again from suffering because of their own sin. We have kings to come who will make Israel great and they will sin in bold and awful ways. We have kings who will lead God's people into blatant idolatry And we have kings who will repent and turn the people toward God. And then Israel will fall under Roman rule while they continue to wait on a Savior who will come. And most will not recognize or believe in him. And yet he will come and be friends with men and call certain men to follow him closely. Even though one is possessed by the devil, and the others give in to sins of envy and rivalry, just like Jacob's sons did. And Jesus will raise up these weak men to be martyrs for his church and be given seats around the throne of Christ in heaven, along with Jacob's sons. making for those twenty-four elders surrounding the throne, singing holy, holy, holy, while casting their crowns at the seat of Jesus in the book of Revelation Think back upon Jacob's life and rehearse all that he has seen and done in total. In doing so, you see a sinful man who behaves sinfully and raised sons who behaved sinfully as well. And no doubt Jacob was tempted to be embarrassed by the behavior of most of his sons, but then his sons were likely tempted to be embarrassed by their father. I say tempted to be embarrassed, for I too have felt the temptation to be embarrassed by my offspring. Only to realize that they too could be embarrassed by some of the things I have said and done. But the knowledge and awareness of our sin is to enable us to resist the temptation to be embarrassed. For the sins of our children are our sins. In the sense that we have passed on many of our weaknesses to them and thus we bear the same guilt. What am I saying? I am saying that in the life of Jacob and his children we can see ourselves. We can see ourselves and know that God used Jacob and his sons to begin the nation of Israel. Even why while they had so many flaws and so many sins. God used them and he uses us to be his church To build his kingdom on earth as it is in heaven. If you and I were to write down our sins, not the small ones that not many know about but the larger ones that have hurt other people. And we were to combine our lists together as a church, making one long spreadsheet. Would we look at the length of that list and conclude that God is among us and that he is using us for the sake of building his kingdom? Or would we look at the list just the size of it and say that these people can't be used by God? They are not worthy. We would likely conclude the latter, and yet God uses us in our our little corner of Carroll County. To boldly stand for biblical morality and practice as best as we can God-fearing worship. As pastor serving for a number of years in the same place, you become aware of particular sins of particular people and couples and families as a whole And I dare not even hint to you at those sins, because the devil would tempt us to look around and wonder who is responsible for what sins. The point is, we are all sinners in need of forgiveness and grace, and God chooses to use us. Like he uses other churches, which also include sinful people, he uses all of us to build his kingdom Have you ever heard of two Christians who will no longer speak to one another? That's not the Christianity Jesus taught. What about a church where the youth minister has had an affair? In this one church, a Sunday school teacher contradicts the teaching of the pastor. At another church, one businessman cheats another church member in a business deal. In another church, a youth is partying dangerously behind her parents' back. And yet in another church a wife has left her husband because, well, she said she just fell out of love. These are all sins within the Christian church that Jesus says he loves and that he uses to minister his truth to the world. Christians can sin and sin boldly, and Jesus gives grace and uses said sinners to build his kingdom. I know of a church where a young man had an affair with his stepmother. At the same church, parishioners were getting publicly intoxicated at church socials. At the same church, cliques were being formed based on which minister they preferred. And throughout the church, there was a strong resentment toward their bishop, whom they said thought himself quite bold when writing his emails, and yet quite weak when he spoke to them face to face. Of course, you know, the church I am describing, I merely modernized the sins of the Christians at Corinth. They are us. And we are them. Their sins are the fruit of them choosing to be the main authority over their lives. They chose their will over God's will. Now I started this sermon asking about the mystery of where the will of men begins and ends and when it comes in contact with God what will wins out. After examining Genesis 48 and 49, I still can't answer that question. But I can know and you can know that when humanity as a whole and individual persons use their will, their ability to choose, it doesn't seem to end well. But the amazing grace of God uses us just as he used Jacob and his sons to be his church and to build his kingdom. Recently I sent a questionnaire to the vestry that described the character and gifts that are to be of our next bishop One Vesterman asked me if we had enough men in our diocese to choose from who met the criteria listed. It is a great question. The most honest answer is no. No, we don't. In fact, if you look at the standards required of men to be pastors, let alone bishops We wouldn't have anyone meet all of those requirements. But God still uses men to pastor his church and to build his kingdom. And he uses husbands and wives to sanctify one another, even with their many flaws. And he uses sinful parents to raise sinful children to his glory. He uses sinners. And are we not grateful for it? Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God Through the lives of these men chosen by you, we do indeed this morning see ourselves And with that confession, we simply say we are grateful that you still include us, no matter our sin, that you redeem us and you use us to redeem your world. And we say to you, we are thankful for it. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen

sermons.title: Genesis as Foundational
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. Do well to turn in your Bibles to Genesis chapter 50, but it began with a story Most of us know well enough the story of Martin Luther, the German monk who in 1517 started a religious revolution. It would challenge some of the false teachings that had risen up in Christianity and in particular the Roman Catholic Church When Luther was eventually successful at challenging the authority of the Roman Church over all of Western Christianity, naturally there sprang up a number of religious leaders and teachers. who wanted to go even farther away from Rome than Luther did. One such group was called the Anabaptists Because they believed that for a person to be truly baptized, he or she needed to be baptized as a confessing adult hence uh these professing Christians were rebaptized or baptized again, the word Anna meaning again. But among those who tried to move themselves away from Rome, there were teachers and leaders who wanted to move even further away. And these groups are best described as fanatics or fanatical Anabaptists The city of Münster in Germany at the time of the Reformation was a unique city that it was not governed by the church, but was instead independent, answering primarily to King Charles V. But it was indeed heavily influenced by the Roman Church. Within the town of Munster, there began a rebellion against the Roman Catholics and their influence, so as eventually to remove them physically from the city with their so-called idols. This was 16 years after the beginning of the Reformation. The success of the Lutheran rebels was noted by fanatical Anabaptists who soon entered the city of Munster and took over the city by forcing new elections and bringing in many Anabaptist followers, resulting in the election of a man by the name of John Matthias in 1533. John Matthias was known to promote violent rebellion. With the Roman Catholics pushed out, Mass conversions by way of rebaptism took place inside the city. And by the way, the city was a walled-off city. So you could restrict who was coming in, keeping the Roman Catholics out, and who could go out, keeping the Anabaptists in. Well, this walled city then was surrounded by a Roman bishop who gathered an army and ordered a blockade of the city Hoping to bring panic within to break the rebellion. Although the Anabaptist leaders tried to extend their supplies within the city, the people got desperate. On Easter Sunday in April, Jean Matthias, who recognized the people's panic, said that he had a vision from God and that he was to go out and fight the army of the bishop single-handed. He of course failed and was beheaded. Within the city walls, a man named Jean von Leyden declared himself the new leader Who insisted on the citizens of Munster giving quick and unquestioned obedience to his leadership? Von Leyden next declared a new word from God that decreed that polygamy was now lawful. Meanwhile, he took fifteen women as his own brides, including the wife of the former leader Matthias. All who opposed him would be killed, including any wives that tried to leave him. Meanwhile, another other Anabaptists from the surrounding areas were siding with the leaders because they hated the Roman Catholics. siding with the leaders inside the city walls of Munster, and many tried to sneak in and help. With the siege lasting over a year, Many barbaric behaviors were practiced inside the city simply for the purpose of survival. Some people tried to escape from the city only to be killed by the army that was waiting outside. The bishop's army finally broke through after a year-long blockade on a rainy night and took back the city. What they did with the leaders of this rebellion, I will leave for you to go home and Google and do some research. And I bring this sordid story to your attention on our last look at the book of Genesis, because Genesis is a book about beginnings. Establishing a foundation, yes, a foundation for our Christian faith, which is the covenant God has made with mankind. And to venture away from this foundation, to venture away is to go the way of fanatical Anabaptists. And you and I must be warned. Yes, what they did could happen to anyone who leaves behind what is foundational in the Christian faith. How people get from believing in confessional baptism to accepting murder and polygamy is first cause by leaving what is foundational. So I want you to look back with me at Genesis chapter 50. to see what is foundational from this chapter, foundational to our Christian faith even. In verse 1 Jacob has just died and Joseph weeps bitterly. This is to remind us again that death came into the world by way of the sin of humanity, our first parents, Adam and Eve. Death was the punishment of that sin. Death was not God's eternal plan in what God, although he knew what Adam and Eve would do, God wanted life for his creation. Therefore, death is painful. The forty days given for mourning shows that Jacob was mourned as a royal Egyptian. And this is part of God's promise to Abraham, as God has made his name known through his descendants, the descendants of Abraham, and made God's people a blessing to other nations, just as he promised. Next, Joseph assures that his promises to his father are fulfilled. In his actions of assurance, we see God of promise. Making sure that his promises are fulfilled. Joseph uses his authority and influence to assure these promises, just as God uses his authority and influence to assure us of his promises. And he has promised by way of his descendants that there will be a man to crush the serpent's head. By way of Joseph taking back the remains of his father, Jacob, we see the hope of the resurrection. God is a God of the living. Jesus said as much. Abraham is alive, although the world only knows him as dead. Isaac is alive. Jacob is alive, for God preserves the souls of his people until the day of resurrection, when all of the ground and the sea will give up those dead bodies to be reunited and renewed. With those who will have heaven as their home. When Joseph buries the body of his father, he does so as a testimony of our resurrection hope. And we do the same. We Christians bury our dead with the hope of the resurrection And the great mourning that occurs for Jacob is symbolic of the sinfulness of humanity. As we are reminded that all have fallen short of the glory of God, and therefore all must mourn for their sin so that they can seek forgiveness and receive it. When the brothers of Joseph don't have their father as a buffer of love between Joseph and them, they fear that Joseph will enact vengeance. The fear is unwarranted as Joseph reveals himself to be a Christian man. If you are not used to my expositions, it may sound funny to hear Joseph, great grandson of Abraham, be called Christian. But I argue that the Christian covenant is a fulfillment of the Jewish covenant, making Joseph a Christian, as was Abraham, who saw the day of Jesus and was glad. As a Christian man, Joseph knew he was to forgive, and forgiving his brothers, he had already done. As a Christian man, he is to trust that the will of God, no matter what life circumstance brings, that God has shown him that what man meant for evil, God meant for good. Christian men see the greater purpose of God in all of life circumstances, and so they trust in what they cannot see. And finally, we can say that what we see in Genesis is foundational to the Christian faith, as Joseph can speak words of confident faithfulness that what God has promised Will most certainly come to pass. God will deliver his people no matter how much time passes, and we remember it's 400 years. He did that for Israel, and he's keeping that promise for you and I. Now you might wonder Why I am compelled to defend the book of Genesis in the manner of it being foundational It is because I recently listened to a podcast of a popular Christian evangelist who put forth the idea That Christians today should unhitch, and that's his word, unhitch themselves from the Old Testament. His argument, and I don't want to present a straw man, so I'm trying to give it to you as he put it forward. His argument is that although the Old Testament is divinely inspired, it should not be a main source for Christians regarding any practiced behavior of the faith. He argues that Acts 15 is proof As you remember, that's when all of the apostles gathered together for uh uh making decisions in regards to the Gentiles. He argues that Acts 15 is proof that early Christians did not use the Old Testament to explain or justify their faith, but only stories of Jesus we now find in the Gospels. He believes that the new covenant, the covenant we have with Jesus, is the only thing necessary to understand what it means to be Christian and to live as Christians. This teacher confesses that what he is teaching may be unnerving to some, but in actuality he says it is quite liberating because It makes the message that Jesus brought into the world much more simple. In an article I read about this teacher, It is revealed that he believes people are leaving the Christian faith because of their embarrassment over stories in the Old Testament. Stories like six days of creation, Abraham being asked to sacrifice Isaac, the extermination of entire tribes, and so on. Well for those of you who have heard most of my sermons on Genesis and have heard my sermons on the Epistle to the Hebrews, do you know that the position this evangelist takes, and again he's popular. It's far from my own. And when I tried to understand his point, and believe me, I tried to listen without all of my mind being made up I could hear the heart of an evangelist, an evangelist who is trying to think of a new or at least reworked idea of how to make the gospel message more appealing to modern ears. And yes, I can get that, but only to a certain extent. It is true that the devil can use difficult narratives in the Old Testament to obscure God's intended truth. or to distract what is bothersome to modern minds. And so these people find reasons to dismiss the Bible in its entirety. But a simple answer to that concern is that no one is going to believe in Jesus unless the Holy Spirit has dropped the scales from their eyes, and with that truth we should accept that ignoring the Old Testament is not the answer for helping the spiritually blind to see But I want you to agree with me on something else. I want you to agree and live out the truth that rightly understanding the Old Testament is what is truly liberating, especially to see through the typological study that we are finishing here today. Consider again. Consider again, there is the seed typology, the seed typology that St. Paul expands upon to the Christians at Galatia. A seed or descendant, God promised, would crush the serpent's head. The serpent, the devil, and the seed, Paul teaches, is singular, not plural. It was to be one man. And he was to be one man and the only person ever to fit the description of a descendant of Adam and Eve who could crush the devil. And he is Jesus, who not only bound the straw man as he entered this earth, but stepped on his head while dying on the cross. There is the covenant of Abraham typology that has God choosing a man with no descendants as the patriarch of all of God's people to come. Where men are not fruitful in offspring is like men not fruitful in righteousness, and God provides. Abraham is called out of a sinful land to a new land, just as all Christians are called out of darkness and into the light of righteousness. God makes the covenant with Abraham and his descendants symbolized by the cutting away of the foreskin, which is a precursor to the cutting away of the stone-laden hearts of every person. God also called Abraham to sacrifice Isaac. Reminds you not to see what was in Abraham's heart, for God already knew Abraham's heart. Now he called Abraham to offer his son and then withheld the knife-sealed hand that was going to bring down the blow. He did it to show Abraham that he, God, is not like the other gods that require such a sacrifice of their people, the false gods around Abraham. God was showing that in truth God was the only one Himself who would require such a sacrifice. And there is also the very important struggle between works and grace typology. In the life of Abraham As Abraham performed many obedient deeds for God, like leaving his father's homeland, like offering Isaac, like cutting the sacrificial offerings, you remember as God prescribed and the torch walking through them? Like the act of circumcision. And yet God said it was not all of these works, but because of what Abraham believed, it was his faith that God counted to him as righteous. The difference between man-made works, righteousness, and righteousness by grace through faith is spoken throughout the letters of St. Paul. And Abraham is the primary example to us about faith versus works. By grace we are saved through faith. And so was Abraham. And then there is Israel as the church typology. It is first the Ark of Noah, it is like the church, the only vehicle by which any person can be saved from God's wrath. Then it is the family of Jacob who is chosen to bring forth the people of God as they are made a nation. And the foundation of that nation begins with women at strife trying to have more children than the other. It is siblings being jealous and envious of the favored one of God Just as the Pharisees were of Jesus. And Joseph is so much like Christ, a type of Christ, that I dare not try to describe it all again. It is very plain to see. This family of Jacob reveals that life within and without the covenant with God consists of conflict. And the conflicts are within each person and between parties as well, even brothers. against brothers, as the person of Judah reveals, within and without As rehearsed last sermon, the sins of the family of Jacob were numerous, they were heinous, they were deplorable, with no expectation that God would use them, and yet use them he did. And so in them we see us. We see the church. We are sinners in the hands of the living God, and yet we are not crushed. But sanctified and used for God's glory. If we don't have Israel of the Old Testament to understand what it means to be and not be God's people Then how are we to understand the church in its history and in its modern state, a state riddled with hypocrisy, envy, half-truths, blind spots to sin, and the like While also containing men and women who love God and love their neighbor and pray for his kingdom to come. Israel is as the church. Consider these questions. When you start reading Matthew's gospel, how do you understand the lineage of Jesus starting with Abraham if you don't know Genesis? How do you understand the meaning of repentance from sin and faith toward God preached by Jesus if you don't know Genesis and the fall of man? How do you understand the need to shed blood and sacrifice for sin if you don't know Genesis? How do you understand Jesus to be the word that was in the beginning? If you don't know the book that is about beginnings, Genesis. How do we understand that we are saved by grace through faith alone and not by our own works if we don't know Genesis and that Abraham had faith and God marked it as righteousness. What difference would it make to us for Jesus to say, Abraham saw my day and was glad if we don't know Genesis? And how do you understand, truly understand, so that your hope is in the kingdom of God to come, if you don't understand that in the book of Revelation, the covenant of God made in the Garden of Eden is fulfilled. as the tree of life is found smack dab in the middle of New Jerusalem. That doesn't mean anything profound unless you know Genesis. When pondering this sermon, I remembered the book titled All I Really Need to Know I Learned in Kindergarten. I have not read the book, but I learned of its content. It is a number of essays about life lessons, and the title of the book comes from the first chapter where the author puts forth the premise that the basic things one learns in kindergarten like sharing and being kind to others and cleaning up after yourself and living a balanced life between work, play, and learning. that all of these are foundational to anyone having an enjoying life. Well, as you may know the many parodies of that title, I guess I'm going to join the fray. All I really need to learn, I learned in Genesis. Not probably saying too much, but But when we learn from the gospels about Jesus and what atonement is, what holiness is, what faith is, and so on Knowing Genesis and all of the Old Testament allows for the other things we know to make a great deal more sense. And so together we thank God for Genesis. Don't unhitch, for you will go the way of the fanatic. Stay hitched and find true liberty. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God We thank you for this book and for all the truths that are revealed therein, that are found in the New Testament. Father, you have revealed yourself in such a gracious manner, and we thank you for the lessons learned in this book these past months. We thank you in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Tenable Faith
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Today, we start a series of sermons That I am calling the summer of the saints. I thought that was rather catchy. The summer of the saints This is a different type of series for us, but I am not going to be expounding on a different text from the Bible. But instead, I'm going to reveal to us how early Christians, and by early, I mean Christians who lived up to the third century how early Christians understood the Bible, and how they lived their lives according to that understanding. So the Scripture is our authority in this series as it always needs to be, but we are going to be looking at Scripture through different lenses. And to help you understand what has motivated me to do a series like this, I begin with a story. Shortly after I arrived as the new rector here at St. Stephen's, which by the way was 20 years ago this weekend. I heard about the connection this parish and Bishop Cummins parish had to the Erickson family, and I'm so grateful that Kathy's here and Tyler and could catch us up on what Johnny is doing. I had heard the story of Johnny Erickson, now Tada, several years prior, how she broke her neck in a swimming accident and how she learned to do extraordinary things with her teeth And most importantly, how she had a powerful testimony regarding her faith in Jesus while going through the most difficult testing of her faith in accepting her paralysis. I wanted to learn more about her and her story, so I, when I got here, picked up her autobiography titled Johnny. And in this autobiography, Johnny tells about a young man named Steve Estes. Steve is now a pastor, he's a counselor, he's an author We when he came to know Johnny, he was but a young man with no theological training. But he became a confidant and spiritual counselor for Johnny as again she wrestled with God to accept a life of faith in him while facing a lifetime of paralysis. What I remember well about the effect Steve Estes' counsel had on Johnny was when he confessed to her that all the truths that he was teaching her and reminding her from God's word, that all of these were a mystery to him. Because the counsel he was giving her, even though it was from Holy Scripture, he didn't know if it actually worked. He didn't know if a person could endure suffering like Johnny's and not lose faith. He didn't know if a person could count sufferings all joy as we are told to do in Scripture. Or if a person could worry only about today and trust that God would take care of all the days ahead As an inexperienced young man, he didn't know if applying biblical principles actually changed a life for the better. He didn't know it until he saw it work in John. And I love the honesty of such a confession, for I have had a similar experience. I have counseled people telling them how to apply the scriptures to their particular struggle or trial. when I myself had not been through what they are going or were going through. And I'm sure all of us have had at one time a moment where we have wondered whether the principles for living the Christian life really do give a person peace of heart and mind. If I forgive as I should and love as I should and be patient, patient as I should, will it bring me inner joy and peace of my conscience? Does the Christian life applied provide victory over sin in my life? Can faith in Jesus give me peace over inner struggles and difficult people? I am trusting in this series that the lives of the saints of old will tell us the answers to these questions. We begin with looking not at one particular saint, but all of the apostles The original 12, who you know became 11, and then back to 12, and then 13 when adding the Apostle Paul. We start with the 12 by examining a document that is believed to have come from their teaching. And it's called the Dida K. The Dida K spelled D-I-D-A-C-H-E and pronounce Dida K. The date of the Didique is hotly debated. We are going to settle on the year 100 A. D. as that is the most popular scholarly date as of today. Now I have outlined the document as follows. It begins by underlining necessary moral behaviors by Christians, again, from the scriptures. Next, it gives counsel on how to live the Christian faith in the context of the sinful world around you. It then warns Christians about false teachers and certain sins that lead to death. That is followed by the centrality of the sacraments in the lives of Christians. Discussing the sacraments leads to how Christians are to properly treat one another, and that leads to how Christians are to treat clergy, and it ends, as you might expect, with the call to look for Jesus' second coming. So in the first section, we hear the words of Jesus in the Sermon on the Mountain. That's why we read it, part of it today. As the apostles believed the standards of morality Jesus set for his followers, they believed it was to be seriously followed. Here are some of those instructions. This is from chapter 1 titled The Two Ways and the First Commandment. Quote: There are two ways: one of life and one of death. But a great difference between the two ways. The way of life, then, is this. First, you shall love God who made you. Second, love your neighbor as yourself, and do not do to another what you do not want done to you. And of these things, the teaching is this: Bless those who curse you, and pray for your enemies, and fast for those who persecute you. For what reward is there for loving those who love you? Do not the Gentiles do the same? But love those who hate you, and you shall not have an enemy. Abstain from fleshly and worldly lusts. If someone strikes your right cheek, turn to him the other also. And you shall be perfect. If someone impresses you for one mile, go with him too. If someone takes your cloak, give him also your coat. Sound familiar? Notice the trust in the words of Jesus in these instructions. The first Christians believe that as Jesus said it, so should it be done And that when it was difficult, God would provide. This type of faith believes that when you give someone your coat, God will provide you another. It believes that when you turn the other cheek, God will help you endure the pain. This type of faith believes that the enemies of God are to be faced with kindness. And gentleness, and yes, with the love of God. We Christians are to love our enemies. Who teaches that? Jesus does. We are to love our enemies in every age and as long as we serve our Savior on this earth. Now these next instructions focus on how to love your neighbor and follow the same moral standards as Jesus taught, which you know were the standards of the Ten Commandments, only Jesus interpreted them much more specifically. Hear this, quote. And the second commandment of the teaching, you shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not commit pedastery, that's for me, pederasty You shall not commit fornication. You shall not steal. You shall not practice magic. You shall not practice witchcraft. You shall not murder a child by abortion, nor kill that which is born. You shall not covet the things of your neighbor. You shall not swear. You shall not bear false witness. You shall not speak evil. You shall not bear a grudge. You shall not be double-minded nor double-tongued, for to be double-tongued is a snare of death. Your speech shall not be false nor empty, but fulfilled by deed. You shall not be covetous, nor rapacious, nor a hypocrite, nor evil-disposed, nor haughty. You shall not take evil counsel against your neighbor, you shall not hate any man, but some of you shall reprove, and conquering some you shall pray. And some you shall love more than your old life.
