Please notice how these first Christians applied the law of Christ. to their particular sins, the sins of their day. The sin of pederasty is older men behaving sexually with boys. It is a form of homosexuality that has men finding pleasure in not just males, but pre-pubescent males. Such a sin was practiced by the more well-to-do in the Roman and Greek cultures. Modern homosexual apologists claim that such practices prove homosexuality has been an acceptable form of behavior in such advanced cultures. The truth is that such behavior was never acceptable in terms of being considered normal. It was merely ignored because it was mostly practiced by the wealthy. And I trust you have noticed also that it is the same sin practiced by the Roman Catholic priest, by some Roman Catholic priests who have scandalized Christianity. And I also trust you notice the clear condemnation of abortion. There is no question that early Christians understood life to begin at conception. And there is no question that women have been tempted to forcefully terminate pregnancies because of poverty or scandal. But human life has always been precious to God at every stage of existence. And there is no child that is to be labeled unwanted, regardless of the circumstance in which it was conceived. Can I get an amen? For these early Christians, we can see a wisdom that is lacking in the teachings of some who consider themselves Christian leaders of today. I have heard one such teacher claim that Jesus didn't condemn homosexuality because he never spoke about it. And another claim that Jesus didn't condemn abortion because again he didn't speak about it. But the first Christians understood Jesus. That when he had when he said to love your neighbor as yourself, that it fell under the commandment of God not to kill. And it fell under the further teaching of Jesus that we were to not entertain hate in our hearts, because that's where killing begins. And so the commandment not to murder includes the unborn, and that would include the newly born as well. Jesus didn't need to speak specifically about it. And when God commanded that his people not commit adultery, that was to include any sexual coupling with anyone that was not your spouse. Since the Bible only knows marriage could be between a man and a woman, the condemnation of adulterous acts would include homosexual unions, which include the condemnation of pederasty and the like. The logic is not hard to follow. The next sin warned against are where sins begin. And Jesus touches on that. These are warnings against what goes on within us, as our minds think upon things that we could do or may want to do while our conscience tries to wrestle with our desires. Hear these instructions. My child, flee from every evil thing and from every likeness of it. Be not prone to anger, for anger leads to murder. Be neither jealous nor quarrelsome, nor of hot temper, for out of all these murders are engendered. My child, be not lustful, for lust leads to fornication. Be neither a filthy talker, nor of lofty eye, for out of all these adulteries are engendered. My child, be not a liar, since a lie leads to theft. Be neither money-loving nor vainglorious, for out of all these thefts are engendered. My child, be not a murmurer, since it leads to the way of blasphemy. Be neither self-willed nor evil-minded, for out of all these blasphemies are engendered. Again, warnings about what starts from within. The next sins listed warned Christians never to play with the spiritual. The spiritual world is real and it is not to be trivialized. Quote, My child, be not an observer of omens, since it leads to idolatry. Be neither an enchanter, nor an astrologer, nor a purifier. nor be willing to look at these things, for out of all these idolatry is engendered. The first Christians Would never play with Ouija boards or magic eight balls or look at their daily horoscope for guidance This next quote I provide for us because it is not practiced today as it should be We might say that all things we own are from God, and yet we treat them like they are our own to use only. But if all we have is from God, should it not be available to all Christians who are God's people And so hear this. Quote, do not turn away from him who is in want. Rather share all things with your brother. And do not say that they are your own. For if you are partakers of that which is immortal, how much more in things which are mortal? Again, such instruction should be within our conscience when we know a brother or sister in need, and that we can help that person Or when people ask of us and we can provide, we should. If we are not our own, but we are Christ's Then we, then what we own is not ours to withhold, especially to a brother or sister in Christ. Now concerning the sacraments, the instructions are both pragmatic and ritualistic. Baptism was to be done as an act symbol symbolizing conversion and new life, of course. Interestingly, it was recognized that rivers and lakes were not in abundance, so whatever form of water was available was to be used for the baptism, and they specifically mentioned the act of pouring the water. Now concerning the Lord's Supper or Holy Communion, it was to be done at least weekly and include the Lord's Prayer, which interestingly is to be said at least three times a day. After receiving the bread and wine, a particular prayer of thanksgiving is to be said. And such instructions show that our human natures need ritual. We best function under ritual. We have security in what we do on a regular basis and when we practice ritual in our faith instead of being dead, which some say comes with ritual. Instead, it makes us place our meeting with God as a priority in our lives because we cannot do without it. We feel less until we do it. The first Christians understood this principle, and so should we. Now the next concern is how clergy are to be treated The concern is the presence of false teachers within the church. And you remember that's the concern in Paul's letters, in John's letters, and in Peter's letters. Hear this. But if he, a visiting preacher, if he teaches so as to increase righteousness and the knowledge of the Lord, receive him as the Lord. But concerning the apostles and prophets, act according to the decree of the gospel. Let every apostle who comes to you be received as the Lord. But he shall not remain more than one day or two days, if there's a need. But if he remains three days, he is a false prophet. And when the apostle goes away, let him take nothing but bread until he lodges. If he asks for money, he is a false prophet. Did you hear that? Let us underline the standard that if a clergy teaches people to live righteously, that is the primary evidence that he is from God. But if a man tries to make his visiting a means of financial gain for himself, he is automatically disqualified to the office in which he claims. And folks, this is no joke. No man should preach the truth of Jesus for financial gain. And no Christian should give his or her money to anyone who asks for it, no matter how dramatic the plea. And yes, that applies to radio and television personalities. Or shall we not call them by what they are, false prophets? These next passages show how Christian life is to be lived in community with fellow Christians. Hear this. Quote, so also a true teacher is himself worthy, as the workman of his support. Every first fruit, therefore, of the products of wine press and threshing floor of oxen and of sheep, you shall take and give to the prophets, for they are your high priests. But every Lord's day, gather yourselves together and break bread, and give thanksgiving, after having confessed your transgressions, that your sacrifice may be pure. But let no one who is at odds with his fellow come together with you until they be reconciled, that your sacrifice may not be profaned. For this is that which was spoken by the Lord in every place and time offer to me a pure sacrifice, for I am a great king, says the Lord, and my name is wonderful among the nations. End quote. They are to support their spiritual leaders in prayer and in giving. They are to be sure to be together at least every Lord's day, which is Sunday, and still is Sunday. They are to include in their regular gatherings the Lord's Supper, confessed sin, prayers of thanksgiving, and a standard of peace in which we are forgiving one another So that our spiritual sacrifice that we're offering right now is pure before God. But we should not say they, we should say we We are to support our leadership, and for us, that is highlighted by praying for our future bishop. We are to be sure to gather together on the Lord's day. And when we gather, we are to share in the Lord's Supper, to confess our sins, to pray prayers of thanksgiving, and to be sure we forgive one another. And we are to do it all with the hope that Jesus will return again and we will forever be in his presence. So what do we learn from this document? Is the Christian life, as Jesus put it before his followers, tenable, reachable, livable in all situations? The answer from the first generation Christians as they left instructions to the second generation Christians, the answer to that is yes. Yes, and there is a qualifier. It is a necessary qualifier Because we don't gather with God's people as we should, because we don't forgive as we should. Because we choose to sin instead of obey, there is also the need to face our practice of falling short of the standards that Jesus has set for us. The teachers of the Didic said it this way. Quote, See that no one causes you to err from this way of teaching Since apart from God it teaches you. For if you are able to bear the entire yoke of the Lord, you will be perfect. But if you are not able to do this, do what you are able. Let me read that qualifier again. But if you are not able to do this, do what you are able. Regardless of what we fail to do or what we do that we should not have done, we are then to do what we are able. To do what you are able is to stay on the narrow road, even though you stumble, even though you stall. To do what you are able to do is to stay on the road. To do what you are able to do is to be honest with God and your fellow man, that you are weak internally and externally. But that you still believe in Jesus. And that is enough to press forward. To do what you can is to stay in the battle. It is to fight to the end. You can do it. You can do it. The Savior has declared it. Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious God, we thank you for the testimony of the early church, for their ever confidence that the standards that you set in your holy word Are to be pursued without a doubt. And that the holiness that you require of your people is given to us by Christ, and we are to follow in his steps. May we never, ever remove those standards, no matter how difficult the traveling is. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Freedom and love
sermons.speaker: Deacon Ricky McCarl
sermons.text: Let us pray. May the words of my mouth and the meditation of all our hearts Be acceptable and pleasing in thy sight, our rock and our redeemer. In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. Amen. I uh was reminded this morning of the first time I read the gospel after being ordained as a deacon As some of you may know, you can't read the gospel in the Eucharist until you're a deacon. And I was newly ordained, my first Sunday as a deacon. And I go down amongst the people, and I began to read the gospel, and I'm thinking to myself as I'm reading the gospel, this is so cool. I'm reading the words of Christ. Uh and and then I realized, no I'm not. I was reading the epistle lesson for the morning. Um so I I quickly apologized and uh went to where I was supposed to do, but um I bring that up because, as you probably have noticed, all of the readings this morning were not what was in the bulletin. And I have to apologize to you all, the gospel and epistle lessons listed are incorrect because I had to write two sermons this week and at the last minute decided to preach this one instead of the other If you, however, do want to hear the other one, you're more than welcome to join us at Westminster Church of the Brethren tonight at 4 p. m. I promise it's a good one too. When I was in college, there was a local megachurch in town that most of my classmates attended One day, mostly out of curiosity, a friend and I attended worship there. It was a patriotic holiday of some sort, and the stage, as they called it, was decked out in a huge American flag. Now, I'm not sure if I remember this right or not, but I also think that there may have been fireworks. Or maybe it was just angry incense. I don't know. On this particular Sunday, they also took a good 15 minutes out of the service to recognize each and every veteran in the church. Now, I believe that in and of itself these aren't bad things. I love our flag. Fireworks. And am eternally grateful for all of the things our service men and women have done for our freedom I'm just not comfortable with taking any time out of our worship of God and giving it over to our federal government. So that's not what we're going to do here today But I would be remiss if I didn't take this 4th of July weekend and use it as an opportunity to discuss what it means for us to be Christians living in this great country. With all of our freedoms, liberties, and privileges. The history of our great church and our great nation are intertwined To be Anglican and to be American are in a lot of ways connected historically speaking. After the war for independence was over, most of our clergy went back to England. There were no bishops, and the church was in danger of becoming destabilized as a result. There was even talk. God forbid, of the church becoming Presbyterian or even Congregationalist in polity. Where's Phil? Another problem arose as well. If we were going to get bishops, then they would need to be consecrated in England. And the trouble with that is that in order to be consecrated by the Church of England The prospective bishop needed to swear allegiance to the reigning monarch. In this case, that would be King George III. And as you can see, this became a pretty large problem for us. But where there is a problem for the covenant people of God, God has always provided a solution. The solution came in the form of bishops in the Scottish Church, who in the beginning of the reign of William and Mary refused to swear allegiance to the new co-monarchs Because they had already swore allegiance to King James and his children. As a result, these non-jore bishops, as they were called, were able to consecrate our new bishop Bishop Seabury, without the customary oath of allegiance to the king. We had our bishop, and the episcopacy was saved. Thanks be to God. And so with our country's independence came our church's independence as well. And though we as Reformed Episcopalians have departed from the Protestant Episcopal Church This is our story as much as it is theirs. And so being American and being Reformed Episcopalian are in many ways connected. But being Reformed Episcopalians should change the way that we are to be Americans. It changes the way that we are to be Americans because we are first and foremost Christians. And to be a Christian American means something vastly different than being a Muslim American, or a Jewish American, or an atheistic American. Our allegiance as Americans is contingent upon our higher allegiance, our allegiance to Christ. And now my thesis for this morning is this. Freedom is the fundamental tenet of what it means to be an American. But freedom does not work without faith in the one who provides it. And the words of John Adams, our Constitution was made only for a moral and religious people. It is wholly inadequate to the government of any other. Turn with me to the Gospel of Matthew chapter 5, beginning in the 43rd verse, and we will discuss this in more detail. Our gospel lesson appointed for today comes from our Lord's Sermon on the Mount. And I can close my eyes and picture in my mind Jesus And his disciples gathered around him on the beautiful rolling hills of the Galilee as the sun shines down and the breeze from the sea blows softly in the background. He begins to preach. Blessed are the poor in spirit. And this is hands down the greatest sermon ever preached, because it came straight from the lips of God. And one of the things that Jesus clearly communicates in this sermon is that the standard of the law is much greater than the teachers of the law have taught. He says, You have heard that it is said, you shall love your enemy, or love your neighbor and hate your enemy. But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you. Wait, what? But there are enemies. Exactly. He says to love them. And this is pretty radical stuff How can we love our enemies? Why should we love our enemies? They're our enemies, not our friends. And the answer is simple because he said so. But also because in loving our enemies, we reveal ourselves to be children of the Father in heaven. Loving our enemies is what separates us from them. It's what sets us apart as in the world, but not of the world. This in fact goes against everything the world says. The world wants us to despise our enemies, to desire our enemies' destruction, to see our enemy as, well, our enemy. You see this most clearly in modern political discourse. If you disagree with the prevailing winds of culture. Instead of live and let live, you're called a racist, a Nazi, or phobic in some way And this, of course, is the first step in not only ignoring an argument, but in dehumanizing the person that disagrees with you. Dehumanizing those who disagree with us is not love, and in extreme cases has led to the destruction of entire people groups in the history of the world. And this is not something that we as Christians are to be engaged in. We are, as Christ has commanded, to love our enemies. We are to pray for those who persecute us, remembering that God makes his son to rise on the evil and the good alike. And that he sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous alike. In other words, our God is sovereign. He is in control, therefore hating those who hate us is wholly unnecessary For if God is sovereign, if he is in control, if he is our king, then he will deal with our enemies by either changing their hearts and making them our brethren, or by judging them and giving them what it is that they have always deserved. Prayer is the only thing we need to do. So if all we need to do is pray, what then is left but to love? We don't need to get revenge because vengeance is the Lord's. We don't need to win them over with our well-thought out arguments. Because it is the Lord's job to turn hearts to him. And we don't need to defend ourselves, for as the book of Exodus says, the Lord will fight for you. You need only be still Be still and love. But it is hard to love our enemies, one might protest. They are so enemy-like Well, yes. In fact, Jesus says that himself. He says, For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not the tax collectors do the same? Loving those who love us comes easy, but the real challenge is in loving those who hate us, those who wish us ill. Loving people like that shows the world around us that we are, quite frankly, weird. Jesus calls it being perfect as the Father is perfect So in loving those who hate us, we actually reveal the Father to the world around us. Remember the words of St. John, we love because he first loved us. We are transformed not by our love for God, but by God's love for us. John goes on to say in 1 John 4. 10, herein is love, not that we love God, but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. He did this when we were his enemies, when we were at enmity with him. But God loved his enemies so much that he gave up his beloved son for them. And this love transforms life, and this love is the example for us in our own earthly relationships. The other day I witnessed a conversation on social media. It's a terrible place to witness conversations. in which someone had made the suggestion that the Judeo-Christian moral ethic is the foundation of Western civilization, and that that was superior to other ethical systems. Now, up until that point, the conversation was a friendly philosophical debate. The suggestion about Western civilization and its moral ethic changed the tone, however, and the conversation significantly. It was suggested by one person, a former hospice co-worker of mine, that the person making this statement about Western civilization was a racist. And that I was probably going to block her and have nothing to do with her as a result. Now I had to formulate a proper response to her assumption and her assertion. One that did not stoop to that level and honored Christ. And I chose to go the route of the Christian moral ethic I explained that I did not plan to block her and that I considered her a friend, despite her opinion of the perspective that the other person put forward. Now, believing that the Christian moral ethic on which Western civilization is built is superior isn't a racist thing to say. If we thought it was, we wouldn't be sitting here today. In fact, I think it's clear from this very text that we are examining that the Christian moral ethic is fundamentally opposed to racism and hate. And I'm even going to argue that it was the developments brought about by this moral ethic that ultimately exposed racism and hate for what they are, namely sin. We cannot forget that Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was first and foremost a minister of the gospel. And that the gospel was what influenced that entire movement And so we decided to get to respond in love and mercy. And I highlight this story not to toot my own horn. I am, after all, a sinner saved by grace, and have not always elected to respond in a Christian way to people like this I am a son of the Scotch-Irish settlers of Appalachia, so I've gotten my dander up before and have regretted it later. But instead, I bring this up to illustrate the difference between a Christian response to an opponent and that of non-believers. Calling someone racist is dehumanizing. It does more than denigrate the argument, it denigrates the character of the individual as well. It is, in the words of Jesus, a form of murder. Look at Matthew 5, verse 21. In the same sermon that Jesus implores us to love our enemies, he also says, Ye have heard that it was said of them of old, thou shalt not kill. Verse 22. But I say to you, who whosoever is angry with his brother without cause shall be in danger of the judgment. And whoever says to his brother Racha shall be in danger of the council, but whoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire. Now you can take this extremely literally and conclude that Jesus is just saying that he doesn't want us to call people stupid, but the whole thrust of what Jesus is saying in his sermon is much deeper. He's talking about what we might call in modern times character assassination. We aren't to do that The Christian isn't to denigrate his enemy. To do so is in the mind of the great lawgiver himself, Jesus Christ, murder in the same way as using a knife or a gun. Instead, we are to love our enemies and to pray for them, trusting in God's sovereign power over us all. In fact, I'm even going to argue that to kill someone's character is the first step in a process that leads to physical murder. Hitler, in the beginning, simply lied about the Jewish people. He engaged in a dehumanizing propaganda campaign blaming the Jew for all of the world's problems. And this ultimately led to gas chambers and mass graves. It was a murder that started in the heart. And the mind. It poured out of his mouth and ended in the loss of thousands of lives. And Christians need to avoid this at all costs. And we will do that by striving diligently to love our enemies, even though we might disagree with them. And so this brings me back to my thesis. Remember what President Adams said. Our Constitution was made only for a moral and religious people. It is wholly inadequate to the government of any other. So then it is no stretch of the imagination to connect these two ideas. To be moral and religious is to follow Christ. And to follow Christ is to what? We remind you every Communion Sunday, you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the first and great commandment, and the second is like unto it, thou shalt love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets. And that, friends, right there is the Judeo-Christian moral ethic summed up in a nutshell. Love God, love your neighbor. Freedom will never work. America will never work unless we are living that out as a nation. And it starts with us. We are Christ's body and his representatives in this great land. We are to set the pace We are to be the example of what it means to be a religious and moral people. The Constitution was written for us. And now I want to say more about this. Secularism, which defines our current governmental structures. Are not capable of providing the kind of freedom that this nation was founded on It strives to divorce all public life from the Judeo-Christian moral ethic on which our society is founded. But if we do that, though, we no longer have as the source for our laws the objective truth of the command of God. Love God, love thy neighbor. And so what replaces those commands? Only the subjective whims of the people Which is, quite frankly, a scary concept, because without the law of God, we become a law unto ourselves. And so let me ask you this. Why would we want the Ten Commandments removed from courthouses and town squares? Why would we want to ask prospective judges about their religious views and then suggest that they are unfit for office because they believe in the God of the Bible? Is God's law bad? Is there something inherently problematic with following Christ and the ethic he has set before us? Not unless it isn't freedom that you're after. Let's look at those countries who unhitched themselves from the Judeo-Christian moral ethic of the West. Communist Russia was a prime example First, they killed the priests, and then they killed personal freedom. People stood for hours in breadlines, the poor got poorer, and the rich got richer If you ever questioned the government, a mass grave became your final resting place. They divorced themselves from the teachings of Christ, and tyranny followed not far behind. Kill the priests, and you ultimately kill freedom with them. I'm not telling to kill priests. That's bad for me. It is only a moral and religious people who can handle freedom. And we must strive as Christians to protect that freedom. But more importantly, to model what it looks like by loving our enemies and praying for them. In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

sermons.title: Clement
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. This is the second installment in our series That I have titled The Summer of the Saints. And in it we are looking at the epistle or letter known as 1 Clement. 1 Clement is a letter written to Christians in Rome, and to whom all it would be distributed after Rome. According to the third century Christian historian Eusebius, this letter by Clement was widely read and popular in Christian churches. Which may cause us to wonder why it is not in the canon we call Holy Scripture. The main reason would be that Clement was not an apostle And therefore, his writing had no apostolic authority behind it, which was an unwritten criteria to be included in the canon. The letter, however, is consistent with all of Scripture in its doctrine and moral standards. It can be said to be a confirmation of what the Bible teaches. But who was Clement? Well, we don't know for sure. What we do know is that he was either a student of St. Paul or a student of a student of St. Paul. He was likely a presbyter in the church and likely serving the church in Rome. Some say he was the third bishop of Rome. His life and letter are either second or third generation Christian, for he lived somewhere between 80 to 140 A. D. The feel of his letter is as if Christians have been so busy suffering martyrdom And holding on to the faith, as the apostles instruct for us to do, hold on, so busy that they needed a refresher of what the Bible teaches regarding how Christians are to live. Outside of surviving persecution. The letter mentions the suffering and death of both Saint Peter and Saint Paul, who died under the persecution of Nero So the letter of Clement is either written in the midst of Christian suffering under Emperor Domitian or shortly before said persecution began. What is highlighted for me, and therefore will be highlighted for you in this sermon, is the attention Clement pays to young adults. You can see a focus on young adults throughout the letter, and that is why it has a feel for being a letter that recognizes that some things that should have been said to young Christians has not yet been emphasized as it should have been, and so here is Clement's opportunity to do so. Youth. Youth has many of us looking at it as if it is in the review mirror. And yet youth is a most precarious time, and the devil knows as much, and therefore does everything to use that precarious time to his advantage. I know some young adults, no names needed, who seem to need to learn not learn, I should say, who seem to need to not learn from their parents mistakes, but want to be sure to learn things on their own, even if it threatens to kill them And so they repeat the same sins as their parents, or near the same sins, and it is all so unnecessary. Such sins are the ones that the Bible refers to as the sins of youth Sins of youth refer to both the time of the sin in their youth and the kind of sins committed. These are sins that are committed when the power of lust is at its strongest. And animal energy is at its greatest. Dr. Timothy Horton describes said sin as, quote, vanity both of spirit and of conversation. Flexibility to do evil, easily wrought upon and drawn away and enticed to what that which is evil Unteachableness, wax to temptation, and flint to admonition, impetuous intemperance and uncleanness. Sounds pretty bad, doesn't it? And then there are the young adults who are addressed in the book of Proverbs because they are prone to laziness. Many young men fall into that category. Sins of laziness leave the fields unplowed as winter settles in. Sins of laziness include indifference, self-indulgence, and cowardice. Resulting in a refusal to take personal responsibility for the outcome of one's life. Sins of laziness find a young man walking down the street of prostitutes because, well, there's nothing else to do. And while we think that because of the technology of our day, the sins of youth are different Let us not think too highly of our current situation. For example, our elders say that kids have their heads buried in their phones or in their tablets. And the result is that our culture no longer converses with one another as we did back in the day. But I recall a painting by Norman Rockwell that shows a young husband having his head buried in his newspaper while his wife looks away in great disappointment. And I have seen photographs of crowds of people also burying their heads in newspapers as they stand on a street corner to catch up on the news of the afternoon. They came after the news from the morning paper, and still there would also be an evening paper to read as well. No, our proneness to sin is the same, and it's to the same sins we only find different ways to practice those same sins. Well, the first thing that Clement does, addressing the youth, is to praise them for their faithfulness. This is not false praise as in simply using words to encourage what was not actually taking place. in their lives in order to psychologically manipulate them to behave in a godly manner, being described. This was true praise because of true obedience to God and to their conscience. This is what he wrote, quote, and you were all lowly in mind and free from arrogance Yielding rather than claiming submission, more glad to give than to receive, and content with the provisions which God supplieth And giving heed unto his words, you laid them up diligently in your hearts, and the sufferings of Jesus was before your eyes. Such words are high praise. And considering the suffering many Christians endured in the early persecutions of the church. To remain faithful as described is a great testimony of the presence of God in their young hearts. And I confess to you my own sin of not praising my children enough I was prone as a father to notice flaws before I noticed virtue. I regret it, and yet I rejoice when I see my sons being better fathers than I was as they make effort to praise their children when their children do well. May that continue. We all need a pat on the back from people we respect and admire. We need to be told that we are doing well so that the devil cannot discourage us by tempting us to doubt ourselves and especially doubt the voice of the Holy Spirit. Young adults need such encouragement most of all, for there is no greater time in life to doubt yourself. than when you are young and trying to make decisions as if you are mature. Finding that vocation you should pursue and whom you should be with the rest of your days are daunting decisions. To be given confidence that their walk with God is being lived well will help young adults be confident in the decisions they make for the future. Clement also understood how necessary good examples of faith are for young adults. He wrote, quote, Let us set before our eyes the good apostles. There was Peter, who by reason of unrighteous jealousy, endured not one but many labors. And thus having borne his testimony, went to his appointed place in glory. By reason of jealousy and strife, Paul by his example pointed out the prize of patient endurance. After that, he had been seven times in bonds, had been driven into exile, had been stoned, had preached in the East and in the West He won the noble renown which was the reward of his faith. The sin being talked about in these two examples was jealousy by others And the way such sin was endured by each. And Clement believed young adults need such good examples to follow, to imitate. We addressed two weeks ago the need for each of us to know that what we say we believe comes to a good end. We need to know it works. We need to know if people truly can forgive, that people can love unconditionally. That we can overcome fear, sin, and strife. We need to know that women can submit to their husbands and not be taken advantage of. We need to know that men can sacrifice for their wives and still be respected. We need to know that if we take the time to both properly discipline our children and properly train them to know the Lord, that they will always remain Christian. We need to know that God truly does provide our daily bread, no matter our present circumstances, and we need to know so much more. Young adults need to see fruit from the Christian life of those who are older. Receive this truth from me as a clergy who has observed many Christian homes. A devastating blow to the faith of a young person. is to see hypocrisy in his or her parents and other Christians they respect. And I don't mean a hypocrisy that reveals that their parents, that their elders are sinners in general. Of course we all are. I mean hypocrisy where a parent or elder declares to believe in a moral standard and then fail to live up to that standard, which happens. But not own up to that failure, to not confess that failure, and to not repent of that failure. That type of hypocrisy allows the young mind to think the Christian faith is all a scam. It must be a ruse or something that people play at but never actually believe. I am reminded of an interview I recently heard from Dr. Jordan Peterson, who I have mentioned before. Dr. Peterson has a strong following of young adults as he teaches them necessary skills to be successful in the culture such as we have now. In the interview, Dr. Peterson addressed the question of whether he believes in God. He answered by saying that to say you believe in God Places a great burden on yourself because then your life needs to show that what you say you believe is true, your life reflecting what you believe To live not as you believe is to be a liar, and he doesn't want to be a liar. And so he says, he tries to live as if God exists. And he said it with such humility and angst in his tone. He caused me to respect his point a great deal. However, a Christian who knows what the Bible teaches understands that he or she will not live up to what he says he believes, as we are continually falling short of the glory of God We are not perfect as our Heavenly Father calls us to be perfect. But that only means that we are to live in a perpetual state of asking God for forgiveness. And receiving said forgiveness by the means of Jesus our Savior. That's the Christian life. And that points us to these words of Clement. Quote, let us fix our eyes on the blood of Christ. And understand how precious it is unto his Father, because being shed for our salvation, it won the whole world the grace of repentance. He then goes on to review that throughout Holy Scripture, God has always included the grace of his call to repentance. I ask, can we see the value of seeing the call and act of repentance as grace to us? We more often speak and think of grace in terms of the forgiveness of God and not the call to and the act of repentance. But it is good for us to think on the call to and the act of repentance as grace to us. For we we must see it as an opportunity we would not otherwise have to be right with God and to be right with our fellow man. When you hear the call to repent, it is to ring in your ears as good news to you. It is good news that you have an opportunity to turn away from what leads to destruction. It is good news that you can get back on that narrow road that leads to eternal life. Now for young adults, it is most important to change your thinking about the call to and act of repentance. For in young adults is a strong temptation to be defensive rather than teachable. To claim you know something when you clearly don't. And so your first inclination when someone says you are doing something wrong is to stiffen your neck and defend your honor. But such defensiveness does not coincide with understanding that repentance is grace to you. Repentance necessitates that you admit you do not have it right, that you did not do it right, that you are in the wrong, and that you need to change. And to admit these things is to do what Clement next says to be done. Christians are to pursue the virtue of humility. Clement uses the phrase, quote, to obtain a good report. He uses it as a goal which all young adults should pursue, to obtain a good report. To obtain a good report is to have others speak about you in terms of respect. And no one but a fool speaks negatively about a humble man or a humble woman. In order to obtain a good report from others, you must be humble Clement says the following, quote, you see, dearly beloved, what is the pattern that hath been given unto us? For if the Lord was thus lowly of mind, what should we do? Who through him have been brought under the yoke of his grace? After describing the humility of the saints of the Old Testament, he said, quote, The humility therefore and the submissiveness of so many and so great men who have thus obtained a good report Have through obedience made better not only us, but also the generations which were before us, even them that received his oracles in fear and truth. Humility as a chief Christian virtue There is sound reasoning in the fact that most moral stories are addressed to children and have children in them. For it is in childhood that bad habits can be addressed and sound virtues instilled. And so we learn from our bank of moral stories of a boy named Dick who needed to say please. We read of Godfrey Gordon Gustavus Gore, who needed to learn to shut a door And of Rebecca Offendoort, who made sport of slamming those same doors. There was Jim who ran away from his nurse and was eaten by a lion, and Dirty Jim, who it was reported of him, was never seen clean. And we all know of Jack, who was at first thoughtless, but then with courage slayed a giant And we uphold the virtue of a boy who people loved so, and when people asked why, it was because he never told a lie But when such lessons are not learned well when we are children, they are much more difficult to learn when we are adults and still young. The difficulty of being young, young adults, again with lusts that are at their strongest and energy at its greatest. Makes it difficult to fight off temptation and to follow a path of righteousness rather than personal pleasure or gain. But God has great hope for the young Let us not forget passages in the Bible that speak directly to the young adult. St. Paul instructed Timothy to not allow others to look down on him because he was young. When commissioning Jeremiah to prophesy, God would not let Jeremiah have the excuse of being young. God said to him, Do not say, do not say, I am only a youth. For to all to whom I send you shall go up, you shall go up, and whatever I command, you shall speak And hear this from Ecclesiastes. Rejoice, O young man, in your youth. And let your heart cheer you in the days of your youth Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, in your youth And from the prophet Joel, as repeated by Saint Peter. God said, And it shall come to pass afterward that I will pour out my spirit on all flesh. Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy. We are to see from such passages that God has a call on a young person's life. As age is not a determining factor regarding what can be accomplished in the name and power of Jesus Christ. The second generation Christians needed to hear such a truth and Clement gave it to them. And we need to hear the same truth. And so I pass it along, and may it be repeated to every generation until the Lord returns. Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious God, we thank you for the call on young men and young women to be fruitful in your kingdom, to be used by you for the sake of your kingdom. To do things that you are calling them to do that are standing up to the temptations of the world and being a witness to the grace you so freely offer. May that be true for our youth, we ask, in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Ignatius
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I know with age the memory fades. Have we sung that song before? That was new to me. She smiles, yes. Begin with a little narrative this morning. The two teams on the field that Saturday afternoon were equal in size and strength and skill. They were not bitter rivals, but because key players knew one another, the victor would thoroughly enjoy the moment while the loser would surely taste bitterness. The home team had a sound lead going into the second half, but a few mistakes led to the score being tied at the end of the game. In the first overtime, both teams scored, and both teams missed their extra point In the second overtime, both teams scored touchdowns and two-point conversions, leading to a third overtime. Where the visiting team scored first and then failed on their extra point try. If the home team scored a touchdown on the next possession and Scored their extra point, the victory would be theirs. The home team got the ball down to the opponent's four-yard line. It was third down The coach sent in the play. Trips right, rifle right. Rifle is a quick screen to a wide receiver. Because the play had been called earlier with little success, the receiver that was to get the ball decided that he would run a slant route instead. When the quarterback looked to throw the rifle pass, no one was there. He then spotted the receiver running a slant route and Only it was run in the drop zone of an outside defender who easily intercepted the pass. Game over. Home team loses in triple overtime on a play that wasn't to be what it was. Of all the team sports to play, football provides the greatest need for teamwork And as such, plays can become disasters when just one player does his own thing. In other team sports, teamwork is certainly needed for success, but it is usually teamwork that requires adjustments in the middle of a play. In basketball, teams run plays, but the plays are never done without someone improvising. Lacrosse is the same, soccer is the same. But with football, a specific play is called, and even if the play is changed at the line of scrimmage, it is still the same play for all the players. And when there is improvisation needed, it is usually known improvisation For example, when a pass play is called and and the defense lines up in a particular coverage that would impede the receiver's route. The receiver knows and the quarterback knows the adjustments. They've already been planned, they've already been practiced. If a running play is called and a and a defense aligns itself differently than expected, The offensive linemen make different calls to one another to change the way the play is blocked. If a player doesn't understand the call, doesn't understand What the call is supposed to have him do, or doesn't care to hear the call, the play is not going to work. And I often think of the lessons the game of football teaches when I observe and participate in church ministry. That has people running their own plays instead of running the play the director has called. And no, I'm not talking about St. Stephen's My observation is more on the diocesan level or in the denomination level. And my football analogy will serve well as we learn about Ignatius of Antioch. In this third installment in our series, Summer of the Saints, Ignatius was another second-generation Christian after the apostles He is thought to have been a disciple of John the Baptist. I'm sorry, John the Baptist, John the Apostle. He is thought to have served the church as bishop of Antioch in the city of Antioch, and thus he was called Ignatius of Antioch. Ignatius died a martyr's death having been eaten by lions, although it is not verifiable whether him being fed to the lions was inside or outside an arena. Before his death, Ignatius served the persecuted Christians around the world by writing to them letters of encouragement and instruction And it is from his letters that we get to know the most about him. And what stands out to me from the seven letters that are available to us Is first the dedication Ignatius had to the hierarchy of the church and the need to obey said hierarchy. And second, his call for Christians to be stalwarts in any society in which they were citizens. The Christian call to be stalwarts, to be firm, to be steadfast The unwavering citizens of a society is primarily found in Ignatius' letter to Polycarp, who was a co-laborer, and we will touch on him very soon. The call for Christians to be stalwarts in the societies in which they live is akin to the teaching of Jesus, where he describes his followers to be salt and light of the earth We heard that in our gospel reading. We know salt to be both a preservative and to adding flavor. We know light as a beacon in darkness to expose what is true and to expose what is real. Christians are to preserve what is holy and righteous, what is morally upright and virtuous for societies in which they live. The United States and some of Europe are still being blessed by the residual effect of the dominant Christian ethic that permeated those cultures for hundreds of years. The farther away we go from such an ethic, the more shameful our culture becomes Hear these instructions for Christians to be strong in their faith. Ignatius said this, stand firm, as does an anvil which is beaten. It is the part of a noble athlete to be wounded and yet to conquer. And especially we ought to bear all things for the sake of God, that He also may bear with us. Be ever becoming more zealous than what thou art. Weigh carefully the times. Look for him who is above all time, eternal and invisible. Yet who became visible for our sakes, impalpable and impassable. End quote Because of these instructions, we should be reminded of the words of Jesus in that high holy prayer, where he prayed to the Heavenly Father. That his followers would be in the world, but not of the world. In order for Christians to stand firm, we must not be influenced by the ever-changing spirits. that tried to lead us to trust in anything except for God. Our standards are of old And our God is the God of ages past and the future that lies ahead. And he does not change, and therefore, neither does his standards of right and wrong. of truth and falsehood, of what is holy and what is unclean. It is necessary, during these troubled times in which we live, for Christians to be unmoved. Regarding the moral standards God has established for all people. It is for us to remain steadfast So that when people of the world get tired of chasing their tail, get tired of reaping a great deal of pain from what they have sown. Get so diseased that their bodies no longer feel pleasure. Get so lowly of conscience that they can't stand aside of themselves. And if they dare at that moment to seek God and turn from their sin, the church, the Christians, are to be there to turn to and model. Model the way of mercy, healing, and holiness. Consider if we don't remain stalwarts for the societies in which we live. Who is going to exemplify truth in teaching and living if Christians do not? The answer is no one. It really is up to us to preserve a semblance of a society that can retain a common sense of decency and decorum toward our fellow man and toward ourselves. And we need such societies for the gospel to be heard so that God's kingdom can be established, because that's what Christ came to do. Ignatius also understood that for Christians to be the stalwart of the societies in which they live, it must begin with the husband and the wife. He wrote this, quote, speak to my Christian sisters that they love the Lord and be satisfied with their husbands in both flesh and spirit. In like manner also exhort my brethren in the name of Jesus Christ that they love their wives, even as the Lord the church. Now these words are the same, written by St. Peter, written by St. Paul. For Christians to be a preservative for society, we must lead in being examples in our homes. And that does not mean that there is not sin in our homes, that there's not disappointment in our lives. Of course, there is. It means that no matter what our circumstance, no matter what sins are committed, no matter what disappointments come our way, self-inflicted or otherwise We remain true to our marriage vows, to our baptism vows, to our duty to be the husband and wife and parents God has instructed us to be. And don't listen to the devil. Don't listen when he tells you that because you struggle, that you cannot fulfill your duty or your vows. Rebuke him and such lies, and keep on trying. Stay in the fight. Keep trying until your days on this earth are done. And if you do, and if you do, The devil will stay under your feet, for that's where Jesus placed him. In his continuing instruction on marriage being a foundation for a good Christian witness to the world, Ignatius turns our attention slightly by saying the following, quote. It becomes both men and women who marry to form their union with the approval of the bishop. That their marriage may be according to God, and not after their own lust. Let all things be done to honor God. End quote Such words are not familiar to our hearing. We don't often think of ecclesiastical hierarchy having any involvement in choosing who we marry, our husband or our wife. But Ignatius expected as much from Christians and much more when it involves the authority of ecclesiastical officers. The mentioning of the authority of a bishop then leads Ignatius to address the issue of ecclesiastical authority to a greater extent. He says this next. Give ye heed to the bishop, that God also may give heed to you. My soul be for theirs that are submissive to the bishop, to the presbyters, and to the deacons. And may my portion along with them be in God. Have you ever considered that the manner you treat your bishops Your pastors, your deacons, will be returned to you in the manner that God treats you. If you haven't considered such, please know that Ignatius considered it and believed it. In each of the seven letters we have, as Ignatius the author, we find a section in every one of them. dedicated to how Christians are to treat their ecclesiastical authority. To the Smyrmayans, he instructs Christians to do nothing without the bishop. Specifically he said, Let no man do anything connected with the church without the bishop. Let that be deemed a proper Eucharist, which is administered either by a bishop or by one to whom He has entrusted it. Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude also be. Even as wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the church. To the church at Philadelphia he said essentially the same. To the Trollians he instructed that their submissiveness to their bishop is as the same as their submissiveness to Christ. To submit to their proper bishop, their proper presbyter, their proper deacon was to protect them from false teachers. To the Magnesians he said the same, and to the Ephesians he said the same. And again, such teaching is foreign to our ears. It is, however, the same instruction St. Paul gave when he said that we are to be imitators of him, following him, for he, our leader, follows Christ. It is the same as is taught in the letter to the Hebrews, where it says, if you remembered, obey those who rule over you and be submissive. For they watch out for your souls as those who must give account. Let them do so with joy and not with grief, for that would be unprofitable for you. American Christian ears don't hear such a connection between our obedience to our bishops and other clergy and our obedience to God But the second generation Christians did. They saw the connection. Now I now bring these two themes together for us that I'm highlighting from Ignatius. Christians are to be stalwarts, the salt, the light, the unchanging truth for each society in which we live. And in order to do so, we must be submissive to our ecclesiastical authority. In the history of the Christian church, the ability of Christians to be stalwarts of their respective societies has been repeatedly undermined By laity who disrespect and refuse to submit to their church authority Sure, and I I give this, sure. We have different denominations because we have many different personalities with certain types of appreciation for certain types of worship expressions. Sure. But many of those denominations sprung up because of people who were unwilling to submit to the ecclesiastical authority over them. And yes, there have been good reasons for Christians not to obey certain leaders because those leaders were ungodly. I get that too. But I submit that the majority of denominations that have arisen in North America and Europe were because someone wanted to be in charge instead of submitting to their church authority. Lament with me this morning. Lament with me about the damage that has been done to our Christian witness because so many people in the church refuse to submit to their church authority. Lament because our contribution as Christians Lament because of our contribution as Christians to the fact that abortion is considered a right and sex outside of marriage is thought to be normal in our society. And you say, how have we Christians contributed to such sins? It is because We have divided ourselves in multiple ways that the Christian church has no voice that is heeded or even paid attention to. Answer this. What is the Christian Church's view on the topic of abortion? One denomination will say they are against it. Another denomination will say they're for it. Another denomination will say nothing for fear of offending. One independent church will have one pastor against it and another for it in certain circumstances, with the biggest independent church in town never speaking on the topic. How can an unbelieving people who don't know moral truth find any type of moral compass if the church has no voice to lead them Lament with me how times have so drastically changed from the turn of the 20th century unto today. I was just reading a book that was describing at the turn of the 20th century that a local town had headlines in their local paper About a new Christian church being built. And there was regular updates, front-page news of a new Christian church being built in the town of Fort Dodge, Iowa And there were editorials about this new building that this new building was going to serve the entire community well. That is what happened in 1915 in Fort Dodge, Iowa, and many towns across America. But no more. It seems that the only time a Christian church gets a headline is when there's another scandal that's revealed. As the prophet Isaiah said, Woe is me, for I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and I live amidst the people of unclean lips. But what is to be done? The problem is rather large and we are rather small compared to the problem. Yes, we are small. But the Lord our God loves the small things. God uses small seeds to grow large plants. He uses a small group of men to spread his gospel over all of the world. God uses small things. He uses a staff He uses a jawbone. He uses a young boy's lunch to do big things. Thus he can use us. We will have a new bishop soon enough. And we will be challenged to submit to him. And that means to follow his lead when he says, go this way. It won't be easy to submit, but we must, for in such submission we are trusting God. We are obeying Him, just as Ignatius taught We are a relatively small parish in this community, and yet if we stand firm in the faith And that means firm in the moral truths of Holy Scripture, even while all moral truth is crashing down around us If we stand firm, we will be used of God to guide the lost to the truth as God reveals it. Regardless of how confused our culture becomes regarding morality, if we remain the stalwart of South Carroll County, God can use us to guide the lost To the light, to the truth, to eternal life. You see, folks, God has already called the place We're just supposed to run them. We're supposed to do as we have been instructed. We are not to run our own plays. We're not to make up new ones. were to do what he has already installed. To run the plays God has called, and to do so as a team. Is the only way, the only way we will make a difference in our small corner of the world. Amen. Let us pray. Our God, our help in ages past, our truth for that which is to come. We thank you for not changing We desperately need to understand that we too must stand where you do. Father, help us to be used by you. To hold on to the truths that you have revealed. To do so, ever ready to speak the truth as the world seeks it. As we ask and pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Polycarp
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated Our series again is The Summer of the Saints, and I want to force upon you a commercial. of sorts. Last week after uh dwelling and and conversing with Bobby Lynn after the service I realized that the sermon that I preached last week is a good description of how I see St. Stephen's in the future. of what we stand for, what we strive for, of what we want to do and be. So I encourage you to Take advantage of that sermon online if you haven't. It gives you opportunity to get a picture of where I am going as a rector in regards to leading this parish. Today, again, we look at another saint, but we start with the Apostle John. John was the last surviving apostle. He moved to Ephesus to serve the church by writing his gospel. He was nearly a hundred years old when he died, but it was John who ordained a man named Polycarp as bishop of Smyrna, which was a city just north of Ephesus. Ignatius, we learned about last week, passed through the city of Smyrna on his way to his martyrdom when Polycarp was 35 years old. Polycarp took it upon himself to collect the letters of Ignatius and have them passed throughout the Christian church. Several Christian historians record that very fact. Polycarp was martyred himself at age 86, which means that he was given a good amount of time in life to minister to the Christian church. His martyrdom is important to repeat to each generation of Christians, for it was not the simple fact that he was willing to die for His Savior, but the manner that he died is to be appreciated by all The events that led to the martyrdom of Polycarp saw many young Christians dying in the arena during the reign of Domitian, Emperor of Rome. Many were tortured before they were fed to the wild beasts. Because so many young Christians suffered bravely, the crowd got a little anxious and started to cry out for more Christian blood. And the crowd got so excited at one point they started to chant for the blood of Ponycarp, a well-known leader of the Christians. When Polycarp heard of their chant, he wanted to remain in town, but members of the church persuaded him to leave and distance himself from the city. While away three days he spent every day praying, until he had a vision of a pillow burning, which he interpreted as his necessary fate. Although Polycarp was not yet captured, a young man who knew of his whereabouts was captured and tortured until he confessed what he knew. Troops with weapons as if they were arresting a robber came at night to the sleeping place of Polycarp, and although he was given enough time to escape He relented, saying, The will of God be done. When he met his captors, they were so very impressed by his health and by his mind and by his graciousness that they stayed with him to eat and drink, and even allowing him a personal time, an hour of prayer alone. When his prayer was done, they placed him on a donkey and brought him back to the city of Smyrna When in the city, the captain of the captors tried to persuade him regarding the easiness to have the charges dropped against him if he would only burn incense to Caesar. Of course, he refused. At his refusal, all decorum was lost amongst his captors, and they started beating him. But he did not let out a cry, but made his way swiftly to the stadium. And when he came into the stadium, The noise was so loud, they say, that not a single human voice could be heard. But there was a voice, and it was heard, but it was not from men. It was heard by those around Polycarp, a voice from heaven that said, Be strong, Polycarp, and play the man. Once again, the leaders who condemned him tried to persuade Polycarp to give allegiance to Caesar and to condemn the Christians. He refused. Instead, he asked if he could have a chance to testify what it means to be Christian. The proconsul said that he could speak to the crowd, but Polycarp, hearing their chants for his blood, knew that they were not there to listen to him speak. He requested an audience of the pro-council personally, but that was denied. Again, a magistrate tried to persuade him to swear an oath to Caesar and to revile Christ And Polycarp responded with the following. Quote, 86 years have I been his servant, and he has done me no wrong How then can I blaspheme my king who saved me? By threat of being torn apart by wild beasts to threats of being burned alive, they continued to call him to repent, ironically, of his Christian faith. Their hope was that if a leader of his stature, of his importance, of Christians If his leadership he would turn from them, well the rest of the church would follow Soon the crowd called for him to be burned alive, and the followers of Polycarp remembered his vision. What happened next was with great speed, the crowd immediately collected timber and sticks from workshops and the baths, and the Jews more especially assisted. He removed his clothes so that the flames would touch his skin quickly. They desired to nail him to a stake, but he insisted that he would not flee the flames, and that he would remain unmoved. Before the fire was lit, he prayed a loud prayer, thanking God for the privilege of knowing Jesus as his Savior, and for the privilege of dying a martyr's death, to honor his God. After his death, there was great disagreement as to what to do with his body, for some leaders feared the remains would be worshipped by his followers His bones were eventually collected and placed in what they said was a suitable place. Afterward it was said that Polycarp, even by unbelievers, That he gave up his life in a distinguished manner. Polycarp did indeed play the man. Yet I wonder when I read that quote from the voice of God, for Polycarp to have courage and to play the man, how many of you were curious as to exactly what does that phrase mean? The phrase is a translation similar to what is translated in the King James Version of 1 Corinthians 16 verse 13, where Paul said this. Watch ye stand fast in the faith. Quit you like men, be strong. Now the word quit has changed quite a bit. The meaning in the Old English used to mean to conduct oneself in a specified way. Not to give up, but to conduct oneself in a specified way. The specified way in the Corinthian passage is like a man. Today we might translate it more loosely to mean be like a man should be. That is not politically correct, for today we are told that men are not masculine by nature or by calling, but by social constructs that need to be torn down But we here are not politically correct. We embrace what it should mean to be a man Which is to say we believe in courage, in bravery, in fortitude, and being steadfast in the truths that God has revealed to us. That is what God calls men to be. And so quit like a man is to live like a true man. And thus to play the man is to live up to the standards God has set for men. And in the context of Polycarp, it was to remain firm in the faith, in his faith, in the Lord Jesus Christ, in the midst of suffering. In the midst. The need, the need to remain steadfast was not new to Polycarp when God's voice instructed him. In his writings, specifically his letter to the Church of Philippi, he instructs deacons to be servants of God, and he says, be servants of God, not men. Ministers can become servants of men when they fear men, for when a minister fears men He will work to appease them, and that will cause him to compromise. When a minister compromises, he doesn't instruct directly what the scriptures say. He doesn't touch on the sins of those in his congregation because they might disapprove and show that they disapprove. He doesn't rebuke and exhort as he should because men are more comfortable being told how righteous they are as opposed to how they need to repent. Many a church has floundered and then died, and families have gone to hell because ministers have compromised the truth for fear of men. To play the man in the church is to serve God first, middle, and last. But playing the man did not mean for Polycarp that he didn't need to be gentle and understanding. Playing the man means that as well For to the presbyters he said, quote, Let the Presbyters be compassionate and merciful to all, bringing back those that wander. Visiting all the sick and not neglecting the orphan or the poor, but always providing for that which is becoming in the sight of God and man Abstaining from all wrath, respect of persons, and unjust judgment, keeping far off from all covetousness. not severe in judgment as knowing that we are all under a debt of sin. End quote Thus, to play the man, to be strong as a man, includes being as God, as God is. which is slow to anger, having compassion on the weak, and desiring people everywhere to repent and find mercy. A person who plays the man understands he is a sinner, and therefore he has compassion on sinners. Polycarp understood that playing the man also meant to practice the fruits of the Spirit in all circumstances. It meant persevering in our hope. It meant being imitators of the patience of Jesus. It meant to exercise all patience, all clothes from Polycarp. Hear these words describing what it means to play the man. He said, Stand fast, therefore, in these things, be firm and unchangeable in the faith. This type of message we remember from Ignatius. It is very easy to bend to the ways of the world, for that is what most people are doing around us. To be on the narrow road as Christians are to be means that we cannot bend with the wind. We cannot shift with the shadows. When Jesus asked the rhetorical question that when he returns, will he find faith on this earth? He did so to imply how difficult it is to remain faithful amidst an unbelieving world that doesn't like people remaining faithful, especially religious people remaining faithful. In remaining faithful, if it wasn't difficult, then no one would be called to do it. Polycarp writes about a presbyter who gave up his call and therefore left the narrow road. His name was Valens V-A-L-E-N-S. Polycarp said of him, quote, he so little understands the place that was given to him in the church. He continued, I am deeply grieved, therefore, brethren, for Valens and his wife, to whom may the Lord grant true repentance. Although we don't know what Valens did to give up his calling in the church, Polycarp alludes to it by his instructions in the context of mentioning this valence. He said, I exhort you therefore that ye abstain from covetousness, and that ye be chaste and truthful For if a man cannot govern himself in such matters, he shall how shall he enjoin them on others? If a man does not keep himself from covetousness, he shall be defiled by idolatry And shall be judged as one of the heathen. But from these words we are to understand That to play the man is to live with a fruit of the spirit that we know of as self-control. Being a man means To be under control. And a major part of self-control is controlling the tongue. It is the opposite of living virtuous, to let your tongue wag as you feel it should. The devil gets people to think that they are being virtuous when they are bold to express their feelings about something, or to get something off of their chest, as we like to say. Bold expressions of opinion are not godly, but of the flesh. And such expressions of the flesh usually lead to having to apologize later. A person who is playing the man doesn't need to express his passions in words, but he is instead self-controlled. speaking when it is appropriate and to the advantage of those who would hear him. Being self-controlled in the context of Polycarp's words about balance was to appreciate that one has what one has as opposed to what others have. The sin of covetousness is so easy to practice. It is a natural part of our fallen sinfulness to want what we don't have and want it just because we don't have it. As a minister, it can be difficult to know that people who might have much less of an education can make twice as much, even more, than you do. But that is the way of it, and has always been the way of it, television false prophets being the exception But I have never been in need. My daily bread and that of my children when they were under our roof has always been provided. The way political candidates talk today, you would think that most Americans go to bed every night hungry. The truth is we are the most wealthy people the world has ever known, and that's a historical fact And poverty around the world is at its lowest point ever. The point being that we have what we need, despite what the devil places in front of us, tempts us to covet. Those who witnessed Valens betray his clerical call because of coveting needed to be warned against such a sin, and so do we. With the call to live under self-control, we can see that to play the man is not just a masculine thing to do, but rather a call for all Christians. in all circumstances. And this gives us insight to be able to say that to play the man is more than to behave like a man should, it is to be like Jesus. who was and is the very essence of what God intended humanity to be. Hence we can conclude that when God told Polycarp to play the man, It was more than a reference to behaving like a man should. It was pointing to the man who was also God. Now the martyrdom of Polycarp played a very important role in our Anglican Way heritage. But before I get to that, I want to say a word about being Anglican. There are some Christians who don't like titles or distinctions such as Anglican. They seem to think that such distinctions betray the purity of what it means to be a Christian. Without any distinction. Such thinking is ideal, I agree, but is without a sense of reality Being Christian today and for quite some time means different things to different people, many different things. For example, there are people who claim to be Christian who do not believe Jesus was God Which is a primary doctrine for Christianity. There are people who confess Jesus as Savior who do not trust what the Bible teaches. There are people who say they are Christian and who have been ordained as clergy to serve the church who say that the resurrection of Jesus never occurred and that Jesus wasn't even a historical figure. Thus, to say we are Anglican is to say that we are following a certain understanding of the Christian faith that is rooted in the Holy Scriptures. and in the liturgy of the church handed down by Christians of the English-speaking world, that's Anglican. As Reformed Episcopalians, we are identifying as a unique expression of Anglicanism that expresses our Christian faith by teaching and preaching the whole Council of God, all of the Bible. And worshiping God according to the order of the historic book of common prayer. The historic book of common prayer. In short, to say I am Anglican is like saying I am Jorgensen or I am Smith or whatever your surname is. By identifying with the same name Jorgensen doesn't say I'm not a part of the human race. It is merely saying that I am a particular tribe of the human race. Thus to say I am Anglican is to say I am Christian of a particular tribe. But back to Polycarp's contribution to our Anglican heritage. In 1555, moving way up on the calendar, Hugh Latimer was a former Bishop of Worcester And an influential priest-preacher of the Protestant way. Nicholas Ridley was Bishop of London and a supporter of Lady Jane Gray to be Queen as opposed to who we now know as Bloody Mary. When Mary took the throne, both men were arrested for treason, and both were declared guilty after their trials and sentenced to death. Before the judgment was carried out, they were called to repent of their Protestant ways, but they refused They were next chained to their respective stakes, and a bag of gunpowder was hung over each man's neck, around each man's neck. And it was at some point during that time that Hugh Latimer said, quote, Be of good comfort, Master Ridley, and play the man. For we shall this day light such a candle by God's grace in England as shall never be put out. Vladimir was remembering the martyrdom of Polycarp as he was being martyred. It is a story to tell every generation. As a conclusion to remembering St. Polycarp, we can be challenged to commit to being willing and able to die for the gospel. After several years teaching introductory philosophy at college-level classes I will remember most how the majority of students confessed that they could not think of anything that they were willing to die for. Not even a family member was worth their own life being sacrificed. This means that for some people they do not have in their lives enough love for something That they would do anything in order to keep that something alive. How sad. And yet that is what the good news of Jesus does for us. It gives us something to love so much, we are willing, and for some, even happy to die for it. May we, along with Polycarp, play the man every day we are given in this world, and may we be able to say in the end something similar about Jesus as All my days have I been his servant, and he has done me no wrong. How can I then blaspheme my King who saved me? Amen. Let us pray. God, we thank you for the persons like Polycarp. We thank you to see how much the gospel affects lives to the point of giving up those lives. Father, we see the standard and we embrace it. May it be so for all here. We pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Justin the Martyr
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I spoke briefly last week about defending why Christians can use identifiers like Anglican And I am going to expand on that explanation here to show the value of our next Saint in our Summer of the Saints series. Let us imagine you want to be able to say that to be a Christian for you is to love Jesus, and that is the only distinction that you need. You love Jesus. Or perhaps you're a part of a local church that says in bold letters in his bulletin each week, we have no creed but Christ. It's a very catchy phrase indeed. But when you are asked a series of questions that go as follows, let's see if that stands up. Questioner says, okay, you say that you love Jesus. Can you tell me who Jesus is? Answer, your savior, you say. Questioner, yes, but who was he? What was he? What did he do? How is he your savior? Answer. Oh, um, well, he was conceived by the Holy Spirit and was born of the Virgin Mary. Questioner. So he was God because he was conceived by the Holy Spirit? Answer. Well, yes, but Not only God, he was the son of Mary, his mother also. Questioner. Oh, so he was half God and half man. Answer. Well, no. He was fully God and fully man. Questioner. Wait, what? How can that be? Answer. Yeah, I don't know, but that is what the church decided that the Bible teaches. Questioner. Wait, what church What are you talking about? Answer. Oh, well, yeah. The church uh had a number of gatherings of its leaders to clearly spell out what the Bible teaches to combat a number of heretical teaching about Jesus and God in general. And it was at those gatherings that it was agreed that the Bible teaches that Jesus is both fully God and fully man. Questioner. But what about what you said about you loving Jesus was the only distinction you need? Answer. Okay. Yes, that is what I said, but now I see that I need to clarify who Jesus is before such a statement can help anyone believe in Jesus. Questioner, okay, okay, I can accept that. Let's try another approach. You said that you need to love Jesus, and that was enough, but why do you love Jesus? What did he do for you to love him so much? Answer. Aha, yes, that's easy.
