He died for my sins, and therefore I can be forgiven and go to heaven. Questioner. Yes, of course. Of course. And did he die for only your sins? Answer: No, he died for the sins of all humanity, for the whole world. Questioner, oh, so then does the whole world go to heaven? Answer, well, no, the Bible doesn't teach that. It teaches that you have to believe in Jesus. Questioner, believe what about Jesus? Answer: That he was the Savior who died for the sins of humanity, and all that believe in him would receive a heavenly reward. Question. But how does one believe? Answer. Oh, again, I can easily answer that. You confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, you believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, and then you are baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. And you're saved. Questioner, what does it mean to be baptized? Answer. Well you are dumped in water while the three names of God are proclaimed. Questioner. So you have to be dumped to be baptized? Answer. Well no. There's other ways, such as pouring water and sprinkling water. Questioner, but what about those three names you mentioned? I thought it was just that you needed to love Jesus. Answer. Yes, well, again. Perhaps that wasn't the most helpful way to explain the Christian faith. There is also the doctrine of the Trinity that why don't we close the curtain on that discussion and recognize that Being Christian and just loving Jesus and having no creed but Christ is not an effectual testimony to the world, nor is it a defense of what Christians believe. Our saint this morning is known as Justin Martyr. Justin Martyr Was one of the first apologists or defenders of the Christian faith after Jesus and after Paul And once again, we are confronted with the word that has an old meaning to it. Apology used to mean defense, rather than saying, I'm sorry. Justin Martyr was a defender of the Christian faith. Personally, he was born at the end of the first century to non-Christian parents. His lineage was either Greek or Roman. His young education was unsatisfying to him, leaving him hungry for greater inspiration. He gravitated toward the study of Plato in his older years, and that seemed to give him the needed paradigm to better understand the world around him. By providence of God, Justin was walking by a seashore when he met an old man And the man told him that the path of the philosopher was ultimately barren, and that true enlightenment could come only from understanding and embracing Christianity. After listening to the old man, Justin concluded that he must follow both his wisdom and his own desire for the divine. So he started to study Christianity. After being exposed to Christians who were living an honest and chaste life that revealed a true faith in God. Justin committed himself to spread the knowledge of Christianity as the true philosophy, as he called it. Justin started out going from town to town, debating philosophers publicly. He founded a philosophical school in Rome where he himself taught the students. Because of his mission work to spread Christianity, because of his teaching of Christian doctrine to these young students It was the conclusion of Roman leaders that Justin was corrupting young minds with what they called godlessness. For Justin rebutted the Roman belief in many gods, teaching that there was just one. He and some of his students were arrested, and after a sham trial, were beheaded His death was somewhere between 162 and 168 A. D. , hence the name Justin the Martyr. Justin faced his martyrdom with the same bravado and confidence in God's grace as did Polycarp. When he was told that he would be tortured without mercy if he did not obey Rome, he replied this, quote, that is our desire. to be tortured for our Lord Jesus Christ, and so to be saved, for that will give us salvation and firm confidence at the more terrible universal tribunal of our Lord and Savior. In his writings, Justin Martyr left the church what is called first apology. Which is a defense of Christianity. And it was written personally to the Roman Emperor Antonius Pius and his sons and the Roman Senate. He next wrote the second apology written to the Roman Senate only. He wrote several other works, but only a few we have today. One was called a discourse to the Greeks and was a discussion with Greek philosophers about the character of their so-called gods. And another described the sovereignty, the doctrine of the sovereignty of God. Now from Justin's first apology, we learn the following from this third-generation Christian. First, Christianity is rational, and that can be demonstrated when compared to other religions of the world. Second, Christians uphold a higher moral standard, and that should be evident to both those fellow citizens and to their rulers. Third, a logos can be seen in all of men and is a uniting reality for all human beings Fourth, false gods are used by demons to corrupt humanity and should be seen as such. And fifth, what Christians are actually doing when they worship. So first, Christianity is rational. To say in general that God exists is most certainly rational. Christians need to stop being embarrassed or feeling inferior because we believe there is a God. Concluding that all of creation is a byproduct of a chief designer who created all things is not irrational. It is most certainly not improbable. Honest scientists confess as much. Early Christians faced a different argument. Because they believed in only one God, they were actually called atheists. Their rejection of the many gods of Greek and Roman mythology was deemed to be a threat to the culture of the Romans. And Justin responded in this aggressive manner. He said, and we confess that we are atheists. So far as gods of this sort are concerned But not with respect to the most true God, the Father of righteousness and temperance and other virtues, who is free from all impurity. I hope you hear from such words what I hear, which is an aggressive defense of the Christian faith, defending it in a bold manner, not being shy. Sometimes Western Christianity has portrayed itself as effeminate when it comes to standing up for our faith. For some, there appears to be an embrace of a necessary softness, as if Jesus was only kind. only soft-spoken, only polite in all circumstances, and so Christians must be the same. But that was not the perspective of early Christians, for they needed to be tough in living out their faith and in speaking their faith. Nothing was going to be given to them that made life easier for them to live. There was no hate crime laws back then. There were no cultural condemnations against being prejudiced. And Christians were the new minority in the world, and that new minority required that they turn the other cheek. But turning the other cheek and giving an extra cloak when asked does not mean Christians should not be bold in proclaiming the truth of Christ and defending against lies spoken about them. Like the Old Testament prophets, Justin was bold to compare the God of Christianity to the many false gods that were worshipped in Rome. He said, quote, and neither do we honor with many sacrifices and garlands of flowers such deities as men have formed, and set in shrines and called gods. Since we see that these are soulless and dead, and have not the form of God, but have the names and forms of those wicked demons which have appeared. And then regarding the idols themselves carved to honor the gods, he wrote, We consider such carvings not only senseless, but to be even insulting to God. who having ineffable glory and form, thus gets his name attached to things that are corruptible and require constant service. Does not Justin show a bravado in these words that is lacking today Coincidentally, I read an article on Tuesday of this week about an international weightlifting competition that was under protest Because it was won by a transgender male who self-identified as a female winning this female weightlifting contest. That is ridiculous. It's absolutely absurd. And I'm not talking about the fact that women shouldn't be having weightlifting competitions. I bring the topic of transgender up at this point, of showing bravado, because our culture has turned itself upside down regarding sex and gender issues. And Christians should speak up and say so. Not only do we have God's word on our side, we have common sense. God is installed within the created order What is called natural law allows us to say to such a confused culture that men are designed to be men and women are designed to be women. That is the way of it, and it is good To teach and practice otherwise is to harm and eventually destroy the human race. We have every right to say that, and we should. Regarding the morality of Christians compared to unbelieving people St. Justin explained that Christians are the best of citizens, and the crimes that they commit, such as not worshiping the gods of Rome and other such laws that are broken Those laws do not corrupt society. Breaking them does not corrupt society. But when such laws as stealing, conspiracy, whoredom, and alike are committed, these are what undermine a society. And such sins are overlooked, Justin said, compared to the manner that Christians are treated. And while we agree with St. Justin on this point, We need to be careful. For we cannot claim that Christians live consistently according to the moral standards that God has set for us. The devil has gotten away with the claim through his servants that Christianity can be disproven by the hypocritical lives of those who claim to love Jesus But it does not follow that the moral standards taught in Christianity are false because there are people who fail to meet such standards. Our faith is placed in the one man who met all the standards and yet was hung on a cross. We place our hypocrisy We place our hypocrisy at the foot of the cross of Jesus crucified and plead for his mercy every day. And he promises to give such mercy to all who ask of him. Saint Justin also argued that the truths of the Christian doctrine can be seen in the teachings of others who did not know Jesus as the Christ. He argued that there is a Logos that is revealed to all, and that Logos is a universal truth fully revealed, fully revealed in Jesus. He wrote, quote, If therefore on some points we teach the same things as the poets and philosophers whom you honor, And on other points are more fuller and more divine in our teaching. And if we alone afford proof of what we assert, why are we unjustly hated more than others? He then refers to the teachings of Plato and of the Stoics to show just how similar Christian doctrine is to the wisest of secular minds. Another bold expression of how St. Justin exposes what is behind the teachings of the Romans and their myth gods. He said, But those who hand down myths Which the poets have made, adduce not proof to the youth who learn them. And we proceed to demonstrate that they have been uttered by the influence of the wicked demons To deceive and lead astray the human race. He goes on to identify all false teachings of other gods, but Jesus as being of the devil. And if he did, shouldn't we? It is not yet against Western law to publicly say that Allah is not God And that Muhammad is not God's prophet. And even if it becomes law to forbid such statements, Christians must still say it. We can and should say that the Jesus of the Jehovah's Witnesses and the Mormon Church is not the true Jesus. And the Jewish faith is incomplete in its faith, for it is only fulfilled by believing in Jesus as the Messiah. Christians should never shy away from stating such truth. It is part of our pilgrimage to say such truth St. Justin also takes the time to explain to the Emperor and the Senate what Christians are doing with their rituals. Baptism, they didn't understand. He said is an act of using water to regenerate sinners to live new lives. He interprets Jesus' words that his followers must be born of both water and the Spirit to be referring to the ritual of baptism. After baptism, it is the Christian duty to gather together for corporate worship, where Justin describes the memoirs of the apostles. being read and taught. Prayers are offered at length, and the sacrament of eating bread and drinking wine is practiced, but only by those who have been baptized. Thus Christians are not performing rituals in secret, which they were accused of doing, and they were especially not practicing cannibalism. And that accusation came out of quoting Jesus, this is my body, this is my blood. Now, from all of this that I've described of Justin Martyr and tried to portray to you, from all of this, I want you to hear what was part of our epistle reading this morning. Words from St. Peter. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope you possess. Always be prepared. It is understood that not everyone has the same oratory skills, not everyone can articulate the faith in the same way, nor should they But we all can articulate our hope in the way God has given it to us. St. Justin the Martyr is an example of thoughtfulness and bravado. But we do not all have to be the same as him, yet we can all be similar using the gifts God has given each of us. Each of you has a story to tell about God's mercy in your life. Each of you can at least articulate what you believe by reciting a creed. Each of us can confess what we believe to those who ask of us. And we can do so without embarrassment or shyness. For as St. Paul said to Timothy, for God has not given us a spirit of timidity, but of power and love and discipline. So love Jesus, do that, absolutely. And tell the world, when you do, who He is. Dream of that day where there are no distinctions such as Anglicanism or Presbyterian or Baptist. And in the meantime, confess the creeds, hand it down to you. Many died a martyr's death, so that you could. Let us pray. Our Father, for the bravado of Justin the Martyr, we thank you. We know that is your spirit in him working to stand for the truth. And Father, give us each the same courage. Help us to understand the spirit you've given us. And help us to be brave to articulate what you have shown us to be true. to confess Jesus as Lord and Savior. It is in His name that we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Irenaeus
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. Our next Saint in our Summer of the Saints series Is named Irenaeus, Bishop of Lyons. Lyons was and is a well-populated city in France. And in the second century, it was a place of constant Roman persecution against Christians. Irenaeus was a third generation Christian. He testified that he had heard the preaching of Polycarp Who we know as a disciple of the apostles, as the Bishop of Smyrna, and a martyr for Jesus Christ. What we know about Irenaeus personally is very scarce. He tried the monastic life for a time, but it was not fitting for him. He served the Christian church as a missionary, pastor, and bishop. His lasting contribution to the church is where he stood against heresy, and in general, heresy, but specifically Gnosticism. Specifics about his death are unknown. The first known writing of Irenaeus is titled Against Heresies It is an attack on pseudo-Christian groups that embrace Gnosticism and Marcionite doctrines. Before we get to what those are, please hear the following qualifier. We are going to hear why it is important to think biblically, which is rightly. About God, about God the Father, thinking rightly about God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit. We are also going to hear the dangers of thinking wrongly about the same. What you're not going to hear is that a person's salvation is determined by how he or she rightly understands Christian doctrine. Right Christian doctrine doesn't save anybody from sin and death itself. It is by, as you know, the blood of Christ. and the grace of God, and those two things are not to be separated, it is by that that we are forgiven that we have eternal hope. We say by grace alone, by faith in Christ Jesus alone, is anybody saved? Why it is necessary to challenge false teachings called heresies and why it is important to embrace right teachings about Christian faith we call orthodoxy is because where the false teaching leads a person, they can lead us down a road that is wide And many travel on it, when in fact the road for Christians is narrow, and few travel on it. Thus, to be Orthodox in our understanding of the Christian faith is to be amidst a small number of people and a more difficult road to travel. Perhaps it is fair to say that if a Christian teaching, if a movement, if a teacher is popular, you are either in heaven Or you're hearing heresy. So now that we are clear on how we are saved and are not saved, let us look at the teachings of Irenaeus. First, we note that he quotes Holy Scripture profusely and freely. And I read the following to you so that we can all sense the urgency of his teachings against these heretics. Quote, inasmuch as certain men have set the truth aside and bring in lying words and vain genealogies which, as the apostle says, minister questions rather than godly edifying, which is in the faith, and by means of their craftily constructed plausibilities, draw away the minds of the inexperienced and take them captive, these men falsify the oracles of God and prove themselves evil interpreters of the good word of revelation. They also overthrow the faith of many, and by drawing them away under pretense of superior knowledge. Well the words I highlight from that are draw away, captive, and overthrow the faith. In these words are the end concern or the end reality of people hearing and believing false doctrine. These concerns are what Jesus described when he said, For false messiahs and false prophets will appear and perform great signs and wonders to deceive If possible, even the elect. In another place, he said, be on guard against the yeast of the Pharisees and Sadducees. And the gospel writer explained this. He said, then they understood that he was not telling them to guard against yeast used in bread, but against the teaching of the Pharisees and the Sadducees. In Acts, when Paul was leaving the the church in Asia, he left them with this warning. He said, I know after I leave, savage wolves will come in among you and will not spare the flock Even from your own number, men will arise and distort the truth in order to draw away disciples. When referring to the teachings of Paul, St. Peter warned the church this way: Be on guard, so that you may not be carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your secure position. And finally the warning against false teachers from St. John, who said, They are from the world And therefore speak from the viewpoint of the world, and the world listens to them. We are from God, and whoever knows God listens to us. But whoever is not from God does not listen to us. This is how we recognize the spirit of truth and the spirit of falsehood. These are warnings, and there are more, of course, but they suffice to show that Irenaeus and his warning fits the warnings of Scripture. But what are the heresies that he is most concerned about? I have mentioned the dangers of Gnosticism several times from this pulpit And in my other teaching venues, but I want to give you the official description of Gnosticism. It is the belief That the material world was created by a lower God called the Demiurge, and that the divine is a divine spark Trapped within each human, and it can only be released or liberated by gnosis or spiritual knowledge. Thus, Gnosticism doesn't address the subject of sin, since they say sin happens in the physical world and they don't care about the physical world. It only addresses ignorance being overcome by spiritual knowledge. Hence it focuses on the spiritual, not the physical. You might remember how this is a problem, for it was God who created matter and said it was good. It was God who made himself of no reputation, taking on the form, matter of a man, so that he could lead, teach, and sacrifice himself for the sins of humanity. To deny the physicality of Jesus is to call God a liar and to denigrate the humility and sacrifice Jesus provided for our sins. Now from this understanding, we can say that Gnostic beliefs and Christianity do not go together, and therefore Christians label Gnosticism a heresy. And that's all we need to do, right? Just label it a heresy and move on. But it's not that easy. It is not that simple. It is never that simple. While Gnosticism doesn't present itself today as an organized teaching, it has a place within the Christian church today without being identified as Gnosticism, as heresy, and not being rejected. For example, traces of Gnostic belief can be seen in the manner that we treat church buildings. If you have thought that the church building doesn't matter to anything concerning the Christian faith, then perhaps you have been influenced by Gnosticism. At the core of such a thought is that it is the spiritual that matters most, and not the physical. But that is not what the Bible teaches. In fact, St. Paul said that it was first the physical and then the spiritual That is how God created us. He created the physical body of man first, and then breathed into him life, a spirit, his spirit. Consider how the human spirit reacts to buildings that have been clearly set aside for holy use. When you enter cathedrals that were painstakingly built to communicate both beauty and awe Beauty and awe of God and beauty and awe of the gospel that He gave to humanity. The physical beauty of those cathedrals affects your inner spiritual nature. And thus, when you're in those facilities, you act differently, which is to say, you act accordingly, which is to say, you act as you should. And this is preached after hearing the news that in the month of July The second oldest cathedral in England, Rochester Cathedral, had its nave redesigned to be a putt-putt golf course. The stated reason was so that families would come and have fun while considering their spirituality. That is taking the principle of first the physical and then the spiritual to a different end goal or end whole as in whole of one. Alas, that's more tragic than humorous, isn't it? If you are not challenged by the Gnostic tendencies some have and understanding the use of church buildings, then examine if you have ever appreciated or thought about or maybe even wanted a wedding on on a beach or or on a mountain in the mountains or some other venue that was not a physical church A rejection of a church building for nature can also be caused by Gnostic seeds For the church building is the physical image of the body of Christ, and it is by the authority of the church that a couple is pronounced married. Not the state, not a nation, not an individual, but the church only has the authority to pronounce a marriage valid. And the church's symbol of authority is its buildings. If you are not challenged by where weddings take place, consider How you appropriately clothe yourself for worship, or how you view the bread and wine used in Holy Communion. Does your dressing for church services reflect the particular and unique presence of God amidst his people when we gather to worship, focusing solely on him? If not, why not? Consider a seed of Gnosticism as the cause. Is the bread used at Holy Communion like any other bread or tortilla, even though it has been consecrated for holy use and has been called the body of Christ? Is it merely bread and therefore to be treated as mere bread? Is the wine used for holy communion just wine and nothing else, even though it has been consecrated for holy use and called The blood of Christ shed for you. I am well aware of how sensitive some of us can be about the use of wine versus grape juice. If you think it doesn't matter, I ask that you consider if Gnostic thought has influenced you. Jesus took the cup full of wine and said, this is my blood. He didn't take the cup of grape juice. He took wine. I say it with a fatherly heart, asking each of us to examine ourselves to see if seeds of Gnosticism have taken root within us Irenaeus focused on two Gnostic teachers because of their popularity. One of them was named Marcion. Marcion was a contemporary of Irenaeus and was made bishop by his father, who was a bishop. The position of bishop gave the teachings of Marcion authority. Marcion being influenced by Gnostic thought taught a coexistence of Christian teaching and Gnostic teaching, which we said don't go together His first conclusion was that the God of the Old Testament was not the God of the New Testament, for the God of the Old was barbaric. and of condemnation, whereas the God of the new was loving and forgiving. Thus Jesus was not the Son of God of the Jews, but was instead the Son of a good God. The good God was another God. He called it the supreme God. While the God of the Old Testament could be described as the demi-urge from Gnostic thought. It all means nothing to you, I concur. If it all means nothing to you, I concur that it doesn't really mean anything to us. What should matter to all of us is the rejection of the Old Testament, for that meant a rejection of much of the New Testament. It meant that any use of the Old Testament by Jesus in his teachings was to be rejected. Any use of the Old Testament by the teaching purposes of St. Paul and others, rejected. Thus the Marcian doctrines of God and salvation looked a great deal like the doctrines of liberal theologians of today. And the doctrines of theologians today are minimal and non-invasive. They are rejections of what the teacher doesn't want the Bible to say. In short, Marcionites and liberal teachers of today make up their own Bibles as they pick and choose the teachings of Holy Scripture that make their lives more comfortable. Now before I expound on this point, I want to acknowledge that I have preached about the God of the Old Testament being the God of the New Testament many, many, many times. We just finished the book of Genesis, where we saw the person of Jesus throughout the stories of that great book. And thus Jesus can be found in the Old Testament and God used those stories to prepare us for the Jesus to come. I then do not need to say more about that here. What I am concerned about is how susceptible we are to following the Marcion lead and choosing for ourselves our own versions of the Bible. May you and I never have a phone conversation that goes as follows. You. Hi, Pastor Eric. It's been a while since we've talked. Do you have a minute or so? Me? Yes, yes, I do. How can I be of help? You. Well, I wanted you to know that my soul is at peace, more peace than it has ever been, and I have been finding my way back to God. Me. Oh, that sounds wonderful. You. Yes, I I was recently rebaptized, but I had to leave that church because the pastor started preaching against sexual sin And I couldn't handle that type of negativity in my life. So I left. Me. Silence. You. Now I am at another church, and they are very accepting and open, which has made me feel at home, and as I said, at peace. Me. Can I ask why you're calling me? You. Yes, I have been learning some things that I think you should consider, such as the Bible actually doesn't condemn people's sexual preferences. Me. You are aware that I believe it does, and that it always has, and that the Christian Church has always taught that the Bible condemns sexual practices outside of a marriage covenant. You. Oh no. I have learned that it actually doesn't, and that it can be interpreted much differently. My current pastor teaches from the Bible all of the time. And shows us how it doesn't condemn certain behavior, but focuses instead on how we are to be loving and accepting. Me. Silent. Again. I don't have a reply. What reply should I have? I recognize such a conversation for what it is The person talking to me has found a teacher that makes him comfortable in his sin. I have no words that can match such teaching, for such teaching tickles ears. My words will not. I can use sexual sin as an example because it's so prevalent We can leave the sin blank and you can put whatever is your struggle, for we all are tempted in different ways And you can be sure that there is some teacher, some teaching, some pseudo-faith that will tell you, you can do as you like and God will not condemn you because he loves you. And love you he does. Only his love is so great that he calls you out from being in bondage to sin and loves you so greatly. That he provided a way out of that bondage, which is by way of his only son, and loved you so much that he desires you to live a self-controlled life. That allows you to resist the temptations of the flesh. That is the true love of God. The other is a lie The devil is a liar from the beginning. He has not changed his ways. When he tempted Eve in the garden, he called her to question what God has said. Has God indeed said, you shall not eat of every tree of the garden? The seed of doubt as to what God actually said took root in Eve and she sinned. The devil asks the same question today, has God really said? And there are many who allow that doubt of what God has clearly said to take root Irenaeus wrote a great deal against specifics of Gnostic heresy and its teachers. And when he summed up his teachings, he said the following. I have pointed out the truth and showed the preaching of the church, which the prophets proclaimed, as I have demonstrated, but which Christ brought to perfection. And the apostles have handed down, from whom the church, receiving these truths, and throughout all the world alone preserving them in their integrity, has transmitted them to her sons. Then also having disposed of all questions which the heretics proposed to us, and having explained the doctrine of the apostles, I have clearly set forth many of the things which were said and done by our Lord in his parables. I close with that quote because it shows the confidence Irenaeus had of the Holy Scriptures as interpreted by the Church. Such scriptures do not change, and we can spend a lifetime studying them and lifetimes more, and never exhaust the truths therein. Nothing is to be taken away from them. Nothing is to be added to them. A third generation Christian proved as much, and if it was good enough for him. It is good enough for us. Let us pray. Our God We thank you for men like Irenaeus, and we take up the charge that he took up, to be true to your word. To trust in it is the true knowledge of you and of how men can be saved. May that never, ever be denied. I pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Tertullian
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. This next saint in our Summer of the Saints series is not a saint. At least according to Roman and Eastern Orthodox traditions, he has not been canonized a saint. Biblically, he is a saint, for he is of the priesthood of all believers. His contributions were many. But before we get to those, I want to read a quote that was reported two weeks ago in the news about a popular Christian, at least popular in modern Christian music. This person publicly questioned his personal Christian faith and questioned Christianity as a whole. He said the following. This is a soapbox moment, so here I go. How many preachers fall? Many. No one talks about it. How many miracles happen? Not many. No one talks about it. Why is the Bible full of contradictions? No one talks about it. How can God be love and yet send four billion people to a place all cuz they don't believe? No one talks about it. Christians can be the most judgmental people on the planet. They can also be some of the most beautiful and loving people, but it's not for me. And I shared my thoughts about this announcement of a public falling away from the faith during Bible study two weeks ago. With the concern that there may be some of us in this parish who have read books by men who have recently denied the faith or listened to their music or their teachings And when you hear that they have renounced their faith, it burdens you and causes you, perhaps, to doubt your own. As I stated two end days ago, I hate Christian fads. Hate them. And I am leery of popular Christianity, wherever it is. When it was popular to do so, I never bought anything that had WWJD on it. Even though the intent was positive, plus I had too much sarcasm remaining in me at that time of its popularity, that I would answer the question, what would Jesus do I would answer it this way. He would become human, teach us the way to the Father, die for our sins, and raise it, rise again, because that's what he did. And I always thought the question should be, what would Jesus have me do? That question is always worth asking and trying to answer But WWJD is a lot more pithy than WWJHMD. Other things in Christian popularity in the last two decades are books like The Purpose-Driven Life The Left Behind series, the prayer book of Dibets. And I don't know all the what else because I don't again follow Christian Fads. But if you do or have I want to care for you as I don't want you to be discouraged by popular teachings and leaders and singers who turn away from Christ. Their behavior is not new as men and women stop following Christ likely every day. And that is just how Jesus warned it would be. That's why he gave us one of those lines, many are called, but few are chosen. We started this series trying to uphold Christians of the first three centuries Who did truly and honestly believe in Christ Jesus, and their lives and their writings proved that they believed. This was our focus because there is in the back of our minds, we all have to be honest about this. We all in the back of our minds have questions regarding whether Christianity actually works as it promises it will work. We need some examples to encourage us as well as examples to follow. And we have heard from such examples this summer, thanks be to God. But this man, Tertullian, will be a challenge for us because he contributed a great deal of knowledge for Christianity to go forward. And yet there was an apparent discontent that he had about the faith that pushed him towards a tertiary group of Christians Who were out of the mainstream of the church and who sought a new revelation from God. You will have more about them later. Where Tertullian will challenge us is where the apostles and leaders of the Christian church in the New Testament were challenged. Consider that passage in Mark that we read, Mark chapter 9, beginning at verse 33. In the passage St. Mark, we heard Jesus coming to the city of Capernaum, which is in northern Israel. He hears his disciples disagreeing and he asks them, what were you talking about? They are quiet because they are embarrassed, for they were presenting arguments to one another about themselves, explaining how they were better or greater in the eyes of Jesus than the rest. Jesus next gives a most profound lesson about humility by picking up a child. And claiming the child was an example of how to follow him, of how to be humble A child, you see, can be hungry for knowledge. He can more easily admit that he does not know and he wants to be taught And a child in the first century of the ancient Near East was not considered of value because he must be cared for while providing nothing to contribute to the family's well-being. He is considered as low as a servant until he comes of age. So before them is a child. A great image of an honest servant, and therefore a lesson in humility. But the disciples don't learn quickly, and John speaks up about A man who used the name of Jesus to cast out demons. John is concerned that the man was not one of them. He wasn't one of the apostles. The man in question was a byproduct of being in the crowds and hearing Jesus, or maybe he just heard of Jesus. And John didn't like it. He wanted to control it. Mark seems to have included this part of the story to show just how much these disciples, these apostles, struggled with pride. They were the closest to Jesus. And John was even closer than the rest of the apostles. They wanted to control the privilege that they had, and yet Jesus wants nothing of the kind. They had yet to understand humility even after the lesson of a child. Mark puts these stories back to back to show how the apostles had yet to truly listen to Jesus about humility. Now Jesus tells John that such a person using his name very well very well may become a believer. And then he caps it with this quote that we should always remember. For the one who is not against you or us is for us. For the one who is not against us is for us. Oh, how desperate the church is for such maturity today The Christianity lived within the church today seemingly competes for people to fill the seats more than they are concerned for glorifying God and making disciples. I know the temptation all too well. Now regarding Tetolian, he is known more for what he wrote than what he did. He encouraged other Christians to explore previously uninvestigated thought. He wrote works in defense of the faith, especially against Gnosticism, which we talked about last week. He also wrote the first Christian book on baptism, and then a book on the Christian doctrine of man. He wrote on essays on prayer, on devotion In addition to apologetic and polemic works, he addressed himself to the whole a whole range of moral and practical problems, issues facing the Christians of the first three centuries. He talked about what is appropriate dress for a Christian. What about wearing of cosmetics? Service in the military? Whether one should flee under persecution He wrote on marriage and remarriage, on the arts, theater, and civic festivals. And I suspect all of us would like to hear what he had to say on those issues. His range of topics showed that Christianity is to permeate all aspects of a Christian life. And where Tertullian contributed the most from my studies was his understanding of the Trinity. Tertullian's definition of God was, God is one substance or essence, and God is three persons. The word essence comes right from the Greek. The word is ousia. The word substance comes directly from Latin, substantia. Even the word person is Latin from Latin personae. And these distinct distinctions have remained the most helpful for theological students to come as close as possible to understanding God in three persons, blessed Trinity. Where Tetullian troubled Christians of his day was his choice to leave the Orthodox or established church and become a part of a sect. A tertiary group called the Montanists. The Montanists. Now remember, in his day, the early third century, there was no quote established church. Christianity was outlawed. Christians had to stay together to be safe. To break away from the main Christian body was very troubling to the body as a whole. Especially a person of Tertullian's ability. But break away he did He did so because he was dissatisfied with how his Christian contemporaries, he called them, lackadaisical in their Christian lives. You and I would never call Christians of his day lackadaisical, for to be a Christian then was to put your life in danger every day. But such was Tertullian's perspective. Instead of the main body of believers, he appreciated the Urgency of the mountains, for they gave messages of the imminent end of the world, and they combined their message with a strident and demanding moralism. Montanism stood in judgment on any compromise of anything of the ways of the world And Tertullian gave himself fully to the defense of this new movement, and he was their most articulate spokesman. Eventually, eventually, the Montanus were not rigorous enough for Tetolian. He broke away from them and found his own sect, a group that existed until the fifth century in Africa. According to tradition, he lived to be an old man. His writings date approximately, last writings date approximately about 220 A. D. And yet there is no Date for his death. Tertullian was awed to his contemporaries because he left them And thought he needed something different than those who were a part of the church and who made up the church People make such decisions every day, and we may not like it. I certainly don't like it when people no longer want me to be their pastor, but it happens. There are souls that become discontent with their spiritual condition and think, like Tertullian, that they need something else to increase their spiritual well-being. They seek a new spiritual high, a new emotional experience. But they are not leaving the faith. They are struggling in the faith, they are different in the faith, but they are not denying the faith. And that is important to agree upon. Let us go back to the words of Jesus. If they are not against us, then they are for us. Let us face it. Overall, people are odd. You've noticed that, I trust. People are odd I know a guy who hates elevators and would prefer to walk the stairs in most buildings that offer stairs or an elevator. Now think about that. How does a person want to pass on a free ride to go higher, preferring to perspire while plodding upstairs? That guy is weird And the same guy has trouble falling asleep, so he often moves his feet to the bottom bedboard to rock himself to sleep. This guy has problems. And if you want to know just how odd, really odd this guy is that I'm talking about, and you don't know who I am talking about, but this guy It's so odd that when he eats Doritos out of a bag, he searches for the chips that have the most cheese dust on them. And if the cheese dust is not enough, he puts it back and looks for another. That is an odd duck. And I know a woman. You don't know her, of course. She is anonymous. But she thinks that there are ice machines that make the best ice. And so she chooses places to eat that provide the best ice for her to chew on after her drink is consumed. Sounds like someone headed for the loomy bin. Another woman I know, and this is truly a different woman than the first, this woman loves peanut chocolate and MMs. But when she eats them, she eats the chocolate around the peanut and then spits the peanut in a bowl. Lock her up Now let's stick to eating. Some people have to eat their meal in a certain order, and they make sure that each part of it is separate from the other parts. No touching. And so it's the meat, and then the vegetables, and then the potato. No mixing of the food, even though it's all mixed up in the digestive tract. Leaving what we eat. There are odd words that people pronounce, or pronounce them oddly. Have you ever heard someone say Wednesday instead of Wednesday like the rest of us? Or how about February instead of February like everybody else? It is almost as if some people want to appear odd. And let us only briefly mention how strange people are who talk to their pets as if they are their children. You're such a good little boy. Did you go peep? Mama is so proud How do we survive as a society with such people? But we do, we survive. Tertullian was awed. He wanted to express his faith in Christ, and that faith in Christ expressed was different than most. But he never denied Jesus as Savior and Lord. He never preached or taught heretical doctrine. He was a Christian. As are many people who know, we know, who profess Jesus as Savior, but walk the narrow road in a different or unique manner. The message I hope that you are getting is that when we encounter people who claim Jesus as their Savior, but walk an odd path. That we are to have charity for such people. Again, I'm not talking about seeing people as Christian who have denied the faith as the first example was given. Or if they're walking in disobedience to God's commandments, I'm not talking about those. I'm talking about people who are Christian but are, in our eyes, a little odd. The Bible is filled, filled with instructions on how Christians are to treat one another, even others with oddities. We are not to judge one another, even if our judging is concluding that someone is odd. St. Paul said to the Corinthians Therefore, do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness, and will disclose the purpose of the heart. Then each one will receive his commendation from God. Have you ever considered that an oddity of another person may be his or her way a coping mechanism and the Lord helps them use such a mechanism to handle the stresses of life To come to such a conclusion is to express charity to one another. To the Colossians, Paul wrote. Bearing with one another. And if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other, as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive I trust you heard in those words that we as followers of Christ are to forgive in place of complaining. Forgive in place of complaining. But what if someone does a clean up after themselves in the church kitchen? Forgiving, replacing, complaining. But what about those kids who leave balls and equipment in the gym? Forgiving replaces complaining. But what about the family who was part of our fellowship, counted as members of our parish, fellowship with us regularly, and then with no biblical warrant, left our fellowship for wanting a new experience? Forgiving replaces complaining. What we are addressing here from the life of Tertullian is a real and prominent problem. And the life of Tertullian shows us it always has been Fellow Christians do odd things for odd reasons, and we don't like it, and we wish they didn't, but that does not make them non-Christian. The call for Christians to have charity for one another, even when the other acts odd, is a call from Christ Jesus Himself. Do I believe Christians make poor decisions in their churchmanship that will have negative ramifications in the future? Yes, I do. And I have examples to verify my conclusion. Tertullian's decision immediately affected his influence amidst the majority of Christians of his day He lost influence and the church lost a great mind. But he was still a Christian and should have been treated as such. Consider the maturity displayed by Saint Paul with these words. Some indeed preach Christ even from envy and strife. And some also from goodwill. The former preach Christ from selfish ambition, not sincerely, supposing to add affliction to my chains. but the latter out of love, knowing that I am appointed for the defense of the gospel. What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is preached. And in this I rejoice. Yes, I will rejoice. Oh, how the church today longs and needs such maturity displayed among us How the Holy Spirit must be grieved by Christians who are unwilling to rejoice that Christ Jesus is preached, for that is enough. And so while we lament that Christians don't always stay together, we still can and still must rejoice that Jesus is preached. Let us pray. Your son, our Savior, that those who are not against us are for us. And we thank you for the example of St. Paul, concerned most for the preaching of Jesus. So Father, may that be our focus as well. May we be a people who love all Christians, all who are on that narrow road. And Father, may we forgive as we've been forgiven. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen

Which should convict us that when we look around and believe ourselves to be lacking, Paul spoke to a church our size and spoke differently. It should be convicting to us to realize that what we need as far as speaking and knowledge is already before us. What we need regarding spiritual gifts is present with the people we are sitting around. Perhaps we are guilty of asking God for the things that we already have. Another lesson from the abundance of knowledge, wisdom, and spiritual gifts owned by the Corinthian Church Is that the ability and gifts must accompany hard work and maturity In sports, in academia, in the arts, it is the saddest tale to know of persons who are gifted but lazy, talented, and yet immature. The apostle has begun by describing what the Corinthian church is, and follows by listing what they are gifted to be, and then next explains. What is hindering them? What their problem is. Their problem is that there is division in the church. The appeal by the apostle is for all of the people to agree with one another Such an appeal sounds virtuous, but I believe it is fair to ask if complete agreement with one another is possible. If by agreement he means that all of God's people are to think alike, well we might as well immediately ignore this appeal, for that is not possible. And this is where translations help us. The New King James translates agree That we should agree with one another. It says that we should speak the same as one another. That's a better translation. We are to speak or confess the same things. This is where our minds can be united. We can agree to confess the same things. Regardless of what our culture testifies to us, it is not bad for us to divide according to our ethnicity, our tastes, or personalities. It is quite natural to befriend people who have similar backgrounds than you do. When we come together as a church, however, These divisions are to be left outside the door. For when we come together, we are united by our confession. That is to say, we are united by what we say and believe about Christ. And this is why it is troubling That so many independent churches do not recite the Apostles or Nicene Creeds. The creeds allow us to confess together the same beliefs. It appears for the Christians at Corinth that there was a temptation to divide along more distinct lines. Which were lines seemingly drawn by those who taught Christ. There was Paul. A gentleman named Apollos, and Cephas, who's Peter, and I'm sure there were others. As a pastor in this day, I am well aware that my voice is competing for your attention within the Christian world. Where some historical contexts have dictated that the only educated man in the town would be the minister, and there were no churches for miles. Today I compete to be your primary teacher of the Word of God with radio, television, internet preachers. Then there are Bible studies not sponsored by our church or in detail agreement with our denomination, as well as teachers and preachers from your past. This can lead to legitimate problems. A smorgasmorg of food is before you. You decide what is healthy and what is not. You develop your own taste for certain teachings and you reject others. We cannot avoid this reality. It is the way it is. What we can avoid is that such differences would divide us. Our divisions occur when we insist That Martin Luther's view regarding the nature of the elements of Holy Communion is the only view. Or that John Calvin's view about soteriology is the true biblical view. Or that Thomas Cramner's view on liturgy is the only acceptable form for the church. Now we may be proven right about those as we stand before the Lord But none of these are acceptable points of division. To confront our sinful tendency towards division, Paul makes a simple point. Simple point for the whole sermon. Christ cannot be divided. Christ cannot be divided. To choose up sides and insist everyone must come over to my side of thinking and follow my preferred teacher is an attempt to divide Christ. But we say again, Christ cannot be divided. Because of this fact, it is necessary to understand that when we divide over such issues, we are not dividing Christ, we are dividing ourselves from Christ. I don't see how that can be an overstatement. Remember in grammar school when We all have been a part of choosing up sides. If you were captain of the day, you chose your best friends first, and then those who you thought could help you win the game, whatever the game was Those chosen last didn't feel so good about themselves. Thus there was a pecking order of who thought they were on the best side. For the body of Christ, it is different. There is no best side. For the only good side is the side that Jesus is on, but because he does not divide, he sides with no one. Either we side with Jesus or we are alone. When we divide, Christ Jesus will not play. We are what he has made us. We are what he has enabled us to be. Thus let there be no division among us, for there cannot be, for he does not divide. A. W. Pink. A. W. Pink is a hero to many Calvinists and Reformed thinkers. especially because of his book titled The Sovereignty of God. Pink was an English Bible teacher who lived from 1886 to 1952 As a young man, he desired to become a Christian minister, but did not want to attend a liberal theological college, and he viewed all colleges in the United Kingdom as liberal. After a short time at Moody Bible Institute, he took his first church as pastor in the state of Colorado. He lasted less than two years. He next was co-pastor to a church in California lasting less than four years. This became a habit. He went from church to church, both in the United States and in the UK. Eventually he decided that it wasn't him that had the problem, it was the church that had the problem. He spent the last two decades of his life alone with his wife. He was so recluse that in the town he lived, the people knew him little other than a certain day and time he would walk through the town. Because of his voluminous writings, his fans describe him as a great Bible teacher, but his contemporaries found him offensive and aloof. While it may be said that he was a great Bible teacher, he almost ignored a fundamental teaching of Holy Scripture, which is love your neighbor as yourself. Even though God has said to all confessing Christians, do not forsake the gathering together of the saints, Pink describes such instruction as not applying to him. In his writing during his last two decades, he criticized all evangelists for not doing it right when he didn't even say hello to his neighbor. He died, as I said, in 1952, alone with his wife. His wife, afterward, spent a couple of decades enjoying fellowship with other Christians. But he had to die before she could. We are to understand, as Paul did, and as the Christians at Corinthian needed to understand That Jesus cannot be divided. If you do, if you try, you will be left alone. Let us pray. Our God, we thank you for this admonition to the Corinthians. Mindful how easy it could be for us to divide as well. And how easy it is for the devil when he divides to then tempt just as he did Adam and Eve. Father, wherever we can find unity among ourselves, may it be done. May our humility before you win the day We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen

sermons.title: The Message is the Cross
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles to 1 Corinthians chapter 1, beginning at verse 18 Be mindful that it is your responsibility to follow in God's Word and be sure that the preacher is preaching the truth. So check it out. 1 Corinthians 8, chapter 1, verse 18 and following. We are to recall St. Paul's instruction in verse 10. of chapter 1, for the Christians in court to have no division among them regarding what they confess in terms of the Christian faith. It is with that goal in mind that we are to look at the remaining verses of this chapter. So follow again with me. In verse 18, Paul summarizes his entire message and the gospel itself as, quote, the word of the cross. There have been many attempts made through Christian history, and they are being made well as today, to refashion Christianity into a message that does not focus on the cruel death of our Redeemer. But for Paul, for the Bible, for the New Testament, the gospel message is about the cross. Without embarrassment, we say that we have a Savior who died for us. Verse 19, the word wisdom, or the Greek Sophia, is used for the first time quoting the prophet Isaiah. It is used 17 times in 1 Corinthians, and six of those times it is used in the first three chapters. Elsewhere in Paul's letters, Sophia is used only 11 more times. So obviously this idea of wisdom is a matter of concern for these Corinthians. Corinth, you recall, was steeped in Greek culture. And for Greeks, Sophia referred to philosophy together with rhetorical eloquence. The men who could think and speak well were the most respected. These Corinthian Christians apparently had fallen prey to the temptation to want their newfound Christianity to compare well with Greek philosophy and the morality of those eloquent sophists, as they were famous for their teaching. Paul's message is that Christianity could not be born of human wisdom. Its message is of a crucified Messiah. No worldly wisdom would ever come up with that. So Paul begins with this citation from Isaiah. reminding them that the world's wisdom, far from being the pattern that Christians are to emulate, and not something that Christians are to embrace for themselves That wisdom stands, in fact, under the judgment of God. In fact, God said that he would destroy human wisdom In verse 20, the word scribe is a reference to a Jewish rabbi or teacher of the law. Both Jews and Gentiles are to be the focus of his remarks in the remaining verses. From verse 21, we are to understand that the world's wisdom and God's wisdom cannot be reconciled. The wisdom of the world keeps people from God. It does not bring them to God. In verses 22 through 24, The word stumbling block is the word scandal, which has here mean a meaning, not something that makes a person stumble, but something that is deeply offensive. The Jews sought miraculous signs because that is what they expected the Messiah would deliver for them He would, they believed, be like Moses and repeat the triumph of the Exodus, but on a greater scale. Their Messiah would shake off Rome like Moses shook off Egypt. The Greeks, in comparison, wanted reason and Sophia Theirs was a great civilization that astounded the world with its progress. It was their very advances that had caused many to abandon the belief in their traditional gods. and pursue philosophy and reason instead. People still do the same today. Instead of signs and Sophia, God gave them a crucified Savior. For both the Greeks and the Jews, it was like trading grandeur for humiliation. For the Jews, the crucified Messiah was an oxymoron, like jumbo shrimp. To the Greeks, it wasn't so much irreverent as it was ridiculous. In verse 25, the wisdom of God is compared to the wisdom of men. Some may ask Why didn't God just give them signs and a wisdom that would have impressed the world instead of this silly story of a cross? The reason for Paul is that it is in this weakness and foolishness that salvation comes. Here in this foolishness we find the true wisdom, and in this weakness is true power. In verses 26 through 28, we see that there is another way in which the gospel defies expectations. Not only is its message totally contrary to what the world expects of a religion that is worth their attention, It does not find its converts among the beautiful people, the great people of the world, but it finds its converts among the least of these. This included the Corinthians themselves. There is a third-century pagan critic of Christianity who made this very point when he said, he wrote. In offense, Christians included in their midst the uneducated, the dishonorable, the stupid, the slaves, even women and children All were thought to be third-class citizens. And of course, Jesus takes such criticism as a compliment. In verses 29 through 30, we are given the reason why God chooses the lower class. It is to destroy every human pretense. of our merit before God. Every human idea that we have something that will make God sit up and take notice of us. It is done to destroy our pride, the very thing that destroyed Adam and Eve. From verse 31, we can sum up the point by noting that everything we have and everything we are that is good is from the Lord. Only He is deserving of our praise. As Christians of today, we may think of our faith as repeatedly laughed at Scorn by comedians, Hollywood in general, neo-atheists, the liberal press, liberal professors, and so on. But still, we face nothing like what believers faced in the early days of the church The message of the cross was genuine foolishness in the view of a great many, especially the cultured elite. The Jews, of course, were incensed by the claim of Christians that the Messiah had come, but that he had come to be crucified. They had an expectation of the coming of the Messiah, but crucifixion, weakness, suffering for sin had no place in their expectation. The Messiah's coming would be in a glory, not humiliation. Add this to Deuteronomy chapter 21, where God says to curse anyone who hangs on a tree The Christian doctrine of Jesus Christ was such a complete repudiation of Jewish thinking about the Messiah, it is no wonder that they found it profoundly offensive. At the same time, we have the Gentiles rejecting it for different reasons. The notion that the meaning of the world should be found in a Jewish rabbi who was crucified outside of Jerusalem, in their view, that was ridiculous. Christian faith and experience has over many generations since cast such a halo around the image of the cross That we have a very difficult time appreciating what a cross symbolized in the first century world. We make crosses of gold and hang them around our necks. Our churches are decorated with crosses. We sing of the blessed cross, the glorious cross, the rugged cross. We pray that God would keep us near the cross or beneath the cross. But citizens of the first century would have thought such expressions madness. For a moment, consider it from their perspective. Jesus was a convicted, sentenced, and crucified criminal. No criminal deserves to be worshipped and certainly does not deserve to be thought of as God. In a fascinating and important study on crucifixion in the ancient world. A German scholar named Martin Hengel Points out that references to crucifixions were few and far between in the literary remains of the culture. The sophisticated were ashamed of crucifixion, and having witnessed it, they had a deep aversion to it. And he states the following, quote, For the men of the ancient world, Greeks, Romans, barbarians, and Jews, the cross was not just a matter of indifference, just any kind of death It was an utterly offensive affair, obscene in the original sense of the word. There is a graffiti that has been discovered by archaeologists on the Palatine Hill in Rome. It dates from the third century. It is a drawing of a youthful, it is drawn by a youthful hand, and it depicts a boy standing in the posture of worship with one hand raised. The object of his devotion is a figure on the cross. And the figure has the body of a human and the head of a donkey. And underneath the picture is scrawled the words, Alexamenos worships his God. Thus the graffiti is a young Christian's beliefs being mocked And chief among those beliefs that made the boy's faith so silly to his peers was this notion that he worshipped someone who died on a cross. And here I wish to say something about modern Christianity that goes back at least to the 70s and into the 80s. Even though God did not intend for the Christian faith to be popular or mainstream, and that God knew that it would be the opposite of every cultural fad, Some Christians have tried to make it popular with the apparent concern to make it appeal to younger generations. And so we have Christian radio with Christian rock and even Christian rap. We have Christian celebrities who try to be fashionable and trendy. We uphold any celebrity or any professional athlete who claims to be a Christian as models for our teenagers We have cool pastors who wear skinny jeans and wireless microphones while talking real to the people. We have latte bars and vestibules and entertainment for the kids. who will we would never expect to sit in worship. And we have wacky youth pastors who try to make Christianity fun. And none of this has anything to do with the gospel. And if I may, appears to be ashamed of Jesus on the cross. What St. Paul believed would reach the younger generations is what reaches every generation of believers. It is the historic, detailed facts of the gospel story, the story that Jesus lived in detail. It is those details that include his gruesome death along with his glorious resurrection. There is a reason why people don't believe and why they find the cross offensive. And St. Paul said it to us in verse 18. He said, For the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing. They are perishing. They are perishing precisely because they do not know themselves to be perishing and have therefore no conception of their being in desperate need of redemption. As Paul says of himself in Romans chapter 7, Christ never made sense to him until he realized himself a sinner, in bondage to sin and in desperate need of redemption. Christ and the cross is for those, Paul says in verse 18, who are being saved. These Christians in Corinth had experienced the transformation of their lives. They had changed in many happy ways. But they had changed because they had embraced the message of the cross, received the forgiveness of their sins, the power to repent of those sins and to live a new life and to have hope for a life to come. Paul came to Corinth with no other message than the message of the cross. The message of our sin. God's wrath, Christ's substitution of himself for us, and bearing our punishment. He came with that message in defiance of the fact that it was ridiculous to the Greeks Because it was the truth. And the only way they could get out of their sin was to hear that truth and accept it. The fact that they did not know they were perishing didn't stop Paul He preached their sin and God's wrath and Christ's redemption and the Holy Spirit worked that truth in some of their lives and transformed some of them. But some might say he could have appealed to them differently and been more successful. And the only answer is no. No, he could not have. Considering the Jews in comparison to the Greeks, they thought about life to come and how to get there. But they didn't think in terms of salvation, of their being deserving of God's wrath, of their being unable to escape it by themselves. and of their being rescued by a loving and powerful Redeemer who had to take their place and die for their sins. They thought of heaven as something that they must earn in the ordinary ways of ceremonial and moral obedience. But by God's will, some among them also fell under the Holy Spirit. Their own terrible sin and guilt they understood. The exquisite holiness of God and being Christ for them, sin for them, made their plight becoming righteous for them It is only when our sin and God's wrath is revealed to the conscience that suddenly the cross makes perfect sense. And Christ is seen for what he and he alone can give. The message, of course, fell on deaf ears in Corinth many more times than it was embraced. But God had converted people in that city. And the Holy Spirit opened the eyes and ears of them all, of what they would never have believed before, suddenly became to them utterly self-evident. Also surprising and wonderful. And so we make a complete circle. Paul reminds these Christians that worldly wisdom has nothing to do with the gospel. Worldly wisdom, such as it was prized and sought of in Corinth, has self-sufficiency and self-congratulation and self-love shot through it. It promotes itself as the answer to man's needs, and that of course is for us genuinely ridiculous. For we have been living with that wisdom now for thousands of years and have not gotten much of anything from it. There was no gospel, no good news in Judaism or Greek philosophy. There was advice, advice that didn't amount to much, as it turned out. But no wonderful news of God's love and our rescuer from sin and death. True wisdom Is much more honest, painfully honest than the wisdom of the world. It forces us to recognize that our problem is not our circumstance, it is not other people Our problem is ourselves. We are sinners. Selfish, disobedient, unkind. We do not by nature live in a way that pleases God. Our Creator's greatest purpose in us, we do not fulfill. We are utterly careless of God and His interests, His law and His commandments, His holiness and purity. And all that sin must pay a wage. It provokes the holy wrath of God, his justice. This may not be what people think about their lives. It's certainly not what people want to think about their lives, but it is in fact the truth about their lives. There is a dilemma of epic proportion. What can be done? How can I face God with my sinful life? And then comes the wonderful good news, the word of the cross. You can do nothing, but Christ has done everything. On the cross he bore in your place the punishment of your sins. Believe in him and you will be saved. Saved in this life and saved to live and love and rejoice forever. That was the message Paul brought to Corinth. Salvation for sinners through God's love and Christ's sacrifice That is the message of the cross that has been proclaimed throughout the world ever since. It remains foolishness to most human beings even to today. But to those whose minds the Holy Spirit illuminates, it is the most clear and compelling, the most self-evident and self-authenticating, the most heartwarming and soul-stirring truth in all the world. The message of the cross is that mankind is perishing in sin, and that Christ and Christ alone can deliver men and women, boys and girls from guilt and sin and give them eternal peace. It may not be hit. It may not satisfy the tastes of the sophisticated. It may not appear to vast numbers of people to be a message of any immediate relevance. They may well prefer to think about many other things, and they do. We know the basic temptation of Satan is what he said to Eve in the garden. Did God really say? The devil has deceived many people by having them doubt what God said. And he is a master at making that first question a domino question so that if he can get a person to doubt one thing God has said, Then many other things God has said are next doubted. He did so in the Episcopal Church in the USA Presbyterian Church. By doubting God actually said that he did not want women to hold leadership over man in the church. And once that was doubted, the whole Christian ethics was doubted, and we have those in those churches today who both teach immoral things and are immoral themselves. Another form of did God really say is I wish God would have said it differently or done it differently. Those who think and say such things are listening to the whispers of the devil. Repent from such thinking and accept what God actually said and did. He sent his son, Jesus, to die on the cross. That is what he said, and that is what he did, and that is what he wants us to tell the world. I listened to a gentleman named Jeff Walton this week. This gentleman lives in Washington, D. C. , and he works for a think tank. That in part evaluates trends in religion. He stated that religious communities grow when they offer people something that no one else is offering. And the serious people want something that is counter-culture. The message of the cross Is something that no one else has, and it most certainly is counterculture. What we must do better is lift high the cross without shame and believe in its redemptive authority. If we pass that confidence in the cross On to the next generation. We will see God's kingdom come in our lives. Believe it. Amen. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Staying On Message
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles, if you would, to 1 Corinthians chapter 2. We are covering verses 1 through 5. 1 Corinthians 2, 1 through 5. I'm going to let you in on a Jorgensen story that is legend, at least legend in the Jorgensen world. It is a story about telling a story. Ten years ago, my fiance Whom is now my wife, was telling the family, her family, a story about a traumatic accident that occurred when she was in high school. She began by informing us that she wanted to tell us the cantaloupe story. She went on to list a series of events. That caused her to be late for a bus that had taken her school choir on a trip. And seeing the bus, worried that it was about to leave. As she ran to the bus, she described herself, and these are her words, as running too fast for her legs. Now I question the possibility of such a running style, because it defies the definition of running, and that's when she became a bit defensive in her story. She then described herself as losing her balance, falling forward as she was running. She then described herself as hitting gravel pavement face first And sliding, again in her words, the distance of one hundred yards When I laughingly protested that there is no possible way she could have been running fast enough to slide 100 yards, let alone survive sliding one hundred yards yards, she became defensive again, and then finally conceded that it was probably more like 100 feet. Of course, I still protested that such was too far, but at this point in the story she was not in the mood for my reasoning. She then described her injuries, which consisted of bloody scrapes and bruises to her arms and to her hip bones and to her legs. When she was finished with the story, her brother naturally queried, why do you call that the cantaloupe story? To which she naturally responded, Oh, I had a cantaloupe in my hand. To this day when she is asked about this story, and again it is legend in our family, she has a defense, or perhaps What some would just call a mere explanation as to the details of the story. My wife's defensive explanation is not unlike all of us when we have details in a story that is questioned or are questioned. It is difficult to know whether it is appropriate to defend one's self by way of further explanation or just keep quiet. Saint Paul mostly defends himself, while Jesus usually kept quiet. The answer to the question of whether to defend or keep quiet is likely found in the two Proverbs in Proverbs chapter twenty-six. Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you also be like him. And then right afterwards it says, answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes. Well, which is it? The answer is it depends. In a different approach, Jesus had many opportunities to defend or explain himself And it appears, according to my count, that he opted not to defend or explain more than he explained. In fact, it is very rare that Jesus explained himself except to his disciples, regarding miracles he performed and lessons that he taught. One particular instance we heard about when we studied the Gospel of John It is in John 6, where Jesus says to those following, Unless you eat of my flesh and drink of my blood, you cannot be my disciple. The passage describes most of the people confused and maybe even disgusted by what Jesus just said, and so they leave him. And nowhere, nowhere is Jesus described as chasing after them to explain what he meant. It should not surprise us, therefore, when we learn that early Christians were accused of cannibalism. I am sure that the word spread fast. as to, that's how gossip lines spread, as to what Jesus Christ said without context. No matter that there was a greater depth of meaning to what he said, gossip lines are viewed as infallible. Of course, the greatest example of Christ unwilling to defend himself was at his trial before the Sanhedrin when false accusations were made And the scripture describes him as silent as a lamb to his shearers. In contrast, as I said, the Apostle Paul made great efforts to defend or explain himself. I dare say that the majority of the second epistle to the Corinthians is a defense of his ministry and of his authority. One of the complaints toward the apostle was that he had harsh words in his writing and soft words when he is physically, was physically in their presence. And perhaps this accusation of him being too harsh and then too soft is behind these words in 1 Corinthians 2. His comments are support for what he has said previous, which is that he was not ashamed to look the fool and preach Christ crucified. His attempt is to get his hearers beyond the manner of the message and to the content of the message. And this is what we are going to be challenged to do as well. Again, verse 1 of chapter 2 reads, And I, brethren, when I came to you, I did not come with excellence of speech or wisdom. In this passage, the apostle differentiates between two Greek terms, logos and sophia. The first word is usually translated word, logos word, and the other, Sophia, wisdom. Excellency of words or speech, you remember, is associated with a rhetorician, which is someone who is trained in rhetoric or public speaking. As stated last week, the Greeks highly respected men who could reason well and speak well A trained rhetorician uses different techniques and assimilates vocabulary to his audience depending on how he wishes to sway them. A skilled rhetorician is usually going to sway the masses in a direction that would manipulate them where he wants them to go. But there is a pitfall to his discipline. Because rhetoric is a technique and style of speech, the audience can reject the points of the speaker based solely on the fact that they do not like his style. Essentially what has happened in such instances is that the technique and style of the speaker overshadows his message. This happens all too often in modern day Christian churches. Parishes Grow in number or shrink in number based on the personality of the preacher and the particular style of his speaking It is a dangerous practice of a listener to receive the message based solely on the technique and style of the orator. If we reject words spoken to us based on technique, style, or manner that they are spoken, we are likely to miss the message that God wants us to hear. The apostle instructed the church at Ephesus, you remember, to speak the truth to one another in love. Too often we wrongly interpret love to be soft-spoken and careful wording. If we are not spoken to in what we consider kind, loving. A type of tone that we prefer, we are likely to reject the message altogether The mature person of faith, however, is most concerned about the substance of what's being said. Balaam Balaam, for example, could have easily rejected the rebuke of his donkey when it spoke because he did not like his tone. If he were to do so, he would have been slain by the angel that stood in his path. David could have thrown Nathan out of his chamber and missed the chance to repent and be forgiven. Because Nathan was direct and forceful when he insisted that David was the guilty man. Peter could have walked away from Jesus and justified in his own mind that Jesus had wronged him. Because Jesus said to him, get thee behind me, Satan, after Peter had told Jesus not to go to Jerusalem. From these examples, we can interpret that speaking the truth in love can and does include being direct, being forceful, and even being offensive if necessary.
