Although a local pastor like ours chooses to call a minister, that church cannot turn around and uncall the same minister because they do not like what he is saying Hence the minister is free to do Christ's bidding without the concern that his paycheck will not be forthcoming because he's made some people in the congregation uncomfortable. There is, of course, means within the Episcopal government that allows a parish to submit complaints to their bishop if their minister is not remaining true to God's word. This is not only available, but it should be done to preserve the purity of the gospel. Well, along with being a servant, the minister, as I said, is also a steward. A steward is one who cares for and distributes. In the case of a minister, he cares for and distributes the mysteries of God. The word mysteries means truths once hidden that are now being revealed Jesus spoke this way to his disciples from Luke chapter 8. He said, Unto you, his apostles, his disciples, is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God. In the first chapter of St. Peter's first epistle, he describes these mysteries as hidden from prophets and angels, although the prophets and angels longed to look into those mysteries. Because a minister is a steward of God's mysteries, he is given certain gifts by the Spirit that allow him to illuminate the Word of God into the lives of the people of God, the people he's been given responsibility to care for. He is not given such illumination because he is a more perfect man or has more perfect brain matter, but only because of the office he holds. Hands are laid on ministers at ordination to pass on the gift of the Holy Spirit that he might more effectively minister God's word. I have personally experienced occasions where the Word of God has come to me in times of counsel and teaching, and I have been able to apply it directly to the need of a person to whom I am speaking with. Not because of anything other than the office that I hold. And I believe such words are granted me, again, not because of my abilities, but because of the Holy Spirit. and the office of a minister. As a steward, no glory is to be given to any minister when a word is spoken well or spoken at an appropriate time. A steward, again, merely cares for and distributes what is owned by someone else. These mysteries are God's. He alone is to receive the glory. The most important requirement to be met of a minister is that he be faithful to the stewardship he is assigned. The judge of his faithfulness is to be no other than God. The faithfulness of a minister is accomplished by being the servant, the steward we have just described. And ministers can become entangled in many other activities that would tempt him to be pulled away by his primary duty. He may become involved in the finances of a church. He may become a contractor for a building project. There are many things that could draw his attention away. The apostles recognized this early on. If you remember, there were squabbles going on in the early church, and we find this story in Acts chapter 6. And the other disciples were trying to figure out these squabbles, and it was taking them away from studying Christ's words and teaching them to the people. And so they got together and they chose certain men that they might worry about the needs of the people so that the apostles could worry about working and serving the Word of God These men eventually became official officers, and we know them today as the office of deacon. The disciples did this again so that they could give themselves, the scripture says, to prayer and ministry of the word. A minister is thus faithful when he preaches and teaches and counsels the Word of God. Now, a difficulty relating to the faithfulness of a minister is the subjective rather than objective criteria that he lives by. If he is a servant to Christ first and a steward of God's mysteries, how does anyone else know that he is being faithful to such a service and such stewardship? Now going back to our prior example of a minister teaching and preaching about eternal judgment, we can imagine some in the congregation who would question whether Christ was bidding him to address such a topic. Maybe he's wrong. Maybe he didn't hear Christ. How do you how do we know he is doing Christ's bidding and not his own? The preacher has one of a few callings that has quite a few people believing that they know how he needs to perform his task. I know that to be true, for when I was a layman, not even considering pursuing the ministry, I used to second-guess the content of my pastor's sermons every once in a while I would say to myself, I wouldn't have said that. I would think to myself, well, he could have said this Or he's being a little bit too soft on that point, or he's being a little bit too hard on that point, or he forgot about this exception to his third point As you can see, I understand how some people listen because I have done the same. What I needed to learn Is that the men I was critiquing knew that there was a different approach to take. They knew that there were qualifications to make Yet they chose to mention or not mention them according to the direction they best understood, having received the message from their master, who is Christ. You and I may say he is mistaken, but such outside judgment cannot matter to the man who is trying to listen to his master, who is Christ. The apostle speaks personally to the Corinthians as he shares his own perspective on how others judge him. See that in verse 3. He refers to their judgment as a very small thing. He's saying it doesn't matter. I can think ill of you, and you can think ill of me, or we can think ill of one another, but what matters is not how we judge one another. If I was to walk into your place of business and tell you that your work on a current project Or proposal is unsatisfactory, or if I was to tell you that your calculations on a particular project were incorrect, you would likely look at me with some surprise, shake your head, and ignore me You would do so because you know that I do not know all I need to know to make such a judgment about your work. And this is what Paul is saying The people of God, the local magistrates, and even his own judgment is inadequate to the task of knowing all there is to know to judge him in his ministry. Of his own guilt, the apostle is not aware. Has he been an unfaithful servant? Has he been too soft? Has he been too bold? Has he compromised? Has he been overbearing? He does not believe he has, but he confesses that he does not truly know. What he does know is that even if he is free from personal guilt, That freedom of guilt does not save him. It does not justify him. This got me thinking, I I recall watching a Kery Grant movie years ago called Bringing Up Baby. In one scene, Catherine Hepburn is accusing Kerry Grant of speaking falsely. And he responds by stating Quote, privately I do not believe such to be true about myself. And I loved the line privately when I heard it. Privately, I have an understanding about my service to God and the stewardship with which I am responsible. When someone disagrees, I must be respectful and take inventory If I cannot agree with the person who disagrees, I must confess I cannot see all things, but I know privately I do not believe such to be true about my character or my choices. This is what Paul is saying. Privately he knows nothing against himself, and he is trusting that God, as the final judge, will reveal all truth in the end. And those of you who are enjoying our study of Job, we recognize that Job makes the same point to his friends who insist that he he must have sinned to deserve his suffering. Privately, privately, he knew nothing of a sin that deserved what he endured. Now the final admonition along this subject is that we participate in no judgment before the time until the Lord comes. It's in verse 5. It is important, of course, to keep this admonition in context. For the apostle is not telling us to cease from judging anything. We make judgments as part of everyday life. We judge what we are going to wear, what we are going to eat, what we're going to say. And we get mixed up when Jesus said, judge not lest you be judged. His meaning is not that we don't judge someone who is practicing wrong behavior. Of course we're to judge that and say it's wrong. We are to judge when someone has sinned, for it is important to call sin. What we cannot do is make judgments regarding another man's heart. Is one man being faithful to his calling and another not? If there is nothing outwardly to point to such evidence, then we are not to judge. If the polity of a church is set up properly, a man who is living an unfaithful life outwardly will be and should be subject to judgment over him. We may think that one man is better to follow than another because he is more faithful. But that type of judgment we are not to get into. Because we cannot see it. We cannot see the heart. And that's where the church is divided, and that's where Paul is correcting them Although judgment cannot and should not be made of one person to another, this does not mean that there will not be a time of judgment. The apostle makes it clear that there will be a day when the Lord comes to this earth and places all men before him, and the things unknown will be known, the things hidden will be revealed. This promise is to put fear and hope together in the heart of every minister and of every person. The fear is to drive us to repentance and to drive us to obedience. The hope is to be placed in the mercy of God by the blood of Christ. A minister must be keenly aware that his judgment will consist of his faithfulness as a servant and as a steward. And all persons must be keenly aware that the Lord will reveal the innermost secrets of their heart. Too often we can spend an eager amount of time and energy criticizing and judging others while overlooking our own sin. Applying St. Paul's concern here in 1 Corinthians 4 to the present state of the church It is important to see that there is most certainly time to judge clergy when clergy have sinned publicly, either by sinful behavior or sinful teaching. There are false teachers who claim giving them money in sea faith so that they can live a luxurious lifestyle is God's will. I even ran across a teacher who promised that he could help people get out of credit card debt by charging their credit cards $1,000 and sending it to him. Amazing. Amazing. You can't make such a thing up. And yes, there are perverted preachers who use their position of authority to take advantage of vulnerable people. It is all true, it needs to be exposed, judged, condemned in this life, if possible. Outside of such blatant sin, Other judgment that takes place within the church is unnecessary and out of place. Instead, it divides Christians, and such division is Supporting the devil's cause. It may surprise you to know that in the end, God is not looking forward to judging and then condemning. But God instead is looking forward to praising his people. He's looking forward to praising their heart. Those who have focused upon God's judgment and not judging others are the ones he will praise with those precious words, Well done, good and faithful servant. Enter your rest. Be it known, dear parish, that God is looking, looking for people He can praise with those words. A minister is no more than a steward. He is not to be treated as untouchable. He is not to be judged by another man when he has only been a steward. Our energy to judge is to be focused upon God's judgment. For in the end, that is the only judgment that will matter. Let us pray. Our Father, we want to pray as is the concern of the Apostle. that we let nothing divide us that would be one man, one person judging another. But Father, we do say, all of us say, that if there is sin that needs to be revealed, may it be revealed. And if there is judgment of another man, let us repent and put it aside. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Choose Humility and Suffering
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I invite you to pick up a Bible and turn to First Corinthians chapter four. 1 Corinthians chapter 4. Our reading started at verse 8, but we're going to be starting at verse 6. Verse 6. The phrase these things refers to being a servant and a steward, as we spoke about last week. The phrase beyond what is written applies to a minister being no more than what is written, which is a servant and a steward. That they would be pumped up addresses their temptation to think that following one man over another made them superior. In verses 7 through 10, 7 through 10, we find an unusual but effective sarcasm. I have had conversations over the years with fellow Christians who have said that they don't like sarcasm, with some insisting that God would not use sarcasm. But the fact is there is a great deal of sarcasm in Holy Scripture. The Corinthians are not wise while Paul and his companions are fools. They are not distinguished while St. Paul is dishonored. But Paul was treated like a fool, and he was dishonored by the Jews and the Greeks. His sarcasm is to humble the Christians who are dividing themselves from one another, while he and his companions Are concerned first and foremost about the gospel being preached. Verse 11 through 13 This is not here a list of complaints, but of reality. Working with our own hands, he says. That refers to making a living to support his own ministry. Paul describes himself elsewhere as a tent maker. Also, the point must be seen that while Christians are de-fellowshipping from one another, Paul and his companions are giving love to people who mistreat them. The contrast again is to humble them. Verses 14 through 15, Paul reminds them why he is able to say these things directly To say he is their father is not a violation of Christ's command that we are to consider no one, no man, father. Paul is a father to them and that he is God's representative as God their father. Because he brought the gospel to them, he has a right to be honored and respected as their spiritual father. When Jesus warns against calling a man father, he is not referring to giving a man and he is referring to giving a man and his teachings authority above the Holy Scriptures. He is not rejecting the relational title of father. That is why it is biblically acceptable to call a minister father if you believe him to be your spiritual father. Verse sixteen through seventeen, there to imitate the apostle is to listen to the teachings of Timothy, who comes on the apostles' behalf. What Timothy will teach them to do is how they are to imitate Paul, to live out their Christian life daily. Not on Sundays, daily. Verse eighteen through nineteen, those who are called puffed up are arrogant. They're arrogant because they speak as though they have more understanding and insights than the Apostle Paul. He used the term word, not referring to the word of God, but the words of men. Again, contrast, words of God, words of men. In verses 20 through 21, the kingdom of God is not in word, again the words of man The power of the kingdom of God is displayed in the words of God and in his deeds, what he has done. The apostle can come to the Corinthians displaying both. How he comes will depend upon the attitude and actions of those who are arrogant. Those brief notes on this passage will serve as a background for highlighting two main subjects that are being contrasted in this section of Scripture. The first is the contrast between humility and arrogance. The other is of suffering versus kingship. Suffering versus kingship. Now the story of God's kingdom consistently places the spirit and ethic of every age on its head. Every culture of every age experiences and accepts the ethic that might makes right. The strongest and the fittest receive the power and the glory of man. The boy with the biggest fist and the meanest nature rules the playground. Whether it be a third-world culture that pays homage to a man who can throw a spear the farthest Or a first world that pays millions to a man who throws a ball. They are all controlled by the same ethos. I realize that those who are being blown by the winds of our day are trying to say that the meekest make right, or that the immigrant is to receive the greatest respect But please look critically again. While the progressive holds up the victim for praise, they hold up the victim as more righteous. The most pure. And thus they are still holding up that which they define as the greatest. And they bully you if you don't agree. To our age and every age, the voice of God speaks to this in the same tone with the same message If you want to be great in God's kingdom, you have to be a servant. If you want to have eternal life, you must become like a weak child. In a Darwinian culture such as ours, where the survival of the fittest is not only taught in our classrooms, but practiced in our boardrooms, this makes no sense. Eat or be eaten, killed or be killed are the slogans that the kingdom of God replaces with, he who tries to save his life will lose it, and he who gives up his life will save it in the end. The Bible forces us to examine the manner the world thinks and to transform our minds to think in the manner of God. On the issue of humility, we are forced to recognize that those who are arrogant are blind to reality. Only those who are humble see things as they actually are. In verse 7, the apostle challenges those who are arrogant to re-examine why they are so high on themselves. If they are as smart as they think they are, how did they become so? The answer, of course, is that any gift they have has been given to them. They have nothing that they have not received. It reminded me of an interesting exchange Between Mark Cuban, the owner of the Dallas Mavericks, an MBA team, and Shaquille O'Neal, who is a former NBA center. O'Neill was criticizing the owner of the Mavericks by stating to a reporter that the owner's wealth was not earned but gained by lucky investments in the stock market. Cuban, when he was told that about this comment, shot back sarcastically by saying, Oh, and Shaquille O'Neal is over seven feet tall and weighs over 300 pounds because he earned it I think such is a very good comeback. Far too many people are arrogant because they do not recognize that what they are, the gifts they have, have been given by God. Those who are puffed up, as the apostle describes them, are in such a state because they believed they had greater understanding about God than others. They believe themselves to be more perceptive and perhaps even more learned than the apostle. Such an attitude is not much different than our neighbor or co-worker Who knows that we attend church regularly and that we participate in Bible studies, and they perceive us to be blind and themselves having sight You're wasting your time. You're wasting your money supporting a church by your giving and by your attendance. To them, you look the fool. To them, you are a weaker person because you need, as they say, a crutch. The truth is Those who consider followers of who are considered followers of Christ, those who consider them fools, are themselves foolish. They are foolish because they are bound by their sin. They carry guilt wherever they go. They're burdened by a load of sin, vices, and they have no hope beyond the grave. They call the call of the grave screeches like nails on a chalkboard, like a haunting echo down an empty hall, and they refuse to acknowledge those horrible sounds. They cover their ears as they harden their hearts. Their denying of their fear of death simply leads to greater expressions of sin in desperation, which again causes the grave to beckon. This vicious cycle is unending until it ends in death. The only hope, the only possibility for the sounds of the grave to be silenced is if arrogancy is turned to humility. Humble yourself before the Lord, and he will lift you up. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted, said the Lord. He does not ask of us what he himself has not done. He humbled himself, Philippians tells us, and became obedient even unto death. Jesus' death at the hands of those who are his creation, think about that, he died by the hands of those he created, that defines humility. He, having set the standard, expects all who would follow him to have the same humble mind. Let it be heard this way. A follower of Jesus cannot hear the call for humility to be an option. It is a requirement. To be Christian is to be humble, humbled by the reality of your sin and your desperate need for a savior. To be a disciple of Christ, you have to be humble to confess that you don't know God, and you need to know Him. It requires humility to allow others to teach you and to remain a student the rest of your days. God is opposed to the proud, but gives grace to the humble. The second contrast, as I said, is suffering versus kingship. When I was 11 years old, I was a sixth grader in Lakeland Elementary School. In my class was a boy named Mark. Mark was teased repeatedly. He was punched, poked, belittled by his classmates. On the final day of school before summer break, He was surrounded by the boys of his class. His pants were taken off of him, passed around as he cried in the playground, standing in his underwear. Later that summer, I was over at my best friend's house, who was a year younger than me. He probably still is a year younger than me. I looked at a group picture he had taken at church camp when he returned. In that picture was Mark. The boy that had been teased in my class all year. I asked my friend about Mark, and he told me he was a nice guy to get to know. I was stunned. I thought those who suffered such teasing and torture that they were deserving, not nice average guys. There were some within the Corinthian church who had a similarly warped understanding regarding the virtue of suffering for the sake of righteousness. Because they are comfortable, meaning they didn't lack anything such as food, shelter, clothing, wisdom, and influence, because of all that, they perceive themselves to be royalty To be important. To be a king is to have rule. So they thought they should be in control. Their condition had fooled them into thinking that God had placed them in a position to rule. And this mistake is not uncommon. When persons take inventory of their lives and they like what they have, they can wrongly assume that God is pleased with them. Others who suffer are perceived to be receiving their just reward. We have been referring to this line of thinking in our study of the book of Job. For it is a system of thinking that seemingly transcends time and global regions. Throughout the history of man, people have believed that those who have wealth and power are blessed of God, or of the gods. And those who have little, well, they're cursed. One of the dangers of this way of thinking we can summarize as: you get what you deserve in this life. It is as if you are comfortable, then you can become complacent because God is well pleased. But complacency contributes to you forgetting that you will stand before God on judgment day Remember that in order to wake these Corinthians out of their complacency, the apostle uses sarcasm as he calls them rich, wise, strong, and honored while he and his fellow servants are poor, foolish, weak, and dishonored. Here again, the manner of this world is turned on its head. As the apostles, those whom Christ had chosen to lead, they go hungry, they go thirsty. They wear rags and they are physically mistreated They are cursed, persecuted, slandered, and considered the refuse of the earth. In the kingdom of God, such a life is the outcome of being first. Suffering is a product of following Christ. Those who think of themselves to be reigning as kings do not know the power of God. The power of God is not expressed in the words of a man. A person can be conniving, manipulative, and influential within the world, but such is not true power. The power of God is given to those who suffer. Jesus said to his disciples, that everyone who has left houses and brothers and sisters and fathers and mothers, children, or fields for my sake, will receive a hundred times as much as they inherit eternal life. Thus, true power is not something that can be manipulated, but is instead given by God. An article in the Harvard newspaper from nineteen eighty two nineteen eighty two An article in the Harvard newspaper described the reception of a featured class speaker to their upcoming graduates. The speaker spoke strongly against premarital sex, against abortion, spoke in favor of prayer She prayed that the graduates would go into the world and work for Jesus. She said, it is unbelievable that today mothers can lawfully murder their own babies. She praised virginity as the most beautiful thing a young man or woman can give one another, and thus they should give such only on their wedding day. The writer of the article said that the woman spoke with mesmerizing conviction and that she received a long-standing ovation before an unusually large crowd. You likely have guessed that that speaker was Mother Teresa. Such a story gives a clue. Why many long for the old days when people would respond to such a speech in such a manner? But why was she received in the manner described? It had to be because she spoke with power. Power coming from years of suffering with the least of humanity. Such suffering can even bring the respect from those who don't believe, because it's obvious that there is goodness in such suffering. From suffering comes power. Power of God. Power that demons cannot deny. Because power in the kingdom of God comes by suffering, of course no one has greater power than our Savior. He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, familiar with suffering, like one from whom men hide their faces, he was despised and we esteemed him not. Surely he took up our infirmities and carried our sorrows, yet we considered him stricken by God, smitten by him and afflicted. Therefore, therefore, God exalted him to the highest place and gave him the name above every name. That at that name Jesus, every knee shall bow and every tongue confess. If a person thinks he has kingship, his kingship is in his own mind. Only a person suffering for the name of Christ has the power of God. St. Paul ends this portion of his letter by telling the church that he plans to come to them. Yet those who are puffed up converse and behave as if he's not going to come. Paul then gives this direct warning. When he comes, he will either come with a rod, which refers to judgment, or he will come in love. The manner in which he comes will be determined by the humility and suffering of the Corinthians, or by their arrogance and their perceived royalty. In the same manner, our Savior comes to every man. Before he does, before he comes to each of us, he gives us this warning. He shall come with the rod of judgment or in love and grace. What determines how he comes to us is whether we choose humility over arrogance and suffering over royalty. To choose humility and suffering is to choose Jesus Christ. Beloved, we do not have a visit from the apostle approaching. What we have is a visit from our Lord. He is here in spirit as he has promised, and he will come again in glory as he promised. May our choice of humility and suffering be a welcome that for his entrance. Amen. Let us pray. Our Father, we thank you for the courage of St. Paul, for him addressing directly the problems in the church. And recognizing that those who humble themselves will indeed be exalted, embracing the promises of Christ, may we do the same. May we uphold those who suffer. May we uphold those who are humble in spirit. That all of us might be just that. Father, we do anticipate your coming. Come again, Lord Jesus, and help us to be humble In Jesus' name we pray. Amen

sermons.title: Passionate for a Pure Church
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, yo quiero que lo me lo quiero. In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles to 1 Corinthians chapter 5. We are looking at verses 1 through 8. 1 Corinthians chapter 5, verses 1 through 8. It's uh a good thing to go through a book of the Bible. It forces you to address subjects you might not feel comfortable addressing otherwise, and here is one passage. But first I want you to know that I have come to regret my involvement in social media for various reasons One of them is how it is used by the devil to tempt us toward coveting We can easily covet when we view pictures of someone else's meal. I don't know why people post what they're eating But they do, and you're not eating that. But there are other things like people posting pictures of a party That you were not invited to, but all of your friends are attending. And as they post pictures of how much fun they're having, the devil can whisper to us that we should have been invited Bitterness and resentment can set in by those who feel left out because of a face-baced post. I know it's not called face face, but I didn't want to give any social media a plug. But one good thing about social media is that it seems to have reduced the use of the annual Christmas letter. Because we are already knowing so much about each other because of my book. You know the uh Christmas letters I am talking about, those letters you used to get when They would tell everyone how fantastic their life is and how great their children are, and you would compare them to you and you would feel very inadequate. I had a friend who received a Christmas card from a friend of his who told of all the ski trips he had taken to Tahoe the previous year. And he enjoyed was enjoying his pontoon plane that enabled him to land on the sh shoreline of his lake property. My friend and his family on his teacher's salary could not relate In my first year of youth work, Bobby Lynn and I received a Christmas letter from a family that was unknown to us. It told of Aunt Beatrice and her gallbladder. We learned of Uncle Fred and his ringworm. We were informed of the insights, of the insights to a family squabble. The problem was we didn't know any of the people that were referred to in the letter. And this made us indifferent at best. After being at the church for a year, we finally came to know the family better and finally cared about what was told, although, you know, a little bit too much in the letter. And this is a problem when you're reading someone else's mail. Imagine randomly going through the mail of a person you did not know. Now, of course, I'm not suggesting you do that, but to make this point When you found something interesting, you would be frustrated due to the lack of details, not knowing the parties. Other items would not appear interesting because, again, you didn't know the persons involved The persons and situations referred to most likely have been written by the writer as if they could be understood by the parties that are reading it as well as the parties being referred to. People being in the know. You would have to read between the lines if you wanted to be in the know. Well, such a scenario is exactly what we have when we pick up chapter 5 of Paul's letter to the Corinthians. Paul is aware of a sin within the church that the people of the church were also aware of, which allows him to not go into much detail. But simply point to how they should respond. The description of the sin by St. Paul is described enough for us to get a general idea. And vague enough for us to speculate with several theories. The apostles' response to the sin is also vague enough for us to wrestle with his wording and try to imagine what he means. It is because of these reasons that our approach to the text will be a little unique this morning. We're going to Try to break it down in in verse sections, then try to have a running commentary with verses one through eight Hopefully this will help clear up some ambiguity while at the same time providing some necessary insights in order to interpret and then apply the message to our contemporary context. At the close of the sermon, we will summarize the passion of this section, which I believe is a passion for moral purity. Moral purity. At the end of the last chapter, the apostle warned that he could either come to the Corinthians with a rod of chastisement or with love and gentleness. The manner of his coming would be determined by the humility or the pride exhibited by these Christians at Corinth. Now the apostle is going to address a specific sin amongst them. So in chapter 5, verse 1, we learn that there is fornication. for sexual immorality amongst them. The phrase sexual immorality is translated from the Greek from the Greek word pornea Pornea. From this word we receive our English word, as you can imagine, pornography. The word is comprehensive in that it covers all sexual sin falling under the seventh commandment, which we know as thou shalt not commit adultery. When our heavenly father gave his ten commandments, he did so without extensive commentary on each one Later, within the laws given to the Levites and the second law given to Moses that we know of as Deuteronomy, God does expound on each one of the Ten Commandments. Regarding the seventh commandment, the Lord lists numerous acts of sexual behavior that are forbidden. Knowing Knowing that without such case laws described, his people would have justified their sin by proclaiming that God wasn't clear enough. Now adultery has been wrongly interpreted to refer only to the forbidding of sexual intimacy between a person who is married and a person he or she is not married to. With this understanding, those who are not married would be free to be sexually active as long as they were not with a person who was married. The command to commit not commit adultery, however, is actually a positive And the positive is it encourages sexuality only within the context of marriage. Any sexual intimacy practiced outside of the context of marriage is sin. That's not complicated. Pretty straightforward. Sexual intimacy is even sin when practiced by an engaged couple For no vow has been made before God and his witnesses, and therefore such activity falls under adultery. Because of possible ambiguity, it is necessary for a list to be written of all the sexual intimacy that God forbids. Therefore, in the Levitical law, we read that bestiality in all its forms is forbidden. Homosexuality and all of its forms is forbidden. Incest in all of its forms is forbidden. And unfortunately, this latter category is where the Corinthians have their guilt. So again at verse 1 of chapter 5, the sexuality or fornication being practiced in the church He says is so corrupt that not even it's not even accepted within the Gentile or unbelieving culture. And this is a telling criticism The first century of the Greco-Roman world, and especially in Corinth, had a reputation for all kinds of sexual impropriety. This devastating criticism places the morality of the Gentiles on a higher level than God's people at Corinth. The sin criticized is described as a man having his father's wife. The phrase to have a woman in the New Testament in certain places refers to marriage. The man may have thus married his father's wife. The chosen phrase of the apostle father's wife gives us help interpreting, for at first it may appear that this man has married his own mother. Because the father refers, because the apostle refers to this woman as his father's wife, it is most likely the woman is not his mother, but his stepmother, divorced from his father, now married to this man. Regardless of whether there is no blood relation This type of relationship is strictly forbidden in the book of Leviticus, chapter 18. There the law states that a man should not look upon the nakedness of his mother or his father's wife. Verse 2. Just as bad as the sin itself was the Christian response. Paul says they were puffed up. We described a week ago that to be puffed up is to be proud. Whether the Corinthians are actually proud of the sin itself, which is weird. Which they may have perceived as evidence to their tolerance. They're putting up with it. Or they were proud for other reasons already listed It is because of their pride that they ignored the sin of this man. Today you and I can identify certain groups who still call themselves Christians Who believe their tolerance of sin in their midst is a virtue more important than sexual purity or just moral holiness They are puffed up just like these Christians at Corinth. But regardless of the reason of their pride, grief, grief, not arrogance, is the appropriate response to sin. The right answer to this sin is not only grief, but grief followed by action. The man must be removed from among them. In a tolerant culture such as ours, this action seems too harsh. It is no more harsh now, however, than it was then. The removal of the sinful party is in line with God's law, which requires a guilty party of egregious sin to be executed. That's Old Testament law. Like Achan and his family from the book of Joshua, those who are guilty must be removed, for the remainder of God's people not to be polluted by their sin. That problem still exists today. People as a whole can be polluted by the egregious sin of others if those sins are not addressed. The New Covenant has done away with capital punishment within the church. We don't put people to death But instead, the church is called to practice a spiritual discipline upon members who are sinning, continuing to sin. Not have sinned once, but continue in their sin. Our Savior spelled this discipline out in Matthew chapter 18. You remember it read today, we were to confront someone once and then and then twice and then the third time before the church If no repentance is made, the man is to be outed and treated as a sinner. This type of discipline is known to the church as excommunication. The person is excommunicated, that is barred from partaking of holy communion until he or she repents and shows fruits of repentance. Because the partaking of Holy Communion is so readily associated with being a part of the church, the discipline has been practiced since the first century. But you and I know it has fallen out of practice in today's church. To be barred from the Lord's table was to be treated as an outsider, and for some who are nervous and frightened, Such discipline appears too harsh. In verses three through five The previous background we've been looking at is necessary for us to understand what the apostle was doing in these verses. When he refers to judging, although he is absent and delivering the guilty party over to Satan. By referring to being absent in the body, but present in spirit, it is apparent that the apostle is applying those words that Jesus said in Matthew 18. There in verse 18, remember Jesus tells the disciples, assuredly I say to you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven. Similar words are spoken in John chapter 20 when Jesus' spirit breathes upon them the Spirit And he says to them, if you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven, and if you retain the sins, they are retained. Paul seems to be applying that truth, Matthew 18 and John 20, to this situation in 1 Corinthians 5. As an apostle and spiritual father to the Corinthians, Paul has the authority the spiritual authority to bind or loose, to forgive or retain the sins of this guilty man. The description of delivering the man over to Satan, that's important to understand. It's a bit more complicated. This is a unique description he gives. And again, in light of Matthew 18, it is likely that a man delivered to Satan is one who has been ordered out of the church Satan, we know, along with his principalities and powers, rulers of this age, Satan has jurisdiction in the world. Within the Christian church, where the gospel is proclaimed, Satan is defeated. He has no rule in the church. This is protected territory. To turn the man out of the church and over to Satan would be to remove him from the safety of the church and to send him back to the onslaughts of satanic powers. It's quite dramatic. The purpose, however, of turning the man over to such an onslaught is not that he may be forever thrown out of the church. It is not the desire of the apostle that his soul be destroyed. It is the destruction of his flesh. That is what is desired. And this should not be far from our understanding. For anyone who has had a loved one who needed to reach bottom before he could get help, well, you know what the apostle means. A drunk or drug addict, a rebellious teenager, or a philanderer must reap the painful rewards of their sin before they are humble enough to seek help and mercy. We may think that the best thing for us to do is to help their flesh when it is it is their very flesh that needs to be destroyed In the end, the apostle believes that this discipline will save the soul of the guilty man, and that's what matters most. Paul is hoping that the difficulties the man encounters outside the church would motivate a change of behavior, repentance, and the possibility of being reclaimed by the church. Prior to the second coming of Christ. In verses six through eight of this passage, The apostle moves from speaking specifically about one man and his sin into a passionate plea for the whole church. The plea begins with the metaphor that all of us know well because it's part of our everyday diet. Spread. A little leaven leavens the whole lump. With leaven, the bread does not rise in only one spot, but the whole loaf is affected. Be not unwise, we are being told, in thinking that sin in the church will only affect those who are closest to it. Sin, unless it is dealt with biblically, as Christ has instructed, if it remains, will affect all of God's people. Understand, church. Understand that you are in Christ. You are the leavened, the unleavened, the unleavened, which means you are the pure ones. You as Christ's body are to operate out of sincerity and truth. Sin is not a part of who you are in Christ. To keep the feast is to continue to feast on Christ who is pure. To allow leaven is to allow the world in, which pushes Christ out. Have you ever wondered, if only for a moment, what would happen if the church, which is you and I Actually believed everything that is written in the Bible and attempted to follow it as best as we possibly could. Oh, I know that there are certain passages that are not as clear as we would like them to be, but let us be honest with ourselves that that is an excuse planted by the devil. Who wishes for us to give up the premise that we cannot understand certain passages or that we cannot do all that God requires Church. There are certain things that are clear, and we are able to do them. This is one of them. It is clear what type of sexual intimacy is sin and what is not If it is with your spouse, it is holy. If it is with anyone else beside your spouse, it is sin. If you become married to another who is forbidden by God's law, it is sin. If a person within the church wishes to live in sin, it is the church's responsibility to discipline that party in such a way as to move. To move him or her to repentance. That's the point. And here I need to address the sin of our day. Which is giving sexual urges such prominence of importance that some have decided to identify with the sexual urge that they have They describe themselves by their sexual urge. For the Christian, a sexual urge of any kind is not our identity. Our identity first and last is our place in Christ as we are children of God, inheritors of God's kingdom, little Christs, which is what the word Christian means Again, imagine for a moment what the church would be like if we believed and obeyed what the Bible clearly says. Would there be less people in the church? In the beginning, perhaps. Would there eventually be more of God's people forgiven and ready to meet Jesus on that last day? Absolutely. If we believe the word, the Bible, and follow its teachings as best we can We would be, as Paul describes us, of sincerity and truth. In the end, the holiness of the church would usher in the second coming of Christ. I believe that. But alas, for so many reasons that have nothing to do with the Scriptures or God's leading, too many churches do not confront sin in the manner that God prescribed. We fear that we will turn people away. We fear we will alienate. We fear a reputation of being judgmental. We may even fear that with such standards we could be next. Such fears, I will be bold to say, are from the pit of hell. For they focus on the immediate and not the eternal. I have asked whether you have imagined such a church. I have. And I'm tired of imagining. Let us not merely imagine, but start believing and start obeying. Amen. Let us pray. Our God, we do confess what is clear in your holy word. And we confess it goes against the spirit of our age. It always has. But Father, make us a people who are committed to your word without apology and without fear. Father, where we need to be disciplined, discipline us. Where we need to be holy, make us holy. And may you come again. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Associating With The Immoral
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We are covering First Corinthians chapter 5. Working from verse 9. The passage reminded me of working with youth, and so Uh that got me to thinking uh working with youth within the church provides opportunity for many lessons to be learned Youth have a great ability to be serious with their faith and humorous at the same time. There was a particular instance when I was leading a Bible study with a group of teenagers, and several girls became distraught after hearing the news that a boy, acquaintance of theirs from high school had died. I asked how it happened and they stated that he was cleaning his family's pool and became electrocuted Of course, that sounded like a horrible way to die. So before we started the Bible study, we included his family in our prayers. I asked one of the girls who was upset to pray for the family of the boy, and she solemnly did so. She began with these words. Lord, we bring before you this shocking death of our friend. And as she continued, there began to be snickering throughout the room. And before the prayer was over, all of the teenagers were laughing quite heartily. Now please don't hear that as a morbid laughter. They showed genuine concern about the family and his friends The gaff in the prayer, however, provided tension relief. The interesting observation for me was to notice how quickly the mood had changed, serious to laughing. Teenagers seemed to like to ride the edge between faithfulness and sin. As a parent of teens past and present can attest, many teenagers want to know where the line is drawn so that they can lean as far as possible over that line without actually going over it. And I have a theory that overt teenage behavior becomes the continuing subconscious of an adult. As adults, we still have the same tendencies towards the same sins as we did as teenagers, only we have conformed those tendencies according to the culture in which we live. One of the common questions asked by Christian teenagers is, can I have non-Christian friends? Another popular question is, can I date non-Christians? In the adult world, these questions are still applicable, as many adults still struggle with the influence their non-Christian friends and co-workers have upon them. The dating question as adults turns into the marriage question. Can I marry a non-Christian? I have criticized the contemporary Christian church in the past for treating the Word of God as a how-to manual. You know, how to be a better parent, how to be a better how to be get a better job, how to influence people. When Christians are exposed to such sermons, the teachings they tend toward using the Word of God rather than being transformed by it. God's Word is so much more than a how-to description It is the story of God redeeming his people from sin and death, and should be preached and taught in such a manner. However, there are passages that provide a little how-to information. Our passage today addresses the question of how Christians are to relate to unbelievers. This is not described by the apostle in a step-by-step manner. But provides principles for answering the questions of both teenagers and adults involving God's redemption and the warning of how not to be influenced towards or by unbelievers. So there are two groups of unbelievers that are described by the apostle in this passage in Corinthians. The first group is unbelievers in the world. The second group is unbelievers in the church. In regards to unbelievers in the world, the apostle needs to clarify some apparent misunderstandings from his previous letter. And you'll note This is interesting. This is 1 Corinthians, and he mentions a letter previous. So it's really 2 Corinthians. We don't have that first letter, so we assume it wasn't or didn't have evidence of being inspired like First Corinthians and 2 Corinthians do. And as a personal note, it is encouraging to me that the apostle confesses a misunderstanding of his words. If the great apostle Paul can be misunderstood, how much more can a small town preacher like myself be misunderstood? Easily is the answer to that question. As we must read into what St. Paul is responding to, it seems that the confusion occurred when the apostle told the church. not to associate or keep company with those who were sexually immoral. How that was understood was that the people of the church Could not associate at all with sexually immoral people outside the church. When we consider the moral climate in Corinth in that day Such non-association would exclude a whole lot of people. While we were in ancient Corinth last spring, We were told that the ancient palace that sits at the highest peak above ancient Corinth was in Paul's day a temple to honor Aphrodite, the goddess of many lovers. The practice in that day was for the temple prostitutes to look out over the peak of the mountain. And if they spotted ships coming to port, they would make their descent down to the city to meet up with the men and offer their bodies in exchange for money. Such was a common and accepted practice. Thus to not associate with sexually immoral people in general. would be to the exclusion of many people in the city and visitors to the city. And we asked, is that what God truly wanted? Imagine if you and I were not to keep common company with any sexually immoral people outside of our church today. Our co-workers and neighbors would have to become strangers. The Center for Disease Control reported in 2017 That over half the teenagers in the United States have had sexual intercourse by the age of 17, and a third of teenagers in the United States are sexually active on a regular basis. A census in 2018 showed that 15% of Americans are living together with their significant other, and that's up 3% from 10 years ago. And trending upward. This would mean that our children's classmates and teammates must become estranged. It would mean a number of young people in our lives are to be socially ignored. Therefore, to interpret the apostles' directive to these categories places some impossible expectations on God's people. How could the church minister the gospel to a world full of sinners when it doesn't even know the sinners? Of course, the apostle realizes this impossibility by stating at the end of verse 10 that Christians would need to keep out of the world itself If they were required to not keep company with the sexually immoral, Jesus told his followers that they were to understand themselves to be in the world. Being in the world means that we have been placed here by God to serve Him and engage the lost. Yet He also distinguishes from being in the world and not of the world. To be of the world is to be a product of the world's thinking and of the world's morality, which God's people ought not be. Being placed in the world means that we have a purpose, a calling to transform the world with the gospel. Christians are the city upon the hill. Christians are the salt of the earth. The people of God, the church, are to be about transforming the world by proclaiming the living gospel. When we pray the Lord's Prayer, we ask for God's kingdom to come on earth as it is in heaven. You're asking for the world in which we live to be transformed by God. You're not asking that he would help us escape the world, but by his sovereign will change it. And this understanding of the church's responsibility is why many reformers rejected monasticism. Monasteries communicated a spiritual elitism to the masses who understood that escaping from the temptations of the world was more pleasing to God than living out one's faith within the world. The Reformers believed that the seclusion of Christians did not transform the culture and usher in the kingdom of God, but actually stifled the growth of the church. And a similar criticism we may make upon the Amish and communities like them. Well, we can respect and appreciate their covenant hearts towards family and local community They appear to reject the call of Jesus to engage the world with the gospel. It appears from the outside looking in that Jesus, when he said, Go into all the world and preach the gospel, They don't believe such directive applies to them, but it does. As usual, Christ is our finest example on how we are to relate to the world. Christ related to the world in a redemptive manner. He was criticized and scrutinized by the Jewish religious leaders for keeping company with known sinners. He did not just converse with them as our gospel reading reveals. He ate with them. And eating with them, however, he had a purpose, not just to have polite conversation or to consume food. Christ's presence among the known sinners was a testimony that God had sent his son for persons such as these. Jesus never compromised his message to the sinners. He called them to repentance and belief, just as he calls all men. What the Pharisees and scribes failed to see was that their own sin made them just as guilty as those known sinners. When Jesus ate with the Pharisees, he was also eating with sinners. Christ came for them all. A Christian's friendship with those in the world should always first and foremost have the goal and purpose of testifying to the gospel. If you were looking for a reason as to why you have the neighbors you have, the co-workers you have, and the old acquaintances you have Understand first and foremost that you are a witness to the truth of Jesus as God's Son. If you are not a witness of Christ, then you don't care for your friends as you say you do. Each of us is a missionary where we live and where we work. Our manners, conversation, and character are a testimony to the gospel for good or for ill. Whether we want it to be or not, when we claim Christ, we are witnesses of Him to sinners that God has placed in our lives. Now turning to the second group. The second group is how we deal with unbelievers within the church. And I do not use the term unbelievers when referring to those within the church as I do when referring to those outside. By unbelievers within the church, I mean those who confessed Christ as their Savior, yet live a life that is not equal to their confession. Notice how the apostle calls them brothers. They are brothers in Christ. But he also calls them fornicators, covetous, idolaters, revilers, drunkards, or extortioners. Well, that's a strange combination. Brothers and. But by calling the sinful inside the church brothers, it presents a powerful lesson that Christians of every age need. It is a lesson of loving someone so much that you need to do what is needed to help them get away from their sin before it's too late. Moderns call such love tough love. Tough love is called so because it means we might have to watch someone feel rejected and hurt by our insistence that they repent. And seek help to live righteously before God. When confronted, the sinful brother may reject us and even blame us for their troubles and then accuse us of not loving them But the end product, the end goal of heaven over hell is to be our priority for our brother in Christ. And this is to cause us not to be devastated by immediate reactions. While we are not to judge persons of the world because of their sin, but instead present them the gospel, Paul is telling the church that we are to judge people within the church who will not repent. This is the tough love. By judging, he does not mean for us to conclude whether these persons are saved or not. Our judgment is to be an honest assessment as to whether such a person's lifestyle is once again consistent with what he or she is confessing. It is not by accident that the apostle does not simply refer to possible sins, but attaches a person's identity with their sin. For example, a person who is living a sexually immoral life is not described as merely behaving in a sexually immoral way, but is identified as a fornicator. He or she is a fornicator, an adulterer, a thief, a covetous person, a liar, a drunkard, etc. This is not simple name-calling But a lesson that teaches us how our identity is either in Christ and that we are Christians, or it is wrapped up in the sin we chose to live in. This type of identifying a sinner communicates that by living in a particular sin, a person is serving that sin. The sin becomes a false god, an idol to the brother who refuses to repent and seek help. This is why the Apostle John says so boldly in his first epistle that he who sins is of the devil, and that whoever is born of God does not sin. And by sin he doesn't mean one sin. He means living in sin. It's not a one-time thing. It's a lifestyle. The person who lives in sin is not identified with God, but with the sin he or she has chosen to live with. And such a person is still a brother in Christ? So we do not forget him or her, but call him or her to the higher standard. A brother living in sin is a Christian who needs to repent. And live by the identity Jesus has given him, not by the identity that the sin has given him. The restriction the apostle places upon the Christians is that they are not to eat with confessing Christians who live in sin. The apparent concern is that eating with such persons would appear to be condoning their lifestyle. And this standard We should notice is much higher than how we are to treat unbelievers outside the church. This is consistent with how Jesus treated those who should know better We remember that Jesus ate with sinners, but it was the Pharisees he called hypocrites and whitewashed tombs. It was the Pharisees whom Jesus called sons of the devil. These were the ones who believed themselves to be righteous, but never examined what was inside their hearts. Christian brethren who choose to live in sin fall under the same category as the Pharisees. But understanding this passage and how it applies to us can be very difficult to hear We all have loved ones, whether they be friends or relatives, that we know are not living a lifestyle that is consistent with their confession. How are we to treat them? We cannot refuse them meals, a listening ear, or a hug. I do not believe such is required, especially those who are family. However, those who are placed under church discipline and have been publicly proclaimed unrepentant should require such treatment as hard as it is. Principally, it is important for all of us to consider how our treatment of loved ones, whom we know are not living consistently with their confession, should be treated. For their benefit and for the benefit of the gospel, we must not in any way condone the sinful lifestyle of a loved one. The most practical way to do this is to lovingly share the truth of God's word, leaving no misunderstanding of what is sin and what is righteous. A scheme of the devil today is to have someone close to us claim to be a sinner And the loving thing to do is proudly accept the person who wishes to be attached to their sin. But such is not the love of God that accepts the behavior of a person who claims the homosexual lifestyle style or the fornicating lifestyle, which is just as bad. The love of God calls people out of such lifestyles in order to be free, free from the chains that desires of the flesh can place them in. What God desires for us is that we do our very best to stay away from an identity that connects us to sin. There is an old story of a king that serves us well here. There was a king who lived in his castle perched on a hilltop high, on looking the homes of his subjects. The king was committed to descend from his castle every day to be amidst his people. When looking for a charioteer to take him down that windy road, he interviewed three men. The king's main question to each was How close can you come to the edge of the road without falling off the cliff? The first man said, I can come within a foot without falling off the rocky cliff. The second man said, I can do better. I can come within an inch. And the third man said, I will never come close to the edge. The third man was higher. The whole purpose of eating with unbelievers of the world and not eating with Christians who are behaving like unbelievers is to lead the sinner to repentance. The purpose of excommunication, of discipline, of not eating, of disfellowshipping, of leaving no misunderstanding is to lead the sinner to repentance. Remember, our whole mission of our lives is to get from this life to the next. It is not to have everyone like us. It is not to be the most popular. It is not to wink at sin for the sake of being accepted. It is not to have the greatest following. It is to get from this life to the next and to help as many people as would like us to help them to do the same. Let us pray. But God, we thank you for the challenge of the apostle. No compromise does Paul have, even in the midst of such sinful men and hypocrisy within the church. Father, help us hold the same standard, believe in the same way that you will meet us as we do, because we want to get from this world and the next, and we want others to do the same. Pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: We Must Get Along
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Kindred have a great and I'm an evil remote. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. We are examining 1 Corinthians chapter 6, starting at 1, going through 11, continuing our series in 1 Corinthians. Can't we all just get along? Most adults remember those words from a convicted felon as chastisement to the city of Los Angeles and the country as a whole. Although reworded for grammatical reasons, a similar question can be asked of the Christian church. It was several years ago that I heard a statistic compiled by the Barna Institute finding that one in six families church hop annually. With megachurches increasing in number, it makes it that much easier to slip in and out of church with no one seeing you and no one caring for you. Such hopping makes it appear that we can't get along. The apostle addressed in the previous chapter the issue of treating those who are unbelievers outside the church and those who are behaving like unbelievers inside the church. We concluded that we are to treat both in a redemptive manner. We care about the soul. Experientially, we may note that it is seemingly much easier to be gracious and patient and kind to those outside the church than it is to those within the church. Pastor Ron Greer served an evangelical church in Madison, Wisconsin. Greer was a bi-vocational pastor, as he also worked for a local fire department. He was fired from his second job at the fire department for passing out tracts which described homosexuality as a sin. When the city's homosexual activists found out about the pastor's tracks, they stormed into Greer's church, disrupted the service throwing condoms at the communion table and shouting obscenities. Ron Greer responded by graciously inviting them to join the worship service. Later, later, when the press asked how he had kept his cool, he smiled and said, I have no more reason to be angry with them than I would a blind man who had stepped on my foot. What a great perspective. Donald Waite was a former Navy chaplain who was named the new pastor of Emmanuel Baptist Church just outside of Boston. Pastor Wade began his ministry in earnest by sitting down with every family in the church to hear their story. Pastor Wade, however, heard more than personal stories of each family. He also heard stories of gossip and slander of other families. He not only had an ear for such stories, but encouraged them. Soon the church became a distrustful community. as the pastor used the information he had he had gained to sway the decisions of the church to his favor. Subsequently, the people became distrustful of one another, and of course, their pastor. A congregational meeting was called by the deacons to take a vote of confidence over the pastor. Baptists can do that. The pastor, however, would not allow an announcement for such a meeting to be made. On the fourth Sunday of the pastor's stonewalling, two deacons attempted to control the microphone during the announcement to announce the meeting. A shove from the pastor and a punch from a deacon began what was literally a Donny Brook within the sanctuary. After the police arrived to restore order, the key players were called before the local courthouse for a hearing. The presiding judge was David Goldstein. A member of the local Jewish synagogue. After assessing the charges, Judge Goldstein said Quote, no charges will be pressed at this point, but I urge you to work this out within your own church. Your Jesus Christ may allow this sort of thing in his followers. But the Commonwealth of Massachusetts will not permit fistfights as a regular part of a church service. And we say out. With such stories of church conflicts in our minds, let us now turn to 1 Corinthians chapter 6. After addressing the immoral problem within the Corinthian church, the apostle addresses his third issue of concern. He is upset with the church for not being able to work through and settle their disagreements Again, like a lecturing father, the apostle forcefully chastises the church. He desires them to feel shame for bringing the world into the church to solve their disputes. Admittedly, the apparent dispute likely had something to do with a good deal of money or or valuables But for the apostle, no amount of money can ever justify Christians not being able to settle their own disputes The passage is unequivocal in its denouncing of Christians who would bring other Christians to a court of law. The reasoning of this prohibition begins with the realization that such judges are incapable of ruling according to God's law. And an equally important concern for Paul, and hopefully for the church, is a witness to the gospel that that is to be maintained before unbelievers. In verse 1, the apostle refers to the unrighteous. And this description of those magistrates within the world can be translated unlawful. Or those without the law of God. It is certain that the Corinthian culture was not learned in the Mosaic law Without knowing the Mosaic Law, secular judges have a very hard time achieving justice by God's standards. Certainly each of us has heard stories of how justice is passed down in courtrooms today with no consideration of God's law and in too many cases no consideration of even the Constitution. Consider cases that judges allow to go to trial. In 2011, a monkey grabbed a hold of nature photographer David Slater's camera and snapped a selfie of himself. The animal rights group PETA filed a lawsuit claiming that the copyright for the photograph should belong to the monkey. After years of courtroom drama, both parties eventually came to a settlement regarding bad rulings in New Jersey of this year. A 16-year-old boy raped a drunken 16-year-old female classmate, filmed it, and titled the film Rape. The judge found the boy innocent because he judged rape being defined as being held at gunpoint. The judge also said that the boy was from a good family, he had good grades, and he had a bright future. An appeals court overruled the judge writing a 14-page rebuke of his prejudicial ruling. You can easily find more examples of incompetent rulings by judges and frivolous lawsuits by citizens that have nothing to do with true justice. And no wonder. For the magistrates of our day have no reference point for morality. What is right or wrong is determined by the wind Created by local media and polling data. The Constitution has more and more become a document of personal interpretation by judges more concerned about a personal agenda than the original intent of our founding fathers. And I know none of this, none of these examples are a surprise nor is a return to God's moral law or an original reading of the Constitution something I think will ever be regained. The truth is, when the parameters of God's law are removed, there are no boundaries to keep the sinful tendencies of mankind hemmed in. Placing ourselves before secular magistrates to settle disputes with one another is similar to launching dice in Atlantic City hoping for good luck. Where we should go to settle such disputes should be determined by those who know the law of God and are therefore have the mind of God. Thankfully, we have a form of church government that allows us to look to our pastor, our priest, and our wardens. If no decision can be reached, we may appeal to our bishops and then to the College of Bishops. And if we are God-fearing in our Christian walk, We will submit to their leadership and abide by their ruling. Such is rare. Rare to hear about in these times, but it is set up to be used if we cannot settle a dispute. It is not altogether clear what the apostle means in verses 2 and 3, where he describes Christians judging the world and then judging angels. Such judgment is elsewhere left up to Jesus as he is the one who is found worthy. The Apostle's reference most likely is that we as his children will indeed sit at Christ's right hand. And because we are seated with Christ, who reigns above all, we become participants in his judgment of the world. The angels to be judged could refer to the angels who have fallen, as Saint Peter describes, or all angels who become subject to us who are faithful in this life. Because the apostle does not go into great detail regarding these judgments, it is likely that he wishes for us to get the main point. If such large responsibilities will be placed upon us in the end, should we not be able to complete our duties now with the smaller things? It is to the church's shame that not only do we struggle to get along and handle our own disputes, But we can't even decide who among us is good enough to be a judge. Are we that distrustful of one another? Most certainly the inability to answer who is best among us to judge tells us how unhealthy we can be. Upon going to civil magistrates to settle disputes within the church, we have already failed as faithful witnesses to the gospel. One can only imagine how long it would take for the Jewish judge in that second story to overcome the bias that was undoubtedly engendered by what he witnessed by these Christians in his courtroom. This is what the apostle means by referring to it as an utter failure. They have utterly failed as witnesses to the gospel. They have failed to be faithful and they have failed to glorify God. What would be better for the apostle, the apostle says, is to endure the wrong suffering rather than be found unfaithful. And it is here, at that point, that we find the Christian ethic that goes beyond any teaching that is known by the world. Christians are called to endure a wrong suffered to prevent a wrong from being perpetrated. What else did Christ mean when he told us to offer the other cheek? Provide an extra coat or go an extra mile We as followers of the Lamb, led to the slaughter in silence, are called to endure wrong done to us for the sake of the gospel. Witness. Now again, the context is within the church. The wrongdoing suffered is within the church. Paul is not saying that Christians can't use secular courts at any time. The Apostle Paul, after all, appealed to his Roman magistrates for his release from prison to preach the gospel. It was not Christian involvement with magistrates altogether that the apostle is concerned for. He was concerned with Christians charging and suing Christians. No doubt there are many Christians who will be noted on that great day of judgment of their enduring wrong for the sake of the gospel. Many of these wrongdoings are only known by the ones suffering them, but they nonetheless endure quietly for the sake of the church's witness and the unity of God's people. Remember, no greater love as any man than the one who lays down his life for a friend. This includes laying down one's pride and one's rights as well. Verse 8 and following is a break in the text as Paul gets to what some call the nitty-gritty of the issue. Apparently the reason why there are disputes within the church is the same reason why there are disputes before civil magistrates. The reason is sin. You yourselves do wrong, he says. The number of sins headlined by types of sexual immorality are sins that reflect a person's character. It is sin and sin alone that causes Christians to go at one another with unrighteous fervor. And our first story, the love of Christ, was readily expressed to those who were violently opposed to the pastor. His patience and understanding, with their blindness to their own sin, is commendable and biblical. Our second story showed no patience, no righteous character, as lines within the church were drawn due to the sins of gossip and slander. And I suspect as well that the sins of gossip and slander were merely the sins that were known, that are likely those that were unknown that needed to be revealed. As sin dominated the relationship between the pastor and some of the members of the congregation, it exploded as we should expect in Mahem. And here is another problem with the modern church that must be addressed if our witness to the truth of the gospel is going to be effectual. We must work not to wink at sin. Not to wink at sin. Too many Christians today wink at sin. Now the phrase wink at sin refers to a realization between two people as they are looking upon something or talking about something. That there is a wrong being done, but one party winks to the other party as a signal that it's wrong, it's immoral, but it's not a big deal. And so parents allow their children to explore their sexuality with their girlfriend or boyfriend because, well, it's all part of growing up. Wink, wink. Adults smoke marijuana because it's just like drinking alcohol when it isn't. And besides, no one is prosecuting it anymore. Wink wink. A father finds evidence that his son is looking at pornography on his computer and well he reasons at least he's not gay. Wink, wink, and again, wink. Every week breaks down the truth that we say we believe. And not only does the world see us as hypocrites, so do our children. And when Christianity is not seen as real in the life of parents, it will not be real in the life of their children. The sober reminder of the apostle to the church is that those who practice such sins listed will not inherit the kingdom of God. And of course, that's a nice way of saying they are bound for hell. The list of sins begins with what most cultures would recognize as unacceptable behavior. And because idolatry was combined with sexual immorality within the Corinthian culture, it is understandable why it would be licid amongst fornicators and homosexuals and others The other section of the list seems to be a grab bag of sins with no apparent theme. And this is due to the fact that the apostle is not making an exhaustive list of sins. but is highlighting perhaps some he is aware of in the midst of the Corinthian church. It is easy for a preacher to mention these types of sins because the sexual ones get all the attention. But notice among the list is covetousness. Covetous is the sin of not being satisfied with what God has provided. But instead waiting, wanting what others have, even though we don't need it It is especially rampant this time of year. Being covetous begins with being ungrateful to God. It then turns to jealousy of others And then wants what others have, even though it is not theirs to have, and then it turns into stealing or extortion or whatever means necessary to get what you want. It begins with the heart and ends in death. Now the glory of the text Is that the apostle says, and such were some of you. And such were some of you. This first means that these Christians are removed from such sins and are, for the most part, leading moral lives for Christ. And second, it means that such sins can be overcome, can be placed in the past. Such is the hope of the gospel. Drunkards can no longer be drunkards. Sexually immoral can no longer be sexually immoral. The gospel of Jesus Christ provides a person to no longer be attached to the sin. Sins that our culture informs us are part of our psychological makeup and hence cannot be overcome can be overcome by the gospel of Christ. The fact that it only takes confession of mouth and belief in the heart that Jesus is the Savior. And God disrupts the lie that we can earn anything by his favor. We can't, we don't. The moral requirement of us is to live our lives according to what we say we believe. And that begins with how we treat one another. And changing how we treat one another to be loved first and last is a great way to prepare ourselves for his coming again. Let us pray. Our gracious God, we see the standard here. We see what needed to be corrected in Corinth, and although We don't know of such sins in our midst. We certainly see the need to forgive one another, to handle our disputes together, to guard from sin and not wink at it. And first and foremost, care about our witness of your gospel to the world. Keep that in our conscience, we pray, in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Sexual Immorality Again
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated and turn in your Bibles to 1 Corinthians chapter 6, working from verse 12 through 20 And as you do that, I want to start off by saying that I do not wish to preach about or against sexual immorality for a third week And I can easily guess that you don't want to hear another sermon about or against sexual immorality. But here we are. The Apostle Paul has addressed three major sins within the church in the first six chapters. They are disunity, immorality, and lawsuits against the brethren.
