The second is the transitory nature of all earthly things. And the third is the comparative freedom From care in being unmarried. The address begins by referring to virgins. It is assumed that those who are not married and are in the church are virgins. This does not mean that the unmarried are disqualified if they are not virgins. God can make all of us virgins by his grace. The apostle precedes his comments again with a qualifying remark that he has no command from the Lord about this topic. Christ Jesus did not speak about the issue. He did not counsel his apostles either about it. Paul then is making it clear that he is giving his opinion. And again, his opinion is based on the belief that Jesus and his return is imminent. And so this is what we should do. So, in the apostle's opinion, the first reason a person who is unmarried should stay the same is due to the possible suffering marriage could bring. And it's not the suffering you might be thinking about. This suffering is not due to the torment one suffers from a burdensome spouse. In the apostle's words, he calls the suffering the present crisis. As I said, the apostle believed the words of Jesus. He believed The Lord's words when Jesus told his disciples that the about the signs of the end of the age, which we read from the gospel according to St. Luke, there was a promise there that The generation that was following Jesus would not pass away until all of these things took place. The Apostle Paul lived and taught and preached as if any day could be his last day and the last day of his peers. He of course was correct in this belief, but it happened differently than what he expected in terms of Jesus returning When Jesus prophesied as to what would happen at the end of the age, as we read in Luke, He was describing what was fulfilled in A. D. 70 when the city of Jerusalem was destroyed at the hands of the Romans. False cries appeared at that time. Wars and rumors of wars alarmed the masses. There were earthquakes and famine. Christians were persecuted to their death. It was a dreadful time for those in the city of Jerusalem as they fled to the mountains, as pregnant women were especially susceptible to mistreatment. All of this was what the Savior warned about to the generation that he was speaking to. So although this was fulfilled in AD 70, these warnings apply to us as much as they did to the first century church. But we have lost a sense of urgency. Every age has its moments of crisis. Every age has signs of the end. They all eventually lead to the real end of time and the return of Christ. Yet today we are easily lulled into casualness. The return of Christ has been spoken about for almost 2,000 years, and still he is not here. The message no longer has the intensity it once had, especially for the first generation. Our behavior in everyday life usually does not reflect a belief that Christ is coming and he's coming soon. But look around you, my friends. Pay attention to the world in which we live. As already stated, each age has signs of the end. We right now hear of wars and rumors of wars, Iraq and Iran. We have numerous false Christs, false teachers. The information age has brought us these false teachers to our front door daily. Morally right is called morally wrong, and morally wrong is called morally right. The younger generation thinks they are awake when they call females males and males females, or simply ignore gender differences altogether. They are not woke, but sleepwalking at best. Such are signs of the end, signs of Christ coming again. And as many people may perceive, Christ not coming soon, we often forget that he comes to people daily. As men and women have their lives snuffed out unexpectedly. A man who is swept away by a storm crushed in an accident or taken out by a heart attack is a man who has had Christ come again specifically to him Do not forget what the apostle tells us. With the Lord, a day is of a thousand years. A thousand years is like a day. The Lord is not slow in keeping his promises, as some understand, slowness. He is patient with you, not wanting any to perish, but for all to come to repentance. This is why the apostle thinks it is good for us to remain as we are. To be married places us in a susceptible position. Fleeing to the mountains, enduring persecution, and suffering hardship is better done as an unmarried person, without a doubt. The heartache of watching a loved one endure suffering is much more difficult than bearing such suffering yourself. The second reason to remain unmarried is the transitory nature of earthly things. This is expressed in the apostles' words, those who marry will face many troubles in this life. Such troubles include fleeting moments of joy in marriage, but also mourning in death, trials for each day. Those who use the things of this world will find them passing away all too quickly. We must be honest and confess that the merry life can be one of monotony. That is to say, that there is an aspect of married life that is tedious and time-consuming. The tedious things we do do not always appear to have lasting value Keeping the kitchen clean, washing clothes, paying bills, caring for the lawn, or like the jobs we become engrossed in by sweat and worry. And the end of time as we do them doesn't seem to matter. In the moment there appears to be no connection between mowing the lawn and eternity. Except for sometimes mowing the lawn seems to take an eternity. Much of what we do within the context of our homes seems to have no immediate value. The great irony is that this world is in its present form passing away. And we spend a large portion of our lives trying to maintain it. But that perception is false, as I will soon address. As an unmarried man, the apostle had little investment in the present form of the world. He was a tent maker, you remember, who only worked enough so he could earn money to travel and to eat He was free from the responsibilities of a wife and children. He was free to invest his life in that which would not pass away, the kingdom of God. And this moves us to the third reason for remaining unmarried. The unmarried have freedom from the cares of this world. Monasteries and nunneries were developed with this thought in mind, with this principle in mind. A nun within the Roman Catholic Church is understood to be married by vow to Jesus Christ. As a full-time servant, she is able to be concerned solely with the Lord's affairs. A monk is concerned to have the same is is considered to have the same freedom as he devotes himself solely to studying, preserving, and teaching the Word of God. Of course one does not have to join a monastery or a nunnery to be wholly devoted to God. The description the apostle uses in verse 39 regarding a wife's responsibility to her spouse. Leaves little room for doubt that married life restricts one's freedom, at least as Paul is describing it. The wife is described as bound to her husband. She is bound by her vow. Her vow to her husband requires her to perform certain duties. And restricts her ability to move freely about as the Spirit of God might otherwise call her to do. That's a reality. In saying all of this, it may appear to some that the apostle fails to see the glories of marriage. And we confirmed two weeks ago that he certainly does understand the glories of that marriage covenant. He also understands that when a wife is bound in her duties to her husband, she is glorifying God. He understands that when a man is working within a With the concern about the things of this world, he is doing so for the benefit of his family, and God is well pleased. What undergirds the opinion of the apostle is again what is articulated to the Ephesian church. He is telling them to redeem the time, make use of the time. For the days in which you live are evil. The apostle is like a prophet In earnest. He feels the end of the age approaching. He senses the calling of the Lord in his own life and the lives of those around him. With his personal end approaching, he wants nothing to interfere with his devotion to Christ. If time is going to be redeemed, the church must act now. But what does this mean for us in this now new year twenty twenty? An obstacle before the church today that St. Paul did not have is that reality again. that it is almost 2,000 years having passed and Jesus has not returned. And because of that reality, it gets easier with each passing decade to be less urgent about his return. But Jesus didn't tell us to be urgent about his return. He simply told us to be ready. And as I stated, his return will at least be personal to each of us as we all face our own mortality. Because of our individual mortality, Jesus will return to us, and we are to be ready. And so we are to redeem our time, we are to redeem our days, our hours, we are to make them count. But how do we redeem our time? Well, this may sound a bit different than what the Apostle Paul is pointing to when he reveals that a married person gets tied up in worldly responsibilities, but I think he's pointing to a greater Responsibility, a greater principle. To redeem the times we live in, we must start by fulfilling our personal obligations. That's what he means by staying where you are. If you are in a present position, stay there and do your responsibilities. For those who are married or wish to be married, take care of your spouse. Do your job well. Learn in school if that's where you are. Train your children in the Lord if that's where you are. Pay your tithe and your bills, and yes, even your taxes. Do the basic things of responsible living in this world in order to train yourself for the world to come. The things of this world are passing away, and so we don't cling to them, but instead we use them to better our preparation. I heard an exchange from psychiatrist Dr. Jordan Peterson and a young college student that makes this point so glary. The college student challenged Peterson about his teaching that people should concern themselves first and foremost about their personal responsibilities rather than taking up social and political issues of today. The essence of the challenge was that young people should concern themselves with pressing global matters rather than trivial responsibilities such as cleaning their rooms. Peterson's response was simplistically brilliant when he said the following. People who don't have their own houses in order should be very careful before they go about reorganizing the world. He went on to say that, quote, generally, people have things in their personal lives that are more difficult to deal with and that they are avoiding. That generally they avoid them by adopting pseudo-moralistic stances on large-scale social issues so that they look good to their friends and neighbors. Such a diagnosis is dead on when describing the self-righteousness being expressed in our present day by mass media and again the woke generation. And I am arguing, it is what St. Paul is arguing to the Corinthians. Instead of getting caught up with the issues of the world, we are going to go about redeeming the time in which we live. By doing the things that matter eternally, and to prepare ourselves for the things that will ultimately last for eternity. If we get good at our personal responsibilities, we are indeed preparing ourselves for the coming again of Jesus. And this goes to the principle Jesus taught in the parable of the talents, where we learn to be faithful in the small things, and he will make us responsible for greater things. And those greater things are eternal things. And so, clean your room. Care for your spouse. Be accountable for your personal responsibilities. And when Jesus comes again to you personally or splits the eastern sky You are ready. Let us pray. Our Father, we are challenged by The simpleness of Paul's message of how to stay where we are and to be our best where we are. That in the end we might be prepared for your coming, whether it be personal or whether it be for your whole church. May that convict us enough, Father, to move, to change if need be, or to continue in faith as you call us to be. Above all, Heavenly Father, we want to be ready. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen

sermons.title: Knowledge and Love
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Open your Bibles to 1 Corinthians chapter 8. Follow along with me as we cover that chapter. 1 Corinthians chapter 8. As many of you know, I love chocolate chip cookies. Better stated, I love homemade chocolate chip cookies. I can give up dieting And eat when I'm not hungry, when my beloved wife cooks a new batch of her special recipe and method of chocolate chip cookies. And I cannot divulge what those special things are. Years ago I analyzed my love and devotion for chocolate chip cookies. I once thought I actually loved the chocolate chips, and the dough was a necessary evil. This, however, is false. The dough, I have come to realize, adds flavor to the chocolate chips and holds them together for a perfect order. Each on its own, the dough and the chip is good, but much better when they're placed together And please, please do not ruin a chocolate chip cookie with any type of nut. Can I get an Amen? This example, believe it or not, segues to our text, where the Apostle Paul addresses another issue that the Corinthians had written him about. The apparent question they asked was what the congregations should do regarding the controversy as to whether it was appropriate to eat meat that was first offered to idols. This problem was very common for the Corinthians as the city market was filled with meat that was first used to worship idols. The meat offered to idols was consumed by the offerer, then by the priest, and then the priest would take what was left over and sell it on the open market to subsidize his income. Why eating such meat would be questioned was primarily for two reasons. First, some were concerned That buying and eating such meat would be, in a spiritual way, participating in idol worship Second, a part of the worship of idols was the belief that eating the meat used in worship is a consuming of the power of that spirit of that idol Thus, there was a concern about the spiritual power within the meat. It is easily assumed from the content of the apostle's response. That the Corinthians added to their question comments about their knowledge of idols, stating that they did understand that these idols Representing gods, because those gods did not exist, the idols really didn't mean anything. The possible logic of their thought process was that If an idol represents a god that does not exist, then the meat offered to something that does not exist And is therefore not actually meat offered to an idol or a false god, it's just meat But to answer the question, the apostle appeals to what will we refer to, or I will refer to this morning as Christian maturation. A particular problem is placed before the apostle. He addresses the problem while at the same time addressing issues of Christian maturity. It can be easy, and all of us are guilty of this, to focus on the example of the particular problem. and not learn the general lesson or the the principle of the problem that needs to be applied. And the example I just I previously gave shoots the point Upon hearing my love for chocolate chip cookies, you may disagree with me entirely, and you do so on the basis that you don't like chocolate chip cookies. You may be one who insists that chocolate chip cookies need walnuts. Others may insist that the whole cookie experience is not complete without a nice cold glass of milk. And upon taking such positions, my point of emphasis has been lost to you because the focus has been placed on the particulars of the example and not the general truths. If we get caught up with the particular issue of meat offered to idols, we lose the general lesson of Christian maturation. Lessons can be bogged down by qualifications that answer the what-if questions. What-if questions, there is no end to them. The purpose of my chocolate chip cookie analogy was to show the relationship between knowledge and maturity. One can be good without the other, but when they come together, something is created that is better than good. Knowing truth and practicing truth without maturity makes the knowledge incomplete. And here's a key ingredient. Christian maturity adds love. It adds love to the truths that are known and then practiced. The Christian life is always one of maturing, never arriving on this side of heaven. And I want to say that again for emphasis. The Christian life is always one of maturing on this side of heaven. When we learn something about Christ, a part of every lesson is that there's always something more to learn. Those who are truly educated, truly educated, are humbled by what they do not know It is not until we are glorified that we will be able to know all truth, or at least spend eternity learning all truth. This is all a preface by the apostle before he answers directly the question posed to him. The Corinthians must understand the benefits and weaknesses of knowledge by itself. They must be challenged to add the love of God to their understanding, which will enable them to make mature decisions regarding such issues as offering meat to idols. The apostle is providing what many refer to in a negative way as a pastoral answer. Such answers come in the form of essays rather than yes and no. Ask a pastor a question, oh, here we go. And it is understandable that a parishioner would like a yes and no answer. However, without understanding the why. We have a tendency to become like Pharisees. We become legalistic. Questions such as: Should a Christian woman wear a bikini bathing suit in public? Should a Christian mother work outside the home? Can a Christian attend a football game on a Sunday without breaking the Sabbath? Today we can add, can Christians smoke weed? It's a popular question. When these are answered with a yes or a no, it appears to create a law for all of us to abide by when there isn't a law. Yes and no answers do not take into consideration the many possible variables. To provide an elongated answer helps establish principles which respect possible variables. So we look in verses 4 through 6. The apostle breaks down what the Corinthians know. We know, he says. And what they knew is that an idol is nothing. And what he means by that is that the idol is a non-entity It is only what it is made out of. There is no personality or power behind the idol. The only power an idol has is what the worshipper ascribes to it. It is the same logic that some have applied to guns and other weapons. The only danger lies in the one who handles the weapon. The only authority in an idol that it holds over men is the power that men give to it. To take this thought further, excuse me, we see, we must see, I believe, the great irony of idol worship. If idols only have the authority that is prescribed to it by men, then what we end up worshiping is an idol that is very much like ourselves. Man with his personality gives life to idols. And this has been revealed in how some indigenous tribes would use totem pole-like images that have carved heads of different animals that carry certain virtues that the particular tribe wants to emulate. The ideal person that is brave, loyal, and such is who that people want to be or who they think they are. Thus, the personality of our idols is self. When a man worships an idol, he is either worshiping himself or what he desires to be. Even though idols are non-entities, the apostle recognizes the spiritual forces behind idols. He recognizes not the gods these idols represent, but the demonic forces behind them that call them to false worship. And these so-called gods are demonic, and they are real, and therefore they must not be underestimated. They also must not be overestimated, for above them is the one true God, God the Father God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, have the position of reigning above these false idols or so-called gods, for they are the creators. The Trinity is the creator, the sustainer of all life, including the demonic. Sadly. Even though the leaders in Corinth, or at least the writers to Paul, understood the true nature of idols, these so-called gods, but some in the church did not. Not everyone has the same knowledge, and that results in frustrating conversations. It disrupts unity. It might easily be assumed that all who attend this church understand the principles of historic Anglican liturgy. And might also be understood by those on the outside that each of us understands the episcopal form of government that we practice. But such assumptions would be wrong. Would you like to have an experiment? How about an assignment? Let's have each of us write a 500 words or less paper about why the Anglican liturgy found in the Book of Common Prayer is more biblically responsible than other modern worship orders Ready go. Or how about a 500-word or less paper on why the episcopal form of government is to be preferred as opposed to the congregational or presbyterian? Ready, go Personally, I didn't know these differences until someone held a grade over my head and threatened to flunk me until I studied these issues. So let us be honest and admit that we choose a parish based on relationships with other believers We also base our decisions to be a member here or elsewhere on personal feelings we have about the services or the minister. The majority that have come through our doors and chosen not to make our fellowship their home Base their decision on what they like or what they don't like as opposed to what they know Formalism as we practice it, for many, communicates a dead faith. I know it does because that's exactly what it spoke to me when I was a new convert. Ignorance, or more gently stated, immaturity, causes us to make decisions based on what we like or how we feel, not on what we know. Because there were those Christians in Corinth that did not understand the issues of idols fully, they responded to it immaturely. Some could not disassociate the meat offered to idols with the idols themselves. They believed in their conscience that they were participating in idol worship by eating the meat offered to the idols. Paul refers to these Christians as weak. Their weakness was in their conscience. And this weakness, however, does not remove them as having a personal relationship with Christ. They are still Christian. They are still members of Christ's church. The conscience of a person is a powerful deterrent and should not be cast aside lightly. The Holy Spirit speaks to every Christian, guiding him or her to all truth. Those messages, however. Are deciphered through the past experiences of a person and lingering guilt of past behavior The voice of God can be muddled and interfered by that guilt. The apostle knows the truth should be obvious Whether a person eats meat offered to idols or does not eat meat offered to idols does not matter either way. Neither way is a sin. He may sin, a Christian may sin if he acts against his own conscience Understand that if a man goes against his own conscience, he will find it easier to go against God's law. If a man's conscience is not heeded, neither will he heed the voice of God. And those two statements are hard for some people to accept, but life experience verifies them. If you go against your conscience, your conscience becomes hardened, and the voice of your conscience is harder to hear. This flows over to your ability to hear the Holy Spirit as he too becomes harder to hear. How not to treat Christians with a weak conscience can be seen in this following example. A church was attempting to move from drinking grape juice for Holy Communion to drinking wine, something we will be talking about at our next annual meeting. The pastor was convinced that when Christ took the cup of wine and said, Drink this in remembrance of me, he was implementing wine as the most appropriate symbol for his blood. Therefore, the pastor reasoned, wine should be what the church uses just as Jesus commanded. Upon the first service where wine was used, the elements were taken to the nursery workers. The two women in the nursery stated that they could not drink the wine, for they did not consume alcohol. The response of the pastor's wife, who happened to be in the room at the time, was stated bluntly. Jesus drank wine, and he told us to do the same, so get over it. Now, the knowledge of the pastor's wife was and is irrefutable. True, Jesus did drink actual wine. True, he did tell his disciples to do the same. And true, it would be best if the young ladies got over it. However, there is something obviously missing within this knowledge. What is missing is the love of God. In verses 9 through 13, the apostle recognizes the knowledge of the Corinthian leaders and the freedom that knowledge brings. This, however, is not where a mature Christian stops. A maturing Christian adds to his freedom responsibility. A maturing Christian takes into account the weakness of his brother in Christ. This, my friends, is adding love to our knowledge. Christian maturation is the process of understanding all the facets of our faith. Understanding both freedom and responsibility within the faith. That's following the example of Christ. As much as I am to obey the command the Lord gave Peter, which is to get up and eat, Even eat food that was once considered unclean, I am also to obey the Lord's warning that if I cause a young one, an immature one, to stumble Well, it's better that I had a stone cast around my neck and thrown into the sea. Christ takes issue with those who tempt and lead astray the weak and the young. He takes it personally, and so should we. The mature in Christ give way to the weak. It is as Christ has done. He refused to regard equality with God a thing to be grasped. He took on the form of a servant. He added love to his knowledge, and that made him most lovely. Complete devotion to Christ includes sensitivity to the conscience of a brother or sister. It includes a denial of our own freedom for the strengthening of another's weakness. Okay. All of this sounds good, but the question has still not been answered. Which is it, Pastor? Can we eat meat offered to idols? Can Christian women wear bikinis? Can Christian mothers work outside the home? Can men go to football games on the Lord's Day? What about whether it is acceptable as a clap in church? Can divorced Christians remarry? Is it a sin to drink hard drink? Does the Bible forbid Christians seeing rated R movies? Does it? Is it? Can we? I mentioned the question, should Christians smoke marijuana? Because we should be wrestling with how we are to apply God's law to certain behaviors, we should try to answer that question. More dilemmas of a similar nature are going to be placed before us. We need, as a church, to have answers. Well, I'm not going to answer that question about marijuana smoking today, but stay tuned. It can be answered, and the principles in 1 Corinthians 8 can be used to help us answer the question. My best answer to all such questions and the many of their type: if the chips are knowledge. And the dough is love. I think we need more dough with our chocolate chips. Let us pray. Our Father, we thank you for the courage of Saint Paul to address issues that are pressing in the moment for your people. We confess today that we have them and we wonder, but we thank you for the model here of taking what is true and what we know and applying that love. Father, help us to be mature in you and toward one another. Pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Free for the Truth
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated and turn in your Bibles to 1 Corinthians chapter 9, our epistle reading, 1 Corinthians. Chapter nine As all of you would agree, certain social conversations can be awkward. It can be awkward for a myriad of reasons, especially when you are getting to know someone. You don't know their moral standing, their political affiliation, their marital status, their the cookies they like, you don't know much of anything about them. And such issues are important for if we speak in favor of something our new acquaintance opposes We have offended before we have befriended. This is especially true in this day of President Donald Trump. It is difficult to diagnose all persons as to why they get emotionally hysterical over their hatred for the president. Whether you agree with his policies or not, as Christians, we are not to be emotionally hysterical about anyone or their policies. Because Jesus Christ is seated at the right hand of the Father, and thus nothing outside of God's sovereign will, including the rise and decline of political leaders, nothing is outside of God's will. There are also so many people today presented to us in the media who are quickly offended at certain types of speech. I am aware that much of what I preach each Sunday would be labeled by the current media as offensive and even hate speech. So be it. But offensive speech can occur between two friends as well One can babble on, pontificating about one issue after another, not even realizing they have just offended a friend. We all, by experience, can confirm the proverb: When the words are many, sin is not absent. Unfortunately, much offense occurs between friends because what was stated was poorly stated, and what was heard was poorly heard. One of the more difficult responsibilities is public speaking. When you speak publicly, there are multiple possibilities to be misunderstood and to make offense. In the ministry, the possibility to offend is greater because a minister is expected to say everything well without misspeaking, stumbling, or being too personal. You seem to forget that Jesus himself made great offense to his audiences. Consider that he spoke directly to religious leaders and called them hypocrites. To others, he spoke in parables that they did not understand. And still to others he spoke in a grotesque manner. Remember that unless you eat of my flesh and drink of my blood, you cannot be my disciple. The result was people walking away in disgust. It is a difficult task to speak truth to an audience while at the same time encouraging them to follow you. When you read the book of Hosea, for example, you will note the bravado in the prophet's message. Comparing his bravado to preachers of today. You will easily identify how men do not speak the truth within their own pulpits When speculating as to why ministers do not stand up and speak the truth to their congregations today, you may think that there is a fear of hurting the feelings of those in the parish. When feelings are hurt, parishioners become angry. When parishioners get angry, well, enough of them, a minister could lose his job. Some ministers don't preach by conviction for fear of losing their paycheck. C. S. Lewis calls such ministers who give in to such fear as men without chests. Men without chests can be caused by in part by congregations without ears. As Paul warned Timothy There would be a time when men will want to not want to hear sound doctrine, but prefer to have their ears tickled. It becomes a revolving cycle that is hard to jump off. Pastors don't preach the truth because congregations become angry. The people don't hear the truth because the past pastor is afraid to preach it. The result is a congregation remaining comfortable in their sin and a pastor uncomfortable in his calling. To turn this around, someone has to take up the mantle and speak the truth, regardless of the consequences. Even when someone tells you that he wants to hear the truth, I want to hear the truth, experience has taught us that most underestimate how much they can handle. What husband hasn't been in a quandary when his wife asks him if she looks fat in this new dress If he says no, he is lying. If he says yes, he gets boiled cabbage for dinner. A wise husband. Must realize that his wife doesn't want to know the straight-out truth about weight gain. She wants to know if her husband still finds her attractive. What he should say is, honey, you look great in everything that you wear. Of course, the same scenario can be described of a balding man. All of this that I've said thus far is a setup. To examine what St. Paul faced as a founding preacher, pastor to these Corinthian Christians. The Apostle Paul found freedom in preaching the truth. He was comfortable to say what needed to be said, regardless of how it was to be received. And this is not to say that he desired to run Rushd over the people of God. He is called to be a minister, a caretaker. He is the one who instructed the Galatians to be rebuked, but to do it in love. Such reveals his heart as a pastor. This is after he stated to the Galatians that the church was bewitched. The apostle, nonetheless, had a reputation for being much more harsh in his letters than when he came and talked to them in person. And this shows us that although he was right in what he said, he was gentle in the way he communicated it. His ability to say what needed to be said came from his confidence in his calling in Christ and his freedom to not be dependent upon man. If you remember from our look at 1 Corinthians chapter 8 last week, the apostle instructed for the strong in the faith. To give way to the weak for the sake of the kingdom of God. He now uses his own life as an example of how he has given way to the weak for the sake of the kingdom. For the Corinthians to understand just how much he has given, he reminds them of his position as an apostle. That's how he starts the chapter. The office of apostle commanded immediate respect from the Christian community. These were men that were chosen by Christ personally to continue his work. Honored as he ascended to heaven. First, you remember there was the twelve. One was a traitor. Another was added immediately after Jesus ascended. The integrity of the twelve was known by all within the faith. They had seen Jesus. They knew him intimately. And most importantly, Jesus personally commissioned them. So the Apostle Paul comes along claiming to be an apostle It's clear he's not part of the first twelve. He makes thirteen. That's odd. An interesting note. on the question of where he fits in, is that with the twelve tribes of Judah, you remember that Joseph's his tribe was split in two. Being represented by his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. Thus there were thirteen tribes, just as there were thirteen apostles. But it was due to the manner of Paul's conversion and his effectiveness in ministry soon after. It was impossible to deny, even by the other twelve, that Paul was an apostle The twelve recognized his legitimacy on a number of factors, including his dramatic conversion, where Jesus appeared to him personally and commissioned him personally. This personal commission was verified in his effectiveness in ministry to the Gentiles. This effectiveness was written firsthand by the Corinthians. They knew his labor. They knew the results of his apostleship. Paul then appeals to the personal testimony of the Corinthians. Others may deny his apostleship because it was not procured like the first twelve, but surely the Corinthians knew differently. To confirm Paul as an apostle to the Gentiles, one needs to look no further than the Corinthians themselves, who were saved out of the darkness of paganism and into the light of Christ. It must be concluded that if the office of apostle commands immediate respect, then Paul himself commands immediate respect. The respect of his office commands includes freedom in behavior. He says he is free to drink as he wishes Eat as he wishes, and take a believing wife as he wishes. As an apostle, no one stands in judgment over him regarding such matters. Now, regardless of what the Roman Catholic Church would have us believe, the apostles, along with presbyters and deacons, had a right to take a wife. In fact, we should consider it a great irony that the Roman Church would so doggedly hold to the practice of celibacy amongst its priests when Peter was the first supposedly the first pontiff. We know that Peter had a family, as he is referred to here as Cephas by the Apostle Paul. He had a wife and extended family to care for. And there was most certainly nothing wrong with having a wife. It is within their rights. Another right of the office of apostle and/or preacher of the gospel is the right to be paid. In verses six through twelve, the right is explained as natural and scriptural. Apparently, Paul and his companion Barnabas were expected in some circles to have to work in order to continue supporting their own ministry while the other apostles were paid by the church. Paul points out that other occupations, such as a soldier and a farmer and a shepherd, allow the workmen to receive the benefits that they help produce. He gives another example in the law of Moses of when an oxen was feeding on the grain that the oxen was treading. These mills, some of them are still used today in the Middle East, consisted of a pole sticking straight up, and then another pole perpendicular to which the oxen was attached. And the oxen goes around in circles milling the grain. During the work, the grain would come out and be on the ground, and the law then forbids a cruel master from muzzling the oxen to prevent him from eating the grain on which he is working. The Apostle Paul claims this law to have been written for the application to ministers. A minister of the gospel deserves to eat from the fruit of his labor. A minister sows spiritual seed. The righteousness, blessings, and souls reaped from such seeds are a harvest for which he has a right to receive. Verse 12 closes the point by reminding the Corinthians that others have received financial support from them and Paul, although deserving it more Paul has not. Now one would think that the apostle has said enough to make his point, but he says more In case he has not been emphatic, he reminds them that the workers in the temple were to receive a share of the offerings. And this fact allows him to brazenly state that the Lord has commanded that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel. With that argument being emphatically made by the apostle, he now explains what he is getting at, what his point is. He has not used any of the rights that are afforded to him as an apostle. He does not drink or eat whatever he wants. He does not have a wife. He does not receive financial help from those whom he has sown into spiritual seeds. This is Paul's elongated example of how he, as an apostle, has acted out of charity, the same charity he previously charged the church to practice. That charity, that love we discussed in chapter 8, was to give way to the weak so that they can become strong. Paul has given away his rights. Many of the pleasures this life offers could rightly be claimed by him, that he refused them in order to be strong for those who were weak. So that they can become strong. The result of the apostle denying himself of his rights has greater consequences than strengthening the weak, as if that was not enough. For the apostle, a greater consequence is freedom when preaching the gospel. Upon denying himself of earthly pleasures, the apostle has nothing to lose when he preaches the truth. There is no pressure of offending, for those who are offended cannot hurt him. They can't take anything away from him. The only pressure the apostle feels is the Lord Himself, who by His Spirit has pressed upon Paul the necessity to preach. It is as if the apostle cannot escape the need to preach the truth. In fact, the only time he feels relieved of that pressure is when he preaches. A repeated word of advice that I give to men who are speculating about pursuing the ministry comes from St. Paul's words here. If a man is to pursue the ministry He first must be confident that he can do nothing else, because his conscience won't let him do anything else. He must preach, or he will not be in right relationship with God. We spoke in the beginning about how difficult it is to speak without offending. Freedom to speak without offending is not the same as freedom to speak the truth. There is no freedom like that of speaking the truth. The same can be said for freedom to hear and believe the truth. I mentioned in Sunday school recently how the Roman Catholic Church has it right when they regularly implement confession. Well before I go on, please don't misunderstand me, confession should not be thought of as a sacrament. It is not necessary for a person to confess and then follow up with a bunch of repeated prayers or something, some type of act of contrition. What I'm speaking to is the simple act of confessing one's sins to someone else because it has a very freeing action, a very freeing feeling. When you confess your sins to another, someone else knows, and there is freedom in that knowledge. The confessor isn't hiding anymore. The devil can't use our hiding to beat up our conscience. Once a conscience is clear, the person has the opportunity to not be concerned about what other people think about them. When you and I are not concerned with what other people say or think, we are much more ready to hear what Jesus, the Holy Spirit, the Heavenly Father, has to say to us. When we are confident in our position in Christ, we find freedom to hear Him and speak the truth about Him. Too many men and women are weighed down by the opinion of others. They are concerned about how they will be perceived. Some will think you are too religious. Some will think you are too radical. Some will think you are stupid for believing all that Bible stuff. Some will call you hypocritical. Please see that when you concern yourself with the opinions of others, you rob yourself of freedom to hear, speak, and believe the truths of Christ. Bobby Lynn and I enjoy an occasional walk through graveyards. I know some of you like that as well. Imagining the lives of the people buried there in relation to the what the gravestone says about them. Bobby Lynn has an affinity to a headstone that reads, See, I told you I was sick. Along with that witty headstone I have heard of a particular pastor's epithet that reads, He did not say half of what he wanted to say. I think that's more sad than clever. Especially if what he wanted to say was what he should have said. When denying himself of his rights, the Apostle Paul freed himself of the bondage of men. He could not be accused of preaching with a false motive. He was not bound by the need to be accepted. He was free to preach the truth. The church needs more, like the Apostle, more men who are free to preach the truth. And we need more parishioners who are free to hear the truth and speak that truth to their neighbor. May the Spirit speak to each of us this morning as to what rights we need to give up in order to speak and to hear uncovered truths of the gospel. To our Lord and Savior be glory in the church forever. Amen.

sermons.title: To Not Be Disqualified
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn with me in your Bibles to 1 Corinthians chapter 9. We'll be working through four verses, 24 through 27. And in case you're wondering why we're wearing white today This is a Sunday in which we mark that Jesus was brought to the temple and by law his parents offered two turtle doves. in response to him being included into the kingdom of Israel forty days after his birth. I know most people think it's holy writ to say it's Super Bowl Sunday, but it's actually the offering of Jesus at the temple. This morning, interestingly, we are dealing with a sports metaphor. Surprising to me, some people don't like sports metaphors In defense of those of us who use them often, the apostle offers one, extends one himself, so it's in holy writ, so it's certainly legitimate. Before we examine the apostles' metaphor more closely, we must remind ourselves of the context in which this metaphor is found. The Apostle is concerned for the weak in faith within the Corinthian church. The weak are disturbed by fellow Christians eating meat offered to idols, even some of them sitting at banquet tables that reside in pagan temples. Paul has been describing his own self-sacrifice for the strengthening of the weak and his sacrifice for spreading the gospel. He now moves to a sports metaphor in order to give a picture of what type of sacrifice he and all Christians should be making for the sake of the gospel. The old saying, history repeats itself, appears true when a general comparison is made of the cultures such as the United States and Ancient Greece. Greece was a culture made up of many independent states. The greatest of these states was Athens. Athens was the first state to practice democracy. Each man within the state had a right and responsibility to vote over political issues. The major cities of these Greek states flourished with incomparable learning, farming, and trade. Success brought more leisure for the people, and they combined their leisure with their religion. In order to honor their many gods whom they believed resided on Mount Olympus, the Greeks organized athletic games. The victories of the athletes were thought to bring honor to the gods. The Games became known as the Olympic Games and began in 776 BC. These games took place every four years. The city of Corinth resides west of Athens. And because the Olympic Games had been going on for over eight centuries at the writing of the Apostle Paul, the people well understood the use of this sports metaphor. In fact, the Corinthians, the people loved these games so much that they started their own. The Isthmian Games, as they were called, by some accounts overshadowed the Olympic Games when they were started. The Isthmian Games occurred every three years, and like the Olympic Games, consisted of running, jumping, and throwing contests, as well as chariot races. Like the Greeks, we too find ourselves living comfortably from our success as a nation. Our leisure time enables us to enjoy all types of sports. Although we do not organize and participate in sports to honor other gods, some worship their chosen sport. as a God. We know that many choose a seat in a stadium over a seat in the house of God Like these Greek cultures, we uphold our athletes as blessed of the gods. The point being that if any culture Could relate to the apostle using a sports metaphor, it is our culture. From his chosen words We can sense the apostle giving us a pep talk and a locker room before the great contest. In verse 24, We get the sense that God is speaking through the apostle, and we must understand this. It's not just to these Corinthian people, but to all who would read these words in the future if Christ tarries. He tells us to run in such a way that you may obtain the prize. And he is talking to each of us personally. This is the second person singular you. You as an individual. You are to run the race in such a way that you may obtain the prize. The great Newt Rockney, football coach of Notre Dame, was known for his talks that would inspire men to play beyond their known capabilities. Sports can do that for a man. It can push him beyond what he knows as his capabilities. And the most famous of his speeches is in regards to George Gip. Gip was the greatest running back Notre Dame had produced up to his time. By many accounts he was a selfless man who gave up his time to those who requested of him When he gave up his time to a group of boys during a rainstorm, he developed complications of a common cold, which resulted in pneumonia and resulted eventually in his death On his deathbed, he reportedly made the request that when the boys were down, could Rachney encourage them by asking them to win one for the Gipper. At halftime against the then powerhouse Georgia Tech, Rockney suspended talks of strategy and technique and told the story of George Gip and his request. This is supposed to be the line with Rockney speaking. And the last thing he said to me, Rock, he said. Sometime when the team is up against it and the brakes are beating the boys, tell them to go out there with all they've got and win just one for the Gipper. The Notre Dame team went out the second half and beat favorite Georgia Tech on the wings of inspiration. Rockney never confirmed that the death-bed story of the Gipper was a true story. But the story proves to us that pep talks can move men. And the first point in our pep talk is that we are to run the race to win. Only one can receive the first prize in a race. Second and third prizes are modern day concessions. In the first days of the Olympics, there were only one winner per contest. The others simply lost regarding regardless of which place they came. Personally, I tried to drill that into my children as they matured, telling them that second place was only the first place of losers. Interestingly, when when playing cards with my mother-in-law I noticed a particular strategy she was using and I asked her if she was trying to win. She said no. She was just trying not to come in last place. Some of us don't relate to that type of thinking. Mr. Vince Lombardi was the famous football coach for the Green Bay Packers in the 50s and 60s. And he was attributed to have said, winning is not everything. It's the only thing. With modern-day sensitivities the way they are, the attitude of Coach Lombardi is understood to be misplaced testosterone and a byproduct of centuries of male patriarchy. And all that stuff is supposed to be bad. I remember the first volleyball game I ever played at a church function. I was a college student. My first chance to spike the ball, it brought down the ball on the face of the pastor's wife, who was on the other side of the net. And the piercing eyes of those playing communicated as their lips blurted out. This is just for fun. Fun for me has always been about winning. Personally, I've never found fun in simply playing a game. All of these years later, I'm still trying to learn how to play something just for the fun of it When it comes to my faith in Christ, I pray I never learn to be in the race just for fun. It is all about winning. It is all about winning because the reward is eternal, and so is the penalty for losing. In verse 25, the apostle compares the prizes of an earthly race to that of an eternal one. The prize for winning a foot race or a discus thrown at the Isthmian Games was a wreath made out of Isthmian pine. It was a plant from which the reeds were made and for which the games were named. These reeds, as you may imagine, were not poorly put together. They were carefully crafted. They were coveted by all who competed in and all who watched the contests. The winners were honored also with an image carved in stone, but it was wearing the wreaths that mattered to them. And this may sound as if the Greeks immortalized their victors, but such was not the case. They purposefully chose wreaths of perishable material For as the leaves perished in the crown, the crown became more corrupt, and the image was pressed upon these victors that their glory was fleeting. Another wreath would be rewarded to another victor three years later. We of course are not running a foot race, we're not throwing a discus or jumping into a sand pit. We are running a race for the life of our souls. This is not a race in which competing is all that matters. It is not a race in which the outcome is inconsequential. What we are running for is an incorruptible prize. The only ones who will receive such a prize are the ones who win. That prize is referred to as an incorruptible crown. No passing of time can wither its rigidity. No earth-born substance can eat away at its virility. The apostle Peter calls it an unwithering crown. Paul described it to Timothy as a crown of righteousness. James in his epistle describes it as the crown of life. All who enter into the presence of God after the final judgment will receive this crown and will have won the race. And we must underline that winning the race is more than simply competing. Today, children who participate in sports can become confused because they are rewarded for simply participating. Because of all of our boys playing sports, we did have a large share of trophies. Within our trophy display, we had divided the trophies that had been earned From the trophies that had simply been handed out. The trophies earned were given out for winning championships and being a valuable player Those trophies were set aside from the rest that were received just because our son had a warm body and showed up. We all know that the reason why trophies are given out to all participants is so that they can not go away with hurt feelings. A serious problem with being so concerned about hurt feelings is that few participants strive for greatness. They don't know how to work harder for a prize that is earned Because we compete as Christians to win rather than simply participate, we must embrace a regimental life that consists of calculated training. In verse 26, the apostle describes his race as one that is run with certainty. He is certain he is certain that he knows why he is running. Success as a team or individual in competition begins with knowing what you're competing for, setting goals. We must know what we are fighting for. With a goal in sight, our practical everyday behavior is then dictated by what it takes to achieve that goal. It is a given that a Christian's goal is eternal life. This is, however, where the sports metaphor can break down. Or an athlete may or may not choose to pursue an ultimate prize. A sprinter may choose not to run in the Olympic Games. If he does, he will most certainly not win the gold medal. But that does not mean he will not run in another race and be a victor in that race. When it comes to the race for eternal life, for our souls, there is only one alternative result. Those who win receive the prize of eternal life. Those who lose reserve death, eternal death. The goal is singular and obvious for the Christian. The apostle runs the race with certainty of that goal. And he boxes with a target before him. Boxing as a sport was also a part of the Greek Olympic Games. The punches the apostle was throwing were not at the heir, but at an opponent. And that opponent could be a demonic force, or it could be the old man within Paul that tempted him to sin. It was more likely both. But he was never just punching air. Verse 27 describes his regiment as the disciplining of his body. Those who competed in the Greek Olympic Games were not much different than those who are highly trained and skilled today. The original Olympians were given time and resources by their fellow countrymen. Trading for the Games began ten months prior. All athletes had to take an oath that promised fair and hard training, not just in the competition, but in their training. Part of their training consisted of regimented diets. Olympic athletes were restricted as to what they could and could not eat during their training. Before competition, they were required to take an oath swearing that they had abided by all the dietary and training restrictions. And using this description of a disciplined athlete, there is no possible means for a person to understand that their Christianity can be just a Christmas or Easter affair. In fact, there is no room to understand Christianity as a once-a-week Sunday-only affair. To discipline oneself in order to bring one's body under complete submission is to be full-throbbed, sold out, 100% giving Oneself to living for Christ. And the final clause in this passage digs deep into our psyche. As the apostle explains why he does live like this, it explains why he gives way to the weak in faith. He explains why he denies himself his rights as an apostle. He explains why he is all things to all men. He explains why he disciplines himself as a world-class athlete. He does it so that he himself would not be disqualified, so that he himself would not lose. And I wonder if this surprises us. Are we surprised that the apostle might be concerned that in the end he might not make it? He might not win. And here we have a powerful message that cannot escape our notice. It must not escape our notice. The apostle is helping us understand that our salvation The eternal living of our soul is never to be taken for granted. Because we are saved from hell in which all men Due to their sin deserve, and saved unto eternal promises that we've done nothing to earn, we are to be living in a state of gratefulness. We are to be secure in the grace of God to be sure. He will in no wise cast us out. And at the same time, we must never lax into a self-assurance that would allow us to take a day off. There is no tomorrow in the Christian life. We are to live as if we have no assurance of anything but the grace we are given today. That is the mentality we must have. That is the urgency the Apostle Paul lived with. And I will take it as providence and timing that the helicopter accident in California That took the life of a world-class athlete, his daughter, and seven others, occurred as we were about to touch on this passage. May God have mercy upon them. All who were in that accident, all of their races Their life races were over in an instant. And that's an important difference when using a sports metaphor. In sports, we know when the game is over. It is over when the distance to run has been reached, when the attempts have been completed, when the clock expires. Our lives are not so sure regarding our finish line That is one message we have for the world that should always be a part of our testimony regarding our Christian faith. We all will die. We just do not know when. We know it that we will die. And we embrace it because our Savior did. We are to say regarding our own personal finish line, not my will, but thine be done. Because we will die, and because we don't know when our personal finish line will appear, we are to train as if it is today. And train that way every day. When it comes to our Christian life, your very solo. Winning is the only thing. Let us pray. Now Father, we thank you for the confidence of the Apostle Paul. And we thank you for his example to live life in such a manner that every day is the finish line. And we take it as a charge to our lives. May it be resonating in our souls each day we wake. This is our finish line. Let us live That winning is the only thing that matters. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen

sermons.title: But, God's Faithfulness
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles to 1 Corinthians chapter 10. I remind you that as the Berean Church exemplified, we as Christians are to examine the scriptures as they are preached and taught. And we are to be sure that what is being preached and taught is from the Holy Scripture. 1 Corinthians chapter 10, 1 through 13. Once again, before we continue further in the book, we must be reminded of the context we find our passage today. The apostle is still discussing what he began in chapter 8, which is living sacrificially for the weak in faith, for the spreading of the gospel, and ensuring Ensuring his own salvation. The need to live sacrificially is so important. He is finding different ways to make it understood. A number of years ago, I stumbled across what became a monumental moment life lesson. I had struggled for years since the beginning of my theological training with the issue of predestination versus free will. From my vantage point early in my studies, the Bible spoke clearly that each human had the responsibility to choose or reject Christ as his or her Savior. That responsibility to choose was enough free will for me to reject the reformed doctrine of predestination. For those of you who are not theology students, the doctrine of predestination, according to students of John Calvin. Is a teaching that says that all that occurs regarding the salvation of an individual is determined by God. And was determined at the foundation, the beginning of the world. Initially, I couldn't accept that Still, I was honest enough to admit that the Bible did speak of God predetermining a plan for each man. And that was quite clear, still is. Passages such as Romans chapter 8 and 9 undeniably teach the doctrine of predestination as understood by St. Augustine of Hippo and John Calvin and others. So what is a young student of the scriptures to do? The lesson I stumbled across gave me a freedom in my biblical studies that I had never had, and it changed the direction of my ministry that remains with me today. The discovery concerning the right reading and interpretation of the Bible. And unfortunately, this right reading is not found in any textbook that I know of. Yet it is a principle of true, what I consider, true Christian maturity. What I am describing is called by the Reverend Robert Rayburn, who introduced me to this approach. It is called the dialectic hermeneutic. That sounds pretty fancy, doesn't it? This manner of interpreting scripture Recognizes that the Bible presents doctrines in terms of their polarities, their opposites The truth concerning any particular subject or theme is taught now in one place and then now in another. In terms of the poles that lie at the opposite ends of a particular subject. Dialectic means putting together, side by side, conflicting ideas. Now, of course, in terms of the Bible, Dr. Rayburn uses the term dialectic in a guarded way. He is not saying that doctrines are in actual conflict. He is using the term dialectic in order to describe how particular doctrines appear at least to you and I, who are on this side of the sun. Thus when we read such passages as Proverbs chapter 2 26 verse 4 that tells us to not listen to a fool's folly, and then verse 5 tells us to listen to a fool's folly. We have what at first appears to be contradictory statements Which are in reality pulling against one another to bring about a proper, we may even say a needed tension. Think of it as a net in volleyball put together in your backyard. If one side is too tight, the net leans to that one side. When each side is in proper tension, the net and poles are straight up. The immediate application of the tension for me was the doctrines of free will versus predestination. Using the dialectic approach, I could uphold one end of the doctrine, personal responsibility, what we are responsible for in making choices before God. While at the same time upholding God's predetermined plan of salvation for humanity. Both are upright and both are intention. Why this dialectic approach is important for us this morning is as we examine 1 Corinthians chapter 10. We are presented two doctrines pulling against each other in this one chapter. The first doctrine is the warning of the possibility of losing our salvation. versus the doctrine of security in our heavenly hope. So losing versus being secure It is a simple question that does not have a simple answer. The question is: can we lose our salvation? Can a person, whoever that person is, lose his or her salvation? The answer, I believe, should be an emphatic no. And yet, our no should be followed by a warning from the example of those who have apparently lost their salvation. You will recall that the apostle started this manner of speaking in chapter 9 when he examined the last Lord's day. In his comments, he stated that he practiced a sacrificial life so that in the end he himself would not be disqualified from the race, the race towards eternal life. The metaphor of winning the race refers to our heavenly hope. The apostle did not want to lose his place in heaven. Even though we read elsewhere that such is not possible, Jesus will never allow anything to be taken from his hand, he desires to live with the understanding or motivation that it is possible. To press this same understanding upon the Corinthians, he gives them an example. The example is found in verse one through five. And is followed by a reference to it being an example in verse 6. In verse 1, he refers to the Israelites exiting Egypt and wandering in the desert under the leadership of Moses. We remember from that biblical story how God led the Israelites in the direction they were to go by placing a cloud before them by day and a pillar of fire before them by night. As the people walked, they followed the cloud and the pillar of fire. One of the first places they were led was the Red Sea. Of course, the people could not cross the Red Sea. They didn't have a boat to accompany them all. With Pharaoh's army chasing them down, a miracle was needed for the people of God to be saved. You remember Moses raised his staff above the waters, and they were parted before the people, and the ground below dried up. As the people of Israel walked through the sea, the walls of the sea, the great waters, were held back on each side. So they were completely immersed into the sea, but not drowned. After crossing through the waters of the Red Sea, the cloud continued to guide the people through the desert. The cloud thus then became a provision of both shade in the day and for rain when needed. This is why both the Red Sea and the Cloud are described by the Apostle as having baptized Israel. Whether it be immersion or sprinkling of the people, the people were baptized. The apostle refers to their baptism as being baptized in Moses. This does not mean that Moses was their savior, but he was their clear leader. In their baptism, they became disciples of Moses. It is Moses, after all, whom we learn later through the prophecies of Abraham and others in the New Testament that Moses was a type of Christ Jesus to come. Verse three describes all the people of Israel eating the same spiritual food. The food, you remember, was manna, which was bread that came down from heaven, the miracle of food being provided for the people so that they might be able to travel through the desert and not grow hungry or weary. Verse 4 describes the drink in which the people were provided. Water, of course, is scarce in the desert, that's why it's called a desert. The people thirsted, and God miraculously provided water from them from a rock which he instructed Moses to strike. The provision of water followed them through throughout the journey in the desert. Now, personally, having taken a walk through the desert in Israel, such rocks are actually viewable as it seeps out of the walls When you go through a particular region. And such provision of water in a dry and thirsty land is obviously a gracious provision by God. The examples of baptism, spiritual bread, and spiritual drink are striking in how they apply to us in our New Testament context. We are baptized into Christ, just as the people were baptized into Moses. We are given heavenly bread at the Holy Communion table, just as the people were in the desert. We are given heavenly drink after the bread, just as the people were given spiritual drink in the desert In the Gospels, by his own account, Jesus refers to himself as manna from heaven. The apostle calls him, interestingly, the rock that was struck. These Israelites were chosen to receive the heavenly blessings God only bestowed on his people, his people who were his own. Yet, what was their outcome? How did they turn out? Verse 5 described them as displeasing to God. And as a result of God's displeasure was their bodies being scattered in the wilderness. The very place where God provided for them heavenly bread and heavenly drink became their gravesite. The Israelites took part of all the sacraments that you and I enjoy. We call them means of grace, which is to say, each is a vehicle by which God's grace is received. And yet the eventual lust of the people of Israel made their partaking of God's grace null and void. It didn't count. We remember from the beginning part of our study of Corinth that the environment in which the Corinthians lived was no better, and in fact Much worse than that of the people of Israel who died in the desert. Temptation for physical lust was easy for the Corinthians to encounter. Yet those in the desert continually found a way to express their lustful desires. And lust does not have to only refer to sexual desires. We remember that when Moses was on the mountain receiving the law of God, the people made an idol for themselves. In honor of their idol, they feasted and they played. To play is an expression of dancing provocatively. Their eating and drinking turn into dancing. Their dancing provocatively turned into sensuality, and their sensuality turned into sexual immorality. Anyone think of Super Bowl halftime at this point in the sermon? Idol worship and sexual immorality usually came together. The people of Corinth knew well this connection. They had witnessed and in some cases participated in it themselves before their conversion. There was certainly a great temptation to enjoy the lust of the flesh once again. As it was before them and always available to them. God's displeasure on such behavior is clear. In verse 8, the Corinthians are reminded that in one day, with one swipe of God's hand in judgment, twenty-three thousand people, God's supposed chosen people died. Along with idol worship and sexual immorality, the people were also guilty of murmuring. The people complained seemingly about everything. They complained about the bread from heaven, believe it or not. They became weary of its taste as it was no longer special. They became discontented with their leadership, believing that they themselves could do a better job. Even Moses' own sister and brother tried to displace Moses, believing that they knew leadership better than him. They complained when God called them to go forward and conquer the land He was blessing them with. The complaint was that the job was too big and their resources too small. After considering these sins, in particular that of murmuring, it would be easy for this preacher to stop and start meddling. I will not do so, but allow the Holy Spirit to speak to each of us regarding how we might have murmured about the bread offered. the leadership placed over us, or the conquering we are called to do, and how difficult it can be These sins are no less possible for us to commit than they were for the Israelites in the desert or the Christians living in Koranth. For him who has ears, let him hear. The description of these sins as verse eleven states is for our benefit There are warnings of how we today must not commit such sins, or else we might find our bodies scattered in the desert. It is the devil's tool to convince you to believe this could not happen to you If he can get us to shake our heads at the sinfulness of others without seeing our own trespasses, he, the devil, will win the day. That voice that causes you to think of another person who is caught in his or her sin as being less than you, please know now that such a thought is not the voice of God. That thought that encourages you to make a list of how you are more spiritual than others, that's not the voice of the Holy Spirit. And let me be clear and state that there is nothing wrong with professing when we hear a vile and unrepeatable sin. That we will not be guilty of the same. Of course, we should say that we would never cheat on our spouse or curse God or other such sins. We should make it such a profession and a determination that such sins will not be ours. What we should never profess, however, is that we are not capable of such sins. For we are all capable. Thus the words: let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he falls. As soon as you have trusted in your own standing, you are then standing alone You remember the story of the Pharisee who stood before God claiming his own righteousness because of the deeds he had done. That Pharisee stood alone. His salvation was determined on his own merits, and like any other man, he was found wanting When you trust not in your own standing, but in the mercy and grace of God, you no longer stand alone, but Christ Jesus stands with you. When you beat your chest and mourn your sin, your acknowledging Christ alone makes you righteous. Now the Pharisees are an interesting lot. They would be considered religious conservatives of our day. They kept the Jewish faith according to biblical standards. They considered themselves harbingers of the covenant of Abraham and Moses. When the priests were selling their positions for political influence, the Pharisees were calling the people to a biblical standard. Unfortunately, while being seen by the Jewish people as harbingers of their faith, the Pharisees became arrogant with their responsibility. With their arrogance, they decided to add to the law of Moses, with their religion being outward, so that others could see them and praise them. What God saw was most important, however. What God saw were haughty eyes. Now regarding those polls in tension, I began this sermon talking about the poll representing possible loss of salvation is firmly planted here in 1 Corinthians 10 by the Apostle Paul. People do walk away from the faith. Some do it saying they no longer believe. And that's the end of it. Well, others do it, saying they believe, and yet they don't go to church, they don't pray, they don't think upon God's grace anymore. Thankfully, there is another pole. The words used to describe this pole are not many, but they do not need to be. Here is the other side of that dialectic. Here is that other side of people denying Christ and moving away from their faith. Here is the other pole. God is faithful. Every temptation we face is common to all men Whatever temptation we face, no matter how difficult, we can always find another who has experienced the same. In the midst of those common temptations, God is faithful. God will not allow any of his people, us, to be tempted beyond what we are able to endure. He will provide a way of escape. God is faithful. If it takes getting out of a situation of temptation, God will provide it. If it takes enduring a moment of temptation, God will strengthen us to endure it. God is faithful. God's faithfulness is what saves us. It is not our own. For as has been stated, if it was, we could not survive. I have wondered in my older days. Why I ever wanted to insist, I was a Christian because I made the decision for myself. I have never been faithful to anything by my own strength. If my salvation was determined by my own strength, wisdom, and abilities to keep promises, woe to me and woe to you. On our own, we are scattered across the field of wilderness. Because God was faithful in suffering death upon the cross, because of that we are saved. Because he is faithful by abiding among us in his Holy Spirit, we are saved. Because he will be faithful, he will be faithful in coming again to raise us up, we are saved. Thus the two poles stand apart from one another in tension. The one pole has the possibility of us losing our salvation because of our own foolishness and sinfulness. On the other pole, we have the faithfulness of God. On the one pole we have idolatry, immorality, and grumbling. On the other pole, we have God being faithful. Lay that tension Move us to live responsibly, placing our faith in the faithfulness of God. Amen. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Real Reality in idols and Communion
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.source_file: Real Reality in idols and Communion.txt
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. It was suggested after our annual meeting or during our annual meeting that we address some of the issues about Holy Communion from the pulpit And I mentioned that we were indeed going to be doing so simply by walking through 1 Corinthians. And so here we are. And this passage will explain a great deal. 1 Corinthians chapter 10, beginning at verse 14, once again encourage you to turn there. And again, I begin the sermon with a reference to context. What Paul has been addressing in these last few chapters, he continues, having been spurred on by other thoughts that connect the previous chapters. The chapter in chapter eight, he addressed the issue of eating food offered to idols. The overall principle is that because the idols worshipped by the pagans Do not represent real gods. The meat is nothing more than meat. However, he spoke to the strong, telling them to think first of the weak, for the weak may have a problem with their conscience. And Christians should not want other Christians to go against their conscience. And it is not wrong to be weak in certain areas of the conscience. That is part of the message that seems hard to hear. As an example, St. Paul uses his own life to show how to care for others whose consciences are not clear. In order to impress upon the Corinthians the necessity of living sacrificial lives for the sake of others, he describes the fate of the Israelites Who did not live sacrificially. This was a warning to the Corinthians that they too could suffer such a fate In verse 14 of chapter 10, he comes back around to the issue of eating meat offered to idols and provides new light on the subject. In his previous discussion about eating meat offered to idols, the apostle briefly mentioned in chapter 8, verse 10, the fact that there were some in the church Who were eating this meat within the very temples in which the pagan gods were worshipped. This was disturbing for the consciences of the weak, so Paul discouraged the Corinthians from such a practice. In chapter 10, he now addresses another reason why eating such meat in these temples is poor judgment on the part of Christians. He begins his remarks with the call. The call is to flee idolatry Idolatry is the sin described in the second commandment. Thou shalt not worship any graven image. In the old world, the worship of idols required more than a mere genuflecting to a statue. Worshiping idols required the giving up of something in order to appease the God that was represented by the idol. One might be required to give up something as common as money. Another may be required to give a moral sacrifice, such as his or her virginity. And amazingly, others were required to give human life, in particular their firstborn child. Each sacrifice depended upon the god worshipped. The call to flee is an instruction to have nothing to do with these idols in any way. By fleeing, we are staying away from the idols and their associations. Like Joseph, who tore away from the lustful claws of Potiphar's wife and ran for his moral life. So Christians are to take flight away from sinful associations with idols. But why? We may ask why? For if gods represented by the idols don't exist, what exactly are we running from? In order to understand the reasoning behind the apostles' call to flee, we must think. Paul is being respectful to the Corinthian church as he treats them as adults, expecting them to think. He trusts that they will not react on emotion or first impression, but to think. In order to get the Corinthians to think, the apostle presents what we are calling the real reality. The real reality.
