Such a redundancy is necessary, for too often we think that we are in reality when, in fact, we are not. Certain subjects and certain circumstances blind us. An obvious example is how parents can easily see the sins of other people's children But turn a blind eye to the sins of their own children. In such instances, we are choosing our own reality. The real reality of the issues of idols can be seen in the service of Holy Communion. Verse 16 refers to both the cup of wine and the bread offered to worshipers in the service of Holy Communion. He is challenging us to realize that what is actually taking place as we bless the cup and the bread during this service When we bless the cup, he questions, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? It is understood as a real spiritual communion, unlike any other communion that we have with Christ. The bread we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ, he asked This passage is not, as the Romanists might argue, a verification of the doctrine of transubstantiation. What it is is a clarification that something very real and spiritual is happening when we participate in receiving the presented body and blood of Christ. The spiritual presence of Jesus, our Savior, is with us in a manner unlike any other time or any other thing that we do in worship. We cannot see him. We may or not may or may not feel him, but at those moments of blessing, gathering and partaking We are in as deep a communion with Jesus and one another as we possibly can be on this earth. Deep spiritual communion is occurring like it does at no other time. That the contemporary church does not realize this or understand this Is, I believe, one of the bigger problems today facing Christians in regard to Christian worship Too many Christians and Christian groups do not see, and hence do not believe, that anything is going on during the service of Holy Communion, other than people sipping. grape juice and eating unleavened bread. That's it. Period. The apostle, however, is here telling us that so much more is going on. It is spiritual and it is deep. I suspect that the reason why some struggle with the frequent offering of bread and wine Is caused by more than a reaction to Roman Catholicism and the doctrine of transubstantiation. We do not believe that Jesus is especially here, really, spiritually here, offering us deeper communion with Him Unfortunately, as Bishop Sutton has described, too many believe in the spiritual absence of Jesus rather than the spiritual presence of Jesus. Thus, how would anyone naturally react if he or she did not believe Jesus was uniquely present when celebrating Holy Communion? We wouldn't care about the bread, what it was, or how it was distributed. We wouldn't care about the wine or the grape juice, how it was or how it was distributed. We wouldn't care how often the bread and wine were offered because the only unique thing about the experience is how we individually feel about it. And the focus on how we feel about it is because the whole ritual is what we do for God rather than what he does for us. I have tried to stress to all of us at various times in the year that we need to understand that it is Jesus Himself who offers us the bread and the wine. We clergy stand in robes of white not because we look good in them, I don't think we do, but because we do not represent ourselves. A minister who blesses the bread and the cup and offers them to God's people is a mere instrument to do the offering. As I have said, it is Jesus that offers the bread, it is Jesus that offers the wine to you and to me. If we truly understood this, we would never, never refuse this offer. If it was Jesus that held out the bread and the cup, who could refuse? Who actually believed? What I'm saying to you is that each time we partake of communion, he is offering it to you For he is spiritually here, both in the offering of the bread and wine and in the bread and in the wine. And if you ask, how? How pastor? How is he in the bread and in the wine? I carefully respond, I don't know. It is a mystery. We just know this. How do we know this? Jesus said, unless you eat of my flesh and drink of my blood, you cannot be my disciple. But what does that fully mean? It's a fair question. I don't know what it fully means. But I know in part it means take and eat, take and drink. I know that much. To understand further how the spiritual and the physical worlds are not divided and thus are connected as we partake in Holy Communion. The apostle reminds the Corinthians of the Israelites and their sacrificial offerings. This is an important connection, Old and New Testament. Before Jesus' death, the sacrifice offered were accepted by the Spirit of God, who was present in the temple, and all who ate of the sacrifice received the benefits of the sacrifice. Those benefits were God's pardon and God's presence. The physical right has never been disconnected, but is necessarily entwined with the spiritual. This is the real reality. It is a reality that we cannot see, and yet it is as real as what we can see. With this understanding being set before us, remember he's calling us to think. He now turns to the real reality of idols Verse 19 repeats what the apostle said in chapter 8, which was a denial that the gods represented by idols actually exist. Verse 20 explains the real reality, the spiritual reality, of the demonic presence when pagans worship their false gods. When false gods were worshipped in these temples, something spiritual was occurring and it was not good. When sacrifices were made and the food distributed to those in attendance, there was a communion, a deep spiritual communion between the worshipers and the demonic forces present. This was different than just buying the meat offered in the open market after the pagan feast. Once again, the spiritual reality of demons in those temples could not be seen, but they were nonetheless real. For the Corinthians at Corinth, the presence of demonic forces was not considered. The apostle now is calling them to consider. The Christians, as Christians, they cannot partake participate in both spiritual realities. They cannot eat with demons and then with the Lord. Verse 21 reminds us of our Savior's words that we are either for him or against him. The kingdom of God follows one of the laws of logic that is called the law of excluded middle. You are either of God or of the devil, there is not a third option. Today, Christians are just as guilty as the Corinthians of not considering demonic influence. Although we do not have idle banquets in temples from which we feast, there are plenty of other demonic spiritual influences that deceive us being inconspicuous. There are television shows that practice divination or the telling of the future. There are television shows that present mediums and spiritists who supposedly talk to the dead. What comes in the form of entertainment are actually demonic spirits cloaked in popular culture. There are popular children's books such that can be dangerous if children get the idea that sorcery is trivial and something to make sport of During my school days, the popular game Dungeons and Dragons was understood to be an innocent fantasy game. Until teenagers became obsessed with the roles that they played. One teenager named David Fisher now converted to following Christ Has publicly shared of the influence of Dungeons and Dragons upon him. He played the game from the age of 12 to 18. He said, I have been through years of filling my mind with warfare, elves, magic, powerful swords, and gloating demons. He goes on to testify that such influence, quote, left deep scars on me, including physically, which God has been dealing with in lovely ways. Today, Christians dabble in meditation, yoga, hypnotism, and fantasy. Without examining the root of such practices or understanding the spiritual influence undergirding their success. Although we do not want to be a people who overreact, attempting to see the devil under every rock. We certainly do not want to be the fool and provoke God's jealousy. He cares for our souls He desires that we fall under no demonic influence. Yet he knows how easily we are led astray. Hence the instruction of our Savior: be wise as serpents and gentle as doves. It is necessary advice for us when it comes to knowing where demonic forces reside. Verse 23 through the end of the chapter explains where all the glory in our lives is to be placed. If we commune with demons, the glory is misplaced. It is a natural tendency for our logical minds to conclude that if there are demons present when one eats at an idle banquet, Then the demons must be present within the food itself. The logic we hear in the political realm today as weapons are blamed for crimes, alcohol blamed for alcohol abuse, and so on. Within these passages, the apostle explains quite clearly that the meat itself is neutral. Our contemporary setting allows us for a close-to-home example. Weapons, meat, alcohol, drugs are amoral. That a crazed man would use a weapon to kill the innocent does not make the weapon evil. Only the man. And dare I say that politicians who insist on focusing on the weapon are confessing that they don't have a clue as to what to do with the human heart. They have no answer. Again, meat, weapons, alcohol, or any other type of drug is actually amoral. There is nothing moral or immoral about such things. What is moral or immoral is how they are used. And how they are used is determined by the human heart. Participating in idol ritual is dangerous. Not because of the meat offered itself, but because of the demons present. and the influence over the worshippers and their hearts. For meat offered to idols sold later in the market, the influence can only be in the conscience of a man. If a man believes himself guilty for eating the meat, the answer is simple. He should not eat the meat If another perceives guilt within a man because the same man is eating the meat offered to idols, the man eating should cease for the sake of the other. That is dying to self. The summarizing instruction is to do all for the glory of God. And here we are given our primary motivation for life, for all things. It is certainly appropriate for such motivation to be stated in this text, for the subject of eating is one that is done daily and out of necessity. If that which we do daily and out of necessity is to be done with the primary motivation of glorifying God, how much more? Should we seek to glorify God in our unique and given tasks that we are each assigned? And each of us in our individual lives have specific tasks God has assigned us to do. Everything. All in every way we live. These modified nouns cover every possible aspect of our lives. In every way we are to live to glorify God. We can no longer underappreciate or underestimate the spiritual reality which we are involved with. And everything we do, we are to carry the Spirit of God with us and give glory by our actions. At this time I call you to remember that special story in 2 Kings chapter 6. About the prophet Elisha and his servant, who were being hunted by a large army. We are like the servant. Who cannot see the spiritual army upon the hill? We can only see the physical realm, and thus the physical army that seeks to destroy us. We thus allow our emotions to be dictated by what we see in the physical realm. We appropriate our actions by what we see in the physical realm. When Elisha's servant looked up to the hills, did he see reality? It was certainly the reality of this world. It was the reality of the physical world. That reality was his reality, but that was not all there was to see Elisha's prayer was actually a prayer for his servant to see the truth, and as we have described it, the real reality. The truth was that there was much more than the carnal eye could see. There was and is an eye of faith that sees beyond this world and into the next. The eye of faith understands that there is a substance of things hoped for and a conviction of things that are not seen. And so let me ask you each of you this, as if God was asking you personally Do you believe that whatever you do involves the Spirit of God? Do you believe that whatever you unite yourself with You are uniting with the spirit, and that spirit you unite with may or may not be God Do you believe that there is a world that consists of more than you can see, and yet it is as real as anything that you've ever seen? If you do believe, then make every decision, associate with every person, be involved with every activity. With such a reality in mind. And in our case, in worship believe that when you eat of the bread and drink of the cup, there is a spiritual reality that is real reality. Believe it to the glory of God. Amen.

sermons.title: Propriety in Head Coverings
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We are continuing our series in First Corinthians, and we are, as was read, First Corinthians chapter eleven, and I begin by saying that verse one really applies to chapter ten, fits into the context of Saint Paul denying himself his Christian freedom Being concerned about those who are weaker in the faith in terms of meat offered to idols, and he continues that theme of caring for the weak Now the following story is true, only the names have been changed to protect the guilty. A youth minister was assigned the duty of reading the New Testament lesson on a particular Sunday that we know in America as Mother's Day. The pastor intended to preach a sermon on the virtues of motherhood from 2 Timothy 1. There in that chapter, the apostle praises God for the faith of Timothy's grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. The sincere faith of the two women, besides the Holy Spirit, is considered the primary reason for the faith of Timothy. The youth minister, who, in his own testimony, had stayed up much too late the night before Open the Bible to 1 Timothy instead of 2 Timothy. He read to the congregation from 1 Timothy 1. That the law was given for the unrighteous, the sinful, the ungodly, and the killers of mothers. The text for Mother's Day had now become about murdering mothers. Instead of the faux pas being of good humor, the pastor was a serious type. He approached the pulpit and said, All scripture is God breathed, and proceeded to preach from 1 Timothy 1. Story number two. A rather round, jolly, and brilliant professor of mine in seminary Shared a story of the time during family devotions when he was reading to his then young children from the book of Genesis. One particular night he was to read from chapter 38. In that chapter, Judah, one of Jacob's sons, had a daughter-in-law who became a widow. Judah first attempted to have Onan, one of his other sons, lie with her so that she could have a child. When that did not work, the daughter-in-law disguised herself as a prostitute so that her father-in-law would lie with her. Obviously a very sordid tale indeed. As the professor was reading, his wife protested about the improper content for the children. Shush! Shush! Stop! Stop! she was saying, as he was trying to read the story. The professor boldly proclaimed that the story was in the Bible, and therefore respectable to read And she retorted, Well, I wish it wasn't. And such is my feeling, tongue-in-cheek, about 1 Corinthians chapter 11, 2 through 16. Head coverings. I was uh greeting people at the door, having finished uh a wonderful service last week. And good old brother Alan Graham said to me, Good sermon. Can't wait to hear what you have to say next week I didn't catch on then until I sat down Monday and went, oh, okay, here we go. Now this chapter has been uh one that has stirred up great controversy amongst Christians. In fact Much of what is said in this epistle from chapters 11 through 15 has been fodder for much debate over centuries. The following are just a sample of many questions that come as a result of this text. Are traditions of men inherently evil? Is it acceptable for women to prophesy in a church service? Must a modern woman cover her head in worship services? Is a short-haired, i. e. shaved woman, truly a disgrace to God? What do angels have to do with a woman covering her head? Can we objectively learn from nature what is disgraceful? Is long hair sufficient for a woman to wear as a head covering in worship? I will not attempt to directly answer these questions today Bummer, you say. Cop-out, you say. Well being a cop-out is not my normal modus operandi. Fact is, I do not believe that this text is attempting to answer any of those questions. If we are not careful We can approach Scripture as a book of rules and regulations, as if it's telling us what we are to specifically do and what we specifically cannot do in our daily lives. The end result of such labor is that we become legalists who have literally choked the Spirit's breath out of Scripture and made it of stone resembling our hearts. The easiest way to interpret the message of the apostle in this chapter is to discount it entirely as relating only to the primitive culture of the Corinthians. Such an approach, at its root, actually denies the validity and the authority of Holy Scripture. Persons who interpret in this way are in essence saying that these passages are not the Word of God. Those of us who believe that all scripture is God-breathed reject such an approach and determine ourselves to find the truth, value, and application of such texts. We can easily reject this type of approach, for the apostle does not use his contemporary culture, but actually makes his argument from Scripture itself. The issue addressed is not overtly stated, but obviously implied. During the worship services within the church at Corinth, some women were not wearing head coverings. During their participation in the service, from praying to speaking, the women did not have their heads covered. The issue for the apostle was one of propriety and custom, as well as spirituality. For that is the connection that we can find with the subject in chapter ten. The presence of Christ in the Sacrament of Holy Communion. And the presence of devils in a service of meat offered to idols is connected to this chapter. Therefore, what St. Paul is addressing is what is appropriate to do during a Christian worship service. With the variable of men and women and their various roles within the kingdom of God and their various roles in formal worship. With the recognition of the what we called last week the real reality, which is our spiritual reality as we worship. According to historians, the head coverings referred to by the apostle can be better understood as veils. These veils did more than cover the top of the head, as they had the ability to cover the face as well, similar to what we can presently witness in Muslim countries. We may know them better as shawls that can cover the head and be pulled down to cover the face if desired. Although it was not always necessary for the face to be covered by the shawl, the covering was large enough for that to happen. The custom of the apostles on this matter is explained to the Corinthians. In verse 2, the Apostle Praises the church for holding on to the teaching, or as the New King James Version translates, holding on to the traditions. The Greek word is paradosis, which can be translated tradition or custom. These customs were handed down from generation to generation, both oral and written. The same word for traditions is used by Jesus to condemn the Pharisees for the traditions that they held. Keep in mind that Jesus, contrary to modern interpretation, is not condemning the idea of tradition itself to the Pharisees. But that the Pharisees were choosing their traditions above God's law. The traditions or customs of the apostles We're not in the place of God's law, but an application of God's law. An example today will serve us well. We uphold the custom of the apostles today when we worship on Sunday, and by the way, we order our worship with the creeds, the confession, and so on. Customs can be a valuable tool as they grant us security and consistency with the practices and teachings of the apostles, who again were the closest to Jesus. Customs are beneficial as long as they maintain their meaning A custom becomes dangerous when it is no longer practiced for the greater good, but is followed simply to honor the custom itself. Let me explain my meaning by giving another example. We covered the elements of holite communion with several layers of cloth. Each layer represents a point of the story of the burial of Jesus and his resurrection. The white cloth below represents the purity of Jesus and his offering. The Paul represents the cloth that covered his body when he was buried. The chalice veil represents both the church season in its color as well as the holiness of the bread and wine offered. The removal of it, exposing the bread and wine, represents the spiritual presence of Jesus among us in the bread and in the wine. We, as we witness this, are spiritually fed simply by observation. If, however, these become legalistic acts where we feel that we have to do them in order to truly partake of holy communion, then the custom replaces law, and that is sin. Another example is how we follow the custom of collecting all pieces of bread and crumbs after consuming the Holy Communion bread. In doing so, we follow the belief that the bread is no longer just bread, for it represents the body of Christ, having a spiritual component or a real reality. We also followed Jesus' instruction to his disciples at the feeding of the 5,000. You remember, after they were all fed, the apostles came and collected all the leftover bread. The point being, when we are educated about customs such as processionals, the sign of the cross, crucifers, vestments. They become an enriching part of our worship as they proclaim the gospel without words. A properly structured worship communicates the gospel to all of the senses. If the meaning of a custom is not known, well then it becomes a dead work. So regarding our subject from 1 Corinthians chapter 11, the custom of head coverings proclaims truth without words. That truth is that the glory in worship is to be reserved for God alone. The reason for the custom of head coverings is that God is to receive the glory in our worship. How that happens with a woman's head being covered is then explained. What must be emphasized here before we get to that explanation is that God is the sole audience in our worship. Our worship service is for God alone. It is for Him to be pleased. It is He that is to be glorified, and He alone. After my sermon a few weeks ago, which described how we are to be all things to all men that we might save some I was questioned whether we should be all things to all men in our worship. And the answer is emphatically no. We are all things to all men as we meet our neighbor, as we talk with our co-worker. When we worship, we are to be all things to God. There is a dramatic distinction between evangelism and worship. To great misfortune, that distinction has been blurred by many modern expressions of the Christian faith. In the culture of the first century, a head covering was a symbol of modesty and submission. For a woman to discard the covering was to renounce her modesty and her submissiveness to her husband. A woman thus uncovered brought attention to herself, for she was saying she was submissive only to herself. She received the attention, hence misplaced glory. Within this, as an understood cultural reality, The apostle explains why a woman should have her hair covered during a worship service. There is an order of creation. God created man first, and thus man is the glory of God. Woman was created from man, and thus she is the glory of man. Both, of course, as the apostle readily points out, are mutually dependent upon one another. Both could not have existence without the other. In Christ, they are equal. In creation, however, they are to remain in order. If a woman is the glory of a man, then her head ought to be covered during worship, for the glory is to be proclaimed. To only be toward God. A man being first in creation should not have his head covered, for he is the glory of God. The overriding principle for all of these instructions is that no one is to come to corporate worship seeking attention for themselves. The attention and thus the glory is to be to God alone Leaving aside the argument of creation order, the apostle then pleads the reasoning of his custom by the evidence of the natural world. Nature, he says, teaches us that a man with long hair brings disgrace upon himself. A woman with short hair likewise brings disgrace to herself And this may be surprising to some who think of Jesus having long flowing hair. The truth is we don't know what Jesus' hair was like. We don't know even what the apostle means by long hair. The adjective long is is too vague. What we can appreciate and understand is the apostle's point that there is a certain dress and style in every culture that is identified as effeminate and/or masculine. We all know what those are, whether we are willing to verbalize them or not, and whether we are going to be honest with ourselves or not. It does appear observable that women on the average can grow their hair longer than men. Note that I said on the average. And this may be what the apostle means by the nature of things teaching us. A woman's long hair is described as her glory. And this statement, like some of the others, is unclear. It is unclear how long hair is a woman's glory, other than the plain meaning that it is evidence that she is feminine, that she is female. I think it necessary to understand her glory here to be a proper one, as the long hair serves as a natural covering or a natural veil. Her natural veil brings glory to God, thus it is proper, because it is feminine, because it brings glory to the man who brings glory to God. This all being said, it is fair to ask what application is here for us Well, first we can say that all customs are to be practiced for the sole purpose of bringing glory to God. We should not practice a custom that brings attention or glory to any man. All customs should be practiced with the purpose of proclaiming God's truth and focusing our attention on Him alone. Second, there are principles of propriety to learn from the apostle. There is a certain type of decorum in dress that is acceptable and not acceptable when the people of God gather together. What that is, we should be thankful the apostle doesn't give us line item. Once again, we may apply the goal of glorifying God. Where What glorifies God? A woman to dress and decorate herself as a woman. A man should dress and groom himself as a man. Neither should appear in the fashion of the other. Also, a woman should not wear a garment that glorifies her figure. A man should not wear a garment that glorifies his bravado. And neither should wear a garment that ignores the presence of Almighty God within our midst. Thirdly, and finally, there is glory in submission. That submission makes a person less than a person or threatens the freedom of an individual is a lie from the devil's lips. Our Savior submitted himself to the Heavenly Father. We are called to submit to Jesus as our Savior. Wives are called to submit to their husbands as unto the Lord. The head covering was a sign in the first century of willing submissiveness. Submission is not for the weak, but for the strong. It takes one strong of character to submit to another. One who submits according to the will of God is one who follows in the footsteps of Christ, the greatest of submissions. It is the devil who has made submission a dirty word, even among Christians. May the Lord forgive us and give us better minds. The glory of Jesus, after all, was in his submission to the Heavenly Father. Every Christian is to live a life of submission. Submission to God first, then to one another, as St. Paul instructed the Ephesians, submit to one another in love. And then submission to our various roles as women and men in Christ. If you have negative thoughts toward the word submission, those thoughts are either of your flesh or of the devil. And both the flesh and the devil are destined for fire. We began by considering the customs of men and their place in Christian corporate worship. Regardless of customs, the overriding principle of this passage is that our worship is to give glory to God and no other. That principle remains the same whether you're at Corinth in the first century or Eldersburg in 2020. Let us pray. Father, we are humbled by what was going on in the Corinthian church that we're not aware of. But humbled by the fact that it's so easy to get caught in all the different ways in which this can be interpreted, and yet we want to see the most important thing. That our worship always gives glory to you and to you alone. May that be true until you come. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: New Beginning at the Table
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Do I want to do this? In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. He be seated. Turning our Bibles to First Corinthians chapter eleven, we pick up at verse twenty-three as was read. This being the first Sunday of Lent 2020, we are reminded how the Christian life is a repeated offer of new beginnings. Lent provides for us the upfront message that repentance and the receiving of forgiveness from the Lord Jesus Christ is ever present as an offering for a new beginning. My hope is that we will see in our text from 1 Corinthians eleven a verification of Christianity being about new beginnings. When I was a child, my grandparents from my father, the father who raised us, they made a long trek from Pennsylvania to Washington State to visit us at our home My mother insisted on the usual cleaning duties so that our guests would feel welcome. After their arrival, my grandfather made an offer to me and my four siblings He would give us fifty cents if our rooms were not only kept clean, but kept clean underneath our beds. Now fifty cents in nineteen seventy was a lot of money. Why Would he want to look under my bed? I wondered. Never once had I cleaned my room and cleaned under my bed. In fact, the underneath area of my bed became that cat-all for loose items when you were cleaning the rest of the room and you didn't know what to do with some of the stuff you had left over The only time I bothered to look under my bed were during rainy days when I found treasures that I had been missing for such a long time, now rediscovered. So my brother and I frantically went to work cleaning under our beds only to discover how difficult it was to keep the room clean and underneath our beds clean at the same time It took, I remember, three inspections by my grandfather before we received our coveted 50 cents. What would a seeker find, I wonder, if he was to go to each of your homes and look under your bed? And what about your couches? Those who are diligent cleaners sweep and vacuum under their couches consistently. Others do so only when the furniture is moved. And what if the seeker was to look underneath or behind your refrigerator? What would he find there? Several years ago, Bobby Lynn and I moved our refrigerator and we found a check that had been given to us over a year ago. We didn't cash it. We thought that wouldn't be a good thing to do Do many of us live under the delusion that if we cannot see the dirt, that it isn't there? Our cleaning consists of vacuuming and dusting around, but never under and within the mess that is actually there but not seen. Understand that this description of cleaning is not to make you feel guilty about your house cleaning. My apologies if that's what you understand. This description of cleaning can be used as a metaphor to identify that we too often miss Certain sins in our lives, having them swept in the proverbial under the bed. We clean the outside well enough so that it looks as though we are clean But inside, where we hope no one else will see, there is dirt that has been there for many years. We have become so good at this cleaning technique of cleaning the outside only that we actually see ourselves to be clean when deep down we know we are not. Why would anyone want to look underneath, we wonder, and so we do not bother looking within ourselves. The Corinthian church had a lot of dirt underneath its bed, its couch, its refrigerator. The church was fractured over loyalties to different teachers. There were lawsuits being filed against one another. There were different convictions about divorce, remarriage, and the eating of meat offered to idols. These differences resulted in hard feelings. In the section we are dealing with, there was a problem of failing to maintain gender distinctiveness. This was occurring in the worship service In our reading this morning, the apostle continues to address the subject of worship services by rebuking the Corinthians because of their behavior during Holy Communion. And before we get to that rebuke, it is important to note, if you are keeping score at home, that the Corinthians have more problems needing to be addressed than the apostle has encouraged them regarding their right behavior. This church was by no means a perfect church. Yet if you were a Christian in Corinth, you did not have the choice of going from first church of Corinth And transferring over to second church of Corinth because you didn't like what was going on at first church of Corinth. As a Christian, you were either a part of the body of the fellowship of believers at Corinth, or you were not. There is much that can be said about this lack of choice, the inability to church hop. The very least of which is that it is amazing what the people of God can work through and what we can put up with regarding one another when we do not have another choice. The apostle has already called the Corinthians sanctified. They are holy. He has given thanks for their faithfulness. He has eased into some very difficult subjects. Now he can speak directly to them, as we see in verse 17. When they come together for worship, it is not for the better, but for the worse We have already recognized the apostles' dispelling of the myth that all worship is good worship. Doesn't matter what it is. We have recognized that God receives some forms of worship and rejects others. And just in case the people still believe that God is pleased simply because they decide to come together. The apostle quickly dispels that notion. He does so by stating that it is in fact worse when they come together due to the manner in which they come. This is a terrible thing to say about a worship service organized and led by confessing Christians. Yet it was true, and it is true for bodies of believers today. Verse 18 through 19, there are continuing divisions among the Corinthians. These divisions are not the same as the ones originally mentioned by the epistle. Where the epistle they were divided over loyalty to certain teachers. This division is among Christians because of status. Because we are fallen by nature, we are prone to exclude. Whenever a significant number of people are gathered, clicks usually form. These cliques were mostly based on socio-economic boundaries. This is what the apostle is referring to when he mentions those who have God's approval. In the New International Version, this is more of an interpretation than a translation. In the New King James Version, it states For there must also be factions among you, that those who are approved may be recognized among you. Approved. What does that refer to? The approval in this case comes from the people themselves. Notice that the evil one causes a spirit in every age to look upon the beautiful, the fit, the wealthy. Those are the approved of God. And man, simply because they are beautiful and fit and wealthy, also approve of them. The result was a click of people who find a commonality and their status and leave others out of their social world. That this would happen in the midst of Christians is quite unfortunate. It appears, however, that it was most certainly what was happening. The well-to-do were enjoying their surplus together to the point of excess while others were left out. When the less fortunate finally arrived at church for worship, well, they had so enjoyed themselves that there was literally no food left. Because the feast and worship service were so intimately tied to one another, the dishonoring of the less fortunate carried over then to the dishonoring of those same people at the Lord's table. The situation described is not common to us today. Early Christians participated in what they called the agape or the love feast. This was a sharing of food between one another, very much like a potluck today. Because these Christians did not have a fellowship hall, they would all meet together in one large room for the social event, and then that would move itself into the worship event in the same room. By almost unanimous opinions of scholars, the early Christians are understood to have celebrated Holy Communion every time they gathered together. Thus, the love feast would then evolve into a worship service, which consisted of partaking of the bread and the wine at Holy Communion. These two feasts, the agape and holy communion, became so intertwined that it was difficult to know when one had ended and the other had begun. The result was a worship service where people continued to practice gluttony, drunkenness, and separatism. The result of the gluttony and separatism, according to verses 21 and 22, is that some of the people were left hungry and others were drunk. The gathering together of God's people, that is the church, is then despised. And regrettably, shame is brought upon those who were left out. This is why the apostle cannot praise the Corinthians about their worship, and it is why their gatherings are worse than if they had not gathered at all. And I must speak about politics in relation to this passage, which some social justice warriors hold up as an example of how all things should be shared among all walks of life. That's the Christian ideal. That is not what this passage is saying. It is simply condemning the selfishness of those who had an abundance. While not caring for those who had very little. So, beloved, capitalism as an economic theory is morally neutral, and yet it can become a tool of the devil if it is not governed by the Christian ethic to love one's neighbor as oneself and to care for the poor and the widow. Christianity, however, is not socialism. Never has been. Giving for the needs of others is to be organic. It is to come naturally from the heart. Because we are Christian, we give organically, not because it's government-mandated End of political speech. And verses twenty-three through twenty-six We have the words that are very familiar to us as we read them, or read them in our Book of Common Prayer, and also read them from our gospel reading. Much has been written and debated regarding these words of Christ and the Apostle. We do not have time to dissect all that is said here. In general, it is sufficient to note that the Apostle is reminding the Corinthians how the Holy Communion service is to be done. We are to remember his body broken for us. We are to remember Jesus' blood spilled for us. We are to eat and drink them respectively to proclaim his death until he comes again. What the Corinthians were doing was coming to the Lord's table, and it is the Lord's table. They were coming in a careless, irreverent spirit, having no desire to commemorate the death of Christ. These Corinthians treated the Lord's table as if it was their own table. The many came to satisfy their hunger, and not to humbly feed on the body and blood of Christ. Because of the manner this meal was being eaten, the apostle gives warning that whoever eats and drinks in this way, the selfish way, will be guilty of the blood and body of the Lord. The Lord is requiring the church to look under the bed, to look under the couch, to look behind and under the refrigerator, to see what needs to be cleaned up. And notice please that he is not merely pointing to individuals, but the church as a whole. We're all accountable, even if it's you that's got a dirty couch underneath. Historic and contemporary reactions to this passage have too often focused on discouraging Christians from partaking of the elements of the Lord's Supper altogether due to fearing God's wrath. The medieval church had a saying in Latin, sacramentum et mortis articulus aquiparenter. Which translates, the Lord's Supper requires the same seriousness as the very moment of death. Chrysostom, a church father, spoke of sitting up the whole night before partaking of Holy Communion for the purpose of prayer and vigil, because it was such a solemn occasion. Now such attitudes towards the Holy Communion are not wrong, mind you, but they are an overreaction to what the apostle is warning in this passage. Yes, a man is to examine himself. He is to look under his bed, his couch, under his refrigerator. That examination, according to this context, is to not see if there is anything at all that needs to be cleaned up. If this were so, none of us would be able to partake of the elements of Holy Communion. The examination is to see whether we come to the table in a careless, irreverent Spirit, not desiring to commemorate the death of Christ. If we do, we then eat and drink in an unworthy manner. The elements of bread and wine are what we call means of grace We spent a few weeks ago discovering the presence of Christ among us as we partake of those means Thus, the best place for sinners to come to the Lord's table to receive the means of grace necessary to be free from the burden of sin. The best place is to come with a heart that only focuses on what he is giving to us This passage is not to hold you back from the table, but to call each of us individually and collectively to examine ourselves before we eat of that bread and drink of that cup. Why would God want to look there, underneath your metaphorical bed? That is the question answered by the fact that he wants to offer you forgiveness there and cleanse you from all unrighteousness. To bar oneself from the communion table is to focus on the opposite of what the apostle here is teaching. The Holy Communion is about Christ and what He has done for our salvation. It was not about the wealthy Corinthians gorging themselves, and it is not about us feeling guilty about our sins. It is about repentance and forgiveness. Receiving the body and blood of Christ is a means of receiving forgiveness. When this passage is used to focus on our unworthiness only, then we once again have taken the spotlight off of God in our worship and placed it upon ourselves. This is an instance where self-deprecation can actually be self-serving. The warning of judgment in verses 27 through 32 ought to be taken very seriously. It is not, however, a warning to discourage us from partaking of Holy Communion. Instead, it is an opportunity for us to confess our sins. When Bobby Lynn and I were new parents, I would find myself at times struggling with embarrassment about the behavior of my boys. When they would do something wrong, I believed their behavior reflected on my parenting. As I matured, I began to realize that the misbehavior of my children could be viewed as a positive. For it was an opportunity to train. If I did not take advantage of those opportunities, then that would reflect on my parenting. The Holy Communion can be seen in the same manner. Yes, our sin is before us as we are hear the commandments proclaimed, and we examine ourselves to find, yes, we are wanting. Yet there is opportunity to pray, a prayer of forgiveness, and to receive the means of grace embodied in the bread and wine. There is good news in this pattern, for as the apostle states, if we judge ourselves, we would not come under judgment. The service of Holy Communion is an opportunity to judge ourselves. And that opportunity is a means of grace offered to us weekly, if not more. It must be seen that way. In October in eighteen seventy three A bishop from Kentucky was a participant in the worldwide convention of Evangelical Alliance in New York City. This convention brought Christians from different denominations together to acknowledge a shared goal of reaching the world for the gospel of Christ. The bishop from Kentucky presided over an interchurch communion at the Fifth Avenue Presbyterian Church. The service was a powerful demonstration of the unity within the body of Christ. The next day, this bishop, a George David Cummins, Awoke to find in the New York newspapers attacks on his integrity and threats of trial and deposition for having violated, as his accuser saw it, the laws of the church The very thing that communion is to provide for all Christians, unity in Christ, was being used as a charge to depose the bishop. Because these charges were laid atop a great deal of grief for Cummins previous, he resigned his bishopric. And announce the organization of a new church, the Reformed Episcopal Church. This is our tradition. This is our heritage. It is a heritage that sees the service of holy communion as a point of unity, not division. It is a heritage that allows God to look under the bed. And everywhere in our individual and corporate lives, with an understanding that He is doing so for our benefit. It is a heritage that sees the Lord and His table as a means of grace A grace offered to all, with the exclusion of no one, who would call upon the name of the Lord. That is our heritage. May it be continued. One final point. This passage focuses on a warning to not partake of Holy Communion in an unholy manner. If one does partake in an unworthy manner, the judgment of God could occur in this life. That's why some have slept. But we can reverse that. If we partake of the Holy Communion in a worthy manner, which is a humble manner, consisting of repentance and forgiveness. Then the bread and wine can be a blessing for life to us, as opposed to judgment. Being unworthy, which is being our own righteousness, that we are condemned Being worthy, which means being forgiven of our sins, and being righteous in Jesus, that's where we receive new life. A new beginning. And we always need new beginnings. Amen. Let us pray. My Father, from this we truly want to receive that message of our need for new beginnings. And how you offer them to us, oh so freely and oh so regularly. May we humbly receive it with great appreciation that even after we receive it. We get to be made new again and again. In Jesus' name we thank you. Amen.

sermons.title: Otherness of Spiritual Gifts
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We continue our series in 1 Corinthians. Now I begin with an apology of sorts. I have divided this chapter, and some of you might think that that's not a good way to go about interpreting a text. You don't want to divide it up and take something out of context, and and I agree I agree, and I will do so. I will keep everything in context, but I believe we need to focus on something today and then something else next week. The first main point from 1 Corinthians chapter 12 is that different parts of the body of Christ are given specific gifts, and those gifts are different from one another. The second main point is the metaphor of the body parts of a human being similar to how a Christian body of believers is to work together That will be examined more fully next week. Thus, our focus today is on that first main point. Which is that the Christian church is made up of people with different gifts that participate in the body of Christ as a whole. I'd like you to walk with me through the first 11 verses of this chapter, and you will stay awake better if you follow along in your Bible. I will be mentioning each verse and making comments about each verse. So put your finger on verse 1 of chapter 12 and follow along with me. In verse one, the phrase now concerning indicates That Paul is taking up another subject that the Corinthians likely addressed to him about in their letter to him. But as the text unfolds, it will become clearer that this particular discussion in chapter 12 is part and parcel with the abuse of spiritual gifts And those abuses marring the worship of the people. And that's going to be addressed even further in chapter 14. So with all of these abuses being dealt with, this is the third one. We're finding that he is laying a groundwork for proper worship in chapters twelve through fourteen. In verse two, the Corinthians are to remember their past influences, which included The dumb or non-speaking idols that honored no such gods and uttered to them no such truths. In verse 3, we understand the implication of there being people who were claiming to speak by the authority of the Holy Spirit. Who were saying things that were incongruent with the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ? The hyper example would be someone who would say that Jesus is accursed. Now, this may have been something actually uttered during the false idol worship of the pagan Corinthians Or it serves as an example of how absurd people can be when they say they are being inspired by the Holy Spirit to speak When in fact they say nothing that is true of God, nothing that is actually from the Holy Spirit. The final point being that the truth is that Jesus is Lord, and that And that truth can only be uttered by the revelation and power of the Holy Spirit. Anything less said is not from God. In what follows, we have the specific question of the use and abuse of inspired speech placed in a larger context. Paul is going to describe the nature of the body of Christ, that is the church, and the unity that is characterized by diversity. This diversity is necessary for the church's health, and it comes directly from God via the Holy Spirit and is expressed, among other ways, by the diversity of gifts. I recognize that some for some of us, I include myself, the word diversity can trigger negative feelings. Because certain false teachers of today use the concept of diversity as an end to itself and not a means to a godly end. Paul, however, is using it as a means to a godly end. In fact, it is a means that is Not forced upon the church, but is simply the nature of the reality or the very nature of the church is going to be diverse. As we notice the beginning of each verse from verses 4 through 6, we can see a pattern that is similar to the three persons of the Trinity. Within the Trinity, there is a diversity of will, and yet they all come and work together as a unit. And more profoundly, the diversity and unity found in the church is found first and ultimately in God Himself. God is both diverse and one. In this section of passages, there is an important demonstration of the Trinity doctrine in the New Testament. What I mean is that by looking at such gifts in a threefold manner, shows the Trinity to be a natural expression of the body of Christ, because it's a natural expression of the Godhead. There is a diversity of gifts, yet there is the one same Holy Spirit. There is the difference in ministry, yet the same Lord Jesus There are diversities in activities, meaning who is responsible for what, and yet the same God, the Father. Such a Trinitarian reference is not here by chance. Verse 7 is a linchpin verse. As it sums up the whole purpose of the variation in gifts, the variation in ministry, the diversity of responsibility. All of these are for the purpose of profiting the whole body of Christ. That's the main point. And we're going to revisit that later. Verse 8 provides a description or title of certain gifts that are difficult to understand, especially since we are 2,000 years removed from their practice. What exactly was a word of wisdom? What was a word of knowledge? That is not clear to us today Some rogue scholars and ecstatic independent church leaders say that they know what these are and they practice them, they say, today. But their claims don't stand up to thorough examination. Regardless of what they were, the main point from St. Paul is that the gifts and they may be the same gift That is wisdom and knowledge. They were from the same spirit, the Holy Spirit The description in verse 9 reminds us that faith itself is a gift of God, as the Bible confirms elsewhere, as is the gift of healing. The main point, however, regardless of the gift, is that all of it comes from the only Holy Spirit. One God, one Spirit. From verse 10, we can speculate that the working of miracles would be separated from the gift of healing and may consist of turning water into wine. multiplication of bread, for those were the miracles that Jesus performed in his ministry. The gift of prophecy does not need to be a new word from God But an application of God's word to the people in their present state. That's mostly what the Old Testament prophets did. But I would say also that the church was young, so perhaps there were new words to understand. The gift of discerning spirits might refer to evaluating prophecy. I would say it is not, it was not and is not the ability to know the hearts of individuals And I say this because I know people who have claimed that they have that gift and they're able to judge the hearts of men. That is not given to any man. The final two gifts mentioned are speaking in tongues and interpreting tongues. It is necessary for us to address these two gifts. more forwardly because they were so popularly popularly pursued uh in evangelical circles in the 70s and the 80s and the 90s, early 90s The fact that the gift of tongues and the interpretation of tongues are listed here, and then are first listed in chapter 13, verse 1, suggests that the abuse of these gifts was a primary problem. And unfortunately, the choice of translators to use the word tongues represents a failure of nerve. In any similar context, the word would be rendered languages. Only once in the New Testament are we actually given to see the gift of tongues in operation. And it is the Spirit given ability to speak a language that has not been learned. And so with interpretation of tongues, which is most naturally we would take it to mean A translation of languages, that was the actual gift. Verse 11 brings all the gifts mentioned back into the focus into focus, for they are to be used for the purpose of God's will, by the power and authority and inspiration of the one and only Holy Spirit. Now I had to skip then to verse 28, jumping over that metaphor of the church being as the body. We'll touch on that next week. We get a list in verse 28 of Paul mixing together offices of the church and gifts. And the gifts are a bit different in the way that they're given in verses 8 through 10. The gift of helping others and the gifts of administration or Counseling or ruling. These are mixed together in a list that is largely supernatural in their gifts, obviously coming from God Some traditions have linked these gifts to the office of ordained ministry. Now, the general sense of the text, I think, is clear enough. The Corinthians were taking God's gifts and glorifying themselves with those gifts. Gifts that were intended to be for the church as a whole, not for individual grandiosity. What they had been given for, the common good, instead were being used to stroke selfish pride. They interpreted the spiritual gifts that they had been granted, especially the flashier ones, the ones that involved ecstatic speech. They use them as marks of God's special commendation upon them. The lack of a servant spirit among the Corinthians had, of course, already been addressed on several occasions in the letter to this point. This is just another instance of a similar fundamental problem: selfishness. There is a particular message from these verses that is most important for us in the time in which we live. But before I get to that message, I need to say a few words about what so many Christians ask regarding these verses, especially young Christians. When I was a young Christian, I had similar questions. Such questions are: Are the gifts described here still practiced today? Does the Holy Spirit give out the same gifts today as he did to the Corinthian church as Saint Paul describes? And should we see said gifts on a regular basis within the church? Other questions are variations of those view. As a Christian in college, as many of you know. I was part of an independent Christian church that insisted that the answer to those types of questions was an emphatic yes. The church insisted that all of its members tap into the Holy Spirit to find his or her manifestation of the Holy Spirit While also insisting that Christians be re-baptized, water rebaptism, followed by being baptized in the Holy Spirit. And that was to show evidence, you were to show evidence of such a baptism of the Holy Spirit by speaking in an unknown tongue. As a young-minded and young in-the-faith Christian, I followed the leaders of the church and was rebaptized. and then imitated their manner of speaking in tongues by moving my tongue in an unpredictable but imitative manner to sound as those I heard around me. I was next claimed by the leadership to be baptized in the Holy Spirit. During the next two years, I witnessed so-called words of knowledge that stated such things as God wants someone here who is depressed to be healed. We even heard one such word of knowledge that God wants those who are suffering from the blaz to be healed. I myself suffered from an ingrown toenail that that hurt uh very badly during spring football practice. And I was healed after much prayer and after much soaking of my foot in warm water and Epsom salt What wasn't healed was an assistant pastor's wife who died of terminal cancer. What wasn't healed were marriages that were torn apart by adultery. What wasn't healed was the senior pastor who also died of cancer a few years after Bobby Lynn and I left that parish. That is my experience, and it may not be yours. To be clear, I do not believe in what theologians call the cessation view. That concludes that the gifts of the Holy Spirit are no longer to be seen in our midst, thus ceased or cessation. The Bible does not teach any such cessation, nor does it teach continuation. The best wisdom that I have regarding the Holy Spirit and its gifts is given to the church in St. John's Gospel, where Jesus teaches Nicodemus. Remember he said, The Spirit is as the wind, for it blows as it wishes You may hear the sound of it, but you cannot tell where it has come from or where it is going. The Holy Spirit has the will of the Godhead. What I am most certain of is that when the Holy Spirit does move in a miraculous way, such as the changing of a life from a sinner to a saint, The evidence is unquestionable. When the Holy Spirit performs miracles as a testimony to Jesus being Lord and Savior, you will know it is from God. For it can be from no other. As for the message of our day I would like these words of Saint Paul to confront what is popular in independent Christian circles. And I would like to label this popularity as being of the devil. It is a focus in corporate worship and in Christian living That believes that every truth of the gospel of the Lord Jesus is first and foremost for the benefit of the individual. I don't know of a better example of how false teachers of today who call themselves Christians Have turned the gospel of the Lord Jesus into meditations about self-help and narcissism. The example I'm referring to is from a pastor in California who spoke to a congregation in his skinny jeans and untucked button-down shirt. amongst the satellite production displaying on what they call other campuses. And what he spoke about was how the high priestly prayer of Jesus that we read part of this morning is actually a message about how each of his listeners can be better versions of themselves. Please consider what I just told you. The prayer Jesus prayed as recorded in John's Gospel, chapter 17. Where Jesus is praying just before he is betrayed by Judas and the cogs of the machine starting to turn towards his destined crucifixion. There, Jesus first prays that God the Father would be glorified by him. He then thanks the Father for giving him authority to save men. He then states that he and the Father have done to bring light into the world so that the world may know the truth. He then proclaims that he has given his followers truth and prays that they would not stray from the truth, and specifically that they would be in the world, but not of the world. This includes a prayer to keep his followers from the influence of the devil. And that includes for them to be sanctified by the truth from the words Jesus has taught them. He next prays for not only his current disciples, but for those who would follow those disciples, thus he prayed for you and I. He closes expressing his desire that his followers would be in him as he is in the will of the Heavenly Father, and that all of us would share in the same love. Thus, we may easily conclude that the focus of Jesus in this prayer and in his whole life was a focus for others and otherness, which is what the Christian life is to be Now take that truth and apply it to a modern pastor, so-called, who tells his congregation, so-called, that John 17 is, and I quote All about your most abundant life, your most full, your most complete life. Now we may have grace for such a summation. It's terribly poor. And he just might have misspoke. Perhaps he was going to preach about how Christians should glorify God first and foremost on how they are in the world and not of the world. And that they should be made holy by the truth of the words of Jesus, and that we may find our identity solely in Jesus while sharing in the love that He and the Heavenly Father have And and that most certainly could be their most complete life. But that is not what he went on to teach. He went on to teach in summary that the prayer of Jesus wants you to have a great paying job, a great many friends. No trials in life, and the ability to give more money to his church. I'm paraphrasing his teaching. Because if he is going to bastardize Jesus' prayer from John 17, then I'm not going to be kind to any points of his sermon. What I am highlighting for us is how the devil deceived the Christians in Corinth to believe and behave as if they were being given by the Holy Spirit Gifts for their own personal pride and for their own personal benefit In the same way, you can see the devil's work in taking a prayer by Jesus that is most certainly about others. And the priority of the church, first About the church before the individual, and the devil making it about personal pride and personal benefit. The devil's strategy is not new. It is simply rewritten to our modern context. And unaccountable preachers and laymen fall in line. I close with a reminder. that we will finish these points with the metaphor of the church being the body next week. And I close with the reminder of Jesus being in the desert 40 days. Just as we recognize during Lent. Jesus in all of his temptations, especially the ones highlighted in the Gospels, never put himself first. Satan said, Eat Jesus, prove your Godhead, and satisfy your hunger. Satan said, show off God's favoritism of you, Jesus, and jump down and save yourself to impress all. Satan said, Bow down to me, and all the power within the world shall be yours. When Jesus thought not for himself in all of those temptations, he ended up saving the world. When you and I think not for ourselves, we help Jesus save the world. Let us pray. O God, we are humbled by the problems of Corinth, because we are not above them, and we know it, and we confess it Wherever there is opportunity to put ourselves first, to get praise of ourselves by men. May we die to it. And where there is opportunity to use any gifts, to use anything that you have blessed us with for the sake of others, for the sake of your body May that be the priority of each of us in this house. Dear Jesus, be glorified in us and among us. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Being the Body
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated We are continuing our series in 1 Corinthians, and you may wonder should we have a special sir uh sermon for the time in which we're living? Well, you will see that God's word applies to every situation. Turn, if you would, to 1 Corinthians chapter 12. We are working with the body metaphor. The oft-repeated phrase, I know I am somebody because God don't make no junk. Is attributed to Ethel Waters, an African American singer, songwriter, and actress The phrase echoes Psalm 139, where the psalmist praises God for forming him within his mother's womb. Thus granting believers with the faith that God is intricately involved in the forming of every human being as each of us can confess that we are fearfully and wonderfully made. There is a catch. Of course, there is a catch. The catch is that not everyone feels or perceives he or she is somebody, somebody that is important enough for God to care about. Secular solutions to people not seeing themselves as fearfully and wonderfully made by God have been to manufacture self-esteem. in people, especially young people, so that they view themselves as valued. What is not sufficiently answered is the question, valued by whom? Self-esteem without God as the primary component of a person and how he or she views himself. Leaves a crater so vast that all psychiatrists in the world cannot fill it. Consider the unavoidable conclusion a person struggling with self-esteem realizes. She is told that she is of great value, and she is of great value because her teachers and counselors tell her she is. She is then picked on by classmates and told that she's not pretty enough or skinny enough, and she starts to feel bad about herself only to be told by another teacher, another counselor, that she is in fact pretty and that she is shaped appropriately, and this is the counterbalance message to that of her peers. But the problem remains in that she is to base her self-worth on what other people say about her. Even if she was to listen only to her teachers and counselors and believe them alone, she is still basing her personal value on what other people say. It will eventually be asked, what authority or perspective do my teachers and counselors have that makes what they say more important or more valid than what my peers say? The answer to that question is simply chirping. There is no legitimate answer. The irony of taking God out of the conclusion that every person is of value. Is that there was no value placed upon the lives of every individual person until Christianity became the dominant religion in the world? That truth is not hard to look up. Consider how non-Roman citizens were treated in all of the Roman Empire before Christianity. Consider how slaves have been treated within every nation during all times of recorded history before Christianity. Human worth was not understood until Christianity taught that every human being is created in God's image. And because they carry God's image, they are owed respect. From their fellow human beings. Human value was not accepted until Christianity proclaimed that forgiveness of sins and a hope of heaven was for each gender For every person of every age, and for every person, regardless of ethnicity, social standing, political standing, or financial standing. The only, only counter-argument against the dramatic influence that Christianity has had upon the worth of every human being was how people who claimed to be Christian in the West and in Europe treated African slaves. Such historical realities teach us That there is one thing to say that you are a follower of Jesus Christ, and another thing to live all aspects of your life with Jesus as your Lord. When men make money their God, they will justify all other behavior. Thanks be to God. That most of the leaders of the abolitionist movements in Europe and in America were vocally Christian. This introduction brings us to verse 12 of chapter 12 of 1 Corinthians. There, St. Paul summarizes his point, stating that although we make up many different parts or members of the body of Christ, we are all still one body. This point is further described in verse 13 as all who are Christian are not distinct by nationality. or social struct social structure, but we are understood to be all of the same and both our self-worth and kingdom worth because we are Christian. We are all part of the body of Christ. This truth was stated by the prophet Joel, where God said Even on my men servants and my maidservants I will pour out my spirit in those days. In John 7 it reads, On the last and greatest day of the feast, Jesus stood up and called out in a loud voice, If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink. The word anyone is inclusive. In Romans chapter 3 verse 22, St. Paul said, and this righteousness from God comes through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe there is no distinction. The all inclusive. In Galatians chapter 3, 28, Paul said again, there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free Male or female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. When it pertains to salvation and inheritance, we are all considered sons of God. To the Ephesians he said, Because you know that the Lord will reward each one for whatever good he does, whether he is slave or free, all are free in Christ Jesus. And to the Colossians, Paul said, Here there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave or free But Christ is all and in all. Thus there is no mistake to proclaim that in Christ Jesus All of humanity is the same. And thus each person is to be afforded the same rights, respect, and dignity as a human being. No other faith, other than those faiths that borrow from Christianity, no other faith has provided a similar value of each individual person. This being established, we can more closely examine the body metaphor used by Paul to explain the intrinsic value of each member of Christ's body. As stated in verse 14, there are simple observations, noticeable differences in the members of the body of Christ, and each of those differences are represented by a person and many persons. What we are to notice in verse 15 and 16 is the poor logic of the foot and the ear. The foot can conclude that because he cannot do all that the hand can do, that he is not as important as the hand. The ear can conclude that what he does is not as important as what the eye does, meaning that his value is not as great as that of the eye. Both the foot and the ear extend their logic to conclude that because they are less important because of their functionality That they can be understood to not have a true value and thus not are really a part of the body at all. The apostle will reveal the reason why such a conclusion is wrong, but we must first be critical of the foot and the ear. Both the foot and the ear make their observations from their limited vantage point, and they trust in their conclusions. The foot and the ear trust in their own testimonies about themselves, which they have no authority or responsibility to do. The simple fact that they are part of the body and thus do not stand away from the body should tell them that they cannot have an objective opinion. How true it is that the same problem occurs with individual Christians who, by their own evaluation of their own gifts, and placement within their family, within their community, within their church, conclude that they are not good enough to be considered important. Individuals similar to rogue body parts step out of their jurisdiction and make conclusions about their own personal value. With no such authority or responsibility to do such given to them. God has said that such a valuation is his to make. And what he says of all his body parts is that they are all of the same value, which is a precious value. A value he has made, a value he has claimed, and a value that he insists upon In verses 17 through 20, the metaphor allows for each of us, regardless of whether we consider ourselves a foot or a hand, an ear or an eye. To realize how we can be used of God just as God wants us to be used. I shared with the confirmation class a couple of weeks ago about when I was in college and I busted my little toe trying to show off my walking on my hands. I came down on the corner of a couch on my left little toe. No big deal, right? Well, you don't realize until you heard it how much a little toe can cause pain throughout the body and in the mind. You don't know how much your little toe is used for balancing the whole body until you have to use it while it is broken. Like body parts. The Christian church is made up of many different people with many different functions, and each of those functions is to be valued by both the part itself and the work that they do, and by the rest of the body, who may not appreciate just how important each part is. No better place is all of this exemplified than in verse 21, where the hands might not appreciate the work of the eyes until the eyes are not working And the hands can only grope. In the reverse, the eyes easily see what to do, but without the hands, seeing only Seeing only becomes less useful. Now the next struggle that needs to be addressed is when body parts are viewed as weaker or unnecessary. There are troubled people and troubled times for certain other people who see themselves as an appendix for the body of Christ. You don't feel needed. You believe that if you were to be cut out, the body wouldn't miss you, and so you feel down about your self-worth. Well perhaps this is where a metaphor breaks down, trying to explain the value of each individual, or maybe not. The appendix can act as a storehouse for good bacteria in order to help repair the digestive system. I read that this week. Never knew that. What it most certainly does is cause pain when it becomes infected, and that pain will not subside until it is cared for. And there are people in the church who can do their part by providing pain for the rest of the body. There are Christians who have contrarian personalities, and those personalities test the patience and unconditional love of other Christians. There are Christians who are natural pessimists, saying about every ministry program, it'll never work. And this stretches the faith and stamina of other Christians. Such people are always needed For they do not allow the Christian other Christians to walk by the flesh while only being concerned about earthly success They challenge fellow Christians to look deeper and harder at personal motivations and to try to be as pure as possible when it comes to the purpose of our many different ministries. And finally, a person who sees themselves as unnecessary, that person can sanctify the entire church. Because the church is to see that such persons are to be given even greater care, because that care is what they need. The standard of verse 20's fix is for all of us to be moved by For it teaches us that as part of the body of Christ, we are not just concerned about members who are like us, you know, the right hand caring more about the left hand because they're more alike Or the foot caring more about the toes because, well, the toes are part of the foot. As members of the body, we are to care about all members of the body. You see, Christians can be deceived by the devil to think that as long as they work in the church somewhere, that they are doing God's work and they don't have to worry about anybody else, that's all God requires. But what is always required, no matter if you work only in the nursery or only fixing broken things in the building, is that all of us are to care about one another when someone needs to be cared for. When one member suffers, verse 26, all suffer, or at least all of us should. We do so because Jesus suffers when just one suffers, and we are in him, and he is in us. St. Paul ends the metaphor in verse 27 with the simple statement of summation: you, all of us, are the body of Christ. What we are individually together makes us united as the body of Jesus on this earth. The church universal and local is the continuation of the incarnation of Jesus on earth. From this metaphor, we must remember the main point of the chapter. As stated last sermon, when we learned about the diversity of gifts in the church We underline that such gifts are for the benefit of the church as a whole, as opposed to being for the ego of individuals. Thus, we are to continue that lesson when considering ourselves a part of the body of Jesus. Whatever part of the body we are. The purpose of our part is for the benefit of the church as a whole. The function of our particular body part is not for ourselves, it is for others. Our bodily function in Christ is otherness. Being reminded of this principle of otherness. As we live our Christian lives within the church, we are to see two things that clearly come against the spirit of our age. The first thing is the intrinsic value of every person made in the image of God, for we underscore that said value as only true in terms of God as our Creator. The modern psychologist wants each person to live by slogans such as, You're enough. Live your truth. Love yourself. Embrace your flaws. You are perfect just the way you are. None of these mantras make sense by themselves. But we can love ourselves based on God's love for us. We are not perfect the way we are, the way we are, and we never will be in this life. But we are still loved by God. With an unconditional, everlasting love that is so strong it doesn't matter how we see ourselves or how others perceive us. And the love of God has for us is so powerful, so unique, and so empowering that we are able to live for others while not being concerned about ourselves. That is another way, another contrary truth to the spirit of our age. We are told a lie, that we are empowered by how good we feel about ourselves, while Jesus teaches us That we are empowered by not thinking about ourselves at all, but instead thinking about the needs of others And a crisis like a dangerous virus tempts us to be concerned about ourselves first and last. But the power of the gospel is being so other focused, so otherless, that we care for the sick first before self. We make sure the least among us is fed and filled before we fill ourselves. And I guess I need to say that we make sure other people have toilet paper before we have some ourselves. In time of crisis, the church ought not close her doors to be sure that no sickness gets in, but instead opens her doors to help and heal the sick. In times of crisis, may the body of Christ and all of its parts be used by God for caring for others, first and last. Amen. Let us pray. Father, we thank you first for how well this passage of scripture comes into play considering the days in which we live. We are so grateful that you have made us a part of the body, that you have given us intrinsic value and you have claimed it. For yourself.
