sermons.title: Easter 2020
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Crime and Punishment is a mid-19th century novel written by Fyodor Dostoyevsky. That used to be required reading in all American high by all American high school students when said students could Read good literature and understand it, and yes, that is a dig at modern education. Dostoevsky is one of the greatest novelists of all time. With a keen understanding of the human condition. Most important, Dostoevsky was a Christian. The main character in Crime and Punishment is Rodin Raskolnikov. He was a law student at St. Petersburg. When he was forced to drop out because his family's money had depleted. In order to right his life, so he thought, he planned a murder of a woman pawnbroker. Dostoevsky takes us into the mind of Raskolnikov as he wrestles with moral convictions and lack of courage that prevent him from actuating the crime. When he finally does the deed by cracking the woman's head open with an ax, there is a witness to his crime. Who stumbles in just after the deed is done, requiring that she too be murdered Raskolnikov flees the scene with the money in his pocket without being seen by another witness. Suffering from a mental fog, he decides to hide the money under a building rock to be retrieved later. He then wandered the streets while becoming more physically ill. He makes his way back to his small flat and falls asleep. He is found later by his landlady, who notes that he is feverish. His illness then becomes a cover-up of sorts as no one expects him of the crime because of his alibi of being ill and remaining in his flat But Raskolnikov is not physically ill. He is mentally, emotionally, and spiritually ill. His guilt becomes so great that he is racked with confusion, paranoia, and self-hate. Soon, an investigator looks into the past of Vaskolnikov, discovering an article Vaskolnikov had written while in high school. In this article, Raskolnikov argued that certain gifted persons, he uses Napoleon as an example, Certain gifted persons should be allowed to commit certain crimes, particularly people of high intellect, who offer superior assets to society. In the same article, he describes how a person getting away with a major crime might also give a might also give away his guilt by manifesting the same guilt through physical illness. Thus the article Raskolnikov had written was being played out by Raskolnikov himself Knowing that the investigator was close to exposing his crime, Razgolnikov visits a woman He had come to know who he admired and was attracted to, but did not think that he could love because she had participated in prostitution. Sonia, Sonia the prostitute, is the daughter of a jobless man who remains lost in alcohol until his death. After her father died, Sonia became the primary source of financial support for her family, being forced to choose between prostitution or destitution. Her only choice, she perceives, is to sell herself to feed her family. What is remarkable about the character of Sonia is how she maintains her faith in God even in poverty and even as a reluctant and guilt-ridden prostitute After Raskolnikov lamented with Sonia regarding the poor state of her family, he challenges her belief in God. Noticing a New Testament on a nearby table, he brought it to her. Now I realize thus far this is not the Easter sermon that you participate anticipated, but hang on. We will get there. I will now read from the novel. Where is the story of Lazarus? He asked suddenly. Sonia looked obstinately at the ground and would not answer. She was standing sideways to the table. Where is the raising of Lazarus? Find it for me, Sonya. She stole a glance at him. You are not looking in the right place. It's in the fourth gospel, she whispered sternly, without looking at him. Find it and read it to me, he said. He sat down with his elbow on the table, leaned his head on his hand, and looked away sullenly, prepared to listen. In three weeks' time, they'll welcome me in a madhouse. I shall be there if I am not in a worse place, he muttered to himself. Sonia heard Raskolnikov's request distrustfully and moved hesitatingly to the table. She took the book, however. Haven't you read it? she asked. Looking up at him across the table, her voice became sterner and sterner. Long ago, when I was at school, read And haven't you heard it in church? I haven't been. Do you often go? No, whispered Sonia. Vaskolmikov smiled. I understand. And you won't go to your father's funeral tomorrow? Yes, I shall. I was at church last week, too. I had a requiem service. For whom? For Lizaveta, she was killed with an axe. His nerves were more and more strained. His head began to go round. Were you friends with Lisavetta? Yes, she was good. She used to come. Not often. She couldn't. We used to read together and talk. She will see God. The last phrase sounded strange in his ears, and here was something new again, this mysterious meeting with Lizaveta, and both of them religious maniacs. I shall be a religious maniac myself. It's infectious. Breathe, he cried irritably and insistently. Sonia still hesitated. Her heart was throbbing. She hardly dared to read. He looked almost with an exasperation at the unhappy lunatic. What for? You don't believe? she whispered, softly, and, as it were, breathlessly. Read, I want you to, he persisted. You used to read to Lizavetta Sonia opened the book and found the place. Her hands were shaking. Her voice failed her. Twice she tried to begin and could not find the first syllable. Now a certain man was sick named Lazarus of Bethany. She forced herself at last to read, but at the third word her voice broke like an overstrained string There was a catch in her breath. Raskolmakov saw, in part, why Sonia could not bring herself to read to him, and the more he saw this, the more roughly and irritably he insisted on her doing so. He understood only too well how painful it was for her to betray and unveil all that was her own. He understood that these feelings really were her secret treasure, which she had kept perhaps for years. Perhaps from childhood while she lived with an unhappy father and a distracted stepmother crazed with grief in the midst of starving children and unseemly abuse and reproaches. But at the same time he knew now and knew for certain that although it filled her with dread and suffering, yet she had a tormenting desire to read, and to read to him that he might hear it, and to read now whatever might come of it. He read this in her eyes. He could see it in her intense emotion. She mastered herself, controlled the spasm in her throat, and went on reading the 11th chapter of St. John. She went on to the 19th verse. And many of the Jews came to Martha and Mary to comfort them concerning their brother. Then Martha, as soon as she heard that Jesus was coming, went and met him. But Mary sat still in the house. Then said Martha unto Jesus, Lord, if thou hast been here, my brother had not died. But I know that even now whatsoever thou wilt ask of God, God will give it to thee. Then she stopped again with a shamed face, feeling that her voice would quiver and break again. Jesus said unto her, Thy brother shall rise again. Martha saith unto him, I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day. Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection and the life He that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live. And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this? She saith unto him. And drawing a painful breath, Sonia read distinctly and forcibly as though she were making a public confession of faith. Yea, Lord, I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world. She stopped and looked up quickly at him, but controlling herself went on reading. Raskolnikov sat without moving, his elbows on the table and his eyes turned away She read to the 22nd verse. Then Mary was come where Jesus was, and saw him. She fell down at his feet, saying unto him, Lord, if thou hast been here, my brother had not died. And Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews also weeping, which came to her. He groaned in spirit and was troubled, and said, Where have they laid him? They said unto him, Lord, come and see. Jesus wept. Then said the Jews, Behold, how he loved him. And some of them said, Could not this man which opened the eyes of the blind had caused that even this man should not have died? Raskolnikov turned and looked at her with emotion. Yes, he had known it. She was trembling in a real physical fever. He had expected it. She was getting near the story of the greatest miracle, and a feeling of immense triumph came over her. Her voice rang out like a bell. Triumph and joy gave it power. The lines danced before her eyes, but she knew what she was reading by heart. At the last verse, could not this man which opened the eyes of the blind, dropping her voice, she passionately reproduced the doubt. the reproach, a a censor of the blind, disbelieving Jews, who in another moment would fall at his feet as though struck by thunder, sobbing and believing And he, looking at Raskolmakov, he too is blinded and unbelieving. He too will hear. He too will believe. Yes, yes, at once now. Was what she was dreaming, and she was quivering with happy anticipation Jesus, therefore, again groaning in himself, cometh to the grave. It was a cave, and a stone lay upon it. Jesus said, Take ye away the stone. Martha, the sister of him that was dead, saith unto him, Lord, by this time he stinketh, for he hath been dead four days. She laid emphasis on the word for. Jesus said unto her, Said I not unto thee that if thou wouldst believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God? Then they took away the stone from the place where the dead were laid. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me. And I knew that thou hearest me always, but because of the people which stand by, I said it, that they may believe that thou hast sent me. And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth. And he that was dead came forth. She read loudly, cold and trembling with ecstasy, as though she was seeing it before her eyes. Bound hand and foot, with grave clothes, and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto him, Loose him and let him go. Then many of the Jews which came to Mary had seen the things which Jesus did, and believed on him. She could read no more, closed the book, and got up from her chair quickly. That is all about raising of Lazarus. She whispered, severely and abruptly, and turning away, she stood motionless, not daring to raise her eyes to him. She still trembled feverishly. The candle end was flickering out in the battered candlestick, dimly lighting up in the poverty stricken room, the murderer and the harlot. Who has so strangely been reading together the eternal book? Such a scene is so very powerful As we can imagine, two sinners, racked with guilt of their sins and lacking hope for any happiness in this life. Reading of a miracle that provides new life. Critics say that Dostoevsky uses the story of Lazarus to anticipate the needed and future resurrection of Raskolnikov. That's true in part. What Dostoevsky also does in this scene is preach the gospel. The scene allows us to place ourselves with the murderer and the prostitute in the room listening to the story of a man that was dead, dead four days. So dead that his body had begun to decay, and with the decay would have caused a putrid smell in the cave that would overwhelm anyone who was near it when it was opened The point being that the man was dead, and Jesus made him alive again. But none of us is a murderer, right? None of us is a prostitute, right? Wait, wasn't it Jesus who said that if you hate another human being, any other human being, you are guilty of murder in your heart? Wasn't it Jesus who said that even lusting after another person sexually, you have committed adultery in your heart? With such standards, there might be more murderers and prostitutes within my hearing. I am one. There are a number of reasons why Dostoevsky includes the story of Lazarus in his novel, and a number of reasons why St. John includes it in his gospel. The story of Lazarus being raised from the dead is an emphatic statement that Jesus had power over death and life even before his own resurrection. The story of Lazarus being raised from the dead also pointed to another resurrection. A resurrection that would take place after three days. Only it would be Jesus raiself. That resurrection would point to the future resurrection of anyone who would believe that Jesus is the promised Messiah and God incarnate. Recall the words of Jesus to Martha. I am the resurrection and the life. He that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live. And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. These words are as true to us as they were to Martha. And Jesus asked each of us, believest thou this? Ah. Ah, indeed, we do, sweet Jesus. We do believe. And that is why we celebrate this day, this most holy day. We as believers in Jesus Christ can mock death. We can mock the devil. We can mock anything that would claim any authority related to sin and death. In Christ Jesus, there are no murderers, there are no prostitutes, no fornicators, no adulterers, no thieves, no haters, no liars, no cheaters. No persons that will be identified with their sins of the past, for all has been forgiven, and what is dead is made alive. And if we can mock death, we can mock anything that brings about death or threatens death, including pestilence or a virus. And the story read, there were two people in a room alone. Quarantined, if you will allow. Quarantined by their sin and guilt. They had quarantined themselves away from God and away from the rest of society because of their immorality. And yet the good news was right before them as they heard that Jesus brings the dead back to life. He brings the dead in sin and the dead in body back to life. That means that he reverses evil. He turns despair into joy. He turns fear into trust. He turns hopelessness into faith. He turns feelings of loneliness into feelings of being loved. To live in the reality of the resurrected Jesus is to live with evil reversed. What the devil means for evil, God means for good. We can apply said truths to our current state of affairs. Jesus is risen from the dead, no matter a worldwide virus. No matter a government ordered shutdown, no matter people alone, people tempted to despair. Jesus is alive forevermore, and no virus and no government can remove that truth. If you don't know Jesus, know him today. Embrace a future testimony. that will say you became a Christian on Easter Sunday during a pandemic because you, like a murderer and a prostitute, need new life. Jesus is the only one who can give it. Let us pray. Father, we thank you for this good news. We thank you for how a simple story can bring so much to life in terms of the hope of a resurrection. And because of Jesus, we stand victorious. And we pray for anyone who would call upon your name Trusting that they will be heard, trusting that you will save them, because they now believe. We praise you in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Things Above
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. We are taking a break, at least one more week, a break from First Corinthians, because of the predicament in which we are all experiencing. Let's begin by talking about what is good about these past several weeks of being in lockdown. Most parents are now involved in their children's education, and that is as it should be. It was God's commandment that parents take responsibility for their children's education. Parents are growing a greater appreciation for the work of teachers. I heard of a parent. being seen scraping off a my kid is an honor student bumper sticker after just one week of trying homeschool I have heard of another family who packed up the suitcase of their child and sent him to the neighbor with a note that read This is a homeschool exchange student. Please take care of him for a few months. In contrast, we are so very proud of our teachers and staff at St. Stephen's Academy. Headmaster Dykes has done a great job organizing our teachers and our teachers are working hard, harder than they probably would when the children are in the building because they want to keep the quality of education high. We can all be proud of them for that. Another positive: people are more aware of how disease is transferred and more diligent about personal hygiene. Another positive, churches have become more tech savvy and resourceful in order to minister to God's people. People are attending virtual churches that they have never been to and are in another state because those services are even being recorded. My mother-in-law says that she hears three sermons each Sunday as she listens to our service and then the service of her son and then her other son-in-law. Now that is dedication. Another positive is how older people who have tried to stay away from technological advances are now learning. and that learning provides greater opportunities to stay in touch with loved ones. Our family has learned to play games online and We can include people in Richmond and North Carolina, and it's almost as good as them being in the house with you. Another positive is the time families must spend together There is greater opportunities to practice unconditional love and forgiveness, as well as being long-suffering toward one another. Another positive is the Sabbath rest that lakes and rivers and oceans are getting. The land needs a Sabbath year, and at least it's getting a month or two. Another positive is people reaching out to one another, checking in to see how each other are doing. Hopefully, such a practice will remain long after the worst of this pandemic has passed And another positive that I hope will remain is the hunger God's people have to be together. to be together in his house. May we never take it for granted and may we teach our children never to take it for granted. Of course, some of these positives could be negatives. For example, people could get used to attending virtual church and no longer attend to a service in person. That would be unfortunate. The decision to comply with the government shutdown, as you can imagine, has not been easy for you or for clergy. There have been some headline news regarding the constitutionality of the government forcing churches to keep closed and even fining financially those churches that are not complying. And finding citizens who attend those services. I assure you that I do not agree with those fines. I am aware of some who think that we pastors are being frightened to close our doors and that we are cowards for not standing up against our governor. Thankfully, our Episcopal government structure does not allow me to take my own, to make my own decisions as I am covered by a bishop. Who is covered by a college of bishops, and they make decisions for us, and we are expected to follow them with our input, of course. Just as the apostles made decisions for the church to follow, so too do our bishops make decisions for us to follow And our bishops want us to be good neighbors because we don't know fully, even now, over a month later, we don't know fully about the dangers of this virus There will, I am sure, if this stay-at-home order continues for months on end, there will be a time when our bishops and other branches of Christ's Church We'll have to decide whether complying is loving our neighbor. Is that going against tending the flock of Christ? After all, Jesus' primary instruction to Peter to bring him back into the fold, Jesus said to him three times, you remember, feed my sheep. We feed by word and sacrament. The word is still going forth, thanks be to God, but the sacrament is not. Many of you have not been able to receive communion. Baptisms are being postponed. Our granddaughter was to be baptized next week by her grandfather. That little girl deserves to be baptized. I had never imagined a scenario. Where as a citizen of the United States, I would not be able to gather God's people for a baptism. But here we are. It all can be quite frustrating. And yet, and yet there is something that we can do To help us via people who are living out the resurrection of Jesus rather than being restricted by the time in which we live. The verse that I believe God wants us to hear and practice this day was actually a part of the epistle reading from last week. As it comes from Colossians chapter 3, where St. Paul says, and you want to turn there in your Bibles to Colossians chapter 3. St. Paul says there, set your mind on things above, not on things upon the earth. Now I chose as our epistle reading from Philippians today a verse that matches this idea that our citizenship is not here, it is in heaven. And St. Paul says to the Colossians to get our minds thinking about that place. I want us to examine these verses in Colossians more closely, for it seems to me that the more frustrated I become about the restrictions placed upon me. The more I am focusing on things upon the earth, I need to begin to start thinking about things above. In verse 1 of Colossians chapter 3, St. Paul reveals to the Christians at Colossae That living in the reality of the resurrected Christ is to have a dramatic change on our ethical obligations. We are no longer who we were. And that means we are no longer to be doing what we had been doing. For the Colossians, according to verse 5, if you look down to that verse, according to verse 5, this meant that they were no longer to practice fornication, which you know as sex outside of marriage. They were to no longer participate in uncleanness, which is anything against God's law in practice or thought. They were to no longer practice passion, which is to act out any desire of the flesh. They were to no longer practice evil, which is those which are those fleshly desires, and you simply add pride to it. And they were to no longer practice covetousness, which for them was a desire to be like the heathens around them. This last one is what we can be easily tempted to do during this time of quarantine. I wonder if there is anyone else who is tired of commercials or shows on television. That have celebrities encouraging viewers, you and I, to stay at home because, quote, we are all in this together. We are not all in this together. They are roaming their mansions and swimming in their pools. and enjoying their fortunes while bemoaning that they cannot be on the television screen or the movie screen, meaning that they cannot be the center of attention Well, we are doing none of those things. But the temptation then is for us to want to be them. Christians can wonder what it is like to have too much money, too much fame, too much influence, too much availability to do as you please. What is their life like? We may wonder, and so the coveting begins. But here's the truth. Their life is actually like our lives, only they have more means to sin. We can practice the same sins as they practice, the difference being that they have greater means to practice more of it. But the results are the same. When you practice sin, you become a slave to sin. And it doesn't matter how much money you have for a slave is a slave. A slave serves its master, and when sin is your master, the end goal is to take your life. Before St. Paul tells us to set our minds on things above, he tells us to seek those things that are above where Christ is sitting. And before that he says, quote, if then you were raised with Christ. This is an important conditional. It is another way of saying that you must be born again. The Bible uses different phrasing to describe coming to new life in Christ. We are born again. We are given new life We are resurrected with Christ. We are adopted into God's family. All of it means the same thing. It is the first step, the necessary first step. Next, we are to seek what is above. And what are those things above? Future blessings preserved in heaven. Our minds are to be focused on eternal felicity, which is intense happiness. Heaven described in the Bible includes what it is not or what there will not be. The book of Revelation tells us that there will be no crying, for there will be no reason for sorrow. There will be no pain, for there will be no illness and thus no death. All that was brought into the world because of the sin of mankind will no longer exist. Because the old will have gone away, all things in heaven are new. There will be no rough seas, because the rough sea represents the rebellious nations. There will only be a sea that is so very calm it is as glass, for Jesus has calmed the nations. And there will be a new holy city, a new Jerusalem. And new houses to be inhabited by God's people. They are even called, in certain translations, mansions. And everyone gets one, so that you are not tempted to covet. And there will be vineyards and fruitful gardens that will provide all that is needed both for aesthetics and for our daily bread. And there will be perfect peace, so that we can freely love and be loved without regret, without fear, and only forgiveness. Such things we are to seek, and we are to set our minds upon But I must reveal to you that I do not often think about such things. I have not thought about such things during this pandemic crisis. I have thought about my bank accounts. I have thought about my food supply and my toilet paper supply, and not always in that order. I have thought about each parishioner of St. Stephen's and the people that I know are joining our worship services online and those who perhaps I don't know but are joining us. I have thought about webcams and sound systems and computers and YouTube channels and Facebook and Zoom and anything else that is needed to broadcast our services and Bible studies. I have thought about the church finances and your finances, especially those who I know are out of work. I have prayed about these things when they come to mind, asking the Lord to help those in need and to sustain us all as we walk this road. I have thought very highly of Mr. Ryan Hammett and all the remarkable work he has done getting us and keeping us online. I thought about the Reverend Bowles and Diana and how strong a support they have been during this crisis, and now the Neviuses and Grapes and how helpful they have been And of course, my beloved wife Bobby Lynn, who is the model of servanthood. These things I have thought about. But not much, if at all, have I sought or thought about setting my affections on things above. And I need to examine why. Why have I not sought things above or set my mind on things above? Why have I not thought about a place where pain and sorrow do not exist, and where all things are at peace, and where there is all that is needed? And where there is love given and freely received. It must be Why I have not thought about these things. It must be, it has to be the simple truth that I am being disobedient to God I am doing what Jesus told his followers not to do. I have been seeking things of this world, things that are momentary, things that will pass away Things that I was told would be provided for me, that I didn't have to worry about. Therefore, I have not sought first the kingdom of God and his righteousness. As I should be doing during this crisis. I have sinned, I have fallen short I have failed my Savior by not seeking God's kingdom first and setting my affection and my mind on these things as He has promised things above. I confess this to you because it is true, and because you may need to do some confessing yourself. This is where we are all in it together. And maybe I have also bought into the saying That people who are heavenly minded are no earthly good. That saying is supposed to convict us of not caring enough about this life and about the needs, what needs to be done in this life, or the needs of others like the widow, the orphan, the hungry, the homeless. But from Holy Scripture, it sounds like the opposite is true. It sounds like Jesus and Saint Paul have taught that When you set your affection and mind upon heavenly promises, you actually then become more earthly good. And you become more earthly good because what you worry about down here becomes less and less of a concern Because you know what God has provided for you when heaven is your home. And when you care less and less for things of this world, You are not going to hoard. You are likely to practice, not likely to practice your lust of the flesh. You are not so eager to fill up your pantry to protect from that doomsday scenario. Instead, you are more likely to defer to others You're more likely to provide for others. You're more likely to help others because you have nothing to worry about down here because you are just passing through This quote is from C. S. Lewis in his book, Mere Christianity. He says, a continual looking forward to the eternal world is not, as some modern people think. a form of escapism or wishful thinking, but one of the things a Christian is meant to do It does not mean that we are to leave the present world as it is. If you read history, you will find that the Christians who did most for the present world were just those who thought most of the next. The apostles themselves who set on foot the conversion of the Roman Empire, the great men who built up the Middle Ages. The English evangelicals who abolished the slave trade all left their mark on earth precisely because their minds were occupied with heaven. It is since Christians have largely ceased to think of the other world that they become so ineffective in this. Aim at heaven and you will get earth thrown in. Aim at earth, and you will get neither. End quote Considering our current predicament of being under this stay-at-home order, we are to have faith in Jesus Christ. That being heavenly-minded can push out despair. Being heavenly-minded can reduce loneliness. Being heavenly-minded will calm anxiety. Being heavenly-minded can move you closer to heaven itself. Seeking heavenly things and being heavenly minded is a choice to make. It is something we are to seek, something we are to ponder, something we are to care most about. As Christians, we are to live in the resurrection of Jesus. And that means we are to think about a place of promise that allows freedom to love and be loved. In our gospel reading, Peter was only thinking about this world, and it brought about a quick rebuke from Jesus. If you have been like me during this crisis, not thinking about things above, receive this sermon as a rebuke. Think about a place where there is no sin, no pandemic, no unhappiness, no loneliness, no despair. But instead, all that is needed for mind, body, and spirit. May this be our answer, To our children and our children's children and all who had asked of us, how did you make it through that time? May we be able to say, I set my mind on things above. Let us pray. Father, we thank you for this challenge from your word. It is so very applicable to today. Help each of us to set our affections, set our minds on things above Knowing that that is the place you eventually want us to be. Help us, dear Lord. Holy Spirit, help us, we ask. In Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Ordered Worship
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We come back to 1 Corinthians chapter 14, picking up at verse 26. We've been working through 1 Corinthians before the Easter season. We pick up at verse 26, and you will be well served to grab a Bible and walk through with me these verses. I mentioned last week that an advantage for us during this pandemic is to be able to worship with other Christians via the internet. And I have, no doubt, you have been, like me, I have viewed other churches and how they are handling this worshiping online. As I have viewed how other churches and ministers are coping, I have abstained from making any judgments regarding whether they are doing well or poorly, for I accept that all of us are literally making this up as we go and doing the best that we can. But what I have noted is that for some branches of Christ's church, nothing much has changed. For some churches, when congregants could physically attend services, you know, be in the building Their service order was announcements, followed by music, some of it quite loud, but done by talented people. A short prayer followed by a 20-minute sermon, closing prayer, end of service. Other churches sing a few songs, usually contemporary songs. Followed by a 45-minute sermon and then a closing prayer. How someone needs to preach 45 minutes, I don't know, but some do it But what these churches have in common is that their congregations are mere spectators. They are, for the most part, audiences. This has puzzled me because usually these churches are anti-Roman Catholic, and what they fail to understand, or perhaps they simply don't know Is that they are very close to the practice of the Roman church in the Middle Ages. In the Middle Ages, it was common for a local Roman parish to have a chancel screen Which was a large wooden screen or wall or barrier that would cover the entire chancel. The barrier had holes or openings that allowed congregants to view the priests performing ceremony within the chancel where the priests would pray. bless the elements for holy communion, and partake of the bread and wine for themselves as representative for the people. And all of it done in Latin, a language that the priest may or may not have known, with little emphasis on a sermon, and all of this occurring while the congregants were mere spectators. No lay participation was allowed or thought to be necessary. So too, some Protestant churches today treat their parishioners as mere spectators. Whether they are in the building or online. And my point for describing this to you is to provide an observation with a tad bit of criticism, no judgment, no condemnation. Just a tad bit of criticism, because Christian worship should never be a performance for an audience. And that is true even if you think that God is the most important audience member. I will come back to that point later. With this introduction and with our reading from 1 Corinthians 14, no doubt you've concluded that this sermon is about corporate worship. It is. But I'm not going to emphasize liturgical worship like I usually do. Let's first address the several questions that most people have when reading this section of scripture. First, a general question What was going on in the worship service of these Corinthian Christians? The simple answer is confusion. There was no order to their worship. The primary message of this passage is that God desires to be worshipped in an orderly manner. That's verse 40, verifying that point. Apparently the confusion was caused because people were speaking, praying, prophesying, speaking in tongues at the same time, or at least just two people doing two different things at the same time. It is not difficult to imagine how confusing that would be for a congregate to wonder where they should place their attention. Another question is about the tongues mention. What does it mean to speak in tongues? As I said a few weeks ago, the last time we heard from this letter, we talked about this issue. The gift of tongues was the ability to speak in another language a human language without ever being taught that same language. This gift was apparently more common among these Corinthian Christians, as it is not mentioned by Saint Paul in any of his other letters except to Romans and that more briefly. Some say they have the gift today, that again, the tongues I have heard are not languages of men. A language of an of an angel is for another time. I perceive that the gift of tongues can be seen today and those believers who work on translating the scriptures to other languages, and in those who can speak several languages Such is a great advantage when sharing the story of Jesus. The next question may be: why the need for an interpreter? The need for an interpreter is simply to know what the person who is speaking in tongues are saying. Remember, this is in the context of corporate worship. Corporate worship is for the edification of God's people. That is what I was alluding to earlier when I mentioned that God is not to be understood as our only audience when we worship corporately. You have heard me teach and preach many times that it is God who we should be most concerned about regarding our worship. And that is true. And that point is emphasized by me to fight the silliness that is going on in modern worship services. Those services, as I describe, is where the congregants are treated as paying customers who want to be entertained. rather than God's people who are called together to honor him. The point being is that God doesn't need praise, for he is no narcissist No. Instead, we benefit from worshiping him. I know that sounds odd, but it is true, and we will come back to that point. Regarding tongues, the Holy Spirit needed to gift someone to interpret the message that the foreign language-speaking Christian was giving so that all who were present in worship could hear the good news of Jesus being proclaimed. The next question is most likely: why does Saint Paul forbid women to speak? Even saying it is shameful for a woman to speak in a church worship service. This is a tougher question to answer. And it is tougher because Just a few chapters earlier, Paul instructed women that they were to wear head coverings when they pray and prophesy. Well, we all know that you can pray without speaking as you pray in your mind and heart, but you cannot prophesy without speaking. So what is Paul talking about? Well, the context might help, for when he gives women instructions not to speak, it is in the context of people speaking out of turn. And it may have been that some women were interrupting the worship service with clarifying questions that they needed to wait to ask when they were at home. This goes together with the purpose of order. And it tells us for submission. Which I remind us, submission is not a bad word. Another reason for this instruction for women to be silent is the possibility of the church government structure being usurped by certain women who wanted to be elders After all, Corinth was a place where women had influence as a city. The city used statues of women to worship their pagan gods. The lust for women was at a high level because a number of prostitutes in the city served many of the sailors who came to their port. It would be to the shame of the church to allow women to take leadership in the church, for it would mean that the men had abdicated their responsibility. I realize that saying such a thing does not sound right to the modern ears, but it is what the Bible teaches. Finally, I anticipate questions about verse 36 and 38. Take a look at those two verses. You might be asking, why does Paul accuse some Christians of thinking the gospel originated with them, and then tell the ignorant to stay ignorant? The straight answer is that St. Paul was being sarcastic and doing so to put the self-righteous and the stubborn people in their place. Again, I realize that such a rhetorical device as sarcasm is not easily received by modern ears. This is a time, our day and age, of what we can call soft Christianity, which is a Christianity that only wants to hear of God as loving. As comforting, as kind, having no judgment, no condemnation, no sanctifying fire. But God is all of those things and more. Sarcasm and telling people to stay in their ignorance if they are going to insist on seeing things their way Is not heard as godly according to the soft ears of our day. And yet, here it is It is here because those who are faithful will receive the rebuke well, and those who are not faithful will be offended and reject it. Having answered anticipated questions, we now turn to what underlines this section of Scripture. Which is the concern the Apostle Paul had for the Christians to worship rightly. Rightly. And what underlines worshiping rightly is the fact that we as human beings must worship. We must worship This again is hard for modern ears to hear and modern minds to understand. Independent is what we are told we are We think we are free agents who don't need to worship anything if we don't want to. We have convinced ourselves that our worship of God is voluntary. And therefore we can pick it up or lay it down as we please. But let us examine if that is true. Being ordered to stay at home is a vehicle for contributing to other things we might worship. You don't call it worship, but it is worship. Pornography is an example. Online pornography use has gone up since the stay-at-home order has been made. Pornography can be a very addictive force, causing men mostly to bow down to it and serve it. Alcohol consumption is another example of what has gone up during this stay-at-home time. Alcohol and other drugs that allow people to escape into a fog can be a god that insists on our servitude. Such things as pornography and drugs are readily worshipped by many. But of course, there are other examples A person can worship food. People can even worship exercise, computer gaming, gambling, simply looking at their phone over and over again. These are all examples, etc. , etc. , etc. All of these examples are to prove that we are programmed by God to worship. And the only thing that benefits us in worshiping Is the one true God. All other worship destroys us, body and soul destroys us. Let us examine next the idea of our independence. Are we the free agents we think we are? How much power and or freedom do you have to choose your preferred path in life? When I taught philosophy at Stevenson University, I used to put the students through a series of challenging questions about their freedom, the freedom they think they have. There are the simple questions like, are you the height that you want to be? Are your facial features a result of choices you've made? The simple point being that how we look and our physical stature, besides our weight, is determined by genetics and not by our free will. I would next ask a particular student, pick one out, how many universities did you were you accepted to? Let's say the student answered three. I would next ask, well, which of them could you afford? Let's say they answered two. And I would next ask, what was the deciding factor for you to come to Stevenson? And one might say, well, they offered this particular program that no not the other university didn't offer, and so I needed to come here, or I I came here for this particular sport in this particular position that was open. But using just three questions, they would realize they did not have much freedom to not be at Stevenson. And you can't hear saying that they could have chosen not to go to school at all. That is true But what made them want to go to school? What gave them a desire to want to pick that particular major? These things had causes behind them. And perhaps it was their parents that caused them to want this school or want that major or that particular path in life. Or maybe it was just gifts inside that they had or desires that had causes that were not their own. Consider your life and the choices you make. How many options do you have when you make those choices? The cars you drive are determined by, number one, what you can afford. And what you need the vehicle for, and if the vehicle is available. All variables you can't control. Even your spouse was in some ways determined. How many of you had a number of choices to pick out a spouse? Not me. I didn't have a number of women lined up that I got to interview and look them over and decide what I wanted to order for a spouse. In my case, I pursued a girl because I was physically and emotionally attracted to her, and I had to become dependent on her responding to my pursuit. My point is that I was not the determining factor, but neither was Bobby Lynn. There were other factors that neither of us had control over. There is, therefore, a great deal of determinism in our lives, whether we are willing to acknowledge it or not. How much? I do not know. Nobody does. And so we bring these two truths together. We are worshipers by the very nature of being made in the image of God and thus automatic servants of God, whether we want to serve Him or not. And there is a great deal of our lives that is restricted by the variables around us. And no other time in our lives is that more true. Which brings me to my final point, which is that we are to worship God where we are. God has determined for us to be in our homes. And so we need to be worshipers in our homes. Not worshippers of lust of the flesh that are used to distract us, but worshipers of God A God who wants us to embrace the moments that He has given us. St. Paul told the Ephesians, Redeem the time, for the days are evil. We can slightly modify that and say, Redeem the time given to you at home for the days are possibly evil. They are possibly evil and possibly righteous, depending on how they are used. In this time of pandemic, what type of worshiper have you been? How much influence has the news media had in your life over God's Word? If you listen or watch what is called mainstream media, and if they are liberal in their politics They are trying to cause fear within you. Their goal, and don't doubt me, their goal is to have you fearful of the virus. And with that fear convince you that you need to listen to them in order to get through the crisis. They are fear mongers because they are ratings mongers. Rebuke them and get them out of your life. You and I are worshipers of God. We trust in Him. We love Him. We do not fear life or death. We do not fear because of him. Jesus overcame death and fear by being the acceptable sacrifice for our sin, and the grave could not hold him. And it is not going to hold us, we who believe in Jesus. So worship where you are and worship formally every day. Every day. Grab your Bible. Grab your book of common prayer, grab your spouse's hand, and worship God every day. You say you don't have a spouse's hand to grab. Very well. Grab your other hand, fold them together, and allow God to be your comfort. But worship formally. That is what you were made to do. You say you don't have a Book of Common Prayer. Download the Book of Common Prayer. There's an app called I Pray. I Pray. It is a good one because it has all of the Bible readings for each day, including the prayers for the family. That is what Bobby Lynn and I use. Or go to our denomination's website and download the Book of Common Prayer from there. And then pick a time, pick a place, and grab your spouse's hand. And worship formally as in orderly. Do it every day. Such is how you remain heavenly minded. Amen. Let us pray. God, we thank you for this challenge. From the Apostle Paul's words to our current condition, and we see the opportunities before us to do what we are created to do, which is worship you. May each of us redeem this time. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen

sermons.title: Necessity of the Resurrection
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. It is a providential reality and something to celebrate that we are studying 1 Corinthians chapter 15 during the Easter season. Turning your Bibles to 1 Corinthians 15, where our epistle reading came from, begin by talking about pop culture, which is a fascinating phenomenon. Simply Because of how people, items, and behaviors quickly rise to prominence and then just as quickly disappear There are people listening in on this sermon who do not know what a pet rock is or was, and that is a good thing. According to Trend Hunter, the most popular trend for the month of April was non-plastic noodle packaging. where you can buy your top ramen noodles in biodegradable packaging. The second most popular trend was a hand sanitizer made by a company that is best known This information is brought to you by things you don't need to know What popular culture also does is put out false information that is too easily believed. I am referring to comedians and celebrities who will throw out a line regarding what they consider to be factual or a truth, and it is never challenged or rebutted. Specifically, I am referring to statements such as Jesus never existed, or the Bible contradicts itself. Or such stories as Noah and the Ark obviously never happen. I hear such things said in interviews, and the interviewer never counters, never questions Not even asking on what basis, what factual evidence is there for these popular people to say such things? Nothing. And it is so very easy for modern minds to hear such flippant comments about religion and in particular the Christian religion and think, yeah, that's what I figured. And dismiss it altogether. And go on accepting what was said, again, with no factual evidence to back the claim. True historians, however, true historians, as in people who study history, using data that allows them to determine What in history can be verified and what cannot, and what actually can be debunked, those people never doubt the historicity of Jesus. Because evidence of his existence in history fulfills all the necessary checklists for verification And what makes Christianity so compelling is that it goes to great lengths to establish itself in history. This is especially true compared to other religions such as Islam and the false Christian representative such as Mormonism. One very important box to check, to verify that something happened historically is to hear, or in most cases read, the testimonies of those people who were eyewitnesses to the events of the persons being examined. What St. Paul provided in 1 Corinthians chapter 15, after he so brilliantly summarizes the gospel of the Christian faith. He next refers to eyewitnesses who saw Jesus after his resurrection from the dead. Now, I cannot simply refer to in passing Paul's summary of the gospel because it is so brilliantly stated and so very useful. For us to confirm our faith as to what we believe, and also to be a tool that we can share it with non-believers so that they can understand what a Christian believes. And what do Christians believe? Well, as St. Paul says, we believe that Jesus died for our sins just as the Bible describes. We believe his body was buried in a tomb. We believe the grave could not hold him. Thus he was raised from the dead on the third day, which is now called the Lord's Day. And it is called the Lord's Day because he owns that day forevermore. sermons.title: Facing Death
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. Turn in your Bibles to 1 Corinthians chapter 15. Again, seeing God's providence that we are in this chapter during this Easter season, picking up again at verse 20. Our current panic demic, which a phrase my wife coined and I wholeheartedly agree with it, and our current panic demic It has given us opportunity for deeper reflection in regards to issues of life and death. A few weeks ago I saw a video clip of an older man getting out of a car And the person driving asked if he was sure he wanted to go. I assumed he was going to a store. And the man said, if I die, I die. Well you can't argue with that. But I admire such simplicity of thought. Life in this world automatically means death That is the way of it. A governor of a nearby state, no names need to be used, was asked whether there was clear justification for all of the stringent restrictions he was placing upon the state's citizens, considering the financial and mental toll it was taking on people. And his answer was It's either the restrictions or death. And what's worse than death? Nothing. Nothing is worse than death. Well, let's examine that statement. First, the stringent restrictions versus death scenario is a bifurcation, a logical fallacy, for it allows for only two options and there are many more Second and most importantly, we must point out that there are plenty of things worse than death Just from a humanistic perspective, we can point out that elongated suffering can be worse than death. The founding fathers of this country thought that not having liberty was worse than death And we Christians know that unbelief, rebellion against God, being enslaved to sin, and eternal fire are all worse than death So the answer is yes, there are things worse than death. What this panicemic has revealed is that Western societies, once steeped in Judeo-Christian ethics, have not only thrown off a biblical sense of morality, but have lost the ability to face death. And not run scared. What we are seeing around us is people, a great mass of people, and their leaders who are afraid to die. Are you afraid to die? We'll come back to that question. Let us look at our text. And answer some important questions that easily arise from these verses. In verse 20, there is a mention of first fruits. First fruits is a phrase that comes from the Old Testament as it refers to a command of God that the Israelites were to give the first fruits of their crops and the firstborn of their flocks as offerings to God. The offerings were a statement of faith that said that the first yield was owed to God with the trust, with the faith, that God would provide for what comes after. Well, Jesus is the first fruit of the resurrection, becoming a promise that God would bring forth More fruit later. And what comes later is that all who believe that Jesus is God, all of them will be raised from the dead. This is why we say in our confession that we believe in the resurrection of the dead. First the resurrection of Jesus, and then our own, which is to come. The mention of Adam next is to verify how God's kingdom works. In Adam, all of mankind sinned. Well, some have wondered that if that is true and Jesus was born into the human race, how come he did not inherit a sinful nature like the rest of us did from Adam? The answer to that inquiry is in here. For St. Paul explains that God is a God of covenant. The covenant of Adam was marked as guilty and dead because our covenant had Adam sinned. Jesus was sent to establish a new covenant, making him a new Adam, who was sinless and yet fully human. Making him the perfect sacrifice so that all who believe in him could come under his covenant, being found forgiven of sin, and therefore righteous before the Heavenly Father. The authority Jesus has been given is described in verses 24 and 25 Reminding us of that wonderful chapter in the second chapter of Philippians, where we are told that at the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, every tongue confess, that Jesus is Lord. What he is doing even now and has been doing since his ascension, and will continue to do until the devil is thrown into the lake of fire. He is fighting the spiritual battle so that on the that final day all of his enemies, all of them will be placed under his feet, meaning that they will no longer be able to tempt, they will no longer be able to sin Or destroy. And that final enemy, death, will also be destroyed because the devil will be destroyed. So will sin be destroyed, and thus so will death be destroyed. In verse 27, there is a clarification that although Jesus will have all things placed under his feet for judgment The one who puts it there, the Heavenly Father, he will be an exception. He will not be under the feet of Jesus. That God will be all in all, as stated in verse 28, is a reference to the mystery of God the Father and God the Son being two persons and yet one God. The greatest mystery of this section of Scripture is in verse 29, where it describes the baptism or the baptizing for the dead. We are only able to speculate what was occurring, and it may have been a similar practice to what the Mormon religion does. which is baptize living people in order to save or have the sins forgiven of those who have already died. Paul doesn't tell us what the practice was or why it was, but only uses it to say that those who are arguing that there is no resurrection of the dead and then practicing Baptizing for the dead are behaving incongruently. It is the simple rhetorical question: what's the point? Well, the point made in verses 30 through 32 is similar to what was preached last week, which was looking at the life of Paul. and recognizing his remarkable sacrifice in life for the sake of the gospel of Jesus, and identifying it as remarkably foolish if Jesus is not raised from the dead. Again, recognize sarcasm by Saint Paul as he rightly reasons That if there is no resurrection, that all of his suffering in this life and all of his refusal to express his lusts of the flesh, they provide now no advantage. One could and should simply eat and drink and do whatever the flesh desires because death is certain and nothing comes after. The warnings in verses 33 and 34 describe what occurs when a belief in the resurrection of the dead is abandoned. It is natural for a person who does not believe in the resurrection of the dead to conclude that their behavior Their lifestyle in this life has no consequences beyond this life. Those who were denying the resurrection were corrupting others And even though they said that they had a knowledge of God, the denial of the resurrection, and their corrupting lifestyle, well, they were their shame. They should have known better. Without a belief in the resurrection of the dead Non-believers come up with various ideas of what they think happens to a person after death. There is a belief in reincarnation, where the soul of a person takes on or is inserted into another bodily life form to continue on infinitum. In the philosophy of Plato, he taught that the soul of a human being travels and makes choices regarding what it wants to embody. Various beliefs in reincarnation can be seen in Eastern religions and North and South American nativism. Conjectures and speculations regarding an afterlife for the human soul is necessitated by an accepted understanding that human beings have an essence An essence that goes beyond their physical presence. In ancient Greece, there was a legendary king Named Theseus, excuse me, who supposedly founded the city of Athens, Since he fought many naval battles, the people of Athens dedicated a memorial in his honor by preserving his ship in one of their ports. This ship of Theseus stayed there for hundreds of years. As time went on, some of the wooden planks of Theseus' ship started rotting away. To keep the ship nice and complete, the rotting planks were replaced with new planks made of the same material. And here is the key question. If you replace one of the planks, is it still the same ship of Theseus? You see, for philosophy it's a question of identity It asks that if something changes, does it maintain its original identity? Visitors to the ship treated it as if it was original, its identity. And while the issue of identity is interesting, I think it reveals how things, especially people, have an essence to them that is strictly their own, your own. We are told that every cell in our body changes every seven years, and yet we maintain an essence, an identity that is our own, like no one else. Such an essence is also referred to as a soul. It is who a person is. It is not confined to the body. Thus, when the body dies, which it will, there must be a place for the soul to go. And so the human mind comes up with different answers as to where the soul may go, except atheists. But the atheists are a troubled people, for they don't want to acknowledge a soul that will live on, and yet they explain, seemingly all of them explain. That how they will live on is in the memories and in the emotions of those that loved them But how can they live on in the memories of others if, as they say, they will no longer exist? No one can have a memory or emotion about something that doesn't exist Of course, their decaying body is one way that they will continue to exist. But they don't have any other language to describe what will happen to them. To their essence, to their soul, after they die, other than to say they will simply no longer be. What St. Paul is acknowledging while imagining that Jesus is not raised is what is called nihilism, which concludes that nothing in this world has a true existence. Therefore, nothing in this world has a true or important meaning. Therefore, nothing that we do matters. Therefore Do whatever you want. Eat and drink, for tomorrow you die. Atheists argue veheminently against necessary nihilism, insisting that ethical and moral standards can be upheld and followed because of simple observation and coming to conclusions. They can observe, they say, that treating others as you want to be treated is a maxim that works and therefore should be embraced by all. They don't need the Bible or religious teaching to come up with such conclusions. But of course, such a maxim does come directly from the Bible. And it is based on the revelation that every human being is made in the image of God, and therefore is to be treated as an image of God. And as images of God, we cannot simply no longer exist, but we must continue, even after death, the death of our body. The only question is, where do we continue to exist? St. Paul will explain at the end of the chapter. What it will be like for our souls to be rejoined with heavenly bodies, and we will get to that next week. What I am concerned about for us Is are we confident about our souls after death regarding where they will be, which is either with Jesus or with the devil and his angels? Having a fear of death and being a Christian can seem inconsistent and even hypocritical. But fearing death has its degrees. What we most fear is the unknown. I have been asked many times in my pastoral role, what happens to Christians after we die? Well, there is no clear answer to that question. We have Jesus describing the death of another man named Lazarus, not the one he raised from the dead, another man named Lazarus, and a rich man. Lazarus was faithful to God in this life, although he suffered from disease and poverty. He was rewarded by being comforted in the bosom of Abraham. Whatever that is, it sounds very comfortable. And the rich man was sent to a place of torment for living a life of selfishness and pride. The two places are separated by a great chasm, and they can be seen by each other. Jesus also taught that those who die having faith in him will be immediately with him Although in soul only, as we wait for the second coming and our new heavenly bodies, that is about as much as we can know. It is only after the second coming of Jesus and our own resurrection from the dead that we will experience the fullness of heaven, a new heaven, and a new earth. And no, we will not be angels, and no one becomes an angel after death, regardless of how angelic we think the person was in this life. So what we fear is likely what we don't know. And so we deal with our fear, having faith in what we hope for but cannot see. And there is another way with dealing with the fear of death. I asked Bobby Lynn, what she would do if she knew that her death was imminent She said she would make sure she was in right relationship with God and with her fellow man. That is a great answer. It reminded me of a country song some years ago by Tim McGraw titled Live Like You Were Dying For in that song he talks about reading the good book and giving forgiveness that he had been denying. And so Bobby Lynn and Tim McGraw agree. But what does St. Paul say? Go back with me to verse 31 of chapter 15, verse 31. It reads, I affirm by the boasting in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die daily. What does it mean to die daily? It must mean at least that we assure that we are in right relationship with God and with our fellow man. What else would Jesus have meant when he told his followers to pick up their cross daily and follow him? And what else does it mean for us to die daily other than to love God with all of our heart, soul, mind, and strength, and to love our neighbor as ourselves? Like many of you, every day I read the news headlines and I read all of the New positive tests for the virus and the new death count for the virus I believe to focus our headlines on these numbers is to fear death. Let's do something different. Regarding all death around the globe, for whatever reason, statistically, what is called the crude death rate That crude death rate presently sits at seven point seven people dying for every thousand people dying. Say that wrong. 7. 7 people dying for every thousand people living in a year. That is point zero zero seven percent of the world's population die each year. That doesn't sound like much, however, in 2019 the world population was 7,577,130,400. 0. 0077% of 7,577,130,400 is near 58 million people in the world who die each year. Fifty-eight million. About two point nine million of those people are citizens of the United States. I suggest that instead of just reporting how many people have died from this current virus, That news outlets report every day how many people die all over the world for various reasons. That should be a headline every day We would look at that every day and be reminded that we are all going to die. I am reminded of a quote by a previous Surgeon General under President Clinton, Jocelyn Elders, who When testifying before Congress about the danger of the AIDS epidemic, she said, quote, we all will probably die with something sooner or later. End quote. Yes, we will. Yes, we will. And the best way the Bible teaches us to face that reality is to have already died. And the best way to have already died is to die daily Remember the words of St. Paul: it is no longer I that live, but Christ Jesus that lives in me. And the life I now live, I live for Him. Panicdemic or not, let these words be ours. If anyone asks us, Aren't you afraid to die? Our answer, I already have. Let us pray Our Father, there is so much sobering truth in the reality of our mortality. And we want to be a people who do not run scared, but ever trust and have faith. That you overcame death so that we can overcome death. Father, cast out any fears that we have. Help us to die daily. And to realize there's no reason to fear, for we have died and Christ lives in us. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: A New and Better Country
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. I do confess to you that this is a bit surreal for me right now. And um got a little bit choked up singing that first hymn together. Turn with me if you would to 1 Corinthians chapter 15. We're picking up at verse 35. And we're starting off with the question, what is heaven going to be like? Whenever any of us pose such a question, we shouldn't expect a succinct answer Curiosity regarding the itinerary and topography of heaven, including our own physical characteristics as in what will we look like? Causes wonder for Christians of of all ages, of all stages of life. The young seem to enjoy allowing their imaginations to run fanciful as they dream of a world. similar to what they know, but much more grand in beauty and in scope. Fun is envisioned in abundance and the imagination can take us where we want to go. When we get slightly older, say in our teen years, we become a little bit more cynical about heaven. The anticipated itinerary in heaven resembles the average emotional state of a teenager, which is up and down. Their activities are either really exciting or really boring. Heaven then is thought of as something that is likely boring. making it a bit of a downer as they imagine that there will not be really anything fun to do The fear is that heaven will be like a church worship service with mellow music, lengthy teaching, with a lot of sitting and standing. Some churches have tried to overcompensate this attitude, making church exciting with contemporary music and pastors who present something that looks like a TED talk rather than a sermon. Modern Christian music has been compared to those knockoff colognes you get at a discount store. It's not good, but it smells Anticipating heaven to be boring reveals we need a greater understanding of our sin And a greater understanding of the mercies of God, and how privileged we are to know Him, to call upon Him. As we mature into adulthood, our inquisitive thoughts of heaven evolve into looking at the subject more from a relational view. We think of the joy of standing before Almighty God, where we can marvel at His majesty and learn from His depth. We can see ourselves hugging, yes, literally hugging Jesus, seeing him face to face, and at least being able to say, thank you. The older we get means the more feeble we get, and that leads to us looking at passages like 1 Corinthians 15 in order to see what our new bodies will be like. The older we get, we become like children, as our imaginations ask such questions as, what will I look like? Will others recognize me, and will I recognize others? Approximately what age will I be? And a more important question to some is, will I have to go number two? Now, that curiosity I realize is not feminine, but I guarantee you the masculine side does wonder, is that necessary? Well let's see if St. Paul has any answers for us. Thus far in the 15th chapter, the apostle has established well the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead. Where he steers the discussion now is toward helping the curiosity of the Corinthians while at the same time keeping a sense of mystery. We get an idea that we will recognize others and be recognized ourselves, yet it appears that the age of our bodies will not be an issue because the material for which our bodies are made Is has no ability to show where. And plus, age is a reference of time And time will be no more, as it is a part of the created order that will have passed away. The fact that we will inherit new bodies is fascinating in terms of living eternally, and yet it should be noted that the idea would be contrary to Greek culture with which the Corinthians lived. Corinth was a hub of Greek culture, and in Greek philosophy the soul of a person was thought to be eternal, while the body is temporal. At death, the soul is believed to be escaping its prison, which is the human body, and better able to be a truer form, a truer form of itself. In verses thirty-five through forty-four, the apostle gets in the face of Greek thinking. By stating what is doubted is easily understood. Christianity, true biblical Christianity that believes what the Bible teaches. gets in the face of every culture of every age. In the past, missionaries have been maligned for appearing to promote the Western culture. Just as stridently as they're promoting the gospel of Jesus. And while that may be true in some cases, it is also true That if the gospel is brought to a culture that allows, say, men to take many wives and to steal other people's property without penalty To lie under oath and to be rewarded for laziness? The message of the gospel is going to contradict such behaviors. and call them out as sin, sin to be turned away from. The more people that believe the gospel, the more the culture of those same people is going to change. The Western culture changed for the better because the gospel of Jesus was embraced by so many people. And we still see the residuals of that Christian influence today, although distorted. Do not think for a second that the Greek culture would have been concerned for their elderly in a time of pestilence and famine. It is the gospel of Jesus that teaches humanity to care for the most vulnerable among us. Today the devil has turned the care of the least among us into a self-righteousness where governors and other politician leader, political leaders are trying to out care other governors and leaders to show how much more they love their citizens as compared to other governors and other political leaders. And personally, I would praise such love if it also applied to the unborn. Beloved, we can pray that God would relieve us of this panicdemic, and He will likely But until we as a nation condemn abortion, we are in no position to ask God to do anything for our nation. That is a road of confrontation that we must go down, for it is an egregious sin that is haunting us. And the points made in this section of Scripture take the existence of new bodies as a natural occurrence. And they do so as if the listeners should know better. Paul is saying, don't you know that what you sow you will reap? And don't you know that God will do as he pleases? And don't you know that there will be a certain type of flesh that is incorruptible? Don't you know all of that? Well now you do. Except we we really don't, because we do see through the glass dimly, we de we are on this side of the sun. The flesh we now have is the flesh we know, and it is difficult to divorce our thoughts from anything else. By referring to the flesh of men as compared to the animals and reminding the Corinthians of the glory of the new heavenly bodies. The apostle is stating that the resurrection of the body will be of a genuinely human type, as it is not the body of some different order of being. Remember that when God created the universe, including humanity, he looked upon it all and called it good. A main difference, however, is that with sin brought weakness and limitations on the human body. And those limitations with our new bodies will be no more. The new body will be immortal, glorious, powerful, spiritual, which seems to mean that it will be animated and empowered by the Holy Spirit. It will be a supernatural body. In verse 44, the apostle puts two words together that the Greeks would be unfamiliar with and probably repulsed by. This idea of a spiritual body had not been conceived by them. As you recall, to them the body was corrupt. It was temporal. There was was and is nothing to be saved or made new about our bodies. But God brings these two words together. And we can conclude that this was always his plan, a plan for us to have spiritual bodies that would last forever. At creation, God made man being united to his body In fact, chronologically, Adam was a man of flesh before he was a man of spirit. You remember God created him out of the dust. And then after he was created out of the dust, it was then that God breathed into him and made him a living being. At that time, Adam was not considered a person merely housed in a body, but a person who was both body and spirit united forever. When sin entered the world and Adam was no longer allowed to have access to that tree of life, the flesh became susceptible to the elements and to aging. Disease, bodily injuries, and the aging process are all a result of man living in a fallen world. Because of sin, as the Bible says, it is appointed for each person to die once and then judgment. Christians, of course, have a hope beyond that first judgment, and it is the hope that our souls will continue. We rejoice as we should in the midst of our sorrows that loved ones who have fallen asleep in Christ Jesus are with him the very moment they take their last breath. We should not, however, make the mistake of understanding that the salvation of our loved ones and even ourselves has been completed on the day our bodies stop breathing. At that moment, the salvation of God's people is not fully consummated. It will not be completed until the sea gives up the dead and all flesh is resurrected. And the people of God are given new bodies. We must understand that the separation of the soul and the body is an unnatural tearing away. From the flesh, and is not the ideal that God had for humanity. The loss of a loved one by death is painful to all who are left behind And one of the causes of that pain is the inherent uncomfortable feeling we get by gazing upon a lifeless body. Whether the body be very old or very young, one cannot help but realize how difficult it is for the body to not be associated with the soul. To clarify what I am saying, let me emphatically state that all who die in Christ Jesus are with him at the moment of their death, and they continue with him. They too, however, are waiting for that final day when their salvation will be complete and they will be body and soul together forever. To get a glimpse of what our new bodies will be like, we can look to Jesus, as verse 49 states. It says that He is the heavenly man. How the resurrected body of Jesus appeared is a bit of a mystery, for you recall that he first looked like a gardener to the women who showed up at his tomb. The men walking on the road to Emmaus did not recognize him until they rested and sat down and partook of a meal and then saw that it was Jesus. Later, he appeared to his disciples as we read inside a room that was securely locked, implying that he was able to go through walls in some way. And then he revealed himself to all the disciples. He shows them his hands and his wounds. In one moment, when Thomas doubts, he tells Thomas to touch his wounds. We're not told if Thomas ever did. Another moment he tells his disciples not to touch him because he has not yet ascended. What did these instances tell us? A whole lot, and still not enough, to make a composite sketch. In comparison, the ascended and heavenly Jesus is described in the book of Revelation as glorious and humble. He has feet like brass, eyes like fire. He then appears as a lamb that was slain. In the end, he is a rider on a white horse with his garments dipped in blood. None of these pictures is succinct enough to help us understand details of our promised new bodies at the final resurrection. The very least we can say is that they are going to be very much better than the ones we now have. Well, the remaining verses of the chapter are descriptions of victory not yet realized. But they are not too early of a celebration either For the future of sin and death being forever extinguished is the showcase promise of our Savior. And we are to note that the mocking of death with the rhetorical questions as to where is its sting. Is only first to be understood after sin has been fully overcome and forever banished. The sting of death is still real to us. But it is not as real as it could be if we did not have the promises of Jesus that we will be with him until we are resurrected and given new bodies. I summarized the final verses because I want to get to what many of us need, which is a description of heaven, where we are going. Excuse me. The best possible description I have read, besides the streets of gold, Jesus gave to us. The best description I have read is from The Last Battle, which is the final book of the Chronicles of Narnia series by C. S. Lewis. Before I use his description, we need to hear a qualifier. When C. S.
