Lewis was asked if he thought heaven would be close to how he describes it in his writings He said this, no, I don't wish I knew what heaven was like, because if we knew that, we should know it was no better. The good thing, good things even of this world are far too good ever to be reached by imagination. Even the common orange, you know, no one could have imagined it before he tasted it. How much less heaven! And so we recognize such a sentiment as a very important point Lewis believed that the sky and stars above are used in Scripture to cause us to picture heaven as above and beyond us. It is why mountains are used so freely in Lewis's Chronicles. He wants us to look up. The following is a paraphrase of an article written by Professor Peter Shackle of Hope College. He says, in the last battle, forces of King Tyrion, with the two children, Eustace and Jill, among them. Are going against impossible odds, nearing the battle's end as the Calamarines begin seizing Narnians and throwing them into a stable Thinking they were giving them as sacrifices to their fearsome God Tash. The door, however, becomes a symbol of death and a portal to another world. When the Narnians go through it, they find themselves not in a smelly, dark stable, but in a huge land of light and joy. It is a place of youth, as Jill puts it. The professor and Aunt Polly aren't much older than we are here. Of health, Edmund's knee ceases to be sore, and the professor suddenly feels unstiffened. Of abundance, they have crowns on their heads and are in glittering clothes. And of freedom, it feels like, quote, the country where everything is allowed. And it is a place of beauty and of bounty. They see groves of trees thick with leaves, and under every leaf there peeps out the rich colours of fruits. Quote, such as no one has seen in our world. Fruits compared in our world, where we are now, are the freshest of grapefruits you've ever eaten are actually dull, and the juiciest orange is actually dry. There is in Oslin's country heaven, but only on the outskirts They need to travel further up and further in to reach the deep heaven. That description is often repeated further up and further in. As they go, traveling higher into the mountains, things began to look familiar. They see all the old places they loved in Narnia. And the old professor from the first book explains it all in Platonic terms. He said, Listen, Peter, when Aslan, the Christ-like figure. Said you could never go back to Narnia. He meant the Narnia you were thinking of. But that was not the real Narnia. That had a beginning and an end. It was only a shadow or a copy of the real Narnia, which was always and has always been here and always will be here just as our own world. England and all is only a shadow or copy of something in Oslan's real world. After trying his best to say what it was like, the narrator confesses he can't describe it, saying You can't grasp fully what it is like unless you get to that country and experience it for yourself Most of all, it is a place where those who love and long for love, Aslan, the Christ, find fulfillment. Soon entering Narnia, Tyrion sees a brightness and turns around. Quote, there stood his heart's desire, huge and real, the golden lion, Aslan himself. In the words of Jewel, the unicorn, quote, I have come home at last. This is my real country. I belong here. This is the land I have been looking for all my life, though I never knew it till now. Those who have a deep desire for Narnia and for Osman discover that they now have found both. Lewis again holds the prospect out before the reader enticingly. Quote, I can't describe it any better than that. If ever you get there, you will know what I mean. Dear Lord Jesus, help us all get there. Amen. Let us pray. Our Father, by these descriptions, may our hearts not grow weary. But may we be enticed. May we increase our hope. May we more and more let go of a fear of death and trust in you for all of our days. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen. As stated, we are not going to be taking the offering as we usually do. We are going to take a short time to prepare the table and then the ushers will be dismissing you. Again, be mindful that you will come up to the right on the right side as they dismiss you.

sermons.title: Removing what is Obscuring
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We're in First Corinthians chapter sixteen I begin by complaining that it's difficult to believe that we are still struggling with telemarketers. Telemarketers are still calling us, even now that we have cell phones, no longer the home phones that everybody used together as a whole family. No, we have individual phones and they're still getting away with calling us and bothering us and trying to get us to buy their products. And it shouldn't be happening. After all we we have caller ID, and if you don't recognize the number, you don't have to answer it. And so we should be able to not have people calling us, and yet they still do. And telemarketing has become more and more ingenious because somehow They know what numbers you answer and which ones you don't. For instance, anytime I see a number from New Jersey Or Grand Prairie, Texas, I have to answer those numbers because New Jersey is usually Bishop Gillen and Grand Prairie, Texas is usually Bishop Sutton So I have to answer these phone calls, and it amazed me that the after I answered my first phone call from Bishop Sutton from Grand Prairie, Texas. I then received phone calls from telemarketers from Grand Prairie, Texas. That's amazing. How do they do that? The telemarketers also continue to make the same mistakes. They don't listen to you. I answer the phone like this. Hello, this is Eric. And what do I hear on the other end? A pause, a click, and then, hello, I'm looking to speak with Eric Jorgensen. I just said this was Eric. They are not paying attention and you get to realize with the clicking sound and the delay that they're making many, many phone calls And that you just happen to be the stupid one to pick up. And so now they're getting to talk to you. And if you don't pick up, they're calling somebody else. Telemarketers have ulterior motives. They're not there to talk to you about how you're doing. They don't care about your current health situation. All they care about is to sell you on whatever product they are assigned to sell. Ulterior motives. It is Aristotle who told us that there are three Primary types of friendships. And each of them, at least the first two, have ulterior motives The first type of friendship is based on what he called utility. Another is based on pleasure or delight. And the third one is based on virtue. It is the one based on utility that is, first of all, understandable, but second of all can be very painful. Aristotle observed that we make friends with people in a utility or useful manner, such as making friends at work because it makes the work more bearable. Thus we have work friends with people who we might not otherwise care to have a friendship with, but because we are at work and because we're helping each other get through work, we are work friends. I can say also that it's painful because we can discover that a friendship that we thought was based on delight and maybe even virtue. Is actually a friendship in which we are the person being used. Once we are of no use or value to the person we thought was a good friend, The friendship is dissolved and we are emotionally hurt. I have been used in such a manner. And it has hurt a great deal when I found out that I was indeed just being used. I also admit that it's likely that I have used other people, and I pray that God would reveal to me if there's a way I can apologize to anyone in my past that I have used as a friend The point of describing telemarketers and utility friendships is to identify the danger of ulterior motives within relationships and especially within relationships in Christian ministry. When we use the word ulterior in describing relationships, it is usually done in a negative manner. We're likely talking about a person or persons who are hiding a more selfish or sinister reason why they are in the relationship One of the worst and yet most common ulterior motives within the relationship between a Christian minister and a parishioner is based on money. I say it is a worse motive because the ideal that is held before Christian ministers is to follow the life of Jesus, who only gave while not receiving. And followed the life of the Apostle Paul, who worked with his own hands for the support of his ministry, so that no one could accuse him of preaching for the paycheck. And even though these two models are all Christian ministers have to follow, we still have men who claim to be preachers of the Lord Jesus Christ. Who shake down widows and the sick and the go-able for money, that they may keep up lifestyles that are an embarrassment to the Lord Jesus and an embarrassment to his bride, the church. Why people give to these charlatans is beyond my understanding. I just hope none of you are giving, and if you have in the past, I plead that you will do so no more. The Bible cannot be more clear when describing such false teachers, such as St. Peter did in his second letter when he said. Having eyes full of adultery, they never cease from sin, enticing unstable souls Having a heart trained in greed, they are accursed children. St. Paul writing specifically to pastors warned of false teachers who are, quote, Men of depraved mind who are devoid of the truth, these men regard godliness as a means of gain. Those who want to be rich, however, fall into temptation and become ensnared by many foolish and harmful desires and plunge them into ruin and destruction. What more needs to be said except to tap these men and their wives on the shoulder and say, hey, these warnings, they they apply to you. In our text, Saint Paul is talking about collecting money for the saints, for the people of God. And as a side note, I need to point out the charity that Paul exhibits when he calls these Christians saints. A saint is someone who is holy, and if we are honest, we don't act very holy all of the time. We don't act as saints. And if we are honest, not every Christian acts as saints all of the time. Not every Christian lives like a saint, talks like a saint, thinks like a saint. And some in the church may not be believers at all. But Paul calls them all saints. Why? Because Christian love compels him to consider all who profess Jesus as saints until they prove otherwise. It is an example of humility and charity for all of us to follow Before I get upset with another Christian or emotionally disagree with another Christian or am tempted to distrust another Christian, I am first and last to remember that he or she is a saint Remembering that he or she is a saint will change how I interact with my fellow Christian. If I know I am interacting with a saint, I am sure to treat that person differently. Now the history behind this passage is quite simple, although it is never fully spelled out for us, and thus reminds us that we are still reading someone else's mail. What appears to have happened was that after the gospel was preached by St. Peter, as recorded in the book of Acts, 3,000 believers were added to the church. The Holy Spirit poured itself out. It was then that the power of the gospel was so fresh and real. That these new Christians, they created a community where all earthly wealth was shared. I remind you that when the book of Acts describes the first century Christians as having all things in common, There is no evaluation of this new commune as in whether it was good or bad. It simply states it as a fact. They shared all things in common. Nobody comments whether that was a good thing or a bad thing. And many read into the text as if it was a good thing and that maybe Christians should be doing that continually. But the problem of assuming it was good is found in a passage like this in 1 Corinthians 16, where the Christians in Jerusalem, who had all things in common, We're now in financial trouble. They needed financial help for various reasons, and one being That having all things in common is not a sustainable political or financial model As we learn elsewhere in Scripture, a person who wants to eat needs to be a person who puts in a good day's labor. We also learn that Christians cannot use their preparation for Jesus returning to excuse them from work. And we also learn from another letter of St. Paul that a man who does not provide for his own family is to be understood to be worse than an unbeliever. The virtue of hard work is taught throughout Holy Scripture. Having all things in common gives greater opportunities for people who are prone to laziness To take advantage of those who work hard for their daily bread. A common factor that makes socialism and capitalism Broken economic and political models is the sinful nature of each person that makes up that community. Socialism allows for lazy persons to continue in their laziness while also not pursuing the greatest expression of their gifts. While capitalism allows for the greedy to forget the most vulnerable of societies while using them for selfish gain. Socialism crushes the human spirit given to us by God to strive toward excellence, while capitalism necessitates a Christian ethical standard. So that money is not a root of evil. The Christian perspective is the only source that can provide such an analysis in our current political climate, and we need to speak up more and speak out more. What St. Paul has had decided to do was take up a collection of money from the various churches that he visited. And to deliver the collected money as an offering to the Lord by giving it to the Christians in Jerusalem His instruction to the Corinthians was to take the collection on each day, the Lord's day, that they met, until Paul arrived, so that when he arrived, he would not have to ask for any more money. He didn't want to make anything in his relationship with the Corinthians or the Christians at Corinth. He didn't want to make that relationship about money. And we will come back to that point. I need now to make another sidestep, and I'll do this quickly. You remember that the first Christians were Jewish Christians. They worship God on the Sabbath day, the Jewish Sabbath day. They did it in the synagogue and in the temple And then they got together on Sunday to celebrate the resurrection of Jesus. So they worship Saturday and they worship Sunday. On their Sundays, they got together, they heard the word of God spoken that Jesus spoke, they repeated those words, and they gathered together to eat bread and to drink wine. When the church became primarily Gentile in places like the city of Corinth, the majority of Christians did not observe the Jewish Sabbath. They weren't Jewish. So they only honored Jesus, our God, on Sunday. The first day of the week came to be known as the Lord's Day. Thus we worship on Sundays as the first day of the week, the Resurrection Day, the Lord's Day, because that is what the first century Christians did. We do not do it because it was commanded of us. We do it in solidarity with the church historic and the church triumphant. In our tradition, we do not worship in a vacuum, meaning we don't practice our worship as if the church started when we started. We worship with the presence of mind that the Christians who have gone before us are just as important as the Christians of today and just as important as the Christians in the future. They still have a say in what the church is and does. Verse 3 addresses the handling of the money, and Paul is careful once again not to appear to have an ulterior motive in regards to money And so he instructs them to choose their own representative to take the money to these Christians in Jerusalem. And so we come back to the point of Saint Paul doing his best to assure that money does not become a stumbling block in regards to his relationship with the Christians at Corinth. There is a clear teaching in Scripture that the love of money is the root of many evils. It is the gateway drug to greed and covetousness. When money is an idol, it causes you to bow down to it repeatedly as you count it every day. You display it in what you drive, the size of your house, and the manner that you furnish your house In the schools you attend, in the wardrobe you wear, in the quality of food you eat, the clubs you belong to, the socializing that you do, all of it can reflect a love of money. But the Bible could not say more about the dangers of the love of money. And if it did, it would still be ignored by those who have already ignored it. St. Paul's priority is first the gospel, it is last the gospel, in between it is the gospel. Because money can so easily be an ulterior motive to minister in the name of Jesus, Paul stays away from any possible scenario that would associate him with money Instead of with the gospel of Jesus Christ. I could continue to warn about the love of money and the dangers of it being an ulterior motive within Christian ministry. But I need to address what is presently before us. Just as St. Paul avoided the possibility of a distraction like money obscuring the gospel message of Jesus Christ, So too must we avoid issues that would obscure the same gospel. And what the devil is trying to get Christians to focus upon today Is who is responding to the current pandemic responsibly and who is not? Or even now, who's responding to the death of an of a man by brutality of a policeman? Personally, I have my opinions derived from the news sources that I listen to, and my proclivity for examining facts and interpreting them with logic. Which reminds me that those who are touting that we should trust in the science fail to properly categorize science. Science works to test theories and to find consistencies in those tests in order to draw conclusions and to adjust behaviors accordingly. Finding consistencies, drawing conclusions, and adjusting behaviors is using logic. Follow the logic Coming from a logic professor. But my point is that I don't voice my many opinions about this virus. about the news media, and about politicians and their many decisions, because my message must be first and foremost about the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ. And anything that would cause you not to hear that gospel because you don't like my pandemic position, that's a serious problem, and that problem would be my fault. If you are a person that insists that masks should be worn in all public settings, you are likely becoming frustrated by those who are not wearing masks. If you are a person that insists that the requiring of wearing masks in a public setting is an infringement on your constitutional rights You are frustrated by businesses that won't allow you in without a mask, and frustrated by the dirty looks you get by people who think you should be doing what they're doing. And did you hear Thursday the World Health Organization came out and said the only people that should be wearing masks are people who are caring for COVID-19 patients What are we supposed to do? Who are we supposed to listen to? Very frustrating. But let's say you win. Let's say your position wins. Let's say your side wins. Everyone is required to wear a mask at all times when out in public and inside amongst other people. Your side wins. Well, let's take it the other way. No one needs to wear a mask. It's a free-for-all. No one can force another person to wear a mask at any time. Your side wins. Which of these sides, which of these wins helps the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ be heard? That's a rhetorical question. And if you go beyond my reasoning and you say, well, the gospel can't be heard if no one wears a mask and all get sick and all die. Well, that would be a fair response if that was happening, but that is not happening. As Christians, as the Church of Christ, as the body of Christ, the gathering together of the saints We ask you to be precautionary, to care about others around you in response to this virus, not because we know for sure that it helps or that it doesn't help or anything like that It is the receiving from the wisdom of those who say they study this and now don't know again which study is correct. And we adjust our behavior. Why do we adjust our behavior? Because it works? No. We adjust our behavior because we need to preach and hear the gospel. That's why we do it. Because that is our priority, or at least it should be Anything obscuring the gospel, whether it be ulterior motives, like the love of money Or taking a particular political position, or how to respond to a pandemic. None of those, none of those lead you to Christ None of those save your soul. None of those forgive your sins. Consider this. Wearing a mask when you don't think you need to, wearing gloves when you don't think you should have to, limiting your time traveling when you don't think you need to is an ever-present opportunity to die to yourself. These restrictions Allow us to say to our fellow Christians who are struggling, who are in fear, that I care more about my relationship in Christ with you than I do about my constitutional rights. Consider this. Accepting people who do not wear a mask is giving you an opportunity to practice the love of God toward your fellow Christian by enduring By forgiving, by long-suffering. It also teaches you what we have been learning in our study of Ecclesiastes. But there is a great deal we must accept that is beyond our control. Our differences offer us opportunities to practice our Christian morality. Because it is the right thing to do. And because it is the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ that matters most. Paul knew that. And now so do we. Let us pray. Our Father, there's no way that we cannot find ourselves in this message of how easy it is to take sides, to divide, to be angry. To confess other people's sins. And Father, we want to simply say we see our own. And we also see ways in which we can be the love of Christ to others. May we all care first and foremost about the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ. It is in his name that we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Do Not Quit
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We are in First Corinthians chapter sixteen and we are actually coming to the end of the epistle. And while you turn there, I uh will say if you're wondering why did the pastor leave the chancel, Because I looked over and saw that my sermon wasn't here and I don't have it memorized. So I needed to get my sermon. First Corinthians chapter sixteen when I was a sophomore at the University of Idaho, our head football coach at the time. resigned after the season to take the head job at the University of Wyoming. It was a step up for him, oh or so he thought. But to us, to the players equit on us, we were a team. He recruited us to play for him. He made promises to us regarding the team's success with him at the helm. And he quit. It is understandable that the players he left behind would question if there was any sincerity at all in the man who made all of those promises. Did he ever mean what he said to us, or was it all so that he could get another coaching job that paid a lot more? Was he a true Vandal? Vandal is the mascot for the University of Idaho. His quitting proved he was not. I won't say the man's name, but to show his loyalty, he coached at Wyoming for only one year. And without notice took the head job at Washington State. He was there two years until he took the head job at the University of Miami. He then took a job for the Seattle Seahawks, next Oregon State, next the San Francisco 49ers, and again one year at Idaho until he quit on them again and took a job at Arizona State. There is no question that he knew how to coach football and how to quit. What is troubling with people who quit in a similar manner is their motivation. Their motivation appears, and I say appears because I admit I don't know the heart, appears to be only about self. If a leader quits and he or she says it is the best thing for him or her, then there is no doubt that the motivation is self-serving. And if it is difficult for a football team to be disappointed at a coach for quitting on them, how much more is it difficult for a body of believers to have a pastor quit on them? And so you know it is difficult for a pastor when a layperson quits church. I am talking about quitting because I anticipate questions within many of you. And I anticipate these questions because I often have them myself. They are questions such as Is the Christianity that I preach, teach, and strive to live, is it real? And when I ask such questions, I do so knowing well the person that I was before I became a Christian and the person I am now. And I know that the only good that is within me is because of the Lord Jesus Christ. But what troubles me still is how many people have claimed what I have just now claimed about what Jesus did for them and later quit. They quit the faith. They sold out. They gave up. Another aspect of asking a question such as Is it even possible to live the Christian life as the Bible describes it? Another aspect of that question is the disappointment. Of hearing Christian leaders sound a great deal like secular leaders when they try to address contemporary issues. The language they choose and the approach that they take are like warmed leftovers of the secular mind. They sound as if they they don't believe the Christian life is possible to live without political movements, without injustices being highlighted on our television screens These Christian leaders give in saying that the church can't help. They quit They quit using biblical standards and biblical identifiers and instead settle for what the secular mind has decided the standards and the identifiers should be. And so I I do ask questions about whether people truly believe what the Bible claims and what Jesus taught. Just as I stated last week at the beginning of our service, the Bible doesn't use language like racism and social justice. Instead, it warns against sins that go against God's justice, which means the sins that go against his laws. And yes, it is true that oppressing the vulnerable goes against God's laws. God's laws warn against withholding food from the hungry and clothes from the needy. withholding justice from the poor and the wealthy alike, because people are formed in the image of God and they are to be treated as such. God's law goes against withholding justice from a person because of his or her skin color. To treat people in the opposite manner that God requires is to hate. and to hate those made in God's image and thus to hate God. Jesus spoke directly against the sin of hating our fellow man, and he gave us the standard of love, even to love our enemies. He also put warnings that if you were to live by the sword and put your trust in the sword, you would die by that same sword. And he told us to turn the cheek when we are persecuted for his sake, because his good news of offering forgiveness of sin and eternal life to all who would believe in him Was and is more important than any of our cheeks. In days like we are now living, when the world seems to be moving so very quickly to an abyss, that we cannot adjust our minds for what is now accepted or said to be the new normal, we can more easily doubt that our Christian beliefs are still relevant. We are tempted to quit. Consider that in my adolescent days, premarital sex among teenagers was actually rare. Now, virginity is rare. Consider that just a few years ago, men competing in sports as women was thought to be absurd. Now it is defended in our courts of law. Consider how the past few years the subject of abortion was hotly debated and emotionally charged, and today the possibility of infanticide is seen as a defensible progression. Consider that less than a decade ago, many Christians said they believed what the Bible teaches regarding sexual morality. And with a span of a few years, our society tells us the new norm is the opposite. And if we believe what the Bible says regarding sexuality, we are now the haters. We are the oppressors, the bigots, the guilty. So very many Christians have abandoned their biblical standards for what society insists upon. Consider that we want to say that police brutality is wrong, no matter the situation, and that police hatred toward any human being because of race is sin against God. But we are told that we have to say it while also not condemning those who would burn down businesses to the ground and after they take what is not theirs. The Bible condemns both behaviors, but our society, at least through the media, tells us we cannot. As Pastor Doug Wilson stated, we are living in a time when people want to reconcile good and evil, and that can never be. Again, we are tempted to quit. The gospel does not seem relevant to a society that does not want to hear it. These questions, these temptations to doubt, to quit, I was reminded of when reading 1 Corinthians chapter 16, verse 13. In St. Paul's last comments in the letter, we call First Corinthians, he expectedly tries to organize the Christians so that His ministry toward them would continue into the future, even if he was absent for a time. He wants them to know of his plans of being with them in the future, even possibly spending a whole winter with them. But he says the Lord's will for the future is what he trusts in. He wants them to know that there are difficulties ahead, but he is willing to face those difficulties. And he is to remind them of those difficulties when he writes what we call Second Corinthians. They become upset because he didn't get to them as he had once promised. Now he wants them to accept and encourage Timothy, for Timothy was doing the very work Paul was doing and should be treated as Paul was treated. Paul also wanted them to know of his efforts to have Apollos come to them, but Apollos had his own reasons why he could not do so, at least not yet. After all of the instructions about who, when, and where, we then read these words as the Corinthians read them. He says, watch, stand fast in the faith, be brave, be strong, and I add, don't quit So let us do yeoman's work and break down these words of encouragement so that we do not quit Some translations have watch, others stay alert, be alert, be on guard, be vigilant. It is the same Greek word found in the context of Jesus warning about his second coming. Those who watch will be ready. It is also found in the context of Jesus telling Peter, James, and John to watch and pray while he goes to the garden alone. Their watching was to be done in regards to protecting Jesus and protecting themselves spiritually. The word is also found in the book of Revelation, when Jesus says that the people who watch in preparation of his coming, they will be the people he will receive. Thus, to watch in all of these ways is to live the Christian life. We are to be prepared for our Lord to return and receive us while we watch against temptations. For us to be lazy, slothful, and too tired to resist. We are to watch like a watchman who is responsible for the city He is to warn of the coming danger. And from the watchman's warning, we are next told to stand fast. To stand fast is to stand firm, which is not to be moved, not to be moved either by fear or because of physical attack from the enemy. The verb expresses Christian manliness, such as is expressed in the call to play the man. It is a verb for both genders as women also are to play the man. The same meaning is found in Joshua 1, verse 6 Where the Israelites were to be strong and of good courage when they faced their enemies in the promised land. Christians then need not only not to back down But to dig in and fight. We are to fight as if we are the last line of defense, and what we are defending is our very souls and the souls of our loved ones. To stand fast is also to persevere. To persevere is the opposite of giving up. It is to stay in the battle, no matter how many bullets are flying around you, no matter how much how hurt you are or how how tired you are, no matter What your ammunition gauge says, no matter how tired you become, how thirsty you are, how hungry you are, how much you would rather be anywhere else. To persevere is to endure it all and not be moved. And we are to stand fast, to play the man, to persevere in the faith. The faith is in the Lord Jesus Christ. And it consists of trusting, being fully committed to the person of Jesus Christ even when there are seemingly no substances to cling to or convictions to see. Next, we are to be brave, which is to act manly. This is the second time we have used the male gender Now, those who are gender-sensitive in regards to certain adjectives like manly, please be calm. In the Greek world, wars were only fought by men. To be manly was to be brave in the midst of war. The adjective uses the male gender, but the context speaks to all Christians. Christians are to be like men at war who as stated, hold their ground and gain ground also. To be strong is the offensive part of the call. We are to stand our ground and to take some ground as well. And every time the gospel of the Lord Jesus Christ is preached, there is ground being gained. Every time a person hears the gospel and believes, precious, precious ground is being gained. Every time a child is birthed and baptized and raised in the Christian faith, greater and greater ground is being gained. And every time a professing believer gives into a life of sin and is then brought back to new life because of true words spoken by God's saints, more and more ground is gained. There was a woman that I knew several years ago who had a friend over from high school. They shared about what their lives had been like since graduating from high school. My friend had two children and was very involved in her church. Her high school friend was not married, sleeping with several men and experimenting with drugs. My friend told her friend very plainly that she needed to repent and live for Jesus The two women knelt on that living room floor with heads bowed over the sofa on which they had been sitting and prayed for God to forgive her and give her new life in Jesus. The story is so powerful because it was a simple afternoon that resulted in ground being gained for the kingdom of God. It also teaches us that the front line of the battle is anywhere a Christian chooses to stand firm and be strong. Now, if you would look back with me at the text. And notice that verse 13 does not stand alone. It may sound like it could stand alone. Watch, stand fast in the faith, be brave and be strong. That might prepare an army for battle or prepare a team to play hard. But in the Christian world, none of it has lasting meaning if there is not love. Love is what remains. And so we have verse 14 that tells us to do all that we do, that is our watching, our standing fast in the faith, our being brave and strong, all of it is to be done with love. And beloved, this is one reason, a very big reason. I know that Christianity is true and real and can be lived out. Consider how quickly homosexuality has become mainstream in our society, and consider that Christianity is the only faith. The only worldview, the only teaching that can condemn certain sexual behaviors while still loving the people who practice such behavior and love them enough. To help them find forgiveness and give them an identity that goes beyond their sexual desires. God's love is the only thing that does that. Because of the necessity of love, the love of God, and all that we do, only Jesus has the answer to what the secular world calls racism. As I have argued, racism is masked hatred of humanity and of God. And the devil wants to keep such hatred in the political world. So that we can continue only to address the hatred by means of legislation, shaming, pandering, and promising, but never ever address the issue of the human heart. The devil wants to keep it in the streets. The devil wants to keep humanity trying to reconcile good and evil. But it will never be. Jesus wants to change hearts. Another phrase being popularly used today is systemic evil. They say the problem is evil within the system, so we must change the system. That is true on several levels. But beloved, as Christians, we know that the system won't be changed. It won't be any different if it is changed. Without hearts being changed. Because what created the old system and what creates new systems are people with hate-filled hearts. Consider that the people that created Jim Crow laws didn't have a system problem first, they had a heart problem that created an evil system. The people that don't hold police accountable for abuse are part of a system made up of people with a heart problem. And people who are allowed to return evil for evil are part of a system made up of sinners who need the love of Jesus in their hearts. So while others quit, I cannot, because Jesus filled my heart. And I want others who are trapped in hatred and bitterness and strife to know the freedom a Jesus-filled heart gives. This morning I'd like to do something different for closing. I would like you to join me in closing this sermon. By repeating the simple phrase taken from the faithful Joshua, as he took a stand before the people, a people who were ready to quit. You remember that he said this phrase, as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. I ask that you repeat that as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord after each line that I give you. There's just four of them. Excuse me. As men hate as men as men hate men who do not look like them As for me in my house, we will serve the Lord. As people choose looting over protesting and wrath over love As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. As people quit on love, quit on forgiveness, and quit on God. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. As people harden their hearts, refusing to let Jesus in. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. Amen and Amen.

sermons.title: Hard Words Needed
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turning your Bibles to Luke chapter four, we pick up at verse sixteen And we're gonna be going beyond what was read, so uh follow along as you are able. Uh Might sound obvious, but it's not to many. Stating your opinion is not truth telling I find it necessary in marital counseling to remind couples that when you state your opinion, you are not virtuous because you think your opinion is telling truth. When a wife asks her husband if she looks chubby in a particular dress, the husband is not a virtuous truth-teller when he states his opinion that yes, she looks chubby. Neither is a wife a virtuous truth-teller when she tells her husband that she wishes he made more money. While such statements are truth in that they express a person's opinion, they are not objective truth, and they are also not kind and for the man's part not very wise. Which should matter more, being kind and wise. Love, as the scripture says, is kind. In contrast, Jesus didn't confess opinions. He confessed truth. He was true, and what he said was true, and it was objectively true, and it needed to be said. This is the third installment in our series, Thinking Like Jesus. And today we are looking at how Jesus Thought that hard words need to be spoken. Jesus spoke hard words But they were necessary hard words. People needed to hear them. You and I need to hear them, and we need to hear them again and again. Hard words confront. Hard words cause conflict. People get offended by hard words. But hard words give opportunity to change. Stop having sex with that woman who is not your wife. Hard words. They are hard because they address another person's personal behavior. What busin business is it of mine to tell another person to stop committing adultery? None, other than to help stop such a person from going to hell, which is where adulterers go. Hard words again. Addressing the subject of people being judged because of their sin and judged harshly makes people uncomfortable. Some people get uncomfortable even when the charge sin doesn't apply to them. They don't like the confrontation. So they don't like hard words in any form. But soft words don't save. Jesus didn't say to the woman caught in adultery, Go and sin no more, or keep on doing what you desire, it's all the same. Instead, he said, go and sin no more, and he meant it. Sin truly does have consequences, and when a person continues in his or her sin with no repentance, with no forgiveness, then hell is their destination. Hard words. Again, many people don't like hard words. The way modern the modern media presents this current cultural climate, it appears that most people don't like hard words. The same people, they like their own words, of course, but not opposing words. Opposing words are hard words for the sensitive Posing words hurt even before they're uttered. Don't even try, they say. I've been thinking about the manner Jesus responded to political and social uprisings of his day. And there were a lot of them. Barabbas, the man released instead of Jesus, is believed to have been part of a group of rebels who attacked Roman soldiers. The Jews hated Roman occupation of Jerusalem. They hated to pay taxes to Caesar. They hated being treated as second class, for they did not receive justice before the Roman courts unless they were Roman citizens. They hated their Roman occupiers so much that a rebellion took place that led to 1. 1 million. Catch that number. 1. 1 million Jews being killed by the Romans During the siege of Jerusalem, just 40 years after Jesus walked this earth. Jesus saw their anger He saw the anger of his fellow Jews. He heard their disillusionment. He prophesied about the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the temple. But he did nothing to support or discourage the rebellion. And why do you think that was? It was because he was about his father's business. It was because he was commissioned by the Heavenly Father to speak hard words about the kingdom of God. And that is what he did. In our text, Jesus has come back from the desert, having been tempted in all ways by the devil, and having not sinned, he comes back to Nazareth. The town in which he was raised. His custom was to attend services at the local synagogue. He went to church. It was his custom. It was what he did on a scheduled basis. Whether he was asked to read or whether it was his turn to read or whether he was a regular reader, we don't know. We're not told. But in the service, he read the holy scriptures, which is what was done and is still done in the synagogue. He chose a passage that day, and it was a passage from Isaiah chapter 61, verses 1 and 2. The passage Sounds like a personal statement by Isaiah speaking about himself. Jesus reads it and sits down. Now don't put our present setup in your mental image of that scene. Jesus didn't read and then go back and sit in a pew. Synagogues were made with a table or podium to place the sacred scrolls and to read them, and next to that setup To the side was a seat called the seat of Moses, a chair called the seat of Moses. It was from there that a teacher would teach in reference to the text read. Jesus sat down at the seat of Moses in the synagogue that he frequented in his hometown, and he said, Today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing. His clear meaning is that Isaiah was talking about him. He also went on teaching. And we can infer this by the for the text says that the people marveled at the gracious words that came out of his mouth. Well, let us look more closely to the words from Isaiah that describe Jesus. We are told that the Spirit is upon him. He was particularly anointed for the particular task of preaching, teaching, and sacrificing. It was his task alone, and he was empowered by the third person of the Trinity to do it. Jesus was anointed to preach the good news of his offered forgiveness of sin and the promise of eternal life in heaven to the poor. The poor were the least respected in both Jewish and Roman communities. The poor were the humble. They were poor in spirit as well as pocket money. They knew they needed a Savior, and Jesus wanted them to be his disciples. Jesus also came to heal the brokenhearted. The brokenhearted are also humble. They too know that they need a savior, for the world has been harsh on them. They don't know where to turn for help. Jesus offers his love, his forgiveness, his hope to them. He and he only can heal them from their brokenness. The captives. The captives are those caught in sin. They cannot free themselves. They are the addicts. They are the desperate. They are the deceived. They think their sinful lifestyle is their only choice. Jesus came to them so that they could be free from the lies that they have believed. Then there are the blind, and there are the literal blind. And we know Jesus healed blind people. But the blind are also those who don't see their sin. They are the older sibling in the parable of the prodigal son, which was so well preached last week. They think they are in good standing before God, but they are deceived. Jesus came to help them see the truth, and for them to respond to the truth by way of repentance and having faith in Him as their Savior. Then there are the oppressed. That may be a reference to a political concern by Jesus. But no. No. Jesus recognized that there were people in his day that were politically oppressed, no question. But his answer for them was that they could find liberty in having faith and trust in him Rather than in a political system, Jesus has set many a person free in spirit and in truth who remained politically oppressed. Finally, Jesus was present at the acceptable year of the Lord. It was the year that God had chosen to reveal himself in the person of Jesus. It was a time like no other. It was a time to be seized. At first, as is described, the people in the synagogue took kindly to the teachings of Jesus, but it didn't last. He started on hard words. What those exact words were, we are not told, but the response of the people reveals that they were hard words. They started to say to one another, hey. Isn't this guy the same guy we see each Saturday who comes from a lower-class family who is just like us? Certainly no better. Who is he to be teaching in this manner? What authority does he have that we do not have to interpret the sacred texts? Jesus sees the change in the people. He knows their hearts, and so he addresses it. He says hard words. He continues to speak hard words that address the heart condition of the people. They wanted miracle proof. But even with miracles, they would not believe. The situation was a proverb being lived out. Those closest to a prophet, those who have known him since he was a young lad, they cannot accept that God has called him to a greater task. They only see a little boy with a runny nose. And so they reject him. Jesus accepted this, but not without warning. He continued with hard words. He warned them of their foolish ways by way of example in the sacred text, where Elijah is said to have chosen one widow instead of the possible many to know the truth about his power. And then there was Elisha, who healed but only one leper, because the rest did not believe and obey. Such is the case with so very, very many people who have heard the truth over so many years since the days of Jesus. But do not, did not believe. Well, the warning given by Jesus was not received well The synagogue gathering turned into a broo-ha-ha as they drove Jesus out of the meeting house and tried to throw him off a cliff. All because of hard words. But it was not the time for Jesus to die. There were more hard words that need to be spoken. So he was able to free himself from them and walk past them by the power of God. Jesus thought it important to speak hard words. He said that we are to be holy as his heavenly father is holy. Hard words. Hard standard. Who can live up to that? No one by themselves. Only in Jesus can we be holy. Jesus said that lust and hate begin in the heart. Hard words. If they begin in the heart, they are a product of us. And thus, when we commit sin, we are responsible. We need clean hearts. We can only have clean hearts if the blood of Jesus cleans them. Jesus said to his followers, You must hate your father and mother and brother and sister, wife and children, yes, even your own life. Hard words. But Jesus knows how easily we humans can place anything and everything in front of God. Unless we are conscientiously putting him first, we will repeatedly break the first commandment. Too many parents have adjusted their morality based on the behavior of the lifestyle of their children. That is what happens when you don't love God first. Hard words, but true words. Words that need to be spoken, heard, and lived Gay is not okay when your son or daughter or friends say they are gay. Hard words. Fornication is not okay when your son wants to move in with his girlfriend. Hard words. Truth does not become subjective because your daughter took a class in philosophy while away at college, and now you have to accept her brainwashed, woke ideas in order to have a relationship with her. More hard words. You ask, why do I focus on parent and child relationships from the hard words of Jesus? It is because I know too many stories. Jesus said the first must be last and the last first. He said the same thing when he said that his followers must pick up their own cross and follow him. He said the same thing when he said that a person who tries to save his own life will lose it, and that a person who tries to lose his life will find it in the end. Hard words. But such words don't match the spirit of our age. Such words go against being told to get what is yours. Or to do what is best for you, or that your earthly happiness is what is most important. Hard words. Jesus said to Peter, get thee behind me, Satan. Hard words. Personal hard words. But Peter was only trying to prevent Jesus from getting harmed. Peter had good intentions. No. No. Peter had earthly intentions. Peter said what his emotions told him to say. Peter became a mouthpiece for the devil when he wanted to preserve Jesus in this life, in exchange for what Jesus would accomplish for eternal life. The hard words of Jesus snapped Peter out of the fog of only considering this life as opposed to the life to come. What words? What words does Jesus need to speak to you to snap you out of your concern to preserve this life as opposed to the life to come? Whatever those words are, they are hard words, and they are needed words. To think like Jesus, we need to receive hard words. Jesus said, Many are called, but few are chosen. He said the same when he said that the road to hell is wide and many travel on it. While the road to heaven is narrow with few traveling on it. Hard words. It is much easier to think of the gospel of Jesus as free love and wide roads and easy travel. But no. It is a road that few travel upon because it takes great courage, sacrifice, and faith, because the rewards in this life are few. To think like Jesus, you have to have faith that everything you give up in this life will be rewarded for eternity, with no earthly evidential proof of it being true. Well, no proof that we presently see. I started this sermon addressing the subject of opinions not being objective truth. I did so because with the hard words of Jesus we could interpret and apply what he said like a Pharisee would. We could treat his hard words as if they are specific laws that must be followed. But the hard words of Jesus Are not regulations such as not being able to walk past half a mile on the Sabbath? They're words that look to govern the heart. Only you and God know whether you are lusting, hating, coveting, or loving your children more than God. Only you and God know if you believe without seeing and have hope without knowing. To think like Jesus. We have to want to hear hard words. We need to want to obey hard words. We need to want the preacher to say hard words. And we need to want to say them ourselves if given the opportunity. No, there is no guarantee that people will believe the hard words that you say Many more people have rejected the hard words of Jesus than have accepted them. That truth is also a hard word. But the words still need to be said and still need to be received by us. So let us think like Jesus. Wanting to hear, wanting to receive, wanting to speak hard words. For the kingdom of God, the kingdom of God is at hand. Let us pray. Our God, we are humbled by the reality that for all of us There are hard words to take, hard words to hear, hard words to process, and yet we want to think like Jesus. We want to receive them, we want to hear them, we want to obey them. Father, help our weaknesses, help our unbelief. I pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Forgiveness as Priority
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen may be seated. Cornelia Arnolda Joanna Corey Ten Boom He was born the 15th of April, 1892, died the 15th of April, nineteen eighty-three. She was a Dutch Christian watchmaker and later a writer who worked with her father, Caspar Tenboom, her sister Betsy Tenboom, and other family members To help many Jews escape the Nazis from the Holocaust during World War II by hiding them in her home. She believed her actions were following the will of God. They were caught, and she was arrested and sent to Robinsbrook concentration camp. By evidential providence, God, of God, by the evidential providence of God, she was released from said camp because of a clerical error. Shortly before, all the women of that camp were sent to the gas chambers. After the war, Corey Tenboom was invited several places to share her story, and many people came to hear her speak. The following are her words. It was in a church in Munich where I was speaking in 1947 that I saw him, a balding. Heavy-set man in a gray overcoat, a brown felt hat clutched between his hands. One moment I saw the overcoat and the brown hat. The next A blue uniform, a visored cap with its skull and crossbones. Memories of the concentration camp came back with a rush. The huge room with its harsh overhead lights, the pathetic pile of dresses and shoes in the center of the floor. The shame of walking naked past this man, I could see my sister's frail form ahead of me, ribs sharp beneath the parchment of skin Betsy and I had been arrested for concealing Jews in our home during the Nazi occupation of Holland. This man had been a guard at Robinsbrook concentration camp where we were sent. Now he was in front of me, hand thrust out, he spoke. A fine message, Fralein. How good it is to know that, as you say, all our sins are at the bottom of the sea. It was the first time since my release that I had been face to face with one of my captors, and my blood seemed to freeze. You mentioned Robinsbrook in your talk, he was saying. I was a guard there, but since that time, he went on. I have become a Christian. I know that God has forgiven me for the cruel things I did there, but I would like to hear it from your lips as well, Frolein. Again, the hand came out Will you forgive me? And I stood there and could not Betsy had died in that place. Could he erase her slow, terrible death simply for asking? It could not have been many seconds that he stood there, hand held out, but to me it seemed like hours, as I wrestled with the most difficult thing I had ever had to do. For I had to do it. I knew it. The message that God forgives has a prior condition. That we forgive those who have injured us. If you do not forgive men their trespasses, Jesus says, neither will your Father in heaven forgive your trespasses. Still, I stood there with the coldness clutching my heart, that forgiveness is an act of the will, and the will can function regardless of the temperature of the heart. Jesus, help me, I prayed silently. I can lift my hand, I can do that much. You you supply the feeling. And so woodenly, mechanically, I thrust my hand into the one stretched out to me. And as I did, an incredible thing took place. The current started in my shoulder, raced down my arm, sprang into our joined hands. And then this healing warmth seemed to flood my whole being Bringing tears to my eyes. I forgive you, brother. I cried with all my heart. For a long moment we grasped each other's hands, the former guard and former prisoner. I had never known God's love so intensely as I did then. End story. We have been examining the manner Jesus thinks and learning how to think in the same manner. I begin with the story of Corey Tenboom forgiving a prison guard because Jesus thought forgiveness was the highest of priorities. In the text read from Luke chapter five, Jesus heals a paralytic man. Such was a miracle. No doctor then nor now could explain how it happened. First there was a man who could not walk, and then the same man could suddenly walk And the primary factor was that Jesus told him to arise, take up his bed, and go home. And everyone involved in the story focused on the miracle of healing a paralyzed man. As you recall the story, no doubt you have heard in other sermons or in Bible studies, the details of the men who brought the paralytic man to Jesus. Finding a way into the house of Peter through Peter's roof. Poor ancient Near East houses used thatched roofs. The house was crowded with people who wanted to see and hear Jesus. The men carrying the paralytic did the only thing they could do to get their friend in front of Jesus. With the faith that Jesus could heal him, could make him walk. I love the small detail in verse 20 Where we are told that Jesus saw their faith, their faith, the faith of the men carrying the paralytic and the paralytic himself. The faith of the man who brought the paralytic to Jesus was impactful. It was meaningful. It mattered. Such is a great lesson on one of the reasons why baptizing children is legitimate before God. God sees the faith of the parents and the sponsors, and he blesses the child because of the faith of others. Don't ever underestimate the power of your faith in Jesus. As it can have a great impact on others, even those who have no faith at all. So Jesus sees their faith. And says to the man, the paralytic man, your sins are forgiven you. But late. The men who carried the paralytic came for the healing of legs, not for words of forgiveness. The paralyzed man had faith in Jesus for healing his legs. Jesus sees them, and instead of thinking about legs that don't work, And making them work again, Jesus thinks about the need for the man to have his sins forgiven. Jesus sees forgiveness as the highest of priorities. Now, the scribes and Pharisees are thinking about forgiveness as a high priority, but in a different manner. They know that forgiveness can only come from God. And that only God has the power to say to a sinner, your sins are forgiven you. They recognize that for Jesus to say this man's sins are forgiven, Jesus is saying that he has the authority of God. That is why they say to one another that Jesus is speaking blasphemy. And as a side note, if you're ever wondering where in Scripture does Jesus say he is God, well there's plenty of them, but Here is one of those places. And the scribes and the Pharisees knew it. Jesus, knowing their thoughts because he is God, calls them out. He says hard words. And his challenge is for them to determine what is more difficult. Is it more difficult to forgive sins or to heal a paralytic? We know now, we know now because we know the full story of the Gospel of Jesus that to forgive sins is harder because it takes the sacrifice and death of the Son of God. But Jesus wants to show them that he has power to do both. So he heals the paralytic. And people go away giving praise to God because of the power they had seen in the healing. But the real power and the real healing was forgiving sin. The closest disciples to Jesus know how important forgiveness is. To the Ephesians, Paul instructed Quote, be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving one another as God has forgiven you in Christ. To the Colossians, Paul wrote, Bearing with one another and forgiving one another, if one has a grievance against another, as the Lord has forgiven you, so must you also do. When St. Peter instructs Christians to not return evil for evil, but instead return evil with a blessing. He was describing what forgiving one another looks like. It is blessing someone who doesn't deserve to be blessed. Jesus described it later in Luke by saying that forgiving is loving our enemies. And what that looks like is to do good to those who hate you and to bless those who curse you. Notice that such forgiveness is not limited to be practiced between Christians one to another, but also for Christians to practice it toward non-Christians. For the Christian, forgiveness of sin is threefold in priority. We are first to be sure that we are forgiven ourselves for our own sins. We are to be a people of repentance. When confronted with the reality of our sinful behavior, we are to seek God for forgiveness and have faith that we receive it because of His love and sacrificial blood, the sacrificial blood of Jesus. The second aspect of our forgiveness is that we are to forgive our fellow Christians. Such forgiveness is sanctifying in a lifestyle Being in a church means that we bump into one another emotionally and verbally, and that requires a pattern of forgiveness. You cannot be healthy in a parish without practicing forgiveness one to another. And the third aspect of our forgiveness as Christians is to offer forgiveness to unbelievers. This is where our opportunity to be a city on a hill, light in darkness, is when we offer forgiveness even to our enemies Those who would like us to close our church doors and close our mouths and offer that forgiveness, we are to offer it to them even when it is not asked for. And I don't know of a better time to be such a witness in our culture Than in these times when people do not know how to forgive the sins of the past. What we can model to them is the priority of forgiveness, a forgiveness that is in the name and power of Jesus. Recalling the testimony of those like Corey Tenboom, she didn't forgive for the purpose of forgiveness itself. She didn't forgive because her psychiatrist told her it is more healthy to forgive than to hold a grudge. She forgave because Jesus forgave her. And that is the sole reason why we should forgive, even forgiving our enemies. If Christians do not model forgiveness to a dying culture, no one else will. On June seventeenth, twenty fifteen, a group of Christians gathered for their weekly Wednesday night Bible study. At Emmanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in downtown Charleston, South Carolina. The Bible study started late, then its usual time because of a church meeting. At 8 p. m. , 12 people gathered in a basement room at the church for their study. At around 9 p. m. , a man by the name of Dylan Roof, R-O-O-F Enter the building with a loaded Glock 45. When he finds the 12 people ending their Bible study, he opens fire. He shoots all but one person, a woman named Polly Shepherd, because he wants her to share the story of the massacre. Of the eleven that were shot multiple times, eight die within moments of the shooting, with three others severely wounded, with one dying later. From what the man shouted and what the police found about him later, his motive was hate toward the black race. One of the victims that night was a woman by the name of Myra Thompson. And she was the Bible study leader for the first time that evening. She was the wife of the Reverend Anthony Thompson, an ordained minister in the Reformed Episcopal Church. After his arrest, Dylan Roof made it clear that he was proud about what he had done. He stated that he was not sorry. He had no regret and no remorse At the first hearing after the shooting, the judge placed over the case made an unusual move. The following are the words of the Reverend Anthony Thompson. Quote, I glance at my watch and yearn to leave when Judge Gossnell suddenly surprises the courtroom with a highly irregular courtroom move. Without advance warning, the judge begins calling out the names of the victims one by one. He then asks the family members of each victim to step forward if they wish to speak. Several family members take opportunity to address the court. During their testimonial, those emotional tears flowed. The gunman keeps still, quiet, his eyes unmoving and slanted downward. I have already made up my mind not to say anything When Judge Gossnell calls on a representative of the family of Myra Thompson, I freeze. I don't want to speak. I have no idea what to say. I glance at Dylan Roof, and that's when I hear a familiar voice calling my name, speaking directly to my heart I have heard it before, and I know without a doubt it is the voice of my Heavenly Father. I have something to say, Anthony, the voice whispers. I obey immediately and stand up. I still have no idea what will happen. The judge looks at me and asks, Sir, do you want to say something before this court? Yes, sir, I respond. Please come forward, Gosnell says, motioning me to the front of the room. Out of the corner of my eye, I see my children's eyebrows lift, their mouths dropped open. The court is deathly quiet, the raw pain and tension within the room almost palpable. When I reach the podium, I stop and look intensely at Dylan Roof's face on the flat screen of the monitor. I can see him, but through the detention hall's camera lens, Dylan can only see Judge Gossanal. But he can clearly hear everything said to him in the courtroom I take a deep breath, and God puts his words into my mouth. I forgive you, I say to Dylan, and my family forgives you. I pause, unsure what my next words will be. Quote, but we would like to take this opportunity To repent, to call you to repentance, to confess. Give your life to the one who matters the most, Jesus Christ So that he can change it and change your attitude. And no matter what happens to you, then you'll be okay. Do that and you'll be better off than you are right now. While I speak, I note that Roof's eyes are fixed on bleaking and focused on the floor. Throughout the hearing, he has not once looked up. But at the very mention, the moment I mention the name Jesus Christ, Dylan unexpectedly raises his eyes to the camera. And for a split second, I am allowed to peer deep into this young man's soul. I am shocked by what I see. For one unforeseen millisecond, a thousandth of a second, evil becomes careless, accidentally dropping its impenetrable guard, its mask. I am allowed to see in Dylan's eyes a small fissure in which the unanticipated, wretched look of guilt and shame slips through. The hardened racist who killed innocent church members only because he hated the color of their skin becomes yet another unremarkable sinner. Who has allowed, nay, cordially invited evil to enter into his soul to pitch a tent and take up residence there. Before his eyes again glaze over with diabolical hardness, they become a brief window into the killer's pathetic soul. When I catch a sudden glimpse of Dylan's deep sense of degradation, something immediately happens within my heart and mind. I mentally drop the heavy stones of anger, despair, and hate, and I experienced the unmistakable peace of Christ's love filling my entire being. At that moment I feel free as light as a feather. As I return to my seat I sense God calling me to a new purpose in his kingdom, a new beginning, a new mission in Christ, to spread the gospel of unconditional biblical forgiveness. Powerful, powerful words. Powerful because of the priority of forgiveness. Jesus thought it was a priority, and so should we. Certainly, you heard from both stories what occurs in a person's heart when we truly forgive. That is God's presence felt so very real because God forgives and he dwells with those who also forgive. Forgive because you have been forgiven. Amen. Let us pray.

sermons.title: People as Priority
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. For God so loved the world. Such is the beginning of the most well-known verse in the Bible. For those around my age or older, you will remember the guy with the rainbow hairdo Attending televised professional sporting events, holding up a sign that read, John 3, 16. His name was Roland Stewart. He and his sign were seen on television at World Series games, the Major League Baseball All-Star Game. behind the goalpost on Monday Night Football at Indianapolis 500, the Masters Golf Tournament, the Olympics, event after event. He said he did it because he was a born-again Christian and he wanted the world to know about Jesus. Unfortunately. Roland became mentally unstable, committing crimes of terror, resulting in a prison sentence that he is still serving. But Rowland's unsteady behavior does not detract from the message of John 3. 16, which is that God loved the world so much. That he gave his only son so that the world might be saved. But what is the world? Some have interpreted the saying of Jesus to mean that all people in the world will eventually be saved. But that is not what it means. Scripture must interpret Scripture. And so we interpret John 3. 16 in light of passages like Matthew 22, verse 14, where Jesus says, many are called. But few are chosen. Not all people will be saved. Jesus' teaching on the reality of the punishment of hell confirms this. So what does the word world in John 3. 16 mean? In general, it means that God loved his created order, what he called good after he created it And so he has set in motion a process to save it after the sin of mankind and the devil corrupted it with sin and the curse that comes with the sin. What Jesus promised would be saved are all people who believe in him, and he will save the physical world in which we live, for he has promised that one day it will be made new. This leads us to examining the way Jesus thinks in our series, How Jesus Thinks How Jesus thinks about his fellow man, and how he puts humanity as his top priority. Thus, we are examining how Jesus viewed his fellow man in terms of the disciples that he chose. Jesus made specific choices regarding what disciples would be closest to him as confidants and future leaders of the church. From the gospel reading this morning, we heard how Jesus called Matthew to be a disciple. Prior to that, he had called James, John, Andrew, and Peter, also known as Simon. James and John were brothers who worked alongside Andrew and Peter. All four were fishermen, and you remember that Jesus told all four of them that he would make them fishers of men. Peter and Andrew were early followers of John the Baptist. It was Andrew who first introduced his oldest brother Peter to Jesus when they were in the wilderness along with John the Baptist. It is thought that they became spiritual followers of Jesus at that time. Also known as Simon, Simon Peter also, or Cephas or the Rock. Peter, we know as the gregarious, the natural leader, an obvious spokesperson for the twelve. Peter's name is mentioned more than any other disciple in the New Testament. He was the older brother of the two brothers and the only married disciple. His wife was known to travel with him on his missions, as according to 1 Corinthians 9. His assignment, we know, is to bring the gospel to the circumcised, to the Jew. Peter is also well known for denying Christ three times before Jesus or after Jesus was arrested. After his own arrest, many years later, he requested to be crucified with his head down. He didn't believe he was worthy to be crucified in the same manner as his Lord. He died a martyr's death in Rome during the reign of Nero, and some believe it was likely near the same time in which St. Paul was beheaded. An early disciple of John the Baptist, Andrew and John, the son of Zebedee, were present when John the Baptist said, Behold, the Lamb of God, pointing to Jesus. Andrew was the first to follow Jesus, and his enthusiasm was evident in his desire for his brother to know Jesus He had a deep love for God, and that was revealed by spreading the word about Jesus. He is referred to as the quiet apostle. Andrew died a martyr's death. He faced crucifixion with boldness and courage, and we have a quote from him historically. O cross, most welcome and longed for, with a willing mind, joyfully and desirously, I come to you Being a scholar of him which did hang on you, because I have always been your lover and yearn to embrace you. He said that about the cross. James is the elder brother of John. He also was rather quiet, part of the inner circle, and we don't read much about him. Yet he was part of that inner three as he was permitted to be alongside Peter and John when Jesus raised Jairus' daughter from the dead. He also witnessed the transfiguration of Jesus on the Mount of Olives, and he was in the Garden of Gethsemane with Jesus. James was the first disciple to be martyred, he was beheaded, and the only disciple to have their martyrdom recorded in Holy Scripture, Acts chapter 12. John is known as the disciple Jesus loved, being also again part of the inner three. He wrote, as we know, a large portion of the New Testament, 1, 2nd, 3, John, and the book of Revelation He wrote more about love than any other New Testament author. He was exiled to the island of Patnas under Domitian. but was allowed to return to Ephesus, where he governed the churches in Asia until his death around A. D. 100. Then there was Philip, of whom we know very little. Although he was a Jew, we actually know him by his Greek name, Philip He showed a heart for evangelism as he was anxious to tell Nathaniel that the one foretold by Moses and the prophets has been found. Philip was stoned and crucified at Hieropolis Phrygia. Also known as Bartholomew, Nathaniel came from Cana in Galilee. He expressed a local prejudice against those who come from Nazareth. Jesus recognized how sincerely his love for God was, for when he saw Nathaniel, he said, Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit. Nathaniel may have preached in India and translated the book of Matthew into their language. It is recorded that he was beaten, crucified, and beheaded. I guess one wasn't good enough. He died as a martyr while serving at Albinopolis in Armenia. Levi, about whom we read, is the son of Alpheus. Levi or Matthew, we know is a tax collector, and you certainly know that that was the most despised people in all of Israel. They were known for taking extra money and paying off the Romans as well as patting their own pockets And then it happened that as Jesus was reclining at the table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were dining with Jesus and his disciples, and there were many of them. When the scribes and Pharisees saw that he was eating with sinners and tax collectors, they said to his disciples, Why is he entertaining drinking and eating with tax collectors and sinners. And upon hearing that, Jesus said to them, Is it not those who are healthy that need a physician, but those who are sick? I did not come to call the righteous, but the sinners. Matthew brought the gospel to Ethiopia and Egypt. Hardanus, the king, had him killed with a spear. Usually nicknamed doubting Thomas, Thomas was also called Didymus, although whether he had a, Didymus means twin, whether he had a twin brother or sister is not recorded in Scripture. He was an outspoken skeptic to the point of being known as a pessimist. No details are given about Thomas in the first three Gospels other than the mention of his name. John first mentions Thomas in chapter 11. Lazarus had died, and the disciples feared for the life of Jesus themselves, and they didn't want to go back to Bethany. Thomas speaks up and says, let us also go that we may die with him. He is Seeing with great character and quality of courage and loyalty to Christ. And that's not usually attributed to Thomas, but that was him. His devotion to Christ is further displayed when Jesus told the disciples that he was going to go away and prepare a place for them. And he was a little panicky, saying, We do not know where you are going or how to get there. Thomas didn't want to be left behind. And then Thomas's love for Jesus and his desire to see and touch before he believed It was after that he declared, My Lord and my God. Tradition strongly suggests that Thomas started the Christian church in India Some suggest that he was run through with a spear, which is to be ironic, because he wanted to touch the side of Jesus. There was another James, he was the son of Alpheus. His mother's name was Mary, another Mary, and he had a brother named Joseph. Except for a few details about his family, there is nothing more mentioned about him in Scripture, and this may be the reason why he is referred to as James the Less. Tradition says he was crucified in Sinai or possibly stoned in Jerusalem. There was also another Simon who was further identified as the zealot. He was probably a political activist in his younger years. He was a man of fierce loyalties, amazing passion, courage, and zeal Simon had believed the truth and embraced Christ as his Lord. The fiery enthusiasm he once had for Israel politically, he transferred and expressed in his devotion to Christ. There is some speculation about what happened to Simon. Tradition says that after preaching in the west coast of Africa, he went up to England. where he ended being crucified in 74 A. D. The eleventh name on the list of disciples is Judas, but we don't want to get him confused. He's also known as Jude or Thaddeus. We will call him Thaddeus. Thaddeus lives in obscurity as one of the twelve. He did ask Jesus a question. We have that recorded in John 14. He said, Lord, why are you going to reveal yourself only to us? And not the world at large. He seemed overly concerned with this question. Christ responded by saying that he would reveal himself to the world, he would reveal himself to anyone who would love him. Most early traditions say that Thaddeus, son of James a few years after Pentecost, took the gospel north to Edessa. There he healed the king of Edessa named Adgar. Eusebius the historian said the archives of Edessa contained a visit of Thaddeus and his healing of Abgar, but those records are now destroyed. The traditional symbol of Thaddeus is a club because tradition says he was clubbed to death for his faith. And the final of the twelve was Judas Iscariot. Jesus said to the twelve, Did I myself not choose you, the twelve, and yet one of you is the devil? Now we know he meant Judas, the son of Simon Iscari. He was the traitor Nothing is known about Judas' background. His encounter and call by Jesus is not recorded in Scripture. He was not from Galilee, that much is known.
