He obviously became a follower and stayed with Jesus three years. He gave Christ three years of his life, but he certainly didn't give him his heart. And Jesus knew this Judas betrayed Jesus, we remember, for thirty pieces of silver. We take the time to describe each apostle. To realize how God uses many different personality types and people with different gifts to establish his kingdom on earth Contrary to popular belief, we do not have to be perfect for God to use us to work through us. Look no further than the twelve disciples whose many weaknesses are forever preserved throughout the pages of the New Testament. Jesus chose ordinary men, fishermen, tax collectors, political zealots, and turned their weaknesses to strike, producing greatness from utter uselessness. And Jesus did this for the 12 because his priority is the human race, and in particular those who believe in him as Savior and God. The value of the human race is seen in how Jesus prioritizes it and how the devil attacks it. And because there is something inherent in us that wants to value human life, the best way to devalue human life is to dehumanize it. And so the Jews have historically been demonized, making them less human, and then persecuted in some part of the world in every generation. Blacks in the Western world and slaves all over the world, regardless of skin color, were and are dehumanized by being given a lower percentage of humanity to justify how they are treated. And today the unborn are given identifiers like being called a fetus or a bundle of cells or a choice. So that their humanity is still to be determined, and their treatment has no more of value than trash. All of this is the devil's work, and his followers accept it without challenge. But we Christians are to be like Jesus, and that we think upon our fellow man as not only fully human, but full bearers of God's image. No matter skin color, no matter patriarchy, no matter global origin, all are to be valued as human beings and thus worthy to hear the good news of Jesus Christ. I wonder if any of you, upon hearing the description of each disciple, did you hear a description of yourself, at least somewhat? Are you passionate like Andrew? Are you the romantic like John? Are you the quiet one like James? Are you boisterous like Peter Are you a person with a salacious past, like Matthew? Are you quizzical like Timothy? Excuse me. Not Timothy. Thomas. Whatever your personality type, Jesus knows you and wants you to be a part of his kingdom. But let us ask better questions than did I find myself. When you hear the descriptions of each of the disciples, do you hear at least somewhat descriptions of people that you know in church? Another way to put it is, do you know people in church who are passionate or romantic or quiet? Or boisterous, or have a salacious past, or are quizzical. And if you do, and I know you do, do those people get on your nerves? Or do you love them because they are people and specifically God's people? You see, that is the challenge To think like Jesus, we have to love people and love them despite all the things about them that can annoy us and even cause us to avoid them. But Jesus put up with all of their personalities, all of their sins, all of their quirks. They all had little immature faith. One didn't believe until he had empirical proof. Another didn't want Jesus to go to Jerusalem, but to remain safe. And of course, we know of the one who betrayed him. And Jesus knew he would betray him, and Jesus called him to be his disciple still, and Jesus loved him Some of us are boisterous. We speak before we listen. Some of us are quiet, too quiet. Some of us are quizzical, so much so that we always second guess every decision. Some of us are passionate and romantic. And so much so that we put too much feeling to verify truth. And many of us lack a strong faith. But Jesus calls all of us, regardless of our failures, to follow him, to be used by him. And some of us are scared, almost scared to death about a virus, while some others are overly cavalier. And Jesus calls all of us. Jesus calls all of us, regardless of what news we listen to. And who we believe, he calls us to follow him and be used by him. Our challenge last week was to forgive. This week it is to love one another. We are to forgive because Jesus forgave us. We are to love one another because Jesus loves us. Let us pray. Our God, we thank you for the example of Jesus and the priority of the human race. And in particular, to love those who love you. And even though we are so very different in very many ways. That challenge is still before us to love one another, to love our brother, our sister in Christ. If we are not, bring us to repentance. If we are, enable us to love more. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen

sermons.title: On Sanctification
sermons.speaker: Rev. William Vowles
sermons.text: Let us pray. May the words of my mouth and the meditations of our hearts be acceptable in thy sight, O Lord, our strength and our pre redeemer, in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost. May be seated. As we look into our second reading from Romans chapter six this morning, it is important to understand the placement of our passage into the whole of the book of Romans. It is always helpful whenever we look at a passage of Scripture to understand its surrounding verses, chapters, and context. But with the Romans, it is certainly the case. As there is this progression that leads from one point to another, from one doctrine to another I like the way Anglican theologian N. T. Wright describes the book, and I think I've mentioned this before. He likens the book of Romans to a great symphony. Which has four very distinct movements, each movement being a division of chapters, first movement being chapters one through four, then five through eight, nine through eleven, and the last movement twelve Each division differs in terms of style, layout, and mode of argument, but there's this consistent line weaving through the whole of the book. Leading up to chapter 6, it is consistent among commentators to note that having explained the doctrine of justification by grace Through faith in the first four chapters, Paul begins a discussion in chapter five on sanctification that will carry on into chapter eight. As we look up this sixth chapter, we are in the middle of this very important topic. Over the past three weeks, we have been tested by our current sermon series to understand and practice the way Jesus thinks. And this can only be done through a mind being sanctified by his Holy Spirit. What we're talking about here is the issue of spiritual transformation. In the early chapters of Romans, St. Paul makes it very clear that in our natural condition, we are dead in our sins. Why? Because all have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God. And thus, Paul says, the wrath of God was revealed from heaven against all ungodliness. But thanks be to God, He sent His own only Son, Jesus Christ, to be a propitiation for our sins. Amen? As Abraham was justified by faith, so we who have faith in the death, resurrection, and ascension of Christ are justified. So spiritual transformation began for us with this great doctrine of regeneration, when in our deadness we were given new life. And in this new life, the process of sanctification is or should be giving us a new way of thinking and acting. For the apostle says later in his epistle that we are to present our bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God. Not being conformed to this world, but being transformed by what? The renewing of our minds. And this renewing ought to Control the way that we think and the way that we act. Conversion launches us into a lifelong experience of sanctification, which literally means being set apart unto God. So follow with me the flow of Paul's argument in this passage because I think it's helpful to understand the marvelous spiritual transformation going on in the life of a believer. The apostle begins this part of the passage with what some commentators note as an apology for using the illustration of slavery. But Morris adds in his commentary that the apostle is not so much apologizing for using the illustration as he is explaining why he uses it. Even in that day, slavery was regarded as a degrading state. And using this illustration might not normally be regarded as acceptable Yet he goes on using the term because he says in our human weakness, it helps us to understand the points he's trying to convey. Now in today's tension, it's not only hard to use this type of illustration or metaphor, but it's hard sometimes to even have a civil conversation on difficult subjects Feeling that you might be regarded as either insensitive or worse, a bigot. I saw a poll the other day that says 63% of those polled were afraid to share their views publicly for fear of repercussion. Yet how can we understand other people's hurts, present and past? Or how can we grow as individuals or as a people if we cannot have these conversations Sometimes even in our own families. Well, Jesus Himself said back in John chapter 8, verse 34, whoever commits sin is the slave of sin. Jesus introduced this idea of being a slave to sin, and he does it so that we might understand that sin can be a dominating master. Sin can dominate us to the degree that it controls all thought, all motives, all speech, and all of our actions Which is why the apostle tells us there are none righteous. No, not one. There are none that naturally seek after God. The whole human race is born into slavery to sin with the ultimate outcome of spiritual and eternal death. Sin is that internal force that corrupts the whole person. It is like raging cancer in every organ of the body. It is incurable. It's terminal. And worse, because without the blood of Christ, death provides no relief. It only casts that simple soul into a state of eternal suffering. There's no relief. Sometimes When someone has suffered at the hands of cancer or some other dreadful disease and dies, we hear someone say, and I said this myself, well at least the suffering is over, right? Well, while that is true from a physical point, for sinners apart from Christ, the suffering has only begun. So Paul spends much of the beginning of this great book helping us to understand just how pervasive the dominance of sin can be. Those who have come to grips with its debilitating and devastating effects, who understand its potential to doom us to painful suffering forever Who have the desire to be rescued and who want sin's bondage broken. They should be drawn to this text like bees are drawn to pollen or ants to a sweet melon. Because this text offers an amazing offer. In the verse just before our passage, in verse 18, and again in 22 of our passage, we are told that having been set free from sin And having become slaves of God or slaves of righteousness, we have our fruit to holiness, the end of which is everlasting life with our Lord and Savior. Amen? This is the promise of this passage. God's promise to those who are in Christ, to those of us who have come to faith in Him. It is the greatest gift ever given. It is a gift that has no equal. Freedom from sin, its penalty, its power, and someday even its presence The text before us is all about being freed from sin and bound to righteousness So Paul unfolds two types of slaveries: one that began at our natural birth, a slave to sin, and one that began at our new birth, a slavery to righteousness Verse 19. I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your bodies as slaves to uncleanness and of lawlessness, leading to more lawlessness So now present your members as slaves of righteousness for holiness. Paul speaks of the slaves of righteousness in order to show the reality of the devotion which Christ demands Again, he uses this slavery illustration to essentially say that Christians are to be in bondage of Christ. That's not a common term that we might want to use. Amongst other than ourselves. But we are to be no less earnest in our serving Christ than we have been in our service to sin. We are to submit our wills as completely to righteousness as we had before to uncleanness and unlawfulness, which was once something that alienated us from God. And there should be no middle ground in this position, which is why he says back in verse 15, What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law, but under grace? May it never be. Do you not know that when you present yourselves to someone as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin resulting in death, or of obedience resulting in righteousness? The apostle tells us that we are not to pass from one master to no master, but from one master to another master, from one slavery to another slavery. When sin ruled, sin was our master, and Christ meant nothing to us. Now, if Christ rules, he must be master, and sin must be put away. So this imperfect illustration illustrates more completely the absolute need for our Christian duty. Another word, people don't like to hear. And we miss the point if we look for an easier road of and a middle ground of obedience, which so many do today. Which brings us to the culmination of this short passage and one of the most powerful verses in the whole of the book, matter-of-the-bible, verse 23: the wages of sin is death. But the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. This verse is at the center of almost every evangelical tract, Christian apology. It's right in the middle of the Romans Road. Remember that? Paul in this passage conveys two types of wages: the wages of sin and the wages of Christ. Sin has wages. Sin has its end. And both its wages and its end lead to death. The wages are the immediate. The end is the final consequence of sin. The immediate consequence of sin is that it diminishes our capacity for intellectual, moral, and spiritual life. Sin darkens our intellect, it dulls our conscience. These consequences are wages, similar to our human wages, in that every sin has its compensation. And just reward. Yet the wages of Christ are unique in a couple of ways. First, the wages of Christ bear fruit. They proceed from the Spirit and through the sanctification process produce love, joy, peace, long-suffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control. All you kids remember that? And finally, everlasting life. Sin bears no fruit, but rather it is the blight that destroys the tree, the blight that destroys the soul. Also, the wages of Christ are a free gift. They are free because the life of a Christian is not the consequence of their goodness, but the gift in spite of their sinfulness. Eternal life can never be deserved. It is the precious free gift of God. Paul touches on this fruit in verses 21 and 22 when he says, beginning in verse 21 What fruit did you have then in the things which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is dead. Now here's the reality Even though we progress in righteousness, we still sin. We still fall short of his glory. Why? Because we walk in a fallen world whose ruler is the devil himself. And as we are still in this fleshly vessel We don't always yield up those parts of us that we should. That's why we are told here to present ourselves Because we have to do it. We have to seek holiness. It's not just going to happen by osmosis. It doesn't happen automatically because of the presence of this evil flesh in the world. Yet we are not to think that we're alone in this pursuit. Beginning and continuing his talk about sanctification in the next chapter, the apostle says it's hard. He says it's very hard. He begins in verse 21 of chapter 3 saying, I find then a law that evil is present with me, the one who wills to do good. For I delight in the law of God according to the inward man, but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members. Then in verse 24 he says, Oh wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? Then he says, I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Through this journey of sanctification, we will always feel that wretchedness to some degree, because we are not complete in our sanctification process. Many years ago, when I worked regularly with the youth ministries, young people would ask me all the time: will I ever have victory over this sin? Will I ever stop falling into the same temptations? Mature Christians ask the same thing. But young people Get tempted in very intense ways, and we know that. And they want to know if this is going to be the case for their whole life. Is this the way it's going to be? And my response to them is yes, it will. Even as you grow or mature in your faith, temptations and failings will come. I would remind them, as I remind us, that when Paul said that he was a wretched man, he was a very mature believer, an apostle. John Calvin, commenting on this verse, said As soon as the godly begin to be enlightened by the Spirit of Christ and the preaching of the gospel, they freely acknowledge that the whole of their past life, which they live without Christ, is worthy of condemnation. So far from trying to excuse themselves, they are in fact ashamed of themselves. Indeed, they go further and continually bear their disgrace in mind so that the shame of of it may make them more truly and willfully humble before God. Now poor Paul's point here in verse 21 about being ashamed is that although we sin less We feel worse when we do sin. Why? Because it's a natural part of sanctification as we grow deeper in love of righteousness. We grow greater in our animosity towards sin. So even when you sin less, you feel worse. Antidote? Yield or offer up those fallen areas to the Lord through confession and repentance. One of the great benefits of Anglican worship is that every time we meet, whether at Holy Communion Or going through the daily offices here or at home. We offer prayers of confession, repentance, and thanksgiving, and these things help us in our sanctification process. They help us to yield to the spirit and not to the temptations of the flesh, not to the temptations of the world and its ruler. And as we do that, we are more and more conformed into the image of Christ. And the fruit of that is holiness. Look at verse 22 again as we close. But now having been set free from sin and having become slaves of God, you have been you you have your fruit to holiness. and the end, everlasting life. One of those aforementioned fruits of Christ's wages is peace. And peace is certainly a fruit that we need today, is it not? Joel Smith in an article in this month's edition of Table Talk. Sound like a Presbyterian this morning, don't I? States why a believers place is secure and should abound more and more through the sanctification process He says, we have been reconciled to God through the Lord Jesus Christ, who endured the unpeaceableness and cruelty of the world for our sake. He took on flesh and secured salvation through his atoning death for all who believe. Our peace has been purchased by the blood of the Lamb. Through Christ and the indwelling Spirit, we have been made right with the Father, and that peace with God is the source and foundation of peace in God. Our peace is in God's providential care, which is what the apostle tells us in chapter 8 when he calls us his adopted children, who are not left as orphans. But are instead entrusted to his care in all things. Jesus beckons weary and heavy-laden souls to come to him for rest, regardless of their circumstances. Jesus gives us his peace. And we therefore are to be peacemakers in the world. Conflicts Disagreements and harsh words are to be resolved quickly so that we can restore the unity and peace of our relationships. Harmony with God requires love And accord with one another, 1 John 4. 20. This is especially true in marriage and in the body of the church. Well, this also applies to our relationship to the greater world. It may not always be feasible, which is why Paul adds a little caveat. In Romans 12, 18, he says, if possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceable with all. Sometimes we have to make a stand. Sometimes we have to fight. Yet apart from groups of anarchists, most of this nation and the world for that matter desperately desires peace. But the true peace can only come and be found in the peace of God, secured through the Prince of Peace and given as the fruit. Of the spirit of peace. So when Pastor next raises his arm and pronounces the blessing of peace to you, receive it with gladness and rest in this wonderful fruit given to you. In the name of the Father, Son, and the Holy Ghost. Amen.

sermons.title: Internal Holiness
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. It is difficult to know how Jesus thinks today because so much has changed since he walked Deserve. This series on how Jesus thinks and our call to think like him hits a roadblock when we are facing matters of morality today. Well we have a much different landscape than when Jesus taught his disciples We have a culture that has learned that it is much more healthy for couples to fornicate before marriage in order to see if they are sexually compatible. before they ever consider marriage. And living together is a much better option in order to see if the same two people can have Guiltless sex outside of the marriage commitment while also sharing the same toothpaste. Jesus didn't have the foresight to see how necessary it is to play at being married before you are actually married. Also, Jesus didn't consider being constrained by the days in which he lived to see how male on male intimacy could be just as fulfilling as male and female intimacy. Although the male sexual anatomy is not built for such intimacy, Jesus was not enlightened enough To know how the emotional fulfillment such intimacy provides outweighs any deficiencies of the anatomy. Also, Jesus was not aware of the importance of personal rights when it comes to the value of an unborn child. He was not aware of the science. That allows us to label such a child as an embryo or a fetus. He mistakenly assumed that such gathering of cells was a human being. instead of what we moderns know now to be, well, a choice. And Jesus didn't have the awareness, nay He did not have the experience to understand the human struggle. If he did, he would not have taught the way he did He did not see the value of harboring anger and hatred and bitterness in the heart, making it necessary to spill out into the streets and to destroy personal property and commit violence on strangers so that your emotions can be expressed in whatever manner you choose. Jesus never took a psychology class where he would have learned that expressing your emotions instead of controlling them is the best way for mental health Because Jesus lacks so much knowledge, a knowledge that we moderns have, with all the confidence that there will be no greater generation than the one that is rising today We should not listen to what he had to say regarding modern ethics. What we now know about ethics is the most that any generation will ever know. We know that we are to live and let live. I'll do what I want to do, and I'll respect that you will do what you want to do. And neither of us will condemn the other for doing so. If everybody would live by such a motto as live and let live, Really and truly live by such a motto, then the world would be a wonderful place to live. Such was the understanding of the flower children. in the nineteen sixties, but no one listened to them enough or their plans were carried out as was designed. We as a society need to try again to apply those same principles in order to be free. However, there seems to be a problem with the live and let live motto For as it is carried out, it always occurs that what I want to do will eventually interfere with what another person wants to do. It appears impossible for me to let you live as you want to live without your choices interfering with my choices. After all, we we both can't own the same property. We can't till the same land. We can't marry the same woman You can't grow the same business or eat the same foods. Someone's choices in living the way they wish is going to interfere with another person's choices. It cannot be avoided. And because the live and let live way of living presents no rules, no boundaries, no ultimate standard. There is no means to oversee who has the rights to live when such living interferes with the living of others. No matter the generation, no matter the cause, no matter the new social agenda, no matter the new government structure What we humans run into time and again is the reality of our sinful condition. We, all of us, of every age, until Jesus returns, all of us are sinners. And that means that we will think first and foremost about ourselves and we will protect our own welfare before we will consider living in an altruistic manner. Now the logic that I used to throw out the teachings of Jesus is not an exaggerated argument, even though you may have Detected sarcasm in my voice as I presented it. The position of seeing Jesus as naive regarding ethics is very real. And a great many of people who call themselves Christian have accepted the argument and its conclusions. But here is one of the points that I want us to agree to in regards to how Jesus thought and how we have to think like him. That first point is that Jesus believed in the ethics of the Old Testament. Hear that again. Jesus believed in the ethics of the Old Testament. Does he believe in the authority of the Old Testament? And please do not take that point lightly. A great deal hangs on that point. Those who argue that Jesus was not as enlightened regarding ethics as we are today make the strange point that Jesus never spoke against something like homosexuality. I hope you see a problem with such argumentation where you cannot say that Jesus was not enlightened in one premise and then say that his lack of argument proves an acceptance of the behavior. For either what Jesus said regarding sexual ethics and what he didn't say is the standard, or it is not, and you don't refer to him at all. But Jesus did say something about homosexual behavior, just as he said something about every manner of sexuality. He said something about such things when he said, Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets. I have come not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them. Such a statement. Verified that the law of Moses is the law of God, and therefore the standards set therein are the ethics all of God's people are expected to live by. Jesus didn't mention, need to mention every form of sexual immorality because they are already mentioned in the law of Moses, that Jesus obeyed and fulfilled. Jesus didn't need to mention the abomination of bestiality or incest or abortion because God had already described such sins going against his will. And Jesus came to verify the same standards and then even to raise the bar There is a great deal of frustration that I have experienced in my ministry when dealing with Christians and Christian groups that do not respect the Old Testament. Some groups outwardly profess their disdain for the Old Testament by speaking about it in terms of the law within it. being a burden as opposed to pointing us to Jesus which it does time and time again Such a rejection of the Old Testament seems to result in a rejection of church history as well, as such groups only see the Christian faith through their eyes, through their modern experiences. It is a shame. But I mentioned that Jesus raised the bar. And that is the second point I am making today regarding how we are to think like Jesus. In our reading from Matthew that records the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus addresses the ethics of hatred of our fellow man and sexual lust. Jesus begins to address these issues by challenging his listeners that their righteousness must exceed the righteousness of the scribes and the Pharisees. And let us not gloss over that standard. For the lives lived by the scribes and Pharisees were disciplined lives. The scribes after the exile became not only copiers of the sacred text, but interpreters as well The Pharisees laid out the rule book of applying God's law to their everyday lives so that they were to be sure not to break God's law and for everyone to see that they weren't breaking God's law. For Jesus to say that the righteousness of his followers is to exceed these two groups is to say a great deal. I'm quite certain that few of us live as disciplined and cautious lives compared to the Pharisees. And it is a temptation to interpret these words of Jesus in light of our understanding of his atoning work as a righteousness we receive from him, what is called imputed righteousness. Imputed means that our righteousness is the righteousness of Jesus, and therefore that exceeds the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees. But I don't think that's what Jesus is saying. I am confident it's not what Jesus is saying I am confident because Jesus doesn't stop when he sets that standard. He goes on to describe the type of ethics he expects of his followers. Look at verse 21. 521. Jesus recalls the sixth commandment: thou shalt not murder. He confirms the commandment and then adds the higher standard. He states that when one person is angry at another person without cause, and when a person curses another person, both instances are worthy of God's condemnation. To understand this standard, we must first rid of the excuse that whatever has bothered us is good enough to cause us to be angry. No. The cause we must have is in accordance to God's law, not our own preferences or our own feelings. And to curse another human being is to claim them as useless or worthless. Both behaviors are worthy of eternal fire Hard words. But why does Jesus need to add such a standard to an already clear commandment? In verse 27, Jesus refers to the seventh commandment, thou shalt not commit adultery. And then he says that the standard for that law is lusting within the heart. I admit to you that as a young man this law really troubles me. In my explanation of this standard, I want you to know that I am not giving anyone license to Ogle women. And let's face it, this is mostly a men's male issue, although not solely a male issue. But Jesus is not saying that it is sin to notice a woman is physically attractive and even sexually attractive. What Jesus is warning is that if a man looks upon a woman and makes plans within his mind to seduce such a woman or simply imagine himself being intimate with that woman That is when adultery has been committed. And even that interpretation is difficult for men to live up to. But why does Jesus need to add such a standard to an already clear commandment? Similar to the standard not being unjustly angry or cursing another human being, the standard of not lusting is dealing with issues of the heart. This principle is echoed in the letter of James, where he explains that sin has a beginning point, and that beginning point is within the individual who is being tempted to sin. Sin begins in the internal of a person, and therefore holiness must begin there as well. These thoughts of Jesus tie in nicely with the sermon last week by the Reverend Bowles regarding the need for Christian holiness. The holiness Jesus thinks is necessary is internal, personal holiness. And because the battleground of temptation is within the individual, It is for each of us to be honest and speak to our own hearts. It is true that Jesus speaks in a hyperbolic manner when he says that if your right eye causes you to sin, pluck it out, or your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off. If he were speaking straightforwardly, there would be a lot of us blind with no hands. But hyperbole isn't to be dismissed either, for it is an exaggeration to make a dramatic point. It is important that we do not give into internal struggles that motivate us to sin. Now, you can throw yourself naked into a thorn bush to avoid the temptations of a woman That's what Saint Benedict is said to have done. But I suggest a different way that is more internal because again, that's where the battle is. My pastoral counsel for personal and internal holiness is for us to talk to ourselves. My example is Jesus talking to the Father while in the garden right before his arrest. In one sense, he was talking to himself, and in another, he was not. But what I mean by talking to ourselves is that we address the inward battle. I testify that I have tried it, I have practiced it, and it works. For example, while you are in a conversation that is not going well, and you find yourself wanting to raise your voice and become argumentative or defensive, tell yourself to calm down. Tell yourself to be humble. Tell yourself that God is your defender. Remind yourself that you are a child of God. And as a child of God, you have been instructed to be quick to listen. And slow to speak. And that is what you're going to do. Now please don't hear me saying that to talk to yourself is to replace talking to God. Not at all. Talk to him. But also talk to yourself and remind yourself of God's revealed truths. Spending time on the internet can be like walking down the street of a wanton woman. Tell yourself not to go down that street. Turn off your phone. Turn off your computer. Remind yourself that you have been warned by the dangers of going down such streets. What I'm trying to describe is that because Jesus thought the battle over sin and righteousness was internal, we are to begin internally. That is where the battle should be fought. And the best way to fight such battles is to speak to yourselves, to yourself truths that apply the temptations that are inside of you. If inside you desire to shout another person down and even punch him in the mouth, you have a word from Jesus that reminds you that you are to love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you. If internally you have a desire to steal, to withhold, to be judgmental, prejudicial, lustful, untruthful Be honest with those temptations, with the thoughts you have. Identify them as sin. Confess them to God and pledge to turn away from them Rebuke yourself. Internally rebuke yourself. Our righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, not by doing outward deeds that receive praise from men, but battling inwardly where the root of sin begins. And here is a practical and necessary application of this internal battle to sin or to resist sin. When you hear a voice in your head that says you are more righteous because you care about people more, because you wear a mask. Rebuke that voice, for that is the righteousness of the Pharisees. And on the other side If you hear a voice that says your faith is stronger, and thus you don't need to wear a mask, rebuke that voice, for your righteousness is no greater than that of a scribe. One call upon preachers is to warn God's people where the devil is currently prowling. He is currently prowling on the subject of masks, social distancing, the opening of schools, or the closing of schools, businesses, and churches. Don't be a tool of the devil. Rebuke self-righteousness. Practice Christian charity. Give no space for the devil to linger, beginning within your internal self. Let us pray. God, we thank you for this standard, and we humbly confess that we fall short of it. Do we internally struggle both with our personal temptations but also with self-righteousness? May that be far from us, and may we purposefully, internally, choose charity. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Thinking Against the World
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Keep me seated. As an addendum, I want you to know that Uh I mistakenly had written down, uh failed to write down the verses prior to the Matthew reading. where uh Jesus talks about uh marriage and divorce. Uh so that's going to be part, if you turn to Matthew chapter five, that'll be our focus, uh, those three sections of Scripture Uh talking about marriage and then oaths. When I was in middle school I was part of a group of guys that I thought were friends. And one day I found myself excluded by them. I didn't know why. I didn't know what I did, but I was on the outs. My friends, my group, left me out. I remember being frustrated. I remember being sad. But I remember being resolute as well. I was resolute that no matter what happened in my social life, I would not allow what other people thought of me to determine my identity I didn't take such an outlook on life because I was raised to do so or because of my Christian faith. I didn't have that faith. I didn't know Jesus then, but Jesus knew me, and I see that now. When I left middle school to attend high school, I made new friends and reacquainted myself with old friends. My senior year in high school, we played our crosstown rivals. And many of their players were my former friends from middle school. I intercepted a pass on the final drive, a pass that was intended for my previous friend. We won the game And I could say that revenge is sweet, but I didn't care. Well maybe I did, I'm telling you the story, so I cared a little bit. But Jesus was introducing himself to me, and I was caring about a great deal more than a middle school social shunning. I share that story knowing the possibility that some of you hearing me might have a similar experience of being left out or shunned or mocked as a young child or teenager and the sting of that treatment remains even into how you perceive yourself as an adult. I was imagining this past week how there are likely students in middle school and high school who are glad that public schools are being held virtually this fall because they don't feel like they fit into any social group at school. And that feeling of not fitting in eats away at their confidence and their self-worth. Social problems in high school are petty and silly when viewed objectively. We grow up physically and emotionally and we move on. But when in the midst of them, they can feel like the most awful thing we could ever experience. But it's a lie. Jesus tells us it's a lie. And he tells them that it's a lie in many different ways. And I believe he was telling his disciples that fitting in socially is not important when he preaches on several issues on what we call the Sermon on the Mount. In our series, examining how Jesus thinks and how he shows us how we are to think, We come to his teachings on marriage, on oaths, and justice, where each of them appear to be separate subjects But in fact, they have a relationship to one another in regards to how the standard Jesus sets goes against the ways of the world. Jesus thinks differently than the world, and so should we. And when we think differently from the world Then the world and those who are of the world will not be our friends. And that is as it should be. For some Christians, the teaching of Jesus regarding marriage and divorce, as found here in Matthew, is the definitive teaching No other passages of Scripture are needed. Jesus said that divorce among his followers was not allowed except if one spouse commits adultery. Then the only Then and only then may the afflicted spouse divorce the guilty spouse. But But St. Paul added to the teaching of Jesus by stating that if an unbelieving spouse abandons a believing spouse, Then the believing spouse may rightfully divorce the abandoning spouse and be free to remarry you. So those are the only two reasons. But there are many scenarios that don't fit perfectly into the adultery or abandonment categories. Like spousal abuse. Thus it is helpful to turn to the Old Testament, just as we talked about last week, to see what the law of Moses says. My point is not to go down that line of thinking today to discover all that the Old Testament says on the subject of divorce, but only to mention that there is more to consider. But the point Jesus makes is not to focus solely on the issue of adultery and divorce But to compare how the world thinks about marriage and divorce in contrast to how his followers should think, you and I. Later in the ministry of Jesus, as recorded in Mark chapter 10, the Pharisees asked him about marriage and divorce by citing the law in Deuteronomy that allows a man to divorce their wives, allows men to divorce their wives by simply writing a letter of dismissal. That's all that was required. Both references to the law here in Matthew 5 and in Mark 10 are referring to Deuteronomy chapter 24. Where it goes to great lengths to describe what is allowed and not allowed when it comes to writing a letter of divorce and then remarriage. Interestingly, the passage in Deuteronomy 24 assumes that letter writing will take place. The law is not given so that the Israelites could know about how to go about divorcing. It is given because God knows the hearts. He knows it was already happening. And Jesus says to the Pharisees that God allowed such letter writing for divorce because of the hardness of their hearts. Another way to say it is that God knew that to place a higher higher standard upon Israel Giving them a law that was much greater than those around them would be too difficult for the Israelites. It would be too much for them. He knew they could not live up to the standard, a standard that Jesus changed. Because of Jesus, God's people can live up to the standard God had always intended. Which is for a man and a woman to remain faithfully married. And one of the reasons for the new standard It's for the followers of Jesus to think upon marriage differently than the world around them In the ancient Near East, the Gentile world saw marriage as a binding contract that closely simulated a business contract. Because it was a businesslike contract, the relationship could also be broken in a businesslike way. A letter of dismissal. God allowed Israel to behave like the world for a time. And when Jesus came, that time was up. No longer are God's people to behave like the world when it comes to marriage and divorce. We are to think differently than the world. We are to live by a higher standard. One of my political heroes is Ronald Reagan for a variety of reasons. First president I ever voted for. But what Governor Reagan did in 1970 lessens him in my eyes. In 1970, Governor Ronald Reagan of California signed the first no-fault divorce bill in the United States. Similar bills have since been passed in every state of the Union. For Christians, divorce is where we find all parties at fault. Next, where Jesus forbids us to take oaths based on certain truths, we find another way to think differently than the world. The ungodly say that a person can make a promise and not keep that promise because that promise might be based on something that is not binding. What is implied by the restrictions Jesus teaches is that people were swearing promises while invoking objects such as I swear by heaven or I swear by the city of Jerusalem, as if As if those things had the power to bless or curse, depending on whether the oath was kept or not. Apparently, it was also a practice to swear on one's life, as if the person had the power to curse himself or bless himself. Thus, Jesus was addressing baseless superstitions and replacing them with a standard that meant that a promise is a promise is a promise. Your word as a follower of Jesus is to be fulfilled because as followers of Jesus we are followers of the Word, as Jesus was the Word, and because when God speaks It comes to be. Thus we are to be the same. What we promised comes to be simply because we spoke it. Thus, thinking like Jesus is to throw off superstitions and to be people of our words. We too then must throw off superstitions and only trust in God to fulfill the words we promise. Perhaps it's not a surprise to many of you, but it is to me that of the four regions of the United States, you have the West, you have the Midwest. You have the South and you have the Northeast. That the South is the most superstitious, according to percentage of people, 42. 7% of the people in the South are superstitious about something. But what's surprising to me is that the East is not far behind. 42. 2% of people are superstitious in the East. A 0. 5 difference. In the South, some believe, quote, women should never put their purse on the floor, or they'll go broke financially. Also, you are never to clean, especially sweep, on New Year's Eve, or on New Year's Day, or you sweep good luck out of your life. Also, when two people are walking down a street and there is a pole in front of them, they're never to split the pole by each walking on the opposite sides. If they do, they will receive bad luck. In the South, some believe that if you see a red cardinal, someone you love is coming to visit. Others say, never tell anyone the dream that you had the night before until you've had breakfast, unless you want it to come to pass. Others believe that painting their porches blue wards off evil spirits. Generationally, baby boomers don't walk on cracks in the sidewalk to preserve their mother's backs. They also don't walk under ladders or open umbrellas indoors or go camping on Friday the 13th. Generation Xers knock on wood, believe bad news comes in threes, pick up four-leaf clovers, and avoid breaking mirrors. Millennials so far only believe in crossing their fingers and trusting in beginners' luck. As Christians, we are not to put our trust in what looks like an omen or some ritual or prescribed danger, but instead we are to trust in the only one who has true power. Power is not contained mysteriously in numbers or artifacts, but instead is only found in the God who made all things, and supposedly And supposedly those things that have mysteries and scary powers, those also were made by God as well. Jesus wants us to see a rabbit's foot for what it is. A rabbit's foot. He wants us to see the constellations for what they are. They are not there to predict our futures or to determine our steps. They are heavenly bodies that he placed there for us to envision his greatness and his glory. Our yes needs only mean yes, and our no only means no. The next difference from the world Jesus wants us to have is our thinking and our sense of justice. The world's sense of justice is as the Old Testament states: an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. You hurt me, allows me to hurt you back. You damaging me allows me to damage you. That makes everything equal. This standard of justice was well known in the ancient Near East. The Code of Hammurabi, for those who do not know, was a carved-in-stone set of rules that predate the Exodus by almost 300 years. These codes of laws that govern Babylon have a line that reads, quote, if a man knocks out the teeth of his equal, his teeth shall be knocked out. It would read for us teeth for teeth. Thus, such justice, this eye for eye, tooth for tooth, Israel already knew before God's law, and this is likely why God continued it. But Jesus is calling us to think differently, to think differently about the subject of justice. Jesus says not to resist what a person is trying to do to you. Jesus said that if someone smacks you on one cheek, offer the other cheek for them to slap. If someone wants to take the very clothes off your back, offer even more clothes. If someone wants you to take your time and effort for their sake, give them your time and effort and give them more than they ask for. I pause here to say that with these instructions, Jesus most certainly is asking us to think differently than the world. And maybe even too much differently. It could be that Jesus is speaking speaking in a hyperbolic manner again, just as he did when he told us to pluck at our eyes or to cut off our hands. What we can be certain of is that Jesus wants us to think differently about justice toward our fellow man. Consider what someone is doing when they slap your cheek. The person is expressing anger toward you in that particular moment. They want their justice now. A person who wants your tunic for time and labor wants it now. They are concerned most about the moment, the present, and getting what they think they have a right to get. Christians, in contrast, we are in the moment people, but not in terms of justice. In terms of justice, we are eternal people. Our concern, our thinking is to be about eternal justice. And that means we are concerned about heaven and hell. Like many young men, I struggled with this passage as a I questioned if God wanted me to be a wimp, allowing people to bully me. But wisdom from life and scripture has taught me that this passage is about one person seeking justice from another person. And Jesus is wanting us to be a witness about him when we are in such moments. This passage is about living as a testimony to him. When a person wants to hurt me because they want to steal from me, or simply harm me, or harm someone I love, or someone that needs help. Jesus wants me to step in and protect and defend and even harm if that is required in order to protect and defend. But if someone wants to hurt me because of my Christian faith, and that Christianity threatens them like it threatened the Jews and the Romans, a threat that was conjured in their minds, never real. It is then that I am to offer my other cheek, offer my tunic, my cloak, offer my two miles Because when offering my willingness to suffer, it is then that I am Christ Jesus to that person. And there is no more powerful way to witness the gospel of Jesus Christ. Than to be a suffering servant in the name of Jesus. This passage meant a great deal to the martyrs of the church because they knew they were being Jesus. As they were given opportunity to show Jesus to those who oppressed them. Where the world thinks of justice now, Jesus is thinking justice forever. And we are to be thinking about justice forever when it comes to sharing our Christian faith. St. James informs us that friendship with the world is hostility toward God. When you are friends with the world, you think like the world. Covenant promises in marriage can be abandoned according to worldly thinking because earthly happiness is the priority. Keeping your oaths is not necessary because what is best for you in the moment matters most. And justice in the eye of the self-righteous. Who get to determine when justice has been served, they want justice now But Jesus tells us to think differently. Marriage is a lifetime binding, a lifetime binding of souls. Your word as a believer in Jesus is binding. And your willingness to suffer injustice for the sake of your testimony of Jesus is priority. Your friends of this world will abandon you when you think in these ways. But Jesus won't. Let us pray. Our merciful God, we thank you for the standard that Jesus has set for all of us. It is undeniable that it is different than the world And yet our minds need to be opened. We need to be transformed and be renewed in our minds to think in these ways as we do. May you be glorified. Pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Holy Secrets
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. John Smith, and yes that was his name, spelled S M Y T H was a British barrister, which to us is a lawyer, who was a Christian evangelical advocate He ran youth camps for boys, upholding high moral standards as taught in the Bible, and he fought politically against homosexual marriage and sexual indecency. That his ministry had some unfortunate twists when a public schoolboy died in the care of one of his camps, being found naked and drowned. John Smith was not charged, but later Smith was accused of abusing several boys while running his Christian summer camps. Details included swimming naked with teenagers, showering with them in the nude, and encouraging them to talk about masturbation. One alleged victim from South Africa named that said that Smith administered savage beatings with wooden bats. which was a chilling echo of what was also said to have occurred in Britain. But Smith, a former friend of the Archbishop of Canterbury, Justin Welby Who was said to have no knowledge of any abuse claims, had the case against him dismissed a year later in Zimbabwe. Court documents from the time reported, quote, the particular allegations against Smith made the complainants walk naked to the swimming pool at night. That he took showers with them in the new, that he talked to them about masturbation, and told them to be proud of their anatomy because Jesus Christ was a man. Smith was also accused of assaulting the complainants on their rear bare buttocks with a tennis bat, table tennis bat. Smith left Zimbabwe in 2002 to move to South Africa, where he became a religious campaigner against gay rights. In summary, the schools, the camps, the churches Smith worked with all had reason to question Smith's behavior and tactics And to investigate the allegations made against him, but chose instead to trust in Smith's public personae. It was not until 2017 that Hampshire British Police reactivated the inquiry and found that the eyewitness accounts were credible. A spokeswoman said that no report was made to the police at the time of the first allegations, not least because the parents of the victims felt that their sons should be spared more trauma. The college involved had never sought to conceal these dreadful events, it said in a statement. In 2017, Smith refused to cooperate with investigators by refusing to return to Britain to face his accusers. He died in his home in South Africa in 2018 by undisclosed causes. Secrets, secrets are no fun. Secrets, secrets hurt someone. Mr. Smith had a secret, a very deranged and perverted secret, and it caught up with him in this life. For many people, their secrets don't catch up with them in this life, but as we believe, they will be accounted for in the life or death to come. All of us. All of us are tempted to have secrets in our lives. To have parts of our lives that only we know about Some secrets, such as drug and alcohol abuse, can be physically dangerous and damaging. Others, such as lust and envy and bitterness, can be internally dangerous and damaging. But when Jesus thinks secrets, he thinks of them in a holy manner. Secrets to Jesus are to be holy. It has been our attempt to examine how Jesus thinks and to align ourselves with the way of that thinking. And last week we saw how Jesus thinks differently than the world in very specific ways. Well, I don't imagine you can think much differently than the world by thinking of secrets in terms of holiness as opposed to having secret sins. From Matthew chapter six, verses one through four, it is implied that the self-righteous or hypocrites, as Jesus calls them made it public knowledge when they gave their money to aid the poor. Later Jesus teaches us about the widow's might and that What she gave was so much more than anyone else of wealth, because what she gave was all that she had, and she gave out of faith, and that was more valuable to the kingdom of God. The point of this giving, as Jesus describes in secret, is to rece I'm sorry, as the hypocrite after as the hypocrites gave, was done to receive praise from our fellow man. For doing a good deed. In John's Gospel, we learn that the hypocrites Jesus describes are the Pharisees. As John commentates, they love the praise of men more than they love praise from God. The Pharisees. Are a complicated bunch because at the time of their service, they were the conservative people. They were responsible for preserving the daily faith of the Jews when the Greeks and the Romans tried to control that region of what we now call Israel and control the city of Jerusalem. It was the Pharisees who kept the law of God before the people. At their origin, the Pharisees were contrasted by the people of Israel against the Sadducees. The Sadducees were the wealthy, priestly, ruling class, whereas the Pharisees were seen as the leaders of the local regions. They were the leaders of the average citizen. Because of their popularity amongst the average citizen, they grew in number and they grew in arrogance. By the time of Jesus walking among men, they had established themselves as the religious order to emulate, to idolize, and at some times to fear. Their notoriety, the praise of their fellow citizen, went to their heads. As fallen human beings. When we prioritize the praise of other fallen human beings as being the most important thing we can achieve in this life, the problem is grave indeed. Being an idol in the eyes of others can become an idol itself. We can too easily bow down to a system that will allow us to be praised by men. And our culture is so brazen about the importance of the praise of men that we have a national contest that uses the actual term idol. But in the kingdom of God, idols are smashed, idols are crushed and burned until every one of them is at the foot of the cross of Jesus Christ. Unfortunately, young people today have polled that over 50% prefer reaching the goal of being famous more than they desire achieving anything else in this life. And it doesn't seem to matter how the fame comes. The praise of men can be a drug. as is proven by a quote from one popular singer who said that she wished that fame was an IV that she could hook up to whenever she wanted, and that she lived for the applause. As Jesus said of the Pharisees, so he warns of all who seek earthly fame. Your reward will go no further than the praise you receive in this life. So Jesus thinks differently about the praise of men. Jesus thinks it should be avoided. Jesus thinks what other people do to be praised, his followers should do in secret. And so the secret life of a Christian is to begin with the money we give for the needs of others. Giving to help the needy is a religious duty. And those who give to those who have little, much praise is given to them, especially When we see people on the television, which we see every Thanksgiving, usually an athlete, given praise for handing out turkeys to the poor on Thanksgiving. The press loves to uphold such people and to show them as such giving people, but they do so, and you and I know this, for the praise they receive. But what we do as Christians must come from an inward principle, which is that we may be approved by God, not that we be praised by men. And we are told to take heed of this sin because it is a subtle sin. And vainglory creeps into what we do before we are aware. But the duty of providing for the needy isn't to cease because of the threat of hypocrisy. The doom of Christ Jesus that he describes at first seems like a promise. But it is their reward. Not the reward God promises to those who do good, but the reward of hypocrites promising to themselves, and a poor reward it is. That is the reward to be seen by men, and men do see them. And thankfully, there is a reverse truth. That when we take lesser notice of our good deeds, God takes more notice of them. In the end, He will reward us. Not as a master who gives to his servant for what he has earned and no more, but as a father who gives abundantly to his sons who serve him well. And next, Jesus said, we are to pray in secret. Perhaps it is taken for granted that all who are disciples of Christ pray. After all, to become a Christian, if you're not raised in the church, you have to pray. And if you are a sinner, which you are, you have to pray daily. You have to personally talk to God. It has been said that for the Christian, prayer should be like breathing. You should no sooner find a living person not breathing than find a Christian not praying. Because prayer should be so natural to the Christian, it would seem difficult to be hypocritical about it. But no, it also is easy to do in order to receive the praises of men. The scribes and the Pharisees were guilty of two great faults in their praying. They did it for vain glory and in vain repetition. Praying to God is a privilege. Praying to God in the name of Jesus is an even greater privilege. To do so in order to impress others is to burn cow dung having smoked rise as putrid incense. Of course, the persons who are most susceptible to pray for the praise of men are spiritual leaders. We can seek praise for the affluent words that we say. We can seek praise for how well we say those words. We can seek praise for the volume and the tone in which we pray And here is the truth. Any such praise received is of no value, for the prayers, regardless of content, are not heard. What we learn in Holy Scripture is that when we pray, we are to humble ourselves by asking God's favor upon us that we do not deserve. And the most powerful intercessions are those that are made of groanings that cannot be uttered. Next we are to practice is the practice or habit of repeating words. Repeating words is like the world, it's like the heathen. It was the idol worshippers who would chant the same phrases over and over, believing that the more they pray, the more they repeat the same prayer, the greater chance to be heard. by their false gods. Let us well study what is shown of the frame of mind of which our prayers should be offered, and learn daily how Christ prayed. Jesus went to be alone to pray. He prayed in secret. And while in secret, he praised his father. While in secret, he called God his Father While in secret he prayed the words, Not my will, but thine be done. While in secret, we are to do the same. The next thing we are to do in secret is to fast. The word fast literally signifies to abstain from food and drink, whether from necessity or religious observance. It is, of course, commonly applied in the Bible to religious purposes. It was then unusual Excuse me, it was in a usual expression of grief or sorrow. And we know this to be a natural response of the body that in times of grief and sorrow we are not disposed to eat, for we have no appetite. The grief of the soul is so absorbing as to destroy a natural appetite of the body People in deep affliction eat little and often pine away, falling into sickness because the body refuses on account of that deep sorrow of mind to take care of its own health. Fasting, then, is a natural expression of grief. It is not arbitrary. It is something that we naturally do when we are Depressed. It is therefore appropriate in times of penitence, of godly sorrow, of suffering When we are in pandemic, tempest, pestilence, plague, it is useful to humble us to bring us to reflection, to direct our thoughts away from the temptations of this world. It is therefore not acceptable except to be a real expression of sorrow. The Jews, interestingly, fasted often. There were four unofficial annual fastings One was the commemoration of the capture of Jerusalem, that's in Jeremiah 52. Another was for the burning of the temple in Zechariah 7. Another was for the death of Gedaliah, Jeremiah 4 41, and finally the commencement of the attack of Jerusalem in Zechariah 8. In addition, the Pharisees were known to have fasting at fasted twice a week. To fast with a sad countenance is to have a sour, morose look about you. But it is unfelt sorrow. The Pharisees fasted with disfigured faces. They tried to look the part of fasting They did not anoint and wash themselves as usual. They remained uncombed, filthy, and haggard It is said that they were often in the habit of throwing ashes on their heads and faces and mixing these with their tears. This all served to see suffering on their faces. So much pains were taken and so much suffering would they undergo and so much that was ridiculous would they assume to impose upon God and his people That they deceive neither God nor the people. God sees through such flimsy veils. Human eyes can pierce so thin a disguise. Hypocrites overacting their part, not having genuine principles of piety of heart. Not having the genuine expression, and hence they appear supremely contemptible and abominable Never should people exhibit outwardly more than they feel. And never should they attempt to exhibit anything for the mere sake of being praised by men. In such praise as Jesus said, they have their reward. They have all they desire, the praise of men, and the pleasures of arrogant display. So our fasting is to be done in secret, while our countenance are to appear as to be quite full and satisfied For what we do in secret is our holy living, and our Heavenly Father will reward us openly. The Greek there is properly translated in the future tense. It is for God to choose when and how to reward us openly who are faithful. And finally, we are to place our greatest wants and desires and hopes secretly in heaven, where the world clashes with one another over earthly power, over earthly wealth, over earthly justice, our treasures, which include Heavenly powers, heavenly wealth, heavenly justice are to be laid up in heaven, where they await for us who finish our journeys of faith in this life. To store up treasures on earth is also to love the praise of men. For much of what we store up is to display so that others can covet. Secrets, secrets are no fun. Secrets, secrets hurt someone. In terms of the sins of mankind, that saying is true. In the kingdom of God, Jesus wants us to think of secrets as opportunities to live righteously before God. So be challenged to live secretly. Secretly give to those who are in need. Secretly give so that your right hand doesn't know what your left hand is doing. Secretly pray, secretly fast, trusting and believing that God is the only audience you need. And as you do, treasures will naturally be stored up for you in heaven. Let us pray. God, we thank you for these truths that are to be done in secret And we confess how easily our flesh is drawn to do that which gets praise from men. Help us to see secrets as an opportunity to be holy. And to trust that you, as our only audience, is more than enough. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Anxious Distraction
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I encourage you to turn to Matthew chapter 6. As we pick up at verse 22, we'll be covering the entire section that was read for our gospel reading this morning, Matthew chapter 6. Speaking of at verse 22. Here is a story of a couple who received a phone call that informed them That the wife had won a raffle from a bride expo that she was attending for her future daughter-in-law. The prize was a $250 gift certificate and a three-night stay at a resort. Great, they thought. We will take it. Oh, but to get your prize, or prize is, you need to attend a 90-minute presentation. The presentation is in Williamsburg. Well, they were planning on being in Williamsburg for a three-night stay already, so hey, why not? Upon arrival, they found the pitch man to be very nice. He had seven kids. He was a Christian. He was going to give them a deal they could not turn down. The company's timeshares were available nearly all over the world. Their time, share card gave discounts at almost every national chain of stores and gas stations, but he couldn't tell them the price. Everybody vacations. Most families usually take vacations once a year. The cost is usually high. Why not take advantage of a low-cost vacation? Harvard did a study on vacations, and guess what? They're good for you The next step was to see their properties, which were under construction, but you could get an idea. The model condo was beautiful. There was nothing to dislike about it. But still, no price was given. They had to wait. Secretly, the pitchman whispered that they were going to be offered a special COVID price, but he wouldn't tell them what it was. That was for the boss to reveal. So 90 minutes now turned into two hours. And when the first prize came out, it was $32,000. But that was just a cover offer. When the boss came, he tried to seem desperate to offer them their special COVID offer of $9,900 with $2,300 down. It was an unbelievable offer, the couple was told. But the husband doesn't make such decisions in the moment. But the offer was only for today. That's the timeshare code. Only one day. The husband became irritated. He gave a counter-offer. He told them to waive any maintenance fees and he would take it. No, they can't waive maintenance fees. They can't tell you how high those fees will go up over time The husband, clearly irritated, says he's done. Keep your $250 card. He was done. Oh no, they said. The gift is yours. Please let us take you to where you can retrieve your gifts. So they go to another building where they sit down and talk with a woman who takes a departing survey and then gives them an even lower offer than $9,900. It was rejected, and the couple walked away, having a 90-minute presentation turned into over three hours, receiving a gift card that they regretted a lot. That night, or actually early morning, the wife could not sleep as she replayed the whole ordeal in her mind, feeling sorry for saying no and disappointing the pitch man. She didn't want to take the offer, but she didn't want to be disappoint a man who had seven children. Some people do that They replay conversations and events over and over again. Such obsessing seems to be a type of therapy. Thoughts like that keep people up at night. Our thinking, what we think about, attempts to overwhelm our days. We can obsess about uncomfortable situations, awkward conversations, arguments that we should not have had, events that disappointed us. And to this, and to this we add the things we worry about. And it is a wonder that some people can get any sleep at all. And our examination of how Jesus thinks, and then how we should think like him We come to passages of Scripture where Jesus tells us not to think about things we all too easily think about. As I read and reread these passages in Matthew chapter six, and I examined myself, I had to come to the conclusion That of all the passages of Scripture that I fail to live up to, these passages I struggle with the most, at least in everyday living. And I wonder how many in my hearing struggle as well, worrying about everyday things every day. These instructions by Jesus may fit in the category of being such a high standard to live up to that we conclude that Jesus didn't mean what he clearly said. So let's look at these verses, starting with the eyes. To best understand verse 22 and 23, we can look to Proverbs 20, verse 27. And there it reads that the Spirit of Man is the candle or lamp of the Lord. In other words, that which, under the name of conscience, the moral sense, the inner man. discerns spiritual realities, distinguishes right from wrong, giving the light by which we see our moral way. If conscience is single, and its understanding of right and wrong directs the whole body, including the life of a man, in all of its complex variety Singleness of intention to do right before God will preserve us from the snare of a double treasure, and therefore a divided heart. Right and wrong, according to the thinking of Jesus, is not double-minded. A moral standard cannot be good for one person and not good for another person. Morality in the thinking of Jesus is absolute. In regards to morality, Jesus isn't closed-minded, he is single-minded Remember that phrase. Not closed-minded, single-minded. All of us should be the same. This interpretation of the lamp of the eye being the single-minded morality is bolstered by the verses that follow. No human being can serve two masters, for no human can serve two masters as they should serve them. We will fall short if we try to serve both. Thus, no human being can be a follower of Jesus Christ and love something, anything other than Jesus. To think like Jesus is to be single-minded. It is to love Jesus and nothing else. Now, yes, of course, you can love your spouse, you can love your kids, but never before Jesus. You love them because you love Jesus. This refers to the instruction of Jesus for us to even even hate our closest family members in terms of being sure that he is first in our lives. And again, such is not a selfish request on the part of Jesus, for he knows that if we don't love him first and last, we will serve idols. Thus, the background of what Jesus is about to teach regarding our daily needs is how our moral conscience works, and that we cannot serve two masters. These two lessons set up what is possibly the most difficult standard of living that Jesus teaches, and that you and I fail to obey. The thinking of Jesus is that you and I should not think about our daily needs. And yes, I said needs, not wants. Look at verse 25 with me. It is fair to ask what he means by the word life. What he means by life is what I eat and what I drink and my body in general as to what I wear in regards to clothing. Yes, we say, life is more than food and clothing. We get that. Yes, we see the birds of the air and how they are provided for, without thought about how they are provided for. And yes, we believe God values us more than those birds. And yes, we humbly accept that we cannot add a qubit of measurement of anything to our lifespan by worrying about our life. That is what we eat, what we drink, what we wear. So why do I worry about my clothing? Good question. But I do. And I do, even knowing these words of Jesus. Yes, I can see the lilies of the field. They are indeed beautiful. And yes, I accept that Solomon was given more beautiful garments than those lilies. And yes, I believe God will care for me regarding the clothes I wear more than he cares for the lilies. And yes, Jesus, yes, Jesus, I am a man of little faith. Because as easy as it is to say I believe God will feed me and clothe me, As I need, I still worry about what I eat, what I drink, and what I wear. I worry about them every day. Verse 31 begins with, therefore. It means that what Jesus taught in the matter of rhetorical questions that it has a conclusion. We are not to worry about what we shall eat or what we shall drink or what we shall wear. Again, yes, the Gentiles, the unbelievers think about what they will eat and drink and what they will wear. They worry about such things. We're not to be like them. But we are. We do. The alternatives, Jesus states clearly We are to focus our attention. We are to think about the kingdom of God and the righteousness of God by believing. That all things will be eat, what we drink, what we wear, will be provided And then we get a second therefore, which is another conclusion. The argument goes that when you think about the kingdom of God and about God's righteousness and make those your priority That not only will all your daily needs be met, but when they are met, you will not need to worry about them the next day or the next day after that. Everything will be taken care of. You only need to focus on what is in front of you this day, the moment in which you are living. And we sigh when we hear these words. We can think of how freeing it would be to not be concerned about tomorrow. But we are. We are concerned about tomorrow and the day after tomorrow and next week and next month and next year. Consider how our worry is our motivation. I have seen young men have their lives turned for the better when they started to worry about how much they care for the woman they love and the life they wanted to build for them both. Those are good worries because they're good motivations. While I was in seminary, I got up at 5 a. m. in Kansas City, Missouri, during the winter months. to start a school bus so that I could take public school children to school, so that I could get paid, so that I could support my wife and children, providing them food, drink, and clothing. And my flesh wanted nothing to do with getting up at 5 a. m. and starting a school bus in the middle of a Midwest winter. But my worry, my concern, my responsibilities motivated me to get up and go to work. That was a good thing, right? But how does that scenario match up with the words of Jesus here? The answer must be in the teachings about our conscience. And our inability to serve two masters. And it must have something to do with the word that we translate here, worry. The Greek word translated worry is merima, which is better translated over-anxious and distracted. Over anxious and distracted. Jesus then thinks that being anxious about our daily needs distracts us from loving God. Jesus thinks that our motivations matter. Jesus wants us to think first about God and what we do in this life in regards to where we place our efforts. That is to be motivated by serving God. The teaching of Jesus here is against all anxious Immoderate, perplexing, and distressing thoughts and cares that arise from despair and unbelief, which are all dishonorable to God. We cannot say that we believe in God and next fret about our daily needs when the God we believe in says that He loves us and wants us to call Him Father. And as a father, he has said that if we ask for a fish, he will not give us a stone. That would be absurd. Just as absurd as thinking that God will not want to do good to us. To believe you will not be provided for your daily bread is to not know God. He instead is a father who provides for his children. And that includes providing for your health during a pandemic. Concern about our daily needs are the same as concerns about staying alive. We want to eat, drink, and be clothed to stay alive We want to live, but as Christians, we are to want to live for the sake of honoring the Heavenly Father, not to simply stay alive for the sake of staying alive. Beloved, let me state the obvious because the obvious is not stated enough. You and I are going to die. Our bodies will rot away in our own personal graves. And as I shared at the funeral of Mary Lauer, While in our graves, other generations will rise up if the Lord tarries. Other generations will rise up, and then they too will die, and the memory of our lives will fade away. Within a few generations, we may no longer be spoken about or remembered in any meaningful way. That's the truth. That is not a criticism of anyone. My children know little about my great-grandfather on my father's side They know little about him because I know very little about him. My parents, grandparents rarely spoke of him, and my parents never spoke of him. He is, for all purposes, forgotten. If you are challenged by that point to do better at telling your children about their great-grandparents, that's great. But that's not my point. My point is that while we will be forgotten in this life, our hope is only for God to not forget us. And you can know God won't forget you when our conscience is clear before Him, having confessed and confessed and confessed again our sins We can know God won't forget us when we serve only Him. And we can know God won't forget us when we are not anxious about what we eat, drink. Or where, but believe instead that God will take care of us. Like the wise I described at the beginning of this sermon. who is tempted to stay awake at night because she can't stop thinking about failed encounters and worrying about misunderstandings I am tempted to stay awake at night to worry about the state of the Christian church, including our parish.
