I am not worrying as in being overly anxious or distracted. I am worrying in terms of great concern. We are in the middle of a pandemic and we are Christian. We are believers in the Lord Jesus Christ, who said he would never leave us or forsake us. We are promised that to die is gain for us. We are instructed to fear nothing but God Himself, who can send both our souls and bodies to hell. We are to look at life in this world as us already being dead because Jesus said whoever tries to save his life will lose it, and whoever loses it for his sake will save it in the end. We are all about death as Christians, because we are all about eternal life. So if you are anxious about this pandemic, I call you to repent. It is a sin. Be honest with your Heavenly Father and repent. It is a sin to be anxious about such things. Such anxiousness distracts from being faithful. Trust your Heavenly Father, because of Jesus, to provide for what you need in this life. And even if your life is cut shorter than most, it is still a gain for you. Several years ago, we had a men's meeting where we invited the Reverend David Crumb, former pastor of Bishop Cummins, to speak to us He used the opportunity to tell us of his experience when he was wounded in battle as a Marine serving in Vietnam. He stated confidently that since that time he has never been afraid to die. Upon hearing him, I humbly confessed to God and to others That I could not share that same testimony. There was still something about the unknown upon dying that I feared. Yet, through this pandemic, I have been given the confidence today that I too am not afraid to die. And it is not because of anything about myself that gives me that confidence. It is instead the fear that I have seen in others that has made me realize how Christians are to live. In Jesus, we are free. We are free indeed. And that includes fear, fear of death. And beloved, this sermon is not about wearing masks. Wear them, don't. But fear God and God alone. I told you the devil was in wearing masks. He is. Hear that and be warned. I close with the following quote. It is the last line of a poem about fear written by G. K. Chesterton. He said, Like emptied idiot masks, sins, loves, and wars, stare at me now. For in the night I broke the bubble of a great world's jest and woke, laughing with laughter, such as shakes the stars. Let us as Christians wow. Amen. Let us pray God, we accept these challenging words from your son. And we say that We see how easy it is to be anxious about tomorrow, to be distracted about tomorrow Father, forgive us and give us strength to care about today and only today, and to trust that you have everything cared for. And that yes, we take the challenges to die is gain, to live is Christ. It is in his name that we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: The Heavenly Father Loves Us, but
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.source_file: The Heavenly Father Loves Us, but.txt
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. May be seated. The title of this sermon Is the Heavenly Father loves us, but dot dot dot. You will see in a you will see why in a moment Perhaps there is no greater feeling in life than when one person is romantically sweet on another person, and when that interest is known and is then reciprocated. I pursued my beloved the old-fashioned way. I wrote her a letter asking if she would be willing to correspond via mail, i. e. the United States Postal Service. During her senior year in high school and my sophomore year in college. And I cringe that there is a generation that does not know what it means to correspond by the United States Postal Service. But she said yes, and the joy that I had was almost indescribable. But that was just the beginning of my pursuit. After months of correspondence, we had our first date. It was a snow ski trip on Thanksgiving break I picked her up and we drove three hours for her stay at her brother's home with the plan of skiing the next day. The conversation was awkward, but the awkwardness was worth it During that weekend, we prayed together for the first time. When we drove back Sunday night, we held hands for seemingly the whole three hours. It was incredible to be liked so affectionately by another person who you yourself liked very much. Eventually that light turned into committed love, and there is no greater security emotionally than to be committed in love to someone who is committed in love to you Such a description of committed love as a relationship brings us to think like Jesus Thinks. That's our series, Thinking Like Jesus Thinks. Which includes Jesus thinking how much God wants to be in a committed relationship with his people. The best way that I know to summarize the meaning of life as the Bible teaches it is that God wants to be our God and he wants us to be his people. Describing it another way. The purpose of humanity being created, of being tempted in the garden, of humanity being promised a deliverer after Coming worthy of death, the purpose of a flood preserving humanity, of a man named Abraham being chosen, of a nation Persevering of God giving his law and giving Israel land and giving them kings in the line of David And giving his only son, Jesus, the purpose of Jesus dying, being raised, and ascending to heaven, of the Holy Spirit being sent to dwell amongst God's people. The purpose of Jesus coming again, all of it, for the purpose of God being our God and for us to be his people. Hear this from Jeremiah 31. God said, This is the covenant I will make with the people of Israel. After that time, declares the Lord, I will put my law in their minds and write it on their hearts. I will be their God and they will be my people No longer will they teach their neighbor or say to one another, know the Lord, because they will all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the Lord. For I will forgive their wickedness and remember their sins no more. And from the book of Revelation, we hear the fulfillment of that prophecy in Revelation 21. John wrote, Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth passed away, and there was no longer any sea. I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, Look, God's dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain. For the old order of things has passed away. From these verses we can say that Jesus Wants us to think about God the Father in the manner of him wanting to be our God, which is to be the most intimate of fathers. As Jesus continued the sermon, he describes God as a father who eagerly and expectantly wants to hear from his children. The instruction for his followers to speak and knock is for his followers to make his kingdom their priority. And again, we revisit the why of God's kingdom being a priority, it is because if it is not, we will fall into idol worship. And Jesus wants us to think about the Heavenly Father in comparison to earthly fathers to encourage us to knock so that the kingdom of God would be open to us and to encourage us to seek so that the kingdom of God would be found. And I would tell you that those words, their tenses in the Greek knock and seek, communicate a repetitive action. We are to knock and keep on knocking, seek and keep on seeking. These words are to encourage us to do these things, for Jesus wants us to think about God as freely opening the kingdom of heaven as we knock, and freely revealing the kingdom of God as we seek. The thinking is that if earthly fathers would provide simple requests of their children, how much more would God provide for his children? At the end of that teaching, Jesus' point then is to think as if God will care for us. In a committed love relationship from a Heavenly Father, and that after we receive that from Him, we should reciprocate it by doing for others as we want them to do for us. Thus, the golden rule is in the context of trusting our Heavenly Father as our caretaker and in a committed love relationship And once I have faith in God as my Heavenly Father providing for me, I will then turn and give to others freely. Speaking of the golden rule, I once watched a panel discussion about ethics, and the panel included a Christian, a deist, an agnostic, and an atheist. The atheist argued that the golden rule was a byproduct of ethical evolution. When he was told that it actually came from Jesus, He said, well, humanity would have come up with that rule eventually. And we can all respond, well, humanity didn't. I said that Jesus wants us to think and to understand and have faith that the Heavenly Father loves us and that all of what has occurred in the world since the beginning of creation occurred because He wants us to be His people. And that is a very deep and profound answer to the why of life. Questions regarding the meaning of life can be answered with that answer. But I also titled this sermon with the conjunction dot dot dot dot. For while Jesus wants us to think in these ways, he wants us to realize that all that comes with a price Both on his part and on our part. Jesus follows up his golden rule with a contrast between the gates that lead to two contrasting paths. The first gate is narrow, he says. But he quickly turns to contrast it to the wide gate, because the wide gate is the more popular gate It is the gate that many, let us say, most people go through. But that gate and that road lead to destruction, eternal destruction. In contrast, the narrow gate is hard to get through and leads to a path that is difficult to walk. And thus few find that gate and go through that gate, even though behind that gate is reward of life, eternal life. Jesus then wants us to think that converting to be his disciple is the most difficult thing you will ever do because when you convert to following him you are to leave the person you were behind you Your old person is to stay outside the narrow gate while the new person walks the narrow path. And that means leaving a lot of friends Who you want to stay friends, but leave them in their sinful world while they walk the wide road. Converting to follow Jesus means you cannot be close friends with people on the wide road because they are going a different way than you are going. That truth is especially hard for young people to accept, for them to want to be not true. They want to have it both ways. They they want to be Christian, of course, but they also want friends Friends who reject Jesus. And eventually one of those relationships is going to win out. It is thus necessary for Christians to think of their life as naturally counterculture, counterculture to the world. St. Athanasius said that if the world stands against truth, that as a Christian, I must stand against the world. And in case you have not been paying attention, the world is more and more standing against the truth. Thus, Christians must more and more stand against the world. That is not easy. It does not get you invited to many social gatherings. People don't want you to speak at their public functions. They know what you stand for, and what you will say will not be what they want to hear. If you care to know how easily the world wants to silence you once you go against it, Consider this brief account of what happened to Christians in Russia after 1917 under the Soviet leader Vladimir Lenin. When Christians stood against the socialist world of the new Russia. Quote: In order to draw attention to this merciless war Show trials for clergy and lay people who the Soviet Union claimed had resisted their confiscation orders were held. Some trials featuring more than a hundred accused at a single trial. The verdicts were a foregone conclusion, with executions happening nearly immediately after the sham trials were completed. Two-thirds of Russia's 1,025 monasteries were closed. Initially, they permitted a few public debates between Christians and atheists. the most skilled debater for the Christian side being an evangelical Protestant professor named Martin Skowski, but they shut them down once it became apparent that these debates had the potential of backfire. Martin Stofsky was arrested and sent into exile in 1922 because of his ability to persuade people of the truth of Christianity. And the authorities informed him that he would be allowed to return once people were wise enough to see through his lies. He was, of course, never allowed to return. The wave of terror unleashed by the Bolsheviks was unprecedented in scale and viciousness. Archbishop Andronik of Perm was forced to dig his own grave and then shot Bishop Germogin of Tobolsk was lashed to the paddle wheel of an enormous steamboat and twisted to death by the blades. The communists also established their first major concentration camp in Solovitsky Islands, a former Orthodox monastery, which they ominously redubbed the Camp of Special Purpose. The house of special purpose had been the place where the Tsar and his family had been kept and then executed. Between 1917 and 1935, over 130,000 Orthodox priests were arrested And 95,000 of them were shot by execution squads. More than 8,000 were murdered in the initial skirmishes over church treasures. It all sounds so extreme. So extreme that you would think it's not true. But it is. Such is the possibility when you go against the world. Another reason why I say that Jesus wants us to think, to understand, to have faith, that God the Father wants to be our God and does care for us, and then use the conjunction but dot dot dot. Is that Jesus next warns against false prophets? False prophets are also why the gate is narrow and few pass through it. It is easy to be deceived. The devil raises false prophets who seem to be saying the right things. They even use the name of Jesus. They can sound like true teachers, but that is the devil's way. He puts a little lie with more truth. And the lie eats away like a small amount of leaven and a large lump of dough. We are to test the people we allow to influence our faith We are to look at their lives and evaluate whether they have good fruit or bad fruit. And today I would argue that bad fruit is too much fruit. In other words, preachers who are living up in the upper 1% tax bracket are guilty of simony and should be pointed out as false teachers. Their too much fruit is fruit for themselves as they miser money out of the poor and the widow. They should be cut down and thrown into the fire, for they will be thrown into the fire of judgment. And finally, the word but is used for the warning Jesus gives that not everyone who calls him Lord will enter the kingdom of heaven. In fact, there will be people in the last day, the day of judgment, who believed they were following Jesus and they were not. They prophesied in the name of Jesus. They cast out demons in the name of Jesus. They did wonders, miracles in the name of Jesus. And after all of that, Jesus surprisingly says to them, I never knew you. Depart from me, you who practice lawlessness The real truth being that there are people who do many things in the name of Jesus, but live sinful lives otherwise. We have heard about the priests who oversee Mass while scheming to molest young children, but it is not just in the Roman Catholic tradition. There are evangelical churches that harbor ministers with the same perverted schemes to molest children. There are ministers who scheme to have affairs with staff and lonely parishioners. And there are people who dwell in the Christian world. to experience the power of God while avoiding the holiness of God as they lie and steal and cover their sins. And there are ministers who use the name of Jesus to build worldly empires. But these are the most obvious. There are also people who sit in pews, not making money off of Jesus, but using the name of Jesus to soothe their conscience. To look good in the community, to experience religion without honestly knowing who Jesus is. They don't know him, and therefore he does not know them. Preaching a sermon like this is concerning because it can be interpreted that Christianity is a conditional religion. Meaning that conditions have to be met in order for people to truly know that they are saved. That would make it like every other religion, in that it appears that humans earn the favor of God. But we know elsewhere that we are saved by grace through faith. It's not of our own works. It is but by the blood of Christ. But, dot dot dot. Jesus said the gate to heaven is narrow. Jesus said that false teachers will try to lead us astray. Jesus said that there will be many that will think they know him, but truly and honestly never did. This requires us to go against the crowd, to protect ourselves from false teachers. To be sure that we know Him. The Christian faith requires service to God. It requires us to reciprocate the committed love that God shows us. It requires us to live, to live out our faith, even during difficult and confusing days. So let us do just that and live out our faith. Let us pray. Our God, we thank you for the challenge that is so very clear in your word as Jesus spoke them, and it does require us to change our thinking. To understand that this is not something we casually do, but is something that we are to be committed our whole lives to, every day. Father, deepen us in our understanding of that commitment, that we might be known by you, that we might hear our name in the last day. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Thinking the Opposition of Jesus
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: That is a fantastic hymn for these days, is it not? In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. May be seated. This is my last sermon in the series of Thinking Like Jesus. I started the series because there was so much unrest in our culture, and I saw it bleeding out. into the Christian community, so much so that I perceive that we were being tempted to approach Cultural problems, in the same manner the secular world approaches cultural problems, and that is not how Jesus approached cultural problems. Jesus thought and acted differently than the world around him The Greek word ecclesia refers to a gathering of God's people for a particular task. The word is at the root of what we call the church. We are a people called together for a particular task, and that task is to glorify God and enjoy him forever. It is to love God with all of our hearts, all of our souls, and all of our minds. And it is to love our neighbor as ourselves. And that second part is where Christians get confused. When you see a man, a black man, pinned down by a policeman, And the man is clearly in distress, and nothing is being done about it, you perceive as a Christian that you are not loving your neighbor if you do not speak up. And then when you speak up against such treatment by police, the message gets hijacked by other people who have. A political agenda that far outpaces anything Holy Scripture condones. Thus examining how Jesus thought and how he reacted Allows us to recenter ourselves within the kingdom of God so that we don't get carried away by the whims of sinful men. Well such as well there is much more, excuse me, to examine and learn from how Jesus thought I need to close this series because it could delve into so many nuances that it might not ever have an end. And I want to close it by examining, or better said, imagining, what it would be like to live in a world that felt the opposite way of Jesus. Perhaps, just perhaps, if we were to consider living in a world that thought the opposite of Jesus, then we would increase our appreciation all the more regarding how Jesus actually thinks. And with that increased appreciation, we would strive to think more like him. You would think that to live in a world where people thought the opposite of Jesus, that that would be a very difficult thing to do. I anticipate that it would be so hard to live in such a world that we cannot imagine it to its fullest extent. Such a realization, this imagining what it would be like to live in a world that thought the opposite of Jesus. I started to consider this after reading the following post on social media. This example provides perspective regarding the days in which we live. It started out like this. Imagine you were born in nineteen hundred. When you were fourteen, World War One starts. and ends on your 18th birthday with 22 million people killed. Later in the same year that war ends, the Spanish flu epidemic hits the planet and runs until you are 20 years old. 50 million people die from it in those two years. Yes, fifty million. When you are twenty-nine years old, the Great Depression begins, unemployment hits 25%. The global gross domestic product drops to 27%, and that runs all the way until you're 33 The country nearly collapses along with the world economy when you are when you turn twenty-nine um thirty-nine, and then World War II begins, and you aren't even over the hill. When you're 41, the United States has fully pulled into World War II. Between your 39th and 45th birthday, 75 million people perish in the war, and that doesn't include the six million that die in the Holocaust. At fifty-two years old the Korean War starts and five million more people perish. At sixty-four the Vietnam War begins and it doesn't end for many years. Four million people die in that conflict, approaching your 62nd birthday. You have the Cuban Missile Crisis, the tipping point of the Cold War. Life on the planet as we know it could have ended right there. As you turn 75, the Vietnam War finally ends. Still ahead is the Watergate scandal, terrorist attacks. your Cold War standoffs, and as you reach 101 years old, you get to see planes flying into skyscrapers. And the decades I just described are called the good old days. And in those days Most people in America were supposedly, supposedly, God-fearing Christians. Again, what would it be like if there were not God-fearing Christians? If everyone thought the opposite and then acted the opposite of Jesus. In Matthew 18, which was our gospel reading this morning, Jesus thinks it is best. To approach life like little children. The virtue in little children that he wants us to emulate is their humility. But let us be careful. Let us be careful here not to place our 21st century perspective on little children into this teaching of Jesus. Children in the ancient Near East were never coddled. Children in the days of Jesus were truly to be seen and not heard. Children in the days of Jesus were considered considered servants to their parents. They were not treated above how a household servant was treated until they came of the age, and that age was turning thirteen, when a boy was considered a young man and a girl was considered eligible for marriage Before the age of 13, a boy or a girl was to be subservient to his or her parents and fully dependent upon the parents for their daily living. Thus, such children, being humbled by their life circumstances, were eager to learn, to mature, to receive from their parents. This is how Jesus wants his followers to be towards him. We are to be humbled and thus eager to learn, eager to mature in the faith and to receive from our God. But what if we were to do the opposite? The opposite would be to be prideful, as pride is the opposite of humility. What if we were to think that instead of being subservient, we should be served? What if instead of being eager to learn, we were eager to have others learn from us? What if an eagerness to mature that we became determined to remain immature? What if instead of receiving from our parents, we were to take from our parents and think that their wealth is rightfully ours, because we are younger, we are more wise about the world? Perhaps that world is not hard to imagine after all. Supposedly today's new generation, some are calling them Generation Z believes they are owed leadership positions in our culture because those of us who have gone before them have botched things like climate change. We have run the economy into the ground, allowing corporate greed. And we have embarrassed ourselves by not accepting that there are more than two genders. Thus, we are disqualified at this time to hand, and we must hand over the keys to those who can finally make this world the utopia that only they can make it. However, in truth, not much has changed. I'm old enough to remember the 1960s. That young generation of the 1960s thought the same way And they're still running the country. How's that going? Jesus next reveals that he thinks that the youngest people among us are to be the most protected when it comes to their spiritual health. Little children believed in Jesus. They approached him and were held by him. Jesus truly does love all the children of the world. And they are also so special to him that he warns that if anyone is responsible for causing a little child to sin, that person who does so will be judged harshly. So harshly that he will prefer to have a heavy stone around his neck and thrown into the sea than to endure the punishment that God has set aside for him. The sin referred to, causing a child to sin, is primarily referring to unbelief, as in causing a little one not to believe in Jesus. I believe there are two primary causes for a child not believing in Jesus. The first is what he or she is taught or not taught. Parents who put their children in schools that do not claim Jesus as Lord and Savior are dangerously teaching their children. Parents who do not themselves teach their children about Jesus are not fulfilling their baptismal vows. Decide what a child is taught or not taught. The second cause of a child not believing in Jesus is parents who are living as hypocrites. A child quickly comes to the conclusion that if his or her parents don't practice what they say they believe, then why should I? And as soon as such a child is able, they stop attending church and start behaving like an unbeliever. There are, of course, other ways to cause a child to sin, which leads us to imagine if we were to think the opposite of how Jesus thinks. Instead of protecting children, let us instead make their spiritual health vulnerable. Let's tell them all the reasons why they shouldn't believe in Jesus Let's point to all the hypocrites of today and throughout the history of the church. Let's get them to think that no one actually believes that Christianity stuff. Let's get them to question the history of the Bible. Let's get them to even question if Jesus was a real person Let's get them to think that miracles are not possible. Let's get them to think that the other Bible stories are in the same manner that our culture thinks about fairy tales. Treat them all the same What would that culture be like? What would that world be like? I wonder if it would cause children not to treat life itself Sacredly. I wonder if not treating life sacredly would result in children taking guns to school and killing their fellow students I wonder if it would increase the rate of suicide among teenagers. I wonder if we would see an increase of cyberbullying. I wonder if there would be an increase of child pornography and child molestations and children being exploited sexually in movies. Hear about that? But there is no proven correlation between getting children to doubt the existence of God and not treating life sacredly, so I guess it's only in my imagination. Hmm. Thinking about the need for all of his followers to be humble like little children causes caused Jesus to think about adults, causing children to not believe in him, which led him to think about the judgment that such people would come under if they would lead such a child astray. That thought leads to him thinking about the seriousness of sin and how serious he wants his followers to think about sin. He uses the hyperbole once again to get the point across. Cut it off. Pluck it out. And we can say unplug it if it causes you to sin. Habitual sins affect us in our relationship with God and one another. Affairs destroy families. Stealing dismantles reputations. Lying breaks trust. Coveting corrupts and hardens the heart. None of it is harmless All of it requires death, and when you live in sin, you live in death, both death in your spiritual life and death in your relationship with the Heavenly Father. But let us think the opposite of Jesus. What would the world be like if we didn't take sin seriously? What if sleeping with another man's wife was perfectly normal if both parties are consenting? What if being able to steal another person's property fits the same rule as finders, keepers, losers, weepers? What if lying was perfectly acceptable both by governing authorities and the general public? Documents you sign don't have to be accurate. Promises you make are never binding, written, or oral. News reports can be simply made up for political gain. Criminals wouldn't need to cooperate with the police, and the police couldn't be trusted Gee, I wonder what that world would be like. Would there be chaos in the streets? Would it mean that neighbor would fight against neighbor and sibling against sibling? I wonder if people would ever think about Jesus' warning of being cast into hell. Think it's really no big deal because well that's where all the people the cool people are going to go anyways. I wonder what that world will be like. Next, Jesus turns his attention back to the little ones. To despise is to look down upon and disregard it is to see children as not having intrinsic value. But the value of children is so great, Jesus says that God keeps special watch over the angels that are assigned to those children. Children truly do have guardian angels. The love Jesus has for children is next next expressed in the parable of the Good Shepherd, who would without question, seek out and find just one sheep that was lost, even with ninety-nine still in the pen The rejoicing by the shepherd after finding the lost sheep should bring a smile to our faces, as we can imagine Jesus rejoicing when a child confesses him and loves him and follows him. But we are imagining what it would be like to live in a world that thought the opposite manner of Jesus We would then think of children having no intrinsic value. With no value, it would not matter how we treated them. We could molest them. Exploit them, abuse them, enslave them, ignore them, and even go so far as to kill them. What would it be like to live in a culture that molested, exploited, abused, and killed its own children, even killing them before they were born? Hmm, I wonder. And yes, here I go again mentioning abortion. It is a plague upon us, and any culture, cultural confusion we fall into, I believe, is connected in some way to the sin of abortion. That sin that plagues this country and our world. And don't doubt me when I say it. And if you have had an abortion, don't be wrapped with guilt. You have been living in a world that has told you that such behavior is natural in its right. The sin of abortion can and does and will be forgiven by God Don't let your past stop you from standing up against abortion. We need to confess it as a personal and national sin. Upon thinking again about children being led to sin, to unbelief, Jesus next addresses what his followers are to do when a brother sins and does not repent. That part we did not read in our gospel reading. I will not rehearse the steps because that is not the point of this sermon. We are examining how Jesus thinks about such occurrences, and his directives tell us that he thinks it is most important for a wayward Christian to be brought to repentance and to be brought back into the church. The primary goal of church discipline is so that the guilty person would be saved and be forgiven. It is not to humiliate, it is not to embarrass or shame, it is to bring someone to repentance and be forgiven. But we are thinking the opposite and imagining what that would be like what that would be like to live in such a world If Jesus thinks church discipline is for restoring a lost sinner, then we are to not confront the sinner, but instead leave him in his sin. Who cares what he does? It's none of my business and none of yours if a man in the church cheats on his wife or drives drunk or steals from his neighbor or even murders another human being Let live and let live as the motto goes or in case of a sinning brother having murdered someone, we can say live and let die. That was a really bad joke. Can you imagine living in a world where you didn't need to concern yourself about people that you know that they're going to hell? Imagine a world where you didn't care enough about a brother or sister in Christ to mention to them that their current lifestyle is dishonoring to God. Imagine not confronting a fellow Christian who is blatantly living in sin because, well, you're just a little bit too shy and embarrassed. What would that be like to live in such a community? We don't know anyone who is not caring about the souls of his brother or sisters, do we? Hmm. I know I have been obvious with my examples, as I've tried to show that We don't have to imagine any of these things because they are all around us. We have been describing our culture. I am being obvious to show how our culture has fallen so very far from thinking like Jesus and how life could be so much richer. fuller and peaceful in spirit if we were to start thinking like Jesus. Jesus thought that little children mattered. Mattered a great deal. He thought sin mattered and mattered a great deal. He thought sinners being repentant and being brought back into the church mattered a great deal. Simply stated, so should we. Let us pray. Our God, we are once again challenged by these words of our Savior, your Son. And we come to them quite humble, knowing that the standard is not being lived up to. Certainly not by our culture, but perhaps even not in our individual lives. Let us all together be as one and take these standards as our standards. Father, help us to think like Jesus. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Our Resources In Christ
sermons.speaker: Rev. William Vowles
sermons.text: Let us pray. The words of my mouth and the meditations of our hearts be acceptable in thy sight, O Lord, our strength and our redeemer. In the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost. Amen. Maybe seated. If we open our Bibles up this morning to our first lesson from Ephesians chapter 3, we are encouraged. With a wonderful prayer from the Apostle Paul. It is actually the second prayer given to us in this letter to the Ephesians, the first one we find back in chapter 1. The apostle has told us that we are possessors of the unsearchable riches in Jesus Christ, that our resources are limitless And that we are more than conquerors. In chapter one of his letter, he prayed that we would understand that. And in chapter three, he prays that we would apply it. In chapter 1, we have a prayer for enlightenment. In chapter 3, a prayer for enablement. In chapter 1, he prayed in verse 17. that we would have an attitude of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Christ. And in verse 18, that the eyes of our hearts Would be enlightened that we might know. In other words, that we might come to the realization of our riches in Christ Jesus. Unfortunately, many Christians today are seemingly ignorant about the resources that are available to them in Christ. sermons.title: Typology
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Recall with me The conversation Jesus had with the two men on the road to Emmaus after his death and resurrection. Remember that the two men did not know that they were talking to Jesus. From the Gospel according to St. Luke, the text reads And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he, Jesus, explained to them what was said in all of the scriptures concerning himself. Of course, we are not told exactly what the passage of Scripture Jesus referred to, but those words of summary by Luke Should be devastating to any argument that would say that the Old Testament is irrelevant to Christians or even less important to Christians than the New Testament reveals. Consider, please, that when it reads in Luke the phrase all the scriptures, that there was no other scriptures at that time but the Old Testament. Thus, Jesus himself used the Old Testament to describe himself, which for me begs the question. What scriptures are best to describe the person of Jesus? And there is this question. If you were going to explain who Jesus was and is by only using the Old Testament, which ones, which verses would you choose? Now, before you attempt to answer that question, think in general how difficult it is to describe Jesus using any recourse you wish. When you say one thing about him, you also have to say something else, almost the opposite, because you don't want to convey that he is limited by any one description For example, we could say that Jesus is loving, which he is, but we should also be saying that he is a judge of righteousness. Which he is. And we should also say that he touches, converses, and socializes with the unholy Which he does. But we could say also that he is holiness itself, which he is Jesus was caring to those who wanted to be healed, and he was withdrawn from those of his own hometown who would not see him as the Messiah. Jesus spoke gently to the woman caught in adultery and harshly to the Greek woman who wanted her daughter released from demon possession. Jesus came to save his own people, but found greater joy in seeing the faith of the Gentiles. Generally stated, Jesus, knowing him and explaining him is like nailing jello to a wall. Jesus is difficult to describe. He is more than complex. He is eternally mysterious. His depth of character is, on the one hand, unsearchable And yet, on the other hand, he is very much searchable. He is, after all, eternal. He is Almighty God. He is the creator and sustainer of all creation. And yet we, in contrast, are finite. We are merely part of the creation. We are his created beings. What we can know and verify about Jesus in this life is only found in Holy Scripture. And it is even found in the Old Testament, the same passages Jesus used to teach the men on the road to Emmaus. When we look into the Old Testament, we discover that there are several layers to the stories that are told and the commands that are given. Looking at the stories and commands initially is like looking at the scenery provided by a green pasture that we look at from afar off. As a whole, we can take it in and we can enjoy its vastness and its greenery, but when we come closer and explore the pasture, we see the dips in the ground, the crevices, the burrows, the patches of grass, here and there, the rocks, both jagged and smooth, the trees and the bushes of several different species. Thus, we can realize that there is more to the pasture than we initially saw, than we initially understood. I thought about this from our plane ride home last week. I was blessed to have a window seat, and we flew over in clear skies the Cascade Mountains. And then the dry plains of eastern Washington and then Idaho and then flying over the Rocky Mountains What I was viewing was awe-inspiring, but only a general view from above without experiencing the many details that make up those mountain ranges and those vast plains and by the way the state of Wyoming is really ugly just for the record The point being that all of the details of that scenery make up the scenic beauty that is seen from afar off, but the details of that beauty matter. The details are what makes up the scenic pasture, the grand mountains, the vast plains. The details make it beautiful, even though you cannot see them. In the same manner, for Holy Scripture and for Jesus Himself, the details make up the beauty that is seen. Now many of you were trained as children to know the stories of the Bible, and that is our focus today in our parish school and in our Sunday school, our focus is that our children know the stories of the Bible. They should know who Abraham was, who Isaac was, who Jacob was, in chronological order. They should know the placing of Rehoboam and God's calling of the kings. They should know the era of the prophets and the messages of Micah and Isaiah. They should know the difference between Elijah and Elisha. They should know why Jeremiah preached the way he did, and why Ehud stabbed King Egon. It is important that both adults and children be biblically literate so that when we talk amongst ourselves and reference Biblical stories, we know what we are talking about so that we can build up one another. I am romantic about the story. of the British forces being trapped on the beaches of Dunkirk during World War II. As British officer as a British officer realized the possible devastation that could have occurred if the Germans attacked while they were gathered in masses, with little to shield them as they radioed London for rescue. When it was not clear how these 338,000 British and French troops were to were going to get off that island. A British officer at Dunkirk messaged back to the authorities in Britain three simple words. He radio to them, but if not. During that era in British history and culture, the message was immediately recognized as a reference to the book of Daniel. Lord Nebuchadnezzar was going to punish those three Hebrews, Shabbrach, Meshach, and Abednego, by throwing them into the furnace because they would not worship that golden image. They defied the king's command and professed that God would save them, and then they added, but if not Meaning that if God doesn't choose to save them from the fire, they still would not bow down and worship the image. The biblically literate officer. And Great Britain at large were encouraged and strengthened because they knew God's word and how it was to be applied in that historical moment. Oh, how we wish the same could be said today about our culture. But alas And just as it is beneficial to know the stories of the Bible, it is also beneficial to know the particulars of the stories or the details of the stories. It might be asked if it matters exactly what offering Cain gave to the Lord in worship. Does it matter that Esau was hairy? Does the number three have any significance when Peter denied Jesus? The answer to each of those questions is a loud yes. The details matter. But let us be honest with one another. Sometimes the Bible bogs us down with their details. If you have ever read through the entire Bible, you no doubt, and I'm going to confess to you, I'm there. I'm guilty. You no doubt have been tempted to skim over the names that are listed in the book of Numbers. Come on. We've all done it. You have likely concluded that it's not necessary to remember or even know who begat whom. But it does matter. The names matter. Each name listed confirms a lineage back to Abraham, which is aligned back to God's promises, and each of them confirms an inheritance which is directly linked to the promises of God. Each name also leads to and communicates, yes, communicates, Jesus. Summarily stated, Christ Jesus is the key to understanding all of Scripture. Consider how important Jesus is to understanding the story of Abraham offering Isaac as a sacrifice. Modern atheists use such a story to portray the God of the Old Testament as barbaric. And we can easily admit that expecting a man to sacrifice his own son is barbaric Until we know that God sacrificed his own son. It is from that sacrifice that we have an understanding of the faith and devotion God expected from Abraham. Without the revelation of Jesus, the Old Testament would be no more than moral tales, a sort of Hebrew version of Aesop's fables. Unfortunately, it is presented to many as being just that, a book of moral stories and no more. I cringe with clenched teeth, and I assume so do you, when you hear preachers tell the stories of Holy Scripture as if they are moral lessons and no more. Moral lessons such as Jacob teaches us that we shouldn't be deceived. King David teaches us that we should not lust. Gideon teaches us that we when we come to making a decision, well, we should pray about it. Even the New Testament stories are glossed over. From the woman at the well, we learn that we should not change the subject. From the woman caught in adultery, we learn to not judge. From Jesus, while hanging on the cross and telling John that Mary was now his mother, we learned there to care for widows. I trust you can hear my sarcasm. And I say, come on. Come on. You cannot be serious. Surely these preachers don't think that a moral lesson is all that we can get out of these biblical stories. We should hear, shouting from our memory banks, the words of Jesus, that the law and the prophets speak of him. We should be adhering to the admonishment of the preacher from the book of Hebrews, where he states, therefore, let us leave the elementary teachings about Christ and go on to maturity. Let us go on to maturity. Beloved, there is so much more of Jesus to see in Holy Scripture that is already available to us We're willing to dig into the gold mine to find those precious nuggets What I have been alluding to is the beneficial use of typology to study Scripture. The most obvious example of typology is found in the book of Genesis in the person of Joseph, the favorite son of Jacob. Joseph was envied by his brothers. Jesus was envied by his Jewish brethren. Joseph was cast down into the pit, left for dead. Jesus suffered, was dead, and buried. Joseph was raised from the pit and was seated at the right hand of Pharaoh. Jesus was raised from the pit of death and seated at the right hand of the Heavenly Father. Typology is exemplified in the New Testament by Saint Paul in his epistle to the Galatians, and we read that as our epistle lesson. In Galatians chapter 4, Paul uses the person of Sarah and Hagar as types of grace and law, respectively. You will remember that Sarah was Abraham's wife, and because she could not conceive a child, she initially gave her servant Hagar to Abraham so that a son could be born into their household. Because Hagar and her son Ishmael were born outside of the covenant promise, St. Paul describes them as types of the law that are bound by slavery. Sarah, her son to be born, and her son to be born Isaac were part of the covenant promise, and therefore a type of grace, receiving all the benefits that grace offers St. Paul's lesson taught that Christians who are born into grace are not subject to the law and therefore are not bound by the law. We also hear typology teaching from the preacher in the epistle to the Hebrews. In his example or explanation of Jesus being a great high priest. Greater than those who served in the tabernacle. He says this for if he, Jesus, were on earth, he would not be a priest, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law, who serve the copy. That's a word for typology. Copy and shadow of the heavenly things. The words copy and shadow are typological words. Later in the same epistle, it's described the earthly high priest's entrance into the holy as symbolic for the present time. Being a symbol is being a type. Although used in Holy Scripture, you should know that interpreting the Bible by way of typology is not popular among certain scholars. The main reason for this lack of popularity is the work of an early Christian scholar named Origen. Origen was a church leader from Alexandria, which is at the tip of North Africa. His approach to the Bible was more apologetic. He was trying to explain to non-believers why they should trust the Bible. Origen was concerned that the stories and the laws of the Old Testament were so gruesome and violent that it makes God to look to be an unjust savage. Because of this, he thought it best to explain such stories and laws as allegories. Allegory is a close relative to typology. Allegorical interpretation applied to a text such as Genesis 3, which describes Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden and God walking in their midst. He describes it as a made-up story to explain in a dumbed-down fashion how man is responsible for sin entering the world. In other words, it's not seen as a historical account. Origen rebuffed the literalists who believed, who he believed were distorting God's image. And as you are aware, liberals have followed Origen's example by questioning every story told in the Holy Scriptures, doubting everything from miracles, even the resurrection of Jesus. Because of this alliance of origin and liberals, conservatives have rejected Origen's approach, seeing no good outcome. What responsible typology does in comparison to Origen's allegorical interpretation is acknowledge the stories of the Bible to be historically accurate. As well as being an initial layer that can be peeled back, exposing deeper and deeper meaning My chosen example this morning to reveal how this works is from the book of Exodus. The main message of the book is the exodus of Israel from Egypt It is the exiting of Israel from Egypt where they were bound as slaves. And such exiting is a type of salvation. Each of us who have been saved by the truth of the gospel has left our state of bondage to sin and been given freedom and new life. Also, within the book of Exodus, there are various stories within the main story. There were ten plagues that were that we are to understand to be symbolic of God's sovereignty over the ten false gods of Egypt. There was the crossing through the waters of the Red Sea, which we are told later by Peter is representative or a type of our baptism. There were giants inhabiting the promised land. There were types of the fears that man has. There were enemies that need to be driven out from the promised land. And those enemies were types or shadows of our besetting sins that need to be driven out of our lives. There was the promised land itself, which is described as plentiful, providing all of Israel's needs, making it a type of our heavenly hope, where no man will be in want of anything, especially of peace and joy. Then there are smaller, seemingly less important stories, and yet they reveal the will of God. In Exodus, the incident at Mara is an example. Just after passing through the Red Sea, the people of Israel came to a water supply at Marah, but the water was bitter. The Israelites would be poisoned if they drank it. After Moses prayed, the Lord told him to place a certain tree in the water. Moses obeyed, and soon afterward the water was no longer bitter. In the New Testament, we read that we are to understand Jesus as the tree of life. We learn from the Psalms that water is symbolic of the Gentile nations. Putting the two together, we see that the tree Moses used to make the water sweet was a typology of Jesus who would convert the Gentile nations, making them sweet. In another instance, when the people complained to Moses about the lack of water, Moses sought the Lord. And the Lord told Moses to strike the rock, and after striking the rock, the water flowed. It should be obvious to our ears that because Jesus is referring to himself as the rock and a source of living water. That the rock struck was a type of Jesus who was struck so that we might receive water that will cause us to never thirst again. I hope you notice that none of these typologies identified, take away the historicity of the stories. There really was a Moses. There really was a Pharaoh who forgot Joseph and enslaved Israel. There really was an exiting from Egypt. In fact, I love this story. Archaeological finds include the Arama letters, which were written to an Egyptian pharaoh asking for help. As Palestinians were being overrun by what are called, what were called the Habiri people, H A B I R I. The Habiri are understood to be a name given to what we know as the Hebrew people. The date of those letters match the same time as Joseph's conquest in the Promised Land. My hope is that these examples of typology have piqued your interest and increased your appetite for more. Over the next few weeks, we will be examining how the offerings found in the book of Leviticus were types and shadows of the offering of Jesus on the cross The thinking is that the more we see Jesus in those offerings, the greater love and devotion we will have for him. And that will always be a good thing. Let us pray. Father, we would see Jesus. We want to see Jesus. And so as we go through this series of examining the offerings in Leviticus, help us to see Jesus. To know that all the time, since the time you promised that seed would crush the serpent's head, that you have been pointing to Jesus, may he be seen by us, and may our devotion to him increase. We ask this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. You may be seated I realize that I started a series two weeks ago with an introduction to typology. With my plan to examine the law offerings from the microscope of typology But I have to postpone that series for just this Sunday. In just over two weeks, we will be participating in an election process That will determine who will be the next President of the United States and who will control Congress. If you fear, at hearing my voice, that this is going to be a partisan sermon, I hope to calm your fears by telling you it is not. I vehemently disagree with any pastor that sides with one party candidate From the pulpit. Unless the Apostle Paul is running against Joseph Stalin There is no reason for Christian ministers to preach about anything other than Almighty God I am called to be a pastor, which means I am called to bring the Word of God to bear into the lives of God's people. What that means is that I am to help you understand and apply God's word to your everyday life. And that includes a democratic election. In case you haven't noticed My approach to this pandemic era has been to keep the church doors open as much as possible So that the Christian Church in general is seen and understood to be essential when it comes to political, social, and cultural crises. Obviously by my actions, I do not agree with those church leaders who have either closed their doors and pointed their people elsewhere Or who have gone online solely. What I see by such choices is a surrendering to a crisis Making the church only relevant when skies are blue and the public is safe. I also see An agnostic and therefore heretical approach. I'm sure I also say a Gnostic, better said Gnostic and therefore heretical approach to ecclesiology that concludes that the physical presence of the church in a time of crisis is unnecessary And even more troubling can be viewed by society as a danger to society. My approach to this time of pandemic has been to say that not only is the church relevant in such a time, but the church itself must make itself relevant. We must act in order to be relevant. After all, beloved, in a time of pandemic When people feel the fear of death, we are to stand taller and to speak louder, because death is what the Christian faith is all about. Death is our nomenclature. We speak death. We speak death in terms of being dead in our sins and trespasses. We speak eternal death in terms of what we deserve. We speak of overcoming death in terms of the resurrection of our Savior and our own personal hope for resurrection. We speak of death in terms of dying to ourselves, which is to die to our personal desires, our personal preferences, our very self Even dying to our fears. We do this because Jesus said, for whoever would save his life will lose it. But whoever loses his life for my sake and the gospels will save it. Christians and Christians alone have been promised the ability at our resurrection to to look death straight in the eye and say, O death, where is now thy sting? For it will be gone, thrown into the lake of fire, and condemned for all eternity. For we are not only about death, we are about overcoming death. And that includes overcoming the fear of it. And just as the church is to be relevant to society in a time of pandemic So too must we be relevant in times of general and local elections. It is being said by the talking heads in our media that this is the most important election in our lifetime. Well, so was 2016, so was 2012, so was 2008, so was 2004, and so was 2000 and and Let us get some perspective. Consider that in the eighteen thirties in America Winning elections was so important that campaigning politicians offered voters generous amounts of liquor during the campaign, and as a reward For right voting on election day. You can go vote the right way and get your bottle. On the frontier, one evangelist noted that a house could not be raised, a field of wheat cut down, nor could there be a log rolling, a husking, a quilting, a wedding, or a funeral without the aid of alcohol. In eighteen sixty, the country was so divided there were four possible candidates on the ballot for president. As the issue of the sin of slavery weighed the country down, Abraham Lincoln received only 39% of the popular vote. 39%. The other three taking up the remaining 61%. But Lincoln dominated the Electoral College. That election seems to have been important. If you think our country is divided now, consider the election of 1868, where the incumbent president Andrew Johnson, who had succeeded to the presidency after Lincoln was assassinated In 1868, Johnson tried to run as a Democrat, even though he was a incumbent Republican president. He did so because he was a Southerner and he disagreed with the Reconstruction decisions of the Republican Congress. The Democrats criticize the Republican Reconstruction policies and campaign on the platform of anti-black and pro-white. Grant won that election by a mere five percent of the popular vote, but he dominated the Electoral College. And if you think the morality in those days was better compared to today, this is a fact. The smallest towns in America and the American frontier boasted 30 saloons to one church in a city. 30 to one. And where there were saloons, there was prostitution. And where there was prostitution, there were abortions to keep brothels more profitable. The biggest difference of the sins of the United States in the eighteen hundreds compared to today is the number of them. Not the difference in terms of the type, but the number of them and the fact that we are no longer ashamed of them. My point is that the election of eighteen sixty-eight was just as important as the election of 2020. Again, all of this has been pointed out to provide perspective. I have heard Christians pontificate about how voting for a particular candidate who is immoral because of his immorality Excuse me, I'll say that differently. I have heard Christians pontificate about how voting for a particular candidate is immoral because of the immorality of the candidate I have heard other Christians pontificate about how not voting for a particular candidate is voting in favor of abortion. A response to this seemingly insurmountable impasse, I heard recently in a sermon by the Reverend Tony Evans, a sermon preached prior to the election of 2016. There he used the analogy that described the Republican Party as a type of one football team. And the Democratic Party as an opposing football team, and the Christian Church in the position of being the referee The analogy works when we understand that referees are going to make decisions that neither side of the aisle agrees with. Both teams are going to think the referees are against them. That is true for the Christian As both political parties can see the Christian church as not buying in to all that they stand for. The analogy also works because just as referees refer to a rule book that is their standard for making their decisions, So too do Christians have a rule book, the Holy Scriptures, that we look to as an objective standard for the decisions we make. The analogy provides a needed perspective, where the analogy breaks down. is all too obvious. The only way referees in a football game can enforce their rulebook is if both teams agree to give the referees authority. Our culture and our major political parties have not given Christians any authority to decide political or moral issues. It is quite the opposite. In fact, as Christians today, we are looked down upon as being foolish fanatics for believing the Bible for what it plainly teaches. For believing in miracles and for even concluding that Jesus was a real person. So, yes, the analogy doesn't go very far. But where it helps is to show Christians that when it comes to political warfare, we are to play a different role than to be strictly partisan. I confess that I know what it means to be partisan. I was a partisan in my past. I was a Reaganite in the 1980s. I was a card-carrying member of the Republican Party. Once I was ordained to the ministry, I chose not to affiliate with any particular political party because I was convicted that I was called to help usher in the kingdom of God. Rather than usher in a political party for the United States government, I gained new perspective. But that doesn't mean it is wrong for a Christian to be a part of a political party. I'm simply sharing my journey so that you can understand and hopefully relate in a meaningful way. What I realized this year was how wrong I have been to put my trust in political leaders to turn the United States around and away from the pagan direction it is going. Or not where it's going, where it has arrived There is this argument that says that if you vote for a certain candidate and that candidate wins and then he or she will then choose judges who will then make proper moral decisions, and those decisions will save our culture from the impossible immoral slide it is on And yet what happens is that the judges are chosen by the candidates you voted for, and those judges don't make the moral decisions that you think are best for the country. And that leads to voters throwing up their hands in disgust and asking, What's the point? Perhaps Christians should get out of politics altogether. And let the culture go the way the devil wants it to go. Perhaps we can say to our neighbors that if they want to kill their unborn, go ahead. If they want to sodomize one another, have at it. If they want to burn their cities down, we will move aside. If you want to continue in debt so that foreign nations own your very land, just keep on living how you're living. After all, God says that he gives people over to their desires that they insist upon until those desires destroy them. Wouldn't we be doing the same if we just got out of politics altogether? The argument against such a position Is that if the church pulls out of politics, that the church will soon be outlawed, as has happened in socialist states, and the church will have to go underground. But what's wrong with that? The church has flourished in the past when it has gone underground. I realize that such is a radical perspective. But the rebuttal to the church pulling out of politics and having a social moral voice is more than just the threat of being outlawed. It is the call to love our fellow man. Even if our fellow man doesn't love us back, or even if he doesn't want to be loved at all We speak against abortion, against sexual immorality, against leaving debt to our children, because such are dangers to the soul of humanity The more sin we accept, the farther away we remove ourselves from God's image, the very image that is in each and every human being. And so we stay in the culture, attempting to have a relevant voice, because that is what it means to love our neighbor as ourselves. That is a biblical perspective. So what is going to happen if your candidate doesn't win the next election? Or what if he does? Or what if the powers within Congress change? Or what if they do not? Consider the passage read from 2 Chronicles, and I invite you to turn back to there, 2 Chronicles 15. That was our first scripture reading. In that passage, Azariah, who was a lesser-known prophet in the early years of the kingdom of Judah, He came and bravely spoke a word to king to a king Asa who was brimming with success after a great victory over the Ethiopians. In the 9th century B. C. , King Assa of the Kingdom of Judah had enjoyed a significant victory over a mighty army. It would be easy to think that he had a permanent claim to God's favor and to God's blessings in the future. Speaking through the prophet Azariah, God wanted Asa to know the importance of abiding in the Lord. He spoke of a faith principle that is taught throughout Scripture, which is this: if you seek God, you will find him, but if you forsake him, he will forsake you. That principle is true for nations, for organizations, and for individuals In his excitement over a victory, Asa needed a new perspective. He needed God's perspective. Azariah goes on to describe the troubles of Israel that they had in the past and how those troubles were caused by the people not seeking God. When they did not seek God, the influence and presence of priests and teachers of God's law lessened and lessened until there were none. Where there are no teachers of the law, nations are destroyed. Men rise up against each other. Azariah next explains that when there is such conflict and destruction, we are to know that it is caused by the Lord. Look at verse 6 again. He said, So nation was destroyed by nation and city by city. Sound familiar? For God troubled them with every adversity. Let me emphasize the phrase: God troubled them. The idea of God causing trouble between individuals and between nations and within cities May be hard to hear, but but if you were with me at the beginning of this pandemic when we studied In in Bible study, the prophet Joel, the Book of Ecclesiastes, and finished with Job, you are aware that God wants you to know and to be confident That whether it is good or evil, God is in control of it. Now don't hear that I said that God is responsible for evil. Evil is the corruption of good, and God is good. What I said was that God is in control of evil. It does not get away from him He allows it when humanity insists upon it, that that evil has its borders. It can only go so far until God denies it. This is an important perspective that Christians need to have. And we need a different perspective than the world. That is the point of this sermon. We need a different perspective when pundits predict that a coup is going to take place if their candidate doesn't win. Anarchists promise more riots if their candidate doesn't win. And in the midst of this political jousting and chicken little screaming, We can read news headlines like Tier 2 lockdown, what you can and can't do in high-risk areas. Next, scientists raise vitamin D alarm over COVID. Next, this state has the worst COVID outbreak in the U. S. Next, 41 states have uncontrolled spread of COVID-19 or are trending poorly, data shows. Next, here's the eight states that have the worst coronavirus case spikes. And hear this one. CDC report indicates masks may increase chance of infection with COVID or other respiratory illnesses. All of those are real news headlines this past week. Are you scared yet? Take the principle taught in 2 Chronicles 15, in the prophecy of Joel, in the book of Ecclesiastes, in the book of Job, and apply it to today. God is not watching rioting in the streets or plan coups as a spectator, surprised at what is happening, but is instead troubling the people. Troubling the people. Remember, God troubled them. While it appears to be chaos to us Such chaos has borders and limits that are according to God's will and his plan of salvation. When St. Paul said that all things work together for the good, for those who love God and are called according to his purpose. That statement has to include all political raging, all political drama. It has to include worldwide events as well as individual trials. As I stated several sermons ago, the goal of the gospel is that God would be our God and that we would be his people. And what Jesus did for us, and what the Holy Spirit continues to do for us is according to that end goal. God is troubling the people for the sake of the salvation of his people. Believe that and have perspective. The Christian Church is essential because we provide a necessary perspective for believers and unbelievers. Where there is chaos, God can provide peace. And where there is fear of death, God can promise life after death. And the only means of peace and life is the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. Let us pray. Our God, we take this challenge from 2 Chronicles 15 to accept that you bring the trouble. And to accept that, knowing that your plan is to redeem your people. We accept that, we are humbled by it, and we will not be deterred, no matter which direction an election goes. To the fact that you are indeed under control and your will will be done. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Burnt Offering
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. You would do well to turn to Leviticus chapter one, that is the base passage of Scripture that we will be looking at. Three weeks ago I introduced us to the biblical interpretation methodology of typology. Typology is used to see how an image in the Old Testament points to the reality of the New Testament. One of the more obvious examples is the person of Joseph. As Joseph was despised by his brothers. So Jesus was despised by his fellow Jews. Joseph was thrown down into the pit, similar to Jesus descending into hell. Joseph was raised out of the pit to sit at the right hand of Pharaoh, and Jesus was raised from the grave to sit at the right hand of the Heavenly Father. Therefore, the life points of Joseph point to the Christ to come. I warn those of you who have trouble staying awake during sermons that typological studies take time Be sure to have some caffeine before you come to church. The late comedian George Burns Once gave the following advice to preachers when he said, the secret of a good servant is to have a good beginning and a good ending, and to have those two as close together as possible My attempt will be able uh will be to make the middle part as interesting as possible. Have you ever wondered why God commands the Israelites to offer different kinds of offerings? That is what we are attempting to answer. When studying the offerings described in Leviticus as typology, we are operating on the assumption that each offering presents an image of the sacrifice of Jesus on the cross. But not only His offering on the cross, but his very life that he offered unto God. Each offering in details gives a greater insight into what Jesus has accomplished for us. What makes this study so fascinating is that Jesus plays every role in the offerings that God commanded. Bishop Andrew Jukes, whom I am indebted for these sermons, identifies Jesus in three parts of the offering. Jesus is the offering itself. He is also the priest who intercedes when giving the offering And he is the offerer who presents the offering that God requires. As offerer He is the sinful man under the law, fulfilling the requirements of the law. As priest, he is the mediator, God's messenger between himself and his people. As the offering, he is the innocent victim, a sweet and unblemished savor to God, as he bears the sins of man. In general, Jesus is the sum of the offerings. He is the burnt offering, he is the meat offering, he is the peace offering. He is the sin offering. He is the trespass offering. He is all of them by himself, one oblation once offered, as our liturgy says. You will also see that he is further identified in the distinctive differences of each of the offerings. Jukes describes the variety of the offerings to be different aspects. of Jesus' work and different aspects of his person. The distinctive differences reflect the depth, the the width of the sacrifice of Jesus that was once offered and effectual for all time. The truth is the work of Jesus is so encompassing and has so many different aspects to it, and in contrast, we are finite, we are limited by our maturity. that we have a hard time seeing all there is to see in Jesus as the offerings. And even so, regardless of our limitations, we must press on to perfection. We must increase our understanding to what Jesus has done for us. And so we first examine, as I said, Leviticus 1, the burnt offering mentioned in Leviticus. Essentially, there were two classes of offerings. There was the sweet, savor offerings, and those other offerings that were required as payment for sin. The sweet saber offerings are the burnt offerings, the meat offerings, and the peace offering All of these were offered on the brazen altar which stood in the court of the tabernacle, not inside the tent, but outside. The Savor offerings were not sin offerings, meaning that they were not made unto God because of sin or to pay the price of sin. It is therefore important to separate in our minds offerings given for sin and ones given to God for his pleasure. Most people think of offerings in the tabernacle and then in the temple as all of them offerings for sin. With the burnt offering, the meat offering, the peace offering, the offerer comes not as a sinner. But comes as a worshiper with the goal of simply worshiping God. In the sin offerings, he comes as a sinner, needing to pay a penalty for the price of his sin. And the differences are stark because the burnt offering was a sweet savor offering. We need to examine it in light of the atonement of Jesus. But not in the terms of paying for sin, but being pleasing to the Heavenly Father So the first point to be made about the burnt offering is that God finds earthly food, earthly food, satisfying and pleasing. The altar of God is described by the prophet Malachi as a table of the Lord. And according to Leviticus 21, the food that is placed upon there is food of God. In the burnt offering, fire falls from heaven and consumes the sacrifice. The understanding is that God consumed the offering. It is God that consumes it. It is God that is satisfied by the offering. Of course, we are speaking in anthropomorphic language. God does not hunger or thirst like a man. He does not need to be replenished. But his consuming is relatable to us because we are told later that we are to consume him. Remember these words of Jesus, unless you eat of my flesh and drink of my blood, you cannot be my disciple. Pleasing God is not normally connected to understanding the sacrifice offerings in the temple or excuse me in the tabernacle or the temple. Appeasing God, yes. That's how we understand the sacrifices, but pleasing him? No. But the burnt sacrifice pleased him, as did Jesus please him. Did not the Father say at the baptism of Jesus, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased? He was obedient, and his obedience was a sweet smell unto the Heavenly Father. His devotion to the Father and his love for humanity was most pleasing to God. Along with being a sweet savor unto God, the burnt offering was given to secure the acceptance of the offerer to God. To understand this, we must remember again that Jesus played three roles. He was the offering, he was the priest, he was the offerer. As offerer, he played our role. He stood for man as man stood under the law. The difference is that Jesus was acceptable because of his sinlessness. He fully obeyed and thus fully fulfilled the law. Since the time of Adam's transgression, the question of whether man in and by himself could bring anything to God that was acceptable, the answer was repeatedly no. For there was no one obedient, not one, until Jesus. Now we said that the burnt offering was not a sin offering, and yet if you look at verse 4 in chapter 1 of Leviticus, there is the word atonement. But that word atonement means making satisfaction. That's the definition. The satisfaction can be made in terms of sin or in terms of meeting the requirements that God has established. In this case, it is meeting the requirements of what God commanded, of what God was pleased by. Jesus was obedient unto death. He met the requirements. The third point of the burnt offering was that it was life offered. Life. Part of the instruction was that blood from the bullock was to be sprinkled on the altar. We can say that life itself was sprinkled because the Lord says in Leviticus 17, for life of a creature is in the blood. Now this is not superstitiously in the blood. It is symbolically in the blood. Physiologically, we know that blood runs throughout our entire bodies. It encompasses all that we are. Blood is essential to the life of creatures. Blood sprinkled on the altar was symbolic of life offered in worship. I give you my life. Jesus personally embodied the offering of life. He worshipped God in the way he lived. He testified of himself that he did nothing other than what the Father desired of him to do in his thoughts, in his manners, in his eating, in his sleeping. And whatever else that you would think of that makes a person's day, Jesus lived a life of worship. In comparison You and I struggle to live our lives for God even at certain times and certain ways. We are tempted to compartmentalize our lives by putting on a face, an attitude, a persona when we are at work that is different than when we are at home. And that one is different than when we are attending church. Jesus didn't need to put on a different personality because he was serving the Heavenly Father in everything he did. He was the same person. His life lived for the Heavenly Father, made it so that he did everything the same, whether private or public. Considering a life offered in worship and Jesus standing in our stead as the offerer, we are challenged to realize What a privilege it is to worship God in spirit and in truth. As a parishioner in my early days of walking with the Lord, I can personally testify that my worship was selfish. It was selfish until I began to appreciate what a privilege it is to call upon the name of the Lord. That change happened when I stopped thinking about what I like and didn't like about attending church on Sundays. Finding things to complain about is the easiest thing to do. When a person comes to the realization that in their own standing, their own character, They have no right to call upon God's name and expect anything but judgment and damnation. And yet God chooses to hear us and enjoys hearing from us when we come in the name of Jesus. When realizing this, our attitude toward worship changes. The Heavenly Father loves his Son. And because we love his son, he chooses to hear us and receive us as his own. That is nothing, nothing but remarkable. Understanding this as remarkable prevents us from thinking about the ballgame we would rather be attending on Sunday, or the sleep we wish we could catch up on, or whichever one of a million excuses we can come up with.
