To miss attending worship. We get to call on God and we get to be heard by Him because of Jesus as the offerer. Because he was well pleasing to the Heavenly Father. If there is a thought in your mind, no matter if it comes out upon your lips or not, if there is a thought in your That formally worshiping God is a have-to rather than a get-to. Such thoughts need to be rebuked And you need to choose to see worship as a privilege of calling the Creator of the universe Father. The fourth feature peculiar to the burnt offering is that it was wholly burnt or entirely burnt. This is original for it differed from the meat offering and the peace offering, which were which were offered and burnt only in part And the importance of this being wholly burnt, entirely burnt, is a great importance Because man's duty to God is not just to give up one aspect of our faculties or one aspect of our resources or one aspect of our time, we are to surrender all. This is why it needed to be burnt entirely. When Jesus summed up the commandments by saying, You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul. With all your mind, that is leaving nothing uncovered. We are summed up in our entirety by heart, soul, and mind. Although it was not part of our reading, you should know that all the burnt offering was to be accounted for. The head, the fat, the legs, and the in-words are specifically mentioned. And think of the typology here. The legs are symbolic of our walk or our physical exertion. The inwards represent our feelings and our affections from the heart. When we say we feel something for in our gut, we are talking about our inwards. The meaning of the fat may not be so obvious, but in the Psalms we learn that it represents our general health, our vitality. It is our energy. All of these are given to the Lord, and all of it was to be burned. All of it. We have already mentioned that Jesus also gave himself entirely to the Heavenly Father. He held nothing back. That is why he could tell us to love God the way he taught us. He truly expected it of us to love God with all of our heart, soul, mind, and strength. He expects us to surrender our whole self to the Father. That is what it means to pick up your own cross and follow him. He expects us to pick up a dying instrument every day, every day, not just Sundays, not just Bible study days, every day, and follow him. It is why he said to his disciples that unless you hate your mother and brother and sister and father, you cannot be his disciple. And too many weak scholars try to say that Jesus didn't really mean hate as we understand it? No We are to honor our parents to be sure, but we are to love him first and foremost, and if any love comes between us and him, that love is to be hated until we love him the most Try. Try to think of one thing, just one thing that you can have or that you can do that does not need to be given over to the Lord Jesus Christ. Just one thing. One thing that you can keep just for yourself. Maybe it is what you like to do when you have free time. That's your time, right? Do what you want. The Lord doesn't care, but the Lord says to you, redeem the time, for the days are evil. Maybe it is your private thoughts that you keep only to yourself. After all, they're just thoughts. They don't have to mean anything. No one is hurt by them. Yet the Lord says that we are to be transformed by the renewing of our minds, that we are to keep every thought in captivity. How about your bank account? After all, it's your money. Maybe it's a little extra money you made from an odd job, or perhaps it was given to you as a gift, and therefore you can do whatever you want to do with it. Surely the God of all creation doesn't bother with being Lord over extra money. And yet, when the Lord says he owns the cattle on a thousand hills, He is describing that he owns all things, even things of those who don't worship him. But what about my football? I love watching my favorite football teams. Surely the Lord does not want to take away what I enjoy, but here is the inside scoop. The Lord wants us to surrender everything to Him, and He wants what we don't want to give up. He wants that even more And let me remind you, in case you start to think that God is sounding a bit uptight or that he is being presented as a killjoy, or even an egomaniac, for wanting all the attention. God, good people, wants us to give all of ourselves for our own benefit. It is for our benefit that we love Him with our whole being. If we don't give him all, we will end up worshiping that which will destroy us. Today, we remember the Reformation. Part of the purpose of the Reformation is that the Roman Catholic Church had compartmentalized the Christian faith for its followers. It was a thing you did on Sunday, and confession of sin only came when you committed odious sins. It was not a life that you live where you give all that you were. Listen to what Martin Luther said in his 95 Theses. Quote, when our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said repent, he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance. Repentance to Jesus, faith in Jesus, love for Jesus, commitment to Jesus was not for certain days or in certain circumstances, but was for all days and all moments. Jesus gave his all. He was the burnt offering. So too are we to give our all. There is no other standard. Let us pray. Our God, we come before you seeing Jesus in the burnt offering and seeing it as an example for all of us to follow, confessing that When we hold something back, we hold everything back. Help us to have the courage to say, what if, what if I was to give all that I am? What would God do with me? We entrust that you would make us holy as your Son is holy. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Burnt Offering Cont
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. It is a blessing when a holy day falls on a Sunday. It is harder to get people to come out and celebrate Holy Days when they don't fall on Sundays. I wish that were different. And I may be to blame for perhaps I don't emphasize it enough for you to want to come out. All Saints Day is a day we recognize those champions of the faith who led exemplary lives in honor of Jesus, our Savior. There are so very many of them that the church made one day a day of honoring them all, hence All Saints' Day. Imagine with me if any one of the saints we recognize today were to turn return to us in the 21st century and attend a Christian worship service, what would their reaction be? Let us get beyond all of the 21st century wonders that they would experience being distracted by all of our electronic devices, and instead focus on the substance of our worship. Which is our prayers, our songs, and our words preached. What would their reaction be? I suspect that their reaction would be disappointment, and disappointment for two reasons: the lack of substance and the lack of reverence. Personally, I've done a few searches on the internet to see what other local churches are doing in their worship in light of the pandemic, and I have been appalled. The worship in music is akin to a local band playing in a pub. The ordained clergy dressed like they are eating at McDonald's. The sermons are counseling sessions for the depressed. In general, there is no evidence that the people leading such church services There's no evidence that they believe they are in the presence of Almighty God. The following is an account that reflects the confusion of Western Christian worship in our time Chet Samuel became the worship and arts pastor of Farmers Branch Outreach Center, a large independent church in Bergeron, a Dallas suburb. Now as a side note, I am only familiar with bishop, presbyter, and deacon. I don't know where scripture mentions a worship and arts pastor. Anyways. Chet initially felt at home in his new setting, and the church seemed to be receptive of his ministry. His problem started when he began to open the weekly worship practice with a brief devotion based upon the devotional Our Daily Bread. Some of the worship team felt it was a waste of time. And the others felt it was being legalistic for him to read a devotional. Chet's real problem surfaced when he began to insert a hymn into the forty-five-minute worship set, and yes, I used the word set The final straw came when he directed the congregation away from the PowerPoint screen and instructed them to turn in their hymnals. Many did not know what he meant by turning in their hymnals, and so they began to pass their hymnals up to the front, creating chaos in the church. Soon Chet was dismissed from his position. Senior pastor Sam Smucker explained Hymns are generally regarded as not cool, and this And in this extremely competitive Dallas church market, we can't afford to be identified as anything but cutting-edge cool. Well that story is satire, but it's not exaggerated. The Christian Church in America and in Europe is so desperate to be cool it does not look at anything like a saint. would imagine. We as a culture are even the Christian culture have ADD. We are afraid to be bored. And perhaps we think that God is bored with our worship. After all, he is supposed to be the primary audience of our worship, isn't he? As we will see in our second look at the burnt offerings from the perspective of typology, God does like variety in worship. He likes to change things up a bit He gives options, but not the type of options modern worshipers think of. When God gives room for variety, he does it because each option points To another aspect of his character and points to the sacrifice of Jesus, who is the one that enables us to worship God in the first place. We discovered much about the burnt offerings last week. I remind you that the burnt offerings were not for sin, but were for the simple purpose of worshiping God, of honoring Him. I remind you also that each part of the offering was to be understood as symbolic of each part of our human existence. The head represents our mind, the fat represents our vigor, and so on. And we spent time understanding that the offering was holy or entirely burnt. There was nothing left of it. It was fully given to the Lord. That is what Jesus did. He gave all of himself, and that is what we are to do as well. So we continue our discovery of the burnt offering by looking at the varieties that were allowed under the law. There were three grades of burnt offerings that could be offered. A worshipper could offer from the herd, from the flock, or from the fowl. The term grave refers to the monetary value of the offering as a person was to offer what he or she could afford. Each of these grades communicates something different. From the herd is the bullock, and the scripture says of the bullock that it is strong to labor, and great increase or wealth is by the strength of the ox. Such verses describe service or untiring labor. Regarding the flock, we have the lamb, which represents a different picture. We know the lamb to be passive and submissive, as it can suffer without murmuring. Regarding the fowls, we have the turtle dove, which is altogether different from the bullock or the lamb. Bishop Jukes describes the dove as having a mourning innocence. That is a innocence of depression or empathy. For the scripture says we mourn like doves and that we are to be harmless as doves. And we can add peace as the dove is used to present the olive branch. And we could add the Holy Spirit, as the scripture says that the Holy Spirit descended on Jesus as a dove. Looking at what each type offers, we find that the bullock refers to Jesus' ability to work as an ox and bear our burdens. He carried mankind on his shoulders from the time he swept blood in the garden through the stripping away of his flesh as he was whipped, through the carrying of the wood beam on the cross upon up to the hill to his death To the time his father turned away, through it all he tirelessly labored. From the Lamb we learn the submissive character of Jesus To do what needed to be done for the salvation of mankind. We also learn of his uncomplaining character, as he uttered not a word during his physical suffering. From the doves we learn of his sorrow. He mourned. He had empathy. He mourned for mankind as he witnessed us suffer the pains of death. Remember at the death of Lazarus, he wept. He also mourned the holy city of Jerusalem, saying, Oh, Jerusalem, Jerusalem. Jerusalem was filled with the people of God that God chose, but they were too stubborn to accept the Savior that God had sent them. He also mourned for the people who stood at the feet of his cross, who mocked and scorned him. He mourned that they did not know what they were doing. And it is with these images and examples found in the one man Jesus that allow us to now turn and examine ourselves. We are to be what he was and what he is. We are to be laborers. He said that the fields are ready for harvest, but the laborers are few. Who will go to the harvest? The answer is you and I. We are to go out to the harvest, and the harvest is our workplace where men and women can know Jesus can set them free from the bondage of sin, guilt, and shame. The harvest is your school where fellow students need to know that they do not need to be alone because Jesus will be with them and never forsake them. The harvest is your neighborhood where families can experience peace between one another because the peace that Jesus brings to individual hearts. We are also to be lambs. We are to be gentle, turning the other cheek and giving more of what we have to those in need. We are to return a curse with a kind word. We are to endure suffering at the hand of others. We are to not murmur under God's chastening hand, but instead we are to stand fast so that in us others might see Jesus. And we are to be doves. Jesus tells us to be wise as serpents and gentle as doves. As doves symbolize mourning, empathy, we recall that we are to weep with those who weep and mourn with those who mourn. As the doves symbolize peace, we recall that we are to be peacemakers. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall inherit the kingdom of God. Besides the variety of sacrifices under the burnt offerings, there are distinctions to be made about how each is to be handled. We notice that while the bullock and the lamb are divided, that is cut apart, and all the parts accounted for and burnt. There is a restriction regarding the bird, which was not to be divided. It can be determined that such a division would be impractical because of the small size of the bird But that would not communicate what God intends. It is the devil who would like us to think that when worshiping God we should consider what is practical. What is practical is to have a worship service limited by time. I remember an older gentleman Who told me he would no longer attend services here because a service should go no longer than one hour and we consistently go over one hour. What is also practical is to promote what is the most popular amongst the people, in and outside of the church. What is practical is to keep parishioners happy. Being popular and keeping people happy fills the pews. It keeps the coffers ringing. But God is anything but practical when it comes to what he expects his people to do in worship. We said that all parts of the offering representing represent something of Jesus, i. e. , his thoughts and his feelings, his energy, and so on. When a sacrifice is not divided, We acknowledge that there is something to the sacrifice that remains hidden or unknown. This is the part of worship that is purposefully mysterious. It is true that mysteries can scare and make some nervous. Not knowing what is happening or will happen can be unnerving. But we must acknowledge, whether we wish to or not, that there will always be mystery in our worship. To worship without an awareness of mystery is to become bored with familiarity. For example, let us examine the sacraments. In baptism, we say that the water symbolizes a cleansing of sin and that we are buried with Christ and we have circumcised hearts. It is understandable that we would ask, well, how? How does the water bury us with Christ? How does the water circumcise our hearts? And the honest answer is we don't know We can only go by our sense experience, and we don't experience a burial or a circumcision of the heart, and yet we can believe it. We believe it because the Bible tells us that is what is happening, and we believe what the Bible says because we believe in the person of Jesus Christ, that He is the Son of God. Regarding Holy Communion, we know the warning from St. Paul that if a person eats or drinks in an unworthy manner, he or she eats or drinks damnation unto themselves. This communicates that there is power in the drinking of the bread and the wine. Again, it is understandable to ask how. How is there power to judge or to bless in something as simple as bread and wine? The honest answer is we don't know. What we know is what the Bible says. The Bible says that by faith comes, but faith comes by hearing the Word of God. And again we ask how. And again we say we don't know. But that is how God has designed it. Beloved, there are things in our worship that are to remain a mystery. They are to remain undivided. Of course, there is not enough time for us to mention all of the things we don't fully know about God and what he does when we are at worship. But that is because of the very nature of God Himself. They have tried to explain to philosophy students that uh this point about God, that if there is a God Then by definition, you would not be able to understand or comprehend him fully. For if you could comprehend him fully, he would not, by definition, be God. Mystery in our knowledge and worship is not forced. It is a reality. We don't need to conjure up mystery. It's there by God's nature. It is always there for us, this side of eternity. Our worship should reflect that mystery, the same mystery that the saints embraced. Another distinction about how the offerings were handled is that the bullock and the lamb, the inwards and the legs, were to be washed in water. We noted last week that the legs represent our daily walk and the inwards represent our affections. The water represents the Holy Spirit acting through the Word of God. Remember these words of Jesus. Sanctify them through thy truth. Thy word is truth The scripture says Christ loved the church and gave himself for it that he might sanctify and cleanse it by the washing of water by the word. Jesus being a man submitted to the sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit by God's word. So too are we to submit to God's word and be washed by its cleansing power. We should be reminded from this how important it is for us to be a people of God's Word. Reading, meditating, and studying the Holy Scriptures cleanses us. Another distinction with these types of burnt offerings is that a person offering is to lay his hands on the bullock when offered. To lay hands on an offering is to fully identify with it. Jesus as the incarnation reveals, fully identify with mankind. He knew our sorrows and our joys. He knew our temptations, yet without sin. We too are to fully identify ourselves with sacrifice You remember Jesus told us to pick up our cross. He called us to deny ourselves. He called us to think of others before ourselves. All of these are ways to identify fully with the sacrifice. And the final distinction we will make note of is that with the first type of offering, the bullock The offerer, the one who brings the bullet for worship, is responsible for killing the sacrifice and preparing it for burning. With the other offerings, the killing and preparation was done by the priest. But with the bullock, it is the offerer who does the work. And from this we are to remember that Jesus played the role of priest, the offering itself, and the offerer. When describing his Upcoming sacrifice for our sin, Jesus said it this way. No man takes my life from me, but I lay it down myself. What Jesus did was a willful choice. He was not forced. He willingly gave of himself. And his example is the greatest challenge of all. In some ways, it is easiest to do something we don't really want to do because we have the excuse of saying that someone else told us to do it. It is quite another to take full responsibility for the decisions we make. And by way of the burnt offering, we see Jesus as our example, choosing to sacrifice, choosing to die for others. We can talk a lot about what it means to be predestined and what it means to be chosen of God. The Bible uses such language for important lessons. But personal responsibility for our choices is part of the faith. We make choices And we can choose. No, I need to say we must choose whether we are going to sacrifice ourselves. We are to offer ourselves to God. No one else can offer us. Our parents can't even offer us. They can offer us at our baptism as infants, but ultimately we have to own that baptism and then end by offering ourselves The saints we acknowledge today did so. They offered themselves. They picked up their own cross and they followed Jesus And you and I can do no less. Let us pray. We thank you for the example of the saints. And we thank you for the image of the burnt offering and all the details that point us to a Savior and then point us to the Christian life. May we take it up to challenge to follow that example and to be like Jesus a burnt offering, well offered. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Jesus as Grain
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: The name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turning your Bibles to Leviticus chapter two Leviticus chapter two, our first reading this morning. If you are like me When you have read through the Bible, you have glossed over the details of the offerings prescribed in Leviticus, because the details were boring. And unseemingly and seemingly unnecessary. Even this morning as it was being read, I was going, Wow, what a detail. What we are trying to do in this series of sermons is to see just how necessary those details are, because they describe the details of Jesus offering himself. Today we move on from the burnt offering to the grain offering, which is the second of the sweet savor offerings, which are also called meat offerings in the King James Version. The New King James, uh in the New King James it is more understandably the grain offering, the word meat. Conjures up thoughts of beef round chuck steak sausage and all the rest when it really simply means a substance that is consumed. The consumed meaning refers to the portion of the offering that is consumed by the priests. I was asked why the burnt offering was not a sin offering. And the same can be said being asked about the grain offering. The question is especially important because many Bibles contain footnotes that say that the burnt offering is a sin offering. I realize that I am at great risk of going against what the footnotes say, although I trust you recognize that the text is inspired and not the footnotes. But I do disagree nonetheless with such footnotes because I believe the point of them not being offerings for sin is correct. Now, before I explain in more detail why the burnt offering, the grain offering, the peace offering are not for sin, let us acknowledge that the study we have embarked on is a bit deep. It is deep in terms of thoughtfulness and studiousness. The Bible uses the metaphor, you remember, of Some people needing milk because of they are young in the faith or immature, and others of the faith needing meat, meaning that they are wise and mature in the faith. Using the same examples, we can say that this study is a study about meat. It is for the wise, it is for the mature. You will not hear these things preached in many churches, especially in churches today. Most congregations can't handle the depth of such a study, and they are certainly not used to it. But you are different and you are to be commended. I say this as a preface because when good and insightful questions are posed, we need to be thoughtful and ready to have our minds altered with the answers. The first three offerings mentioned, that is the burnt offering, the grain offering, and the peace offering, are also called sweet savor offerings. This description of being sweet savor can be found in verse 9, verse 13, verse 17 of chapter 2. The New King James translates savor, the word aroma. The offerings are a sweet aroma to the Lord. The three sweet aroma offerings have a few distinctions about them that show that they are not offered for sin specifically. First, they are offered on the brazen altar, which is an altar that stood in the court of the tabernacle. The court of or the outer court was outside of the holy place, and that was outside of the Holy of Holies, which is where that once-a-year atonement offering was brought by the high priest. Thus, the simple difference is the location of these three offerings. They tell us that they are different. Secondly, we note the description of the offerings. They are a sweet savor. They are a sweet aroma. The description indicates that they were pleasing to God. They are what he enjoyed. That is why we have said that The person offering these offerings comes in order to be accepted by God. He comes, his very self, comes to be accepted to be pleasing to God. Perhaps that's where the confusion lies. We know that we ourselves, by ourselves, are not pleasing to the Lord, and therefore we cannot possibly come to Him without having our sins forgiven. In fact, we can easily see that if it was not for the sin of mankind and our individual sins, there would be no need for sacrifice at all, for any offering, whether it be birth, peace, or sin offering. That is undeniably true. So to say that all of the offerings are in some way connected to sin is absolutely correct. But what we should see is that the manner of offerings differ, and what the Lord requires of the priest, of the offering itself, and the offerer Are significantly different enough to know that some are necessary for specific sins and others are simply offered to be pleasing to God. And this is where we get into our personal day-to-day faith. Think of it this way. If the offerings were all about sin specifically, there would be only one type of offering that needs to be made. But the sacrifice that Jesus made was more than just being on the cross. Well, that is in no way stated to undermine in any way the value of the cross. But his offering was also his life before mankind. It was everything he did. It was in everything he did. And we are learning that it is to be in everything that we do. If it was just about one sacrifice for sin. Then we would simply need to do what many do, which is only concern ourselves with our faith on Sundays We would only need to go to church each Sunday, confess our sins, receive evidence of forgiveness, and go on living our lives in the week. being only concerned about ourselves with the idea of coming back again the next Sunday and receiving forgiveness again for all the purposeful sins we committed the week prior. But Jesus' life was more than that. And the sacrifices offered that were pleasing unto the Lord reflect a life lived that was pleasurable to God. Behold, my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. In summary, the sacrificial life that Jesus lived shows us that there are sacrifices that are not specific for sin. But for the purpose of pleasing God. The burnt offering, the grain offering, teach us this. In general, we can know that the grain offering provides us another aspect of the perfect offering of Jesus. We will be looking at the grain offering and how it differs from those other offerings. First, as stated, the grain offering was a savor, it was a sweet aroma offering to God. The sweet savor offering represents man in perfect obedience as he yields his life to God. It is an offering that God accepts as pleasing to him. And that certainly describes Jesus. Second, the grain offering differed in regards to the material of which it was composed. It was flour, oil, and frankincense. Flour and oil, we know. Frankincense, we usually hear about in reference to the wise men who came from the East bearing gifts for the Christ child. Frankincense is an aromatic resin obtained from certain trees in the Middle East. We should not think for a moment that God is not concerned with the sense of smell in worship. In fact, it is important to recognize that God desires every one of our senses to be engaged as we worship. The materials listed matter because there is no giving of a life in contrast to the burnt offering. The one offered life, the burnt offering, the other, the grain offering, offers fruit. The distinction between grain and life It's first found in Genesis, as God explains to Adam that the fruit of the herb and the trees were man's allotted portion to eat and be fed by, whereas life was reserved as a portion only offered to God. The word life refers to every animal species. We find that it was only recorded after the flood that man was permitted to eat the flesh of animals, to eat life. That the creatures were referred to as life indicates that what they owed God was their life, for he is the sole creator. The fruit of the earth, the grain that is grown, is a gift from God, and it is owed to our fellow man. The grain offering is something we share with our fellow man First, it is shared with our families as we eat together what is harvested. Second, we exchange goods with our neighbors so that all might have their needs met. And third, and importantly, the law of Moses directs that we leave that which was not harvested out in the field so that strangers who pass by might have something to eat. If we summarize the burnt offering and the grain offering, we could see that the first, the burnt offering, expresses our love and duty toward God, and the second expresses our love and duty toward our fellow man. The New Testament confirms this, as you know, when Jesus summarized the law as loving God and loving our neighbor. We remember that these two offerings are the same as those offered by Cain and Abel. Abel offered a blood sacrifice, and Cain offered fruits of the earth. God received Abel's offering and rejected Cain's. The offering of fruits as an offering itself is not bad. But the offering had to accompany the shedding of blood, for that was necessary to approach God. The shedding of blood was the offering of life, and Cain was willing to offer what was for himself And for his fellow man, but not what was expected by God. Offering grain alone can be best described as offering a tithe. 10% of a person's income without the worshiper offering himself. Beloved God does not want your money without us offering ourselves. He does not need our money, and he does not need us for that matter, but he tells us to offer ourselves because we need him. As we consider the grain offering in relation to Jesus as the priest, as the offerer and the offering, we notice that Jesus presented himself as nourishment to man. He offered himself like grain in order to be consumed. How can we help but not think about Holy Communion and our consuming of the body and blood of Jesus? From this offering of grain. Now I predict if some of you wonder if I'm ever going to stop referencing Holy Communion, believe me, please, I am not forcing the issue. The picture here is very clear. There is a consuming of the sacrifice that is to occur. The priests were to consume part of the grain offering according to the instructions regarding how it was to be prepared. And if we Protestants believe St. Peter that we are priests, if we are priests, we are to consume a portion of the grain offering. And it was then, and we cannot help but see how this is fulfilled in the sharing of Holy Communion, according to the New Testament instruction. Now the third difference that we notice about the grain offering is that it was wholly burnt. As a as the burnt offering, excuse me, I said that all wrong. The third difference we noticed about the grain offering is that it was not wholly burnt as the burnt offering. It was partially burnt and offered to the Lord and the rest given to the priests to be consumed. And this is another insightful picture of Jesus. Jesus gave himself fully to the Lord first, as he was also consumed by man. Mankind consumed his wisdom, his patience, his power to heal. And above all, his grace freely offered. All of Israel was intempted to be the same. All of Israel was to be a nation that was set apart. By God to worship Him solely and to be a blessing to the world, to be consumed by the world. The people chosen by God were to be a lighthouse to the world. But we know they fell short. They worshipped other gods of their time. And again, they never fulfilled their role to be a beacon in a dark and stormy world. And then comes the church. The church is to be what Jesus was, the city set on a hill, the salt of the earth. The church is the place where the Holy Spirit dwells and from where the kingdom of God spreads and grows. Like Jesus, the church consisting of God's people, you and I, are offered to the Lord and offered to our fellow man. Although we said that the grain offering was not wholly burnt, it was instead wholly consumed. It was totally consumed by God and then by man. That describes Jesus and it describes the church. The function of the church in the world is to be pleasing to God as an aromatic worship and to be consumed by the world. And by consumed, I do not mean overwhelmed. The church is to be in the world, but not of the world, meaning that we are to participate in ministering to the world and enjoying the blessings of God in the world, but the world is not to form our beliefs or our character. With the word consume, I mean that we are to be a nourishing source. We are to provide nourishment to the world. Churches can easily err on either side of these two responsibilities, which again are being pleasing to God and being consumed by the world. A church can be completely focused on pleasing God so that its singing is angelic, its architecture heavenly, and its liturgy flawless And yet rarely do they feed their fellow man who lives next door or who begs on the corner. A second church can be completely focused on Meeting the needs of the hungry and lonely, and providing for the sick and destitute, without a thought of how God might be pleased in their songs and in their prayers. The truth from the grain offering is found to be a both and rather than an either-or. We are to be both pleasing to God and consumed, and we can use the word used. Consumed or used by our fellow man. The final contrast we will notice this morning is between the grain offering and the offering of the first fruits at Pentecost. The difference is described in verse 12 as the grain offering is not to be burned. We read in Leviticus 23 regarding first fruits. They was to be offered on several feast days, the first being the feast of the Passover. With each feast, there is a specific instruction as to how the offering was to be made For example, at Pentecost, the first fruit offering was consist of unleavened bread and was a sweet aroma offering, while the next offering of first fruits was part of the sin offering, and that one was to be mixed with leaven. That is not as complicated as it might sound. For all it all that it means to us is that the grain offering on the Sabbath was unleavened, and the grain offering offered on the day after the Sabbath was leavened. The second offering, the one that was leavened, clearly represents the resurrection of Jesus, as he is the first fruit offering of them that slept. In him, when first sacrificed, there was no sin, no leaven, just as the first grain offering. He was the sweet savor to the Father. The leaven mixed after the first offering allowed the bread to rise as Jesus arose, overcoming sin and death. In regard to the church, we need not find ourselves in every aspect of the grain offering or of the feast offerings. Most of this is describing the work of Christ. But we may find ourselves in the grain offering offered at Pentecost, for it is at that feast that the church was empowered on high to fulfill its mission as the Holy Ghost came upon Christ's disciples as flaming tongues of fire. So in closing, I want you to know that I am aware of how fascinating and how mind-bending all of this is. Seriously, I have had to read over my own sermons a few times just to understand what I'm saying to you now. If you find yourself getting lost in all of the details and cross-references, don't be discouraged. I simply ask that you be in awe. We can be in awe at all of the minute details Jesus fulfilled as the grain offering. Think of it this way. We say that Jesus' sacrifice for sin was once offered, and so it was. But his sacrifice as a sweet aroma and as a grain offering that feeds men That feeding of men still continues. He has vouchsafed to feed us, as our liturgy says, and so he does. Amen. Let us pray. Oh God, we are humbled by the details of this offering. And how Jesus, your son, our Savior, fulfilled them, fulfilled them all, even in ways that we can hardly articulate. But we are grateful for it. We're grateful for the detail that you place in our lives that saves us from our sins and saves our souls to live forever. Continue to increase our understanding and thus increase our faith in the offering of your son. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Jesus as Peace
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. Several years ago, back in two thousand five, and that is a long time ago I was coaching our high school basketball team, and we were about to play Rombom. A Jewish school in Northwest Baltimore. Before the game, I was talking to their athletic director at Center Court, who was wearing a Yarmaka. And I, of course, was wearing my clergy collar. A man came out of the stands and said to both of us, it occurred to me, as I watched you both talking, that there's a joke here somewhere There always is. Consider this one. A church bell's ringer passed away. So they posted the position, and a man came in with no arms, wanting the job. The priests weren't sure he could do it, but he convinced them to let him try. They climbed the bell tower, and the guy ran toward the bell and hit it with his head. The result was a beautiful ringtone. They gave him the job. The next day, he went to ring the bell. He tripped and bounced off the bell and fell to the sidewalk below. A priest and a rabbi were walking past. One asked, do you know this guy? The second guy responded, no, but his face rings a bell. The next day the next day the dead bell ringer's twin brother comes in for again the vacant bell-ring position. He also had no arms. They led him up to the bell tower. He ran at the bell, tripped, and fell to the sidewalk below. The same two guys, the priest and the rabbi, were walking by. The first asked, Do you know him? The second guy responds, no, but he's a dead ringer for the guy we saw yesterday. The whole point of those jokes is to introduce you to the idea that we are priests You know, I have been uh paying attention to my presence on uh YouTube and and uh on sermon audio. And I think sometimes as I listen to my sermons, you take yourself way too seriously. So I thought, you know, that's what uh Ecclesiastes talks about, that uh some people can be too religious And uh sometimes we can. It's important to laugh. The comments I received regarding last week's sermon Tell me that you are getting the point of Jesus being these offerings in the Old Testament, but it's not always easy to follow. And I'm with you. I remind you that the end game is to be in awe. To be in awe of how Jesus, our Savior, fulfills the law as he is in the offerings we are examining. Today, we examine the peace offering from Leviticus chapter 3. In general, we know that the peace offering was an offering that was connected to the burnt offering. It too, it too was a sweet aroma offering. It was the third offering that was not for sin, but an offering that was to be pleasing to God. It was connected to the burnt offering, and that it was to be offered after the burnt offering And it was to be burned on top of the burnt offering, which we can understand to mean that it was burned after the burnt offering, although we are not told how long after. As with the other offerings, we can see Jesus in the details and in the three aspects of the offering, which I remind you consist of the priest. the offering and the offerer. Of the different types and grades of the offering, specifically that we will explore next Sunday. We begin today by examining what it means for Jesus to be the priest and what it means for us to be children of the priest. Jesus' position as priest in an offering makes him the official mediator between God and man. In the case of the peace offering, we notice that the priest eats of the offering, and therefore he himself is satisfied by the offering. Jesus as the offerer is the one man, the only man, who stands before God and is himself, in of himself, is pleasing to God. Jesus as the offering focuses not on his person but on his actions, what he did in life. When we examine Jesus as priest, we don't see his person, we don't see his actions, but we see instead his office. There were some offerings where the priest was to receive food. For example, With the sin offering the priest was to consume some of what is offered according to the law, while the offerer consumes nothing With the peace offering, God, the priest, and the offerer eat together of the offering. The priest is to be considered both a friend of God in eating together and a friend of man. And is that not what a mediator does? He is a friend to both parties Our Savior loves the Father and He loves humanity, and therefore He finds great joy in bringing the two parties together. And this makes him more than a friend, as he is a son to the first and a savior to the second. We should here recall Jesus' words to his disciples when they reclined for the Passover meal. He said With fervent desire, I have desired to eat this sacrifice with you. He desired The moment, the moment that began his earthly sacrifice, he desired that Passover meal so that he could share with both God and man the very first Eucharist. He felt that way before the first Holy Communion, he continues that fervent desire as he looks to eat with us each time we gather around that table. Each time we gather is a shadow of what he ultimately looks forward to, which is to eat with us around that great banqueting table. When old things have passed away and all things, all things have become new. Jesus as priest Provides a great insight into this peace offering. For part of the instruction for this offering was to include the feeding, and this is the main point of this sermon The feeding of the priest's children, children of the priest. Leviticus 7. 31 states, and the priest shall burn the fat on the altar. but the breast shall be Aaron's and his sons. From verse thirty-four of the same chapter, From the sacrifices of their peace offerings I have given to them to Aaron the priest, and to the to his sons. From the children of Israel by a statute forever. Fast forward to the new covenant in Christ Jesus. We remember from St. John's opening words of his gospel that those who believe in Jesus are given the right to be called children of God. In Galatians, St. Paul describes us as sons of God, sons, because we are inheritors who would receive the kingdom of God. Thus, the church is the family of God, and all of us are benefactors of his redemptive work. As benefactors, we are like the children of the high priest. We are fed from the sacrifice. We as the children of the priest get to feed off of the peace offering sacrifice And I would also like to point out that there is no age restriction when the children were fed, which is why some Christian traditions allow infants to partake of the Lord's Supper. Let your children partake. They need the means of grace as much as you do. As children of a priest or high priest, as the book of Hebrews refers to Jesus, as children of a priest, you and I are different. Every teenager who lives out their faith openly learns very quickly that Christians are different. And it's not just that we obey the Ten Commandments, which is different enough. Christians are different because of the way we view the world. We understand the world through the knowledge of God as creator and savior. We see the world as not moving in a purposeless manner, but according to God's Restumptive plan. And we see the world as not our home. We remember that the Levites, the priests of Israel And their children were not given a land for their inheritance. With their consecration to the Lord's service, the Levites We're not allowed a territorial inheritance of their own at the division of the land God promised Once established in the promised land, they were supported by the agricultural economy of the time, by the tithes that That were produced in the land paid by the other eleven tribes. The Levites were assigned towns to live in from the inheritance of the other eleven tribes. Of the 48 total cities of the 12 tribes, 13 were set aside for the families of the Levites. And so we, you and I, as children of the high priest who is Jesus, we too look to God for our inheritance. We do not store up treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and thieves break in and steal. We long for a better country. As the book of Hebrews states, a heavenly country. The mind of the priest was that was that we are to be of service, that we are to live lives of sacrifice, personal sacrifice. Priests could not concern themselves with building up their own property or collecting goods. They could not join in with their fellow countrymen and say that the land they sowed was the land they owned and the land they would pass on to their children. No, the priest was concerned with passing on the law, which for us is passing on the faith. As children of the high priest, we are to have such an attitude in that our concern is to be for heaven. And to live sacrificially as privileged people who are able to feast on the peace offering, that we are able to actually enjoy the offering to God. An important point about the peace offering is the word peace. In the Hebrew, it is shalom. Which has various meanings according to its context. The context here is an offering That has three participants eating together, and this leads to the word peace Peace, for it is a meal offered that symbolizes peace between all the parties involved. God, the priest, and the offerer. We know that Jesus is referred to as the Prince of Peace. He is referred to as the Prince of Peace because he is the one who overcame enmity between God and man. And Jesus brings peace to individual lives. He brings peace as he calms the troubled heart, racked with guilt, brought on by individual sin. He brings peace by allowing men to be forgiven and then allowing them to forgive. The need for peace is a challenge for us as we remember from the words of Jesus that we are to forgive our fellow man 70 times seven. And we remember from St. Paul's warnings to the Corinthians that we are never to eat or drink from the Lord's Supper in an unworthy manner. An unworthy manner includes not being at peace with our brother or sister in Christ. Therefore, being at peace with one another is something to take quite seriously. In a book titled The Body, written a bit ago, written by now deceased Charles Colton. He tells the story of a pastor ministering in Boston, Massachusetts, who took a fist to the chin during the announcements before the worship service. The punch started a brawl that only ended when the police arrived, and it was preceded, and according to Colton, caused, by the pastor Who use private information about members of his congregation to sway them toward his way of thinking and his way of spending. I am not aware of any punches being thrown here at St. Stephen's, but I have received looks that are similar to punches. From eyes that if they were able would burn holes in my head. I am aware of dour expressions that communicate a dislike given from one parishioner To another, for whatever reason that seems justifiable in the moment. We are not immune from the reality of contentions We are not immune because as St. James describes, there can be jealousy among God's people. What causes the jealousy is not important, as it is most important that we recognize it for what it is. It allows us to see at the table with God Himself as we sit with Him and with one another that we need to sit and eat in peace. Because it does that, because of what Jesus did, we can and should be at peace with one another. It is the fact that we can be at peace with God and with one another is where we should focus our attention. We could hear Chastising words about how we should be at peace with one another, and if we are not, what consequences there are. But that motivation was already clearly stated by St. Paul What we need as motivation in the positive as we come together is a greater realization about how privileged we are. To be able to sit at the peace offering and be at peace with God and our fellow man. I repeat again that when a peace offering was offered, it was God, it was the priest, it was the offerer that ate together. This is only the case with the peace offering. It's the only offering in which all three are gathered and all three eat. Because Jesus played the part of offerer, which is to say that he played our part, we are to understand that we are part of the peace offering. We participate. We are given a seat at the table. In the peace offering, every participant is satisfied. Every participant receives their fill. We then, you and I, are to be satisfied. We are to receive our fill. I I give you an insight that there was a debate in an online meeting early on in this pandemic. Where we as clergy were in disagreement as to whether we should offer Holy Communion And if our doors are closed, we debated over how we should offer the bread and the wine. It was my position then as it is now. That we need our fill. And that means that we need both. We need the Word of God read and preached. And we need the Eucharist. We need the bread and wine. We need to be fed by Christ. Like the peace offering, we are offered our fill by receiving both the word and the sacrament. As an off of my notes, I know that uh you have heard that there is a spike going on around the country, and certainly in Maryland. And there is that threat of us being shut down once again, not being allowed to enter this building less than twenty-five or more than twenty-five And I'm determined, no matter what happens, that this word of God would be read and preached in this place And that whether I have to shuffle you in twenty-five at a time, that you will receive the body and blood of our Lord. Because we need to be at peace. And we need to be filled. And so you will always be filled as long as the Lord allows. And we can receive our fill because Jesus did this for us. And by the phrase for us, I mean instead of us. He did it as us. Thus, when he was judged, he was judged as us. When he kept the law, he kept it as us. When he was found guiltless, he was found guiltless as us. When he was accepted by God, he was accepted as us. When we talk about being in Jesus, you know that phrase people talk about in Jesus. Scripture describes us as being in Christ. We are attempting to communicate that what Jesus accomplished is what we accomplished by way of him. As Bishop Jukes states, what he did, we reckon to have done, for as us he did it. So what he enjoys, we enjoy, for as us, he enjoys us. I fear that too many Christians do not begin to grasp this. I fear that too many think that of their own merit, of their own experience by God, that they are the thing that God is enjoying. Yes, they say that they are saved by grace through faith, and then they choose to think that God is viewing them according to how good they're being. Because of their various good deeds and behaviors, God is favorable towards them. The truth is, beloved, we are prisoners who have been rescued. We are outcasts that have been been given baths and white robes and a seat at the banqueting table. We are privileged. We are privileged to be called sons of God, and therefore we are privileged to eat of the peace offering. We are privileged to not call this world our home. But instead to have the kingdom of God as our inheritance. We are privileged to be at peace with God, to be at peace with our fellow man, and This is not often stated, to be at peace with ourselves. We get to call God our Father. We get to forgive our fellow man 70 times seven. We get to do that. And we can be secure in our privileged state. Because we have not done it ourselves. Jesus has done it. He has been the peace offering. Therefore, we are secure and we are at peace. Amen. Let us pray

sermons.title: Jesus as Peace Again
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: It didn't have the right sermon on it. And I woke up in a sweat. And here, this morning, I look up and my iPad is nowhere to be found Dreams really do come true. Oh boy. When couples are looking to be married, the last counseling session I have with them includes looking over the vows they are about to make. When parents want to baptize their child, I implore them, along with the godparents, to look over the vows they will make. Vows are important and should be revered because we are saying them to God, and if we break them, we have taken God's name in vain, and we have become bearers of false witness. Today, some people play with bows. Some people perser perceive the traditional wedding vows to be boring, and therefore they try to provide an upgrade. For example, one couple changed the traditional vows, being inspired by Dr. Seuss. The minister says to the groom, Will you take her as your wife? Will you love her all your life? The groom responds, Yes, I take her as my wife. Yes, I'll love her all my life. The minister again, will you have and also hold just as you have this time told The groom says, Yes, I will have and I will hold, just as I have at this time told, yes, I will love her all my life, as I now take her as my wife Another couple, in order to be clear on touchy subjects that they might face, added the following promises to the traditional vows. The groom added, I promise to try to remember to put down the toilet seat and to replace the toilet roll when it is finished. I promise to remember this day with love and roses. I will love you always. The bride added, I promise to learn how to change a tire and how to refill the window washer fluid when it runs out. I will comfort you when your team loses and drink beer with you when your team wins. I will love you always. In one wedding, it was the officiant who joined in the gag He said to the bride, Do you promise to love, honor, cook for, clean up after, surrender your share of the blanket to? Live with flatulence of, relinquish the remote to, and lift the toilet seat after until death do you part. And then to the guru he said, You have the right to remain silent. Anything you say may be held against you. And you have the right to have an attorney present, you may kiss your bride. Cute, right? Funny? Sure. Appropriate? No. No, they are winking at the idea of vows. The word vows simply means a promise, and in case of the peace offering And a wedding, for that matter, and the promises we make to God, regardless of the situation, we are to treat them never haphazardly. We are never to treat them lightly. We learned last week that the peace offering is the only offering where God, the priest, and the offerer eat together. Each of the participants receives their fill from the offering. We learned that Jesus as the offerer in our stead receives his fill, which means that he receives it as us, which means we receive our fill. From this and from what the children of the high priest receive, we acknowledge that we are privileged to have a seat at the table and to be fed sitting next to God the Father and Jesus the Son. What we did not discuss and what we are challenged to learn today is the varieties that can be offered And the reason why the offering is made in the first place. Why do we need a peace offering? Regarding the varieties, there were the 11 cakes that were to be offered with the sacrifice. Because leaven cakes were offered with the offering for praise. We can see it to be an offering of the church, for it is the church's role to bring praise to God. The leaven cakes could not be offered by themselves, but had to be offered with a sweet savor offering or another sacrifice This meant that by themselves they were not sufficient. But when offered with that which was acceptable, the shedding of blood, they became sufficient. That is who we are before God. We are not acceptable in and of ourselves, but when we come with Jesus, when Jesus is with us, when He is our propitiation What we then offer to God is graciously and I would say readily accepted. Another aspect of these cakes is that some were leavened and some were unleavened. We know leaven in Scripture is considered less clean or less perfect. The fact that the priests would eat both types of offerings The leaven and the unleavened, and the fact that Jesus plays the role of the priest for us teaches us that Jesus feeds on both the unleavened and the leavened bread. This means that Jesus is filled by his own blessed and perfect offering, the unleavened, and he is filled by the offering of the church. Which is the less perfect offering or the leavened offering. The same principle can be found in Leviticus chapter 22, where it is said that an animal that has a defect Could be offered as part of the peace offering. That God would accept leavened caked offerings and our defective animal offering is most assuredly good news for us, for we cannot help be honest with ourselves and notice how leavened and defective our worship can be. What I am referring to, when I say that our worship can be leavened and effective, in part, I mean How much trouble we have keeping our attention on the Lord as we formerly worship. What I'm describing is the lofty words we say and the serious confessions we make and the promises we make and all the while we are struggling to understand and truly with no doubt truly believe In regards to our attention, I trust I am not alone when I mouth words that I don't fully pay attention to. Or seeing phrases I don't coincide, that don't coincide with the images in my head. And you might think that as a minister of the gospel, I don't have such problems. You might think that I am always engaged in everything I am speaking, everything I'm reading, singing, and praying. Sadly, such is not the case. I too have thoughts that drift. I have a stomach that growls. I have flesh that grows weary in certain postures. I have prayed out loud while my mind wandered about, gee, I wonder what we're having for Sunday meal today. I have listened to the Ten Commandments, read while I am thinking about how my right knee hurts more than usual while I am kneeling. And let not any scoffer say that such a wandering mind is the fault of the prayer book or the fault of a liturgical worship in general. No, it is the fault of a heart that is sinful and a flesh that is weak. It is at those times in worship When my worship offering is filled with leaven and my sacrifice is defective And then there are the times when I might sing a song about God's sovereignty over all of our comings and goings. And I find myself questioning if that is actually true, considering the suffering of a loved one that I know he or she is experiencing. That is an unfaithful thought. It is a thought that needs to be confessed as sinful and turned away from. It is a defective offering. I believe, but I need God's help in my unbelief. The good news is In all of this is that Jesus, our priest, eats the offerings. He eats the leaven cake and the unleavened. He allows for the defective goat to be offered. And that means that he accepts our offerings of praise and thanksgiving. We bring the sacrifice of praise into the house of the Lord, and he accepts it as we offer it. Again, I say that we are certainly a most privileged people. From variety, we move to the reason for making a peace offering. In Leviticus chapter 7, we read that there is a peace offering given for a thanksgiving, which is also called for a praise. And there is an offering given for a vow. The praise offering or the thanksgiving offering was an acknowledgement of the mercies received from God For example, Israel would offer a peace offering in the form of praise when David slew Goliath and the Philistines fled from them. An individual could offer a peace offering as a form of praise when he recovers from a serious illness or an accident These are just a few of the many mercies that God grants his people, and the peace offering was a way to give thanks to God for his mercies, specific mercies. As God's people who stand on the A D side of history, we are all the more aware of God's mercies towards us. We know what Psalm 22 is describing. We know who the suffering servant, as described in Isaiah 53. We know who he is. We know, or at least we are learning, why each of these sacrificial offerings was necessary and how they all point to Jesus. Therefore, because of the position as God's people, and because to whom much is given, much is required. We are required to give many offerings of praise and acknowledgement of God's mercies to many that you and I have received. Allow me to remind you of some numbers that demonstrate what God is doing right now as a mercy to us. Presently, you and I are traveling through space or orbiting around the Sun at approximately 67,000 miles an hour We are doing this while at the same time spinning on a particular axis at 1,041 miles per hour. We do this while maintaining an average distance from the sun of 93 million miles. Any closer it would be too hot for life to survive. Any farther it would be too cold to cultivate and maintain life. We add to this a gravitational pull of 9. 8 meters per second That you and I are prevented from flying off the earth into the atmosphere, or if stronger, it could crush us And in the midst of all this moving and flying and spinning, you and I have a sense of stillness. You and I can properly use the word calm, even the word peace All of this God has designed for us. All of it God maintains every day, every moment of every day. And why? Why does He do this for us? It is because he loves us, and his love is merciful. What else do we have to be thankful for in regards to God's mercies? Is he not the one, the one that is responsible for keeping our minds working so that our lungs breathe in and out? Does he not oversee our nervous system, which allows us to enjoy physical pleasure while also protecting us from harm? Is he not the one that keeps our hearts beating at an average of 103,800 times a day That means that on an average our heart beats thirty-seven million eight hundred and eighty-one thousand times in a year, and if we live to be seventy-five years of age, our hearts will have been beaten Two billion eight hundred and forty one million five hundred twenty-five thousand times. God does that. We can't do it ourselves. He keeps us going. In him we live and move and have our very being. Considering all of this, can anyone honestly say that God has not done anything for us? Or that He seems to stand idly by and not concern himself about us? What utter nonsense! We now know what the prophet Jeremiah means when he said that God's mercies are new every morning. Beloved, if you don't earnestly desire to bring God a praise offering after contemplating what he does for us each and every moment in our lives, then I am fearful that you truly do not believe in him. Bend your knees to these truths, for to praise him would be to save your very soul. We now turn to the second reason for presenting a peace offering, which was to make a vow. I stated in the beginning that a vow was a promise, a simple promise, only not so simple, in that it was a promise made to God. Naturally, we know the difference between a plan and a vow. I can say that I plan to be home at five. And if I do not make it, I did not break a vow, but instead miscalculated my responsibilities and my travel time. St. Paul had to explain something similar to the Corinthians when they became very upset at him for not keeping what they thought was a promise for him to come to them, only to have his plan, not his vow, thwarted. A vow is a promise for service unto God. In the case of Jesus, it was a vow to be obedient to the law and to be that propitiary sacrifice for mankind. If Jesus did not fulfill his promised service, you and I would have no hope. But he did fulfill his promise, and thus you and I can know God. What God expects of his people is the same reverence for vows made. And this brings us to Jesus' teaching on letting your yes be yes and your no be no. While it is true that Jesus gives the instruction in order to call men to a higher standard of promise-keeping in general, It is also true that he wanted his followers to be people of their word because he was a keeper of his. And we cannot overlook the importance of the word word in this section of Scripture. Jesus was the Word made flesh. In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God and was God. The word word describes God well because when God spoke, he created. Or better stated, he created by speaking words. God spoke and the earth was formed. God spoke and the heavens were formed. God spoke and the earth and the water divided. What God spoke came to be. It therefore ought to be the practice of Christians to fulfill what they say they will do. In fact, it should be considered already done, because a Christian has promised to do it. Our yes and our no commitments should carry the weight of the name that we bear, that we're marked by. We are Christian, followers of Jesus Christ. What we promised should be in his name, simply because he promised it, and we are his. This is one reason why marital vows are so important. And why baptismal vows and confirmation vows and ordination vows and any other that we formally make before God and man are vitally important. When we keep them, when we keep them, we are offering our worship to God. Just by keeping our promise, we are worshiping God. I mentioned the vows we make during rituals because of the way Jesus used his words and his life. If we vow to serve in a certain way, then we must serve I would expect you to think less of me. You should think less of me. If I showed up Sunday morning unprepared to preach, unprepared to lead. Not that I forgot my iPad. My ordinal vows include overseeing the worship service of God's people. But my failure to do so is no more serious than a layperson vowing to teach Sunday school class and being unprepared, or a layperson vowing to minister in the nursery and choosing not to show up. I ask it this way. If we worship God by keeping our vows, what are we doing when we don't keep them? Are we not taking God's name in vain when we don't keep a promise to serve? I know that that is a heavy charge to hear, but it cannot be avoided. My desire as your pastor is that you see first that God is worthy of our praise, for he does so much for us that his mercies cannot be counted. And one way we can worship him is to keep our vows, our formal ones and our less formal ones, our big ones and our seemingly less significant ones. As Christians, there is not to be a difference. The last point to make about the peace offering is that it it is voluntary. It was voluntary. It was offered for praise or to make a vow voluntarily On the part of Jesus, we know that he gave himself up voluntarily. No one forced him to lay down his life. He gave it up freely. And no one forces you and I to give God praise or to make promises of service. But I submit to you that if we don't want to offer praise, if we don't want to make vows of service, that there is something vital missing in our souls. If you don't want to, if you find excuses not to, then Jesus needs to deliver you. If you don't desire to praise him or to make vows to serve him, then you don't really know him, and you need to. Confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord. Believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, and you shall be saved. God wants us to offer a peace offering. And we do so in praise and we do so in vow. Amen. Let us pray. Our God, to you we come learning so very much about what it means to be a part of the peace offering. And as we look at our responsibilities to give words of praise and to give vows and to keep them, give us the courage to do so. We ask this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Merry Worship
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Although It is an integral part of our Advent season. The history of the Advent wreath is not well known. One story says it began with John Johann Heinrich Weikern. Who lived from 1808 to 1881? He was a Protestant pastor in Germany and a pioneer in urban mission work for the poor. During Advent season, children at the Mission School, founded by Wykern, in Hamburg would ask daily if Christmas is yet to arrive. In 1830, Vikern built a large wooden ring made out of an old cartwheel with 19 small candles, red candles, and four large white candles. A small red candle was lit successively each weekday during Advent, and then on the Sundays the large white candles were lit. All of this allowed the children to count the weeks and days remaining until Christmas. The custom gained ground among Protestant churches in Germany and evolved into the smaller wreath with the four candles and then the one in the middle that we know today. Roman Catholics in Germany began to adopt the custom in the 1920s, and in the 1930s it spread, the custom did spread to North America. I always find it interesting when Catholics borrow from Protestants when it comes to symbolism. The modern Advent read has a great deal of thought put into it. And each part is to represent something greater than itself. Our advent candles are uh don't have the frills uh that most can have. Uh it's meant to be seen at a distance without the frills. But traditional reeds have would have been various evergreens, and of course that symbolizes the continuousness of life Some have laurel that signify victory over persecution and suffering. Others have pine and holly that symbolize immortality. Some can have cedar symbolizing strength and healing. The Holly can connect the Christmas story to the sacrifice of Christ, as it reminds us of the crown of thorns that was placed on his head. Then there is the wreath being a symbol again of having no beginning and no end, which represents God, and it also represents the immortality of the human soul. The everlasting life found in Jesus. Any pine cones, nuts, or seed pods used to decorate the wreath can symbolize life and resurrection. Altogether, the wreath of evergreens depicts the immortality of the human soul and the new everlasting life promised in Jesus Christ. As we know, the four candles represent the four weeks of Advent. Interestingly, there is one tradition that says that each week represents 1,000 years. Supposed to be the sum total of years from creation to the time of Jesus being born. Of course, that's speculative calendars. Three candles are purple and one is rose or pink. The purple candles symbolize prayer, penance, preparatory sacrifices, and good works to be undertaken during the Advent. The rose or pink candle is lit on that third Sunday, also known as Gauday Sunday, or rejoice Sunday for that Sunday is a Sunday for rejoicing because half of the wait is over. We are past the midpoint of Advent, telling us that Christmas is that much closer. The progressive lighting of the candles symbolized the expectation and the hope that surrounds our Lord's first coming into the world and the anticipation of his second coming to judge the living and the dead. I hope all of this is somewhat interesting and helpful. What is most important, however, is the candle in the middle It is most important because of who it represents. All that the other symbols communicate mean nothing if Jesus is not the focus of it all. The candle in the middle, the white candle, symbolizes the sinlessness of one man. It is what all the other candles and all the other decorations are to point to. The Advent candles are very much like the lampstands described in the book of Revelation surrounding the Christ who is in his glorified state. In contrast to focusing on Jesus, one of the most ridiculous trends in modern celebrations of Christmas are the mind-numbing television shows and movies and songs that insist that it is not Christmas unless you fill in the blank It is not Christmas until Rudolph leads the sleigh. Unless Sandra gets good cheer. Unless there is enough Christmas spirit. It is not Christmas unless it snows, unless Santa gets a wife, unless the Grinch gives back the presents, unless the cranks decorate their house And the all-time favorite, it is not Christmas because Grandma got run over by a reindeer. The list of songs, movies, and shows goes on and on. Regarding songs, there's one in particular that is very hard for me to listen to. And I realize I could get into some trouble for this because some of you may like the song. Try not to be offended. But I take this opportunity to insist that the song Where Are You Christmas To be the silliest, sappiest Christmas song ever written or recorded, right next to it is the Christmas shoes, a close second. Just hear some of the lyrics to Where Are You Christmas? Where are you, Christmas? Why can't I find you? Why have you gone away? Where is the laughter you used to bring me? Why can't I hear music play? My world is changing. I'm rearranging. Does that mean Christmas changes too? Where are you, Christmas? Do you remember the one you used to know? I'm not the same one. See what time's done. Is that why you have let me go? And so I stop because I can't stomach anymore of that. Of course, Christmas can't go anywhere. Christmas doesn't change. Christmas doesn't let anyone go. And Christmas doesn't need Rudolph, Santa, presents, lights, carols, or fluffy emotions to be Christmas. The word Christmas itself tells us what is needed. The word for Christmas in late Old English is Christas Maese or the Mass of the Christ, which was first referenced by Christian fathers in 1038 A. D. The term Mass is not just a Roman Catholic term. It is derived from the Latin word misa, translated dismissal. which was a word used to conclude the Christian worship service stated in Latin, ete misa, est, meaning go, it is the dismissal. The word has taken on a deeper meaning for Christians as it now describes the entire worship service. Christmas then refers to formal worship of Jesus Christ. The centricity of Jesus in Christmas is what makes Christmas Christmas. When Christians focus on worshiping the Christ child, then it is Christmas. The Holy Scriptures have the same focus. Quite often we read stories in the Holy Scriptures and we have the details glossed over, not realizing that therein is found great lessons. For example, we read in Genesis 4 that Cain was the firstborn to Adam and Eve, and then Abel. It was then Abel who was killed out of spite because God was pleased with Abel over Cain. Can we see a correlation between Adam, who was the first son, and Jesus, who is called the second Adam, who was killed by Adam's race because of spite? And then there is Isaac, who was the second born to Abraham. The first was named Ishmael, whom God did not choose. And it was Ishmael who mocked his half-brother Isaac, just as the Jewish people, half-brothers to Jesus, mocked Jesus as he hung on the cross. And then there is Esau and Jacob, where God chose the second born, Jacob over Esau, from whose line the Messiah would come. All along God was showing his people by choosing the second born Son that the second Adam would come to be born to them and he would do what the first Adam did not, which was be obedient to the Heavenly Father. And going back to Eve, we see in her words an understanding that it is all about the child to be born that will overcome sin and death by crushing the serpent's head. You will remember those words as words of promise as God was cursing Eve. God would bring forth a seed from the woman, and that one seed or child would crush the serpent's head, who is the devil. Eve recalled the promise after Abel was killed and Seth was born to her. She said this, for God has appointed another seed, child, for me instead of Abel. Every faithful Jewish woman was to have the same hope as Eve, which was that this child that she was about to give birth to is going to save mankind. So we see from the tradition of the Advent wreath to the stories in Holy Scripture that the focus of Christmas should be upon the Christ child, our Lord, our Savior. But I want to add one more point. The focus should be about worshiping Jesus as Lord. And that is what we are doing now. And that is what we should be doing today and tomorrow. Yes, Christmas includes opportunities with family and friends. It can include presents and eulogues and carols and good cheer. It can include traditions practiced for generations and memories shared But for it to be Christmas, it must focus on the worship of Jesus as the Christ. We are not to worship family. We are not to worship friends or traditions or whatever else might be important to us on Christmas time. We are to worship Christ Jesus alone. Think about it. Many Christians get upset when people say, Happy holidays, and we whisper, Merry Christmas. Because we want our Christmas. And that's justifiable. But realize that when you wish someone Merry Christmas, you are hoping for them to have a grand time doing what? Worshiping Jesus. After all, it's the Mass of Christ. Remember the word Christmas, the Mass of Christ. Christ is to be the center of our celebration. He is to be the focus of our worship. Where are you, Christmas? That's really easy to answer in worshiping Christ. Amen.

sermons.title: Sin Offering
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. The scriptures clearly warn that there will be a time in history When good will be called evil, and evil will be called good. Apologist G. K. Chesterton said something similar when he said We shall soon be in a world in which a man may be howled down for saying that two and two make four. in which people will persecute the heresy of calling a triangle a three-sided figure and hang a man for maddening a mob with the news that grass is green He said soon, but for us the day is here.
