The Book of Proverbs speaks to this cockeyed manner of looking at the world when it states that a parent who does not discipline his or her child, that he or she is, in God's sight, an abuser Our culture presently boasts that it is enlightened to not spank a child because spanking is an abusive act. Whereas God's word states that if a child is not spanked for ill behavior, that the parent is neglecting the child by not providing the discipline the child needs in order to become self-controlled. Therefore, the scriptures say that such neglect is actually hating the child. The subject of spanking a disobedient child. is just one example of how the Bible comes in direct conflict with the culture that you and I now live Such direct conflict can also be seen in how the Bible and our culture treat homosexuality. What I'm about to say in this sermon is considered, in our predominant culture, to be hate speech. Their reasoning progresses as follows. I am fearful of homosexuals because I have homosexual temptations. I then speak harshly against homosexuality because I'm fighting those temptations. I next speak harshly. Or hatefully against homosexual behavior because I hate myself for having such desires and temptations And what is sad about such accusations is that there are examples of exactly what I just described There are examples of politicians and preachers who have spoken against the homosexual lifestyle and have then been caught in a homosexual affair. What is frustrating about such examples is that a person's hypocrisy doesn't change the morality of homosexuality. This gets to Chesterton's point. If I treat a mathematic problem by concluding that 2 plus 2 equals five, my final answer doesn't change the fact that two plus two equals four, and it always will A politician's behavior or a preacher's sin doesn't change the morality of such behavior or such sin. And here is another point to be understood regarding standing against certain sinful behaviors Where our predominant culture hears hate when speaking of homosexuality as sin, the Bible sees it as grace. For the Christian, speaking against homosexual behavior is like warning a person of a cliff that they are about to encounter. By natural law, we say that we are responsible for one another, and that if I can save you from falling off a cliff that you're not aware of, Then I should do what I can to warn you and thus protect you from harm. It is the same for sexual sins. If you are about to fall into one, then it is my responsibility to warn you of the harm that you are facing. To warn someone of intimate and ultimate danger is a loving thing to do. It is the opposite of hate. But our present culture says differently. It is then the greatest of ironies that warning against homosexual behavior is called hate speech. If there is a legitimate criticism of modern Christianity, it is how politicians and preachers focus on the behavior of homosexuality and ignore and even deny the sin of fornication. Fornication or heterosexual acts outside of the marriage covenant are treated as less offensive to God. and are even winked at as inconsequential. Such winking weakens the moral authority of a preacher For he can justifiably be criticized for not preaching the whole truth of God, but instead only preaching what he believes is safe in terms of what his congregation wants to hear. In truth, the sin of fornication is practiced at a much greater rate than the acts of homosexuality. When it goes unaddressed, we give license for other sins to go unaddressed, and soon there is nothing that is serious enough to be turned away from. If you think I am exaggerating, consider how easily our present culture divorces, terminates pregnancies, coronates homosexual unions, and practically encourages adultery. Such behaviors have increased while the voices of preachers have become softer and softer. Another irony to note is that when a preacher such as myself condemns fornication and calls fornicators to repentance, it is not deemed by anyone, anyone, as hate speech. If such preaching got any traction, if the audience grew larger, the devil would work to get it to be labeled to be hate speech in order to shut it down. The devil doesn't want fornicators to hear the truth and thus repent. The same for homosexuals. He wants them to be seen as victims Victims of preachers like me who call them to change their life by giving their life to Jesus I've spent this time focusing on sexual sins of our day because of our culture's obsession with sexuality and thus making our expressing of sexual desires the most prominent sin of our day. Today, we are examining the sin offering required in the book of Leviticus. When acts of sin take place, something needed to die. Blood needed to be shed. We read from Leviticus 4 that throughout Leviticus are different directives in regards to the sin offering. But our goal, our most important goal for this look at the sin offering is to see Jesus. To see Jesus in the sin offering. With the sin offering, there was a variety of animals that could be offered. Like the burnt offering, the Lord allowed for bullocks, lambs, goats, and turtle doves that could be offered. Added to these for the sin offering were male and female youth goats, which we call kids. And a possible female lamb or pigeon, and sometimes even flower. We remember from our study of burnt offerings that a variety was in relationship to what the offerer could afford, as the offering had greater value or monetary value. Regardless of its value, God accepted what was offered as a legitimate sin offering. With each graded offering, there was a distinction as to how each was to be offered, and we read a distinction in chapter 4. The distinctions reveal the many ways in which Jesus suffered, and those many ways are to move us. They are to emotionally change us so that we might have a deeper understanding to what Jesus did for us. Consider that each year during Passion Week we recount the sufferings of Jesus, and each year we can focus on something different, a different aspect of that suffering. To see it anew, again. We are to be assured that each different aspect of said suffering is a different reason For our sins to be forgiven, as each aspect meets the law requirements and fulfills God's wrath, justifying us who offer. From the sin offering, we notice that there are many persons involved. There is the priest, there is the congregation, there is the ruler, and then there is the common Israelite. First, we have the sin offering for the priest, then the sin offering for the whole congregation, then the sin offering for the ruler, and then finally for the individual. Each person or persons involved in the sin offerings brings a different perspective regarding the offering. From the standpoint of the priest, he is the anointed one. He is in the position where he is chosen to be. He is the head of the priestly family and appointed as mediator between God and man. He is clearly then a type of Jesus, as we know Jesus is our mediator between God and The next perspective is that the whole congregation, the whole people, stand before God and receive the benefit of the sin offering as a group, as a people. Jesus then stands before the sin offering as representative of the whole people, as covenant head He receives the benefit of his own sacrifice, and therefore we receive the benefit of his sacrifice because we are under him. The whole congregation is the church, and the church, the ecclesia, the called-out ones have a headship who is Christ. Once again, we have another proof of how important it is for God's people to gather as a group each Sunday. It is at our gatherings that we receive the benefit of the sacrifice as a group, as a people. It is better than staying at home. Going fishing or going to a ballgame or whatever else we might choose to do instead of gathering together. The third perspective is of a ruler. As a ruler, he is a king. That is his rightful office. As ruler, he is responsible to lead. In the case of Israel, it was to lead them to holy service before God. In the case of the church, it is the same. The throne of David, that line is never to leave the throne. And Jesus is the fulfillment of that line, of that throne, of that eternal kingdom. And the fourth perspective is that of the common people. And here is where we get involved as individuals. The individual is a benefactor of the sin offering. We know that Jesus was an individual. He was like us, and therefore he enables us to stand before God as individuals. And again, I remind you why we say in our in our confession of faith In the Nicene and in the Apostles' Creed we say, I believe, rather than we believe. No one can confess our faith. We have to confess it for ourselves. And from each of these four perspectives, we see Jesus fulfilling each role, and we see ourselves benefiting. And each of these perspectives is necessary. One does not overshadow the other. Each is important and each gives way to the others. The church, then, is a good image before us regarding how all of this works. In the church, there are individuals who are saved from sin and considered children of God and will stand alone before God on judgment day, but those individuals will also be saved together as a whole. When God comes back for the whole church, for his bride as one. Thus you can't have the whole without the individual parts, and the individual parts don't make sense without being part of the whole. The third variety in the sin offering refers to the blood The higher grade, the more valuable offering, required the blood to be sprinkled on the incense altar, whereas the blood from a lower grade or cheaper grade was to be sprinkled on the brazen altar which was in the courtyard. Remember that in the tabernacle there were two altars. The brazen altar stood in the outer court, while the golden altar stood inside the tent in the holy place. The outer court with its brazen altar and labor represent the earth and man's service to God on earth. Any Israelite that was ceremonially clean could make an offering there at the brazen altar, while in the holy place only the priests could go to offer the incense at the altar. Now besides the obvious need for blood to be spilled in order for God's wrath to be restrained, the fact that blood was sprinkled outside and then inside the holy place Shows that Jesus' blood meets us where we are and then moves us closer to the throne It is his blood that men are dependent upon. It is his blood that cleanses us as we are in the outer court and then it enables us to go into the holy place as priests. The fourth and final variety we note of the sin offering is that the higher, more valuable grade of offering is to be cast out of the camp. We read that from Leviticus 4. And yet the lower grade offers nothing, nothing is mentioned regarding their removal from the camp. And in fact, in Leviticus 6, it gives instructions for the lower grade offerings to be eaten by the priest. Now the significance of this is great, for it is a tension that you and I know very well. Within the sin offering, there is a rejecting outside, taking it outside the camp, and there is an accepting, keeping it within the camp, and even consuming it. And thus, it's a rejection and an accepting of a sinner. Jesus was both rejected and accepted by the Father He was cast out and he satisfied the Father at the same time. In like manner, you and I, as we linger in this world, are both rejected and accepted. Even though we are saved and call God our Father, we are still sinners who need to confess our sins and be forgiven. We sin and are saved at the same time. That tension will remain with us until we are taken into God's heavenly kingdom. So, having now examined these varieties and understood them for what they represent. I want us to take a step back and look at the bigger picture of the Lord's instructions regarding the sin offering. The variety of offerings acknowledges variety of human beings. The variety acknowledges and accepts the fact that we come from diverse backgrounds. We what some can afford, others cannot. And the Lord comes to all, for Jesus has paid what you and I cannot pay to be forgiven. Variety of offerings is variety in species, and this recognizes that we come from different cultural backgrounds Variety in offerings also recognizes the diverse sins that we struggle with and the diverse sins we commit. Each requires a blood sacrifice, even though some sins are more destructive than others. Diversity from the vantage point of our God is not that he accepts people as they are and accepts them when they behave in a manner they want to But instead, his diversity is displayed in his loving act of coming down to them, to us, where we are, and providing for us what we need to become a child of God. When St. Paul says that there is no partiality with God, he is referring to how God views mankind. He views all persons as sinners, sinners who carry his image. He doesn't see race. He does not see works of righteousness He does not see personality types. He does not see us as fat or skinny, handsome or homely, gifted or handicapped, wise or foolish, wealthy or poor. He simply sees sinners, sinners made in his image. And because he sees sinners, and because he is love, he gives what is needed for men to get out of their sin. He gives his only begotten Son so that people don't remain sinners. Diversity, according to our media hype culture, is giving rights to people. That will allow them to feel accepted in their sin. God's diversity is to reach out to any man or woman through the sin offering of Jesus So that they might be forgiven of their sin. Beloved, I submit to you again that the most beautiful picture that you and I have That we are able to witness occurs each Sunday. It clearly displays true diversity. For it is the time in which we come up together and take our place at the Lord's table to receive the same bread and to receive the same wine and the same forgiveness. We come up because our Lord has ascended into the heavens and sits at the right hand of the Heavenly Father. We come up because it is in heaven that we will sit at the victorious banquet table to celebrate God's final victory over sin and death. We come up because we respond to his call to eat with him. And so we come up. We come up old and young. Some come up slowly and some with a spring in their step. Some come up needing a little help and others a little more help. We come up with our own unique ethnicity. We come with our individual knowledge and understanding. We come up with our various and private sins that need the blood of Jesus applied. We come up with our various financial, emotional, and relational needs. It is, as we watch one another ascend, a truly beautiful image of God's meaning of diversity. Diversity is not found in the variety of ways we sin, but in the atoning work of Christ applied to each and every individual. That is what we celebrate when we come up. So let us prepare to come up. Amen. Let us pray. God, we thank you for the sin offering, reminding us what is needed each time we sin. And yet we thank you for eyes to see Jesus and to know that He is that sufficient sacrifice for our individual sins and our sins as a people. And so bless us in our consciousness as we prepare our hearts to receive the body and blood of you, Jesus, prepare us to receive it in faith, always in faith. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Trespass Offering
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. May be seated I remind you that our goal has been to look at the offerings from Leviticus and all of their requirements and to find Jesus. If you have waded into a few Christian ponds different from where you are now, you have discovered when praying the Lord's Prayer that there are differences Most Presbyterians and Baptists pray for the Lord to forgive us our debts, while all Anglicans historically pray that we be forgiven our trespasses. Why this is so is not easily discovered. One guess is that it was caused by the English gentry being concerned about their land And because one of the greatest sins, according to the English, was trespassers poaching on their land, thus they chose the word trespass. Whereas the Scottish, who are connected to Presbyterianism, being tight with their money and who considered failing to repay a debt to be a great sin, chose the word debts. Others have speculated that the Scots changed the word just to thumb their nose at the Brits. What we will find in our study of trespass offering Is that both New Testament meanings for the words trespass and debt have a role in describing the offering that we call the trespass offering? Today we begin looking at the trespass offering, which is the next prescribed offering in the book of Leviticus. We can contrast the trespass offering with the sweet savor offering, as the sweet savor offering was for making the worshipper pleasing to God. Whereas the trespass offering was for the pardoning of sin. The trespass offering further distinguished itself from the sin offering we examined last week And that the sin offering was for a person or persons being in a state of sin because of unknown sin committed Whereas the trespass offering was for specific sin committed. The sin offering addressed the very nature of each person. being born into sin, and therefore being sinful. And the trespass offering being for specific behavior which were specific sins committed. Another slight difference between the sin offering and the trespass offering is that while both could be for sins committed unknowingly. The trespass offering could include sins that were knowingly done and sins of a particular level of seriousness. Now, saying that there were some sins placed on different levels of seriousness than other sins may surprise some of us. After all, the New Testament tells us that if we have broken one law, no matter what law it is, we've broken the whole law. The Greek word, usually translated into the English as sin, means falling short of the mark, homartia. And we know that we come short of the mark of perfection all of the time. So it can seem that all sins can balance on a teetotter, teeter-totter, what's a teetotter, teeter-totter, as they appear to be equal in weight. That conclusion is accurate insofar as to conclude that all sins need the grace and mercy of God. But it is also true that some sins practiced clearly indicate that a man has gone down Farther into depravity, and as such, is going to have a more difficult time getting out Lesser sins can lead to more depraved sins. Life is filled with slippery slopes waiting for us. I used sexual sins as our examples last week, and so I do again. Looking at a naked woman can turn a man's thoughts to lust. If he does not stop there, he will turn to what is called soft core pornography, which can tempt him toward hardcore pornography pornography, causing all women to be sex objects for his viewing pleasure, and for some people the slope keeps going, turning into bisexuality The point is that some sins act as a gateway drug to more depraved sins until nothing satisfies the flesh. In the Old Testament, we can see that some sins demanded a sacrifice, while other sins, more depraved sins, demanded a sacrifice and a ransom While still other sins demanded the very life of the sinner. Our discussion about the law offerings is the discussion about the grace of God. Because the offerings all point to what Jesus accomplished in one sacrifice, his own life. There are, however, sins committed that required By God, the life of the offender, the life of the sinner. Such sins were idolatry, blasphemy. Offering of a child sacrifice, conjuring up the dead, adultery, cursing one's parents Even Sabbath violations require death by stoning. Such sins loom in the back of our conscience, making us apprehensive of other sins. For these judgments tell us that God takes certain sins gravely serious, and that they require immediate and permanent judgment in this life. In the book of Numbers, chapter 15, verse 30, such sins are called presumptuous sins. And verse 31 explains that such actions are a despising of the Lord's commandments. Despising. Essentially, such sins are committed with the full knowledge that they are against God's commandments, but the sinner chooses to go against those specific commandments to make a statement that he and he alone is going to be king of his life. Regarding sins committed unknowingly or carelessly, if you look in Leviticus chapter 5, verses 1 through 6, we have examples. And those verses are examples of a person who can be a witness to an oath made, but keeps quiet about it. Such a person has chosen to remain quiet and is therefore guilty of bearing false witness by an act of omission, which is not doing what you know you should have done. Next, we have the example of a person who unknowingly touches a beast that God has declared unclean. Guilt is present even though the person was at the time unaware that they were doing something wrong. Next is the example of a man who makes a rash promise by oath and later realizes that his promise was indeed rash. He too is guilty, and therefore he must make a trespass offering. In Leviticus chapter 6, verses 1 through 7, we have other sins described, sins that were premeditated. In those verses, we have described a man who knows that he is lying, and yet he does it anyways, because the lie will personally benefit him. That they benefit by making themselves richer. Such are examples of how money can be the root of many evils, and such guilty persons are to offer a trespass offering. What is unique and most vital to these trespass offerings being accepted is that it was of the guilty sinner for that person to confess. their sin, to confess. In Leviticus 5. 5 we read, he shall, the offerer shall confess. To confess is to take ownership or full responsibility for the behavior, for the act. Now, when we are young, we have a difficult time taking full responsibility. We see in here the young being quick to blame. The many factors they believe forced them to commit a sin they obviously committed, and those factors allow them to push away personal responsibility. But God says, no. We are to confess our sins as only our sins, and not the sins or faults of others We are to take full ownership of our sins and not to blame others as if their behavior forced our behavior. We are not even to hint at such things. As a young child, I remember vividly a confession forced upon me that I did not do, the behavior I did not do, and the forcing confession did not change my behavior. We had in our basement a large ironing machine. It was not an iron or an ironing board, but a machine operated by the person who would sit in front of it. It had a large roller that was covered with a large pad. It also had a heated piece of metal on which the roller would come down. The operator would move levers with his knees or her knees that brought the roller down and caused it to turn, forcing the clothes to run between the hot metal plate and the padded roller. Unfortunately, the iron would at times be turned on and left on when the roller was in the down position, causing the padded roller to burn. And it was costly to replace. One time when this happened, none of us four children, I being the youngest, Would confess the crime. My parents lined us up according to age for the interrogation, and it didn't take long for my oldest sister to cave and confess with these words I cannot tell a lie, and then pointing to me, said, he did it. Even as a five-year-old, I recognized this was a setup. If I was responsible, I had no recollection. Thankfully, we have a Savior who does not confess Our sins as our sins, but confesses our sins as his sins. He stands before the Heavenly Father with us and says that our guilt is his guilt He confesses as us. It does not take long when reading the New Testament to understand the importance of confession. We are told that if we confess Jesus as Lord and that God raised him from the dead, we will be saved. Jesus tells us that we are to be brave and confess him as our Savior before men, whether friend or enemy. And he warns, as you heard in our gospel reading, that if we deny him before men, then he will deny that he knows us before the Heavenly Father. This agreement is most reasonable because Jesus first confessed us by confessing our sins as his. In doing so, he was the offerer in the trespass offering. In confessing this way, he reasonably and passionately expects us to confess him. I anticipate that some of you might wonder that if Jesus confessed our sin as his sin And that all we have to do is confess Him as our Savior in order to be forgiven our sins, then why do we continue to confess our sins? The answer is in accord with St. John, who states in his first epistle that if we presently say that we have no sin, we are liars. And that it is our responsibility to confess our sins. And after we do so, God can cleanse us from all unrighteousness. What we are to understand is that as we confess our sins each day as individuals, and as we do so corporately each Sunday, We are to confess Jesus as the one who satisfied the trespass offering. We are confessing that the sins we commit now and in the future Are applied to the confession of Jesus as the offerer and the trespass offering. In fact, when we confess our sins to God, we are stating our faith that Jesus is all of the offerings. And as such, our confession is sufficient to be forgiven because Jesus was and is sufficient. Another distinction made in the trespass offering is that it was to include a restoration of what had been stolen. And it was to include one-fifth extra or one-fifth beyond the value of the estimated worth of that which was stolen or marred. Now about this there are many things to say and it would take too long to say it in this one sermon. I will summarize the first point, which speaks to the failure of our modern prison system. We say that when someone is incarcerated, that they are paying a debt to society. But that by that we no doubt mean that such a person is being humbled. And that such humility is a payment of a debt. The Bible, however, would differ. Payment of a debt is actual payment of a specific amount. How does a man being incarcerated for theft, for example, destruction of a car, for example, and being in prison at taxpayer expense, how does that pay a debt? He in no sense pays a debt to the victim. The great irony of our system is that the person whose car was stolen is a taxpayer. contributing to the incarceration or providing room and board for the man who stole his car What the Bible declares is that a wrong done is only made right when full payment has been made. Full payment has been made when all that has been put back, or all that was taken, is put back to its original condition. That, beloved, is what Jesus does for mankind. He is payment as the trespass offering And that means he can pay in full what mankind owes to God for corrupting the human condition and cursing the earth. It also means that Jesus set in motion the restoration of the earth and humanity so that all things will indeed pass away and all things will indeed become new. The proclamation is that Jesus, as trespass offering, did more than enable sins to be forgiven. He began the process of restoration of all the created order. That restoration will assuredly be completed. Now, another aspect to the trespass offering. Is the fact that it was the priest who decided the value or worth of what was owed by the man who was sinned against. This was a subjective judgment, and it was not a subjective judgment. The priest, you will remember, was chosen and anointed by God to decide the value. Therefore, he's not doing it on his own. God himself is helping him find that value. The final distinction we are to be made aware of is the requirement of a fifth of the offering returned That is above and beyond the original value of that which was marred or stolen. A fifth. To say it succinctly, With the trespass offering, the original wrong or evil was remedied by the value, the original value being given back, plus a fifth of the value added to it. To understand the meaning of the fifth of value, we must go back to Genesis. In the story of Joseph being elevated to the right hand of Pharaoh, you will remember. There was a great famine in the land, and because God had given Joseph a vision to warn him of the coming famine, he wisely set aside seven years of fruitful crops to be stored up the grain to be stored up. When the famine came and the people needed to buy the stored up grain from Pharaoh, Joseph bought their land and then allowed them to return to it to cultivate it. And then he required one-fifth of their profit to be returned to the Pharaoh each year. From that time on The one-fifth offering was an acknowledgement that all had been given over to the superior authority, and that one-fifth was an offering of acknowledgement of true ownership. An acknowledgement of true ownership. Mathematically, stay with me. Mathematically, we recognize that one-fifth is 20%, which is double tithe. Double tithe. Thus, within the context of the trespass offering, the offering of one fifth the value over and above what was owed Was not a free gift, but instead a debt that acknowledged who was the true superior, who was the true owner, and thus who was owed a double tithe. Jesus as the trespass offering was like what was just described. Jesus as the trespass offering was above and beyond the value of humanity He was above and beyond, therefore his offering acknowledged that the Triune God was the true owner of humanity. Jesus was a double tithe offering. And so Jesus, as the trespass offering, provides benefits above and beyond our value. We are saved from guilt of sin because Jesus was our trespass offering, and we are given the promise of heaven because Jesus double-tithhed. The earth is saved from the curse of man because Jesus was the trespass offering, and the whole heaven and earth is promised to be renewed because Jesus double-tithhed. We who believe are given the promise of the presence of God in our lives because Jesus was the trespass offering, and we are empowered from on high by the Holy Spirit To live lives of righteousness because Jesus double-tithhed. Beloved, I trust you are not hearing me say that you are to double-tithe. This is not a fundraising sermon. I am proclaiming that Jesus double tithed, and we are the benefactors. After covering much this morning, Let us take a step back. In summary, the trespass offering. First, it is an offering for specific sins known and unknown. Second, it required confession of the sins committed. Jesus as our mediator confessed our specific sins and still does. Well he requires us to confess our sins in his name. For in doing so we are confessing him as our trespass offering. Third, the trespass offering requires preparations There is a reparations. There is a value to every sin committed, and Jesus has met every value. Fourth and finally, the trespass offering required one-fifth the value of the reparations to be paid above and beyond what was owed, and Jesus paid that as well. So, how do we respond to such an offering? Well, we read from Romans 12 this morning, simply stated, St. Paul said. To give our lives as a sacrifice. And that is our reasonable service. Let us pray. God, we thank you for these revelations. Most of all, we thank you for Jesus as our trespass offering and all that that means. Deepen our understanding and thus deepen our faith, and may we never let it go. It's in Jesus' name we pray.

sermons.title: The Day You Die
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. As you know, Advent means coming, and for the Christian Advent season We celebrate the first coming of Jesus as a lowly infant while also looking to the second coming of Jesus when he will split the eastern sky and be accompanied by the heavenly host and all who have died in this life with faith in him for eternity. Because we have finished our book, our look, excuse me, at Jesus as the fulfillment of the law offerings. I am taking advantage of these next two weeks in Advent to do a re-education or a primer on the second coming of Jesus. I begin where people get confused. In Mark chapter 13, in Matthew 24 and 25, and in Luke chapter 21, We read the prophetic words of Jesus about what is going to take place in the future. And we read this quote from Jesus. This generation shall not pass away until all these things take place. Such phrasing has caused many a disagreement amongst biblical scholars One camp argues that Jesus was referring to a specific generation in the future that will witness all that will take place at his second coming and his final judgment. And it will all occur in the span of one generation. A criticism of this understanding, a criticism that I agree with, Is that such interpretation doesn't connect the warnings of Jesus to the destruction of Jerusalem and the horrible suffering that occurred under the hands of Roman soldiers who literally tore down the temple. In the Gospel of Mark, Jesus begins his description of the violence that will take place in the future because His disciples asked him to comment about the beauty of the temple that Herod had built in the days of Jesus, or before the days of Jesus and during the days of Jesus. Jesus then uses the topic of the temple to describe the sufferings that will take place for those who follow him. And then he prophesies of the destruction of that very temple that he was asked to admire. Historically, shortly after the death and resurrection of Jesus The mad Caesar, Caius, nicknamed Caligula, attempted to desecrate that very temple. Everywhere else in the Roman Empire, people were subjugated and forced to conform to the cult of Rome and acknowledge not only Caesar as Lord, but also fall in line by adopting all of their Roman gods. The Jews had previously been left alone, and for Caligula, it was time they began to conform. Kaligua gave an order to set up his statue, his own statue, in the Holy of Holies in the temple. Understand that this Caius Caesar grossly abused what he inherited, making himself to be God and desiring to be called a God And to cut off those who denied his divinity. Accordingly, he sent a Roman courtier named Petronius with an army to Jerusalem to place his statue in the temple, and commanded Petronius, in case any of the Jews would not allow it, that he should slay those who opposed it, and carry all the rest into captivity. The Roman writer Tacitus wrote that Caius did indeed command the Jews to place his effigy in the temple. Josephus records that the Jews pleaded with Petronius not to do it. The Jews, in their stubborn monotheism, were willing to sacrifice their whole nation before they saw the temple defiled. Petronius marveled at their courage and ceased with the process, so the confrontation was temporarily averted. And arranged Caligula next commanded that Petronius be put to death, and Josephus records that Caligula himself died soon thereafter. And due to bad weather in the seas, the letter by him ordering Petronius' death arrived three weeks after the news of Caligula dying. Petronius was not executed, and the temple was spared the abomination. What followed was a tit-for-tat response between Jewish zealots who wanted to cast off any official Roman presence. From the city of Jerusalem, and Roman officials who wanted to force their might upon these Jewish citizens. Thus, a more organized Jewish revolt began. At the outset of the revolt, Herod Agrippa II, grandson of Herod the Great, gained control of the upper city of Jerusalem. But the high priest Eliezer took the lower city and a Jewish civil war began. Agrippa gathered the people in a chamber of hewn stone in a futile effort to restore peace The rebels set fire to the palaces of the king, his sister's palace, and to the house of the high priest. Agrippa fled from Jerusalem, along with the zealots As the fortress of Antonia and Herod Palace also were destroyed. Four years after that civil war was started, on the 10th of August in A. D. 70, Began was called the Jewish reckoning. It was on the very day. The very day when the king of Babylon burned the temple in 586 BC Here now in 70 A. D. , the Romans again burned the temple. Jewish historian Flavius Josephus. was present in Jerusalem when the city was captured and burnt. He described the events of the siege with these words. The Romans, though it was a terrible struggle to collect the timber, raised their platforms in 21 days having described before, stripped the whole area in the circle around the town to a distance of ten miles. The countryside, like the city, was a pitiful sight For where once there was a lovely vista of woods and parks, there was nothing but desert and stumps tree and stumps of trees No one, not even a foreigner, who had seen the old Judea and the glorious suburbs of the city, and now set eyes on her present desolation, could have helped sighing and groaning at so terrible a change For every trace of beauty had been blotted out by war, and nobody who had known it in the past and came upon it suddenly would have recognized the place. When he was already there, he would still be looking for the city. Josephus next speaks of the house-to-house fighting that occurred. Quote, the Romans put the Jews to flight and proceeded as far as the Holy House itself, referring to the temple At which time one of the soldiers, without staying for any orders, and without any concern or dread upon him at so great an undertaking And being hurried on by a certain divine fury, snatched somewhat out of the materials that were on fire, and being lifted up by another soldier, he set fire to a golden window through which there was a passage to the rooms that were round about the holy house on the north side of it. As the flames went upward the Jews made a great clamor, such as so mighty an affliction required, and ran together to prevent it. And now they stirred not their own lives any longer, nor suffered anything to restrain their force, since that holy house was perishing. Thus it was the holy house burnt down. Nor can one imagine anything greater or more terrible than this noise. For there was at once a shout of the Roman legions who were marching altogether, and a sad clamor of the seditious who were now surrounded with fire and sword. The people under a great consternation made sad moans at the calamity they were under Yet was their misery itself more terrible than this disorder, for one would have thought that the hill itself on which the temple stood was seething hot, as full of fire on every part of it. And next, and finally, Josephus lists the horrendous outcome. To give a detailed account of their outrageous conduct is impossible. But we may sum it up by saying that no other city had ever endured such horrors, and no generation in history has fathered such wickedness. In the end, they brought the whole Hebrew race into contempt in order to make their own impiety seem less outrageous in foreign eyes And confessed the painful truth that they were slaves, the dregs of humanity, bastards, and outcasts of their nation. From the words prophesied by Jesus and the historical accounts that I just read, the fall of Jerusalem. There would be no doubt that Jesus prophesied that the generation hearing his voice would not pass away until the events of that destruction took place. And critics say that such an interpretation of what Jesus promised with that phrase, all things will take place, that that phrase included the coming judgment day. And since that most certainly did not take place, they say that we must conclude that Jesus was describing something different than the destruction of Jerusalem. And that something different has yet to take place. But an alternative is that we interpret the phrase all these things to be referring to all the events of the destruction of Jerusalem and not the events that will mark the end of time. There are good and sound reasons that we could interpret these prophecies by Jesus to be describing what would occur in the near future and what would occur in the far future. That is the position that I take. The words of Jesus are both for his contemporaries and for the future Regarding the second coming of Jesus and how the events will take place, we are given an order in St. Paul's letter to the Thessalonians that was read our first reading this morning And you will remember, these Christians at Thessalonica were concerned about the second coming. They had loved ones who had passed away, and they thought, well then they missed out on Jesus' second coming. And so Paul is explaining how it will take place, what events will occur. How it will take place, he says is that Jesus will return being seen in the eastern sky, bringing with him the souls of those who have died with a faith in him. It is the bodies of those souls that will be raised first, and then those who are alive will next be raised, and all be found in the presence of Jesus. It is after that judgment that takes place after that resurrection that those who are in Christ will receive eternal bodies and next be ushered into the new heavens and the new earth. Which is their eternal reward, while those who refuse to believe will be thrown into the lake of fire. There are, of course, of course there are. Differing opinions regarding the millennial reign that is referenced in the Book of Revelation, chapter 20 Some believe it means that after the second coming of Jesus, that he will reign a thousand years on earth, thus establishing an earthly kingdom. where righteousness shall reign, and that after a thousand years the devil and his followers will receive their eternal judgment. Such a perspective is called pre-millennial. The prefix pre-refers to Jesus coming before the millennial, the thousand-year reign. Others believe the thousand-year reign is metaphorical, and that since the resurrection and ascension of Jesus, that he has been slowly but surely taking over the earth as his gospel spreads. Once his kingdom is established on earth, he will then return and create the new heaven and the new earth. Such a perspective is called post millennial. As the prefix post means after, as in Jesus returning after the metaphorical rather than literal thousand-year reign. Still others believe that the events described in the prophecy of Jesus and in the book of Revelation are cyclical, and that each generation experiences their own warnings of the end of time And the ebbing and flowing of the gospel of Jesus, finding a foothold on a people for a time, and then faith waning away only to have a resurge a generation later. Thus, a millennial reign is seen as symbolic in the sense of ebbing and flowing of the Holy Spirit until Jesus returns and final judgment takes place. There are, of course, nuances to these three camps I have described, but what I have said is enough. Regardless of what position you take on how the second coming of Jesus will take place at the earthly level, I want us to focus our attention on when each of us We'll have our own personal meeting with Jesus because that will be, for us, like his second coming. In a pandemic year, our little parish has had three deaths, and none of them directly related to the pandemic. With each of those persons, Bill Schneider, Mary Lauer, and Austin Foreman, I had every confidence at their death that God's grace was evident in their lives. I have no doubt that each of them believed the gospel and are presently in the presence of Jesus. What I want each of us to consider is how we, each of us Need to be prepared to see Jesus even before he splits the eastern sky. And that preparation is simply being prepared to die. In order to be prepared to die, the first thing we need to have faith about is that we will only die when God wills for us to die. Ephesians chapter 1, verse 11 says, God works all things according to the counsel of his will. The phrase all things means all things. And all things includes the day we are born and the day that we die. In Acts chapter 17, verse 25, it says that God is not, quote, served by human hands as though he needed anything. since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything. Everything includes when we are born and when we die. In plain speech, only if God wills do I live another minute. Therefore, the Lord decides when I die. Consider in the letter of St. James, we are told that we ought not make plans in life without considering what is the will of God. From James 14, 13, and 15, he says, you ought to say, if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that. And then James adds, as it is, you boast in your arrogance, meaning he thinks it is arrogant to presume we live one second longer than God wills for us to live. All such boasting, he says, is evil. The point is, only if God wills do I live another minute. Thus, God's sovereign will includes when we are born and when we die. Remember what Jesus said? Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground, meaning die. Not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not, therefore, you are much more of value than the sparrows. What is the point? The point is, if the time for the death of a tiny bird in the remotest part of a forest is of concern to our God and determined by God, how much more so it is for us? Included in what is determined by God as when we are born and when we die The psalmist said, Your eyes saw my unformed substance. In your book were written every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there were none of them. Which means what is written in God's book is when we are born and when we die. Let us consider this point of faith another way. Who else would you want to be in control of when you were born and when you die? That's a rhetorical question. Job confessed the right answer when he said, Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return. The Lord gave, and the Lord taketh away. Blessed be the name of the Lord. What does he take away? Takes away life. Moses says the same thing when he quotes God in Deuteronomy 32. See now that I, even I, am He, and there is no God beside me, I kill and I make alive, I wound, and I heal, and there is none that can deliver out of my hand. According to Job and Moses, God chooses the day we are born and the day we die, and we would not want it to be any other way. I am proposing to all of you that having faith that God has chosen the day we are born and the day we die to be empowering Empowering. It is empowering because it is freeing. We can prepare to see Jesus. By being freed from the knowledge that He controls my daily bread and my daily breath. And you will notice that I am not saying that you don't have to take precautions in life because God knows the day you were born and the day you're going to die. I am saying that if you don't take precautions in your daily life to preserve your life, God may use that slacking and take your life by way of your lack of precautions. And I am saying that if you take precautions, all the ones that are in your power to take, you will still die on the day God has chosen for you to die. I would never tell anyone not to wear a seatbelt or not to wear a mask or any such advice. We all should do as we perceive necessary. But as Christians, whatever we do, we do so being free to trust God for every minute we breathe And we continue to trust him the moment our breathing stops. Remember the question that Jesus posed. He said, when he returns, will he find faith on earth? We are to ask it this way. When you die, and the second coming of Jesus comes to you face to face, will he find faith in you? Next week, we will hear about how to prepare for Jesus' coming by way of humility, by way of confession, and repentance. Let us pray. Our God, with this being confronted with our mortality, the reality that you have chosen that day for us to be born, a day that we celebrate annually And the same you have chosen that day, that very day, that very hour, that very moment that we will die. May that be embraced by all who have ears to hear, that we might find freedom to live. And to trust you and to build up our faith, knowing that that day is written and that day is determined. We are to live freely until that day. May this be true for all of us. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen

sermons.title: Idol of self-preservation
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I taught introduction to philosophy at a university for six years During the section on ethics, I would assign students to write a paper on two ethical dilemmas. One of the dilemmas was pretending you are a part of a religious group that is hiking in the Rocky Mountains When a freak snowstorm hits, leaving your party stranded, with no one knowing where you are or how to get to you. After several days your party runs out of food. After several weeks, a couple of members of your party have died. Now remember I said you are with a religious group. You yourself are religious. And part of your faith consists of understanding that cannibalism is a sin. But you are starving, and others in your party are starving. Do you commit cannibalism to stay alive until help comes, or do you face death by starvation? Within those six years, I would guess that twenty students a semester wrote about said dilemma Making for an average of 40 students a year times six, making for about 240 answers to this dilemma. Not one of them said they would not eat of their fellow travelers because of religious convictions. Not one. And when I pressed a few students on their answers, I received a very sad response, such as one student telling me that he had never met a person that takes their religious convictions so seriously. That was a testimony I did not expect to hear, and yet I am fearful how true a statement it was. Of those students who would not commit cannibalism, the major reason for most of them was because it's gross. The majority of students said they would not hesitate to eat their fellow travelers for the sole purpose of self-preservation. When I would press students on their caring foremost about self-preservation, their defense was simply an inherent need to care about themselves first before they would think about caring for others. My hope is that each of us is challenged by my example of about 240 students on at least two levels. The first level I hope challenges us as whether people we know would say that you are the type of person that takes your religious convictions seriously. If not, why not? And if not, then something must be done So that people you know can say that they know of at least one person who takes his or her religious convictions seriously. The second level where I hope for each of us to be challenged is to have faith that there are worse things than dying in this life. One of those worst things is purposefully sinning in this life for the sole purpose of self-preservation. Going back to my account from the philosophy class, when a student would present her paper saying she was a religious person, but she would commit cannibalism. Her justification when pressed, along with a few other students, thinking the same way, was that she would eat her fellow travelers and then ask for forgiveness later Such manner of thinking was predicted by St. Paul, who said, Shall we go on sinning that grace may abound? His answer, may it never be. If my students over the la those six years span are a fair sampling of the mindset of young adults today It is then fair to draw the conclusion that self-preservation is an idol of our day. And the larger said idol becomes, the more it dominates our personal lives, the more drastic measures will be taken in order for people to preserve their own life. And those measures include giving up personal freedoms, personal rights, with the end goal of being like the Bee Gees and staying alive. It is then for us Christians to see an opportunity in this climate of self-preservation to be a witness to the gospel of Jesus Christ by living lives that are not afraid to die. Not being afraid to die is part of a Christian's DNA. Consider these words of Jesus, who said, Remember Lot's wife. Whoever tries to keep their life will lose it, and whoever loses their life will preserve it. Now, this sermon is a follow-up from last week's sermon. Which was on the subject of preparing for the second coming of Jesus. And last week we learned that there is a second coming of Jesus that we all personally face And that second coming is at our death. We also learn that God has already chosen the day of our death. That knowledge is to empower us to live freely, for there is nothing we can do to thwart God's will. He has chosen when we are born and when we will die. We can then be freed up, even more With the knowledge of God, knowing the day of our death, by heeding the plain teaching of Jesus, that we are to live our lives as if we are already dead. In Luke chapter 21, where Jesus refers to Lot's wife, he is teaching his disciples what those days will be like before his second coming. People will be living lives as if nothing dangerous is going to occur, and then suddenly judgment will come upon the wicked, just as it did in the days of Noah, when people were swept away to their death by the floodwaters. Next, the warning comes to not be like Lot's wife, who you remember, when fleeing from God's judgment of fire and brimstone, decided to look back. And thus, by looking back, she yearned to return to that way of life. She tried to keep her old way of life in her heart, and the judgment was instant. The warning for we Christians, followers of Jesus, is to desire a way of life that we have already died to. We have put the old man, the person we once were, down for the count. And we should not want him to get up again. In Matthew chapter 10, verse 39, Jesus said the same thing, only from a different angle. Quote, whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. Previous to those words, Jesus challenged his followers to take up their own personal cross and follow him. Prior to that challenge, he taught his followers that they could be nothing that came between him and them. For he had to be the priority of their life, even a priority over their own life. These teachings are why I say that dying is in our DNA. It is a DNA that allowed St. Paul to say, to die is game, to live is Christ. It is then our calling, in our day of living before the idol of self-preservation, to live lives that testify to our own deaths. These deaths include being dead to our old sins, being dead to concerning ourselves with our own needs and desires first, and being dead to fear Fear of our earthly demise. It is living out a testimony that we are serious about our religious convictions. I have been criticized by someone who told me that I don't preach enough on evangelism. Well, here is an evangelism sermon point. Take the challenge to live out a life of dying to self. A life that rejects the idol of self-preservation and let your neighbors see Jesus in you. So, as preparation for the second coming of Jesus, we destroy the idol of self-preservation in our lives. And here I present the second idol that must be destroyed. Stephen Frye, not spelt the way we know the Fry spelling Stephen Frye is a British comedian, author, and television host who was interviewed a few years ago. And was asked about his views on God. Fry is a well-known atheist. The host asked Quote, suppose it's all true, and you walk up to the Perthy Gates and are confronted by God, what will Stephen Fry say to him, her, or it? The 57-year-old replied, I'd say, bone cancer in children, what's that about? How dare you? How dare you create a world to which there is such misery that is not our fault? It's not right. It's utterly, utterly evil. Why should I respect a capricious, mean-minded, stupid god who creates a world that is so full of injustice and pain? That's what I would say. The host asked a second question. And you think you are going to get in like that? But I wouldn't want to, Fry insisted. I wouldn't want to get in on his terms. They are wrong. When I watched the clip of the interview, I immediately went to the comment section. That's the most entertaining part of these things. And I found person after person applauding Mr. Frye for his bravery and his logic. I hope instead of bravery and logic, you can identify self-righteousness and ignorance. And I am not just criticizing Mr. Frye. This is not personal. But he has made himself a spokesman for those who hate God. And I am called to speak against such moral arrogance and theological stupidity, for it is the idol of self-righteousness that needs to be smashed. We do this to prepare for Jesus coming to us. Let us examine first what underlines the thinking of Mr. Frye and others who are like him. He has set up ethical standards that he believes God should abide by. And he accepts those ethical standards without saying where they came from and why they are to be understood as universally accepted. Consider the world that was before the Judeo-Christian ethic, before that became dominant in the Western Hemisphere. Pillaging, rape, incest, child sacrifice, land stealing, man stealing, virgin sacrifices, assassinations, genocide. These and much more immorality were the norm before Judeo-Christian ethics. It was not until the gospel of Jesus Christ invaded such lands that such norms were challenged and moral standards changed. What Mr. Fry does is what most judgments on God do today, which is borrow from God's ethical standards and then turn around and condemn him without acknowledging the source of those standards. Pointing to further ignorance in this manner of judging God is for Mr. Fry not to question how something like cancer. Even bone cancer in children, how it came into this world. The Bible plainly and clearly teaches that the earth is cursed and that humanity is condemned to death because of original sin. Adam and Eve, our buried parents, the parents of us all. Sinned against God, and thus brought death into this world. Death in all its various forms. We don't get to choose what deaths are fair or just and which are not. This is another example of the pot questioning the pot or asking why did you make me this way? Who are you, Mr. Fry? Or who is any person who thinks they can insist God does things in ways that only you and I prefer? Shows some humility, even just a little. The final criticism of thinking like Mr. Fry is on regards to his theological ignorance of not knowing what God has done to rectify what humanity has destroyed. God sent his only son to save the world. God made it so that we can no longer be under the covenant of death and suffering that was brought on by the first Adam. But instead, he sent a new Adam who brings us under a new covenant of forgiveness and hope of eternal life. And God didn't need to do that. But he did. And we are given an inward hope and an eagerness to know a God who would do what he has done with the understanding of what the self-righteous complaint about in this life Is so very much small compared to the glorious promises of eternal life to come. Last week During our Sunday school class, where we are looking at the teachings of the prophet Jeremiah, and specifically chapter 6, I encourage you to listen to those lessons on our YouTube channel. I was personally convicted by Jeremiah addressing false prophets who will only tell people what they want to hear rather than the truth about the sins that were so prevalent among the people. And this led me to question myself as to what are the sins I am not confronting in the pulpit, and why am I not confronting them? I start with why I am not confronting them. There are people within these days of a pandemic that are genuinely concerned about infecting loved ones. Who are vulnerable to the virus. They perceive it to be a life and death situation for their loved ones, and so they live a life of quarantine. Each of us must respect that. What I have been concerned about is that if I preach against the fear of death, That those who are fearing the death of a loved one will become angry with me and no longer be willing to hear me, rejecting my pastoral voice with bitterness in their hearts. And if I preach about the freedom we have in Jesus as we are empowered to know the day of our death, that it's set according to God's will. That people will hear me criticizing them for remaining hunkered down and conclude that I am not taking the virus seriously as I should. Any criticism like the ones I have described, I don't like. I want to be a pastor to as many people as possible. I don't want to push anyone away, especially over a virus. If you want to push me away because of the gospel I preached, then that's the way of it. But I won't accept broken relationships over how we each respond to a pandemic. That is the devil's work when it happens, no question about it. Regardless of what criticisms I don't like, I cannot before God fail to preach against the idols that are so prevalent in our day. I cannot say, peace, peace, where there is no peace. I would not be preparing you for the second coming of Jesus, whether personal or universal, without condemning these sacred idols. Self-preservation is an idol that Christians must smash first in our own lives. Allowing us to be a clear witness of the gospel of Jesus Christ, who sets men free from fear of death. I said this early in the summer, and so I remind you here, the testimony of every Christian, if ever asked if we fear death, is to say no, for I have already died. As St. Paul said, it is no longer I who live, but instead it is Jesus who lives in me. That is the standard. There is no other. The second idol to smash for the preparation we are to have for the coming of Christ Jesus is the idol of self-righteousness. Last Sunday evening, as we looked at 1 Corinthians 4, where Paul addresses those who judge him, we noted that arbitrary rules are seeds for self-righteousness. The Pharisees in the day of Jesus had that very problem. They created arbitrary rules and laws that were their own. And this allowed them to condemn others who did not follow those rules as the Pharisees followed them. That is what we are seeing from our civic leaders today. They have created arbitrary rules that enable them to condemn others who don't follow those rules, even when some of them are caught not following them themselves. This happens in a post-Christian culture for when we cast Jesus out of our courtrooms, out of our public squares, out of our public schools. We cast out righteousness. So the only thing we have to replace true righteousness is self-righteousness. When we are self-righteous, we condemn others for not being as we are. We think that we care more about the well-being of others. We wear the damn mask, as our governor has said. But self-righteousness is actually no righteousness. It is meeting the laws and standards of men which fall short of the righteousness of God, a great deal short. Self-righteousness may get you praised by the media. It may get you awards from the local lodge. It may even get you elected to political office. But it will never, not even close, will it ever get you into God's favor. Our works are as filthy rags before God, so says the prophet Isaac. So the challenge for us today is to check our hearts. Pray to God that if self-preservation is in any way an idol in your life, that you smash it inwardly and outwardly, and may your life from now on be a witness to others that you have already died. And next, let us check our hearts for the idol of self-righteousness. And if there be any manner of us thinking we are more moral, More caring, more loving, more sacrificial than any other person. Oh, beloved, confess that as sin. Identify it as self-righteousness and practice it no more. Let the righteousness of Jesus be enough. Because it is. Let us pray. You simply ask Holy Spirit for those who have ears to hear, let them hear. And may we all take these challenges to our personal lives and live them out, for we know it is your will. Bless us in that endeavor, we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Santy Claus Mystery
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I remind you that this is the Christmas season. We Westerners treat the days before Christmas as Christmas instead of Advent. I remind you that Christmas officially begins with Christmas Day and lasts until Epiphany. Today is also the feast of St. John the Apostle, and tomorrow is the commemoration of Holy Innocence. Where Christians are to remember the sacrifice of children for the sake of Jesus. I remind you that of all of these days that they are within the season of Christmas because my sermon this morning is still focused on Christmas My children will verify that the Jorgensen household did not mention Santa Claus at Christmas I grew up in a household that focused solely on Santa with no mention of Jesus. I was going to raise my children differently. Santa was not going to overshadow the story of the birth of Jesus, the holy incarnation of God. Our focus was on God becoming man. Looking back and critiquing my parenting, I was much too animated about keeping Santa Claus out of our Christmas celebration. The true Saint Nicholas was born in modern Turkey and became the Bishop of Myra. Several miracles were attributed to him, including the raising to life of three boys who had been murdered by an evil innkeeper. He is also said to have calmed a storm while at sea. As a result, he became the patron saint of both children and of sailors. The name Santa Claus is Dutch for Saint Nicholas. There's also the tradition that Nicholas inherited a great deal of money from his parents, which he gave to the poor in secret. One of the stories you are familiar with, he gave three bags of gold to a father of three girls who could not afford their dowries for them to be married. Nicholas is said to have dropped the gold down the chimney to preserve the secrecy of him being the giver. The gold then fell into the socks and shoes that were hanging by the fireplace to dry. It is thought that this gave rise to the custom of children hanging their stockings at Christmas Eve. From this story, Nicholas became the patron saint of the poor and of pawnbrokers, and to this day the pawnbroker sign is of three golden balls hanging from a frame to represent the three bags of gold given to those three poor girls. St. Nicholas was also a fighter for truth As there is a story of him becoming so angered by the false teachings of Arius in the fourth century that while being present at the Council of Nicaea, where the church was debating the teachings of Arius Nicholas decided to punch him in the face. I am surprised from that story he was not named the patron saint of Pugilus. And when I wrote that line, I looked it up, and sure enough, it's not official, but there are some fighters who claim St. Nicholas to be their saint. Such stories of Santa should be heard and emulated, even the punching, for there are false teachers that need a good smacking around. And I admit that there are many modern preachers that I would enjoy slapping around, and I don't think the Lord would be displeased, but maybe that's just me. My point is that instead of avoiding Santa, there is much of him that needs to be embraced by Christians. There is, of course, magical mystery in the true story of Christmas, and there is also magical mystery in the stories of Santa. There is even an argument made that the modern Santa character has a possibility, possibility not probability Possibility of being able to do all that modern folklore says that he does. For example No known species of reindeer can fly, but there are 300,000 species of living organisms that have yet to be classified, and while most of them are insects and germs, This does not completely rule out flying reindeer, which obviously only Santa has ever seen. Much has been made about the impossibility of Santa visiting the houses of all the children of the world, about two billion. But since Santa doesn't appear to visit Muslim, Hindu, Jewish, or Buddhist children, this fact reduces the workload to just 15% of those two billion, making the number about three hundred and seventy-eight million children to visit. At an average census rate of 3. 5 children per household In the world, Santa would need to visit 91. 8 million homes, presuming there is at least one good child in each of those households Because of the time zones, Santa has 31 hours of Christmas to work, assuming he's traveling from east to west, which would be the logical thing to do He would have to visit 822. 6 households per second. And considering the distance needed to go between households, Santa's sleigh Would need to be able to travel 650 miles per second, which is 3,000 times past the speed of sound. Now, no vehicle has ever traveled that fast, and no normal man could survive traveling such speed. But again, we're not talking about probability. We're talking about possibility. Even if the possibility is very, very, very small. For such a character to be real, he would have to be sustained by God, for only God can suspend the natural law he created. For such a character to be real, it would take a miracle. But that is precisely what the story of God becoming man is. It is a glorious miracle. So let us look at that glorious miracle. The first aspect of this miracle, from our vantage point, is that God would even consider becoming like us. The psalmist wonders at God when he says, What is man, O God, that thou art mindful of him? Which is to say, Why God would you be concerned about mankind? After all, the mortal condition we are in is of our own doing. God gave us all things needed for life and godliness, and we gave it away Gave it away for the only thing, the one thing that was forbidden of us. And we continue to give what is good in our lives. We continue to give it away for what is forbidden. And yet God still continues to be mindful of us. That is amazing. That is miraculous. It is marvelous to consider, and it is marvelous to be considered. The second aspect of this miracle from our vantage point is that God would become like us in all ways. Jesus did not become similar to a man, but instead became fully man. He made himself of no reputation, taking on the form of a servant. And he didn't become a man for a short time, but he became a man for all time and beyond time, making himself fully man and fully God forevermore. The third aspect of this miracle, from our vantage point, is that God would become a vulnerable infant. As a grandfather who has held his share of infants, I know the frailty of a newborn child. And how fully dependent they are upon parents to provide for them warmth, comfort, food, and safety. Infants can do nothing for themselves, and that means that for a time the Son of God, Jesus our Savior, the one who created all things, could do nothing for himself. Him whom we are dependent upon to live and to move and to have our being made himself utterly dependent to remain alive upon his being begotten. That is amazing, that is profound, and that is incredible to consider. The fourth aspect of this miracle from our vantage point is that Jesus was born in a stable in Bethlehem. At first, it sounds understandable for him to be born there and in that way. After all, people have to be born somewhere. And it is understandable that the rooms at an inn would be full. That happens. But consider he was born in a city that he was not from. God had to move upon a king to insist on a census to give reason for Joseph and Mary to travel there. And it required someone to suggest or offer a stable, not giving up their own room, mind you, for them to find a place to rest. Both of these providential occurrences first teach us about the kingly line of Jesus, for both Joseph and Mary were of that line, and thus Jesus was born in the city of David, Israel's first king. These providential occurrences also teach us of the humility of Jesus, for he came to do what Adam failed to do. And the fifth aspect of this miracle from our vantage point is that Jesus was spared death. As I said, tomorrow we honor the day of holy innocence. We know that an angel necessarily spoke to Joseph to get him to take his family to Egypt, to avoid the jealous wrath of Herod, who was the henchman of the devil. Without that special dispensation, Jesus would have been a victim of mankind at a much earlier age. There are more aspects to this overall miracle of the birth of Jesus that we know. That we do not know. The beauty of it is that because it was a miracle, we stand in awe without having the need for all of it to be explained to us Dr. Peter Craft, in his book titled The Best Things in Life, imagines there the character of Socrates coming back to modern life. Having a conversation, Socrates, with a contemporary college student named Peter, and they have a conversation in one chapter on the subject of Santa Claus. Socrates confesses to Peter that he did not know whether he should or should not believe in Santa Claus. Peter is incredulous at hearing this, for he knows the mind of Socrates that it is ruled by logic. And to Peter, the existence of Santa Claus is not logical. Socrates challenges Peter by asking how he knows there is no Santa Claus. Peter responds by challenging why Santa Claus has never been photographed. Socrates answers that Santa has been photographed many times. Peter counters that those pictures are people dressed up pretending to be Santa. Socrates counters again, asking the question, how do you know that? Have you investigated every one of those people? The point being that to be absolutely certain none such men were actually Santa Claus A person investigating would have to investigate each case, which would cause him to be in many places at one time and in many ages. and and be able to know all things about all the persons he investigates. Because no person is able to investigate such things, there is not one person who has the authority to say for certain that Santa Claus doesn't exist. The same argument can be made about the existence of God. Peter then takes up a different argument by asking How could reindeer fly? And how could Santa visit all those houses and do all the things I previously described that must be done for Santa to do his job? Socrates answers, why, by magic, of course. By magic, Dr. Crace imagined Socrates does not mean power displayed by a witch or a sorcerer, but instead he means mysterious powers that overcome natural laws. What the character of Socrates leaves open is the possibility to accept something, to believe in something that cannot be explained. The skeptics among us, the wise in their own minds among us, hear such logic as complete nonsense. They are already convinced that miracles and magic are nonsense and a product of having delusions. What the unfaithful fail to address when examining their lives is the question of purpose. What is the purpose of it all? If we ask for the purpose of why God would humble Himself in the form of a servant, why Jesus would become a human being in the most vulnerable of conditions. We get the answer that God did it because he loves us. But that is not enough because we don't get, along with the truth that he loves us, the answer as to why he loves us. And we will never get that answer. He chooses to love us when he does not have to. It is only for us to be in all that He does. It is to believe in something that cannot be explained. That is what we celebrate today and these 12 days of Christmas. Something that cannot be explained. Let us pray. On this third day of Christmas, we acknowledge that which cannot be explained, but that which we truly believe, that you became man. Born of a virgin, born as an infant, to be like us, to save us from our sin. And to this we give you our lives. In Jesus' name that we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Covid 2020
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. I want you to know that I titled this sermon before I wrote it. The title is COVID 2020. I titled this sermon Using Two Separate But Related Passages of Scripture. The first was read in our gospel reading, and the main focus for me is on the words of Jesus when he says. And do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul, but rather fear him who is able to destroy both the soul and body in hell. The next passage is in the Gospel according to Saint Luke, chapter 13, where Jesus is asked about a historical event. And the main passage to focus upon are his words, but unless you repent, you too will perish. I begin by sharing with you a conversation I had with my daughter-in-law, Alexis, on the day after Christmas, the feast of St. Stephen. I share this because I anticipate that your family has either had similar conversations or you have asked similar questions as to the one that I asked And I anticipate that you have wrestled with many issues related to COVID-19 and the vaccinations currently being offered. Alexis, as I trust some of you know, is a physician. She is a resident at Virginia Commonwealth University Hospital. Well, you and I have opinions about health, and we say in the middle of a conversation, well, I'm not a doctor, but And we keep talking as if we were a doctor. She doesn't have to say that. She's a doctor. My question to her was, Should I receive the COVID-19 vaccine? Her immediate answer was, why shouldn't you? Not a great start to a conversation. So I explained myself. Speaking in general And from the vantage point of not knowing all that is going on inside me right now, I am in good health. I don't have any nagging pains or symptoms of anything that is a serious serious health risk. I have never gotten a flu shock, and I suspect that I have only had the flu one time in my life, and with that infection I only missed a half a day of work. I have lived now, these past ten months, within the presence of a pandemic virus, and I have not come down with it. All of that speaks to me that I don't need a shot to protect me from the virus. Her argument to me was that the virus is real It is deadly, and there is still a strong case, a chance, excuse me, that I will be infected by it. I countered With a number that seems to be a point of contention. But the number's still there, so I don't know what to do with it. But over 99% of people infected by this virus survive She countered that there are still a number of people who have died from the virus, and those deaths should not be treated lightly. I countered that the current death rate increase in the United States is no greater than the previous twelve years.
