Meaning to me that those who have died would likely have died whether they had COVID-19 or not She counted that there is currently no knowledge of what being infected by COVID-19 will do to a person later in life. I countered that the same could be said about any viral infection that we are exposed to. Not much progress so far in the conversation. My son Isaac then chimed in and asked, if getting the vaccine would enable you, speaking to me, to minister in person to more people in your congregation, would you get it? Ah, got me there. Yes. If taking the vaccine would make just one of my parishioners more comfortable around me and maybe even make them comfortable enough to remove their mask while we share our lives together. Then yes, I will be first in line to get the vaccine. Oh Not first, because that would be selfish, but I will be somewhere in line to get the vaccine. Besides the arguments presented to me by my daughter-in-law, What struck me in our conversation was how passionate Alexis was about assuring the health of other people. She had a look of being incredulous toward me because I didn't seem to take my own health and the health of others as seriously as she takes it. And I respect that. I respect it because physical health is important, and I respect it because she takes the calling of being a physician seriously. But I confess to you that I was tempted to think that Alexis said all that she said because she has to. She is a doctor, and doctors are naturally going to take the position of being health cautious. As I reflected on the conversation on our drive home, I suspected that some of you have a relationship with me like I had with my daughter-in-law. When I speak urgently about the need for your spiritual health to have a checkup and for you to be regularly receiving the vaccination of Word and Sacrament. No doubt you are tempted to listen to me and say to yourself, of course he's going to say that. He is a preacher after all, and preachers say those things. But the logic of such thinking, mine towards Alexis and perhaps yours towards me, is faulty. It is the fallacy of identifying the source Which is to dismiss the opinion or position of someone simply because of their background or their occupation or their politics It is not listening to the actual argument or opinion of a person, but dismissing them for other reasons besides the argument or the position itself. The logic referees throw flags at such faulty thinking. While physical health is important. I am going to argue today that spiritual health is even more important, and I'm going to combat the temptation that you will have to dismiss me simply because what I'm going to say is what you would expect a preacher to say The context of Jesus telling his disciples to not fear those who can kill the body But not kill the soul, but to only fear him who can both kill the body and the soul and send them to hell The context is where he warns them of the persecution that they would face as his followers. He promised them that when they are persecuted, they would receive a guarantee of God's presence among them. And God would give them the words, the proper words that they needed at those times of persecution. And he would give them the necessary inner courage to face their suffering. His warning next was that if his enemies accuse him of being of the devil and performing miracles by the power of the devil How much more will his followers be falsely accused and falsely maligned? And the answer is a great deal more. He follows that reality check with a call not to fear because what is hidden will be revealed. Such is to encourage us that what people think they are getting away with The injustices they are practicing will be revealed for all to see, and injustices will be made right. Jesus next encourages his followers to speak what is not spoken out loud and to reveal falsehood when it tries to hide. Now we might fear to do so because of the repercussions that await us, threatened by the enemies of God. But again, Jesus tells us not to fear men who can only harm the body. In saying this, Jesus was not discounting the difficulty of physical pain and physical death. He himself, you remember, wished that the cup of his death might pass by him. But what he was for sure saying is that physical death has no priority over spiritual death. What we can take from these words is that if ever, if ever we are given the choice of sacrificing our spiritual life in order to preserve our physical de our physical life. We are to choose our physical spiritual life every time. And I'm imagining some of you at this point in the sermon might be questioning internally something like, So what are you saying, Pastor? Are you implying that I should sacrifice my physical body during a pandemic to assure my spiritual life is healthy? My answer, if your spiritual life is in danger, the answer is a resounding yes. By all means endanger your physical life to assure your spiritual life. Am I arguing that anyone should unnecessarily endanger their physical life? No, I am not. Chapter 10. But I challenge each of you to come up with an answer as to how are the words of Jesus that tell us not to fear him or it Not to fear it that could harm the body, but not the soul, but instead to fear only him who can harm the body and soul, how such words are to be applied in a pandemic The application I see is that we are not to fear what a virus can do to us, but instead do whatever is necessary to assure our spiritual life. But I'm a preacher, and of course I'm going to say that. There is an argument that concludes that we should take extra precautions during this pandemic, if not for ourselves. But for those who are more vulnerable, health-wise. I get that argument. I won't argue against it But there is in that position a pastoral concern. Those who join us for weekly Bible study may remember this next point. In the section of family prayers in the Book of Common Prayer, there is a portion of a family prayer that goes as follows. It's in the evening prayer. He pray this, and grant us grace always to live in such a state that we may never be afraid to die, so that living and dying we may be thying. Through the merits and satisfaction of thy Son, Christ Jesus. One evening after we prayed that prayer, I challenged those in attendance to change the wording slightly. We should be praying in this manner as well. And grant us grace always to live in such a state That we may never be afraid to die, or be afraid of a loved one to die, so that living and dying we may all be thine Let us all be honest with ourselves by being aware of ourselves that our fear of a loved one dying is not a fear for them, it's a fear for us And how difficult that death will be for us. The emotional pain we think would be too great, and so we fear such deaths But as followers of Jesus Christ, we must be convinced that fearing death for ourselves or a loved one is not what it means to be a follower of Jesus Christ. Does that mean that you should not be concerned about infecting a loved one with the virus? No, again, that's not the point I just made. The point made is that we are not to fear death for ourselves or for our loved ones, but instead we are to fear God alone. The point is about who to fear and who or what not to fear. That stated, the second passage I want to look at is from Luke chapter 13. It's right at the beginning of that chapter where Jesus says, but unless you repent, you likewise will perish. The context of that warning is a conversation. started by some unidentified followers of Jesus who wanted to know his opinion about Jewish worshipers who were from the Galilean region just as Jesus was, who were violently attacked by Pilate's henchmen while they were making offerings to God in the temple. We presently have no record of such an attack, but there are records of other such attacks commanded by Pilate, so the scenario is quite believable. Jesus addresses the logic that he reads into their mentioning of that event, and he adds another one. Evidently, there was a tower, probably a tower for storing water, in a town just outside of the old city of Jerusalem. The town was called Siloam, and so was the tower. Again, there is no known historic record of this incident, but Jesus and his contemporaries knew of it. Not unlike a disaster we would hear about today The water tower collapsed and those who were near it, 18 people, died as it fell on top of them. So with this mention, Jesus increases the intensity of the example given to him to make the point more obvious. Jesus knew the logic behind the questioners was that those who suffer such tragedies are deserving of what came upon them. It is the same logic argued in the book of Job, where Job's companions spent a great deal of time trying to convince Job that he must have done something immoral, something offensive to God. to find himself in such dire physical and emotional pain. Such thinking is to believe is to believe we live in a world governed by the proverbs like, you get what you deserve in this life. God in the book of Job makes it clear that such is not the world that He created or the world that He governs And although that message God has made clear in the teachings of Job, but also through the prophets as well, such thinkings still exist amongst Christians. Someone is diagnosed with cancer, and we are tempted to wonder what the person has done to deserve such a diagnosis. Someone gets into an accident, and we are tempted to think that such suffering must balance out some ill behavior or some character flaw. Someone gets COVID-19, and we are tempted to think that they are being judged like the Egyptians because only sinners suffer under a plague. Such conclusions are grossly arrogant and ignorant, but such thinking is still among us. But what does Jesus say? What does he use to combat such faulty thinking? He goes to the one priority that will give spiritual life. He calls people to repent of their sins. And he warns them that if they do not, They too will lose both their physical lives and their spiritual lives. And I want us to notice that Jesus doesn't break down how bad their thinking is. He doesn't get philosophical with them. He doesn't challenge their thinking of the universe like it's a yin and yang or a good force versus bad force balance. He doesn't schedule a counseling session with them. He gets to the heart of what changes a soul, which is to repent of our sins. which is to turn away from our immorality and our false beliefs and to turn to Jesus. It is the devil who wants us to wonder about why a tragedy happens to certain people. It is the devil who wants to distract by questioning if God really did say what he said, just like he did to Eve. He wants us to talk about the origin of the virus and the usefulness of masks and the self-righteousness of caring more about others. About getting the vaccine or not, and all that we spend so much time debating and judging others about, as long as we do not mention repentance away from sin and faith toward God. If you have wondered what Jesus has to say about a pandemic, if you have questioned what relevant teaching Jesus may have for us, who are now over ten months into a plague, The answer is Luke chapter 13, verse 5, but unless you repent, you will all likewise perish. Consider this question. How did those cut down by Pilate and those who had the tower fall upon them, how did they perish? What was similar? They perished unexpectedly. They were not ready. But of course, I'm going to say all of this because I am a preacher, and that's what preachers have to say. My response to that conclusion, for anyone who would listen, is first, not every preacher today is saying such things. I fear not many have called people to repentance during this pandemic, and that is precisely what preachers should be doing. And my second response is that I didn't say these things. Jesus said these things. And that should be enough for us. Fear only the one who can harm both the body and soul into hell. That person is God. Repent of your sins, believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and that will be enough to save your soul. Let us pray. Our God, to these words we want to be true. We want to be true to the call to not fear men and to not fear viruses and to not fear death for us or for our loved one. And we want to be true to repent and to believe. Father, help our unbelief. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Introduction to 1 Peter
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, Son, Holy Ghost. Amen. Leave you seated. Please be like the Bereans and open your Bibles to 1 Peter chapter 1. You're starting a series. Through the two letters written by Saint Peter. I want you to follow along with me as we go through the first six verses We note that Peter begins his letter with an introduction, although a very brief one. He uses the name given to him by Jesus, whereas elsewhere he is referred to as Simon and also Simon Peter. Peter also identifies himself as an apostle. Remember that Jesus chose twelve, lost one, assigned another, and then added the apostle Paul, making for thirteen apostles. The title apostle at the beginning of the church was not as grand as it is used today. It did speak to the authority that Jesus gave the leaders of his church For it was to the apostles that he says, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound, and whatever you loose shall be loose. But because the word apostle means a person sent, The men who were given the title did not see it as a badge of authority within the church, but instead saw it as a duty given to them to spread the gospel. Peter embraced his primary responsibility as an apostle, which was to spread the gospel He first calls Christians pilgrims, others translate it sojourners. Such a description speaks to the belief that this world is not the home of Christians. And because it is not our home, we are not to be concerned about our lives in this world, but instead we are to be more concerned about our home in heaven. Having the mind of a pilgrim traveling through a particular place allows us to care less for the land in which we are presently occupying. It's not to be important to us Nor are the troubles found in this land to be so disconcerting to us. We care some, to be sure. We are good stewards of what we are given in this world. But here is not where our lasting treasures are to be placed. Jesus told us to set our affection on things above, not on things on this earth. The traveling Christians Peter writes to are dispersed amidst several districts. Peter understood his ministry to be primarily spreading the gospel amidst Jewish people who were his primary disciples. Thus the word choice of being of the dispersion Would have been known to the people he pastored, for the Jews had a history of being dispersed away from the promised land. I take the word choice to be symbolic, for we cannot imagine Peter limiting his audience to the districts he mentions, for there were others who could have used the teachings he offered. The districts also are Greek districts rather than Roman provinces, which is likely chosen by Peter to further describe a people that were in this world, but not of this world. And then he refers his readers as the elect. This is the same doctrine of election we read about from St. Paul. Primarily in his letters to the Roman Christians and then to the Ephesian Christians. As I have been emphasizing in our study of Ephesians, the primary purpose of the doctrine of election is to assure the readers and listeners that their place in the faith, the covenant of Jesus, their place in that covenant is secure. Just as Israel was chosen of God, and that choice means that they are God's people forever, so too are Christians to see their place in the covenant of Christ Jesus to be forever and always. How we came to be a part of the elect and how we remain a part of the elect is next described. We came to be a part of the elect by the foreknowledge of God the Father. From this, we are to be assured that God is not simply making this up as he goes He is not winging it, crossing his fingers. He is sovereign and therefore controls all things. His will cannot be thwarted, and even it cannot be known without him personally revealing it. And then how we stay within the elect is by the sanctification of the Holy Spirit And we should notice that Peter just taught the doctrine of the Trinity without much effort, as he made equal the Spirit to the Father and the Spirit working with the Son. The sanctification or purifying of us is not a one-time thing, but is ongoing and continuing. The mention of obedience and the sprinkling of the blood of Jesus then connects the new covenant of Jesus to the old covenant under Moses. For the same act of sprinkling blood was done upon the people in Exodus 24, when they committed to do all that the Lord was commanded, then the blood of God of a sacrifice was sprinkled upon them. That too was a blood covenant, but that blood covenant need to be repeated. With Jesus, the blood covenant is filled once for all time. Next is the greeting that we are familiar with, and that it is similar to that which we find in St. Paul's letters. The grace referred to is comprehensive in that it includes the presence of mercy and love in the forgiveness of sin. Grace is what God extends to us. The peace is what we can have internally when we are in right relationship with God and with our fellow man. They go together, grace and peace. The former grace causes the latter peace. The emphasis of praise toward God the Father is next. And this is because of the work of Jesus. It was for the purpose of people having relationship with God the Father. Jesus did the work so that you and I could know the Father. And here Peter is placing us as being a part of the family of Jesus, as Jesus is our Christ, he is our anointed one, he is our Savior. And because of Jesus, we have hope. But hope in what? Hope in God's mercy, yes. But overall, our hope is eternal life. It is heaven. And we have that hope because of the resurrection. Jesus overcame death and thus overcame the destruction sin brings with it. His resurrection and our election make us inheritors of what he accomplished, which is receiving the incorruptible and undefiled. Which are the rewards promised us in heaven, or again where our treasures are to be laid up. Those rewards are kept incorruptible and undefiled by the very personal power of God And the faith we are to have in what Jesus has done for us, making us all sons of God. But none of this has fully come to pass yet. We still await for the truth of all of it to be revealed in God's chosen time. And all of this we can rejoice about. But for a little while, we are grieved from time to time with various trials, as verse 6 states. The word grieved includes the meaning of being sorrowful or in distress. The word is in the present tense, so it was something that Peter knew had h a past tense, excuse me. It is something that Peter knew had happened in the past. But all suffering that we experience down here is to be seen as nothing compared to the promises given to us for eternity. Any and all suffering is brief compared to the eternal glories in Christ Jesus. And trials, hard times. Emotional hard times, physical pain, are to be understood as being from God. They are not There are not any trials that occur outside of God's will. And note that a trial from God is not a temptation from God. He tempts no one. If we are tempted to sin while under trial, that temptation is within us. We are to blame. And so the St. Peter's epistle begins. With pointing us toward the heavenly promises that await us while we sojourn in this world, while encountering trials of various sorts that bring grief to us. So which is it for you? Where do you choose to live each day? Are we to live as heavenly beings or troubled earthly sojourners? I hope you know the answer, so I'm delaying speaking it. David Livingston was born on March nineteenth eighteen thirteen in South Lincolnshire, Scotland. And he grew up with several siblings in a single tenement room. That sounds like a bit of a grievous trial. He started working at a cotton mill company as a child and would follow his long work schedule by schooling during the evenings and weekends. More grievous trials. He eventually studied medicine in Glasgow before going on to train with the London Missionary Society for a year. He completed his medical studies at various institutions in 1840 in London, England. A little taste of heaven. In the official role of a medical missionary, he set forth to Africa, arriving in Cape Town, South Africa, in March of 1841. Again, touch of heaven. A few years later he married Mary Moffat. The couple would have several children, more touches of heaven. Livingston eventually made his way north and set out to trek across the Kalahari Desert In eighteen forty nine he came upon Lake Ngami, and in eighteen fifty one the Zambezi River Over the years, Livingston continued his explorations, reaching the western coastal region of Luanda in 1853. In 1855, he came across another famous body of water, the Zambezi Falls called by the native population Smoke That Thunders, and which Livingston dubbed Victoria Falls after Queen Victoria, all little bit touches of heaven. In 1856, Livingston had gone across the continent of Africa from west to east, arriving at the coastal region of Colomain in what is present-day Mozambique. Another touch of heaven, but I haven't mentioned some trials along the way. Upon his return to England, Livingston received accolades and in 1857 published Missionary travels and researches in South Africa. The following year, Livingston was appointed by British authorities to lead an expedition that would navigate the Zambezi More touches of heaven, also it seemed. However, the expedition did not fare well, with squabbling among the crew and the original boat having to be abandoned. Other bodies of water were discovered, though Livingston's wife, Mary, would perish from fever upon returning to Africa in eighteen sixty two. Terrible, terrible, grievous trials. Livingston returned to England again in 1864, speaking out against slavery, and the following year published Narrative of an expedition to the Zambezi and its tributaries. In the book, Livingston also wrote about his use of finine as a malaria remedy and theorized about the connection of malaria to mosquitoes. Touches of heaven while under trial. Livingston undertook another expedition to Africa landing in Zanzibar in 1866 and going on to find more bodies of water with the hope of locating the source of the Nile, which he never did find. He eventually ended up in the village in Guanghui, where he witnessed a devastating massacre where Arabic slave traders killed hundreds of people. Touches of heaven and grievous trials After these events, Livingston was not heard from and thought to be lost, resulting in the transatlantic venture that was developed by the London Daily Telegraph and the New York Herald Stanley, Henry Stanley, was sent to Africa to find Livingston. Stanley located the physician in the Ugiji In late 1871, and upon seeing him utter those well-known words, Dr. Livingston, I presume. A touch of heaven or no Many times in life, it's neither. Livingston chose to stay, and he and Stanley parted ways in 1872. Livingst died from dysentery and malaria in 1873 at the age of 60. Final grievous trial. His body was eventually transported to and buried in Westminster Abbey. But I did not mention was that much of the grievous trials experienced by Livingston were of his own doing, as he placed himself and his family in too many dangerous situations. while having a fallout with other missionaries because of his harsh personality. Another person to consider is Chief Sichu Sichiyo. Pronounce that right. Sichiyo. Chief Sichiyo of the Queen of People. Of the Twansa clan, primarily found in South Africa. For you see, although Livingston is known as the Africa's greatest missionary, he is recorded as having converted only one person. Chief Sitchil. So let us look at the life of Chief Sitil to see if he lived in heaven or in grievous trial. Sichul was born in 1812. His father died when Sichuel was 10. And two of his uncles divided the tribe, which forced Sichuel to leave his home. A grievous trial. When Sitchio returned, he took one of the tribes by way of his uncle, touch of heaven. It was at this point that he met Dr. Livingston. Livingston was known through a large part of Africa as treating the natives with respect, and the tribes that he visited returned his respect with faith and loyalty to him. He could never permanently convert the tribesmen to Christianity, however, among other reasons for his failure and reasons that also troubled Sitio. It was because Livingston could not demand rain from God like the tribes rainmakers could, who said they could demand rain if they requested it of their gods. A grievous trial for Sitchiel and for Livingston. Livingston immediately became interested in Sitchiel and especially his ability to read Being a quick learner, Sitchiel learned the alphabet in two days and soon called English a second language, Touch of Heaven. After teaching his wives the skill, he wrote the Bible in his native tongue. Touch of heaven with some trial. After a long hesitation by Livingston, who wanted to be sure Sichi ill was committed to Jesus, he baptized Sitchiel and the Christian community fully embraced him. Touch of heaven. Sitchill was now a part of the church, but he continued to act according to his African culture, which went against Livingston's teachings, such as believing and practicing polygamy. Tough, grievous trial. Sitchil had five wives, and when Livingston told him to get rid of four of them, it shook the foundation of the Kwina tribe. That was a grievous time, a grievous trial. After he finally divorced the women, Livingston baptized all of them and all was well, touch of heaven. However, one year later, one of his ex-wives became pregnant, and Sitchill was the father. A grievous trial brought on by self. Sitchiel begged Livingston not to give up on him because his faith was still strong. But Livingston left the country and went north to continue his Christianizing attempts, grievous trial for both men. After Livingston left the Quena tribe, Sitchiel remained faithful to Christianity and led missionaries to surrounding tribes as well as converting nearly the entire Queen people. Touch of heaven. In the estimation of Neil Parsons of the University of Botswana, Sitchiel, quote, did more to propagate Christianity in the 19th-century South Africa than virtually any single European missionary. Although Sichu was a self-proclaimed Christian, many European missionaries disagreed. The Queen of Tribe leader kept rainmaking as a part of his life, as well as polygamy. Touch of heaven and grievous trial at the same time. These summations of these two lives reveal the point we can get from St. Peter's opening words in his first letter. The Christian life is living between the tensions of experiencing touches of heaven, but only for a time, and experiencing difficult trials, but only for a time. I use the life example of Dr. Livingston because he was doing the Lord's work, or he believed, and although he had a great deal of success in the public eye His ability to spread the gospel is greatly limited. When we are doing as we know God would have us do, whether it be homeschooling our children, Or serving at a church function, or being hospitable, or providing a meal for someone, or a thousand things we can do to serve Jesus by serving others. We might have the false assumption that God is going to make such service easy for us. And when we face a trial while serving, our expectations are dashed. The problem is God never promised such a life. What he promised is that his heavenly promises would be enough to give us hope while we suffer various and grievous trials. I use the life of Chief Sitio because the trials that were mentioned were caused by his own sinful behavior. Let us not hide from the fact that Christians sin, and some of those sins are public, and some of those appear quite scandalous. Was Chi Sitchio a Christian? Think upon that. Some missionaries said no. But I think we need to say yes. And he was a disobedient one Some of our grievous trials cannot be avoided, and some are brought on by our own choices, our own behavior. That is the reality of the Christian walk. We live in tension with our eyes on heaven and our feet still walking this earth. The call of God upon each of us is to stay in that tension. Keep your affection on things above while walking the narrow road. The journey really isn't that long. Let us pray. Oh God, with these examples before us and the words of Saint Peter We do want to keep our affection on things above our heavenly hope while remaining here and remaining faithful. But Father, we do sin, and we come here each Sunday to confess those sins, but to do more, to turn away from them. And so we ask once again for you to give us the power and the courage to do so. We thank you for your faith and your bloodshed. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: The Story is Jesus
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, the Son, the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. You will be well served to turn in your Bibles to 1 Peter chapter 1 starting at verse 6. 1 Peter 1 starting at verse 6 Let us all imagine together that Jesus has returned. The dead have been raised. And all of humanity stands before him at final judgment. But before that final judgment Each person that has ever lived receives a special specific book that has his or her name written on it With the date of your birth and the date of your death. You and I, all of us, receive our own book. And we are told that each book is uniquely about our lives. And so we eagerly open them. I open mine, you open yours. And as you start to read yours, you get confused. You are in the book, all right. You are a character in the story But the story, the main character in the story, isn't you at all. The main character is Jesus. And so you think that there has been a mistake, and so you look around to whom you could complain. And then we start to talk to one another, and we realize that in all of our books, in the book of every person who ever lived, the main character in that book is Jesus. And then it dawns on you this world and the way of history that it has played out hasn't been about nations rising and falling. It hasn't been about accumulated wealth or political power or social justice, or individual freedoms, natural disasters, world wars, plagues, or anything other than Jesus You next look back at your book and start to read specific stories from your life. You read about the time you got into a fight with your sibling because he played with your stuff. And you told them specifically not to touch your stuff. And you complained to your parents about the unfairness. And your brother is always touching your stuff. And during that whole scenario, one afternoon in your childhood, you thought the events that happened were about you. But no, they were about Jesus and Jesus establishing his kingdom. Next you read a story of a broken relationship that you at one time thought would end in marriage. The pain of that breakup was almost unbearable at the time. You thought half of your heart was ripped out, and you remember well the internal turmoil you went through. Those were tough days for you. But those days were never about you. They were about Jesus and how Jesus was establishing his kingdom. And then you read about the time that you posted on social media after a terrorist attack, praying for France! You type over the picture of a French flag. And here, in the book of your life, you learn that the tragedy in France was never about France. It was about Jesus and him ushering in his kingdom. Next, you read of a time when you decided to stay home from church for what you called me time, after all psychiatrists insist that such times are healthy. Now, as you read that story, you learn that what you thought was a time for you wasn't about you at all, but it was about Jesus and his coming kingdom. And now it dawns on you, all of those times in your life where you thought what you were doing was the most important thing in the world. When the thoughts you were having and the emotions you were feeling were the apex priority of your life, now you see that none of it was ever about you. It was always about Jesus and will forever be about Jesus You next ponder how your life would have been different, how your thoughts would have been prioritized, how your lusts would have been under greater control. How your conversations would have been so very different, how goals in life would have been better focused, how so very Much, very, very much would have changed if you would have known that the ways of this world are all about Jesus and his kingdom being established on earth as it is in heaven But then you catch yourself. You actually did know that all of your life was about Jesus, or at least you knew it should have been. And now you face judgment. How is that going to go? As we look at 1 Peter 1, verses 6 through 12. We learn that all of life being about Jesus was initially a secret. A secret angels longed to look into, longed to see. Last week we looked briefly at verse 6 and the reality that although heaven is our destination, life is filled with various trials that grieve us. But consider how easier it is to endure various trials, even the most grievous ones, when we accept that what we suffer is not about us And that the Heavenly Father is using such trials to reveal Jesus as Lord and to bring about his kingdom, his eternal kingdom. How much easier or quicker our trials would be if we no longer saw ourselves as being unjustly treated or wrongfully accused or suffering for no reason Angels long to see the purpose of suffering, and you and I get to experience it. Verses six through nine are actually a part of one long running sentence that starts at verse three. Translators break it up for clarity, and preachers break it up because we can't handle all that is said in this one sentence. In the midst of trials, we can easily focus on self because we simply want to survive the trial. But we lack right perspective when we do this. The trial, as was said, is not about us. is how God wants to use those trials to establish the kingdom of God, the kingdom of Jesus, in both this world and in our lives. When we watch a child go through a trial, let's say a toy is taken from her, and she begins to whimper and cry. We don't feel necessarily sorry for her because we know that the injustice that she feels will soon pass and that her emotional pain will not last long. But she doesn't know that. She has not matured enough to know that her trial will soon pass. We too often are like that little girl. But we are to mature and know that our grievous trials are only for a little while. And there is a goal to our grievous trials. There is always a goal. Peter says it is to prove our faith to be genuine and to increase its value to be more precious than gold. As it is being refined by us staying in the trial, while allowing the fire of the trial to burn away that which is impure. And so if we were to ask, what is going on with me right now? What is happening to me, referring to a trial that we are experiencing, the straightforward answer is that you are being sanctified. God is making you more holy through your trials. And here is fair warning. This is by experience, more than scripture Here is fair warning. If you do not allow God to make you more holy, to improve on your virtues as you go through a particular trial, You should know that you will have to go through another and another until you allow God to burn away the dross, for you are his child. He has elected you, as verse 2 states, and therefore he is not going to allow you to remain imperfect, but he is always striving to perfect you until you enter into his glory. But some of this that I've just said sounds like it's about us. After all, Peter is describing our trials and our faith and our being tested. That is about me, you, right? Well no. The sentence continues May be found to praise, honor, and glory at the revelation of Jesus Christ. Consider how the devil plays with individual people, convincing them that the life they live is solely and primarily about them. He convinced Eve that her knowing good and evil from the side of evil was about her. He convinced Cain that his offering being accepted by God was about him. He convinced the people as a whole that building a tower to reach the heavens and to protect them from another flood was about them and their survival. He convinced the citizens of Sodom and Gomorrah that their lives that they lived were for the purpose of pleasure of their flesh. He convinced Sarah that she couldn't conceive because she trusted in her perspective. And on and on it goes. We are all of us easily deceived that our lives are about us. Examine the secular world today where people have their minds On only what is for them. Even when they perform what they consider an altruistic act, it is a lie. For the motivation is for how the act makes them feel. Christians are not called to behave in a virtuous manner because of how it makes them feel It was a number of years ago that a popular atheist named Christopher Hitchens, now deceased, publicly debated the Reverend Douglas Wilson. And Hitchens was quite confident in his challenge for Wilson to name a virtuous behavior that is practiced by Christians and not practiced by atheists. The challenge was to make the point that a person doesn't need to be a Christian or a believer in God in general to behave virtuously. And I was never happy with the response of Doug Wilson, not to criticize him, but he did not point out an obvious distinction between virtuous behaviors performed by Christians and those practiced by atheists. The obvious distinction is the praise, honor, and glory of Jesus Christ The Christian can practice virtuous behavior to the glory of Jesus, while the atheist cannot. My point is that while Peter is seemingly focused on the lives of his hearers while he speaks to their trials and their faith, by continuing on, he makes it clear. That the trials and the purification of the faith of these Christians is done for the praise, the honor, and the glory of Jesus Christ. For as Jesus is revealed, the faith of the Christian is purified. At the beginning of John Fox's Book of Martyrs, written in the sixteenth century from a Protestant perspective. We have this paragraph from the first chapter, introduction. It is, quote, as it is not our business to enlarge upon the Savior's history, either before or after his crucifixion. We shall only find it necessary to remind our readers to the discomfiture of the Jews by his subsequent resurrection. Though one apostle have had betrayed him, though another had denied him under the solemn sanction of an oath, and though the rest had forsaken him, unless we may accept the disciple who was known unto the high priest The history of his resurrection gave a new direction to all of their hearts, and after the mission of the Holy Spirit, imparte new confidence in their minds. The powers with which they were endued emboldened them to proclaim his name, to the confusion of the Jewish rulers and the astonishment of the Gentile proselytes. I want our focus to be upon that opening remark, the proclaiming of the name of Jesus. All martyrs who appear in John Fox's Book of Martyrs died in order to proclaim the name of Jesus. They did it for the praise, honor, and glory of Jesus to be revealed. The martyrs have been given Have been given a special place in the book of Revelation, being under the altar, calling out for vindication, because they understood that their lives were not about themselves. They saw the story of humanity. Even their story, their personal story, was about Jesus. Peter continues by graciously assuming that the elect, to whom he writes, love Jesus, even though they have not seen him. And this gracious assumption reminds us of the words of Jesus to his disciples, you remember, as he tells Thomas. Thomas needing to touch, needing to see, that more blessed were those who had not seen and yet still believe. Such a belief can only be generated and fostered by the Holy Spirit. Because such faith is generated and fostered by the Holy Spirit, the joy that results can be inexpressible and full of glory. If it was a joy generated by us and for us, it would most certainly be expressible and contain no glory, especially no glory of God. Moderns find it quite easy to express joy as it flows out of them in their music and self congratulations I looked it up this week. The words love and baby continue to be the top ten words used in popular songs, such as how moderns express joy. But if your joy is not about you, if it is from God, it cannot be expressed with human words. It is far too deep, far too wide, far too rich to be uttered by earthly words. Peter continues his long sentence by getting to the point of our salvation. The beginning of the sentence was calling for God to be blessed. The middle of it was about grievous trials that we go through. The ending is our salvation. And once again we are challenged by the point of it not being about us. And once again we note that our salvation is actually not about us, even though we are the great benefactors of it. No, our salvation is about the establishing of the kingdom of God in which Jesus reigns supreme. St. Peter's final point in this section is to reflect on how privileged we are to know what we know about the story of Jesus. When Paul tells Timothy that all scripture is God-breathed, he was initially referring to the Old Testament. When Jesus revealed God's plan from the scriptures to the men walking on the road to Emmaus, he was showing them the gospel from the Old Testament. The good news of God sending his son to redeem the world has always been evident but not clearly seen. Even the prophets who spoke the words of God did not see what you and I now clearly see. Jesus is the seed promised to Eve. Jesus is in the life of Seth. Jesus is the secondborn to Adam, to Abraham. Jesus is the persons of Jacob and Joseph. The gospel story is in Moses and then in Joshua and then in Saul and then in David and then in Solomon. It is continued in Elijah and Elisha. It was described by Isaiah, Jeremiah, and all the rest. The prophets also didn't know the story of the world, the universe, that it was all about Jesus. Not even the angels knew that they longed to see it. The same word for see, to see it, same word for see we find in the gospel accounts of the resurrection. People came to the garden that Easter morning and stooped down to appear, to see into an empty tomb. That is the idea, that is the image here. Angels peering down, with studied gaze, longing to know more of this great salvation. They longed to peer, even though there was no salvation for them. The angels that fell were damned. Those that did not were established forever in the fellowship of God. And that was all. But for the elect, men and women, in so many ways, lower beings than the mighty angels, God shows us his extraordinary love and grace and mercy. From this desire of angels to see, to peer into, consider how important perspective is and how it can seemingly change everything. If you stood up in front of the tomb of Jesus at the entrance, as it was shorter than your eyes, you would only see a foot or two inside. giving you a perspective that suffering and death continue. But if you stooped down and peered inside, you would see a tomb empty and all things have been made new. A life-changing perspective. The perspective that your life is not about you is a privileged one to have It is stooping down. It is peering inside. It may get you off your phone and thus off your social media sites. It may get you to not care if you are slighted, if you are judged, even if you are forgotten. It may get you to care first and foremost about the kingdom of God and his righteousness. A passage from our study of Ephesians is appropriate to close on. Here is a summary of the Christian life from St. Paul, Ephesians chapter 4. He said. Walk worthy of the calling with which you were called, with all loneliness and gentleness, with long-suffering, bearing one another in love. From the perspective of seeing your life primarily about you, St. Paul's summary looks unlikely. It's not going to happen. You can't do these things. With the perspective of your life and everyone else's life being about Jesus, living a life of lowliness, of gentleness, of longsuffering. Putting up with one another in love. That seems doable. It's that simple. Let us pray. Our God, we thank you that we are a part of this story. But we also thank you That we can realize we're not the focus of the story. We're not the main character. And for that revelation that it is Jesus, that our lives are to be about Jesus and his kingdom. Father, for that revelation, we thank you. We thank you for perspective, an eternal perspective. It's in Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Holiness Standard
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn your Bibles to 1 Peter chapter 1. We're picking up at verse thirteen. It was our first reading this morning. A powerful residual that comes along with believing in and following the Lord Jesus Christ is a sense of identity, especially for young people. Christianity provides identity for all ages, of course, but it is especially important in the lives of young people The young among us struggle with identity. We all do when we are young. Educators and psychologists have encouraged young people to ask themselves Who they are, as if their personal identity can be found within them. The reality is that when we are young, finding out what is inside of us is like peeling an onion One layer looks like another until there's nothing left. The more important question instead is who do you want to become? When that is answered, a person can then make strides in life to come closer to whom he or she wants to be. I remember a specific instance of wanting to be like someone. When I was in seventh grade, our junior high school had seven, eighth, and ninth grades, and there was a ninth grade boy who most of the girls liked. He was successful in athletics. And so I studied his mannerisms, his gait, his attitude, and tried to alike myself to who he was. I don't know how well it worked, but I well remembered the desire to establish an identity that I would strive to live up to. As I said, we all struggle in a similar manner. We established last week that the story of the world, the universe, of all of creation is centered on the main character who is Jesus. We play a role in the story and we thank God for that, but we are not the center of the story. Never ever are we the center. It has been, is, and always will be about Jesus. A beautiful aspect of the gospel of Jesus is that while he is the central character, he bends down and cares for us. He cares about us individually and corporately. He is the center of the story, and yet he treats us as if we are the center of him. That is a beautiful thing. We also established last week that we are privileged to understand what God was doing by sending Jesus and by Jesus suffering as he did. We get to know what angels longed to look into, longed to understand. We get to see the finished product while understanding what was going on all along, down throughout history. And so it is with the revelation that the story of all creation is about Jesus, and that we are privileged to know the story. With that in mind, It brings us to St. Peter's next point in verse 13. The word therefore starts us off. Because of all before, therefore Peter is saying, because of what he just described, here is what we as Christians are to do about it. The first thing we are to do is gird up our loins. Thankfully, we don't wear loins anymore in our culture. But the expression simply means get ready to be active, and that's not even enough. It also means get ready to fight, get ready to go to battle. And it is the loins of your mind that is to be ready for a fight. Thus, we are to be sober, which does mean not having alcohol impede us, but it also refers to being mentally aware. As opposed to what is called today being spaced out or simply not paying attention. Our minds instead are to be focused on the hope that we have in the grace of God, which includes the hope That our sins are forgiven and that our heavenly reward awaits us. And because we are God's children We are to behave as God's children, and that means not to live as we used to live before Jesus became our Savior. The simple logic is that if you are called holy, which Christians are called because Jesus has made us so by forgiving our sins, then we are to live as holy. Connecting this to my opening comments, our identity is being holy. That is our standard and nothing else. God has said to his people in the book of Leviticus, be holy, as I am holy Jesus repeated the standard when he said, Be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect. No apology followed, no excuse accepted. No qualification offered. The holiness of God is our standard and thus our identity. The standard of holiness, being God the Father, means that all commandments forbidden are not to be practiced. And all commandments directed are to be followed. The standard being God the Father means that all inner turmoils are brought under the authority of the Holy Spirit. As our attitude and our emotions are to be governed by the love of God. Thus we are to be holy both outwardly and inwardly. There have been very different approaches since the time of the ascension of Jesus on how Christians were to go about and are to go about living holy lives. I'm going to group these responses, these approaches, into two camps with the awareness of the many variations that reside underneath these two camps. I do so only to make a greater point than being concerned about those variations. The two camps I'm using are labeled liberal and conservative. The terms liberal and conservative I am not using in a political sense, but rather a theological sense, that politics play a role. Politics always plays a role. The liberal camp sees the standard of holiness being God the Father and concludes that such a standard cannot be reached And therefore, God can't really mean for us to meet that standard. This then allows them to focus not on the laws of God to obey, but instead look for a spirit Behind the laws. Because the spirit of each law is a subjective thing to identify, it allows for all sorts of interpretations and goes along well Goes along well with the line given by the devil to Eve in the garden when he asked, Did God really say you should not eat of the tree of life? From a liberal perspective, we get questions such as, did God really say you should not sleep with your neighbor's wife? Did God really say that He hates divorce? Did God really say that life begins at conception? Did God really say you shouldn't obey the lust of your flesh? Did God really say that we should not have idols in our lives? Did God really say that you were to not behave like the unbelieving? Did God really say that he was one God and there is no other? What is implied, of course, is that what we thought God said likely has a different meaning than we first heard it or understood it. From the New Testament context, we get such questions as: Did Jesus really say he was God? Did Jesus really say that no one receives a heavenly reward unless they go through him? Did Jesus really say that God's kingdom is established in him only? Did Jesus really say he and the Father are one? And then from the letters of Paul and Peter, did the apostles really teach that God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit are all divine and yet one? Did the apostles really teach that the moral standard of the Old Testament continues to be the moral standard for God's people? Did the apostles really teach that men and not women are called to the priesthood to be bishops, elders, and deacons? And then the overall question. Did God really say anything at all of value or truth that should change the way you want to live? Just as where the scriptures say that when you have broken one law, you've broken all the laws, so too it can be said that when you question One clearly stated truth or moral standard of Holy Scripture, you have questioned them all The conservative camp, in contrast, sees the standard of holiness being God the Father and concludes that when the standard is set, it is set There is no deviating from the standard. Truth is truth, is truth. Either you obey it all or you toss it all out. From the conservative perspective, truth morally, historically, statistically, remains constant and objective. Such also describes the God of the scriptures. He is truth, he is constant, he is objective. He is the opposite of shifting shadows that deceive the eyes. He is the opposite of the weather vein that always points to the direction the wind is blowing. Examine the character of God Peter describes when he speaks of God as a judge who shows no partiality. To show partiality is to shift. It is to change, to adjust laws, to fit desires and personalities. That is not our God and not our standard. We are to conduct our lives, that is what the phrase, throughout the time of your stay here, it's talking about your life in this world. From verse 17. We are to conduct our lives in fear. That's a holy awe of God's infinite authority and authority and power. And we are to live before a God who does not change, which means his standards never change. And let me tell you why this is so important to grasp, this understanding from a conservative perspective. It is because the devil has ways, he has strategies, he has methods that he uses to get as many of us as he can over to the liberal side, which is his side. What I'm going to do this morning is what the Ravens should have done last week. The Ravens last week faced a defensive strategy that forced them to turn to the passing game, but the Ravens weren't ready for the game scheme, and therefore they lost. Well, it is the same for us when we are not ready for the game schemes of the devil. We lose, and that means we give in to sinning. One of the game schemes the devil prominently uses today is syncretism. Now remind you that syncretism is the combining of the Christian faith with morality or other beliefs that are in conflict with the Christian faith. Syncretism can be seen in the behavior of a young man who claims Jesus as his Savior and yet he is sleeping with, having sex with his girlfriend. And sees no conflict with his state of belief and his behavior. Syncretism can be seen in a person praying to Jesus on Sunday and reading her horoscope for guidance on Monday. The synosyncretism was what Jeremiah the prophet repeatedly addressed when he prophesied to all of Israel As they repeatedly offered their offerings to the only true God and then turned around and trusted in the honoring of their family idols. And the most subtle asyncretism is worldview. It is when Christians pray their prayers, give their offerings, sing to and hear from the one true God. and then embrace socialist politics or fight for libertarian ideals or be obsessed with consumerism or whatever social ideal or political policy they stand for that is in opposition to biblical standards. There is no righteous tension when evil tugs a war against holiness. Holiness always has to win and will in the end. Another game scheme the devil has is to make what is clearly objective become subjective because of family. The most common practice of falling for this scheme is when parents raise their children to not have sexual relations before marriage. And when the son or daughter decides to move in with his girlfriend or her boyfriend, the parents look the other way and either do not condemn the behavior, be silent. Or actually condone the behavior because they don't want to lose the relationship they have with their child. A more obvious example of making what is clearly objective become subjective because a family Is when a family member announces that he or she is a homosexual. And for the same reasons mentioned previous, now homosexuality is an accepted lifestyle by the entire family. Note that nothing has changed in terms of what the Bible teaches. The only thing that has changed is a person's subjective experience, your family now embracing homosexuality. And now the subjective rules over the objective. The Church of Corinth did something similar when a man began sleeping with his father's ex-wife, and the church turned a blind eye. And the result could have been the loss of the man's soul. Someone needs to sacrifice likability and speak the truth in love in such situations. Another game scheme of the devil is to get us to think that righteousness in one aspect of our lives Is sufficient or a balance for the unrighteousness in our lives. We are seeing this played out in our culture. as the political left not only approves of killing the unborn at all stages of development and even after birth has taken place, but will give up their lives to defend seal pups from hunters and poachers. But it doesn't have to be seal pumps. It could be the environment they claim needs saving, or the social justice that needs changing, or the sexual perversions they want protected. It is anything that they can use to make them feel more righteous. But their righteousness is in their own eyes. It is certainly not the righteousness of God. Such self-righteousness is believing in corruptible things, like verse 18 describes. When it comes to understanding true righteousness, We are to be taken back, as Peter does in verses 19 through 21, taken back to the sacrificial death and the miraculous resurrection of Jesus. It is only by the death, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus that any person can be made righteous. And it is because of what Jesus accomplished that we are to live righteously. And we don't continue our righteousness because of how we live. We continue because the sacrifice of Jesus continues to be effective in our lives, and we are reminded of that continued effective sacrifice when we take the bread and we take the wine The past year that included a presidential election and a once-in-a-lifetime pandemic revealed how easily human beings can fall into the sin of self-righteousness. We have heard people say that they love their fellow man more than others because of how they have responded to the pandemic. We have heard people say that they love the world more and the environment more because of who they supported for president. We have heard those who claim to be Christian say that the manner of a candidate Is more important than the policies by which he governs. Apparently, even when such policies allow for no restrictions for the killing of the least among us, the unborn. I prophetically say to you that there will be no sin more hypocritically obvious on the day of judgment than the one that is uttered by those who say that they love their fellow man and then support the right for a person to kill an unborn child. The God that Peter describes, the God that you and I are to emulate in his holiness, is a God who died for the sake of the child in the womb, the very least among us. I began this sermon talking about the importance of identity, and so I shall end there as well. Our identity is to be holy as our Heavenly Father is holy. We can only achieve that by way, not by way of earthly politics, not by way of personal behavior, but only by way of Jesus, being our Lord, being our Savior. It is only after surrendering to Him as our Savior that we can be motivated to be righteous as God is. The sacrificial life and death of Jesus is to be our primary motivation. To do and not do as God has commanded. The resurrection and ascension of Jesus is to motivate us further that our life lived here is to emulate the glory of the promise of the hereafter. I have been reading a biography about Eric Little, who most of you know from the movie Chariots of Fire. He was an Olympic champion and a missionary to China, where he was also made a martyr. The author spends a great deal of time describing the character of Little. And it is an impeccable character, even compared to the upstanding persons of his day. And the author interrupts his description of Little's character anticipating that the reader is going to think that he's exaggerating. He assures us that he is not. And there was not one person who was interviewed about the character of Eric Little that did not agree. When I heard the character describe of little, I thought it was an exaggeration. But I realized I only did so because I was aware of my own character flaws in comparison My simple point in sharing this with you is that we truly can live more holy lives than we are currently living. And that is why Peter wrote, Therefore, gird up the loins of your mind and be holy as God is holy. Let us pray. Our merciful and gracious Lord, we are grateful for the courage of Peter to remind us of the standard That will always be there, never changing, because it is you who never changes. And that is what we cling to in a day that tosses us to and fro. Father, help all of us have the courage to take up the standard and live it. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Abortion 2021
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: The world was so practice singing sharks and In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Shortly after the new President of the United States was sworn into office He overturned all the previous abortion restriction policies of the previous administration. Whereas funding was withheld from non-government agencies that provided and referred patients for abortion, now the funding is restored. Another policy that did not allow U. S. financial support for foreign groups that provided abortions was also reversed so that Our tax money once again helps other nations kill the unborn. The policies for the next four years at least are summed up By the man that so many people have treated like a health pope. Quote, it will be our policy to support women's and girls' sexual and reproductive health and reproductive rights, meaning abortion, in the United States as well as globally. Anthony Fauci said to the World Health Organization. But I preach today Is one of the most uncomfortable topics of our day. And no doubt you may have stayed home, those of you who are here. Some of you may click it off as you are home. Because no one feels comfortable addressing this issue. And one of the reasons we are not comfortable Is that the church has done a very poor job of providing pastoral care with or about the topic of abortion? I confess to you that the church has done a poor job first by not assuring that women who become pregnant out of wedlock Be welcomed as part of the body of Christ. They should be welcomed because the sin of fornication can be forgiven by the blood of Christ. And those who commit fornication Should not feel any more guilty than those who have fantasized about fornication. Let that one seek into our psyches deeply. There is no question that if Christians in the home and in the church made their daughters believe that the sin of fornication can be forgiven, that they would more likely not hide their unplanned pregnancy. For any of you in my hearing who has been pregnant out of wedlock and perceived that I, as a pastor, would not receive you with loving care, I ask for your forgiveness And I turned from my sin by publicly stating that I will receive you. The other reason why this topic is so uncomfortable for most of us is that there are people we know, people that we love, who have had an abortion. And that person or persons very well may be someone who is hearing me right now Again, the church has done a poor job of helping people who have had an abortion know that such sin can be forgiven by the grace of God when confessed. The church, and I am preaching to myself now, the church needs to do a better job at understanding how easy it is to commit the sin of abortion, for we live in a culture. That does not identify the unborn as human beings. The dominant portion of our culture insists on individual rights so that they can kill the unborn. At will, with no opposition present in legislation, in media, and especially not in person. With the lack of evidential love from the Christian Church and an unencumbered access to abortion, we have made the sin of abortion much easier to practice and therefore much stronger of a temptation. Lord, have mercy on us all. This morning, we take the time to declare our belief in what the Bible teaches about the sanctity of life in all of its stages. And we accept the responsibility, our responsibility, to stand up and defend the unborn. It takes only a moment to know what the Bible teaches about the unborn. In Psalm 139, the psalmist makes it clear. That it is God who forms life in the womb, and thus it is only God who can create life, and thus it is His only to take away. In the Gospel, according to St. Luke, as we read this morning, John the Baptist leaps in his mother's womb because he is in the presence of Jesus, who is also in his mother's womb. The exchange clearly shows how the eternal spirits of both persons were present while in their mother's womb. Jeremiah confirms this very truth when he describes that he also knew God when he was in his mother's womb. These examples prove that the Bible teaches that children in the womb have obvious personhood and not something else. Thus, all laws within Holy Scripture that condemn killing clearly apply to the unborn. And this is why the strategy of the devil has been to deny personhood of the unborn in order to disregard those laws saying they are non-applicable. Again, we have another example of the devil as he did with Eve. Say again, did God really say? We are to answer, yes, he did say. Like Jesus, we are to care for the least among us, and there are no persons more vulnerable, more weak, than the unborn. May God raise up a generation that repents of the sin of abortion. Now, alongside the biblical evidence that clearly teaches that a child in the womb is a human being made in the image of God. and thus should be afforded all rights as a human being. I also want to provide for us reasonable arguments to present to the world, the worlds in which each of us live, and by that I mean our social circles. Mind you, these arguments do not supersede holy scriptures, but they are reasonable to people who do not want to hear what the Bible has to say. And we give credit to advancements in science that allow us to use these arguments. The first argument I propose is based on genetic code. Consider what the difference is between a child when he is five years old compared to the same child when he is ten years old. There is a change in size, but not a change in the genetic code. Now consider the same child when he is twenty years old. There is a great change in size, again, and more hair on the body, but again, no change in the genetic code. Now consider the same person at conception when the tiny, tiny sperm enters the egg cell. What takes place is an established genetic code that goes unchanged all the way to death. Thus it is there is no genetic code difference between a newly fertilized egg in the womb of a new mother and of a 20-year-old man that lives and moves among us. Again, consider the science that we know. A sperm does not have a complete genetic code by itself. It is called a haploid, as it is half of the chromosomes needed to be a complete person. The unfertilized egg is also a haploid, having half of the chromosomes needed to be a complete person. It is only after the sperm joins the egg that the transmission takes place. That is what we commoners call the moment of conception. It is the only time when the genetic code is established, and that code is uniquely different in every person. Thus we can say it is at that moment that human life begins. No counter-argument to accepting that a child in his or her mother's womb is a human being. Is that the genetic code is irrelevant if we accept that the child being it's in its mother's womb is a part of her body. And therefore it is within the woman's power to do as she wishes with her own body. In logic, we use the phrase transitive relation, which in mathematics, you remember it, it says that if A equals B And B equals C, then A equals C. In everyday life, we understand that if Carol is an ancestor to Ben, And Betty is an ancestor to Susie, then Carol is an ancestor to Susie. When we apply this to a pregnant woman who wants to claim an unborn child as part of her body, there are logical inconsistencies that don't fit the transit the transitive relation principle Scientifically, you know that we all have, as human beings, 23 pairs of chromosomes, totaling 46. For every person, 46. And how many feet do we have? How many hands do we have? Well, last we check, two each. But according to the theory that an unborn child is a part of a mother's body, The woman then has 96 chromosomes, four hands, and four feet, making her something other than a human being. Perhaps she could consider herself a superhuman being, but not a simple human being. Thus the transitive relation principle doesn't fit Another popular argument for an unborn child not to be considered a human being is its viability. Viability is defined by abortion advocates to be the ability to remain alive separate from its mother. This allows for abortions to be justified up to or close to the third trimester, whereas before such a time the child would likely not live outside the womb. The problems with this argument are many. First, to mention a few, a fetus is not dependent upon its mother for its identity. For as we have already established, the genetic code is set at conception. Second, every child is dependent upon its mother for sustenance immediately outside the womb and long after birth no matter when it is born. Third, if a child being dependent makes it a non-person Then killing it at any age in childhood can be justified because a child is dependent on its mother daily. Hopefully our culture will never go that far, but there's no guarantee. Fourth The sick and elderly can also need aid to remain viable, and we still consider them to be persons. And finally, all of us are dependent upon one another to remain viable. That is understood when living in a society. Another argument put forth, even by such persons who consider themselves religious and part of the Christian tradition, Is that a child must breathe on its own before it can be considered a living person? Now this position is defended from the Bible, where in Genesis God breathes into Adam, making him a living human being. Because we can now look into the womb, we know that a child can suck its thumb, open its mouth, express laughter and crying It is dependent on oxygen to live by just as it is outside of its mother's womb, as it receives oxygen from the mother. The real argument such people are making is really actually an argument of geography. Supposedly an unborn child is not a person while in the womb and is a person when out of the womb. This is like saying a human is a person while living outside of California. But when he crosses into California, he is a non-person. And while it is tempting to think less of Californians because of their licentious living, the geography argument is invalid Logic has the category of informal fallacies, and under informal fallacies are fallacies of distraction. All other pro-abortion arguments can be categorized as distractions. Abortionists want to insist that If we pro-liferers care about abortion, we should also care about the poor among us as much as if those two things, poverty and killing of an unborn baby, are comparable. They are not. Then there is the argument against capital punishment, with the belief that they are catching us in an inconsistency if we are against abortion but in favor of capital punishment. Once again, such is a distraction, an attempt to get us off the subject. And again, killing unborn babies is most certainly not comparable to killing of a violent criminal. It is also not comparable because it is the state that puts the violent criminal to death, while with abortion it is the mother that is judge and jury, while the doctor is the executioner. Abortion today is no less abhorrent to God than the pagan ritual of offering infants to the false god Moloch. Statues of mullet depicted today look like a cross between having a dog head and a horse head, with arms like humans stretched out. The idols were made from a type of metal that was heated from the inside. A priest of Molech would take the offered infant and place it on the searing hands of the idol And he and his gathered worshippers would watch the baby burn to death, all in an attempt to earn the favor of their gods. And today, we don't even want the favor of false gods, but instead we want votes to achieve places of power. I ask that you turn again to Psalm 94 in your Bibles. I chose Psalm 94 today for our Old Testament reading. as it is an example of an appropriate Christian response to the sin of abortion and a proper prayer against those who uphold the abhorrent sin as a political and even moral right. And I offer this example of prayer for us reluctantly at first. I had a mind during this past summer and fall. To really say to hell with them all. Let them kill their children if they want to Let them live out their lusts upon each other. Let them propagandize their children. They will all soon devour one another. But such is not the mind of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, who told us to love our enemies and pray for them. But how should we pray? We continue to pray the same prayers for our government leaders as written in the Book of Common Prayer, no matter who is in higher office or which party has the political power. But I am convinced that we need also to add prayers that are more aggressive in defense of the least among us. Look at Psalm 94. It begins with a cry for God to bring his vengeance forth. Such is a prayer no different than asking for God's kingdom to come. After all, when God's kingdom is fully seen, vengeance will be his. And so we pray for God to render punishment upon the proud, for they will not repent. We should pray that wickedness like that which is practiced with abortion should be triumphed over We should pray that God would silence the speech of those who afflict God's people while also afflicting our heritage and while they murder the fatherless. They believe that God does not see them, for they don't believe in God's existence at all. We are to pray that their mouths be stopped. For they will have nothing to say when God is revealed and ready to judge. Notice the psalmist has no trouble or doubt that he should call what he should call his enemies. They are senseless and fools. They can be identified so because it is the fool that says there is no God. They will soon learn that God knows their thoughts because God is all-knowing and he will rightly judge those thoughts. In contrast, we also pray for God to bless his people as they learn from God's instruction out of his law. We then remind ourselves in our prayers of God's promises to his people. For no matter how well the enemy enemies of God succeed in this life. God will indeed never, never leave his people. And since God will never leave his people, and the rebellious will be swallowed up by his own rebellion, We can be assured that righteousness will prevail and those who follow after God will have upright hearts. We next are to be reminded that God is also our helper when we slip, or when we are at the mercy of evildoers, for God's mercy is much greater. This shall calm our anxieties as our faith increases. We close the prayer with the realization that evil and iniquity cannot dwell with God It will have to be conquered. Evil gets more evil. It wants to see the life of the righteous snuffed out. It wants the innocent killed. And we would panic, but instead we look to God, for He is our defense, He is our rock refuge. In the end, God will do to them what they want to do to us. The Lord will cut them off even by their own wickedness. Amen. We need to pray this way. We need to pray this way and to pray other prayers like it. Our souls need the aggression. Hear this. There can be no conscientious objectors when it comes to spiritual warfare. All are to be engaged. Love your enemies, beloved. Pray for their repentance. And pray that if they do not repent, that God would bring them down, that God would cut them off. He will. You know that he will. Let us pray. Our God, we thank you for this example of aggressive prayer, of identifying the enemy. And praying that he be brought low if he does not repent. And so we say for all who march for their right to kill their own children. And for those who insist on the right to for others to kill children, all of it we ask that they be brought low The vowels be silenced, and that those who will not repent be judged. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Christian Home
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Join with me in looking at First Peter chapter three, the first seven verses. We come upon the section in 1 Peter that is labeled by scholars to be a household code. We find something similar in the letters to the Ephesians, to the Colossians, and in 1 Timothy. The household codes address expected Christian behavior from wives to husbands, husbands to wives. Parents to children, children to parents, servants to masters, and masters to servants. Because the family unit has been and will always be the foundation of a healthy society and culture. It was necessary for certain behaviors within Christian households to be a point of emphasis. This morning we are going to examine the technical aspects of these verses and then speak openly and frankly. about how these passages passages should be applied to our modern lives. So verse 1 The word likewise has the apostle move on from the relationship of master and servant as one element of social life to the other more universal and involving from the Roman point of view almost a greater subordination which is of husband and wife. Wives are to be subject to their own husbands. While the word own as in own husbands, did not apply in the first century that that women are only required to submit to their husbands and not other men That is emphasized today to calm the distrust our modern minds have on such an instruction. The words that follow indicate the frequency of the cases in which the wife was the only one converted to Christianity in the home.
