And little parishes like ours could spend days, weeks, months, and a great deal of money defending ourselves for the right to say and practice what the scriptures teach. Again, the devil wants us to compromise or close our doors. When the fighting starts, I'm going to need your fervent love. We each are going to need our love for one another to cover a multitude of sins because we will be fighting an enemy that will do whatever it takes to win. We will not have time to address all the failures and faults that we see in one another. Love will have to bury such things. There is something special that takes place when a sports team finds success, especially success that comes after hardship. When you go through hardship on a field with teammates, you learn to trust one another as you learn to grind together and to pick one another up, and that creates camaraderie. And that camaraderie remains. Camaraderie is why teams have reunions. The bond is still there far past the time that they were on the field together. And such is what is needed to be forged between Christians, a camaraderie in Christ, so that we will not be compromised and we will not surrender. I need to be able to trust that you will not compromise, that you will not quit. And you need to trust that I will not compromise, that I will not quit. If I go to jail for what I preach or what I teach, I expect every one of you to come and visit me. COVID-19 or not. And when someone tries to cancel you, because of the principles you stand for and the life you live, I will stand by you, I will pronounce my love for you. I will have you in my home. We will pray against the enemies of God, and we will build up one another because that is what followers of Jesus Christ do. We don't compromise and we do not quit. We don't quit because we get our feelings hurt. We don't quit because I don't have a best friend in church. We don't quit because no one liked my casserole at the church picnic. And we don't compromise because my son came out and said he's bisexual. We don't compromise because my daughter wants to move in with her boyfriend. We don't compromise because my boss will fire me. We don't compromise because we fear men. We fear no man. I realize I sound like a coach in a locker room before a big game, and what we face is much bigger than any game. But we need pep talks every so often. St. Paul told us that we are to run the race of life to win. It is losers who compromise. It is losers who fear men. We are willing to suffer. We are willing to deny ourselves of earthly pleasure We will stand and face people who revile us, and we will love one another, because that is what is needed to resist the devil and remain faithful. If that is what it takes, that is what we will do. That is my promise to you. Let us pray. Our Father, all of us confess you are a God of no compromise. And we confess how easy it is for us to compromise. And so we pray. Dear Holy Spirit, help us to keep our word, to be a people who stand for the faith, will not be moved, come what may. And Father, help us to do it together. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: It is No Longer Friday
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: The name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. It would appear that the human nature has a need to celebrate. This is most evident in our post-Christian culture in the West Where we have replaced religious celebrations with sports celebrations. Fans dressed up in a proper attire Parouding on their team, just as when I was a boy, we would dress up in proper attire for Easter. Fans gathered to participate in the sport with Religious devotion and zeal. They desperately desire to celebrate. And if their team wins It becomes a ruckus scene with laughing and applauding, cheering, and a trophy elevated. I remember on Easter Sunday how Christophers would Enter the sanctuary with the cross held high, and all in attendance would bow in reverence with their hearts celebrating. This was part of our American culture, but such is God. But we still need to celebrate So we now have replaced such religious devotion with celebrating our favorite ball teams. My point again is that we all have an inherent need to celebrate Although as a boy growing up in a Roman Catholic family, my mom was Irish Catholic and my dad converted. And I attended Mass and CCD and went through the rituals of confession and first communion. But after my parents passed away, we became Christians only on holy days. We were Christmas and Easter attenders only. Easter, though, remained a big deal. We boys were given new blazers every year. I even have a picture of me wearing a new blazer, a blue blazer, while sporting a blue derby hat. The girls were given new dresses. We all received a basket of goodies on Easter morning, followed by an Easter egg hunt around the house. After Mass, my grandparents who were staunch and faithful would take the whole family to an Easter brunch For these reasons the Easter holiday has grand has granted me grand memories from my childhood The holiday was a stark contrast to the Friday previous. Being with my Roman Catholic grandparents on Good Friday was a dark experience Their solemnity and introspection was quite contrary to the gaiety of Easter Sunday. In fact, my grandmother treated every Friday in the calendar year as a solemn day. Many Roman Catholics continue to do so. Historically, beyond Roman Catholics, many Western Christians approach Friday in the same manner. The tradition of refusing to eat red meat on Fridays reflects the desire to remember what occurred on that one Friday in history when God's Son was placed upon a cross. to die as a sacrifice for the sins of the world. This solemnity for every Friday has its merit for if we Wish to celebrate the resurrection of our Savior every Sunday, we ought to recognize his sacrifice every Friday. Because our culture is no longer driven by religious convictions, but rather by economic concerns, the contemporary weak is divided up into segments dictated by the workplace. Monday now begins the week and that day is perceived to be drudgery for we have to get back into the work mode. Wednesdays have been given new attention because of an older advertisement that places a camel in an office announcing that it's hump day The hope is to get over the hump in the week and to look forward to Friday. Friday is understood to be The end of the week and hence a day of celebration because Saturday and Sundays will those are me times filled with activities That I need to recover from when Monday comes around once again. Needless to say, the biblical ideal to approaching a week conflicts with our modern day. It will be our attempt this morning to go back in time in our minds that we can better relate to certain weekdays that work toward our redemption. From our gospel text, we receive an emotional description of how the women who were closest to Jesus reacted after his death. In John chapter nineteen, the events of Friday were fast and furious, and no doubt were gut wrenching. The man that these average men and women had put their hope in for not only their happiness in this life, but for their happiness in the life to come, he had been arrested, he had been beaten, he had been ridiculed, he had been mocked. Most of the followers of Jesus did not see him after his arrest. It was not until Friday came that they saw what the San Henred had reduced him to, which was a common criminal. No moment in their lives could have been more surreal than watching helplessly as Jesus was placed by Pilate before the multitude And those people were given the power to release him or call him to death. When the crowd was swayed toward crying out for the death of Jesus What could these lowly, average, non-influential followers do? Such a day was no doubt haunting They must have assumed that they were the only sane people on the planet. We've all had those moments where we feel that either everyone else is insane and we are sane. Or we are insane and everyone else is sane. There are days. Christians can call them Fridays They can be haunting. Like the disciples of Jesus on that Friday, we face situations where we are powerless We wake up believing we have a handle on our life and thus control as to what happens to us and those that we love, but then an event occurs that shakes us so deeply We can now see that we actually never had any control at all. In chapter 19, verse 16 of John, the scriptures say that the soldiers Hear this phrase, they took charge of Jesus. Let us pause and consider how profound that statement is Someone else, not the Father, not the Holy Spirit, not even Jesus Himself, controls Jesus Who could take charge of the Son of God and yet take charge of Jesus? They did. They made him carry his cross to the place of his designated death They placed a mocking sign above him. They nailed him naked and then gambled his clothes. This is what happens when the unbelieving world takes charge. During all of this there was nothing, nothing any man opposed to such treatment could do to stop it. All of us can fall into the trap of believing we actually control our individual lives. Our days in the future are set and we think we have control over them, but we don't. One day our home is established, the next we find the government or the bank is going to take it away. You feel in tip top safe one day and the next day the doctor says We are definitely sick. These are but a few examples of moments when we come to realize we have no control, or at least not the control we thought we had. Such moments are like a certain Friday. Then there are days that are seemingly the worst of days when you feel like you literally want to die. And I'm not speaking about those days when we suffer from a cold. And when I say we, I'm referring to men like myself who when we get sick we act like we're dying. The actual days you want to die happen when you lose hope. Depression is a nasty experience for anyone to go through. Consider when Jesus died on that cross, what hope did his followers have? When you lose hope, the purpose for continuing to live can feel lost as well The hope for the disciples of Jesus for that present day, for their tomorrow, or even being able to make sense of their yesterday, all of it had vanished when their Savior breathed his last. This happened on a Friday. And it did not get better. Well Jesus well they took Jesus down And hurriedly buried him in the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea. They did it because the Sabbath was approaching. The spiritual dark world was having a party. Satan was dancing on the rooftops. He was mocking the hosts of heaven. He danced around thinking he ruled the world. It was Friday. And Friday to him was a beautiful day. Darkness had covered the face of the earth Satan had stolen hope, even stolen faith from the hearts of men. It was Friday. And it belonged to hell The scriptures do not speak of Saturday. It was obviously a quiet day after the death of Christ. The Jewish people, according to both custom and law, could do nothing regarding the body of Jesus. As far as the followers of Jesus were concerned, Saturday was no different than Friday. Worship in the synagogue was no doubt painful rather than joyful. For these disciples of Jesus every day in the future looked like it would feel like Friday. How true it is that the difficult flights we find ourselves in seem unending while you're in the midst of them. From the small things such as financial debt. To the more significant tragedies such as a debilitating illness, it is hard to see beyond the moment. A new day dawning does not seem possible. We are under the sun. We see as if looking through a cloud of glass. Our perspective is flawed. When the first day of the week came, as described by Saint John, it could not have come sooner for the women who were closest to Jesus. While it was still dark, we are told that Mary of Magdala went to the tomb. Her mission was simple She was going to complete the anointing of the dead body of Jesus so that it would be fully prepared for a permanent burial. And for this woman, it was still Friday. Nothing had changed. No flicker of hope was present No doubt the images of her dead Savior were seared into her mind, yet when she arrived at the tomb where the body of Jesus was last place A still small voice whispered from the evidence of the rolled away stone It was no longer private. The voice was not audible, of course, but the evidence stated it clearly. The hangover from Friday was obviously great because Mary didn't hear the small voice. For her, the glass was half empty. Friday had stolen her optimism. She continued to think in her mind that it was still Friday. She ran as fast as she could to one of the disciples that she knew would do something. She ran to Peter and told him that some someone had taken the body of Jesus out of the tomb. Now at that moment, a still small voice was whispering to Peter, It is not Friday. Peter was a man whom desperately needed to hear such news. His Friday began on the night of Thursday when Jesus was arrested. That is the night he denied knowing the Savior, we know, three different times. From then on, Peter was in the background of the disciples He was shamed publicly. For him, Friday was a tragic on another level. He had denied knowing Jesus, and now Jesus was dead, along with any hope of being reconciled to Jesus. Unlike Mary, Peter heard the voice, and a glimmer of hope stirred within him. He and the another apostle, whom we believe was John, ran to the tune. The running indicates the desire to celebrate. When they arrived, the voice was louder It is not Friday. Each of them saw the burial clothes as evidence that it was a new day. The strips that were around the body of Jesus were lying there as if a body was removed while not tearing the strips. They simply collapsed onto the other. Interestingly, the burial cloth placed around the head was neatly folded and off to the side. Like a young Jewish boy would have been taught to do while tidying up. The voice now spoke with greater volume. It is no longer prior The Gospels make it clear that Peter and John did not grasp all that they had witnessed. They still did not understand that Death had lost its stink. They did not know at least this one thing, however, they did know, excuse me, they did know at least this one thing It was no longer Friday. The scene next shifts back to Mary. She has No hope. While she is present outside the tomb, two angels, one sitting at the head where the body of Jesus once lay, and the other at the feet, ask her why she is crying What is implied to Mary by the angel is to look. She was to see the evidence for herself. Jesus was not there. It was no longer Friday. There was no longer a reason to mourn. Mary justified her tears by describing the treachery of someone having stolen the body of Jesus. At her words, she turns around and Jesus is standing before her. Unfortunately, but naturally, Mary is blind with her tears. Evidence around her is confusing so much so that she Does not see the hope that is alive. It is no longer driving. We cannot be so busy. Feeling sorrowful not to understand how glorious a day it is now. Because of that day, all of us can say, It is no longer Friday Even when it is Friday. It is no longer Friday. And because it is a new day, we can see things for what they really are The empty tomb means hope has returned with a vengeance. And such hope is to be applied to this life and the next. The folded burial clothes mean that the sorrow I experienced on Friday. is but for a passing moment and the sun has risen never to descend again it is no longer private Which means that all of us can be as Mary Magdalene and go back to our loved ones and say, I have seen the Lord. It is no longer Friday, for Sunday has come. Because it is Sunday, Christians, because it is Sunday, we are not to live as if it is Friday ever again. I challenge you to consider what cataclysmic events, what painful news, what poverty, what illness can occur on Friday that cannot be overcome by Sunday Church, people of God, regardless of what Fridays have brought you, you must understand, you must believe, getting the tears out of your eyes, that it is no longer Friday. Sunday has come. And because you now live in Sunday, you must put all of your Fridays behind you. From our first reading this morning, we received these instructions. Hear them again. Since then, you have been raised with Christ. Stop there. We must stop and comment that if it is Sunday, that means Jesus has risen, and that also means you have risen. Death shall no longer have dominion over you. Death and all of its pretenders shall no longer sting your soul. St. Paul continues, set your hearts on things above where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Here we are reminded that the only place that will grant us ultimate healing, ultimate joy, ultimate peace is the presence of God. Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things, for you have died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God. Church God's people, this morning, the words of the apostle cry out to us, it is no longer Friday! Even though we are in the midst of events in life that remind us of Friday, pandemic, masks Sixteenth, beloved, Sunday has come. Your life is now hidden with Christ in God. So celebrate. Rejoice. And again I say rejoice. Amen.

sermons.title: Judges 1
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Our reading our reading from Judges didn't go as far as we will be going this morning. We get into chapter 2. This is The start of a series of sermons on the book of Judges, using typology as an interpretive method The book of Judges seems to be perfect for such an endeavor, and yet there is something daunting about the book that makes me concerned. The book, as you have read it no doubt before, is rather depressing and in many ways salacious Never does the author, whoever he might be, some believe it was Samuel, never does he clearly teach us a lesson from the depressing and salacious narratives, but implies the lessons in the manner that he writes. That last point is important for it means that much is required of the interpreter. We have to pay attention. We have to stay awake. For some of you, that can be hard. We have to pay attention to the details of the story to understand the gospel found within. A brief history is needed. We are looking at a time around the 13th century BC, a long time ago. Joshua had just died. The Late Bronze Age was giving way to the Iron Age, meaning that there were few large nations, but many smaller tribes and villages that made up the region. The land of Cana, the promised land, housed many small tribes. There is a general type that can be understood from the book of Judges as a whole, and by type, by type I mean likeness or similarity. Types are not the actual person or the actual truth, but are likenesses that prepare us for what is to come. Recall the types we studied from the book of Leviticus as we noted how the different offerings commanded were types of the offering of Jesus that He made for us for sins. As a whole, the Book of Judges is a type because of the stories are cyclical. The cycle goes as follows. Man falls into sin. Man suffers the consequences of his sin. Man cries out to God. God sends forth a man to save him, or in one case, a woman And then man overcomes. The cycle is repeated over and over in the book of Judges, and is also the overall story of salvation From the beginning of mankind, when Adam and Eve fall into sin all the way to the coming of Jesus Christ as the Savior of mankind to defeat all of God's enemies. Hence, each story of a deliverer in the book of Judges is a type, is a shadow of Jesus Christ. Another general type is how each of the judges used by God delivers the people that he uses by God to deliver the people from their enemies. Just as the patriarchs in Genesis reveal a characteristic of the coming Messiah, remember Abraham was a type of faith, Isaac a type of quietness. Jacob a type of wrestling with God, Joseph as a type of Jesus descending and ascending. So too do the leaders and judges resemble aspects of how we are redeemed by Jesus. These types, of course, are, again, woefully inadequate, and that is part of the lesson of the author. We are to see that although God raises up men, and in one case a woman, to deliver Israel from their enemies, the leaders raised up are only successful for a time, and eventually Israel falls back into sin. Toward the end of the book, we will read the author saying that there was no king in Israel, seemingly implying that if there was a king in Israel, they would not continue to fall into sin. Such a conclusion should not be jumped to so quickly, for we should remember from 1 Samuel that although the Lord allowed Israel to have a king, that is not what he preferred. He personally preferred to be their king. He wants to be the God of his people. For the writer of judges to say then that at that time Israel had no king We are to get a double meaning. Israel had no earthly king, nor did they follow the Lord God as their king. What this all reveals, of course, even the narrative of Samuel, is that there needs to be a king over Israel, who is greater than all the judges and greater even than David. He is to be the king of kings. The king was born to a virgin and revealed to the magi. Also, the entire book of Judges is an example of personal helpful typology. The nation of Israel is a type of each of us who claim to be Christian We repeatedly move towards sin, only to be rescued by our Savior, only to fall back into sin we thought was behind us, only to be saved once again by our Savior. People can talk about their salvation as if it is finished, declaring a time and a date that they were, quote, saved. But the Christian life is actually a series of saving moments. As our Savior rescues us from ourselves, again, and then again and again. These are times of sanctification that all of us need and will continue to need this side of heaven. Now that is enough for a general introduction to the book of Judges. Now we will examine the first chapter and go briefly into chapter 2. This section should be treated as a whole, for it gives a general message using a number of separate stories. Upon careful examination, we notice that the beginning of this book is similar to the end of the book of Joshua The last nine chapters of Joshua contain the same general stories as we find in this chapter, only in Joshua they're of a more positive tone. The negativity of judges tells us right off that the author intends for us to focus on something different than we had before in Joshua. The tribe of Judah is chosen first as a fulfillment of the prophecy of Jacob to lead the Israelites against the Canaanites. Judah goes to battle with the tribe of Simeon, of whom we learned from the last census was actually the smallest of the tribes. Their victories at first are dominant. A brief description of Adonai Bezek, which likely refers to the Lord or King of Bezek. Is useful in describing God's judgment upon a ruler who treated his defeated enemies like dogs. So now he too is to be treated in the same manner. In the midst of the description of Judah's conquest over pagan tribes and in specific the Canaanites, we are given the story of Caleb and his daughter. The story may seem benign, and yet it is the fulfillment of what God had promised Caleb, you remember, and his descendants. For being one of the only two spies of the twelve that were faithful when scouting out the promised land. The description of Judah's conquest picks back up in verse 16. They, of course, conquer again and at this time seem invincible until they come up against the people with iron chariots. The inability to drive these Canaanites out because of the iron chariots should not be understood as if we can simply appreciate how difficult it must have been. For in Joshua chapter 17 it is recorded that the people came and they told Joshua that they feared going against these particular Canaanites because of the chariots. And Joshua responded there and said, Though they are strong, you can drive them out. Well, they did not drive them out. The faith of the tribe of Judah failed, and they allowed pagan people to remain in the land God promised them. The author is now beginning to describe the failures of the Israelites to take over the promised land as they had been instructed. These failures will mount on top of one another as the narrative unfolds. The Benjamites are the next to fail, followed by the tribe of Manasseh. Because of the difficulty in driving these determined tribes of Canaan out of the land, the stronger tribes of Israel decided to accommodate by forcing the people into labor. This forced labor served as an answer for the moment, but was an obvious mistake, as the author implies by such a phrase as never drove them out completely. Never drove them out completely. And continued to live among them. We must understand that forced labor is not a replacement for extinction If pagan people are allowed to remain alive, then their pagan practices remain alive with them, even though they are enslaved. The angel of the Lord described in chapter 2 as appearing before the people verifies the failure of Israel to take over the land as God had required. The mention of Gilgal is significant, for that is where the conquest of the Promised Land began. It is where Joshua first met the angel of the Lord who appeared to him before the battle of Jericho. And where Israel was circumcised after entering the promised land, that angel would appear at the same place. Reminding us of the promising conquest that began there and Israel then quickly failed. It will, I hope, give us perspective to learn more about these Canaanites and their culture. For it occurs to me that we might have a hard time stomaching what the Lord commanded Israel to do. If a modern-day reporter was on the scene, he would certainly use the word genocide to describe what Israel was commanded to do to the Canaanites. And that word falls under the category of immoral in our modern culture. It is likely for some of us not only to question God's directive to commit genocide on the Canaanite people But conclude that if it was up to us, we would have taken a different approach. Hence, we would be more upright or righteous than God We don't come out and say such things forthrightly, but our thoughts give us away. Let us then understand the Canaanites Though we think of them very negatively because of how the Bible describes them, they were actually a very accomplished and sophisticated people, relatively speaking. It may surprise you to know that we owe our alphabetic system of writing to the Canaanites, who combined the Mesopotamian system With the Egyptian hieroglyphics inventing a more simple form of writing. Canaanites were also exceptional and exceptional engineers, as evidenced by their building of fortified cities. They were gifted artisans creating jewelry of all types from gold and silver. They were metallurgists. I don't use that word very often. Casting tools and weaponry from bronze as well as iron chariots mentioned in the text. We could go on, but the Bible shows that God is not impressed with their sophistication. What is interesting to the Lord is the wickedness of the people. They were idolaters and notoriously wicked when practicing their idol worship. As Deuteronomy describes, the Canaanites burned their sons and daughters in fires as they sacrificed to their gods. It was for this reason that Israel was commanded to exterminate them. And still, even with this wickedness known, it is difficult. From the view of our modern sensitivities, to understand how God could command his people to completely destroy another people It is important, however, to remember that God's command for this destruction came only after hundreds of years of witnessing their wickedness. God, you remember, is patient. He is slow to anger. He is abounding in love. He is not willing that any should perish, but that all would come to repentance. It is not as if God had rushed to judgment upon the Canaanites. It is quite the opposite. Another reason for their needed destruction is the obvious effect this culture had upon God's people. The effect led to the destruction of the Israelites by the hand of the Assyrians, 722 BC, and then the Babylonians in 586. Whether we can stomach God ordaining the destruction of a people or not, wickedness such as characterized by the Canaanites always leads to destruction and death. And God will not be mocked. Whatsoever man sows, he will also reap. We see this truth written in bold letters over the world today as it ever was. Judgment can come upon a wicked people by the hands of another nation or by a natural disaster. The point is it will come. The events of this past year, the pandemic, must be mentioned for the number of lives that have been affected. Please understand, I have no specific word from God that states that this pandemic is a form of punishment for wickedness. What I do know is that every man should fall on his knees in humility when such a thing like a pandemic occurs, and acknowledge that we are sore dependent upon God for everything. Without warning, what we do and how we live could drastically change, and what man could stand before God and say that such is not fair. Fair according to whom? What is fair is death for our sins. That these types of trials do not happen more often. Means that we are all benefactors of God's patient grace. There is much that is good in the world today As less people are impoverished and less people are malnourished, percentage-wise more than ever before But again, God, as revealed in the Bible, ignores cultural or political achievements of people and focuses on their moral and spiritual life, and that is what determines his judgment. His end goal is to move people to repentance. Instead of concerning ourselves with the fairness of God judging a people like the Canaanites, It will be more valuable to evaluate our situation today. We also live in an advanced culture that dazzles the world with scientific and commercial achievements. And the wickedness follows closely, much like it did in Canaan. We are a culture that is devoted to its gods of sex and mummy. That pornography, abortion, and overall hedonism provide. Sin is now a source of revenue, mainstreamed and judicially defended. Computer language easily has had the same effect as the Canaanite alphabet. Probes to Mars are just as impressive as iron chariots. All of this goes on while for over a generation we have allowed babies to be barbarically chopped up in their mother's womb. How I ask rhetorically, is such a practice any different than offering our sons and daughters to the fire for the idols? We, of course, had no command or to exterminate the pagan people around us like Israel did. We are to be like Christ to the world. Thus we are not a political nation. We are scattered as Christians from all corners of the earth. We must live with and among the pagans. Because we live with and among them, we are also in just as great a danger from the Canaanites around us as Israel was in the Promised Land. Their failure to drive out the Canaanites is our failure to keep ourselves unspotted from the world It is not easy, of course, to be in the world, but not of the world as Jesus prayed. We all know it's not easy. It is a matter of thousand temptations a day in which we are the day in which we are called, in our own way, to be faithful to God's covenant. To heed his word, to count on his power on our behalf, to drive out the Canaanites before us, our own personal sins. Where Christians fail is where Israel failed. Instead of driving out the worldly influence, we accommodate. Like the Israelites who made the Canaanites their slaves, instead of destroying them, we allow worldly influences into our lives, thinking that we can tame them, that we can control them. We can't. Each of you knows very well some of the places where the world has got a grip on you and where you are accommodating You know very well how the wealth or sophistication or sensuality or humanistic outlook has influenced you. And still, there are many ways that the world has influenced you that you are not aware of right now. What this amounts to is a downward spiral. Greater than you can imagine, one that absorbs you and your children to the point where you gradually become more worldly, more Canaanite, then Christian. The book of Judges provides typological lessons on two levels. The first level is that of the corporate body. In the text, it is Israel as a people who fall into sin, a body of people. God delivers them as a body of people. The second level is that of individual, for each of us can see ourselves in the behaviors described. As we study this book, the Lord is going to place a finger upon areas in our lives, both corporately and individually. Where we have accommodated, allowing the world to influence our lives both as a church and as individuals. When God does place that finger, It is for us to confess the sin of accommodation and purify ourselves in the blood of Christ. Let us start doing that today by receiving the body and the blood. Amen.

sermons.title: Judges 2
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. Turn your Bibles to Judges chapter 2. We pick up at verse 6. From our study of Judges chapter one through chapter two verse five last week, we emphasize the accommodations that had taken place by God's people. I remind you that to accommodate is to adapt oneself to your surroundings, and in Israel's case Instead of changing their surroundings, they became like their surroundings. Another word for this type of behavior is syncretism. Which is the fusing together of different systems of belief. The accommodations of the Israelites to the Canaanites led to a decline in a in their faith and a people becoming more and more like the Canaanites, or as the New Testament describes, more and more like the world. I stated last week that each of us knows of ways we individually have accommodated to the world, and that we must realize that There are accommodations we have made consciously and subconsciously. The subconscious accommodations are the most dangerous For they have seeped into our psyche slowly, unannounced, unrecognized, and therefore they are not addressed. None of us is immune to this stealth accommodations. Some of them come in by way of education. Personally, I was educated in the public schools through high school and then attended a state college afterward. While in high school and college I was exposed to all types of literature that was ungodly. It was required of me to know the thoughts of well-known psychologists such as Rogers, Freud, and Skinner. I was told how the earth and human form evolved by chance I was indoctrinated by teachers who propagandized political issues such as abortion, nuclear power, and animal rights, to name a few. I had one teacher in middle school that hated and feared nuclear power and thought it was his calling in life to get his students to hate and fear it as well. None of these beacons of thought or educators knew the Lord Jesus Christ. They were ungodly, and they pointed me to the ungodly. How I approached the teaching profession my first few years out of college was no doubt influenced greatly by those that I allowed to enter into my mind. It took a great deal of time to re-evaluate what I had learned in light of holy scripture. Being educated by pagans and studying pagans is not, however, what I am concerned about. In many cases, it is a road that must be traveled. What is said by educators and those who study, however, should always be strained through a very fine colander We as Christians have an extra task in our studies. We must be diligent to study what is set before us and decipher the truth from the lies. There are many, many other ways we are influenced of which we are not aware or not aware enough. For example, television has a numbing influence on us as we become entertained by that which is blatantly ungodly. Soon we find ourselves laughing at something that we know the Bible condemns. Also, as I have stated before, I shudder to think how many people have adopted the Parenting philosophy of Oprah and Dr. Phil before and instead of Holy Scripture Parenting practices, in my view, are a glaring area where the people of God have been influenced by so many other venues instead of the Word of God. The danger of this accommodating or syncretism is great, for it inevitably helps God's people become more and more like the world rather than becoming more like Christ. The passage read this morning from Judges does well, exposing the manner in which the Israelites allowed the lifestyle of the Canaanites The ways of the ungodly to seep into their psyche. These passages are a brief summary, really, of the entire book of Judges. The author obviously wishes for us to understand what went wrong in Israel before we read about the specific sins of the people and the characters of the chosen men who were to deliver them. The very next generation, the very next generation that followed the great leader Joshua, the leader who challenges all of us to say, As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. After him, the entire nation of Israel is described as not knowing the Lord personally and not knowing what the Lord had done for the entire nation of Israel. The result of not knowing the Lord or what he did to deliver Israel out of bondage in Egypt is that the people follow the gods that are around them. But how did they not know? One failure was education. The parents did not purposefully and forthrightly train their children in the ways of God. And they did not do so because they themselves fell into disbelief. But they had to worship something, because that is the human condition we have to worship. So they combine their Judeo worship with idol worship. The result of their idolatry is for the Lord to hand them over to their enemies. Each time after the people had suffered, God raised up persons to save Israel from her enemies. Once a leader died, Israel repeated the cycle, going back to following false gods. Unfortunately, as the cycle repeated itself, there became a more and more corrupt people, more and more corrupt behavior. Tired of the cycle, the Lord allowed these nations to remain among them, to test them, to prove who they truly believed in. The test was to see who was faithful to him and who was not. As described A clear sign that accommodation had occurred fully was the intermarrying of the Israelites with the pagan nations around them. It was giving their sons and daughters to unbelievers. The nation of Israel is described in the book of Judges as a type, as a metaphor for the New Testament church. These people had been delivered out of bondage and called to overtake the pagan nations in the promised land. In like manner, the church has been delivered from the bondage of sin and death. And is called to overtake the unbelieving world with the gospel. As Israel was to usher in God's kingdom into the promised land. So we too are to usher God's kingdom into the world by preaching and living the gospel. That is what Jesus meant by being a city on a hill. Because this type is so clear, the lessons from Israel's struggle in this text are very easily applied to our current state. From this chapter, we learn first of all the importance of the centrality of the church of God's people You will notice that all that occurs in the text revolves around God's people. The people of God are chosen to destroy pagan nations. When the people of God, when the church fails, other nations are allowed to remain only because, again, the Lord wishes for them to test his people. These nations would never want us to think of themselves in this manner. Their accomplishments are great in their eyes, and they believe their nation is of central importance. But once again, the Lord cares nothing for these accomplishments. He bases his decision about a nation on how he will use it to sanctify and redeem his church. And this is an important way for us to think about current events and the history of all nations. The significance of any nation is based on how it bears out the kingdom of God. We can talk about how defeating ISIS frees an oppressed people. We can speculate about how it opens up a free market in the Middle East, as well as providing oil to the West. We can even hope for democracy amongst nations led by religious dictators. But the real issue and focus always is the effect a war or a nation has upon the kingdom of God And the establishment of the Church of Jesus Christ. The New Testament Teaches this plainly, as the apostle tells us that Christ Jesus is head over all things, quote, for the church. It is the church that matters most. It is the church for whom Jesus prepares his kingdom. It is the church for whom Jesus is coming back. Whether it is a political warfare defeating terrorists or a catastrophe in Southeast Asia or a pandemic feared throughout the world We should be thinking about nations and events in terms of how they affect the kingdom of God, for that is the focus of God. We should have faith that God is using the chaos, using the chaos in which we live for his plan of redemption of his church. That's what it's all for. And from this passage, we also learn the importance of worship in the life of God's people. Again, the nature of man is to worship. Even those who claim atheism worship a god, only their god is no bigger than themselves. As human beings, we are worshipers. Remember that old song, I've quoted it here before. Bob Dylan, you gotta serve somebody. It might be the devil, it might be the Lord, but you've got to serve somebody. You're going to serve somebody. The greatest evil that Israel commits in judges and elsewhere Is the worship of false gods. Idol worship is clearly forbidden by God and clearly practiced by the people. It should be understood that moral failings come from how we worship Psalm 115 describes those who worship idols, idols that cannot speak, cannot see, cannot hear, cannot smell, cannot feel. Psalm 115 describes the worshippers of these idols as becoming like them. Those who make them will be like them, he says. And judges, Israel becomes lifeless, blind, deaf, and powerless, just like the false gods they bowed down to. And do not be fooled. That worship of an idol has to be specifically identified, physically represented. If you are not in God's house on Sundays amongst God's people because of a recreational endeavor, then you have chosen to worship an idol without declaring it as such. Another lesson learned from this passage is the importance of each generation to pass their knowledge of God on to the next. Israel's unbelief, her wickedness did not spring out of nothing What was the result of a generation failing to teach its children the law of God as they walked by their way, as they rose in the morning, as they laid down at night? Thus we are back talking again about education. The generation of Joshua walked with God, witnessed many miracles, and was used as a weapon to slay God's enemies. And yet they failed to instill this witness of God into their children. I'm afraid that the reason for every dark age of the church can be traced back To the failure of parents to train up their children in the fear and admonition of the Lord. I recall Several times, how I question my practices of passing my faith in the Lord on to my children. Do they know the Bible stories? Do they know their catechism? Were they able to witness to others about the salvation in Christ? Did they know why we do what we do in worship? Were they able to answer skeptics in disciplines of science and other religions? And if I could not answer yes. Not just to some of those, but all of those questions that I knew I was failing to pass my faith on to my children, and I feared that they would not know the Lord. If such statements sound like works-oriented salvation, please forgive me. Every one of us is saved by grace through faith in Jesus. But when raising Christian children, I believe we need to work as if their salvation is up to us and pray as if it's up to God. An aspect of this failure to pass the knowledge of God on to the next generation is the unwillingness to be nourished by the past. This is true in the church and in families. Israel had a past that when we she remembered it and applied it to new situations, it brought her blessings and prosperity. When she forgot her past, she lost her way. For the pagan world we live. In the study of history, to them it's a waste of time. When am I ever going to use this? Is the common question of a high school student around our land. Colleges today are getting rid of their humanities programs. That's true, folks. They're getting rid of their humanities programs because humanity includes history. And according to modern academia History is written by the oppressors, and thus it is irrelevant to the woke generation. But, for Christians, history contains the imprint of God. History testifies of God. From history, we learn the ways of God, and our faith grows in the present because of what we know God has done in the past. Unfortunately, our American culture is not concerned with such nonsense, for it it is singularly guilty of the pride of believing that our present age is so sophisticated so technologically advanced that we need not pay attention to the past. But unless Christians have a knowledge of the past, we cannot possibly put in proper context what we face in the present and the future. God thought the past of Israel so important, even their great sins of the past, that he inspired men to record the past as sacred text. Just as sacred to be treated, just as important to be treated as the law he gave. Another unfortunate way the church has failed to pass knowledge on to the next generation. Is worship order or what we call liturgy. A discussion several years ago now that I Was made privy to amongst Christian adults, voiced a concern that they had lost their children to the world. It seems that many of their children had rejected their traditions The parents testified that their children didn't want to come to church services because they were bored. For those that continued to attend church, they preferred a more contemporary expression. They thought their children would still be in church if the worship was contemporary In comparison, this is not unlike Israel, who seemed to have preferred the Canaanite, highly expressive, and even erotic worship preferred it to their own. Many young persons are like Mark Twain's character Tom Sawyer, who said, church ain't shots to the circus. Indeed, it is not. The brief word of wisdom I had for these people I pass on to you, because I believe strongly that it is from the Lord. Our children do not wish to participate in worship because they do not have a correct or proper understanding of their own depravity. By our own works we are sinners in the hands of an angry God. Because of our personal sin, we find ourselves hanging ever so thinly above a cauldron of hellfire. It is perfectly right and just for us to be released into this fire by a holy and righteous God. We deserve nothing but condemnation from Him. We have no right or means by which to approach God in and of ourselves. It is, of course, by the blood of Christ and his offering of forgiveness that we can approach his throne and call him ourselves. Father. Jesus Christ enables us to approach God in worship. It is a privilege. As a privilege, it matters not whether I enjoy it. If I truly appreciate the privilege, I will enjoy it simply because it is a privilege. This week, according to the church calendar, we are still in Easter season Which is for the Christian a time to focus on celebrating the victory of Jesus over sin and death. That victory is understood better and appreciated more when we see and understand how it is not something we deserve, and that there is nothing we can do to deserve it. We are privileged to call upon the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. We are privileged to do so as a people, as a church. We are privileged to pass our faith on to our children and our children's children. We are privileged to be the true Israel. Let the lessons given to us by the nation of Israel be learned, and let us allow the world to deceive us no longer. Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God, as we read the failings of your people, we acknowledge that they are not your failings, but they are ours. And we are bound to repeat it unless we learn these lessons. Help us all individually and corporately to take them to heart. To believe and trust that we can mature and be the people you desire. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Judges 3
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles if you would to Judges chapter three. Judges chapter three Where our reading our Old Testament reading was from. As I stated the last two weeks The first two chapters of Judges are a summary of the entire book. The first chapter covers the failure of Israel to drive out the pagan people of the Promised Land. as the Lord had commanded. The second chapter summarizes the cycle of sin that Israel falls into as they lived with these pagan nations. The section read from chapter 3 this morning is an account of the first judge used of God to deliver Israel from the oppression of the enemy. Historically, it may be helpful to know that the time period between the exodus from Egypt and the reign of King David Which was approximately 1,000 B. C. , Moses likely led Israel away from Egypt around the 13th century, and again David came to the throne around 1000 B. The evil that is attributed to the entire nation of Israel is the serving of Baals and Asheras. Both of these names describe the primary gods of the Canaanites. Baal or Baal or Baal, all possible pronunciations, he was the sun god. Human sacrifices were offered to him in order to appease his anger during times of plague or during times of famine. The name was also given to other gods of local regions, which meant that there were false gods with names such as Baal Hermon or Baal Lebanon and so forth. But Israelites, the name Baal, came to summarize any false god that was worshipped by pagans. Asherah was the name of a goddess that was widely worshipped in Canaan. Originally, she was the wife of the war god Asur, or Who was the god of the Assyrians? She was later identified as the goddess of fertility. She was also the goddess of love and not war. She was the yang of the yin-yang She was the balancing power of the male figure God or gods. Israel's worship of Asherah is a perfect example of the syncretism we've been discussing. As she was thought to be the female counterpart to Yahweh or Jehovah. It is worthy to note that little is known about the sin of Israel. Other than this general description of idol worship, no specifics are given. It is assumed that they did as the other nations did around them. Also, no specifics are given of the judge chosen to deliver Israel. It is true that we are given a brief description of the lineage of Othniel. But we are told nothing about his personality, nor why he was the chosen one to deliver God's people. The brief description of Israel's sin and its consequences under the king of Aram purposefully communicate that the details are not important. How Ofniel overpowered a king and kingdom, most likely larger and stronger than Israel, is also not important. The two most important points of this story are that it was the Spirit of the Lord that came upon Othniel to deliver Israel. And that it was the forgetfulness of the people of Israel that got them in disfavor with the Lord to begin with. First, we shall examine the Spirit of the Lord coming upon Opniel This is stated plainly enough to disable any thoughts or come to any type of conclusion that we are to give credit to Off-Neel. The lack of detail regarding the character of Othniel and the emphasis that it was the Spirit of the Lord that came upon him tells us that Othniel could have been any man And that it was God who was solely responsible for the deliverance of Israel out of the oppression of the king of Aram. The doctrine, and I'm not a Calvinist, but the doctrine of irresistible grace is found here, as it is so clearly articulated in the New Testament. Atniel is a vessel made for glory, as described by the apostle in Romans chapter 9. The God of Israel is the God or God with a capital G. He is the definition of a sovereign God as he rules over all things. He moves the hearts of men and women towards the establishment of his kingdom for his glory alone. We, as in all of us, are fallen creatures, dead in our trespasses and sins. We are dependent upon the Spirit of God to come to us, overwhelming us, pulling us out of the slew of the spawns. Early into my conversion, I would speak about how I came to know Christ. In terms that would flatter me more than God, it was understood and communicated that I came to Christ and that I chose to follow him. It took a great amount of humbling for me to realize that he came to me. I was a dead man. A dead man cannot choose anything of life, for his ability to choose is dead along with his spirit. I had to be brought to life. I had to be dragged to the Lord. Because I was dead in sin, the only choices I made regarding what mattered to me is what pleased me. I could not choose anything but sin until God chose me. It is clear, then, that there is no glory to be given to Othniel for delivering Israel, because he did nothing that was not enabled by the Lord. And so it is with us. The next important point describes how Israel came to serve false gods. And caused the anger of the Lord to burn against them. The passage says simply that they forgot the Lord their God. I spoke at length last week about the result of Israel failing to pass the knowledge of the Lord from one generation to the next. Because the second generation or the generation after Joshua did not know the Lord as their parents did, Israel followed and worshipped other gods. The word used now to describe their lack of knowledge is that they forgot. Although they forgot God, he did not forget them. He did not forget his covenant with them, nor his promised punishments if they did not follow him. Memory is an important spiritual subject in the Bible. Psalm 78 explains how Israel betrayed the Lord and his covenant. It says they forgot what he had done and the wonders he had shown them. Forgetting contributes to unbelief and even leads to unbelief. Forgetting in itself is an act of unbelief. An opposite, as an opposite, remembering feeds faith, and in many ways is akin to faith. In Deuteronomy 32, 18, the Lord says, You deserted the rock that fathered you. You forgot the God who gave you birth. Through Hosea the Lord said, I cared for you in the desert, the land of burning heat When I fed them, they were satisfied. When they were satisfied, they became proud. Then they forgot me. On the positive side, the Lord commands it commands Israel to remember in Micah chapter 6, verse 5, the Lord said My people remember what Balach, king of Moab, counseled, and what Balaam, son of Boor, answered. Remember your journey to Shittim and Gilgal, that you may know the righteous acts of the Lord. The people of God were to remember the history of their own people, how the Lord had delivered them long ago, and that was to make a difference for them in that day. Taking these texts and many others, we conclude that faith in God feeds Feeds on the recollection of what he has done in the ancient past and in our individual lives. Some of you will remember that my wife surprised me on my 40th birthday by flying in a childhood friend named Jay Ward. That was way too long ago, by the way. It was quite a surprise. And because he had never been to Washington, D. C. , before he departed, we took a trip Down to view the major monuments of the mall. It was the first time I had been to the World War II monument. It was then that it became my favorite I will not do justice in describing it to you if you have not seen it, so I will not try. Of the many things that moved me were the battles listed on each end of the monument under the Pacific Theater and the Atlantic Theater At that time I was not well read on the subject of World War II, so that much of what I was learning from the monument was new to me. I have since had a budding interest in its causes, in its battles, and its heroes. But I was humbled then that I did not know anything of half the battles listed. Because there were men who died to preserve what I so richly now enjoy in those battles and scenarios. I was not ready to appreciate. That lack of knowledge unnerved me. For I know how I am motivated and how you are motivated. We are motivated by our memories. I have since read Band of Brothers, which covers major battles on the Atlantic theater starting from D-Day. I have read With the Old Breed, which tells of battles on the Pacific Front, and the book Helmet for My Pillow, which is another first-hand account of battles on the Pacific theater. And finally, a general treatment of the war, simply titled World War II by Joseph Stromburg. All of my readings Was to increase my appreciation made in that war, the sacrifices made in that war. I am convinced that if we have a greater understanding of what was sacrificed For our benefit, we have a greater desire to serve out our appreciation I remember being in awe of the testimony of our own Tom Sloneker, a veteran of World War II, now gone from us a number of years. He shared with me that he was on a tourist cruise of the Potomac when the terrorists attacked on 9-11, now almost 20 years ago. He told me that there were other men of his generation that were with him on that cruise, and when they heard of the attack, they were ready to fight. Ready to protect their country. Ready as they had been in December of nineteen forty one. They remembered. And because they remembered they were motivated to serve again. There are some wonderful examples in Scripture of faithful servants of God who made the extra effort to remember. Samuel set up a memorial at Mitzpah to commemorate a great victory that the Lord had given Israel over the Philistines. The stone formation was to be a constant reminder to all who passed by what God had done for them. It was also to serve as a constant spur to the people to trust the Lord today. Samuel called the formation an Ebenezer. Ebenezer literally means stone of help. Recognizing that a monument to remember is a help to those who appreciate it Some among us have very good memories, and others of us rather poor. We are naturally impressed by people who have good memories. Abraham Lincoln was said to have an outstanding memory, delighting friends with his ability to recite long verses from Shakespeare and other authors. He also had an uncanny ability to remember names and faces. My beloved wife remembers names well, and she remembers what they said and how they said it. As for me, I have forgotten more than I can remember. And the most amazing among us is Bishop Cox still. Who not only remembers names and faces, but the past needs and burdens of those he has ministered to over the years. And then there are some of us who remember trivial matters and we don't know why. But we are not talking about remembering names, faces, facts, directions, or trivia. We are speaking about a spiritual memory. Such is a memory that places us on an equal playing field with those who might have a natural gift at memory, and yet may not have one in the spiritual realm. And it places us next to the poor in memory of facts of the past, but have a spiritual memory in abundance. This spiritual memory is one that recalls where we have been in our sins and trespasses and how God delivered us from self-imposed peril. Spiritual memory is a relational memory that recalls the work that God does to our souls, enabling us to say that we were once lost and now we are found. It remembers what it was to be without hope and how hope came to be within our hearts. It is the memory that recalls our first love of God. A spiritual memory, unfortunately, because it is relational, is not always positive. We all know by experience how our memory can focus on the bad rather than the good. Relationships can be numbered with positive words, great moments of laughter, and even shared burdens. But it is those moments of slight or hurt feelings that we remember the most. I am amazed how many relationships I have had that appear congenial and even durable That can turn on a negative moment, and that is all that is remembered. You know what I am talking about, for you have experienced them as well. We all have. Having a positive spiritual memory takes purposeful effort. We are to work at remembering what is good rather than bad. For the devil would gladly have us pulled to his side and heed his words of negativity. One way to help our spiritual memory towards the positive is to purposefully recall our sins. That sounds negative, but it is not. Remembering past sins does not need to be specifics, as in replaying them in our minds. But in general, we should remember them. By Israel remembering God delivering them out of Egypt, they were remembering their bondage as well Consider our Psalter reading. The psalmist who wrote Psalm 106 encourages the people of God to remember the past. He realizes that he cannot rightly ask the Lord, that is the psalmist, to remember his covenant promises to bless his children if he does not recall how these same children failed to uphold God's law. After all, it is only in remembering our failures to keep his laws that we can repent and enjoy all the benefits of his covenant faithfulness. For if a man does not repent, God will whet his sword and execute judgment. Psalm 7 Remembering past sins is unique to the Jewish and Christian faiths. If you looked at Psalm 106 through verse 43, You see that it rehearses the history of Israel as a means of recalling the past and implicitly calling those who pray the psalm not to repeat the nation's history of sinfulness. Recall it so you don't repeat it. The low points that the psalmist recounts include the worship of the golden calf at Horeb. That episode of idolatry was especially heinous because it occurred not far from the place where the Lord was revealing his covenant law that established Israel as a holy nation. About 3,000 people died as a result of God's judgment for that particular sin. And many more suffered from a plague sent by the Lord. But note, but note that the psalmist also recalls how the entire nation was not destroyed, but rather rescued through the intercession of Moses as a covenant mediator. And this reminds us that even when God's people have sinned and sinned greatly, forgiveness is available for those who repent through the work of a covenant mediator. Who has now been revealed to be the Lord Jesus Christ. The psalmist recounts many other sins of ancient Israel. Including their failure to drive out the Canaanites, the sacrifice of their children to pagan gods, and more. Yet the psalm, Psalm 106, does not end on a note of doom, but a note of hope. The Lord remembered his promise to bless his covenant people when they cried out for salvation. And he continues to remember his promises when we turn to him in faith and repentance. The importance of remembering the good and the bad is highlighted in Bunyan's book, Pilgrim's Progress, a book that all persons before they die should read. It is an allegory of the Christian life, describing our walk with Jesus as a near perilous journey as we fight spiritual battles on our way to heaven. The main character is Christian, named Christian, who travels the narrow road to heaven. In the second part of the story, we are told more specifically about the battle between Christian and Apollyon, a great demon slash dragon. In the valley of humiliation, just beyond the place of the forgotten green. Of this place, the forgotten green. Greatheart, a guide for Christians, says this, quote, indeed that place, the forgotten, or excuse me, the forgetful green, is the most dangerous place in all these parts. For at any time these pilgrims meet with any brunt, it is when they forget what favors they have received and how unworthy they are of them. We know such wisdom to be true, do we not? When we do not remember what God has done and how undeserving we are that He has done it. We are too weak to resist the whispers of the devil. We are less inclined, if inclined at all, to forgive as we have been forgiven. In summary, we are at our strongest when we remember what the Lord has done for us, and at our weakest when we forget. There is no magic to remembering or working our spiritual memory. It merely takes effort. It is choosing to remember When we arise in the morning, we choose to remember that in Jesus we live and move and have our being. It is choosing to thank God at every meal for the food that nourishes us. For every piece of bread he provides for us. It is choosing to remember during our private devotions and corporate worship that we are sinners and that Jesus offers sinners forgiveness. It is believing in what we read, in his word. Beloved, we have seen what happens when the people of God forget as Israel did. Now let us see what happens when God's people remember. Let us pray. And Father, we confess it is of no strength of ours that we remember. But we do know that you have given us every opportunity and every power to do so. And so we take, or we do not escape responsibility, but take on the responsibility to remember as you have instructed. For what you have done is worthy for us to remember every moment of our lives. We confess this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Stabbing the Fat
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Join me in turning in your Bibles to Judges chapter 3. Covering the stories of Ehud and Shamgar I hope, thus far, in studying judges, that we have learned a little from the style of the writing of the author. Regarding what message he is trying to convey, not just what he tells the reader, but in the style that he tells it We can learn much from the details he gives us as well as the details that he does not give us. Last week we learned that the lack of details regarding the sin of Israel and the personality of their judge. is important for it calls us to focus on what the Lord has done. In the account of Ehud that we have here, there are details given, and they are of course important. For a reason. On the other hand, regarding the sin of Israel and the judge Shamgar, nothing more than a mention is given, which again The silence carries a message with it. The sin of Israel that placed them in need of another deliverer or judge is simply stated. Once again, the Israelites did evil in the eyes of the Lord. The lack of description regarding their sin. As well as taking into account the descriptions of idol worship mentioned previously, tells us that these are simply repeated offenses. It conveys an attitude we might have toward an alcoholic who continues to fall back into drunkenness after periods of sobriety. Or an adulterer who says he has changed his ways only to be found with another woman a week later. When behavior is repeated, we come to expect it. And the unfaithfulness of the sinner no longer surprises us and isn't even worth describing any longer. The description of the king of Eglom that is his oppression over Israel. That description is important for it explains that his victory was accordance to God's providence. Eglom, no doubt, did not see it this way. To him, the victory over Israel was proof of his strength and his good leadership. He is the one who created the coalition of the Ammonites and the Amalekites. He is the one who ordered and carried out the attack on Israel. From his vantage point, he is solely responsible for the victory. The writer of Judges, however, fills us in on the truth. The Lord gave Israel over to Eglon and the Moabites. None of this would have happened if Israel had remained faithful to the Lord, but of course they were not, and the result was 18 years of subjection. We would hope that the cry of Israel to the Lord was one of repentance, but alas it was not. This cry can be compared to a child who is caught with his hand in the cookie jar. A great way to escape inevitable punishment is for the child to begin to cry. In order to receive compassion from his parents rather than a rod. The child, of course, is not crying because he broke a house rule or that he dishonored his parents The child cries because he is afraid of the consequences. So it is with Israel. Their repeated sin and their repeated cries unto the Lord reveal that they are not so much upset that they have offended God. But rather that they did not like the consequences of their sin. 18 years of subjection. God, of course, is compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in love. He knows that if he delivers Israel from the oppression of Eglon, that they will fall back into their sinful ways, but that does not discourage him from delivering them as he promised he would. As I have stated, the details of this story are important. Ehud was a left-handed man, or better translated, ambidextrious. He originated his plan to kill the king by strapping a foot and a half long double-edged sword to his right thigh for a quick cross-draw. This reveals to the reader how he was able to get away with carrying the weapon into the king's presence Because most people were right-handed, a sword, even a dagger would have been placed on the left hip, and that's where the soldiers would have looked for a sword. Ehud, his sword was on his right thigh and hidden under his clothes. Also, the element of surprise was on Ehud's side for he was likely the only one who knew about his plan to assassinate the king. Ehud was sent to the king by Israel's leaders to give tribute or to give something in honor to the king Ehud is the one who had other plans. The details of the king are no less important in this story. Eglon was a fat man. Not like many of us, mind you, who battled the bulge, Iglon was grossly obese, hence rendered slow afoot. Obesity in Scripture symbolizes the sin of gluttony. To be obese, think of this, to be obese, obese around 1300 BC. In order to do that, a person had to have given himself over to the desires of the flesh. Having fed himself on the pleasures of this life off of the backs of others. Eglon symbolizes the nation that he rules And that they prosper off of the backs of the Israelites. Along with being obese, Eglon had become lazy of mind, For he agreed to hear of Ehud's secret without any protection from his guards. This was, of course, very unwise As a decision, but it reflects how slow Eglon had become of mind and body. Eglon is a sad character And in a sense, is being made fun of by the author of Judges, for there is nothing describing of him that is appealing physically or mentally. The blade, being described as double-edged, reminds us of how the writer of Hebrews describes holy scriptures. God's word is said to be a double-edged sword. To defeat the enemy, any enemy of God, his word is to be invoked, just as Jesus did in the desert. The manner that Eglon is assassinated is a metaphor for how the church is to slay the principalities, powers, and rulers of every age. God's word is to be embedded into the fatness of our culture. God's word is to be buried into the recesses of the world that has become obese by indulging in the flesh. Like Eglon's belly, the world swallows the Word of God up as if to overwhelm it with its fatness. But properly placed as Ehud's sword was, the word of God brings the world down. The manner that Ehud escapes is another description of the incompetence of Eglon's reign He is probably so unreasonably feared by his own protectors that they cannot even disturb him when he is on the toilet. By their reasoning to stay out for a long time, period, it appears to be a place where Eglon spent much of his time. The victory of Israel over the nation of Boab was swift following this assassination of Eglon by Ehud Verse 29 describes the striking down of ten thousand men, which is a large number for any battle. This all occurred in a manner that was truly spontaneous. People didn't know what Eglon, or excuse me, what Ehud was going to do. The men of Moab, Moab are described as in the NIV as vigorous, but that's an unfortunate translation, for the Hebrew word is synonymous with fact. The word also can be translated stout or stubborn as the New King James translates it. But considering the description of Eglon, it is very likely that the writer is describing an An army that is similar to the king. They were fat with their spoils of the land and in no manner ready to fight. The fattening of these people by the Lord made them ripe, as we say, for the picking. The defeat, we note, was complete. For we are told that peace reigned in Israel for 80 years afterward. 80 years. Such a peace is a true gift of God lasting two generations. Immediately following the description of peace for 80 years is the verse that might seem out of place. Shamgar is mentioned as the next judge, but nothing specifically is said about his person. His name, his name is a clue, and it is debated whether he was even an Israelite His victory is no less impressive than Ehud's, for he is given credit for striking down 600 Philistines with an ox goad. An ox goad is not much of a weapon. It is a stick to prod animals. It can be many sizes, but it is not made for battle Striking down 600 Philistines with a stick is even more impressive, shall we say, than Samson killing numerous Philistines with a jawbone of a donkey. The placement of this verse and the brief description of Shamgar's victory, preceded by a lengthier description of Eva's victory, communicates, I believe, two things. First, the people of God overestimate the enemy. The ease by which Ehud was able to approach Eglon and then kill him Allows us to ask why was this not done earlier? The ease at which Ehud was able to assassinate a foreign king Assemble an army to defeat an organized army and maintain peace for 80 years allows us to conclude that Israel was superior to their enemy For those eighteen years they were under oppression, and yet they did not exercise their superiority. Add to that story the one of Shamgar being able to kill 600 Philistines with a stick, and it is confirmed that the enemy cannot stand against the chosen people of God. It is then embarrassing when the people of God speak about an enemy, whether it be political or spiritual, as if any can stand against the anointed of the Lord. We know well and have quoted such passages as: I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me. And if God is for us, who can stand against us? And greater is he that is in me than he that is in the world. Applying these to life circumstances is more difficult than mere recitation. We have to believe and we have to live it out. There is no political party or leader, whether in this country or one foreign, that can stand against the anointed of God. There is no earthly army or terrorist organization that can take a single life of one of God's people without it being according to God's will. And regardless of what they do to the body, they can never touch the soul, especially the soul of those who have been redeemed by the blood of the Lamb. There is also no spiritual power, whether obviously demonic or disguised as an angel of light, that can cause us to do evil or threaten our salvation in any way. Such statements are in opposition to the great temptation of many to view the world in a dualistic manner. The battle of good versus evil is believed by some, even Christians, to keep the universe in balance. This Star Wars philosophy is carried into Christianity as some believe that the devil himself has similar, even equal power to our Godhead. And the two are thought to be in battle trying to win supremacy over this earth. One of the more horrid experiences of my childhood was when a neighborhood family took me and my brother to see the Exorcist in a drive-in theater Driving theaters when you're in a car, you're watching a movie. Unfortunately, I was not a Christian at the time and my my parents were ignorant about messages conveyed in such a movie. I remember cowering in the back seat of the car, wishing I did not have to watch.
