My mind, Young Mind, concluded from the movie that God had limited power over the devil. Scripture, of course, tells us something quite differently. Jesus needed to say a mere word, and the demons were gone. Those who spoke in his name were able to overcome the devil, and in some cases, Jesus simply approached a person demon-possessed, and the demons shuddered in submission. Realize, dear church, that Jesus has paid the debt of sin and overcome death itself. Such a victory was total. And the devil has no authority in the lives of those who call Jesus Lord and Savior. Although the devil prowls around like a roaring lion. For the people of God, it is as if he has no teeth. Let us not give him any more credit than he deserves or assume power he does not have. The second lesson communicated in these stories is that God uses means to accomplish His will. Although he could simply strike a man dead, he could have struck Eglon dead like he did Ananias in the book of Acts. He chooses men like Ehud to carry out his providence. This concept can be tricky, and rightfully so, for Christians struggle almost with the same question as non-Christians regarding Divine involvement in tragedies such as a terrorist attack or so-called natural disasters or pandemics Each time a natural disaster occurs or when there is an outbreak of a virus, there are unbelievers who take to the airways or write articles in newspapers or online That one that convinced everyone that there is no God, for no God would allow such suffering. That claim We Christians have they they claim excuse me they claim we Christians have no answer. But we do. They just choose not to listen. What happened in the case of Ehud and Shamgar, and what happens when disasters and pandemics occur are identified by theologians as examples of concursus. Concursus is a subdivision of the category under God's providence. The teaching of divine providence is that everything that happens in the world is ultimately ultimately according to the will and purpose of God. He has a plan. And everything that happens is according to that plan, even the number of hairs on your head at any given time. The doctrine of concursus is the teaching that God uses means, ways to accomplish His will. It may be that there can be a natural explanation for what has occurred, but God uses that natural explanation to accomplish His will. A natural disaster is both caused by God and caused by an earthquake under the ocean floor. A car fatality occurs because God has numbered our days and because a man was driving drunk. Chance is a part of this world, but it is a world God created and a world he controls. Spin the chambers of a gun, having only one out of six chambers filled, and pull the trigger. The odds are one in six that a bullet will be fired. Those odds must concur, however, with the will of God. As Proverbs 1:6 states, a lot is cast in the lap, but every decision is from the Lord. In the case of Ehud, he was the means by which God would deliver his people. Ehud was clever, he was brave, and God used those attributes Shamgar was brave and skillful, and God used those attributes. These skills concurred with God's will regarding timing and victory. We cannot achieve victory unless it is according to God's will. And He chooses to use us, His church. As a means to accomplish his victories. There is a very comforting and hopeful understanding of both tragedy and victory For all of it is according to God's will. On a side note, I would include that the doctrine of concursus helps us understand the importance of Bible study The importance of attending church, the importance of the sacraments of the church. For these are also means, ways by which God uses to give out his grace. Those who would convince themselves that these things are not necessary have failed to understand God's ways. He gives grace and the means of grace, God gives them both Combining these two lessons, we see that God uses means, he uses ways by which he achieves victory over evil and establishes his kingdom against an enemy. Any enemy that is no match for him or his people. When we experience tragedy or defeat, we must recognize the cause of consequences. or the cause of chance, or the cause of nature, along with the will of God. The will of God is always being fulfilled using another word, concursus. When experiencing good fortune and victory, the same elements are involved. During the bad times, may repentance take place and lessons be learned. During the good times, may all praise be given to God, for it all occurs according to his will. Amen and Amen. Let us pray. Our Father in Heaven, as much as we state these things to be true, we recognize that our minds and our hearts do not always go there. We trust in circumstance too often. We trust in chance too often. We don't readily see your hand in the moment. Increase our faith, Holy Spirit. Help us to be relieved of the blinders that we might see your will always being done, and that we might always trust in it. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

Last week we learned that the lack of details regarding the sin of Israel and the personality of their judge. is important for it calls us to focus on what the Lord has done. In the account of Ehud that we have here, there are details given, and they are of course important. For a reason. On the other hand, regarding the sin of Israel and the judge Shamgar, nothing more than a mention is given, which again The silence carries a message with it. The sin of Israel that placed them in need of another deliverer or judge is simply stated. Once again, the Israelites did evil in the eyes of the Lord. The lack of description regarding their sin. As well as taking into account the descriptions of idol worship mentioned previously, tells us that these are simply repeated offenses. It conveys an attitude we might have toward an alcoholic who continues to fall back into drunkenness after periods of sobriety. Or an adulterer who says he has changed his ways only to be found with another woman a week later. When behavior is repeated, we come to expect it. And the unfaithfulness of the sinner no longer surprises us and isn't even worth describing any longer. The description of the king of Eglom that is his oppression over Israel. That description is important for it explains that his victory was accordance to God's providence. Eglom, no doubt, did not see it this way. To him, the victory over Israel was proof of his strength and his good leadership. He is the one who created the coalition of the Ammonites and the Amalekites. He is the one who ordered and carried out the attack on Israel. From his vantage point, he is solely responsible for the victory. The writer of Judges, however, fills us in on the truth. The Lord gave Israel over to Eglon and the Moabites. Like Eglon's belly, the world swallows the Word of God up as if to overwhelm it with its fatness. But properly placed as Ehud's sword was, the word of God brings the world down. By their reasoning to stay out for a long time, period, it appears to be a place where Eglon spent much of his time. The victory of Israel over the nation of Boab was swift following this assassination of Eglon by Ehud Verse 29 describes the striking down of ten thousand men, which is a large number for any battle. This all occurred in a manner that was truly spontaneous. People didn't know what Eglon, or excuse me, what Ehud was going to do. The men of Moab, Moab are described as in the NIV as vigorous, but that's an unfortunate translation, for the Hebrew word is synonymous with fact. The word also can be translated stout or stubborn as the New King James translates it. But considering the description of Eglon, it is very likely that the writer is describing an An army that is similar to the king. An ox goad is not much of a weapon. It is a stick to prod animals. The ease at which Ehud was able to assassinate a foreign king Assemble an army to defeat an organized army and maintain peace for 80 years allows us to conclude that Israel was superior to their enemy For those eighteen years they were under oppression, and yet they did not exercise their superiority. sermons.title: Past What We Don't See
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn your Bibles to Judges chapter 4 Judges chapter four I am grateful That the story from judges we are examining today falls on Mother's Day. You might think that I will You may think that I will draw parallels between the courage of mothers needed in order to be mothers and compare that with the same courage of Deborah needing to lead Israel. I will draw comparisons but not parallels. What needs to be done first of all is to provide a literary examination of chapters four and five. We did not read chapter five today, but I will refer to it But chapter five covers the same material as chapter four, only as poetry rather than prose. The chapter 4 prose are like most Old Testament narratives. The story is told with an emphasis on the facts Logic is a driving force in what is told. This is quite different from the poetry in chapter 5. Hebraic poetry does not emphasize rhyme, which we are familiar with in the West. It is instead impressionistic. and dependent upon parallelisms, which are lines that say the same thing, only in a slightly different way. Our study of this story will focus on the prose and be informed by the poetry. We will save a close examination of poetry for another time. You have noticed how important facts are in telling of these stories of the individual judges, and how important it is to note when facts are not told to us, for that too provides lessons. Last week we learned that Israel too often overestimates an enemy, and that God uses means to perform his will. We were introduced to the doctrine of concursus, which is God concurring with the natural world to complete his plan. The story of Deborah is another example of concursus, while highlighting a different lesson for us today. The story of Deborah has become a very important one for those who have a feminist agenda. As you know, the issue of women ordination within many Christian circles is hotly debated. Despite what certain passages in the Old and New Testaments clearly say regarding a masculine place behind the pulpit, The story of Deborah proves to some that women are also called to lead God's people. A counter-argument, also using this passage, In Judges, is that Deborah is an anomaly due to the sinful state of Israel. And as the text says, Barak was supposed to be the leader But in acquiescing his responsibility, the glory he would have received is lost to a woman Hopefully, as we consider what we have learned thus far about the message the author of Judges is trying to convey We are able to realize that this narrative in chapter 4 has nothing to do with women ordination or women in ministry, either pro or con. As far as the narrative is concerned, once again we are told that after the death of the previous judge, Israel falls back into sin. The consequence of their sin is the Lord, God himself, selling them into the hands of a foreign king. And again we see that Israel overestimates the enemy, for the kingdom that now rules them was defeated by Joshua just a few generations earlier. Israel's failure to get total victory over their enemies means that they came back again like a thorn in their side, again and again. We also learned that the iron chariots are a problem once again. When Israel cries out to the Lord because they do not like the consequences of their sin, Something different is in the land than was before. A woman named Deborah, called a prophetess, is acting as a judge for the people. Deborah is different not simply because she is a woman, but she is not said to have been raised to judge Israel like Uthniel and Ehud. They were raised up by God. Deborah was not. She just is. She just shows up The judging that she does in Israel is also different than the ones previously mentioned, for she delivers no one and does not judge an oppressing power. Deborah speaks on behalf of the Lord, which is why she is called a prophetess. She is in the same line as a Miriam in the story of Exodus. or Anna, who identified the infant Jesus to be the Christ child. As a spokesman or spokeswoman For the Lord, Deborah calls Barak as the Spirit of the Lord led her to do, and commands him in the name of the Lord to form an army and then overcome the enemy. Barak does not stand well on his own, and so he insists that Deborah goes with him It is obvious to him that the Lord is with Deborah, and so he believes her to be the guarantee for a victory. Deborah agrees to go, but states that because Barak has responded this way, the honor that would be afforded to him will now go to a woman. It is natural to conclude that Deborah is referring to herself, but she is not. In fact, Deborah is with Barack just before the battle, and then no longer is mentioned in the narrative. Almost like she disappears. Deborah's willingness to stand in the gap between the people of Israel and God is comparable Comparable to wives and mothers of every age who stand in the gap between God and their children because their husband will not. A wise woman knows she can never be the earthly father to her children and their needs, but because teaching a child to pray is a desperate need And teaching the children biblical stories and how to live out a faith in Jesus are also essential needs. A courageous woman finds her inner Deborah and provides those spiritual needs to her children. Well all the while praying, her husband will find the courage to lead, like Barak needed, just as God has told him to do. But getting back to our narrative, the description of the battle is brief, as Israel's victory is swift and definitive. The story now follows Sisera, a highly regarded general of the Canaanites, who tries to flee for his life after the defeat of his army. The character JayL comes into the picture and by means of some deception and inappropriate behavior by a woman, she is able to rend Sisera defenseless. When the time is right, she takes advantage of the moment and kills the general by driving a tent pig through his temple. As she was plotting this killing, Baroth was searching for Sisera, and when he finds him, he is already dead. The honor then was JL's. As the poetry notes in chapter 5, verse 24, it is the same honor prophesied by Deborah. Hear these words starting in chapter 5, verse 24. Most blessed among women is Jael, the wife of Haber the Kenite. Blessed is she among women in tent. He asked for water. She gave milk. She brought out cream in a lordly bowl. She stretched her hand to the tent peg. her right hand to the workman's hammer. She pounded Sisera, she pierced his head, she split and struck through his temple. At her feet he sank, he fell. He lay still. At her feet he sank, he fell. Where he sank, there he fell dead. The reference to a crushed head should hearken us back to the Lord's prophecy to Eve after she ate the forbidden fruit. The prophecy was that her seed, a son, would crush the serpent's head. The Lord's prophecy referred to the coming of his son, who would crush the head of the devil And every mention of such a killing in Scripture, like David cutting off the head of Goliath, or Jael driving a tent pig through the head of an enemy. All of it is a precursor to what God will do by way of his son to the ultimate enemy, the devil. The other details of the story are worth mentioning again. JL, you recall, is a married woman. For her to invite a man that is not her husband into a tent would have been scandalous to anyone who knew of it She is able to lure Sisera in because he is desperate to be hidden. The milk offered is a means to comfort Sisera. Milk was considered a luxury and had a nurturing connotation as it still does today. The hospitality of J. L. shows to Sisera a lull it lulled his senses and it made him vulnerable. That a woman who is neither a warrior nor an Israelite was able to kill the general confirms the emphasis in chapter 4, verse 23. Which is that God was responsible for subduing Jabon, the Canaanite king, and making Israel stronger. God did it until the Canaanite king was completely destroyed. God was responsible. Not Barak, not Deborah, nor Jael, but God. This lesson we are going to hear over and over again. God was responsible for the victory of the first judge, the second, and the third, and now the fourth. We are going to hear this lesson over and over again because Israel was slow to learn it. And when they did learn it, it did not stay with them. Each sermon from this book thus far has mentioned, in light of this lesson, that God alone is responsible for our salvation. All praise goes to Calvary, the hill on which Jesus died. Added to that lesson is that God uses means to accomplish His will, our salvation. The lesson for us this morning is that God uses means, he uses people as means, people who have faults. Each of the characters in this story is flawed. The most obviously flawed is Barak, who is a man of weak faith, and in a true sense, he's a coward. Deborah says this to his face, mentioning the way he is responding to the Lord's command. And because of his cowardice, a woman who is not even an Israelite Will finish the deed he was commanded to do, and she will receive the honor of the victory. But here's the thing. Here's the thing. Despite Barak's dependence upon Deborah in both to have faith and courage, when we read Hebrews chapter 11, where men of faith are listed, Barack is on the list. He's there with Abraham. He's there with Isaac. He's there with Jacob. We might expect Deborah or even Jael, who can be compared to Rahab. But it is neither of these. Barack, the man of seemingly little faith, is in the whole of faith. The message then is clear, is it not? God uses men who are flawed, even men with but a mustard seed of faith. Upon closer examination of that list in Hebrews, we also notice that Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were flawed. There is not a man or woman in the Hall of Faith who was not flawed. Being an idealist at one time in my life I had expected that the persons God had chosen to lead his people would be near perfect. Certainly not perfect like Christ Jesus, but near perfect as in better than average. I recall my first reaction upon learning the history of our traditions, Anglican traditions, as found in the prayer book and the 39 Articles of Religion. My reaction was one of embarrassment. The Church of England was started because King Henry VIII wanted to get a divorce. Such a start is certainly not as noble as that of Martin Luther, John Calvin, John Knox, and even Ulrich Zwingli Some have tried to get away from this beginning by stating that the Church of England was established much earlier, possibly in the first century, and it was, at the time of King Henry VIII, simply reclaiming its independence. We like that version because it sounds more noble. The truth is that the beginning of Anglicanism is flawed. But so was Luther flawed, as he had repeated bouts with depression and crises of faith. Along with contributing to a riot during the peasant wars where many poor people were slaughtered. Calvin was flawed with poor judgment, leading to a man's death. Knox lacked charity as he condemned all other Christians who did not believe in the same doctrines that he believed. In the same arrogant spirit, Zwingli, in a similar fashion to Calvin, approved of the drowning of a man named Felix Manns, one of his former students and a leader of the Anabaptist movement. Thomas Cramner, the primary architect of the Book of Common Prayer, was also flawed. You are aware of the story of him recanting his Protestant beliefs while imprisoned under Queen Mary He only recanted his recanting when they still planned to burn him at the stake. Cramner was brave when facing the flames, but flawed when he was imprisoned. One of my heroes in my early studies was John Wesley. His discipline, intellect, and servitude would put many contemporaries to shame. And yet there was a time in his life when his jealousy got the better of him. While he was a missionary in Georgia in the United States, he fell in love with a woman named Sophie Hopke. Sophie either did not return the admiration or was impatient with Wesley's slow advancements, and she ended up marrying another man. Wesley was heartbroken. It so happened that during his ministry in Georgia, Sophie and her husband missed one Sunday service, just one. Imagine that. Missed one Sunday service without inquiring as to why the Reverend Wesley placed both of them under church discipline and did not allow them to receive Holy Communion the next Sunday His petty motivation for such action was clear. Certain behaviors at certain times in no sense outweigh the many godly attributes of these Christian leaders down through the centuries. The godly men God has used, by and large, have much more godly attributes to highlight than sinful ones. And yet the sin is there. Personally, I used to be overly hurt and embarrassed when someone would point out that I was flawed. I have been told that I am too prideful. I have been told that my manner at times is careless. Such were blows to my self-image indeed. Eventually, however, I came to understand that my flaws serve a greater purpose. First, they humble me, which causes me to go to the cross and seek God's forgiveness. Second, they prevent any misconception that might arise believing that I am anything more than a sinful man being used of God for the building of his kingdom. As a minister, I am a tool in the hand of God. I am flawed and useless unless God is using me. It's actually rather humorous to be offended by someone believing it is necessary to tell me my faults. I can no longer be surprised that I have them, and no one else should be surprised that I have them either Throughout the Bible, we are taught not to put our trust in man or princes, neither a believing man or a believing prince. God is the only one that can save us, and we need to be sure that we never put our trust elsewhere. Men are merely broken reeds if leaned upon. We can only lean upon the Lord. There would not be so great a disappointment and disillusionment in the church if we would learn not to place our hopes in men as we tend to do. The Bible gives us the following warnings precisely because we are susceptible to this error. Isaiah chapter 2, stop trusting in man. Who has but a breath in his nostrils? Of what account is he? Jeremiah 17. Cursed is the man who trusts in a man and makes his flesh his strength. Psalm 49. But man, despite his riches, does not endure. He is like the beasts that perish. This is the fate of those who trust in themselves. Psalm 118. It is better to trust in the Lord than to put confidence in man. It is better to trust in the Lord than to put confidence in princes. Time and time again, the Lord is reminding his people that they are trusting in the wrong thing. The wrong thing is usually another man or themselves. It is good then for us to be asking ourselves who we might be trusting in or giving praise to other than God. It is easy to give credit to a man when he may have helped you come to the Lord, or when you are shown a truth that is life-changing. I might say of a man that without him I would not know the Lord today. Such a statement is humble, but it is also untrue. God can use a man or a woman, a child or a donkey to bring his will to pass. Regardless, it is the Lord who is responsible. Barak is a lesson in faith. It teaches us to look past the things we can see. To the God who is there, but we cannot see, and the faith we need, even though it be small. It is mighty. We are to look to God, even with our small faith, every hour of every day that we live in this world, until we are before God face to face. With no possibility of failing to give him credit, credit where it is deserved. Let us pray. Our God, we only want to give you credit for all the good that is in our lives. We want to give you and you alone praise. We want to put our trust solely in you. And so we receive these warnings and we receive these examples. And we say, Lord, we believe. But helped our unbelief. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen

The first commands God's people that they should have no other gods before him. If there are gods And those gods are made in the form of idols, and those idols are worshipped by our parents. Commandment five is forfeited until numbers one and two are corrected. This principle is simply stated in the book of Acts. We are to obey God rather than men. Gideon Must apply that principle here, for he cannot obey God unless he defies his father's idol worship. Many Christians struggle here, not knowing when it is appropriate to sever themselves from parental authority. The same dilemma occurs in a marriage when a wife who is called to submit to her husband is asked by her husband to do immoral acts or to stop even worshiping God. Neither option is plausible, forcing a wife to obey God rather than men. Jesus warned of this type of tension between family members when he asked rhetorically He said, Do you think I came to bring peace on earth? No. No, I tell you, but division. From now on there will be a Five and one family divided against each other, three against two and two against three. They will be divided father against son and son against father. mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against daughter-in-law, and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law. We are assured by these words that the gospel of Jesus causes tension in relationships It can be concluded that if the gospel can cause division in familial relationships, it certainly causes division in non-familial relationships. The pull of the family, the pull that it that it can have on us is so very, very strong. And Jesus recognized this when he said in Luke 14, if anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, Wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, and his own life. He cannot be my disciple. I don't think there is a more dramatic statement made by Jesus regarding the cost of following him But if we are to view our actions and our words objectively, we would see how how too often we favor family over following Jesus. It is very easy to do, requiring Jesus to make such a bold statement. He made it because we need to hear it. Gideon is blessed by the Lord to receive the response he did from his father. His father comes to his defense, and as much as this brought joy to Gideon's heart, We must recognize that such a response was not guaranteed. Gideon, in following the Lord rather than those around him, Had to trust that God would meet him, that God would bless him. Going against the tide or going against the ways of the world, which may mean going against family That takes faith. You have to believe that God is going to bless you on the other side It is intriguing to psychoanalyze Israel at this time, for Gideon's words to the prophet indicate that He and the people as a whole understood themselves to be chosen of God, and yet at the same time they participated in idol worship. How could they justify that in their minds? This way of living and thinking We have seen in Christian history, as people continue in their Christian traditions and practices And yet, for all intents and purposes, they are living and relating to God like those in the world around them. The Christian Church has a similar history to Israel, and that it has a cycle of following the Lord for a time. only to drift back into philosophies and behaviors that are more akin to the world than the kingdom of God. It does not take long to identify how worldviews such as Darwinian evolution, Freudian psychology So-called sexual liberation, moral relativism, and so on have influenced Christian thinking alongside Scripture That these professing Christians do not see blatant contradictions in their thinking is disconcerting and even mind-numbing. It takes a great deal of faith, faith that only can come from God to separate oneself from the world and live as God has instructed. Gideon was given that faith and enabled to step away from his family's idolatry. It is only after he stepped away that he could see the contradiction in which he previously lived. He didn't see it until he stepped away. In our contemporary setting, we can see that it takes a great deal, a great deal of strength and faith and courage for a teenager to step away from his peers and follow the morality of Holy Scripture. He knows that by doing so he could be an outcast and socially persecuted But this he must do in faith, trusting that God is going to meet his social needs on the other side. Going the opposite way of the world takes courage, but it can be done. A parent must courageously instill discipline in her son Rather than place him on drugs as the doctors suggest, believing that God will instill discipline in his heart. A worker must trust that in standing up for honesty against a corrupt boss, that God will provide his daily bread when being fired is a possibility. When it comes to being in the world and not of the world, there is no merge lane. Many times you are going to go against traffic, and the only one going the right way will be you. It is hard to tell at times that we are going the right way. But as Jesus said, his road, the road to eternal life, is narrow, and few travel on it. So when you look to your left and you look to your right and there's nobody there, it's because there's few that travel on it. There are no promises given to us when we go against the world in favor of God that everything to enjoy in this life will be ours. Some preachers say we will prosper in this life while asking for your money, so that they can prosper, but that is the only motivation: your money The primary promise made to us for not being of the world is eternal life after death. As we take our individual and corporate stands against the ways of the world, we have to have faith that God will meet us on the other side. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Thankful for the Struggle
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I received several concerns last week as I was standing on these little podiums that you feared that I was going to fall. Well Ben Weinwright was uh gracious enough to uh loan this to us, so I much safer now. Although our readers and liturgists they're still in very much in peril. We are in Judges chapter 8. I start off by mentioning Ludwig von Beethoven. If you know anything about his biography, he was considered an ornery and bitter man. And perhaps it was because of his deafness that he was socially rude. Whatever the reason, we are told by others that he was difficult to be around. Yet there is a story about him that sheds light upon another side of his personality. When Beethoven heard of the death of a friend's son, he hurried to the house overcome with grief. He had no words of comfort to offer the family, but he saw a piano in the room For the next half hour, he played that piano, pouring out his emotions in the most eloquent way that he could. When he finished playing, he simply left. The friend later remarked that no one else's visit had meant so much. It is remarkable that a person seemingly so bitter Could do such a kind gesture. But Beethoven's inconsistent personality is not unlike our own. Those of us who are considered generally kind have moments of meanness. Those of us who are temperamental can have moments of serenity. I always question statements at funerals that depict the deceased as having never spoken an unkind word. Is that possible? I ask I also have been among family who speak about a deceased relative, wondering if a kind word was ever spoken. Is that possible? I wonder. Like the apostle described to the church at Rome, it is as though there are two persons inside of us, one who wishes to do good, and the other that is easily prone to evil. This is not a personality disorder, nor a Dr. Jekyll, and Mr. Hyde nightmare. It is the reality of being Christian in a fallen world. It is the reality of being saved, but not saved altogether. It is the reality of being justified while still needing to be sanctified. We can be confident in our salvation because of the sacrifice, because of the victory of Christ Jesus And yet we fail to live every moment of every day as a person who has been saved, as a child of God. We read a familiar story at the end of Gideon's life. It is familiar because it mirrors each of us. It is a story of a man of faith who does not behave as a man of faith should. From the sermon last week, we learned that God was controlling the circumstances that would enable Israel to realize that God was responsible. God was responsible for the victory over the Midianites. This was God's concern from the beginning that Israel would take responsibility for this impossible victory. So he made it evident that he was the one responsible by lowering the odds greatly, causing the Midianites to turn on themselves. As the victory became a route, Gideon called for reinforcements to help him chase down the enemy, who of course was fleeing. At that point, Gideon was going beyond what God had instructed. And as we highlighted last week, we no longer read of the Lord speaking to Gideon. The story picks up in chapter 8, after most of the leaders of the Midianite army are captured. Gideon now has to deal with leaders of the tribe of Ephraim who are upset because they were not given credit for the victory they thought they deserved, the credit they thought they deserved. Gideon has to play politics, and as he does, he humbles himself before the complainers. It is a great irony that such a complaint is made immediately after Israel has experienced a great victory and God caused it all to happen. The whole point of the lesson, as we stated last week, is that it was God only that deserved the glory. Regarding Ephraim's complaint, I read an article recently by a pastor who was having trouble in his congregation. He had ordered some books on the subject of church problems, and in reading a few of these books, he realized that they were all the same. That is, the problem in the churches was all the same. This led him to compare the people of God to a stage production in which each person seems to play a role. There are the heroes, the antagonists, the counselors, the do-gooders, the complainers, the villains, and then extras that make up the production. Every church has these characters, no matter the stage. In this play, Ephraim is playing the part of the complainer. Going back to the narrative, we see that Gideon has kept together the original 300 men that God had originally chosen. As he pursues the last remaining leaders of Midian, the officials of Sukoth and Paniel tribes do not treat Gideon with respect. In response, Gideon promises that he will pay for their, they will pay for their disrespecting of him. After successfully defeating a much larger army, once again, Gideon returns to the tribes that had dispersed and disrespected him, and he punishes them. His vengeance was personal, and as the storyteller reveals, it was also heartless. In verse 20, we read of Gideon turning to his eldest son Jether, ordering him to kill the military leaders he had captured. And Jethur's response reminds us of a younger Gideon who was at one time not willing to enter battle and not willing to shed blood. Now, Gideon is a different man and is willing to be judge, jury, and executioner. As a different man, Gideon is a conflicted man. At one moment, he is a reluctant judge, and the next he is in the heat of battle At one moment he is doing as the Lord commanded, and the next he is going beyond what God instructed. At one moment he is making peace, the next he is killing all that are in his way. Because of this inconsistency, one commentator has called Gideon the unbelieving believer. The unbelieving believer We cannot doubt that Gideon was a man of faith. He is described as such in the book of Hebrews, chapter 11. The unbelief within him is expressed in taking credit for that which belongs to God. Gideon essentially takes over for God, making decisions that we can call bloodthirsty. And God had warned him that this would happen. God helped decrease the chance that Gideon would take the glory, and still Gideon thought of himself as the conqueror. There is, of course, a great spiritual lesson in all of this. Consider that we are a success-oriented people in America We glamorize success and we ridicule failure. The more success we have, the easier it is to see ourselves as responsible for it. Gideon was not above the sin of taking credit for what God had done, and neither are we. Success, of course, is not ungodly. The covenant in Deuteronomy promises prosperity for God's faithful people. On the other hand, the negative side of prosperity, as we all know, is very real. Poverty has slain its thousands But prosperity, it's tens of thousands. Jesus said it was harder for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven than a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. He never said that about a poor man. Judges 7 reveals that the Lord anticipated that Israel would lose her faith in the midst of her prosperity. And I remind you of the prayer of Augur from Proverbs chapter 30, who prayed this, Two things I ask of you, O Lord, do not refuse me before I die. Keep falsehood and lies far from me. Give me neither poverty nor riches, but give me only my daily bread. Otherwise, I may have too much and disown you and say, who is the Lord? Or I may become poor and steal and so dishonor the name of my God. This is not a common prayer of today. It is unfortunately not common among Christians, even. It is more likely that we would hear, O Lord, cause me to win the lottery. Or you may remember the popularity of that prayer of Jabez, remember that bad, increase my territory. We want prosperity. We do not imagine that it would be a bad thing, only a good thing. We lay our heads down at night with visions of being able to pay our bills without a pinch. Have time to pursue our pleasures. Enjoy relationships with no tension. Watch our children soar to success, never failure. Surely such prosperity can only be a good thing. But actually the Bible is against such ways of thinking. God knows our fallen nature. He knows how easily we can take for granted whatever blessings come to us. The last thing we would have expected in chapter 6 of Judges, if we had not read ahead, was for Gideon to turn into a confident, overbearing, bloodthirsty tyrant. But that is what success had brought to that once timid Gideon. Strangely enough, there is great encouragement in this story of Gideon's transformation. It is the encouragement from a different angle. Gideon was better off when he struggled than when he was victorious. And that is the encouragement we, you and I, have struggles We would rather not, but we do, and some quite a lot of them. We have increasing disappointments, worries, and frustrations with ourselves, our finances, our relationships. Our health. And we learn by experience in the Word of God that it must be so. Without these struggles, we would forget God. We would begin to live as if we had no debt to Him and no dependency on His mercy and on His grace. I greatly respect those who serve the church by writing books that help people through difficult times. Much time and effort, as well as money, has been spent on answering questions such as, why do bad things happen to good people? But there is really no need for multiple chapters and multiple books. The answer lies in two primary truths. The first is that we live in a fallen world and therefore are subject to consequences of this fallen state. The second answer, and the one that is pertinent to our examination of Gideon, is that we need bad things or struggles so that we continue to acknowledge our utter dependence upon God. Of course, not all of us have the same struggles. God cares for his children individually He knows each of our needs and our individual weaknesses. We might believe someone has it easier than we do. As we struggle to pay our bills, for they don't seem to struggle and drive a nice car. What struggles they might have that we cannot see might be ones that we do not have. The point is that struggles are universal, and they are universal because they are necessary for our spiritual health As you know, states are finding more ways to entice their citizens to hope for big payouts With state and regional lotteries as well as opportunities to gamble, both online and in person. These get rich quick opportunities Should cause deeper conversations amongst Christians. We should know about the morality of gambling. It is popular to excuse playing the lottery or the slots or the racehorses by stating that it's simply entertainment. Whether one plays the lottery or participates in other forms of gambling, out of compulsion or out of entertainment, all of us can't help but have dreams of striking it rich. When we allow ourselves to dream of striking it rich, there is also the reasoning that if we do, the money will solve most, if not all, of our problems. In truth, it merely creates other problems, if not more problems, and the greatest problem is the temptation to think and behave as if we no longer are dependent upon God. God knows our fallen nature. He knows how easily we can take for granted whatever blessings come to us. No doubt you have heard stories like that of Jack Whitaker, who in two thousand two bought a lottery ticket on Christmas Day that won him $314 million. A take-home of $113 million after Uncle Sam His previous vices of drinking too much alcohol and paying spippers only increased. He spoiled his granddaughter with a large monthly income and four cars. The granddaughter's boyfriend soon overdosed on drugs, while the granddaughter herself died of mysterious causes a year later. The granddaughter's mother was found dead seven years after the jackpot was won. Whitaker's wife also divorced him. Whitaker lost the people he loved in his life and the money that he won. Whitaker testified, quote, Since I won the lottery, I think there is no control for greed. I think if you have something, there's always someone else that wants it. I wish I'd torn that ticket up. William Post III pawned some items in his house so that he could buy forty lottery tickets. He ended up winning sixteen point two million dollars from the Pennsylvania lottery. Post spent his money wildly. The majority of the first year installment of his winnings, which totaled $400,000, was spent in the first two weeks. After a year, he was half a million dollars in debt. His girlfriends sued him, claiming that they had agreed that they would share the money that he won. When she won in court, he couldn't pay. So his lottery payout was frozen. He had to declare bankruptcy, and he only managed to hold on to about $2. 6 million, which he immediately spent. He was next arrested for assault for firing a shotgun at a man who was pestering him for money. Even worse, his brother hired a hitman to kill him and his wife so that he would inherit the money He was on wife number six by that time. Thirteen years later, this lottery winner died alone and penniless, living off welfare payments. And each of us is tempted to think that it if it happens to us, we would not make such mistakes. I say it again. God knows our fallen nature. He knows how easily we can take for granted whatever blessings come to us. Take a moment and rehearse the many ways we are dependent upon God rather than earthly wealth. Dependent upon God so that we might receive a heavenly reward. There are several things that are absolutely essential to our spiritual health and perseverance The first is the intercessory prayer of our Savior. He sits at the right hand of the Father and mediates to the Father on our behalf. Would any of us remain faithful to the end of our days without his prayers? And then there are the ministering angels who are responsible to watch over us as God directs. Would any of us complete our heavenly pilgrimage without these ministering spirits hedging the road before us? Included with these essentials is the need for trials and tribulations. When you think that struggles are a part of the devil's plan and that success is always good. Remember Gideon. God warned Gideon of the dangers of a great victory, and still Gideon succumbed to the temptation by taking the battle in a direction that he wanted. rather than having confidence in what God had done for him. Although Gideon achieved great success as a leader, and he did, The nation of Israel enjoyed peace under his leadership for forty years. Yet Gideon's faith Left him in the end as he became an idolater. The success we dream of, and the persons we would become because of the success of Might be difficult to acknowledge. If we could have opportunity to see what type of person we would become if great success would come our way. Many of us would look the other way. We would be horrified to see what success made of us This is one reason why the prosperity preachers are so dangerous, for they present only one side of success. While completely and purposefully ignoring that those closest to Jesus died poor in this life, but wealthy in the next. Therefore, Christians are never to be ashamed of struggles. Remember, Gideon, when the Lord sprinkles your life with struggles Remember that success did him in. And remember the faithful man he was when he struggled. The ability to stray from the Lord and shun his offerings to us is within each of us. The struggles that God brings to our lives work in our favor to prevent that old man, the sinful nature, from winning the day. We struggle in this life to enjoy the success offered in eternal life. Never forget that, so that you remain faithful to the end of your days. Beloved, I end this sermon with a bit of a pitch for next week. I believe it is my essential duty, my calling. To help any who would have me help them to get from this world to the next. That's my job. That is why I preach sermons like this one here. But next week I am interrupting this series on judges, as I will throughout the summer interrupt this series. To answer questions that Christians struggle with. So next week, the first question I will attempt to answer is why does evil exist? I do so because I don't want such questions to shake your faith. I want you to be confident that answers to difficult questions are accessible. So wake your kids, phone your neighbors, and be with us next week as we try to build up our faith. To get from this world to the next. Let us pray. Father, we thank you for the standard The standard is set by Christ, and as we recognize those of faith who fail, like Gideon. We take warning. And we do so knowing that we are completely and utterly dependent upon you. And that is as it should be. We confess it in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Why Does Evil Exist?
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. As promised last week, in interrupting our series in the book of Judges To answer some difficult questions, questions posed by so many, those in the church and those outside the church. And perhaps this one question is the most prominent and yet not so easy to answer. The question is, why does evil exist? This general question has its siblings, such as why do bad things happen to good people? And if God is all good, why does he allow the devil to exist? These and others can be summarized by that question, why does evil exist? What concerns me most about such questions are the hearts of those who ask it. It has been my experience that many people who ask such questions, whether they are within the church or outside the church, They seem to already believe that they have an airtight argument against either the existence of God or they are in a position to condemn God. And they want to deny God's existence or condemn God because they want to live in sin without guilt. And because God is the source of guilt for sinners, they either want God to not exist, or they want to see themselves as morally superior to God. Whatever the reason, such persons use the existence of evil to reject having faith in God. I realize that I cannot reach such people. Their hearts are not open to hearing answers to their questions. And although I cannot know their hearts fully, I can see parts of their hearts by the fact that they do not want to stay around to hear answers to their questions. As I have stated to those involved in our Wednesday Bible study, it is not a virtue to ask tough questions. But it is a virtue to hear tough answers. My preaching this morning is not for those outside the church. I realize that the Holy Spirit can use this sermon to awaken a dead soul, and I hope that such happens. But my focus is on all of you. As I stated last week, my primary role in your life is to help you get from this world to the next. And to help do so, I need to engage along with you against the devil, against your conscience To do battle with your conscience and the devil and his minions when they try to put doubt in your mind by questioning the purpose of evil. That is what I'm trying to do this morning. The question, why does evil exist, falls under the philosophical category labeled by philosophers and theologians as the problem of evil. The category recognizes that God is defined as all good, and yet he allows evil to not only exist. But to cause pain and heartache upon those he created in his own image. The logic goes as follows If God is good, which we say he is, and if he is all-powerful, which by definition he is, then he would naturally prevent evil and only do what is good for his people, the people he created. It is a good argument on the surface. After all, if we were all powerful, we would assure that all good things were done for our children and nothing bad. But we should question whether doing good and not allowing anything painful or hurtful to happen to our children If that is actually good for our children. We wrestled last week with the reality that Struggling and suffering consequences for actions in this life is necessary. Because if struggles and sufferings were not present, we would deny a need for God. However, to simply conclude that evil exists, that is existing in the form of suffering and struggling, just so that we do not forget God. That does not get to the heart of why good why God would allow the evil of us having the ability to forget God. That's still present. And I frame the argument in such a manner because I believe it should be confessed by all, even the greatest of minds. That we cannot know fully in this life why God has chosen to do what he has done in terms of creating us in the manner that he did To placing humanity in the Garden of Eden, to allowing the devil to be present in that garden, taking on the form of a serpent? Because God has been defined as that by which nothing greater can be conceived, or as he describes himself, the I am. With either definition, we must conclude that there are things about God and ways about God that we cannot know, at least in this life. Realize, please, that if we could know all about God, then he would not, by definition, be God. Because by definition God is greater than what the human mind can conceive. And so we accept that we may never know God fully, even when we are with Him for eternity. That being said, there are some things that we can know. Helpful things. As we can be confident that God wants us to know these certain things. And so let us look at what we can know. In brief, we can know that God created Adam and Eve with the ability to make choices. We should not, however, call it free will. Don't use that term, that phrase. Because the word free can simply can imply that all choices are available. And having all choices is not possible. The ability to make choices means that there are at least two things that we can choose from. When I taught philosophy at the university, I would use a random student to demonstrate that free will As in having all choices before you is not a reality. I would ask a chosen student, how many colleges did you get accepted into? And they would usually say something like three. So the choices to go to college were limited to three. Not all. I would then ask why they chose Stevenson. They would usually say because of the financial package and the programs offered, it's what they could afford, it's what they wanted. So actually, because of other circumstances, the student really only had one college to choose. So in reality, when we consider other choices we make in life, it usually comes down to choosing between two things and not an unlimited number of things. So God gave humanity via Adam and Eve the means to make choices. Humanity, in his innocency, chose evil. Knowing the warning that if they did, death would enter the world. So death, because of their choice, entered the world, along with the earth being cursed. And I must pause here to embellish what it means for the earth to be cursed. Weeds and plants poisonous to humans grow because the earth is cursed. Weather patterns causing dangerous flooding, powerful winds, dangerous avalanches, freezing temperatures, droughts, lightning that ignites forest fires. Waves that swallow inhabited shorelines, rivers that wash away villages, are all present because the earth is cursed I believe that one of the most underrated results of the fall of humanity, underestimated in the Western with Western Christians, Is the earth being cursed? And understanding what that means for us. Too many Christians today speak of what is natural. Being more godly than what is unnatural, when the natural is actually cursed and in need of redemption. When Jesus said, if the people did not praise him, that the rocks would cry out. It is because the earth is in need of being born again. Just as we humans are in need of being born again. This is why the Bible describes our final redemption in terms of a new heaven and a new earth. So death entered the world, but God did not leave humanity to ourselves but made a promise that a seed, a son, would be born to a woman and eventually destroy, crush. The devil. He did not need to do so. He was not obligated to do so. But God loved the human species so much that he set in motion his plan to redeem his people. Meanwhile, we still have the ability to make choices Again, it is not a free will. We cannot choose to believe in God or follow Him or obey Him out of the recesses of our own consciences. And that is because we are dead in sin. As all who are born into the covenant of Adam are spiritually dead. But we do have the ability to choose, and many, many times people choose to do evil. Consider all the evil that falls upon human beings, and you will notice That a great deal of evil and suffering that we experience, we do to one another. Even the sickness we experience like a pandemic, some say humanity did it to himself in a laboratory Consider the many wars that we were started by humanity. Even the crusades, which were done in the name of Christ. Were not done because they were commanded by God, although some had godly motive, but rather by men who insisted they were speaking for God. but base their call to arms on political and emotional appeals rather than appeals from the Word of God. Some of you remember the disaster that we know of as Katrina, when so many lives were lost in the city of New Orleans, because of that hurricane And some prominent people at that time spoke out against God for allowing such a catastrophe. Instead of examining humanity and questioning the arrogance of the citizens of Louisiana, For building and living in a city below sea level. Simply question what natural disaster prominently occurs in the Gulf of Mexico? Answer? Hurricanes. And what happens to cities built below sea level when hit by a hurricane? Answer. Flooding And yet arrogant humans denounce the existence of God because of suffering caused by man that could have been and still could be avoided. Another aspect of this question of the existence of evil is to consider what type of relationship we would have with God and with one another. If God saved us from the repercussions of the evil we commit. As we discussed last week. We know ourselves well enough to know that we would continue purposefully to sin because we would not need to be concerned about the consequences. But sin corrupts, and sin ends in death. And God, who loves us, will not allow us to wallow in corruption and death. And so He allows us to suffer consequences. For we need to, in order to give us an opportunity to turn away from that sin and to turn to God. I am aware of an objection lurking within the back of our minds That questions why give us any ability to choose in the first place? Why not make the why not make humanity Robotic, rather than give him the possibility to fall, to choose evil rather than good. The answer cannot be fully known in this life, but we can know that the answer lies in what we call relational. God's ultimate end, you remember, is for him to be our God and for us to be his people And it appears that for us to be relational with God, we must choose to love Him just as He has chosen to love us. Consider the following. We would not know love if evil were not present. Because love is a choice requiring a great deal of vulnerability and humility. Now I need to be careful here because there is most certainly a way to know love without evil being present. We know this because God the Father loves the Son and the Holy Spirit, as does the Spirit love the Son and the Father, as does the Son love the Father and the Spirit. And there is no sin amidst between or within them. And I believe Adam and Eve could have loved, could have chosen love before they chose to sin. But because they chose death, God had to act. What God has done with the presence of evil within his creation is to use it. He uses it to redeem us only from the side of pain and suffering as opposed to the side of perfection. Thus, the ability for humanity to make choices gets to the heart of what it means to love in a fallen world. When we choose to love someone, we choose to suffer for them. We choose to be kind. We choose to be humble. We choose to think no evil of them. We choose to bear all things, to believe all things, to endure all things for someone besides ourselves. And because we choose to love another person, the relationships we have that are based on love go so much deeper into our psyche, into our souls, and matter to us so much more. Than other relationships that are merely cordial when it comes to blaming God for tragedies such as natural disasters, Pandemics, grave illness, and even man-made tragedies such as planes flying into buildings Let us take a moment to consider how many tragedies do not befall upon us. I recall a night when a son, whom shall not be named, had received his driver's license. And his older brothers forced him to run the errand that mom requested. And thus, not wanting to, he was driving in a foul mood. It was winter and so the roads were slick. He decided to take the right turn too quickly between lice, or then food lion, and fairy queen And the family van slid across the road, hit the curb, and slid down into the small ravine on its side. When I was contacted, I quickly went to the scene where I found this particular son standing outside the driver's side of the van as it laid on its side. He was physically fine, but emotionally, understandably shaken. What I noted next was a telephone pole, maybe three feet from the curb area where he had slid into. Meaning that three feet more, he would have smashed himself into a telephone pole instead of sliding down a shallow ravine. Where was God? He was right there. How many natural disasters God has saved people from is not known. How many illnesses God has protected you from, you cannot know in your lifetime. How many accidents have we been spared from can only be imagined. What this point gets back to is the wisdom that Joseph, son of Jacob, the wisdom that he had when he finally confronted his brothers who had sold him into slavery. A slavery that God used to raise him to the second highest position in Egypt. Remember what he said to his brothers. What you meant for evil, God meant for good. Let us have faith and let us give our praise and thanksgiving to God that we have been spared the consequences from the many stupid and thoughtless and careless things that we have done. Instead of noting that God could have prevented evil from entering the world or concluding that he should have done something to stop it, We should instead consider how God uses evil to achieve his redemptive plan. Simply examine the last days of Jesus. And see how God used evil to redeem his people. He used the evil of Jewish plotters to capture and place Jesus on trial. He used Satan's prompting to betray Jesus and the will and character of Judas to carry it through. God used Roman injustice to capture and try an innocent man. He used the cowardice of Pilate to give in to the will of the masses. God used the brutality of the soldiers to make Jesus that suffering servant. Of course, the Jewish leaders, Satan, Judas, Pilate, and the soldiers were all ignorant of the role they played. In fulfilling the divinely prophesied redemptive purpose of the cross of Christ. God is the one responsible. Which leads us to the most helpful passage of Scripture that should be highlighted and memorized by every Christian. It is from Romans 8. 28. And we know that for those who love God, all things work together for good. For those who are called according to his purpose, all things work together for the good. Next is a quote that helped Bobby Lynn and I get through some difficult days. It is as follows. Quote, hope is being convinced that you are surrounded and pursued by the goodness of God. That he works all things for good in the end. So if it is not good, it is not the end. And that there is no story or tragedy or grief where he won't have the last word. So instead of taking a posture of questioning God's existence or his goodness or simply seeing ourselves as more righteous than God, because we would do it all so very differently Let us be humbled that a great deal of evil in this world is by our own doing, and that God uses that evil to redeem us. And to redeem this world until we are perfect and fit for eternity. Amen and Amen. Let us pray. Our Heavenly Father, we thank you for the truths spoken in your Holy Word that lead us to these conclusions. That it is us that needs to repent for evil, and it is you that we need to turn to for the good. May that truth be ever in our hearts. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Sins of the Fathers
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. And again, you are encouraged to open your Bibles to Judges chapter 9. We're not only going to be covering the verses read, but also covering beyond what was read It would appear necessary to identify the characters in this chapter before I speak of the message that we may receive from it. Jerubaal is Gideon. The author uses this name for Gideon to show that Israel had become Canaanized, meaning that they had become like the nations around them, and that means that they were worshiping false idols. He does this by referring to Gideon's Canaanite name, which is Drew Baal, and the meaning of Drew Baal is he who defends Baal. Abimelech, whose name means my father is king, was a son of Gideon, as the text says, and his mother was a Canaanite woman. This meant that Abimelech was half Hebrew. Shechem was a city within the territory of Ephraim. It was the home city of Abimelech's mother. Jotham, we remember from chapter 8, is also a son of Gideon and a faithful Israelite With the characters and primary place of these events identify, we now turn to what is unique about this story The story so far has been about judges or men and one woman chosen by God to deliver Israel from an oppressive enemy and bringing peace to the land for a certain amount of years. Abimelech, however, is not a judge. There is no oppressor. He delivers God's people from no one, and he most certainly does not bring peace. This would lead us to wonder why the author would tell us about Abimelech and use so much detail in telling this story. I said a few weeks ago that the story of Gideon covers all of three chapters, the longest story in Judges. Actually, we can count chapter 9 as the fourth chapter in Gideon's story. What we have read so far this morning is just a portion, as I said, of a very long chapter. And yet it covers, conveys, excuse me, to us the character of Abimelech and explains directly, without specifics. That Abimelech is a product, a product of his Canaanized father, Gideon. Since we did not spend time this morning reading the rest of the chapter, I would like to summarize the story at this point. By his actions, it is obvious that Abimelech made a plan to become king. He gained the support of his mother's hometown by deception. When he gained a following of immoral men, he used them to kill his seventy brothers for the simple reason that they would not be able to claim the throne that he wanted to claim. The only brother to escape was Jotham. When people of Shechem were ready to crown Abimelech king. Jotham appeared and told a fable to the people to communicate what they had done and are doing by crowning Abimelech. And in case you missed it, Abimelech is the thorny bush that is preferred over the other great trees. And he is arrogant enough to think that he, as a thorny bush, can provide shade for great trees, which of course is absurd. Jotham finishes with a prophecy regarding the future sufferings of Shechem's citizens caused by the choice they made on that day. Soon after Abimelech is made king, God turns the hearts of the people away from Abimelech as their leader. Plots soon spring up amongst the people of Shechem to go against Abimelech. Abimelech, of course, is not going to give up without a fight, so he organizes his men for battle. Initially, Abimelech is successful in turning back the uprising. He does not, however, stop, but pursues the rebels. The king who was supposed to care for these people has now entrapped them. He quickly surrounds the tower that the people were hiding in with branches and sets them on fire, causing the people from within, men, women, and children, to die. Later Abimelech chased another group of people down. After trapping them in another tower, a wise woman took a stone from above the tower and dropped it on Abimelech's head. The blow proved to be a fatal one, but with the pride of Abimelech, knowing he was going to die, He ordered his armor-bearer to kill him with a sword, so that others would not know that he was killed by a woman. So ends the reign and life of Abimelech, son of Gideon. The story of Abimelech unfortunately requires us to recall the sins of Gideon. When the Lord warns in the second commandment that those who worship false idols will have judgment passed down upon them, and not only them. Upon their children, even up to a fourth generation. When God said this, He did not make an idle threat upon intended. Gideon gave into idol worship at the beginning and the end of his life. It was told to us in chapter 8 that idol worship was a snare to him and to his family. When we read of Abimelech's life, we understand him to be an arrogant man who does not fear the Lord. There is no doubt that the author wishes for us to see the results of Gideon's sin by describing to us the fate of Gideon's sons. and the behavior of the one who wanted to be king. What Gideon likely did not anticipate, or at least underestimated, was how quickly the judgment of the Lord would come upon his family. The judgment upon Gideon's family came swiftly as one son killed seventy of his brothers by dashing them, it says, upon a rock. The judgment of Abimelech comes more slowly, but the outcome is the same. The effects of Gideon's sin is evident in the life of Abimelech. For his level of depravity goes beyond that of his father. Gideon refused kingship, but it was offered to him, but then he goes and names a son, my father is king. That same son then forced himself to be king. Gideon put to death men who he felt did not respect him, while his son Abimelech put to death men, women, and children. Gideon asked for his son to be put to death, I'm sorry, for his son to put to death leaders of armies that they had defeated. Abimelech forced a young man to kill him to save his own pride. The sins of the Father are here visited upon the Son and expressed in greater horror. It is the horror of every God-fearing parent and the ignorance of every godless parent to understand that sins are passed on to the next generation. Angry husbands often had angry fathers. Silent men had silent fathers and alike. Controlling mothers often imitate their own mothers. Parents who abuse are often products of abuse, and they have children who end up abusing. Generational sin is even more profound than that, for in very mysterious ways The sins of the fathers are visited upon their children, ways we don't readily identify. In many cases, sins are not expressed in the same way, but they are still the same sin. The sin of pride may be dominant in a parent's life and manifested by showing off wealth. A child from the same parents might manifest the same pride in the pursuit of a career over family, pursuit of athletics for the glory, etc. The sin of a loose tongue might be expressed in the form of gossip by a mother and in the form of backbiting and malicious lying in her daughter. These obviously are just a few of many examples of sin being handed down from one generation to the next. Besides the examples of how sin of one generation is passed down to the next, we also have in this story an example of divine retribution. Verse 5 tells us that Abimelech killed his seventy brothers by throwing them upon one rock. How this was done is not clear. It is up to our imaginations. Likely they were thrown from a height that place them upon a rock below. The mention of such a rock is necessary in order to point out God's retribution when Abimelech is killed. As the adage has it, he who lives by the sword dies by the sword, or he who lives by the rock dies by the rock. In a Dante-esque manner, Abimelech dies also by a rock, only in his case, a woman tosses it. It is a great irony that Abimelech would try to cover up For all not to see that he was killed by a woman, when all who have read this story since know that not only was he killed by a woman, but he tried to cover it up The typology in the story might be highlighted for Jesus is referred to in the New Testament as the rock. He is the chief cornerstone. He is the foundation stone. He is the spiritual rock from which the Israelites drank. He is the rock of offense. Those who are crushed in the head by a rock, such as Abimelech and Goliath, are types of the devil who was promised by God to have the devil's head crushed by the seed. A chosen son who is Christ the Lord. Such a victory over Abimelech is a precursor to Jesus' victory over the devil. And finally, where our focus will aim this morning is upon the consequences of following an ungodly man. In verses 24 and verses 56 and 57, we have repeated reasons as to why God turned the people of Shechem away from Abimelech. Look at verse 24. It reads, God did this in order that the crimes, the crime against Jerubaal's 70 sons. the shedding of their blood might be avenged on their brother Abimelech and on the citizens of Shechem. I assume it is agreeable to each of us that Abimelech was judged so harshly because of what he had done. His demise seems fair or in line with our sense of justice. He got what he deserved. You will notice also that the judgment being handed down by God is not just upon Abimelech, but upon the people of Shechem who made him king. In verse 57, the writer says, God also made the men of Shechem pay for all their wickedness. Their wickedness. But what wickedness had they done? It is understood that their wickedness was making Abimelech their king and turning a blind eye to his murderous ways. In doing so, they were taking part in Abimelech's sin. They had become responsible, as he was, for the death of those 70 sons of Gideon. The scenario here is very much like that of Adolf Hitler and the citizens of Germany in the 1930s and 40s. We can only speculate as to why so many supposedly God-fearing people chose to follow a leader like Adolf Hitler. We know that the country of Germany was in dire straits financially. It was also politically divided, making it easier for a man like Hitler to rise through the ranks of a small political party Evidently his speeches and confidence gave pride to the citizens of Germany who were embarrassed, you will remember, after World War I and the subsequent reparations required of them. They were also weak leaders governing the country. At the time, they could be bullied by someone like Hitler. You combine those factors with godless philosophies being taught in the schools and embraced by the elite in the country, and we can understand why they would be so susceptible to choosing such a leader When Hitler got into a position of power and began to implement his sense of justice, the citizens turned a blind eye to his many atrocities. But can we understand why they did it? Why they turned a blind eye? Was it because they believed if they spoke out that they would suffer as others were suffering? Were their own lives more important than the lives of those who were being murdered and treated as experiments? Was it because the people of Germany actually agree deep down in their consciences with what Hitler was doing to millions of Jews and thousands of professing Christians? Regardless of the reason why the citizens of Germany followed Hitler We learn from the Lord's judgment upon Shechem that in following an ungodly man, the people are culpable for the sins of the man they follow. The pandemic we have been experiencing has revealed a great deal about ourselves. And one of those revelations is how and why, the how and why of who we choose to follow in response to a pandemic. Some follow news anchors. Some follow celebrity positions. Some follow politicians. Few, very few, follow the church, the Bride of Christ, the Redeemer. Why is that? I cringe when considering the likely answer or answers. Jesus said that his church will be the judge of nations. And yet we do not look to the church even for a hint of wisdom during a crisis. Some of us tried to lead, lead by telling Christians not to panic, but to have faith in Jesus, remembering that fear is the opposite of faith. Some of us tried to lead by reminding Christians that to die is gain, to live is Christ, and that as we follow Christ we are already dead, dead to ourselves and most certainly dead to the fear of death. And now we are, according to our state politicians, out of a state of emergency. And that means, according to them, that things can return to what they were prior to the pandemic. I try to avoid the term normal. And in the meantime, the church calls and has been calling its people to come and worship the Lord, to be in his presence, which is amongst his people. So that some will no longer forsake the gathering together of the saints. And still the voice of the church is ignored. Those who are ordained to cry out so that the voice of the Lord can be heard can only do so much. For it is the people of God that need to respond to the voice of the Lord and allow the church to have authority in your life once again. There is culpability both ways, meaning that the church leaders are culpable for what they speak, and the individual church member is culpable for how he or she responds. This culpability is also in smaller settings, such as a county that allows its judges to be bribed and certain citizens to be discriminated against. This culpability is in the church where a minister preaches and practices immorality. If a congregation hears a man speak against what the Bible clearly teaches Rejecting the Bible's authority, it is the responsibility of every man and woman to speak against such blasphemy. If they do not, they are culpable as much as the minister for the sins that follow. This culpability is also in the home. A woman should never turn a blind eye to physical abuse, whether it be toward her or her children. A husband should never ignore a sign of his wife or children abusing alcohol or drugs. When we fail to address such sins as they should be addressed, which is by exposing them, we become part of the problem and thus accountable to God for those same sins. Choosing someone to follow is not an easy decision. Every leader has his flaws. The Apostle Paul said to the Corinthians, be followers of me as I follow Christ. The key to that verse is, as I follow Christ. We are to follow men who follow Christ. When they stop following Christ, we are to stop following them. Perhaps from what we have uncovered this morning, you have concluded that we are all in it for the worst. After all, if my sins are going to be passed down to my children, then I can only pity my children. If I will be judged by a standard proportionate to my sin, then I may as well end my life now. And if I am culpable for the sins of the men I follow, I have no plea. But God anticipated our dilemma. For when the prophet Jeremiah described the covenant of the Messiah, he said this. He said, in those days, days of the Messiah. It will no longer be said the father has eaten sour grapes and his the teeth of his children are set on edge. Instead, each will die for his own iniquity. If anyone eats the sour grapes, his own teeth will be set on edge. It's not said very positively, but it's actually good news. The good news is that we do not have to be trapped by the sins of our parents. But there is a requirement. We must place our faith solely in the Lord Jesus. Not in a celebrity doctor, not in a politician, not a scientist, but solely in the Lord Jesus. The glory of the new covenant is that because of the sacrifice of Jesus Christ, our sins can be forgiven both by God and by one another when we confess them. enabling my children to be free of my sinful burdens. Because Jesus took on the proportionate judgment of my sins, I do not have to bear them myself. And finally, because I have the courage to follow only men who follow Christ, I can be confident that I will speak up when necessary. And know when a man has stepped off, has stepped off the only road that leads to eternal life. And when he steps off, I no longer follow. Beloved, Gideon's sin of idolatry carried the story of his family to a bitter end. It does not have to be so for any of us. Because we do not know when our end will be, it is best that our trust is placed completely in the Lord Jesus Christ. It is in him only that bitter can be turned can be turned sweet and death into life. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God, the great tragedy of Gideon and his family is here written for us.
