To not follow the example. But to see what hope there can be in having our sins forgiven and having our children released from our sins. For we confess this day, as you will us to do, that it is only in the Lord Jesus Christ. May that be said and confessed by all of us And our children, and our children's children, until you come again. It is in Jesus' name that we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Why Anglicanism?
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I begin with comments from our first reading, First Corinthians chapter three. I have thought in the past that the Apostle Paul got away with a great deal that I myself have not nor could not get away with. An example of what I am describing is from 1 Corinthians chapter 3, where he describes the Christians at that church. as babies in the faith, of whom he had to feed milk only, because they were not mature enough for solid food. But I now realize that Paul actually didn't get away with anything, and that I actually have had it much easier The Christians at Corinth were highly critical of Paul, and one reason was for this character That they believed had that they believed Paul had given them that there's a character of being immature. But that is not our focus this morning. Paul explains further that they are not ready for solid food because he says they are carnal. The word carnal means flesh. Therefore, Paul is saying that the Christians who are part of the church at Corinth live their faith by being ruled by their flesh. Evidence for living by their flesh is that there are behaviors that reveal envy, strife, and divisions between people in the church. Evidence to that is that one group says they are of Paul, and another that says they are of Apollos. Evidently, to say you are of someone is to say that I follow that person and in doing so I have a particular identity that is separate from my identity with anyone else even though we all are to be one in Christ Jesus. Paul next reveals why saying you are of someone is a gross misunderstanding of what it means to be Christian. It is because the men that are being divided over are only ministers used by God, so that the people of Corinth would believe on the Lord Jesus Christ. A minister is simply a person who does the bidding of someone higher. Paul next uses the metaphor of growing a plant. Paul is the planter, because he first told the Corinthians about the gospel of Jesus Christ Apollos watered by following up while teaching in greater depth what it meant to be Christian. And while the two ministers were serving these people, God was working within them, within their hearts, their souls, their minds, establishing their identity as His people. Next, Paul uses the metaphor of a building where different people contribute to raising the building. But make no mistake, with each building God makes, and buildings that represent converted persons, Jesus is the cornerstone of each and every person, of you and me. The focus then is to be on the unity, what unites Christians in Corinth, not upon what is different about them. I use these passages to answer a question. As I stated a few weeks ago, I'm using the summer months. By interrupting our series on the book of Judges to interject some questions that I anticipate need to be answered. The question I am answering today is why Anglicanism? Or why be an Anglican? There can be unfortunate but real parallels between the scenario Paul was addressing within the Corinthian church and what we know today as denominationalism. Before I address the issue of denominationalism, I need to tell you what this sermon is not about. I do so because the subject can be so broad as to be daunting, both in scope and in the time needed to address it. This is not a sermon that looks at Anglicanism as opposed to Roman Catholicism or Eastern Orthodoxy. The history and issues with those wings of Christ Church are too grand to be helpful to us today. I am also not looking at Anglicanism as opposed to the mainline denominations who have denied the authority of Holy Scripture and have instead aligned themselves with progressive and liberal theologies. I, for the most part, do not see us as having the same gospel as them, therefore it would be a fruitless examination. Instead, what I am addressing in this sermon is the why of Anglicanism versus Presbyterian groups like the PCA or the OPC. Lutheran churches like Missouri City, Baptist churches like those that are part of the Southern Baptist Convention or independent churches who usually have Baptist-like doctrine but want to be labeled as a community church. And finally, some Methodists, some Methodists, Who have hung on to most of the gospel message. So I'm asking the question: why Anglicanism as opposed to any of the others that I have just mentioned? And let's get into some full disclosure. I am aware that there are faithful people among us. who do not identify as Anglican in your Christian expression, and that you are here worshiping and serving at St. Stephen's for a variety of reasons that are not essentially connected to being Anglican. I'm also aware that there are some here, or some who are listening to this sermon. Who dislike identifiers or labels that convey a distinctive look or perspective of Christianity that would separate you from other looks or perspectives In other words, you just want to be Christian. The spirit behind that desire is true and it is noble It is part of what St. Paul was teaching the Corinthians. The reality behind that desire is that you and I have to make decisions Decisions like baptizing babies, or no. You need to decide about communion, such as how frequent What type of bread? How is it to be received? What type of wine? How is it to be received? And what about your statements of faith? Where do they come from? And what about your government structure? Bishops or no? Women priests or no? And there are many more decisions to make, and once you have made them, you then can see who you line up with, what denominations you are most like that already exist That are following the same look as you just chose. Hence we are all something Some identify identity, we are all some identity or label that falls under a more general category of being Christian. We may not like it, we might not like the labels, but they cannot be avoided in this life. But again, the spirit behind wanting to be just Christian or being a mere Christian, as C. S. Lewis put it, is still true, it's still noble. Therefore, regardless of the decisions we make regarding the many issues before us to organize a church They are not to pit us against one another, and we are most certainly not to look down upon one another when we cho choose differently. I have been guilty of doing so in the past, and I announce publicly that I am committed to not do so in the future. I will still agree with my decisions, but I am in no position to think less of those who make different ones. We truly are all one in Christ, even when we don't admit it. So we now get to the meat of the answer to the question, why Anglican? First, Anglicanism provides a connection with the historic church while living in the present age. This is related to the point made by G. K. Chesterton when he said the following, quote, Traditions mean giving a vote to the most obscure of all classes, our ancestors. It is the democracy of the dead. He went on to say, quote, tradition refuses to submit to the small and arrogant oligarchy of those who merely happen to be walking about. All Democrats object to men being disqualified by the accident of their birth. Tradition objects to their being disqualified by the accident of their death. Democracy tells us not to neglect a good man's opinion, even if he is our groom. Tradition asks us not to neglect a good man's opinion, even if he is our father. The informal fallacy of chronological snobbery is ever present today And is especially practiced by those who are young, who have concluded that all that is older is asleep. But Anglicanism answers that the church triumphant is a living body of believers who are waiting for Jesus to return. So that they can receive their eternal forms and live forever in the presence of God, both in body and in spirit, just as the Heavenly Father desires and has planned. Anglicanism orders its worship services according to the scriptures that describe 24 elders around the throne, 12 from the old 12 from the New, singing praises of holy, holy, holy. A chorus that continues when we worship and when we start our worship services We join into a service that has already started and never ends. Within the ideal of tradition Anglicanism orders its worship services according to what has been handed down to us, both in structure and in content. When Bishop Cramner wrote out the daily services of morning and evening prayer, he borrowed from what early Christians practiced. And from the principles established in the morning and evening sacrifices offered to God in the Old Testament. In other words, traditions. When he wrote out the main worship service of Holy Communion, he based it off of the practices of Christians who were first generation followers of the apostles. One of his principles followed the axiom, what is closest to the source of water is the purest. Hence, what is closest to the practice and teachings of the apostles is the purest form of worship He used sources such as the Apostolic Constitutions, which were collections of writings from the Apostles and their followers Writings that describe liturgies used in Christian worship, even the very words used by the priest in presiding over Holy Communion. The vestments that are worn by bishops, priests, and deacons today are all influenced by the priests of the Old Testament and priests of the early church. What we wear today is not comfortable. It may be aesthetically appealing to some, not to me. I sweat a great deal in these garments, which is ironic because they became more commonly used in places like England, where priests liked to wear them because they kept them warm. But priests are not to wear vestments because of what is liked or not liked. The vestments instead are to point to that which is greater than self, who is Christ Jesus. For the white symbolizes his perfection, and the colors are to symbolize the church seasons, and the church seasons are to point to the works of Christ, the works for the salvation of his people. It is to be all about Jesus. This is in contrast to those who wear jeans Sit in schools, excuse me, sit in stools to preach, who refer to their elevated platform as a stage? And all of it to cause attention to self. And that is not a criticism, it's a mere description. I conceive that such an approach can help bring unbelievers to Jesus, but I am not convinced that the same can sanctify disciples. I believe Anglicanism can and does sanctify disciples by reliving the traditions of the historic church. A second reason for why Anglicanism is that it provides a solid answer to the most prevalent heresy of our time, which is Gnosticism. I remind you that Gnosticism is derived from the Greek word gnosis, which means knowledge. It was a disorganized heresy in the early church that seems to rise up again, at least every other generation. Today, it is a term that covers a great deal of definitions, so we will focus on one particular definition, which is the belief that the spiritual world is good while the physical world is evil. This belief resulted in a bifurcated approach to the physical world, where many Gnostic teachers taught that the physical world and any pleasure derived from that world is to be avoided. But not because a belief in right or wrong, but a belief that to enjoy the physical world was to give power to what was called a demi-urge or a lesser God. There was, however, another approach to Gnosticism that viewed the physical world as of no consequence. Resulting in its teachers and followers enjoying all the pleasures of the flesh because the flesh was useless and powerless. What both camps within Gnosticism believed was that only the spiritual world mattered. Of course, as I have argued from this pulpit several times before, to care only for the spiritual world is to deny the importance of Jesus becoming flesh and dwelling among us. It is to deny that the resurrection of the flesh mattered. It is, beloved Foundational to the Christian faith, that both the physical and the spiritual are to be believed as of the same importance. But again, modern-day Christians struggle to believe in the importance of the flesh. They say it doesn't matter how you dress for worship They say it doesn't matter what postures you take while you worship. They say that the aesthetics of a building inside and out are of no value. They say the need for weekly communion is not there. It's not necessary. And what is at the root of all such conclusions? What do they say matters more? They say it is the spirit that matters more. They say what is most important is how a person feels, which is an aspect of the human spirit. Anglicanism in comparison says that the physical world matters. And so we arrange our sanctuaries in a cruciform manner to point to the gospel. Crosses are boldly displayed. Communion tables are central We have symbols on all of our walls and windows to point to different aspects of our salvation and how it was won and how we are to live it out. We take postures that are to lead our hearts, as for St. Paul said to the Corinthians, first the flesh, then the Spirit. For the Spirit follows the postures of the flesh. I could go on, for the physical is before you each and every Sunday, giving us an opportunity to hope for a new heaven and a new earth. Which is to hope for victory in the spirit and victory in the physical world. Finally, my last answer for this sermon as to why Anglicanism Is how our form of government and our form of worship provide the opportunity to form a level of reverence That is so deep desperately needed today and is definitely owed to God. A few weeks ago within our Wednesday Bible study Where we are answering objections to God, we discussed the various ways God motivates his people. We noted that the two most frequent motivations in Scripture are God's love and a fear of God. The Hebrew and Greek words for fear range from great reverence to great terror. A positive of fearing God is it can immediately dissuade us from doing what is wrong or from continuing to do what is wrong Fear of God can also humble us, which is an internal state of being that God requires of us. Fear also gives us a desire to warn others about God's wrath unless they repent. But the majority of Christians today are not motivated by a fear of God. And that is because the church and its prophets, its preachers, do not preach today for people to fear God. It doesn't sell. What was revealed this past year is that too many people fear viruses. Fear politicians, fear bad media, more than they fear God. Fearing God is not something that comes naturally, but is instead something that is learned. And we can learn by respecting the authority of the church. And the governing authority of the church. Bishops truly are men ordained by God for specific tasks that only they can perform. When we respect them, we have greater reverence/slash fear for God. Hearing God's law and of his punishments for breaking those laws is also needed. And it is something we Anglicans do when we recite the Ten Commandments and then pledge to keep them. And to learn a proper fear of God, we need to hear how God punishes his people when they sin. just as we have been doing when we have studied the book of Judges. Another way to to grow our fear of God, having nothing to do with Anglicanism is to look at the world and its results. What not fearing the Lord brings is chaos culturally and morally. And cultural and moral chaos brings great pain and suffering. And so I have answered the question: why Anglicanism I did not say it was entirely better. I did not say that what we practice is altogether better. I simply said that it is better in certain areas of our Christian expression. When Paul addressed the divisions in Corinth, he was witnessing men giving praise, praise to men, that was to go to God alone. No one should give praise to what is Anglican or Presbyterian or Baptist or name your church here. Anglicanism is a branch of Christ Church that provides things some other branches of Christ's Church do not. That is why. Let us pray. Father, we thank you for the traditions. We thank you for the challenge to Gnosticism. We thank you, Heavenly Father, that you grant us a fear that is most desperately needed. Continue to bless us in our attempt to honor you and all that we do. And may we always love other branches of Christ's Church. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Jephthah Saved by Grace
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. It is inevitable that each of us will say something stupid in our lifetime. Many things, many times. Saying something stupid could mean that we spoke out of turn. Said something offensive, or simply gave information that we should not have. Also, we say things that are stupid, meaning dumb. Someone sent me a while back a list of quotes from famous people that are stupid, as in dumb. These quotes are collected to make us feel smarter, at least smarter than those who made the quotes. Miss Alabama, 1994. This USA contest, she was asked, if you can live forever, would you and why? She answered. I would not live forever, because we should not live forever, because if we were supposed to live forever, then we look would live forever, but we can't not cannot live forever, which is why I would not live forever. In an interview, singer Mariah Carey offered this observation. Whenever I watch TV, I see those poor, starving kids all over the world. I can't help but cry. I mean I'd love to be skinny like that, but not with all those flies and death and stuff. Former mayor of city of the city of New York, David Dinkins, answered accusations by saying, I haven't committed a crime. What I did was fail to comply with the law. Actress model Brooke Shields said against smoking Smoking kills. If you are killed, you've lost a very important part of your life. Good old Arnold Schwarzenegger He was asked some years back if he supported gay marriage. He said, No. I'm I'm I'm not gonna do an impression of oh suppose. No, I think gay marriage is something that should be between a man and a woman. And finally, the former notorious mayor of Washington, D. C. , Marion Barry advertised our nation's capital by saying, outside of the killings, Washington has one of the lowest crime rates in the country The narrative read today from Judges tells us a very stupid statement was made by Jephthah. He made a vow to God that whatever the first thing was that came out to greet him after his victory over the Ammonites, he would sacrifice unto God. It might be fair to speculate that Jeff anticipated a loyal dog or some form of livestock would be the first to greet him when he arrived home victorious. Alas, it was not livestock, but a human being, and not just any human being, it was Jeffka's daughter His only daughter, his only child, as the narrator wants to be sure we understand. Jefftah is a complicated, complicated biblical character. His pedigree is impure. He was the son of a prostitute. His person was not well liked, and this was evident by those in his hometown asking him to leave only to call him back because when the Amra Amara Ammonites became too oppressive, they needed his leadership. Apparently the only thing that was redeeming about this man was his skill as a warrior. When asked to lead Israel in battle, Jephthah looks out for his own interest because he wants to secure a position as a leader once the battle is done. Jephthah, however, eventually reveals a noble side of his character when he attempts to negotiate with the Ammonites. His desire is for peace, and any God-fearing man should desire peace. We are given more information about the claim to the land in question from the book of Joshua. We are told there that the land once belonged to the Ammonites, but they had it taken from them by the Amorites When Israel crossed the Jordan to enter the promised land under Joshua, it was from the Amorites that the land was taken. Jephthah's account of how the land was transferred to Israel is well stated to his credit. Jephthah knows the history of God's redemptive work, and he's working to save the nation of Israel and to keep that redemptive work going. Good for him. This arguing over the land reminds me of another stupid statement, one made by the now deceased actor John Wayne. Wait a minute, going after John Wayne? That's not very American, but he did say this. About the American Indians. I don't feel, he said, we did wrong by taking this great country away from them. There were a great number of people who needed new land and the Indians were selfishly trying to keep it for themselves That's one way to look at it, I guess. When the king of Ammon pays no attention to Jephthah's argument, the Lord responds by sending his Holy Spirit upon Jephthah God is stepping into the matter at this point, choosing to bless Jephthah with heavenly authority. As verse 32 states, the Lord gave the Ammonites into Jephthah's hands. God is again responsible for the victory of Israel. It was between that point of God anointing Jephthah and Jephthah defeating the Ammonites that he made his stupid vow. Now I will take a short time to comment on the particulars of Jephthah's fulfilling his vow It is the view of some that Jephthah is acting virtuously by fulfilling his stupid vow. It is my view that he is acting stupidly by fulfilling his stupid vow. His vow was similar to those pagans around him who asked special favors of their false dogs while promising to sacrifice their own children. The law of God gives people like Jephthah an out by allowing certain vows, such as those stated in Leviticus 27, to be annulled. Certainly a vow that is sinful falls under the annulment category. Just as response to his daughter greeting him has him falling back to his selfish ways. He appears to place blame upon her by stating, oh daughter, you have made me miserable The narrator allows her to be seen as more virtuous than he by accepting the vow made The time allowed for her mourning is to emphasize that because she is not married and without child, by sentencing her to death, Jephthah is sentencing himself. For he will have no offspring to inherit his name or his newfound position of authority. Now it has been speculated by modern evangelical commentators that the vow fulfilled was not Jeff's daughter being sacrificed. but her remain rema remaining a virgin and in secl seclusion for the rest of her life. Such an understanding has merit in that the writer does not tell the reader when or how the sacrifice was made. And the end of Jesse's family line would be the same. For others, such a reading is a G-rating of the story, and it does not match up with a natural reading of the text. It is possible that she was sacrificed, only the narrator does not wish to recount the details of her final breath. Like Gideon before him, Jephthah leaves us in a state of quandary. He will remember that we called Gideon an unbelieving believer. Jephthah is the same. We know this because once again his name is written in the book of Hebrews, chapter 11, as a man of faith. He is mentioned with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses. Jesta was a believer. A Christian, if you will. He was a man of faith, a faith in the redemptive plan of God, by also being a man who did not always behave consistent with what he said he believed. So how we question are we to understand such faith? We say the scriptures teach that you are either in the kingdom of God or you are not You are either a believer or you are not. There is no third option. If you are a believer, then you behave, you make decisions, you act like a believer. Jeff did not always make decisions or not always act like a believer. The scriptures tell us That for those who come to Christ Jesus, repenting of their sins and believing on Him, old things pass away. All things become new. Being born again means to us that we are new persons. As new persons, we should make decisions and act like children of God rather than children of the flesh. But alas, we find ourselves and we see others reverting back to old sinful ways. We don't like things so confusing. We prefer a cut and dry world. If a person behaves a certain way or makes a particular decision, it tells us whether or not he or she is truly a Christian. He stupidly kept his stupid vow, and therefore he is not a Christian. Yet the Bible tells us otherwise. This makes us uneasy, but that does not make this untrue. There are Identifiable reasons why Christians make stupid decisions and behave in an unrighteous manner. First, we can say that the times in which we live has something to do with the quality of a man's spiritual life. We wish this were not true, but we know that it is. We usually highlight those who are brave and faithful enough to rise above their times. Which shows that we recognize certain times as more difficult than others. Such people that rise above the times are special and highlighted because they are so uncommon. Jephthah lived in an idolatrous age amongst idolatrous people. He was foolish, selfish, and influenced by pagans just like the rest of Israel around him. Personal experience confirms the point that we are affected by the times in which we live. We can look at the many sins that men fall prey to today that they would not have decades previous. A generation ago, a man would have to go into a CD theater to see pornographic movies The fact that such behavior would be public kept the man away from such a sin Today, he can either sit as at his computer or stream it on his television Easier, more private access gives greater opportunity to sin in many ways. Divorce is another example. At the most, two generations previous to our own, divorce was rare and shameful Now it is common and in some cases said to be virtuous. A man years previous would stay in a loveless marriage because of duty toward his wife and children and fear of God. Now he finds it easier to be concerned for his own happiness because sages of modern society tell him that his happiness in this life is the most important thing. Again, the point being that we are products of our time. A second reason Christians make stupid decisions is that some believers have a harder time living out their faith than others. There is more to this point than I can unfold this morning. It is sufficient to point out that faith is a gift of God. Some have more than others Wisdom comes from God. Some apply it more than others. Each situation and circumstance combined with ability and maturity is different for every individual. We don't respond to situations the same as another person would. We probably don't respond to situations the same as we did compared to the other day. I have retorted to those who have said to me that they don't always agree with me by saying, uh, well, I don't always agree with myself either. It is admittedly difficult to watch those who have a harder time living out their faith. I have been a minister long enough to be able to know when a family or individual is going about life the wrong way. There are subtle signs that give me concern, although there is no obvious sin. The signs are just there. I see couples not seeking counsel. I know of parents that don't want help. I have heard single people speak to that which they do not know. It is like watching a car go into a ditch, sometimes off a cliff, with no ability to stop the outcome. But noting the stupid decisions people make does not make me a more sincere Christian. It is quite possible that the blinders I notice in someone's life are simply different than the blinders in my own that everyone else notices. The third reason why Christians make stupid decisions and behave in an unrighteous manner is because we are in a battle between the flesh and the spirit. All Christians are in this battle St. Paul explained to the Galatians, for the flesh, lust against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, and these are contrary to one another, so that you do not do the things you wish to do. Such a battle reveals that we are saved, but not entirely. It is what theologians call the already, but not yet. Saved, yes! But not yet. But not yet means that there is some saving, some sanctifying yet to be done. Our flesh must eventually go to the grave. We are to be raised, body and spirit, only when the final trumpet blows. It is only then that death will be fully vanquished Until then, the flesh will influence our behavior, our decision-making, our actions. And we will reap the fruit of the influence of the flesh. In truth, some Christians simply fight more valiantly against the flesh than others. This does not mean that the ones who fight harder are the true Christians, and those who do not are the false Christians. We don't know. We cannot know. But we do know, because God tells us, is that those who fight harder will win more battles in this life. Those who apply more faith and use the wisdom of God will find greater peace in this life. Those who do not do these things will struggle with great intensity and suffer more setbacks. Greater struggles and setbacks do not determine one's place in the kingdom of God. They simply confirm the principle that a man will get his come up and Christians and non-Christians are subject to the law that we will reap what we sow. Christians will make stupid decisions, some really bad decisions, like Jephthah. And they will have to suffer the consequences for those decisions. As a pastor, where I have the greatest burden is when parents make decisions that endanger their children. This is where modern people can be no better than jepta when they offer their children up to the state or offer them to false teachers who worship earthly idols. In the end, and by end I mean the actual end of time itself, when all creation stands before the judgment seat of God. There will be those who enter his kingdom who spent the rest of their days on this earth in a jail cell, in poverty, in shame, in isolation, because of the sins they committed on this earth. These will be entering side by side with those who lived sober, responsible lives, having been good citizens of their country and faithful to their families. Side by side We understand from this that all of us are saved by grace through faith. That sentence Rolls very easy off the preacher's tongue, and we hear it so often that the depth of it can be obscured Christians are saved from the punishment of hellfire by the grace of God through faith in Jesus Christ This is true even if we go through life doing stupid things and saying stupid things and suffering all the consequences we deserve. We are sinners saved by grace. Yes, some are more stupid than others. Some have longer wrap sheets than others We could spend our time comparing lists and making ourselves feel better about the sin that we have. We could quote more celebrities celebrities saying stupid things and feel better about our intelligence compared to theirs. We could examine the jeptas around us and conclude that they are all fools But this does us no good. We too are fools. Fools saved by the grace of God. The following lyrics are from a song by Zach Williams, who sang this song live in Nashville's Harding Prison. I thought it fit well here before we come to the communion table. I hope you can envision this song being sung, two prisoners, in jail. And them singing along. There's a chair that awaits for you, and a friend who understands everything you're going through But you keep standing at a distance in the shadow of your shame. There's a light of hope that's shining where you come and take your place and bring it all to the table. There's nothing he ain't seen before. For all your sin, all your sorrow, and your sadness, there's a Savior, and he calls. Bring it all to the table. He can see the weight you carry, the fears that you hold at your heart. But through the cross, you've been forgiven. You're accepted as you are So bring it all to the table. There's nothing he ain't seen before. For all your trials, all your worries, and your burdens, there's a Savior and He calls. Bring it all to the table. Bring it all. You can bring it all. And come on in, take your place. There's no one who's turned away. All you sinners, all you saints, come right in and find your grace. Come on in and take your place. There's no one who's turned you away. All you sinners, all you saints. Come on in and find your grace and bring it all to the table. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God, we thank you for characters like Jeff. You remind us of how stupid we can be, and even suffer in this life because of our stupidity. And yet, by your grace, you make us people of faith, men and women of faith. We thank you, Heavenly Father, that in the midst of our stupidity, you call us to the table and you make us white as snow. This we give our praise and thanks for in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Is the Bible Trustworthy?
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. May be seated. We interrupt our series of sermons on the book of Judges to answer the following question. Can the authority of the Bible be trusted? I wrote that introduction three weeks ago. God has had other plans. But I come back to this question because of how important it is. This past year and a half has forced us to examine who and what authorities do we trust. As stated several weeks ago, That what has been revealed is that very few people trust the church as an authority in their lives. This is very sad indeed. As I also stated, the church will be the judge of angels. This point was made by Saint Paul when he rebuked the Corinthian Christians for suing one another instead of being able to solve their differences. If we cannot judge between one another, how can we expect to judge angels? That is an obvious rhetorical question. It is further ironic that Christians do not look to the church as the authority, let alone unauthority. For one of the last instructions given by Jesus was for the church to have authority. So that when the church binds something on earth, it would be bound in heaven. And when the church looses something on earth, it would be loosed in heaven. And still, very few look to the church for guidance, direction, even small decision making. And in case the devil is tempting you to think that I am preaching such a point in order to gain some type of authority in your life, well, first of all, I'm not the church. And second of all, I hear this as me needing to heed my bishops more and more. I ask that each of us would examine ourselves regarding what different authorities we allow in our lives and why. Who do you listen to for news and information? And why do you choose that particular source? Who do you believe when it comes to disagreements between sources? And why do you believe one source over another? By what standards do you make your decisions to trust the resources you trust? The toughest challenge to answer, honestly, is this. How much does the authorities you trust say what you want to hear? And is that why you choose them? If you choose authority sources that already sound like you, well, you've made yourself your own authority. All of this discussion and questioning about the authority, about authority, leads us to question, the one at the beginning, can the authority of the Bible be trusted? My daughter Christiana emailed me about two months ago saying that she was concerned about raising her children and not having the answers that would help them stay in the faith. She did not feel prepared to answer. She'd been reading the Mama Bear Apologetics, which Some are studying this summer, she came to realize that if her children asked certain questions, she didn't have certain answers Now I was a bit disappointed in hearing this. I uh felt confident that I had answered such questions that she was having in confirmation class. She responded by pointing out that she was 12 years old when she took confirmation class and doesn't remember a whole lot on the topics. But I gave her notes, especially notes on the Bible and its authority, and I thought she would keep those notes. I'm sure all of you who have taken that class have kept those notes. You know where they are right now, right? Yeah. I recognize that uh my idealism is a bit weak And so this issue about the authority of the Bible needs to be reiterated. It needs to come up time and time again. We need to be strengthened in our understanding of how important it is to know the Bible can be trusted. We forget. We need to come back to simple truths. We need to realize that the devil continues to say, just like he did to Eve, did God really say? And I think upon this young lady Hazel, how she's been marked by Christ and now a A target is on her back by the devil and he she's going to go through life with people in her life questioning the authority of the Bible Do you really believe that book? It's written by men, you know. It's really old. You can't trust the truths they're in. She's going to hear this time and time again. Will she be ready? So let us begin. The first reason that the authority of the Bible can be trusted is because it says so itself. When it says that the words therein are inspired by the Holy Spirit. Hear these words again from St. Paul to Timothy. All scripture is God breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training and righteousness. So that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work. Next is from Saint Peter. He said Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one's own interpretation, for no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man. But men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. This proclamation of Scripture about itself is not just in the New Testament, for we have passages such as Psalm 1, Psalm 19, where we read, the law of the Lord is perfect. Converting the soul. The testimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple. The statutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart The commandment of God is pure, enlightening the eyes. But the magician The logician responds to this argument making the point that simply because the Bible says it is the authoritative word of God does not make it the authoritative word of God. That's known as a circular argument And circular arguments can be proven invalid. A proper response to such a rebuttal is acceptance that a circular argument can be proven invalid, but only If that argument stands alone. If there are other valid arguments, then the circular argument can stand. So what are the other arguments? One other argument is that a great deal of the Bible was written by primary sources. A primary source is someone who was an eyewitness to the events that transpired, to the words that were spoken as well. We do not have this, of course, with the book such as Genesis, which is said to have been written by Moses by use of oral tradition and being inspired by the Spirit of God. But it can be said about the book of Exodus, which was written and experienced by Moses. It can be said about 1 and 2 Samuel, which were written and experienced by Samuel. It can be said about the books of the prophets who experienced the events, heard the words of God, and wrote them down. In the New Testament we have these testimonials. This is from the Gospel according to St. Luke. He said, Many have undertaken to draw up an account of the things that had been fulfilled among us. just as they were handed down but to us by those who from the first were eyewitnesses and servants of the word. With this in mind, since I myself have carefully investigated everything from the beginning, I too decided to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus. that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught. And then again from Peter, 2 Peter chapter 1. For we did not follow cunningly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty. And then from 1 John 1, verse 3, the Apostle John said, that which we have seen and heard, we declare to you, that you also may have fellowship with us, and truly our fellowship is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ. And again from Peter, this is from his sermon in Acts chapter 2. Peter challenges the people hearing him preach. He said, Men of Israel, hear these words. Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested by you To you by miracles, wonders, and signs, which God did through him in your midst As you yourselves also know. They saw Jesus, they heard Jesus, they knew. Being their own witnesses, that what Peter preached to them about Jesus was true. And still another argument regarding the authority of the Bible. Is the numerous prophecies spoken in the Old Testament that were fulfilled in the New Testament? We have the prophecy that the Messiah would be born in Bethlehem We have the prophecy that the Messiah would be born in the line of Judah. We have the prophecy that the Messiah would spend a season in Egypt We have the prophecy that the Messiah would heal the sick and give sight to the blind. We have the prophecy that the Messiah would be preceded by a prophet in the likes of Elijah. We have the prophecy that the Messiah would be rejected by his own people, that he would be sold for money, that he would have his clothes torn from his body, and those clothes would be gambled over. That his body would be disfigured and that his hands and feet would be pierced. We have the prophecy that the Messiah would be resurrected from the dead, ascend into heaven, and seated at the right hand of his Father. But you say that such evidence is still not enough for all of it is internal, meaning that it's what the Bible says about itself. What evidence for the authority of the Bible is found outside of the Bible? Such is called external proof. What we can first look to are the many archaeological discoveries that confirm a great deal about what the Bible describes. For example, there is the Myrnita Stele, which is an inscribed stone from the 19th dynasty of Egypt that describes the Israelite people. This comes from the 13th century BC. And corresponds quite well with the earliest possible archaeological evidence of a settlement of an Israeli people as a tribe in Canaan. And next we have on the northeastern shore of Mount Ebal, just to the north of modern-day Shechem Neopolis, on the west bank. Israeli archaeologist Adam Zerdl discovered a site dating to the early Iron Age, the period, again covering the late 13th and early 12th century BC. Zirdal suggests that there is a cultic site that is uncovered, that is likely an altar. Erected by Joshua on Mount Ebel, recorded in Joshua chapter 8. Zerdo suggests that it served as a central cultic site. For the earliest Israelite settlers in that region east of Canaan. Next are the many discoveries within the old city of Jerusalem. Among the most noteworthy finds that are relevant that were found during the Iron Age remains come from marking the city of David. The original beginnings of the city are there, fortifications, water systems, houses, and even a possible palace. It is believed even today that on the site of the old Temple Mount, you can find evidence of the first Temple Mount. And as we were so privileged to visit, it is believed that what is called Herod's Tower now was likely David's original Palace, and it is uncovered that during the time of Herod he would take those who had been arrested down to the very bottom depth. It's likely where we stood was the same place Jesus stood the night he was arrested. Next are fragments of a monumental inscription written on basalt in Aramaic. These were discovered outside the gate of the Iron Age Tildan in northern Israel in the mid-1990s. It is written there of a king, an Aramean king, boasting of killing the kings of Israel of the house of David. Most scholars believe that this inscription was written under the orders of Hazael around 840 B. C. And describes his victory over the kings of Israel, most likely Joram, son of Ahab, and the house of David, most likely Ahaziah, son of Joram. As such, it is seen as the earliest mention in the extra-biblical text of the name David, specifically referring to the kingdom of Judah, the house of David, some hundred and fifty years after the time. While there are numerous discoveries worthy of mentioning, I close my examples with the discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls. These are still being rescued, studied, and preserved today. These ancient texts verify the accuracy of the translations of our day, showing that the sacred texts of Holy Scripture were not carelessly written and collected, but were painstakingly written, copied, and cared for as if they were the very words of God. The many archaeological discoveries repeatedly confirm the historistical accuracy of the many historistical narratives told in the Bible It can also be said that there are no historical narratives in Scripture that have been proven false by archaeological discoveries. And while the absence of proof is really no proof, when the people argue that the Bible narrative is false, they also do so without proof. And this brings us to the most important proof that the authority of the Bible can be trusted. It is not enough to say it is authoritative because it says it is, as we have admitted. It is not enough to say it uses primary sources. It is not enough to say that many of its prophecies have been fulfilled. It is not enough to say that the archaeological discoveries have verified its veracity What is enough is the person of Jesus Christ. Jesus himself is the most valid proof that the Bible is the Word of God. It is the sinless character of Jesus that causes us to trust him. He was a perfect man who became a perfect sacrifice for the sins of man. It is the words of light that he uttered that causes us to listen to him and listen with ears to hear. It is his humility that caused us to have faith that he was who he said he was and was able to do what others witnessed him doing. And because Jesus was all that he was, when he speaks of Abraham, speaks of Moses, speaks of Elijah as real men, living out a true faith, we believe him. When Jesus refers to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah and the reign of King David as historical, that is how we understand them as well. Because Jesus accepted the Old Testament as inspired by God and thus true, then we do as well. And because Jesus of the New Testament is spoken about as his words of truth, that he had words of eternal life. And because Jesus said the Holy Spirit would guide us into all truth, the result is his people writing down those truths, what he uttered, what he taught, what he proclaimed. I am more convinced of the power of this argument that the authority of the Bible can be trusted based on the person of Jesus. Because of how popular it is today to challenge whether Jesus ever existed. According to this argument, if Jesus can be doubted As a historical figure, then all of Scripture should be doubted as well. But we have evidence outside of the Bible that Jesus existed. The Jewish historian Josephus mentions Jesus as a historical figure twice in his writings around 93 A. D. The Roman historian Tacitus, from his work about 116 A. D. , tells of the burning of Rome around 64 A. When he said Nero blamed the persons commonly called Christians who followed their founder named Christus, who was put to death under Pontius Pilate. Other mentions are similar in referring to the person the Christians pray to, the person that they worship, the person that they follow. Is such enough evidence that Jesus existed? Is all of this enough to be confident in the authority of the Bible? Perhaps the true struggle is not determining whether the Bible is a trusted authority, but whether we want to allow it to have authority in our individual lives. The struggle is common. We are tempted towards sin, and we are tempted to live in sin. We are tempted to live a life according to the desires of our flesh. But the Bible tells us we should not. It warns against such a lifestyle. When we choose to live according to our flesh, the message of the Bible brings guilt to our conscience. But we don't want guilt. And we still want to live out our fleshly desires. And so we find reasons not to allow the Bible to speak guilt into our lives. We doubt its accuracy. We deny its authority. We hear the argument that it is written by men. And that sounds like a good enough reason to reject it entirely. But it is not. The Bible is a perfect example of Jesus. For it too is fully of God and fully of man. At the very least, each of us needs to be honest when we doubt the authority of the Bible in our lives. There is more than enough evidence for us to be confident that it is from God. My charge to each of us is to allow it to have full authority in your life and watch the Holy Spirit make you more and more like the man who gives its authority. Amen. Let us pray Our gracious and merciful God, we thank you for the confidence that we can have in the Holy Scriptures. There is much that has been said this morning, but we all confess it comes down to your Son, Jesus, our Savior and our Lord. May his authority always reign in our hearts and in our consciences, that we might trust him and thus trust in his word. This we ask and pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: COVID-19 True Righteous
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. It has been over twenty-two years since I first preached behind this pulpit. And I estimate, amidst that time, that the following sermon is the most pastoral sermon that I have preached. This is like one of those meetings when my children were young, and I would call them up all together and say we need to have a family meeting. All sermons, of course, are pastoral, each dealing with what I perceived the Lord would have me say from a particular text. But this one has been written to address a great concern that I have among us. In this sermon, I will directly address issues related to the COVID-19 virus. I begin with the testimony of Bobby Lynn and I Unbeknownst to us, we were exposed to someone with COVID on Sunday, July 18th. This person was fully vaccinated, but was exposed himself. And therefore exposed us. When he called us to inform us that he had tested positive, Bobby Lynn had already started feeling symptoms. This was two days after exposure. That Thursday, she tested positive to COVID-19. Her primary symptoms included nose and chest congestion with a severe, raspy cough, headache, fatigue, and she did lose her sense of taste for a few days. I had felt a couple of symptoms, so I tested that Saturday and received a negative result. I tried to continue life as normal while also choosing to quarantine together Which meant that I would not go to church or enter the church building until all symptoms were passed. But I never felt strong. I started to have more severe symptoms the next week, continuing with body aches, dry coughs, sweats, chills, fatigue, leading to exhaustion. We knew I had the virus and that was confirmed that Friday by a test. While the improvement started that next day, Saturday, we would have better moments followed by setback moments. More than two weeks after exposure and both having finished quarantine, we still had lingering effects that reminded us that our bodies were still recovering. When informing people that we were sick from COVID-19, those that we had exposed, the repeated response or question was, are you vaccinated? No, was our reply. No one who responded in like manner followed up with a why not question, and I anticipate that such was so because it opens up a List of controversial topics that is too long to be addressed in one sitting. So I want to address some of those topics this morning. But first, I want you to know why I think it should be addressed. Within the Christian church lurks the devil. Who is seeking to divide and then devour Christians with the idea that responding to the pandemic in specific ways Results in greater righteousness before God and our fellow man, while not responding in those same specific ways results in being unrighteous before God and being unloving toward our fellow man. I trust you know as a Christian that such thinking is unbiblical and even heretical But the temptation to think in this manner is prevalent. But back to the pressing question, why did we not get the vaccine? Well, full disclosure, I signed up on two different websites to get in line to either get the Pfizer or the Moderna. The Johnson <unk> Johnson was not an option because it is connected to using aborted fetal tissue, and I will have nothing to do with that. While on those lists, I was updated, but never told an appointment could be made. I was only asked if I wanted to remain on the list, and I was asked that several times And finally I turned down being on the list in May. My thinking by that time was that I had survived over a year through this pandemic all around me and had not been infected. The odds seemed in my favor that such would continue. And I believe that I was healthy enough to survive the virus if I became infected. Natural immunity sounded better than manufactured immunity to me. I also didn't think the virus would be difficult to endure as I was in fairly good physical shape. That last thought proved to be irrelevant, by the way. The main counter-argument to my reasoning that I am frequently hearing is that I am now a part of the problem as to why the pandemic remains as the pandemic is now not about COVID-19 virus, but about those who are unvaccinated. It is now the pandemic of the unvaccinated. Those who currently diagnose the pandemic in such a manner Conclude that the vaccinated have proven that they care about their fellow man, while those who are unvaccinated do not. The disdain for the unvaccinated continues to grow with news headlines insisting that when the unvaccinated contract the virus They should suffer more than the vaccinated, and they should either be refused hospitalization or forced to pay their hospitalization out of their pocket. What is most notable, or notably missing, from this reaction to the unvaccinated, is the idea or consideration of grace being given. As historian Tom Holland in his fantastic book titled Dominion has proven The concept and practice of being gracious, one human being to another, is a Christian ideal. The effects of human beings being gracious to one another has essentially created Western societies that care for the least among us while also affording equal rights to one another. Such carrying and affording of rights is not found in cultures that have not been affected by the Christian ideal. Practical application of being gracious to our fellow man is to not condemn but help people who, let's say, are obese, or people who are chain smokers, or people who are addicts. Or anyone who contributes to their own suffering. But such graciousness is seemingly not afforded to those who are unvaccinated. Why is this? There is likely truth to the speculation that the unvaccinated are now a replacement for the ire that was focused on a particular former president. With a political pariah no longer in the daily news, the unvaccinated are the easiest targets to gang up on with blame and anger. Another possibility is that the unvaccinated allow the psyche of those who are angry to feel morally superior. This need for moral superiority relates to my belief that every human being has an innate desire to be righteous As that desire stems from being made in the image of God, who we know is righteous by nature. Because we are living under a curse of death because of the sin of Adam. Our need for righteousness cannot be fulfilled using our own devices, but we can feel righteous. And we can feel righteous when we do something we think is morally superior to others, such as show our care for our fellow man by wearing a mask, staying six feet away, and getting vaccinated. The temptation to be self-righteous, to perceive oneself to be morally superior as compared to others That's a very strong temptation. And that strong temptation is evident by how often Jesus had to address self-righteousness while dealing with the Pharisees. Surprisingly to me, the Pharisees were not a self-righteous group of men at their inception. Their beginnings would have attracted most of us here, as they desired to retain the law of Moses while continuing to live in a Roman culture. They perceive the wisdom literature and the prophetic messages of the major and minor prophets. They consider those as important. in order to understand how to apply the law of Moses in their modern world. What evolved, however was a strain of teaching that tried to apply the law of Moses to modern-day events that eventually treated such teaching as just as authoritative as the law itself. The very specific example addressed by Jesus that we read this morning to get the point across regarding the sin of self-righteousness. That was in regard to what they called Corbin. Essentially, the Pharisees had established what they thought was a loophole in the law of God. And that loophole was to their benefit. It was, of course, the responsibility of all Jewish people to honor their father and their mother. When a father and or mother became financially needy, part of that honoring was to provide for them. However, the law of Moses also allows for specific gifts, special gifts, either money or property. To be given to the temple treasury and be used in the manner seen fit by the priests, and some of those were Pharisees. This resulted in Pharisees teaching that Jewish faith that the Jewish faithful could give Corbin, special gifts, to the treasury instead of providing for the financial needs of their parents. The result was disobeying the law of Moses and replacing the law of honoring father and mother with giving of a financial benefit to the Pharisees. When Jesus rebuked them for this practice, he made it clear that they had chosen to disobey a clearly stated law, honor thy father and thy mother, and replace it with a man-made law. that was formed for selfish gain. And all the while pretending that obeying their man-made law was actually more pious, more God-fearing, than obeying God's fifth commandment. I stated earlier that we all have an innate desire to be righteous. And this innate desire is corrupted by our fallen natures, allowing us to perceive that righteousness can be something we attain for ourselves with our own strength, by our own devices. But such thinking is in error, egregious error. For the Bible tells us that our good works, the things we do where we think we are pleasing to God, That those works are as filthy rags in the eyes of God. And the description of a filthy rag is that of a woman, what she would use during her menstrual cycle. And I tell you this to make the point clear. Our works cannot in any form make us righteous before God. In truth, when laid before him, our works disgust him. And why wouldn't they? Our works are tainted with impure motives. Our motives are Mostly impure because we think of ourselves to be good, which is to say better than others. We easily praise ourselves, seeing ourselves as praiseworthy of others. We are not honest with ourselves regarding what is truly going on with inside of our hearts We think about ourselves and what adulation we deserve and what credit we should be getting and how much more we care than other people do. And how much better we look doing our good works, and how our family is better than other families because of how much we praise one another for all the good works that we do And as God watches our behavior and knows our hearts, it is rather disgusting to him. In truth, there are very clear works Jesus commanded us to do that have nothing to do with masks. Six feet apart for vaccines. Let us each take inventory regarding the words and actions these past 18 plus months. How many times have you spoken about the virtue of wearing a mask compared to how many times you have shared with someone, anyone, about salvation through Jesus Christ as the Son of God? How much have you thought about, talked about, and have been concerned about the effectiveness of COVID-19 vaccines? compared to how many times you have thought about, talked about, and have been concerned about people who do not know the Lord Jesus Christ. And how much holiness have you gained in your mirror as you watch yourself obey the science while harboring personal pride in your heart? Hear this perspective. If you believe the evolutionists, the Earth is 4. 5 billion years old. If you believe the creationists, the earth is no older than 10,000 years, the average life expectancy in the United States is between 76 and 81 years of age. According to evolutionists, your life does not even register as a percentage as compared to the age of the Earth. According to the creationists, your life registers 0. 008 compared to the age of the earth. Either way, the earth barely registers your existence. And yet Jesus lived, died, and rose again for your eternal existence, and he did so for all persons who would hear his voice and believe. What then is more worthy of our time on this earth? Should we spend our time sharing about the effectiveness of vaccines? or about the person and teachings and victory of the Lord Jesus Christ. Certainly you hear that as a rhetorical question. The survival rate after contracting COVID-19 remains very high. Even now among the elderly, there Has been quite a bit that has been learned on how to treat those who are elderly who have contracted the virus. And the survival rate is even high for those who have pre-existing conditions. But there remains a very low eternal survival rate for those who die without knowing the Lord Jesus Christ as their Savior. Each of us must ask ourselves which one we care about more: eternal life or earthly life. And what have we talked about and how we have lived these past eighteen plus months reveals what we actually care more about. Now, if you have been made comfortable with me addressing people who are tempted to care more about COVID-19 prevention than they do about the souls of their fellow men and women Let me make you uncomfortable. For just as people are tempted to be self-righteous because of the masks they wear and the vaccines they jab into themselves, So too can Christians be tempted to be self-righteous because of the masks they don't wear and what they won't allow jabbed into them. Anti-vaxxers can think too pure of themselves, believing the world to be more holy when it is naturally embraced. But the world is not holy because it is natural. It is cursed along with humanity. The nature of the earth is corrupted as it too longs to be made new. It too longs for a savior. Even the rocks cry out. There is no inherent righteousness in the natural earth, and thus no one can find righteousness within nature. When it comes to righteousness, true righteousness, which is a righteousness only from God, there is no human being that is righteous except Jesus. As St. Paul said to the Christians at Rome, there is no one righteous, no, not one. But you and I, we can't see God. We can't know God without being righteous. And so we are utterly dependent to be made righteous by another St. Paul continued to the Romans. He said, and this righteousness from God comes through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe. There is no distinction. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God and are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. God presented him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in his blood in order to demonstrate his righteousness. Because in his forbearance, he had passed over the sins committed beforehand. He did this to demonstrate his righteousness at the present time. So as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus. Where then, he asks, is the boasting? It is excluded. On what principle? On that of works. No, but on that of faith. For we maintain that a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law. There is no better, are no better words that a preacher can preach than the words that inform that God makes righteous His people when they have faith in Jesus. And because such righteousness is so freely given and so freely received, the answer to the question about boasting is obvious. There is no room for boasting for everything that I have that will last forever has been given to me. Masks will pass away. Vaccines will no longer be needed. Six feet will only refer to our burial. But the righteousness we receive will be eternal. And this is where the lesson of to whom much is given, much is required. Here is where it is applied. We have been given righteousness by the grace of God, and it is for us to use that great amount of righteousness by grace. And be forgiving to one another with an abundance of graciousness toward one another. Jesus said that the unbelieving world will know we are Christians by our love for one another. And that love must include being gracious to one another, and especially now within the context of a pandemic. If you do not have grace for people who are Christian, who are living through a pandemic differently than you, you are not behaving as a Christian should, and you need to repent and you need to start loving. That is what living through a pandemic as a Christian looks like. We're about to take communion. We are going to gather around the same table with the same need for God's grace, but to receive that grace you must have it for one another as well. The time is now, the moment is here, to be gracious to one another, and to keep on being gracious to one another If you want to know God's will, His will for you and I is to be gracious to one another. Can I get an amen? Let us pray. Father, we come humbly, knowing that there's not much that we have done right through this pandemic, whether it's from within our hearts or whether it's plans that we've made. We confess that we do see through the glass dimly, and we are desperate to see you face to face. Father, what it is clear in your will, what we do see clearly, is how we are to love one another and be gracious to one another. May that message rule our hearts and this church. This we pray in Jesus' name.

sermons.title: Using Sinfulness
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We are finally making our way back to the book of Judges. We have missed it for over four weeks. And we read from chapter 13, but I will actually be covering information from chapter 13 through chapter 15. Want to open your Bibles and follow along. Chapter 13 begins with a usual description from the book of Judges. Again, the Israelites did evil in the eyes of the Lord. The time of oppression by the hands of the Philistines is said to be forty years. That number is always significant. It was forty days that it rained upon the earth in the days of Noah as a judgment of God. It was 40 years that Israel wandered in the desert as a punishment for not trusting in the Lord when they first came to the Promised Land. 40 here is another set time in which God's people are judged for their sin. To symbolize God's judgment and his son's holiness, Forty was the set number of days that Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, coming out having not sinned, and being pleasing to the Heavenly Father. The scene of the announcement of the coming birth of Samson, we are all familiar with. We remember it from the story of Sarah and the angel visiting her and Abraham. We remember it from the story of Zachariah and Elizabeth. Each couple had difficulty imagining that what they were being told would come to pass. The instructions to Manoah and his wife were that they were to raise the child as a Nazarite. The word Nazarite is not related to the city that will be named Nazareth. It is instead a description for someone who is set aside for sacred service. Samson is the first in Scripture to be raised in such a manner. The primary restriction was that the boy's hair could not be cut. The other restrictions given are for Manoah's wife. She was told not to drink wine or any fermented drink or unclean food while carrying the child. It is worthy to note that the purpose of abstaining from alcoholic drink was not to condemn the consumption of alcohol even for a pregnant woman. But instead, it was to recognize that such abstaining was to be abstaining from the luxury That was a result of living in a land controlled by idolaters. Notice that Manoah's wife was not to eat anything that came from the grapevine. Making freshly picked grapes and the juice of those grapes off limits. Grapes symbolized fruit cultivated over time. Because the Philistines had been in control of the land for 40 years, the grapes consumed would be a result of a foreign rule in the land of God's chosen people. The restriction was a symbol of rejecting the Philistine rule. The restrictions of cutting Samson's hair had a similar purpose It was common among the heathen, idolatrous nations, to shave the heads of their children as a symbol of a consecration to their idols, to their shrines. This was primarily done for children dedicated to serve before the idols. In other words, serve as a worshiper in front of the idols. For an Israelite, it became a virtue to do the opposite and grow one's hair long. Growing the hair long meant complete devotion to God instead of idols. Long, untouched hair was a sign of personal devotion. stating that all of the person belonged to God. It was from God that all strength came, and the hair was a symbol of that strength. And said symbol will play an important part in Samson's life later. Like many of us would feel, Manoah apparently was not confident in what the angel instructed him to do. He inquired of the angel of the Lord, not realizing to whom he was speaking, and discovered that the messenger was more than a man speaking for God. The messenger was actually from God's throne. What happens in the following dialogue is mysterious and it's One of the more than a few examples in Scripture of what theologians call theophanies. Theophanies are times in which God appears among men. He is not a man like other men, but his appearance is such that he is spoken to like one man would speak to another. By some revelation not described to us, the reader, the heavenly messenger is soon seen to be more than a man and then is called an angel. Angel, as you may know, means simply means messenger of God. Then whether it is the word spoken or some other supernatural occurrence. Those receiving the message conclude that they have not only been in the presence of a heavenly being, but actually been in the presence of God Himself. This happened when the heavenly messenger came to Abraham and announced that Sarah would give birth to a son. You remember that three messengers came, and after two left to go down to Sodom, one remained. And Abraham spoke to him, calling him Lord. Also, when Jacob wrestled with the heavenly messenger until the sun rose, he said afterward that he had seen the face of God. A similar understanding happens with Manoah. After having spoken with the heavenly messenger and realizing he was more than a man, Manoah wants to eat with him. The messenger instead encourages a burnt offering. Manoah is a persistent man and asks the angel's name. The reply might as well have been, I am. For Manoah understood it to be God himself, as verse 22. Look at verse 22, chapter 13 reveals. Of course, we know that no man can see God, that is, see God for who he truly is, and then live. We remember from Exodus how Moses was privy to see the manifestation of God from his backside. But could not encounter him face to face. How does a man, any man who is finite, come face to face with the infinite? It is not possible. The Ophanes are also called Christophanes, for they are actual pre-incarnations of Jesus. The third person of the Trinity is the one who wrestled with Jacob. Bartered with Abraham, walked in the fiery furnace with Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and here he is speaking to Manoah. Now I wish to summarize the rest of Samson's story, at least that we're covering today. You could call what I'm about to do the ELT. It stands for Eric's Living Translation. There are a lot of bad English translations of the Bible being printed today, and the ELT may fall into such category. Nonetheless, here we go with the ELT. Samson had an eye for a Philistine girl, which he shouldn't have. His parents helped him get her, which they shouldn't have. Thankfully God was using their behavior the whole time for his glory. When going to meet the girl, Samson was attacked by a lion and killed it with his bare hands. When he later came upon the carcass of the same lion, it had a beehive in it Samson took honey from the beehive, which he shouldn't have. He gave some of his to his parents, which he shouldn't have. During his wedding party, Samson played a game with the Philistines, which he shouldn't have. They could not answer the riddle, so they got the answer from his wife. God used Samson's anger toward them for the sake of his glory. When Samson's wife was taken from him, he set out to get her back. In his anger Samson burned up the crops of the Philistines, which he shouldn't have. When his own people knew Samson was the cause for the anger of the Philistines, they turned Samson over to them to keep the peace. Samson then was able to be in their midst, and grabbing a donkey jawbone, which he shouldn't have, he killed a thousand men. Once again, God gave Samson strength for the sake of his glory. At the end of the day, Samson was thirsty and complained to God, which he shouldn't have, and God revived him. In my translation, you no doubt noticed that there were a number of times when I said he shouldn't have, making it more of an interpretation than a translation. What I am referring to when I say that Samson should not have done these things is the fact that he was a Nazarite. As a reminder, a Nazarite was someone set aside as a special servant of God with restrictions placed upon him. Samson was set aside according to the angel of the Lord to be a servant of God. Thus he was to obey the law of God. God's people are clearly instructed not to marry foreign women, but Samson does. Parents are not to aid in such marriages, but Samson's parents do. God's people are not to touch the carcass of an unclean animal. Samson does. He also should not be feeding honey from such a carcass to his parents, but he does. Samson should not have been carousing with the pagans, but he does. Again, he should not touch a dead carcass of an unclean animal, but Samson does by picking up a jawbone of a donkey. Such were the things that Samson did in violation of his Nazarite vows. Because of this behavior It is fair to wonder how or why God would use such a man as Samson. He most certainly is not a man to emulate. In fact, while studying this passage, I recalled when my older boys were young, there was a series of Bible action figures available at the local Christian bookstore. Samson was one of those figures and he was labeled a Bible hero. Now, of course, it depends on how you define the word hero to justify Samson being in that category. At the end of his life, he performed a heroic act, but he is not a person of character that any child should emulate. In Samson, we have a man of sinful character being used of God in a sinless way. It was the Reverend William Still who described something like this as God using sin sinlessly. Or the case here using a sinner sinlessly. Just how sinful was Samson? One commentator described him in the following manner. Samson is disrespectful of his parents, callous toward his Nazarite calling, without any loyalty to his own people. Compromising in his ethic, rude to his wife, flippant with his tongue, and driven by lust, appetite, and eroticism. The only way that good can come from this man is by God overpowering him with his Holy Spirit and driving him to the task of delivering his people, something he is not naturally inclined to do. What God does through sinful Samson is disturb the status quo A detail of this story not yet highlighted is the fact that Israel had not cried out to God while they were oppressed by the Philistines for 40 years. From this we could conclude that they were comfortable enough under Philistine rule to remain there indefinitely. This conclusion is further bolstered by the behavior of the Israelites when they turned Samson over to the Philistines. Samson in a rage killed thirty men and destroyed acres of crops of the Philistines. The reaction of the Israelites, instead of letting him lead them into battle against their oppressor, Was to become upset at Samson for disturbing the peace. But of course, there was no peace. Israel was being oppressed for 40 years. Yet, like many who live in sin for an elongated period of time, they do not know any better. They do not know that they are dead in their sin. They do not know that they are spiritually blind. They did not cry out to God for deliverance, yet God, by his grace, delivered them. The point is made this way to highlight God's initiation. He is the one who is responsible for Israel's deliverance from the Philistines. He's responsible in every way. The New Testament reveals God's initiative in this same way, when we are told that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. Obviously, no one was crying out for God to send his son as a sacrifice so that men might be saved from their sin and have a heavenly hope. If there was any crying out in the first century, it was by the Israelites who wanted to be delivered from Roman political oppression and occupation. It was not to be delivered from sin. But being delivered from sin is what God had planned all along. Jesus explains God's initiative when he says No one can come to me unless the Father draws him. The word translated draw has been rightly interpreted to be drag. No one shall come to me unless the Father drags him. It is what Jesus is saying. Because we think upon how does a dead man come to God? He must be dragged. In his spiritually lifeless state, he is dragged. In his rebellious state, he is dragged, kicking, and screaming. This is all part of God's mode of operation. He initiates, he chooses. And he is free because he is God to bring about the salvation of those he chooses by whatever means he desires. Thus he can use the sinful in a sinless manner. The Lord uses sinfulness to accomplish his holy will. And this is not the first time God uses men in this manner.
