sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. I have a confession to make to you of sorts this morning. I have been a renegade preacher For the past 22 years. The ideal Anglican preacher oversees morning prayer every day with the readings coming from the lectionary. And then at night, oversees evening prayer with readings coming from the lectionary. For example, if you turn in your book of common prayer to Roman numeral 42, page 42. You will see the readings assigned for morning prayer on the week of the sixteenth Sunday after Trinity, which is this week And on the next page, Roman numero 43, you will see the readings for evening prayer of the same week. If these services are followed and all of God's people attend all services, we would hear the entirety of the Bible read in one year. For Sunday worship, something else is to take place. If you turn to page 232 in the Book of Common Prayer, You will see that there is a collak, which simply means prayer, and then there are two readings: the epistle reading and the gospel reading, and these are called propers. These readings are to be read each year on their assigned Sunday, and then the sermon is to come from those two readings. Thus, there is a great deal of idealism that precedes the Book of Common Prayer If followed as it is written, God's people would be hearing all of the Bible read each year and would be exposed to the same themes of the scriptures each week. Such idealism, however, doesn't match the culture of America. We don't attend morning prayer and evening prayer every day We have televisions after all, and they demand our attention. That is said in jest My assessment as a pastor is that most professing Christians are relatively biblically illiterate, and thus I consider it my calling to expose You to all that the Bible teaches, all of the stories it tells. For example, I took the time to read to you three chapters from the book of Judges. and preach about those passages because I anticipate that when you come to such chapters, you find them so strange that you gloss over them until you get to books and chapters you more easily understand. I anticipate such because I have done the same. My point is that I have chosen to preach through entire books of the Bible so that you can hear how passages of Scripture You're attempted to gloss over can be understood and applied to your Christian life. Over the years, we have covered a good number of books of the Bible, reading every word. Today is a change. I will not be a renegade, at least from now until the end of December. We will be hearing sermons that will incorporate the collect of the week and the propers assigned for specific Sundays. Today, as I said, is the 16th Sunday after Trinity. And so we will be looking at the epistle reading from Ephesians chapter 3, beginning at verse 13. And then from St. Luke, the gospel reading, chapter 7, beginning at verse 11. And so if you would turn in your Bibles to Ephesians chapter 3, beginning at verse 13, we're going to walk through that passage. We must consider that when Paul tells the Ephesian Christians not to lose heart, that when he wrote that, he was himself in jail. For a person to tell you not to lose heart when he himself has a reason to lose heart, well that message is very powerful indeed. Paul lived his whole life after conversion with a passion to bring salvation to his own people, the Jews. What placed him in jail, I remind you, was when, on a strategic visit to Jerusalem, he had the opportunity to preach to a vast crowd on or near the Temple Mount. According to Acts chapter 21 and 22. But the opportunity ended in disaster Because the Jewish crowd could not stand the idea of the good news of the Messiah being extended to the Gentiles A riot ensued, putting Paul in a legal dilemma, from which he used his right as a Roman citizen to appeal to Caesar At the writing of this letter to the Ephesians, Paul was imprisoned in Rome awaiting for his trial before Caesar. And there, because he knew God wanted Gentiles to share in the good news of the Messiah, he wasn't afraid to preach that truth. But what does it mean to say that his tribulation is their glory? That's what he writes. His tribulation is their glory. The answer is that their glory must be a reflection of the dignity of St. Paul in the midst of suffering and a reflection of the glory of the gospel itself. Paul was being used and probably in a greater way than he even imagined. This Roman imprisonment produced the letters of Ephesians, Colossians, Philippians, and Philemon. And they all most certainly have had a place in the eternal plan of God. In the same manner, each of us has a place in the service of God's eternal plan. Knowing this and working towards it is a great guard against losing heart, as he says, do not lose heart in the midst of tribulation. Paul next prays on the basis of Paul's prayer was his knowledge of God's purpose. This means he confidently prayed according to God's will. Paul prayed in the posture of bowing his knee. This position of utmost humility was in contrast to the normal posture of the day, which was to stand and raise up your hands. Thus consider others who prayed while kneeling. Solomon prayed on his knees, first Kings chapter eight. Ezra prayed on his knees, Ezra chapter 9. The psalmist calls all of us to pray on our knees, Psalm 95. Daniel prayed on his knees, Daniel 6. People came to Jesus kneeling, Matthew 17 Stephen prayed on his knees, Acts chapter 7. Peter prayed on his knees, Acts chapter 9. Paul prayed on his knees, Acts chapter 20. And the other early Christians prayed on their knees, Acts 21. Most importantly, Jesus prayed on his knees, Luke 22. St. Paul directed his prayer to the Father, who is presented as the planner among the members of the Trinity. Prayer is usually directed to the Father through the Son by the empowering and direction of the Holy Spirit. And remembering that all God's family is called after his name, Paul showed that his mind was rather taken with this idea of the essential unity of the body of Christ. God is father of both the Jews and the Gentiles. Such unity is not manufactured, but is instead a spiritual reality. Paul prayed for God's will, which is what it means to be according to the riches of his glory. The prayer focused on being strengthened in the inner man, which is the character of each individual. Such strength is needed when considering the tribulations that lie ahead. There is an inner man, an inner person within each of us, and that person is who we really are. When such a person is exposed without being strengthened by the Holy Spirit, we can see ourselves weakening under pressure. Paul next asked that Jesus would live in these believers, just as Jesus promised. When he said, If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. This is the fulfilled promise of the Holy Spirit filling each believer. Of course, it is through faith that Jesus dwells within us. As one commentator said, quote, The indwelling is, from one side, the sovereign gift of God, from the other, it is a matter for the simplest and most personal reception by man. And then the form of that reception is just this: faith, reliance, submissive trust, not animated action, not exalted aspiration, but acceptance. Paul next asked that all this would take place as they were rooted and grounded in love. As Charles Spurgeon stated, two expressions are used. Rooted, like a living tree which lay hold upon the soil, twists itself around the rocks and cannot be upturned. Grounded like a building which had been settled as a whole and will never show any cracks or flaws in the future through failure of the foundation. Paul next prayed that they might be able to understand together in community, that's important, in community, every dimension of the love of Jesus. Paul wanted them to know it by experience, that love by experience and not just in words. By saying that that love has strength, that length, excuse me, by saying that love has length and depth. Is showing that it is objective. It is not something you feel, but something that is. However, he is also using such phrasing metaphorically, as such love does not have limitations, it really, truly cannot be measured. Paul asked God to fill these Christians unto all the fullness of God. The word unto is a better translation than the word with. Paul wanted Christians to experience life in Jesus Christ, the fullness of God, and to be filled to their capacity with Jesus. Even. As God is filled to His own capacity with His own character and attributes. And what we are filled with spills out of us. And so the prayer includes asking that God would spill out of these Christians, of you and I. The prayer is followed by a glorious doxology that we will return to in a moment. What is striking is how bold St. Paul's prayer is. He expects God to answer it, and he expects it because of what he knows about the character of God. He knows that God wants all of what he prays for. But how does Paul know the character of God and know it to be so benevolent? That is answered by the story told in our gospel reading. Turning back to the Gospel of St. Luke chapter 7, picking up at verse 11, we see mentioned the city of Nain. which was in the region of Galilee, in the boundaries of the tribe of Issachar. It was about two miles south of Mount Tabor and not far from Capernaum. There are three miracles recorded in the Gospels describing Jesus raising people from the dead. The three noted, however, do not mean that those are the only ones that Jesus raised from the dead. We are told by John that Jesus did so many miracles that it was not possible for them to write them all down. There are a few points that we must underline while examining this miracle. The first one is that there were many witnesses to what Jesus did. For this occurred after Jesus had preached the Sermon on the Mount, meaning that many people heard that Jesus did indeed have the words of eternal life. Thus his crowd was growing. It was becoming large The fact that many people would see his miracle, his miracles, and hear his teachings, and still not believe, is quite mysterious. It appears to be a coincidence, but we in faith know that it was providence that Jesus would be confronted by a burial procession. He went to the city of Nain. We're not told why. It was simply because the Father instructed him to do so. He encountered a burial procession because the father wanted him to. Nothing was done by chance. Of all that Jesus encountered, what was most notable in the procession was the mother of the young man who had died. We are told that a widow, that she was a widow, excuse me, and now alone at the death of her son, as he was her only child. We are to remember that widows were to be provided for by their sons. Having now no son, she was not only alone, but likely financially destitute. I would normally take a story like this and insist that the main message Jesus is showing us by raising this young man from the dead. Is that he is pointing to his own resurrection and the resurrection of all that will believe in him. That is, after all, the main message to receive from the story of raising Lazarus from the dead. But what Luke has us focus upon is why Jesus raised the young man. Look at verse 13. Jesus saw the woman and had compassion on her. Luke underlines this compassion of Jesus in verse 15. By noting that after the young man became alive again with the proof of him sitting up and speaking, we are told that Jesus himself presented the young man to his mother. Jesus took him to her so that she might personally receive the blessing from him. And we are also to notice that no one asked Jesus to raise the young man from the dead. No one praised such a request. No one asked for a miracle. And yet Jesus was ready and willing to do it for one main reason: He had compassion on the mother. Thus we have the answer to the character of our Savior and the reason Saint Paul is so confident that Jesus will pray to the Father. on our behalf that we might be strengthened by the Holy Spirit in the inner man and that we might be rooted and grounded and loved It is then from the knowledge of Jesus having compassion and the faith that God will fill his people with himself That St. Paul breaks out in a song of praise that is one of the more glorious worded songs in all of Scripture. How is it one may ask that God can do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think? The answer is that God, by definition, is that by which nothing greater can be conceived. Thus He can do those things that we cannot conceive. He is the Alpha and the Omega. He is all-powerful, all-knowing, and in all places at all times. Consider that you can ask for every good thing you have ever experienced, and God can do above that. You can think of or imagine things beyond your experience, and God can do above that. You can imagine good things that are beyond your ability to name, and God can do above that. Hear what Charles Spurgeon had to say about Paul's language. Quote, he, Paul, has instructed here in the Greek an expression which is altogether his own. No language was powerful enough for the apostle, I mean for the Holy Spirit speaking through the apostle. For very often Paul has to coin words and phrases to shadow shadow forth his meaning, and here is one. He is able to do exceeding abundantly, so abundantly that he it exceeds measure and description. End quote. While name it-claimant preachers want to use such phrasing as a defense for why God should do our bidding and why we should ask for worldly goods. We are to recognize that God has already done more than we can ask or imagine. For many of us, we didn't ask for or imagine our salvation. Well, being dead in our sin, we didn't know we needed God or that we were even lost until he dropped the scales from our eyes and showed us the cold, dark hearts that we had. That we are presently experiencing the love of God and the love of being in God's family is also more than we have asked for or imagined, and aren't we grateful for it? According to the power that works in us. This means that not only is God not far off from us, but he is within us and working to make us holy. When we are baptized, when we confess Jesus as our Savior, it is then that God starts a work within us to make us more and more into His image. He doesn't wait until we are in heaven to purify us, but he does so now and continues as we cooperate with him. The things Paul prayed for in the previous verses, spiritual strength, the indwelling of Jesus, experiential knowledge of God's love, and the fullness of God. All of it belongs to us as children of God in the present. However, they must be received by believing prayer And can be furthered in the lives of others by our prayers for them. And finally, to him be glory in the church by Jesus Christ. This is the only fitting response to this great God. And we emphasize that it is to be done in the church. It is to be done in every age of the church. This is where we are to see ourselves as connected to the church historic for what has been done in the past by the church, giving glory to God. It's also to be done in the present and the future. I once again emphasize how important tradition can be, for they connect us with the church of the past age and allow us to be a link for the church in the future. What Paul's doxology shows is how the love of God, understood and applied to the Christian life, results in expressions of beauty. Beauty in our individual lives and in our corporate life. Beloved churches sing better when they corporately receive the love of God The countenance of an individual, Christian, brightens and endures when the love of God is fully received. All of us need more beauty in our lives, and to experience it, to experience beauty inwardly and outwardly, is to experience and believe in the love of God. Through Jesus Christ. Amen. Let us pray. Gracious and merciful God, the depth and the power of St. Paul's words we recognize to be truly inspired by knowing the love of Christ, the compassion of Christ. His desire for us to be healed and whole and full. For this heart, we thank you. May our hearts be full and may our Beauty increase as we dwell upon the love you have for us. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Take the lesser seat
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. This sermon we will be looking at Ephesians chapter four and Luke chapter fourteen In May of 1991, Michael Jordan, the great basketball player for the Chicago Bulls, had won his first NBA championship. While also winning the MVP of the same championship series and being named the MVP of the entire NBA for the 1990 and 91 season. He was wealthy beyond most of our dreams, along with being the most recognized athlete in the world. Just after winning the NBA Championship, Jordan appeared on the skit comedy show Saturday Night Live. The most memorable of the skits was the one he did with Al Franken, when Al Franken was funny. Where Franken played a self-esteem counselor named Stuart Smalley. Stuart Smalley was the host of a show called Daily Affirmations And on that show, he welcomed as a guest the great Michael Jordan. The highlight of the skit was when the host instructed Michael Jordan to look into a mirror and talk to himself, repeating the words, I am good enough, I am smart enough, and doggone it, people like me. The great irony was first that the character, Stuart Smalley, was so very insecure that he was in no place to give anyone counsel about self-esteem And of course, the greatest irony was that Michael Jordan would need a self-affirmation conversation with himself. And what is ironic today is that such self-affirmation is being touted as mentally healthy within Christian circles. There are self-affirmation slogans you would speak to others, such as, you are good enough. You are enough. Others you speak to yourself, such as, I am an overcomer. I can do all things. And this doozy, I am my own superhero. What is unfortunate is that Christians are satisfied with such slogans instead of being satisfied with what God has said about them. And not seeing the conflict of such statements as, I can do all things, as it comes in conflict with St. Paul saying, I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me. What I hope for all of us to see is how m such self-affirmation not only comes in conflict with what God's Word says. But also carries a spirit of narcissism that is contrasted with the biblical ideal that all who follow Christ Jesus are to die to themselves. While putting the needs of others before their own. As we look at Ephesians chapter 4, verses 1 through 6. We remember that Paul spent three chapters spelling out in glorious detail all that God did for us and noting that he did it freely by his grace. Now he brings a call for Christians to live rightly, but only after explaining what God has done for us. He says we are to walk worthy of the calling with which you are called The apostle gives Christians such instruction again directly after describing God's work that He did for us to motivate us, to motivate us by that work. If we are not serving and obeying, then we are not grasping what God has done. The idea is that we don't walk worthy so that God will love us. But we walk worthy because He already has loved us. Our walk is how we live. How we live our lives each day. And we are to walk each day with all, he says, lowliness and gentleness. A worthy walk before God will be marked by lowliness and gentleness Which is not a selfish desire to defend our own rights and advance our own agenda Consider that before Christianity, the word lowliness always had a bad association to it. In the minds of many, it still does But for the Christian, it is a glorious virtue exemplified by Christ Jesus Himself It means that we can be happy and content when we are not in control, when we are not steering things our own way. When practiced as Jesus did it, it is a major part of our witness to the world lowliness. In our lowliness we are to be long-suffering, bearing with one another We need this so that the inevitable wrongs that occur between people in God's family will not work against God's purpose of bringing all things together in Jesus. Long suffering goes against a dominant spirit of our age that calls Christians to quit on one another. John Chrysostom defined long-suffering as the spirit that has power to take revenge but never does. It is a characteristic of a forgiving, generous heart. And long-suffering is to naturally spill out of us because God is so very long-suffering toward us. A result of long suffering is endeavoring to keep the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace. This humble, forgiving attitude towards each other naturally fulfills this gift of unity of spirit. This unity is a natural byproduct of being ruled and led by the Holy Spirit. But what must a Christian do to have unity in spirit? We must realize that we do not create such unity. God never commands us to create unity among believers. He has created unity. His spirit of unity. Our duty is to recognize it and keep it. And this is a spiritual spiritual unity, not necessarily a structural or denominational unity. But that of the Spirit. It is more easily seen in the quick fellowship among Christians of different races, nationalities, languages, and economic classes. We can also understand this unity of spirit by understanding what it is not. In a sermon on this text, Charles Spurgeon pointed out of the things that the text does not say. It does not say to endeavor to maintain the unity of evil, the unity of superstition, or the unity of spiritual tyranny. It does not say endeavoring to keep up your ecclesiastical arrangements for centralization. And we should also say what this unity is. It is centered on the person of Jesus Christ in the complete revelation of who he was and what he did, as stated in the creeds. To center it on anything else is not to be Christian, but something else that is irredeemable and lost. Next is described the unity where it factually exists. He says, there is one body and one spirit. We have unity because of what we share in common. In Jesus we share one body, which is to say both the body of the church and the body of Jesus in the sacrament. We also share one spirit, one hope of our calling, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one Father. The danger is that each of these can be used to divide. When we are one body And yet we won't submit to certain ecclesiastical authorities because we simply don't want to. We are one spirit, and yet we disagree as to what extent the spirit is going to govern our lives. We are of one hope, with many not understanding heaven proper. We are of one calling with some not accepting the doctrine of election. We are of one Lord with some who call themselves Christians, not allowing Jesus to rule them morally. We are of one faith with some rejecting the doctrine of Solafidae, faith alone. We are of one baptism and yet some Do not recognize baptisms of others because of mode or age. We are of one father, and yet some prefer having a woman lead them. We have a great distance to go to truly know or experience the unity that is described by St. Paul. But the lack of unity, I lament, does not displace the truth that there is unity of God's people, prepared for them and existing for them, but requiring each person to submit to it. Beloved, there is great power in seeing one another as having God within. I may not like what you just said to me, but if I believe God is within you, I will always love you and forgive you. I may not agree with where you stand on vaccines, on masks, on public schools, but if I know God is within you, I will love you and overlook what we see differently. I may not understand your marital dynamics, your child rearing practices, your choice of profession, or the friends you choose. But if I agree that God's within you, I will love you as part of God's family, a family that will be forever. Again, there is great power in seeing people as having God within. We now turn to Luke chapter fourteen, and we see the social dynamics that are described. They are not of unity. They are not of love. And most certainly not seeing God within one another. Luke sets the scene as being in the house of a Pharisee. We know that the majority of Pharisees, or the Pharisees as a group, were greatly suspicious and jealous of Jesus. Jesus had garnered a great deal of popularity, which came along with influence amongst the people, and it was the same type of popularity and influence the Pharisees wanted for themselves. Luke tells us that lawyers were also present. The Bible uses the term lawyer in a religious sense. These men were scholars of the law of Moses. We also know them as scribes. Thus the men who influenced the Jews religiously were present, Pharisees and scribes, present for a meal after a worship meeting in a local synagogue, for we are told that this took place on the Sabbath. They likely would have been at a synagogue and then come together for a meal. The setting also includes a guest or a crash visitor, we don't know which, who had drops C. The term Luke used was a technically was a technical word in the Greek, hydro picos, which we would expect because Luke was a physician. In general, it is a swelling of the body, usually caused by heart failure. Jesus quickly sizes up the situation and recognizes it as a setup. And so he takes the case to them rather than waiting for them to take it to him. He asks: Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath? No one speaks. No one answers. Of course they don't. They don't see God in him, and he knows God is not within them. If God was within them, they would not put Jesus to a test. The issue for the Pharisees and scribes was their understanding of healing being an act of work. And as we know, the Sabbath was a day of rest, not a day on which to work. To be sure, not to break the Sabbath law, the Pharisees had come up with a list of actions That could not be practiced on the Sabbath, for such acts would be defined as work. Such laws developed into a great list called the 39 Creative Activities And they included planting and reaping, spinning and sowing, trapping and killing, riding and erasing, only to mention a few. A reason for such a list is the perception the Pharisees and Scribes had about the law of Moses, which was that it was written to be served as opposed to being written to serve God's people. Jesus does not respond to their silence, but instead focuses on the ill man first. Luke simply says Jesus took him and healed him. Next, Jesus provides two common analogies that cause continued silence from those testing him. An accident such as a donkey or an ox falling into a pit could be imagined by all that were present. These were domesticated animals that wandered and did not always recognize the next dangerous step Because such animals were expensive and very useful for a family, it was necessary for them to be rescued, even on a Sabbath. The logic of Jesus is response-proof. If the life value of a donkey or an ox is great enough to do an act of work on the Sabbath, how much more is the life value and healing value of a human being? And none of this testing, mind you, of Jesus includes the accepted reality that Jesus has the power to heal. Evidently, such healing occurred so much it was no longer a marvel to them. But Jesus wants to dig a little further into their consciences, into their souls. The souls of these self-righteous men. What he gets to is what is at the heart of them making these lists, what is at the heart of them testing Jesus. What is at the heart of the problem, the sin that they have not overcome is pride. It is personal selfish pride. They think they are good enough, smart enough, and doggone it people like them. To reveal this pride, Jesus describes an event that they had all experienced. They are to imagine that they are at a wedding feast, and at wedding feasts in the ancient Near East, the closer you sat to the person putting on the feast, the more honorable a place you had been given. The advice of Jesus is not to expect to be honored, but instead to take the place of the least honored. In other words, be humble. Take the lowest place, and if you are asked to sit at a more honorable place, all the more happy you will be. This teaching matches the words of St. James, who said in his epistle, humble thyself in the sight of the Lord, and he, God, will lift you up. Put another way, Christians are not to lift themselves up, but are instead to wait until God does it. Lifting ourselves up, proving our own self-esteem, is speaking only empty words that do not change our inner struggle, which is pride. Self-esteem, as it is defined today, is greatly deceiving, for we are told in this therapeutic age that we don't think of ourselves enough when the truth is we think about ourselves too much. The downtrodden remain downtrodden because they are obsessed with how downtrodden they are The insecure remain insecure because they are comparing themselves to others and concluding that they are not measuring up while failing to see how obsessed they are with thinking about how they don't measure up To all of this, Jesus provides us this maxim to live by: whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. But you say that you don't struggle with pride as others do. Well, such a conclusion is prideful. Let us do some self-examination. What is it within you that refuses to learn something new? Whatever it is, the root of it is pride. What would you call that feeling of resistance to new practices while concluding that your old way of doing things is good enough? I would call it pride. What is it within all of us that doesn't want to admit that we are wrong, or that doesn't want to admit a mistake, or doesn't want others to know of our ignorance? Or becomes embarrassed because of weight gain, or a torn dress, or from taking a tumble. You guessed it. It's pride. It is sinful, selfish, personal pride. And the only answer is to repent of the sin as pride and to take the lesser seat. It is to walk in this world with an attitude and perspective that sees self as lowly and meek. It is to be long-suffering and forbearing to fellow Christians. It is to endeavor toward unity centered on the goodness of Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. There is no other answer. There is no savior named Tony Robbins. For those of you under 30, Tony Robbins is a famous positive attitude speaker. For Christians to be in the world and not of the world, which means to be a product of the world, Christians need to take the lesser seat. We need to embrace humility. Thirteen years ago, Google released a searchable database of five point two million books published Since 1500. It's a long time. Researchers discovered that between 1960 and 2008 Nineteen sixty and two thousand eight, individualistic words increasingly overshadowed communal ones. I instead of we. The usage of kindness and helpfulness had dropped 56% in books. 56%. Similarly, modesty and humbleness dropped 52%. Our language reflects our culture. And no doubt in 2021 it's gotten a lot worse. Consider the person of Jesus. He was born lowly, lowly of a state. He owned no property. He had no offspring. He had no earthly wealth. He did not have a place to rest his head. At his most difficult hour, his closest friends abandoned him, even some denying they knew him. But the effect of his life that he has had on the world, on the many lives that have accepted him and rejected him, is measureless. He changed the world and continues to do so. And it all started with him taking on the form of a servant, taking the lesser seat. Of course, I do not know what troubles your life finds. I don't know all the relationships that are strained. I don't know the sins that you are trying to overcome or the feelings you are trying to heal, but I know, and you know, the power of humility. Be humble and let the Lord lift you up. Amen. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God, as we see the sins of the Pharisees and Scribes and the pride that they displayed. And how it was a barrier that would not allow them to see Jesus as who he was. And we see the call of St. Paul for us to think upon ourselves as lowly and to be long-suffering. We embrace it. We embrace the call to be humble. And we acknowledge that it is the only way to your kingdom. And so build us up. Help us to be humble that we in the end might be lifted up. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Jesus as Judge
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. You may be seated. I want to commend my oldest son for his reading this morning. Although he read the wrong passage. We are looking at 1 Corinthians chapter 1, verses 4 through 8, and then Matthew 22. It is likely that you have not heard of the name Paul of Samusara. Samusara was a small town in southeast Turkey. Paul was born of humble beginnings, but rose in the ranks of the Christian church, being made a bishop in 260 A. D. Paul of Salmusada had a pupil by the name of Lucian of Antioch. Lucian was also from the town of Salmusada. Lucian was known for his scholarship and was ordained as presbyter within the Christian Church with the date unknown. There was a student of Lucian that you may have heard of. His name was Arius. As a seminary student, we are taught about Arius, about Arianism. And the Nicene Council and the beginnings of the Nicene Creed, with no mention of Paul of Samosada or Lucian of Antioch. But new teachings and bad doctrine have a beginning, and the teachings of Arius that were eventually labeled heretical Began with Paul of Salmusada, and the reason behind his teachings we will address in a little time. Allow me to remind you of the teachings of Arius. Arius and his followers believed that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, who was given birth by God the Father, with the difference That the Jesus as the Son of God did not always exist, but was made God's Son within time. By God the Father. Therefore, Jesus was not co-eternal with God the Father. In simpler terms, Jesus had a beginning, whereas God the Father never did. Why Jesus needs to be understood to not have a beginning, we will soon see. Let us now look at the two texts that were our epistle reading from 1 Corinthians chapter 1. And the gospel reading, respectively. So, first the letter written to the Corinthians by St. Paul. The purpose was addressing a number of sins that were continuing in the church But before St. Paul gets to those sins, he begins on a positive note. As he is able to see What the grace of God has done to these Christians in Corinth, and if you know what Corinth was like, God had to do a great work. He was positive about their Christian faith and their love, and he wants to build upon it. St. Paul puts an emphasis on the origin of the grace that they show, thus an emphasis on Jesus Christ in them. Jesus Christ truly does change lives. And it is especially evident that lives are changed when a person knows nothing of God and is then surprised by the truth of who God is and thus who Jesus is and the forgiveness and love only He can provide Thus everything changes. It did for me personally, and I know it does for you continually. Being enriched by Jesus includes all utterances, which is what we confess to believe and how we articulate our faith. Knowledge includes our understanding about God, which also implies our doctrine or our core beliefs about God. And because these Christians articulated the right things about what Jesus had done and who he is and what he has done with them, all of it confirms that they are Christian. These are God's people. The statement and confirmation continues as Saint Paul wants the Corinthian Christians To be confident that anything they need to continue in their Christian faith will be provided for them They are to continue in the faith while awaiting the revelation of Jesus, which is another way of saying awaiting his second coming. There is no question that first century Christians believed Jesus was going to return in their lifetime. St. Paul believed that, and that is what he taught his fellow Christians to believe. Christians are to always be ready for the second coming of Jesus, no matter how long ago it was promised. At the mention of the revelation of Jesus, Saint Paul again uses the word confirm, which means in this context, to sustain. It is a stamp of guarantee, similar to what St. Paul says to the Philippians when he describes the good work God is doing in them, and that God will be faithful to complete it. And the stamp of guarantee is to give them confidence that they will be blameless, which is to say, without sin, in the day of Jesus' second coming. Their blamelessness, but our blamelessness and the blamelessness of every Christian is because of the atonement of Jesus made for our sins. and our confession of our sins so that the atonement can be applied to each of us personally. But why should anyone be concerned about being blameless in the day of the Lord Jesus Christ? After all, he is just a man. We will come back to that point as well. Our gospel reading begins in Matthew 22, after Jesus has put the Sadducees in their place. I remind you that there was a dispute between the Sadducees who only looked at the first five books of the Bible as authoritative. And seeing no doctrine of the resurrection, they did not believe in a life after death. The Pharisees saw differently, believing that all the books of the Old Testament were pres that we presently have To be authoritative. And thus seeing testimonies of the life and death and life and death in the words of King David and in the prophets, they see that there is life after death. When challenging the Sadducees, Jesus uses just the book of Genesis, a book they accept. To show that God is a God of the living. And that means that the patriarchs continue to live. Thus there is life after death. Now one would think that by putting the Sadducees in their place, that the Pharisees would be appreciative. They were not. Matthew tells us that they heard what Jesus did, and their response was to test him once again. The greatest commandment question has been asked prior to this instance, with Jesus asking a scribe who answered it correctly. Now, I think some background is helpful to know why such a question was popular, which is the greatest commandment According to rabbinical teaching, there are more than six hundred precepts or laws in the law of Moses, with the understanding that a considerable number of them could not be observed. So which were the absolute obligation and which were not? The rabbinic schools made a distinction between what they called heavy and light commandments. As though some were of less importance than others, and thus some might be neglected with impunity. Some even taught that if a man rightly selected some great precept to observe, he might safely disregard the rest of the law. This was the kind of doctrine which St. James addressed when he said, Whosoever shall keep the whole law and yet stumble in one point, he is becoming guilty of all. Thus, the Pharisees may have desired to discover whether Jesus knew and sanctioned these rabbinical distinctions. Such was the possible mindset of those who wanted him to answer the question. The point of the answer Jesus gives should be quite obvious, but it should again be stated. When you love something with all that you are, you are not going to go against that something. And in fact, you are going to do all that you can to honor and protect it. But God is more than a something, he is more than an it. He is three in one and is wholly relatable. For us to love with all of our heart, soul, mind, and strength is to be in right relationship with God. And that's what God desires most. We are created, after all, to enjoy him forever. He wants to be our God and he wants us to be his people. And as his people, his children, he wants us to love one another just as aggressively and faithfully as we love him. And when we love one another with all that we are, we also forgive immediately and think positively of one another, expecting the best to come out of one another. It is true that such standards of love will only be fully fulfilled in heaven, but before we get there, we are to work and practice loving God and loving our fellow man. Instead of Jesus being on the spot, he decides to turn the tables and places the Pharisees on the spot. Jesus knows that they're looking for the Messiah, the Christ, so Jesus asks them, whose son is he? Or who is the father of this Christ? They think they have the answer, for they have been taught that the Messiah will come from the lineage of King David. In this they are correct, but Jesus points out the unstated Why would King David speak in the Psalter with such phrasing as, the Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand till I make your enemies a footstool? The conflict is stated. David's son cannot be his lord in any manner that is humanly possible. What Jesus is intimating for those who have ears to hear is that he, as the Messiah, is eternal. He is the Lord of David, and will be seated at the right hand of the Father. It can also be read as follows: The Lord Yahweh said to my Lord the Messiah, Sit at my right hand. Such was a prophecy respecting the exaltation of Jesus. To be raised at the right hand of a king was significant of favor, trust, and power. Authority. And that power, that authority included returning to judge both the quick, the living, and the dead. Thus the equality of Jesus to the Father is here displayed. The Father had already pronounced That all glory would be given to his son, and he makes it clear here that all authority will be given to his son as well Jesus is clearly said to be co-creator with the Father, as described in the opening of John's Gospel, and in the words of St. Paul to the Colossians. And here in Matthew's gospel and in St. Paul's words to the Corinthians, we are to know that Jesus has the power to redeem his people and cast his enemies into the eternal fire. What we see in both 1 Corinthians reading and in Matthew reading is the place Jesus has to exercise authority in terms of redemption and eternal judgment. This is the scary Jesus. This is the Jesus with feet like brass and eyes like fire. This isn't the comfortable Jesus who is portrayed by some as a pal or a buddy, someone you can snuggle close to. No, Jesus on the throne with the nations before him, ready and willing to lift his people up while throwing down all who oppose him. That is this Jesus This is a Jesus not often described in a 21st century church, but it should be as it once was. Some speculate that the rise of Mariology, the veneration of Mary, grew in the Middle Ages. Because Jesus was portrayed as an eternal judge rather than a loving Savior. Mary seems to soften the gospel for many who only understood Jesus as the final judge. It is the opposite today, however, as the modern church has softened the gospel by not underlining Jesus as their final judge. But what danger? What danger is there in not understanding Jesus as the divine final judge? I have one example, and it is the character of Paul of Samosata. Who you should recall began the string of false teachings that led Arius being excommunicated and his teachings being labeled heretical. Paul of Salmosada did not believe Jesus to be co-eternal with the Father, and thus did not see him as the final judge. And Paul of Salmusada was also a money-grabbing charlatan who used the church and its people for personal gain. He was described by English the English historian Edward Gibbons in the following manner, and I quote, The wealth of that prelate, Paul of Samusada. Was a sufficient evidence of his guilt, since it was neither derived from the inheritance of his father, nor acquired by the art of honest industry. But Paul considered the service of the church as a very lucrative profession. His ecclesiastical jurisdiction was venal and rapacious He exhorted frequent contributions from the most opulent of the faithful and converted to his own use a considerable part of the public revenue. By his pride and luxury, the Christian religion was rendered odious in the eyes of the Gentiles. His council chamber and his throne, the splendor with which he appeared in public, the suppliant crowd who solicited his attention. The multitude of letters and petitions to which he dictated his answers, and the perpetual hurry of the business in which he was involved were circumstances much better suited to the state of a civil magistrate Than to the humility of a primitive bishop. When he harangued his people from the pulpit, Paul affected the figurative style of the theatrical gestures of an Asiatic sophist. While the cathedral resounded with the loudest and most extravagant acclamations in the praise of his divine eloquence, against those who resisted his power or refused to flatter his vanity The prelate of Antioch was arrogant, rigid, and inexorable, but he relaxed the discipline and lavished the treasures of the church on his dependent clergy, who were permitted to imitate their master in the gratification of every sensual appetite. For Paul indulged himself very freely in the pleasures of the table. And he had received into the Episcopal Palace two young and beautiful women as the constant companions of his leisure moments. End quote I ask you if such things could be said about a person who truly feared God No person being given such responsibilities within the church who truly believed Jesus was returning to separate the sheep and the goats. To open the heavenly gates for his people while also casting the guilty into eternal fire, no person believing such would live in such open sin. Now I recognize that it may be said that there is no way of knowing if the false beliefs of Paul Osamusara were the direct cause of his chosen life and debauchery. A direct cause I accept cannot be proven. But because we know our fallen natures, we know how much our theology affects our living. How we think about God affects our behavior. The callet that we prayed today in light of these verses Knows the connection to our temptation. It asks that the God, the good Lord, would grant us grace. To withstand the temptations of the world, the flesh, and the devil, and that we might have pure hearts and minds to follow God. We need such prayers because when we do not take into account Jesus as both Savior and our judge, it is our tendency to focus on Jesus as Savior only. Jesus as Savior only makes us want to be forgiven of our sinful pleasures, but not delivered from them. Jesus as our judge increases our desire to want to be rid of our sins. In Florence, Italy, legend proclaims that it is physically impossible upon entering the Baptistry of San Giovanni Not to look up. Langdon, despite having been in this room many times, now felt the mystical pull of the space and let his gaze climb skyward to the ceiling. High, high overhead, the surface surface of the baptistry ochnical bulbs spanned more than eighty feet from side to side. It glistened and shimmered as if it were made of smoldering coals. Its burnished amber gold surface reflected the ambient light unevenly from more than a million smalty tiles Tiny ungrouted mosaic pieces, hand-cut from a glassy Cilicia glaze, which were arranged in six concentric rings in which the scenes from the Bible were depicted That's a passage from Dan Brown's Inferno. He is describing a mosaic in a church that actually exists. In that mosaic, Jesus is seated on the rims of paradise, stretching his hands to direct the separation between the righteous and the damned. And showing marks of his crucifixion. The position of the legs and feet, as well as the complex pleats in his dress, are highlighted by the glittering gilded mosaic pieces. And they make the Christ as judge daunting and majestic. At his sides, arranged in three parallel registers, are located two groups of angels Which carry the symbols of the passion and everything they need for the last judgment. They sound the trumpets of the apocalypse that wake up the mortals from the tomb. In the second register are two long benches decorated as thrones on which are seated the Virgin Mary, the Saint Giovanni, Batista and the Twelve Apostles, each of them with a written book with many different alphabets to symbolize their evangelation of the world. Among the saints are heads of angels looking out from behind the backrests. The lower register shows the representation of paradise and then hell. The resurrected souls are immediately taken by angels or devils. The righteous are pushed toward a group that, in gratitude toward God, is accompanied by a large angel holding a scroll toward the heavenly Jerusalem. You can see that another angel opens the door to a little man, dragging him by the hand, while the heavenly city, three great patriarchs, hold the sweet breads in their lap And the heavenly city grows extraordinary and colorful with plants, symbolizing by a band as little green meadows dotted with flowers. Among the righteous is the first row we can see a king and a Dominican friar, followed by three virgins and a bishop. In contrast, ugly devils with black wings of a bat push the damned to the right, where they jostle each other, trampling and covering their eyes and their mouths in disgust. The representation of hell is dominated by the great horned Satan on a throne inflamed, nibbling on a man, while two snakes that are snapping two of the damned come out of his ears. This is the depiction of Jesus as judge. That the Christians of the Middle Ages understood. It was not a balanced depiction, but one that is sore needed today. Jesus is our Savior, even our friend. But he is also coming to judge both the living and the dead. And our response, the only appropriate response, is Amen. Come, Lord Jesus. Let us pray. Gracious Heavenly Father, we do want to be a balanced people. We do accept Jesus as our Savior. Well, we want to also accept him as our final judge. May both of those things be before our consciences, be before us as a as a congregation. That we might accept both as true and very hopeful, that your will might be done, and that the enemy might be put down and the righteous raised to eternity. This we pray because we know it is your will. In Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Choose to put it on
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. May be seated. You want to turn in your Bibles to Ephesians chapter 4. We're looking at verses 17 through 24. Ephesians chapter 4, verses 17 through 24. Last Sunday, a news organization interviewed a woman who is being called the Facebook whistleblower. Believe me, I am no defender of Facebook or any of its social media outlets. Get that straight. I am no defender. I think it is obvious that such social media can be a danger to many, especially the young of mind, who put so much importance in what their peers Think or say of them. When a young girl posts a picture of herself and gets critiqued or gets only a few people to push that like button Such can be devastating to her self-awareness. That companies would take advantage of young persons' frailties is upsetting and it is immoral. But I had several problems with the interview of the Facebook whistleblower. She started off saying that Facebook Repeatedly chose what was good for Facebook as opposed to what was good for the public in general. But she never defined what was good for the public Consider that the same argument could be made against the Mars Incorporation, who put profits before the good of people. By producing candy bars that make them profitable while also making us fat. There has been no whistleblower from Mars Incorporated She also accused Facebook of allowing hateful and polarizing rhetoric. This may be true But hateful rhetoric was never defined, and neither was polarizing rhetoric. In fact, it's very likely That if you were to post on social media that Jesus is the way, the truth, and the life, and no one can come to the Father but through him. That she and many others would label such rhetoric as both hateful and polarizing. Again, I am in no way defending any social media outlet. In no way. My simple point is that there is very little critical thinking going on today, and I want that not to be true of Christians. We of all people need to be critical thinkers with our ears and minds doubting what the world is saying and comparing it to the standard of what the Holy Scriptures are saying We are going to dissect Paul's words to the Ephesians that were from our epistle lesson, only we are focusing on, again, verses 17 through 24. St. Paul has been describing the church as a body, and where our reading picks up is his use of a metaphor being a new man instead of an old man. Thus we are to put off the old man as if he is a garment worn too often. But to know what to take off is important. And so the apostle describes what that old man is and what we should take off. He begins with, therefore, which makes the connection not only with the glorious spiritual privilege laid out from Ephesians chapter 1 through Ephesians chapter 3. But also with the high call of a unified, mature body, as described in Ephesians 4, verses 1 through 6. Because of this high calling, he says we should walk, which is to live, in a different way than the world walks and lives around us. There is an ever-present temptation for Christians to display to the world that we really aren't different after all. This is usually a misguided effort to gain the world's respect or approval This must be resisted at all costs because the goal in itself is both undesirable and unachievable. Paul says we are to no longer walk as the rest of the Gentiles walk. The Gentile walk is characterized by, he says, the futility of the mind. In the end, their thinking is futile. Why? Because their understanding is darkened. Why? Because they are alienated from the life of God. This does not mean that mankind in his rebellion against God is not capable of mighty intellectual achievements. Of course it is. By God's grace it is. What it does mean is that all such achievements fall short of true wisdom, because the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Thus, with no fear of God, there is no true wisdom. As one commentator said regarding the word futility, quote, the thought is not that unregenerated minds are empty, it is that they are filled with things that lead to nothing. As Christians, we have a proper way and place to walk or live. It is as if Jesus turned us around and put us in the right direction. And now we are to walk and progress in that direction. And yes, we get lost at times, and we need to be put back on the right road, and so we confess our sins, and Jesus is gracious to us time and time again. St. Paul continues his description of the old man or the unbelieving man, saying, Because of the blindness of their heart From this we learn that fundamentally the ignorance and lack of understanding of humanity that does not believe all of it is a heart problem. It is shown not only in a foolish denial of God, but also in moral failures They are listed here as lewdness, uncleanness, greediness The unbelievers, we are told, who are the old man Paul speaks of, were either atheists or they believed in gods who were themselves immoral. Therefore, in their denial of the true God, they denied any standard of morality, and in doing so, they are without excuse. Paul next describes the unbelieving as people being past feeling, which has the idea of a person's skin becoming callous. No longer sensitive to pain, such as understood as the logical result of the blindness of their heart. Blindness can also be understood here as hardening. And this ancient Greek word is used medically to denote the callus formed when a bone has been fractured and then reset. Such callous can be even harder than the bone itself. Lewdness is sin that flaunts itself. Throwing off all restraint and having no sense of shame, no sense of fear. Uncleanness is a broad word, mostly with reference to sexual impropriety. The phrase in verse 20, you have not so learned Christ, is a repetition of the idea. That shows that putting on the new man has a strong aspect of learning and education. You have heard him and have been taught by him as the truth is in Jesus, says St. Paul. This is what he means to be renewed in the spirit of your mind, as directed in verse 23. Thus before we knew Jesus Or let Jesus in our lives, we did not think right. We did not critically examine the world and our place in the world. We are allowed, excuse me, we allowed false teachers in our minds and we believed them. We listened to entertainers tell us what is most important in life and we trusted them We allowed news sources to tell us what reality is and we didn't question them. We heard the psychotherapy world tell us that self should be priority and we allowed that message to comfort us. But what did Jesus say about what is most important in life? Or what reality is, or what our personal priorities should be? St. Paul says that we Christians have heard Jesus and that we have been taught by him. And thus the plea by St. Paul is to go and see what Jesus said. Jesus said that there would be false teachers who have the sole purpose of leading God's people astray. He said that seeking the kingdom of God and the righteousness of God was the most important thing to do in our lives. He said that reality is only possible to realize when you put our faith in him as Savior and Lord. He said that our priority in life individually is to glorify God in everything that we do If any teaching, if any doctrine, if any proposal says anything in opposition to what Jesus has said, it is to be rejected and marked as false and a lie. Of course, our Christian life must go beyond head knowledge, but it must absolutely include head knowledge and influence our whole manner of living. What we know should influence how we live. This is not just in the sense of knowing facts, but the ability to set our minds on the right things as Jesus has taught them. Beloved, this is so fundamental to the Christian life that Christian maturity is described as renewing of the mind. If you want to know how you're growing in Christ, is your mind being renewed? But head knowledge is more than just knowing about Jesus. For just knowing about Jesus isn't enough to keep us pure. As Charles Spurgeon, the great preacher, said, quote, so if you want to know the Lord Jesus Christ, you must live with him. First, he must himself speak to you, and afterward you must abide in him. He must be the choice companion of your morning hours. He must be with you throughout the day And with him, you must also close the night. And as often as you may wake during the night, you must say, When I awake, I am still with thee. The metaphorical language of putting off the old man and putting on the new man informs us that to do so is a matter of the will. To put off the old man and to put on the new man has the same idea of putting off or putting on a set of clothes. The idea is to change into a different kind of conduct. Think of a prisoner who is released from prison but still wears his prison clothes and acts like a prisoner and not a free man. The first thing to tell that person would be that they should put on new clothes So just as putting on different clothes will change the way you think about yourself and see yourself, even so putting on a different conduct will start to change your attitudes. This means that we shouldn't wait to feel like the new man, but we should put on the new man It is the individual will of every Christian to put on the new man and to do so get this every day. It's an everyday choice. Fundamentally, Paul says that for the Christian, there must be a break with the past. Jesus isn't merely added to our life, but the old life dies, and Jesus within us becomes our new life. In verse 24, Paul says, put on the new man, which was created according to God, in true righteousness and holiness. Thus, this new man is a new creation, just as Paul described to the Corinthians, where he said Old things have passed away and all things have become new in Christ. We become closer and closer to how God intends us to be. This new man, this new person is created according to the image of Jesus, and thus it is instinctively righteous, it is instinctively holy. Now this is again in contrast to the old man who is the person inherited from Adam who instinctively rebels against God. My first Christian album that I purchased after being renewed by Christ at the age of 18 was by a group called Petra. And on that album titled Never Say Die, ironically was a titled song Killing the Old Man. So which is it? Do I Never Say Die or Do I Kill the Old Man? The lyrics are as follows. I think it's gone far enough. I can't take it anymore. I've got to even up the score. Before he sweeps me off the floor. I've really got to find a way of taking care of him for good. I know he'd kill me if he could So I'll nail him to the wood. Killing my old man. You may not understand. He's a terrible man. Got to make a stand and kill the old man. Every time that I think he's gone and I finally won, he just just keeps coming back. Puts me on the run. I think I'd better do it now. Get my hammer and a nail. Pray to God that I won't fail, lest he keep me in jail, and I don't want to stay in jail. Killing my old man. You may not understand. He's a terrible man. Got to make a stand and kill the old man Sounds right, doesn't it? That is what we should be doing is killing the old man, correct? Actually, no. Petra had some nice songs, but their theology wasn't quite informed. What Christians are to understand, how we are to think, is what the Holy Scriptures say. And what they say is that the old man, your old man, my old man, has already been killed. Hear what St. Paul wrote to the Christians at Rome. He said, Knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, Jesus, that the body of sin might be done away with. This means that the power of sin, which is that that holds on to us individually as sin, is our sin nature. It was overcome by the death of Jesus, for he was the perfect sacrifice to satisfy the wrath of God, and therefore all persons that put their faith in him also have their old man. Our sinful nature, inherited by Adam, crucified also. Thus, the only life the old man has is what we give him. What we give him when we don't take him off and fail to put on the new man that Christ Jesus has made for us. And the truth is, no one puts the old man on us except ourselves. We put him on. He can be like a comfortable old pair of shoes that you can't throw away because of how well they mold to your feet. They are ugly, they are worn out, and useless, but they are too comfortable to be rid of. So it is with our old man. He is too comfortable to be rid of. We return to him when life is stressful. We put him back on when current relationships are strained, and when we need to protect our emotional state. We put them on when we are insecure in a new job, or a new school, or with new people We put them back on when the newsman tells us that all is not well and it is not safe to leave your house. We put them back on when we are told to fear death more than to love life. We put them back on. Wow. That's preaching. We put them back on when the newswoman tells us it is more dangerous to go to church than it is to go to the grocery store We put them back on when we trust doctors over the Word of God, much like Israel trusted in horses and chariots over God's promises. But that person who bows to the stresses in life, who hides from emotional pain, who hides from change, who believes every word of a news anchor, who fears death, that person is not who you are. It is not who anyone is who follows Jesus Christ. Each of us has been made new, and thus we can put on our new person. And again, it is a choice we make. We can put on the new person Jesus made, the person who has all had all things made new. And we can overcome the stresses of life and even see them as challenges to be conquered. We can embrace emotional pain as a means by which we mature. Our new man can embrace changes because we now see them as blessings specific to us by the hand of God Himself. Our new man can critically think in terms of what media tells us, and thus we can discern when it is right to be cautious and when it is right to obey God over man. And here is the important point. Once again, you must put on the new man every day. Because the old man remains with us until heaven is our home, and we have been given new bodies that will never die. Thus it is easy to return to our old ways, to return to faithless days, to return to who we once were. No one who speaks the truth has said it is easy to follow Jesus Christ. The Christian road is narrow, having few that travel on it, and that means it's not easy. But it is it is the only road that leads to the heavenly shore. So put on the new man every morning and don't take him off. You need him. You need him to walk the narrow road. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God This metaphor that St. Paul has developed, we easily see ourselves. We know when that old man is calling us, we know when he tells us to put him on. The temptation is real for all of us. We confess it. But we want to be thankful to you each and every day that you've given us a new man, that you make us new each and every day. And with that hope and with that gratefulness, may we put him on and keep him on until you return to us. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

And on that album titled Never Say Die, ironically was a titled song Killing the Old Man. So which is it? Do I Never Say Die or Do I Kill the Old Man? The lyrics are as follows. I think it's gone far enough. I can't take it anymore. I've got to even up the score. Before he sweeps me off the floor. I've really got to find a way of taking care of him for good. I know he'd kill me if he could So I'll nail him to the wood. Killing my old man. You may not understand. He's a terrible man. Got to make a stand and kill the old man. Every time that I think he's gone and I finally won, he just just keeps coming back. Puts me on the run. I think I'd better do it now. Get my hammer and a nail. Pray to God that I won't fail, lest he keep me in jail, and I don't want to stay in jail. Killing my old man. You may not understand. He's a terrible man. Got to make a stand and kill the old man Sounds right, doesn't it? That is what we should be doing is killing the old man, correct? Actually, no. Petra had some nice songs, but their theology wasn't quite informed. What Christians are to understand, how we are to think, is what the Holy Scriptures say. And what they say is that the old man, your old man, my old man, has already been killed. Hear what St. Paul wrote to the Christians at Rome. He said, Knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, Jesus, that the body of sin might be done away with. This means that the power of sin, which is that that holds on to us individually as sin, is our sin nature. It was overcome by the death of Jesus, for he was the perfect sacrifice to satisfy the wrath of God, and therefore all persons that put their faith in him also have their old man. Our sinful nature, inherited by Adam, crucified also. Thus, the only life the old man has is what we give him. What we give him when we don't take him off and fail to put on the new man that Christ Jesus has made for us. And the truth is, no one puts the old man on us except ourselves. We put him on. He can be like a comfortable old pair of shoes that you can't throw away because of how well they mold to your feet. They are ugly, they are worn out, and useless, but they are too comfortable to be rid of. So it is with our old man. He is too comfortable to be rid of. We return to him when life is stressful. We put him back on when current relationships are strained, and when we need to protect our emotional state. We put them on when we are insecure in a new job, or a new school, or with new people We put them back on when the newsman tells us that all is not well and it is not safe to leave your house. We put them back on when we are told to fear death more than to love life. We put them back on. Wow. That's preaching. We put them back on when the newswoman tells us it is more dangerous to go to church than it is to go to the grocery store We put them back on when we trust doctors over the Word of God, much like Israel trusted in horses and chariots over God's promises. But that person who bows to the stresses in life, who hides from emotional pain, who hides from change, who believes every word of a news anchor, who fears death, that person is not who you are. It is not who anyone is who follows Jesus Christ. Each of us has been made new, and thus we can put on our new person. And again, it is a choice we make. We can put on the new person Jesus made, the person who has all had all things made new. And we can overcome the stresses of life and even see them as challenges to be conquered. We can embrace emotional pain as a means by which we mature. Our new man can embrace changes because we now see them as blessings specific to us by the hand of God Himself. Our new man can critically think in terms of what media tells us, and thus we can discern when it is right to be cautious and when it is right to obey God over man. And here is the important point. Once again, you must put on the new man every day. Because the old man remains with us until heaven is our home, and we have been given new bodies that will never die. Thus it is easy to return to our old ways, to return to faithless days, to return to who we once were. No one who speaks the truth has said it is easy to follow Jesus Christ. The Christian road is narrow, having few that travel on it, and that means it's not easy. But it is it is the only road that leads to the heavenly shore. So put on the new man every morning and don't take him off. You need him. You need him to walk the narrow road. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God This metaphor that St. Paul has developed, we easily see ourselves. We know when that old man is calling us, we know when he tells us to put him on. The temptation is real for all of us. We confess it. But we want to be thankful to you each and every day that you've given us a new man, that you make us new each and every day. And with that hope and with that gratefulness, may we put him on and keep him on until you return to us. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Game Time
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. If you'd like to turn in your Bibles to Ephesians chapter 6, we will be focusing on that reading this morning, Ephesians 6, 10 through 20. In John Milton's Paradise Lost, the backstory of Satan and his motivation is provided, which is, of course, speculation. But it is also believable. Satan attempts to make himself equal with God. But is unable to gather the following of angels he so desperately craves, God punishes him for his insurrection by creating hell as a place of punishment. Afterward, God creates the heavens and the earth as well as mankind and places Adam in a beautiful and awe-inspiring garden. Satan looks upon God's creation and the dwelling of Adam, and he becomes bitter and jealous. Adam is now his enemy because God's favor upon Adam. And I say it again to underline it. Adam is the enemy of Satan, not God. Satan then morphs himself into a serpent to surprise Eve in the garden and to tempt her to eat from one of the trees, which is forbidden. He succeeds and then succeeds in tempting her to fear that God will replace her with another. So she tempts Adam, and again the devil succeeds. What Milton does well with his speculation is show how, again, mankind, the family of Adam and Eve, is his enemy, the enemy of the devil. Again, God is not his enemy, but mankind is his enemy. But we know that the devil has first been defeated by the Heavenly Father by kicking him out of heaven. and then by the Son of Man who was obedient unto death, death upon the cross. His only means now to have victory in any manner is over the souls of mankind. Thus, if we are the enemy of the devil, he has made himself an enemy of us, each of us and all of us. He is our enemy individually and corporately. Remember, as you have heard me say before, the devil wants you either dead or a denier of the faith. Either way, he thinks he wins. But you cannot die unless God wills it. So the only other opportunity the devil has, the only approach he has to us, is to tempt us to deny faith in Jesus Christ. In the passage read from Ephesians, we have explained the various armory we are to put on, and we will touch on each piece that is mentioned. But the focus is the purpose of the armor. The purpose is clearly stated in verse eleven. Where it states that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. This is repeated in verse 12, where we are instructed to stand therefore. St. Paul has described in the first three chapters in this letter to the Ephesians the beautiful manner in which God has saved his people. Followed by how his people are to respond to what God has done, to the manner of salvation given to them, by living lives of holiness to God. But living holy lives is not an easy task. There is a great deal of struggle and warlike experience that takes place in the lives of Christians. That too often don't appear or resemble a physical battle, but the intensity of what is occurring is most certainly warlike. No literary work captures this warlike reality of a Christian life better than the allegory, The Pilgrim's Progress. Written by a non-conformist John Bunyan in the seventeenth century. I find it ironic that I'm quoting such a work considering I'm an Anglican, and Bunyan was persecuted by the Anglican Church for preaching the gospel without a license, which is why he was recognized as a non-conformist In fact, Bunyan wrote The Pilgrim's Progress while in jail for preaching the gospel. But there are several books that every Christian ought to read, and The Pilgrim's Progress is one of those books. What Bunyan captures so well is the spiritual battles that are ongoing in every Christian life. The main character of the allegory is named Christian. His life is your life and mine. Your battle with depression as a Christian is captured by Christian falling into the slew of despond. Your struggle to listen to God's word over the wisdom of the world is described when Christian heeds the counsel of Mr. Worldly Wise Man. Your battle with personal pride is depicted in Christian's fight with the fearful demon Apollyon. Your being tempted by pleasures of the flesh is depicted when Christian arrives at Vanity Fair. The presence of people, like faithful and hopeful, show how important Christian fellowship is as you walk the narrow road that leads to heaven, or as Bunyan calls it, the celestial city. The trials Christian experiences in Dowding Castle represent all of our doubts concerning the Christian faith. Which consists of wondering if all of what we say we believe is actually true, and our questioning of whether anyone is truly following on this narrow road. In the end, Christian must cross the river of death where faith is greatly tested, but on the other side is everything he's been striving for. When facing all that Christians face, while they walk the narrow road that leads to heaven, it is necessary to put on the armor that God has so graciously provided. It is evident by the order in which the armor is identified that it is clear the order of which the armor of a Roman soldier would actually put on. In fact, it nearly corresponds with the order in which the poet Homer describes over and over again with the army of his heroes. First the belt and girdle to cover the waist, which came together forming the body of armor, then the sandals, next the shield, and after this the helmet itself And only after this was the soldier armed with the sword. It is good to note that the sword, representing the Word of God, is taken up last. For it is necessary that each Christian have his or her defense in place before going on the offense. The defense the armor gives to us needs to be in place because of the constant attack we are under. And we note also that putting on all of this is similar to putting on what is called in Scripture the armor of light, which is to put on the Lord Jesus Christ. We can also see the various parts of the defensive armor are the various parts of the image of the Lord Jesus Christ. Hence, they are properly his, it's his armor, but freely offered to us. Thus, the righteousness is clearly the righteousness of Christ realized in us The Samuels which give firm footing are the gospel of peace in him. The salvation is his salvation. Work out in us. Even the sword is in no sense our own. It is the Word of God, wielded by us, but in itself living and powerful and sharp. With the mention of loins and breastplate, there is an obvious reference to two passages in the prophet Isaiah, from the prophet Isaiah. Which state respectively from Isaiah 11, righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins. And from Isaiah 59, he put on righteousness as a breastplate. Excuse me. Thus, truth and righteousness are virtually identical or at least inseparable. Thus they are compared to the strong belts and the breastplate continuous, forming together the armor of the body. Perhaps truth is taken as the belt because it is the one bond both of society and the individual character. But it is the two together that men stand armed with honesty. Again, all of this is necessary in order for each of us to stand. Which is to not give way to the devil. When Eve was tempted by the devil, who again disguised himself as a serpent, It only took one word of doubt about one thing God said that led to her demise. Forgive me. In this parish, we have seen an unfortunate number of people walk away from the faith. And there is no doubt that it started with the devil being successful, with tempting those people to doubt merely one thing that God said. For Eve, it was to question if God really said what he said when she was told not to eat of the forbidden fruit. Eve remembered God saying that they should not eat nor touch the fruit from the tree of knowledge. Adding that phrase, nor shall you touch, complicated the whole matter. The devil seized upon it and noted how ridiculous it all was. It was a silly law. It didn't actually apply to Eve's life. Surely the devil reasoned, God said it in a context that didn't mean what he thought it meant He argued to Eve that having knowledge of good and evil, well, that is a good thing for Eve to have. To say that she was not even to touch it shows that God was exaggerating his instructions. So reasoned the devil. Of course, the reasoning was all a lie.
