To know good and evil from the side of evil was what God did not want, but rather that we should know good and evil from the side of obedience. Eve failed, and then Adam, neither of them understanding beneath, for girdles of truth, breastplates of righteousness. Shoes of the gospel of peace, shields of faith, helmets of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit. But we, being on the other side of their fallen state, now have the knowledge of what is needed. And you will note that these items of armor are what the soldier willfully put on. They are God's items of armor, as has been stated, but it is for us to put them on. It is according to our will that we put them on. And to put one piece of armor on is not enough. To leave just one piece out is not enough We must put it all on and keep it on until we are at rest. And it is necessary to say this because St. Paul warns in verse 18, perseverance is necessary. Beloved, the devil doesn't try, doesn't try us once and fail and never try again. The devil is, as St. Peter described, a roaring lion, as a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. The word seeking Is a present passive verb, meaning that he has been doing so and is doing so now. The devil has been tempting you from the start and continues to do so in the present. The warning to persevere fits with the warning for us to hold on. In Revelation chapter 3, Jesus said, I am coming soon. Hold on to what you have so that no one will take your crown. We are to hold on to our faith because Christ is coming soon. In Revelation 2, Jesus said, only hold on to what you have until I come. To him who overcomes and does my will to the end, I will give authority over the nations. It is said another way by St. Paul as he talks about finishing the race. Too many, too many people who say the prayers of Holy Scripture and the prayers from the prayer book for years suddenly drop out of the race. They not only stop running the race, they also start on another road. A road that is wide and many travel on it. This is my pastoral heart to you. This is where I don't care if I get a paycheck. I don't care if you like what I'm about to say. Hear this as a great warning. Sign to you. Stand. Hold on. Finish the race. It cannot matter to you that so many drop out. It cannot matter to you that so many let go. It cannot matter to you that so many sit down. You be the one to stand, to hold on, to finish the race. Do you need motivation? A couple of weeks ago, Sports Illustrated did a story about the Kiwi Dome and its uniqueness. It is the home of the Idaho Vandals. And since I played in that dome for four years, I'm going to take you inside, specifically inside the locker room. There you are, sitting on a bench with your locker directly behind you. It has your last name on it. Everyone calls you by your last name. That is a college football thing for some unknown reason. You have your uniform on. The pants are yellow gold. The jersey is black and bright yellow. And having a number that represents you. Your right leg is bouncing up and down, almost like a twitch. You cannot help it. Your breathing is shallow, as you seemingly forget that you need to breathe. Your thoughts are on what you need to remember for the game plan. But they keep being interrupted when the door to the stadium is open and you hear the roar of the crowd. They are excited. You are excited. You yawn. Why are you yawning, you wonder? You're not tired. Now you're worried that you're going to play tired, but no one told you that you yawn because you're not breathing properly. That would have been nice to know. You next hear shoulder pads clash. Your teammates are slamming their shoulder pads against each other and yelling exclamations. There was another teammate walking up and down the aisle of the locker room, repeatedly hitting his helmet against his thigh pad while chanting, Let's go, baby! Let's go, baby! You yawn again. Stop that, you say to yourself. Next you hear a wrenching sound. It's your head coach. He always throws up before a game. He enters the meeting area in the locker room and tells you how much you need to give if you're going to win. It is going to take your every effort, both body and soul. You have to face your fears and overcome them. You have to offer your body literally in order to defeat the enemy. And in the end, if you do give up yourself as needed, you will be victorious. You have made your decision. You are all in. Live or die, you will give yourself up for the battle. The call is given and you rise and you join the rest of your team chanting I D A H O Idaho Idaho Go Go Go The door opens and you run out to the roar of a crowd that is eager to see what you will sacrifice. This roar makes what you do, what you're about to do, all worth it. Well, in heaven proper, we are told that there is a crowd of angels who cheer regarding a Christian's salvation. We are told that elders who surround the throne of God are chanting holy, holy, holy. And you have been given instructions on how to be victorious, on how to win. You must take up your armor and put it on and stand firm. You are to stand firm in what Jesus has taught you while not being swayed by the false teachers who say it was all a myth and that you are a fool for believing it. You were to stand firm in what Jesus did, even while people laugh at the idea of someone rising from the dead. You are to stand firm and swing your sword to beat back the lives of the devil. This you are to do again and again as long as it takes. Which is the day that the angels come to take you away to the place where Jesus is. And it is his presence. That makes what you do all worth it. Let us pray. Our gracious God, we do thank you for the hope of heaven. We thank you for the armor that helps us to stand, that helps us to persevere. May that be true for everyone who hears my voice in this place. May we all persevere until we see your face. It is in your name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Necessary Forgiveness
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. If you'd like to follow along with me, you can turn to Matthew chapter 18, beginning at verse 21. Matthew 18, verse 21. My only other pastoral ministry was in Pullman, Washington. under the denomination of the Church of the Nazarene. The congregation felt at times That it was made up of misfit toys. If you remember Rudolph the Red Nose Reindeer's Stop Motion Special You will remember that reference. One example was a couple in their late 80s who lived in a rundown home and who played in a kitchen band With a wash tub plucking string and a washboard to scrape. And yet they traveled the globe, having been to Israel four different times. We also had a few widows with a variety of backgrounds. One particular widow I called upon because she had missed attending church for a number of weeks. When she answered the door, she did so halfway, which communicated to me that I was not going to be invited inside. She then told me that she was not coming back to church I asked her why, and she answered that I had told her that she needed to forgive her brother, and she was not going to do so. I inquired as to when I said that she should forgive her brother, and she said that it was when I preached on the need to forgive others. And that I said we need to forgive all persons, no matter what they have done to us. She took that to heart and applied it to her brother and decided that she was not going to forgive him Mind you, I did not know what her brother did to her that needed forgiveness. It may have been as horrid as molestation Or he may have stolen from her. She did not confide about that part of her story. What I was compelled to say was a doubling down of sorts. I did say she needed to forgive her brother, and though I did not know what horrid thing or things he had done, I did know that it was not for her to condemn her brother to hell. Which is what it means to forgive someone. And allow me to be clear before we press on and look at the teachings of Jesus on forgiveness. Forgiveness is not forgetting what has been done to you. It is not putting your trust back into someone who dishonored you. It is not treating a relationship as if nothing happened. Such would be absurd and damaging to the person who has been sinned against. What forgiveness does mean is that I am no longer condemning that person in my heart. I am no longer wanting damnation for that person. I give the judgment of the sinner over to God, who is the only just judge. Let us keep that in mind as we examine Matthew 18, beginning at verse 21. Where we pick up in the gospel narrative is where Peter must have been greatly surprised with what Jesus had just taught about reconciliation. And how we are to forgive those who have sinned against us. And in Jesus' teaching, he uses the title brother. Which communicates a fellow Jew, in the case of the apostles, and in our case, a fellow Christian. Thus, as a brother, it makes the offense done to us that much harder emotionally. We expect our enemies to sin against us, but not our brothers and sisters in Christ. Peter wanted to know what limits were it to be imposed on this generosity expressed by Jesus Especially, it might be if the offender has made no reparations for his offense, not even acknowledging that he's done wrong. Peter likely thought that he was unusually liberal and generous in proposing such a measure of forgiving someone seven times. Seven, you remember, is the number of completeness. And Jesus had used it when giving his sentence in Luke about forgiveness. Jesus said If he trespasses against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turned to you again and says, I repent, you are to forgive him. Some rabbis had fixed the limit of three, from an erroneous interpretation of Amos chapter 1 and chapter 2, where we read the same phrase, for three transgressions and for four. But the usual understanding about forgiveness is of three offenses only. Drawing the line there, and having no pity on the fourth offense. The scribe Ben Sira bids a man admonish an offending neighbor twice, but he's silent on any further forgiveness. In general, we can say that the Jews were very fond of defining and limiting moral obligations, thinking that they could accurately prescribe their morality by a number. And Christ demolishes this attempt to define by law and measure of grace. And are we not thankful for that? Grace cannot be measured. In his response, Jesus gives the full weight of his authority to his teaching, which is a distinction from Peter's suggestion of other rabbinical teachings. Of course, seventy times seven is not a specific number, but it's practically unlimited Thus, for the Christian, there is no measure of forgiveness. It must be practiced whenever the opportunity arises. Interestingly, some translate this 70 times seven to be seventy-seven times Which makes an allusion to the retribution exacted by Lamech, you will remember in Genesis chapter four, where he said, If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold. This connection would mean that Christian forgiveness must be extended as far as old world vengeance. In short, it can be summarized that mercy rejoices against judgment And St. Paul caught the same spirit of Jesus when he writes, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven you. Forgiving one another as Christ has forgiven you. What a standard. In the time of Moses, there was a foreshadowing of the doctrine of forgiveness in the laws that restricted harsh treatment of debtors, as well as the enactment of the law of Jubilee. However, we also remember that there are laws that allow for retribution, especially when an act of one loved one one loved individual has brought personal injury on another individual. And that enacting of revenge reminds us of the difference between the law and the gospel. So Jesus answers fully in giving a parable. Jesus is an illustrator. with his parables, which means that he causes us to picture in our minds the scenes described, knowing at least two things about the use of parables. The first is that they can cause us to consider what is being meant. A plain understanding is not always available. An easy understanding is not always available. In fact, when the apostles don't understand at first his parable about the sower, he explains by quoting Isaiah. That he does not want people to quickly understand and turn from their sin. And that sounds kind of strange. It doesn't sound like the teachings of Jesus. But it does not mean that he does not want people to turn from their sin, but only that he wants them to consider the cost before they turn from their sin. He wants them to take account of what they are doing. Jesus wants serious disciples. And so parables are told so that the listener would strive toward a greater understanding. The second reason for these illustrations is the result of the illustration means that we draw pictures in our heads that stay with us longer than lessons taught by rules. And so Jesus tells the parable of the unmerciful servant, picking up at verse 23. We notice that the word like in verse 23 allows us to compare the kingdom of heaven to the story in the parable, but not but not to understand there to be a direct parallels. The king is unnamed because he does not need to be named, for the scenario in the parable is quite common in the ancient Near East. It was common for the king to call forth debtors and to extract from them what was owed to him, whether in part or in whole. They are called servants in the New King James Version, but the word could be slave as subject. All subjects, which were all citizens in the ancient Near East, were considered slaves to their king, according to the king himself. So this first man couldn't pay a debt of 10,000 pounds. In the day of Jesus, a talent was a lot of money. Multiplied by 10,000 would mean the man is way, way over his head in debt. The judgment is swift. All of the debtor's family is to be sold into slavery, and whatever is garnered from the sale will go to pay for what is owed. And we can imagine that the family being sold into slavery would never reach 10,000 worth of talents, but the king wants to get something in return. Now, as stated earlier, these are not to be considered direct parallels from the parable of the kingdom of heaven. God is not the king, master in this parable. But the king is like God, and that all of his creation owes a great debt to God, even for their very existence, let alone for all the sins that we have committed. And we, like the debtor, are never near being able to pay off our debt. Again, like the debtor in the parable, our only hope is to plead for mercy. Plead for mercy with the fated hope that the debt might be reduced or at least we could make payments on the debt The debtor knew, and the king knew, that payments would never amount to enough money to pay off the debt. It was too much. The king slash master seeing the state of the debtor on the ground and seeing there was no way the debt could be paid. And considering the desperation of the man, decided to cancel the debt, which is to forgive. It is to treat it as if it no longer existed. What a stunning turn of events. No one could have guessed that the scene would turn out the way it did. unless they had seen the king do the same before, which the debtor had not. Now surely each of us has had worldly debt cancelled or paid by another. And we get a sense of lightness about us as we feel like a burden has been lifted off of our back. Take that feeling and multiply it a million fold. However, the manner that Jesus tells the story has us understanding That immediately after the once debtor had left the presence of the king, having just had his debt forgiven, That he spots someone called a fellow servant, a fellow slave, who owes him money Thus, he sees a peer who owes him a hundred denarii. A denari was an average day's wage. I looked it up. The average day's wage today in America is somewhere around two hundred and forty dollars. That would make the debt owed today twenty-four thousand dollars. Now that's a pretty good sum The average American credit card debt is around $6,300. So the amount owed is three times what the average credit card debt is today. It is a tough financial situation this second debtor is in, but it's not impossible. For the first debtor, it was impossible to pay back the debt. For this second debtor, the debt can be paid with hard work and time. Now Jesus pours it on in this parable. Whereas the king, in a much greater authoritarian role, did not physically abuse the first debtor, the first debtor physically abuses the second debtor by grabbing him by the throat. Jesus also has the second debtor use similar words as the first debtor. He fell to the ground. He begged, he asked for patience, and then made the promise that he would repay the debt. The difference is the first debtor said the same words and knew that it was a lie. Whereas the second debtor could be true to his word. The judgment is swift, again, with no compassion. The second debtor is thrown into prison by the first debtor and will remain there until the debt is paid. Which we assume it will have to be paid by the second debtor's family. But the second debtor is the breadwinner of the family The likeliness of the family being able to pay is similar to the likeness of the first debtor being able to pay off his debt. It will not happen. So the first debtor has made it so that the debt owed him will never be paid. Verse 31 refers to fellow servants. Which are fellow slaves or just fellow citizens, when they witness the comparative injustice before them, They join together because they are all in this slavehood together. They recognize that if such injustice can be done to a fellow citizen, then they could be next. And so they tell the king. When the king finds out about the first debtor's hypocrisy, he calls the first debtor to stand before him. And it is easy to imagine that nervous walk of the first debtor to go before the king. Now the logic is simple by the king. The king is straightforward. I forgave your great debt out of compassion. And therefore, whoever owes you should have received the same compassion. To not do so is to not appreciate the compassion from the king. The sentence is for life. The first debtor is to be imprisoned and tortured for life For he will never be able to pay off the debt, so he will remain in torture the rest of his days. Again, we have a scene in which no one saw what was to come. I remind you that the king is not parallel to God. The debtors are not parallel to us, but the king is like God, and the debtors are like us. The only parallel is that what the king did to the first debtor in the end will be what God does to any person who does not forgive his brother his sin. But Jesus could not mean all sins, right? What about that woman I described at the beginning of the sermon? What if she was molested by her brother repeatedly and regularly? And let us say he stole from her as well, stole her savings, stole her retirement. Is she still required to forgive him? Again, I remind you that to forgive is to no longer condemn or desire a person to be condemned. It is to turn all judgment over to God. That does not mean that the woman needed to be in the presence of her brother. nor to trust in him ever again. What it does mean is that she should not want or hope for his eternal demise, nor should she place him in an eternal demise in her heart. And why? Why? Because God has forgiven her Pardon this example. But have you made the same mistake as I have gotten older and less aware of how old you look? You can look at another couple like Bobby Lynn and I do and conclude that they must be older than us, and then we go home and look in the mirror and go, oh my, I think they're actually younger than us It is the lack of self-awareness regarding how we look, and a lack of self-awareness regarding the depth and the breadth of our sin. This lack of self-awareness regarding the depth and breadth of our sin is common to all of us. How do each of us calculate our sins, considering there are so many of them? Let us look at it generally. How many times have you done what you ought not to have done? Which is to say, done what God has instructed and commanded you should not do. How many times have you left things undone, which is not doing as you ought to have done, because God told you to do it, only you decided not to? Let us look at such sins more specifically. What you ought not to have done is talk about another person unkindly. What you ought not to have done is gone to bed angry, spent money frivolously, envied your neighbor, consumed food and drink greedily. And lusted immorally. What you ought not to have done, well excuse me, what you ought to have done, was attended worship of God faithfully. Found ways to support the bride of Christ, his church, lovingly. Supported your hurting brothers and sisters in Christ prayerfully. Set a good example to your children in a manner of life and not keep record of wrongs done to you. Have I hit a nerve on anyone? I could go on, and yet enough has been said to get us to realize that we are sinners who not only need the forgiveness from God, but we need to forgive others as we have been forgiven. I want to confess to you this morning, at the funeral yesterday I saw someone I hadn't seen in a while. It stirred up some anger and frustration in my heart. And I realized, Lord, I'm preaching a sermon that I need to hear. I need to forgive. I need to see my sins as much greater than theirs. And so I confess to you that I need to hear this sermon and I need to forgive The key point for me in the parable is that the king saw the absence of appreciation for the mercy he had shown. This can be our standard. We are to show appreciation for the mercy that God has bestowed upon each of us. May such a lack of appreciation not be found in our hearts. Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God, so much has been forgiven of us, and our lack of self-awareness of our debt is unfortunate, but we take opportunity through this parable to count it and to understand that to whom much is given, much is required And so may we each be a people who forgives and does so readily and willfully. We ask this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Breaking Bands
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. You'll do well turning to Colossians chapter one with me. In the Gospel according to St. Matthew, chapter twelve, which is three chapters after our reading this morning. Jesus is accused of healing people by using the power of the devil. Jesus explains that such would be impossible because the healing he does is a reverse of what the devil has done. He goes on to explain that in order to overcome a strong man in his own house, you must first bind the strong man and then plunder his house. The example explains how Jesus was able to reverse the destruction of the devil. Jesus, by way of his resistance from the temptation of the devil in the wilderness, has bound the devil. Making him restrained and powerless, and thus giving Jesus free reign to cast out sickness as well as the demonic. We then understand the New Testament saying that to bind someone is to restrain them and make them weak and powerless. The truth is, all of us, all Christians, are restrained, weak, and powerless without the presence of the Holy Spirit within us. Left to ourselves, we would have no ability to shed the sins that can so easily bind us. But the truth is also that there are sins that bind Christians, and that makes us similar in a way to those who do not claim to know Jesus as Savior. What makes us different than the unbelieving is that God can break those bands that bind us Therefore, we need to know what sins are there that have restrained us and weakened us. We know that some people's sins go before them. meaning that they are obvious to everyone who knows such a person. An older man's potbelly, for example, can give away his love for rich food and drink. A woman's tongue, for example, can give away her love of gossip. And the sin of gluttony and gossip can bind someone, meaning that such sins cannot be controlled or overcome. But there are sins that come after as well, meaning that other people don't know what sins presently bind a person. Lust is a more common sin that can be hidden, and along with it are sins of pride and anger, and the sin we addressed two weeks ago, withholding forgiveness. Such sins can be as binding as those of gluttony and gossip. They can restrain us and weaken us until we feel powerless against them. There is another sin that is not often enough referred to as sin, but it was something that needed to be corrected with the Christians at Colossae. Such sin was the lacking of knowledge, wisdom, and a right understanding about Jesus. You might wonder how such is a sin. Well, first we define sin as falling short of perfection The Greek word harmortia, translated sin in English, originally meant missing the mark, and it was used to describe an arrow missing the mark or missing its target If the Christian's target is the will of God, and it is, and if the will of God is for us to have a proper and correct understanding of Jesus, and it is. Now to not have a correct understanding about Jesus is sin, falling short of the mark. Thankfully, it is easily repented of, and those who have done it can easily be restored, but it requires learning. And learning requires humility. If we remain prideful so that we do not learn, then the ignorance is a band that binds us, making us restrained and powerless. Look with me, if you would, at Colossians chapter 1. We're going to be going through each verse, starting at verse 2. To the saints and faithful brethren in Christ who are in Colossae, grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. An important fact about Colosse at this time of the letter was that there was a sizable Jewish population in the city. Some of those, perhaps good, a good number of those who heard this letter read for the first time were Jewish Christians. That fact is a significant thing to know or understand when it comes to the false teachings that were being given there. Verse 3. We give thanks to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, praying always for you. Thanksgiving that begins the letter is more elaborate than in Paul's other letters, but notice the theme of the whole paragraph. The first sentence begins with thanks, and the last sentence, beginning at verse 11, includes giving thanks found in verse 12, making a very good section to cover during Thanksgiving Day. Verse 4. Since we heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and of your love for all the saints, this is a gracious compliment. And an example for Christians of every age, for we are commanded as Christians to love one another. Verse 5 Because of the hope which is laid up for you in heaven, of which you heard before in the world of the truth of the gospel. So we glean from this that Epiphras, the missionary, who first evangelized Colossae, had recently brought Paul a report about the church. In that report there was much that was good, but some that was concerning. The Colossians, who knew Epiphas well, would have understood that Paul knew of their situation because Epiphers was their source. Paul understanding the human condition begins with praise and gratitude. He'll have some more controversial things to say as he proceeds, but he wins the ears of the people with his gracious introduction. The manner that Paul addresses these Christians causes us to guess that Paul had not been to Colossae, or at least had not been there since there was a Christian church in the city, as we find out. In chapter 2. It is also helpful to know how Paul uses the word hope. He uses it as a synonym for salvation. That is, here hope is salvation when it is fully realized in heaven, which Christians hope for. And understand also that hope is made the foundation of their faith and their love. These three things remain. We must understand that the gospel, in summary, is a message about the future. The power of the gospel in present day depends entirely on the promise of things to come and a believer's confidence that those promises will be fulfilled. Realize this. Without a true heaven, there is no gospel and there is no Christian life. Verse 6, which has come to you as it has also in all the world, and is bringing forth fruit, as it is also among you the day you heard and knew the grace of God and truth. So Paul here is underlining the power of the gospel, a power displayed in its triumphant advance throughout the world, which is called the fruit. Just remember how remarkable this was that a message that no one had heard before and was so alien to the thought world of the Greco-Roman world that it was taking over that world. Tertullian, a second to third century Christian theologian, famously wrote to some pagans and said this We are but yesterday, and yet we already fill your cities, islands, camps, your palace, senate, and forum. We have left you only your temples. Verses 7 and 8. As you also learn from Epiphas, our dear fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf, who also declared to us your love in the Spirit. Paul seems to be saying that what they learned from Epiphras is what they would have heard from Paul himself. And that there was nothing lacking in the message Epiphus brought them, as the false teachers have apparently insinuated. It was also important to express the love of the people toward Paul. Verse 9. For this reason, we also, since the day we heard it, do not cease to pray for you, and to ask that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding. At the beginning of his letter, Paul usually moves from giving thanks to making petitions. Here he prays that the Colossians might continue on the course they began when they first became followers of Christ. This confirms that something has derailed them for a time. As will become clear as the argument proceeds, His point is that they don't need to take a new direction, but rather to continue to follow the one they have been on from the beginning. There have always been Christians, so-called, who think they need a new direction, even when they were never good at following the old one. Today there are more groups that have tried to redirect Christianity than there are groups who followed the original course. This verse also reminds us of how important regular prayer is. It is the battleground for the souls of humanity. Verse 10. That you may walk worthy of the Lord, fully pleasing him, being fruitful in every good work, and increasing in the knowledge of God. A prayer to walk worthily is a prayer that implies that such can be done. Also, within this prayer is the need for the knowledge of God's will. And God's will is not what is in the future. But what is in the present? In the present, they need all wisdom and spiritual understanding, and that includes an increase in their knowledge of God. The prayer continues in verse 11, strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, for all patience and long-suffering with joy. Here is a short list of what is described to the Galatians as fruits of the Spirit, evidence of the Holy Spirit governing their lives. Verse 12. Giving thanks to the Father who has qualified us to be partakers of the inheritance of the saints in the light. This phrase, who has qualified us, that's unique to Paul and unique to this letter. Obviously a person would need nothing more than for God to qualify him. And it tells us it is never our work, it is God's work in and through Christ Jesus. Verse thirteen He has delivered us from the power of darkness and conveyed us into the kingdom of God, of the Son of His love. The prayer moves from what is needed to what Jesus has done to meet those needs. To deliver is to save. It is to rescue us from what we were, what was binding us, and where we were going. The word conveyed is also translated transferred. Meaning that we have been placed in a completely different world, a real world, an everlasting world. We have been placed into the kingdom of God, and our citizenship in that kingdom is assured and eternal. And of course, the son of his love is Jesus. And we sense when St. Paul is passionate, he gets rather poetic. Verse 14. In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins. This verse provides a clarity as to who is responsible for our deliverance. Deliverance from the devil's binding to the freedom of the kingdom of God. It is by the work of Jesus, the spilling of blood, that procures our sin being forgiven, which is also having bands of our sins broken. As one commentator stated, quote, taking the letter as a whole, it appears that Paul used this his customary introductory section of Thanksgiving and petition. To assure these Christians that they had been properly established in the truth of the gospel, and that their place within the Christian community was well known and an honored one It was also his way of subtly reminding them that the gospel had already done its great work in them. They themselves were evidence of its power. It is that same hope and love that releases every Christian from the bands we place on ourselves when we practice sin. And I use the word practice purposefully, for it is not a sin committed and then turned away from that binds us But instead are those sins that we repeatedly fall back into, whether such sins are outward or inward, as described earlier. Now I turn your attention to our gospel reading from Matthew chapter 9, and you may not see a connection immediately from Paul's words to the Colossians to The descriptive of Matthew chapter 9. Matthew chapter 9 tells of two miracles in one narrative. St. Mark and St. Luke tell us that the name of this ruler who approached Jesus, his name was Jairus. Identifying him as a ruler refers to his position in his local synagogue. He is a Jewish leader who worshiped Jesus. Luke tells us more in that the girl was the only child of Jairus and that she was 12 years old. In Matthew's narrative, Jesus does not hesitate to go and heal the young girl. While traveling, Jesus is pressed on every side by people wanting to be with him, to hear him, and to be touched by him. As he is pressed on every side, a woman who has suffered from female bleeding for 12 years, notice the girl was 12 years old. Suffering from bleeding for twelve years touches him. The temptation for such a woman to be frustrated was likely very great, and she was enduring the stigma. Of suffering from being declared unclean for all those twelve years. No doubt she was in great fear and humbled by her life circumstance. When she approached Jesus, but Jesus was her only hope. And there's that word again, hope. So she touches Jesus and is healed Luke tells us that Jesus felt healing power go out of him, which is again unique to this story, and yet it was also likely that he felt faith touched him. When Jesus arrives at the house of Jairus, music is being played to mourn the loss of the child. Jesus tells them that such is not necessary. for the girl is only sleeping, and his words receive laughter and scorn. Matthew tells us that Jesus merely took her hand and she was made alive again. Now instead of combing over the details of these miracles, I want us to take a look at these two miracles from a different angle. First, let us look at the woman who bled and was considered unclean. Why would Jesus heal in this manner? What is the purpose of such a healing? Was it out of mere kindness? Well, that likely has something to do with it, but it seems fair to assess that not every woman who lived in the day of Jesus who had something similar going on was healed. So, does that mean that Jesus was unkind to them? Was it the faith of the woman only? Meaning that it had nothing to do with the will of Jesus Well, that would be inconsistent with all the other healings by Jesus that are recorded. And the young girl, why raise her from the dead? Was it because Jairus asked and Jesus liked him? You might say that the purpose of healing is obvious. Death is painful. Everyone wants to remain alive as long as possible. I suppose that is so, especially this time in history where people seem more afraid of death than ever. But consider that this young girl will have to face death again at another time in her life. And thus she will have to face death twice. In summary, she was raised from the dead only to die again later. The same point could be made with the raising of Lazarus, especially since Lazarus was older and therefore had less of a life ahead of him to live. So I'm going to answer my own curiosity questions as to these two miracles The answer, I believe, is that both of these miracles point to what St. Paul was describing to the Christians at Colossae. Both of the miracles are metaphors for what Jesus truly wants to do to those who believe in him. He wants to break the bands of sin that restrain us by giving us new life and making us clean. While false teachers were telling the Christians that Jesus wasn't truly a man and then telling them that he wasn't truly God. Paul was calling them back to the basics of the faith, which is to believe that Jesus was and is both man and God, and that his suffering and death were sufficient to give them new life and to make them clean. And while television preachers say that the gospel is about making you rich in this life and never getting physically ill The basics of the faith remain, which is to believe that Jesus is fully God and fully man, and that his blood spilled is sufficient to give you new life in the Spirit and make you clean morally, thus breaking the bands of sin that bind us. Beloved With faith in Jesus, all bands of sin can be broken, and all things in our spiritual lives can be made new. Listen to our call act this week again and apply it to your life wherever sin tempts you, whether sin within or sin without. We pray this prayer. O Lord, we beseech thee. Absolve thy people from their offenses That through thy bountiful goodness we may be delivered from the bands of those sins which by our frailty we have committed. Grant this, O Heavenly Father, for the sake of Jesus Christ, our blessed Lord and Savior. Amen. And we say, Amen. Let it be so, let it be done. Allah do God take this time and prepare our hearts to receive the bread and wine that Allah Allah will.

sermons.title: Being Heavenly Minded
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. The sermon this morning is derived from our reading from Jeremiah twenty-three And then from a reading of the Gospel of John chapter 6, so you can bounce back and forth with me. Oliver Wendell Holmes, Sr. , is credited with this quote, some people are so heavenly-minded they are of no earthly good. The same sentiment is found in a song by Johnny Cash called The Rambler, where he sings, You're shining your light, and shine it you should. But you're so heavenly minded you're no earthly good. The criticism that some Christians are so heavenly minded that they are not, or no earthly good It's a catchy turn of a phrase, but is it warranted? Is it a true criticism? Amy Grant had a similar thought in a song early in her career called Mountaintop. Here are some of the lyrics. I love to sing and I love to pray. Worship the Lord most every day. I go to the temple and I just want to stay, to hide from the hustle of the world and its ways. And I'd love to live on a mountaintop, fellowshipping with the Lord. I'd love to stand on a mountaintop, because I love to feel my spirit soar. But I've got to come down from that mountaintop to the people in the valley below, or they'll never know that they can go to the mountain of the Lord. Again, it is fair to ask, is this really a problem? Are people spending too much time with the Lord Jesus in worship? and devotion that they have become neglectful of their fellow man. No person was ever so heavenly minded than Jesus of Nazareth, and yet he was also very helpful to his fellow man. So let us look more closely at how helpful Jesus was in the feeding of the 5,000. Again, John chapter 6, we pick up at verse 5. So Jesus sees the multitude and he turns to Philip and he asks Philip a question. And we know why he asked Philip, because Philip was from that region. We learn this from chapter one, that he was from Bethsaida. He would have known the food vendors in the area, and perhaps even knew somewhat of their inventory. Verse 6 tells us that something was about to happen. Philip anticipated something was about to happen. He raises the stakes on the situation and points out that it would take 200 days of wages in order to feed all of the men who were there and their families. Philip seems to be challenging Jesus to reveal himself by pointing out the odds against him of successfully feeding over five thousand people. In verse 9, we hear of two of the disciples. Only John among the four gospel writers mentions Philip and Andrew by name in this pre-miracle moment. The others refer generally to the disciples. And only John mentions that the boys' loaves were barley loaves, the inexpensive bread of the lower classes. The fish were no doubt small. We can think of pickled small fish. And these were added to a lunch to make that coarse bread a little bit more interesting. Verse 10 reveals what all the gospel state, and that 5,000 was the number of adult men present. That means that adding women and children, there may have been several times that number actually present to be fed. In verse 11, we are to notice that the word for gave thanks is the verb form of the word Eucharist. Many readers of John's Gospel would not fail to make the connection to the sacrament of Holy Communion Though, truth be told, John does not take advantage of every possible way relating the miracle itself to the Lord's Supper For example, he doesn't mention that Jesus broke the bread, which the Gospel of Mark describes. Jesus took the bread and broke it. John's emphasis falls rather on the supply of food, stating that everyone ate as much as he wanted, and there was still much left over. The instruction to gather up the food left over led to the tradition of clergy consuming the communion bread entirely after it has been distributed. As verse 13 states, there was indeed much more left over than they had in the beginning. All four gospel writers mentioned the number 12 in regards to the baskets, which must be a significant number, for there was enough food for all of God's people, pointing to the 12 tribes of Israel. There is enough left over, but there was no waste by the express command of the Lord. The gathering up of the food is a sign of its preciousness, just as it is with Holy Communion. The men mentioned in verse 14 is generic, so we can interpret it to mean those who received the bread concluded that Jesus was not just a prophet, but the prophet. And that prophet is the one described in our reading from the prophet Jeremiah. He is the righteous branch and the king. That will reign and prosper, executing judgment and justice in the earth, and his name is the Lord our righteousness. The context of the passage from our reading from Jeremiah finds the citizens of Israel threatened by the big bad Babylonians. The Babylonian captivity is the period in Jewish history during which a large number of Judeans from the ancient kingdom of Judah were made captives in the Babylonian Empire. The captivity followed after a defeat known as the Jewish Babylonian War and the destruction of Solomon's temple in Jerusalem. These events are described in the Old Testament, and we should know We should know the historicity of these stories because they are proved both archaeologically and other non-biblical evidence. Where Jeremiah chapter 23 fits in is after a warning given to the sons of Josiah, and specifically Jehoiakim, king of Judah. Jeremiah's words were fulfilled after the Battle of Carchimish in 605 BC, when the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar II besieged Jerusalem, which resulted in tribute being paid by the Judean king Jehoiakim. However, in the fourth year of Nebuchadnezzar II's reign, Jehoiakim refused to pay further tribute. which led to another siege of the city in Nebuchadnezzar II's seventh year. That cultivated in the death of Jehoiakim and the exile to Babylonia of his successor, Jaconia. along with his court and many others. Jaconia's successor, Zedekiah, and others were exiled in Nebuchadnezzar II's eighteenth year A later deportation occurred in Nebuchadnezzar II's 23rd year. The dates, numbers of deportations, the number of deportees given in biblical accounts is not exactly known. Thus in the midst of the threat of deportation, Jeremiah describes a time When God's people who are scattered abroad will be brought back into the land, being led by a man whom God will raise to lead them According to the book of Ezra and Nehemiah, a number of decades later, 538 BC, almost that 70-year prophecy plan. The Jews in Babylon were allowed to return to the land of Israel due to King Cyrus's decree. Initially, around 50,000 Jews made the trip to the land of Israel. following that decree by Cyrus, as described by Ezra, whereas most remained in Babylon. Later an unknown number of exiles returned from Babylon with Ezra himself. That's the important part. The return of the deportees to Judah during the next 110 years is known as the return to Zion, an event by which Jews ever since have been inspired. Thus it is fair to ask whether such a return, led by Ezra, is or was a fulfillment of Jeremiah's prophecy in chapter 23. After all, the people returned from the north country, and Babylon was north of Israel, just as the prophecy describes. They returned from all surrounding countries, again as the prophecy describes. Ezra was a righteous man who insisted that the law of God be followed even to the extent you remember the story even to the extent of forcing interfaith marriages to be broken, for such was breaking of the law of God. Could he be considered the man called the Lord our righteousness? Could he be the fulfillment of Jeremiah 23? Some can easily think so. But we can answer no, because Israel was not of the house of Judah, which the Lord our righteousness must be. Now, if the Lord our righteousness is Jesus, we still have another problem. Jesus did indeed fulfill the title of being righteous. He also was of the house of Judah, so that requirement can be checked off. And while Jesus has brought into God's kingdom people from all points of the earth He has not brought all to Judah, nor are all of his people safe, as the prophecy describes. You ask, preacher, what is your point? The point is that even though we can identify Jesus as the person being described by Jeremiah We must also recognize that what is described about Jesus has not been wholly fulfilled. Whether you are an all-millennialist A premillennialist? A post-millennialist? Those are words referring to how you interpret end-time prophecies. You are able to recognize that there is a good deal more that needs to be done to fulfill the prophecies about Jesus. And where these prophecies will ultimately be fulfilled is in heaven. This is underlined based on the point I made last week, which is that Christianity is a faith about the future. And the ultimate future is heaven. Saying again that without heaven, as our hope, there is no Christian faith. Now, the heaven that I speak of is not what is now. What we know about heaven in the present is that it is where Jesus resides, and the souls of those who have died having faith in him also reside. It is not the heaven of First Corinthians fifteen and Revelation twenty-one. Those heavens are when all of the faithful are gathered, all with eternal bodies, all within the eternal kingdom of Jesus, forever and ever. Turning back to the miracle of the feeding of the 5,000, there is a more important point to make. Which is that the miracle itself was important at revealing who Jesus was, as it was not important to just feed a large group of people one meal. That Jesus could break bread and it would multiply was an unexplainable miracle that had to seem like a sleight of hand being pulled off. There is no manner of Hollywood magic that could do justice to what Jesus did here. And any Jewish person who knew their scriptures would remember that the promised Messiah was to lead the people as a type of Moses. And so just as Moses seemingly provided the people with bread from heaven, so does Jesus provide the people with bread. Again, another box to check off to assure who Jesus was. But the people The people who received that bread did not understand that Jesus was pointing to something much bigger than a meal for the day. He was pointing them to heaven from where the first manna fell. And we can know that the people did not understand what Jesus was doing by feeding them, for after this miracle, Jesus feels the tension among the people. They're going to try to make him an earthly king. They want him as their king because he can feed them their daily bread. He can provide for them so that they don't have to depend on the Romans or their crops or their fishing nets. They think Jesus is the perfect king because he is intelligent enough to reason past the Romans, and he gives people free stuff. Sounds familiar? But Jesus avoids this political rally by escaping and finding a place to be alone. When John continues the story, and we didn't read this part, you can read on. When John continues the story about bread, he describes a multitude of people seeing Jesus and going after him. And when the crowd finds him, Jesus confronts them regarding their motivation. John writes this. Jesus answered them and said, Most assuredly I say to you, you seek me, not because you saw the signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled. Do not labor for the food which perishes, but for the food which endures to everlasting life, which the Son of Man will give you, because God the Father has set his seal on him. That Jesus practiced this type of confrontation is not heard of in churches today. Many don't know what to do with this type of confrontation. Think about what's going on here. Such is difficult for modern Western Christians to consider. Jesus Points to their motivation to follow him and identifies it as selfish and says it without apology, without hesitation. Jesus knows the hearts of men. And when he reveals what he knows, it can be difficult to take. In the time which we live, and the type of people our culture is producing, this type of confrontation would not be received. Jesus, at the moment such was spoken, would be canceled. We don't allow for people to reveal who we really are. We prefer who we want people to think we are. But let us notice the instruction Jesus provides He tells his followers who are following him, following him just to get another free meal, that they are not even to work for food In this life, because it perishes. But instead, they are to work for food that gives eternal life. And Jesus is the source of such food. And this is where we connect our reading from Jeremiah to the people eating miracle food. Both are telling us to get our eyes off of the earthly and look to what is heavenly. Look to the hope of your salvation, which is heaven, as opposed to what can be collected on earth. But what about those warnings against being so heavenly-minded, you're no earthly good? Ignore them. Don't listen to them. Amy Grant was was never and is not a source of ripe biblical knowledge. Here is the truth. Those who think upon heaven first are more free from concerns of this life, and those who are more free can be more effective and constructive for the kingdom of heaven. Consider that those who focused on earthly things would have believed Ezra was the Messiah prophesied about in Jeremiah 23. Those who focused on Jesus being an earthly king stopped believing in him and following him when he refused them. One of the reasons Jesus was crucified was how he had disappointed those who followed him based on their political aspirations to overthrow Rome and make Israelites governors of their own land. And people continue to look to Jesus politically to this very day and expect him to establish his kingdom by some political means. Consider how many ways Jesus teaches his followers not to focus on things of this world. The woman at the well was told not to be concerned with the water from the well, but instead be concerned about the eternal water that Jesus represented. In his first public teaching, Jesus told those who would listen not to worry about their daily bread or the clothes that they will wear, but instead pursue the kingdom of God, which is heaven. But what about wars and earthquakes and fires and floods? Jesus said those are just birth pangs. Concern yourself with the kingdom of heaven. What about the type of work we should do on the Sabbath? His answer: focus on heaven. What about paying taxes? Give to Caesar what is Caesar's and focus on heaven. What about if we have more than one spouse? What's heaven going to be like then? Don't worry about your spouse's focus on heaven. What about my parents' estate that I need to take care of? Focus on heaven. What about my fishing business? What about my tax business? Focus on heaven. What about my own life? Focus on heaven. There are some things that are unclear in Scripture, such as what type of mode of baptism is best, or how will the second coming unfold. But there are also many things that are painstakingly clear. And of those things, one is to focus on heaven. The colic for today, the Sunday before Advent, was a favorite of Bishop Cox. And I was remembering that fondly this week as I prepared this sermon. Stir up, we pray. Who here needs to be stirred up? We can become so very caught up with worldly thoughts that we are no heavenly good. The prayer asks that we be stirred up to do the works of God so that so that we are plentiously rewarded. That is heaven, folks. Heaven is our plenteous reward. So let us be heavenly-minded so that we can do some earthly good. Let us pray. A gracious and heavenly Father, we thank you for the words of your Son. And we thank you for the work of your son and all that he pointed us toward. May that be where our attention is, to your kingdom in heaven, that we might be some earthly good. We pray this in Jesus' name, Amen

sermons.title: Jesus is Dangerous
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: We don't want to know the highest full warriors. Name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Happy New Year. For those who are fairly new, To liturgical services, you should know that the first Sunday of Advent is considered the first day of the church calendar. The purpose of the church calendar is to tell the story of God's salvation through Jesus Christ by marking certain dates in a calendar year that tell us Of what God has done to redeem his people. The four Sundays before the birth of Christ are days to look forward to the first coming of God in the person of Jesus. culminating in the celebration of Jesus being born in Bethlehem and thus the incarnation of God fully realized. What is curious to me are the chosen lessons given to us in the Book of Common Prayer for this first Sunday of Advent. Why did the church leaders choose Romans chapter 13, 8 through 14, and Matthew chapter 21, verses 1 through 13? Why did they choose it for the first Sunday of the church new year? There is no clear answer other than that most of the selected teachings were handed down by Saint Jerome, who lived in the fourth century. So when we read and examine these Bible readings, we are doing so with 1700 years of Christians doing the same. So let us look at the sins St. Paul lists in Romans chapter 13. He begins with adultery. Adultery is defined as sex outside of marriage. Any sexual intimacy with another person outside of marriage, outside of a marriage covenant, is considered adultery. And what results do we see from adultery? Guilt and shame on both sides, as one side is in the wrong, and the other figures that she must have done something wrong. Adultery also results in loss of trust and loss of intimacy. Loss of trust and intimacy result in divorce. Divorce results in loneliness. Loneliness leads to illness, both mental and physical. They still say that in the West, 50% of marriages end in divorce. With up to 40% of those being ended because of infidelity. Next is to kill To kill is to murder, which is the taking of an innocent life. To be a murderer, a person must take on a godlike complex That sees himself as the authority over another person's life. Such is deranged egoism at best. Then there is the thief. To live the life of a thief, a person must distrust everyone because he cannot trust himself, because he is aware that he is a thief. Such a person cannot believe in his own private property because he doesn't believe in the right of private property of others. Then there is the liar. To be a bearer of falsehood, a person must get used to building untruths upon untruths, for a lie is easily revealed by simply one truth. A life lived by lies causes false realities that cause a person to remove himself from the real world, becoming detached from honest and needed fellowship with other human beings. And then there is coveting. To covet is to not be satisfied with just one thing, but soon all things. To allow coveting within the heart means that it takes root and grows, and soon nothing is enough. Nothing satisfies. Everyone has a better spouse, a better home, a better job, better kids, better opportunities, even better hopes and dreams. There is no happiness experienced in a covetous life. What leads you and I to such things as Paul described is first to live like you are sleeping. It is to treat your life experiences, life experiences as though they are but a dream and will soon be forgotten. It is to lazily live, which is to not be aware of how we are mentally and then morally influenced by the world around us. It is to adopt the ethics of the world with no awareness that you have done so. What leads us to such sins is to treat life as one brief opportunity to enjoy the pleasures of the flesh as much as possible. Get it while you can, they say. Love the one you're with, they sing. Eat, drink, and be merry, for tomorrow we die, they yell. And you can do it without much thought It is the easiest thing to do, to give in to what you desire to do in the moment. It takes work, however, to cast off the sins that we so easily fall into. It takes effort to put on the armor of light, which is the very presence of Jesus in your life. That must be done. To fight off the temptations of the devil so readily and willingly he places before us. To put on the armor of light requires the removing of what was dark within and around us. And that armor must be put on daily, for the battle against the sins of the flesh are daily, and in some ways just a click away. But let us now stop and back up and re-examine those sins listed. What do we think the reasons are for God to command us not to practice such things? Is God to be considered the ultimate killjoy? The ultimate party pooper? The greatest wet blanket known to man Because he does not want us to enjoy the pleasures of this life. If we think in such a way, if we think at all in such a way, we are greatly, greatly mistaken. God, beloved, is not affected in any meaningful way by the sins we commit. And that's a profound statement that I've never heard anybody else say. Our sinning does not change God's will. It does not change His plan of salvation. It does not change His sovereignty over all of creation. Our sins do not change God's glory. He is never tainted by our sin. Any sin that mankind practises changes nothing about God, except Except for resulting in a heavy heart as he watches us destroy our own lives and destroy the lives of others. That point is why I started by listing the sins that St. Paul lists and then describing the negative outcome of practicing such sins. Think of it this way. God knows the human condition. He knows how depraved we can become. He knows the earth and the laws that govern it. And because he knows these things, he places warning fences around parts of our lives where the danger is. Consider an example regarding the commandment not to steal. A people who do not respect the private property of one another will result in social chaos. It's inevitable. And another example, a people who do not guard against covetousness will be a society that is unhappy and bitter, and the result will be stealing and murder. Again, God knows our fallen human condition and what we need. He knows what we need to protect ourselves from ourselves and from one another. And there is good news that shows God is not a killjoy, for he says that you can run around within the parameters of the fences he has put up. Enjoy yourself within the parameters. But alas, most men and women want to be their own God. And that means to have no boundaries placed around us. Soon Augustine stated in his grand work, The City of God, that men reject Christ because they want to pursue pleasures of the flesh without having their consciences challenged. Beloved, he stated that in the early fifth century. And you and I know that the rejection of Jesus as Savior and God today It's for the same reason that St. Augustine described all those years before. Now we turn to our gospel reading, Matthew chapter 21. And in that gospel reading, we have a narrative given of events that transpired, which is different than the teachings by Jesus. But the events do teach us a number of important things. And so we walk through chapter 21. In verse 1, we read of Bethpage, which was a Jerusalem suburb, a site which today is not exactly known. But at most, it must have been no more than two miles away from the city of Jerusalem, traveling from east to west. Because Jesus had walked all the way from Galilee, he obviously did not need a ride for the last two miles. In fact, this is the only occasion in the Gospels where Jesus is recorded to travel in another way besides by foot. From what takes place in verse 3, we can assume Jesus knew the owners of the animal, for as in the Gospel of Luke, we learned that the disciples were in fact stopped by the owners of the animals. And the disciples said what Jesus told them to say, and the owners were satisfied. The citations in verse five are from Isaiah sixty two, verse eleven, and Zechariah chapter nine, verse nine. Matthew tells us that Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey precisely to fulfill these prophecies of Israel's coming king. The important point of the prophecy here is that the king is gentle as he comes riding on a donkey. It is a picture far removed from what the politically motivated wanted of Jesus. We note That he does not ride a war horse like Julius Caesar did when he conquered Rome, but instead rides on the foal of a donkey, which represents humility. In antiquity, a king would not normally enter his capital on a donkey, but on a steed, or perhaps marching at the head of a column of troops. Jesus had a very different view of what the Messianic king would be and do, different certainly than his contemporaries. Who were, we remember, waiting for a powerful man to lead them in victory against these Roman oppressors and throw them out of the country. Physically, the text gives a picture of Jesus surrounded by people as he rode down the road that led from the summit of the Mount of Olives to the bottom of the Kidron Valley and then up again to the city gate. Some of these people had been walking with him before he began to ride the donkey's cold, and some of the people had heard of this arrival and came out of the city to greet him. There was great noise and happy excitement as they greeted the miracle worker. And by their reaction, we can know that they began to believe that he would proclaim himself king and deliver them from the Roman army. Hosanna to the Son of David means hail to the Messiah and indicates that the people were ready to proclaim Jesus the one whom the prophets had told them to expect. For them, the day of Israel had been waiting for for centuries, had at last arrived. The next citation is from Psalm 118, verse 26, and that is followed by another acclamation. Verse 10 describes a city stirred up by the commotion caused by the entrance of Jesus. The people were asking one another, what is this all about? Remember that there would have been thousands of Passover pilgrims jamming the streets of the capital, many of whom had come from quite a distance, even from foreign lands. They would have not known as much about Jesus, and Jesus was much less familiar a figure in Jerusalem as he was in Galilee. Though by this time, it is doubtful anyone had not heard of this miracle worker from Galilee because he had just raised Lazarus from the dead a few days earlier. Answering the question of who Jesus was by stating a prophet from Nazareth may sound anticlimactic, coming after a crowd was shouting Hosanna to the son of David But we remember that Moses had foretold of the coming of a great prophet in Deuteronomy 18. And the arrival of that prophet was a significant part of the expectation of many Jews Who were looking for a fulfillment of these Old Testament promises of the Messianic Age We can view the triumphal entry of Jesus into Jerusalem in at least two ways. For it was at least two things at once. It was first a public declaration of his messiahship, which was a grand gesture that challenged the Jewish religious leadership. We know before this that he had repeatedly attempted to keep claims that he was the Messiah quiet, so as not to provoke a confrontation with the priests and the elders before it was time Time meaning when he would be crucified. But the narrative Matthew gives, Jesus is openly receiving the adulation of the crowds, letting them proclaim him as the Son of David at the top of their lungs. He came into Jerusalem as a king and was in fact daring the religious authorities to do something about it. His hour had come. There was no longer any need to quiet the witness of his lordship. But at the same time, the manner that Jesus entered the great city revealed that he was not the Messiah that the people were expecting. Meaning that he had not come to do for them what they thought the Messiah would and should do. That he had come to give his life as a ransom for their sins. Not to lead them in victory over the Romans in the field of battle. He entered Jerusalem as a king, to be sure, but as a meek and lowly king. Riding on a donkey, not a war horse, at the head of a little company of disciples, ordinary men, all of them, to commit to a battle of a different kind. That battle is a spiritual battle, and it is being waged for you and within you and within the church as a whole. It can be simple to take a passage like Romans 13 and all the sins that are mentioned and make the point that Christians need to stop sinning in order to be ready for Jesus to come. But that creates a false picture of God. It is important that we no longer view God as a taskmaster that has a clipboard marking down each time you break a commandment. He doesn't need a clipboard and he is not keeping score. He has fought and is fighting to change his church. And each person in his church from the inside out, so that his commandments, which are his righteous character, Are willfully followed as naturally as we love our spouse and love our children. That the people wanted an earthly king without Show that they did not know what was going on within, within each of them, and within them as a people. They needed a king to change the very nature of who they were. And that is what Jesus came to do. This is why Jesus used language like new birth and new life. Provides us images of what needs to happen within For while the body ages, the spirit is made new when it surrenders itself to Jesus as Lord and Savior. For such newness allows our spirit to quickly cast off, to quickly cast off works of darkness. Cast it off with disdain of such works. And we are not just renewed once. We are not given new life as a one-time thing. New life is always available when sin is acknowledged and turned away from, along with a confessed faith in Jesus, a confessed faith in his blood sufficiently washing away our sins. That Jesus does battle within to make things new is where he is dangerous. For he disrupts what we are used to about ourselves and about the world around us. What we are presently is what we are most comfortable with And when he makes us new, people may not recognize us, and some may not like the change. The change may reveal the works of darkness they are wearing, and they might not be ready for such to be revealed to them. Again, this is where Jesus is dangerous. I remind you of what St. Augustine said. Men reject Christ because they want to pursue pleasures of the flesh without having their consciences challenged. Jesus challenges the conscience, which is from within, so that we can cast out darkness that is without. And he does so not because he needs it, but because we need it. Our lives, our families, our communities, our country, our world needs the works of darkness cast away And for the light of Christ to be put on. And so we begin this new year, contemplating within the commandments of God that He has given for our good. And appreciating the battle, he continues to fight within us for our good. Accept it, beloved. We are in a battle for our souls and the souls of humanity. And it begins within. Let us pray. Our gracious God We thank you for your commandments, as they reveal your character, as they reveal a standard that is best for us, and we thank you for the victory of Christ. That we can hail him our King, and we pray for your will to be done that He is King within and without, so that your commandments are loved by us as we walk in them. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Raging Nations
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. You may be seated. The Church of the Nazarene, a denomination I served for over nine years. Elects ministers to a position titled District Superintendent. The position of District Superintendent gives a man the responsibility to oversee a number of churches within a particular region. The position is very much like a bishop Only it is not an ordained position or a permanent position like a bishop, but is one that is voted on every few years. In 1996, 25 years ago, at a district council meeting where we were to elect the next district superintendent to a region in the Northwest. A minister by the name of Steve Fletcher, a man I did not know personally, preached the sermon for the worship service that day. He began by describing a plane flight he was on that had television screens that were displaying World news. Back then flights had video screens every ten rows or so and everyone watched the same video, whether a news or or a movie. Today we are quite spoiled with screens on the back of seats or using our own devices. But he described spellbound the people at that worship service. as he depicted a newscast that showed the separate nations of Europe with their various boundaries, and then showed those boundaries wiped out and the whole Europe becoming one nation. What the newscast was anticipating was what is known as the European Unification. What the Reverend Fletcher did was use that newscast to describe the end times The belief in the end times that the whole world is going to come under one government ruler who is the Antichrist. And from him, people would be forced to receive the number 666 in order to be able to buy food, shelter, and clothing. Those who refuse the number of the beasts would be refused basic sustenance and would suffer in the great tribulation. The Reverend Fletcher painted such an urgent message that he was elected that day to be the next district superintendent. And I remember listening to that sermon and watching the reaction of the members of the council be spellbound, and I realized how obsessed people can become about the subject of the end times. If you want to make money off of Christians, write a convincing book about the end times. Our gospel reading From Luke chapter 21 is very similar to what is called the Olivet Discourse in the Gospel according to St. Matthew, which are a series of teachings by Jesus about what is to come And many interpret it to be describing a future not yet seen. Looking at verse 25 from Luke 21, We can add from other passages that the sun will be darkened and the moon not give light. The moon not giving light would be the result of the sun being darkened. The perplexity of the nations would be the mental confusion, for if the sun is not shining, there would come upon all persons on earth a confusion regarding day and night. and the inability to see clearly to perform everyday tasks. The sea and the waves roaring is a clear metaphor for nations being in chaos, which means that individuals will be in chaos. We can be sure of this metaphor because elsewhere in the Bible where it describes the exodus of Israel from Egypt, the waters are gathered up. So that Israel could pass through on dry land and that's a metaphor for the nations giving way to Israel as she enters the promised land? The metaphor is further taken up when the book of Revelation describes Jesus sitting on his throne, and before him is a sea of glass, which is the way of describing how Jesus brings calm to the nations. In verse 26, we hear of the reaction of those alive who witness the lights of the universe going out. The phrase, men's hearts failing, literally means that their souls are going out of them, which is another way of describing a person who dies. The powers of heaven being shaken is a repeat of what is described in verse 25. Verse 27 clearly describes Jesus returning to earth to judge the nations. It is his second coming. With that second coming, there will be no doubt who it is or what he has come to do. Jesus encourages his followers that when that day comes, they are to look up and lift their heads, which is an expression of anticipation and hope. They are to anticipate and hope because their final redemption will be a present reality. I want to pause here for a moment, for it is important for us to know that simply dying while believ while being a believer. In Jesus Christ is not when our final redemption is a present reality. The Bible tells us that believers in Jesus Christ at their death will be with Jesus That is for sure. That is their spirit will be with Jesus. But the final salvation of God's people is still yet to come. At that final salvation, our bodies, in whatever form or shape they are, will be raised, and Christians will receive new bodies and receive a heavenly reward. And that is the time where there will be no more tears. Until then, those who have died in Christ are with Jesus, and they are awaiting that final resurrection. So when Jesus returns, it will be the final redemption of all believers. Jesus' next point points to what is very natural. Excuse me, Jesus' next point. Next points to what is very natural to them, as they lived in a part of the world that readily grew fig trees. The time of year Jesus said this would have been in the spring where everything was growing around them A modern image for us who live near the United States Capitol might be the blossoming of the cherry trees. Times in life provide signs that something else is coming. Thus, when the nations become disturbed and distressed, so we can know that something else is coming, and that something else would be Jesus. Where some Bible readers get tripped up is the promise in verse 32. Such a verse has led some interpreters to believe that the destruction of Jerusalem was the subject of this prophecy By Jesus, for that occurred in 70 A. D. , and there certainly were people who heard those words of Jesus and who witnessed the city fall to the Romans. But of course, the fall of Jerusalem did not immediately usher in the return of Jesus as judge. So, what are we to do with this apparent discrepancy? Well, we take the time to answer this apparent discrepancy because we believe the words that Jesus speaks in verse 33. Which is that the words of Jesus will not pass away, meaning that all he says will be true This lines up with St. Paul's words that we read from Romans regarding the Word of God. After quoting Psalm 69, Paul reminds the Romans that all that was written before, which was called the Old Testament, Was written for the comfort of the Christians, being able to see how God's word was fulfilled in the person of Jesus And it is the person of Jesus, I remind you, that causes us to conclude that the Old Testament is God's word, for Jesus confirmed that it is. But believing in the Bible to be the very words of God, both the Old and New Testament, doesn't go far enough. The scriptures have to be read, understood, and in order for them to be edifying and comforting and informative, we must read them and understand them. One very important tool of rightly interpreting the scriptures is to begin with the original audience and the historical events that transpired and would soon transpire. For example, at the time of Jesus speaking these words in Luke 21, nations were already raging. As Rome was engaged in a civil war just a generation earlier, while also being at war with every nation around until they conquered the land of the tribes that would make up the Roman Empire. From Israel's perspective, Rome wasn't an enemy, Rome was the enemy. Their occupation was a gross injustice to the freedoms of every Jewish citizen. The only way Israel gained political clout was to be ruled by Herod the Great, who was loyal to Rome while also being loyal in a political manner to Judea. In fact, Herod saw himself as a Messiah for Judea, which is why he was so brutal regarding the killing of babies when Jesus was born. And why he interrogated the wise men as they followed the star. He didn't want his messiahship to be challenged. But when Herod died, Judea lost a great deal of favor from Rome and were given over to selfish governors who mostly wanted to feed their own pockets. But the Jewish historian Josephus tells us that for a number of years prior to that, from at least about 60 A. D. up until the outbreak, that there was growing tension over the last few governors of the countryside. He tells us that they were pretty abusive and corrupt administrators, robbing people again in order to lie in their own pockets. Josephus also tells us that there was another source of growing tension in the country at this time because there was an increasing number of bandits and rebel types coming out of the woodwork in the country. And so between growing banditry and the rise of zealots, an urgency movement, and then the corruption of the administration, the situation in Jerusalem was becoming very, very tense indeed.
