By the year 66 A. D. , it would break out into a full-scale war, a Jewish revolt against the Romans. Now, allow me to continue a little bit of history. We need to know all this in context. Apparently there was a riot in the city of Caesarea, and the Roman governor required Reparations to be paid. The Jewish inhabitants of Caesarea had apparently gotten angry over their relationship with their Gentile neighbors and had gone on a rampage. The governor naturally wanted them to pay for the damages. When they refused, he went to Jerusalem and demanded the money should come out of the temple treasury. And for the Jews, that was the last straw, and that started the revolt. Unfortunately for him, the governor didn't count on the level of popular sentiment that had grown against him. He thought he could take a bully approach and the people would cower and he would get what he wanted. He was wrong and was rebuffed. When he called for reinforcements and tried to march on Jerusalem, again he was ambushed on the way, and apparently some Jewish men thought Such was a sign that God was now ready to deliver them from the Roman rule. That this was the coming of the Jewish kingdom. And so quickly a small skirmish burst into an open revolt and consumed the entire country. The war lasted from 66 A. D. to 70 A. D. The Roman general Vespian, who would soon become the next emperor, led the troops to occupy Galilee and stop the revolt Vespian basically decided to divide the country into two parts. He thought he could get control of the north and then move south toward Jerusalem. Jerusalem was his ultimate target, but he wanted to isolate it before he ever tried to take it. In the year 68 A. D. , the Emperor Nero was assassinated. leaving leading to a Roman civil war with three people claiming a right to the throne. Because of the interfighting of Rome, some Jewish men once again thought it was a sign from God That God was acting in their favor to be free from Rome. Vespian eventually was recalled to Rome and was made emperor. His son Titus, who would succeed him a few years later and be emperor himself, was left in charge of the armies It was Titus, then, who would proceed to undertake the siege of Jerusalem and finally end the war in the year 70 A. D. It is the siege of Jerusalem that we have been leading up to. For if you look at the prophecy of Jesus prior to our gospel reading, You will read him describing the very city of Jerusalem being destroyed. If you would turn to Luke chapter 21, and we'll pick up at verse 20. Luke 21, verse 20. He says, this is Jesus, but when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation is near. Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains, let those who are in the midst of her depart, and let not those who are in the country enter her For these are the days of vengeance that all things which are written may be fulfilled. And he goes on. The Jewish historian Josephus was an eyewitness to this siege that Jesus prophesied about. He tells of some of its events in gruesome detail, and I'll get into that later on tonight. Josephus describes walking around the walls of Jerusalem and pleading with people on the inside to give up rather than go through the suffering and agony that would come from a long, protracted siege. Josephus also tells us that there was a lot of infighting going on in the city among the different rebel factions who occupied different parts of Jerusalem. The loss of life during the siege before the Roman attack was catastrophic to the Jewish population as a whole. For two years Jerusalem was under siege. Starvation, disease, murder were the order of every day. In the month of August in the year 70 A. D. , the fate of Jerusalem was sealed. On one fateful morning, the Romans attacked Josephus describes the armies breaking through the walls of the city and the Roman soldiers running through the streets, going from house to house and killing everyone they found. Interesting for us today is that there are a lot of evidence between the artifacts scattered throughout this layer of archaeological record. Discovered were arrowheads and spears and other kinds of instruments that indicate a pretty serious hand-to-hand combat in all parts of the city. The lower city of Jerusalem remains to this day largely uninhabited, but in Jesus' day and up to the time of the first revolt, that was the most popular part of the city. But in those final hours of the battle, it was burned to the ground, including the temple. Again, all of this Jesus warned about. So what does all this mean? Well, it means that when Jesus promised that the generation he was speaking to would experience what he was describing, he was referring to the fall of Jerusalem. But that fall did not mean that Jesus would return soon after. It was just one sign. A pretty painful sign, to be sure, but a sign of many to come that precede the second coming of Jesus. What we must do is not make the mistake of making our Bible reading generationally centric, meaning that we interpret Bible passages in the lens of our own personal generation. Consider this embarrassing example. In the late nineteen eighties, some preachers were teaching that the locusts coming out of the smoke in Revelation chapter nine are actually Black Hawk helic helicopters Which meant that the machines of modern warfare of the late 20th century were being described by John, the revelator, meaning that Jesus was coming back late in the 20th century. There are preachers and teachers and bloggers today who are claiming our political unrest in the West And the pandemic around the world are fulfilling end times prophecies and indicating that Jesus is returning soon. He may be. I hope so. But the signs we see are no more relevant than the signs seen by those who lived during the Revolutionary War, the Civil War, the First World War, the Second World War, the tumultuous 1960s. And so on. What we have that generations before did not is modern media that can easily draw up a map of a one-world government Causing the gullible to be sure Jesus is returning in our generation. Beloved, according to the scriptures In the book of Acts, Saint Peter quotes the prophet Joel and confirms that the last days were inaugurated with the first coming of Jesus, and that we have been living in them ever since. And because, from God's perspective, a day is as a thousand years, we are about into the third day. I want you to follow my logic. Because of a calendar error, if you're not familiar with this, we know that Jesus was actually born around 4 B. C. , because Herod died in 4 B. C. and Jesus was born during Herod's reign. If he started his ministry at the age of 30, which we believe he did, then he started his ministry in 26 A. D. He was crucified after three years of ministry, making his resurrection in the year 29 A. D. Again, if a thousand years is a day to God, then 1029 A. D. was a day to God. Finished. And that means that 2029 A. D. will be a day to God finished, meaning that 2030 will be the beginning of the third day from God's perspective. And we all know what he did at the beginning of the third day. You get where I'm going? I should write a book. But beloved, what does the scripture say? The scriptures say no one knows the hour, and that includes the day, and that includes the year. We are to be ready always What we are to be certain of, without a doubt, is that all that has been promised about Jesus coming again will be fulfilled. In the meantime, as our collect says, we are to hear, read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest the words of the Lord. But that is what a Christian is doing while he waits for Jesus to return. Amen. Let us pray Our God, we thank you for this call to digest your word. And that is what we need to do. Through our Bible studies, through our Sunday schools, through our daily readings, digest your word and trust that all of it's going to come to pass in your time at your will. May it be done, may it be so. In Jesus' name we pray, Amen.

sermons.title: Stewards of the Mysteries
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: The name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. This sermon will be covering both the epistle reading and the gospel reading, the first reading and the second reading. We'll start off with 1 Corinthians chapter 4. To the Christians in Corinth, St. Paul says that it is a very small thing that he should be judged by them or by any human court. It is therefore understandable that we would inquire why the Corinthians would judge him. Context, context, context. It is all about context. Previously, in the same letter, Saint Paul addressed the factions that had developed in the church Some held their faith allegiance to Paul, others to Peter, and still others to Apollos. Such divisions, Paul said, were of the flesh. The Christians were behaving like fallen men, instead of men of God, who are to see each other as the same in faith and in virtue. He sums up his unifying point by using this phrase: You are Christ's, and Christ is God's. So the judging that Paul refers to, that is, those who judged him, likely included those who claimed to be either followers of Apollos or followers of Peter, or also known as Cephas. Those people may have judged Paul as not being worthy of being followed, or at least not as worthy as Apollos or Peter. The judgment may also have included that Paul was not a good steward of his calling to preach the gospel, for that is what he refers to in verses 1 and 2. And we're going to come back to that point. I want to take a moment that I usually try to steer away from in sermons, which is to make a personal point of reference. I have become aware of some criticism of me during and related to this pandemic I have been told that the practices we initially installed with the wearing of masks and distancing and then relaxing those practices, that I was a danger to the community I have also been told that our interpretation of the mask mandate being the same as that which was allowed in restaurants, which is where you wear it into the establishment and then take it off That that was in defiance of our governor. I have been told that the sources I pass on to you via email to help perspective with help with perspective on the virus that they are not proven trustworthy. In general I accept that such differences of opinion are part of what it means to see through the glass dimly and to be under the sun. Both biblical metaphors accept the reality that we are limited. All of us are limited as to what we can know for sure. And with the fourth wing of our government, the mainstream media, laying down on the job, it is much, much harder to know what truth is to be accepted. I realize that there are people who are positive that if they had to make the decisions the Vestry and I have made, that they would lead differently. So be it. But I want you to know that there are a few things that I believe the Holy Spirit has convicted me about that I cannot disavow. The first is that the doors of the church should never ever be closed again. I understand. And I'm glad that we did what we did initially when the pandemic started But meeting in person for worship and to continue to receive the sacrament should be a choice that people make, as opposed to shutting them out. And I believe that this should be done regardless of what lockdowns are passed down from government institutions The second is related to the first, which is that the sacrament of holy communion should be made available every week, regardless of what is going on outside the church. A few moments in cinema have captured my conviction, and one of those was in the movie Pearl Harbor. Now I hesitate to use this example because it's not a good movie. So I'm not recommending it. But there is a scene near the beginning that shows bombs exploding on the ships. in the Hawaiian harbor and men's bodies being broken and split into pieces as they fell into the water And at one scene there is a minister, priest, wearing his vestments, and performing last rites on the men fallen and dying. And he is doing it in the calmest of manners. That is what I am convinced the church should be. We should be offering God's mercy and the hope of heaven in the name of Christ Jesus. in any and every crisis, and doing so while there is danger all around us. The third conviction I have had Is how ministers are to teach God's Word and apply it to any crisis. At the beginning of the pandemic, for those who join me online, We were so enriched by studying the prophet Joel. And to understand that no matter what was happening around us, that God is sovereign over it all. And that the outcome was his outcome and no other. I do have other opinions that I know will bother some of you. And I said it's opinions, it's just opinions. I will state them only as examples. I am not against vaccines, not whatsoever But I am against mandated vaccines. I believe that such mandates set precedents that is difficult to come back from. I'm not against wearing masks, but I am against mandating them for the same reason. But none such issues will I die on. I will not divide on them either If you choose to divide with Christians over such issues, I can only warn you that God from His holy word speaks against such division, and you will be judged by Him on such a choice. I shared with some of the vestry that people need to realize that I am not as bad as they think. I am actually worse. And I mean that sincerely. I rush to judgment too often about a situation or about a person, and not in a loving way. I judge people who judge me, and that's just sin for sin. I do the very thing I said I would not do, and I don't do the thing that I should do. I am undone. And yet I continue to confess my sin and get up and keep going. And you know, that is another spiritual lesson that I've gotten from Hollywood In the fabulous series Band of Brothers, a story about the use of the 101st Airborne in World War II, there is a scene where snipers are firing At the troops who are invasing invading a small town. And the leaders of the troop invasion are yelling, keep going, keep moving. And the frightened are hunkered down and frozen by fear. But the logic is that if you keep going, you keep moving, you're more difficult of a target. And so I keep going. And we should keep moving. But let us get back to Paul. When he says it is a small thing to be judged by the Corinthians, and that he does not judge himself, he is not saying that he does not judge himself in other ways. For what he does not judge himself on is his stewardship of the mysteries of God. He is not saying that he is perfect inwardly and outwardly. But the one thing he does know and is certain about is that he has been a good steward of what God has called him to do, which is to preach the gospel to the Gentiles, and the Corinthians are fruit of that labor. Consider St. Paul's resume as an apostle, written in his second letter to the Corinthians. For his Christian faith, Paul received from the Jews five lashings. Three times he was beaten with rods. Once he was stoned. Three times he was shipwrecked. He suffered perils on water and perils via robbers. And in perils via the Jews and the Gentiles, while suffering in cold, in weariness, in nakedness, in hunger, in thirst, and deep concern for the churches. Paul understood what it meant to pick up his cross daily. And what did he do it for? What was the purpose? He did it to preach the gospel to the Gentiles and to stand up to his fellow Jews who would deny Jesus as the Messiah and try to shut the mouth of Paul. And while we might think that Paul was a gifted man, which he obviously was theologically We must not think of him as someone too far removed so that we think that we cannot do as he did. In Sunday school last week, we heard a good overview of Paul's life, learning that before he took on his missionary journeys, he was a like likely an average man, small of stature, perhaps And the skill of being able to mend tents. The nine to ten years he spent from the time of his road to Damascus conversion to his first missionary journey are not even worthy to record. He did as you and I do, which is to live out our Christian faith within our everyday lives with a call to share Jesus. As we move to examine the gospel reading from Matthew, I ask that you keep in mind Paul referring to the gospel as mysteries of God. So we look at John and John sending his disciples to see who Jesus was, and and I like some other interpreters understand John the Baptist to be Sending his followers to inquire about Jesus so that his followers would no longer follow John himself. There may have been Summed out in John, only because he did not see Jesus perform the miracles he was supposed to perform, what was expected of the Messiah. And that's why Jesus wants his disciples to tell John about the miracles to convince John. So there could be mixed motives. There usually are in the things we humans do. The statement in verse 6 is a clever way to warn that people will be offended by Jesus. And we know Jesus said some offensive things. He was provocative on purpose. He was sarcastic on purpose. He was confusing on purpose. He wanted disciples who would pursue him in humility and who would not stop because of petty issues. Next, Jesus asks his disciples, what attracted them to John in the first place And this assumes that those who were then closest to Jesus were at one time either followers of John or at least interested in John's ministry. Jesus has them examine what their expectations were. John was a prophet, yes. But he was more than a prophet. He was the prophet, meaning he was the chosen prophet to usher in the days of the Messiah, just as the prophet Malachi described. The focus of this passage in Matthew from Matthew is the purpose of John the Baptist His purpose was to prepare the way for Jesus. Now imagine if your life, the primary reason for your existence is for another person. And that person is separate from you, meaning that he is not even someone that you was a mainstay in your life. Now, of course, we don't know what type of relationship John the Baptist had with Jesus growing up. They were extended family, yes, they were. But just how close they were is unknown. Most certainly John did not know Jesus was the Messiah before his baptism. Remember these words from the gospel according to St. John, starting at John chapter 1 verse 30. John the Baptist testified, quote, This is he on behalf of whom I said, After me comes a man who has a higher rank than I, for he existed before me. I did not recognize him, but so that he might be manifested to Israel, I came baptizing in water. And John continued, I have seen the Spirit descending as a dove out of heaven, and he remained upon him. I did not recognize him. But he who sent me to baptize in water said to me, He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit I myself have seen and have testified that this is the Son of God. End quote. So again, imagine the main purpose of your existence is to introduce the world Of who the Messiah is, and then fade into the background, not even able to be an eyewitness to all the miracles that confirm Jesus as the Messiah. Would you want such a life as that? Well, in a certain way, you do have a life like that because you are a Christian. A Christian is a follower of Jesus Christ, and that means that you no longer live, but instead you live for Him. Your life is for another. Your purpose is to honor Jesus in a way I want you to consider today. Your purpose is to lead the way for Jesus in the lives of the people that you know. Notice that I did not say that you were to be John the Baptist. There was only one John the Baptist. And I did not say that you were to be the Apostle Paul, being called to sail the seas doing mission work. But you are a person who knows the mysteries of God. And you do have a call upon your life to be prepared to share that hope that lies within you. The word mysteries in 1 Corinthians 4 1 means truths, truths once hidden but now revealed. As in Luke chapter 8, Jesus said, Unto you it is given to know the mysteries of God. But what exactly, what precisely are those mysteries? They are, in no particular order, God becoming man, Jesus as the Son of God, Jesus as divine, the Holy Spirit as divine, and yet separate from the Father and the Son. Jesus dying, thus God dying, the Son being separate but co-equal with the Father, God remaining one but three Jesus rising, death losing its sting, Jesus ascending, and the Holy Spirit descending, and the church given the duty to continue the presence of God on earth until Jesus returns. None of that was known until God revealed it through Christ. Yes, it may be said that it was revealed in pieces in the Old Testament. We have covered that in different ways in our study of the Levitical sacrifices, in our typological study of Genesis, where we found types of Jesus in every patriarch. But all of that pointed to what was revealed in and through Jesus and was understood by Paul and the first century church. It is a mystery revealed that you and I know But your neighbor likely does not know. Your co-worker likely does not know Beloved, we are, we may be, we may be, living in the most Bible-ignorant culture since the colonizing days of North America. I looked up studies done on the average American's knowledge about the Bible, and I couldn't find any done within the last decade. So instead of pointing to the Bible ignorance of the unbelieving world, I thought I would challenge each of you. And I want you to conjecture that if you don't know the answers to these questions Then your non-church neighbor, co-worker, is for sure not going to know the answers to these questions. Please answer these five questions internally, of course There are a number of places where the Bible says that Jesus is God, but where does Jesus explicitly say he himself is God? I'm pausing for a fact. Where in the Bible does it say Jesus is God while describing God dying? These next questions can have more than one place in the Bible. Where does the Bible confirm that human beings are sinners? What and where in the Bible are sinners told what to do to have their sins forgiven? Where in the Bible does the Holy Spirit referred to as God? Beloved, answers to these questions are main parts of what it means to be stewards of the mysteries of God. I close referring to our prayer for this third Sunday of Advent. We pray That the church might reveal the mysteries of God in order to turn the hearts of the disobedient to the wisdom of the just, and that by doing so we might please God. Beloved, we have a lot of work to do. And so we better get to it. Let's pray. Our gracious and heavenly Father, for what is placed before us as being stewards of your mysteries. We take it to heart and we take it seriously. Understanding that before us is a is a is a test, a trial of our faith to say, do I actually believe this word and do I want to share it with others And so we take this as a commission that each person that we know in our lives that doesn't know Christ, that we may introduce them, that they might too know those mysteries. May this be true for all of us, we pray in Jesus' name, Amen.

sermons.title: The Peace of God
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Certain passages from Holy Scripture can be difficult to hear Where they stir up emotional frustration because they sound so easy, but are actually very difficult for some people One such passage for me is St. Paul's directive to be not weary in well-doing. I've commented before that such instruction is frustrating because we are not told how we are not to be weary and well-doing. Another passage, again, for some people, may be St. Paul's instruction to count it all joy when you encounter various trials. Again, how do you count something as joy when you feel no joy, but in fact you feel the opposite? In our passage from Philippians chapter 4, verse 6, we are instructed to be anxious for nothing. That is not easy to do for some people. Anxiety overwhelms some people so much so that just thinking about their anxiety makes them anxious. Now, to Paul's credit, he does say that we are to replace our anxiety with prayer, supplication, and thanksgiving. For those who suffer from greater anxiety, prayers, supplications, and thanksgivings don't balance out the feelings of anxiety I hope to help with such a dilemma in this sermon. So let's look at Philippians chapter 4, looking at verse 5. The word gentleness might be rendered forbearance, allowing it to carry with it the ideas of patience and graciousness. When we consider that the church at Philippi was facing some opposition, specifically persecution for their faith, Paul was then reminding them to be gentle-spirited as Jesus himself was. In 2 Corinthians chapter 10, Paul refers to, quote, the meekness and gentleness of Christ, using the same word here. A reason why Christians should be gentle is given, which is that the Lord is near. The phrase at hand is ambiguous in the Greek as it is in the English. It can mean near in terms of space or time. Either understanding would make sense here. Either understanding would serve as an excellent reason for Christians to face the difficulties posed by other people with patience And with grace. Either the Lord is at hand to help and protect us, or he is near to returning, and we have only to be faithful servants until he comes. The latter case is favored by most commentators as it is a reminder of the Lord's admonition to be like faithful servants who are waiting for their master to return. is worth pointing out that the sentence, the Lord is at hand, is not grammatically connected to anything else. It stands by itself. So it is just as possible to provide motivation for the exhortation that follows it or from the exhortation that precedes it. Or it's likely both. Consider this point. There is a reason not to be anxious because the King of Kings will soon be here and put all things right. and reward his people for anything they have endured in his name. In verse six, the anxiety That Paul is commanding Christians to lay aside is defined as unreasonable worry that detracts, that distracts, excuse me, worry that results from a forgetfulness Of God and a forgetfulness of his promises. There is, of course, a proper kind of worry, the worry that comes from love and concern for others The proof of this type of worry-anxiety is actually in verse 6 and in chapter 2, verse 20, it describes Timothy being concerned about the Philippians' welfare. So there is simple advice to us here. Take your troubles to God and let the Almighty take care of them. The practice of your faith in Jesus to have all things under control is to counter the worry that tempts us. And we are to remember to thank God for what He has done for us, which will sweeten your spirit and keep your troubles in perspective. This is not the only place where Paul combines peace and thanksgiving. In Colossians chapter 3, verse 15, he says, Let the peace of Christ rule your hearts And be thankful. But you say, What if I don't feel at peace? What if I don't feel thankful? What does my lack of feelings combat my anxiousness? How does that work? We will get back to such dilemmas. In verse 7, we are given a promise, a result of not being anxious. The result is that God's peace will keep them, meaning it will replace the anxiousness and it will be sufficient for them. This peace is something that no one will understand who imagines it that it somehow takes some human effort There is something godlike about it, making it more wonderful than a person can know until such a person experiences it. A vast multitude of saints through the ages will say to that, Amen. They have found the peace of God like a like a garrison of soldiers protecting them and warding off the enemies, allowing them to rest. In the serenity while the world creates more chaos. Peace is both a very important word and idea in the human life Having a very elastic concept and definition. I grew up, as many of you did, with the word peace being used politically. as in wanting peace between the Soviet Union and the United States, or wanting peace in the Middle East. Today there is talk of the need for peace in the inner cities and between the races. Even when there is no real conflict, people still talk of the need for peace. But peace is also an intensively personal and private condition. Soldiers at war who are facing death every day can have peace, while people living in political and social conditions of quiet and prosperity still think they need more peace. People mean different things when they use that word piece. Humorist writer P. G. Wodehouse once quipped That the peace that passeth all understanding can only be experienced by the man who gives up golf I think golfers would get that. Some people define peace as simply the absence of inner turmoil or frustration or worry. That obviously is part of anyone's definition of peace, but Paul certainly means much, much more by peace than that. Because he held That a person could have peace in the midst of many trials and troubles of different kinds, and even have it during the most profound disappointments in life. Of course, the peace that Paul is describing is not a peace achieved from ignorance of a cold heart. Man can achieve such peace in the flesh by caring nothing about the world or his own self. The most evil man in the world can have such a peace But it is only the peace in the sense that a man in a coma has peace. Instead, Paul is talking about a different thing. He calls it the peace of God But what is the peace of God? Well, it is first a gift. It comes from him. Jesus, you remember, told his disciples, My peace I leave with you. And here in Philippians chapter 4, verse 7, we have a similar idea. The peace of God Actively guarding our hearts. Second, we can know that the peace of God necessarily includes having peace with God Himself. Such peace is what every human being needs, whether they acknowledge it or not. To have peace with God is to be forgiven of sins and being able to call him Father. It is laying one's head down at night, trusting that your soul is in his care, whether you awake the next morning or not. Thirdly, the peace of God is a supernatural reality. Thus it is not something that we can create on our own work or or work up to it by some technique such as Practicing yoga or some other transcendental meditation. This is where it is found as surpassing all understanding. Such peace lies in the spiritual world, and that is why it can touch our souls Is where we have deep communion with God, and such communion lies beyond both our comprehension and our vocabulary. Corey Timboom, whom I have mentioned in this pulpit before, endured a concentration camp of the Nazis during World War II. Joined by her father and her sister. Her father died only two weeks after being captured. Her sister Betsy lived for a significant time before expiring as well within the camp. In Corey's book titled A Prisoner and Yet She writes about the peace of her sister as an otherworldly thing. As Corey and Betsy were becoming acclimated to life in a concentration camp. Corey observed the following as she watched her sister Betsy in the barracks sitting on a bed a few rows over doing some mending. She described her sister as follows. There was something home-like about the way she sat there. Her face was so peaceful and sweet. The pleasant atmosphere which Betsy always seemed to create at her about her at home had not left her even here. That she lived a life devoted and in service to the Lord before her imprisonment, which shone on her face and in her actions while imprisoned. It is hard to imagine using the word peaceful when describing anything about the experience of a person imprisoned in a Nazi concentration camp. But there it was. I get concerned when Christians do not have peace. The supernatural kind. I conjecture that a lack of peace is from an incorrect way of understanding ourselves. And the expectations we might have that do not come from God's Word. I am thinking of expectations such as how we should feel on the inside. I have mentioned Dr. Carl Truman's book before, titled The Rise and Triumph of the Modern Self, where he argues quite convincingly that we moderns are living in a therapeutic age Where we see ourselves and the world, including its history, through therapeutic lenses, where everything is diagnosed psychologically, and all that comes back to how we feel And by feel I mean our emotions. What I'm getting at is that the peace of God transcends and descends our emotions. It goes higher and deeper than how we feel at any given moment. Think about how we talk to one another, whether in a deep conversation or chit-chat. How are you feeling? We begin focusing on emotion. Oh, I'm so happy for you, we respond. Again, emotion. That sounds sad. I'm sorry to hear that. Again, focusing on emotions. I have the worst Bible study question ever asked. Here it is. It sounds something like, how does that passage make you feel? But it is not just feelings in the therapeutic age, it is also desire. What we desire is suddenly who we are. Our identity is what or who we desire. Beloved, this elevating of feelings and desires are idols to be smashed. Please hear these truths Feelings can be controlled and even changed. Not with ease, I would never pretend it is done with ease. Desires can be controlled as well, and yes, even change. Again, not easily, but it can be done. And being ruled by feelings or desires is the opposite of God's peace, which is again a gift spiritually given. In fact, the peace of God has a defiance about it, which again points to its supernatural nature. For Paul, the peace of God acknowledges the many things that tempt anxiousness, but instead of crumbling under all of life's weight The peace of God fills the heart in defiance of negative expectations. No matter the existence Of reasonable fears and even crushing disappointments, the peace of God overcomes. Consider that Paul does not encourage Christians with the peace of God so that all things will go well from now on. Things were not well for the Philippians, nor for the Apostle Paul, who was riding, we remember, from prison. The only motivation Paul gives is that the Lord is near. Again, God's peace is supernatural. It rests on the reality of God as known, loved, and trusted by his people, and upon the reality of his second coming. And the heavenly hope, which is the happiest conceivable ending to one's life as a follower in Jesus Christ. There is a Latin phrase that we Christians should get to know better. It is pronounced hub specie eternitatis. It means literally under the aspect or from eternity. What it means practically is viewing a thing in terms of eternity. And that is what Paul is pointing to here. Christians are to live their lives each day, soup speci eternitatis, in view of eternity. With a view to what will be soon, with a view to how that soon-coming future ought to profoundly change our view of our present circumstances in life. Things have a very different meaning and a very different aspect if they are considered in reference to what they mean for eternity. Be anxious for nothing. The Lord is near. Troubles can be very heavy, but they get much lighter if they are viewed. From the sight of eternity. The Lord Jesus had to go to the cross. A greater suffering no man has come near to enduring in this world. And yet he was strengthened to endure it, for the scripture says, for the joy that was set before him. On the other side of the cross was a future so magnificent, so wonderful, so happy that the prospect nerved him to bear up under the crisis, though he had To pass for our salvation. Well, says Paul, you are to think of your own life, your own problems and troubles and sorrows in this same way. Sub space eternitatis in view of eternity. The Lord is near Perpetua and Felicity, a young noblewoman and her slave, were martyred for their faith in A. D. 203 under the Empress Severus. At the time of their arrest, Perpetua had an infant son and Felicity was pregnant. While she was in prison, Perpetua wrote about the circumstances leading up to their death. in a diary that was later published as the Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity, one of the earliest writings by a Christian woman. In her diary, Perpetua describes an interaction with her father as he came and begged her to recant her faith. While we were still under arrest, my father, out of love for me, was trying to persuade me and shake my resolution. Father, I said, Do you see this vase here, for example? Yes, I do, he said. And I told him, could it be called by any other name than what it is? And he answered, no. Well, so too I cannot be called anything other than what I am, a Christian. Prior to their arrest, the women had been studying the scriptures and preparing for baptism They were baptized in prison by their teacher, who was imprisoned with them. The prison warden was so inspired by their faith, he also converted. A penalty for professing the name of Christ, perpetua and felicity were sentenced to death. Yet with God's peace in their hearts, they remained serene in the face of their fate. A note from an editor at the end of Perpetua's diary describes the day of their victory dawned, and they marched from the prison to the amphitheater joyfully, as though they were going to heaven. with calm faces, trembling, if at all, with joy rather than fear. Propetua went along with shining countenance and calm step, as the beloved of God, as a wife of Christ Putting down everyone's stare by her own intense gaze. Perpetua and felicity were thrown into the arena of wild animals, but they were not killed. Tragically, the Emperor Severus then commanded that they be put to death by the sword. Beloved, the martyrs are for our encouragement. And that what we face in this life, we can do so with the peace of God in our hearts, as it was in their hearts, making our trials but shadows. But we can face even our shadows with the peace of God and our eye on eternity. Let us pray. Our gracious God, for these challenges we accept them all. Seeing the standard is set before us by our Savior and by those who have followed him to martyrdom death. Encourage us this day to face all of our fears for they trust that you are not only near, but there is eternity waiting. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Cross on your Tree?
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Is there a cross on your tree? I asked the same question sixteen years ago. And when I have visited parishioners' homes during the Christmas season, many have wanted to show me that they did indeed have a cross on their tree. But there are a number of you who are new with us, compelling me to ask again, is there a cross on your tree? Do inventory for a second. I'll give you a moment. Look to your wife, look to your spouse, see if there's She can guarantee that you have a cross on your tree or not. If you have a Christmas tree up in your home to help you celebrate the Christmas season, Is there a cross as part of your ornaments? Amidst all the sprinkling lights, these shiny ornaments, and maybe some tinsel, is there a cross? I realize that at Christmas time we are celebrating the birth of Jesus and not commemorating his death. Or are we? Let us consider what we are celebrating in order to capture the true nature of Christmas. The idea of baby Jesus is comfortable for everyone. Baby Jesus threatens no one. Jesus as a baby is meek and mild. As a baby, he is sweet and tame. Worshiping God in his humble estate is much easier for some people than worshiping him while he is naked upon a cross. We stress in this parish the importance of following the church calendar for the primary reason that it walks us through the redemptive story of God. Just as God instructed Israel to formulate its calendar year-round around God's redemptive acts that saved them from slavery in Egypt and provided them atonement for their sin. So too do Christians follow a calendar year-round where God's redemptive acts are shown to save us from the bondage of sin and eternal damnation. Israel's calendar, you remember, is highlighted by two primary holy days. The first is Yom Kippur, or the Day of Atonement. It was on the Day of Atonement that the high priest was to go into the temple and then into the Holy of Holies behind that grand curtain. And present a once-a-year sacrificial offering to the Lord for the sins of the entire nation. The other holy day is Passover On Passover, the Jewish people remember by way of a meal how God delivered Israel from Egyptian slavery. In between those two holy days are other days that remember how God preserved them in the desert for over forty years, providing for them daily bread and regular meat. And every generation of Israelites is warned by God to not forget what He has done to save them, and the holy days they are to commemorate are a means by which they can remember. The holy days remembered by Christians serve the same purpose. They help us not forget what God has done and through Jesus. We are reminded at Advent, the beginning of the Christian calendar, that God became man and dwelt among us, and that He's coming again. He came once, and He's coming again. At Christmas, we are reminded that when Jesus came the first time, he came to take on the human nature. It was what Christians called the incarnation, God becoming flesh. And we remember that when taking on the form of man, he did so for eternity, meaning that he didn't become a man and then went back to being God, but instead he became a man To identify with us forever. We are to be humbled by this act of humility that He chose to be like us. This is so very, very important to understand. After we celebrate his incarnation, we also remember what might be considered the smaller things, such as his circumcision and his dwelling in the temple at age of twelve. We then remember his baptism and his fasting in the desert for forty days. Then, of course, there is his passion, which included the institution of holy communion, his washing of feet, his arrest, his trial, suffering, and death. These solemn events are then brightened by the Easter Sunday celebration where we proclaim He has risen. He has risen indeed. The story does not stop there, of course, because we have to recall his ascension into heaven and the sending of the Holy Spirit. Each of these are important watermarks in the story of God redeeming his people The story of redemption is thus told within each calendar year, and that story is rehearsed by Christians each year until the Lord comes again, so that we do not forget Consider the words of Jesus in response to Pontius Pilate asking him if he were a king. Jesus said You say rightly that I am a king. For this cause I was born. The cause he is referring to is all that his life and death and resurrection meant to the world. The question about a cross on your tree is to help us see that although we focus on God becoming man this time of year, we do not do so separately from the whole redemption story. We celebrate Christmas as part of the redemption story. And you and I need redemption. For redemption means to buy back. And you and I have been given over to sin and to the devil, be born in a sin covenant. We cannot help but sin because being of the human race means we want to do what we are told not to do, and we don't do what we are told to do. Thus, all of us have sinned. All of us need redemption. And the celebration of the birth of Jesus is to celebrate the story of how God redeems his people. By celebrating the life, the death, resurrection, ascension, and the coming again of Jesus. It's all included. You see, while we might focus on one thing this night, we do so in light of all that was to come. Every story, by definition of being a story, has a beginning, middle, and end One of my favorite holiday movies is Planes, Trains, and Automobiles. You remember Dell, played by John Candy, is a talker. Neil, played by Steve Martin, is finally fed up with Dell's talking. In a rant, Neil says to Dale and I cut this down. And by the way You know, when you're telling these little stories, here's a good idea. Have a voice. It makes it so much more interesting for the listener. How many times have you wanted to say that to someone in a conversation? Well, good stories have a point. Truth is, the beginning of the story does not have its fullest impact upon the listener until the end is known. The end grants greater understanding to the beginning. Consider the popular poem, Twas the Night Before Christmas. It starts as follows, you know it, 'Twas the night before Christmas when all through the house Not a creature was stirring, not even a mouse. The stockings were hung by the chimney with care in hopes that St. Nicholas would soon be there. The children were nestled while snug in their beds, while visions of sugar plums danced in their heads. And mama in her kerchief and I in my cap had just settled down our brains. Original, for a long winter's nap, when out of the lawn there arose such a clatter, I sprang from my bed to see what was the matter. Away to the window I flew like a flash, tore open the shutters, and flew up the sash. Do you know what comes next? These opening words make so much more sense as to why we should know the details of a couple going to bed when we know what comes next. The words are exciting and we have a heightened anticipation because we know what comes next. It is St. Nicholas, who is referred to previously, who had caused the clatter. In a similar way, the birth of Jesus has a greater effect upon our emotions, upon our faith, when we know what comes next. The story is heightened because we know the end. The death of Jesus, his crucifixion, gives us insight into why he was born into the human race, into a lowly stable into the town of Bethlehem, and how a star led men from afar to seek him. He was born into the human race because it was necessary for a perfect human being to die for the sins of the world. He was born into a lowly stable to contrast the modern men who anticipate what they anticipate regarding the birth of a king. He was born into Bethlehem because, like the lowly stable, Bethlehem was a lowly city. And Bethlehem was the city of David. And the Savior was to be born from the lineage of David, which both Mary and Joseph were from, the lineage of David. A star led men from afar to seek him as a sign that the whole universe celebrated the event and that the birth of Jesus was for the redemption of men from afar, as well as men who were near. Which meant he came for both Jews and Gentiles. You can see from these examples that the details of the Christmas story are better understood regarding their importance when we know the end of the story. And a major part of the end of the story is a cross. It might seem like bringing up the story of a cross at Christmas is like discussing world hunger at Thanksgiving. But I submit that amidst the sentimental ornaments and the modern symbols of overweight men wearing red, there should be a cross. In a unique and mysterious way, there is as much joy to be found in the cross as there is in the nativity. There are buttons worn this time of year and stickers placed on cars that say he was born to die. I wouldn't want to say more than that, but For Jesus was born to do everything that he did, everything. But the slogan summarizes an important truth. The manger and the cross are the same story. One is not valued without the other. On this night we remember God becoming man as a baby, born in a lowly stable. And we remember that he died to set men free from sin and death. Hence, it was truly a holy night. It was holy and is holy because God became man, and it is holy because he died to set men free. So make sure that there is a cross on your tree and make it empty. An empty cross. So that tells the end of the story. He is not there. He is risen. Amen.

sermons.title: A Punch from Stephen
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. May be seated. I stated in the homily I gave for Bishop Cox's funeral That the early church fathers praised the saints in their eulogies because the lives of the saints, and in particular the way that they died. Made them examples for all Christians to follow. Well, today is the feast of Stephen And in honor of our namesake, we will make him an example for us. And that example specifically is his willingness to speak the truth when it was needed. Thus it is his courage that we will uphold today. What happened to Stephen needs to be understood in the context of what Jesus promised would happen to those who followed him. Recall what he said to his disciples, similar to our gospel reading. Behold, I send you out as sheep in the midst of wolves. Therefore, be wise as serpents and harmless as doves. But beware of men, for they will deliver you up to councils and scourge you in their synagogues. You will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles. But when they deliver you up, do not worry about how or what you should speak, for it will be given to you in that hour what you should speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you. Now, brother, will deliver up brother to death And father his child, and children will rise up against parents and cause them to be put to death And you will be hated by all for my name's sake, but he who endures to the end will be saved. Stephen experienced the truth of the warning Jesus had for him and for all of us firsthand. There are a number of similarities I want us to notice between the reasons for the arrest and trial and execution of Jesus and of Stephen. First, both were full of faith and the power of the Holy Spirit, allowing them to do great miracles as a witness to the people that God was indeed with them. Second, because of the attention the men received by the populace, others became jealous, and especially the religious leaders. We must recognize that jealousy is a terrible and cowardice sin that tempts men to do unconscionable things. Third, because of the wisdom of Jesus and the wisdom of Stephen, no one was able to refute them in public, and so false charges were made against them. Again, that is what jealousy will tempt a man to do. Notice the similarities between Jesus and Stephen are specific, such as the same charges brought against them. Jesus was charged with having said that he would destroy the temple and replace the law. And in 614, chapter 6, verse 14 of Acts. Stephen is charged with repeating what Jesus was accused of saying. Where the similarities end is the response of Stephen to the question posed by the high priest. Jesus, remember, was a lamb to the slaughter. Jesus said nothing in his defense Stephen, however, spoke in answer to the question, are these things so? He spoke because Jesus had commissioned him to speak. He has commissioned all of us to speak when he said that we were not to fear when put on trial, but that we are to have faith that the Holy Spirit would give us the words we needed in times of persecution. And so Stephen spoke, and he spoke quite courageously. Because Stephen's answer, we which is actually a sermon, is 53 verses long. We cannot break it down verse by verse, and it would not be helpful to use several Sundays to examine its details because its effect is to be experienced in one hearing So it will be my job to underscore the highlights of this sermon, and I'm going to do so with some sound effects. By sound effects, I mean like those that were implemented in the old Batman and Robin television show. You remember when Batman and Robin would get into fights and and with the bad guys and when they threw a punch the word pow or or bam or boom would come on the screen indicating that the good guy good guys were giving it to the bad guys. Well, Stephen pulls no punches in his answer to the high priest. What he gives is a sermon with a lot of pow, bam, and boom. Stephen opens with a couple of well-struck jabs. Bam, bam, bam. His focus is on Abraham leaving his homeland for a land unknown but promised. Which is an implied lesson that the men of the Sanhedrin needed to do the same regarding their understanding to the Christian faith. They were unlike their father Abraham. They had no courage, they had no faith. The description of Abraham's father dying is like old things passing away and all things becoming new in the new covenant. The Sanhedrin needed to die to their old understanding. There is a warning in verse 7, whereas he is quoting from Exodus and referring to a promise by God toward Egypt. The same words will be applied to the Jews who already have started putting Christians into bondage. Whereas God judged Egypt for putting his people in bondage. He will soon judge Israel for rejecting Jesus and putting his followers in bondage. The next pow is the result of a left hook by Stephen. When he doesn't merely provide a history lesson when he describes Joseph being sold into slavery, but instead gives another example of how similar the unfaithful Jewish fathers were to the present Sanhedrin. In other words, the treatment Joseph received from his brothers is the same as how the Sanhedrin treated Jesus. The mentioning of being Joseph's brothers being jealous and selling Joseph into slavery is the same as the Pharisee being jealous of Jesus and handing him over to Pontius Pilate. And it is why Stephen is on trial. He was accusing them of petty jealousy, but they will need to get hit in the head by a sledgehammer to get the point. The telling of the story of Moses was a bam, bam, like a right and a left combination. There are many similarities to the person of Moses and the person of Jesus. The birth of Moses and the birth of Jesus resulted in infant genocide. Both were rejected as leaders by their own people. Both were chosen by God to deliver the people of God. And both performed miracles as signs that God had called them. But of course, Jesus did much more than Moses, for Moses delivered the Israelites out of earthly bondage, whereas Jesus succeeded in delivering mankind out of eternal bondage. This section of the Sermon of Stevens is also a defense against the charge that Stevens spoke against Moses. That was part of their accusation. He shows that he understood Moses better than they did. The prophecy quoted in verse 37 was obviously referring to Jesus, at least it was obvious to anyone who had ears to hear. The next POW is a sneaky uppercut in verses 39 through 43, where the Israelites are described as having rejected the deliverance God had provided for them And God in return gave them what they wanted. That was happening as Stephen was speaking. The same thing was happening. They were rejecting their opportunity to believe what Stephen is telling them. And Stephen let them know it. The Sanhedrin was willing to accept what was false in the place of what was true. making them no better than their fathers who worship the golden calf instead of the one true God. Well just as a boxer Sizes up his opponent before he delivers the knockout punch, so Stephen begins circling and winding up. He mentions the prophecy from Amos, which was not for the purpose of speaking against the offerings of sacrifices as a whole, but to show that God was ultimately pointing to the sacrifice of his son. Because that sacrifice, because of that sacrifice, the people of God could be perfect in heart. The mention of the prophecy of Isaiah is not against the temple, as much as it conveys that Solomon conveyed, what Solomon conveyed when he built the temple. The temple was always pointing to Jesus. The tabernacle was pointing to Jesus. Abraham and Moses were pointing to Jesus. And then boo, he says, You stiff necked and uncircumcised heart of heart and ears It was a right cross to the head, and Stephen landed it hard. As stiff-necked people, they were stubborn. They were proud. They were too stubborn and proud to see what was clearly before them. Jesus was the Messiah. They had prayed would come, and they chose to deny it. They chose not to hear the truth. And then boom, again, a left cross. The so-called spiritual leaders of Israel were just like their unfaithful fathers before them. What Stephen implied earlier is now plainly stated. And then another boom, an overhand right to the temple of their heads, as he calls them lawbreakers. Stephen could have called them many things and received no response, but they were not going to be called lawbreakers. They took great pride in the manner that they kept the law of Moses. It was their thing. In their minds, they were anything but lawbreakers Stephen knew this was in their minds. He knew what the knockout punch would be, and so he did not hesitate to deliver it. He was not afraid to make people mad. He was not afraid to call attention to their hypocrisy. And he was not afraid to suffer the consequences for it. Here is true courage, beloved. He said what was true. He said what needed to be said And he said it with full awareness of what they were going to do to him. True courage displayed. Where does courage need to be displayed in our day? Considering how far our culture has slid from where it once was. And doing so with the belief by those who are leading that they are more virtuous than those who led before. Meanwhile, we see looting of department stores in the middle of the day Being reported and no one stopping it. And some won't even call it stealing, but rather redistribution. We hear of public schools teaching children, children, that a boy can be a girl if he wishes, and a girl can be a boy if she wishes. With some parents considering paying for sex change operations before the child hits puberty. Such is child abuse of the most serious kind. When adults do wacky things to their bodies, it may be right for us to ignore them, let them harm themselves. But when such is taught and practiced on children, Christians need to object. And then there is our culture confusion on marriage. Our culture is so backward, Christians should now embrace the concept of separation of church and state So as to get the government out of the business of what they say can be a marriage. But what of a time in the future? When they not only say who can be married, but require the church to sanction it, facing fines and even jail time if we refuse. I trust you are with me when I say bring it on. It is time the church shakes up this backsliding on a toboggan sled to hell culture. I say bring it on because it will require people standing against the culture to cause people to question how far it has fled down the hill. Beloved, the same spirit of courage as Stephen is alive and well in each of us. Consider St. Paul's words to Timothy. For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and love and of a sound mind. We are given courage from the Holy Spirit. It is courage that is going to be needed to make a difference in our culture for the gospel of Jesus Christ. I continue reading from Acts chapter 7, picking up at verse 54, reading about how these people responded to Stephen and his right and left hooks. When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart and gnashed at him with their teeth. But he, being full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God. And Jesus, standing at the right hand of God, and said, Look. I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God. And they cried out with a loud voice, stopped their ears, and ran at him with one accord. And they cast him out of the city and stoned him. And the witnesses laid down their clothes at the feet of a young man named Saul. And they stoned Stephen as he was calling on God and saying, Lord Jesus, receive my spirit. Then he knelt down and cried out with a loud voice, Lord, do not charge them with this sin. And when he had said this, he fell asleep. Should we weep for Stephen? Should we cry bow and demand justice? It does not appear that we need to do anything for him. Heaven opened up for him. He saw Jesus waiting for him. He was like his Savior Jesus at the end of his days on earth when he asked that his executioners be forgiven. No. Stephen needs nothing from us. But we need something from him. We need to follow him in courage. Beloved, we have had a front row seat to watch the devil corrupt our culture and the church Consists of too many Christians that have bowed to the spirit of this age over and over again as the church strives to look more and more like the world. And the devil will work and work and work until the gospel of Jesus Christ is heard no more. Which means Christians have to work and work and work and work. Am I an alarmist? Am I mimicking Chicken Little? Am I crying wolf when there is no wolf? If I preached this sermon in 1981, it would have sounded like I was crying wolf. Maybe even so in 1991. Maybe, maybe in 2001. But here we are in 2021 with spiritual carnage all around us. I remind you of the letters to the seven churches in the book of Revelation, where Jesus repeats to his churches to hold on. If that is the least we can do, then that is what we must do. Hold on. We must hold on And we need courage to hold on to what the Word of God says about salvation, about heaven and hell, about who Jesus is and what We must believe about him and what the Bible teaches on morality, on what is right and wrong. And to hold on is not just doing this for ourselves, it's for our children. And our children's children and our children's children's children. I pledge to hold on with you, and as we hold on, I want the persecutors to bring it on. And I want to pray like Stephen, Lord, do not charge them with this sin. And I want to see Jesus. And the only way to see Jesus is to speak the truth and hold on. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God, we thank you for this patron saint, Stephen. And for the courage you gave him, and for the words that you gave him, and for what they mean to us today as we face our own persecutions. Heavenly Father, grant us the courage that you granted him, and may we stand the test of time and hold on. Pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Blessed Resolution
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Again, Isaiah, the Spirit of the Lord of God is upon me because the Lord has anointed me to preach good tidings to the poor. He has sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound. To proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of vengeance of our God, to comfort all who mourn, to console those who mourn in Zion, to give them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning. The garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness, that they may be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that he may be glorified. There are some who believe the words in Isaiah to be describing Isaiah himself. Well, if they do, that is saying a great deal about Isaiah. But Isaiah knew he was speaking of someone besides himself. After all, he was a prophet, a very mouthpiece for God. I trust you noticed that the description of the ministry of the Messiah is virtually repeated by Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount as recorded in the Gospel according to St. Matthew, starting at chapter 5. So that's where we're going this morning, Matthew chapter 5. And I encourage you to turn in your Bibles with me And follow along. It will be to your benefit. Matthew chapter 5, beginning at verse 1. Why study the prophet's words when we can study how Jesus fulfilled the prophet's words? The section we will look at is also known as the Be Attitudes. which is a word derived from the Latin meaning blessed or happy. If we use happy, we should not think about smiling or emotions or a mental state, but instead a person's entire life. It is a more objective description than a subjective one. Some would use the phrase gladness of heart. Verse 12 captures it by the phrase, rejoice and be glad. Because this sermon was preached to the Lord's disciples, the Beatitudes are in a way a description of the Christian character or the attitudes and commitments a Christian makes in his or her life as he or she lives out the favor of God that he has placed upon his or her life. We also can't help but notice that the opposite way of thinking and living would be the life of a worldly man Thus there are also warnings in these beatitudes, in that to live in the opposite manner is not to be living out the favor that God has made upon your life. And consider the structure of each be attitude. The first half provides us with what a disciple is, the second half provides what a disciple obtains. And I would like to make a challenge before we examine each one of these. The challenge is to acknowledge that every person claiming to be Christian should be living out every one of these beatitudes in some measure. It is the immature mind that works on some of them but not all of them and it is the stubborn character to say that you are the way you are and you're not changing And thus everyone has to put up with you. No, you are to work on each of these if you confess Jesus as your Lord. In Matthew chapter five, verse one, Jesus sets the stage quite literally. As he chooses a spot to preach that can hold a crowd and provide a theater type setting so that the most possible people can hear his voice. If you visit Israel, where it is believed this sermon took place, you will see a very beautiful setting that has been commercialized to an extent, but done tastefully As the natural beauty of the area is respected. In verse 2, the phrasing is a Hebraic expression That is the opposite of chance. And what I mean by that is that everything he is about to say is purposeful. It's not just speaking off the top of his head. So verse three. Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. The word poor refers to poverty of spirit, not of material wealth. Though the Lord elsewhere teaches us that the rich have a greater difficulty being poor in spirit, the trapping seems to be that we can become self-sustaining. Simply put, you don't pray because you can pay. This allows us to see a connection between material poverty and the poverty of spirit. The poor, whether spiritually poor or monetarily poor or both, are precisely those people who have no other recourse but their hope and trust in God. They rely upon the Lord because they know they cannot rely upon themselves. Their resources are inadequate or depleted. Disciples of Jesus are to know themselves to be morally and spiritually destitute. That has to be understood before you can seriously follow Jesus. That's where the Christian life begins. It is no accident that this beatitude comes first. Remember, Jesus says that the kingdom of heaven is theirs. Is theirs. Present tense. It is not only that it will be theirs at some point in the future. It is already is, even though when we look around and the world is the same as before when we started following Jesus. In the following Beatitudes, there's going to be more emphasis that will fall on fulfillment in the future. But that future is already present in principle As the Bible so often reminds us, theologians like to call it the already, not yet position of every Christian this side of heaven. Verse four. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. The idea of mourning here is primarily that of suffering, but not suffering for the sake of suffering, but for reasons of faith. Again, we can clearly see that the first two beatitudes are drawn, influenced by Isaiah chapter 61, where both the poor and those who mourn are mentioned. They mourn, note this, they mourn not selfishly, as if their only interests were greater peace, happiness, and prosperity for themselves. But they mourn for the apparent slowness of God's justice. God's justice is what delivers a person from his own sins. And to bring righteousness to the world. Thus, their mourning, or better, our mourning, is on account of loyalty to God. And a desire to see his glory revealed to the world. The writer of Psalm 119 says it this way. My eyes shed streams of tears because men do not keep your law. That's the same heart. There is the idea that such people will have their comfort in due time. And please note that comfort and the kingdom of heaven are describing the same thing. Verse five. Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. The meek Are those who are content to wait upon the Lord for the accomplishment of His will, even while experiencing disappointment and suffering, personal disappointment and suffering? Jesus describes it elsewhere as dying to self or taking up your own cross to follow him. It is a willingness to not insist upon your own rights, your own needs, or your own wants. The same word is used to describe the Lord's own character later in Matthew 11. It is not weakness as the world often thinks of weakness, for it requires a the greatest spiritual strength to be meek in a world like ours With hearts like ours. And now again, I qualify that this is not a meekness that is necessarily practiced in all situations. It is in the context of the gospel being preached and the gospel being stood for. Jesus doesn't call us to be meek on the basketball court or while hunting. But there can't always be more meekness about us in everyday life. This beatitude is almost a direct quotation from Psalm 37. There in the Old Testament, the meek will inherit the land, and by that he means the promised land. And so we see Jesus here repeating the same principle but universalizing the promise. They will receive the entire earth. God will give the meek what they did not and would not grasp for themselves in this life. And note that inheriting the earth is connected to the kingdom of heaven, is connected to being comforted. Verse 6. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. There is an unfortunate debate. Whether the righteousness here should be taken to refer to a social righteousness, what we would call social justice, or personal righteousness or personal holiness. In the context of the beatitudes that follow, perhaps especially from chapter 5, verse 20, it is likely that Jesus here means a desire for personal holiness. The they will be filled, indicates that God's grace is necessary for this righteousness to be experienced. For righteous living in itself. In other words, it's not a human achievement. Our righteousness comes from Jesus Himself And it's also something we should purposefully desire. And again, to be filled is to inherit the earth, is to be comforted, is to have the kingdom of heaven. Thus, the first four beatitudes can be said to express a disciple's utter dependency on the Lord while also promising the greatest of futures a human being can hope for. Verse seven. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. There is a principle here for the Christian to show mercy to his fellow human beings, and that principle is taught in the Lord's Prayer. Or we are to forgive as we have been forgiven. And we are told that to whom much is given, much is required. When you take inventory of how much you have been forgiven, it is much harder to withhold mercy. And receiving mercy from God is connected to inheriting the kingdom of God, the kingdom of heaven, to being comforted, to inheriting the earth, to being filled. Verse eight. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. This beatitude is drawn from the well-known Psalm 24, where those who have kept themselves from idols are said to be pure of heart. Purity here refers to that quality of undivided loyalty to God expressing itself in moral uprightness. This purity, Jesus teaches, goes down to the bottom of a believer's life and controls a believer's attitudes and thoughts as well as a believer's actions. It is in the heart, deep inside, in the secret place of a person's life, that most people do not expect to find, do not even think is necessary to find purity. But Jesus requires it there, first of all, because out of the heart, he says, flows the choices we make in life. Believers already see God, in a sense, in this world by faith, seeing him who is invisible, as the writer of Hebrews puts it But they will see him literally and in a fully realized sense in the world to come. It is as Jesus said to Thomas, Because you have seen me, you believe. Blessed are those who have not and yet still believe. The promise to see God It's the same as obtaining mercy, which is the same as being filled, which is the same as inheriting the earth, which is the same as being comforted, which is the same as having the kingdom of heaven. Verse nine. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God The absence of self-ambition, which is found in the earlier Be Attitudes, now comes to expression in a life devoted to blessing others. The merciful, the peacemakers, bringing peace to others as God has brought peace to them The Father, the Heavenly Father, is a peacemaker, and his children bear his resemblance. There is no greater inner joy to be had than having peace with God. And having that peace with God and a love for others makes it natural to want to bring peace to others. The reward is being called sons of God. And sons of God have the kingdom of heaven. They are comforted. They inherit the earth. They are filled. They obtain mercy. And they will see God. Verse 10. Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Initially, it might seem absurd that a righteous person would be persecuted. It would seem more justified to persecute a self-righteous person. For self-righteousness and arrogance is quite ugly. But the fallen world we live in does things backward. The self-righteous get applauded while the truly righteous are hated They are hated because they remind sinners of the very fact that they are sinners. And prideful sinners don't like to be reminded of their sin, and so they persecute the righteous to quiet their own conscience. But Jesus warned us that if we follow him, we would be hated by the world, for after all they hated him, the man without sin. The promise of having the kingdom of heaven gives a book end to these beatitudes. I mentioned this on Christmas Eve. Knowing the end helps us understand the story. And the end of the Christian life is heaven. And that is summarized in verses 11 and 12. He says Blessed are you when they revile and persecute you and say all kinds of evil against you falsely for my sake. Rejoice and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven. For so they persecuted the prop the prophets who are who were before you. We should remember That Matthew's original readers were Jewish Christians who, no doubt, were suffering severe persecution from their fellow countrymen for their loyalty to Jesus as the Christ. We will read more about this in the book of Acts. Jesus expands this last beatitude about persecution because it has such special revalence to the situation his disciples will soon find themselves. If they are being persecuted by the unbelieving Israel, well, there's nothing new about that. The faithful have suffered at the hands of the unfaithful in the church many times before. Persecuted Christians will always find themselves in good company. And I can't help but think what it was like to hear Jesus preach this sermon. Not in terms of being able to see him or hear his voice, but to realize just how mind-changing it was For he said things that no one else had ever said, and in the context, no one else has ever been it. How these words and warnings must have returned to the disciples' consciences again and again. When they were experiencing the persecution Jesus warned about. They had to return to these words of Jesus For what they experienced in this life was not heavenly or comforting or merciful or any of that which Jesus promised. Remember, all the twelve except Judas suffered severe persecution, and only John survived his torture. To endure, they had to remember these words of Jesus, having their eyes on heaven, where all the promises of Jesus would be realized. I am not much for New Year's resolutions. The Gregorian calendar we follow doesn't universally determine when a New Year begins. But I am taking the challenge this year to have the Be Attitudes in front of me on my mind and hopefully eventually in my heart every day this year. If I am Christian, which I say that I am, and my baptism confirms, I am to be poor in spirit. Which means I am to recognize, acknowledge, and pray regarding the reality of my utter dependence upon God for anything that is good and holy. I am to mourn, which is to desire that God's justice be done, which includes having his righteousness revealed. I am to be meek, which is to care first for God's will to be done, regardless of what happens to me personally. I am to hunger and thirst for righteousness, which is to cast out things in my life, within me and without me, that do not reflect the holiness of God. I am to be merciful, which is to match what has been forgiven of me to the people in my life. Which means I am to be quick to forgive and forgive 70 times seven. I am to be pure in heart, which is to be loyal to the Savior, who deserves nothing less than my undivided commitment to build his kingdom on earth as it is in heaven. I am to be a peacemaker, which has me focused on helping people to be first at peace with God and then at peace with one another. And finally, I am to accept the fact that if I succeed at any or all of these, there will be those people who hate me. The logic is simple. If they hated the perfect man, they will more easily hate someone like me who is imperfect. And so here is the list, and I put it before me this year. Be poor in spirit, be mournful, be meek. Be hungry and thirsty for righteousness. Be merciful. Be pure in heart. Be a peacemaker. Accept persecution. Such is what it means to be Christian and nothing less. Let us pray. Our gracious and heavenly Father, from these words of the prophet Isaiah, to Jesus teaching us what it all means and exemplifying it in his life. We take the charge. We take it as you speaking to us, the standards that you place before us. May we settle for nothing less. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Think Different
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. You will be served well to turn to Romans chapter twelve in your pew Bibles. Romans chapter twelve, picking up at verse one. The verb translated present from the instruction to present your bodies Is the same Greek verb found in Romans chapter six, verse thirteen, sixteen, and nineteen There, Paul had said that Christians were not to present their members to sin as instruments of righteousness, as once they had been doing.
