That instruction by St. Paul was very general. Now he will proceed in greater detail to describe the life that followers of Jesus Christ ought to live. It is a reminder that the final chapters of Romans have already been anticipated in a general way. We have already heard of the Christian life, at least in general. And now we are going to find out what specifically it is to be. It is interesting, by the way, and will become clearer as we proceed into this chapter. that the description of the Christian life that Paul gives us is a further explanation or practical explanation of the ethical teachings of the Lord Jesus as we read them in the Gospels. They are, as Paul twice labels his ethical teachings, the law of Christ And in particular, they follow a number of details from the teachings of the Sermon on the Mount. So you can think of the Sermon on the Mount as being a general way in which we should live, and then Paul is getting to more specifics. The term bodies, present your bodies, again from the instruction, present your bodies, is not a specific reference to the physical part of a person, but actually to one's entire life. We are to hold nothing back, but instead we are to give ourselves to God as a sacrifice. Which is to say we have to offer ourselves to God in recognition that we belong wholly, all of us to Him And we must strive to be worthy of him. That is why he gives us the phrase acceptable to God. I want to say this off of my notes. We often hear Christianity too often today as just it's to be a part of your life. Paul didn't understand it that way at all. It's to be all of your life. It's to affect all of your life. All of your thinking, all of your doing is your Christianity. Anything else to Paul is not Christianity. The phrase reasonable service is also translated spiritual worship Which sums up Paul's main point. Our lives are to be the worship and service of God at all times and in every way. The worship practice in the Lord's house, as we do today, and on the Lord's day, is simply to be a corporate and focused concentration. of that constant self-surrender expected of every Christian every day. No exception. Verse 2. By renewal of mind, Paul means the gaining of moral perception and moral sensitivity. that will direct a believer's path to godly living. The renewal of the mind is, of course, the Holy Spirit's work, as Paul has already said in chapter 6, 7, and 8 in Romans. But it is a work in which we participate. We're not bystanders. Those of you who have been Christians for some time and have read the Bible through a number of years will know that what we have before us in Romans chapter 12, verses 1 and 2 Is perfectly characteristic of Paul's writing. There are two great areas of biblical truth: doctrine and then practice. Theology, and then ethics. It is a description of what God has done for us and an account of what we are to do for God. Romans chapters 1 through 11 is doctrine or theology, a theological account of what the Lord has done for us, saving us from sin and death. Romans chapters 12 through 15 is how the theology is to be lived out by the Christian. And the connection between the two sections of Romans and the two areas of the Christian faith is this single word. Therefore, it means that what has been established allows us to say what follows. And here is an important point. Doctrine is never taught in the Bible for its own sake. Doctrine is never taught in the Bible for its own sake. It is taught to produce a response by the believer. And that response ought to be love and gratitude that seeks to express itself in a life of obedience and service offered to God because of what He has done for us. This, therefore, is Paul's way of saying what Jesus said to his disciples in the upper room the night of his betrayal. He said, if you love me, you will keep my commandments. The Christian life comes out of the believer's love for God. And Christ, which itself is the result of what God has done for us. This does not make doctrine secondary, but it only points to the end or the purpose of doctrine. And it also teaches that if your doctrine is poor, meaning that you think incorrectly about God, then your ethical practices will also be poor. Said another way, when you think in a poor manner about God, your life will be lived in a poor manner. Again, our Christian life is to be lived in response to the gospel and the forgiveness of our sins. But of course, it isn't just Paul who connects the gospel to the Christian life in this way. In remarks very similar to those of Paul here at the beginning of Romans chapter 12. And after giving the account of our salvation, in 1 Peter chapter 1, Peter uses similar language. He says this: therefore, gird up your loins of your mind. Be sober and rest your hope fully upon the grace that is to be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ. Thinking first and then acting. In summary, you can't live the Christian life until first you are a Christian. In the first two verses of this chapter, we are given a very general statement of the Christian life The setting aside of ourselves to God in gratitude for his saving love and renewal of our mind, which is our inner life Leading to a transformation of behavior that will demonstrate itself in an increasing separation between our way of life and the way of life practiced in the world around us. Verse 3. The first part of this verse is easily understood, but most difficult to practice every day. Because we underestimate the very pride we have in ourselves. We readily think more highly of ourselves than we ought to. It's natural to the human fallen condition. Pride is a daily battle, even for those who think they have low self-esteem. What is curious in this passage is the phrase measure of faith. The main point of referring to a measure of faith is that Christians are not to compare themselves to one another. But are instead to see that we are all the same, which is to say we are all in this together. We are all fundamentally the same before the Lord. Verses 4 and 5. As we remember the metaphor of believers together forming the body of Christ, it is a dominant theme in Paul's letters. Sometimes, as in Ephesians and Colossians, the point of the metaphor is to describe the dependent relationship of the body to Christ Himself as the head. In 1 Corinthians chapter 12, as is the same here, the point is to describe the interdependent and interconnected relationship between the parts to one another as a whole body. We all belong to the same body, and each has his own contribution to make. You remember how Paul stretches this out in 1 Corinthians 12. Someone is an eye, someone is a hand, someone is an ear, and so on. It is a wonderful and easily understood metaphor. We all need each other. In general, what we can say from these verses is that a great deal of the ethical change in our lives and the ethical difference we are to have from the world has to do with our minds. Which is how we understand the world around us. It is not solely on the mind, of course, for a great deal more of our ethical change and ethical difference has to do with the grace of God. Personally, my conversion, I never saw myself as prideful or selfish Until the Holy Spirit dropped the scales from my eyes so that I could see myself for who I truly was and who God truly was. But consider in these short five verses of chapter 12 how the mind is a major focus. He says we are to be transformed by the renewing of our mind. We are to prove what is good and acceptable and perfect will of God using what? Our minds? We are not to think more highly of ourselves, but instead we are to think soberly, which is to be aware of our surroundings and how God is not a respecter of persons. Which is to say that God favors no person over another, but sees us all equally, which is how we are to see one another, how we are to think about one another. This passage from Romans fits nicely with our gospel reading because Jesus at the age of twelve Knew the value of properly developing his mind. And I say properly because as G. K. Chesterton once said, I don't fear the uneducated. I fear the poorly educated. There are many people who walk about having letters after their names. to indicate the degrees that they have earned who are poorly educated, but think that they should be making decisions for the uneducated. Such people are to be feared most. But back to the gospel reading from Luke chapter 2. We don't know hardly anything about the boy Jesus. This is the only story we have. But it is obviously a necessary one because God inspired it to be recorded. That Jesus went missing from the family. may seem rather strange to our modern ears, especially when we see children liter literally tethered to their parents. With the anticipation that that they would run away like a dog if the tether was released. But when families made the trip to Jerusalem, especially From as far away as Nazareth, which was about ninety miles, such a trip would take about five days. And when families traveled on such journeys, they would take extended family and friends along As it was either the Passover Feast, Pentecost, or Tabernacle Feast, when the families would worship together in Jerusalem. And the families would not always stay together when they traveled. So it was easy for the family to assume that if Jesus wasn't with Mary and Joseph, he was with some aunt or uncle or cousin. When they gathered to take inventory of their party, it was discovered that Jesus was missing. Their journey back did not necessarily take three days. But instead the writer of Luke could be counting the days Jesus was in the temple. A day and a half travel before Jesus is discovered missing, and a day and a half travel to retrieve him is more likely. The Talmud says that within the temple walls there were three synagogues, one at the gate of the court of the Gentiles another at the entrance of the court of the Israelites, and a third at the southeast part of the inner court. It was in these synagogues that the rabbis would expound on the law. Among the famous doctors or rabbis then living and teaching in Jerusalem were the famous Hillel. who would have been a very old, nearing a hundred years at that time, and the equally well-known rival Shemai Others would have been Gamelael, the master of Saul of Tarsus, who we know as Paul And Jonathan, the complier of the Chaldee paraphrase of the sacred books, and Simeon, the son of the successor of Hillel, and possibly Nicodemus. Who, some years after, came to Jesus by night, and when the end was come, reverently assisted in laying the Son of God with all honor in the tomb. We may with great probability assume that amongst those doctors whom the boy Jesus questioned at the Passover feast, some, if not all, of these well-known men were sitting before him. And while it is touching that Jesus was in the temple and thus the place where his parents should have first looked. It is most intriguing that he pursued the development of his mind. We should remember that Jesus himself told us to love God with all of our heart, soul, mind, and strength. To love God with our mind is to do as Paul describes, which is to prove what is good, acceptable, and perfect will of God. And again, as I have said before, when St. Paul refers to the will of God, he is not talking about God's will. in terms of whether you should buy that particular house or join that particular gym or eat that particular candy bar. He is talking about discerning good and evil. He is talking about knowing the voice of God versus the voice of the world. And I wonder How many of us allowed God to transform our minds and search out the good, what is good, acceptable, and perfect will of God concerning how we should respond to a pandemic. Many searched out secular news in order to learn how to respond, and many of us look to our trusted news sources to know how to respond. But how many confessing Christians allowed their minds to be renewed in order to find the perfect will of God to respond to a pandemic? That is a challenge for all of us to take up. Consider all of the ethical decisions you have had to make. And how you have had to decide which decisions are actually ethical, and how you are to respond to people who understand the issues differently. Vaccines are especially difficult to decipher regarding the ethics involved. And here I am not just referring to COVID vaccines. Some Christians don't want to have anything to do with vaccines because in the development process aborted fetal tissue was used. That is a legitimate concern, and yet other Christians recognize that the principle of what man meant for evil, abortion. God meant for good a vaccine that can prevent illness. As a pastor, I support both sides because I don't want people to do things or not do things that will go against their conscience. were to do all things by faith. What I do know, however, with certainty Is the will of God in the matter which is to not condemn my fellow Christian for the decisions he or she makes? And it is not for me to disfellowship with Christians that see things on such matters as different from me. Once again, being on this side of the sun and seeing through the glass dimly Accepts that I am in no position to charge, try, convict, and condemn anyone on such matters. This is why the metaphor of all of us being one body is so helpful. Because it is not just about vaccines. It's the many different choices we make, different, that is, from one another in the same body of Christ. Differences that make it a feeding ground for the devil and his minions to find ways to create discord. Let us consider the many ways our present culture thinks differently than how Christians are to think. Our present culture says cancel anyone who has sins in their past that are no longer acceptable. In contrast, Christians say repent and be forgiven. And don't ask for forgiveness for something you haven't done. Our present culture says, look out for number one and get what is yours. In contrast, Christians say, think of others before yourself Our present culture says, pursue your pleasures, especially the sexual ones, and identify yourself with your desires. In contrast, Christians say flee sexual immorality and practice self-control while identifying first and last as a Christian. Our present culture says, fear death and accept any restraint on your freedoms to avoid death. In contrast, Christians say to die is gain, to live is Christ. Our present culture says there is no God, there is no devil, there is no heaven, and there is no hell. So eat, drink, and be merry. In contrast, Christians say, eat, drink, and be merry, because there is a God, and He provided your meal, and there is a devil, so resist him. And there is heaven. So look to it as your reward. And there is a hell. So warn people who are lost in their sin. Beloved, the devil is going to continue to come up with many ways to get you to think differently about your faith, about morality, about what to fear. And you're going to have to continue to prove what is good, acceptable, and perfect will of God. That is the Christian life. Stay in the fight and allow your mind to be renewed. Here is a new thought for you. When you look around and conclude how successful the devil has been by using this therapeutic age. He has developed to get people to change their minds on what is sexually immoral and what is a lawful marriage. And what is decent regarding entertainment, and what is to be feared most, consider this, how God will use all of this to usher in his kingdom. Consider God's track record. A womb was vacant and a couple very old, only to become parents of millions. Joseph, son of Jacob, was in a pit only to be raised to rule Egypt. The people of Israel were being mocked by a giant. Who no man could defeat until a kid with a rock took him down. Jesus was dead. The disciples were scattered. All of it appeared to be a victory for the devil, all of it until day three If we get our minds off of COVID numbers and on to what God does when all seems very, very bad. That is getting your mind renewed. Let us pray. Our gracious and heavenly Father, we thank you for the renewing of our minds. We thank you for dropping the scales from our eyes. We thank you for the perspective that is needed to be saved. Now we ask, give us the courage to live it out. To live out this renewing of our mind, that we ourselves might be transformed, and that we might help transform the world. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Overcome evil with good
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: I have to say, I tuned in last week as we were in Tacoma, Washington, and uh I I so much appreciate Reverend Voles and his faithfulness. But it's just not the same as being in person. It's good to be in the house of God. We attended a church that is the oldest building in Tacoma, Washington, and it houses an Anglican church. And we just so happened to attend there's about probably ten of us there, and we uh attended where the uh the priest had COVID, so he couldn't be there, and a layman read morning prayer, made an attempt at a sermon. And uh and we were dismissed within forty-five minutes. Um again, good to be here in the house of God. We're going to be covering two sections. The first is our reading from the Gospel according to St. John, and then we'll go into Romans chapter 12. So join me in both of those. Regarding the narrative in John chapter 2, where Jesus attends a wedding with his disciples, there are several interesting tidbits to take away, thus reminding us Of the likely reason for telling the story. First, Jesus attends a wedding This is pointed out in our prayer book in the wedding ceremony liturgy. The fact that Jesus took the time to attend a wedding. Verifies the importance of a wedding ceremony and the celebration that follows. Weddings are a type of what kind of relationship God wants with his people. The book of Revelation describes a great wedding banquet as a heavenly reward after Jesus is properly wedded to his bride, which is the church, who is us. The Anglican tradition refers to marriage as sacramental, meaning that it is not a sacrament in the way that Baptism and Holy Communion are sacraments, which refers to rituals that all Christians are to participate But it is like a sacrament, and that those who do participate in it are to treat it as a sacred thing. We say in our wedding liturgy that marriage is, quote, not to be entered into, nor taken in hand unadvisedly lightly or wantonly to satisfy men's carnal lusts and appetites, but reverently, discreetly, advisedly, soberly, and in the fear of God Second, when Jesus is spoken to by his mother, he calls her woman, which seems to be a reference to Mary's position as the new Eve, for Eve simply means woman. Third, when Jesus refers to his hour, he is talking about the time that his messiahship is revealed with the knowledge that when it is revealed that he is claiming to be the Messiah, the Jewish leaders will come after him to take his life. This is why when Jesus performs miracles and asks that what he did be kept quiet There was a time he was going to accept his fate on the cross, but that time was specific and was not to be hurried. Fourth, Mary ignores this concern and instructs the servants to do as Jesus says. And this confirms the danger Mary was willing to enter into. It is dangerous for Jesus to work a miracle and thus begin the journey to the cross. Mary is willing to begin that journey, and so is Jesus. Fifth, Jesus fills six water pots representing the six days of creation. Six, that the master of the feast notices the difference in wine quality confirms that this is not Welch's grape juice or grape juice plus This is the wine that people would drink to make the heart glad, just as we do today And when the heart was glad, the quality of wine didn't matter, except to Jesus, for he thought it did matter, and therefore turned the water into better wine. And our reading from Romans chapter 12, beginning at verse 16, and I encourage you to turn there in your Bibles. I question the wisdom of the liturgy to begin at verse 16 because it needs to be examined. with the knowledge of verses 14 and 15 addressed last week. The instruction to bless those who persecute you, verse 14. And to rejoice with those who rejoice, and to weep with those who weep, verse 15, are very difficult things to do For they call us to do what does not come naturally to the human sinful condition. We naturally want to get back at those who persecute us. And when our enemies rejoice or weep, we don't naturally want to rejoice or weep with them. Many of you didn't weep with Steeler fans when they lost last week. And I know there are some Steeler fans here, so I said many, not all. The point is St. Paul is setting a standard that is difficult to live up to But he sets it anyways, and we are to strive to that standard. As most of you know, I came to a saving faith in Jesus Christ while a senior in high school. And when I would share my new faith with my peers, a primary objection to being a Christian was that life would be boring. Of course, the definition of boring in high school, public high school, was the inability to party freely, which means abusing alcohol, using drugs, and engaging in fornication My objection to such an objection was that my eternal life needed to be more important than my immediate gratification of the flesh, and so I would settle for Bory. But having walked the narrow road for 39 years, I have experienced how free the Christian faith allows me to be. For I can be at peace with God and peace with my fellow man while gratifying the flesh in the context of the marriage covenant, while also being challenged to live a better life than I naturally am inclined to do. Nothing else in the world, no religion, no guru, no counselor will instruct me to bless those who persecute me. Or weep with my enemy. And yet that is exactly what I'm supposed to do as a follower of Jesus Christ. Striving to practice such behavior is not only the opposite of boring, but it is a dangerous life. Because it sets itself against the world that is going the opposite direction. It is within the context of verses 14 and 15. Where we are told in verse sixteen, to be not wise in your own opinion. This is similar to Proverbs 3, verse 7, where God's people are told, Be not wise in your own eyes, fear the Lord, and turn away from evil. What is implied there is that to be wise in your own eyes is to trust too much in yourself. So much so that you think you can figure things out on your own. And that means that you are not fearing the Lord. Because if you feared the Lord, you would seek his counsel. Without seeking the Lord for counsel, you will fail to turn away from evil. Paul's instruction also reminds us That humility is necessary to the Christian, not only in our dealings with others, but also to keep our mind open and teachable. A person who sees his errors learns from them. And let us be reminded that these instructions to think and act differently than the world are connected to the instruction at the beginning of chapter twelve, which was to be transformed by the renewing of our minds. Beloved, in our natural state as sinners, we don't think right You may wonder how people of this world can look at a baby in a womb and not see a human being and therefore justify abortion at any stage. And you may wonder how a union between Adam and Steve is seen as just as natural as a union between Adam and Eve. And you may wonder how a natural born man can be called a woman, and vice versa But people do think in such a manner and march and protest for their right to do so. But we are descendants of Adam and Eve. Thus we are under a sinful covenant. For Adam and Eve thought they could know good and evil from the side of disobedience. Thus, we needed a Savior who died and rose again in order to show us good and evil from the side of obedience. But because we were first born in sin under Adam and Eve, before our spiritual eyes were opened, we therefore need to work at having our minds renewed. In verse seventeen, it says, to repay. To repay is to give or return what is given to you. Again, this is one of the most difficult standards for a human being to follow. And yet it is the standard for the Christian. It takes moxie to live in such a manner. He says regard means properly to think or meditate beforehand Thus, we are to consider how to respond to the evil done to us, and that means we are not to be a people who suddenly react. We are not to be a people who act out of passion first. Instead, we are to have a settled plan on how we react to the evil done to us and our thinking. is to go along the line of what would be good in the eyes of most men, what most people would understand to be a good response. The phrase good things means actually what is beautiful or comely, attractive. Consider again how high of a standard this is. The world might be impressed if we simply didn't give back evil for evil. But we are to do something beautiful to the person who is evil to us. That sounds ridiculous. Until we remember that our Lord prayed for those who put him on the cross, asking that they be forgiven. What is more beautiful than that? Thus, that is what we are to pray when evil is done to us. Forgive them, Lord, for they know not what they do. And if returning beauty for evil is not difficult enough, we are then told to live peaceably with all persons if possible. Unfortunately, I can testify that it is at times not possible. I have reached out to several people who have left our parish being angry with me for what reasons I was not never told. I have reached out via email, physical letters, and even when I have seen them face to face, and I have asked, what have I done? That they no longer speak to me, and I am given no answer. But we are to try, which is what the phrase, as much as depends on you, means. Again, such is not an easy thing to do. We risk the likelihood of being rejected. Our pride will likely get hurt when we try to apologize or at least discover what we should apologize for. But our pride being hurt is to be sacrificed because the standard is to be at peace with every person we can be at peace with. And peace means forgiveness. Peace means we don't hold any anger or animosity toward another human being. And impossible that we give opportunity for others to not be angry or have animosity toward us The instruction not to avenge means that we have been wrongly and justly treated, and yet we are not given the freedom to equal the wrong. To give place is to stand aside. It is getting out of the way to allow God to enact whatever justice he wills. With the knowledge that he will repay the evil that has been done to his people who are his. Beloved, we are to be as confident in God's avending justice as we are. confident about our salvation. And it only makes sense for God to enact his justice, for he is the only one by nature who is just But what are we to do in the meantime as we wait for this justice? It can take a while before we see God's vengeance, and it may not even be in our lifetime. So what are we supposed to do? Verse 20 says that while we wait for God's justice We are to feed our enemies and provide for them drink. I say it again because it does not sit well. While we wait for God's justice, we are to provide food and drink for the very people who wrong us. This is that boring Christianity I described earlier. The phrase, heap coals of fire. I have heard it said that such would be a blessing because People supposedly would carry hot coals in some type of container on their heads in order to have fire when they arrived at their destination. I found such a teaching on various evangelical websites, but not one respected historical commentator mentions it. What makes the most sense to me is that because coals of fire is used elsewhere in Scripture to communicate God's judgment To heat coals on a person's head is a metaphor for not fully condemning them, but giving them a wake-up call for their conscience. So, whether it is to keep a fire going or to burn a person's head, the main message is to awaken their conscience to further highlight how evil they have been. And the main point of St. Paul's teaching on how we are to treat our enemy is to overcome their behavior by being good to them. But who would live this out? Seriously Who would practice this type of behavior to overcome evil with good? First It would have to be someone who actually believed the gospel of Jesus Christ. This is to believe that Jesus was God incarnate. That what he taught was true, that the miracles he is said to have performed were real, and that he really did die on the cross while asking his enemies to be forgiven. It also would be to fully believe that he did indeed rise from the dead and ascended into heaven and sent the Holy Spirit. All of it you would have to believe was true to overcome evil with good Second, for such a person to live this type of life, you would have to not be concerned about self. To not think about self, you would have to place other people's needs before your own. And that includes the needs of your enemy. To put other people's needs before yourself, you would have to get phrases out of your life, such as, I like. I want, I prefer, my desire, my needs, what about me? Out of your speech. Third, for such a person to live this type of life where you work to overcome evil with good You would have to seize every moment where it is possible to do good instead of evil done to you And this last point I make because we are almost two years total in living within a pandemic, and two years of a human being's life is a great deal of time. Take myself, for example. The average age of death for an American male is 79. Let's round it up to 80. I was 55 when the pandemic started. That meant that when the pandemic started, I was I had 25 years to live. Thus the pandemic and the government restrictions has taken eight percent of my lifetime left. Eight percent. And how much more does it want to take? As the writer of Ecclesiastes says, the human life is like vapor. It is here, and then it is gone. We see it, so we know it has substance, but then it evaporates and it is gone. At a cemetery in Tacoma, Washington, lie my parents, who died when my father was 32 and my mother was 29. My grandparents on my father's side are also there, with my grandmother dying at 61, my grandfather at 74. On that same plot is my aunt who raised me, who also died at 61. And with all of them is a stillborn boy named Josiah, son of my sister and brother-in-law. Across the way, maybe 30 yards, are my grandparents on my mother's side with a surname Barrett. My grandmother died at 72, and my grandfather died at 89. On their plot is their son Thomas, my uncle, who died at the age of sixty. Tears came upon me suddenly when I visited them last weekend. I didn't expect that. I thought of what could have been. What would have been so different? It is vapor, beloved. It is all vapor. I wonder if any of you know anyone that is living their life to overcome evil with good Do you know someone who believes the gospel of Jesus Christ? All of it, without a doubt? Do you know someone who is not concerned about self but instead puts the needs of others before their own? Do you know someone who seizes every possible opportunity to overcome evil with good? Do you know someone like that? I know Betty Moores. That is about as close as I've gotten to knowing someone like that. And yet that is the standard for Christians for living this boring Christian life. In trying to live this life, you will fail. You will fall short. You will sin. And the Bible says to confess such sin, turn away from it, and try again. And then again. And then again. And then again. Until your vapor disappears. Allow me to provide something practical. The next time you feel an injustice was done to you, and done on purpose, because the evildoer doesn't like you. When that feeling of vengeance rises within you, tell yourself, overcome evil with good. Tell it to your inner self, overcome evil with good. And pay attention how your emotions change, how your eyes will be open to see how to react in other ways. besides vengeance. And perhaps, perhaps you will become the next person you know that does live this way. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Jesus is Sovereign
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. He be seated. We'll be looking at both the Romans section, Romans chapter 13, and I'm sure many of you are curious about this in light of all that we've had to do in regards to our government. And then we will be looking at Matthew chapter eight. In order to begin to understand Romans chapter 13, We must see it in light of what we learned from the chapter that immediately precedes it, and in specific the end of chapter twelve. We sometimes get mesmerized by the chapter numbers and forget that these are texts that succeed one another in a continuous narrative. There at the end of chapter twelve, we are taught that Christians are not to avenge themselves They are never to avenge themselves, but leave room for God's wrath. He will repay. Vengeance is his. Other factors needed for understanding Romans 13 is the history of Israel For most of her history, Israel was subject to powers, governments, and empires far greater than herself. In the era immediately before the New Testament, Israel's greatest feat as a people was accomplished under the Maccabees, who led a resistance movement, what we moderns would call a guerrilla struggle. Against their Greek oppressors. But how does that square with Romans thirteen? At the time of the writing of the New Testament, the Jews were subject to the Roman government They were not free to practice their faith, but depended solely on the Roman Imperial Empire to give them that permission. And then on such would be the case for the Christian Church, as it would have to make its way in the world quietly, being careful not to offend unnecessary powers that be By the end of the first century and thereafter, the number of Christians executed by the state for no other reason but that they were followers of Jesus Christ grew grotesquely. It is with these truths in our minds that we can now look at the passages in question, chapter 13, beginning at verse 1. What is fundamentally taught in this passage is that the rights of an individual are a second priority for the Christian. What is to be regarded more than personal rights are duties of Christians. And what is also fundamental is that those duties are founded on theological realities. The reason Christians must obey the state is because it has been instituted by God. Thus, its authority derives from the Christian's own Heavenly Father. Verse 2. Because all governing authority comes from God, to resist it is to resist what God has put in place And whatever punishment we receive is simply getting what we deserve. Verse 3. To avoid punishment is to avoid fear of governing authorities. And to avoid fear, you must do good. Such is not complicated. Verse 4. The term sword is a metaphor for any punishment handed down by a governing authority. Some people believe it is a justification for capital punishment. But the main point is that God uses governing authorities to exercise his wrath. Verse five The conscience is usually overlooked, and yet it is remarkably necessary to consider for much of our physical and social health is related to our conscience. If we are doing what we should not be doing, we are jeopardizing our well-being. Verse 6. It should be no surprise that taxes should enter the discussion regarding obedience to the state, because from the very beginning taxes have been a chief means By which states impose their power upon their citizens while also being the chief complaint of those citizens against the government. The Revolutionary War, after all, was ostensibly about taxes. But the same argument wages today. As someone once said, if our forefathers thought taxation without representation was bad, they ought to see what it is like with representation. Verse 7. There may be even here an echo of the Lord's remark, rendering Caesar the things that are Caesar's and to God the things that are God's. We know that Paul was thoroughly familiar with the substance of the gospel accounts and the words of Jesus. He would have had those words echoing in his mind. Now, the great irony of this whole section of Scripture is that St. Paul would soon find himself in jail by the Romans for doing the very thing he says not to do. For Paul did disobey his governing authorities by preaching the gospel. This then must take us to Acts chapter 5. Where the Jewish high priests and the elders of the Sadducees placed Peter and the other apostles in what is called the common prison. But the Holy Spirit broke them out, and they went straight to the temple to teach the crowd about Jesus. When they were discovered to be out of the jail, they were once again captured and told not to teach about Jesus, which brought this reply, we ought to obey God rather than men. And that is the crux of the matter, is it not? The context of Paul's instruction allows us to summarize his teaching about Christians obeying governing authorities in the following manner. Christians are to lay low when it comes to matters of the state that would interfere with them preaching, teaching, and obeying the gospel. This doesn't mean that Christians can't be involved in state affairs. Not at all. Again, the context is not pursuing vengeance, but instead returning evil with good. And then trusting God will enact vengeance, which he does many times through governing authorities. And because God controls governing authorities, we should obey them, which allows us to keep a good witness before them. All of that makes sense until Until a governing authority forbids what God commands. If you wonder how this can be lived out, I have an example for us. In a letter written by a man named Wang Yi, a Christian pastor and now a prisoner in China, sentenced to nine years for preaching the gospel. He asked that this letter be read if he could not be found, for it would mean that the state had arrested him. The translation is a bit broken and it's a little bit lengthy, but it's really good. He says, according to the teachings of the Bible and the mission of the gospel, I respect the founding powers of God in China. Because the King of Waste and the King of Kings are all in God. To this end I obey God's arrangement of Chinese history and institutions. As a pastor of the Christian Church, I started from the Bible and had my own understanding and views on social, political, and legal fields, what is justice and the governance of goodness. At the same time, I am full of disgust and hatred for the Chinese government's persecution of the church, the deprivation of human faith, and the freedom of conscience. However, the change of all social and political systems is not the mission of my calling, nor the purpose of the gospel being given to the people of God. Because all the ugliness of reality, the political injustice, the arbitrariness of the law show that the cross of Jesus Christ is the only salvation that every Chinese must have. It also shows that true hope and perfect human society does not exist in any institutional and cultural changes of the earth. But simply how humans' sins are forgiven by Christ and have the hope of eternal life As a pastor, my faith in the gospel and the teaching of the people and the blame for all sin are out of Christ's command in the gospel Out of the unmeasurable love of the glory king. Everyone's life is so short, and God is so eager to command the church to lead and call anyone who is willing to repent, to repent. Christ is so urgent and willing to forgive all who turn from sin. This is the purpose of all the work of the Church in China. It is to witness Christ to the world, to witness the kingdom of heaven to China, and to witness the eternal life of heaven to the short life of the earth. This is also my pastoral call To this end, I accept and respect the Chinese regime as a temporary ruler allowed by God, as the Lord's servant John Calvin said, The ruler of evil is God's punishment for the wicked people, and the purpose is to urge the people of God to repent To this end, I am willing to obey their law, enforcement, behavior physically, as if obeying the Lord's discipline and training I also believe that the persecution of the church by the Chinese communist regime is extremely evil in crime. As a pastor of the Christian church, I must sternly and openly blame such sins. The calling also requires me to violate all human laws. that violate the Bible and God in a non-violent form in peace and patience. Christ my Savior also asks me to joyfully bear all the costs of the transgressing evil laws. But this does not mean that my personal and church disobedience is a political act, in any sense of activism or civil disobedience. Because I have no intention of changing any of the Chinese systems and laws, as a pastor, the only thing I care about is the disobedience of faith, the shock of sinful humanity, and the testimony of the cross of Christ. As a pastor, my disobedience is part of the gospel mission. The great mission of Christ requires our great resistance to the world. The purpose of existing is not to change the world, but to witness another world. Well said. Clearly, what Pastor Yi accepts is the sovereignty of God. What Pastor Yi has faith in is that God is sovereign. And he's going to accomplish his perfect will. And that means suffering under an unjust political system, trusting that all of it contains God's love And this is where we can transition now to our gospel reading. What is remarkable about the two characters highlighted in the two stories of healing in Matthew chapter 8? Is the faith that both of them have. The leper has faith that it only takes the will of Jesus to determine whether he can be healed. Which is an acceptance of the power of Jesus to heal when and how and where he wants to When Jesus proclaims his will, he then touches the unclean man. And as Matthew describes, the leper is immediately healed, on the spot. That the leper was to tell no one is similar to our discussion last week, and that it was not yet Jesus' hour. We recognize that when too many people would witness the power of Jesus, they would want him to publicly claim his messiahship, and Jesus still had much to teach and much to do. We know that the centurion described next had even more faith than the leper, for Jesus said the same as it was greater than any Israelite that was following him, even greater than the apostles. A centurion was an officer in the Roman army, and as their title gives away, he was a commander over a hundred men. The centuria is Latin for 100. Various paths led to becoming a centurion. Some were appointed by the Senate or the Emperor, or elected by their fellow soldiers. But most were enlisted men promoted through the ranks after 15 to 20 years of service. As company commanders, they held important responsibilities, including training giving out assignments and maintaining discipline in the ranks. When the army encamped, centurions supervised the building of fortifications, a crucial duty in enemy territory. They also escorted prisoners and procured food and supplies when the army was on the move. As his words displayed, this centurion talking to Jesus knew what it meant to be under authority and to be the one in authority. And if he can, if he can get, this is his thinking, if he can get what he wanted when he wanted it, so too could Jesus and much more. He understood that Jesus didn't have to touch the leper to heal the leper. He didn't need to touch the tongue to give a man speech, or to touch ears to give a man hearing. Jesus did those things to demonstrate to his followers what he was healing. But in truth, he simply needed to will it to be so, and it was so. And as I said previously, this is a belief in the sovereignty of God, and specifically the sovereignty of Jesus, who was and is the God-man. This is why believing that Jesus is fully God and fully man is so important. For if it were not so, then Jesus would be a simple magician. And it would be his father doing the healing. But the centurion understands that it is the sovereignty of Jesus that is doing the healing. Thus, you and I are to have faith in the sovereignty of Jesus. That word sovereignty comes from the Latin having various pronunciations but with a consistent meaning. It is to be the superior ruler. It communicates that there is no one who can be above said ruler. The power of the knowledge of the sovereignty of Jesus is one of the more comforting doctrines that we can embrace. Consider what it means for each Christian. First, nothing can happen to you that is not the will of God. Nothing And that is comforting because God loves you and He wants to do good for you. But not all things are good right now, you say. All right. Well, remember the quotable verse from Romans chapter 8. All things work together for the good, for those who love God and are called according to his purpose. Thus, a wise person said, if things are not good, then God is not done. When in Tacoma, Washington, two weeks ago. Bobby Lynn and I were driving alongside the inlet waters of the Puget Sound when I received an emergency alert on my phone. That there were conditions for a tsunami to hit the Puget Sound and for everyone to stay away from the shorelines. Well, we were driving along the shoreline. I thought it ridiculous to imagine a tsunami hitting the Puget Sound, but later there I found that was recorded an eruption of a volcano in the Pacific Ocean near Tonga. And though I thought it ridiculous to be hit by a tsunami, still my mind played out what it would be like to get hit by a tsunami on a shoreline in Tacoma, Washington. And my following thought was: well, if that is how God wants me to depart this world, then that is what's going to happen. And that thought was comforting to me. After all, what does Psalm 139 mean to Each of us, when the psalmist says, Of all of us, your eyes saw my unformed substance. In your book were written every one of them the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them. And these words by Job speaking of all human beings, quote, Since his days are determined, and the number of his months is with you, speaking to God. And you have appointed his limits that he cannot pass. And these words recorded by Jesus, you remember in Matthew chapter 6. And which of you, by being anxious, can add a single hour to his span of life? And from Job again. In his God's hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind. Are such passages humbling? Yes. But they are also comforting, for they tell us that we do not control our lifespan. They tell us we don't have to be anxious about tsunamis. They tell us we don't have to be anxious about blank. Put your concern here. And please step away from all the questions that naturally come up when we talk about God's sovereignty Yes, you should still pray because God wants a relationship with us. Yes, you still make decisions, but never outside of God's will. And no one knows exactly how that works. Yes, there is a permissive will of God and a sovereign will of God, and it is a sovereign will that cannot be thwarted. The point still is that God is sovereign. Jesus, our Savior, is the superior ruler over all nations. All governments, entities, all big tech, all political parties, all laws and regulations, all religious institutions. He's sovereign over them all. I recently listened to a podcast that warned against using Google and other big tech listen as they are listening to our conversations and trying to influence how we think. Yeah, probably. But Jesus is still sovereign. Beloved, humanity today, especially in the West Thinks that we are quite important, thinks that we are influential, so much so that we could even change the weather. But we are not. We are none of those things. For nothing we do is outside God's will. And so we trust him. We trust him no matter what he said, what it some excuse me. We trust him no matter what is said on the news or what threatens us. We trust him. We trust in Jesus. Amen. Let us pray. A gracious God, we are reminded of the man who stood before Jesus and said, I believe, but help my unbelief. No doubt there are people here who are struggling with the idea, Lord, that nothing can happen outside your will, even their very lifespan. Father, give them faith and trust in you, that indeed they can put their full trust in you that no matter what happens, it will be for our good because you love us. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: There's a Fight Going On
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Our focus once again is on the two readings, the epistle reading and the gospel reading. And I want to begin by highlighting for you the call X, or For those of you who are new to us, the prayers for the week that we pray each week, this week being the fifth Sunday after Epiphany. On the third week of Epiphany, we prayed that God would mercifully look upon all our dangers and necessities. By stretching forth his right hand to help and defend us. On the fourth Sunday after Epiphany, we prayed that God, who knows our frailties May grant us strength and protection to support us through all dangers and temptations. Today we pray that the church may be kept in the true religion While being defended by God's mighty power. I trust you see a theme in these prayers, or at least a recognition that you and I, as individuals, and as a church lumped together are in need of help. We are in danger. And without the help of God, we are doomed. And I'm not being overly dramatic. In the 1980s, a series of books became popular among evangelical Christians that depicted the Christian life as unseen warfare. The novels were written by author Frank Peretti, who described the daily life of a Christian as unaware of the spiritual battles that were occurring around them. As he or she went about his or her daily life. Feretti described angels fighting with demons over what influences an average Christian while being tempted to engage in sin. Ferretti describes a demon attacking an angel with a fiery weapon in order to have an advantage over a woman. He is trying to tempt While the angel returns fire with heavenly weaponry that would thwart the demon Now how accurate Paretti was is unknown, but his writings seem to awake an awareness within Christians Of an awareness that was not present before. At least that was true for me. These prayers for the past few weeks have also had a similar effect on me, waking up something about the danger we are in. How much danger I am actually in each day, I have not been aware of. But as a pastor, I am observant to the dangers parishioners face. Consider The devil tries to make you unhappy in your marriage, thinking that maybe you married the wrong person. The devil and his minions work to make you unhappy in your work Wanting you to conclude that you have pursued the wrong vocation. Demons are working to make you unhappy in your church by calling you to follow your emotions rather than your convictions. Spiritual warfare is being raised over your desire to pursue sex over covenant, to pursue food, over self-control, to withhold forgiveness over love. To accept doubt over faith, to surrender to fear over the sovereignty of God. But we don't see the warfare, we don't see the danger. The devil doesn't appear before us in a red suit with a pitchfork in his hand, speaking audibly to us about the temptations he's going to put before us. He is subtle. We don't like something about someone or something, and we still and so we allow it to fester within our conscience. We feel slighted, uncared for, disrespected, even though it was not done to us intentionally. Still we know we don't like how we have been treated. We might talk to others about it and and when we find someone that thinks similarly about the person we are upset at You're upset with. We now have an ally that testifies and justifies why we are upset. Soon everything about that person or about that organization or about that leadership, everything they do now is wrong And gives us additional reason why not to like them, or him, or it. And it all adds up to canceling said person or said organization out of our lives. What we don't see, what we think was just us and our will, was actually a series of demons. coaxing us along, encouraging every evil thought and every evil emotion, every hate, every anger. What we failed to see was the danger we were in, and our need to be protected from such danger. In the passage read from Colossians, we have to notice how important it is for Christians to work on relationships with fellow Christians. It is the recognition that if we cannot practice the Christian charity we are to be given in Christ and to give in Christ, if we cannot practice it toward fellow Christians Then the world cannot know the truth of the gospel because we are not a witness to it. And it further is evidence that the love of God actually is not within us. That Christians don't forgive and love other Christians is a real problem within the church, and I have felt it firsthand. As a pastor, I am a walking pariah for some people. People see me in public And having not been in church or no longer pretending to walk with the Lord, the sight of me, not me personally, but the office that I hold reminds them of their not being in church or not walking with the Lord and brings guilt and so they avoid me. They look the other way or if they have to engage me they act like they are quickly going to the bathroom. What they don't see, what they don't know, is that there is a spiritual warfare going on within them that yells, get away from him. In one voice, and be reconciled to him in another voice. Unfortunately, the voice that says, get away from him, is the voice most heeded. Let us look at Colossians chapter three, beginning at verse twelve. Paul has previously told the Colossian Christians what to put off, which are the sins of malice and sins of the flesh. He now turns to what they should put on. And these things to put on are to be done as being a part of the, he says, the elect. Most references to Christians being the elect is to connect them with the Israelites who were the elect, while also teaching each Christian that his or her salvation is determined by God, not by man. And are we not grateful for that? He then calls Christians holy. Calling Christians holy is to call us what God has made us, for the holiness that we have is his work. To call us beloved reveals the heart of God toward us. He so loved the world that he gave us his son. And now being the elect, being holy, being beloved, we are to put on tender mercies, which is us passing on the grace of God to other people. We are to put on kindness, which is to be to others as we wish they would be to us. We are to put on humility, which is not to think highly of ourselves. We are also to put on meekness, which is being gentle to one another, which is to be gentle in the realm of physical gentleness, spiritual gentleness, and emotional gentleness. We are to put on long-suffering, which is bearing with one another, having the heart that says, even in your flaws, I will love you and respect you. And we are to put on forgiveness, which is a willingness and eagerness not to hold someone's sins against them, even when they hurt us personally. But to forgive someone of their sins even if they do not ask for said forgiveness. And our standard for forgiving others is how we have been forgiven. That is why we pray, forgive us our trespasses. As we forgive those who trespass against us. He then tells us that we should put on, above all that has been mentioned, we should put on love. He calls this love the bond of perfection. That means that the love is like an upper garment. which completes and keeps together all the rest, which without it would be loose and disconnected Consider that grace is practiced where love is wanting are mere hypocrisy. And we remember from 1 Corinthians 13 that this love we are to put on consists of being patient, being kind, keeping no record of wrong, just as Paul has described to the Colossians. In truth, you cannot put on kindness, meekness, long-suffering, and all the rest unless you put on love, for such things are the substance of love. And look at the result in verse 15. We have peace with God as He rules in our hearts. And how does he do that? By us putting on love. Now I know from some Calvinists that statement doesn't sound right. All that saves us comes from God. And I say, absolutely. But the instruction for us to put on all the attributes of love is Holy Scripture. So it is something that we do, and yet our salvation is entirely what God does. Yes and yes. How does that work? I don't know. But I know what the Bible says, and you read it with me. We are responsible to put on all that is associated with the love of God, even while He secures our salvation. Practically, it is remembering that love is our standard. And then remembering what love is: patient, kind, merciful, etc. And then it is choosing to practice that standard in all my dealings within the church. So that email that I am writing because I am frustrated and angry has to give way to love. That speech I want to give to put someone in their place. has got to be silenced and replaced with words of encouragement. That ignoring that I want to continue must be replaced by giving another person my time and my energy. That withholding of forgiveness, while keeping record of wrong done to me, needs to be acknowledged as sin, and I need to choose love, which is to choose to forgive. Consider this. Just as I was talking about the spiritual dangers that surround us, so we must realize that the emotion You have to be angry, to be bitter, to insist justice for yourself. Such emotions and the defense of such emotions are voices of the devil And his minions calling you out to lash out. But the voice that says, be patient here. Or the voice that says, Be meek there. Such is never from the devil, but only from God. Thus voices and emotions that are not love are not of God and must be rebuked. Jesus in Matthew 13 provides a parable for us to understand the battle that rages over our souls. We should remember first that Jesus told the, in the same chapter, told a previous parable about the sowing of seeds. In that parable, the sowing was the preaching of the gospel, and the ground was the hearts of those who would hear the gospel. Some hearts are rocky and no seed takes root. Other hearts contain weeds which choke out the healthy plant. Other seeds were received with fertile hearts, where they took root and grew healthy. This parable, this parable we examine. Seems to be more about Christians and their lives as they already have growth and health and salvation In the parable, it is the enemy of the sower who sows the tares, the weeds, amidst the wheat. In our lives, as Christians, it is the devil himself who sows tares, weeds in our lives that grow along with what is fruitful and healthy. Teres can be false teachers, deceitful men, and those who simply make life difficult. We can want them out of our lives, asking the Lord to remove them, but a good farmer knows that if you harvest the tares too soon, you also are going to damage the wheat. This reminds us that not every everyone who says they are a Christian actually is a Christian. Jesus Himself. Said that many will say in the day of judgment, Lord, Lord, looking for him for salvation. And he will say, I have never known you. One of the more fascinating stories in the Bible is that of Judas Iscariot, who we knew we know portrayed Jesus. And people like to ask difficult questions such as, could Judas have chosen not to betray Jesus or was he destined to do so? We can answer that and not be absolutely sure. What was always fascinating to me is that when Jesus sat down with his apostles and Blessed the bread while breaking it and passing it and saying to each, This is my body. And then blessing the wine and passing to each of them, saying, This is my blood. He shares it with all of them alike, which is to say that Jesus communed with the man he knew would betray him. Such was truly love and sorrow mixed. Having at the time knowledge of what was in the heart of Judas and what he would do. Jesus talks elsewhere about separating true believers from those who say they believe. But that too is only to occur at the day of judgment and not before. Because the hearts of individuals are unknown, The day of judgment is not only going to surprise many because they thought they believed, but they did not. Observers of such surprises will also be surprised, because outwardly we were certain that this person was a Christian. But there was no inward faith. And there are others that look outwardly like they don't have faith, and yet there is a saving faith within Because we are susceptible to deceiving ourselves, thinking we have a faith when we do not, the words of our collect this week are necessary to pray. Again, we are to pray these words. That the church may be kept in the true religion while being defended by God's mighty power. The easiest and most haunting example we have is the mainline Episcopal Church. We could point to the ordaining of women, which began in 1974 But we have to go back even further to understand what justified the ordination of women. During the 1950s and 60s, Episcopal seminaries, along with mainline Presbyterian seminaries, were following the teachings of a man named Rudolf Boltmann Who was following the tradition known as Higher Criticism, which dates back to the 17th century? Higher criticism was looking at ancient texts such as the Bible. From twentieth century lenses, and denying what did not hold up to contemporary scholarship Its fault, higher criticism's fault, of course, was that no ancient text can hold up to 20th and 21st century standards For there was no using of footnotes, no checking of quotes, no bibliographies for cross-reference, no means to historically verify stories The end goal of these higher critics was to demythologize the Bible. So texts such as Paul saying to Timothy, I do not permit a woman to teach or to have authority over a man. These were to be viewed by modern Christians as misogynistic and thus stuck in their historical context. It then became a common practice in seminaries to look at a biblical text in light of modern sensitivities, allowing the sensitivities to lead the way. Hence, a bishop looked at the justification of ordaining women and concluded that ordaining openly homosexuals fell under the same argument. Soon there is nothing in the Bible that speaks to morality that carries any authority The very existence of Jesus of Nazareth falls next, falls next, giving us today leaders in the Episcopal Church who care more That happened that happened this year, who care more about speaking about climate change than preaching the gospel to a lost and dead world Meanwhile, the devil smiles and the demons cackle. Maybe you have noticed, maybe you have not. But I have a ritual before I preach. I kneel and I first rebuke the devil and his minions from this sanctuary so that the people of God can clearly hear the voice of God. I then ask the Holy Spirit to anoint my words, and that I cross myself three times, first on my forehead, asking that my mind might be blessed. Then I crossed my lips, asking for my speech to be blessed. And then I crossed my heart so that my heart would believe the truth of God's word. It is my way of saying, as St. Paul said, so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified from the prize. I do this because, as we have prayed these past few weeks, we need God to mercifully look upon all our dangers and necessities. By stretching forth his right hand to help and defend us. We need that God, who knows our frailties, may grant us strength and protection to support us through all dangers and temptations. We need that the church may be kept in the true religion while being defended by God's mighty power. Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious and heavenly Father, we submit all of these prayers together to you. Confessing that we are indeed in danger. Help us, dear Lord, to keep our wits about us, to pay attention to the fighting that goes around us. And to engage in it, that the devil might not have his way and that we might not be disqualified. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Covetous Herat
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Our focus this morning will be primarily on 2 Corinthians chapter 11. We will also be touching on our gospel reading, Luke chapter 8. When I was a boy of 13 years, I watched a movie that inspired me and that it helped me focus on what I wanted to be and do as a young man The movie was called One-on-One, starring Robbie Benson and Annette O'Toole. It was about a young man who had received a basketball scholarship from a major university being a basketball star in high school. Coming from a small town to a large university was a difficult transition, and the Robbie Benson character named Henry Steele didn't play well. The coach was disgusted with Henry's play, and so he tried to force him to quit the team and give up his scholarship. Meanwhile, Henry was falling in love with his tutor, played by Annette O'Toole. In a scene of romance, Annette's character named Janet calls college sports garbage. Henry responds with the following: quote, Maybe college sports, the way they are run, is garbage. But playing sports and sports itself is beautiful. You see, when I am working out and I hear myself and I feel it and it hurts and I don't think I can take one more step. And then I do. I know my legs are listening to something inside of me, something I didn't even know existed. Such a line echoed with me and stayed with me through my high school and college days And I still think of it when I am working out or playing a sport, and my body yells within me, stop, rest, quit. And the same lines, the same lines from that movie came back to me as I read the epistle and gospel lesson for this week. The Apostle Paul didn't know what was inside of him until he did what God was calling him to do. And he was able to do it. And I know that it is true for all of us who call ourselves Christians. We can be pushed beyond limits that we have set upon ourselves. So let us look at what Saint Paul endured as described in 2 Corinthians and see where we fit in when it comes to being pushed beyond limits that we set upon ourselves Our reading picks up at verse 19, but it is necessary to know that Paul was previously addressing the presence of men within the Corinthian church That were calling themselves apostles and therefore proclaiming to have the same authority, if not more authority, than St. Paul. He points out, Paul does, that he came preaching the gospel free of charge while the others expected a wage. He next pointed out that their deeds were not righteous, nor did they endure suffering for the sake of the gospel. He next apologizes for what he is about to explain, but he sees it necessary to prove his calling as an apostle so that the Christians at Corinth would not be led astray by false teachers. Again, picking up at verse 19. And there we find biting sarcasm. Modern ears don't appreciate this type of language, and many would stop reading because of the offense But Paul is goading them to make them angry in order to get their attention, in order to get them to see just how serious a thing it is to listen to false teachers. Jesus said that we would know false teachers by their fruit, which is a way which is the way which they live Well, these false teachers sacrificed nothing while also wanting to be compensated. In contrast, Paul sacrificed everything and asked for nothing. Thus the fruit between the two should have been obvious. Verses twenty and twenty-one The sophist philosophers of that day, traveling philosophers, were rough on their audiences. The people of Corinth were allowing themselves to be abused by these speakers who tried to humble their audiences in order to convince them that what they had to say was better than anything they had previously heard. Paul did not come to them berating them, and from some people's perspective that showed that he was weak. But he could be bold if they think that is what would be convincing. Verse 22. The false teachers obviously made a great deal about their themselves being authentic Jews. But Paul was first a disciple of Gamile, a Pharisee that was very respected in the day, as we read in the book of Acts. Paul was a student of the Pharisee of the Pharisees, therefore he could make the same boast. Verse 23. What follows is a more elaborate list than what was already given in chapter 6. Here is described the hardships of the apostle's life As proof of the privilege he considered it was to serve Jesus while he was given the empowerment to do so. The false teachers obviously saw Paul's suffering as a sign of his weakness. He saw it, and he wanted the Corinthians to see it as a sign of God's strength. Verse 24. We remember that forty lashes was the maximum allowed in the Old Testament law. The rabbinical principle was to give 39 so as to assure of not breaking the law by miscounting. To judge in such a manner is similar to our system that considers certain laws broken to garner certain many days in jail. Thus, certain laws broken earned a certain amount of lashes. What was not taken into consideration in every situation was that there were given lashes to an innocent man. Verse 25. Rods were used by the Romans for beating. So Paul got it from the Jews and from the Romans. And he shouldn't have been beaten as a Roman citizen, but we know from the book of Acts and first century evidence that citizenship did not always protect a person as it should have. Verse 26. One scholar has calculated that Paul would have traveled nearly 10,000 miles, making the trips that we know about in the New Testament. He would have shared the roads with and ships with governing officials, pilgrims, letter carriers, sightseers, runaway slaves, athletes, businessmen, teachers, and students. In just this one verse, we learn that all that Paul did is not actually recorded in the book of Acts, for there is only recorded one shipwreck. But because of the Pax Romana, or what we know as the Roman peace, and because of their infrastructure that provided significant roads to every known region, Traveling the Roman Empire was done by many and done often, and yet not without its dangers. With St. Paul's travels, we add the danger of bringing a controversial message, the gospel of Jesus Christ. So he had also to deal with the wrath of mobs in the streets and the cities in which he preached. Verse 27 Paul gave all of himself on behalf of the gospel. He held nothing back In this, of course, he was a faithful servant of his master, which resulted in him losing nights to prayer and many times going without food and drink because of the calling God had placed on his life. Verse 28. His motivation for suffering in all of these manners is stated here, with the hope that the love of God is communicated to these wayward Corinthian Christians. Understand, Paul wasn't only about starting churches or about even growing churches He was mostly about keeping churches, and that means keeping the people in those churches, keeping them in the faith. Too many were being deceived and walking away just as is occurring today. Verse 29. His concern for the people is further described. He identifies with the weak in order that he might make them strong. And he burns with anger over those Christians who are made to stumble by these false teachers. Remember. Jesus said that if a little one is caused to stumble, that the one who caused it might as well have a millstone be around his neck and thrown into the sea. Jesus didn't put up with deceivers, and neither did Paul. Verses 30 through 33. Here, the apostle is aware of how the devil can twist what he has been describing so that the Corinthians might dismiss his suffering as boasting. It is easier to dismiss a prideful man. And so Paul wants them to know about his weaknesses. He verifies that what he is about to tell them is a true story. And we know this story from the book of Acts. In summary, he was going to be arrested, and so he fled like a scared squirrel. Being secretly lowered outside the city gates of Damascus. He takes no pride in that, but he has been genuine with them. That should be testimony of him telling the truth. St. Paul, of course, has not been the only Christian to suffer greatly while working to share his faith in Christ. I want to introduce you to a man named David Brainerd. David Brainerd was a product of the great awakening of the 18th century. Because of his outgoing zeal for the Lord, he was kicked out of Yale. And back then a man could not become a public preacher unless he had a degree from Yale, Harvard, or a European institution. So Brainerd changed course and studied to become a missionary to Native Americans. When he qualified for the work, he was sent to evangelize Native Americans along the Delaware River. The work was grueling because of the living conditions, along with the language barrier, along with natives not trusting him. Brainerd also traveled to surrounding tribes, but the people initially were unresponsive to his message Fighting tuberculosis, cold, lack of sleep, hunger, Brainerd fought to continue his ministry among the Indians. And he wrote this to summarize. Quote, to an eye of reason, everything respecting the conversion of the heathen is as dark as midnight. Yet I cannot but hope in God for the accomplishment of something glorious among them. And the Lord was gracious to him by allowing him to see a good number of Indians coming to having a saving faith in Christ. One year counting 130 new converts. The natives grew to love Brainerd, but his health could not sustain him. One day he called as many natives as he could to hear him as he read from the Psalter and prayed with them. He then traveled on horseback to the house of the famous preacher Jonathan Edwards, where he was cared for by Edward's daughters. He survived only two more months dying from tuberculosis at the age of twenty-nine And of course, Brainerd's story is one of many others about people who served God through hardship, disappointment, loneliness, and temptation, inward and outward. What is a concern is when we 21st century Christians living with the many comforts that we do. When we hear the listing of the many sufferings of the Apostle Paul, or the commitment of a David Brainerd, or we hear about the martyrs who kept the faith even while losing their lives We can see them as super Christians who are able to do things we could not do or things we purposefully choose to avoid. But if we think we are incapable, I am calling you today to tell you you are mistaken. You are capable of enduring suffering. You are capable of having zeal, the zeal of a David Brainerd. You are capable of facing your death while keeping your faith in Jesus Christ. And this sermon is not my attempt at a Tony Robbins speech. Just like my silly little example of a silly movie I saw when I was young. You actually can endure beyond what you thought you were capable of doing. Consider how necessary coaches and teachers are in our lives. Not many of us as teenagers would pick up a book titled Mice and Men and read it. And write a summary of it unless a teacher instructed us and held a grade over our heads as the incentive And then when the teenager reads the book and realizes reading can be enjoyable, he begins reading other literature he otherwise would not have considered. It only took one teacher to get the student to want to learn. Consider also how many of us would practice playing the piano every day for an hour. Except that we had an instructor that held us accountable. And then when the piano student gets the basics down, music becomes a joy rather than something that has to be done. Consider the track runner who doesn't want to run 10, 50 yard sprints because he's tired and he's sore. And his coach hearts on him until he gets the workout done. And after 10 50-yard sprints, the coach asks him for one more. And the runner doesn't think he can do it. He thinks he is done, but the coach harps some more, and the runner runs another 50-yard sprint The coach helped him get more out of himself, more than he thought he had in him. That is what God wants to do for you. Because he loves you. Wanting you not to be what you think you are, but what he can make you. Consider all the lies that defeat people. All the lies they believe about themselves. And consider what Paul was able to do as a non-super Christian. If Paul can endure being whipped five different times, then you can be faithful to your wife. If Paul can suffer being beaten by rods on three different occasions, then you can overcome that addiction, so-called. If Paul can survive being stoned as in rocks being thrown at him, then you can survive your in-laws by showing love and forgiveness to them. If Paul can go without food and water, then you can go without visiting that inappropriate website or go without visiting the local bar. If Paul can endure perils, then you can endure not gossiping about other Christians. And if Paul can do all of it for the sake of the church, You can ignore what you want, what you prefer, and instead make decisions for the sake of others, especially for the sake of your family I speculate that some of you hearing my voice have believed that you are not capable of sharing your Christian faith with your co-workers because, well, you just don't have the right words. Hear this truth. Yes you can. I also speculate that some of you have not stood up for Christian truth because you thought you would be socially alienated. Hear this truth. You can stand up for Christian truth, and you can endure being socially alienated. I also speculate that some of you have kept quiet that you are a Christian because you think you could lose your job. Hear this truth. If that happens, God will find you a better job. All too often Christians are living in fear. We fear being rejected, being alone, losing what we think we need, being exposed as a fraud. But none of what we fear is justified. For God has told us to trust Him in all things. And that includes where we get our daily bread and how we maintain our mental and emotional health. And even when you are found to be a fraud, we have faith in God for his forgiveness and what we confess and that he can make us new again. The parable that was read this morning, Jesus tells regarding the sower and the seed and the ground. And it can first make it appear that there is nothing we can do about the soil. Either we are good soil or not. Either the seed grows deep within us or it does not.
