But the seed planted among thorns represents a plant being choked, Jesus says, with cares of riches and pleasures of life. Pursuing riches and pleasures of life are choices we make While the devil, by means of the world, tells us that our dispositions to this sin or that sin are what we are, genetically or psychologically The gospel of Jesus Christ breaks us free from any disposition the world places upon us. Beloved, whatever it is that God wants you to overcome, to stop doing, or to endure, it can be done Because the Holy Spirit is within you, and Jesus overcame for you, and St. Paul was an example for you. You can, like Paul, do all things through Christ who strengthens you. Amen and Amen. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God, as we read the strength you gave the apostle and all that he had to endure, and as we recognize our responsibility, To cultivate a heart that is receptive of your grace, Father, help us to have the courage to do so. To walk the roads you have placed before all of us. So that in the end you might be glorified and we might be saved. Through Jesus Christ our Lord, we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Love is not Blind
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Begin this morning by looking at Luke chapter eighteen, picking up at verse thirty-one. Luke eighteen, picking up at verse thirty-one. In the therapeutic age in which we live, it is quite tempting to hear the words of Jesus from Luke 18 And wonder what it would be like to know what your end days on earth would be like, and then conjecture how you would face them. Jesus knows how the next days are going to go. And we may be tempted to wonder what such was like. This is a type of what Sigmund Freud called projection. It is unfortunate because it is also a form of narcissism Because it fails to allow someone else's story or experience to be their own, but instead has a person only experiencing an event from the hearer's anticipated experience. Saying it another way, the person who hears about the experience doesn't concern himself with what the person went through, but only thinks about what it would be like if they went through the same. Such, to be blunt, is extremely self-centered, but unfortunately encouraged by modern preachers. Who think it is more appealing to imagine what an experience felt like so that we can all have a personal feeling about something rather than simply acknowledging the difficulty of what was experienced by another. Other examples include what it might have been like for the woman caught in adultery to be told by Jesus, Go and sin no more. Or be being told to imagine what it would have felt like to run to the tomb of Jesus and see that it was empty. Truth be told, what feeling such persons had at such times is objectively irrelevant and inconsequential to the facts of the accounts. But preachers go there with an attempt to connect emotionally with listeners who are, unfortunately, being programmed to think that how they react emotionally to a biblical story is what matters most. I realize that I may have just turned some of you off to what I am preaching today because you react more to what is emotional than what is factual. I don't want to turn you off. But I am also fighting against the spirit of our day that wants you to stay emotional and go no deeper. To go deeper is to go to what is at principle. And what is at principle is everlasting. Also, emotions change from person to person, but facts do not. In our gospel reading, Jesus was on his way to Jerusalem. We have heard Jesus warn. those that he healed and and those that he cast demons out of, that his true identity was to be kept hidden until the right time. The right time was according to the Heavenly Father, which was when he was to be handed over to the Gentiles, to be beaten, whipped, and hung on a cross. Jesus says here that he is going to Jerusalem to fulfill what was written by the prophets concerning him. And what was written. Honestly, we don't have time this morning, or the next, or the next, to list all that is explained by the prophets said about Jesus. It is sufficient, however, for us to name the following. Jesus was, according to the psalmist, to be a reproach to the people His bones were to be placed out of joint. Like dogs, people were to surround him. His hands and feet were to be pierced, while his clothes were being auctioned by lots. According to the prophet Isaiah, Jesus was to be despised and rejected. He was to be the carrier of sorrows and seen by his fellow man as being stricken and smitten by God. He was to be led to the slaughter like a lamb who was silent. According to the prophet Jeremiah, Jesus was to suffer all that he did so that God could make a new covenant with his people. Which was God placing his law upon the hearts of his people, making them always his people, and him being always their God, meaning that all of his people would know intimately him personally. That is the end goal. God wants to be father to those who call him father. What Jesus warns about next, no way did the apostles understand. He was to go to Jerusalem to suffer. We know from their bickering that they anticipated events would be much different. Remember that they bickered with each other about who was the closest to Jesus and thus who would sit on his left hand and his right hand. That meant that they thought Jesus would establish an earthly kingdom. Perhaps they thought it would be something similar but greater than what the Maccabees did when they thwarted the Greeks and established rule over the region of Judea, which included the city of Jerusalem, just a generation prior. Whatever their vision, they were sure it was going to be a physical rebellion and a physical rule led by Jesus. These words of Jesus of his suffering and his death were not understood until after his resurrection. Picking up at verse 35. Verse 35, there is a connection between this story being told and what Jesus said about his upcoming suffering and death. We're going to get there and connect them soon. He said, then it happened. Luke says, then it happened. This refers to what happened next, remembering that Jesus was on his way to the holy city of Jerusalem Jericho was known as a city of palms, and there is today many palms within and without the city. And it is and was approximately 18 miles from Jerusalem. Of course, there was no welfare state to fall back on, so average families in the ancient Near East who had someone blind in the home They could only afford to feed the people who could work in the household. A blind person in the days of Jesus couldn't work So begging is all that they had, and family members would take their blind and set them in places where the most people would pass by, and the road from Jericho to Jerusalem was well traveled. Verse 36, there was a number of disciples following Jesus for various reasons. And that is why the blind beggar could tell something was happening that was unique or someone special was passing by Hence the question likely to a family member or family members that have brought him there regarding what's going on, what's taking place. The they referred to as likely the family members that brought the blind beggar. Verse 38. No doubt the reputation of Jesus had spread throughout the region. All who needed healing would have wanted to be in the presence of Jesus, to be healed by Jesus. It was understood that the Messiah was associated with physical healing, and the connection of the Messiah to David was well known. Hence the cry, Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me. Verse 39. The scene allows us to see from the eyes of those who were following Jesus by the manner they speak to the blind beggar. Jesus was understood to be an important man, a future earthly king, and thus he would not have time, in their view, to be bothered by a common beggar. The faith of the beggar is to be underlined. He cried out all the more, not being detoured by anyone who would have him be quiet. What is more, he understood that his healing would have to be by the mercy of God. This does not mean that he understood his blindness to be directly connected to some sin that he had committed. Too often people think that way. They think bad people have bad things happen to them, and good people have good things happen to them. That was the worldview of Job's friends, and it continues in some people's minds today. But such a worldview is false. Bad people can be quite successful in this life. Good people can experience hard times. Such cannot be refuted. A saving faith like the one of this blind beggar understands his own sinful condition. He understood that just within himself was sin. Not without within. He was a sinner. And that means that he thought of himself first. He made decisions for his benefit first and last. He preferred his needs over the needs of others And because of his handicap, he was likely bitter in heart, maybe against God, against those who claimed to speak for God, because he resented God for his blindness. Having that knowledge of yourself that you are a sinner is all too rare But the result of that knowledge is crying out to Jesus, Have mercy on me. Verse 40 Hearing the man, Jesus stops walking. He is responding. He is stopping in his journey to the cross to respond to a man most people thought was cursed by God. The man needed to be brought to Jesus first because he was blind and second because of the crowd that he had to wait wait through. Verse 41. Jesus is direct in his question. And consider what options there were. He could have asked Jesus for money. But Jesus knew what he wanted, and Jesus wanted to be asked. Remember, beloved, as Christians, we are in relationship with God, which means we are to communicate with him. He wants us to ask of him. He wants to give to us. He wants us to say thank you. Verse 42. Jesus next announces his healing and then connects it to the faith the man expressed. Now let us be careful here. Too many preachers connect the praise of Jesus regarding the man's faith to a formula. That says that personal faith is the sole cause of a person being healed. Such teaching is shamefully false Such allows false teachers to claim that when they pray for a person to be healed and the person is not healed, well that means that the person that needs the healing but didn't get it, that person has failed to have faith. It's not the healer that failed, but the person who is sick or lame or remains sick or lame, that person has failed. Instead, consider the examples of people who were healed by the faith of someone else. You remember the story of the Cripple, that was lowered down from the roof of St. Peter's house, placed before Jesus. And the text says that Jesus saw their faith and healed the man. Their faith was the faith of those who lowered the man. Then there is the daughter of the centurion who was healed because of the faith of her father. Not her faith, the faith of her father. And then remember the instructions in the book of James for elders of the church to pray for the sick, anointing them with oil in the name of the Lord. And it says, James says, and the prayers of the elders. In faith will save the sick. Again, not the faith of the sick, but the faith of the elder who prays. That is the faith needed. I am sorry to spend so much time on that point, but the falsehood that is so widely repeated, I needed to counter it. Verse 43. Here is a true disciple of Jesus. The blind beggar is healed. He gives rightful glory to God, knowing that praising God is praising Jesus. Celebrating such healing and the healing itself is infectious. Now, here is the connection between why the event of the healing of a blind man and Jesus telling his disciples that he is on his way to Jerusalem to suffer and die. Remember that Jesus' followers did not know what he was describing. Luke says it was hidden from them. His suffering and death was hidden from them. To be hidden is not to see what you could possibly see until something that's blocking it is removed. For a blind man, everything is hidden from him in the sense that he is not able to physically see. And then Jesus uses the ability to physically see as a metaphor for faith. Seeing and having faith in Jesus is the same. Consider why Jesus healed the blind man. Jesus cares about the man because he is a human being, and because to heal the man teaches everyone who is following Jesus that they too need to be healed from their blindness. What they are blind to is why Jesus is going to Jerusalem. Again, they thought they were following a Messiah who would establish an earthly kingdom. They thought they would rule, or at least the people they believed in would rule, and they would be the benefactors. But that is not the kingdom Jesus is going to establish. His kingdom was to be built with people who have had their hearts of stone cut away and given new hearts that beat with the love of God. And the a kingdom that is built with people whose hearts beat for God cannot be anything but beautiful. There is a reason, beloved, why atheists don't have cathedrals. As comedian Steve Martin sings, atheists don't have songs. This love of God within the hearts of believers is highlighted in our epistle reading from 1 Corinthians 13. A passage I have used as part of my own testimony, and that when I first read the chapter, my heart was cut quick, and I knew three things. First, I have never loved anyone as described in that chapter. Second, I have never been loved by anyone as described in that chapter. And third, I wanted that love. My next step was to confess Jesus as God. It is difficult to preach on love in our culture because the manner we presently use the word. Love is sung when the word sex could be substituted for it. Love is used to describe how a person feels about his dog. His car, his job, and then his spouse. What is powerful about the manner the Bible uses the word is both in action and in description. Love is seen by Jesus willingly going to Jerusalem with the full knowledge of what he would suffer. Love is exhibited when Jesus hears the cry of a blind man And love is seen by the blind man who cries out for mercy from Jesus with faith that Jesus can grant that mercy. And love is practiced by Jesus when he heals the blind man. And love is expressed when the blind man glorifies God in the name of Jesus. Love is revealed by Jesus sending a message to his followers that they too are blind to who Jesus really was. And what he was planning on doing. And therefore they needed to be given sight, which is to be given love. As far as the description of love in 1 Corinthians 13, we get the positive in that it suffers long, is kind. Bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. And then its negatives. Love is not envious. It is not conceited. It is not rude. It is not selfish. It is not provoked. It does not think evil of another. These beloved are the standards by which Christians are to live. There is no higher standard, no other relatable standard. Imagine if you were required to read the definition of love before you got into a conversation with anyone. Consider how our word choice, our tone, our body language would change with the definition of love in our memory. As we enter the season of Lent, let us ask God to heal us from blindness. So that we may love the Savior with a better understanding of why he went to Jerusalem. May God heal us from the blindness of how we treat certain people poorly. Or blindness to a forgiveness we have withheld. Or blindness to how desensitized we have become to what is immoral. Or blindness to the needs of a brother or sister in Christ, or blindness to what is actually blasphemous. Of course, the devil wants you to stay blind. So such healing can only occur because we have faith. Faith that Jesus can heal our blindness and help us to love. Let us pray. Gracious and merciful Father, such a standard you have placed before us, and we know it is a standard of you. It is your love to us. And for that standard may we not shrink, but fight for it, strive for it, recognize that without it we are blind, and so heal us from our blindness and make us holy once again. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Purposeful Christianity
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I want to go off notes to begin with. When I was in seminary We had a homiletics class where we would meet in the chapel, a small little chapel area, where we would practice our preaching. And before we would the student would get up to preach, we would sing one line from a hymn And someone chose to sing this hymn. And the first line, as you know, ends with, For still our ancient foe doth seek to work us woe. His craft and power are great. and armed with cruel hate, on earth is not his equal. We finished and sat down, and the student said, We can't stop there. You gotta keep singing. So uh indeed you gotta you gotta keep singing. Alright, turn if you would to 2 Corinthians chapter 6. We're going to be covering verses 1 through 13, and then we'll make our transition to our gospel reading, which was Matthew chapter 4. So 2 Corinthians chapter 6, begin with uh referencing the movie Goodwill Hunting. The movie was set in 1959 at a fictional, elite, conservative Vermont boarding school named Welton Academy. It tells the story the movie does of an English teacher who inspires his students through his teaching of poetry. On the first day of classes, students are surprised by the unorthodox teaching methods of the new English teacher, John Keating, who is played by Robin Williams. A wealthy alumnus himself, Keating encourages his students to make your lives extraordinary, a sentiment he summarizes with the Latin phrase Carpe diem, meaning seize the day. In an early scene, Mr. Keating takes the students to a separate room and shows them an old photograph of former students and gives a rousing speech with an important message. He said this. They're not that different from you, are they? Same haircuts, full of hormones, just like you. Invincible, just like you feel. The world is their oyster. They believe they're destined for great things, just like many of you. Their eyes are full of hope, just like you. Did they wait until it was too late to make from their lives even one iota of what they were capable? Because you see, gentlemen, these boys are now fertilizing daffodils But if you listen real close, you can hear them whisper their legacy to you. Hear it? Carpe. Carpe diem. Seize the day, boys. Make your lives extraordinary. Because we are food for worms, lads Because believe it or not, each and every one of us in this room is one day going to stop breathing, turn cold, and die. Are you motivated? I thought about that phrase, carpadium, while studying Paul's words in 2 Corinthians chapter 6. With further study, I discovered the original usage of the phrase carpe diem was not related to what Paul was communicating. The first usage of Carpe Diem was by the Roman poet Horus, who advocated for getting as much enjoyment out of each day as possible, because the next day is unknown. Mind you, Paul is not against enjoying a day. It was simply not the message he was conveying to the Corinthian Christians. So let us examine that message from chapter 6, beginning at verse 1. Paul has already said in chapter 5, verse 20. That God makes his appeal to men through Paul himself. He wants the Christians at Corinth. to be assured that it is God himself who stands behind the message he gave them What is hard to know is precisely what Paul means when he speaks of someone receiving God's grace in vain. How is it possible to receive God's grace in vain? It may be best to think of him appealing here to the Corinthians here to stand firm in the grace they have already received. Just as he once said of himself that after preaching, he himself could possibly be disqualified. Verse 2 It is being underlined that God has visited these people with his salvation and have done so through Paul's own ministry. Paul's authority, which had been disputed by the Corinthians, was demonstrated by the work that God did in them through him. The word now drives this thought home. This is the time. The very moment of this letter was God's favor toward them. This is the time for them to give heed to his words. Not tomorrow, not next year, but now. A similar thought can be found in the prophet Isaiah: Seek the Lord while he may be found. Call upon him while he is near. Verses 3 and 4. In these verses, Paul both denies the charges that the false teachers have been making against him. And asserts the faithfulness of his ministry, largely by indicating how much he has suffered, suffered on behalf of the ministry God gave him to fulfill. He begins by saying that his personal behavior has not been inconsistent with his message, as this had again been one of the charges against him. We know very well today what damage is done to the credibility of the gospel and the reputation of Christianity when ministers are exposed to have purposefully gone on sinning. Paul was painstakingly careful to avoid giving any offense by the manner in which he lived. He did not want to put any obstacle in the way of people believing the message that he was bringing them Now, the list of hardships that Paul endured for the sake of the gospel has been called an apostolic identification card. We remember from a few weeks ago that this page is elaborated on in the same letter in chapter 11. We can see how this shorter summary prepares the way for that longer, more detailed account that Paul gives. Verse 5. I want you to notice the first triplets that are here: troubles, hardships, and distresses. Those are general terms to describe what he's been through. The second listing the triplet, beatings, imprisonment, and riots. Those are more specific to what we know In the New Testament, of what Paul went through, especially from the book of Acts. The third triplet are hard work, sleepless nights, and hunger. Those are difficulties more of a voluntary nature, which means that they were difficulties that Paul imposed on himself, believing them to be a testimony to others. His reference to labor may refer to Paul's practice of supporting himself by the trade of tent making while devoting himself also to preaching. The fasting was at times voluntary in order to increase his godly self-control At times to demonstrate to God the sincerity of his prayers, and at other times fasting was involuntary, being caused simply by the lack of food. Verse 6. Paul turns here from sufferings that he endured for the gospel's sake to the virtues of the Christian life. If the false teachers had pointed to Paul's hardships as a sign of his weakness, he points to his character as a Christian, showing that it had remained unchanged even with the difficulties of life. Verse 7. The phrase by the word of truth is best taken to be a reference not to the way that Paul speaks, but what he proclaims. The gospel. He preached the gospel, as they well knew in the power of God. Chapter 8, excuse me, verse 8 through 10, we have here the first of what we call antithesis. He says, as deceivers and yet true. It is the first of the seven antitheses that follow, in which the perception is contrasted to the reality, or the judgment by the flesh rather than judgments by the spirit. And then verses 11 through 13. Paul has demonstrated his affection for his spiritual children in Corinth. All he is asking is that they return the affection. So let's now turn to Matthew chapter 4, the gospel account of Jesus fasting in the desert 40 days. A passage we are very familiar with. I want us to see a connection between Paul's words in Corinthians to what Jesus is experiencing in the desert. What we note first is that Jesus was led by the Holy Spirit. So let us ask and answer why, what does it mean to be led by the Holy Spirit? The phrasing of being led by the Spirit occurs in two other places. The first is in Romans 8, where Paul is contrasting being led by the Spirit as opposed to being led by the flesh. They're opposites. The second is in Galatians, where Paul also contrasts Christians being led by the flesh as opposed to being led by the Spirit. So from these we know what being led by the Spirit is not. It is not living according to the desires of the flesh. And related to that, it is not avoiding godly counsel or godly teaching or godly preaching that would expose sins of the flesh. That's what we tend to do. We don't want to hear it, and so we just stop listening. Hence being led by the Spirit is doing things that are contrary to the living by the flesh When Jesus makes his way to the desert, he is consciously going to live out the discipline of his flesh. To show that he is not only led by the Spirit to the desert, but led by the Spirit in all of his living on earth. Jesus was going to the desert to bind the strongman and then plunder his house. And let us not ignore the antithesis in this account. For whereas the nation of Israel wandered in the desert forty years because they did not have faith in God to enter the promised land, So Jesus was in the desert 40 days to practice faith in God so that you and I can enter heaven Whereas Israel, while in the desert, complained of not having enough food or drink, Jesus goes without food, taking the human body to its limit. Whereas Israel tempted God with their discontent, Jesus withstood temptation of all types. And along with contrasting Jesus with the nation of Israel in the desert, we should also contrast Jesus in the desert and Adam in the garden. Adam was in paradise, where life was abundant and all was at peace, whereas Jesus was in a parched land with death and the means of death all around him. Adam could and did eat as he willed, except one particular fruit, whereas Jesus did not eat at all. Adam was tempted Adam was tempted by one thing and failed, whereas Jesus was tempted in all ways, his flesh being tempted to eat, then his mind being put to the test, and then his heart being tempted to bow. And Jesus was obedient. Jesus was without sin, and when Satan left Jesus in the desert, there was no more tempting him, for he had overcome it all. I'm now going to bring these two things together, these two passages, but I need to introduce you to something that I'm calling purposeful Christianity. Purposeful Christianity. When we teach parenting, we talk about purposeful parenting. Purposeful parenting is When you are not just going along in your day while accepting moments to teach and train a child as the moments come up, but instead you are planning ways to train your children. I might call my five-year-old son over to me and tell him I want him to pick up after the dog who had just chewed up a toy. I'm asking my five-year-old son to do so because he needs to learn how to be a part of the home, which means to do his part in the work that's needed. But I am also checking his heart to see if he is willing to obey me. If I sense hesitation or resistance or even a slight complaint, such as, well, why me? I then know that my son's heart needs more training, so that he obeys cheerfully and right away. To answer criticism, that this personal parenting approach seems to have the goal of the dad running the household like a tight ship, and all are to obey him as captain. That's not it at all. Instead, the end goal of purposeful parenting is to make it natural for my child to obey his governing authorities, the first one being God. So when he is being led by the Spirit to befriend a neighbor or to do service work for the troubled, he has a heart that's trained to do such. Also, purposeful parenting has the goal of giving your child, which I think is the greatest gift you can give besides faith in Christ, to give the child self-control. By being able to say no to what the flesh wants to do, but instead to do what the spirit wants to do. Now take those simple principles in purposeful parenting and apply them to the Christian life and you get purposeful Christianity. Look again at verse 12 of 2 Corinthians chapter 6. Paul and his companions had hearts that were open wide for a free exchange of Christian love. But the Corinthians were closed of heart. He says, restricted by their own affections. They could not control their affections They could not rightfully direct where their affections should go. They did not have self-control In order to grow out of their immaturity, remember he spoke to them as if they were children, in order to grow out of their immaturity, they needed to make decisions purposefully Do things that would free up their hearts to love and be loved by Christ Jesus. The season of Lent gives us opportunities to purposefully discipline our flesh So that we become more sensitive to the leading of the Holy Spirit while also increasing our self-control, so that we less and less live in obedience to the desires of our flesh. As opposed to the spirit. But of course, we need to be disciplined in our lives throughout the year, to be sure. But Lent grants us an emphasis of discipline. So what does this look like practically? I love to answer my own questions. Those are the easiest ones to answer. Practically, I can purposefully fast from food so as to learn how I am not to be a man led by my stomach, but is fed by the Spirit of God. And I can know that to do so is where the Holy Spirit leads because it would be the opposite of where my flesh leads and where the devil wants me to go. Fasting, and this point I can't underline more, fasting also helps me control other desires of the flesh. I learn how to deny myself in always. For example, and this is my testimony to you, I can be a very impatient man. Surprise, surprise. Especially while while driving in heavy traffic. But fasting has helped me say no to the feelings of anxiety that I have when traffic is slow and all the other drivers are stupid. And it doesn't take going into the desert 40 days to officially fast. Jesus did that so that no one else has to. In the year 604 A. D. , in a letter to St. Augustine of Canterbury Pope Gregory the Great announced the final form of abstinence that soon actually became law, that had Christians abstaining from flesh meat And from all things that come from flesh, such as milk, cheese, eggs, and butter. This was during Lent. This applied also, except to those of ill health Many Christians, especially in the East, still fast in this manner. For Christians today, what you do is up to you. You can fast a meal. You can fast a day. You can fast multiple days. You can fast from certain foods that you crave, fast from certain drinks you like It is between you and God. But once you make that commitment to fast, keep it, or there is no benefit from it. But even if you fail, try again. That's the Christian way. Then there is fasting from entertainment. One of my sons, when young, fasted from swinging on our swing set. He made it all the way to Easter Sunday, and the first thing he did after church was swing. But you and I have more distractions than swing sets. Our distractions we carry around with us or look at them on our desks or in our living rooms Denying ourselves of unfruitful habits is a means to be sensitive to where the Spirit is leading and help us see where and how we have been desensitized. And be assured, good Christian, that the devil wants you to watch more television, spend more time online, be more distracted by political hacks. Anything and everything he would like you to do besides being still and to know God In one sense, this sermon is very practical. I am calling us to be led more by the Spirit of God. The way to do that, as Paul said to the Romans and Galatians, is to no longer commit sins of the flesh. Such sins were part of the Greek and Roman culture. They were what everyone else did. The same is true for today. Our American culture, having thrown off its origins of Christian ethics, promotes sins of the flesh So we, like the Roman Christians and the Galatian Christians, are to live by the Spirit and not by the flesh conscientiously. And to do better at living by the Spirit, we have to purposefully do things that train ourselves to listen less and less to the flesh and more and more to the spirit. But we must do so now. Now is the time and not tomorrow. Today is the day of salvation. In closing, the following words from the combination service that were read on Ash Wednesday fit well with our passage from 2 Corinthians 6. We say there, therefore, brethren, take we heed be time, while the day of salvation lasteth. For the night cometh when none can work. But let us, while we have the light, believe in the light, and walk as children of the light. That we be not cast into utter darkness where is weeping and gnashing of teeth. Let us not abuse the goodness of God, who calleth us mercifully to amendment. And of his endless pity promiseth us forgiveness of that which is past, if with a perfect and true heart we return unto him For though our sins be as red as scarlet, they may be made white as snow. And though they be like purple, yet they shall be made white as wool. Turn ye, saith the Lord, from all your wickedness, and your sin shall not be your destruction. Cast away from you all your ungodliness that ye have done Make you new hearts and a new spirit. And I add, do it today. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God, as we think upon our weaknesses, and we recognize how much more discipline we need to say no to the flesh and to be led by the Spirit. We give you thanks for every opportunity you give us to turn away from the direction of our flesh and turn to you. And we see today this is another opportunity May it be done to our salvation and your glory. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Persevering Faith
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We are looking at both passages read this morning, 1 Thessalonians 4 and then Matthew 15. The following story was told by Father Robert Hart and found in Touchstone Magazine 2004. The name of the subject is withheld. The lady seemed to be very healthy. She lived in Turner Station, an old suburb of Baltimore, practically in the water of Baltimore Harbor. A very traditional black neighborhood. It has a church of some kind on every corner, and in a way, characteristic of the city's black community. The Christians speak with an unashamed faith that quickly names Jesus in any place at any time. This joyful lady, young as a widow, made no secret of her love for Christ. It was difficult to believe that she already had been murdered by her late husband. And not only by him, but also by the laws of the United States. As understood and carried out by the Maryland Department of Corrections. Her husband was imprisoned for a fairly lengthy time, and she waited for him. Raising the children by working at menial jobs for small pay and keeping the house ready for the day on which he would come home. She would take the children as often as possible to the prison to visit their father, reminding them that he was coming home someday. She waited for that day, and it finally came Long imprisonment has the unfortunate effect all too often of providing men, even girl men, with a temptation they could not have prepared for. After a few years of being away from women, locked up like animals, they find that they are drawn toward other men. This unexpected temptation had overcome her husband during his years in prison. He gave in He engaged in sexual acts with other men, no doubt only after a very long time of being locked up. He had a faithful wife at home, a better wife, no doubt, than many of his fellow prisoners. Most of them, if they had been married, found themselves divorced shortly after beginning their term. Perhaps their wives' actions is not hard to understand Why be alone day in and day out doing time as a celibate spouse? All too often to endure proves to be too much for a wife of a jailbird But not for this Christian woman. Her commitment was not only to her husband, but to her Lord. She waited I, Robert Hart, have always supplemented my income by working on special cases for an attorney who helps uninsured patients obtain eligibility for medical assistance programs. Medicaid. Many of them are strippers on Baltimore's infamous block who have been infected by HIV to a life of heroin addiction and often prostitution. And eventually die of AIDS. I suppose someone could, lacking charity, shrug off their deaths as simply the consequence of their deeds. But this client had lived a virtuous life, from all that I learned about her and her time on trial. This infection was no consequence of careless living. Her husband was a criminal, but that was not known to her until he was caught. He became capable of perverted acts with other men, but this was kept hidden also from her. Hidden as well was the disease that had been diagnosed by the doctors at the prison hospital. To reveal to anyone that a person has AIDS is strictly illegal. And so fearful are medical providers of giving any perception that confidentiality may have been violated that I have sometimes had trouble getting them to fill out forms even at a patient's own request when he needed them to obtain medical assistance. The husband had engaged in gay sex while in prison, and that is a fact that the prison doctors were afraid to reveal. He was coming home as a man unworthy of such a wife, a faithful Christian woman of good character. His right To sexual pleasure, even then, even with a disease that would surely infect and eventually kill her, was thus created by a legal right to special confidentiality. So she must die. Perhaps no sacrifice is too great for a society that worships the creature more than the creator, and specifically the creature we call sex. The law has been made the servant of this worship, and this lady was only a small sacrifice. She was no one rich or famous, no one to be missed just the widow of a deceased convict living in a small, poor neighborhood. Policy required that she must die if necessary, infected by a man whose right to confidentiality was a higher priority than the life of his wife. She had done no wrong, mind you, that the state would seek to punish. The authorities had no intention of killing her They simply believed that they had no legal right to try to save her. This amounts to complicity on their part in her death. But by the legal definition, they were not murderers. They obeyed the law. Now read this story Not to undermine the legal concerns of the author, but to highlight what we might miss, which is a woman Who maintains faith in Christ Jesus while her husband is in jail, remaining faithful to God and her husband until he returns home. Only to be sentenced to death in spite of her faithfulness because of the acts of sexual immorality. And it is it is easy to question where was Jesus for her? The warning against sexual immorality in our reading from 1 Thessalonians seems to some to hamstring Christianity. Is one of the few subjects that turn people away from Christianity. They like all the love spoken about, They love the teachings of Jesus when he speaks about loving God, loving your neighbor, and God loving them They embrace the teaching of not worrying about tomorrow and that God will supply all that we need for today They like that their past sins can be forgiven and that the yoke that Jesus places on them is light. Being born again sounds liberating. But then there are teachings about strict sexuality and suddenly the burden of Jesus does not appear light at all, but actually as a millstone that is not worth carrying around Thessalonica was a Greek city. To understand what Christian churches in historically Greek cities were up against culturally regarding sexuality I want you to hear this description from an article written by Jeffrey R. Stone, a law professor from the University of Chicago. Quote, from the sixth to the fourth century BC, Greek culture attained its most impressive achievements in literature. philosophy, politics, science, and the arts. The Greeks of this era generally eschewed the legal enforcement of moral or religious notions of right sexual conduct. Classical Greek morality and law focused not on sexual sin, but on whether an individual's conduct was harmful to others. To the ancient Greeks, Eros was a primal force that permeated all facets of life. The Greek gods indulged freely in sexual pleasure in Greek mythology. Zeus variously became a bull, a swan, and even rain with the goal of seducing mortals. Aphrodite was the goddess of love and of sexual rapture. They called it the things of Aphrodite. It is said that during the festival of Aphrodite, her priestesses had sexual intercourse with strangers as a form of worship. The Greeks approached the human form with no sense that nudity was inherently shameful. To the contrary The phallus was a potent symbol of fertility, a central theme in Greek religion. A pillar topped by the helmet of Hermes, adorned with an erect penis, stood at nearly every Athenian's front door. Vases and terracottas depicted explicit scenes of vaginal and anal intercourse, masturbation and fallacious Moreover, the Greeks had no concept of obscenity, a legal notion that would not come into existence in Western culture for another 2,000 years. Thus, there is a reason why St. Paul's letters written to churches in Greek cities necessitated a call to sexual purity. And perhaps there is no time more similar to today than what early Christians were exposed to in the first century. Whereas in our time decades ago, sexual exploitation and sexual gratification of all types were found in just a few Particular cities in the United States, such as Las Vegas or New York. Now it is in every city, and in our living rooms and on our phones. But this is not a contest regarding who lived in a more salacious time. Regardless of how salacious our culture is regarding sexuality, the same teaching applies. This is God's will for you, your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality. Mind you, it would be enough to say this is God's will for you, your sanctification. That is to say, God's will for each of us is to be made holy, which is to grow in holiness, which is to be made more and more like Jesus. And that means holiness would apply to every area of our lives. This is a go-to verse for me when people want to know what is God's will for my life I know what his will is, and so do you. It is your sanctification. It is for you to be made more holy. It is to be made more and more like Jesus. But because of the sexual culture the Thessalonians were surrounded by, Paul goes into greater detail detail of pressing concern He calls them to be made more holy in their sexuality. Now a careless and faithless reader can see Paul's words and quickly conclude that he is a killjoy. And nothing more. But there are reasons for the call to sexual holiness that are beyond being anti-pleasure. One of those reasons is found in the text. And noticed during our Sunday school class a couple of weeks ago when we looked at this very passage. Paul calls for the Christians to be sexually sanctified, and then he coaches the Christians not to behave like unbelievers in their sexuality. And then in verse 6 says, no one should take advantage or defraud his brother in this matter. In what matter? The matter of sexuality. The meaning is that if you participate in sexual immorality with another person, the word brother here can be male or female Then you are taking advantage of them by defrauding that person, meaning you are the transgressor against them. In simple terms, you are hurting the other person. And we know from St. Paul's teaching to the Corinthians that there is a spiritual component to our sexual intimacy. Thus our souls are injured, and we injure the souls of others when we are not sexually sanctified God does not want our soul injured, and he doesn't want you injuring others, and so he calls us to be sanctified in general, and then specifically in our sexuality. Consider our opening story. The husband's immoral sexual behavior and his not disclosing it to his wife resulted in her being transgressed against. And the result of that was the taking of her life. But again, we can ask, where was Jesus for her? To answer that, we turn to our gospel reading and see a Jesus that some do not recognize nor like. Some commentators try to soften the story by insisting that Jesus ignored the woman and then spoke to the disciples about her and then called her a dog, all with a wink. As if he was simply joking with her. But there is no joking suggested in this story. No one is reported to have laughed. Consider that the woman was a Canaanite. She was a Gentile. Gentiles were unclean people according to Jewish law. Jesus didn't have to speak to her, and most certainly he didn't need to do what she asked him to do. There was no law that required it. And when he was encouraged by his followers to rebuke her, which would be to send her away, he doubles down, reminding them that he was sent for the chosen people of God, the Jews. In response to her worship of him, he does indeed call her a dog, or at least having some of the same worth as a dog, and then her response. Her willingness to take the place of a family dog is remarkable, and it shows no personal pride in her heart. as well as a love for her daughter that will take her to the lowest of positions in society. And she was also wise, very wise. What she said is true. Dogs are permitted the crumbs that fall from a family table. And a faith, a faith that trusts that the crumbs of Jesus can heal her daughter is a great faith. The Greek word here for woman, what Jesus next calls her, can also be used for wife or lady. She is indeed not a dog, and Jesus makes that clear. But let us not think that Jesus was surprised by her response. He knew what was in her and he also knew how to get it out. We see this by his unwillingness to answer her initially, to remain silent. He is testing her. This is one of the ways Jesus disciples his followers. He is showing us what is inside of us, and one way is not to answer initially. Jesus then speaks to his followers, reminding them that he is there for the Jews only. But he wasn't, and he knew he wasn't. But they didn't know this, and so he tests them. And then the woman's biggest test of all: what humility was within the woman that she would have faith in crumbs? Her response revealed a faith in the crumbs of Jesus, and Jesus calls that faith great. Remember that Jesus is usually complaining about the faith of his followers, complaining of their lack of faith, especially the disciples closest to him. This is the only time he uses the phrase great faith. It is the only time he uses the Greek word megalay. To describe someone's faith, Meghalay means large or in the widest sense, thus, her faith is vast. The great lesson from this story is the need for persevering faith, which is a great faith. A persevering faith does not quit, but keeps knocking, keeps seeking. A persevering faith is not detoured by silence. A persevering faith is willing to go as low in humility as possible in order to be heard by the Lord. In general, a persevering faith is not derailed by circumstances. As Minister Rob Rayburn said. True faith must believe, excuse me, true faith must believe the Word of God sometimes in defiance of appearances. That woman, whose husband infected her to a death sentence, while being faithful to him, needed to believe in God in defiance of appearances. And I will answer the question. The question, where was Jesus for her? Where was Jesus for her? He was with her, being infected by AIDS, and suffering with AIDS until her spirit left her body. So that she could be with Jesus, awaiting a natura reward promised to her. God's will for us is to be sanctified, and in particular, sanctified in our sexual expression. And that may seem too difficult in the age in which we live and the culture in which we live. But persevering faith is not derailed by circumstance. True faith in Jesus defies appearances. When I was a youth pastor, I was green, really, really green. I had not taken one Bible class. I was making it up as I went. One of my first days as a youth pastor, I was visiting a home where there were a number of teenagers from the church. A parent asked me to speak to them. I had not planned to say anything formal. But I had to prove myself. So as they gathered around sitting in a circle, I said something like You have all heard that God loves you and loves you just the way you are. And that is true, that is correct. But He wants to do something more for you. It is like the old saying. And then I stopped. I stopped speaking because I forgot the old saying. And I looked to one of the mothers who was listening in and I said Do you remember the old saying? And she said, I have no idea what you're talking about. And I swear she wanted me to squirm. But it did pop into my head. And I said it again God loves you just the way you are, and he loves you enough not to let you stay that way. That is an informal manner of God saying, This is God's will for you. Your sanctification. Let us pray. Our gracious God, we thank you for this specific word to a people who are surrounded by immoral sexuality. And no doubt tempted in many ways to give in to their desires of the flesh. And so we don't live much differently in the culture we now reside And so we pray that you'd help all of us overcome those desires of the flesh, that we might be first ruled by the Spirit, and that we might be truly sanctified in all ways. guarded by your wonderful Holy Spirit, to protect our hearts, to protect our minds, and to protect our souls. Sanctify us all, we pray, in Jesus' name.

sermons.title: Our Choices Matter
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Okay. Believe it or not, I don't have these sermons memorized, so uh yeah Luke chapter 11, pick up at verse 14. We're going to go verse by verse, but I want to begin by talking to you about a repeated argument against the existence of God. And that argument is what philosophers call the problem of evil. The problem of evil essentially states that if God exists Then he must be benevolent, or simply stated, he must be good. If God is benevolent, then he would prevent evil from occurring. But evil exists. Therefore, God either doesn't exist or he is not good This argument carries a great deal of authority when suffering occurs upon the innocent, so-called. The innocent are children, the elderly, and the sick, and the handicapped. What this argument fails to address is the involvement of the will of humanity. The will of humans is a major factor. in the evil experienced by the innocent, again so-called. Calculate, if at all possible How much evil occurs upon the innocent because of the will of fellow human beings? A primary example for today is the war between Ukraine and Russia, considering that it was started by the wills of men And not just the wills of the two present heads of those states. There were wills of men historically that created and built on tensions already existing between those two nations. But what about natural disasters, you say? Yes, natural disasters occur outside of the will of men. But the curse caused by Adam and Eve resulted in such disasters because all of creation was cursed. Also, much of the decisions we make contribute to those disasters. The most obvious choice of the will of man is to build a city below sea level so that when a hurricane comes, and they do come, hundreds, if not thousands, of people are devastated. Yes, there are wildfires that occur by lightning strikes, and some of those fires cause damage to people's homes and property However, according to the National Park Service of the United States, 85% of wildfires are caused by humans. Humans who have a will to be careless or not. I could go on, but you get the point Now consider the alternative of humanity not having a will. If each individual was not given choices in life, but was programmed to do good always There would be no sincere relationships, but only manufactured ones. There would be no actual love, or even humanity itself, as we now define humanity. Because there would be no capacity to share in charity one with another. Without a doubt, there is great power in the love one person chooses to share with another person. But with the ability to choose, with the presence of the human will, people don't always do what is right or what is good. And when we are descendants of Adam and Eve, who are cursed because of the choices they made in paradise. We actually find it easier to do what is wrong or bad. Bad for us and bad for our fellow men. But why would God allow Adam and Eve to make such choices, the critics ask? The obvious answer is that To not allow them choice is to take away their will, which is to take away their capacity for a relationship. Okay, says the critic, but why do we have to suffer because of the choices made by our original parents? The Bible reveals two reasons. First, Adam and Eve represent us all, meaning that we would have done the same thing that they did. After all, the word Adam means mankind. Second, God is a covenant God, and so we come under the covenant of Adam and Eve. And so we inherit sinful natures and the sting of death from them. But why does God have to be a covenant God? This is where the questioning must stop. God, from our position as created beings, is Who he is, having revealed himself to be, and he is a covenant God. It is not for us to ask questions about what God has not revealed about himself. We are, I remind you, after all, under the sun. We are part of creation. We have no place to question how God relates to us. What we are to be grateful for is how God has provided another covenant, the covenant under his son, his only son, Jesus. This is why Jesus is called the second Adam, for he provides a covenant in which we can have our sins forgiven and be adopted as children of God. I bring up the presence of the will of humanity because we see the fruit of the human will. being displayed in our gospel reading by those who choose not to believe Jesus to be the Messiah, even when he presents evidence to them that cannot be denied by any objective observer. But that is a serious problem. The problem of not being able to objectively see truth. So let us now look at the gospel according to St. Luke, chapter 11, picking up at verse 14. The Gospel according to St. Matthew tells us that the man was blind as well as mute. Luke's account allows us to imagine how when Jesus did such miracles, the response of the onlookers was always fascination. The people, it says, they marveled at Jesus. Naturally, they marveled because what they witnessed was not something they had ever seen before. Such power was utterly unprecedented in their experience. That is why it is so hard to believe for people today. We must see it for ourselves, even when a multitude sees it, and there are still skeptics. But this first audience realized that they were in the presence of something they did not understand and yet it was still awe-inspiring. A man who couldn't speak suddenly spoke freely. How was Jesus able to do it He did not utter any incantations. He did not perform any magical ceremony. He simply gave a commandment to the demons, and they unquestionably obeyed him That Jesus was a deliverer was obvious, but how was unknown. Verse 15 Here is the will of human beings who had cold and hard hearts. They chose to believe that Jesus performed miracles, miracles of God's grace. Performing them by the power of the devil. Beelzebub was the name of a heathen god of the cult of Baal, the same false god we hear so many times about in the Old Testament. In the first century, the name had been attached by the Jews to Satan, the archenemy of God. It was actually a slur, as it probably literally means Lord of the Flies. It is a sort of thing that you might call someone who is a traitor, you call them Judas, or a deceitful woman, you call her Jezebel. It was a name to mock the devil, just like we try to do when we picture him with horns and a pitchfork and looking rather impotent. Luke describes those who were making such accusations as he calls them some of them. But we know from Matthew and Mark that the them were once again scribes and Pharisees from Jerusalem. Hence it was religious leadership, as it is so often even today. Religious leadership Who took the lead in suggesting another explanation for how Jesus did what he did or assuming he had evil motives They seem to have been thinking that only by placing the miracle worker Jesus in a bad light could they preserve their own leadership and preserve how they thought people saw them. Verse 16. The others who wanted him to do something else extraordinary and amaze them in some other way seem to have wanted a show And seem to have a standard of what would it take for them to actually believe Jesus was the Messiah. Again, we will Have the will of humanity at work, and their choosing is not so good. Verse 17 and 18 We know this famous statement from our own American history as it was used by our Abraham Lincoln during a famous free war speech. It is by itself a simple point of logic. Why would Satan work against his own kingdom by emasculating his own servants? What Satan would be choosing to do is engage in a civil war against himself. Even by evil standards, that strategy is unreasonable. The only logical conclusion from the miracles of Jesus is that God was working through Jesus to bring about his kingdom. And we are to recall that this exorcism does not stand alone. For the gospels records several miracles just like this, as well as other healings. Jesus likely did this for two years straight. All of this by a man who warned against the devil and commended all men to have faith in God's grace. Such a message the devil could never ever utter. Verse 19 Perhaps this teaching by Jesus sounds a little strange to us, but it meant a great deal to the original audience. Stretching out the point for clarity, Jesus is saying that if his power over the kingdom of evil is because he is in a a league with the devil himself Then by what power or authority do Jewish exorcists of that period, by what power do they cast out demons or at least attempt to do so? What is inferred, and from what we read in all of the Gospels, demon possession at this time was widespread. And although we read nothing about it in the Old Testament, At the time of Jesus, it was a scourge that great thought and effort had been devoted in finding ways to deliver those who were possessed. We read of a Jewish exorcist as well in Acts chapter 19, where men attempt to cast a demon out. Hearing the name of Jesus from the Apostle Paul. When they did so, the demon proclaimed that if that he did indeed know the name of Jesus, and he knew the name of Paul, then he didn't know the name of them. And this resulted in the possessed man jumping them and injuring them and causing them to flee. So the point of Jesus is that if he was casting out demons by the mere utterance of a word, If the demons are invariably obeying him, and he is delivering one person after another from the scourge of demon possession, because they say he is in league with the devil Are they then ready to declare that all Jewish exorcists are in league with the devil? If he succeeded only with demonic power, then those must be succeeding as well. And that point they were not willing to accept. Verses 21 through 22. Jesus, of course, is in no relation to the devil in exorcisms or healings that he is practicing. Far from being in league with the devil, the Lord was spoiling Satan's kingdom and delivering those who were Satan's captives. Thus, Jesus is the strong man. Let us not underestimate what Jesus accomplished in the desert when he resisted the devil fully. He showed himself to be the stronger man. Therefore, what he required and requires of devils, they must do. Verse 23. The point is that, as the Lord's power over the demonic realm demonstrates his divine authority, there can be no neutrality about him. And that includes no neutrality about those who follow him. His work was too demonstrative, too unique, and too much of a blessing to those in need for a willful decision about him not to be made. For the first century onlookers, there are neither, they are either for him and enthusiastic about it, what he is doing, or they are against him. Which is to say they are either on God's side or the side of the devil. Now some commentators have said this is Luke's version of the dilemma argued by C. S. Lewis Stating that Jesus must have been either a lunatic, a liar, or Lord. The argument presumed that what Jesus said about himself as recorded in the Gospels makes him a lunatic, meaning that he was delusional when he said something like, I and the Father are one. Or when he said, before Abraham was, I am. Or Jesus knew that such statements were not true, but like any cult leader, he did whatever he could to get a following. thus making him a liar. And then the last option, Jesus was who he said he was. And because the wisdom taught by Jesus showed he was not a lunatic, and the character of Jesus showed that he was not a liar, the third option is all that is left. The point being is that when you rationally limit the possibilities, you more easily come to the right conclusion. From what Jesus is arguing in Luke, he is either from God or he is a bad man Hard to believe he is a bad man, teaching the way he did, delivering people as he did, and living selfishly selflessly as he did. Hardly anyone down through the ages has ever thought or claimed that Jesus was a bad man or mentally ill. So if not bad, then what is left? We are left with the confession that Jesus Christ is Lord. Verses 24 through 26. You see here that Jesus is not done teaching on demon possession and the need for the human heart to be filled. This teaching is a warning and is just as important to grasp as the lesson that Jesus cast out demons by the power of God Himself. The lesson is that both those who had been delivered from demons and those who had witnessed the deliverance, they must not assume that such deliverance is enough. This is from commentator George Bradford Caird, quote: The heart of a man is a house which must have an occupant. And the only way to ensure that it is not taken over by disreputable squatters is to see that it is inhabited by God who made it for himself. Exorcism is not enough. The spiritual world, like the natural, abores a vacuum. End quote. The mistake is easy to make. Just getting some bad habit out of your life appears enough until it is replaced with something virtuous. Until then, there is room for another dangerous vice. In the case that Jesus describes, the demonic possession is worse than before Should this be a warning that scared them? Yes. Should this scare us? Yes. The man who had unclean spirits go out of him was likely a willing participant for the unclean spirits going into him. The going out of him was by the grace of God. The going into him was by his will. And I don't think it is complicated for evil spirits to enter a person. People who play with the occult in games that include casting spells and addressing the demonic are wilful participants in welcoming evil spirits to be entertainers in their lives. Those who look to horoscopes for guidance and predictions of the future are allowing evil spirits to have influence in their lives. Those who read the philosophies of men without using Holy Scripture as the standard for truth allow demonic space in their minds. Which soon takes up space in their hearts, resulting in a denial of God and a denial of anything that is good. And then there are those people, easily more than any who dabble in the occult or read horoscopes or read the philosophies of men. They, these people instead are the people who allow sin to fester in their lives, which is allowing evil spirits to take residence. Such people allow anger to turn to hate, and then hate to bitterness, and the evil spirit of bitterness now takes control. And notice that in such instances the will of the person was involved initially. A man chooses to be angry, but that is not the problem. The book of James says, be angry, but sin not. Don't let the sun go down on your anger. It is one thing to choose to be angry, and still another to let the sun go down on your anger. And such does not have to be literally applied. It simply means to hang on to anger, again, willfully. And while the anger is willful and the hanging on to it is wilful, when it turns to bitterness, the evil spirit of bitterness has taken control and deliverance is needed. But anger is just one example. We could describe how coveting turns into envying, which turns into bitterness as well. Sexual lust has its own slow development ending in fornication and adultery. Pride has its own slippery slope leading to idol worship of self. All of them, all of them begin with the will of a person choosing to sin and then remain on the slope that just keeps picking up speed. We are not passive in how our lives are lived, beloved. God has given us a will And if you claim Jesus Christ as your Savior, he has given you the Holy Spirit, who strengthens your inner will, so that you can say yes to its leading and no to the temptations of Anger and bitterness, coveting and envy, lusting and adultery. That is what it is to fill our hearts, the Holy Spirit filling our hearts So that we are filled with God's perfect love, and perfect love casts out evil. Beloved, our liturgy is a gift of God, giving opportunity to confess the sins that we have allowed to take hold of us and to ask God to forgive us. That is the cleaning out that we need. But we don't leave our hearts empty. We ask the Holy Spirit to come into our hearts and to fill us up. And then we eat with our God as we receive the bread and then the wine. Every time we worship corporately is an opportunity to be cleansed Filled and have fellowship with God restored. So let's get to it. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God, you are thankful for these warnings. You are thankful for the reality of the spiritual world that we need to understand and know about. That we give up all these sins that we allow to fester, that we avoid anything that would speak of the occult, and that we allow you to fill us up. And so we look to that now, the confession of our sins. The allowing of the Holy Spirit to fill our hearts, and then to be able to sit and receive from you the bread and the wine. May this day be a restoration day for all of us. Pray this in Jesus name, Amen

sermons.title: Rest, Relax, Recline and Eat
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. He'd be seated. We will be looking at first our gospel reading and then our reading from Galatians. But I want to start off with a story. The old gray donkey Eeyore stood by himself in a thistly corner of the forest. His front feet well apart, his head on one side, and thought about things. Sometimes he thought sadly of himself, why? And sometimes he thought, what? And sometimes he thought, in as much as which. And sometimes he didn't quite know what he was thinking about So when Winnie the Pooh came stumping along, Eeyore was very glad to be able to stop thinking for a while in order to say, How do you do? in a gloomy manner to him And how are you? said Winnie the Pooh. Eeyore shook his head from side to side. Not very how, he said. I don't seem to have felt at all how for a long time. Dear dear, said Pooh, I'm sorry about that. Let's have a look at you. So Eeyore stood there gazingly sad gazing sadly at the ground, and Winnie the Pooh walked all around him once Why, what's happened to your tail? he said in surprise. What has happened to it? said Eeyore. It isn't there. Are you sure? Well, either a tail is there or it isn't there. You can't make a mistake about it, and yours isn't there. Then what is? Nothing. Let's have a look, said Eeyore. And he turned slowly around to the place where his tail had been a little while ago, and then Finding that he couldn't catch it up, he turned round the other way until he came back to where he was at first. And then he put his head down and looked between his front legs. And at last he said with a long, sad sigh, I believe you're right. Of course I'm right, said Pooh. That accounts for a great a good deal said Eeyore gloomily. It explains everything. No wonder. You must have left it somewhere, said Winnie the Pooh. Somebody must have taken it, said Eeyore. How like them, he added, after a long silence. Such was the exchange of Pooh to Eeyore in A. A. Milne's Winnie Plu. I have included this reading Because I've concluded during Lent season, historical liturgical churches like ours are the aeor of the Christian church. Our readings each Sunday during Lent can be described as gloomy. Our prayers could be described with sad eyes and with our heads down. In the call X for each week so far in Lent, we have prayed for God to defend us from our enemies, because we cannot defend ourselves. And we pray that we need help because we cannot help ourselves. And we pray for help to abstain from sin because we cannot abstain from sin ourselves And we pray a lament of our sins with an acknowledgement of our wretchedness. Such prayers seem to require poor posture. Sad eyes and a gloomy voice when prayed. Meanwhile, modern Christian churches with their rock bands and torn jeans and therapeutic sermons Use Lent as another theme to tell the congregation all the positive things God wants to do in their lives. And still others don't even mention Lent at all, but focus also on the positive things God wants to do in the lives of his people. So as I said, we are the Eeyore of the Christian Church. However, the writers of our liturgy did not want the middle of Lent season to be marked with gloom and sadness. But instead wanted it to be seen as a time where we can see Easter on the horizon and be encouraged by prayers for comfort and food for refreshment. And so we turn to the gospel according to St. John chapter 6. I have preached on this gospel reading text before. Not too many years removed, when we walked through the Gospel of John. We noted then why the great crowd followed Jesus. He was performing miracles of healing, mostly, particularly healing the sick, of course. And we note again that Jesus did his healing in the open for any witnesses to see him, as opposed to in a stadium on a stage where the sick are controlled by handlers. That the Passover was near, no doubt played a factor in the large crowd getting larger. And no doubt the Passover reminded all of God, all of God delivering Israel out of Egypt And God leading the people into the desert, and God providing for them manna, bread from heaven. Remembering for six days, and then the seventh they were to take off, gathering more on Friday, so that Saturday could be a day of rest. And likely when thinking upon the manna God provided the people, some remembered that the Messiah to come was to be like Moses. And if Moses played a part in providing bread for the people, so too would the Messiah provide bread. And Jesus takes this challenge, but not because it was a challenge, but because he had a genuine concern for the people. He saw the size of the crowd. He knew there was no store or vendor that could provide for all of the people, and so he plans to feed them. For as verse 6 states, he may have asked Philip to help to buy bread, but he knew what he was going to do. Jesus, like his father, takes what is little and uses it to accomplish great tasks. We have been studying in 1 Samuel chapter 17 in our Bible study on Wednesdays, and we noted that David picked up five rocks when encountering Goliath. Those who have been a part of the Bible study will recall that we speculated that David picked five rocks Knowing that he only needed one, but also knowing that Goliath had four brothers. Thus one rock for each of them was picked. With that miracle and great victory in mind, we note that the lad in the story has five barley loaves and two small fish. Perhaps he too was one of five siblings that was going to share a lunch together. Five rocks to kill five giants, five loaves to feed five thousand. And two fish to represent the old covenant and the new. Peter asks, I'm sorry, Andrew asked, referring to the lunch of this one family, what are they Among so many. He being like King Saul, seeing only the outward of Goliath, and having no faith So too does Andrew see only what is in front of him. And what is in front of him is limited. Only it is not. For Jesus was in front of him. Jesus instructs the disciples to have the people sit down. He wants them to rest. He wants them to be resting as they are nurtured. His desire for them is to be rested and nurtured is a desire for them to be strengthened. When we are hungry, truly hungry, where our bodies lack the nutrients needed, our minds do not think clearly, and we are preoccupied with what our flesh desires For the people to digest the words Jesus has spoken to them, they needed to digest actual food so as to be able to think only about what Jesus has said. And what has Jesus said? If you look in your Bible, you will look at chapter 5, and you will see there a great deal that Jesus has said. He has described his unity with the Heavenly Father. He has insisted that he, as the Son of God, be honored. He has referred to himself as the Son of Man, which is the title for the Messiah in the book of Daniel. He has promised everlasting life to all who listen to him and believe. He next explained that the miracles he does are to be a witness to all regarding who he is. And then he confronts the unbelievers and warns them that Moses will be a witness against them, for Moses knew him and had faith in him. Such teachings were and are a great deal to comprehend at the time they were heard and even for us today. Time is needed to process the teaching. And a meal on a hillside where families can rest and think and discuss, that is what was needed. There is a repeated theme in Scripture that has God teaching, speaking, acting, and then the people sitting and eating. What did Abraham and his men do after Melchizedek revealed to them who he was? They ate bread and drank wine. What did Abraham and Sarah do with the angel who revealed God's will to them regarding having a son? Let's eat and drink together. And what did Isaac do when blessing his sons but recline, eat and drink? And what did Joseph arrange for his brothers after each trip to Egypt? But a place to recline and eat and drink. And what did God do with the elders of Israel after their many years of bondage and ten plagues that set them free? After having Moses read his covenant to the people, and they all agreed after it was read, it says in Exodus 24, then Moses went up. Also Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel. And they saw the God of Israel, and there was under his feet, as it were, a paved work of sapphire stone. And it was very like the heavens in its clarity. But on the nobles of the children of Israel, God did not lay his hand, so they saw God, and they ate, and they drank. Such a repeated theme I have previously overlooked in regards to Jesus feeding the 5,000, which we know was likely more of 15 to 20,000, counting family members. Preachers can focus on Jesus being like Moses, as was mentioned before, or the imagery that Jesus later reveals, which is that He Himself is the bread of life, from which all who follow Him must eat. We can make note of the stewardship of Jesus when he commissioned all of that was left over, the fragments to be collected. Israel was commanded something similar when they were not allowed to leave any of the manna on the ground. In our tradition we are reminded of our stewardship each time we have extra bread and wine for Holy Communion, we save it and we consume it. And preachers can focus on the last words of the section where Jesus is confirmed by the disciples to be a prophet. But another focus not often mentioned is the fact that Jesus wanted his followers to rest, to be relaxed, and to be fed. Such is not an understanding consistent with what our focus has been during Lent. It is not consistent with the attitude of Eeyore, but it is what Jesus was concerned about. It is what God desires for those who follow Him. And I hope for you to keep that in mind as we look to our epistle reading from Galatians chapter 4. Paul has already rebuked the Galatians for following another gospel. That gospel was one of works, as in believing that by following the Moses or the Mosaic ritual law, that they can be in right relationship with God. They were wrong, and the teaching they were allowing among them was false. Paul makes that clear for over four chapters before he gets to the allegory he wants to use to stamp the point home. As we read this allegory, I I I want you to work to not get caught up in the actual person of Sarah and the actual person of Hagar The historical account of these two women is found in the book of Genesis and is very unfortunate and emotional, as petty jealousy results in a woman and her boy being cast out of their home and defend for themselves. That story is separate from the allegory they provide. Sarah In the allegory is the free woman. Hagar is the Bondwoman. Hagar, as a Bondwoman, was born into bondage. She was required to do what she was told to do, and if she didn't do it, was punished for her disobedience. Sarah, being free, could do as she pleased. And according to law, a son born to a bondwoman was a slave also. A son born to a free woman was free also. The allegory is stretched farther. with the comparison of Hagar being like Jerusalem of this world and Sarah being like the heavenly Jerusalem. So the implied question is, do you, Christian, want to be born of a free woman or born of a bondwoman? Do you want to be of the city of this world or the city of heaven? To attempt to find God by obeying the law, which is referring to the ceremonial law, is choosing to be born of the bondwoman and of the city below. To be right with God by the grace of God through faith in Jesus is to be bored of the free woman and to be of the heavenly city. And while the choice seems obvious, it is not so. For like the blanket of Linus in the Charlie Brown saga, people find comfort in the law. It is what they can control and thus perceive they are controlling, controlling their own destiny, even their own afterlife. But such is a lie. A lie from the devil himself, who also wanted to control his own destiny, which he never will The grand truth is that God wants his people to not just be born of the free woman and not just be of the heavenly city, but to live as being born free, and to live as being of the realm of the heavenly city. And although we cannot do so fully until we are resurrected, God still wants us to be free, to rest, to recline, to eat, and drink. So that we are strengthened. To live as being born of the free woman and live as being of the heavenly realm. Our consciences can be free to rest, to recline, to eat, and to drink Yes, it is true.
