There are still 17 more days of Lent, not counting Sundays And we are to discipline ourselves in fasting and be reflective on our fallen human condition, and bettering ourselves to listen and follow the Holy Spirit All that remains. But today, we are called to rest, to recline, to eat and drink, to be strengthened For those 17 days ahead, with Easter finally on the horizon Of course, we must come back and find out what happened to Eeyore and his tail. Pooh went to Owl to ask for help. Owl had an idea of writing up a notice for a reward. The rest reads. Owl went on and on, using longer and longer words, until at last he came back to where he started, and he explained that the person to write out this note was Christopher Robin. It was he who wrote the ones on my front porch door for me. Did you see them, Pooh? For some time now Pooh had been saying yes and no in turn, with his eyes shut to all that Owl was saying, and having said Yes, yes. Last time he said, no, not at all, now, without really knowing what Al was talking about. Didn't you see them? said Owl, a little surprised. Come and look at them now. So they went outside, and Pooh looked at the knocker and the notice below it, and he looked at the bell the bell rope And the notice below it. And the more he looked at the bell rope, the more he felt that he had seen something like it somewhere else, sometime before. Handsome bellrope, isn't it? said Al. Pooh nodded. It reminds me of something, he said. But I can't think what? Where did you get it? I came across it in the forest. It was hanging over a bush. And I thought at first somebody lived there. So I rang it, and nothing happened. And then I rang it again, very loudly, and it came off in my hand. And as nobody seemed to want it, I took it home. And Owl, said Fu solemnly, you made a mistake. Somebody did want it. Who? Eeyore, my dear friend Eeyore. He was he was fond of it. Fond of it? Attached to it, said Winnie the Pooh, sadly. So with these words he unhooked it and carried it back to Eeyore. And when Christopher Robin had nailed it on its right place again, Eeyore frisked about the forest, waving his tail so happily that Winnie the Pooh came over all funny and had to hurry home for a little snack of something to sustain him. And wiping his mouth half an hour afterwards, he saying to himself proudly, Who found the tale? Aye, said Winnie, said Pooh, at a quarter to two, only it was a quarter to eleven, really, I found the tail. So, as Pooh needed to rest, recline, eat, and drink after working hard to find Eeyore's tail in order to be strengthened. So too do we need the same as we look for Easter Sunday not far off from now. Amen. Let us pray A gracious and heavenly father, we thank you for this day for it allows us to Have a reprieve to receive from you the nourishment that we need to continue on during this lent season, seeing that Easter is not now so far off. Encourage us, strengthen us this day, we pray. In Jesus' name. Amen. Please be reminded of our giving, of our tithes, and our offerings to the Lord. Let us now prepare our hearts to receive the body and love of Satan.

sermons.title: Passion Sunday
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Bueno, bueno, bienvenido finismo. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. You may have noticed that in the prayer book The title of this Sunday is Twofold. It is the fifth Sunday in Lent, as well as being called Passion Sunday. Because some Christian traditions call Palm Sunday Passion Sunday, for us to call the Sunday prior Passion Sunday can be a bit confusing. But it is important to separate these next two Sundays because the focus is different for each of them The reason why this Sunday is also called Passion Sunday is the focus that is placed on the suffering of Jesus. With the acknowledgement that when he sets his sights on going to Jerusalem, the whole purpose of his mind was to suffer and die. Thus, in the mind and heart of Jesus was his suffering even before it physically began. And because it was on the mind and heart of Jesus, so too it should be on our hearts and minds. What can be difficult is to understand why his death was necessary. After all, when someone has wronged us Done evil to us, and then asks for our forgiveness, we grant it and we go about our lives, not counting that wrongdoing against another person. And we hope that people will do the same to us when we wrong them and seek from them forgiveness. So, why doesn't God just accept the apologies of all who have sinned against him and allow us to go about our lives? To be able to answer such a question fully is to delve into the nature of God that has not been revealed. What we can know is that God has revealed Himself to be just. And in fact, the definition of just and justice in Western civilization is based off of what God has said is just. Both in the Hebrew and Greek The words we translate as justice and righteousness have so much connection and overlap that they are nearly synonymous and necessarily connected. When studying the Bible, we must recognize the connection between words like righteous, righteousness. Justice, justified, and justification. Like Scripture says, God is righteous It is saying God is just. And when it says He is just, it is also saying that He is righteous. In the letter to the Romans, for example, Paul speaks to the righteousness of God. And it could be said that Paul is describing God's administration of justice. As it relates to human humans, righteousness is not just about our relationship with God, but also about our relationship to our neighbors. For example, Jesus said, when you give to the needy, you are practicing, practicing righteousness. Matthew 6, 1 and 2. We can understand that giving to the needy is also practicing justice because it is a righteous act. Of course, all of us are guilty of injustice, which is the same as saying all of us have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God. We have all fallen short of what God's justice demands. But what does God's justice demand? Let us look at the answer in four different ways. First, biblical justice means personal accountability. Such is not accountability to self, but a taking of responsibility for one's actions It is taking the blame for what has been done without trying to make excuses or include others as being responsible for our behavior. The guilty individual may have been negatively influenced by others, but the blame cannot be shifted. Each person must be held personally accountable for his own wrongdoing. A clear example of this is in the law of Moses from Deuteronomy 24, verse 16. Quote, fathers shall not be put to death because of their children, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. Each one shall be put to death for his own sin. Now, such has been lost on Western societies, for we hear of current generations being responsible for the sins of their forefathers. The Bible knows nothing of such responsibility. And those who perceive themselves as victims play it the other way as well, insisting that their sins Their failures are caused by their forefathers. Again, the Bible knows of no such responsibility. And personal accountability also means that when we are the wrongdoer Justice demands acknowledging our culpability, accepting the consequences, and attempting to correct the damage we caused. Next, biblical justice means fairness. Fairness means giving the same advantage to each person. This is not the same as giving the same outcome, as progressives today insist, but is giving the same opportunity. Thus doing justice also means not giving an unfair advantage to some people over others Consider how the Bible often uses terms relating to measurements, balances, and weights to express fairness as justice. People traded with goods like grain and oil. There was a natural temptation for merchants to give a slightly better exchange rate to certain people over others. After all, who would notice? The answer is that God notices. He noticed every time people use an unequal weight or measurement This is from Proverbs 11:1. A false balance is an abomination to the Lord, but just weight is his delight. God notices every time someone withholds fair wages from a laborer, God commands his people, you shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as a native among you. And you shall love him as yourself, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt. I am the Lord your God. You shall do no wrong in judgment, in measures of length or weight or quantity You shall have just balances, just weights, a just epha, and a just hen. Leviticus nineteen But biblical justice as fairness, again qualifying, cannot possibly be applied in all circumstances, again as progressives would have it. Not all persons are granted the same intellect, or the same health, or the same body strength, or the same personality. Some disadvantages have to be overcome by the individual. It is what can be made fair. What can be made fair is what should be made fair. Next, biblical justice means collective responsibility. This one we must be careful with. Because we can think collective responsibility with the modern notion of systemic evil, such as what is being called systemic racism. As some of you have heard me state, racism is not a biblical term. The biblical term is hate, and it is a damnable sin when it is focused on human beings. You might want to get that. The concept of systemic evil as it relates to sin is also not a biblical term. And it is contrary to biblical teaching. Consider that if systemic evil was real, then Jesus would be a sinner. For Jesus was part of a Jewish system and a Roman system, and both practiced injustices. Consider that the Jewish system of Jesus' day was unjust in condemning him If systemic evil is applied, then Jesus is not only guilty of being a part of the system, he is guilty of condemning himself, which is absurd. In truth, in truth, the idea of systemic evil is a means for academics to condemn societies while disconnecting themselves from accountability. Everyone is guilty except the academic, identifying the guilt of the system. Instead What collective responsibility means is that each of us is part of something beyond our individual self. We are part of a family. And then a church. And then a city. A county. A state. A country. Where we work is another community, and so on. And within those communities, we have responsibilities towards others. And that could mean ensuring fairness in the community Standing for the weak in the community, exposing wrongdoing and treating others as we want to be treated. Said simply, it is not about ensuring justice for ourselves, but also for those in our several communities. From Isaiah chapter 1. Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean, remove the evil of your deeds from before my eyes Cease to do evil, learn to do good, seek justice, correct oppression, bring justice to the fatherless, plead for the widow's cause. Next, biblical justice means merciful generosity. We must accept the truth that the biblical concept of justice doesn't pit mercy against justice. but brings them together. Biblical justice is loving, merciful, gracious, generous, restorative. As mentioned earlier, Jesus considered charity and act of doing justice, practicing righteousness. When we provide food, clothing, and shelter for those in need, we are doing justice or acting righteously. We see this in the justice laws in Israel, such as in Deuteronomy chapter 24. He says, When you reap your harvest in your field, and forget a sheaf in the field, you shall not not go back to get it. It shall be for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, that the Lord your God may bless you in all the works of your hands. In the book of Ruth, when Boaz provided food for Ruth and Naomi, he was caring for the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow And when Boaz found out Ruth and Naomi were his relatives, he did justice by redeeming them. Boaz did not do such a thing as Because he had a crush on Ruth, as some moderns think. He did such things for them because it was just, and he aligned himself with justice. Next, biblical justice fulfills the law of God. From the book of Numbers, chapter 23. God is not a man that he should lie, or a son of man that he should change his mind. Has he said and will he not do it? Or has he spoken and will he not fulfill it? From Isaiah 55. God says, So shall my word be that goes out and from my mouth. It shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it. Jesus explained it as follows. Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them. For truly I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the law, until all is accomplished. Matthew chapter 5 And the law says, the law that Jesus came to fulfill says the wages of sin is death. It is not for us to question whether such a wage is necessary, but instead to accept that it is, and then marvel at God fulfilling that wage with his own son. The preacher to the Hebrews in chapter nine, which was our epistle reading Reminds us of some of the details prescribed to the high priest of Israel when offering the sin offering according to the law, the law Jesus came to fulfill. There was the ark, which was golden laid, having cherubim at its top, from each end, with their wings folded toward one another inside Having the tablets of the law, Aaron's rod, and the pot of manna, all reminding Israel of what God did to deliver them from Egypt and bring them to the promised land. Then in the holy place were furnishings, including a table of showbread and the golden candlestick, respectively pointing to the Savior to come, who would be the bread of life, the light of the world. Further outside the tent was the altar upon which the sacrifice was placed. And going back into the temple, there was the altar of holy incense. It is mentioned last because it is believed to be of high importance and it has symbolized the needed prayers rising to the mercy seat of God. And we must mention the priesthood, for it was a necessary office relating to both God and man, and serving as a mediator between the two. And what the preacher to the Hebrews captures is that the Trinitarian God we worship was involved in the offering of the suffering and the sacrifice of Jesus. It was the Father to whom the offering was made. It was the Holy Spirit rising to the throne of God with the smoke from the incense and the smoke from the offering itself. It was Jesus acting not only as the offering, being sacrificed on the cross, but as a priest who prepared the offering and shed the blood. With this we are to remember that Jesus said that no one else lays his life down, but he lays it down himself by his will. The involvement in all of the Godhead when the sin offerings were offered in the tabernacle and then in the temple and then in Jesus is summarized by St. Paul, 2 Corinthians 5. God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. So God was just when Jesus became unjust. By taking on the sins of the world. But because he was not personally unjust, the injustice of the world could not hold him in the grave. That's a great sentence, by the way. I believe we can all agree that the exchange read this morning for our gospel lesson was uncomfortable. More uncomfortable than a rich actor striking a rich comedian. Jesus tells his listeners that because they do not believe him, they are not of God They reply, obviously offended, and tell him he has a demon. Jesus retorts that because they dishonor him, they dishonor God. He then makes a promise that whoever believes in him will not see death. Of course, he's referring to eternal death. They mock him because even Abraham has seen death Then Jesus makes a statement that requires him to be stoned, for he took on the very name that God revealed to Moses by saying, before Abraham was a goamine, I am But what was this exchange really about? It was about being right before God. And who is right before God? And to be right before God is to be righteous. And what we have learned this morning is that to be righteous is to be justified and therefore just. I believe every human being has a need for justice and righteousness within them. Because every person is made in the image of God, and God is righteous and just But because that image of God is marred with sin, the sin of Adam and our own personal sin, we cannot achieve righteousness on our own. We can only achieve righteousness by the way of Jesus. And if we reject the righteousness of Jesus, then we have to find our righteousness and our justice from some other place. And this is where self-righteousness arises. Self-righteousness can be claimed when a person obeys the rules better than others Self-righteousness can be claimed when a person follows more rituals than another person. Self-righteousness can be claimed when we think we care more than most other people. But such righteousness is no righteousness and is rewarded no farther than the length of a person's life. What Christians are to do is to receive the righteousness of Jesus Christ and to be thankful for his righteousness. And during Lent, we are to meditate on what suffering Jesus endured in order that we might be made righteous. And when I say what suffering Jesus endured, I am talking about more than the cross, which might be enough. More than the scourging, more than the abandonment of his closest disciples, more than the crown of thorns. Jesus' endurance was taking on human form, which included the weaknesses of men, which included the susceptibility to disease, susceptibility to bodily injury, susceptibility to emotional struggle, along with peer and family disappointment The suffering of Jesus that he endured included people who witnessed him perform unexplained miracles and still did not believe who he was. Jesus endured people who could not refute his teaching and yet still would not agree with him. Jesus endured false teachers who lied about what he taught. Jesus endured spiritual leaders who were jealous of him being able to heal. Jesus endured people saying he had a demon and did miracles by the power of the devil. Jesus endured people who followed him only because of what they could get from him. Jesus endured his own disciples, not understanding what he was teaching them. Even having been around him for three years, they still bickered about who was going to sit next to him on what they thought would be an earthly throne. All of it. Plus events in the Passion Week, Jesus endured so that you and I and all that believe in him could stand before God and be called righteous and just Beloved, our concept of justice and righteousness comes from God. Without Him, the only righteousness we have is self-righteousness. And the only justice we have is what men fight for on the streets. If we have true righteousness It is the righteousness given by Jesus who suffered and endured for our righteousness. Let us only think upon his suffering. Let us pray. Our gracious God, we thank you for granting the world a right definition of justice and righteousness. And we mark this day all that you have done to achieve that for us. May our minds be upon that suffering, that enduring. These next two weeks, as we look to that glorious Easter Sunday, it is in Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Palm Sunday
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. A mature gentleman shared with me a number of years ago that he had a personal test To see whether the Lord was going to give him a good day or a bad day. While in his office in the morning, he would take a crumpled piece of paper and throw it, attempting to make it into the trash basket a few feet away from his desk chair. Let's say it was six feet away just to keep it current If he made it, he believed the Lord would give him a good day. And if he missed, he wondered what the Lord had in store that would trouble him. He admitted that it was silly, but he did it nevertheless. I assume most of us Bible-believing Christians Don't think about God in precisely the same manner described, but I conjecture, because I have heard from many of you, that some of you believe in omens An omen is a supposed sign about the future, about a change that is going to take place Omens have been detected in anything from the flight pattern of a bird to residue left in the bottom of a teacup, also known as tea leaf reading. A belief in omens tells us something about ourselves and about how we think about God. Notice, please, I did not say that a belief in omens tells us about God. They do not. But it says such a belief in omens tells us of how we think about God. And I'm convinced that too often for too many of us we think about God. What we think about God is not who God truly is. It is important that we only think about God in the manner he has revealed himself to be and nothing more. For instance, we are not to view God as a taskmaster who gives us commands and then stands above us with his hand raised, ready to chastise us if we fail Instead, we learn from his weeping alongside Mary and Martha at the death of their brother Lazarus that Jesus chooses to enter into our life experiences. He suffers with us when we are struggling emotionally and even when we are failing in life. He weeps with those who weep, he mourns with those who mourn. And because we have more good times in life than bad, and we truly do, he rejoices with those who rejoice. My concern is that such a message about who God has actually revealed Himself to be gets drowned out by the former ways of thinking about Him. Simply put, some of us have thought about God in such a particular way for such a long period of time that it is difficult, very difficult, to get such thoughts out of our heads. Without trying to sound like Norman Vincent Peale, and if you don't know who that is, you don't need to, I must highlight the principle found in Proverbs chapter 23, which states As a man thinks in his heart, so is he. Now let's start with what this verse does not mean. It does not mean that if you have a positive mental attitude, positive things and only positive things will happen in your life What it does mean is found in the context. The context is a warning against gluttony and covetousness. It is the stated reality that if a man sets his mind solely on what he will eat and drink, then those desires will dominate his thinking. He will become dominated by that upon which he chooses to focus. Under such a principle about how the mind and the will of an individual works, We can also be warned that how a man thinks upon God, that is how he will perceive God is to him, like the man shooting the crumpled paper in the basket. To state it practical practically, if a man thinks that God is a taskmaster, then everything negative that happens in his life is going to be viewed as a form of God punishing him Or if God is seen as an idle observer to our struggles in life, then silence in the midst of pain and trouble is going to be interpreted as God being indifferent and uncaring. It would seem that the way we think about God is vitally important because of the repeated instruction in Holy Scripture for Christians to be renewed in our minds. Our minds need to be renewed, meaning improved upon, how we understand God and how His kingdom is ruled. All of this pioneering about the importance of the manner that we think about God is exemplified in the story of Jesus entering Jerusalem on what we call Jerusalem. Palm Sunday. Consider, if you will, the type of thinking about God that was going on among the people who lined the streets shouting, Hosanna! And among the Pharisees who observed the spectacle with contempt, perhaps there is no better narrative than this to show the dangers of how we are thinking and where it can lead. We know, for example, that the disciples were anxious for all of Israel and Rome to believe what they had come to believe. They wanted Jesus to prove himself. We can easily speculate that it was this was the case for Judas, who was likely trying to force the hand of Jesus by causing him to show his power at his arrest and trial. Judas thought he understood Jesus' plan, and in the end the confusion and guilt led him to hang himself. The rest of the disciples had witnessed Jesus perform miracles of such a magnitude that they could envision the kingdom of God being established on earth, where bread was provided daily, just like the days of Moses. They even argued about who would sit on his left hand and right as he sat on his earthly throne like that of King David. They could imagine Rome being brought to its knees just like Egypt was brought to its knees under Moses. After all, was not Moses said to be a type of the Messiah to come? Before Palm Sunday, they had witnessed Jesus delay the revealing of his identity time and time again. As Jesus finally accepted the praise given him upon the entrance into the Holy City, we can feel the excitement of the disciples as they understood the time had come for all men to know the truth. The truth of God was about to be revealed. However, it was not what the disciples and what the crowd eventually wanted. Speaking of the crowd, historian Alfred Edersheim speculates that those who displayed palm branches and laid garments for a makeshift carpet were reacting like most crowds do. They were responding to rumors and getting caught up in the moment. And here is Edersheim's description, quote. They had been greeting him with hosannas, but enthusiasm, especially in such a a cause, is infectious. They were mostly stranger pilgrims that had come from the city, chiefly because they had heard of the raising of Lazarus. We can imagine it all how the fire would leap from heart to heart. So he was the promised son of David. The kingdom was at hand. End quote. The description reminds us that excitement in a moment does not indicate true belief. We now turn to the Pharisees, who we know were among the crowds. While the crowds cried Hosanna, they turned to one another with angry frowns. See, they said, the world has gone after him. It is always so this side of heaven that men turn against one another with malice and jealousy of heart. Some of them appealed to Jesus perhaps as a test, or simply because they could stand the praise no longer. They appealed to Jesus to rebuke those who were singing. Jesus' response tells us that something more is happening than mere enthusiastic greetings. In Jewish writing, reference to rocks crying out, Was a witness to the sins of those that cried out of those who had been in the city. Jesus turns the idea into a testimony of righteousness. Creation is about to be redeemed and praises must be heard. From the attempts of trapping Jesus, the negative comments made throughout the Gospels and the plotting that led to the crucifixion of Jesus. We know well how the Pharisees felt about Jesus. We also know what they thought about God. First, we know that they thought that whoever God was, he was not Jesus. Second, we know that they understood God to be in favor of their legalism. They thought that God could be appeased and even impressed by their extensive interpretations of the law. When God revealed Himself as He truly is, their hearts and minds were not ready because their Of their preconceived ideas of who they thought God should be. Ideas, mind you, that were not the result of holy scriptures, but their own imaginations and what they added to the scriptures. So thus far we have examined three groups of people with specific ideas about God and about Jesus, and none of them on that first Palm Sunday had a proper understanding of God. And yet, God has supplied for them all that they needed to know, for what He has supplied were signs. Not omens, signs. First was the sign of the donkey upon which Jesus rode. We know that he did so as a fulfillment of the prophecy of Zechariah. There was, however, more to the use of a donkey than to fulfill prophecy. We know from various stories in the Old Testament That donkeys were used to carry burdens, or the weight of what a man needed for daily living. So as the donkey carried Jesus into Jerusalem, so Jesus carried the burdens of men upon him. We also know that from the story of Balaam, a donkey was used to carry a prophet, and was given the ability to speak in order to warn of impending doom. In like manner, this donkey was used to carry a prophet, but not just a prophet, the prophet. Who also had a word of warning. The warning was that to reject Jesus as the Messiah was the same as rejecting the Heavenly Father, and woe to any man or any city that would do so. We also know that the use of a donkey from the story of Samson was to slay Philistines with the jawbone of a donkey, a thousand Philistines, mind you And of course, the jawbone of a donkey was not a common weapon. It would be unexpected that a man could defeat an entire battalion with such a weapon. The devil thought similarly when Jesus entered Jerusalem. He did not understand that the weapons of Jesus' warfare were not and are not carnal. Besides the Old Testament references to donkeys, we should also note that the Romans used the same animal. Donkeys were not animals merely associated with the poor, but were owned by poor and rich alike. Besides being used from for domesticated purposes, they were used as symbols of political and militar for political and military leaders. A watchman, a watchman assigned to the high tower of a city would view an oncoming political or military leader and communicate whether he was coming in peace or in war If in peace he would be riding on a donkey. Further signs tell us more about the Savior who was coming to Jerusalem in peace. Jesus was riding on a donkey that had not been broken. Anyone who had to train a donkey knows that they do not like to be ridden. That Jesus was able to calm the animal so that it could be written, is to remind us that before sin entered the world, beasts lived in harmony. Prophecy tells us that in a redeemed world, the lion will lie down with the sheep. Such an image reflects the peace the Messiah will provide to the world. Thus, Jesus is able to bring peace to this chosen donkey. The second major sign was that of palm branches. The palm branch was a symbol of triumph and victory in pre-Christian times. The Romans rewarded champions of games and celebrated military successes with palm branches. The motto was Palmom qui marit fermat Which is Latin for let him bear the palm who has deserved it. It then appears that the Jews adopted this usage of palms. Jews carried and waved palm branches during festive celebrations. What the Romans rightly understood, along with other headreaths awarded to their champions, was that such plants withered and died, symbolizing the fleeting glory of men. While the people used the palm branches to celebrate Jesus' entrance, they did not understand how fleeting that celebration would be, as their own lips would turn Hosanna's into shouts of crucify him crucify him. The branches they waved were once green and fresh. Those same branches soon turned yellow and dry and eventually became dust. Just as will happen to all who reject Jesus as Savior. These signs, these symbols Jesus used on the first Palm Sunday, tell us who God is. But not all of who God is. The symbols of Palm Sunday are to be understood in light of what they represented from the past and what they pointed to in the future. In the book of Revelation, we see Jesus on a horse again, and we see palm branches waving again, but the horse is not a donkey. The horse is white, symbolizing both the purity of its rider and the victory that is his. Jesus in that same instance is described as having eyes like fire. And from his mouth comes a sharp sword. His robe has been dipped in blood, and he is said to make wars. And we say, but wait, what happened to the Jesus of peace? What happened to the mild donkey and the calm stroll into Jerusalem? And what happened to the man who said by the prophet Isaiah to have nothing physical about him that would draw attention to him? And here he is with eyes of fire. If we didn't know any better, we could conclude that the Jesus of John's revelation is not the Jesus that rode into Jerusalem. We might tend to wonder to what Jesus we are referring to when we call upon him. We might struggle to wonder what image we are to have of him when we picture him in our minds, listening to our prayers and our praises. The answer I believe is both and. Both and means that Jesus is both the God of peace and a God of war. It means that when we pray to him, we pray to him as meek and gentle, and as a warrior bent on destruction of the enemy. The and means that there is more to him than being meek and being a warrior. He is all in all. He is the I am, which is to say that there is no word that can fully describe him. There is no word that can clearly identify all that he is. It says in Revelation that he has a name that no one can pronounce. Now, beloved, I ask you plainly and pastorally, what type of God do you have in your mind when you invoke his name? What type of presuppositions do you have about him that match up to who he truly is? I suspect that whatever he is to you, he is more. And whatever presuppositions you have about him, they need to be renewed. When you think upon him riding a donkey, remember that he also rides a white horse. When you think he is silent, know that his voice causes mountains to quake. When you think he is standing idle, rethink by remembering how he identifies with us in all ways. When you think that your days are determined by omens, we consider signs that show Jesus to be greater than time, space, or circumstance. I suspect that when we allow the Holy Spirit to form in our minds the true expanse of the Triune God, that even our understanding of ourselves Will improve as well. I mentioned earlier that palm branches are also in the book of Revelation. Today we waive them limited by time, space, and understanding. One day we will wave them if we remain faithful to the end of our days. We will wave them with thousands upon thousands around the throne, and then we will truly know him, truly understand him, and see him as he truly is. Let us look forward to that day. Amen.

sermons.title: Maundy Thursday
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. The following scenario has likely played out in your home several times. You wake up in the middle of the night terribly thirsty. Your mouth is dry and sticky. But the air outside the covers is cold. So you don't want to get up and get a drink. But you can't sleep because the only thing you can think about is how thirsty you are. So you get up and stumble to the kitchen. Sounds like a Dolly Parton song. You open the cabinet and grab a glass, immediately followed by turning on the cold water at the faucet. You quickly fill your glass with the cold water and without hesitation raise it to your lips and drink. You feel it go down your throat and confirm to yourself that it satisfies. You then enjoy one more drink before going back to bed. When back in bed, you enjoy the feeling of the covers again, along with the satisfaction of no longer being thirsty. It was such a simple and quick common act, and yet as you do it, and so many other things like it. You are unaware that you are acting as God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Ghost. In his book titled Through New Eyes, biblical scholar James Jordan outlines the pattern of God's work. We see the pattern in creation, where God saw a need and he chose to meet it. The earth was void and it needed to be filled. To fill it, God first took hold of creation. He was the hovering spirit that was over the face of the earth before life was given to it. The preacher of Hebrews describes the Godhead, the Godhead as upholding all of creation. God lays hold of it to mold it according to his will. And so the second thing God did after taking hold of creation was to restructure it. We remember that he separated the light from the darkness. The waters above from the waters below, as well as separating the waters below to become land and sea. The third thing God did was distribute creation. He filled the sky with light, and the seas with fish, and the land with plants and animals. The fourth thing God did was evaluate his work. His evaluation is a good lesson against the heresy of Gnosticism. Gnosticism says that the physical world is inconsequential, even evil. God evaluated his work, which was the physical world, and he said it was good. Fifth and finally, God enjoyed his creation when he rested on the seventh day. That is what the Sabbath day is for. We are to enjoy, find peace and rest with the good that God has done. The scenario of getting up in the night for a drink of water Follows the pattern of what God does when he works, his pattern of creation. The need preceded everything There was a void and God filled it. We are thirsty and we get a drink. First, we lay hold of the glass of water. We restructure the cabinet by removing the glass, and we restructure the sink and water by turning on the spigot. We then distribute by drinking the water, we then evaluate its effect and determine that it was good And finally, like a brief Sabbath, we find enjoyment in the satisfaction of quenching our thirst. Such a simple act, and yet so profound. If we were to open our eyes to see how much of what we do resembles the work of God, our God would, excuse me, the work of our God. We would agree with Mr. Jordan when he says, every calling in life, indeed every action in life, thus has immeasurable dignity. When it comes to man rightly imitating God, however, something must be added to these steps of God's work. Recall these words of St. Paul from Romans chapter 1, verses 20 and 21. He said, For since the creation of the world God's invisible qualities, his eternal power and divine nature have been clearly seen, being understood from what has been made, so that men are without excuse. For although they knew God, they neither glorified him as God, nor gave thanks to him. But their thinking became futile, and their foolish hearts were darkened. We must make note from these verses that men had their hearts darkened because they knew of God by way of creation, but failed to give him thanks. They were not willing to glorify God for being the Creator, nor were they willing to thank Him for creating them and all that was around them. A necessary part then of man's work, a part that must be added to the five acts of God already described, is the act of giving thanks. Men are to give thanks. A good identity for a Christian church is to embrace the institution of preaching the Word of God, the Holy Scripture, and then rightly distributing the sacraments and practice proper discipline. Of the first identity, the preaching of Holy Scripture, we find the six parts of man's accepted work. The void is not knowing God, and that precedes everything. To know God, the word of God is first laid hold upon by the one who reads it to the congregation. Thanks is then offered after the proclamation that what was read is the word of the Lord. The word read is then broken down and expounded upon for greater understanding. The word preached is then distributed among the people listening. as the Holy Spirit makes for specific application in individual lives. The people then evaluate what is preached to first determine, like the Bereans in the book of Acts That what was said was truth and to evaluate how it fits within their lives. That's your job Finally, once the word has been evaluated, it is to be a source of enjoyment and nourishment as it brings health to weary souls. The next place we find these six parts of a man's work is in the sacrament of holy communion. The void precedes it, which is the need for the grace of God. To receive that grace, Jesus first took the bread. And he took the cup. He laid hold of them. He had plans to restructure them. Jesus then gave thanks for each element. Think upon that. Jesus, the Son, who was with the Father creating the world, gave thanks for creation. Jesus, who was the bread of life and the wine of joy, gave thanks for each. He did as man should do. He did the work of man. Jesus then restructured the bread by breaking it. And he restructured both the bread and wine by calling it his body and his blood. It is at this point that it can be said that Jesus did not need to make it his actual body and blood, as some have needlessly taught, for his own body and blood was sufficient for the sacrifice. But we will not labor by saying what the bread and wine was or was not. We say what Jesus said. He restructured it when he said, This is my body broken. And this is my blood shed. Jesus then distributed the bread and wine to all who were present while giving them a monde, a command, do this in remembrance of me. The disciples, of course, obeyed and tasted the bread and drank from the cup, and by doing evaluated it saying, in effect, it is good. And finally, Jesus and his disciples enjoyed the remainder of their time together around the table, as is evident by them singing a hymn. Thus they took a brief Sabbath, having received the means of grace. It is to be noted That when that each time we do as Jesus instructed, we are working as God worked. We are taking hold. We are giving thanks. We are restructuring. We are distributing. We are evaluating its goodness. And finally, we are resting in his grace. It is something so simple and yet so profound. Join me in imagining What you would come up with in order for people to remember you. Imagine being given a promise that whatever it is that you come up with, people will perform it on a regular basis and do so to remember you and the life you lived. Think about what you would come up with. What would you come up what would you want other people to do to remember you? Maybe it would be an annual golf tournament in your name. Maybe a play with scenes that symbolized your stages in life. Or how about a banquet to be held annually with a seven-course meal and speakers and songs sung? Whatever you would choose, I am confident, it would not be eating bread and drinking wine. And that that is what Jesus chose. It was something so simple and yet so profound. Perhaps it is profound in part because it is so common. It is a concern by many That to participate in the rite of Holy Communion regularly will lessen its importance in the hearts of believers. The concern is valid because we know ourselves too well. We know how easily we slip into habits, and so the liturgy becomes a habit that we can recite without being engaged consciously or emotionally. We know how easily we can take the greatest of blessings for granted. This concern is even more understandable in that what we do is very, very simple. We take, we eat, we take, we drink. That is all. But there is a great irony in all of this. What is so simple has immeasurable dignity because we do as God does. What we need to do is recall each time we do it that we are doing what God does. Another reason why we can take Holy Communion for granted is because we may see it as an act that we do for God. But what we do, we do as God doing it. It is God offering to us to take the bread. It is God offering to us to take the cup. It is God offering both to us. He is present with us in Holy Communion like no other time. How is he with us in holy communion like no other time? Is not fully understood. But it is true and it is real. Beloved, when we are convinced that what we are doing is what God does, and that He is present with us like no other time. The importance of what we do will not be lessened, but become more and more profound. What we do as we take and eat, as we take and drink, has immeasurable dignity. The following is a sort of catechism about the Book of Common Prayer Liturgy. It was written in 1942 to answer common questions about Anglican liturgy. I want you to hear the dignity. in the answers to common questions about the service of Holy Communion. This is about the prayer of humble access. We are not worthy, we say, to God. The prayer of humble access, so-called, because of the humble confession of unworthiness which the priest here makes both for himself and as the representative of the people who approach God's table with him. Question: For what is the prayer of humble access a preparation? Answer: For the reception of the Blessed Sacrament Therefore, in the early English prayer book, this prayer was used very properly, the last thing, before partaking of the consecrated elements. Question. What follows the prayer of humble access? Answer. A hymn may be sung, and the priest, after partaking of the communion himself, delivers it to the people with the words prescribed. Question. What are people directed to receive the Holy Communion? Why are people directed to receive the Holy Communion kneeling? Answer. It is considered the more reverent way, and reverent actions are best not only to express, but to deepen reverent feelings. Question, what should the consecrated elements, excuse me, how should the consecrated elements be received by the communicants Answer. The bread should be received in the palm of the hand, never with the fingers. The cup should be taken firmly by the stem or base with both hands Question, is it proper to receive the blessed sacrament with gloved hands? Answer: No. It is a mark of reverence to remove the gloves. as we would do in receiving a precious gift from the hand of a loved and honored human benefactor. Question What follows in this service after the people have communicated? Answer. A prayer of thanksgiving and a hymn Question, what hymn is generally sung here? Answer, the hymn called Gloria in Excelsis. Question. What is the propriety of singing this hymn at the close of Holy Communion? Answer By singing a hymn, we follow the example of our Blessed Lord and His disciples, who sung a hymn at the close of their first Eucharist feast. And by using this hymn, we welcome the Savior to our hearts in the same words with which the angels welcomed him into the world. Beloved, let us welcome Jesus into our hearts tonight. Amen.

sermons.title: Seven Words
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: The Christian Gospel is the story of mankind sinning against God from the very beginning of time. It is then God promising to send forth a man who would shed his own blood to pay for the sins of mankind. It was God who, after the sin of Adam, sent types of the Messiah to come, types like Joseph. Who was rejected by his brothers, handed over to the Egyptians, thrown into prison, only to be raised up from prison to be seated next to Pharaoh, to be the most powerful man in Egypt. Jesus too was sold by his fellow Jews, his brothers, thrown into prison, murdered on a cross, buried in a grave, only to rise to be seated at the right hand of God the Father. Moses was a type of the Messiah to come. King David was a type of the messiah to come. But none of them were the Messiah. It wasn't until Jesus of Nazareth performed miracles, taught openly about the kingdom of God, that the true Messiah was revealed. That they rejected him, and as the life of Joseph prophesied, rejected him up to the cross and unto the grave. When Jesus was on that cross, the event that we remember so emotionally every Good Friday. We recall that he made seven statements, which are called seven words. The first was, Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. The least we know is that these were the first recorded words from this tragic scene, but to call it tragic is not fully accurate. For it was a tragedy that had to take place. Thus it was a glorious scene as much as it was tragic. But for the words to be the first recorded, tell us that they had to be spoken and we had to hear them. When they were spoken, meaning what was going on when they were spoken, it is clear, not clear, but some commentators have speculated that in a dramatic fashion They were spoken while the nails were being driven into his hands and into his feet. Could anything more dramatic have occurred in the history of mankind or since? I think not. What is a profound truth to acknowledge is how different the words are from other holy men dying. For even men we would call holy compared to ourselves still need to ask God to forgive their sins. But Jesus had no need to say, forgive me. We repeatedly say that Jesus was sinless, but to realize such was true, even at his death, that he had no need to be forgiven. is so very remarkable from our perspective that we have few words to comprehend it. But Jesus was not on the cross for himself. Jesus was on the cross for others. And so as always, thinking of others, he utters this prayer. uttering it too with the same consciousness which he had formerly expressed when he said, Father, I know that thou hearest me always. And we must note that his intercession has this for its ground, though in meekness it is not expressed. Father, I will that you forgive them, but instead, Father, forgive them. With all the faith that what the Father would do is what Jesus asked of him. But the reason for these words striking me so hard For they know not what they do. I ask, what difference does that make? So what if they didn't know? For they should have known. Is all that it takes to not be guilty of your evil deeds is to plead ignorant and all is forgiven? Try that with a police officer who pulls you over for speeding or having an expired license Sorry, officer, I had no idea. Now I you can be sure that I will not do it again. That's not going to work But of course, Jesus isn't saying that their ignorance lessens their guilt. The people are guilty even chanting for his death and chanting for the blood guilt to be upon them. Which is to be upon their ledger that they will answer to God for. They are as guilty as anyone ever has been So Jesus isn't justifying their ignorance, but forgiving them by his mercy. Jesus is being merciful to them despite their ignorance, not because of it. The second of the seven statements Jesus made while on the cross, today shalt thou be with me in paradise. His words were in a response to the one thief who took a chance to believe Jesus to be the Messiah, asking Jesus to remember him. Considering the request of the thief to be remembered, no strength given by an angel could have been more welcome to this dying Savior Jesus than these words of intense and sincere penitence. with strong faith. One commentator suggests that the crucified king cannot see these two criminals, cannot direct his glance to this last request without adding to his own agony by movement upon the cross. But that pain he forgets and turns with an impulse of joy as well as he can to the soul that speaks to him, thus making the nails more firm That is how the cross suffering was designed. The more you fought against it, the more agony you would feel, along with the tension that would increase with each movement. The request from the sinner was for Jesus to remember him. A very simple request with faith that says that a mere remembrance by Jesus would be salvation enough. And to this prayer Jesus answered, and we can say that the Lord's answer was very striking. Remember him, yes, but not in a far-off second coming, but on that very day. Before the sun scorching then their tortured bodies set, he would not merely be remembered by him only, but would be the closest companion, Jesus says, with me. You will be with me. Not in a future time, on a day not even known by the Son of God, when all men will be required to give account for their sins in this world. Not on the day of judgment when all worlds and actions of men will be re revealed, but this guilty sinner will be almost directly in the fair garden once known as Eden The quiet home of the blessed, the object of Jewish hope. There he would be remembered, and there in the company with his new found Lord. Interestingly, this is the only instance we have of Jesus using that well-known word, paradise. In the ordinary language used by the Jews of the unseen world, it signified the Garden of Eden, or Abraham's bosom, they called it It is the representative locality where the souls of the righteous would find a home after death where the body is separated from the soul. So let us not be confused. Paradise is not the heaven proper that Jesus promised. Heaven is a place Jesus went to prepare, and a place where we will live in the final resurrection. Until then, the paradise is for all who are in Christ, and they will experience it in peace as Abraham's bosom, closest to the Heavenly Father, a place to be cared for until his second coming. But what truly matters What truly matters in those words is that a sinner was forgiven and given the reality of eternity. It is for that that the angels in heaven rejoice. It is because a sinner at the last moment is saved that you and I have hope Because the angels rejoice, so too can we rejoice. A sinner is saved. Hallelujah. With the next words Jesus spoke, he saw his earthly mother Mary, and then looked to his disciple John and said, Woman, behold thy son. In this address by Jesus, the term woman was not on the lips of Jesus, excuse me, was on the lips of Jesus as an honorific title. rather than an expression of coldness, as a few have read it to be. Mary was indeed the woman whose seed would crush the serpent's head And Jesus hanging on the cross while beneath him was a hill called the skull was at that very moment crushing the serpent's head. So in using woman, in no part was there any disrespect or failure to show affection to his very mother. Jesus said unto his mother, Woman, behold your son. Meaning not himself, but the disciple John, who was now to be her son, not by nature, not by adoption, but he who would show himself a son by his sonship affection for her, a care for Mary, with honor and respect unto her. Again, Christ calls her not woman Out of disrespect, or because he's ashamed of her, but partly that he might not raise or add strength to her passions by a tenderness of speaking. And partly, partly to conceal her from the mob, lest she be exposed to their rude insults, as also to let her know that all natural relations was now ceasing between them. Profoundly Jesus, fully human and fully God, thought of his mother while breathing his last, and thought of her on how she would be cared for, even when he knew that he would rise only two nights later. He secured her basic needs, even when he will walk in her midst again forty days before his ascension. He gave her a son, even when he knows that the Holy Spirit would be her comforter. Simply stated, Jesus cared for his mother. The next statement Jesus makes, he says, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? It is generally understood that our Blessed Lord, continually praying upon the cross and offering himself a sacrifice for the sins of the whole world, was referencing the whole of Psalm 22 with those words. That psalm was to show what would come of the Savior. The purpose of that being so that the Jewish scribes and the people might examine that psalm and see the cause of why he would not come down from the cross. Namely because that very psalm showed that it was appointed that he should suffer these things. Stated more simply, he was witnessing to them the truth of the gospel, so that if they chose, they could know the truth about him. Listen to Psalm 22. But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by men and despised by the people. All who see me mock me, they sneer and shake their heads He trusts in the Lord. Let the Lord deliver him. Let the Lord rescue him. Since he delights in him. Many bulls surround me. Strong bulls of Bashan encircle me. They open their jaws against me like lions that roar and maul. I am poured out like water, and all my bo bones are disjointed. My heart is like wax, it melts away within me My strength is dried up like a pot third, and my tongue is fixed to the roof of my mouth. You lay me in the dust of death For dogs surround me, a band of evil men encircles me. They have pierced my hands and feet. I can count on my bones. They stare and gloat over me. They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing. Psalm 22, written some eight hundred years before the death of Jesus. How could his suffering be more accurately and specifically described? It could not. But their hearts were hardened to the plain truth, the only truth that could save them. The next statement Jesus made on the cross was, I first, I first Could it be that in dying for humanity, Jesus was speaking for humanity? Thus it is humanity, the human condition, that firsts And what is it that we thirst for? We thirst for living water. We thirst for that which can cleanse our palates so that we never thirst again We thirst for Jesus. But many, many people don't drink Jesus. Instead, they settle for a dry and thirsty land. They think they can be satisfied by this world. The statement I thirst also implies that John, who wrote it, purposefully omitted the other statements to allow these two words to suffice as a synopsis. For John wrote in full, he said, after this, Jesus, knowing that all things had been now finished, said, I thirst, in order that the scripture might be fulfilled. Thus John heard in these two words the comprehensive cry which gathered up all the yearnings and agonies of the soul of Jesus, which fulfilled this great tragedy. expressing the awful significance of his suffering, and strangely filled up the prophetic picture. They gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink. His thirst is our thirst. The next statement Jesus made on the cross was, it is finished. The other gospel writers record more words than what John writes here, such as Father, into thy hands. John simply adds the climax. And leaves the divine, unmistakable, and mysterious fact that the suffering is indeed finished in all of its awful grandeur. In summary, the world's debt was paid. The types and symbolisms of the old covenant with all of its ritual requirements and bloodletting had been adequately fulfilled. The mighty work undertaken by him who would realize the expectations of the oldest prophets and the unconscious prophecies of the satanic world, all of it was done Every iota, every tittle of the law had been magnified in what Jesus accomplished on the cross. In Greek, tetalethi. In Latin, consumatum est. It is finished. From the ground of the human nature, from the heart of man in whom all wants, perils, sins, mysteries of the human race were gathered up He endured the wrath of the righteous judgment of God against humanity in his most vulnerable state. But there is a great irony at this finished moment, as death itself does not become the shame of Jesus, but his veritable glory. The sin of humanity is branded with an eternal curse more deep than any previous manifestation of divine justice that it ever could have produced. And yet Death loses its sting on what C. S. Lewis called the deeper magic still. God reconciles the world to himself by the death of his son, by this curse, thus falling upon his only begotten. In the death of an innocent man, the earthly judges are condemned by their victim The great and last enemy is itself wounded unto death, thus death has a death. And the final words of Jesus on the cross were, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit. The description of Jesus crying with a loud voice is the solemn setting of the departure of his spirit when he commended it to his father. The object of the receiving, the refreshment of the vinegar, the sour wine, was that his natural strength weakened by his Long suffering was to be restored sufficiently for him to render audibly the last two sayings, it is finished. That was his farewell to the earth. This commending his spirit to the Father has been accurately termed his entrance greeting into heaven. Doctrinally, to commend his spirit to the Father is a saying of vast importance, for it emphatically asserts that the soul will exist apart from the body in the hands of God the Father. This, at least, is the soul's proper home until the old body is raised and the soul's given a new body to live for eternity. Our passage in Luke goes on, and having said thus, he gave up the ghost. This setting his spirit free was his own voluntary act. He already told his disciples of his own independent power to lay down and to take up his life. It may not be fitting to speculate on the physical cause of our Lord's death, but it is known that the human heart has a sack of water around it to protect it And it has been argued that when the spear went into the side of Jesus, that water and blood flowed out, making the symptoms agree with a rupture of the heart. Such as might be produced by intense mental agony. We call it a broken heart. Such are the last words of Jesus. May we use them to deepen our understanding of his suffering and thus increase our love for what he did for us. But focusing on Good Friday must stay on Good Friday, because Sunday is coming. Good Friday is not good unless we celebrate his resurrection on Sunday. Beloved, Good Friday is here with all of its suffering. A Sunday is coming. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God We thank you for the suffering of your son. We thank you for these words spoken so insightfully to touch on all that he suffered. And yet, Father, as we focus on that suffering, we also look forward to Sunday when we know the promise that suffering will be no more. Let us look forward to that day in Jesus' name. Amen. We continue our worship. After the sermon. The Lord be with you. Let us pray for you.

sermons.title: The Church Confirms
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. You may be seated. Growing up in the Roman Catholic Church. You are allowed to take your first communion at the age of seven because it is said to be the age of reason. But to partake of the bread at Holy Communion, you are required to have been baptized and have said your first confession. Now, confession for Protestants is something only seen in movies. And what is depicted in movies isn't far from what actually happens. You go into a booth, you kneel before a screen window where the priest is on the other side, and you say words to the effect. Forgive me, Father, for I have sinned. It has been however many days since my last confession. For seven-year-olds, however, the priest can dispense with the booth and simply have the child speak directly to him. The challenge of confessing sins when you are seven years old is great, because while it is said to be the age of reason The concept of sin versus righteousness is not altogether clear, and most seven-year-olds do not keep track of their sins. So most seven-year-olds go into this scenario trying to think of sins to confess, and where their reasoning applies is that a seven-year-old thinks of things He might have done or that sound plausible to have done, but not things that sound too bad or evil. So a seven-year-old might confess that he swore, but not the really bad words, just the D-word. Then he might confess that he fought with his brother over a toy while leaving out the cheap shot to the head. Then he might confess that he did not obey his mom when told he must clean his room while leaving out the part of throwing a tantrum and slamming the bedroom door. The priest, having experienced such a confession more times than he can remember, assigns certain prayers to be said as penance and then pronounces absolution by saying the following I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. The basis for the scenario I have described comes from John chapter 20. Our second reading, chapters 9, verse 19 through 23. I'd like you to look through that those verses with me this morning. So John 20, picking up at verse 19. Then the same day, at evening, being the first day of the week, when the doors were shut Where the disciples were assembled for fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the midst and said to them, Peace be with you. This was at the close of the day on which the Lord had risen. It came to be called that day because it was so memorable in the history of the church. After the most astounding and independent revelations had been made to several individuals having seen Jesus personally, now at about 8 p. m. There occurred that which John now describes. The note of the time identifies it with the scene and events of Luke chapter 24. Thus, John had the former account of Luke before him as he reminisces about this moment. To understand the full force of the passage, we must bring to it the statements of Luke, Mark, and Paul The disciples had been prepared by the reports of the women that the grave had been opened and was empty, and that angelic appearances had confirmed the resurrection of Jesus. There was also the impression made on Peter and John when they found it, as Mary and the other women had said, the disappearance of the body of Jesus confirmed by four independent lines of testimony. is strangely difficult to account to account for on any hypothesis except for that there was a resurrection The disciples were evidently confounded by this fact. The Pharisees and Sadducees were quite aware that such an event would be a checkmate of their supposed victory over this scorned and embarrassed rival. The Roman soldiers were pledged in honor and by pride and passion not to allow themselves to be reduced to impotence. Hence, there is no explanation of the body being absent from the tomb except the historical fact of the resurrection. The well-known words of greeting, peace be with you, would come to them at this fearful gathering bringing familiar tones of his voice, falling upon their hungry ears, the assurance of the Master's presence in their midst. But the words would also have a fuller meaning of a message from the spiritual world. It is a voice from the darkness beyond the grave, into which the living have tried in vain to see. And the voice is one of peace. It is the message of the conqueror of death to those who were then conquered by fear. Now declaring that the victory is won. It is the message of atonement, declaring the peace which flows from pardoned sin and reconciliation with God. To the disciples themselves, and through them as the apostles of peace to all mankind. A peace we will come back to. Verse 20 When he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Then the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord. Besides the beautiful tone and meaning of his words, Jesus provides further evidence that it is indeed him who stands before them. His hands and his side show the wounds that verify that the same body that hung upon the cross less than just three days prior was standing before them very much alive. He did indeed die. Thus he did indeed rise from the dead. The word glad can be rejoicing. And the wording of the verse can be, when they saw it was the Lord, no further proof was necessary. Verse 21. So Jesus said to them again, peace to you, as the Father has sent me, I also send you. Then Jesus to them again, the words he said before, peace to you, which he repeated Understanding that they had yet to respond verbally, but only by emotion. The first piece was to bring them back into the fold. Remember, they had abandoned him The second piece is to call them to mission. Jesus then says, as my Father has sent me, I also send you. It must be realized what an honor this sending forth was. The same honor Given to the Son, who was sent by the Heavenly Father, is now given to the apostles. No greater honor could be bestowed in this life. And by the sacrifices made by each of the apostles, they understood the privilege. The similarities of the mission of Jesus And the mission of the apostles lies in these following things. Their authority is both divine. They are both sent into the same place, the world. And in much of the same condition the world was mean, despicable, hated, and persecuted were they? And in part for the same end, to preach the gospel and work miracles for the confirmation of the gospel they preached. But the difference was not to obtain redemption, that being the work done solely by Christ, in which he has no partner, and to whom all the glory must be given. Verse 22. And when he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, Receive the Holy Spirit. Beloved, the very same Greek word here, only in the New Testament here, is used by the Greek Old Testament of God breathing life into Adam. Jesus breathes into his apostles as God breathes into Adam. This gospel of the new creation. of Jesus, look back at the beginning of human life, and then to Jesus symbolically breathing a new life into his people We are probably to regard the breath here not merely as the symbolic of the Holy Spirit, but as the means by which the Spirit was imparted to them. Receive, combined with the action of breathing, implies this. This is all the more clear in the Greek because the word pneuma means both breathe and spirit. A point which cannot be preserved in the English. But at least spirit is better than ghost. We have here, therefore, an anticipation of the day of Pentecost. Just as Christ bodily returned from the grave and his temporary manifestation to them was an anticipation of his spiritual return to heaven and abiding presence with them, the Holy Spirit, which would be even unto the end of the world, is symbolic here. Verse 23. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them. If you retain the sins of any, they are retained. The authority to forgive sin and to withhold forgiveness is directly connected to the apostles and then the church at Pentecost receiving the Holy Spirit. Meaning that the ability and authority to forgive or withhold forgiveness comes from the Holy Spirit. And we differ from our Roman Catholic friends in that we do not interpret this passage to be referring to an individual being given authority to give or withhold forgiveness to or from another individual or another group of people. It is best to understand this passage to be giving authority to the apostles and then to the entire church, authority to preach the gospel of Jesus Christ and declare and declare forgiveness of sins To all who believe, and to withhold forgiveness of sins, to all who reject the message It is similar to when Jesus sent out the 70, you remember that story, telling them to preach the good news. In Luke chapter 10, Jesus said the following: Quote: Whatever city you enter, and they receive you Eat such things as are set before you, and heal the sick there, and say to them, The kingdom of God has come near you. But whatever city you enter, and they do not receive you, go out into its streets and say, The very dust of your city will clean which clings to us, we wipe off against you. Nevertheless, know this, that the kingdom of God has come near you. But I say to you that it will not be tolerable, it will be more tolerable in that day for Sodom than for that city. In the same manner, in John chapter 20, where Jesus is said to breathe on his apostles, Jesus is sending them into the world. And wherever they declare Jesus as the Messiah, they will also declare forgiveness of sins. And wherever Jesus is rejected as the Messiah, the opposite declaration is made By connecting these sections of Scripture, we are seeing a consistency in how Jesus uses the church and what the church is to be doing. There are people, and you know them, who think they can be Christian without being in the church. They think that the church is only political, because sometimes it is. They think that the church is only social, because sometimes it can be. They think that the church is only hypocritical, because sometimes it is. Such people think that they can stand outside the church and therefore judge it And judge themselves as better than the church. But while the church can behave politically, behave socially, behave hypocritically, which is to say, sinfully. It is also the body of Christ, the city on a hill, the family of God, and the bride of Christ. The church is what God has chosen to use to continue the work of Jesus. Again, that is what Jesus was doing by breathing upon them. He was giving them the charge to continue his work. And then providing a precursor to the day of Pentecost when all who call upon Jesus to be saved are baptized into his name and recipients of the Holy Spirit. This interpretation connects well with the promise of the Holy Spirit as recorded by John just four chapters earlier. When Jesus tells his followers that the Holy Spirit will guide them into all truth, Jesus says, the Holy Spirit will guide you. But that word is plural, meaning you all, meaning the church. This is why we put our trust and faith in the doctrines and confessions of the church. For we believe the promise of Jesus was fulfilled and continues to be fulfilled in keeping a remnant, always a remnant, of believers within the truth. The church is fulfilling its role when it is preaching the Word of God while declaring sins to be forgiven when men and women confess their sin and believe on the Lord Jesus Christ. And And declaring condemnation when unbelief is continued. The church is also fulfilling its role when it divides falsehood from truth Which maintains the essential teachings of Jesus and his apostles. And another thing the church does is confirm faith in Jesus. This leads us now to our epistle reading from 1 John chapter 5. In that epistle reading John addresses three primary things. First, what is legitimate testimony regarding Jesus Second, how the testimony is legitimate. And third, how each person can know he or she is saved First, a legitimate testimony is verified by three witnesses, for the law of Moses requires two or more to verify a truth. According to verse 7, the Father is one testimony, the Word who is Jesus is the second testimony, and the Holy Spirit is the third. Second, those three who testify together show their testimony to be legitimate because they appeared together at the baptism of Jesus Where God the Father spoke approval of the Son and the Holy Spirit descended upon him as a dove. This is what is meant when John says that Jesus came by water and blood. Which is by baptism and his death. And the nature of the three witnesses is one. The nature is one, and what they agree upon is one. The third part of a legitimate testimony is how a person can know he or she is saved Which means said person has his or her sins forgiven while being given a promise of eternal life. John says that because the three agree in regards to who Jesus is and what he did for the salvation of mankind to be saved, a person must agree with their witness. If you disagree with their witness, then you are not saved. If you agree with their witness, then you are saved. It is that simple. But each of us knows that sometimes we believe more strongly than other times. Too many times our behavior and our tongues don't match what we say we believe. And so we question, and the devil helps us question, whether we are truly believers. Maybe we are not. Maybe we don't believe Maybe we are playing a game with our psyche. Maybe in the end we will be revealed as phonies. Beloved, this is where the church comes in. This is where the purpose of the church is further revealed. The church exists to provide different means for you to continue in your faith, to renew your faith, to confirm your faith, and to mature your faith. The authority Jesus gave to the church is to proclaim salvation to the unbelieving and the believing world. That is what the early Christians did, and what we continue to do today. I read for morning prayer this week from Acts chapter 20. Where Paul preaches so long that a man falls asleep and then falls out of a window. It's a good thing some of you are not sitting on a windowsill right now But that scenario is the church helping Christians mature in the faith, teaching the Word of God, even though it bored someone almost to death. It is to the church that we are to go to hear God's word taught and preached by those God has ordained to teach and preach it. It is to the church that we are to go to hear proclaimed after we have confessed our sins. God have mercy upon you, pardon and deliver you from all your sins. And from these words, we note the difference between saying, as the priest of Rome says, I Forgive you of your sins. We say, God, have mercy upon you, pardon, and deliver you. It is to the church that we go to sing songs and hear spiritual songs in order to encourage one another. It is to the church that we go to bend the knee and receive from Jesus the bread we are to treat as his body, and the wine we are to treat as his blood. With insight into how he uses such means to communicate his grace to us as we inwardly digest it and say it is good. How can we know we are saved? Because of our commitment to the Bride of Christ. Who is beautified by our presence and engagement with her. While people in the church may spoil her innate beauty, The purpose of the church in this life is to confirm the salvation of its members until Christ returns and makes his bride forever spotless. It is for us to be a part of her until that day. And all of God's people said Amen. As we prepare to receive the body and blood of our Lord, remind him of our offering plate tonight.

sermons.title: Suffering Identity
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. It did not Get reported this morning in terms of announcements, but in case you did not know, our parish has a softball team And they played on Thursday and the slaughter rule was applied for each game, not to our favor. And basically, by the report of my sons, um our junior warden couldn't pitch a strike. So hopefully next week we will improve. Because yours truly will be on the mound. We're looking at both uh first Peter chapter two. From our epistle reading and then from our gospel reading, John chapter 10. The modern obsession with identity. Who am I? What am I about? Is actually not modern at all, for it has its roots in the nineteen sixties. Where the youth culture was telling everyone to do your own thing, or do you In the 1970s, the same spirit told everyone, define yourself or be your true self. The problem was, and is, how does a person know who he or she is in order for you to do you? Such slogans led many to what is called an existential crisis, with people not knowing what they really wanted or what was truly important in life. As you have heard me say from this pulpit these past two years, I agree with Dr. Carl Truman, who argues that we are currently living in a therapeutic age. Which is a time in which human identity is understood through psychological analysis where each and every hang-up Habit or hurt emotion must be therapeutically treated.
