But the therapeutic age is actually no different than doing you or finding your true self I recently read one author who believes such self-obsession goes back to the 4th century BC in the teachings of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. Each in his own way explained the apparent power of each individual to manipulate the contents of his or her own mind. It was no longer the gods' voices that they heard inside their heads, but it was now their own voice. And a similar shift of identity took place when early Christians began to emphasize each person's soul and its private salvation or damnation. A shift took place in no longer focusing on tribal identity, but the identity of the individual. Who made choices to know and follow Jesus Christ or to continue to follow the devil The truth of individual identity before God was then corrupted, as most Christian truths are corrupted. In the Western world, in the era known as the Enlightenment, where men became so enamored by the power of the human mind that thinkers declared themselves independent from the external world. having the power to make their own identity, which took away the power from the church and even God. Although this modern Western self went through its adolescence in Europe, it reached its full maturity in the United States of America. And the fact the first time the word individualism appears in print is in the Alex Destocville's book. Democracy in America, published in 1835. And how much larger does the individual loom today in America? The land of individual license plates, personal podcasts, and personal pages on a website that I will not name in this pulpit. With all this individualism, we still struggle with personal identity. Who am I? In a Gallup poll released this past February, 7. 1% of Americans now identify as non-heterosexual That's a double from a poll in 2012. How does such identifying change so drastically What we have yet to understand and may not be able to understand for some time is the impact of social media that it has on young minds and immature minds. Most of us can still remember our middle school days. And we can remember them because they were so very dramatic to us and traumatic to many. Middle school is when the body changes and resembles something that is not envious. For young men, voices change and sound like nothing they had known before and would know after. For young girls, emotions change and they start to care more about what they cared little about before. How they dress, what people think of them, becomes more important than they could have imagined. For all middle schoolers, interest in the opposite sex, or just sex itself, increases beyond their preparation. Emotions fluctuate, resulting in happy children turning into brooding teenagers. Mind you, I did not have to look up what adolescents go through to come up with these descriptions. The changes are fresh in my mind from my own adolescent days and having raised six children. That there are adults today who want to give adolescents and even children the power to change their sexual identity Allows me to question if I have been locked up in some type of mental health facility that doesn't have walls For anyone who understands what an adolescent, let alone a child, goes through, should understand that without knowing fully what changes they are experiencing in the moment Makes them in no sense capable of deciding what gender they should be for the rest of their life. As if that can actually be changed. But that our culture has arrived at such confusion about sex, gender, and individual identity should not be a surprise to Christians. For the scripture clearly warns that when humans turn away from God, that God may turn them over to their own desire. And the desire today in our culture is to be sexually and morally confused This lengthy introduction on the crisis of identity is to lead us into what St. Peter communicates in our epistle reading. Where he wants Christians to identify with Christ and follow his example, particularly when it comes to enduring suffering. And even more particularly enduring undeserved suffering. Peter wants Christians to be thankful for suffering endured wrongfully. The argument that follows is how obvious it is that all respectable persons should endure suffering patiently when the suffering is deserved. Because of what you have personally done. You get what you deserve. Many examples can be made such as a person driving while intoxicated, and then crashing and totaling his car while being physically injured. Such suffering is a common cause and effect reality. The cause was you, the effect was because of the cause, and you get what you deserve. But to suffer patiently When no personal wrong has been done, is a call above what is commonly expected. St. Peter says that to suffer wrongfully is to follow in the steps of Christ. Peter gives another reason for why Christians should suffer wrongdoing and suffer it patiently. In doing so, it is commendable, he says, before God. What is commendable is the reward promised to all who are faithful to the end. It is the words, Well done, thou good and faithful servant. In summary, Peter teaches us that Jesus is an example for us to follow. In patiently suffering wrong, we are taking on the identity of Christ. Peter finishes his teaching on such patience by showing how Jesus did what he did. For the salvation of others. Thus, our suffering wrong and doing so patiently is to be for the sake of others. But what does that look like practically? It may surprise you that the context of this teaching by Peter is directed at servants. But it is not limited to servants. And ironically, we are actually all servants, servants of God. But I want to show how modern-day suffering can and cannot be for others. Let us imagine a boss at a paper sales company. Who comes up with the idea to entice their clients to buy more paper by challenging them to find a hidden golden ticket? That will give them 50% off their next order. Only the gimmick backfires as one company gets all three tickets offered, getting them almost free paper. When management of the paper company wants to know what has happened, the boss with the idea wants a salesman to take the blame. And then when the idea actually increases sales, the boss wants the credit to be given back to him, but the salesman won't give it back. In such a scenario, no one is suffering patiently, thus no one is showing to have a good character. By the way, I just told you an episode of The Office, in case you didn't know that. But when a person does allow another to get their credit, to get their praise without protest, those who know have such character standard impressed upon them. That's impressive to watch another person die to himself. I realize that such suffering is not the suffering Peter refers to. But we moderns don't know the type of suffering Peter and his first audience knew. So let's talk about the different kinds of suffering that many of us do know. It is the suffering we do for those we love who are either walking foolishly in their life or not living the Christian faith at all. Parents know the suffering I am describing. We don't know exactly how our children have come to make foolish decisions, for we don't know what we have done to contribute to those decisions. Decisions like getting involved in drugs, bad dating choices, premarital sex, eloping. Playing video games for many hours, lacking ambition to achieve anything in life. Watching your children be foolish is a gut punch to the conscience. And a weight truly hangs from the heart as you stoop down to the realities your children are making for themselves. And even greater pain is experienced by parents and other family members when you see someone they love no longer live a life that reflects a Christian faith. Church attendance ends. Personal prayers are no longer offered. Talk of God in any meaningful way is no longer heard. We want to continue to think that our loved one is still a Christian, is still heaven-bound. But their life shows no current proof. Again, the weight of that falls upon us when we face the spiritual life of a loved one. It feels too great to bear. Some people cannot think about it because it brings them so emotionally low, they fear they won't be able to come out of that loneliness. And we are tempted to beat up ourselves, wondering what wrong did I do that my child, my brother, my spouse, my parent no longer believes. With the burden of an unbelieving loved one, we are suffering wrongfully, and yet we are told that we need to do so patiently. Two Wednesdays w Wednesdays ago, during morning prayer, we read from Psalm 119. Where the psalmist says, quote, Before I was afflicted, I went astray, but now I keep your word. And quote, it is good for me that I have been afflicted, that I may learn your statutes. You and I understand those words. The psalmist knows he has done wrong and accepts the discipline he received and sees it as a good thing because it helped him learn God's law in a manner that he did not know it before. Again, we understand his thinking, but suffering when no wrongdoing has taken place is a suffering on a different scale. It is entering into the arena of the man we know of as Job. If you have studied Job, you know it is a repetitive book. At least after Job loses everything that he loves in life, except his faith in God. What Job's friends, if we can call them friends, what they do is insist he must have done some sin that was deserving of his suffering. What Job insists is that he has done nothing wrong. He knew of no sin in his life that deserved his suffering. His friends insist again, and Job insists again, and no one is moved from their arguments. Now, mind you, Job does not insist that he is not a sinner, but only that he has not suffered That his suffering is not equal to what he has done to offend God. In the end, Job is right, and yet he is not right. He is right in that he had not done anything that offended God so that he deserved what he suffered. But to question God's wisdom, While in the midst of his suffering was a wrong done, a serious wrong. What a Christian must do when suffering without wrongdoing is to be patient. In the suffering, which is to trust in God. This is why the reading from Peter is matched up with our gospel lesson from John A Christian must trust in Jesus as the Good Shepherd. In the gospel reading, Jesus is the Good Shepherd. We can suffer wrongdoing patiently because we trust in our good shepherd. Jesus as our good shepherd means that he is fully devoted to his sheep. Shepherds in the ancient Near East led sheep in lands that were desolate and where sheep were exposed to fierce beasts and robbers. Our shepherd is committed to providing for his sheep in desolate lands and to lay down his life for the protection of his sheep. His devotion to his sheep comes from his ownership of his sheep. As he himself points out, he is not a hireling. He will go after the lost until he finds it. And Jesus as our good shepherd means he is intimate with his sheep. Jesus does not simply know of his sheep. But he knows who they are and where they are. He knows their weaknesses and thus how they are in danger. He knows their weariness, their foolishness, and their temptations, which is their aptness to go astray. And with his intimacy with them, the sheep know his voice. The union Jesus develops with his sheep can be compared to a healthy father and son relationship. The sheep are known by Jesus, and Jesus is known by the Father, and thus the Heavenly Father knows the sheep. Jesus as our good shepherd means that as we go through suffering patiently, even when doing no wrong to deserve that same suffering, We go through it having our hands held by our shepherd, who wills we make it through our suffering, and that our suffering would transform us more and more to the image of Christ Himself. The suffering of a Christian, beloved, is never for the sake of suffering itself. Hear that The suffering of a Christian is never for the sake of the suffering itself. Our physical pain is never for the pain only. Our emotional pain is never for the emotion only. God can use our pain to mold us and refine us, melting us as gold. And I say can. Can because we have choices to make when we suffer. We can choose the negative which includes complaining, resisting, and anger, which always turns into bitterness. When we choose the negative from our suffering, our suffering has no eternal value. No glory is revealed, but only more pain and more suffering, because suffering experienced without patience results in continued suffering. Consider suffering like a broken leg. The pain is immediate, the correction increases the pain, but soon the physical pain subsides and the healing process takes place. But also it takes time. If such suffering is endured with complaint, impatience, and frustration, there is no value in the suffering other than continuing the emotions of the devil. When dealing with emotional, relational suffering, where love between family and friends is broken or marred, and we insist that we can't get over the hurt placed upon us. Insisting that no forgiveness or reparations can be made to ease our pain, we also continue the emotions of the devil, and nothing is redeemed. For our suffering to include redemption, we must rebuke impatience Resist anger, accept our situation as God wills, and choose to be like Christ. The great irony of us moderns who struggle to understand our identity is that our first parents Did the same, wanting to be like God. They wanted to know good and evil just as God did, only they didn't care how they would come to know good and evil. And the devil convinced them it is best to know good and evil from the side of evil. Jesus reversed their behavior. Showing that man can be like God and knowing good and evil only from the side of good. Now we are given the ability to have our identity to be in Christ Jesus. While knowing good and evil from the side of good, just as Jesus did. That means that we may suffer with no wrongdoing. But we are to be suffering patiently. There is no identity holier than that. Let us pray. God, we thank you for the example of Jesus. We thank you for the clear identity that you provide every Christian. That we don't have to struggle with what desires we have or or who we are or be ourselves or whatever that may be. But that we see you, and we see that identity, and it is that that we strive for. For those who are going through suffering at this time with no wrongdoing. Give them the patience they need. Give them that identity of Jesus Himself. It is in His name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Heavenly Home
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Before we get to the text, I want to report to you about our softball team. The starting pitcher this week was me. I walked the first three men. The fourth guy hit a triple. And I couldn't pitch a strike after that. So I pulled myself in the first inning. And we lost both games. So we are now You're defeated. You haven't won a game. But we're having a lot of fun. We're looking at 1 Peter chapter 2, primarily verses 11 and 12. So please follow along in your Bibles. 1 Peter chapter 2, looking at 11 and 12. In this Peter's first epistle, his attention at our reading from verse eleven shifts. To the place or position of Christians in the world and among the Gentiles If they are, if Christians are God's chosen people, a holy nation, and a royal priesthood, which he just stated that we were in the previous verses How should Christians relate to the society around them, to the governments of this world, and in particular, how should they respond to the world's animosity And rejection. Christians may be God's chosen people and his servants in the world, but the world hardly believes it or sees it that way. So, how are Christians to relate to the unbelieving and hostile world? All of this is to come in the following paragraph from verse 11 to the end of chapter 2. The word beloved and the phrase I beg you indicates that a new set of exhortations is going to be given. Peter begins by repeating what he said about these Christians in brief in his address at the beginning of the letter. That they are sojourners, that is, resident aliens, people who do not have a permanent place in the world. They are also exiles, foreigners. That is, they don't belong to the world's native population. They are outsiders. They will never fully fit in. Of course, this way of speaking about Christians is not original to Peter. Abraham and Jacob thought of themselves as strangers and pilgrims in this world, that is, as people who had no permanent home in this world but were passing through to somewhere else. That's important. Which is a great irony to me, considering the promised land was to be home to Abraham and his descendants, which we now know that the promised land was a type or shadow of our heavenly home. One example of the fathers seeing themselves as sojourners is when Pharaoh asked Jacob how old he was. Jacob replied, The years of my pilgrimage, pilgrimage, are a hundred and thirty. As the book of Hebrews reminds us, to refer to his life as a pilgrimage was a confession of faith. Jacob was a man looking for a better country, and he knew that it was not to be found in this world. He lived on this earth, but never felt at home. Hence he was but a pilgrim in this world. And not surprisingly, King David. In Psalm 39, verse 12, he used the idea of being a stranger and an alien to describe a spiritual point of view. Hear my prayer, O Lord. Listen to my cry for help. Be not deaf to my weeping, for I dwell with you as an alien. Stranger as all my fathers were. But what we know of David doesn't have him being an alien or stranger physically He owned property. He had a family. He had a position in the world. He was a king, after all. When David's son by Bathsheba died, he said that he could not then go to where his son now was, but there would be a time where he could go. That is faith that there is another home where we can be with those we love who fear God So David was a stranger and an alien as his fathers were, in the sense of having faith in another home. Here in 1 Peter 2, again, verse 11, Peter uses the idea of being alien in a slightly different way. His is an ethical application. Because Christians are sojourners and exiles in this world, and because it cannot be our home, We cannot get our ethics, our way of life, from the world around us, but we are instead to get it from our true home only. Resulting in the Christian life and thus culture being very different than the lives of our neighbors and the culture that they have developed. But let us stay away from going as far as the Amish, who, when they hear these words of Peter, they hear a defense of the lives and culture they have created. I ran across an article by a former Amish man answering why the Amish live the way they do. He said, quote, Well, it's different for everyone. For me, it was a safe, fun, and sheltered childhood But as an adult, it just didn't make much sense anymore. I think to myself that everyone should start out Amish It's a great boot camp to life in general. It makes you decide what is really important instead of going through life blindly, or at least so for me I have to admit he may be on to something there. But Peter is not recommending that our clothes be different and that we should never read books of the world or that we should not be educated about the world. Both Peter and Paul in their sermons and letters reveal an awareness of literature and teachings of their day. They even use such knowledge to address the unbelieving world with the gospel. In fact, verse 12 indicates that Peter fully expected that the Christian sojourners and exiles he was writing to would be living their lives in full view of the unbelieving world. So what is the focus Peter is speaking about in verse 12? It is Christians as sojourners and exiles in the moral and ethical sense. The lives of Christians are to reflect the principles and practices of that place and that world to which they are heading. And because there is such a difference between this world and that world, the heavenly realm, it is inevitable that each world should produce a very different type of life. A difference so stark that unbelievers want to join you or despise you. The subject of abortion is an example. After the Supreme Court leak, the despising of those who have a different ethic on the subject of abortion was ramped up to a fever and still is. Such is to be expected. Consider why. All of the laws and mores that have been overturned, implemented, and accepted in just two decades are focused on sexual expression. which is sexuality without restraint. Saint Paul says this very thing to the Philippians chapter three. He says, Brethren Join in following my example and note those who so walk, that is how they live their life, as you have us for a pattern, you have us for an example. For many walk, live their life, of whom I have told you often, and now tell you even weeping, he's mourning how they walk and how they're affecting the world, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ Remember Jesus said, You're either for me or you're against me. Whose end is destruction, eternal damnation, whose God is their belly. Belly is a euphemism for any desire of the flesh. And whose glory is in their shame. They think they are right, but they will be condemned. Who set their mind on earthly things, what is not eternal. For our citizenship is in heaven, from which also we eagerly wait for the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ. Again, Peter is basing our Christian way of life on the fact that we are sojourners and exiles in this world. In verse 11 and 12, the accent falls on distinguishing our lives from the life of the world around us. Here is another important definition of the Christian life. It is not the life that the world lives. It is not the life this world teaches us, encourages us, and tempts us to live. It is a different life, a distinct life, a life apart. And this is why the Christian life can be so difficult for the young. One of the greatest temptations in the Western world facing young people. is to fit in, to be a part of the crowd, to be considered accepted and liked. Living out the Christian life could actually cause the opposite to occur, because living out the Christian life openly causes unbelievers to notice that you are different. Such is also why youth groups and youth gatherings are so important to some parents who see them as a means for their teenager to fit in. Truth be told, such fitting in begins and ends at home, where children can have their social world fulfilled by being under Christian covenant with parents and siblings who love and stand by them and who also prepare them for a world hostile to their Christian faith. But let's get back to the point. Our lives are to be different, purposefully different. And we can examine ourselves to see if we are living different. To examine ourselves, we must ask the following: In what ways is it obvious that you and I do not live the world's life That we belong to another country, that our speech, our customs, and our habits are quite different from those of this world. It is passages like 1 Peter 2, 11 and 12, that each of us must take inventory of our individual lives. Inventory of our family of our parish. And ask honest questions and accept honest answers So that if confession and repentance are necessary, then we can get to it. The quicker the better. In general, have we gotten our ethics from this world or from heaven? Are our business ethics those of this world or those of heaven? Are our family interactions worldly or heavenly? And one of our thinking about and using about the use of money and time or choice of entertainment How about just how we think about other people? Do we think about people as God's word instructs us, or do we mimic how the people around us think? What would a private investigator say of you after watching you for a week Would there be enough evidence from his notes to convict you if you were to be put on trial being accused of being a Christian? If these questions make you uncomfortable, then good. Do something about it so that you are comfortable the next time you are called to examine yourself. A beautiful part of the Christian faith is that wrong done can be made right in an instant. I can at one time hoard my money. I then can see that I have made money an idol Next, I confess such idolatry, receive God's mercy in Christ Jesus, and be done. I'm a new man. The same can be with relationships. Excuse me, I can say. I didn't have a good conversation with you the last time we spoke. I was offended, and I have been shunning you Please forgive me for my behavior. And you can say, thank you, friend. I forgive you. We shake hands and it is done. We are in right relationship. Christianity encourages quick turnarounds in life, and that is so very, very freeing. What is also helpful about speaking about our Christian life as sojourners, in addition to the fact that our lives are to be obviously unusual, distinct from the unbelievers around us Is that we are to have where we are going in our minds. Where we are going in our minds daily I have preached recently how that phrase, being heavenly-minded does no earthly good, just how ridiculous that is. Jesus told us to store up treasures in heaven. Well, can that be done if I'm not thinking about heaven? St. Paul said to the Colossians, set your affection on things above, not on things on this earth. Well again, how can I set my affection on what is above, which is heaven, and not have heaven at the forefront of my thoughts? Those are my affections for crying out loud. They are what I care about most. But let us be practical and concrete. What about heaven is to be on our minds? Well, let's remember what Jesus promised. He promised eternal life, which is absence of death, which is the absence of sin, because the wages of sin is death. So that is really, really good. No more sin means no more temptation to sin, which is great by itself. And no temptation to sin means no more wrestling with inappropriate thoughts or feelings. No more questioning someone's intentions or promises or motives. There will be no more wondering if you are loved and no obstacles to love others. And the word Jesus uses repeatedly in our gospel reading when describing what the apostles will experience is joy. The feeling of joy is a freed heart, an uplifted heart that feels that everything good can and will happen. It is the feeling that all that is hoped for will be completed. And according to St. Matthew, Jesus said the following about heaven. Truly I say to you, that you who have followed me In the regeneration, when the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or farms for my name's sake will receive many times as much and will inherit eternal life. Thus we are to think about thrones, apostolic authority, and everything human beings need to be healthy and happy. According to the book of Revelation, thinking of heaven is thinking of seas of glass, singing, not being restricted by physics. Rainbows fully formed and connected, streets of gold, and a tree from which we can freely eat that gives life and nothing but life. Beloved, Peter is simply telling Christians to live as strangers and aliens. Each of us must ponder what that means and how best to do that. You must turn your heart and mind heavenward. You must often contemplate your life there and compare it to your life now here. And you must do what the godly have done, always done. Take those steps from time to time to attach yourself to that city and to that world above. Some of you do this already, I know. You go to the cemetery and stand before the graves of loved ones. Who are now in heaven, among the spirits of just men, made perfect. And you stare at that stone until you think you can see your own name written there. It is both sobering and necessary. With my mind on my heavenly home, I want to do what is necessary to conform my life to that home. And that means that my ethics and morality are to match that home, and we are to take a lifetime to match it, however long that life is. A few weeks ago, I was recalling the feeling I would get when in college. And finals week was always a burdensome time. But after I would take my last final before summer break, My car was loaded down, ready to go home, and I would remove the sunroof of my yeah, you did remove the sunroof back in the day. From my 1979 cherry red turbocharged Mustang. I would then roll the windows down, put on some Christian rock in my tape cassette. Crank up the volume and head home, which was 300 miles away. That feeling was like no other. I have not experienced those emotions since the last time I did that. But I want my dying to be like that. I want to feel the burdens lifted. Nothing but freedom ahead and a desire to be home. Amen

sermons.title: Authority of Words
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. Turn with me in your Bibles to James chapter 1. Our epistle reading, James chapter 1, picking up at verse 17. We're going to be walking through each of these verses that was read. So join with me. In doing so, James chapter one, starting at verse seventeen. Verse 17 makes it clear That if there is anything good in your life, if there is anything that brings you joy rather than sorrow, peace rather than despair, comfort rather than pain, It is because of God. The sin of mankind is so very underrated in terms of consequences. That we see humanity repeat sins again and again as if we are suffering from insanity because we expect a different outcome. God warned Adam and Eve that the wages of sin was death. We moderns read such a warning and conclude that God only means physical death. Adam and Eve were going to live forever in paradise, but they chose to sin, and thus they were sentenced to die, which meant only a physical death. But a physical death was only part of their suffering. God cursed the ground, and because of the sin of Adam and Eve, and thus all of the created order, it is in chaos. Yes, the result of the ground being cursed is that Adam had to till the ground and yield any fruit from it, but it also means that the physical world is out of balance. And thus brings forth earthquakes, fires, and floods. It is suffering because of the sin of our parents, and thus our sin. And thus the created ordered also looks to be redeemed. For that is what Jesus said on the day that we call Palm Sunday. That if the people didn't sing his praises, that the rocks would cry out. And it is why Jesus says that God in the end will create a new heaven and a new earth. Because it needs to be redeemed. The earth that God created and said it was good will be recreated. When the dead in Christ will rise at the return of Jesus and all will be made new But for now, because the earth is cursed, we are to recognize that anything that we experience that is good in this life has its origin in God. This is why Christians are to live a life of thanksgiving. It is good to say the general thanksgiving from the Book of Common Prayer, morning and night. For it does well to sum up all that we are to be thankful for. The fact that God can be described as having no variation. Or no shadow of turning emphasizes that the gifts he gives are not arbitrary nor given on a whim. He is consistent on his provision and his love. Verse eighteen confirms that our God is a God of intention. What he has done and is doing and wills to do for us is purposeful. It has an end goal, and that end goal is in his heart. By sending his only son, he sent truth, ultimate truth, which was everything necessary for the salvation of humanity. And because it was done by his will, and not ours, we can be sure that it will be accomplished. I have preached repeatedly that a good understanding of the doctrine of predestination is to know that our salvation is not determined by Our own will, but instead the will of God. We are to be so very, very grateful for this because our wills are fickle We are too inconsistent day to day that we cannot depend on ourselves for our salvation. Going by our own will would surely damn us all. If you are tempted to think differently, please examine yourselves. See how inconsistent you are in your own thinking. You allow certain behaviors in your life today that you didn't allow yesterday. You think certain ways about certain subjects that you dared not think about in prior days Please, please examine closely the COVID-19 restrictions we allowed ourselves to follow with no science behind it. Why was it important that when we entered a restaurant we had to wear a mask, but when seated we could take it off? And why was it acceptable to go to the store, but not to church? Though I remember the reasoning. It was argued that when in the store we are not stationary, but when we are in church, we are stationary. Okay. Well, when you are entering a restaurant, you are not. Stationary and yet you needed to wear a mask, but when you were stationary sitting down, you didn't. Beloved, the lies we tell ourselves, or that we allow ourselves to believe, are remarkable. So let us listen to God, who only speaks truth. Verse 19 begins with, so then Which is to say that because every good gift comes from God and can be trusted, and because all is being done for our salvation according to His will We who call ourselves Christians are to be slow to speak and slow to wrath Such is very practical advice with a great deal of spirituality behind it. The warning to be careful in what we say and the protection that silence gives us goes beyond James and even beyond the Bible. The phrase slow to speak is a common piece of Jewish wisdom, reminding us of statements in the book of Proverbs. For example, compare James to Proverbs 17, 28. Even a fool is thought-wise if he keeps silent. and discerning if he holds his tongue. And there is the verse just before it, Proverbs 1727. It links hasty speech with anger, just as James does here. A man of knowledge uses words with restraint, and a man of understanding is even-tempered. In other words, an angry person rarely controls his speech as he should. We all share in having regrets for words spoken in anger. As I stated, like so much of biblical wisdom, this council is also something you will find in non-biblical sources. In one of the Inter Testament books, part of what is called the Apocrypha, in the book of Ecclesiasticus, we read Be quick to hear and be deliberate in answering. If you have understanding, answer your neighbor. But if not, put your hand over your mouth. Outside of Scripture in the secular world we find Plutarch, a a Greek moralist, telling of us of Simonides who used to say that he had never been sorry for having kept silent. But many times for having spoken words to remember and live by. In the same way, the reference of being slow to anger is also proverbial. And Proverbs 15, 18, a hot-tempered man stirs up strife, but he who is slow to anger quiets contention. And in chapter 16, verse 32, whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city. Hopefully you remember from our preaching series on Proverbs that there are a number of Proverbs devoted to anger in one way or another. Interestingly, we can hear from Seneca, a Roman contemporary of James, first century, a Stoic philosopher and a moralist. He wrote an essay on anger. He said this Anger is the most outrageous, brutal, dangerous, and intractable of all passions. The most loathsome and unmannerly, nay, the most ridiculous also. If I were to describe it I would dress it up as the poets represent the furies with whips, snakes, and flames It should be sour, livid, full of scars, and wallowing in gore, raging up and down, destroying, grinning, bellowing, and pursuing Sick of all other things and most of all itself. The fruit of anger was obviously something he experienced. And finally, on anger in Greek mythology, the anger of Hercules is described as a warning. Hercules, you remember, was a child of Zeus and Alchemenes. Hera, wife of Zeus, detested the unfaithfulness of her husband and tried to punish him by punishing any offspring that resulted from his unfaithfulness. Hercules was an offspring. When Hercules was older, having a wife and children, Hera manipulated him into a time of rage where he ends up killing his entire family. The story is supposed to be a lesson in the dangers of anger and the dangers of allowing influences that anger you. So, the point. The dangers of anger are not new to the Bible But the motivation to not let anger control we Christians is that it does not produce the righteousness of God. Verse 20 assumes that such righteousness matters to us, and thus we would refuse uncontrollable anger. And think about this. Replay times in your life when you were not swift to listen and you were fast to speak. No doubt you said what you should not have said because you allowed anger to rule you. Wrath. Anger Bad speech are most certainly connected, and we all have experienced that in one form or another. But bad speech can be avoided, and that is when we control our anger, which can be done, which takes us to the next verse. Verse 21. Verse 21 gives us the means by which we can be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to wrath. He says we are to lay aside all filthiness and overflow of wickedness. To lay aside is to have nothing to do with it, whatever the subject is. It is necessary to ask how laying aside filthiness and wickedness helps us to be swift to hear. The word filthiness is pollution and defilement. It is what corrupts other things. So that is that is the idea. What other things we might be doing and allowing to influence us is polluting us. So that we are quick to speak and slow to listen, leading again to wrath. And the idea overflows And the idea of overflow, excuse me, is easy enough to understand. It is simply too much, or way too much. Wickedness, however, includes depravity or malignity or trouble or all three. It's bad. There is nothing good in it. It is usually used when describing doing harm to another person. So we are to have nothing to do with evil that looks to harm, whether it be emotionally or physically, because it pollutes all other things we do. And then we are to receive with meekness, he says, the implanted word, which is, of course, the living word, the word of God, spoken through Jesus, and allow that word to grow within us. The Bible loves agricultural metaphors because they are so versatile. They speak to life and healthy life and newness and growth and even judgment. We have here the principle of replacement, which is that if you want to replace something bad, you need to replace it with something better. But where I wish us to go this morning is to examine the power of words. And thus why it is so important that we are to be slow to speak. Because it is more, it has to be more than simply not getting into trouble because of what you say. It is that, but it has to be more than that. Because God created everything we know to exist by means of words. His words spoken, created. And then Jesus takes on the title of being the word, the Logos, the Word for Wisdom. The word logos is used as divine expression. So that it has a definition, but it it is to be taken in an expressive manner. Jesus, by calling himself the Word or Logos, is expressing us an identity And then Jesus has this section in the Sermon on the Mount where he tells his followers that they are to let their yes be yes and their no be no. And it is too simple to hear that instruction and take it only at face value. As if We are to only learn that when we make a promise we are to keep it and that our word is good enough to make a promise, meaning nothing more, meaning we shouldn't swear by anything There is all that, but again, there has to be something more to it. There is a reason why God wants us to keep our word and that our word alone is enough. And I believe the reason is the spiritual authority that is embedded within our words, because we are Christian, which I remind you means little Christ. As image bearers of God and Jesus in miniature, there is spiritual power in the words that we speak. Something happens when we speak that we cannot see, but is real nonetheless, just as real as what we can see. Something is happening that is effectual towards our spiritual health, and we must admit that the effect can be good or bad. Consider the primary means God chose for his gospel to go forth into the world It was and still is by preaching, which is speaking, speaking God's words. And the mysteries, the things we cannot see, is what is going on as those words go forth and are heard by the ear, translated in the mind, and either cut to the soul. And loosen it to believe and have faith and love for God, or it goes forth And clangs off the soul like metal hitting metal, as heart, the heart remains cold and as stone. Even the truths I speak to you today are doing something within you that no one can see. Or not doing something within you because your mind is elsewhere or your eyes are droopy or whatever the case If what I speak is truth and you believe it, and you want it to shape you because the Holy Spirit has convicted you and convinced you. Well, it can change you a great deal, a great deal about your life, because you go from here caring about the words you speak. And as you care about the words you speak, it profoundly affects you speaking differently so that people notice. I have seen this since attending meetings online. I'll be in a meeting and someone asks a question. And someone else is quick to answer. And then someone else responds to that. And then another person responds to those responses, and it can be quite lively. Especially when you are dealing with an important issue that must be solved. Meanwhile, I I haven't said a word. And the host is inevitably going to say something like, Eric, you have been quiet. What are your thoughts? Beloved silence says a lot. It can fool you, as Proverbs says, into thinking that the person being silent is thinking well and thus more rationally. It may not mean that, but if you have any type of positive reputation at all, people are going to want to know what you have to say. And it can be more meaningful, more wanted when you keep silent and listen. And while that is very practical, there's also something very spiritual about it because it provides an extra authority to your words that you would not have had. Had you spoke before you thought. Consider how careful God was when he spoke creation into existence. We know that he simply could have spoken once, and all that we know of matter could have appeared at once, and he could have done that because by definition God means that he could do that But he took time, six days exactly, to create all the matter that we experience. And he did it in such a way so that such matter could interact and then be built upon. After all, you need dry land to have a sea, and you need a sea to have dry land. And consider when God has been silent on Sue, and you also beast need the field and field needs the beast. But consider when God has been silent, and Israel longed to hear from him, and as they were enslaved and in need of deliverance, God then spoke. First he spoke to one man, Moses, and then to all of Israel, giving them what were originally called the ten words. And the next time God was silent, Israel yearned again to be free from another oppressor, Rome. And when God spoke, it was his son. And the timing was perfect. The language of Latin and Greek were what was spoken in the day, languages that allowed Christianity to organize itself and then flourish. The Roman roads were in place to allow men to walk them and spread the good news. The system of capital punishment was in place. So that the means of the Son of God offering himself as a sacrifice for sins was enabled. And all of that brought with it a spiritual authority. That changed the lives of people, that changed the lives of nations, that changed the trajectory of the world. The main lesson, beloved, treat your words carefully. Treat them as having spiritual authority with them. Treat them as having creative power. You will rarely speak the same again. And listen to words carefully. We live in a great time in history for many reasons. But one for me is our access to knowledge. I listen a lot, a lot, to books on tape and lectures on my phone through each day, and I see its effect upon me. Listening to and listening to words read in order to learn is older than private personal reading. But I notice my writing is faster, my thinking is greater, my conversations more interesting, I think. Because of the words I am absorbing, such a gift continues to give. So let us be quick to listen and slow to speak. And when we do speak, may we speak living words. Let us pray The gracious and heavenly Father, we are challenged here to a discipline that does not come natural to our fallen condition. But nonetheless, we have a desire to see how powerful our words can be, and that there is a spirituality, an authority behind it that you grant. And so as we carry the name of Christ everywhere we go, may this discipline increase more and more in us. And may we absorb good words and speak them as well. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: 40 Years
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Forty years is a long time in the life of a human being. The number 40 is used several times in Holy Scripture. In the Hebrew Bible, 40 is often used for time periods. 40 days or 40 years. With the purpose evidently to separate two distinct epics or two time periods Rain fell for 40 days and forty nights. Noah waited forty days after the tops of the mountains were seen, after the flood, before releasing a raven. Spies were sent by Moses to explore the land of Canaan and were gone forty days. According to Stephen from Acts chapter 7, Moses' life was divided into three forty It's three 40-year segments, separated by his growing to adulthood, fleeing from Egypt, and then to lead the people out of Egypt. The Hebrew people lived in the lands outside of the promised land for 40 years. Several early Hebrew leaders and kings are said to have ruled for 40 years, again representing a generation. Examples include Eli, Saul, David, and Solomon. Goliath, if you remember, challenged the Israelites twice a day for 40 days before David defeated him. The prophet Elijah had to walk 40 days and 40 nights before arriving at Mount Porab. The New Testament similarly uses 40 to designate important time periods. We remember that before his temptation, Jesus fasted for 40 days and 40 nights. 40 days was the period from the resurrection of Jesus to the ascension of Jesus, which we will recognize this week. In modern Christian practice, we know that Lent consists of 40 days preceding Easter. Such references may not be connected one to the other, but it is an interesting survey nonetheless. And it is not really certain why the number 40 appears so many times in the Bible, other than mention briefly, in that it separates periods of times or epochs Giving each their own significance. And as far as years go, it refers to a generation passing Today it is accepted that a generation is twenty-five years, counting the average time elapsed when an adult has a child. In different cultures, however, the number could be a bit longer as an older male marries a younger female. That time could be around 40 years. Regardless, the Bible wants us to think of 40 years as representing a generation. And so as we mark 40 years today, we can say that a generation has passed at St. Stephen's and a new one is beginning. That sounds good, positive, and healthy. And we can also use the example of Israel wandering in the desert for forty years, and after forty years, they were able to enter the promised land. And that metaphor sounds good. At least the end part, because it says that we were going wandering the desert for the last forty years. I don't think we've been doing that, have we? No, we haven't. We have and are still having fruitful years. So the metaphor doesn't work all the way. But if we were to take the positive part, the entering into the promised land We could say that after our first forty years, there are even more blessings ahead. And that sounds really, really good. Until you examine the book of Joshua. And realized that entering the Promised Land was not easy, but instead it took great sacrifice, personal and public loss, and a great deal of faith that was not found amongst the previous generation. Remember when the first spies went into the promised land, only two believed that it could be taken Forty years later, Israel didn't have a more organized army than before, and they were facing the same odds. The next generation knew that what they faced would be difficult. But they had a faith that their fathers did not have. And they were not perfect. It was a mustard seed of faith, but it was a faith. And what they faced teaches us a very important lesson. Following God, living the Christian life, doing as God commands, leads to conflict In life, there is inevitable and unavoidable conflict. And the conflict can be both inside and outside the body of believers. Having passed through these many years, I believe we know a conflict outside better than we are aware of it being inside, though I might be wrong about that because too many Christians get hurt from conflicts outside because, well, they're not ready for it. And being ready for conflict gives better odds of survival. And I don't mean being ready physically as having bigger weapons, but being ready by listening to God. Israel first encountered inside the Promised Land, they went against the city of Jericho. And such is a great example on how to be ready to win a battle. Israel had to listen to God and be quiet, silent even before they could shout. And they had to do so orderly as they walked around the city. And we can know why, because although Israel of that epoch were a very different culture than our own, we still know the human condition. And we know them because we know their parents. Their parents couldn't wait for Moses to come down, so they fastened that golden calf and called it Jehovah. Then when God spoke to them audibly, they were so frightened they asked to never hear God's voice again. Talk about an impetuous people. And so we can imagine the next generation being given the game plan to defeat Jericho and what type of murmuring they were tempted to do. I thinly imagine how Joshua would have given that speech. Okay, guys, here is what God said. We are going to march around the entire city one time a day for six days. And then on the seventh day we're going to walk around seven times. And we're going to do it all not saying a word, not making a noise. Then after that last time around which will be our 13th, I will give the signal and you all are to make as much noise as possible. There is no way that speech was going to fly or the plan to work unless there was that crucial component they couldn't say a word. Because we all know how it works. One guy murmurs, another guy mumbles, another guy then whispers, and soon everyone is complaining. That was not going to happen. And with obedience, by doing exactly what God commanded, those walls came down. And there is no question, beloved, that walls are being built right now to keep Christians out. And with that internet fad still going, subtle humor there, such walls are being built faster and faster. The Christian faith being kept out of the public schools. Wall. The Christian faith being kept off certain social media. Wall. Christian values being maligned in the public. Wall. Political parties wanting to reach into Christian offering plates. Wall. Politicians wanting to make certain speech illegal. Wall. All of this means there is still a lot of marching to do. I mean that metaphorically. And faith to be applied in order for us to see those walls come down. And there must be no complaining or arguing, but only obedience. And for the Christians, such obedience is to keep ourselves pure from idols, idols of our day. Just as God arranged his laws to Israel so that they be kept separate from the nations around them regarding their morality. So too are we to be kept pure, which is to be in the world but not of the world, just as we heard from 1 Peter two weeks ago. Strangers to this world we are and will always be And so there are enemies without, and those who live the Christian life will be in conflict with those enemies. And there is a conflict, are conflicts within. And there are two main types of conflicts within. The first type are false teachers, and the New Testament writers had to deal with those types as every generation of Christians has to do. False teachers of today are not much different than they have been in the past. They tempt God's people to doubt the authority of the Bible, to deny the deity of Christ, and to accept the morality of the world. The simple way to combat such is with truth. The truth prevails when Christian laity insists it be heard from the pulpits and clergy do the work of study and proclamation. The other main type of conflict within is seen in the next battle in the book of Joshua, going into that promised land. Even before describing the lost battle to the tribe of I, the author of Joshua tells us that an Israelite named Achan kept some of the spoil or loot from the victory over Jericho for himself. This was a sin. And because there was sin amidst the people of Israel, God did not fight for them. What this teaches us, without the need to kill someone, because Achan needed to die, but what it helps us anticipate is that there will be sin among us. And when we do sin, whether it be sin against God or sin against one another or both, the sin creates conflict. And it's how we deal with the conflict that matters. And by matters, I mean how we get beyond the sin and into better relationships. But you say, I don't want that. I don't like that. It shouldn't be that way. I have heard many, many times Christians say to others, in the church. Well, Christians don't act that way. Well, the person you are referring to is a Christian, and he did act that way. And so yes, Christians do act that way. Such acknowledgement is not accepting the behavior or overlooking the behavior, but is an acknowledgement that the person we are referring to is a Christian. He's been baptized in the triune name of God. He confesses Jesus as his Savior. Because his behavior in a moment does not match up with his Christian profession doesn't exclude him from being a Christian. At the moment it makes him a disobedient Christian that needs to repent. But the point is that sin occurs within the church, and sin causes conflict, whether we want it or not. I have been thinking and contemplating about this a lot these past few months as I have surveyed my time as rector at St. Stephen's And counting the number of people that I have served who moved on from us because of conflict. Not because of unbelief, but that has happened. Not because of life changes such as moving away, which has of course happened. But I was thinking mostly on those who moved on because of conflict, and they saddened me the most. Not that I don't miss any of the others, but they saddened me the most because they avoided conflict rather than engaging in it and wrestling with it until the outcome is good. This got me to think upon Jacob, who wrestled with the angel, who many believed was the pre-incarnate Christ. The incident is referred to as Jacob wrestling God. Which it was. And that was part of the meaning of his name change, Israel or Yitzrael, which means in the Hebrew, wrestling or fighting with God. And Jacob won, you remember, although he didn't because he was given a limp. But he won because the outcome was good. And it was good because Jacob in his wrestling with God got to know God. For coming out of that fight, he no longer referred to Yahweh as the God of his fathers, which is what he called God. He would use language like the God of Abraham and to the God of Jacob, but he would never say my God. It was not until after he wrestled with God that he finally saw Yahweh as his God. And this relates to Christians because we are children of Abraham. For our faith in Jesus is the same faith that Abraham had. Jesus even said, Abraham saw my day and was glad. And as St. Paul notes, the righteousness of Abraham was from the faith he had in God, just as is our righteousness by our faith in Jesus Christ. Remember why we say, glory be to the Father, to the Son, and the Holy Ghost, after we read the Psalter. For the Psalm Book of Israel is our Psalm Book. Only we state it with the revelation of the God, the three and one. But what that also means is that as we identify with Israel, as we are a continuation of Israel, We also identify with wrestling with God. We identify with the struggle we have living the Christian faith to the standards that Jesus sets for us. Because every time we don't Every time we choose sin, every time we suffer and murmur, we are wrestling with God. And every time we struggle to love one another and forgive one another, we are wrestling with God. And it is good to wrestle with God because the outcome is good. And so I lament a little this 40th celebration. over those who didn't want to wrestle, who didn't want to have an outcome that was good. And another detail about Jacob wrestling with God is that it took all night I have never participated in organized wrestling. I am only familiar with wrestling my brother, and as a boy I cheated with kicking and scratching to survive But because I have talked to and watched wrestlers, I am aware of what it takes to be a good wrestler, especially the physical and mental stamina it takes to engage another person's body And try to control their movements while they try to control yours. It's exhausting. So, what does it tell us that Jacob and God wrestled all night? Well, some conflicts are really, really hard to get through. Some take a great deal of stamina mentally and emotionally. There is a lot of pushing and shoving going on without quite knowing who is in the right. Jacob could have quit and no one would have thought less of him. But he wanted the greater blessing. He wanted the good, and so he stayed in the fight. And consider this. Again, the details are important. It was God who tapped out. Tapped out as a phrase in mixed martial arts where let's say a guy's being choked and he can tap the opponent and it's over. But God tapped out for the text says that God said, let me go, for the day breaks, essentially saying, I've had enough. It's over. But Jacob won't let him go. And God loves that. God loves that Jacob won't let him go until there is a greater blessing, a good outcome. Beloved, consider how many great blessings we have missed because we avoided conflicts. And the story of Jacob wrestling is an even greater lesson in working through conflict, because right before Jacob wrestled with God, he was on a collision course to meet his brother Esau, the one he had stolen the birthright. Jacob was certain Esau was coming for revenge, and so he kept sending valuables and servants and even his own family ahead to smooth something over with Esau. And so when Jacob is about to face Esau, again face conflict, he wrestled with God, which was an embracing of conflict, followed by finally meeting Esau, conflict embraced again, and the outcome was one of peace. It must be noted that Jacob doesn't meet up with Esau unless the previous conflict he had with God was faced and won. One conflict faced and a good outcome makes the next conflict faced much easier. Again, without facing conflict, there is no greater blessing, no good outcome and no peace. There is a beautiful section in Genesis chapter 20, or 33, after Jacob meets with Esau. He goes his way to Shechem, which is in the promised land, and just outside the city he builds an altar and he calls it El Elohe Israel, which is translated the God of Israel. The building of the altar is Jacob's celebration that the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, is now the God of Israel, which is the God of the one who wrestles with God. Forty years is a long time for a human being. It is a blip in the history of man. And it is but a nanosecond of time compared to God. But it is a long time for us. Forty years from now, my oldest son will be 73 years old. I will be dead and buried, and remembered only by my family. But from that time until this time There will be many walls to bring down and many conflicts to face. May it be done, all of it, to the glory of God and the salvation of his people until he returns. Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God, we thank you for these standards and these challenges in your word. To press on after 40 years, to press on and bring down walls, and to recognize the enemies without and within, and the conflicts that we have to face and wrestle with Recognizing that we are indeed wrestling with you. And with that confession, may we never give up because we want the good from you. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Fear God
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. From our epistle reading, Saint Peter said The end of all things is at hand. That is quite a phrase, and one that provokes a picture in my mind. Of a man dressed in faded white rags holding a sign that says something similar like, the end is near. I don't know where such men come from or what their logic is. They must expect their message to accomplish something. But the most common response of passers-by is with a shrug of the shoulders. The context in which St. Peter says It is just says the same, is just after he warned against living after our lusts. Living according to what our fleshly desires desires is quite easy to do. We see the piece of chocolate cake. We like the taste of chocolate cake. We like the feeling of a full stomach, and so we eat the piece of chocolate cake. Not too much argument goes on within us. We see, we like, we partake. The flesh wants it, and so we go get it. What is realized later in life is that the more the flesh governs us, the less we listen to the Spirit of God And the result is being less godly until there is no restraint within us, only lust. We eat too much, we drink too much, We allow sexual pleasure to rule us, we allow our emotions to govern us, so much so that our identity is more aligned with the world than it is with the Christian gospel. But by the grace of God, lust will have the victory. And so Peter wants Christians to consider that the end of all things is near. It is to be a motivation for us. When we think upon the end of time, when we will stand before God and give an account of our lives. It is quite daunting and even frightful. Such consideration is to scare us straight. It is to change the course of our lives so that we desire to live godly and righteously as opposed to living according to our lusts. To emphasize his point, Peter tells us to be serious and watchful. Serious, we know, at least we know it when life forces us to be serious But the world only wants us to laugh. And laughing is great when something is actually and naturally funny. But the devil wants us to laugh at the holy. At the sacred, at the profound. The more we laugh at such things, the less holy, the less sacred, the less profound they become. With such topics holy, sacred, and profound, we should always be serious. To be watchful is to be aware of the temptations of the devil and to be prepared for them. Being prepared allows us to fight against such temptations and to be victorious over them. You know where you are weak. You may not be tempted to eat the piece of chocolate cake, but the gossip you have been told may be your tripping wire. You may not be tempted by sexual images, but holding in bitterness, well, that comes natural to you. Whatever your weakness, you are to be watchful against them so that the devil doesn't have the upper hand. And why? Because the end of all things is near. But it isn't. Peter wrote this nearly 2,000 years ago. In St. Peter's second letter, he realizes this conundrum. And so he tells the church, with the Lord, one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. And this teaches the church that Christians are to live in another tension. The tension is that we are to live as if Jesus is going to return and judge the world at any moment. And we are to live as if it may be a while for that any moment to take place. Be ready, be patient. Such attention is to change how we live, because otherwise we might become lazy in our expectation or impatient in our waiting. An impatience that could lead to unbelief. Such tension is similar to what was addressed at our Wednesday Bible study a few weeks ago. If you tune in on Facebook or Zoom or attend in person, you will find our Bible study quite lively when our own Bob Weinright tries to stump the pastor. My mother-in-law joins us online from time to time, and she was curious several months ago to know who this Bob guy is. For example, when praying prayers from the family prayer section in our Book of Common Prayer, we pray these words. Imprint upon our hearts such a dread of thy judgments and such a great sense of thy goodness to us as may make us both afraid and ashamed to offend thee. And above all, keep in our minds a lively remembrance of that great day in which we must give a strict account of our thoughts Words and actions to him whom thou hast appointed the judge of the quick and the dead, thy son Jesus Christ, our Lord. After praying this prayer, Bob asked the pastor something like, You say we are saved by grace through faith. And that such grace covers our sins, and yet we are praying to keep our minds in our minds that we will be judged for what we say and do. So which is it? The pastor's answer is both. We are to live in the tension That we are saved by grace through faith, and that we will have to give an account in the last day for our thoughts, our words, and our actions. The tension of realizing both is absolutely necessary. It is necessary on one hand That we are saved by grace through faith, because our thoughts, words, and actions in our past are enough to condemn us, let alone what we will do in the future. On the other hand, knowing that we will give an account for our thoughts, words, and actions restrains us from the evil we are capable of doing. I have been reading the Gulag Archipelago, which is the testimony of Alexander Solsenitsyn And his first-hand account of the injustices of the Soviet Russia and their communist system What is verified in his account is how evil the human spirit can be. We underestimate ourselves, beloved, on how devilish human beings can be without the restraint of the Holy Spirit And it is remarkable to me, to all of us, I think, that anyone, anyone would consider socialism to be a rational form of government Because wherever it has been instituted, it has resulted in crimes against humanity that are tragic at best, if not originating from the very pit of hell. The following is a description of Sultan Easton's of his polit of the political prisoners who were average Russian citizens. Who were treated how they were treated even before being convicted during the reign of Stalin. This is a long quote, but well worth it. Quote The overcrowding of the cells not only took the place of the tightly confined solitary box, but also assumed the character of a first-class torture in itself. One that was particularly useful because it continued for whole days and weeks with no effort on the part of interrogators. The prisoners tortured the prisoners. The jailers pushed so many prisoners into the cell that not everyone had a piece of floor. Some were sitting on others' feet. And people walked on people and couldn't even move about at all. Thus, in the Kishnav Cells for preliminary detention in 1945, they pushed 18 prisoners into a cell designed for the solitary confinement of one person. In Lub Enst in nineteen thirty-seven it was fifteen, and in nineteen thirty-eight Raz Munich found 140 prisoners in a standard cell built for 25 With toilets so overburdened that prisoners were taken to the toilet only once a day, sometimes at night. And the same thing was true of the outdoor walk as well. It was Razmunik who in the Lubnik Yaka reception kennel calculated that for weeks at a time there were three persons for each square yard of floor space Just as an experiment, tried to fit three people into such a space. But this, too, is no miracle In the Vladimir Internal Prison in 1948, 30 people had to stand in a cell 10 feet by 10 feet in size In this kennel there was neither ventilation nor a window, and the prisoners' body heat and breathing raised the temperature to 104 to 113 Fahrenheit. And everyone sat there in undershorts with their winter clothes piled beneath them. Their naked bodies were pressed against one another, and they got eczema from one another's sweat They sat like that for weeks at a time and were given neither fresh air nor water, except for gruel and tea in the morning. And if at the same time the latrine bucket replaced all other types of toilet, or if on the one hand there was no latrine bucket for use between trips to an outside toilet, As was the case in several Siberian prisons. And if four people ate from one bowl, sitting on each other's knees, And if someone was hauled out for interrogation, and then someone else was pushed in, beaten up, sleepless and broken, and if the appearance of such broken men was more persuasive than any threats on the part of the interrogators, and if by then death and any camp whatever seemed easier to a prisoner who had been left unsummoned for months Than his tormented current situation. Perhaps this really did replace the theoretical ideal of isolation and solitary. He goes on. Abegamov himself could beat in nineteen forty-eight, yes, Minister of State Secretary Abinikov himself did not by any means spurn such menial labor. He was not averse to taking a rubber truncheon in his hands every once in a while, and his deputy Ryuman was even more willing. He did this at Sukhunabka in the General's Interrogation Office. The office had Imitation walnut paneling on the walls, silk portiers at the windows and doors, and a great Persian carpet on the floor In order not to spoil all this beauty, a dirty runner bespattered with blood was rolled out on top of the carpet when a prisoner was being beaten. When Ryuman was doing the beating, he was assisted not by some ordinary guard, but by a colonel. And so, said Rayuman politely, stroking his rubber truncheon, which was four centimeters an inch and a half thick You have survived trial by sleepless with honor, Alexander Dogan had cleverly managed to last month without sleep by sleeping while standing up. So now we will try the club. Prisoners can take more than two or three sessions of this. Let down your trousers and lie down on the runner. The colonel sat down on the prisoner's back. Alexander Golgan was going to count the blows. He didn't yet know how m how about a blow from a rubber truncheon on the sciatic nerve when the buttocks have disappeared as a consequence of prolonged starvation. The effect is not felt in the place where the blow is delivered. It explodes inside the head. After the first blow, the victim was mad with pain and broke his nails on the carpet. Ryumin beat away, trying to hit accurately. The colonel pressed down on Alexander Dolgan's torso. This was just the right sort of work for three big shoulder broad stars. assisting the all-powerful Rayuman. After the beating, the prisoner could not walk and, of course, was not carried. They just drug him out along the floor. What was left of his buttocks was soon so swollen that he could not button his trousers, and yet there were practically no scars. The descriptions in the book of suffering and torture go on and on. It is a difficult book to read because of the evil practice by persons not much different than you and me. The point of me reading this to you is that in order for the consciences of both the leaders of the Communist Party in Russia and those who carried out their orders, To be able to carry out the evil and injustices they practice, it was necessary for them to rid themselves of any consideration that they would ever be held accountable before God. The following is from a Wikipedia page on Communist Russia. Quote, Under the doctrine of state atheism in the Soviet Union, There was a government-sponsored program of conversion to atheism conducted by communists. The communist government targeted religions based on state interests. And while most organized religions were never outlawed, religious property was confiscated, believers were harassed, and religion was ridiculed while atheism was propagated in schools. And we ask why. Why be so concerned about religion in general and especially Christianity, which was at one time the state religion? It was because Christianity provided a fear of God rather than a fear of the state, and such a fear of God would have convicted those who carried out those crimes against humanity. If they were to ever consider that they needed to answer to God for their actions. A lack of fear of God and his judgment is on display in our country. As we see people protest for the right to abort babies even up to the moment of birth. And as a side note, I have to question whether a young man would have done the horrors that he did this last week if he had the fear of God within him. For those who are in favor of abortion to the moment of birth, the logic is evidently and absurdly geographical. As if a child is not a human being at one moment because it's in the womb, and it is a human being at the next moment because it is outside of the womb. But there is more. There are some, not many right now, but some some people who propose that Mothers should be able to kill their children even after birth, even after a few months, because it is still her right to choose And if you wonder how such thinking could be considered or even spoken, it is because people do not understand that the end is near. Which means that they will be held accountable by God for all that they have said and done. We will all be judged by God for what we say and do in this life. That was the point I began with. You may have thought I have gone down some rabbit hole from these examples and forgot what text I was preaching from All that I have spoken was for the point of how evil we human beings can be without the fear of God in us, without understanding that the end is near. I remember being dumbstruck a few years ago while watching a documentary on the experiments that were performed on United States citizens For the study of eugenics in the early 20th century, I was horrified That there were political and social leaders who were abdicating and performing medical experiments on the poor and disabled while also supporting forcible sterilization on the same. I submit that the only possible way a culture can allow such actions and attitudes towards the most vulnerable among us Is by ridding ourselves of any fear of God and any fear of his judgment. Beloved, this is where scientism has gotten us. Scientism not is not science. Scientism upholds all science, moral or immoral, as an idol to be bowed down to And scientism makes no room for any fear of God. But it isn't only scientism or communism that behaves as if the end is not near. It is believism as well. Believism is the distorted practice and teaching of solafide, or faith alone. It is the understanding that a person merely needs to say he or she believes in Jesus, and that that belief is the determining factor for his or her salvation. Believism denies that a person's behavior, his actions, his lifestyle needs to match up with what he says he believes. But we all know that life doesn't play out that way if we are honest with ourselves. I have no argument to convince anyone that I love my wife if I am being unfaithful to her. No one should believe me. Just the same, I cannot say I believe in Jesus while not praying to him, not praising him, not following his life of holiness. And not aligning myself with his teaching, and not adoring his bride, the church, with my presence and support. And I certainly won't align my life with the teachings of Jesus if I don't believe I will have to give a strict account for my thoughts, words, and deeds. In the Book of Ecclesiastes, King Solomon wrote, quote, because the sentence against an evil deed is not executed speedily, The heart of the children of man is fully set to do evil. In other words, I have no understanding of judgment before me. So I am not restricted. I can do what I want. Such a teaching is at the same root of what I have been describing to you this morning. On the last day, all sins will be judged, and the sins of all Christians will be forgiven. All sins will be judged, will be revealed, held accountable for, and all sins of Christians will be forgiven. It's both. And we need it to be both, lest we go on sinning with no fear of judgment, while taking for granted the great mercy God has granted us. Shall we go on sinning that grace may abound? St. Paul asked with the answer: May it never be. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God, we thank you for these words of St. Peter. The end of all things is near. May that be in our consciences as we go through this life, in every moment of our lives, that we truly might have a fear of you that is healthy, that leads to holiness. That leads to your bride, the church, being pure. And Father, as you keep that before us, help us also to keep before us the mercy and the grace you bestow upon us. So richly and so greatly that we have every hope that we will be forgiven in the end. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: You have it good
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We're going to be looking at 1 Corinthians chapter 12. So it would be well for you to turn there, 1 Corinthians chapter 12, our reading, starting at verse 4 Just how bad is it out in the world right now? Terrible, right? I mean the mass shootings one this morning, right up. Look at the headlines, another shooting in Philadelphia. The shootings, the viruses, the unrest, the hate. Wow, it's bad. But is it? We as fallen creatures, we humans, are drawn to hear bad news and to be pessimistic. And bad news sells. And each of us is buying. News organizations would not lead with bad news if bad news didn't sell. And the worse the news is, the better. News organizations have loved COVID-19 pandemic.
