Loved it Initially, you and I wanted to know if we were going to die. And they wanted us to depend on them for that news. Shootings, they love shootings, especially if they are racially motivated. The more they can divide the general public the more they want to tell the story, even if they don't have all the facts. Can you tell how I perceive the news business? But I am trying to make another point. The world right now is not terrible In fact, this may be the best time in the history of the world to live. The best time to live. Consider the data. Battle deaths, people dying from state-to-state conflict has declined significantly since 1946, which as you know was the end of the Second World War. Since 1994, large-scale violence around the world is down significantly. And while human population grows, there are fewer famine deaths in the last decade than any time in recorded history. Extreme poverty is being tracked and said to be declining nearly every day. And what about terrorism? I couldn't believe this when I read it. Terrorism, really bad, right? More people are dying each year by bee stings, you know, business stings. Than they are by terrorism. What about heart disease, the top killer in the West? Actually, the number of people dying from heart disease has been declining in number since 1978. Even chances of dying of cancer are less than ever before in history. Outside of death and overall health, consider how wealthy we are in the West. I eat better than any king before the 20th century. I can order what I want to eat from a variety of different menus and cuisines, more than any sultan prior to the 21st century. And I don't just have one chef, I have multiple chefs at my disposal. And I can have the food delivered, I can pick it up myself, or I can visit my chefs in person. While being served at a table, I do not have to clear or clean. And if my transportation fails, I can pay any number of quality mechanics to help me And considering what the internet provides and what delivery services do, if I want something, almost anything, I can buy it, have it delivered without even standing up. And if you live in Eldersburg, you have access to auto stores and pizza parlors on every corner. And entertainment. You want to watch a Broadway show? Click. You want to watch a popular movie? Click. You want to binge watch a documentary? Click. You want to listen to lectures on World War I? Click. There is no better time to be alive. And can we say the same about being Christian? I say there is no better time in the history of man to be a Christian. You say, but what about the moral corrosion of our culture? What about the public schools that have deserted Christian principles Yeah. Compared to when I went to school, it is certainly more secular and even more so than it was, say, 70 years ago. But there was a lot of problems 70 years ago, hypocrisy amongst Christians being a main problem. And those problems resulted in what we see in our culture today. What is positive about being a Christian, at least in the United States, I I can't say the West because Canada is going off the rails, so we have to disclude them But in the United States, you still have freedoms that are maintained that allow us to meet, to organize, to read, to hear. Teach and learn what the Bible says, and the many, many resources that allow us to know the Bible better than any generation before our own. And because our secular culture is making the battle lines clearer for us, there is no better time to stand up to be a Christian and not lose your life. You have it good. We all do. And that is part of what St. Paul was saying to the Corinthians When he was describing to them the diversity of gifts given to them, given to the church by the Holy Spirit. Our reading picked up at verse four of First Corinthians chapter twelve. In the previous chapter The Apostle Paul addressed some problems that were occurring in the church when the people gathered for worship. This is other evidence that shows there were serious problems in the first century Christian church, and they therefore should not be idolized as if that was the best time for Christians to be alive. The new faith had a lot of growing pains to experience. For the Corinthians, it was getting together and sharing a meal before formal worship. And when doing so, food was not shared equally. As likely the poor and the widows were being neglected as was common in cultures in the ancient Near East. Also, people were coming to the Lord's table, Holy Communion, in an unworthy manner. And God was judging them for it. That is the background of the comments Paul makes about spiritual gifts. He says in verse 1 of chapter 12 that he did not want them to be ignorant about such gifts. For such gifts were to be applied when the people gathered for worship. Because of their past lives of idol worship, Paul first sets them straight. That no one can mix Christianity with the false religions that they left behind. And the Holy Spirit enables each person who confesses Jesus to make such a confession. Which verifies that everyone who does confess Jesus has the Holy Spirit within them But with the Holy Spirit present in a Christian's life, that presence is going to manifest itself differently in each person. So verse 4 begins by stating that although there is a diversity of gifts, it is the same Holy Spirit that empowers each person. Differences in ministry, but the having of the same God is similar to having different gifts, but the same spirit. Verse 5 mentions activities, which are events that occur as a result of the working of gifts, which are a result of the Holy Spirit's presence being manifested. For example, let us imagine a scenario where a married couple is struggling to get along With no counsel, helping, but a minister prays with them and learns from them that the wife is harboring bitterness for the past sins of her husband. The bitterness being revealed, the husband becomes contrite. The husband asks for forgiveness. The wife forgives. The relationship is restored. Such is an activity by the Holy Spirit to move a couple towards reconciliation. But we can be more dramatic. Let us say a couple is in a dire situation financially. They pray for God to bring help. They receive an anonymous donation because the Holy Spirit moved on the heart of a person who could help. The activity is receiving money desperately needed, and the gift was hearing the Holy Spirit speak knowledge previously unknown. Do I believe such activity of the Holy Spirit happens? I do indeed I do because the Lord has allowed me to witness such activity, and I do because of passages such as this. God, Paul says, works all in all. God works all in all. And that is an expression Meaning that when it is good, God is involved, and when God is involved, it is good, and even when it is bad, God is still working to make it good. And therefore it if it is not good, then God is not done. That's a place for an amen. Amen What verse 7 does is remind us what the diversity of gifts is for. It is for the benefit of all. Thus, thus, no gift is for the individual. No gift is for the person who has the gift. And this is a much different teaching than the charismatic world that I dwelt in for a time in my college years. The focus in my circles, as I remember it, was upon the person with the gift, and what that gift can give that person rather than give to those in need or even give to God. Next is the listing of the gifts that are for others. That are for others. The first is a word, is a word of wisdom. The second is a word of knowledge. One commentator I read this week said that no one really knows the difference between the two. I have always thought that a word of wisdom was similar to The scenario I described that had a minister who was able to find bitterness in the heart of the wife not previously found. A word of knowledge might be slightly different, as it could be coming to know something or someone without any investigation, such as A person of financial means who thinks he hears the Holy Spirit tell him that a couple he knows is in financial need without actually knowing their financial records. Whatever the difference, it is insight of a people, of a person, of a situation not previously known, but come to light for the purpose of helping another. Next is the listing of faith as a gift. In general, faith is always a gift For everyone who has faith in Jesus Christ, that faith has been given to said persons. And we know this because the only thing we inherited from Adam and Eve Our souls that are dead to God. We are all born dead in our trespasses And sins, because our first parents broke the first covenant, and that means we inherit the repercussions of that broken covenant, which is having dead souls. For our souls to have life, they must be made alive by God. As St. Paul summed up To the Ephesians, by grace, through faith, each Christian is saved. And that grace, and that faith Not being from ourselves, but they are both instead gifts given to us by God. We think that our salvation is due to us believing in Jesus by our own volition as if we just figured it out while others have not Then we would boast about having faith. And that would be giving glory to self as opposed to where it must go, which is to God and God alone. And unfortunately, there are some Christians who do boast about their faith with testimonies Such as I chose to follow Jesus, or I became a Christian when I understood my sins and the gospel. Beloved, the opposite is true. It is never what I did or what I do, but only what God did, what he does, and what he will do. The point is that the faith I have been describing is a saving faith. And that is not the faith that Paul is describing here in verse 9. We can be assured of this because these gifts are for others and not for ourselves, whereas my saving faith is for myself. This faith, being for others, we all have experienced, even if we have not identified it as such. For example, if you and your spouse are going through a difficult time that may or not be your fault, and you don't see a way out of your pain, You don't see a future. And your wife can. She can see a way out. She can see a future. She can encourage you that there is a way out, that there is a future that God wants for you. That is practicing the gift of faith. It is a faith that is present within a person or persons when most people don't see any hope. It is a faith that overcomes odds. It slays giants with one rock. It calms lions in a den. It walks amidst a fiery furnace. It walks on water. The next two gifts may seem like they overlap, like wisdom and knowledge. The gift of healing is a gift of miracles, and yet the gift of miracles does not have to be a gift of healing. And St. Paul participated in the miracle of healing, such as healing the crippled man and Lystra. And he had experienced miracles such as casting out evil spirits. Having the gift of healing does not need to be a miracle for today. There are many Christian doctors who have the gift of diagnosing health and prescribing for the sake of better health. Along with having a thorough education about healing, the miracle aspect of healing does not occur today as it did during the ministry of Jesus and the apostles, and that includes Paul. I say that only because the evidence is clear. And I am not a cessationist, which is someone who believes that miracles have completely stopped when the gospel was established. It is clear again by the way of biblical accounts and church history that there was a change in the manner the Holy Spirit worked in the church after the apostles. And I have been a part of churches that claimed the opposite, that claimed there had been no change, while insisting on miracles still occurring, and yet they did not. What I have witnessed, of course, is limited. So I make no claim of what the Holy Spirit will or will not do. And I still pray for miracles Because I trust the Holy Spirit will always do what is right. And if He wants to do a miracle, by all means let us witness a miracle. Next is the gift of prophecy, which most make the mistake of interpreting as speaking forth what is to come, speaking about the future. But the prophets of Scripture primarily, primarily spoke forth the word of God to the people of their day, showing how God's word is to be applied to their lives. Such as Nathan rebuking King David about his murder and adultery. So any man who has been called to speak God's word to his contemporaries is a man gifted With prophecy. Next is the gift of discerning spirits, which is someone who can see through another person's words and hear the truth. And it is more than a feeling, although it can be that way sometimes. But it has to be more than a feeling because feelings are subjective. It is noticing gestures, reading into lines spoken, sizing up posture or handshake. It is seeing a false teacher for what he is, false, even though he is cunning in his words. Next is speaking in tongues and the interpretation of tongues, and I am not going to get into that topic and end up in the weeds. I wrestled with the topic throughout the 1980s and I am done wrestling. Today, tongues and interpreting tongues is being able to speak and interpret different languages. in order to communicate the gospel to different cultures. It is for others. Remember, the gifts are for others rather than being for a person who wants to speak the language of angels. The variety of gifts listed here by Paul does not exhaust the list of gifts that people can receive from the Holy Spirit. What it does is promote these two things. The gift of the Holy Spirit are for others as established. And are sufficient for overcoming sin and remaining faithful until our days are ended. You, Christian, live in great days. But here is my beginning point. You and I are prone, pre-programmed Inheritors of Adam, to focus on the bad, to play the Eeyore, to think the worst. Remember these words from St. Paul to the Ephesians. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Who has blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ. All spiritual blessings. Whatever your past sins Whatever past sins have been done to you, whatever the devil has told you that you have to pay for, the gifts of God via the Holy Spirit are sufficient for you to overcome. And know this final point. The gifts to overcome are scattered throughout the church, so you must stay in the church. Such gifts are for others. So whatever you have to offer, give it. And what others have to offer, receive it. For that is how God has ordained it. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God, how grateful we are for the coming of the Holy Spirit. How it empowers us, not only as individuals, but in the church, that all things are before us, that all things can be overcome. May we practice these gifts, and may we receive the benefit of others and their gifts, that all in all the church might function as your bride. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Created to Worship
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. May be seated. Amen. The prayer book epistle reading for Trinity Sunday is from Revelation chapter four. Verses 1 through 11, and I invite you to turn in your Bibles. You will be well served to follow along with me this morning. While studying the passage this week, I was tempted to teach about all of the symbolisms that are within, as I love the book of Revelation, because of the symbolism But to do so in depth, that I prefer will cause us to miss the primary point of the passage, a point That is good for us to hear and emphasize on a day we confess the doctrine and fundamental doctrine of Christianity, which is that we worship a God that is three in one. But let us dip our toes a little bit into the symbolisms presented here in order to get to the truth of Trinitarian worship. First, there is a door. Just as there was in chapter 3 a door, only Jesus is not knocking at this door in chapter 4 because this door is open. It is a contrast in that the door in chapter 3 is on earth and it is closed. And the door in heaven is open, reflecting the welcoming God is giving John and all who would read his vision. Next, there is a voice as a trumpet. Trumpets herald good news, as our own Dan Nevius displays. The voice tells John to come up, just as the Garden of Eden was elevated Just as God called Moses to come up to receive his commandments, just as Jerusalem was a city set on a hill, so God wants to communicate that when we meet with him, we are to come up. And this is why in our tradition we come up to receive Holy Communion. To come up is to go where God is. Next, the stones mentioned are the first and last, respectively, on the breastplate of the high priest. A rainbow is next, and it is complete, symbolizing that What was meant as a promise of God's mercy after the flood is now fully completed, showing that God has kept his covenant promises. The rainbow surrounds the throne just as the 24 elders do, and the number 24 brings together the 12 tribes of Israel and the 12 apostles chosen by Jesus. So that the number represents all of God's people, old and new. Next, the elders are clothed in white robes. Not in ties or suits or casual wear because Jesus wants to hang out with his people White robes represent formality and purity. These men are around the highest of thrones, and they have been made pure by the blood of the one they worship. Which is why they wear white. Next are the flashes of lightning, identical to the flashes of light when God was on Mount Sinai. The seven spirits of God represent the ministry of the Holy Spirit, which is the fullness of God's activity. Next is the sea of glass, which is calm and smooth, looking like crystal. Because the nations are described as raging waters elsewhere in Scripture, we are to understand that Jesus has brought calm to the nations. He has brought peace. What is described next is similar to stories in mythology or characters out of a Tolkien novel There is a circle within the circle of the rainbow and the elders that is made of four living creatures. The eyes of these creatures are noted first. A creature covered with eyes obviously is responsible to see. Each of these creatures is responsible to see or to watch over all of God's creation. That there are four living creatures causes us to connect their duties with the entire world. The Bible in various places describes the earth as being four-cornered. It does not do so because the writer believes that the earth is flat. It is because the earth is to be understood as an altar for God. Just as the altar on which sacrificial worship was offered in the temple, that that table had four corners, so is the earth described. The earth is the Lord's. It is a place upon which God is to be offered praise and sacrifice. When there are mentioned four corners of the earth, or four winds, or four directions, or four rivers in Eden. Which are we are to understand each to be a reference to an altar on which God is to be honored Also, the four creatures are living, living as opposed to being creatures of stone or carvings of stone. The four living creatures also correspond to the points on a compass, and the earth as an altar upon which God is worshipped Their numberless eyes represent their watchfulness over every part of creation. And here is where we will take our time to examine the appearance of each creature. The first has an appearance like a lion, the second like an ox, the third like a man, and the fourth like a flying eagle. These distinguishing characteristics represent the four animate powers of creation. Animate powers of creation. The lion represents the beast of the field The ox represents the cattle or domesticated animals. Man represents himself as an intelligent creature. And the eagle represents birds of the air. Together they represent the powers of creation in their physical strength, daring courage, keen intellect, intuition, and freedom of movement with majestic flight. In summary, they represent creation in all of its fullness of its power and talents The number six, and then six wings, also ties into creation, for it was in six days that God created the heavens and the earth. The six wings thus indicate the fullness of creation in its development. Well, once we understand What each creature represents, we must then notice what they are doing. They are worshiping God. In fact, they never stop worshiping God. The words are repeated over and over again. Holy, holy, holy is the Lord, God Almighty, who was and is and is to come. Verse 9 tells us that there is an antiphonal to this saying, which is a song sung in response. As the 24 elders fall down in response to this cry of holy, holy, holy, falling down before the one on the throne. Worshiping him forever and ever by laying down their crowns before him. Crowns, crowns that were given to them by the one who is on the throne. They lay those before him and respond, You are worthy, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things. By your will they were created and have their being. As we imagine this scene in our minds, it's quite common To be in awe, while at the same time wondering how these beasts and these elders could worship day and night in the same way, in repetition. Verse 8 describes the worship as being done day and night and never ceasing. They say these words over and over again, and the elders respond to the words over and over again. Before we focus on the worship emphasis, I know it is necessary to address what many of you are thinking To worship in this manner described would be monotonous, and monotonous is boring. My first official ministry in a church was towards college students, and I remember a college girl with whom I was trying to share the Christian faith with. And she asked me, why would you want to go to heaven? And I'd never been asked that question directly, and it took me a moment to collect my thoughts. And I answered in two ways, and neither of the answers helped her at all. First, I said that it was better than going to hell. I certainly believe that is true, but the statement doesn't say a whole lot about heaven. Living in a sewer is better than living in hell, but I would not compare a sewer to heaven. I then said that in heaven we will worship God for eternity. This, as I said, did not strike her as a selling point, and we all can understand why. She did not know of God's mercy at that time and therefore was not moved by any conviction to worship God. Also, like most of us, she found that worship services in churches were not all that exciting. In my younger Christian days, I thought worship in church should be exciting, so I was involved with churches that clapped and danced and played loud music and shouted every now and then. What I came to experience from those worship scenes was pumped up excitement generated out of a modern spirit. That did not sustain my faith. And if I was not emotionally excited in worship, I thought something was wrong with me A problem with such worship is the point where you come down off of your self-generated emotional high and you lose the motivation to stay in a mindset of worship. I had to learn that by experience and more in-depth Bible study, that life is not a constant high, and our flesh reminds us of that continually. Liturgical worship like our own and happy clappy worship like I described are both limited by our flesh. As Paul said, the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak. We have a hard time imagining ourselves worshiping God day and night because we get bored. And our flesh cries out for something different, even if our worship only lasts an hour and a half every Sunday. A desire for something different is caused by a misunderstanding about heaven compared to our present earthly state. But the elders and beasts around the throne are able to worship continually because they are not bound or restricted by flesh that is weak and susceptible. That's our flesh Our flesh, having been born of Adam's race, is dying. That is part of the curse. Our time here is short. Resurrected flesh does not have the same concerns, and in fact, such flesh is able to fulfill what it was created to do when it worships continually. That may be a hard concept to grasp considering the dominance of our flesh in this life. But it can be proven when you consider what you are. But each person is created to be the purpose of each human life. And this is where we agree with the Presbyterians. The purpose is to glorify God and enjoy Him forever. We are created for worship. In fact, I accept that we worship all of the time without either realizing it, realizing we are worshiping, or willing to admit that we are worshiping. When we put our desires before the law of God, we are worshiping our desires. When we put our personal will before the will of God, we worship our personal will. When our dreams are future, when it does not glorify God, we worship our dreams. Consider please that whatever we are choosing to prioritize in our lives has an essence of worship. You're worshiping with that choice, choice of our priority, and in our actions And it can be said that unregenerated people, people who are not Christians, worship their priorities also, only theirs is false worship. Christians, on the other hand, are to do all things in their individual lives as acts of worship. The infamous atheist Christian Hitch Christopher Hitchens tried to argue that there was nothing good a religious person could do. that an atheist also could do. The answer to his challenge is to find something that contradicted his claim, saying that, yes indeed, there is something that we Christians can do that that they cannot. And that answer is that we can do good for the glory of God. Or to put it in our context this morning, we can do good as an act of worship. Everything we do can give glory to God. And we are built, we are engineered for worship And those who remain faithful to the end of their days will be rewarded with eternity in a state of worship of the one true God. Not only are we created to worship God, but we are created to worship in a certain way. And here is where much of modern Christendom has failed. For the vision that John has of the exalted Savior being worshipped is a model for us. What John describes is a worship service of the risen and glorified Savior, Savior of mankind, a worship service in heaven. It is for us who are below heaven, beneath the sun, to duplicate such reverence by our actions and by our words while being on this side of the sun. I began by referring to the call for us to come up. And how we follow that call is when we receive Holy Communion. We also duplicate the white robes for clergy, symbolizing the clergy's duty before God. Today we make note of the words spoken around the throne as the elders and beasts Speak their roles responding. The beasts cry out, holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty. The cry is Trinitarian. No cry is more appropriate on Trinity Sunday as to recognize the holiness of the Father, the holiness of the Son, the holiness of the Holy Ghost. The cry is heavenly as it contains words inspired by the presence of Almighty God. Because the words are heavenly, And thus inspired, the same words should be words spoken by us as we abide on earth. We should use the words of heavenly worship. As we do, we should humbly acknowledge that we are not starting the song, holy, holy, holy, and we are not alone when singing it. And that each time we sing such words, we are joining in the chorus that has already begun and continues forever and ever. I am concerned that it can be an arrogant act to ignore heavenly words of worship Found in the prophets, found in the Psalms, found in Revelation and other places, and to replace those words with contemporary expressions. Now that is not to say that contemporary or extemporaneous expressions are bad or inappropriate. I'm not saying that at all They can be helpful as long as they do not replace the heavenly words provided for us in Scripture. For example, I remain completely confused as to why modern churches Today, who claim Jesus as their Savior do not pray the Lord's Prayer. They do not pray the very words that Jesus told us to pray. The apostles coming to him, how shall we pray? Jesus answered, Pray this way, our Father who art in heaven. If Jesus said, Pray this way, that is the way we should pray. To acquiesce our preferences and personal expressions for the words of the heavenly creatures and elders around the throne is one way, just one way. We can lay our crowns down before the throne. After all, part of worship is surrender. We surrender ourselves unto God and say, Not my will, but thine be done. We surrender by asking the Lord what he would prefer rather than what we would prefer in our worship. The words of the beasts and elders speak of God's righteousness. He is holy, as each person of the Godhead is holy. The words speak of God's power. He is almighty. The words speak of his work of salvation. He is worthy. The words speak of his ultimate victory. He is to receive glory, honor, and power. The words speak of his creative and sustaining power. He created all things and by his will and in him each has their being. Such words should be the exact words, and such themes should be the same themes in our worship For they are inspired words and inspired themes, and thus our worship is to be inspired. But St. John's description, with that description, we are able to peek in on a heavenly service. What we see is the answer to why we exist. We exist to worship God, which is the one appropriate response his creation should have when in his presence. Worship, true worship, is wholehearted, awe-inspiring, and loving. This scene in the throne room of God establishes a foundation from which the rest of the visions of John flow. Every vision in Revelation from here to chapter 22 is related back to this scene here in heaven. And one final thought. I have been asked by several persons through the years: why does God insist on our worship Is it as if he has an ego to be stroked? Do such questions reveal how we tend to see God? We see him in terms of how we view mankind. This is how mankind would do it. It's to be stroked. God, by definition, needs no validation. As St. Anselm defined him, God is that by which nothing greater can be conceived. Being greater means you have no equal. No one can compare to him We worship God not because he needs it, but we need it. Because again, if we don't worship God who is true, We will worship anything else, and anything else is false. So join the chorus, brothers and sisters in Christ. Join the chorus. The service has already begun. We are a bit late, but still privileged to be a part of it. Sing the words, inspired by heaven, and fulfill your proper use. Amen. Let us pray. For this challenge, our Heavenly Father, we are grateful Humbled by it, really, understanding that our words should be heavenly, and that we have not started this, nor will we finish it, but we are simply a part of it. And may we all feel privileged to be so. Pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Father's Day 22
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. For those of you near my age You will remember the sitcom from the 1970s, All in the Family. Every now and again I will run across clips of that show, and I still find it very funny, especially the character of Archie Bunker. Who is the center of the show? And who displays a great deal of wisdom and insight from modern fathers on this Father's Day. It did not take me long to find quotes from the show about some very pertinent topics regarding marriage. Archie said The only thing that holds a marriage together is the husband being big enough to step back and see where the wife is wrong. And this a woman should cleave into her husband. Right here in this house is where Edith cleavage belongs. On parenting, Edith, Archie's wife, says, Maybe we should take the stroller back and exchange it for a bassinet. Archie responds Don't be ridiculous, Edith. The kid can't learn to play one of them until he's 13 On religion and his grandson's faith, he says, raise him a Lutheran if you want, raise him a Norman with seven wives, a holy roller, or a seventh-day adventurer. On creation, he says, the Bible, if you read it, you'd know. It's right there in the beginning, there in the book of Genesis. And on God's providence he says, God don't make no mistakes. That's how he got to be God. And finally, on the unity of faith, he says, God made us all one true religion, Edit, which he named after his son Christian, or Christ for short. It is characters like Archie Bunker that make us feel better about ourselves as we realize that we may not know what we are doing as husbands. And or fathers, but there are a few people who are worse than we. Celebrating fatherhood as we do on this day is a bit complicated Because of the undeniable reality that earthly fathers can leave scars on the psyche of their children. If a father is neglectful, immoral, abusive, or simply absent, the negative psychological effect upon children can be immeasurable. I have heard many times, as no doubt many of you have, just how hard it is for people who had a bad father to overcome those negative emotions when trying to relate to God as father. The negativity they have about the role of father is automatically transferred to God as Father, and that is a relationship they think they cannot have. The work we must do for such people is to reverse the roles. We are to define the image of Father in general By our Heavenly Father instead of our Earthly Father, and thus how we relate to the Heavenly Father goes back to how we again deal with our earthly father and overcome the negative experiences we have with our earthly father. It was surprising to me that God is referred to as Father in the Old Testament only ten times. He is described first as Father in relation to him being the creator of heaven and earth, and thus he is the father of all that exists. He is also described as father in that he provided for his people as he helped, fed, and aided Israel, and called Israel his son. And then there is the fascinating passage that is often overlooked in terms of God being father. Isaiah 9, verse 6 contains a prophetic description of the coming Messiah, who is a child born to us. A son given to us who will have the government on his shoulders and who will be called wonderful counselor, almighty God, everlasting Father, the Prince of Peace. How often do preachers and teachers of the Bible expand on Jesus being known as the everlasting Father? Of course, we are not to confuse the person of the Heavenly Father with the person of Jesus the Son, as the Athanasian Creed reminds us. But we should always think of the son in relation to the father, and the father in relation to the son. After all, there is no father without the son, and no son without the father. The unity of the Father and the Son is described in the words of Jesus regarding his own actions. He said that he did nothing but what he saw the Father having him do. And we remember St. Paul's words, that the Father was in Jesus, reconciling the world to himself. And may I add, although this is not our focus, that within these verses and others like them, there is a clear revelation of the Trinity without using the word Trinity. As we come to the New Testament, the relational title Father takes on an exalted and primary title. It is evident that we who are God's people are to think of God Almighty as our Father. Jesus teaches this to us by describing first how we pray. We are to pray in secret, he says, to our Father. We are to recite a script that begins with our Father who art in heaven. And when we seek forgiveness, we are to seek it from the Father through the Son. When we think of our daily needs, Such as food and clothing, we are to know God as Father, a Father who will provide When we are motivated to serve in God's kingdom, we are to be motivated by the love of God as our Father. And going back to the Lord's Prayer, we should be struck by the privilege we have to call God our Father. After all, we are a race that was afar off. Under the covenant of Adam, we abandoned God as our father and placed man as the author of life, as the Lord of the future. Consider, every time a man tries to clone himself, he is trying to be his own father. Every time a child is ripped from the womb, man is trying to be his own father Every time public prayer is squelched, or a manger scene is removed, or a display of the Ten Commandments is taken down, Or a law is passed to mainstream sexual immorality, man is trying to be his own father And such behaviors would be our own if God had not revealed Himself to be our Father I remind you of St. Paul's words to the Ephesians as he describes our relationship to God. He said In love, he, God, predestined us to be adopted as sons, his sons, through Jesus Christ. in accordance with his pleasure and will, to the praise of his glorious grace, which he has freely given us in the one he loves. The emphasis on the role of God's love in our adoption communicates that God is not a reluctant stepfather. Who only adopted us because he thought our mom was pretty? No. God's love came first, and then came the act of his adoption. He desires to call us his sons and daughters, and he desires us to call him Father, our Father, to be precise. I pause on that phrase once more for us to notice that it is a word that begins with a plural possessive. God is our Father. And as we say that together, we acknowledge that each of us is a child of God. That makes us siblings. It makes us family. Which is one of the more prominent metaphors used in the Bible to describe the church. And as St. John's first letter explains, because we are God's family, we must love one another. As an older preacher, friend of mine used to say, you have to love me if you want to get to heaven. We will have to unwrap that point on another day. Although we are adopted, we have full privileges just as we would if we were blood. And we are blood, actually. Jesus made it so. Because of the blood of Jesus covering us, we are called children of God. And not just children, but heirs. We are all of us, male and female alike, all of us like the firstborn Son, because of the Heavenly Father Because of the Heavenly Father's only Son, Jesus, we are heirs of his eternal kingdom, and we say, thanks be to God. Having accepted our adoption and being made heirs, we need to be challenged to better relate to God as Father. I remember lamenting with my brother-in-law several years ago when our children, of course, were younger. How frustrated we both were with our children, especially our sons, he had four, I have five, who would not come to us before or while they were having trouble. Instead of afterward, when nothing could be done but pick up the pieces. His style and gifts of parenting were different than mine But between us, you would think that one of us would be fathering well enough so that our children would confide in us more readily. But alas. And I bring this up not to lament, but to confess that what I wanted of my children, what I wanted them to do freely, come to us when they were in need. I myself have a difficult time doing with our Heavenly Father. I do not go to Him easily and readily when I am struggling. I can live in denial with the best of them. I can convince myself that I am holding, that I'm not holding a grudge. I have forgiven them. When I really have, I can convince myself that I'm winning the fight over my flesh when I'm actually losing it I can convince myself that I have the situation under control when I do not. And I can see the Heavenly Father shaking his head as I lament about the apprehensions and blindness of my own children, when in fact they are my own apprehensions and my own blindness. Beloved the Heavenly Father wants us to come to Him The context of our gospel reading is a focus on prayer, which is us coming to God. The primary lesson is that we should be repeatedly seeking God for our needs and without hesitation. The second lesson is the reason why we can seek God for our needs. It is because God is a loving Father. And for us to know how much God loves, Jesus compares him to earthly fathers. Earthly fathers are who are of a right mind Would never refuse a child of their own who asks for bread and instead be so unkind as to offer a stone or a serpent. To be sure, there are earthly fathers who are addicts or mentally ill and failed to provide for their children. But Jesus is describing an average earthly father who sees it as his duty to provide for his children. Such men, Jesus says, are evil. That seems strange to us initially, for Jesus to call men who provide for their children evil. But Jesus isn't referring to their actions of providing as evil. He is instead describing the nature of men. He is reminding his disciples that mankind is evil by fallen nature and by practice. Preachers like myself have been accused of being too negative because while I mention man's favor with God, I also remind us of man's sinfulness. Some like to hear good only without a caveat that refers to the bad. I respond by noting that in the case, in this case, these are the words of Jesus. He is giving the caveat and doing so using harsher words than I have ever used. And let us be honest, when examining the words of Jesus, he is no wimp. When he calls Peter Satan, and a begging woman a dog, and men in general evil. He is being brutally honest, and he expects us to take it because it's the truth And the harsh truth makes the grace and love he bestows upon us who are evil all the more amazing. By referring to men as evil, Jesus is contrasting that truth with the amazing love of God as Father. He wants to be our father, not just in title, but in true relationship He wants us to ask of him. He wants us to trust him. He wants to be our guide, our protector, our caretaker. He wants us to say Abba. The title Abba is an intimate reference to God as Father. We know that Jesus and his disciples read And wrote in Hebrew, especially in the synagogue, but in everyday speech and in their preaching, they spoke Aramaic. In Biblical Hebrew, Ab A B means father, but in Aramaic, Abba is father, and it was derived from baby talk. As the rabbis said, a small child learns to say Abba, which we can translate daddy, and ima for mommy. In the pre-Christian era, the usage of the word Abba was broadened so that the use of the word was no longer restricted to just children. The idea of it only meaning daddy actually receded. And the word acquired a warm and familiar ring, which would more align with saying My dear Father. And we are to know that nowhere in the entire devotional literature of ancient Jerusalem Is Abba a way of addressing God? And yet the teaching of Jesus and the practice of Jesus made saying Abba for Christians the norm. We can call God my dear father because Jesus has enabled us to have such a relationship. Finally, as God is our Father, and we are His children, we are to be imitators of Him. This seems to come naturally to children to follow the example of their fathers, and it's expressed in a little poem titled Little Eyes Upon You. It goes, it begins as follows. There are little eyes upon you, and they're watching day and night. There are little ears that quickly take in every word you say. There are little hands all eager to do anything you do, and a little boy who's dreaming of the day, he will be like you. It goes on to remind fathers just how important they are in the molding of the lives of their children by imitation. It is, of course, a good thing for us to be imitators of the Heavenly Father, but as we get older, we appear less inclined to do so. Because of our perceived personal maturity and our awareness of our own autonomy, we are easily tempted to do as we please. Even mature Christians find it easier to choose their own way. But imitating God the Father is the best for us. And a manner of imitation that is lacking today, especially on the heels of COVID-19, is presence. Our God is a God of presence. It is His attribute. It is His will. Regarding his attribute, we know him to be omnipresent. He is everywhere to the point that we can go to the depths of Hades and to the highest of the heavens, and God is there. And then there is his presence by his will. He chooses to dwell with men. He chooses to be uniquely present when his people gather. His unique presence when we gather makes our time of worship more sacred. It makes the breaking of bread and the drinking of wine all the more intimate and effectual towards our salvation. His unique presence means the devil has no place to sit among us because when we invoke the name of Jesus, he must flee. I am glad and grateful that we are able to stream our services online. And I have benefited by the services being streamed as Bobby Lynn and I have participated in the few Sundays we have been absent these last two years. But there is nothing that can replace being physically present with the body of Christ Taking the same postures together, reciting the same words together, and taking the bread and the wine together. A way to imitate God as our Father is to be present when his people gather. Hopefully, most of you will remember a series of sermons I did about God being our Father. It was during a time of social unrest when our civil fathers were being maligned. A primary point I made is what I close with today. Evangelical Christians talk about the importance of Jesus being the individual savior of each person in order for such persons to be saved. That is all well and good, but it must not stop there. For Jesus Jesus himself wants to be our Savior so that, dot, dot, dot, so that we would have God as our Father. That was the end goal of Jesus, and that should be our end goal as well. Look to God the Father. Place your needs and your care in his hands Follow his example, and you will be whole. Let us pray. Our gracious and heavenly Father, we thank you for that privilege to call you our Father. We ask your mercies upon us as we have failed to put our whole trust in you and to believe that you want to hear our prayers and meet our needs. May we be humble children, always looking to you for what is needed, always trusting in you for your guidance, always trusting in you for your care. This we ask and pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Everyone Must Submit
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. May be seated Turn in your Bibles to 1 Peter chapter 5, beginning at verse 5. That is where we will be landing this morning. But I begin by giving away a counseling secret that I had practiced. of every one of my premarital counseling sessions, the first one, what I do is I turn to the book of Ephesians, chapter 5, starting at verse 22. It reads, Wives submit to your husbands as to the Lord. For husbands For the husband is the head of the wife, as also Christ is the head of the church, and he is the Savior of the body. Therefore, just as the church is subject to Christ So let wives be to their own husbands in everything. Such a passage collides so violently against the culture we now have. So that I need to emphasize how radical and necessary it is for Christian wives to embrace such a passage. Submitting to a husband in the same manner a woman is to submit to God is difficult indeed. To acknowledge the husband is the head or leader of the wife is also difficult, not just because it is hard for any personality to release their autonomy to another, but because the culture around us would call a woman who accepts this position to be a fool. And finally, the standard is made clearer for the woman's submission in that she is to be subject to her husband in all things. Just as the church is subject to Christ in all things. I then challenge the future wife to reject the modern culture that condemns words like submission and simply accept what the scriptures say. As you can imagine, the counseling sessions start off a little tense I then move on to verse 25, where husbands are instructed to love their wives. With that, I say something like: so the husband doesn't have to submit, right? And they both shoot me a confused look, not knowing where I am going. I then point out that I should have started reading at verse 20 21, excuse me, 21, where Paul says, submitting to one another in the fear of God. The point I make is the same I make here, looking at 1 Peter 5. All Christians submit. We first submit to God, and then to the authorities over us, and yes, even within the home. A husband submits. As well as a wife, he simply submits in a different manner, such as being willing to sacrifice his life for his wife, because that is how Christ loved his church. Our reading from 1 Peter instructs Christians to all be in submission to one another. It comes at the back portion of the passage which starts with the instruction for young people to submit to their elders. Why that instruction is given to young people specifically is easy to answer. As one commentator suggested, the generation gap didn't begin in the first century. Some young people, having just been free of their parents' rules, don't want new parents, whether it be a boss, a teacher, or a church elder. But in referencing the need for young people to submit to those elders, Peter is moved to remind all Christians that we are to submit and specifically to one another. And in order to submit to one another, we have to clothe ourselves, he says, with humility. Now cloth the clothing metaphor is helpful because clothes are something that we choose to put on Unless you are an infant, you know how to dress yourself, and therefore you are responsible for what you wear because you choose to wear it. Humility is something Christians are to choose to wear. And why? Why put on humility? Well, he just said that we are to submit to one another. And humility enables us to do so. But in case we need further motivation, he says, God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. To resist is to oppose, which is to go against what is going the opposite way. To be proud, then is to oppose God. To be proud is also to think you are better than others. What every one of us needs is God's grace. To be given grace is to be acted upon by God's mercy. To be humble is to think, to accept a lowly position before another human being. Now, beloved, you do not want to go against God. We talked about wrestling with God a few weeks ago, and that is something different than going against God. As stated, going against God is going the opposite way and thus the wrong way. Whereas wrestling with God is staying in the fight in order to receive that greater blessing Going against God is to strive toward perdition. As sinners, we must choose to be humble in order to receive the grace that we need. With the word therefore, he starts verse 6, meaning that because God is opposed to the proud, but gives grace to the humble, and you don't want to be against God Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God that He may exalt you in due time. The instruction starts off with us making a choice We are in control of humbling ourselves, and that simply means taking the low position when such is possible. We do so recognizing that the hand of God, or the simple use of his finger and thumb Can crush our bodies to dust and cast us to hell with justice served The hope at the end of the verse is the saving hope, for it tells us that God does indeed want to exalt us in his time, not our own. This is the opposite of our personal pride, which wants to be exalted now. And God's due time, maybe, maybe, not in this life. But when we are resurrected and the eternal heaven is our home, the need to cast our cares upon a God who ultimately cares for us is because of the fear we might have When we think about all that could be done to us when we take the position of humility. People try to take advantage of the humble Yes, they do. They try to fool or deceive or plainly lie to the humble and expect the humble to take it. Yes, they do. So, so in the midst of our fears of being injured physically, socially, economically, and in other ways, when we take the position of humility We are to cast our cares upon God with the faith that He cares for us, and that means He will take care of us even when people take advantage of our humility. This is where we must see a connection between the Sermon on the Mount given by Jesus, as you know, recorded in Matthew chapters 5 through 7. See the connection between that sermon and these words of St. Peter two weeks ago I read Leo Tolstoy's book titled What I Believe, also titled A Confession Tolstoy was not a Christian most of his life, even though he was raised in a Christian culture. He came to embrace the teachings of Jesus later in life, and some critics called it a midlife crisis. Tolstoy focused his understanding of Christianity on a literal interpretation of the teachings of Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount. Which meant that when Jesus said, do not resist evil, that he meant it in every scenario. Our modern translations add person in order for the passage to read, do not resist an evil person. But the actual text can read, do not resist the evil. But regardless of the translation, in order to follow Christ, you are not to resist the evil being done to you or the evil person that is doing the evil. And such an interpretation is still a very, very high standard that Christians don't want to accept as an interpretation because of how radical it is. I have always interpreted those words of Jesus to be in the context of my Christian witness. For example, when I am sharing. Preaching or teaching the good news of Jesus Christ, and someone wants to persecute me by slapping me on the cheek, that is when I can turn and offer him the other. When I am being a Christian witness and am being treated harshly because I am a Christian and a piece of clothing is asked of me, I am to give two pieces of clothing. This is in contrast to an insistence where I am simply walking down a public street and I'm picked out by some ruffians to be bullied. and stolen from, not because I am a Christian, for they don't know what I believe, but simply because I look like their next victim. In such a scenario I have thought that I have every right to fight back. But Tolstoy doesn't see the teachings of Christ as I've just described. He sees that Jesus is saying that all forms of violence are evil. For violence and such is never God-honoring and is always sinful. Now, I am not a pacifist, and Tolstoy hasn't convinced me to be one. But, but, I am challenged to take the standards Jesus put before us in a more serious and straightforward manner. Consider how many nations that claim some Christian heritage went to war in the 20th century. And no, they didn't go to war in the name of Jesus, as some poor historians and critics have claimed. But they did go to war justifying their aggression. with the words of Jesus, or at least with the interpretation of the words of Jesus by their national church It is quite a challenge to imagine a world where Christians sacrificed their individual lives, the lives of their loved ones, and those in their Christian fellowship For the purpose of being witnesses to the ways of Christ Jesus and caring about that only. What if we did give what was asked of us, even when it is unjust? Or actually love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us. How many of us actually do that? As you have heard from this pulpit over the years, I can claim some bravado with my willingness to say what God's word says and accept the criticism and persecution that may come. And I know Paul's warning that for any man to think he stand, take heed lest he fall, meaning that where you think you are strong, you may actually be weak. Thus I am aware that I can be weak, but I am determined to speak the truth, come what may, and yet I have had to ask myself These past weeks, after reading Tolstoy, do I have enough courage to love and pray for my enemies? For those who would rather I be dead because of the words I preach. What Jesus preached in the Sermon on the Mount was truly, truly radical. And not radical in the sense of taking to the streets and working to cause political change. But radical in turning individuals inside out. Jesus tore down the internal practices of everyday persons and said that we were not to hate. That we were to make our promises based on our character, to keep our vows, especially those in marriage, to remain sexually pure. And to allow others to mistreat us and bless those who curse you, and to do it all knowing that every human being is no less than you are in value, no matter their behavior, their actions, or their beliefs. In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus was pointing to the norms of his culture and uprooting them for the purpose of higher, holier standards. In the simplest of interpretations, Jesus was saying in that sermon, you know how you like to be liked by your neighbor? No more. Expect and embrace being persecuted by him. You know how you like being part of the crowd? And going along to get along, no more. You are to be the salt of the earth. And let your light shine so that people see clearly that you are different because you follow Jesus Christ. You know, you think only the true truly religious can be righteous. No more. Your own righteousness must exceed the most religious person that you know You know how you have enemies, you hold grudges, you say mean things, and choose not to be reconciled to one another. No more. You are not to hate in your heart. You are not to speak unkind words. You are not to worship God. Even pray to Him until you are in good fellowship with your fellow man. You know how you lust for sexual pleasure? No more. You are to guide your eyes continually You know how you are flippant with your vows, even your marriage vows? No more. You are to keep your word and especially those promised to your spouse. You know how you hate your enemies just like everyone else does? No more. You are to love your enemy. Pray for their forgiveness and give them what they ask of you. But who does these things? Who who lives like that? Some of you will remember this story, but I tell it again. Because it exemplifies the times in which we live, what must be and what must must be done about it. When I taught philosophy at the university, I assigned students an ethical dilemma that had them stranded on a mountain in a winter storm because their plane had crashed. They are with a religious group that believed the Bible as holy and true. But the group was stranded for many days without food And some who survived suggested that the rest of them eat those who had perished in the crash. The simple question to answer was Do you eat those who have perished in order to survive, even though you believe that the Bible is holy and true, and the Bible clearly speaks against cannibalism? Now, the scenario I came up with doesn't go into how the Bible condemns cannibalism. Cannibalism in the Bible is usually associated with idol worship or desperate people under the curse of God But again, the scenario is an ethical dilemma, it's not a Bible lesson. And I would say eighty percent of the students said that they would eat the perished passengers and the justification was their own personal survival because their primary moral objective they believed should be their own personal survival. When their answers were defended, I would try to counter argue to expose the weaknesses and their position. I remember one student, I tried to corner, reminding him that in the scenario, he is a religious person. He believes what the Bible says is true. So how can he justify going against his faith? He countered that he could cannibalize the dead passengers and ask God for forgiveness later. That was an argument repeated by many. I countered that his personal faith won't allow such because he doesn't want to offend God. And what he countered back is what stuck with me He said, I don't know anyone who takes their religious faith that seriously He got me. I had no counter. I was undone. And I am guessing that he was speaking accurately. He probably didn't know anyone who takes their Christian faith seriously enough to sacrifice for it, to obey its principles, and to defend its creeds. The tough question is, do the people that know you know someone who takes their Christian faith seriously? In the gospel reading, Jesus begins the lost chapter. There is first the lost sheep. Then there is the lost coin, and then the lost sons. It is a chapter of motivation Jesus wants us to know what God does for us and how much he wants to do it for us. God finds us and he celebrates our being found. He does so because we are as dumb as sheep who wander, making ourselves vulnerable to the devil and to our own temptations. But God searches for us and finds us to save us from the devil and from ourselves. God does that when he doesn't have to. And we in turn are to love him for it and follow him, which is living as he desires us to live. We are to live seriously for him. And that begins with being humble before him. And that leads to submitting and walking honestly with God. It is true that you are going to fail to live up to the instructions of Jesus even in that Sermon on the Mount. But there is to be no quitting. There is confession again and repentance again and a commitment to overcome again and again and again. And that is repeated until you cross the river of death into the hands of God. Where we only want him to say, well done. So put on humility and let's be serious about it. Let us pray. A gracious God, we recognize these standards to be out of our reach without you, Holy Spirit, empowering us, strengthening us. And helping us to be obedient to you in all things. And so we confess our sins again this day, and we receive Your symbols of forgiveness. May we once again strive to live out as you have commanded, to honor you for finding us. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Necessity of Forgiveness
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. May be seated. Our focus this morning is on Luke chapter 6, our gospel reading. So you are encouraged to turn to Luke chapter 6, beginning at verse 36. There is a letter written in the mid to late second century, around 145, they believe. By an unknown author who identifies himself as a student or disciple of the apostles. The person receiving the letter is named Diognetus. But nothing more is known about him. The letter is considered one of the first apologies or defenses of Christianity. It would appear that Dionytus had previously inquired about Christians, and the writer is answering his questions. The description of second century Christians should be the goal of every Christian of every generation. If the following could be said about us today, we would indeed be the city on a hill, the salt of the earth. Part of the letter reads as follows. Christians cannot be distinguished from the rest of the human race by country or language or customs. They do not live in cities of their own. They do not use a peculiar form of speech. They do not follow an eccentric manner of life. Yet although they live in Greek and barbarian cities alike, they follow the customs of the country in clothing and food and other matters of daily living. At the same time, they give proof of the remarkable and admittedly extraordinary constitution of their own Commonwealth They live in their own countries, but only as aliens. They have a share in everything as citizens and endure everything as foreigners. Every foreign land is their fatherland, and yet for them every fatherland is a foreign land. They marry like everyone else, and they beget children, but they do not cast off their offspring. They share their board with each other, but not their marriage bed. They busy themselves on earth, but their citizenship is in heaven. They obey the established laws, but in their own lives they go far beyond what the law requires. They love all men, and by all men are persecuted They are poor and yet they make many rich. They are completely destitute and yet enjoy complete abundance. They are reviled and yet they bless. When they are affronted, they still pay due respect. They are treated by the Jews as foreigners and enemies, and they are hunted down by the Greeks. And all the time, those who hate them find it impossible to justify their enmity. In the same way, Christians love those who hate them. Such a description doesn't have to be describing all Christians individually, for all have not mastered all that Jesus has taught. But It is a general reputation like no other. And every Christian should strive for such a reputation. And if we did, we would be fulfilling the Great Commission without using words. I challenged each of us with a question last week, which was, Do the people you know know someone who takes their Christian faith seriously? This is another way of asking forthrightly. Are you taking your Christian faith seriously so that it is obvious to others? In our gospel reading, Luke 6, we find Jesus teaching what is called the Sermon on the Mount, which we looked at more closely last week. It is connected to the teachings of St. Peter. Only in Luke's version of the sermon, which is slightly different than Matthew's, though not different enough for there to be a question about its accuracy. Our gospel reading begins with the word therefore, which is unfortunate because it starts with a conclusion without context. Previously, Jesus had changed the norm, which was hating your enemy and withholding anything good from him. Instead, Jesus instructs his followers to love their enemies and to give them whatever is asked in order to be drastically different than their fellow citizens. After all, sinners without prodding hate their enemies and do good to those they love. That is not difficult. But those who follow Jesus are to exceed such behavior by doing more. And the more, in the end, is being merciful. That is what verse 36 concludes. Be merciful, Jesus says, just as your heavenly Father is merciful. And so the standard is set, with no exception. The next verse, verse 37, judge not lest you be judged, is one of those few passages in the Bible that people know without ever reading the Bible. The sinners will quote it to Christians in order to put Christians in their place and to have us back down from a platform they think we have stood upon. But I need to take some time on this passage in order to properly interpret it and thus properly apply it. The word judge is not simply identifying that something is good or evil or even bad, as in concluding that you're eating too much and that's bad or drinking too much and that's bad. No, the word judge here is to condemn, which is to conclude that something, whatever is being judged, is worthy of punishment, which for the Christian understanding is hellfire. So when Jesus says we are not to judge or condemn, he means that we are not to play the role of prosecuting attorney and then judge and then jury. We are not to conclude an ending to a person's soul, regardless of behavior or motive. So I am not judging when I say you shouldn't have committed adultery or hit your wife or lie to a police officer or the many other immoral things we might do. I am judging when I say that you who are worthy of eternal damnation is guilty before God. That's when I have stepped too far. This is why Jesus follows those words, not to judge, with the instruction to forgive, and you will be forgiven. And this is the crux, is it not? We follow Jesus first and primarily because we need our sins to be forgiven. Thus, it should be easy for us to forgive others because we in turn are forgiven. Which again is why we follow Jesus. It is why we say we are Christian. What is the most important thing for these children baptized here today? It is for their sins to be forgiven. Thus, the Christian life is made up of faith in the blood of Jesus, confessing sins, asking God for forgiveness, and striving to live as Jesus instructed. With the expectation to need to have to have faith again, to confess again, and to ask for forgiveness again. Because when each of us stands before the judgment seat of Christ Jesus to account for our lives, it is the forgiveness he provides that is our only eternal hope, our only eternal hope. We are next to give. And what he desires us to give is forgiveness, which implies that it is a choice we make. We are to choose to forgive others. And Jesus promises a good return on the forgiveness we choose to give. With all the benefits offered to us when we forgive, it is befuddling how many people who call themselves Christians withhold forgiveness. When you ask such persons why they withhold forgiveness, it is always about themselves. Well I can't I can't trust them. Or I'm too hurt. Or he doesn't deserve my forgiveness. The pronouns give the problem away. We use too many I and my words So many, too many Christians miss out on the blessings Jesus offers when they don't forgive. Too many siblings don't get along, won't even speak to each other, because one or both choose not to forgive. Too many Christian marriages break up. Well, just one is too many. Because one or both choose not to forgive. And too many churches have revolving doors when it comes to membership because too many Christians choose not to forgive one another. In order to convince us how important forgiveness is for us, Jesus motivates us by extending his explanation on how blessed we can be if we give forgiveness. Commentator Joaquin Jeremiah gives some background into the corn measuring process in the ancient Near East. He says, the measuring of corn is a process which is carried out according to an established pattern. The seller crouches on the ground with the measure between his legs. First of all, he fills the measure three-quarters full and gives it a good shake with a rotary motion to make the grains settle down. Then he fills the measure to the top and gives it another shake. Next he presses the corn strongly with both hands. Finally he heaps it into a cone, tapping it carefully to press the grains together. In this way, the purchaser is guaranteed an absolutely full measure. It cannot hold more. That is the point Jesus makes. He will guarantee to you a full measure of reward for the forgiveness you choose to give. Next, we can understand the mention by Jesus of the blind, leading the blind, to be a person who has sin in his life. Trying to judge or condemn another person who has sin in his life. The next image provided by Jesus is both absurd and comical A plank is a substantial piece of wood, and it would be comical to watch someone walking around with a large piece of wood sticking out of their eye, although not comical to imagine how it got there, but to see such a person walk around, let alone try to help someone get a little piece of sawdust out of their eye. But Jesus becomes more serious, not just comical, but serious again when he calls the person a hypocrite. And why would the man be a hypocrite? The difference in sizes is to note that the person who is trying to remove the speck is guilty of a greater crime than the person he is offering to help. The crime is greater because the crime is the unwillingness to forgive. If a man is guilty of larceny And seeks forgiveness only to be stolen from, and in turn refuses to forgive the one who stole him, his greater sin is the unforgiving. His action is what defines hypocrisy. The final point by Jesus is for the hypocrite to take the board out of his own eye, which is the choice not to forgive. He's taking that out and forgiving. And now, after forgiving, it is much easier to help another. Now to forgive other people of sin done to you, or sin not done directly to you, but the result hurts you. Such is not easy, and no one should ever say it is. Such would be a lie, making the forgiving all the more difficult. I have shared the story of the forgiveness practiced by Corey Tenboom toward her Nazi captors before, and I found one similar in a series of stories about people living out their Christian faith. A Turkish officer raided and looted an Armenian home. He killed the aged parents. and gave the daughters to the soldiers, keeping the eldest daughter for himself. Sometime later she escaped and trained to be a nurse. As time passed, she found herself nursing in a ward of Turkish officers. One night, by the light of a lantern, she saw the face of this officer. He was so gravely ill that without exceptional nursing, he would die. The days passed and he recovered. One day the doctor stood by the bed with her and said to him, But for her devotion to you, you would be dead. He looked at her and said, We have met before. Why didn't you kill me? She replied, I am a follower of him who said, Love your enemies. From such stories, we confess that to forgive may be to suffer. It may be to make the heart vulnerable and thus possibly hurt again. But the motivation to put up with such suffering is given to us by St. Paul in our reading from his letter from Romans chapter 8. To endure suffering when we take up the upper road and forgive. We are to consider that all of our suffering in this life combined is worth it. All of it. When it is compared to the glory that awaits us as a heavenly reward. When we forgive, we are to consider the promise of heaven, which includes our sins being cast into the lake of fire Death having no more authority. Temptation to sin swallowed up, and the love of Jesus Christ shared with one another without interruption. When we forgive, we are to consider that the earth itself, all of creation, even the moon and stars, groan. For they too suffer because of the curse of man. But they know what is coming and why the created order groans. The created order sees itself made new and wants to be made new Referring back to the description of Christians in the second century, we can admit that those Christians had one thing better than we do today, and that is They didn't have a history of failure that has scarred the witness Christians have before the world. The Lord has been my shepherd since I turned 18 years of age. And so it has been a while since I have looked at Christianity from outside in I don't remember having many thoughts about Christians before the Lord found me. But I can guess that what the unbelieving world sees of Christians isn't very lovely and perhaps very ugly. What they see is likely scandal. What they see or hear about is abuse. That is what the media shows them. What they see are rich preachers wanting to stay rich. And so they tell their audience what they want to hear, and people still give. They prophesy that they can blow away COVID-19 and people still give them money. They say they need private jets and people still give them money. And then there are the hit pastors who wear designer clothes with designer haircuts, and who are made Christian celebrities by their churches, who later, we find out succumb to the sins of the world and then publicly renounce the faith. Such are the easiest things to see about Christians. And so reading a letter like written to Diagnetus, not likely today. But there is one thing that Christians could work on and become better at, so that if anything can be said about Christians today, it may be that we are people who know and practice. Forgiveness. Such is not going to change quickly because forgiveness takes work. It takes a fight against evil and the evil one. It takes daily diligence from the for the devil and his agents will place memories before you. Just when you think you've got this forgiveness thing down, a flood of pain and anger comes storming back. And a desire to see your enemy suffer follows. And the giving of forgiveness has to begin again. But like anything else worth doing, it must be done until it is completed. Consider this a possible future letter. Dear Diognetus Christians are people with whom you shop at a local grocery store and sit in traffic with every day. Some own shops and some work in shops. Some live in large houses and some in modest houses, just like you and your family. And Christians dress like people around them. In other words, you cannot tell who a Christian is when comparing them to those in their communities. But if you are around them, if you visit their churches, or if you deal with them pup in public, and there is a dispute. Christians can be spotted by how willing they are to forgive and ask for forgiveness, wanting to be at peace with their God and their fellow man. May such a letter be written about us. Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious God, we receive the call, the standard. To forgive and be forgiven. May that be on our hearts each and every day we have opportunity to forgive and to love. In Jesus' name we pray, Amen

sermons.title: Leaving All
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles to Luke chapter 5. We will be going over our gospel reading today. Luke chapter 5. According to the liturgical calendar today is the fifth Sunday after Trinity Or the sixth Sunday after Pentecost, and whichever Christian calendar you follow, it is also known as ordinary time. I realize that by referring to the Christian calendar, I have already bored many of you Incidentally, the ordinary time or the weeks after Trinity are sarcastically referred to as boring time instead of ordinary time. The reason this time in the Christian calendar is considered boring is because of the themes that are focused upon other times in the Christian year. With the first focus on the birth of Christ, we have Advent, Christmas, and Epiphany With the next focus on the resurrection of Jesus, we have Lent, Holy Thursday, Good Friday, Easter Sunday, and Ascension Day. In between those two themes, the primary focus is on ordinary time with a lot of green to be seen. The importance of ordinary time, which is named after the word ordinal or numbered, which is referring to how we Count the first Sunday after Trinity and then the second Sunday after Trinity and so on, and I'm boring myself telling you this. But The importance of this time in the Christian year is the focus on discipleship in general. The coming of Christ and the new birth in Christ are the focus of our Christmas season. The forgiveness of sins and the hope of the resurrection are the focus of our Easter season. But the Christian life is made up of a great deal of downtime Where we live our faith day to day, with no focus other than on our relationship with God through Jesus Christ. And the chosen reading from the Book of Common Prayer for this ordinary time reflects that focus on our faith day to day. That is why we spent time focusing on the importance of forgiveness last week, because it is so very fundamental to our everyday Christian walk Christians must lead a life of forgiveness, both in seeking it from God and giving it away to others.
