If we do not lead a life of forgiveness, we are not Christian. For today, from our reading in Luke, we will focus on discipleship specifically as it what it means to be a student of Christ. Which is what the word disciple means, a student of Christ. It was several years ago now that I learned the truth about what it takes to be a student or a learner First, you must admit you don't know something, which requires humility. Every young student Even excuse me, even young students have a hard time admitting that they don't know something. Bobby Lynn taught at the academy here for a number of years and can remember The many students five or six years old who when she would teach them something new, they would respond, I knew that Saying it in a proud sort of manner, revealing that there was not a humble heart that was needed. To truly learn is to be truly humble. Next, a learner must receive what he or she did not previously have, and that continues to require humility, for it is taking from another what is lacking in you. With new knowledge, a person is made new, for he or she is more advanced than he or she was before. And I hope you see closely how being a d student or disciple, how closely it is to being a convert. A convert needs to humble himself before God, acknowledging his sinfulness and his need for a Savior. He then must receive the forgiveness God offers in Christ Jesus. With such forgiveness, the convert is made new, and is therefore not what he or she was before So putting this together, we can conclude that to be a student, a disciple, is to be continually made new. In the gospel reading, we find followers of Jesus crowding around him and pressing in on him, and interestingly The followers did not include Simon Peter, did not include James, did not include John. Prior to this, Luke records Jesus being at the house of Simon Peter. So We know that they knew each other, and we know that Peter had witnessed Jesus as a dramatic and effective healer. But the three lives of these future apostles had not changed in priority until the events in Luke chapter 5 described. We first must notice why the people are crowding around Jesus. They have a good motive. Luke says it is to hear the word of God. There are hungry hearts among mankind that want to hear truth, want to know truth, and want to follow truth. Jesus fed that hunger and still feeds that hunger, and people who are hungry today can still be fed when Christian pastors are faithful to preach what Jesus said and what he did. Being the creator of all things, Jesus was aware of how calm waters can be a natural sound conductor. To sit in a boat and to be pushed out a little would provide a needed sound conductor for a large group. It is curious why Luke does not tell us what Jesus taught. Perhaps he repeats it elsewhere, but what Jesus said is not the focus of this story. The focus of the story begins with Jesus seeing Simon, who was not yet called Peter, and tell him to go out into the deep and put down their nets. We know that Simon, along with James and John, were professional fishermen. They knew the lake, also called the Sea of Galilee. They knew it well. They knew that the best time to fish that time of year was at night. And they knew that if they had failed to make a significant catch at night, there was no chance of catching anything in the morning. Peter knew that, and Peter repeats that to Jesus, but Peter had something to make him a disciple. A learner. He had humility. He had humility in that he was willing to accept the instruction of Jesus, even though his professional wisdom told him differently. And Peter had faith in Jesus. And that is revealed by his response, saying, At your word. At your word. To say at your word is similar to Amen. It is to be saying, let it be so It is a phrase we would be well served to have in our vernacular on a daily basis. It is telling the Lord Jesus that although the circumstances as I see them are not in my favor, And do not appear to have a good outcome in the future. I will trust at your instruction, and therefore believe you, Lord Jesus, over what I see. To say at your word is to walk by faith and not by sight. Jesus said That to forgive, we will receive blessings at the fullest measure. And we must only respond with, at your word. Jesus says to love our enemies and we must only respond saying at your word. Jesus says not to worry about tomorrow and we must only respond by saying at your word Jesus says that he will provide our basic needs. Regardless of the stock market, regardless of how high gas prices go. Or what type of policies the administration has in store, we must only respond by saying, at your word. And Simon not only needed to have faith in the Word of Jesus, but he needed to do specifically as Jesus said. He needed to go into the deep waters. Go to the deep. The deep waters are the more dangerous waters because of what could happen to the boat and the time it would take to get back to shore. Also, the deep waters are where the wind makes the waves taller, for there are no barriers to slow it. The deep waters are more dangerous indeed while having a greater reward. Simon also needed to let down their nets. These were the same nets that needed mending after each outing because of what the water and the growth within the water would do to them. And so Simon does as he was instructed, and the number of fish was much larger than they had ever caught before. And we can know this because the nets couldn't handle the count or the weight. Not even the boats could handle the number of fish, for they began to sink because of the weight of their content. And Simon responds. Notice that he does not respond to the sinking boats. But response to the authority of Jesus and the blessings that Jesus bestowed upon him and his partners. Simon's humility is further displayed by falling to his knees before Jesus, which signaled his unworthiness to be before Jesus And then expressing that unworthiness by recognizing his own sinfulness and thus his unworthiness to be blessed by this holy man. Simon's words here are similar to those of Isaiah in Isaiah chapter six. When standing before the Lord, Isaiah said, Woe is me, for I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips, and dwell among a people of unclean lips. It was similar to Daniel, who when encountering a vision of God, he said, no strength remained in him, as his vigor had turned to frailty. If you ever wondered what it would be like to stand before the Lord, the Bible has stories that give you an answer. Jesus is then gracious to Simon, as God is always gracious to the humble. As Simon was in awe, and as James and John were in awe, Jesus gives them a direction for the rest of their lives, for eternity. They are to become fishers of men. So we have clearly learned through Simon the importance of humility when being a disciple of Jesus. But what about verse 11? Look at that verse again. It says that when they brought their boats to the land, they forsook all and followed Jesus. The all would include their fishing nets, their boats. Their knives, their baskets, all that was needed to make a living via fishing. And the word all may have included their family and friends. For Jesus would say later that unless his followers hate their father or mother or wife or children, they cannot follow him. He also says elsewhere that each of his followers must accept Jesus, who will die on a cross, and then they must pick up their own cross. So, how literal are we to take these requirements for discipleship? I certainly don't hate my wife Nor my children. And so am I disqualified from being a learner of Jesus? I have no physical cross that I have picked up to actualize my devotion to Christ. But the disciples, the disciples left all. It says it right here in Luke 5. 11 and in Matthew chapter 4. They left even their families behind, and they say so later in Luke 18, when Peter reminds Jesus of all that they have left to follow him. But what does leaving all and leaving quickly really mean? Well We know that just after Jesus calling the three fishermen in Luke 5, Jesus is next in a Galilean home where a crowd has gathered. So the three fishermen could not have immediately left all to follow Jesus because they were still in Galilee where they all lived. And it is further likely that the house they were in where Jesus taught, and you remember the story of some other disciples dug a hole in the roof and Lower down a paralytic man so that Jesus could heal him, scholars agree that it must have been the home of Simon Peter. For Jesus was previously there and healed Simon Peter's mother-in-law So Simon Peter did not just up and leave without a word to his family, but they did eventually put their old lives behind them and follow Jesus for three years. No doubt there was great sacrifice on their part, but I have no doubt it was an even greater sacrifice on the other end. I want to personally share my own story of leading a life behind. I have been praised by some. Who know my story regarding what I did in taking my family from Washington State to Kansas City, Missouri? and attending seminary full-time while working two jobs while my wife stayed home and cared for the home and for the children. For on the surface it does sound like a great sacrifice But it was not. Not compared to what my bride, Bobby Lynn, sacrificed. We went from a spacious three-bedroom home To a cramped two-bedroom home with the boys sleeping in the attic. We went from being 40 minutes away from her parents to 1,500 miles from her parents. She went from me helping her with the kids every day to me being gone 12 hours a day only to come home, play with the boys, eat some dinner, and study until bedtime. That was for three long years. And she had two more children while we lived in Kansas. Kansas City. And both times she gave birth, she needed to be taken to the hospital by someone she didn't know because I was working. That gave us five boys when we left seminary. For three years she battled loneliness, depression, exhaustion. When her parents arrived for the graduation ceremony, I took Bobby Lynn with me to the closing chapel service for the students. With just her and I in the car, I stopped short of the campus where we parked and we could see the bell tower of the seminary. I stopped because I wanted to thank her for her sacrifice, and we cried, and we cried, and we cried Is that the type of leaving Jesus wants of his disciples? Is it to follow Jesus going where He has gifted us to go and convicted us to go with the willingness to sacrifice and endure the cost. I think it is. A little side story. When I was a senior in seminary, an anonymous person put a brochure in my cubby, which is where we would receive our tests and our papers back That brochure was for the Reformed Episcopal Church. I had never heard of the denomination before, but someone must have heard me argue or speak my mind in class and thought I would be a good fit. I read it, I took it home, and told Bobby Lynn that this church, the Reformed Episcopal Church, is where we should be. She looked at me bug-eyed and said, I'm not doing this again. So I guess sacrifice has its limits. What we must see is that the Bible is not above using hyperbolic language to make a point. The description to leave all, the teaching that we must hate those closest to us in life, the directive to pick up our own cross. Are ways to get across to us what the first commandment of the Ten Commandments means. There is to be No God before the only true God. And if anything is before him, whether it be your profession, your family, Your reputation, your personal wants and needs, all of it must be second to the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Again, I have been praised because I picked up my family and moved again halfway across the country from Texas to Maryland to pastor this parish. But again, the real sacrificing was Bobby Lynn. She had a baby less than a year prior She had no family close, no immediate friends, and was responsible to homeschool our children all under the age of ten. And some of the people at St. Stephen's didn't like her husband As many of you know, it is hard to love people who don't love your spouse. But she has died to herself many, many times while serving her Savior through her husband and through her church. And my point is not to praise my wife. It truly is not. It is to give an example of how everyday folks like us can leave everything to follow Jesus, even if we stay right where we are. We are not part of the twelve whom Jesus told to follow him. The calling of the apostles and their destinies were extraordinary and never to be duplicated again. But their hearts, like the heart of Simon, who would be called Peter, their hearts were humble, and their faith in Jesus as the Messiah was real. So that following Jesus was first in their life. Such hearts, my brothers and sisters in Christ, well, that can be duplicated again. Let us pray. Our gracious God, we thank you for the model of the apostles. And they're sacrificial living. And they're giving of all. And we see ourselves that there are plenty of times that we're not giving our all. But we can. We know we can. And so convict us where necessary that we might truly serve you. Truly serve you as you have called us to do. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Abhorring Sin
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I needed that hymn today. What a wonderful, wonderful hymn. We are looking in Romans chapter six, primarily 15 through 23, we will be referring to what would have been our gospel reading also in Mark chapter 8, verses 1 through 9. Romans 6, starting in verse 15, even prior. Where the Bible gives promises such as being in Christ means that all things have passed away and all things have become new, it is speaking about sins. That we were once guilty of that will no longer be counted against us. We have a tabula rasa conscience. Our slate is clean. However, We all know that we don't forget what we were once guilty of doing, and sometimes the desire to commit those same sins remains. And the disconnect some people might have, that is different, say from the first century Christians in Rome, is that we may have grown up in the church and thus grown up to know Jesus as our Savior always in our lives. As was different for those Paul wrote to in Rome, who were all new converts to the Christian faith But even Christians who grow up in the faith or have been Christians for many years know what it means to get caught up into sin and needing to be forgiven. And if you don't think that is true for you, I will say that you're simply deceived. What Paul argues in chapter six of this letter to the Romans Is that Christians need to put their sinful ways behind them, and to convince them of this, he uses logic and an emotional argument. With the logic argument, he uses what seems to be a rhetorical question. Should Christians go on sinning that grace may abound? The question comes out of the true reality that God's grace can overcome any sin, which is fantastic news. But the temptation would be to either say, well, if grace is always more, then I can continue sinning so that God can continue giving more grace, thus be given more praise. Or I can think that to keep on sinning isn't dangerous anymore because grace is always there to grant me forgiveness. Both ways of thinking are in error. And that is why Paul answers his own question with certainly not. Which is to say that we certainly should not go on sinning. His emotional argument, which also includes logic, is to use the analogy of being slaves. Now, slavery in the ancient Near East was very common, although not the same slavery as what occurred in the United States. Let's be clear on that. Americans, they only think of slavery in one manner. I have lectured before in Sunday school and in Wednesday Bible study that slavery in the Bible was so common because it was out of necessity. If you were a slave, you were either sold into it by your family, or you sold yourself to pay off a debt. Or, or you were born into it because your family had been enslaved because of debt, or because of war. Warring nations either enslaved those whom they conquered or killed them so that they would not come back and play war again. To say, as a famous atheist has done publicly, that the Bible is in favor of slavery is purposefully ignorant. The Bible isn't in favor of it, but only acknowledges its existence. So Paul appeals to the analogy of being slaves by describing the Roman Christians as being enslaved to sin. Because of their prior unbelief, they could only sin. They had no choice in the matter In Christ Jesus, they had been set free from the guilt of those sins and thus were now free in terms of their standing before God. But Paul recognizes that people get pulled back into the sins they were once enslaved by. The flesh can be and is weak. And because there can be temptations all around us, it is easy to fall back into the sins that were once forgiven. For the Romans, sexual immorality of all types existed, and the phallic symbols were ever present as they were used for witchcraft and the public religion. Children and women were no more than objects to be used. But Paul wasn't just worried about outward sins, for he knew the teachings of Jesus Sins such as jealousy, lying, envy, hatred The love of money, vainglory, hypocrisy, and the like are all sins that persons can easily return to. Thus, the emotional appeal Paul makes is to ask: what fruit did you have then in the things which you are now ashamed? And that question is asked in a careful manner. For he did not ask, what enjoyments did you have, or what immediate outcomes did you have, because Those enjoyments and outcomes would be in the moment. He asks instead, what fruit did they have? Meaning, what eventual outcome did you have? which is an outcome after the initial one. And those outcomes are always those that fruit is always bad. Because we are guilty, and that guilt doesn't go away without the blood of Jesus Christ. Remainder of the appeal is to know what has been done for you as you now profess Christ Jesus and thus call Upon his name to have your sins forgiven and be placed in the past. Paul then summarizes his appeal by reminding them that the wages of sin is death. It's always death. And if the opposite reward is for those who cling to the cross of Christ, then that opposite is eternal life. The purpose of this teaching by Paul, and he's been trying to make this point in different ways in this letter thus far. Is that Christians at Rome and all Christians of every era are to live their lives according to what they say they believe Christians are to live their lives according to what they say they believe. That point got me thinking about Mr. Talkative and the Pilgrim's Progress. By talkative, Bunyan, the author, is not merely describing a character who likes to talk. Even if you recall the story for those who do not, allow me to set the scene. Christian, the main character of the story, catches up with a man named Faithful. Faithful is fleeing an enemy, causing Christian to move faster so that they can travel together on their way to the celestial city. When walking together, they share about their different experiences, and in this conversation, Bunyan shows the importance of Christian fellowship. And how our journeys while walking the narrow road will not all be the same. As the two travel, they come upon a man named Pocketev, who is traveling the same direction. Faithful engages him while Christian stays back, and there's a reason. Talkative is excited to talk to faithful. As Talkative begins with the statement that too many people like to talk about trivial things, but he likes to talk about things of value. To say such a thing is a warning sign to those who have lived longer in this world, but faithful believes what he hears People who actually talk of things of value simply do so rather than tell you so. Talkative impresses more by stating that Any good thing a man can say or do comes from God alone, for nothing is by works but only by grace. Faithful soon realizes that Christian has stayed back, and so he slows to talk to him in private. He learns that Christian knows talkative And that he is a man not worth listening to. Christian summarizes his opinion of Tokadiv by saying that his religion is only On his tongue. Christian goes on, quote, when he talks of prayer, repentance, and faith And the new birth, he is not speaking of his own personal experience, but merely repeating what he has heard After learning that his life and family in no way resemble a faithful Christian life and home, Faithful understands the lesson that saying and doing are two different things entirely. Christian then challenges faithful to put Talkative to a test by speaking to him about the power of God within that changes a man to where his heart and life is truly and obviously made new. Faithful takes the challenge and re-engages talkative. The first thing talkative reveals is that he doesn't know the difference between crying out against sin and aboring sin. Talkative next reveals that he thinks of the gospel only in terms of what he says, but not by faith that is revealed by his doing. Faithful further challenges Takhadiv to examine his heart, to see if he has experienced the love and mercy of God. Talkative response by calling faithful rash, rude, peevish, fault-finding, and unfit for wholesome conversation. And he quickly makes his exit. Characters like talkative are nothing new, and even Christians who are true Christians and have true faith. An experience can fall into a talkative approach to the faith. And the Holy Spirit has to awaken us from our sinful slumber and bring us to repentance. What got to me personally was the character talkative and where I think this story applies to Paul's teaching. Is talkative not knowing the difference between crying out against sin and a boring sin I know myself well enough to recall times I was crying out against sin, while not abhorring the same sin and actually participating in it. I know this to be true about myself, and I'm focusing on my sin, so none of you take this as a personal attack. But I have done the same about sins such as gossip. I have discovered that someone had gossiped about me. Don't worry, I'm not aware of anything recently. But I have found such out and immediately I start to slander and gossip about the person who is gossiping about me. He said, what? That's not a Christian thing to do. That guy can never be trusted. He lied to his wife three weeks ago about where he was going at night. That guy what a loser. So there I am crying out about the sin of gossip, but practicing it that very moment. Who's the loser? Me. A bore is to be disgusted with hatred. We have to hate the sins we commit or are tempted to commit. We have to hate them to be rid of them. And to hate a sin that you were once a slave to is a difficult thing to do. Once again, walking the narrow road takes work. It is facing the same temptations over and over again and working to hate what you want to do. By doing as Paul teaches, which is to consider the pain and guilt brought upon you when practicing the sin you have in your past, and ask that question, what fruit has it brought you? Nothing but bad things. And that is reason enough not to do them again. What Paul does with his slavery analogy and with his reference to the fruit of such slavery is refer to earthly things in order to communicate spiritual truths. You remember when Jesus speaks to Nicodemus, he uses earthly analogies to communicate spiritual truths. Jesus used the earthly example of being born to the point of a new birth spiritually. When Nicodemus was confused, Jesus said to him. If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? What a great question. The earthly things point to the heavenly things. Consider Mark chapter 8. It is the story of Jesus, Mark's account of Jesus feeding the multitude. And why did he feed them? That is easy to answer, for the text says that Jesus had compassion on them. They've been following him for three days, and now they have no food. They were hungry. Some of them were so far from home that they might have fainted before they could reach home. So Jesus feeds them. But that was only the immediate, that was the practical reason. The earthly things, the fish and the bread, were also analogous to Jesus being Lord of all living. And Jesus being the sufficient Savior who would supply all needs of mankind. And it pointed to Jesus himself, who is the bread of life. This fundamental truth of understanding earthly things to understand spiritual things is why I repeated White but repeatedly point to the types and shadows of the Old Testament and their fulfillment in the New You remember we studied at length how the temple offerings, which are earthly, how they revealed spiritual truths by the sacrifice of Jesus, which is heavenly. Take, for example, circumcision of the flesh. There was nothing more earthly, but it was a type of the symbol of baptism. Which is also earthly, but more clearly pointing to the new birth offered through Jesus Christ as believers have their sins washed away. Unfortunately, there are contemporary Christian teachings that say that baptism isn't necessary because it is earthly. And some even say that Gentile Christians should only be concerned with the teachings of Paul because the Gospels were written for the Jews. Such nonsense shows how easy it is to stray when you do not understand how the earthly things can teach the spiritual truths. Earthly slavery reveals slavery to sin, and the good news of Jesus Christ is that believers are freed from that sin, for they need to learn how to live in that freedom. For those who repeat unwanted sin again and again, a common threat exists with all who do so. And it is not to look at the pain and guilt from the past sins like we should, but to stay in the past, as if the guilt and sin remain a part of them, a part of their identity. When giving counsel, I hear people talk about their past as if it defines them. And I counter that it only defines you if you let it. A passage of scripture every Christian should have memorized is Philippians 3. 13, which reads, Brethren, I do not count myself to have apprehended But one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind and reaching forward to those things which are ahead. But what has Paul not apprehended? The answer we get from the previous verse, which reads, not that I have already obtained all of this, he was referring to the resurrection. Or have already been made perfect, it was being perfect that he did not apprehend. But I press on to take hold of that for which Christ took hold of me. By saying this emphatically, he is saying that he doesn't care what other people think of him, nor does he care what they think of themselves. Some accuse him of being a man not true to his word and thus not perfect. Some claim to be more devout and more holy than Paul. For Paul, none of that mattered. For he was choosing to put the past behind him and aggressively reach for and attain that which was ahead of him. And Paul made this a lifestyle choice because Kronos is linear and not stopping. And thus we must always be forgetting those things that are behind, reaching only for that which is ahead. Always Placing things behind us and going forward always is an often repeated theme in both the Old and New Testaments. Consider these words from Isaiah 43. Do not remember the former things, nor consider the things of old. From 2 Corinthians 5, 17. Therefore, if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature. Old things are passed away. Behold, all things are become new. Hebrews 10, 38 through 39. Now the just shall live by faith, but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him. We are not of them who draw back into perdition, but of them that believe to the saving of the soul. Later in Pilgrim's Progress, Christian walks with a character named Hopeful, and they come upon Lot's wife. Who you remember was made a pillar of salt. And they say to one another, remember Lot's wife. But why remember her? It is because what she did is so easy to do. She looked back at Sodom and Gomorrah, and instead of abhorring that life, she remembered it fondly. St. Paul would ask, what fruit did it bring for her? Her everlasting condition is her answer. And it is ours. Let us pray. Our gracious and merciful God That message to leave that which is behind behind, and to press forward to what is ahead is such a hopeful message in Christ. And so we embrace it, each of us on our own journey, each of us at different levels in our own journey, but still all of us needing to leave that which is behind and press forward, grabbing at that which is ahead. For what is ahead is your forgiveness, is your mercy, is everlasting life. May it be ours. In Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: False Prophets
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: The name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turning your Bibles to Matthew chapter 7. We're looking at our gospel reading, starting at verse 15. The Sermon on the Mount in St. Matthew's Gospel, as you know, begins in chapter 5 with what are called the beatitudes, and it ends in chapter 7. The first part describes what it means to follow Jesus. It is the Christian life. And the second part, which was our gospel reading in part, Is set is a set of warnings for not following Jesus or not following Jesus properly In verse 13 of chapter 7, Jesus describes the way of following him as narrow, as in it is a narrow gate that gets you on the right path. He then describes the way as difficult. And because it is difficult, few people find the end. These passages in our liturgical readings for these Sundays in Trinity have fit so very well with our study of John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress. And I so wish more of you could have joined us for this summer for Sunday school, but I certainly understand that that can be difficult. But you will have to oblige me with another reference to the story. This one is of Christian and now his companion, hopeful. As they make their way to the celestial city, which is heaven, and on the path, they climb the direct of the mountains. I have interpreted the delectable mountains to be symbolic of an elder Christian who has walked with the Lord many years and is therefore able to receive some reprieve by being blessed by the mountains. And getting a closer glimpse of the celestial city. There were four shepherds on the delectable mountains. that first made sure that Christian and hopeful had come through the right way, and then proceeded to help them prepare for the latter part of their journey while also giving them warnings in the following manner. This is a quote. Then I saw in my dream that the shepherds led them to another place where there was a door in the side of a hill. They opened the door and bid the pilgrims to look in. Peering in, they saw that it was very dark and smoky. They also thought that they heard a rumbling noise of fire and a cry of some who were tormented, and that they smelled the scent of brimstone. What does this mean? Christian inquired. The shepherds told them, this is a byway to hell, a way That hypocrites go, namely such as sell their birthright with Esau, and such as sell their master with Judas, and such as blaspheme the gospel with Alexander. And such as lie and deceive with Ananias and his wife Sapphira. Then hopeful questioned the shepherds I perceived that all of these once had a reputation as being pilgrims, just as we do, had they not? Shepherds, yes, and some held to it for a long time, too. Hopeful. How far they went on a on on in pilgrimage, yet notwithstanding they were thus miserably cast away. shepherds, some not as far as these mountains, and some went further. Then the pilgrims said to each un to each other, We had need to cry to the strong one for strength Shepherds, yes. And you will also have need to use that strength when you have it Bunyan there captures the need for fear, a healthy fear of God and his judgment, so that we do not stray from the narrow way. Now mind you, there is a fear that is unhealthy and dangerous, as it is a fear of man and a fear of death, and such fear slows us, even freezes us, so that we are no good to anyone. But the perfect love of God casts out such fear and allows us for a right fear, which is a fear of God alone. Keeping that right fear helps a pilgrim to stay on the narrow way even toward the end of the journey. And going back to Jesus' Sermon on the Mount, Jesus continues by warning his followers of false prophets. As if referring to the way to heaven as narrow and that few travel on it, it is now, we come to find out, that there are false prophets on the way. These false prophets don't look like false prophets, but the opposite. They are gentle and mild as sheep, but are in fact wolves who want to devour true sheep. Jesus next tells us that there is a way to tell who are wolves in sheep's clothing. You will know them, he says, by their fruit. Fruit in the Bible refers to the deeds of men. And thus the warning is to note the hypocrisy of these so-called prophets. The principle is an easy one. Good trees produce good fruit. Bad trees produce bad fruit Bad trees cannot produce good fruit, and good trees cannot produce bad fruit. These truths are then followed by a warning of judgment. And all who plant orchards know that bad trees must be uprooted and burned in order not to corrupt the remaining trees. The word therefore in verse 20 ends this portion of Jesus' teachings, but in our book of common prayer, the authors decide to continue one passage more, verse 21. Verse 21, with the spine-tingling reality that there will be people who will stand before God on judgment day and think confidently that they were pilgrims on the narrow road. And revealed this confidence by referring to Jesus as Lord. But in truth, they were lawless and will be judged as such. As you know, St. Paul addressed many false prophets, many false teachers in the first century. Those false teachers consisted of men who said things such as, the resurrection has already taken place. Another said that Christian Gentiles must obey the Jewish ritual laws. Another said that Jesus was just a man and not God. And others said that Jesus didn't come in the flesh, but only appeared to come in the flesh. Those are then. What about now? What false teachings of our day do we hear? Some are the same and have been labeled Gnostic. The word Gnostic comes from the Greek word gnosis, which simply means knowledge. But the Gnostic teachers meant special knowledge Which was a knowledge of the Spirit being superior over the flesh. And therefore, any truth is only known in the Spirit. Such teachings, I hope you see, collide head-on with Christian truth. For God created the world and said it is good. And Jesus came in the flesh and remains in the flesh for eternity. And God Himself made the promise that the earth, the physical world, will be made new. With the incarnation, God becoming flesh, and with the promise of a new heaven and a new earth, God reveals that he cares for the physical world as much as he cares for the spiritual world. And for eternity he will live with his people in those worlds as one reality. Unfortunately The Gnostic understanding remains among us, especially amidst the evangelicals who do well to want to share the gospel of Jesus Christ with others but who fail to see the value and beauty of the physical world. Whereas Christians of old would carefully plan out their buildings so that they communicated Christian truths in many different ways, such as stained glass windows. with Christian symbols and saints, as well as carvings on the walls of wood and stone, and sanctuaries built in a cruciform shape so that if you look down upon it from on high, you would see the shape of the cross. Such planning is rare if not abandoned completely by modern evangelicals. For Western evangelicals, buildings are for practical use only. This results in what some have called a sancta catha gymatorium, which are multiple purpose rooms where you can play a basketball game and then move some chairs around and hold a worship service by and then follow by moving the same chairs around and bringing tables in and share a potluck meal Such practices fail to see the beauty of the physical world while only focusing on the spiritual. For those of you who are not inclined to care much about how buildings are designed or how beauty is to be used or how the physical world can be sacred I submit to you that if you were to see me break for lunch and leave my study and plop in front of the Holy Communion table and place a bag lunch on it and crack open a Coke can on it. Even you would conclude that such was an inappropriate action. It is that sensitivity that I am appealing to. Other false teachings of our day can be found primarily in the mainline churches who still call themselves Christian But who no longer insist that Jesus is the only way to heaven and teach that the ethical teachings of the Bible are no longer applicable. What is frustrating about such denominations is that they still call themselves Christians while completely abandoning what the Bible identifies as Christian and what most of history has called Christian. It was hoped that such leaders who abandoned the basic tenets of Christianity would simply start another religion instead of corrupting the one they are within. But alas. But let us examine how these denominations went rogue, and in particular what happened to the Episcopal Church in America. There were multiple reasons why the Episcopal Church is no longer Orthodox Christian, but we will only look at one of those reasons. In 1976, after many years of rumblings, the Episcopal Church voted to ordain women into the priesthood. Even though the Bible, historical practice of the church, and reason were against it. But how did they get there One origin for the change was how they interpreted the Bible. A prominent passage on the subject of women's ordination is from 1 Timothy 2, verse 12 and following. It reads Paul says, I do not permit a woman to teach or have authority over a man, but to be in silence. For Adam was formed first and then Eve, and Adam was not deceived, but the woman being deceived fell into transgression. The instruction is straightforward enough, and the church historically interpreted the instruction for its plain and obvious meaning. For Paul uses scripture, the reference to the creation of mankind and the fall of mankind. That is the base of his decision not to allow women to have authority in the church. Add this to Paul's instruction to the Corinthians not to allow a woman to speak out in the church, and Jesus calling only men, an Old Testament priest only being men And the desire for God to be relatable as our Father, and such is enough to conclude that only men should serve as priests. And on a side note, be careful what you wish for. For a woman to want to do as men do in callings such as priests. The duties can come with great burdens and greater judgment before God. As we prepare to call a new bishop. I have worked close enough to Bishop Gillen as president of the Standing Committee, allowing me to see the great responsibilities and great difficulties That come with the calling of a bishop. And I have concluded that it is not a position anyone should think of as a promotion. As far as the painful work and needed commitment, it can be seen as a demotion But back to our examination of what went wrong regarding women's ordination in the Episcopal Church in America Episcopal scholars started listening to the teachings of those who worked in the field of what is called biblical criticism. Biblical criticism was created to examine the Bible through modern scholarship means. It attempts to place the Bible in modern literary literary categories and then break it down with a modern understanding of the world. For example, biblical criticism starts with the premise that miracles do not occur. With that premise, they then toss out any mention of a miracle as being non-historical, placing such stories in the category of fantasy or fiction or both. It was philosopher David Hume who convinced the educated world that miracles are impossible because causality cannot be experienced. While never addressing that the very definition of a miracle is to overcome the impossible and be without Addressing the issue of experience. So biblical criticism as a discipline looks at Paul's instruction that women should not lead in the church. and forces its own interpretation by reading into the text what is not there. They say that Paul himself was misogynistic And therefore had prejudice against women, and that disqualifies him to comment about the subject. Next, they say that women were not allowed access to the same education as men, and therefore they could later rise to lead the church when that education was available. Next, they say that other texts seem to show women as leaders in certain churches, such as Priscilla and Aquila explaining together to Apollo. What he lacked in understanding about Jesus. All of it together was cause to change the polity of the church while also changing the authority of Holy Scripture. Beloved, there is a reason why idioms such as, if a camel is allowed to get its nose inside of a tent, it will be impossible to prevent the rest of it from entering. It is similar to the Western saying, if you give them an inch, they will take a mile. Such thinking is said to be fallacious because it doesn't always come true. But it came true in the Episcopal Church. Once such passages of Scripture were allowed to be dismissed because the motive of the instruction or the character of the author could be questioned Then any teaching or instruction could be called into question and eventually dismissed. Beloved, the very same method of interpreting the Bible, what is called hermeneutics, That was used to ordain women was also used later to accept immoral sexual behavior practiced by priests and also practiced by bishops The camel got fully into the tent. I realize I have taken you on a higher level of thinking journey, so allow me to simplify the point about false prophets that Jesus warns about. They do as the devil did in the Garden of Eden. They simply ask us to question if God really said what the Bible says he said. To Eve the devil said, Has God indeed said you shall not eat of every tree of the garden? This was followed with a bold-faced contradiction saying, You shall not surely die. The devil continues the same tactic today. With such questions, the devil repeatedly succeeds in getting people to doubt what God has said. Clearly said, and to accept an alternative that is false and leads to the false prophets and those who follow them to be cut down and burned. But we are told to look for the fruit of these false prophets. Since the nineteen seventies, false prophets in the Episcopal Church have taught publicly that Jesus was not divine, that he was not raised from the dead, and that the God of the Old Testament was guilty of bloodlust. And no ecclesiastical condemnation of such teachings has come forth with no conviction of betraying their ordination vows. The Episcopal Church had a peak membership in the 1950s of 3. 3 million people. They now number half as many, and that tally was taken in 2019 before the pandemic. Another survey shows that from 2009 to 2019, the Episcopal Church averaged just over 5,000 people in attendance on a given Sunday, while dropping nearly 3% every year through that decade. And the average age of an Episcopalian is 69 years old. Six years ago. It was reported that one of the largest congregations in the Episcopal Church consisted of 300 Muslim men who met for prayer in the Church of the Epiphany in Washington, D. C. , every Friday. And no, they were not praying to Jesus. If you want to see fruit, there is your fruit. We pray in the call it for this week to have hurtful things put away from us. Hurtful things include false teachings. Beloved, we have been gifted to have the Bible given to us by God through his church, just as he promised, to guide his church into all truth. We have been gifted with traditional interpretation of the same scriptures for almost 2,000 years. That is why many of us will not put up with false prophets and teachers who say that they have something new. No, they do not, and they have never mastered what is old. Let us master the old so we can quickly identify the fruit of those who are false This next analogy is older, but it still works. Before the technological advances we have today, federal agents in the United States were trained to spot counterfeit money. Not by examining the counterfeit bills, but by examining what a real bill was. The theory was: if you know a real bill well, a counterfeit will be obvious We can apply the same to our Christian faith. When you know well what the scriptures say, you will more easily identify a false prophet. And young people, young people, the church needs more men who care about this. It needs more men who want to know the scriptures and teach the scriptures and to identify those who are teaching falsely. Few answer such a calling, but such a calling has great reward. Let us pray. Our most merciful Father, we thank you for the warning of our Savior, your Son. We pray that we would be diligent followers of Him, noting the false prophets. And not allowing them to speak and mislead your people. And for anyone, dear Lord, who would Feel the calling to pursue the ministry that they might stand for the truth against these false teachers. May you move upon them, Holy Spirit. Encourage them to seek, and they will find. This we pray in Jesus name. Amen

sermons.title: Ignorant Righteousness
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I encourage you to turn in your Bibles to 1 Corinthians chapter 10. 1 Corinthians chapter 10, we will spend most of our time there, verses 1 through 13. I begin by sharing a story with you that few have heard before. I am neither proud nor embarrassed by this story. I graduated from seminary with honors as my grade point average achieved Magna cum laude status. I'm not bragging because I follow that up by telling you that I graduated from college with no honors, sitting in the back of class whenever I could. And my college counselor looked at my transcripts and he said, Well, I have always said anything above a C grade is wasted effort I thought it was a great line, honestly. But back to my story. I took a class in seminary titled Pastoral Counseling. The professor was training us on the latest methods of counseling, only putting a Christian spin on the techniques. He rarely brought the Holy Scriptures into the curriculum. Toward the end of the class, he gave us an assignment. We were to choose any book on counseling and write a review. This was great for me because I had just bought a book titled Psychobattle by Richard Gance. The book takes a harsh view of modern counseling techniques and instead challenges the reader to approach psychological issues from a biblical standpoint only. My report was highly in favor of the book, and when I received my written review back, the grade I received was a C I immediately set up a time to meet with the professor to discuss the grade. In summary, he said to me that if I agreed with what the book said. That I had disregarded all that had been taught in the class. I scrambled in my brain I then said that I thought the assignment was to write a review as if you were the author of the book, thus writing from the author's perspective. He looked surprised and said, well, if that is the case, then I can see why you wrote what you wrote. And he changed my grade to an A. Now again, I said I am neither proud nor embarrassed about that story. And my reasoning is that I have learned to play the game of higher education. And that game is still going on as I learned while teaching at the university. If you give them what they want, they will give you what you want. It is not about truth, not about knowledge, not about learning, but is instead about indoctrination. I have come to the conclusion that higher learning is neither higher nor is it learning. Most institutions should be abolished, but I state that as just a subjective opinion As G. K. Chesterton put it about a hundred years ago, it is not the uneducated that I fear, but the poorly educated. I told you this story because I read a lot of psychology in St. Paul's letter to the Corinthians, and in particular in chapter 10, as we read the Epistle Lesson. The modern definition of psychology is the study of the mind and behavior of a human being. The origin of the word, however, is different It is that addressing the psyche or the soul of a person and what can be known about a person's soul. First, let's have some background about the Epistle lesson. In chapter 9 of 1 Corinthians, St. Paul teaches how to approach the subject of eating meat offered to idols. Corinth was a city that worshipped many gods by means of offering sacrifices, and then such meat would be available to buy and consume in the public market. Jews, of course, would have nothing to do with such meat, but it became a question of whether Gentile Christians could eat such meat Paul uses the question to talk about freedom in Christ, and yet there is a principle to care for those who might be offended. The concern for those possibly offended was not in regards to their feelings, as it is in our culture today, but about offending the faith of others. Offending the faith. Paul talks next about making himself a slave for the sake of others, even though he is free in Christ. And then he adds to that metaphor that he treats his Christian life as if he is running a race so that he might win, and the win is a heavenly reward. It is with that discipline of training his body to live a disciplined life for the sake of a heavenly reward. that he begins to use the history of the Israel people as an example of a warning of how not to run the race. What I want us to keep in mind is that the primary purpose of all of these metaphors and references is so that the Christians at Corinth would receive their heavenly reward. This means that we need to get out of our heads The idea that God is as a taskmaster with a clipboard making marks every time we sin with the plan of making a case against us when it comes to final judgment. We also need to get out of our heads the idea that God is somehow crushed in spirit when we sin, as if our sin takes something out of him or away from him. We likely get this from bad preaching that says that our sins put Jesus on the cross. No, Jesus put himself on the cross for us. And while he needed to do so because our sin has condemned us, our sin never takes away from God. Anything from God. He is the same yesterday, today, and forever. What God cares about regarding our sin is what it does to us and what it does to our fellow Christian. With those truths in our psyche, within our souls, we look at Paul's words in 1 Corinthians chapter 10. In verses 1 through 5, he describes the Israelites who were delivered from bondage in Egypt And describes how they had a type of Christian experience and that they were baptized when under the cloud Which represented the presence of God, and baptized while walking through the Red Sea, as it was walled up by God, and the ground they walked on was dry. For those of us who believe that God made the heavens and earth out of nothing, it is not hard to imagine this miracle. And so Israel, Paul explains, was baptized, all ages baptized, and it wasn't by the mode of immersion. As one writer put it, the Israelites were baptized without immersion, while the Egyptians were immersed without being baptized. Also, the Israelites experienced the second sacrament, which is Holy Communion, in that they ate spiritual food, which was manna from heaven And they drank spiritual drink, which came from the rock that Moses struck. And then St. Paul mixes his metaphors by referring to Jesus as the rock, who was not only strong as a rock, but was also struck. But even though all of these good things happened to those Israelites, even though they walked with God through baptism and through holy communion, They still do not walk as God had commanded and therefore were judged in this world And this reminds us of the Protestant warning stemming from the Latin ex opere operato, meaning by the works performed. It is a caution that the effectiveness of the sacraments are not in the partaking of the sacrament only, but require faith, faith from the one whom is receiving the sacrament. Sacraments are a means of grace to us when faith in Christ Jesus is included, not just the work itself. According to verses 6 and 7, the simple problem with the Israelites, even after receiving the sacraments, was that they lusted after evil things. We remember the story to be that when Moses remained on the mountain for a significant period of time, the people complained, and then they concluded that Moses was dead. And that God wanted to be worshipped in a similar manner that the Egyptians worshiped their false gods. And so they put their gold together and molded a golden calf. And then they worship the same calf while performing sexual acts as they saw the Egyptians doing. From this we are to be well warned about negative influences all around us They call us to do as they do. And it is easier to be like them than it is to break away and to live a life of sacrifice. But breaking away every Christian must do. The word sexual immorality in verse 8 and following covers all sorts of sexual sins. We moderns get focused on homosexual acts, whereas sexual immorality includes fornication, adultery, and others. And the citizens at Corinth were regularly confronted by sexual immorality. It was freely practiced as a part of their religious and culturally accepted behavior. For the Christian to act differently was a call to come out from among the sinners and to be noticeable saints. The mention of serpents was how God judged those Israelites who committed blatant sexual immorality. The murmuring describes, those were complaints against Moses and Aaron. God punished those guilty with a plague which is described to the Corinthians as an angel of destruction. Paul then teaches that all of that which occurred to the Israelites is now to be understood by the Corinthians as being an admonition not to do as they did. That point takes us back to what I said earlier, which is that God wants us to receive a heavenly reward. We are told elsewhere that God has no pleasure in the death of a sinner. God wills, he says, for all persons to be saved. But he also respects the will of individuals and respects it enough that those who choose to be against him, they will get what they desire. It is out of love that we are warned that if we think we will not be tempted to go after our lusts, That such is like thinking that we stand by ourselves. And to think that way will end up in us falling. Which is to fall into the sin we think we are strong enough to stand against. And with that We are to understand that we can indeed endure temptation, not by ourselves, but because God will be there for us, ensuring that no matter how hard the temptation He will make sure it is not more than we can endure, and he always promises us an escape. A key phrase to understand where God is when we are tempted is God is faithful. In the context of us being tempted, it means that God will do his part. He delivers us from evil just as he told us to pray. He is watching over us to be sure we are not overwhelmed by temptation. He will indeed, without a doubt, without question, provide an escape for us. Evidence that God wants to be understood by us to be benevolent We have from our gospel reading, where we are told of two men who react to their promised inheritance quite differently. The youngest wants his inheritance while his father is still alive, thus treating his father as if he were already dead. The father had provided everything the youngest son needed to live comfortably in this life, and yet the young man wanted more. He wanted to pursue his lusts. The oldest son stayed behind, doing as he had done before, for he was dutiful and proud to be dutiful. When the youngest son spent all his money, and he had been reduced to the lowest of servitude to stay alive. All the while his father waited for him to return, for there was always opportunity to return. Once the young man understood the benevolence of his father, he returned to be a servant only to be received as a son, as an inheritor. That is how God sees all who are his children. It is why God calls all of his children, male or female, to be sons, because we will all, regardless of our gender, be inheritors. But the story Jesus tells isn't about the young son only. There is the older son who stayed behind, but for the wrong reason. He stayed behind because he thought he was earning his inheritance and thus the favor of his father. But his father always had favor for him because he was his son. Not because he didn't go off whoring or spending his inheritance, but because he was his son. In verse 28, Jesus says that the older son was angry. His anger was self-righteous. He believed he deserved the celebratory meal. Such a celebration should have been about him being loyal to his father. While he is angry, his father is always giving opportunity for the son to come to the celebration. And to get out of his self-righteous ways. And remember how the story ends. The father refers to the younger son being alive again. Being found after being lost. And as far as we know, the Father is still outside, outside the celebration Waiting for his oldest son to repent of his anger and come in and celebrate. God is still waiting. The author of the book I mentioned at the beginning of the sermon is Richard Ganz, as I said. In chapter 11 of Cycle Babel, he tells the story of a man named Harry. Who came to see the doctor in order to help him stop his countless sexually immoral escapades while he worked as a traveling circus acrobat? He had recently become a Christian, and a major reason for becoming a Christian was to be delivered from his sexual temptations. What he was coming to Dr. Gance about actually was to complain that Christianity was not working for him. He explained that although he was living a celibate life, his desires for sexual satisfaction were as strong as ever. He believed he could not continue as a Christian if the desires were not removed. In summary, he thought Jesus would remove his sexually sinful desires, and when that did not occur, he concluded that Christianity did not work for him I hope you can see the similar thoughts of both Harry, the acrobat, and the oldest son in Jesus' parable. Both think that life should be about them. The oldest thought that if there was to be a celebration, it should be about him. And Harry thought that Christianity and the power of the gospel should be about him and how his desires needed to be eradicated. Such is what modern psychology promotes. It feeds the soul, the psyche, with the lie that life should be about you. And thus you can create your own realities and your own perceptions of God or gods as long as it feeds your feelings. Modern man says that modern self is king, and yet Christianity proclaims that Christ is king and there can be no other king. But when we make ourselves our own king, we follow after our own lusts, and in the end, that results in hurt and guilt, embarrassment, and painful memories. But when Jesus is King, we have everything at our disposal to be overcomers of sin inwardly and sin outwardly. Upon reflecting on his patient Harry, Dr. Dance shares what he had learned since. He says this, I came. To see that the glory of our faith is not that we have no desire to sin, but that we do not have to act on those desires. I also came to learn that it was God who gave us the power to say no to sin. It was God who made us both to will and to work his good pleasure. Philippians Chapter 2, verse 13. And so I close with one final example from our study of pilgrim's progress. Christian, our main character, tries to convince a man named Ignorance that he cannot rely on his own strength to be righteous. And that he has misunderstood why he is to place his faith in Jesus alone. The next quote from Christians summarizes the main error of this character, ignorance. Christian says to him, your beliefs make Christ a justifier of your actions, but not of your person. You think that your person is justified for your actions' sake, which is false. Indeed, it is false. Jesus wants to justify your person. And we only need to ask him to do so. And then let him. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God, for the power to overcome sin, for the power to say no to sin. For the ability to live as you have called us, we thank you, knowing that it is your work. It is your desire, it is your will. May we match our wills to yours. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Standing Afar Off
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated I am going to read our gospel lesson again while interrupting myself with commentary. So Luke chapter 18, verse 9. Also he spoke this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous. and despised others. The manner this parable begins reveals that it does not have a necessary connection to what came before it and what came after it. Luke, our author, was told about the parable and decided that it fit between the persistent widow and the rich young ruler. Perhaps it is an example of persistence on the part of the tax collector needing forgiveness, and the Pharisee being rich in self-righteousness, again which is told after. The verse also gives the purpose of the parable. The persons who trusted in themselves And these are not specified to be the actual Pharisees. It could be anyone that has such an attitude. The Pharisees are the easiest example. The word for despise means count for nothing. And is again one of those words which St. Luke's has that the other gospel writers have not. This arrogant depreciation of others by the Pharisee would seem almost an exaggeration. If experience and history did not show how easily men and women of religious societies and orders drift into it. And how hard it is to set any limits on religious egotism. Verse 10. Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. As bad a rap as the Pharisees get in the New Testament, it should be known that they started out to be a very important sect. as they began for the purpose of maintaining piety amidst the Jewish people while most were going the way of the Greeks. By the time Jesus arrived, their piety resulted in some massive egos. That the Pharisee would go to the temple to pray is not surprising. That is where he expected himself to be. The tax collector, however, is a different story. Tax collectors in the first century, I remind you, were considered traitors by their fellow Jews, and rightfully so. They were employed by Rome to take money from their fellow Jews, and many of them demanded extra fees and took the raised amount for themselves. Their reputation is why it was a surprise for Jesus to risk calling Matthew as an apostle and for him to dine with Zacchaeus. Verse 11. The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust Adulterers, or even as this tax collector. That the Pharisees stood indicates nothing For the tax collector stood as well. It was and is a respectful posture of prayer. The phrase with himself can have a double meaning. First, it means that he stood apart from others, thus making himself a self-perceived superior Second, the phrase can refer to his prayer. The man may as well have been praying to himself. If he had faith in God and thus a right definition of God, he would have known what God knows, and thus he didn't need to list all of his good works. But he wanted others to hear, as well as his own ears, to hear about himself. We also notice that he first lists what he is not rather than what he has done Of course, we know that there is no righteousness without sacrificial blood, for death is required where there is sin. And we also know that men are poor at judging themselves. It will be God who will determine if the Pharisee has extorted or been unjust or committed adultery. After all, Jesus identified Pharisees as stealing from widows. Verse twelve. I fast twice a week, I give tithes of all that I possess. Here are the positive things the Pharisee did, and he did them beyond what was required. They were only to fast, required by law, according to Mosaic law, to fast two days out of a whole year. He fasted twice a week. There was only a tithe required of certain goods, not of everything. Yet he tithe of all that he owned Thus, in his conscience, he not only was righteous, but he has righteousness stored up. Verse thirteen. And the tax collector, standing afar off, would not so much as raise his eyes to heaven But beat his breast, saying, God, be merciful to be merciful to me, a sinner. Of course, the contrast is obvious to display the importance of humility whenever one approaches the throne of God. The standing afar off and the not lifting up of his eyes all speak to a humility That fears God standing before him, but knows that in order for his soul to have peace, he must stand there before God. The pounding of the chest seems to imply a tension of the vessels of the heart, such as we all feel in deep emotion. To which fist pounding seems in some measure to relieve. So men strike their chest When they suffer from cold to quicken the circulation of the blood. And it could also symbolize where sin buries itself and how we need to have our hearts cleansed. The tax collector refers to himself as a sinner, but it literally can read, To me the sinner. As though, like St. Paul, he singled out his own guilt as exceptional and thought of himself as the chief of sinners. Verse 14, Jesus says, I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted. The Greek word for justified implies a completed and abiding justification, which is a recognition that all men are saved by grace through faith alone. There is also something suggestive in the fact that the house is made the test for each of these men. Jesus said both went home. Home life is the test of the reality and acceptableness of our worship for God. Are we truly who we say we are? And that is proven in the home. The Pharisee, in spite of his self-congratulations, betrayed a conscience that focused more on the sins of others than that of his own The tax collector, not in spite of his self-condemnation, but by reason of it, went home with a new sense of peace, which will show itself in a new gentleness and cheerfulness. The latter part of the verse is a proverb within a parable. It is an axiomatic truth within the kingdom of God where Jesus reigns. Persons can only be exalted by humbling themselves. There is no other way to be exalted. There is no other way to see Jesus and be glad to see him but by humbling yourself. And we notice again that such humility is a choice we make. And no one can make that choice for you. Either you accept that you are a sinner in need of a savior Who can and will forgive your sins, or you die in your sin and suffer damnation But such can be said in a more positive manner, as St. Paul does to the Corinthians, which was our epistle reading. Paul says in chapter 15, verse 3 to the Corinthians, for I delivered to you, first of all, that which I also received, that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures. Because the wages of sin is death, someone has to die for your sins to be forgiven you. And if it is you that dies. For your own sin, there is no atonement because you are not a spotless sacrifice. Your death is only what is deserved because of your sin. What you need is someone paying atonement. Atonement is an offering for the purpose of purity The sacrifice makes what is being sacrificed for pure, which is to have no sin counted against you To say that Jesus died for our sins is to say that he atoned for our sins, and to say it was done according to the scriptures. He is not just talking about the gospels, but all of the Old Testament, what it required when it comes to fulfilling the law, which was both the moral law and the ceremonial law Jesus was sacrificed according to and in accordance with the scriptures. But how do we know? That the sacrifice of Jesus was sufficient for the atoning needs of our sins. Paul goes on. And that he was buried, and that he rose again on the third day according to the scriptures. Such is the evidence of what Jesus accomplished These are stated historical facts. Jesus was buried. Buried in the tomb owned by Joseph of Arimathea. He was buried according to the law, as the sun was setting on Friday, and thus entering into the Jewish Sabbath, which was a day he could not have been buried according to the law. Further proof of our sins being atoned for is that the same Jesus who was buried was next raised from the dead on the third day. Which means Friday counts as one day, Saturday as day two, and Sunday as day three. But how do we know that Jesus was raised from the dead? Someone could have stolen his body, or Jesus wasn't really dead but snuck out of the tomb, or someone took the body and buried it somewhere else. So Paul goes on. And that he was seen by Cephas, who is Peter, then by the twelve. So there were eyewitnesses to Jesus being alive. A stolen body cannot appear alive. Jesus being tortured and nailed to a tree would have no strength to sneak away. But what if the apostles got together to tell a big lie? A lie upon which each of them swore to keep hidden in order to start a new religion upon which they all would die for. First, who in their right mind would start a religion that they knew they would have to die for while knowing the religion is based off of a lie? Second, Paul has another answer. After that, he, Jesus, was seen by over 500 brethren at once, of whom the greater part remained to the present, but some have fallen asleep. That is a lot of witnesses who could verify everything Paul was describing. And there were many still alive who could be questioned about all that Paul had stated. So to my surprise, I ran across ten different theories as to how Jesus did not rise from the dead. I mentioned the stolen body theory. This was the earliest theory put forth by the Jewish religious leaders, you remember, in the Gospels. Claiming that the disciples came and stole the body of Jesus away and then started to spread the lie of a resurrection. The rebuttal to this story admits, first of all, that there was an empty tomb. This theory was never accepted, however, by the Jews, and it could easily be dismantled. First, we are supposed to believe that the disciples, mostly fishermen, were able to overpower battle-hardened Roman soldiers. Second, we know that they were cowards. They fled when Jesus was arrested, and when he was suffering and in the grave, they were hiding for their lives. Fourth, as we have asked, why would the disciples willingly die, which they did, for a lie that Jesus had risen from the dead? And so the only conclusion we can come is that the truth remains, Jesus is risen, so your sins are forgiven. Then there's the swoon theory. This theory gained traction with the Passover plot book in 1965 and a film in 1976. The concept is that Jesus did not die on the cross, but rather swooned or fainted. The unconscious body of Jesus was removed from the cross and placed in the tomb. Later, he just woke up and got out of the tomb. And the disciples saw him, they thought he was resurrected from the dead. The rebuttal again is that there was an empty tomb. And we also consider that Jesus was whipped 39 times by a cat of nine-tails, tearing his back to pieces. Jesus was then nailed to a cross with large stakes. After death, he was placed in a tomb with no medical attention for at least 36 hours. If he did revive, how could he even gotten out of the tomb which was sealed by a large stone? The only conclusion again we can come to is that Jesus is risen, so your sins are forgiven. Then there's the hallucination theory, and this theory says that they were all hallucinating together, thinking that Jesus had been raised from the dead. The rebuttal is that medical evidence has shown that a group of people cannot hallucinate the same thing. It's an individual thing, not a group thing to do And so, again, because of a silly theory, we can say that Jesus is risen and your sins are forgiven. Then there's the mistaken identity theory that wasn't the right guy. Someone else was on the cross. Well that means that Mary couldn't recognize her own son, that John, who followed him for three years, couldn't recognize His identity. Again, Jesus is risen, so your sins are forgiven. Then there's there's a theory that says, well, this is just a copy of pagan myth. There are others who said to be raised from the dead. The only problem with this is that those so-called stories similar to Jesus actually came after his death, not before his death. And so we say again, Jesus is risen. Your sins are forgiven. Then there's the wrong tomb theory. They went to a tomb. They thought it was Jesus. It wasn't his, but they thought he was gone. Therefore, that's silly. Joseph of Arimathea knew where it was. The Pharisees knew where it was. The Roman soldiers knew where it was. Thus again, Jesus is risen, so your sins are forgiven. Then there I hadn't heard this from the twin theory. Jesus had a twin. And it was him that was on the cross. And of course, if you're twins, we have some in our church. Can imagine twins talking it one talking another into actually going on the cross. Not quite And so we say Jesus is risen, your sins are forgiven. And again, this next one I hadn't heard. An alien theory. Jesus was an alien and actually was put in the tomb and beamed himself out of the tomb. Of course, in the times of Jesus, the first century, they knew nothing about aliens. And so we say Jesus again is risen, so your sins are forgiven. Then there's the contradiction theory. This simply states that the disciples had made a mistake. They were just basically telling a lie, uh wanting it to be true. But the answer to that is that it could easily Jesus' body could have easily been brought out and Paraded before the people, and evidence would show that Jesus was not alive. And thus we say again, the conclusion is Jesus is risen. So your sins are forgiven. And the last theory is the only theory. It's that Jesus did come alive again. And I thought about how to close this sermon this morning. I thought, you know, I need to come up with something clever. I need to come up with something memorable. And then I thought What better message do I have for any of us today? What do you need to hear? What do I need to hear? I need to hear that Jesus is risen and my sins are forgiven. And I know you need to hear that as well. That's the good news of the gospel. That we celebrate every Sunday, gathering together to celebrate. That Jesus is alive and my sins can be forgiven. Let us pray. Gracious and Heavenly Father, we thank you for this simple message. We thank you that as we pictured that That Pharisee and that tax collector standing before you, both of them needing forgiveness, but only one of them understanding. We have been privileged to hear the gospel of Jesus Christ, to know that we do need forgiveness. And then you give us that hope. That hope that Jesus has risen from the dead. And because of that, what we confess, what we ask for, forgiveness can be received. This day together, we give you thanks. In Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Hearing it andLiving it
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. You will be well served to turn in Mark chapter seven, starting at verse thirty-one, our gospel reading, Mark seven, verse thirty-one. Cindy. Cindy was faced with a dilemma. She was currently living with her mother, who was ill and bedridden And they were alone as her father passed away a few years prior. Her mother became so sick That she needed around the clock care. And they were finally able to find a nursing home that her insurance would pay for But with her mother moving out, Cindy would have to pay the rent for the current home in which they lived, and she could not afford it. The only option that she could see was to move in with her boyfriend. It made sense. They were practically engaged, which is practically being married, and they could more easily share the financial load together, so they did. They became roomies There was a problem, however. Both Cindy and her boyfriend claimed to be Christian. So, yes, their decision didn't reflect what they religiously claimed But their intent to be married someday seemed to allow their consciences not to be overburdened. And they concluded, they are saved by grace through faith. Their sins are covered by the blood of Jesus, and that includes their acts of fornication. Chris didn't have a dilemma at all. Chris had heard all his life that God was sovereign And that meant to him that it didn't matter what he did or didn't do, because God was in control, and there was nothing he could do or say that would change God's will. But Chris was in a rut. His life was mundane. His marriage was on life support. His kids were dabbling in sins of the flesh, experimenting with drugs and alcohol. Chris lived by the motto, let go and let go. And so he did. And nothing in his life changed. His marriage not only didn't get better, it got worse. And the distance relationally with his kids kept growing Chris began to see the Christian life as one false hope fading into another false hope until there was no more hope. Martha's life wasn't much better than Chris's. Her marriage was also on life support. Her children were also distant relationally from her. And her husband. But Martha wasn't going to just let go and let God. No, she believed in trying harder. If life wasn't the way you want it to be, just try harder. So she prayed harder. She read her Bible harder. She went to church harder. She worked on her marriage harder. She addressed her children harder. Unfortunately, no matter how harder Martha tried in all aspects of her life, her marriage didn't get better, and her children never drew closer to her. Either Christianity doesn't work, she concluded, or God has ceased to care for her. Now the first person I described, Cindy, who chose to live with her boyfriend, can be considered a nominalist. A nominalist doesn't necessarily equate ideas or doctrines with reality.
