As a Christian She can see that God's law condemns people who choose to live in sins such as adultery, but she can also conclude that such condemnation is an idea that doesn't result in anything real. Thus, Cindy doesn't need to fear God, but only appreciate his warnings. The second person described Chris Who just lets go and lets God, we can call a pacifist. Pacifists who are Christian Believe that the fate of the world, and thus their own personal fate, has been determined by God, and therefore there is nothing that they can do to alter that fate. So they do not need to take responsibility for their lives or the lives of those they are in relationship with. Thus, when such people like Chris live lives of despair, there is nothing they can see that can be done about it. Our last person, Martha, who just tries harder, can be called a moralist. Moralists who are Christian Subconsciously think that they can earn the favor of God, even though they say outwardly that they cannot. Such people will claim to be saved by grace alone while inwardly being convinced that if their life is good, then they are doing good things. And if their life is difficult, it is because they are sinning in some unknown manner or that God has abandoned them. My question for each of us today is which one are you closest to being? Are you closest to being a nominalist where you believe in this Christianity stuff, but not to the point that it should regulate every aspect of your life? Or are you closer to being a pacifist, thinking that there is only so much that you can do, and even that doesn't make much of a difference? Life simply comes at you, and you deal with it when it brings you, not overcoming anything, but just surviving. Or are you closer to being a moralist, which has you convinced that you can get what you earn, even in the spiritual realm? So if things are not going well, you simply have to work harder. The problem with each of the persons described is that they have not, have not encountered, truly encountered the transforming reality of the gospel of Jesus Christ. In our gospel reading, we are told of a deaf man who has a transforming encounter with Jesus. Now the setup we should go into prior to where our gospel reading began, Jesus was outside of Galilee among the Gentiles, and in our reading, he is still there. From the vicinity of Tyre, where he met the Syrophoenician woman, he traveled with his disciples northward towards Sidon and then southeast Down the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee into Decapolis, another Gentile region His traveling made a horseshoe-shaped trail about the distance of 120 miles Interestingly, the telling of this healing that we read today is only in Mark's gospel And so we see verse 32. We see in verse 32 that the Lord's reputation as a healer had been established on the previous visit to Decopolos, which is described in Mark chapter 5. The man who had been delivered from a demon, according to 5 verse 20, had told his story in all of the surrounding area. The people that believed in the man's story brought to Jesus this man who was deaf and mute. We are aware how difficult it is for people to learn to speak who cannot hear. In verse 33, Jesus removes the man from the crowd. Apparently for the same reason, he would later order those present at the healing not to talk about it. Remember that Jesus had a time frame for his ministry and he would stick to that time frame It is curious why Jesus chose specific physical techniques to carry out his miracle healings. We remember at one time he put mud on a blind man's eyes. What Jesus is obviously doing is physically touching the areas in which he is going to be working. First the ears and then the tongue. And this teaches us again how important physical touch is and how personal Jesus is. Why the saliva is more difficult to answer. In verse 34, we read that Jesus chose an Aramaic word to command the miracle Likely so that those around could be a witness, as Aramaic was the language known by Jews and by Gentiles. By looking up to heaven, he is making it clear where he came from, where he was going, and where the power was coming from that allowed him to do such a miracle. In verse 35, Mark makes it clear how quickly the miracle took place. At the words of Jesus, the man was healed. The Greek translated, his tongue was loose, is literally the chain of his tongue was broken. And a part of the miracle often overlooked is that the man could speak plainly. In normal scenarios such as this, a person would have to have speech lessons because he had not spoken before. But Jesus gave him the ability to speak plainly, which is to be understood in his speech. Verse 36, once again the Lord attempted to keep the popular excitement under control. He had as much to worry about from Philip the Tetrarch, who controlled Decopolis, as he had to worry about the Pharisees in Galilee. And once again, his effort to keep people quiet was futile. Jesus did not want people to make too much of his miracles. It was the understanding of his person, who he was, and the work that was he was doing that was most important. From verse 37, we get a great summation of who Jesus was. He was a man who did all things well. The last part of the verse is a reference to the prophet Isaiah, who said, Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped. Then They will leap for joy like a deer, and the mute tongue shall shout. We all likely know persons who have suffered great hearing loss. Watching a loved one disengage from social life because of hearing loss is terribly sad. Whenever my father-in-law has trouble with his hearing aids, he is no longer able to ask how you are? To tell you how he is doing, to enjoy the family storytelling and the laughter we all share when we get together. He is alone at those times. Not even able to enjoy the evening news on television. That is one type of deafness. But the Bible broadens the idea of deafness when it includes spirituality. What Mark makes reference to, the words of Isaiah, even more expansive, is that it is in the context of the promise of eventual triumph of God's salvation in the world. For just before the verse I read from Isaiah 35, there's a phrase that says this, the glory of Lebanon will be given. Well, what does that matter? Well, the regions of Tyre and Sidon, through which the Lord just passed, that's Lebanon. In other words, this miracle of giving hearing and the power of speech to a deaf mute, Mark understands to be a great picture of the salvation That the Lord would bring in the age of the Messiah, which is a fulfillment of biblical prophecy of the coming of the salvation of the world, not just the region, the world. That this miracle of healing a deaf mute has that symbolic significance of the world A picture of salvation from sin and death, a picture of the dawning of a new day, a new creation, a new world. is further confirmed by the way Mark speaks of hearing as a spiritual capacity. It is to be noted how often the word hear or hearing occurs in the Gospel of Mark with spiritual overtones. It's referring to grasping or understanding the significance of Jesus and the good news about him. The word occurs many times in Mark's account of the Lord's parables, and you will remember in chapter 4, it includes that citation from Isaiah chapter 6, where Isaiah says They may be seeing, but never perceiving, and ever hearing, but never understanding. Hearing, hearing then, in the Bible, is a metaphor for understanding. And so the opposite is true, as deafness is a metaphor or an illustration of mental and spiritual stubbornness. Both an incapacity and an unwillingness to understand what Jesus is saying, and an unwillingness to respond to him in faith. The problem wasn't that Jesus wasn't clear or that his teachings were too complicated so that it confused those who heard him. The problem wasn't in what Jesus said or how he said it. The problem was in the heart of the believers or unbelievers, I should say. The problem was that the people who heard him were spiritually deaf. They weren't capable of hearing the simple and wonderful news of salvation and eternal life. All of it that Jesus brought to them. So later in chapter 8, verse 18, when the Lord challenges his disciples, he says, Do you have eyes, but fail to see? And ears, but fail to hear? He is obviously using physical sight and physical hearing as an image of spiritual capacity. Multitudes of people saw Jesus and heard Jesus, but were blind as bats and deaf as posts. When it came to seeing who and what Jesus really was and hearing what he really said What I want us to try to imagine is how the life of that man who was once deaf and mute, how that life changed. To go from not being able to hear and speak, to being able to hear most clearly and to speak most plainly was likely day to night, I'm sorry, night to day for him. He was able to engage and interact with the world as he had never done before. And in a manner that was personal, intimate, and liberating. In short, his life was transformed and most certainly for the better Those of us who claim Christ, who claim to be Christian, we are not deaf, not physically or spiritually. But we can be, like me, half deaf. As most of you know, I am completely deaf in my left ear. I have been all my life, and so I don't know differently. It only becomes a handicap when people talk from my left side and I don't know I am being spoken to and then that person speaking to me may conclude that I am rather rude for not responding. The other handicap is that I don't know where certain sounds are coming from. Thus finding something that is beeping is quite difficult for me. So I can hear, but not always, and not always correctly. Which brings us back to the lives of Cindy, Chris, and Martha. To be a nominalist like Cindy, you have to be hearing because you acknowledge Jesus to be the Christ But you do not have the knowledge that reveals how a full embrace of Jesus as your Savior empowers you to live a life that matches what you say you believe. To live in sin is to be deaf to the wages of sin, and how real those wages are, which is why Jesus had to die. To be a pacifist like Chris, you have hearing because you believe in the highest nature of God in Christ Jesus, which is that he is sovereign. But you are deaf to your own responsibility to choose love, to enact forgiveness, to care for the downtrodden, to model a living faith. To be a moralist like Martha, you have hearing because you have faith that Jesus was who he said he was, but you are deaf to your inability to improve on the grace of God. As the Apostle Paul wrote, are you so foolish after being with the Spirit? Are you now trying to attain a goal by human effort? Christians are called, and it can be said that Christians are identified, to be a people who love the Lord our God with all of our heart, soul, mind, and strength This means that our hearts are fully transformed, beating for the love that God has given us. It means our souls are alive and ready to live for eternity. With the freedom from sin given to us by the blood of Jesus. It also means our minds are transformed to believing, hearing, and seeing things we could not before, prior. But that God has revealed and healed our spiritual eyes and ears. Finally, it means that we are to give our very lives, our living, our moving, our being, to serving God. That's a transformed life. From our epistle reading, we hear Paul convincing the Corinthians of the sufficiency of the gospel to transform lives. Such is compared to the sufficiency of ourselves. How much do you trust yourself to overcome vices? Or to be consistent in expressing love, or to stand your ground when persecuted for your faith. I can only speak for myself and confess that I am not sufficient. To live a faithful Christian life, but, but the Spirit that gives me life gives it and makes it sufficient that I can live and be an overcomer. Thus the Holy Spirit gives life so that the Sindhis of the faith will say no to compromise, and the Chris's of the faith will re-engage and be active in their pursuit of God And the martyrs of the faith would work to glorify God only. If you have ears to hear, you can ask Jesus at any time to transform your life. Anytime. Let us pray. A gracious and heavenly Father For this example of healing, for this empowerment to heal a man from being deaf and mute. We thank you. We thank you for that, man, but we thank you for what it means to us that you can transform lives, that you can change us and make us new. That spirit that you give us is sufficient to the task. May it be for all of us. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: The Radical Samaritan
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Okay, what about the people? In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. You will be well advised to turn to Luke chapter 10. Luke chapter 10, our focus this morning will be on the grand parable known as the Good Samaritan. Interestingly, it comes in the context of a man asking Jesus, what must he do to inherit eternal life? And we don't know if the man asked a sincere question, meaning that he was truly searching Or if he was asking a question to trap Jesus, as some other Christians were wanting to do. When the scribe stood up to address Jesus, such was a demonstration of respect. And calling him teacher was another demonstration of respect. But it is the follow-up question that has some scholars questioning his ultimate sincerity. It can be fairly speculated that the scribe knew the answer to his own question, but it can also be speculated that he wanted to see if Jesus thought the same way. And so when Jesus throws it back to him, he answers with the summation of the law. When Jesus is asked this at another time, he doesn't have the scribe answer as he does here, but answers it himself with the same answer, a summation of the law. The answer comes from the book of Leviticus and the Book of Deuteronomy. So the law of God provides New Testament truth to an everlasting covenant. But for a moment, let us examine what it is being required of all persons in order to be saved. People are to love God with all of their being. Which is summarized in heart, soul, strength, and mind. That phrasing covers all of what it is to be a human being. God is to be first and foremost in our lives. That is asking a lot for us, placing God first and foremost. It does not come naturally. Having inherited the sinful state of our souls from Adam leads us to put ourselves first. Our thoughts and our priorities are about us first. And even when we put God first, it is likely because we want something from Him, and so we're trying to earn His favor. For those who have walked the Christian life for several years, you know by experience that you will spend the rest of your living days striving to put God first in your life while trying to put yourself a distant third. And I say third because we are to also love our neighbor as ourselves. This too is a tall order. If we fail to put God first time and again, then how can we put our neighbor at the same level we put ourselves? Again, we need to accept that we will spend the rest of our living days striving to live up to this summary. And so in Luke chapter 10, verse 28. It was common in Jesus' day for Jews to think that the way to gain eternal life was to keep the commandments. Do as you're told. Statements to that effect can be found wherever one looks in the literature at this period. An older contemporary of Jesus, the famous Rabbi Hillel is quoted in the Mishnah as having said the following Who has gained for himself words of Torah has gained for himself the life in the world to come This scribe that's speaking to Jesus, the one questioning Jesus, had done nothing but repeat the common teachings of his day. But as with the Lord's conversation with the rich young ruler in Luke chapter 18, Jesus knew how to unmask self-righteousness and hypocrisy that was inherent in their understanding of gaining salvation. Whether for the purpose of debate or as a statement of hypotheticals Jesus agrees that a life of perfect obedience to God's law will indeed lead to salvation. The problem, of course, is that no one lives such a life That is what man did not understand, and that is what Jesus was about to show him. Verse 29. The typical Jew of the period did not doubt that the law of God could be kept well enough to earn salvation. The rabbis even spoke of people who kept the law in all of its specifics, and so naturally they talked at a great length about precisely how to keep the law Perhaps then the scribe genuinely wanted to know how to determine who his neighbor is in order that he might keep the law as it is summarized. It should be noted before we look at the answer given by Jesus that the Jews at the time did not include Gentiles as their neighbors, no matter how closely they lived to them. And so Jesus answers by describing a man going on a trip. The 17-mile descent from Jerusalem to Jericho has always been dangerous. The Roman general Pompeii had to wipe out stronghold brigands near Jericho, and the Crusades, a thousand years later, had to build a fort. At the halfway point to protect pilgrims traveling the same road. There are even some 19th-century accounts of pilgrims traveling the road with an armed guard and still being attacked. Stripped and robbed. To describe the victim as half dead is to say that he was unconscious and unable to call for help or even identify himself to any passerby. All of this is significant as we will see. The fact that he was stripped is not inconsequential. A person's ethnic religious community can be identified in the Near East today as it could be in the Near East in Jesus' day. either by his speech or by his dress. In this case, the man could not be identified by a passerby as to who he was or where he was from. They were certainly not all Jews that traveled that road, though many Jews did. And the hearers of the parable would have probably assumed that this man was a Jew. But no one could know for sure. Without clothing, he could be reduced to simply being a human being. Verse 31 The original hearers would immediately know that the priest of the Jews in those days belonged to the upper class of the nation. This priest would have been writing. In the Near East of that time, or for that matter, of this time, no one has who has any status would take a 17-mile hike through the desert. They rode, and this is the natural assumption of the parable. He had a donkey. The Samaritan also was riding, as we discover only after he is introduced. Because there was no need to mention the fact right here. But the point is that the priest was writing, and that's important If we were, if he were writing, excuse me, if he were not writing, he would not have been able to do what the Samaritan did for this man, and the comparison would be lost on us. Not only did the priest have an animal upon which to put the wounded man, as a member of the upper class, he had the means, the money, to do the very thing that the Samaritan did. But for whatever reason, the priest did not regard the wounded man, the victim, as his neighbor. Perhaps he was not a Jew Who could tell? Perhaps he was dead or would soon be dead, and that would mean the priest defiled himself by touching him. The ritual to remove such ceremonially uncleanness was time-consuming, expensive, and in some cases humiliating. These were reasons for the priest to think that the man was not his neighbor. For this priest, life was lived according to a codified system of do's and don'ts, of lesser and greater obligations and of qualified and unqualified commandments. The priest was not simply indifferent or cruel. He was likely weighing the matter in terms of rabbinic legislation. Which had largely forgotten the truth of the Old Testament, which is that he serves a God who loves mercy more than sacrifice. Verse 32. The nature of the road, its contours still visible in our day, and of travel in the desert at the time Led Near Eastern peasants today, when hearing this parable, to assume that the Levite knew that the priest had already passed the wounded man, and passed by himself in large measure because the priests did also. It helps to be reminded that the priests were derived from the tribe of Levi, but not all Levites were priests The Levite would have had the means, would not have the means that the priest had to care for the dying man, but he should have had the conviction to do something. Verse 33. The Lord's audience, those listening to the parable, original parable Would naturally expect Jesus to mention a Jewish layman to be the next passerby. First the priest, then a Levite, and then a Jewish layman. That is a natural progression Instead, to their shock, their amazement, and no doubt their offense, the third man on the road to come by the wounded man was a hated Samaritan. To the Jews, the Samaritans were the scum of the earth, and that's not an exaggeration. And it wasn't simply because of their ethnicity. The Samaritans were heretics, peoples whose religion was a mixture of Judaism and false teachings. They were the worst because they corrupted the Jewish faith. It is striking to our sensitive ears how bitter Jewish speech was toward the Samaritans in those days. We read in a Jewish commentary on the law, he that eats the bread of the Samaritans is like to one that eats the flesh of swine. In the synagogue, if you can believe it, prayers were offered that the Samaritans might not partake of eternal life. The hate was real and it was accepted. The key word in this verse is compassion. The Samaritan had it, while the other two men did not. To have compassion is to have both sympathy and pity. It is to be moved inwardly so that you must help outwardly. It is what all men need to have towards one another. Verse 34. The Samaritan acted on his compassion. And used his resources to bring the man to help. It was the least he could do. Verse 35. Because Jericho was a Jewish town, it would not have been friendly to the Samaritan, no matter how much means he had with him. What he does is in entering the town and assuring provisions for the victim combines compassion with great courage. Verses 36 and 37. Jesus has answered the scribe and answered him well. Even if the crowd objects, and they would object, because of the hate they had in their hearts, but not because of the truth of the example There are several lessons of course from this parable. The first I wish to point is not profound, but simple, a simple lesson on how Christians are to participate in charity. Needs are placed before all of us on a regular basis. There are people who are poor and in need in our own country And there is a great deal of need abroad that we are made aware of by the many me news sources that try to get get our attention every day. We can't possibly give to all of them, but we feel guilty when we don't give to any. But what this parable teaches is that charity Begins with those who are right in front of us. And I don't mean by in front of us, those on our screens. Where money is sent and someone we don't know makes choices as to how it's to be distributed after they take their cut. I mean in front of us as in people we encounter in the flesh. The Samaritan encountered the victim in the flesh and was able to have personal compassion on a specific person. Now I am not speaking against organizations such as Samaritan Purse or Anglican Relief. We should give to them as we are able But biblical charity is first and foremost caring for those you encounter in your life who are in need. Those are people you are to treat as your neighbor. The second lesson I underline is the recognition of just how high a standard the law places on all of us. That is part of our epistle lesson. When the law of God is applied to our lives, we recognize that it exposes our desire to break it and our inability to keep it. Even when it is summarized, we fall woefully short, both in loving God as we should, and loving our neighbor as we should. That is why Jesus is our Savior. He did not and does not fall short in anything. And the only way we can match the standard of God's law towards him and our fellow man is to have faith in the righteousness of Jesus. For it then becomes our righteousness, and it is that in how which we are saved. Thanks be to God. But there is another lesson I want to underline for all of us today. It is the lesson on how radical in our faith Jesus is calling us to be in this parable. The manner Jesus set up this parable of the Good Samaritan can be accurately described as radical. The priest going by and ignoring a dying man is radical. He was, after all, assigned to be a communicator to the people about who God is. And that God had revealed Himself, even in the law, as being slow to anger and abounding in love. God had revealed Himself As having the goal of being God to all he calls, and for them to be his people, meaning he wants to have a personal relationship with his people. God has revealed Himself in the Psalms as desiring to be amidst his people, even the sick and the broken and the victim. But when the priest passes by the victim on the road, he has none of that in his conscience, but only self-preservation. The Levi, I said, was not a priest, but was of a tribe that was assigned to serve the people. He was to be sensitive to the needs of people. But instead, he follows the poor example of the priest. And as we've noted, the people would have thought Jesus would present to them a simple Jew. As coming along and helping the victim, but instead he chooses a Samaritan for his example. And as has been shown, that was radical. And then the Samaritan uses all of his resources to have compassion on a man who would likely have hated him before he became a victim. Radical. And then the Samaritan goes beyond what he can do in the moment by securing help for the victimized man in the days to come. Radical again. And he does it in a city where most of the residents would not only socially reject the Samaritan, but would beat him if they had the chance. Radical again. So Jesus sets a radical example of faith and action before all who would follow him. Remember that he did something similar in John's Gospel when he told the crowd, unless you eat of my flesh and drink of my blood, you cannot be my disciple. And many stopped following him. Radical. But Jesus' radical standard is a call for a radical faith That turns away from the sins of the world and claims Jesus as Savior and Lord. You young people today You young people have opportunity to be radical about Jesus before your peers by refusing to follow fads and being pure in your moral living. You women have opportunity to be radical in your faith by refusing gossip, by submitting to your husbands, and by praising one another instead of backbiting as the world does. You men have opportunity to be radical in your Christian faith by laying your life down for your wives, by avoiding sexual immorality, and by loving your children unconditionally. But wait, how is such living radical? Young people being pure in moral living is what is expected if we claim to follow Jesus. Wives refusing to gossip and submitting to their husbands. Well, that's instructed by St. Paul in several places. Husbands avoiding sexual immorality and loving their children unconditionally. Are to be husband and father priorities. What is so radical about doing what is expected of you? Well, it has always been radical because it is a calling to do as the world around us does not It is understood that to live by such a standard will show you to be different. Salt of the earth. City on a hill. It shows to the unbelieving world that though you are in the world, you are not of the world, which means you are not a byproduct of the world. And beloved I tell you, the Lord brought this vision to me late in the evening. Christians Living obediently is so radical today because it is so very rare. We can even say that the Christian church is like the victim on the road to Jericho. There are so few who are actually following the way Jesus has taught that the church has been stolen from, beaten, and stripped, and left for dead. And it needs someone who will radically clothe her, pick her up, bandage her wounds, and see that she is cared for. That is radically done by Christians living as God has instructed and as Jesus has modeled. Let us pray. A gracious and heavenly Father, for this parable that is everlasting and the truths therein, we thank you. And I pray, dear Lord, that we as your people would see our opportunity to heal the church by living as you have called us to live, regardless of what the world does. To be the light, to be the city on a hill, to be the salt of the earth. May we all consider this a radical way to live In Jesus' name we pray, Amen.

sermons.title: In the Minority
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. It is a privilege, an honor to be behind this pulpit. The Lord has blessed me to be behind this pulpit a few times in my now over 23 years at St. Stephen's. And I do realize that we are getting quite older. I am currently helping coach our local football team in Eldersburg, the high school. And I sat there during a practice and realized that the age of these players is about seventeen years and that it will be forty years Before they are my age. And I will be ninety-seven years old. Probably not making it to ninety-seven. Time does go by. It is as a vapor, the writer of Ecclesiastes says. And so we need to receive every moment of it with gratefulness. I bring you greetings from our good bishop Raymond Charles Gillen. He thanks you for allowing me to be with you in his place and for your support of the diocese. It is my honor to be in his stead. God has used him profoundly, and I have witnessed such firsthand as the president of the standing committee. There have been rogue ministers who have disrespected his office and tried to take churches with them, and he has handled the instances with grace and godly care. There have been wolves that have tried to enter into our fold with fake credentials while fooling some sheep. And our bishop has remained steadfast and patient, and God uncovered their falsehood. Beloved, no bishop is perfect, and no bishop should be overly praised. But it is appropriate to be thankful to God when a bishop does the work of holding to sound doctrine and protecting the church. Amen. I also bring greetings from St. Stephen's Parish. We are your daughter, parish, and your sister, church. Bobby Lynn and I appreciate you and appreciate the friendship we share with your rector Cedric and his wonderful wife, Sarah. Spent many a meal together when we go on pastors and wives retreats, enjoying one another's company. But let us now look at our text from the gospel reading, Luke chapter 10 and the 10 lepers, Luke chapter 17, excuse me. Luke chapter 17 and the 10 lepers. Politically, I am probably more conservative than I need to be. But witnessing the Black Lives Matter upheaval over two years ago. Was difficult because I tried to understand it through the perspective of one of my daughters-in-law. And she is not near politically motivated as I am. But she knows at least one thing, one very important thing that I do not, which is what is it like to be a racial minority? Let us be honest and admit that life is much easier when you are in the majority. And the majority doesn't need to be based on race. You can be in the majority based on wealth, intelligence, status, arrogance, appearance, arrogance, and the like. Whatever the reason you are in the majority, you know that life is much easier Being in the minority is hard. When in the minority, the majority look upon you suspiciously. The majority can question the minority as if there is something wrong with them. The logic is that if you are in the minority, then you have Done something that has has you deserving to be in the minority, and you must change in order to be like those in the majority. It means that people are comfortable are comfortable around you when you are in the majority. Being in the minority is the opposite. You are not accepted and people are not comfortable around you. The account in the gospel according to Saint Luke, Jesus healing of the ten lepers, and only one returning to give him thanks and praise. Is a story about being in the minority. In verse 11 of Luke chapter 17, we we catch up with Jesus in the midst of his travels. The last time we knew for sure where he was, he was in Perea, the area east of the Jordan River. Now he is back on the west side of the river, but still moving slowly toward Jerusalem. We understand that he was not in any rush to reach the city, only needing to be there somewhat before the Passover. So it seems that he went this way and then another way, visiting various towns and villages along the way, following no natural north to south route. Verse 12 tells us that he entered a certain village. Which one? It doesn't matter. That is not the point of telling this story. The lepers met Jesus at the entrance to the village because lepers were required by law to keep their distance from the general public. They wanted to be healed by Jesus, but needed to cry out in order to keep their distance. They had heard of Jesus, surely most lepers had by that time, and they called him by name. From verse 14, we note what Jesus did not do. He did not touch them as he did when he healed other lepers. He did not make a show of this healing. He only told them to go show themselves to the priests. Such was required by the law of Moses, for those who were healed of skin diseases must show proof of such a healing in order to be received or get permission to be received to return to society. It appears then that Jesus was putting their faith to the test to see if they would go to the priests with the confidence that they would be healed. It seems also that the cure for their disease would not come until they were on their way to see the priests. Jesus shows again that his power was unlimited. Just as he had shown in chapter 7 of this same gospel when he healed the centurion servant Just by speaking it into being. What is curious is how our reading Can assume that the man who returns to Jesus went to the priest, was pronounced healed, and then returned to Jesus with thanks. But the text doesn't say that. It says that the one man of note saw that he was healed, which means that on his way to the priests, he noticed that he was healed. Thus, he did not go to the priest to have it pronounced that he was healed, but he knew it himself, and therefore he first went to Jesus. He went to Jesus to give thanks for his healing. So the man did not go on to see the priest until he had first returned to Jesus to offer his thanks. The fact that he praised God, as others who had been healed by Jesus had done before him, indicates that he saw in what Jesus had done for him the power and mercy of God. And we can know that he had every confidence that he was healed because he approached Jesus falling at his feet. Falling at his feet. For he no longer needed to keep his distance. And we might assume that the fact that the man was a Samaritan is an afterthought when in fact it is an important detail. Remember that the Jews and Samaritans did not like one another or associate with one another. For this man to fall down before a Jew was a further mark of his humility. And it was a further demonstration that faith in Jesus is nothing else. That nothing else matters. The language of verse 18 suggests that the other lepers who had been healed were Jews And that it was only the Samaritan who was not only happy to be healed, but grateful to the one who had healed him, so grateful that he had to express his gratitude immediately. It is very important for us to know that the phrase in verse 19, has made you well, can also be translated from the Greek has saved you. Thus the passage can read, arise, go your way, your faith has saved you. This is to remind us that the healing of Jesus always had a much greater end in mind, which was the salvation of souls. Jesus healed the body so that people would believe he was the Messiah and that he would put their faith in him for their sins to be forgiven. I always need to be reminded myself that Lazarus, whom Jesus raised from the dead, died again. Thus, the point of Jesus raising him was so that people would believe in him as the Messiah. It was never for the purpose of Lazarus simply being alive in this world. And in this story, it was never for the purpose of simply being healed of a skin disease, as difficult such a skin disease can be. The end goal is always the salvation of the soul. So the man who has his skin healed and his soul saved was a minority. He was a minority in that he was a Samaritan, and he was a minority in that he was a leper, and he was a minority in that he he alone He alone, one out of ten, fell at the feet of Jesus to worship him. Applying this story to our contemporary context, I ask, what did you come here to do today? Did you come to fall down at the feet of Jesus and give him thanks? In doing so, you have placed yourself in the minority. Gallup research from 2010 Says that just over 20% of the United States population attend church weekly. You can do the math That was 12 years ago and 10 years before the pandemic. No research has been reported recently, but we all know that church attendance is down since 2020. Also, that that 20% statistic included synagogues, mainline churches, and Mormon churches. Thus we can speculate that the percentage of people in America who attend Bible-believing churches each Sunday is half of that 20%, meaning 10%, meaning 1 out of 10. By coming to worship this morning, you are like the Samaritan leper who was healed by Jesus and returned to Jesus to worship him and be saved. And that also means that you are in the minority. And what do we say about being in the minority? You are not accepted, and people don't trust you. One of the most difficult decisions my wife and I made as parents was where to send our children for high school. It was difficult because we were keenly aware of how vulnerable their minds are as teenagers and how different their high school experience was going to be compared to first being homeschooled and then attending St. Stephen's Academy. I am very grateful to God that He impressed upon us as parents to prepare our children to be different. Whereas we might be tempted to help our children fit in with their peers, we purposefully told our children Not only not fit in, but be ready to be treated as if you are not accepted and that people do not trust you We did this not only to help them deal with peer pressure they would face in high school, but also what they would face for the remainder of their days on this earth. Because if you live the Christian life as Jesus instructed, you will not be accepted and people won't trust you. Now when I say won't trust you, I realize that that may not sit right with some of you, for it sounds like people won't trust you to watch their dog or collect their mail when they are on vacation That is not what I am referring to. Fact is, most non-believers will trust Christians more than other people to watch their dog and collect their mail. When saying people won't trust you, I am referring to what you stand for, which is the reason for your living. It is the same reason why the Pharisees didn't trust Jesus. He was too good, and they hated him for it. And this brings us to our epistle reading for this Sunday. As you know, Paul wrote to the Galatians because they had compromised the Christian faith by accepting the law as a means to their salvation. After Paul rebukes their understanding, he goes on to argue how it is by grace alone, through faith alone, that they will be saved. He also argues how the works of the Holy Spirit are superior to the works of the flesh. What he means by works of the flesh are simply the attempt of people To keep God's law while failing to do so, either in the heart or in the actions. In our epistle reading, he describes that what works of the flesh turn out to become. They become adultery, fornication, uncleanness, and lasciviousness, which can be related to sexual immorality He then adds witchcraft, hatred, envying, murder, and the like, which are all sins that desire hurting our fellow man. So we may summarize our human behavior without God in terms of sexual immorality or causing suffering upon our fellow man. And such rightly summarizes the plight of our inner cities in the United States today. In contrast, he then lists the fruits of the Spirit Love, joy, peace, and non-suffering. These reflect a flesh that is under control. These are fruits that come supernaturally as they have allowed the Holy Spirit to reign in a person's life. So that it is not the person's will that is in control, but the Holy Spirit Himself guiding and leading an individual to lead a holy life. Such is what Jesus meant when he said that we are to die to ourselves. To die to self is to let the Holy Spirit rule your life. Fruits such as gentleness, goodness, meekness, and temperance are what are practiced toward our fellow man. So that we are enabled to love our neighbor as ourselves, which was the lesson given to us last week in the story of the Good Samaritan. And the Good Samaritan was in the minority. He was a minority ethnically, but mostly he was a minority in terms of his having compassion on a man no one else would. And Jesus placed him as our standard for which Christians ought to strive. Of course, men like a Samaritan are placed in the minority because of how they were born. We cannot change our ethnicity or our gender, no matter what corrupt modern minds want to believe. And others become a part of the minority because of what happens to them, such as a person contracting leprosy. In both cases, minority status is thrust upon such people, and they have to learn to cope. To be Christian, in contrast, is something we choose, and thus we choose to be in the minority. When a young Christian, eighteen years of age, I read the following words of Jesus from St. Matthew's Gospel, chapter 7. Jesus said, Enter through the narrow gate, for wide is the gate, and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many enter through it. But small is the gate, and narrow the way that leads to life, and only a few find it. Those words bothered my young mind. Why would Jesus explain the way to his promise and the Christian journey as one that is not walked by men? That seemed to me at the time pessimistic and unattractive. If Jesus was taking a marketing class, he would fail. We Christians fall prey to the spirit of the age time and again when we base success and failure on how many people we attract. I have been asked too many times when we hold a special worship service or start a new outreach program, questions like, well, how many people were there? What is implied in such questions is that success is based on popularity. If such were true, of course. Jesus died as one of the least successful public figure figures in human history. I have heard as You have testimonies of ministries growing from a small Bible study in a home to thousands of people now attending, and we are to be convinced that such is evidence of success. But the real evidence of God's blessings, of his presence, of his victory over sin and death, for the benefit of those who follow him, the real evidence is love. Joy, peace, long-suffering, gentleness, and goodness. Displaying such fruits is living in the minority The real evidence of God changing a life is for that person to return to Jesus, to fall at his feet, and to worship him with thanksgiving. As that one leper did. To do so again is to live in the minority. To be Christian, beloved, is to be a minority. And it is to embrace a minority status. After all, why would Jesus tell us that the road to his kingdom is characterized by few traveling on it? How does such a knowledge help us? And elsewhere he says, many are called, but few are chosen. What is the purpose of him saying such things for those who follow him? It seems unnecessary information. Unless, unless we are to realize that to walk the narrow road, to display gifts of the Spirit To return to Jesus with thanksgiving is a rare thing to do. And we may think what we are doing is wrong. Or unaccepted or foolish because so many are not doing what we are doing. But Jesus warned us that we would be in the minority. Beloved, to be Christian is to be in the minority. And that is to be expected and embraced. And here is how here is how you stay in the minority When Saint Paul explains to the Roman Christians how people stray from God by exchanging, he says, the incorruptible for the corruptible He said it all started because although they knew God, they did not glorify him and they did not give him thanks. To stay in the minority, we must do as the one leper did. Glorify Jesus and give him thanks. Let us pray.

sermons.title: No Worry Necessary
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be deceated. Our focus this morning is from our gospel reading, Matthew chapter six, verses twenty-four through thirty-four. With the manner in which our present Western culture behaves, an objective observer could conclude that emotional anxiety Was introduced in the twenty-first century and has reached a pandemic status. Currently There are five hundred and eighteen thousand eight hundred and forty mental health professionals in the United States. This is compared to the number of ordained ministers in the United States. I excluded those churches that have become apostate. So the number is an estimate, but the number is almost half of those in the mental health field, coming in at 283,000. So there are roughly 283,000 ordained Christian ministers who believe the Bible to be true. And who teach and preach it for the sake of Christians in the United States, while there are 518,840 mental health professionals who treat troubled minds. I choose to say nothing about the number of mental health professionals, but I will say that the church is currently understaffed. We need more men to instruct Christians on how to apply the Word of God in their lives And I suspect many Christians do not know that Jesus spoke directly about anxiety that is experienced by many people. And for those of you who suffer from or are tempted by anxiety, you must know that the great physician Jesus has a remedy. First, Jesus knows of our weaknesses and of our worries We worry, all of us do, about tomorrow. We worry about where our daily bread will come from. Now, mind you, we Western Christians don't worry like those people did in the times of Jesus or in third world countries today. In Jesus' day, each day required a trip to the market for the evening meal. There were no refrigerators to store extra food. Pantries were not full of food with preservatives. Daily bread was a daily thought and pursuit. And making money each day was a thought because there were not salaries paid or contracts negotiated. You earned and were paid by the day. Almost nothing was guaranteed. This being understood, we can more easily imagine how tempting it was for the average person to pursue money. Because greater wealth meant lesser worry about each day. Human beings of all generations and from all cultures appreciate the blessing of having a mind at peace. Where worries are taken from you. Wealth can do that. It can give you greater peace of mind. I know this quite well as I was tempted to worry a great deal when there were eight people in our home and each of them wanted something to eat. Imagine that. And each of them had clothing needs, and each of them had wants for what their peers had. And my salary only went so far. The great irony of being older and making more money and being empty nesters is that now I can afford to have eight people in my home, but instead now there's only two But the temptation to pursue money means that money is a primary motive and desire of our hearts. And God has always been about changing the hearts of humans so that we can care about the right things as opposed to those things that are destructive. In Matthew chapter 6, verse 24, Jesus, our physician, identifies a problem. It is the same one found in the first two commandments and the same one recognized by Bob Dylan Each human being is created to serve something. Each human being is engineered to worship something. If a person doesn't worship the one true God, he or she will worship something in his stead. But you cannot worship both, as Jesus says, you cannot serve both. If two things are competing in your life, you will eventually hate and despise one and love and be loyal to the other. When God says, Thou shalt have no other gods before me, he is giving a warning and a truism. A truism. You will remember that the phrase before me means next to me, in front of me, behind me, in proximity to me. We can say that we are not to have any gods, little g come anywhere near or around the one true God. In verse 25, Jesus tells us that we are not to worry, which is to be anxious about basic needs in life. We all need to eat in order to live, and we all need to have clothing in order to be proper citizens and to have protection from the elements And Jesus tells us not to worry about such things, and we still worry about them. Yes, even we who live in the wealthiest country in the world, the world has ever known, even we worry about such things. Even though we have food in our refrigerator and freezers, an abundance of clothing in our drawers and closets, not to mention how many shoes we have. With all that we have, we still think that our next meal may not come, or our next ensemble may not be right, unless we worry about such things. Next, Jesus asks a rhetorical question: Is not life more than food and the body more than clothing? Yes, we say in our conscience, and then we go back to worrying about such things Did you know that the body can go between 8 to 21 days without food, depending on the condition of the body, before starvation? Did you know that a pair of Levi jeans can keep you covered and warm for two years being worn and washed daily The challenge found in the words of verse 26 is how we think about our God. We are to understand him to be a heavenly father, which means that he cares about his people. The point of examining the birds is that we are of much greater value to our Heavenly Father, having been made in his image compared to the birds of the air, and yet God provides for them naturally Thus, how much more will he assure that we are provided for? Besides, verse 27 points out, besides, what person can add anything to his being? to his height or the length of his days. Who can do add anything by worrying about your needs? Again, we answer in our conscience, no, we can't add anything, nothing to our stature by worrying, and yet then we go back to worry. Verse 28 provides another rhetorical question, and we answer it again in our conscience. We shouldn't worry about our clothing. And another example of God caring for his creation is given. He clothes the fields with beauty, and the fields do nothing to earn such clothing, but only receive it with thanks. These fields compared to the raiment of Solomon are more beautiful. Where I went to college at the University of Idaho. The school is in an area called the Palouse, with rolling hills that grow any number of crops. When you get a chance to see these hills from a bird's eye view, you see how beautiful they can be as their fruit is revealed in the richness of their soil. Such is clearly more beautiful than anything a person can wear. Verse 30 provides another opportunity for us to be shamed by a rhetorical question. Yes, our conscience says, God will much more clothe us who are made in his image than he will the fields around us. And his point at the end of the verse is the true problem, O you of little faith. Be challenged today and ask how big is your faith in God to provide what you need, what you daily need? If you do not have such faith, but instead replace it with worry, the simple answer is for you to repent. Repent and thus turn away from not having faith that God will provide for you what you daily need. And believe, have faith that He cares for you and can provide for you. In verses 31 and 32, Jesus makes the point clear that we are not to behave as the unbelieving world behaves. They concern themselves with what they will eat and drink daily. They concern themselves for this because they are their own masters. They serve themselves. They believe in themselves. They see themselves as the most sufficient provider. But God, the only true God, wants those who follow Him to trust in Him and Him alone as sole provider. And God, being who He is, which is all knowing, knows what your needs are better than you know them yourselves. It makes the most sense to put our faith for our daily needs into the one who owns the cattle on a thousand hills. In verse thirty-three, Jesus provides the alternative to worry To anxiousness about how our next need is going to be met. His answer is to seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness. But what does it mean to seek the kingdom of God? The simple answer is that followers of Jesus are to search for ways to express the love of God in their lives. A practical answer is to walk a journey that works to understand how to to how the love of God is to be applied to my employment The employment I have, to the spouse God has given me, to the family of which I am a part of, and to my fellow man who crosses my path. Thus, the kingdom of God is to be pursued in my home, where I strive to love my wife as Jesus loves his church I am to raise my children as inheritors of the kingdom of God. I am to treat my fellow Christians in God's church as beloved of God and saints. This means that I am to be a repeated offerer of forgiveness and respect, as well as a repeated requester of forgiveness and grace. In living my life in such a manner, I am part of God's kingdom being built here on earth as it is in heaven. And we note that Jesus added on to his instruction to seek the kingdom of God, which is to seek the righteousness of God as well. This means that my morality is to match my confession. The manner I live my life is to match up with the righteousness of God. Thus I am to be faithful to my wife, both emotionally and physically. I am to avoid the sins of the flesh and any contribution to those such sins. I'm to live my life in accordance with God's commandments, and if ever I become guilty of violating them, any one of them I am to confess my sins to God and to turn away from such behavior and once again be clothed by the righteousness of Christ Jesus. From these instructions, Jesus makes a very bold promise. If any person seeks the kingdom of God first and foremost, while also abiding by the moral standards God has set, All of his needs will be provided for, no worry necessary Thus, as was described, people are tempted to pursue money because money alleviates worry, and all human beings want to alleviate worry. But Jesus points to a different way, a way much different than the world around us. And he wants us to be different than the world around us. It is a way that has faith in God as the true provider, and so it ceases to worry and trust in our own strength, but instead seeks what is most pleasing to God. Which is for his kingdom to be revealed in our individual lives and for us to live wholly in honor of him. Verse 34 is a conclusion and a summation of what Jesus has said about worrying, about being anxious Do not worry about tomorrow. Easier said than done, right? Well, not if you apply faith in the Lord Jesus The logic is certainly there. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble. A more clear translation reads: each day has enough trouble of its own. And all of us say, Amen to that. We know by experience. Each of us, every Christian, should be living in the moment and dealing with troubles in the moment, and stop worrying about tomorrow. A tomorrow we cannot control. To do so is to have faith that what God has supplied for you in the moment is sufficient for you to find joy and to find peace. Now you might think these verses of Scripture would forbid planning for the future, such as having savings accounts or other investments for retirement. That is not what Jesus is speaking about. Other scriptures speak of receiving a reward for planning carefully for the future. Proverbs says, Go to the ant, O sluggard, consider her ways and be wise. Without having any chief, officer, or ruler, she prepares her bread in summer and gathers her food in harvest. Joseph, son of Jacob, in the book of Genesis, saved seven years of grain for the future, seven years of famine. So God is good with us planning and preparing for the future. But what Jesus is speaking about or against is worry and or anxiety about the future. He is speaking candidly about what it means to live day by day with faith in him, not in your bank accounts, in him. A life of faith in Jesus Christ is trusting of God to provide what we daily need while we use our energy to seek his kingdom and his righteousness. I have attempted to minister to people with various forms of anxiety And my experience has taught me that not all anxiety is the same, and some are treated differently than others. I don't attempt to speak authoritatively about different medications, whether needed or not needed. What I do say is what Jesus said. The formula for treating all forms of anxiety, all temptations to worry, is to seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness. But, someone might protest, you're saying anxiety can be cured without medication. No, I am not. I simply said what Jesus said, which is, seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness. I did not say more than that, but I will not say less than that. Some of you will remember a sketch That Bob Newhart did. He plays a therapist and explains to a new patient That he charges five dollars for the first five minutes and nothing after that. The woman patient is surprised but agrees. She then explains that she has a fear of being buried alive in a box. Just thinking about it gives her panic attacks. And disables her from going into tunnels and getting on elevators. The therapist, Bob Newhart. Diagnoses the patient as having claustrophobia, and then proceeds to give her two words of advice That he wants her to take with her and be a reminder to her whenever she thinks about being buried alive. And those two words are stop it. The patient is confused. She doesn't understand. He yells it again. Stop it! He then reasons with her saying, you don't want to go through life thinking about being buried in a box. I mean, that's frightening. So stop it. But she says, I have had this fear since I was a child. No, said the therapist, we don't go there. Just stop it. Reading some of the comments next to the video, you will find a number of people who claim to have mental issues say it is the best advice they've ever received, and that they frequently come back to the video to remind themselves simply to stop it I don't know if the sketch is being positive or negative about mental health or mental health counseling, but Jesus gave us more than just stop it. He told us to seek his kingdom first and his righteousness. And in doing so, not only will all that is needed in this world be given to you, But you will also rid yourself of unnecessary worry and fear. Again, to seek first the kingdom of God is to walk a journey that works to understand how the love of God is to be applied. to the employment I have, to the spouse God has given me, to the family of which I'm a part, and to my fellow man whose path I cross. No mental health person will tell you that, but it is the most important counsel you will give. You will get. Seek first the kingdom of God. And be not like the world around you. Let us pray. Our gracious God, we thank you that you do more than just tell us what not to do, but you tell us what we can do To overcome the weaknesses of our flesh, to overcome the fears that this world tells us to follow. And so help all of us apply in our lives to seek Your kingdom first and your righteousness. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen

sermons.title: The Sympathy of Jesus
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We will be dissecting Luke chapter seven, starting in verse eleven, our gospel reading this morning. Prior to our gospel reading, Jesus had just healed a servant of the centurion Prior to that, Jesus had preached the Sermon on the Mount. Thus, Jesus had revealed himself in his authority by word and by healing. Verse 11. Now it happened the day after that he went into a city called Nain, and many of his disciples went with him and a large crowd. Once again, we are reminded that since the ministry of Jesus went public everywhere, he went, he was accompanied by a great crowd. He was a phenomenon, and everything he did served to further increase the people's enthusiasm Interestingly, Luke is the only one of the gospel writers to include this particular story. Nain was a town some twenty miles southwest of Capernaum. It would have taken a day to walk there, for Capernaum is where Luke says Jesus was prior But what we are being reminded of is that the Lord didn't simply stay in Capernaum, but was in fact walking throughout Galilee and visiting all of its towns while preaching and healing. Verse 12. And when he came near the gate of the city, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother. And she was a widow, and a large crowd from the city was with her. Such was a unique and unplanned situation, at least unplanned as far as any expected itinerary. A widow was bearing her only child, which meant it was a woman Who faced a future without help in a time when women alone were particularly vulnerable to economic hardship And a woman who had to hear had to bear the burden of knowing that her family was coming to an end. The large crowds suggest that the people of the town appreciated what this woman was facing. Verse 13. When the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her and said to her, Do not weep. The wording of Luke is quite revealing. When he wrote this account, it was post-resurrection and post-ascension of Jesus. Luke had interviewed the apostles. He had interviewed Mary, the mother of Jesus. Thus, he had heard first-hand accounts of what Jesus said and what he did. The result is Luke referring to Jesus as the Lord. The Lord, he says. And it is odd from my view that any Christian would struggle with understanding that the Bible teaches the divinity of Jesus. When so many eyewitnesses and first century followers accepted that he was God without a doubt Verse 14. Then he came and touched the open coffin, and those who carried him stood still, and he said, Young man, I say to you, arise. Luke recalls how the dead man was being carried in a what he calls an open coffin. The Jews sometimes used coffins, but often they did not. Likely the body was wrapped in a cloth and the resting on an open what they called a briar or a burial plank Making it easy for Jesus to touch him. We remember from Jewish law that touching a dead body led to being ceremonially impure. But of course, Jesus touched the leper previous. But by touching the dead son, the Lord rendered the boy alive, thus no defiling took place. Verse 15 So he who was dead sat up and began to speak, and he presented him to his mother. We should note the almost poetic manner Luke describes the miracle. He tells us that the dead man sat up, which is something that dead people do not do. Then he began to talk, which again is something dead men do not do. It is here that we should remember how the boy The prophet Elisha brought back to life how he sneezed seven times, which again is something the dead do not do. And finally, the Lord gave the boy back to his mother, and the wording is precisely the same used in the case of the prophet Elijah returning the dead son to the widow of Zarephat. Who again he made alive. Verse 16. Then fear came upon all And they glorified God saying, A great prophet has risen up among us, and God has visited his people. The people could not have been expected to understand that God was standing before them Remember that the Lord's own disciples didn't understand. But with true insight, they gathered at least these two things. First, Jesus had displayed the same power that Elijah and Elisha had displayed over 800 years before. That put Jesus on the same level of the great prophets in Israel's past. That is a high compliment indeed. The Jews knew that there had been no such prophet in Israel for close to nine centuries. But such a miraculous occurrence proved that there was once again a prophet in Israel. You would have to be a Jew, living then under the thumb of the Roman state, hoping against hope as your parents, grandparents, and great-grandparents had hoped. For some divine intervention on behalf of God's people to realize what an important impact this realization would have had on all who were there to see it. And then on those who simply heard of it second hand. Second, they knew that the power Such men had at their disposal was not their own. It was from God Himself. And so they very rightly, if not fully understanding drew the obvious conclusion, Almighty God had come among them and was working through this person, Jesus of Nazareth. Verse 17. And this report about him went throughout all the Judea and all the surrounding region. Verse 17 says that we've what we would expect to occur. People would have to share what they had witnessed, and the excitement about what God was doing was understandably contagious. Having looked at each verse of this miracle account, that again is unique to Luke. I want to make the following observations for some important meditation. First, we observe how serious Jesus was in spreading his good news. The kingdom of God had come and was being revealed in the person and actions and words of Jesus Christ. And he was making every effort within him to go from town to town. Revealing himself as many as possible could hear him and see him. He was not a guru who rented out an auditorium. Or who sat on high, expecting everyone to come to him, Jesus came to the people Jesus made himself vulnerable in being out in the open, having no handlers, but only men who were closest to him so that they could be eyewitnesses to his works and to his words. Second, we observe that a large crowd followed Jesus We learn elsewhere that people of these crowds had various reasons for following him, and Jesus was always challenging them to examine their motivation. Jesus was never about simply having a large crowd, but was repeatedly trying to widow that crowd so that people who followed him would not be deceiving themselves. One of the approaches I have in ministry, and one of the reasons I have embraced the Anglican way, is because it is not popular. We do nothing in our ministries or services at St. Stephen's to appeal to the flesh. Instead, we do what most do not. Which is to be formal and reverent and not make our worship about what we like. We govern our Sunday school, our Bible studies, and All that we do when it comes to scriptures by what the Bible says rather than what we wish it said We catechize our children old school style, which has them memorize and recite. Not many churches do that, and not many parents out in the community want it. We do these things because we believe that such is most pleasing to God. He is our first and our last audience. For churches in our denomination that are struggling to keep their doors open and because of low attendance and increasing debt, I want them to embrace being different because it is pleasing to God and no one else is doing it. Few churches are liturgical, reverent, sacramental, and biblical in their preaching and teaching. And there are Christian souls out there who want to be liturgical, reverent, sacramental, and biblical. We just need to let them know we are here. Third, we observe the details Luke includes about the family and the funeral encountered by Jesus and his followers. Luke tells us that the man is dead, and all who are part of the funeral are certain of it. The dead man was the only son of his mother. As stated, this spoke to the troubled um the trouble faced by his mother. She was a widow. We are told, which tells us that she had already suffered tragedy through death of a loved one. Widows didn't receive pensions or social security in the first century There was no life insurance paid out to pay off her debt. Her only financial hope was her son caring for her, and he was on a pallet, likely wrapped in a cloth, and being taken to a tomb. The woman's prospects for any future financial security were being taken to the same tomb. Fourth, we have already observed that Luke called Jesus the Lord. But we can add to that observation that Jesus had compassion on the woman. The Lord, our Lord, had compassion on a woman he did not personally know, and he had it in a moment when all he could do was observe a funeral procession. Now, we can easily easily conclude that there were many, many funeral processions that took place in the lifetime of Jesus, having lived 33 years. And many that took place in his three years of ministry, and certainly some of those he witnessed firsthand. But in this instance, Jesus chose to express his compassion by performing a miracle. And it can be asked, and I think fairly Why Jesus didn't have compassion on all who faced the tragic death of a loved one, so much so that Jesus raised them all from the dead. The simple answer is that such was physically impossible. By becoming a man, Jesus Had chosen to limit himself as all human beings are limited by time and space. And Jesus chose only certain ones to raise. Because in raising the ones he did, he was pointing to a greater resurrection. One that would be the final resurrection to eternal life. But this widowed mother would benefit in this life by her son being raised, just as we have described. But consider that this son would indeed die again. He would have to face his mortality all over again, sometime in the future. Which again tells us that Jesus wasn't bringing the young man back to life only for the sake of this life But was pointing to something much greater than the raising of one young man in one moment in time. Fifth, we observe that Jesus enables the once-dead man to immediately move He sat up and immediately communicated. He began to speak, giving obvious evidence to all who were there that what Jesus did was a true miracle. In making the miracle obvious to all, he is making it obvious that he is pointing to something greater beyond the miracle. He was pointing to himself to be the Messiah, the one of whom they had been waiting for, and the only thing that was required is for them to believe in him 6. We observed that Luke observed, which was that fear came upon all who witnessed a man rise from the dead. The Greek word for fear here is phobos, which can mean awe, it can mean reverence, and it can mean terror. It fits well here because the people expressing expressed being in awe, as some said, God had visited his people. But it could include terror, because the power to raise a person from the dead, that power was within Jesus. And that type of power Should invoke some sort of terror because, as Jesus said elsewhere, such power includes being able to send a person's body and soul to hell. My turn excuse me. Yeah. I turn now back to the Lord having compassion on the woman. The Greek word for compassion is to have pity, and it's to feel compassion as an emotion. We would say that Jesus felt for her, which means that his emotions identified with hers. Jesus had empathy for her plight. Now, I have been arguing that this healing was more than for the purpose of for one young man to live. And we can say the same about raising Lazarus from the dead. And Jesus felt compassion before that miracle as well, for we are told that Jesus wept when seeing the emotions of those who had loved Lazarus and who had watched him die. But Lazarus, after being raised, would also die again in the future. As Scripture says, it is determined that all men die once. Well, Lazarus and this young man in Luke chapter seven actually died twice. C. S. Lewis Faced death twice. Two years after his wife's death, Lewis began to have problems with his heart. He fell into a long coma and then unexpectedly recovered. Regarding the whole ordeal, Lewis said, quote It would have been a luxurious, easy passage, and one almost regrets having the door shut in one's face. To be brought back to life and have all one's dying to do again was rather hard In the cases of this young man in Luke 7 and Lazarus, I'm sure it was rather hard for each to face death again. And in both cases of their first death, the compassion, the empathy Jesus showed was for those who were still alive, but suffering from the pains of death. And I argue that the compassion Jesus showed, the empathy he had in this story, points to a greater compassion he has for all who call him Lord and Savior. Charles Spurgeon says the following about this Greek word for compassion Quote, it is not found in the Septuagint. The fact is, it is a word coined by the evangelists themselves. They did not find one in the whole Greek language that suited their purpose, and therefore they had to make one up It is an expression of the deepest emotion, a striving of the bowels, a yearning of the innermost nature with pity. That is how Jesus feels about those who follow him and call him Savior and Lord. And just as being raised from the dead points to something greater, which is the final resurrection, so too does the compassion of Jesus point to something greater, which is the compassion he has for us. As we struggle in this life to remain faithful to Him. Beloved, the compassion of Jesus expressed here is to get you through days when you don't want to get out of bed. When you don't know how the bills will be paid, when you don't want to have to change another dirty diaper. When you don't want to watch a loved one suffer, when you don't want to suffer yourself, when you have to stand by and watch a loved one slowly damage themselves And that compassion is for when friends abandon you. And all such things, Jesus has compassion for you. Understanding Jesus having compassion for you is to be in contrast to seeing him as having feet like brass and eyes like fire, as he is described in the book of Revelation. He is thought by some to be eager to return and pass judgment on all sinners. Some have speculated that one reason for the rise of Mariology, which is the worshiping of Mary, the mother of Jesus, It was because of how Jesus was being preached and how he was being presented in art in the Middle Ages, which was as a divine judge who was eager to condemn. Depictions of Mary and prayers to Mary were to a gentle woman who would pray to Jesus for the people, and Mary would hear the prayers of the people because she had compassion. But as we have learned of Jesus in this story in Luke 7, Jesus had compassion and has compassion, a great compassion, and a desire For you to endure the difficulties of this world because the promises in the next world are there for you, where you will have no need for compassion because you will be like him. Beloved, Jesus wants us to know him as our Savior who has compassion on us. And that compassion, that empathy, is to motivate us to trust him. To place our faith solely in him and to love him even more. We may note again that there were mourners who joined the widow, and thus they had compassion. Many went out to mingle their tears with hers, but the sympathy of all could only go so far. They cannot be expected to enter into the privacy of her woe. Human sympathy is at best imperfect, sometimes selfish, and always finite, always temporary. Not so with the compassion of Jesus, who joined that funeral procession. He could say, as no one else could, I know your sorrows. The condolences of the kindest friend on earth knows limit, but Jesus knows none. Jesus is compassionate toward you, and that should make all the difference. Let us pray. A gracious God, for this example of compassion that you placed in your son. For all that he revealed to us about who you are, all of this we are very grateful. And may it be used in our motivation to love you more, to trust in you more. That we might trust you to the end of our days. This we pray in Jesus' name

sermons.title: Jesus Owns Sundays
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We are going to be looking at the first part of our gospel reading, Luke chapter fourteen. Reading one through six, verse one. Now it happened as he went into the house of one of the rulers of the Pharisees to eat bread on the Sabbath, but they watched him closely. They were not given the name of this host But we are given the impression that this Pharisee was an important man, being a ruler among the Pharisees Perhaps he invited Jesus to his home to thank him for some kindness. Or because the presence of Jesus in his home would be an honor to him and his family. But we remember that the Pharisees were also keeping an eye on Jesus And no doubt hoping that he would say something that they could use against him. Imagine being our Lord. Knowing that your enemies were hanging on every word, hoping that you would say something, however innocent, that they could use against you. No doubt there was never a man in the history of the world who chose his words more carefully as did Jesus of Nazareth. Verse 2 And behold, there was a certain man before him who had dropped sea The man with drugs he may have been an invited guest, or he may have been brought there by his family who had heard that Jesus was going to be there Or maybe something more sinister. Dropsy is a condition in which the body swells from accumulation of fluids. Verse 3. And Jesus answering spoke to the lawyers and Pharisees, saying, Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath? The verb responded or answering, describing what Jesus said, has led some commentators to suppose That the man had been put there by the Pharisees themselves precisely to see whether Jesus would perform a healing on the Sabbath. So Jesus responded to what he gathered they were doing. The question Jesus asked posed a dilemma for the Pharisees. We remember that this scenario happened often. They set traps for Jesus, but were caught in those same traps themselves. According to rabbinic regulations, which is the interpretation of the law of Moses, it was not lawful to heal on the Sabbath unless The person's life was in danger. This man would not have died if Jesus had waited until the evening when the Sabbath was over to heal him.
