The meal to which Jesus was invited was after the morning worship in the synagogue, just like any of our homes each Sunday after worship service sharing a meal So it would have been it would have been a few more hours until the evening and the Sabbath was ended. And the point being that Jesus could have waited Jesus didn't, and he doesn't mind confrontation. When Jesus asked if it was possible to heal on the Sabbath, he was directly challenging their rabbinical interpretation of Sabbath law. For priests, the priests knew there knew that there was no such a law forbidding such healing on the Sabbath according to the law of Moses. Furthermore, the Pharisees were the bad for wanting them not wanting the man healed Finally, if they had purposefully planted the man there and then argued that he shouldn't be healed, they would be both devious and spiteful. Verse 4. But they kept silent, and he took him and healed him and let him go. They remained silent, presumably because they didn't know what to say. They hadn't anticipated the question of Jesus. This is the last, interestingly, the last Sabbath healing that is recorded in the Gospel of Luke. The phrase Let him go should convince us that the man was brought to the meal just to test Jesus. Once again, because of the hardness of their hearts The Pharisees missed a chance to give glory to God for a miraculous healing. So much of God's glory is missed because of the pride of men's hearts. Verse five. Then he answered them, saying, Which of you having a donkey or an ox that is fallen into a pit will not immediately pull him out on the Sabbath day. You'll notice in the marginal notes of the pew bible that some manuscripts actually read son instead of donkey. When you use donkey the argument goes as follows If you take care of your animals in need on the Sabbath, how much more is it right to take care of a human being in need? The argument is more blunt if it reads son, for it has Jesus saying to them, You would do precisely what I have done if the person or animal in need happened to be yours. Verse 6. And they could not answer him regarding these things. Really, what could they say? The Lord was left standing before them, having demonstrated that even on their premises, deeds of mercy are appropriate on the Sabbath day. It is fitting for us to remember elsewhere. When Jesus is accused of disobeying the Sabbath, you remember when his apostles were eating grain from a field and the Pharisees considered such actions to be harvesting, which is work, and thus breaking the fourth commandment. Jesus answered the accusation with the example of David and his men eating the bread offered in the tabernacle and arguing that desperate times can make use of sacred of the sacred, it becomes necessary. And then Jesus says, what all Christians remember, the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Such words by Jesus are quite freeing to Christians, but not in the way most people of today might think. For the modern Christian, we might hear such words by Jesus about the Sabbath and conclude that the Sabbath doesn't matter. That it is no longer applicable as a law to us. But that is not what Jesus said or what Jesus implied. Nor is it what the majority of Christians have understood since the first century. I read a theologian this past week who insisted that the victory that Jesus achieved by dying on the cross and overcoming death was that all the laws of the Old Testament were abolished, including the Ten Commandments. That would have been news to the apostles and their followers in the first century. What we know from the book of Acts is that the apostles continued to worship in the synagogue on the Jewish Sabbath And then added to their gathering on Sundays where they would worship as Christians, gathering together on what they came to call the Lord's Day. It was called the Lord's Day because it was the day upon which Jesus showed his victory over death. Thus, Jesus owns Sundays When the gospel spread into the Gentile world, they didn't have the practice of worshiping on Saturdays, but they easily followed the tradition of worshiping on Sundays, and it became a natural transition for Christians to call Sunday their own Sabbath day. And to do so is actually what is foreseen in Jewish practice. In the book of Leviticus, God commands Israel to celebrate what was Called the Feast of the Tabernacles or Booths, which is to remember God providing for his people while they were in the desert, living in tabernacles or what we call tents. God specifically specifically tells them to sacrifice to him during the celebration for seven straight days. Then on the eighth day to have what he calls a holy convocation, which is a gathering of all the people to worship together, and when they do, God calls it a sacred assembly. Early Christians saw a connection with Jesus being raised on what could be called the eighth day. And this they called a sacred assembly of God's people on the eighth day of celebrating. And thus they referred to Sundays as the eighth day of celebration, with an emphasis on Christians gathering to worship. What early Christians and generation after generation that followed them did not do or teach or say is what Jesus did not do or teach or say Which is that it doesn't matter what you do on Sundays. Or if if you have something more important to do, then go on and do it. Go ahead. It's just another Sunday Such gatherings were commanded and necessary. Some history buffs will remember That the French, after their secular revolution, tried to change the calendar by using 10-day weeks and removing all religious references to their calendar year and it failed miserably. Turns out we humans are engineered to live seven-day weeks Author Jeremiah Jocks writes that the human biology proved the seven-day week, predates all societies. Mankind has long understood that our bodies operate on a circadian, daily, monthly, and annual rhythms But chronobiologists have only recently discovered seven-day patterns are written into the biology of people, animals, and plants. According to a book titled The Secrets Our Body Clocks Reveal, written by Susan Perry and Jim Dawson The blood pressure cycle, coping hormone cycle, immune response to infection cycle, production of blood and urine chemicals And even the heartbeat operate on seven-day patterns. Experiments conducted by scientist Franz Holberg also proves that seven-day cycles govern fundamental aspects of the lives of flies, rats, and other critters. Research by Holberg, Perry, Dawson, and others have uncovered no cycle between daily and monthly frequency that occurred five days, six, eight, nine, or any other number only. Only seven. A rat can't tell the Talmud from the Huffington Post drops continu So if the seven-day week was invented by people, as historians maintain, what explains these biological seven-day rhythms. An excellent rhetorical question. And our bodies, minds, and spirit need to follow those God made rhythms. And thus we need to include our worshiping of God in the person of Jesus Christ, his only son. But one of men's excuses. What of men's excuses? I have heard plenty. It's the only day we have free. Well, whose fault is that? It is the devil beloved who wants us to fill our schedules so that Sunday is the only free time to do what we want. But what is this self-governing of our calendar while confessing Jesus is our Lord? We cannot do both and be truthful. Next. It's the only time the family can get together. Again, whose fault is that? Was it not Jesus who said we must love him first and foremost, and that includes over and against our closest family members? Next, it's the only day our kids soccer league plays. There are always choices to be made in life. And the best choices made are by priority, not by circumstance. Not prioritizing the worship of the Savior of the world By allowing circumstances such as sports leagues to come first will affect your child's priorities when he is older. And your missing of ten times a year Sundays will become your child only attending on Christmas Christmas and Easter And the next generation not worshiping at all, at least not worshiping the one true God. Beloved prioritizing anything but Jesus is idol worship straight up. Next. We are on vacation. That one was hard for me to hear, because the rebuttal should be obvious. There are no vacations, vacation exceptions in Holy Scripture. Every Sunday is the Lord's Day, whether it falls on your vacation time or not. Next, we have Raven tickets. Can't go there with me. Nope. And I've been to games. People show up to those games late all the time. And one last excuse this one got me. Well, this year Christmas falls on Sunday, and we are with family on Christmas. First, refer to the comments about loving Jesus more than family, and second There is no more appropriate place to be on on Sunday Christmas morning than to be in church participating in a holy convocation. No better place Let's go back to what Jesus said. The Sabbath was made for man. Let's give a commandment that is for our personal, cultural, and societal benefit. When we use it as instructed, rest and worship, we have greater health in all aspects of our lives. To not use it as instructed takes away from what God has gifted to us in this life while also pointing to an eternal rest that He promises for all who believe. Through the prophet Isaiah, God makes it clear how favorable he makes life for those who keep his Sabbath. Isaiah 58, 13 through 14. If you turn away your foot from the Sabbath, from doing your pleasure on my holy day, and call the Sabbath a delight. The holy day of the Lord honorable, and shall honor him, not doing your own ways, nor finding your own pleasures, nor speaking your own words. Then you shall delight yourself in the Lord. And I will cause you to ride on the high hills of the earth and feed you with the heritage of Jacob your father, the mouth of the Lord has spoken. The Sabbath delight. This Sabbath delight is in stark contrast to thinking and approaching the Sabbath as a day governed by rules and all of it being boring. No fun. One of the more impressionable moments during our trip to Israel, some seven years ago now. Was observing an entire culture observing the Sabbath. The carefulness that parents took in laying out the family meal on Friday evening to the willing participation of all businesses and eateries, if they were practicing Jews or not It was inspired. The day matter. Each family member matters. And it's a rhythm for them, for they practice the same every week, every Sabbath. Sundown to sundown. Elevators are put in special modes that allow them to go up and down by themselves because of the conviction of not pushing any electrical buttons on the Sabbath. All public transportation is shut down from sundown to sundown. And while restaurants shut down, certain rooms in stores and hotels are open. for families to freely use to share a meal while even being joined by strangers. But I am sounding like a commercial for Sabbath keeping. We shouldn't need commercials to get us motivated to treat the Lord's Day as the title says. It is the Lord's Day. What became unfortunate in the day of Jesus was what the Sabbath had become. Like other laws of Moses The restrictions placed upon the Jewish people by the Pharisees and scribes were extra-biblical and highly questionable. Picking grain was harvesting, healing the sick, which no one in the history could do in the manner Jesus did it, that was considered working We humans seem capable of turning rule, regulation, or law into our own righteousness. And you know and I know that when we give account of our lives before the face of God Almighty, there will be no reward for being the best social distancer. Recall again what Jesus said after informing us that the Sabbath was a gift given to humanity by God for our benefit. He said, therefore, the Son of Man, who is Jesus, is also Lord of the Sabbath. Modern ears hear such and conclude that they don't have to practice the Sabbath as was done before. We think that because Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath and he didn't follow the rules of the Pharisees, that we don't have to follow any rules either. The contrary is true. Because Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath, we are to do what it is intended for, which is to worship and rest. What each of us should be asking after hearing Jesus say he is Lord of the Sabbath, we should be asking, is Jesus Lord of my Sabbath? And I should get the word my out of it and ask the question, if Jesus is Lord, of the Sabbath I say I practice. Let us end with an emphasis on the phrase, the Lord's Day. It is not Eric's Day. It is not Mark's Day. It is not Stan's Day. It's not Margaret's day. It's not Patricia's day. It's not Lucy's day. It's not Sam's day or put your name here day. It is the Lord's day. And as such, what is done on that day, on every Sunday, is what the Lord would have us do. Amen.

sermons.title: The Grind
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. You will do well to turn to First Corinthians chapter one, picking up at verse four. Which was our epistle reading this morning, 1 Corinthians chapter 1, starting at verse 4. The section of scripture Chosen for our epistle reading has been uncovered by modern biblical scholarship to be a familiar Greco-Roman rhetoric revealing how Saint Paul adapted such style to structure his letters that they might be most effective. In Greco-Roman rhetoric before Paul, there was a literary device known as the exordium. Which was an introduction to a speech or letter by which the writer or speaker would attempt to elicit the goodwill of the listeners or readers by way of praise and encouragement. Before this, Cicero and Quintilian, two masters of Greco-Roman rhetorical style, both recommended the use of what is called the opening. Such an introduction paves the way for stating the main thesis or purpose statement of the letter, which in this case will come in verse 10, which reads. Now, I plead with you, brethren, by the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you. But that you be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment That statement is called the propositio or proposition, and is followed by the ratio, which is the statement of facts that spell out the problem In this case, that would be verses 11 through 17, which is a brief summary statement of the fact that Paul has learned that there are deep and dangerous divisions Within the Corinthian church. The narratio is in turn followed by the probatio or proofs. These are the arguments of the letter, and it takes us from chapter 1, verse 18, all the way through to chapter 16, verse 12. They provide the reasons why the hearers or the readers should take up a specific course of action that is being recommended. The final section, characteristically brief, is the paroratio or summary, the final exhortation, which is found in chapter 16, verses 13 through 18. It is a brief recapitulation of Paul's basic thesis stated again in chapter 1, verse 10. Such is a fancy way of outlining the letter But I think this is a very helpful way to understand the letter. The exact similarities between these various rhetorical forms of Greco-Roman writing and speaking And Paul's structure here in 1 Corinthians puts it beyond doubt that Paul has employed this well-known and accepted structure of writing a letter to influence people. Adopting contemporary styles of rhetoric is not new in the Holy Scriptures. We can say that the Holy Spirit and Moses Used the structure of the ancient Near East political treaties to state and describe God's covenant with Israel. The prophets used a standard legal form of speech and argument to indict Israel for her crimes against God, against the covenant he made with her. Thus, Paul, like many other biblical writers, used the literary and rhetorical forms common to his day. just as Christian writers and speakers today use the forms of our secular culture to speak and write on behalf of the Christian gospel. While Paul adopts the style of his contemporaries to influence, as stated prior, he also makes an overarching point that is often missed. First, he praises them and encourages them by describing how they have everything they need in this life to be holy and pleasing before God And next goes on to describe their various sins and problems resulting from those sins, which reveal how they are not using everything they have been given. And thus an overarching lesson is their dependency on God to use the gifts they've been given. So let's look at each verse. Verse 4, chapter 1. I thank my God always concerning you for the grace of God which was given to you by Christ Jesus. Here is an expression of thankfulness. The emphatic use of the singular, I thank my God, is in contrast to the plural previous in verse 1, where Paul is saying he is joined by Sosthenes, but now Paul is the author of this epistle. And instead, he's writing this letter in his name alone and with his sole authority. Verse 5 That you were enriched in everything by him, in all utterance and all knowledge. The word everything refers to every gift which equips a Christian to live the Christian life. The word utterance is Rhema, Logos, meaning discourse and reason. Knowledge refers to that what was needed to understand in order to be saved. Verse six. Even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you The testimony, the testimony referred to here is what the apostles shared with the Corinthians concerning Christ, their own testimony and the truth of Christ. And then it showed also that the Corinthians, what they showed to Paul is that they believed and they exhibited fruits. That also was the testimony. Verse 7. So that you come short in no gift, eagerly waiting for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ. To say come short in no gift can be stated in the positive, you have every gift that you need. We know that outward expressions of the gifts of the Holy Spirit were healing, prophecies, speaking in unknown languages, and then words of wisdom. The revelation of the Lord Jesus Christ is referring to his parousia, which is his second coming. Verse 8. Who will also confirm you to the end that you may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ? The Who in this verse is, of course, Jesus. He will confirm which is to keep or establish or maintain, which refers to their position in the faith. Jesus will keep them in the place of having all that they need to live the faith up to the time Jesus returns, which is what the phrase, the day of the Lord Jesus Christ, means. In our adult Sunday school class, we've been studying the Ten Commandments in light of our gospel reading, which tells us that the greatest commandment Are to love God with all of our heart and soul and mind, and to love our neighbor as ourselves. I argue the first five commandments tell us how to love God. No other gods, no idols, no name in vain. Honor the Sabbath and honor your father and your mother, which translates into honoring God. And the next five tell us how to love our neighbor. No murder, no adultery, no stealing, no lying. And when we get to the commandment number ten, I explain of all the people in the world. And all the people in history of the world, we have no excuse for coveting. As I've explained from this pulpit before, we are kings and queens. We live better than most kings down through history. We can pay for people to clean our homes. We can travel around the world. We can order most any food we desire and enjoy a different cuisine each day of the week. We can cool our homes in the summer And heat them to our comfort during the deep winter freeze. And we can be entertained at the click of a button There is no need that we are in want for. Thus, covening should not have a pull on us, and yet it does. It does because our hearts are wanting. We lack in our hearts a gratefulness for what all that we have. To know such is true, consider that the richest men in the world, that the world has ever known, still want to be richer. It is a heart issue What St. Paul has explained to us in his opening to the Corinthian Christians is how all Christian people have everything they need in order for them to live faithfully The Christian gospel that they profess they believe. We Christians lack nothing, which is to say, we have been given everything we need to walk faithfully with God And yet, and yet, like a coveting man who has everything, we don't like, we don't live like we have everything we need. As described, Paul is complimenting and encouraging these Christians at Corinth before he presents the probatio, or proofs, that describe the problem. And the major problem was that there was division among them. The division was expressed in groups who insisted that they were followers of certain teachers only. such as Cethas or Peter, and then Apollos, and then Paul, and some only Jesus Now, we would think that those who said they followed Jesus only were in the right. That's the right group. But in order to follow Jesus, they had to have the teachings of Paul and Peter and Apollos. But the point wasn't who was right. The point was that there was division, and that division contributed to their problems. The following were problems in the church caused by them choosing sides. Their division left them susceptible to worldly wisdom against God's revelation Their division led them to not know how to deal properly with unholy living among them. Their division led them to suing one another in secular courts. Their division confused them on marital roles and the sin of divorce. Their division caused a lack of wisdom when dealing with meat offered to idols. Their division had them going against their consciences Their division led them to disrespecting those weak and poor among them, which led them to disrespecting the service of Holy Communion. Their division led them to not properly use the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Their division prohibited them from rightly and properly loving one another. Their division disrupted their corporate worship, which is the very thing that all of us are created and called to do. Their division disabled them from properly knowing and understanding the hope of the resurrection of the body and the hope of eternal life. It should be known, but it must be said, that unity is an important part of the Christian life, but it isn't the most important part. Unity at all cost is the rowdy cry of those Christians who have not defended the Christian faith, but have allowed their denominations to become corrupt. In their doctrinal teachings. And when you become corrupt in what you say you believe, you next become corrupt in how you live. You lose your moral compass. A man denies the virgin birth, which leads to questioning the authority of Holy Scripture Which leads to no longer believing that Jesus is the Son of God, that his death on the cross paid for their sins, that there was a resurrection, and even leads to doubting whether Jesus lived And finally, people no longer believe they are sinners. Instead, they believe they have all the beauty inside them, as Whitney Houston sang. It is truly a slippery slope that so many have slid down, reminding us why Jesus said that the road to heaven was narrow and few travel on it. But when, but when, if ever, is it appropriate for Christians to divide from one another? First, Christians should never divide over personality differences, and yet that is what Christians mostly divide over. The church being called a body, a bride, a family, a nation, means that we have to remain united while being so different. And we are, as Christians, defined by our obligation to forgive one another, even when it's over and over again. And being Christian is loving one another, for Jesus said, you remember, the world will know we are Christian by our love for one another. And that love is patient and kind. And both of those are to be put into practice when we encounter differing personalities within the church. So again, personality differences are not to divide Christians. The only division that is justified, which means rightly done before God, is when the leadership of a church Will not address and correct known immorality or false teaching When such is not addressed from the top by those God has given authority to in order to protect his bride, the church Such as has already spiritually divided the church, and such a church will not stand. When I refer to known immorality, I am referring to sex or money abuses that people know about, whisper about, and in general most people in the local church know about, but it is never addressed. Beloved, the proverb, a little leaven leavens a whole lump, is true. Any sin not confronted and confessed and repented of infects all the souls around it. When I refer to false teachings, I mean anything that goes against the substance of the Apostles and Nicene Creeds, which summarize what is necessary for a person to believe in order to be saved. Other than leadership not addressing known immorality or false teaching, I see no other reason to divide from others who call themselves Christians. But we have today in our Western Christian culture softies. Softies don't want to work through personality issues. Softies want to bounce from church to church, usually every three years, getting in only so deep into other people's lives. before they softly go away and find another church where they can again get in only so deep into other people's lives for another three years until they are off again Such Christians are not soldiers in God's army, but are only pretending, only plain, only making the Christian life easy for themselves. That is why they are softies. Beloved, living the Christian life is facing the grind. The grind of loving and forgiving over and over again. While you yourself are being loved and forgiven over and over again, because you need to admit That you're not so easy to get along with all of the time. Try to recall the Greco-Roman literary outline I described at the beginning of the sermon. The last part was called the pero ratio, which is the summary of Paul's answer to the problem of division. He states his answer in chapter 16, beginning at verse 13. This is what he says. How to handle division problems. Watch. Stand fast in the faith. Be brave. Be strong. Let all that you do be done with love. To watch is to watch out. It is to be purposefully looking for dangers that divide. The watchman, when on duty, must always be awake and alert, convinced that one moment of lacking awareness will doom the entire city. And the devil is always working to divide Christians. Most of us knew with the first mask mandate How the devil would use it to divide Christians. He will use anything he can To stand fast in the faith is to be firm in holding and defending the truths of the gospel. It is not yielding to any foe, but instead maintaining the truth And adhering to your confidence in God and to the doctrines of the gospel with unwavering constancy. It is to be firm in maintaining what you believe to be true and in holding on to your personal confidence in God Notwithstanding all the arts, the insinuations, and teachings of seducers and friends of false doctrine. To be brave. To be brave and strong is stated next, and it is a reiteration of standing fast. It is an underlining of what needs to be done in order to live the Christian life, a life that does not divide over the trivial. Soft people don't stand fast. They run away. Soft people do not defend truth, but give in to what is contrary. Soft people don't have confidence in God, but only trust in their ability to flee. And next we are given the summary of what enables us to stand fast, which is the love. The love given to us. By Jesus Himself. And such a love is to be with us, motivating all that we do. Such is the same love that is described in three chapters prior. It is that love that is patient and kind. It is a love that is not boastful, that is not proud, it is not envious, it keeps no record of wrong and it thanks the best of others. Soft people can't love in such a manner. To love in such a manner takes courage. It takes moxie to stare down your own insecurities, about your own inadequacies, and choose to die to such feelings and instead choose to love. Beloved, it takes courage to not have divisions among us. It takes a hardened nerve not to be moved. We have been equipped by God to do so. So let it be done among us until he comes. Let us pray. Oh God, we thank you for this challenge. We thank you for the courage of the apostle to address the problem of division that continues to this day. But you have given us an answer. You've called us to stand fast and you've called us to love. May each of us take this challenge upon us and live it out until you return. This we pray in Jesus' name.

sermons.title: Putting off and on
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: I got locked out of my iPad and it didn't recognize my face. Sometimes I wake up in the morning and Turn it on and it looks at me and goes, I don't recognize it. We are in Ephesians chapter 4, part of our reading from Ephesians 4, starting at verse 17. The epistle reading assigned to us this nineteenth Sunday after Trinity finds us in the middle of St. Paul's letter to the Ephesians It is a letter that I least like to preach from because it is so perfect a letter that I feel inadequate To comment about it. But that is my job. And so I reluctantly try. In the first three chapters of this letter, Paul reminded these Christians of their great salvation Which is given as a free gift by God the Father, accomplished by God the Son, and placed in their possession by God the Holy Spirit. At the beginning and at the end of those three chapters, he prayed that they would come to appreciate the greatness of God's love for them and to appreciate how much the triune God has done for them. Then, with the so often used word therefore, Paul turns from theology to ethics in chapter 4, verse 1. From God's grace and gift to us, to our expected response of love and obedience to Him His main point is that we Christians must walk worthy of the gifts God has lavished on us. And what Paul is proceeding to tell us is how to do that and what it looks like. In verse 16, in the first 16 verses of chapter 4, he focuses on the unity of the people of God And they're maturing together into a loving fellowship that works fruitfully in his service. He has reminded us Christians that we derive the strength to live this holy life from Christ Himself, to whom we are connected as the body is connected to the head. We have no excuse then if we do not live as we ought. Now, in the section that we are looking at today, Paul is going to speak in general before descending to the particulars of the Christian life. He is going to talk about putting off the old man and putting on the new man. That is, he is going to describe the Christian life as new creation. Christians are as new creatures. New men and women. God has made them so by the Holy Spirit. Now they must live according to that new nature. That is how a mature Christian lives. Paul spoke about growing up into maturity in the previous section and now defines how that is done in the verses we are about to read, starting at verse 17. This I say therefore and testify in the Lord that you should no longer walk as the rest of the Gentiles walk in the futility of their mind. The section begins with another therefore. This is a continuation of the therefore in verse 1 of the chapter. It is, as the grammarians say, a resumptive. And indicates that he is still building his ethics out of his theology. That is indicated further by the fact that Paul once again uses the word walk Again, in verse 1, walk. We must strive to walk in a certain way because Christ has saved us to walk that way. If we have been saved to grow up into Christ and become mature in Him, if each of us as part of Christ's body, we must build itself up, the body entirely This is what we must do. This is what we must set out to become. We will have another, therefore, in chapter 4, verse 25. where Paul finally descends from the general statements of the nature of the Christian living that occupied his first 24 verses of the chapter. to the particular of Christian living that will take him to the end of the letter. But before we move on, we must appreciate Paul's insistence on this connection between doctrine and life. Our daily living ought to always flow from what we say we believe. Who we know is God, and what we know He has done for us. And we must understand what the end goal is, where we're trying to go. If your daily Christian life does not flow naturally from what you say you believe, and if you still find yourself envious of the world, These words by Paul are for you, and for all of us who will be tempted later in life to fall back into the sinful habits we thought we laid aside so many years before. He says the futility of the mind. The futility of the non-believing mind mentioned in this verse is thinking That sins of the flesh are natural, and that the futility is exposed when people prefer to be defined by their sins of the flesh. Futility of the mind is further thinking that the meaning of life is solely subjective and thus self-determined. Futility of the mind is in the thinking that each individual person is the master of his own fate, including the fate of his or her own soul. For many, such thinking will be found futile only at their day of judgment. Verse 18 Having their understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart. The problem with the life of unbelief is that it has lost touch with reality. Those of us who came to the Christian faith with years of unbelief behind us, we marvel at how foolish we were in our thinking and in our actions. What really mattered, which means eternally mattered, didn't matter to us at all. And what was fleeting and harmful was what we cared about most. But, as Romans 1 also says, the ignorance of an unbeliever is no excuse, which means that non-believers are responsible for their unbelief. Verse 19 Who being past feeling have given themselves over to lewdness To work all uncleanness with greediness. The past feelings mentioned are feelings of shame and guilt from sin. The longer a person lives in sin, the more callous they become to God and thus to truth. We also notice that lewdness refers to sins of the flesh, and greediness is a love for money. Sex and money were idols then, and they still are today. And we notice that Paul describes the unbelieving world as very dark and void of meaning. As Dr. Rayburn points out in his comments about this verse, quote, Paul says nothing at all about the positive features of that life. that have long been very impressive to those who have studied the classical period. We hear from Paul nothing about their achievements in art or building or government or civilization. Paul is interested in the moral dimensions of life and in that dimension as viewed from God's perspective and the perspective of the last judgment. You can build remarkable buildings that are still the amazement of the world. You can engineer an aqueduct that still, these thousands of years later, carries water hundreds of miles You can write literature that still moves men's minds and hearts in our modern world. You can do all of these things and still go to hell In verses 20 through 21, Paul reminds the Christian Ephesians that what they have learned about Jesus is the opposite of the unbelieving world. In verses 22 through 24, Paul summons Christians to grow up into Christian maturity by putting off the old man. Or the old self and putting on the new self. Christian readers of the Bible instinctively know what Paul, what St. Paul is talking about Even if theologians and preachers preach around the idea. The theologians and preachers' problem is created by the fact that in the New Testament, even the writings of Paul, the old man, or equivalent terminology for the human being still in sin and unbelief, not yet renewed by the power of Christ and the Holy Spirit, not yet reborn. Not yet a new creation as spoken of as dead and destroyed. In Romans 6 Paul says that because we were in Christ when he died and rose again from the dead, we have been freed from sin. Is that your experience? Saint John in his letter, first letter, puts it even more strongly. He says, no one who is born of God will continue to sin because God's seed remains in him. He cannot go on sinning because he has been born of God. 1 John 3. 9 Is that your experience? And Christians know what this teaching means. If they became Christians after living as unbelievers for years, they know very well how dramatically their lives have changed when they said, I believe. They know that a revolution has taken place in their morals and their desires and in their behavior itself. Isn't that all of our experience? They know they are new creatures, and that the old things have passed away, and all things have become new. Isn't that true for all of us? And even if a person has been a Christian for as long as he or she can remember, they know very well how fixed and how inescapable is their commitment to Christ. Isn't that it for you? They can compare even within themselves the life of sin and the life of righteousness, and they know very well that they are unalterable. Committed to righteousness, that they belong with the Lord, and that they must live for Him and cannot do otherwise. Isn't that true for all of us? They have died to sin just as surely as the man or woman who has dramatically converted in their twenties or thirties and who underwent a remarkable and obvious revolution in their life when she or he or she became a Christian. We all have that identity, don't we? But if the old man is dead, If the old man is dead, how is it that we are commanded to put him off? If he is dead, shouldn't he just fall off? I think that is a very important question to ask. For thus far I have been describing an ideal Christian life. Where a person, whether converted later in life or growing up in the faith, truly loves God and truly hates sin, and the fruit of their life reveals as much. Whereas many of us find our lives not so victorious and our living not so self-controlled. We speak poorly to our spouse. We eat what is unhealthy and unnecessary. We talk disparagingly about someone out of turn. We are ungrateful for the blessings we clearly don't deserve. And we don't give God the glory that He deserves from us. And that last sin of not giving God the glory he deserves from us is quite dangerous. For Paul teaches us in Romans that Abraham was strengthened in his faith by giving glory to God, whereas prior he explained that the people who did not give glory to God were turned over to the power of the sins they so desperately wanted to serve. And I hope you have noticed that all the sins I have described thus far, I did not mention sexual immorality or the love of money, because those sins are usually the focal point But there are so many other sins that we commit and return to without considering that, although not as popular, are just as damning. The good news of Paul having to tell the Ephesian Christians to put off the old man and to put on the new man is that it is necessary for all Christians to do. Meaning that it did not happen without needed instruction and needed obedience. And that means that all Christians struggle to live as they should. All of us do The old man may be able to be be put off, but we need to do so again and again Earlier when I spoke ideally about how Christians should be living as compared to their unbelieving days, or how Christians should be able to see clear improvements in their lives as they walk with Jesus. Some of you may have checked out on me psychologically, concluding that such maturity may be for others, but not for you. And that there must be something spiritually wrong with you because such described victories over sin are few. Even though evangelists can present the Christian life as victorious and carefree, because all guilt and shame are set in the past. Because of the forgiveness and thus freedom Jesus offers, those of us who have lived the Christian life know differently. And that to walk with Christ is to be blessed at one moment and suffer blows the next moment, with most of those blows being self-inflicted. And such a cycle repeats itself again and again. Consider how many ways the epistles in the New Testament instruct Christians to break away from sin, especially sins of the past. And then to receive what God has made new for us. This wouldn't happen unless it was a problem. The Romans were told to be transformed by the renewing of their minds. Paul didn't write that unless they weren't being transformed by the renewing of their minds. The Corinthians were to be strong and courageous against being divided. And he wrote it because they weren't. The Galatians were to walk in the Spirit and not the flesh. Why? Because they were walking in the flesh and not the Spirit The Ephesians were to put off the old man and put on the new. Why? Because they weren't. I trust you get the point. All Christians have sins to confront and to move past. All Christians have something to die in them and something to be made new. And I don't preach this because misery loves company, and therefore I want you to have company. I preach this way because the devil tempts us to give up. I see it all the time in coaching, whether it be an older player or a young child. You teach them a new skill skill, and they don't do it properly the first few times, and there is a fear of failure that quickly can be seen in the player's face And the next temptation is to quit. The worst part of being a pastor The worst part of being a pastor, worse than all the complaints about your personality, about your hard words, about song choices. About hymnals chosen, about service times, about Sunday school demands, about counseling the obstinate, about masks About being made aware of sins in the home, none of it is as difficult as watching people quit the faith. Some do it outright, telling me they no longer believe. Others do it by claiming To still be Christian while no longer worshiping God and then living with the boyfriend and then not thinking about God in any serious sense Thus, their life is then lived as if they officially denounced the faith. Regardless of how you are constantly taking off the old man, And because you keep returning to your former sins and constantly putting on the new man because you want to be that new man, Regardless of how many times you repeat the cycle, do not quit the faith. Never, ever quit. In our gospel reading, we have another example of imputed righteousness in the form of healing. The text says that Jesus saw their faith, which would have been those who carried the paralytic and the paralytic himself. And because of that faith, Jesus chose to forgive the paralytics' sin. The carriers And the paralytic were likely initially confused because they came for a healing of the body. And they got a healing, but not the type they initially came for. Of the type that they all needed, that we all need. Let us be reminded of why the scribes accused Jesus of committing blasphemy. Only God can forgive sins, and by Jesus claiming to be able to forgive sins, he is also claiming to be God. And no man is God, therefore Jesus committed blasphemy. But he didn't, because he is God. He then asked, Jesus then asked, what is easier? Which is to ask what is harder. Is it harder to forgive sins than it is to heal? For healing in this life is a momentary power of God, restoring a body, only for that body to become sick or injured again and then die. But to forgive sins requires death by sacrifice. And a sacrifice that is sinless. And such a life is repeatedly and constantly saying no to desires that go against God's law and to your own personal will. And all of that sacrificial living leads to sacrificially dying by willing to give up one's life, give it over to the authorities to be beaten, mocked, and then crucified. That is why forgiving sins is harder. And that forgiving of sins is not in this world only, but in the next. And thus it is eternal. And the eternal forgiveness of sins is why you do not quit. What Jesus offers is forgiveness for your eternal soul. And your eternal soul will never quit. It will continue, and it is for you to decide whether it will continue for eternal life or death. If it is for life, never quit. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God for this message, for the reality of those who have quit. We pray that they would repent and be given better minds. And we pray here for all who are hearing this sermon, hearing this message. May they never quit. May they always turn to you and find forgiveness of sins. This we pray in Jesus' name and all of God's people said, Amen.

sermons.title: Celebrating with God
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. You may be seated. We are looking at Saint Matthew's Gospel, chapter twenty-one. Verses 1 through 14. We'll also be turning to Ephesians chapter 5 as well. But Matthew 21 is a good start. The parable that was read as our gospel lesson is the last in a series of three that are aimed at what we will call the religious establishment, which consisted of the Pharisees. the Sadducees and the Scribes. All three parables illustrate the unbelief of the religious leaders and predict divine judgment as a result of that unbelief. If you remember the series of parables began with the Lord saying that while the religious leaders in their pride were refusing to enter the kingdom of God by believing in Jesus The outcasts of society, the tax collectors and the prostitutes, were doing the opposite by repenting and thus entering the kingdom of God. This parable of the wedding banquet, as we will see, reflects that same reality. Starting at verse 2. As we read elsewhere in Matthew 8, verse 11, and Matthew 25, verse 10, the banquet or wedding banquet represents the blessings of salvation, the blessings of eternal life. In the case of this parable, it is a banquet of a king prepared for his son. Sons figure prominently in all three of these three parable series. Verse 3. Verse 3 presupposes a previous invitation that had been accepted Of course, we would expect the citizens would be honored to be invited to the king's son's wedding banquet But their hypocrisy of the religious leaders is now revealed. They said they would come with no intention of attending. Their reason to not live up to their word reveals their malicious hearts. In verse 4, we have a second appeal. Which is gracious as it gives opportunity to see the effort that the king has put forth for his guests to enjoy the celebration. To know what the king has done for them and to still refuse the invitation reveals the hardness of their hearts. In verse 5, we see that the invited guests have refused at least now twice. Remember that the first parable of the three, called the parable of the two sons, featured a son who refused to do what his father demanded of him and then regrets his refusal and goes into the field while the second son said he would go into the field and did not. Do as he promised. The challenge to us is which son will you be? The second parable was about vine dressers who were to give to the owner of the land proceeds from their vineyards, but thought that the landlord didn't deserve what they had grown, So they beat the servants sent to them and eventually killed the owner's son. Obviously, all three parables describe the religious leaders and their bad character This third one we are looking at shows that God wanted to include them in the celebration of his son. But incredibly they considered other things more pressing, more important For these trivial things, for these trivial things, they were willing to risk the wrath of the king. There was no urgency to their business, they simply didn't care. Their shallow pedestrian excuses revealed hearts of stone and a taste for things only in this life, with no care for what was eternal. While some of the invited in verse 6 responded with mocking smirks, others were engaged with anger to a level of violence. Showing that Jesus was fully aware of what these religious leaders intended for him. As stated, the mistreatment of the king's servants was previously described in the parable of the vine dressers and that mistreatment uh by these that was still to come. Clearly, the parables are dealing with the same themes. There was no respect for the king, no fear of his wrath, and thus no respect for God or fear of his wrath. From verse 7, we learn that the servants of the landowner and the servants of the king represent the prophets. The anger of the landowner and the anger of the king is the anger of God toward those whom he seriously wants to join in the celebration. He wants that But instead they mock him for his kindness. It is clear from verse 8 that the celebration will not be canceled Because the invited guests refuse to come, God graciously looks for others to celebrate with him. Verses 9 and 10 describe the theme of the kingdom being repopulated by unexpected people when the citizens of the kingdom, the Jewish people originally chosen by God They failed to respond and were cast out. Verse 11 indicates that the king's servants had gathered all the people they could find, both good and bad, the text says The presence of the bad in the new group requires further clarification. The new tenants of the kingdom of God were those outcasts. That the Jews despised and thought themselves better than those tax collectors and prostitutes who were replacing the so-called religious of the kingdom But who repeatedly refused the invitation of the Lord. But those attending, those attending must themselves bear fruit. Or their fate will be no better than those who rejected the king before them. We are to understand that if a person stood out not being dressed properly, that everyone else was dressed properly, meaning that all of them had a chance to change their clothing. Verse 13 shows, as elsewhere in Matthew, it will only be at the final judgment when it will be revealed who are the true guests. of the king at his banquet. The judgment may sound harsh, being cast out, gnashing of teeth, and all that But it only sounds harsh because our ears are too used to being tickled. Verse 14 is an easily memorized passage. That summarizes the parable and the two parables prior. It isn't proof. It isn't proof of the doctrine of predestination, however Because the parable prior speaks to people making decisions for themselves and then suffering the consequences of those decisions. Predestination and the idea of free will are mysterious to us, for we don't know where the will of God and the will of one human being connect and or disconnect. What we know from this parable is that people who were expected to attend the celebration did not. And those who were not expected did. But even with those who did, some did not properly prepare themselves What we should first get from this parable is how much a privilege it is to be invited to celebrate with God. There is no requirement for God to invite you to the celebration of his son and his son's bride. Nothing compels God to invite us and enjoy his company other than his love, which is stated in that most often repeated verse. For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son. To be invited by the means of God's love is to recall how we have done nothing to earn God's favor. But only by him choosing to reveal himself to us are we able to be invited to join him. The statement that all have sinned and fallen short of the glory of God includes us. Without Him awakening our spirits and showing us the futility of our minds prior to knowing Him We would still be wallowing in our self-righteousness, thinking that we are deserving of love, deserving of health, deserving of happiness, because, well, we're just better than most. The failure of the Jewish leaders to appreciate the privilege they had to be chosen of God, chosen of God to bring forth the Messiah. To have the character of the Messiah revealed in the law of God. To have leaders that revealed the will of God. To have prophets that God had given them. Showing the virtue of humility over pride, it is all too easy to conclude that being chosen by God means that we have done something to earn his favor. The devil makes it easy to conclude as much, but the opposite is true There is nothing within us that is worthy to be chosen over another, but only God's will. Being humbled by that reality is to make all of us more grateful and thus more loyal. To the Savior. The second truth to be revealed from the parable is all of the trouble that God goes to ordering To ordering the fatakha, to invite the people, to create this celebration. Consider that God could be satisfied to celebrate by himself. He is triune, after all. He is sufficient within himself to enjoy the company of himself, and yet he desires to have people among him. He desires to be a loving, caring, and providing God to the people made in his image He wants to celebrate with his people so much that even when a spoiled and privileged people reject his invitation, he goes out again to find a different people Again, with the final goal of celebrating with them. I will be their God, and they will be my people, he said through the prophet Jeremiah. That is what he wants. And to fulfill what he wants, he sacrifices to get it, even sacrificing his own son. The third truth to be received from this parable is that God loves to celebrate. The end goal of our salvation is described several times in Holy Scripture as a feast, which shows that God wants us to enjoy pleasures of the flesh only in due time and in due order. To feast. To feast is to enjoy taste and fullness, and to drink is to enjoy mirth. We should always appreciate moments around our kitchen tables when food and drink are being enjoyed by the people we love. Such are glimpses of our heavenly celebration. The fourth truth to be received from this parable is that we are individually responsible for how we ready ourselves for the celebration. In the parable was a man who did not properly dress for the occasion, which showed himself to be disrespectful about the occasion. To say he was speechless is to say that he had no justified reason as to why he was not properly dressed, which means that he purposefully did not go out of his way to prepare for the occasion. His was a heart that understood the king, offering cheap grace. He thought of the invitation as requiring nothing of him other than to accept it and enjoy the bounty. With no sacrifice or respect on his part. Such thinking leads us to our epistle lesson Where Paul gives direction on how Christians are to get ready for the wedding feast. And before we look, That Paul's instruction further. Let us acknowledge that the Christian faith is not for slackers. Those who follow Christ and call him Lord are told to count the cost because it costs a good deal to follow him. It costs friends. It costs family. It costs lost sleep because of prayer burdens. It costs forgiving others when you do not want to. It costs time because we give up our days and our hours to serve the church, his bride. It costs money because Christians faithfully give to his bride. It costs patience because we endure others. It costs endurance because we choose not to quit. It costs self, for it is self that we are to die to. And all such sacrifice does not come naturally. When in college, my freshman year, playing on the football team, I played on what they call the scout team. Which was the team that ran the offensive plays of the opponent that we were to face that weekend. One of the defensive backs, a starter, I will not name him publicly When I would line up as a wide receiver, he would whisper, Jurg, Jurg, that was his pronunciation of my last name, Jorgensen. He would say, Jurg, Jurg, what's the play? Where's it going? And if it was going to the other side of the field, then he would slack off. He would be lazy. If I told him it was coming his way, then he would give full effort, knowing that the coaches would be watching. Beloved, there is no place in the body of Christ for slackers, for there are no place where you can be lazy. And so Paul, in his letter to the Ephesians, chapter 4, says, chapter 5, excuse me, says, for us to walk circumspectly Which is to live one's life strictly or accurately. The word is generally used in the context of intellectual accuracy or thoroughness In this context, it means to look for the traps of the devil. Thus, you cannot live circumspectly and be a slacker. And why else should we walk strictly and wisely is because he says the days are evil The days are evil is to be understood in a general sense, which is to say that there are temptations to sin at all times and in all places. And thus you cannot live strictly and judge the world accurately and be a slacker. A common manner of evil to be strict about is drunkenness For the alcohol dulls the senses and fogs the thinking while weakening a person's constitution. Whereas the sin Being tempted no longer looks dangerous, and the strength to say no to earthly desires is overwhelmed by the desire to satisfy the flesh. The answer, instead of drunkenness, is instead to be filled with the Holy Spirit, which grants the opposite effect of the wine. It is the Holy Spirit that renews the mind to think God's thought. And strengthen conviction and enables a person to say no to self and yes to God's commandments. To do so is to go against the spirit of this world. And to go against such a spirit is in no way enable you to be a slacker. And while being filled with the Spirit, he says we are to sing to one another psalms, hymns and spiritual psalms. The Psalms are clearly what we have in the Old Testament, considered the first hymn book of the church, which are also songs accompanied by musical instruments The hymns are those songs which are sung without accompaniment, and the spiritual songs seem to be a catch-all category for other types of songs. That these songs are to be melody in the heart is an encouragement towards emotion, which is our passion. Thus, our passions are to be poured out to God in song rather than being poured out in our flesh. To control our passions takes discipline, and discipline is unknown to slackers. And as mentioned last week, giving thanks to God is giving glory to God, and such is what we must do, for that is what we are created to do. And finally, there is the last instruction in the section of scripture read, which tells us to submit to one another, which is to be accountable to one another. And that is and that is in place before Paul continues about the proper roles of the Christian household. To be accountable to one another takes a great deal of courage. A person submitting to one another says, look at my life, and critique it. See what I see. See what I do. See what I write. Know what I say and correct it where it need be. Who says such things? No one I know, except it should be all of us. It is the slacker who submits to no one Going back to our parable, we realize that we have been privileged to be invited to the wedding of God the Father, to celebrate the wedding of his only begotten Son, to the church. And admits that privilege is a warning to prepare properly and thus not be a slacker. And Paul directs us on how to prepare. Beloved, you and I have been invited to a wedding, the greatest wedding of them all. It is time to look for a new dress, or a new suit, or a fancy sport coat. It is time to get the hair done. To cut the nails, to bathe thoroughly, to shine the shoes until you see yourself in them. Press the slacks until the crease can be clearly seen. The dinner has been announced as ready, with the oxen and fatted calf having been cut, cleaned, and cooked. I ordered the filet. Many of you probably ordered the crab cake, I imagine. But we all want to be there. Let us pray. A gracious God, for this image that you have placed before us For the excitement of joining the wedding feast. May all of us feel that privilege and be motivated by it to serve you All of our days that we will enjoy that day and enjoy it forever. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Motivated by the Kingdom
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I encourage you all to turn to John chapter 4. Our gospel reading, John chapter 4, beginning at verse 46. We're actually going to be going beyond our gospel reading. We are going to go into chapter 5. We're going to be comparing These two events that John records. So John 4, 46, starting. In the ethics class That I taught at the university, I introduced to the students Kohlberg's theory of moral development The premise of the theory is that there is a universal development sequence to structures of moral development that extend across all cultures. The theory is actually a simple observation. Stage one. Stage one is punishment and obedience orientation. Where decisions are made based on the understanding of the authority and its ability to carry out physical consequences. A child obeying because it does not want to be spanked is an example. Stage two is the relativist orientation. Where a person is pragmatically driven, being concerned primarily with self-interest and that which satisfies the self. If good is done, it is for the purpose of having good done in return. Stage three is the good boy, nice girl orientation Where a person tries to live up to the expectations of others while searching for approval. Stage four is the law and order orientation where a person is concerned with maintaining social order. It is obeying the law because the law keeps society in order. It is concerned with the duty of all citizens. Stage 5 is the social contract orientation, where laws are understood to be a means to a greater end. Laws are to be examined, formulated, and even changed to bring about the greater good. The final stage, stage six, is the universal ethical principle orientation. Ethical decisions are made with personal ethical principles and logical understanding of consequences both for the individual and the universal. Are you taking good notes for all of this? None of these stages, mind you, are exclusive to one another We are, as a sinful race, a combination of many motivations regarding why we obey rules, why we obey laws, and why we disobey the same. And many people get stuck in one or two of the stages, never maturing out of them so they might be motivated for the sake of the good of others rather than just thinking about themselves. I reference Kohlberg's theory here because the two stories we are looking at from John's Gospel have a number of different motivations being described. And these motivations will tell us about ourselves, that is to say, who we are and who we identify with. And it will be a call for us to repent of certain motivations we may be embracing. Recall that John is very particular regarding what stories he tells. Remember, his gospel is written much later than the first three. He only chose seven miracles of Jesus to describe, and he did so keeping in mind the juxtaposition of each of the stories. Not just in the relation to each other, but in relation to the discourses, those teaching moments of Jesus, those that he records. And so we mentioned the juxtaposition of the story of the woman at the well and the Samaritan people who believed Jesus to be the Messiah. Recall that Jesus stayed with the Samaritans two days, and many believed on him because of his word. That reason, because of his word, is very important. It is important because of what they needed in order to believe and what they didn't need. They needed Jesus to reveal himself through his teaching and by simply being among them. That is to be compared to what the Galileans said they needed. After Jesus, after the stay of Jesus in Samaria, he goes back to the region in which he performed his first miracle. Remember turning the water into wine. Apparently, having just arrived, Jesus is contacted by a government official, likely a servant of Herod Antipas. For the purpose of healing the official's son, the response of Jesus speaks to motive. The reference to you people is to the people of Galilee. Jesus reveals their moral development. They are stuck at stage two as being pragmatically selfish. If it is about them, if it will benefit them, then they will follow, they will believe If it is not about them, then it makes no difference to them. And so Jesus calls them out. He confronts their motivation. But the nobleman, the nobleman is undeterred. His son is dying, and that is all he cares about. The nobleman then is motivated both for himself and for another. That is where most of us find ourselves when we pray for a loved one. We want them to be healed for their own sake and for our own hearts not to be hurt by watching them suffer. Jesus refused the man's request to go down with him to see the man's son. And incidentally, the request to go down is topographical As Cana was about 1,500 feet below Capernaum in elevation. But the refusal of Jesus to go down was not a refusal to heal the boy Jesus does what the centurion knew Jesus could do. He only needed to say a word, and the healing occurred. A key point in exchange is that the nobleman believed the word of Jesus. His believing is a result of him maturing spiritually. He trusted Jesus. That is no small thing to trust Jesus. It very well could be an eternal thing to trust in him. We don't know right now. Was the faith of the nobleman a saving faith, or was it in the moment of crisis? And once his son is back to full strength, they forget all about Jesus and go about their lives taking their health for granted. Crisis faith is an immature faith. It too is stage two in moral development as it is concerned primarily with self-interest. Crisis faith is so very easy to practice, for it provides a quick bandage to stop the bleeding. Many of us noticed Christ's faith after 9-11. People came to church to pray, to hear hope. They were earnest about faith, giving an answer to their soul, for the world was too confusing, and they needed a void to be filled, and the why questions answered But the faith, crisis faith, didn't last. Once the threat faded into our memories, and once we were assured by our president that the military would hunt down the terrorists, Many put their trust in chariots and horses, and their need for God faded. Crisis faith leads us to start attending Bible study more frequently or worship on Sunday more regularly, Christ's faith prods us to open up dusty Bibles and read, looking for anything that gives the soul hope. Christ's faith gets us on our knees and has us praying for longer periods and more earnestly than other times in our lives. There is truly nothing wrong with Christ's faith if it is the beginning point for us. Jesus knew this for the nobleman. The man needed Christ's faith to wake him up to the possibility of knowing God, personally, knowing God. And so the boy became sick. But not sick outside of the knowledge of the Heavenly Father. The boy's sickness grew worse, but still not outside the will of the Heavenly Father. And once Jesus heard of the boy's sickness, even though the motive of the people was to see miracles, and the motive of the nobleman was a crisis faith, Jesus knew the will of the Father and thus proclaimed healing for the boy, and the boy was healed. You see, beloved, God knows what motivates us. He knows that death and the fear of death are motivating. When Jesus warned that people who are not allowed into the kingdom of God will experience weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth, That was to be a motivator, and the motive was the first stage development, which is the stage of fear of punishment. And it is perfectly legitimate motivation to turn away from sin, but it is a beginning point. John tells us that the beginning point of the nobleman led to a belief in Jesus that spread to his whole family. And then John tells us that it was the second sign Jesus did in Galilee. By saying such, John is noting that there is a goal, a goal beyond the boy being healed. And beyond good wine being served at a wedding. The story of the boy being healed from the jaws of death Is next to or right before the story of the paralytic being healed in John chapter 5. The setting is much different. And obviously at a different time, but John wants us to hear the stories back to back. He wants us to relate to each of them. John doesn't specify what feast is being celebrated in chapter 5, verse 1, but since they are back in Jerusalem, we can guess it's another Passover. The mention of a fifth colonnade likely describes the dividing colonnades between two pools, which have been revealed by archaeological excavation. Verse 4 is controversial, for it does not appear in some manuscripts, and it appears a scribe put it in later to explain what was believed at the time. Regarding the sick man, it appears that he was lame and in not being able to walk. The mention of thirty-eight years May be a reference to the time Israel wandered in the wilderness, or it may simply mean that he was lame for a very long time. The motivation of this man was likely quite desperate and, frankly, depressing. His only hope was a miracle from heaven. Based off of a legend that has no accounted record of being true. An angel stirring the water And to add to his problem, he could not even tempt the fate of the legend because of his inability to move quickly. That Jesus quickly tells the lame man to walk after the man explains his dilemma shows us that Jesus is telling him that no angel from heaven is needed Only the Son of God, who is from heaven and will return to heaven, is needed. And all that the Son of God needs are words of life. The word immediately is used to assure the reader that it only took the words of Jesus to act out this miracle in all of its fullness. There was no slow growing of muscles or time for the straightening of bones and the stretching of ligaments. It was instant. Jesus can do that. Note that nothing about the character of the lame man has been revealed to us yet. Nothing about his motivation or his maturity level has been revealed, except that he wanted to be healed and that he was desperate. When John mentions that that the the day of healing was the Sabbath, it sets us up for an inevitable conflict. The Pharisees, we remember, were the police force against Sabbath breakers as they would watch for violators of their interpretation of the Sabbath law. And their interpretation was that no one was allowed to carry his sitting mat around the temple court because such was working, and God's people are not to work on the Sabbath. Now we are going to assume in the name of the love of God that these legalistic Jews who questioned the once lame man did not know that he was at one time, for a long time, lame. And so confronting the man for carrying his mat seems a little understandable. But then the man tells them that he is carrying his mat because the man who healed him told him to do so. And notice that the legalistic Jews completely gloss over what they were just told about the man being healed. They ignored that a miracle man is among them. They didn't care if the lame walk. They didn't care if the blind see. They only cared about their narrow interpretation of the Sabbath law. Remarkable. Remarkable. Next we have Jesus running into the once lame man again and instructing the man to understand what a blessing it is for him to be healed. And that the man should see to it that he sins no more, or something worse, something worse would come upon him Now we have already heard Jesus say in other places that people are not necessarily sick because of a specific sin committed. But the word necessarily is useful because of what Jesus implies here, which is that some people do indeed get sick because of sins they have committed St. Paul confirms this when he warns against people taking the Lord's Supper in an unworthy manner. It is the responsible Christian, the mature Christian, who will ask the Lord to search His heart to see if there is any sin therein. What occurs next forces us to question the maturity of the healed man. As soon as he learns that it was Jesus that healed him, he goes and tells the Jewish legalists, and they follow up by finding reason to persecute Jesus. We could read into this and conclude that the healed man was an immature man and that he was only concerned about getting not getting in trouble with Jewish leaders, or maybe he was mature enough to want to be thought of as a good boy. But either way, his actions do not seem to care about what his telling would do to Jesus. And then there is the motive of the legalistic Jews. The maturity level we can place them in is stage four. Which is again law and order orientation, where a person is concerned about maintaining social order. These men are more mature than the heeled man or the citizens of Galilee, but they are stuck at stage four. In fact, they are so very stuck that the law and their interpretation of the law itself has become an idol to them. They worship it. Their legalism is such an idol that it blinds them from seeing the Messiah. They say that they are looking for. Amazing. But that is what legalism does. It blinds persons from seeing their own hypocrisy. That is why legalists so easily strain a gnat and then swallow a cattle. It is why they try to take a speck out of someone else's eye while having a board stuck in their own eye. Legalism helps a person see the sins of others more easily while increasing their blindness to the sins of their own. Legalism also breeds jealousy. Legalism doesn't like other people expressing freedom. Legalism doesn't like people having a good time. Legalism wants everyone to stay under the weight of the law, for misery does indeed love company. Well, we have seen the motivation of the people in these two stories, and we have been able to place them in stages of moral development and found them all to be wanting. Except one, of course. What was Jesus motivated by? We can assume he was at stage seven in his moral development, which, if you recall, the stages is higher than the stages I listed. And at that stage of moral development, a person is motivated, motivated by the coming of the kingdom of God. The primary reason Jesus healed the nobleman's son was for a sign for the people that the kingdom of God, Jesus Himself, had come to them. His healing of the lame man within the temple walls was a sign to the people that the kingdom of God had come to them, even to the ones who had tried to destroy it. And because Jesus was motivated by the kingdom of God, so too are his followers to be motivated. We are to be motivated by the kingdom of God. We might miss it because we say it so often, but when we pray the Lord's Prayer, we pray for God's kingdom to come. That is the end goal. It is so simple, making it so profound. It is all, it is all for the kingdom of God. Why do I want my children to believe and have families where their spouses and their children believe? I want it for them as individuals, of course, to be sure, but the true motivation should be the kingdom of God. I want, I am to want the kingdom of God to come Why do I want all of your marriages to survive and thrive? It is for you, to be sure, but it is most importantly for the kingdom of God to be established on earth as it is in heaven. Why bother with a school? Do you know how much hassle it is to run a school? Why do it if it is that much of a hassle? Why do I prepare sermons for each Sunday? Why? Why not just go through the motions and spend time talking to you about what interested me in the news this past week? Why not? Why bother to show care and concern for the sick, the hurting, and the lonely? Why befriend people when people will get mad at us and leave the church? Why bother indeed? Well, you know the answer to these questions. It is because of the kingdom of God. It is because of the kingdom of God that we minister the way we do. We care about what we care about. The kingdom of God is to be our motivation. Sure, you and I can be motivated by fear of punishment, by wanting to be considered a good boy or a good girl, or because we want good social order. But all such motivation must grow up. All such motivation must move to the last motivation for Christians, which is to see the kingdom of God, to see God's will be done. That was the motivation of Jesus, and it is to be ours as well. So let it be our motivation. Let us grow up and care most about the kingdom of God. Let us pray. Father, for this standard, we thank you for revealing it to us through the Gospel of John And for him to point to your kingdom to come and your will to be done. May that be our constant prayer, our constant goal, and that which we praise you for. In Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Reliability of God
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Forgive my voice. Some of you know that I helped coach the Liberty High School football team. We had a playoff game last night and I was yelling out the plays to the players, the numbered plays, and then I woke up with this whatever it is inside my throat. So it's a little rough this morning. Oh, and we lost forty-five to forty-three. It was a terrible loss. We're looking at Philippians chapter 1, starting at verse 1, our reading started at verse 3, but we're starting at verse 1, and then we're going to jump over to the Gospel of Matthew I purchased a boat just over two years ago. I should say we purchased a boat. Three of my sons invested with me I did it for the sake of the family. Fun. Family fun with the hope of spending summer Saturdays out on the water with the family towing the grandchildren around on ski tubes. The boat is 21 feet long, has a stern drive engine, and packs 220 horsepower. We put in a new floor, new seats, and new wiring for the trailer. I took a required course to get a boat license. I got a trailer license from New Hampshire because if you don't want to pay a lot of money to to the state of Maryland, you go through New Hampshire In the two summers, oh, we bought life jackets and ski tubes and a tow rope. In the two summers that we've had the boat, we have taken it out four times. And no one has been tow, and no fun has been had. There are various reasons for that that I will not go into. My main point in telling you this is to show how easy it is to have plans, to make plans, and never fulfill your plans. The book of Proverbs tells us that many are the plans of a man's heart, but the Lord's purpose prevails.
