Examine yourself and consider how many events you have wanted to attend, how many things you have wanted to experience How many purchases you have wanted to make, how many items you have saved up for, how many places you have wanted to go, and you haven't done any of it. Just how reliable are we? Even reliable to ourselves. Many Christians have a difficult time with the doctrine of predestination. The problem seems to be about the understanding of an individual person's free will and an apparent injustice being done by God by not choosing all people. If God chooses who will be saved, where does that infringe on a person's ability to choose for themselves? And how is it just for God to choose some to be saved and not others? Well the Calvinists have answers to these objections. Because every person before he or she is saved is dead in their sins and trespasses, no one has the ability to choose God. Thus, God must intervene and enable people to choose the good, which is to choose Him. To the second objection made by babies and others, the base truth is that if justice were fulfilled Then no one would be saved because all persons deserve damnation. That God would save anyone shows him to be merciful. For he fulfilled his own standard of justice by sacrificing his own son. Such answers are logical and reasonable to the objections But none of what I have just said gets to the heart or the purpose of the doctrine of predestination. The heart or purpose of the doctrine of predestination is security in salvation. Security in our salvation. It is for Christians to be at peace with the fact that our salvation and our heavenly hope are so solely dependent upon God as opposed to ourselves. And for that, we are to be most grateful. Let us now examine how this is declared by Paul to the Christians at Philippi. The opening verse of St. Paul's letter is unique in that it includes Timothy as a source of Paul's writing. We learn later in the letter that the people of the church requested that Timothy be sent to them. So Paul assures them of his present condition, which is ministering next to Paul. To refer to all of them as saints is gracious and loving as a reference. Were all of them behaving like saints? We can say no, because there was some disunity among them that Paul needed to confront. But Paul was loving and gracious to all of them, regardless of their troubles, and it is an example for all of us. In fact, I speculate that if we were to refer to each other as saints, it would have at least two effects. If we greeted one another, if we greeted one another in the manner of good morning, Saint Stan or Saint Fran. Or good morning, Saint Suzanne. Or Saint Larry's not here. Not going to call him a saint. Those who were called a saint Would be encouraged to act like a saint, and those who call people saints would be encouraged to treat them like a saint. Either way, it's a win win. Next, the line, Grace to you, and peace. That's a typical greeting by Paul. Years back when there was some social tension in this parish, and I noted two things about the tension. Some people were not being gracious to others, nor were they practicing feast, but were instead unnecessarily riled And so I started ending my pastoral correspondence with the phrase grace and peace. Because we all need grace in terms of getting it and giving it. And we all need to be at peace because there is nothing worth being disturbed about except your own sin. And Paul closes his greeting by giving God the Father and Jesus the Son the same billing. For in the Father and the Son is the source of grace and peace. Verses 4 and 5 reveal the intimate relationship Paul had with the congregation as a whole And that affection displayed reveals how important such relationships are. When Paul prays for them, he has memories that are filled with joy. And such speaks to the impact that these people had had on his life. They had fellowship with him Which is a sincere friendship where he could trust them and they could trust him. Such is a genuine relationship, which is where honesty can be expressed without condemnation. And with commitments made to one another that will be fulfilled without reservation, and where love, true Christian 1 Corinthians chapter 13, love is exchanged And at the center of it is the good news of Jesus Christ, which is that sins are forgiven and heaven is our certain hope. Because of the genuine fellowship just described, Paul turns to the confidence that he has in their salvation. Not because of how good a people they are, or because of how much he feels loved by them, or how much they have helped him in the past. No. He is confident in their salvation because of God. God, he says, who began a good work in them. Which means that he revived them and revealed the truth of himself to them and brought them to be converted to the Christian faith That such was the beginning point, and that God is sure to complete, which is to keep them in the faith until Jesus returns to take all of his people to their eternal home. And so I take you back to my voting plans. Or maybe we can look at your travel plans. Or house renovation ideas, or the new garden that you have been wanting to start, or maybe you started it but didn't finish it. I recall growing up with several of my father's projects going unfinished, and I always wondered how he accepted it. We had a stairwell that was half painted. And I would think that such a reality would feel like it was mocking him every time he walked up and down those stairs. If the walls could speak, they would say to him every time he walked those steps Yeah, I'm still here waiting for that spackling to be sanded, waiting for that first coat to be finished. I'm not going anywhere, still available anytime that you need me. The point being that we humans, our species, are not reliable. We should not depend upon ourselves because we cannot depend upon ourselves. Thus we are to say, thanks be to God, that it is He who will finish the work He started in us, and it is only Him that we can trust. How grateful we are to be that God is solely responsible for our salvation is underlined and highlighted by the parable of the unforgiving servant in our gospel reading. The story is familiar to us, so I am simply going to place a spotlight on certain aspects of it. Jesus tells the parable in response to the question about forgiveness. How many times should I forgive a brother who sins against me? With the possible number of seven. And so we ask, why seven? The number is sacred in that it is the days in which God used to identify time And it is the numbered day in which he rested while calling his creation good. Thus it is a number of completion. Number of completion. Jesus answers with the same number multiplied to a much greater number of completion. Which was his way of exaggerating the point to absurdity, which tells us that there is no number to completion regarding how often Christians are to forgive one another. To explain how forgiveness is to work within the lives of those who followed him, Jesus describes a king making a common business action. A king wants to settle his debts, which means he wants people to pay him what they owe him. This is unlike the world economy today. Which seems to have countries indebted to one another with no one able to settle debts, but that commentary is for another time. So this wealthy man or king calls those indebted to him to pay up. And one man owes a lot and could not pay. So the king, the wealthy king, treats the situation like any business transaction, or any businessman would, and calls for the man to be thrown in prison as a thief, because that's what he was. It was not personal, merely business. The debtor panics and asks for mercy, with a promise to pay the debt eventually. The wealthy king sees the humbleness and desperateness of the debtor and rescinds his call for justice, and next extends mercy by canceling the entire debt. Such was unexpected. The debtor didn't even consider asking for such forgiveness Such as the second example of human fickleness in the story, with the first being the debtor who took out a debt he couldn't afford. Having then been freed from the debt, which we can all empathize with, or we can feel what that must have been like emotionally, having, as they say, a great weight taken off your back. The debtor also has people indebted to him and decides to settle those debts, being now the collector. So he comes upon a fellow debtor and demands his money, money considerably less than what was just recently forgiven. And the fellow debtor also cannot pay, and also asks time to pay it. But the first debtor refuses to be patient and has his fellow debtor thrown in prison. Such is a display of grace received, but not given. And Jesus warned elsewhere that to whom much is given, much is required. I found an article this week titled Presidential Promises Broken Since Nineteen Sixteen. Here are some of the highlights. Woodrow Wilson ran for re-election in 1916 on the slogan, He kept us out of war. The result, just 29 days after he was sworn into his second term, Wilson asked a joint session of Congress for a declaration of war against Germany Citing Germany's broken promise to suspend unrestricted U-boat warfare and an attempt by Germany to talk Mexico into joining an alliance against the U. S. Congress granted the request two days later. Then there was Lyndon Johnson taking office, as you know, in 1963 after the assassination of JFK. Running for re-election in 1964, LBJ painted his opponent, Barry Goldwater, as a war hawk And promise we are not about to send American boys 9 or 10,000 miles away from home to do what Asian boys ought to be doing for themselves. The result? Johnson sent combat troops to Vietnam and escalated the war many times. After public opinion turned against him LBJ pulled out of the 1968 race. Then there is the first George Bush. In his acceptance speech in 1988, He said to the crowd, you remember it, read thy lips, no new taxes. The result, the Bush administration found itself plagued by a persistent recession while the federal deficit increased. After months of trying and failing to hammer out a deal, Bush admitted his failure and raised taxes. And then there was a president who I can't remember, but he said something about his healthcare system and that you could keep the doctor if you wanted to keep your doctor. And then there was a president who said he would build a wall and then that didn't happen. What's the point? People don't keep their word. In fact, we could even say they can't keep their word. There is no one beside the Lord Jesus Himself, the Apostle Paul, who understood the human condition more clearly than Augustine of Hippo. In his work titled Confessions, he thoroughly explains his outward struggles with lust of the flesh and inner pride. After he turned his life over to the Savior Jesus and became a new man, he explained how difficult it was to control earthly desires still when you sleep. This is what he said. Speaking to the Lord, he says, This Verily thou calls me to continency from the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of the world. Thou calls me to continency from concubage and wedlock itself. Thou hast cancelled something better than that. Thou hast permitted. And since thou gave it, it was done, even before I became a dispenser of thy sacraments. But there still lives in my memory whereof I have much spoken. The images of such things as my ill custom there fixed, which haunt me, strengthless when I am awake, but in sleep not only so as to give pleasure, but even to obtain agreement. And what is very like reality? Yea, so far prevails the illusion of the image in my soul and in my flesh. That when asleep false visions persuade to that which men waking they cannot be true. Am I not then myself, O Lord my God? And yet there is so much difference between myself and myself within the moment wherein I pass from waking to sleeping, or returning from sleeping to waking. Such sentiment is very close to the description St. Paul gives to the Romans in chapter 7. describing that he does what he does not want to do and fails to do that which he does that he knows he should do In the end, all of us are to say, along with Augustine, along with St. Paul, woe is me. And so we can't trust others. And we can't trust ourselves even when we're asleep. Thanks be to God. We are not left to our woeful condition. But instead we celebrate the deliverance Jesus offers and provides, along with the power of the resurrection, to overcome sin when awake and when asleep. But while we struggle in this life with the flesh and the spirit, and while we admit our inconsistent character, And an inability to be altogether true in keeping our word and doing as we should, we come back to the promise given by Paul. He, God, who began a good work in you. Which is to open your eyes to the spiritual world and the realities of the destruction of sin, and to believe Jesus is the Son of God who overcame sin and death. That's what he woke you up to do. Such a faith is what he began in you. Will be, God will be, faithful to complete it. To complete it is to be standing before him while he extends himself to us and says, Well done. Thou good and faithful servant, enter into your rest. God did the saving, is doing the saving, and will complete the saving. And our lives are to be lived, reflecting the gratefulness we have in our hearts that He will complete it in us. Let us pray. A gracious and heavenly father We thank you for what you started, we thank you for what you are doing, and we thank you for the promise of completion. May our hearts be increased all the more this day to serve you faithfully until the end, until our end, until you greet us and welcome us home. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Open your Bibles to the book of Revelation. Revelation chapter one. Today we began a series of sermons from the book of Revelation. I preached from this fascinating text near twenty years ago And there are a number of new faces among us, so I am taking up the challenge again. There are a number of points to remember as we study this last book of the Bible. Let it be understood. The book is first a letter to first century Christians. Addressing the suffering they were enduring for the sake of the gospel. This is as opposed to 20th and 21st century teachers. Who treat it as a prophecy only, and a prophecy that applies to our modern context only. Such a reading is ego-centric, narcissistic, and ill-informed. The original audience was the primary audience, and while the Holy Spirit had in mind all Christians who would follow, we must learn what these words originally meant to the original audience. Also, knowing Old Testament texts such as the Book of Exodus, Daniel, Isaiah, and Ezekiel are crucial to interpreting the book of Revelation. Also, there is a great deal of imagery and metaphor that should keep us from interpreting certain texts literally. Because they were not written to be interpreted literally. Finally, most everything you might remember from the left behind series is wrong. And for those of you who do not know of the left behind series, I encourage you to keep it that way. Let us now turn to what we know about the writing of the book and what we don't know. We know that it was written by John the Apostle, brother to James. He is also known as the one whom Jesus loved. John referred to himself in such a manner. Frustratingly, we don't know when it was written Some believe it was later in John's life, around 90 A. D. Others believe that because the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of the temple are not mentioned. Which occurred in 70 A. D. , it must be before that fall, making the writing at least 21 years earlier. Again, we don't know The title of the book is Apocalypse or Revelation. It is both a revelation of John And of Jesus, because it was given to John by Jesus, and John wrote it down. So let us begin. Verse 1. The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show his servants things which must take place, and he sent and signified it by his angel to his servant John. A revelation is an unveiling, and this is the case, an unveiling of divine mysteries. There is a curious reference to God here, saying that God gave Jesus a revelation, which he was to pass on to a servant of Jesus, who we learn later is John. But Jesus is God and will be shown to be God in this entire text. So God gives this revelation to Jesus, who is God. And part of the three and one. This type of what I'm calling mixed, mixing descriptive, mixing descriptive, we will find several times in this book. What is being revealed, he says, are things. And the things will take place shortly, which means they are events, and events in time. The word shortly can be translated immediately, which leaves no doubt that what he is about to describe is relevant to the Christians who first read these words. Another character is added to the scene. It is an angel who is given the duty of relaying to John the revelation. Verse 2: Who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ to all things that he saw The person who bore witness is John, as he is the subject at the end of verse 1. John uses judicial language as if he is on trial or at least giving a deposition It is his way of swearing an oath to what he is writing. A reference to the Word of God is another mixed descriptive. As it can refer to Jesus, whom John is witness, or the actual words God was then telling him. What he saw was Jesus. The whole revelation will be about Jesus the Christ, the Messiah. Verse 3. Blessed is he who reads, and those who hear the words of this prophecy, and keep those things which are written in it, for the time is near. Here is a rare promise of blessing to the reader, and with such a blessing promised, you would think more Christians would focus on this book. But many are either scared off or confused or both. Note that there are conditionals for the blessing. You either have to hear or read the words, which is that you cannot just hear words about the actual words, but hear or read the actual words. Next, you have to keep those things which are written therein. To keep is to follow their guidance, it is to have faith in their truth. We may summarize by saying the reader or listener is to believe and obey. Verse four. John, to the seven churches which are in Asia, grace to you and peace from him who is And who was, and who is to come, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne. Here we see that John is writing the letter, but he is not the origin of the letter. The original audience was seven churches, but such were not the only churches of that day. Seven, you will remember, is a number of completion. So the number represents all Christian churches. And not all that only existed in the first century, but all churches for all time. These churches named existed in the first century, but so did other churches, and they had similar problems. My point is that because the number of churches are seven, it symbolizes that the messages go beyond those churches, even though Even though I started off saying that the original audience is most important. It still is, but so are all the churches that existed then and will exist. When it comes to the issue that are addressed to these seven churches, we're going to find ourselves in these addresses. The greeting of grace and peace is Pauline, but the author John is giving it, and the greeting was quite common. The identity of from him is Jesus. And the early church recognized how important this introduction was because Jesus didn't have a beginning in terms of being part of the Godhead. He is identified as who is, presently existing, and who was previously existing, and who is to come, future existing. As he will be appearing on earth again at what is called his second coming, and there is no better verse for Advent than this one. The letter is said to be from the seven spirits, which can be confusing if you take the number literally. There are not seven Holy Spirits, but one. Again, the number seven symbolizes completeness. So it is saying that the letter is from the Holy Spirit in its completeness. Verse 5, and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler over the kings of the earth. To him who loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood. The letter, it says, is also from Jesus Christ. Christ is not his last name, but it is his title. It means anointed, which is another word for Messiah, which is our Savior. Jesus is the faithful witness in numerous ways. He was a faithful witness, for he revealed the essence of the Heavenly Father. He said, If you have seen me, you've seen the Father. He was a faithful witness to the moral law of God as revealed in the Holy Scriptures, for he kept it all. He was a faithful witness in carrying out the will of the Father even unto death. And he was a faithful witness showing that death cannot hold down a soul that is guiltless. And it says, Jesus is the ruler over the kings of the earth. Not a ruler, not was a ruler, not will be ruler Jesus Christ is the ruler, the ruler over the kings of the earth. And it is passages like this that get me closer to being a post-millennialist. I won't bore you with too many details, but there are three primary camps of scholarship regarding the end of time and how it will go down according to the Bible. The first is the premillennial camp. The word millennial means a thousand, referring to a thousand years, and it is derived from Revelation chapter 20. Where it describes a binding of the devil and the reign of Jesus on earth for a thousand years. A pre-millennialist believes that Jesus will come back to the earth, and that is when the devil will be bound, and Jesus will have a literal, which means physical, reign over all of the earth. Then there are the odd millennialists, and they believe that the thousand-year reign is not to be understood as literal but metaphorical. And that the reign of Jesus has begun ever since he overcame death. But it is a spiritual reign, and those who believe in him experience such a reign personally. When Jesus returns, the final judgment will take place. Then there are the post-millennialists. Who also, like the all-millennialists, don't believe in a literal interpretation of Jesus reigning on earth, but believe that the physical reigning is to be done by the church. The church is to Christianize the world before Jesus physically returns. Thus, you have groups of Christians who believe in building up schools of good learning. Who believe in starting good businesses with Christian owners, who help build Christian communities, who make stronger Christian churches Who disciple families and exemplify Christian faith by supporting one another. There is now, if you don't know, a movement called Christian nationalism. Christian nationalism believes America can be pulled back from the gutter of smut and greed where we have been lying for some time And re-establish itself as a God-fearing nation. And the conviction that such can be done comes from passages that tell us that Jesus is the ruler over all the kings of the earth. I am not going to tell you which of the three millennial camps I fall under But I will tell you that I get pumped up. My testosterone level spikes when I read that Jesus Christ is the ruler over all the kings of the earth. And he received said status not by wielding a sword or commanding an army or having access to a nuclear arsenal. He did it by submitting to the will of the Heavenly Father. He did it by giving up his own life to a people, to a people who thought they deserved to be chosen by God. And he gave it to an empire that thought it was the most powerful in all the world. And he gave it to the devil, who thought once he had Jesus on the cross, that he himself would rule the kings of the earth. But as C. S. Lewis in his Narnia series describes, there was a deeper magic still. The earth could not hold him, hell could not hold him, and so he went from fully identifying with sinners In hell, to the very heights of heaven, where he reigns, and where no principality or power or ruler of any age can challenge him. And so we can say, we can say, Go ahead, devil, steal your elections. Get into political offers office the perverts and the immoral and the dishonest and the thieves and the scammers. Get them all elected And doing your bidding. And have them help you think you have power. True earthly power. But you know, devil, and I know devil. And we all know, devil, that there is a firstborn from the dead that rules over all the kings of the earth, proving that your power is not true power, but a mere illusion. Now let us continue reading what a true God with authority does. Again, reading the rest of verse 5: to him who loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood. What does the ruler of the kings of the earth do? He loves his people. Jesus loved us. And what does a person do for those he loves? He saves them from their demise because of their sin. And so Jesus washes us from our sins with his own blood. Remarkable. Unconditional love displayed and exemplified with no rival, he offered himself He freely bled and died, and he uses that blood to cleanse from sin all who accept him as Savior and Lord. Remarkable indeed. And what does the blood of Jesus do for those he washes? Reading verse six. And has made us kings and priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen. Who has he made kings and priests? Us? Yes, us. Because Jesus rules over all the kings of the earth, he can replace them. And being priest, what advantage is there to being a priest? Priests get to serve There is like me no other profession that is more privileged to serve than a priest. We get to help people at their most joyous times, a baby being born and then christened. To most painful times, deathbed of a loved one, saying goodbye at a funeral. We get to speak the good news of Jesus Christ to a dying and lost world. Here it is explained that such a privileged position is for all of us. All of us can enter the Holy of Holies and see God face to face. That is what being made a priest allows, and so we respond accordingly. We say as the verse ends, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen. And as Paul reminds us. When it comes to being saved from sin and death, God does not know male or female. In glory All our kings and all our priests, regardless of gender, and God was no progressive. Such is as it always has been. Verse 7. Behold, he is coming with clouds, and every eye will see him, even they who pierced him And all the tribes of the earth will mourn because of him. Even so. Amen. How many things, how many things are for sure in life? The old saying answers only death and taxes. And as ironic as that may be, it is not the final answer for Christians. We can add that Jesus will return. And at that return, he will solidify his victory over sin and death by raising to new life all who believed in him. That is ultimate victory. That is reigning over all the kings of the earth. That is plundering the devil's so-called domain. So if you follow Jesus and you fret about elections, no more. If you struggle with a vice as if you are on the losing side, no more. Regardless of your life situation, if you are weighed down by illness A broken relationship, financial burdens, social despondency, no more. Regardless of your life situation, Jesus has won the day. And you who follow Jesus need to get your head up and walk straight because you are on the winning side. And so our study of the book of Revelation begins. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God, we need to be inspired by this book as the first century Christians were. We need to see how important it is that in the midst of our sacrifice for you, we are being made whole and prepared for eternity. And so bless this study. May it be useful for your glory and our sanctification. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles to Revelation chapter 1 Picking up at verse 8, follow along with me if you would. Revelation chapter 1. Picking up at verse 8 Before John's vision, the last time anyone physically saw Jesus was Paul on the road to Damascus. And in that vision, it was a light and a voice. Before that, the last sighting of Jesus was of him ascending into heaven But looking very much like he looked on earth. What John sees of Jesus in the book of Revelation is quite different than how Jesus looked While walking amidst humanity. The question we can ask and answer is, why? Why does Jesus appear so different in this vision he gives to John? This will be answered in our study today. The introduction we started last week continues. And we hear Jesus describing himself in verse 8 as the Alpha and the Omega. We know such letters are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, respectively. Thus, the meaning of the reference is repeated to be the first and last, which is an identity of Jesus not having a beginning and not having an end. In verse 9, John identifies himself again with an explanation of where he was when he received the vision he is about to describe. The island of Patmos is off the west coast of Turkey in the Mediterranean Sea. It was a place where political exiles were sent. Thus, John was placed in political exile as Christians were starting to be seen as a danger to the Paks Romana. In verse 10, we are told what day in the week the vision came to John. It was the Lord's day, which is the day of resurrection, which we know of as Sunday. And even rabbis began to call in the first century Sundays as the day for the Christians. John describes himself as being in the Spirit, which is referring to the Holy Spirit. He may have been in a trance, but the details of what it means to be in the Holy Spirit, those details are left to the imagination. Next, Jesus again refers to his eternal identity, and the instruction to write to the seven churches is repeated. with the addition of giving the names of the churches. First, Ephesus is addressed. It was an Asiatic metropolis and was nearest to the island of Patmos. Then the other churches on the west coast of Asia are listed, than those in the interior region. We are going to look at verses 12 through 16 together as they describe the exalted Jesus giving us one grand image. A voice causes John to turn and see, such as what we are attempting to do this very hour. We need to see Jesus as he is revealed here. The seven lampstands are similar to what the prophet Zechariah saw in his vision and those placed in the temple. But these seven lampstands seem not to be connected, but stand each on their own while Jesus is in the middle of them. That the image that John sees is like, he says, like the Son of Man, allows there to remain a mystery to this vision. We remember that the seven churches represent all churches because the number seven means completeness, and thus Jesus stands in the middle of all churches. He is dressed in a robe with a golden band around him. The dress is a combination of what a priest would wear to enter the Holy of Holies. And what a king would wear. Jesus then is appearing as a priest-king. His white hair symbolizes purity and a transfiguration as is fitting for his heavenly state. His eyes, like fire, show his purpose of looking upon both good and evil while consuming both. Turning evil to ashes and the good into purified gold. His feet are brass because he himself has been purified by his own suffering. The description also speaks to the beauty of his glowing feet that are firmly established in truth and in righteousness. His voice is like water, in that it rushes like great rivers, it cascades like great falls, and it roars like violent waves. The stars are explained in verse 20 to be the emblems of the angels of the seven churches. They are described as stars in his right hand. Perhaps appearing as a wreath or as a royal and star-adorned diadem in his hand. The two-edged of or double-edged sword coming out of his mouth is found elsewhere in Scripture. It is his word. The word of Jesus is the sword. And as the preacher to the Hebrews explains, it has the work of putting to death those who rebel against God. and the work of surgically healing those who fear God. In general, it is used to both judge and save, which is the same purpose or persona as the Holy Scriptures. Describing his countenance or what it was like to look upon him as looking upon the sun in its strength. Is using a descriptive that can be understood, and yet we humans cannot look upon the sun in its strength without damaging our sight. Thus, the countenance of Jesus could not be looked upon for long. John's response described in verse 19 is one that all of us would follow. The song so popular with evangelical Christians several years ago titled I Can Only Imagine. speculates as to what it would be like to stand before Jesus as the writer of the song wonders what he would physically do. Well, John has the answer. In response to John falling as a dead man, it is the exalted Jesus who serves to comfort and relieve John's fear. Which we should describe again as remarkable. For here is the exalted one bending low to place his right hand on John. Jesus once again provides the description of himself being the first and the last, only he adds here that he lives, but was at one time dead. This is a profound description and one that you can use to witness to heretical groups such as Jehovah's Witnesses and Mormons. For both groups deny the divinity of Jesus. Here, Jesus makes it clear that he is God by describing himself as eternal while also describing himself as having died. Just ask a heretic, when did God die? And you have placed them in a position of doubt. Jesus next describes himself as having the keys of Hades, which is the dwelling of the dead, and he has the keys of death itself, which means he has authority over death. He is now the deciding factor on who lives and who dies and where they go after death and who will be given new life. What Jesus has revealed about himself in these verses, both in his physical appearance and by his words, is himself as judge. Jesus as judge is not often described or preached or taught in modern evangelical churches. We don't mind learning about baby Jesus, and many people would like him to stay a baby. We don't mind hearing of Jesus teaching in the temple as a youth, for he harms no one. We don't mind hearing about Jesus healing or forgiving or even dying. But Jesus as judge is not as pleasant as the rest of it. But here he is. Dressed and exalted and positioned and equipped to judge both the living and the dead Recall that Jesus warned of judgment several times in the Gospels. He warned us that we will be judged in the same manner we judge others. He warned that all persons will be required to give a justification for every empty word spoken. He warned that those who will not believe in him as Savior have already condemned themselves. He warned that those who ignore the needs of the least regarded in society will be sent away to everlasting punishment. And let us remember these following words from Jesus, where he is teaching his disciples what to expect from the unbelieving world around them. For if they persecuted him, they will surely persecute his followers. And then he says this to them so do not be afraid of them. For there is nothing concealed that will not be disclosed, and nothing hidden that will not be made known. What I tell you in the dark, speak in the daylight. What is whispered in your ear, proclaim from the housetops. Do not be afraid of those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul. Fear the one who can destroy both soul and body in hell. And so let us identify plainly who it is that can send both the body and soul to hell. The answer, of course, is Jesus. I now must balance This emphasis of Jesus as judge, because it can be taken a bit too far. It is speculated by some scholars that the rise of Mariology Which is at the very least praying to Mary, mother of Jesus, and some worshiping her, that it was caused in part by the over-emphasis of Jesus as judge. Jesus, as judge, scared many in the Middle Ages, causing Mary to look more approachable. Paintings from the Middle Ages show Jesus as a large figure at the center of the scene with multiple people either around him or to his sides while he is announcing their eternal fate. Such are not the type of pictures presently made of Jesus. Such are not the type of pictures we would hang in our church today. Prayers to gentle Mary, who was thought then to intercede to Jesus directly, those are not made. Of course, we Protestants see such thinking as quite absurd, for it is Jesus who we want a personal relationship. It is Jesus who is our intercessor. For it was Jesus who said, Come unto me, all ye that are heavy laden, and find rest. That his yoke was easy, that his burden was light. But let us not leave our image of Jesus only as a teacher calling us to be relieved of our burdens. For what we have just read in Revelation and our imaging in our minds is a Jesus who reigns over all the kings of the earth and is ready and able to judge men for their deeds. In totality, what every Christian needs is an image of Jesus as a baby, for that speaks of the love of God along with his humility. And we need a Jesus who teaches with patience, and a Jesus who forgives prostitutes, and a Jesus who suffers and dies, and a Jesus who is resurrected and ascended And a Jesus who is judge. All of those images and understandings of Jesus we need For they keep us balanced in love with him versus adoring him versus fearing him And what our culture so desperately needs is a fear of God, which comes when you proclaim Jesus as judge. I shared in Bible study a few months ago that I agree with those who are warning That the sexual immorality that is being mainstreamed in our culture has an end goal. And that end goal is the sexualizing of our children. Such has been blatantly stated by some who are on the fringe of the culture, but something happened recently That was barely in the mainstream news that shows how pedophilia is working to become mainstream Balenciaga is a clothing brand in the fashion industry that I had not heard of prior to a conservative reporter. Who showed a Balenciaga ad of a little girl no more than five years old holding a teddy bear while wearing a bondage outfit? And that's right, I said a bondage outfit. And if that isn't bad enough, in front of the image of the little girl and her bondage outfit are a number of items Called paraphernalia that looks like it doesn't belong, but it clutters the floor or the table, whatever is in front of the little girl, and scattered In that material, you can find a file. You have to focus in. You can find a file with a court ruling on it. The document is a copy from the Supreme Court case called Ashcroft vs. Free Speech Coalition. A case that struck down a law against against child pornography. In more simple words, the case document said that child pornography could be protected under free speech laws. Not only had I not heard of Balenciaga clothing, but I had not heard of a court case in the United States that ordered in favor of child pornography. But you tell me if there is any other reason for the Balenciaga Company to have a little girl in a bondage outfit with a court document favoring child pornography in the ad. Any other reason other than the promoting and sexualizing of children. If you have wondered just how far down the sleaze hole people can go, here's an example. Thus, not only do we not protect children in the womb, we want to have sex with them if they make it out of the womb. My point in telling you about this perverted clothing company is to ask this one question. Do they not fear God? You will remember that question from the scriptures in the Gospel according to Luke and his account of Jesus hanging on the cross. With one criminal hanging on a similar cross to his left and another to his right, and one of them saying to Jesus, if you are the Christ, save yourself and us. Luke says that such was stated as blasphemy because the man didn't believe Jesus was the Christ, so he didn't believe Jesus could save them, and so instead he mocked him. And Luke says that the other man rebuked the first man and said, Do you not even fear God, seeing you are under the same condemnation? Asking next for Jesus to remember him after death, Jesus made that saving promise that he would be with Jesus in paradise But let us focus on the question and ask. Ask it of the likes of owners and operators of Balenciaga and companies like it. Do you not even fear God? But let us not stop there. Let it be asked of your neighbor who scorns the religious. Do you not even fear God? Let it be asked of the adulterer who flaunts his unfaithfulness before his own children. Do you not even fear God? Let it be asked of the landlord who doesn't care for the apartments he rents but raises the price for rental on a whim. Do you not even fear God? Let it be asked of the politician who buys stocks related to legislation passed. Do you not even fear God? Let it be asked of the violent who stab and shoot his fellow man for anger, for extortion, for revenge. Do you not even fear God? Beloved, just as we love to see Jesus in a manger and read of him eating among sinners. And willing to touch and heal lepers, so too do we need to see Jesus highly exalted with eyes of fire. Fire that consumes sin and the sinner, and with a sword that can strike and disembowel. And that image provides the original question I asked. Why do we need to see Jesus in this exalted manner? Because it reveals him as judge and it tells us to fear him. Amen. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God, as much as we acknowledge your mercy, we here today acknowledge that you are judge. Judge of the living and judge of the dead, the decider of our eternal fate. And with this we say, we fear you and we love you. And we thank you for that fear. In Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Get the Love Back
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles to Revelation chapter 2. Looking at the first letter, Revelation chapter two, starting at verse one. And as you turn there, I I want to I I've looked at myself on YouTube And I've noticed how many times I preach and I'm off kilter. And for those of you who borderline on obsessive compulsive disorder, I realize that that really might bother you a lot. So try to keep as straight as I can If you are keeping score regarding my sermons, you notice that although we read verse 20 last week, I did not comment on it. I did not do so because I see it as an introduction to the seven letters we are starting to examine this morning. What I want us to agree upon is that because the number seven represents completeness, And because we believe these churches are representative of all Christian churches over all of time that we can agree with the Anglican scholar John Stott that the seven letters are seven marks of faithful and godly churches, that all churches should aspire to be. Consider this summary. Love is in letter one, suffering in letter two, truth in letter three. Holiness in letter four, integrity or sincerity in letter five, mission in letter six, and zeal in letter seven. If each of these characteristics is aspired to, the church will be, will be a pleasing bride to Christ. And so we start at verse 20 of chapter 1. John tells, I'm sorry, Jesus tells John that the seven stars in his right hand are seven angels that are assigned to the seven churches addressed in this vision. The beauty of this description is that Jesus wants us to understand that there are spiritual powers that are assigned to each church. Such powers are guardians of the churches, guardians ordained by Jesus, and messengers of his word and of his will. To believe that God has assigned heavenly messengers to lowly parishes such as St. Stephen's is quite comforting and encouraging, which should embolden us in the faith. We confess, knowing that it is backed up by heavenly powers. And so verse from chapter one, I'm sorry, chapter two, verse one It is natural for the vision to begin with the church in Ephesus because Ephesus was a chief city and closest to the island of Patmas Where John received this vision. Ephesus was also the first seaport in Asia Minor and home to the Temple Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. also known as the Temple of Diana. Perhaps forty years before this vision, the dating you remember is not assured. Forty years, the Apostle Paul had spent three years in Ephesus building up the church. Later, Timothy had an extensive ministry there. Then late in the first century, the Apostle John, the man receiving this vision, lived in Ephesus and made it the center of his ministry. No doubt there were many in the congregation that received this book of Revelation who knew John personally. Some of them probably knew him very well. And perhaps A number of them, a number of people, could remember the ministry of Paul, who were among the first to receive this letter. Twenty years after the writing of Revelation, Ignatius, the chief minister of the church in Antioch Wrote a letter to the church at Ephesus that is full of praise for what he calls that deserved, happy church, which is known everywhere, he says. For it known for its good deeds, its brotherly love and unity, under a man, this is so fascinating, under a man of inexpressible love, their bishop Onisimus. That name, you might remember, is the same Onesimus, according to ancient tradition, that was the runaway slave and then Christian convert whom Paul sent back to his master Philemon, as we read in the New Testament letter that bears Philemon's name Ignatius also expresses praise for the Ephesian Christians because he says no false teaching could gain hearing among them. Quite a history indeed. Verses 2 and 3. If Jesus were to write to St. Stephen's today and pin these very same words, I would be tempted to be overly proud, sinfully proud, perhaps. For you who have been within my ministry in this parish for any number of years, the one thing you know is that I strive to abide by the truth of the gospel And have made it a priority to be a defender of the gospel as it has been handed down to us from the apostles. The phrase the book of Jude uses is the faith once delivered to the saints. That same faith is what I am willing to defend to the death. I do confess that I have been tempted to be weary several times in the fight to defend it. But I find strength beyond myself and press on. What has been endured by the Ephesians from the words of Jesus were false teachers who have claimed to have the same authority as the original apostles, but then have proven themselves to be liars. And the only way to prove people are liars is to compare their teachings to the truth, and then only stand for the truth. The laboring praise of them is their due diligence to compare the false teachings they had heard, no matter how clever the teacher And to conclude that the teachers were to be rejected. Today, considering how much the devil has continued to use false teachers in every medium possible. It is a testament to the Holy Spirit that even a few remain faithful to that faith once delivered to the saints. Verse 4. What comes next is cold water to the face, but it is also a template for each of the seven letters. In Ephesus, something is missing. Something needs to be addressed. It can be concluded that standing for the truth isn't all that makes up the Christian faith. These Ephesian Christians have left their first love. Those Who think too much have questioned what Jesus meant in saying this to the Christian, to these Ephesian Christians. They questioned, what is the love that the Ephesian Christians had lost? Some argue that what was lost in Ephesus was brotherly love. In their zeal for doctrinal purity, a very good thing in itself And a zeal that they are actually commended for later on in the letter, they had allowed an uncaring and critical spirit to grow among them. As one commentator put it, the eagerness to root out all the staken men had ended in a sour and rigid orthodoxy. And such a problem is not original to the Christians at Ephesus. Others have chosen truth over brotherly love. Other scholars, however, argued that what is meant is that the Ephesian Christians had lost their love for God, for Christ Jesus Himself. That was their first love. They were doing the right thing still, but were no longer motivated by a devotion to the Lord They liken the statement in verse 4 to that of Jeremiah 2, chapter 2, verse 2, where the Lord says to Israel, I remember the devotion of your youth, how as a bride you loved me. But others argue a third possibility, which is that the statement refers to neither brotherly love nor a love of God and Christ. But to a love for the lost world, and specifically to sharing the gospel and bearing witness to others, which these believers had loved to do when first they became followers of the of Christ, as I said, such conclusions are from people who think too much As the great Anglican Archbishop Richard Trench stated, after discussing various interpretations Quote, the suggestion that this leaving of the first love can refer to the abating of any other love but that to God and Christ grows out of entire ignorance of the whole spiritual life. And this makes good sense. Because brotherly love comes from loving our God first and foremost. Caring for the spiritually lost comes from loving our God first and foremost. Love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, soul, mind, and strength. And what follows from that is a love for our neighbor as ourselves. The human need to love God is similar to the first commandment of the Ten. We are to have no other gods before him. To put something before him is to choose to love something before him, and to do so is to set up an idol in our lives, and that is always self-destructive. That is why some see the first two commandments as the same. To put something before God is to make a graven image. And a graven image is an idol. And when we make an idol, we worship said idol. And this leads me to a passage of scripture in the Gospels that is avoided by many who call themselves Christians. It is from Luke chapter 14, verse 26, Jesus said. If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. Such words are especially troubling to our Western culture, which has placed the nuclear family as a centerpiece in fulfilling personal existence. The first time Jesus said anything like this was in the Gospel of Matthew, and he said it to the twelve apostles. When he says it here in Luke, it is to a in in in the context of him being followed by a large crowd. It's almost as if he's walking along and he realizes how many people are following him and he stops. And he looks upon them, the multitude, and he says, If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes. And his own life also he cannot be my disciple. And of course he knew he knew it would be a jarring thing to say and a jarring thing to hear. He knew it would trouble the people. But he said it because first it was true, and second, because he wanted to get across to any anyone who would consider being his disciple, that they must be willing to die to anything. To anything in order to put him first. That is how serious he is. And please notice that I said how serious he is. Not how serious he was. He doesn't say such things to his apostles only. He says it to all who would want to call themselves Christian. And we need to ask why Jesus would choose the closest family members, our immediate family members, to be a testing ground of our devotion to Him. C. S. Lewis sheds light on this in his book about the four loves, which is the study of the four Greek words used to express the one word we have for love. One of the loves under the general category is affectionate love. Lewis calls under that category gift love. He has a fictional character named Mrs. Fidget, and she is a master of gift love. She does for her children in their older age what they had eventually learned to do for themselves, but Mrs. Fidget keeps on serving them because she has trouble, a terrible need. To be needed. Thus, what she thinks she does in love is actually done with selfish motivation to be relevant in the lives of those closest to her. There is also a caring love, which is a concern for the safety of family members, so much so that you do not want them to take risks in life. Such love thinks the worst day possible is to hear that a loved one had died, not because of the death of a loved one, but because of the emotional toll it would take on the one who is practicing caring love. Again, caring love is no love at all, but selfishness in disguise. These are just two examples of why we must love God over family. So let us ask and answer ourselves what it means to love God. Well, as stated, it means to have no other gods. Which is to have no other loyalties, priorities, and authorities besides Him. It is not only to place God as our priority, But to do so in every aspect of our lives. Every aspect, and no, I did not stutter. Every aspect of our lives Preacher, you may be asking, preacher, do you really mean every aspect of my life? That I do. You want to challenge for specifics. Preacher, you say again, do you mean God is to be first in my work? I do. Do you mean God is to be my first priority in my pleasure? I do. Do you mean God is to be first in my TV watching? I do. Do you mean God is to be first in my sexuality? I do. Do you mean God is to be first in my money spending? I do. Do you mean God is to be first in my eating and drinking? I do. Do you mean God is to be first in my conversation? I do. Okay, okay. You challenge. Do you mean God is to be first in my business in the bathroom? I do. That is what it means to have no other gods before him, and what it means to love him. The Ephesians had lost that love, that priority, because they morphed into a people who saw themselves as gatekeepers to the truth. Without remembering that part of that truth is to know a living and loving God who wants to know them and for them to know him. We celebrate the coming Messiah this Advent season for many reasons, including the knowledge that God wanted to be like us so that we could know Him. Remember the connection Jesus wanted his followers to see between him and the Heavenly Father. He said, If you have seen me, you have seen the Father. He also said that to love him was to love the one who sent him, which is the Heavenly Father. And so we are to grow in love more and more with the Son of God. But let us get practical. How do you return to your first love? Well, the text says the first step is to repent. To repent is to acknowledge that you have been going the wrong way, and then you purposefully and sincerely go the opposite way you've been going. The call to repentance also includes the acknowledgement that a choice of the will needs to be made. And this is in opposition To modern thought, which conveys that love is something that comes upon you and then controls you. As opposed to you making a choice, as opposed to love being a choice. Any righteous husband or wife will confess. that they have had to make a choice to stay in a marriage because love is not always not always there in terms of emotion. Love then becomes a choice And because it is a choice, and a choice to repent, when it is not enacted, it is also a responsibility. We are responsible to love God. And I am aware that saying such can sound like a duty, and a duty can become something to resent, but again, if you choose to resent, that's your choice. Loving God is a duty. And for those who are to love him, it is a response to how he has loved us. He that loveth not knoweth not God, for God is love. The letter closes with a warning of Jesus removing their lapstand, which means to remove them from the position, their position in his kingdom. And it's conditional unless they repent. Such a warning is out of love. For it is to be a jarring motivation to take seriously how Christians are to love God. He next praises them for hating the Nicolacians. And said group will come into play later on in these letters. Who were the Nicolaitians and what they were teaching or doing is not clear, but we know this. It is likely that they were syncretists. Syncretists wanting Christians to blend into the pagan religions around them rather than standing out against them. This then seems to be an encouragement for the Ephesians to continue to stand fast against false teaching. And that's further conveyed in verse 7, where he says that those who overcome will eat of the tree of life in the paradise of God, which we know is a description of heaven, and that will be described at the end of the book. So what are we to make of this praise for remaining steadfast in the faith and then condemning their lack of love and then praising them again for standing strong against false teachers? There are two things I close with that I wish for us to pull out of this. First, the first is That we are never finished in this life in our sanctification. There are always places in our lives where we can be made more holy. And that will be seen throughout these seven letters. The second and most important from this particular letter to the Ephesians. Is that love for God is essential to our faith in Him. Our God is a relational God. He wants to be our God and he wants us to be his people. With the motivation of love, thus we are to choose to love him. There is no better way to prepare for his coming this Advent season than to choose to love Him. Let us pray. Our God, with that call to choose to love you, we recognize that the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak. We want to do our own thing. We want to go our own way. We want to live the way we want to live. That is what our flesh calls us. But our spirit says no. Our Spirit says to love you first, and so that is what we will choose to do. And we will do it in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Confess Before Men
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turning your Bibles to the Book of Revelation. The Book of Revelation, chapter 2, we're looking at the second letter. To of the seven letters to the seven churches, Revelation chapter two, beginning at verse eight This second letter begins as the first, which is addressing the angel assigned to the church identified. Interestingly, the word angel simply means messenger, and because of that, some scholars have noted the possibility Of these seven letters being written to the pastors of each church who were deemed messengers If that is the case, then your pastor can be considered an angel in your life. And your reaction is similar to when I suggested the same twenty years ago. Nothing much has changed. Smyrna was a city due north of Ephesus, only 35 miles. It too was a port city and thus a strategic one for war and for trade. Polycarp, a disciple of John the Revelator himself Was a bishop there and was martyred for his Christian faith. Jesus introduces himself in a similar manner as chapter 1. With an emphasis on him being divine. He says he is the first and the last. And the emphasis also on overcoming death by resurrection. It may be asked why would those two things, those two attributes, be important to the Christians as Smyrna? Well, Christians at Smyrna were suffering persecution for their faith in Jesus Christ. To know that Jesus suffered even to the point of death, death on a cross, is a most helpful reference point. To point to and to hold up when suffering, as well as knowing that he suffered even though he was divine. Next, because Jesus has eyes of fire, which enables him to see the bad and judge it and the good and reward it, Jesus tells him that he sees them. He sees them, saying that he knows their works, tribulation, and poverty. Their works include living out the gospel, which is having faith in the good news that Jesus is the Christ, and that to follow Him is to love Him, and to love Him is to obey Him. Jesus said himself that if you love me, you will keep my commandments. And it is because of their work that they suffer tribulation. The first to persecute the Christians were Jewish, as this is well recorded in the book of Acts. We first read of the apostles being thrown in prison by order of the high priest only to be miraculously freed. We next read of Stephen being accused of blasphemy and then being stoned after confronting the hypocrisy of the Jewish religious leaders. After Paul's conversion, he is the target of many conspiracies to kill him because he confounded Jewish arguments, proving that Jesus is the Messiah. Herod, wanting to please the Jews, decided to get in on the persecution, killing James the Apostle. Wherever Paul went, there were Jewish leaders trying to quiet him and stone him, but God kept giving Paul a way of escape. But the people who converted to Christianity in the cities that Paul was chased away from were left for persecution. And again, most of it came from Jewish religious leaders, and most of the persecuted were Jewish having converted to Christianity. And one of the tactics of persecution was what we would call today canceling. Christians were financially frozen out of society. The Jewish leaders convinced Jewish businessmen not to exchange with Christians. That is why Jesus also, he says, knows of their poverty. Their work is their faith in Jesus. Their tribulation are because of the Christian faith, and their poverty is because of their tribulation. And Jesus knows who the persecutors are. Now before I continue, I need to make a disclaimer, especially in light of the anti-Semitism that has been spewed by certain entertainers of our day. When I refer to Jews in the context of the book of Revelation, I am mostly referring to Jewish religious leaders. And I am most certainly not saying that the Jewish people as a race are guilty of persecuting Christians, nor am I saying that they behave as a cohesive unit So the persecutors Jesus knows are the blasphemers, and they are blasphemers because they say they are Jews, which is to say they are the people of God. But they are not, and in fact, they are actually of the synagogue of Satan. Such is harsh language indeed, and harsh language for any culture or of any generation, but especially our generation that sits on this side of the Jewish Holocaust. To better understand the divide between early Jews and Christians, we must know our history better. As Paul wrote to the Corinthians, the Christians were an embarrassment to the Jews First, the Hellenistic world thought that Christians were just another sect of the Jews After all, the first to follow and proclaim Jesus as the Messiah were Jewish. And they continued to worship in the synagogues and appear at the temple while also worshiping as Christians. And so no wonder the confusion. And this confusion embarrassed the Jews, who could not accept that God Would become flesh, and most certainly could not accept that he would purposefully subjugate himself to the powers of men. And the Christians wouldn't leave the Jews alone. Every time the apostles would go to a new town, they would go into the synagogue and preach Jesus as the Messiah. They were a nuisance. And if you can get rid of a nuisance, you do so. This meant that Christians were to be persecuted, and Jewish people were warned. Not to befriend them, not to do business with them, and certainly not to convert and become like them. Know this also. The Christians believed themselves, and they should have believed, that they were the chosen people of God. The Jews were also the people of God, but to believe in Jesus was to fulfill all that was promised in Judaism. To believe in Jesus as the Messiah is to believe that the promised seed that will crush the serpent's head, as prophesied in Genesis 3, that had been fulfilled. To believe in Jesus is to see how God's promise that the kingdom of Israel will come from the line of David and reign forever. Has also been fulfilled for Jesus is of that lineage, and Jesus will reign forever and ever. To believe in Jesus is to have the same faith as Father Abraham Which is a saving faith. So a Christian saw themselves as a do complete. To deny Jesus is to be incomplete, and then to speak against Jesus, well, that's taking the side of the devil, and that must be condemned. And the source of unbelief needs to be identified. And the source is Satan, hence the phrase, the synagogue of Satan. To say that such is unkind or even anti-Semitic is to not understand the times it was written And to forget that Jesus himself was a Jew, as was John, who was given this letter to write down. It was never about being a Jew physically. But about being a Jew spiritually, which was and is to be under the covenant God established with Abraham and fulfilled in Jesus. Remember when Jesus said this in John eight forty-four? You You are of your father the devil, and the desires of your father you want to do. He was a murderer from the beginning and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources, for he is a liar and the father of it. Jesus said such to a crowd of Jewish people. And interestingly, in that text, prior to Jesus saying that The text says that the people following him believed in him as the Messiah. But the higher his standards became to follow him, They started to resist, and in their resistance, they clung to the fact that they were Jewish, claiming that Abraham was their father. Thus, in their doubt, they went back to leaning on their ethnicity, and Jesus would not have it. Within the harshness of Jesus' words, we can learn just how serious faith in Him is, and how serious it is not to have faith in Him. I don't think I can overstate how important it is to have faith in Jesus as the Christ, and to confess that same faith to all who would hear. The Apostle Paul went to great lengths in his letter to the Romans to explain how having faith in Jesus as the Messiah was God's plan all along. And that Abraham himself had such a saving faith, and thus God made him righteous. So too does God make righteous those who confess Jesus as Savior and God. And the opposite is also true. If you do not have faith and do not confess Jesus as the Christ, your soul is under the authority of the devil, and hell is your destination. Remember these words of Jesus. Therefore, whoever confesseth me before men, him I will also confess before my Father who is in heaven But whoever denies me before men, him I will also deny before my Father who is in heaven. The word therefore announces the crux of the matter. He comes after Jesus telling his disciples to shout. what he says from the rooftops. And then like we discussed two weeks ago when we spoke of Jesus being judge. He tells his followers not to fear those who can harm the body, but to fear that which can harm the body and soul. And that is to say we are to fear Jesus. The point is that if you shout what he says from the rooftops, some people, perhaps many, are not going to want to hear it. Sinners who want to remain sinners do not like to have their sin pointed out. That is why sinners want their sin to be made culturally normative. Normalized sin calms the conscience. Christians are a threat to the conscience when they insist that certain behaviors, certain beliefs, are an abomination to God. Our culture's abandonment of the concept of absolute morality has been a slow gas leak, undetected, and quite an accomplishment by the devil himself. Even though not everyone agrees with our cultural confusion of gender and gender roles and what sexual immorality actually is. There is an acceptance of such confusion because it allows for people's personal fetishes to be acceptable as well. For example, a person may not agree with homosexuality being normative, but such acceptance of sexual immorality allows His conscience to be free while living with his girlfriend or having multiple partners. The logic is: whatever calms my conscience is acceptable. And the devil smiles at such a conclusion. To have a true faith in Jesus Is to agree with his moral standards, which are clearly stated in the Ten Commandments and further expanded upon in the Sermon on the Mount Which teaches that such commandments are to be internal as well as external. To have faith in Jesus is to do so outwardly as well as which is to I'm sorry, to have faith in Jesus is to do so outwardly as well, which is to confess it. To publicly confess him and not be ashamed. There was a story rumored back in the nineteen eighties. It might have been before that, but that's when I heard it. When the government in China was trying to slow Bible trafficking in China, and many underground Christian churches were starting up and growing It was told that in that country in those years a government official broke into a Christian worship service just beginning and pointed a gun at those who were attending the worship And threatened to kill everyone there for their insurrection against the state, and that if they wanted to remain alive, they would leave immediately. Some did, and some stayed. And when those who feared death over fearing God left, the government agent put down his gun and said, Now we can begin the service. Such a scenario allows us with our imagination to place ourselves in such a position and to question: what would we do? We cannot know for sure, but we certainly can want to be the ones who stayed and to accept their end if it meant confessing Jesus as Savior and God After Jesus warns against denying him before men, he says the following: Do not think that I came to bring peace on earth. I did not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to set a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man's enemies will be those in his own household. He who loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. And he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. And he who does not take his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me. He who finds his life will lose it, and he who loses his life for my sake will find it. I ask, is there or has there been anyone more radical than Jesus He sold out his life for the sake of the salvation of those who would confess him, and he expects those who follow him to sell out as well. I don't know how else it can be explained or understood. And why his followers must be sold out is if they are going to be tested. Jesus tells those in Smyrna that the devil is about to throw some of them into prison, and that experience will test their faith. Will they still love Jesus while suffering? That had yet to be determined. The ten days he mentions is a reference to the ten days Daniel and his companions were tested. It is symbolic of such testing having a determined end. The end reward for remaining faithful is the crown of life, which is heaven. Which is being in the presence of God with all beauty and glory for eternity. And the opposite is true To not remain faithful to the end of our days is to suffer the second death, and that second death is described elsewhere as wailing, weeping, and gnashing of teeth. Now, I've been calling us to confess Jesus and to do so publicly, but when confessing Jesus, we are not called to be donkeys about it The cashier at the grocery store doesn't need to know you love Jesus unless you are asked, or it's a natural part of your conversation. To say, I believe in Jesus to someone who is not asking or caring is not what it means to confess him before men. What it does mean is that in every live context where we are given opportunity to testify what we believe and who we follow, we are to state it. And to take whatever consequences are required. That is what it means for a Christian to overcome. I close with the reminder of how powerful God has made speech. He used words to create something, the universe, out of nothing, the void. God is characterized by his speaking and his acting, and both of them being indistinguishable. That is why it is fitting for Jesus to be called the Word of God, for his actions and his words mirror themselves. And the same is to be for us who follow him. Our words and our actions are to be the same. What we confess, we believe, is to be mirrored by the lives we live. There is no other Christianity. Let us pray. A gracious God. For the standard you put before the church at Smyrna For the standard you set for us, all of us. All of us are convicted to live by. And we know you've given us the spirit of authority and power to live such lives. May we never be cowardice to not confess you before men, and may our lives follow that confession. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Christmas Day
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We know the following verse well, especially because it is read, before an infant is to be baptized, from Mark chapter 10. And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, Let the children come to me, do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. Truly I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it. And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them. And the following is like it from Matthew chapter 18. At that time the disciples came to Jesus, saying, Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven? And calling to him a child, he put him in the midst of them and said, Truly I say to you, unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me. Preachers and teachers have tried to explore what it means to be as a child when receiving the kingdom of God and humbling oneself to receive it. Those who identify a wonderment in the child and a desire to be taught, a desire to be led, a desire to be instructed are likely the closest to what Jesus wants us to see in those who follow Him The older we get, the more stuck we become in how we think and understand. Things new are not as exciting as they were when we were younger. But there is also a gentleness in a child and a vulnerability in a child that must be part of the analogy Jesus gives us. In the book of Revelation, This vulnerability of a child is captured in chapter twelve, where a vision of a woman giving birth is described. while a red dragon having seven heads and ten horns stands before the woman, ready to devour the child as soon as it is born. But the child is caught up and taken to the throne of God. It is thus the child versus the dragon, or versus the tyrant, that repeats itself in literature and lore. It is a simple observation to note that Christian writers are obsessed with child versus tyrant motif. But the characters can also be childlike, such as the lead character in Don Quixote, who is said by Sancho Panza to have a childlike innocence. But the standoff between a child and a tyrant isn't only fascinating because it should not even be a contest. The tyrant should defeat the child. It is fascinating because the opposite occurs. And therefore the storylines are fascinating because of the irony in them And God loves irony. He loves his son to be born of a virgin, and the bloodline of his son to include a prostitute. And his son Jesus loved to say the last will be first, and the first will be last. And it is things like that that turn the world downside up. We see the use of iron of the irony of child versus tyrant in Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol. Which is a surprise to some, for Dickens made himself a part of the Unitarians who denied the divinity of Christ, which interestingly Did not prevent Dickens from saying that Jesus was his Savior. G. K. Chesterton considered a Christmas Carol to be Dickens' best work. Consider how insightful he was in choosing his characters. The Apostle Paul in Romans 7 uses the analogy of being old. To be similar to being under the law. And being under the law was being dead. Paul also instructed the Ephesians in chapter 4 of that letter to put off the old man. Of course, the old man doesn't know he is old until he is made new. Ebenezer Scrooge didn't know he was old either. And Scrooge would never be charged as a lawbreaker, for he was a strict lawkeeper, while condemning anyone who would receive a handout. Scrooge is described as old in every way. He is bone skinny, confined to his office and flat. Struck in a dreary routine that made him a part of the walking dead. We are introduced to him at a funeral of his dead partner, Jacob Marley. Both of them were collectors of debt, getting as much money from the poor as the law would allow. Death and law was the identity of Scrooge. What Scrooge could not see was that he was a man in debt himself, in debt to God and his fellow man in terms of love and morality. Hear this description given by Dickens. Oh, but he was a tight-fisted hand at the grindstone Scrooge A squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous old sinner, hard and sharp as flint. from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire. Secret and self-contained and solitary as an oyster The cold within him froze his old features, nipped his pointed nose, shriveled his cheek, stiffened his gait. made his eyes red, his thin lips blue, and spoke out shrewdly in his grating voice. A frosty rhyme was on his head, and on his eyebrows and his wiry chin He carried his own low temperature always about with him. He iced his office in the dog days and didn't thaw it one degree at Christmas. We are next to contrast Scrooge at Christmas to his nephew Fred. Who greets his uncle cheerfully and is described as ruddy and handsome. And with his greetings, he says, God save you. And God must save Scrooge. For he cannot save himself, but only becomes colder and more alone as the clock ticks. Fred's cheerfulness is childlike, for it will not be daunted. This is the first bah humbug we hear from Scrooge. When Scrooge challenges Fred asking, whatever good did anyone receive from Christmas, Fred responds with childlike wonder. There are many things from which I might have derived good, by which I have not profited, I dare say, returned the nephew Christmas among the rest.
