But I'm sure I have always thought of Christmas time when it has come around, apart from the veneration due to its sacred name and origin If anything belonging to it can be apart from that as a good time, a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time, the only time I know of in the long calendar of the year, when men and women seemed to be one consent to open their shut up hearts freely, and to think of people below them as if they were really fellow passengers to the grave and not another race of creatures bound on other journeys. And therefore, Uncle, though it has never put a scrap of gold or silver in my pocket, I believe that it has done me good, and will do me good, and I say, God bless it. The clerk, hearing such an answer, instinctively applauds only to be shamed by Scrooge We know the story has Scrooge arrive at his flat with his plain meal and a restless sleep ahead, as he will be visited by four ghosts. The first is Marley, followed by the ghost of Christmas past, and then present, and then future Where a child plays a role in the story next is Ebenezer himself, as he sees himself as a child being taken there by the ghost of Christmas past. There he was at a boarding school, and Ebenezer was sent there by his father, his angry father, only to be alone twice. first by his father and then being rejected by his peers. In another scene, we hear and watch him struggle to stay in a relationship with a woman that might have given him children. It is Bell, who is the one he is to marry, but he will never fully commit as he is busy building his business and learning to prioritize money Bell says to him, You are changed. When it was made, their contract for marriage, you were another man. I was a boy, he said impatiently. A boy his now older self rejects. Another saga of the child against the tyrant. Only the tyrant is rejecting himself as a child. With the Ghost of Christmas present, we are given another chance to compare and contrast Scrooge with a child. And this is the center child of the story. Tiny Tim. The scene is Bob Cratchit carrying his son Tim, who is crippled, and that is made obvious by a crutch and an iron frame on his legs. They were coming home from a church service, and Mrs. Cratchit asked how Tim fared. As good as gold and better was the answer. And it was noted that Tim said to his father during the service, he had hoped people noticed him at the church because he was a cripple. And it might help people remember Christmas as a day to celebrate a man who made the lame beggars walk and blind men to see. Scrooge, the tyrant, is smitten with the child, for the child may be a part of the surplus population and a liability But his heart reveals a love for humanity that Scrooge does not yet know. But is then, right then, while watching the child and listening to the heart of the child is having something grow within him that was not there prior. And a fear has developed in Scrooge. He wants to know if the child, if Tiny Tim, will live. The answer is a hint. The ghost confesses seeing a vision of a chair in a corner that is empty and a crutch that has no owner. When Scrooge objects to the vision, his own words are quoted back to him. If he'd be like to die, he had better get to it and decrease the population. Dickens here reveals the value of a child, even a crippled child, as compared to a crotchety old man who cares only for his bank account. Christians are called to be born again, which is to become a child, and to receive Jesus as a child. Because the heart of a skin flint is difficult if not impossible to turn around Next is the ghost of Christmas Future, which reveals to Scrooge how people will dishonor him at his death. And if such is not difficult enough, Scrooge is shown Bob Cratchit returning to his home at a much slower pace than when carrying Tiny Tim. It is clear that Tim has passed, and the family is very much in the grips of grief With the following words, Bob tries to console his family and raise up the child as an example for all them, saying this But however and whenever we part from one another, I am sure we shall none of us forget poor tiny Tim, shall we? Or this first party that there is among us Never, father, cried they all. And I know, said Bob, I know, my dears, that when we recollect how patient and how mild he was, although he was little, little child We shall not quarrel easily among ourselves and forget poor tiny Tim in doing it. No, never, father, they all cried again. I am very happy, said little Bob. I am very happy. Mrs. Cratchit kissed him, his daughters kissed him, the two young Cratchits kissed him, and Peter himself shook his hand The spirit of tidy Tim, thy childless essence, was from God. Of all the spirits that visited Scrooge that night, and of all the things he witnessed, both past, present, and future, and of all the warnings of his own demise, nothing moved him like the life and possible death of Tiny Tim. The child, the child once again tamed the tyrant. We know the rest of the story, how Scrooge awoke. to find himself on Christmas Day and able to rectify the evils he had perpetrated on those who had tried to wish him a Merry Christmas just a day earlier, as well as committing himself to make merry the rest of his days. But likely, likely you don't remember or glass over the words Dickens wrote for Scrooge when realizing the night of the spirits was over. Scrooge said to himself, I don't know what day of the month it is. I don't know how long I've been among the spirits. I don't know anything. I am quite a baby Never mind. I don't care. I'd rather be a baby. Hello, whoop, hello here. It is here that we are challenged, yea, encouraged, to rather be a baby. For this is the time of year we get to call out of ourselves the children we once were. And how much we loved life and loved others and loved God. On this day we say, unto us a child is born. Allowing us to be vulnerable children again. And Amen.

sermons.title: Where we are Lacking
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I highly, highly, highly, highly, highly encourage you to turn in your Bibles, your pew Bibles, your personal Bible. To Revelation chapter 2, beginning at verse 12. It's going to make more sense if you follow along. I realize even hearing what was read this morning for the epistle lesson, it can be very confusing. So we're gonna clear it up. There are a number of mysterious references in this letter to the church at Pergamum. So you know Pergamum lay just north of Smyrna, which was just north of Ephesus. It may appear that a compass pattern is developing with these letters, but that will change with the next letter. With so many mysterious or initially unknown references in this letter, it is my perspective that we should address each of them first Before we get to the primary message Jesus had for the church at Pergamum and what he has for us. Well, so we begin with the mention of the double-edged sword. That takes us back to the description of the risen Savior in chapter 1, verse 16. The sword comes out of the Savior's mouth, giving us an obvious reference to his word, or as we say, the word of God, the word spoken of God. You will remember the writer to the Hebrews uses the same imagery in chapter 4, verse 12 of that epistle. There, the word of God is said to be a double-edged sword used to divide between the bone and morrow of man. It is likened to a surgeon's scalpel. God cuts into a man with his word, having the ability to mend and heal Like a surgeon, or harm and mane like a warrior. The Word of God, His law, and His revelation is our standard We are judged by it for heaven or condemned to it or by it for hell. The description then has a positive and a negative aspect The Word of God is positive because it can be used to justify, sanctify, and defend us, or it can be a testimony against us. Next is mentioned Satan's throne. That is a unique description and no doubt a unique place. Because Pergamum was a seat of government for the Roman province of Asia, the description may be a jab at Rome. The city was also the center of worship for the serpent god Aslepius, who was said to save people from diseases. The city was also the site of the first temple of the imperial cult, a cult that worshipped the present and former Caesars as gods. This temple was built among a cluster of other temples for Zeus, Apollo, Athena, Dionysius, Aphrodite, and others These all lay together in a beautiful grove. With all of the idolatry surrounding these Christians in this city, we can see, can imagine why it was called Satan's Throne. Of the person of Antipas mentioned, mentioned as being a martyr Nothing is known other than he was esteemed by his church for suffering unto death for the truth of the gospel. There may be a link between describing the area as Satan's throne and the death of Antipas, meaning that Antipas died at the judgment throne of the devil residing in Pergamon. The description next of the teachings of Balaam to that of Balach leads us back to the book of Numbers. And reminds us how important it is to have a full knowledge of Scripture. We cannot understand what we should about the New Testament, including the book of Revelation Unless we know the Old Testament. Balaam was a prophet for hire, with a reputation for having heavenly authority in his words. He started off, you remember in Numbers, planning to curse Israel, only to end up speaking forth a blessing when the Spirit of Almighty God intervened. His story unfortunately continues, for he counsels Balach, the king of Moab, to entice the Israelites to commit fornication. Which they did, as recorded in the book of Numbers, chapter 31. Balaam does this for a price. He sells his prophetic gift, his influential power to the highest bidder. He is corrupted by fame, money, and sex. Sounds as if he comes from Hollywood or professional sports. The influence of Balaam is similar to the sins of the Nicolatians You will remember them being mentioned in the letter to the church at Ephesus. The Nicolatians are believed to have been given the name because they followed the teachings of a disciple who is mentioned in the book of Acts. Tradition has him following the heresy of Gnosticism, which when united with Christianity taught that freedom in Christ placed men above the moral law. It taught that not only were Christians not subject to the condemnation of the law, Christians were taught to be able to disobey the law with no consequences. What you did in the flesh didn't matter. The last two mysterious references in the letter are in the context of heaven To those who overcome hidden manna is promised. This is likely a reference to the manna that is stored up in the Ark of the Holy of Holies. This is also connected to the true bread that came down from heaven to be revealed on the last day There is a theme throughout the New Covenant that the glory of the heavenly promise is a mystery to be revealed Such as stated in 1 Corinthians by St. Paul, he said, No eye has seen, no ear has heard, no mind has conceived what God has prepared for those who love Him. Next, we are promised a new name upon a white stone. Nowhere else in Scripture can we find reference to such a stone. There were stones upon the breastplate of the high priest, and two of those stones, possibly like diamonds, hidden behind the twelve stones representing the twelve tribes. Another reference is the description of God's people as being like stones within the temple of God, being built in the heavenly realm, Jesus as the cornerstone. This is most likely the reference as white represents our purity in Christ, and the new name is that which is given to us because we have been born anew of the Spirit. The themes of new and white are abundant in the New Covenant. This letter to the church in Pergamum is similar to the ones to Ephesus and to Smyrna, as each begins with a with a positive, encouraging word. The people of the church in Pergamum have stayed true to the name of Christ in the midst of an extremely hostile environment. As we have discovered, the environment was hostile politically because it was the seat of a government authority of the Roman Empire It was hostile religiously because of the number of gods given a place of honor by the non-Christians of the area. In the midst of such pressures, the Christians of Pergamum did not deny their faith in Christ. For this, they are commended. Jesus warned, you will remember that if his followers did not acknowledge him before men, he would not acknowledge them before God. And once again we had that reference to do not fear The ones who can harm the body, but fear him who can harm the body and soul by casting them into hell. It is no small thing to overcome the fear of men. Many have shrunk for fear of suffering at the hands of men. The shrinking can be caused by a threat of physical torture. It was Bishop Cramner, the author of our Book of Common Prayer, during the reign of Queen Mary, who being left alone for days to consider his fate. sinned by signing a letter of recantation of his Protestant beliefs because of the physical suffering he faced. In our circles, it is more likely that shrinking will be caused by peer pressure. Teenagers know well the intensity of peer pressure. It's one thing to have just a few friends and quite another to be laughed at and ridiculed because you are different. The insecurities that come along with puberty are volatile. Add to that being ostracized by peer groups, and you have a young boy or girl who walks around with a heavy heart. And such fear does not end after puberty, as so many a man has fallen at the heels of stronger influences. Behaving in an immoral and immature manner because he wants to be just one of the guys. Many young women have dressed themselves in styles inappropriate and misleading, as well as participated in gossip and slander in order to fit in with the crowd. When a person is able to stand against such pressure, it is to be commended. Standing up in and for the name of Christ is what God expects of all of us. In spite of what is commended among the Christians at Pergamum, there are also serious problems. There are two problems, none of which is less serious than the other. The two sins are having people in the midst of the church who hold to the teaching of Balaam, and also having among them those who hold to the teachings of the Nicolaitians. The two sins are actually the same sin. And the same sin is actually two sins. The first sin is allowing false teachers to remain in their midst. Whether they are teaching the ways of Balaam or the Nicolaitans, the sin is allowing false teachers in the church. And teachers and the teachers do not have to be formal teachers. Their informal influence upon other members of the church places them among false teachers. Allowing such influences is the opposite of what the Christians at Ephesus did. You will remember how Ephesus was commended for not allowing false teachers to remain among them. With this same concern, the Epistle of Jude calls for Christians to contend for the faith against men who have rushed for the sake of financial profit into Balaam's error. I find by personal observation that there are certain people who strive to be in confrontation with their fellow man, and others who avoid it at all cost. Most of us fall somewhere in between. The personalities who strive to be in confrontation are looking for a fight. They love to draw lines in the sand and dare someone to step over. Others want peace at all costs and will compromise the very core of their convictions to keep that peace. There is, of course, a necessary middle ground. Those who live for confrontation tend to live alone because every issue is as important as the next And most do not want to be around such persons because we do not have the energy to fight over everything Those who want peace at all costs, and with nothing meaningful to show in their lives, as every belief system or moral stance has been compromised, garnering no respect from their fellow man For Christians, our breaking point is clearly defined. It is revealed in the Holy Scriptures Which defines who Jesus was, what he did for the sins of men, and what men are to do in response, and the laws that are to govern our lives as followers of the same Jesus. When anyone purple shirted, that means he's a bishop, or in blue jeans, because he's a cool pastor When anyone purple shirted or in blue jeans tells us differently, we are to stand against such teaching and stand for the truth as it is in Jesus. This may mean casting him out. Casting him out may mean bringing him up on charges before the church, barring him from the Lord's table. It may mean politely asking him to leave the premises, or it may mean picking him up and literally throwing him out. The point being is that we have standards. We have a breaking point that cannot be compromised. There are a myriad of reasons, cowardly reasons, why persons are allowed to remain in the church even though their life or doctrine is heretical. The leadership of the church may not want the publicity caused by casting out a false teacher. The leadership may fear the extended family of the false teacher The leadership may have their own sins they are covering up, and so they choose not to expose others. They also may not care enough about the truth to preserve it. Whatever the reason, it is not good enough, and unless the church rid herself of false teachers or false influencers, then Jesus will rid himself of the church, placing Outside of the lampstands. The second sin included in the one sin is called syncretism. Syncretism was a sin committed by Balaam and by the Nicolaitans, and by Israel, who committed it repeatedly. Moreover, it is as prevalent today as it was then. Syncretism is an attempt to reconcile two different Opposite belief systems and make them one. In the case of the teachings of Balaam, it was the combining of idol worship with a belief in one God in three persons. In the case of the teaching of the Nicolaitans, it was the combining of immoral behavior with the purity of Christ. In the case of Israel, it was the combining of any other tribe or nation's gods with their worship of the only true God. The Sino Syncretism was part of Israel's identity shortly after they entered the Promised Land, and was the primary cause of them being taken into exile less than a millennium later. Syncretism is perhaps the most deceptive of sins and is used by cults because of its effectiveness. In simple terms, it takes truth and mixes it just with a little lie, resulting in the corruption of the whole. Christianity with a little lie is no longer Christianity. When the Apostle Paul wrote to the church at Galatia. His clear edict was for them to turn away from any other gospel. And adding to the gospel is another gospel. Most of the syncretism we know is identified as such because it is formally presented. In other words, it is a formal teaching. When a certain group claims Jesus as their Savior and includes in that belief the requirement of dietary or ritual laws We can say that such is a sin of syncretism. When a religion claims Jesus to be a son of God, And includes other sons of God, such as Joseph Smith, we again easily identify the sin of syncretism. But what about secretism that is not formal? What if the teachings or understandings are in our heads, in our consciences? It is quite possible that we could mix occultist practices with our faith in Christ if we read and follow horoscopes. It is likely that we follow humanistic philosophies about sexuality and abnormal behavior if we turn to psychologists before we turn to Scripture for guidance. That is syncretism. A number of years ago, I was exposed to the film series and book How Shall We Then Live by Dr. Francis Schaeffer. It was an eye-opening moment for me to recognize how many of my views on life had been influenced by philosophies of the world. They had seeped into the core beliefs, my core beliefs, and I did not recognize them to be contrary to Scripture. Examples are in the way we raise our children. Pragmatism is present when we think that because we were raised a certain way and we turned out all right. Then we should raise our children in the same manner. And why anyone would conclude that they turned out all right is beyond me. Behaviorism, a worldly philosophy, is present when we try to change the behavior in our children rather than change their hearts, where sin is harbored. Examples are also in the way we worship. Individualism is present when I care first and foremost about what I like and what is right for me. Existentialism is present when I base truth upon my experience and I evaluate others in terms of my experience. I ask, dear church, how different are we from the church at Pergamum if we combine the philosophies of men with the gospel of Christ? When Jesus tells us, tells the church to hear what the Spirit is saying, that is a warning. To hear, in the manner he is describing, we must examine all the ways in which the sin he identifies might apply to us. Thus, this is not the type of message that we should respond to immediately. We must allow the Spirit to speak to us regarding the many ways we have put up with and even embraced false teachings, placing them alongside the gospel The implied joy he mentions in such a letter is that it is not too late. Like Pergamon, we can be commended for not denying Christ in the midst of hostility. We can be encouraged that Jesus will reward us before our Heavenly Father for not denying our faith in him before men. Like Pergamam, we can also be challenged to identify areas where we have allowed systems of thought and practice that are contrary to Scripture to be a part of our faith. May this prayer be our prayer as individuals and as a church. Heavenly Father, search our hearts and know us. Try us if there be any belief or practice among us that is contrary to your gospel. Reveal it and purge it out of us so that we might be the church you long for, a church without spot or wrinkle. Amen and amen. Better.

sermons.title: Hold On
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles to Revelation chapter 2. Revelation chapter two, picking up at verse eighteen Each of us has personal and peculiar sins with which we struggle Although culturally we may view one sin to be more serious than another, the Scripture treats sin the same in terms of each of it and all of it bringing forth death. The adulterer is viewed and rightly so as a pervert who commits sin against God and his family But according to Scripture, he is no worse a sinner than a Sabbath breaker or a man who covets a Harley Davidson motorcycle. Churches have sins they struggle with as well. The parish can practice great reverence in worship, but not fulfill the command of Jesus to feed his sheep. Another feeds sheep well, but does not evangelize in their community or support missionaries outside of their walls. Such are corporate sins. Individuals who sit in pews may not be consciously sinning in the manner described as the whole church But if the sin is taking place within the parish and nothing is being done to combat it, each person contributes indirectly by standing by and saying and doing nothing. The manner I am using the word sin is important, and using it in the most general of senses, sin is missing the mark, the Greek harmartia. It is failing, excuse me, it is falling short of God's perfection. A person or church that falls short of God's perfection in any way is guilty of sin. And in need of God's forgiveness through Jesus Christ. Acceding to the truth that we all struggle with personal and corporate sin, we look to the church at Thyatira. And immediately notice that their sin is almost the exact opposite to the church at Ephesus. You will remember that Ephesus was commended for holding firm to the doctrines that they had been taught, but found guilty of forgetting their first love. Diatira, on the other hand, shared the love of God with all, but failed to protect itself from false doctrine. In this address we are looking at today, we are to notice that Jesus does not treat the sin of the church to be any more serious than that of Ephesus. Sin is sin. And when it is revealed to us, we are to repent and lean on the mercies of Christ. In the three previous letters addressing Ephesus, Smyrna, and Pergamum, we found ourselves heading due north. Diatira takes us southeast. Thyatire was a trading post very close to the main road leading to Rome. It had the usual false idols like most cities of Asia Minor. One idol that was unique to the city and actually considered the guardian of the city was to the son of Zeus. Thus it makes sense that the first word Jesus says to the church at Thyatire is to proclaim that he alone is the Son of God. This is the only place in the book of Revelation where Jesus uses that title to describe himself His title is uncompromising against the false son of Zeus. He is here proclaiming it. Jesus emphasizes in his introduction two parts of himself that were used to describe him in chapter one. The eyes of fire remind us again that he sees all. Nothing can be hid from him His feet of bronze have us to recall the beautiful feet of those who bring good news. Jesus brings good news to the churches in a glorified state And the fact that he is glorified is part of the good news. This awe-inspiring vision of Jesus in chapter one may not communicate good news initially Because his exalted image tends to engender fear. However, the fact that the exalted Christ addresses the church and gives those that are guilty of sin a chance to repent That is most certainly good news. Being confronted with sin is hard on the pride. And our initial response tells us that the situation is bad. When our pride is overcome, we can then see opportunity for repentance and restoration more clearly. Thus, Jesus speaks to the church and he brings good news. The personal address to the church begins with a commendation. They have been living out their faith and love by deeds and acts of kindness and service. Moreover, they had persevered while doing these deeds. What the deeds were exactly is not listed, meaning that these specifics are not necessary. Acts of love, kindness, and service are not limited to certain things. Such can be anything when a person puts the needs of others before his own. Such deeds have to be unconditionally done for them to be out of love. To serve another person expecting nothing in return is what our Lord did to his fellow man. Christians perform such deeds because the love of God dwells within them to the extent that they can't do anything else. It is to be natural for Christians to forgive, to serve, to nurture, and to show concern for others because the loving Spirit of God dwells within. To persevere while expressing their love through service is most impressive. It is impressive because it is all too easy for us to become discouraged. Considering how the flesh wars against the spirit. Although we live by the Spirit of God that dwells within us, we also battle with the flesh and our fleshly desires. We grow tired. We become weary. When someone refuses to receive our overtures of kindness, we are tempted to just give up. When someone steps on our acts of kindness, expects them from us, or shows no appreciation, we are given another reason to cease to stop doing them. To do so to be giving in to the desires of the flesh, and that caused us to be concerned with self first and self primarily We do not know all that the people of Thyatira suffered in return for their deeds of love, but we can be encouraged that they did not stop their deeds, even while being mistreated. The Savior is aware of their good works, done in faith and love, regardless of whether the recipients of that love were appreciative, and Jesus loves them for it. In addition, the church is further commended for their maturity or growth in their deeds. The growth could have been by quality, quantity, or both. The important point is that they were performing greater deeds than they were at the beginning of their faith. The church's maturation is an example to us all, individually and corporately. Many have been tempted in their latter days of life to view their deeds of the past as enough. I did my time in the nursery, some have said, and it's time for someone else. I showed up for work day once three years ago, and so I've done my part. I shared the gospel with my neighbor across the street, someone else can reach out to the neighbor next door I provided sandwiches to the homeless last year, someone else can provide for them this year. For the church of Thyatira, there was no expiration. or uh for doing good deeds, and one was not enough, nor was one hundred. Jesus reveals in this letter that a church is supposed to mature And the way it expresses its worship and its outreach. A person should be able to visit St. Stephen's ten years from now and see maturity. The maturity should be expressed in greater sincerity, in greater piety, and greater reverence. We should be friendlier towards strangers and more hospitable to one another. We should have more missionaries we support and more people who have become a part of the kingdom of God through the sharing of the gospel by membership by members of this parish. From deep mature love comes an increase of good deeds. Ryatira had not forgotten their first love. Unlike the Church at Ephesus, the love of God compelled the people of Diatira. But not all was well. Also, unlike Ephesus, they did not fight stridently to resist false doctrine. Where Ephesus was commended by a tira, failed. A plain and simple reading of verses 20 through 23 would have us understand that there was a woman in the church whose name was Jezebel. This Jezebel called herself a prophetess, and by her teaching had misled the people of God and influenced them toward sexual immorality and a participation in idol worship. Considering the salacious connotations of the name Jezebel and the metaphors the Savior uses in these letters. It is more likely that the Jezebel referred to is either a real woman that Jesus refers to in a derogatory manner, or a compromised teaching of Scripture that Jesus gave a proper name. You will remember that the Jezebel in Israel's history was the wife to King Ahab. Thus she was queen of Israel in the 9th century BC. By the accounts recorded in 1 and 2 Kings, we learn that she was a wicked queen who led God's people into idolatrous worship of pagan gods, false gods. The proper noun Jezebel is thus fitting to describe a person or a teaching that would lead people astray, people of God astray. Evidently, this person or teaching was not embraced or taught by the elders of the church, but it was tolerated. Tolerance is a modern virtue that has extended its influence on much of our culture. Tolerance is a modern virtue that accepts all faiths and religious practices except those that are intolerant. Thus, modern tolerance is actual intolerant toward the intolerant, giving it an inherent contradiction. Let us be open and honest and confess that Orthodox biblical Christianity is intolerant, for we believe that Jesus is the truth, not merely a truth. He is the only way to heaven, not one of many ways. This makes modern tolerance intolerant of Christianity. Because God is intolerant of churches that are tolerant of sin, we stand in the fork road. Going one way makes us tolerant of the world, but intolerant of God. Going the other way makes us tolerated by God, but intolerant of sin. Taking into consideration who the Bible says will win in the end, it is the church's well-being that we are intolerant. Imagine the effect of tolerated sin upon a church When a person is living in open sin and not being required or called to repent If a man, for example, is leading an adulterous life, and this life is known by the elders who do nothing to call the man to repentance, and he continues to escort his family to church each Sunday, The stir such behavior would cause would be a slow corruption and a silent uproar. Imagine further such a man coming up for Holy Communion. Despite the warning in 1 Corinthians chapter 11 that such sinners eat and drink damnation to themselves, the man still comes forward. What respect is garnered by the people toward the minister who distributes the bread and wine? How can the people trust that such a man would care for their souls if he does not stand strong before a known sinner? The prayer book states specifically that if anyone who comes forward were a known sinner, meaning a person living in sin who will not repent, the elements are to be withheld. To tolerate such sin in our midst opens the gate for the weak and impressionable to pursue the lust of the flesh with no fear of earthly or heavenly retribution. Such a slope is very fast and slippery. The example I used of a man committing adultery was not by accident. The sin of Jezebel is the leading of people into the sin of sexual immorality and the eating of food offered to idols. It is not known whether the sin of sexual immorality is used figuratively, as the name Jezebel might have been being used, or if it's literal. It makes sense that it would be literal because of how intertwined sexual immorality and idol worship were in the scriptures. Fornication and idol worship are almost used as synonyms in the Old Testament to describe the sins of the Gentiles. We know well from either our own experience or the culture around us about the large role sexual immorality plays in most sin. It was true in the New Testament times, and it is true today. In Acts chapter 15, when the disciples decided to bring the Gentiles into the church, The summary requirement was for them to restrain from sexual immorality and from eating of food offered for sacrifices to false idols. Such sins were dominant in the world around them, and to refrain from such sin was to be separate from the world. The punishment that the Lord plans for Jezebel is poetically appropriate. It is to put her in her place. Since she will not repent and wants to be in bed with sexual immorality, then the Lord will cast her there where she will suffer her death. The principle is the same as Jesus' words to Peter, that a man who lives by the sword will die by the sword, and those who live by sexual immorality will die by their sexual immorality. The final instruction in verses 24 and 25 refers to Satan's so-called deep secrets. This is likely a reference known only to those who had submitted to the teachings of Jezebel. We do not know what the secrets are, and it would provide little help for us to know. The faithful at Fiatira did not believe the secrets, and neither should we. What is helpful to us is the instruction to hold on to what we have until Jesus comes. And so I ask, do you realize what you have? I form the question to cause you to examine yourselves. Do you realize what you have? What you have in the freedom you express, the Bible you possess, the traditions that have been handed down to you Hold on to what you have. You have been given great gifts. The first and foremost is your faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. Others include the Bible in a language you can understand. You also have been given a reverent form of worship to follow Many of you have parents you are to honor and children you are to train. Hold on to what you have. Don't treat it for less than what it is worth. It is worth your soul and the souls of your children and the soul of your children's children. Modern Christianity can be confusing as there are many expressions of worship, Bible interpretations, forms of church government, and some wild ideas about outreach. In the midst of the confusion is the temptation to wonder if the grass is greener on the other side. Thus, the very least we should do is hold on to what we have. The Christian life is not about what is new. It is about the old paths. The old paths that converge with only the only path. The only road that leads to heaven. While being enchanted with what is new or more exciting, we are tempted to grab a hold of the new and letting go of the old Those who hold on to the old, to what they have, those are the ones who overcome. Those who overcome are given authority over nations. Those who overcome will rule. Jesus received authority from the Heavenly Father and gives it to those who hold on. I ask again, do you know what you have? Hang on to it until Jesus comes. Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious and heavenly Father, we give thanks together for what we have, for the riches that have been bestowed upon us as a people of God. Help us to have the courage to hold on, to be thankful, and to hold on until you come. Help us, dear Lord. We pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Coming to You
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles to Revelation chapter 3. You're looking at verses 1 through 6. Revelation 3, 1 through 6. Of the seven letters written, and unlike the churches addressed thus far There is no praise for Sardis. If you have ever received a complaint from someone about your person And there are no words of praise within the complaint, you find yourself with nothing to grasp onto emotionally to keep yourself steady. In such a predicament, you become desperate for something, anything to hold you steady. You can tell me I am a false prophet. Fine. You can tell me I'm a lousy pastor. Fine. You can tell me that I am a poor leader. Fine. All of this and more you can tell me as long as you give me something to hang on to, to grasp. Just tell me that you like my shoes or my wife, something, anything, and I will hold on to that compliment. Sardis gets nothing There is nothing for which to praise them. This no doubt will bring them low, and obviously low is where God wants them to be. Sardis was a small city just south of Thyatira. It was a city protected by mountains, making it seemingly impervious to enemy attack And yet, the city was overthrown at least twice in its short history twice because the people took too much comfort in what they thought was natural protection around them The history of Sardis is a fitting metaphor for the Christian church established there. They took too much comfort in their lack of persecution, and the enemy overthrew them. We have noticed that the description of Jesus as highly exalted in chapter 1 is continued in each of the seven letters With special emphasis given to specific characteristics, he wants particular churches to notice. Ephesus and Thyatira, for example, were reminded that Jesus has eyes like blazing fire. Those eyes were highlighted because Jesus was emphasizing to those churches that he could see them and that he could sanctify them as he examines them. The fire being the sanctifier. Sardis is reminded that Jesus holds the seven spirits and the seven stars. We learned at the beginning of our study that the seven spirits refers to the seven endowments of the Holy Spirit placed upon the Messiah as told by the prophets. It also tells us that the Spirit of God is within each church. The seven stars represent the church in its fullness, its entirety. Seven represents the universal church, and therefore Jesus holds the whole church in his hands. Because he holds them or it, the church, in his hands, he controls them, it, the church as a whole. Because he controls them, he is sovereign over Sardis. And he is sovereign over the whole Christian church. And the people of Sardis needed to know this. Jesus begins his address to Sardis' particular situation by referring to their reputation. They had the reputation of being alive. Contemporary Christians continue to use such an expression to describe other Christians. We speak about certain people or churches being alive in the faith or dead in the faith. To be alive in the faith is to be expressive in word and active in deed. A person who says, praise the Lord a lot, and is active in his or her church is thought by others to be alive. A person who does not mention the Lord and shows no evidence of being a Christian unless asked is thought to be dead. Today, churches are given the reputation of being alive if they have outreach programs, activities for families, lively worship, and large attendance numbers. What gave the Church of Sardis the reputation of being alive is not mentioned. But the important point being made was that their reputation was mistaken. What others thought of them was incorrect. They were dead. Even though we admit we cannot judge the heart of another man and confess that only God can. We remain guilty of looking on the outward and concluding that what we see on the outside is what's going on on the inside as well. The outward appearance of Sardis caused other Christians to conclude that the church was alive with faith. Perhaps it was large attendance. Perhaps they had members who were civic leaders. Perhaps they said, praise the Lord a lot. Whatever the cause, other Christians understood Stardust to have a faith that they did not have. The Lord looks at the heart, and the heart of the Christians at Sardis was dead. The remedy for the dead condition of Sardis reminds us again how simple the Christian life can be. Wake up, he says. Like the citizens who should have been ready for an attack, wake up! The Christians are unaware of their dead state. They are caught up in their own perception of themselves. They think they are alive, but are revealed by the definition of God to be dead men walking. In one sense, we all live in our own perception of reality. We think of ourselves differently than others perceive us. We think we are in the right regarding a particular subject when many around us think we are wrong. We might perceive ourselves to be brighter than we are or more handsome than we are. The real danger is not being in your own reality, it is being in your own reality and not acknowledging that you are. When we are in such a state, it is necessary for us to wake up. Wake up. A problem with the command wake up is how such phrasing is used today. Those who consider themselves woke. Perceive themselves to be awake while the generation before them and every generation before them is asleep. Jesus points to Christians in Sardis. And he tells them that you might think you are woke, but you are not. After waking up in response to the voice of the Lord, we are to strengthen what remains, he says This instruction is similar to the emphasis we placed on the Lord's message to Thyatira to hang on to what they had. This is based on the principle that we cannot mature in every way at once. The things we can mature in We are to do so quickly in order that we might have a foundation upon which we can build. We're an individual it may be that While the moral constitution has broken down, there is still a belief in the righteousness of God and the power of the blood of Jesus Christ. That belief needs to be strengthened in order that all might not be lost. Once faith is strengthened, it can be built upon so that a person's moral constitution might improve. For a church, it may be that the practices are in place so that worship is God-honoring and programs are meeting the earthly needs of the people But these do not involve faith in what is hoped for and a conviction of that which is not seen. The answer for such a church is not, as some have erroneously concluded. To cast out the practices of something and include something that is contemporary. The answer, according to our Lord, is to strengthen the practices you have, to strengthen what remains, and then build upon it. Once again I submit, as I did two weeks ago, that God's people are to long for the old paths, for those old paths were effectual to the salvation of men. The instruction of our Lord goes on with the notification that he has found the deeds of the church incomplete. This charge can be placed on most, if not all, churches, for each branch of Christ's church has its strengths and weaknesses. We see it in our denomination. The Reformed Episcopal Church, for example, rightly emphasizes reverent worship. And biblical doctrine, but is poor in my estimation at sending out and supporting missionaries both locally and abroad. Abroad, we only have a few that fall under the jurisdiction of our denomination. Locally, we are slow in planting churches. How often I hear from you and those who have moved from us the difficulty in finding churches that have what we have. If we believe that what we practice is God honoring and what we believe leads to the salvation of men, we ought to be planting churches in our surrounding communities. That we do not is, in my estimation, how we are incomplete. Where Sardis is incomplete is not known. It's not said. It is fitting with the holiness of the Lord that he does not publicly write down where the people of Sardis are incomplete. He tells them they are, and if they are honest with themselves, they will know what he is speaking about. Like King David, Christians are to pray these words Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me and know my ways. And then when God does, to accept it and repent from it. Only pride prevents us from offering up such a prayer, and the same pride will keep us out of glory. For the remedy for being incomplete is to remember what they have received and heard. After remembering, they are to obey it and at the same time repent for not obeying it to begin with. As with the first remedy, we are shown again how simple the Christian life is. To repent is to turn away from the direction one is going. If you believe one way and you repent, it means you now believe the opposite way. If you are behaving one way and you repent, it means that you behave the opposite way. The Christian life can be described in the following manner. Jesus Christ is the Son of God who died for the sins of men. Believe in him. Followers of Jesus Christ are baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost. Be baptized. Christians are to obey the commandments of God while they wait for his second coming. Obey His laws and wait for Him. The only reason such a life becomes complicated is when a person who says they are Christian or wants to be Christian lives by the flesh rather than the spirit. Our flesh provides excuses as to why we cannot believe or obey at this time or at that time or any time in the future. Circumstances in life become excuses that place the Christian life on hold. Because sinners live by their flesh so often they try to become Christian by their flesh. They try to live by the laws of God using the strength of their flesh. They fail and conclude that it does not work for them when all the while the one who holds the seven spirits is able to empower them. To receive the power of the Spirit, the sinner must wake up. Wake up to the call of Christ. Wake up to the simple trust and obedience that is needed to be saved. Wake up and repent for being asleep. Repent for being dead. The warning to those who are asleep Is that the Lord Himself will come to them like a thief, meaning at a time they do not expect? If they are not ready, their eternity is sealed. The coming that our Lord describes here is not necessarily his second coming, where the eastern sky is split, and all will bow before him, and the dead will rise. Instead, his second coming can refer to a specific coming, which means that he comes to specific people at a specific time. And we can think of it in this way. If you are struck down today or tomorrow by an accident or a disease that takes your life, in a very real sense, the Lord has come to you. And the coming of the Lord to us includes more than this: more than his second coming or the point of our death. It will occur when we do not expect it. And we are to expecting it, we are to be ready. An example I've used before is an instance such as driving down the road. You become tired and perturbed with the slow driver ahead of you, and so you honk and you make disgusted expressions. And when you finally are able to pass, you look at them and give them a scowl of your disapproval, only to realize to your embarrassment that the person you are passing is the neighbor to whom you have been trying to witness your Christian faith. In that instance, Jesus has come to you and you were not ready. I've been not ready a lot of times Jesus could come to us in the form of a beggar, employer, stranger, or person who is ill. If we do not receive him, then we were not ready. The good news in the address to Sardis is that there are those in the church, a few at least, that have not fallen asleep. A few are not dead. A few are ready. The image of soiled clothes is in contrast to the white robes promised to believers as a symbol of purity. that the blood of Christ accomplishes. The image of Christians dressed in white is repeated in Revelation. The reason these faithful are mentioned is to cause us to recall how God consistently holds a remnant for Himself We've been studying that in Romans and it reminds us of the prophet Elijah and those that God kept back from worshiping Baal. God always keeps a remnant. For those who have remained faithful, the risen Savior provides encouragement. The squeaky wheel gets most of the attention in this life. In the kingdom of God, the quiet wheel gets just as much. The Lord knows the deeds of the quiet ones. He is well aware that you have remained faithful. He says to the man who has worked most of his adult life at the same job to provide for the family that he is pleased. He says to the man who has been faithful to his one wife all their married days, that he is honored. He says to the man, Who ha who was in church whenever physically possible and paid his tithe habitually that a robe of white is waiting He says the same thing to a woman who devotes her life to raising her children in the faith instead of making a career for herself He says the same to the woman who submits to a husband that is not always kind or caring. He says the same to those who visit the sick or serve soup to the poor with no recognition and no expectations. These people and many others like them do not get the attention that the boisterous sinners and the self-proclaimed saints do in this life But our Lord promises to honor them much greater in the life to come. In his promise to those who have And we'll remain faithful. The call for the sinner to wake up and for the faithful to be strengthened come together They come together in his promise that he will not blot out the names of those who are faithful from the book of life. The reference to the Book of Life has cultural and Old Testament significance. Culturally, the Book of Life was the register of the living in every town. When a citizen died, you simply erased the name. In the Old Testament, the book of life is the register of God's people. In the case of the Christians at Sardis, like the books of every town, if a member of the church were dead, then his name would be erased. For those who were faithful, Jesus promises their names would remain. Implied in the promise is the possibility that Christians from Sardis could lose their salvation. Having their names blotted out of the book of life, if they do not wake up. This implied possibility has caused some to conclude that Christians can lose their salvation. Although such a conclusion goes against our Lord's promise that those who are his will not be cast out, and nothing can separate us from his love, and that those he has chosen he will save Still, some believe salvation can be lost. Otherwise, they reason God would not imply it as a possibility. In response, we must realize that such implied warnings are not for causing insecurity or to end the salvation where God has begun in us. Direct warnings or implied warnings are a means by which God stirs up the hearts of the faithful. It is how He wakes the faithful up who have slumbered. Those who are not God's people will continue in their ways. Those who are God's people will hear the warning and respond appropriately. The summary instruction for the church is simply wake up and strengthen what you have. Although the church has sinned, there is opportunity to turn around. The true believer will hear the call to wake up and do so. The unbeliever will continue to sleep regardless of how loud the alarm goes off. It can be said loud or soft. It can be said with implied warning. In the end, only those who have ears will hear. Thus I can say I can say it softly, and still the faithful will hear. Wake up and strengthen what you have. Amen. We continue in our worship by the giving of our tithes and our offerings, and we're mindful that the Lord loves a cheerful gifts.

sermons.title: Be Encouraged
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. May be seated. I have heard that title before, but I've never sung it before, that song. And I still haven't sung it. I don't know how that goes. But we'll keep trying. We are in Revelation chapter 3, picking up at verse 7, the letter to the Christians in Philadelphia. If you need to be encouraged this morning, you are in the right place. You may have noticed that these seven churches addressed are collective examples of individual personalities and seasons of life Personality-wise, we know people like Sardis who have a reputation of being alive in the faith, but are actually dead. Like Thyatira, some people serve their fellow man well, but are lazy theologically. Others are strident theologically, but do not serve their fellow man. Seasons of life are reflected in churches like Smyrna, who were going through a time of poverty. and Philadelphia, who were being persecuted by the Jews. In such seasons, it is not a time for rebuke. It is not a time to have all of our shortcomings listed. It is a time to be encouraged. Philadelphia needs to be encouraged, and the Lord provides such like no one else can. Each word, phrase, and reference is specifically chosen for encouraging the Christian Church at Philadelphia. In addition, we should note that such encouragement is for the church as a whole. Just as an entire church can be confronted and rebuked for sin It can also be encouraged for its obedience. Certainly, some may have been involved in the life of the church more than others, but that does not make them more important. If we are going to embrace the metaphor of the church being like a body, we must acknowledge that the little toe contributes to the body running fast just as the hamstring or the quadricep. I acknowledge this for your hearing, that you might know how important each of you is in making up the local body of believers. Even if the only thing you provide is your presence on Sundays, you matter. You are what is needed to make the body whole And it is to each of the parts of the body, the church, that the Lord writes these words of encouragement. Jesus begins his encouragement to the church by referring to himself as holy and true. He is comparing himself to the false idols that were worshipped in this pagan city of Philadelphia. Jesus is pure. He is sinless and is therefore unlike the idols of that day. Being unlike false gods, he does not ask people to sin. Jesus is true. He does not teach lies or represent lies. The Christians in Philadelphia could count on him. He then uses a description of himself that has not yet been given in this revelation. But is another way to encourage as he reaches back to what he has revealed about himself through the prophet Isaiah. In Isaiah chapter 22, God accuses a royal steward of falsehood, of betraying his trust. He then promises to replace the false steward with a faithful one. This is what he said. He said, I will clothe him with a tunic and tie your sash securely about him. I will entrust him with your authority. And he will become a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of David. Then I will set the key of the house of David on his shoulder. When he opens, no one will shut. When he shuts, no one will open. Jesus takes that passage and applies it to himself. He is announcing that the officers of apostate Israel are false stewards. They have to be removed from authority and replaced by the one who is holy and true. The key of David refers to God's covenant with David and the kingdom to be established through David's line. Jesus is of that line and the one given the key. The Jews believe they own the rights to David's line, but the Heavenly Father owns it and he gives it to the Son. All who believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, whether Jew or Gentile, are allowed through the door and into the kingdom of heaven by the authority of the Son, the owner of the key. The Savior holds the door open for the Christians at Philadelphia because he knows their deeds. When he told the church at Sardis that he knew their deeds, it was bad news, for they were dead in their faith. They were incomplete. In the case of Philadelphia, the fact that the Lord knows their deeds is a positive. It is worth noting that the deeds of the Lord that the Lord knows are not front-page news. They did not run the largest soup kitchen in Philadelphia. They did not have well-attended crusades. Their deeds were simply keeping God's word and not denying his name. It appears that in light of the persecution, Christians were under the spirit of the day that dominated the city, and it was enough that the people remained obedient and courageous. Sometimes, many times, the Christian life needs to be no more than doing what you are told and staying true to what you believe. The Apostle Paul said as much to the church at Rome when he instructed them to live quiet lives. And when it was within their power, they were to be at peace with all men. Once again, we hear our Lord commending those who are of a simple faith. He does not require an understanding of super lapsarianism. Works of supererrogation, transubstantiation, venial versus mortal sin, or whatever egg-headed words theologians can conjure up. He doesn't require a church to hold crusades, bring in Christian musicians for the purpose of outreach, or hold thoughtful seminars. Not to say there's anything wrong with such things. The point made is that what God requires is a simple faith in difficult times. A simple faith is the most effective faith. Because of their simple faith, the Lord says he opens the door to the kingdom of God for them and will not allow it to be shut. And here is a statement for eternal security. As a believer on the Lord Jesus Christ, he has started a work in you and he will complete it. He has paid for your sins by the blood of Christ, and that blood is too valuable not to retain what is purchased. He has marked you as his own. He has promised he will never leave you or forsake you. No one can reverse what he has done, not even our so-called self-wills. For we are his, and the door remains open. As part of the security promised to believers, the Lord Jesus makes a commitment To humble those who are guilty of persecuting the Christians at Philadelphia. He refers to them as those who are of the synagogue of Satan. Who claim to be Jews, though they are not, but are liars. Hard words. You will remember that in the sermon regarding the church at Smyrna, he identified the synagogue of Satan as those of the Jewish faith. Who not only rejected Jesus as Savior, but also did everything within their power to rid that city of the Christian faith. From these words, we conclude that the primary persecutors of Christians during the time of the writing of the book of Revelation were Jewish. And once again, I remind you, as I did when discussing Smyrna, that the words here are in no way anti-Semitic. The words of our Lord do not give Christians in any way the authority to retaliate against the Jewish race. The reason why our Lord calls them the synagogue of Satan and says that these people are not real Jews but liars. It's because a real Jew would believe Jesus to be the Savior. Those who say he is not the Savior, whether they be Jewish or Gentile, are of Satan. For Jesus clearly applied this truth to all when he said that you are either for me or against me. Those who are against them are of Satan, because there are only two sides. Continuing this line of thinking, we can conclude that there is no such thing as an Orthodox Jew or an Orthodox Judaism. That is to say that the term Orthodox refers to that which should be believed within the faith The Jewish religion of then and of today does not believe in Christ Jesus as Savior, and therefore they are not Orthodox. Likewise, we should not describe people of Jewish descent as only believing in the Old Testament, but not the New Testament. After all, the Old Testament spoke of Jesus. The law, the Psalms, the prophets clearly described his birth, his life, his atoning sacrifice, and placed at the right hand of the Father. To believe in the Old Testament is to believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. Furthermore, when a Jew believes On the Lord Jesus Christ, becoming a Christian, he is not, quote, a Jewish Christian. He is a Christian. Any further distinction confuses the covenants. There is one covenant more fully revealed in the New Testament, but the same covenant that God made with Abraham. Abraham believed and was made righteous. He saw Jesus day and was glad. At the time of this letter to Philadelphia, the Jews clearly had the upper hand in that city. Nevertheless, Jesus promises a time when they will be forced to come and bow down to the feet of the city. Of Christians. Those who falsely claimed to be Jews were initially in the position of the persecutor. But they will be forced to acknowledge the covenantal status of the Christian church on the day of God's choosing. It will be that way for all the enemies of God's people. A Christian's place in authority and honor is described by the Apostle Paul in his letter to the church at Ephesus. Where he speaks in the first person plural, saying this: God raises us up with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus. In order that in the coming ages he might show the incomparable riches of his grace expressed in his kindness to us in Christ Jesus. So we know that after his ascension, Jesus was given the seat at the right hand of the Father. Every knee will bow and every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord as He sits on that throne Putting these two descriptions together from Ephesians and what we know of Jesus' place, the Christians are seated with Christ, who is seated at the right hand of the Father. The same homage then given to the Savior by those who are enemies of God in this life will be given to Christians who sit with Him. Hence, if you cannot rejoice in your position in this life, you will rejoice in the one promised, the position promised in heaven. You may not be winning in this life, says the Lord, to the persecuted Christians in Philadelphia, but you will in the life hereafter. And I realized that that statement is quite contrary to the preachers who claim heaven on earth to their followers and then ask for that seed offering. But the Christians that received this message in the first century, they knew persecution and they knew poverty and they clung to the hope of heaven. And thus that is what I choose to preach. Another promised honor to the Christians of Philadelphia, because they had been patient as the Lord instructed, is for them to be cared for by the Lord when the great trial comes. From my perspective, the great trial that is going to come upon the whole world is one that came upon the whole world, the whole known world, when Rome began to burn under Nero. When Nero looked for someone to blame for a fire that was likely started by him And continued because of him, he found the Christians to be easy targets. Christians soon became enemies of the state of Rome as well as enemies of the so-called Jews. Be reminded again that the original audience of these letters were first century Christians going through persecutions. Certain Christians who hold to a dispensational view of the Book of Revelation believe that this passage alludes to a rapture of the church before Armarged. The great final battle. An obvious problem with such an interpretation is that if this promise to the Church of Philadelphia were referring to Armageddon, then the battle would have already taken place. If it is referred to a battle that does not involve Philadelphia, then it is at odds for it to be mentioned to them, for they would be long dead before such a battle occurs. If we don't care about such an oddity and believe this refers to a promised rapture, there is another problem, and that is with the word keep. To keep is to preserve, to safeguard, to defend. It is the same as found in the Epistle of Jude, where the Lord is said to keep Christians from falling. Defending the rapture, excuse me, excuse me, defending and a rapture are not the same. This promise to keep is like the others before it, in that it confirms to the heart of weary Christians that God governs their days. He is their shield. He is their defender. Since God is for them, there is no foe who can legitimately, legitimately threaten them. The remaining promises bring together the garments of a high priest and the architecture of the temple. According to 1 Kings, the two pillars of the temple are given names. The first name of a pillar is He Shall Establish, and the second pillar is in him is strength. The pillars corresponded to the shoulder pieces of the high priest that he had written on them the names of the sons of Israel. The headdress of the priest had inscribed the name of God just like the beams that overarch the pillars. Great confidence swells the heart of all believers as our Savior identifies us with the high priest and with the pillars in the temple. We are worthy to enter the Holy of Holies as would the high priest. At the same time, we are given a grand sense of security because we are like the pillars in the temple. Like the first pillar, God has established us. Like the second, God is our strength. For every Christian that remains faithful to the end, there is an assurance that he or she has a place in the very presence of God. No one can remove you. No one can take your crown of glory. Only you can willingly throw it to his feet. Because of all this, because of all this, we can say to the devil and his angels, bring it on. You can try your best. You can stake your claim upon red light districts, communist nations, Washington, D. C. abortion clinics. You can even claim my body with disease, but you cannot harm my soul, for the Lord Jesus Christ owns me. He has marked me. He has placed his name upon me. He has placed a name upon me so holy, so righteous and pure that it cannot be uttered with evil lips. He has written upon me his new name, and I am his. Such words can be uttered and uttered defiantly by you to the devil. Such words can be uttered to any voice in your head, to any blasphemer in your ear, or any persecutor that believes he has the upper hand. Dear friends, there are times to be encouraged in the faith, and today is one of those times. As it is true every Sunday, I do not know what each of you is going through. Each of you has personal trials that are very different from one another. And yet in those differences we all need the same encouragement. In the midst of your struggle, know that the glorified Savior has a door open for you He will bring your enemies to your feet. He will give you a crown. He will mark you and establish you in his presence so that no one can remove you. And he will mark you, mark you with his most holy name. For you who have ears of faith Hear what he is saying to the churches. Let us pray. Our gracious God, for this most holy of encouragements, certainly in times of trial for each that are here within my voice. We do pray that these words might go deep, that we might be confident before the devil, before any trial, before any situation. To know the door is open, to know we've been marked, to entrust that our soul is owned by you. May this be an encouragement to all who believe. We ask in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Be Good for Something
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles to Revelation chapter 3. Revelation chapter 3. You'd be much served to uh to follow along. To understand the symbolism that's being used here, Revelation 3, beginning at verse 14. Last week we were encouraged by the Lord when we studied his letter to the church at Philadelphia. But every Sunday we can be encouraged because of the Easter story Jesus is no longer dead. He is risen. He tasted the bitter so that we could taste the sweet. Encouragement is good for the soul and often needed. From the other side, rebuke is needed also. Rebuke does not draw crowds or sell tickets, but it is as much needed as encouragement. The Church at Laodicea was lukewarm in its faith, and encouraging words would have allowed the church to remain in its present state. There is a saying that goes something like, God loves us just the way we are, and too much to let us stay that way. The saying applies to the church at Laodicea. The city itself was a prosperous one, and likely the most prosperous of the seven cities addressed by these seven letters by the risen Lord. The city had great wealth and financial independence. It had a textile industry which produced a very fine quality of black, glossy wool. It had a renowned scientific community with a prestigious medical school and an ISAV that is produced, known as that was produced, known as Phrygian powder. Which was well known even in the days of Aristotle, some 300 years prior. It appears from the content of this letter. that the prosperity of the city contributed to the church being lukewarm. Before he addressed the problems within the church, Jesus describes himself as the Amen. The faithful and true witness and the beginning of creation. These three titles have a Trinitarian reference as well as providing a resume. For his right to bear testimony against the church. The Amen is used by us after we pray and after we sing. It literally means so be it. The force of the phrase is much stronger than simply so be it. It is actually an oath. To say amen means to call a curse down upon oneself, meaning that if what is being said or promised is not true or goes unfulfilled, the person in question is to be damned. As the Amen, Jesus is making an oath that what he says and promises, he will do. As a faithful and true witness, he can be dependent upon to speak the truth. He is an infallible witness. As the beginning of creation, he is the ruler of all. St. Paul said the same in Colossians, speaking of Jesus, he says he is the image of the invisible God. The firstborn of all creation. For by him all things were created, both in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, rulers, authorities, all things have been created by him. And for him. Having properly introduced himself in regard to the authority he has to judge the church, Jesus begins describing their standing before him. He describes them as lukewarm, and does so in relation to preferring either being hot or cold. In my younger days, I understood Jesus to be telling the church that he would prefer them to be hot for him, on fire for him, meaning that they were on-fire Christians, as we like to say. or cold for him, meaning that they were antagonistic to the gospel. Such a conclusion reveals how conditioned I was by my culture in the manner I understood what hot implied or what cold implied. I did not try to answer why the Lord would prefer a church being antagonistic, other than it might be an easier way to know what to do with such a people. Like me, you will likely be interested to know that the city of Laodicea was situated between two other important cities Hieropolis and Colossae. Colossae was in a valley surrounded by mountains, supplying it a fresh and cold water supply. Hieropolis was situated on the other side and higher up, and it was famous for a natural hot spring. People would come from around the region to bathe in its mineral-laden pools. From Hieropolis, the hot spring would flow down to Laodicea, where it cooled on the way. Thus, the point was that the waters at Laodicea were neither hot and healing, nor cool and refreshing. Like the waters that flowed through the city, so was the condition of the church. Compared to the cities that surrounded her, the church at Laodicea neither cured illness nor soothed dry lips. The church was good for nothing. The church was ineffectual For Jesus to say that he would prefer them to be hot or cold means that he would like them to be effectual in one manner or another. Instead, the church had no influence upon the society around her. From this rebuke, we can conclude, dear church, the Christian calling is not to blend in with pagan society, but to convert it And reform it, making it God's kingdom on earth as it is in heaven. In my opinion, of the seven churches addressed in Revelation The one most American churches identify with is the church at Laodicea. My opinion is fostered by the divorce rate in churches, abortion rates in churches Premarital sex rates amongst Christians, these today mirror the culture we are called to transform. It's quite popular, as you know, for Christians to gather on Sundays at what are being called mega churches. The leaders of these churches have one primary goal: get as many people in through the door as possible and make sure they give you some money. Reportedly, there are local churches that attract close to 2,000 people on a given Sunday, and there are churches across the United States, one that attracts 40,000 on a given Sunday. Thus, these institutions are successful at drawing a crowd, but how successful are they at changing the culture in which they worship? Where is the impact these megachurches have on the morality and faith of Carroll County? Where is the impact of these mega-mega churches upon the inner cities, suburban areas, or simply the homes of the families who attend those same churches? If a church does not provide a place of healing or a place of refreshing, it is lukewarm If a church does not strengthen families or turn the hearts of men from immorality or feed and clothe the sick and disease or convert lost souls, it does not have to do all of these, but at least one It is lukewarm. It is fair to ask that if a church is not transforming society, if it is not Christianizing the culture, or at least challenging the prominent sins of the culture, What good is it? If the salt has become tasteless, our Lord said, how will it be made salty again? It is good for nothing except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by men. This is why Jesus says he will spew, spit, vomit the church. out of his mouth. There is no taste worth savoring. There is no effect worth digesting. As you know, the pandemic has put a lot more churches online to stream their services. Upon examining a few, I have discovered a pattern. Many of these churches are performing concerts with emotionally oriented music, followed by a short prayer and a sermon that is more like a counseling session. Beloved, the people of God don't need to be manipulated, they need to be fed. But the danger at Laodicea is more than being lukewarm. Laodicea has a perception of herself that is false. If you if you have ever dealt with a person who has a false perception of himself, you know how difficult it is to change his mind. A man who thinks he is funny will continue to tell jokes and laugh the loudest at himself than anyone else in the room. A man who is a poor athlete will continue to tell others how good he was in his day, not knowing that he is simply blowing smoke. A man who believes he is special because he has wealth will tell anyone who will listen about his newest car, his latest cruise, while the poor sap listening is trying to figure out how nicely to get out of the conversation The church at Laodicea thought she was rich and in need of nothing. Jesus breaks the news that the church is actually wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked. Earlier we described the economic wealth of the city. It is interesting that the categories of wealth shared by the city and the poverty that Jesus describes are the same. The city makes fine black wool, but the Christians there are naked. The city makes world-renowned eye salve, but the Christians there are blind. It is typical for our Lord to turn our perceptions of ourselves upside down. Where the Pharisees thought they were righteous, they were actually sinful. Where they thought they were humble, they were actually prideful. Jesus does the same to the church, proving that Christians are susceptible to the same sins as non-Christians. The blessing for us, the blessing for us is the opportunity we have been given to change, to repent. What Jesus offers the church in place of their poverty can only come from him. It is an offer of mercy. He offers them gold refined by fire, light garments to clothe them, and I salve to anoint their eyes so that they can actually see. The symbolism should be obvious. True faith and genuine works in response to God's mercy are described in Scripture as jewelry. The trial of faith, St. Peter says, is more precious than gold. Works done in faith are described by St. Paul to be gold, silver, and precious stones. Jesus can make what we do on this earth worth something beyond immediate gratification. The symbolism of white garments describes purity and covering as opposed to filth of sin and nakedness, which is shame. The ability to see is a description of true sight that identifies godliness and righteousness. Again, these are only available in Christ and no other. For a church that has been harshly criticized, these are actually hopeful words. It is hard. I know it is hard because I have been personally rebuked. It is hard to understand rebuke and discipline as an act of love. We falsely understand that saying nothing and requiring no repercussions is loving or merciful. Many times, including this time between the Lord and the church at Laodicea. Love and mercy are expressed in rebuke and discipline. This does not make sense to our flesh. It certainly is not how we would choose it to be for ourselves. And yet here is the Lord Jesus saying to the church that those whom he loves he rebukes and he disciplines. If our flesh tells us that we are not being loved, well our flesh is wrong. What the Lord requires of his people when they are confronted with sin is of course repentance. Repentance is not merely something done at conversion, never to be practiced again. If you came to the faith later in life and repented of your sins, that was just the beginning. The Christian life is a life of repentance. We repent corporately in worship and privately in prayer. And such prayers are not only daily, but frequently throughout the day. We are to be a people who repent. We confess our sins to the Lord and to one another, for we have to. The remarkable image we are given when the Lord tells us to repent. Is that he is at the door.
