Here I am, he says with emphasis. I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in and eat with him and he with me. Evangelists in the 20th century used this image to call the unredeemed sinners to the faith in Christ, saying that Jesus was at the door of their heart and he's waiting for you to open to him. I'm not against such a use, but it is most important to understand that Jesus stands at the door of a Christian, the life of a Christian, and the life of the church. He is knocking on the door of Christians. Because he is knocking at the door, we realize that he is outside. And that is truly sad. The Lord is standing outside of his own church. He is the head of the church. It is his body. It is his bride. It is his namesake. And yet he stands outside. How did he get outside? The people who claimed to be for him and claimed to follow him shut him out. This is a grave circumstance indeed. But when we take pride in our wisdom and when we put trust in our flesh, we tend to go against the very thing we said we are fighting for. The remarkable aspect of this image is that Jesus would bother knocking. He has every right, I'm sure you will agree, to break the door down. He has every right to turn over the tables as he did in the temple. It is his house. Yet he stands at the door and knocks. As he knocks, he politely waits. He waits for the church for the Christian to answer. Moreover, we notice the intimacy he offers. He offers us his presence, and not just a presence that floats around like a ghost and watches us. He offers us a presence of eating with us. He will eat with us and us with him. As you know, eating a meal with another person, especially someone outside of the family, according to Jewish custom Was the greatest act of intimacy. Here is the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the ruler of God's creation, saying to us that He wants to eat with us. He wants to eat with his creation. He wants to eat with those who believe they are rich when they are not. He wants to eat with those who have pushed him out of his own house. He wants to eat with us who are in need of constant repentance from sin. In addition, not only does he want to eat with us He wants to give us the right to sit with him on his throne in heaven. Remarkable. Dear Church, What have we done to deserve his presence at our table, let alone a place at his side as he rules the nations? We have done nothing, and yet the offer is here for us to take. Words cannot express the graciousness of our God. Our hymns are all of a sudden inadequate. Our tunes are not worthy of his ears. Our prayers are utter nothing but babble when contrasted with what he is worthy to receive. And yet he still stands at the door and knocks. You will notice, dear church That the description he gives of himself standing at the door does not include a clause or a phrase that describes him ever leaving. He knocks and he waits. This reminds us that he takes no pleasure in men perishing. He has no pleasure in sinners not responding, and so he stands and waits for us to answer. Dear Church, if we have been ineffectual in the world, we are supposed to reform Let us repent and open the door. If we have perceived ourselves wrongly, believing that we were rich when in actuality we were poor before God, let us repent and open the door. If we have become like the world we are supposed to leave behind, let us repent and open the door. Upon reading this passage, he has knocked, and now he waits. Amen. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God, give us the courage to open the door, to properly examine ourselves. And to allow you to come in, allow you to make reform. Allow you to make us more in your image. Father, eat with us this day. As we come around this table, may we recognize it is you that offers us the bread, it is you that offers us the wine, it is you that joins with us. We thank you for it. In Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Come Up!
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: And thus we are nation raised all the way in third glory. And when we create our ways, will we bless our three boys? In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles to the book of Revelation, chapter 4. Really, really, really implore you to follow along. You will get lost in this sermon if you're not following along in the scriptures. There's a great deal of imagery we are trying to understand, and it's important that you read along as I explain it. If a homiletics professor or New Testament scholar was in the congregation this morning I might not do what I am about to do. I'm going to divide chapter 4 of the book of Revelation into two parts. Technically, this should not be done because the whole chapter is a description of one particular scene, and each part is as important as the next. However, and I admit that the however would not satisfy a high-strong PhD, there is simply too much in this chapter to explain and digest in one sermon. The first part we will hear from this morning is covering verses 1 through 6 of chapter 4. The beginning of the chapter brings us into Revelation proper, meaning that what we had had so far has been an epistle or letters to the seven churches. From here on out, the visions that we read are of a different genre and are on a different level spiritually. It cannot be helped by us to notice the juxtaposition between the ending vision of chapter 3 and the beginning vision of chapter 4. In chapter 3, Jesus, you remember, was standing at the door of the church and knocking. In chapter 4, there is a door in heaven standing open. This means that while men have shut the door of the church, leaving the Savior on the other side. God has opened a door up for John and for us so that we might look into heaven. Look into heaven and increase our faith. Because heaven is described as having a door, we can know that it is a place. Because the door can be opened or closed, we are able to conjecture that some will be left out while others allowed in. The one who owns the voice that speaks to John is not identified. But the voice is described as sounding as a trumpet. The sound of a trumpet represents triumphant glory. I'm sure you are like me. I look forward to Mr. Dannevius playing his trumpet. For it provides a triumphant glory feel that we do not get otherwise. Of course, it's especially liked on Easter Sunday. The sound is appropriate on special occasions because it represents something very unique. In this context, it represents the triumphant glory of the Son of God. The triumphant glorious voice tells John to come up. This is not an incidental call. We are called up because that is where God is. The book of Genesis describes the Garden of Eden as up on a mountain from which four rivers flow down. God called Moses up while on the mountain. God gave Moses the commandments while up on the mountain. Jerusalem was a city set on a hill, thus it was up. To be called up is to be where God meets his people. As we worship using the prayer book, you will hear the Sersum Corda as the minister says, Lift up your hearts. And we respond, we lift them up to the Lord. Our sanctuary is built with the communion table and rails elevated because of the call of God to come up to worship. He, God, is high and lifted up, and we come up to him in his response to his call. Looking to the text, we see the phrase, what must come next? I'm sorry, what must take place after this? Such a phrase has caused unfortunate angst between Christians, for some have translated it to be an emphasis on future events. But I remind you that this does not have to be, for it was the first century Christians who were the first audience and the primary benefactors of this vision. They need to know what must happen as well as we need to know. The phrase can simply mean events that will have Have to take place with an emphasis on the word must rather than after. In other words, we are going to hear a description of what God assures is going to happen. What it means for John to be in the Spirit is not clear to us. It is safe to assume that John is explaining how he could be viewing this vision while remaining on the island of Patmos. Nothing more is said about what it is like to be in the Spirit, and so it is safe to say that we are not meant to know. We are to notice that the throne scene next described and the one that sits on it, we are told is like or as, meaning that he cannot be seen by man. And thus he has an appearance to John that can only be a simile of his true being. The three stones identified represent three of the tribes of Israel and are found on the breastplate of the high priest as described in Exodus chapter 28. as well as being mentioned as jewelry that littered the ground of the Garden of Eden, as mentioned by the prophet Ezekiel. Jasper is the first stone on the breastplate and is clear in color, representing purity. While Cornelian was the last stone on the breastplate and is red, representing sacrifice. The emerald is green, representing nature, and symbolizes God redeeming all of his creation. Next is the rainbow, and it is connected symbolically with the emerald For it was the rainbow that was made a promise by the Lord after the flood that he would not judge his creation in the manner of the flood again. The rainbow is a covenant symbol, and here this is important, and here it is described as encircling the throne of God. The fact that it is a circle is greatly significant for us because it ties into the number of elders seated around the throne, as well as the sea of glass. The rainbow circle symbolizes that God's covenant is complete. We normally see the rainbow as a half circle. It is incomplete to our eyes. Now, surrounding the throne is a full rainbow, and as a complete circle, it confirms that what we are seeing is a glorified Christ. The same Christ who has promised to split the eastern sky upon his return. But God had set out to do at the fall of mankind is completed by symbolized by the circular rainbow The circle is closed around the throne of God. The image that John is seeing is not bound by time. It is an image that is eternal. We might wonder when this image is to be realized, and the answer is that it is realized now, but not yet quite. The victory over death and sin of our Lord has always been a heavenly reality. The scripture says that the Son of Man was slain from the foundation of the world. Beloved, what John is being allowed to view and what we are allowed to imagine as he describes it is the end of the puzzle. We are imagining, and John is seeing the completion of God's redemptive work. We are seeing heaven. That idea that this image represents the completion of redemption is further bolstered by the identified number of elders that surround the throne. And nowhere in the Bible is the term elder given to anyone but men. Elder or presbyter designates leaders among the people of God. They are leaders within the church. But why 24? Why 24? We know beginning with the Old Testament that the number 12 represents God's people. There were twelve sons of Jacob who became covenant heads, known as the 12 tribes of Israel. The twelve tribes made up God's chosen people. In comparison, when Jesus walked the earth, he chose twelve apostles. The apostles were given charge of leadership over God's chosen people. The church. Simple addition of God's people represented in the Old Testament and God's people represented in the New Testament, give us a total of twenty-four Thus the elders that surround the throne, in the same manner as the rainbow surrounds the throne, symbolize the old and new covenants coming together in one covenant. What God started and promised through Israel is completed in the church, which Jesus is the head. The adornment of these elders with crowns reminds us of the promise by Jesus to Peter, who had asked about leaving everything to follow Jesus Jesus said that his disciples would receive back in the life after a hundredfold of what they had left behind. He also said that they would be seated next to him. And here they are. The adornment of these elders is duplicated by churches such as our own that have us the custom of presbyters wearing albs while overseeing the service of Holy Communion. The white owl represents the purity of Christ. It is a purity he has himself as well as a purity he provides to us. The white robes point to Christ and point to the heavenly scene around his throne rather than pointing to the man who wears it. It is this church's belief that a man who officiates the worship of Almighty God should be clothed in a manner corresponding with the task assigned to him. You will notice that there is no mention of business suits and ties being worn around the throne or even black robes as some preachers wear. The described visual effects of lightning and thunder capture what is first mentioned in Exodus 19, when the Lord is on Mount Sinai, speaking to his people. From the throne described here and from the mountain described in Exodus, there came flashes of lightning and voices as peals as thunder. These are associated with the awesomeness of God. The effects represent God's presence You remember that his presence was so very awesome before the Israelites that they cowered before him and asked Moses to speak on God's behalf, for they feared God's revealed power. Christians, in contrast, know they can fear God and still be in His presence. Like the lampstands with lamps burning in the holy place in the temple, so there are seven lamps of burning before the throne. The seven lamps are symbolic of the seven spirits of God mentioned in chapter one. This is another reference to the Holy Spirit in his sevenfold fullness of activity. Putting visual and audio effects together, we see that there are three aspects of God's glorious image. His voice is one, his radiant glory is two, and his spirit is the third. The final image we will discuss this morning is the glassy sea. It is a sea of glass, it says, like crystal. To the human eye, nothing can be more pristine and calming than a sea of glass likened to crystal. Many of us dream of sitting on the beach in front of a clear ocean water with waves calmly rolling in. Lakefront property is valuable because of the calming effect water has upon the human spirit, especially when the water is at rest. What we should first notice from this description of this glassy sea is that it is similar, the vision is similar to the one described by the prophet Ezekiel. Ezekiel, however, sees the crystal sea from below, whereas John is seeing this from above. The difference of perspective allows us to conclude that what John is seeing, again, is the finished covenant. It is the kingdom as it is and will be at our resurrection. The description of a glassy sea is also a reference to the peace that Christ will bring to the nations. At creation, you remember, God chose to use land as a symbol of his people and water as a symbol of the nations that threaten his people. At creation, he separated the land and the sea. When he chose Abraham and his descendants, he aligned Abraham with a promised land, and the Gentiles, he aligned them with troubled waters. It was troubled waters that the Lord punished his creation in the flood. It was the lack of fresh water that drove Israel to Egypt. And it was troubled waters that God parted so that his people could be freed from slavery. After 40 years, the Lord then held back troubled waters. Like he hold back troubled nations to allow Israel to cross over into the promised land. The psalmist King David poetically describes the troubled nations as troubled waters in the following verse of Psalm 65. He said to the Lord, You answer us with awesome deeds of righteousness, O God, our Savior, the hope of all the ends of the earth and the farthest seas. Who formed the mountains by your power, having armed yourself with strength, who stilled the roaring of the seas, the roaring of the waves, and the turmoil of the nations. Thus the Crystal Sea is a sea that is calmed by the gospel. Combining all of this imagery allows us to summarize that the power of the gospel brings the plan of salvation to completion As the covenants are brought together and revealed as one, and the peace, the peace that the gospel brings to all the nations The peace provided by the risen and glorified Savior has no ripple. There is no wind that can move it or rock that can disturb it. The image that John sees is that of an ultimate peace. The peace described is a peace that every human soul longs for. Some try to find it in chemicals, others try to find it in gratifying the flesh, still others by forced meditation or good deeds to the earth or to their fellow man. In reality, everlasting peace is provided only by the risen and glorified Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ. In C. S. Lewis's series, The Chronicles of Narnia, he repeatedly describes the reaction that people have when they first encounter Aslan. the great lion, who is the Christ-like figure in the stories. The reactions are of great fear, along with a strong sense of comfort and security. The reactions include awe from His Majesty that would cause a person to look away, and at the same time a feeling of warmth. An invitation that causes a person to want to always remain in his presence. It is that reaction that is intended here when we look into heaven. What reaction each reader or listener has is dependent on what you hope for. If your hope is in Christ, it is in this vision that the hope is realized It is in this vision that the hope is of peace. He said, Jesus said to his disciples when he visited them after his resurrection, peace be to you. He says the same as we gaze upon the encircled throne and the crystal sea, he says, peace be to you. The book of Revelation is a book we return to again and again because of images given to us here that cause us to see why we are following Jesus Christ. Allow yourself to be a first century Christian living in Jerusalem, where there is a great deal of tension between Jews and Roman leaders. Tension. Tension that boiled over into a siege, and then into starvation, and then to a slaughter of thousands, and the fear that you feel having witnessed it all. What came to be called the fall of Jerusalem? Such fear is palpable. And then you are given this vision of John Of Jesus on the throne and nations at peace, true and eternal peace. Surely such a vision would stay with you because you need it to bring you peace. Or maybe you are a first century Christian in the city of Corinth. And the Greeks and the Romans don't much care about your faith, but the Jews do. And as a result, they won't share commerce with you and they ridicule you and and bring you up on false charges before the state. And you are hearing about Your leaders, the apostles of the Christian church being killed in horrible ways, like being crucified upside down or pierced through the heart. And you get this letter from the Apostle John, and you read of a door opened in heaven and a throne. And the one who is Jesus sitting on the throne. And Jesus is shining on the throne. And you remember the rainbow. God's promise in Genesis, a full circle, now being fulfilled. And you hear of 24 elders around the throne dressed in clothes of white with golden crowns on their heads. And from the throne comes lightnings and thunder, and you are told of a sea that is like glass, like crystal. And a peace comes over your soul. A peace in the midst of turmoil, a peace in the midst of persecution. A peace given to you because you have seen heaven. Yes. We need these scenes of heaven. And we need to come back to them because that is the reality we strive to experience. That is where our hope lies. See the door of heaven open and know that such vision gives hope for now. And may we never give up on it. Let us pray. My gracious and merciful God, we thank you for being privileged to Read of this vision, to imagine it within ourselves, and to receive that peace that only you can give For this blessing, we thank you, but we pray that you would always bring us back to it when the nations are in turmoil, when our lives are not So smooth that we might see this vision again and be at peace. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: We Can Imagine
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I encourage you, as is typical in the book of Revelation, to follow along in your Bibles. You will be fed much more sufficiently if you follow along, the imagery is uh sometimes complicated You remember a number of years ago the popularizing of the song I Can Only Imagine? Even though it is clearly a Christian song, it was actually played on secular radio stations The song has been sung by a number of artists since, becoming popular in Christian, contemporary, and country music circles. A movie was even made about the writing of the song. The song's premise appealed to many as the writer of the song asks the Lord what his personal reaction is going to be. the day he stands in heaven before his Lord and Savior, Jesus. The chorus goes, you remember Will I stand in your glory, or to my knees will I fall? Will I dance for you, Jesus, or in awe of you be still? Like sing Hallelujah or be able to speak at all, I can only imagine. The song touches the souls of many and sparks the imagination. Because other Christians have likely asked similar questions. How will I respond? Christians anticipate that the sight of the glorified Savior and the unmerited position they will have before him will overwhelm their emotions and to their knees they will fall. But they also anticipate the possibility that they will want to dance while caring nothing of what others think about their dancing. They anticipate a freedom of their body and soul that they have never experienced in this life. While it is true that we can only imagine the scene in heaven, It is also true that our imaginations are not left to their own devices. The scene that is described to us in Revelation chapter 4 directs our imagination to what it is like to stand before Jesus. As I stated last week, it is not the best approach to study this chapter in two sections. What limits us each week is time. I know that I'd only have a short time to keep your attention. And when there is so much to discover from such passages, we can easily be overwhelmed with the information to the point of missing what is most important. Thus we have divided the chapter up into two parts. The first part taught us that the covenant of God was completed, being symbolized by the rainbow that is now a circle. And the elders who represent both tribes of Israel and the apostles who represent all of God's people. These symbols bring the new covenant and the old covenant together. Our emphasis last week was upon the crystal water before the throne. We learned that the water in Scripture represents troubled nations. And because the water is clear and crystal, we proclaim that Christ has brought peace to the nations. Our emphasis was that we get to peek into heaven with this vision, which provides us peace, peace available in every situation. What is described next is similar to stories in mythology or characters in a Tokian novel. There is a circle within the circle of the rainbow, and the elder is made by four living creatures. The eyes of these creatures are noted first. A creature covered with eyes obviously is responsible to see. Each of these creatures is responsible to see or watch over all of God's creation That there are four living creatures causes us to connect their duties with the entire world. The Bible in various places describes the earth as being four-cornered. It does not do so because the writers believed the earth was flat, but because the earth is understood to be an altar unto God. As an altar on which sacrificial worship is offered in the temple, that had four corners. And so the earth is described as having four corners. The earth is the Lord's. It is the place upon which God has offered praise. When there are mentioned four corners of the earth, or four winds, or four directions. or four rivers in Eden, we are to understand each to be a reference to an altar on which God is to be honored. Also, the four creatures are living as opposed to creatures of stone. The four living creatures are also correspond to the points of a compass. And the earth as an altar where God is worshipped. The numberless eyes of the four creatures represent their watchfulness over all parts of creation. We now next turn to examine their appearance. The first has an appearance like a lion. The second like an ox, the third, like a human being, and the fourth, like a flying eagle. These distinguishing characteristics represent the four animate powers of creation. The lion represents the beasts of the field. The ox represents the cattle or domestic animals. Man represents the intelligent creatures. And the eagle represents birds of the air. In summary, they represent creation in all the fullness of its power and of its talents. The numbered six wings also ties into creation for it symbolizes the six developments of creation or what we call days of creation. Once we understand that each creature represents, we must notice what they are doing. They are worshiping God. In fact, they never stop worshiping God. The words are repeated over and over again. That's why we sung them in our opening hymn. Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come. Verse 9 tells us that there is an antiphon to this saying given by the 24 elders who represent the covenants. An antiphon is a sung response. They respond by falling down before the one who sits on the throne, worshiping him forever and ever, by laying their crowns before him, crowns that were given to them by him. They lay those before the one on the throne and respond, you are worthy, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power. For you created all things, and by your will they were created to have their being. As we imagine this scene, in our minds it is quite common to be in awe. While at the same time wondering how these beasts and these elders could worship day and night saying the same thing and doing the same thing Verse 8 describes the worship as being done day and night, never ceasing. They say these words over and over again, and the elders respond to the words over and over again. Now before we focus on the worship emphasis, I know it is necessary to address what many of you are thinking. To worship in the manner described is monotonous, and monotony is boring. I remember my first ministry assignment was to college students at the Nazarene Church that we attended in Moscow, Idaho. Where I had recently graduated, a college-age girl to whom I was attempting to witness the Christian faith asked me directly, why should she want to go to heaven? I had never been asked that question directly, and it took me a moment to collect my thoughts. I answered in two ways, and neither of them helped her. First, I said that it was better than going to hell. I certainly believe that to be true, but such a statement doesn't say a whole lot about heaven. Living in a sewer is better than living in hell, but I would not compare a sewer to heaven. I then said that in heaven you will worship the Lord for eternity This, as I said, did not strike her as a selling point, and I can understand why. She did not know of God's mercy at the time and therefore was not moved emotionally or with gratefulness to worship God. Also, like most of us, she found that worship services in churches were not all that exciting In my younger days, I thought that worship should be exciting, so I was involved with churches that clapped and danced and played loud music and shouted every now and then What I came to experience from those worship scenes was a pumped-up excitement generated out of guilt or simply manipulation. For me, it was a desire to have worship exciting that caused me to excite myself. If I was not excited in worship, I thought there was something wrong with me. The problem with such worship is the point where you come down off of your self-generated high, and you are reminded once again how difficult it is to stay motivated while worshiping God. The guilt returns. I learned by experience and biblical example that life in this world is not a constant emotional high, and our flesh reminds us of that truth repeatedly. Liturgical worship, like our own, or happy clappy worship, like I just described, are both limited by our flesh. The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak. We have a hard time imagining ourselves worshiping God day and night because we get bored. And our flesh cries out for something different when we worship for an hour to an hour and a half on Sunday morning. Such a conclusion is caused by our misunderstanding about heaven and our present earthly condition. The elders and beasts around the throne are able to worship continually because they are not bound or restricted by flesh that is fallen. Our flesh, having been born of Adam, is dying and thus limited by time. Resurrected flesh does not have the same concerns, and in fact is fulfilling what it's created to do when it worships continually. That may be hard, a hard concept to grasp considering the dominance of our flesh in this life. But it can be proven when you think about what you are created to be. The purpose of each human is to glorify God and enjoy Him forever. We are created for worship. In fact, I argue that we worship all of the time without realizing we are worshiping We worship our desire. We worship our self will. We worship our dreams, our aspirations, we worship our relationships, our emotions. My argument is that almost everything we do has an element of worship involved It just so happens that unregenerated people, people who are not Christians, worship falsely Christians, on the other hand, are to do all things in this life as an act of worship. When we do not, we are worshiping the wrong things, and yet we are still worshiping. It is that simple. We are built for worship, and those who follow Christ will spend eternity worshiping the true God. Not only are we created to worship, we are created to worship a certain way. And here is where much of modern Christendom has failed. For the vision that John has of the exalted Savior being worshipped is a model for us. What is occurring in the mega churches today, or the community churches that want to be mega churches, was exposed in a documentary series about Hillsong Church, which started in Australia while planting many churches in the United States. What made Hillsong scandalous was their celebrity focus and their sex scandals with their leadership. What stood out also was their documented knowledge. Of how to manipulate people with their music. Their praise and worship style was based on the distortion of Psalm 22, verse 3, which reads. Yet you are holy and thrown on the praises of Israel. From such a verse, they preach that God not only inhabits the places of the place of his people when they sing his praises, but that God actually rushes to them when he hears their singing. With God's presence ensured, the song leaders lead songs of uplifting sounds and words of thanksgiving. Which then leads to songs of love and then leads to songs of quiet contemplation, allowing the worshippers to feel an emotional presence of God without being able to know the difference between the true presence of God and their personal emotions. Such practice has been called musical sacramentalism, which says that God's presence is primarily in the singing of his people. rather than in the words read and preached and in the bread and wine. Unfortunately, the praise and worship approach sees God similar similar to a genie in a bottle. Who has to be conjured up before he can they can get what they wish for. What John is describing in Revelation is a worship service of a risen and glorified Savior of mankind in heaven. It is for us who are on earth to duplicate such reverence by our actions and words while we are here. Last week we spoke of the call to come up to worship and how that is to be duplicated in our services. We also mentioned the white robes which symbolize the office of an elder and his duty before the throne of God. Today we make note of the words spoken around the throne as the elders and the beasts worship. The beasts cry out, Holy, Holy, Holy is the Lord God Almighty The cry is Trinitarian. It recognizes the holiness of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. The cry is heavenly, for it contains words inspired by the presence of Almighty God. Because they are heavenly and inspired, these should be our words as we worship here on earth. We should use the words of heavenly worship. And as we do, we should humbly acknowledge that we are not starting this song of worship. And we are not alone in singing this song. In fact, whenever we sing or chant these words in our service which we do when we follow the Holy Communion service. We are joining in a course that has already begun and continues forever and ever. It is, I perceive, to be an ignorant act, to ignore the heavenly words of worship found in the prophets, the psalms Revelation in other places, and to replace those words with contemporary expressions. That does not say that contemporary or extemporaneous expressions are bad or inappropriate. These are helpful as long as they do not replace the heavenly words provided for us in Scripture. To acquiesce our preferences and personal expressions for the words of heavenly creatures and elders around the throne is one way we can Lay down our crowns upon the throne. After all, part of worship is surrender. We surrender ourselves unto God and say, Not my will, but thine be done We surrender by asking the Lord what he would prefer rather than what we prefer. The words of these constant songs speak of God's righteousness. He is holy. They speak of his power. He is almighty. They speak of his eternal nature. He was and is and is to come They speak of his work of salvation. He is worthy. They speak of his ultimate victory. He is to receive glory and honor and power. They speak of his creative and sustaining power. He created all things by his will, and in him they have their being. Such words should be the exact words and themes of our worship in this life, for they are inspired, and as is our worship to be inspired. With this scene, as described by John, it has allowed us, allowed us to do This imagining. Our imagining, however, is inspired. We have been able to peek in on a heavenly service What we find is the answer to why we exist. We exist to worship God, which is the one appropriate response His creation should have to His presence. Worship, true worship of God is wholehearted, awe-inspiring, and loving This scene in the throne room of God establishes a foundation from which the rest of the vision John describes is to flow. Every vision we see from here on out is related back to this scene in heaven of God's people worshiping him. One final thought. One final thought that relates to our purpose to be worshippers is necessary. Some of you have heard this point made. It was asked of me, not by a young college student, but by a mature male, why God would want to be worshipped? Does he have an ego problem? Implied, and the question is whether or not God is on an ego trip when he calls his people to worship him. Such a question reveals how we are limited to think about God in terms of ourselves. We need validation from others, so we speculate that by making his preachers worship him, God needs validation as well. By definition, God needs no validation. We worship God not because He needs it, but because we need it. We need to acknowledge the one who has saved us from ourselves. We need to be used for the purpose He made us. Just as a cup formed from a potter needs to be poured out or poured into, so we too must be worshippers of God. For in doing so we are fulfilling our purpose. What we are made to be. So join the chorus, brothers and sisters in Christ. Join the chorus. The service has already begun, and we are privileged to be a part of it. Sing the words inspired by heaven and fulfill your proper use. Amen. Let us pray.

sermons.title: Ash Wednesday
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. This year marks the 361st anniversary of the 1662 Book of Common Prayer. An edition of said book that was to endure for centuries with little or no modification, and from which of today's Anglican prayer books From Edinburgh to Toronto, from New York to Singapore, from Nairobi to Wellington to the Reformed Episcopal Church descended. 1662 version was descended from the work of Thomas Cramner in the 16th century. Itself a reformed Anglicanized version of the middle midieval Latin used Sorum, which is the Roman Catholic ritual. The sixteen sixty two Book of Common Prayer, which is the closest to the R. E. Book of Common Prayer, includes, for Ash Wednesday, A combination, literally meaning threatening of vengeance, descended from the 1549 Book of Common Prayer on the first day of Lent. This service literally breeds fire. Those of modern taste don't care for it I am keenly aware that the megachurches today that won't curse anything, but insist that God has called them to affirm only Preachers of such perspective don't fear God, but there will be a day when they will be forced to do so. The combination service proceeds to list various sinners the Bible calls accursed. Not just idolaters or cursors of parents, but those who moved their neighbor's landmark as well. Most of us would agree with someone who listed these sins. We would agree that they are bad Those who purposefully divert the blind, adulterers, fornicators, murderers of innocent for profit, those who trust humans rather than God and the rest. But we are to be careful today when we use the word cursed for those who commit these sins as if being cursed for eternity. Only those persons who commit such sins and then cling to such sins without repentance, those are the ones that remain cursed. The purpose of this service, as with much medieval and reformed proclamation of sin, is to call sinners to repentance. No doubt the Mosaic version in Deuteronomy has much the same purpose. Sin is a reality and it has real consequences. That is the point of services right tonight. Part of the purpose of Lent, at least in the Western view, since the Middle Ages, is to repent of our sins. The list of sins taken from the book of Deuteronomy starts off cursing those who make carved images and worship them, because such is a clear breaking of the first two commandments of the Ten Commandments. To curse a father and mother is the breaking of the fifth commandment. To remove a neighbor's landmark is to steal from him, which is taking part of his property and making it your own. To make the blind go out of their way is to not love one's neighbor. To withhold justice from the fatherless and widow is to not only not love one's neighbor, but also not care for the most vulnerable among us. To injure a neighbor secretly is to both lie to God and to hate thy neighbor. To lie with a neighbor's wife is to break the seventh commandment and the tenth commandment. To be paid to harm a neighbor is to love money more than God, and it is also to break the sixth commandment as well as failing at love. To put trust in a man is to break the first commandment and failing to love God. The final curse covers the many perverted and heartless ways One man can harm another, thus breaking all of the commandments. If the list of sins seems a bit much to us, Perhaps that is good. Perhaps we need a reminder of our own wretchedness to use another Book of Common Prayer word. Once we stand face to face with our own depravity, then we can all the more rejoice in God's grace. This is the end goal of healthy medieval and reformed piety. Not for us to spend our lives in sackcloths and ashes. rubbing excrement on our faces like King Priam upon the death of Hector. No, rather it is for us to acknowledge our own brokenness And to turn to the Redeemer for the grace he gives, and to be transformed into his likeness. I find it necessary to draw our attention to just how depraved human beings can be, and then show you how twisted we can become because of that depravity Considering that evil now is good and good is now evil. The evil of Jeffrey Dahmer was recently documented on a popular streaming application Dahmer killed and dismembered at least 17 men and boys between 1978 and 1991. Many of his later murders involve necrophilia, sex with the dead, cannibalism, eating of human flesh. And the permanent preservation of body parts, typically all or part of skeletons. It is said to be one of the highest-view documentaries of all time. People's fascination with Dahmer may be caused by the unbelievability of it all. I only mentioned Dahmer because of the popularity of the documentary. For as you know, there are many, too many examples of men committing evil, vile and inhuman acts against their fellow man, proving just how vile and demon-like human beings can be. What has risen its evil head recently is this trend of adults influencing children to be confused about their gender and sexuality. And then while contributing to that confusion, consenting for a child, a child to go through surgery, resulting in the mutilation of a child's genitals. And thus forever altering the child's body that looks neither male nor female nor functioning as either male or female for the rest of their days. Again, these are children, children who may think themselves as a dog one day while crawling around on all fours. These are children that might fancy themselves one day a girl and another day a horse. These are children who don't know what true sexual desire is and who are needing to be molded to understand what it means to be male or female And they are cursed to have adults in their lives that claim to love the child so much that they want to affirm their child's confusion and immaturity. and affirm it to the point of consenting to genital mutilation. Beloved, such is not love. But is instead demonic deception, revealing the perversions within the adults who express their perversions on their own children. I shared with you via email the email that I was sent as I responded to objections regarding this very subject. I have since received other emails that call me evil. Evil for making a statement of protection for children. Who are subject to their parents' perversions and demonic understanding of the good. I remind you of the words of Jesus again. Then Jesus said to his disciples, It is impossible that no offenses should come, but woe to him through whom they do come. It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea, than that he should offend one of these little ones. The word phrase little ones is another word for children. To offend is to entrap, to trip up, or entice to sin. Can the warning be more clear? Jesus does not want us to come near tempting children towards sin. And encouraging children to follow unabated toward lusts of the flesh, that's sin. If we fail at defending children From such evil we fail our God and we show no faith in him and we deserve to be accursed. Truly we are living in days when evil is called good and good is called evil. Thus, we take this day as an opportunity to be sober regarding our sinful natures and the human proclivity to rebel against God. For those who think this sort of call against sinners is Old Testament only or too medieval or reformed, take note of the list of sinners who will not partake of the kingdom of God according to St. Paul Take a look at Tertullian's work on modesty. Observe Leo the Great's call to sinners. Read the Eastern Greek Mark the Monk, fear of his own salvation despite his life of asceticism. Services such as this are a healthy balance to our joy, not something to abandon because of certain excesses at particular times, places, and traditions. These services are needed. We need to be reminded that there is evil and that there is good. And the only way to stay away from evil is to cling to the good. And the good for us is to repent of our sins against God and believe the blood of Jesus forgives us and saves us for eternity. Amen and amen.

sermons.title: Four Horses
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I do really I truly encourage you to turn to Revelation chapter 6. We're covering verses 1 through 8, and if you're not following along in the scriptures, it will get confusing. So encourage you, Revelation 6, 1 through 8. Up to this point in Revelation, I believe I have not said anything regarding the meaning of the book that is controversial. I have inferred a certain position about the end times, and I know scholars who disagree with my position, but I have not overtly stated it because the text has not required it. That will change today. Before we discuss the breaking of each of the first four seals and the horses that appear in the Revelation as a result of the breaking of the seals, I want to go back and briefly discuss the content of the scroll Be reminded that the scroll taken by the lamb is written on both sides. We said that such description is similar to the Ten Commandments as described in the Book of Exodus That relation means that the scroll contains God's words and thus God's will. It is worth noting that the scroll, even after all of the seals are broken, is never formally read. The content of the scroll is never explicitly revealed. Because each seal reveals a dramatic scene We are to understand the scene and what it symbolizes as God's word or God's will being fulfilled. Thus, the very least we can say is that the scroll contains the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, and the mysteries are revealed with each seal that is broken. Another important point to understand before we begin to understand the meaning of the four horsemen is that nowhere in this chapter is there a reference to time. I point this out because some scholars have interpreted these revealed horses to be successive chronologically, but such an understanding does not come from the text At the end of this sermon, you will understand why it is not necessary to perceive these horses to appear chronologically. After the first seal is opened by the lamb, who is the only one worthy to open the seals of the scroll, immediately the white horse and its rider appear. John takes notice of them after being directed by a living creature around the throne. John had numbered the creatures in chapter 4, and he stays with those numbers. as a reference in his description. The first beast, you remember, had the face of a lion. It is that beast that tells John, Come. The direct to come is emphatic. It is the same cry God uses to call his people to worship. It is the same directive that God uses at his second coming advent when he will tell his bride to come to him. What John is about to see is related to the salvation of the world. It is fitting that that beast with the face of a lion, symbolic of Jesus as the lion of the tribe of Judah. Thunders forth the directive for John to come and behold. White represents purity and is a dominant color in heaven. Horses throughout the Old Testament and in ancient Middle Eastern cultures were symbolic for war. A man who rode a horse toward a city was a man coming in war. Watchmen were instructed to alert authorities in a city if a man were riding toward the city on horses because it was culturally understood that they were coming against the city. A man who came on a donkey, like Jesus did when he entered Jerusalem on Palm Sunday, it meant he was coming in peace. If a man was coming to a city on a white horse, he was doing so to declare victory It was Roman custom for a Roman general or Caesar himself to switch horses after a battle by climbing on a white horse, ride into the city, and declare victory. Remember, Christians, the revelation of John is written not only to describe the victory of Jesus over sin and death, but to declare it. Jesus won the victory at his resurrection. The white horse and its rider are symbolic of the victorious Christ. The psalmist gave a prophecy about this very scene in Psalm 45, where it reads, Gird thy sword on thy thigh, O mighty one. In thy splendor and thy majesty, and in thy right hand teach thee awesome things. Thine arrows are sharp, the peoples fall under thee. Thine arrows are in the heart of the king's enemies. That the rider represents Christ is further clarified by the crown that is upon his head No crown is given to anyone in the book of Revelation that is not thrown back to the one who is worthy to wear the royal symbol. The worthy one is Christ alone. The white horse being revealed first is not chronological, but it's theological. For it proclaims that all that is to come from the next six seals comes under the banner of the victory of Christ. This is a needed message for persecuted Christians in the first century and Christians of every age Who would become anxious over wars, over famines, over pestilence, over persecution, over disease, over pandemics What comes with the next three horsemen does not come outside of or instead of the authority of Christ, but is a reflection of the victory of Christ. These come because Christ is victor. After the second seal is opened, the second living creature that had a face like an ox or cattle instructs John to come His directive is also emphatic. The second horse is described as fiery red. The rider of the horse was given power to take peace from the earth and make men slay one another. To further symbolize his purpose, he wields a large sword. This second horse, this red horse, symbolizes war. We must remember the words of Jesus at this point, saying, I did not come to bring peace, but a sword. Also, he said, he who lives by the sword will die by the sword. Some have interpreted this horse, and others that follow as being evil or a release of the demonic. This is unnecessary and is caused by a false perception of God. Some refuse to acknowledge God as an avenger. But God has always revealed Himself as an avenger. He brought a flood upon the earth because of the evil practiced by men. He rained fire from heaven upon Sodom and Gomorrah because they would not repent. He conquered cities within the promised land, ordering the death of all citizens because they continued to bow in honor of false gods. The horse in red that symbolizes war is a horse that is of God and given power by God to perform the assigned task. It is beneficial to our weak minds and our feeble hearts to know that wars on earth are not outside of God's will. When Christians hid from the wrath of Nero, when they marched against the Muslims, when they put a red coat in their gunsight. When they found shelter from the bombings of the Nazis, when they made their way to the beaches of Normandy, when they fought in the deserts of Iraq and Afghanistan. Each and every one of them had to know that such wars around the world were not outside of God's plan. War can be confusing regarding the cause and objectives, but for Christians, wars always fall under the mysteries of God's kingdom. They are confusing because man is confused in his sin. But such confusion is also a part of God's plan. When the third seal is open, the creature who has a face of a man says to John in the same emphatic way as the other creatures before, Come, he says. The horse that is revealed next is black in color. The rider holds a pair of scales The scales are balancing scales. The scales are used to judge and determine value. Black is typical of woe and mourning. Woe and mourning in this case involves scarcity of food. A voice from the throne, unidentified, announces the price The measure of food was what was allotted to soldiers for a day. Thus, a man can only afford to feed himself from day to day. The cost is too great for a man to feed his family. There will not be enough money to spend or save beyond that which is necessary. The common man will suffer, the poor man will starve. Graciously, there is a restriction placed upon the horse and the rider. They are prohibited from hurting the oil and the wine. The oil is used to make bread and to soothe wounds. The wine is to make glad the hearts of men. Their prohibition is both practical and spiritual, for oil and wine are part of the church's ministry. Oil is used to anoint the sick, and wine is used to remember the poured-out blood of the Savior. Historically, not long after this vision given to John, there was a famine recorded in the region under the reign of Claudius. The famine did not overlook the Christians, as many suffered and hungered, and died. But the famine under Claudius was not the last famine There have been famines all over the world, and Christians, along with non-Christians, have suffered because of lack of food. It is worth noting again that the events symbolized in these horses are not chronological and may actually occur concurrently. War and famine often occur side by side. One may even cause the other. In the history of man, many have suffered because of war and famine. The fourth seal is then broken. Another call to come is made to John by the fourth beast, who we remember to have the face of an eagle. The horse is described as being pale. The Greek word for pale is chloros, literally meaning greenish white. It is a color of a person who is stricken with disease or with death. The Greeks used the word to describe people who were afflicted by a plague. The color is consistent with the name of the one who rides the horse, whose name is death. Directly associated with death is Hades. who in this vision is the dwelling place of the dead personified. We are told that Bay, the Bay meaning death and Hades were given power over a fourth of the earth to kill by sword, famine and plague, and by wild beasts of the earth That death and Hades are restricted to a fourth of the earth is significant for hopefully obvious reasons. First, they are not given authority to judge the whole earth, although the whole earth is worthy of such a judgment. God's grace, exhibited by a restrained hand, is practiced here. Also, the number four is symbolic of the whole earth, as in the four corners of the earth, which you remember is to refer to the earth as an altar to God. These two thoughts together allow us to conclude that death and Hades have authority that is restricted to a fourth of the earth, and the fourth of that earth is spread throughout the globe. Another interesting reference to sight regarding the authority of death and Hades is Ezekiel 14, verse 21. God proclaims through Ezekiel that he will judge Jerusalem by those four dreadful judgments: sword, famine, plague, and wild beasts. These are the same manners of death brought on by the riders of death here listed. The people of Jerusalem were to suffer because of their rebelliousness before God by the four judgments listed by John and receive the description of the four horses The following application then cannot be avoided. In seventy A. D. A little less than 40 years after the death and resurrection of Jesus, the city of Jerusalem was overrun by Roman forces. Thousands of Jews were killed, and many more were thrown out of the city. The temple was desecrated, and Roman forces occupied the holy places as well as the seats of local government. Could the fall of the city of Jerusalem in 70 A. D. be the fulfillment of the prophecy of Ezekiel and the vision of the pale horses? Who rider is death followed by Hades? I believe the answer is yes. I also believe that its fulfillment does not begin and end with the fall of Jerusalem. It is necessary for us to remember the words of our Lord to his disciples When he warned them that they will hear of wars and rumors of wars. Such things will happen, but the end is still to come. He warned that nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be famines and earthquakes in various places. All of these are the beginning of the birth pains, which means the beginning of the end. From the time of Christ's resurrection until today. We could map the wars of men and their outcomes along with the famines that have swept through certain lands There are body counts too numerous for us to comprehend and disease that every culture has struggled to overcome. Each of these periods could be said to be a result of the first four seals having been broken and the release of the four horsemen and the apocalypse. Take, for example, the upheaval in the Iraq War three decades ago When America first engaged Iraq in war in 1991, numerous books were written by Christian communities confirming that Armageddon had begun. What we may call those books now is a fulfillment of Jesus' words, which is wars and rumors of wars. Because these horses of the apocalypse are general in their description, every decade in history is being described by the authority given to these respected writers. Every age of man has consisted of men fighting against and killing one another. Every age has suffered times of famine and disease. Every time there is a war, famine, or disease, death and Hades are present. The four horsemen of the apocalypse. are symbolic of every age of man even before the time of Christ. Take, for example, the time of the plague in the Middle Ages The Christians of that day believed the end of time was at hand, because the four horsemen, the one that was pale, whose rider was deaf, had obviously been released upon them. But such a time was not the end of time. The period of mass deaths eventually ended in Europe and was then followed by wars between Christians and famines again. And famines again. And wars again. So that you are clear about the application of this passage for us, I will be clearer about what I am saying. The first four seals of the scrolls have already been broken. The four horsemen have been released and have practiced their authority since the day of John's vision. Our focus, however, is not to be upon the latter three horses, but upon the one who was first. We are to believe in the one who was in white, who wore the crown and carried the bow. He is the King of Kings and the Lord of Lords. He will come into the revelation again toward the end, claiming to be King of Kings and Lord of Lords. What is to be understood by Christians who were being persecuted in the first century, and Christians from that day until this one, who have been persecuted? Put to death, suffered in war, suffered in famine, suffered in disease, and mourned because of the death in this life. What is to be understood is that all of this is done. In opposition to Christ victorious. It is all coming under the authority of the first horse of the first rider. It is all coming under the authority of Christ as victor. Christians who can wrap their hearts and minds around such a truth will not will not shake a fist at God when a loved one is killed in battle or by disease. Or death that comes to a loved one too early. Such is part of God's plan. All of it comes under his authority. It might not appear so to our perspective, but our perspective be damned. The vision of the four horsemen is not to frighten Christians, but to encourage them. What is painful in this life is a necessary part of God's plan towards our salvation. The white horse and its rider lead the way. Those that follow follow under his authority What we may fear from the vision of these horses are troubles in life that we have experienced. But there is nothing new under the sun. Nothing new under the sun when we f when referring to the troubles of men. What we as Christians are to understand is that all surrender to the white horse and its rider. It's rider who wears a crown. It's rider who carries a bow. It's rider who is victorious now until the end of time. And so we say, No matter what comes our way, thy will be done. Amen. Let us pray. Gracious and heavenly Father, this is truly a vision that is beyond our scope, even beyond our imagination. But it is also a vision that is clear, and that the white horse comes first and the white horse comes last. And he who rides upon it is our Savior and our God. And so it is in his name that we entrust ourselves to you. May Christ, victorious, reign forever. Amen and Amen.

sermons.title: Martyrs Cry
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Turn if you would to Book of Revelation, chapter six. Again, very helpful if you follow along. With me, Revelation chapter six, starting at verse nine. I find motivational speeches to be a fascinating topic. You never know how effectual you can be to a people. Newt Rockney, the well-known football coach of Notre Dame from nineteen eighteen to nineteen thirty Shared with the press one of his halftime speeches that he used to motivate the team to victory. Part of it went as follows. Men We're going inside of them, we're going outside of them, inside of them, outside of them, and when we get them on the run once, we're going to keep them on the run. And we're not going to pass unless their secondary comes up too close. But don't forget, men, we're going to get them on the run. We're going to go, go, go, go. And we aren't going to stop until we go over that goal line. And don't forget, men, today is the day we're going to win. They can't lick us, and that's how it goes. The first platoon men go in there and fight, fight, fight, fight, fight. What do you say, men? Such vigor supposedly inspired the boys to play harder. And I admit to you that there are many sermons that I have suffered over on how to inspire you. I question how my words can move you to strive harder, become more committed, and give your all for Jesus and his message of salvation. We can identify the many different ways we are motivated. The very first motivation is the lowest form, which is fear. I say the lowest in terms of emotion. Other forms of motivation include negatives like greed, revenge, and selfishness. Good forms of motivation include caring for others, gratefulness, and the highest, which is love. But the basic, most fundamental motivation is fear Because it is the most basic, doesn't make it negative. It is very useful as Jesus uses it to start people on the right path. Be reminded of these warnings that cause fear, Jesus said And do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul. Rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Matthew chapter 10 verse 28, Jesus describes the signs of the ends of men seeing fearful sights. Jesus used fear that resulted from his miracles, such as after raising the son of the widow of Nain, Luke says. Then fear came upon all, and they glorified God, saying, A great prophet has risen among us. These examples show that fear motivates But such fear needs to turn into something more substantive, like gratefulness and love. But gratefulness and love might start out with fear. And our passage from Revelation, particularly at the breaking of the sixth seal, what is naturally generated in us is fear, fear of God's wrath And that is a good thing. So let us begin with verse 9 of chapter 6 It reads, When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony which they held. Note that this is the first seal where there is no creature calling out. The souls described are under the altar. Just as the blood sacrificial of sacrificial vis victims slain on the altar was poured and flowed to the bottom of the altar, so the souls of those sacrificed For Christ's testimony, they are symbolically represented as being under the altar in heaven. And what they say is similar to what was said by Abel after being slain by his brother Cain for blood, often represented as crying for vengeance. These martyrs were slain because of their commitment to the Word of God and for what they believed, which is called their testimony. The Word of God was both personified in the person of Jesus, as well as being written the written word, which at the time of John would have at least been the four Gospels. To say they held the testimony means they did not deny it when confronted, and their fate was at stake. Beloved, holding on to the faith, regardless of what happens in your life, is just as important as confessing Jesus as Savior and Lord the first time. Holding on to your testimony may be the hardest thing you will do in life. And today it seems to be a popular thing to let go. The coach in me comes out when I come to passages such as this because I want every Christian to hold on. To hold on to the very end of your days, because your days are short and full of evil, and the reward is everlasting. So hold on. Verse 10. And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, until you judge and avenge our blood on these who dwell on the earth? The first words of the martyrs is giving honor to the one true God who is holy and true. Again, the martyrs speak as able, for their blood is crying out for vengeance. And this is a surprise to some who only view being in the presence of God, being in heaven. to be a peaceful place and a place where you're you're simply grateful with certainly no concern for vengeance. But justice, justice is a holy thing, and it must be satisfied. And Jesus made it clear. That murderers who don't repent will experience weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth. Vengeance is the Lord's, and he promises it will be accomplished. Verse eleven. Then a white robe was given to each of them, and it was said to them that they should rest a little while longer, until both the number of their fellow servants and their brethren Who would be killed as they were was completed. The white robes symbolize the holiness given to them because of the sacrifice of Christ Jesus And because of their faithfulness to that sacrifice, even faithfulness unto death, the call to wait a little longer Is understood in the context of a day being as a thousand years and a thousand years as a day from God's perspective What they are to wait for is those fellow servants who will join these early martyrs by facing their own deaths while holding on to the Word of God and holding on to their testimony. Such a number is still to be added to. The voice of the martyrs is an organization worth being informed by in order to pray for those who suffer in this present day And an organization to donate to for those who are struggling to hang on to their testimony. When you consider that one of the seven seals was Opened only for the sake of the martyrs reveals how important they are in the sight of God. Verse 12. I looked when he opened the sixth seal, and behold, there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black as sackcloth, a sackcloth of hair, and the moon became like blood. It will serve us well to keep in mind the parallel imagery of the Old Testament. The shaking was spoken of by the prophet Haggai, who said, Yet once for all shake I not the earth only, but also the heavens. And the phrase once for all signifies the removing of things that are shaken. As for the sun turning black as sackcloth, the prophet Joel had a similar thought. He said, the sun shall be turned into darkness. And the prophet Isaiah, I clothe the heavens with blackness and I make sackcloth their covering. The moon as blood is also repeated by the prophet Joel. Verse 13. And the stars of heaven fell to the earth as a fig tree drops its late figs when it is shaken by a mighty wind. The falling of stars of heaven has a parallel in Isaiah, who said, All the hosts of heaven shall be dissolved. The fig tree analogy works, but it is expanded in our minds to imagine what type of wind would have to blow for stars to fall from heaven. Verse 14. Then the sky receded as a scroll when it is rolled up, and every mountain and island was moved out of its place. This verse also is a reflection of Isaiah chapter 34, which reads, All the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the heavens shall be rolled up like a scroll. All their host shall fall down as the leaf falls from the vine and as fruit falling from a fig tree. Having an idea that we might try to have of what it takes to create mountains, to have them moved from their place Would be a disruption of everything we know about on this earth and its inhabitants. Perhaps this is the beginning of a new heaven and a new earth. Verse 15. And the kings of the earth, the great men, the rich men, the commanders, the mighty men, every slave and every free man hid themselves in the caves and in the rocks of the mountains. John is able to reflect on who could stand in the midst of such upheaval of nature and not be scared out of his mind Scared for his present state and a future that has a darkened sun and a blood moon, a starless sky and mountains displaced. Will kings stand in place? Will great men stand in place? Will rich men stand in place? Will commanders stand in place? Will mighty men stand in place? No, no. They will be joined with the slave and free men And hiding themselves and covering themselves to shield themselves from the realities that they are witnessing. Verse 16 And said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who sits on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb. Here we have them hiding and hoping to be crushed. To be crushed rather than face what changes the earth is going through. But it is here we learn that it isn't the changes of the earth that scare them. They hide and they cow And they would ask for death because of the fate of him who sits on the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb. Beloved, as we come to this final verse in of the chapter, I allow myself to share my motivation. I spoke about being motivated by fear, and I believe verse seventeen is calling us to be motivated by the fear of God's wrath. It reads, For the great day of his wrath has come, and who is able to stand? It is the lack, it is the lack of fear, fear of God, a lack of fear of God's wrath That I believe has steered our culture into the ditch which we now lie. In historian Tom Holland's book titled Dominion, He carefully argues the dramatic difference Christianity has meant to the world. Whereas the world before Christianity celebrated might makes right And the idea of fate being the causal factor of the weak being weak and the poor being poor, Christianity in opposition says the opposite. The weak are to be treated as strong. The poor are to be understood as wealthy. The wealthy are to be understood as dead in spirit The mighty are to be seen as weak spiritually. God now favors the poor in spirit. God favors the meek. Such teaching was so radical that it literally shook up the world. It changed how cultures treat the weak, treat the poor, treat the needy, treat the sick. It became virtuous to treat the poor and the needy and the disenfranchised with dignity and respect. Because of Christian doctrine and belief, the minority in societies became a priority. No other culture before the ascent of Christianity cared about the minority. Such is factual and well documented. But there is a problem. And it has labeled itself woke. We know the devil's tactics. They are scripted, they are predictable. He takes the truth and sprinkles it with a falsehood and confuses many. So there is the truth of caring for the least among us and seeing such care as virtuous, and the devil takes that truth. A truth Christianity has revealed and sprinkles it with the falsehood so that it is a corrupt understanding of the world. So now instead of the least among us being the poor and the fatherless or the widow or the sick or the lame, the woke tells us that the least among us should be included with the sexually immoral. And the sexually confused, and the gender confused. When I taught at the university several years ago now I tried to introduce the concept of absolute morality, which is simply the acceptance that there is a right and that there is a wrong. There is good and there is evil. There is moral and there is immoral. And when doing so, I tried to find an act that a human being could do that we all, teacher and student, could agree was immoral or evil. And I asked the students if we could agree, all agree, that being sexual with a child pedophilia was immoral. I would guess that half of the class agreed visually with me shaking their heads, and the rest of the class showed no emotion or no nonverbal response. And that struck me as odd until I read of a movement in modern psychiatry that wants to relabel people. Who are identified as pedophiles to be minor attractive persons, so as to lessen the stigma of such persons. So, as to lessen that stigma, relabeling them from the perspective of modern psychiatry for the purpose of caring about the minority. My point is that the devil has done a masterful job at taking what is good and holy within the Christian gospel, which is caring for the least in societies. And relabeling the least among us to be the immoral. And I explain all of this to argue That none of this would be possible in our culture or any culture that has a proper understanding of the wrath of God, and because of that wrath, a proper fear of God. The answer to how a culture can withstand the lies of the devil and the relabeling of evil versus the good is to have a proper fear of God's wrath. The answer to how a family can keep marriages intact and keep children from walking away from Christ Jesus and his church is to have a proper fear of God's wrath. The answer to how you, as individual persons, can remain faithful to Jesus in your personal behavior and your confessed faith is to have a proper fear of God's wrath. While it is true that a mature Christian faith would move you to more than just fearing God's wrath, But to loving Jesus and his sacrifice and his mercy towards you, you will always need to have a healthy fear of God's wrath. Such a need for a fear of God's wrath is why I have such a disdain for songs Christians sing that present Jesus as a boyfriend. Or pictures of Jesus that paint him as effeminate. And while I understand the need for Jesus to be seen as approachable For we all need to approach our Savior, bearing our hearts, bearing our souls to him. He must be also at the same time that we see him as approachable. He must be understood. By us to carry the wrath of God with him. And so I point our attention back to verse 16. I have been referring to the wrath of God at this point in the sermon, but it is important to remind you that the wrath of God is actually the wrath of the Lamb. The Lamb is the one from whom the wrath of God will come, and so we have the greatest of ironies before us. The weakest, the least frightening of any animal is to be feared because of his coming wrath. Thus we have before us as our focus of worship the approachable God who calls us to come to Him and to trust Him and to be comforted by Him while at the same time fearing Him So much that we would rather have rocks fall upon us than to be suffering under his divine judgment. John Dunn had been appointed Dean of St. Paul's Cathedral in London in 1621. Rather than fleeing the city as the bubonic plague ravaged its citizens, he remained and devoted himself to preaching and ministering to the flock. When Dunn became ill himself, he was certain it was the plague. That's when his wrestling with God began. Although he had earned a doctorate in divinity degree, a doctorate of divinity degree from Cambridge, served as a minister, questions of fear tormented him. Dunn's wrestling ended up focusing on fear. He knew how much the Bible spoke about not giving in to fear. As Moses led the Israelites out of Egypt, and later when he gave them the Ten Commandments, he admonished them not to fear. God's message to Joshua was to be strong and courageous and not to fear. David said that he would fear no evil. The prophets repeatedly exhorted the people not to be given to fear, reminding them that God was with them. In the face of invading armies, God sent messengers who delivered his assurance. Do not fear, do not be dismayed. But knowing all of this didn't relieve Dunn's fear of suffering and dying. Finally, Dunn identified the antidote to his fear. The antidote was in the fact of another form of fear, that is the fear of God. The formula is simple. Resist all other forms of fear by embracing the one necessary fear. This led Dunn to pen a devotion on the right fear, and part of his prayer in that devotion goes as follows. Give me, O Lord, a fear of which I may not be afraid. The truth in such a prayer Is that the fear of God relieves us from all other fears? Let us pray. A gracious and heavenly Father, for this vision of the broken sixth seal We ask that you would give us that healthy sense of fear that always puts us before you, humble, that always puts us before you ready to worship, that always puts us before you obedient. May that fear always be with us until you return. In Jesus' name we pray.

sermons.title: 144 Thousand
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We are looking at Revelation chapter 7, verses 1 through 8. Always helpful to follow along, making sure your pastor doesn't slip up, keeping him accountable. We talked about uh Jehovah's Witnesses in Sunday school, and so it's appropriate that we bring them up again. If you have ever entertained a Jehovah's Witness at your door and engage them in conversation You likely have heard about the 144,000 who will make it to heaven In modern times, the Jehovah's Witnesses have identified themselves with the number one hundred and forty four thousand The Jehovah's Witnesses faith is fairly young, beginning in the late nineteenth century under the leadership of a man named Charles Russell. It found footing in America in the early 20th century under the leadership of a man who went by the name Judge Rutherford. The primary distinction between Jehovah's Witnesses and Christianity is that Jehovah's Witnesses deny the Trinity, the doctrine of the Trinity, and deny the idea of eternal damnation. They believe that 144,000 people exactly will spend eternity in God's heavenly kingdom while the rest of us will continue on this earth Said doctrine is based on the passage we have before us from Revelation chapter 7. Let me dispel any possibility that we will come to the same conclusion. We discussed last week that the calamity described at the end of chapter six after the breaking of the sixth seal was part of the response God had to the question posed to him by the revealed martyrs after the breaking of the fifth seal. They asked, how long? How long would it be before there was vengeance taken upon those who were responsible for their death? A little longer, the Lord said. That answer was followed up by a description of a catastrophic end to the world as we know it. And The rhetorical question remains, who can stand?
