The words that begin chapter seven indicate that there is an interlude between the breaking of the sixth seal and the breaking of the seventh That interlude sets up a dramatic pause, causing the reader to anticipate the breaking of the seventh seal even more. The chapter begins with after this, which is a short phrase, but important to distinguish what he saw after the sixth seal and what he is currently seeing. The next vision begins with the appearance of four angels standing on the four corners of the earth. Let me remind you that the earth was not believed to be flat This is a reference to the four corners of the earth, granting two analogies. The earth, as you know, has four directions, north, east, south, and west, associating it with a compass. or four corners. The earth is also referred to as an altar upon which God is worshipped and served, and the altar in the temple had four corners. The angel standing at the four corners, do the bidding of God, God Almighty, who of course is depicted as reigning over his creation. We are given no description of the angels other than that their posture and their responsibility. They are standing and they are holding back before winds of the earth which is to say the winds that come from the four markers of the compass. They are there to prevent the wind from blowing upon the land, the sea, or any tree. And blowing upon them for destruction. The Bible consistently uses trees to describe men, as in Psalm 1 Where a righteous man is described as one who is like a tree planted by the waters, who yields fruit in good season. Thus, the reference here of a tree is likely to say that the wind will not blow upon land, sea, or men. The world described here is much different than the one seen at the breaking of the sixth seal. With the sky being rolled up, stars falling from the sky, mountains laid low and islands being moved. There is nothing from the breaking of the sixth seal but upheaval and chaos. Here Chapter 7, the winds are held back. Calm is brought to the world. Calm is enabled by the sovereign rule of God. And you will remember Jesus holding up his hand and calming the seas, and at doing so his disciples knew that he had the power of God. While the devil brings confusion and chaos, God brings peace and calm. After calm is brought to the earth, John sees another angel. This is one, this one is also not identified, but his actions are Christ-like. He comes from the east, just as Jesus said he would do at his return to the earth He promised he would come on a cloud of glory splitting the eastern sky. As the angel comes, John notices that he has a seal of the living God. The seal is not like the one on the scroll. Our English translations are sometimes too simple to reveal the differences. A seal in this context signifies power, guaranteed protection, and a mark of God's ownership The seal that the angel bears is one that marks what is owned by the true and living God. This is as opposed to those who mark themselves for the sake of their pagan gods. We see such markings continuing today as people tattoo themselves with all sorts of cultural icons. The purpose of this marking by the angel is hinted to is hinted to in the instruction by the angel. who is coming up from the east and says to the other angels, Do not harm the land or sea or trees until we put a seal on the foreheads of the servants of God. Because it is harm that the seal is to protect God's people from, that recalls Ezekiel 9, our Old Testament reading. where God commissions executioners to destroy everyone in the city. But first, he commands another angel to go through the city and put a mark on the foreheads of the men who have sighed and groaned over the sins that were being committed in their midst. Thus the godly were marked for protection so that their fellow citizens might be destroyed. And we stop here to examine our Old Testament reading, allowing its context to inform us. The prophet Ezekiel, you will recall, was a prophet to Israel during the exile to Babylon. Israel had committed acts of idolatry over and over again, so much so that God finally allowed the Babylonians to overrun the great city And take into captivity the king of Israel and his court while also destroying the city and the holy temple. With the many people taken from Israel and made slaves to the Babylonians, there were few left behind, and even fewer. left behind or in captivity that were living faithfully to the Lord. Ezekiel's audience was primarily his fellow exiles living in Babylon. And his primary rebuke was to those in exile who had conformed their lives to be similar to the lives of their captors. Which meant that they took on the sins of their captors, which meant they continued in their idolatrous ways. Such behavior is a temptation for every generation of God's people. Christians, whether conscientiously or not. can easily take on the morals and behaviors of their unbelieving neighbors to the point of living no differently than their neighbors. In similar ways of the days when Israel was in captivity under the Babylonians, so Christians today are captive to the secular world. You know the drill, you know the story. Where once public schools opened each day with a prayer to God in the name of Jesus Today, every religion is mentioned in the classroom except Christianity. Whereas Christian morality such as Heterosexual marriage, abstinence, not bearing false witness, not stealing, not coveting, were upheld as standards to live by So now sexual immorality is taught as a norm. And lying, stealing, and coveting are acceptable. Well Because life isn't fair, and somehow because life isn't fair, it makes such behavior acceptable. But morally lying down and adopting such standards is not acceptable to God. It was not acceptable in the days of Ezekiel, nor is it acceptable today under the banner of Christ Jesus. Again, in Ezekiel chapter 9, the prophet tells of a vision he was given of the city of Jerusalem. It is a vision of judgment against those who insisted on their idolatrous ways. God had convicted them of their wrongdoing. God had given them warning after warning again and again. God had called them to repentance again and again, and still the people insisted on rebelling against him and behaving like the unbelieving people around them. There is a time when God's patience ends. He is, as he said he is, long-suffering. He takes no pleasure in judging sinners. But there is a time and there is a place where justice must be practiced. For if it is not, it is not justice. But before that justice is handed out, God does something for those who have remained faithful. He marks them so that they do not suffer As stated in verse 4 of Ezekiel 9, a man clothed with linen is instructed to mark the forehead of each person who laments about the sins of the people of the city. Such people, by their emotional expressions, reveal that they care. They care about the sins committed by their fellow citizens. And they mourn the fact that God is not honored as he should be. You know, I say to you, there was a time a few years ago. Where I was so sick and tired of hearing about the sins of our culture on the television, on the radio, that I thought just leave them to themselves. If they want to abort their children, let them abort their children. Commit acts of sodomy, let him commit acts of sodomy, whatever. Just let them let them go to it. But here God is marking those who lament the sins of the people around them. He is telling us to care about the people around you. That they are sinning against God, dishonoring Him, should be lamented not because just because they're hurting God, but because they're hurting themselves. And we should care. The marking of the forehead, both in Ezekiel 9 and in Revelation 7, is also a reminder of the marking of the high priest. The high priest whose forehead was marked with gold letters, proclaiming that he is holy to the Lord. From these two Old Testament accounts, we may say that the seal in revelation given to the servants of God marked their protection and marked their status as holy to the Lord. But you might be thinking, it says that only 144,000 received the mark. Well, no. No. The number 144,000 is a symbolic number representing all of God's people. You will recall that we interpreted the 24 elders around the throne of God to be representative of the 12 tribes of Israel and the 12 tribes of, or excuse me, the 12 apostles of Jesus. And combining the two, representing all of God's people, Old and New Testament. So 12 plus 12 equals 24, and 12 times 12 is 144. Add to that the fact that John in his revelation doesn't use a number larger than the word thousands. Meaning he doesn't use millions or billions to represent a large number. He only uses thousands. Then we are given this number, 144,000. To be symbolic, to represent the multitude of God's people. And if you look at verse 9, which we'll get to next week, it's further confirmed for God for John looks again and sees a great multitude that no one could number. 144,000 representing that number that no one could count. So God marks his people. And if you are a part of God's people, God has marked you. And He has marked you for two reasons. The same two reasons. He marks you to protect you from the wrath to come, and he marks you to declare that you are holy to the Lord. God has a thing for marking and protecting. He marks Cain so that no other man would be free to have vengeance on him. He marked Abraham and his descendants with a sign of circumcision so as to symbolize his covenant with his people by way of the male organ. From which the seed would come and come forth the Messiah. God had the homes of his people marked by blood, painted over their doorposts, so as to protect them from the angel of death. And with the new covenant, Jesus practiced and Paul taught us that baptism is the new circumcision So that those who have been baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost have been sealed, marked for eternal salvation. Our tradition allows us to acknowledge that marking in baptism when the priest takes that consecrated water and gives the sign of the cross. On the forehead of those who have been baptized. And we who remember that at certain times and places in our services. Give the sign of the cross to be reminded that we have been marked by God. But how can your life be affected now with the knowledge that God has marked you? What difference should that make? I know of parents who created their own catechism where they would provide identity for their children. In order to prepare them to face the world that will tempt them to deny their faith in Jesus and conform them to their morality, the morality of their peers. Such catechism could sound something like this. Let's say that there's a little Eric Jorgensen running around. He would be asked, what is your Christian name? Answer, my Christian name is Eric William Jorgensen. Question, and who gave you that name? Answer. My parents at my baptism. Question, what does Jorgensen mean? Answer. Jorgensen means son of George, named after St. George. Question, and who was St. George? Answer. St. George was a slayer of dragons. Question. And who is the great dragon in the Bible? Answer: Satan. Satan is the great dragon in the Bible. Question, and being a son of George, who are you to slay? Answer: I am to be a slayer of Satan and his works Question. And what are Satan's works? Answer. Satan's works are disobeying God, teaching falsehood, and tempting men toward evil. Question, and how do you slay such works? Answer: I slay such works by obeying God, believing truth, and loving my fellow man. The hope with such catechism is to provide such a strong identity within a child. That it would be strange, a strange thing for him or her to behave in a different manner than the identity given him or her. Thus, in the same way, we can take on the identity Jesus gives to us by his marking of us, and with that identity live as becomes that identity. And as our culture has recently proved, if we don't receive our identity from the marking Jesus has placed upon us, we will be told from where our identity comes. And some of you know there is a part of our culture that is obsessed with identity. They want to insist on an identity that puts their sexual desires first. Their preferred gender next, followed by their preferred pronouns, with a spastic expectation that everyone follow their identity demands. But such persons are self-identified, and therefore they can ignore what others see about their identity and live in their own reality. But a Christian's identity is given to them. It is God who marks us. It is God who calls us to own that marking It is God who labels us holy to the Lord. And that identity is to be known to us, so connected to us, that it'd be a strange thing to not live according to it. And so this morning I ask you to join me. Turn in our Prayer book prayer books. Turn in your prayer books to page five hundred eighty-three. We do this every year, but we're doing it a little off schedule this year. We're only going to be doing the first four questions, 583, a catechism. Question. What is your name? Answer? Question Who gave you this name? Answer? Question What did your sponsors then do for you? Answer. It is not really earth and counts the devil and all the words, God and the safety world, and all the simple thoughts of the flesh. And we should believe all our same all Jesus Christ. Question, do you not think that you are bound to believe and to do as they have promised for you? Answer. Yes indeed, my God, and I am getting after the power that can be all into the state of salvation. And all of God's people said, Amen

sermons.title: The God Who Saves
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We're looking at Revelation chapter seven, picking up at verse nine. Revelation seven. Picking up at verse 9, and I begin the question. Of course, you answer this to yourself: what Do you praise God for today? Why did you come to Sunday morning worship? I have been involved in Christian churches that will use Sunday morning worship as a time of testimony sharing. Testimony sharing is when a minister or song leader asks the people of the congregation If there was anything they would like to share with the rest of the congregation regarding what God has been doing in their life Some testimonies were quite emotionally moving. Others were quite, well, long. There were actually services where the minister decided not to preach his prepared sermon because the testimonies had taken up so much time In the denomination I served for a few years, it was common for the preacher to allow testimonies to supplant his sermon. Serving my first year in said church, I was told about such services where the testimonies dominated the service. And parishioners would describe it as being wonderful that the preacher didn't have to preach. These comments were stated before I was scheduled to preach, and I always wondered whether there was an implied message. In my three years pastoring in that denomination and at the local church where I served, no testimony supplanted my sermon. But you assume that already And I hope you don't feel that you want testimonies to replace my sermons, but even if you did, well, I would still preach. But back to my original question. What do you praise God for today? During the services dominated by testimonies, inevitably someone would stand up and thank the Lord for his or her salvation. I thank the Lord that he saved me. And when I first heard such a testimony, I truly did think to myself, come on, that's an easy one. Anyone can testify about how thankful they are for his or her salvation. Let's hear some of the dramatic stuff. Let's, you know, get really get really honest here. I thought about those simple testimonies while studying this end of chapter 7 in the book of Revelation Because of the content of the song that is sung by the great multitude standing before the throne and in front of the Lamb. The content of the songs and proclamations in this chapter should be the reason why we praise God today, and every day we gather for worship. Before we get into specifics of the song sung, we need to establish who these people are that are beginning singing. Last week I proposed that the number 144,000 was a symbolic number symbolizing all of God's people under both the old and new covenants. You will remember the number 144,000 is the result of 12 representing the tribe of Israel And twelve, representing the twelve apostles, multiplied together and expressed in terms of a multitude or thousands. What we pointed to last week that affects our interpretation of verse 9 this week is that John heard the number 144,000. He heard it. He did not see the people and count them off one by one, counting all the way to 144,000. What happens in verse 9, which is the same vision that began in verse 1 of chapter 7, is after John hears 144,000, he then sees It reads, after this hearing, I looked, and there before me was a great multitude that no one could count. From every nation, tribe, people, and language standing before the throne and in front of the Lamb Because of the symbolism of 144,000 being heard and the subsequent seeing that John does after hearing I propose that the great multitude he sees is the same multitude that he hears is numbered. This multitude consisted of so many people that no one could count the number. But that statement is not made in an absolute sense. When saying no one could count, he does not mean that the number was not definite It most certainly is definite, for God knows whose are his, and he knows us in every way. Instead, it is a description like the one promised to Abraham. When God said to Abraham that he would have descendants greater than the sands of the seashore and greater than the stars of the heavens. Those numbers are greater than a man can count. And I want to take opportunity now to explain once again. The importance of noting the similarity between the described fulfillment of God's covenant here in Revelation and the one promised to Abraham. I have said numerous times that I do not believe that the Bible speaks or treats the salvation of the Jewish race separately from that of the Gentiles. This separation of salvation has been popularized in past years, and I do believe it has an effect upon the church, and that effect is not benign. When God promised Abraham a number of descendants that could not be counted, he was not speaking about descendants of Abraham's loins. Although that is what some Jews and even some Christians believe. The Apostle Paul could not have stated this doctrine more plainly. Than he did in his words to the church at Rome, found in chapter four chapter four, beginning at verse thirteen, and they read It was not through the law that Abraham and his offspring received the promise that he would be heir of the world, but through the righteousness that comes by faith. For if those who live by the law are heirs, faith has no value and the promise is worthless. Therefore, the promise comes by faith, so that we may be by grace and may be guaranteed to all Abraham's offspring, not only those who are of the law, but also those who are of the faith. The faith of Abraham. He is the father of us all. As it is written, I have made you a father of many nations. The Apostles' words state plainly that Abraham's offspring are a people of faith. Whether we are Jew or Gentile, we are all one in Christ Jesus because we have the same faith. John's description of the multitude being from every nation, tribe, people, and language makes perfect sense in line of the faith of Abraham, for that brings us all together. The description of the multitude is also the fulfillment of what God set out to do when he sent his son. We know the verse well, John 3. 16. God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believes in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. God's love for the world was further seen in his command to his disciples to go throughout all the world and preach the gospel, baptizing those who believed. It was also his promise that he would not return, not return until the gospel had been preached to all nations Thus, the description of every tribe, people, and tongue present in heaven in Revelation 7 is a fulfillment of John 3:16. The multitude is described as wearing white robes and holding palm branches. This would have been a good sermon for next week. The white robes are the same as those worn by the martyrs under the altar in chapter 6, who were revealed after breaking that fifth seal. The white represents purity and holiness, and by wearing white, the multitude is said to be as worthy as their exalted Savior who wears the same white. The branches, like the ones waved as Christ entered Jerusalem on a donkey five days before his death, and a week before his resurrection. Symbolize a restoration of God's people, a restoration to paradise where Christ Jesus reigns as King. In verse 13, one of the elders that sits around the throne asks John to identify the multitudes in white robes. Who are they? And where did they come from? He asks. John, not knowing, acquiesces to the elder, who informs him that the multitude consists of those who came out of the Great Tribulation. Now the punctuation in the New King James Version helps us understand what is meant by coming out of the Great Tribulation. It means that they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. A natural explanation confuses us because blood cannot make a garment white. Christ's blood, however, is a blood that was innocent. It was the blood of a perfect man, and thus a perfect sacrifice, making all who would accept his sacrifice to be clean from their sin. Because blood represents sacrifice and forgiveness, and white represents purity and righteousness, those who washed themselves in the blood of Christ were made pure and righteous, and thus white as snow. Though your sins are scarlet, said the prophet, I will make them whiter than snow. By referring to the multitude as coming out of the Great Tribulation, we must not perceive them as separate from the martyrs revealed in chapter 6. nor separate from the Christians who have suffered and preserved in the faith up to and through today. The purpose of the description is once again for the comfort of those first century Christians and all that follow. That God rewards them for their faithfulness, and he will reward all who remain faithful to the end of their days. Because God has rewarded the faithful. Their response is one of praise, of worship, and it is the words, the words in their praise that I wish to focus on this morning. The multitudes are the first to cry out. We are not told whether this is a song set to a tune, so apparently it doesn't matter. The words, the words that they sing are what is most important. From verse 10, salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne and to the Lamb. Their words focus on the salvation that God brings through the Lamb. The Lamb that represents the sacrifice of Jesus They praise God for their salvation. These words are followed by those of the angels and elders and four living creatures around the throne. They all fall face down and then say, Amen, praise and glory and wisdom and thanks and honor and power and strength be to our God forever and ever. Those words are in response to praise given to God simply for salvation. They describe the God who saves. The final words of this scene are spoken by the elder who asked John to identify the multitude. His words describe the salvation of the multitude. He says, they are before the throne and serve him day and night in his temple. Never again will they hunger, never again will they thirst. The lamb will be their shepherd. God will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Such words describe the salvation that the multitude will experience. And together, the three cries of praise consist of praising God for salvation, describing Him as the one who saves, and describing what it means to be saved. These cries take us back to my description of the testimonies people give in churches regarding their salvation. When I ask or describe it as easy, it is actually to do so, to stand up and give testimony to your salvation is the most profound thing that you can do. Think of it this way. All other testimonies we give, whether we be praising God for our daily bread. Or for our spouse, or for our children, or for our job, etc. , etc. And none of such things match up to the salvation we have in Christ. Because all those things are in this life. Even those things we call miracles, such as a healing from a debilitating and even malignant disease. Does not compare to our salvation. And please don't misunderstand me. God is to be praised when He answers prayers. regarding our daily sustenance, regarding even miracles that save lives. But all of these concern such things that occur in this life, and in this life we are just passing through The words of praise, the cries of the multitude, and the testimonies of God's people in heaven do not consist of words regarding a new job, a good report from the doctor. They contain descriptions of our salvation. So perhaps we need to rehearse in our mind why salvation is so important. God created an earth on which people could live in paradise. But man, represented in Adam and Eve, chose to rebel against God. The sin of man meant that the justice and wrath of Almighty God, who was holy and righteous, had to be satisfied Man was forced to offer blood sacrifice and have his days cut short upon the earth because he was not worthy to be in the presence of the one, true, holy, and living God. The Bible tells us that because of the rebellion of angels and the sin of man, a place called hell was created by God to punish for all eternity those who have rebelled against him. When God looked upon the world, he found none that were righteous, not one. If left to ourselves, eternal damnation would be our destination. The description of weeping, wailing, and gnashing of teeth would be for us to experience were not for the moment God satisfied himself taking on the punishment that we deserved. The only thing that satisfies him is perfection. And because we are not perfect of our own device, eternal damnation is what we deserve. What argument, what explanation or justification could be presented to Almighty God that would stop him from casting us into eternal lake of fire to join the devil and his angels? What explanation? What justification? This is why the revelator Johns asked the question, who can stand? No one. No one can stand. What we have just described is what we are saved from And we have only touched on the punishment of hell and generalities. There are specifics to the punishment perhaps specified to each sin that will be experienced by those who do not willfully bend the knee to the King of Kings. And the Lord of Lords. There's also described in brief what we are saved to experience. The saved will have eternal purpose, as there will be no questions such as, why am I here, or what is my purpose? We exist to serve God The saved will never hunger or thirst, but will be forever provided for. The heat of the day or the cold of the winter will not be a concern. What Adam and Eve were barred from having access to will be ours to eat, to drink. And finally, there will be no reason to shed a tear This is the salvation awaiting the multitude that remains faithful to the Lord Jesus Christ. So I began this sermon by asking you why you came this morning. What do you praise God for today? We, of course, have a multitude of things to give God praise for in this life. But what we should always give praise for, what we should always be at the forefront of our thoughts, and the first thing on our lips in our praise to God is for our salvation. The multitude, praise God for salvation. The multitude is us. Let him be praised because he has saved us in Christ Jesus Amen. Let us pray

sermons.title: Silence
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. He be seated. Turn in your Bibles to Revelation chapter eight. We'll be walking through verses one through five. I freely confess today that interpreting this book, the Book of Revelation, gets difficult from here on out. If you think it has been difficult thus far, chapters one through seven will soon seem like grammar school. And as the difficulty increases, we must pull out those cliches that motivate us. If it was easy, everyone would do it If it wasn't hard, it wouldn't be worth doing. When the going gets tough, the tough get going. I warn you of the tough road ahead because I want you to work at staying with me. I don't want you to be discouraged if it does not all come together in your mind. Remember that there is a great reward promised to us, to anyone who would hear and understand the prophecies written in this book. Many scholars have spent the majority of their lives trying to understand the truths in this book. Our understanding will only increase the more we keep at it. We are dependent on both reason and revelation when we study this book. Reason is needed to pull together passages of Scripture from other books of the Bible. Helping us make sense of the vision John is describing. Reason also helps us make decisions as to whether a passage should be understood symbolically Or literally, or both. We often use reason without realizing what we are doing because it comes naturally to us when we put thoughts together. My favorite question asked of me while teaching logic, and it was asked seemingly every year. When I would explain how to identify the rules of logic in an argument, a student would inevitably raise his hand with all sincerity and ask the ubiquitous question, when are we going to use all of this stuff? To which I would regularly reply, obviously you're not using it right now. We do use this stuff. We necessarily use logic and reason Hopefully often, and it is needed when we study Holy Scripture. Revelation, not the book, but the guiding of the Holy Spirit, is necessary because the Holy Spirit reveals truths that we cannot see. Reason helps us put together what has been revealed. Without revelation, we would have nothing to put together. Revelation takes us beyond our reason to see things that cannot be seen by the human eye, but only by the Holy Spirit. So let us now depend on reason and revelation to understand the book of Revelation. Remember That we treated Chapter 7 as an interlude between the breaking of the sixth seal and the seventh seal Chapter 6 described the climactic end of the world as we know it after the breaking of the sixth seal. Chapter 7 describes the multitude that no one could count surrounding the throne, giving praise to God for their salvation. Chapter 8 connects us back to chapter 6 as it describes the breaking of the seventh seal and its results. Revelation is needed to understand this passage in the book of Revelation because my reason leads me to anticipate that the breaking of the seventh seal would bring everything together. The scroll had seven seals, and the opening of the seventh seal would naturally bring about the end. After all, the world came to a cataclysmic end at the breaking of the sixth seal. I expected the breaking of the seventh seal would reveal the content of the scroll And the end of time and the beginning of eternity. That does not happen. What happens is a new series of events that are marked by the blowing of seven trumpets. With the description of the trumpets, we now enter the tricky zone. With the trumpets being blown, we have a new catastrophe coming upon the earth, with each one blown. This causes us to conclude that the breaking of the seals and the blowing of the trumpets are not chronologically in succession. They cannot be. If the catastrophic end of the earth was described after the breaking of the sixth seal, there could not be more catastrophes to come. There are, according to my reason, two alternative interpretations. Either the description of the destruction of the earth in chapter 6 was not as grand as I thought Or the events described in accordance with the seven trumpets overlap the events described at the breaking of the seven seals. Because the wrath of God is described in chapter 6 as universally cataclysmic, I must conclude the latter. The events that follow the blast of each of the seven trumpets overlap the events of the breaking of the seven seals. As we begin examining the first five verses of chapter 8, we would be helped to keep this in mind. So after the seventh seal is open, we are told that there was silence in heaven for about a time of about a half an hour. The pause is a dramatic one and relates to several instances in the Bible The instruction of God through the prophet to be still and to know that he is God comes to mind, to be quiet. The question Jesus posed to his disciples in the garden regarding prayer also comes to mind. Can you not wait and pray an hour? Here is half of that hour, and is fitting as the silence relates to the prayers of God's people symbolized by the incense. Some commentators propose that the silence relates to the time when the high priest entered the Holy of Holies during their service within the temple proper. Others say it describes the peace of God brought upon by all of the creation. The silence certainly could refer to these, but the connection the silence has to the prayers of God's people and the trumpets that will be blown are the most important detail to help us interpret this meaning. When we think of trumpet blasts, we think of royalty. Trumpets were and are used to announce royalty. When exalted praise is given to God in the Psalms, trumpets are usually naturally used. Trumpets were not used only for royalty, but for battle as well. Recall the scene at Jericho when God's people were commanded to go around the city and blow the trumpets while shouting. The Lord then knocked the walls of Jericho down, and the people of God charged in and overwhelmed that once impenetrable city. The story of Israel overcoming Jericho is connected to this scene in heaven, not only because of the trumpets, but the number seven and the silence. For six days the Israelites compassed and walked around the city of Jericho once each day. They were led by seven priests who carried seven trumpets. The same number as the angels and trumpets in John's vision. As seven priests led the way, they blew the trumpets On the seventh day, the people of Israel went around the city seven times. At the end of the seventh time, on the seventh day, the seven priests blew the seven trumpets while the people shouted in unison as Joshua commanded. The end result, as you know, was the wall falling down. Where silence connects is the instruction Joshua gave to all the people before they began to walk around the city on that seventh day. He said to them, You shall not shout, nor make any noise with your voice, neither shall any word proceed out of your mouth until I bid you to shout. There was an obvious reason of this silence, considering the likely words that would have been spoken by the people As they walked each day around the city and then seven times on the seventh day. The parents of these people were complainers They doubted Moses at every turn. They did not think they would make it through the water or the desert, and they did not believe they could overcome the cities like Jericho within the promised land. That is why they were not allowed to enter the Promised Land. Griping and complaining come from the flesh. When our flesh controls us, we begin to complain about the conditions we are living in, or the food we are eating, or the leadership that is over us. We can easily imagine that the words of the people would have been if they were allowed to speak. They would have looked at the walls of Jericho and expressed their doubts to one another about their ability to be victorious. They would have said to one another, what a dumb plan it was, and how foolish Joshua was for trying it. They would have complained about the rocky walk the rocky walk they took each day and the waste of time being made going in a circle. Instead of complaining, however, the people were forced to be introspective, which is what you have to be when there is silence. They had to keep their thoughts to themselves and personally wrestle with their own flesh. The silence allowed the Spirit of God to speak to them. It caused them to face their lack of faith and personal struggles without interfering or confirming comments of others. This is what silence provides. There are no doubters to feed off of. There are no gossipers or slanderers to listen to and agree with. Silence brings us before God and allows us to see ourselves for who we are. It has been a warning by many preachers and prophets that our culture is suffering because of its inability to be introspective. We have difficulty being silent. We have televisions in our computers, in our cars, in our cell phones. We have music available as we walk, drive, work, read, sleep. We are a culture of gadgets going from one toy to the next. The temptation to have something always before us to keep our attention is too much for some. Many young minds view having to sit and be silent as punishment. The silence described in verse one is not punishment, but a prelude Like the silence of the people surrounding Jericho, it is a prelude before the trumpet sound and destruction follows. God uses silence to bring about his victorious kingdom Understanding the description of silence in this way helps link it together with the prayers described with the golden censors and incense. Now a censor is a bowl-shaped utensil used to burn incense. The ancient ones came as goblets held at the bottom or at the handle holding the bowl out in front. Burning incense was a regular part of the rituals by the Lord for the priests to practice while worshiping in the temple. The meaning of the incense was clouded during the Old Testament until John's revelation The censors contain incense, and the incense burning results in smoke. The rising smoke is the prayers of all the saints. The vision of John takes us into the temple worship. Only it is the temple of heaven. And there we find an angel of the Lord assigned to carry a golden censor and burn the incense given to him. The incense is burned before the golden altar, before the throne of God, and the smoke, the prayers of the saints, rise up to God. The saints referred to are not those that are sanctioned by the Roman Catholic Church. The term saints refers to all who have had their garments washed in the blood of the Lamb and thus are made white. They are the multitude. They cannot be counted. They are us. Have you ever wondered what happens to your prayers? Especially prayers that appear to go unanswered. Because we are children of God and because we speak And what we speak has power to bind or to set free. Our prayers have everlasting effect. In fact, there are only two outcomes of a Christian's prayer possible. Our prayers are fulfilled or they are denied. We are told that they are denied when we ask of the Lord out of selfish motivation. I can ask the Lord for a new motorcycle. Please, Jesus, provide for me a new motorcycle. But I don't need a new motorcycle. I don't need an old motorcycle. And if I asked for one, it would be for my own pleasure. I should not expect such a motivation to be rewarded. In fact, James tells us that too many times we do not have because we do not ask, and then we when we do ask, we ask out of our own lust. Let such a man not expect to receive anything from the Lord, said James. When we ask with proper motivation, we are promised to be heard and to receive a yes. What we often don't understand is that the yes may not be in this life. We ask, for example, to be relieved of a disease in this life And the Lord answers such a prayer with, yes, only the relief is in the life to come. What is being taught to us who try to understand this passage is that our prayers, the prayers of Christians, do not disappear into the stratosphere. Christians of the first century who asked God for protection, justice, and for his kingdom to come And overcome their enemy, certainly wondered whether God had heard them as they saw their brethren be persecuted and even martyred. Let there be no doubt that not only does God hear the prayers of his people, they are a sweet aroma to him. In the prayers of the saints, he finds pleasure. Revealed in this vision is how the prayers of the saints play a role in God's kingdom coming to earth. Verse 5 describes the angel with the golden censor that is filled with incense, taking fire from the altar. In Leviticus, we learn that the fire from the altar originated in heaven, and it was the priest's responsibility to keep the fire going. When other holy fires were to be started in Israel, they were to be started by the embers from the altar. The altar on earth was a type of the heavenly altar that we see in this verse. The angel takes the fire of God from the heavenly altar and ignites the incense, meaning that the fire of heaven ignites the prayers of God's people. The angel then throws the censer with the burning incense upon the earth. The result is thunder and lightning and earthquake. And these phenomena, again, should be familiar to us because they accompanied the glory cloud of God's presence in the book of Exodus. When the Lord appeared in the glory cloud, he was accompanied by thunder, lightning, and earthquake And so here we we reason here. We reason here. We put the pieces together of this vision with the Old Testament And we conclude that the prayers of God's people bring about God's presence on the earth His personal, powerful, all-inspiring presence is upon the earth when his people pray. When two or more are gathered in my name, Jesus said, there I will be in the midst of them. From all the drama and symbolism of John's vision at the beginning of chapter 5, the core message to God's people is that our prayers are a powerful force In the coming of God's kingdom. Our silent prayers, when our thoughts are being spoken to the Holy Spirit, are a powerful force also. Our verbalized private prayers are heard by God's ever-present ear. Our corporate prayers, when things are agreed upon, are given priority before God's throne. These and other mutterings, too deeply felt for words, are mixed with the fire of heaven and bring about the kingdom of God from heaven to earth. Think of it in the following manner. St. Peter quotes Leviticus saying that all who follow Christ are a priesthood. It's called the priesthood of all believers. You likely don't feel like a priest and just a couple of us have been ordained to be a priest. But when you pray, you are a priest in that you are doing a priestly thing. Your prayers are a priestly thing to do. Your prayers are incense to God and are part of his ushering in the new heaven and the new earth. And believing this, beloved, beloved, please listen. Believing this is more important today, having just witnessed a fatal tragedy in Nashville. Where three Christian children and three Christian adults were gunned down because their Christian faith was perceived a threat to a troubled and possessed individual. The mockers have come out And they have laughed at Christians and questioned how could our Christian prayers have been answered by God when such a tragedy has been allowed by God? But what such mockers only consider and this is key what such mockers only consider is what happens in this life What such shooters only consider is what happens in this life. What such persons who try to be like God and change the gender of themselves or others And choose who will live or who will die, what they consider is only what happens in this life. But there is a life and a death to come Where our prayers are like incense to God, and his vengeance is assured. And in that life and in that death, justice will be served. Christians in the first century needed to know that, and Christians of three nine year old children And Christians who love three adults from Covenant Presbyterian School and Church near Nashville, Tennessee, need to know it today. God stores up our prayers, and they rise before him as incense, and they will be part of his coming again. Believe it, beloved, believe it. Amen and Amen.

sermons.title: Easter
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Every Easter Scott Hollenbeck will shake my hand and he says today It's a day Christians can gloat. Unless we're sure about that. I have a number of embarrassments to reveal to you. Embarrassment number one. The Egyptians had a story of a god named Osiris that is so similar to the story of Jesus. That it can be said that Christians borrowed from that story. Osiris and Jesus were identical in a number of important ways. According to Christian critics, Osiris was called Lord of Lords, King of Kings, God of Gods, Resurrection and Life, Good Shepherd, Eternity and Everlastingness. And the God who made men and women to be born again. Osiris' birth was allegedly announced by three wise men known as the stars on the belt of Orion. Osias had a star in the east, Sirius, that signified his birth, and his followers enjoyed a Eucharist ceremony of sorts in which his flesh was eaten in the form of communion cakes of wheat. Skeptics also claim Osiris taught much of the same material as Jesus. The claim is that many teachings are identically the same, word for word. Osiris was allegedly killed and resurrected, providing hope that every believer might also be resurrected into eternal life. These similarities, when offered in succession, cannot by chance, be by chance, and thus they are embarrassing to Christians. We look like a bunch of copycats. Embarrassment number two. Christianity as a religion is based on the claim that Jesus rose from the dead. Even the Apostle Paul reasoned that if Jesus did not rise from the dead, then what every Christian has said or done for their faith in Jesus has been in vain. But Jesus could not have risen from the dead, because such would be the greatest of miracles, and philosophers have proven that miracles cannot happen. Simply stated, a miracle is a violation of mathematical, immutable, and eternal laws. Consider within the very exposition itself A miracle is a contradiction in terms. A law cannot at the same time be immutable and then violated. To acknowledge that miracles cannot take place is to live in a fantasy that is occupied by people who are an embarrassment. Embarrassment number three. Jesus was not sinless, but was obviously cursed by God because No sinless man would be found guilty of offending the state or his own religious authorities, and no guiltless man is going to be put to death on a Roman cross. The Roman cross was created to put to death the most vile of criminals and the cruelest and least humane manners, and all who witnessed such killings were horrified by the spectacle of such judgments. In short, bad things happen to bad people, and good things happen to good people. The crucifixion of Jesus was a bad thing. Embarrassment number four. Christianity is based on a conspiracy. And it is a conspiracy that is pretty easy to imagine and pretty easy to pull off. Jesus was indeed crucified. Jesus was placed in the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea. And the guards were placed at the tomb after the tomb was enclosed, but they were temple guards, they were not Roman guards. Temple guards were not disciplined. Temple guards would have easily slept on the job, especially on the second night If the apostles were able to roll the stone to cover the tomb, they were certainly capable of rolling it back to open the tomb. They could have easily stolen the body of Jesus. and then started spreading the rumor that he had risen from the dead, starting with, say, five hundred people, and then continued to add that following until a public day of celebration, the day of Pentecost where they could make a bold public claim and add to their new church, their new religion, 3,000 people. They did it for power, they did it for prestige, they did it for money. And the money argument is easy because once they got those 3,000 converts, those new converts starting to give the apostles money, and supposedly it was to be shared. But if the apostles would conspire to hide the body of Jesus, they could easily pretend to share the money given to them and keep it for themselves. It was all the ruse, and it is embarrassing to have ever believed it. Scandals are embarrassing. When a particular parish or ministry has a scandal, it can lead to doors closing and men being shamed and names and reputations being destroyed. One of the more popular apologists for Christianity around the world was named Rabbi Zacharias, and his ministry organization by the same name was exposed a couple of years ago and thus fell under scandal. After Ravi died, accusations of sexual perversions were made and an investigation was done, and it was discovered that his practice perversions and cover-ups occurred in multiple places and countries with multiple victims. As a result, his once thriving ministry issued a public apology and subsequently announced that they would undergo a name change and remove all material related to Zacharias. The Christian and Missionary Alliance denomination posthumously revoked his ordination after conducting their own investigation. Again, scandals are embarrassing. And strangely enough, St. Paul admits to the people at Corinth that Christianity, a religion, is based on scandal. St. Paul said we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block, and that word stumbling block in the Greek is scandalon, where we get our word scandal, and to the Greeks foolishness. So when is the embarrassment of Christianity going to be enough to quit this Christian gig and simply eat, drink, and be merry the rest of our days? And here is where I abort my ruse. I am not embarrassed in the least about the Christian faith, and you anticipated as much. But arguments I put forth as embarrassing are indeed believed by many. For instance, I have heard comedian and talk show host Bill Maher make the argument That the story of Jesus is a myth, and that it was based on the myth of the Egyptian god Osiris. And I can picture young men staying up late. Smoking their wlackie tobacke and drinking their Harl Seltzers and watching Bill Maher's show And believing every word that comes out of his mouth, including how Jesus never existed, and Christianity was simply a copy of some Egyptian god. And the same young men swearing off Christian heritage of their family and of their country. So let us look at the facts The facts are the names used for Jesus were not used for Osiris. Names used for Osiris were Lord of all. Good being, Lord of the underworld, Lord King of eternity, ruler of the dead, Lord of the West, etc. And those same titles were used for other Egyptian deities as well. Instead, we know Jesus as the Son of Man, the Son of God, King of Kings, and Lord of Lords. Scholars also say that while the belt of Orion is connected to Osiris, the three stars are in no place connected to the three wise men of the Bible, and plus the Bible never says there were three wise men, it just says there were three gifts. The claim that Osiris instituted a communion-like meal for his followers has no scholarly evidence. The claim that much of Osiris' teachings were the same as those of Jesus has no scholarly evidence. The claim that Osiris was killed and later resurrected, that's a complex story. The actual story is that Osiris was murdered and his body was dismembered and scattered. Later, his body pieces were recovered and rejoined, and he was rejuvenated. Osiris then journeyed to the underworld where he became Lord of the Dead. That is hardly what we gather to celebrate today. The life, death, and resurrection of Jesus is wholly unique. May God deliver our culture from people who get their theology, their knowledge of God, from comedians who merely repeat poor and unfounded arguments So that they can quickly dismiss what actually scares them. The second embarrassment claim was regarding the impossibility of miracles. 18th century philosopher David Hume is considered the father of this argument. It basically says that there are laws set in place in nature that all humans have experienced. And that those laws are unalterable, and we know this also by human experience. The law of gravity, for example, has been experienced by all humans, and no one can alter it. One of the problems with such an argument is the claim that all humans have the same experiences. First, That is impossible to say, for it is impossible to confirm, because of how spread out the human race is and how long the human race has existed. Obviously, the human experience of the apostles was that they saw Jesus dead, they saw him buried, and then they saw him alive three days later. And we add to that all the other miracles they witnessed Jesus do, and then experiencing being miracle workers themselves after the Holy Spirit fell upon them. Also, there is a serious flaw in the definition Hume gives of a miracle. He states that such is a breaking of unalterable laws of nature. But that definition isn't sufficient. Theologian Thomas Aquinas from the 13th century defined a miracle as an event beyond the powers of natural order. Such a way of looking at the world is similar to C. S. Lewis in his series The Lion, Witch, and the Wardrobe, when he describes the resurrection of Aslan. He calls it a magic deeper still. Which is what beyond the powers of natural order is. The third point of embarrassment I pointed to was That how Jesus was treated and punished was deserved, because only bad people are treated in such a manner That sounds like a deeply and obviously flawed argument, but consider how quickly and easily we come to such a conclusion. We hear of someone contracting a disease or getting into an accident, and we wonder quietly what they did to deserve such a judgment by God. As if God passes his judgment in this life by way of disease and accident. And if you don't admit that you are tempted to think in such a manner, then you don't understand the book of Job. For in Job, we are forced to deal with the very real and mysterious question of why bad things happen to good people. Jesus, of course, was innocent, but when taking on the sins of the world, he became a person worthy of death. By bearing the burden of sin and death, he was becoming like us so that we could become like him. In a quirky and mysterious sense, Jesus got what he deserved because he got what we deserved. And besides, innocent people are wrongly judged and condemned by the state on a repeated basis. The fourth point of embarrassment I pointed to was the possibility of disciples conspiring together to make up the story of the resurrection of Jesus. Those who make this accusation and are convinced of the plausibility, interestingly accept the historicity of Jesus without question. And even accept the way in which Jesus died and was buried. And this leads me to address the historicity of Jesus. It has become popular with the dismiss crowd, and I the dismiss crowd are those who accept unsubstantiated arguments and dismiss the gospel altogether. But it became popular to say that Jesus never actually existed. And to say such is usually related to Osiris comparisons or other myth comparisons. To say Jesus never existed is to speak like a fool. Scholars who do not believe Jesus to be God, who do not believe in miracles, do not question whether a man from Galilee Named Jesus existed, had a small following, and was killed by the Romans on a cross. But back to the conspiracy theory. Consider what would have had to happen in order for the apostles and other followers of Jesus to make a plan of action and then execute it to create the largest religion In the world and continues to convert followers today. They would have had to create the story of the resurrection of Jesus and the purpose of that resurrection. That would have been done before the death of Jesus, and that's contrary to what the gospel says, because the disciples are said to not even understand the resurrection of Jesus. Because they did not know what was going on in terms of Jesus rising from the dead, they could not know the purpose of Jesus rising from the dead. Jesus needed to rise from the dead because death needed to be vanquished, and God's eternal kingdom needed to be established as opposed to a kingdom on this earth. And I know the counter-argument is to say that since the apostles wrote the gospels, they merely put that in later, that they didn't understand the resurrection. And that's fair enough. But such is a very humble way to tell a false story. And it is necessary to rebut by asking why none of their contemporaries refuted their version. Also, the conspiracy theory doesn't include temple guards but Roman guards. And the tomb is sealed by a Roman insignia To imagine that the guards fell asleep, enabling the apostles to steal the body of Jesus would mean that they either outwitted or physically overwhelmed the Roman guards and broken the seal. Such were crimes against the state punished by death. Not to mention that the guards would have been put to death for their failure to guard the body. None of that happened. With the apostles unable to steal the body of Jesus, that fact alone brings down the whole conspiracy theory, not to mention the inability of the apostles to face their fears, to be organized, and to keep their stories straight. And there truly was no incentive monetarily or otherwise to conspire together. In fact, the Apostle Paul makes it his duty to collect money for the church at Jerusalem from other churches outside the city because the Christians there have become so impoverished Because of the prejudice against them in that city. No apostle became wealthy for following Jesus, and all of them sacrificed their lives to follow him. Beloved, there are many arguments against the resurrection of Jesus, and I guarantee you, guarantee you that there are solid and well-researched answers to all of them. All of them I quoted earlier that Paul admitted the scandal that is the gospel. Here is the verse in its entirety. For the Jews request a sign, and Greeks seek after wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified. To the Jews a stumbling block, scandal. And to the Greeks foolishness. But to those who are called, both Jew and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God, because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men. To say Jesus rose again is part of that stumbling block, that scandal, and is to be embraced as a scandal as opposed to being embarrassed. Don't run from it. It is scandalous to say God became man. It is scandalous that the God man Jesus died because it is saying God died. It is scandalous to say a man on a cross died and was buried, but came alive again to live and reign forevermore, because that doesn't happen. But it did happen. If you are an unbeliever, I want you to admit that you don't believe because the story can't be true, because it can, and it is. But you must admit that there is another reason why you choose not to believe. And if you confess that reason to God. And are sincere about knowing him, he will show himself to you by way of his son. I looked up how to overcome embarrassment One way is to reach out for support. If you're feeling like you can't cope with your embarrassment on your own, do not be afraid to reach out for help. Another way is to comfort yourself, as you would expect a parent or a friend to do. Don't be hard on yourself. Be kind. Another way is to practice deep breathing. Deep breathing helps us relax. After an embarrassing moment, sometimes we need it just to take a moment with a few deep breaths. Another way is to journal. Counter the negative thoughts that are living in your head after an embarrassing moment by writing them down. Another way is to give yourself a pep talk and create helpful statements to yourself. Well, you could all do all that. Or believe that Jesus is risen, is risen indeed, and embrace the scandal, a scandal that will be for eternity. Let us pray. Our gracious and heavenly Father We are given all the confidence in the world that what we say is true, that your son Jesus has risen, that he has risen indeed. There is no argument that can go against that statement of fact. And so we face it with excitement of our own resurrection, with appreciation for the great victory you've had over death. But we pray for those who do not believe. May whatever impedes them be removed, so that they too can rejoice that you are risen, risen indeed. Amen.

sermons.title: Identifying with Suffering
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, Amen. Please be seated. I very much encourage you to turn to Revelation chapter 8 in your pew Bible or your personal Bible. Revelation 8, taking up at verse 6, we're going to get into the weeds, folks. We're going to get into the weeds when it comes to understanding this vision. I have started walking again, trying to get my body in shape for bathing suit season. I am doing my best so that when I am on the beach, fellow swimmers won't try to roll me back into the ocean having mistaken me for being washed ashore In my walking back and forth from my home to the church, I once stepped over a small bird. It was likely a young robin. It was on the road, dead looking, as if it had never learned how to fly. As I stepped over it, I hardly paid notice until I realized That the dead bird that made little difference to me had the attention of our Heavenly Father Jesus used birds as an example of how if the Heavenly Father feeds them, how much more will He provide for our needs? It is quite profound to think upon the fact that what we might consider unworthy of our time and attention is cared for and counted by the God of all creation. As I was struck by such a realization, I began to ponder what had likely happened to the bird. It is possible that it was tossed from its nest during a storm the night before. This got me to consider the irony of its death. It is counted by God, and yet God is the one responsible for the wind. and the rain that tossed it out of its home, leading to its death on the roadside. There is a theological argument against such a conclusion For it could be countered that because humanity brought sin into the world and thus corrupted creation, it is actually man who is responsible for storms and resulting of dead birds. But God is sovereign over what man does and the results of what man does, so God is still responsible in some way. Such irony bothers the emotions of many, leading them to conclude that either God does not exist because a loving God would not be the cause of such irony Or the God that does exist is evil, making the universe a vehicle for him to inflict pain upon his own creatures. Neither one of those conclusions matches up with Scripture. It is likely that what is ironic to us is consistent with God's moral and loving character. What I am hopeful we understand from our study of this rest of chapter 8 in Revelation is the care that God has for his creation, even though, even though he is the cause of the events that transpire at the blowing of each of the seven trumpets. As I explained two weeks ago, I do not believe we can understand what occurs at the blowing of each of these trumpets as chronologically successive from the seven seals open previous. The events occurring at the opening of each seal are contemporaneous with the events occurring at the blowing of each trumpet. They may not be exactly parallel, but they most certainly occur near the same time. I have been trying to persuade you in this study. That the breaking of the seals does not start these events, but reveals these events, reveals where and are and will be. It is the same with the trumpets and the bulls to come. To understand what is occurring, we must keep everything in context. Meaning that the seven trumpets blown are linked theologically to the seven seals. In fact, the seven trumpets are a part of the breaking of the seven seals rather than being separate. Also, we discussed last two weeks ago, excuse me, we discussed two weeks ago, we must recall the meaning of the blowing of the trumpets. Comparing the events at the beginning of chapter 8 caused us to recall the battle of Jericho Trumpets announce battle. And each of the first four trumpets that are blown here announce battle. The four trumpets, like the four seals in the first four seals in chapter six, are to be understood as one unit They are distinct from the last three trumpets. First the four, then the last three. The first trumpet sounded brings hail and fire mixed with blood. The falling of hail and fire are the exact description of what occurs, remember, in the book of Exodus at the seventh plague over Egypt. The target, however, of this hail and fire is not limited to one nation. It's not limited to Egypt, but one-third of the earth. At the blowing of the second trumpet, something similar to a great mountain, whether it is an actual mountain or what mountain it is is not clear, but it was on fire and cast into the sea. The result of such a catastrophe is a third of the seed turning to blood. Now that should cue your memory To realize that that reference to water turning to blood takes us again back to Exodus, the book of Exodus, and Egypt. In that play, which we read about this morning, the great body of the Nile was made blood, and fish of the Nile died The body of water turning to blood at the second trumpet is a third of what is on the earth It boggles the imagination to consider the stench and destruction blood in the Nile must have caused. And here we have a third of the earth's water. And remember that the earth is primarily made up of water. The underst Excuse me. Understandable result of such water turning to blood is the death of men on the sea and creatures that live in the sea. And again, to imagine the stench. At the blowing of the third trumpet, another third of the earth's water bodies is corrupted by a star from heaven. The star falls as a lamp, meaning that it can be seen falling. The star has a name, wormwood. Wormwood is a bitter plant that produces oil which can poison water. Bitterness is symbolic of sorrow and disaster. Literally, it results in death for all who would drink it. And again, this takes us right back to the book of Exodus. For something similar occurred when Israel was walking through the Red Sea, walking for three days and finding no water. When they finally came to a body of water, they discovered they could not drink it because it was bitter. The people as We come to expect complain again to Moses. The Lord instructs Moses to cut down a tree and to cast it into the water to make the water sweet The meaning should be available to our faithful minds as we remember Psalm 1. Jesus is the tree planted by streams of water which yields fruit in good season. He was the one cut down as a sacrifice, and he turns the bitter into sweet. For all who drink from him, he is the living water. At the blowing of the fourth trumpet, a third of the light of the sun, moon, and stars was taken, so that a third of the light of day was taken as well. Again, back to the book of Exodus, back to the suffering of the Egyptians, back to the darkness that fell over Egypt, as recorded in the book of Exodus. The darkness covered the area of Egypt only at that time, and in this way it covers a third of the earth. It is evident from the comparison of the catastrophes that occur after the blowing of each of the four trumpets and the account of Israel's exodus from Egypt. That our God wants his people to understand something about what he is doing here in Revelation 8 Just as in the days of the Exodus, when God was delivering his chosen people out of the bonds of slavery and into the new land, that he would provide all that they needed to do so He is doing the same in the last days. He is using his creation to bring forth judgment upon the wicked in the earth for the purpose of delivering his people from the bonds of sin. The use of the fraction one-third is evidence of God's purpose You will remember that the breaking of the sixth seal and the release of the fourth horseman, we recall that the rider was given authority to harm one-fourth of the earth Here, there is given authority to harm one-third. It is a small fractional increase, but an increase nonetheless. One commentator attempts to make the argument that a fourth of the earth being harmed by death was a natural occurrence He argues that a fourth of a population is always dying and being replenished, even the beasts of the field and the fish of the sea. I looked up the annual rate for deaths to birth in 2022, and births almost doubled the number of deaths, so that commentator is is wrong. But it is interesting still to notice that the fraction, one-third, is a definite increase from the fourth horseman. The higher fraction is a verification that the increase in catastrophe and death is part of God's redemptive plan. And I can't say that enough. The increase in catastrophe and death is part of God's redemptive plan. And as increase occurs, whether in the lives of the first century church, whether in our lives or the lives of our children's children, we are to understand such increase in a different light, in a different light than the unsaved world While they see such a catastrophe purposefully, purposeless, excuse me, purposeless and undeserved, we see it as redemptive. We see God doing something. Now, verse 13, our last verse, is a controversial verse in this chapter because the translation of the word angel. Manuscripts are equally divided with half containing the word angel and the other half having the word eagle. As Job describes, the eagle is a creature that hastens to its prey. The appearance of an eagle announces swiftness and certainty of woes to come. Translating the creature who cries out the woes to come to be an eagle also fits with the warning of Jesus as recorded in Matthew chapter 24. Jesus there is warning his disciples about false Christs who will do signs and wonders to lead people astray. When someone tells us that the Savior is in the desert, so go and meet him, or that he is in a secret place, so go and meet him, we are told not to listen. Jesus said, For as the lightning comes out of the east and shines even unto the west, so will the Son of Man be. For wheresoever the carcass is, there will be the eagle gathered together. The appearance then of an eagle at this point in John's Revelation communicates that there is a carcass. It is dead. What we learn from these verses is that there will be days when violence, death, and destruction will increase upon the earth. Because division refers to the fraction one-third, however, we know it is an increase, but an increase that does not overwhelm. There are still two-thirds not affected, meaning that God is not doing away with all of mankind. He is not giving us more than we can endure. Because the vision is similar to the plagues recorded in Exodus, God's people can go to that story, believe it or not, that story of Exodus, for comfort. Because there was a greater cause than the plagues themselves, which was Israel's relief from bondage, there is comfort. There is comfort in the midst of plague. Because the plagues that came down upon Egypt did not harm the Israelites, there is comfort. You remember they lived in the land of Goshen The land of Goshen was given light while Egypt was in darkness. The cattle of Israel were healthy while the cattle of the Egyptians were infected. The hail and fire fell upon the Egyptians, but not upon the Goshans. God thus spare the Israelites from the more difficult plagues. But such sparing should not lead us to conclude that the Israelites did not suffer during the plagues. They too depended upon the Nile for their water, and they too had to dig elsewhere for a fresh source, just as the Egyptians did. They too had to endure the stench from the blood of the Nile, as well as the stench from the frogs that piled up. And most important to note, the Israelites had to suffer repercussions of the first nine plagues whenever they went into Egypt. The flies bothered them. The frogs bothered them. The hail bothered them. The locusts and darkness bothered them when they were in Egypt. Because this world is not our home, and because our promised land is heaven Means that being where we are now, we are in our own type of Egypt We are like the Israelites, traveling from Goshen to Egypt during the plagues. And because we are in Egypt The events occurring with the blasting of the first four trumpets will not elude all Christians. Because we are in Egypt, the catastrophes represented by the blowing of the trumpets occur around us Repercussions of the plague-like events are visited upon those in the land. And we are in the land. However, What we are to gain from John's vision is a confident perspective regarding the events in the world around us. Christians are never to be a people who panic. No matter what happens around us, we are never to be a people who panic. Certainly we mourn when lives are lost. Certainly we bear arms to defend our home and our country. And certainly we defend the defenseless around the world when we can. But we do these things out of out of fear for the end, not out of fear for the end, because we know no matter how bad it gets. No matter how many towers fall, no matter how many nations are corrupted, no matter how many markets crash, no matter how many dictators place Christians in their gun sites. No matter how many plagues or pandemics occur, we are to have faith that it is part of God's plan and God's eye is upon us. Simply because a sparrow falls does not mean that the bird is out of God's care. So it is with his people and much more. What we are faced with almost on a daily basis is the difficulty we have reconciling God's people suffering and God's caring for his people. When we say that God watches the sparrow, we do not mean that he is simply a casual observer He identifies with his creation, and most importantly, he experiences life with us, the good and the bad. Some of you have heard this example before, but it still stands out to me I was in a counseling session when I was very green in the ministry. A young woman was having difficulty being intimate with her husband. I could not find a way to help her until she decided to share with me what had happened to her when she was 16 years old. She was raised in a Christian home and said she felt very close to God in her young teenage years. Her older sister was more rebellious and adventurous. When the parents were gone for a long weekend, the older sister went to a party where there was drinking and drugs and decided to take her younger sister with her. The 16-year-old Christian girl found herself in a world she had never been before, and she did not want to be there. Within the context of drinking and carousing, she was raped by a boy a couple of years older. After she told me the story through tears, she ended with a piercing question: Where was God when I was being raped? As I said, I was young and I struggled for wisdom. It took a while, but it came to me where God was. God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. He was taking on the sins of the world. He was identifying with the poor, with the weak, with the downtrodden. In other words, Jesus was being raped as well. And I know that sounds shocking and scandalous to say it in that way, but we truly can come to no other conclusion When Christ took upon him the sins of the world, he identified with the priest who offered the sacrifice, he identified with the sacrifice itself, and he identified with the people who needed the sacrifice. He identified and still does identify with the victim. St. Paul said it plainly in his letter to the Romans, we suffer with Christ. It is a joint suffering resulting in us also sharing in his glory. As we read the catastrophic events described at the blowing of the first four trumpets, We may wonder what is to become of God's people. Some want to believe we are raptured into heaven before it all starts. But there is no rapture here. The first century church, suffering as it did, was not raptured. The Christians during the many plagues were not raptured. The Christians under Stalin were not raptured. The Christians in the Holocaust camps were not raptured. Christians in terrorist attacks today, we're not raptured. Christians in pandemics, we're not raptured. Whatever would happen to us or those who witness such calamity as described here in Revelation 8, we know at least this. His eye is upon us. He identifies with our suffering, and that identification is enough to save us. Amen and Amen. Let us pray. A gracious and merciful God You give no greater example, no greater example in that you suffer with us even today. And for that, we give back to you ourselves, for that is all that we have. May you be honored as we worship you this day in Jesus' name. Amen

sermons.title: Woes
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. We are looking at Revelation chapter nine It's always good to follow along in your Pew Bible or your personal Bible. Revelation chapter nine. It is common in our vernacular to give evil a personal identity. We speak of evil as if we know who it is, where it is, or what it does. We might say that is evil. Or there is evil in that man. And our speech makes it sound as if evil has its own existence outside of the man who practices it. Speaking about evil in this way is helpful because we generally understand what the speaker means Technically, however, evil does not exist outside of the people who practice that evil. Thus the existence of evil is relationally connected to those who practice it. There are different types of people who practice evil. For the sake of time, I am placing them in only three categories. There are those who are purely evil. The motives and behaviors of such people have no redeeming value. Their hearts are closed to God, and they follow the devil's lead. Then there are those who play with evil. It excites them to sin, and such sin is usually done in private or secret While the rest of their lives they are embracing the common moral standards of the society around them The third group abores evil and attempts to cling to what is good while confessing that they participate in evil when they follow the desires of their own heart. These people are like the Apostle Paul, who confessed to the, in his epistle to the Romans, that he does the very thing he does not want to do. In response to recognizing their internal hypocrisy, the people cry out for a savior.
