sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. That was a a new hymn to uh to us. Didn't quite know how to sing that one, but uh It it it it had two words to it anyway. Alright, we are in Revelation chapter twenty and uh we're starting at verse one and again I encourage you to follow along in your Bibles. It'd be quite helpful. During the Christmas season, our family used to put together a puzzle in the living room. We would place a card table in the living room and Whoever wished to join in gathered around and chose a section of the puzzle to put together. We would start each puzzle with a lot of family participation, but the number dwindled in about an hour It usually took a few days to a week before a puzzle was completed. On a few occasions it took longer because, well, some puzzles are just downright difficult. There are certain background scenes, such as those that are all white or all black or a mixture of colors that require numerous pieces, and each one looks like the other. In some cases, you have to make a stack of puzzle pieces that look alike and try one piece at a time until you have no more to try And yes, it usually ends up being the last one you try. There have been times, and I am sure it is because I am impatient. But there have been times when I thought for sure a puzzle piece fit when it did not After I placed it where I thought it should go, the rest of that particular part of the puzzle became all the more difficult. There are some pieces that you are confidently placing in the puzzle while ignoring the firmness, the extra firmness you need to get it in there. A forced puzzle piece is the best example I could come up with to describe what some writers As scholars have done with Revelation chapter 20, as they try to put together the puzzle of the end times. While this chapter, chapter 20, should fit well with the glorious message of John's vision, it has become the focus point of disagreement and division amongst Christians. A simple warning. The sermon this morning will consist more of teaching than preaching. The text and the controversies that relate to it necessitate such an approach. I hope you will bear with me. The title placed at the top of the chapter by Zombergan, not our Bible publisher, but the one who publishes the NIV, the New International Version, reads on the top, a thousand years. Such a title showcases what is controversial about this chapter, but I think it focuses on the wrong message of the chapter. While it is true that verses 2, 3, 4, 6, and 7 contain the phrase a thousand years, or the word millennium, And while it is true that this is the only place in Holy Scripture that that phrase is used The millennium or thousand-year reign of Christ is not the primary message of this vision. Before we get to that message, however, we must respectfully examine what others have focused on and see if there are any puzzle pieces that have been forced into position. In the educated circles, you will hear terms related to the end times, such as pre-millennialism, post-millennialism. Aw-millennialism and dispensational premillennialism. These are the labels given to the four primary interpretive perspectives of the end times. And, as you can see by the names given to each position, the identifying birthmarks are in relation to how they view the millennium. The thousand-year reign of Christ. The one that was most popular in the 20th and into the 21st century, being heard in most modern evangelical churches and In narrative form, and the very popular, once very popular Left Behind series, is dispensational premillennialism. Those who take such an approach to understanding the end times believe something similar to the following They believe all the promises the Lord made to Israel and the genetic line of King David in particular will be literally fulfilled. This means that the literal physical nation of Israel will receive back all the promised land that was originally promised to Abraham and his descendants. including the Temple Mount currently occupied by an Islamic mosque. Also A descendant of David will take the throne of Israel and re-establish a monarchy for that nation. After these events, the Israelites will receive a special revelation regarding Jesus as the Messiah, resulting in all that are of the Israelites' heritage being saved. In the meantime, or in another dispensation, hence where they get that name, the Christian Gentiles will be raptured from this earth at a secret return of Christ. That return will be followed by a great tribulation, where war and death will reign on earth. Wars will then cease at the announced second coming of Jesus. Which will be done in public and in dramatic fashion as he splits the eastern sky. He will next establish his throne on earth, and physically reign over all creation, along with those who had been raptured earlier, after his thousand-year reign, The final judgment will take place. Satan will be thrown into the lake of fire, and the believers of Jesus as Messiah will be given their heavenly reward. Those who believe such a scenario of the end times begin with Revelation chapter 20, verses 1 through 6. Understanding the reference to a thousand years. They also interpret the mention of a first resurrection literally and believe it to be referring to the rapture. With these verses, they include 1 Corinthians 15, verse 2, which describes Christians being changed in a twinkling of an eye. They also include 1 Thessalonians 4. 15, which describes Christians who are alive being caught up in the air to be with the Lord after the resurrection of those who are dead in Christ. They also include, and we will end with this one, they also include Jesus describing in Matthew 24 of two men being out in the field where one is taken and the other is left behind. With these pieces, those of this perspective put together a puzzle of the end times that is unlike any other Before it or after it. There are problems, however, with putting these pieces together. First, Israel forfeited the rights to God's promises when she went after other gods, as Deuteronomy 28, our Old Testament reading. Clearly warns against and the prophecies of Jeremiah and Isaiah. Second, the Apostle Paul teaches in the epistle to the Romans and Galatians. That those considered true Israelites are people who are of faith in Christ, just as Abraham was. This means that all who believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, whether Jew or Gentile, are considered a part of the true Israel. Third, the thousand-year reference can and needs to be interpreted symbolically rather than literally. Fourth, the first resurrection is referring to being made alive in Christ after being dead in sin, not to a first coming and then a second second coming of Christ. There is only one second coming. Fifth, the passages used to help understand Revelation 20 do not describe a rapture that occurs separately from the second coming of Christ. Thessalonians is merely describing to the church what will happen to the bodies of those who are already dead before the second coming of Jesus. And what will happen to those who are still alive at the second coming of Jesus. And in Matthew chapter 24, Jesus is actually describing judgment, not rapture. Those who will be taken from the field will be swept, Jesus says, swept up just like those in the flood in Noah's day. Where they go is to judgment, not the presence of the Lord. Although I have rejected the conclusions of such an approach to the end times My goal this morning is not to malign such an interpretation of this passage, but to explain why I disagree with what is predominantly taught in modern evangelical churches and to focus on what I believe is the true purpose of this point of the vision. To grasp the purpose, we must remember that we have just had described to us the final demise of both the false prophet and whom we previously called the harlot, and the beast, who we interpreted to represent all who persecute Christians. As both of them, it says in chapter 19, were thrown into the lake of fire. As John's vision has already revealed, the final judgment of those two, the harlot and the beast. Does mean that the presence of evil does mean that the present of evil is no longer upon the earth. Does not mean, excuse me, saying that wrong. Does not mean The devil has presented his nature as Trinitarian in order to mock the Godhead For he wants to be like God by making the beast like the Son, the harlot like the Holy Spirit, and the devil like the Father Christians have been encouraged by John's vision so far because they learn of the certain demise of the harlot and then the beast. There is still one judgment left, however. And the vision in chapter 20 provides us the scene of the devil's final days. That is the purpose of the vision. That is the message of this passage. The devil's end is ordained by God and it is seen by John. The first part of the vision describes an angel coming down that has the keys to the abyss. The abyss is not the lake of fire. It is the place of darkness and is also known as the bottomless pit where the devil and his angels direct their operations. The authority of this heavenly angel to be able to bind the devil, and the very act of binding him should remind us of Matthew chapter 12. Where Jesus explains the binding of the strongman. He said if a house is going to be plundered, the strongman, that is the man who is to protect the house, must be bound. Jesus was explaining that if he is able to plunder the devil's house by casting out demons, he must first bind the strongman, which he had done. In the gospel according to St. John, Jesus said, Now shall the prince of this world be cast out, and later the prince of this world has been judged. These were all statements in the present tense and applied to the time Jesus walked the earth. By resisting the devil in the desert and causing him to flee, Jesus achieved victory over the devil. Because of his sinlessness and authority received from the Godhead, the devil was bound by the will of Christ. After Jesus' death, resurrection, and ascension, his power then was over the devil both in life and in death. And that power is given to those who follow him. That is why the scriptures say, Greater is he that is in you than he that is in the world. That is why Jesus said, Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound, whatever you loose shall be loosed. That is why when we resist the devil, he will flee from us In summary, I am saying that the binding vision John sees is something that has already been done. It began when our Savior walked obediently on earth and after his resurrection, and it applies to those who follow him today. What is meant by the thousand years or millennium fits well in this interpretation When the phrase, the phrase is understood to symbolize a quality of time, not a quantity of time. We have already understood the number 10 as it is used in the revelation to symbolize completeness. The number 1000 is 10 to the third power. It is a Trinitarian ten. It means that Satan, the devil, the dragon, that old serpent, is bound for a time that is complete or perfect in terms of God's redemptive plan. You will also notice that the binding of the devil is not absolute. The devil is bound so that he cannot deceive the nations. Thus he is still prowling like a roaring lion. He is still a great deceiver. Yet he cannot carry out his great plan of deception entirely. For he is brought under the mighty reign of God and therefore cannot thwart the coming of the kingdom of God. While it is true that Satan is bound and is controlled by the will of God, it is also true that he will be loosed for a little season. The meaning is likely that he is allowed to work his will during that period. That period will be used to gather up the nations just as described in chapter 19. And just as chapter 19 describes, the battle is over the same time it begins. You remember it, fire comes down from heaven, and the war is over. And there is no casualties to count on God's side. After the battle, the devil himself will be thrown into the lake of fire, along with the harlot and the beast. Their end will be torment, and their torment will never end. For Christians who are being persecuted for their faith, And for Christian families who have lost loved ones because of their faith in Christ, the message is that those these things, excuse me. Though these things have to happen, it all comes under the sovereign will of God and is part of his redemptive work. The harlot will have her day, but she will be thrown in the lake of fire. The beast will have his day, but he too will be thrown in the lake of fire The devil will make his last stand, but his end will be the same. He will be thrown into the lake of fire. In the meantime, in the meantime, those who are alive in Christ have authority over the devil, for he cannot steal the soul of a man. If we resist him in the name of Christ, he has to flee. In the meantime, those who have died in the faith are given a place of honor and responsibility. Those of us who are still alive on this earth can be assured that the loved ones who have died in Christ are presently secure with Christ. And in the end, we must know that the day of judgment will come for all the enemies of God I use the following analogy because I think preachers of the gospel can never refer too much to C. S. Lewis. In the book The Silver Chair, which is part of the Narnia series, a little girl Named Jill comes face to face with the great lion named Aslan, who is a type of Christ in the stories. Jill was terribly thirsty, and needed a drink from the stream, but Aswan was in her way She asked him if he would promise not to do anything to her. He responded by saying that he makes no such promise. She then asked if he eats girls. He responds, I have swallowed up girls and boys, women and men, kings and emperors, cities and realms. Next, Lewis comments, the lion didn't say this as if it were boasting, nor as if it were sorry, nor as if it were angry, it just said it. And that is our God. To know what type of God He is shakes our knees and blesses our souls. Those who want a clear blueprint for the end times come away from Revelation with a belief that they have found what they are looking for, a piece of the of the puzzle that must fit. And yet, nowhere does the scripture promise such a blueprint or puzzle piece. For those who are in the battle, Who walk faithfully before God, who live every day as if it is the last day, a blueprint is not needed, nor is a puzzle piece. In the last installment of the Narnia series titled The Last Battle, there is a time of great sorrow when the small band of faithful Narnians. Realize that Narnia is no more. Quote I'm sorry. In response to that realizing that the unicorn Animals speak in Narnia. The unicorn says, nothing now remains for us but to go back to Stable Hill, proclaim the truth, and take the adventure that Aswan sends us. We would do well. We would do well to imitate such an attitude toward the end times We do not know what remains for us except to take the adventure God sends us. Knowing that the devil will be undone And the lake of fire is his destination, giving us the only puzzle piece we need. Amen. Let us pray. Our gracious and faithful God, we thank you for the hope of the devil's demise. We thank you that evil will be done away with. And we have that promise that we can cling to each and every day of our lives. Help us to look forward to that day every day, knowing that you are sovereign over all. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Hell as a Positive
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. He be seated. That hymn is not often sung, but most appropriate for our passage this morning, we are looking at Revelation chapter 20 Looking picking up at verse 11, Revelation 20, picking up at verse 11. Hell on earth. Hell on Earth was how Albert Evans from Brighton Ferry summed up his experience of the First World War. in a BBC interview in the 1970s. He was 19 years old when he fought in the now infamous Battle of Mametz Wood. in northern France in 1916. One of two thousand three hundred excuse me two hundred and thirty-seven thousand men and boys from Wales To serve in the Great War, he survived. Tens of thousands didn't, and one of the bloodiest battles of the Psalm 4,000 men from the 38th Welsh Division were killed or injured in Mammoth's Wood In BBC archive footage, Albert Evans recalls how the line of men which advanced toward the wood withered away before his eyes The machine guns of the Germans were just spraying fire over the open site, he said. You couldn't get near the wood. Control was instead given to Major General Herbert Watts, and a second attempt was made. Quote, the wood was very thick and dense. The soldiers became very disoriented, but they pushed through and forced the Germans out. The enemy may have been cleared, but the 38th Division paid a heavy price Lord Thomas Gresfold recently highlighted the role of the division in the House of Lords, describing the loss of men in the battle as a huge tragedy for the whole of Wales. He said 1,000 men of the Rhonda Regiment went in battle that day, but only 130 men answered the roll call the following day. The rest were either missing or wounded and most likely dead. Personally I have read several first-hand accounts of battles fought in World War II from books such as Band of Brothers, Helmet for My Pillow, and With the Old Breed. And all of them, all of them would describe their experience as hell on earth. It is on, is it not? That such a description would be used, and most say it is appropriate, and yet so many, so many do not believe hell exists. Before we take the time to finish chapter 20 in the book of Revelation, I have the hope of generating a greater appreciation for the fact that there is a hell. And please, please do not anticipate this sermon to be negative, troubling, or remote. Parts will be, parts have to be. But overall, unsettling reality of hell as a means is a means of grace to us. In verse 11 of chapter 20, it could have been identified as the beginning of a new chapter. It is starkly different from described judgment of the devil in verse 10. of the chapter. There is seen by John a great white throne. This throne is a new vision. It is white for obvious reasons, but it should be said that as a throne, the color speaks to the rain of purity now that evil has been done away with after the devil has been thrown into the lake of fire. We can't immediately identify the one who sits on the throne as God the Father, for it is his holy face that no one can see. And live. And therefore we would expect that the earth in heaven would flee away at the revelation of his face His face is holy. Earth and heaven have been corrupted by the fall of man and the continuous sin of men. Therefore, they cannot remain before the presence of his holiness. It might surprise us that heaven would pass away, but we understand by remembering that heaven is also a name for the sky. Before God created, there was nothing, and it was on the first day of creation that He created the heavens, skies, atmosphere above us, and the earth When Adam sinned, both the heaven and earth changed, for all of it became under a curse, a curse caused by Adam and Eve And the earth passes away, so does everything on the earth. Material goods, including food, clothing, shelter, monuments, monies, valuables, collectibles, and such pass away. Bodies of nature also pass away, including grand mountains, mighty rivers, and other bodies of water, great and small. Everything, literally everything, that we are tempted to place, our comfort, our security, our identity will be gone. You are like me. You use places and items of this world to give you comfort and security Whenever I travel, especially when I travel alone, I use the memory of the front of my home, my own bed, the love of my family, and the arms of my wife to motivate me To put up with the many hassles of airports and interstates. When we witness someone use a cup of tea, a particular chair. Hold the hand of their spouse to calm anxieties and fears. We can be confirmed that we use things of this world to give us comfort. It is remarkable how a particular shirt, a piece of music, or family tradition will set us in a mood of peace and tranquility that we long for. Such are moments that God gives us. They are a gift of Him in this life. But all these things, all of them will be removed at the revealing of the face of God. With everything removed, mankind alone is all that there is. All that there is that stands before God is mankind standing before his face for judgment. As judgment commences, John then sees the dead, small and great, stand before God As mankind takes its place before God in John's vision, the books are open. The books are records, recorded records of the works of men. These books are evidence. They are multiple because they contain the evidence of the works of men, both great and small, both righteous and evil. They contain evidence that will determine what names are written in the most important book, the Book of Life. The book of life is first mentioned in chapter 3, verse 5, also in chapter 13, verse 8, and 17, verse 8. As much as we anticipate the opening of the book with the seven seals, we anticipate the opening of this book all the more. For it contains the names of those who will have heaven as their eternal reward. Before we examine the books, we should bring verse 13 into our explanation. Verse 13 is a further description of verse 12 rather than a separate event or judgment. The C Giving up the dead is described because Christians in John's day wondered, like we do, what happens to bodies of men and women who end up at the bottom of the sea. Similar questions are asked about the bodies of those who are shredded, torn, burned, and mutilated in accidents, or about bodies cremated and then spread upon the earth, or simply bodies that become dust. as they decay and eventually become a part of the ground that encompasses them. What these passages reveal is that the earth must give up the bodies of the dead in whatever form they become. For they are to become human form again and be judged for eternity. Both the flesh and the soul of men come back together and will be judged. Just how that will look, how these bodies will come together, is not described. It is enough for us to accept that God will do it. If he can create something out of nothing, if he can create humans out of dust, putting bodies back together doesn't seem all that difficult. In both verse 12 and 13, we are told that men are judged according to their works. This might unnerve all of us at first reading, for it is our understanding that our faith in Christ Jesus is what saves us, not our works. What is confirmed here is that ultimately we are judged by our works, especially those who have refused Christ as Savior. God's judgment is not without cause. Those who have defied his offered son will be called to give an account for their lives. They must answer for every moment God has given them upon the earth. If there is one thought that was evil, One act that was selfish, one look that was lustful, one yearning that was covetous, or one moment where another God was followed or worshipped, it will have to be accounted for As scripture states, if man breaks one law, he is guilty of breaking the whole law. The punishment for that broken law is death. It is eternal death, which is death of both body and soul. For those who have not accepted the sacrificial atonement of Jesus to pay for their sins, the judgment of God will fall upon them. The case against them will be overwhelming, and all will see that God's judgment is true and right. For those whose names are written in the book of life, they will be judged also according to their works, although their works will be seen as the works of Christ. Better said, the works of Christ will be seen as theirs. Because of what Christ Jesus has done, those who believe in him have his works counted toward their works. That is why Paul refers to the Christian as being in Christ or of Christ. From the Heavenly Father's view, when he looks upon us, he sees us as being in his Son. We are in the covenant established and fulfilled by Christ. The works of those in Christ will also be counted as a way of glorifying Christ. James reminds us in his epistle that faith without works is dead. As followers of Christ, we are to continue his work on earth, meaning. Meaning that we feed the hungry, we heal the sick, we care for the orphaned and widowed, we go the extra mile, we give the extra coat. We give from our money accounts. We love our enemies and announce his gracious name to all who seek him. All such works are recorded as praise to the King of Gory. This is how works will be accounted for toward those names that are written in the book of life. Verse 14 describes the end of both death and Hades. It's curious that death and Hades, which we think of as abstractions, are here personified They are described this way so that we understand the totality of Christ's victory and the totality of God's judgment. Death is referred to by the Apostle Paul as the last enemy. Hades is the place where those who had died dwell until the final judgment. Both death and Hades are a result of the sin of man and the rebellion of the devil. Because the devil is already thrown into the lake of fire, and the judgment of mankind's sin is finalized Death and Hades also have a demise, which is along with the rest of evil, into the lake of fire. The reference at the end of verse 14 of the lake of fire being the second death is to clarify that the first death occurs when man passes from this life. This is the death that all are assured to face. The second death, the death that occurs in the lake of fire, is assured only for those who have unrighteous works Sin unaccounted for, and who are therefore not named in the book of life. Verse 15 is the final statement on the subject If anyone's name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire. The judgment of fire, the reality of hell, the thought of everlasting torment is written here for the following reasons. First, it is to be a motivation to spread the good news It is natural that men are spurred on to turn away from that which is dangerous, dangerous to them or those they love. A love of one's fellow man and the knowledge of hell as a destination for unrepentant sinners is to motivate us to tell others the good news of the Lord Jesus Christ. The description of hell as a place of eternal torment is to overcome any fears we have in this life of people who would reject us because of the message we proclaim. Practically speaking, when you are tempted to consider how a person might react negatively to you because you share the gospel with them. The feeling is to be overcome by the sense of urgency that you have for the souls of others to be saved from eternal fire. You must ask yourself, is being called a religious zealot or having a reputation of being a Jesus freak As bad or as big a concern as the souls of the people you know are going to hell? It should not be When it comes to family members, whether it be parents to children or children to parents or one sibling to the next, you must ask yourself. Is the anger I will receive and the possible shunning that will occur because I confront a loved one who is in sin? Is it worth the eventual saving of a loved one, saving their souls from hell? It should be. From my vantage point as pastor, too many parents watch their children wander from Christ. Know they are living in sin and say nothing. Say nothing because they do not want friction in the relationship. What is worse? What is worse? Having friction in this life or being separated for eternity in the next? The answer again should be obvious. Second, the description of hell as final judgment is written here to proclaim the righteous judgment of God. Sin is defiance against Almighty God. The punishment for sin is death. Sin must be accounted for. God requires a penalty of death. If it is not met in this life through his son, it is required for eternity of those who do not repent. Beloved, God is not like men. He does not go back on his word. He made a covenant with men. That covenant included the requirement of death for sin. It must be fulfilled. The world needs to know this People outside the covenant who might entertain that God exists continually place expectations on him regarding how it this world is being run and never acknowledged, or perhaps Are not told about the expectation that they have failed to keep. This must be known, and God's judgments must be proclaimed as right. The message of a real hell for punishment of evil does that. The third and final reason for the description of hell is to place a righteous fear into God's people. Hell is to be a deterrent for us We are all motivated by fear. Fear conjures up an inherent reaction, an innate reaction within us. You know what it's called? Fight or flight? When frightened, we either fight off that which scares us or run from it. Hell can either be fought off, which occurs by people denying its existence Or we can run away from it. To run away from it is to run away from sin. One way to not take God's grace for granted is to not go on sinning while assuming God's grace will abound. This is why hell must be real to us. Christians are to live with the tension that on one side of our spiritual state we are secure in Christ. And we have every confidence in heaven. On the other side, we have warnings that if we choose to walk by the flesh and remain unrepentant to sin, we are in danger of hellfire. One tension keeps us secure. The other keeps us at the task of resisting temptation. The description of hell, as revealed to John and written to the church, is a healthy, necessary grace to us. As you well know, it is quite popular today for ministries to focus on only the positive aspects of the Christian faith. For various reasons, certain ministries stay away from any mention of hell and stick with that they consider a positive and uplifting message. What I have presented to you today is an argument for the positive and uplifting message of hell It is a means of grace to us, as a motivation to proclaim the gospel, as a proclamation of God's righteous judgment And and as a deterr deterrent to redis it of the Had a little brain freeze there. Let's start that again. What I have presented to you today is an argument for the positive and uplifting message of hell. It is a means of grace to us, as a motivation to proclaim the gospel, as a proclamation of God's righteous judgment, and as a deterrent to resist the devil and flee from sin. It is healthy for Christians individually and the church in general to live in tensions with the security that we have Christ. And the reality of hellfire. Let us keep that tension for the sake of our souls and the sake of Christ's church. Amen. Let us pray. A gracious and heavenly Father, for this vision that you've given John For this revelation of a true hell that burns with fire, that suffers those who will not repent. May that always be with us. And may the security in Christ that you give us also always be with us. We might live in that tension and serve you faithfully through our rest of our days. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: God Among Us
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Turn in your Bibles to Revelation chapter 21. Picking up at verse 1, Revelation 21, picking up at verse 1. We need to become better storytellers. Storytelling, especially within a family, provides a necessary sense of identity. Over 15 years ago now, I learned that I have a great uncle named Arthur J. Hope on my mother's side. Who attended the University of Notre Dame to study physics? While an undergrad student, he became interested in theology and eventually decided to pursue the priesthood. After being ordained, he went back to Notre Dame, where he served as a professor of philosophy During his time as a professor, he wrote a book entitled The First 100 Years of Notre Dame. The last printing was 1999. And serves as the primary resource for the university's history. I like knowing about such relatives Gives me a better idea of the stock I come from and thus a better idea about myself Another example of telling stories is my grandmother on my father's side, who used to tell a story about her family's brush with fame. Although her uncle was a minister within the Lutheran Church, that was not considered noteworthy compared to the story of the infamous Jesse James hiding out in the family barn. Evidence was left behind to confirm he and his gang spent the night in the barn while hiding from the law, but the family was not aware until they had gone What this says about my stock, I am not quite sure, but she always seemed to enjoy to tell story. Storytelling within the family should be healthy, fascinating, and joyous. It also serves another purpose. Storytelling can be likened to our salvation. Storytelling is how we understand our salvation. This is nowhere more evident than in Revelation chapter 21. From this chapter, we learn about the heritage of man, both under the covenant and outside the covenant. We learn certain symbols, how they're used throughout Scripture. We are also reminded of our beginnings and learn about how time will end. If you have ever wondered Why men like to tell and hear stories, the answer is in Holy Scripture. Originally in history, family stories were orally handed down to succeeding generations. From the time of Moses, men wrote their stories down, enabling them to be consumed by the millions Today, we are exposed to stories via audio recordings, live productions, movies, television, and song This shows that we love stories. And it shows enjoying stories is how God has programmed us. And the good stories, the stories we all enjoy are those that start with a dilemma or a conflict And work toward a resolution with a character that saves or restores what has broken down. Such stories are types and shadows of the gospel. The great dilemma that all good stories resemble Is the broken relationship between mankind and God because of the sin of man. The resolution is found in the Savior, who is first promised and then brought forth. He gives up himself, his own life, for the sake of restoring what is lost. And the end truly can be described as happily ever after. As we examine chapters 21 and 22 of the Book of Revelation, we must see them as the end of the greatest story. It is the only true story. It is the story toward which all good stories point. Verse one of chapter twenty-one begins with John seeing a new vision. In the revelation, we have gone from one new vision to another. Sometimes they overlap, and other times they are completely different. This one is now contrasted to the previous vision of all that is evil being thrown into the lake of fire. Because the first heaven and earth necessarily passed away before the face of God, a new heaven and earth are brought forth, and from this we are reminded of the first creation. When God had created all and said that it was good, He placed Adam and Eve in the garden in order that they might govern the rest of his creation. He was to be their God, and they were to be his people. The sin of man delayed what God designed. Now, in Revelation 21, as John describes it, what God had planned for is being achieved. An important distinction between the new creation and the old is that there are no longer a seed John revealed to us in chapter 17, verse 15, that the waters represented the Gentile nations The land has always represented or symbolized the people of God, while the waters that were all consuming in Genesis imparted in Exodus symbolize nations that were in rebellion against God. Now, in this chapter, at the revealing of a new heaven and a new earth, there is no more water. There is no more sea. There are only the people of God. Finding its place of rest within the new creation is the holy city. The Garden of Eden was the first holy city, and from it all rivers flowed, and in it God walked. Subsequently, after man was kicked out of the garden and God chose David to lead his people Jerusalem, Jerusalem became a type of the holy city. For it was also a city set on a hill, like the garden, and housed the temple of God, which symbolized God, localized God's presence among his people. The holy city that John sees here is called the New Jerusalem. There is a remarkable difference, however, from this city and the ones before it. This city, the heavenly city, is actually a bride. We remember the people of God being referred to as a bride in chapter 19. As the people of God, we take on a submissive role to the Savior and are therefore typed as a bride. The people of God are not only identified as a bride, but a beautiful adorned bride Our adornment is fitting for the day that is being described and the place of heaven in which we live. Thus the people of God are identified as both a beautifully adorned bride and a holy city. The New Jerusalem. Thus, there is a mixture of metaphors used here to help us grasp the profundity of our heavenly state. It has been an emphasis of mine throughout our study of Revelation to proclaim the identity of the Christian Church here and in all of Scripture as the true Israel. I have been saying that the true Israel, the true chosen people of God, are made up of those who are descendants of Abraham by faith. Those that make up the church, the called-out ones, the peculiar people, the chosen ones, are not those who are merely of the bloodline of Abraham, but those who are of the faith line of Abraham. In this vision, the New Jerusalem is a holy city made up of people of faith, faith in the Lord Jesus Christ for salvation. Nationality is irrelevant. Faith in Christ is all that matters. To deepen our understanding as to what it means for the people of God to be referred to as the New Jerusalem, a voice from the throne, the same white throne on which the judge of all sits says with a loud voice, Now the dwelling of God is with men. He will live with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. As mentioned before, the first holy city was the Garden of Eden, where God walked amongst his creation. Then it became Jerusalem, where God dwelt inside the temple, within the Holy of Holies, above the Ark of Covenant. He dwelt there as a means of grace for his people in order to have his presence among them, although limited. It was limited because man could not be in the presence of Almighty God without a blood sacrifice for the atonement of sins. Only the high priest could go before God, and that was limited to once a year. To understand the people of God as a city, the holy city, we are to understand that God dwells among and within us. For this New Jerusalem, there are no more limitations. Just as in the Garden of Eden, the Lord God Almighty walks, physically, dwells among his people. Now, as depicted here in Revelation 21, the dwelling of God is with men. The redemption of mankind and the description of heaven bring the story of God and his people back to the place where he intended. In heaven, we live in a place together with God where we can dwell in peace before Him. We can dwell in peace because our sins are no more. And God dwells with us because He has made us His sons. A favorite description of many regarding what heaven will be like is in verse four. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain. What this will be like, we can only imagine, and imagine we are allowed to do. To appreciate what it would be like to live without a reason to mourn, we must do some inventory. Think for a moment about all the times you mourn and cry. I am not referring to tears of happiness. Those are much different. I'm referring to times when tears flow and our soul aches. Those times are usually, if not, caused by death. And I don't mean that death actually has to occur in order for us to mourn in such a manner. We cry because someone we love almost died. And we emotionally imagine what it would be like to be, to lose, to be without or lose him or her. We also cry because a loved one has been diagnosed with a disease that may take his or her life We also cry because someone we love died some time ago, and something we associate with reminds us of him or her and how empty we are without them. Recently I reflected on my love for my wife and I am moved emotionally because I am aware that one day one of us will likely have to say goodbye to the other Recently, she told me she thinks that I am going to go first, but that is a discussion for another time. And speaking of saying goodbye, why do we become so emotional when we say goodbye to someone who is moving away or simply going on a long trip? It is likely that we become emotional because we consider that we may never see that person again in this life. Such emotions of mourning are conjured up because of the possibility of death, even though it may be many decades in the future. We cry because we are vulnerable to death in this life. In heaven, however, in heaven it will not be so. With death gone, having been thrown into the lake of fire as the last enemy There will be no more reason to cry in mourning. Truly we can say with defiance, as the Apostle Paul says, Mocking, O death, where is thy sting? We can mock death because surely the sting will be no more. We will no longer know absence within the heart. We will no longer fear loneliness. We will not cower because of cancer test results. We will not fear that a loved one has been in an accident. We will not even remember the aches and pains of old age. We will no longer desperately hang on to each moment as if someone is trying to steal it from us. Time will be no more. Eternity is all that we will know. Verse 8 is for the purpose of contrast. While those who are citizens of the New Jerusalem will be having their sorrow turned to joy and their mourning to laughter. There is the reality that those who would not receive Christ as Savior will suffer eternal punishment and the second death. These are summarized in adjectives such as cowards, unbelieving, abominable, murderers, sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and liars. Sinners will be identified with their sin for all eternity. And this will be so because the sinner chooses it to be so. Thankfully, this passage does not call us to focus on the suffering of hell. What I wish for us to underline and to highlight is the second phrase in verse 3. They shall be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. And I would also add verse 7, I will be his God, and he shall be my son. It was God's initial desire at the creation of man for Adam to be his son. This desire is described throughout Scripture in a similar way to what is stated here. One similarity is ownership When God made his covenant with Abraham, he planned to make Abraham's descendants his own people. In the Exodus, we find the use of a singular pronoun, my. My is used over and over again when the Lord refers to Israel as my people. Let my people go so that they may worship me, he said. When the Lord was angry with Israel, Moses reminded the Lord of it that Israel was owned by the Lord. Thy anger, Moses said, is hot against thy people. Consider this nation is thy people, said Moses to the Lord. Through the Psalms and the prophets, the Lord takes his ownership seriously, and he continually refers to Israel as his people, even when they do not act like his people. In the deepest sense, the relationship was one-sided with Israel. From the time of the Exodus on, the Lord has waited for a time when his people would be his own and he would be their God. He wanted to be their God in every way. He wanted his creation to enjoy what he had created and created them to be, and that consisted of having an intimate relationship with him. In Leviticus the Lord spoke to such a time. He said to Israel, I will put my dwelling place among you, and I will not abhor you. I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be my people. Although Israel continued to sin either by following other gods or not trusting in the one true God as their deliverer. God continued to entrust himself to them. He continued to call them his people and look forward to the day when he would be their God. As the psalmist said, Happy is that people whose God is the Lord. Through Jeremiah and Ezra The Lord used the same phrase, the same phrase to describe the future he did in Leviticus. I shall be their God, and they shall be my people. The preacher in the Hebrew epistle used the same phrase to describe what occurs with all those who follow Christ. He becomes our God, and we his people. And now, here in the Revelation, when the heavenly rest is realized, it is stated by God Himself that He is our God. And what can be better? Where the story began, we're talking about stories. Where the story began, God was walking amongst his people. And here, in the end, God is walking amongst his people. And yet the end is the beginning of eternity There is nothing, truly nothing, in this life, that is as profoundly meaningful than an intimate relationship. To know and to be known by another human being stirs up godly desires of service and sacrifice, of passion and freedom. Such a relationship awaits all who call on the Lord Jesus Christ to be saved. This is how it should be. It is how it was written to be. It is the story of our God. Until that time, until that time when he walks among us, we tell the story of God's love and his plan of salvation. Until that time, until that time we say Amen. Let us pray. A gracious and heavenly Father We thank you for this great story, and we thank you for the privilege of being a part of it. And as we thank you for it, We know the commission is that we tell it, and tell it again and again to our children and our children's children and all who would have ears to hear. May all of us be a part of that story to the very end. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen

sermons.title: Further In
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Join me in turning to Revelation chapter twenty-one. We are picking up at verse nine. Things are not always as they appear You knew that, of course. Of course, you did. We base a law of what we understand by appearance. Even though we know that what appears cannot always be trusted. I have dabbled a little in what are called sleight-of-hand tricks Sleight of hand tricks are based on the premise that people are used to seeing things a certain way and tend to be caught off guard. When a particular motion is made, resulting in something unexpected. Take this lot of tissue, and I go to grab it And it's not there. And you expected it to be there, and you're wowed. Right? You know how many years it took me to practice doing that? I can do such tricks, but I have no idea how illusionists make a statue of liberty disappear The point is that things are not as they appear to the eyes. Plato, the Greek philosopher, attempted to explain life in this world as a type of illusion. He described the realities we know around us as perceptual. All of creation, including humanity, and the souls of men, are perceptual and thus Imperfect. He said that the perceptuals are imperfect forms of the reality Forms are the true reality having an existence as an idea. They have an almost spiritual quality about them existing eternally outside of the physical world. When you see a table, for example, A table is merely a perception of a form or idea of table that has a perfect Eternal existence apart from the actual table that you see before you. Plato applied his philosophy to morality As he identified goodness to be a form that has existence outside of a good deed that a man does. It is for man, according to Plato, to attempt to replicate the form of goodness in life and thus be in greater relationship with eternity. As with most philosophies, there is some truth in Plato's understanding of life mixed in with a lot of confusion and distortion. As Christians, we understand life by means of revelation, the revelation given to us by God. God reveals to us that He is creator. God reveals to us His law. He reveals to us our sin, which is the failure to keep His law. He reveals to us his nature by sending his son. He reveals his love by sacrificing his son for our sins. He reveals to us our need to believe and be baptized in the name of His Son for our salvation. We are utterly, utterly dependent upon God's revelation to understand any truth in this life and the next. What Plato got right, at least in a passing reference, was the existence of a reality beyond the one that we see in this life. That existence is not separate, however, from what we actually see, but what we actually see does not do justice. Does not do justice to what God has prepared for his people in heaven. That was the point of all this. One of the dangerous results of Plato's philosophy was Gnosticism, which we have discussed several times before. I remind you that Gnosticism is a belief that matter or material existence is in its essence evil. Because it is evil, it is to be discarded, and the spiritual alone is to be pursued, much like Plato. But the biblical worldview understands matter, and we want the biblical worldview. The biblical worldview understands matter or the created world to be good. For God created it and said it was good. It is corrupted. It is corrupted only because of the sin of man and the curse that followed. Creation is now under a curse, and like mankind, all of creation must be given a new birth. It is in Revelation chapter 21 that we get to hear a description of the new birth of creation. There is going to be a new heaven and a new earth, and thus what we see in this life can be likened to what we see in the next. But is so very limited for what is experienced in the next life is only beautiful and never dreary. It is only bright and never dark. It is shiny and never dull. It is prosperous and never poor. What we learn from John's revelation is that what we know in this life is going to be more beautifully expressed. And intimately experienced in the next. In verse 10, chapter 21, John is carried away by The angel who poured out one of the seven bowls of the plagues and shown a mountain that is great. We know that the Garden of Eden was on a mountain, and we know that God met Moses on a mountain, and we know that Jerusalem, the city of God, was established on a hill. Each of these was like this mountain, only they were not this mountain. This mountain was great, being higher than all the rest. From heaven, John saw a city coming down. The city is called the holy city, for it is like Jerusalem. When Jesus chose the twelve disciples and God chose the twelve tribes of Israel, we knew that he was bringing together the covenants. By calling Gentiles into the faith, we understood that the promise of salvation through Christ was given to more than just the Jews. We did not know, however, just how close the covenants were. And the measurements of the city that comes down confirms the unity of the old covenant and the new. There are twelve doors, twelve foundations, and the measurement is twelve thousand stadium. The overall measurement of the city that comes down is 144 cubits. 12 squared is 144. Twelve tribes of Israel multiplied by the twelve apostles of Christ equal 144. We recall from this that there were a hundred and forty-four thousand counted being around the throne. These are all proven by this passage to be a symbolic number of God's covenant within his people. The old covenant and the new covenant make up one covenant which includes all of God's chosen people The unity of the covenants is further described in terms of the city's decorations. The chosen decor are the very stones placed on the breastplate of the high priest Which he wore entering the Holy of Holies. Those were beautiful stones, but they are not these stones. The beauty of the gates is said to be twelve pearls. We have to remember that Jesus compared the kingdom of heaven to being a pearl of great price. But there are no pearls on this earth like these pearls. The great street of the city is said to be pure gold. Gold was the standard for national economies for years because of its value. But no gold on the earth is pure enough to be as glass. No gold that we know is like this gold. The fact that John does not see a temple in the city teaches us the purpose of the measuring of the city. The city is said to be a perfect cube. The Holy of Holies, the room within the temple in which the Ark of the Covenant rested and God was said to have dwelt, that also was a perfect cube. But that perfect cube is not this perfect cube. We are to understand by this comparison that the holy city that comes down in John's vision is The heavenly holy of holies. Where God dwells is now where all of his people are allowed to dwell And the presence of God in the Son, who is to us the Lamb, is permanent amongst his people. He is the light in which we will walk. His presence guarantees that only purity of heart and purity of life will be practiced by all within the Holy City. Adam knew what it was like to walk in God's presence and for God to walk in his presence. So did Abraham, Moses, and the prophets. The disciples knew what it was like for the Lamb of God to illuminate the world Even we, even we who are so far removed from the time the Savior walked this earth, have an idea, an idea of what it is like for God to dwell among us For he is now here in spirit. And yet those manifestations, those times in which God was with men, is not like this time that John describes. Everything we know and have experienced of what is good, right, proper sensible, beautiful, meaningful, colorful, bright, cheery, playful, exuberant, and so on is going to be overwhelmed by what heaven has to offer The difference between earth as we know it now and the heaven we will know is expressed better, I think. In C. S. Lewis's Chronicles of Narnia series, in the book titled The Last Battle. Many of the characters in the series are brought together to see the end of Narnia. Narnia was to these characters a sort of heaven on earth. It was promised land. Although Ashwin, the Great Lion, had warned them that all worlds must come to an end, none of them had thought, or at least they had hoped, that he did not mean Narnia. But Narnia did come to an end. After its end, while characters such as Lucy and Jill cried, because Narnia was so beautiful to them Aswan shouted as he ran from where they were all standing, he shouted, come further in, come further up. They did not know where they were at the moment, nor did they know where he was going, nor could they keep up with him. As they walked together to follow Aslan's path, they noticed a freshness in the air. The beauty all around them was breathtaking and made it hard to continue on because of what there was to see right in front of them. They said to each other that the place reminded them of somewhere but they could not think of its name. Edmund said it was like somewhere in Narnia, in the Narnia world, only the mountains were bigger and the waterfalls more powerful and beautiful. The more they saw, the more they recognized that the land they were in was very much like Narnia, only not like it. It was then that Farsight, the eagle, spread his wings and soar 30, 40 feet up into the air, circled round and then alighted to the ground. Kings and queens, he cried, we have all been blind. We are only beginning to see where we are. From up there I have seen it all. Narnia is not dead. This is Narnia. Diggory, the oldest character in the story, explained to the others that the real Narnia was before them, and the Narnia that they had known was only a shadow or a copy. Quote, all of the old Narnia that mattered, he said, all the dear creatures have been drawn into the real Narnia through the door. And of course it is different, as different as a real thing is from a shadow or as a waking life is from a dream. Lewis goes on to confess to the reader that it is hard to explain how the newly discovered Narnia was different from the old. He explains it by saying, quote, You may have been in a room in which there was a window that looked out on a lovely bay. of the sea or a green valley that wound away among the mountains. And in the wall of that room opposite to the window there may have been a looking glass And as you turned away from the window, you suddenly caught sight of the sea or that valley all over again in the looking glass. And the sea in the mirror, or the valley in the mirror, were in one sense just the same as the real ones. Yet at the same time they were somehow different. Deeper, more meaningful, more wonderful, more like places in a story that you have never heard, but very much want to know If what we experience in this life will be shown to be of limited dimensions, of what is more beautiful and rich in the life next. We may wonder, at least I wonder, why we find so much enjoyment in this life. I have even questioned if it is wrong to enjoy myself as much as I do in this life. as if I am not aware that this is not my home. Am I somehow clinging to the shadow of a world if I want to grow old with my wife? Watch my children, have children, and look forward to each Christmas day. Such questions are also answered in Lewis's story. It was the unicorn who summed up what everyone else was feeling. He stamped his right front hoof on the ground and neighed and then cried, quote, I have come home at last. This is my real country. I belong here. This is the land I have been looking for all my life, though I never knew it till now. The reason why we loved the old Narnia is that it sometimes looked like this. Thus I conclude, along with Lewis, that we can enjoy moments in this life that are right, holy, and good, because they look a little like the ones we will know more fully when heaven is our home. For some people, it is difficult to imagine heaven because it is hard to think upon one's life without struggle without the sweating of the brow, without overcoming obstacles, without having to fix something or build something But nowhere does God say that some such things won't be a part of heaven. What he assures us is that what is painful in this old earth will be no more And with new bodies, who can know what God will have us do with them? But when we do have those moments of heaven on earth where we are nearest to our spouse Or laughing with our children, or enjoying fellowship with other Christians, we can know. We can know that God wants us to enjoy such moments because we get an idea. a taste of the good that awaits as God will be among us. It is here that we should rehearse to whom John is first sharing this vision. It was with first century Christians who were suffering persecution because of their faith in Jesus Christ, as their lives were physically threatened as well as their livelihood. Such Christians were rejected socially and politically by both the Jews and the Gentiles. There was no greater need that such people had in that day than the hope of heaven. I suppose there are many practical applications to be made of John's vision of heaven We could allow it to be a vision for us in times of trouble in this life. We could examine each stone or each numeric symbol in relation to the many others like it throughout Scripture as We've begun a little bit to do. We could even make up a special study of heaven and call it heavenology. And we could do a lot more, I suppose. And yet it seems to me that one thing we should do, the least of these things we should do, is rest in the knowledge that there is such a place and that we will go there someday. Amen. Let us pray. A gracious God, for this vision we are grateful. It is a gift to your people to imagine what it will be someday when all is finished and you raise us and you give us everything new. And we rest in you. May this vision help us conquer all our demons, help us conquer all of our sins, and help us live for you to the end of our days. As we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Reasons to Look East
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We're looking at Revelation chapter 22. We're winding down our series on the book of Revelation. How do you know when someone is telling the truth? You cannot really know unless the person has a track record. If I have lied to you in the past Grossly exaggerated a story, sugar-coated a message, or misrepresented myself, your first inclination would Be to not trust me when I spoke. Everything I said would carry a background voice That would drown out my words. You would be saying to yourself, he is probably lying, or I can't believe a word he is telling me. When we have known people for a long time, we tend to weigh their words. We learn when they are likely telling the truth and when they are exaggerating. We can believe what someone says in certain instances and doubt what they say in others. For instance, when our emerettis senior warden Would tell me something about the building or church finances or a story concerning a ministerial need within the church, I would believe every word he uttered But when he would tell me about his exploits as an athlete when he was younger, well, I tend to listen with different ears When the subject is the Holy Scripture, we should always be confident in that what we are reading is the truth. And yet, some struggle believing the visions and miracles. I knew of a young adult convert to Christianity that he said he believed in the Lord Jesus Christ as his Savior, but the stories such as Jesus walking on water and the feeding of five thousand people with only Five loaves and two fish, those were harder to accept. It took the young man time, walking with the Lord and seeing personal miracles in his life. To relieve any doubts that were first there. Applying all of this To the vision of John that we've been reading about in the book of Revelation. And the passing of time works in the favor of our confidence and then works against our confidence. The passing of time, since John wrote this epistle, has allowed us to see God's promises, his word through his prophets come to pass. We are told, for instance, through the prophet Isaiah, that a sign would be given of a virgin giving birth We were told through the prophet Micah that Bethlehem, although a small city, would be chosen as the place of the Savior's birth Some 700 years later, Isaiah's prophecy was fulfilled. Some 500 years later, Micah's prophecy was fulfilled. I was just reading this week how both secular and Christian scholars believe Jesus was indeed born in Bethlehem within a cave. A cave that was written about by historian figures dating back to the 2nd century A. D. , and where the Church of Nativity sits today. Our Christmas depictions are usually of a wooden stable, but in the days of Jesus, wood would have been scarce. Stables were likely small caves. But back to the dating I was referencing. As we examine John's revelation, his vision of the second coming of Christ and the new heaven and the new earth. We are approximately one thousand nine hundred and sixty-eight years removed. I get that number speculating that John received his vision, his revelation at A. D. 55. That is over. Twice the amount of years that it took for Isaiah's words to be fulfilled, and almost four times longer than it took for Micah's prophecy to be fulfilled While time has proven God's word through his prophets to be true, before the vision of John, it seems like a long time coming in John's vision, comparatively. Thus it can be asked, can we still trust in John's vision? And simply ask, is Jesus actually really going to come again? So far, we are given no reason not to trust. We can recognize John's words of warning and judgment and apply them to the fall of Jerusalem in 70 A. D. We can identify the suffering of Christians that John describes as those that were experienced by the first century church We can also draw connecting lines from John's described persecution of the church to every century since his day as somewhere in the world Christians have been a chief target of oppression. Even today, in Muslim, communist, and pluralistic countries, John's message of enduring under persecution brings hope to Christians Although much of what John describes has already taken place, again, what about the return of Jesus? Is he simply slow in keeping his promise? Does the delay tell us that it has a chance of not being fulfilled? Well, before we answer such questions, let us look more closely at the beginning of Revelation chapter 22. The beginning of the chapter 22 finds John in the middle of being shown what heaven will be like when all that is evil has been thrown into the lake of fire. And the Son of God dwells permanently with his people. What John sees is paradise restored. This is Eden, only it is not Eden. It is the heavenly Eden, or we can say the true Eden. In Eden, four rivers flowed, giving needed nourishment to all life. Now there is one river, the river of life. The prophet Ezekiel described such a river. Jesus testified that he had water from the river, calling it living water, to give to those who followed him. And here is that living water that nourishes all who are living in the true Eden. Next, the tree of life is described. Described as spread all along the great street of the holy city and by the river of life. What was once forfeited by Adam and Eve and denied to succeeding generations is now fully restored. In Ezekiel, there are multiple trees bearing fruit monthly and growing leaves for healing. Those many trees are here, one tree. The healing power represents the far-reaching power and effect of death and resurrection of Christ. From the tree and in the holy city, eternal life only found in God is perpetually available to his people. With the described river and tree of life available to all within the city, the curse that was placed upon the human race because of Adam's sin is here forever lifted. The reference to the throne of God and the Lamb being in the city is similar to the description in chapter 21 of them being physically present among God's people. This is more intimately described as the people will be able to see God, to see God face to face. Such closeness to God could not be known before because man was in sin Simply seeing the face of Almighty God, who is holy and true, would strike a man dead. Now that sin is removed, there are no more barriers between man and God. Men may see God and serve him Although perpetual service does not sound appealing in this life, let it be understood that with the chains of sin having fallen off Men will know for the first time that freedom is service, and that mankind will fulfill what he was created to be. We should notice that although John is shown the river of life and shown the tree of life, he does not actually see the face of God in his vision. From verse 4 on, he speaks about these events in the future tense. Even though what John sees is in one sense real, It is also yet to be realized in its fullest measure. This is why verse 6 is necessary and where we today must receive our confidence. The angel said to John, and so he says to us, quote, these words are trustworthy and true. The Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, sent his angel to show his servants the things that must soon take place. It was necessary for the angel to speak these words to John and to us, for while living in the present. It can be difficult to imagine and even appreciate the heaven that is to come. And as stated earlier, with the with the passage of time, our confidence can be weakened that what is promised here regarding the return of Christ The defeat of evil and the coming down of a new heaven and a new earth come to pass? Will it come to pass? So how can we know that what we read here will actually take place? First, we can have confidence because God spoke these words himself. These are not the words of men, but of God. As a person of simple faith might say, God said it, I believe it, and that settles it. But a logician would not let us get away with such reasoning because it is circular. Logically, we cannot defend God's promises by arguing that God said it. To say I can believe what God says because I can trust what God says is not an airtight argument. Although it might be enough for some, there is more we can offer. The second reason we can have confidence that these things will come to pass is the prophecies that have been fulfilled. Have already spoken of two of them, both regarding the birth of Christ, and of course there are many others. No one can read David's words in Psalm 22 or the prophet Isaiah's words in chapter 23 of his prophecy, and not know that the suffering of Jesus on the cross is being described. The point being that since God has a track record of always keeping his promises, we can have confidence that he will keep these promises of his second coming. This only works for a while, however, and as time passes, our flesh becomes discontented. We may even argue that God has never waited this long to fulfill his promises. After all, God's prophecies to Abraham took about a thousand years to fulfill through Moses. His promises to Isaiah took, as I said, over 700 years. His promises regarding the coming of the kingdom of heaven are now, again, 1,968 years and counting. It would appear that God is off his average. But actually, but actually he is not. But the first promise, the first prophecy was that a seed would come from Eve, that is a sun, and that sun would crush the serpent's head. That seed was Christ making the promise fulfilled over 6,000 years earlier. If God's track record is not enough, then we can look at the veracity of the Bible as a whole For to doubt this word in the book of Revelation regarding the coming of Christ and the kingdom of heaven is to doubt Holy Scripture as a whole. Archaeological discoveries have again and again confirmed the stories told in the Bible The city of Jericho has been uncovered. Tablets from Egypt referencing the Haburi people sweeping through the land of Canaan have been found. Secular documents have corroborated the gospel accounts of the regions described, the customs of the people, and the political leaders of the day that the Bible describes. And although there are not artifacts that confirm the kingship of David, for example, or actual writings of St. Paul. There have been no discoveries that disprove David's reign in Israel or that Paul wrote 13 letters that are now a part of the New Testament. As I challenge my confirmation class and new members class every year, try and uncover an archaeological find that contradicts anything in Holy Scripture. Not one exists. Another reason we can trust in the veracity of the Bible are the eyewitness accounts. John's vision, for example, was seen by John, who then wrote it down. He did not write down what other people saw. He wrote down what he saw. It is the same for his gospel. He states his eyewitness account in the first chapter of his gospel. Quote We have seen his glory, he said of Jesus, the glory of the one and only who came from the Father, full of grace and truth. Matthew. Matthew was an eyewitness to what he wrote. Mark wrote down what Peter witnessed. And Luke wrote down what the rest of the disciples remembered. These are not the words of what someone else said about what someone else said. They are the accounts of those who lived amongst Jesus, tasted the food that he ate, heard the words he spoke, and embraced him when they greeted and when they parted. Another reason we can trust in the veracity of the Bible is its moral consistency Even though there are differences in moral behavior, such as man of old having more than one wife and even having concubines, The condemnation of extramarital relations is for every age. In certain places, the Lord said that He overlooked the sin of man for a time. That means that he waited for the right time to call men to a higher moral standard. The standard was always there. Whereas men of old might have more than one wife, the Lord then called his people to have only one wife, and after that he called each man to no longer lust after another woman besides his wife Other moral standards were raised as well, such as going from thou shalt not murder, to warning us that if we hate a man, we have committed murder in our heart. The moral consistency is a high standard of morality for those who claim Christ as their Savior. Thus far we have quite a case built up For believing the promises of God regarding the coming again of Christ and the establishment of the kingdom of heaven. But above all Above all that we have said so far, the primary reason why we can believe the promises and all that the Bible says is the person of Jesus Christ. Jesus is the primary reason we believe the promises of heaven. In fact When it comes right down to believing anything about the scripture, it is the person of Jesus Christ that validates it all. You see, the skeptics may convince themselves that the creation account in Scripture is a fable, and that the existence of this earth and all its inhabitants are a result of chance But they cannot deny the person of Jesus. Literary scholars can doubt that John wrote the three epistles attributed to him and the book of Revelation, because they see variations in the style of the Greek. That they cannot deny the person of Jesus. Scholars can doubt the integrity of the Apostle Paul And portray him as a man out for power, power over this small band of Christians of the first century, but they cannot deny the person of Jesus. All of these issues can be cause for doubting the scriptures, but every man who is honest must answer the question of Jesus. Who was he? Who was Jesus? That question gets more and more important. For today, it is popular to question whether Jesus ever existed at all, which actual historians, actual historians do not doubt. In fact, in a debate between John Lennox and Richard Dawkins, Dawkins frustratingly admitted that historians do not doubt the existence of Jesus. But who was he? Who was Jesus? If you settle for the answer that Jesus was only a man who taught good things, You then have to account for the miracles that are attributed to him. If you for a moment believe the miracles were made up, then you must account for the eyewitnesses. Consider that the most important miracle, his resurrection, could have been easily proven false if it were false. If you settle for Jesus being a madman or Jesus being a liar, then you must make account for the wisdom of his words and the integrity of his life. When the person of Jesus is looked at honestly and sincerely, there is only one conclusion a person can come to. He is who he said he is. Once that is established, Jesus' verification of the Old Testament is good enough for us. Jesus' teachings and standards are good enough for us. And Jesus' words that he is coming back. And coming quickly to establish a new heaven and a new earth are words that we can place our confidence in. Jesus is coming, bet your life on it. Let us pray. Gracious and heavenly Father, the evidence is before us, and we thank you for it. And we do put our confidence in your word that Jesus is indeed coming again. And so we can say adamantly, as John did, Amen. Come. Lord Jesus, Amen

sermons.title: Thanksgiving 2024
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the introduction To his book The Screw Tape Letters, C. S. Lewis says the following We must picture hell as a state where everyone is perpetually concerned about his own dignity and advancement. Where everyone has a grievance, and where everyone lives the deadly, serious passions of envy, self-importance, and resentment. Of course, for the Christian and for the Christian life, the opposite of each one of those descriptives is to be true. That is the brilliance of C. S. Lewis's book. The opposite is true. The enemy in the book is actually God And the master, so-called, is the devil. So if the Christian life and the church in general is to be the opposite of what Lewis describes of those in hell, We are to be perpetually concerned about the dignity of others and the advancement of others While holding no grievances against our fellow man, and where we live with lively passions of gratefulness for others along with self-denial and a joy for the success of others That is indeed a tall order, but it is also the life that Jesus lived. What stands out in the description of hell in comparison to what we have come to do tonight, which is to give thanks. are the ugly sins of envy and resentment. Envy and resentment are the opposite of giving thanks, but they are easy to do, easy to practice. To prove how easy it is to fall into the sins of envy and resentment, we merely need to look at how the mainstream media in the West does its job. The questions posed have the goal of conjuring up envy and resentment rather than pursuing any truth that will help the audience Consider this question. How did the election make you feel The questioner knows very well how the election made the person being interviewed feel They simply want the person being interviewed to spew out envy and resentment. It makes for good television It gets a lot of hits on the internet. And it likely puts a voice to how the media itself feels while also trying to pretend to be objective. Envy and resentment do well to describe why the tenth commandment is necessary. Have you ever considered just how unique the last commandment is We say that the first five deal with our relationship with God. We worship God only We revere his name. We set a day aside to corporately worship him. And by honoring those in authority over us, we honor him The last five are to deal with our relationship with our fellow man. And note that they are all commandments against actions we take. And commandments six through nine are physical actions we take. Murder, adultery, stealing. And bearing false witness are things we do with our minds and our bodies. I say minds and bodies because as Jesus taught The likes of murder and adultery begin in the heart. That is why he calls his followers to address issues of the heart before they become actions of the body But the tenth commandment is different. It deals primarily, if not solely, with the heart and the spirit of a person. Consider that you can covet what your neighbor has and take no action. You can break the commandment without doing anything physically. It can be practiced in your mind and heart, and no one can know. Coveting is a sneaky sin, for there may be no empirical evidence it is taking place or that it took place, and yet God has placed it in his top ten.
