If it makes the top ten, we can be assured how important it is Although I have given the following example many times as it is a staple in our confirmation class, and Scott, who is here, will attest because I think Scott spent in 20 years of my confirmation class. I give it again because I can think of a no better example, although this time I changed the gender and the item to covet. Let's say a girl has an older sister, and it is her older sister's birthday For her birthday, she received a Barbie doll. And she loves on that Barbie doll, playing so many imaginary scenes and lifestyles. Well grooming her blonde hair and living in her toy Malibu Beach House. Our little girl watches her older sister play with her doll and desperately Wants one like it. But it is not her birthday, and Christmas isn't close. So our little girl gets her Our little girl sets her sight on playing with her older sister's doll She asks her mother if she can play with the doll when her sister is away, and her mother forbids her, because it is up to the older sister to decide who plays with her doll. Well, one morning both the older sister and mother were shopping, and the young girl takes advantage and sneaks into her older sister's room and begins playing with the doll. She even takes it outside for Barbie to ride in her toy convertible car. Only the car Starts to go too fast down the driveway and ends up smashing into the garbage can, cracking the side of the car. Our little girl panics, knowing that her older sister and mother will return home soon. She quickly gets back into the house and returns the toys to their proper place. While saying nothing. When the older sister returns home, she immediately checks her toys, having a suspicion that her sister would play with them when she was gone. She notices the cracked toy car and runs to her mother. Next, both mother and older sister are standing in front of our young girl, with mother asking our young girl if she played with her sister's Barbie doll toys. And our little girl responds emphatically with a no. In that brief scenario, how many commandments did our young girl break? Well, she coveted by wanting the toys her sister had. She stole from her sister by damaging part of the toy and therefore taking value away from the toy. She dishonored her parents by ignoring her mother's clear instructions. She then lied about it to her sister and mother. And finally, we can say it all occurred on Sunday, so she is also a Sabbath breaker. That is five commandments broken. And we can add that whenever you break one of the commandments, you have broken the first commandment, because God was not your God at the time you sinned. So six commandments out of ten were broken. And it all started. It all started with breaking commandment number 10, coveting. It began with a sin in the heart and in the mind As you can see, coveting, which we are defining as envy and resentment, is a dangerous sin. Think upon all the things we can cover. The list in the commandment itself shows how extensive the sin can be. And again, it it doesn't have to be a physical thing. We can covet the time of others. We can covet relationships that others have. We can covet another person's ethic or good fortune or personality. Or opportunities, or background, or history, or family tree, or education, or moral fortitude, and we can go on As the example given shows, once that sin is committed, a domino of sins can fall Of course, I do not describe the dangers of coveting to be only discouraging, but as a mere warning. The way to combat coveting is what we came here to do. We are here to give thanks. We're here to give thanks to God and to praise Him for providing all that we need and certainly more. And know, beloved, know that the devil hates it when we give God thanks. When we are satisfied with what has been given to us, what we have been blessed with And I realize that when living in a consumer society like ours and having disposable income like we do We can be tempted much easier to buy what we don't need and to want what others have. But such temptation is easier to resist and contentment is much easier to achieve. When we count our blessings and give God thanks for each one of them, and to know, to truly know. That the only thing he promised to those who follow him, as was read in our gospel reading, the only thing he promised was clothing for each day and our daily bread. I close with this truth. As we come to give thanks tonight and possibly give public testimony For what we are thankful for, it must be said that just as envy and resentment begin in the heart, which is to say, internally, So does being thankful begin internally. And as long as we are thankful internally, God is honored and praised Amen.

sermons.title: Love your wives
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated I have called this series of sermons the Rambling of a Rector, and that gives me the opportunity to preach on what I think I need to preach on. That which is Weighing on my heart. Husbands, I wonder how you would respond Two weeks ago, I arrive home from the parish, and as I walk up the stairs, as our house is a split level, I see My 58-year-old wife, with her back turned to me, sitting on the counter that separates the kitchen proper from the dining room. She is sitting on the side of the kitchen sink with her feet in the sink itself. As I walk around, I then see a three-year-old girl smiling from ear to ear, also with her feet in the sink. With both having large smiles on their faces, it is next announced that they are giving themselves pedicures and thus soaking their feet in lavender soap. Seeing that moment and remembering it brings a rather large smile to my face. Such love, such care, such vulnerability. I have become well aware of how my love for my wife affects how she loves and cares about and serves others When she is secure in my love for her, she is free to be what she needs to be for others. Unconditional love, uninhibited love, does that. It frees the recipient. It secures them and helps them to be free to love others. And so, husbands, are your wives free to love others Husbands, are your wives secure in your relationship with them so that they can be free to be themselves and not perceive life with you as a burden? I have become aware recently of Christian marriages dissolving, and not because of the sins Holy Scripture allow for divorce, which are infidelity and abandonment These marriages, marriages of confessing Christians, are ending in divorce because of falling out of love and becoming disconnected from one another. What seems to be missing for many Christians is the moral weight of what it means to be married, and the immoral weight of what it means to break vows Vows made to a spouse and vows made to God. I qualify this sermon stating that while writing this sermon, I did not think of any particular couple who has divorced, nor am I thinking of any couple that is headed for divorce. What I am concerned about is the truth being heard from the pulpit Regarding what it means to be in a Christian marriage, and for you to hear before being tempted to perceive yourself no longer compatible to your spouse. I want to address this in a sermon while the fire is hot, as we just celebrated a new Christian marriage yesterday. The reading from Ephesians is popularly read at wedding services, and understandably so. However, modern readings at modern weddings like to avoid the word submit when reading verse 22 of chapter 5. So they choose wordings such as, entrust, entrust yourself to your husband. When it is next read that husbands are to love their wives, the focus is on the romantic love that Sinatra Air Supply and Shiran have sung about. But that love, the romantic kind, is not what is being described in Ephesians or anywhere else a husband is called to love his wife The love here does come from the Greek word that is used to describe God's love. But it is not the meaning of that love that is important as the analogy of that love. Which is to love in the same manner, in the same way, that Jesus loved and loves his church, his church, who are his people. And how did Jesus love his people? Paul says it clearly in the verse. Jesus gave his life for his people. The conclusion that I am preaching is that the stability and sanctification of a Christian marriage is first and foremost dependent upon the husband loving his wife. Thus, on the Sunday before Father's Day, men are being called to stabilize and sanctify their marriages by better loving their wives. A husband, a husband's love must come first because God's love came first. This includes leading and not abdicating. In St. John's first cited letter, we read this from chapter 3, verse 7. Beloved, let us love one another, for love is of God, and everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. He who does not love does not know God, for God is love. In this, the love of God was manifested toward us that God has sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through Him. In this is love. Not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his son to be the propitiation for our sins. To make the point more clearly, some translations read: But God first loved us. The emphasis that God's love came first is essential. He is the initiator in our relationship with him. He is the person in the relationship that sent his law. He then initiated again and sent his prophets. He then initiated again and sent his only son. He then initiated again by sending the Holy Spirit, which we commemorate today, which means that God is with us always. This example of initiating is to be copied by husbands. The man is to pursue the woman before marriage, and the husband is to pursue the wife in marriage. This means that husbands are to show love for their wife first, and when love is forgotten, the husband is to be the one who initiates its restoration in the relationship. Now, husbands, I know this is not easy. I know by experience. Let us be honest that when we are in a serious disagreement with our wives, Not getting them to agree with us, we are tempted next to feel disrespected. And when we allow that emotion of feeling disrespected to take over our hearts and minds We don't want to initiate anything with our wives, especially not the restoration of love. But that is exactly What we are to do. We are to be the ones who first die to ourselves and pursue our wives so that love is restored. Because. Because God's love came first. Also, a husband's love must meet the standard spelled out in 1 Corinthians 13. This means to never take advantage of a weaker vessel, a woman, physically, emotionally, and certainly not spiritually. It is absolutely appalling to hear testimonies of women who have been abused by their husbands in the name of Jesus, for the justification of Paul's instruction for wives to submit to their husbands. The logic of the husband seems to be that if she is to submit to me in all things and I am not getting from her physically what I desire, then I can just take it when I want it. This attitude for body is mine. Paul says so in First Corinthians chapter seven. The logic of the husband seems to be that if I'm not getting emotionally what I want from my wife, then I'm going to take my emotions out on her, because she then is the cause of my anger and my bitterness. Beloved men are cowards who think and act in such a manner. And ministers who do not rebuke such men are worse than cowards. So let us take this type of thinking and compare it and contrast it to what is taught in 1 Corinthians chapter 13. After listening the gift of tongues, the gift of prophecy, the gift of power to perform miracles, the feeding the poor and being willing to die for the faith He says, if love is excluded from such gifts and practices, those gifts and practices are useless. He then says what love is: love suffers long. Husbands, do you suffer long with your wives by enduring their longer stories or putting up with their supposed annoying habits or simply accepting that women are naturally different than men? Love is kind. Now the kind that is being referred to here is not the same that are on signs, you know, placed on telephone poles and street corners that say be kind Those signs are nothing but confusing. Should we be kind to child molesters? Should we be kind to arsonists? Of course not. The instruction to be kind needs to have a context. And this context is to be kind to our fellow Christians, and to do so in order to bring glory to God. And so, husbands, you must ask yourself if you are kind to your wife, who asks of you to do chores and then prods you when you delay. Are you kind when she puts things away that you were using and now you can't find the thing because it is now where it is supposed to be? You can guess that such scenarios I did not make up. Next, love does not envy Husbands, do you envy your wife for the friendships she has while you have few and maybe none? Envy includes jealousy Husbands, do you become jealous of your relationship with your wife that your wife has with other men only because you are too insecure in your masculinity? Next, love is not proud. Husbands, do you think you are better than your wife? Do you think you are smarter, wiser, more capable of getting along in this world? Next, love does not behave rudely. Husbands, are you appropriate with your wives even when no one else is around? Do you make fun of your wife to friends? Do you tell stories of your wife that embarrass her? Next, love does not seek its own Husbands, do you decide on how the money is spent without consulting your wives? Do you say yes to every motorized toy you want and no to her desire to have some perfume? And how about intimacy? Do you seek your own only? At this point in the sermon, if you are a husband here today, you are probably feeling a bit ticked on. And some of these questions and their implications have likely landed like a gut punch. So let's breathe a little bit by turning to the positives of what love does instead of what it does not. Love rejoices with truth. You husbands are the pillar of truth, to be the pillar of truth in your home Truth is to be loved by you, expressed by you, and a standard you expect everyone in your home to live up to. Now I always need to qualify whenever I speak about truth because too many of us think that truth is telling others what we think. That is not truth. It is instead your opinion. If someone asks your opinion, then you should tell it. But some sugar on it, if it's painful. Just because you go around telling people your opinion does not make you a bastion of truth. But facing up to what is true And being willing to speak the truth about God and morality is being a bastion of truth. Next, love bears all things. This is similar to suffering long, but includes taking on the emotional and spiritual burdens of your wife. Husbands are to help relieve their wives of the pressures that life places upon them. Husbands regularly say, I got this, when their wives are overcome with emotion. Next, love hopes. Husbands are to keep hope in every aspect of life Both husbands and wives worry about the faith and spiritual health of their children and their children's spouses and their grandchildren and other loved ones. And as they pray together, it is to be the husband that reminds the wife that it is not where their children are in the moment that matters most, but where God is going to place them. when things finally work to the good. And next, husbands are to endure all things. To endure is to never quit, to never give up, to never lose hope, to stay the righteous course until the end, which is the end of the husband's days on earth. Husbands are to be the most consistent presence in every home. They are to be the ones that everyone in the home looks to in times of crisis, worry, and confusion. And part of that need to endure is in husbands taking on the sins that occur in their relationships with their wives. Now I I have been scoffed at by men when I counsel them in this truth. But I did not make it up. I got it from Paul's instruction in Ephesians 5, where he tells husbands to love their wives as Jesus loves his church. All we need to do is note all the ways that Jesus loves his church, and one of the very large and important ways he loves his church is to take on the church's sin. He makes our sins his own by applying his atoning sacrifice to them. And so husbands are to take responsibility for the sins in their marriage. This does not mean, as some have argued, that I am saying that the woman has no responsibility for the sins within the marriage. She most certainly does, but she is to stand before God for her own sins. The husband is to stand before God, being responsible for both their sins within the marriage. Thus, his role is to be a priest to his wife Which is to guide her with him to the foot of the cross and seek the forgiveness of God when there is failure. in their marriage and to seek wisdom of God on how to repair the hurts that came from the failure. And it is the husband's role to make every effort to change the character of the marriage So that the same failures will not occur again. I hope you see that taking on such a role should not be controversial, but instead beautiful. And speaking of what is beautiful, my final point in order to strengthen Christian marriages is to know that a husband's love is rewarded by a beautiful wife. It is said in our culture that beauty is subjective. The Bible does not agree. The Bible describes beauty as objective. Esther, Rebecca, and Bathsheba were all called beautiful in reference to their outward appearance. And the passages don't say that the people thought they were beautiful, but instead it is stated in an objective truth. And it may be true that the manner a husband treats his wife may add to her outward appearance. Because she is motivated by the love of her husband, a wife may take care of herself and her appearance. She may put on a happier countenance. She may look younger than she is because the love of her husband makes her feel younger. But no outward appearance will improve unless the husband speaks love to his wife. A woman can't know how much she is loved by her husband unless she is told, and not just a quick I love you. Time needs to be taken to explain what a husband loves about his wife. And I know that for many men such words do not come naturally. But that is why we have been gifted with passages such as in the Bible from the Song of Solomon. And why other men are gifted in the secular world with poetic thoughts, such can help free the tied-up tongue. But say something, good man, say something. But the beauty I am referring to is not outward. For no matter who the woman is, she will age, and outward beauty will lessen. The beauty I am referring to is what Peter describes in his first epistle, chapter 3, where he instructs wives with these words. Your beauty should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes, but from the inner disposition of your heart The unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in God's sight. For this is how the holy women of the past adorned themselves. They put their hope in God I swear to you that in my fading eyes, my wife is without a doubt more beautiful than when I first fell in love with her, and it is because of what she has adorned herself with inwardly. She has adorned herself inwardly so much so that she can climb up on a kitchen counter along with a three-year-old granddaughter and soak their feet in lavender soap. Husbands, love your wives as Jesus loves, loved, and loves his church. It is a lifelong calling, and no one else is called to do it. But you. Let us pray. Gracious and heavenly Father, we know that standard is there. We've read that passage many, many times. And we recognize that there's no doubt we fall short as men. But Father, give us the courage to act like men, to act like godly men, and fear you and love like you And love our wives, that they may be beautiful inside and out. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen

sermons.title: Where do we go from here?
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.source_file: Where do we go from here.txt
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated I want to start off by thanking Father Bill for filling in so ably. One of the warnings of going on a sabbatical is that the congregation might be or get used to you being gone and they don't think they need you anymore And uh Bill gives us that sense, to be sure. It became fairly clear to Bobby Lynn and I before we left for England That our oldest child did not have confidence in our traveling acumen, having the question unspoken, how are they going to get there? Having traveled with us to Greece a few years ago and believing in our inability to communicate effectively, he anticipated some costly mistakes along the way. And a few did happen. But thankfully, they were not costly. For instance, our first meal in London was fish and chips in a pub. In those scenarios, you order at the bar, and they bring the food to you. So I ordered at the bar, and the woman taking my order said No paid my paid stop and I froze, I didn't know how to respond Seeing my look, she got a little upset and said the same faster and more terse. The pays by pays out Still looking puzzled, she said, You get a side. So pays my page or south. I didn't realize she was giving me side options Which I did not expect because in America the chips are the side. I chose the peas because I wasn't sure what the rest of the options were. When I told Bobby Lynn what had happened, she told me that about mashed peas, mashed peas, and that she was encouraged to try them The next time we had lunch, we did try them and guess what they they taste like peas The next instance was in Paris, where they are truly rude to you if you don't speak French. Bob Lin was frightened to speak to anyone, so I did most of the communicating because I am used to not being liked. When I engaged a French person, I did as I was told. I said bonjour, and I ended with merci. With the rest of my communication being hand gestures, you know, nodding, shaking my hand, shaking my head. And that works. Until we got back to London, directly from Paris. And I went to order at the Hotel Café while we waited for our room. And I was still in Paris mode. So I ordered using hand gestures. And the woman stopped me. She said, are you trying to use sign language? I then spoke in the English that I know And finally this last example, when I arrived when we arrived in Iceland on our way home, that's where our stopover was. We were waiting to deplane and I asked Bobby Lynn what our next connecting number, flight number was Understand that when we are in public, we don't like other people hearing our conversation, and so we speak in quiet voices. Problem is we can't hear each other. So this is how the conversation went. Me. What number is our connecting flight? Her answer, 1463. Me, I hear, 4063. As we get off the plane and make our way to the gate, she asks Did I say our flight number was 1461? I say, no, 4063. And she says, okay. Thankfully, there are reader boards that confirm how ridiculous we can be. So I suppose it is understandable. That there would be questions as to how are they going to get there. After the first few visits to cathedrals in England There was a similar reoccurring question that I kept asking myself, which is how have we gotten here? The we, I am referring to in the question, is modern Christians. And the here is the manner we express our faith as compared to how Christians expressed their faith thousands of years ago and even prior to the 1980s. I am aware that I have addressed similar types of questions in the past, especially being influenced by the likes of Dr. Carl Truman. Who correctly diagnosed our age as the therapeutic age, which means that we want to solve our spiritual problems By way of professional counseling, positive thinking, pharmaceuticals, and personal acceptance for love. In other words, it is having faith that our personal struggles that used to be called sins are healed by those who know Freud without knowing Jesus And who are adept at writing new prescriptions. That being understood, I want to broaden our diagnosis of ourselves and the rest of the modern Christian church. With that question, how did we get where we are, considering where we have been? And yes, I begin with my experience at viewing several cathedrals When considering the work necessary to build such structures, and the time to build them, and the sacrifices made by the builders and those who contributed but never even saw the completed structure. How did we go from that to Kathagymus sanctatorius? Cafetym is sanctatoriums. I am referring to those structures that can be a cafeteria for lunch, a gym after school, a sanctuary on Sundays, and an all-purpose room for other gatherings. It appears that no thought when designing and building these buildings included what is beautiful and most honoring to God. What appears to govern the thoughts of those who are responsible for such structures is what is most practical. And making what is practical as a priority is following the idol of pragmatism Pragmatism says that what works, what works is most important. What is the easiest is the thing to do. Pragmatism tells the builder that knows the material he is using is some far to use it anyway. Pragmatism has parents bowing to it when they choose to buy a large home instead of paying to ensure that their children have a Christian education. Pragmatism is followed when a young couple decides to live together to save money. And even Christian couples deciding to have sexual relations outside of marriage because they are going to get married someday So pragmatism is one reason we have gotten to where we are now. It is the philosophy for those who are compromisers. In sticking with the theme of isms, I am making this next one up. We have gotten where we are, because too many bow to happy ism Happyism is believing that God, first and foremost, wants me to be happy in this life. The number of times I have heard the justification of behavior practiced and decisions made that go directly against Holy Scripture because people believe that God wants them to be happy Would astound you. First, there is no agreement as to what is meant by happy. And second, there is not one scripture that backs such thinking. Happy defined by Scripture would be to be at peace with God and your fellow man And to be at peace with God, you have to be in obedience to God, having your sins forgiven. To be at peace with your fellow man is to forgive him his wrongs Toward you, and to live in such a way that expresses the love of God toward him. Thirdly No martyr, no martyr would know what you are talking about when you say that God wants his people to be happy. And that means in this life happy. And that means to enjoy desires of the flesh and movements of emotions. They are the ones, the martyrs who cry out even now, how long, O Lord? How long? Because the happiness they know is when death is defeated in finality and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire, and they see God face to face, having having received New bodies that will last for eternity. So another answer to the question, how do we get here? Is the idol of happierism. The next answer to the same question is a better known ism, and that is subjectivism This is another example also of Christians following the culture and its norms instead of walking in the kingdom of God. Subjectivism says that truth is an oppressive concept that can only be experienced by the individual who defines what truth is. And so Christians mimic phrases such as, my truth, or speak your truth. Of course, there is no such thing as individual truth. There is truth and nothing else but falsehood. Subjectivism, when bowed to, makes you call one person they and them Subjectivism when worship forces girls to compete with boys and to agree that anatomy is a social construct rather than a most ugly protrusion So another answer to the question, how do we get here, is the idol of subjectivism. And finally, for this sermon, anyways, is the idol of individualism. Individualism is closely related to subjectivism with a special emphasis on the individual and what the individual likes. A poster child for individualism would be Veruga Salt. in Willy Wonka and the Chocolate Factory, who wanted what she wanted without exception, and she wanted it now Some preachers decades ago tried to point out the selfishness in individualism that had Christians making choices on how they wanted to worship God by insisting on what they like. And didn't life in music, prayers, service flank, even sermon topics But many Christians didn't stop, and soon churches became like corner stores that create an inventory based on what consumers would buy. And conversations after church services continued to consist of statements such as, I didn't like that chorus we sang, but I enjoyed the first one. And did you like the sermon? I thought his last point was weak, but he told a funny story. And preachers like myself Keep saying, what's the difference if you liked anything in the service? It's not supposed to be about you, and especially not about what you like. But the comments about what it's like continue. And so another answer to the question, how do we get here, is the idol of individualism. You will be thankful to know, I trust, that I know my job is not to be simply pointing out what is wrong within the Christian church. But it is also to have answers for what we can do about what is wrong. And so I point us to a passage of scripture that was read in a worship service here during my absence It was from 2 Timothy chapter 3, where Paul lists to Timothy characteristics of the ungodly, characteristics that people will display near the end of time. He says that they will be lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents. ungrateful, unholy, unloving, unforgiving, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, without love of good Traitorous, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, and then he says this about them They will have a form of godliness, but deny its power But what is it to have a form of godliness? A form of godliness is to outwardly portray oneself as godly Without actually believing that how you behave outwardly has anything that results in the power of God being displayed. And add this next point to the mix. To be able to outwardly portray oneself as godly, you have to know what godliness is. And even non-professing Christians can know what godliness is and deny its power. Years ago, I witnessed an atheist debating a Christian, and the atheist tried to make the point. That the evolution of man came up with the idea of loving your neighbor as yourself And even though the Christian in the debate pointed out that such a statement was first made in the Bible, the atheist still insisted that evolving man would eventually come to the same conclusion. But what he didn't know is that there is inherent spiritual power in the godly act of loving your neighbor as yourself. What I am ultimately saying is that Christians need to repent. Repent of the sin of not having faith in the power of godliness. And then we need to start having faith that when we choose to live godly lives, God effectively moves in our lives and in the lives of those we touch. That spiritually awakens, spiritually teaches, encourages, and improves our trust, our faith in Him. That is what is meant by the power of godliness. Let me use an example I have already mentioned. The Christian couple who is fornicating together with the justification that they are going to be married someday, so that makes their behavior acceptable. Consider that they become convicted about their sin and confess it as sin and vow to remain celibate until they are married. What we are to believe about such choices and following through with such choices is that God brings power to such godliness. So that their consciences are clear and they are able to be more freely loving to each other and have respect for each other. And they are more free to bear up other people's burdens because their yoke has become light. And they are able to be more easily to forgive others, the wrongdoings done to them because they have been forgiven much. That beloved is power in godliness. Consider how many Christians, how many Christians deny the power of godliness? Christian couples become convinced that their differences cannot be overcome and divorce is unavoidable. To come to such a conclusion is to deny the power of godliness, which is to deny the power of forgiveness. The power of unconditional love, the power of keeping your vows, the power of dying the self, the power of putting other people's needs before your own. Let us go back to our isms. We discussed the dangers of the idol of pragmatism But what can make pragmatism fall like the idol of Degon fell before the Ark of the Covenant is caring about aesthetics, which is pursuing beauty. Beloved, the sanctuary we are beautifying will carry godly power In it, we are communicating to God and to ourselves and to anyone who visits us that beauty matters when we worship God corporately. And that we want to give him the best room we can afford so that we honor him in every way we know how. Believe that there is godly power and beauty, and then pursue it. The idol of happyism Can also fall when we choose to pursue the kingdom of God first and not pursue personal happiness in this life. I realize, in saying such, that the devil, if you are willing to listen to him, will tell you that I just said that God doesn't want you to be happy in this life. But I most certainly did not. I simply said that such is not to be our pursuit, and in fact, I am simply quoting Jesus. And we must believe that there is great power in pursuing first the kingdom of God, and there is great power in being willing to sacrifice our lives for the sake of the gospel spreading. That power, that power is revealed in saying that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church. The idol of subjectivism was next, and can also fall when we live by truth, which is speaking truth and never lying. Even when speaking will reveal our own sins. It is accepting truth even when it is uncomfortable and goes against our emotions We must believe that there is power in preaching, teaching, and praying of truth, even when, even when but a few are listening. We must believe that truth is worth losing friends for, worth losing our job for, worth losing our status, because Jesus Himself is the truth. And finally, the idol of individualism. The idol of individualism will fall When we believe in the power of living as the apostle described when he said, It is no longer I that live, but Christ that lives in me, and the life I now live, I live for him. Such is the proper standard for how Christians should use the pronoun I. For in each instance, Paul is not the focus, but instead the focus is Jesus first and last. And so there is power, power in dying to self, in picking up one's cross. And not caring for how other people perceive me, treat me, speak of me, or provoke me, because it is not me, but Christ. Beloved, do not doubt the power of social sacrifice. When people witness it, they know how it influences, and they either admire it or hate it. They hate it because they can't do it. And so the answer to the question, how do we get here? now shifts. It shifts to how do we get to where not only do we know the form of godliness, but that we also believe in its power. Lord Jesus, give us faith to know the power of godliness. Amen.

sermons.title: Small Righeousness
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. We are looking back at Ecclesiastes. We're back in the book of Ecclesiastes. And it is best for you to follow along in your Bibles, because you will get lost if you do not stay with me. And I put a sign there on the Bible pile To say, grab a Bible today. This is a good day to have a Bible. And if you need to sneak over there, because you didn't listen to my little note there, you can go ahead and do that and we'll we'll watch you as you go. I feel I must preface this sermon with a confession that the subject of righteousness can be both ambiguous and dry. I preached last week on the power of righteousness because Christians are to believe in such power. And too often we behave like the world and do not believe in such power. And I gave examples of righteousness, which is first What Jesus makes us because of his sacrifice on the cross, our righteousness is a result of his obedience, his suffering, his death, because he is our payment for our sins. Simply put, the righteousness of Jesus is imputed to us, which means it is counted for our righteousness. And then there is the righteousness that we practice, which is simply living lives as God would have us live. I use the last sermon, the examples of being celibate before marriage and forgiving others who have wronged us and keeping our vows in marriage and pursuing the kingdom of God first and foremost in our lives What I did not do was describe how living righteously also applies to everyday situations, everyday things that we make decisions about. For example, Bobby Lynn and I recently spent a few days with her parents in Olatha, Kansas, which is just outside of Kansas City. When we visit them, they give us their basement, which has a bedroom with a large bed and a separate bathroom and living room. It is quite comfortable for us. When I was writing the sermon that I preached last week, I was making trips up and down the stairs and using different rooms in the basement. And I was tempted simply to leave the lights on in each room until I was done with the sermon and no longer needed to be working. But with that temptation came a question in my conscience. What would I like a person to do who was staying with me? And the answer was obvious. I would want them to turn off the lights in the rooms they were not occupied. I realized that such an example sounds simple and maybe even outside of what we would call a moral decision. But here is the truth. When you are faithful, and being faithful is a righteous act, when you are faithful in the small things, you are more likely to be faithful in the larger things. When our oldest started attending McDonough School way back in the 2000s, I went there one evening to hear the chaplain of Princeton speak. I knew then that Princeton had left their Christian roots behind long ago, but I was still curious of what he had to say. And I only remember one point of his speech. Which was that when he was young, a young man, he would bring his report card home from elementary school, and his father would take it and look first at the penmanship grade That's right, young folks. Yes, back in the day, penmanship was taught and graded. Now this chaplain didn't know why the penmanship grade was so important to his father until he was older. And his father shared with him that it was important because he believed that if his son was careful with his penmanship, Which is being careful with small details, then he would be careful in the rest of his subjects. The speaker said that his father was right. And the teachings of Jesus confirm that he was. We are to be righteous in the small things, to be sure to be righteous in the larger things. Now, turning to Ecclesiastes, although I preached from the end of chapter 5 the last time we looked at the book of Ecclesiastes, which is over a month ago now I wish to rehearse the end of that chapter again in order to keep what we read in chapter 6 in its context. The point made in chapter 5, we'll pick up at verse 10. The point made in chapter 5, we have heard in various forms in both teachings of the Old and New Testaments. We learn, starting with verse 10, that loving money instead of God, regardless of the density or shininess of the coin, will neither satisfy. It is vapor. It appears to have substance, and then it is gone. From verse 11, with more wealth comes greater responsibility. And a man may find himself concerned more about those responsibilities than enjoying the wealth that he watches others enjoy. From verse 12, the contrast is made in regards to those who labor but are not wealthy. They may live day to day or paycheck to paycheck, but at least they are at peace with themselves and others. From verses 13 through 15, here is the plain reality of living in a fallen world. A man of riches has no guarantee that they will last. If riches are his idol, it is right for God to crush that idol, and the result is leaving nothing behind. From verses 16 through 17, the preacher calls the emptiness of money evil. And it is evil on several different levels. Mostly it is evil because it results in nothing of eternal value. To labor after wind is to want something that cannot be captured, cannot be controlled. Cannot be contained. And then in verses 18 through 20, here is the truth of it all. And it must not be lost. God's people are not to engage in class envy or class warfare. We are to do what is at the heart of the tenth commandment We are to appreciate and then enjoy what we have been given and say it is enough for the moment because God is good and all things good come from Him. When a man is rich, he is rich because God would have him be. A man's riches could be a curse to him. or blessing depending on how he responds to God's wisdom and God's commandments Now before we get to the heart of chapter 6, I wish for us to examine as objectively as possible Where we find ourselves in regards to that scale, that range from poverty to riches. According to the U. S. Census Bureau, a study done in 2022, there are 37. 9 million people in America that fall below the poverty line. In the US, poverty is officially defined as income insufficient to buy basic necessities of life, including, among others, food, clothing, and shelter. My pause because after inflation this past year, maybe there's more than thirty-seven point nine million Unfortunately, this statistic or these statistics remain ambiguous, for it does not state how much food, how much clothing, what type of shelter. Around the world, in comparison, poverty is understood by a different set of standards. In developing countries, it is estimated that two billion people do not have safe drinking water, and 3. 6 billion lack access to safely managed sanitation. As of today, a quarter of the human population in the world lives without electricity in the home. Considering such living conditions and those that fall below the poverty line in our beloved U. S. of A We can see that the word poverty can be used with a wide range of definitions. When we consider also where we live in this state of Maryland, And where we live in the state of Maryland, Carroll County, and neighboring counties, we must acknowledge that we are the wealthy. We are those that the preacher is describing. And I assure you that I am aware that there are those in the United States and abroad who have wealth that dwarfs my own. I have walked the docks of Annapolis and seen boats that cost four or five times as much as my home. I've seen the estates of the rich and powerful in Baltimore area alone, and I have an idea of my wealth in comparison. But I would have you consider your wealth in comparison to the people who have never owned property, who have no running water, no private sanitation. No regular income, no means of transportation beyond walking, no education, and are without government over them that cares to create an environment So that a responsible citizen could get out of such conditions. Does not our wealth dwarf theirs? And so turning to chapter 6. While considering the wealthy, the preacher has noticed something about them that he says is common. This then is not a casual observation or one that is short of examples. This happens to many And what happens is that a man is given everything that he could need in his life, including public honor, which we must note is hard to come by in any culture. Yet the same man lacks something that makes it all worthwhile. These men who lack are not given by God the ability in this life to enjoy their riches. We notice in response that the preacher laments this reality. He does not chide the rich for being rich or think that their inability to enjoy their riches is what they deserve, as if they should be suffering like the poor. But instead he laments this reality of not being able to enjoy what is good in this life. He calls it vapor. And then he calls it of an affliction. And I didn't Mention his use of the word evil in verse 1 because I wanted to get to this verse which better explains how he is using that term evil The word affliction. The word affliction helps us know that the preacher is referring to the curse mankind is under because of Adam. This is why the preacher calls it evil. It is evil reaped by those who come under Adam's curse. It is evil. Because it is not God's perfect will, but is instead God's punishment for mankind's disobedience The dramatic description in verse 3 expounds on the point made in verses 1 and 2. Believe it or not, there was a day when a large family was considered a blessing. Even though there were more mouths to feed, it was believed that more children would pay off and contribute to the wealth of a family as they grew older and worked at the fields or in the family business. And so the preacher exaggerates imagining a man with a hundred children and a long life, and yet his soul cannot be satisfied by his blessings. But why is this man not satisfied? The preacher does not say, but Jesus expounded upon it. When he told his disciples that they must hate their family members in comparison to their love for God in order to truly follow him. This was, of course, a dramatic thing to say, as family is the bedrock of the promises to Abraham. The promises were to each man and his descendants. For Jesus to demand this letting go of the first place of importance of family and insist upon God being first in every single life of his followers Tells us that the first commandment is an absolute necessity to be obeyed It is helpful to note that the goodness the man does not see is not in what he enjoys about his family The word is used in terms of purpose. Goodness refers to purpose. It is the purpose of it all that the wealthy man does not see. The reason then why it should have been better for such a man to have not been born at all is because he does not see the true purpose of such wealth, of such heritage, for to him it is vapor, it is like darkness to him. The ending of verse 6 is the reasoning of a man who does not know purpose. Do not all go to one place, he asks. Yes, in a manner of speaking, they do. But the grave is not all there is. We know this, but the rich man does not. Here is a plain truth within the broader teaching. What we consume in the moment does not and cannot satisfy the soul, if it is only the substance itself that is our focus. A good steak is a good steak. A fine wine is a fine wine. The best of pasta or the best of vegetables, if there is such a thing. Or the best of fruit, or whatever you crave to eat and consume, is good in the moment, but it should never be looked to for satisfying the soul. The remaining verses, verses 8 through 12 of the chapter, cover a wide spectrum of observations regarding the futility of man in terms of what he believes will satisfy him Or what he believes he can control. Which one knows how to live life better? The rich or the poor? The wise or the fool? In the end, both don't have an advantage. To say whatever one is, he has been named already, for it is known that he is man. That is simply another way of saying that there is nothing new under the sun in the context of how each man struggles to overcome his given lot in life. Let us be honest. That the debate of nature versus nurture and how they both contribute to who we are and what we become, both sides have to accept that there are limitations placed upon each of us. We can only be so tall, so strong, so smart, etc. And we cannot overcome a certain amount of our social and economic limitations without outside help. And most importantly, we will not climb high in society or find great success or live long life if the Lord God does not will us to do so. The summation of verse 12 appears to be quite a downer in terms of our inability to know exactly what is good for us. And how fleeting our lives can be as each of our lives seems to disappear like a shadow. We have to answer the last question by admitting that no indeed We cannot tell what will come after us. We are under the sun and therefore have a poor vantage point to see the future of our own life, let alone the world as a whole. Now, I don't want us to end this sermon on such a down note. We know the preacher is right about all that he has said, but he is not finished. Remember, we are in the middle of his sermon. The whole book is a sermon, one sermon. And even though I don't want to be a spoiler for where he is going, I need to say it to you. That's where he is going in general is to point our attention to the beauty of faith. The beauty of faith and how it plays a major role in us. Making sense of the world in a short time we are given to live. What I want each of us to take away today Is the importance and responsibility of pursuing the thirst and hunger we have for righteousness The preacher alludes to such pursuit in verse 9, when he laments about the wandering desires of men. Men who live by the flesh wander. It has been described as a hole in the soul that each man tries to fill with everything but what is needed, which is the Lord Jesus. It is described here in a similar manner as an appetite. We want something, but we do not know what it is. And every time we think that something might satisfy the appetite, we come away still hungry. This idea of appetite reminds me of one of C. S. Lewis's arguments for the existence of God. From his book titled The Weight of Glory, we read this, quote, A man's physical hunger does not prove that man will get any bread. He may die of starvation on a raft in the Atlantic. But surely a man's hunger does prove that he comes of a race which repairs its body by eating and inhabits a world where eatable substances exist. In the same way, though I do not believe, I wish I did, that my desire for paradise proves that I shall enjoy it I think it a pretty good indication that such a thing exists and that some men will. A man may love a woman and not win her. But it would be very odd if the phenomenon called falling in love occurred in a sexless world And a more simple summary, if I may, he is saying that a desire for something is an indication that that something exists The existence of righteousness is also evident to those who settle for self-righteousness. When Jesus said, Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled. He was not speaking about a righteousness that exists in and of itself. He was speaking about a righteousness that exists in the context of following him as his disciple. And he was not speaking of a righteousness that we can achieve on our own merits or by our own will. But instead, it is a righteousness he provides for us. And this points us back against the point made last Sunday regarding our need to have faith in the power of righteousness. That power exists because of Jesus, and we can know it is real because Jesus exemplified such power. So the righteousness we pursue and the power that comes with it is not a theory. And God doesn't call us to it without His help, His presence, His provision. In the book of Jude, we can call it a letter, but in the book of Jude, he compares the judgment of God That God will have upon fallen angels. And then he compares it to what God does for those who are faithful to him. He says that God sanctifies his people, which is to make them holy. He then says God preserves his people, which means they cannot wander. He ends his letter praising God, who keeps his people from stumbling, and a God who yearns to present them faultless to a heavenly reward. That God wants his people to be righteous. And this is expressed in a clever poem that I came across Angels fallen, give us pause. It is wise for us to consider their cause Heaven and God's very presence was theirs, but they wanted more and greater shares. They chose to revolt to rebel, and the result was a casting down to hell. God's dealing with men is not the same. He desires men to stand and not fall in shame God is able, desirous, and willing to keep men from tumbling, from falling. And so we learn from angels cast down that the Lord prefers we wear a crown. Beloved, he cares about our righteousness in the small and in the large. He cares because he wants us. He wants us to wear a crown. Let us pray. A gracious God, it is so very helpful to know that you are not a God who simply gives his laws and his standards and stands by and watches us fail. But a God who wants our righteousness, who gives our righteousness, who enables our righteousness. Who wants us to wear a crown? May we see you in that light always and forever. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Where Wisdom Points
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: The name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated and grab your Bibles and turn to Ecclesiastes 7. It is very important that you follow along this morning Ecclesiastes 7, we'll be working through the whole chapter. And as you turn there, I do want to give thanks to all those who participated in our vacation Bible school this past week It was uh quite a successful time of ministry for the children that attended. It was so well done, well put together, the teachers and the and the helpers were so proficient And what they did and sincere, and so we give the Lord thanks for all who served and all the children that were affected by last week. Since the preacher of Ecclesiastes is changing up his style a bit in chapter 7, it is appropriate for this preacher to change as well. Chapter 7 extols a certain virtue. The four cardinal virtues of history are justice, prudence, temperance, and fortitude. These virtues are listed that listed date back to the most well-known Greek philosophers and were believed to be sufficient guides for moral living in every culture. Our own Benjamin Franklin felt the need to add to the list with the following additions: silence. Order, resolution, frugality, industry, sincerity Moderation, cleanliness, tranquility, chastity, and humility These can be considered wise additions, but I argue that each of these added can find a home as a subdivision of one of the first four. For example, silence can fall under the category of temperance, and resolution can fall under the category of fortitude. Now, regarding the four cardinal virtues, I speculate that the most neglected of all, now I mind you I can't prove this point completely. But I speculate that the most neglected of all is prudence. Prudence can also be defined simply as wisdom. I speculate that prudence is the most neglected because of my own personal failings, and I speculate it as a pastor. Who has viewed many a life and many a relationship that have become strained because of the lack of prudence And I speculate it because the Bible spends a great deal of time helping us to apply basic wisdom to various circumstances of life. I thought it interesting to review the gifts of the Holy Spirit as listed in the book of Galatians, chapter 5. And those begin with love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, and the rest. But what is noticeably lacking in the list of gifts of the Holy Spirit Is wisdom. Wisdom, prudence is not then a gift of the Holy Spirit Now that does not mean that the Holy Spirit doesn't provide wisdom in a given moment, but as far as gifts simply given by God's grace without any work on our part, wisdom is not included. This led me back to realize that one the one book of the Bible that speaks most to the subject of wisdom, the book of Proverbs. is a book of instruction to help us be wise because well because it is not a gift and therefore it is something we need to work at It is something we need to learn to apply to the many situations in life that occur without us being able to anticipate them. If you consider how many situations we find ourselves in that are disappointing or heart-wrenching or heartbreaking, and consider how much we contributed to our own troubles, it becomes quite humbling. For instance, and I have used these examples before, think about how much blame God has received over the years for the devastation caused by hurricanes. Hurricanes such as Hurricane Katrina. People still ask, how can we say that God is love if he would let such suffering happen to so many people? But think about it for a moment from God's perspective, if that is at all possible. Man built a city below sea level. What else can be expected when there is a violent storm? If the sea rises, the city will flood. God has not hid such wisdom from men. It is available to us. If an area is below sea level and the sea rises, the area referred to will be covered in water. Let's look at another example of a more personal nature. If a person smokes cigarettes and gets lung cancer, it is not God's punishment. But a natural reaction to the susceptibility of the human condition and cigarette smoke. I will be even more personal I smoke a pipe now and then. And even though pipe tobacco doesn't have the same dangers as cigarettes. If I overindulge and end up getting mouth cancer, I have no one to blame but myself Wisdom tells me the possibility of getting sick, and thus I should not be surprised with the outcome. Dare I venture into the example of the homosexual lifestyle, if I could be so bold. Is it not obvious that the male body was not created to have sexual intimacy with another male body? And if that does occur, and there are communicable diseases as a consequence, if a communicable disease is a consequence, should we be surprised? No, we should not be surprised because wisdom tells us so. I mentioned wisdom and relationships, so I want to give two examples there. If I gossip about and then slander another person, And then find that the same person is uncomfortable and even awkward around me, and frankly doesn't want to be around me, it is not fair to think I have, is it not fair, excuse me, to think that I have reaped what I have sown? If I call a person a foul name and criticize him repeatedly, it seems fair to assume that I will not be getting any love or affection in return. Believe it or not, some people don't connect such cause and effect dots and go day to day wondering why people don't like them. They do not apply wisdom. What I have given are more extreme examples. There are more common ones that will be touched on as we walk through chapter 7. So let us begin at verse 1, reading each verse and commenting. Now, I want you to notice, please, also, that there are provocative statements made here, to be sure, and then there is a given explanation. Verse 1. A good name is better than precious ointment, and the day of death than the day of one's birth. A good name over precious ointment. The idea of a good name is not understood until the rest of the verse, which references death. A good name, at the end of one's life, is better than precious ointment. Alabaster was an ointment used at death. The provocative statement of death versus birth can trip us up. I can testify that pastoral visits after a birth are much better than those of visiting a house of mourning. Verse 2 Better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for that is the end of all men, and the living will take it to heart. The point is made again and expounded upon. The first part is provocative and not relatable in terms of personal experience. If you were invited to such parties, to which one would you go? All would go to the house of feasting versus the house of mourning. But that is not the preacher's point. The point is that there is an end of all men. All men will die. Hebrews 9 reads, it is appointed for men to die once, and then judgment. The end of the verse reads: All the living will take it to heart. Here is the main point. This is where it matters. I have come to suspect that the most important sermons we can hear are eulogies. I wrote my dissertation. on the structure of a proper eulogy because God had visited my ministry with many deaths and funerals during my early years here at St. Stephen's. In my first six months of a small parish, I presided over the funerals of Ruth Montgomery, Greg Ladke, Evelyn Gray, and Lucille Chapman. Adding to those, one of the saddest funerals was for a 13-year-old boy dying of cancer. The father came to me in tears, desperate to find some solace with God and his son, as he was dying, and he had nowhere else to turn. Ten years after his son's death, I received a call from the funeral home asking me if I would do the service of the father, as he had recently died. And they had no other minister that they knew but me. As you can imagine, I have many more stories of funerals that were very difficult to preside over because the deaths were so hopeless. Death brings about a sober reality. And those moments are indeed more important and more opportunistic for us, and opportunistic for anyone who has ears to hear Hear the gospel, the truth, the truth that God loves us and wants to save us from sin and death At a feast, at a feast, such contemplation does not occur. At a house of mourning, in contrast, we are given the opportunity to face our need to be saved from sin. And from death. Verse 3. Sorrow is better than laughter, for by a sad countenance the heart is made better. The main point of verse 2 is now driven home by these observations. The first part is troublesome, but it is explained in the second statement. When is sorrow better? Sorrow brings us to the point of understanding what matters most in life. Sorrow helps us evaluate the meaning of our lives. by contemplating, considerating, considering, excuse me, and evaluating. Verse 4 The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth. Here is the same said again, in case it was not understood. Author Lucy Bregman argues that we are coming out of an age of silence When death and its pain was not talked about in Western culture. It is popular today to refer to funerals as a celebration of life. That is all well and good, but it can never deny that death has occurred. Take inventory about your own conversation regarding death as you grew up and even now As Christians, we should be a people who talk of dying well. The death of a Christian should be a testimony of God's mercy and love to all who know you. Let us read verses 5 and 7 through 7 together. It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise than for a man to hear the song of fools. For the lack of crackling of the thorns under a pot, so in the laugh is the laughter of the fool, this also is vanity. Surely oppression destroys a wise man's reason, and a bribe debases the heart. Because fools prefer mirth or partying to serious contemplation, the thought continues in regards to honesty. A rebuke by a wise man is to be preferred to a man who sings praises. That famous Hollywood line, you can't handle the truth, should never be said about the God fearing. We can and should handle the truth. In verse 6, here it has us preferring the truth as opposed to what would make us laugh. Is this speaking against laughter? No. But when is laughter good? Laughter is good when seriousness is not needed. What is to be preferred to laughter, however, is when honesty, truth, and the reality of human mortality need to be accepted and not avoided. What happens when you burn thorns? Is there any heat generated? It is only noise. Useless noise. Entertaining, perhaps, but of no use. It is vapor. We see it, in this case, hear it. But we cannot grasp it or control it or use it for any good. It is here and then gone without achieving any purpose or good end. And then in verse 7, we hear the preacher responsible in recognizing how easy it can be to be distracted by oppression, or as translated elsewhere, affliction. And with it comes a heart that gives in to bribes, the bribes of a fool. This understanding, however, is then rebuked in verses 8 through 10, which we read again together. The end of a thing is better than its beginning. The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit. Do not hasten in your spirit to be angry, for anger rests in the bosom of fools. Do not say why were the former days better than these, for you do not inquire wisely concerning this. So the end of a thing is what we strive to experience. A person gives in to a bribe in the moment because of difficulties occurring in a short period of time instead of seeing the greater purpose in life. Being patient for the end of things is the wisdom given here. How many unfortunate young men and young women have given into a moment of lust in the back seat of a car without seeing the end? How many have allowed their emotions to carry the day without considering the consequences? And that brings us to verse 9. The wisdom here is repeated in the book of James and is obviously needed advice because it is a widespread problem. The fool lets anger Rest. It lets anger sit within the heart without rebuke or resistance. And anger, like a shaken bottle of soda, has pressure that needs to be released. And when it does release, because it has been inside for so long, it blows. And woe to those who experience the aftermath of it. Verse 10, the result of anger kept inside is complaining, or better said, whining A whiner wonders why life is not as good as it used to be. He wonders why bad things keep happening to him. She wonders why others have it better. And can we reason with the preacher why such considerations are not wise? It is because we look at the past with blind eyes Not seeing how they were with their own problems and not as rosy as we think they were. Here is an honest assessment. If we cannot make sense of the present, how can we make sense of the past? And finally, verses 11 and 12. Wisdom is good with an inheritance and profitable to those who see the sun. For wisdom is a defense as money is a defense. But the excellence of knowledge is that wisdom gives life to those who have it. And so, what is our duty in all of this contemplation? Is it simply honesty and truth? Is it to extol wisdom for what it can provide us in this life? We know from the life of Solomon, our preacher, that wisdom cannot save the soul. Only Jesus can save a man's soul from sin and death. Only Jesus What wisdom can provide is some profit in life for those who live looking up at the sun, you and me? Verse 12 ends with, Wisdom gives life to those who have it. From what we have expounded upon in these verses, we can conclude that the life referred to is a better life. But what is a better life? It is a life of peace with God and peace with our fellow man. A better life is when we avoid troubles that can be avoided. And all of this is good, very good, but it must be qualified. A failure of modern preaching and thus modern Christianity is seeing the Holy Scriptures as a self-help book. And that faith itself as a way to avoid hardship in life. That is not what this wisdom is about. This wisdom is not a recipe Do this, and this is what you will get automatically. No. Wisdom as it is described here does two things First, it teaches us what it means to live in the tensions of two worlds. The tension of the first world is that we live in a fallen world, and thus we are suspect to all the that curse. That it brings upon us because of Adam. Disease, misunderstanding, limitations. The tension of the second world is that we are victors in Christ Jesus Sin and death do not reign over us. We have victory in the name of Jesus The tension between these two realities will be with us until Jesus comes again or we go to be with him. And second, the wisdom here points us to the cross, to the cross of Jesus. That is because the greatest wisdom a man can have is to believe in the person who is truth, who defines truth, and that is Jesus. Wisdom that does not acknowledge Jesus as Lord and Savior is not eternal wisdom. Consider that our preacher, none other than Solomon himself. who when he was told by God that he could ask for anything of this world, and he asked for wisdom. And so he ruled with the greatest gift of wisdom man had ever known up to his day. And yet he strayed from God and pursued sins of the flesh, even falling into idol worship. So no, wisdom did not and cannot save a soul In chapters 5 and 6 of Ecclesiastes, he explained how earthly wealth could not save his soul. Now we know that wisdom also cannot save his soul. And so what have we learned? Money is nice, nice to have, but it does not lead to eternal life. Wisdom is nice to have. In fact, wisdom is better, better than money. But it must lead somewhere other than itself. To be meaningful, to be eternally useful, wisdom, money, anything that we have, worked for, or get been given must lead to Jesus the Christ. Amen and Amen. Let us pray. Gracious Father, we thank you for the gift of wisdom. And we sorely need it. Need it in our individual lives, need it in our relationships, need it for the rest of our days. But most importantly, we want it to lead to Jesus, whom you gave. as our truth. May it be so in Jesus' name. Amen

sermons.title: God Makes Thing Crooked
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated, and I encourage you to turn in your Bibles to Ecclesiastes chapter 7. We pick up at verse 13. Ecclesiastes 7, picking up at verse 13. Now imagine Imagine, if you will, someone giving this task to a preacher. Here is your task, preacher, and you don't have a choice but to accept it. It is your task, and it must be done. For you are not who you say you are, nor are you doing what you have been commissioned to do. So here is the task Explain in careful detail the beauty, denseness, and vastness of the Amazon rainforest. Including how mysterious and complicated and dangerous it is, so that God's people can clearly imagine it. And to help you along, here is a small plant plucked from the same forest to give people a visual idea of what you are describing. And next, explain the distinct distinct words, the distinct words of the great height of the Rocky Mountains, including an exact description of the pure white snow caps, the feel of the crisp winds that blow, the awe that is inspired when looking up from their bases. and the amazing view when standing at their peaks and looking down and across. And to help you out, here is a picture of the Rocky Mountains. taken from Interstate 70 in Colorado just last year. And finally, provide for God's people A sense of the great depths, vastness, and power, anger-expressing and peace-providing calm of the earth's oceans. And to help you out, here is a cup of ocean water retrieved only a few days ago from the Atlantic to serve as a tangential aid. Go to it, man. Don't stand there and be idle. These tasks, as assigned, are not mere impossible, they are impossible. They are impossible because Picturing the Amazon rainforest from a description can only be fuzzy in our imagination, and that is even after a person has visited there. The grandness of the Rocky Mountains can never be exactly described, nor can a sense of the depths of the earth oceans be realized, even if we were to dive into one. And most certainly, the visual aids would fail to capture anything close to these places, and in fact, the aids may lessen their true reality. as they communicate limitations more than the greatness they are supposed to help describe If these places are difficult to describe, consider how strenuous it is for a preacher, any preacher, to describe God. While a man can place a measurement on the height of mountains and the depth of an ocean, what man can measure God? While a man can come up with the resemblance of snow-capped white mountains or lush green trees with an above-average vocabulary, what man can describe God? who has no physical or spatial boundaries. And then there are attempts to describe God not in terms of physical attributes, but in terms of his actions. The preacher of Ecclesiastes may have tried to do this. I speculate, because what we read at the end of chapter seven. is a recognition that what he sees has been done by God is not what he would have expected And because it not is not what he expected, he doesn't know what to do with what he sees. He doesn't know what conclusions to draw. Have you ever seen something occur? Only it never actually occurred, but you thought you saw it because you expected to see it. Have you ever heard something only you really didn't hear it, but thought you did because you expected to hear it When we expect to see something and then think we saw it, or expect to hear something and then think we heard it, we have to do a double take or a double listen. To erase our pre-programmed minds in order to register what truly we have seen, what truly we have heard. We also do something similar when we don't want to believe what we have seen or what we have heard. We want to think better of someone, and so we disbelieve what we have seen them do. Spouses can do it with each other, and parents can do the same regarding their children. For many, it is easiest to stick their heads in the sand, as the saying goes, and refuse to accept reality. Poet T. S. Eliot got it right when he wrote, humankind cannot bear very much reality. At the end of Ecclesiastes 7, we have a description of what the preacher actually sees, and it is not initially as beautiful as the Rocky Mountains. But it is most certainly deeper than any ocean. First, he challenges man by pointing out that no one can make straight what God has made crooked. And in saying this, he is also pointing out the reality that God makes things crooked. It is worth repeating. God makes things crooked. God is good, we say, all of the time, is the response. If that is true, which it is, then we have to put a syllogism together which concludes that when God makes things crooked, it is good. That may sound logical in theory, but it is most difficult to reconcile in the mind of a human who is under the sun. Because we don't like or want to accept that God would make things perfect The easiest, most simple way to look at the world is to conclude that all good things come from God and all the bad things come from the devil. But the preacher doesn't see it that way. God, he says, makes things crooked. Now I am well aware that I am stepping on some images of God that we have, and I admit that I am not comfortable with all of it. I too can get comfortable with what I understand about God. And I don't like that the preacher is stretching my understanding to an extent that I have never done before. But the text says what it says. God makes things crooked. In verse 14, the preacher adds to this acceptance of God making things crooked. We are to be joyful when we are prosperous. That's good to hear. God wants us and expects us to enjoy the pleasures of life when they come to us. There is nothing wrong with such enjoyments. And in fact, if we do not enjoy, we are offending God, for it is God who has given them to us to enjoy. But then there is the other end of the truth. When adversity occurs, we are also to understand that those times as well come from God. The end of that verse, although a bit awkward to translate in English, states that a mankind that in mankind's position he will never be able to be assured of the future. What will happen in the future is only in God's mind and God's will, and he does not share it with man. Commentator Jeffrey Myers says the following: quote: God answers to no one but himself. He shares his power with no one. He has not relinquished his control to the forces of nature or the randomness of chance of the whimsical nature of the human will. In verse 15, the preacher shares some observations that prove his point: that God's nature in ways extend beyond our understanding. He says that he has seen, making him an eyewitness, he has seen a just man die living righteously before God, which is doing as God has commanded. While at the same time, he has seen a wicked man live longer, longer than most, and never turning from his wickedness. And it is implied in noticing this that our understanding of God would have him turn around such circumstances. The way we understand God, the righteous man should live long, and the wicked man should die because of his wickedness. And now we must understand verse 16 and 17 in light of verse 15. The righteousness of verse 15 is an outward righteousness. He is describing someone who believes that because of the manner he is living, God is automatically going to give him long life. And he expects that because he is living better than an outwardly wicked man, that God is going to end that wicked man's life sooner. Naturally, of course. That's the way it's going to be. That's how we understand God. What the preacher points out is that he has witnessed God doing the opposite. And so as we attempt to understand the instruction to not be overly righteous or overly wicked in verses 16 and 17. We are to know that it is a type of righteousness that is outward and believes itself to be earning God's rewards. And a wickedness that is living as though there will be no consequences to wicked living. Outward righteousness alone will not be rewarded, and outward wickedness will not go unpunished. The underlying wisdom of these points is at the end of verse 18, he who fears God will escape them all. Our responsibility as Christians is not to earn long life by outward living, nor is it to live wickedly and expect nothing in return. Our responsibility is to fear God. The undertow of wisdom in the remaining verses of this chapter is an encouragement to accept the fact that there are so very many things that we cannot make judgments about because of what we do not know. As human beings fallen, we all have weaknesses. There is not a just man, a man who does good and yet does not sin. Such a man does not exist Therefore, when we go to pass judgment on an economic inferior, we are to recognize that the sin we judge is the one we are guilty of ourselves. Again, what we think we know and understand, we come to find out later, is sorely lacking We can say along with the preacher, as for that which is far off and exceedingly deep, who can find it out? This is true about God and what we see happen in the world around us. The remaining verses of the chapter, verses 25 to 29, are comparing the woman of wisdom to the woman of folly. This is not a section on courtship, not a section on dating. It is using the feminine title for both wisdom and folly.
