To show how each is something that men try to win over, just as a man tries to win over a woman Only there is a great consequence of bitterness and death if folly is pursued instead of wisdom. Ending at verse 29, and then into chapter 8, we see that there are some conclusions to come to, but no mysteries of God are solved. God has made man to stand upright. Man is in God's image. But man also goes about scheming his way through life, even scheming against God. What we can know at the very least is that man benefits from wisdom. What that wisdom is and what it looks like. In all circumstances, like we said last week, is to be discovered, pursued. The best thing we can learn from wisdom of this chapter Is that there is much more to know about God than we can possibly experience in this life, and much of it can be hard to accept. I had a professor in seminary tell a story of his family devotions growing up. His father, he said, would read through the Bible, never skipping a chapter or passage, regardless of its content. He remembers what his father read from Genesis chapter 38, which he remember tells the story of Judah not keeping his promise to his daughter-in-law Tamar that she should marry his next son because her first husband had died. In response to this failed promise, Tamar dresses up like a harlot and deceives Judah into sleeping with her She later reveals herself as his daughter-in-law, and it is learned that she is pregnant by him with twins. I am summarizing to remind you how scandalous the whole story is. Well, as the father of my professor started reading this story, the mother told him to stop. The father asked why, and she responded by saying that the children didn't need to hear of such behavior. The father retorted, but it's in the Bible. She responded, Well, I wish it wasn't. Many would agree. We might wonder why such salacious details are necessary to be recorded. And some of you might agree with the mother that it is not necessary to read such behavior to children. But the story and its details make sense much later when we read the genealogy in St. Matthew's Gospel St. Matthew gives a family tree of Jesus, starting with Abraham, who had Isaac, who had Jacob, who had Judah, who had Perez, by his daughter-in-law Tamar. Yes, God chose the product of an incestuous relationship to be the bloodline of our Lord and Savior and His only Son Jesus, the second person of the Trinity. God makes things crooked. And we want to make things straight. But God makes them crooked. We want to sugarcoat what God has done. On something goes down easier. Many of us Many of us want a cartoon version of God and His way and the world because cartoon versions are much easier to witness and accept. And the children can witness them, and we need not be concerned, for in the cartoon versions of God The whole point is mirth, and the colors are crisp, and the coyote never gets seriously injured when the anvil falls on his head. But we can't make the crooked straight. Our God is a God who makes things crooked, and we cannot change that. One of the more crooked stories in all of Holy Scripture is found in Genesis also, Genesis chapter 22. Where we read of the Lord commanding Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac. And while we know most of the details of the story, many of us don't focus on the things that are crooked and scary. We focus on the end, which was that Abraham did not cut the throat of his son, and that God provided a ram for proper sacrifice and worship. Which meant that for Abraham all of it ended well. That's all we want to know. We conclude that God never really did want Abraham to sacrifice his son, Isaac. It was just an important test, we say. That is the G-rated version. That is the cartoon version. A closer look at the details of the story reveals a more harsh reality. The Bible narrative is actually very frightening. Without qualification, the Lord commanded Abraham to commit an obvious abomination, passing Isaac through fire. In Leviticus, which comes later after Abraham, God revealed this law. You shall not let any of your descendants pass through the fire of Molech, nor shall you profane the name of your God. Such law requires us to ask what has happened then with God's instruction to sacrifice Isaac. It seems as if God suffered from a split personality. Had he given up on the promises he made to Abraham? Had he given up on being God? What hope is there for any of us if God himself has become madness? To have his chosen servant Abraham kill his son is apocalyptic. But it's a test, we say. God really didn't mean it, we cry. But Abraham and Isaac didn't know any of that. Yahweh wasn't straightforward with them. To take Yahweh at his word would mean that he actually planned to have Abraham sacrifice Isaac. In truth, we know the end. It actually increases the horror of the story. The whole thing is a staged play. Yahweh wants Abraham to work through the idea of killing his son, and yet there were other options. He could have been plain-spoken and avoided the ruse. He could have just reasoned politely and respectably with Abraham, perhaps laying out a hypothetical ethical dilemma for Abraham. And then judge him by it. God could have said, What would you do, Abraham, if I asked you to sacrifice your son Abraham's reply, I would do it, Lord. And God, knowing the hearts of men, would have known if Abraham would have done it, would have done what he said he would do. That could have been enough. But no, that's the G rated God. That's the God that makes life straight, not crooked. The Yahweh of this story, Genesis 22, wants to play this whole thing out to the very last moment. Along, allowing Abraham to experience all the turmoil of not understanding God at all To not being sure of the promises he received from God, to facing a future of guilt that knows it was his hand that killed his only son. God played with Nyes. He played with innocent Abraham. What kind of God does this We cannot answer that question in full. We are going to spend an eternity understanding what kind of God does such things. A part of the answer, however, we already know. We know he is a God that doesn't just play out scenarios up to the very last moment and then hold back the hand that holds the knife. No. He lets the knife fall. He lets the whip snap. The nails be hammered, the spear go into the side of his only son. He carries through the story, the crooked story. He carries through the crooked story so that you and I can have life and life eternally. Every one of us knows what a crooked life is. None of us has a straight life. What we are to hope in is that God redeems what is crooked. In the end, he makes everything straight. Amen. Amen. Let us pray. Gracious and heavenly Father, we thank you for this truth, although difficult to swallow. Recognizing that even what Christians present today is certainly not a God who makes things crooked. But we understand that to be true, and we accept it to be true. And now we ask that you would redeem all that is crooked in our lives, that we in the end might be straight. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Growing in Secret
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated and turn in your Bibles to Ecclesiastes chapter eight. Ecclesiastes chapter eight. In C. S. Lewis's Third and final book in his space trilogy titled That Hideous Strength. We are introduced to a heroine named Mrs. Jane Stubbick Jane is a conflicted character as she is married to a man she does not admire nor respect. And she had yet, at least for the majority of the story, submitted herself to Christ Jesus as her Lord and Savior. Much of her reasoning for resisting the faith was her dislike of men and her fear of men, of men lording their masculinity over her. Eventually, she finds the ability to trust one man by the name of Ransom. He is the hero of the entire trilogy. In this quote, Ransom sets Jane straight regarding her dislike of anything masculine. He says, quote, the male You could have escaped, for it exists only on the biological level. But the masculine, none of us can escape What is above and beyond all things is so masculine that we are all feminine in relation to it. You had better agree with your adversary quickly. You mean I shall have to become a Christian? said Jane. It looks like, said Ransom. By the manner of God's masculinity, as it is described by Lewis, is showing that God is much more than a particular gender. God's masculinity is most noted in his authority. It is to the shame of humanity that we all struggle so very greatly with submitting to authority. And it is to be understood that the importance of a wife submitting to her husband and children honoring their parents And all citizens obeying their particular governing authorities is not for the sake of peaceful living only, but for an inevitable transference to God. We are all to understand that our willingness to practice submitting to those who have authority over us is ultimately related to our submission to God. How we obey or disobey authority is akin to how we obey or disobey God. How we treat authority is akin to how we treat God. How we feel about authority is akin to how we feel about God. And how we speak about authority, again, is akin to how we speak about God. The wisdom provided in Ecclesiastes chapter 8 begins with the importance of submitting to authority. The reference is to submitting to kings, but the principle relates to all who have authority over us. It relates to parents if you are a child. It relates to to husbands if you are a wife. It relates to teachers if you are a student. It relates to employers if you are an employee. It relates to governing authorities if you are a citizen. And yes, it relates to ecclesiastical authorities if you are a citizen of God's kingdom. The preacher is saying essentially the same thing that we read from Romans chapter 13. Where St. Paul instructs us to obey those who have authority over us, for they are God's instrument to protect those who do right and to punish those who do wrong. In some ways, life is really not that complicated. If you obey the authorities, things will go well for you. If you do not obey those authorities, expect dire consequences. The preacher turns in verses 8 through 10 to observe those who are in authority. And he notes that some are evil. Such leaders cannot be avoided. He notes that all leaders are limited. That, too, cannot be avoided. Stating it as simply as possible, we are to obey those in authority, but we cannot come close to trusting them in the same manner we trust God. As a nation, we need to be reminded every four years that no person elected president should be given our hope or entrusted with our future. It is only in God that we can place our hope and our future. This is important to remember for once again. Once again, we are inundated with the message that this is the most important election in our lifetime. And yet supposedly the same was true four years ago, and four years before that, and four years before that, and still nothing has changed culturally We still kill our unborn and mutilate their genitalia if they survive the womb. Hard words. True words. There are shadows that obscure when dealing with governing authorities, as the preacher points out in verses one through fourteen. Evildoers do not always receive their just due, and if proper punishment is received, it is not necessarily in a timely manner. Thus men can perceive that they can get away with evil deeds without suffering any serious consequences. When men think they can get away with evil, the occurrence of evil deeds increases. What is best, the preacher reminds us, is for persons to fear God first and last, because there will be a day of reckoning for all who do evil In the meantime, the wicked can get treated like the righteous and the righteous like the wicked. In the meantime. We now come to the final lesson concerning submission to authority. To learn it well, we turn to the Gospel of Mark chapter 4. I read from verses 26 through 29. And Jesus said, The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. and should sleep by night and rise by day, and the seed should sprout and grow. He himself does not know how For the earth yields crops by itself, first the blade, then the head, after that the full grain in the head. But when the grain ripens, immediately he puts in the sickle because the harvest has come. Now the connection between these two passages may not be immediately obvious. But hopefully you will see it in the end. The parable is peculiar to Mark's gospel. It is a parable that teaches us how the kingdom of God works. Because as believers in Jesus, we are part of God's kingdom, he gives us insights regarding how it is governed. From this parable, we learn what we can do and what we cannot do in God's kingdom, and we learn what we can know and what we cannot know. First, what we can do is cast seed upon the ground. The seed, we know, is God's Word. The seed is the truth that Jesus is the Son of God and the Savior of the world. God has chosen for each and every one of us to be planters of such seed. The ground in the parable is the hearts and lives of our fellow human beings who have fallen away from God's truth and are in need of new life. We are to provide the Word of God to the lives of people we encounter in this world so that they can grow new life. Each of us is given holy orders to plant the seed wherever we go Each of us has a sacred service, and that we are to be given access to people that God places in our lives that we might plant the seed of God in them. This is within our capacity to do, and we are to be about doing it. And then there comes what we cannot do. We cannot make the seed ourselves. It has to be given to us. It has to come from elsewhere and not ourselves, for we cannot manufacture it The seed is not born of a man, nor produced by man, but must come from God. We are to be stewards of the seed, but stewards only I recently read some quotes by a left of Orthodoxy pastor within a certainly more liberal church. Who thinks himself to be quite clever in asking such provocative questions such as, what if Mary, the mother of Jesus, wasn't technically a virgin? Would that change your love for Jesus? Or what if Jonah wasn't actually swallowed by a great fish? Would that affect your trust in Holy Scripture? The questioner is trying to get to the heart of why we believe what we believe, to show, I suppose. That there are many things that are not at the core of what we believe, and such shouldn't be treated the same as what is essential of the faith. From this preacher's perspective, such questions are completely out of place. For the questioner does not appreciate Does not appreciate that to know such a thing as Mary being a virgin when she gave birth to the Christ child is by revelation Revelation, not by our imagination, and we are privileged to know it and privileged to confess it It is true that a Christian's faith in Jesus as Savior is not dependent upon the virginity of Mary. The virginity of Mary is a part of what is revealed in God's truth and is never separated for who Jesus is. We don't need to invent questions, for we do not invent what is revealed to us. It was given to us just as all parts of the gospel, the seed, were given to us. The next thing we cannot do, along with not making the seed, is that we cannot cause life to grow where the seed is planted. This is clearly seen in our gospel reading where we have an older son and a newer son, and each of them respond completely different to the news of God's grace. We might think we can cause life to grow where the seed is planted. We might think we can cause something to grow because of what we do to the soil or how we water the plant But in truth, we are only aiding it to grow, not causing it to grow. For a plant to grow, it is dependent upon that which no man can supply We cannot cause it to germinate, to sprout, to grow leaves, to change color, or to ripen. Modern men and modern churches do not agree with what I have just described. They believe they can make seed grow. They believe they have the skill and power to grow the gospel in the hearts and lives of people. And so they market the seed. They treat it like it is a product to sell on Fifth Avenue. They use the wisdom of the world, and they appeal to the flesh in order for the seed to be purchased. They put the seed to popular music. They surround it with coffee shops. They package it in young verbiage. They say it will make you wealthy, healthy, and happy. But the seed can't be born of blood, nor the will of the flesh, nor by human decision. It can only be born of God. If anything does grow from what modern men manufacture, it is either weakly ill or malformed. It is something that is dependent upon being repeatedly fed with what caused it to grow in the first place. If it was born by entertainment, then it always wants to be entertained. If it was born by high emotions, it always wants another emotional high. In the end, things that grow in such manners go the way of the grass withering and the flowers fading. Alongside of what we cannot do is what we cannot know. The heavenly seed grows in secret. We cannot know the heart of another man or woman. We barely know of our own hearts. We cannot fathom why a seed would grow so readily and willingly in one heart and not another We cannot come close to correctly identifying why one man can eagerly receive the Word of God and another man scowl at the preacher and mock everything he says. Like Samuel, we expect the oldest and the strongest of Jesse's sons to be the next king. We expect that what we see on the outside is what is going on on the inside. Have you ever heard someone say of another individual, gee, he sure would make a great Christian? I don't believe people are thinking clearly when they say such things. Oh, yes, I know what they are trying to say They're trying to say that a person who has gifts such as public speaking or intellectual reasoning would provide God's kingdom with great assets. But this type of reasoning is also not thinking clearly, for God has a record of choosing poor speakers like Moses and common intellects like Peter to build his kingdom And I ask you just what person wouldn't make a great Christian? That is probably a question that shouldn't be answered. The reality that we cannot know certain things about the kingdom of God is quite unnerving to some people, perhaps all people. In my pastoral role, I confirm to people going through trials that nothing happens to us by chance, and because of that we can trust that God has greater reasons for what we suffer through. The difficult question to answer, and the question will inevitably come is to understand what God's reasons are right now. A person going through a grave trial wants to know right now what God's reasons are And even though I am anointed to teach and preach God's word and give words of counsel and wisdom, I cannot answer such a question. I can only project that in the future days you will be able to look back and to see what God was doing. I trust that is the case. But the truth is there are things beyond our ability to know right now. And so, what do we do with the knowledge that there are things in our lives we cannot control or know? Here is the lesson of the parable and the lesson of Ecclesiastes 8. We accept it by faith. We accept the fact that there are things we can neither control nor understand. There are things done only by God, and there is knowledge only known by God. We accept it by faith. We have faith in the Lord Jesus, that He has us in His will. That he will make all things work together for the good, that he will never leave us or forsake us. That at the end of it all we will walk streets of gold and live in mansions made in heaven. Faith in such things is the foundation of what it means to be Christian. We accept the fact that there are things we cannot control or know, and we accept it by faith. And what does God do with such faith? Well, again, go back to the parable Although no one knows how it happens, we are to understand and be assured that there will be a crop, a crop that grows, and it will grow until it is fully ripened, and when it is fully ripened, it will be harvested. For us to be harvested is to be taken home, home to heaven. Thus we can say, in every trial There is at least one purpose God has, and we can know it right now. It is for us to be harvested, for us to be taken home to heaven. From the perspective of the preacher of Ecclesiastes, it is good, good to enjoy what we can of this life, because there are many things that we cannot understand. And it is futile to try. He says, so drink out. Eat, drink, and be merry. This advice is fine, at least in terms of moderation, as long as we have faith, faith to accept that moments of enjoyment in this world are to give us a little taste. Of what we have to look forward to in heaven. My family, like your family Has had to accept over the years that there are things in life that we cannot control and we cannot know fully It is tempting to try to fully control and to fully know. We can try to control things by surgery, procedures, treatments, counsel. We can think we know things by looking at recovery percentages and medical advances, all that might give us a sense of hope. But in truth, we control nothing and we know nothing. Only God is truly in control. Only God knows all things. And only in God are we to place our hope. And because he is the first and the last, the beginning and the end, and because all things have been placed in subjection under his feet. Placing our hope in God alone, in Jesus the Savior, is a privileged thing to do. May we have faith. May we have faith to be comforted that He alone controls and knows all things. The true masculine one will have his way. Beloved, I do want to say this before I close. As we prepare to receive the elements of Holy Communion, Please know that there is a reason, a deep spiritual reason Why the last supper scene was mocked at the opening ceremonies for today's Olympics in France There's a reason why they went there. The devil hates what we are about to do, and so he mocks it, thinking we will shy away from it. On the contrary, we boldly approach the table of our Lord, because in receiving it we proclaim Jesus' death until he comes. Amen.

sermons.title: Whatever your hand finds to do
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.source_file: Whatever your hand finds to do.txt
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated and turn with me to Ecclesiastes chapter 9. Ecclesiastes chapter 9. I will be walking through each of the ten verses, and I'm not going to read them, but but commentary have commentary on them So you'll want to follow along in your Bibles. Our approach for this chapter will be in two parts. We will begin with notes concerning the interpretation of the verses we are covering, and then focus our attention on a particular message I believe the Lord has for us. So beginning with verse 1 Here is a carry-over from chapter 8. Even though we are limited in what we can control and what we can know, we can still make observations. We can still observe. The love and hate description means that God finds favor and displeasure. with the behaviors of men. Verse 2. The good are good morally The clean are clean ceremonially, as in worship. The sacrifices are done to God alone, and as the law prescribes And the one who fears an oath is compared to a man who makes an oath rashly with no intention to comply. The observation made in this verse should be noted by all. The most obvious example we have is the attack on our nation in 2001. People who put their faith in the Lord Jesus Christ for salvation died that day, along with people who were atheists, backsliders, Muslims, and likely of other faiths. We know that accidents and injuries and murders and disease come upon all walks of life. The devil will tempt us to discern why tragedies befall one person as opposed to another. And the judgment is usually a speculation that such persons have done something wrong and therefore God is punishing them. But the book of Job and the accusations of his friends teach us that this is not the case. We must be careful. We must be most careful to not make such accusations For to say that a person experienced tragedy because God is displeased is to think that we earn his labor and earn his displeasure. If it is by grace through faith that we are saved and not by our own works, then we can contribute nothing to God's favor toward us. It is by grace alone. Also, to say a person has deserved their tragedy is to say that we don't deserve the same fate. If I am in an auto accident with another person and that person dies, do I have any right to conclude that I deserved to live and he did not? And I know that sounds horrible to say out loud, but it is. It is the preacher's job to say what men can be faking. And thus to challenge that thinking when it is unbiblical and unrighteous. The lesson from the Tower of Siloem, if you remember that in Luke chapter 13, the Gospel of Luke chapter 13. That there repeats the point. People came and questioned Jesus. What they spoke out loud is what all of us think. They wanted to know if the Galileans who were killed by Pontius Pilate while they worshiped, they wanted to know from Jesus if those people who were killed deserved it. What Jesus taught them by referring to a particular tower falling on 18 people and 18 people dying, a tragic death, Jesus taught them that that can happen to anyone. What Jesus is most concerned about is that people repent and that people believe. Men need to repent because we are all sinners. And if we truly received what we deserved, we would all die tragically without hope. Verse 3. The evil referred to may as well be translated curse. For it is the result of the fall of men that tragedies befall the righteous as well as the wicked. It is the consequence of man disobeying God and death being brought into the world. With sin and death as part of the world, there is also madness in the heart of many men For Christians, these verses can seem outdated, for they do not describe what Jesus can do to the heart of a man and how he can heal both the spirit and the body. But the wisdom of the preacher here cannot be denied. Yes, Jesus gives new life to the soul of a man. And Jesus can heal a man or a woman of any disease. But even if those alive in Christ, and even those who have been healed, all of them go to the dead, as the phrase says. A Christian is not required to be an optimist, a pessimist, or a realist when it comes to matters of health, wealth, and healing or disease, tragedy and death. There is both in Scripture. We are called to believe what the Bible says. Does it say that by the stripes of Jesus we are healed? Indeed it does. Does it say that all go to the dead? Indeed it does. As always, as always, thanks be to God, the scriptures do not leave us to focus solely on death. Verse four. We can say yet to him, for this is a change of perspective. And we should know to the Eastern mind that dogs were not domesticated but contemptible. They were dirty grounders who depended upon the scraps of others This is compared to the lion who was considered grand and powerful. And if you have ever been near a lion, even a tamed lion. When he roars, you understand why such are looked upon as something to fear. Verse 5 This is not an insightful revelation regarding what happens to people after they die. It is a simple observation. That what you can know when you are alive is not to be compared to what you know when you are dead, at least as far as what goes on in the world. Perhaps such a statement destroys the idea that our dead loved ones are looking down upon us as we go through our lives. But to think such a thing is only emotional reasoning, for it is only God who can know all things and be in all places. Verse 6. Here is a sobering thought that does not provide much comfort for people who mourn the death of a loved one. It is truth, but it is hard truth. Verse 7. The joy described is by choice. The wine, yes, it's fermented. Drinking wine and being merry or happy is never a problem biblically. Drinking wine and being angry, abusive, belligerent, or committing debauchery is always sinful. Verse 8. White, white was usually worn for a celebration and represented to the Eastern mind both joy and purity. Oil was used lavishly to provide a softness to the skin that could not otherwise be attained. and to provide a fragrance that was otherworldly as compared to the odor of daily Eastern living Verse nine. Some Bible versions do a great disservice to this verse Some translations say to enjoy life with your wife, as if the author wants you to enjoy life and be sure to include your wife. Instead, what it instructs is for a man to enjoy life by means of his wife, and for him to have his wife enjoy life by means of him. As we understood when beginning our study of this book, the word translated meaningless in the NIB and vanity in the New King James is best translated to be vapor. Life is vapor. Vapor communicates the shortness of a human life and the inability of a person to capture it. Verse 10. Whatever your hand finds to do is that which you can accomplish. It is understood that what you can accomplish would fit under what God would have you do. And here again is a comparison of what we can do while you are alive, as opposed to what cannot be done when you are in the grave. Now in this next section of the sermon, I'm going to be an advocate for Christian freedom. However, considering the political landscape of the day, I must qualify what I am about to preach. Some modern politicians are currently promoting themselves as a candidate for freedom. But their definition of freedom is much, much different than what the Bible teaches and what I'm about to preach. Their definition of freedom is to be able to live sexually immoral lives with no consequences. Their definition of freedom is to kill babies in the womb. Their definition of freedom is to live lives of debauchery with no social condemnation. Beloved, such is not freedom, that is actually imprisonment. Imprisonment that leads to eternal hellfire. And the devil knows it. So let us set about understanding what freedom actually is. From the perspective of those outside of the Christian faith looking in, it can easily appear that Christians don't have fun. This is especially true when we face when the when the buffets of Christianity are fringe groups Who emphasize a particular lifestyle to be necessary in order for a person to call him or herself a Christian? Having personally been a member of such a group, I have been provided a perspective that I have needed in order to find true freedom in Christ Jesus. I was once within a denomination that required its members to refrain from smoking, dancing, drinking alcohol, and going to movies. Why these four restrictions were specifically chosen were because of their association with the lascivious living. Dancing and movies were considered vehicles, vehicles by which the devil tempted the flesh. Alcohol broke down inhibitions of the flesh And smoking was done by all people who went to dances, movies, and drank alcohol. It is helpful to know That most Christian groups that prohibit such living came out of the suffrage movement, which also contributed to the prohibition laws that we have in our history. What so easily happens when emphasis is placed upon a restriction of certain types of behavior is how the refrain from those behaviors become the identity. The identity for what it means to be called Christian. And so it becomes embedded in the minds of some that Christians look a certain way. Eat a certain way, act a certain way, and behave in a certain way. For those on the outside it looks like oppressive living. And for those on the inside it becomes, it becomes legalism. And the irony, from my vantage point, of such groups is how far they are, they try to remove themselves from the apparent dangers of Roman Catholicism. claiming that the Roman Catholicism is a works-oriented religion, while at the same time making their own legalism a type of works doctrine What the preacher hones in on in this section of scripture is the response God's people are to have to the reality That there are things that occur in life that are according to God's dispensation and sovereign will that we cannot understand. Even though the things we observe are grave and troubling, our ability to fathom all of God's reasoning and plans is simply not possible. And considering the length of a man's days and the fact that our days will come to an end, it is both reasonable and from the directive of the preacher necessary, and here's the point. Necessary for us to enjoy each and every moment we are given. The instruction to eat, drink, and be merry is not often repeated in the Bible. And it is not often preached in pulpits. The reason is obvious, for we are all well aware of the tendency for mankind to abuse what is enjoyed by the flesh. We can take anything that is fun, that feels good, that is enjoyable, and make it an obsession With that admission, we are to still embrace the wisdom of enjoying life to the fullest enjoyment possible. Let us then think upon our eating and our drinking with the understanding that the principle of moderation is understood. It underlines everything. We don't need a lecture this morning about what not to do. This text tells us what we should be doing, and we should be enjoying what we eat and what we drink. The power of an individual contributes to what is aesthetically pleasing. What is aesthetically pleasing is one of the highest expressions of experiencing God that we can have in this life. What I mean by that is that as we mature in our faith, our relationship with God becomes less and less about what we should be doing, what we should not be doing And more about experiencing the beauty that is all around us. As a child We think as a child, which means that we focus on what is immediate and most pleasing. We focus on what we like to eat, what we like to play with, what entertains us, and what satisfies us. It is a rare child who looks up and sees the blueness of the sky or notices the greenness of the grass. It is the rare child that notices how awe-inspiring mountain ranges can be Or how a painting can capture the meaning of life better than a photograph. Or how a song can move the soul because of the serenity it expresses. As we mature, as we mature, we understand the importance of beauty. In beautiful aesthetics, we can see God. And the palate, the palate contributes to us experiencing God. The scripture says: O, taste, and see. That the Lord is good. Taste! Of course, we taste the Lord in a particular way when we receive the bread and wine each Sunday. But we also taste him in a good steak, or good bread, or well prepared salmon. Or pasta with a tangy sauce, or sweet chocolate, or whatever is carefully prepared. God wants us to enjoy such things and not feel guilty about it. When the food melts in our mouth and we savor each bite as if it is our last In good food and good drink, we experience a satisfaction the eternal soul longs for. When food nears perfection, it makes us long for heavenly food. And then there is the instruction for us to concern ourselves with what we wear, and this surprised me a bit. Again, we know that being obsessed with what one wears is an abuse, but that is not what this is being not talking about. How a person appears is to be enjoyed as well. As was stated earlier, white, for the Easterner, was what was worn to celebrate and represent purity. And there are no other persons who should be able to wear white but those who have been forgiven of their sins and had their sins washed by the blood of the Lamb. There are no people more worthy to enjoy being well-dressed and well groomed than those who are fitted for heavenly garments. And next, we are instructed to enjoy our spouse. And while the world struggles with understanding the definition of marriage, The people of God are to participate in the institution of marriage with freedom and uninhibited joy. While it is true, while it is true that men tend to look forward to the marital bed more than women, It is the husband's responsibility to ensure that his wife finds intimacy mutually satisfying. It is not often that intimacy is discussed from the pulpit, and that is to the shame of preachers. There is likely nothing more needed in marriages than an appreciation for the satisfaction that can be enjoyed in marital intimacy. The lack of mutual enjoyment and marital intimacy is most certainly a contributor to the high divorce rate and the use of pornography among Christians. What needs to be understood is the pleasure that can be experienced by a married couple that learns to be intimate with one another. The years that pass by are to be filled with memories of learning from and enjoying one another The beauty that develops from years of intimacy defines what it means by the phrase love making And the final instruction from verse ten is simply summarize enjoy life. It is a simple instruction to do whatever is placed before us to do. Enjoy life Such a simple instruction, but difficult when our faith in God and our following of Jesus has consisted mostly of understanding what we cannot and should not do. The best description I have been given to understand how we are to view God's commandments is to enjoy life. With and in that commandment, to treat God's commandments as a fence, a fence that protects us from the dangers that are on the outside. Within the fence, within the boundaries, there is plenty of room to run around. For example, as I just gave. We are commanded not to commit adultery. But there is plenty of running around that can be done inside the fence of marriage. We are commanded not to covet, but there is much that we can enjoy within the things God has given us. The point is, there is much to enjoy about life. And the wisdom of the preacher is to tell us to enjoy it. It is given to us to enjoy. God wants us to enjoy it. Jesus died and rose again and went to the Father so that we can enjoy life Yes. Yes, our lives are vapor. They are here and they are gone But the preacher instructs us that because they are vapor, we are to enjoy every moment possible. Such a direction we can all willingly obey. Enjoy life. That is what our Savior wants us to do. Let us pray. A gracious God, we confess how much we hear from the pulpit and even what we read in your holy word of what we shouldn't be doing. We should not get into And so we thank you for this that encourages us to enjoy what we've been blessed to enjoy. And may we do that in the freedom that only Christ Jesus can give. This we pray in his name. Homet

sermons.title: Pursuing Immediacy
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Once again, I encourage you to turn to Ecclesiastes. Ecclesiastes chapter 9. We're picking up at verse 11. This is a series of sermons that it is most helpful if you follow along in your Bible. It's going to be explaining a lot of what might seem to be obscure statements in these passages. I'm wondering if you are on the boat, do you remember what you wanted to be when you grew up? You want to be a doctor, a lawyer, an astronaut, a policeman, fireman, teacher, politician, engineer, or any one of the other popular professions? And did you achieve what you wanted? It'll mean to pour salt and a wound if you didn't and that you have regrets. I ask this because studies have been done since 2010, and every year since then has come out to be the same, that half of teenagers When they are fully grown, they have the vision, the goal of being famous. When learning of this, it was new to me that being famous is an occupation. Thanks to social media, there are those who have achieved fame and made a lot of money. based on nothing more than being salacious contributors to social media. For Christians, the idea of pursuing fame should be seen as a contradiction To what we are to be pursuing in the short-spanned lifetime that God has given to each of us. The catechism teaches us that our purpose for existing is to glorify God. Our songs say, to thine be the glory, meaning to God be the glory. And we sing, if I receive any praise, let it go to Calvary. And all glory, praise, and honor to be Redeemer King. The Bible tells us to worship God alone and to seek his kingdom first. From these examples, there doesn't seem to be room for anyone who follows Jesus to seek out personal fame. Of course, it is not that easy to simply say Christians are not to seek personal fame, but it is with the same breath that we tell our children To do all for the glory of God. Whatever you do, do it to the very best you can do it. We read it last week from chapter 9, verse 10 of Ecclesiastes, where it says, Whatever our hands find to do, do it. We are told elsewhere that we have to live out our days, being fruitful and multiply. And so we are to be successful in this life. And with a certain amount of earthly success, someone can find personal fame. But with personal fame comes along greater responsibility, especially for Christians, because we claim to represent more than ourselves. We claim the name of Jesus. And with that, people expect that we live up to what we claim to be. And many, unfortunately, hope that we don't. Because it gives them another reason to reject the Christian faith. I remember the likes of athletes like Tim Tebow. becoming famous because of his football skills while also claiming to be a Christian while also publicly stating that he was going to remain a virgin until marriage Plenty of people were hoping for his downfall so that his Christian witness would be marred, so that those same people who hoped for his downfall could justify their own moral failings. Another fault line of fame for Christians is the elevating of Christian pastors to celebrity type status. Just last week, I saw another headline of a pastor of what are called mega churches being forced to step down because of indiscretions And the fact that him stepping down made headlines with certain media groups shows how some people are looking Looking for such hypocrisy in order to denigrate the Christian faith and to make themselves feel better about their own hypocrisy. But the problem is not only the indiscretions of men who are pastors, but includes the congregations that give their pastors celebrity-like status. We cannot sing if I receive any praise, let it go to Calvary, while also thinking And let it go to Pastor Mike as well, because he is just so wonderful. He understands me and he's so funny. I love his last sermon. The pattern seems to be that men with outgoing personalities and oratory skills with some feminine tendencies, let's be honest about it are elevated to the point of being praised by their congregations while also being allowed to live lives that have no accountability, for they have no one in leadership above them. And such fame feeds their ego to the point that they start to believe they are untouchable. It has gotten bad, but it has also gotten good when such men are exposed. But such exposure should include the members of those churches that elevate such men to that celebrity status. In our reading of Ecclesiastes, we have heard this morning about the superiority of wisdom. Instead of pursuing fame, God's people are to pursue wisdom. Because Solomon is our preacher. We remember that when the Lord said that he could ask for anything, and it would be given to him, Solomon asked for wisdom. And the Lord was so pleased, so pleased he gave Solomon enough wisdom to be claimed by all who met him to be the wisest man they had ever known. But wisdom, like most anything else we pursue in this life, has its limitations. It doesn't bring about all that we had hoped it would The observations made in Ecclesiastes chapter 9, verse 11 describe what wisdom cannot explain. We would expect a race always to go to the swift, and the battle to the strong, and the bread to the wise, and riches to the smartest, but that does not happen. The use of the word chance is to be understood as referring to events that happened that no one could have foreseen. And those same events change the outcome from what was expected. And wisdom also does not determine the time a man will die. We all know too well that people who have left us too suddenly and unexpectedly, wisdom also cannot foretell the future. Wisdom seemed great to the preacher, to King Solomon, but he provides a story next to show again the limitation of wisdom. It starts in verse 13 by presenting a contrast between a small city and a large kingdom. A great king would be a king who had a great army. It would be a king who had at his disposal the finest of weaponry. It would be a king who had the wisdom and skill to use his great army to defeat most kingdoms around him. For such a king to besiege a city would be quick and simple. Such a king and his army could quite easily make a full assault on a small city without losing many men. But this king, apparently wanting to give the people of the city a chance to survive, decides to surround the walls with men and traps. In order to keep the people inside the gates and force them to surrender. Why this city was besieged, we do not know But we can guess by the manner it was saved. We can speculate that there were a few bombastic citizens that would not give homage to the great king We can surmise that there were rich men in the city who thought themselves to be kings and who were unwilling to submit to the authority of this great king. We can imagine that their pride got the best of them and their tongues displayed their pride. And the king responded how any great king would respond, which is to bring the prideful to their knees. Within the city, however, there was a wise man. He was wise but poor. Just as the preacher said earlier, there are those who are wise and still have need of bread. And so this wise man rightly suggested that he go and try to reason with the great king. The wise man, excuse me, the wise man. Would not have been regarded in the city because he was not wealthy, but he did have a reputation of being wise, and so it was given to him permission to intercede He may have likely gone to the great king, found out what the great king wanted, and compromised with the great king for what was reasonable, and brought the information back to the elders of the city. The elders likely heard what was reasonable and concluded that it would be a small thing for them to comply as compared to losing their lives. and losing their families to the swords of the great king's army, and so they conceded to the compromise. The city was saved And there was likely great rejoicing and great feasting and much to be thankful for after the seed was over. But when all the celebrating died down, No one remembered the poor, wise man that saved them. So, wisdom does not always bring fame. No, it does not. So what is the point of being wise? Such a question would be hard for young minds. to answer today, again, because of the obsession for fame. The scenarios that follow in the text describe a world That does not work in the manner we hope or expect. Wise words should be heard over the shouts of a fool. Wisdom should be preferred over war, but it takes but one man to destroy peace. Perfume can be pleasing until it is corrupted by flies. One foolish word can sully a wise man's reputation. Fools can rise to great places of authority while wise men sit in low places. The digging of a pit can be useful, but a place of misfortune if the one who dug the pit falls into it. A man can break through a wall to defeat his enemy only to be bitten by a serpent on the other side A man can clear land of rocks only to be crushed by one of them. A man can split wood to warm his home, only to be impaled by a shard. One of the points of all these observations is that an entire plan can be thwarted by one small oversight or an event outside of a man's control. This is not stated, mind you, to dissuade a man from making plans or from digging or building or clearing or cutting. It is again simple observations of how the world actually works. In verses 11 through 15 of Ecclesiastes chapter 10, the lesson for wisdom is a comparison between the careful words of a wise man and the senseless talk of a fool. These words remind us of the wisdom in the Epistle of James as he warns us of the sin that is brought about because of the tongue. A foolish person reasons that because he or she lacks knowledge, they can make up for it by out talking others. A fool makes confident statements regarding life and his understanding of it. He believes he has it figured out and that he controls what is out of any man's ability to control. The last section of chapter 10, verses 16 through 20 teaches us that what we think we may want politically and socially is not always what we think it will be. We might think we want a ruler as innocent as a child, but innocence does not necessarily provide wisdom. We might think we don't want someone born of prestige and position as a ruler, but with prestige and position comes education, life experience, and these provide wisdom. Verses 18 and 19 provide another lesson on the virtue of work versus idleness. And the phrase money answers everything. can be interpreted to mean that you are only able to enjoy a feast when you are able to provide for a feast, which is to be able to pay for it. The last verse of the chapter brings us back to our relationship with our leaders. Again, there is no wisdom in a person setting himself up to be an adversary of a ruler or an adversary of those who hold high positions because of their wealth. For this preacher, there is a primary lesson for us. From this section of scripture, we have covered. The preacher of Ecclesiastes has instructed us that it is best to pursue wisdom in this life. And then And then he spends a great deal of time explaining how wisdom has its limitations. It does not provide fame. It can put you in conflict with foolish rulers. It can confuse you about the world around you, because what you expect to happen doesn't always happen, and what you expect should be doesn't always occur. The lesson for this generation is for us to recognize how much we have been influenced to pursue what is popular, prestigious, and trending and to pursue wealth by any means necessary. And speaking of what is popular and trendy Those of you who are seasoned might not be aware of how quickly information is disseminated and wrong information is disseminated via the Internet The young are able to receive information through tweets or Instagrams within seconds to their phone devices And what is happening is that a story breaks and it's reported in a tweet or on X or WhatsApp or WeChat or TikTok And that story is regurgitated with alarm and shock or immediate opinion without knowing any more of the story than the original two sentences. And because this information is so fast, those who are swimming in this social media ocean move on quickly To another social media story without bothering to follow up on the first story to find out more information The result is that nothing is thought about thoroughly. No opinion is substantiated with necessary facts. The devil, the devil has fostered a spirit of immediacy that tempts people, especially young people, to want to keep up, to never be out of the loop. And what is really happening to the devil's glee is that people are chasing their proverbial tales. What is needed? What is needed is wisdom, but wisdom that is sought after because of where it eventually leads. What is needed is wisdom that leads to Jesus. Jesus is the way, the truth, and the light. The wisdom of Ecclesiastes can only be understood and applied when understanding and embracing the gospel of Jesus Christ. As followers of Jesus Christ, we can be aware that the world does not operate in a manner we would hope or expect, that there are certainties of life. For while there are many things that we don't understand and cannot understand in this vaporous life we live, we can know Jesus. Jesus brings sense and perspective and peace to issues in our lives we cannot grasp. But on second thought. On second thought, following Jesus isn't the wisest thing we can do in this life, if it is this life we care about most. Jesus divides. Jesus sets standards we cannot achieve on our own. Jesus will have no other God before him. Jesus is not put up with people who step on his road to heaven and then look back. When Jesus prays for us to not be taken out of this world so that we might be witnesses, he also says that he has made his followers not of this world. To be of the world is to be a product of the world. It is to be pushed along by the evil spirits of each age. It is to go the way of the wide road that most people travel off. To pursue fame simply to be famous. To support a candidate for office because famous people do? To form an opinion about a moral issue because a popular person tweeted the same? To not test every spirit, which is to say every fad that comes along, is to place yourself right in the middle of the wide road that most people are traveling on. I tried for several days to find a story about a person giving up fame to follow Jesus. But I realized that such a story would continue to focus our attention on the allure of being famous. And so I decided to tell you a story from my own average life. I came to know Jesus and confess Him as Savior just before I turned 18 years old. And just after that, deciding to follow him, I went to a high school basketball game, involved in that, and afterwards Usually got with my buddies and did things teenagers shouldn't be doing. And as I walked out in the parking lot and my buddies pulled up, get in, let's go! I said to myself, are you gonna follow Jesus? Or follow them. And I decided to follow Jesus. And so I said, no, not going today. And I went home. Sat in my basement with my parents. I watched TV. Choosing to follow Jesus. Give me as simple as going home and watching TV. I believe every Christian, whether you grow up in the church or not, needs to have moments like that. And I say moments as in plural instances because there could be several instances where you need to make a choice that leads to Jesus. That is the wisest decision a person can ever make. Amen. Let us pray Gracious and heavenly Father, we thank you for that goal of wisdom, but we also thank you for the testimony of this preacher. It tells us that wisdom has its faults, wisdom has its shortcomings. And so we thank you for where it needs to lead ultimately to your Son, our Savior. May all of us make that choice. To follow Jesus. Amen.

sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Today, we begin a series of sermons based on the pastoral epistles, or more specifically. St. Paul's Letters to Timothy and Titus. This sermon is an introduction to those letters. And I trust you will find it to be more interesting than the word introduction. We begin with some basic information. We confirm that these letters were written by St. Paul, because first the letters claim to have been written by St. Paul. Further, the first letter mentions Timothy as Paul's known companion twice in 1 Timothy 1:2 and chapter 6, verse 20. What is more, the critical and direct manner of the book as it is written is Pauline, along with the likes of Galatians and Colossians. Finally, the doctrinal content is Pauline with its stress on sound doctrine. The primary reason why Paul's authorship is questioned is because of the content of these letters. Critics say that the vocabulary is different from his other letters, but an obvious answer to that is that the subject matter is different. What is consistent with Paul's letters is his concern for right doctrine. And that is stated in 12 different places in these letters. A serious problem with modern scholarship is the approach to biblical texts that do not agree with the scholar's morality. If a moral teaching or doctrinal teaching does not agree with a scholar's moral or doctrinal belief, they question its authority, and they do that by questioning authorship. Remember that one of the clearer criteria for a letter or a gospel to be accepted as part of the Bible was apostolic authorship. So if a liberal scholar can prove to himself and those who will listen to him that Paul did not write these letters, then their content can be dismissed. But it doesn't stop there. If authorship cannot be disproved, these same liberal scholars question the motive of the author. And this will we will see most clearly in the weeks ahead. We'll wait for you to get that. The date of these pastoral officials begins with 1 Timothy, and it is believed that Paul wrote 1 Timothy from Macedonia between A. D. 65 and A. D. 66. During his release from prison, it was in between his first imprisonment and his second imprisonment. So who was Paul writing to? Well, the original audience and direct audience was, of course, Timothy, who Paul called his son in the faith. Timothy was Paul's personal representative, as stated in chapter 3. He was often Paul's companion, as we see in 2 Corinthians 1. Philippians chapter one, Colossians chapter one, and first and second Thessalonians chapters one respectively From Acts chapter 16, we learn that Timothy had a Greek father and a Jewish mother. His grandmother was named Lois, and his mother was named Eunice, as told to us in 2 Timothy. He was converted to Christianity through Paul at the city of Lystra, as we see in Acts chapter 14 and again in Acts chapter 16. He was young and timid early in his ministry, and Paul mentions that in 1 Timothy 4 and 2 Timothy 1. Timothy also appears to have often been sick as described in 1 Timothy 5. Yet he was one of Paul's most trusted associates. And while these two epistles were to Timothy, they were about how some false teachers believe in myths. Stressed genealogies and tried to impose their ascetic tendencies on these new Christian converts. It is believed that the false teachers were pretend Jewish converts who also denied the future resurrection. taught contradictions between the Jewish and Christian revelations, and engaged in endless and aimless disputes about words. They also denied Christ's humanity, which is at the root of one of the most widespread heresies the church had to address And also, while this was written to Timothy, Paul was well aware that the content would be distributed amongst the Christian churches. Because his other letters had been distributed, meaning he was writing to the church as a whole. What was the exact purpose of these letters? Well, there were a number of reasons for writing 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus. Number one, Paul wanted to encourage Timothy to oppose those false teachers. Number two, he desired to furnish Timothy with written apostolic credentials of his own authority. Number three, he wished to exhort Timothy to diligence in the ministry of Christ And number four, he wanted Paul, I'm sorry, Paul wanted to instruct Timothy in church conduct But an overriding purpose, an overriding purpose of all three letters is the subject of sound doctrine. And that is where we will focus our attention this morning. As stated in these letters, the concept, the concept of sound doctrine or right doctrine, is mentioned twelve times. It was a concern and remains a concern today. And by sound doctrine, the Bible means reveal the truths that confirm the teachings of Jesus And that will always be true, regardless of the year, the place, or the culture. And it is the idea that sound doctrine exists That goes against the spirit of our age. Modern sages and internet influencers talk of each individual person having his or her own truth. And use phrases like, speak your truth. And the implication is that truth comes in many different shapes and sizes. But if truth comes in many different shapes and sizes, then there are truths that will inevitably contradict each other. To anticipate those contradictions, the modern sages and influencers came up with the idea of individual truths, with the belief that you cannot argue with a person who insists on their own truth. For what is real to them is real to them. And unless you are them, you cannot question it. Of course, that line of argument is delusional. If I were to say that my truth is that I am the president of the United States, and such was true because it's true to me. And everyone should treat me as such, which means that I should be able to live in the White House, collect my $400,000 a year. sign bills into law, have a secret service duty protect me, although I don't know how well they're doing these this lately, and sleep with your writing But that is absurd, you say. Of course it is. Just because you claim an individual truth doesn't mean everyone around you has to do your bidding to help keep up your delusion. That is one of the reasons why announcing your preferred pronouns and expecting others to adjust to your preferences is not only presumptive, but will also lead to the absurd. To prove that truth exists, meaning that there are universal truths that exist, regardless as to whether they are recognized by some people or not, we can look to the rules of logic. There are three primary rules that I remind you of to confirm that universal truths exist. The first rule is called the law of identity. It states that if something is true, it is true for all persons, in all places, at all times. For example, if the globe is a sphere, then it was a sphere a thousand years ago, and it is a sphere now. It cannot be flat to you and a sphere to me, and both of us are speaking the truth at the same time. That there are objections to this and they are little legitimate objections. What if things change? What if something catastrophic happens to the Earth that no longer makes it a sphere, such as a very large asteroid hitting the Earth The answer is that it would not change the identity that the Earth is a sphere when saying it was a sphere before the asteroid hit. If an asteroid hits the planet and anyone survives, they simply could not state that truth anymore that the Earth was a sphere. Another objection is stating an error. For example, this is just an example. If scientists say that the earth is warming, And it is warming, and its warming is caused by human modern living, and such warming is a danger to the existence of the planet. And if we don't do something, we will all be underwater within twenty years. And that truth twenty years later doesn't happen. Then how was that truth a truth? Again, just an example. Made it up. I made it up. Well the simple answer is that that truth was never a truth It was always a falsehood not properly identified, meaning that the identity of what then was believed to be a truth was actually a falsehood and always was a falsehood The second rule of logic is the law of excluded middle. This law states that a statement or a truth or a falsehood is either true or false with no third option. If a statement is made that says sodomy is immoral, such a statement is either true regarding its morality or false regarding its morality. There is no third way or third option or something in between moral and immoral. Also, we can examine it another way. You can say that sodomy is moral And that statement also doesn't have a third option. It is either a true or false statement with no ambiguity possible. And finally, the third rule of logic is the law of non-contradiction. And this rule really breaks the mind of the rebellious because it insists That if something is true, it is true for everyone. If something is false, it is false for everyone. If stealing is an immoral act, then it is immoral for all people. It cannot be immoral for me, but not immoral for you. Truth, in other words, does not bend the knee to your unique circumstances. Thus, statements such as God exists or God is real Are either true for everyone or false for everyone. Such statements cannot be true for me and false for you. If truth could contradict itself, then no scientific discovery could be made, no morality could be agreed upon. No societies could be governed. No conversations between human beings could be trusted or useful. But how you ask, how does the unbelieving or the pagan mind get away with defying these rules of logic? If they are laws, then they are to be obeyed, right? I answer first that I set out to prove that truth exists, and these laws help us see its existence. But laws being in place never guarantees that they will be followed. When teaching ethics for a college course I had to study the subject matter more deeply than I had in my college days. And I learned that philosophers have labeled the method of getting around these rules of logic They labeled it utilitarianism. It would be helpful for your own sanity to know about the practice of utilitarianism Because it is how some people, many people, approach moral dilemmas. Have you ever asked yourself, for example, how a politician Who is Roman Catholic defends and even supports laws that allow for abortion to be legal and for abortions to be eagerly sought after When the Roman Catholic Church has a clear and anopolitic stance against abortion? The answer is utilitarianism Utilitarianism states that the primary goal of any moral or political position is the greater good. What is the greater good is that which is what is best for the most amount of people, they say. And what is good for the most amount of people is to be pursued at all costs. There are, you know, nuances to utilitarianism. One is called rural utilitarianism, which states that While the greater good is the priority to pursue, there are some rules that need to be followed, such as respecting other people's individual rights. But the other more popular nuance followed today is titled act utilitarianism, which means that any act or action done is acceptable As long as the goal is the greater good. Such an approach to life also is known by the phrase: the end justifies the means. The primary critique of utilitarianism, whether it be rule or act, is who is to say what is the greater good? By what standard is the greater good determined? It appears to this preacher that the greater good for Western politicians today is whatever will get them elected. But thanks be to God, the Christian Church has an anchor, or better yet, a foundation stone by which we can determine what is the greater good. The greater good for the Christian church is, of course, the establishment of God's kingdom on earth as it is in heaven. The means to establish God's kingdom on earth is by placing our faith in Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. And the one reason we should do that is That Jesus claimed ownership of truth. Jesus himself is sound doctrine. Allow me to remind you of the many verses in the Bible that connect Jesus to truth and connect truth to Jesus. John alone in his gospel is determined that when we think of truth, we think of Jesus. In John chapter 1, verse 8, Jesus is called the true light. In John chapter 1, verse 17, we read For the law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ The Greek word, in all of John's uses of the gospel, of the word truth, excuse me, in his gospel, is the same word. And to give you a sense of how the Greeks use that word, I lifted a quote from an article about the Greek word elithea, meaning truth. Quote, Parmenides refers to truth, Elethea, as revealing, unrevealing. For ancient Greek philosophers, Alethea uncovers the structure of human reality, making it the opposite of illusion. In other words, knowledge does not come from idleness, but from proactive engagement with human reality. And we can say, we can say that no one addressed in his teaching and showed in his actions more care about human reality than Jesus. So the Greeks thought that the concept of truth was something to actively pursue and actively engage. And so when Jesus says to Thomas, when asked that Jesus show the place where he is going, Jesus said in John 17, 6, I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one can come to the Father except through me. So notice how going the way is to be active. And when active, going the way, we are to go after truth, and Jesus Himself is that truth. So Jesus, knowing how the Greeks used the word truth, refers to himself as the truth, meaning that to follow him is not to be idle, but to have a proactive engagement with him. And then there is this most famous quote from Jesus from John 8, verses 31 through 32. If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free. Before saying this, Jesus had established himself as truth personified. Thus, the one who will set you free is Jesus. And that is why we believe in Jesus. It is not because of archaeological discoveries, it is not because of how we were raised, it is not because Christianity is a part of our American heritage. We believe in Jesus because he speaks the words of everlasting life. No one has ever spoken like him. His words give life to the soul. And his actions, his actions display a perfect man and a perfect sacrifice for sin. Having faith in Jesus means having faith in his sacrifice, which was giving up his life to pay for our sins. There is no other truth that provides forgiveness of sins and a clear conscience, and that is how he sets a person free. In Jesus, old things pass away, and all things become brand new. In John chapter 18, you will remember verse 37, Pilate, who was given the responsibility to condemn Jesus or release him, Asked Jesus if he is the King of the Jews. The passage then reads, Jesus answered. You say rightly that I am a king. For this cause I was born, and for this cause I come into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice. And Pilate said to him, What is truth? There is, of course, undeniable irony in Pilate asking such a question when the truth is standing before him. And the same can be said to so many churches who have abandoned Jesus as the only way to the Father. And treat their so-called Christian faith as one of many religions, all of them being the same in their hearts and eyes. And the same can be said for Western culture that has a Christian heritage with no appreciation for how it has helped create the prosperity that they enjoy. But we, we happy few, we band of brothers, can answer Pilate's question, what is truth? Truth is Jesus. Jesus is sound doctrine. And he is what we will uphold. Let us pray. Gracious and Heavenly Father, we accept this revelation of the truth of Jesus, of who he was, and what he said, and what he did. And as we accept that truth, may we not put up with false teaching and false doctrine. May we stand, even if we stand as one of many, may we stand on that truth. It's in Jesus' name we pray. Amen.
