In John chapter 1, verse 17, we read For the law was given through Moses, grace and truth came through Jesus Christ The Greek word, in all of John's uses of the gospel, of the word truth, excuse me, in his gospel, is the same word. And to give you a sense of how the Greeks use that word, I lifted a quote from an article about the Greek word elithea, meaning truth. Quote, Parmenides refers to truth, Elethea, as revealing, unrevealing. For ancient Greek philosophers, Alethea uncovers the structure of human reality, making it the opposite of illusion. In other words, knowledge does not come from idleness, but from proactive engagement with human reality. And we can say, we can say that no one addressed in his teaching and showed in his actions more care about human reality than Jesus. So the Greeks thought that the concept of truth was something to actively pursue and actively engage. And so when Jesus says to Thomas, when asked that Jesus show the place where he is going, Jesus said in John 17, 6, I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one can come to the Father except through me. So notice how going the way is to be active. And when active, going the way, we are to go after truth, and Jesus Himself is that truth. So Jesus, knowing how the Greeks used the word truth, refers to himself as the truth, meaning that to follow him is not to be idle, but to have a proactive engagement with him. And then there is this most famous quote from Jesus from John 8, verses 31 through 32. If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free. Before saying this, Jesus had established himself as truth personified. Thus, the one who will set you free is Jesus. And that is why we believe in Jesus. It is not because of archaeological discoveries, it is not because of how we were raised, it is not because Christianity is a part of our American heritage. We believe in Jesus because he speaks the words of everlasting life. No one has ever spoken like him. His words give life to the soul. And his actions, his actions display a perfect man and a perfect sacrifice for sin. Having faith in Jesus means having faith in his sacrifice, which was giving up his life to pay for our sins. There is no other truth that provides forgiveness of sins and a clear conscience, and that is how he sets a person free. In Jesus, old things pass away, and all things become brand new. In John chapter 18, you will remember verse 37, Pilate, who was given the responsibility to condemn Jesus or release him, Asked Jesus if he is the King of the Jews. The passage then reads, Jesus answered. You say rightly that I am a king. For this cause I was born, and for this cause I come into the world, that I should bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice. And Pilate said to him, What is truth? There is, of course, undeniable irony in Pilate asking such a question when the truth is standing before him. And the same can be said to so many churches who have abandoned Jesus as the only way to the Father. And treat their so-called Christian faith as one of many religions, all of them being the same in their hearts and eyes. And the same can be said for Western culture that has a Christian heritage with no appreciation for how it has helped create the prosperity that they enjoy. But we, we happy few, we band of brothers, can answer Pilate's question, what is truth? Truth is Jesus. Jesus is sound doctrine. And he is what we will uphold. Let us pray. Gracious and Heavenly Father, we accept this revelation of the truth of Jesus, of who he was, and what he said, and what he did. And as we accept that truth, may we not put up with false teaching and false doctrine. May we stand, even if we stand as one of many, may we stand on that truth. It's in Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Cultural Accommodation
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated and turn in your pew Bibles To First Timothy chapter one. I will be walking verse by verse. To First Timothy chapter one. Just this past week, I witnessed a woman on social media pretending to be a pastor. Preach a sermon in which she claimed that if Jesus were with us today, which he is, but again she thought she was a pastor, so such what you get But her claim was that if Jesus were with us today, that he would be a counselor at abortion clinics. where he would hold the hand of those getting abortions in order to make them feel loved and make them feel good about their decision to abort the fetus or what we would call a baby. I don't give you her name and I won't give you any other information about her because she doesn't deserve anyone's attention, but I use her as an example to ask once again How did we get here? The sermon so-called, where she said such awful things, was in a supposed Christian church. And it's hard to realize that people listened to her and allowed what she said to influence their lives. Again, how did we get here? We started last week a series of sermons from what are called the pastoral epistles. And so we begin with 1 Timothy 1, verse 1. Paul begins by referring to Jesus Christ as our hope, which is unique to the New Testament. The Greco-Roman world was truly a world without hope, very much in the same way that our culture over the last generation has become increasingly, noticeably, profoundly a culture without hope. Proof of such is how much emotion we put into our political candidates Almost as if we are electing a new Savior every four years. Then perhaps the most profound evidence of our culture losing hope is the plunging birth rate in Europe and North America. Such is a result of not seeing anything in the future that excites or is important. So there is apparently no hope to pass on to future generations. But for Christians, for Christians, Christ has opened a sure and certain way to heaven. Indeed, he has gone to prepare a place for us. Our lives can be lived in the confidence of that beckoning future. And that is what the New Testament means by hope Not a wish, but a firm and confident certainty about the future. That is hope. This kind of hope was then and has always been one of the one of Christianity's outstanding. And absolutely unique features. For there is no hope in the lives of Islam. There is only hope with a lowercase H You hope it will go well for you when you die, but you don't really know whether it will or not. And to presume to know is arrogance in Islam In Christianity, such confidence is faith. Verse two For Paul to refer to Timothy as his son in the faith strongly suggests, though it doesn't absolutely prove, That Timothy became a Christian under Paul's influence, likely on Paul's first missionary journey But the statement also confirms Timothy's authority as one close to Paul and having his confidence And having Paul's confidence is important because though the letter is addressed to Timothy in a variety of respects, it is undoubtedly a personal letter. There is much in it that seems to have been addressed to the church in Ephesus, where Timothy was then ministering, and it was also sent to Christians everywhere, as I mentioned last week. The greeting at the end of the verse is most certainly Pauline, as it shows he greets fellow Christians in all of his letters. Verse 3. What seems to be suggested here is that at some point Paul and Timothy had met face to face. after Paul had left his younger associate in Ephesus to deal with the false teaching there. Timothy had left Ephesus to consult with his mentor and his oversight. Perhaps in hopes of rejoining him in his itinerant ministry, because apparently there wasn't much texting going on back then. But Timothy had been told to return to Ephesus and to complete his work there. He wasn't an officer of that church in Ephesus But something like an apostolic delegate, we might even call him a bishop, for he was doing the work of what a bishop is called to do. The fact that he is writing this letter after the two men had talked face to face is no doubt at great length about the situation in Ephesus. It's an indication again that this letter to Timothy was intended to be read by the whole church. But who were these false teachers? And what was their point of view? The following is a quote from Bible commentator William Mounts regarding the false teachers. Quote, it appears to have been a form of aberrant Judaism with Hellenistic Gnostic tendencies. That over-emphasized the law and underemphasized Christ and faith, taught dualism, in which the spiritual was emphasized at the expense of the physical Asceticism, denying the physical resurrection, a viewpoint that often went with dualism, was unduly interested in minutiae of the Old Testament Produced sinful lifestyles and irrelevant quibbling about words, and was destroying the reputation of the church at Ephesus. Verse 4. Myths and endless genealogies describes at least some of the different teaching mentioned in the previous verse. Apparently these teachers, as I have a number of false as a number of false teachers have throughout the ages Studied the Old Testament genealogies and their host of names, and fashioned from them stories that were then used to teach a certain way of life. A way of life quite different from that which was taught by our Lord Jesus. Verse 5. I will be coming back to this verse as it will be the foundation of what I want to emphasize today. The text says the word command. without pointing to any particular command, so we can interpret it to be a short way to reference the commandments of the Old Testament and specifically the Ten Commandments. What I will say now is that it is a very odd for Christians to discount the importance of the Old Testament and the commandments of God. Paul makes it clear in his letter to the Galatians that the law or commandments of God lead us to Jesus. We can't fulfill all of them, and even the ones we think we can fulfill, we don't do so in our hearts, which is the fundamental place they are to be obeyed. And that reality is what leads us to Christ Verse six. The description here of people having turned aside from the commandments of God and turning to idle talk is correctly referenced in your pew Bible as being explained in chapter 6, verses 4 and 5, where the idle talk is described as being obsessed with disputes and arguments over words that are said to be useless, meaning they solve nothing and certainly do not bring glory to God or righteousness to men. Verse 7. That there was trouble in Ephesus is quite clear, which again was where Timothy was serving at the time of this letter. How much teaching there resembled that which was troubling the Colossian Church sometimes before this is difficult to say, though clearly there are similarities. The false teaching was Jewish in origin, but mixed in elements of Hellenistic or Greek thought as well. The teachers encouraged lax moral living and a variety of religious speculative superstitions that had nothing to do with biblical truth or the historical record of the good news of Jesus Christ. And what is more, provides no encouragement for the holy life that the apostles had taught his converts. Like most Christian heresy The false elements came from the culture. Either Jewish or Roman, it doesn't matter. Came from the culture. Jazz up the apostolic message in a way that would prove attractive to people at that time and in that place. And it is that last statement about this section of Scripture that false heresies and false elements came from the culture, is what needs to be addressed by the Christian church. A few years ago, I read Ross Duthat's book titled Bad Religion: How We Became a Nation of Heretics. Duthath has a unique take on Christianity, being a confessing Christian while also a columnist at the New York Times, believe it or not. His book is a very depressing narrative, thoughtfully and convincingly told. He recounts the decline of the mainline Protestant denominations in the second half of the 20th century. Having accommodated the faith to the culture, they were soon left only with the culture and no faith And then the similar accommodationist project pursued in the Roman Catholic Church after Vatican II with similar dismal results. He then goes on to describe the resurgence of evangelicalism and conservatism in the Roman Catholic Church in the late 20th century. And that would seem to be a happy outcome, but then he goes on to describe how once again that momentum was squandered. when cultural accommodations continued to weaken the influence of the evangelical part of the church. In an effort to make Christianity attractive to the world, the church or churches became too much like the world to remain of any interest to the world. And that is hard, really hard to admit. The world, in other words, came to think that it already had, albeit in a different form, what the Christians were offering. Whether it was health and wealth, which is a baptized materialism the world already had, or a highly subjective message in which God within, the God within, or our experience Of what we call God became more important than God Almighty, who made the heavens and the earth, and who reveals Himself and His will in His Holy Word. The world was left thinking that it could do what the church was doing and do it even better So allow me to give you examples of where the Christian Church is much like the world, to attract the world, when in fact it turns the world away. Emotionalism. Much of Christianity has adopted the language of the psychological world. So that we sound more concerned about how we can heal a person emotionally rather than spiritually We talk about our feelings as if they are to determine who we are and what we stand for. We discuss the importance of identity and how important it is for our children to have their own identity. We put faith in personal acceptance so that we don't feel bad about our body type. We talk of accepting ourselves and to be accepting of others. But the Bible doesn't use that language. And the gospel doesn't preach such self-esteem. In fact, it can be argued quite forcibly that it preaches the opposite of some of the things I have described. The opposite is in Holy Scripture so that we don't base our faith on how we are feeling at any particular moment. Because we all know our feelings change. They change as the wind blows, changing in both direction and strength. And this is where the false teachers snatch up the deceived. They prey on our emotions. They know what to say and how to say it, so that you are deceived while you testify that what you heard was the best sermon you've ever heard. But in that sermon, in that sermon you were never called to greater holiness, never called to greater faith, never called to deeper love, but only made To feel good about yourself. Truth is, because the idol of emotionalism, false teachers have us worshiping ourselves without us knowing it. Another place where Christians are too much like the world is our love to be entertained. And I am not referring to how we love to watch television. I'm referring to Christians who love to be entertained during or in their so-called worship services. Take an objective look at a church band and compare it to a secular band. The instruments are the same, the outlets are the same, the music is the same, only the lyrics might be different. But as some critics have noted, there are songs that churches sing today where the name Jesus can be replaced by my girlfriend or my boyfriend, and no other change would be needed. Personally, I like to shop at stores that accept knockoff brands and overproduce products that they buy from mainstream stores. At these knockoff brand stores you find cologne that tries to smell like more popul the more popular and well-known cologne colognes. And that is what modern Christian music can be compared to. It tries to be the same as secular music, and it is not. And the most dangerous place where Christians are too much like the world is our shifting morality. As I stated last week, if a statement is true, it is always true, regardless of time, place, culture, or person. If sexual immorality is a sin, then it is always a sin, and for all time a sin, and for all places a sin, and for all cultures a sin, and for all persons a sin. What I didn't make clear last week is that there is a difference between saying something like, I think sexual immorality is a sin, and simply saying, sexual immorality is a sin. By taking the I think out of it. The former statement is simply a testimony. It is a person telling what they think or believe, and that's simply personal. But when a moral statement is made that leaves out what a person thinks or believes, it is necessary then to recognize that it has a truth value placed upon it. And so if the Bible states that sexual immorality is the breaking of God's commandments, such has a truth value that is either truth or false. Thus it is then true for everyone in all places at all times, or it is false for all people at all places at all times. The truth value of sexual immorality being a sin that is not determined by whether a couple they plan to be married, thus their adultery can be overlooked. And I didn't make that one up for I have heard Christians say such things. And the truth value of such a statement is not adjustable because the person you love, maybe it's your nephew or niece. They're attracted to the same sex and because you love them, you're going ahead and affirm their sin. Such thinking leads me to a necessary point that goes back to my opening example of a false teacher claiming that Jesus would encourage a woman to get an abortion. The word love. The word love has been compromised, hijacked, and been used in a blasphemous manner. Love and the manner Jesus used it and practiced it was to rescue people from their slavery to sin and to rescue them from the fires of hell, which is where they were headed before he called them to follow him. The love of God does not make people feel good or feel comfortable about their sin or their sinfulness. Instead, the love of God pulls a person out of their sin so that any guilt attempted afterward is a false accusation. All that I've said is to take us back to verse 5, which was the positive understanding of God's commandments. Instead of being disputed or argued about, they are to be loved and with sincerity. So what I leave you with that I want you to remember is that the Christian faith is to be one of the Christian faith is to be one that is sincere and without compromise. Sincerity comes from within. It is a confirmation that we truly believe what we say we believe. And the greatest sincerity detectors are the young. They know when someone is telling the truth or does not believe in what they say they are believing. And they are the most important people to be sincere with, because they will not believe what we are teaching them to believe unless they know that we believe it ourselves. To be sincere is to be honest with ourselves and with God. It is to say to God on a repeated basis, I believe, but help my unbelief. And for our Christian faith to be without compromise, we must willfully choose to not allow circumstances or the spirit of the age to change our convictions. Stealing another person's goods does not all of a sudden become acceptable. Damaging another person's property does not become normative because of political differences. Hating another human being is not understandable, no matter their ethnicity or political affiliation. As Christians, we both stand for what we believe, and we are willing to die for what we believe A Christian being willing to die for what he believes is the best witness to the truth of the gospel that the church has ever had. So receive this charge. Regarding our faith in Jesus Christ, be sincere and without compromise. Amen.

So receive this charge. Regarding our faith in Jesus Christ, be sincere and without compromise. Amen.

sermons.title: Sound Doctrine
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Leave me seated. We are looking at 1 Timothy 1, verses 8 through 11. So turn there in your Bibles if you would. 1 Timothy 1, verses 8 through 11. There is a story I heard several years ago from an eyewitness So I hope it is true. A deacon of a Baptist church was told that he was to do the reading from the Bible for the Sunday morning service Which was the preacher's chosen text for Mother's Day. The text was to be from 2 Timothy 1, where Paul encourages Timothy To be built up in the faith, which was a faith passed down to him through his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. The obvious point the preacher planned to make is how important mothers are to their children following the Christian faith. But the deacon got confused when he turned to 1 Timothy instead of 2 Timothy He then found the place where mothers are mentioned and read, as we heard earlier, that the law is made for the ungodly And for sinners, for the unholy and profane, and for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers Now one would think that the preacher would simply announce the mistake and then read from 2 Timothy about Lois and Eunice. But this particular preacher told the congregation that all scripture is inspired, and so he simply and dutifully made up a sermon on the spot on Mother's Day about the law being for people who murder their mothers. Again, I heard it from an eyewitness, so it has to be true. The passages that we read from First Timothy are straightforward enough for us to understand what immoral behavior Paul is condemning, but it has confused Christians over the years Regarding just how much a Rukta, how much of a role the law of God plays in the Christian life We will go through verses 8 through 11 and then we will circle back. So verse 8 Here the apostle continues his thoughts from the preceding verses regarding how false teachers had entered the church and were partificating on the law of God, and apparently We're teaching lax morality. It is understandable that upon hearing the Christian gospel and emphasizing grace and faith that a person would conclude they no longer needed to heed the law of God. Words like being free in Christ And that the yoke of Christ is easy and light. Sound, sound like obedience to the law of God is no longer required. And so Paul here turns the point back to the Christian to point out first that the law is good. Interestingly, there are two primary Greek words for the word good, and Paul uses both of the Greek words for good 34 times in these two letters to Timothy. Clearly, Paul is focused on Christians being good morally and doctrinally in order to stay in the faith. But what does Paul mean by saying the law is good if it is used lawfully? We will come back to that point. Verse nine. The beginning of this verse reminds us once again that Timothy was a real person with a close relationship to Paul and his teachings, and that is this in this letter, with that relationship in mind. And so we wonder if Timothy knew exactly what Paul was saying When he states that the law is not made for a righteous person. It sounds like he is referring to a previous conversation they both had about the law. What it means to us has several possibilities. It could mean that those who are in Christ Jesus, meaning those who are Christians, have been made righteous and are living righteously and therefore don't need the law. And some have taken that meaning and decided that they no longer even need to read the Old Testament because the law does not apply to them. For those of you who have heard me preach and teach for any length of time, you know that I've despised that understanding. Another possibility of its meaning is that he is speaking in a facetious manner, meaning that he knows that there is no one who is righteous on his own or her own merit, and therefore the law is needed for everyone. The third possibility is that he is referring to the righteous who are made righteous by Christ, and then showing how the law can continue to be used. For turning the sinner to their need for a savior in order to be righteous, and that understanding turns them to Christ Jesus. That is an argument Paul makes clear in his letters to Romans and to the Galatians We now turn to the sins Paul chooses to list in regards to how the law of God can address those who choose to be or remain subordinate to sin. The lawless and insubordinate to the law are those who refuse to abide by any restrictions upon their lives. They want to do what they want to do with no authority, political or religious. None of it is going to rule over them. Such people live selfish lives while also living with no self-discipline. They are the type of people that most other people don't want to be around. The identification of ungodly and sinners is the most general listing. It includes everyone who does not know Jesus Christ as their personal Lord and Savior. It is people who either don't believe there is a God or refuse to acknowledge Jesus as God. Next are the unholy and profane. To be unholy is also to be ungodly. Being unholy is a result of not having Jesus as your Savior and thus having no propitiation for your sins. To be profane is of a different type of sin. It is to be willfully wicked. This moves the list to a second type of lawlessness Whereas the sins before could be passive, the sin of being profane is doing something to purposefully dishonor the God you say you don't believe in. And so the profane moves us to be murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers. I wish to take a bit more time on this listing of such sins, for they truly are wicked. To kill father or mother, or just one and not the other, for the reason of simply being wicked, is a breaking down of what it means to be human A person's father and mother are the closest thing to themselves. Not only are they humanly responsible for the existence of their children, but they are also responsible for the sustaining of their children. If this is done with any type of love and caring, the Bible tells us that such parents are to be honored and nothing less. God takes the honoring of parents so seriously that in his law is a command that if a child curses his parents, he is to be stoned to death. Interestingly, such a stoning is never recorded to have happened, but the law itself shows how serious God is about parents being honored. And there is a fundamental reason for that concern. The first God-like figure a child has is his father and his mother. As described, parents are the caretakers of their children, providing food, shelter, clothing, and protection. Parents also provide an education for their children, and by that I don't mean sending their children to school. I am referring to teaching a child manners, teaching them how to clean up after themselves. Teaching them to keep themselves healthy and to understand things of the world and of course of God. Like God Himself, parents provide all that is needed for a child to be self-sustaining. And as a child honors the god-like figures in his early life, so he or she will honor God when they are on their own and even starting their own family. It is called transference, and it is real when it comes to children honoring their parents and then also honoring God. When children do not honor their parents, such is an inevitable breakdown of society. It will not be avoided. Next is listed is manslayer, which is simply someone who takes the life of another. One of the greatest breakdowns our society continues to witness is our insensibility to the value of another person's life. We don't value human life as we should, and the result is abortions, school shootings, street shootings, public knifings, and random violence. That seems more rampant because of the many street cameras we now have. Such violence and murdering has an evil. Spirit behind it. It is a spiritual problem as much as it is a physical problem. Next is listed fornicators and sodomites. It is important today for us to have these two listed together. Fornication is simply sexual intimacy outside of a marriage covenant. It includes sexual intimacy of all types. Whether it is with two persons who are married, but not to each other, or when one person is married and the other is not, both are called, as we know it, adultery And fornication includes two people who are not married being sexually intimate. Too often we hear preachers condemn acts of homosexuality, but say nothing about heterosexual immorality. Both are sins in the eyes of the Lord. And I appreciate here the term sodomite It describes what is going on in a homosexual relationship, and it takes us back to the biblical language, instead of bowing to the language the devil prefers, which is like gay or same-sex. Next listed is kidnappers. Some translate it to be enslavers. The idea is what the law of God condemns in the Old Testament, which is called man stealing. Such is similar to murder in that the lives of another human being is not honored, but instead is used to profit the thief when selling a person into slavery or buying an enslaved person. Next, listed are two words that apply to the legal system of a society. Liars are those who bear false witness. The manner in which these words are used is not addressing conversations where you tell someone you you didn't have breakfast when you did, or you did play with your brother's computer when you said you didn't No. These words apply to being in a justice setting where criminals are being charged and being examined and witnesses are not telling the truth, which is perjury. And the guilty are withholding the truth or bearing false witness. And the reason such sins are serious enough to be mentioned here is because a society cannot function Cannot function when it cannot enact justice on the guilty or cannot free the innocent. When the courts can't be trusted, a culture ceases to be functioning and healthy. Thus the law of God is needed to restore order and dignity to people What is fascinating, and perhaps a bit surprising to some is how Paul connects sound doctrine to moral living. Put another way, how we think about God and what we believe about Him is going to affect how we live our lives. I asked last week when describing a woman who thinks she is a preacher and she teaches blasphemous things about Jesus. and then justifies her three abortions as right moral acts and thus a righteous thing to do. I ask the question, how did we get here? Well, Paul answers the question here. We get to immoral life behavior because we abandon sound doctrine. We get to immoral life behavior because we abandon self-doctrine, sound doctrine. And let us be honest with ourselves, as there are some of you who don't like to talk about or be taught about or think about sound doctrine. You might say it is too detail-oriented for you. You might say that the language confuses you You might say you don't have the time to think about such complex things. And yet, and yet The proof of the need for having sound doctrine is stated right here. And if you don't have sound doctrine, your life will be affected negatively by it and if the church doesn't have sound doctrine, their last stand will be justly blown out But where does sound doctrine start? Well, Paul says it in verse eleven It starts with the glorious gospel. And the glorious gospel is the revealed truth that God so loved the world that he gave his only Son. He gave him to humanity to teach us, to exemplify God to us, and to be a sacrifice on the cross for us. We can place our trust in that sacrifice for our sins, for our sins to be forgiven, and then for our lives to be lived out according to his teachings and according to his example. Such a summary leads us to the plain message of this passage of Scripture, and that is, Christians are to live good moral lives. The living of good moral lives is expected of us, and the one who expects it is Jesus. For Jesus himself lived a perfect moral life and taught us how we can follow his lead. And I must say at this point the obvious: living a good moral life is not easy. There are temptations to compromise our morals all around us. The spirit within us is willing to live a good moral life, but the Bible also says That the flesh wars against the spirit, and the flesh is weak. And so the temptations are plenty and strong The flesh is weak, and the unbelievable world doesn't want us to live a good moral life. They are rooting against you. They are like the mean girls who all of a sudden hate the prom queen when they very much liked her before. But now that she was elected prom queen, they hate her. And say they don't hate her because she was elected prom queen and they weren't. So that's precisely why they hate her. When Christians lead good moral lives, the world hates you Because you remind them that they are not living good moral lives. Misery does indeed love company. And they want Christians to be miserable in their own sin just as they are miserable in their own sin. And they also don't want you to live a good moral life because they like their sin Even though it makes their conscience feel guilty, they enjoy the pleasure enough to keep sinning and be spiritually miserable. I have heard just this past week that this year's elections are primarily about the economy and abortion rights. Supposedly, such are the two subjects voters care most about. But I question that summation in regards to abortion. I recently heard a woman confessing that abortion isn't the issue for her. The issue is her having the ability to live a sexually immoral lifestyle. and not have any consequences for that lifestyle. An abortion gives her another option to not have consequences. At least she's being honest. People truly do cling to their sin. So temptations are all around us, and they are strong. Our flesh is weak. And our unbelieving friends, our unbelieving neighbors, acquaintances, and even some of our family members hope we fail. Doesn't sound like a recipe for successfully living out a good moral life. It isn't. It is hard And because it is hard, because it is hard, we need men to lead their families, both in words and in actions. We need men to speak the truth, stand up against falsehood, and lead by example And we need strong women. We need wives and mothers who will also speak the truth while letting their husbands lead as they are called to by God. We also need women who will help their husbands live good moral lives. And finally, we need children, children who are willing to be different from their peers if their peers do not know the Lord. Being different from one's peers can be the hardest thing a young person can do, but it will be the most rewarding thing to do for your soul. Remember that Jesus described his followers as being in the world, but not of the world. To be of the world is to be a product or result of what the world believes. To be of Jesus, to be of Jesus. Is to be a product or result of what He has done for us and within us. He has made us holy, and so let us live out. Holy lives. Amen

sermons.title: Get all you can out of life
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen

sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated and turn, if you would, in your Bibles to Ecclesiastes. The book of Ecclesiastes, chapter 11. We're looking at chapter 11, verses 1 through 6. Ecclesiastes eleven, verses 1 through 6 Please be mindful of what I said early on in our study of this book of Ecclesiastes. The book as a whole is one sermon. It is thus difficult But not impossible, but still difficult, to take sections of the book and make each section a separate sermon. A good sermon ebbs and flows. It hits hard in some places and slows down enough for reflection in others. Taking a step back and looking at what we have covered the last several months, we can see the ebb and flow In chapter 7, we learned how wisdom is better than foolishness, and that when we choose foolishness, we should not be surprised by the consequences. In chapter 8, we learned the importance of submitting to authority, and in specific submitting to God's authority regarding the things we cannot control. In chapter 9, we were challenged to not only accept that there are things we cannot control, but to have faith in God in the midst of our trials and our tribulations. Next, we learn that we are free to enjoy the good gifts God has given us. And last week we were informed about the limitations of wisdom. And that wisdom must lead us to Christ for it for that wisdom to have lasting value. To transition to the lesson in chapter 11, we must keep in mind that there is a temptation to respond to the fact that there are limitations to wisdom. And that response might be to sit and do nothing. The question could be asked If wisdom doesn't lead to fame, if it doesn't give clarity to strange things that occur in life, then why pursue it? There are two general responses to life circumstances that appear ruled by determinism. We can say, what's the point of trying? We can't do anything to change the outcome. Or we can say, let's get all we can out of life since God, since we know God has everything. under control. And from the lesson given in the beginning of Ecclesiastes chapter 11, we can see that the preacher Solomon prefers the latter approach. Get all we can out of life. A literal reading of verse 1 can cause a bit of consternation. Cast your bread upon the water. If a person casts bread upon water, we know by experience that the only thing that is going to come back to him is soggy bread. And that would happen only if the birds and fish didn't get to the bread first. So what does this verse mean? If you struggle to answer that question, you are certainly not alone. The following are quotes taken from various commentators regarding Ecclesiastes 11, verse 1. From commentator Albert Barnes quote, the verse means show hospitality Even though the corresponding return of hospitality to you may seem improbable, nevertheless be hospitable in faith. Some interpreters not unreasonably understand by bread the seed from the produce of which bread is made. seed cast upon the fertile soil flooded by the early rains would be returned to the sower in autumn with a large increase. End quote From commentator Adam Clark, quote, Cast thy bread upon the waters, an allusion to sowing of rice, which was sown upon muddy ground, or ground covered with water. and trodden on by the feet of cattle. It thus took root and grew, and was found after many days in a plentiful harvest. End quote. From commentator John Gill, quote, Cast thy bread upon the waters, as the wise man had often suggested. That nothing was better for a man than to enjoy the good of his labor himself. Here he advises to let others, the poor, have a share with him. And as he had directed in the preceding chapter how men should behave towards their superiors, here he instructs them what notice they should take of their inferiors. And as he had cautioned against luxury and temperance, intemperance, he here guards against tenacity and covetousness and exhorts to beneficence and liberality. That which is to be given is bread, which is put for all the necessaries of life, food and raiment or money. That answers all things, but may be a supply of wants, a support of persons in distress, what is useful, profitable, and beneficial. So which is it? Is the verse referring to hospitality? Is it seed or rice? Is it food for the poor? From these three commentators, there is at least one thing we can be assured of. The meaning of the verse is that we are to be giving. It could be hospitality, it could be sowing rice for a future harvest, or it could be giving directly to the poor. Whichever It is there is a consensus that we, God's people, should be giving. The reference To the number seven and then eight in verse two helps us to better understand verse one. The number seven we are to remember represents fullness or completeness. Thus to give a serving unto seven is to give unto completeness or to give as much as is needed. To give eight is to give beyond what is needed. It is to give in an overflowing manner With this information, we can conclude with commentator Mr. Gill that this verse one is indeed talking about giving to the poor. The natural events that are described in verses 3 and 4 are also events that man cannot control. The manner they are described contains a warning against idleness. A man who is idle and simply observes the events of life is a man who does not sow seed. He doesn't give. He does not cast his bread, and so he does not sow, and finds that he will not reap. If he does not cast bread upon the water, it will not return to him. If he does not give, then nothing will be given back to him. The facts stated in verse 5 first remind us of the words of Jesus regarding the Holy Spirit. You remember from John chapter 3, verse 8, Jesus said, The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound. But you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit. Next, we are reminded of Psalm 139, where David states, quote, My frame was not hidden from you when I was being made in the secret. Intricately moving in the depths of the earth, your eyes saw my unformed substance. In your book were written, every one of them the days that were formed for me when as yet there was none of them. The blowing of the wind and the forming of a child then in the womb are both mysteries to us. And both are acts of God, making him the one who knows the secrets. The difference to be made in understanding that God knows the secrets and that God is doing the things that men are not. privy to watch is that we are able to be free to sow our seed in the morning. Also as instructed in verse 6, we are to sow seed in the evening. But why? Why the morning? Why the evening? Because we don't know which sowing will end up prospering. Will it be the work we do in the morning that will prosper, or will it be the work we do in the evening that will prosper? Whichever it is, God knows, and he would have us sowing at both times. So we stop at verse 6 and try to summarize what we have been taught. We are to give of ourselves. Give what is essential to life to those who are in need. And we are to give beyond what is needed. We are not to sit back and observe life, but instead we are to be actively involved in giving with the understanding that there is going to be a return. on what we are giv giving, even though we cannot control it or see how it's going to come back to us By faith, we are to be giving at all moments of the day with the faith that God will bring about an increase. Sounds pretty simple. Sounds like good advice. We are to give We are to give especially to those who have needs. The problem is, if we are honest in examining ourselves, we don't give as much and as often as we should. Solomon preaches this advice to God's people after having witnessed much of life. And has viewed how men don't spend enough time caring about their fellow men. When Jesus was amongst men, he said literally the same thing. Jesus said, give and it will be given to you. Good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over, will be put into your lap. For with the measure you use it, it will be measured back to you. What we need to be reminded of today are the more difficult words. Jesus spoke before his admonishment to give. Remember that the Sermon on the Mount was a ratcheting up of holiness. He was not simply repeating the moral law of the Old Testament, but setting a higher standard of holiness. Remember these words. Give to everyone who begs from you. And from one who takes away your goods, do not demand them back. And as you wish that others would do to you, do so to them. If you love those who love you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. And if you do good to those who do good to you, what benefit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. And if you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners to get back the same amount. But love your enemies. And do good and lend, expecting nothing in return. And your reward will be great. And you will be sons of the Most High For he is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. Be merciful, even as your father is merciful. I suspect that many of us, when we hear such words of Jesus, we scoff a bit under our breath. It's kind of like what most men do when they hear the words of Jesus explaining that lusting is the same as committing adultery. We stop and say, yeah, right, like it's possible not to lust. Well, to these words about giving, we say, yeah, right Like I'm going to j just give good things to my enemy. Like I'm going to just give to anybody who asks of me. Like I'm going to lend my money and expect nothing in return. There is no way. We can't imagine it. Christians have debated for centuries what really was going on in Acts chapter 4, trying to dissect what it meant for Christians living in Jerusalem to share all things in common. It is described as people not treating the things they possess as their own, and that when land, for example, was sold. The monies made became property of the body of believers and not of any individual From this description it is debated whether a person's spiritual maturity and health could be detected in the manner that he or she allows others to use what they own The point can be made via a question. Can a Christian be living faithfully and at the same time withhold the sharing of his property? The challenge is difficult for people of a society that values material goods as much as you and I do. We speak about homes and cars and valuables using words like my and mine It is my house. It is my car. That television is mine. We even use those words to describe time, using phrases like, you're wasting my time. It appears that by our verbiage that ownership or at least claims to ownership are very, very important to us. Perhaps we could should consider how Jesus understands us when we say what we own. Perhaps we should consider Jesus' perspective when I claim that it is my house or my car. Perhaps we should consider that it is quite absurd for a person who lives under the sun and has a vaporous life for me to claim ownership of time. This obsession about ownership of material goods is sometimes justified with the argument about being a good steward. We argue that it is good for us not to loan out our things because we are being a good steward by ensuring that what we have is not damaged or misused. The problem with that argument is that nothing in Jesus' words seems to foster a concern about being a good steward over giving freely of what we have. Jesus said, give if it is asked of you. That's it. No qualifications. I proclaim to you emphatically, based on the wisdom of the preacher of Ecclesiastes and based on the commands of Jesus, that a Christian cannot live faithfully and be close-fisted. Which means to be unwilling to share freely of what you have been given freely. The ability to give freely is all too rare amongst us today. We are too suspicious, too stubborn, too selfish with the things we claim to own We need to repent. Repent from this obsession with ownership and be freed from such bondage and listen to the preacher and cast our bread upon the water. All too often, when we hear lessons about giving, we think monetarily. I briefly mention our claim of ownership over time. It is also our time that we are to give freely when we are asked for it. We are to give freely of our time without expecting anything in return. Because I give my time to someone doesn't mean they have to give me time in return. And again, this goes against our culture, for we are a people that expect a dinner invitation from the people we have had over to our house for dinner. We expect a card from the people who send us cards, or people we send cards to. The act of giving without expecting a return is a new world to us, and yet it is God's world. It is how citizens of God's kingdom are to live. We are to give of ourselves in whatever capacity is asked of us, and we are to expect nothing in return. And please notice that when the preacher describes planting in the morning and in the evening, that can be interpreted to mean planting early in one's life and later in one's life. Stated plainly, we are to be giving of ourselves all the days of our vaporous life, whether we are 10 years old or 100 years old. We are to be giving, freely giving. The importance of living a life of giving is seen in the numerous times that it is encouraged in the New Testament. To the Galatians we read, let us not become weary in doing good. For at the proper time, we will reap a harvest if we do not give up. To the Hebrews we read: God is not unjust. He will not forget your work and the love you have shown him as you have helped his people and continue to help them. To the Corinthians, we read, the point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully. Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. To the Philippians we read, I am full, said Paul, having received from Epiphroditus the things which were sent from you. a sweet smelling aroma, an acceptable sacrifice, well pleasing to God, and my God shall supply all your need, according to his riches, in glory by Christ Jesus. You see, beloved, casting our bread upon the water is not just an advice of a sage. It is a description of what it means to say we are Christian. We are givers. We give whatever we have. And we believe that it will come back to us and even more. Let us pray. A gracious God, we thank you for these mysterious words, words that do call us To be mindful of how much you gave, and that because of that model you set before us to give your only begotten Son, we ourselves who follow you are to be givers. May that conviction reign in us until our days are ended, knowing how much will be returned to us. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Good Warfare
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Open your Bibles to 1 Timothy chapter 1 First Timothy chapter one beginning at verse twelve. Once again, we will be going through this verse by verse. First Timothy chapter one beginning at verse twelve. Comedian Nate Bargetse has a bit where he talks about his parents being Christians and states that they still are Christians. But when he was growing up in the 1980s and 90s, he says that they were the most Christian. And then he states that Christian parents in the 1980s and 90s were the most Christian of all Christians. And I get that humor because I began to walk with Jesus at the end of 1982, and it was somewhat popular, somewhat popular at that time to be a Christian. And one of the popular things Christians would do was to read books by Frank Peretti His first book was published in 1986, titled This Present Darkness. It depicts a fictitious town called Ashton Where a skeptical reporter and a pastor begin to compare notes and suddenly find themselves Fighting a hideous plot to subjugate the townspeople and eventually the entire human race by way of demonic forces. Caretti helps the reader understand that what we see physically is nothing compared to what is happening spiritually. As a person prays, angels and demons are fighting by the sword in the spiritual realm And the depiction of the battles would have the reader picture in their minds the greatest swords play imaginable They were and perhaps are still very entertaining books, although the Bible doesn't describe spiritual warfare in the same style as Peretti. But just as there is warfare in Peretti's books, so does Paul use the word warfare when writing to Timothy. And that is where we will end our focus this morning. But we begin with examining verse 12 through 20 of 1 Timothy 1, verse 12. The manner this verse is worded may make it sound as if Paul was chosen by God to minister in the church because Paul was faithful. But that interpretation would discount what Paul says next about himself, which is that he was a blasphemer, and thus not faithful to God at all, but instead Paul was an enemy of the gospel. And so we look for another understanding of what Paul means, a more likely interpretation Is that after Paul was knocked down by the appearance of Jesus on the road to Damascus and was blinded by the presence of Jesus, And then was rebuked by Jesus and then called to repent and follow Jesus that Paul was made, made faithful. We know by the manner God calls people to himself to do his ministry that he doesn't base such callings on the person's ability. Moses, for example, was a poor public speaker and a man who was guilty of murder. King Saul was a very poor leader, but was made the first king of Israel by God. The nation of Israel itself was insignificant when God called them to be his people, and they were repeatedly unfaithful to that calling. My point being that God chooses the unlikely and makes them to be what he needs them to be. Verse 13. After stating that Paul himself was faithful, he needed to confess that he was what he was before he was made faithful. A blasphemer is someone who speaks falsely and offensively about God. I insist that what I am about to say is not not Not anti-Semitic. We may side with those who are of the Jewish faith because we confess the God of the Old Testament But we are not the same because they deny the God of the New Testament, and to do so is to blaspheme God. And again, to say so is not being anti-Semitic Is simply telling the truth about God. For God revealed Himself in and through the person of Jesus God offered his only son, and Jesus offered himself as the only, the only possible sacrifice for our sins to be forgiven. To reject God's offer and the offered life of Jesus is to blaspheme God. Such is true for Jews and Gentiles alike. I too was a blasphemer until Jesus revealed the truth to me. All who do not believe are blasphemers. As a persecutor, Paul is referring to the days before his conversion where he persecuted Christians. The account, as told in the book of Acts. has Paul holding people's tunics while they stoned Stephen for being a Christian. We then learn that Paul had a reputation for dragging Christians out of their homes and out of synagogues. And changed and charging them with blasphemy if they confess Jesus as their God. Certainly some of us could be called persecutors of Christians if we have ever made fun of Christians or wanted them to be quieted. But Paul truly was a persecutor in every possible sense. To call himself insolent is likely connected to being a persecutor. For to be a persecutor in the manner Paul was, you had to be rude and arrogant, and that's what being insolent means At the end of verse 13, we once again could read it incorrectly. For it could sound to some that God overlooked what Paul did because Paul was ignorant. As if being ignorant is a good excuse for being for behaving, excuse me, poorly or sinfully. In Holy Scripture, ignorance never excuses sin We are told elsewhere that God overlooks the sin of people for a time because of the ignorance of the people, but the sin still needs to be dealt with. That is why Paul uses the word mercy as in I obtain mercy. And it is why he uses the word grace as in, and the grace of our Lord was exceedingly abundant. Both mercy and grace of God are needed to forgive sins. In fact, Paul refers to all that is needed to forgive sins, for in verse 14, he goes on to describe the abundant grace He was given along with faith and the love of Christ Jesus. What Paul has done in these two verses is described the one and only manner he was saved from sin and death. And it is the same way and the only way any of us is saved from sin and death It is by grace, through faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, because of the love of God, that anyone is saved from the guilt of their sins and there deserved eternal judgment. Verse 15. It is very likely that this saying was shared amongst Christians early on. It is short and pithy and memorable. What Paul adds at the end, the confession of his own unworthiness, is compared to others that is also memorable. Interestingly, this verse played a key role in the life of a man named Thomas Bilney, who was one of the earliest English reformers. and earliest to be martyred for his faith in 1531, during the reign of King Henry VIII, before Henry became a friend of the Reformation. blindly said this about this verse. I chanced upon this sentence of St. Paul in 1 Timothy chapter 1. It is a true saying, and worthy of all men to be embraced, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the chief and principal. This one sentence, through God's instruction and inward working, which I did not then perceive, did so exhilarate my heart Being before wounded with the guilt of my sins, and being almost in despair, that immediately I felt a marvelous comfort and quietness Insomuch that my bruised bones leaped for joy. After this, the scriptures began to be more pleasant to me than honey or honeycomb. And such a response is evidence of a tougher and stronger time when men could face come face to face with their failings And then face to face with the gospel of Jesus Christ, and instead of being crushed by their guilt or embarrassed by what others knew about them. He can rejoice that what he is and what he has done can be forgiven and he can be made new. Paul had that toughness as well. May we have it also. Verse sixteen Paul here explains how his suffering, his sufferings, and he had a great deal of it as he lists them to the Corinthians. But those sufferings were used by God as a testimony to the unbeliever. For if he, Paul, could overcome the pains and trials of life while having faith in his Savior Jesus Christ, so could they. And this thought causes Paul to break out into a doxology. And we know that Paul considers the value of his calling to be about bringing sinners to God. And it appears that the pr that the privilege of doing so causes him to praise God even more. Because of the Amen at the end of verse seventeen, we should summarize Paul's point. Paul has already argued that these men Who are false teachers, that they have seriously misunderstood the nature and purpose of the law of God. And now he reminds Timothy to remind the Ephesians that salvation is by grace and by Christ. Not by human achievement of any kind, and certainly not by the program these new teachers are recommending. Paul's point can be put simply. I came to Christ not although I am a sinner, but because I am a sinner. And being a sinner, only God could save me. And it was God who did save me by his grace through faith in Jesus Christ. With that established, verse 18. Has Paul passing on his calling to retrieve the lost by reminding Timothy of the time there were prophecies about him? We could call such a time his ordination, such as when a man is set aside for the work of the church in a formal capacity. They even likely included hands being laid on Timothy, for we know that such was done at ordinations. For Paul later instructs Timothy to not lay hands on any man suddenly, which means quickly, as in, be careful who you ordain to the ministry of the church. Regarding the prophecies, we should remember that a prophecy could be a new revelation that God calls his prophet to speak. Or it could be a word God has already spoken, and the prophet shows the church how to apply it. Verse 19. Here Paul is concerned that Timothy live out what was prophesied about him. For if he does not, he will not be living by faith. And if he does not live by faith, he will not have a good conscience. To not have a good conscience is very difficult, both spiritually and psychologically. Many turn to substance abuse to drown their conscience. A guilty conscience drives people to other sins to distract their conscience. The end result is a faith that becomes shipwrecked. He says shipwrecked, which is a metaphor. For not only something that no longer works, but also for something that is abandoned. And such a metaphor leads Paul to remind Timothy of the example of a no longer working and abandoned faith. In the lives of a person named Himenaeus and another named Alexander. We don't know intimately who these men were That Paul mentions men who have gone astray and turned to idle talk in chapter 1, verse 6. And in 2 Timothy, Paul mentions Himeneus by name again and calls him out for saying that the second resurrection had already occurred. That teaching disturbed a great deal of people, for if it was true, those who were alive still had missed it. And would be left to die without hope. And this now brings us back to Paul charging Timothy to wage the good warfare. It also connects us back to last week, where we taught that sound doctrine is connected to holy living. Thus, good warfare occurs both in the doctrines we understand and believe and in the lives we live. I began with mentioning author Frank Ferretti and his novels about spiritual warfare because they awaken me. To the reality that there is warfare going on in the spiritual realm that is occurring on a daily basis, and the war is about the will of God and for the souls of men. I have witnessed too many Christians just in this small parish be unaware, unaware of the spiritual warfare that was going on. And the end goal of the battle was their soul. And I have witnessed people lose. Just like Himenaeus and Alexander, Paul describes their faith being shipwrecked. It is broken and abandoned. I have confronted young women about them living with their boyfriend, and I did so because I feared for their souls. As they were compromising their morals for earthly love and affection. One young woman I confronted left my study and never darkened the doors of St. Stephen's again. Another young woman I confronted about the same sin, left the church, and her parents left with her. None of them understood that there was a spiritual warfare going on over their souls, and they were losing. I don't want to be cartoonish about it as if each of us has a demon on one shoulder and an angel on the other shoulder and each is whispering in our ears what we should or should not do But when we heed false teaching or don't have sound doctrine at all because we don't read our Bibles, We don't attend Sunday school. We don't attend Bible study. We don't read good teachers about the Bible. We are susceptible to our own faith being shipwrecked. There are spiritual winners and spiritual losers when we make moral decisions. When we decide to withhold forgiveness because of how hurt we feel, we might as well picture an angel getting thrust through with a sword. When we are too prideful to be rebuked or corrected, we may as well picture a demon with his foot on the neck of God's spiritual servants. When we choose to side with envy, with greed, with lust, with pride, selfishness, or falsehood, the enemy smiles. And our own spirit is vanquished. But I can't end here. I can't stay on the side of the sinfulness of our spiritual battles For that is not who wins in the end. We just sang about that. The following is from Peretti's first book. As the demon started to enter the church, suddenly, as if colliding with a speeding wall, the creature was knocked backward. And into a raging tumble down the steps, the glowing red breath tracing a corkscrew trail through the air With an eerie cry of rage and indignation, it gathered itself up off the sidewalk and stared at the strange door that would not let it pass through. Then the membranes on its back began to billow, enfolding great bodies of air, and it flew with a roar headlong at the door, through the door, into the foyer, and into the cloud of white, hot light. The creature screamed and covered its eyes, then felt itself being grabbed by a huge, powerful vice of a hand. In an instant, it was hurling through space like a ragdoll, outside again, forcefully ousted. The wings hummed in a blur as it banked sharply in a flying turn and headed for the door again. Red vapors chugging in dashes and streaks from its nostrils, its talons bared and poised for attack. a ghostly siren of scream rising in its throat. Like an arrow through a target, like a bullet through a board, it streaked through the door, and instantly fell itself felt itself inside, tearing loose. There was an explosion of suffocating vapor, one final scream, and the flailing of withering arms and legs. Then there was nothing at all except an ebbing stench of sulfur. And two strangers suddenly inside the church. The big blonde man replaced a shining sword as the white light that surrounded him faded away. A spirit of harassment, he asked. Or doubt, or fear, who knows? And that was one of the smaller ones. I've not seen one smaller No indeed. And just how many would you say there are? More, much more than we, and everywhere, never idle. So I've seen the big man sighed. But what are they doing here? We've never seen such concentration of them before. Here. Not here. Oh, the reason won't be hidden long, he looked. He looked through the foyer doors and toward the sanctuary. Let's see this man of God. They turned from the door and walked through the small foyer. The bulletin board on the wall carried requests. for groceries for a needy family, some babies babysitting needed, a prayer for a sick missionary. A large bill announced a congregational business meeting for next Friday. On the other wall, the record of weekly offering indicated the offerings were down from last week. So was the attendance from 61 to 42. Down the short and narrow aisle they went, past the orderly ranks of dark stained plank and flat pews, toward the front of the sanctuary, where one small spotlight illuminated a rustic two by four cross. hanging above the baptistry. In the center of the worn carpeted platform stood the little sacred desk, the pulpit, with a Bible laid upon it These were humble furnishings, functional, but not at all elaborate, revealing either humility on the part of the people or neglect. Then the first sound was added to the picture, a soft, muffled sobbing from the end of the right queue. There, kneeling in earnest prayer, his head resting on the hard wooden bench. And his hands clenched with fervency was a young man, very young. The blonde man thought at first young and vulnerable, but all showed in his countenance Now the very picture of pain, grief, and love. His lips moved without sound as names, petitions, and praises poured forth with passion and tears The two couldn't help but just stand there for a moment, watching, studying, pondering. A little warrior, said the dark-haired one. The big blonde man formed the words himself in silence, looking down at the contrite man in prayer. Yes, he observed, this is the one. Even now he's interceding, standing before the Lord for the sake of the people, for the town. Almost every night he's here. At that remark the big man smiled. He's not so insignificant. But he's the only one. He's alone. No, the big man shook his head. There are others. There are always others. They just have to be found. For now, his single vigilant prayer is the beginning. He's going to be hurt, you know that. And so will the newspaper man, and so will we. But we will win? The big man's eyes seemed to burn with a rekindled fire. We will fight. We will fight, his friend agreed. They stood over the kneeling warrior on either side, and at that moment, little by little, like the bloom of a flower, white light began to fill the room It illumined the cross and the back wall slowly, brought out the colors of the grain of every plank of every pew, and rose in intensity until the once plain and humble sanctuary came alive with an unearthly beauty. The walls glimmered, the worn rugs glowed, the little pulpit stood tall and stark as a sentinel backlit by the sun And now the two men were brilliantly white, their former clothing transfigured by garments, they seemed to burn with intensity Their faces were bronzed and glowing, their eyes shone like fire, and each man wore a glistening golden belt from which hung a flashing sword. They placed their hands upon the shoulder of the young man, then, like a grace, fully spreading canopy, silken, shivering, nearly transparent membranes began to unfurl from their backs and shoulders and rise to meet the overlap above their heads gently undulating in a spiritual wind Together, they ministered peace to their young charge, and his many tears began to subside. Again, beloved, this is the opening of Frank Peretti's book titled This Present Darkness Warfare. God's people. Warfare. Stay in the battle and fight. Stay and fight. Amen. Let us pray. A gracious and heavenly Father, open our eyes to that which is spiritual. Open our eyes to the battles that are raging for our souls and the souls of our fellow men. Open our eyes and give us faith to fight. We pray this in Jesus' name.

sermons.title: Necessary Paradoxes
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. And I encourage you to turn in your Bibles to 1 Timothy That's right before 2 Timothy. 1 Timothy chapter 2, we're working through verses 1 through 7. 1 Timothy chapter 2, working through 1 thro Seven I wonder if any of you have heard of a theologian named Jacob Hermanson. Well, that is his Dutch name. Some of you may recognize his Latin name, which is James Arminius. If you have not heard of James Arminius, I will introduce you. Try not to mix up his last name. with being an Armenian, which are people who hail from Armenia, which is a country north of Iran. It can be confusing because people who called the teachings of James Arminius are called Arminians, and those who hail from Armenia are known as Armenians. With the difference between the two names being an E instead of an I or an I instead of an E. So James Arminius was a Dutch theologian Serving the Protestant Reformation in the 16th century in the capacity of a professor of theology at the University of Leiden. He became renowned for his teaching against the Belgic confessions, which makes claims consistent with the teachings of John Kelvin regarding the doctrine of predestination. Arminius wanted to reform the reformers regarding doctrines such as total depravity, irresistible grace, and perseverance of the saints He claimed he only wanted to teach and believe what the Bible teaches. He wanted to emphasize that all persons are given an opportunity to believe on the Lord Jesus for their salvation. And that is done by God's prevenient grace. He called it prevenient grace, or grace that goes before To enable a person to make a choice to be a Christian or not. At the time of the Reformation, some believed that such teaching was heretical. And Christian leaders were pressured several times to claim James Arminius as a heretic. Arminius died in 1609 while in the middle of a public debate about his teachings. He was survived by his wife and nine children. And we are going to come back to Professor Aminius' teachings after we look at verses 1 through 7 of 1 Timothy 2. So verses 1 and 2. These two verses flow together, so we will look at them together. Paul has just encouraged Christians to fight the good fight, and he gave examples identifying those who had lost the fight and thus lost their souls. He stays within the church operations by instructing Timothy, who again was leading the church at Ephesus, to pray. Simple enough. He does so by listing the types of prayers that should be prayed in the church. Supplications. Supplications are prayers that request God's help while also taking a humble approach Thus, it is the type of praying that is concerned with both what is said in the prayer and the inward approach of the person praying. Next, the word prayers is a simple and general term where the rest fit under. Intercessions are simply prayers on behalf of others. But this is important. To be Christian is to simply not simply pray for yourself As Christians, we are to be part of a body, part of a bride, part of a city, part of a nation. Our existence in Christ automatically puts us in relationship with one another and with other Christians. Next is giving thanks, and that's straightforward for us. The general thanksgiving prayer in our prayer book for morning and evening prayer is one of the better prayers ever written for giving thanks. And then Paul includes with that instruction to pray for all men. That can be tough. for some Christians to do, for there are people that are evil and people who are simply not likable. There are people who want us to abandon our Christian faith or to be arrested for what we believe. Such people are most difficult to pray for. But such a teaching is derived from what Jesus specifically said. Jesus said Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you. Jesus exemplified his words by praying for those who put him on the cross. You remember this. Asking the Father to forgive them, for they did not know what they were doing. Next, included in the instruction to pray for all men, is to specifically pray for kings and all who are in authority. Again, not easy to do. Part of our morning prayer service is a prayer to be prayed daily that asks God's blessing on those who have authority over us. And this instruction by Paul is especially powerful considering that Nero, that name, Nero, the first great persecutor of Christians, he was on the throne. Of Rome, when Paul gave this instruction. Pray for those who ferociously persecute you? Yes. Pray for them. But why? Paul gives the answer. He says at the end of the verse that we, we Christians, may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and reverence. Living a quiet and peaceable life means that Christians are able to live out their lives, their convictions, without government interference. This verse, this verse has guided my personal political voting over the years. Rich of the candidates locally, statewide, and nationally are going to give Christians an environment where we can live quiet. And peaceable lives in all godliness and reverence. Answer that, and you will know who to vote for. The beginning of verse 3 confirms that what Paul has just described is what God wants. It is good and acceptable in the sight of God, our Savior. And then Paul says, who, referring to God, desires all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Such a passage James Arminius loved to focus on. In that passage, we have an insight into the heart of God. If this is what God wants, then we too should want it, and we too should pray for it. That is how such a passage is interpreted by many. But is that what it actually is saying? We will come back to this verse With the thought of all men being saved and coming to the knowledge of the truth, leads Paul to state plainly what that knowledge is and what that truth is. Starting at verse 5, it is clearly stated that God is one and that Jesus is the only mediator between God and man. There is no other. No matter what the coexist stickers say, or what the liberal mind wants to believe, there is no other way. Jesus himself again said it plainly. I am the way, the truth, and the light. No one comes to the Father but by me. Such a statement cannot be made more plain and the interpretation of it more obvious. Paul then goes on to explain what Jesus did to be the only mediator between God and man. He paid the penalty, the ransom for the sins of mankind. So that we do not have to pay it, which would have cost us our lives in this world and in the world to come, which is for us to suffer eternal death. Paul next finishes his comments on the subject of praying for all men by stating emphatically his call to preach the truth and to teach the truth. And from these words, we can be assured that Paul cares, and we can say he is even obsessed about the truth. It sets us free. At this point, I'd like us to go back to verse four, where we are told that God desires all men to be saved. Such a verse rests comfortably with these other verses from the Bible. To the nation of Israel through the prophet Isaiah. He said, Yet the Lord longs to be gracious to you. He rises to show you compassion. And these next words are from Jesus as he looked upon the city of Jerusalem. O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it. How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under wings? And you would not. Matthew 23 Through the prophet Ezekiel, the Lord God said, For I have no pleasure in the death of anyone, declares the Lord God. So turn and live. From 2 Peter chapter 3, we read, the Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise, as some count slowness. But is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance. All of these, along with more well-known passages such as John 3. 16, describe the heart of God Almighty And they should move us to be smitten by him because of that heart toward his creator, his creatures, those he created in his image, you and me. There is a problem. There is a problem. Such passages collide Into other passages of Scripture that speak of a different reality, at least different on the surface. Ephesians 1, verses 4 and 5. Paul said, Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him. In love, he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will. And then from Romans chapter 8, verses 28 through 30, Paul said, And we know that for those who love God, all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers And those whom he predestined, he also called. And those whom he called, he also justified. And those whom he justified, he also glorified. But Paul didn't make any of this understanding of predestination up on his own. Jesus from John chapter 15, verse 16, Jesus said. You did not choose me, but I chose you, and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you. And then from John chapter 6, verse 44, Jesus said, No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day. This gets Paul to think in this manner, and he says in 2 Timothy 1, verse 9 Again, Paul speaking of God the Father, who saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works, but because of his own purpose and grace. Which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began. And then from Ephesians chapter 1, verse 11, Paul said, of Jesus In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will.
