For me, this is an anniversary of sorts each Christmas season. It was just a few days after Christmas. of 1982 when I surrendered my life to Jesus the Savior. And it was the Christmas message that sent me over the edge. It was too much to resist, too much to take in, that God would humble himself in such a form of an infant. How does a person say no to that type of love? And what words are there to say in response? And yet you can't just sit there and say nothing. Mary couldn't hold it in. My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has rejoiced in God, my Savior, for he has regarded the lowly state of his maidservant For behold, henceforth all generations will call me blessed. For he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name. If she can't hold in Christmas, why should we? There is no reason to. But imagine the tension of living under the covenant in centuries before the Messiah. The mental conflict would be stark. The psychology is twisted as the heart and mind longed for relief The prophets proclaimed justice. Israel will certainly be judged. But the prophets also proclaimed grace. God will come to redeem his people. Even though Israel sin, they're worse than those of the pagan nations of Cana. Even those of Sodom and Gomorrah, which we know God destroyed. We would expect that God could do nothing less than wipe Israel out entirely. Yet the promise of grace came again and again. God will surely redeem his people. But how can he wipe them out and redeem them at the same time? It seems as though God's justice violates his mercy in the other way around. God, it seems, is in a bind. If he redeems, he is winking at sin. If he judges, he does not fulfill the promise of salvation. God seemed to be wanting to build attention and build it and build it and then came Jesus. Can we feel the agony of life without Christmas? No wonder Mary sings. She carries life from the dead, light from darkness, home from exile. Seeing, O baron, you who have not born, break forth into singing and cry aloud, you who have not labored with child, for more are the children of the desolate than the children of the married woman. Imagine sitting in the deserts of Babylon and Assyria, counting the stars, juggling mercy and justice. O come, O come, Emmanuel, and ransom captive Israel, that mourns in lonely exile here, until the Son of God appears. Rejoice, rejoice Emmanuel shall come to thee, O Israel. And Mary sings on, and his mercy is on those who fear him from generation to generation. He has shown strength with his arm. He has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts. These words speak of fulfillment and victory. I wonder how much victory we have spoken this year. How much victory has the church proclaimed this Christmas season? Our Christmas celebrations are no longer accepted in our culture. They are no longer regarded as religious. It's a winter song fest at the school, not a Christmas concert. The greeting, as you know, is Happy Holidays, not Merry Christmas. It's a winter break for college, not Christmas vacation. So settle down, you who get all excited with your unwanted and unwarranted Christmas cheer. Save it. It's not wanted. But the beauty of the story cannot be hid, for old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new. In the incarnation, we see that in him was life, and the life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. Light light overflows, overpowers, and blinds like its creator The triune reveals himself as a God of excess, the God who gives all, the light that chases away darkness. The Son. The Son gives all for the Father and the Spirit. The Father gives himself over to the Spirit and the Son. The Spirit returns more sacrifice and love back to the Father and the Son. The coming of the sun is the expressed image of God bursting into the old world. He dwelt among us. And how lovely is your dwelling, O Lord of hosts. My soul longs, yes, even faints, for the courts of the Lord. My heart and my flesh cry out for the living God. Words of King David. David fainted and cried at the excess he saw. How he would have burst forth if he had seen the sun. The excess of the incarnation bridles my tongue each year as I attempt to preach with words that seem impossible to express. I see parents struggle as their little children grow older to ask questions. They struggle with how to explain what we are celebrating. Some have come up with the birthday idea. Jesus was born this day, and so we wish him happy birthday. But as well-meaning as that is, we must understand it to be more than a birthday. We are not celebrating that Jesus is 2,025 years old today. We are celebrating that God became man and walked among us Singing Happy Birthday does not provide the required awe that the story contains. And so and so we rely on readings of old, the songs of old, and we use them again and again, and somehow. Somehow, unlike everything else that becomes passe and tedious, the readings always say more than they did before, and the songs never, never disappoint. It is obvious why the message cannot disappoint. It should not surprise us that Christmas contains the most traditions and most symbols of any of our holy days. We need them, for they attempt to express the depth of God taking on the form of a man. The Christmas tree, for instance, causes us to look backward and forward. For it all began at a tree. The need for a savior began at a tree, as Eve ate first and then Adam. Judgment was passed on a tree as the Savior was nailed to and hung from one. And it ends with the tree, as the tree of life takes center place in the new heaven. What goes under the tree is a type of excess we worry about during Christmas. It's too much. We care about earthly goods too much. The extravagance of the wrapping with its bright and shiny colors and bows is beautiful and stirs the imagination The content inside those boxes excite the mind of a child almost to a frenzy and cause many excited stomach aches. The older and seasoned among us say they don't get excited for gifts as they once did, but they love watching their children and grandchildren get excited. And part of the reason is because they remember the emotions and stomach aches they had as children. But all of it can seem so secular and materialistic The gifts are only matter. Matter we see a thing burn in the fire on judgment day. And we are spirit. We are destined to live in the heavenly realm as spiritual beings We should be shouldn't be concerned. We shouldn't be concerned about earthly things. But those wrappings are still pretty, and my stomach still aches with excitement. When we spiritualize our celebration in such a manner, we have missed what we are celebrating. We are celebrating matter. You are celebrating that God became matter, flesh and blood, man. In doing so, he redeemed his creation, his matter, his world, that he called on the sixth day of creation very good. And Mary sings on. He has put down the mighty from their thrones and exalted the lowly. He has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent empty away. She still bursts forth. Her song continues. And that's another thing we do to excess during Christmas. We eat a lot this time of year. And we eat what is rich in sugar and fat. We eat sweets in the form of candy canes, chocolates in all shapes and textures, cookies with frosting, pies and cakes that fill up our eyes and then our stomachs. We eat too much. We eat more than we need. And yet Jesus was sent to fill us, fill us with good things. If we were to spend all our days eating and reclining in like manner, it would certainly be to excess. But this day, on this day, it cannot be to excess For it is only in the grace of God that we see true excess. He has given more than we can ask for or imagine. And Mary sings. He has given help to his servant Israel in remembrance of his mercy. That's the word, isn't it? Mercy. In his mercy he remembered man. How do we express it? What synonyms or Greek lexicon can help unravel it? Can a word study or a theological encyclopedia help us understand mercy? No, it must be experienced. For Mary, a song burst forth from her womb just was filled with the Savior of the world For each of us, a song bursts forth within our hearts, for Jesus is in our hearts. This takes us beyond speech, for what we are saying is not only did God come to dwell among us, but within us. Even saying it in a casual manner that I just did embarrasses me. I don't have better words. There is not enough oratory skill within me to express this reality. And so I turn to the old readings. And I say, unto us, a child is born, unto us a son is given. And he shall be called wonderful counselor, Almighty God, everlasting Father, Prince of Peace. Mine eyes have seen thy salvation, which thou hast prepared before the face of all people To light a light to lighten the Gentiles and the glory of thy people, Israel. And then I turned to the old songs and sing as we did today. Joy to the world. The Lord has come Let earth receive for king. Let every heart repair him room and heaven and nature sing. And heaven and nature sing. O come all ye faithful, joyful and triumphant. O come ye, O come ye to Bethlehem. Come and behold him, born the king of angels. O come, let us adore him. Oh come, let us adore him. Oh come, let us adore him. Christ the Lord. Hark, the herald angels sing. Glory to the newborn king. Peace on earth and mercy mild. God and sinners reconcile. Joyful all ye nations, rise. Join the triumph of the skies. With angelic host proclaim, Christ is born in Bethlehem. There is more to say. Yes, indeed, there is. But these help. They help us burst forth. And we are allowed to. Nay, we cannot help but do so this day. Merry Christmas.

sermons.title: Worship pass it on
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Imagine a little bit and over the In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. I preached this series of sermons several years ago. And I made a booklet out of it and handed those booklets out to each family in the church. So some of you have heard what I am about to preach today and the next four weeks, although modified. I was visiting with um Howard Mosier Who I told him I was going to be repeating a series and he said well a sermon isn't good until it's been preached a hundred times. So take that advice But what I'm about to preach, I believe, is very important, and perhaps I'll preach it every three years. I have preached and taught many times the warning that a man's conviction can become his son's tradition, which can become his grandson's elimination. This usually occurs because the first man did not pass down well enough the basis for his convictions. The common example is a man's patriotism. Imagine a grandfather who loved his country and expressed said love by flying his U. S. flag on Flag Day, Veterans Day, Memorial Day, Independence Day. He hosted a family picnic every year on the 4th of July. He prayed to God to bless the United States and its citizens. He was proud to vote in every election and he rooted heartily for the United States of America every Olympic Games. And his son did the same. His son loved the traditions of his father, and so when he had a family Of his own, he displayed the U. S. flag on all the days his father did. He hosted his own 4th of July picnics, and he prayed for his country and called himself blessed to be living in the greatest country in the world. But his son, who is the first man's grandson, isn't so sure about how great this country is He hears from his teachers that the history of the United States is not honest, and that generations before him overlooked the sins of their forefathers. Our forefathers' treatment of Africans and Native Americans was abusive at best and murderous at worst When this son asks his father about why he thinks the United States is the greatest country in the world when it has such terrible sins in its founding, his father cannot answer Because in truth he loves the country because his father loved the country. And his father never explained what foundation Of that love was beyond the way he displayed it, that love. Conviction to elimination happens quickly. Second generation, third generation, and it's gone Of course, there is nothing wrong with being upfront and honest about the sins of our forefathers. I have preached about our culture's failures to address the sins of our forefathers. But we can only address the sins of our forefathers with an understanding of the Christian gospel. The sins of our forefathers teach us how to apply the gospel and how the gospel is to permeate all aspects of our lives and our culture. But I turn back to passing on convictions. Passing on convictions requires explanation, cogent explanation for the traditions you have. For without understanding traditions, they become dead on arrival to the next generation. That reality is very easily seen in Christian traditions examined, examined in the context of how we worship. Take a quiz. Why do older churches use pews for sitting? And why are they placed in rows one behind the other? Don't know? Change it. Why is the pulpit on one side and the lectern on the other? Don't know? Change it. No, don't just change it. Get rid of them both. Why is the communion table in the middle? Why is it back behind the lector and pulpit? Why do ministers wear dresses? Why is everyone so somber and serious when they receive the bread and the wine? And what really is the Lord's Supper You don't get your hunger or thirst satisfied, so what good is it really? You don't know? You don't have answers to these questions? Then change them. Get rid of them. Do what is most practical. After all, God doesn't care how he is worshipped. He only cares if we are sincere and honest when we worship. Stop. And there it is. There it is. The understanding that reveals why everything is questioned regarding traditions of the church. It is the belief that God doesn't care how he is worshiped, but only that he is worshiped in sincerity of heart and mind. The problem with this belief about God is still that it doesn't have biblical merit. God never says that it does not matter how he is worshipped. And he never said that he is only concerned about sincere hearts and minds. Such an interpretation of God is reading into Scripture what some want it to say rather than what it actually says. People have argued that God does not care how we worship, but only that we do so in sincerity of heart and mind. They point to passages such as David saying to God in Psalm 51, verse 16 For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it. You would not be pleased with a burnt offering The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit, a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise. For some people, these words teach that God doesn't delight in any sacrifice at all. But that conclusion doesn't wrestle with the reality that God is the one who commanded who commanded the offered sacrifices for sin. For some people, the latter part of the verse reveals that God actually wants, which is a broken spirit and a contrite heart. But that conclusion doesn't take into account what David says next in the same psalm, which is the following. Then Then you will delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings, and whole burnt offerings. Then bulls will be offered on your altar. This last verse makes it clear that it is not sacrifices that God is displeased, but sacrifices made without a broken and contrite heart. God wants both from his people. He wants sacrifices as he commanded them in his law, and he wants hearts of the people as they obey. The problem with Israel is that they either repeatedly trusted in the rituals without their hearts being given to God, or they did not obey the rituals as commanded. Another passage often quoted by those who think that God does not care about the form in which his people worship is from Hosea chapter 6. Which says, For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offering. To conclude from that that God does not like the very thing He has commanded is simply illogical And it fails to take onto account what God is truly after with the sacrifices He had commanded to be performed. His end goal has always been for the people of Israel to be his people and for him to be their God. And what that looks like is that the people would love him. And accept his love, and that would be expressed by obeying the law, not out of the trust in the law itself, but a trust in the giver of the law, which we you and I call faith. In case you are being tempted to think that such is my own interpretation, listen to these words from the prophet Jeremiah. Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat the flesh. For in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, I did not speak to your fathers or command them concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But I command the command I gave them, obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people, and walk in all the way I command you, that it may be well with you. Of course, the offerings were essential to worshiping God, because they all point to the fulfillment, which is the sacrifice of Jesus upon the cross, which of course is essential to our Christian worship. Their faith pointed forward. Our faith points backward, and yet it's the same thing. The Christian life is to be what God wanted for the Israelites, which is forgiveness of sin, and that includes sacrifice. In obedience to his will, and that means that the Christian life is a life of worship. Another biblical argument against the worship of God In any matter we choose, is the number of times God rejects worship not commanded We learn quickly in Holy Scripture that God does not indiscriminately accept all forms of worship. Recalled a lesson about faith in the book of Hebrews About how God accepted the offering of Abel, but not that of Cain. Cain did not bring forth the first fruits, and it was because he lacked faith that he did not bring them. Abel brought the firstborn of his flock to worship God, and yet it wasn't that fact alone that he brought forth the firstborn, but that he did so in faith. In faith that God would receive it and forgive. And this example teaches us that God does discriminate when it comes to worship, worship that he will accept. Interestingly, the offerings of Cain and Abel can be considered both private worship and corporate worship. They're private because each brought separate offerings. They're corporate because they were the only family worshiping God. The next example comes from the book of Leviticus, where the Israelites received commandments primarily regarding corporate worship And from Leviticus 10, we read, now Aaron's sons, Nadab, and Abihu, took their censors. Put fire in them, placed incense on them, and offered unauthorized fire before the Lord, contrary to his command. So fire came out of the presence of the Lord and devoured them, and they died before the Lord. There are several points of information we are to identify. from these two verses that were violations of the law, the law just given to them regarding corporate worship. First They each took his own censor rather than the sacred utensil that was to be used in the sanctuary. Second, they both offered their censors together, whereas the incense was only to be given by one person. Third, they performed an action that was only to be performed by the high priest, who was their father. Fourth, they offered incense at an unauthorized time. Fifth and finally, they offered these incense offerings as worship directly in front of the Holy of Holies, which was a breaking of a specific commandment. In summary, Nadab and Abihu worship in a manner that they were not instructed to do, and in a manner they were specifically instructed not to do. But they were worshiping, so that should be to their favor, right? They were calling upon the right God, so that should count for something, right? Apparently not. You see, by worshiping in a manner that God did not command, they were presuming upon God. That any way God is approached is a sufficient and acceptable manner. It wasn't, and it still isn't. If you are still convinced that sincerity of heart and mind is what God is most concerned about when it comes to the worship of Him, let us reflect on the story of King Saul and Israel's victory over the Amalekites. At the beginning of 1 Samuel chapter 15, God speaks to King Saul through the prophet Samuel, telling him to go and fight against the Amalekites. To avenge the manner that Israel was attacked after Israel had been freed from bondage while escaping Egypt. God instructs Saul to kill every Amalekite, as well as the oxen, sheep, camels, and donkeys. Nothing of the people was to be left. The directive was clearly stated and agreed to. And yet after God gave Israel a resounding victory, We read that the people took the plunder they were to destroy, particularly taking the sheep and oxen, and then used them as sacrifices to worship their God And let that be underlined. The people use the best of the livestock from the plunder of the Amalekites to worship God. That sounds like a good thing they were doing. They were praising God for their victory. They acknowledged that God was responsible for their victory It all seemed so very right because they were worshiping God in sincerity. But here is what Samuel the prophet says to them after discovering what the people had done. Samuel said to King Saul, Has the Lord great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and presumption Presumption is as iniquity and idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, he has also rejected you from being king. From that example in 1 Samuel, let us not next make the mistake of thinking that God must only be concerned about obedience when it comes to corporate worship. The prophet Malachi brought forth God's word to the Israelites while the temple was being built, rebuilt by Ezra and Nehemiah. He began his prophecy by condemning the priests of Israel for their defiled offerings. But the offerings were defiled not because the priests were worshiping an idol or a false god. No, they were worshiping Yahweh. And they were worshiping in the right location and were offering the sacrifices according to the law. All was good. But all was not good because the poor were being oppressed. The starving were not being fed. The widows were not being cared for. The lame and the sick were being ignored. Thus the rituals of corporate worship being followed, but the laws of loving God and loving one's neighbor were forgotten. Corporate worship had become ritual for the sake of ritual, which can happen to any form of worship that does not include loving God and loving your neighbor. I anticipate that by now some of you might be frustrated at the points I have made, because it can appear that there is no way to please God when it comes to corporate worship. If God is concerned about our hearts and minds as we worship, but not to the point that they are what is most important, and then he cares about obedience. But that that is what is not his only concern. And then that obedience is not just in what we do in worship, but what we do outside the temple, i. e. feeding the hungry Then it appears that he is easily offended if we lean too far one way as opposed to another And if you perceive God to be easily offended when it comes to worship of his people, I can emphatically say that he is not. But getting you to that point of questioning whether God is easily offended has actually been one of my goals The very least I want you to conclude is that God does not accept any and all worship that uses his name. That should be clear enough from the examples in Scripture. I can say that God is not easily offended by the worship of his people because our worship, our corporate worship, is not for God. It's for us. God is concerned about our manner of corporate worship because He cares for us. How we worship God is how we think about God. And how we think about God is in what and where and how we put our faith. If we view God as only concerned about our hearts and not our obedience, then we worship God by the way of our emotions. If we view God as being most concerned about obedience, then we put our faith in ritual. If we view God as only concerned with what we do within the walls of his sanctuary, we fail to love our fellow man. So we have spent a lot of time in the Old Testament this morning, but remember the point made from the book of Hebrews Which is that Jesus is in all of the Old Testament, and therefore he is our model for worshiping God. He is the epitome of sincerity of heart and mind, while being fully obedient, while loving his fellow man. So we look to him first in our worship, and we look to him in this series of sermons regarding how Christians are to properly worship. Now I started by describing a grandfather's conviction becoming his son's tradition, becoming his grandson's elimination. Because I'm concerned that such will occur in my own family and in the families of St. Stephen's. I've started by trying to convince you that sincerity and effort to worship God is not enough. My end goal is to convince you that the traditions we have been given within the Anglican way, which is part of the great tradition, are actually convictions and worthy to be passed on. Traditions can actually be convictions if we understand and remember why we do what we do. Let us pray. O gracious and heavenly Father, we put forth this word, hoping it is received and spoken to by the Holy Spirit. That all that is true might be convicting and might motivate us to move in action, to move in worshiping you in spirit and in truth, in faith and love. And so bless us in this day and bless us in this series. May it be helpful to passing on conviction. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Worship Symbols
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Be seated. We are in the middle of a series of sermons on corporate worship, Christian corporate worship. And thus far we have established that God does indeed, does indeed reject certain forms of worship. We learn that there is a preferred order of worship by God Himself established in Holy Scripture. And we saw how our Anglican traditions follow what God established, making our Anglican traditions heavenly relevant. In this sermon, we will look at the power of symbolism and how God has used symbols in the context of how his people worship him. But first, a joke. A Jewish father was very troubled by the way his son turned out, and he went to see his rabbi about it. Rabbi, I brought my son up in the faith, gave him a very expensive bar mitzvah, and it cost me a fortune to educate him. Then he tells me last week he's decided to be a Christian. Rabbi, where did I go wrong? The rabbi strokes his beard and says, Funny you should come to me. I too brought up my son as a boy in the faith, sent him to university, and it cost me a fortune. And then one day he comes to me and tells me he wants to be a Christian What did you do? asked the man of the rabbi. I turned to God for the answer, replied the rabbi. And what did he say? Asked the man. He said, Funny, you should come to me Some of you it takes a little bit longer. I like the joke because it mixes together the old covenant and the new covenant. In Bishop N. T. Wright's book titled Paul, a biography, his argument that I so much appreciate is that the Apostle Paul did not have a conversion experience to Christianity on the road to Damascus when Jesus appeared to him in that blinding light, but it was was instead a right progression. For it was God's plan all along for the Jewish people to follow Jesus as their Messiah. God promised a Messiah to the Jewish people within his covenant promises. And Jesus was and is that Messiah. To believe in Jesus was to believe in the covenant God made with Adam. And then Noah, and then Abraham, and through Isaac, and Jacob and Judah, and then Moses, and then David, and then Jesus. That Jesus is the fulfillment of what it meant to believe in God's covenant with the people of Israel is dramatically stated in the book of Revelation. Where Jesus calls Jewish people who reject him, who reject him as being members of the synagogue of Satan. This oneness of the Old and New Testaments allows us to glean from the Old Testament principles regarding how God prefers to be worshipped And we did that extensively last week looking at Exodus chapter 24. Now we peek into the tabernacle. And into the temple and their worship to understand just how powerful symbols can be while God's people worship him. To appreciate symbolism, we must first address the second commandment, which condemns the making of graven images, so that such images can be bowed to and worshipped. And here I remind you of that commandment in full. It reads, You shall not make for yourself carved images. Or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth, you shall not bow down to them Nor serve them. For I, the Lord, your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me But showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments. The middle part of the commandment is important. For some Christians have interpreted the first part to so strivantly that they believe it is a grave sin. For a Christian to make any image at all of anything in the likeness in heaven or on earth Historically, such people have been called iconoclasts, for they were of the conviction that it was their duty to destroy images that Christians would use to worship God. It would not be useful for us or possible for us to address all the issues regarding sacred images, for the issues continue to divide the Christian Church. What we can know for sure is that God was not commanding that no images of any kind should be made. And we can know this because God Himself God himself commanded that images of cherubim should be made of gold and placed on top of the Ark of the Covenant, with their wings pointing to one another. Also, the curtains for the tabernacle were to be decorated with elaborate embroidery, also depicting heavenly cherubim, which were angelic-like creatures, symbolizing God's protection. God therefore was not hypocritically commanding that there be no graven images whatsoever, and next commanding that the images of cherubim be used in his holy tabernacle, and then in the temple worship. So, God allows for images, symbols to be used for us to worship Him. And we underline worship Him. As opposed to worshiping an image. Consider how God uses images, symbols for his people to worship him The Ark of the Covenant, as mentioned, was a profound symbol for God's people, as it represented God's presence amidst the people. It also contained the Ten Commandments as the central document of God's covenant with his people. It contained Aaron's rod that budded so that God's wrath would be turned away It contained a pot of manna to remind God's people of how God provided for them in the desert. Each item was a reminder, a symbol of God establishing covenant with his people, Israel. as a whole. Now regarding other furnishings that served also as symbols, there was the outer wash bin in the temple court that was used for ceremonial cleansing So that the priest could properly present the offerings. It also pointed to the washing that God would give believers at their baptism when Jesus the Messiah was revealed. There was also the altar where the chosen animals were sacrificed because of the wages of sin is death. And that altar was pointing to the cross. Inside the curtains of the temple and later the temple was, oh excuse me, inside the curtains of the tabernacle and later the temple. was the table of showbread that contained twelve loaves representing the twelve tribes of Israel. It was an offering of thanks to God for grain. Grain, as well as representing God's presence amidst his people as their provider. It also pointed Israel to the Messiah to come, who would offer himself as the bread of life. The lampstand across from the showbread table served as a source of light while also representing God's presence as he went before the Israelites at night in the form of a heavenly flame It also refers to God revealing himself to Moses as a fire that burns but does not consume. And most importantly, it pointed to the Messiah who would be called the light of the world. Then there were the garments to be worn by the priests, and especially the high priest, who wore a breastplate of precious stones that were symbols according to God's commandments, representing both God and the people, and especially the beauty of God and how beautiful He wanted to make His people. All of these reference symbols are related to what God had done, was doing, and was bringing about, which was the salvation of his people. The use of symbols representing God bringing salvation to his people is tenfold in the book of Revelation There, Jesus is exalted with feet of brass, eyes like fire, upholding the seven churches as they surrounded him like lampstands. Next, we find ourselves in a throne room where Jesus is on a throne and also appears as a lamb before the throne. Then there are the 24 elders surrounding the throne representing the old covenant and the new covenant while singing holy, holy, holy, the Trinitarian praise. While they throw their crowns at the feet of their Christ, their Savior, their God. In the scriptures, a violet sea is a symbol of a troubled nation In heaven, in Revelation, the sea is as smooth as glass, dressed before the throne of the exalted Christ, telling us that Jesus brings peace to the nations. Also, there is a rainbow. And it can be seen only the rainbow is not a half-circle as we view them on earth, but is a full circle meaning that God has fulfilled his promises to his created order. Each depiction of Heavenly scenes tells a portion of the story of how God saved and is saving his people All of these symbols from the tabernacle worship to the throne of Christ Jesus are heavenly relevant. And the question remains, are we heavenly relevant? Remember, I quoted a proverb of sorts in the first sermon in this series that says that a grandfather's conviction Can become a son's tradition and eventually his grandson's elimination. An example is a trend within contemporary Christian worship that has pastors wearing casual clothes while standing on a stage speaking to the congregation like Tony Robbins at a you can do it positive mental attitudes seminar And we ask, how did that happen? Notice that the traditional setting of chancel furniture has the pulpit on one side of the sanctuary, the lectron on the opposite side, with the Holy Communion table in the center and back in the chancel. That is purposeful, for it gives a cruciform shape, a shape of a cross, more clearly seen from a bird's eye view. The shape of the cross is thoughtfully made, for it is the cross that enables us to call upon the name of our God. The central position of the Holy Communion table communicates the primary importance of the Holy Meal. The holy meal to be consumed each week to commemorate the covenant God made with his people, and where God manifests himself as we eat his flesh and drink his blood. As an overreaction against the Roman Catholic tradition and the doctrine of transubstantiation Certain Christian gatherings from the time of the Reformation decided that the Holy Communion table should not be central, focused, but instead it should be the preaching of the Bible. The result was placing the pulpit at the center of the chancel. Such placing of the pulpit communicates priority, the priority of preaching. With some modern churches, the pulpit is removed, communicating a different priority. What or who is the priority? When a man stands on a chancel that they call a stage, Alone with his microphone headset, his blue jeans, his untucked shirt, and his talking points. What is the focus? The answer is the focal point is the man himself. We should be asking Is the priority of a preacher's personality heavenly relevant? I submit that it is not. But it sells, right? It markets well. There are even Christian gatherings that display a video of a man who is in another city and maybe even another state. Wearing his blue jeans, his untucked shirt, cordless microphone, and displaying his talking points. It is modern church on the big screen. Thousands of professing Christians appear to prefer such a setup, for they attend most Sundays to watch their church service. These things have happened because nobody knew why the pulpit was placed in the middle of the chancel, because no one remembered that the preaching of the Word of God was the priority. And the pulpit was placed in the center because people didn't understand why Holy Communion was so important. Because they didn't hear it taught that God preferred to end his time with his people with eating and drinking. I submit also that the Holy Communion table was removed from the center of the chancel and the focal point of the worship service. Because people stopped believing that Jesus was uniquely present among his people when they broke bread and shared a cup. An absence of faith and the real presence of Jesus at the Holy Communion table has resulted in placing the personality of a man center stage. And we can call it a stage because it is not treated as a chancel. The word chancel is from the Latin meaning crossbars. It describes the barriers that were used in the Middle Ages to distinguish the area that the clergy and the choir worshipped. Distinguish it from the nave where the congregation worshipped. And it also distinguished it from the altar where the bread and wine were consecrated and consumed In the Anglican tradition, the chancel is a type of the holy place in the temple, and the altar or communion table is a type of the holy of holies. What was done in the chancel area was the leading of worship for God's people with the utmost reverence. Because the clergy pursued reverence, it was necessary that their vestments not represent themselves, but rather represent the office they held, and more specifically the God they worshipped. Clergy in the Middle Ages learned how effectual their vestments could be at helping the worshippers see God. Wearing two cloaks for warmth turned into wearing a cassock that is black to symbolize the sinfulness of the man. With a surplus over the cassock that is white to symbolize the purity given to us by Jesus. The tippet or stole Worn over the surplus came to represent a yoke like that was placed on the oxen to plow a field It was and is to help the clergy know he is first and last a servant. For some clergy When leading a full Holy Communion service, a white robe called an alb became the clear choice, for it symbolized the presence of Jesus as the people break bread and drink wine. I have instructed you as a parish many times before that Holy Communion proper has Jesus offering us the bread and offering us the wine And the white being worn by the clergy, symbolizing that reality. Now I mentioned the nave, which is where the congregation worships. The word nave comes from the Latin word navis, which means ship. Traditionally, Christian sanctuaries lined their naves with rows of seats or pews to replicate a galley of a ship. Where the servants would row in unison to keep to keep the ship moving toward the heavenly shore The concept of a sanctuary being like a ship comes from Noah's Ark, which was the vessel God used to save his chosen people from his condemnation. of humanity by way of the flood. The church then serves just as the Ark of Noah did, for each are vessels by which God saves his people. Consider that if you remember each time you enter a sanctuary, that you are on this journey toward the heavenly shore together with other Christians You are less likely to be selfish, to be unkind, to be unforgiving, etc. , because you can't row alone. We need one another, and we need to stay in the boat. There are other important symbols. That when understood, add to our appreciation for what God has done for us to receive His salvation The fine linen cloth on the communion table is to remind us of the cloth that was used to cover the body of Jesus at his burial The veiling of the chalice or covering of the chalice and placing of the patent are symbolic of the clothes that once covered Jesus in the grave And were next found folded and placed to the side because he was no longer there. He had risen from the dead. And if you pay close attention, you will see water being poured into the communion wine. That symbolizes that at the suffering of Jesus on the cross Both water and blood poured from his side after being pierced by that spear. It's interesting and it has been speculated. That the water that poured out of Jesus was from the pericardium sac that surrounds the heart, meaning that Jesus did indeed die of a broken heart. There are other symbols and movements you might witness the clergy performing that are part of Anglican custom, that are not prescribed in any book of the church or in the book of common prayer. They include crossing oneself, bowing while professing the names of the Trinity. You might see clergy and lady striking their chest while confessing their sin As a reminder that we are the same as the publican in the story Jesus told about the Pharisee who stood before God with a self-righteous heart, while the publican stayed in the back of the room while pounding his chest. in recognition that he was a sinner in need of God's forgiveness. There are other symbols that are too numerous to review in this one sermon But the point of it all remains that each contribute to telling the story of how God has redeemed, His redeeming, and will redeem his people. Are they necessary for worship? No. Are we better Christians for using such symbols? No, for there is no such thing as a better Christian. Can they be useful tools to heighten our attention while we worship? Well, God thought so. Let's pray. Father, we thank you for the traditions that have been handed down, some written, some not. But all of them help us to focus our attention on what you have done, what you are doing and will do to save us And for these traditions, we thank you. May we never bow down to them, but may we use them to bow down to you. This we pray in Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Worship Being Peculiar
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. He be seated. One of the characteristics my wife Bobby Lynn and I tried to instill in our all of our children. Was to embrace being peculiar. And by peculiar, I do not mean socially awkward I mean peculiar in the sense of standing out because they did not follow the crowd in terms of what was popular or expected. I wanted them to get used to being thought of and treated as different or odd because as Christians living in a secular world If we are being faithful to the Holy Scriptures in our day-to-day living, we are going to stand out. We are going to be seen as being different. When you don't join the mob think, people notice and pass judgment. When you don't curse or gossip or slander or complain, people will notice, and they may even accuse you of being arrogant. When you bow your head in public prayer before each meal, people will notice and murmur about your piety. As a teen or young adult, when you simply obey your parents, people will notice, and some will think you are a suck-up. When you don't smoke weed, don't do drugs, don't get drunk, don't commit adultery, people will notice And conclude you are either under the thumb of your parents, dying to get away from them, or you are self-righteous and will soon be a hypocrite. That is what my children faced when they attended a private but secular high school, and I wanted them to be prepared for it. I prepared them by telling them how different Christians are to be and how people will notice and by standing out in the manners I just described, they could be a witness, could be a witness to the truth of Jesus Christ without uttering a word. By my children embracing being peculiar They were able to park with pride a rusted-out $300 pickup truck next to the Mercedes, Lexus, and Jaguars their school peers drove. The younger ones, when it was their time to attend high school, were able with humor to drive a 25-year-old Cadillac that drove like a boat and could not go in reverse. They were able to laugh at peers who would ask them what they thought were trapping questions such as, What would your dad do if you told him you were gay? They were able to say yes when peers would ask, hey, if I die and don't believe in Jesus, am I going to hell? And when you know you are different, you expect others to treat you differently It keeps reality before you and it helps you stay different. Mind you, yes, there is a danger in being different because people can be different just for the purpose of being different. But Christians are different because of our nature. We are awake, which has a different meaning than it used to We are no longer dead in our trespasses and sins, but instead awake by the life-giving Holy Spirit to better able know God, love God, and love our fellow man. We have God in us, animating our spiritual selves, while those who do not believe remain spiritually crippled and, yes, dead. My premises are that we are different by our nature, and that we are to embrace being different, leading to the conclusion that our worship of God should be different as well. In this series of sermons on worship, and for this sermon, I am espousing a very simple point, which is that our worship should embrace being peculiar. The logic from the opposite view I am espousing goes something like the following: Christians need to corporately worship God. Many Christians do not attend church services to corporately worship God. Many Christians don't attend because church services are boring. The church then needs to make services exciting. Church services are more exciting when the people are entertained. No one knows entertainment better than the secular world, so the church should replicate what the secular world does, only make it Christian, so that it is Christian worship with a secular style. Fundamentally, the logic of this approach to corporate worship is not flawed. Worship as entertainment can and does attract a crowd. The problem with this type of reasoning and worship is not the logic applied, but the question it fails to address. Which is whether or not God is pleased with worship that is entertaining. We know that God would not be pleased by worship that is entertaining if it contains something barbarous, pornographic, or salacious or heretical? But what about circus-type stunts or or special effects? Such things don't break any of God's commandments, do they? What some people are not questioning is whether such questions should even be asked. The point is not whether God would allow circus stunts and special effects in a Christian corporate worship service It isn't spent to determine whether what is being done in Christian corporate worship is heavenly relevant. In previous sermons in this series, we have established that God does indeed reject certain types of worship We have concluded that our worship of God must include obeying Him and loving our fellow man. We have learned that God has given us an order of worship in Exodus chapter 24. Which is the very first time Israel worshiped as a people, and we have seen how our Anglican traditions follow that same given order. What I want to convince Christians is for all of us young and old to embrace what it means to worship as a peculiar people. So let us examine where this is spoken about, where Christians are described as peculiar. It is from St. Peter's first epistle, his first letter, so 1 Peter chapter 2 is where we are coming from this morning. And in 1 Peter 2, he exhorts Christians to lead lives that are morally separate from the unbelieving world. Christians are to put aside, he says, malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy And slander for all are sins of their former lives and sins of the people around them. What they are to replace with such sins is the Word of God. To further implore Christians to live a different kind of life, Peter uses several metaphors, such as Christians being as babies longing for pure milk. Or hungry so as to want to taste the kindness of the Lord. And because Jesus is the cornerstone, he is to be approached by us as a living stone. that although rejected by men is precious before God. And as Jesus is a living stone, so too are Christians to see themselves as stones who are being used by God To build a spiritual house in order to offer up spiritual sacrifices in the name of Jesus. Jesus as the cornerstone of all that is built up is either the rock upon which all earthly and heavenly lives will be built, or a rock upon which all who do not believe will stumble over or crash into. So after mentioning those who do not believe and therefore stumble and crash upon the eternal rock who is Jesus, Peter wants to get back to the reason why Christians are to live separate moral lives away from the unbelievers around them by identifying them as God's chosen people. According to Peter, Christians are to identify themselves with Israel, for he quotes Exodus 19, verse 5. Where God called Israel out of bondage in Egypt to be his very own people. They are chosen by God, just as God chose Abraham and credited Abraham's faith as righteousness In the same manner, God has chosen an entire people to be his very own. It is God's choice and no one else's. Christians are next called royal priesthood, a royal priesthood. As royals, Christians belong to the one kingdom. As priests, Christians have been washed clean of sin and are able to stand before God as clean and are able to hear God speak and are able to serve God as his representative. Christians are next called a holy nation. The term holy is to be consecrated or set aside to be used by God for his glory. The term nation reminds us that Christians are not believers separate from other believers, but are instead an entire people who must love one another to continue as God's people. We are chosen, we are part of the royal priesthood, and we are holy and a nation only if we are a body and not mere individuals. Christians are next, and finally called a peculiar people. Now that word peculiar is from the King James Version translation. The phrase literally means a people of special reservation. A people of special reservation. It is a most personal phrase to describe what God owns for his own personal care. It is saying he will not share us with anything else. And what are Christians to do with this unique identification given by St. Peter? The why question needs to be answered. Why see ourselves in this manner? What is the point of being chosen, royal, priestly, a holy nation, and peculiar people? The answer is in the next phrase. To declare the praises of God. To proclaim the excellencies of him who called you. In other words, it is to worship God. So if Christians are chosen, royal, priestly, a holy nation, and peculiar, it follows that the worship of Christians should reflect who we are. To put it another way, Christian corporate worship should reflect the people God has made us to be It should reflect that we are chosen. It should reflect that we are royal, priestly, a holy nation. It should reflect that we are peculiar. To put it another way, Christian worship shouldn't reflect who we are not. We are not unbelievers. And therefore, our corporate worship shouldn't look like we are unbelievers. A glaring flaw of the Christian Church for at least the last four decades has been an inability to differentiate between Christian corporate worship and outreach. Modern Christian churches have made times of Christian corporate worship a time of outreach to justify worship styles and times of recharching professing Christians and sharing the gospel with of Jesus Christ with unbelievers They have done so because they understand the purpose of the church. It's to grow its membership. It's to evangelize, to get to be a large church. And yet, while evangelism is a responsibility of the church, it is not the why, it is not the purpose of the church. I say again, the purpose of the church, the end goal of the chosen people of God is to glorify God. To glorify God and enjoy Him forever, it is to worship God. Christians from every tradition, East or West, Should not have a problem whatsoever with Christian bands playing music that sounds like secular music only with words devoted to Christ when it is played and used for outreach to unbelievers Who might like such music? Christians from every tradition should not have a problem with a pastor wearing a cordless microphone, blue jeans, and an untucked shirt and talking points When it is in the context of outreach. There are indeed unbelievers who are more apt to attend a gathering of people who play rock music and speak in a casual manner and entertain. That seems to be true. But when such settings are called Christian corporate worship, the Bible does not know of such worship, and the church historic does not know of such worship. And those are only the only sources of authority that can teach us what proper Christian corporate worship is to be. Let us consider the words Saint Peter has chosen for God's people to worship. Being chosen means that we are going to have a security in our salvation and a trust in God that an unbeliever is not going to have. But chosen means we are able to celebrate that our salvation, our very salvation, is not determined by our ability to keep a promise, but it's determined by God's ability to keep a promise. Being a royal priesthood means that we are going to take our corporate worship seriously by behaving in a manner proportionate to our status. A royal does not behave like a pauper, because the privilege demands more. The priesthood, with its privilege, calls for dignity to be shown and seriousness to be maintained. As St. Paul has said when addressing Christian corporate worship, but all things should be done decently and in order. As a peculiar people, we are going to have a verbiage that only we use when we gather together. This is one of the reasons why we use an older text for our Book of Common Prayer. Those who prefer a modern language version have put forth a purpose That no one today uses the language used in the old prayer books. The fact is, no one used said language when the prayer book was first written For no one used it as a common vernacular. The formal language of the prayer book was originally chosen because it reflected corporate worship as a unique time For God's people to gather. And it communicated the formality the church believed was needed for such gatherings. Now, admittedly, some of the words are quite archaic to us, and some sound strange and even funny. Do you hear the word sucker and chuckle because the way it is pronounced, and then wonder what it means? It means to give assistance or aid to someone. How about the phrase, dissemble nor cloak? The simple means to hide true motives, and cloak is to cover rather than reveal. How about absolution and remission? Absolution is a declaration of God's forgiveness, and remission is a canceling of debt owed. How about inestimable It means too great, too great, too large to calculate. What about the use of thou so often when reading the Ten Commandments? To be sure, thou is an archaic form of the more simple word you, but when it is used in the context of God's God's founding document for his covenant with his people And is expected to be followed without excuse, thou is most appropriate. And what about the word oblation? It refers to the thing that is being offered by, or excuse me, the thing being offered to God. And the mouthful word, propitiation, what does that mean? The word propitiation is a mouthful word, and yet there is not another word in the English language that can express that God was in Christ. Reconciling the world to himself, appeasing his own wrath. Yes, there are certain words that Anglicans use in corporate worship that unbelievers have a hard time understanding, as do Christians who are not a part of the tradition. The hope is, the hope is That an unbeliever who participates using Anglican worship traditions will at least know that those who are familiar with the traditions have their attention upon God. And if the unbeliever is seeking God, if he is seeking God, he will find him, for the liturgy points to him. I recall an advertisement in the local newspaper here several years ago now where a church was starting up and meeting at the local Freedom Hall just as St. Stevens did many years ago. The advertisement showed a cartoon drawing of a church setting where a man was asleep in a pew And the caption read something like, If this is what you think church is, come visit us where you will never know you are in church. Now, any reasonable person could or should respond that there is no purpose in going to church if you don't know you are in church. Obviously, I am taking the position that when Christian worship, when in Christian worship, they should know they are attending church. Because we do what we do in worship is altogether different than what we do at any other time and any any other place each day of the week. Sundays are for worship and it's different. What we do in worship is to reflect That we have been chosen, made royal priests, and made a holy nation, and made a peculiar, a peculiar people. I began these sermons warning that if we do not pass on the justification of why we worship in the manner we do, the matter will be lost. And replaced by the practical. And what is what is practical will be less and less meaningful The following quote summarizes the burden I believe God has laid upon my heart. It is from the Reverend Dr. Kerr Marquette, a Lutheran theologian, who has since passed on. But he said the following If the liturgy is boring to children, it is usually because the parents do not find it interesting either. If children saw adults treating the Sunday service as the most important activity of their lives, they would respect it also, and would never dream of treating it as a pop event. to be tinkered with by every Tom, Dick, and Harry. A church which has won a conscientious loyalty of parents, particularly fathers, will have the devotion of their children also But a church which objectively capitulates to the whims and tastes of the adolescents will have and deserve neither. In these sermons, I strive to gain the consciousness, loyalty of parents, so that they would pass on the principles of proper Christian corporate worship to the next generation. So that a standard can be maintained that is received by God because it is heavenly relevant. What I put forth is the best I have, for it is to be passed on. Let what is true and what I have said be established in the hearts of God's people, and let what is manufactured Burn with the chaff. Let us pray. Our gracious God, we thank you that you have made us A people identified by our peculiarities. That you have made us specific, given us an identity, granted us a picture of what it is to be different through Christ our Lord. May we not be afraid to be different in the world and certainly not of it. In Jesus' name we pray. Amen.

sermons.title: Advent 2024
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Although it is an integral part of our Advent season, the history of the Advent wreath as we have here, is actually obscure. One story is that it began with Johann Henrik Wickern, 1808 to 1881. He was a Protestant pastor in Germany and a pioneer in urban mission work among the poor During Advent, children at the mission school, Rahas House, founded by Wickern in Hamburg, during the Advent season would repeatedly ask daily if Christmas had arrived. In eighteen thirty-nine he built a large wooden ring made out of an old cartwheel with nineteen small red and four large white candles. A small candle was lit successively every weekday during Advent. On Sundays, a large white candle was lit. All this allowed the children to count the weeks and days remaining until Christmas. The custom gained ground among Protestant churches in Germany and evolved into the smaller wreath with four or five candles that we know today. Roman Catholics in Germany began to adopt the custom in the 1920s, and in the 1930s it spread to North America. And I always find it interesting when Roman Catholics borrow symbolisms from Protestants. The modern Advent wreath has a great deal of thought put into it as each part of it is to represent something greater than itself. The wreath is made of various evergreens, signifying continuous life. The laurel, if it has laurel, can signify victory over persecution and suffering. Pine, holly, and yew can symbolize immortality. Cedar can symbolize strength and healing. Holly also has a special Christian symbolism. The prickly leaves remind us of the crown of thorns that Jesus wore for the sake of humiliation. And there is an English legend that tells of how the cross was actually made from Holly. The circle of the wreath, which has no beginning or end. Symbolizes God as eternal, also symbolizing the immortal soul and the everlasting life found in Christ. Any pine cones, nuts, or sea pods used to decorate the reef also symbolize life and resurrection. Altogether, the wreath of evergreens depicts the immortality of the human soul and the new everlasting life promised through Jesus Christ. As we know, the four candles represent the four weeks of Advent. A tradition is that each week represents 1,000 years, to sum up the 4,000 years from Adam and Eve until the birth of the Savior. Of course that dating is speculative. Three counters are purple and one is rose or pink. We have pink The purple candles in particular symbolize the prayer, penance, and preparatory sacrifice and good works undertaken during Advent The rose or pink candle is lit on the third Sunday, also known as Gaudet Sunday, for Gaudae is Latin for the word rejoice. Now, Sunday is the Sunday of rejoicing because the faithful have arrived at the midpoint of Advent, when their preparation is half over and they are all so close to Christmas. The progressive lighting of the candles symbolizes the expectation and hope surrounding the Lord's first coming into the world in an anticipation of his second coming to judge the living and the dead. All of this, all of this is interesting and helpful to know, but what is most important, of course, is the candle in the middle. It is the most important because of who it represents, for all that the other symbols communicate mean nothing unless Jesus is the focus of it all. The candle in the middle. The candle in the middle, the white candle symbolizes sinlessness and is what all the other candles should be pointing to. The Advent candles are much like the lampstands described in the book of Revelation that surround Jesus as he appears in his glorified state. In contrast to focusing on Jesus, one of the most ridiculous trends in modern celebrations of Christmas are these mind-numbing television shows and movies that insist that it is not Christmas unless dot dot dot you fill in the blank It is not Christmas until unless Rudolph leads the sleigh, unless It is not Christmas unless Santa finds some good cheer. It is not Christmas unless there is enough Christmas spirit. It is not Christmas unless it snows. It is not Christmas unless Santa gets a wife. Unless the Grinch gets back the presents. Unless the cranks decorate their house, unless the spoiled child gets the right present, unless the turkey is properly cooked. And my all-time favorite, and yours too, it is not Christmas until Grandma gets run over by a reindeer. The list goes on and on. Bobby Lynn actually wrote down a list of Christmas movies she wanted to watch during the Advent season, and it has been a long four weeks for someone like me who says, Ba humbug. To the sappy movies played this time of year. And it's not just television and movies. The sentiment is in modern songs. Personally, I must change the station if the song Christmas Shoes is being played I'm not going to quote any of those lyrics, but simply ask why does a child's sick mother who is bedridden need a pair of shoes? But I don't consider that song to be the sappiest. I realize I could get into trouble for this one because some of you may like this song, but I take opportunity to insist that this the song Where Are You Christmas To be the silliest, sappiest Christmas song ever written or recorded. Listen to some of the lyrics. Where are you, Christmas? Why can't I find you? Why have you gone away? Where is the laughter you used to bring me? Why can't I hear music play? My world is changing. I'm rearranging. Does that mean Christmas changes too? Where are you, Christmas? Do you remember the one you used to know? I am not the same one. See what the time have done. Why you let me go I will stop there because such songs are just too painful for Scrooges like myself Of course, Christmas can't go anywhere. Christmas doesn't change. Christmas doesn't let anyone go. And Christmas doesn't need Rudolph Santa, presents, lights, carols, decorations, or fluffy emotions to be Christmas The word Christmas itself tells us what is needed. The word from Christmas or for Christmas is the late Old English is Christas Mesa. Which is the Mass of Christ. It was first found referenced by our church fathers in 1080 A. D. The term Mass is not just a Roman Catholic term. It is derived from the late Latin word misha, which means dismissal. A word used in the concluding formula of Christian worship services. The last words in the service were it misa est, translated go. It is the dismissal. It has taken on a deeper meaning for Christians as it describes the whole worship service, as some describe Christian worship as the Mass. Christmas then refers to the worship of Jesus as the Christ. And that worship is corporate, not individualistic or familial. The modern trend of putting family first and foremost at Christmas misses the meaning of the day itself. But I get the importance of family at Christmas. I get the importance of family traditions at Christmas. We had our own when our children were young and we still try to keep some of them going But family is not to be worshipped at Christmas or any other time. Family is not to be the priority on Christmas. And did I just say that in a church on the east coast of the United States? I did. The priority is to worship Jesus Christ for becoming man and remaining man for all time. Traditions and familial love mean nothing that lasts unless Jesus is at the center of our celebration. The centricity of Jesus in Christmas is what makes Christmas. When a Christmas focuses on worshiping the Christ child, then it is Christmas. The Holy Scriptures have the same focus. Quite often, we read stories in Holy Scripture that have details we gloss over. Gloss over, not realizing that within them is found a greater lesson. For example, we read in Genesis 4 that Cain was born first to Adam and Eve and then Abel. You know that. It was then Abel who was killed out of spite because God was pleased with the offering Abel brought to him and not the offering of Cain. Instead of Cain wanting to learn what he could do to be accepted by God, he instead focused his anger on Abel and murdered him. We can learn lessons about anger spite and coveting from the actions of Cain. We can also see things more profound in that story. Remember that Adam was the first man, and Jesus is called the second Adam Can we see the correlation between Adam, who was the first son, and then Jesus, who was the second son, and was killed by Adam's race because of spite? just as the second born Abel was killed at a spite. And then there is Isaac, who was the second born to Abraham. The first was named Ishmael, whom God did not choose. And you will recall in that story that God instructed Abraham to send Hagar and Ishmael away from the camp because Ishmael had mocked Isaac. The same happened to Jesus, who was a half-brother to the Jews, having been born of a virgin. He too was mocked by the Jews, his half-brothers, as he hung on the cross. And then there was Esau and Jacob. God chose again the second born, Jacob over Esau, to bring forth the Messiah, the second Adam. All along God was showing his people his redemptive plan by choosing the second born. The second born, that a second Adam would be born to them, who would do what the first Adam did not, and that is be obedient to the Heavenly Father. Going back to Eve, we see in her words an understanding that it is all about the child to be born that will overcome sin and death while crushing the serpent's head. You will remember that such was the promise within the curse placed on Eve, which is a strange place to find a promise in the midst of a curse. God would bring forth from a woman a seed. And by that promise is for a child to be born who will crush the serpent's head. The serpent, of course, represents the devil, and such was fulfilled when Jesus hung on the cross, and below him, beneath his feet was the hill that he was hung upon, which was called Golgotha, meaning the hill of the skull, which represents the serpent's head. The greatest of ironies was that Jesus died. While he died, he was also being victorious. The devil thought he had won by killing the Son of God, when in truth he had lost and lost for eternity. Eve herself recalled the promise of the seed being born to crush the head of the of Satan. After Abel was killed and Seth was born to her, she said. For God has appointed another seed for me instead of Abel. Every faithful Jewish woman was to have the same hope as Eve had Which was that she would be the chosen one to bring forth the child that would save mankind. And now we know that God chose a virgin named Mary. Along the same way of reflection, we follow the life of Joseph, who was the firstborn to Jacob and Rachel, but the eleventh son overall, which places him in obscurity and yet he was favored by his father. Such favoritism made him an enemy of his brothers, who resented him for having his coat of many colors made by his father. They envied him, and so they plotted to destroy him. Does such a story sound similar To that of Jesus, who was hated by his half-brethren because he was favored by his Father, the Heavenly Father? They hated Joseph so thoroughly, they plotted to kill him. But when that was debated, they agreed to throw him in a pit. And if that wasn't enough, then they sold him into slavery, staged a killing by putting blood on his coat, and then lied to their father about the whole ordeal. Beloved, we should never underestimate how low the human soul can descend when it comes to jealousy and bitterness. Consider that the very people who were eyewitnesses to the miracles Jesus performed as a testimony to God's favor of him. Even people who heard a voice from heaven saying, Of Jesus, this is my beloved Son, of whom I am well pleased. Even those witnesses Turned on him, shouting, crucify him, crucify him. Knowing this about the human soul and where it can go We should never be the witnesses on television saying, we never thought our neighbor was capable of such an evil, or parents that tell a teacher his child to never do something wrong. We are all capable. We are all capable. But my point is that the life of Joseph was lived out the way it did for the salvation of Israel as a nation. And that life was also lived out as a testimony to the Savior to come, who is Jesus the Lord. Consider Moses as living a life that points to Jesus. Consider Joshua living a life that points to Jesus. Consider Samuel living a life that points to Jesus. Consider David, David crushing the serpent's head while cutting off the head of Goliath, which pointed to Jesus. Consider Solomon as ruling a nation that was at peace with all nations, living a life that points to Jesus and what he will eternally accomplish. Peace In all nations. The point being made is from all of Holy Scripture, we see it surrounding the person of Jesus. So we see the traditions of the Advent Reef to the stories of Holy Scripture that the focus of Christmas should be upon Jesus our Lord. And what I want to add, one more point, it should also be about worshiping the Lord. That is what we are doing today, and that is what we should be doing on Christmas Day. Consider the description that St. John gives again in the book of Revelation. He tells the readers that his vision included seeing seven golden lampstands, which represent the seven churches to be addressed, and those seven churches represented all of the churches. And those churches were not lined up in a row, but were encircling someone, encircling the Son of Man. John describes him as having been clothed in a golden band with hair as like wool, as white as snow. He had feet like brass and eyes as fire. Out of his mouth came a double-edged sword, and his countenance was like the sun shining in its fullest strife. And John's only natural response, John's only natural response to that vision of a glorified Savior was to fall at his feet and worship him. And Jesus is today glorified, but calls us to remember that he humbled himself to be born as a man. and die a man in order that we could be made new men to live forever Yes. Christmas includes opportunities with family and friends. It can include presents and eulogues and carols and good food. It can include traditions practiced and memories, memories shared. But it must be our focus to worship Christ Jesus. We are not to worship family, friends, traditions, or whatever else is important to us on Christmas. We are to worship Christ alone. Now I want you to think about this. Many people, such as myself, many Christians, get upset. When people say, Happy holidays, instead of Merry Christmas. And that is justifiable. I understand the angst about that. The wishing of happy holidays takes Jesus out of Christmas But realize when you wish someone a Merry Christmas, you are actually hoping for them to have a happy time worshiping Christ. You are not simply saying, enjoy your Christmas. No, you are you are telling them worship Jesus. Remember, the word Christmas is the Mass of Christ. Christ is to be the center of our celebrations. He is the focus of our worship. The question that that happy song asks, Where are you, Christmas? That is an easy question to answer Christmas is found in worshiping Christ the Lord. Amen. Let us pray. Gracious and Heavenly Father, for that very word Christmas we thank you for, reminding us that it is about celebrating and worshiping you for your great gift of your son. May that be in all of our hearts and all together as we worship together. In Jesus' name. Amen.

sermons.title: Worship Knowing Good and Evil
sermons.speaker: Rev. Eric W. Jorgensen
sermons.text: And wonders of you done, and wonders of his love, and wonderful. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen. Please be seated. Last week I started A series of sermons that I've preached before, but the importance repeats itself over and over again. My main message last week was to say that our traditions need to become our convictions Otherwise, they will be tossed aside. Having established that God, that the God of Holy Scripture Does not accept just any form of worship, but instead is insistent that worship be by first his commandments What he has ordered us to do in worship, but also including a heart that loves him, and also including a heart that loves our fellow man. Any worship that falls short of said standards, any one of those three said standards, is rejected worship. A number of years ago, I visited a home of a parishioner who attended this parish, but her husband did not. I visited the home because I wanted to see if I could convince this husband to believe in Jesus and next to become a part of St. Stephen's For the sake of his own soul and the soul of his wife, who so desperately wanted her husband to be a Christian and attend worship with her The husband thought himself a good thinker, and so he posed to me this question: why does God need to be worshipped? It appears, he said, that God has an ego problem when he commands that he be worshipped Up to that time I had not been asked such a question, but I surmise since that many people who struggle to have faith Have asked or thought something similar. Certainly, if any human were to demand to be worshipped We as Christians would be appalled and see it as a sinful ego expressed. And as we look back at the pharaohs in Egypt, the Caesars of Rome, and the likes of Hitler and Mussolini, We righteously disdain their egos and their insistence on being praised by their followers, and then we make the mistake of thinking That God might be worthy of similar disdain because of his commandments to be worshipped. That type of thinking is a very serious problem. For it reveals that we are tempted by the devil to understand God in the same categories as understanding ourselves and understanding our fellow man. It is a struggle for human beings to comprehend that God is holy, W-H-O-L-L-Y, and Holy H-O-L-Y, different from humanity. And in being wholly different, he is beyond our comprehension, the comprehension of humans, because being beyond our comprehension is part of what it means to be God It fits the definition. If we who are finite could understand, fully understand God, then he would have to be finite as well. For the finite cannot fully comprehend the infinite. To realize God in his totality is beyond our comprehension Helps our faith to increase as we contemplate his revelations to us, which at the center is his glorious incarnation, which we celebrate Christmas season. Christian apologists have rightly described God as separate from his creation by explaining that everything that has existence Either exist as being caused by something else, known as causality, or by the necessity of its own nature. I say it again. Everything exists, has come into being by the cause of another thing, or it exists by the necessity of its own nature. Thus it is argued that while all things that exist require an outside agent that caused its existence. There is the possibility of God, because God exists by the necessity of his nature, which is an eternal nature. To put it another way, God does not have to have a beginning, because the word beginning implies the existence of time. And it was God who created time, making God before time. And we only say that to help us comprehend God's eternal existence, since there could not have been a before. before time, because the word before only makes sense in the context of time.
